Series title page

**Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal Library, complete, uniform, convenient, economical, of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprint of all surviving monuments of Catholic tradition through the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, compared with one another and with certain manuscripts, and corrected with the utmost care; continuously elucidated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by the discovery of all works completed after the most extensive editions issued during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following the individual volumes or authors of some importance; arranged with chapters properly set within the text and with headings at the upper margin of each page indicating its subject matter; expanded by works both doubtful and apocryphal, yet possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one an index of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written upon any topic may be seen at a glance; the other an index of Holy Scripture, from which the reader may readily discover which Fathers have commented on each passage of the individual books of Scripture, and where in their works they have done so. A most accurate edition, readily to be preferred to every other, if one considers: the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the completeness of its correction, both the variety and number of reprinted works, the highly convenient format of the volumes and its consistent uniformity throughout the work, the modest price, and, above all, this single, methodical, chronological collection of six hundred fragments and minor works hitherto scattered here and there, but now for the first time gathered in our library from works belonging to every age, place, language, and form.**

**Second Series**, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Prepared by J.-P. Migne, editor of the *Universal Clerical Library*, or *Complete Courses in the Individual Branches of Ecclesiastical Learning*. The Patrology has been printed in two editions: one Latin, the other Greek-Latin.—The twelve hundred volumes of the Latin edition are sold for one thousand francs; the thirteen hundred Greek-Latin volumes for eighteen hundred francs.—The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the latter, however, are provided in it only in Latin translation.

[Col. 0013]

**[On the Glorification of the Trinity and the Procession of the Holy Spirit.]**

[Col. 0009]

**Letter of R. D. D. Rupert, Abbot of Deutz, to the Roman Pontiff, Prelate of the Apostolic See**

1–3 Before your presence, O prince, most blessed Peter, witness of Christ and leader of the Christian faith, and likewise before the presence of your vicar, the pope, our lowliness asks to find a broad way and to have room. For one of the wisest of princes says: “A man’s gift makes room for him and brings him before princes” (Prov. 18). Therefore, lest I should come empty-handed, I have presented a gift such as my hand was able to find—would that it were a perfect gift, or a good gift, so that you might say: “This is from above, descending from the Father of lights” (Jas. 1).

For this gift consists not in perishable gold and silver, in which the princes of this age chiefly delight, but it is a work produced by the grace of God—the sole delight of holy princes, past and present—to whom the King of kings and Lord of lords has given everlasting rule in his heavenly kingdom (Rev. 5). It bears this pleasing title upon its front: *On the Glorification of the Trinity and the Procession of the Holy Spirit*.

Perhaps someone will say: “Our princes now have enough gifts, or offerings, of this kind.” You should recall that, when the tabernacle of the Lord was being made and the people were diligently bringing offerings every morning, the craftsmen were compelled to come and say to Moses: “The people are bringing more than is necessary.” Moses therefore ordered an announcement to be proclaimed: “Let neither man nor woman bring anything further for the work of the sanctuary.” Thus the people ceased bringing gifts, because what had been offered was sufficient and more than sufficient (Exod. 36).

To this I say: Certainly I remember it; but what is your point? Do you mean that, because that handmade tabernacle was made according to the pattern of the unmade, or heavenly, tabernacle shown to Moses on the mountain (Exod. 25), we too should, following the pattern of that prohibition, be forbidden and cease from offering gifts for the work of the heavenly sanctuary—cease from exercising the graces or charisms which the Holy Spirit distributes to each as he wills: the word of wisdom, the word of knowledge, kinds of tongues, and interpretation of utterances—because others before us have spoken wisely enough and knowledgeably enough, and have interpreted God’s sayings abundantly? (1 Cor. 12.)

Because there it was proclaimed that neither man nor woman should bring anything for the work of the sanctuary, do you wish likewise, as it were by allegory, to shut us up, so that now we may offer no gift from the riches of salvation, from the treasury of the Lord’s word, for the work of the heavenly sanctuary? Please, do not be too allegorical.

You too should remember what the holy Fathers before us understood concerning that passage about the simple Jacob: “Jacob,” Scripture says, “took green poplar rods, almond rods, and plane-tree rods, and partly stripped them; and when their bark had been removed, whiteness appeared in the portions which had been stripped, while those which remained whole continued green, and in this manner a variegated colour was produced” (Gen. 30). Accordingly, following that mystical model, we do not everywhere indiscriminately remove the bark of the letter and retain the whiteness of allegory. In many places we do; but in some places, without seeking allegory, we preserve the moral sense in the greenness of the letter.

For example, the Lord says: “Fire shall always burn upon the altar; the priest shall nourish it, placing wood upon it every morning, day by day; and, after laying the burnt offering upon it, he shall burn the fat of the peace offerings. This is perpetual fire, which shall never fail from the altar” (Lev. 6). What value would the bark of the letter have in this command? Therefore we strip away the bark and retain the spirit of allegorical understanding, when we understand the altar of God to be our heart, and the fire which must always burn upon it to be the flame of charity.

I confess to you, great priest, that I offer and judge—indeed wish to have judged—this present work, and whatever works I have so far completed with similar zeal, as wood by which the fire of charity or love may be nourished upon the Lord’s altar, in the heart of any reader or hearer who desires, through reading or hearing, to advance in love for the Lord’s name. Nor do I esteem this gift, by which, as I have said, I seek to have a way or room made for me before princes, as highly as gold, silver, and precious stones; or as blue cloth, purple, scarlet twice dyed, and fine linen, which are spiritually offered in the construction of the spiritual tabernacle.

All is well with us if these writings of ours are judged at least to have the value of wood by which that fire, already mentioned, may effectively be fed upon the Lord’s altar in the heart of some little one. But in Moses’ order that it be proclaimed, “Let neither man nor woman bring anything further for the work of the sanctuary,” as in many other matters, let the literal sense remain; just as in parts of the rods [Col. 0011] the bark remained green, because spiritual offerings have not ceased as they ceased there.

It belongs to those who do not see well—indeed, to the envious—to employ such an analogy and say: “As the people then brought more than was necessary, so now more books are written than are necessary.” It always has been permitted and always will be permitted for anyone, preserving the faith, to say what he thinks; and no one compels anyone unwilling to accept our writings.

I would wish, since the law of the Lord commands it, that these offerings of a faithful soul should be approved and accepted by you, the high priest, as first-fruits truly worthy to be received for the Lord’s work. Where does the Lord’s mystical law command this? In the construction of the tabernacle mentioned above, in these words: “Speak to the children of Israel, that they may take first-fruits for me; from every man who offers willingly you shall receive them” (Exod. 25).

And who is this “every man” who willingly offers first-fruits, except one in whom faith—the first virtue—works through love? (Gal. 5.) Certainly such a one is rightly called willing. “For God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. 9); and consequently, whether he offers little or much, his offerings are rightly called and truly are first-fruits.

For this reason it should also be observed that offerings of lesser value in themselves are not named last by the Lord: namely, goats’ hair and skins of rams dyed red; rather, they are placed almost in the middle of all the offerings. Thus you find gold, silver, bronze, blue cloth, purple, scarlet twice dyed, and fine linen set first; while spices for anointing oil and sweet incense, onyx stones, and gems for adorning the ephod and breastpiece are set last; and, as has been said, goats’ skins and red-dyed rams’ skins are placed in the middle (Exod. 25). Are we not usefully instructed by this arrangement also, that things which appear small to human beings are sometimes more acceptable to God because of the offerer’s good will, and are reckoned by him among the first-fruits?

Receive, then, from me, a willing man, these first-fruits which I have offered: first, this present work, divided into nine books, *On the Glorification of the Trinity and the Procession of the Holy Spirit*. There are other works which I have not yet been able to present: a work in thirteen books, *On the Victory of the Word of God*; likewise, *On the Glory and Honour of the Son of Man*, in the same number of books; thirty books on the Twelve Prophets; twelve books on the Apocalypse; fourteen books on the Gospel of John; forty-two books *On the Holy Trinity and Its Works*; fifteen books on Samuel and David; and seven books, in honour of the Blessed Virgin Mary, on the Song of Songs. Before all these I had also written a little work, *On the Sacraments, or Divine Offices, Through the Cycle of the Year*, divided into twelve little books or volumes.

This gift, as I recalled at the beginning from Solomon’s saying, “A man’s gift makes room for him and brings him before princes” (Prov. 18)—who ought to forbid this gift from making room for this man and bringing him before princes, especially when divine authority cries from above: “From every man who offers willingly you shall receive first-fruits”? (Exod. 25.) I profess by a true declaration that I am indeed a willing man, because I laboured upon this gift, to be offered for the work of the Lord’s tabernacle, not hired for human wages but delighting solely in the sweetness of the divine Word. For this reason I remembered these things and poured out my soul within me: “For I shall pass into the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God, with the voice of exultation and confession” (Ps. 41).

[Col. 0011]

**Rupert’s Prologue to Cuno**

[Col. 0011A] 5 What shall I do, O all you lovers of Christ, kindly hearers, since my mind does not allow any subject set before it, however far beyond its strength, to depart uninterpreted or unworked? Behold, at the urgent request of a certain friend of the bride or bridegroom, such as the voice in the Song of Songs speaks of: “We shall make you golden ornaments, studded with silver” (Song 1), I had published a little work in three books on the subject which he proposed to me: *On the Sacraments of the Faith, in the Form of a Dialogue between a Christian and a Jew*. Because of its subject or character, I thought fit to call this little work *The Ring*; and, having done so, I believed I had satisfied his good and praiseworthy desire.

But he, according to Wisdom’s saying, “Those who eat me shall still hunger, and those who drink me shall still thirst” (Sir. 24), after eating and drinking this very little, hungering and thirsting further, and with the palate of his mind, as it were, stimulated by the taste of good flavour, added this request, this insistent demand: that I should further undertake to speak against Jewish unbelief, first concerning the three persons of the one supreme Divinity, and to show him—though unwilling—that the glory of the Trinity is attested from the Law and the Prophets, Scriptures which he himself reads and receives.

Then, that I should show why or how the assumption of flesh pertained especially to the person of the Son. Then, that I should demonstrate that the time in which this Jesus Christ was born—whom we confess and know to be the very Messiah whom the holy Fathers awaited as promised to them—does not differ from the truth, but indeed accords fully, with the prophecy which the patriarch Jacob uttered beforehand: “The sceptre shall not be taken from Judah, nor the ruler from his thighs, until he comes who is to be sent” (Gen. 49).

In proposing these three matters, did he seem to have set before me a small or easy subject? On the contrary, he imposed a great and difficult task; and the more nearly the mind approaches it and desires to fulfil the requests, the more it feels its weight and almost recoils—except that it has long been accustomed, with God’s help, to deal with matters greater than its strength.

What, then, shall I do? Certainly this is expedient and best: having a friend, I shall go to him at midnight and say, “Friend, lend me three loaves, because a friend of mine has come to me from a journey, and I have nothing to set before him” (Luke 11). My mind is my friend, though it often withdraws so far from me that I rightly cry: “My heart has forsaken me” (Ps. 39). Thus it may truly be called both friend and deserter. It is a friend when it holds itself within; a friend when it calls and turns toward one of the saints; a friend when it thinks more deeply that the Son of God became the Virgin’s son for our sake; a friend when it looks still more deeply upon the mystery of the cross, by which the same Son of God drew all things to himself (John 12); a friend when it still most certainly desires to behold the glory of the Blessed Trinity, as through a mirror and in an enigma.

Indeed, it once saw this course of its own in a certain image, and now experiences it to some extent in actual things. After much searching of the Scriptures for testimonies concerning Christ, the Son of God, it now finally desires to utter something sweet or pleasing concerning the glory of the Holy Trinity and the procession of the Holy Spirit.

In what respect, however, is it also a deserter? Certainly a deserter in frequent distraction; a deserter in forgetfulness of its purpose; a deserter in the windows through which it ought not to go out; a deserter in sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch. Such a mind, behold, has now returned to me from its journey, as it has often done. But what shall I say? I have nothing, as I have already said, to set before it: I have no good, sound, and well-resonant word from myself by which I may worthily carry out the proposed work.

It remains, therefore, as I have said, that I go to that true friend, that unique friend, who, though he was God, became man for our sake—friend and brother—and say to him: “Friend, lend me three loaves” (Luke 11). Friend, give me a word which both refreshes and delights my heart and edifies whatever worshippers of the Trinity may read or hear it.

Formerly, when you, my most beloved Cuno, venerable bishop of the Church of Regensburg, had shown certain of our works to the legate of the Apostolic See, Lord William, bishop of Palestrina, and he, being a studious and exceptionally learned man, had read them attentively and embraced them, he was pleased, among other things, to inquire whether I had published any work on the procession of the Holy Spirit. Because he made this inquiry with considerable desire, you, out of good will, were almost grieved that I had nothing which could be carried by him to the feet of the holy Apostolic See on this subject—something which might be like a pearl upon that work which, as you thought, he had desired and taken with him as gold: namely, the exposition of the first six of the Twelve Prophets.

That copy, through your agency and at his request, I lost, as I also lost many other copies of our works which you took away when you departed for the episcopate. Therefore, when I wished to enter upon the requested subject concerning the glory of the Holy Trinity, the memory of that day came simultaneously to my mind; and it seemed that some usefulness, however slight, would be added if, in the course of the same work, I should mingle the sweetness of discourse on this subject of the procession of the Holy Spirit.

I confess that, as soon as this thought or suggestion occurred—which may it indeed be that of the Paraclete himself!—of whom the Lord says, “He shall teach you all things and bring to your remembrance all things whatsoever I have said to you” (John 14), it greatly pleased me, drew the face of my mind toward itself, and made it glad.

But how could a Jew suitably stand here in dialogue, as that friend requested, before the face of a Christian who, with unveiled face, contemplates the Holy Trinity, and propose questions whose solution might reveal ever more fully the face of Moses, when he has been accustomed to flee immediately from the very first revelation? Therefore, setting him aside, let Christian faith alone, in quiet and tranquil leisure, proceed through the sacred pages, so that he may not interrupt, and you, Christian, may nevertheless have what you desire, so far as this can be done through us with God’s help.

**On the Glorification of the Trinity and the Procession of the Holy Spirit, by R. D. D. Rupert, Abbot of Deutz**

**Book One**

**67 Chapter I**

**That the mystery of the Holy Trinity is a desirable treasure, and that this treasure is hidden in a field**

[Col. 0013D]

You are a desirable treasure to us, O wondrous mystery of the Trinity; and indeed a hidden treasure, yet hidden in such a way that you may be found by the attentive person who seeks you, having the eyes of his mind enlightened by faith. For where is that hidden treasure? In a field. Thus the Lord says in the Gospel: “The kingdom of heaven is like a treasure hidden in a field” (Matt. 13).

A wonderful thing! It is not hidden in a purse, in a lodging, or in an inner room—where people usually hide their treasures, since they fear thieves—but “in a field,” that is, in the open. What kind of concealment, I ask, is this: to be hidden in public? Yet it is so, and it is entirely true.

We have now undertaken this work, and the purpose of our present work is to demonstrate how, or in what manner, this treasure is hidden in the field. Let us therefore say that we have found this treasure hidden only from the blind; and that we may, as it were with a pointing finger, show it to those who have eyes but perhaps have not yet seen sufficiently and desire to see.

**Chapter II**

**That Holy Scripture of the Old Testament is this field, and why it is fittingly signified by the name of a field**

[Col. 0015B]

This field of which we have spoken is Holy Scripture of the Old Testament. It is rightly called a field because it is indeed a public thing: a thing placed in the open and set before all people, indeed all nations, who wish to read or hear it. Hence the truthful saying in the Psalm: “The Lord shall recount in the writings of the peoples” (Ps. 86). What does he mean by “in the writings of the peoples,” unless it is as if he said, “in the writings set forth for the peoples,” or “which may be read by all peoples”?

It would not have been necessary to say this unless there were certain Scriptures or writings which are not the writings of peoples: for example, the writings of Platonists and Aristotelians. Certainly, in contrast to what they wrote, the sacred Scriptures are rightly called the Scriptures of peoples, because they do not drive peoples—that is, the simple—from reading them. Even if they do not quickly grasp the mysteries, they at least easily grasp the literal sense and the moral understanding as well.

But the writings or sayings of those philosophers evade by slippery windings and exclude the simple. For example, if you say, “A man has died,” they say, “A dead man is not a man.” In one respect they speak truly: if he is a man, he lives; but if he is dead, he has ceased to be both a man and a soul and an animate body. The peoples—that is, the simple—do not attend to this and stand astonished. Nevertheless, it is true to say, “A man has died,” in the sense in which we are accustomed to signify the whole by a part. We rightly call the human body deprived of life “a man”; and both ordinary people and our Scriptures accept speech of this sort. On account of such simplicity, they are Scriptures of peoples.

Similarly, concerning what we have proposed here about the treasure, saying that it is hidden in the field, that is, in public, those men would say or write that there is a contradiction in the qualification, and other such things which ordinary people do not understand. Yet it is true; and not in the sense in which, in the earlier statement, a part signifies the whole. Rather, understand the whole of the whole: namely, that the whole is open or public to those who see, while the whole is hidden or closed to those who do not see.

**Chapter III**

**How, or from what sort of persons, a treasure of this kind is hidden in such a field, and by what sort it may quickly be found**

We have said in what field this treasure is hidden: namely, the glorious distinction of the persons of the Holy Trinity. We must now say how it is hidden there. For we proposed above to demonstrate both matters: in what field it is hidden and how it is hidden.

No distant example is needed for this demonstration. A suitable one is at hand, if you look at the basis for the saying: “The Lord shall recount in the writings of the peoples” (Ps. 86). You will certainly tell me that he said this concerning what he had earlier introduced in the form of a question: “Shall a man say of Zion, ‘A man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her’?” (ibid.)

In the same manner, and to the same degree, in which this great portion of the hidden treasure—this talent of great weight, this sacrament of the Incarnation pertaining solely to the person of the Son—is hidden in the often-mentioned field, the mystery of the whole Trinity is also hidden there, no more obscurely. It was hidden only from the unworthy, those who chose to be envious rather than to see, so that it could not be found while they sought it, and so that the good pearl, not to be trampled by swine, might not be cast before them.

Therefore he says: “O Zion, shall this man say, ‘A man was born in her’?”—that is, in his own city, concerning which he had previously said: “Glorious things have been spoken of you, city of God” (ibid.)—“and the Most High himself founded her.” Shall a man say this, that is, someone wholly earthly, such as a Jew or heretic? The implied answer is: No. For to say this belongs to gods and to all sons of the Most High (Ps. 81): that this man, who was born in holy Zion—the one city of all saints and elect angels and human beings—“himself founded her as the Most High” before he was born in her.

A merely human person will not say this; no one devoted to earthly understanding will understand it. Therefore, the treasure is hidden. Similarly, concerning all the sacraments and the distinction of the persons of the Holy Trinity, which is the great treasure, one must understand that its manner of concealment is such that an unbelieving person does not find it, while the faithful multitude of gods or sons of the Most High quickly apprehends it.

**Chapter IV**

**That this treasure is hidden not in one part of the field but throughout the whole field of Holy Scripture, and is found, or quickly discovered, by the worthy while remaining hidden from the unworthy**

In what part, finally, or in what parts of the field ought this hidden treasure to be found? Someone may perhaps suppose that the treasure is hidden or is to be shown in a part or parts, rather than in the whole field. To this I say: Not in parts, or by parts, but in the whole and throughout the whole, through every boundary of this field, this treasure has long been found and is still to be found.

What is this whole? Certainly, everything which God has done from the beginning of creation until now. I shall briefly run through the boundaries of the field: the divisions of useful works upon which all Holy Scripture rests; and I shall now promise that the co-operation of the Trinity, signified by the very letter, is absent nowhere in all these things.

First comes the creation of heaven and earth; next, the creation of the angelic creature; after this, the forming of man with the blessing of the fashioner or Creator; then, after the flood, the blessing for restoring the human race from a few human beings; after this, the promise made to Abraham concerning the blessed seed, which is Christ; then, God’s descent into Egypt to deliver his people; after this, the form of blessing by which Moses was commanded, when the tabernacle was completed, to bless the children of Israel; then the word spoken to David concerning the building of the Lord’s house, together with the sacraments of the Psalms and the proclamations of the prophets; after this, the consolation, or return, from captivity in Babylon; then the victorious battles of the Maccabees.

Through all these boundaries the field extends, and in all of them this treasure is hidden. To state it more plainly: from these works of God the holy Scripture of the Old Testament was written, and it is certain that the co-operation of the Holy Trinity was not absent from any one of them; this must be demonstrated in the present work.

When this has been demonstrated, the most radiant work of the Lord’s Incarnation, Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension, and of the coming of the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, will follow. Our modest discourse will then be able to sound forth with all the greater freedom and force in praise of the glory of the Holy Trinity, which began thereafter to be proclaimed publicly throughout the world, insofar as it has been fortified by more testimonies from the sayings and deeds of preceding ages. Therefore let us now begin the course of our undertaken work from the beginning of creation.

**Chapter V**

**On the opening of the book: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth”; how this treasure is concealed there; and that the Son is the Beginning, as he himself said: “I am the Beginning, who also speak to you”**

“In the beginning God created heaven and earth. But the earth was formless and empty, and darkness was upon the face of the deep, and the Spirit of God moved over the waters” (Gen. 1). Behold how the treasure is concealed. Let neither we be wearied nor anyone be disgusted by this frequent use of the names “treasure” and “its concealment.” There is joy in discovery; and joy over what has been discovered gladly repeats the same things as it ranges about, for it makes one speak from the abundance of the heart (Matt. 12).

Behold, then, how the treasure is concealed. When the Spirit of Holy Scripture intends the Holy Trinity to be understood in this opening of the book, it hides only one person beneath a slight veil and thereby conceals the face of the same Trinity from the wise and prudent, while intending to reveal it to little ones. Under what veil, and which person, does it conceal? Certainly the person of the Son, under the veil of the name *beginning*.

For the wise and prudent—that is, the proud—such as those who said to the incarnate Son of God, “Who are you?” (John 8), found nothing else, or wished to find nothing else, in the words “In the beginning he created,” than “He created first” or “He created at first.” In this sense even the distinguished pagan poet could say:

> In the beginning heaven, earth, and the flowing fields,  
> The shining globe of the moon, and the Titanian stars—  
> An inward Spirit nourishes them.  
> (*Virgil, Aeneid* 6)

But, attending to the little ones who would hear him, when they asked, as has been said, “Who are you?” he replied: “The Beginning, who also speak to you” (John 8). In saying this, he certainly unfolded this passage, this opening of Holy Scripture, so that you need not doubt that he wished you also to recognize what he says of himself in the Psalm: “At the head of the book it is written concerning me” (Ps. 39).

For what is the head of the book except this beginning of all the Scriptures of truth? Every sacred Scripture, every canonical Scripture, is one book, because it tends toward one end, proceeds from one God, and is written by one and the same Spirit. Conversely, all writings which do not come from the same Spirit of truth are many books. Therefore the wise Ecclesiastes says: “There is no end to the making of many books” (Eccl. 12).

Thus: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth, and the Spirit of God moved over the waters” (Gen. 1): the splendid head of the book proclaims the glory of the Holy Trinity. Let those who hate him flee from this face, as carnal Israel then fled and feared to approach when Moses’ face became radiant through converse with God (Exod. 24).

**9 Chapter VI**

**Why it was fitting that the Son, or Word of God, should be called the Beginning**

Why, then, was it fitting that the Son, or Word of God, should be called the Beginning? Certainly because all things were made through him. Yet, for the present purpose, too little has still been said. For all things were made not only through him, but also for his sake. Thus the Apostle says: “For it was fitting for him, for whom are all things and through whom are all things, in bringing many sons to glory, to perfect through sufferings the author of their salvation” (Heb. 2).

This is the true reason, the reason worthy of this great name, *Beginning*: because he is “for whom are all things and through whom are all things.” He, I say, is the principal and efficient cause of every creature.

Someone says: “And is not God the Father a beginning?” Certainly: the Father is beginning, the Son is beginning, and the Holy Spirit is beginning. Yet there are not three beginnings, but one Beginning, just as there are not three gods but one God.

Why, then, did the inspirer of Holy Scripture, the Spirit of God, wish in this opening of the book to call only the person of the Son “Beginning”? For this reason, I say: This entire book, all Holy Scripture, whose heading is “In the beginning God created heaven and earth”—for what creature, or for the sake of what creature, was it written? Certainly Holy Scripture was composed for the human creature, for the instruction of the human creature.

Without doubt, this one person, the Son of God, is Beginning to that creature in three ways. In two ways he is Beginning both to the angelic and to the human creature: namely, because all things are both for his sake and through him, as has already been said above. In a third way he is Beginning to the human creature alone, because through his Passion he was perfected as the author of our salvation: he is the prince and Beginning of our salvation.

This future reality did not escape Moses when, instructed beforehand by the finger of God, he began to write this Scripture. Therefore, rightly and reverently, according to the truth of the matter, he used *Bresith*—“beginning”—in place of *Ben*, “son,” calling the Son of God “Beginning.” He through whom and for whom he created us, saw us, and foresaw that we would be saved.

Accordingly, one should consider that, although the Father too is Beginning, and although the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are, as has already been said, one Beginning, “from whom are all things, through whom are all things, in whom are all things” (Rom. 11), nevertheless nowhere is either the Father or the Holy Spirit read to have named himself Beginning so manifestly as the Son named himself, saying to the Jews: “I am the Beginning, who also speak to you” (John 8).

**Chapter VII**

**On the Father’s saying to the Son in the Psalm: “With you is the Beginning in the day of your power, amid the splendours of the saints; from the womb, before the morning star, I begot you.”**
In the Psalm the Lord says to the Lord—that is, the Father to the Son:

> “With you is the beginning on the day of your power, in the splendours of the saints; from the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Ps. 109 [110]).

This is to be understood as though God the Father said to David’s Son, David’s Lord: “I, the Beginning, am with you; I work with you on the day of your power, in the advance of your victory or resurrection—the day, that is, on which the saints shone after darkness had been driven away and remission of sins received. I, I say, am the Beginning: namely, the Father, who ‘from the womb, before the morning star’—that is, before every creature—‘begot you.’” For Lucifer, who fell because he wished to be a beginning, was indeed “the beginning of the ways of God,” but he came after you (Job 40).

Nevertheless, this exposition, by which the Father is understood as “the beginning” in this verse, is troubling to weak minds, as we have learned by experience. For from this they think it may freely be said that the Father is the beginning of the Son; and they attempt to force into the same sense the Apostle’s statement: “But God is the head of Christ” (1 Cor. 11). Therefore, so that every stumbling-block may be removed and faith may proceed upon an unharmed path, it must be known that the wording of the cited verse imposes upon us no necessity to understand the Father by the name “beginning.”

For when it says, “The Lord said to my Lord,” that is, the Father to the Son, God to Christ, “With you is the beginning,” this is rightly understood as if it said: Therefore “sit at my right hand”; therefore “rule in the midst of your enemies,” because you are God and not merely man, Word and not merely flesh. In short, this is what “With you is the beginning” means: united with human nature—according to which you were seen or reckoned the least of men—is the divine nature, the ancient and uncreated Beginning (Isa. 35).

What else does Peter say in the Acts of the Apostles, speaking of this same Lord: “He went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, because God was with him” (Acts 10)? Certainly we do not understand it as it could be said that the Lord was with Moses, or as the Lord says to Joshua: “As I was with Moses, so I shall be with you” (Josh. 1). No: when it is said, “because God was with him,” namely Christ, we understand it as though it said: because he was not merely man, but God and man.

Likewise, when here you hear God the Father saying to Jesus Christ, the mediator between God and men, “With you is the beginning,” let Arius not suppose that an opportunity has been offered him to say: Since the Father here calls himself the beginning, therefore he is the beginning of the Son, and hence the Apostle says, “But God is the head of Christ” (Eph. 5). Bring the dispute to an end briefly: understand that the Beginning—that is, God or the Word—and the assumed man are one person, Jesus Christ; and that, for his human nature, the divinity of the Word inherent in him is Beginning, Head, and God. Moreover, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—the undivided Trinity—are one Beginning, one God, and one Head.

## CHAPTER VIII

Concerning the reason for the name “Beginning,” and concerning the Apostle’s saying: “For whom are all things, and through whom are all things.”

Much could already be said here from faithful testimonies gathered out of the treasury of the Scriptures. But since we have undertaken to proceed according to the order of Scripture, we must be brief, and must now demonstrate by another comparison why it pleased Moses the writer—or rather, him who spoke through Moses and wrote by the finger of God—to call the Son, or the Father’s Word, “Beginning” in this chapter of the book.

It has already been said that “all things are for him and through him”; and for this reason he is rightly designated by this name. But the same reason will be more agreeable when a comparison is introduced. The Apostle says that a man is the head of a woman because “man was not made for woman, but woman for man” (1 Cor. 11). For God said: “It is not good for the man to be alone; let us make for him a helper like himself” (Gen. 2). The latter is like the former.

For what other model did he have, so as first to make the man, and then, for the man and from the man, to make the woman, except his own Word, his own Son, “for whom and through whom all things were made”? Finally, what one woman was to one man, that was—and was destined to be—the one Church of all holy angels and chosen human beings to the one Son of God.

Yet in these acts of making there is a difference, just as there is between grammatical prepositions, and so also in the truth of the understanding. For the woman was made both for the man and from the man; but the Church is for the Son, not from the Son. No creature, I say, has been created from the divine substance itself. Hence the Apostle rightly said: “For whom are all things, and through whom are all things” (Heb. 2). And the Evangelist says: “All things were made through him” (John 1).

By this comparison, then, the mind can in some measure grasp how rightly the Son of God was called the Beginning at the beginning of creation. For if a man is rightly called the head, that is, the beginning, of woman because the woman was made for him, then much more undoubtedly does Scripture rightly call the Son of God the Beginning, because all things are for him and through him.

## CHAPTER IX

That the name “Beginning,” spoken to the Jews, has a loftier meaning than if he had said, “I am the Son of God,” or, “I am Christ.”

When, therefore, he declares himself to be the Beginning from this testimony at the head of the book, answering the Jews in this way—“I am the Beginning, who also speak to you” (John 8)—it is holy and venerable to consider how he both eludes their malicious intention and does not merely fail to conceal the truth of his essence, but reveals it more profoundly.

For this name, “Beginning,” has a loftier meaning than if he had said, “I am the Son of God,” or, “I am Christ.” To which angel or human being is it permitted or fitting that he be called Beginning? This term is incommunicable to every creature. The one who dared to say, “I made myself” (Ezek. 29)—for he is rebuked by the prophetic Spirit for having said this in Ezekiel, which is the same as saying, “I am the Beginning”—for that very reason fell as an angel and became the devil.

But the name “Son” is communicable; he himself communicated or shared it with his children, because they shared in his flesh and blood. Thus the Holy Spirit testified long beforehand in the Psalm: “I said: You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High” (Ps. 81 [82]). Nor does this conflict with what the Apostle says: “For to which of the angels did he ever say: You are my Son?” (Heb. 1). For he immediately adds, “Today I have begotten you”—words which in their entirety were never said, nor ever will be said, to anyone else.

“Christ” too is a communicable name. For example, God himself, speaking in the Psalm about the fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, says: “Do not touch my anointed ones [christos]” (Ps. 104 [105]). Thus, as has already been said, in calling himself Beginning he revealed the truth of his essence more profoundly than if he had said, “I am the Son of God,” or “I am Christ”; and he so evaded their malicious intention that they could not accuse him before the Roman authority as though he had assumed a royal title.

So also elsewhere, when those surrounding him said, “How long do you keep us in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly” (John 10), he did not immediately rise against them by saying, “I am Christ.” Rather, as though moving around behind them, and having said certain things about himself as the Shepherd and his sheep—a profession for which the Romans would not have cared greatly if he were accused on its account—he finally said: “I and the Father are one” (John 11). This is certainly far loftier than saying, “I am Christ,” because, as has already been said, many have been called christs, so much so that David did not hesitate to call even Saul, though rejected, “the Lord’s anointed [christus]” (1 Sam. 24).

## CHAPTER X

How the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one Beginning; and why it was more necessary that the person of the Son be known to be the Beginning.

So far, according to our ability, we have spoken of the person of the Son and why he ought rightly and reasonably to be called Beginning. Concerning the person of the Father, that he too is Beginning, it is not equally necessary to demonstrate this by the testimonies of Scripture. For every controversy of heretical perversity or Jewish unbelief has customarily erred not so much regarding the person of the Father as regarding that of the Son.

Among these the Arians were the fiercest. They not only resisted in words the truth held by the Church of God concerning the co-eternity of Father and Son, but also persecuted the same truth with swords, wishing the Father to be called or regarded uncreated, but the Son a creature.

If someone wishes, at the beginning of John’s Gospel, when it says, “In the beginning was the Word,” to understand the Father by “beginning,” so that the meaning becomes “the Word was in the Father,” he does violence to the text and leaves no place for the following statement. For after “In the beginning was the Word,” it is immediately added: “And the Word was with God.” What work, then, does “and the Word was with God” perform if you understand the same thing in “In the beginning was the Word”?

Therefore we understand “In the beginning was the Word” more aptly and directly as though it said: Before the ages was the Word, the Lord Christ, who appeared as man at the end of the ages. For the purpose of that holy Gospel is to defend and proclaim the antiquity of Christ the Son of God: that he did not begin to exist from Mary, as certain heretics were then saying and beginning to contend while that beloved disciple of the Lord was exiled on the island of Patmos; and for this same reason he wrote this Gospel last.

Thus, as has been said, it should be understood: “In the beginning was the Word”—Christ did not receive the beginning of his existence from Mary, but was God before the ages, and became man at the end of the ages. I say this not because the Father is not also Beginning—for I have said above that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, the blessed Trinity, are one Beginning—but because, on account of and against heretics, it was more necessary to defend the person of the Son than that of the Father through the testimony of Scripture and by this name Beginning: namely, that he was not made or created, but that all things were made for him and through him. This was the purpose of Moses—or of the finger of God in whom Moses wrote—when at the head of the book he placed this statement: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.”

## CHAPTER XI

Concerning the Holy Spirit, or the procession of the Holy Spirit: that it occurred in three ways—first, to create all things, as it is said, “And the Spirit of God moved over the waters”; second, so that the rational creature might be adorned with spiritual gifts; third, so that he might be given for the remission of sins, which did not occur before Christ’s coming.

You have found, then, O human being, a treasure here: your treasure is the Holy Trinity distinctly expressed, immediately followed by the words, “And the Spirit of God moved over the waters.” For the God who created is the Father; the Beginning in which he created is the Son; and “the Spirit of God who moved over the waters” is the Holy Spirit.

Regarding this third person of the Holy Trinity, it is not irrelevant to ask—indeed, it is worthy of inquiry and knowledge—why both here and through almost all the pages of the Old Testament he is called the Spirit of God or Spirit of the Lord, whereas in the Gospel, and from the very beginning of Luke’s Gospel, he is called the Holy Spirit without reference to God or the Lord. You will perceive that this is so if you survey with mental or diligent attention the Scriptures of both the Old and New Testaments.

If you ask this, you quickly find a useful answer: the procession of this Spirit, whom the holy Church of Christ calls “proceeding” on the authority of Christ himself, who says, “When the Paraclete comes, whom I shall send you, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father” (John 15)—his procession, I say, occurred in three ways according to the Scriptures of truth.

First, in order that all things might be created in the beginning, of which we have already spoken; second, in order that the human creature might be adorned with spiritual gifts, among which the greatest is that he spoke through the prophets; third, in order that he might be given for repentance and remission of sins, which did not happen before Christ’s coming.

Having first considered these matters, you plainly understand that when he first proceeded in order to create all things, as here: “And the Spirit of God moved over the waters” (Gen. 1), he was rightly called the Spirit of God. By this name, as Father Augustine says, it is understood that he is God’s own goodness: “For because God is good,” he says, “he therefore created all things.” And where he distributes his gifts, there the Spirit of the Lord is written; for example: “And the Spirit of the Lord departed from Saul and moved in David” (1 Sam. 16).

And when he began to work remission of sins, namely from the advent of Christ the Son of God, he began to be called by the glorious title Holy Spirit. Before the advent of that same Son of God, he was indeed given in distributions of graces, but not also for remission of sins. Hence the saying: “The Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John 7).

Since he himself is remission of all sins and our sanctification, he is beautifully honoured from our lips by the title Holy Spirit—not because he is sanctified, but because he sanctifies, or is the Sanctifier, and is Sanctification itself. But this will be discussed more fully in its proper place; for the present, preserving the order, let us return to the chapter.

## CHAPTER XII

Since both the Father is Spirit and the Son is Spirit, why this substantial name itself, namely “Spirit,” is more often assigned in the Holy Scriptures to this one person.

Although Scripture here calls this person alone Spirit, saying, “And the Spirit of God moved over the waters,” nevertheless both God himself, whose Spirit is here proclaimed, and the Beginning itself—that is, the Son, in whom “God created heaven and earth”—are Spirit; and there are not three spirits but one, just as there are not three gods but one God.

Hence in the Gospel, after the Son of God had said, “True worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and truth; for the Father also seeks such as worship him,” he immediately added: “God is Spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth” (John 4). In these words the intention is not that “Spirit” is the subject and “God” the predicate, making the sense “The Holy Spirit is God”—though this too is rightly proclaimed in its proper places. Rather, God is the subject and Spirit the predicate, so that the meaning is: God is Spirit.

For the Holy Trinity—understood here, as has been said, in “In the beginning God created heaven and earth, and the Spirit of God moved over the waters”—is, just as one God, so also truly proclaimed and understood to be one Spirit. Why, then, is this substantial name itself, Spirit, more frequently assigned in the Holy Scriptures to this one person? Is it because his nature is more subtle, though the Trinity’s nature or substance is one? Certainly not: it is not more subtle, for there is no dissimilarity of substance. Rather, this person has an operation of his own, exceedingly subtle.

For this Spirit is understood in God as, in the soul, its consciousness or intention. Thus the Apostle, after saying, “Who among men knows the things of a man except the spirit of the man which is in him?” immediately adds: “So also no one has known the things of God except the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. 2).

This Spirit is the power of the Most High, of Father and Son; for both persons are rightly understood in the name of the one God when the Spirit of God is spoken of, both in this chapter of the book and throughout the whole book—that is, Holy Scripture—where the Spirit of God or Spirit of the Lord is proclaimed everywhere. If, however, a distinction of persons is desired in this very relation, an example is ready at hand. In the Gospel the Lord says: “It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. 10). And the Apostle says to the Galatians: “Because you are children of God, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts” (Gal. 4); and elsewhere: “If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him” (Rom. 8).

He is, I say, the power of the Most High, just as the Son is the strength or arm of the Lord. His particular operation is this: through the arm of the Lord, that is, through the Son, all nature was made and every creature or substance formed; through this Spirit every chosen rational creature, angelic as well as human, is made alive and lives for God.

## CHAPTER XIII

Concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit: that its beginning was when the Spirit moved over the waters, and how far this Spirit of God has proceeded in his work.

Above, mention was made that the holy Church customarily calls this Spirit of God “proceeding,” in a solemn designation, on the authority of the Son of God himself, who first used this word when he said: “When the Paraclete comes, whom I shall send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father” (John 15).

From where, do you think, was the authority for this word or title taken, if not from this very chapter of the book, where it is said: “And the Spirit of God moved over the waters”? What was moving over the waters if not already proceeding? Everything that the Son of God, made man, walking and teaching among men, spoke had authority from the Holy Scriptures; and even when he was thought to speak new things, he looked to his own Scriptures, as the Beloved in the Song of Songs had long before said of himself: “His eyes are like doves beside streams of water, washed with milk and resting beside abundant waters” (Song 5).

Therefore, just as we are certain that when he said, “I am the Beginning, who also speak to you” (John 8), he looked, as was mentioned above, to this chapter of the book where it is said, “In the beginning God created heaven and earth,” so likewise, when he called the Holy Spirit proceeding, let us not doubt that he looked also to this passage, because it was written: “And the Spirit of God moved over the waters.”

The procession of the Holy Spirit is a great matter. Its beginning was that moving over the waters. Let us lift up our eyes—the eyes of the inner person, the eyes of faith that loves and seeks by understanding—and see how far this Spirit of God has proceeded in his work. Then we shall be able to weigh somewhat the dignity, or weight, of this saying concerning “the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father.”

Certainly, when he began to proceed, when he moved over the waters, the earth, made from nothing, “was empty and void, and darkness was over the face of the abyss” (Gen. 1). But what is the earth now, and what has been made in it through the omnipotence of him who proceeds?

It is too little merely to observe that first intellectual light was made; then the firmament in the midst of the waters dividing waters from waters; then, from the dry land called earth, the bringing forth of every green plant and every tree bearing fruit and having its seed in itself; then every adornment of the firmament or heaven, with sun, moon, and stars disposed in wonderful order; then every creature that swims in the waters, flies over the earth in the air, walks upon the earth either on four feet or two feet, or crawls without feet; and, finally, whatever was made at God’s word and created at God’s command. Last and most beautiful among these was the human creature. Of them all it is written: “God saw all things that he had made, and they were very good.”

It is too little, I say, to observe these things in the procession of this Spirit of God unless, having lifted up your eyes as stated, you see how far he has proceeded and will still proceed in his work: namely, until the Son of Man sits upon the seat of his majesty, possessing authority to make judgment on the right and on the left. This Son of Man is the Beginning of creation and the summit of this creation or procession of the Spirit of God, because all things were made for him and through him, as was recalled above with the testimony of the apostolic saying: “For it was fitting for him, for whom are all things and through whom are all things, who had brought many sons into glory, to perfect through suffering the author of their salvation” (Heb. 2).

## CHAPTER XIV

Again concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit: how it differs from the procession of the Son, since the Son said, “For I proceeded from God and came.”

Let us follow more attentively, with the glorification of the Trinity, the majesty of this procession. Let it be for us to fashion—or, by priestly right, to offer—the loaves of presentation from the table of the heavenly sanctuary which the Lord has prepared before us (Ps. 22 [23]); that is, by faithfully handling the Scriptures of truth, we may, so far as we can, make offerings of beautiful praise worthy of God.

We must first say what procession, or proceeding, itself is; then how the procession of the Holy Spirit differs from that of the Son. For the Son himself, speaking of himself, used this word when he said to the Jews: “If God were your Father, you would love both [him and me]. For I proceeded from God and came. For I did not come of myself, but he sent me” (John 8).

He used two words: “I proceeded and I came.” It is far too narrow to understand one and the same thing in these two words—namely, nothing more than that, coming into this world, he who had been invisible with God appeared visibly through assumed flesh. The meaning is broader, and its light of understanding greater, if you receive two births in these two words, “I proceeded and I came”: the birth of his divinity, by which he was begotten from the substance of the Father before the ages; and the birth of his humanity, by which he was born from the substance of his mother in time.

Yet his coming forth from the Virgin’s womb was also a proceeding, as it is written: “He himself is like a bridegroom proceeding from his chamber” (Ps. 18 [19]). Again, in another Psalm it is said to him: “Press on prosperously, proceed, and reign” (Ps. 44 [45]). This is rightly understood of his present life in humanity, according to which it was truly said: “The child Jesus advanced in age and wisdom” (Luke 2)—advancing, that is, until he appeared in words and deeds to be Wisdom itself.

And as it was said, so it happened: he proceeded prosperously through a little more than thirty years, and, after so brief a time had passed, behold, he now reigns with great power, as he says: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. 28). But here we deal with that more ancient proceeding of his, concerning which he said with no slight weight: “For I proceeded from God” (John 8).

What was that progress or procession, if not the wonderful and ineffable love of the one saying: “Let there be light; let there be a firmament” (Gen. 1); let there be lights, and all the other things, of which the Psalmist, contemplating that saying or Word, says: “He established them for ever and ever; he gave a commandment, and it shall not pass away” (Ps. 148)?

Therefore, as we proposed above, we must first say what procession or proceeding itself is, and then in what respect the procession of the Son, who said, “For I proceeded from God,” differs from the procession of the Holy Spirit, of whom the same Son said: “Whom I shall send to you, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father” (John 15).

## CHAPTER XV

What procession or proceeding is; and why, speaking of himself, he said “I proceeded” in the past tense, but of the Holy Spirit said “proceeds” in the present tense.

A procession is the solemn going forth of persons of the highest distinction, who make their presence manifest with a certain festival gravity, so that they rightly deserve reverence from the crowds who meet them, as often happens, with great delight and escort them with great joy.

Our own proceeding, because we are local beings, is a journey from place to place. But divinity is not local, although a place is sometimes assigned to it; for example, when someone says: “Truly the Lord is in this place, and I did not know it” (Gen. 28). The procession of divinity, however, is the effect of a wondrous work. Through it the majesty of so great a dominion is perceived and contemplated by the mind, just as the dignity of a venerable man proceeding reverently from place to place is known from his appearance.

Therefore, if we are teachable, attentive, and well-disposed to contemplate the beauty of so great a procession, the effect of the work can teach us to know the Lord of majesty: the Lord of majesty, I say, the Son, who proceeded long ago; and likewise the Lord of majesty, the Holy Spirit, who still proceeds.

Finally, this distinction in the tenses of the word must be heard carefully. Speaking of himself, the Son of God said in the past tense: “For I proceeded from God” (John 8); but speaking of the Holy Spirit, he said in the present tense: “Who proceeds from the Father” (ibid., ch. 15). It would therefore be most unsuitable to call both the Son and the Holy Spirit “proceeding,” since *procedens* is a present participle, as is the verb *procedit* (“proceeds”), which was said of the Holy Spirit alone.

The Son, however, proceeded long ago, as has been said. His procession was that effect of work from which God, who created all things through him, long ago rested, as Scripture plainly says: “God rested on the seventh day from all the work which he had accomplished; and he blessed the seventh day and sanctified it, because on it he had ceased from all his work which God created in order to make” (Gen. 2). For afterwards he created no new kind of creature which he had not created in its kind before that rest.

## CHAPTER XVI

That neither did the Son proceed to create all things without the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, nor does the Holy Spirit proceed to sanctify without the cooperation of the Son.

Do we, then, separate—or allow to be separated—the procession of the Holy Spirit, by which he still proceeds to the sanctification of the rational creature, from the procession of the Son, which, as has been said, proceeded long ago and ceased to proceed, that is, ceased to produce or accomplish new species of creatures? Do we say, or allow it to be said or thought, that the Son proceeded to create without the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, or that the Holy Spirit proceeds to sanctify without the cooperation of the Son? Far be it!

For the operation of the whole Trinity is inseparable: one God, one and inseparable sovereignty. Even then, when the Son proceeded from the mouth of the Father saying, “Let this or that be,” the Holy Spirit was the director of the whole work. And now, as long as the Holy Spirit proceeds to sanctify and moves over the waters of baptism—the same one “who moved over the waters” in the beginning, as Scripture says—the Son is the deciding and efficacious cause of that sanctification.

There, where God the Father with the Holy Spirit created all things through the Son—“all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made”—and here, where God the Father with the Son sanctifies the chosen rational creature, delights are prepared, or accomplished, through the cooperation of the whole Trinity: namely, those delights of love of which the Wisdom of God, the Son of God, speaks, remembering it as we say of his own procession:

> “When he prepared the heavens, I was there; when he enclosed the abysses by a fixed law and circuit; when he strengthened the upper air and balanced the fountains of the waters; when he set its boundary around the sea and gave the waters a law not to pass their bounds; when he laid the foundations of the earth, I was with him, arranging all things; and I delighted day by day, playing before him at all times, playing in the inhabited world, and my delights were to be with the children of men” (Prov. 8).

What is this except as though he said: When God said, “Let there be light”; when he said, “Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters; let the waters under heaven be gathered into one place”; when, I say, he said these and the other things and saw each day “that it was good” (Gen. 1), I proceeded from his mouth, for I am that utterance, or his Word.

Therefore the procession of the Son is not separated in time or place from the procession of the Holy Spirit, because these things were made when the Spirit of God “moved over the waters.” And, just as the Father, so also the Son and the Holy Spirit are one God, everywhere present and enclosed in no place.

Only this difference between the two processions, of Son and Spirit, must be recognized in the effect of their work. From the creation of creatures or substances, which were indeed made through the Son—for all things were made through him—“God rested on the seventh day.” But from the sanctification of the rational creature, a work accomplished through the Holy Spirit, neither the Father nor the Son has yet rested or ceased. Hence the same Son of God said to the Jews: “My Father works until now, and I work” (John 5).

Of those delights of Wisdom, who says, “My delights were to be with the children of men” (Prov. 8), there will be fuller discussion in its proper place, in that special work of the Trinity: namely, the making or formation of the human being.

## CHAPTER XVII

Against those who said that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone and not also from the Son: the saying of Wisdom, “Behold, I shall bring forth for you my Spirit and reveal my words.”

That same Wisdom says to the little ones: “Behold, I shall bring forth for you my Spirit and reveal my words” (Prov. 1). What is this except what incarnate Wisdom foresaw that it would do, and has now done? For when he had risen from the dead, standing in the midst of his disciples, he breathed on them and said: “Peace be with you; receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20). And, as another Evangelist says: “Then he opened their understanding, that they might understand the Scriptures” (Luke 24).

Was this not Wisdom—that is, the Son [‘of the Son’] of God—giving or bringing forth from himself his own Spirit, the Holy Spirit, proceeding from himself, and revealing his words? Again, in the same book it is written: “Wisdom built herself a house; she hewed out seven columns” (Prov. 9). What does this say except that the Word of God, the Son of God, assumed a nature, or a human body, and infused into that assumed man the sevenfold Holy Spirit?

We say this because there were certain persons, especially Greeks, who said that this Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone and not also from the Son. Yet the holy Roman Church, pillar of the Latin Church—long ago, through many councils, shining with evangelical light and firmly established on the rock of faith—so refuted them, having as a fellow-singer from among the Greeks Athanasius, catholic and orthodox, that it is no longer necessary for us to add anything, except that in our discourse we offer willing service to this procession, and in writing on such a subject chew over a certain sweet delight upon the palate of the heart.

But this delight is doubled, and gladdens more abundantly the beholder of so great a procession, if reason also supplies support together with the authority of Scripture, so that inward faith may not doubt that this Spirit of both proceeds no less from the Son than from the Father: God from God, not differing in substance, equal to both in majesty, not equal in glory.

Therefore, so that we may delight profitably in this procession and speak delightfully of profitable matters, we must first say how many, and what, are the modes of procession of this Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER XVIII

That the following saying of the Son, on the night when he was betrayed, greatly supports the same truth: “But I tell you the truth: it is expedient for you that I go away; for if I do not go, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go, I shall send him to you.”

Already mentioned above, but the subject now calls for repetition and fuller explanation: according to the Scriptures of truth, the procession of the Holy Spirit takes place in three ways. First, so that all things might be created in the beginning—that is, in the Son or through the Son. Among these, where it is said, “And the Spirit of God was borne over the waters,” the greatest and most beautiful creature is related to have been made: namely, intellectual light, the angelic creation. Secondly, so that the human creature might be adorned with spiritual gifts, among which the greatest is that he spoke through the prophets. Thirdly, so that he might be given for repentance and the remission of sins, which was not done before Christ’s coming. Who could doubt to say concerning this effect of procession—namely, being given for the remission of sins—that in this respect the Holy Spirit proceeds also from the Son? For concerning that gift likewise, by which the same Spirit distributes the divisions of graces, something must be said later; for in that mode too he proceeds from the Son. For the present it is preferable to speak of his being given for the remission of sins, without which gift no human being ever could be or can be saved.

The faithful hearer, I hope, will willingly and effectively receive this first point. The Son of God himself says: “I go to him who sent me, and none of you asks me, ‘Where are you going?’ But because I have said these things to you, sorrow has filled your heart. But I tell you the truth: it is expedient for you that I go away. For if I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go away, I will send him to you” (John 16). I know, indeed, and marvel that this passage has been treated by certain great and holy Fathers [Col. 0030C] in such a way that they said Christ’s apostles could not have spiritual love for the Lord himself unless he withdrew his bodily presence; and that this is what he means when he says: “For if I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go away, I will send him to you.”

Finally, such an exposition of this present chapter does not attain to the summit of the matter, or the majesty of the mystery being treated at that most sacred supper. Thus I do not hesitate to say that, considering the greatness and weight of the matter, this interpretation is good indeed, but seems much too slight. Moreover, it may also be said that what he here foretold did not happen for this reason: “Sorrow has filled your heart,” because, ascending into heaven, he removed his bodily presence [Col. 0030D] from their eyes. On the contrary, they rejoiced all the more for that reason, as Luke relates more clearly: “And it came to pass,” he says, “while he blessed them, that he departed from them and was carried up into heaven; and they, worshipping, returned to Jerusalem with great joy” (Luke 24). Whence, then, ought they to have been sorrowful, or whence did sorrow fill their hearts? Certainly because of his death, over which they mourned so long, until Mary Magdalene came announcing that he had risen—to those, Mark says, who had been with him, mourning and weeping (Mark 16).

Was this, then, he asks, going to the Father—namely, dying—since he said, “And now I go to him who sent me”? Clearly, this was going to the Father, from whom he will also be crowned with glory and honour on account of that same passion [Col. 0031A] of death (Heb. 2). Does not the Evangelist also say this at the beginning of the same discourse? “Jesus, knowing,” he says, “that his hour had come, that he should pass from this world to the Father” (John 13). And again: “Knowing,” he says, “that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he had come forth from God and goes to God” (ibid.).

## Chapter XIX

Again concerning the same saying; and that the Holy Spirit was then first called Paraclete, that is, Comforter, because he himself is the remission of sins—a remission which he did not previously bestow, Jesus not yet having been glorified.

Therefore, if we are to say something worthy of the great solemnity of the Lord’s own utterance, when he says, “But I tell you the truth: it is expedient for you” (John 16), it is also worth considering [Col. 0031B] that nowhere before that most sacred Supper, at which he delivered this discourse, did he call the Holy Spirit “Paraclete.” It belongs to an instructed mind to discern the reason for this name, “Paraclete,” which in Latin is called *consolator*, “comforter.” Whoever perceives that reason will at the same time understand that it greatly concerned the matter that he should call the Holy Spirit Paraclete particularly at such a time—something he had not previously done, whether through himself or through the prophets.

For what sort of time was it then, or what was being accomplished at that time? It was the time of the Passion, the time of glorification. For his hour was at hand, when, through the passion of death, he would pass from this world to the Father; and by this passage he was shortly to pass in such a way that we might receive [Col. 0031C] remission of sins. For our sins neither were nor are forgiven otherwise than through his blood. And what, I ask, is the first or greatest consolation of all the saints, if not remission of sins?

Therefore, when he says, “For if I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you,” he wishes it to be understood as though he had said: If I do not pass from this world through the passion of death, the Holy Spirit will not be given to you, nor to those before you, nor to those who will come after you, according to this gift which is the remission of sins. For this reason he is rightly called, and truly is, the Comforter. And when he immediately adds, “But if I go away, I will send him to you,” he plainly declares that this Comforter proceeds from himself: this Holy Spirit, the forgiver of sins and remission itself.

And who, except an unbeliever, would wish to doubt or be ignorant that remission of sins has proceeded to us from this person, from this Son of God? Does not the truth of the Gospel make this clearer than light to us, when he himself who had said, “But if I go away, I will send him to you,” after he had gone away, returned and stood in the midst of his disciples, breathed on them, and said, “Receive the Holy Spirit,” immediately adding, “Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them” (John 20)?

The Holy Spirit is not, indeed, a bodily breath. Nevertheless, by the word “he breathed,” two things are made intelligible to us: that this consolation proceeds from him, and that through this Holy Spirit all sins can be forgiven as easily as anyone can breathe when he wishes. Many considerations reasonably serve this truth; but lest a lengthy discourse become too wearisome, it is fitting, as it were, to take breath by bringing this little book to an end.

# Book II

[Col. 0031]

## Chapter I

Concerning the treasure of the Lord’s name: those who store it up for themselves are, according to blessed Job, kings and consuls, or princes.

O Trinity, God: those who faithfully store up for themselves the treasures of your name are kings, consuls, or princes. Blessed Job, wishing that he were like such rich men, says: “For now, sleeping, I should be silent and take rest in my sleep with the kings and consuls of the earth, who build solitudes for themselves; or with princes, who possess gold and fill their houses with silver” (Job 3).

What then of one so insignificant, who thinks that he has found this treasure hidden in a field, as I described in the preceding [Col. 0031D] book? Do you suppose that I dare hope that, when I possess this gold and fill my house with such silver, I shall sleep in silence and rest in my sleep with those kings and consuls of the earth—those who knew, each in his own time, how to govern themselves and to give counsel to others? “With those princes,” that is, with the holy teachers, who, in order to possess this gold and silver, built for themselves the solitudes [Col. 0032C] of holy contemplation, in accordance with that true saying: “Write wisdom in the time of leisure, and he who is diminished in activity shall acquire it” (Ecclus. 38).

Oh, may the old prophecy of the memorable Otomas [reading uncertain] be fulfilled as it was foreseen! Jesus Christ, Lord of all dwellings, who are yourself both the doorkeeper and the door, bring me into their house, even to their feet—not to say, to sit among them: namely, those kings, consuls, and princes already mentioned—with this promise: “You shall enter the grave in abundance” (Job 5). With this hope, therefore, let the faithful discourse that has been begun complete its course and, as far as it can, sound forth the praise of the proceeding Holy Spirit with the praise and glory of the supreme Trinity; let it search out testimony from the holy Scriptures.

## Chapter II

That the Holy Spirit proceeds no less from the Son than from the Father; and concerning the Son’s saying: “Whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father.”

A few things have already been said concerning the procession—because he proceeds for the remission of sins—and more remains to be said [Col. 0033A] in support of this truth: that this one and same Spirit proceeds no less from the Son than from the Father. For the Son himself said: “For if I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go away, I will send him to you” (John 16). This has already been discussed.

It remains to bring forward for this very question another saying of the same Son, upon which those who maintained that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone and not also from the Son seemed to themselves to rely strongly: “When the Paraclete comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father” (John 15). “See,” they say, “how he distinguished the matter, how carefully he expressed it. For he said merely, ‘Whom I will send to you,’ but added, ‘from the Father.’ Nor, content with saying it once, lest he should seem to have expressed it insufficiently, he added: [Col. 0033B] ‘Who proceeds from the Father.’”

Therefore, in order to establish that the Holy Spirit proceeds equally from the Son as from the Father, it is insufficient for them that the Son said in several places, “I will send him to you,” unless we give the reason why, or with what intention, he added, “who proceeds from the Father.” This is indeed a great question and difficult to resolve, if it were already established and conceded that whenever “Father” is named, only one person must be understood: God the Father of the only Son, Jesus Christ.

But since, as the Apostle says, “One God and Father of all” (Eph. 4), and since in the Lord’s Prayer we say, “Formed by divine instruction: Our Father, who are in heaven,” the name “Father” must be understood distinctly: at one time as the Father of all the children of adoption; at another as the Father of the only [Col. 0033C] and consubstantial Son. Thus, for us who are not born but adopted, the one and same triune God—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—is Father. But for him who alone is the natural Son, the Father is one person, and is called Father relatively to that only Son.

The mark of this distinction is as follows. In the Gospel there are places where this Son says, with a possessive pronoun, “my Father” or “of my Father”; and there are places where he says “Father,” “the Father,” or “from the Father,” as here, without adding such a pronoun. If you distinguish these carefully, it is most beautiful to observe that when he expressly says “Father” or “of the Father” with “my” or “of my,” the matters then spoken of far exceed the common fellowship of our brotherhood; that is, the things he then says are such as no one of us who are named and are his brothers or sons of God through grace is permitted or allowed to say.

For example: “My Father,” he says, “works until now, [Col. 0033D] and I work.” And: “Amen, amen, I say to you: the Son can do nothing of himself, except what he sees the Father doing.” And immediately after: “For as the Father raises the dead and gives life, so also the Son gives life to whom he wills” (John 5). Who among the children ever was or ever will be permitted to say these things and what follows, except this only Son of God?

But where he says “Father” without the possessive pronoun, he speaks more humbly concerning himself, in such a way that his words are nearly suited to, or capable of imitation by, our littleness—of us whose brother he deigns to be or to be called. For example: “And as the Father gave me commandment, so I do” (John 14). These are more humble words and express the humility of assumed humanity, in relation to which the one God—the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—is undoubtedly greater. Such also are the words he speaks in the same place: “If you loved me, you would indeed rejoice, because I go to the Father; for the Father is greater than I” (ibid.). “I will no longer speak much with you, for the prince of this world comes, and has nothing in me” (ibid.), and so forth.

It would be easy to demonstrate this distinction, observed almost everywhere in the Gospel Scriptures, were it not too long for the reader—especially since, instructed by these few examples, he can investigate the rest for himself.
