Yet he who is accustomed to sing in the person of the Son, “I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete” [Col. 0034B] (John 14), and likewise, “My food is to do the will of my Father” (John 4), should know that the Evangelist did not write, “My food is to do the will of my Father,” but “the will of him who sent me”; nor did he write, “I will ask my Father,” since asking belongs to an inferior nature and his request was to be the sacrifice of his Passion. Rather: “And I will ask the Father,” he says, “and he will give you another Paraclete.”

## Chapter III

Again concerning the same saying, against the heretics: from the statement “who proceeds from the Father” it does not follow that the Holy Spirit does not proceed from the Son; rather, it follows that the Holy Spirit is God, because he proceeds from divinity.

Therefore, since, in speaking of the proceeding Holy Spirit, he said, “whom I will send to you from the Father,” and did not add “my”; and likewise, “who proceeds from the Father,” and did not add “my”; secure and provident faith rightly understands “from the Father” as though he had said “from divinity”—that divinity, namely, which is the one substance of Father and Son.

Let us now inquire into the intention or reason why this faithful witness said that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father. Then this saying will sound and be heard by one “who has ears to hear” as truly the voice of the firmament, truly the sublime sound of God. What is the intention or reason, except that for which he was born and came into this world: namely, to bear witness to the truth? For thus he said: “For this I was born, and for this I came into the world, that I should bear witness to the truth” (John 18).

What is the sum of this truth to which testimony is to be borne, if not that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one true God? Surely, in bearing witness to this truth, that which the same Son of God said magnificently concerning himself has great relevance: “For I proceeded from God” (John 8); and that concerning the Holy Spirit: “who proceeds from the Father” (John 15).

For what, O Arian heretics, who said that the Holy Spirit is a creature; and you, O Macedonians, who said that the Holy Spirit is not God—what, I say, O senseless ones, proceeds or has proceeded from God except God? “That which is born of flesh is flesh; and that which is born of Spirit is spirit” (John 3). So beyond doubt, what has proceeded and proceeds from God is God. The Son proceeded from God; the Holy Spirit proceeds. Therefore the Son of God is God; therefore the Holy Spirit is God.

See how brief the saying is, yet how great a testimony it resounds! “Therefore, I proceeded from God” is a brief saying, but it bears great testimony to the truth that the Son of God is God. “Who proceeds from the Father” is a brief saying, but it bears great testimony to the truth that the Holy Spirit is God. This is the great voice of the firmament, as said above; this is the great sublime sound of God, thundering over the ancient serpent, who was conquered and cast down from heaven to earth (Rev. 12), and over the water of wicked teaching which he sent from his mouth like a river after the woman—that is, the Church—that he might cause her to be swept away by the river. Strengthened by this voice, the earth aided the woman by opening its mouth and swallowing that river: that is, the Fathers from the whole world assembled and opened their mouths so greatly that through scriptural testimonies they annihilated the blasphemies of the heretics, of whom the worst were the Arians and, after them, the Macedonians, who said that the Son of God was a creature and that the Holy Spirit was a creature and not God.

## Chapter IV

Again concerning the same statement: why, at that most sacred Supper at which he was betrayed, not content with saying, “Whom I will send to you,” he added, “who proceeds from the Father.”

Thus, when the Son of God said, “I will send the Paraclete to you from the Father,” and added or repeated, “who proceeds from the Father,” this does not mean that he does not proceed from the Son. Rather, it demonstrates that the majesty of him who proceeds must be magnified still further, lest someone think and a heretic say that he hopes from a man and does not proceed from the very substance.

This comparison which we shall give is of some help to the understanding of faith. In the Gospel according to Mark, after saying, “Whoever receives one of such children in my name receives me,” he immediately added: “And whoever receives me receives not me, but him who sent me” (Mark 9). For he was humble: among human beings he appeared as a man, among mortals as mortal; he seemed merely human and was not acknowledged as God. Therefore, lest anyone say or think, “Why do you count it a great thing that you are received? Or what is great about receiving someone in your name, when you too are a man like those whom you wish to be received in your name?” he rightly and aptly continued: “And whoever receives me receives not me, but him who sent me.”

Similarly, when he said these things, when he promised the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, did he not appear even more as a weak man and, as it were, the least of men on the evening in which he was betrayed, at that most sacred Supper? Did he not then especially labour in our weakness, and have neither form nor beauty? Hence the prophet says: “And we saw him, and there was no appearance; and we desired him, despised and the least of men, a man of sorrows and acquainted with infirmity; and as it were his face hidden, and despised” (Isa. 53). Therefore, lest the majesty of the Holy Spirit seem less, whether to those then present or to those yet to come, because such a man had said, “Whom I will send to you,” he rightly and necessarily added, “from the Father,” and repeating: “who,” he says, “proceeds from the Father”—that is, from the most high divinity, from which it should be believed or known what the Most High himself is.

Therefore, by this comparison, as has already been said, faith ought to be helped so that it may be firmer. Especially since, unlike the place where he said, “And whoever receives me,” he did not here introduce a kind of substitution by saying, “He does not receive me, but him who sent me.” For here he did not use such language as to say: “Whom I will send to you—not I, but he who sent me, will send.”

## Chapter V

That the Son is a fountain of this procession, just as the Father is, as the Psalmist says: “For with you is the fountain of life.”

Therefore, that we may draw life and, drinking, may never thirst, let us approach this proceeding one as intelligently as confidently, not doubting that the Son, equally with the Father, is the fountain of this procession. Thus let us say with the Psalmist to you, O Lord: “For with you is the fountain of life” (Ps. 35). For the Holy Spirit is life; the “fountain of life” is the Son of God; and the Lord to whom these words are addressed—“O Lord, your mercy is in heaven,” and so forth, down to “They shall be inebriated from the abundance of your house, and you shall give them drink from the torrent of your delight, for with you is the fountain of life” (ibid.)—is God the Father.

Thus in this psalm we understand the fountain to be with the Lord as, in the Gospel, the Word is with God. A river runs forth both from the fountain and from the fountain’s spring; the Holy Spirit proceeds both from the Son and from the Father. A river, for example Pishon or Gihon, flows from the fountain that is by Paradise (Gen. 2). “The rush of the river which makes glad the city of God” (Ps. 45) proceeds from the fountain that is with the Lord, from the Word which is, or was, with God.

Yet this comparison is not altogether perfect. Paradise and fountain, earth and water, are different substances; and a river emerges locally from the fountain or that earth. But the fountain and the Lord with whom is the fountain of life, and life itself—that is, the Holy Spirit—are one substance.

Now consider the sequence and connection of the words. After saying, “They shall be inebriated from the abundance of your house, and you shall give them drink from the torrent of your delight,” he added the reason why this ought to happen and whence it could happen, saying: “For with you is the fountain of life” (Ps. 35). For the present connective makes such a construction in reference to ability or possibility: “I said, ‘You shall give them drink from the torrent of your delight’”—that is, you will give them perfect and inestimable joy—and you can fittingly do this, “for with you is the fountain of life,” from whom proceeds the Holy Spirit, who himself is the torrent of your delight.

In reference to cause, however, it is thus: “I said, ‘You shall give them drink,’ and you ought to do this because they believe and confess that with you is that fountain of life.”

## Chapter VI

Relevant to the same truth is what that fountain, the Son himself, cried aloud: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink”; and concerning the opening of that same fountain.

Is this not what that fountain, the Son himself, cried aloud? “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. He who believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly” (John 7). To whom does it suit more fittingly than to a fountain to say, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink”? For a fountain has that which it pours forth from itself. The fountain of life which is with you, O Lord, has life—that is, the life-giving Spirit who proceeds from it—and, by abundant condescension, flows into the mouth of one who thirsts or can drink, that is, into the inward parts of the believing, desiring soul that wills to live.

Hence it is written in the prophet Zechariah: “On that day there shall be an open fountain to the house of David and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for the washing of the sinner and the menstruous woman” (Zech. 13). We rejoice that Christ, the Son of God, is designated by the name of fountain in this argument, because we are establishing what no one ought to doubt and what the Catholic Church now firmly believes: that the Holy Spirit proceeds no less from the Son than “from the Father.”

First, he proceeds for the remission of sins. Concerning this gift of the Holy Spirit, the prophet himself plainly says: “for the washing of the sinner and the menstruous woman”—that is, of both peoples: the sinful Gentile people and the menstruous Synagogue, one of whose nobler sons, Isaiah, confesses and says the same: “We have all become as unclean, and all our righteousnesses as the cloth of a menstruous woman” (Isa. 46 [citation as printed]).

Nor should it be unknown when, or from what day, this fountain was opened and washed the sinner and the menstruous woman, since it was said: “On that day there shall be an open fountain to the house of David” (Zech. 13). Surely that day is now the day of the glorification of Jesus Christ our Lord (John 12), from the time when, lifted up from the earth in order to draw all things to himself, he gave up the Spirit and “one of the soldiers opened his side with a spear, and immediately blood and water came out” (John 19). Then this fountain was made open, and from then on it is open, because not before then but from then on the Holy Spirit was given for the remission of sins.

For, as has already been said and must often be said and always known, the same Spirit had indeed been given to the Fathers and prophets in divisions of graces; but until then both the sinner and the menstruous woman had been deprived of this gift, which is washing. Hence comes the saying: “For the Holy Spirit was not yet given, because Jesus was not yet glorified” (John 7).

## Chapter VII

Concerning the special nature of that fountain which is with you, O Lord, and the equivocal use of “fountains” in Scripture, so that there one may draw waters with joy from the fountains of the Saviour.

Perhaps someone says: “Fountain” is a mystical name shared by many; for many fountains are named in Scripture. Many holy people—prophets and apostles, namely—are signified by the name of fountains. For example: “You shall draw waters with joy from the fountains of the Saviour” (Isa. 12). Again in the Psalm: “And the fountains of waters appeared” (Ps. 7). The Saviour himself also says to the Samaritan woman: “Whoever drinks from the water that I shall give him shall never thirst; but the water which I shall give him shall become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life” (John 4).

How, then, when seeking evidence for the procession of the Holy Spirit and maintaining that the same Holy Spirit proceeds no less from the Son than from the Father, do we rejoice so greatly in the signification of the Son by the title “fountain,” because it is written, “For with you is the fountain of life” (Ps. 135 [citation as printed]), and “On that day there shall be an open fountain to the house of David and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for the washing of the sinner and the menstruous woman” (Zech. 13)?

To this I say: there is a great difference between the fountain which is with God and the other fountains, all of which received from his fullness in order to become fountains. Although they differ greatly from him in this—that, as already said, all received from his fullness—and there are still many differences among them, the greatest distinction is the one I shall immediately state.

From the one fountain, which was and is with God (John 1), from the very deep heart of the Father, proceed not merely voices or words, but the very substance of the Holy Spirit. From the other fountains, however, only the voice or words of the same Holy Spirit proceed, not his very substance. What are the voice or words of the Holy Spirit? Surely all the Scriptures of truth, which the Spirit, inspirer of truth, spoke through the mouths of holy people (2 Pet. 1).

Therefore consider carefully these words: “But the water which I shall give him shall become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life” (John 4). This is correctly understood thus: the grace of the Holy Spirit which I shall give, or can give, to him—for that Spirit proceeds from me—is not and shall not be like the spirit of this world or the wisdom of this age, which does not give life. Like the water of this well which you draw, it does not prevent you from thirsting again. Rather, that same grace will produce in him an understanding of the life-giving Scripture; and this understanding continues as water does not cease flowing from a fountain, so that by speaking or also by writing it may, as through certain streams, water many meadows—that is, the souls of many people. Thus may come about what the Psalmist said: “Making its streams drunk, multiply its offspring; in its drops it shall rejoice as it springs forth” (Ps. 64).

Each of the fountains—that is, the holy people—can indeed do this, because they are inspired by God: they can pour forth a little stream of teaching and bring out a good discourse. But none can convey the Holy Spirit himself to a human being, however abundant he may be in the gift of that same Spirit, except that sole and unique fountain of life which is with you, O Lord.

## Chapter VIII

Concerning the Evangelist’s words: “But this he said concerning the Spirit, whom those believing in him were to receive.”

Therefore one must consider very carefully what happened when that fountain, as mentioned above, cried aloud in the Temple on the great day of the feast: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink; he who believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly.” The Evangelist immediately added: “But this he said concerning the Spirit, whom those believing in him were to receive” (John 7).

It may indeed simply and without offence, in fraternal peace, be accepted or understood that he cried all this concerning the Holy Spirit. But where there is disagreement, one must speak against those who disagree. Accordingly, while we deal here with the procession of the Holy Spirit, we must distinguish carefully: the Lord said, in a manner, not merely one thing but two things. For in the literal sense, drinking is one thing and pouring out rivers another, just as receiving is one thing and giving or rendering another.

Therefore, since the Evangelist did not write, “These things he said concerning the Spirit,” but “This he said concerning the Spirit,” an unconstrained exposition is available. What the Lord cried—“If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink”—he undoubtedly said concerning the Spirit, testifying that the Holy Spirit proceeds from himself. But when he added, “He who believes in me, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly,” he likewise spoke concerning the Spirit, but in the sense that it is not the Spirit himself, but the voice or teaching of the Holy Spirit, that pours itself forth from the belly or mouth of the inspired person, according to his saying elsewhere: “The Spirit breathes where he wills, and you hear his voice” (John 3).

For just as the voice sounding through a person inspired by the Holy Spirit—such as a prophet or apostle—and uttering a discourse of wisdom or knowledge, or any of the kinds of tongues, is not the very substance of the Holy Spirit breathing in the soul where he wills; so the rivers flowing from the believer’s belly are not the very substance of the water which that fountain gives, or to which he invites when he says, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink.” Nevertheless, both the voice which you hear and the rivers dispersed through the voice of a speaking person are rightly denoted by the name “spirit,” according to that mode of speech by which we often express the cause through its effect—for example, when we call hot iron “fire,” and water frozen by cold “winter.”

## Chapter IX

That from the belly of the believer in the Son of God flow only the mysteries of the Scriptures, administered through the Holy Spirit; but from that fountain—that is, the Son of God—the very substance of the Holy Spirit also proceeds.

Therefore, as has already been said, all other persons called, or worthy of being called, fountains differ greatly from that fountain which is God and man. From those fountains there flow only “rivers of living water,” which are not the very substance of the Holy Spirit, but the mysteries of the Scriptures administered through the Holy Spirit. From that fountain, however, the very substance of the Holy Spirit proceeds, because he is God; and rivers of Scripture flowed forth in bodily voice, because he is man.

There are many such “rivers from the belly” flowing both from his belly and from the belly of the believer in him. But there are four heads of all the rivers—that is, four principal rivers; rivers, I say, meaning mysteries. For just as there is one fountain, or “river which,” Scripture says, “went out from the place of delight to water Paradise, and from there is divided into four heads” (Gen. 2), that is, principal rivers, so among the many and manifold mysteries there are four chief mysteries of Christ, to which all divinely inspired Scripture directs its attention: his incarnation, his passion, his resurrection, and his ascension.

These rivers do not cease flowing both from his belly and from the belly of one who believes in him. The whole world has heard the voice of the Holy Spirit proclaiming these mysteries, both through his mouth and through the mouths of the apostles who believed in him—with this exception, again, which must be established in addition: these mysteries were both instituted and proclaimed by him; the others, however, were ministers and helpers in conveying this proclamation to us.

Now concerning what has already been mentioned—“The Spirit breathes where he wills”—that is, concerning the procession itself or the person who proceeds, namely that he is God and Lord and has the same majesty or power as the Father and Son in this very procession, further discussion is required. For now, the discourse concerning his proceeding no less from the Son than from the Father has been carried thus far.

## Chapter X

Concerning the Holy Spirit himself as he proceeds, and his divine power, according to the saying: “The Spirit breathes where he wills.”

The following very brief clause, “The Spirit breathes where he wills” (John 3) [Col. 0040C], declares splendidly to us who believe in him both the divine nature and likewise the divine power of that same Holy Spirit; and it is plainly a definition distinguishing him from every spirit which is not God or which breathes under God. For no spirit besides this Spirit, who is God, “breathes where he wills.” Every created spirit, whether good or evil, breathes where it is sent or permitted to breathe; nor does it breathe in such a way that the spirit itself enters into the substance of our spirit, except the Creator Spirit alone.

“What then,” someone asks, “does it mean that a man is said to be full of an evil spirit?” Just as we read of a certain holy or faithful man, for example, “Stephen, full of the Holy Spirit” (Acts 6) [Col. 0040D], so we read that Judas was influenced by an evil spirit—not in some indeterminate fashion, but so that the evangelist says of him: “Satan entered into him” (John 3). Likewise, concerning good spirits, there is this example in the prophet Zechariah: “And the angel who was speaking in me said to me: I will show you what these things are.” Again: “And the Lord answered the angel who was speaking in me with good words, consoling words” (Zech. 1). And afterward: “And behold, the angel who was speaking in me went out, and another angel went out to meet him” (ibid., 2).

I say in response to these things: neither these testimonies of Scripture compel us, nor reason itself permits us, to say or suppose that the spirit of a rational creature ever could have been, or can be, infused substantially into another rational spirit [Col. 0041A], or that a rational spirit is capable of another spirit except the Spirit of God alone. A spirit sent or permitted merely into the dwelling of the body inserts itself there. The evil spirit infects the captured human spirit with the poison of wickedness, or agitates it with frenzied scourges; but the good angel, appointed guardian of the human spirit, soothes it with good words, with consoling words. Neither infuses itself into its very substance. For the angelic spirit is not so much subtler than the human spirit that one is capable of the other, or one capable of being received by the other. The Creator Spirit alone—alone, I say—and the one God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, is capable of being received by the human spirit, because he is incomparably subtler.

“If anyone loves me,” says the Son, “my Father will love him, and we shall come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14) [Col. 0041B]. But concerning this Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, he said: “You will know him, because he will remain with you and will be in you” (ibid.).

## Chapter XI

On that mode of his breathing by which, breathing where he wills, he penetrates the very substance of the soul and traverses its abyss; and on the fact that in this life it is given to very few to experience this condescension.

Therefore this Spirit is God, and the present saying also confirms it: “The Spirit breathes where he wills.” When he wills, he breathes outwardly through an angel—that is, he gives a command or counsel. And when he wills, he breathes inwardly through himself—that is, he sensibly traverses the substance of the soul. But this last thing which I have spoken of belongs to very few while we live in the body [Col. 0041C] and are away from the Lord. The first thing which I mentioned—that when he wills he breathes outwardly—belongs to so many that it can sometimes happen even to evil persons.

For example: “Saul sent officers to seize David. When they saw the band of prophets prophesying, and Samuel standing over them, the Spirit of the Lord came also upon them, and they too began to prophesy” (1 Kings 19). Other messengers prophesied, and a third group prophesied; Saul himself went, and the Spirit of the Lord came also upon him, and he prophesied. For there is a certain effect capable of opening the inner eyes even of one who does not deserve the entrance into himself of the same Spirit of the Lord, so that he sees what he had not known and understands the will of the Lord—doubtless to his own judgment.

So also Balaam, speaking of himself, says: “Balaam son of Beor has spoken; the man whose eye is closed has spoken; the hearer of God’s words has spoken, who has beheld the vision of the Almighty, who falls, and thus his eyes are opened” (Num. 24) [Col. 0041D]. Concerning this Balaam, it must be observed for the present argument that, although it is said or written once and twice that the Lord, meeting him, put a word in his mouth (ibid.), nowhere is it said, “He put it in his heart,” as is said to the worthy and faithful man: “The word is near you, in your heart and in your mouth” (Deut. 30). For he did not in his heart, through love, savour the things which are of God, though with his mouth, through knowledge, he uttered the things which are of God (1 Cor. 2).

To experience this mode of breathing of which I began to speak—by which “the Holy Spirit, manifold, as Wisdom says, subtle, mobile, discriminating, undefiled, sure, gentle, steadfast, secure, more mobile than all things mobile” (Wisdom 7) [Col. 0042A], penetrates the very substance of the soul and traverses its abyss—belongs to very few so long as they are in this life, away from the Lord. Even if one of them has scarcely experienced it, he cannot express what he feels in words if he wishes, because it is ineffable.

Such a person has no need for someone to teach him that the Holy Spirit is God. The very anointing of his infusion teaches him, as John the apostle says in his epistle: “And you have an anointing from the Holy One, and you have no need that anyone should teach you; but as his anointing teaches you concerning all things” (1 John 2) [Col. 0042B]. He plainly says this from experience within himself. And he knew that some among them possessed something of this wonderful, ineffable anointing, through which the blessed soul understands that it is pleasing to God, as he afterward says: “By this we know that we remain in him, and he in us, because he has given us of his Spirit” (1 John 3).

## Chapter XII

If this Paraclete wills to breathe where the consolation of the present age is neither sought nor received; and concerning the Lord’s saying: “I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete.”

Where, I ask, does the Spirit will to breathe such an inspiration? For we believe and know that, as God and almighty Lord, he breathes where he wills [Col. 0042C]; but a loving mind does not inquire without purpose where he wills, or is accustomed, to breathe. I answer: he wills to breathe, and does breathe, with that wonderful inspiration of which I have spoken, where there is no consolation of the present age; where there is one who says, “My soul refused to be comforted” (Ps. 76). Again: “Woe is me, because my sojourning has been prolonged; I have dwelt among the dwellers of Kedar; my soul has been a sojourner for long” (Ps. 119).

But to whom is this groaning known, except to God or to his Spirit? Therefore he says more profoundly: “My secret is mine, my secret is mine; woe is me!” (Isa. 24). For what reason? “The earth shall be utterly broken, the earth shall be completely crushed, the earth shall be violently shaken, the earth shall be fiercely agitated” [Col. 0042D]; and understand: therefore my soul refused consolation, because stable consolation is not found upon an earth that is to be broken, crushed, shaken, and agitated. This has already happened several times in particular places, but at the last judgment it will happen universally and irreparably.

Where, because of such a cause, there is grief or groaning, there this Spirit, the Paraclete—that is, the Consoler—wills to breathe. All persons of this age have another consolation of their own: “Woe to you rich,” says the Lord, “because you have your consolation” (Luke 6). But to his disciples he says: “And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, that he may remain with you for ever” (John 14). He said “another Paraclete” because there are two Paracletes [Col. 0043A], greatly unlike—indeed, opposed to—one another: on the one side, the Spirit of God; on the other, the spirit of this world.

Therefore, after saying, “He will give you another Paraclete,” he added, “whom the world cannot receive, because it neither sees him nor knows him” (John 14): the world, namely, having its heart comforted and made fat by its own paraclesis, its own consolation. Indeed, it is a good and acceptable interpretation which has been stated before us: the Holy Spirit is called another Paraclete in relation to the Son because the Son himself is Paraclete—another in person, not another in nature. Yet the sense now proposed is likewise pleasing, indeed more straightforward.

For in the blessed Trinity there is indeed, and must necessarily be confessed for salvation, a plurality of persons; but there is no duality of paraclesis, that is, of consolation [Col. 0043B]. But here, in this opposition in which the world is set against God, when he says, “The Father will give you another Paraclete, the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive because it has not seen him,” the duality of paraclesis is evident. For, just as there are two spirits—one of the world, the other of God—thus reason permits us rightly to speak of two Paracletes having nothing in common: one, the spirit of this kind, which consoles the children of this age amid transitory delights; the other, the Spirit of God, in whom alone the children of God, the children of the Bridegroom who has been taken from them, have consolation (Matt. 9).

## Chapter XIII

Again, on the same condescension of the Spirit breathing where he wills, in accordance with that passage in Proverbs: “Do not give wine to kings, O Lemuel; do not give wine to kings. Give strong drink to those who mourn, and wine to those bitter in soul.”

Therefore the saying, “The Spirit breathes where he wills,” is to be understood reverently in this way: he wills at one time to breathe, and at another not to breathe, not by chance but according to the rationale of judgment. Wisdom indicates this rationale to us in Solomon’s Proverbs in these words: “Do not give wine to kings, O Lemuel; do not give wine to kings, because there is no secret where drunkenness reigns, lest perhaps they drink and forget judgments, and alter the cause of the children of the poor. Give strong drink to those who mourn, and wine to those bitter in soul. Let them drink and forget their want, and remember their sorrow no more” (Prov. 31) [Col. 0043C–D].

Lemuel, which is interpreted “in whom God is,” is Christ himself, in whom God truly was, as the apostle says: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. 5). Yet God was not in him as he is in us, but in a far different manner: namely, such that God the Word and the assumed man are one Christ, one person. The wine given by this Lemuel is undoubtedly this Holy Spirit. When he had been given to the apostles by him who said, “I will send upon you the promise of my Father” (Luke 24), and they spoke in tongues, those who heard were astonished; not knowing themselves what they said, they nevertheless spoke truth: “These men are full of new wine” (Acts 2).

The kings to whom this Lemuel does not wish to give this wine are the rich of this age, proud in their very riches; to them, as was already said above, this Lemuel himself says: “Woe to you, because you have your consolation” (Luke 6) [Col. 0044A]. And as though the same Lemuel were asked why he does not wish this Paraclete to send such wine to such persons, he says: “Because there is no secret where drunkenness reigns,” calling their pride drunkenness, their very abundance or confidence of consolation. There is surely no such secret there as this wine requires, as this Paraclete seeks.

What kind of secret, then, does he seek? Surely that a man bearing the yoke from his youth should sit alone and mourn (Lam. 3), keeping before his eyes the present reason why he ought to mourn: namely, that, mortal as he is, he lives in sins or in dangers of sin [Col. 0044B], and must render account before the tribunal of the dreadful Judge, where no consolation whatsoever of the present age, however great, will be of any use (2 Cor. 5). Therefore, because he truly despises that vanity, saying with the Psalmist, “My soul refused consolation” (Ps. 76), and because there is no such secret there, he says: “Do not, O Lemuel, give wine to kings,” that is, to the proud.

It often happens that one of such persons, having tasted, as he imagines, some small portion of this wine—having received, that is, a word of wisdom or knowledge, prophecy, kinds of tongues, or any of the other gifts distributed by the same Spirit, “the same Lord, the same God, apportioning to each as he wills” (1 Cor. 12)—uses it in pride and produces heresies and schisms. This is what he says of those kings: “Lest perhaps they drink and forget judgments, and alter the cause of the children of the poor” (Prov. 31) [Col. 0044C]. Heretics forget judgments when they judge or think wrongly concerning the holy Scriptures; and this is to alter the cause of the children of the poor—namely, of Christ, who, though rich, as the apostle says, became poor for our sakes (2 Cor. 8).

To whom, then, or to what sort of persons is the wine of this consolation due? “Give,” he says, “strong drink to those who mourn, and wine to those bitter in soul.” Those who mourn, those bitter in soul, are those who are weary of the present life and long for the future; and therefore they praise the dead more than the living, as Ecclesiastes says, “those who recognize their tearful exile” (Eccles. 4), according to the words: “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept, when we remembered Zion” (Ps. 136) [Col. 0044D].

Let these drink; let these receive the Spirit, the Paraclete, “and forget this their want, and remember such sorrow no more”: made certain by this pledge (Eph. 1) that the feet of the saints already stand in your courts, Jerusalem, where there is no want and sorrow will be no more (Rev. 12).

## Chapter XIV

That the sorrow of the saints and the bitterness of their souls proceed from great strength of faith, and that for this reason they are worthy of the consolation of the Holy Spirit.

O sweet sorrow, therefore, and O lovable bitterness of soul, possessing so great a recompense of holy joy [Col. 0045A], so delightful a visitation of so great a Lord, so sweet a consolation of so great a Paraclete: whence does the human spirit have you, and whence did you promise yourself to it? Surely from the strength of faith; and you bear it true witness that its faith is great. For unless it had faith in its inmost parts, it would not go about mourning, would not be bitter in soul, would not know itself needy and poor, and would not say, for example, what the mighty king, splendid in the glory of his kingdom, said: “Behold, as the eyes of servants are upon the hands of their masters, as the eyes of a handmaid are upon the hands of her mistress, so our eyes are upon the Lord our God until he has mercy upon us” (Ps. 122).

It would not know how to say, “We are greatly filled with contempt”; it would not know what honour, or how great an honour, it lost in Adam [Col. 0045B], or what reproach and how great a contempt it inherited in him. To know this is a matter of faith; and faith itself is the life of a human being (Hab. 2). Therefore the Lord says in the Prophet, and the apostle recalls it: “But the righteous lives by his faith” (Rom. 1), or: “My righteous one lives by faith” (Heb. 10).

It is therefore beautiful and devout to behold this entrance of the Paraclete: faith opens the door to him as he stands at it and knocks; having entered, he stoops in most gracious condescension into the embrace of faith, and dines with it, and it with him. Is it appropriate for the Son of God alone to say, “Behold, I stand at the door and knock; if anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will enter to him and dine with him, and he with me” (Rev. 3) [Col. 0045C], and not also for the Paraclete Spirit? Indeed, it is appropriate also for him. For the Son of God, or Word of God, is never accustomed to enter here to remain except through the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit is the guide of the journey, or of the entrance; and in a wonderful and ineffable way, although he himself is the gift of Father and Son, when he enters in the manner now under discussion—namely, through sensible grace, which is a great prerogative—he gives the Father and the Son with himself: that is, he brings about knowledge of the Father and Son.

## Chapter XV

On the distinctions of faith: why great faith, little faith, and least faith are so called in the sayings of the Lord.

Nearly all of us, indeed, have faith, for “without faith,” says the apostle, “it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 11) [Col. 0045D]; but not all have great faith, and consequently not all have received such grace. For there is great faith, little faith, and least faith. If this were not so, the Lord would not say elsewhere: “Great is your faith” (Matt. 15); elsewhere, “Why are you fearful, you of little faith?” (Matt. 8); and elsewhere, “How much more you, of least faith!” (Luke 12).

Something must briefly be said, by way of clarification, concerning these three distinctions. Least faith is found where people are indeed Christians and confess Christ, yet live in worldly conduct and think and are anxious about tomorrow, saying, “What shall we eat? What shall we drink? With what shall we be clothed?” (Matt. 6). Because of this excessive anxiety, they avoid undertaking a stricter life, and almost despair of God’s care if they lack any one of these things even for a time [Col. 0046A]. Therefore the Lord says: “But if God so clothes the grass, which is here today and tomorrow is cast into the oven, how much more you, of least faith!” (ibid.).

Little faith, however, is found where, through fear of death, someone suppresses the voice of Christian confession at the crisis of persecution. Peter did this when he denied Christ (Mark 14), as did the other apostles, who all fled after abandoning him. Therefore he said to Peter, when he began to sink because he saw the strong wind and was afraid: “O you of little faith, why did you doubt?” (Matt. 14). Likewise, in the other storm, he said to both Peter and the other disciples: “Why are you fearful, you of little faith?” (Matt. 8).

For both storms signified the coming disturbance caused by the Jews. The first, where it is written, “But he was sleeping, while the boat was being covered by the waves” (ibid.), was a sign that, while the Lord slept the sleep of death, the faith of the disciples would be endangered [Col. 0046B]. The second, where “he came to them walking upon the sea” (Matt. 14) and grasped the hand of Peter as he cried out because he had begun to sink in doubt, was a sign of the resurrection: in that he walked upon the sea, he was to walk upon the waves of death, as it is written: “He who ascends over the setting, the Lord is his name” (Ps. 67). And it signified that he would console that same Peter, so that he would not lose his apostolic rank. Peter then cried out because he had begun to sink when, going outside, he wept bitterly, and the Lord looked upon him as he wept.

Great faith, moreover, is found where both the apostles and the other saints not only did not fear death but even chose to die for the sake of eternal life (Luke 22), following the example of the three youths who, when they said to King Nebuchadnezzar, “Behold, our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the furnace of burning fire and to free us from your hands, O king,” added further: “But if he does not will it, let it be known to you, O king, that we do not worship your gods, nor adore the golden statue which you have set up” (Dan. 3) [Col. 0046C].

## Chapter XVI

Again, on the sorrow or bitterness of great faith, and on Solomon’s statement: “A heart which knows the bitterness of its own soul—no stranger shall mingle in its joy.”

Surely that grief of those who mourn, or who are bitter in soul, belongs to this faith, because while living in the body they remain long away from the Lord (1 Cor. 2), and they refuse to receive any consolation from this age. They groan, they groan; and they do not groan merely because they are going to die, but because they live. They weep for life itself because they fear that in living they may sin. Here is the place; here the cause demands that the Spirit, “who breathes where he wills,” should breathe in the manner already described.

With what fruit? With what effect? Surely, that by his infusion he may bestow some gift of himself, and, in bestowing it, may as it were soothe the face of the weeping soul with the hand of pious consolation, wipe away its tear, and cause it to receive certain firstfruits of joy: “that he may give it rest from evil days” (Ps. 93) [Col. 0047A], and that it may live patiently until the time of its calling comes; so that, sitting alone, a person may speak with God whenever he wishes and exercise himself in the gift he has received.

This is the meaning of the saying: “A heart which knows the bitterness of its own soul—no stranger shall mingle in its joy” (Prov. 14). What is the bitterness of the soul but this pilgrimage, on account of which, or in view of which, the Psalmist says, as has already been mentioned: “Woe is me, because my sojourning has been prolonged; my soul has been a sojourner for long; my soul refused consolation” (Ps. 119)? Yet not every heart knows this bitterness. Many hearts are so dull that they do not feel it; indeed, they consider bitterness sweetness, and reckon the brief stay of this life not a pilgrimage but a homeland [Col. 0047B].

Death of the body is bitter to them, indeed even the mere remembrance of death; as the Wise Man says: “O death, how bitter is the remembrance of you to the man who has peace in his possessions, to the tranquil man whose ways prosper in all things, and who is still able to take food!” (Sir. 49). But they do not consider the cause of death—the fact that death entered this world through sin. Therefore, by no small separation, he separates those who mourn from those who do not mourn, saying: “A heart which knows the bitterness of its own soul—no stranger shall mingle in its joy.” This is the same as the Saviour’s saying: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5).

For what is the joy of that heart except the consolation of this Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, visiting that heart because it knows its own bitterness? And he rightly says of this joy that “no stranger shall mingle in it.” For he is the Spirit of truth, teaching all truth; and, as the Psalmist says, “Your good Spirit will lead me into the right land” (Ps. 142) [Col. 0047C], he guards the soul so that the spirit of deception—the true stranger, because contrary to truth—may not creep in. This, then, is the fruit of great faith, which, as stated above, opened its door to this Paraclete so that he might enter: it did so by mourning in bitterness and by refusing temporal consolation.

## Chapter XVII

On the Lord’s addition, after “The Spirit breathes where he wills”: “You hear his voice, but do not know whence he comes or whither he goes”; and on the fact that the coming Spirit displays some sign appropriate to the grace he brings.

What then follows when the Spirit has breathed where he wills with such great condescension? “And you hear his voice,” he says, “but do not know whence he comes or whither he goes” (John 3) [Col. 0047D]. True is the saying, “You hear his voice.” For one who has received such grace cannot keep silence, even if he sometimes wishes to be silent because of some reason or danger.

For example, Jeremiah says: “I have become a mockery all day long; everyone derides me. For for a long time now I have spoken, crying out injustice and proclaiming devastation. And the word of the Lord has become to me reproach and mockery all day long; and I said: I will not remember him, nor speak in his name.” When he had said this and, by this declaration, resolved to keep silent [Col. 0048A], what immediately follows? “It became,” he says, “in my heart like a raging fire, shut up in my bones; and I grew faint, unable to bear it” (Jer. 20).

The same sense appears in the Psalmist’s statement: after saying, “I set a guard upon my mouth when the sinner stood against me; I was mute and humbled, and kept silence even from good,” he immediately adds: “And my sorrow was renewed; my heart grew hot within me, and in my meditation fire burned” (Ps. 38). Truly, therefore, you hear his voice, because he cannot be silent and does not dare to hold his peace. For there is within him a master who has given him the trumpet of voice and says: “Cry aloud; do not cease” (Isa. 58), and other similar words.

But perhaps you do not know that he has such an inward monitor; and therefore you ridicule him as he speaks and mock him as he cries. It follows: “But you do not know whence he comes or whither he goes” (John 3) [Col. 0048B]. Truly you do not know whence he comes. Perhaps you were in another chamber and asleep when that Lord, that Paraclete, saw the person whose voice you hear keeping watch, as the Psalmist says, “My eyes anticipated the watches” (Ps. 76), and in great condescension bent down to him either like a river of milk or like a torrent of fire, according to the prophetic saying: “For thus says the Lord: Behold, I bend toward them like a river of peace, and like an overflowing torrent of the glory of the nations” (Isa. 66).

For he who proceeds is accustomed, wherever he proceeds, to make an array appropriate to his procession and, according to the grace which he brings among the many divisions of graces, to present to the senses of the soul—or even to the eyes of the body—a sign suitable to his coming or presence [Col. 0048C].

## Chapter XVIII

An account of certain signs with which, in our own days, the Holy Spirit graciously infused the visitation of himself into certain persons.

For the moment I shall be silent about greater signs: namely, the sign or manifestation by which he appeared over the Lord in the form of a dove (Matt. 3), and over his apostles in fire (Acts 2), since he was to mitigate the wrath of that Judge for us and kindle with good zeal the hearts of these men, hitherto weak. Let it not trouble us to write, or anyone of good will to attend to, the lesser signs which we have seen in our time, whoever he may be who deigns to read these things.

A maiden named Waldrada was making preparations for marriage, though the marriage did not please her in heart. One night, while she was awake and the others slept, this Paraclete breathed upon her in such a way that those who slept awoke because of the greatness of the heat and cried out, thinking that the house itself was burning [Col. 0048D]. She lay beside her widowed mother, who had undertaken the purpose of holy widowhood. Through the upper window of the house, behold, a great fire came and entered; descending to her, who alone saw these things, it slipped into her mouth and into the hidden parts of her womb.

Her mother was the first to be shaken from sleep by the greatness of the burning heat which touched her powerfully, and she cried more loudly: “Rise, rise! We are burning, we are burning!” But that fire did not burn; it illumined. It did not consume the body; it shone within the soul. Therefore, while they were disturbed and felt the heat but did not see the fire, the mother at length perceived that the heat issuing from her daughter was spreading itself. The daughter, now inflamed with divine love and wounded in heart, wept abundantly, so that from that hour she did not cease for a long time to pour forth tears [Col. 0049A].

And from then on, who heard her voice? For what happened to her was in accordance with this very chapter now under discussion, in which the Lord said: “The Spirit breathes where he wills, and you hear his voice, but do not know whence he comes or whither he goes” (John 3). What voice of hers, then, did anyone hear from that time onward, except her vow, resolve, and observance of holy virginity? She remained in that resolve until old age and led a solitary life in seclusion; finally, after completing her course, about four years ago, she passed, as we believe, from earthly marriage, from whose midst she had been called, to heavenly marriage.

Another man, who mourned almost inconsolably that his sojourning was prolonged (Ps. 119), praised the dead more than the living with Ecclesiastes (Eccles. 4), and—like Hannah in the account (1 Sam. 1)—whose countenance was no longer changed in different directions [reading uncertain], one night gave himself to sleep, full of pain and wholly in mourning. Behold, he saw the heaven above somehow opened a little; and from it something like a shining talent of ineffable, living substance was swiftly sent down, quicker than speech. Entering into his breast, it immediately shook him from sleep by its greatness or weight—heavier than gold, sweeter than honey [Col. 0049B].

When it had entered, it first rested for a little while and held itself still from every movement; he too remained still, lying perhaps on his back, and awaited what would happen. Then it began to move and circle about the womb of the inner person, the womb of the soul, which, he confesses, he had not known until then to be capable of so much. Thus, in a wonderful manner, the living thing and true life moved in circles; and each ensuing circuit was greater and much wider than the preceding one. At last the final infusion, like a great overflowing river, made him understand or feel that the entire receptacle of the soul or heart was full and could receive no more.

When this had happened, it again rested briefly, so that it neither flowed in as it had done nor flowed out as it afterward did [Col. 0049C]. Meanwhile the inner person wished, as it were, to see more clearly the face of that living substance; but in some manner it concealed itself so that its face could not be seen, though it was felt with very great weight and with great sweetness. Afterwards it began to turn back; making its circuit toward another direction in the manner of a river, it flowed out through the left side, in sight of the eyes of the inner person. As it flowed out with its final waves, it paused a little; and behold, he says, “I saw that that most beautiful substance was like liquid gold” [Col. 0049D].

## Chapter XIX

Again, on his saying, “You hear his voice”: that the voice of the inspired person is full of groaning; what it means not to know whence he comes, and what it means not to know whither he goes.

Therefore, because no one knows any such grace except one who receives it, Truth itself rightly and truly says: “You hear his voice, but do not know whence he comes or whither he goes.” You hear the voice of one groaning; you hear the voice of one speaking the words of God; but you do not know from what furnace the voice of groaning has been formed, or by what river the voice of exultation and confession has been imbued and gladdened. This is not to know whence he comes.

And what is it not to know whither he goes? Surely, not to know what he desires, why, exulting, he groans, or, groaning, he exults. He himself knows toward what he tends, and speaks truthfully according to that knowledge: “As the deer longs for springs of waters, so my soul longs for you, O God” (Ps. 41), and other similar words [Col. 0050A].

Perhaps, while he considers himself to be in secret, or believes that he has a secret which he loves, so that without witnesses he may groan freely according to his desire and hear the sound of his own groaning—which hearing delights him just as eating bread delights him, so that he can truthfully say, “My tears became bread to me by day and night” (ibid.)—perhaps, I say, you happened to be lying nearby without his knowing it [Col. 0050B]. As he wailed on high and gave free rein to his groans, you heard and wondered; you heard and felt compassion, because you had not yet experienced such a wound and did not know what cause, or what sort of cause, produced so great groans. And you could indeed wonder. For who can groan as intensely over any bitterness of this world as does one of this kind because of the sweetness of the love of God?

Here plainly is what the apostle says: “For we do not know what we should pray for as we ought; but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings that cannot be expressed” (Rom. 8). And truly it is wonderful and ineffable that, although this Spirit is given as Consoler to those who say, “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept, when we remembered Zion” (Ps. 136), and is therefore called or named Paraclete, yet this same Spirit, when he comes and has infused himself and brought the whole dwelling-place of the soul into his possession, increases groans, multiplies tears, and produces more frequent sighs [Col. 0050C], while the face nevertheless remains exceedingly joyful. Thus you greatly wonder at the cheerfulness of a person’s public countenance when, lurking as though by stealth, you had heard in private that person’s groans.

Therefore, just as you do not know whence he comes, so you do not know whither he goes; nor can you ever sufficiently know it unless the same thing happens to you likewise, unless you receive a similar wound from this Spirit of loving-kindness [Col. 0050D].

## Chapter XX

In the case of one who groans under inspiration, proof of the saying which Truth spoke in promise: “Amen, amen, I say to you, if you ask the Father for anything in my name, he will give it to you”; and concerning the apostle who asked the Lord three times.

In this man, then, was proved what Truth promised when it said: “Amen, amen, I say to you: if you ask the Father for anything in my name, he will give it to you” (John 16). For on what grounds, or by what right, does it come about that one receives what one asks, except because one asks only according to God? Hence, after the Apostle had said what was mentioned above, “the Spirit himself intercedes for us with inexpressible groanings,” [Col. 0051A] he immediately added: “But he who searches hearts knows what the Spirit desires, because he intercedes for the saints according to God” (Rom. 8). Therefore not everyone ought to hurry, upon hearing, “If you ask the Father for anything in my name, he will give it to you,” to expect that what he asks will be done for him. For this does not apply to all, but only to those who have received that Paraclete, who intercedes according to God for the saints. This, indeed, is to ask in the name of the Savior, whom at that time in the same discourse he promised to his apostles.

But someone says: the very Apostle who wrote the foregoing words, “the Spirit intercedes for us,” and the rest, and who possessed an eminent grace of that same Spirit, as he says there: “But we ourselves also, having the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan within ourselves” [Col. 0051B] (ibid.)—he, I say, asked, and it was not granted to him. For he says: “There was given to me a thorn for my flesh, an angel of Satan” (2 Cor. 12), “on account of which I asked the Lord three times that it might depart from me; and he said to me: ‘My grace is sufficient for you’” (ibid.). “For strength is perfected in weakness.” Did he not ask according to God? Or was he not himself one of the saints for whom he said that this groaning Spirit intercedes? Yet it was not granted to him.

To this I say: whence do we know that it was not granted to him? Does he himself say this? We know, indeed, that our elders, far better than we, have said and written that he was not heard, and have labored to show that it was not useful for him to be heard. Yet even if someone wishes to press us by the authority of those who are held in great esteem, we nevertheless do not hesitate to say that he was heard. What if he was not heard immediately—not at the first, not at the second, not even at the third petition? For the Savior did not say: If you ask the Father for anything in my name, he will give it to you immediately. Nor did he intend it to be understood in that way. For when he was about to say, “Ask and you shall receive; knock and it shall be opened to you” (Matt. 7), he first set forth a beautiful example of perseverance: “Which of you,” he says, “will have a friend, and will go to him at midnight, and say to him, ‘Friend, lend me three loaves,’” and so forth, down to: “Yet because of his persistence he will rise and give to him” (Luke 11).

Therefore do not tell me that he was not heard, and that such a hero [Col. 0051D] was buffeted by that wicked angel until the end of his life. It may indeed have been part of the divine dispensation that he should be buffeted for a time, lest the greatness of his revelations should exalt him while still young; but that, once he was a mature man and a veteran soldier, he should thereafter be made secure from such buffetings. This well befitted him who disposes all things sweetly (Wis. 2), the Ancient of Days with gray and venerable head.

## CHAPTER XXI

Whether, after this Paraclete has once poured himself in through a familiar visitation, it may happen that he withdraws himself and utterly and irretrievably abandons the soul he has kissed.

It is now asked whether or not this Paraclete, [Col. 0052A] after he has once poured himself into the inner chamber of the soul by that familiar visitation of which we have spoken thus far, may afterward withdraw himself from it, offended by some sin, so as utterly to forsake a soul once kissed by his consolation and leave it desolate with everlasting desolation.

On this point I wish to answer briefly: excessive confidence is dangerous. The Apostle does not wish anyone to be overconfident; he said of himself—and surely said it as an example for our benefit—“For behold, I do not reckon myself to have attained” (Phil. 3). Yet elsewhere, after saying, “We also glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces patience, patience testing, and testing hope,” he immediately adds: “But hope does not disappoint, because [Col. 0052B] the love of God has been poured out into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5).

Therefore we do not dare proclaim security to anyone of this kind who has received such a grace of the Holy Spirit as we are discussing, which the Apostle calls “the firstfruits of the Spirit.” Yet we do not hesitate to say that his hope is—or ought to be—firmer because of such a conscience, because he has already experienced that he has as guardian him of whom it is written: “Behold, he who guards Israel will neither slumber nor sleep” (Ps. 120). This is said to whoever has been made like Israel. In what respect? Surely in that, as he wrestled with God (Gen. 32), was strong against God and prevailed, and said to him while weeping and entreating him—which is true strength—as Hosea recalls, saying: “He prevailed against the angel and was strengthened; he wept and entreated him: ‘I will not let you go unless you bless me’; and he blessed him in that same place” (Hos. 12). So this man also has wrestled somewhat with God, weeping because he knew himself to be an exile; and he was strong against God, and God could not overcome him. He could not restrain himself, while that man wept and entreated him, from pouring out upon him, from the abundance of his mercies, the Spirit, the Paraclete.

Therefore he who guarded Israel and his race, so that the confirmed blessing, though offended by the many sins of that people, did not fail until Christ should be born from it—“Behold,” says the Psalmist, “he will neither slumber nor [Col. 0052D] sleep” (Ps. 120)—will also guard you, a true Israelite, so that you do not sin; but if you do sin, you may quickly lament your sin, in accordance with the saying: “Amen, amen, I say to you: he who believes in me, even if he has died, shall live” (John 11).

## CHAPTER XXII

That no one ought to have excessive security; and concerning the Apostle’s saying, “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God”; and that David, because he had grieved him, said, “Restore to me the joy of your salvation.”

Therefore no one, while living, ought to possess or presume upon excessive security. Rather, the more familiarly one has experienced that kiss of the consoling Paraclete, of which, as we mentioned above, the Apostle said: “Because the love of God has been poured out into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” [Col. 0053A] (Rom. 5), the more vigilant one ought to be lest one grieve that same Spirit, as the same Apostle says: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption” (Eph. 4). Explaining by what occurrences he is accustomed to be grieved, he says: “Let all bitterness, wrath, indignation, clamor, and blasphemy be removed from you, together with all malice” (ibid.).

The nature of the Holy Spirit is indeed incapable of suffering; nevertheless, when the gift of that same Holy Spirit dwelling in a human being stirs itself, the person himself, in that stirring, experiences less sweetness and more severity if he has acted carelessly in any respect. Those who have experienced it know this better.

For example, David had experienced these things. He said: “Do not take your Holy Spirit from me,” immediately adding: [Col. 0053B] “Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and strengthen me with a ruling spirit” (Ps. 50). Certainly, although he had sinned grievously, the Spirit of the Lord had not departed from him [Col. 0054A]—of whom it is written: “When Samuel anointed him, the Spirit of the Lord came directly upon David from that day onward” (1 Sam. 16)—but thereafter it did not show itself so joyful or pleasant in its movement or attraction as it had formerly been accustomed to do. Nor did he recover that joy or delight so quickly, except after suitable satisfaction, while he endured meanwhile great tribulation both outwardly and inwardly, so that scarcely anyone more fittingly than he could say: “I found tribulation and sorrow” (Ps. 14).

For it must be understood that he grieved inwardly because he had grieved the Spirit of the Lord (2 Sam. 13); and the outward tribulation that followed, namely the disaster within his household, undoubtedly struck him sharply. And although in body he escaped the sword of his son, nevertheless the sword reached even to [Col. 0054B] his soul: “Iron passed through his soul” (Luke 2).

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 0053]

## CHAPTER I [Col. 0053B]

That we ought to bless the Lord as much as we can, and that he is greater than praise; for many things are hidden, and we have seen few of his works.

“Blessing the Lord,” says a certain Wise Man, “exalt him as much as you can, for he is greater than all praise. When exalting him, be filled with strength; do not grow weary, for you will not attain. Who has seen him and described him? And who has magnified him as he has been from the beginning? Many things, greater than these, are hidden; for we have seen few of his works” (Ecclus. 43).

What few things had this man seen when he said these words? “The height of the firmament and its beauty; the splendid sun, a marvelous vessel, the work of the Most High; the appearance of the moon and the glory of the stars, which illuminate the world”; as well as the other works of the Lord. Then he had read or heard of glorious men, whom—or in whom—he began to praise the Lord, saying: “Let us praise glorious men and our fathers in their generation” (Ecclus. 44). Judging all these few and small in comparison with greater or more numerous things, he says: “Many things greater than these are hidden; for we have seen few of his works.”

What are those greater or more numerous things, hidden and unseen? Surely, before the height of the beautiful firmament from which he began to praise, very many angels had been made, distinguished into nine orders. Concerning them, or their ordered and manifold glory, he could rightly say: they are hidden from us. And after “the glorious men,” whose praise he set forth in order down to Simon son of Onias, the Son of God, Christ, was to come, doing such great things in his first and second advent that, concerning everything he knew or everything that had been done before him until then, he could rightly say: “For we have seen few of his works.”

And we, according to the purpose which we proposed—to seek out or display in the field of the Scriptures the hidden treasure of the holy name [Col. 0054B] of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—have paused for some time at the beginning of the book where it is said: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth, and the Spirit of God was borne over the waters” (Gen. 1). But the diligence of contemplating the procession of the Holy Spirit has led us farther afield. We now return to that beginning and intend to say something concerning the happiness of the holy angels, concerning that same Holy Trinity whom they bless without ceasing.

## CHAPTER II

Concerning the angelic creature: that it was made where God said, “Let there be light”; and concerning the judgment of the Holy Spirit in the condemnation of the darknesses, or of the prince of darknesses, the devil.

Where God said, “Let there be light, and there was light; and God saw that the light was good, and he divided the light and the darknesses” (Gen. 1), weighty authority from many persons, and especially from Father Augustine, establishes that the angelic creature was made, that good angels are signified by the name “light,” and bad angels by the term “darknesses.”

But in another work we have treated more fully of this marvelous creature and of the other things which the sequence of Scripture afterward narrates as created or made; and, as far as we could, we have carefully followed the order of things. At present it belongs to our purpose to celebrate, with the pious and pleasant festivity of discourse, the blessedness of this light as a mirror of the supreme Trinity; and to praise and admire the judgment of the Holy Spirit in condemning the darknesses, or the devil, prince of darknesses. For this contemplation belongs to the praise of his procession, of which we have already said something, and to the glorification of the Trinity, of which we proposed to speak together.

## CHAPTER III

Concerning what the Lord said to blessed Job: “Do you know the order of heaven, and will you establish its ordinances upon earth?”

“Do you know the order of heaven,” says the Lord to [Col. 0055A] blessed Job, “and will you establish its ordinances upon earth?” (Job 38). It is understood: as I do; and you must answer: No. For no one except God alone knows this order of heaven, the whole extent of which is here indicated by the name “light,” when Scripture says: “And God said: Let there be light; and there was light.”

Yet the Holy Spirit revealed to some persons that, while still living in the flesh, they might partly, as it were through a mirror and in an enigma, see (1 Cor. 13) that work of heaven of the blessed Trinity, distinguished into three times three choirs, whose names are these: angels, archangels, thrones, dominions, principalities, powers, virtues, cherubim, and seraphim (Rom. 8).

This order of heaven, ordered for seeing and praising the glory of the Holy Trinity, possesses such blessedness that the Apostle rightly marvels and says to all who, according to God’s foreknowledge and predestination, are called to fellowship with them, justified and glorified, and arrive or shall arrive there: “Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him.” He immediately adds: “But God has revealed them to us through his Spirit” (1 Cor. 2). To which “us”? Surely, to human beings remaining on earth, inhabiting this earthly dwelling of the body. Who else could reveal these things to them except God?

Therefore, when he says, “Do you know the order of heaven, and will you establish its ordinances upon earth?” it is rightly understood, as has been said, “as I do,” and the answer is: No. Now our childlike understanding desires to express, for little ones like ourselves, as far as we can and as far as we have received from God—or from those to whom God has revealed it through his Spirit—what this order of heaven is, and how God himself, who spoke these words, established its ordinances upon earth.

## CHAPTER IV

What the order of heaven, or the order of the heavens, is; and concerning the verse of the psalm: “By the Word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their power.”

The order of heaven, or order of the heavens, is that firm establishment of them concerning which the Psalmist says: “By the Word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their power” (Ps. 32). For who are those heavens except all the saints in whom God dwells? For this reason they are called—and are—heavens, because God dwells in them.

A narrower interpretation understands only the apostles of Christ, whom the incarnate Word established by his presence, and to whom, sitting at the Father’s right hand, he sent the Holy Spirit from heaven for the perfection of their confirmation. Before these very few heavens, there were very many heavens, innumerable to us—that is, saints. And David lifted his eyes toward them, saying: “To you I have lifted up my eyes, you who dwell in the heavens” (Ps. 122).

Therefore especially in the present passage, when it is said, “By the Word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their power,” we understand the holy angels. This is especially so because, just as there, where it is written, “God said: Let there be light; and there was light,” there follows: “God said: Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it divide waters from waters.” And shortly afterward: “God said: Let the waters which are under the firmament be gathered together into one place, and let the dry land appear” [Col. 0056A] (Gen. 1), so here too the previously cited verse is immediately followed by: “Gathering the waters of the sea as in a wineskin, placing the abysses in storehouses. Let all the earth fear the Lord; let all the inhabitants of the world be moved by him. For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. 32).

In these sayings, although a beautiful allegory lies beneath, the true literal sense of the magnificent history nevertheless remains and is not nullified. Therefore, “By the Word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their power”: that is, the holy angels, having within themselves the blessed Trinity dwelling in them—one God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—stand firm in their order. For the Lord himself is the Father; the Word of the Lord is the Son himself; the Spirit of his mouth is the Holy Spirit himself: the one and only firm establishment of holy angels and elect human beings, so that the foot of none of those already ordered, or still to be ordered there, may ever again be moved.

## CHAPTER V

That in that holy order of blessed spirits the order of the Holy Trinity must first be contemplated; that the glorious city, of which Holy Scripture so often speaks, has God as its lover with ineffable love, and that this lover complains in Jeremiah that he is despised by the unfaithful soul.

This is the glorious city of which Scripture speaks so much to us. For example, the Apostle says: “But you have approached Mount Zion and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and the assembly of many thousands of angels, and the church of the firstborn who are enrolled in the heavens” [Col. 0056C] (Heb. 12). Likewise, to the Galatians: “But that Jerusalem which is above is free, and she is our mother” (Gal. 4), and many similar things.

In this blessed city, in this order of blessed spirits which the Lord knows, we first desire to contemplate, though with a small eye, the glory of the Holy Trinity, and to trace some likeness of the beauty of that firm establishment by which the Lord, the Word of the Lord, and the Spirit of the Lord’s mouth established this our mother, this glorious city, by joining her to himself. By the likeness of what, or of what thing? Surely, by the likeness of a lawful husband who greatly desires to propagate his race or offspring, and for this cause takes a wife. For example, such was David: undoubtedly a strong man and a lawful husband in every marital union, except in the matter of Uriah the Hittite.

For indeed, apart from that case, he lived lawfully with all the wives he had, since he needed many children and relatives, because he had undertaken a great matter—the reins of a kingdom—while being a man of such a kind that he himself said: “But I am a poor and insignificant man” (1 Sam. 18): poor, namely, in possessions, and insignificant in the smallness of his household.

Nor should we, through excessive modesty, hesitate to take from this man, or from someone like him, a likeness based on the marital relation in order to contemplate the purpose of God for which [Col. 0057A] he both created and joined to himself our mother, the heavenly Jerusalem. For in many places of Scripture he himself wishes it to be recognized that he is a lover. For example, when he says in Jeremiah: “As a woman despises her lover, so the house of Israel has despised me” (Jer. 3). Therefore, conversely, you may truthfully say: “As a woman gladly receives her lover, so the true house of Israel, the true city of Zion, the heavenly Jerusalem, has gladly received me.”

Accordingly, by such a likeness it is permissible to contemplate the cause or work of God, the work of the Holy Trinity, in that order of heaven, in that holy and thrice-blessed Jerusalem. For there is in these things a likeness, though an unlike one: flesh is unlike spirit, indeed, yet there is some likeness between these unlike things. “What is born of flesh,” says the Lord, “is flesh; and what is born of spirit is spirit” (John 3). But now let us come to the matter.

## CHAPTER VI

That, according to the likeness of a lover—in whom are these three things: the lover himself, his love, and the increase for which, through his love, he is moved to propagate offspring—the lover himself is God the Father, his love the Holy Spirit, and his increase his Word.

In a lover there are three things: the lover himself, his love, and the increase for which, through his love, he is moved to propagate offspring. Likewise, in our Creator, who calls himself a lover, as was said above, there are three: himself, and his love, namely the Holy Spirit, and his Word, which is nothing other than [Col. 0057C] his increase, his seed, his Son.

This likeness, although, as has already been said, it is very unlike—so unlike that spirit is unlike flesh, and flesh spirit—is nevertheless so true that it is written also in Isaiah: “Shall I, who cause others to bear, not myself bear?” says the Lord. “Shall I, who grant generation to others, be barren?” says the Lord your God (Isa. 66). For he was speaking to this order of heaven, to this great and holy city of Jerusalem of which we are now speaking. Hence he immediately says: “Rejoice with Jerusalem and exult in her, all you who love her. Rejoice with her in joy, all you who mourned over her, that you may suck and be filled from the breast of her consolation” (ibid.), and so forth.

We would know nothing of such an order or generation unless he who knows had established its ordinances upon earth. And how did he establish them? The Spirit of God himself, who was then borne over the waters when God said, “Let there be light,” is also now borne over the waters while we are baptized in Christ. And this is God’s saying, “Let there be light”: he regenerates us, so that we who once were darkness are now light in the Lord.

This is regeneration: God, the aforesaid lover, impregnates the believing soul with his Word, making her worthy of his love. For the Word is his seed, as the Apostle James says: “Of his own will he begot us by the Word of truth, that we might be a kind of firstfruits of his creation” (Jas. 1). This seed is received only with love; this Word is introduced only through the Holy Spirit. This Trinity is one God: God, the lover of the rational creature; his seed, which is his Word; and his love, which is the Holy Spirit.

Therefore, although flesh and spirit are unlike, as has already been said, there is nevertheless some likeness here. For just as the generation of flesh is effected by a person’s seed and love, so the generation of spirit is accomplished by God, his Word, and the Spirit of his mouth. And even if the saying already cited—“Do you know the order of heaven, and will you establish its ordinances upon earth?” (Job 38)—may be expounded otherwise, nevertheless the sense we have stated has force and lacks no weight. For in no way did God establish more splendidly upon earth the ordinances of the order of heaven than by regenerating through water the children of light, who are to go into that order of heaven among the angels of light. “For they shall be,” says the Lord himself, [Col. 0058B] “like the angels of God” (Matt. 2).

## CHAPTER VII

Concerning the Apostle’s statement, “For it was fitting for him, for whom are all things and through whom are all things”; and that it is too little for us to know that the angelic creature and every creature were made through him unless we also know that they were made for him.

The following also aptly belongs to the aforementioned likeness: as we read that a man takes a wife only for love of offspring, so God the Father created the rational creature—the angelic creature of which we now speak, and the human creature of which we shall speak afterward—only for love of his Word. Hence the Apostle, speaking of that Son of God, says: “For it was fitting for him, for whom are all things and through whom are all things, who had brought many sons to glory,” and so forth.

He did not say only, “through whom are all things,” but first said, “for whom are all things,” because he is the cause of all things. This light was made through him, because it is written: “God said: Let there be light; and there was light.” If he spoke and it was made, then surely it was made through the Word. But it is too little to know this. For this statement of faith contains greater delight when we know that it was also made for him: namely, that this creature might have him within itself, and by having him might become light.

For he is light—certainly not made light, light illuminated by another, but illuminating light, and therefore true light. In comparison with him, whatever kind of light it may be, any angel of light, is rightly and faithfully denied to be light.
