Hence John the Evangelist says of John the Baptist: “He was not the light, but that he might bear witness concerning the light.” But of Christ the Lord himself: “He was the true light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world” (John 1).

John, and any angel of light or human child of light, is called or is light as a lamp is light: that is, a light not without material. But the Word of God, God the Word, is the very substance of light. For for him, being and shining are not different things; for these others, however, being and shining are different. By loving the light, they themselves are light; just as, conversely, apostate angels become darkness by hating the light.

## CHAPTER VIII [Col. 0059A]

Again concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit: that it is poured out upon us human beings through two gifts, one for the remission of sins and the other for distributions of graces; but upon holy angels through one only, namely for distributions of graces.

Concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit, which effects this both in those blessed spirits and in us human beings—that, by having the Word of God, the Son of God, remaining in us, we may be called and be sons of God (John 3)—we said above that it is poured out through two gifts, or by two gifts: one given for the remission of sins, the other for distributions of graces.

But it is given in these two ways only to us human beings. Upon holy angels, however, it has been lavishly poured out in one way only, namely for distributions of graces. For it was and is the righteous judgment of that same Holy Spirit that he should never be given to apostate angels for remission of sins. For they sinned with their prince, the devil, not through weakness or ignorance, but through pride.

The prophetic Spirit, in Ezekiel, marks the greatness of that pride in words such as these, reproving the devil under the name of the prince of Tyre: “Because your heart was lifted up, you said: ‘I am God, and I sit upon the throne of God’; and you gave your heart as though it were the heart of God” (Ezek. 28). Again, under the name of Pharaoh, king of Egypt: “Behold, I, Pharaoh, am the great dragon, who lie in the midst of your rivers and say: ‘The river is mine, and I made myself’” (Ezek. 29).

For such pride he received the sentence of eternal condemnation: cast out of heaven (Rev. 12), he became the devil, prince of darkness, though he had been a splendid angel. Hence the same prophet says to him: “You, the seal of likeness, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty, were in the delights of the paradise of God,” and so forth, down to: “Your inward parts were filled with iniquity, and you sinned, and I cast you out from the mountain of God” (Ezek. 28).

By these words, surely, three instruments of his terrible pride are proclaimed: wisdom, beauty or comeliness, and especially where, under the name of Assyria, it is said of him that no tree of paradise was comparable to him and to his beauty, because “I made him splendid.” The third was his greatness: for “the cedars,” it says, “were not taller than he in the paradise of God; the fir trees did not equal his height, and the plane trees were not equal to his branches” (Ezek. 31).

But true greatness is God; true wisdom is the Word of God, the Son of God; and true beauty is the Holy Spirit. This blessed Trinity is the greatness, wisdom, and beauty of the holy angels. But the devil did not honor that greatness, did not embrace that wisdom, did not love that beauty. How then can he be said to have been full of wisdom, perfect in beauty, extended and protecting, except ironically? (Ps. 48). For sacred Scripture contains very grave ironies.

For example, when the Holy Trinity says: “Behold, [Col. 0060A] Adam has become as one of us” (Gen. 3), whereas in truth, because of sin, “he was compared to beasts and made like them” (Ps. 48); and when the daughter of Babylon is called a virgin though she is a harlot (Isa. 47). Thus we understand that it is also said to him reproachfully there: “Every precious stone was your covering—sardius, topaz, jasper, chrysolite, onyx, beryl, sapphire, carbuncle, and emerald” (Ezek. 28). These are the nine holy orders of angels; yet he arrogated them to himself, setting, as was said above, “his heart as though it were the heart of God,” and saying, “I sit upon the throne of God.”

For such a covering of every precious stone belongs to God alone: that is, every translucent order of angelic dignity. As it says in the psalm: “You have put on praise and beauty, clothed with light as with a garment” (Ps. 103). That is: you are so clothed and adorned by the beautiful confession of the saints—all of whom are light, that is, children of light—as a person is by his garment.

This is too little if understood only of human beings, the children of light; for holy angels too—indeed, first of all they themselves, the light and children or angels of light—have clothed their Creator with their beautiful confession. They are those concerning whom the same Lord says to blessed Job: “When the morning stars praised me and all the sons of God rejoiced” (Job 38).

## CHAPTER IX

That by the right and just judgment of God the Holy Spirit judged the devil unworthy of his regard and guilty of an eternal offense; concerning the fall of that same devil; and that he was placed on the holy mountain of God.

Therefore, because he sinned through pride, by a right and just judgment the Holy Spirit, proceeding from the Father and the Son, did not proceed into him as into the elect angels, but utterly turned far away from him. He endured from him the same rejection which he endured, or endures, from human beings like him, saying: “As a woman despises her lover, so the house of Israel has despised me” (Jer. 3).

For just as he drew that people Israel to himself and gave it the law, or the tablets of the covenant, on the mountain—which for this reason was called the mountain of God (Exod. 20)—requiring this in return for all his benefits, that they should love him, and saying: “And now, Israel, what does the Lord your God ask of you except that you fear [Col. 0060D] the Lord your God and love him?” (Deut. 10), and many similar things; so also he placed that evil one in heaven, as he says: “I placed you in the midst of the holy mountain of God; you walked in the midst of fiery stones” (Ezek. 28).

He required this from him: that, as a rational creature, he should give thanks to his Creator and such a great benefactor; and that, like a stone set or prepared in its sockets, he should receive the bonds of gold, the bond of the love of God. For this is what the same Scripture says: “Gold, the work of your adornment, and your sockets were prepared on the day you were created” (ibid.).

But because, through excessive pride, as has already been said, he rejected from himself God the lover and endured the Spirit of love’s contemptuous rejection from him—for he never receives him into himself, although it is written, “Gold, the work of your adornment”; for “was” or “was ready” must be understood—by a most just judgment the Holy Spirit did not will or purpose ever to proceed into that creature and its evil angelic accomplices in the way that he proceeds to us sinful human beings for remission of sins and afterward adds distributions of graces.

On this matter I wonder that some argue that he fell immediately upon being created, although no authoritative Scripture has handed this down; indeed, what is written here sounds contrary. For after saying, “Your sockets were prepared on the day you were created”—that is, you were created rational and endowed with subtle intelligence, so that you have no excuse for your sin—it immediately adds: “And I placed you on the holy mountain of God; you walked in the midst of fiery stones; you were perfect in your ways,” understood hypocritically, from the day of your creation, “until iniquity was found in you” [Col. 0061B] (Ezek. 28).

Since there are many such statements, which cannot be resolved away because they are words of divine authority, it must necessarily be understood that some interval elapsed between his creation and his being cast out, or falling from heaven, in accordance with the words: “And you sinned, and I cast you out from the holy mountain of God.”

## CHAPTER X

Response to one who perhaps asks: Why did he place the devil on the holy mountain of God, and why did he bestow so much upon him, when the Holy Spirit, “who searches all things, even the deep things of God,” knew him?

[Col. 0061C] Here perhaps someone may ask: Why did He place him, such as he was, upon the holy mountain of God? Why did He bestow so much upon him? Did not “the Spirit, who searches all things, even the depths of God” (1 Cor. II), know that this stone, most hard and rebellious, would not receive into itself the gold—the work of His adornment? Why then did He place him there, to walk in the midst of fiery stones?

Whoever asks this should also ask why the same Lord placed man in paradise. For He did not make him in paradise, but brought him there. Thus Scripture says: “The Lord God made man, and placed him in the paradise of delight, to work it and keep it” (Gen. II). Let him then say: Did God not know that it would come to pass that he would not work it and keep it? Why, then, did He place [Col. 0061D] him there?

To this I say: God was not ignorant; but unless He had tested the angel in heaven and man in paradise, so that, for ages yet to come, either what was in the angel [uncertain] or what was in the human heart might become known, we would not know how to praise His judgments, and we would lack much in the knowledge of God—whose knowledge is eternal life—as the Son of God Himself says: “And this is eternal life: that they may know thee, the true God, and Jesus Christ whom thou hast sent” (John XVII).

What we have said is better understood by a comparison. When the Lord sent Moses to Pharaoh, saying, “The cry of the children of Israel has come to me; come, I will send thee to Pharaoh,” and so forth, He also said: “But I know that the king of Egypt will not let you go, except by a mighty hand” (Exod. III). Yet He did not immediately exert that mighty hand; He did not at once strike down Egypt’s firstborn, or the Egyptians themselves with Pharaoh. Rather, He first addressed him with many good words, tested him by many signs and lighter plagues, until those who saw him might know—and we too, who read, might know—the glorification of the Lord in Pharaoh’s chariots and his army: for the Lord is just, whereas Pharaoh and his people are ungodly.

So likewise the same Lord, although He knew how evil that angel was, ought not immediately to judge or condemn him before the eyes of the rest, but first to test him; and likewise man, so that we too, together with the holy angels, might know from the outcome, or from their works, what God alone already knew, while no evil merits had yet preceded; and, knowing His righteousness, might praise it either in the fall of that angel or [Col. 0062B] in the punishment of man.

## CHAPTER XI

Why he was condemned by so terrible a judgment; and concerning what is said in the Apocalypse: “One of the heads of the beast, which had seven heads, as though slain unto death; and the wound of its death was healed,” or, “it has the wound of joy and lived.”

We have already said above that the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, and the wine or strong drink of His consolation, according to the vision of Lamuel, is to be given “to those who mourn and are bitter in soul” (Prov. XXXI): that is, to human beings who, conscious of their sins, steadfastly refuse and reject consolation according to God and consolation from this world.

But how far those apostate angels, together with their head, the devil, were or are [Col. 0062C] from this praiseworthy mourning and this sweet bitterness, the Scripture of the book of the Apocalypse wonderfully intimates—a book in which almost as many mysteries are contained as there are words. Indeed, one might say even more; for, according to the worth of the volume, too little has been said. Blessed Jerome says that manifold meanings lie hidden in almost every single word.

How then does that Scripture speak? “And one,” it says, “of its heads”—namely, of the beast which had seven heads—“was as though slain unto death; and the wound of its death was healed” (Apoc. XIII).

We understand the seven heads of the beast, which it raised against the woman with child—who cried out in travail and was in anguish to give birth, so that, when she had brought forth, it might devour her son—to be the seven principal, or most famous, kingdoms of this world. From the time of the promise of the blessed seed, which is Christ, these kingdoms stood in this cause, under the devil’s agency (whose body they are rightly understood to be as heads, just as all the wicked are rightly called and are his members): that the promise might not be fulfilled, that Christ might not be born, or that, once born, He might die and His name perish.

The first was the kingdom of the Egyptians, which commanded all the male offspring of Abraham’s seed to be killed or drowned in the waters (Exod. I). The second was the kingdom of carnal Israelites, which—especially while Jezebel reigned and acted—wished to abolish the Word of promise, adding the worship of Baal to the calves which Jeroboam had made, and for their sake killing the prophets and digging down the altars of the Lord (III Kings XIX). The third was the kingdom of the Babylonians, which [Col. 0063A] carried that people captive and cast into the furnace of fire the three youths who refused to worship the statue it had erected (Dan. III). The fourth was the kingdom of the Persians and Medes, which, through Haman’s agency, wished to destroy the entire Jewish race (Esther III). The fifth was the kingdom of the Greeks, whose powers the devil especially appropriated to himself through Antiochus Epiphanes, as the books of Maccabees recount (I Macc. I). The sixth was the kingdom of the Romans, which killed Christ and His martyrs. The seventh kingdom will be that of Antichrist; and it is of this that you should rightly understand the saying: “And one of its heads, as though slain unto death, and the wound of its death was healed” (Apoc. XIII).

For the devil is, or will be, the one who received in heaven the wound of eternal condemnation; but, it says, “the wound of his death was healed,” or, as it is repeated later, “he has the wound of the sword and lived.” Thus, as said above, Scripture wonderfully indicates his hardness. For what is it to say, “He has the wound of the sword and lived,” except that he has both been condemned and remains proud? And what is it to say that the head was as though slain unto death and its wound healed, except that he does not care about—indeed, despises—his own destruction and separation from God, which is true slaughter and true death, and defends himself as though alive, that is, righteous? For he does not truly live, nor has “his wound been healed”; but this is said because the wretch thus arrogates it to himself and thus consoles himself.

## CHAPTER XII

Concerning what was said to blessed Job: “His Spirit adorned the heavens, and by His midwifing hand the twisting serpent was brought forth.”

Therefore we say, no less knowingly than faithfully, in praise of this proceeding Holy Spirit, that just as now, so also then, in His procession He held the path of judgment over every impenitent heart, adorning with the gifts of His graces the humble and submissive angels, and leaving the proud devil, together with his accomplices—all spirits, sons of pride.

Hence this most beautifully and truly [Col. 0063C] said to blessed Job: “His Spirit adorned the heavens, and by His midwifing hand the twisting serpent was brought forth” (Job XXVI). For although the saying, “His Spirit adorned the heavens,” is rightly understood of the blessed apostles, it is no less true to think or say this of those blessed angels, whom the same Spirit adorned, distinguished into nine orders.

And although the twisting serpent was then “brought forth,” when the Lord said, “Now is the judgment of the world; now shall the prince of this world be cast out” (John XII)—which was still future when this Scripture was composed—it is no less true that he had already then been brought forth from heaven by that fearful expulsion which the Lord Himself recalls, saying, “I saw Satan falling as lightning from heaven” (Luke X).

Indeed, this same twisting serpent, adversary of the supreme Trinity, is still to be brought forth a third time; and therefore he has been condemned and is to be condemned by a threefold judgment, namely on the day of judgment, when what the Lord likewise says to blessed Job shall take place: “Behold, his hope shall disappoint him, and in the sight of all he shall be cast down” (Job XL).

Now observe how great a matter, how weighty an act, is signified in so brief and sparing an expression when it says, “And by His midwifing hand the twisting serpent was brought forth,” after first saying, “His Spirit adorned the heavens” (Job XXVI). What is it to act as midwife except to receive newborn infants and, by careful handling, preserve them for life? When, therefore, it says this, it wonderfully indicates what care our Creator had or has for His chosen creature, both angelic and human, because of the humility of that creature; as it is written: “The Lord preserves the little ones; I was humbled, and He delivered me” (Ps. CXIV).

Accordingly, when He adorned those heavens, which are the holy angels, He brought forth [Col. 0064B] the twisting serpent—that is, He cast the devil out of heaven—so that, with the stumbling-block removed, He might make peace and concord in His high places. And when He adorned other heavens, that is, the apostles, He therefore brought forth the same twisting serpent—that is, cast him out—as He Himself said in the Gospel, so that, freed by His blood from the stumbling-block of sin, we might know and be able to serve our Creator and Redeemer.

And when He shall so fully adorn all the heavens—that is, all the saints, both angels and human beings (John XII)—that the angels will no longer have the work of ministry which they now perform and will perform until that day (whence the Apostle says, “Are they not all ministering spirits, sent to minister for those who shall receive the inheritance of salvation?” [Heb. I]), and human beings, or human spirits, having resumed their bodies, shall receive the double glory of body and soul: then He will utterly bring forth the same twisting serpent. For in the sight of all he shall be cast down, so that every stumbling-block may be removed from His kingdom and that rest may have peace—the rest of which it was likewise said to blessed Job: “Who has declared the order of the heavens? And who makes the harmony of heaven sleep?” (Job XXXVIII).

## CHAPTER XIII

Concerning what was said to the same blessed Job, “Who has declared the order of the heavens?”; and why not even Moses ought to have described the order of the heavens—that is, the orders of the holy angels—though he was the first to declare the order of the earth and the generations [Col. 0064D] of the children of men.

Upon the most beautiful and most firm foundation of this text, we have willingly and delightfully built, so far as we are able, the gold or silver of our present discourse—or something of precious stones—in praise of the Holy Spirit, who adorns heavens of this kind. But meanwhile a question arises, since one may ask why no one up to that point ought to have declared the order of these same heavens.

For when the Lord says, “Who shall declare the order of the heavens?” it is understood: no one; but I shall declare it. Thus Moses, who before blessed Job received the first letters—namely, the Hebrew letters—written and delivered to him by God, or by the finger of God, recounted almost nothing of the order of those heavens except this alone:

“And God said: Let there be light; and light was made. And God saw the light, that it was good; and He divided the light and the darkness. And He called the light Day, and the darkness He called Night” (Gen. I).

The question, then, as already stated, is why no one up to that point declared the order of the heavens—not even Moses, who, intending to describe the order of the earth, that is, of man, recounted concerning those heavenly beings only this very briefly, so uncertainly and, as it were, under a veil, that scarcely any of the spiritual Fathers could understand it. Especially since Father Augustine interpreted the name “light” as denoting the holy angels and the name “darkness” as denoting the evil angels; and their division, in the words “And God divided the light and the darkness,” indicates that judgment which the Catholic Church firmly maintains: that the angels of light will never again return into darkness, and the angels of darkness will never again return into light.

Whoever asks why not even Moses wrote, or ought to have written, more or something more manifest about those heavenly beings should also ask why he drew so thick, dense a veil over his face in the heavenly mysteries of the Scriptures—those things which were thereafter to come about or be accomplished concerning the human race. It was so dense that not only those carnal children of Israel who then beheld his horned face could flee from it (Exod. XXXIV), as their descendants flee even to this day, but even the spiritual children of Israel, among whom we too are numbered, can scarcely, by working and reworking his Scripture, perceive where the brightness of his countenance tends or where the rays of his horned face are directed.

To one who asks this or that, we must answer: the almost wholly carnal world of that time could not bear heavenly mysteries. For the world was then like a wanton and unruly boy or youth. On behalf of those to whom the inheritance was promised in Abraham’s seed, which is Christ, a pedagogue could scarcely be found who might restrain its unbridled ways by present punishment and vengeance close at hand—so that fire consumed many of them, the earth swallowed them, and the bite of serpents devoured them (Num. XVI).

Since, then, the world was such, how could it have been fitting for the order of heaven to be declared to it with unveiled face or in plain words, or for the orders of holy angels to be described, when even those things which pertain especially to human beings had to be veiled beneath the wonderful splendors of spiritual mysteries? Therefore, whoever asks why not even Moses, to whom God “spoke face to face” (Exod. XXXIII), declared the order of these heavens, should consider himself answered.

## CHAPTER XIV

Concerning what was said to the same blessed Job: “And who makes the harmony of heaven sleep?” and what, or of what kind, that sleep is.

Now, returning to the chapter mentioned here and above: what is this harmony of heaven, and what or of what kind is its sleep? For He said: “And who makes the harmony of heaven sleep?” (Job [Col. 0066A] XXXVIII).

Clearly, harmony is a concordant song, discordant in nothing; and the entire symphony of that angelic song is praise of the holy Trinity. The sum of this praise we hear in Isaiah: “Holy, holy, holy, the Lord God of hosts; the whole earth is full of His glory” (Isa. VI), or, “the heavens and earth are full of His majesty.”

This is a true and beautiful harmony, with every string well stretched and every voice rightly consonant. From it, as was said above, the twisting serpent was brought forth: discordant in every voice, opposed to every harmony; a hissing creature, not a singer, not a leader or responder in song—indeed, so far as lay in him or lies in him, a corrupter of all sacred music.

How did, or does, the Lord God make this harmony of heaven sleep? Certainly by casting down or casting out from the rank or choir of singers that oft-mentioned and oft-accursed twisting serpent. For when He cast him down, He established peace and made concord in His high places. Is not that peace, that concord, sleep?

For what else does the holy and mystical law promise us human beings except that ineffable security under the name of sleep? “You shall eat,” it says, “your bread in fullness, and you shall dwell in your land without terror. I will give peace in your borders; you shall sleep, and there shall be none to frighten you.” And immediately, showing how or by what our sleep is brought about: “I will take away,” He says, “evil beasts, and the sword shall not pass through your borders” (Lev. XXVI).

The evil beasts are the malignant spirits; and the head of the evil beasts is that serpent, that is, the devil. The sword—that is, the sentence of eternal condemnation, of which we have already spoken—has now crossed their borders. What, then, is more beautiful in expression, more precious in reality, than this: “And who makes the harmony of heaven sleep?” O thrice and four times blessed harmony of heaven, where the whole multitude both sleeps in singing and sings in sleeping! For it keeps Sabbath; and its sleep in the Sabbath is the very rest of the Lord, the Lord’s seventh day. Into that rest it entered with unending harmony, with an ineffable voice, with tireless stretching.

## CHAPTER XV

[Col. 0066D] Again concerning the same harmony, and concerning the words of that harmony or song which we heard in Isaiah: “Holy, holy, holy, the Lord God.”

We have heard, as already said above, certain words of that harmony or song: “Holy, holy, holy, the Lord God” (Isa. VI). How beautiful and even is the tenor of the words; how certain and stable! Here there are no degrees, no moment of increase or decrease in these voices.

Whence, then, did hostile heresy derive its degrees? For as if that harmony had sung, “Holy, holier, holiest,” and had added in the plural “lords and gods,” rather than “the Lord God” in the singular, it made degrees for itself—especially through the mouth of Arius—so as to say that the Holy Spirit was indeed great, but that the Son was greater than the Holy Spirit and less than God the Father.

Whence, I say, did that impious, serpentine heresy derive these degrees, except from the serpent himself, the father of lies, whom the hand of the Lord brought forth and cast out from that harmony because of his discordance? Therefore such a heretic is guilty of an eternal offense, like his father the devil, who made these degrees by which one does not ascend to the heights but descends to the depths.

It is written in Hosea: “Thy calf, Samaria, has been cast away; my wrath has been kindled against them. How long shall they be unable to be cleansed? For it is itself from Israel. A craftsman made it, and it is not God” (Hos. VIII). The sense is this: Do not wonder that the filth of Israel, namely the calves which Jeroboam made, could not and cannot be cleansed; because it itself—that is, the calf, or the worship of the calves—is from Israel. For it did not take from elsewhere the practice of worshipping a calf as God, as it took Baal and Astaroth, and so forth, monstrous idols of demons, from neighboring nations—perhaps many of them wandering and sinning through ignorance. But a craftsman made it: that is, Jeroboam or Israel, knowing that the craftsman is not God.

For Scripture plainly says: “And Jeroboam said in his heart: Now shall the kingdom return to the house of David, if this people go up to offer sacrifices in the house of the Lord in Jerusalem. And, having devised a plan, he made two golden calves” (III Kings XII). Because he devised this plan, the prophet—or God—called him a craftsman: for he sinned not ignorantly but maliciously. Therefore those sins could not be cleansed, so that Israel might depart from its calves even during the reign of one of its kings.

The same must be understood of Arius and the other heretics, who refused to understand that harmony of heaven and preferred to rend the unity of the song. They will no longer hear that harmony of heaven, nor will they have part or fellowship with those who proceed by the plainness, or equality, of faith, without those degrees of inequality, so that they may sleep and sing there, according to the words from the Songs of Ascents: “For thither the tribes went up, the tribes of the Lord, the testimony of Israel, to give thanks unto the name of the Lord” (Ps. CXXI).

For they cannot be cleansed, but shall be unclean both in this age and [Col. 0067D] in the age to come, and shall labor forever, as that serpent, their deceiver, labored: with his nostrils pierced by stakes and a ring in his nose (Job XL). Thus he never keeps Sabbath, never sleeps, but goes about the earth, wishing indeed to conceal but unable to conceal his weariness, when, being asked, “Whence comest thou?” he answers and says: “I have gone round the earth and walked through it” (Job I). And especially at this time he has great wrath, because he knows that he has but a short time and will not long be allowed to go about.

## CHAPTER XVI

The judgment of blessed Pope Gregory concerning those heavenly orders of holy angels; and which or what kinds of human beings obtain fellowship in each order.

Blessed Pope Gregory, speaking of those heavenly orders of holy angels (Homily 34 on the Gospels, no. 11), and rejoicing in the hope that we shall come into their fellowship—or, as the Lord Himself says, their equality—says among other things:

“Those who do not cease devoutly to announce to their brethren the small things which they grasp run in the number of the angels. Others are able both to grasp and to announce the highest secrets of heaven. Into what order, then, are these reckoned, except among the number of archangels? Others work wonderful signs and act with power. To what lot and number do these belong except that of the heavenly virtues? Some also cast malignant spirits out of possessed bodies by the power of prayer and the force of received authority. What lot do these obtain for their merit except among the number of the heavenly powers?

“Some, having received virtues, are themselves better even than the good and preside over chosen brethren. What lot have these received except among the numbers of the principalities? Some so rule over all vices that they are rightly called gods among men; of this kind was Moses, to whom the Lord said: ‘Behold, I have made thee a god to Pharaoh’ (Exod. VII). Into what number do these run except among the dominations? Some have received this gift of power, that they may rightly judge others. What are these except the thrones of their Creator?

“Some are so filled with love of God [Col. 0068C] and neighbor that they are rightly called cherubim; for cherubim is said to mean ‘fullness of knowledge.’ And, as Paul says, we have learned ‘that the fullness of the law is love’ (Rom. XIII). All who are full of charity toward God and neighbor have received the lot of their merits among the cherubim. Some, set aflame by the fires of heavenly contemplation, burn in loving, kindle others in speaking, and make those whom they touch by their word immediately burn in the love of God. Those, therefore, who have thus been set ablaze in the love of their Creator—into what order have they received the lot of their calling except among the seraphim?”

## CHAPTER XVII

Reply to those who say that multitudes fell from each individual order, because, according to that judgment of blessed Gregory, some human beings are assumed, or are to be assumed, into one order and others into another.

When he says these things—namely, that some human beings are reckoned among angels, others in the number of archangels, others among the heavenly virtues, others among the heavenly powers, others among the principalities, others among the dominations, others among the thrones, others among the cherubim, and others among the seraphim as receiving the lot of their calling—some commonly maintain that multitudes fell from every order, and that the losses in each order must likewise be repaired from human beings.

What could we, or can we, say to this? For this belongs to those orders concerning which it is written and quoted above: “Dost thou know the order of heaven, or canst thou establish its ordinances upon the earth?” (Job XXXVIII).

We say, therefore: if they could confirm from any canonical Scripture the opinion which they have prematurely adopted—namely, that those angels or spirits were established in their respective orders as soon as they were created, and that immediately some fell while the others remained in their ranks—then the opinion would have to be granted. But this is not so. No canonical Scripture supports that opinion; indeed, prophetic truth in Ezekiel strongly opposes it (Ezek. XXII), as we recalled far above.

Therefore we rightly ask in return: what reward did those blessed spirits receive because, when the apostate spirits sinned, they themselves refused to sin? For if they were then already, as they are now, established and perfected in their orders as angels, archangels, thrones, dominations, principalities, powers, virtues, cherubim, and seraphim, how could so many thereafter fall?

For example: if they were in the order of seraphim—that is, of those angels who burn with, or kindle, the fire of divine love—how could they thereafter fall away? Indeed, how could they be thought never to have burned with the sweet ardor of that love? It is therefore truer and more reasonable to say that, as reward because they did not sin and preferred to be subject to their Creator, they received the orders which they now possess. They were ordained for this very purpose and made firm by the word of the Lord and the Spirit of His mouth, so that they could no longer fall—that is, sin—just as the stones mentioned above, held fast by gold, are maintained in their appointed ranks according to the knowledge of the craftsman: bound in being ordered, ordered in being bound, so that they cannot fall out. Nor does the discourse of the doctor cited above properly compel us to understand otherwise.

## CHAPTER XVIII

Another consideration from the likeness between the nine orders of angels and the nine charisms of the Holy Spirit given to human beings according to the Apostle, who says: “To one indeed by the Spirit is given the word of wisdom,” and so forth.

Now, because the same discourse has made us rejoice according to the form which the Lord Himself established, saying, “For they are equal to the angels, since they are children of the resurrection” (Luke XX), and because we are to be disposed into the same nine orders, it is most beautiful to consider that, as many as are there the adornments of the heavens by the Spirit of the Lord’s mouth, so many are here among holy human beings the divisions of graces by the same Spirit.

For the Apostle says: “But to each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for profit: to one indeed is given by the Spirit the word of wisdom; to another, the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another, faith in the same Spirit; to another, the grace of healings in one Spirit; to another, the working of miracles; to another, prophecy; to another, discernment of spirits; to another, kinds of tongues; to another, interpretation of speeches. But one and the same Spirit works all these things, dividing to each as He wills” (1 Cor. XII).

Whoever considers this—that the election drawn from human beings is adorned with as many varieties of charisms as those beings are known to be distinguished into orders by the blessed Spirit—may also fittingly infer, from those same charisms, which persons, and what sort of persons, ought to be considered like which angels or angels of which order.

Thus, those who have interpretation of words, so that in at least one language they may set forth the meaning of the Scriptures for the benefit of hearers—are they not angels? “For the lips of the priest,” as the Lord says in Malachi, “keep knowledge, and they shall seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. II).

But those who have also received kinds of tongues, so that they can accomplish this not merely in one language but in diverse languages, and carry, extend, and spread the Word of God from nation to nation—something granted especially to the holy apostles—are they not rightly called and indeed archangels?

In discernment of spirits you rightly understand judicial dignity, so that such people are rightly called thrones, because, with God presiding in them, they know how to judge concerning spirits, according to the words: “Do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits whether they are of God” (1 John IV).

In the grace of prophecy, the authority of dominations is not incongruously recognized, for prophets truly exercised dominion even over kings, especially Elijah and Elisha. Indeed, the king cried out to Elisha: “My father, my father, the chariot of Israel and its charioteer!” (IV Kings XIII). Prophets exercised dominion over other kings also; and to Moses, the greatest of the prophets, it was said: “Behold, I have made thee a god to Pharaoh” (Exod. VII).

Does not faith merit a principality? Thus Abraham (Rom. IV), Isaac, Jacob, and David, because of faith—or the righteousness that comes by faith—were called patriarchs, that is, princes of the fathers. Peter the apostle too deserves to be called prince of the apostles because of the excellence of his faith. Therefore all whose faith is held to be more illustrious are rightly called principalities, and they are held worthy to rule—that is, preside—over their brethren or the Churches of Christ.

The grace of healings and the working of miracles differ chiefly in this: the grace of healings is exercised upon infirm bodies, whether by the laying on of hands or by some other means. But the working of miracles is displayed outwardly in external things, in the elements of this world, as especially occurred through the hand of Moses, who is read to have done only this concerning bodily healing: he healed the leprosy of Mary his sister (Num. XII). Those, then, to whom the grace of healings is given—are they not among the powers? And those to whom the working of miracles is given—are they not rightly counted among the virtues?

Further, those who have the word of knowledge are as cherubim; and those to whom the word of wisdom has been given are as seraphim. The Apostle Paul especially shone in the former grace, for he possessed knowledge not only of God but also of the world. In the latter shone John, the beloved of the Lord, whose entire discourse concerns charity, which is true wisdom, and who aims to kindle his hearers with the fire of God’s love, in accordance with the very name *seraphim*.

## CHAPTER XIX

Concerning the Apostle’s saying: “For nowhere does He take hold of angels, but He takes hold of the seed of Abraham.”

Add also what the same Apostle says: “For nowhere does He take hold of angels, but He takes hold of the seed of Abraham” (Heb. II). To what end is this? For we said far above that the Holy Spirit is given to us human beings in two ways: first, for the remission of sins; second, for divisions of graces. But He was poured out upon the holy angels in one way only, namely in divisions of graces, by generous condescension. For the judgment of the same Holy Spirit was, and is, true: that He should never be given to apostate spirits for the remission of sins.

Therefore, that you, O human being, may consider how much you owe to the Creator and discern your own cause more clearly, add that “He nowhere takes hold of angels,” but takes hold of human nature from the seed of Abraham with such a taking hold that the Author of your salvation deigned to be perfected through the passion of death.

How great a share of the thanksgiving you owe is contained in this? He both created the angels and magnified those who did not sin; but He both created you and, when all had sinned in Adam, justified and furthermore magnified you. He justified you, I say, by giving that gift of the Holy Spirit which is the remission of sins—a gift which the election of angelic creatures did not need, because it had not perished. He magnified you by the other gift of the same Spirit, which is the division of graces, by which He first adorned and magnified those heavenly spirits.

God, therefore, is the God of angels; but to you that same God is also High Priest. Yet the one and same Son of God is King both of angels and of human beings. Since these things are so, do you think that you have more wood upon the altar of your heart than an angel has, to nourish the fire of divine love? For it is written in the holy and mystical law of the Lord: “A fire shall always burn upon the altar; the priest shall feed it, laying wood upon it every morning, day by day” (Lev. VI).

To lay wood upon the fire is to keep continual remembrance of the benefits of the holy Trinity, and because of them to advance more and more in His love, burning meanwhile for a little while until that which is perfect comes, as it is written in Isaiah: “The Lord has said, whose fire is in Zion, and whose furnace is in Jerusalem” (Isa. XXXI).

For Zion is the present Church; but Jerusalem is that heavenly city, that is, the whole company of holy angels, of whom our discourse has hitherto treated. Therefore, “the Lord’s fire is in Zion, and His furnace in Jerusalem”: that is, the abundance of divine love which exists there surpasses present love of God just as a great furnace, strongly kindled, is more powerful than a small fire, however little it may be.

## CHAPTER XX

Again, the judgment of blessed Gregory upon that verse of the Song of Deuteronomy: “He set the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God”; whereas, according to the Hebrew truth as translated by blessed Jerome, we read: “He set the boundaries of the peoples according to the number of the children of Israel.”

The same aforementioned doctor says: “The woman had ten drachmas, which are the nine orders of angels; but, in order that the number of the elect might be made complete, man was created as the tenth.” And again, after some intervening remarks: “That heavenly [Col. 0072A] city consists of angels and human beings; and we believe that only so many of the human race ascend to it as there remained there elect angels, as it is written: ‘He fixed the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God.’”

I confess that I doubt whether this Scriptural testimony is sufficiently apt to confirm this point. Especially since, according to the Hebrew truth, as blessed Jerome translates it, it is written thus: “He fixed the boundaries of the peoples according to the number of the sons of Israel.” What sense this wording may yet bear we shall say later. For the moment it is preferable to say this: because of the words, “But, in order that the number of the elect might be made complete, man was created as the tenth,” many are accustomed to suppose that, if all the angels had remained steadfast and no fall had occurred among them, man would not have been created, nor would there have been any reason why man ought to be created.

If this is granted, [Col. 0072B] one must beware lest we be so childish as to imagine that before the fall of the angels God had no purpose concerning the creation of man, but that only after that fall happened did such a plan finally occur to him—namely, to make our race in order to restore the number of his household or family that had fallen. It is therefore more correct to say that man was not made for the angels; rather, the angels too, like all other things, were made for a certain man, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “For it was fitting for him, for whom are all things and through whom are all things” (Heb. 2). We did not pass over the remembrance of this chapter in the first little book of the present work, when we spoke of “the beginning” in which God created heaven and earth.

For if the Evangelist speaks truly—indeed, because he speaks truly—[Col. 0072C] when he says, without exception, “What was made in him was life” (John 1), having first stated, “All things were made through him, and without him was made nothing,” how much more was this beautiful man, to be assumed by the Word himself into the unity of his person, life in him before the angels came to be? Wisdom itself, which is nothing other than the Word himself, also testifies to this when it says: “The Lord possessed me at the beginning of his ways,” and so forth down to, “when he laid out the foundations of the earth, I was with him, ordering all things and delighting before him at all times, delighting in the inhabited world” (Prov. 8). It immediately adds: “And my delights [Col. 0072D] were to be with the children of men.” What is this, unless it were as if it had said: Before God made anything from the beginning, and while he made this or that, this was his purpose: that I, the Word of God, God the Word, should become flesh and dwell among human beings in great love and supreme humility, which are true delights.

## 33. Chapter XXI

That it may more plausibly be said that not so much man was made to supply the number of angels, as both angels and human beings were made for the man Jesus Christ.

Therefore we say more plausibly that [Col. 0073A] man was not so much made to supply the number of angels as that both angels and human beings were made for the one man Jesus Christ, so that, since he who was born God from God was also to be born man, he might have a household prepared from both sides: on this side angels, on that human beings; and that he himself, both God and man, might stand forth as Lord and Creator of angels, and as Lord, Creator, and Savior of holy human beings—Lord, I say, in them as in his own house, King in his own nation, God in his majesty. For, as has already been said, “all things are both for him and through him.”

With this in view it is also beautiful to observe [Col. 0073B] that not before, but after the Word of promise had come to Abraham concerning that most blessed seed (Heb. 2), concerning the coming or birth of so great a man, the holy angels began, rejoicing together with human beings, sometimes also visibly to perform that ministry of which the Apostle says: “Are they not all ministering spirits, sent for ministry?” (Heb. 1). They did so with such familiarity that they even deigned to be received as guests and to take food set before them in the manner of human guests (Gen. 18); and many benefits were administered through them, as the whole course of the sacred historical and prophetic writings testifies everywhere.

We have, however, said something elsewhere [Col. 0073C] concerning those benefits and ministries of theirs, in the work entitled *On the Victory of the Word of God*. Here it has pleased us only to recall that, rightly, from the Word of promise made to Abraham concerning his seed (Gen. 12), in whom all nations were to be blessed—that is, Christ—the ministries of angels among human beings began to be exercised and frequently performed, as though Scripture were saying to us that angels rightly served those fathers from whose seed the Lord of angels was to be born.

## Chapter XXII

What sense this wording may bear, which, according to the Hebrew and as translated by blessed Jerome, we read: “He fixed the boundaries of the peoples according to the number of the sons of Israel.”

We proposed above to say what sense this wording may bear, which, according to the Hebrew and as translated by blessed Jerome, we read: “He fixed the boundaries of the peoples according to the number of the sons of Israel” (Deut. 32). For the reading in another edition, “He established the boundaries of the peoples according to the number of the angels of God,” would have a stronger meaning through the authority of the aforementioned eminent doctor if the Hebrew truth also read thus, as the Seventy translated it: “according to the number of the angels of God.”

First, therefore, we must seek Moses’ intention [Col. 0073D] in these words of the song of Deuteronomy:

> “Ask your father and he will tell you; your elders, and they will say to you: When the Most High divided the nations, when he separated [Col. 0074A] the sons of Adam, he fixed the boundaries of the peoples according to the number of the sons of Israel. But the Lord’s portion is his people; Jacob, the line of his inheritance” (Deut. 32).

Clearly, in these words and in what follows, while recounting God’s benefits, Moses intends to attract that people’s goodwill toward the worship of God, or toward love of its Father. “He possessed you,” he says, “and made you and created you.” But from what beginning, or from what number, did he begin to possess them as such a possession, so that the one man Jacob became a nation or a people? Clearly, from Jacob’s entrance into Egypt, when the Lord said to him: “I am the most mighty God of your father; do not fear; go down into Egypt, for there I will make you into a great nation.” And shortly afterward it is written: “All the souls of Jacob’s household who entered Egypt were seventy.”

Now Joseph and his two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh, were in Egypt. [Col. 0074B] Again it is written: “Therefore all the souls of those who came forth from Jacob’s thigh were seventy-five” (Gen. 46). Assuredly according to this number of the sons of Israel—who then began to be a people—the Lord had long before “fixed the boundaries of the peoples,” when, as is said in the same place, “the Most High divided the nations” and separated the sons of Adam because of their pride, when they were building the tower of Babel.

By that division, [Col. 0074C] seventy-three nations, as the writers say—or rather, as reason shows, seventy-two nations and an equal number of languages—began to exist throughout the lands; growing, they filled provinces and islands. Hence blessed Jerome, where the Lord said to Peter, “Do you think that I cannot ask my Father, and he will now provide me with more than twelve legions of angels?” (Matt. 26), recalls that aforementioned multitude of nations or peoples in this manner:

> “Among the ancients one legion was completed by six thousand men. Because of the brevity of time, we do not hasten to explain the types of the numbers. Let it suffice to have said that seventy-two thousand angels—the number into which the language of human beings was divided among the nations—are manifestly made up by twelve legions.”

Accordingly, [Col. 0074D] this wording has some weight in this sense: “He fixed the boundaries of the peoples according to the number of the sons of Israel.” For how greatly it serves to demand Israel’s goodwill toward God that, when God already had seventy-two nations, he left them aside and chose for himself as a nation seventy-two men, or a few more, because Joseph was in Egypt with his sons. Hence it is rightly read with astonishment because of their small number: “But the Lord’s portion is his people; Jacob, the line of his inheritance.”

## 34. Book Four

[Col. 0075]

## Chapter I [Col. 0075A]

A proposal to say something concerning the human creature, in praise of the Holy Trinity and in honor of the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father and the Son, whose very bright gifts shine forth in this creature.

It belongs to a wise man, while building his house, to dig deep and lay foundations upon rock. “The rain fell,” says the Lord, “the floods came, the winds blew, and they rushed upon that house; and it did not fall, for it had been founded upon rock” (Matt. 7). We too earnestly desire in some measure to be made like that wise man.

For whenever, wishing to construct some edifice of good and faithful discourse [Col. 0075B], we seek and retain some fitting or suitable passage from divine authority—canonical authority, whether of prophets or apostles—so that we may build upon their foundation, we surely dig deep and lay foundations upon rock. Accordingly, if the wordy rains of worldly people descend, especially those of hateful sophists, to whom their own straw and hay are pleasing while our gold and silver seem cheap, and our precious stones contemptible; if, I say, the floods of heretics come and rush against our house, it will not fall, because it is founded upon rock.

Therefore, as we are now about to say something concerning the human creature, to the glory and praise of the Holy Trinity and in honor of the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father and the Son, whose most bright gifts shine in this creature, we seek this foundation [Col. 0075C]; and in every small portion of our discourse we desire to retain a sure passage from Holy Scripture. For this, as we have already said, is to dig deep and lay foundations upon rock. This is the first passage.

## Chapter II

On God’s purpose in saying: “Let us make man in our image and likeness.”

“Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1). [Col. 0075D] Hence faithful David says: “Your hands made me and fashioned me wholly round about” (Ps. 118 [119]; Job 10). Digging deep here in order to lay foundations, what rock do I find except the intention of the blessed Trinity itself, saying: “Let us make man in our image and likeness”? What was its intention, or what was in its intention, except he who now sits at the right hand of the Father, “the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Tim. 2)?

For if, as has often been said and must always be known, [Col. 0076A] all things are not only through him but also, as the Apostle says, for him, how much more was the human creature made for him! Therefore, when it says, “Let us make man in our image and likeness,” it is insufficient, for the fulfillment of God’s purpose, merely to observe that all the elect—“who are called saints according to the purpose” (Rom. 8)—were created rational and will be like God, their Father, as sons, according to the saying: “Beloved, we are now children of God, but what we shall be has not yet appeared. We know that, when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3).

This, I say, is insufficient unless you consider this man, who himself is, as the Apostle says, “the image of the invisible God” (Col. 1), and as he says elsewhere, “the radiance of his glory and the imprint of his substance” (Heb. 1). For when the blessed Trinity said, “Let us make man,” and the rest, had it thought or purposed nothing concerning this man, only afterward, when Adam sinned, did God finally devise that the Son of God should become man in order to redeem humankind?

We spoke of this earlier when we discussed the angels: [Col. 0076B] if the Evangelist says truly—indeed, because he says truly—“What was made in him was life,” excluding nothing, since he had first stated, “All things were made through him, and without him was made nothing” (John 1), then much more was this man, to be assumed by the Word himself into the unity of his person, “life in him” before the angels came to be. This was his delightful purpose, as Wisdom speaks—Wisdom which is nothing other than the Son of God himself: “The Lord possessed me at the beginning of his ways, before he made anything, from the beginning,” and the rest, which it concludes thus: “And my delights were to be with the children of men” (Prov. 8).

## Chapter III [Col. 0076C]

On what blessed Job says, and David after him: “Your hands made me and fashioned me.”

It was therefore a great undertaking, a very laborious matter, and it required the great counsel of the Holy Trinity that it should say in this manner, “Let us make”; and that, in so speaking, the one divinity of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit should, as it were, exhort itself to work. Thus those holy men mentioned above, rightly considering the matter, say: “Your hands made me and fashioned me; give me understanding” (Ps. 118 [119]); and: “Your hands made and fashioned me wholly round about” (Job 10).

For what such thing was created in the first days? [Col. 0076D] What such thing was made in those generations of heaven and earth? On the day when the Lord God made heaven and earth and every shrub of the field? Beautifully, therefore, and with great reverence, must it be heard that, while Scripture in recounting each of the kinds of God’s works says, “And God said, Let this or that be,” it recounts only of man that God said, “Let us make” (Gen. 2).

We have treated the individual days and their works more fully elsewhere. [Col. 0077A] There our diligence also did not pass over the fact that God said “Let there be” seven times and, though not in the same words, nevertheless used the same manner of speech which grammarians call the imperative mood; and seven times his work pleased his goodness, Scripture saying: “And God saw that it was good” (Gen. 1). This goodness of God is nothing other than the sevenfold Spirit of God.

But concerning man he did not say, “Let man be,” or, “Let the earth bring forth man”; rather, he said, “Let us make.” And afterward it is written: “Therefore the Lord God formed man from the mud of the earth and breathed into his face the breath of life” (Gen. 2). Clearly, where it says, “He formed from the mud of the earth”—which is to fashion—it provides occasion for our wonder and imparts knowledge to our humility, so that he may say: “Your hands made me and fashioned me.”

O great spectacle, great miracle! [Col. 0077B] Do you suppose that the holy angels, who had already been created, knew what God the fashioner was beginning to make with such great exertion? Clearly, that mystery was hidden from them, if the Apostle speaks truth—indeed, if Christ speaking in the Apostle does. For he says:

> “To me, the least of all the saints, this grace was given: to preach among the nations the unsearchable riches of Christ, and to enlighten all concerning what is the dispensation of the mystery hidden from ages in God, who created all things, so that through the Church the manifold wisdom of God may be made known to the principalities and powers in the heavenly places” (Eph. 3).

The fashioner alone knew, and he alone held hidden within himself [Col. 0077C] the dignity of the future work, foreshadowing it by the character of his operation as he worked with his hands.

## Chapter IV

That God does not have hands or feet as we do, as those called Anthropomorphites thought because of rustic simplicity; and on what is written in Isaiah: “Who has weighed the mass of the earth with three fingers, and weighed the mountains in scales and the hills in a balance?”

We do not say or suppose that God has hands or feet [Col. 0077D] as we do, as those whom rustic simplicity caused to be called Anthropomorphites thought. Rather, by the plurality of hands, when it is said, “Your hands made me,” a plurality of persons is indicated, just as elsewhere by the plurality of three fingers. For it is written in Isaiah: “Who has weighed the mass of the earth with three fingers, and weighed the mountains in scales and the hills in a balance?” (Isa. 40). “With three fingers,” that is, with the three persons of the one true, supreme Godhead.

Therefore, when he says, “Who has weighed with three fingers?” the wise man requires an answer, that you may say: “You, O God, have weighed it.” And when you have answered, he is pleased that you should further ask and say: “Where? How? What mass of earth? What mountains? What hills have been weighed and balanced?” (Ps. 148).

To one asking thus, it is beautiful to answer: “Lord, if I say that you have hung the inanimate and insensible earth which we tread beneath our feet upon nothing—for it is upheld by no pillars [Col. 0078A], but you established it by the decree of your command that it might be stable—and that you commanded mountains and hills, which are the swellings of the earth, to stand firm: I speak truly, but it is too little for the glory and praise of the Trinity, which you wish to be indicated to us by the three fingers, and of which this inanimate and insensible earth is not capable.

“Therefore I shall say more: where or when you said, ‘Let us make man,’ and from the mud of the earth created or fashioned male and female, and blessed them, saying, ‘Increase and multiply’ (Gen. 1)—there, or then, you ‘weighed the mass of the earth with three fingers’ and ‘weighed the mountains in scales and the hills in a balance.’ Then you weighed that mass of earth which was worthy to be weighed by your three fingers: namely, that great mountain [Col. 0078B] which, according to Daniel’s vision, filled the whole earth (Dan. 2). And you weighed in the scales those mountains and those hills of which the Apostle says:

> ‘For those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brothers. And those whom he predestined, these he also called; those whom he called, these he also justified; and those whom he justified, these he also glorified’ (Rom. 8).

“Most truly, none of these things was lacking in foreknowledge and predestination when you said, ‘Let us make man in our image and likeness,’ and created male and female, and blessed them, saying, ‘Increase and multiply.’ You had predetermined the number of their multitude; you had foreknown the measure of their increase—that is, the merit of each person—and you weighed the weight of merit in the balance or scale of just recompense.”

But what of those [Col. 0078C] whom these three fingers did not touch in such a weighing—that is, those whom you did not predestine in this word of blessing, “Increase and multiply,” whose superfluous multiplication came from sin or because of sin, when you said to the woman: “I will multiply your sufferings and your conceptions” (Gen. 3)? If the children of blessing, whom you commanded to be born by saying, “Increase and multiply,” are rightly called and are mountains and hills weighed or balanced by three fingers, what does the Holy Spirit immediately judge of those whom corrupted flesh brought forth, or brings forth, beyond measure, and who are multiplied beyond the number? “Behold,” he says, “the nations are counted as a drop from a bucket and as the slightest weight on the scales; behold, the islands are as fine dust. All nations are as though they were not before him; they are counted by him as nothing and emptiness” (Isa. 40).

What, I ask, or how much is a drop from a bucket [Col. 0078D] in comparison with great mountains? What is fine dust, carried away by a light wind, compared with stable hills that are moved from their place neither by earthquake nor thunder? Thus all the children of this age, however lofty they may seem and however great in their own eyes, are nothing in comparison with the children of blessing, who, according to your purpose, O God the Trinity, “are called saints” (Rom. 3). You foreknew and predestined them before the ages; each in his own time you called, justified, and glorified in your name. Their greatness will appear most clearly when it is said to them: “Come, blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25).

## Chapter V [Col. 0079A]

On what the Lord God said: “Behold, Adam has become as one of us, knowing good and evil”; and to Adam himself: “For you are dust, and to dust you shall return.”

Let us proceed further. [Col. 0079B] For our purpose is to traverse the field of Holy Scripture, to seek and display the treasure of this holy name—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—hidden in this field, yet so as to be found by those who desire to be rich toward God.

“Behold,” God says, “Adam has become as one of us, knowing good and evil” (Gen. 3). “Now therefore, lest perhaps he stretch out his hand and take also of the tree of life and live forever,” the Lord God [36] sent him out of the paradise of delight, to work the earth from which he had been taken. And he said to Adam himself: “For you are dust, and to dust you shall return” (ibid.).

What he said to one person, he clearly said to the entire human race. And human humility assents to his saying or judgment—indeed, to his most merciful providence—when it says in the psalm: “In the morning let him pass away as grass”—understand, man or human nature—“in the morning let him flourish and pass away; in the evening let him fall, grow hard, and wither, because we have failed in your wrath and have been troubled in your fury” (Ps. 89 [90]).

And the sense is: [Col. 0079C] “I said, ‘Do not turn man away into humiliation’; yet I do not pray that man should become immortal and impassible as soon as he is born. Rather, I assent to the divine sentence by which you said, ‘For you are dust, and to dust you shall return’: namely, that he who appears ‘like grass in the morning,’ clearly green and beautiful, should ‘pass away,’ that is, fail after the manner of that grass, in this manner and order. Like grass in the morning, so a man in his youth should flourish—that is, be vigorous—and afterward pass from the morning bloom of youth into the evening of old age; and, placed in that evening, should fall—that is, die—and after death grow hard, that is, become a rigid corpse; and afterward wither, that is, become dry dust.”

This is a right and very prudent assent. [Col. 0079D] For it is not merely to be accepted, but in every way to be praised: the provident counsel of the Holy Trinity, whose voice is this in the plural number, “Behold, Adam has become as one of us,” just as was the voice previously discussed, “Let us make man in our image and likeness.” The human mind does not suffice to praise or adequately consider the height of this divine counsel, by which the blessed Trinity provided for a human being dead by the death of sin, which is the death of the soul, the necessary death of the body, having ready with itself an instrument of good art by which, through the death of the body, the death of the soul might be destroyed.

## Chapter VI [Col. 0080A]

An exclamation after the prophet who, immediately after the statement, “Who has weighed the mass of the earth with three fingers,” added: “Who has helped the Spirit of the Lord, or who has been his counselor and shown him?”

Here therefore one wishes to cry out with the prophet who, after saying, “Who has weighed the mass of the earth with three fingers, and weighed the mountains in scales and the hills in a balance?”—a passage which we recalled above—immediately added:

> “Who has helped the Spirit of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor and shown him? With whom did he take counsel, and who instructed him, and taught him the path of justice, and trained him in prudence, and showed him the way of understanding?” (Isa. 40).

This exclamation or wonder, O God, is fitting [Col. 0080B] in your other wonderful works also, but it has its greatest place in this counsel of yours, or because of this counsel, by which you took such good counsel for humankind that you said, in the gravest irony: “Behold, Adam has become as one of us”—because the serpent had said, “You shall be as gods” (Gen. 3)—and immediately added: “Now therefore, lest perhaps he stretch out his hand and take also of the tree of life and eat and live forever” (ibid.).

You spoke this, O blessed Trinity, with counsel. For counsel is with you; if counsel were not with you, the prophet would not say, “Lord, let your ancient true counsel come to pass,” nor would the Psalmist say, “But the counsel of the Lord remains forever” (Ps. 32 [33]). Therefore counsel is with you, O God, in the Holy Spirit, just as might is; hence the same Spirit is called the Spirit of counsel as well as the Spirit of might (Isa. 11).

Let each person see what he thinks; [Col. 0080C] for my part, in nothing do I admire more, in nothing do I more embrace the height of the divine counsel, than in this saying and act: that he said to man, “You are dust, and to dust you shall return” (Gen. 3), and sent him away lest he should eat of the tree of life and live forever. I therefore dare to dwell on that counsel and to answer these inquiries. For although the Apostle speaks truly when he says, “For who has known the mind of the Lord?” (Rom. 11)—and you should understand, “No one”—yet elsewhere the same Apostle says: “But we have the mind of Christ” (1 Cor. 12 [2]).

Thus, before God entered upon this ancient counsel, [Col. 0080D] no one knew his mind and no one from without was his counselor. But now, after it has been accomplished, many have known it; and, to use the words of the same Apostle, “Great indeed is the mystery of godliness: it was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, appeared to angels, believed in the world, taken up in glory.” Therefore I shall inquire, as the prophet himself taught us to inquire by asking, and I shall answer as the Christian faith has instructed us to answer.

## Chapter VII [Col. 0081A]

Again on the same exclamation, “Who has helped the Spirit of the Lord?” and on the obedience of the Son, which helped the Spirit of the Lord.

Who has helped the Spirit of the Lord? For the Spirit of the Lord was laboring. Indeed, if anyone else made him labor, so that he might say to him, “You made me labor in your iniquities”; if any human being grieved him, so that the Apostle rightly says, “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption” (Eph. 4), then above all Adam grieved him and made him labor through his iniquities, by which he involved and condemned in advance all his posterity before it was born.

Who, in such labor, helped the Spirit of the Lord, who desired to overthrow the author of sin and restore justice for the children of blessing yet to be born, lest the blessing by which he had blessed them, saying “Increase and multiply,” should perish? Who, I say, helped him? Truly no one from without, but only the wisdom of God within: the obedience of the Son of God.

Suppose, therefore, that in that counsel [Col. 0081B] the Spirit of the Lord said: “Behold, if man, or the human race, dead according to the soul, should live forever in bodily life, there will be no way by which he may be restored.” What then did the wisdom of God—the Son of God—say to this? “You did not require a holocaust or a sin offering; then I said: ‘Behold, I come’” (Ps. 7 [40]). “I myself, from ancient times, before the earth was made and while this or that was being made, while I was with you ordering all things, had long held as my delight ‘to be with the children of men’” (Prov. 8).

“But behold, all the children of men must die the death of the flesh, because they are dead by the death of the soul. I shall not evade the purpose and refuse to be with the children of men. Rather, in greater necessity I shall confirm greater love. And ‘behold, I come,’ so that for their sake I may become ‘a holocaust and a sin offering.’”

Who was counselor in this, and showed him? [Col. 0081C] Truly no one from without; but the Son of God, offering voluntary obedience, was counselor—indeed, is counselor. Hence the prophet says: “And his name shall be called Wonderful, Counselor” (Isa. 9). With whom did he take counsel and instruct him? Truly with no one from without; but within, in the hidden place of the Trinity, it was reasonably determined that it was fitting for him—as the Apostle says, “for whom are all things and through whom are all things,” who had already, by foreknowledge and predestination before all ages, brought many sons into glory—that their author of salvation should be perfected through suffering (Heb. 2).

What, I ask, is more fitting than this perfection? What is more beautiful than this reasonable [37] love? This is the path of justice which no one outside taught him; this is the knowledge in which no one instructed him; this is the way of prudence which no one showed him, but which he himself discovered.

See then: [Col. 0081D] if it had not been provided that man should not also take from the tree of life and live forever, what delights would there be, or could there be, for this Wisdom of God in “being with the children of men” (Prov. 8)? For if the children of men, dead according to the soul, did not die according to the flesh, and if the Son of God, deigning to be with the children of men, did not die according to the flesh, what delight would it be to him, or what benefit to us, that he should be with the children of men? None. For just as a grain of wheat falling into the earth remains alone unless it dies (John 12), so, unless we all, the children of men, died according to the flesh, and he who wished to be with the children of men had spoken this one thing to us by means of likenesses—that he would die according to the flesh—he would remain alone, and there would be nothing in which or through which the Godhead could be propitious to us.

But now, because God said to man, [Col. 0082A] “You are dust, and to dust you shall return,” Job says: “I have found a means by which I may be merciful to him” (Job 33). And what is that? Clearly: that I ought to be made like my brothers in all things—understand, except sin—as is said elsewhere: “Tempted in all things according to likeness, yet without sin” (Heb. 4). O wondrous discovery: that for this reason the Son should be delivered to death, so that the Lord might have to be made propitious again to the servant!

## Chapter VIII [Col. 0082B]

Again on what is written there in the prophet: “With whom did he take counsel, and who instructed him, and taught him the path of justice, and trained him in knowledge, and showed him the way of prudence?” And an answer to that inquiry according to the Apostle’s saying, “We speak wisdom among the perfect,” and elsewhere, “But God has revealed it to us through the Spirit.”

Who taught him this path of justice? Who showed him this way of prudence? For “there shall be a path and a way there, and it shall be called the holy way” (Isa. 35), says the same prophet. For some it is indeed a path, that is, a narrower way; for others, however, a way—that is to say, level or broadened. And for whom, or for what sort of persons, is it a path? For whom likewise, or for what sort, is it a way?

Clearly it is a path for those who do not understand the things of God, [Col. 0082C] namely, for the wise of this age. Of these, or of such persons, the Apostle, after saying, “For the Jews ask for signs and the Greeks seek wisdom, but we preach Christ crucified: to the Jews a stumbling block, and to the nations foolishness” (1 Cor. 1), afterward says:

> “But we speak wisdom among the perfect; yet not the wisdom of this age, nor of the rulers of this age, who are brought to nothing. Rather, we speak God’s wisdom in mystery, the hidden wisdom which God predestined before the ages for our glory, which none of the rulers of this age knew; for if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2).

Clearly, for these and all who are such, this rationale of justice of which we are now speaking is a path: a way so narrow that few of them are or have been found who found it.

But the way of prudence is a way—indeed, a way more than merely a path—[Col. 0082D] for those who love him. Such a one is the same Apostle, who immediately adds: “But God has revealed it to us through his Spirit,” and the rest down to: “The spiritual man judges all things, and he himself is judged by no one. For who has known the mind of God, that he may instruct him? But we have the mind of Christ” (1 Cor. 2).

O then, how beautiful is the way of prudence; [Col. 0083A] how great is the beauty of justice in the word of the cross! Of this word the Apostle was then speaking when he said: “For the word of the cross is foolishness to those who perish; but to those who are being saved, that is, to us, it is the power of God” (1 Cor. 1). This word of the cross is what now comes to mind as we contemplate that counsel of the Trinity which we admire with the prophet saying: “Who was his counselor and showed him?” (Isa. 40).

We dare to join those who say, “But God has revealed it to us through his Spirit.” For we have heard the Son of God say, when he deigned to be baptized by John—clearly with a baptism of repentance—“For thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all justice” (Matt. 3). We have also heard the Apostle say: “For it was fitting that the author of salvation should be perfected through suffering” (Heb. 2); and that suffering was the completion of the repentance which he undertook in order to fulfill all justice.

## Chapter IX [Col. 0083B]

On that irony of God, or of the Holy Trinity, by which it said: “Behold, Adam has become as one of us, knowing good and evil,” after it had already said, “For you are dust, and to dust you shall return”; and how that irony was turned into earnest when the new Adam, Jesus Christ, became one person of the three persons of the Holy Trinity.

[The supplied source ends here, with Chapter IX incomplete.]

Nor, therefore, do we doubt that, as soon as the holy Trinity uttered this irony—“Behold, Adam has become as one of us, knowing good and evil”—after it had already said, “For dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return,” and had made coats of skins for Adam and his wife and clothed them, it was determined in the same counsel as follows: Adam has not become, as he supposed, like one of us; rather, he has lost what he had, or might have had, from us. But it befits us to fulfil all righteousness in such a way that one of us may become like Adam: that is, may become man in such a way as also to be mortal according to the flesh, like Adam, and may die such a death as a criminal, as Adam is, and be reckoned among the wicked (Isa. 53), of all whom Adam is the exemplar.

For by this means it shall come about that many sons of Adam may become as one of us, not at all deceived in their hope, as Adam was deceived; that they may become, I say, “as one of us,” that is, may become sons of God by grace, brothers and co-heirs of the only-begotten Son, who is one of us. Did it not thus come to pass? Therefore we do not doubt that in that counsel of the Trinity it was thus said or considered: the Son of God, one of those three Persons, rendered good for evil—that is, grace for robbery—to humankind, by becoming like Adam. Hence he says: “I am forgotten as a dead man from the heart,” that is, dead by the death of the soul, “and I am become as a lost vessel” (Ps. 30), namely as Adam was; “and I am reckoned with those who go down into the pit,” of whom Adam was made the first; and “I am become,” that is, I am reckoned, “as a man without help”—understand, divine help—“and like the wounded sleeping in the graves”: that is, oppressed both by actual sins and by original sin, which Adam committed when he was free among the dead, namely having power to take up my life after death, a freedom not possessed by the dead.

Thus indeed it came to pass, and that irony was thereby turned into earnest, so that you may truly say: O God, Trinity, “behold, Adam has become as one of us”; that is, humanity [Col. 0084A] was advanced into unity of person in the Son, who is one of us. Humanity, I say, became the Son of God; and this is the new Adam, father of many sons, whose whole company “is as one of us,” that is, like the Son of God. Hence is that saying: “We know that, when he shall appear, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3).

## Chapter X

Concerning faith, which is one and the chief of the gifts of the Holy Spirit; and that it was in the first holy ancient Fathers a preparation for so great a mystery and so great a salvation.
