For so wonderful and ineffable a mystery, a great preparation was surely necessary. What preparation, or what kind, except faith? For through the fault of unbelief and excessive ambition Adam had made himself unworthy of God, believing the serpent rather than God and aspiring to that exaltation which he first desired who said in his heart: “I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14). For what else did that liar promise when he said: “You shall be as gods”?

On the contrary, a preparation of faith and humility was needed, so that, with the order of justice preserved, the children of men might render themselves worthy of that grace which Wisdom had purposed—Wisdom whom we understand, and indeed believe, to be the Son of God himself, saying, as was mentioned above: “My delights are to be with the children of men” (Prov. 8). Whence came this preparation, namely faith, except from thy gift, O Spirit of the Lord? For among the distributions of graces which thou workest, this is one and the best, as the Apostle says: “To one indeed is given by the Spirit the word of wisdom; to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another faith in the same Spirit” (1 Cor. 12), and the rest. We have, as I think, aptly said above that the number nine of these graces corresponds to the nine names of the orders of angels.

Therefore, when the same Apostle says: “By faith Abel offered to God a more abundant sacrifice than Cain, by which he received testimony that he was righteous, God bearing testimony to his gifts; and through it, though dead, he yet speaks. By faith Enoch was translated so that he should not see death, and was not found because God translated him; for before his translation he had testimony that he pleased God. But without faith it is impossible to please God” [Col. 0084D] (Heb. 11)—when, I say, he said these things and the rest, our wonder is increased, so that we say more and more, as the prophet cited above says: “Who has helped the Spirit of the Lord?” (Isa. 40). Or rather, where were those helpers of thine, O Spirit of the Lord? Of such helpers the Apostle speaks when he says: “For we are God’s fellow-workers,” adding: “You are God’s field, God’s building. According to the grace given to me, as a wise architect I laid the foundation, and another builds upon it” (1 Cor. 3).

Where, I say, were they when thou wast laying those foundations of the earth: those first Fathers of the Church according to faith? For today, wherever this foundation is laid, wherever faith is founded, there are many such helpers: many voices of preachers, many books of prophets and apostles, many frequent signs confirming what is spoken. But then, “who helped thee, O Spirit of the Lord?” What help of this kind didst thou possess? Thou alone, without books, without signs or wonders, didst write—as thou art the finger of God—this Scripture in their hearts, that is, the knowledge of faith, through which, or “in which, the elders received testimony” (Heb. 11), as the same Apostle says: namely Abel and the other ancient Fathers down to Moses, in whose hearts this foundation was laid by thee without books and other aids.

## Chapter XI

That at that time not only faith but also prophecy was given by the Holy Spirit to those holy men before the Flood, according to his will; and concerning the mystery of the number in which Lamech says: “Sevenfold vengeance shall be taken for Cain, but for Lamech seventy-sevenfold.”

The same Holy Spirit then apportioned to those elders or fathers, according to his will, something also of the other charisms: namely prophecy, or divine knowledge. For we are not here concerned so much with human knowledge, which even those without faith or expectation of this Paraclete often attain through human ability. An example is music, which Scripture thus mentions in him who was seventh from Cain: “The name of his brother was Jubal; he was the father of those who play the harp and organ” (Gen. 4).

But we call divine knowledge that which has some divine or spiritual savor, such as this: “Sevenfold,” says Lamech, “vengeance shall be taken for Cain; but for Lamech seventy-sevenfold” (ibid.). For the Lord himself deigned to remember this saying and refer to it. He spoke scarcely anything without the authority of Scripture. When Peter said, “Lord, how often shall my brother sin against me and I forgive him? Until seven times?” he answered thus: “I do not say to thee, Peter, until seven times, but until seventy-seven times” (Matt. 18).

For a divine meaning lies hidden in these words, which may readily be gathered from the rationale of the numbers. The number seven, in which Cain’s sin is placed by the words, “Sevenfold vengeance shall be taken for Cain,” is indivisible: it has no half, third, or other parts apart from units alone. But the number seventy-seven [Col. 0085D], besides units, also has other parts into which it may be resolved: namely seven and eleven; for seven times eleven, or eleven times seven, is seventy-seven. Therefore, rightly and beautifully, just as by the number seven—in which, as we have said, Cain’s sin is marked—is understood the unremitting vengeance inflicted upon him because he was impenitent, so by seventy-seven—in which Lamech’s wound or bruise is placed, when it says “but for Lamech seventy-sevenfold”—is understood a remitting vengeance: that is, one which forgiveness will at some time limit or end. This is what the Lord said to Peter: “I do not say to thee seven times, but until seventy-seven times”; that is, thou shalt forgive not every impenitent person, but everyone who does penance.

That prophecy was not wholly absent from the people of that age may be established by this example or testimony which we read in the canonical Epistle of the apostle Jude: “But Enoch, the seventh from Adam, prophesied concerning these, saying: Behold, the Lord comes with his holy thousands to execute judgment against all the ungodly” (Jude 14), and so forth. Although this prophecy has no example in writings known before that apostolic Epistle, nevertheless it cannot lightly be disregarded that an Apostle of Christ wrote that it had been prophesied, and could have known it through the Holy Spirit.

## Chapter XII

Likewise concerning the charisms of the Holy Spirit: that at that time, and afterward before the advent of the Spirit given for remission of sins, he had not been given in that way; that the gifts then bestowed were preparations for the regeneration by which they are now sons of God; and concerning what blessed Job says of them, that those conceived did not see the light.

By enlightening people with these and other charisms of his, the Holy Spirit undoubtedly already made a multitude of sons of God, although Scripture plainly names only a few—only two or three—before the Flood. “For when men began,” it says, “to multiply upon the earth, the sons of God, seeing that the daughters of men were beautiful, took wives for themselves from all whom they chose” (Gen. 6): calling those sons of God who were of Seth’s stock, and daughters of men those who were descended from Cain’s stock.

Nevertheless, although they were already called sons of God because of faith and the other charisms of the Holy Spirit which we have mentioned, those same charisms did not then yet accomplish that they were sons of God. Rather, they were preparations for the begetting—or indeed the rebirth—of sons of God, in which both the old and the new were perfected; for God, says the Apostle, provided that they should not be perfected without us (Heb. 11). For through the blood of this one alone, both they and we received the Holy Spirit in this grace which is remission of sins.

In this distinction, namely between the old and the new, it is pleasing to observe that, since, as we have said elsewhere, there are two gifts of the Holy Spirit, one for remission of sins and the other for distributions of graces: the ancients received the latter before they received the former; but the new, namely we who are reborn or have been reborn after Christ’s Passion, received remission of sins before distributions of graces. The exception is Cornelius in the Acts of the Apostles and those with him, upon whom, before they were baptized “for remission of sins,” the Holy Spirit fell, and they spoke in tongues and magnified God (Acts 10).

For the circumstance of the time required this, on account of those who believed from among the Jews, lest, if Gentiles were not circumcised, it should be lawful for those Jewish believers to say more stubbornly: “Why did you enter in to men having the foreskin?” And so that Peter might have greater freedom to say to them: “Who forbids these to be baptized, who have received the Holy Spirit as we have?” Therefore of those ancient saints or sons of God, especially those who lived before the Flood, you may rightly say the mystical saying of blessed Job: that, conceived, they did not see the light.

For the grace of the Holy Spirit, which is the very blessing of Father and Son, by which God blessed male and female, saying, “Increase and multiply,” was never afterward barren, as a maternal womb that conceives sons of God. Yet because they had not come to the day of the reward mentioned above, and indeed were not made known to the world through any narrative of Scripture, they were, as it were, conceived persons who did not see the light. Therefore, leaving these matters, let us now proceed to the rest.

## Chapter XIII

Concerning Noah’s three sons, through whom the world was restored; and, a point very worthy of notice, concerning the threefold utterance over them of the word of blessing which God pronounced over the first human beings; and that Noah cursed Canaan rather than Ham himself.

“Noah was a just man and perfect in his generations. He walked with God and begot three sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth” (Gen. 6). From these three men the world was restored; and, what is very worthy of notice, the word of blessing which God had pronounced over the first humans was renewed over them in a threefold utterance. “Go forth,” God says to Noah, “from thy ark, thou and thy wife, thy sons and thy sons’ wives; and enter upon the earth. Increase and multiply upon it” (Gen. 8–9). Again, secondly: “And God blessed Noah and his sons, and said to them: Increase and multiply and fill the earth.” Then thirdly: “But you, increase and enter upon the earth and fill it” (ibid.).

Does not, then, the Trinity which there showed itself in speech here show itself in deed? For there, in saying, “Let us make man in our image and likeness,” and, “Behold, Adam has become as one of us,” it showed itself in speech. Here, preserving Noah’s three sons and blessing them with a threefold blessing, that they might be the beginnings of so great a matter, namely the restoration of the human race, it surely showed itself in deed.

Nor does the fault of one of those three men diminish this mystery, any more than Adam’s transgression destroys the mystery of his words: “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh” (Gen. 2). Hence the Apostle says: “This mystery is great; but I speak concerning Christ and the Church” (Eph. 5). Accordingly, it is very noteworthy that when father Noah learned what his son Ham had done to him, he did not say, “Cursed be Ham,” but: “Cursed be Canaan; he shall be a servant of servants to his brothers” (Gen. 9).

For it was not fitting that a wise man should send the blow of a curse upon one in whom God had bestowed blessing among his brothers, blessing all three together, as has been said, and saying: “Increase and multiply.” Just as God himself, after blessing Adam and Eve in the same manner, saying, “Increase and multiply” (Gen. 3), did not turn the word of blessing so completely to its opposite as to say to Adam what he later said to Cain: “Now therefore thou shalt be cursed from the earth”; and to the serpent: “Because thou hast done this, thou shalt be cursed among all animals and beasts of the earth.” Rather, he said: “Cursed is the earth in thy work” (Gen. 4).

Thus, just as the unchangeable God did not judge it fitting to say “Cursed” to the very person whom he had blessed, but preferred to say “Cursed is the earth in thy work,” so the man of God avoided saying, “Cursed be Ham,” whom God had blessed, and preferred to say, “Cursed be Canaan.” Why, however, Moses wrote that this son rather than another of Ham’s sons should be under the curse—although Ham also had other sons, as Scripture says: “The sons of Ham were Cush, Mizraim, Put, and Canaan” (Gen. 10)—would be superfluous to discuss now. Yet it must briefly be said: at that time Israel, having come forth from Egypt, was being led into the land of Canaan, and the sins of the Canaanites were being fulfilled. Therefore Israel needed to know that the Lord’s help in destroying them would not fail it, and also that this race had been cursed before it was born.

## Chapter XIV

Concerning the purpose of that judgment, namely the Flood: that the splendor of the holy Trinity shines forth there for one who examines the text of Scripture more closely.

But that we may know more certainly that Noah’s begetting three sons, and the restoration of the world from persons of this number, occurred not by chance but by the providence of the holy Trinity, let us examine more closely the letter in the purpose of that judgment, namely the Flood. For after it has been said: “The sons of God, seeing that the daughters of men were beautiful, took wives for themselves from all whom they chose,” there immediately follows: “And God said: My Spirit shall not remain in man forever, because he is flesh.” Then, after the complaint about that mixture of the sons of God with the daughters of men has been repeated, there directly follows: “But God, seeing that the wickedness of men was great upon the earth,” and the rest, down to, “For it repenteth me that I made them.”

Scripture immediately adds: “But Noah found grace before the Lord, and begot three sons”; and so says: “And when God saw that the earth was corrupt, he said to Noah: The end of all flesh has come before me; make thee an ark of planed wood” (Gen. 6). Who, in keeping with the manner and purpose of the present work, would not delight that even here, where perhaps it was not thought to shine, the splendor of the holy Trinity appears? For in so brief a passage, behold, the name of God occurs a third time: “And God said”; “But God, seeing”; “And when God saw.”

What is lacking here for the manifestation of the Trinity, except that, because—as we said at the beginning—this treasure had to remain hidden in this field of Scripture, the relative names were left unspoken? Thus it was not said: “God the Father said”; “God the Son saw”; “God, the Spirit of Father and Son, saw.” For if all this had been written, the world could not then have borne it; Moses’ face would have been too horned—that is, too radiant (Exod. 34)—and scandalized Israel would have fled farther from him.

Now it is permitted to lift the veil from his face and show that this passage proclaims the holy Trinity seated upon the throne of judgment, for the great judgment, namely the execution of so terrible a judgment upon those giants and exceedingly numerous people whose wickedness and iniquity filled the earth. Let us therefore consider here the judgments, the judgments of the individual Persons of the holy Trinity.

## Chapter XV

Concerning the first sentence of that judgment: “My Spirit shall not remain in man forever, because he is flesh,” and how it suits the Person of the Father.

“And God said: My Spirit shall not remain in man forever, because he is flesh.” Surely it suits that Person who said, as was discussed above, “Behold, Adam has become as one of us; now lest perhaps he take also of the tree of life and live forever,” to say: “My Spirit”—that is, made or given by me—“shall not remain in man forever.”

Indeed, this sentence confirms the earlier sentence and in some measure satisfies those who hear it: it shows that he truly and wisely, and most beneficially, closed the tree of life to humanity, lest humanity should live forever. As though he said: What would human beings do if they lived forever, when through a comparatively long life—for example, nine hundred or eight hundred years—they have become so corrupt and so proud? Therefore, as I then said, “lest he take of the tree of life and live forever,” so now I say: “My Spirit shall not remain in man forever, because he is flesh,” that is, because he is corrupt. Indeed, I shall also diminish his years: they shall no longer be so many years, but shall be one hundred and twenty years.

Others indeed lived fewer years after the Flood, but Moses, who wrote this Scripture, was of that number when he died, namely one hundred and twenty years old. There is another interpretation of this number, but this seems preferable. Yet we are bound by our purpose and cannot dwell upon such matters, especially since we have treated them more fully in another work. Therefore this sentence of judgment most properly belongs to the Person of the Father. For the sentence which follows belongs to the Person of the Son, and the consideration of this is sweet and pleasing to us.

## Chapter XVI

Concerning the second sentence: “God, seeing, repented that he had made man upon the earth; and, looking ahead to the future and touched inwardly by sorrow of heart, said: I will destroy man whom I created”—and how this suits the Person of the Son.

“But God, seeing that the wickedness of men was great upon the earth and that every thought of their hearts was bent toward evil continually, repented that he had made man upon the earth. And, looking ahead to the future and touched inwardly by sorrow of heart, he said: I will destroy man whom I created from the face of the earth, from man even to animals, from creeping things even to birds of the air; for it repenteth me that I made them” (Gen. 6).

This sentence, I say, more properly suits the Person of the Son: namely, to execute judgment upon human beings, because he was to become the Son of Man, as he says in the Gospel: “And he gave him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man” (John 5). The fact that that Son of Man had not yet been made does not make the execution of judgment upon human beings—that is, the bringing on of the Flood—less fitting to him, since he was most certainly to be the Son of Man and this work was already before him, as it is written: “Behold, his reward is with him, and his work before him” (Isa. 40, 62).

Likewise, was not already before him the repentance, or baptism of repentance, with which he was to be baptized in the form of a servant, consummating that same repentance by the Passion and death of the cross? And our sicknesses and pains, which he was to bear; the wounds by which he was to be wounded for our iniquities; the bruising by which he was to be crushed for our crimes (Isa. 53); the chastisement and bruise, or stripes and welts, by which his most sacred body was to be cut—were these not already before him?

If the prophet, while these things were still future, saw them as though already past and declared all of them in words of the past tense—“We saw him, we considered him, and did not esteem him; he bore our sicknesses, he carried our pains, he was wounded, he was bruised, by his bruise we were healed” (ibid.)—how much more were they present before him, although not yet done!

Therefore, the words of Scripture, “It repented him that he had made man upon the earth,” and this saying, “For it repenteth me that I made them,” surely suit this Person, namely the Son. Rightly this sentence may be taken as prophecy, and “it repenteth me that I made them” understood as though it said: I shall perform repentance “unto death, even the death of the cross” (Phil. 2), because I made them; or, I shall be beaten—that is, I shall most certainly be beaten—for no fault of my own other than that I made them. This surely will be to render evil for good. Therefore I shall destroy them: these now through the present Flood, and all the impious in the future judgment by fire. Therefore, I say, because for this very reason I have just authority to execute judgment, because I am the Son of Man; or it must be understood at the same time: I have been slain, that is, shall most certainly be slain, by them or by persons like them.

But what is this which Scripture says: “Touched inwardly by sorrow of heart”? What is meant by “inwardly”? For God is not like a human being, whose body is outward and soul inward. Therefore, “inwardly” signifies the secret of which the Apostle says to the Ephesians: “To enlighten all men concerning what is the dispensation of the mystery hidden from ages in God, who created all things, that it may be made known to principalities and powers in heaven” (Eph. 3). Since that sorrow by which he was to suffer for us, and which he saw as already present, as has been said, was hidden from both angels and human beings, it is rightly said: “Touched inwardly by sorrow of heart.”

And what, moreover, is meant when it says: “Looking ahead to the future”? Surely, in the same sense, it is as though it said: Foreseeing that his suffering would have much fruit. To the same foresight or providence belongs also that which he says in the Psalm: “What profit is there in my flesh, when I go down into corruption?” (Ps. 29). For unless the human race had been destroyed by that Flood and filled with many other miseries, and unless our necks were soon brought down into the mire, how should we receive the yoke of Christ’s humility? Even now affliction scarcely gives understanding to the hearing (Isa. 28), when “man born of woman, living for a short time, is filled with many miseries” (Job 14), and “the days of our years in them are seventy years” (Ps. 89).

## Chapter XVII

Concerning the third sentence: “And when God saw, he said to Noah: The end of all flesh has come before me; make thee an ark”—and how this suits the Person of the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0091B] What follows: “And when God saw that the earth was corrupt, he said to Noah: The end of all flesh has come before me; make thee an ark of planed wood” (Gen. 6), and the rest, among which it is written that “the dove came to him in the evening, bearing in its mouth an olive branch with green leaves” (Gen. 8), surely belongs to the Person of the Holy Spirit. Thus you may here truly say the Davidic words: “Mercy and truth have met one another; righteousness and peace have kissed” (Ps. 48). For the Holy Spirit himself is mercy, as we sing in the Psalm: “My God, my mercy” (Ps. 58); and the Son of God himself is truth, as he himself said: “I am the truth” (John 14).

And who does not know that, just as it was truth that “God, seeing,” as has been said, “that the wickedness of men was great upon the earth, said: I will destroy man whom I created from the face of the earth, from man even to animals, from creeping things even to birds of the air” (Gen. 6), so it was mercy that he said to Noah: “I will establish my covenant with thee, and thou shalt enter the ark: thou and thy sons, thy wife and thy sons’ wives with thee. And of every living thing of all flesh thou shalt bring two into the ark, that they may live with thee, male and female, that seed may be preserved upon the whole face of all the earth” (ibid.).

Thus, both by words and deeds, in that great business of so great a judgment, the Trinity at once showed and concealed itself. In the other principal places of this field, that is, of holy Scripture, we hope the same: that this treasure may without doubt be found by those who seek piously. Therefore let us proceed, and with watchful eyes examine and search every place as far as we can.

## Chapter XVIII

Concerning God’s words: “Come therefore, let us descend and confuse their languages there,” because this is the voice of the Trinity, just as was the plural saying: “Behold, Adam has become as one of us.”

“But the Lord descended to see the city and tower which the sons of Adam were building, and said: Behold, they are one people and all have one language. And they have begun to do this, nor will they cease from their thoughts until they complete them in deed. Come therefore, let us descend and confuse their language there” [Col. 0092A] (Gen. 11).

And indeed, as in Adam’s transgression, so great a matter had occurred that the holy Trinity had to oppose itself to it, so also here. For what were the sons of Adam intending when they said: “Come, let us make for ourselves a city and a tower whose summit may reach to heaven” (ibid.)? Surely they were being deceived by the same daring pride by which Adam had been deceived, aspiring to be like God; and he who said in his heart, “I will ascend above the height of the clouds; I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14), was stirring them up. Because of the pride which they were imitating, Scripture aptly marks them out by calling them sons of Adam: “But the Lord descended,” it says, “to see the city and tower which the sons of Adam were building.”

Indeed, this manner of speech intends to excite wonder that the sons, although already bearing their father’s punishment, still breathed such great audacity. For it is surely more astonishing to be proud after punishment, or while under punishment, than before punishment. It is pleasing, therefore, to marvel at their audacity also in the words of the pagan, namely the distinguished poet, who, eager to describe the punishments of hell, says:

> Here the ancient race of Earth, the Titan brood,  
> struck down by thunderbolt, rolls in the deepest abyss;  
> here also I saw the twin Aloadae, monstrous bodies,  
> who undertook with their hands to tear apart great heaven  
> and to thrust Jupiter from his heavenly kingdom.  
> —Virgil, *Aeneid* 6

But should we suppose that God feared this, and for that reason said: “They have begun to do this, nor will they cease from their thoughts until they complete them in deed”? Even if they were still living today and had never ceased building—or never would cease—could they reach even halfway to the height of heaven or the firmament? By no means. But let it be granted that they reached, or could reach, that height of the firmament which they call the *Aplanes* [the sphere of the fixed stars]. What harm could they do to the invisible Majesty, even if they were not cast down or struck by lightning?

Therefore there is no doubt that God foresaw something, since it was written above (Gen. 6): “Looking ahead to the future.” Nevertheless, he did not foresee their hands; rather, he foresaw their tongues. In what respect? Let us attend, because this passage demands no slight understanding. God said: “They will not cease from their thoughts until they complete them in deed,” yet he did not cut off their hands but confused their tongues. Let us therefore say what construction of the proud he foresaw, since it was truly said above: “Looking ahead to the future.”

## Chapter XIX

Concerning the words: “They will not cease from their thoughts until they complete them in deed”; how they completed them in deed.

The Holy Spirit was to compose the Scriptures of truth for the sake of humble people—the Scriptures which we now read—and in them he had proposed to conceal the treasure (Jer. 48) which we both find now and desire to find: the treasure of his name, the treasure of the mysteries of Christ, the Son of God. For he knew the height of Satan, who reigns “over all the children of pride” (Job 41). He foresaw that the construction of that tower, their vain and false knowledge or loquacity (2 Thess. 2), exalting itself against the truth of God (2 Cor. 10), was an image of it.

He therefore said: “They have begun to do this, nor will they cease from their thoughts until they complete them in deed.” From what thoughts would they not cease? Clearly those which he declares in these words: “Let us make for ourselves a city and a tower whose summit may reach to heaven” (Gen. 11). Did they not do so? For as soon as the holy Scriptures were widely published among them, they raised the tower of contrary knowledge even to blaspheming the Creator. Hence the saying: “They devised and spoke wickedness; they spoke iniquity on high. They set their mouth in heaven, and their tongue passed over the earth” (Ps. 72). That is: being earthly, their tongue, by blaspheming all earthly things, passed even to God himself. For they spoke wickedly not only concerning earthly things, but also concerning their Creator.

I say, therefore: if, after the lips of those who rise up had been divided or confused and their thoughts scattered, they did and said such great things that scarcely could stand or resist the one to whom it is said in the Song: “Thy neck is like the tower of David, built with battlements; a thousand shields hang from it, and all the armor of the mighty” (Cant. 4), what would they have done, what would they have said, if their tongues had never been confused and their lips never divided?

Rightly, then, and providently, when the time was at hand for the Scriptures of truth—the Scriptures of the Law and the Prophets, in which is the treasure of truth—to be written, that division of languages or nations occurred, so that this treasure might be concealed in one language or nation alone until the appointed time. But could even that have sufficed? Certainly not, unless, in that one language of the Hebrew people, the subtlety of concealment had been accomplished under figures and riddles, in parables and allegories. For even those to whom the utterances of God were entrusted could not have borne them, as was signified when the sons of Israel fled or feared to come near, seeing the radiance of Moses’ face (2 Cor. 3; Exod. 34).

## Chapter XX

Concerning that plague of confusion, in what respect it was beneficial, and to which Person it more properly belongs to have said to the others: “Come, let us descend and confuse,” and so forth.

Thus a great blow indeed befell the world when the confusion of languages took place; yet it was of no small benefit in this respect: pagans, Jews, and especially heretics, scattered through Asia, Europe, and Africa, were less able to build their tower, liable to confusion, against the truth than they would have been had they all been of one speech and the same language. To which Person, however, is it more fitting that He should have said to the others: “Come, let us go down and confuse their language”? Do you suppose it was the Person of the Son? For where the wound of that confusion was to be healed, this Person—that is, the Son—speaks to His apostles: “And I,” He says, “will ask the Father, and He will give you another Paraclete” [Advocate] ([John xiv](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=John%2014&version=VULGATE)). And so it happened: the division of languages, which had come about through pride, was restored by the coming of the Holy Spirit, that same Paraclete, so that every kind of language sprang forth in their mouths ([Acts ii](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Acts%202&version=VULGATE)).

Since this was to come about at the Son’s request, and did come about, we are pleased to ascribe to this Person the saying addressed to the Father and the Holy Spirit: “Come, let us go down and confuse their language” ([Gen. xi](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Genesis%2011&version=VULGATE)); for, plainly, both these new things and all those ancient things were made for His sake ([Heb. ii](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Hebrews%202&version=VULGATE)). Yet we no longer understand the words “Come, let us go down and confuse” as the words of one asking, since asking belongs to one who is lesser. But He, namely the Son, was not then lesser; rather, when He became man, then He was made a little lower not only than the Father and the Holy Spirit, but even than the angels ([Ps. viii](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Psalm%208&version=VULGATE); [Heb. ii](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Hebrews%202&version=VULGATE)), because according to His human nature He could suffer and die—which, indeed, was to ask. For by dying He was made a sacrifice for us.

Therefore we understand the words “Come, let us go down, let us confuse” better and more faithfully as those of Wisdom taking counsel and ordering all things with God—as we have in the Proverbs; that Wisdom ([Prov. viii](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Proverbs%208&version=VULGATE)), namely, is the Son of God. Let us proceed further.

## CHAPTER XXI

Concerning the faith of the father Abraham, who believed the promises of the blessed seed; and concerning the fact that he saw three and worshipped one.

[Col. 0094C] In the part of the field that we now touch, in the place of Scripture into which we now advance, shines the faith of our father Abraham, believing the promises of the blessed seed. Here too, O blessed Trinity, God, Thou dost shine forth most brightly, and the treasure of Thy name is not greatly hidden—namely, designated in three great men and in three angels.

The three men who are the beginning of the great nation are Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, concerning whom even today we hear Thee declaring: “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” ([Exod. iii](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Exodus%203&version=VULGATE)). Of the three angels Scripture says thus:

> “The Lord appeared to him in the valley of Mamre, as he sat at the entrance of his tent in the very heat of the day. And when he had lifted up his eyes, three men appeared to him, standing near him. When he saw them, he ran from the entrance of his tent to meet them, and bowed himself to the ground, and said: ‘Lord, if I have found favour in thy sight, do not pass by thy servant’” ([Gen. xviii](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Genesis%2018&version=VULGATE)), etc.

The more familiar and celebrated is the feast of that day, the poorer is all our discourse for celebrating it jointly. For who does not know, who has not heard, that Abraham, our father according to faith, on that day, in the very heat of the day, saw three and worshipped one? He saw three men; yet, meeting and worshipping them, he did not say, “Lords, if I have found favour in your sight,” but: “Lord, if I have found favour in thy sight.” This was to worship one while three were in view.

But what is meant by that banquet of the three angels, who promised that Isaac would be born, and who were received as such guests with laughter and joy? A little earlier the aged Abraham had laughed, as Scripture says: “Abraham fell upon his face and laughed, saying in his heart: ‘Shall a son be born to a man a hundred years old? And shall Sarah, who is ninety years old, give birth?’” ([Gen. xvii](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Genesis%2017&version=VULGATE)). Here, when the Lord who had appeared in the three persons of angels said, “Returning I will come to thee at this time, life accompanying me, and Sarah thy wife shall have a son,” Sarah laughed behind the entrance of the tent—she laughed, I say, secretly. And when the Lord said to Abraham, “Why did Sarah laugh, saying, ‘Shall I indeed, old as I am, give birth?’” Sarah, terrified by fear, denied it, saying, “I did not laugh.” But the Lord said: “It is not so; rather, thou didst laugh” ([Gen. xviii](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Genesis%2018&version=VULGATE)).

What, I ask, is meant by that banquet of such guests, celebrated with the laughter and rejoicing of old people, in which He who is promised to be born is commanded to be called Isaac—that is, “laughter”—and the parents to whom the son of this name is promised are named Abraham, that is, “father of many nations,” and Sarah, that is, “princess”? Let us say something worthy of faith, that we may deserve to feast with eternal laughter with the blessed Trinity, according to the signified mystery of that banquet.

## 43. CHAPTER XXII

Concerning the three fathers, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; how, in those three angels feasting together and promising that Isaac would be born, the sacrament of faith in the Holy Trinity was prefigured—a faith by which the world was illuminated through Christ’s coming.

In the prophet Amos [Hosea], the Lord says: “And I spoke through the prophets, and I multiplied visions, and in the hand of the prophets I was represented” ([Hos. xii](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Hosea%2012&version=VULGATE)). Now these three fathers—Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—were, or rather are, the chief and greatest of the prophets, with whom the Holy Trinity, the one God, established His covenant. Thus the Psalmist sings, having first said:

> “He remembered for ever His covenant, which He made with Abraham, and His oath to Isaac; and He established it for Jacob as an ordinance, and for Israel as an everlasting covenant” ([Ps. civ](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Psalm%20105&version=VULGATE)).

Afterward he adds:

> “He permitted no man to harm them, and for their sakes He rebuked kings: ‘Do not touch my anointed ones, and do no evil to my prophets’” (ibid.).

Therefore, if we are to be accounted worthy of the mystery of that banquet, we must know by what likeness the Holy Trinity was represented there in the hospitality of father Abraham. This does not require our assertion, for it is known almost everywhere to nearly all that Isaac, the son of aged Abraham—whose name means “laughter”—by being born and living bore the type of our Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the ancient and eternal Father, who is the laughter of holy human beings and the joy of all blessed angels.

According to the dispensation of times appointed beforehand with God, it was to come about that the Holy Trinity should become known to the world by public preaching not before Christ’s coming, but in the noon or brightest heat of the day of His very coming, when our Isaac Himself began to speak with the Gospel voice. For example, when He says: “I and the Father are one” ([John x](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=John%2010&version=VULGATE)); and: “But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, He shall teach you all things” (ibid., xiv); and many other things pertaining to this rule of faith. The best known and most illustrious is that saying at the end of Matthew’s Gospel:

> “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” ([Matt. xxviii](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Matthew%2028&version=VULGATE)).

Most beautifully and most holy, therefore, not before but when the time had now come for that Isaac, the figure and form of this Isaac, to be conceived or born, those three men—that is, angels—appeared to father Abraham. To him as he ran to meet them, worshipped, and said, “Lord, if I have found favour in thy sight,” and all that follows as far as “I will set before you a morsel of bread,” they promptly replied, “Do as thou hast said”; and most familiarly they ate “three measures of fine flour, a most tender and excellent calf from the herd, butter also and milk” ([Gen. xviii](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Genesis%2018&version=VULGATE)).

In what other way more intimate than this could father Abraham wish to feast the citizens of the invisible fatherland, or could a faithful man, reckoned righteous through the merit of faith, wish to minister to the holy and indivisible Trinity? Likewise, in what other way could the multitude of nations, of whom he is the father according to faith, wish more familiarly to minister to the Holy Trinity than by offering on the holy altar the sacrifice of the Lord’s body and blood, standing beneath the tree—that is, in faith in Christ’s cross—as it is written there: “But Abraham stood beneath the tree” (ibid.)?

Much material offers itself here, and the greatness of the matter demands abundance of speech; but we have spoken elsewhere according to our ability. Therefore, satisfied to have recalled or demonstrated in accordance with our purpose the testimony of the Holy Trinity, which shines forth magnificently here, let us end the present little book, immediately to proceed further according to the tenor of the same purpose by which we undertook, in this most spacious field of sacred Scripture, to show believers the treasure which unbelievers cannot see or find.

# BOOK FIVE

[Col. 0095]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0095D] Concerning Solomon’s saying in the Proverbs: “The name of the Lord is a most strong tower; the righteous runs to it and shall be exalted”; and concerning the fact that he is righteous who is justified by faith in this name.

Thou art our hope—indeed, the crown of our hope—O name of the Lord, name of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; the crown, I say, of hope, as the prophet says: “O Lord, Thy arm is exalted, O God of hosts, the crown of hope adorned with glory.” For what other than Thee do we hope for, or ought we to hope for, while in speaking and writing we preach and glorify Thy name? What else, I say, ought we to hope for except that, loving Thy name, we shall glory in Thee? “For,” says the Psalmist, “all who love Thy name shall glory in Thee” ([Ps. v](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Psalm%205&version=VULGATE)); and Wisdom says: “The name of the Lord is a most strong tower; the righteous runs to it and shall be exalted” ([Prov. xviii](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Proverbs%2018&version=VULGATE)).

But who is righteous, or whence is he righteous? Is it from works? Certainly, if the question is of works, the Psalmist objects, saying: “For no living person shall be justified in Thy sight” ([Ps. cxlii](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Psalm%20143&version=VULGATE)); and the Apostle agrees when he says: “By works no flesh shall be justified before Him” ([Rom. iii](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Romans%203&version=VULGATE); [Hab. ii](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Habakkuk%202&version=VULGATE)). Whence, then, is he righteous? From faith, because it is written: “But the righteous lives by faith.” Abraham was justified by faith, as Scripture says: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him for righteousness” ([Gen. xv](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Genesis%2015&version=VULGATE); [Rom. iv](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Romans%204&version=VULGATE)); and then, as we have mentioned, he deserved to see and receive the mystery of the Holy Trinity in the three angels.

Let us therefore also glorify Thee in this hope of righteousness, O name of the Lord; and let this be for us to run to the most strong tower and to be exalted: that we strive to build a faithful discourse upon the foundation of faith, so that it may be a tower in timely help and that this hope may be firm.

## CHAPTER II

Concerning God’s words, as He began to speak to Moses: “Thus shalt thou say to the children of Israel: ‘The Lord God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, hath sent me to you’”; and concerning the name *Adonai*, “which,” He says, “I did not make known to them.”

As God began to speak to Moses, He said among other things: “Thus shalt thou say to the children of Israel: ‘The Lord God of our fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, hath sent me to you. This is my name for ever’” ([Exod. iii](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Exodus%203&version=VULGATE)). Elsewhere He says to the same man: “I am the Lord who appeared to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as God Almighty, and I did not make known to them my name *Adonai*” ([Exod. vi](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Exodus%206&version=VULGATE)).

There it must be supplied: “as I shall make it known to thee.” For then the Lord gave Moses a certain grace of His Spirit, namely, the working of miracles, which He had not given or made known to those fathers. For they did not work miracles of this kind, but were glorious by faith alone. Whoever considers this assuredly understands rightly the saying: “And I did not make known to them my name *Adonai*.” Likewise he understands the saying in Isaiah, where, after first saying, “Where is He who brought them up from the sea with the shepherds of His flock?” he immediately adds: “Where is He who placed in the midst of him the Spirit of His Holy One?” And then: “The Spirit of the Lord was his guide” ([Isa. lxiii](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Isaiah%2063&version=VULGATE)).

He understands these things rightly, I say, who considers that Moses, owing to the circumstance or necessity of the time—because Pharaoh would not let the people go except by a strong hand—received this grace from the Spirit of the Lord, namely the working of miracles, which the Apostle places in the middle, that is, fifth place, in the order of the nine charisms of the same Holy Spirit ([1 Cor. xii](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=1%20Corinthians%2012&version=VULGATE)). Assuredly by this grace, by the working of miracles, God made His name *Adonai* known to Moses, and through Moses to us all—that is, *Adonai*, which, blessed Jerome says, we generally call “Lord.”

Hence it is that Isaiah, in the passage mentioned above, after saying, “Where is He who placed in the midst of him the Spirit of His Holy One?”, immediately adds, in order to make clear what operation of the Holy Spirit he means there: “Who led Moses at His right hand by the arm of His majesty; who divided the waters before them, to make for Himself an everlasting name; who brought them through the depths, like a horse in the wilderness, without stumbling, like an animal descending into the plain.” And, having inserted what we said above, “The Spirit of the Lord was his guide,” he says again: “Thus Thou didst lead Thy people, that Thou mightest make for Thyself a name of glory” ([Isa. lxiii](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Isaiah%2063&version=VULGATE)).

## CHAPTER III

That it was no diminution of glory or merit for those fathers that He said: “And I did not make known to them my name *Adonai*.”

[Col. 0098B] What then shall we say? Are the holy fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob of lesser glory or merit than Moses because He did not make His name *Adonai* known to them, but made it known to Moses in the sight of Pharaoh, the Egyptians, and other nations through the working of miracles? Thus the Psalmist sings: “Thou art God who dost wonders; Thou hast made known Thy power among the peoples; Thou hast redeemed Thy people, the children of Jacob and Joseph, by Thine arm” ([Ps. lxxvi](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Psalm%2077&version=VULGATE)). And the Lord Himself says to Pharaoh: “For this reason I have set thee up: that I may show in thee my strength and that my name may be proclaimed in all the earth” ([Exod. ix](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Exodus%209&version=VULGATE)). By no means.

Indeed, their great faith shines all the more precious before God in our eyes because it did not need to grow by signs of this kind—which the Jews seek even today—or by languages, which, as the Apostle says, “are for a sign, not to believers, but to unbelievers” ([1 Cor. xiv](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=1%20Corinthians%2014&version=VULGATE)). Hence the same Apostle, recalling their faith, says: “Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God” ([Heb. xi](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Hebrews%2011&version=VULGATE)). And truly He is not ashamed, since He even freely assumed this name for Himself, calling Himself by their names, as we mentioned above: “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob; this is my name for ever, and this is my memorial from generation to generation” ([Exod. iii](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Exodus%203&version=VULGATE)).

Therefore, when He says, “And I did not make known to them my name *Adonai*,” this is beautifully understood: “and yet their faith was great.” Conversely, when I shall now make my name *Adonai* known to this people—indeed: “Now thou shalt see what I will do to Pharaoh; for by a strong hand he will let them go, and by a mighty hand he will drive them out of his land” ([Exod. vi](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Exodus%206&version=VULGATE))—their faith will not be great. Rather, they will be rebellious, unbelieving, and a stiff-necked people, so much so that thou also, provoked by them, wilt have to make a distinction with thy lips and speak like a man not of great faith.

For the Lord already knew that Moses, after He had made known His name *Adonai*, would say: “Hear, ye rebellious and unbelieving: shall we draw water for you out of this rock?” The sentence immediately followed: “Because ye did not believe me, so as to sanctify me before the children of Israel, ye shall not bring these peoples into the land which I will give them” ([Num. xx](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Numbers%2020&version=VULGATE)).

I have said these things in order that it may be plainly evident that what He said—“And I did not make known to them my name *Adonai*”—was no diminution of glory or honour for those fathers, but rather a mark of dignity. Rather, theirs was the greater merit: Abraham departed from his land without that manifestation of so great a name and without seeing such mighty operations, whereas these people scarcely believed and followed even after such mighty works had been performed, in order to dwell in the land given them by Him—especially after they had cried to the Lord and had been brought out from the house of slavery, from the prison-house of the Egyptians, from the iron furnace.

Moreover, this also is to be wondered at in a man who had not seen the resurrection of the dead, nor received the working of miracles such as the others received. For, as the Apostle recalls: “By faith Abraham, when he was tested, offered Isaac; and he who had received the promises offered his only-begotten son, to whom it had been said, ‘In Isaac shall thy seed be called’” ([Heb. xi](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Hebrews%2011&version=VULGATE); [Rom. ix](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Romans%209&version=VULGATE); [Gen. xxi](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Genesis%2021&version=VULGATE); [Gal. iii](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Galatians%203&version=VULGATE)); judging that God is able even to raise from the dead. But let us now return to the chapter mentioned above.

## CHAPTER IV

Concerning the fact that the Lord, answering the Sadducees regarding the resurrection of the dead, fittingly recalled these fathers when God said, “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob”; from which He thus argued: “He is not the God of the dead but of the living; for all live to Him.”

“Thus shalt thou say to the children of Israel: ‘The Lord God of our fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, hath sent me to you’” ([Exod. iii](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Exodus%203&version=VULGATE)). Mindful of this passage, the Lord answered the Sadducees who were testing Him and who say that there is no resurrection:

> “Have you not read, concerning the resurrection of the dead, what was spoken by God, who says to you: ‘I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’? He is not the God of the dead but of the living” ([Matt. xxii](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Matthew%2022&version=VULGATE))—“for all live to Him” ([Luke xx](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Luke%2020&version=VULGATE)).

Some are accustomed to doubt concerning this answer, as though it did not adequately establish the resurrection against their sect, or heretical opinion. For they say that even if the dead do not rise again, nevertheless the statement remains true and firm: “He is not the God of the dead but of the living; for all live to Him.” For what then? Do Peter and Paul not live to Him because they have not yet risen? Did they not, while they were in the body, desire to depart from the body ([Phil. i](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Philippians%201&version=VULGATE)) and to be present with God, in order that they might live more truly?

This question would be more difficult to resolve if the Sadducees said only that there is no resurrection of bodies while conceding that the spirit or soul lives after laying aside the body. But they concede neither. Hence the passage in the Acts of the Apostles:

> “But Paul, knowing that one part were Sadducees and the other Pharisees, cried out in the council: ‘Brethren, I am a Pharisee, the son of Pharisees; concerning the hope and resurrection of the dead I am being judged.’ And when he had said this, dissension arose between the Pharisees and Sadducees, and the multitude was divided. For the Sadducees say that there is neither resurrection nor angel; but the Pharisees confess both. Then a great outcry arose, and some Pharisees stood up and cried: ‘We find nothing evil in this man. What if a spirit or an angel has spoken to him?’” ([Acts xxiii](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Acts%2023&version=VULGATE)).

Therefore, because the Sadducees denied the resurrection of bodies in such a way as to believe that souls have no life after bodies, the Lord beautifully and reasonably asserted that there is life after bodies so as at the same time to assert the resurrection of bodies. Once it had been granted—which necessarily had to be granted—that God said, “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (for the Sadducees accepted the Pentateuch), and once this irrefragable proposition had also been assumed, “He is not the God of the dead but of the living,” the conclusion followed that there is a resurrection of the dead. For just as it is unfitting—indeed impious—to call God the God of the dead, so it is equally absurd and impious to call Him the God of the half-living or the God of the half-dead. Yet this follows if bodies do not rise from living souls.

## CHAPTER V

Concerning the chapter of the prophet Hosea: “I have spoken,” says the Lord, “through the prophets, and through the hand of the prophets I was made like unto [something]”; how the Holy Trinity was represented in these fathers: God the Father in Abraham, God the Son in Isaac, and God the Holy Spirit in Jacob’s supplanting.

We cannot sufficiently praise these men, our parents according to faith—Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—to whom the Trinity God gives such great glory that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit deigned to have Their own name designated under their names. This name the world plainly could not yet bear. Truly these three are the prophets of whom the same God spoke especially in Hosea: “And I spoke through the prophets, and I multiplied vision, and in the hand of the prophets I was represented” ([Hos. xii](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Hosea%2012&version=VULGATE)).

We must therefore say, though briefly, how or by what deeds God the Father was represented in the hand of the prophet Abraham, God the Son in the hand of the prophet Isaac, and God the Holy Spirit, cooperating with mother Rebecca, in the hand of the prophet Jacob.

Abraham is interpreted “high father”; Abraham, “father of many”—understood: nations. And who is truly the high Father except “the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies,” as the Apostle says, “and the God of all consolation” ([2 Cor. i](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=2%20Corinthians%201&version=VULGATE))? And who is truly the Father of many nations except this same God, by grace the Father of us all who believe, from whatever nation?

He joined the ancient Church to Himself. For the Church according to faith, from the beginning until the birth of our Lord Jesus Christ according to the flesh, was His spouse; and the faithful virgin bore to Him this Son, conceived of the Holy Spirit, promised long before and awaited for a long time. Was this not like Abraham’s receiving in old age from his barren wife Sarah his long-awaited only-begotten son Isaac? Finally, in Sarah—whose name means “princess”—faith is rightly understood, whose pre-eminence before God is great. In the handmaid Hagar—whose name means “stranger”—is understood the law, which first gave birth in slavery and brought nothing to perfection, until the Son of God was born according to the flesh ([Rom. xiii](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Romans%2013&version=VULGATE)) from the freedom of faith.

Isaac means “laughter”; and what laughter is like the Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God? At the birth of that Isaac, and before his birth at the final promise, both his parents laughed—above all his mother, who, after his birth, said: “God has made laughter for me; whoever hears will laugh with me” ([Gen. xxi](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Genesis%2021&version=VULGATE)). Is this not like the fact that, when the Son of God was born from the Virgin’s womb ([Luke i](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Luke%201&version=VULGATE)), the mother, the heavenly Jerusalem, laughed? For she laughed—that is, she sang, “Glory to God in the highest,” and by singing proclaimed her joy, our joy, great laughter to people of good will.

“God did not spare His own Son, but delivered Him up for us all” ([Rom. viii](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Romans%208&version=VULGATE)); and it is superfluous to prove that He was represented by Isaac in that Abraham, at God’s command, offered his only-begotten son as a burnt offering ([Gen. xxii](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Genesis%2022&version=VULGATE)).

Jacob is interpreted “supplanter.” And who is such a supplanter as the Holy Spirit? For the word “supplanting” is not unfitting for God, especially since it is written in the Psalm: “Arise, O Lord, go before him, and supplant him” ([Ps. xvi](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Psalm%2017&version=VULGATE)). The Jewish people are understood: that it may be taken away from them and given to others—not only that which they possessed in a figurative likeness when they said, “The Romans will come and take away our place and nation” ([John xi](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=John%2011&version=VULGATE)), but also those things which are their chief privileges: “the adoption as sons, the glory, the covenant, the giving of the law, the worship, and the promises” ([Rom. xi](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Romans%2011&version=VULGATE)).

## CHAPTER VI

Again, concerning Rebecca’s counsel, which Jacob accepted to salutary effect; why we rightly understand that the grace of the Holy Spirit was represented in it; and concerning the very good garments with which she clothed him, and the verse of the Psalm: “He chose for us His inheritance, the likeness (*speciem*) of Jacob whom He loved.”

Therefore we rightly understand the Holy Spirit to have been represented in the counsel Rebecca gave to her son Jacob and which he accepted to salutary effect. For Rebecca herself, in that deed, signifies the grace of the Holy Spirit. In her two sons, one of whom, “Esau became,” as Scripture says, “a skilled hunter and a man of the field; but Jacob was a simple man, dwelling in tents. Isaac loved Esau because he ate of his hunting; but Rebecca loved Jacob” ([Gen. xxv](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Genesis%2025&version=VULGATE)), the Apostle found a true example or proof for his words to Timothy:

> “Exercise thyself unto godliness; for bodily exercise is useful for a little, but godliness is useful for all things, holding promise of the life which now is and of that which is to come” ([1 Tim. vi](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=1%20Timothy%206&version=VULGATE)).

For Esau exercised himself by bodily exercise, and this was useful to him only for a little, so that finally, weeping with a great outcry, Isaac said to him: “In the fatness of the earth and in the dew of heaven from above shall thy blessing be” ([Gen. xxvii](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Genesis%2027&version=VULGATE)). By these words he received, indeed, a promise of the life which now is alone.

But godliness, in which Jacob exercised himself, was useful for all things. It held the promise of the present life in these words: “May God give thee of the dew of heaven and of the fatness of the earth an abundance of grain, wine, and oil.” But it held the promise of the future life in what follows: “May peoples serve thee and tribes bow down before thee. Be lord of thy brothers, and may the sons of thy mother bow down before thee. Whoever curses thee, let him be cursed; and whoever blesses thee, may he be filled with blessings.” For by such a blessing Christ, who is eternal life, was promised to be born of his seed.

What, or what kind of, was that counsel of Rebecca with Jacob, in which, as we said above, the Holy Spirit was represented? “Now therefore, my son, obey my counsels,” etc., as far as: “And she clothed him in the very good garments of Esau which she had with her at home” (ibid.). Those very good garments were priestly garments. Scripture called them Esau’s garments because he was the firstborn, but Rebecca knew that he was not worthy of such an office.

According to the mystery, the garments with which the worthy son ought to be blessed are those charisms of the Holy Spirit which we mentioned earlier from the Epistle of the Apostle Paul: the word of wisdom, the word of knowledge, faith, gifts of healings, workings of miracles, prophecy, discernment of spirits, kinds of languages, and interpretation of utterances ([1 Cor. ii](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=1%20Corinthians%202&version=VULGATE)). Garments of this kind the grace of the Holy Spirit had and has at home, according to the likeness of Rebecca. How at home? Certainly in the power of giving or distributing them, as the same Apostle immediately says: “But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each one as He wills” ([1 Cor. xii](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=1%20Corinthians%2012&version=VULGATE)).

At first He distributed these charisms, as He willed, to the election of that Israelite people; then, however, after an exchange had taken place according to the likeness of those twins, He distributed them to the election of the nations, as is written in the Psalms: “He chose for us His inheritance, the likeness (*speciem*) of Jacob whom He loved” ([Ps. xlvi](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Psalm%2047&version=VULGATE)). In saying this, he sends us back to our history. For just as Esau, the elder in birth, was rejected by God and Jacob was loved, so the Israelite people, formerly acceptable to God in a certain familiarity, was afterward rejected; while the nations, who initially had no knowledge of Him, deserved or received His blessings. This is what “the likeness (*speciem*) of Jacob” means: according to the likeness of Jacob whom He loved. “But Esau,” He Himself says in Malachi, “I hated” ([Mal. i](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Malachi%201&version=VULGATE)).

## CHAPTER VII

Concerning the charisms of the Holy Spirit, prefigured by those good garments; the mystical dimness of Isaac’s eyes when he blessed; and Moses’ saying: “Either forgive them this offence, or blot me out of Thy book which Thou hast written.”

Clothed in those very good garments, Jacob entered, by his mother Rebecca’s counsel, to his father Isaac, who could no longer see, in order to receive the blessing. Nor would he have possessed the blessing by inheritance because of those garments unless he had also entered to the father, as has now been said, who could not see, and received from his mouth the words of blessing.

Similarly, equipped with the aforesaid charisms of the Holy Spirit, every simple man dwelling in tents, every faithful man having hope in the word of promise—of whom one of the best was Moses, who wrote this very mystical Scripture—entered through faith, by which all things are present, unto Christ the Son of God as though unable to see: that is, dying on the cross. There the royal lights, lights intimating laughter and joy according to the name Isaac to those who love Him, were darkened by the gloom of death, in order that he might receive forgiveness of sins. For no one could have received that blessing, namely forgiveness of sins, through those charisms unless this our Isaac, His eyes closed in death, had already given it.

Knowing this, Moses, most faithful in all His house, spoke thus: “Either forgive them this offence, or, if Thou dost not, blot me out of Thy book which Thou hast written” ([Num. xii](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Numbers%2012&version=VULGATE)). Again: “Thou commandest me to lead out this people, and Thou dost not tell me whom Thou wilt send with me” ([Exod. xxxii](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Exodus%2032&version=VULGATE)), especially when Thou hast said: “I know thee by name, and thou hast found favour before me.” And afterward: “Unless Thou Thyself go before us, do not lead us out from this place” ([Exod. xxxiii](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Exodus%2033&version=VULGATE)).

Concerning this chapter, to speak in the Apostle’s words, “we have much to say and difficult to explain, because,” as he says, “you have become weak in hearing” ([Heb. v](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Hebrews%205&version=VULGATE)). For very many even today are little children because they have not yet known, with that knowledge which belongs to the perfect, the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Let us therefore question Moses, the most faithful one. What is this statement which thou hast spoken: “Either forgive them this offence, or blot me out of Thy book which Thou hast written”? When you have asked this, suppose that he replies to you in words such as these: in the words of a man of the same faith, the words of faithful David: “I am afflicted and greatly humbled; I roared because of the groaning of my heart.” Then, immediately turning to the Lord: “Lord,” he says, “all my desire is before Thee, and my groaning is not hidden from Thee” ([Ps. xxxvii](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Psalm%2038&version=VULGATE)).

This saying suitably belongs not to David alone but to all the saints. For the desire of all was one groaning desire: that Christ should be born, that the Saviour, the Son of God, should come, to give the blessing, to give the Holy Spirit in the forgiveness of sins. This was that desire. Hence Jacob himself says to his son Joseph: “The blessings of thy father have been strengthened by the blessings of his fathers, until the desire of the everlasting hills should come” ([Gen. xlix](https://biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Genesis%2049&version=VULGATE)).

Therefore Moses, roaring from the groaning of his heart according to this desire, said: “Either forgive them this offence, or blot me out of Thy book which Thou hast written.” What does this mean? If Thou dost not forgive them, if because of their sin Thou cease to fulfil Thy promise, so that, once they have been destroyed, the seed Thou didst promise to Abraham does not come, it is one and the same thing as if Thou blottest me out—and clearly it follows that Thou blottest me out of Thy book which Thou hast written. For unless He comes, no one can be saved. Therefore: “Unless Thou Thyself go before us, do not lead us out from this place.” For what purpose is it for us to enter any land, unless from that people there be born, according to Thy promise, One who may lead us into eternal life?

## CHAPTER VIII

Again, concerning the charisms of the Holy Spirit; that the blessing by which our Isaac blessed us is the grace of the Holy Spirit proceeding from Him; and, against the Monothelites, concerning that wonderful mystery by which Isaac blessed not the one whom he himself wished, but the one whom mother Rebecca wished to be blessed.

Of all the charisms mentioned above, the best is fragrant faith; and it has especially aided and especially advanced all those whom the Holy Spirit, according to the comparison already made, has deigned to clothe in Rebecca’s gifts, as though in very fine garments [Col. 0104B]. Scripture commends this faith in such a way as to say: “And as soon as he perceived the fragrance of his garments, he blessed him and said: Behold, the smell of my son is like the smell of a field full of blessing, which the Lord has blessed” (Gen. XXVII). The mystery—that is, the sacrament—of faith is more pleasing, because among all the charisms of the Holy Spirit it is faith that is accustomed to make us more fragrant to our holy Isaac, the Son of God, so that He cannot contain His tender feelings but pours forth the abundance of so great and so necessary a blessing, so great a grace of the Holy Spirit: namely, the forgiveness of sins, which proceeds from Him.47

And it came about through a wonderful mystery that he did not bless the one whom he himself wished, but the one whom Rebecca his mother preferred to be blessed. Was there not in this a mystery of evangelical, or catholic, truth [Col. 0104C]? For in the one and same Lord Jesus Christ, just as we proclaim two natures or substances, so also we proclaim two wills and two operations: one of divinity, the other of humanity. Such is the meaning required by faith, and there are many proofs in the words of our Lord Himself.

For example, when according to the will of human weakness He had said, “Now my soul is troubled; and what shall I say? Father, save me from this hour,” immediately, countering Himself according to the will of His divinity, He said: “But for this cause I came unto this hour”—that I might not be saved from it, but suffer death. “Father, glorify Thy name” (John XII).

Likewise, according to the will of His humanity, when He saw the city He wept over it; for He would have wished it to be saved. Hence He said: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, [Col. 0104D] how often would I have gathered thy children together, as a hen gathers her chicks beneath her wings, and thou wouldst not” (Matt. XXIII). But according to the will of His divinity, having made a scourge of cords, He drove all from the Temple; and by His words He also made plain what He signified by the deed: “Amen, I say unto you,” He said, “the kingdom of God shall be taken from you and given to a nation yielding its fruits” (Matt. XXI).

Much could be said here against the error of Eutyches or the heresy of the Monothelites. But since we are bound by our subject, let it suffice to recall the two wills or operations in Christ; and, following the comparison with Isaac, because he blessed not the one whom he wished but the one whom he did not wish, let us continue what we began.

## CHAPTER IX. [Col. 0105A]

On the operation of miracles, which is great among the charisms of the Holy Spirit; on the saying, “There arose not a prophet thereafter in Israel whom the Lord knew face to face”; and on the fact that working miracles meant making known the name Adonai.

Above we began to speak of the operation of miracles, which is a great grace among the divisions of the graces of the Holy Spirit, while remembering at the same time that saying: “I am the Lord who appeared to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as God Almighty; but by my name Adonai I did not make myself known to them” (Exod. VI).

After what we have already said on this matter, it remains to say that Moses is deservedly held great on account of this grace, so that Scripture says of him: “There arose not thereafter in [Col. 0105B] Israel a prophet like Moses, whom the Lord knew face to face.” For it continues: “In all the signs and wonders which He sent by him to perform in the land of Egypt against Pharaoh and all his servants and all his land, and in all the mighty hand and the great marvels which Moses performed in the sight of all Israel” (Deut. XXXIV).

Therefore this statement must be understood in reference to this grace—namely, the operation of miracles—and not to the entire grace of the Holy Spirit: “There arose not thereafter in Israel a prophet like Moses.” Otherwise it would seem to conflict with the sentence which the Lord pronounced concerning another: “Amen, I say unto you, among those born of women there has not arisen one greater than John the Baptist” (Matt. XI).

It should therefore be observed that Scripture does not say, “There arose not thereafter a prophet as great as Moses,” but “like Moses”; and it specifies also the quality or mode in which he arose, by saying, “in all signs and wonders.” For truly, in this respect neither John himself nor anyone else arose like Moses. Of John, indeed, it is written in the Gospel: “Many came to Jesus and said: John indeed performed no sign; but all that John said of this man was true” (John X).

Perhaps someone asks: What do you make of the great prophet, our Lord Jesus Christ? Did not at least that prophet arise in Israel like Moses? Did not Moses himself speak and write concerning Him: “The Lord thy God will raise up for thee a prophet from thy nation and from thy brethren, like me” [Col. 0105D] (Deut. XVIII)?

To this I say: certainly, if greatness is in question, as He is truly greater than Jonah and greater than Solomon, so He is also greater than Moses (Matt. XII). Yet, in the judgment of inquisitive people, He was not here “like Moses.” Thus, when He performed many wonders, even when He had satisfied many thousands with a few loaves, and said to them, “This is the work of God: that you believe in Him whom He has sent,” they said to Him: “What sign, then, dost Thou perform, that we may see and believe Thee? What work dost Thou do? Our fathers ate manna in the wilderness” (John VI).

In short, whatever He had done or wished to do, He would not have been to them like Moses unless He fed their curious eyes with miracles of this kind and continually filled their idle bellies with food. [Col. 0106A] Therefore, when Moses said, “The Lord thy God will raise up for thee a prophet from thy nation and from thy brethren, like me,” this is rightly understood as said of the truth of human nature. For the Son of God was to become—and indeed did become—like Moses in this respect: that is, a true human being, as is written in Job, and as we recalled much earlier: “If there be for him an angel, one speaking among a thousand” (Job XXXIII).

But in all other respects He is far greater than Moses. And to complete our begun discourse on the charisms of the Holy Spirit: according to every operation or ministration of that same Holy Spirit, He performed many good things, except that He did not personally exercise the varieties of tongues—a grace of the Holy Spirit which He afterward gave to His apostles—and, moreover, He alone effected the forgiveness of sins through the same Holy Spirit. [Col. 0106B]

## CHAPTER X.

Again, on that grace of the Holy Spirit which is the operation of miracles: how the magicians before Pharaoh imitated it, and, being unable to withstand it, said, “This is the finger of God.”

The spirit of falsehood imitates, even now, the illustrious grace of the Holy Spirit—namely, the operation of miracles—in which Moses was truly great; just as it then imitated it before Pharaoh as far as it could. As it is written: “When he cast down the rod and it was changed into a serpent”; and again: “When he struck the water of the river with the rod and it was changed into blood”; and: “When for the third time he stretched out his [Col. 0106C] hand over the waters of Egypt, and frogs came up and covered the land, the magicians did likewise by their enchantments.” But this was deception in appearance, because it was not reality in experience.

When it came to gnats—when the dust of the earth had been struck so that gnats came upon both people and beasts, troublesome not merely to the sight but painfully biting to the touch—the magicians could not stand, and said: “This is the finger of God” (Exod. VII–VIII).

We wonder how men of this sort knew to call this efficacy of the Holy Spirit, namely the operation of miracles, “the finger of God”; just as we also wonder how Nebuchadnezzar knew to name the Son of God. For he said: “Behold, I see four men loosed and walking in the midst of the fire, and the appearance [Col. 0106D] of the fourth is like the Son of God” (Dan. III).

As there the spirit of falsehood imitated, through the activity of those men, this power of the finger of God—that is, the operation of miracles—so it will especially imitate it in that lawless one “whose coming,” says the Apostle, “is according to the working of Satan, in all power and signs and lying wonders, and in every deception of iniquity for those who perish, because they did not receive the love of truth so that they might be saved. Therefore God will send them a working of error, so that they may believe the lie, and all may be judged who did not believe the truth but consented to iniquity” (II Thess. II).48

For unless they had been like that Pharaoh, and, to use the words of the same Apostle, unless they had “held down the truth of God in unrighteousness, because what is known of God is manifest among them” [Col. 0107A] (Rom. I)—unless, I say, they had purposed to enter houses and lead captive little women, that is, wretched souls burdened with sins, after the likeness of that Pharaoh, whose purpose was not to know the Lord and not to let Israel go—the Lord would not send, nor permit to come to them, a spirit of falsehood: lying people resisting the finger of God and, so far as they can, opposing the Holy Spirit.

They are rather like those of whom he immediately says: “But as Jannes and Mambres resisted Moses, so these also resist the truth” (Tim. III). And what finally? “Their folly,” he says, “will become manifest to all, as theirs also did.”

## CHAPTER XI. [Col. 0107B]

On the threefold blessing of the name of the Lord, which, after the Tabernacle had been completed, the Lord commanded Moses to pronounce, saying, “Thus shall you bless the children of Israel”; and on His saying, “They shall invoke My name upon the children of Israel, and I will bless them.”

After Israel’s departure from Egypt, when the Tabernacle had been completed and the law of ceremonies prescribed: “The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to Aaron and his sons: Thus shall you bless the children of Israel, and you shall say to them: May the Lord bless thee and keep thee; may the Lord show His face to thee and have mercy on thee; may the Lord turn His countenance toward thee and give thee peace. They shall invoke My name upon the children of Israel, and I will bless them” (Num. VI).

Here also Moses hides his face and has a veil placed [Col. 0107C] over it; but, as the Apostle says, “in Christ that same veil is taken away” (II Cor. III). How is it taken away in Christ Himself? “Go,” He says, “teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII).

What is it to baptize the nations after instruction has gone before, except to bless the children of Israel? For from whatever people or nation they come, those who believe in Christ are, precisely because they believe, themselves children of Israel, just as they are children of Abraham.

Therefore, the name of the Lord repeated here three times in the formula of blessing is, for the unbelieving Jew, partly veiled, because it is not distinguished or expressed in this manner: “May the Lord the Father bless thee; may the Lord the Son show thee His face; may the Lord the Holy Spirit turn His countenance toward thee.” For “the children of Israel could not gaze upon the face of Moses” [Col. 0107D] (Exod.
