XXXIV), so expressly manifested was the glory of his countenance. But, as has already been said, it is revealed in Christ (II Cor. III).

The sons of Aaron the high priest are the apostles and priests of the great High Priest, “Jesus Christ, who has passed through the heavens” (Heb. IV). It belongs to them to bless under the threefold name of the Lord—that is, to baptize in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit—yet in such a way that they know themselves to be not the givers but the ministers of the blessing. This is what He immediately says: “They shall invoke My name upon the children of Israel, and I will bless them.”

Accordingly the provident Apostle, writing to the Corinthians, says: “Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?” [Col. 0108A] (I Cor. I). Again: “When one says, ‘I am of Paul,’ another, ‘I am of Apollos,’ and another, ‘I am of Cephas,’ are you not human beings? What then is Apollos? What is Paul? Ministers through whom you believed, each as the Lord gave. I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the increase. Therefore neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but God who gives the increase” (I Cor. III).

Surely this is the meaning demanded by the authority of truth which says: “They shall invoke My name upon the children of Israel, and I will bless them.”

## CHAPTER XII.

On the blessing with which Jacob blessed his son Joseph under the threefold invocation of the holy name: “God, in whose sight my fathers walked; God, who has fed me from my youth; the angel who delivered me from [Col. 0108B] all evils”; and on the fact that this angel is the person of the Son.

A certain part of this field has almost escaped me and been left behind, in which, as we have often said, this hidden treasure lies concealed: that is, this most holy Scripture, in which we continue to proclaim that the mystery of the Holy Trinity both shines forth wonderfully and remains hidden. We rejoice exceedingly at finding it, saying with the Psalmist: “I will rejoice over Thy words as one who finds great spoil” (Ps. CXVIII).

When Israel the father was ill in Egypt, and Joseph, having heard this, went to him with his two sons Manasseh and Ephraim, it is afterward written: “And he blessed Joseph’s son and said: God, in whose sight my fathers Abraham and Isaac walked; God, who has fed me from my youth [Col. 0108C] to this present day; the angel who delivered me from all evils, bless these boys” (Gen. XLVIII).

Beginning thus, he first blessed Joseph’s two sons, and then his own twelve sons, each with particular blessings. Once he said, “God, in whose sight my fathers walked”; a second time, “God, who has fed me from my youth”; but a third time, “the angel who delivered me from all evils.”

And who is that angel who delivered him from all evils, except the angel of great counsel, God the Son of God? (Isa. IX). Do not doubt that the person signified by the name of the angel “who,” he says, “delivered me from all evils,” is this person. That person, I say, appeared to him at the beginning of all his evils, when he was fleeing from his brother Esau, who said: “The days of mourning for my father will come, and I shall kill my brother Jacob” [Col. 0108D] (Gen. XXVII).

How did He appear to him? Or by what indications can it be recognized that the person who appeared to him was the Son of God? Scripture says: “When he came to a certain place and wished to rest there after sunset, he took some of the stones lying there, put one beneath his head, and slept in that place. And he saw in a dream a ladder standing upon the earth, with angels of God ascending and descending by it, and the Lord leaning upon the ladder and saying to him: I am the Lord God of Abraham thy father and the God of Isaac,” and so forth, down to: “And I will be thy guardian wherever thou goest” (Gen. XXVIII).

Indeed, there is here a great sacrament of the Son of God, if you rightly recognize the ladder and rightly consider what it means that the Lord [Col. 0109A] was leaning upon the ladder. For, without prejudice to the moral interpretation—by which we may say that the ladder is the progress of our life, its two sides our body and soul, and its rungs the ascents of diverse virtues—without prejudice, I say, to that moral interpretation, the generation of our Lord Jesus Christ must be understood through that ladder. Its two sides, as it were, are the two great patriarchs, as the Evangelist writes: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, Son of David, Son of Abraham” (Matt. I).

To these fathers God promised on oath that the same Christ would be born from their seed (Gen. XLIII [probably XXXII or similar reference uncertain]). How was the Lord leaning upon the highest rung of the ladder? Surely in this way: that, as an orphan—that is, born in this world without a father according to the flesh—He needed Joseph as an adoptive and foster father. Therefore, “the angel who delivered me,” says Jacob, “from all evils,” is God the Son of God; and consequently, because he prayed in this manner, naming God three times, it is plain that he invoked the Holy Trinity. [Col. 0109B]

## CHAPTER XIII.

That in those blessings of the ancients the relative names—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—had to be kept silent; that speech had to be closed, so that they might not bless as openly as we now bless or baptize in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and on what is written in Isaiah: “The vision of all things has become to you like the words of a sealed book.”

Therefore, when we are baptized or blessed in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, this is not a recent practice. For in much the same manner people were blessed in ancient times too, under the Law and even before the Law, except that, because the time required it, the relative names—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—were kept silent.

For speech had to be closed—indeed, sealed. Certain of them, namely the prophets, testify that they were commanded to do this. After Isaiah had spoken of this name—“The Seraphim cried one to another and said: Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts” (Isa. VI)—and then had said much about the name of Emmanuel who was to be born and about His appellation, “Hasten to take the spoil; make speed to seize the prey,” he writes that near the end of the vision he was commanded: “Bind up the testimony; seal the law among my disciples” [Col. 0109C] (Isa. VIII).

Daniel also, after many and very great visions, writes that he was commanded: “But thou, Daniel, close up the words and seal the book until the appointed time.” And again: “Go, Daniel, for the words are closed and sealed until the time appointed” (Dan. XII). And as though Daniel asked why these things were written if they had to be closed and sealed, it was said to him: “Many shall pass through, and knowledge shall be multiplied” (Matt. VII [citation as printed]).

Was this communicated only to these men, and not also to Moses and all the prophets: that it was expedient for them to speak under closure and seal? For Isaiah speaks, both for himself and for all, because of—or against—those who would not honor the words of heavenly sacraments as pearls, but would instead trample them underfoot: [Col. 0110A] “The vision of all things shall be unto you like the words of a sealed book, which, when they give it to one who knows letters, they say, ‘Read this’; and he will answer, ‘I cannot, for it is sealed,’” and so forth, down to: “The wisdom of its wise men shall perish, and the understanding of its prudent men shall be hidden” (Isa. XXIX).

Moses, therefore, having thus far spoken of the mystery of the Holy Trinity, rightly and fittingly closed his discourse, merely suppressing, as has been said, the relative names Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Nor did he merely close it: he also sealed it. How did he seal it?

## CHAPTER XIV.

On the saying, “Hear, O Israel: the Lord thy God is one God”; on the three things immediately added, “Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy strength”; and on love being threefold and one—not three loves, but one love.

“Hear,” he says, “O Israel: the Lord thy God is one God” (Deut. VI). Is not this saying like the seal of a closed book to one who knows letters—namely, to the Jew who professes to know the Law and the Prophets?

For when you set before him this book so that he may read this plural-sounding passage, “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. I), and ask him to notice the distinction of three persons in the words which immediately follow—“And God created man in His own image; in the image of God He created him; male and female He created them, and blessed them” [Col. 0110C] (ibid.)—when, I say, you offer him these and other passages, some of which we have already examined, to read or understand, he says to you: “I cannot read the book in this way, for it is sealed, having this seal: ‘Hear, O Israel: the Lord thy God is one God.’ But you want me to read of three gods; this statement forbids me to do so.”

When he says this, the book is sealed—sealed indeed. He speaks truly in part, because for him it is thus closed and sealed. Yet he is without excuse. For he has not seen, or has not wished to see, the Lamb whom John saw and whom we too have seen by the same faith, opening the book and unsealing its seals. That Lamb has made intelligible to believers alone, as He has the other sacraments, this also: that there are three persons and nevertheless one God.

This the true Israel heard, and always hears: that there is no God outside God; the Son is not outside the Father, nor the Father outside the Son. “I and the Father are one” [Col. 0110D] (John X), says the Son; “I am in the Father and the Father is in me” (John XIV); and “the Holy Spirit, whom the Son sends and who proceeds from the Father” (John XV), does not proceed anywhere outside the Father and the Son. For this one substance of the Trinity is not circumscribed or localized, nor does any other accident attach to that substance so that it may be changed from itself, as a human being is changed from himself: for example, once an infant, now a child or youth; formerly an old man, now a decrepit man of extreme age.

Someone asks: Whence is an example by which God’s Trinity in persons and unity in substance may be understood? To this I say: surely from what Moses immediately added beneath the veil of his face. For after saying, “Hear, O Israel: the Lord thy God is one God,” he immediately says: “Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy strength” [Col. 0111A] (Deut. VI).

This wording, indeed, according to the Septuagint interpreters, has four elements, as do many passages of Scripture that vary; the translation of these passages the apostles and evangelists sometimes adopted as the circumstances required, as blessed Jerome testifies. And for this reason I think the Evangelist Luke records these four: “Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy strength, and with all thy mind” (Luke X).

But according to the Hebrew truth there are only these three: “Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy strength.” Therefore take from this your example, O lover of the Trinity, worshipper and lover of the one God. Is not love “with all thy heart,” love “with all thy soul,” and love [Col. 0111B] “with all thy strength” a love that is threefold and one? So thy God, O Israel, is three in persons and one in substance. As there are not three loves but one, so there are not three gods but one.

## CHAPTER XV.

That there are three operations of the one love, which Moses immediately arranged in order; that the first operation, corresponding to what he had said, “Thou shalt love with all thy heart,” begins thus, “These words shall be in thy heart”; and that this operation is the contemplative life.

Let us follow this text and attend more closely, in the present passage, to the glorious face of Moses. For immediately after he said, “Hear, O Israel: the Lord thy God is one God,” he added what we have already cited: “Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy strength.” Thus he wished the three persons of the one God to be understood as there are three operations of the one love.

Let us follow on, then, for here truly is the joy of faith, like a person’s joy at finding hidden treasure. For he immediately arranged in order each operation of the threefold love, so that you may understand that he did not vainly invite Israel to hear that the Lord thy God is one God.

This, then, is the first operation of love which follows, corresponding to what he had said: “Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart. These words which I command thee this day shall be [Col. 0111C] in thy heart; and thou shalt tell them to thy children, and thou shalt meditate upon them while sitting in thy house and walking on the way, sleeping and rising; and thou shalt bind them as a sign upon thy hand, and they shall be and move before thine eyes; and thou shalt write them upon the threshold and doors of thy house,” and so forth, down to: “Take great care lest thou forget the Lord, who brought thee out of the land of Egypt, from the house of bondage” (Deut. VI).

Does not the radiant face of Moses in these words indicate that operation of love which the Israel of God is accustomed to call the contemplative life? For there is fulfilled in it what was said here: “Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart,” while the words of God are in his heart, while he meditates upon them and recounts them to his spiritual children; while he is not anxious and troubled about many things (Luke X), but is “sitting in his house” and “walking on the way”—that is, rejoicing in the hiddenness of his conscience and advancing from virtue to virtue [Col. 0112A] (Ps. LXXXV); while, with a right intention, he sleeps that sleep of which the soul that had sought rest in all things says in the Song of Songs: “I sleep, but my heart watches” (Song V), and of which Christ says in the Gospel: “Mary has chosen the better part, which shall not be taken away from her” (Luke X).

If at any time the beloved Lord God, whom he thus loves with all his heart, gives His voice and knocks at the sleeper’s door, saying, “Open to me, my sister, my friend, my dove, my undefiled one” (Song V), and she rises to open to Him—that is, to teach some persons by preaching, so that He may enter through faith and be in them—then her hands also drip with myrrh, and her fingers are full of the choicest myrrh.

This, surely, is to do what was said: “Sleeping and rising, thou shalt meditate upon them, and thou shalt bind them as a sign upon thy hand” (Deut. VI): that is, thou shalt offer examples of right living, while thy good works firmly adhere to good words. If this Israel, exercised by long and constant meditation, should progress so far that he can treat and expound the divine words not only by reading and speaking but also by writing, for the benefit of the Church entrusted to him, this indeed is to do what follows: “They shall be and move before thine eyes, and thou shalt write them upon the threshold and doors of thy house.” [Col. 0112C]

To this operation of love, to this contemplative life, honorable support is due from royal houses and from the territories of nations, so that it may be free to keep a festival day and hold sacred leisure. Then especially those in this profession must labor, lest they forget—or rather, so that they may diligently keep—their purpose.

This is what is immediately said to this Israel: “When the Lord thy God shall bring thee into the land for which He swore to thy fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and shall give thee great and excellent cities which thou didst not build, houses full of every good thing which thou didst not construct, cisterns which thou didst not dig, vineyards and olive-groves which thou didst not plant, and thou shalt eat and be filled, take great care lest thou forget the Lord who brought thee out of the land of Egypt, from the house of bondage” [Col. 0112D] (ibid.).

For beneath the veil of the letter there is a mystical meaning. When thou hast entered by faith into the land of the living, to which the first entrance is the sacred understanding of the Scriptures, and God has therefore given thee the regions of the nations, and thou hast possessed the labors of peoples, so that thou mayest keep His statutes and seek His law (Ps. CIV), beware lest thou be ungrateful. Beware, I say, lest with the resources of righteousness which God has given thee, thou shouldst wish to serve in sin’s army.

## CHAPTER XVI. [Col. 0113A]

The second operation of love, corresponding to what he had said, “and with all thy soul,” is the active life, which he begins to set forth thus: “Thou shalt fear the Lord thy God, and shalt serve Him alone, and shalt swear by His name.”

Immediately follows the second operation of love, corresponding to what he had said: “And with all thy soul: thou shalt fear the Lord thy God, and shalt serve Him alone, and shalt swear by His name. You shall not go after the strange gods of all the nations which are round about you, because the Lord thy God is a jealous God in the midst of thee, lest at any time the anger of the Lord thy God be kindled against thee and remove thee from the face of the earth,” and so forth, down to: “And the Lord our God commanded us to do all these ordinances and to fear the Lord our God, that it might be well with us all the days of our life, as it is today” [Col. 0113B] (Deut. VI).

Does not the radiant face of Moses in these words, as was said above, indicate that operation of love which the Israel of God is accustomed to call the active life? For in it is fulfilled what was said: “Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy soul,” while it “does not go after the strange gods of all nations,” which is the sin of adulterous souls; but fears the Lord its God as its sole and lawful husband, and serves Him alone with free service.

For its fear is not the penal fear which perfect love, as the Apostle John says (I John IV), casts out; rather, it is a religious and reverent fear, “a holy fear,” as the Psalmist sings, “enduring for ever and ever” (Ps. XVIII). Accordingly, when he now says, “Thou shalt fear the Lord thy God,” you rightly take it as a repetition of the earlier saying, “Thou shalt love the Lord thy God.”

For just as in the saying, “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. CX), fear is not separated from wisdom but joined to wisdom as the beginning is joined to the completion of every thing, so also when, after saying, “Thou shalt love the Lord thy God,” he adds, “Thou shalt fear the Lord thy God,” his discourse does not depart from love but lays down the beginning or foundation of love.

In another respect, even for a true soul loving God as her husband, it is useful to fear the penalty or punishment of adultery. For after saying, “You shall not go after strange gods,” he immediately adds: [Col. 0113D] “Because the Lord thy God is a jealous God in the midst of thee, lest at any time the anger of the Lord thy God be kindled against thee and remove thee from the face of the earth.”

What follows—“Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God, as thou didst tempt Him in the place of temptation”; and then, “When thy son asks thee tomorrow, saying, ‘What do these testimonies, ceremonies, and judgments, which the Lord our God commanded us, mean?’ thou shalt say to him, ‘We were Pharaoh’s servants in Egypt, and the Lord led us out of Egypt by a mighty hand’” (Deut. VI)—these things, I say, and those following are fitting instruments of a loving soul, as of a chaste mistress of a household. Such a soul should not display curiosity and wandering eyes, but modesty and reverence toward her untemptable husband, carefulness in guarding her household, and the discipline of chastity in raising her children.

This operation of love is second in dignity but first in order, exercising the active life; whereas the operation above mentioned is first in dignity but second in order, constituting the contemplative life. For we do not descend to the active life after the profession of the contemplative, but ascend to the contemplative after the practice of the active.

Mercy is owed to this operation when it exceeds its measure, because it is anxious [Col. 0114A] (Luke X) and troubled about many things; for, drawn out through the five bodily senses, it labors. Mercy is owed to it precisely because, diligently engaged in frequent ministry, it fed the hungry, gave drink to the thirsty, received the stranger, clothed the naked, visited the sick, and came to the one in prison (Matt. XXV).

Thus, beautifully making known her hope to her children, she says at the end of her discourse: “The Lord our God will remember us mercifully, if we keep and do all His commandments as He commanded us” (Deut. VI). [Col. 0114B]

## CHAPTER XVII.

The third operation of love, corresponding to what he had said, “and with all thy strength,” is to overthrow altars and break statues. This operation is the crown of martyrs, though in a different manner, because they did not fight with a material sword.

[Col. 0114C] There follows the third operation of love, corresponding to what he had said: “And with all your strength.” — “When,” he says, “the Lord your God has brought you into the land which you are entering to possess, and has delivered many nations over to you, you shall strike them down unto utter destruction. You shall make no covenant with them, nor spare them, nor contract marriages with them. Rather, you shall do this to them: overthrow their altars, break their statues, cut down their sacred groves, and burn their carved images, because you are a holy people to the Lord your God,” and so on, down to: “And the Lord your God shall give them into your sight, and shall slay them until they are utterly destroyed. He shall deliver their kings into your hands, and you shall destroy their names from under heaven; no one shall be able to withstand you until you crush them. You shall burn their carved images [Col. 0114D] with fire. You shall not covet the gold and silver of which they are made, nor take anything from them for yourself, lest you stumble; for it is an abomination to the Lord your God. Nor shall you bring anything from an idol into your house, lest you become accursed, as it too is” (Deut. 7).

Does not the radiant countenance of Moses, in these words, direct attention to that operation of love in which, with all their strength, both the ancient saints before Christ’s coming—namely, the illustrious judges, glorious kings, splendid prophets, among whom Elijah was especially renowned in this contest, and the memorable Maccabees—and, after Christ’s coming, the holy apostles and so many glorious martyrs, fought? For all these, loving their Lord God “with all their heart and with all their soul,” [Col. 0115A] and likewise “with all their strength,” did these things: they overthrew the altars of the nations, broke their statues, cut down their sacred groves, and burned their carved images. And, as is there said among other matters—which it would take far too long to set down here in full—“you shall devour all the peoples whom the Lord your God is to give you,” they devoured many peoples throughout the world, being sent to devour, though with a different kind of devouring. For the ancient saints devoured with the mouth of the material sword; the new saints devoured with the mouth of the spiritual sword. Indeed, the ordering of that age was one thing and that of this age another—a distinction between the two ages, according to the reasons for suffering and acting, which we treated more fully in the work we wrote *On the Victory of the Word of God*.

To this [Col. 0115B] operation, together with the crown of righteousness, belongs also the tribunal of judgment and the authority to judge, as it is written: “The saints shall judge nations and rule peoples” (Wis. 3). Fittingly, therefore, he concluded these words with such an ending: “You shall detest it as filth, and regard it as defilement and uncleanness, as an abomination, because it is accursed” (Deut. 7). What is this, if not as though he said: “You shall judge, or condemn”? This they indeed do now in part, where they themselves seem to be condemned and many to have been put to death; but universally they shall do it on the Day of Judgment, visibly appearing as judges over every filthiness, every defilement, and every abominable uncleanness, so that they may cast them into an unclean place, into the depth of hell.

## CHAPTER XVIII

That, by the likeness of these three operations of the one love, we ought to be aided in understanding that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are three persons and one God.

Here, I think, we have a striking image by which we may contemplate and know in part the inscrutable splendor of the eternal sun. For behold: there are three operations of love, yet not three loves, but one love. And behold: there are three breathings of a human being—soul and heart, and the strength of both—yet not three spirits of one human being, but one spirit. Thus, O Israel, there are three persons of your God: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; yet there are not three gods, but one God.

Does not the soul do one thing, and the heart or human mind another? The soul indeed gives life to the whole [Col. 0115D] body and administers all the body’s functions through the five senses; but the heart or mind is in the presence of the soul, walks with it, and prescribes to it all that it should usefully do. Thus, in some manner, God the Father, living in himself, is eternal life; while his Son, or Word, is in him and was in him, providing that he should make all things very good. Hence the Word himself, Wisdom herself, says: “When he prepared the heavens, I was present; when by a fixed law and circle he enclosed the abysses; when he strengthened the upper air and weighed the springs of waters; when he set its boundary about the sea and imposed a law upon the waters that they should not pass their bounds; when he suspended the foundations of the earth, I was with him, ordering all things” (Prov. 8).

[Col. 0116A] Almost in this way might the heart or mind of the architect who built this basilica or that fortress speak of his soul: “When it forethought the measurements of this building’s length, breadth, and height; when by a fixed law of numbers it distinguished its columns and the spaces between columns, or its towers and the spaces between towers; when it chose the squared stones, or stones to be squared, which it would place in the foundation, I was with it, ordering all things.” For it could not otherwise have thought these things beforehand, unless the heart or mind had been with it—that is, unless it were a rational or skilful soul.

But why say more? “Remember,” says someone, “that you do not know his work, of which men have sung. All human beings see him, and each beholds him from afar. Behold, God is great, surpassing our knowledge; the number of his years is beyond estimation” (Job 36). If man does not know his work—that is, himself, for he was made in God’s image and therefore is called, as it were, God’s own work—how much more does he not know God himself? For men did not sing him himself, but sang about him: namely, this Moses and the other saints who possessed the greatest knowledge of God. Thus one of them says: “Who has seen him and described him? Who has magnified him as he has been from the beginning?” (Ecclus. 43). All see from afar; each beholds from afar—from afar, I say, that is, “through a mirror, in an enigma” (1 Cor. 13). But to see face to face does not belong to the present age; that hope is reserved for the future.

## CHAPTER XIX

That the Son of God and the Holy Spirit proceeding from him are represented in what the Lord said to Moses: “Gather for me seventy men, and I shall take from your spirit and give it to them.”

A fuller treatment, according to the passage set down above, might be given concerning the glory or brightness of Moses’ countenance, or the opening of the book once sealed. But, content to have found in this place the treasure of your name, O Trinity God, let us remember our purpose, and consider that feature of the glory of Moses which concerns the procession of the Holy Spirit (Heb. 11). For above we stated in what way the triune and one God was represented in the prophets and patriarchs, whose God he is not ashamed to be called—namely, in Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Now, according to this mystery of the Holy Spirit, it is easy to say in what manner he was also represented in the hand of Moses.

As Moses’ glory increased, the envy of the people increased also, to such an extent that the matter seemed unbearable to Moses, and he said to the Lord: “Why have you afflicted your servant? Why do I not find favor before you? And why have you imposed the burden of this whole people upon me?” and so on, down to: “But if it seems otherwise to you, I beg you, kill me, and let me find favor in your eyes, lest I be afflicted by such great evils” (Num. 11).

It is worth attending carefully to what we are saying: Moses, the example of all prelates who rule well, suffered excessive envy from those subject to him, so that the burden of this torment seemed unbearable. Although he was the meekest of all men dwelling on earth, he was slandered by detractors and murmurers as though he were an arrogant man and excessively greedy for glory. His own brother Aaron and his sister Miriam did not spare him this injury. “For they said: ‘Has the Lord spoken only through Moses? Has he not also spoken through us in like manner?’” (Num. 11). From his own words to the Lord—“But if it seems otherwise to you, I beg you, kill me, and let me find favor in your eyes, lest I be afflicted by such great evils”—it is easy to recognize how great a storm of grief was in his heart.

“And the Lord said to Moses: ‘Gather for me seventy men from the elders of Israel, whom you know to be elders of the people and teachers; lead them to the entrance of the tabernacle of the covenant, and make them stand there with you, that I may descend and speak with you. And I shall take [Col. 0117B] from your spirit and give it to them, that they may bear with you the burden of the people and that you may not be burdened alone.’ Moses therefore came and told the people the words of the Lord, gathering seventy men from the elders of Israel, whom he caused to stand around the tabernacle. And the Lord descended in a cloud and spoke to him, taking from the spirit that was in Moses and giving it to the seventy men. And when the spirit rested upon them, they prophesied, and did not afterwards cease.”

Wonderful is God’s mercy; wonderful is Moses’ kindness. For in what other way could he have better satisfied the people, so that he might not appear to wish to glory alone? Yet even this seemed too little to him: that he was judged worthy to have seventy men share in his glory, unless he also desired that the whole people might likewise be able to glory in the Lord. “For when a running boy [Col. 0117C] announced to him, saying, ‘Eldad and Medad are prophesying in the camp,’ Joshua son of Nun, Moses’ minister and one chosen out of many, immediately said: ‘My lord Moses, stop them.’ But Moses replied: ‘What? Are you jealous on my account? Would that all the people might prophesy, and that the Lord would give them his Spirit!’” (Num. 11).

## CHAPTER XX

That the seventy men received a part of Moses’ glory—namely prophecy—but not also the working of miracles, as Joshua did, of whom the Lord said, “And you shall give him a part of your glory”; and that this was what he meant when he said, “I shall take from your spirit.”

Before we enter into the mystery of this event, according to the tenor of our purpose—by which we have proposed to glorify the Holy Spirit as proceeding equally from the Son as from the Father—it is pleasant to linger a little over the literal sense. For the Lord said: “I shall take from your spirit and give it to them”; and again Scripture says: “And he spoke to him”—that is, to Moses—“taking from the spirit that was in Moses and giving it to the seventy men.”

What then? Could he not give them his Spirit without diminishing Moses’ spirit—that is, the spirit which he had given to Moses? You would rightly ask this if he had said, “I shall take from you.” But now he simply said, “I shall take,” which is nothing other than as if he had said: “I shall take from your spirit and give it to them”; that is, I shall give them, not as much as you possess among the distributions of the graces of the Holy Spirit, but some portion of your glory. Thus later the Lord himself says concerning the very famous Joshua: “You shall give him commands in the sight of all, and a part of your glory, that the whole assembly of the children of Israel may hear him” (Num. 27).

And so it came to pass. The waters of the Jordan were divided, when the Lord said to Joshua: “Today I shall begin to exalt you in the sight of all Israel” (Josh. 3); and all the people passed through the dry channel. This was a part of Moses’ glory, who was glorified by raising his rod and dividing the sea, so that the children of Israel might walk through the midst of the sea on dry ground. It was, I say, a part of his glory. For in this glory—namely, in the performance of so great a miracle—Moses did something more: he again stretched out his hand against the sea, “and the waters returned and covered the chariots and horsemen of Pharaoh’s whole army; not even one of them remained” (Exod. 14).

If you remember the other matters as well, you will see that the statement concerning Joshua was true: “You shall give him a part of your glory.” For he was not as great in all the signs and wonders which the Lord performed through him before Pharaoh and the Egyptians, and before all Israel, as Moses was. Therefore what the Lord said—“I shall take from your spirit and give it to the seventy men” (Num. 11)—must be understood in no other way than as if he had said: “I shall give them a part of your glory,” just as he said of Joshua. For prophecy was a part of Moses’ glory, apart from which Scripture recalls that those men received no glory, saying: “And when the spirit rested upon them, they prophesied and did not afterwards cease” (ibid.).

What we intend to say can readily be shown by the analogy of a small thing: behold fire. Though it is a body, it is divided without being diminished and spreads itself without loss to itself, however many portions we take from it. But do we take anything away from it—whether the fire is large or small, a great lamp or a little one—when, lighting as many lamps as we wish, we seem to take portions from a single one? Certainly, however many portions are taken, the undivided fire suffers no loss from the light lent out from any lamp. So the Lord could say, “I shall take from your spirit and give it to them,” as though saying: “Of the many graces bestowed upon you, I shall impart to them one grace: the grace of prophecy.”

# BOOK SIX

[Col. 0117]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0117D] Concerning what is written in Micah: “And we shall raise up over him seven shepherds and eight principal men”: who these shepherds and principal men are; what it means to raise them up over Christ; and that Moses is one of those shepherds.

Whenever, while speaking of the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, we call to mind anything which the great fathers and judges of Israel performed as a type of him, we do—or desire to do—that which, among other things, was said concerning him through the prophet Micah: “And we shall raise up over him seven shepherds and eight principal men” (Mic. 5).

Who are or were the seven shepherds, unless Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph, who, when bringing his brothers before Pharaoh, commanded them to make this profession: “Your servants are shepherds from our childhood until the present, both we and our fathers” (Gen. 46)? They spoke truly, for their fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and Joseph himself while still a boy, had charge of feeding flocks. Thus Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph. Also Moses, whom the Lord called from the bush [Col. 0119B] while he was feeding the sheep of his father-in-law Jethro (Exod. 3), and David, whom the Lord took from the sheepfolds—“he took him from following the ewes with young” (Ps. 77)—are they not six shepherds? Add Abel, who was himself the first shepherd of sheep (Gen. 4), and there are seven shepherds.

Moreover, the eight principal men are the eight chief judges who overcame enemies in renowned and memorable battles and delivered Israel from the slaughter wrought by devastators: namely Joshua, Othniel, Ehud, Barak, Gideon, Jephthah, Samson, and Samuel. And what does it mean to raise these seven shepherds and eight principal men up over him—that is, over the ruler and supreme judge of Israel, “who shall come forth from you, O Bethlehem of Judah,” as is written there in the same prophet? What, I say, does it mean to raise them up over him, unless to show that they bore his type before them and that he fulfilled in reality what happened to them in figure? (1 Cor. 10).

Let us now, therefore, raise up Moses the shepherd over him in this manner; according to the mystery of the event which we have related, let us confess what is true, pious, and catholic: that the Holy Spirit proceeds from God the Son just as from God the Father.

## CHAPTER II

Again concerning the word “raising up,” since that which had been dead and comes to life again is said to be raised up.

Nowhere does Holy Scripture narrate that anything of this kind was said or done concerning any of the shepherds or principal men, such as was said by the Lord to this Moses: “I shall take from your spirit and give it to them”; and again, “he spoke to him, taking from the spirit that was in Moses and giving it to the seventy men” (Num. 11). All the more, therefore, do we desire to raise him up over him from whom, according to the mystery of this event, the Holy Spirit proceeds—he “from whose fullness,” John the Baptist says, “we have all received, grace for grace; for the law was given through Moses, grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1).

But first, an inquiry concerning the word “raising up” is not out of place. For that which was dead and comes to life again is raised up, or said to be raised up. Was, then, that which was so done in Moses dead? (Exod. 34). Certainly it was dead, in comparison with the surpassing life which is in the grace and truth of our Lord Jesus Christ. For just as the Apostle said, speaking of that literal brightness of Moses’ face at which the children of Israel were afraid, “For that which was glorious has not been glorified in this respect, because of the surpassing glory” (2 Cor. 3), that is, in comparison with the surpassing glory; so you may rightly say also of this outpouring of Moses’ spirit that it ought not to be called alive or life-giving, because of the surpassing life—that is, in comparison with the surpassing life.

“Let us raise up,” therefore, is rightly said; that is: we shall show that what happened in Moses possessed less life and usefulness, whereas in Christ there is true life. But why did he not say, “We shall raise up in him,” but preferred to say, “We shall raise up over him”? Surely because of the abasements of our Lord Jesus Christ himself. For he was not only made “a little lower than the angels” (Ps. 8), but was actually seen as lower than Moses and all the prophets. Far above that form in which he appeared upon earth and conversed with human beings—above the form of a servant, in which he could even be crucified—are those things which we testify concerning him according to the Scriptures of truth, first of all according to the Scriptures of this Moses.

Knowing this, when he spoke of the coming of the Holy Spirit, he said: “He shall glorify me, because he shall receive from what is mine and declare it to you.” And immediately he added: “All things that the Father has are mine; therefore I said that he shall receive from what is mine and declare it to you” (John 16). What does he mean when he says, “All things that the Father has are mine,” unless as if he said: “All the Scriptures, which the Father undoubtedly composed through his messengers Moses [Col. 0120C] and the other prophets, tend toward me”? Therefore, when the Spirit of truth makes you understand anything “written concerning me in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms” (Luke 24), this indeed shall be to receive from what is mine and declare it to you. By doing this, he shall glorify me—namely, among you and among all who shall believe through your words—when you think greater things of me than you now think, beyond what you now see in me or hear from me.

## CHAPTER III

How this mystery of the shepherd was raised up over the Lord Christ in his being commanded to gather seventy men at the entrance of the tabernacle of the covenant, that they might receive from his spirit.

Therefore Moses, gathering seventy men from the elders of Israel whom he himself knew to be elders and teachers, in order that a gift shared from his spirit might be given to them for ministry, signifies our Lord Jesus Christ. He gathered the disciples whom he chose, knowing them to be elders—that is, to possess the faith in which, the Apostle says (Heb. 6), the elders, that is, the holy fathers, received testimony—in order to make them participants in his Spirit. This Spirit is in him not by measure, as in any one of the saints, but, as the Apostle says, “in him the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Col. 2).

That dove, seen descending upon him when he was baptized, teaches us this; Luke writes more clearly that “heaven was opened, and the Holy Spirit descended upon him in bodily form like a dove” (Luke 3). Certainly both that bodily form—something whole, entire, and indivisible—and the Apostle’s statement, “In him the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily,” affirm this: the Holy Spirit was not given to him by measure, but is wholly in him and remains wholly in him with all his gifts, just as the bodily form of the dove descended wholly upon him with all its members. This is not to say that the Holy Spirit then began to be in him or to remain in him, but that this form demonstrated that he was and remained in him.

Finally, if someone considers his human nature, it is certain that the Holy Spirit remained in him from the beginning of his conception, since the undefiled Virgin conceived him by the Holy Spirit. But if the discourse concerns the divine nature, it is foolish to doubt whether the Holy Spirit is in the Son, since Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one substance, separable in no place and changeable by no accidents.

Where did this lawgiver and giver of blessing gather these men, that he might give them from his Spirit? At the entrance of the tabernacle of the covenant, and there he made them stand with him (Num. 11). What is the entrance of the heavenly tabernacle not made by hands? For it ought not to be unknown that one tabernacle was pitched by God, not man, and another was pitched by man at God’s command, according to the pattern of the former—God commanding and saying: “See, and make according to the pattern shown to you on the mountain” (Exod. 25).

What, then, is the entrance of the heavenly tabernacle except the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, in which his side was opened by a soldier’s lance, whence blood and water flowed? For we know no other entrance; nor is there any entrance or passage for us “into the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God” (Ps. 41), except through faith in this sacrament. To that entrance, indeed, all of us who have been baptized in Christ Jesus are brought; for, as the Apostle says, “we have been baptized into his death” (Rom. 6), and there we received the Holy Spirit.

But it is fitting here to consider those leading men whom he then brought there in person, saying among other things, with eyes lifted up to heaven: “Those whom you gave me I have kept, and none of them has perished except the son of perdition” (John 17). How did he make them stand with him? “You,” he says, “are those who have remained with me; and I appoint for you, as my Father appointed for me, a kingdom” (Luke 22). Thus they stood with him at the entrance of the tabernacle—not, I say, seventy men, but now one hundred and twenty men—when the Lord descended and, taking from the Spirit of Christ, gave it to them; when “there suddenly came a sound from heaven as of a violent rushing wind, and tongues divided as though of fire appeared to them” (Acts 2).

## CHAPTER IV

Concerning the fact that the Lord had patiently endured them until then, but after so many people received from Moses’ spirit he began to strike the murmuring people; and concerning the reality of which this occurred as a figure.

It is highly relevant to consider what happened, and what kind of things happened, to that people after they had received from Moses’ spirit and those seventy men had prophesied and did not afterwards cease. Even before this they had tested the Lord many times and had spoken wickedly amid God’s very benefits; they asked for nothing without murmuring, beginning thus: “What shall we drink?” (Exod. 15). Again, murmuring, they said: “Would that we had died by the hand of the Lord in the land of Egypt, when we sat over pots of meat and ate bread to fullness” (Exod. 16).

The Lord patiently endured their murmuring and evil speech, even when Moses said to the Lord: “What shall I do with this people? A little more, and they will stone me” (Exod. 17). Their hardness was so great that Moses was already afraid in this way; yet the Lord did not himself strike them with any plague, except that Moses, on account of the guilt of the calf which Aaron made (Exod. 32), of his own accord and without being commanded, ordered the sons of Levi, and each killed his brother, friend, and neighbor; and on that day twenty-three thousand fell.

Yet there Moses was zealous for the Lord. But we are now concerned with the fact that the Lord was angry on behalf of Moses. Nothing of this kind is found, either said or done, before so many people prophesied after receiving the gift shared from Moses’ spirit. But from that point onward, because their murmuring against Moses did not cease, the Lord heard and was angry, so that first he covered his sister with leprosy, white as snow (Num. 12); and the wrath of the Lord struck the people with an exceedingly great plague. “And all the men,” he says, “who have seen my majesty and the signs which I performed in Egypt and in the wilderness, and have tested me now ten times and have not obeyed my voice, shall not see the land which I swore to their fathers; nor shall any of those who have reviled me behold it” (Num. 14).

And so it happened. The earth swallowed some of them (Num. 16); fire consumed others; some perished by serpents; and that whole generation which had come out of Egypt, from twenty years old and upward, [55] except Joshua and Caleb son of Jephunneh, was consumed by various disasters and laid low in the wilderness (Num. 14). What does it mean that God’s judgment or wrath over them became so terrible not before, but after the diffusion of Moses’ spirit? “For all these things,” says the Apostle, “happened to them in figure” (1 Cor. 10); and therefore we ought to inquire more carefully what was prefigured by this ordering of time.

## CHAPTER V

Concerning the Lord’s answer when the Pharisees said, “This man does not cast out demons except by Beelzebub, prince of demons”: “But whoever speaks a word against the Holy Spirit shall not be forgiven, neither in this age nor in the age to come”; and that the event occurred as a figure of this judgment.

While we attend to this question or chapter, and at the same time hear the Apostle saying, “But we have the mind of Christ” (1 Cor. 2), behold, the mind of Christ himself graciously meets us in these words which he answered the Pharisees when they said: “This man does not cast out demons except by Beelzebub, prince of demons.” “And if I,” he says, “cast out demons by Beelzebub, by whom do your sons cast them out? Therefore they shall be your judges.” After a few intervening words, he says: “Therefore I tell you: every sin and blasphemy shall be forgiven to human beings, but blasphemy against the Spirit shall not be forgiven. And whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man shall be forgiven; but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit shall not be forgiven, neither in this age nor in the age to come” (Matt. 12).

In these words the mind of Christ meets us while we attend to the foregoing chapter concerning Moses: why God was angry with murmurers and detractors, and did not spare them, only after—not before—something from his spirit had been given to the seventy men; why his wrath rose against them and consumed them terribly in diverse ways, as was said above.

Let us therefore say: so long as our Lord Jesus Christ appeared to be the sole witness to himself, he could in a sense seem justly to be lightly regarded by those who said: “You bear witness concerning yourself; your testimony is not true.” Though he could truly answer in return: “Even if I bear witness concerning myself, my testimony is true, because I know whence I came and where I go” (John 8), nevertheless this patience judged their sin forgivable for so long, saying to them: “Whoever speaks against the Son of Man shall be forgiven.” For they could still be excused on grounds of ignorance; hence, when he suffered, he said: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23).

But when the Holy Spirit came to bear witness, as he himself promised, saying: “When the Paraclete comes, whom I shall send to you from the Father—the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father—he shall bear witness concerning me, and you also shall bear witness” (John 15), from that time onward they had no excuse for their sin. Foreseeing this, he said: “But whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit shall not be forgiven, neither in this age nor in the age to come” (Matt. 12).

And so it happened. For not before, but after he sent the Holy Spirit to his disciples, and those who had been unlearned and ordinary people began to speak in various tongues the mighty works of God and to bring forth from the Scriptures—which are indeed the voices of the Holy Spirit—the testimony of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, they were judged with eternal judgment: it was not forgiven them “either in this age or in the age to come.” Indeed, in this age they perished when the Romans conquered, and in the age to come, when evil spirits dragged their souls to torments.

Certainly, as a figure of the event to be enacted, it happened to those who afflicted or provoked the spirit of Moses that not before, but after something from his spirit had been given to the seventy men, the wrath of the Spirit of the Lord was angered against them and destroyed, in so many and such diverse ways, that whole generation which came out of Egypt. The same is true in the case of individual persons—that is, the same judgment. For as long as they oppose sound teaching through ignorance, the sentence of eternal judgment from above is held suspended over them; but when, knowing the truth, they oppose truth through pride—for example Arius and the other heretics, or the many founders of heresies—from that point they are judged to be blasphemers and to speak a word against the Holy Spirit, and this sin shall not be forgiven either in this age or in the age to come.

## CHAPTER VI

That David was the seventh of the aforementioned shepherds; that with him not only is God’s name tripled, as with Moses, but also the relative names of the Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—are found expressly stated; and that he was the first to name the Holy Spirit, previously called the Spirit of God or Spirit of the Lord.

The seventh of the shepherds mentioned above was David, whom both sacred history most plainly narrates to have fed his father’s sheep (1 Sam. 16), and who himself sings in words of this kind: “He chose David his servant and took him from the sheepfolds; he took him from following the ewes with young” (Ps. 77). How many great teachers have raised this shepherd up over him in the manner mentioned above—that is, over our Lord Jesus Christ.

We too, though last, have raised him up over Christ to the extent of our power, both in many other places and especially in the work which we wrote on the first and second books of Kings. With David, concerning our purpose, we find the treasure of our faith in the Holy Trinity expressed more openly. In what way more openly? Surely not only, as with Moses, by the threefold substantial name, “God.” For example, when he says: “May God bless us, our God; may God bless us” (Ps. 66). But also by the expressly stated relative names—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

For Christ himself speaks in that Psalm: “The Lord said to me: You are my Son”; understood as Son by nature, not by adoption. For it follows: “Today I have begotten you” (Ps. 2). We understand “today” as though it meant “in eternity,” “in immutability.” For just as, for him, there is being, and not having been or being to come—whence he said to Moses, “I am who I am” (Exod. 3), and to the Jews, “Before Abraham came to be, I am” (John 8)—so our faith’s understanding admits in his begetting neither yesterday nor tomorrow, but only today.

What follows—that the Lord Father also said: “Ask of me, and I shall give you the nations as your inheritance and the ends of the earth as your possession” (Ps. 2)—is plainly said with reference to the humility of our nature. For according to the form of a servant this is fitting for him, and it was necessary for us that he should ask the Father—that is, suffer for our salvation. For we wish to understand nothing else here by the word “asking” except obedience, whose summit is the sacrament or sacrifice of his most holy passion.

Likewise, in another psalm, when the same Father says, speaking in vision to his saints—among whom David rejoiced to count himself—“He shall call upon me: ‘You are my Father, my God, and the upholder of my salvation’; and I shall make him the firstborn, exalted above the kings of the earth” (Ps. 88): when, I say, he says these things and states the relative names of Father and Son, he also expresses both natures of the only Son. For according to the divine nature, “he,” he says, “shall call upon me: ‘You are my Father’”; and according to the human nature, likewise “he,” he says, “shall call upon me: ‘You are my God and the upholder of my salvation.’”

In accordance with this meaning, this firstborn, now made exalted above the kings of the earth—that is, now raised from the dead, now about to sit in eternal session at the right hand of Majesty on high—says: “I ascend to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God” (John 20).

David was the first to name the Holy Spirit, saying: “Do not cast me away from your face, and do not take your Holy Spirit from me” (Ps. 50). For until then it had been written “Spirit of God” or “Spirit of the Lord.” But David was the first to name him “Holy Spirit,” a more resonant expression; we have already mentioned the dignity of this title in the first little book of the present work. Thus he openly declared the relative names of the Holy Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—which neither Moses nor anyone else before him had expressed so plainly.

## CHAPTER VII
Of the promise made to him with an oath: “Once I have sworn by my holiness,” and of the threefold name of the Lord addressed to him when it says: “I will give you rest, and the Lord will foretell to you that the Lord will make you a house.”

To this man, as to Abraham, a promise was made with an oath concerning the blessed seed, which is Christ: that he would be born from his seed. Hence, singing of the mercies of the Lord, he said from the mouth of the Lord himself: “Once I have sworn by my holiness: if I lie to David, his seed shall remain for ever” (Ps. [col. 0125C] 88 [89]). It should therefore be reverently observed that the blessed Trinity, which presented itself to Abraham in three angels for the confirmation of the promise, or for the greatness and dignity of what was promised, almost expressed itself in three words to David in the promise concerning that same seed, namely Christ: “Thus says the Lord of hosts: I will give you rest from all your enemies, and the Lord will foretell to you that the Lord will make you a house” (2 Sam. 7).

For in these words, at the beginning of so great a promise, as is understood from what follows, when he says: “And when your days are fulfilled and you sleep with your fathers, I shall raise up your seed after you, which shall come forth from your womb; and I shall establish his kingdom. He shall build a house for my name, and I shall establish the throne of [col. 0125D] his kingdom for ever. I shall be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son” (ibid.), in these words, I say, the one divinity of the supreme and indivisible Trinity openly shows itself through the distinction of persons.

For who, or which person, says: “And I will give you rest from all your enemies,” except the person of the Father? For he continues and says afterward: “I shall be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son.” Therefore, that person of whom the Lord Father says, “And the Lord will foretell to you,” is the Lord, the Holy Spirit, who foretold through the mouth of the holy prophets, as Zacharias also says: “As he spoke through the mouth of his holy prophets from of old” (Luke 1). And the person of whom he immediately says, [col. 0126A] “That the Lord will make you a house,” is the Lord the Son. Not three lords, but one Lord.

So far as this holy Scripture could or ought, it both preserved this mystery for future generations and concealed it from those who then lived while it was being composed; for they could not bear the distinction of the three persons, as we have already said elsewhere, if it had been openly preached to them.

## CHAPTER VIII

That when the Paraclete, the Spirit of truth, was sent to the apostles—or indeed even before he appeared in tongues of fire, which occurred on the day of Pentecost—when he had opened their understanding so that they understood the Scriptures, the first testimonies concerning Christ were drawn from David’s psalms.

How much, do you suppose, does the Father have in this Psalter? For the Son said—and we recalled it above—“When the Paraclete, the Spirit of truth, comes, he will glorify me, because he will receive from what is mine and announce it to you.” And immediately he added: “All things which the Father has are mine; therefore I said: Because he will receive from what is mine and announce it to you” (John 16). How much, then, do you suppose the Father has in this book? How much did the Holy Spirit receive from it and announce to the apostles, so that the Son of God might be glorified?

It is very delightful that after Christ, the Son of God, ascended into heaven—even before the Holy Spirit proceeded forth visibly in tongues of fire—the first thing that he brought forth was taken from this book and announced to Peter, so that he might say: “For it is written in the book of Psalms: ‘Let his habitation become desolate, and let there be no one [col. 0126C] to dwell in it’; and, ‘Let another receive his episcopal office’” (Acts 1; Ps. 108 [109]).

For what the Evangelist John narrated had already occurred: “When he had said this, he breathed upon them and said to them: ‘Receive the Holy Spirit’” (John 20). And Luke, recording the events of that same day and that same evening, said among other things: “Then he opened their understanding, so that they might understand the Scriptures” (Luke 24).

But when the days of Pentecost were fulfilled, and the Holy Spirit proceeded from the throne of majesty and “sat upon each one of them as fire—for divided tongues, as of fire, appeared to them—and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in diverse tongues, as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance” (Acts 2)—when, I say, this sound occurred and, at this sound, the confused multitude assembled, was not the first thing which the Holy Spirit brought forth through the mouth of the apostle Peter taken from this book?

For after first citing the testimony of the prophet Joel, that they were not drunk as those people thought who “mockingly said, ‘These men are full of new wine’” (ibid.), he immediately set forth the proposition concerning the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ and supplied this proof: “For David says concerning him: ‘I kept the Lord always before my sight’” (Ps. 15 [16]), and the rest. “For David did not ascend into heaven,” but he himself says: “The Lord said to my Lord, ‘Sit at my right hand, until I place your enemies as a footstool beneath your feet’” (Ps. 109 [110]).

As has already been said above, it is very delightful that, when we wish to say that the Father has many things in this book which belong to the Son—as indeed all else does, for all Scriptures tend toward the Son—we observe that the first things which the Holy Spirit brought forth through the mouth of the apostle Peter on the very day on which he was given were taken from this book, in which God the Father stored up for his Son very many faithful testimonies.

## CHAPTER IX

Likewise, concerning the saying, “That Spirit will glorify me, because he will receive from what is mine and announce it to you”; and concerning the verse of the fourth psalm: “The light of your countenance, O Lord, has been marked upon us; you have given joy in my heart.”

Here in the fourth psalm he says: “The light of your countenance, O Lord, has been marked upon us; you have given joy in my heart.” For the fourth psalm, bearing this title, “For the end: a psalm, a song of David,” if you consider it rightly, looks toward that [col. 0127B] day on which the Holy Spirit, as was said above at §57, proceeding from the throne or majesty of the Father and the Son, so filled Christ’s disciples with joy that they appeared full of new wine, speaking in tongues and unable to keep silence because of the joy which thereafter no one could take from them.

For understanding this, it helps to survey the meaning and sequence of the psalms preceding it—the first, second, and third psalms—together with this fourth psalm. For they proclaim to the attentive ear the four mysteries of our salvation, in faith in which our life consists: the Incarnation, Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension of Jesus Christ, the Son of God; and likewise the joy with which the Holy Spirit, as has been said, filled the disciples of that same Lord on the day of Pentecost.

For these, O Son, the Holy Spirit received from what is yours and announced to us, so that now, in this façade or vestibule of your Father’s treasury, we may demonstrate these four badges of your nobility: namely, that, born a man without sin, you lived among men and, though not a sinner, suffered death in obedience to paternal love; that you rose from the sleep of death by the power of divinity; that you ascended into heaven, to return on the day of judgment and strike the ungodly, because they opposed you without cause.

Accordingly, leaving aside for a little the verse written above from the fourth psalm, “The light of your countenance, O Lord, has been marked upon us; you have given joy in my heart,” we shall begin with the first psalm and briefly demonstrate these matters, so that, when the façade or vestibule of the sanctuary—which is exceedingly spacious within—has been seen, whatever unlearned spectator like ourselves may be present may say: “O how much the Father has here, and how much the Spirit of truth can receive from here, in order to announce to us those things which the Father has stored up for his Son; for at the entrance there is so resplendent and orderly a prospect, adorned with the mysteries that belong to life.”

## CHAPTER X

That through the meaning of the first psalm the Spirit of truth announces this to us concerning Christ: that he both came into this world without original sin and lived in this world without actual sin.

The first psalm, the first utterance of the Psalter, says: “Blessed is the man who has not gone in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way [col. 0128A] of sinners, nor sat in the seat of pestilence.” Who is such, or so great, a man except the one alone?

And indeed, if actual sins are in question, to say nothing for the moment of the greatest and latest saints, who could count the multitude of innocent little children who have not gone in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of pestilence? But if you reflect upon original sin, there is no one at all except this man; for, as the Apostle says, all sinned in Adam (Rom. 5).

This, then, is that truly blessed man, whose conception and birth came about through the operation of the Holy Spirit (Luke 1), as is beautifully suggested by this saying: “And he shall be like a tree planted beside streams of waters” (Ps. 1). For by the plural expression “streams of waters” we understand the distributions of spiritual graces, all of which were poured out together upon this God-bearing man, or blessed man, from the beginning of his conception. But upon other human beings, whoever may be worthy of them, they are bestowed or distributed neither in such fullness nor in anything comparable to it, but far less abundantly.

Yet let us on this occasion draw back the foot of our mind from the depth of these waters. For we proposed briefly to demonstrate in this psalm that the most holy humanity of our Lord and God Jesus Christ was without both original and actual sin; and for the present it is enough to accomplish this through these three antitheses.

“He did not go in the counsel of the ungodly,” but “his will is in the law of the Lord.” “He did not stand in the way of sinners,” but “he shall meditate in the law of the Lord day and night.” “He did not sit in the seat of pestilence,” but he is—or “shall be”—“like a tree planted beside streams of waters,” which “shall give its fruit in its season.”

Let us now demonstrate, then, the two opposing counsels, whose threefold effects are so contrary. What was the counsel of the ungodly into which that unhappy man—the old Adam—went, that is, by which he departed from God? Surely this: that he who was dust presumed to desire to be like God (Gen. 3). What, conversely, was the counsel of the godly into which this blessed man—the new Adam—did not go, that is, by which he did not depart from God? Surely this: that he who was God by nature deigned to descend into our dust. The former was the counsel of the spirit of the devil; the latter, the counsel of the Spirit of God.

Hence these three antitheses of which we spoke: according to that counsel the former went away, whereas the will of the latter, according to this counsel, was in the law of the Lord—indeed, as the Apostle says, “He was made under the law,” though he was Lord of the law (Gal. 4). The former stood in the way of sinners, for he displayed in deed the evil thought of so great an ambition; the latter meditated in the law of the Lord day and night, so that he might fulfill in the truth of his passion what was prefigured in the legal ceremonies—for example, of the lamb and calf and other things of this kind.

The former sat “in the seat of pestilence,” that is, he left to his descendants as an inheritance the pestilence of the death of both soul and body. But this man, as a fruitful tree, gave this fruit in its season: that, by eating his flesh and blood (John 6), we might be freed from the guilt of that forbidden food.

## CHAPTER XI

That through the meaning of the second psalm the Spirit of truth announces this to us concerning Christ: that he suffered for our sins through obedience, namely by obeying the Father who said, “Ask of me”—that is, by dying. For this was his asking: “And I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession.”

“Why then did the nations rage, and the peoples devise vain things?” (Ps. 2). For he said somewhere to the Jews—and what he said to them, he said and says to all nations and peoples—“Which of you convicts me of sin? If I speak the truth, why do you not believe me?” (John 8). What else is meant by this question: “Why did the nations rage, and the peoples devise vain things?”

For this reason we join this second psalm to the first or preceding one: because, in accordance with our purpose, we recognize in the first that Christ, the Son of God, was conceived, born, and lived as a man without sin; and in this second one we understand to be set forth the reason why he suffered, which the nations and peoples, devising vain things, did not know.

For he says: “The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession” (Ps. 2). Having heard the word, “Ask of me,” we must also know the manner or character of the asking. How did he ask, if not by dying? Undoubtedly the humility of his most holy passion was his asking; it was the sacrifice, apart from which God did not desire any burnt offering or sin-offering (Ps. 39 [40]).

The sense, then, is this: Therefore I, the blessed man, who owed nothing to death because I committed no sin, paid the debt of death; therefore, when “the nations raged and the peoples devised vain things,” when the kings of the earth stood up and the rulers assembled together [col. 0129D] against the Lord and against me, his Christ—therefore, I say, I kept silence, I was always silent, I endured patiently, though I could at any time have said what I said once: “I am he,” whereupon “they went backward and fell to the ground” (John 18). For the Lord Father said to me: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession.”

Among the many things consonant with this saying of the Father belongs also that which Isaiah said among other things: “If he shall make his soul an offering for sin, he shall see a long-lived seed, and the will of the Lord shall prosper in his hand” (Isa. 53; citation printed “Isa. III”). But how could his death be of such worth or such power unless he who was born as a man in time was God before the ages? Therefore, before the Father was to say, “Ask of me,” he prefaced it: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you.”

The sum of the remaining words to the end of the psalm is that which he said: “And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself” (John 12). Again he said: “All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth” (Matt. 28): judicial power, certainly, at the right and at the left, which is signified by this brief verse: “You shall rule them with a rod of iron; you shall break them like a potter’s vessel” (Ps. 2).

## CHAPTER XII

That through the meaning of the third psalm the Spirit of truth announces this to us concerning Christ: that he rose and ascended into heaven; and that this is what he says: “I slept and was in a deep sleep, and I arose,” and: “But you, O Lord, are my protector.”

After the nations—the Gentile peoples and the Jews—raged until they killed him, they rejoiced and boasted in many ways as though they had conquered, taking his very death as a great proof that he was not from God, that he was a deceiver, and therefore that his name had perished and that there was no salvation for him in God.

But he, now dead for three days, spoke—and now, still living, speaks—the words contained in the following psalm: “O Lord, why have those who trouble me multiplied? Many rise up against me; many say to my soul, ‘There is no salvation for him in his God,’” and so forth, as far as: “I slept and was in a deep sleep, and I arose” (Ps. 3).

Who, unless he sleeps with the sleep of sin and is sunk in the deep slumber of deception, fails to recognize that this is the voice of one rising again, that these are words of resurrection? Therefore what follows—“I shall not fear thousands of people surrounding me. Arise, O Lord; save me, my God” (ibid.)—is the voice of one ascending and going to sit at the right hand of God.

He had, however, more briefly touched upon both the resurrection and the ascension in one short verse: “But you, O Lord, are my protector, my glory, and the one who lifts up my head.” The apostle Peter expressed the glorious sense of this verse in this way: “The God of our fathers raised up this Jesus and exalted him by his right hand as Prince and Saviour, to give repentance and forgiveness of sins” (Acts 2; wording closely reflects Acts 5:30–31).

We have done what we proposed: namely, to demonstrate at the very beginning of the Davidic Psalter these four mysteries, without faith in which no one has lived—the Incarnation, Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension of Jesus Christ, the Son of God—so that in a clear sequence we might arrive at the day of the procession of the Holy Spirit, whose grace is sounded by the fourth psalm which immediately follows.

## CHAPTER XIII

That through the meaning of the fourth psalm, which begins: “When I called upon him, the God of my righteousness heard me; in tribulation you enlarged me,” the Spirit of truth announces this to us concerning Christ: that he fulfilled his promise, saying, “Your heart shall rejoice, and no one shall take your joy from you.”

“When I called upon him, the God of my righteousness heard me; in tribulation you enlarged me.” We considered above the verse of this psalm: “The light of your countenance, O Lord, has been marked upon us; you have given joy in my heart.” Having enlarged upon it, we departed briefly to touch on the preceding psalms, in order to demonstrate that in this prophecy there lies hidden and shines forth, in a wonderful way, a clear order of the mysteries of our salvation.

We ask, then: does not the voice of this fourth psalm suit the event and the utterance of that day on which the Holy Spirit came from heaven and filled the praying disciples of the Lord with joy, so that it is fitting for that assembly and for the whole subsequent Church to say: “In tribulation you enlarged me; have mercy on me and hear my prayer”? For “all were persevering unanimously in prayer, with the women and Mary the mother of the Lord Jesus and his brothers” (Acts 1).

Did it not happen to them as this utterance of the prophetic Spirit declares: “In tribulation you enlarged me”? Until then, indeed, both their hearts and their mouths had not been broad but exceedingly narrow. How were their hearts narrow? They were unlettered and unlearned men. How were their mouths narrow? They possessed the rusticity of a single language, Hebrew, so that when they spoke in their native idiom, they were immediately recognized as Galileans.

Those who had been so narrow in heart and mouth were so enlarged that they both understood the Scriptures and spoke in tongues; and, what is greatest, not in peace but amid persecution. “For they went away rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they had been judged worthy to suffer reproach for the name of Jesus” (Acts 5).

Great and wonderful was the enlargement of those who, persevering unanimously in prayer according to this prophetic utterance, “Have mercy on me and hear my prayer” (Ps. 4), were heard in such a way that, attaining firmness in both heart and mouth—in the heart, the Scriptures; in the mouth, languages—they spoke to rulers and said both to the people and to the elders: “Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood? Know that the Lord has made his holy one wonderful” (ibid.).

For what else is the sense of those words, “Men of Israel, the God of our fathers has glorified his Son Jesus,” and the rest, down to: “Repent therefore and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out” (Acts 3)? And how beautifully the words written here in the psalm, “Be angry and do not sin” (Ps. 4), and the apostle Peter’s words there, “Repent, that your sins may be blotted out,” signify one and the same thing.

Likewise, by the words written here, “Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?” that falsehood is rightly rebuked which, before the day on which the apostles began to preach, had been spread among the Jews—the falsehood, I say, which they had sought and purchased by giving the soldiers a large sum of money, so that they might say: “His disciples came by night and stole him while we slept” (Matt. 28).

But now, leaving aside the multitude of things that might be said from this passage, let us examine the verse we have proposed for the recognition of the holy Trinity.

## CHAPTER XIV

Again, concerning the verse of the fourth psalm: “The light of your countenance, O Lord, has been marked upon us”: that the countenance of the Lord is the Son of God, and that the light of the Lord’s countenance is the Spirit of the Father and the Son.

“The light of your countenance, O Lord, has been marked upon us; you have given joy in my heart.” The Lord to whom these words are said—“The light of your countenance, O Lord, has been marked upon us”—is the Father; the countenance of the Lord is the Son of the Father; and the light of the Lord’s countenance is the Holy Spirit of the Father and the Son.

The Son is rightly called the countenance of God the Father because, just as the emotion of joy or sorrow may be perceived in a human being’s countenance, so the will of God the Father became known to the world through the Son. We rightly understand the light of the Lord’s countenance to be the Holy Spirit of the Father and the Son because, just as the light of a brilliantly shining thing opens a way or prospect to bodily eyes—for example, as the brightness of the sun, driving away the darkness of night, makes day for us—so the Holy Spirit, driving away the darkness of ignorance, teaches us all truth. For through him we know both the Son and the Father, and know the Spirit himself as proceeding from both.

Who marked “upon us this light of your countenance, O Lord,” and when and where? Our Lord Jesus Christ, while your countenance was still hidden in that humanity so that he could be crucified. For unless it had been hidden, unless he had restrained himself and ceased to say, “I am he” (John 18), all would have gone backward and fallen to the ground, and they could not have seized him.

Our Lord Jesus Christ, I say, while your countenance was still thus hidden in his flesh, promised that he would mark upon us this light of your countenance, and immediately marked it, truly acting as high priest according to the right of his office, whose function it is to mark not only the forehead of the body but also the forehead of the believing soul. For on the very night in which he was betrayed, he said: “I will send you the Paraclete, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father” (John 15), along with many similar words pertaining to the distinction of the three persons, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
