Then, on the very day on which he rose, standing in the midst of the disciples, after first bringing the good message of peace which he had made between God and men, “he breathed upon them and said: ‘Receive the Holy Spirit’” (John 20), namely for the forgiveness of sins. For it follows: “Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them” (John 20).

And on the day of Pentecost he sent that same Spirit in distributions of graces, with many shining miracles. Thus, having the light of your countenance, O Lord, marked upon them, they began on that very day to call others and bring them so that that same light might be marked upon them through their ministry and the laying on of hands. For on that same day those who received the word were baptized in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and about three thousand souls were added that day.

## CHAPTER XV

On the variation in the same psalm between singular and plural number: that the singularity of believers is that they possess one Spirit and one faith, while their plurality or multitude consists of those who are opposed to, or outside, this unity.

And see how beautifully the prophetic Spirit distinguished believers from unbelievers by the very mode of speech. For of unbelievers he said: “Many say, ‘Who will show us good things?’” But, intimating that a certain unity had been produced out of the multitude of believers, when he had said, “The light of your countenance, O Lord, has been marked upon us,” he immediately preferred to use the singular number, saying in their person: “You have given joy in my heart.” And rightly so, because the multitude of believers had one heart and one soul (Acts 4).

This unity of heart and soul is also beautifully expressed by the adverb: “For you, O Lord, have established me singularly in hope” (Ps. 4). For the Holy Spirit himself makes one out of many. But those who do not have him are many; indeed, they are divided against themselves by diverse opinions and, in most cases, by contrary opinions through sects.

What then does it mean that, after “In peace I shall sleep and rest in the selfsame” (Ps. 4), he adds this cause or reason, “For you, O Lord, have established me singularly in hope,” unless it is as though he said: Therefore, because I now strive for this singularity or unity, of which the Apostle says: “For as we have many members in one body, but all members do not have the same activity, so we, though many, are one body in Christ, and individually members one of another,” and so forth, down to: “Being of the same mind toward one another, not setting your minds on high things, but consenting to the humble” (Rom. 12)—because this unity is made by one Spirit and one faith, I hope, I say, to come to that place where “I shall sleep and rest,” in as great a peace as the expression “in the selfsame” is intended to convey.

For such a meaning, the mode of speech varies according to the variation between singular and plural number: so that, after saying in the plural, “The light of your countenance, O Lord, has been marked upon us,” he immediately says in singular speech, “You have given joy in my heart”; and again, after saying in the plural, “They have been multiplied by the fruit of their grain, wine, and oil” (Ps. 4), he immediately says in the singular, speaking in the person of the distinct multitude of those whose heart is, or ought to be, one and whose soul is one, or whose Spirit and faith are one: “In peace I shall sleep and rest in the selfsame.”

It may indeed be understood as said of the reprobate or earthly-minded: “They have been multiplied by the fruit of grain, wine, and oil,” so that it expresses rebuke, because they rejoice in such things and have multiplied through earthly riches. Yet, conversely, it is reverently understood that they have been multiplied through the fact that Christ, “as a grain of wheat falling into the earth, died” (John 12), and that he multiplied for believers in himself the two gifts of the Holy Spirit, of which we have often spoken, as the fruit “of wine and oil” (addition).

This unity or singularity, which in this psalm speaks in most of the saints, is that which the Lord Christ himself requested on the very night in which he was betrayed: “Holy Father,” he said, “keep in your name those whom you have given me, that they may be one as we are.” Again: “I do not pray only for these, but also for those who will believe in me through their word, that all may be one, as you, Father, are in me and I in you, that they also may be one in us,” and so forth; which he ended thus: “That the love with which you loved me may be in them, and I in them” (John 17). This love, plainly, must be understood as none other than the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER XVI [col. 0134A]

Again, that this unity says, “You have given joy in my heart”; and that where the Holy Spirit dwells, there is eternal and ineffable joy.

Would that—since there is neither leisure nor purpose to examine one by one all that has been said here—we might at least be permitted to penetrate the meaning of this one saying: “You have given joy in my heart.” But who can penetrate it unless he has received that same joy? Meanwhile, we can know and say this: that this joy is the Holy Spirit.

Certainly the Holy Spirit, just as he is rightly called the light of the Lord’s countenance, is also and rightly called the joy of the Father and the Son. Where the Holy Spirit dwells, there is eternal and ineffable joy; and he brings nothing other than joy itself.

David himself, through whom these words were spoken, had experienced this joy. For he had received the full horn, as it is written: “The Lord said to Samuel, ‘Fill your horn with oil and come, that I may send you to Jesse the Bethlehemite; for among his sons I have provided a king for myself’” (1 Sam. 16). Samuel therefore took a horn of oil and anointed him in the midst of his brothers. “And the Spirit of the Lord was directed upon David from that day and thereafter.”

Nevertheless, for a time he diminished this joy for himself; and, to use the words of the Apostle, who says, “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God” (Eph. 4), he then grieved the Holy Spirit when he sinned against Uriah the Hittite (2 Sam. 12). Knowing and feeling this, he said: “Restore to me, O God, the joy of your salvation” (Ps. 50 [51]).

Holy men, whose breasts are dwelling places of the Holy Spirit, know how that happens which the Apostle does not wish to happen when he says: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you have been marked for the day of redemption” (Eph. 4). For there is a certain touch of the same Holy Spirit, by which he sometimes sensibly touches a person when he wishes to arouse that person to work, so that he may not neglect the grace which the Spirit himself has bestowed upon him.

If one then proceeds with a quiet mind, or is alone in private, whether giving himself to sleep for a time or keeping vigil, he perceives that touch as gentle and most sweet, like the familiar call of a present friend. But if it is otherwise—if, for example, a straw rushing into the eye of the mind has disturbed it, and satisfaction has not yet been made—then that touch comes more slowly and feels harsher, so that conscience does not hesitate to say: “Behold, the Holy Spirit of God has been grieved.”

How much more had the Spirit of the Lord been grieved, and how much reason David had to say, “Restore to me the joy of your salvation,” because a traveler, namely the devil, an alien far from the kingdom and city of God, came “to the rich man,” David; and “he, sparing to take from his own sheep and cattle in order to provide a feast for that traveler, took the ewe of the poor man and prepared food for the man who had come to him” (2 Sam. 12).

## CHAPTER XVII [col. 0135A]

Wonder at how wisely the book was sealed until the Lamb opened it; and concerning the saying of blessed Job: “He moves the earth from its place; he commands the sun, and it does not rise; and he seals up the stars as under a seal.”

Behold, while we stand as it were in the vestibule of this great house, and, having viewed the splendor of its façade, discern a brightness like it—indeed greater, and more spacious within—of your holy name, O God Trinity, whom we worship and to whom we sing with this Psalter, we marvel how wisely the book was sealed before the Lamb received it and opened its seals (Rev. 5), and how firmly it is still kept shut against one who, because of his unbelief, is unworthy to read within. Truly, it was wisely provided [Col. 0135B] that in these greater books he should not say what prophets commonly say in the lesser ones: “Thus says the Lord God of hosts: Behold, I will bring upon you a nation from afar, O house of Israel, says the Lord” (Jer. 5);—“Thus says the Lord God of hosts, the God of Israel: Make your ways and your practices good” (Jer. 7).

For who could then bear it, if he spoke similarly in these greater books? For example, if he said: “Thus says the Lord God of hosts: My God, my God, look upon me; why have you forsaken me?” Thus says the Lord: “They pierced my hands and feet.” Thus says the Lord: “They divided my garments among themselves, and cast lots for my clothing” (Ps. [Col. 0135C] 21). The book, therefore, was rightly sealed: omitting expressions of this kind, and intending to utter unbearable mysteries, this first speaker assumed the person of him of whom he spoke, so that, for the time being, he might seem to inattentive hearers to speak of himself, whereas the Messiah—that is, Christ—was speaking in him.

He also calls him “the Word” more often than “the Son,” so that he may conceal the mystery of the same Trinity; as in: “By the Word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their power” (Ps. 32). We mentioned this verse much earlier, when speaking of the angelic creation. This, I say, is what we marvel at; and in this very wonder, so great that none of our speech could suffice to unfold it, behold, we aptly hear behind us, as it were, the voice of blessed Job saying:

> “He is wise in heart and mighty in strength. Who has resisted him and had peace? He removes mountains, and they do not know it—those whom he overthrows in his wrath. He shakes the earth out of its place, and its pillars shall be shaken. He commands the sun, and it does not rise; and he shuts up the stars as under a seal” (Job 9).

We heard this voice while, standing in contemplation of the brightness that shines in the Psalms, we marveled. What are the mountains which God removed, for whose removal he is deservedly proclaimed both wise in heart and mighty in strength? Do you suppose they are the apostles, concerning whom it is rightly understood when elsewhere it says: “The mountains shall be moved into the heart of the sea” (Ps. 45), that is, they shall pass from the Jews into the midst of the nations? They indeed are mountains, but they are not the only ones whom God removed. Moses also, and this David, and [Col. 0136A] all the prophets are mountains—not because of any bodily bulk, but because of the eminence of the Scriptures which, under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, they wrote.

How, from where, and to where did God transfer these mountains? Clearly, by giving kinds of languages he transferred them: that is, through their interpreters he translated their Scriptures from the one Hebrew language into Greek and Latin. By a marvelous judgment it came about that all nations should read and know, while those whom he overthrew in his wrath should not know—namely, the Jews, among whom these same Scriptures had been deposited, and whose eyes he blinded because of their unbelief. Nor did he overthrow them only in this manner; he also scattered them captive among all nations, so that they now have neither prophet, nor prince, nor leader. This is well understood in what he immediately says: “He shakes the earth [Col. 0136B] out of its place, and its pillars shall be shaken.”

Then he immediately adds: “He commands the sun, and it does not rise; and he shuts up the stars as under a seal” (Job 9). For they possess and carry with them in captivity the Scriptures of the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms; but they do not possess Christ, toward whom all the Scriptures tend. What is it to possess [added: the Scriptures] but not to possess the intention of the Scriptures, except to possess the heaven but not the sun? And what is it to read the prophets and refuse to understand them, except to keep the stars shut up as though under a seal? God commands this—that this sun should not rise for them—and for this reason shuts stars of this kind as though under a seal, because their blindness arises not so much from ignorance as [Col. 0136C] from envy. Therefore we safely—indeed, laudably—assent to this command by which he commands the sun not to rise for them, saying with the Psalmist in the person of the sun itself: “Let their eyes be darkened that they may not see, and bow down their back always” (Ps. 68).

## Chapter XVIII

Concerning Solomon’s statement, “Who has raised up all the ends of the earth?”—what his name is, and what the name of his Son is, if you know it; likewise, “Woe to one alone, because when he falls he has no one to lift him up,” and the rest, after which he adds: “A threefold cord is not easily broken.”

Solomon expressed the Son of the Father in such unmistakable language that the aforesaid enemies of truth cannot dissemble when they hear the distinction of persons within the unity of the Godhead. For he says: “Who has ascended into heaven, or who has descended? Who has held the wind in his hands? Who has bound up the waters as in a garment? Who has raised up all the ends of the earth? What is his name, and what is the name of his Son, if you know?” Immediately he adds: “Every word of God is fire-tested; he is a shield to those who hope in him” (Prov. 30).

This is the same as if he said more plainly: The name of his Son is the Word, and every word of God flows from this fountain—the word which “holy men spoke, inspired by the Holy Spirit” (2 Pet. 1). It protects those who hope in it, as did he who said: “Remember your word to your servant, in which you gave me hope” (Ps. 118).

The same Solomon, desiring that a human being should never be without companionship, without meditation upon the [Col. 0137A] word of God, said: “Woe to one alone, because, when he falls, he has no one to lift him up. And if two sleep together, they will keep one another warm; how shall one be warmed alone? And if someone prevails against one, two withstand him.” He immediately added: “A threefold cord is not easily broken” (Eccl. 4).

Is not this saying a star shut up, as it were, under a seal, according to the Scripture mentioned above? Suppose one of those who, in Solomon’s own sense, say, “I am the most foolish of men, and the wisdom of men is not with me; I have not learned wisdom, and I have not known the knowledge of the holy ones” (Prov. 30), is so unlearned and illiterate that he cannot meditate upon the word of God or sleep with it in that sleep of which the beloved says in the Song: “I sleep, but my heart watches” (Song 5). Yet at least he can hold in memory the name of the Lord, in which the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is sealed. Plainly this is “the threefold cord, which is not easily broken” (Eccl. 4). Let him sleep with this name, and he will not be alone.

Speaking of these two, he did not say, “One of these two will never fall”; rather, he said: “If one falls, he shall be supported by the other.” Nor, I say, did he say, “A threefold cord is never broken”; he said, “A threefold cord is not easily broken.” For it never happens that one who has love or meditation upon the name of the Lord falls without having for a time forgotten the threefold cord on which he depended. David too fell. Yet when he falls, he shall rise, his strength restored through invocation of that same [Col. 0137C] name of the Lord. Thus comes about what is said here: “And if someone prevails against one, two withstand him.”

Hence elsewhere he says: “The name of the Lord is a most strong tower: the righteous runs to it and shall be exalted. The wealth of the rich is his fortified city, and like a strong wall surrounding him” (Prov. 18).

## Chapter XIX

That there are three things—faith, hope, and charity—through which a human being is brought to the likeness of God, according to his declaration, “Let us make man in our image and likeness”; and that Solomon composed three books, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs, according to these three.

There are three things through which a human being is brought to God’s likeness, according to his declaration: “Let us make [Col. 0137D] man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1). These three are faith, hope, and charity. For a human being was created in God’s image insofar as he is rational. But he attains the likeness of the same creating Trinity by possessing these three: faith, hope, and charity.

According to these three Solomon composed three books: the book of Parables, or Proverbs; Ecclesiastes; and the Song of Songs. He wrote Proverbs in order to instruct faith; Ecclesiastes, to strengthen hope; and the Song of Songs, to expand charity. Certainly all divinely inspired Scripture tends toward this same end; but in the order of these three books it is especially delightful to observe that they were composed or arranged according to the order of these three virtues: faith, hope, and charity.

By falling away from these, the first man lost the glory of God’s likeness, in such an order that he lost charity, did not retain hope, and did not possess faith. For love of God was first required from him, in that God made him unlike all living creatures. Since no helper like him was found for him, God said: “Let us make him a helper like himself,” namely, for the propagation of offspring so numerous and of such blessedness that they might be like angels; “and he took him and placed him in the paradise of delight.” For such great benefits he rendered no service of love, no utterance of thanksgiving.

Then hope was required of him in the setting forth of the command: “From every tree of paradise eat, but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil do not eat.” [Col. 0138B] For the rational man ought to have hoped, saying: If God has bestowed such great things freely, will he not give greater things if I keep his commands? But he did not hope in the Lord; pleasing himself, as though free and wishing to be as God. For unless he had harbored this swelling pride within, he would not have yielded so easily when tempted from without.

Faith was required of him when God said: “On whatever day you eat from it, you shall die by death” (Gen. 2). But he did not believe this saying; indeed, he believed the serpent more when it said: “You shall by no means die” (Gen. 3), and obeyed the credulous woman’s evil voice more than God’s voice. Thus the old Adam, falling away from charity, hope, and faith, defrauded both himself and his posterity and removed them far from the likeness of the blessed Trinity. Conversely, the new Adam restored us, by the reciprocal steps of faith, hope, and charity, to that same likeness of God. And all divinely inspired Scripture, as has already been said, intends this; but these three books of Solomon do so especially, or more plainly. To demonstrate this, it is pleasing to linger for a little while.

## Chapter XX

Concerning the statement in Proverbs, “Wisdom built herself a house; she cut out seven columns”; and, “The Lord possessed me at the beginning of his ways,” and the rest through, “I was with him, arranging all things”; and that “In the beginning was the Word; all things were made through him” has one and the same meaning.

After a few preliminary words, which serve to win attention, receptiveness, and goodwill, the first task in Proverbs is to cleanse the soul through moral teaching, so that it may receive the mystery of faith. It begins thus: “My son, if sinners entice you, do not consent to them. If they say: Come with us, let us lie in wait for blood” (Prov. 1), and so forth. Whoever considers this carefully soon perceives that this is its purpose: that the vessel may be cleansed from the mire of sin and from love of the world, so that it may receive the precious substance of faith; for otherwise this cannot happen.

Therefore the Lord himself said to the Jews: “How can you believe, who receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from God alone?” (John 5). Much more could he have said: How can you believe, who lie in wait for blood, hide snares against the innocent, and say: “Let us swallow him alive like hell [Col. 0139A] and whole, like one going down into the pit; we shall find every precious substance” (Prov. 1), according to that saying: “This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and the inheritance shall be ours” (Mark 12).

Elsewhere the Evangelist says: “But Jesus himself did not entrust himself to them, because he knew all men, and because he had no need that anyone should bear witness concerning man; for he himself knew what was in man” (Matt. 2). Since, therefore, there is no open place for faith unless the vessels are first cleansed from love of the world, from avarice—which is idolatry (Eph. 5)—and from other criminal vices, especially from the “prudence of the flesh, which is hostile to God” (Rom. 8), and from the esteem of worldly wisdom, which ought rather to be called babbling loquacity than wisdom, he beautifully first recalls from such things the son whom he wishes to call to the understanding of faith.

He repeatedly declares that the same worldly wisdom must be avoided, twice under the name of a harlot, first beginning thus: “The lips of a harlot drip honeycomb, and her throat is more glossy than oil” (Prov. 5). Then he repeats it thus: “Say to wisdom: You are my sister; and call prudence your friend, that it may guard you from the strange woman and from the foreign woman who makes her words sweet. For from the window of my house I looked through the lattice,” and so forth, through: “For she has cast down many wounded; and all the strongest have been slain by her. Her house is the way of hell, penetrating the inner chambers of death” (Prov. 7). These words in a marvelous manner both mark, in the literal sense, the hateful shamelessness of a prostitute, and in the mystery especially detest the ambitious [Col. 0139C] and windy loquacity of worldly wisdom.

Then at last, believing herself accepted by those by whom she has been heard and whose goodwill she has won, she again cries out among other things: “Hear, for I shall speak of great kings, and my lips shall open to proclaim what is right; my throat shall meditate truth” (Prov. 8). Of what great matters do you speak? What right things, what truth will you proclaim? “The Lord,” she says, “possessed me at the beginning of his ways, before he made anything from the beginning. From eternity I was established, and from ancient times, before the earth was made. When he prepared the heavens, I was present,” and so forth, through: “Therefore now, my sons, hear me” (ibid.).

After inserting a few words, she says: “Wisdom built herself a house; she cut out seven columns; [Col. 0139D] she sacrificed her victims, mixed her wine, and set her table” (Prov. 9). Are not these things the same things which John the Evangelist declared more openly in the clearest voice, saying: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made; and the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1)? The voices, names, and words differ a little, but the things are the same.

Here there is Wisdom; there, the Word. Here there is the beginning of ways; there, the beginning. Here Wisdom says, “I had been conceived”; there the Evangelist says not “was made,” but “the Word was.” Here she says, “I was with him arranging all things”; there it is said: “The Word was made flesh; all things were made through him.” Here it is said: “Wisdom built herself a house”; there it is said: “The Word was made flesh,” and the incarnate Word himself calls his flesh his temple. Here it is said: “She cut out seven columns”; there it is certain that the seven spirits dwell in the temple of the Lord’s body. Here it is said: “She sacrificed her victims, mixed her wine, and set her table”; there this was so done, as we have experienced and as all experience: he gave his own body over to death and, in commemoration of that death, daily sets before us bread and wine—his body and blood.

## Chapter XXI

That, after the likeness of a weary traveler, the frequent interruption of books relieves the weary mind of the writer.

Like a weary traveler, I am compelled to sit down and finish this book. I am like one who, on a journey, had perhaps marked out a stopping-place, thinking it a nearby place which he could reach before sunset, and thinking a journey of two or three days to be a journey of one day. Something like this has happened to me. Seeking some image of the Holy Trinity in this mirror of the three virtues—faith, hope, and charity—I set the foot [Col. 0140C] of my mind and the course of my tongue upon Solomon’s three books, thinking that my purpose could be accomplished in the briefest course.

But behold, I see that it cannot be done so briefly; otherwise I shall offend any wise judge, any examiner of good discourse, who, attracted by the good flavor of our proposition but not satisfied by its full abundance, and therefore all the more irritated, will be indignant and say against me something like this:

> Mountains are in labor; a ridiculous mouse will be born.  
> —Horace, *Ars Poetica*

Therefore, like the one already described, who, despairing of reaching his intended lodging, lies down in the middle of the journey, I shall reserve what remains of the road for a future day and now make an end here of the present battle, lest it be much longer than those preceding it. I invoke the Holy Spirit, whose annual feast now returning stirs us to praise his coming, and who likewise “makes glad, like the rush of a river, the city”—that is, the Church—“of God” (Ps. 45), so that under his guidance this traveler may arrive where he tends: “One thing,” he says, “I have asked of the Lord; this I shall seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, that I may behold the delight of the Lord and visit his temple” (Ps. 26).

## Book Seven

[Col. 0141]

## Chapter I

Again concerning the treasure of faith, hope, and charity in Solomon’s three books: that one should rejoice over that treasure of wisdom, but fear because so wise a man fell, or could fall.

Let us likewise rejoice over finding treasure in this portion of the field: in Solomon’s three books, in the consideration of these three things—faith, hope, and charity—through which a human being is restored to a certain likeness of the blessed Trinity, a likeness which, as was said above, he lost in Adam, while God’s purpose remains: “Let us make man in our image and likeness.”

Let us rejoice, I say; but our joy is disturbed and troubled by an unpleasant recollection: the recollection of so great a man’s ruin—that a sanctuary of such wisdom fell so far that, through love of women, he could serve foreign gods in his old age. As Scripture says: “And when he was already old, his heart was corrupted through women so that he followed foreign gods” (3 Kings 11). Does not the recollection of so great and so wise a man, so horribly corrupted in his old age, make the judgment of God fearful to us?

There is indeed a consoling opinion held by some: that he repented and composed these books after his repentance. Nevertheless, this fall makes the tablets [i.e. the Scriptural record] terrifying, in which so great a column fell. For it was not after he fell in old age, but before he fell, that he received such wisdom in youth, when the Lord said to him: “Behold, I have done for you according to your words, and I have given you a wise and understanding heart, so that no one like you has been before you, nor shall any arise after you” (3 Kings 3).

What, then, can we say here? Truly nothing except something like the Apostle’s words: “How incomprehensible are your judgments, and unsearchable your ways” (Rom. 11), O Lord. We must be humbled or bowed beneath him, beneath whom, as blessed Job says, those who bear the world are bowed (Job 9). For even if we understand anything concerning the Most High, who is wiser than this man?

## Chapter II

Concerning the co-eternity of the Father and the Son, according to Wisdom’s words, “Before anything was made, I had already been conceived,” and the rest; and concerning the Incarnation of the same Wisdom, according to the words, “Wisdom built herself a house,” and the remainder.

However matters may have gone with Solomon, wherever such a tree may have fallen—as it says: “If a tree falls to the south or to the north, in whatever place it falls, there it shall be” (Eccl. 11)—whatever his condition at the end, and wherever he may now be, we know and understand that the fruit of such a tree is good, greatly effective for the life of faith, from which the righteous lives (Hab. 2; Rom. 1).

For in the clear name of Wisdom, saying: “From eternity and from ancient times [Col. 0142A] I was established; and before anything was made I had already been conceived; and before all things I was brought forth” (Prov. 8), she declares the Son of God to be co-eternal with God the Father. Wisdom herself requires all the children whom she receives to believe this, saying afterwards: “Therefore now, my sons, hear me,” and so forth, through: “But whoever sins against me injures his own soul; all who hate me love death” (ibid.).

For these sayings—which it seemed far too long to transcribe in full—proclaim both the divinity of Jesus Christ, Son of God, co-eternal with the Father, and that he was born before all ages and without beginning. And the words immediately following, “Wisdom built herself a house; she cut out seven columns” (Prov. 9), and the rest which we sampled above, are spoken mystically concerning the Incarnation of the same Word.

Truly, then: “Whoever,” she says, “sins against me injures his own soul,” or, to put it another way, “all who hate me love death.” For they are heretics. And who so loves death and, by loving death, injures his own soul—or, to speak in David’s terms, David who preceded Solomon, who so loves “iniquity” that he “hates his own soul” (Ps. 10)—as does the heretic and the Jew, who so eagerly and diligently exerts himself in disputes about words in order to seem able to establish rationally that Christ began to exist from Mary and was conceived from Joseph’s seed?

They are inexcusable because, as the sequence of Holy Scripture here relates, Lady Wisdom, after she “built herself a house, sacrificed victims, mixed wine, and set her table,” sent her maidservants to summon people to the citadel and walls of the city. She not only said, “Whoever is little”—that is, humble—“let him come to me”; she also spoke to the foolish: “Come, eat my bread and drink the wine which I have mixed for you. Leave childishness behind, and live; walk in the ways of prudence.”

But what follows? “He who instructs a mocker does an injury to himself, and he who rebukes the ungodly brings a stain upon himself” (Prov. 9). Did not those maidservants whom Lady Wisdom sent experience this? They wished to instruct the mocker, namely the Jewish people, and suffered the injury which we read of and which Wisdom herself foretold: “Behold,” she says, “I send to you [Col. 0142D] prophets, wise men, and scribes; and some of them you will kill and crucify, and some of them you will scourge in your synagogues and persecute from city to city” (Matt. 13).

They wished to rebuke the ungodly, namely the Pharisaic assembly, and brought upon themselves the stain from which our eyes recoil: they blasphemed the Holy Spirit speaking in them, as we have in the Acts of the Apostles. For example: “They contradicted what was being said by Paul, blaspheming” (Acts 13).

What then follows? “Do not,” she says, “rebuke a mocker, lest he hate you. Rebuke a wise man, and he will love you” (Prov. 9). This they did, saying: “It was necessary that the Word of God be spoken first to you; but since you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the nations. Jews ask for signs, and Greeks seek wisdom” (1 Cor. 1). The Jews did this inquisitively when they said: “What sign do you perform? What work do you do?” (John 6). For this reason they are denoted by the name “mocker,” like that Herod who wished to see the Lord Jesus, hoping “to see some sign done by him” (Luke 23).

The Greeks, however, diligently sought wisdom, found it, and loved it; summoned to its citadel or the walls of its city, they came. Behold, they eat from its table and drink its wine. Thus “wisdom was justified by her children” (Matt. 11), because she neither neglected to teach the wise man—that is, the well-disposed hearer—nor passed over the mocker in such a way that he could excuse himself on grounds of ignorance.

## Chapter III

Concerning what follows in the same book of Proverbs: how almost the whole discourse is, as it were, in conflict through the opposition of righteous and wicked persons, who oppose and fight one another, according to the incarnate Wisdom’s saying: “I came not to send peace, but a sword.”

Behold, as I think, the door has been opened and understanding illuminated for this breadth or multitude of Solomon’s Proverbs. For what a great and marvelous spectacle you have here, whoever gives attention! What an onset, what a conflict, is this discourse of the wisest man, consisting in the opposition of two adversaries who fight each other: righteous and wicked. Through their antitheses almost the whole book proceeds:

> “A wise son makes his father glad, but a foolish son is his mother’s sorrow. Treasures of wickedness shall not profit; but righteousness shall deliver from death. The Lord shall not afflict the soul of the righteous with hunger, but he shall overthrow the snares of the wicked” (Prov. 10).

As he begins to set forth such manifold oppositions of righteous and wicked, or wise and foolish, look with attentive eyes; then you will take great delight in this spectacle, if you know the sure boundaries of righteous and wicked, or of righteousness and wickedness. What is our righteousness but our faith? Or who is righteous but one who believes? For “the righteous,” Scripture says, “lives by faith” (Hab. 2). Unbelief, conversely, is unrighteousness, and the unbelieving mocker of the righteous is wicked.

Therefore, after the building of the house which Wisdom built for herself through the mystery of the Incarnation, it is most beautiful in all the divisions or oppositions of this book to understand that sword of which incarnate Wisdom herself said: “I came not to send peace, but a sword” (Matt. 10). From that time onward, and much more than before, righteous and wicked, wise and foolish, divided against one another, were made manifest by their contrary pursuits.

In this rational consideration it is likewise not least delightful that, at the beginning of such oppositions, the opposing mothers are first placed in view: on this side Wisdom, mother of the righteous; on that, Folly, mother of the wicked. For he says: “The beginning of wisdom is fear of the Lord, and knowledge of holy things is prudence. For through me your days shall be multiplied and years of life added to you.” He immediately adds: “The foolish and clamorous woman, full of enticements and knowing absolutely nothing, sat at the doors of her house, on a seat in a high place of the city, to call those passing along the way and proceeding on their journey. Who is little? Let him turn aside to me. And she spoke to the senseless: Stolen waters are sweeter, and hidden bread more pleasant” (Prov. [Col. 0144B] 9).

By the name of the foolish woman he undoubtedly denotes the shameless, excessively talkative, indeed deceptive wisdom of the world, exalting itself against God’s wisdom, especially from the time when that Wisdom built herself a house, as has been said above, sacrificed her victims, and sent her maidservants to summon people to the citadel and walls of the city.

How different—indeed, how contrary—were or are the ends of the children of each, namely the children of Wisdom and the children of Folly, the almost entire sequence of the following book intends to proclaim through antitheses such as this: “A wise son makes his father glad, but a foolish son is his mother’s sorrow” (Prov. 10). Let us lift our eyes straight across the whole world, even to the ends of the earth, where the apostles’ sound went forth, where the martyrs’ blood was poured out, wherever the wisdom of orthodox Fathers contended in speech and writing for the glory of the house which Wisdom built for herself and of its seven columns, against the folly of the Jews, the impiety of pagans, and the wickedness of heretics. It is plain that everything is full of the evidences of these things which are spoken to this end through so many opposed sayings.

## Chapter IV

Again concerning the opposition of the righteous person, who lives by faith, and the wicked person, that is, one who does not possess faith; and what, according to the same book of Parables, is the end of each.

Mindful of our purpose, we shall say again that this book of Parables or Proverbs instructs faith; the following Ecclesiastes strengthens hope; and the third, *Sirasirim*, that is, the Song of Songs, delights—or perhaps expands—charity. Through these three a human being is restored to the likeness which the Trinity proposed when it said: “Let us make man in our image and likeness.”

Faith is plainly necessary for eternal salvation: faith confesses that the Wisdom speaking here—“I was with him arranging all things” (Prov. 8)—is uncreated, never was not, and nevertheless knows that this same “Wisdom built herself a house.” This has no other meaning than the Evangelist’s words: “In the beginning was the Word; all things were made through him; and the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1).

Whoever faithfully believes these things in the heart [Col. 0145A] unto righteousness (Rom. 10; Prov. 8), and confesses them with the mouth unto salvation, is the wise son who gladdens his father; the son whom righteousness shall deliver from death; whose soul the Lord shall not afflict with hunger; whose hand prepares and gathers riches in harvest; over whose head is the Lord’s blessing; whose memory is with praises; whose mouth is a fountain of life; in whose lips wisdom is found; whose faith is the rich man’s substance and city of strength; whose work is for life; whose tongue is chosen silver; whom the Lord’s blessing makes rich, and to whom affliction shall not be joined; to whom his desire shall be given, and who shall be as an everlasting foundation.

Conversely, the wicked person, who is called—and is—wicked precisely because he does not possess, indeed hates and persecutes, this righteousness of faith, shall be as a passing storm and shall not remain; his years shall be shortened; and all the things most abundantly expounded from Scripture against him shall be fulfilled. The last of these in this book is the saying concerning Antichrist, prince of the foolish or wicked, and how foolish he appeared after being lifted up on high; for if he had understood, he would have put his hand over his mouth.

In the three things set in opposition to this one lies the consummation of the praise of the righteous, when he says: “The lion, strongest of beasts, will fear no encounter with anyone”—in whom we understand Christ himself; “the cock, girded in the loins,” which is every order of preachers; “and the ram, and there is no king who can resist him” (Prov. 30), in whom we understand all prelates who have ruled, or do rule, Christ’s churches well. No persecutor has been able to conquer the strength of their faith, nor will that one be able to do so who, after he has been lifted up on high, as has already been said, will appear foolish; in him lies the consummation of the reproach of the wicked.

## Chapter V

Again concerning faith: that it is the strong woman of whom it is written at the end of the same book: “Who shall find a strong woman? Her price is from afar and from the uttermost ends of the earth.”

May my discourse be pleasing to you, holy Trinity; may my praise be sweet to you, O likeness of the holy Trinity—the threefold power: faith, hope, and charity. My soul has “tasted and seen that your merchandise is good” (Prov. 31). And now I hasten toward the end of this book of Proverbs, in which, as I have already said once and again [Col. 0145D], there are teachings concerning faith—as though God had scattered for me, along this road, some light of understanding, and I had clarified something from these depths according to my purpose. And I desire to enter the assembly where the Preacher, Ecclesiastes, sits, wearing the crown of hope—that is, holding the book in which the most wise king, seated as preacher over youths and adolescents, chiefly insists on proving that youth, pleasure, and all their instruments are vain, whereas the fear of the Lord and the keeping of his commandments are the whole being of man, as he says at the end of that very volume: “Fear God and keep his commandments, for this is the whole of man” (Eccles. 12).

But what shall I do? For, at this ending of Proverbs, my mind’s foot is held fast by the worthy praise of a certain great and memorable woman [Col. 0146A], which begins thus: “Who shall find a strong woman? Her price is far away and from the uttermost bounds; the heart of her husband trusts in her, and he shall not lack spoils” (Prov. 31). Who, I ask, is this strong woman? We know indeed that she is the holy Church; but we inquire further. What is the reason that generations of so many ages, such multitudes of human beings or souls, are called one woman, and that out of all of them there is one Church, having God as her husband, whose heart trusts in her? What, I say, brings this about, if not one faith? Finally, just as it is said in Ecclesiastes, and as we recalled above: “Fear God and keep his commandments: this is the whole of man,” so one may rightly say: Hold the one Catholic faith; for this is the whole Church.

Thus [Col. 0146B] let us read and understand here the praise of the strong woman as truly the praise of faith; for assuredly, according to faith, the whole Church, as has already been said, is called one woman, and her husband, who praises her, “whose heart trusts in her,” is the Lord God himself. Who will find this? Certainly, no one fails to find the Church spread throughout the whole world, unless he is such a person as closes his eyes so as not to see it; but few find the secret of faith. For it is neither found nor recognized otherwise than through the Holy Spirit. Therefore he said, “Who will find?” and immediately, wishing to awaken fitting admiration in us, he says: “Her price is far away and from the uttermost bounds.” Understanding this, the apostle Paul said: “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the proof of things not seen” [Col. 0146C] (Heb. 11).

O how far away is this substance, for which this proof is brought forth from the utmost bounds—a proof of what does not appear and is not seen, so many mountains and hills of visible things lying between! For example, the renowned fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and those descended from them—of whom the Apostle says that they were as the stars of heaven in multitude and as the innumerable sand on the shore of the sea—all died according to faith, not having received the promises, but seeing them from afar, greeting them, and confessing “that they are strangers and sojourners upon the earth” (1 Pet. 1). To us also, who are indeed nearer to the reality in time, yet do not see the reality itself, the apostle Peter speaks: “May you be found unto praise and glory and honor at the revelation of Jesus Christ; though you have not seen him, you love him; and even now, though not seeing, yet believing, you rejoice” (ibid.). O then, how far away, as has been said, and from what uttermost bounds is the price of this woman—the preciousness of this Church, the faith of this active woman—who looks not upon things seen but upon things unseen.

## CHAPTER VI

Likewise, concerning the dignity of the same faith: how it is said, “The heart of her husband trusts in her, and he shall not lack spoils; she shall render him good and not evil all the days of her life.”

What glory, then, does she deserve in the sight of God? He says: “The heart of her husband trusts in her, and he shall not lack spoils.” The saying is plain, but must be heard with reverence: God, exalted and immeasurable, is the husband of this spouse, namely faith, and “his heart trusts in her” [Col. 0147A]. How does it trust? In this way, assuredly: that he does not hesitate to show his secrets to her. I shall say more, according to the authority of Scripture: he cannot hide his secrets from her. For he spoke thus to Abraham, in whom he had found this strong woman, this faith: “Can I conceal from Abraham what I am about to do?” (Gen. 18). “For I know that he will command his children and his household after him to keep the way of the Lord.” Great is the confidence of so great a husband in the steadfastness of his most steadfast spouse: he cannot conceal his secrets from her.

But let us consider further the force of the expression. For he did not say, “Her husband trusts in her,” but “the heart of her husband trusts in her.” Indeed, this love is usefully weighed, especially if you do not overlook where, when, and by what event such a statement was proved. For in all the holy patriarchs and prophets faith experienced that God, her husband, trusted in her; [Col. 0147B] [66] for he revealed his secrets to her, and she herself both spoke wisely through their mouths and sealed them prudently and strongly. But there is a place, and there was a time, concerning which you may truly say not merely, “Her husband trusts in her,” but—what sounds more forceful and penetrates more deeply into the innermost mind—“the heart of her husband trusts in her.”

Where do you find this? Certainly in the soul of the holy Virgin Mary. There faith experienced what it heard here concerning itself: “The heart of her husband trusts in her.” For there her husband opened his heart to her. By what opening? Surely one great and ineffable: so that the heart of this husband might accomplish in her what he had foretold through David’s mouth: “My heart has uttered a good word; I speak my works to the king. My tongue is the pen of a swift-writing scribe” (Ps. 44). Thus he opened his heart to her: he sent into the mind and womb of the most faithful Virgin the very substance of the eternal Word, conceived in his heart and begotten from his heart before the ages [Col. 0147C]. Through that very faith of which the discourse now speaks, she conceived such great divine mysteries as the angel announced them. For she received God in her chaste womb and, blessed for ever, bore for us God and man [addition: “bore”].

O holy faith, then, how true is this saying concerning you: “The heart of her husband trusts in her, and he shall not lack spoils.” What spoils, or what kind of spoils, except the words of the Lord, the words of her husband? For thus she herself spoke through David’s mouth: “I shall rejoice over your words as one who finds great spoils” (Ps. 118). Therefore “he shall not lack spoils”: that is, so intimate a husband makes his own words intelligible to the faith known to him, certain of what immediately follows: “She shall render him good, and not evil, all the days of her life” (Prov. 31).

For she is not like that woman previously branded with infamy: “a foolish and clamorous woman, full of enticements and knowing absolutely nothing” (Prov. 9)—a woman, I say, not strong, indeed the opposite of this strong woman. For she is impious heresy, and she has rendered, like Jewish faithlessness or the synagogue of Satan (Apoc. 2), evil and not good, all the days of her life; for she always resists the truth with a stiff neck.

## CHAPTER VII [Col. 0148A]

What good, or what kind of good, faith—or the faithful Church—renders, so that the heart of her husband rightly trusts in her, according to the Hebrew alphabet, whose individual letters are prefixed to individual verses.

What good, or what kind of good, has faith—or the faithful Church—rendered and does it render, that “the heart of her husband” may rightly “trust in her”? Let us ask this Hebrew alphabet, whose individual letters are prefixed to individual verses: Aleph, Beth, Gimel, Daleth, He, Vau, Zain, Heth, Teth, Jod, Caph, Lamed, Mem, Nun, Samech, Ain, Phe, Zade, Coph, Res, Sin, Tau. These are the twenty-two Hebrew letters with which, among them, all Scripture is woven.

What then is indicated to us by the fact that individual letters are prefixed to individual statements, except that all Scripture divinely inspired [Col. 0148B] is the good work of this strong woman, the work of faith which she has rendered to her husband? For not without reason, but as a signification of great meaning, the names of individual letters are prefixed to individual statements in certain Psalms, in the Lamentations of Jeremiah, in his prayer, and also at this end of Solomon’s Proverbs. The meaning in question can readily be recognized from interpretations of the names themselves, as the illustrious man, blessed Jerome, skilled in the Hebrew language, interpreted them.

For he interprets Aleph as “teaching”; Beth, “house”; Gimel, “fullness”; Daleth, “of tablets”; He, “this”; Vau and Zain, “these”; Heth, “life”; Teth, “good”; Jod, “beginning”; Caph, “hand”; Lamed, “heart”; Mem, “from these”; Nun, “eternal”; Samech, “help”; Ain, [Col. 0148C] “fountain”; Phe, “mouth”—not from *os*, “bone,” but from *os*, “mouth”; Zade, “justice”; Coph, “calling”; Res, “head”; Sin, “teeth”; Tau, “signs.”

Let us first set down the direct wording of this interpretation, and then form a construction of that wording according to the sense contained in it:

> Teaching of the house; fullness of tablets;  
> this and these: life, the good beginning, hand of heart.  
> From these: eternal help, fountain of the mouth of justice,  
> calling of the head, signs of teeth.

This is the wording, which is construed thus. Holy Scripture, which is faith’s work, the good work which Catholic faith has rendered to her husband God, is the teaching of the house—the teaching of the Church, which is the house of God. It is the fullness of the tablets, the fullness of the Law: that is, of the ten commandments written on tablets of stone by the finger of God. What are this fullness and this teaching [Col. 0148D] if not life? For the word of God is that in which a human being lives, as he says: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word which proceeds from the mouth of God” (Matt. 4). Therefore: life and the good beginning—understand, the beginning of eternal life. For here in sacred Scripture is the beginning of life: that we may see and walk by faith, not yet the consummation in which we see face to face (1 Cor. 13).

The hand of the heart—that is, the activity of holy meditation—is this teaching of the house, this fullness of the Law. From these comes eternal help. What is truer than this? For through sacred Scripture we learn here what we shall know eternally. Without doubt this very Scripture is for us the fountain of the mouth of justice. From it we draw that which we confess with the mouth unto [Col. 0149A] salvation, and by confessing which we are justified. Holy Scripture itself is the calling of the head for us, because through it Christ the head calls us to himself, that we may deserve to become his members. All these are signs of teeth, because these elements can sound only when formed by teeth and the plectrum of the tongue; thus all Holy Scripture, written in such manifold fashion from so few elements, may be read or heard.

## CHAPTER VIII

On the wondrous power of faith, especially in this saying: “She made fine linen and sold it, and delivered a girdle to the Canaanite.”

Among the other sections of this beautiful praise, since it is not our purpose to examine all of them—for it would be far too long—I cannot allow this to pass untouched [Col. 0149B]: “She made fine linen and sold it, and delivered a girdle to the Canaanite.” The other statements indeed are very splendid and, according to the metaphor of the prophetic and strong woman, highly relevant to the matter or mystery—from the saying, “She sought wool and flax, and worked with the counsel of her hands” (Prov. 31), to the words, “She made fine linen and sold it.” But this saying, “and delivered a girdle to the Canaanite,” stands far above the metaphor.

For what? Does a worthy woman, just as she is accustomed to seek wool and flax and work with the counsel of her hands; just as she is accustomed to bring her bread from afar and to rise by night—that is, early in the morning—carefully considering how to give prey to her household and provisions to her maidservants; just as she is accustomed [Col. 0149C] to open her hand to the needy and stretch out her palms to the poor, and in these and other ways to busy herself constantly with service—is she also accustomed to deliver a girdle to the Canaanite? Therefore this stands above the metaphor.

Let us apply diligence and, as in the other matters, seek understanding in this one also, especially because of what was said in the earlier [67] parables: “An intelligent servant is acceptable to a king; a useless one shall bear his wrath” (Prov. 14). Therefore we say with a voice of thanksgiving that this strong woman “delivered a girdle to the Canaanite” as often as mighty faith renders acceptable to God the Most High, the great King, someone who had been contemptible among human beings.

For the Canaanite was contemptible—indeed, accursed by God—while he was still in the loins of his father Ham, when Noah said: “Cursed be Canaan; he shall be a servant of servants to his brothers.” Again, a second time: “Blessed be the Lord God of Shem; let Canaan be his servant.” And a third time: “May God enlarge Japheth, and may he dwell in the tents of Shem, and may Canaan be his servant” [Col. 0149D] (Gen. 9). Very contemptible, therefore, was Canaan, whose seven nations, when the children of Israel entered, the land had to vomit out by God’s judgment (Lev. 20), as it did.

On the other hand, faith is very powerful and very noble: it could give a girdle to such a Canaanite, or to anyone similarly lowly according to the ignobility of the world, so that, because of the merit of the faith which he received, he may walk girded—while the children of the kingdom who have no faith lie fallen and ungirded, or are even carried away into captivity [Col. 0150A]. As holy Job says: “He loosens the belt of kings and girds their loins with a cord” (Job 12 [printed: 10]). Does not the Apostle also say this? “God,” he says, “has chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; God has chosen the weak things of the world to confound the strong; and the ignoble and contemptible things of the world God has chosen, and the things which are not, in order to destroy the things which are” (1 Cor. 1).

All these—the foolish, weak, ignoble, contemptible, and virtually non-existent—you rightly understand under the single name “Canaanites.” Lady Faith could clothe such a one in her fine linen and, according to her will, give him a girdle; and she did so, and she alone did this, so that one regarded as dishonorable in the world walks honored before the eyes of the Lord and likewise in the sight of great and small persons [Col. 0150B] who belong to the household of that same faith.

## CHAPTER IX

How the following book, Ecclesiastes, pertains to the instruction of hope: “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity.”

The discourse we have pursued thus far has shown that the purpose of Proverbs is directed toward the instruction of the faith by which the righteous person lives. Now, according to our purpose, it must be shown that the purpose of the book of Ecclesiastes is to furnish a sure rationale for hope: namely, to show in what a rational human being ought not to hope, and in what he ought to place his hope. It begins to do this in this way: “Vanity of vanities, said Ecclesiastes: vanity of vanities, and all is vanity. What advantage has a man from all his labor at which he labors under the sun?” [Col. 0150C] (Eccles. 1)—understand: except vanity?

Thus, beginning with the sun, which is the most beautiful work of the Creator and the highest among all the things from which mortal life subsists and obtains its pleasures, he indicts all things of vanity—and with a true indictment, indeed. “For,” says the Apostle, “the form of this world passes away” (1 Cor. 7).

Not content with having said once, “Vanity of vanities,” he repeated it a second and a third time: “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity,” so that you may observe how earnestly he speaks and acts. For he has prefaced the statement with the authority of royal title and the city of Jerusalem. He says: “The words of Ecclesiastes, son of David, king of Jerusalem” (Eccles. 1). By three great names he prepared authority for this book for the benefit of its hearers, naming himself Ecclesiastes—that is, Preacher—Son of David, and [Col. 0150D] King of Jerusalem.

What is the first thing under the sun in which covetous man has placed his hope? Surely the earth. And in this there is astonishing madness: although the habitation of this earth was given to a man driven from the felicity of paradise as a punishment—namely, that he should work it in the sweat of his face—he strives to command it as though for glory. Is this not vanity when he says, “I, a man born from earth and destined to die tomorrow—this much land is mine, and these territories are mine”? Thus he rightly indicts first the desire for, or possession of, land as vanity, saying: “A generation passes, and a generation comes, but the earth stands for ever” (Eccles. 1).

It is as though he openly said: In vain have covetous men striven to subjugate land to themselves and join field to field, even to the boundary of a place—sometimes with horrible conflict, even to the shedding of much blood—for while so many generations pass away and so many arrive, the earth remains here. It did not follow those who have already passed away; nor will it follow those who arrive or are to arrive. A generation has passed away: just as by being born it brought nothing into this world, so by dying it could take nothing away. And the generation that comes—or we ourselves who now exist—may say, in the Apostle’s words: “As we brought nothing into this world, without doubt neither can we take anything away” [Col. 0151A] (1 Tim. 6).

In the saying, “A generation passes, and a generation comes,” and in the remaining things that follow, wherever he indicts vanity, understand wisely that his intention is the same as that which the same Apostle, after saying—as we have recalled—“For we brought nothing into this world, and without doubt neither can we take anything away,” immediately expressed: “But having food and clothing, let us be content with these. For those who desire to become rich fall into temptation and the snare of the devil and into many useless and harmful desires, which drown people in destruction and perdition. For covetousness is the root of all evils; pursuing it, some have wandered from the faith and entangled themselves in many sorrows” (ibid.).

What else does Ecclesiastes say when he so repeatedly says “vanity and affliction of spirit”? This too he says among other things: “What indeed will profit a man from all his labor and affliction of spirit, with which he has been tormented under the sun?” (Eccles. 1). All [Col. 0151B] his days are full of pains, and even by night his mind has no rest.

## CHAPTER X

How all that God made in six days is rightly charged with vanity in comparison with the seventh day, on which he rested.

Great is the subject of this Scripture, and great is the benefit of this preaching when this Preacher speaks, holding before his eyes these two opposites: vanity on the one side and truth on the other, so that you may clearly distinguish between them and define each by a proper definition. The definition of vanity is this, which the apostle Paul expressed almost sufficiently and briefly when he said: “For the form of this world passes away” (1 Cor. 7). For everything that passes away is plainly vain, and in passing away deceives and mocks its possessor or lover.

What other definition of truth can we fittingly give, except to say that truth is that which is always the selfsame? Because it does not pass away, it deceives no one; and in that best part there does not occur what occurs in the realm of vanity for those concerning whom it is written: “They slept their sleep, and all men of riches found nothing in their hands” [Col. 0151C] (Ps. 75). And what is that which is always the selfsame? [68]

Let us go to the head of the book, to the beginning of the Scriptures of truth, because there is a great and evident doorway of reasoning from which we may distinguish truth from vanity by definite boundaries. For in six days he completed all his work—heaven and earth and all their adornment—and on the seventh day he completed his work. Of that seventh day, I remember saying in another work that it is first by nature, though reckoned seventh in order. Hence, concerning the day on which “God said, ‘Let there be light,’ and light was made, and he divided light from darkness,” Scripture does not say, “And morning and evening were made, the first day,” but “And evening and morning were made, one day” (Gen. 1).

The six days are the six primary forms of all creatures, through which the Creator ought to be known. Therefore they are called days: that is, they illuminate the eyes of our heart for knowing the Creator. Of these creatures, the angelic creature is first and human nature sixth. The seventh day, as I have said, is first by nature, because it is Wisdom, in which [Col. 0152A] God made all things; for it is “the Word through whom all things were made” (John 1), and in it God rests. Therefore this day is first, because in it he saw every creature before making it; but for us it is seventh, because we first know the creature and through it know that the Creator is great.

It should therefore be noted that, although it is said, “God completed his work on the seventh day,” it is not said, “All his work which he had made”; rather it is said: “And on the seventh day he rested from all the work which he had accomplished” (Gen. 2). For he rested from all work, in that he would henceforth create no new kind; but if you rightly weigh the sense of the word “completed,” he completed on the seventh day not all his work, but the rational creature alone—and not even all of it, but only the elect who, through humility, rendered themselves worthy of that seventh day.

What is it to be completed on the seventh day in which God rested, except to enter into that rest of the Lord which is the fullness of blessedness? The Apostle also magnificently recalls it: “For we who have believed shall enter into rest, as he said: ‘As I swore in my wrath, if they shall enter into my rest,’” and the rest, down to: “For whoever has entered into his rest has also rested from his works, as God did from his” [Col. 0152C] (Heb. 4).

## CHAPTER XI

That it is not so much the creature itself as the immoderate use or perverse love of the creature that is rightly charged with vanity; as Scripture says: “And God saw all the things that he had made, and they were very good.”

Thus here we have these two opposites, vanity and truth, distinguished by fixed boundaries: vanity, namely, in the sixfold number of creation; truth, in the rest of God, that is, on the seventh day. “Then,” you ask, “is creation vain? Or are God’s works vain, and is God himself the author of vanity? Are not all God’s works rather good, as Scripture there says: ‘And God saw all the things that he had made, and they were very good’?” (Gen. 1).

To this I say: every creature is indeed vanity in comparison with the rest in which God rests on the seventh day; and every rational creature is charged with vanity insofar as it seeks rest in these temporal or visible things and has not founded its hope upon those eternal and invisible goods—the Lord’s rest [Col. 0153A]. Yet it is not so much the creature itself as the immoderate use or love of the creature which is charged with vanity.

For example, when the human mind becomes so entangled in the beauty of the sun that it thinks the sun is God and chooses to serve the creature rather than the Creator; and not this creature alone, but other creatures as well, above all the four elements—fire, air, earth, and water—to which it assigns names of divinity. Therefore Scripture rightly indicts all these things of vanity, and first the sun, saying: “The sun rises and sets, and returns to its place; and being born there, it goes round through the south and turns toward the north” (Eccles. 1).

Certainly, in its rising and setting, in its southern circuit and northern return, there is great changeability and great vanity. For prolonged daylight, when the sun turns northward, is not sufficiently welcome to a person at work; nor, for those who play among birds, is the persistence of darkness always pleasing when it circles through the south. The same is true in the other changes of day and night, summer and winter, spring and autumn. There are indeed many remedies for human weakness, but no less many wearisome anxieties, because there is no sufficiency in these things; rather, in all of them there is great need. Therefore hope or confidence must be placed neither in these things nor in anything that is beneath or done beneath the sun, for all things are vain, all things transitory.

With this purpose he indicts all things of vanity, and finally man himself [Col. 0153B], whoever he may be whose hope does not extend its foot beyond or outside these things. For he says: “Therefore one destruction is shared by human beings and beasts, and the condition of each is equal: as man dies, so they die; all breathe alike, and man has nothing more than beasts. All are subject to vanity, and all go to one place. They were made from earth and return together to earth” (Eccles. 3).

Therefore hope must not be placed in a human being, however godlike, however powerful. Did not father David before him also hold this view? “Do not,” he says, “trust in princes, in the sons of men, in whom there is no salvation. His spirit shall depart and he shall return to his earth; on that day all their thoughts shall perish” (Ps. 145). Does it not follow, then, that man himself is vanity? Hence the same writer says elsewhere: “Nevertheless, every living man is altogether vanity.” Immediately, in two verses, he confirms this very point which the Preacher here unfolds in a longer discussion: “Nevertheless,” he says, “man passes in an image, but he is disturbed in vain. He stores up treasures and does not know for whom he will gather them” [Col. 0153C] (Ps. 38).

Clearly, the same sense occurs in many of the things said here, including this: “Again I hated all my industry and the labor in which I had worked most diligently beneath the sun, since I shall leave it to an heir after me, though I do not know whether he will be wise or foolish; and he will rule over my labors, for which I sweated and was anxious. And is anything so vain?” (Eccles. 2).

## CHAPTER XII [Col. 0154A]

Concerning the saying, “Fear God and keep his commandments, for this is the whole of man”; and that without the fear of God every living person is vanity.

In keeping with the purpose of this book of Ecclesiastes, enough has briefly been said to establish that hope must be placed in God alone, since we consider it sufficiently demonstrated that hope must be placed neither in a human being nor in any other creature. Father David did likewise in many Psalms. Having said, as we recalled above, “Nevertheless, every living man is altogether vanity” (Ps. 38), and intending to show that hope must be placed neither in man nor [69] [Col. 0154B] in human treasure, he immediately says: “And now what is my expectation?” (ibid.). This is as though he said: “In what, then, shall I hope? Shall it not be in the Lord?”

Likewise, when he had said, “Do not trust in princes, in the sons of men, in whom there is no salvation,” he also added the reason why hope must not be placed in them: “His spirit”—namely, that of the human being—“shall depart, and man shall return to his earth; on that day all their thoughts shall perish.” Immediately he exclaimed: “Blessed is he whose helper is the God of Jacob, whose hope is in the Lord his God” (Ps. 145), and so on to the end of the Psalm. By these words he endeavors to awaken hope through rational exhortation, so that you may perceive that the good which remains ought to be preferred to all that passes away.

In the same sense, this Preacher, wishing to recall the multitude of his assembly from an immoderate love of passing things and stir them to hope in eternal goods, and accomplishing this by many arguments, reaches this conclusion at the end [Col. 0154C]: “Let us all hear together the end of the discourse: Fear God and keep his commandments, for this is the whole of man. And God shall bring into judgment all things that are done, for every error, whether good or evil” (Eccles. 12).

How does what he said, “For this is the whole of man,” taste to you upon the palate of the heart? What meaning does this expression produce in your understanding? It should produce the meaning which pertains to the same reasoning by which the eternal and immutable God said: “I am who I am. Thus shall you say to the children of Israel: He Who Is has sent me to you” (Exod. 3).

For from the beginning of the book he had dealt with the corruption of vanity; reproving and examining all things, he demonstrated that everything vain, everything passing away, is indeed as though it were not—even man himself was not excepted, whoever walked in vanity. For he says: “I said in my heart concerning the sons of men, that God might test them and show them to be like beasts. Therefore one destruction is shared by human beings and beasts, and the condition of each is equal” [Col. 0154D] (Eccles. 3), along with the other passages we recalled above, including the Psalm verse: “Nevertheless, every living man is altogether vanity” (Ps. 38).

Therefore, that the whole assembly may know through what means human nature must be freed from the bondage of corruption, so that man may no longer be vanity but may have being, may share in the Selfsame with that eternal One who says, “I am who I am”—“This,” he says, “is the whole of man”: to fear God and keep his commandments (Eccles. 12). Grammarians understand this to be said in the ablative case, as though he said: By fearing God and keeping his commandments, man receives being; and this is grace, by adhering to God, who is being by nature. For one who adheres to God is one spirit with him (1 Cor. 6).

Otherwise, whether a man is king of Israel in Jerusalem or a mighty king in Babylon, however abundant his delights and the goods he enjoys—building houses, planting vineyards, making gardens and orchards, constructing pools of water, possessing male and female servants, herds and great flocks of sheep, heaping up silver and gold for himself, providing himself with male and female singers, cups and pitchers for pouring wine—what does it profit him? All these things are vain, and he himself is vanity [Col. 0155A] (Eccles. 2).

## CHAPTER XIII [Col. 0155B]

That these two—faith, instructed in Proverbs, and hope, strengthened in Ecclesiastes—work through the third, namely charity, which speaks in the Song of Songs.

These two, namely faith, which we have indicated is preached in the Proverbs, and hope, which is strengthened in Ecclesiastes by many arguments for despising vanity, work through the third, namely charity, which speaks openly, beginning thus: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song 1).

Of all the voices in this book, it is not necessary now to demonstrate that they are voices of charity, signifying the affection of four persons: Christ who is desired, the Church who desires, the friends, and the young women who long to hear the voice of the beloved bridegroom and the voice of the beloved bride, and to rejoice joyfully at hearing them [Col. 0155C]. We are reluctant, being sluggish, and we confess that we are reluctant to linger here longer, especially because we published long ago a small work of our own on these Songs of Songs, divided into seven little books, in honor of our Lady Saint Mary, the perpetual Virgin. She is preeminently the true bride of the eternal friend, namely God the Father; likewise bride and mother of the Son of that same God the Father; the proper temple of charity, that is, of the Holy Spirit, through whose operation she conceived him. That Holy Spirit, indeed, is the charity of Father and Son.

Let any kindly hearer who has heard of that work receive it, not as something opposed to the ancient teachers, who in the same Songs expounded more extensively the love of the holy Church, but as something added beyond their exposition: gathering and uniting the voices of so great and widely extended a body, the Church, into the one soul of Mary, Christ’s singular and unique beloved. For nothing of all that can be said or sung concerning the great and holy love of the Church, beloved by Christ and loving Christ, is unsuitable to her [Col. 0155D].

We say this only regarding this Scripture, which is wholly fit for song. For in the other Scriptures many lamentable things resound concerning the repentant Church; in many respects she sinned, and for those matters she laments and groans with fruits of repentance. These things are beneath the dignity of this blessed Virgin, whose most spotless life had no cause for groaning except the wound of charity, because the full and perfect blessedness was delayed during the time of this pilgrimage [Col. 0156A].

## CHAPTER XIV

How, in these three—faith, hope, and charity—we can profitably contemplate how we may be instructed more and more toward the knowledge of the holy Trinity.

We must keep in mind the purpose or intention with which we began to speak of faith, hope, and charity, according to these three books of Solomon: namely, that in this, as it were, mirror of these three—faith, hope, and charity—we might contemplate a certain likeness of the Holy Trinity. For through these three He refashioned humanity into His own likeness, according to the purpose He had set forth when He said: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1). In this brightness, therefore, of the divine likeness—in these three, faith, hope, and charity—is that which we may profitably contemplate, so that we may be instructed little by little, more and more, toward knowledge of that same Holy Trinity, whom we cannot now behold in His majesty.

Behold, we understand and know that faith, through hope and charity, accomplishes those things contained in these three books—Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs; and hope likewise accomplishes them through faith and charity. For faith, through hope and charity, accomplishes this in a human being: that he approaches the house which Wisdom built for herself, to the banquet of the victims which she sacrificed, to drink the wine which she mixed, and to eat the bread of the table which she set forth (Prov. 9), with a mind so prepared that he is willing to render like for like—that is, to lay down his life for Him who first loved us so greatly as to lay down His own life for us (John 19).

Hope, through faith and charity, accomplishes this in a human being: that even if a persecutor is absent—one who is accustomed both to take away earthly possessions and to kill the body—he himself, understanding that all things are vain, that is, transient, voluntarily abandons what he possesses, according to the counsel of Him who says: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you shall have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me” (Matt. 19).

How much can we contemplate in this mirror, or enigma, of the brightness of that most high Trinity, whose face we cannot now see? Certainly little; yet even this itself is already some spark of eternal life for us. “For this,” says the Son of God Himself, “is eternal life: that they may know thee, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom thou hast sent” (John 17).

What, then, is that however small thing which we can now see through this mirror, in this enigma? Surely it is the work which it is necessary for our eternal salvation to believe and know: that God the Father, through His charity—that is, through the Holy Spirit—gave this command to His own Son, that He should suffer for us (Rom. 8); and that the Son Himself, through the same charity—that is, through the same Holy Spirit—received this command, to obey “unto death, even the death of the cross” (Phil. 2).

With what hope? With that, surely, which the Holy Spirit proclaimed to us through Isaiah, saying: “If He shall lay down His soul for sin, He shall see a long-lived seed, and the will of the Lord shall prosper in His hand” (Isa. 53). But the Father Himself—with what or how great a faith? “For He is faithful in all His words” (Ps. 144), and especially in this, and all His works are in faith, and this work most particularly. With what or how great a faith, then, did He give the command of this obedience, the command of this suffering? (Ps. 32.) Surely with such faith as He Himself is: with faith as great as He Himself is; with admirable faith, inseparable faith, most persevering faith, most victorious faith.

By how many evils of human beings was He provoked, by how very great sins? Yet He persevered in the purpose or promise of so great a good, and did not make void those things which had proceeded from His lips (Ps. 88). Hence David too was anxious: “Have mercy on me,” he says, “that thou mayest be justified in thy words and prevail when thou art judged” (Ps. 50). With how many kings and how many kingdoms did the devil, armed, labor to turn them away from this purpose? Yet the most mighty God prevailed; and, as He had purposed, behold, His Son, God and man, sits at His right hand.

From that perseverance of the faithful and strong God comes our work in twelve little books, entitled *On the Victory of the Word of God*.

## CHAPTER XV

That in the ancient Scriptures these names—faith, hope, and charity—are found almost so rarely, although the realities themselves are proclaimed everywhere; just as the relative names Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are either silent, or uttered most rarely and with caution.

Today the proclamation of these three—faith, hope, and charity—is illustrious in the evangelical and apostolic writings [Col. 0157C], and in the mouth of the whole Church. Long ago it was not so. For how many passages are there in the Scriptures of the Old Testament where the manifestation of these forms—faith, hope, and charity—shines forth under their own proper names?
