It is indeed known and certain that all Scripture, divinely inspired, aims at the realities or virtues signified by these names; yet, though this is so, it nevertheless proclaims those same realities almost everywhere in absolute terms, as we have already shown in part. But these relative names—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—it either kept silent, or uttered only very rarely and cautiously, and never joined them together.

For example: since, as has been shown above, almost everything Solomon says in Proverbs pertains to the glory of faith, where did he openly proclaim this very name, “faith”? Likewise in Ecclesiastes, though almost all that is said there through many arguments urges a human being toward the crown of hope, where did he name hope itself? In the Song of Songs, though nearly everything pertains to the sacrament of charity, he named charity itself by its proper name only a few times, saying: “He paved the midst with charity” (Song 3), and elsewhere: “Many waters cannot quench charity” (Song 8). And elsewhere again: “He ordered charity in me” (Song 2).

Yet the word *charity* could be proclaimed or declaimed more freely even to those childish, carnal people, who neither knew nor cared to know what faith, hope, or spiritual love was, and who perhaps considered the carnal love of man and woman, husband and wife, parents, children, and other relatives or connections to be sufficient charity. In divine discourse, however, the subject is that charity whose ecclesiastical definition is this: to love God for His own sake, and to love one’s neighbor—not merely any person, but an enemy—as a human being for God’s sake (Matt. 5). If people had been capable of this love, would the Law have said to them: “You shall love your friend and hate your enemy” (Deut. 15)?

The same must be thought concerning faith. For if people at that time had been capable of the faith by which Abraham was justified (Gen. 15; Rom. 4), would the Law have been given? And, to make this discourse more pleasing by an analogy, would Abraham have taken a handmaid if the free woman had not been barren? (Gen. 16; Gal. 4.) But we have treated these matters more fully elsewhere.

## CHAPTER XVI

Again, concerning faith, hope, and charity: that through these three the Holy Trinity is represented in the Holy Scriptures; and concerning the Apostle’s saying, “Then I shall know even as I am known”—what it is to know or to be known.

The purpose here was to show that these three are the means through which a human being is refashioned into that likeness of God which He set forth in the beginning when He said: “Let us make man in our image and likeness.” Hence also the apostle John says: “We know that, when He shall appear, we shall be like Him, because we shall see Him as He is” (1 John 3).

How much delight, do you suppose, is contained in this demonstration or understanding? For the holy prophets are indeed blessed because the Lord was represented in their hand, as He says in Hosea—and as we have already recalled: “And I spoke through the prophets, and I multiplied visions, and through the hand of the prophets I was represented” (Hos. 12). Yet all holy and elect persons are blessed because the Holy Trinity—the one God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—is represented in them through these three: faith, hope, and charity.

This mode of representation is universal. The holy patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—who were themselves prophets—had certain particular representations in themselves of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, as we have recalled in its place. But this is the universal likeness: that of faith, hope, and charity; and this likeness will remain forever.

We delight in the greatness of the matter, but there is labor in the delight: the feeble discourse fails, and the tongue, though eager to speak, cannot attain what little the Spirit suggests to the mind. For it is a great chapter in which, or around which, the soul—almost wearied out—now hastens to conclude its discourse concerning these three.

What chapter? “Now,” says the Apostle, “I know in part; but then I shall know even as I am known. But now faith, hope, and charity remain, these three; and the greatest of these is charity” (1 Cor. 12). By what voice, by what words, can we grasp the meaning of these words? For the word *knowledge* signifies a certain joining or mutual apprehension of two consciousnesses, having an exceedingly great and intimate confidence in one another, which the soul can sufficiently know not through reading or hearing, but through experience alone.

Holy Scripture speaks much, by analogy, of the mutual knowledge of the Spirit of God and the human spirit. For example: “As the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so shall thy God rejoice over thee” (Isa. 62). Therefore, when he says, “Then I shall know even as I am known,” intending by the word *knowledge* to suggest the everlasting exercise of charity, or the torrent of delight overflowing from the secret place of divinity into the inward parts of the loving soul, who can adequately unfold it in words?

It is hidden from us throughout the whole time of this pilgrimage. Therefore the Psalmist sighs: “How great is the multitude of thy sweetness, O Lord, which thou hast hidden for those who fear thee” (Ps. 30). If it is hidden from every living person—indeed, from everyone who is a pilgrim in this mortality—then he rightly says: “Now I know in part.”

What, then, is “Now I know in part,” especially since he adds, “But then I shall know even as I am known” (1 Cor. 13)? Let us be aided in this sense by the analogy written above, where it is said: “As the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so shall thy God rejoice over thee” (Isa. 62). For a bride never fully knows the bridegroom’s affection except when, through natural union, they become one body. There indeed she can say: “Now I know even as I am known.”

## CHAPTER XVII [Col. 0159C]

In what sense or with what intention the Apostle said, “But now faith, hope, and charity remain, these three; and the greatest of these is charity”; and that these three are inseparable, as is the Trinity itself.

Finally, this too deserves inquiry: in what sense or with what intention did the Apostle say, “But now faith, hope, and charity remain, these three; and the greatest of these is charity”? For in the blessed Trinity—whose likeness, as we have already said, is formed in the human soul through faith, hope, and charity—we know with certainty that there is nothing earlier or later, nothing greater or less; rather, all three Persons are coeternal and coequal with one another.

But here, in this image or likeness, there is greater and lesser; there is earlier and later, and no small inequality. For he also said above: “And though I have all faith, so that I remove mountains, and have not charity, I am nothing” (1 Cor. 13). And then, having joined these three—faith, hope, and charity—he says: “But the greatest of these is charity.”

Furthermore, true faith is never without charity, and true charity is never without faith. As the one and triune God—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—is indivisible, so the one and triune virtue of faith, hope, and charity is indivisible, which is effected in human souls in relation to the Trinity.

But concerning the Apostle we should know this: there are places where he proclaims faith in his own sense, and places where he speaks of faith in the sense of others, so as to rebuke and correct those who presume too greatly upon faith. Thus, in his own sense, he proclaims faith so that he includes faith, hope, and charity together, because these are truly inseparable, when he says: “But to him that worketh not, yet believes in Him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness.” And shortly thereafter: “For we say that faith was counted to Abraham for righteousness.” Again: “For the promise to Abraham, that he should be heir of the world, was not through the Law, but through the righteousness of faith” (Rom. 4).

When he says these things, and the like, he is plainly proclaiming faith—not dead or bare faith, but faith living through the fervor of charity and adorned with the crown of hope. And just as we sometimes invoke the Holy Trinity by the single name of Father—for example, when we say, “Our Father who art in heaven” (Matt. 6)—so here he proclaims faith, hope, and charity under the one name of faith, and wishes them to be understood.

But, speaking in the sense of those to whom he addressed himself, namely the Corinthians, he seemingly separated faith from charity (1 Cor. 13), saying what we recalled above: “And though I have all faith, so that I remove mountains, but have not charity, I am nothing” (ibid.). For they separated faith far from charity, because, although they were without charity, they thought themselves to possess the faith of Christ. Therefore he rebukes them, beginning thus: “Now I beseech you, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you all say the same thing and that there be no schisms among you. For it has been declared to me concerning you, my brethren, that there are contentions among you” (1 Cor. 1).

But it was not expedient from the beginning for this to be preached first: namely, that faith profits nothing unless it works through love (Gal. 5), or that, as the apostle James says, “faith without works is dead” (James 2). He knew that it must be provided with great caution and discernment that, at least initially, the Name of the Lord Jesus Christ should be received by peoples who were unlearned and hitherto idolaters, and that good works should afterward be built upon it. For this reason he rightly compared himself to a wise architect, saying to those same Corinthians: “According to the grace of God which was given to me, as a wise architect I laid the foundation; but another builds upon it” (1 Cor. 3), and so forth.

## CHAPTER XVIII

A prayer that, since through these three we are refashioned into the likeness of the Trinity, the blessed Trinity may increase faith, hope, and charity in us.

Since, therefore, through these things we are refashioned into Your likeness, increase faith in us, increase hope, increase charity, O blessed Trinity. For these are our riches, this our treasure, this our life, O blessed Trinity. This is our wisdom, this our strength, this our glory, O blessed Trinity; this our desire, this our everlasting foundation. This is the light of our eyes, O blessed Trinity. This is our righteousness, this our gladness, this our joy, O blessed Trinity. This is our mercy, this our consolation, this our confidence, O blessed Trinity. This is our honor, this our victory, this our crown, O blessed Trinity. Increase these in us, therefore, so that, living forever, we may bless You.

## BOOK EIGHT

## CHAPTER I [Col. 0161A]

That the confession or praise of the Holy Trinity is the Lord’s song, which ought not to be sung in a foreign land in answer to the questioning of heretics, beside the rivers of Babylon.

We now desire to sing the Lord’s song, a hymn and one of the songs of Zion—the words of songs by which, or in which, the Holy Trinity, God of gods, is praised in You, O heavenly Zion. But weeping interrupts our song while we still sit here “beside the rivers of Babylon” (Ps. 136).

What then? Shall we cease to sing and “hang our instruments upon the willows in its midst,” saying, “How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land?” (ibid.) By no means shall we cease; indeed, unasked, we shall freely sing the words of the Lord’s songs. For we are not questioned, nor do we wish to be questioned, by those who have led us captive.

The Babylonians—that is, the sons of this age, worthy of confusion—are accustomed to ask for the words of songs, not so that they themselves may receive the fruit of faith or that we may be fed, but so that we may entertain their ears; especially so that, at their will, we may twist the voices of Scripture, which are the Lord’s songs, into perversity. Such Babylonians were the Arians, the worst enemies of the Holy Trinity.

Let us strengthen ourselves for singing, not forgetting Jerusalem—that is, maintaining not an earthly but a heavenly intention—and setting before ourselves this heavenly Jerusalem at the beginning of our joy. Let this be our chief reason for singing: namely, for preaching the glory of the Holy Trinity, so that we may deserve to please not people of that kind, but the one true and only God Himself.

Let us strengthen ourselves, I say, and, that we may be steadfast, let us recall what happened here, and what was done, or how it was done, in Babylon. Let us first set down the event itself, or the sacred history, and then append its mystery for our consolation.

## CHAPTER II

Concerning the three victorious boys in the midst of the Babylonian furnace: that in them the Holy Trinity both displayed and signified the presence of its assistance against the head of idolatry.

“Nebuchadnezzar the king made a golden image, sixty cubits high and six cubits broad; and he commanded proclamation to be made by the voice of a herald: ‘To you it is said, peoples, tribes, and languages: at the hour when you hear the sound of trumpet and pipe, harp and sambuca, psaltery and symphony, and every kind of musical instrument, fall down and worship the golden image which King Nebuchadnezzar has set up. But whoever does not fall down and worship shall that very hour be cast into a furnace of burning fire’” (Dan. 3).

Despising this edict and not fearing this punishment, the three boys Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego were cast into the furnace of fire; and the fire did not touch them at all, neither distressed them nor caused them any harm. “Then King Nebuchadnezzar was astonished, and said to his nobles: ‘Did we not cast three bound men into the midst of the fire?’ They answered: ‘Truly, O king.’ ‘Behold,’ he said, ‘I see four living men, unbound and walking in the midst of the fire; there is no corruption in them, and the appearance of the fourth is like the Son of God’” (ibid.).

This miracle had such force upon Nebuchadnezzar that he said: “The most high God has wrought signs and wonders before me. It has pleased me, therefore, to proclaim His signs, because they are great, and His wonders because they are mighty; and His kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and His power endures from generation to generation” (ibid.).

Does not this event, so victorious a deed, proclaim the Holy Trinity as gloriously in these three boys as another event, involving the three angels whom Abraham received as guests, signified the same Trinity? (Gen. 18.) This consideration is exceedingly beautiful and delightful, if you weigh or reflect that the blessed Trinity had one and the same concern in these three fleshly boys and in those three angelic boys.

What concern, and of what kind? Surely this very great concern and exceedingly great care: to fulfill the word of promise. There, it was that Isaac might be born, the beginning of the seed or genealogy from which Christ was to be born; here, that the race of Abraham, or Judaea, parent of the same Christ who was to be born, might have consolation in that Babylonian captivity. For through impious human beings the devil sought to blot out that race, so that the line from which this seed—that is, Christ—was to be born might not exist, as had been promised to Abraham and had already been foretold through many prophets.

Therefore the Most High God performed many signs, and this greatest sign, before the eyes of those who had carried that people of God captive, so that, preserved among the nations, the children of the exile might at length be sent back to the place where Christ had to be born from them. Long before, the prophetic voice had sung of this in congratulation: “Virgin Israel, return to your cities” (Jer. 31); how long will you turn away in grief? You shall bring forth the Lord and Savior.

## CHAPTER III

How the words and mystical meanings of Psalm 136, “Beside the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept,” accord with that history or event.

It is worthwhile to observe how the words of the psalm mentioned above accord with this history or event: “Beside the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept when we remembered Zion” (Ps. 136). For already in David’s time, when he sang that psalm, the prophetic Spirit saw the future captivity of that people in Babylon. The holy persons awaited from this people the fulfillment of the promise, namely Christ’s birth, according to what God had said to Abraham: “In thy seed shall all nations be blessed” (Gen. 22); and according to what the same God had said through the mouth of Jacob: “The scepter shall not be taken away from Judah, nor a ruler from his thigh, until He comes who is to be sent” (Gen. 49).

According to these words, it was established that Christ was to be born from Abraham’s seed, from the tribe of Judah. Where? Surely not in Babylon, but in Zion, or Jerusalem—that is, in the land whose metropolis was Jerusalem, namely, in Bethlehem. The prophetic Spirit foresaw and foretold this very thing. For David himself says: “Behold, we heard of Him in Ephrathah” (Ps. 31). Ephrathah itself is Bethlehem. After David, it was written through another prophet: “And thou, Bethlehem Ephrathah, or land of Judah, art little among the thousands of Judah; from thee shall come forth unto me He who shall be ruler in Israel” (Mic. 5). Between these two, Isaiah said the same thing, beholding the matter through the Spirit: “For from Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isa. 2).

What a just longing, then, those people in captivity, the children of that exile, must have had to return to the land of Judah! Therefore, so long beforehand, the prophetic Spirit said in their person: “Beside the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept when we remembered Zion” (Ps. 136). What other worthy cause could there have been, except the one we have described, for which they remembered that earthly Zion?

For this reason the prophetic Spirit said in the person of each one of those to whom leave to return was granted: “If I forget thee, Jerusalem, let my right hand be forgotten; let my tongue cleave to my jaws if I do not remember thee, if I do not set Jerusalem at the beginning of my joy”; adding: “Remember, O Lord, the children of Edom in the day of Jerusalem, who say: ‘Lay it bare, lay it bare, even to its foundation’” (ibid.).

For the children of Edom were especially detestable, because, although they were Israelites’ brothers according to the flesh (Exod. 15), they were particularly hostile at Israel’s departure from Egypt (Num. 20), frequently stirred up and assisted other nations against them, and mocked their captivity and other calamities. Concerning the persistence of this fury and indignation to the end, he says in Lamentations: “Rejoice and be glad, daughter of Edom, who dwellest in the land of Uz; to thee also shall the cup come: thou shalt be drunk and stripped naked” (Lam. 4). In these words the same vengeance of justice is announced as is requested in these words: “Remember, O Lord, the daughters of Edom in the day of Jerusalem.”

Would he who, for the reason already stated—namely, the hope of Christ’s birth—remembered that earthly land of Zion, not also have remembered heavenly Zion? And would not this beatitude befit one who, out of longing for so great a hope, despised the desires of the flesh and Babylonian delights in order to return, having received leave to return to that land: “Blessed is he who shall seize and dash thy little ones against the rock”? It is not worthwhile to linger on each of these matters; let us pass, as intended, to the mystical sense of the same psalm, which more closely concerns us.

## CHAPTER IV

That we do not have as great a cause for this sort of complaint as the ancient saints had: “Upon the willows in its midst we hung our instruments. How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land?”

First, it should be known that we do not now have as great a cause for this sort of complaint as the ancients had, to say: “Upon the willows in its midst we hung our instruments. How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land?” We must indeed weep, whoever we are who have hope in the age to come, who are children of that Jerusalem which is above, the city of the living God, in which the glory of the Holy Trinity is seen. This accords with the very name Jerusalem, for it is interpreted “vision of peace.”

We must weep, I say, because while we are in the body we are pilgrims away from that vision, and the whole world is Babylon to us. But in that very weeping we have more joy and consolation here, because Christ, whom those weeping persons awaited as one who was to be born, has now been born: the sun of the human race. And so great is the difference between those who weep that one may say: they wept in the night, but we weep as though in the day; and more freely than they, even amid our tears, we can touch our instruments and sing the Lord’s song—that is, open our mouths and publicly preach faith in the Holy Trinity.

They were not permitted to do this, for such preaching could not then be borne. For we speak of the children of that captivity alone; among them the three boys mentioned above are most famous, because by their number they showed that the presence and care of the blessed Trinity were at hand, as it danced in the furnace of burning fire (Dan. 3); but we speak also of all the earlier holy patriarchs, kings, and prophets—whoever knew the mystery of the same Holy Trinity.

For the willows were not only Babylonian, Assyrian, Persian, and Median people, but even persons of Israelite or Jewish descent. Therefore especially because of them the instruments of this song had to be hung up—that is, the glory of the Holy Trinity either had to be kept silent, or spoken in such a way that it could not be heard outside; written in such a way that the sealed book could not be read by the common people.

What, then, happened, or what was done, that we are free to sing the Lord’s song, to sing or cry with the holy Seraphim: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts; the whole earth is full of thy glory” (Isa. 6), and now openly preach here faith in Your name, O blessed Trinity? How did it happen that we could so sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land?

## CHAPTER V

Concerning great Rome: that it was great Babylon so long as it carried out persecution against worshipers of the same Trinity which was glorified in the former Babylon through the three boys.

A wonderful thing: Babylon itself has become a kind of Jerusalem, a daughter of the heavenly Jerusalem; she who was Babylon has also become a new Zion. We mean the city called Rome, because it was Babylon and is now a kind of Zion. It is, I say, according to the faith of the blessed apostle Peter, the faithful mother-city of Zion.

That city was Babylon when Peter himself wrote in his epistle: “The elect Church that is in Babylon greets you” (1 Pet. 5). For this phrase figuratively struck at Rome. While it was still Babylon, and its king was Nebuchadnezzar—that is, Nero, Decius, Diocletian, or any such ruler—it, together with Nebuchadnezzar, set up a great and exceedingly high image, and decreed to peoples, tribes, and languages that they should fall down and worship the image; and that if anyone did not fall down and worship, he should be cast into the furnace of burning fire (Dan. 3).

For as far as it could, that head of the world exalted idolatry on high, and strove more zealously for its images once it had heard the new preaching of the one God—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. From that time it made almost the whole breadth of the world, through public edicts and written laws, into a single furnace of fire, as it were one furnace of manifold affliction and most burning persecution against the Christian name.

But what did it achieve? Just as “the angel of the Lord, descending into the furnace with those three boys, drove the flame of fire out of the furnace and made the midst of the furnace as a wind of dew blowing; and the fire did not touch them at all, neither distressed them nor caused them any harm” (ibid.), so the Son of God, the Angel of Great Counsel, was so present with all His witnesses and confessors of the Holy Trinity in that tribulation. This may be understood even from the fact that He visibly met one of them, Peter.

> [Note: [Col. 0165D] See the *History of Hegesippus*, book III, chapter 2.]

Having been worshiped by him and asked, “Lord, where are you going?” He replied: “I am going to Rome to be crucified again.” Thus He “drove the flame of fire from the furnace and made the midst of the furnace as a wind of dew blowing,” as the martyr Lawrence himself showed by experience when, while being roasted, he said: “O your madness! Unhappy men, you do not know that your coals provide not burning for me, but refreshment.”

Why say more? Just as that Nebuchadnezzar, though then fickle and vain, recognized and confessed the Son of God, saying: “Behold, I see four men unbound and walking in the midst of the fire, and the appearance of the fourth is like the Son of God,” so, much more truly and much more steadfastly, the Roman Empire at last recognized the Son of God, and even now firmly holds and declares that the confession of the blessed Peter ought to be held: “Thou art Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16).

Thus it even compels other nations to make this confession, and in a certain manner says: “Therefore this decree has been established by me: that every people, tribe, and language that shall speak blasphemy against the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego—or, more plainly, against God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—shall perish, and his house shall be laid waste; for there is no other God who can save in this manner” (Dan. 5).

## CHAPTER VI [Col. 0166A]

How beautiful is the mystery in the statement, “Then these three, as with one mouth, praised, glorified, and blessed God,” and in the furnace’s being heated sevenfold more than it was usually heated; and what force the number seven has there.

Therefore the instruments are touched, and the words of the sermons resound, preaching God as Three in unity and One in Trinity, while the psalm’s voice accompanies them: “For all the gods of the nations are demons, but the Lord made the heavens” (Ps. 95).

How beautiful a mystery, how great a spectacle of judgment in heaven and on earth! “Then,” it says, “these three, as with one mouth, praised, glorified, and blessed God” (Dan. 3). For all we human beings whose faith is one and catholic are, as it were, three, and all have one mouth. We are three, I say, because we depend upon three. Upon which three? “There are three,” says the apostle John, “who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit; and these three are one” (1 John 5).

Our song, or the words of our songs, are praises, glorifications, and blessings, as though from the one mouth of three who weep while singing, sing while weeping, and in singing and weeping accuse Babylon’s sevenfold sin. In what sense sevenfold? Sacred Scripture says: “And Nebuchadnezzar commanded that the furnace be heated sevenfold more than it was customarily heated” (Dan. 3).

The number seven is indivisible, for it can be divided into equal parts only by units; and in Scripture it often signifies totality, sometimes of evils and sometimes of goods. Of evils, as in: “From whom He had cast out seven demons” (Mark 16). Of goods, as in: “Seven times a day I have given praise to thee” (Ps. 118). It also signifies an impenitent heart, as in: “Sevenfold vengeance shall be taken on Cain” (Gen. 4).

With this meaning, we may here understand the statement, “He commanded the furnace to be heated sevenfold more than it was customarily heated,” so that we understand the unforgivable sin of the Babylonians—that is, of all impious people who, as far as they could, persecuted the saints and persisted in an impenitent heart. By what voice, with what words, does our song accuse their sin? “Remember, O Lord, the children of Edom in the day of Jerusalem” (Ps. 136), and the rest, of which we have already spoken above.

## CHAPTER VII

Concerning the four beasts—the lioness, bear, leopard, and another, terrible and marvelous, without a name—that against each of them there was set the opposing aid of the Trinity under the sacrament of the number three.

Since we have begun to speak of the mystery of the number three, showing that by this number, in the case of the captives praising God in the furnace, the Holy Trinity splendidly signified to that people the presence of its aid, it is pleasing to pursue the matter somewhat further. For we must know that “when there were four great beasts coming up,” Daniel says, “from the sea, different from one another: the first, like a lioness”—this was the kingdom of the Babylonians; [Col. 0167A] “another like a bear”—this was the kingdom of the Persians and Medes; “another like a leopard”—this was the kingdom of the Greeks; “the fourth, unnamed, terrible and wondrous, and exceedingly strong” (Dan. 7)—this was the kingdom of the Romans.

Against each of the beasts, or beastly kingdoms, you will find set in opposition the sacrament of the number three: that is, the Lord’s help bestowed through three persons, for preserving or delivering the particular people of God in that time. For at that time, as has already been said above, a great matter was being transacted, concerning which the Holy Trinity deigned laudably to show itself solicitous, and to demonstrate a token of that solicitude by such a number—namely, three. For does anyone think it a small thing that Christ, God and man, was to be born according to the [Col. 0167B] promise from that people? Assuredly, for this cause the blessed Trinity showed itself worthy in demonstrating that it cared and was solicitous for the preservation of that nation.

And concerning the first beast, namely the Babylonian kingdom, something has already been said, but something remains lacking. For someone may say that Nebuchadnezzar was overcome and God glorified not through the three youths alone, but also through Daniel, the fourth. Therefore the case of the three youths must be distinguished more carefully from Daniel’s case, on account of which “Nebuchadnezzar fell upon his face and worshipped Daniel” (Dan. 2); and from that on account of which, by God’s command, Daniel was clothed by Belshazzar in purple, a golden chain was placed around his neck, and proclamation was made concerning him (ibid., 5); and from that on account of which [Col. 0167C] the same Daniel was cast into the lions’ den: “And God said: He sent his angel and shut the mouths of the lions, and they did me no harm, because righteousness was found in me before him” (Dan. 6).

From these three cases, I say—in which the one and same God, three and one, glorified Daniel alone—the one case must plainly be separated, on account of which, by delivering the three youths cast into the furnace of fire, that same God glorified himself. For this case of the three youths alone was idolatry—indeed, the very head of idolatry—before which no king or ruler is read to have promulgated laws of death out of zeal for his idol. Is it not therefore all the more evident that those three youths alone were appointed to martyrdom, not by chance but by God’s providence, so that the lioness-beast [Col. 0167D] might be taught, at least for an hour, to take up the voice of a human being and confess God?

## CHAPTER VIII

Concerning the bear, that is, the kingdom of the Persians and Medes: how there the Most High glorified his power under the same sacrament of the number three, that is, through three kings, in the rebuilding of the Temple or city.

Now then, concerning the other beast, which was like a bear—namely, the kingdom of the Persians and Medes—consider how the Most High glorified his power under that same sacrament of the number three.

“In the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, that the word of the Lord from the mouth of Jeremiah might be fulfilled, the Lord stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia, and he caused a proclamation to go throughout all his kingdom, even in writing, saying: [Col. 0168A] Cyrus, king of Persia: The Lord God of heaven has given me all the kingdoms of the earth, and he himself has commanded me to build him a house in Jerusalem, which is in Judah” (1 Esdras 1).

When, after this proclamation had been issued, all those whose spirit God had stirred went up to build the Temple of the Lord, together with the silver and gold vessels which Nebuchadnezzar had taken from Jerusalem, and when they had begun to build the Temple of the Lord, their enemies heard of it and hindered the work of the house of the Lord; and it was interrupted and not carried on until the second year of Darius king of Persia. He, namely Darius, confirming the decree that had been proposed, namely this:

“Any man who changes this command, let timber be taken from his house, set upright, and let him be fastened upon it; and let his house [Col. 0168B] be confiscated. But may the God who caused his name to dwell there destroy every kingdom and people that stretches out its hand to oppose or destroy that house of God which is in Jerusalem”—

thus subscribed: “I, Darius, have made the decree, which I desire to be diligently fulfilled” (1 Esdras 6).

After these words, the third, Artaxerxes, strengthening the same matter, wrote thus:

“Artaxerxes, king of kings, to Ezra the priest, the most learned scribe of the law of the God of heaven, greeting. I decree that whoever in my kingdom wishes to go to Jerusalem with you, from the people of Israel, its priests, and its Levites, may go”;

and so forth, down to: “Teach freely also those who are ignorant; and whoever does not diligently observe the law of your God and the law of the king shall be judged [Col. 0168C] either by death, or exile, or confiscation of his property, or indeed imprisonment” (1 Esdras 7).

Did this wonderful event occur by chance: that the victorious faith of three Jewish youths, in the furnace of fire, which had testified against the head of Babylonian idolatry that he is the true and only God, should command that the house and city of that God—which had been destroyed—be rebuilt by the united decree and goodwill of three pagan kings? Certainly not by chance, but by the heavenly governance of the great and ever-provident counsel of the holy and undivided Trinity.

It seems difficult and almost impossible to say that the Holy Trinity was represented even in the aforesaid three Gentile kings. Indeed, we would not dare even to suspect this, unless the Holy Spirit himself had long beforehand declared it by his authority through the mouth of the prophet Isaiah concerning Cyrus, the first of the three. For, having first said:

“I am the Lord, making all things, stretching out the heavens and establishing the earth; who says to the deep, Be desolate, and I will dry up your rivers; who says to Cyrus, You are my shepherd, and you shall fulfil all my will; who says to Jerusalem, You shall be built, and to the Temple, You shall be founded” (Isa. 44),

he then added: [Col. 0168D]

“Thus says the Lord to Cyrus my anointed, whose right hand I have taken,” and so forth, down to: “that you may know that I am the Lord, the God of Israel, who calls you by your name, for the sake of Jacob my servant and Israel my chosen; and I called you by your name, I have likened you, though you did not know me; I girded you, though you did not know me” (Isa. 45).

Unless, I say, the Holy Spirit had many years beforehand ratified this by his authority, saying to Cyrus, who was to be born so long afterwards, “I have likened you,” and unless reason led us to see that what was said to Cyrus alone—“I have likened you”—suited or agreed with the other kings of the same goodwill, Darius and Artaxerxes, who would dare say that the Holy Trinity was represented in three pagan kings for such a work? [Col. 0169A]

## CHAPTER IX

Likewise, how the aid of the Holy Trinity against Haman, lest he destroy the Jewish people from whom Christ had to be born, was provided through only three persons.

I come to that fierceness of the same bear, that is, to the cruelty and more-than-bestial savagery of the same kingdom of the Persians and Medes, [Col. 0169B] when, under King Ahasuerus, the devil attempted to bring about the uprooting from its very foundations of the root of our salvation. This he did through the most arrogant Haman, who persuaded King Ahasuerus that letters should be sent throughout his whole—and very extensive—kingdom, ordering that the whole Jewish race be destroyed in one day (Esther 3).

How, or through how many people, did the one God, the Trinity, on the contrary provide and show solicitude for that people, the one tree from which the fruit of salvation for the whole world, Christ the eternal life, was to be born? Only through these three: Esther, Mordecai, and King Ahasuerus himself. Therefore I shall by no means hesitate to say that, in this respect, the saying uttered by the prophetic voice long before Cyrus was born applies also to King Ahasuerus: [Col. 0169C] “I have likened you, though you did not know me” (Isa. 45), as we recalled above.

For what? Did not God the Father in some way make him like himself chiefly in this, when it was said to him: “Behold, the gallows which Haman prepared for Mordecai stands in Haman’s house, fifty cubits high” (Esther 7)? “Hang him upon it,” he said; and Haman was hanged on the gibbet which he had prepared for Mordecai.

For, that you may know how true and beautiful this likeness is, remember what the Apostle said of the Lord Jesus Christ:

“And you, when you were dead in trespasses and in the uncircumcision of your flesh, God made alive together with Christ, forgiving you all trespasses; blotting out the written decree which stood against you and was contrary to you; and he removed it from the midst, fastening it to the cross; stripping principalities and powers, he exposed them openly, triumphing over them in himself” (Col. 2).

Therefore in King Ahasuerus God the Father was represented, and in Mordecai God the Son was wonderfully represented. Further, who could doubt that in Esther the grace of the Holy Spirit, or the Spirit of counsel, was represented in so great a matter? For by using wonderful counsel she brought it about that the king’s mind was turned to favor and mercy toward her proscribed people; and that the most arrogant Haman, in whom the devil, a murderer from the beginning, was figured, should be caught—not just anywhere, but at a banquet table—[Col. 0169D] drunk and overcome with feasting, and condemned to death by hanging on the very gibbet “which he had prepared for Mordecai” [Col. 0170A], plainly according to the mystery of that saying which the Lord spoke of the devil to blessed Job: “Can you draw out Leviathan with a hook, and bind his tongue with a cord?” (Job 40).

For he too was as though caught with a hook: he had boasted magnificently of the queen’s banquet, so as to say to his friends and to his wife Zeresh: “Moreover Queen Esther has invited no one but me with the king to the banquet; and tomorrow also I am to dine with the king in her presence” (Esther 5). Thus he dined, thus he bit the little cakes of the feast, so that after the soft flavors of the food he immediately received the iron sentence of death.

## CHAPTER X

Why, for this cause, the Holy Trinity called Cyrus, king of Persia, by name and assimilated him to itself, and gave such goodwill in the heart of the other kings of Persia and Media; and that our Lord Jesus Christ, for whose future birth these things took place, is first set forth in the Scriptures. [Col. 0170B]

Why did the Holy Trinity thus call Cyrus by name and make him like [its servant], and give so great a goodwill in the hearts of the other kings of Persia and Media? “For Jacob my servant and Israel my chosen,” he says (Isa. 45). For which Jacob, or for which Israel? (Gen. 23.)

Certainly it is insufficient if you understand merely that Jacob or Israel [Col. 0170C] of whom we know and read: “Isaac begot Jacob” (Matt. 1), or the rather small multitude of survivors of that people, which is commonly called Jacob or Israel in the Scriptures by the name of its father. And indeed Cyrus understood nothing higher, sought nothing beyond this; and for winning his goodwill toward that people it was enough that their God, so many years before, had through his prophet foretold such great things and recorded such glorious things concerning Cyrus himself, and had promised that he himself would accomplish them for him (Isa. 45).

Nevertheless, there is one true Jacob, servant of the Lord; one true Israel, chosen of God: the Lord Jesus Christ. For his sake the supreme Trinity showed such care as we understand, or desire to understand, in its help under the sacrament of the number three. Hence this has already been said and must still be said.

As we consider this, there pleasantly comes to mind that this servant of the Lord was the first to give thanks to God. Before him you will not easily find anyone, whether in the Law or in the Prophets, of whom it is plainly written that he gave thanks to God. [Col. 0170D] For God’s benefits had not yet been fulfilled; and the greatest of all is that he made this servant of his, Christ Jesus according to the form of a servant. For that deed, surely, thanksgiving is owed to him.

Finally, whoever gives thanks to God without having before his eyes, in that very act of thanksgiving, this reason—that God made this servant of his, and in order to make him accomplished so much, among which he also inclined the minds of Gentile kings to goodwill toward his name—has not yet understood how or why thanks ought to be given.

We have said that this one first gave thanks to God; for before him we recall that the voice of thanksgiving was nowhere heard in the Scriptures [Col. 0171A], though especially in the Psalms you hear so many voices of exultation and confession, voices of blessing and praise, voices of adoration, song, and jubilation. But where, I ask, was the voice of thanksgiving heard—or where ought it to have been heard—before it came from the mouth of this servant of the Lord, this chosen one of God?

## CHAPTER XI

What thanksgiving is, and when, how, and where our Lord Jesus Christ gave thanks.

First, therefore, it must be defined what thanksgiving is; then it must be shown where, when, and how he gave thanks—not by the tongue alone, but in deed and truth; not merely in words, but in words and deeds.

Thanksgiving is a worthy return corresponding to divine [Col. 0171B] benefits, so great that nothing is lacking to its perfection, or than which no greater can be. Thanksgiving, I say, and the worthy return corresponding to God’s benefits, is love, of which “no one has” or can have “a greater,” “than to lay down his life for his friends” (John 15).

Of this love the Spirit says in the Psalm: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me? I will take the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord” (Ps. 115). Conscious within himself of this great love, which, as we have said, is true and perfect thanksgiving, this servant of the Lord gave thanks.

First, according to John, when about to speak at length concerning the sacrament of his body and blood, “he took the five loaves, and when he had given thanks” (John 6), looking up to heaven (Matt. 14), as the other Evangelists report, he distributed them to those reclining at table (Mark 6; Luke 9).

Second, when about to raise Lazarus, he lifted up his eyes and said: “Father, I give you thanks, because you have heard me; and I knew that you always hear me” (John 11). The raising of Lazarus, of course, was the chief cause why the envious Jews sought to kill him.

Third, on the very night in which he was betrayed, after taking bread and the cup and giving thanks, he gave them to his disciples, saying: “This is my body. This is my blood of the New Testament, which shall be shed for many” (Matt. 26).

Thus this faithful and true one could freely profess that he gave thanks, because he gave thanks in truth, being ready, while we were still enemies (Rom. 5), to receive for us the cup which the Father gave him.

For what reason was this servant so ready to give thanks to the Father? We must understand that giving thanks belongs to the lesser nature, namely the form of a servant. Therefore, when he says, “Father, I give you thanks,” we understand not one person but the three persons—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—who are “one God and Father of all” (Eph. 4), as the Apostle says, to whom we too pray: “Our Father who art in heaven” (Matt. 6). But when he says “my Father,” “of my Father,” or “my Father” in the accusative, the only-begotten Son distinguishes his own proper relation by that possessive pronoun, and only one person must be understood by the name Father.

For what reason, then, was he so ready to give thanks? [Col. 0172A] “Because you have heard me,” he says: “And I knew that you always hear me.” Where, I ask, had he heard him? Had he prayed privately, before coming to the place where Lazarus had been laid, and received an answer that he could raise him; and was that why he said, “Father, I give you thanks because you have heard me; and I knew that you always hear me” (John 11)?

This supposition is slight; it does not attain to the dignity of thanksgiving or the majesty of the one giving thanks. For he possesses every working of miracles, not in the humility of petitions, but in the power of the word inherent in him. He recalls to the attentive hearer a far different, much more excellent, and more laborious hearing of himself: namely, that long before this servant of the Lord became a servant according to the form of a servant, or was formed from the womb of the Virgin, he was heard in all the necessities of humankind—heard in the patriarchs, heard in righteous kings and judges, heard in prophets, heard in the children of the captivity, [Col. 0172B] of whom we have already spoken above, heard in the Maccabean brothers, of whom we shall still speak; heard in the cry of every woman who has a child in her womb, who cries out in giving birth and endures anguish in order to bring forth—that is, in the longing of the ancient Church, which had Christ himself in promise, desired his coming, and was as though in labor and pained in childbirth until he came (Rev. 12).

Was not that cry, since it was made on your account, your cry, O Jesus Christ? Therefore one of them said to you, as though already present: “May the Lord hear you in the day of tribulation” (Ps. 19). This is the true cause worthy of thanksgiving: that you might say, “Father, I give you thanks because you have heard me,” because you caused adversity to be born to the whole world. And, you say, “I knew that you always hear”: for you were God, and are now God, and before you were born from the Virgin’s womb you knew that all these things happened on your account.

## CHAPTER XII

Concerning the third beast, namely the leopard, that is, the kingdom of the Greeks: how the Holy Trinity showed against it the presence of its aid through three men, three brother-leaders—Judas, Jonathan, and Simon.

We have spoken of two beasts, the lioness and the bear, and how against them the Holy Trinity signified the presence of its help by the number three. Now we must speak of the third beast, the leopard, and how matters were conducted through the aid of the same number.

Concerning that beast, this must first be remembered: the people of God were not delivered from its mouth without bow and sword. It happened as had been foretold through the prophet Hosea: “I will have mercy on the house of Judah, and I will save them in the Lord their God; and I will not save them by bow and sword, by war, by horses, or by horsemen” (Hos. 1).

For Nebuchadnezzar’s being cast down before the servants of the Most High God, and his being overcome so as to confess once, twice, and a third time that he alone is the true God (Dan. 11, 14); likewise, the rebuilding of the house of God in Jerusalem, which he had destroyed [Col. 0173A] (Ezra 1, 7); likewise, Haman’s malice returning upon his own head, so that he himself was hanged upon the gibbet “which he had prepared for Mordecai” (Esther 3, 5, 7)—these things were not done by bow and sword, not by war, nor by horses and horsemen, but in the Lord God, who alone, having the hearts of kings in his hand, inclined them wherever he wished (Prov. 12), so that the remnant of that people might be saved (1 Macc. 1) and his purpose fulfilled.

But in order that the fierceness of this beast—that is, the kingdom of the Greeks—might be checked, especially in that King Antiochus wrote and sent books by messengers’ hands to Jerusalem and all the cities of Judah, ordering them to follow the laws of the Gentiles (Dan. 8), this was done by bow and sword, in war; yet, as Daniel had foretold, “with a little help” [Col. 0173B] (Dan. 11).

Three brothers were leaders in the wars: Judas, Jonathan, and Simon. They fought indeed with few weapons, but conquered by great faith. We have dealt with them more fully in the work which we wrote on the victory of the Word of God, and therefore we must pass over them now. For the sole point relevant to the present purpose is to consider, in the Lord’s help, the sacrament of the number three: that God the Trinity acted according to his custom, signifying by this number, in helping them, that his care and solicitude were present—fittingly, no doubt, for the magnitude of the matter, namely because of the hope of the promise laid up for all the saints in the advent of Christ, the Son of God, the Savior then awaited.

## CHAPTER XIII

Concerning the justice of the judgment expressed by the prophet Hosea: “I will no longer have mercy on the house of Israel, but I will have mercy on the house of Judah”; and that the house of Judah had three righteous kings, whereas the house of Israel had not even one.

[Col. 0173C] It pertains to the same subject now to inquire into and understand the justice of the judgment in what we recalled a little earlier, the Lord’s saying through the prophet Hosea: “I will have mercy on the house of Judah.” For he had first said: “I will no longer have mercy upon the house of Israel, but I will utterly forget them”; and now he declared: “I will have mercy on the house of Judah, and I will save them in the Lord their God” (Hos. 1). And so it came to pass.

For the captivity of the ten tribes remained irrevocable: “the king of the Assyrians took Israel captive and carried them away into Assyria [Col. 0173D], and placed them in Halah and Habor, by the river Gozan, in the cities of the Medes” (4 Kings 17). But the tribe of Judah, at the appointed time, was saved in the Lord its God and recalled from the Babylonian captivity.

To those who inquire or wish to know the justice of this judgment, the answer is quickly given: although the tribe of Judah, the kingdom of David, sinned much—as did the ten tribes, the kingdom of Jeroboam, which he had torn away from the house of David—yet it fared well in this respect, that according to the oft-repeated sacrament of the number three, in which we take great delight, the tribe of Judah prevailed in judgment over the cause of the ten tribes.

For the Lord God of judgment found in the tribe of Judah three men of mercy, three righteous kings: David, [Col. 0174A] Hezekiah, and Josiah. Apart from these three, all sinned. But concerning the kings of the ten tribes, it is certain that all sinned, and none can be excepted, because none of them departed from the sins of Jeroboam—that is, from the calves which Jeroboam made.

In the tribe of Judah, as already said, three were free and righteous with respect to such sin; and some of the others repented of their sin. But among the kings of the ten tribes there was one and the same worship of idolatry, namely that of those calves. One of them, Jehu son of Nimshi, did indeed abolish the worship of Baal (4 Kings 10). But what good did it do to abolish Baal while nevertheless worshipping calves as God? Therefore that prophetic saying very fittingly applies to those kings of Samaria: “The best among them is like a brier; the upright like a thorn hedge” (Mic. 7). [Col. 0174B]

## CHAPTER XIV

A summary of the deliverances: from the word of promise until the Nativity of Christ, that people from which Christ had to be born was saved seven times; and this pertains to the mystery of the Holy Trinity because each deliverance occurred on account of, or through, three men found among them.

Behold how many times that nation was saved on account of three men found in their midst, under the great mystery of the Holy Trinity, as has often been said already.

First, when they served in Egypt because of the sin of their fathers who had sold their brother Joseph (Gen. 37), they cried to the Lord and were heard on account of those fathers, the three greatest men—Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—as Scripture says: “Their cry rose up to the Lord because of their works, and he heard their groaning and remembered the covenant which he had made with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob” (Exod. 2).

Likewise, when he said that he would destroy them because of the calf they had made, he spared them on account of the same men, Moses standing before him in the breach—that is, in the utmost humility of mind—and saying: “Why, Lord, is your wrath kindled against your people?” (Exod. 32). “Remember Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, your servants” (ibid.).

Then, when they had made two calves, following Jeroboam (3 Kings 12), had been divided from the house of David, and the tribe of Judah too had worshipped the gods of the Gentiles, so that both parts were therefore justly to be handed over to captivity (2 Chron. [Col. 0174D] 28), the same tribe of Judah was saved on account of three men found in their midst: “David, Hezekiah, and Josiah, apart from whom all committed sin,” says Jesus son of Sirach. “For the powerful kings of Judah abandoned the law and despised the fear of the Lord” (Ecclus. 49).

Then, when they were led into captivity and shared the common mourning expressed in the words, “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down and wept, when we remembered Zion” (Ps. 136), they received the greatest increase of consolation through three men found in their midst: Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, because they despised the command of the wicked king and triumphed gloriously in the midst of the burning furnace.

Then, when it pleased God that the captivity should be ended, [Col. 0175A] that the Temple which had been destroyed should be founded, and that the city of Jerusalem itself should be rebuilt, God again accomplished this through three men: through such men as he wished, and such as it was fitting for the work to be accomplished through—not merely through the captives themselves, poor as they were, but through the powerful kings under whom the captives were held: Cyrus, Darius, and Artaxerxes.

Then, when the most arrogant Haman wished to destroy the whole Jewish race, salvation was accomplished through these three: Esther, Mordecai, and King Ahasuerus himself.

Then, when the devil attempted to do the same under the Greek kingdom, the remnant of that people was saved by the martial courage and illustrious faith of the three leaders, Judas, Jonathan, and Simon.

There is a most delightful mystery in these numbers: seven times, as has here been recounted, on account of three men, or through three men, [Col. 0175B] God one and three—that is, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, whom we confess and worship—saved and delivered that people until the word of promise was fulfilled, through which we too have been saved.

## CHAPTER XV

That it is not now so with that people after Christ’s birth; rather, “If these three men—Noah, Daniel, and Job—are in its midst,” says the Lord, “as I live, they alone shall deliver their own souls by their righteousness.”

Now consider what the Lord says through the prophet Ezekiel: “Son of man, when a land sins against me by committing a trespass, I will stretch out my hand over it and destroy from it man and beast. And if these three men, Noah, Daniel, and Job, are in its midst, [Col. 0175C] as I live, they alone by their righteousness shall deliver their own souls” (Ezek. 14).

Not content with saying it once, he repeats the judgment a second, third, and fourth time [Col. 0175D]: “As I live, they shall deliver neither sons nor daughters, but they alone shall be delivered; as I live, they shall deliver neither sons nor daughters, but they alone shall be delivered; as I live, they shall deliver neither son nor daughter, but they alone by their righteousness shall deliver their own souls” (ibid.).

Distinguishing his four judgments—famine, evil beasts, sword, and pestilence—the Lord affixed the same judgment to each. But this applies not to every land, but to a certain land when it sins; not to every land, I say. For after all these things he added: “And even if I send my four worst judgments—sword, famine, evil beasts, and pestilence—into Jerusalem, to destroy from it man and beast, nevertheless there shall remain in it a remnant bringing forth sons and daughters” (ibid.).

Unless he had decreed this, unless in the preceding judgments he had intended a certain land very different from Jerusalem, then surely what he says—“Noah, Daniel, and Job, they alone by their righteousness shall deliver their own souls”—would seem contrary to what has been recounted thus far: that the nation was often delivered on account of three men and through three men.

How then did he distinguish the land from Jerusalem? [Col. 0176A] What else should we understand by the separation of the land—that is, the Synagogue, which even now blasphemes Christ whom it crucified—from Jerusalem—that is, the Church, which believes in Christ?

But someone says: How could these three men, Noah, Daniel, and Job, ever have been in the midst of that land—that is, the Synagogue—which crucified Christ? To this I say: those three men, Noah, Daniel, and Job, lived long before and departed this life long before that accursed land crucified Christ, the Son of God.

But if you rightly distinguish their respective grounds—namely, that Noah built the ark amid a common danger, Daniel led a celibate life, and Job ruled his own household well, being especially known for having been found faithful in temptation—you plainly understand that those three men, Noah, Daniel, and Job, were in the midst of that land, and came to us from the midst of that land.

And if it seems too general a demonstration to show this in all Christ’s apostles, who were in the midst of that land [Col. 0176B] and, coming from it, established for us Gentiles the three aforesaid modes of life, behold, we may point out, as it were with a finger, three of those men—namely, apostles—Peter, John, and Paul, very like Noah, Daniel, and Job. Thus Peter, the chief ruler of the Church, is like Noah (1 Cor. 7); John, the chief example of the celibate or virgin life, is like Daniel (Eph. 2); and Paul, who among the other things in which he labored more than all others also rightly ordered married life, is like Job (2 Tim. 3).

## CHAPTER XVI

From what sword and famine, from what beasts, and from what pestilence the apostles did not save their Jewish kinsmen according to the flesh; and that they themselves were in their midst like Noah, Daniel, and Job.

We must now show from what sword and famine, from what beasts, and from what pestilence [Col. 0176C] they did not save their Jewish kinsmen according to the flesh, but delivered their own souls alone; and for what reason this was justly done.

To make this clearer, we must now proceed in order to that fourth unnamed beast, concerning which it is written: “After these things I looked in the vision of the night, and behold, a fourth beast, terrible and wondrous and exceedingly strong, having great iron teeth; it devoured and crushed, and trampled the remainder with its feet” (Dan. 7).

In whatever manner the Roman kingdom, as a great beast, terribly and wondrously devoured and crushed [Col. 0176D] the strength of the other nations with its great teeth, its iron teeth, this did not greatly concern those captives, to one of whom these things were revealed and through one of whom they were written for us. For their concern was only for their own race; the concern of the prophetic Spirit was for them because Christ was to be born from the same people.

Therefore, just as we know that the other beasts were so described, for example when one was told, “Arise, devour much flesh” (ibid.), on account of the Jewish people, concerning whom Haman said to King Ahasuerus, “If it pleases you, decree that it perish” (Esther 3), so also what is said concerning this fourth beast, the terrible and wondrous beast—“devouring and crushing and trampling the rest under its feet”—pertains to the same people. Under the commanders or rulers [Col. 0177A] Titus and Vespasian, that kingdom devoured and crushed them with a devouring so terrible and a crushing so wondrous that nothing like it had ever happened from the beginning of the age to any people or city, as Josephus the writer sets forth plainly, at once with astonishment and grief (Book 7, *On the Jewish War*). And it trampled the rest under its feet, so that it is apparent even now that those who remained of them were led captive into all nations.

Would these three men, Noah, Daniel, and Job, had they been in their midst, have delivered them? There were, indeed, some like them in their midst—namely, the apostles and many believers in Christ—but they did not deliver them. Rather, so that they alone might deliver their own souls, they were commanded by divine revelation, when the siege was imminent, to depart from their midst. Was this not as though Noah, Daniel, and Job had departed from their midst?

But three others, greatly contrary to them, remained in their midst [Col. 0177B]: Eleazar, John, and Simon, authors and leaders of most cruel, unspeakable seditions. Thus it came wonderfully to pass. And whereas in Babylon you hear: “I see three men walking in the midst of the fire, and the appearance of the fourth is like the Son of God” (Dan. 3), here, on the contrary, in the city called Jerusalem, you might cry out: I see three men holding miserable Jerusalem, tearing it apart and tormenting it in miserable ways by sword and famine—three men, I say, leaders of wickedness and of all brigandage—and the appearance of the fourth is like Barabbas, the seditious robber.

For because they chose Barabbas for themselves, but demanded that Christ, the Son of God, be killed (Matt. 7), therefore every Noah, every Daniel, and every Job withdrew from them. And by a just judgment, while they were besieged outside by the Romans, within they were given as prey to those three seditious leaders, who, divided against themselves, jointly tore apart and vied in ripping open the fasting and hungry entrails of the crowded city. [Col. 0177C]

## CHAPTER XVII

What, or of what kind, was the sin of that land which Noah, Daniel, and Job could not save; and how the Jews blasphemed, or spoke against, the Holy Spirit.

This was the judgment upon that land which sinned—not in just any manner, but as He said: “When a land sins against me by acting faithlessly in faithlessness” (Ezek. 14). For what is to act faithlessly in faithlessness, except to persist in a purpose of faithlessness with an unrepentant heart? This, then, was the exceedingly grave sin of that land, namely, that of the Jews, to whom most especially and in the first instance—and then to heretics as well—belongs that rebuke: “Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart?” (Ps. 4). How did they act faithlessly above all others—that is, persist in faithlessness? They rejected and crucified the Son of God, the Lord Jesus Christ, in their faithlessness. In faithlessness, I say—that is, against their own Law. For Moses had said in the Law: “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from your nation and from your brethren, like me; him you shall hear. But whoever refuses to hear his words, which he shall speak in my name, I will exact vengeance” (Deut. 18).

Therefore, in rejecting the Lord Christ they acted faithlessly, particularly since they possessed the lawful sign by which they could understand that he was that prophet: namely, the sufficient testimony of truth in his deeds and words. Yet perhaps some could excuse themselves on grounds of ignorance, saying that he was great. Thus, when he was blasphemed, he said: “Whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man shall be forgiven” (Matt. 12). And when he suffered: “Father,” he said, “forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23).

But what happened after this? How did that land become inexcusable, or how did it act faithlessly in faithlessness so as to be inexcusable? The Holy Spirit came upon his disciples, whom, indeed, he had indicated when he said to them: “And if I cast out demons by Beelzebub, prince of demons, by what power do your sons cast them out? Therefore they shall be your judges” (Matt. 12). “They cast out,” he said—that is, they shall most certainly cast them out, more than they do now, when the Holy Spirit comes. The Holy Spirit came, I say, with manifest power to bear testimony that he was the Christ; and then was fulfilled what he had said to them: “When the Paraclete comes, whom I shall send you from the Father—the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father—he shall bear testimony concerning me, and you also shall bear testimony” (John 15). Nevertheless, after this they persisted in faithlessness and did not cease to blaspheme; and then at last they were judged to have spoken a word against the Holy Spirit, and that sentence came upon them: “Whoever speaks a word against the Holy Spirit shall not be forgiven, neither in this age nor in the age to come” (Matt. 12).

## CHAPTER XVIII

Concerning which Jerusalem it is of which the Lord says in the same place: “If I send my four worst judgments upon Jerusalem, nevertheless there shall remain in it a salvation of those leading forth sons and daughters.”

But what outcome has that Jerusalem amid all tribulations? For the Lord says, immediately afterward in the same prophet: “Though I send my four worst judgments—sword, famine, evil beasts, and pestilence—upon Jerusalem, to destroy from it man and beast, nevertheless there shall remain in it a deliverance, bringing forth sons and daughters” (Ezek. 14). Wonderful is the difference, wonderful the contrast, between that land—that is, the apostate Synagogue—and this Jerusalem—that is, the faithful and catholic Church.

In that land, Noah, Daniel, and Job, if they were in its midst, could not deliver sons and daughters from any one of these judgments, but only their own souls. Yet into this Jerusalem the Lord sends all these four judgments in such a way, namely, that the patience of the saints may be tested—as has often happened—that, not to say what is less, Noah, Daniel, and Job, if they are in its midst, will deliver sons and daughters; but I say what is greater: “There shall remain in it a salvation of those leading forth sons and daughters.” For it is greater, by dying, to lead forth into eternal life sons and daughters who did not yet exist, than by prayer to rescue from bodily slaughter sons and daughters who already existed.

We have heard and seen how much the whole world, which lies in wickedness (1 John 5), has done against this Jerusalem; and especially how greatly, and through how widely extended persecutions, that same terrible and wondrous beast mentioned above has, as it were with great iron teeth, devoured and ground this Jerusalem. But what harm did it do? For there remained in them a salvation of those leading forth sons and daughters. Just as grain sown and dead in the earth rises again into manifold fruit (John 12), so, very often, when a few died for the testimony of faith, many thousands, considering their rational endurance, came to believe in Christ. Of these one may rightly say that those earlier persons who died were the fathers or mothers of the latter; and thus, as sons and daughters—indeed, truly as sons and daughters—they brought them forth by their own blood.

This, therefore, is truly Jerusalem and truly the house of Judah, to which that saying in Hosea truly applies: “I shall have mercy upon the house of Judah, and I shall save them in the Lord their God; and I shall not save them by bow, sword, war, horses, or horsemen” (Hos. 1). Likewise in Zechariah: “Not by an army, nor by strength, but by my Spirit, says the Lord of hosts” (Zech. 4). Your Spirit, O Lord of hosts, proceeding from you and beginning from the upper room, where it was awaited while a few men were gathered together in one place, came even to the great teeth, the iron teeth, of that beast. That beast, namely the Roman Empire, was truly Babylon; and throughout the whole furnace of persecution the Son of God, showing himself to the devout martyrs “as a breeze blowing with dew,” walked with them through the midst of the fire and kept their faith unharmed, until that beast became a man—that is, admitted reason—and, understanding the Christians’ faith to be rational, received the banner of the cross upon its brow; and, declaring with a human voice that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one true God, it even presented itself as protector to his worshippers.

## CHAPTER XIX

Concerning those three men whose proper names were Noah, Daniel, and Job, and how each came forth in his own time.

Let all, therefore, who desire to belong to these three men—Noah, Daniel, and Job—come forth from that land, and let them see how great is the desolation of that land and how fruitful is the testing of this Jerusalem. For “Behold,” he says, “they shall come forth to you, and you shall see their way and their devices; and you shall be comforted concerning the evil which I brought upon Jerusalem and concerning all that I brought upon it. And they shall comfort you when you see their way and their devices, and you shall know that I have not done without cause all that I did in it, says the Lord God” (Ezek. 14).

A great and almost ineffable mystery. How did Noah, Daniel, and Job, so often named above, come forth to us from that land, since they could not save sons and daughters? Let us first speak of those three men whose proper names were Noah, Daniel, and Job, and how each came forth in his own time. Noah first came forth with his three sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth (Gen. 8). Daniel, however, came forth with three boys, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego (Dan. 3). Job came forth with his three friends: Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite (Job 2).

What was their coming forth like? Noah’s coming forth from the heap of the dead was for the restoration of the human race through his three sons, under God’s threefold blessing, saying, “Increase and multiply” (Gen. 2). Daniel’s coming forth with his fellow captives was for their consolation, together with the three boys whom he received victorious from the midst of Babylon’s furnace; while he himself was glorified by three increases of grace in the sight of three kings: in the sight of Nebuchadnezzar, by the interpretation of dreams; in the sight of Belshazzar, by the reading and interpretation of words which were, in a wondrous manner, visibly written on the wall by an invisible hand; and in the sight of Darius, by a praiseworthy victory, because, as he said, “The Lord sent his angel and shut the mouths of the lions, and they did not defile me” (Dan. 2, 5, 14).

Job’s coming forth was as an example of patience for all ages to come. He was tempted and tested in three ways: by the hidden power which Satan received against him (Job 1–2), by the open speech of his wife, and by the excessive wisdom of his three friends, which afflicted him severely; and, because they had not spoken rightly, he reconciled them to God through sacrifice (Job 42).

Thus these three men—Noah with three sons, Daniel with three companions, and Job with three friends—make twelve; and this is the number of those who, first after Christ, undertook to steer the ark, that is, the Church, upon the waters of baptism; who glorified God among the nations, as in Babylon; and who stood firm in every temptation. Whoever rightly considers this undoubtedly perceives that saying of the Lord: “You shall know that I have not done without cause all that I did” (Ezek. 14).

# BOOK NINE

## CHAPTER I

Concerning what is written: “As one who eats much honey, it is not good for him; so one who is a searcher of majesty shall be overwhelmed by glory”; and that searching the Scriptures is not the same as being a searcher of majesty.

As we speak of your glorification, venerable Trinity, one God, we have long trembled beneath the rod of your fear, knowing both that we must never cease from your praise and that we must nevertheless beware of much speaking. For it is written: “As one who eats much honey, it is not good for him; so one who is a searcher of majesty shall be overwhelmed by glory” (Prov. 2). And elsewhere: “For God is in heaven and you are upon earth; therefore let your words be few” (Eccl. 5).

Yet is searching the Scriptures the same as being a searcher of majesty? Or may one rightly say to him who does not speak beyond the rule or authority of the Scriptures of truth: “Your words are not few, but many”? Therefore my mouth shall still speak the praise of the Lord which it began; and this work, now extended through eight little books, I shall conclude in this ninth little book.

And when I have done so, O Spirit of Father and Son, what reward is there for this work? Or rather, what grace for this grace? Let the inner man be permitted, by briefly and secretly expressing his purpose or expectation, to use the words of blessed Job: “Only two things,” he says, “do not do to me, and then I shall not hide from your face. Remove your hand far from me, and let not your might terrify me” (Job 13). That is to say: Do not exact vengeance for my sins, and let not the princes of darkness confront me; and then, gladdened by the abundance of your benefit, at its departure my soul shall say: Behold, I now see what I desired; I now hold what I hoped for. After putting off the body, I am not hidden from his face—the one whom, while placed in the body, I loved with the whole affection of faith.

Therefore, let the subject of this final book be for me you, most holy house, with your seven pillars, which Wisdom built for herself (Prov. 9). I have indeed mentioned you in some place in the preceding books; but I have deferred until now the mystery of the seven pillars, almost universally known, desiring to add something beyond common knowledge and customary reading concerning this house, which is the temple of the Lord’s body, to the praise of the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father and the Son.

## CHAPTER II

That the house which Wisdom built for herself is the body of Christ; and that within this house the procession of the Holy Spirit was celebrated three times: first, in building; second, in adorning; third, in dedicating.

Here, therefore, it is fitting first to recall that the procession of the Holy Spirit was celebrated three times in this house, according to the type of that made house, or temple, which Solomon built with great wisdom, adorned with wondrous glory, and dedicated with great solemnity. For the Holy Spirit wisely built this unmade house, the temple of the Lord’s body, by himself; fittingly adorned it; and gloriously and blessedly dedicated it (3 Kings 7–8).

He built it, I say, in the incarnation of the Word itself; he adorned it in the manifestation of that true man; he dedicated it in that same man’s most holy resurrection. That dedication is indicated by the title of Psalm 29: “A psalm of a song at the dedication of the house of David.” For the title directs us to the history and to the sacred understanding of the history: just as David, by his expenditure and provision, built a temple to the Lord through Solomon’s hand, and afterward dedicated it with joyful and [alternatively: solemn] solemn ceremonies and words in praise of the Lord (1 Chron. 22), so Christ’s body, in respect of its unique birth and immunity from sin, was built; but after the resurrection, in respect of impassibility and immortality, it remains dedicated in eternal glory.

By that manifestation we mean that in which the Holy Spirit manifested him in the form of a dove, while John proclaimed: “And I did not know him; but that he might be manifested in Israel, therefore I came baptizing in water” (John 1). In these three splendors of grace, which was poured out upon your lips—“more beautiful in form than the sons of men” (Ps. 44)—we so praise and glorify the holy Trinity that we likewise proclaim the Holy Spirit, proceeding from the Father and the Son, as the maker of this house. This house, indeed, are you according to your humanity; and in it he himself rests with all the riches, or treasures, of wisdom and knowledge which he has stored up for you.

## CHAPTER III

Concerning the seven pillars of this same house; and who was the first author of this number in writing of the seven spirits of God.

Who has not heard, from the agreement of other Scriptures, that the seven pillars which Wisdom cut out in this her house—as Scripture says, “Wisdom built herself a house; she cut out seven pillars” (Prov. 9)—are the seven spirits of God? For example, the prophet Isaiah said: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root; and the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. 11).

There are many passages in Scripture which agree concerning the sevenfold Holy Spirit, under the mystery of the number seven: namely, the seven lamps before God’s throne, the seven horns of the Lamb, and his seven eyes (Rev. 4–5). This is no different from what is found in the prophet Zechariah: seven eyes upon one stone, and seven lamps upon a single lampstand, above the top of that one lampstand (Zech. 3–4).

But we seek this—and it is delightful to discover it: who was the first author of this number, to write of the seven spirits of the Lord; and for what reason these same seven spirits ought to have been signified by the equal number of pillars. There is no doubt that everything found in the canonical Scriptures possesses divine authority. Nevertheless, that divine authority itself is more pleasing and gives fuller joy when any divine Scripture possesses at the same time authority or testimony from some earlier Scripture.

For example, what is written in Zechariah, as I have already mentioned—“For there are seven eyes upon one stone” (ibid.)—possesses divine authority, for the Holy Spirit spoke through the mouth of all the prophets. Yet it delights us more because before him the prophet Isaiah, whom we have already mentioned, wrote most explicitly of the seven Spirits of the Lord, so that he even expressed each one by its own proper name (Isa. 11).
