Therefore we ask whether the one who undoubtedly wrote by divine authority, “Wisdom built herself a house; she cut out seven pillars” (Prov. 9), read or heard some predecessor speaking similar words—for example, David or Moses. In seeking this, we quickly discover that Moses was the predecessor of this writer and of all the prophets in this mystery of the number seven. His Scripture, flowing not from a man or from the handwritten literary work of any man, but from Moses’ own mouth, is like the fountain of the Scriptures; all the other prophetic Scriptures are like streams from that same fountain. This is easy to show, if so great a matter can be set forth in a few words.

## CHAPTER IV

Concerning the first seven days; and that from them the Spirit of the Lord, who was borne over the waters, ought to be known as the sevenfold Spirit: first, the spirit of fear, in accordance with the division of darkness and light; and finally, the spirit of wisdom, in accordance with the seventh day on which God rested.

“In the beginning the Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters” (Gen. 1); that Spirit of God is, indeed, the goodness of God himself. In this goodness God created all things in six days and rested on the seventh. Since the Creator is known through the creature, as the Apostle says: “For his invisible things, from the creation of the world, are understood and perceived through the things that have been made—his eternal power also and divinity” (Rom. 1), we especially, who desire, in knowing God, to glorify him as God and give thanks, ought to know from the creaturely order of those days the Holy Spirit himself, who before every day was borne over the waters.

From that day, namely, on which God divided light and darkness—that is, good angels and evil angels—this Spirit is known to be the spirit of fear. For in the believing soul, remembrance of that great and terrible judgment produces fear: the judgment in which the angels of darkness were divided from the angels of light by so great a separation that they can never again be restored throughout eternity. Of this fear, or spirit of fear, it is written in Job: “Power and terror are with him, who makes peace in his heights” (Job 25).

From the second day, on which “God made the firmament in the midst of the waters and divided the waters from the waters,” the Spirit of God may be known as the spirit of piety, if one rightly considers with what purpose God made the fabric of this world, whose beginning was the making of that same firmament, which he called heaven. What did God—or the Wisdom of God—intend when he thus began? “When he prepared the heavens,” she says, “I was present; when he bounded the abysses by a fixed law and a circuit, I was with him, arranging all things, playing before him at all times, playing in the circle of the earth; and my delights were to be with the sons of men” (Prov. 8). And what could be more pious than that he prepared the heavens, made this world, and made the human race within it, because Wisdom herself already delighted that she would one day become man and be with the sons of men?

From the third day, on which God said: “Let the dry land appear,” which he called earth; and, “Let it bring forth green grass bearing seed, and fruit-bearing trees producing fruit according to their kind, whose seed is in itself upon the earth” (Gen. 1)—which was the beginning of the world’s adornment, on account of which Scripture says, “Moreover, the Lord God had planted from the beginning a paradise of delight” (Gen. 2), where adornment, or the adornment of the earth, is understood—from this third day, I say, the Holy Spirit is known to be the spirit of knowledge, indeed even the Lord of sciences. Since Adam, placed in Paradise, already coveted this knowledge in his heart, the tempter was allowed to approach and say: “Eat, and you shall be as gods,” that is, like God, “knowing good and evil” (Gen. 5).

From the fourth day, on which God said: “Let lights be made in the firmament of heaven, and let them divide day and night; and let them be for signs, seasons, days, and years” (Gen. 1), the Holy Spirit is known to be the spirit of might. For who among ecclesiastical writers or pagan philosophers has not marveled at the might, or power, in those two great lights—the sun and moon—and in the stars which God placed in the firmament of heaven? First the Psalmist says: “He made the great lights: the sun to rule the day, and the moon and stars to rule the night” (Ps. 135). After him, investigators of the world, the wise men of this age, said and wrote much concerning this most marvelous creature, the sun, moon, and stars, which keep their courses according to so certain and fixed a law, established by God’s command that he set in place. They even believed that these bodies live and that human destinies hang upon them (Virgil, *Georgics*; Ovid, *Metamorphoses*); a belief which the Church of God neither wished nor ought to accept.

There are other marks of their powers, sufficient to sound understanding for proving that great might is truly present in them. “Five zones hold heaven,” says the distinguished poet (Lucan, *Pharsalia*); and secular writers have expended much notable ingenuity upon their positions and upon the causes of temperateness or intemperateness associated with them [addition: “ingenuities”]. Nor did ecclesiastical discernment reject these matters, understanding the sun to be the principal cause of this diversity, in accordance with the command laid upon it to rise upward and descend downward. “For the sun rises and sets,” says Ecclesiastes, “and returns to its place; and there, rising anew, it circles through the south and turns toward the north. Going around, it surveys all things in its circuit; the spirit proceeds, and returns to its circuits” (Eccl. 1).

By circling and circling again, it tempers two zones: the one which is also central, excessively scorched because it is always subject to the sun; and the two outermost zones, benumbed by cold and perpetual ice because the sun is farther from them, or because in its circling and circling again it does not draw near to them. We would consider it superfluous to mention these matters here, unless we had to say something about the might that is in the sun—especially because the Psalmist also refers to them, saying: “For neither from the east, nor from the west, nor from the desert mountains”—understand, “is an open place of escape”—“for God is judge” (Ps. 74).

From the fifth day, on which God said: “Let the waters bring forth creeping things with living soul, and birds above the earth under the firmament of heaven”; and blessed them, saying, “Increase and multiply,” the Holy Spirit is known to be the spirit of counsel. While his power is borne over the waters, it has produced this wondrous thing in a creature of such a kind as lacks reason: it knows how to provide so wisely for its offspring that rational man cannot sufficiently marvel. The same is true even of the smallest animals produced by the earth on the sixth day: “Go,” says Solomon, “to the ant, O sluggard; consider her ways and learn wisdom. Though she has neither leader, instructor, nor ruler, she prepares food for herself in summer and gathers in harvest what she may eat” (Prov. 6).

Finally, in the human creature it is not so marvelous that it is capable of counsel, since in man rationality stands between sensuality and mortality. But in a creature of this kind, whatever it may be, that is without rationality, although it exercises the five senses, it is exceedingly marvelous that there should be so much mortality—or, as it were, a solicitude of counsel—in it, so that it may serve as an example to man, reproving his sluggishness in many respects.

From the sixth day, or from the human creature made on the sixth day, the Holy Spirit is known to be the spirit of understanding: not only because man is known to be rational, but also—and this is greatest—because he is capable of spiritual understanding. For although the first man did not then understand, and very many after him did not understand, as it is written: “Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared to senseless beasts and became like them” (Ps. 48); and again: “The natural man does not perceive the things which God has made” (1 Cor. 2), nevertheless there have been, and are, many spiritual people. For the Lord is great, and he has filled many whom he willed with the spirit of understanding.

From the seventh day, which God blessed and sanctified, and on which he rested—from this very fact, namely that he rested upon it—the Holy Spirit is known to be the spirit of wisdom, insofar as the nature of that rest can already be perceived or tasted in this life. For he truly leads into great wisdom the one whom he makes teachable by that saying: “Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart, and you shall find rest for your souls” (Matt. 11). This rest is wisdom, which the Holy Spirit produces: that is, participation in uncreated Wisdom, which is the Word of God himself, the Wisdom of the Father.

## CHAPTER V

For what reason the same mystery of the sevenfold Spirit was fittingly designated by the name of seven pillars; and why Isaiah, arranging the same spirits in reverse order, descended from the spirit of wisdom to the spirit of fear.

As far as faithful discourse could, it has reached the clear fountain from which a stream flowed through the mouths of many who said words like those of him who, after saying, “Wisdom built herself a house,” added: “She cut out seven pillars” (Prov. 9). But for what reason was it fitting that the mystery of the sevenfold Spirit, already mentioned, should be designated by the name of seven pillars?

Surely because of the great glory and honor of this most high Son of Man, since the temple of his body is itself the house which “Wisdom built for herself.” A house built upon pillars plainly derives from those same pillars both firmness and beauty, and it is lofty. Therefore, if you look at the pillars which we have now set out in order, is not such a position of the house of Wisdom that exaltation of the Son of Man of which it had long before been written: “You crowned him with glory and honor, and set him over the works of your hands” (Ps. 8)?

For he is Lord of the holy angels; Lord of the firmament—that is, heaven; Lord of earth, or Paradise, and sea; Lord of sun, moon, and stars; Lord of all creatures produced by the waters and of those produced from the earth; Lord of the entire human race; and Lord even of the Sabbath (Matt. 12), that is, of the heavenly homeland in which is the fullness of the rest for which we hope. Truly it is a great house, a beautiful and most lofty house.

The sevenfold Spirit himself dwells there fully and in perfect peace, for he has never suffered there any offense of fault or negligence. This is what Isaiah said: “And the Spirit of the Lord rests upon him” (Isa. 11). But that Isaiah arranged the same spirits differently, placing the spirit of wisdom first and the spirit of fear seventh, has this cause or reason: our Lord Jesus Christ, whose coming was foretold from the most high, wise secret and great rest of the Father’s bosom, descended here even unto obedience and the death of the cross. This obedience, indeed, was in him the religious fear of the Lord. But we, for whose instruction or correction those works of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were written, begin with fear and are perfected in wisdom, as another Scripture says: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110).

## CHAPTER VI

Concerning the building of this house of the Lord; and that there occurred in it what the Psalmist said: “Mercy and truth met one another; righteousness and peace kissed.”

How did this happen? How was this house built? “Hammer, axe, and every iron tool were not heard in the house while it was being built” (3 Kings 6). Rather, in secret silence, with no disturbance from the unrest of human work, the Holy Spirit, who “in the beginning was borne over the waters,” came upon the blessed Virgin and ineffably overshadowed her womb (Luke 1), after the fashion of a bird warming an egg placed beneath it by a most desired brooding.

Yet our weakness might perhaps not dare to use this comparison in so great a mystery unless it had been assumed beforehand. Then, therefore, occurred what the Psalmist, singing, had foretold: “Mercy and truth met one another; righteousness and peace kissed. Truth sprang up from the earth, and righteousness looked down from heaven” (Ps. 84).

For mercy is the Holy Spirit; truth is the Word of God, the Son of God. Likewise righteousness is Christ, the Son of God; peace—that is, the remission of sins—is the Spirit. How, or for what end, did such mercy and such truth meet one another? How, or for what end, did such righteousness and such peace kiss? Who shall ask me this? Or who is fit to answer these things?

I too might ask something far less, which nevertheless cannot be explained in words or comprehended by human understanding. In the nest of a bird, when an egg lies beneath it, how do the bird’s own body and the offspring formed from the egg meet one another? For the body of the brooding bird is not changed into seed, nor diminished from its own nature in order that offspring like it may be born; but by the warmth of the brooding body the egg is animated, and its moisture is formed into a similar bird. Thus they meet and kiss one another—that is, they are joined in inseparable love.

Who is sufficient to dispute about such things? We indeed read that “Solomon discoursed concerning trees, from the cedar which is in Lebanon unto the hyssop which comes forth from the wall; and he spoke concerning beasts, birds, creeping things, and fishes” (3 Kings 4); but we do not read that in disputing and discoursing he comprehended these things themselves. How much less, then, is anyone sufficient to dispute or discourse concerning how the Holy Spirit, coming upon the blessed Virgin and remaining in his own nature or substance—lest anyone suppose that he himself was there as seed—and the Word of God, with the seed-bearing substance of the Virgin’s womb, met one another, according to what has already been said: “Mercy and truth met one another” (Prov. 25).

Let us not, therefore, seek matters higher than ourselves, lest we be accused as searchers of majesty. Let us be content to know this: that Wisdom built this house, the most holy temple of his body, for himself by his Spirit—by his Spirit, I say, that is, by operation, not from the substance of his Spirit. And the seven pillars already mentioned he cut out, as it were, from another mountain, from the person of his Father alone. But Wisdom herself, or the Son of God, and the Father of that same Son, just as they are one substance, so also both inseparably placed their sevenfold Spirit in this house, in this man Jesus Christ, Son of God and Son of Man.

## CHAPTER VII

Again, concerning the same matter: for what end mercy and truth met one another, and what counsel they had there concerning the salvation of the human race, according to that saying of blessed Job: “Would that my sins, by which I deserved wrath, and the calamity which I suffer, were weighed in a balance.”

We have spoken, as far as we were able, of how and where mercy and truth met one another; it remains to say also for what purpose, since this too was proposed above. For what purpose, then, did mercy and truth meet one another? For what purpose did they come together? For what purpose did righteousness, which is truth itself, and peace, which is mercy itself, kiss one another? Surely in order to deliberate and take counsel concerning great matters, to consider the business of a great undertaking: namely, how the human race might be saved.

For it was no slight matter how mercy, which is the Holy Spirit, might excuse and restore humankind to salvation while preserving the claim of righteousness or truth, which is the Word himself, or the Son of God. Counsel was therefore held—or rather, the counsel predetermined before the ages was then brought from the Virgin’s womb into effect—by establishing that a human being had suffered more calamity than he had deserved by his sins.

This, then, was the sum of the counsel in that meeting of mercy and truth, or kissing of righteousness and peace: that this man of divine goodness, the fruit of our earth—that is, of the Virgin’s womb—must be born mortal, die, and rise from the dead; and that he should thus be brought to completion through faith in our hearts, so that we might be two: namely, the sinful human being, condemned to death because of sin; and, in each one of us, the man made mortal without sin, put to death, and thereby made conqueror of death.

Are we not thus, O mediator of God and humankind, man Jesus Christ, you and I, two? Indeed, are we not one spirit and one body? (1 Cor. 6.) Yet in another respect we are two, and Wisdom speaks of us both: “Two together are better than one. They have the advantage of their companionship. If one falls, he shall be supported by the other; if anyone prevails against one, two withstand him” (Eccl. 4).

Where does—or will—this occur? Surely it begins in this life and is completed at the gate mentioned by the Psalmist when he says: “He shall not be ashamed when he speaks with his enemies in the gate” (Ps. 126). In the gate, I say—that is, at the departure from this life—it is completed.

How is it completed there? By standing before Christ’s tribunal, when the balance is set ready: the balance which blessed Job, lamenting that it was not yet set ready in his day, said: “Would that my sins, by which I deserved wrath, and the calamity I suffer, were weighed in a balance! This would appear heavier than the sand of the sea” (Job 6).

This balance was set ready when, as has been said, mercy and truth met one another: when the immortal God became a mortal human being. When, therefore, one comes to the examination of this balance, while standing before the tribunal of this Judge, there are two scales, one of mercy and the other of judgment. Yet there are also two persons, as we have said: the human being who sinned, and Christ, who did not sin, dwelling by faith in that person’s heart (Eph. 3). The sins of one alone are weighed in the scale of judgment; the calamity of two is weighed in the scale of mercy: both the calamity of the death of the one who sinned—for example Job, or another faithful man—and the calamity of the death of the one who did not sin, namely Jesus Christ.

Would not, then, the calamity in the scale of mercy appear heavier than the sins in the scale of judgment? Certainly heavier than the sand of the sea, as twofold against single: because, though we are two and only one has sinned, both pay the debt of death. What then? Surely, as it is written and as we have already recalled: “If anyone prevails against one, two withstand him” (Eccl. 4). That is, if the prince of this world stands against him in order to accuse the departing soul, he seeks defense from Christ dwelling within him, saying: “Take hold of weapons and shield; rise up to help me” (Ps. 34).

## CHAPTER VIII

Again, concerning the building of the same house: what mystery is contained in the saying, “When the house was being built, it was built with hewn and finished stones.”

But now let us fulfill, in the order we proposed, our discourse concerning your house, Lord—your body, Christ. For we proposed faithfully to celebrate in discourse these three matters: the building, adornment, and dedication of this house, “in which all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Col. 2).

We should now speak of its adornment, were we not still held in the section on the building by this passage: “When the house was being built, it was built with hewn and finished stones” (3 Kgs. 7). For the mind does not permit the mystery of this passage to pass untouched.

What, then, is meant by such a house being built “with hewn and finished stones,” except that the mediator of God and humankind, the man Christ Jesus, was conceived from the womb—or formed in the womb—of the Virgin according to the faith and faithful utterance of the patriarchs and prophets, who indeed were, or are, great stones and finished stones?

One of them, Isaiah, rejoices over this and says: “I took for myself faithful witnesses: Uriah the priest and Zechariah son of Barachiah. And I approached the prophetess; and she conceived and bore a son. And the Lord said to me: Call his name, ‘Hasten, strip the spoils; hurry to plunder’” (Isa. 8).

Certainly this one man spoke; yet it is fitting to say that all the holy prophets likewise spoke, or speak, through whose mouths the Holy Spirit has spoken from of old. For all approached that prophetess; the faith of all, the prophecies of all, converged upon that blessed Virgin; and she herself knew what was being done concerning her according to the truth of the Scriptures.

“The house, therefore, was built with hewn and finished stones”: that is, the Lord’s Incarnation rests upon the faith and exposition of the saints and upon the Scriptures of the prophets; and your holy house, Lord, has true testimony from them all, according to that proclamation of the great Prophet: “Your testimonies have become exceedingly trustworthy; holiness befits your house, Lord, unto length of days” (Ps. 92).

How fittingly, moreover, are these finished stones also called hewn. For which of them passed through the course of this life without the cutting of tribulation? Indeed, many of them were hewn even to the destruction of their bodies. Hence God himself says in Hosea: “Therefore I hewed them by the prophets; I killed them by the words of my mouth” (Hos. 6). And Stephen, the first martyr, says in the Acts of the Apostles: “Stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit, as your fathers did, so do you. Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? And they killed those who foretold the coming of the Just One” (Acts 7).

## CHAPTER IX

Concerning the adornment of the same house: with what gold it was adorned when the Holy Spirit descended upon the Lord in the form of a dove while he was baptized by John.

Once this house—or temple of the Lord’s body—had been built, what happened next? How was it adorned or decorated? “Solomon,” says the mystical Scripture, “covered the house before the oracle with purest gold and fastened the plates with golden nails; and there was nothing in the temple not covered with gold. He also covered the whole altar of the oracle with gold, and made in the oracle two cherubim of olive wood” (3 Kgs. 6).

According to the type of that made-by-hands adornment—which it would take far too long to set forth here in full—the house not made by hands of which we are now speaking, namely the humanity of Christ our Savior, was also adorned in the thirtieth year of his age. For until that year he remained unknown among people.

In that year, as the Evangelists plainly say, “Jesus himself was beginning to be about thirty years old when he was baptized by John; the Holy Spirit descended upon him in bodily form like a dove; and he, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan” (Luke 3–4).

What, I ask, does it mean that he returned from the Jordan full of the Holy Spirit, when without doubt he had been full of the Holy Spirit from his very conception? What does it mean, I say, or what did it mean, that he returned from the Jordan full of the Holy Spirit, except that the time had now come for him to exercise in deed those gifts of the Holy Spirit which he had previously possessed in power? (1 Cor. 10.)

This is the true gold, the purest gold; these are the precious stones: namely, the word of wisdom, the word of knowledge, the working of miracles, gifts of healing, prophecy, discernment of spirits, and interpretation of utterances (John 7). From that time he began so to exercise such gifts in deed that no one ever spoke as this man spoke, and no other ever performed works such as he performed (John 15).

Was not that house therefore covered with purest gold, so that there was nothing in the temple not covered with gold? Delighted by such gold, or by the splendor of gold, his bride says in the Song of Songs: “His hands are turned, golden, full of hyacinths” (Song 5).

“Turned” means swift or skillful in working; “golden,” working by the power of the divine nature; “full of hyacinths,” breathing forth heavenly mysteries in outward signs. That this house had been adorned with such adornment had remained so wholly unseen for thirty years that, when he chose disciples and also gave them power to perform works of this kind, astonishment at him became excessive, as Mark plainly relates: “When his own heard it, they went out to seize him, for they said that he had gone mad” (Mark 3).

## CHAPTER X

What was signified by the Holy Spirit’s appearing, when proceeding to this work, not in any form whatever but in the form of a dove.

What was signified by the Holy Spirit’s appearing, when proceeding to this work, not in any form whatever but in the form of a dove? Truly it belonged “to the great mystery of godliness, which,” as the Apostle says, “was manifested in flesh, justified in spirit, appeared to angels, was preached among the nations, believed in in this world, and taken up in glory” (1 Tim. 3).

For you must not attend only to the fact that from that time the Word in flesh, God in man, began to be glorified by miracles. Rather, you must attend to the fact that he then undertook to perform repentance for us: baptized with John’s baptism, namely a baptism of repentance, which he immediately began with a fast of forty days and continued in until death—indeed, death on a cross.

Truly this was a great mystery of godliness, because the Lord laid upon him, in repentance, the iniquities of us all (Isa. 53). For the sacred and mystical law had signified such repentance, completed by death on the cross, in the sacrament of sacrifice, saying: If burnt offerings are offered “to the Lord from turtledoves and young pigeons, the priest shall offer them upon the altar; and, twisting back its head at the neck and breaking open the wound, he shall cause the blood to run down upon the side of the altar. He shall not cut it apart or divide it with iron, but shall burn it upon the altar, on wood with fire placed beneath it: it is a burnt offering, an offering of a most sweet odor to the Lord” (Lev. 1).

For what is signified in this offering of the turtledove and dove, commanded to be offered for sin, and in the requirement that the victim’s head remain attached to the body after death, except the person of our Mediator? The death of our Redeemer availed for the joining, not the severing, of his body—that is, the Church. For the mediator of God and humankind, who is the head of us all, is truly the victim of cleansing. By what he suffered death for us, he adhered to us more truly.

Therefore, after the cutting, the dove’s head remains attached to its body, because not even intervening death divides Christ and the Church. It was thus greatly pertinent to the great mystery of godliness that the Holy Spirit appeared upon him in the form of a dove, of whom the Apostle says: “By the Holy Spirit, offering himself unspotted to God, he cleansed our conscience from dead works to serve the living God” (Heb. 9).

Add also that John the Baptist, in the very place where he bore witness, saying, “I saw the Holy Spirit descend from heaven like a dove, and remain upon him,” proclaimed his gentleness with this utterance and judgment: “Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1). Finally, in the Lord’s sacrifice—the sacrifice of sweet odor—the gentleness of the lamb and the simplicity of the dove alike mystically signify the innocence and godliness of Christ, the Son of God.

## CHAPTER XI

Concerning the day which the Holy Spirit appointed in David, saying: “Today, if you hear his voice.”

From that time onward, that is the day of good hearing, the day on which the voice is to be heard in the gentleness of faith, which the Holy Spirit appointed in David and which the people now recall. Therefore, as the Holy Spirit says: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts, as in the provocation, according to the day of temptation in the wilderness” (Ps. 24).

O sweet and gentle voice, voice of love and grace, voice of turtledove and dove, which in Luke we began to hear thus: Returning in the power of the Spirit into Galilee, when he came to Nazareth and entered the synagogue, and the book of the prophet Isaiah was handed to him, he immediately found this passage: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he anointed me; he sent me to proclaim good news to the poor, to preach release to captives, to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of recompense” (Isa. 16). “Today,” he says, “this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing” (Luke 4).

By this voice our hearts ought today to be softened or made gentle—today, I say, that is, on another day, different from that day on which Israel came out of Egypt through the Red Sea and for forty years tempted and provoked the Holy Spirit in the wilderness.

Did not John the Baptist see this, when at the beginning of this day he saw Jesus coming to him and said, as we have recalled above: “Behold the Lamb of God” (John 1)? Indeed, such language gives us such an understanding: behold him whose figure was the Lamb sacrificed in Egypt, when its blood was taken from the threshold and placed on the lintel and on each doorpost, so as to express the figure of the cross; and the Passover—that is, the passage—took place. For the Lord passed through Egypt, striking the Egyptians and saving the children of Israel (Exod. 12).

Now another Egypt will be struck, another sea divided, another manna given from heaven, another rock give other waters to the thirsty, another land entered, another city Jerusalem inhabited; and all things will be restored anew, as he who baptizes in the Holy Spirit says: “Behold, I make all things new” (Rev. 21).

Therefore the day of holy newness dawned when, with the Spirit of godliness appearing from above in the form of a dove, Christ the Son of God was declared High Priest: High Priest, I say, himself both victim and temple, and from that time most excellently adorned, as we have said above, according to the figure of that temple made by hands—not with corruptible gold but with the true gold of radiant divinity, which then began to shine in him through the working of miracles, the grace of healings, and the other works of the finger of God, the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER XII

Concerning the dedication of the same house—that is, the resurrection—according to Psalm 29, whose title is: “A Psalm of David, a song at the dedication of David’s house.”

The mind hastens, according to its purpose, toward the dedication of the house—that is, toward the glory of the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ—by which the temple of his body was undoubtedly dedicated, so that, with every poverty of mortality or passibility wiped away, an eternal solemnity and everlasting festival may be celebrated in it with the voice of exultation and confession by angels and by all people who are or will be children of the resurrection.

At this point, may the text of Psalm 29 direct our thought and words, a psalm bearing this title: “A psalm, a song at the dedication of David’s house.” But first, it is pleasing to lay down as the foundation of our discourse that the house made by hands, which, as we have said above, was built as a type of this one, was dedicated under a threefold blessing of the Lord’s name, as the sequence of Scripture itself plainly shows.

First, it is written thus: “The king turned his face and blessed the whole assembly of Israel, and said: Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, who spoke with his mouth to David my father and fulfilled it with his hands” (3 Kgs. 8), and so forth.

Again, secondly: “Solomon stood before the altar of the Lord, in the presence of the assembly of Israel, and spread out his hands to heaven, and said: Lord God of Israel, there is no God like you in heaven above or on earth beneath, who kept for your servant David my father the things you spoke” (ibid.), and so forth.

Then thirdly: “When Solomon had finished all the prayer, he stood and blessed the whole assembly of Israel in a loud voice, saying: Blessed be the Lord, who has given rest to his people Israel, according to all that he has spoken” (ibid.), and so forth.

Thus, under the threefold invocation of the Lord’s name, as has been said, he dedicated the Church, or house of the Lord—not by chance, certainly, but with the great reason of the wisdom God had given him, especially since such a rule of blessing had been given. For it is written in the book of Numbers: “The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to Aaron and his sons: Thus shall you bless the children of Israel, and say to them: May the Lord bless you and keep you; may the Lord show his face to you and have mercy on you; may the Lord turn his countenance toward you and give you peace” (Num. 6).

We say this for the glorification of the Trinity, because, as we have taken care to show thus far, the Scriptures of truth record almost nothing celebrated or memorable without the sacrament of this holy name.

## CHAPTER XIII

Again, in the same psalm, concerning the threefold invocation of the Lord’s name: “I will exalt you, Lord; Lord, I cried to you; Lord, you brought my soul up from hell”; and concerning the title of another psalm: “Unto the end, a song of the psalm of resurrection.”

Now consider this very beautiful point: in this psalm, a song sung or to be sung for the dedication of David’s house—that is, Christ’s body—the threefold invocation of the same name, Lord, similarly prevails.

First he says: “I will exalt you, Lord, because you received me and did not delight my enemies over me.” Secondly: “Lord my God, I cried to you, and you healed me.” Thirdly: “Lord, you brought my soul up from hell; you saved me from those going down into the pit.” Immediately there follows the chorus of the multitude with this exhortation: “Sing to the Lord, you his saints, and give thanks to the remembrance of his holiness” (Ps. 29).

Likewise, at the dedication of that house made by hands, after Solomon had first offered threefold adoration of the Lord’s name, there immediately followed an exhortation to the multitude and the sharing of a great universal festival. Solomon continued: “Let our heart also be perfect with the Lord our God.” And Scripture followed: “Therefore the king and all Israel with him sacrificed victims before the Lord” (3 Kgs. 6).

For this dedication is a universal festival, the festival of resurrection. Hence we must not pass over the fact that the title of the psalm set forth above, which runs, “A psalm, a song at the dedication of David’s house,” is almost explained by the title of another psalm, namely the sixty-fifth: “Unto the end, a song of the psalm of resurrection.” It begins with this title: “All the earth rejoices in God, sings a psalm to his name, gives glory to his praise,” and says among other things: “I shall enter into your house with burnt offerings; I shall render to you my vows, which my lips uttered. I shall offer you fat burnt offerings with incense of rams; I shall offer you oxen with goats.”

All these things mystically signify the burning up of vices, purification of the spirit, and complete endeavor toward the destruction of all resistance, as of horned rams; all preeminence, as of horn-thrusting oxen; and all foulness of evil works, as of goats.

For with such burnt offerings one enters the house of resurrection, the house which the most wise Solomon—that is, Christ the Son of God—built through himself: namely immortality and impassibility, which the heavenly spirits already possess, in whom the majesty of the holy Trinity dwells most fully. Into this house the Forerunner entered by the way shown him by the dove—that is, by the Holy Spirit.

For Christ himself, suffering and rising from the dead, began for himself and for us the festival of this dedication, as a head for its body. To hold this faith and work in this hope through love is surely to sing lawfully the song of the psalm of resurrection and already to stand with song in that dedication of David’s house.

## CHAPTER XIV

Why, from that festival of dedication—that is, from the glory of the resurrection—the Holy Spirit appeared not in the form of a dove but in the form of fire; and concerning the spirit of blasphemy, whose sin will be forgiven neither in this age nor in the age to come.

This dedication of the house indeed possesses the joy of a great festival; nevertheless, the form which appeared thereafter ought to instill great fear and awaken concern. For the Holy Spirit did not show himself here to be seen in the form of a dove, but proceeded from that house in the form of fire upon the blessed apostles (Acts 2), sent by him according to the power or nature of divinity, as he said to them: “If I go away, I will send him to you” (John 16).

Why then not in the form of a dove, but in the form of fire? Let all who dare irreverently to behold this house of the Lord after it has been dedicated attend to the great difference between these forms, namely the dove and fire—those to whom he himself said: “Therefore I say to you: Every sin and blasphemy shall be forgiven to people, but blasphemy of the spirit shall not be forgiven. Whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man, it shall be forgiven him; but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit, it shall not be forgiven him, neither in this age nor in the age to come” (Matt. 12).

Let such people attend, I say; or rather, because such people refuse to attend, let us attend to the reason why the one and same Spirit, appearing at different times, displayed forms so different.

First, it must be said what distinguishes blasphemy from the spirit of blasphemy, since he said: “Blasphemy shall be forgiven, but the spirit of blasphemy shall not be forgiven.” Blasphemy alone, and not also the spirit of blasphemy, occurs when someone speaks in ignorance otherwise than truth stands, or does something against justice. For example, Saul acted in ignorance and error (Acts 9).

But the spirit of blasphemy exists where someone knowingly and out of envy resists truth (1 Tim. 1). This is the sin of the Jews and heretics, whom the Apostle declares must be avoided: “Avoid,” he says, “a heretical person after a first and second correction, knowing that one of this kind has been perverted and sins, being condemned by his own judgment” (Titus 3).

Therefore, distinguishing the guilt of each, the Holy Spirit appeared upon the Lord Jesus not in the form of fire but in the form of a dove before his glorification; and conversely, after his glorification, he appeared upon the apostles not in the form of a dove but in the form of fire. For those who spoke a word against the Son of Man could still be excused on account of ignorance, and it was therefore fitting that he should act with them—or endure all things—in a spirit of gentleness.

For example, he did not consent to his disciples when they said: “Master, do you wish us to command fire to come down from heaven and consume them?” Rather he said: “The Son of Man did not come to destroy souls, but to save them” (Luke 9). Further, while he was being crucified, he said: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23).

## CHAPTER XV

Again, concerning the same judgment of the Holy Spirit, together with the Apostle’s statement: “For if we sin willingly after receiving the knowledge of truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins.”

Thus far the patience and gentleness of the Lamb, which the dove had signified, extended toward you, O sheep of the house of Israel, to whom he had been sent; and therefore he said: “I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. 15).

From that time, as you sin, your sin is reckoned as committed in the spirit of blasphemy, and it shall be forgiven neither in this age nor in the age to come. For now there is no sacrifice for you: the Son of God, though he was a lamb, has become a lion; and the Holy Spirit, who had been seen as a dove, has been shown as fire. For you do not sin through ignorance, but sin willingly, perverted and condemned by your own judgment.

Hence the Apostle says: “For if we sin willingly after receiving the knowledge of truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins, but a certain fearful expectation of judgment and a jealousy of fire that shall consume the adversaries” (Heb. 10).

How is there no sacrifice for sins left to us, namely Jews by nature, if we sin willingly—that is, if, hearing his voice and knowing him from the Scriptures, we wish to harden our hearts? Surely in this manner: that neither victim or sacrifice nor place or temple remains in which sacrifice may be offered.

For Daniel had been shown beforehand: “Christ shall be slain, and his people shall not be his—the people who are to deny him—and the people with their coming leader,” understood as Vespasian or Titus, “shall destroy both city and sanctuary; and its end shall be desolation, and after the end of the war desolation has been decreed” (Dan. 9). And victim or sacrifice shall fail, and in the temple shall be the abomination of desolation, and desolation shall continue unto consummation and the end (Luke 15).

See how no sacrifice for sins remains for those who sin willingly—that is, who hate this dedication and the one sacrifice celebrated in it—according to the Gospel parable of the elder brother, who, knowing that a feast was being celebrated inside for his younger brother’s return, willingly remained outside and refused to enter.

But what is that fearful expectation of judgment and jealousy of fire which shall consume the adversaries, still remaining? Their punishment is not only that which they have already received in this age, falling by the edge of the sword and being led captive among all nations. What then is it? “A fire,” says the Lord himself, “has been kindled in my wrath, and it shall burn unto the lowest depths of hell” (Deut. 32).

The same judgment of double punishment is contained in the saying: “It shall not be forgiven him, neither in this age nor in the age to come.” And justly so, because one who sins willingly—that is, knowingly—has no excuse for his sin: one who, as the Apostle says, tramples the Son of God underfoot, calls the blood of the covenant unclean, and insults the Spirit of grace (Heb. 6).

## CHAPTER XVI

How we ought to sing and what we ought to confess in singing to the remembrance of his holiness; and that this remembrance is the mission of the Son of God, who says in Isaiah: “Before they came to be, I was there; and now the Lord has sent me, and his Spirit.”

Therefore, as he says, as we have recalled above: “Sing to the Lord, you his saints, and give thanks to the remembrance of his holiness” (Ps. 29)—the title of which psalm is “A psalm, a song at the dedication of David’s house”—let us sing in harmony and confess faithfully, as children of the resurrection, as priests and Levites of this dedication.

What shall we sing, or what shall we confess? What shall we say in singing and confessing? Is it only what we heard him say here: “I will exalt you, Lord Father, because you received me” (ibid.), and what he said: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke 23)?

Indeed, this and almost the whole text of the same psalm are utterances of the humanity, or human nature, whose God and Lord are the Father and the Holy Spirit, as well as the Son himself who assumed that humanity into the unity of his person.

We sing and confess more deeply not something else, but this very thing which we received from him, which the Prophet himself spoke long before he was born in the flesh: “Come near to me,” he says, “and hear. From the beginning I did not speak in secret; from the time before they came to be, I was there; and now my Lord has sent me, and his Spirit” (Isa. 48).

This is indeed the most profound remembrance of his holiness, which we must confess for our salvation. “I was there,” he says, from whatever time you can remember—or even “before they came to be,” namely heaven and earth. For a little earlier he had said: “My hand also founded the earth, and my right hand measured the heavens” (ibid.).

Or, from whatever time you please—of Adam, Noah, or Abraham; or before Abraham himself came to be; or before any of those earlier—I was there, and from the beginning I spoke not in secret but openly to all the world, whether in Moses or in the prophets; indeed, even before Abraham or Noah. For none of the things which were to come was concealed, as the prophet testifies: “For the Lord God will do no word unless the Lord reveals his secret to his servants the prophets” (Amos 3).

“I was there,” I say, “before they came to be, and now the Lord God has sent me, and his Spirit.” The Lord God, the Father, has sent me: for he willed that I should put on flesh, or assume humanity—he who before the ages generated me according to the divine nature, called me from my mother’s womb, then anointed me at the Jordan, and sent me to preach good news to the poor.

The latter follows the former, and the final statements follow these: “Sing to the Lord, that you may be his saints, and [give thanks to] the remembrance of his holiness” (Ps. 29). We customarily call the churches of martyrs their “memories,” because there we remember their martyrdoms in singing and confessing. Rightly, then, we understand here also as the remembrance of the Lord’s holiness this house, whose dedication this psalm concerns according to the title already given above.

Therefore we rightly give thanks to this remembrance of the Lord’s holiness when, on account of this memorable work, we proclaim, praise, and bless the holy Lord: the holy Lord Father who sent the Son; his holy Spirit who prepared the Virgin’s womb for the Son; and the holy Son himself, who assumed humanity in his holiness.

And who, except one sinning willingly, does not understand you, O blessed Trinity, in these words: “And now the Lord has sent me, and his Spirit”? Therefore such persons have no share in the dedication of this house, but remain outside the measure of the temple, or rule of faith. Though they may seem to be within by confessing Christ, like many heretics they are outside and are reckoned with the pagans, according to the saying: “But cast out the court that is outside the temple, and do not measure it, because it has been given to the Gentiles” (Rev. 11).

## CHAPTER XVII

Concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit according to the following passage of Isaiah: “They did not thirst in the wilderness when he led them out; he brought forth water for them from the rock, split the rock, and waters flowed”; and concerning the voice of exultation by which we are commanded to proclaim this.

It is pleasing to proceed a little further in keeping with the purpose, so that the end of this work concerning the glorification of the Trinity and the procession of the Holy Spirit may accord with its beginning.

Where he said, “And now the Lord has sent me, and his Spirit,” after a few intervening words he says: “Proclaim with a voice of exultation; make this heard; carry it to the ends of the earth. Say: The Lord has redeemed his servant Jacob. They did not thirst in the wilderness when he led them out; he brought forth water for them from the rock, split the rock, and waters flowed” (Isa. 48).

For this rock is the very house of which we were speaking: it is the temple of the Lord’s body, concerning whose resurrection our discourse has been concerned. Another prophet also says of it: “I saw water coming out from the temple on the right side” (Ezek. 47), and all those to whom this water came were saved.

Here and there, water in the singular is the Holy Spirit in the grace by which he is given for remission of sins; and water in the plural is the same Spirit in the grace by which he is given in distributions of gifts.

“He brought forth for them such water, or waters, from the rock” (Isa. 48), because the Holy Spirit is living water: whoever drinks it “shall never thirst, but it shall become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life” (John 4). Surely, as he proceeds from the Father, so also he proceeds from the Son.

In figure of this it happened that the rock struck in the wilderness gave, or poured out, water to the thirsty people (Num. 20). Hence also the Apostle says: “They drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10).

“A voice of exultation,” I say: “Proclaim,” he says, “and make this heard; carry it to the ends of the earth” (Isa. 48). The voice, I say, is the preaching of the exultation of the Gospel. Hence it received its name, to be called Gospel, which means “good news,” because there is truly great exultation and great and true joy in this announcement, whose summary is this: the Lord has redeemed his people.

## CHAPTER XVIII

That the dedication of this house not made by hands was the rejection of that old house made by hands, according to Isaiah’s vision in which, as the Seraphim cried, “Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God,” the house was filled with smoke.

Finally, this too must be understood: the dedication of this house not made by hands is the rejection of that house made by hands, as the Apostle also testifies, saying: “There is indeed a setting aside of the former commandment because of its weakness and uselessness” (Heb. 7). That rejection of which we speak was signified by the smoke which Isaiah saw: “The seraphim,” he says, “cried one to another [Col. 0199A] and said: Holy, holy, holy, the Lord God of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory. And the thresholds of the hinges were shaken by the voice of those crying, and the house was filled with smoke” (Isa. 6).

For so it was to be, and so it came to pass, just as this sacred prophecy foretold. The Lord being seated upon a lofty and exalted throne—that is, after the Lord, the Son of God, ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of God, which throne is indeed lofty—the seraphim, whose name means “burning ones” or “those who attend,” cried “holy” three times. That is, the holy apostles, inspired by the Holy Spirit in the appearance of fire, as was said above, preached the holy Trinity; and behold, the earth is full of the glory of this preaching [Col. 0199B]. Even if another interpretation is possible, this one is nonetheless true and more relevant to the matter.

For John says in his Gospel: “Therefore they could not believe” (John 12), because Isaiah said again: “He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, lest they see with their eyes, understand with their heart, be converted, and I heal them.” And immediately it is added: “Isaiah said these things when he saw his glory and spoke of him” (Isa. 6). Behold the place where Isaiah spoke these things—or rather, where the Holy Spirit spoke in Isaiah. For there it was first stated, “and the house was filled with smoke.” Afterwards it is written thus: “Hear indeed, but do not understand; see the vision, but do not know. Blind the heart of this people, weigh down its ears, and shut its eyes [Col. 0199C], lest perhaps it see with its eyes, hear with its ears, understand with its heart, be converted, and I heal it” (ibid.).

Therefore the vision of the Lord seated upon a lofty and exalted throne was a prophecy of the Lord’s ascension into heaven. And the words, “Those things which were beneath him filled the temple,” mean the same as if it had been said: “The gifts of graces which he gave to men, as it is written, ‘Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; he gave gifts to men’” (Ps. 67), filled the hearts of believers, who themselves are the temple of God, because Christ dwells through faith in their hearts.

Over such a temple stood the seraphim—that is, the apostles and prophets from both Testaments (Eph. 3), who hold pre-eminent rank [Col. 0199D], thinking the same thing concerning the Trinity, which is one God. Their sacred writings testify to this. This is for one to cry to the other and say, “Holy, holy, holy, the Lord God”: the page of each Testament, both prophetic and evangelical Scripture, agrees in the same confession concerning the one Creator. He created all things in the number of six days, and rests on the seventh; and he will grant that same Sabbath to his faithful ones, especially to the preachers of truth, so that when they have completed their works, they too may rest “from their works,” as the Apostle says, “as God did from his” (Heb. 4).

“Thus six wings for the one, and six for the other” (Isa. 65). With as many wings as they flew, with so many they covered his face, and with as many, namely, they covered his feet. For with as great a zeal as they testify from both Testaments to the holy Trinity, so carefully do they conceal both the brightness of the divinity of Christ, the Son of God, and the mystery of his humanity or Incarnation—whether from those unable to grasp it, or especially from those unable to hear because of the torment of envy.

“For,” he says, “the thresholds of the hinges were shaken by the voice of those crying, and the house was filled with smoke.” The rulers and elders of the Jewish people indeed stirred up sedition; and the prophets, wise men, and scribes sent to them, some they killed, some they scourged, and from city to city they persecuted them (Matt. 23). Therefore their house was left to them desolate, rejected and filled with smoke because of the blindness of their hearts [Col. 0200B].

Some of them were pierced to the heart and said to the apostles: “What shall we do, brothers?” (Acts 2). In their person the prophet fittingly said: “Woe is me, because I have kept silent; for I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell among a people having unclean lips; and I have seen with my eyes the King, the Lord of hosts” (Isa. 6). For this was what each of them said: Woe is me, because by crying out and consenting to those who cried, “Crucify, crucify” (John 19), I defiled my lips; and I denied before Pilate my king Christ, whom I saw with my eyes, who came in my days, as had been promised in the Law and the Prophets (Matt. 27).

“And one of the seraphim,” he says, “flew to me, and in his hand was a small stone which he had taken with tongs from the altar, [Col. 0200C] and he touched my mouth” (Isa. 6). “For Peter said to them: ‘Repent, and let each one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of sins; and you shall receive the gift of the Holy Spirit’” (Acts 2).

Peter is rightly understood here as one of the seraphim. For he is first among the apostles, and to him above the rest it was said: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven” (Matt. 16). This is what we hear here: “In his hand was a small stone,” because pre-eminent authority after Christ was given to him, to effect forgiveness of sins for believers. This small stone, [signifying] the glory of the Holy Spirit, had been taken by “tongs from the altar,” that is, from the majesty of Christ—by tongs, I say, that is, through the outstanding faith in Jesus Christ, one and the same God and man.

“And I heard,” he says, “the voice of the Lord saying: ‘Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?’” (Isa. 6), as though he said: They killed and persecuted the prophets, and crucified me, the Lord of the prophets. After so many proofs of their sins and hardness of heart, “Whom shall I send? Who will go for us?”

Here, O thrice and four-times blessed Stephen, first martyr (Acts 6), you offered yourself in willing faith, most faithful hope, and gracious charity, and said: Behold, here am I; send me. Neither commanded nor sent by a human being, nor through a human being, but through the fullness of the Holy Spirit you performed great wonders and signs [Col. 0201A] among the people. You went before the blessed apostles themselves in the battle; and as the first martyr in Christ’s Gospel, crowned victor in accordance with your name, you fell asleep in the Lord.

## CHAPTER XIX

Concerning what is written in praise of the strong woman, that is, holy faith: “her husband praised her,” and “give her of the fruit of her hands.”

Behold, O blessed Trinity, according to our purpose and according to our ability we have glorified your name; and your procession, O Holy Spirit, behold, as you yourself gave it, we have pursued in speech and writing. What reward will you give? For we dare—not of ourselves, but the strong woman within us dares—to behold her price from afar and to summon it from the furthest boundaries.

Who is that strong woman? Is she not faith, through which Abraham pleased you, and through which the whole multitude of the elect is joined to you, the one God, as a wife or beloved woman to her husband? She dares in us, and through her we dare, because we are righteous from no other source but her, and from her we live. Behold, here too, behold in us, “she has opened her mouth to wisdom, and the law of kindness is on her tongue, and she has not eaten the bread of idleness” (Prov. 31) [Col. 0202A].

Let her children therefore arise and proclaim her most blessed, and let her husband Christ praise her. Nor is she less praiseworthy because we, in our wretched condition, are frail, as the great Apostle also says: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” (2 Cor. 4). Where shall her children arise and proclaim her most blessed? Where shall her husband praise her? At the gates: at the departure from this present life, according to Wisdom’s decree, which we have here: “Give her of the fruit of her hands, and let her works praise her in the gates” (Prov. 31).

[Col. 0201]

[COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF ST JOHN.]

## RUPERT’S DEDICATORY EPISTLE TO CUNO

(Absent from the Cologne editions of 1533, 1566, 1577, 1598, and 1602; from the Paris edition of 1638; and from the Venetian edition of 1749. It is found in the 1526 edition of Rupert’s Works, edited by Cochlaeus and published at Cologne by Franciscus Birchmann, 2 folio volumes. It is also printed as a preface to the Commentary on John, separately issued at Nuremberg in 1526 by Johann Petreius, octavo. This was transcribed for us from the Nuremberg edition and sent by Dr Henry Denzinger, professor of theology at the University of Würzburg.)

“I meditated in the night with my heart, and I was exercised” (Ps. 76). My venerable father Cuno, abbot of the monastery of Siegburg, worthy of remembrance: the fruit of meditation and exercise seemed to be that I should write. But behold, this very thing which I wrote has become to me like a flash of flame; it does not permit me to remain hidden, and turns upon me the far-different eyes of different persons.

To those whose eyes perhaps are bleary with evil zeal and who do not know the eye-salve of brotherly charity, all things are black and obscure. But to those whose eyes are bright through goodwill—of whom you, Father, are best toward me—everything that I write is, as I hear from you and from them, white and good. To you therefore and to those like you my soul now recites, concerning its cause and conscience, what the holy Church says of her afflictions: “I am black, but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem, like the tents of Kedar, like the skins of Solomon” (Song 1).

For what is blacker, what more like the tents of Kedar, than that vanity of presumption by which they suppose that I leapt forth in self-exaltation to write? Since Father Augustine, the voice of Christian law and instrument of Catholic faith, expounded the Gospel of John in an eloquent and sweet exposition, they imagine it to be a rebuke or disparagement of him that I have presumed, after so great a teacher, to chew over the same Gospel—that is, the very Word of God. They are greatly indignant at a new man, as though in a spirit of pride I had dared to graft myself into, or even to set myself before, ancient nobility.

But I trust that I have God as witness in my soul that the reason which impelled me to do this—to treat in my own speech so lofty and divine a Gospel after such and so great a helper of Catholic peace—was that “I remembered God and was delighted” (Ps. 76). For to be judged or examined by a human day was, I think, a very small matter to me (1 Cor. 4).

But they have nothing to say, nothing to offer as an argument, except that some of them, wishing to maintain that the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood is merely a sign of a sacred reality, in accordance with the former error of Berengar of Tours, think that even blessed Augustine held this view—which is wholly false. But I maintain that the body of Christ which was given for us is true body, and that the blood which was shed for us is true blood, as the Catholic Church holds. Because they have attempted to establish their view, they disparage blessed Augustine by thinking against him, whom Berengar used to cite in defense of his error, tearing apart his sayings in an evil sense. Yet now scarcely anyone dares openly to profess or defend this, since the entire Catholic Church knows that it is the true body and true blood of Christ.

Another charge which they loudly bring against me as a great crime is that I dared to doubt whether Judas the traitor participated in communion in that same sacrament, as Father Augustine maintains, or whether he did not participate but should be thought already to have departed, as St Hilary firmly affirms.

This is that great blackness, O my father, and O all you daughters of Jerusalem—this is the blackness by which, in their eyes, my soul says, “I am black like the tents of Kedar” [Col. 0203]. They say that I am arrogant and unbelievably puffed up, that I allow no worthy cleric to live—by which term a person notably learned in letters, of whatever order or habit, is customarily designated—without accusing him of being a heretic. This indeed is to be, or to be called, black like the tent of Kedar, concerning which it is written: “His hand against all, and the hand of all against him; and opposite all his brothers he shall pitch his tents” (Gen. 16).

What was I to do, Father? One sought to take from me the truth of the Lord’s body and blood. Another charged me with intense hatred because I would not say that the writings of one of our teachers possessed canonical authority equal to the Scriptures of prophets and apostles. Another preached that God wills evil. That same man, and some others, contended that Christ the man—the new man who was created according to God (Eph. 4), assumed into unity of person with God the Word, and who before the Passion, according to his humanity, was lower not only than the Father but even than his angels (Ps. 8)—had in no way attained equality with God.

Concerning all these matters I have explained sufficiently in my apologetic writings, which I composed before these works for the students of ecclesiastical learning and faith, with you, O most worthy of abbots, and those men themselves as witnesses and privy to the fact that I reported what was most true. What then was I to do, except pitch my tents opposite all these men, and deem their gratuitous hatred preferable to peace with them? Let them attack me without cause and call my tents black like Kedar: in the end truth shall prevail, in whose bright mouth my judgment is laid up—that my soul is rather beautiful in faith and intention, like the skins of Solomon, which he stretched from dead animals, from those who were put to death by the violence of persecution for righteousness’ sake (Heb. 11).

I shall now briefly disclose to you what, and how, I understood when I treated those words of the same Lord by which he commends the life-giving sacrament of his body and blood, since this was the first of the causes mentioned above. The body and blood of Christ exist in three modes of essence; in a fourth respect they differ. They exist in name, reality, and effect; but they differ in outward appearance.

They exist, I say, in name, because the supreme priest of heaven, who, being Truth itself, does not customarily assign empty names to realities, impressed this name so forcefully that he did not merely say, “Let this be called my body; let this be called my blood,” but, “This,” he said, “is my body; this is my blood” (Matt. 26). They exist also in reality, because it is indeed the Holy of Holies; and truly, under that appearance in which he was handed over and pierced by the lance, he himself is the Holy of Holies. They exist nevertheless in effect, because just as truly, under the appearance in which he hung upon the cross, he effected forgiveness of sins for all who awaited him from the beginning of the world in faith—whether through all the legal sacraments of faith, from righteous Abel to the thief whom he received as he confessed upon the cross—so truly under these appearances of bread and wine he effects the same forgiveness of sins for all who have entered, or enter, into that same faith, after that appearance passed from here and withdrew into heaven.

In the fourth respect, the same body and blood differ in appearance; and this is greatly beneficial, not only lest the colour or taste of human blood cause any horror to those receiving it, but also that the excessive credulity of our first parents may be cured by a fitting antidote. For they believed the deceiver, the devil, concerning what they did not see: namely, that the tree possessed an effective power for attaining divinity; and by eating they died. Let us, conversely, believe God our faithful Saviour concerning what we do not see: namely, that bread and wine have passed into the true substance of body and blood; and, eating and drinking, let us live for ever.

## 90. RUPERT’S PROLOGUE TO THE GOSPEL OF JOHN

[Col. 0203]

[Col. 0203A] The disciple whom Jesus loved, who also reclined at supper upon his breast (John 21), gives true testimony in his Gospel to his same loving Lord: that Christ is the Son of God—that is, not merely a man born from the Virgin’s womb at the end of the ages, but before all ages God begotten from God the Father.

All divine Scripture, inspired in a more than human manner, indeed bears testimony to this truth; but both the cause and the text of the work plainly establish that this is especially the purpose of this Gospel. The cause was that, after he had been sent by Domitian into exile—Domitian being the second persecutor of Christians after Nero—heretics had rushed into the Church, like wolves into sheepfolds bereft of their shepherd: Marcion, Cerinthus, Ebion, and the other Antichrists. Denying that Christ existed before Mary, they stained the simplicity of evangelical faith with perverse teaching [Col. 0204A].

Thus, compelled by almost all the bishops of Asia at that time, after a fast had been proclaimed for all, he prayed to the Lord and, intoxicated by the grace of the Holy Spirit, wrote this Gospel. By the sudden disclosure of the light of truth, it scattered all the darkness of the heretics.

The text of the work itself is such as the proper order of testimony altogether demands. For he calls in another witness with himself, no less suitable, namely John the Baptist, so that there may be two witnesses. “Every word shall stand only in the mouth of two witnesses” (Deut. 19). Having thus called in John, who came “for testimony, to bear testimony to the light,” he frequently calls both John’s words and his own “testimony.” At the end of all, he says of himself: “This is the disciple who bears testimony concerning these things and wrote them; and we know that his testimony is true” (John 21).

This, therefore, is the singular and pre-eminent witness of the Son of God. In the public court of heaven and earth, when the issue was not so much the boundaries or laws of a kingdom as the very birth of our King, with other witnesses exhausted and violently silenced by the outcry of opponents, he suddenly stepped into the midst. With the great thunder of his evangelical voice and the lightning-flash of the resplendent Word, he terrified and scattered the whole council of vanity and the entire assembly of evildoers throughout the earth [Col. 0205A], openly declaring that he is the only-begotten and consubstantial Son, and therefore the legitimate heir of the eternal Father.

This testimony magnificently supports our hope—that is, the hope of all orphans whom he appointed as his heirs in an eternal testament written with his blood—which was endangered by such disparagements from opponents. For how can the testament by which he bequeathed to us a heavenly inheritance be valid (Heb. 9), if he himself was not the lawful possessor of heaven? And how was heaven his possession, if he did not come from heaven but took his beginning from Mary?

Appropriately, therefore, as was said, this faithful Witness comes to the aid of our hope, proclaiming the ancient rights of the freeborn testator: he declares not only that heaven, but all things that exist, are his; indeed, that all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made (John 1).

Therefore for us, who, testifying to the Son of God, testify to the Scriptures, and delight in the way of his testimonies as in all riches (Ps. 118), this testimony especially must be searched out and sought with the whole heart [Col. 0205C]; it must be desired with the whole soul and loved above gold and topaz. For if we are evangelical merchants seeking good pearls, behold, one precious pearl has been found (Matt. 13). For where can any pearl of greater value be found?

God, the true lover of souls, fixed this pearl in the heart of his beloved John’s soul as a memorial of his special love: so that the Word which the Virgin Mary alone brought forth in flesh might be brought forth by this fellow virginity, above all saints, in a living voice for mortals. Therefore all things must be given in order that this one pearl may be purchased; and all the filth of fleshly desires must be wiped from the eyes of the heart in those who study the venerable writings in Christ’s school, so that they may be able in some measure to follow this eagle. Purity of heart enabled it, more than the other living creatures of divine vision, to contemplate with the unblunted gaze of the mind the brightness of the eternal sun [Col. 0205D].

[Col. 0206A] For the Lord speaks through Isaiah concerning one who tends toward true wisdom by the way of purity: “He shall dwell on high; the heights of the rocks shall be his stronghold; bread is given to him, his waters are sure. His eyes shall see the King in his beauty; they shall behold the land from afar” (Isa. 33). Or rather, more plainly relevant to the matter, this was said to blessed Job in different words but the same sense: “At the Lord’s command he shall be lifted up; like an eagle he shall place his nest in the heights; he dwells on rocks and abides on precipitous crags and inaccessible cliffs. From there he surveys his food; his eyes look from afar” (Job 39).

John, the lofty contemplator of this Word and eternal Principle, attained all these things magnificently. For he was lifted up like an eagle, fixing open eyes upon the rays of the Divinity; and he placed his nest in the heights—that is, he established the stronghold of this his eternal Gospel upon rocks, that is, upon the solidity of truth. From there he contemplated the food, namely the glory of this eternal Word, which he also deserved to touch.

Yet, as was said above, “his eyes shall behold the land from afar,” and here likewise it says, “his eyes look from afar.” For even this elevated eagle does not yet see God by direct sight, but “through a mirror in an enigma” (1 Cor. 13). “Now,” he says, “we are children of God, but it has not yet appeared what we shall be” (1 John 3).

Although his young ones lap blood (Job 39)—that is, although his hearers are satisfied merely with knowledge of the blood of the crucified Lord, because they cannot receive the mysteries of the Divinity—still we are not altogether rightly blamed for attempting in some measure to behold the flight of so great an eagle. For the young are fed in their nest precisely so that one day, after their mother, they too may fly out to the same food.

Therefore we shall strive to follow, by the same path though not altogether in the same footprints, the lofty mysteries through which the great teacher Augustine flew in this brilliance of the Gospel like a great eagle. He flies over the lofty summits of mountains; we shall sometimes occupy ourselves even about their lowest roots. He hastens to pluck the higher fruits of a tall tree; we shall endeavour to reach also those branches of the Gospel text near the earth which he left for little ones. Thus, because fuller-grown persons have been satisfied by the lofty explanation of mysteries, the continuous exposition of the text may now also assist the little ones—that is, those like ourselves [Col. 0206D].

## FOURTEEN BOOKS OF COMMENTARIES BY RUPERT, ABBOT OF DEUTZ, ON THE GOSPEL OF ST JOHN

[Col. 0205]

## BOOK ONE

[Col. 0205D] 91. “In the beginning was the Word.” Behold, “Truth, which sprang up from the earth” (Ps. 84), assumed flesh from the Virgin [Col. 0206D] in order to free us from the devil; that same Truth is begotten from the virginal soul of John, putting on a bodily voice [Col. 0207A] in order to fight for us against every heretical perversity.

For he who “poured forth a good word from his heart” (Ps. 44) into the virgin’s womb, so that the invisible God might become visible and true man, by his chaste embraces impregnated the adopted soul of his beloved John with that same Word, so that the ineffable Word might issue forth, audible and intelligible, through John’s voice and writing.

He therefore says: “In the beginning was the Word.” We do not, then, worship a recent Lord, as Cerinthus, Marcion, Ebion, and the other Antichrists falsely alleged. For what they said—that Christ did not exist before Mary—is false. Christ, who is now a man at the end of the ages, was in the beginning and before the ages the Word. He was not all that he now is, namely flesh and Word; but he was the Word alone. Now he is one person of a twofold substance and a twofold operation, a giant of two substances; but in the beginning he was the Word, of one substance and one operation. Therefore Christ existed before Mary, because “in the beginning was the Word.”

But “Word” here is not to be understood childishly, that is, according to the etymology of the term, as we learned from Donatus when boys: that *verbum* is so called because it is formed by air struck with the plectrum of the tongue. A word of that kind passes through the air in sounding. But the “Word” which was in the beginning—that is, before the air itself and before all things made—“remains forever” (Isa. 40) [Col. 0207C].

For this Word is perpetual Reason, everlasting Wisdom, incomprehensible Understanding, unchangeable Truth. Yet among us *verbum* is predicated equivocally both of articulated speech and of the silent counsel of the mind. Why then should eternal Reason not rightly be called the Word, from which we possess rationality—that is, the whole faculty available to us for producing words?

“Do not become children in your understanding,” says the Apostle (1 Cor. 14). For the Word, although not aerial—that is, not formed by struck air—the Word, I say, although not affective, as our words are, but [elsewhere: “and”] substantial, was Christ: “in the beginning was the Word.” Where, however, was this Word? What was its place? “Man does not know its price,” as is said through blessed Job (Job 28). Yet, through the Spirit’s revelation, it is gradually known through what follows, and first through the statement which shows, as it were, its place—where it then was in the beginning—when it adds: “And the Word was with God.”

Behold, these are the Lord’s arrows, in whose light we go; this is his flashing spear, in whose brightness we walk, as it is said to him through the prophet: “They shall go in the light of your arrows, in the brightness of your flashing spear” (Hab. 3). For by the arrow of the first statement which he cast, he pierced all those heretics who, with differing blasphemies but an equal spirit of malice, denied, as already said, that Christ existed before Mary. But with this following arrow he strikes the Patripassians, who, denying the Trinity, asserted that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were only one person, not three [Col. 0208A].

For he says clearly: “And the Word was with God.” You need not doubt concerning the persons when you hear that one was, or had been, with another. By saying, “He was with God,” he magnificently indicates the dignity of this Word. For what does “he was with God” mean except that he was in great honour, supreme dignity, and great love?

“He was with God,” but not as a rich man has his gold with him. A rich man has gold in his chest, not in his own wretched, diseased, perhaps even leprous substance. But the Word was with God as wisdom is with the wise person, strength with the strong. For it is said through blessed Job: “With him are wisdom and strength” (Job 12). The rich man’s gold is in his purse; God’s Word is in his heart. Truly, therefore, the Word was with God.

Now, just as he distinguished the persons by saying, “And the Word was with God,” so conversely he joins the substance by adding, “And the Word was God.” He briefly testified that there is one substance in the two persons, God and his Word. The Sabellians bear this with difficulty; the Arians receive it resentfully. The former, namely the Sabellians, would prefer him to say that God and his Word, as they are one substance, are likewise one and the same person; but the latter [Col. 0208C], namely the Arians, would prefer him to have expressed that, as there are two persons, so also there are two different substances. They wish the Father alone to be God or Creator, while the Son, though great and excellent, is a creature.

But the truth of this present testimony, like the voice of flashing thunder, strikes the earth on both sides—that is, it equally confounds the seared conscience of both parties (1 Tim. 4). Let the Homoousians, that is, confessors of consubstantiality, therefore rejoice: confessing, with the support of so great a witness, two persons indeed, but one substance of the Father and the Word, neither confusing the persons nor separating the substance. “The Word,” he says, “was God.”

Immediately, in one statement, he most beautifully embraces everything which he expressed in the three propositions just mentioned: “This,” he says, “was in the beginning with God.” What then resulted from the Word’s being with God? Or why did the Evangelist not prefer to say, “The Word was in God,” but says—and even repeats a second time—“was with God”? By this phrase he signifies that he intends some great business. For whenever we likewise say in speech that one person is with another person, the propriety of the expression lies in our wishing to signify that a certain business concerns them.

What, then, is agreed between the two through the goodness of both? It follows: “All things were made through him.” This plainly occurred through the goodness of both, which is the Holy Spirit.
