For if you ask, Who made all things? the answer is: God. If you ask, Through what? behold, you have it: through him, namely the Word. If you ask, Why? the answer is: because he is good. And this is the whole Trinity.

“All things,” he says, “were made through him.” O how worthy of praise and reverence is this Word through whom all things were made! Benevolent observers lift the eyes of heart and body to the beauty of things made, visible and invisible; attentively considering them, they cry out in heart and mouth: Great and beautiful is the creative genius of God, which is nothing other than this Word through whom things so great and so beautiful were made: “For all things were made through him” [Col. 0209A].

Another Scripture also testifies: “For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. 32)—namely, those things which invite to praise the Creator: all his angels, all his powers, sun and moon, stars and light, the heavens of heavens and all that is in them; earth and all that is in it; sea and all that is in it (Ps. 148). He spoke, as another Scripture also witnesses: “Let there be light, and there was light;” he said, “Let there be a firmament, and it was made” (Gen. 1). He spoke likewise concerning each of the rest: “Let there be,” and they were made. Therefore they were made through the Word, because they were made by his speaking.

But he spoke not with an elemental sound or bodily voice—for God is spirit—but in that mode of speech by which your soul, whoever you are, a human being whom he made in his image, forms silent speech whenever it wishes.

[Col. 0209C] Take heed, whoever you are, child of light, and despise as cobwebs the notions dreamed up by the children of night—that is, by the philosophers of this age. They said that the matter from which all things were made, which they also called *hyle*, was not created by God but was coeternal with God; God used it as an artisan uses wood when he founded this world, itself coeternal with him. They also imagined that there were patterns, which they call Ideas, at which he looked in order to make all things in imitation of them.

Therefore despise these things, worshipper and knower of the eternal Word. For truth is not so constituted; rather, “all things were made through him,” and “in this beginning,” that is, in this Word, God created heaven and earth and all that is in them.

Therefore, from that which is weak in God—from the birth of the flesh, the confines of the manger, and every condition of mortality—lift the eyes of your mind upward beyond Mary, who herself, without doubt, was among all things made through him. And from the fact that “all things were made through him,” faithfully judge the antiquity of Christ and the majesty of God’s Word, whoever you are who, before hearing or understanding the truth of so great a Witness, supposed that Christ did not exist before Mary.

With what emphasis he said, “All things were made through him,” he immediately impresses by sharp repetition when he adds: “And without him nothing was made.” “Nothing,” he says, “was made without him”: no nature, no substance, nothing whatsoever, however evil it may be. For nothing is evil by nature; nothing is evil except through supervening malice. Even the devil is evil through vice, but his substance is not evil by nature [Col. 0210A]. Thus the Manichaeans’ fable of an evil principle, or of some whole race of darkness—I know not what—is refuted. For, as has been said, “all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.” It follows:

“What was made, in him was life.” Even now the troublesome challengers of the truth—especially those who, as has already been said, have supposed the world to be coeternal with God—are accustomed to press the question and say: Why did a new will arise in God? Why did he adopt a new plan? For if, after the infinite delays of his eternity, he at some point made the world, this is a new will and a new plan, and it is quite evidently an indication of changeability in him. Likewise, if it is certain that Christ existed before Mary and that “all things were made through him,” [Col. 0210B] whence came the new will that, after so many thousands of years, he should come for the restoration of humankind? Indeed, if, when he made the world and fashioned the first-created man, he wished the human race to be saved, why did he not foresee or guard against its falling into the shipwreck of perdition? For in the one case he may be charged with changeability, in the other with lack of foresight.

The truth, seeing on every side, cuts down these also—the portions of the opposing contention—like the heads of a hydra as they spring up anew, adding, as befits the majesty of wisdom, calmly and briefly: “What was made, in him was life.” The meaning is this: Whatever was made, before it was made, existed in his foreknowledge; and that foreknowledge is nothing other than life. For to the Godhead, living is not one thing and knowing another; nor in God is living wisdom [Col. 0210C] other than wise life. It is otherwise in the soul: it lives substantially, indeed, but knows accidentally. God, however, both lives and knows substantially, for nothing accidental can befall the Godhead.

Therefore life—that is, the living knowledge in him from the beginning of all things which he was going to make—was already in him. This is true, probable, and necessary. For whence does the rational soul derive this capacity: whenever something is to be put together by the craft of building or architecture, it first sees the entire structure inwardly in its art before displaying it outwardly in its work? If it wishes to construct an ark or the framework of a spacious house, it first turns over the image of it within itself; and already the mind and thought are such as the material arrangement of the work will later be seen to be. Thus you rightly say: what is to be made is already life in the craftsman’s mind. Whence, I ask, does the rational soul possess this, unless because God created the human being in his own image—“in the image of God he created him”?

But the image and radiance of God, as the Apostle says (Heb. 1), and the impress of his substance, is this Word: this Son, God from God, called an impress by reason of likeness. For the Father and this Word are one God, just as gold or ivory and the king’s image impressed in it are recognized as one seal. Yet we are marked with this impress not according to the outward human being, [p. 93] as the Anthropomorphites supposed, but according to the inward one. Hence we are rational—that is, capable of receiving teaching or instruction. If, then, the features of reason are so beautiful [Col. 0211A] in the soul which has been formed, how bright and certain is divine Reason itself, which is not formed but is itself form! If the shadow is thus vividly conscious of its art, is Truth itself not much more provident and constant in its purpose or work? Clearly, incomparably more steadfastly and perfectly, the order or nature of all things that were to be made lived in this Word. Nor did he merely know from the beginning what things he would create, or how he would create and arrange each in its proper condition; he also knew how he would recover certain lost things for his glory.

Hence every nature maintains its fixed course, and there is nothing new under the sun (Eccl. 1). For once, by his unchangeable will, he established the command; and once “he created all things together, he who lives for ever” (Eccl. [Col. 0211B] 18). Thus the unsurpassable height of the divine counsel concerning the salvation of the human race remains wholly intact. For he did not call, justify, and glorify any elect persons other than those whom he foreknew and predestined before the ages (Rom. 8); nor, as though caught unawares or outwitted by the devil, did he devise something new when he sent this Word to be incarnate. Rather, it was so predetermined; it was so altogether pleasing before the Father because it was beautiful and fitting: amid the enmities of the opposing devil, ever looking toward what would better serve our salvation, divine beneficence should attain the summit of its dispensation.

Why, then, do you charge God with impotence or rashness, heretical rashness? Make a division here after “What was made,” and then add: “in him”—that is, in the Word—“was life.” Or certainly, to speak now in accordance with another Scripture, what was made was a delightful and beautiful play before God in his wisdom. For Wisdom itself—which is this Word of God—says: “The Lord possessed me at the beginning of his ways, before he made anything from the beginning, and from eternity I was appointed.” And shortly afterward: “I delighted,” she says, “day by day, playing before him at all times, playing in the inhabited world; and my delights were to be with the children of men” (Prov. 8).

This play is the ineffable delight of divine goodness, by which the Creator, before making anything, already delighted in his Word, in his wisdom. These things are great; these things are lofty. The majesty of such meanings strikes back the eyes of mortals like the brightness of the sun. Yet some likeness of them glimmers in our nature, as it were the image of the sun visible in water. For example: behold, a musician skillfully constructs whatever instruments he chooses, and, measuring them according to fixed numerical proportions known to himself, distinguishing the intervals between tones, compels the sound stirred up in an inanimate object by breath or stroke to imitate the reason implanted in him. What then? Before he constructed the instruments, was not music already present, playing in his mind and voice—playing in the diversity and distinction of modes—and were not his delights in the sweetness of many songs? Music was one, and nevertheless is one even now; nor does it increase or multiply itself, however many lyres the pleasure of the singer may assemble for singing.

[Col. 0212A] In this, as has been said, there is some likeness. For what are we but certain instruments of the great musician, God? Hence we are commanded to praise the Lord “with lyres and organs” (Ps. 150), which are surely our hearts and bodies. Our Lord himself is, above all, the musical instrument of God the Father; and the same Father says to him while, according to the body, he lies in the tomb: “Awake, my glory; awake, psaltery and lyre” (Ps. 56). Indeed, the whole world is an instrument of divine praise, although only a human being or an angel knows how to sing God’s praise; just as in a lyre the string alone, though not without the wood, sounds the melody of song.

Therefore, just as the nature of music is life in the musician’s soul, which art has imitated in an instrument, so the composition of the whole world—which, as has already been said, is an instrument of divine praise—before it was made was life in this Word. Of this it is further said: “And the life was the light of men.” This life, he says—the Word through whom all things were made, this eternal Reason—is the light of human beings, that is, of the best part of all things that were made. For although it shines over all things that have been made, in this visible world it illuminates human nature alone: it expresses its own image in the human soul alone.

For among all things that have been made, some merely are, such as stones; others both are and live, such as trees; others are, live, and perceive, such as animals. But after the angel, the human being alone has been placed in this honor: that he has been made capable of seeking and finding his Creator. Therefore, when he says, “This life was,” or “is, the light of human beings,” it is as though he said: It imparted the light of rationality to human nature alone.

Although this is so, he could have said, “And thus the life was the light alike of angels and human beings.” For the nobility of radiant reason illumined both natures—the angelic and the human alike. We received it because, as was said above, God made the human being in his image and likeness. Yet the Gospel is written not for angels but for human beings alone; for Christ came not for angels, but only for human beings. Those who did not receive him are reproved especially in this Gospel and in the other words of the apostles, the Holy Spirit reproving them through these, according to Christ’s own words concerning him: “He,” he says, [Col. 0212D] “will convict the world concerning sin, because they did not believe in me” (John 16). It is therefore rightly said here: the light of human beings only. For the matter of angels does not concern us at present.

And “light of human beings” is said universally, that is, of good and bad alike. For good and bad alike shine in this respect: that they are rational. Although an evil human being is darkened by sinning and becomes a child of night and darkness, he is nevertheless not deprived of that light of reason by which he surpasses the animals. There is also another light (1 Thess. 5), which could be or can be lost through the darkness of wickedness: namely, the glory of the likeness of God. For God made the human being not only in his image but also in his likeness. In his image, indeed, insofar as he made him rational and eternal; [Col. 0213A] in his likeness, insofar as he made him an imitator of his goodness. He loses this light of God’s likeness when, by sinning, he abandons imitation of the Creator. But the light which he possesses from God’s image does not cease to shine with the brightness of reason.

And by that light he is reproved by God, who also in this respect “makes his sun rise upon good and evil” (Matt. 5): he deprives neither good nor evil of the light of reason. Thus it is the light of human beings, including evil persons, on which account they are without excuse (Rom. 1). Hence follows:

“And the light shines in darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it.” The light, he says—that is, the discernment of the reason mentioned above—shines in darkness, namely, in the consciences of those who have become darkness by acting wickedly. For, to say nothing of the Jews, who together with the light of reason also possessed the lamp of sacred Scripture, the Apostle says of the Gentiles, who did not possess such light: “For what is known of God is manifest among them, for God has revealed it to them. For his invisible things, from the creation of the world, are understood through the things that have been made and are seen” (Rom. 1). [p. 94]

The light of reason, therefore, is that which shines even in whatever depths of the darkness of sins. But, though they were darkness, they did not comprehend this light shining within them, because, although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks to him. The Jews, however, are even more guilty. Although they could recognize the true light present through both the judgment of natural reason and the witness of the sacred Law, they were more darkened and did not know it. For they shut their eyes lest they should see, and stopped their ears lest they should hear (Isa. 32; Acts 28); and they utterly refused to understand, in order that they might do good (Ps. 35).

Behold the sign that was opposed (Luke 2), defended with what peals of thundering truth! What can unclean spirits utter against this, creeping forth from the inner recesses of heretics in the manner of frogs? Yet other enemies and opponents of this sign remain: namely, the Jews, who, as though situated under another sky, are not terrified because they do not hear the crash of this thunder. For heretics are struck, as it were, by lightning from their own sky: while pretending to be followers of the apostles—for otherwise they would not have been heard unless they had been thought apostolic—while, then, pretending to hold or set forth apostolic doctrine, they are smitten from above as adversaries by the testimony of so great an apostle. But the Jews are, as it were, under another climate. Because they do not receive Christ’s apostles (Luke 20), nothing concerning them pertains to the Jews and nothing moves them that our firmament proclaims such great glory of God.

What then? Will they be excusable? Have they not heard, or could they pretend not to have heard? On the contrary, they heard first—not from some indirect source, but from the mouth of one whom they can neither conceal nor refute in any way. For they heard through John the Baptist, whom all know to be a prophet, and they cannot deny that his testimony came not from human beings but from heaven. For John’s name and merit were celebrated even by their own historians: [Col. 0214A] the miracle of his birth and the wonder of his holy life; the dignity of his preaching and authority of his baptism; the testimony, too, which he bore to Christ (John 1), and the cause of his death (Josephus, *Antiquities*, Book XVIII, ch. X).

John himself wrote nothing. Yet, so great was he that he might have been thought to be the Christ; the entire world heard what he said and whom he pointed out with his finger, and this sound of his went forth into all the earth. Therefore this beloved John takes this most suitable witness with him, so that this word of faith may lawfully stand in the mouth of two witnesses (Deut. 17), and so that a large audience may fittingly be supplied, both on account of the witnesses’ lives and on account of the steadfastness of their testimonies. With them he will set forth, in alternation, now his own words, now those of John bearing witness to Christ (John 8), first showing in this manner who and what sort of man John was.

“There was a man sent from God, whose name was John.” Accordingly, when speaking of the eternity of the Word, the Evangelist said, “Was,” and “Was”; but now he says, “There was a man,” turning the little word into the perfect tense. For the being of the Word neither began nor ended; but the being of this man John, since he was now dead, had passed away. For a human being is properly said to be such as long as flesh is united with a rational soul. Wisely, therefore, and properly, “Was” was said of the former and “There was” of the latter: “The heavens shall perish, but you remain,” says the Psalmist, “and they shall all grow old as a garment; and as a covering you shall change them, and they shall be changed. But you are the same, and your years shall not fail” [Col. 0214C] (Ps. 101).

“Therefore,” he says, “there was a man sent from God, whose name was John.” Every word must be weighed as on a balance, since they proceed from the treasures of wisdom. The utterances of wisdom are held to have greater weight when they are not seen to have been spoken superfluously—especially in so great, indeed so principal, a matter, in which the majesty of truth must most fully make itself known, lest it should deign to flow away in words falling idly.

Though it might have been said, “John came as a witness,” it appears superfluous to have said, “There was a man sent from God, whose name was John; he came as a witness,” since other prophets too were human beings, all were sent by God, and many human beings bore the same name John. The words must therefore be weighed more carefully, because they were uttered not in slight speech but in lofty proclamation. That is, a man so named in such a place or cause was one to be received with great regard, far unlike the multitude of human beings: one than whom no greater arose among those born of women, so great that long before he had been called an angel through the prophet. “For this,” God says, “is he of whom it is written: Behold, I send my angel, who will prepare the way before my face” (Matt. 11; Mark 1; Mal. 3).

Thus he was an outstanding and renowned man, rightly to be proclaimed in the contention of all people with full, sonorous utterance and the full voice of the Gospel. “Sent,” he says, “from God.” All the prophets too were sent by God; for if they were not sent by God, they came from themselves. And if they came from themselves and spoke from themselves, they are thieves and robbers (John 10). But far be this from the heralds of truth; far from those to whom the word of God came, concerning whom the Holy Spirit says: “I said, You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High” (Ps. 81). Therefore all the holy prophets were sent from God, because all came with the Word of God.

What, then, worthy of the singular acclaim of such a declaration is contained in the statement that this man was sent from God? Much in every way. First, because the days of the others who were sent “were swifter than a runner” (Job 9). For although it is a runner’s duty to wait at least a little until he sees what message he is to carry back to those to whom he must return, they hastened back from here by the road of all flesh before they deserved to await and see the Lord’s coming. [Col. 0215B] But this man was sent at the time when he could see him: so that, living, he might point him out with his finger to the living; and, dead, might shortly afterward announce to the dead in the underworld that he was about to come.

Further, he was sent in such a way as to come beyond nature, born from the womb of old age and barrenness—which is not the operation of nature but of God alone—so that in being born he might precede the one who was to be born; in preaching, run before the one who was to preach; in baptizing, go before the one who was to baptize; and in dying, precede the one who was to die. He was therefore sent uniquely: he had nowhere to stop, nowhere to turn aside, no leisure to hold discourse with the world; he was to possess neither house nor field, nor acknowledge kindred, but, driven alike by the word of the Lord and by the business of the one sending and following him, to run naked and unencumbered before his face, as one made and born for this alone: to prepare his ways before him (Luke 1).

“And his name was John.” His name came not from human beings nor through a human being, but from God through his archangel; it was not given by chance, but John was his name for a definite reason. Certainly for a definite reason: because the sum of all his preaching was the grace of the Lord. What, indeed, did he preach except that the carnal Law had been abolished and spiritual grace had arisen? For the Law given through Moses lasted until him; but from his days came the grace that was made through Jesus Christ. And once he pointed out with extended finger the Author of that grace, through the same grace “the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matt. 11). Now the name John, when interpreted, conveys this: the Lord’s grace. Therefore the reason why his name was John is manifest and worthy. [p. 95]

But the Jew does not know this, because these things are different—perhaps “such things” [*talia*, uncertain reading]—because he refuses to admit the veil placed over his heart (2 Cor. 3). Yet many other things are at hand, some of which have been mentioned above, by whose compelling force they cannot deny that his testimony or baptism came from heaven (Luke 20).

Thus, after this great man has been displayed as if before the view of a council—or rather in the midst of the crowds and in the tumult of the Jewish people stirred up against Christ—the Evangelist declares firmly: “This man [Col. 0216A] came as a witness, to bear witness concerning the light, that all might believe through him.” This man, he says, so great, so conspicuous [*spectabilis*, perhaps repeated in the source], came for this, was made or born for this, was placed on high for this: that, seen by all and heard by all, he might bear witness concerning the light against the darkness which, as was said above, refused to comprehend the light shining within themselves, saying, “Is this not the carpenter’s son?” (Matt. 13; Luke 4), and “How then does he now say, ‘I came down from heaven’?” (John 6; Mark 6).

Against them this man came to bear witness that he himself was the Light of human beings; that he was the only-begotten Son of God, “through whom all things were made.” All the prophets, indeed, bore witness to this same light. But John’s testimony differs from and surpasses theirs chiefly in this: they testified that he was to come; John, testifying that he had now come, also pointed him out as present with his finger, lest there be doubt about his person, saying: “Behold the Lamb of God; this is he of whom I spoke” (John 1).

What need had the Light of human beings, or what benefit did it seek for itself, that in our assemblies it should so earnestly procure for itself the witness of so great a herald? “That all,” he says, “might believe through him” (ibid.). Understand: that he himself, and no other, that this same Jesus, son of Mary and of Joseph, as was supposed, was from the beginning the Word of God, the Word who was God, the eternal Light. This, then, was the purpose of his love, which did not seek what was his own but what was ours (2 Cor. 13). The Light intended that we all might believe, and that by believing we might come to him and be illumined. We rejoice and give thanks for such gracious benevolence of the Godhead.

It was not, however, because the Light itself shone too little that it required testimonies. Rather, the fault lay not with the Light itself but with the eyes, which could not recognize it through itself. For human eyes had become bleary—indeed almost blind—from the dust of earthly desire; and therefore, the more brightly the true Light shone, the more grievously it offended them. Unable to endure it, they turned themselves away and, as it were, turned their backs upon the rising sun. But they looked more tolerably on John, as upon a mountain illuminated by the rays of that same Sun. This great mountain, clothed in beautiful light, pleased them, and they delighted in it so much [Col. 0216D] that they thought he himself was the Christ.

Against that opinion of theirs there immediately follows: “He was not the light, but came to bear witness concerning the light.” Why is he denied to be the light unless he was thought to be the same Light as Christ? Yet “he was not the light.” He was not, he says, the true light; he was not the illuminating light; he was not the substance of light itself. He was, however, such a light as were the apostles, to whom it was said: “You are the light of the world” (Matt. 5)—a light received from elsewhere, a light not by an essential good but by an accidental gift. But what kind of Light was Christ?

“He was,” he says, “the true light.” He was the true light, that is, the efficient cause of the light by which John too shone. For it follows: “Which enlightens every human being coming into this world.” He enlightens, he says, every human being coming into this world, namely, by that illumination which all human beings lost in Adam. By one kind of light, namely the light of reason, which they possess because they were made in the image of God, all human beings come into the world illumined. But by another illumination, namely the knowledge of God, which they ought to have possessed because the human being was likewise made in the likeness of God, they are born into this world deprived.

Yet not all human beings—not all the children of Adam without exception—attain this grace of divine light. For many are justly left without it; they have wandered from the way of truth, and the Sun of righteousness has not risen for them. Therefore, the words “He enlightens every human being coming into this world” mean the same as if he had said: Christ was the true Light, without whom no human being coming into this world is illumined; and all surely come darkened through their ancestral transgression.

It must be understood, however, that human beings are illumined so as to be holy in God’s likeness by the proper operation of the Holy Spirit. Yet their being created rational in God’s image pertains especially to the Son, “who,” as the Apostle says, “is the image of the invisible God” (Col. 1). Nonetheless, even the coming of the Holy Spirit to enlighten the human mind is effected by the grace of that same Son, who came to give the Holy Spirit, as he himself declares: “I came to cast fire upon the earth; and what do I desire but that it should burn?” (Luke 12). Therefore Christ alone is the true Light, who, as has been said, in both ways “enlightens every human being coming [Col. 0217C] into this world.”

But if every human being, then John also. This is said because this Light, Christ, the true Light, the Word of God, was with God before it came into the vessel of our flesh. How then, you ask, did it enlighten every human being coming into this world before John, while so far removed from God, so far gone into exile in this world? Perhaps you do not wonder about John, because when he was illumined this Light had already come into the world and had already poured itself into its temple, the virgin womb. You may perhaps rightly say that, as the great substance of that Light descended, it also shone upon John in his mother’s womb and produced, by a gentle stirring, that exultation of the infant over which we joyfully applaud.

You ask how, earlier, while it was still with God, it enlightened every human being coming into this world. But let this not trouble you; rather, hear what follows: “He was in the world.” He was with God and he was in the world. For the Word was God. But God, the Creator of all, is not in one part [the printed reading has *in patre*; probably *in parte*], because he is everywhere. Therefore the Word, God, because he is unbounded light and is everywhere, was both with God and in the world. What, then, is surprising about his being in the world? Hear something greater. For it follows: “And the world was made through him.”

Therefore he fills the world in order to govern it; he governs it in order to fill it; by filling it he surrounds it, and by surrounding it he fills it; by sustaining it he transcends it, and by transcending it he sustains it. Thus the statements are not contradictory: this Word, this true Light, both was with God and enlightened “every human being coming into this world.” For, being everywhere, he was both with God and in the world.

But what sorrow, what cause for lament, lies in the fact that, after saying “and the world was made through him,” he immediately added, “and the world did not know him”! O blindness, O ingratitude! For the first human beings, ungrateful as they were, shut their eyes when they thought that they were opening them. The devil, the father of lies, promised them that, if they transgressed the commandment, their eyes would be opened and they would become like gods, “knowing good and evil” (Gen. 3)—that is, possessing what belongs to God alone, knowledge of all things. But instead they were blinded [Col. 0218B] and left their blindness to their descendants as an inheritance. Thus, through blindness, they did not see him “who was in the world and through whom the world was made,” whose knowledge they had presumptuously desired to equal; and through ingratitude they did not glorify him as God or give him thanks, even for so little as they were able to know of him from his works.

The phrase, then, “and the world did not know him,” is the exclamation of one grieving. More grievous still is what follows: “He came into his own, and his own did not receive him.” For he came into his own: either into this world, which was made through him, or insofar as he took hold of Abraham’s seed, from which the people of Israel, peculiar to him, had sprung. For by taking hold of Abraham’s seed (Heb. 2)—that is, by assuming flesh from Abraham’s seed—he came into his own when he lived among the people whom he had acquired for his own inheritance by great benefits.

Yet he came not locally—for he is God, and thus it is certain that he is everywhere. He came, indeed, not by moving from place to place, but by making himself visible though he was invisible. For he was in the world by his divinity, whose property is to be or to remain; but he came into the world by his humanity, whose property is to go and pass from place to place. “And his own,” he says, “did not receive him.” It is the deed of their fathers: they did not receive him; indeed, they even killed him. For who are these his own if not those wicked and doomed cultivators to whom he himself had leased his vineyard? (Matt. 21).

This is therefore more aptly understood: “He came into his own,” so that you may understand that vineyard of which it is written through the prophet: “For the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isa. 5), which, according to the Psalmist, he brought out of Egypt, cast out the nations, and planted (Ps. 79). He set a hedge around it, in that he supplied fortified cities or the protection of angels; he dug a winepress in it and built a tower—that is, he possessed an altar and the splendor of the temple in that people alone. Therefore, when he was sent to this vineyard of his, the master of the house saying, “They will reverence my Son” (Matt. 21; Luke 20), he came into his own. But the evil cultivators, the evil workers of the Law, did not receive him. Indeed, they cast him out beyond the city and killed him more boldly and wickedly than they had killed his servants (ibid.), that is, the righteous and the prophets.

“But as many as received him, he gave them power to become children of God: to those who believe in his name.” He said universally, “His own did not receive him”; but he neither said, nor ought to have said universally: “None of his own received him.” For some of his own, although few, did receive him. And what is worthy of greater grace: although they knew that they too would likewise be cast out because of him, they nevertheless received him.

But especially from a people he did not know, from a nation he had not recognized, namely the innumerable multitude of the Gentiles, people flocked to him when he had been cast outside his vineyard and stained with his own blood. They devoutly laid him upon their bowed shoulders and carried him to their own lodging. “As many, therefore,” he says, “as received him”: as many as went out to him when he suffered outside [Col. 0219B] the gate; as many as, from the nations which had not known him, ran to him and did not blush to bear his reproach (Ps. 17; Heb. 13)—to them he gave great power, illustrious power, namely, the power to become children of God, though formerly they had been enemies of God (Rom. 5; Eph. 2). Such was the power he gave to those who received him.

And what it is to receive him, lest the expression be understood too broadly, he defines more plainly by adding: “To those who believe in his name.” It is as though he said: This power to become children of God is not given merely to those who put a roof over him, set food before him, mix drink for him, and so receive him. For Judas too could have done such things and still have been a devil. In this manner only the flesh is refreshed. But Christ is not flesh alone; he is also the Word, and especially because he is God’s Word he can give the power mentioned above. Therefore, to those who have received him in the way in which the Word of God ought to be received, “he gave power to become children of God”—that is, to those who believe in his name.

For to believe is to receive the Word, the seed of God, with love and carry it in a mind made pregnant. It has such strength and power that, transferring the substance of the soul into its own vigor, it makes gods out of human beings (Ps. 8), children of grace out of children of wrath (Eph. 2), and brings about the fulfillment: “In the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ there they shall be called children of God” (Hos. 1; Rom. 9).

“Who were born not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of a man, but of God.” Let no one, then, boast that he has been carnally begotten from holy parents, as Jews are accustomed to boast that they are Abraham’s seed (Matt. 3). For a person’s carnal birth from these or those parents does not make him more or less numbered among God’s children. This is especially evident in the two twins Jacob and Esau. For although they were begotten from the same bloods—that is, from the union of the same father and the same mother—although they were born by the will of the same flesh, that is, of the woman (for the Evangelist uses “flesh” for “woman,” according to the words, “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh,” Gen. 2), and by the will of the same man, a holy man and great patriarch—although both were thus born from the same holy parents, [Col. 0220A] they were not therefore both predestined or called into the number of God’s children. Rather, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated, says the Lord” (Mal. 1; Rom. 3).

Likewise, children born from Christian parents, however faithful and righteous, cannot receive by birth the grace of being Christians, even though, as has been said, they are born from the most Christian parents. For parents generate not Christians insofar as they are Christians [the text adds: “they generate Christians”], but carnally insofar as they are human beings: that is, not by Christ’s grace but by the nature of flesh. And therefore they generate not in Christ but in Adam.

Accordingly, those born from the circumcision are no less in need than those born from the uncircumcision; those born of righteous parents are no less in need than those born of unrighteous parents [Col. 0220B] to advance to the Catholic Church, through whose ministry they may be born again according to the new Adam, and through him attain the true Father, God. For previously, springing from whatever bloodline of parents, they were born according to the old Adam, through whom they attained the devil, the prince of transgression.

Therefore, to bring the discourse back in its final conclusion to what has gone before: he who, as was said, “enlightens every person coming into this world,” who gave to those receiving him such power that they might become children of God—he himself was the true light. But John, whose diminution was the point of these statements, because he was so great that he was thought to be the true light, should bear the testimony for which he came [Col. 0220C] concerning this very light, by which he himself too was enlightened. For, as was said above, the Evangelist John introduced him here so that, by both his own testimony and John’s, he might defend the true light against the darkness which would not comprehend it.

He therefore continues concerning the Word, of which he had begun to speak, saying: “And the Word was made flesh.” Let Cerinthus and the other Antichrists hear what the conjunction *and*—which is placed here—means; the passage must be connected thus: I said above, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God, and all things were made through him.” Returning to the same subject, after I had introduced another witness: “And the Word was made flesh.” Therefore let the orphans, let the posthumous sons, hear of the noble antiquity of their Father [Col. 0220D]. Let them hear and know that through Christ “all things were made, and that through him the world was made”—he who was said to be so much younger than the world’s origin that heretics and Jews, begrudging the children their nobility, denied that he existed before Mary.

But when we hear that “the Word was made flesh,” no one should suppose this to mean the same as if it had been said, “The Word was transformed into flesh.” For that sense is heretical; that exposition is foreign to the faith. The Word was not transformed into flesh; rather, by assuming flesh he deigned to condescend to those who are fleshly. Thus it was said: the Word which was with God was made flesh—just as you too, when you speak, may rightly say: “The word which was in my soul was made vocal” [Col. 0221A]. Therefore, just as, when your voice proceeds from your mouth to another’s ears, that same word of yours remains in your heart, while through hearing it has also entered another’s mind; so too, when the Word’s visible flesh came forth into public sight, the Word itself remained wholly in the Father’s heart, while it was nevertheless wholly transmitted to us through that same flesh.

Thus the same whole Word, wholly in the Father and wholly in the flesh, “reaching from end to end,” proceeds from the Father’s heart—beyond or above which there is nothing—“like a channel of immense water from a river” (Ecclus. 24), descending through all the ranks of angels to our flesh, beneath or below which, because it decays in the grave through sin, there is nothing more abject.

Nor should this point be passed over: together with the name or substance [Col. 0221B] of flesh, a rational soul too must certainly be understood. For the Word of God did not assume flesh without a soul, as the Apollinarian heretics imagined. “For he came to save that which had perished” (Luke 19); but the whole human being had perished—wholly indeed, that is, both in body and in soul. In body, the human being was mortal; in soul, already dead; and in both was eternally condemned. Therefore, that the Word might save the whole person, he likewise assumed the whole human being: flesh and a rational soul.

Otherwise, if God the Word had assumed flesh alone without a soul, where would he have fixed his root? For only the rational spirit is capable of receiving him. Indeed, this Word is utterance; it is wisdom. Individual human beings too see it only with the mind, insofar as they share in it; they embrace it only with the soul [Col. 0221C]. Much more, therefore, when the universal Word assumed flesh, did he not omit the receptacle suited to himself, that is, the rational soul. Far be this notion from the heart! Far be it from the mouth of all who place their hope in the incarnate Word!

For especially in the soul that Scripture was made by God the Father, uttering forth a good Word, concerning which he himself says in the Psalm: “My tongue,” he says, “is the pen of a scribe writing swiftly” (Ps. 44). For the true and perfect nature of this Word was inscribed upon the true and entire nature of humanity—that is, joined in the unity of one person without confusion of either substance.

Thus was produced that splendid electrum, the price and ornament of the human race, in which the gold of divinity [Col. 0221D] lost nothing of its brilliance, and the silver of humanity acquired an increase of its beauty. Therefore, when he says, “The Word was made flesh,” it is the same as if he had said, “God was made man,” according to the usage customary in the Scriptures. For by the name *flesh* the whole human being is sometimes signified, as there: “And all flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Luke 3). Conversely, the whole human being is signified by *soul*, as it is written: “Jacob went down into Egypt with seventy-five souls” (Acts 7). Therefore God was made man.

“And dwelt among us.” Among us indeed in every respect, having come from his invisible things to our visible things. First, he dwelt among us in the true nature of our flesh, subject to all the laws of human nature [Col. 0222A]. For, with this one exception—that the woman in childbirth brought forth a human being not conceived, in the manner of all flesh, from male seed, and that she was not violated by childbirth, but remained a virgin before childbirth and a virgin after childbirth—apart from this, the true nature of humanity ran through its entire proper course.

If the Jew, or the detestable slanderer the Manichaean, says, “If a virgin gave birth, it was a phantom,” then it follows that they must judge the first parents of humankind, Adam and Eve—because they lacked fleshly parents—to have been not real but phantom human beings. For it is farther removed from the nature familiar to us for a human being to be formed from earth than to be conceived from a woman. It is more marvelous for a man to be fashioned from inanimate and insensible matter than for a man to be generated without a man from animate, sentient, indeed rational substance [Col. 0222B]. The former is certainly more marvelous; the latter is more venerable. The former belongs to divine power; the latter is a work alike of power and grace.

Now some utterly recoil from believing that the God who is Holy of holies could suffer himself to be enclosed within a woman’s womb. But, I ask, do they know the character of their own horror? There is one kind of horror which proceeds from reason, another which proceeds from sensation. It proceeds from reason when we recoil from vice in comparison with virtue, although in sensation we may sometimes take greater delight in vice than in virtue. It proceeds from sensation when we recoil more from touching a serpent than a stone, although in reason we unquestionably prefer the animate and sentient body of the serpent to the inanimate body of the stone [Col. 0222C].

In what manner, then, do they recoil from a woman’s womb: by sensation or by reason? Certainly by sensation, not by reason. For reason can recoil from no substance or nature, from absolutely none of the things God made.

But God, or his Word, being Reason itself, is affected by none of our sensations. He recoils from and hates no creature or nature at all—which without doubt no one other than he himself made—but only the defect of nature. Much more, therefore, should we faithfully and devoutly believe that he did not recoil from the undefiled womb of the Virgin. Therefore God the Word dwelt among us; and in that hidden place of female nature from which each of us came forth not without sin, he lodged for nine [Col. 0222D] months without the contagion of sin. Then, “like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber, and setting his tent in the sun” (Ps. 8), he dwelt among us: clothed, as an infant, in tender flesh; uttering the cries of infancy; made under the Law (Gal. 4); subject to Joseph and Mary (Luke 2); circumcised; and, like a sinner, purified by the legal offering; suffering hunger; enduring the deceits of the tempter (Luke 4); likewise bearing human persecutions (Matt. 16); sorrowful unto death; fleeing from place to place (John 7); and finally made obedient unto death (Phil. 2).

But to what end, at last, did this humility of weakness come? It follows: “And we saw his glory, glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father.” “We saw his glory,” he says: a glory to which we can bear witness precisely because we saw it; and we began to see it from the sign by which, invited to a wedding, he changed water into wine (John 2). For this was the beginning of signs which he performed before his disciples, and he manifested his glory (John 2). Then we saw him enlightening blind eyes (Mark 10), banishing leprosy by his touch (Luke 17), driving away fevers (Matt. 8), raising decayed corpses (John 11), opening the bound tongue and deaf ears, walking upon the waves, calming the winds (Matt. 12 and following), stopping the flow of blood (Matt. 9), and satisfying many thousands [98] from a few loaves (John 6).

We saw also the glory of his transfigured face (Matt. 17), to be revealed to the very choirs of angels [Col. 0223B]. Finally, we saw what is greatest and most glorious: him rising from the dead (Luke 24; Mark 16; John 20). We saw in his hands and feet the marks of the nails; we saw, I say, and looked upon; we touched, and our hands handled (1 John 1) his side pierced by the spear. We ate and drank with him (John 21), saw him gloriously ascending into heaven (Mark 16), and received from him the promised Paraclete, the Holy Spirit (Acts 1, 2).

We saw this glory of his, glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father: that is, such glory as no one among all God’s children was deemed worthy to be glorified with. For all God’s other children were adopted; this one was begotten—indeed, he is the Only-Begotten. All the others are children by grace; he alone and only he is so by nature [Col. 0223C]. Rightly therefore, being “fairer in form than the children of men,” he possesses a glory, which we have seen, different from that of all children.

Let us now hear the final conclusion of this chapter. How glorious did you see him to be? “Full,” he says, “of grace and truth.” O great proclamation, great and faithful testimony! Did you ask what kind of glory that of the Only-Begotten was? It is gold, true gold, the price worthy of our captivity. This rich and noble man came forth from the treasury of the Most High; his little body is a pouch of precious gold. Hold him while it is cut open by the violence of death, and grasp the talent of grace and truth which is in him.

How full Christ is of grace and truth, and how weighty that grace and truth are [Col. 0223D], this same Evangelist John will shortly make clear by the following testimony of John the Baptist, where he will say: “Grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.” For, as was said in the Preface, these two witnesses speak in this Gospel; it is not so much the wall of a History that is being built as an impregnable tower of testimonies being raised.

He therefore says: “John bears witness concerning him, and cries out, saying: This is he of whom I said: He who is to come after me has been made before me, because he was prior to me.” John the Baptist—who, as Truth testifies of him, was neither a reed shaken by the wind nor a man clothed in soft garments (Matt. 11)—stands firmly on a high mountain, where he was fully exposed to the mighty and frequent assaults of a violent wind: neither to be broken by adversities [Col. 0224A] nor bent by praises of himself. For, delighting in no greatness of reputation, he does not allow himself to be thought greater than he is, though the crowds imagine him to be the Christ—the one whom the Evangelist has just declared to be full of grace and truth.

John, indeed, was a minister of grace, but not the fountain of fullness of grace. He was truthful and faithful, but he was not Truth itself. If he had wished or delighted to appear what he was not, he would have been neither a participant in grace nor a companion of truth. Therefore, standing firm as was said, rooted steadfastly and unmoved by empty winds, like a cedar of Lebanon, he rebuffs all the popular breeze with a great cry and says: “This is he of whom I said: He who is to come after me has been made before me, because he was prior to me.”

The Evangelist introduces these words by anticipation in order that, by John’s testimony, he may especially confirm what he had just said: “Full of grace and truth.” For later he will relate when and where John said those things which he now asserts that John said about him. “This,” he says, “is he who stood in your midst, whom you did not know.” This man is the very one of whom I spoke to you—namely, at Bethany beyond the Jordan, where I was baptizing, when you sent priests and Levites to ask me, “Who are you?” For then I confessed, “I am not the Christ,” and said of this one: “He who stood in your midst; he who is to come after me has been made before me,” and so forth.

No one doubts that the Lord came into this world in the flesh after John. For John’s conception—and likewise his birth—preceded the Lord’s birth by six months [Col. 0224C]. Therefore, when John says of him, “He has been made before me,” it cannot be referred to the making of the flesh which the Word assumed. For, as has already been said, hardly had the Divinity begun to put on that flesh as a shoe when his herald leapt for joy enclosed there (Luke 1), as though eager to burst through the doors of the maternal womb and announce that he would soon come after him.

Knowing this, Arius, enemy of faith and foe of grace and truth, snatches this saying from John’s mouth, like one “who lies in wait in secret, as a lion in his den lies in wait to seize the poor” (Ps. 6), so that by drawing people to himself he may tear apart Christ’s people. For he maintains that the Son of God is a creature, and therefore eagerly seizes upon the statement, “He has been made before me,” in defense of his own faithlessness. Yet, truly blinded by rage, he fails to notice what follows. For according to his perverted interpretation, what place is there for the reason that follows: “because he was prior to me”?

To make it still clearer how inappropriately—indeed, violently—he twists this text, let us for the moment question John in accordance with Arius’s interpretation: Why was he created before you, John? “Because he was prior to me,” you answer. What sort of reasoning is this? Was he created before you because he was prior to you? Or do you cry out and bear testimony concerning him in order to announce, according to Arius, that he is a creature, and attach such an elegant reason to your proposition? In vain, then, does the impious man rage, who, leaning upon so slender a branch, does not fear the deep precipice beneath him [Col. 0225A].

For if John had wished, in the same sense in which he said, “He has been made before me,” to use the present or future tense, he would have said, “He is made before me,” or “He will be made before me.” For “He has been made before me” is the same as if he had said, “He has become greater than I.” This was said in the same sense as: “I must decrease, but he must increase” (John 3); or as that which Daniel said in his figure concerning the stone cut from the mountain without hands, which crushed the statue (Dan. 2). “The stone,” he says, “grew and became a great mountain, and filled the whole earth.” For the stone is Christ, who seemed small in comparison with John, but became great above John and above all such mountains.

Therefore, “he who is to come after me,” he says—who will preach to you after me and baptize you in the Holy Spirit after me—“has been made before me”: he has been placed before me and become greater than I; as I have diminished, the great King advances with me as his attendant. And this rightly, because “he was prior to me.” He was far prior to me: not because he was born before me according to the flesh, when I preceded his birth by six months, but because he was prior to me in that he was with God and was God.

For if you wish to know that he was so much prior to me, hear more clearly: “And from his fullness we all received.” All without exception: namely, whoever of us came into this world to be enlightened; all prophets, all patriarchs; absolutely all of us who were sent, whoever received any gift from above (Jas. 1). See how the great trumpets of the two Testaments accord with one another: this John, chief of the Evangelists, and that other John, greatest of the prophets. See how the two cherubim look upon one another, their faces turned toward the mercy-seat (Exod. 37; Heb. 9): this one at the beginning of the New Testament; that one standing as it were at the far edge of the Old instrument [Col. 0225C]. This one an Evangelist and Apostle; that one the last of patriarchs and prophets.

For with their faces turned toward the mercy-seat—that is, with minds intent upon bearing testimony to Christ, “who is the propitiation for our sins” (1 John 2)—they look upon one another because they think the same things and speak harmoniously. For this one says, “In the beginning was”; the other adds, “He was prior to me.” This one says, “He was the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world”; the other, “And from his fullness we all received.” This one says, “Full of grace and truth”; the other says, “Grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.” Therefore, as was said, they look upon one another, and their faces are alike, so that from seeing one it is easy to recognize the other.

Therefore, what this one said above—“In the beginning was”—is the same as what that one now says: “He was prior to me.” Content with saying this with great and fitting gravity, although he too could have said, “In the beginning was.” For this slight lash of modest expression is enough to drive away the flies of heretics who deny that Christ existed before Mary’s childbirth [Col. 0226A] or conception. For when John the Baptist says, “He was prior to me,” nearly all conscious Judaea immediately grants the premise: “But your birth was earlier than his birth by the full six months.” All Christianity concludes: therefore Christ, in that same birth by which he was born according to the flesh, or in that same conception by which he was conceived, was prior. It is thus enough against heretical filth that John said, “He was prior to me”; for if Christ existed before John, he did not begin to exist from Mary’s womb.

But if a loftier utterance delights you, and in this, as in a heavenly melody, you prefer to hear strings more piercing than weighty, behold: here the precentor of truth strikes with the same finger a string that is higher indeed, but of the same mode.

[Col. 0226B] “And from his fullness,” he says, “we all received.” This certainly has a loftier sound. But what is this which we all received from his fullness? Surely—to omit the rest for now—we received from him all that makes us appear admirable to you; especially that for which I, John, seem great: that I came from an aged and barren womb (Luke 1), brought forth amid accompanying wonders; that I am a burning and shining lamp (John 5), so that you wished to rejoice in my light, saying, “This man is great; this is the Christ.” Thus all of us received from him, each according to his good pleasure, so that some among us were deemed worthy of the prophetic spirit; others were found great patriarchs; others kings, chosen, outstanding in faith, distinguished in righteousness [Col. 0226C], long-suffering in hope, obedient in commandments, believing in promises, foreknowing things to come, powerful in speech, resplendent in miracles.

For he was full, as he is now, of grace and truth. Therefore he poured out upon us divisible streams of that same grace from himself, the living fountain. For he was not full as one supplied by infusions sought from elsewhere; rather, like a fountain from his own veins, he was—indeed, is—full of “water springing up into eternal life” (John 4).

Therefore do not say, “God spoke to Moses; but this man, we do not know where he is from.” For Moses too is one of us; from this one’s fullness he received even this: that he should be appointed god to Pharaoh (Exod. 7); that, after Pharaoh had been overcome and all Egypt struck with diverse plagues, he should at last divide the Red Sea into divisions [Col. 0226D] and lead Israel through its midst (Ps. 77; 135); receive bread from heaven (John 9); and draw water from the rock broken open in the wilderness.

And this is that hand of the Lord whose finger wrote the Law which Moses received on tablets of stone (Exod. 32), and of this very one Moses wrote. Therefore do not say to him: “You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham?” (John 5, 8). For before Abraham came to be, this one was—indeed, is. For he himself is the Word of the Lord which came to Abraham and to all the holy prophets. Absolutely all of us to whom the Holy Spirit says, “I said: You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High” (Ps. 81), received from his fullness this very thing, that we are called gods; for we were called gods because the word of God came to us [Col. 0227A]. But he himself is the Word of God. Therefore, as was said, from him we received this very thing, that we are called gods. It follows:

“And grace for grace; for the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.” These words must be understood in such a way that the exposition may proceed as closely as possible with John’s present purpose, as he cries aloud and bears witness concerning Christ. For they may indeed be understood thus: We have received grace for grace—namely, the grace of eternal salvation in return for the grace of present faith, to which he himself called us freely through his preachers, that is, without any preceding merits of our own, and justified us by the gratuitous remission of sins. But, as has been said, we must approach more closely John’s present intention [Col. 0227B].

His intention is to set the Lord Jesus above himself, above all the saints, and above Moses himself, the giver of the law; and to show that his coming was necessary for all, because the law given through Moses had brought none of them to perfection (Heb. VII). He therefore says: “And we received grace for grace,” as though saying: Before he came in bodily presence, all of us received grace from his fullness; and when he appeared in the flesh, we received grace in return for that same grace. We received a better grace for a good grace. For the grace of the law was indeed good; but because it brought nothing to perfection, he, coming, gives the assisting grace of the Gospel. Thus an advantageous exchange takes place: as if someone were commanded to give up silver in order to receive gold [Col. 0227C], or to reject even the clearest water in order to drink excellent wine.

That the law is rightly called grace here can easily be proved. It is called grace because it was freely given. And that the law, or all God’s benefits to the former people, was given freely—that is, without preceding merits—is attested by Moses when he says: “Know therefore that it is not because of your righteousnesses that the Lord your God gives you this excellent land as a possession, since you are a people of very stiff neck” (Deut. IX). But someone may say: “It had already become a debt, because God had sworn to their fathers that he would give them a land flowing with milk and honey” (Gen. XVII); and it was just that he should fulfil his word, or the oath which he had sworn (Exod. XXXIII).

To this we ask whether the very fact that he swore was gratuitous or owed. And beyond doubt it must be confessed that he swore not from obligation but freely; freely indeed he appeared or made himself known to Abraham and the other fathers. For having justly deprived the first sinful man of the glory of Paradise, and owing nothing to all humankind, he had justly hidden his face from them, as from the children of a condemned father (Gen. XII, XV) [Col. 0227D]. This, then, is the earlier grace, which is called simply “grace”; but the subsequent grace of the Gospel is called not simply grace, but “grace and truth.”

That this grace and truth was exchanged for the grace of the Mosaic law is attested by John himself, who says these things. For after first saying, “And grace for grace,” he immediately added, explaining what he had said: “For the law [Col. 0228A] was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.” And if you ask in what respect the grace and truth of Jesus profit more than the law of Moses, he immediately adds: “No one has ever seen God.” Behold the imperfection of the law: for through it no one ever returned to the vision of God, which the whole human race lost in Adam’s sin. Then follows at once: “The Only-begotten, who is in the Father’s bosom, he has declared him.” Behold the perfection of grace and truth. For the Son declared God, being full, as has already been said, of grace and truth; because, by opening the way through his blood, he made God known to humankind.

Therefore, in the words, “and grace for grace; for the law was given through Moses, grace and truth came through Jesus Christ,” the sense proceeds rightly [Col. 0228B] according to John’s intention as he cries aloud and bears witness concerning Christ. For it greatly assists the recognition of his fullness to know that his people first received from him grace—that is, the knowledge of the law and the prophets, through which they possessed a knowledge of the true God, freely given to them—and then grace in return for that grace: truth in place of figure, reality in place of shadow, spirit in place of letter.

Thus grace and truth came through Jesus Christ: grace, namely, because, when we were enemies—when the Jews themselves, I say, were, as the Apostle testifies, “by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Eph. II)—we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, that same Jesus Christ. For in no better way do we here understand grace than as the reconciliation [Col. 0228C] made between us and God through Christ.

This grace, or reconciliation, was only prefigured in the ceremonies of the law—for example, in the sacrifice of the paschal lamb (Exod. XII) and in the other things of that kind; it was not actually conferred. For although all the righteous and holy fathers, when they had fallen asleep, were kept among the dead, yet in great security and blessed hope, no righteousness of that law could break down the wall of enmity by which they were prevented, on account of their ancestral transgression, from beholding the glory of God. Hence it was added: “No one has ever seen God.”

But in Christ’s Passion that wall was broken down, because the bond recording sin was erased by his blood (Col. II). “And coming,” says the Apostle, “he preached [Col. 0228D] peace to those who were far off and to those who were near” (Eph. II): that is, to the Jews, who were near through the earlier grace of the law, and to the Gentiles, who through ignorance of the truth had been exceedingly far from him. Hence, after saying, “No one has ever seen God,” he immediately added: “The Only-begotten, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared him.”

“Who is in the bosom of the Father.” O with what loftiness and beauty the present pillar of truth again touches upon the Father while bearing witness to the Son. Above he said: “Because he was before me.” Now, speaking again of the same one, he says: “Who is in the bosom of the Father.” These words are altogether as if he had said what the Evangelist said of him: “In the beginning he was, and he was with God.”

“The eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear [Col. 0229A] with hearing”: namely, the eye of him who, according to Isaiah, sees the land from afar (Isa. XXXIII), and the ear of him who, with Ezekiel, hears inwardly from the holy living creatures “the sound of wings, like the sound of the most high God” (Ezek. XI). Let us therefore, I pray, distinguish this exceedingly lofty sound with attentive hearing. For he did not say without reason, “Who is in the bosom of the Father,” when he might have said, “Who is with the Father.” Such a phrase is not insignificant; rather, it gives the hearer the greatest radiance of divine beauty, especially in this most weighty theme, in which, in the supreme matter of law and grace, a kind of comparison or contrast is made—not as between good and evil, but as between perfection and imperfection—where it was said: “For the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came [Col. 0229B] through Jesus Christ.”

Let the attentive hearing of faith therefore perceive what the herald of grace and truth intends to convey by this supreme cry. You asked whence Jesus Christ had the power to do what Moses could not do; for what reason he alone, out of so many thousands, was chosen to restore grace and truth between God and human beings—that is, to dissolve enmities and restore peace (Col. I). Behold, the answer is given you: because he is in the bosom of the Father.

What does “in the bosom of the Father” mean? He is in the highest love, in the most diligent care and protection, of God the Father. For what purpose? Namely, so that sin might not find him, as it has found all human beings from the beginning of the age; that sin which, pursuing all souls without exception, finds them outside and seizes each one in her menstrual impurity. They were found outside because, as Isaiah testifies, they had been cast out: “They slept at the head of all the ways” (Isa. LI), like a trapped beast [Col. 0229C]. How, then, could the cast-out bring back the cast-out into grace, or the ensnared set the bound free?

Therefore, a little earlier, when the same prophet had said: “Arise, Jerusalem, who have drunk from the hand of the Lord the cup of his wrath,” he added: “There is none to raise her up [variant: support her] among all the sons whom she bore; and there is none to take her by the hand among all the sons whom she reared” (ibid.). For, as has been said, all had gone out from the bosom of God’s grace, having been born with the sin of the first transgression and, however great and righteous they might be, not wholly free besides from actual sins.

But this one did not go outside; he did not stand outside; he did not sit outside when he entered our region [Col. 0229D]. Adam did not know him. The serpent did not know. Eve was neither delighted nor pained; but God the Father alone was privy to the Virgin. In a wondrous manner he both sent this Son into her womb and retained him in his own bosom; and now and always he guards him with such care and cherishes him with such love that the devil, the tempter, never finds any trace of him, does not know whence he comes, and does not know where he goes.

Therefore, because he is thus in the bosom of the Father, because he did not commit sin nor contract it from elsewhere, he came to stand before the countenance of that same Father in order to reconcile human beings. Therefore grace and truth came through him, as has been said above; therefore he declared God, whom no one has ever seen—that is, he revealed him and made him visible to human beings [Col. 0230A].

This is likewise evident in the Psalm, where, while speaking his works to this king, the tongue—that is, the power of the Holy Spirit—like the pen of a scribe writing swiftly, inscribes this Word of his, this wisdom and entire power of his, upon human nature, and addresses him thus: “Fairer in form than the children of men; grace has been poured out upon your lips” (Ps. XLIV).

For he is fairer in form than the children of men because he is not merely human, but God by nature. Some children of men are indeed gods by adoption, as was said above, on the testimony of the Psalm: “I said: You are gods, and all are children of the Most High” (Ps. LXXXI). But he alone is God by nature; he alone is the Son consubstantial with the Father. His divinity is here properly indicated [Col. 0230B] by the term “form.”

For divinity is form—form, certainly, not formed. God’s substance is neither created nor made; and thus, as has been said, it is evident that it is not formed, but is only form. Things that consist of both matter and form are called, and are, formed. For example, a human being is called formed because he consists of body and soul. The body itself likewise consists of earth and God’s fashioning; or again, some statue consists of stone or bronze material and the sculptor’s workmanship. But God consists of no matter. Therefore he is always what he is, is not changed, and is subject to no accidents. Accordingly, divinity, as has been said, is not formed but only form.

Thus the divinity of Jesus Christ is properly signified by the words: “Fairer in form than the children of men,” as though it were said: Because you are God, you are fair and glorious above all human beings, because human beings are pure. Therefore, when about to say, “Grace has been poured out upon your lips,” it rightly prefaced: “Fairer in form than the children of men” [Col. 0230C]. This is the same as what John the Evangelist says: “Therefore he is full of grace and truth, because in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was God.” Or John the Baptist says thus: “Therefore grace and truth came through him, because he was before me,” or because “he is in the bosom of the Father.”

“And this is the testimony of John, when the Jews sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to him, to ask him: Who are you?” This, he says, is the testimony of John of which I have spoken, which he now bears, which he now cries against all Antichrists who deny that Christ existed before Mary; indeed, which he will bear and cry out so long as evil fish, mingled with good fish, strive to break the nets of faith. This is his true testimony.

I shall now say when and for what reason he was prompted to bear it. For it is highly relevant to know the time and cause, especially since from these it may be discerned (Matt. XIII) whether his testimony is from human beings or from heaven—that is, whether he received the things he testified concerning Christ from human conjecture or from the spirit of prophecy. I say, therefore, that he uttered this testimony, of which we have spoken, when “the Jews sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem [Col. 0231A] to him, to ask him: Who are you?”

He had recently come from the desert, where he had led an eremitic—indeed, an anchoritic—life, so secluded and unknown to human beings that, when he came, he was thought to be Christ, Elijah, or one of the ancient prophets appearing from hidden places known only to God. This plainly supports the truth: namely, that his testimony was, as has been said, not from human beings but from heaven. For he had not come stirred up by Jesus’ fame—for Jesus, still living hidden among human beings, had as yet done nothing renowned—nor had he been summoned by him through any visible messenger. Rather, as Luke relates, he was commanded by an invisible inspiration of the Godhead to come and preach and baptize.

For he says: “In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, Pontius Pilate governing [Col. 0231B] Judaea, and Herod tetrarch of Galilee,” and so forth, down to: “The word of the Lord came upon John, son of Zechariah, in the desert” (Luke III), and the rest. Thus he did not yet know the Lord Jesus according to his humanity, until he saw him coming to himself amid the crowds to be baptized by him in the Jordan. Then, by the revelation of that same Spirit through whom the word of the Lord had come upon him, he knew that Jesus was the proper temple of that same Word of the Lord, before whose face he was sent in order to prepare his ways.

Hence he will say a little later: “And I did not know him; but he who sent me to baptize in water said to me: He upon whom you see the Spirit of God descending like a dove and remaining on him, this is he who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.” He did not fail to know that Christ had come, since for this very purpose the Spirit had driven him out from the desert: that, by coming and preaching and baptizing, and moreover by dying, he might discharge the office of his forerunning before him [Col. 0231C]. Nor was he ignorant of Christ’s power or majesty, since even prophets of lesser rank had not been ignorant of it; indeed, they had testified concerning Christ in their writings—writings not unknown to John—to things no less great than the Gospel itself. But he did not know him according to his humanity, as has been said: that is, what his appearance or bearing was, or where, or among what people, he lived.

Therefore the testimony is so much more trustworthy and worthy of all acceptance because it is shown to be wholly free from every human favor and conjectural presumption. Thus, not without reason, as has already been said, the time and cause of the testimony having been set forth, the words themselves remain to be expounded in order, since we have arrived at that testimony.

The Jews knew from the law and prophets that Christ, a great king, was to come, and that no king or ruler would fail from Judah before the coming of him who was to be sent. For their father Jacob had said: “The sceptre shall not be taken from Judah, nor a leader from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent” (Gen. XLIX) [Col. 0231D]. Now they saw before their eyes that the sceptre had been taken from Judah, and a leader from his thigh, especially since, in a kingdom divided and torn apart, four foreigners ruled over its separate parts.

They could therefore easily be persuaded to believe that Christ had come; always alert and expectant at every report, and eager to hear something new. According to their carnal opinion, they expected to possess a golden and gem-studded Jerusalem, a worldly age, and a victorious kingdom, so that, according to the prophet, they would “take captive those who had taken them captive” (Isa. XIV)—namely, the Romans, under whose rule they were. At John’s preaching they could therefore at once readily suspect this, to such an extent that they judged John himself to be the Christ.

Nevertheless, their carnal hope was considerably offended because he preached the humility of repentance, warned the brood of vipers to flee from the wrath to come by producing fruits worthy of repentance (Matt. III), and they heard him proclaiming that the laws of God’s kingdom would be wholly contrary to the vices to which they gladly clung. [Col. 0232B] Therefore, the evangelist says, “They sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to him, to ask him, ‘Who are you?’” “You,” they say, “a man of such renown, introducing with such authority this new rite of Baptism—who do you say that you are?” They undoubtedly wished to hear from his own mouth whether he was the Christ, as was commonly supposed.

But he was neither a reed, as was said above, able to be shaken by an adverse wind and bent away from the truth; nor was he a man clothed in soft garments (Matt. XI; Luke VII), so as to receive with yielding assent the praises of a fame exceeding his measure, as though they were caressing hands. Such are those who dwell in kings’ houses: possessing power, they delight in being called beneficent by their flatterers. Therefore, when questioned, he immediately shook off the bristling bristles of his mind, much harsher than the camel-hair with which he was outwardly clothed: “I am not,” he said, “the Christ.”

A truthful herald of the Truth, he wisely guarded against the deadly falsification of the divine name. Knowing himself to be the bridegroom’s friend, he would not, by secretly coming to the bridegroom, falsely claim to be the bridegroom himself. We must carefully observe the ornamented circumlocution, taken not without reason from the apostolic mouth, in which he speaks thus: “And he confessed, and did not deny; and he confessed: ‘I am not the Christ.’” For the matter—that is, the virtue of truth and humility which was in John and is here narrated—is so great that its expression is fittingly illuminated, as though by certain eyes, with shining clauses [Col. 0232C] so that we may attend, marvel, and delight in imitating it.

Yet this too must be noted: the evangelist affirms that the negative statement, “I am not the Christ,” is a confession, and denies that it is a denial. Clearly his intention is that, especially at this point, you should recognize John the Baptist as a confessor of Christ—which is altogether probable and true. For had he said that he was Christ, or agreed with those who thought so, he would undoubtedly have denied that he who is Christ is Christ. Thus the opposition is sufficiently firm: while he says in testimony to Christ, “I am not the Christ,” in one and the same saying he confessed Christ and did not deny Christ; consequently, at this point he shone forth as a true confessor of Christ. [102]

Accordingly, Christ’s faithful witness received fitting testimony from Christ’s Gospel, when evangelical Truth declares: “And he confessed, and did not deny”—so that you understand, “Christ,” whom he would indeed have denied had he said anything other than what he said: “I am not the Christ.”

“And they asked him, ‘What then?
