Are you Elijah?’ And he said, ‘No.’” “No,” he says, “according to your understanding or opinion, I am not that Elijah in person who was taken up to heaven in a fiery chariot and is reserved for a future time [to be revealed] (IV Kings II); rather, I am another man, born about thirty years ago of an aged father and a barren mother, herself also advanced in years” (Luke I). This is how the matter must be distinguished, since he could not deny without qualification that he was Elijah. Otherwise this would conflict with the Truth, who said of him to the crowds: [Col. 0233B] “If you are willing to receive it, John himself is Elijah” (Matt. XI; Luke I).

But it is now clear how there is no contradiction. For the Lord’s saying, “He is Elijah,” is mystical and needs interpretation, as he shows by adding: “He who has ears, let him hear” (Matt. XI). Namely, John is Elijah in this respect: according to another testimony of the Gospel, he came in the spirit and power of Elijah, and possessed the same grace or measure of the Holy Spirit. Moreover, the austerity of his life and the rigor of his mind equal Elijah’s. That man was in the wilderness; this man was in the wilderness; and each wore a leather girdle. The former, because he rebuked King Ahab and Jezebel for impiety, was compelled to flee (III Kings XIX); the latter, because he rebuked Herod and Herodias for their unlawful marriage, was beheaded (Matt. XIV).

Or John is called Elijah because, just as Elijah, according to Malachi, is to come beforehand and announce the coming Judge (Mal. IV), so John did this at the first coming; and each is a messenger—this one of the first coming, that one of the second (Mark I; Luke III). Thus it is mystical that John was called Elijah by the Savior. But they were not seeking mysteries; they were asking only about Elijah’s person. Therefore, it does not contradict the sentence of truth that he denies being Elijah: what was true in the mystical sense, as has already been said, would have been false in the understanding of those questioning him if he had said, “I am Elijah.”

“Are you the prophet? And he answered, ‘No.’” This too is plainly true, although the Lord says of him: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet” (Matt. XI; Luke VII). John was indeed a prophet in power, but he was not a prophet by office. That he was not a prophet by office will become clear from the very definition of the prophetic office.

The office of the prophets was, before the Word became flesh, to prefigure in deeds and foretell in words that the Word of the Lord would assume flesh. For although there are or have been very many who deserved to be instructed by the Spirit of prophecy in diverse matters, holy Church nevertheless counts in the catalogue of prophets only those who received in their minds the oracle of the Holy Spirit concerning the highest matters—that is, the mysteries of the Word to be incarnate—and announced it to the world in speech and writing. John, however, did not serve the Word of the Lord in this way. [Col. 0234A] He was not in the shadow of things to come, but in the reality of things present; nor did he utter a prophetic discourse to which men were to attend as to a lamp shining in a dark place. Rather, with finger extended, he pointed out the true sun now risen to those wholly turned away, who were following the setting of their own mortality. For he was almost contemporary with Christ’s humanity, whose rising he had preceded by no more than six months through his own birth.

Therefore he was not a prophet by office, and he rightly denies this when asked; as though the bridegroom’s friend should say to the bride: “I am not an envoy like the others, bringing you gifts or blessings from your bridegroom; rather, the bridegroom himself, having me as master of the feast or fellow guest, comes now to meet you on the wedding day.” Yet by power or grace he was a prophet—indeed, more than a prophet—inasmuch as he touched Christ, the present summit of all prophets, and knew his mysteries more intimately than all the prophets.

But someone may say: Why, when asked whether he was a prophet, did he deny the office but remain silent about the power or grace? Clearly, because those questioning him stood against him as adversaries, as the evangelist shortly afterward subtly indicates when he says: “And those who had been sent were from the Pharisees.” Since, then, they stood opposed in an unjust or treacherous intention, the Spirit of wisdom dwelling in John did not see fit to honor them with an answer of another kind. He answered only what was asked, with irreproachable restraint. For no one justly reproaches a person for failing to answer beyond or otherwise than the mode of inquiry requires.

There are two modes of inquiry. One is properly called *interrogatio*, “interrogation,” and is the only one employed by dialecticians: when something is asked in this manner, one must always answer either “it is” or “it is not.” This is the manner used here by these adversaries: “Are you Elijah? Are you the prophet?” The other mode of inquiry is likewise properly called *percontatio*, “questioning,” which dialecticians do not recognize. When something is asked in this manner, many diverse answers may be given according to the will or understanding of the respondent. Finally, they use this manner when they say: “Who are you, that we may give an answer to those who sent us? What do you say about yourself?”

So long as those who seemed wise and prudent in their own eyes irreverently assailed, with interrogations, the dwelling-place of such great grace, they were dismissed, as was fitting, by a simple denial according to the mode of inquiry. [Col. 0234D] But when they descended, however imperfectly, to questioning, saying, “Who are you, that we may give an answer to those who sent us? What do you say about yourself?” then he gave those chosen priests and Levites such an answer concerning himself as they did not know how to ask, and which they could not comprehend because of the height of its mystery, and therefore could not trample underfoot with their contempt. He said: “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness: ‘Make straight the way of the Lord,’ as Isaiah the prophet said.”

Let the teachers of the Scriptures now go, who have taken away the key of knowledge (Luke XI), professing that the mastery of the Law and the Prophets belongs to them. Let them go and, if they can, discern by their own understanding the sacramental meaning of this passage of theirs; or, if they cannot, let them humbly ask for its solution from the one by whom it was sublimely proposed. But they wish rather to seem wise than to be so; they prefer not knowing to learning—especially now, when they were sent precisely because they were regarded as men able to comprehend every answer and make a certain judgment concerning all that might be said.

Therefore, perversely prudent men turn their minds backward, and these cunning dissemblers pass over the answer with a deaf ear, as though they had not heard it. Let the little ones therefore laugh—those to whom these and similar things have been revealed but concealed from the wise and prudent. Ignorant through pride of the lofty humility of the Spirit, such men are cast down while they exalt themselves; and they busy themselves with the paltry burdens of the letter.

For from John’s saying, [Col. 0235B] “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness,” from this utterance it is granted only to the little ones—that is, the humble—to understand that he confesses himself contemporary with Christ. It is as though he said openly, as I said above: “I am not the Christ; but I am that one whom Isaiah heard crying to you with inward hearing, that you should prepare his ways, because that same Lord, namely Christ, is now present. For I cry to you now: ‘Prepare the way of the Lord,’ because I say to you: ‘Repent, for the kingdom of God will draw near’” (Matt. III). [103]

Since, therefore, my voice is so great that so great a prophet heard it so long beforehand while standing upon his watch—indeed, upon the Lord’s watch—keeping vigil through the nights; and, looking from afar and seeing Christ, he also saw and heard me in the Spirit, and struck with joy cried out: “The voice of one crying in the wilderness: ‘Prepare the way of the Lord; make straight the paths of our God’” (Isa. XL)—since, behold, I am so great that it was also prophesied concerning me, and men have suspected me to be the Christ whom you await, you ought to believe me when I show you Christ.

For as a voice exists so that the word may be heard, so I too was born for this purpose: that through my ministry Christ, who is the incarnate Word of the Father, may be recognized as present. And what do I cry? “Prepare the way of the Lord.” For the Lord is on the way: he has entered the way of this present life. And he who, in himself, is always the same, advances through the changing varieties of our condition toward a great work. He is now on the way: behold, “like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber, he rejoiced as a giant to run his course” (Ps. XVIII). [Col. 0235D] Whence does he come, and whither will he go? “His going forth is from the summit of heaven, and his course reaches to its summit” (ibid.). Do not meet him in opposition; do not resist him; do not place stumbling-blocks in his way. For “whomever he falls upon” (Matt. XXI), he will crush. Woe to those upon whom he will fall into death because of their crime (Luke XXII).

“Therefore,” he says, “make straight the way of the Lord.” But they pass over his cry with the deaf ear already mentioned and, as though he had said nothing, conclude: “Why then do you baptize, if you are neither the Christ nor Elijah nor the prophet?” They might have remembered what they had heard last as well as they carefully reckoned the earlier matters, had they not preferred to begrudge instruction rather than seek it. The evangelist, as was said above, silently indicates this when he adds: “And those who had been sent were from the Pharisees.” “They were from the Pharisees,” he says—that is, from those who sought not God’s glory but their own; who had taken away the key of knowledge, and neither entered themselves nor allowed others to enter (Luke XI).

It was with this fault that they now assailed John: not only were they themselves unrepentant, but they could not bear that others should be summoned to repentance. Thus they said: “Why then do you baptize, if you are neither the Christ nor Elijah nor the prophet?” Therefore, as has been said, when “the Jews sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem,” and they questioned and interrogated him in this manner, while the whole synagogue of Jews and Pharisees who had sent them waited, John then bore this testimony concerning Christ, which has been written and expounded above in great part.

Then “the voice of one crying in the wilderness” was heard—indeed, coming from the wilderness. There he had lived a solitary life, very like Elijah’s, such as befitted a lawful and spotless witness: lest eyes which were to see the presence of the true Light should draw anything from all the lust of the flesh that is in the world; lest the finger which he was to extend in pointing out the Lamb of God, or the hands beneath which that head revered by angelic powers was to submit and be baptized, should touch anything from the whole mass of defiling pitch; and lest the beauty of the mouth from which the testimony of grace and truth was first to be heard should in any way fade by uttering vain or idle speech.

Then that great and splendid voice was heard, coming from the wilderness—indeed, [Col. 0236C] crying from that wilderness [or, “out of that wilderness”] where righteousness once dwelt, but where murderers now dwell. Righteousness, abandoned by them, abandoned them in turn. These were the company from which came those to whom, as said above, he answered when they pressed him in this way: “I baptize in water, but one stands in your midst whom you do not know.”

“I indeed,” he says, “not without reason, not without heavenly authority, not coming of myself but sent by God, baptize in water. Therefore I am an object of wonder to all, and you ask so eagerly who I am, because I come not from among you nor from ordinary intercourse, but from the wilderness, bringing with the voice of preaching a manner and habit of holiness. These things, indeed, are something; but one stands in your midst”—that is, he has long walked amid the multitude of the people, has become accustomed to human society and common habitation—“yet you do not know him.” Him it is expedient to know, necessary to seek, profitable to find, and saving to believe in.

“He it is who is to come after me and who was made before me,” and the rest that has been expounded above. The faithful speaker, proceeding in this order, spoke to hearers who were more attentive than teachable or well-disposed—more attentive, namely, through their own curiosity than through goodwill. And from that time John himself began to decrease while Christ Jesus began to increase (John III); yet, by thus diminishing himself before men, he grew so greatly before God that no human being could grow beyond him.

“I baptize in water,” he says. Already in this diminishing of himself there is great humility: when he had said, “I baptize,” he added, “in water,” so that you may understand what he was shortly to say: “But he baptizes in the Holy Spirit.” Christ indeed also baptizes in water; but this is the third—indeed, the least—element of his baptism. “For there are three that bear witness” in Christ’s baptism: “the Spirit, the water, and the blood” (John V). Of these, as was said, water is the least; and John baptized in water alone, before the Spirit was given after Jesus had been glorified (John VII), indeed before Jesus had been pierced with the lance and his blood poured out.

Greatest is the Spirit, in whom alone forgiveness of sins is given. Since John could not give this, he prepared the people for Christ’s baptism by baptizing them unto repentance. For Christ, coming through water and blood, not in water only but in water and blood, alone baptizes in the Spirit. This testifies how Christ is the Truth, who alone grants forgiveness of sins: marked by water, purchased by blood, and poured forth by the Holy Spirit.

This contrast of greater and lesser, so widely different, was therefore made by John for the sake of his own diminishment. Yet more fully and plainly, in what follows, he diminishes himself so that the estimation of Christ’s greatness may grow. He says: “He it is who is to come after me, who was made before me.” This has been expounded above: Christ comes after John in that John, by being born, preaching, baptizing, and also dying, followed Christ’s birth, preaching, baptism, and death. And Christ was made before him in that he was set above him.

But this is the great and splendid mirror of humility which he then adds: “I am not worthy to loosen the strap of his sandal.” By this saying, employing a familiar comparison for those present, according to what they could hear or grasp, he commends Christ’s excellence with the greatest diminishment of himself; and he most beautifully signifies to us, from the breast of fruitful grace, the widowhood or rejection of the synagogue which we now see.

For it was an ancient custom that if a man refused to take as wife the woman who belonged to him, he himself should loosen his sandal for the man who came to her as bridegroom by right of kinship (Deut. XV; Ruth IV). But to whom could the synagogue more properly belong as wife than to Christ, whose is the whole inheritance of the Father—the entire Church from the beginning to the end of the age? For who is nearer to the Father than the Son? But he refuses to take as wife the one who belongs to him, because he repudiates the synagogue once united to God.

Therefore let that synagogue not suppose, when repudiated by Christ because of its fault, that it has Moses or the prophets. For, as John testifies concerning himself (John IX), none of Christ’s kindred is worthy to loosen the strap of his sandal. That is, none of the patriarchs or prophets can remain with it or save it, since it is unworthy of union with Christ.

This may, however, be understood in another way. Since sandals are made from dead animals, the incarnate Lord appeared, as it were, shod, because in his divinity he assumed the deadness of our corruption. Hence he says through the Prophet: “Upon Idumea I will stretch out my sandal” (Ps. LIX), that is, I shall be made known to the Gentiles through the mystery of my incarnation. But it is not enough to penetrate this very mystery of the Incarnation with the eyes [variant: “eye”]. For it cannot in any way be investigated how the Word takes bodily form; how the supreme and life-giving Spirit is animated within the mother’s womb; how he who has no beginning both exists and is conceived.

Therefore John is unable to loosen the strap of his sandal, because even he, who knew Christ’s incarnation through the spirit of prophecy, cannot sufficiently investigate the mystery of that incarnation. But, O John, fellow minister of truth and grace, can you not at least know why that strap was bound? Do you not know in what or what kind of lodging divinity was shod? Do you not know from what kind of woman the Word was made flesh? Do you, heavenly attendant and friend of the bridegroom, not know what we, the little children of the Church, do know? Why then is “the voice of one crying in the wilderness” silent about this? Why do you not preach this and raise your voice?

Clearly, because the time has not yet come. “For there is a time to speak and a time to be silent” (Eccl. III). The time for speaking these things will be when the Son of Man has risen from the dead. Therefore, not without cause, the affection of one who loves groans and cries with great longing, and imputes to his own unworthiness the fact that he will not have time to run with beautiful feet upon the mountains, evangelizing and “preaching peace, announcing good, preaching salvation, saying, ‘Your God shall reign, O Zion’” (Isa. LII).

Matthew the evangelist no less expresses this vehement cry of his affection in the words: “He who is to come after me is stronger than I, whose sandals I am not worthy to carry” (Matt. III). For what is it to carry his sandals except publicly to announce to the world the aforesaid mystery of his incarnation? The apostles did this, whom the prophetic Spirit blesses, saying: “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament announces the works of his hands. There are no speeches nor words whose voices are not heard. Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. XVIII).

And what is their sound and what are their words? “In the sun,” they say, “he has placed his tent, and he himself is like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber” (ibid.), and so forth. In doing this, the apostles carried his sandals, stretched out into Idumea and among all the foreigners; for this they were judged worthy both to suffer disgrace (Acts V) and to die.

But John foresees in the Spirit that he is not to be preserved until the time of declaring that glory: great indeed and inferior to none of the apostles, yet thinking humbly of himself and regarding as small the grace within him in comparison with those who were to declare that glory of God. For he knows that before Christ lays aside those sandals through his Passion and imposes them upon his chosen ones to carry throughout the whole world, he himself must be brought to completion amid the straits of Judaea and descend to the underworld, in order to perform there also the office of his forerunning.

Thus he groans, professing himself unworthy to carry Christ’s sandals or loosen their strap—that is, unworthy to announce with the blessed apostles the mystery of Christ’s incarnation and the glory of his resurrection. Nevertheless, neither Machaerus, a town of Galilee, nor the prison of adulterous Herod could contain so great a head, so that he did not shine throughout the whole world in the evangelical chariots, declaring with the firmament of heaven the glory of God—that is, bearing with the blessed apostles a resounding testimony to the Word of God.

To this day he does not cease to resound in the Gospel of that Son of God, known and renowned especially for that famous testimony which Christ himself bore of him: “Among those born of women, none greater than he has arisen” (Matt. XI).

“These things took place in Bethany beyond the Jordan, where John was baptizing.” Since in cases one also customarily asks about the place—whether it was famous or deserted, where something is alleged to have been done or said—the evangelist fittingly adds the place in which so great a voice of one crying was heard, saying: “These things took place in Bethany beyond the Jordan, where John was baptizing.”

It is as though he said: O scribes and Pharisees, none of you could have been unaware of this testimony which you cannot deny to be from heaven. For the place was nearby, only fifteen stadia from Jerusalem, and was at that time exceedingly well known: John was baptizing there (Matt. XXI), and, as the other evangelists report, people went out to him (Matt. III; Luke III); nor do your own historians keep silent: “The whole region of Judaea and all the people of Jerusalem went out to him, and were baptized by him, confessing their sins” (Mark I).

Therefore the Word of the Lord does not permit you to be excusable, since beyond the Jordan, so near to you and in such a place, through such a man and at the very time when you sent to him, he bore testimony to the Truth. Yet you did not believe him. But in Bethany—that is, the house of obedience, namely in the Church, which is Christ’s house and obedient to his faith—he likewise does not cease to cry, accusing you of impiety and strengthening us in faith in Christ by his testimony.

Meanwhile, no one should doubt that John’s soul clung to heaven in suspended longing, and that he sought outwardly with intent eyes and continually praying mind the one whom he had recognized inwardly. For, instructed by the Holy Spirit, he had come from the wilderness and, receiving the crowds that flocked to him, baptized, in order that he might openly show to others him who would come among sinners to take away the sins of the world—for this was undoubtedly to occur.

For he himself was soon to say: “And I did not know him; but that he might be made manifest in Israel, therefore I came baptizing in water.” Therefore, as he stood aloft as a watchman, higher than the whole world, wounded by longing and striking heaven with groans, thirsting to see his salvation so that he might show it to the living and announce it to the dead, “the next day he saw him coming toward him.”

“The next day,” he says: after the herald had served the Truth with so great a cry, faith receives its reward and devotion is recompensed. He receives a great reward indeed: that very one who is the crown and reward of all the saints, and who promises as a great thing, saying: “If anyone loves me, he will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him” (John XIV). For how could John, seeing him, have recognized him unless Jesus had in some measure manifested himself to him?

Would he have recognized him if, when he came, he had shown him only the form of a servant, which all saw? Certainly not; for, as has already been said, John himself testifies that he did not know him according to the form of man. Therefore, in the form of a man, John saw that form and beauty by which Christ was “more beautiful than the sons of men”; with a pure heart he saw that grace and truth which he had declared came through him. [Col. 0240B] He saw him and said: “Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world.”

What he saw with an enlarged mind, he wonderfully expressed in this brief declaration. Having tasted with double delight the sweetness of God through Christ’s bodily and spiritual appearance alike, he immediately poured it forth for us to taste in a voice of rejoicing. For he who “leaped for joy as an infant” (Luke I), while still little in the womb, because the King of the ages had descended into the virginal chamber—how greatly did he leap in joy as a young man preaching when that same King, Christ, was present before him to be addressed!

And he who deserved to hold such worthy thoughts about him as he had spoken above, while seeing him only with the mind and seeking him with outward eyes—when he found him, how much more ought he, or could he, utter something worthy in exclamation? Thus, shaken by the mighty impulse of the Holy Spirit, he cried out; and, as though adding a precious gem to pure gold, he added to his earlier words, when the joy of his mind burst forth into speech: “Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world.”

His preceding discourse shines for all like a golden seat in Christ’s evangelical chariot; but this saying, like a most precious stone, is added to increase its beauty. Holy Church eagerly seizes it, setting it upon her forehead and breast, and celebrates it more frequently in Christ’s praises. “Behold,” he says, “the Lamb of God.” When you hear “lamb,” you find an evident entrance into a great mystery.

For it is well known that the people of God were delivered from Egyptian slavery through the immolation of the lamb, and that Pharaoh with all the Egyptians (Exod. XII)—whose hardness the ten plagues had not overcome through Moses’ hand—was crushed by the lamb’s blood alone and by the mystical power of the evening sacrifice, when all the firstborn were slain (Exod. XIV). It also caused the children of Israel to cross the Red Sea, Pharaoh being drowned with his chariots and horsemen.

John, prophet and more than prophet, points with his finger to this shadow of future things, soon to be fulfilled in the truth of Christ: “Behold,” he says, “the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world.” It is as though he said: The ten plagues of the commandments given through Moses did not sufficiently scourge Pharaoh, the destroyer of our freedom and life, unto complete spiritual victory; but the blood of this Lamb—that is, of this innocent man, who committed no sin at all, the true Lamb without blemish, whom neither original sin nor any actual sin darkens—will cause us to pass free from that ruler of death and prince of darkness into the homeland of light and the true promised land which we lost in the first parent.

For neither by resisting the spiritual Pharaoh through the ten commandments, as through ten plagues, nor through carnal sacrifices, could we or our fathers be perfectly justified. But this Lamb will take away the sins of the world when, hanging upon the cross, he cleanses his whole Church—however great it is or shall be, from the beginning to the end of the age—with the stream of blood and water flowing from his side.

With this in view, John the Baptist himself said, according to the other evangelists: “I ought to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?” (Matt. III; Luke III). For both he and all the elect needed to be baptized in Christ’s blood, since the entire Church from the beginning of the world had until then kept watch outside; the judgment of supreme justice did not allow it to enter the heavenly sanctuary while defiled by the guilt of the ancient transgression.

Thus one of those holy ones, the holy and great prophet Isaiah, says: “We have all become as unclean, and all our righteousnesses are like the cloth of a menstruous woman” (Isa. LXIV). Therefore, when John says, “I ought to be baptized by you,” he truly understood this both of himself and of all who are foreordained to life. For through grace alone we are brought back to the kingdom of heaven, which we cannot purchase by any merits of our works.

Abraham indeed could, through his faith or righteousness (Rom. III), escape the punishment of ancestral guilt; but by no merits could he redeem that glory from which he had justly been disinherited in the first parent. The greatness or eternity of heavenly glory is a matter not of merit but of grace. It was freely given to the blessed angels; it was likewise freely given to the first parents of the human race; and it is restored to us entirely freely—that is, through Christ’s grace alone—whoever now have received reconciliation through him.

Therefore he alone and truly “is the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world.” By this saying, the wonderful herald of truth briefly shows the two substances in one person, namely God and man; he declares that both natures must be confessed: the passible nature of humanity and the impassible nature of divinity.

For inasmuch as he is man, he could, like a meek lamb, be led to the sacrifice (Isa. LIII); he gave his body to those striking him and his cheeks to those plucking them, that we might be fed by his flesh and clothed in his wool; and he was nailed to the cross and pierced with a lance, that the doorposts of our foreheads might be marked with his blood (Exod. XII). But inasmuch as he is God, he could take away the sins of the world: ascending to the prey and roaring in the underworld like a lion’s cub (Gen. XLIX), while the ancient plundering tyrant of death could not resist him. And now, having overcome death and sitting at the Father’s right hand, he powerfully forgives the sins of those who believe in him.

Therefore this evangelist, whose purpose is to gather testimonies to Christ’s divinity, rightly judged this saying not to be omitted, especially because it is of such splendor that the earlier declaration, “full of grace and truth,” is most strongly proved from this effect—that he takes away the sins of the world.

It follows: “This is he of whom I said: ‘He who is to come after me was made before me, because he was before me.’” It is as though he said: Do not receive another in Christ’s name as though he were Christ, nor be deceived when they tell you: “Behold, Christ is here,” or “there” (Matt. XXIV). For this one—and no other—this one, I say, is Christ, of whom I told you: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Mark XI). When another comes in his own name, take care not to receive him.

This Jesus, thought to be the son of Joseph, is the Christ (Matt. XXI; Luke III), born at the appointed time and on the predetermined days at Bethlehem from David’s seed—namely, when the sceptre had been removed from Judah and the ruler from his thigh (Gen. XLIX), and the foreigner Herod ruled in David’s kingdom.

“And I did not know him; but that he might be made manifest in Israel, therefore I came baptizing in water.” I cannot sufficiently marvel at the wisdom of God, artificer of all things, possessing all power and foreseeing all things: how, in the highest matters, not disdaining to have secular eloquence as a companion, it uses her as a handmaid and leads her along with itself, while covering her altogether with its own greatness—so completely that the presence of this talkative attendant can be discerned only by the most diligent.

For behold, wishing to catch the wise in their own craftiness, it has most evidently formed a syllogism. Above, through this John the Baptist, the faithful interpreter of his will, it had prudently set forth concerning the absent Christ: “Because he was before me”; “from his fullness we have all received,” [106] “and grace for grace,” and so forth.

Every hearer—the whole people—granted, indeed gladly accepted, that Christ would be a great king, a great and illustrious leader, having the crown of kingship upon his head and ruling from sea to sea and from the river to the ends of the earth (Ps. LXXI). For this was everyone’s single judgment concerning Christ, and this was how the prophets had declared him. Therefore they listened all the more attentively and more readily conceded the point to John as he testified, because, enslaved to carnal affections, they hoped that under Christ’s reign the pleasures of the body, the abundance of all things, and an altogether carnal age would not fail them. Therefore, once this testimony of so great a herald had been firmly established among the hearers,
… in the assertion, when Jesus at last came to John among the other men, the Holy Spirit takes him up, speaking through his mouth: “Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world; this is he of whom I said,” etc.

At this the hearer, who above does not rest at all, but rather disputes with as many arguments as he can muster: for Jesus was a Galilean man, who had hitherto walked among them like the rest of mankind, as though in his own homeland (Matt. 13). Yet certainly that saying is true, “that no prophet is accepted in his own country” (Luke [Col. 0243A] 4). Therefore it is necessary that he who has taken up the cause should contend in this same undertaking—which he does, employing weighty testimonies and finally concluding thus: “And I saw and bore witness that this is the Son of God.”

Accordingly, after he had said, “Behold the Lamb of God,” and the rest, he immediately introduces, for confirmation of his statement and refutation of his opponent, testimony taken from heaven, when he says: “For I saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and remaining upon him.” And in order to show that his testimony is pure, free from every human favor or partiality, he adds: “And I did not know him.” As though he were plainly saying: Why should you think that I was induced by favor or human partiality to bear this testimony concerning him? “I did not know him,” since, while I was an anchorite in the desert [Col. 0243B], I had previously had no association with him and no conversation.

“But that he might be made manifest in Israel, therefore I came baptizing in water.” That is: I did not come from the desert because I knew him; rather, I came for this reason, that I might come to know him.

But you say to me: How could you know even this—that you would find him while baptizing in water—unless you knew him? To this, I say: “And I did not know him”; but he who sent me to baptize in water said to me: “He upon whom you shall see the Spirit descending like a dove and remaining upon him—this is he who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.” Thus I came baptizing in water not by human will but by divine authority.

And just as Samuel was sent to Bethlehem (1 Sam. 16), knowing that among the sons of Jesse there was one whom he was to anoint king, but not knowing which of his sons he was, so I came to the Jordan knowing that Christ had already come, but not knowing in what person Christ was present. And just as that same Samuel recognized David at the sight of his face—“for he was ruddy, beautiful in appearance, and handsome of countenance”—but was made certain when the Lord said, “Rise and anoint him, for he is the one,” so I recognized this man when he came [Col. 0244B] to me and the Spirit revealed him, and I said: “Behold the Lamb of God; and I ought to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?” But I was made certain when the Spirit came upon him in the form of a dove. “And I saw and bore witness that this is the Son of God.”

## BOOK II

[Column 0243]

[Col. 0243C] There are three matters, distinct in this passage, which must be carefully considered: namely, John’s baptism, concerning which he himself says: “But that he might be manifested in Israel, therefore I came baptizing with water.” Likewise Christ’s baptism, concerning which it was said to John himself: “This is he who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.” And the appearance of a dove, in which the Holy Spirit, descending upon the Lord, was shown to that same John. These things, as I have already said, deserve careful consideration. For they are great and lofty matters: by understanding them faith is fed, hope is nourished, charity is kindled, and the whole inward person is made serene, as though by an infusion of morning light.

Therefore, first, with the preceding light of divine grace, we inquire what cause or intention there was for John—signifying Christ’s grace by his name, proclaiming it by his office—to come, as he himself says, “baptizing with water.” The immediate answer indeed occurs: he came baptizing unto repentance in order thereby to prepare the way for him who, coming after him, would baptize unto the remission of sins. But was baptism unto repentance so necessary, as though, once the Lord Jesus had been glorified, no one could receive the grace of his baptism unless prepared? This is wholly foreign to the faith. On the contrary, very few from that people to whom the baptism of repentance was preached attained Christ’s baptism; whereas to us the entire grace of baptism unto the remission of sins passed over without baptism unto repentance.

What then was the intention of the Holy Spirit, who sent all the prophets, each in his own time, when he drove John forth from the desert to preach the baptism of repentance? For barren Judaea did not produce fruits very worthy of repentance (Matt. 3). Nor could the intention of him whom the Holy Spirit undoubtedly sent have been frustrated in this act, whatever that intention was; for whatever undertakings begin at his prompting are brought to completion, with no one at all able to hinder them. Our consideration must therefore be raised above that scant repentance of the people, which, however considerable it may have been, certainly produced nothing worthy of so great a stirring-up of the voice crying in the wilderness: “Make straight the way of the Lord.”

For whoever seeks the same cause in our Lord himself will find it in this way. No believer doubts that Christ Jesus came in the flesh in order to take away the sins of the world and take them upon himself, according to the prophet saying: “And the Lord laid upon him the iniquities of us all; and he suffers for us, and the chastisement of our peace is upon him” (Isa. 53). That this was the true and supreme repentance performed for the whole world is shown by the fact itself, perceived by reason, and confessed by holy faith. For in the very guise of a penitent, the same prophet mentioned above, beholding this Son of God, says: “And he rose up like a shoot, and like a root from thirsty ground. He has neither form nor beauty; and we saw him, and there was no appearance” (ibid.), etc.

Therefore there is no doubt that our Lord came to perform repentance for the whole world, by which he might expiate the sins of all. But he had already reached the age of youth; and although he knew that he had come for this purpose, to undertake for all, as has been said, so great an office, he humbly remained hidden within himself, awaiting, in the form of a servant, the command of his commanding Father: namely, [supplied: “so that”] his entire work might be not of his own will, but of true and perfect obedience. For he knew that in himself he had to give us an example, lest any one of us, trusting in holiness or knowledge, should dare to seize for himself an ecclesiastical office, and especially the rank of the holy and venerable priesthood. This is properly the ministry of Christ the Lord himself, who takes away the sins of the world.

Hence the Apostle says: “And no one takes this honor to himself, but he who is called by God, as Aaron was. So also Christ did not glorify himself to become high priest, but he who spoke to him: You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Heb. 5; Ps. 8). Therefore, while he, as has been said, awaited his lawful and ordered promotion, John the Baptist came preaching in the wilderness of Judaea and saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. 3). That this preaching of John was a summons to him is attested by John the Baptist himself in this Gospel of John, when he says: “Because, that he might be manifested in Israel, therefore I came baptizing with water.”

The cause, then, why John came to baptize with water and to preach the baptism of repentance was no other than this: that the Holy of holies, who alone was fit to bear repentance for the sins of all the elect who had awaited his coming from the beginning of the world, being publicly summoned by this proclamation, might openly approach the heavenly sanctuary in the sight of God the Father and the holy angels. There, with the same Spirit descending upon him in the appearance of a dove, he might be designated High Priest—the same holy and immaculate man who had formerly been conceived when that Spirit came upon Mary. He would have no victim to offer but his own flesh, which, after being afflicted first by a fast of forty days and forty nights (Matt. 4), then by every manner of suffering, he would finally offer to God the Father for our sins, as a “sacrifice acceptable, a sweet-smelling savor” (Eph. 5).

And all this had to be done in such a way that both the inquisitive malice of the devil and the whole synagogue of that Satan might for a time remain ignorant of God’s counsel; while, flashing forth from his very hiding-place in frequent benefits, his wisdom might profit the simple. For it was fitting that at his first coming the Son of God should come hidden. At his second, however, “our God shall come manifestly and shall not keep silence” (Ps. 49).

John therefore rightly, by the counsel of the Holy Spirit, sends his ministry—by which Christ alone was being sought—into the crowd, openly preaching baptism to all and baptizing all unto repentance, so that, while the same rite was seen in many, an occasion for discourse about the one person might for the present be removed. Thus Samuel, mentioned above, was sent to anoint as king him whom the Lord had provided for himself among the sons of Jesse. Fearing lest Saul should hear, he took a calf from the herd at the Lord’s command; and, arriving at Bethlehem, he was met by astonished elders, who said: “Is your coming peaceable?” “Peaceable,” he said. “I have come to sacrifice to the Lord. Sanctify yourselves and come with me, that I may sacrifice.” And he brought them out to the sacrifice (1 Sam. 16).

Thus, indeed, divine providence wished both there to keep the anointing of the chosen king and here the manifestation of the Savior secret amid a great multitude; and the thing was done more discreetly than secretly. For it was done precisely in order that it might be known in its own time.

Of those baptized in the Jordan by John, as Luke says (Luke 1), confessing their sins and producing worthy fruits of repentance (Matt. 3), no one should doubt that this penitent in innocence and innocent in repentance took their sins upon himself, together with the sins of all who awaited him in the underworld. Thus, all who died from this life before his baptism was revealed were afterward to be saved through Christ’s passion—his baptism, whose definition or rule is baptism in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. But all who reached that fullness of time in which it was said, “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28), and did not receive this washing of grace and truth, received no benefit from having been baptized with John’s baptism; nor could repentance, without faith in Christ added to it, save them at all.

For John baptized with water, enjoining repentance alone—having been sent for the cause or intention already stated as far as possible—but did not also grant remission of sins. Christ, however, baptized once indeed in water, and at the same time in the blood flowing from his side; nevertheless, he baptized, and indeed now baptizes, in the Holy Spirit, granting perfect remission of sins through water and the sacrament of that same blood of his. After he promulgated its rule, remission is thereafter granted to no one outside his baptism.

Now we must speak of his baptism, as proposed above: “Upon whom,” he says, “you see the Spirit descending like a dove and remaining upon him, this is he who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.” It must be carefully noted that, although he could have designated him with his proper title and said, “This is Christ,” or, more properly, “This is the only-begotten Son of God,” he preferred to use a description, saying: “This is he who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.”

First, we must define what it is to be baptized in the Holy Spirit, and then say why he especially wished here to say, “who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.” To be baptized in the Holy Spirit is to receive the grace of the Holy Spirit (Rom. 6), which not only shows what sin is but also provides help against sins: blotting out those of the past, repelling those presently pressing upon us, and thus making sons of God out of slaves of sin, sons of grace out of sons of wrath (Eph. 2), and a royal and priestly race out of strangers and foreigners.

For Christ’s baptism is a royal and priestly anointing (1 Pet. 2), by which he himself, anointed above all his companions, is called Christ—*Messiah* in Hebrew, *Christos* in Greek, and *unctus* (“anointed”) in Latin. He alone was so anointed in fullness that he can anoint others in part and make them sons of adoption; and he causes those anointed by him, who is principally anointed, to be called Christians—that is, after Christ. This is signified by the words: “This is he who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.”

Before Christ’s coming this could in no way be accomplished, because the law that had been given was able only to show sin, not also to take it away. Hence the ancient fathers, however righteous, descended to the underworld, bearing the old disgrace of the fatherly transgression and not wholly escaping the mire even of actual sins, so as not to contract some defilement or stain (Rom. 7), which it was impossible to cleanse with the flesh of bulls or the blood of goats (Heb. 9). This was Israel’s reproach, which the uncircumcised enemy, the devil, continually threw in its face, mocking even the righteous ancient fathers and saying, as it were: “Why have you come prepared for battle?” (1 Sam. 17)—because, holding the commandment [variant: “commandments”] of the law as weapons, they did nothing bravely and could not produce from among themselves a man who would enter the unique contest for all.

In vain he strove [variant: “they strove”], by various washings and righteousnesses of the flesh (Mark 7), to erase his reproach, because they did not have a priest able to give the Holy Spirit, whose grace is the true and sole remission of sins. Therefore, when John is given the sign by which he may recognize Christ, he is told: “This is he who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.” This is the same as saying: This is he who removes reproach from Israel, namely by granting remission of sins, which is not granted at all except in the Holy Spirit.

This baptism is not of one power only, but of a double operation. For Christ baptizes in the Holy Spirit first, as has been said, by granting remission of sins. He baptizes also a second time by conferring the adornments of diverse graces. Of the grace of remission of sins, on the very day on which he rose, he himself says, breathing upon his disciples—whom he had certainly already washed from their sins in his blood—“Receive the Holy Spirit.” He testifies that he gives him to them for the remission of sins by immediately adding: “Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them; and whose sins you retain are retained” (John 20).

But of that abundance of gifts by which, as stated, he confers the adornments of diverse graces, he says, as Luke relates in the Acts of the Apostles: “For John indeed baptized with water, but you shall be baptized in the Holy Spirit not many days hence” (Acts 1). This same John the Baptist expresses both things given [variant: “gifts”] in this baptism in the Gospels of Matthew and Luke, when he says: “He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire” (Matt. 3; Luke 3). For he baptizes us in the Holy Spirit when, by the invisible grace of that same Holy Spirit descending into the font of baptism, he forgives all the sins of those who are baptized. He baptizes also with fire when, kindling them by the fervor of the same Holy Spirit, he makes them strong in love, steadfast in faith, radiant in knowledge, or burning with good zeal.

In the remission of sins there is indeed no division; rather, one and the same grace of remission is equally and uniformly present to all, laying aside all our iniquities and casting all our sins into the depths of the sea. But in gifts of grace the same measure is not bestowed upon all; rather, in a sense “the Red Sea is divided into divisions” (Ps. 135), while to one is given faith, “to another a word of knowledge and wisdom, to another kinds of tongues, to another interpretation of utterances,” and so forth—“all these things the one and same Spirit works, distributing to each as he wills” (1 Cor. 12).

In the saints of the New Testament, indeed, we see these gifts of the baptizing one, these splendid marks of glorious baptism; and none of them is recorded as having received them before being baptized unto remission of sins, except Cornelius and those with him. While Peter was still speaking, the Holy Spirit fell upon them, and they were “speaking in tongues and magnifying God” (Acts 10). Some of the fathers of the Old Testament, however, received workings of miracles, and very many received prophecy, though they were not baptized unto remission of sins.

For it is certain that all were baptized when Christ, dying on the cross, poured out from his pierced side a stream of blood and water [Col. 0248C] for the cleansing of the entire Church, however great it might have been from the beginning of the world up to the very hour of his death: from the first of the righteous, namely Abel, to the thief who, on the cross—before that great and most saving stream of cleansing had flowed from Christ’s side—confessed the Lord and believed that his kingdom would come, gaining it by that swift confession (Luke 23).

From that time the sacrament of this baptism was set at the first entrance of that same holy Church, so that whoever wishes to enter the Church must be baptized as it has now been baptized, whether Gentile or Jew. Therefore, when the fathers of the Old Testament received, before Christ baptized, the same gifts of grace that Christ, ascending on high, gave to people of the New Testament (Eph. 4), careful discernment is required, so that Christian faith may not be ignorant what was granted more to the new than to the old—or rather, what was granted alike to new and old in Christ’s baptism.

For when the subject requires a discussion of Christ’s grace or of the Holy Spirit, an opponent entangles a faithful and catholic person in objections, sometimes failing not in meaning but in wording. For the same God worked so greatly through the ancient fathers, and the same Spirit spoke so greatly through the mouth of his holy prophets from ancient times (Luke 1), that, when an opponent raises objections, it is most difficult to compare the new with the old—and contentious to prefer them—unless one first observes the precise point at issue before beginning a circuitous discussion of words.

Therefore we must first say that the glory of Christ’s baptism, by which the holy apostles after the Lord’s ascension were glorified through receiving gifts of diverse graces—especially kinds of tongues (1 Cor. 14), “which are a sign not for believers but for unbelievers,” or prophecy, in which the ancient saints especially shone—is not of such power that perfect salvation lies in those gifts, particularly since both good and evil people can possess them. “For many,” says the Lord, “will say to me on that day: Lord, did we not prophesy in your name? And in your name perform many miracles?” And then I shall answer them: “I do not know you; depart from me, workers of iniquity” (Matt. 7). Saul too was able to prophesy and to be evil (1 Sam. 19).

Were not all the children of Israel baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea, receiving bread also from heaven (1 Cor. 10; Exod. 16), water from the rock (Exod. 32), and glory through other marvels? Yet afterward very many were rejected: some were swallowed alive, others consumed by serpents (Num. 21), and others in many ways; apart from very few, all fell in the wilderness. Indeed, to come to the new: when the Lord Jesus summoned the twelve apostles, gave them power and authority over all demons and to cure diseases, and sent them to preach the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 10; Luke 9, 10), was not Judas among them (John 12)? The very one who sent him called him a devil before his betrayal, because he could not even be faithful with the Lord’s moneybags.

Since, then, not only good people but evil people too can receive gifts of such charisms, let not the splendor of the miracles performed among the ancients make us doubtful; let it not make us blind or dim-sighted in considering the majesty of Christ’s new grace. For he who baptizes in the Holy Spirit gave both the power of such gifts and that without which these avail nothing—namely remission of sins—to us and to them.

The Holy Spirit’s filling of the Lord’s disciples on the day of Pentecost (Acts 2) was not the beginning of this second gift—that is, of the working of miracles or the other such gifts already mentioned—but an additional outpouring of generosity. But the beginning and completion alike of that which is the greatest work and greatest power of Christ’s baptism, namely remission of sins, is Christ’s death. Through the Holy Spirit he offered himself as a sweet-smelling offering (Eph. 5); in this death we are baptized, as the Apostle says: “For all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death; we have been buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too may walk in newness of life” (Rom. 6).

For in his death, pouring blood and water from his side, as has been said (John 19), he washed the whole Church from its sins, giving to the living and the dead the Spirit of remission, as he showed immediately when he appeared to them alive, saying: “Peace be with you. Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them” (John 20).

By this gift alone baptized infants who die pass into the kingdom of God. But by that gift whose addition came on the day of Pentecost, the ancient fathers could be glorified and nevertheless held in the underworld because of original sin—just as Judas could, while exercising that same gift, be called a devil, be a thief of the Lord’s moneybags, and have a place in the deepest hell to which, after accomplishing his transgression, he would depart as a son of perdition.

The prophet testifies that the Lord himself, in the form of a servant, received these gifts, speaking thus in his person: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me” (Isa. 61); “he sent me to proclaim good news to the poor” (Luke 7). That these words were said of his present anointing, in which the Holy Spirit was seen over him in the appearance of a dove (Luke 3), he himself also testifies. As Luke relates, full of the Holy Spirit he returned from the Jordan, was led into the wilderness, and, after every temptation had been completed, returned in the power of the Spirit to Galilee. He entered the synagogue, and the book of the prophet Isaiah was given to him. When he had unrolled it, he found the aforesaid passage and began to say to them: “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing” (ibid., ch. 4).

The Holy Spirit, then, descended upon the Lord Jesus not only in order that a sign might be given to John, but in order that the human nature united to God might exercise the office of evangelizing and the order of the high priesthood. For just as the Son of God did not come of himself, but the Father sent him, that he, Lord of all, might deign to assume the form of a servant, so likewise in that form of a servant (Phil. 2) the Son of Man did not seize for himself the office of evangelizing, but humbly accepted the burden laid upon him by the Holy Spirit.

For it was fitting that he should fulfill all righteousness in this way (Matt. 3): he who had obediently become man was also obediently sent to preach by the same Spirit who sends all others who worthily receive a share in the ministry of salvation, so that some may be appointed apostles, others prophets or evangelists in the Church (1 Cor. 12). Then that great and conspicuous Angel of Great Counsel stood beside the altar of the temple (Rev. 8), namely, called to the sacred order of the high priesthood. The Spirit of piety appeared over his head in the appearance of a dove, so that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest before God and make atonement for the sins of the people (Heb. 2).

Therefore God, creator of all, received gifts among human beings (Ps. 67), being sent to minister—gifts which afterward, ascending on high and leading captivity captive (Eph. 4), he would give to people to be sent forth for ministry in due time. And thus, “full of the Holy Spirit,” as stated above, he returned from the Jordan.

He was full, certainly, not because he then received the Holy Spirit for the first time, since from the very beginning of his human existence he was conceived through the operation of that same Spirit. What, then, now occurred, such that he was said to return from the Jordan full of the Holy Spirit? Surely the fullness already in him [supplied: “up to”] the surface spread forth—that is, to his outward actions themselves—so that we all might receive from it; as if the fullness of living and unfailing water in a very deep well rose upward to the surface of its mouth, so that even little children might be able to draw or drink.

Thus the fullness that he possessed inwardly spread forth even to outward things, and “grace was poured upon his lips” (Ps. 44), so that in his words its abundance might be heard and in his miracles seen—the abundance by which he was full of grace and truth. But he did not receive remission of sins, which, as said above, he gave to human beings when baptizing in the Holy Spirit. For what is greater occurred: he was conceived of the Holy Spirit, so that he possessed neither original sin nor admitted actual sin.

But someone may say: He too had to be baptized unto remission of sins, not his own but ours, so that, once he was baptized, remission of our sins might occur. This certainly must be granted, but only concerning that baptism of his of which, already baptized by John, he himself says: “I have a baptism to be baptized with, and how I am constrained until it is accomplished!” (Luke 12). He said this, namely, concerning his passion, in which the whole Church, which is his body (Eph. 1), was to be baptized.

Otherwise, if remission of our sins took place when he was baptized in the Jordan, why would his passion have been necessary to us? Therefore he received from no human being a baptism for remission of sins; rather, by his passion he became for us the fountain of remission. Hence the holy Roman Church rightly customarily celebrates the sacrament of baptism universally and jointly, not on the day of Epiphany, but in the most holy solemnity of Easter. For, as stated above, “all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death” (Rom. 6).

Thus this is he who baptizes; this is he alone who grants remission of sins; this is he who comforts and enriches, through the abundant gifts of his divinity in the Holy Spirit, the disgraceful and ignoble poverty that has come upon our nature through sin. Why at this place or time so sure and manifest a judgment concerning the authority of baptism was given has long been well understood by the catholic Church.

First it must be known that this great man, sent by God—great in merits and possessing, in proportion to his greatness, a great inward voice of holy longing in his heart—lifted the eyes of his mind toward God and cried mightily to heaven, praying continually that he might soon be permitted to see that consolation of Israel which he knew to be near and which he had greeted in his mother’s womb. His desire was no less than that of the most blessed old man Simeon, whose inward cry and great outcry reached the ears of the Most High, so that God’s mercy could not restrain itself: the Holy Spirit gave him the answer that he would not see death before first seeing the Lord’s Christ (Luke 2).

Therefore this man too, crying out with the great voice of desire and praying continually, obtained from the Holy Spirit this response: “Upon whom you see this sign, this is he who baptizes.” And, as stated above, the catholic Church has long well understood the reason for this sign. For that dove who sent John and had sent all the prophets knew that ravens and kites would arise who, tearing one another with their beaks and rending unity, would stand opposed to one another, swollen with arrogant spirit, and say: “What is given by us is holy. He who has been baptized by that drunkard, or that one by that fornicator, is unworthy. You, baptized by those or those,” says Donatus, “if you have any sense, must be rebaptized by us.”

Against these the dove cries out—the dove that always bears in its mouth a branch of green olive (Gen. 8), that is, always loves and proclaims true peace and unity. From the summit of the most high head of us all it cries and says: “This is he who baptizes.” As though saying: Why do you, ravenous kites and contentious ravens, divide the grace of baptism among so many authors with such obstinate beaks? “One is he who baptizes.” This one and he alone sanctifies; there is one fountain, one stream of saving baptism, whatever channels it may flow through. “This is he who baptizes,” from whose mouth flows the very power of the sacrament, purifying, cleansing, giving life to, and sanctifying the whole faithful person.

Perhaps you did not know how to distinguish a living fountain from a dead marsh or muddy cistern. Behold, as I told you: “Upon whom you see the Spirit descending like a dove, this is he who baptizes.” So now I tell you: wherever you hear these words uttered in their entirety, “I baptize you in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,” there without doubt is this very one, and there he himself baptizes.

For what is Paul? What is Apollos? What indeed is Cephas? (1 Cor. 1). They are ministers in Christ’s sacrament; they are ministers, not authors; servants, not lords; channels, not fountains. For, as stated above, this one alone is the fountain, the one Lord, the one author. He baptizes in water through ministers, but he alone baptizes in the Holy Spirit through himself.

But if, beneath the sacrament of the aforesaid name, a corpse reeks with some heretical corruption, even then the invocation of the divine name is not judged invalid. Yet such a baptism is only such as the dead could administer to the dead [Latin variants: *mortuos*, “the dead,” and *mortuis*, “to the dead”], of whom the Apostle says: “Having indeed an appearance of piety, but denying its power” (2 Tim. 3). For they are branches, indeed, but branches cut off from the vine. They were members of the living body of the Church, but lack life because they have been cut off from the body. Therefore, in baptizing, they conveyed the appearance of piety alone which they possess; but the power of that piety, which they do not possess, they could not convey.

Accordingly, when those baptized by such persons return to the catholic Church, the washing of the flesh is not repeated for their completion; rather, they are brought into the catholic Mother—where what is lacking is supplied—so that through her reconciliation they may deserve to receive the grace of the Holy Spirit. For the Holy Spirit is given in her alone, because God is not in a division of minds but in unity and peace, which is “the bond of perfection” (Col. 5 [probably Col. 3:14]).

And these persons, though begotten as it were from a less lawful marriage-bed, are nevertheless reckoned as children. For from every tribe of the children of Israel were numbered the children known to God, where the servants of our God are sealed upon their foreheads (Rev. 7): namely, both from the tribes of Gad and Asher, born of a handmaid, and from the tribes of Judah and Joseph, born from lawful wives (Gen. 30).

Therefore the grace of baptism is to be attributed to no human beings, nor measured according to human standards. For this one alone baptizes, and we are baptized in the name of him alone, who alone was crucified for us all, as the dove displayed above his head testifies. We must now carefully consider, insofar as he himself deigns to reveal it, why the Holy Spirit wished to appear in that form.

The Holy Spirit is Lord and Ruler of all things done or to be done concerning our salvation; indeed, he is their efficient cause. For why did the Father send the Son into this world except because of his charity (John 3)? Or why did the Son reconcile us to his Father through his blood while we were enemies, except because of that same charity? And what is the Holy Spirit except the charity of the Father and the Son?

Therefore the Holy Spirit, appearing over the Author of our salvation, gave a sufficiently fitting indication, appropriate to the time, of his grace, by visibly showing human eyes the bodily form of a dove which he had assumed. For the dove is a simple and gentle bird (Matt. 10). Charity indeed can rage and be zealous, but it first uses gentleness, so that it rages against no one except one whom gentleness does not bend; it never comes with the rod except to those by whom its gentleness has been despised (1 Cor. 4).

The same charity ordered both things in Christ: his first coming to us was to take place in gentleness, whereas his second is to be in the power of zeal. Therefore, as he came to us in the spirit of gentleness, the same Spirit, appearing over him, rightly designated him as a gentle bird.

But it must be known that before Christ’s coming the Holy Spirit appeared over none of the saints; nor after his coming was he seen over anyone in this form. Before, indeed, he gave gifts, as stated above, and sometimes indicated their quantity or quality by fitting signs. Thus, when he sent the aforesaid prophet to anoint David, his chosen one, as king, he commanded him to take not a flask, as for anointing Saul, but a horn of oil (1 Sam. 10), thereby signifying both the greatness and strength of his gift—that is, the firmness of David’s throne and the loftiness of prophetic grace.

Likewise, when he wished to take Elijah into heaven (2 Kings 2), knowing that Elijah possessed a most fervent zeal for this divine love, he sent a fiery chariot with fiery horses to carry him away, in order to signify the dignity of his good zeal. So also in many other saints he represented, by suitable figures, the gifts that he gave; but, as said, he was seen to appear over none before Christ’s coming.

Afterward, however, he was seen appearing over the apostles—not in his own substance, which is invisible, but as fire, an indication of his presence. Yet tongues divided from that fire were seen (Acts 2), because not all things were given to any one person; rather, by the will of that same Spirit, to each was distributed his own measure of grace.

But over the Lord himself both the invisible substance of the Holy Spirit is present, and what is seen outwardly is not a part or sign of a part, but a certain whole and integral reality. For he alone is the one to whom “God does not give the Spirit by measure” (John 3). “For,” says the Apostle, “in him dwells bodily the fullness of divinity” (Col. 2). He said “bodily,” not because God is corporeal or localized, but because, just as any body is undivided in any place together with all its members, so the divinity of the Holy Spirit is wholly present in Christ with all its gifts.

The prophet, beholding this fullness long beforehand, says: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root. And the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of knowledge and piety, the spirit of counsel and strength; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. 11). For these are all the gifts of the Holy Spirit, like all the members of one body. That none of them was lacking to Christ is testified both by the prophet’s aforesaid proclamation and by the present whole and undivided appearance of the dove.

For the spirit of wisdom rested fully upon him. The first human being, lacking it—or rather, rejecting it from himself through pride—refused to heed or submit to one better than himself; abandoning the true light, he trusted that he could shine for those following him. Like a man by night, he fell among thieves, by whom he was stripped, wounded, and left half-dead (Luke 10).

But this second man, like a dove “dwelling beside full streams” (Song 5), always attends to the divinity inherent in him. Gazing into its clear majesty, he saw the coming deceitful hawk and escaped him, when in the wilderness he refuted all his temptations with a wise answer (Matt. 4). Filled also with the spirit of understanding, he knew to whom to disclose the mysteries of the kingdom of God and to whom to speak in parables (Matt. 13). Deprived of this, the first human being did not discern on the balance of reason how much
For the threats of God were more trustworthy than the serpent’s promises when it said, “You shall be like gods” (Gen. 3). For he was steeped in the gall of bitterness; and, swollen with the spirit of pride, he resentfully bore the command that had been laid upon him. But this one, like a dove, free from every gall of this kind [Col. 0254D], and discerning all things with the sound palate of his heart, neither admitted demons when they confessed that he was the Son of God (Mark 5), nor spoke the mystery of God to the unworthy; indeed, he forbade what is holy to be given to dogs and pearls to be cast before swine (Matt. 7).

Likewise possessing the Spirit of counsel, he concealed “these things from the wise and prudent, in order to reveal them to little ones” (Matt. 11). The first man, wholly lacking this Spirit, held discourse with the adversary and did not hide himself from him in humility. But Christ kept his purpose entirely secret from the devil, so that, although the latter knew him to be the Son of God, he did not know that through his cross and passion he would bring about the salvation of the human race. By that same Spirit of counsel, preaching good news to the poor, he did not repel either Samaritans or Gentiles from mercy [Col. 0255A]; indeed, he healed their sick (John 4; Matt. 8, 15), like a dove which sometimes broods over alien young. And to those coming from east and west he promised to open Abraham’s bosom for their repose.

He also advanced in the Spirit of fortitude. Abandoning this Spirit, the first man was conquered, succumbed without restraint to gluttony, and made himself saleable; indeed, sold for nothing, he stripped and ruined himself of every protection. But Christ, like a dove nesting in the rocks, where the serpent cannot approach, placed those who believe in him in a secure protection—for example, when he said, “No one can snatch [them] from the hand of my Father” (John 10).

He likewise abounded in the Spirit of knowledge. The first man lost it when he desired to know more, as the ancient enemy promised that, once he had become a transgressor of the command, he would possess the knowledge of good and evil [Col. 0255B]. But Christ, having within himself the heap of all the Scriptures, as a dove gathers the whiter grains from a great heap of wheat, brought forth from every Scripture sayings appropriate to the time or circumstance, so that his astonished adversaries said, “How does this man know letters, having never learned?” (John 7).

He was altogether full of the Spirit of piety. The first man had been grievously stripped of it when he consigned himself and his descendants to eternal death; nor, when questioned after his fault, did he pity his own soul so as to repent. Rather, he turned back upon God the evil which he had perpetrated, saying, “The woman whom you gave me gave to me, and I ate” (Gen. 3). But Christ not only killed no one, like the dove, which [Col. 0255C] eats nothing living; he was always intent, moreover, on giving life to the dead: “For,” he says, “the Son of Man did not come to destroy souls, but to save them” (Luke 9).

The Spirit of the fear of the Lord rested upon him. The first man repelled this Spirit from himself from the devil’s first suggestion up to the consummation of sin. But Christ, as a dove has groaning instead of song, so counted it a delight to be filled, in accordance with the Father’s will, with reproaches. From the beginning of his incarnation he said in every circumstance—readily, not only in words but also in deeds—“Father, let not my will but yours be done” (Luke 22).

Therefore the Spirit of the Lord, which hitherto had found no resting-place in the great forest of the human race, at last rests upon this flower. Remaining in him in an eternal station, it never suffered at any time the repulse of any vice [Col. 0255D]. Nor did the divine oracle keep silence in this passage about that resting-place. For when it had said, “Upon whom you see the Spirit descending like a dove,” it immediately added, “and remaining upon him.”

This same Spirit is indeed with us and in us, according to the promise of our same Savior; but it is said to remain in our head himself far more excellently and much more immediately. For it so remains with us and is so in us that there are never lacking in the Church persons who possess the grace of this Spirit, or some gift of it: namely faith, a word of wisdom or knowledge, interpretation of utterances, discernment of spirits, and things like these. But rare is the person [Col. 0256A] who has progressed so far that his soul inwardly feels, even for a moment, that touch of this Spirit signified in Elijah by the whisper of a gentle breeze: “And after the fire, a whisper of a gentle breeze; and the Lord was there” (3 Kings 19).

For that sign expresses a certain inward perception of circumscribed truth, which a holy mind, caught up in contemplation, sometimes deserves to taste by a sudden illumination. But Christ is so full of the same Spirit that it dwells bodily in him, as was said above, ever content with its dwelling in his gentle breast and never disturbed by any tumult of carnal affections.

As though in its first outpouring, he himself poured back upon us the fullness of the Spirits mentioned above when he began the first discourse that he delivered after this manifestation to the crowds gathering around him in this way: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5), and so forth [Col. 0256B]. Here he invites and instructs us to be, in imitation of himself and according to a certain order of the heavenly dispensation: humble through the fear of God; gentle through devotion to piety; discerning through knowledge; free through the fortitude of the mind; cautious through counsel; provident through understanding; and mature through wisdom.

But when the Prophet speaks of heavenly things, he enumerated these stages in descending rather than ascending order: wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, fear. For it is undoubtedly established that one ascends from fear to wisdom, not returns from wisdom to fear [Col. 0256C]. For knowledge has perfect charity, whereas “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110).

But the Lord, because he raises us from earthly to heavenly things, enumerates the same stages in ascending order, beginning with fear, which is understood through poverty of spirit: “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matt. 5). Next he commends piety, saying, “Blessed are the gentle” (ibid.). For it is the work of piety to become gentle and not to resist divine Scripture—whether understood, when it strikes at any of our vices, or not understood, as though we could be wiser or give better commands.

Then one comes to the third stage, that of knowledge, when he says: “Blessed are those who mourn” (ibid.). For that fear by which one reflects upon God’s judgment, and that piety by which one cannot but believe and yield to divine Scripture [Col. 0256D], compel one to mourn oneself. True knowledge makes a person of good hope not boastful, but lamenting.

Then one begins to be on the fourth stage, that of fortitude, of which he says: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness” (ibid.). For it belongs to fortitude to draw the mind so completely away from every deadly delight in transitory things that it is free to hunger and thirst for righteousness. Then, by the counsel of mercy, he cleanses the soul that is in turmoil and, as it were, clamorous against itself through the defilements conceived from the desire for lower things. Hence it follows: “Blessed are the merciful” (ibid.).

From here one ascends to the sixth stage, that of understanding, where he now cleanses the very eye by which God may be seen, insofar as he can be seen by those who die to this world, insofar as they are able. Of these it is added: “Blessed are the pure in heart” (ibid.) [Col. 0257A]. At this stage he so cleanses the eye of the heart that he prefers neither himself to truth nor his neighbor, whom he loves as himself. Such a son ascends to wisdom, which is the last and seventh stage, and in it enjoys peace and tranquility. Hence it is added: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (ibid.). The eighth beatitude is the same as the first.

Therefore, when he in whom the sevenfold Spirit remains and rests like a dove says these things, his purpose is surely that the Church, regenerated by the same Spirit, should be such that he may rightly say of her in the Song of Songs: “My dove, my beautiful one, my immaculate one, is one” (Cant. 5, 6). For the dove is one when the Church, gathered from many persons of every sort, having one Spirit, is of one mind—saying the same thing, thinking the same thing, and not dividing itself through the scandals of sects (1 Cor. 1) [Col. 0257B]. For all who are led by another spirit are ravens: rapacious ravens, contentious ravens.

Such was Macedonius, who, unworthy to be counted among the members of the dove—that is, of the Church—said that the Holy Spirit is not God. Truly a raven, he emerged wholly black and sinister, of dreadful appearance, from the waters of baptism. Nor did that dove which appeared over the Lord regard him with any portion of her gifts, as it is written: “For the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee from the deceitful, and will withdraw from thoughts without understanding” (Wis. 1).

But the dove—that is, the Holy Spirit—proves by a sufficiently firm argument, from that dwelling in which it rests [Col. 0257C], that it is God. For if it were not God, how could it be capable of a human or angelic spirit? A created spirit cannot in any way pour itself into another spirit. An evil spirit may indeed creep secretly into the hidden chambers of the body and drive a person’s soul with frenzies; hence a person is said to be full of a demon. But it cannot in any way infuse its own substance into that person’s substance.
