The Creator of spirits alone, by his subtlety, is capable of a rational spirit, as of his creature; but the latter is capable of no substance except the divine and creative substance.

Yet this “Spirit filled the whole world, and also filled him whom the whole world does not contain” (ibid.) [Col. 0257D], as was said above: “Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan” (Luke 4). And lest the heretic perhaps object that it filled his flesh, not his mind, it must be remembered that this “Spirit of the Lord is the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, counsel and fortitude, knowledge and piety, and fear of the Lord” (Isa. 11). But where do wisdom and understanding, counsel and fortitude, dwell if not in the mind? Where do knowledge, piety, and the fear of the Lord reign if not in the heart? Therefore this Spirit, which is received by a rational mind and searches all things, is God.

Accordingly, the one dove—that is, the holy Church—rejects this Macedonius and all others whatsoever who are of the race of ravens; abhorring their rending kisses [Col. 0258A], she permits them to have no communion with her. She loves peace and embraces peace, since the first dove, the Holy Spirit, brought her an olive branch with green leaves, making peace through Christ, through whom he reconciled us to God.

But now that we have, as far as we are able, completed the three matters proposed, let us hear what John—the witness and champion of truth, strengthened by evident proofs—freely proclaims at the summit in the Spirit of fortitude. “And I saw, and bore testimony, that this is the Son of God.” “I did not,” he says, “hear mere report; I did not learn from uncertain conjectures. Rather, I saw the dove coming from heaven; I saw the Spirit of God, not merely offering the kisses of a dove, but pouring his whole self into this man. And he remains in this [Col. 0258B] temple, from which he has not migrated elsewhere; he is found nowhere except in this his resting-place, where he was received to remain in profound tranquility.”

And, in a wonderful manner, he so remains in this his temple that he ever proceeds from it—namely, so that from his fullness we may all receive, “drawing water which, according to Ezekiel, goes forth from this temple on the right side” (Ezek. 47). For the temple of the great city shown to him, the true temple of the holy Church, is this very Lord, as John the Evangelist also testifies in the Apocalypse: “And I saw no temple in it, for the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple” (Rev. 21). Therefore this temple, as stated above, is shown to the prophet as entered by the dove and as issuing forth like living water, cleansing and saving [Col. 0258C], so that now, as has been said, “we may all receive from his fullness.”

“‘This,’ he says, ‘I saw and bore testimony: that this is the Son of God.’” Let the worthy speaker say this: the king’s friend and noble chief senator of the heavenly court; let him say that this man, “who, as I said above, comes after me, is the Son of God.” For the citizens of the heavenly city hear nothing more gladly; no minstrel do upright children, teachable in song and trained to dance to a good song, prefer to hear (Matt. 11).

For who could confess more clearly than this herald of faith that Christ is God and man? For when he said that the man came after him, he plainly declared that he was a human being born after him. And he called the Lamb of God “a man” more magnificently than “a human being” [Col. 0258D], in reference to what was said of the typical lamb in the Law: “The lamb shall be without blemish, male, one year old” (Exod. 12). For this man is a male lamb, softened by no effeminacy, but steadfast in every virtue, firm and perfect. Thus, in calling him “a man,” he expressed the true nature of humanity together with the integrity of virtue.

Now, however, in testifying that this is the Son of God, he likewise confesses in him the true nature of divinity. For it cannot reasonably be understood that the son is of another nature than the Father who begot him. When does a human being generate anything other than a human being? So too every animal at some time generates nothing other than what it itself is. Nor does any plant produce seed except according to its kind, nor does a tree that produces its fruit ever exceed its species in its seed [Col. 0259A] (Gen. 1). For thus the Creator of all established those things: “He set a command, and it shall not pass away” (Ps. 144). How much more did the Creator himself beget not something other than what he is, but God from God, light from light, the immeasurable from the immeasurable, the Almighty from the Almighty?

For he did not adopt this one but begot him, as John himself clearly expresses when he says above: “The only-begotten, who is in the bosom of the Father, himself has declared him.” Therefore this burning and shining lamp shows us by clear light that Christ is true God and true man—the true light which the darkness did not comprehend: namely, Manichaeus and Photinus, the former denying that this Jesus Christ is true God, the latter that he is true man.

But again we must beware the two-formed monster of the Nestorian heresy, which asserts that, just as two natures or substances, so also two persons must be confessed in Christ: that one is the Son of God and another the Son of Man [Col. 0259B]. This neither reason nor the ordinary usage of our speech admits, as dialecticians especially know. For there is no particular or general name, except that most general one, namely “substance,” by which God and man can both be called generally—just as Moses and Aaron are two human beings, and this ox and that one are two animals or two animate bodies.

Thus God and man cannot alike be predicated as two by any one particular or general term except by that most general term, the name “substance” [Col. 0259C]. For “animal” cannot be predicated of the true God in the same way as of a human being, since the true God is not a body; therefore he is neither an animate body nor an animal. When, then, in the masculine gender you have predicated “two” of Christ, God and man, what subject will you append to that predicate? For a predicate requires a subject; or, as even children know, it always seeks something variable of its own gender, number, and case to have as its fixed noun. Certainly it cannot be a term indicating diverse species or individuals of diverse species; this is impossible in the masculine gender. For instance, since “human being” and “horse” are names of different species, they cannot be expressed under one substantive name in the masculine gender.

Accordingly, of a human being and a horse you say better “these two [neuter]” than “these two [masculine]” [Col. 0259D], because the horse together with the human being does not make up a number of persons, though it makes a plurality of substances. What, then, will you supply when you have predicated “two” of Christ, God and man? Will you perhaps supply “Christs”? Surely that is like calling one horse and its rider “two riders.” For “Christ” is the name not of a nature but of an office. Indeed, there were other christs—that is, anointed ones—of whom he himself says, “Do not touch my christs” (1 Chron. 16); but this one, in whom “the fullness of divinity dwells” (Col. 2), as said above, was anointed above his companions (Ps. 44).

Indeed, God and man are far more unequal than horse and human being. For the only thing common to the true God and a human being, which can be predicated of each, is substance; but of a human being and a horse, not only substance but also body and animal are predicated in common [Col. 0260A]. If, then, the person of the rider so absorbs the person of the horse that the horse, though not united to him, cannot together with him make up a number of persons, how much more does the person of God so absorb or take up the person of the human being in Christ that they are neither called nor are two Christs or two Sons—especially since God is inseparably united to the human being.

Therefore, while the truth of the two substances is preserved, Christ is one—that is, one person: this is the man or Son of Man; this same one is the Son of God. Delighting in his form and beauty, God the Father himself spoke over him from heaven that memorable saying: “You are my beloved Son; in you I am well pleased” (Mark 1) [Col. 0260B].

He certainly did not say this at the beginning when he created the universe, when he stretched out the fabric of heaven or set a boundary to the sea and, as a wondrous craftsman, arranged all visible and invisible things, distinguishing each in its place or order. Indeed, all that he had made pleased him, because “they were very good” (Gen. 1); but nowhere among all those things does he intimate that he was well pleased in himself. But in this one he is pleased in himself and says, “In you I am well pleased.” This is far different from saying, “You pleased me.”

Let us therefore consider what was done in Christ, and we shall see that, in truth, the Father rightly was well pleased in himself in him because of the magnitude and character of the work. When God had made all things [Col. 0260C], he had made nothing at all like or equal to himself. For it could not be that, in the created order, a creature like or equal to God should be fashioned. Therefore the Creator’s good will was not satisfied by the fact that all that he had made was very good, because among all things he saw nothing like or equal to himself. But, as has already been said, something altogether such as he himself is could not be created.

Accordingly, the multitude of creatures, weak because made from nothing, had in part fallen and could by no means be restored by its own strength. Therefore the Father’s gentle and benevolent love—the very love which has now appeared in the form of a dove—suggested that he should unite to his handiwork that very Power, that very Word through which he had made all things, since he had created nothing equal to himself; and thus produce within the order or nature of the creature one thing lacking nothing [Col. 0260D].

When this was done, almighty goodness rejoices and dove-like love, knowing no envy, applauds itself because through its aid human nature has been made equal to it. It judges worthy of praise that it has so aided the needy nature of humanity from the riches of its own nature that humanity is henceforth fit, equally with God himself, to govern the whole kingdom of the Father, administer the entire commonwealth of heaven and earth, and reign upon his throne. This work he praises so greatly, and in it he is pleased in himself to such an extent, that whoever is not pleased with it, whoever does not look upon him with praise and thanksgiving, he repels from salvation and from the kingdom of Christ his Son as ungrateful, truly proud, and envious.

But now let us examine what follows in the Gospel narrative. “The next day John was again standing [Col. 0261A], and two of his disciples [were with him].” Here it is rightly asked how this Evangelist John does not differ in the present account from the other three Evangelists. For Matthew immediately adds, after the Lord’s fast and the devil’s temptation: “When Jesus heard that John had been handed over, he withdrew into Galilee” (Matt. 4). Mark likewise, immediately after recounting the same temptation: “But after John,” he says, “was handed over, Jesus came into Galilee” (Mark 1).

These two seem jointly to affirm that Jesus did not come into Galilee before John was handed over. Luke, meanwhile, says nothing about John’s imprisonment, beginning thus: “And when every temptation had been completed, the devil departed from him until a time. And Jesus went forth in the power of the Spirit into Galilee” (Luke 4), and so forth [Col. 0261B]. But this Evangelist John reports that, before John had been handed over, Jesus came into Galilee, called Philip and Nathanael (John 1), and, on the third day, having been invited to a wedding in Cana of Galilee, made wine from water, manifested his glory, and his disciples believed in him. Later he says: “John too was baptizing at Aenon near Salim, because there was much water there; and they came and were baptized” (John 3). He immediately adds: “For John had not yet been put into prison.”

The question, then, is how they do not differ—though no one dares call them contradictory except one who is opposed to his own soul. The solution would indeed be excessively difficult if Christ had come to Galilee only once, or if every Evangelist had undertaken to describe separately all his actions, all his departures, and all his returns [Col. 0261C]. But the Gospel narrative establishes that our Lord, the minister of our salvation, went and returned more than once; and none of the Evangelists undertook to comprehend everything he did, which would have been impossible.

Rather, each of the heavenly creatures proceeds before its own face (Ezek. 1): that is, each Evangelist undertook, out of his innumerable deeds and sayings, to describe only as much as would suffice to attest the faith and not weary the reader. Matthew, Mark, and Luke were silent concerning the first year, in which, while John was still preaching, Jesus performed miracles and taught certain persons privately [Col. 0261D], but did not yet wish to become so publicly known to crowds by preaching. Otherwise, how could that report have arisen that, when he became known by public preaching, John was thought to have risen from the dead? Thus it is written in Mark: “King Herod heard—for his name had become known—and said: ‘John the Baptist has risen from the dead, and therefore powers are at work in him’” (Mark 6). Luke likewise says: “Now Herod the tetrarch heard of all that was done by him and was perplexed, because it was said by some that John had risen from the dead” (Luke 9).

They were therefore silent about the first year, and began their narratives from his public preaching, which he began after John had been handed over [Col. 0262A]. This can readily be perceived from what follows in Matthew and Mark. For each, having said, “Jesus came into Galilee,” immediately adds the calling of the apostles. Luke does so a little later; for in his account, before the calling of the apostles, Jesus is frequently in the synagogues and teaches on Sabbaths.

Yet in this Evangelist John, what may perhaps raise a difficulty for accepting the preceding statements is that, before John was handed over, Andrew follows Jesus upon John’s judgment, brings his brother Simon to him, Jesus going out into Galilee calls Philip, and Philip brings Nathanael. But once every difficulty has been removed, reason may stand more firmly: this is certainly not the same calling of the apostles which occurs earlier, as stated, in Matthew and Mark, but later in Luke [Col. 0262B]. For it does not follow that, because they followed him, came, saw where he remained, and remained with him that day, they were already perfected and elevated to the apostolic summit. At that time they began to know him; but they did not then already follow him after leaving all things.

The attentive reader must therefore first remove from his mind an impression which almost immediately and excessively preoccupies the minds of nearly all who begin to hear the Gospel Scripture. Since, after the temptation mentioned above, the other Evangelists immediately join the account of Christ’s preaching—as the text is joined, for example, when Luke says, “And Jesus went forth in the power of the Spirit into Galilee [Col. 0262C], and came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up” (Luke 4)—they carelessly suppose that the succession of time or events was likewise unbroken. That this is not so is evident from a nearby statement in Luke himself. For they say to him when he comes to Nazareth, where he had been brought up: “What great things we have heard done by you in Capernaum, do here also in your own country” (ibid.).

Therefore, before that return of his into Galilee from which the other Evangelists, after relating the temptation, begin the account of his preaching, he had stayed and performed signs in Capernaum. But after the disciples heard John speaking and followed Jesus—indeed, after the miracle at the wedding, in which water was changed into wine—those signs in Capernaum occurred. For this was the beginning of the signs; after performing it Jesus went down to Capernaum. Thus this Evangelist adds: “After this, he went down to Capernaum, he and his mother . . . and his disciples” (John 2) [Col. 0262D].

This, then, is the right understanding: that return of Jesus into Galilee from which the other Evangelists begin is the one which John mentions much later, saying: “When therefore Jesus knew that the Pharisees had heard that Jesus made and baptized more disciples than John—though Jesus himself did not baptize, but his disciples—he left Judaea and went again into Galilee” (John 4).

Although Peter and Andrew could hear—and indeed see—so many of his miracles before, called from their boat, they followed that same Redeemer after leaving all things, the ancient teachers nevertheless said concerning these princes and fathers of our faith: “They had not yet seen him perform any miracles, nor heard anything from him concerning the reward of eternal recompense; yet at one command of the Lord they forgot what they seemed to possess” [Col. 0263A]. This should by no means seem contrary to the preceding statements. For it was said with reference to the narrative whose text in Matthew is such that no mention is made before their calling either of his teaching or of miracles (Matt. 4).

Thus this Evangelist differs in nothing from the others. After the manifestation of Christ which took place in baptism, he begins—or rather continues—his narrative with the testimonies to Christ’s divinity that he had begun. “John was standing, and two of his disciples [were with him]” (John 1). In asserting that John stood, the literal sense indicates the posture of a man standing and earnestly doing or saying something pertaining to his office. But in a higher sense it intimates his great and ever intent attention, by which he not only outwardly served our Lord, whom he had recognized in the manner described above, in the office of his forerunning, but also inwardly stood continually beside him with the raised devotion of his mind [Col. 0263B].

For when he baptized him and saw the Holy Spirit descending upon him in the form of a dove, that same Spirit immediately drove him into the desert; and he was in the desert forty days and forty nights and was tempted by Satan (Luke 4). This Evangelist, as he does many other things, omits this, aiming, as stated at the beginning, to present testimonies concerning the divinity of the Son of God; and thus, as from a great heap of things said and done, he gathers only the more splendid items which he knows to be most suited to his aim or purpose.

There is no doubt, however, that John eagerly looked forward to the return of our Lord, so that he might again see him: to see him was salvation to one who recognized him, glory to one who preached him, and joy to one who pointed him out. Thus the watchman of life and salvation, the messenger of redemption and peace, the discerner of grace and truth, stood in the height of his heart [Col. 0263C]. He stood, certainly, higher than Lucifer, the forerunner of the sun, gazing upon the Sun of righteousness hidden in a cloud—that is, awaiting Christ as he endured the assaults of temptation in the desert or, now that the tempter had been overcome, still kept himself in the shadow of his humility. It is uncertain, however, whether John had seen him on his return from the desert before this.

And two of his disciples stood with him, imitating their teacher in their inward disposition; they were the firstfruits of the people whom this forerunner prepared not for himself but for his Lord. “And, looking upon Jesus as he walked, he says: ‘Behold, the Lamb of God.’” The sequence of the narrative deserves careful notice: outwardly it is brief and clear, but inwardly—something little children are not yet able to grasp—it is pregnant with the weight of mysteries [Col. 0263D].

For what is Jesus walking, except the Son of God made a participant in our mutability? Formerly unknown to human beings, he began to be known and loved from the time he began to walk: coming from heaven into the Virgin’s womb, from the womb into the manger, from the manger to the cross, from the cross into the tomb, and from the tomb again into heaven [Col. 0264A]. From then he began to be known and loved, as it is said to him in the Song of Songs: “Your name is oil poured out; therefore the young maidens loved you” (Cant. 1). For what is “oil poured out” except the Word poured forth from the Father’s heart?

If, therefore, our souls are now “young maidens,” and have now, as it were at John’s mature age, learned always to stand with his disciples with a firm step, they recognize Jesus from the fact that he walks, through the judgment of John speaking in this Gospel; and, following him, they finally arrive where he himself abides through his divinity. This is beautifully intimated to us by the advance in conversion of those same disciples. For he says to those standing with him: “Behold, the Lamb of God.” In accordance with his human nature, as stated above, he calls him the Lamb [Col. 0264B]. For just as Pharaoh was formerly overcome and the servitude of the children released through the immolation of the lamb—something which could not be accomplished by the hand of Moses and Aaron through the infliction of plagues—so through Christ’s passion the devil, prince of darkness, was defeated and the redemption of the human race was accomplished, something which could not be effected through the commandments of the ancient Law and the sacrifices of the old priesthood.

“And the two disciples heard him speaking, and they followed Jesus.” They did not merely hear with their bodily ears, but they alone then obeyed [obedierunt], and received his testimony. For he, as a most faithful witness, always spoke of Him with the purpose that his hearers should follow Him rather than himself; and thus what he himself had said might be fulfilled to the glory of God: [Col. 0264C] “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3). Therefore the two disciples heard this intention of his and, as has already been said, received his testimony when, as he spoke, they followed Jesus.

But whenever anyone is converted and begins, as was said before, to follow in mind and in the movement of devout affection the Lord Jesus as He walks—that is, by meditation and by keeping in memory the footsteps of His humanity—Jesus does not immediately turn and show him His face. That is, He does not at once, at the beginning of conversion, reveal to those who follow Him the divine presence of His majesty, which is understood by the face and according to which He walks nowhere. Rather, that same Jesus and those things which for a time concerned Him, and which are now past and have come to an end—namely, what He did or suffered in the flesh—must be pondered with tenacious memory [Col. 0264D] until His most exalted divinity perceives itself to be sought by those who follow, and, as though looking back over His shoulder toward the place from which He departed, by hidden inspiration shows them in some degree His face. For now, presiding in heaven, He perceives the persevering faith of those who follow Him more than formerly, while walking among men, He perceived the crowd pressing upon Him (Luke 8). It follows, therefore:

“But Jesus, turning and seeing them following Him, said to them: What do you seek? And they said: Rabbi (which is interpreted ‘Teacher’), where do you dwell?” Jesus is rightly said to have turned. For before He walked in the manner described above, having gone forth from highest heaven, He was wholly turned away—that is, angry with the entire human race because of human sin. Hence the prophet cries with groaning: “We have sinned, and You were angry, and You turned away Your face” (Isa. 64). [Col. 0265A] But He turns when He deigns to look upon individuals who seek Him in faith. Of this turning of His it is said in the Psalm: “O God, You will turn and give us life” (Ps. 84). Likewise: “Turn, O Lord, and deliver my soul” (Ps. 6).

Jesus therefore turns and sees those who follow Him when He graciously beholds those who confess faith in His incarnation or passion. Yet among them are many who seem to follow Him and do not know what they seek: that is, they indeed believe in Him, as they suppose, but do not know of what spirit they are or what their intention was. For, as the Apostle says, “They profess that they know God, [Col. 0265B] but deny Him by their deeds” (Titus 1); and though they honour Christ with their lips, their heart is far from Him (Isa. 29). For they may follow Christ by the profession of faith and seek something other than Christ; indeed, they may walk in sheep’s clothing while inwardly being ravening wolves (Matt. 7). Thus Judas could follow Christ with the other apostles (John 6) and seek something else; he could be called an apostle and yet be a devil; he could preach or baptize and yet be a most wicked thief of the Lord’s money-bags (John 12). Thus Simon Magus could be baptized (Acts 8) and yet remain in the gall of bitterness; he could confess faith in Christ and nevertheless have no part or lot in this matter.

So too, almost every day, so many reprobate persons enter the churches with the elect that, because of their multitude, the number of the elect appears very small—just as, in a great heap, unless one comes close, the grains can scarcely be seen because of the abundance of chaff. [Col. 0265C] Since, therefore, all do not follow Christ with one mind, He rightly now says to those who first followed Him: “What do you seek?” Whenever we hear this saying, we ourselves ought to look into our heart and each question his own conscience, so that we may know with what intention we follow Christ. For what He says to those two He says to all.

If we truly seek Christ and desire to be where He is, then our desire and the preparation of our heart speak this in His ears: “Rabbi (which is interpreted ‘Teacher’), where do You dwell?” We rightly call Him Teacher, [Col. 0265D] because we belong to His discipline when we truly seek God. And we say to Him, “Where do You dwell?” when we think upon the heavenly homeland, where He sits at the Father’s right hand, glorified with the glory which He had with the Father before the world existed (John 17); He who, while a resident and pilgrim in this world, “had nowhere to lay His head” (Matt. 8).

“I remembered these things,” says the Psalmist, “and poured out my soul within me, because I shall pass into the place of the wondrous tabernacle, unto the house of God” (Ps. 41). We too must remember this, all of us who follow Christ by confession of faith, lest through a vain intention we remain with those of whom He Himself says: “Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward” (Matt. 6). The Psalmist, likewise refusing [Col. 0266A] to be like them, says: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I shall seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life” (Ps. 26). For those who continually ask this and speak in this manner, “Where do You dwell?”, there will someday come to pass what follows:

“Jesus says to them: Come and see.” And then it is added: “They came and saw where He was staying.” For Jesus says, “Come and see,” when, through assisting grace deserved by good conduct, He raises the mind in contemplation and for a time admits it to heavenly joys, so that it may be able to taste that sweetness “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man” (Isa. 64; 1 Cor. 2). Thus they come and see where Jesus dwells; and to those who see the Creator’s dwelling, every creature is narrow and confined.

[Col. 0266B] One of these, as he himself says, “was caught up as far as the third heaven; he was caught up into paradise and heard secret words which it is not permitted for a human being to utter” (2 Cor. 12). Many saints indeed, tasting beforehand by diverse grace the glory of the kingdom in which Jesus dwells, have seen it. But this man was called by such great grace to see it that he did not know whether he had been wholly taken outside the body, or whether, remaining in the body, only his spirit had been raised in ecstasy; as he himself says, “whether in the body or outside the body, I do not know; God knows” (ibid.).

Certainly, this also ought not to be passed over according to the letter, which follows: “And they remained with Him that day.” He used an apt qualification in saying, “that day.” For they did not then leave everything and follow Him, nor did they from that time remain always with Him; [Col. 0266C] but only on that day did they remain with Him, and begin to hear familiarly the words of grace proceeding from His mouth. For Jesus, since John had not yet been handed over, as was said above, neither preached publicly nor is recorded as having given anyone new commands concerning leaving father or mother, or renouncing other necessities. But let us now continue the spiritual interpretation.

Paul indeed, through the surpassing greatness of the revelation, heard, as has already been said, “secret words which it is not permitted for a human being to utter.” But each of the rest is raised according to his own measure: one receives a word of wisdom or knowledge; another kinds [genera; printed also as *generationis*] of tongues [116]; another the grace of healings; and similar gifts (1 Cor. 12). When anyone has attained this, he has become fit [Col. 0266D] both to invite others and, through preaching, to make them followers of Christ. This too is beautifully prefigured in those of whom the present Gospel speaks. For it continues:

“Now it was about the tenth hour. Andrew, the brother of Simon Peter, was one of the two who had heard from John and had followed Him. He first found his brother Simon and said to him: We have found the Messiah, which is interpreted Christ. And he brought him to Jesus.” He who had first heard and followed Jesus afterwards found and brought his brother, already then fulfilling the Scripture which this same John was to declare: “Let him who hears say, ‘Come’” (Rev. 22).

But why is it inserted, “It was about the tenth hour,” at the point where Jesus gathered the firstfruits [Col. 0267A] of our calling? Clearly, because no preceding merit of those called, but the grace of the One calling alone, brings about their salvation, and because in all things age neither distinguishes nor prejudges, it was fittingly signified by saying, “about the tenth hour.” For He is that householder who went out early in the morning to hire labourers for His vineyard, and went out about the third, sixth, ninth, and tenth hour and did likewise; and at last said: “The last shall be first, and the first last” (Matt. 20).

The tenth or eleventh hour is undoubtedly already near evening, which signifies the setting of human life. It is evident, moreover, that great Andrew, who came to Jesus at the tenth hour, and still greater Simon his brother, greatest in the order of the apostles, who was brought later, at an evening still closer at hand [Col. 0267B]. For on the same day Andrew came to Jesus first with the other disciple, then his brother Simon; on the following day Philip and Nathanael came; and, without any mystical marking of hours, on the third day the wedding took place at Cana of Galilee. Therefore what He would later signify in words while speaking in parables, He already signifies in His own disciples, when, drawing by hidden inspiration those whom He wished to make great apostles, He begins to call them in the final part of the day—that is, at the tenth hour.

There is also another reason why it is especially pleasing that this Lamb of God was indicated or recognized at the tenth hour. The lamb by whose immolation the firstborn of Egypt were slain (Exod. 12) and the captivity of the children of Israel was released, and which foreshadowed this Lamb, was commanded to be taken into the houses of the children of Israel on the tenth day of the moon, to be slain after the fourteenth day, on the following evening, when the moon is at its fullest. As I have said, the lamb was commanded to be taken on the tenth day of the moon [Col. 0267C]; Egypt was likewise crushed by the tenth plague; and, moreover, ten commandments of the law were afterwards given for striking the spiritual Pharaoh (Exod. 20).

When, therefore, we hear that this Lamb of God was indicated by John’s finger at the tenth hour, all these things usefully return to our memory: namely, that the tenth hour suggests to those able to understand a mystical harmony of the Scriptures. For now the true Lamb is indeed taken into the houses of the children of Israel, when, at John’s words, “Behold the Lamb of God,” true Israelites begin to follow Him, whose life was like the tenth day of the moon: not yet full and round, because the law [Col. 0267D] under whose ten commandments they had served had brought nothing to perfection (Heb. 7).

And John, like another Moses, having disciples and observing the ten commandments of the law most diligently, was as though resisting Pharaoh—that is, the devil—with ten plagues. But since Pharaoh had not yet been overcome, John pointed with his finger and said: “Behold the Lamb of God”—understand, the Lamb by whose blood, when the doorposts of our foreheads have been marked, we are to be delivered by a mighty hand, and the prince of darkness is to be drowned in the waters of baptism, in which He will baptize us with His blood mingled with the water. It therefore belonged to the evangelist, in recounting the designation of this Lamb, not to pass over in silence the tenth hour at which it occurred.

But let us now consider what follows. [Col. 0268A] “Andrew, who, as was said before, was one of the two who had heard from John and followed Jesus, found Simon his brother.” Behold, as we look from afar, from this word, “found,” we recognize as though from a flying spark that in them there was a great flame of holy longing. And truly, in those whom prevenient grace had predestined to such great glory, there was a great desire, impatient of every delay, to see the Saviour, when they heard from their teacher John’s testimony that He had come: for John had seen the Spirit descending like a dove and remaining upon Him.

When, therefore, John again pointed Him out as He walked, as said above, and Andrew, having followed, saw where He stayed, he doubtless hastened, ran, and sought [Col. 0268B] his brother, so that he who was a companion in longing might become a participant in joy. Seeking, then, “he found his brother Simon, and said to him: We have found the Messiah, which is interpreted Christ.” “We have found,” he says, not one crying aloud or disputing, for His voice was not heard outside in the streets; but, with the lamp—namely, the testimony of John, who is “a burning and shining lamp” (John 5)—we have found the Messiah, concealed in the hiding-place of humility and silence.

For that spotless Lamb, wholly white, lay hidden among black goats in this night in which the eyes of sinners are darkened. But John, the lamp, dispelled our darkness and, showing Him to us, said: “Behold the Lamb of God.” “Which is interpreted Christ” was not said by Andrew, but was added by the evangelist on his own account, wishing to explain the Hebrew word to Greeks and Latins. [Col. 0268C] For *Messias* is Hebrew; in Greek it is *Christus*; in Latin it is called *Unctus*, “the Anointed One.”

“Jesus looked at him and said: You are Simon, son of John; you shall be called Cephas, which is interpreted Peter.” By this first declaration of the Lord, who looked upon and addressed him, great and ineffable joy is foreshadowed for blessed Peter. For if all the apostles and all the saints ought to rejoice in this world because their names are written in heaven (Luke 10), how much more ought this most blessed man to rejoice, who, so to speak, found his own name written at the beginning of the book? For the Lord had not yet called anyone by his own name, nor afterwards did he describe anyone with so intimate a gaze, nor express such friendly [Col. 0268D] attention toward anyone.

We learn the reason for this name from another passage of the Gospel according to Matthew. For when Peter had said, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God,” Jesus answered and said: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven. And I say to you that you are Peter, and upon this rock I shall build my Church” (Matt. 16). As though you were asking why he called him Peter, he added the reason, then hidden for a time in his humility: “And upon this rock I shall build my Church.” It is therefore clear that Christ was going to build his Church upon himself, namely the firm rock; and when he saw—or rather, as the Evangelist says, looked intently upon—him whom he wished to be, after himself, the first foundation of that Church, he named him Peter from himself, the first Rock. For upon him, after Christ himself, the entire structure of the spiritual building was established.

This may also especially be understood from the conclusion of the present chapter. For it ends thus: “Amen, I say to you, you shall see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending 117 upon the Son of Man.” In saying this, he undoubtedly sends us to the history in which “Jacob, having placed a stone beneath his head, saw in a dream a ladder touching heaven, and angels of God ascending and descending by it. Rising in the morning, he took the stone which he had put beneath his head and set it up as a pillar, pouring oil upon it” (Gen. 28). That [Col. 0269B] stone, drenched with oil, signifies him who was anointed with the Holy Spirit. Hence he is uniquely called Christ, because he “was anointed above his companions” (Ps. 44 [45]). But more must be said of this shortly.

Therefore Simon, which is interpreted “obedient,” because he was to be placed first upon that Rock on which the Church is built, is fittingly given a changed name and called Peter from the Rock itself. By this it was signified that all who are built upon that foundation which is Christ should, according to the prophet, “be called by a new name, which the mouth of the Lord has named” (Isa. 62). Nor is it without significance that at such a place and time he is called the son of John. For, just as his name is changed, so he is transferred from a carnal father or lineage to a spiritual one, so that henceforth [Col. 0269C] his father may be that Bridegroom who was to build for himself a bride from his own side (Eph. 5), in whom Peter deserved to be the first son, just as he was the first stone.

“On the next day he wished to go out into Galilee, and found Philip.” Lest you suppose that it happened by chance that “he found Philip,” the Evangelist first stated his will. For nothing comes about in divine providence by chance, nothing rashly, nothing fortuitously: all things present themselves to his seeing eyes. Appropriately, then, before saying, “he found Philip,” he said, “he wished to go out”; which is as though he had said: Wishing to find Philip—indeed, wishing to make water into wine and there make the beginning of signs, where afterwards, according to Matthew, he would first preach and say, “The kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. 4)—wishing in every respect to fulfil the prophecy which says: “At the first time the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali was made light [or: relieved], the way of the sea beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles” (Isa. 9)—“he went out into Galilee and found Philip.”

He found him, as one whom he sought; for he foreknew and predestined him, together with all the saints. And for this reason he went out: that he might then call him whom he had foreknown and predestined before the ages. Yet “he found” him not in the way in which we are said to have found something when we see what we had earlier sought without seeing it; but in the way in which the good shepherd says, “I have found my sheep which was lost” (Luke 15), or the woman says, “Rejoice with me, because I have found my drachma which I had lost” (ibid.); and as he likewise finds each one of us when he gathers us to his faith, though we had been lost. In the same manner and with the same force it is now said: “He found Philip. He said to him: Follow me; and rising, he followed him” [Col. 0270A]. He had foreknown this also: that as soon as he said, “Follow me,” Philip would rise and obey by following. For his grace had already gone before one who did not know him; before directing his voice to Philip’s ears, he had put his hand into his heart to draw him.

“Now Philip was from Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter.” This fact especially commends divine grace: from a sinful city these three were called, great fathers of the righteous and believers. For Bethsaida was a sinful city, so much so that the Lord reproaches it, as Matthew relates, saying: “Woe to you, Chorazin; woe to you, Bethsaida; for if the mighty works done among you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would surely have done penance in sackcloth and ashes” (Matt. 11). Therefore, when from that city, against which the judgment of truth pronounces woe because of unbelief and impenitence, such great fathers deserved to be called and chosen for the joy and peace to be preached to the whole world, whose work and whose gift is this, if not that of the grace of God, which goes before and follows its elect, granting them an undeserved benefit?

It follows: “Philip found Nathanael.” Philip, seeking Nathanael, found him in order to make him a sharer in this present joy; and, in accordance with his name—for Philip is interpreted “mouth of a lamp”—he hastens with the light of good news to illuminate his neighbour [Col. 0270C].

“And he says to him: We have found Jesus, son of Joseph, from Nazareth of Galilee, whom Moses wrote of in the Law and the prophets.” The order of the words is: We have found that Jesus, son of Joseph, from Nazareth of Galilee, is the one whom Moses wrote of in the Law and the prophets [the prophet]. This we have found: we have learned that it is so; by the lamp of trustworthy testimony we have recognized that such and so great a man has arisen from so humble a place, namely Nazareth of Galilee. He used a suitable description, because many were called by the name Jesus; and so, along with his proper name, he gave the name of the city and of his father, Joseph, as he was supposed to be. In this he also maintained the true law of history, which does not omit the opinion of the common people appropriate to time and place. Nor does he incur the charge of lying by calling that man father who was not his carnal father. For if those who adopt other people’s children are not improperly called fathers of those whom they have adopted with fatherly affection, how much more fittingly is this man—the unique and singular foster-father of the Lord—called his father? For the Lord, born an orphan in this world, that is, without a carnal father, used that blessed man as a father in all things; and in the genealogy set forth through Matthew (ch. 1), his human nature, needing every human aid, rested upon that holy Joseph as upon the highest step [Col. 0270D].

When Nathanael heard this, “he answered and said: Can anything good come from Nazareth?” Nathanael was learned in the Law. Hence Philip, announcing the news to him, had said beforehand: “We have found Jesus, whom Moses wrote of in the Law and the prophets.” Knowing from the Scriptures that Christ was to be born from Bethlehem, the city of David, and from the seed of David, he either doubts or asks whether anything of this kind can come from Nazareth. For he did not know, or had not been told—or, if he had known it at some time, it could have been erased from his memory—that in the days of the enrolment “Joseph went up from Galilee to the city of David, which is called Bethlehem, because he was of the house and family of David, to be enrolled with Mary, his betrothed wife, who was pregnant” (Luke 2). Perhaps he knew that Joseph, or Mary herself, who lived in Nazareth, was of Bethlehemite stock and of David’s seed. Thus, however one construes his words, “Can anything good come from Nazareth?” whether as a question or as an assertion, he does not depart from the true meaning.

“Jesus saw Nathanael coming to him, and said of him: Behold, truly an Israelite in whom there is no guile.” Here plainly the Saviour saw with the open eyes of his grace—those very eyes with which he saw and predestined us all before we existed. Nor could he fail to know with what mind Nathanael was coming to him: namely, that he sought God in simplicity of heart, according to what is written: “Your eyes see the things that are in the hearts of men, and all shall be written in your book; man sees the face, but God sees the heart” (Ps. 138 [139]; 1 Sam. 16). Therefore the judgment which he had without error written concerning him in his book, he immediately uttered, saying: “Behold, truly an Israelite in whom there is no guile” [Col. 0271C].

By saying “behold,” he signifies that Nathanael is worthy to be looked upon; and by adding “truly,” and “in whom there is no guile,” he makes the proper distinction among Israelites. For not all who are of Israel according to the flesh are Israelites; rather, only those in whom there is no guile, who are upright in heart and thirst to see God, are reckoned Israelites (Rom. 9). But Nathanael, cheerful in countenance and still more cheerful in mind, was a true Israelite, a son of him who wrestled with God (Gen. 32).

“Nathanael says to him: How do you know me?” By this inquiry he indicates the very point which proves, by the testimony of truth, that he is a true Israelite. For false Israelites take excessive delight in their own praises, not considering whether their praise comes from men or from God. But when this man heard himself called a true Israelite—a title of great praise and great worth—he said, “How do you know me?” That is, as you must understand: How do you know one whom you have not until now seen according to the flesh?

“Jesus answered and said to him: Before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you.” This was what Nathanael sought: God and the Son of God, who according to his divinity is present everywhere and sees even those to whom he is not bodily present. Yet, compared with greater things, it is a small matter that he testified that he had seen Nathanael beneath the fig tree. For he saw not only Nathanael, but all his elect, when they were beneath the fig tree. He saw them with the eyes of his mercy: that is, when their first parent, having become a transgressor of the commandment, covered his shame with sewn fig leaves (Gen. 3) [Col. 0272A]. Already then he saw them and had compassion; already he was mercifully arranging the order by which he would free them from the guilt of transgression.

Therefore Nathanael, a true Israelite in whom there was no guile, because he did not, in the manner of the Pharisees, oppose the truth which he knew, but loved it when known with a simple heart, quickly and briefly receives satisfaction from the Christ whom he sought. For it follows: “Nathanael answered and said: Rabbi, you are the Son of God; you are the King of Israel.”

At this point the mind of one who loves faith pauses and is held fast, looking about and eagerly desiring to know what became of this beloved Nathanael after so resounding a confession of the Son of God. For he appears nowhere, neither in this Evangelist nor in any of the others, except that after the Lord’s resurrection this same Evangelist John mentions him in this manner: “Simon Peter and Thomas, who is called Didymus, and Nathanael, who was from Cana of Galilee, and the two sons of Zebedee, and two others of his disciples, were together” (John 21). Who would not wish that a lamp of so great brightness should by no means be hidden beneath a bushel, but set upon a lampstand (Matt. 5) and shine upon all who are in the household of the Church? Who, I ask, would not desire that so great a confessor of the Son of God should be counted among Christ’s great apostles? For what more did Peter confess, he who deserved not only the apostolate but, above the rest, the keys of the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 16)?

Perhaps someone answering this question will say: Peter was a fisherman, but Nathanael was learned in the Law. Now God’s purpose was to break the strong through the weak and contemptible things of the world, and through things that were foolish to confound the wise (1 Cor. 1). Therefore, remaining faithful to that purpose, he rewarded the faith and confession of the fisherman Peter not only with the apostolate but with the keys of heaven. But he left Nathanael’s confession without the reward of apostolic rank because he was learned in the Law. Yet would one who said this truly satisfy the diligent reader? Certainly not. For “the spirit of knowledge” (Isa. 11), one of the seven spirits of God, while it is an honourable gift of God, in no way diminishes the truth or merit of faith. Indeed, holy simplicity joined to learning excels, as the angel testifies when he says to Daniel: “Those who are learned shall shine as the brightness of the firmament, and those who instruct many unto righteousness, as stars for everlasting ages” (Dan. 12) [Col. 0272D]. Moreover, it is especially contrary to this explanation that the Lord did not reject from apostolic grace Saul, a treasury of great learning and, as he himself confesses, instructed at the feet of Gamaliel (Acts 22): “He who worked in Peter for the apostleship of the circumcision also worked in me among the Gentiles. And, he says, the Gospel of the uncircumcision was entrusted to me, as that of the circumcision was to Peter” (Gal. 2).

We ask, then, where this Nathanael, beloved of God, remained hidden; for, as has already been said, apart from this place and the other mentioned above, no traces whatever of this name appear anywhere in all the Evangelists’ lodgings. But looking again to the twelve seats and those sitting in them, we see Bartholomew everywhere attached to Philip, by whom this Nathanael was called. Yet we do not know when Bartholomew was called, just as we do not know where Nathanael went after he was called. And just as this Evangelist John, who wrote of Nathanael, names all the apostles here and there but is altogether silent about the name of Bartholomew, so conversely the other Evangelists, who everywhere join Bartholomew to Philip, are altogether silent about the name Nathanael.

It is certain that Bartholomew is not a Hebrew but a Syriac name, which in Latin means “son of one who suspends the waters.” Nathanael, however, is Hebrew and means “gift of God.” Perhaps, therefore, this very Nathanael, who was from Cana of Galilee, is Bartholomew, which means “son of one who suspends the waters”: because on the third day, when a wedding took place in his village of Cana in Galilee, the Lord was perhaps invited to the wedding on his account, and, turning water into wine, suspended it, to the amazement of all [Col. 0273B].

But let us hear what the Son of God and King of Israel, one and the same man, answered this confessor of his. “Because I said to you, I saw you under the fig tree, you believe; you shall see greater things than these.” Every believer may plainly hope this concerning himself. For when he faithfully and with good intent expresses the small things which he perceives concerning the Word of God, he shows himself worthy for the Father in heaven to reveal to him greater things, which flesh and blood cannot reveal (Matt. 16). Hence it is written in the Psalm: “I opened my mouth and drew in the spirit” (Ps. 118 [119]). For by opening his mouth, namely by confessing unto salvation that which he believes in his heart unto righteousness, he draws in the Holy Spirit, who may fulfil his good desire through a fuller knowledge of the truth.

“And he said to them: Amen, I say to you, you shall see heaven opened and the angels of God descending and ascending upon the Son of Man.” By these words he promises them that they shall see what they did not know: namely, that by his passion heaven would be opened, and that there would be harmony between angels and human beings, who had formerly been at variance, heaven being closed to humankind and a partition-wall of enmity standing between them because of original sin. For until then there had not been such agreement of angels and human beings that holy angels, coming to the souls of blessed people as they departed from their bodies, carried them through the open gates of heaven, as they do now, reverencing and worshipping in their King and God the human nature that ascended powerfully into heaven without the conveyance of angels, “making the cloud his ascent and walking upon the wings of the winds” (Ps. 103 [104]) [Col. 0273D].

He promises this sight plainly to true Israelites, declaring that what their carnal father Israel foresaw in a figure (Gen. 28) would truly be fulfilled in himself. For “Jacob, going out from Beersheba and travelling to Haran, when he came to a certain place and wished to rest there after sunset, took some of the stones lying there and put one beneath his head; and he slept in that place. And he saw a ladder standing upon the earth, its summit touching heaven, and angels of God ascending by it” (Gen. 28).

That Jacob, who was later called Israel, signifies the true Israelites, such as Nathanael was, concerning whom the Lord had shortly before said: “Behold, a true Israelite in whom there is no guile.” The stone which Jacob put beneath his head in order to sleep signifies this same Christ, the cornerstone, “which the builders,” the false Israelites, “rejected” (Ps. 117 [118]; Acts 4). Whoever puts this beneath his head—that is, beneath his heart—sleeps securely, because he has despised the riches of the world and therefore is not troubled by the world’s sufferings, having in this world nothing for which he may rejoice, fear, hope, or grieve. For the mind is secure when these things are absent for Christ’s sake. And the man who placed his head, that is, his heart, upon Christ the Rock so as to be free from such passions says: “I sleep, but my heart watches” (Song 5) [Col. 0274B].

This especially did those who, hearing his voice then saying, “Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I shall refresh you” (Matt. 11), left all things and came to him, in order to learn from him because he is altogether “meek and humble of heart.” Sleeping in the humility of his heart as upon a solid rock, and finding rest for their souls, they knew the mysteries of the kingdom of God—mysteries which the proud cannot know, among whom there are always quarrels, since they are awake for disputes and contentions. These saw heaven opened by those keys which the Lord gave to Peter, his chief vicar (Matt. 16); they saw the flaming sword extinguished which had been placed at the entrance of Paradise (Gen. 3); and, awakened by the sudden sound of the Holy Spirit coming upon them, they proclaimed it to us in fear and with cries (Acts 2).

They also took up that stone upon which they had rested and set it up as a pillar, so that we might all see it and believe in him, and, built upon the same stone as a spiritual building, as walls of the holy Church (1 Pet. 2), might say: “How terrible is this place” (Gen. 28), namely, to the gates of hell, which “shall not prevail against it” (Matt. 16). “This is none other than the house of God and the gate of heaven”: namely, the gate through which angels ascend and descend upon the Son of Man—ascending to contemplation of his divinity, descending to veneration of his humanity or passion [Col. 0274D].

For through this one and only gate angels descend to the Son of Man himself, their God and King, dwelling through faith in our hearts; and they ascend by those steps of the ladder which we understand morally as the different advances in virtues. By these our two sides, namely our body and soul, are marked, and they reach heaven by the straight way, whither we may be borne by the aid of the holy angels, who have become our friends through Christ’s death.

It follows: “And on the third day a wedding took place in Cana of Galilee, and the mother of Jesus was there. And Jesus and his disciples were invited to the wedding.” The humility of the one same Son of Man always precedes the glory of the Son of God. This is readily recognized in almost everything that he did or endured on earth, as he freely undertook the work of our salvation. Born of a woman, he is nourished at virginal breasts; wrapped in swaddling clothes, he is praised by angels singing, “Glory to God in the highest” (Luke 2); placed in the narrowness of a manger, he is shown by a shining star in the breadth of heaven (Matt. 2); carried to the temple as though a sinner, he is proclaimed by Simeon as the true light (Luke 2); coming among sinners to the baptism of his servant, he is manifested as the Holy of Holies by the voice of the Father and the visible appearance of the Holy Spirit over him (Matt. 3; Luke 3); he endures the deceiver’s frauds, and immediately angels come and minister to him (Matt. 4; Luke 4).

So now also, invited to a wedding with carnal people, he does not disdain to come; and immediately, by turning water into wine, he is proved to be the true God, Lord of the elements and ruler of nature [Col. 0275B]. For as it is glorious to have performed this miracle and by his will alone to have raised an element above the laws of its own nature—a fact which by itself could suffice to establish belief in his divine majesty—so it is a mark of great humility, worthy of proclamation, that he who was conceived without a man and born without violation of his mother’s integrity came to weddings in which virginity is lost and the lower condition of married persons acquires the tribulation of the flesh (1 Cor. 7).

For marriage, however honourable, and the marriage-bed, however undefiled (Heb. 13), belong to a lower rank; but sacred virginity belongs to a higher honour and grace, commended by the lovely beauty of devout humility. We do not defend marriage against certain heretics who disparaged weddings in such a way that, agreeing with others, we make marriage equal to virginity or, with shameless rashness, even prefer it. For who does not know that marriage is good and instituted by God, yet that the nature of married persons itself has been corrupted? For when God made a wife for the first man, as an aid in the propagation of offspring, he blessed them, saying: “Increase and multiply, fill the earth and subdue it” (Gen. 1). And in that blessing thus given was the power of generation, so that the elect alone might be born without any injury from flesh puffed up and resisting the spirit, without any itch of lust, and might be predestined for restoration to the tenth order.

But when man swelled with the poison of the ancient serpent, he was cast down from that dominion over his own flesh (Gen. 3); and he who had been placed in honour “was compared to senseless beasts and made like them” (Ps. 48 [49]) [Col. 0275D]. At once married persons, who had been created rational, began to be moved irrationally; and the flesh began to move the spirit, so that the spirit might serve its impulses, although the flesh’s condition had been such that it itself ought fittingly to obey the rule of the spirit (Rom. 7). Hence, ashamed of themselves, they covered their shame with sewn fig leaves (Gen. 3).

From that time the flesh fights against the spirit even in married persons, however holy or righteous they may be (Gal. 5). However holily they may live at other times and subject the flesh to the spirit, when they come together, the flesh is superior and the spirit inferior; and the whole keenness of the mind is so overwhelmed that it cannot meditate upon God or give itself to prayer. Thus Paul, having said by concession rather than by command, “Do not defraud one another” (1 Cor. 7), immediately added: “except perhaps by agreement for a time, that you may give yourselves to prayer.”

Therefore, although the blessing given before sin remains—as God said, “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” (Gen. 1)—the corruption introduced through sin diminishes this good. And, most grievous to say, in the embraces of marriage that tribulation of the flesh does not cease which God justly imposed upon the woman when he said to her: “I shall multiply your sorrows and your conceptions” (Gen. 3). For multiple conceptions from the earth of the flesh grow beyond number like dense thickets of thorns and briars [Col. 0276B]. So many reprobate persons are born that the elect are few in comparison with them.

Virginity, on the other hand, is concerned with how it may please God, and “thinks of the things of the Lord, that it may be holy both in body and in spirit” (1 Cor. 7), because flesh does not intervene between God and its spirit. Rather, the spirit, superior to the flesh, rules the inferior flesh and is ruled by the God who is above it. The Apostle does not indeed condemn the use of liberty in married persons; but he confidently prefers to that liberty what he judges more useful: his counsel concerning virgins.

Therefore it is a condescension of humility that the heavenly man, born of a Virgin, did not refuse, when invited, to attend earthly and carnal weddings. And his making wine from water is consequent upon this: after humility comes glory, ever new and ever to be proclaimed with the same admiration. For although each year God, by the same power, causes water received into the bosom of the earth to pass into wine in vines, and although our understanding cannot comprehend this efficacy of his, still in this miracle above all we, who praise him, direct our minds in eager desire for divine praise.

For by that natural process it is shown, as all know, that God is almighty; but by this new miracle it is proved, as only believers receive it, that almighty God became man. Moreover, all the other elements cooperate in producing wine from water in vines. First, water is received in the bosom of the earth, without whose aid it could provide no richness to the roots of vines, herbs, or trees. Then, by the mild tempering of the air, it is drawn forth into the shoots; and, with the aid of heat, the shoot puts forth leaves, the cluster flowers, and the grape gradually ripens [Col. 0276D].

But here, where the entire order of nature is absent, the fact that wine was made from water testifies that this man is greater than nature itself: he is Lord of nature. Thus we admire far more the remarkable rod of Aaron, which put forth leaves and flowers that were transformed into almonds; indeed, we admire and venerate it more than all the cedars of Lebanon and every other tree that becomes green again and produces fruit or seed, each according to its kind, by the customary yearly course of nature. Not because these things are greater, but because, together with the miracle itself, they provide evident proof of the divine presence and of his will and watchful care over us.

For we do not so much marvel that God could make wine from water as rejoice that he alone who could do this became man and walked among human beings for thirty years, dwelling within the hidden enclosure of flesh. Therefore, as has been said above, in this deed also the humility of the same Son of Man precedes the glory of the Son of God, so that he may show every rank in his deeds what he taught in words, saying: “Just as everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, so conversely everyone who humbles himself shall be exalted” (Matt. 23; Luke 14, 18). The merit of preceding humility is the gateway to following glory [Col. 0277B].

But now let us come to the very words of the Gospel reading. First, having considered the letter in sequence, let us then seek out the mysteries.

“And on the third day a wedding took place in Cana of Galilee.” The conjunction placed at the beginning refers the attentive reader back to what precedes, in this way: “On the next day John was standing,” and so forth; “On the next day he wished to go out into Galilee and found Philip”; “and on the third day a wedding took place in Cana of Galilee.” The Evangelist wished us carefully to observe that not without reason, but by grace of a definite mystery, our Lord performed the miracle by which he manifested his glory, so that his disciples might believe in him, on the third day after gathering disciples.

For he is the one who, in two ages of the world—before the Law and under the Law—chose a few holy people from the mass of the lost; and in the third age, namely under grace, amid the weddings of people marrying and giving in marriage and wholly occupied with their pleasures, brought in the heavenly wedding of the holy Church. He himself went forth “as a bridegroom from his chamber” (Ps. 18 [19]), so that spiritual children might be born of that virginal marriage. But this must be discussed later. Now, as was said, the foundations of the history must first be laid.

“And the mother of Jesus was there.” This is a great example of humility for all ranks of the holy Church to behold; nevertheless, sacred virgins should not imitate the fact that the mother of Jesus—the virginal temple of the Lord, the inviolate sanctuary of the Holy Spirit—did not disdain to be present at the celebration of carnal weddings [Col. 0277D]. Sacred virgins should not imitate this because the time, the person, and the place are different. “All things have their time,” says Ecclesiastes (Eccl. 3).

For virgins dedicated to God, their vocation ought to burn in the mind, shine in their clothing, and radiate in their speech or public profession. The virginity of the Lord’s mother was hidden from all people, because the circumstances of that time did not permit it to be made public. For free profession of virginity, or proclamation of such an example, could not then exist, while Moses still declared under his veil (2 Cor. 3): “Cursed is everyone who does not produce seed in Israel” (Gen. 38). She therefore chose humbly, while present, to avoid scandal rather than offer to future virgins an untimely example of rigorous purpose—an example that would raise the pride of foolish virgins more than it would instruct the restraint of prudent ones. Among mothers and all other women who had known men, the virgin mother preferred herself to none; everywhere she presented herself as a mother because she had a son, while keeping in her heart the unspoken mystery of her virginity.

For just as it is unfitting—indeed impossible—to secure the roof of a house before its foundation, so before faith in Christ’s incarnation had been received it was impossible to prescribe the rule by which sacred virgins ought to distinguish themselves from secular women. But now the vocation is public, and counsel concerning virgins has been publicly given and received (1 Cor. 7). Therefore sacred virgins would cause a greater scandal to the Church of Christ by attending weddings than by avoiding such a gathering [Col. 0278B].

Accordingly, prudent virgins have inwardly the oil of humility or charity: that is, they do not despise the lawful liberty of those marrying, even though it occupies a lower rank. But outwardly, and especially in that very assembly of a wedding, they do not display their shining lamps. For where can those lamps more quickly be extinguished by the wind of wretched vanity? Or where can they more readily imperil themselves through their eyes or ears, following the example of Dinah, Jacob’s daughter, who was found and violated by the corrupter precisely because in girlish frivolity she went out to see the daughters of an unknown land? (Gen. 34.) They cannot be as secure as that blessed queen of heaven, whose treasure of virginity was hidden from people and fortified by the strong protection of her Son and the faithful guardianship of holy angels.

“Now Jesus and his disciples were invited to the wedding.” This also, undoubtedly, is not rashly to be imitated by men of spiritual vocation. For where reason requires it, it is beyond reproach not only to go to weddings but even to frequent an idol-temple. But where there is a sufficient cause for prohibition, it is unworthy not only to eat with tax-collectors and sinners, but even to say “Greetings” to a brother (2 John 1). This distinction may readily be discerned by a familiar comparison.

As long as a sick person is incapable of acting for himself—suffering from frenzy or lethargy, or disabled by paralysis—so long it is praiseworthy for a prudent and noble physician not to avoid going to a place unworthy of himself to visit the sick person and sitting beside a poor bed; and, though asked—or even struck—by the sick person, to provide help freely. But when sound judgment has returned to the mind or health to the body, if some new ailment occurs, whether phlegm or a troublesome heavier cough, then at last the physician, recognizing his own dignity, does not go down to the filthy huts of the poor sick person. For his own house is known, where he can be sought or found; and the patient can now walk and knows how to speak for himself [Col. 0278D].

So, indeed, when God incarnate came into this world, the great and true 121 physician came down to a patient already beyond hope, who could not come to the physician, did not know how to seek his aid—indeed, who, lying half-dead, thought himself healthy. Just as he did not wait for such a man to ascend to heaven in order to bring himself down, so, after descending, he did not wait for sinners to come and hear him reading in the synagogue or teaching in the temple. Rather, he himself first went down to them, eating and drinking with tax-collectors and sinners, so that the Pharisees said: “Behold, a gluttonous man and a drinker of wine, a friend of tax-collectors and sinners” (Matt. 11).

His apostles likewise acted thus wherever, sent as teachers of the Gentiles, they came as physicians to unknown sick people. But when they had cured the sickness and given precepts for living, they withdrew farther from those whose vices of character were renewed after they had been cured through faith. For Paul says: “I wrote in the Epistle that you should not associate with fornicators—not, of course, with the fornicators of this world, or with the greedy,” and—
And the rest. And a little later: “If [Col. 0279B] anyone called a brother is a fornicator, or greedy, or an idolater, or abusive, or a drunkard, or a robber, do not even eat with such a person” (1 Cor. 5).

Therefore, after the physician has approached those who were ill and, by calling sinners to repentance, has so healed them through faith that they themselves know, or are able, to come to the Church, it is no longer for men of spiritual purpose, following the Lord’s example, to go to the weddings of secular persons. Likewise, following that same example, sinners and tax collectors are not to associate with his apostles, since Christ himself, speaking in them, commanded that with such persons they should neither eat nor say “hail” to them (2 John 1).

This is not because, after the manner of Tatian, Marcion, and certain other heretics, they disparage marriage or equate it with fornication; [Col. 0279C] rather, because, having a vow and a purpose directed toward something better, they have left this good behind them. It is such a good that looking back toward it is not without danger, because leaving it behind is not without labor.

It follows:

“And when the wine failed, the mother of Jesus said to him: ‘They have no wine.’” The blessed Mother of God desires that a gateway of heavenly beneficence be opened for the guests, lest the devotion of those who had invited her should lack its reward, and lest an untimely want bring sadness to the cheerfulness suited to the occasion. For it must be believed that they invited the Lord Jesus, his mother, and the disciples with devout affection—especially since they could not have been unaware of the reports about him which had already begun to circulate [Col. 0279D]. For Nathanael too was from the same village; recognizing him the day before, he had said: “Rabbi, you are the Son of God; you are the King of Israel.”

Therefore, when the Evangelist had said pointedly, “A wedding took place at Cana of Galilee, and the mother of Jesus was there,” he added distinctly: “Jesus and his disciples were also invited to the wedding.” You should understand that, once the wedding had been celebrated and the diners had reclined, once the guests were at ease, Jesus was deliberately invited as a holy man, as a great prophet, whose blessing, it was not vainly hoped, would benefit the descendants of the married pair or the whole company of guests. Thus the blessed Virgin, in order to reward the devotion of those who had invited her, knowing that in the flesh which she had borne there dwelt the creative power of all things [Col. 0280A], says to her Son, her God: “They have no wine.”

“Jesus said to her: ‘What is there between me and you, woman? My hour has not yet come.’” This may be understood in two ways, and either way can build up the mind of the true believer.

The first is that we should judge that, by this saying also, those heretics—who, as has often been said, deny that Christ existed before Mary—are struck down. Against them, above all, all the testimonies of the present Gospel are composed. For the divinity which lay hidden in the temple of his humanity and was now beginning, a little, to display itself in the working of miracles, could truly say: “What is there between me and you, woman?” Since [Col. 0280B] already then the blasphemies of heretics sounded in his ears, who would say: “Christ’s whole beginning is from Mary.”

Thus, in these two brief sayings, he expresses the two natures of one and the same person: the divine, namely, in “What is there between me and you, woman?”; the human, when he immediately adds, “My hour has not yet come.” For he who according to his divinity is without time and without mother, according to his humanity deigned, in being born and in dying, to have times and hours—not fated hours, as the astrologers suppose, but those which he himself appointed.

Yet here one must beware the error of Nestorius, who, thinking that two persons must be confessed in Christ, forbade the blessed Mary to be called *Theotokos*, that is, Mother of God. He said that she was not the mother of God but of a man, because only the human, and not also the divine, nature of Christ was taken from her. [Col. 0280C] But beyond doubt, as the catholic faith maintains, she must be believed and confessed to be the mother of God and of the man. For she truly conceived the incorporeal Word of the Father through believing with the ear of her heart, and bore from her virgin womb the Word made bodily from her flesh.

Alternatively: “What is there between me and you, woman? My hour has not yet come.” The Lord Jesus is not found earlier to have disregarded his mother; rather, he was subject to her, as Luke the Evangelist testifies in a certain passage, speaking of his parents: “He went down with them and came to Nazareth, and was subject to them” (Luke 2). But now, as he begins to work miracles and prepares himself shortly to go through cities and villages and proclaim the kingdom of God, he says to his mother: [Col. 0280D] “What is there between me and you, woman?”

This resembles what, according to another Evangelist, occurred when he was speaking to the crowds. Someone said to him: “Behold, your mother and your brothers are standing outside, seeking to speak with you.” But he answered them: “Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?” And stretching out his hand toward his disciples, he said: “Behold my mother and my brothers. For whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, that one is my brother and sister and mother” (Matt. 12).

Thus he himself did first what he commands us to do. For he commands no one to do anything which he himself did not first fulfil in deed, as it is written of him: “What Jesus began both to do and to teach” (Acts 1). He commands the person who wishes to be worthy to leave father [Col. 0281A] and mother for the Gospel’s sake, and to renounce all that he possesses (Matt. 10). This, therefore, he himself did first: descending from the Father, though he was rich, he became poor for our sake; leaving house, mother, and the kindred of his flesh, he went out to evangelize the poor (Luke 1; 2 Cor. 3).

Therefore, at the beginning of his miracles, with the office of his preaching soon to follow, he says to his mother: “What is there between me and you, woman?” Certainly he says this not according to the flesh, as stated above, but according to his divinity—which did not receive its beginning of existence from his mother. The work of this divinity must altogether take precedence over concern for the flesh. Nor should anyone say this to father or mother according to the flesh, but according to God—namely, where the work of God requires one to disregard all things, even one’s own [Col. 0281B] soul.

In this way he in no respect acts against the Law which says: “Honor your father and mother” (Deut. 5; Exod. 20). For the same Law which says this also speaks again by the same authority, or in the same Spirit: “He who said to his father and mother, ‘I do not know you,’ and to his brothers, ‘I do not recognize them,’ and who did not acknowledge his own children—these have kept your law and preserved your covenant. They shall teach your judgments, O Jacob, and your law, O Israel. They shall place incense in your wrath, and a whole burnt offering upon your altar” (Deut. 33).

Therefore, in order that he might fulfil the Law perfectly, he did not acknowledge his mother while preserving her honor. For there is surely no dishonoring of father or mother when they are set aside not for any ordinary cause, but for the honor or work of God alone [Col. 0281C]. Jesus, intent upon that great and necessary work of salvation, declares that he will not acknowledge his mother until, when that work has been completed, he says to her: “Woman, behold your son” (John 19)—which he was to say at the hour of his death.

Accordingly, when he had said, “What is there between me and you, woman?” he immediately added: “My hour has not yet come.” As though he said: “From the time when I came to baptism and went out into the wilderness, you have sighed with maternal affection because you were deprived of my presence. Now you have me at this wedding and rejoice that you enjoy my presence; but the time is still approaching when, leaving you more and more, I shall not cease to travel through cities and villages. With this present life I shall finish the work which I began. Returning from this expedition, wounded and [Col. 0281D] dying, I shall be received by you. For now the burden of heavenly business presses so heavily that I have no leisure to consider what I owe to your maternal affection. Nor do I have to do my own will, but to bear the obedience laid upon me by the Father. Whatever sort of necessity his command brings, such a son will I show myself to you in that hour.”
