He answered these words, indeed, not the thing his mother had said, “They have no wine,” but the vehement cry of her inward longing, sounding deeply in his ears, because she always burned to see his face present. For he wished no less than she did to gladden by his benefit the guests whose devotion had invited him—especially for the benefit of those whom he knew would believe in him when they saw this miracle. Therefore it rightly follows:

[Col. 0282A] “His mother said to the servants: ‘Whatever he tells you, do it.’” Knowing his will and not doubting his power, she suitably prepares the minds of the servants by her warning, so that they might not regard as madness what he was about to command, since they had not yet experienced his true power. For even his relatives, when he was choosing the apostles and giving changed names to some of them, “went out,” says Mark the Evangelist, “to seize him, saying, ‘He has gone mad’” (Mark 3). Therefore she anxiously warns them, lest through disbelief or even mockery they make themselves unworthy of the grace of the miracle; instead, by obeying the command, they were to make way for the manifestation of God’s glory.

“Now there were six stone water-jars set there, according to the purification of the Jews, each holding [Col. 0282B] two or three *metretae*. And Jesus said to them: ‘Fill the water-jars with water.’” The purifications of the Jews were numerous. Some came from Moses, but very many from the tradition of the Pharisees, concerning whom Mark also says: “For the Pharisees, unless they wash their hands repeatedly, do not eat, holding to the traditions of the elders. And when they come from the marketplace, unless they wash, they do not eat. And there are many other things handed down to them to observe: washings of cups, pitchers, bronze vessels, and beds” (Mark 7).

Because of such purifications, water-jars were placed there so that water might be ready at hand. In this house they are now said to have been of stone. They were vessels so called because they had been prepared to receive water: for Greek *hydōr* means “water” in Latin [Col. 0282D]. Otherwise the name is used improperly, as in: “The jar of meal shall not fail, nor shall the flask of oil diminish” (3 Kings 17). The Evangelist took care to indicate that their capacity was unequal when he said: “Each holding two or three *metretae*.” By *metretae* he means certain measures, as if he had said jars, amphorae, or something similar. A *metreta* is the name of a measure, and this measure received its name from measuring; for the Greeks call a measure *metron*, whence *metretae* are named.

“And they filled them to the brim.” It should be noted that the Lord made neither wine to gladden the guests nor bread to satisfy the hungry crowds from nothing; nor, indeed, did he make anything in the whole series of his signs [Col. 0282D] from things that did not exist. Rather, he either brought existing things into his hands and improved them—making wine from water and multiplying five or seven loaves to satisfy many thousands—or he restored what had been corrupted to wholeness by healing the sick, or restored what had been lost by raising the dead (Matt. 14). But he did not make anything from nothing.

For Scripture does not lie when it says: “He who lives for ever created all things together” (Ecclus. 18). He created all things together from nothing, that is, the first elements of things. But in the six days, when he made the forms of all things, he did not create them from nothing; rather, from those same elements he formed them by the command of his Word. “And on the seventh day he rested from all the work which he had accomplished” (Gen. 2), namely, so that thenceforth he should command no new kind to be produced [Col. 0283A]. Yet he works even now, governing and multiplying those same things, and above all transforming humankind for the better.

Therefore, since, as Scripture testifies, God speaks once and does not repeat the same thing a second time, the unchangeable Son of God, when about to give wine, did not create it from nothing but made it from a fitting element—from water, which every year he changes into wine as it ascends through the vines from their roots, “by the command which he established, and it shall not pass away” (Ps. 148). How he did this may be believed; it cannot be investigated. Yet it is certainly more wondrous to have created water from nothing than to have made wine from water. For it is more wondrous to bring into being any substance which did not exist than to add any accident to an already existing substance.

[Col. 0283B] All liquid, generally speaking, is one substance and one element; color and flavor, however, are rightly classed among the multitude of accidents. Thus, when God created water from nothing, he did something more wondrous because he produced a substance; but when the Son of the same God made wine from water, adding only an accident to the substance of the liquid, he did something more venerable. For, as has been said, it is not so venerable that God could do this as that he who could do it was God made man.

“And he said to them: ‘Draw some now, and take it to the steward of the feast.’” The *architriclinus*, or steward of the feast, is said to be the friend of the bridegroom who, while the bridegroom is free from all business and resting, presides over the wedding, provides necessary things, and has charge over the guests and the whole household. He is called [Col. 0283C] *architriclinus*, that is, “chief of the triclinium,” because he shares the couch of the bridegroom and bride in the dining-room where they recline.

A *triclinium* is so called as though it were a “third reclining-place”—that is, a chamber within a chamber, indeed a chamber within the first and second chambers. He commands that the wine made from water be offered to this man first, so that the lamp of so splendid and joyful a miracle might not remain hidden, but, set as it were at the summit of the wedding feast, might spread its brightness more widely, gladdening the whole house and all the guests and more eagerly kindling the faith of those for whose sake it had chiefly been performed. And this indeed occurred.

“But when the steward of the feast tasted the water made wine,” and so forth. [Col. 0283D] Truly then, as the Lord himself says, “Behold, one greater than Jonah is here” (Matt. 12)—not only greater than Jonah or greater than Solomon, but greater even than Moses or any of the holy and great men whatsoever. For, to pass over the fact that he was born when and how he willed, that he died when and how he willed, rose again, and ascended into heaven—to omit for the moment these greater things—123 what saint, among all those through whom signs and wonders were performed, ever worked a sign by will or command alone?

Moses, indeed, worked signs in Egypt by crying out to the Lord, so that God said to him: “Why do you cry out to me?” (Exod. 14). Thus by crying out—that is, not exercising his own power but acting by another’s command—he struck the waters with the rod and divided them. But this one, seated and silent [Col. 0284A], by a mere nod and by his will alone, turned them into good wine.

“This Jesus did as the beginning of signs in Cana of Galilee, and manifested his glory.” He made a great and illustrious beginning of signs, striking human eyes by that flash as by lightning, so that, astonished, they might raise their gaze to contemplate the face of heaven—that is, so that, as diligent and attentive spectators considering also the other things he was to do, they might turn their believing minds to belief in the coming of the kingdom of God.

“And by this sign,” he says, “he manifested his glory,” so that they might see, and we might hear, “his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father” (John 1); that from afar we might hear and believe unto our righteousness and salvation (Rom. 10). For the lamp had not come in order to lie hidden beneath a bushel, but to be set upon a lampstand [Col. 0284B] and give light to all who are in the house (Matt. 5). So too, where there is worthy fruit—that is, the benefit of souls—we ought to make manifest before people the grace which is in us, so that they may see our good works and glorify our Father who is in heaven (ibid.).”

“And his disciples believed in him.” It is said here that they believed in him, but it is not said that, leaving all things, they followed him. For John had not yet been sent to prison. Jesus himself did not enter upon the course of public preaching before John had been handed over; nor, leaving mother and relatives, did he travel through cities and villages preaching. It is from this preaching that the other Evangelists, as stated above, take the beginning of their narrative [Col. 0284C] after his baptism.

Therefore he had not yet commanded his disciples what he was to command only after first doing it himself: namely, that, leaving all things, we should follow his footsteps, which he had not yet shown them by going before them. Among these disciples we think that this John the Evangelist, leaving his wedding—since almost everyone holds that this was his wedding—began to follow the Lord himself. For histories relate that Christ called him from the wedding when he was intending to marry, and therefore bestowed upon the man whom he had drawn back from carnal pleasure the sweetness of his own more excellent love.

He already had disciples, then, whom especially the testimony of John directed to him. While John himself carried forward the course he had begun by public ministries [Col. 0284D], Jesus revealed to them the private beginnings of his miracles and teaching. Hence it is added: “After this he went down to Capernaum, he and his mother and his brothers and his disciples; and they remained there not many days.”

## EXPLANATION IN THE SAME READING: According to the mysteries of allegory

In the divine works performed concerning our salvation, we believe that a mystical meaning is present, just as we confess that the Father works even now and that the Son likewise works (John 5). This is the worthy and praiseworthy labor of catholic Fathers in the venerable Scriptures: as the eternal Father works [Col. 0285A] nothing without the coeternal Son, so they do not permit any of those things which were bodily done for human salvation, whether in the Law or in the Gospel, to be devoid of spiritual understanding.

“This was the beginning of his signs,” and the rare deeds performed by the same Lord—that is, by the Word incarnate for our sake—brought greater amazement to humanity. Therefore, since we confess the Son in order that we may have the Father, let us, with his help and following the example set by the holy Fathers, contemplate in this great and wondrous work the beauty of spiritual understanding.

“A wedding,” it says, “took place in Cana of Galilee.” This great event, proclaimed beforehand by the praises of many prophets and prefigured by the deeds of the patriarchs, was that the two natures, divine and human, would meet in the one Christ [Col. 0285B], and that he would “set his tabernacle in the sun, like a bridegroom coming forth from his bridal chamber” (Ps. 18). And it came to pass in the bridal chamber of the virgin womb that the bridegroom was joined to the bride: that is, the Creator was joined to the creature by great condescension.

Now Cana is interpreted “zeal,” and Galilee “transmigration.” The name of the place greatly contributes to the spiritual meaning: namely, that God, the mightiest of spirits, was led by great zeal against the adulterous devil. Seeking in this way his creature whom the devil had corrupted, he increased the devil’s punishment by a just judgment, while by his grace he restored to the creature, sought out and found, an undeserved glory.

“Therefore a wedding took place in Cana of Galilee.” The whole household, which is the holy Church, celebrates a feast-day, not vainly believing itself wholly joined to that God who, it believes, assumed its nature in the truth of flesh [Col. 0285C]. “And the mother of Jesus was there.” The mother of Jesus is present where these weddings are celebrated, because the true faith in Christ’s incarnation is surely not lacking to any who deserve to be called and to be children or guests of these weddings.

Marcion, Cerinthus, Ebion, and other heretics, holding their separate assemblies, were not children of these weddings. For the mother of Jesus was not there, because, though by different errors, they excluded from their hearts and assemblies, under the same spirit of wickedness, faith in his Incarnation. Only there is the solemnity of these heavenly weddings celebrated where the mother of Jesus is—that is, where the mother Church is: namely, where the true faith of his Incarnation is daily preached to young women [Col. 0285D] being married to Christ.

There Jesus and his disciples are present when invited: the bridegroom, namely, and his friends. Thus there are four persons who speak in the Song of Songs (chs. 1, 6) of bridal love: the young women whose weddings await them, or who daily marry Christ; mother Church, who gives them birth until Christ is formed in them; Christ himself; and his disciples—that is, the bridegroom and his friends.

What, then, was signified in these bodily weddings that belonged to those spiritual ones? Namely this: something was partly accomplished and partly still future. For by the wine’s failing was signified what had already occurred: namely, that the blessedness or incorruptibility granted to humankind had failed when the first parent [Col. 0286A] sinned. For man was so made that, if he willed, he could avoid sin and could avoid death, eventually to attain what is better and more perfect: namely, the inability to sin and the inability to die. But by sinning he fell into the condition that he could not be free of sin and could not avoid death.

Thus the wine fails because the wretched nature of humankind has been deprived of the blessedness of bestowed grace. What was signified by the six stone water-jars filled with water had likewise already occurred. For the perfect number six of the jars signifies all the holy Fathers, divided through different times—that is, through the six ages of the world—each of whom in his own time was filled with the water of saving wisdom (Ecclus. 15).

Their minds were like stone water-jars: firm in faith [Col. 0286B] and capacious in intellect. Each held two or three *metretae*, because, though the faith of all was one, not all were given the same or an equal measure of wisdom. For more was revealed, for example, to Moses than to Abraham, and to David than to Moses (Gen. 12, 15). This is plainly shown from the words of sacred Scripture itself.

Who does not know that Abraham spoke with God? Yet the Lord says to Moses: “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob; and I did not make my name Adonai known to them” (Exod. 3, 6). Behold, more had become known to Moses than to Abraham, since God made known to Moses concerning himself what he related that he had not made known to Abraham.

The Psalmist likewise, after saying, “How I have loved your law, O Lord; it is my meditation all the day” [Col. 0286C] (Ps. 18), adds: “I have understood more than all who teach me” (ibid.); and again: “I have understood more than the elders” (ibid.). Therefore, the one who says that he meditates upon the Law and testifies that he has understood more than all his teachers and more than his elders makes clear that he received divine knowledge more abundantly than Moses.

Thus the saying of Daniel is fulfilled: “Many shall pass through, and knowledge shall be multiplied” (Dan. 2). Therefore, such water-jars do not have one or an equal capacity, because not all received with equal grace the mystery of the Trinity of the divine name or the other mysteries of divinity. And indeed all drew that water of saving wisdom from the fullness of him who now said: “Fill the water-jars with water.” Yet the water was pale and cold [Col. 0286D] and could not restore human nature to its former strength.

For that Mosaic Law, those gifts of God, had brought nothing to perfection, because they could not grant remission of sins and resurrection of the flesh to humankind; they received only the killing letter of the Law, not the life-giving Spirit (2 Cor. 3). But by the water’s being changed into wine was signified the grace and truth that had come—or rather, that was then beginning to come—through Jesus Christ.

For he had clothed the corruption of our nature with the strength of his divinity (Ps. 92); and not long afterwards, having overcome the passion of death (Matt. 27), he was to consecrate in himself, and in the bodies of many saints rising with him, the homeland of resurrection. Having now ascended into heaven after accomplishing this [Col. 0287A], he shines most brightly from above upon all the water-jars beneath him, and in the waters of holy Scripture he presents his image and power to be seen and tasted.

Thus, when the weakness of our nature has been healed, whoever of us has been baptized in the Holy Spirit and has already come to life in the first resurrection (Luke 24), being transferred in blessed hope to the second, understands, as that same meaning opens to us, the spiritual sense in those same Scriptures.

Now something should briefly be said about the ages themselves, insofar as they concern the weddings of Christ himself or the chastity of the holy Church. Behold, at the beginning of the first age it was said: “This now is bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh. Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh [Col. 0287B]” (Gen. 2). This clearly commends the fidelity and unity of lawful and chaste, yet still carnal, marriage. Nevertheless, so long as it was understood only according to the flesh, it was only water—however sweet to drink and suitable for drinking.

But when the Church, betrothed to him, came to the wedding, “and his voice thundered over many waters” (Ps. 28), as he said through his Apostle—in whom he himself was speaking—“This mystery is great; but I speak concerning Christ and the Church” (Eph. 5), the water was changed into wine. On hearing this, holy souls began to burn with love for spiritual marriage, considering another “man, namely the new man, who was created according to God” [Col. 0287C] (Eph. 4), who in a certain sense left his father when, coming forth from the Father and entering the world (John 16), “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2); and also his mother—that is, the Pharisaic Synagogue and the whole Jewish people—and cleaved to his wife, namely the Church chosen from the Gentiles, with whom he is now one body: head and members, bridegroom and bride, Christ and Church.

For, just as God made Eve not from just anywhere, but from the very substance of the man, so that the ground of natural love might be greater—“for he took one of his ribs while he slept and built it into a woman” (Gen. 2)—so too he caused the Church to be born not from just anywhere, but from the blood and water of his side; nor does he nourish her from any source other than his own flesh and blood [Col. 0287D] (John 19). Hence in both cases there is a greater unity of one and the same flesh. Under this understanding, therefore, as with excellent wine, thirst is quenched, love is kindled, and very many are inflamed even with a desire for virginal chastity, so that they disregard not only the yokes of oxen they have bought and the estates they have purchased (Luke 14), but even marriages of the flesh, in order that they may be more able to devote themselves to heavenly marriage.

The second age begins with Noah. Scripture relates of him that “he planted a vineyard, and, drinking wine, became drunk and was uncovered in his tent” (Gen. 9), and so forth. Taken according to the letter, this is sweet water, suited to cleansing conduct: lest anyone, despising a father’s weakness which he knows, after the example of Ham, should justly incur a curse like his [Col. 0288A]; but, covering it with due honor and love, after the example of Shem and Japheth, should inherit a worthy blessing. In them one must observe that, although all had been preserved in the same enclosure of the ark upon the waters, nevertheless the very different quality of their conduct made a great distinction between them in the sight of their father.

But the literal sense of this Scripture is changed, as water into wine, when it is offered to the children of the marriage in a spiritual understanding thus: Noah, whose name means *rest*, is our Lord, upon taking whose yoke upon ourselves we find rest for our souls (Matt. 11). He planted the vineyard, namely that Jewish people which he transferred out of Egypt (Ps. 80); and, drinking from it wine that was exceedingly bitter—indeed, vinegar mixed with gall (Matt. 27; John 19)—he was uncovered [Col. 0288B] in his tent: that is, he was made in the likeness of men, truly capable of suffering, found in appearance and in the reality of death to be a man (Phil. 2).

Ham, whose name means *cunning*—that is, the contentious and impatient heretic, ready for strife—despises this weakness of the Father; and, because from the weakness of his Passion he understands him to be truly man, he disdains to confess him truly God. Therefore, as Ham was cursed in his son Canaan (Gen. 11), so this man too is cursed in his posterity, that is, in his own soul. But Catholic men, figured by Shem and Japheth, reverence the same weakness of the Father with fitting mysteries, knowing that “what is foolish in God is wiser than men, and what is weak in God is stronger than men” [Col. 0288C] (1 Cor. 1). Therefore they become glorious in the kingdom of their Father and are enlarged in eternal dwellings (1 John 2). For Shem means *glorious*, and Japheth, *enlarged*.

And indeed all those people, namely the heretics, floated with these men in the waters of baptism in the same ark of the Church; yet they were estranged backward, and “they went out from us, but they were not of us.” In the 125th year, the third age begins: Isaac is born to an aged father and a mother long barren and herself advanced in years. He is born of the free woman by promise, Ishmael having first been born of the handmaid according to the flesh. This historical account of a divine work is clear and sweet water, profitably watering the reader’s soul and increasing the growth of his faith by examples. For it was Abraham the father’s faith [Col. 0288D] that he did not consider his own body already dead, though he was nearly a hundred years old, nor Sarah’s dead womb, but believed that God was able to do whatever he had promised.

“But,” says the Apostle, “these things are spoken allegorically” (Gal. 4). “For these are the two Testaments: the one indeed from Mount Sinai, bearing children into slavery, which is Hagar,” and the rest. Therefore, with the Apostle as author—indeed, with Christ, who speaks in him, as he himself says: “Do you seek a proof of Christ who speaks in me?” (2 Cor. 13)—with Christ, then, as author, this water of the literal sense is changed into wine. Drunk with it, faith comes to maturity; the Holy Spirit loves it dearly; and the bridal love of souls is multiplied.

So too all the other things done in that age are changed, like waters into wines, when they are understood spiritually [Col. 0289A], because “all things happened to them in figure” (1 Cor. 10), as the same Apostle says. In the fourth age, besides figurative deeds, such as David’s victory over Goliath (1 Sam. 17), the building of the Temple at Jerusalem (1 Kgs. 7), and the marvelous architectural work of the wise king, many things besides these and others like them were also said mystically. Most of these, taken according to the letter, provide such water of wisdom as is neither sufficiently clear nor fit to drink. For example, this passage in the Song of Songs: “There are sixty queens and eighty concubines, and maidens without number” (Song 6), and similar sayings, which, taken according to the letter (2 Cor. 3), do not in any way build up the chaste conduct of the Church.

They are therefore received according to the Spirit, and water becomes good wine [Col. 0289B], “worthy,” as it is said in the same Songs, “for the beloved to drink, and for his lips and teeth to chew upon” (Song 7). So also that which David sang: “Go forth from your bridal chamber,” and so forth. The songs of the Psalms, likewise the sacred books of the prophets—if we follow the letter alone, we drink in almost everything dead and tasteless water; but, following the Spirit, we marvel at the life-giving savor and power of the finest wine.

In the fifth age the captive people of God are carried away under the king of Babylon (2 Kgs. 24), and chosen men from the sons of the captivity are in the house of the eunuch (Jer. 29). Because of their supreme continence of life, God gave them knowledge and instruction in every book and in wisdom, but especially to Daniel understanding of all visions and dreams [Col. 0289C] (Dan. 1). These things and the rest, on the surface of the letter, furnish a cup of sweet water and offer a great example: that by purity of life one may attain the honor of wisdom.

But the spiritual man understands those eunuchs to have been prefigured who “made themselves eunuchs,” as the Lord says, “for the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 19); and who, in the present captivity in which the king of confusion, the devil, enslaved the human race in our first parents, knowing that “the time is short” (1 Cor. 7) and that “the days are evil” (Eph. 5), approve the Apostle’s counsel that they should remain unmarried. To such persons a clearer understanding of the heavenly mysteries is given—for example, to this John, whose are this Gospel and the Apocalypse, in which almost as many words as there are are mysteries.

This water, then, became wine [Col. 0289D], and, wonderfully intoxicated by it, they forget sensual excess; indeed, they even make themselves eunuchs, that they may be more closely grafted into Christ, the true vine.

The Lord himself filled the vessel of the sixth age from the fountain of water springing up into eternal life (John 5). Certainly, the mystery of his incarnation, and also his sayings and deeds before he rose from the dead, then had the taste of water, though of the clearest kind. For in him our nature was capable of suffering, and the mysteries of the kingdom of God which he signified by his words and deeds were not clearly understood. But when he rose from the dead, water was changed into wine: for our nature, which had been capable of suffering in him, was strengthened by eternal incorruption, so that we too might hope for the same; and he “opened [Col. 0290A] the understanding of his disciples, that they might understand the Scriptures” (Luke 24), and that they might remember the words which they had heard carnally from him as needing spiritual interpretation.

Accordingly, all the distributions of saving waters which were allotted to past generations are brought together at this heavenly wedding feast, and, the water having become wine, the guests rejoice. For this wine “makes glad the heart of man” (Ps. 104), and here is “the intoxicating cup—how splendid it is!” (Ps. 23). On the contrary, in all the assemblies of Jews and heretics, because the Mother of Jesus is not there—that is, because faith in the Lord’s incarnation does not feast there—these waters are turned for them into blood (Exod. 7), so that, corrupt and corrupting, they may drink and vomit corrupt Scriptures—or rather, drink (Jer. 25) and die [Col. 0290B]; and so that “fire and sulphur and a stormy blast may be the portion of their cup” (Ps. 11).

Concerning their punishment the justice of God is praised in the Apocalypse, where they say: “You are righteous, O Lord, who are and who were holy, because you have judged these things: because they shed the blood of saints and prophets, you have given them blood to drink, as they deserve” (Rev. 16). Now, at the Lord’s command, the servants draw the water—that is, diligent interpreters of the Scriptures who expound them spiritually—and carry it to the steward of the feast, since they do not attribute to themselves what they understand, but to the Holy Spirit.

For he is the steward of this wedding feast: he who, coming upon the blessed Virgin, prepared the banqueting chamber of her womb, so that in it divine nature might be united with human nature; and who aids individual souls, so that in the hidden places of conscience they may be joined to God the Father [Col. 0290C], and so that, by the same Word by which the blessed Virgin was made pregnant, they too may be made fruitful from his embraces (Luke 1). This good wine, therefore, must be offered to his praise (1 Cor. 10) and drunk in his honor. It has been kept until now, because it was not given to earlier times, but to us, “upon whom the ends of the ages have come.”

We are forbidden by the authority of the holy Church to doubt at what season or on what day of the year this sign was performed. The Church customarily celebrates the glory of this sign on the same day on which the Lord was adored by the Magi (Matt. 2) and on which he chose to be baptized by John (Matt. 3). If it was performed on that same returning day of the year—or rather, since we must unquestionably yield to the aforesaid authority of the holy Church [Col. 0290D]—we are compelled to confess that throughout that entire year, at the beginning of which he was baptized, namely the thirtieth year of his life, he lived silently without miracles.

For at the beginning of his thirtieth year, namely on the thirteenth day of that same year, he was baptized. Luke says: “Jesus himself was beginning to be about thirty years old” (Luke 3). This is the same as if he had said: When Jesus was baptized, the thirtieth year of his life had begun to run its course. But where he was throughout that whole year, or what he did, is uncertain. For if, after completing the fast of forty days, he returned immediately from the desert and moved among people, how did John—who had recognized him from heaven and had already pointed him out as he came toward him, saying, “Behold the Lamb of God”—how, I ask, did that burning lamp, which had been lit for this very purpose [Col. 0291A], to show him to everyone, remain silent for that whole year and not reveal him even to his own disciples?

For it is evident that John did not point him out to them in that 126th year, since only now, that is, on the third day before the aforesaid wedding, when he again says, “Behold the Lamb of God,” they rejoice that they have found him and say, “We have found the Messiah,” and so forth. It may therefore rightly be understood that, even after his fast of forty days, he remained for some time in the desert. Matthew says: “The tempter left him, and behold, angels came and ministered to him” (Matt. 4). Mark also seems to indicate the length of time more expressly, saying: “And he was with the beasts, and angels ministered to him” (Mark 1) [Col. 0292A].

Therefore, if, as the elders carefully observed and handed down to us, he performed this glorious beginning of signs when his thirty-first year of life had already begun, he also provided in this an example worthy of his followers: that no one should prematurely bring his powers into public view, at the risk of destructive vanity, since the Lord himself—to whom vanity could never creep in—waited for the lawful time, that is, full manhood, before displaying the glory of his omnipotence.

## BOOK THREE

[Col. 0291B] Timid sailors carried across the great sea, praying for a calm breeze, look up at the stars fixed in heaven; when land has been lost, they hold to heaven, and, seated at the helm, steer by the stars. They avoid following wandering stars, lest they run upon shipwrecking sandbanks or be carried into unknown regions and never reach the desired harbors.

We who have entered upon the depth of this Gospel Scripture must do the same. First, we must pray for that more tranquil Spirit of whom the Psalmist says: “Your good Spirit shall lead me into a straight land” (Ps. 143). Then we must keep in mind, with vigilant eyes, the sacred teachers, who, like the bright stars of the never-setting Arcturus, stood always fixed in steadfast faith, poured forth the light of faith, and knew no setting of error [Col. 0291C]. But the wandering light of heretics must be avoided far away. For, as the Apostle says, they are “wandering stars, for whom the storm of darkness is reserved forever” (Jude 13); and whoever follows anything from their error suffers shipwreck in no depth of Scripture more greatly than in this Gospel of John.

Therefore, as he inspires us, by whom all faithful Scriptures were composed, let us follow the blessed stars of Catholic teaching and sail on in the vessel we have begun, fearing nothing from heretical pirates, whom this sea is accustomed not to nourish but to sink in eternal shipwreck. It follows:

> “After these things he went down to Capernaum, he and his mother and his brothers and his disciples; and they remained there not many days.”

With great restraint our Lord, after so great a miracle by which he changed water into wine, remains for a little while and permits John, his forerunner, still preaching, to go before him until his appointed end. He stays in a fixed place, suspending his own preaching from public gatherings and from travelling about cities or towns. This has already been said above: before John was handed over, he delayed the public course of his preaching to such a degree that, when he began to preach, John was thought to have risen from the dead.

Thus [Col. 0292B] throughout this whole year, which was the thirty-first of his life, displaying miracles gradually and apart from public notice, he too prepared the way for his future preaching. After this year, when John was handed over, he began preaching himself, at which point the other Evangelists began their narratives. This John was beheaded (Luke 9) on the fourth day before the Kalends of September, in the thirty-second year of our Lord.

“He went down, therefore, to Capernaum.” This descent indicates not so much the downward slope of the land as the great condescension of his humility: namely, that God descended to human beings, the holy one to sinners. For Capernaum was a sinful city, so much so that he later reproached it also, saying: “Woe to you, Chorazin; woe to you, Bethsaida”; and thereafter: “And you, Capernaum, shall you perhaps be cast down into hell?” (Matt. 11). He reproaches these cities because many mighty works had been done by him in them, and they had not believed.

“He went down, therefore, he and his Mother,” namely, the one whom, once he became occupied with the work of preaching, he was in a certain sense to cease recognizing—to such an extent that, according to another Evangelist, when someone said to him, “Behold, your mother and your brothers stand outside seeking you,” he replied: “Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?” (Matt. 12), and so forth. His brothers, who go down with him, are his relatives, because it is a frequent custom in the Scriptures, especially among that people, that those close by blood—such as cousins or more distant cousins—are called brothers.

Some disciples [Col. 0292D] were already following him. He was, as it were, instructing them in the first elements of heavenly doctrine; they had not yet been brought to that perfection at which they must be commanded to leave everything. This happened especially when, calling some from boats and others from different occupations, he eventually caused twelve, besides others, to be with him. Capernaum is a city in Galilee of the Gentiles (Matt. 4), situated in the borders of Zebulun and Naphtali, beside the Lake of Gennesaret. Capernaum means “village of consolation.”

It therefore rightly signifies the people of the Gentiles [Col. 0293A]. For, with respect to those among them to whom the cross of Christ appeared foolishness, Christ himself deservedly reproaches them; but to those who, believing, received him as the power of God and the wisdom of God, he gives the grace of his consolation, having left the Jews behind (1 Cor. 1). This was prefigured more clearly according to Luke. For when the men of his own city had said: “What great things we have heard were done by you in Capernaum, do also here in your own country,” he said: “Truly I say to you, there were many widows in Israel in the days of Elijah, and Elijah was sent to none of them except to a widow woman in Zarephath of Sidon” (Luke 4).

After these words, when they had led him to the brow of the hill upon which their city was built in order to throw him down, “Jesus,” the Evangelist says, “passed through the midst of them and went on his way; and he went down to Capernaum, a city of Galilee, and taught them there on the Sabbaths” (ibid.) [Col. 0293B]. This Evangelist John will later recount that descent. For by this deed it was prefigured that his own people—the Jews, from whose flesh he was born—would bring him to the precipice of death, and that for this reason he would pass away from them and descend to the borders of the Gentiles, so that there he might be nourished by the faith of the Church.

This was also prefigured in the fact that Elijah was sent not to any of the many widows in Israel but to the widow woman in Zarephath of Sidon; or in the fact that, though there were many lepers in Israel under Elisha, none of them was healed except Naaman the Syrian (2 Kgs. 5). It was not without purpose that he recalled these former events to them with so solemn an oath, saying: “Truly I say to you.” Therefore, after wine had been made from water, the Lord went down to Capernaum, that is, to the village of consolation. For after, by rising from the dead, he changed the water of our mortality into the wine of his immortality and, by giving the Holy Spirit, advanced the watery sense of the letter to spiritual understanding, he passed from the Jews to console the Gentiles. It follows:

> “And the Passover of the Jews was near, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem.”

Thus he remained in Capernaum not many days, as the Evangelist says; that is, perhaps not even for the whole three months. For from the day on which, as stated above, the beginning of the signs—the changing of water into wine—was certainly performed, until the sacred evening of Passover, there were in that year, according to the lunar reckoning, eighty-eight days, or, according to more accurate copies of chronologers, only eighty days [Col. 0293D].

This must by no means be passed over: this ascent of our Lord to Jerusalem, because of what was said and done there, deserved to be written among the testimonies of divinity which this Evangelist especially intended diligently to gather. For many judge the greatest of the signs to have been Lazarus’s resurrection (John 11), the man blind from birth receiving sight (John 9), the Father’s voice heard at the Jordan (Matt. 3), or his displaying on the mountain the glory of one triumphing in transfiguration (Matt. 17) [Col. 0294A].

But to the more discerning, among all the signs he performed, this appears more wonderful: that one man—contemptible at that time, and so lowly that he was later crucified—could, while the scribes and Pharisees raged against him and saw their profits being destroyed, at the blows of a single whip drive out so great a multitude, overturn tables, break up seats, and do things which an infinite army could not do. For something fiery and star-like shone from his eyes, and the majesty of divinity gleamed in his face. Therefore the witness of the Son of God, testifying to the divinity of the same Son of Man, rightly took care not to omit this in order to refute the heretics.

But what does it mean that this Evangelist asserts that he did this now—namely, drove buyers and sellers from the Temple [Col. 0294B] (Matt. 21; Luke 19)—which, according to the other Evangelists, he did when he came to that same city to suffer, with crowds accompanying him and children crying “Hosanna” (Mark 11)? Did he perhaps set down each thing first simply as it first came to mind, as though the time of events need not be considered, provided their truth were established? It might perhaps be more permissible to suppose this: that, gathering testimonies to Christ’s divinity according to his own intention or purpose, he thought it worthy to write this notable deed first because it was greater than the others.

But the following text does not permit either opinion. For further below it is written: “When he had come therefore into Galilee, the Galileans received him, since they had seen all the things he had done in Jerusalem on the feast day” (John 4) [Col. 0294C]. Did all the other Evangelists err in remembering when this happened? Or did they all, by chance and in agreement, hold the same false opinion about the same time? Far be it! Or did they perhaps transfer to the end, for some mystery, what happened in the first year? But the text of their writings forbids this suspicion. For, according to Luke, when he arrived at Jerusalem already about to suffer and wept as he saw it, he entered the Temple and began to drive out buyers and sellers (Luke 19), so that by driving them out in his deed he might signify beforehand the very destruction which he had predicted.

Mark, moreover, determines more precisely even the day on which he drove out the buyers and sellers: namely, the following day, after he had entered the city already about to suffer (Mark 11) [Col. 0294D]. We are therefore compelled from every side to confess that this happened more than once: that he is said to have driven buyers and sellers from the Temple. And indeed it may confidently be affirmed that he did this not only at the very end, when he went up to suffer, but also as often as he went up after beginning to work miracles, whenever he found dealings of this kind—or rather, robberies. He was zealous, and “zeal for the house of the Lord consumed him” (Ps. 69).

Nor without reason did John the Evangelist wish in this respect to differ from the others, asserting that what they say occurred last occurred here in the first year. For an opponent might have said that the scribes and Pharisees were not restrained or stunned by a divine nod, and did not allow their profits to perish, but acted from fear of the crowds, many of whom had come with him and many of whom had gone out to meet him as he came, with praises and palm branches [Col. 0295A]. Therefore, that we may know that the whole event must unquestionably be ascribed to the power of his divinity, John testifies that he did this also at a time when he was still little known and had come with no crowd accompanying him. But let us now examine the words of the Gospel.

> “And he found in the Temple those selling oxen and sheep and doves, and money-changers sitting.”

It should be known that, according to the commands of the Law, in the Temple of the Lord, most venerable in the whole world, and with Jewish people flowing there from almost every region, innumerable victims were sacrificed, especially on feast days: bulls, rams, and goats. The poor, lest they be without a sacrifice, offered young doves and turtledoves [Col. 0295B] (Deut. 12). It often happened that those who had come from far away had no victims. The priests therefore devised a way to make plunder from the people: they sold all the animals necessary for sacrifices, both to sell them to those who had none and to receive back those very animals once they had been bought.

Their scheme was often thwarted by the poverty of those selling, who needed resources and lacked not only sacrificial victims but even the means to buy birds and cheap little offerings. They therefore also established money-changers to lend money on security. But because the Law commanded (ibid.) that no one should take usury, and money lent out could not profit them if it brought no gain and might perhaps sometimes be lost, they devised another *techna* [device], so as to make the money-changers *collybistae* [dealers in *collyba*] [Col. 0295C].

The Latin language does not express the exact meaning of this word. Among them, *collyba* are what we call *tragemata*, or cheap little gifts: for example, roasted chickpeas, raisins, and fruits of various kinds. Therefore, because the *collybistae*, who were to lend money, could not receive usury, they received various articles in place of interest, so that what was forbidden in money they might demand in things bought with money—as though Ezekiel had not himself proclaimed this very thing, saying: “You shall not take usury or excess” (Ezek. 18).

When the Lord saw such commerce—or robbery—in the house of his Father, stirred by the ardor of the Spirit, according to what is written in the sixty-eighth Psalm, “Zeal for your house has consumed me,” he made himself a whip of cords and drove so great a multitude from the Temple. Beyond this outward deed, truly great and to be proclaimed as a testimony of Christ’s true and supreme divinity, it portends another thing for the wretched Jews: a truly great and pitiable evil, truly to be lamented, unless it happened deservedly—the destruction of the bloodstained city and of the profaned Temple. It also signifies beforehand that the rite of the old sacrifice was to be wholly abolished from the sight of God [Col. 0295D].

For what does that cord do in the hand of one mighty, in the hand of one wise? What does it signify except the Roman army: harsh in slaughter, strong in binding and taking captive? He who once said through the prophet, “Woe to Assyria, the rod of my fury; the staff itself is in his hand, my indignation” (Isa. 10), now, acting in his own person, proclaims: Woe to the great beast of the Roman Empire, which, according to Daniel, devours and crushes and tramples the remainder under its feet (Dan. 7). It is the cord of my wrath, the iron strap, and the bond by which this people is to be taken captive.

This ominous sign portended that disaster to them, as is especially clear from the Gospel according to Luke. For, as he relates, before he entered the Temple and performed this sign, he saw the city, wept over it, and said: “Because, if you too had known … days shall come upon you, and your enemies shall surround you with a rampart” (Luke 19), and so forth [Col. 0296A]. Since, therefore, he first pronounced that final destruction and then, in driving them from his Father’s house, employed a whip made of cords, he plainly indicates that by his deed he signified the very evil which he had foretold in words: an evil which he weeps over according to the compassion of human nature and executes according to the just judgment of his divinity.

And vengeance is fittingly prefigured by a cord, because they were to be punished. For they themselves were surrounded by the long cords of their sins (Ps. 139). Matthew in turn expresses the length of these cords. For after saying, “Behold, I send to you prophets and wise men and scribes; and some of them you will kill and crucify, and some of them you will scourge in your synagogues and persecute from city to city,” he immediately added the length of these cords by which they were surrounded, saying: “So that upon you may come all the righteous blood shed upon the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah, son of Barachiah, whom you killed between the Temple and the altar. Amen, I say to you, all these things shall come upon this generation” (Matt. 23) [Col. 0296C].

Therefore, as a sign and portent of their miseries:

> “Having made a whip of cords, he drove all out of the Temple, including the sheep and the oxen; he poured out the money-changers’ coins and overturned their tables.”

He did not care if the profits of priests who committed robbery and despoiled the people should perish.

“And he said to those who sold doves: ‘Take these things away from here, and do not make my Father’s house a house of trade.’” And this is especially to be noted: in the very heat of severity, in the very flame of burning zeal, while, with no concern for the priests, he cast out the merchandise, he spared the poor—namely, those who sold doves (for it is not the rich but the poor who are accustomed to sell such little birds). He therefore spared those poorer persons, so as not to drive out the doves they were selling; for once driven out they would fly away, and the sellers could not catch them, and might at some point be distressed by their loss and rightly lament it.

Nor should this be passed over: whereas in another Evangelist he cites Scripture, bringing forward the testimony, “My house shall be called a house of prayer, but you have made it a den of thieves” (Matt. 21; Isa. 56), here he says, “Do not make my Father’s house a house of trade.” For he said the former to the scribes and Pharisees, or priests, who truly, under the appearance of divine worship, lay hidden as though in a den and, as was said above, made prey and robbery of the people; but he speaks this to the poor sellers of doves, who did not know the difference between their right hand and their left.

But according to mystical understandings, Jesus daily enters the temple of his Father and casts all men out of his Church—bishops as well as presbyters, deacons as well as laity, and the whole multitude—and he regards sellers and buyers alike as guilty of one crime. For it is written: “Freely you have received; freely give” (Matt. 10). “He also overturned the tables of the money-changers”: that is, the altars, called the money-changers’ tables on account of the avarice of the priests. He also overturned, according to Matthew (ibid.), the seats of those who sold doves—something which it would be absurd to understand literally. For the doves were not upon seats but in cages; nor should we suppose that sellers of doves sat in seats. Rather, mystically, the dignity of teachers is indicated by the seats, and it is reduced to nothing when it is mixed with profit.

What has been said of churches, let each person understand also of himself. For the apostle Paul says: “You are the temple of God, and the Holy Spirit dwells in you” (1 Cor. 3). Let there be no trade in the house of our prayer: no commerce of sellers and buyers, no coveting of gifts; lest Jesus enter angry and stern, and cleanse his temple only by applying the scourge, so as to make a house of prayer out of a den of thieves and a house of trade. [Col. 0297C]

How, then, did the Jews, or the heretics Ebionites—that is, “the poor,” poor rather in understanding than in name—and the rest, against whom this evangelical truth according to John thunders most especially, fail to hear the authoritative voice saying, “Do not make my Father’s house a house of trade”? They heard Mary his mother say: “Son, why have you done this to us? Behold, your father and I were seeking you sorrowfully” (Luke 2). And therefore they break out by saying that Christ was born from Joseph’s seed (John 6), and they did not hear him himself saying here: “Do not make my Father’s house a house of trade.”

If they did not hear the gentle bleating of the meek lamb saying, “Why were you seeking me? Did you not know that I must be in the things that are my Father’s?” (Luke 2), how did they not at least hear this roar of the lion, making his way in storm and whirlwind, overthrowing all things by the terror of his aspect, and saying, “Do not make my Father’s house a house of trade”? For it is by no means slight or trivial that, in saying “my Father’s house,” he added “my.” It is more profound indeed than if he had simply said, “the Father’s house.”

This is to be noted almost everywhere in his words: when, naming the Father, he adds “my,” he speaks of the fatherhood of nature, by which he is the sole and only Son; and the things he says are especially high and divine, as in: “My Father works until now, and I work” (John 5). But when, naming the Father, he does not add “my,” he speaks of the fatherhood of grace which is shared with us, or by which we are his brothers. Then he speaks more humbly of himself, as in: “And as the Father gave me commandment, so I do” (John 14).

It follows: “And his disciples remembered that it was written: ‘Zeal for your house has consumed me.’” From that time they remembered that this had been written of him, after he opened their understanding so that they might understand the Scriptures. Therefore they remembered that it had been written of him because they saw it fulfilled: “Zeal for your house has consumed me” (Ps. 68). This is expressed far more resonantly than if it had been said, “Zeal for your house has inflamed or kindled me.” For in that psalm the weakness of his humanity prays—a humanity which so veiled the divinity dwelling within it that, as he walked among men, he did not appear to men as God. Yet suddenly zeal for his Father so stirred him that his very weakness seemed no longer to appear—the weakness which had hitherto served to conceal his divinity. [Col. 0298B]

For what else could he have done if he had not possessed the weakness of our nature? Zeal for God’s house therefore consumed him, when the radiance of flashing divinity, exerting itself, covered or concealed the weak nature.

“Then the Jews answered and said to him: ‘What sign do you show us, that you do these things?’” So long as heaven thundered, the frogs were silent; so long as divinity roared forth from that dwelling-place of his flesh, proclaiming, “Take these things away from here, and do not make my Father’s house a house of trade,” the Jews remained silent and held themselves in the marsh of their silence, daring to utter nothing in reply. But when the thunder ceased, creeping out again—yet still trembling and quivering with something like angry fear and fearful anger—they said: “What sign do you show us, that you do these things?”

For the Jews seek signs, not for God’s glory but their own: in vanity they thirst for that nourishment of miracles on which the infancy of that nation was formerly fed, so that by new prodigies they too might pride themselves, as their fathers had done, and become a spectacle to all the surrounding nations. They do not reflect that their fathers, rebellious and unbelieving, could eat manna and die in their sins. They therefore say: “What sign do you show us?” As though they were saying: Moses showed signs and wonders from heaven and gave manna to our fathers (Exod. 16); you, if you are the Christ—as, with John testifying, people had already begun commonly to say—“what sign do you show?” What do you accomplish, that we may believe that God, whose this house is, is your Father?

As they said these things, it truly did not befit the wisdom of God to give them such signs as they wished, when, becoming no better, they would always seek more and more with insatiable curiosity. He therefore said: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” Then the Jews said: “This temple was built in forty-six years, and will you raise it up in three days?” But he spoke of the temple of his body.

Three matters must be discussed here. First: why, when they sought a sign and he had performed many signs, he answered by giving the power of his resurrection alone as a sign. Second: why he foretold that resurrection or his death, yet concealed it from the understanding of those who sought the sign. Third: why he wished to use, not any sort of figure, but the name or likeness of a temple.

Certainly it was to the point that, when they said, “What sign do you show us, that you do these things?” he should answer with the sign sufficient to distinguish his greatness and preeminence. For he was pressed with the question because he had cast them out of the temple, asserting that it was his Father’s house; and they asked him by what sign they should believe him. Therefore he ought to give the sign that would suffice as proof of his divine majesty—indeed, the sign by which, when displayed to them, he would expel them all from his Father’s house and kingdom, and at the same time scatter them as captives among all nations. [Col. 0299B]

For from what was the truth of his divinity more clearly shown? From what was the justice of their condemnation or dispersal more firmly established, than from the fact that he whom they crucified rose from the dead? Moses and all the other saints died, and none of them rose again; but this man, though crucified through our weakness, now lives by the power of God (1 Cor. 1). And because he “became obedient unto death, even death on a cross, God gave him the name which is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of things in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. 2). But because they crucified him, they were cast out of God’s house and, like the sheep and oxen which they sold and bought in the temple, were justly exposed to plunder and slaughter among all nations.

Jesus therefore rightly replied to their inquiry with the sign: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” You ask: Why did he declare the glory of so great a sign in such a way that those to whom he answered could not understand it? Or, if he did not wish it understood, why did he not remain entirely silent? Clearly, he did not remain entirely silent because here and in many places, sometimes more obscurely and sometimes more plainly, he foretold it, so that those who already were, or would later be, worthy of the revelation of the mysteries of God’s kingdom might in their proper time remember his words, and, aided by his preceding sayings, come to know or believe the ensuing events. Hence it is added: “When therefore he had risen from the dead, his disciples remembered that he had said these things.” [Col. 0299D]

But when he spoke these very words, he removed them from the understanding of those to whom he was speaking because, as the Evangelist says shortly afterward, Jesus himself did not entrust himself to them. He knew that they were such people as were not fit for him to entrust with the mysteries of his counsel. For if, when he said to those to whom he would most fully entrust himself, “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be handed over to be crucified, and on the third day he will rise” (Matt. 20)—if, I say, when he said these things, he restrained their understanding by a fitting moderation so that they should not understand, and so that this saying should be hidden from them—how much more ought he to have hidden this saying from his plotters, to whom he would never entrust himself?

And if he called his own disciples, not yet renewed by the grace of the Holy Spirit, old wineskins and therefore said that new wine should not be poured into them (Matt. 9), how much more ought he not to pour the purity of his counsel into these tombs of the dead, which appeared beautiful outwardly but within were full of rottenness (Matt. 23)? Rightly, therefore, when they sought signs, he neither wholly concealed this sign of his omnipotence nor uttered it in plain speech for them openly to understand.

The third of the proposed questions is this: why did he disclose the meaning of his reply not by any arbitrary image but by the name or likeness of a temple? By this saying he indeed “made his enemies wander in a pathless place and not in a way” (Ps. 106); but he reserved for his faithful those things which they would remember and, at the proper time, understand as the mysteries of his purpose. For those who wandered said: “This temple was built in forty-six years, and will you raise it up in three days?” [Col. 0300B]

As though, in saying, “Destroy this temple,” he had pointed his finger at those great and beautiful walls; or as though God dwelt in no other place than that handmade temple. Yet, on the contrary, Solomon, the builder of that temple, had said: “Can it truly be thought that God dwells upon the earth? For if heaven and the heaven of heavens cannot contain you, how much less this house which I have built for you?” (3 Kings 8). Yet these inwardly deaf persons had heard this, although they looked upon the temple outwardly; much more had they attended to what incarnate Wisdom had said of herself through the mouth of the same Solomon: “Wisdom has built herself a house; she has hewn out seven pillars” (Prov. 9), and so forth.

Since therefore they erred thus in the presence of truth, and their eyes were darkened though the sun was present, they said, “This temple was built in forty-six years,” referring not to the first but to the second construction. For Solomon first completed the temple during the greatest peace of his kingdom, by a most fitting work of seven years (3 Kings 7). When it had been destroyed by the Chaldeans, rebuilding began after seventy years (4 Kings 25), when Cyrus the Persian ordered the captivity released (1 Ezra 1). But the children of the migration could not complete within forty-six years the work they were doing at the command of the leaders Zerubbabel and Jesus, because of opposition from neighboring peoples (1 Ezra 2–3). [Col. 0300D]

They, then, erred in this way concerning the word of truth. But we, not only believing with his disciples the Scripture and the word spoken by Jesus, also draw out—against their will—the meaning of truth from their error when they say, “This temple was built in forty-six years.” For this number, not of years but of days, accords most suitably with the completion of the Lord’s body. Writers on natural things report that the form of the human body is completed in that number of days: in the first six days after conception it has the appearance of milk; in the following eight it changes into blood; then it is solidified during twelve days; in the remaining eighteen it is formed into the complete outlines of the limbs; and thereafter, during the remaining time until birth, it increases in size.

Six, eight, twelve, and eighteen make forty-five. If we add one day—that is, the very day on which the body, distinguished into limbs, begins to receive growth—we find precisely as many days in the building of the Lord’s body as years in the construction of the temple. Thus the handmade temple fittingly prefigured his most holy flesh, which he had taken from the Virgin.

The same number also rightly applies to the holy Church, which is his body, and from which he was about to cast the faithless Jews by the scourge of just condemnation. For it is built from the entirety of the human race propagated from Adam. Now the name Adam, in the four Greek letters by which it is written, yields this same number, forty-six, when calculated in Greek. For α is one, δ four; and again α one, μ forty: together they make forty-six. [Col. 0301B]

It should also be known that by these same four letters—α, δ, again α, and μ—the four regions of the world are indicated, into which Adam was scattered in his children, from whom the whole Church is gathered. For these four letters occur at the beginnings of the names of the regions of the world: ἄρκτος, “north,” begins with α; δύσις, “west,” with δ; ἀνατολή, “east,” with α; and μεσημβρία, “south,” with μ.

Therefore, taking the forty-six years mystically as an aid to faith, we detest those who unbelievingly objected this number of years. For they are cursed because, as had been foretold by the patriarch Jacob in the type of Simeon and Levi, they became instruments of iniquity. “For in their anger they killed a man, and in their self-will they undermined a wall” (Gen. 49). Especially those of the tribe of Levi—namely, the scribes and Pharisees—killed such a man and pierced the wall of so great a temple with nails and a spear.

Having said these things, we should carefully note the Evangelist’s purpose when he says: “But he spoke of the temple of his body.” For why did he add this at last, except to strike also by this saying the heretics who, with viperous tongues, detract from Christ the Son of God? This Gospel, as has often been said, was written especially against them. To make this clear, it is now pleasing to ask these same heretics: Whose temple is it, if not God’s? A temple for any creature neither has ever been made, nor is ever to be made or called such. But here the Son of God calls his own body a temple. For who speaks, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up,” except the Son of God, the incarnate Word? Therefore he is God, because he has a temple—however much gross swine may grunt against it, wallowing in their marshes. [Col. 0302A]

And without doubt this temple of the Son of God is more worthy than that temple of his Father, of which he had said: “Do not make my Father’s house a house of trade.” For this temple is not handmade and cannot now be destroyed forever; that handmade temple, lacking God as its inhabitant, was destroyed. And concerning this temple, according to Ezekiel, “water went out from the right side, and all to whom that water came were saved” (Ezek. 47). But from that temple, the temple of the scribes and Pharisees, blood does not cease to flow—the blood which they invoked upon themselves when they said: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27).

It follows: “When he was in Jerusalem on the feast day, many believed in him, seeing the signs which he did. But Jesus himself did not entrust himself to them.” These persons who believed in him also erred in believing, so that, as was said above, Jesus rightly did not entrust himself to them. They indeed believed that he was the Christ who performed such deeds before them; but, judging his kingdom carnally, they did not deserve to grasp the ways of his humility or the mysteries of his kingdom.

The Holy Spirit rebukes the vanity of such persons in the psalm, saying: “It is vain for you to rise before the light; rise after you have sat down” (Ps. 126). For they seek to rise before the light—which is altogether vain—because they seek to be exalted before the time. They do not strive in proper order toward the feast of glory; that is, they are not first humbled so that afterward they may deservedly be exalted. So these persons, seeing the signs which our Lord performed, believed in him. They vainly wanted Christ to come and reign in such a way that, with him as king, they themselves might, according to their carnal understanding, consume the strength of the nations and pride themselves in their glory. Believing him to be Christ, yet not humbled with him, they already applauded themselves concerning exaltation. [Col. 0302C]

So too the sons of Zebedee, of whom this John was one, not yet humbled, already wished to be exalted, saying: “Teacher, say that one of us may sit at your right hand and the other at your left in your kingdom” (Matt. 20; Mark 10). They went in vain because they wished to precede the light—that is, they sought exaltation before Christ—and hastened by another way to exaltation, without preserving the order appointed by the Light itself. For before they were humbled in accordance with the Lord’s passion, they were already choosing places in which to sit, one at the right and the other at the left.

Why, then, did he not conceal or entrust himself equally to these and to the others? For he immediately begins to entrust himself to the sons of Zebedee, saying: “Can you drink the cup which I am about to drink?” (Matt. 20). Thereafter he gradually commits heavenly secrets to them, and especially to this John, to whom he showed the secrets of the eternal Beginning and many treasures of heavenly revelations. But to these persons who believed in him, “Jesus himself,” says the Evangelist, “did not entrust himself.” Why then did he distinguish these and those by such a different lot? It follows.

“Because he himself knew all men, and because he had no need that anyone should bear testimony concerning man. For he himself knew what was in man.” This is plainly a most firm reason, sufficient to satisfy one who has learned from the Apostle not to have the thing formed say to him who formed it: “Why have you made me thus?” (Rom. 9). First, however, it must be said that this same reason, neither vain nor weak, was set forth against heretics, according to the Evangelist’s often-mentioned purpose.

For who knows all men except God, “who searches hearts and kidneys” (Ps. 7; Jer. 17)? Who has no need for anyone to bear testimony concerning man except God, to whom it is truly said: “You alone know the hearts of all the children of men” (3 Kings 8)? Finally, who knows what is in man except God? Of him it is not vainly said: Man sees the face, but God looks upon the heart (1 Kings 16). Thus here too the Evangelist, in accordance with his purpose, plainly testifies that Christ is God by saying: “Because he knew all.” [Col. 0303B]

But if he knows all men, he surely also knew those who believed in him when they saw the signs he performed. Therefore, according to his knowledge of them, he had to deal with them discerningly: that is, he rightly did not set spiritual things before those who had a carnal understanding, especially since it is not his counsel “to give what is holy to dogs, or cast pearls before swine” (Matt. 7).

For although the potter has power to make from the same clay one vessel for honor and another for dishonor (Rom. 9), our Potter must not therefore be supposed to use this free power toward us without a preceding cause of justice—as though many people are vessels of dishonor because he did not wish to show them the honor of his knowledge. Rather, he does not wish to pour his honor into them because they themselves are vessels of dishonor. To put it more plainly: a person does not act wickedly, and thereby perish, because God predestined him to death; rather, God predestined him to death because he foreknew that he would act wickedly. This has been abundantly argued by God’s helpers against the heretics who deny free will.

For, as the Apostle testifies, just as God’s predestination precedes calling, so his foreknowledge precedes predestination (Rom. 8). Therefore, what the Evangelist says—“But Jesus did not entrust himself to them, because he himself knew all men, and because he had no need that anyone should bear testimony concerning man; for he himself knew what was in man”—is like saying of some prudent man: He would not pour his wine into these or those vessels because he himself knew that they were filled with mud; and he had no need for someone to go and inspect them for him, for he himself took care and was able to see within by himself. Let us now consider what follows in the Evangelist’s narrative.

## Chapter III

“And there was a man of the Pharisees, Nicodemus by name, a ruler of the Jews. He came to Jesus by night and said to him: ‘Rabbi, we know that you have come from God as a teacher. For no one can do these signs which you do, unless God be with him.’”

This man should be considered a man not so much by nature as by reason. Indeed, those to whom Jesus did not entrust himself were all men by nature; but because they did not rationally seek the things they did not know, in a sense they were not men. But this man, by God’s favor, made use of reason in the things he saw and heard—the faculty by which alone we are helped to differ from brute animals. Seeing the signs which Jesus performed and not understanding the things he said, he did not fade into foolish wonder—as did those who had said, “This temple was built in forty-six years, and will you raise it up in three days?” Rather, as a rational man preparing himself to receive the things of God, he bound himself by a strong argument, putting forward: “Rabbi, we know that you have come from God as a teacher”; and then adding the strongest reason: “For no one can do these signs which you do, unless God be with him.”

What grace, what good and praiseworthy disposition does he show in coming to him by night? He is a praiseworthy attendant and venerable servant, very unlike the Jews—of whom he was a ruler—and the Pharisees—from among whom he came—who sent men by night to seize him, whereas he himself came by night to hear him. They sent men by night to seize Jesus without a crowd; he came by night to hear Jesus without a crowd, although Jesus did not entrust himself to them. They made evil use of their hour and of the power of darkness; he well took advantage of the leisure of nocturnal silence, suitable for instruction. They lost Christ the Savior by seizing and binding him; he found and held Christ, the Word of God, by asking and hearing. [Col. 0304B]

Thus this man was a ruler of the Jews; but the Jews themselves were a brood of vipers (Matt. 23). He was of the Pharisees, whose very name means “those who divide” and who were divided from God; yet, leaving them, he clung to the One and joined himself to the one Word of God. Hence there came to pass that proclamation of blessedness uttered by the voice of Wisdom: “Blessed is the man who hears me, who watches at my doors, and keeps watch at the posts of my doorway” (Prov. 8). That is: this man watched at the doors of wisdom by night with all the eyes not less of his soul than of his body; during one night he watched at its doors, closed in the human daytime.

Was not the body of the incarnate Word the house of Wisdom, concerning which Wisdom itself, its inhabitant, had shortly before said to the Jews: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will build it”? Were not the doors of this house or temple closed especially to those who knocked most irreverently, saying: “This temple was built in forty-six years, and will you build it in three days?”—when they were closed even to those who believed in him, as the Evangelist says: “But Jesus himself did not entrust himself to them”? But this man approached reverently; with those removed—or rather asleep—to whom the inner chamber of this temple ought not to be opened, he watched and knocked with a friendly voice, and summoned to himself Wisdom, the inhabitant of the sacred breast, through the opened doorposts of mouth and tongue. [Col. 0304D]

He is therefore blessed because, escaping the children of darkness whom perhaps he still feared, he sought and found the light in the night, and drew from the mouth of Wisdom great sacraments of our salvation. But now, while he asks, let us examine the words of the Lord who answers, and experience his sayings as sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to our throat and mouth.

[Col. 0305A] “Rabbi,” he says, “we know that you have come from God as a teacher.” It could have been written thus: “Teacher, we know that you have come from God as a teacher.” But he used a fitting diversity of languages, not only for elegance of expression but also to make the sense clear. For it is better shown by this wording that he meant: “We know that you have come from God in order to be a teacher.” Rabbi is said because of the excellence of teaching, although it can be translated into Latin—as can the other Hebrew words—just as certain other untranslated words are uttered because of the excellence or dignity of the things they signify, such as Alleluia, Amen, and any others of that sort.

And indeed we rightly praise the man’s rational zeal, because, laying aside the arrogance of the Pharisees, from among whom he came, he approached our Lord and called him Teacher with a true desire to learn. Yet we note this defect: he did not yet know how to call him Teacher and Lord together, so as already to be equal to those whom he himself approved, saying: “You call me Teacher and Lord, and you say well, for I am” (John 13). But he must be forgiven, and his infant, toothless faith must be awaited until it grows and advances; and soon there will be fulfilled in him what is written: “Those who draw near to his feet shall receive from his teaching” (Deut. 33). Meanwhile, we rejoice that we see him drawing near to his feet when he says: “We know that you have come from God as a teacher. For no one can do these signs which you do, unless God be with him.”

Those who withdrew themselves from this same teaching—namely, the Pharisees, from among whom he too came—said: “By Beelzebub, prince of demons, he casts out demons” (Luke 11). Yet they knew the same thing this man knew—precisely the same thing. For he says of himself and them: “We know that you have come from God as a teacher.” They are therefore rightly charged with having spoken a word against the Holy Spirit which will not be forgiven them, either in this age or in the age to come (Matt. 12). For they knew that he cast out demons by the finger of God, something the magicians in Egypt could also know before Pharaoh when Moses performed signs. For they said: “This is the finger of God” (Exod. 8). Knowing, therefore, that he cast out demons in the Holy Spirit, they said: “By Beelzebub, prince of demons, he casts out demons”—which is the same as saying, a thing dreadful even to hear: “The Holy Spirit is Beelzebub.”

Therefore, because he confessed with his mouth as much as he could understand in his heart, Jesus saw—indeed, had seen beforehand—that he ought to entrust himself to this man and admitted him to the secrets of true Wisdom, which he himself is. For it follows:

“Jesus answered and said to him: ‘Amen, I say to you, unless a person is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.’” “Amen, amen” means “truly” or “faithfully.” Incarnate Truth confirms his sayings with an affirmation fitting to himself, so as to rouse and make attentive one who is drowsy and careless concerning the future. It should be noted that, whereas in the other Evangelists this affirmative expression occurs sometimes more often and sometimes more rarely, it is found more frequently and always doubled in this Evangelist alone. For the matters reported by him are greater and more divine, and therefore demand the hearer’s more attentive mind by a more urgent—that is, ever doubled—cry of affirmation.

It may also rightly be understood that Amen is said in the very name of Truth, which is the Son of God himself, according to that passage in the Apocalypse: “Thus says the Amen, the faithful and true witness, who is the beginning of God’s creation” (Rev. 3). Thus, when he says, “Amen, amen, I say to you,” understand him to say: “I, Truth, speak truth to you.” But let us now continue his words, supported by so great a foundation of truth: “Unless a person is born again,” he says, “he cannot see the kingdom of God.” [Col. 0306B]

Here now, be attentive, since it is proposed to you [to us] not only to chew the kernels of the sacraments but also to touch the bark of the letters. We ask first: to what did the Lord make this answer? For, as the literal text of the Gospel stands, he said these things in answer to Nicodemus. Yet Nicodemus seems to have proposed no question to which Jesus could consequently answer about seeing the kingdom. If he had said, “We know that you have come from God, Christ the King,” no question concerning the suitability of the answer would remain.

Therefore we too, dispersing the night of our ignorance and keeping watch with this Nicodemus in the aid [hearing] of truth, first seek from Nicodemus’s own intention a way to hear the great and profound mysteries of God’s kingdom which are spoken to him. No one can doubt, first, that Nicodemus was present among the many who, as said above, believed in him on the feast day when they saw the signs he performed.
