What did they believe concerning him, except that he was the Messiah whom they had long expected to come: a great king, a victorious king?

This, therefore, was the intention of Nicodemus in coming by night: to learn from him when or how he would sit upon David’s throne and restore the kingdom of Israel. Nor should his statement, “We know that you have come from God as a teacher,” be thought inconsistent with this intention. Indeed, even those who did not know the Scriptures to be from God hoped that the Christ would be not only a king but also a teacher of righteousness. Hence the Samaritan woman says to him: “I know that Messiah is coming, who is called Christ. When he comes, he will declare all things to us” (John 4). How much more, then, could this man—who was a teacher in Israel—knowingly, indeed rightly, call Teacher the one whom he believed to be Messiah?

For those who consider these things, this answer shines forth as exceedingly pleasing and wonderful, rendered as suitably as it was truly, as it befitted supreme Wisdom to speak through its own mouth: “Amen, amen, I say to you: unless a person is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.” What could men already grown old, surrounded by their children, who thought themselves already qualified for God’s kingdom by hereditary right through their fathers, and who had begun to open the greedy bosom of their hearts for the riches that, they supposed, would flow into that kingdom—what could they have wondered at more? They were preparing to raise a stiff neck in contempt of all the Gentiles. What could they wonder at more than that, unless they were first born, they would not see God’s kingdom? Would it not have been easier for them to accept that there would be no kingdom of God than that someone who had been born could be born again? Hence:

“Nicodemus says to him: How can a man be born when he is old? Can he enter his mother’s womb a second time and be born [or, be born again]?” Precisely because he is old, because he is the old man: “For he has grown old among all his enemies” (Ps. VI), he must therefore be born anew; he must be changed; he must be renewed by another generation. But he could not penetrate with an earthly understanding the words of the heavenly man, and therefore he said: “Can a man enter his mother’s womb again and be born?” For he considered only that birth or generation (John I) [Col. 0307B] which is from bloods, from the will of the flesh, and from the will of a man; from which people are not born to become children of God, or to see the kingdom of God. Yet he did not raise this objection, impossible or useless for the kingdom of God, in the intention or spirit in which those above had said: “This temple has been built for forty-six years, and will you build it in three days?” (ibid. II). Otherwise Jesus would not have entrusted himself to him either. Rather, he was knocking with eagerness to learn, not clamouring with the envy of opposition. He judged himself deficient in understanding rather than Christ to be uttering empty things.

“Jesus answered: Amen, amen, I say to you, unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.” It is not impossible, he says, for those who wish to enter [Col. 0307C] the kingdom of God, what is proposed. For I did not say that a man must “enter his mother’s womb again and be born.” There is another birth by which it is possible for any man, however old, to be born anew. It is possible, indeed, to apply water to a human being and to invoke the Holy Spirit over the water. Once invoked, he is immediately present and sanctifies the element familiar to him—familiar, I say, for “in the beginning he moved over the waters” (Gen. I). And it is altogether impossible for the invocation of his name to be ineffective, especially for this work over the waters, when he is invoked with the name of the Father and of the Son. Thus a human being may enter, not his mother’s womb, but the fountain of God’s grace, and be born anew.

Yet another truly enters his mother’s womb again when he is restored by true faith to the bosom of this grace. For grace is our mother; the one harmonious and beloved city of God and of all his blessed angels is our mother. We were badly born from her womb and cast out when, in the first parent, abandoning the repose of Paradise, we fell into this exile because of sin. The holy man mystically laments the unhappiness of that birth, saying: “Let the day perish on which I was born, and the night on which it was said, ‘A man has been conceived’ . . . Why did I not die in the womb? Why did I not perish at once when I came out of the womb? Why was I received upon knees? Why nursed at breasts?” etc. (Job III). By these words he bewails the four stages of original sin: suggestion, delight, consent, and defence, [Col. 0308A] by which four modes every sin is consummated.

Thus, having been born unto death, we are rightly said to be reborn unto life when we are immersed in baptism through the sacraments of our same mother—from whom we were divided by sin—that is, the heavenly Church. For thus we have passed from the three stages of the left-hand generation to the likewise three stages of the right-hand generation: from the devil to God; from the old Adam to the new, that is, Christ; from the progenitors of our own flesh to the holy ministers or priests of the Catholic Church, through whom we begin to ascend. Therefore, when Nicodemus said, “Can a man enter his mother’s womb again and be born?” the Lord rightly did not deny that this could happen. For it can happen, not according to his carnal understanding, [Col. 0308B] but according to the truth of the spiritual sacrament; and it does happen.

It must be understood, however, that the efficacy of this sacrament did not begin to be celebrated immediately upon these words, nor while the same Lord, our God—an immortal man among men—dwelt clothed in our mortality. But when, by rising from the dead, he himself began to reign and entered first into the glory of his kingdom, then those who saw the kingdom of God first began to be reborn: namely, by dying and rising again with him through baptism. Then the rule for baptism was first given by him when he said: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII). For neither through John’s baptism nor through any other remedy [Col. 0308C] could this entrance into the kingdom of God now under discussion be opened to anyone before the King himself acquired the kingdom of God by his Passion; before, through the water and blood flowing from his side, he instituted the sacrament of baptism itself, redeeming the whole Church—which, as has been said elsewhere, awaited him among the dead—with that same blood, and washing it with that same water for the remission of sins (John XIX).

But since he spoke these things to a circumcised man and, without any exception for circumcision or uncircumcision, said universally, “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God,” the matter itself seems to demand that we ask—or rather, that we answer with the Apostle those who ask: “What advantage then has the Jew, or what is the usefulness of circumcision?” (Rom. III). For it is clear that, when the Lord said these things, no one had yet entered the kingdom of God. Therefore, since he said without exception, “unless someone is born again,” it is clear that those detained among the dead also had to be reborn “of water and the Holy Spirit,” however holy or righteous they might have been. As has already been said elsewhere, this happened when Christ, dying upon the cross, paid Adam’s debt and regenerated the whole Church that had existed hitherto (Col. II), when in death he wonderfully poured forth blood and water from his side (John XIX), from which she might be reborn—just as he took a rib from the side of sleeping Adam, from which Eve might be fashioned (Gen. II).

Therefore, concerning the reason or usefulness of circumcision, we must argue in such a way as to understand together that it rightly ought to have ceased from the time when, as Christ died upon the cross, the sacrament of baptism was instituted. The Apostle Paul testifies that circumcision was given as a sign of the righteousness of faith, saying: “We say that Abraham’s faith was reckoned as righteousness. How then was it reckoned? In circumcision, or in uncircumcision? Not in circumcision, but in uncircumcision. And he received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of the faith which is in uncircumcision, of our father Abraham, that he might be the father of all who believe through uncircumcision, so that it might be reckoned to them also as righteousness, and that he might be the father of circumcision” (Rom. IV), etc.

This is plain from the sequence of the book of Genesis: Abraham was justified through faith before circumcision, when the same Scripture says, “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness,” and he was called the friend of God (Gen. XV). The Apostle adds that he was marked with the sign of circumcision, saying: “and he received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of faith” (Rom. IV). For he was marked as a vessel of righteousness, containing the treasure of faith which he had already offered to God as the price of the promise, so that by this sign the covenant of that promise might be confirmed and God, who had promised, might rightfully be held as debtor. For when God had said, “Every male among you shall be circumcised, and you shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskin,” he immediately added, “that it may be a sign of the covenant between me and you” (Gen. XVII). The Apostle therefore rightly says that “he received the sign of circumcision, a seal [Col. 0309C] of the righteousness of faith” (Rom. IV).

But what had God promised him, or what had he believed so as to be justified, that he received this sign of faith? God had promised, and Abraham had believed, that his seed would be as the stars of heaven, and that in his seed all nations of the earth would be blessed (Gen. XV). This promise concerning the blessing of the nations in his seed was confirmed in God’s first and last address to him. For at the first appearance, commanding him to depart from his land and kindred, he said: “Blessing, I shall bless you, and I shall multiply your seed, and in you all kindreds of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. XII). At the last, when Abraham offered his son to God, God called to him from heaven and, with the interposition of an oath, renewed the promise of blessing: “Your seed,” he says, [Col. 0309D] “shall possess the gates of its enemies, and in your seed all nations of the earth shall be blessed, because you obeyed my voice” (Gen. XXII). Hence it is called a renewed promise, because first and second a promise was made concerning the nations to be blessed in his seed.

Therefore, since Abraham’s faith, which was reckoned to him as righteousness, consisted in his belief in the promise of the seed, and since God wished this faith to be marked, where more fittingly than in that part of the body through which seed passes should it have been marked? For the Jews are accustomed mockingly to object when we say to them that circumcision was a sign of faith: “Why,” they say, “was this sign placed not rather upon the ear, the lips, or some other uncovered part of the body, rather than upon that part which is always covered, so that it might be more visible if, as you say, it was given as a sign of faith?” Yet they cannot deny, compelled by the authority of their own Scripture, that it was given by God as a sign of faith, as has been stated. We therefore say to them: Since circumcision is a sign of faith, and faith concerned the promise of the seed, should it not more suitably, in accordance with its cause, have been placed upon the very organ through which seed is emitted, rather than upon any other part of the body?

Therefore, as has been said, by the authority of the Apostle—and indeed of the old Scripture—circumcision is a sign of faith. But this faith concerns the promise of the seed. It follows that circumcision is a profession of expectation for that seed; and whoever is circumcised professes that he awaits that seed, which is Christ. For the promise was made not concerning seeds, as though many, but concerning one seed, namely Christ (Gal. III). But whoever professes that he awaits this seed’s future coming certainly denies that it has come. Therefore, all of us who confess that Christ has come in the flesh, circumcision having been abolished, need only the sacrament of that same Christ our Lord, of which he now speaks: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.” If we were circumcised, Christ would profit us nothing (Gal. V), because by that sign we would profess that we awaited his future coming and thereby deny that he has come.

But the Jew replies: What God has once established for eternity, he himself never permits or commands to be changed. We agree: God is unchangeable. [Col. 0310C] He adds accordingly: He established circumcision as an everlasting covenant, an eternal pact. For he speaks thus to Abraham concerning it: “I will establish my covenant between me and you, and between your seed after you in their generations, as an everlasting covenant” (Gen. XVII). And shortly afterward: “My covenant shall be in your flesh as an eternal covenant.” Therefore, he is not from God who both does not keep the Sabbath himself and, through his baptized persons or baptizers, dissolves the everlasting covenant of circumcision.

When the Jews argue thus, we aptly and inaptly sing to them that verse of the Psalm: “Let their table before them become a snare, a recompense, and a stumbling-block” (Ps. LXXXVIII). For in this way it is fulfilled in them: the table of this Scripture and of the other sacred readings becomes a snare to them, so that they are ensnared by wrongly understanding it; and it becomes a fitting recompense to them that, being made to stumble, they are not permitted to attain the light of truth.

What then? Does this Scripture proclaim that God appointed the rite of circumcision for eternity? The succession of birth and generation will not be eternal, yet could the law of circumcision be eternal? What, then? Let us examine the very words of Scripture more carefully, lest we suppose them in any respect excusable. What did God will to be eternal? What did he establish as everlasting? His covenant, his pact. What is that covenant? What is that pact? Is circumcision itself a covenant or pact? Certainly not: it is the sign of the covenant or pact. For when God had said, “Every male among you shall be circumcised, and you shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskin” (Gen. XVII), he immediately added: “that it may be a sign of the covenant between me and you.” Therefore circumcision is not the covenant, but the sign of the covenant. As great as the difference between the writing of a testator and the seal impressed upon it, so great, certainly, is the difference between the promise made to Abraham concerning the seed, which is Christ, and circumcision itself. The promise of the seed, met by Abraham’s eager faith, is the pact or covenant; circumcision, however, is the sign of the covenant.

And God indeed said that the covenant would be everlasting; but when he said, “that it may be a sign of the covenant between me and you,” he did not add “eternal.” For then perhaps it could in some manner rightly be understood that circumcision must be practised forever—though this is as impossible as it is untrue that the succession of generating and being born is eternal. But now the covenant is indeed eternal, because the eternal seed was promised, believed, and given; circumcision, however, which is the sign of the pact or covenant, can neither be practised eternally nor ought it now to be practised, after the coming of that promised seed.

It is still asked why the holy Fathers before Christ’s coming did not enter the kingdom of God. Were they not themselves justified by the same faith? To this we answer: Why are our catechumens not admitted to the communion of the sacrament of the holy Church—for example, of the Lord’s body and blood? Do they not believe in their hearts and confess with their mouths the faith of Christ? (Rom. X). “Of course,” you say, “because they have not yet been regenerated in the sacred font.” Precisely so: the saints of old likewise ought not to have been received into communion of glory and the vision of God by that heavenly Church; nor was it fitting that human righteousnesses of whatever sort should be received among the brightness of angelic innocence or charity, since all of them, Isaiah testifying, were like “the cloth of a menstruating woman” (Isa. LXIV), unless they had first been washed in the flood of blood and water flowing from Christ’s side.

The Jewish adversary nevertheless continues to object: Since your Christ, who gave you baptism, was circumcised, why do you exclude circumcision rather than being circumcised after his example before you are baptized? Why do you not admit that element of our religion which you cannot deny that your Christ accepted in his own flesh? It would be surprising if they did not also object why we do not offer a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons as a sacrifice for our firstborn infants, since Christ himself was purified by such an offering according to the law of Moses (Luke XXII).

But sound teaching of the faith has long since silenced this aforesaid objection and the ignorance of all foolish people. First, with the Apostle, we say that Christ was given as a minister of circumcision for the truth of God, to confirm the promises of the fathers (Rom. V); and for that reason he was made under the law and was rightly circumcised according to the law, so that, as a circumcised, lawful, and blameless minister, he might proclaim the grace of his salvation (Gal. IV). Next we add this: the seed promised to Abraham (Gen. XV) is Christ himself, the one seed. Until he came, generations were counted, tribes and families, kindreds and households separately distinguished and carefully observed (Matt. I; Num. XXXVI), lest, when Christ came, it should be uncertain that he was descended from Abraham’s seed, from the tribe of Judah, from the family of Perez, from the house of David, to whose faith he had likewise been promised (Ps. LXXXVIII).

But Christ himself begot no one according to the flesh. Keeping his flesh in perpetual virginity, he showed that the generations of Abraham’s flesh were completed in himself, the one seed promised to Abraham. And, if you consider rightly, beyond this seed of Abraham, which is Christ, no genealogy of Abraham’s flesh ought any longer to be extended or reckoned. Therefore, just as Christ begot no one according to the flesh, so consequently he ought to circumcise no one according to the flesh. He was rightly born according to the flesh from those by whom he was also rightly circumcised according to the flesh; likewise, he rightly circumcised none of us according to the flesh, since he begot none of us according to the flesh. Where Christ was given as the eternal heir, there, as the generation of flesh ceased in him, so circumcision of the flesh likewise rightly fails. He is the originator of another—that is, a spiritual—genealogy, and consequently of another sacrament for us as well.

For a second—indeed now a third—time God made a covenant with us in Christ. Observe carefully the threefold development of the covenant he made with humankind. First he made it with Noah; second with Abraham; third [Col. 0312C] with Abraham’s seed, which is Christ. In accordance with the reality and faith of each, he varied—or rather brought ever nearer in each—the sign of his covenant. Noah believed the coming flood when God foretold it; believing, he obeyed by building the ark, and did everything God commanded him. He received a sign suited to the reality and faith in question (Gen. VI): namely, the bow set in the clouds of heaven. God said: “I will set my bow in the clouds of heaven, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and the earth; and I will remember my covenant which I made with you” (ibid. IX), because the flood which he had believed would come at God’s word descended chiefly from the clouds.

Abraham, however, believed and obeyed God, who commanded him to depart from his land and kindred and promised to bless and multiply him and to bless all nations in his seed (ibid. XII). He received the sign of God’s covenant no longer outside himself, as Noah had received it in the clouds, but within himself—yet outwardly in the flesh, in that part of the body through which, as said above, seed is transmitted. This was fitting because, strengthened in faith, he had not doubted the promise of the seed (ibid. XVII).

Finally Christ, because he served not only faithfully but knowingly—for he could be ignorant of nothing—“became obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. II). He received—indeed, he gave—the everlasting sign of the eternal covenant: a sign now to be placed neither outside the human being nor in one part of the human being, but one by which the whole human being, inwardly and outwardly, is together regenerated and sanctified by a visible sacrament and an invisible power. To examine this, let us now return to the words of the Gospel reading itself.

“Unless someone is born again,” he says, “of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.” Anyone who knows how to weigh the words of God and recognizes with clear insight the splendour of divine utterance can plainly see that it was said far more carefully, “Unless someone is born again of water and spirit,” [Col. 0313B] than if it had been said, “Unless someone is baptized.” To be baptized seems indeed to mean the same as being born again of water and spirit; yet there is some difference. Everyone born again of water and spirit has indeed been baptized, but not conversely: not everyone baptized has also been born again of the Spirit. To make this clear, we must first seek a definition of one who has been born again.

The one who has been born again is the person renewed in the spirit of his mind, who has put off the old man with his deeds and put on the new man, created according to God in righteousness and holiness of truth (Eph. IV). But many of those baptized in water are not renewed in the spirit of their mind. They do not lay aside the deeds of the old man, although immersed in water they profess to put on the new man. Truth therefore speaks providently when it prefers to say, “Unless someone has been born again,” rather than “Unless someone has been baptized.”

Accordingly, Simon Magus was baptized in water but was not baptized in the Holy Spirit (Acts VIII), for “the Holy Spirit of discipline flees the deceitful man” (Wis. I). Thus he may be called baptized but not born again. So too many others are baptized but are not born again, and therefore are rightly compared to defective fetuses: conceived indeed in the womb but not quickened, or losing the life breathed into them at once and being cast out as miscarriages. These also are likened to those who passed through the Red Sea but fell in the wilderness and did not enter the land of promise (Num. XIV). But those born again of water and the Holy Spirit, who perseveringly enter the kingdom of God, are like those who crossed both the Red Sea and the Jordan and, victorious by the prowess of their battles, obtained the promised land.

Those baptized by heretics likewise have been baptized; the washing of the flesh is not repeated for them. Yet they have by no means been born again: they come forth already dead and indeed have never lived (John XII). Hence they are not even comparable to those fetuses which, having been quickened in the mother’s womb, die before being brought forth. Yet if they return to the unity of the Church and, through confession of the Catholic faith, submit themselves to the one mother Church, then they are quickened by Christ’s Spirit, which is in her alone. Thus they too are numbered among those reborn to see [Col. 0314A] the kingdom of God. They differ only, as it were, in birth from those baptized in the Catholic faith and Church, but they attain fellowship in the same kingdom—just as Gad and Asher, Dan and Naphtali, were born more obscurely from slave-women, yet nevertheless received an equal measuring-line in the division of the land.

Now that the proposition has been heard—that Truth has explained what is necessary for seeing the kingdom of God (ibid. XVI)—let us hear the reason he appended for this hearer whom he had undertaken to instruct. It follows:

“That which is born of flesh is flesh; and that which is born of spirit is spirit.” The good teacher, who had no need for anyone to question him, did not wait for Nicodemus to ask, “Why can no one enter the kingdom of God unless he is reborn?” Rather, of his own accord he gave a very subtle reason in the most subtle manner. “That which is born,” he says, “of flesh is flesh; and that which is born of spirit is spirit.” This argument requires an intelligent and sharp hearer. For, upon hearing this proposition of the heavenly dialectician, he should immediately, prompted by the same Spirit through whom he was reborn, infer and say: But all human beings are born of flesh—of sinful flesh, which does not know God, loves the world, and follows its own desires (Rom. VII). The kingdom of God, however, is wholly in the Holy Spirit; it wholly consists in spirit and truth (1 John II). It possesses nothing earthly, admits nothing perishable, and contains nothing vain or foolish (Luke XVII; [Col. 0314C] John IV; Rom. VIII).

Before all else, you who say these things, King and Emperor of this kingdom of God, were born indeed of flesh, but not of flesh alone. For you were conceived and born from the Holy Spirit and virgin flesh. Therefore you are flesh, indeed true flesh, because you were born of flesh; but you are also spirit, because you were conceived of the Holy Spirit. All other human beings are flesh only, because they were conceived and born from flesh alone. When you, whoever you are, have made this inference, he concludes thus: Therefore, he says,

“Do not marvel that I said to you: You must be born anew.” Do not marvel, he says; rather, it would be marvellous if I had said that an unreborn human being could enter the kingdom of God. For an unreborn human being is flesh, but the kingdom of God is spirit. These—flesh and spirit—are contrary, and, as the Apostle says, oppose one another (Gal. V). The person not reborn does not feel the unpacified conflict and mutual opposition of these antagonists, because he is entirely flesh and has nothing of the spirit opposed to flesh. But once he has been reborn and grows in this new generation, he experiences grave struggles of flesh and spirit. For he delights in the law of God according to the inward human being, yet sees another law in his members, opposing the law of his mind, leading him captive under the law of sin which is in his members; and he groans: “Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. VII).

When the grace of God delivers one who cries out thus continually, even while still living he is no longer in the flesh; he does not know the passions which were working through his flesh. And if the proud handmaid murmurs at all, she is immediately sternly afflicted by her mistress, reason. Therefore, since an unreborn human being, as said above, is flesh, whereas God’s kingdom is spirit; and since flesh and spirit are contrary and oppose one another, “do not marvel,” says the Lord, “that I said to you: You must be born anew.” For it would be more astonishing if I had said that an unreborn person, born of flesh and being flesh, could enter the kingdom of God, which is entirely spirit—that is, spiritual.

Nicodemus could have replied to this—as one inexperienced and unacquainted with the grace of this birth: [Col. 0315B] “Who then can enter the kingdom of God?” So too, when Jesus himself said, “It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for one who possesses riches to enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XIX), his disciples heard it and marvelled, saying: “Who then can be saved?” He immediately came to the aid of their wavering hope: “With human beings this is impossible,” he says, “but with God all things are possible” (Luke XVIII). Thus Nicodemus too might here have fallen away from hope in the kingdom of God, supposing it impossible to be born again of the Holy Spirit. For why would a visible human being think it possible that he could be born from an invisible spirit? This too is impossible with human beings.

Therefore, because “with human beings this is indeed impossible, but with God this and all things are possible,” he immediately adds: “The Spirit breathes where he wills.” By this saying he commends at once the grace and power of the Holy Spirit. That he is under no obligation and yet wills is grace; that “he breathes where he wills” is omnipotence. And truly this Spirit owes nothing to any human being, because Adam, the first father of all, transgressed; by a just law he was disinherited from God’s kingdom, which is now under discussion. Since the kingdom of God was justly closed to all, the fact that it is opened to some by this regenerating Spirit belongs to gratuitous mercy, or merciful grace; but the fact that it is not opened to others belongs to just vengeance, or the justice of the avenger.

He says therefore: “The Spirit breathes where he wills.” As if he said: Do not say in your heart, “Who will ascend into heaven” (Deut. XXX), to bring down this Holy Spirit, so that we may be reborn in him and thus enter [Col. 0315D] the kingdom of God? For he himself graciously and freely deigns, and is able, to breathe upon us. And as soon as, through that power by which “he breathes where he wills,” he sends himself upon the waters, he works the wondrous work of his power: the inanimate element is made alive—not with animal life, but with spiritual power—and becomes the gate of God’s kingdom, the bridal bed of heavenly grace, and the womb of the mother Church above.

For what maternal entrails do, so that received seed may cohere and be quickened, this element does when the Holy Spirit comes upon it: a human being born from the mass of ruin and death is reborn into the assembly of the living and the people of possession (Eph. II). In this manner he breathes equally upon all, regenerates all equally, and gives remission of sins equally to all (1 Pet. II). But he does not give gifts of grace equal or identical to all; rather, he breathes upon each when and as he wills, and divides to each as he wills—giving to one the word of wisdom, to another kinds of tongues, to another discernment of spirits (1 Cor. XII), etc.

Once this has happened, the new person who has been reborn does not cease to speak of the kingdom of God into which he has been reborn, to invoke the Father by whom he has been regenerated, to proclaim the word by which he has been refreshed, and to confess in the Holy Spirit by whom he has been renewed. Hence the Lord now, having said, “The Spirit breathes where he wills,” immediately adds:

“And you hear his voice, but do not know where he comes from or where he goes.” This was said then uniquely to Nicodemus, and it was undoubtedly said truly. For the voice which he then heard, saying, “Amen, amen, I say to you, unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God,” etc., was the voice—indeed, is the voice—of the Holy Spirit. This new man, this heavenly man who speaks these things, was conceived by that Spirit; and all of us must be reborn in likeness to him through the same Spirit (Eph. IV), so that we may see his kingdom. This clearly is the voice of the Holy Spirit. For he does not speak fleshly things but spiritual things; not human but divine things; not earthly but heavenly things (1 Cor. XV).

Yet Nicodemus does not know where he comes from or where he goes, because he is wholly ignorant from what time, with what fullness, the same Spirit rests upon this man through whom he speaks; and he does not know to what kingdom, or in what order, the Spirit intends to bring him. For he does not yet know that from the very beginning of his conception this man was sanctified by the sevenfold Spirit, or that he would reach the point of offering himself to God through the same Holy Spirit as a living sacrifice for the whole world, a sacrifice of sweet savour; and that he would accomplish this in such an order that those reborn of water and the same Spirit might enter the kingdom of God. He therefore rightly says to him, “And you do not know where he comes from or where he goes,” because, ignorant of these mysteries, he expected God’s spiritual kingdom in a fleshly manner.

Nevertheless, this must also be understood of individual human beings, according to the measure or proportion of the gifts which the one and same Spirit works, distributing to each as he wills (ibid. XII). For when we hear someone possessed of some such gifts speaking or prophesying, we hear the Spirit’s voice, because we recognize that what he says is spiritual. But we do not know where he comes from or where he goes, because we do not know when or how the speaker received the grace to utter mysteries, or toward what end or fruit that grace with which he now appears endowed will proceed.

Hence he immediately adds:

“So is everyone who is born of the Spirit.” But this says too little. For not only does the one who hears his voice not know where the Spirit comes from or where he goes; the speaker himself does not know from where, or through what merits, he has received the Spirit. Nor does he know where he goes; that is, he does not know whether he will receive eternal grace in return for this temporal grace. “For man does not know his end” (Eccl. X), and all things are reserved as uncertain for future time. Paul likewise does not reckon that he has laid hold of it (Phil. III), and altogether “a human being does not know whether he is worthy of love or hatred” (Eccl. IX).

“Nicodemus answered and said to him: How can these things come about?” He does not ask, as an unbeliever, how these things can be possible; rather, convinced that the things he heard from so great a teacher would be fulfilled—for he had just confessed that he was a teacher come from God—he asks that it be explained to him by what manner or order they can be accomplished. Indeed, the Lord could have explained much more plainly to this disciple all that he had said from the place where he declared: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” [John 2; Col. 0317B], saying, for example:

“This body of mine is that temple of which I said to the Jews: ‘Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.’ They will destroy it—not because I command it, but because I permit it; they will destroy it, I say, by the violence of suffering and the cross. Then a lance will open the side of this temple, and water together with blood will come forth; and all to whom this water comes shall be saved” [John 19; Ezek. 47]. “Its invisible power also reaches all the elect who are dead, namely those for whose salvation this temple of my body is permitted to be destroyed. This water with blood will also reach all the living who shall believe in me [Col. 0317C]. When I have raised this temple in three days—that is, when I have risen from the dead—I shall give the rule of that necessary regeneration of which I now speak, saying: ‘Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit’” [Matt. 28]. “With the invocation of this Name, this water will come to them, and they shall be saved. For with it, both to the dead and to the living, the Spirit of forgiveness will be given: so that, as sin has been committed through bodily thoughts and the five bodily senses, so they may be cleansed through the bodily element of water and the incorporeal Spirit. Otherwise the entrance into the kingdom of God cannot be opened.”

In this way, certainly, he could have explained his sayings more fully. But Jesus did not yet entrust himself so fully even to him, knowing that he too could not bear such things [Col. 0317D]. For he says also concerning his own apostles of this sort: “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” [John 16]. Therefore, withholding these matters for the time, he says: “Are you a teacher in Israel, and do not know these things?”

Appropriately he knocks down the pride not only of this man, but also of all the scribes and Pharisees who “sat on Moses’ seat” [Matt. 23]. For, loving the chief seats in the synagogues and to be called Rabbi by men, they certainly did not possess the true understanding of those Scriptures whose teaching they professed. If they had been true teachers in Israel, they would have known the Scriptures; how then could they be ignorant of these things? For what else did they read, for example, in Ezekiel when he says: “I will take you from the nations, and gather you from all lands, and bring you into your own land; and I will pour clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed from all your defilements, and I will give you a new spirit” [Ezek. 36; Col. 0318A]? What else, I ask, does this Scripture say than precisely what the Lord now says: “You must be born again of water and the Spirit”? And what land does it promise after the pouring out of water and Spirit, when it says, “You shall dwell in the land which I gave to your fathers,” if not the kingdom of God? For he now says that we cannot otherwise enter it except by being thus reborn.

It is therefore as though he had said: “Unless I first pour clean water upon you and place my Spirit within you, you shall not dwell in the land which I gave to your fathers; indeed, you shall not enter the kingdom of God [Col. 0318B], which I once gave to your first parents” [Gen. 2]. Likewise in Ezekiel, chapter 47: what are the waters issuing from the temple on the right side, by which the other waters are healed and great fish are produced, but the waters of baptism and the gifts of the Holy Spirit? Flowing from the temple of Christ and his Church, they heal and regenerate all peoples so that they may enter the kingdom of God.

I pass over the fact that Zechariah, speaking of this same regeneration in baptism, says: “There shall be an open fountain for the house of David, for the washing of the menstruous woman” [Zech. 13]; and the other such passages scattered throughout the Scriptures. Since the scribes and Pharisees, one of whom this man was, were ignorant of all these things, they are proved falsely to have arrogated to themselves the name and position of teachers. The Lord says: “Are you a teacher [Col. 0318C] in Israel, and do not know these things?” What he says to one, he says to all. It is as though he said: “You are ignorant of these things, and are you a teacher in Israel?” Restraining his own disciples from their presumption, he says: “Neither be called teachers, for one is your teacher, Christ” [Matt. 23].

For Christ alone is truly our one teacher, “in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” [Col. 2]. By the Holy Spirit he opened the understanding of his disciples so that they might understand the Scriptures; he “hid these things from the wise and prudent, and revealed them to little ones” [Luke 10; Matt. 11]. Concerning the truth of his teaching he immediately adds: “Amen, amen, I say to you: what we know we speak, and what we have seen we testify; and you do not receive our testimony” [Col. 0318D].

It should be noted that, although above and below he speaks in the singular—“Amen, amen, I say to you,” and so forth—in this verse alone he preferred to speak in the plural: “What we know we speak, and what we have seen we testify,” and so forth. This is because he declares that he gives testimony and calls his speech testimony; but the testimony of one person is not legally valid, whereas every word is established by the mouth of two or three witnesses. Rightly, therefore, he does not say, “What I have seen I testify, and you do not receive my testimony”; but, “What we have seen we testify, and you do not receive our testimony,” wishing himself and the Father to be understood, as he says elsewhere: “I am he who bears witness concerning myself, and the Father who sent me bears witness concerning me” [John 8; Col. 0319A].

The sense is: We are not, he says, like the teachers, scribes, and Pharisees, among whom you are, who have taken away the key of knowledge and neither enter themselves nor allow others to enter [Luke 11]. We do not speak from conjectural presumption, as those do who speak from themselves, seeking their own glory and prophesying from their own hearts. Rather, “what we know and what we have seen”—a certain reality existing in truth, the true sense of the Scriptures whose teaching we profess—we speak and testify. For what does the one divinity of Father and Son not know? What does it not see—that divinity in which all things subsist, which governs and fills all things?

Nor should this be passed over: although he speaks to Nicodemus alone, he does not say in the singular, as elsewhere, “You do not receive our testimony,” but “You do not receive our testimony” in the plural [Col. 0319B]—that is, you scribes and Pharisees, who consider yourselves wise and teachers merely because men call you Rabbi, and who, fearing injury to your reputation, scorn to hear teaching and to acquiesce in truth. This was not to be said to him alone: he belonged to them indeed, yet was coming out from among them and desired to hear this man as a teacher come from God.

But he proves by argument that they do not wish to receive his testimony, saying: “If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things?” [John 3:12]. It is an earthly thing that a temple made with hands should be destroyed and rebuilt in three days. It is earthly, I say, in your understanding—that is, when it is understood as the words outwardly sound, beyond which your earthly understanding does not rise. Yet you do not believe that I can accomplish this in so brief a time, since you do not know that I am the Word through whom the world and everything in it were created in six days. As I said, you do not believe that I can accomplish so quickly what was done by human beings, though over a longer period—namely forty-six years—and is therefore an earthly work [Col. 0319C].

Yet these things are in truth heavenly: the temple is heavenly, built from heaven, not made by hands but created by God. How then will you believe, if I tell you that you will destroy it by crucifying it, and that I will rebuild it in three days by rising from the dead, and that from then on human beings will begin to be reborn, themselves rising from their sins? If I tell you these things and others like them, which are truly heavenly, will you believe?

It follows: “And no one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven.” And this, he says, is “Amen,” that is, “Truly I say to you”; or, the very thing I have already told you—that no one can enter the kingdom of God unless reborn of water and the Holy Spirit—I confirm again to you by an equivalent argument: “No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven.”

It is therefore beneficial for all to put on the Son of Man by being reborn through water and the Spirit, or to be incorporated into him, so that because they are born of flesh, because they are flesh, and thus cannot ascend to heaven, they may be lifted there by him who alone can ascend into heaven [Col. 0320A]. And as the members follow the head, and “wherever the body is, there the eagles will be gathered” [Matt. 24; Luke 17], so all who, reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, put on Christ and are incorporated into Christ may be lifted into heaven by the vehicle of his divinity and fed eternally by the food of his vision.

At this point the Nestorian heresy is struck with a double blow. Dividing Christ, it wished one person to be the Son of God and another to be the son of man. For how did the son of man descend from heaven, when the angel Gabriel was sent to the Virgin and, by his voice, the Word of the Father penetrated the inward ear of the same Virgin [Luke 1]? Up to that point he was not the son of man, but only the Son of God. And how was the Son of Man already in heaven when he said, “the Son of Man who is in heaven,” though, while speaking these words, he stood upon two feet—or perhaps sat folded up upon the earth [Col. 0320B]?

How, I ask, did the Son of Man both descend from heaven and already exist in heaven, unless the man taken from the earth is one person with the Word that descended from heaven, and unless, with the man speaking on earth, God—who is both in heaven and everywhere—is one and the same person? Therefore he who descended is himself also he who ascended above all heavens [Eph. 4], one and the same Son of God and son of man. He was able to ascend because, as heretics have dared blasphemously to say, he did not take his beginning from Mary; rather, he descended into her from heaven, where he had existed before Mary.

All these things, however, were spoken to Nicodemus in order that for the present they might remain closed, as though covered beneath a veil; for, although he asked, the manner in which these things could be accomplished was not stated. For it was truly night; and so these sayings and whatever like them were gathered together, in order that, when day had risen—that is, when Jesus was glorified through his resurrection and ascension—his words might be compared with his deeds, indeed both words and deeds with the Scriptures, and then at last rightly understood [Col. 0320C].

This too is worthy of reverence in the grace of his lips: though he could have said, “No one ascends into heaven except I, who am in heaven,” just as he says below, “Thus the Son of Man must be lifted up,” though he could have said, “Thus I must be lifted up,” nevertheless, as in almost all other places, it was customary for his mouth to call himself the Son of Man. Indeed, with this title his sayings breathe more sweetly the fragrance of humility. By this example we too are taught to avoid words nearer to boasting.

But beyond this there is another reason why we should delight more deeply in this name, Son of Man. For he wishes us to understand that he is our neighbor and our brother, having so frequently upon his lips the designation Son of Man. And without doubt he shows himself more closely related to us in this manner than if he called himself merely man [Col. 0320D]. To make this indisputable, it is worth answering those who are accustomed to ask why God, in assuming humanity for the restoration of humankind, did not form from the earth the man whom he would assume—as he made Adam from it—but took true human nature from Adam’s own race, from the lost mass, from the seed of Abraham, the stock of David, the flesh or seed of Mary, though she was a virgin.

The brief answer is this: he could indeed have formed from the earth a new man to assume; he would have been flesh and blood, but not our flesh or our blood; a man indeed, but not our neighbor; truly a man, but not the Son of Man. Therefore the ground of our redemption would not have been so just, since the flesh that had not committed sin would not make expiation for the sin committed; nor could the righteousness of one man, unknown and alien to our race, so properly be reckoned ours [Col. 0321A].

But now “mercy and peace have met each other” [Ps. 84], because in one and the same Christ divinity sought us mercifully and our flesh reconciled us justly, since he is both God and man, our Creator and our neighbor. Thus he fittingly speaks to us with kindred affection in that grace which “is poured out upon his lips” [Ps. 54], when he so often and so familiarly calls himself the Son of Man: so that we may render to the one and same Christ, as our Creator, the fear and honor due to him, and may approach him as our neighbor with confident love.

It follows: “And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that everyone who believes in him may not perish but may have eternal life.” See what kind of life, what kind of entrance into the kingdom of God, the Savior gradually reveals to one man awaiting that kingdom, and in that one man to all who await or seek it. He had said that no one could see the kingdom of God unless reborn; and reborn not from just anywhere, but from water and the Holy Spirit blowing wherever he wills, and so forth [Col. 0321B].

These were great and lofty things; yet they had not raised Nicodemus so high that he should think more of him than he first confessed when he said: “We know that you have come from God as a teacher.” But now he begins to hear what he did not expect to hear: namely, that this same teacher is not only man but also God. For in whom else ought one to believe but God? Indeed, in whom, if not in God alone, is belief not ruinous? Yet this teacher who came from God plainly teaches that one must believe in himself: “That everyone,” he says, “who believes in him may not perish but may have eternal life.” Therefore he openly testifies concerning himself that he is God [Col. 0321C].

Consider also, in this testimony to his divinity, how much humility it breathes, though it is the loftiest confession: “As Moses,” he says, “lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up.” He acknowledges that the serpent was made as a figure of himself [Num. 21]; indeed, he testifies that he commanded a serpent to be made as a figure of himself. For who did this and the other things, or commanded them to be done, but God, but the Word of God? Yet this man, this very Christ who speaks these things, is the Word of the Lord which came to Moses and to all the holy prophets. Therefore he who commanded it to be made himself testifies that it was made in likeness of himself.

The history is well known. The people spoke against Moses and the Lord because they were weary of the journey and toil: “Why,” they said, “did you bring us out of Egypt, that we might die in the wilderness?” [Num. 21; Col. 0321D]. For this reason the Lord sent fiery serpents among the people. When they cried out greatly to Moses because of their bites and wounds, and he prayed to the Lord, the Lord said: “Make a bronze serpent and set it up as a sign; whoever has been struck and looks upon it shall live.” And this was done [ibid.].

His humility, mindful of this sign of himself—humility which, in order to lift us to heaven, lowered itself to the earth—says: “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up.” The likeness of that sign, then, which was foretold or recalled to Nicodemus on that night, must be considered by us in clear daylight. There are indeed several features which complete the likeness of this lifting up of the Son of Man [Col. 0322A].

First, it was a sign given against the bites of serpents. Second, it was not just any sign, but the image of a serpent that was set forth. Third, it was made not of stone or wood, but of bronze. Fourth, it bestowed a remedy upon those who looked merely by sight. All these things constitute a certain likeness of our Lord, Prince, and Savior, lifted up to give repentance and forgiveness of sins.

For the bites of serpents are sins, by which the human race was wounded after the devil deceived the first man through a serpent. Against these bites a sign was given: namely, Christ himself, who here speaks of himself. Simeon said of him when he held him in his arms: “Behold, this one is set for the fall and rising [Col. 0322B] of many in Israel, and for a sign that shall be contradicted” [Luke 2].

How, or by whom, was this sign contradicted? Most of all, it was contradicted by the Jews, who called him magician, evildoer, and deceiver [Matt. 27; John 7]. They persisted in crying this out until they counted him, when lifted onto the cross, among criminals, as the prophet had foretold [Isa. 53; Mark 15]. Thus there was a certain likeness to a serpent, because they wished nothing else to be said or thought about him except, “He is a magician; he is a deceiver.”

He could indeed be called and judged such; but just as that serpent was a serpent only in form—indeed, in appearance alone—and did not possess the serpent’s poison, so he, condemned in human judgment in the likeness of sinful flesh and crucified among sinners or evildoers, committed no sin: “neither was deceit found in his mouth” [1 Pet. 2; Isa. 53; Col. 0322C]. The same point would have been understood had the serpent been made of wood or stone. Yet it adds more to the mystery that it was commanded to be bronze: first, because such an image was made not by iron cutting but by fire melting; second, because the nature of bronze is very resonant; and further, because it is enduring and can be corrupted by rust only with the greatest difficulty.

For God-man was conceived not by a mortal operation, but by the melting power of true fire—that is, by the operation of the Holy Spirit. And while speaking with human beings he did not, like true serpents—that is, whisperers or slanderers—hiss something secretly; but, like resonant bronze sounding clearly, he preached publicly. As he himself testified: “I have spoken openly to the world, and in secret I have said nothing” [John 18; Col. 0323A]. And his flesh, like bronze, proved incapable of being dissolved by the rust of any vice whatsoever.

Finally, the perfection of the whole likeness lies in this: just as it was said of that bronze serpent, “Whoever has been struck and looks upon it shall live” [Num. 21], so here it is said of the Son of Man: “That everyone who believes in him may not perish, but may have eternal life.” This likeness has such force among the faithful people, who desire to live with the spiritual bites of serpents abolished, that, as that serpent was visibly lifted up as a sign and viewed with bodily eyes, so the Church should also bodily lift up the sign of this Son of Man; and, while following and searching with the mind for what is hidden in heaven, should also attach bodily eyes to his visible sign [Col. 0323B].

When the Jews see this, they are angry, since their savage conscience is torn apart because their crime is thus made public in the highest degree and is not permitted to lie hidden in any corner of the earth. They are angry, therefore, and sing against us: “The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the works of human hands.” And then: “Let those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them” [Ps. 113]. They think that they are singing a Davidic song. But in truth, whenever they say these words, according to their intention they are serpentine hisses [Ps. 139]. They hiss against the Lord and against his Christ; against the Son of Man and against his sign.

But let them not frighten us, deter us, or turn away our eyes, so that we should cease to behold Christ with the mind and his sign with reverent eyes, in order that we may escape the bites of serpents hissing through their blasphemous mouths [Num. 21; Judg. 5; Col. 0323C]. “The idols,” they say, “of the nations are silver and gold.” We grant that they are silver and gold—that is, without sense and without soul, as silver and gold are. But what is that to us? Indeed, what is it to this sign of the Son of Man, lifted up and rightly to be lifted up? Is it attacked by that Davidic song? Far from it. For it is not an idol of the nations.

The idols of the nations were the idols of Beelphegor, or Baal and Astaroth [4 Kgs. 23], and of the other dead persons whom their fathers, mingled among the nations, worshipped, falsely saying that those beings were or had been gods. Likewise the images of Jupiter and Neptune, Mars and Mercury, Saturn and Venus, and the monstrous forms of the remaining idols, were idols of the nations: they were merely gold and silver.

But this is the sign of the lifted-up Son of Man, whom the nations did not know, whom we did not know when we were Gentiles, “being led away to dumb idols as we were led” [1 Cor. 12; Col. 0323D]. This sign, however, is not merely gold and silver: it is the sign of truth [Matt. 27]. Let them stammer this to their little viper-children, for whom they have stored up the blood of Christ. Let fathers teach it as a category to their unhappy little children, “thinking themselves, like David, to have vessels for song” [Amos 6]; and let them say, “The idols of the nations are silver and gold,” pointing at those basilicas of martyrs where they know that such a sign of the Son of Man is lifted up. Let them tell their children that this saying was sung beforehand concerning this sign, so that lost sons may drink in rivalry from their fathers’ mouths the hatred of Christ.

But the same God whose prophet said this concerning the idols of the nations says through the prophet to us Gentiles concerning this Christian sign: “Behold, I lift up my hand to the nations, and I will raise my sign to the peoples, says the Lord; with their faces bowed to the earth they shall worship him” [Isa. 49; Col. 0324A]. Let them sing as much as they please, and let them themselves be ensnared by their own [variant: “his own”] song, saying: “Let those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them” [Ps. 113]. Let them become like the calf they made in Horeb and the graven image they worshipped [Ps. 105], because they truly worshipped falsehood and spoke falsehood, saying: “These are your gods, Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt” [Exod. 3].

They are rightly like those persons: they have eyes and do not see, ears and do not hear [Ps. 113]. And lest they imagine themselves exempt from this curse and think that it was spoken of others, we do not set before them words which they do not receive—the Apostle Paul saying, “We know that whatever the law says, it speaks to those who are under the law” [Rom. 3]. Rather, let them hear Isaiah the prophet, through whom God speaks: “Bring forth the blind people who have eyes, and the deaf who have ears” [Isa. 43]. Again: “Deaf, hear; and blind, look, that you may see. Who is blind but my servant? And who is deaf but he to whom I sent my messengers?” [Isa. 42; Col. 0324B–C].

Finally, they have become like not only their own idols but also their seditious robber Barabbas, whom they chose while crucifying their peaceful King. They have therefore been almost consumed and scattered by murders and seditions. But we do not refuse to become like the sign we worship: namely, that just as the demons inhabiting them tremble and flee at the sight of this sign, so, when any one of us speaks to “his enemies in the gate” [Ps. 126]—that is, at the departure from this present life—they may be confounded and unable to stand. Let the croaking ravens fly far away, hungering for our punishment [Isa. 9]; unable to overtake it [Col. 0324C–D], they abandon all the sooner the open heaven to the Christian soul ascending and marked with this sign.

Therefore, according also to the other prophetic oracle which says: “Lift up a sign to the peoples. Behold, the Lord has made proclamation to the ends of the earth” [Isa. 62], let us visibly lift up this sign, as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so that the peoples may not forget it, for this is not expedient. Why are they angry? They too have been scattered among all nations so that the peoples may not at any time forget Christ. For he himself says in the Psalm: “God has shown me concerning my enemies: Do not slay them, lest my people ever forget.” But what then? “Scatter them in your power” [Ps. 58].

Thus, although they are angry, both their captivity and the lifting up of this sign will everywhere proclaim Christ [Col. 0325A]. Their crime especially led to this lifting up. For if they had killed Christ in another way, the manifest sign of his death could never have been lifted up so fittingly [John 8]. If, as they once attempted, they had stoned him or thrown him down from the brow of the mountain [Luke 4], or destroyed him by any of the kinds of death with which they killed the prophets [Matt. 23], an image of his death could have been set forth far less plainly.

But now, in the very manner of his death, there is both a miracle of their most audacious crime in people’s minds and a spectacle fit for the eyes, a plain and evident representation. The Son of Man, therefore, was truly lifted up, because it was fitting that it should be so, “that everyone who believes in him may not perish but may have eternal life.”

Let us hear the reason which follows, directed against heretics, whom this Evangelist especially refutes here by recording testimonies to Christ’s divinity. For after the preceding declaration in which he announces that he must be lifted up and that faith must be placed in him, the hearer seeks a reason which will both satisfy Nicodemus, who is present, and stop the mouths of the heretics who were to come. Therefore he says:

> “For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but may have eternal life.”

Hardly even in part can the art of this Master, who came from God in this respect, now be known—hardly can it be seen “through a mirror, in an enigma” (1 Cor. 13)—especially when he wishes to intimate who he himself is, from whom he was born, or for what purpose he came. For when he had said that he must be lifted up and that one must believe in him [Col. 0325C], the hearer silently awaited the reason—he who did not fail to know that belief was due to one God alone, being indeed a ruler of the Jews—by which he might be instructed why belief in the Son of Man was necessary. For if one must believe in him, it follows that he is God. The consequence, therefore, was that he should say: “Because I am God; because I am the Son of God; because I am the only-begotten of God the Father.” And he adds this, but with such a seasoning of wisdom and humility that it is evident that he is not so much commending himself or seeking his own glory as desiring the necessary salvation of his hearers. “For thus,” he says, “God loved the world, that he gave his only-begotten Son.” Does he not, in saying this, reasonably show that one must therefore believe in him, the Son of Man, because he is the only-begotten [Col. 0325D] Son of God, consubstantial with the Father? Accordingly, he aptly repeats what he had said: “That everyone who believes in him may not perish but may have eternal life.”

How much grace and beauty there is in this: when the necessary occasion requires him to confess that he is the Son of God, he avoids display—or rather, by avoiding it intimates that he is what he was—and takes refuge in commending God’s love, saying, “Thus God loved the world.” He could have said, “I am so great that I can redeem the whole world for one who believes in me.” Yet he says: God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son as its price. “He gave,” that is, he handed him over: not sparing his Son in order to redeem a servant (Rom. 8). And who would dare say to him [Col. 0326A], “Why have you done this?” Can the adversary who held the world captive rightly accuse this most merciful love, or this loving mercy, of being without justice or without truth?

Perhaps the proud angel, when we say, “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth,” dares to stir his wing, open his mouth, and snarl (Isa. 10), saying: “It is false. For the fact that ‘God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son’ is mercy without truth; it is unjust mercy.” Against his brazen and foul face we stand as firmly as faithfully, saying: Was it just that God’s love should appear less than the love of any human being? Was not our father Abraham—for he is our father and the father of all believers, whether [Col. 0326B] those of the circumcision or those of the uncircumcision (Rom. 9; Gen. 15)—a man from that mass which wholly perished in Adam, who, justified by faith, handed over his son? Behold: he offered his son to God and did not spare his son for God’s sake. Was it not therefore, without injury to justice and truth, God’s will to become debtor to a human being, so that God too should not spare his own Son for the sake of man, because man had not spared his son for God’s sake?

Thereupon God, accepting so great a ground of justice, proclaims: “By myself I have sworn: because you have done this thing and have not spared your only-begotten for my sake, I will bless you and multiply your seed; and your seed shall possess the gates of its enemies, and in you all the nations of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. 22). Who dares say: Why [Col. 0326C] did you swear thus? Why did you bind yourself by an oath before a man of the condemned race, so that you owed him seed which should possess the gates of its enemies, and in which all nations would be blessed? (Gen. 12.) Certainly, even if it belongs to grace or mercy alone that God first called him and led him out from Ur of the Chaldeans, promising this seed of blessing, it now belongs also to truth and justice that, to one faithful and proven in so great a trial, he promised and fulfilled it with the interposition of an oath.

Therefore God, as truthful as he is merciful, with truth as steadfast as his mercy is irreproachable, “so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son,” that is, handed him over to be lifted up to the height of the cross, so that everyone who believes in him—namely, firmly holding the same faith of that father Abraham—[Col. 0326D] “may not perish but may have eternal life.” For Abraham offered his son by faith when he was tested; and he offered his only-begotten, he who had received the promises, to whom it had been said: “In Isaac shall your seed be called” (Gen. 21), reckoning that God was able to raise even from the dead (Rom. 4). Therefore whoever believes in the only-begotten Son of God—that God gave him as he promised, raised him after he had been killed, and exalted him as Prince and Savior—possesses the same faith with Abraham and receives the same blessing, “that he may not perish but may have eternal life.”

The world which God loved, then, we understand as the human race: that is, the living and the dead. The dead, certainly, who awaited his coming in faith [Col. 0327A]; the living, who were to believe in him, whether from the Jews or the Gentiles. For without distinction between Gentile and Jew he says universally: “That everyone who believes in him may not perish but may have eternal life.” Since this could have troubled Nicodemus or the other hearers of that time, he further supports it by the confirmation which follows:

> “For God did not send his Son into the world to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him.”

This he plainly introduced against the carnal opinion of the Jews, who, as has already been said, hoped that, with Christ reigning, an earthly kingdom and a carnal age would come, bloodied by wars and slaughter among the nations: that is, they would obtain a peaceful victory for themselves through the killing of human beings and would seize [Col. 0327B] those who had previously seized them. In this sense certain heretics too expected, mockingly, the fable of a thousand years: a golden, gem-studded Jerusalem on earth; the rebuilding of the Temple; the blood of sacrifices; Sabbath leisure; the wrong of circumcision; marriages, births, the upbringing of children, the delights of banquets, and the servitude of all nations; and again wars, triumphs, and the slaughter of the conquered.

Against this meaning, I say, in which they expected Christ as such a king: “God did not,” he says, “send his Son into the world to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him.” He did not send him to judge, but to be judged; not to judge or order the things which are in the world, but to be judged and to perform the things that belong to eternal salvation. Thus, to someone who said to him, “Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me,” he answered: “Man, who appointed me judge or divider over you?” (Luke 12.)

Moreover, to the condemnation of those who hoped that the Messiah had come to judge the world and subject the nations to their rule, he testifies elsewhere, saying: “For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9). Yet neither had he then come to judge even these spiritual matters in the manner in which he will judge in his majesty; nor was he in any way to judge secular or carnal matters, but rather that the world might be saved through him. He was to be judged rather than to judge.

Having thus set aside that aspect of judgment, he immediately adds concerning the judgment for which he came: “Whoever believes in him [Col. 0327D] shall not be judged; but whoever does not believe has already been judged.” Behold: how does he whom God did not send into the world to judge the world judge the world, sitting—or rather, already as though lifted up and set forth as a sign? It is therefore clear that he did not say, “God did not send his Son to judge the world,” concerning every kind of judgment. For behold, he judges; behold, he separates: “Whoever believes in him,” he says, “shall not be judged.” Rightly, justly, faithfully.

For whoever believes in him also believes what he said above, what was commanded: namely, that unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God. This he believes, and in believing hastens to be born again. Once reborn, he is already another person, already a new person; he has departed from the old father and come to [Col. 0328A] the new; he is an estranged person, seed of another (Gal. 3; Eph. 4). Why then should he be judged? Why should he die because of Adam? Why should he be found excluded from God’s kingdom because of Adam’s sin? “Far be it,” he says. “He shall not be judged. But whoever does not believe has already been judged.” Where? When? In that father of his, in that sinful ancestor of his. When that man sinned and was judged, when he was clothed in garments of skin and cast out from the kingdom of God (Gen. 3), then this man too was judged and, together with him “in whose loins he was” (Heb. 7), was expelled from the kingdom of God.

And why, you ask, does he thus remain cast out, now and forever? “Because,” he says, “he does not believe in the name of the only-begotten Son of God”; that is, because he does not believe that he must be born again according to the only-begotten Son of God, in order that he may [Col. 0328B] enter the kingdom of God. Therefore “he who does not believe has already been judged,” that is, he remains in that condemnation. But he who believes was indeed judged then as well, yet shall not be judged—that is, he shall not be retained in that condemnation.

This point must be carefully observed. When he says, “Whoever believes shall not be judged,” he does not deny that such a person was judged. The distinction, then, is this: the believer was judged in the mass, but is not judged in his individual person; whereas the unbeliever was judged then in the mass and will be judged in the future in his own person. Now, carried in mind to that day on which the believer shall not be judged and the unbeliever shall be retained in the condemnation in which he was judged—namely, the day of the final judgment—let us question the Judge himself [Col. 0328C] and hear from his mouth the cause or justice of this judgment. He says:

> “And this is the judgment: that the light came into the world, and human beings loved darkness rather than light.”

“This,” he says, “is the judgment”: on this account human beings are without excuse; on this account their condemnation is just, “because the light came into the world, and they loved darkness rather than light.” For if the light had not come today, when it was said to them, “Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25)—for your first father Adam sinned, who listened to the devil’s counsel against me, desiring to be like me, and you were all judged in him because you were in his loins—when this, I say, was said to them, they would answer: “Lord, when our first parents, their eyes opened, knew themselves to be naked [Col. 0328D]; when the light came to them, seeking and reproving them, and said first to Adam, ‘Where are you? And who told you that you were naked, unless you ate from the tree from which I commanded you not to eat?’ (Gen. 3)—were we, who had not yet been born, aware of their guilt or their defense? If the light had come to us and shown us our sins, we would have repented, and, recognizing our evil deeds, would have abandoned them.”

Perhaps they would say this today. But now every accusation has been removed from God and every excuse taken away from them. “For the light came into the world”; it pursued human beings as soon as they had been cast out of the kingdom of God. It kindled for them very many lights, where they were born after their father’s stripping, so that, recognizing their nakedness [Col. 0329A] and repenting, they might recover their clothing or adornment. It kindled very many such lights for them both before the Law and under the Law—namely righteous men, in whose shining deeds, writings, or sayings they might see and recognize themselves. At last it came in the very substance of light itself, showing them the prepared and easy entrance into the kingdom of God; but “they loved darkness rather than light.” Why? “For their works were evil.” What works? Fornications, adulteries, murders, sorceries, revelries, drunkenness, thefts, perjuries, false witness, and things like these (Gal. 5). This light is hostile to all such things, which it forbids to be done and with which it cannot agree.

Therefore, while it shows them the entrance to the kingdom of God, while it commands them to be born again of water and the Holy Spirit [Col. 0329B] and to enter the heavenly generation—in which it is not permitted to prostitute oneself or become drunk, to defile or be defiled, to covet and seize or steal—they flee this light and hide themselves in their darkness, like Adam their father. They cover their shameful deeds with the leaves of a perverse defense; moreover, they blaspheme the light itself and defend their darkness, calling “darkness light and light darkness” (Isa. 5).

> “For everyone who does evil hates the light and does not come to the light, lest his works be reproved.”

Not everyone who does evil, for “all have sinned and lack the glory of God” (Rom. 3), but everyone who does evil persistently, deliberately, and perseveringly—not everyone who sins through ignorance or weakness, but the one who loves iniquity and carefully defends it—hates this light and does not [Col. 0329C] come to it, lest his works be reproved. Such were those whose profits I scattered when I drove the sellers and buyers from the Temple (John 2). For this is why they do not receive this light, why they do not hear me: because I tell them that unless, instead of being greedy, avaricious, rapacious, or adulterous, they become generous, liberal, and diligent, and are wholly reborn so as to become other persons, they cannot attain the kingdom of God.

Those people, seeing me cast out demons and knowing that I cast them out by the finger of God—which even the Magi before Pharaoh could recognize from the works (Matt. 12; Exod. 8)—lie and say, “He casts out demons by Beelzebub, prince of demons” (Luke 11), because they hate me, the true light. Since they are unwilling to come to me, since they flee the present light [Col. 0329D], they wish it to seem that they act from rational judgment rather than from the presumption of hatred or envy.

> “But whoever does the truth comes to the light, so that his works may be made manifest, because they have been done in God.”

“Whoever does the truth,” he says—that is, whoever thinks and judges with God against his own iniquity, which he hates; whoever delights in the law of God according to the inward person, and, seeing another law in his members warring against the law of his mind and leading him captive under the law of sin which is in his members (Rom. 7), confesses, cries out, and groans; whoever thus ascends the tribunal with God and, displeased with himself, judges himself and desires to become another person—such a one “comes to the light,” which tells him what is good for him [Col. 0330A] and shows him the entrance to God’s kingdom, “so that his works,” the words of devout confession and true repentance, “may be made manifest, because they have been done in God.” In God, certainly, not against God; not as are the works of those who sin knowingly and deliberately and defend their sins. For such persons sinned either through ignorance or through weakness; recognizing their sins, they grieved, wept, confessed, and received the counsel of their salvation: that they might be born again of water and Spirit and, preserving this regeneration, enter the kingdom of God.

Certainly he used an appropriate comparison, fitting both subject and occasion. For when he said these things to Nicodemus, it was the time of night and darkness. Just as adulterers and fornicators love the night and flee the day, so all the ungodly love the present age and hate the future, hiding themselves from truth under the protection of falsehood. Conversely, just as industrious and chaste persons disdain the night and anticipate the slow day with eager light, so all who are of God hate their sins, hunger and thirst for righteousness, and, despising the present age, seek everywhere, conscious of the future kingdom of God, the truth [Col. 0330B].

Accordingly, as has been said, he employed the appropriate comparison of light and darkness, commending all who, just as Nicodemus sought the light of truth in the time of night, console the darkness of this present life by the illumination of Holy Scripture, attending to it “as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in our hearts.” But he reproves those who, in order to excuse themselves on the ground of ignorance, do not wish to understand so as to act rightly. Indeed, as the prophet says, “lying on beds of ivory and luxuriating on their couches” (Amos 6), they do not wish to be troubled or to have their pleasures diminished by the threats of the coming judgment, “because of fear and expectation of the things coming upon the whole world” (Luke 21).

At the end of this discourse of the Lord, it must not be passed over that it is commonly asked why God, for love of the world, gave—as was said above—not an envoy or an angel, but his Only-Begotten. Some say: Could he not have defeated the devil through the archangel Michael or Gabriel, or through some member of the principalities and powers, thrones or dominions? Why did he send his consubstantial Son? Why hand him over? [Col. 0330D] Why did he will him to undergo the outrage of death?
