Unless some certain answer is given to those who say these things, proved altogether most firmly by a clear outcome, that the human being could not be liberated from the devil by any creature, however strong, but only through the sole only-begotten Son of God, perhaps God’s spontaneous love or grace will seem excessive, and the humility or humiliation of the Son of God excessively unwarranted.

Indeed, we say to them with the Apostle: “It was fitting for him, for whom are all things and through whom are all things, who had brought many sons into glory, to perfect the author of their salvation through suffering” (Heb. 2). But this is not enough for them. For they go on and say: How was it fitting for him, or why was it fitting, if the outrage of his incarnation or death was not so [Col. 0331A] necessary for us? Many things may be said in answer to this; but for one who is not contentious and who yields to truth, a few things out of many suffice.

First it must be said that the human race could not otherwise be saved by a fair and just redemption, unless the propitiator who came to redeem or save had first put on the very nature which had committed sin, in order that in that nature he might offer to God a satisfaction worthy for all the liabilities of those of the same nature. But this was altogether impossible for an angelic nature: namely, to assume human nature, to clothe itself with a human soul. For the angelic spirit is in no way subtler than the human soul. Therefore neither is capable of the other: the angelic spirit is not capable of the human spirit, nor the human spirit of the angelic.

Finally, God alone—the uncreated Spirit, the uncircumscribed Spirit—though he himself is capable of no other, is capable of every rational spirit, whether angelic or human. Thus, when someone is said to be full of a diabolical spirit, it should not be imagined that the substance of the diabolical spirit has entered the substance of the human soul; rather, it has crept into the hidden caverns of the body and, finding the soul in its dwelling-place, lashes it with infernal scourges, infects it with poisons, or inflames it with fires. How then could an angel assume human nature? How could it clothe itself with a human soul, than which none is subtler?

Furthermore, angelic nature, compared with ours—for we are earth—is not the finest gold; and consequently no angel is so much more precious than a human being that, if sold, he could counterbalance the inheritance [Col. 0331C]. For what is an angel by nature but a rational and immortal creature? And certainly a human being also, according to the soul, is a rational and immortal creature. Besides, the human being possesses the most beautiful structure of a body and can enjoy the blessedness of eternal life in both body and soul. And while the angel has a single robe, the human being will possess a double robe of everlasting glory.

Therefore this one thing was necessary for our salvation: that God, who loved the world, should not send an envoy but should give his only-begotten Son, who by divine power might do what neither envoy nor angel could do—that is, penetrate the human soul by the subtlety of his divinity and unite, or join, the whole human nature to himself in one and the same person [Col. 0331D]; and that he might offer that nature to the eternal Father as a worthy price for Adam’s debt, being as he was far and incomparably more precious than any angel. He was “chosen from among thousands,” because “his head is finest gold” (Song 5): that is, because his Father is the one true God, and he himself is the only-begotten and consubstantial Son of that same Father, and therefore true God.

Was this not fitting for him? Was this not a truly divine work and a sufficient proof of true Divinity? Was this work not an insignia, glorious to his golden head, no less of mercy than of power: that he willed, and alone was able, to assume our nature; that he willed, and alone was able, by immeasurably outweighing all our race in the balance of the cross, to purchase it? Truly, therefore, as the Apostle says, “it was fitting for him, through whom [Col. 0332A] are all things and for whom are all things, who had brought many sons into glory, to perfect the author of their salvation through their sufferings” (Heb. 2). Now let us return to the sequence of the Gospel reading.

> “After these things Jesus came into the land of Judea, and there he remained with his disciples and baptized.”

Wherever the name “baptism” is placed or mentioned, it is of such greatness that it immediately fills the whole mind of the hearer, and of such splendor that it scarcely permits its proper appearance to be discerned except by a practiced observer. For many, having read or heard this narrative—that “Jesus came into the land of Judea with his disciples, remained there, and baptized”—are so filled by the majesty of the name that they have no leisure to consider or inquire whence the power or usefulness of this sacrament first arose.

But for those more fully instructed in the sacraments of faith, there is no doubt that the power or authority of Christ’s baptism took its beginning from the death and resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ himself: when, now dead, he poured out blood and water from his pierced side, as Paul says: “All of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death. We were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life” (Rom. 6). This matter has been discussed more fully above in the second book.

When, then, we now read that Jesus baptized, we ask how or by what power he baptized [Col. 0332C], especially on account of those who, lacking discernment and forestalled by reverence for this name—baptism alone—cannot bear to hear that it has any equivocation except amid the troubles of controversy. Indeed, the resolution of this question would be more difficult to discover, unless the provident Evangelist said somewhat later: “Although Jesus himself did not baptize, but his disciples did” (John 4).

From that saying the solution of the question is now made easier. For since “he baptized” and “he did not baptize” are opposites and cannot both be true at once, it is quite clear that in this place he said Jesus baptized according to the common report, which he again states in order to overturn or correct it when he says: “When Jesus learned that the Pharisees had heard that Jesus was making and baptizing more disciples than John—although Jesus himself did not baptize, but his disciples did” (John 4). By saying this he overturns his earlier statement, in which he now says that Jesus baptized while remaining in Judea with his disciples; and he indicates that this report had been spread by John’s envious disciples, especially while the Jews were envious and stirring up envy. This is made clear in what follows by the dispute reported to have arisen between John’s disciples and the Jews.

For Jesus’ disciples baptized, and this was truly to be ascribed to him because they baptized by his authority. Indeed, they rightly claimed a privilege above John’s disciples because of the greatness of so great a Master. For John performed no sign, whereas Jesus was so great [Col. 0333A] that many believed in him when they saw the signs that he performed. Moreover, John bore witness to him, and was so much less than he and gradually diminished that he confessed himself unworthy to loosen the strap of his sandal (Mark 1; Matt. 3). Therefore what his disciples did in baptizing was to be attributed to Jesus—not by the envious or slanderous, but by those who faithfully believed and rightly cherished the Master’s glory in the teaching of his disciples.

Yet, as we proposed to ask above, how or by what power did Jesus’ disciples baptize, or, if you prefer, Jesus himself baptize through their ministry? Was it by the same rule or efficacy by which his disciples baptize now—or rather, by which he himself baptizes through his disciples or ministers? Certainly not by the same rule. For the same rule of baptism had not yet been given, without which Christ’s baptism can nowhere be performed; for he delivered it not before but after his resurrection, saying: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28).

Nor, therefore, did they baptize with the same efficacy, because the right side of the life-giving temple—of which mention was made above—had not yet been opened, so that water flowing from it together with blood might, according to Ezekiel, heal all waters and bring them the power of regeneration (Ezek. 47; John 19). The Red Sea, that is, the sacrament of this baptism consecrated by Christ’s blood, did not yet exist. How, then, are those baptized through this sea said to have crossed through a sea which did not yet exist? The Lamb had not yet been slain, and yet the children of Israel are thought to have crossed the Red Sea. Why afterwards is this true Lamb slain and the doorposts consecrated with his blood, if Pharaoh’s firstborn and all the Egyptians’ firstborn had already perished and all had been submerged in the Red Sea (Exod. 12; 1 Cor. 10)? That is, if Jesus’ disciples baptized with the baptism by which, when we are baptized now, every sin, actual as well as original, is overwhelmed.

But someone may say: Jesus’ disciples baptized in order that those baptized might become entitled to belong to Christ’s future redemption. This may indeed rightly be granted, provided that no one believes that anyone, dead or living, received before Christ’s Passion by any baptism the remission of sins, which is the Holy Spirit. Hence in this same Evangelist it is written: “The Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John 7).

Therefore, since we have no evidence on evangelical authority that Jesus’ disciples received anything by command or rule concerning baptism except what he had only just said to Nicodemus when he came to him: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God,” it must be held without doubt that, without awaiting the tradition or rule of baptism—for they neither knew how to ask about it nor thought that any other existed than that according to which John baptized, namely for repentance—they too baptized in some manner as they themselves had been baptized by John: namely, without catechesis concerning Christ’s cross, death, or [Col. 0334A] resurrection; without the necessary distinction of persons, in the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. And they did this as long as John survived.

For after John had been handed over and Jesus, succeeding to the office of preaching, came into Galilee—as the Evangelists Matthew, Mark, and Luke plainly testify, as has already been said elsewhere—Jesus’ disciples are nowhere read to have baptized (Matt. 4; Mark 1; Luke 4). Nor did Jesus himself command this to them before his resurrection. Indeed, when he summoned the twelve apostles and gave them power and authority over all demons, sending them to preach (Matt. 10), and likewise when he later sent the seventy-two (Luke 10), he said nothing to them about the ministry of baptism, but only that they should preach, saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of God will draw near” (Matt. 4)—that kingdom which from then onward is within us, since, through the death of our King, Christ God and man—through the death, I say, and resurrection of this great King—the prince of this world has been judged and cast out (Luke 23; John 18).

For where do we find, throughout the whole time of Christ’s preaching—that is, from John’s arrest until the Passion of the same our Lord—that his disciples baptized or that Jesus himself commanded them to do so? Therefore, when we hear that Jesus baptized, or rather that his disciples baptized, let us not be so overwhelmed by the greatness of the name baptism that we fail to distinguish the thing itself or its form, imagining that such a baptism was performed as we do not doubt Christ commanded to the apostles after his resurrection [Col. 0334C].

The Evangelist here calls “the land of Judea,” to which Jesus came or where he remained with his disciples, that fourth part of the Jewish kingdom administered by Pontius Pilate. There Jesus, after those things which had been done or said in Jerusalem, remained, as has been said, and baptized.

> “Now John also was baptizing at Aenon near Salim, because there was much water there; and people came and were baptized.”

Aenon is a place in which is also the village of Salim, at the eighth milestone from Scythopolis, in the plain called Salomias. “There,” he says, “John too was baptizing.” Why John began to baptize has already been stated above: namely, that while John baptized, Christ might be manifested in Israel. Thus he himself said: “I did not know him; but that he might be manifested in Israel, for this reason I came baptizing in water” (John 1).

Why then did he not cease the office of baptizing, since Christ had been manifested? “For John,” he says, “had not yet been sent into prison.” It was more fitting and reasonable that he should withdraw when, sent into prison, he had lost the ability to baptize even if he wished; and thus he would not make anyone uneasy as though he had changed his mind, like one who, having stirred the people with so great a proclamation, had begun the practice of baptism vainly and was soon to abandon it—having perhaps begun it more for one man than for the kingdom of God.

Indeed, at this time it was fitting to know that he had come baptizing in water in order to make known the one man Christ [Col. 0335A]; but it was not yet time to speak so as to say this and everything else. He therefore baptized and preached repentance until he was put into prison. Once that had happened, neither his disciples nor Jesus or Jesus’ disciples are read to have baptized anywhere, until Jesus himself was first baptized with that baptism of which he says: “I have a baptism with which to be baptized, and how I am constrained until it is accomplished!” (Luke 12).

For he was to be baptized by his Passion, since he himself, according to the prophet, still had filthy garments (Zech. 3): namely, the corruptible, passible, and mortal members of the flesh. Having removed or laid them aside through the stripping of death, he would recover the same members, made white through the glory of the resurrection—that is, impassible by the power of immortality [Col. 0335B].

“Therefore a dispute arose between John’s disciples and the Jews concerning purification, and they came to John.” Behold, even now so great and violent a wind blew that not merely some reed, but even a grown young tree might seem able to be shaken by its force. For as Jesus increased and this man now began to decrease—as it was fitting that this should happen, and as he himself had declared—his disciples, while the Jews maliciously provoked them and wished to kindle the flame of envy, became jealous, so that they tried to weaken John’s testimony which he had borne concerning Jesus, namely by extracting from him some statement about Jesus that might appear inconsistent with his earlier testimony.

[Col. 0335C] For example, suppose the Jews had said: “Behold, we have two baptizers: whose baptism purifies better?” “Whose,” John’s disciples say, “if not his who first discovered these waters and first showed them to mortals? Our baptizer learned to baptize not from men nor through a man, but through the Word of the Lord, while he was alone in the wilderness; and then, when he came here, he himself baptized that younger man—to whom everyone now comes—just as he baptized the rest.”

The Jews, on the other hand, say: “Did not your master rank the purification of that man’s baptism above his own baptism, saying, ‘I baptize in water; he will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire’ (Matt. III)? Did he not say that he was unworthy to loosen the strap of his sandal? (Luke III).” Therefore, when a dispute of this sort had arisen, “they came,” he says, “to John.”

[Col. 0335D] Nor is it surprising that disciples still inexperienced should have disputed over the purification effected by the baptisms, or over the dignity of their masters, when even the great apostles, with their Master’s Passion already imminent, disputed which of them seemed to be greater in the kingdom of heaven (Matt. XVIII). They came as far as John. They pressed the question with great persistence and spirit, carrying the windy contrivance of this dispute as far as that tower which was founded upon the highest rock, far more lofty and much stronger than our reeds, which such a wind is accustomed easily to shake in whatever direction.

For, that we may know that they came to him with the intention of calling him away from his testimony concerning Christ, the very words sufficiently and clearly indicate this. They were as follows: “Rabbi, he who was with you beyond the Jordan, to whom you bore testimony—behold, he is baptizing, and all are running to him.”

[Col. 0336A] The substance of what they said, or could have said, is expressed so briefly that in almost every little phrase there lies a force that might have moved him, had it not struck a mind firm, prudent, and, as was said before, well founded in the truth.

First—as a scorching wind often begins with a gentle whisper—they flatter him, saying, “Rabbi.” They knew that the delicate ears of the scribes and Pharisees delighted in this title; as the Lord also says: “For they love the chief seats in the synagogues, and greetings in the marketplace, and to be called Rabbi by men” (Matt. XXIII; Mark XII). Nowhere except in this passage do we find him called Rabbi: neither by those who, seeking from him counsel for salvation, said, “What shall we do?” (Luke III), nor by anyone in any place in the Gospels. Even if it may at some time have been said, it was rightly omitted by the Evangelists as superfluous; yet in this place it absolutely ought not to have been omitted, because of the need to indicate the magnitude of the present flattery.

Accordingly, after placing before him this grand title, by which they thought he could be bent to agree with them, so as to seek precedence over the Lord Jesus, they say: “He who was with you beyond the Jordan,” and the rest. It must be noted carefully with how much art and how elaborate a snare they proceed, in order that John may repent of the testimony which he bore concerning the Lord.

[Col. 0336C] For by two preceding propositions they attach two further points under an indirect pretext, in this manner: “He who was with you beyond the Jordan—behold, he is baptizing; and he to whom you bore testimony—behold, all are coming to him.” He who was with you beyond the Jordan, and submitted himself to your hands as an inferior, behold, he is above you in Judaea and baptizes separately on his own authority. And, “he to whom you bore testimony”: in an excessive humility, subjecting yourself far too much to him and giving your glory to another, behold, everyone, neglecting you, comes to him; despising your baptism, they eagerly seek that younger man in rivalry.

By these and similar utterances, fashioned out of Jewish envy, they sought to turn the mind of the most faithful witness away from the truth to which he bore testimony; so that, once the agreement of those baptizing had been broken, the remedy of baptism or repentance might more easily seem capable of being despised as though reasonably.

[Col. 0336D] For the Pharisees and very many of the Jews “rejected the counsel of God, not having been baptized” (Luke VII) with John’s baptism. For, being false and deceptive, they expected, when the Messiah reigned, to exalt themselves proudly in his kingdom—not to humble themselves for their sins or to repent; to despoil all nations—not to share two tunics or double portions of food with the Gentiles.

## BOOK IV

[Col. 0337]

[Col. 0337A] Since John truly is a burning and shining lamp (John V), we rightly rejoice in his light, provided that we recognize that light of his which the Jews refused to recognize. And therefore, wishing to rejoice for an hour—that is, hastening to snatch from him whom they supposed to be the Christ the temporary joy of an earthly kingdom—they could not rejoice fittingly.

His light, however, is humble truth and true humility. Shining wholly in heart and speech by this light, he could not admit the real darkness of empty glory—which seems to fools to be light. Therefore, when the Jews send—indeed, when they themselves come—to John, raising, as has been said, a question about purification, and he bears testimony to the truth, we rejoice well and commendably in his light: not for an hour, but for a true and complete day; not aiming at time, but at timeless eternity, while we gladly embrace the truth shining through his mouth.

Let us therefore hear what he answered at this point:

“A man cannot receive anything unless it has been given to him from heaven.” It is as though he said: “Why, O importunate supporters, do you call me Rabbi so insistently? Why, as though honoring me, do you enlarge me with a title greater than I am? This is his name, and it belongs to him who alone needs no one, who alone possesses and teaches man knowledge (Ps. XCIII), who gives precepts for living and imparts to the man subject to him the law of life and discipline (Ecclus. XLV).

[Col. 0337B] “And he greatly surpasses men, of whom ‘no one can receive anything unless it has been given to him from heaven.’ For all have received from elsewhere; each awaits his own gift from the fullness of another” (I Cor. IV). “Therefore every man must be forbidden to love being called Rabbi by men; indeed, sacred Scripture is nowhere accustomed to call Moses by this title, since he did not give the law from himself, but received it from elsewhere in order to give it” (Exod. XXXVI).

“Therefore do not call me Rabbi; rather, call me a disciple of truth. For certainly, since I too am a man, I could not have received anything unless it had been given to me from heaven. Or is it only now, for the first time, that I say I am not God, but merely a man?

“You yourselves bear me testimony that I said: ‘I am not the Christ, but I have been sent before him.’ When you sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to ask me, ‘Who are you?’ I confessed and did not deny, and I confessed, ‘I am not the Christ’; and I said, ‘He who is to come after me has been made before me’ (John I), and the rest.

[Col. 0337D] “Therefore, when I now say it thus—‘You yourselves now bear me testimony’—this is what you say: ‘Rabbi, he who was with you beyond the Jordan, to whom you bore testimony.’ Thus I have by no means only now learned that I am a mere man, since you know it, remember it, and now bear me testimony that I said, ‘I am not the Christ.’ Had I said otherwise, I would certainly have affirmed myself to be more than a man. For Christ is more than man, because he is not merely man, but both God and man.

“Therefore call him alone Rabbi, because ‘your one Master is Christ’ (Matt. XXIII), concerning whom I have already said, and you have heard, that ‘from his fullness we have all received’ (John I). Be, then, his disciples together with me. For what have I that I have not received from his fullness? But if I received it, why do you wish me to glory as though I had not received it? (I Cor. IV.) Glory belongs to him alone, because he received from no one; because he is full, and it was not given to him from heaven, because heaven itself is his.

[Col. 0338C] “Let no one now trouble me: though one possessing the power of the Spirit has risen above me, I will not abandon my place. My place, I say: I shall not exceed my measure. I know my place—namely this: that I am not the Christ, but have been sent before him. Do you wish to hear what he is and what I am? Do you wish now to know this through a comparison well known to you?”

“**He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the bridegroom’s friend, who stands and hears him, rejoices with joy because of his voice. Therefore this joy of mine has been fulfilled.**” All of you who have either celebrated weddings or attended them know how great the difference is between a bridegroom and his friend [Col. 0338C].

But why, O John, friend of the bridegroom, have you referred not openly, but as though beneath a veil, to both natures of Christ—namely, the divine and the human? For it could have been said thus: He who is God and man is Christ. For the statement, “He who has the bride is the bridegroom,” is not understood by us as if it had said: It is not I, who am a mere man—as any one of you is—who am Christ, because I am not God; but he is Christ who, before he was man, was God, and, after becoming man, nevertheless remains God according to his nature, while, because he has assumed human nature, he is Christ.

Just as any bridegroom, before he took a bride, was a man; and after taking her, nevertheless remains a man by nature and sex, but is called and is a bridegroom because the female sex has been joined to him. Thus we understand this statement to have been made, and from it we know that Christ is the bridegroom, because we believe and confess that he is not merely man, but God and man. For unless we had first believed that, we should by no means understand today that Davidic proclamation: “And he, like a bridegroom coming forth from his bridal chamber” [Ps. XVIII], and the other testimonies of Scripture of this kind [Col. 0339A].

But they did not yet believe; they did not yet know that Christ was God and man. They did not expect the Messiah in such a way as to believe that he would be God, but only a man—though a great man, still merely a man. Why then, O John, lamp of the world, did you not at least first show your disciples openly that Christ was God and man? You yourself knew their slowness better; yet you spoke mystical and lofty matters to them as though they were perfect and trained in faith in Christ—matters whose very surface they could scarcely grasp.

Clearly, because it was not yet fitting that these things be proclaimed before Christ’s Passion. For the order of divinity does not allow the same Christ to be recognized—who or how great he is—and to be honored or worshiped according to his dignity before, having completed the service enjoined upon him by the Father, he sits at the right hand of Majesty on high [Col. 0339B]. This order was necessary for our salvation: before he claimed for himself what belongs to God, he had first to do or suffer what belongs to man.

Thus, when he gave the twelve apostles power and authority over all demons, to heal diseases, and sent them to preach, he did not command them to preach himself; he commanded only that people should repent and know that the kingdom of God was drawing near [Matt. X]. And so John, because he was being pressed by questions, could not altogether remain silent concerning Christ’s greatness—which is his divinity. Yet, because it was not his office to preach the incarnation of the same Son of God, but only to baptize and say, “Repent, for the kingdom of God will draw near,” he so moderated the words of his testimony that he neither concealed the truth nor exposed it to be popularly judged or trampled underfoot [Col. 0339C].

Therefore he says: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom.” Besides the glory of the inwardly hidden mystery already discussed—of which, according to the Psalmist, the heavens were to declare, so that there were no speeches or words whose voices were not heard, whose sound was to go forth into all the earth and whose words to the ends of the world, saying: “He has set his tabernacle in the sun; and he, like a bridegroom coming forth from his bridal chamber, has rejoiced as a giant to run his course” [Ps. XVIII]—besides this inner glory, I say, the saying has very great practical usefulness on its surface as well. It could build up those present and restrain them from their excessively fleshly rivalry [Col. 0339D].

For there was none among them who did not know that adultery is abominable when a best man, falsely claiming to be the bridegroom, dares to defile the bridal chamber of the bride entrusted to him. For example: Father Abraham, considering his servant faithful, sends him under oath by the God of heaven to take a wife for his son Isaac, giving him gifts to carry from all his goods. The servant addresses Rebecca when he finds her at the well and sees her drawing water; because she was beautiful, he first gives her bracelets and hangs earrings from her ears. Having thus well prepared her mind, he finally obtains her from her parents and sends her, entrusted to his fidelity, to his master Isaac [Gen. XXIV; Col. 0340A].

Would this man, though he is Isaac’s servant, go unpunished if, delighted by the girl’s beauty, he lied that he himself was Isaac and stole for himself the embraces belonging to his master? Certainly there was no one among them who did not know that this was an abominable crime, which, because of its enormity, rightly deserved punishment in the manner of slaves.

But now, since he is about to rise beyond the slave’s condition into the honor of fidelity, he stands as the great best man in the wedding-house of his lord the bridegroom. He hears him and rejoices with joy at the bridegroom’s voice, as the latter congratulates him for his zeal and diligence in bringing him a girl worthy of him. John plainly asserts that his own coming to baptize in water, in order to prepare for the Lord a perfect people, is like this [Col. 0340B].

For after he had said, “He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the bridegroom’s friend, who stands and hears him, rejoices with joy because of his voice,” he concluded thus: “Therefore this joy of mine has been fulfilled.” What joy? Namely, that I am the friend of him who has the bride and is therefore bridegroom; that I was sent before him; and that, having addressed the first Church of his disciples as it drew water from the streams of my baptism, I adorned it with the bracelets of good works and hung earrings upon it, saying, “The kingdom of God will draw near”; and thus I led it on to the only-begotten Son of God the Father, saying, “Behold the Lamb of God.” To him the Synagogue, his mother Sarah—dead through unbelief—will immediately be joined, and he will fill the face of the world with seed.

“**This,**” he says [Col. 0340C], “**is my joy, and this has been fulfilled**,” so that I seek nothing higher. Why do you say to me: Be the bridegroom yourself? Let him be called and be the bridegroom to whom the bride is owed. My joy has indeed been fulfilled in this: that I am the bridegroom’s friend; that I stand in the banquet hall and hear him, rejoicing because of his voice—because of his testimony, which you too will hear, by which he declares me blessed, saying: ‘Among those born of women none has arisen greater than John the Baptist’ [Matt. XI],” and so forth.

When John said these things to those who had pressed him with the aforesaid question and wished, on his own authority, to think of him beyond what they heard and saw from him—some excessively favoring him, others maliciously attempting to weaken or annul, by imitating his voice, the testimony which he had borne to the Lord—when for that reason he set before them the comparison of the bridegroom and his friend, were not his disciples, who favored their teacher too greatly, reproved within themselves? Could not the Jews, who had tried to diminish his testimony concerning Christ but now saw it rather increased, blush inwardly? [Col. 0340D]

Accordingly, as the true and worthy best man of the bridegroom, an unblemished friend, he worthily stands before him in the eternal banquet hall of heaven, hears his voice, and rejoices with joy which will not be taken from him. In every respect this best man is rightly proposed as an example to all who obtain the care and governance of Christ’s bride, the holy Church: they must not look upon her with adulterous eyes and steal her union from her true bridegroom [Col. 0341A].

For as long as they preach the Catholic faith to her, they are called and are the bridegroom’s friends, the bridegroom’s vicars, and also men, because Christ speaks in them, and his seed is the word of faith [Luke VIII], received through them. But when they try to bring anything alien to Christ’s faith to her ears, they are adulterers, because Christ does not speak in them; and the bride is, as it were, defiled by an alien body when she permits herself to submit to such teachers of error.

Paul, one of the chief friends of this bridegroom, sharply rebukes her voluntary inclination to this when he cries out: “Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?” [I Cor. I]. For amid their divisions they said: “I am of Paul; I am of Apollos; I am of Cephas” [ibid.; Col. 0341B]. In this way Paul, Cephas, and Apollos were not themselves adulterating Christ’s bride—for they were his faithful ministers—but souls inclined to her adultery were trying to provoke their bridegroom’s friends into committing adultery.

Yet from whatever side the fuel of adultery arises—whether from that which is called the bride or from those called friends—this testimony is true and cannot be dissolved: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom.” That is, he alone who, though God, deigned to unite human nature to himself—he alone, and no other, among all, is the bridegroom of the holy Church; and anyone else who thrusts himself in can be an adulterer, but cannot be a bridegroom.

For this true friend, whom all the friends of this bridegroom imitate, it is enough—and it is great and brings full joy—that he has been judged worthy to stand, to hear him, and to be conscious of the heavenly secrets transacted with the bride [Col. 0341C].

What then remains? What must be done henceforth? He says: “**He must increase, but I must decrease.**” Until now, he says, I have cried out by the testimony of my voice alone that he is greater than I and that he was before me. Thereafter, by evident realities, it must become certain that I am not Christ but have been sent before Christ, and that he is not, as I am, merely man, but also God. For this is my decreasing and his increasing: not that the measure allotted to me diminishes, or his immensity grows, but that the vastly unequal greatness of each may become known to you.

In another sense, truly according to human nature—for man is made a little lower than the angels [Ps. VIII]—he has an increase: first through signs and wonders; then through the order of death, resurrection, and ascension; and thus he receives “the name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” [Phil. II], and repentance and remission of sins should be preached among all nations [Luke XXIV; Col. 0341D]. This must altogether come to pass; it is fitting and necessary for the human race that he be worshiped as “sitting at the right hand of Majesty on high” [Heb. III].

Meanwhile, I must decrease, so that no one may put confidence in me, a mere man, or make flesh his arm. You will immediately see this when, handed over and beheaded, I descend to the lower world, doing nothing worthy of the name of Christ which you importunately lay upon me [Col. 0342A]. When these things have been accomplished, the comparison between me, whom you thought to be Christ, and him who is truly Christ—against whom you fought through your questions—will at last be sung not only to you but to the whole world. Then it will be known and said how much smaller I am, whom Zechariah begot [Luke I], than he whom you call Joseph’s son [Luke IV; Matt. XIII].

You ignore this because I came unknown from the wilderness, long consigned to oblivion, and so suppose that I am Christ, as though I had come from certain secret and invisible places. Yet without doubt my smallness will be distinguished from his greatness by the distinction of our origins. He whom a corruptible man, mute and unable to speak, begot from his own flesh is, as he is, certainly called less than him whom the incorruptible and invisible God, eloquent and making all things by speaking, uttered from his heart [Col. 0342B].

When these things and the rest begin to be openly preached to the whole world, when the heavens sound forth and declare the glory of this Son of God [Ps. XVIII], it will then unquestionably appear that heaven is higher than every mountain, day fairer than twilight night, and the sun more splendid than the morning star.

The very times of his birth and Passion, together with the manner and place of that Passion, fittingly signify this increase. For he is not born or does not suffer at the seasons when days diminish; nor does he suffer, as I did, at the ill-omened birthday-feast of Herod or Pilate [reading uncertain]. Rather, he suffers at the Paschal full moon; not for the dancing of a single girl, but at the clamorous demand of the whole Synagogue; not in the concealment of a dark prison, but beneath the open sky, openly before all heaven and with the whole world as witness; not beheaded outside the city gate and diminished in head, but raised and stretched out upon the exposed wood [Matt. XIV; Mark VI; Col. 0342C]. In the form of the cross, he declares that he draws the fourfold world to himself.

“**He who comes from above is above all.**” Let them hear this too, and what follows. Let the Jews hear and be covered with confusion; let the heretics hear, against whom this Gospel, as has often been said, is especially written—those who, by a devilish spirit, have fabricated the claim that Christ took his beginning from Mary. “He who comes from above,” he says, “is above all.”

He had said that Christ must increase; he adds the reason, proving why he rightly increases and why the whole world ought rightly to think greater things of him than of John. Why, you ask, does he increase, and why do you decrease as he increases? “He who comes from above,” he says, is above all for this very reason: because he comes from above; because he was not sown by propagation in his mother’s womb, nor came from nothing, nor proceeded from any source other than the Virgin’s flesh, but “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God” [John I]. And because he is God, he is worthily above all—greater than all, more excellent than all—not in place but in dignity; not yet in body but in honor; not yet in the impassibility of flesh but in the fullness of grace and truth [Col. 0342D].

All others are from below, and for this very reason, because they are from below and came from below—from an earthly father, taken from earth, whose substance or beginning is earth—and, though by the Creator’s grace he could have become heaven, he became earth for the serpent to eat. Therefore all are rightly beneath him, and he is above all. Hence it follows: “He who is of the earth is of the earth, and speaks of the earth.”

For what is it to be “of the earth” but to have received the beginning of one’s existence from earth, and to be nothing more than what has been taken from the earthly mass of the human race? He who is of the earth, he says—that is, whose being began from earth—is of the earth; that is, earthly, just like his ancestor of whom the Apostle says: “The first man is of the earth, earthly” [I Cor. XV; Col. 0343A]. Everyone is altogether earthly, because he has an earthly foundation—that is, an earthly beginning—and consequently speaks of the earth: he savors earthly things and is entangled in earthly senses.

What then must happen? How is he aided? He says: “**He who comes from heaven is above all, and what he has seen and heard, this he testifies.**” He who comes from heaven is therefore heavenly, as the same Apostle cited above says: “The second man is heavenly, from heaven” [ibid.]. Therefore, as stated, he is above all; and “what he has seen and heard, this he testifies,” so that we may all receive from his fullness and learn to speak something of heaven, though we spoke only of earth.

See now to what he directs his words—that is, why he said, “He is above all,” and how, or above whom, he is above all. For “what he has seen and heard, this he testifies”: namely, he is above all those who have testified that the kingdom of God would come, that entrance into God’s kingdom would be opened to human beings. The prophets and kings formerly testified to this; the patriarchs and righteous people, expecting and foreknowing it, greeted it from afar and spoke beforehand of it to their descendants and fellow heirs [Col. 0343C].

But did they see that kingdom? Did they hear the voices of that kingdom? Coming from there to this world, did they announce to captives sitting in darkness, to those in chains, what they had freely seen and heard? Did they come from heaven? Or rather, were they born in this captivity, having previously not existed at all, wholly sprung from earth?

Therefore this witness is the fitting witness above all witnesses of the kingdom of God, because he already existed before he came here, and came here from the kingdom of God—from his own kingdom—into our exile. Although he was king of that kingdom of God, he chose for our sake, in order to testify to and open it for us, to be born in the form of a servant [Phil. II]. Thus it is most truly said here: “And what he has seen and heard, this he testifies.”

The prophets indeed saw certain visions of that kingdom, and for this reason they were called seers [Col. 0343D]. But it is one thing to see, through hidden inspiration, figurative and enigmatic visions of God’s kingdom; another to have seen the kingdom itself and, coming from it to us who have never been there, to testify or proclaim it.

But why did he say this to his disciples, or to the Jews with whom the question about purification had arisen? Why, when they said, “Rabbi, behold, he baptizes, and all are coming to him,” did he say it, except that his disciples might cease being jealous on his behalf, that the Jews might cease devising snares against the truth, and that all might rather come with bowed head to him, the true Baptist?

Because, chilled by envy, they refused to do so, he immediately adds with grief: “**And no one has received his testimony**” [Col. 0344A]. O counsel of evildoers, ruined Synagogue, wicked assembly! See what a messenger, what a lawful witness, what faithful testimony they did not receive. The foreknown indignity of the matter deeply moved John’s prescient heart; the bitterness of the sacrilege struck the mind of that great lord who knew it, so that in grief he cried out: “And no one has received his testimony.”

For truly no one received his testimony while he walked among human beings; while he stood bodily present in the assembly of people and bore testimony to the truth, whether in the synagogues of the Jews or in Pilate’s tribunal. The injustice of the cross cries this aloud; the indignity of the death by which he was punished as a false witness proves it.

But someone may say: It is not the case that no one received his testimony, for some received it and some believed in him. We agree; we do not deny that some believed in some fashion, however uncertain and weak. Since they confessed him to be the Son of God, they received his testimony. Yet at that decisive hour of necessary witness, how many dared to testify or subscribe? Did not all flee, leaving him? When the Shepherd was struck, were not the sheep scattered, leaving him alone? [Matt. XXVI; Zech. XIII; Col. 0344B]

Therefore, while this Lord in the form of a servant proclaimed the testimonies of God’s kingdom, although he confirmed the same testimonies not only by words according to the Scriptures but also by miraculous deeds, no one received his testimony. But when, rejected by the council of evildoers, despised by the judges of iniquity, and punished as a false witness, he rose from the dead and ascended into heaven, reporting to God his Father who had sent him what he had suffered, immediately the Holy Spirit came as the helper of his testimony, a worthy defender. From that time onward no one failed to receive his testimony.

Then he was proved and recognized as having been a true witness; then and thenceforward he is to be believed to be the true King—indeed, the true God—and to have brought true laws from the kingdom of God. Hence it follows: “**But he who has received his testimony has sealed that God is true.**” [Col. 0344C]

Who is this blessed one who has received his testimony, except the whole Christian people, that son of salvation, marked by the Holy Spirit through the hands of the ministers to whom it was said: “You shall receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, and you shall be witnesses to me in Jerusalem, throughout Judaea and Samaria, and even to the farthest part of the earth” [Acts I]?

For whoever has heard them—having within themselves the testimony of the Holy Spirit who came upon them and proclaiming it by testimony, for example when they say: “The Word was made flesh and dwelt among us, and we saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father” [John I]—whoever has heard these and other such things preached and has been baptized in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, has received his testimony. And regarding him who did not deny, when questioned before Pilate, that he was King of God’s kingdom, the true King and Son of God, yet was denied and punished as a false witness—such a person certainly declares that God is true: that he is the one true God with the Father and the Holy Spirit [Col. 0345A].

He declares this; he has sealed it in his heart; he has depicted it on his forehead with the sign of the cross, believing in his heart unto righteousness and confessing with his mouth unto salvation [Rom. X]. The foolish Jew or heretic, such as Cerinthus, attempts to dissolve this truth, saying in his heart, “There is no God” [Ps. XIII]. But the receiver of the testimony has sealed—that is, committed to worthy remembrance—the words of his testimonies, by which God is steadfastly defended as true.

For in his Gospel he speaks in the manner in which God speaks. Thus it immediately follows: “**He who is of God speaks the words of God.**” What is it to speak God’s words except to speak in the manner in which God alone may speak? There is something nearly similar in the Acts of the Apostles concerning Herod, where it is read in just rebuke: “When he had taken his seat, dressed in royal robes, the people shouted, ‘The voice of a god, and not of a man’” [Acts XII]—that is, words by which it is right and lawful to acclaim God alone and not a human being. For example: “King living forever, ever mighty, almighty, immortal king and our God,” and similar expressions [Col. 0345B].

But the angel of the Lord struck Herod because he accepted the people’s excessive favor and did not give honor to God. This one, however, when he spoke God’s words, when he uttered God’s voice—for example, “Before Abraham was, I am” [John VIII]; “I and the Father are one” [John X]; and “I am the beginning, who also speak to you” [John VIII]—when he uttered these and similar words belonging to God, not man, the glory of miracles accompanied them, proving that he himself was the true God.

He was not like the aforesaid Herod, who, having accepted God’s words shouted to him, was struck and, rotting, consumed by worms; groaning, he said: “Behold your god”—that is, a false god; namely, a man, not God.

Therefore he says: “**For he whom God sent speaks the words of God.**” As though he said: He who was not, in the common manner of nature, conveyed into his mother’s womb by propagation, but came into this world from God and was sent—who was not, as I and all the prophets were, born in order to be sent, but was sent in order to be born—he speaks the words of God. That is, he speaks as God speaks, and the receiver of his testimony, through his words, receives with believing heart that God is true [Col. 0345C].

This is readily recognized from the works which follow his words. The receiver seals the same words of his divinity in the purse of his heart or memory, so that whenever proud Goliath—that is, Cerinthus, Arius, or another heretic—blasphemes this God of Israel, he may bring forth these words, prepared like David’s smooth stones from the rock, and strike the brow of blaspheming pride [I Kings XVII], testifying that the Son of God is the true God.

For he is no ordinary or common man; he is not bounded by the common measure of Adam’s children, nor by the distributive grace allotted to righteous people. This is what follows: “**For God does not give the Spirit by measure.**” Truly, not by measure: for the whole Holy Spirit, with all his gifts, rests wholly upon him—as the complete form of the dove showed me. The dove showed itself to me above his head with all its members [John I]. The Holy Spirit was not given in this way to anyone among all the thousands from whom this one was chosen [Song V; Col. 0346A].

All of us, people under a condemned head, spared from destruction and death only by God’s mercy—wretched and needy, unhappily born, exiles from the heavenly Father, who gnawed away in the wilderness, foul with calamity and misery, and thought it luxury to live among thorns—we who were formerly dumb dogs, unable to bark because of hunger [Isa. LVI], count it a great thing, and are well treated, that the God of our fathers deigned to be called our God. He placed us among the dogs of his flock, and refreshed from his crumbs [Matt. XV], so that we may be able to open our mouths and bark.

For each of us, a half-ounce of meager knowledge is thrown as though it were rye bread, or a quarter portion of prophetic grace is distributed; content each with our own measure and acknowledging that we have been well treated, we keep watch outside [Col. 0346B]. But this noble man, happily born, appointed Lord of heaven and commander of the holy angels before he was born in this form, is circumscribed by no measure, nor does he display any divided little gift of the Holy Spirit.

But what is this? I will express to you in a brief sentence the vast difference between him and us.

“**The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand.**” Which of us has had ears to hear, and has deserved to hear, what this great herald said, standing afar off and standing humbly as he yielded place to the greater one—the Son of God—in the contrition of his heart? What does this contemplator of the depths of God the Father say? What did he say? What did he pour forth with most reverent heart and most devout mouth? “The Father,” he says, “loves the Son.”

Father, rightly: is it strange or unjust that you love the Son, that you judge your Son worthy of honor? If indeed we speak righteousness, let us judge rightly, we children of men [Ps. LVII], since “no one has ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it” [Eph. V; Col. 0346C]. If each person loves his own flesh, and a lawful father judges his son, begotten from his own flesh, worthy of the same honor as himself, and no one reproves this, how much more rightly does God the Father love his own substance in his Son and judge him consubstantial with himself worthy of the same honor as himself?

What if, coming forth from the Father’s bosom, he put on the corruptible skin of our mortality? Is he therefore less honorable, or ought he to have been less beloved even by the Father who sent him for this purpose? Ought not the Father rather to raise up to the fellowship of his right hand the very man whom he put on at his command?

Therefore he says: “The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand.” The Son, he says, as he now is—namely, clothed with the form of a servant—the Father loves even with that form of a servant in such a way that he has given all things into his hands. The Father himself will never judge anyone, but wills that all judgment be carried out through that servant’s form which his Son assumed at his command [Col. 0346D].

The prophet Daniel bears witness to this same thing long before: “I looked,” he says, “in a vision of the night, and behold, the Son of Man came in the clouds of heaven and came even to the Ancient of Days; and they presented him before him, and there was given to him kingdom and honor, and all peoples, tribes, and tongues shall serve him” [Dan. VII; Col. 0347A].

Why then are you jealous and say: “Behold, he baptizes, and all are coming to him”? All—every one of them, even those who do not wish to come to him—have been given into his hand. When he has been lifted up from the earth, he will draw all things to himself [John XII]. He will make all stand before his judgment: the sheep indeed at the right, but the goats at the left; he will judge both those within and those outside. The Father has given him so great a kingdom, so great an honor, so great a power—an eternal power.

For the Father does not love the Son by measure. If we know what the Father’s love is, it is plainly evident that the Father’s entire heart is full of love for the Son. No corner could remain in the bosom of that immeasurable and uncircumscribed breast in which anything, great or small, of the Father’s entire treasure could be shut away from the Son [Col. 0347B].

For what is the love by which the Father loves the Son, or the Son the Father, but the Holy Spirit, consubstantial with Father and Son? But it was said above that “God does not give the Spirit by measure.” Therefore I know that the Father loves the Son not by measure, but with all his heart, all his strength, all his love, all his Spirit. What then could he retain, or where could he store, what he did not give into his Son’s hand?

If parents lay up treasures for their carnal children, how much more ought such a parent be believed to have laid up heaven and earth, and whatever they contain, for such a Son? Yet how great, or what kind, are these treasures before him? They are “as a drop from a bucket, as tiny dust” [Isa. XL; Col. 0347C].

The narrow and needy minds of mortals esteem these things so highly that they say: Where was God, and how did he exist before making them? In what solitude did he dwell silently, without any riches and without all attendants? We think this because, in our poverty of understanding, we behold only the dregs of his riches—that is, creation—made by him in time and place.

But his accumulation of honor or riches did not increase more through the multitude of creation, nor was it diminished more through the fall of angelic or human creation, than if a single drop fell from a full bucket. Before he made these things, “our Lord was great, and great was his power, and there was no number to his wisdom” [Ps. CXLVI].

Why then, you ask, is the Son so greatly magnified by his herald because the Father gave all things into his hand? Why does the Son himself exult in one place, saying: “All things have been delivered to me by my Father” [Matt. I]? What material for exultation and glory is there here, that the nations are given him as an inheritance by him before whom all are like a drop from a bucket?

Yet the exultation and magnificence are truly worthy. For it is not greed that glories, but goodwill that rejoices; it is not that the kingdom benefits him, but that he benefits the kingdom. He is not exalted by our service; our service is freed through his dominion [Col. 0347D]. When he receives a kingdom in us, he stoops down; when we are subjected to him, we loose the chains upon our necks.

Therefore what John says, “The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand,” is the same as if he had said: We all were by nature children of wrath, but he alone is the Son of love, and God the Father works the salvation of us all through his hand. Hence it follows:

“**He who believes in the Son of God has eternal life; but he who is unbelieving toward the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him.**”

Therefore go, all you Egyptians; go, all of you, to Joseph, and say to him: “Our salvation is in your hand” [Gen. XLVII]. For this is what the herald of the Savior of the world says. This is what the forerunner of the increasing Son says, who runs before his royal chariot with the voice of proclamation: “He who believes in the Son of God has eternal life; but he who is unbelieving toward the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him” [Col. 0348A–B].

What is this? All human beings sinned in Adam; driven out from God’s paradise, they were cast down into darkness and became Egyptians—that is, people of darkness. Behold, they are perishing from hunger; behold, they have not found the bread of eternal life. But now this man rules throughout all the land of Egypt. Whoever believes in him will be fed with the bread of life and understanding, and given to drink from the saving water of wisdom (Ecclus. 15). To such a one will be opened the storehouses of paradise, which had been shut against the gluttonous human being because of the bite taken from the forbidden tree; and, eating from the tree of life, he will possess eternal life. Whoever does not go to him, whoever does not believe in him, “shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him” [Col. 0348C].

This was ordained in the council-chamber of the Trinity, where this Son, begotten, obediently received the command to become the Savior of the world. Our whole earth has been struck with barrenness; the entire mass of humankind has been condemned by the curse of thorns and thistles. What then shall we eat, all of us unhappy Egyptians? Whoever among us, whoever among all Adam’s children, does not believe in this Son of God and does not confess him as Savior of the world, according to the decree of the great Father, the great King, God, who caused him to mount his chariot, “shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him.”

What wrath of God? Surely that which came down upon his father, the transgressor. For he does not say, “the wrath of God comes down upon him,” but, “the wrath of God remains upon him” [Col. 0348D]. Long ago it came down upon all by hereditary right, and “there is no other name given under heaven to human beings” (Acts 4; Rom. 9) through which it can be removed, except this sole and only Son of God. Therefore upon the one who does not believe him the wrath of God remains, because, as has been said, it can be removed only through him.

Clearly this condition of salvation or life is not newly established. For Abraham our father according to faith was justified by the same covenant (Gal. 3; Gen. 12). Unless he had believed in the promise concerning his seed—which is Christ—that in him all nations would be blessed, he would neither have been called righteous nor a friend of God, and consequently could not have been saved at all (Rom. 4; Gen. 17). Likewise, his descendants were saved by the same faith in the seed to come [Col. 0349A], and by the sign of that faith, circumcision, of which something has already been said elsewhere.

But what if very many who possessed the sign of circumcision did not know the meaning of circumcision itself? Even now, after circumcision has been abolished, are there not among us—who are marked with the cross of Christ—some who know nothing of all the sacraments beyond Christ’s name alone? Some, through infancy, do not even know how to invoke the name of Christ, the Son of God; yet, because his name has been invoked over them, if they die at that age, they are saved. For being untaught is very different from being unbelieving.

Let us therefore understand the saying universally—that is, as concerning the entire body of human beings, ancient and modern alike: “Whoever does not believe in the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him” [Col. 0349B].

Thus far this lamp, the preparer of the Lord’s ways, was to burn and shine. Now the sacrilegious deed of murderous and adulterous Herod must extinguish it (Matt. 14), God permitting it, because his light is plainly not suited to the present time. For it is expedient that, before Christ is publicly proclaimed everywhere by such a light, the eyes of the Jews should be darkened; and that, rushing about in darkness with a frenzied mind, they should stumble over this stone of stumbling (Ps. 90; Rom. 9), this rock of offense (1 Pet. 2), so as to be broken and crushed.

Therefore let the venerable one, the friend of the bridegroom, now withdraw, proved and having completed his service, so that at this time our bridegroom, our God, may be a hidden God, and that no one may speak such lofty things concerning him. Nor should he grieve because he is removed as though unworthy to untie the strap of his sandal [Col. 0349C] (Matt. 3)—that is, because he does not reach the fitting time for preaching Christ’s incarnation. For those too who carried his sandals into Idumea (Ps. 59), that is, who preached to the nations faith in his incarnation, were born of women.

Yet the bridegroom himself, whose sandals John desired to carry, declared universally: “Among those born of women none greater than John the Baptist has arisen” (Matt. 11). Therefore he should not grieve that he has been rejected as though unworthy. For wherever these sandals have been carried, his blood too, shed in Herod’s prison and at Herod’s banquet, will cry out; and it will proclaim in a great voice Christ’s faith and the testimonies of chastity.

It follows:

## Chapter IV

[Col. 0349D] “Therefore, when Jesus knew that the Pharisees had heard that Jesus was making and baptizing more disciples than John—although Jesus himself was not baptizing, but his disciples were—he left Judaea and went again into Galilee.”

Jesus himself first does what he, the teacher of humility, is about to teach; and by a reverent example he foreshadows the very thing which, through Paul, the dwelling-place of his grace, he will tell us: that we should be “outdoing one another in showing honor” (Rom. 12). For as long as this lamp previously spoken of—the most brilliant lamp, John—could burn and shine (John 5), and as long as the children of darkness allowed him to stand shining upon his lampstand, the Lord of all judged him worthy of such honor that, just as John did not commend himself by his preaching but Christ, so conversely [Col. 0350A] Christ Jesus, while John was still alive, did not anywhere set before the people the chair of his teaching by the office of public preaching.

Had he wished to do so, his own great brightness would certainly have more quickly obscured John’s reputation, just as the feeble glow of a lamp is commonly overwhelmed by the noonday sun. Carefully avoiding this, the provider of good examples did not even permit disputes to increase because his own disciples also baptized—disputes which, as has been said above, had already begun. Rather, he graciously yielded place and time, so that his Baptist might reach the completion of his course with due honor.

This is what the Evangelist now relates: “Therefore, when Jesus knew that the Pharisees had heard that Jesus was making and baptizing more disciples than John [Col. 0350B]—although Jesus himself was not baptizing, but his disciples were—he left Judaea and went again into Galilee.”

He who knows all things before they happen is said then first to have known this, when the aforementioned dispute arose from John’s disciples together with the Jews. And he is rightly said to have known it then, when, since others now knew, it had to become manifest that he did not delight in the false praises of the envious—by the same maturity of judgment with which he disdained to hear the testimonies of demons crying, “We know that you are the Holy One of God; you are the Son of God” (Mark 1; Luke 4).

The Pharisees heard that Jesus was baptizing and making more disciples than John; but they did not have ears to hear. They were altogether deaf to hearing God’s word and blind to seeing [Col. 0350C] the rectitude of the divine plan. For they, as has been said above, “rejected the counsel of God, not having been baptized with John’s baptism” (Luke 7). “Their own malice blinded them, and they did not know the mysteries of God” (Wis. 2).

Such men heard that Jesus was baptizing: their malicious envy attributed what the disciples did to their Master. For Jesus himself was not baptizing, but his disciples were. Their baptism was enough to furnish an occasion for those eager to slander the Master. They therefore said: “Look, we have two Baptists. Is either of them Christ? It is more credible that neither is. What is this, then, if not the wandering favor of an uneducated mob? It first whispered to us in our ignorance that John was Christ; now, its curiosity sated and John despised, it follows this new man with the same rashness or uncertainty of judgment. Look now how contentiously these two men act, magnifying their names among the peoples in opposition to one another. Which of them will more stubbornly retain the name of Christ among this accursed crowd which does not know the law?”

“When Jesus knew,” says the Evangelist, that the Pharisees had heard what was stated above, “he left Judaea and went again into Galilee”—not because he feared their malice, but because, according to his humanity, he yielded to his predecessor and fittingly awaited his own time, which had not yet come while John was still preaching (John 7).

“He went again into Galilee,” he says. He significantly adds, “again,” because he had gone there long before [Col. 0351A], after the Spirit had driven him into the wilderness following his baptism by John (Luke 4)—namely, when he found Philip and changed water into wine at Cana of Galilee (John 1–2). You should understand that this return to Galilee, from which the other Evangelists begin, was not his first but his second after his baptism.

Let us attentively contemplate this return to Galilee, because it is wholly figurative. By the sayings and deeds which the present reading recounts, he mystically foreshadows, with the finger of God as guide and disposer of his paths, where he will lead and into what channel he will divert that stream of water of which he had spoken in Judaea: “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3); that river of living water which was to flow forth from his temple (Ezek. 47), when it should be destroyed through Jewish sacrilege, just as he then said to them: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” [Col. 0351B] (John 2).

The Evangelist begins it thus: “Now he had to pass through Samaria.” For what reason? Surely the reason stated much later, after this journey, in these words: “For Jesus himself testified that a prophet has no honor in his own country.” Therefore, in order to establish the truth of this testimony of his—that he had no honor among the Jews for no other reason than that the Jews, his own countrymen, despised him as someone familiar out of envy—and, conversely, to prove from the fact that he would receive divine honor in a country not his own that there was no other cause at work than the common vice of proud persons, envy, “he had to pass through Samaria.”

This was necessary; it suited the purpose or plan of his divinity that he should make his way through those foreigners and foreshadow the plan he held concerning us, who were strangers to God and aliens to the covenants. For the Samaritans were counted among foreigners by the Jews, and the Jews were not counted as such by the Samaritans.

There was a long-standing, twofold cause of dissension. The first was that, through Jeroboam’s agency, the ten tribes had been torn away from Judah and the house of David; leaving the temple of the Lord which Solomon had built in Jerusalem, they worshipped as God the golden calves made by Jeroboam [Col. 0351D]. This was at their king’s prompting, because he feared that, if in accordance with the law they went up three times yearly to Jerusalem to appear before the Lord their God, they would be induced by their brothers, the children of Judah and Benjamin, to desert him (3 Kings 12).

The other cause was that, after Shalmaneser had carried those same ten tribes into captivity and settled among their remnants inhabitants gathered from diverse nations, every nation made its own god. Thus Israel’s remnants, mixed with the nations, gave their Jewish enemies greater grounds for contempt, so that they justly seemed contemptible (4 Kings 17).

But the purpose of the Divinity was that salvation should pass to foreigners when the Jews, who were to destroy the most holy temple of his body, as has been said above (John 2), were abandoned because of their unbelief [Col. 0352A]. It was therefore fitting that, in leaving Judaea, he should pass through Samaria. He wished first to speak by deeds what he would later confirm by words. For he was going to say, “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28); and already he indicates that the Samaritan woman ought to seek this same teaching from him, under the name of water springing up into eternal life.

Let us therefore attempt to unfold the mysteries of the present reading—desirable for us Gentiles, who are strangers, more than much gold and precious stone, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb (Ps. 18)—with the help of him whose grace, hidden beneath the bark of the letter, we reverence.

“He came therefore to a city called Sychar, near the estate which Jacob gave to his son Joseph” [Col. 0352B]. Sychar is Shechem itself; but through an error the faulty reading *Sychar* came into use. It is a Samaritan city now called Neapolis. Samaria, indeed, was the royal city now called Sebaste; and the entire region around it had once taken its name from the city.

There, namely at Shechem, Jacob gave an estate to his son Joseph, when, dying in Egypt, he said to him: “I will give you one portion beyond your brothers, which I took from the hand of the Amorite with my sword and my bow” (Gen. 48). In saying that he possessed it by bow and sword, he called bow and sword “justice,” through which he, a sojourner and stranger, deserved to be delivered from danger after Shechem and Hamor had been killed because of the rape of his Dinah (Gen. 34). For, as the history relates, he feared that the neighboring towns and [Col. 0352C] villages would rise against him because of the overthrow of their allied city; but the Lord did not allow them to harm him.

Or rather it should be understood thus: “I will give you one portion, which I bought by my own strength,” that is, with the money which I acquired by much labor and sweat. What he says, “beyond your brothers,” shows that he gave it to Joseph’s tribe apart from the allotment. Indeed Joseph was buried in that place, and his mausoleum may still be seen there today.

Near that estate the Lord Jesus came. “Now Jacob’s spring was there.” This spring was notable and well known, both because of the scarcity of springs and the force [or perhaps “continuous flow”] of its water—since in most places of that land, apart from cisterns, there is a shortage of water—and because of the dignity and memory of so great a patriarch. Especially when the two sides were heated against one another, that is, Jew against Samaritan, the Samaritan, faced with a Jew glorifying in David’s city and Solomon’s temple, found consolation for his distressed poverty by defending himself with the dwelling-places of the earlier patriarchs (3 Kings 8), who had lived in those regions.

“Jesus therefore, wearied from the journey, sat there beside the spring. It was about the sixth hour” [Col. 0352D]. Here mysteries must now be sought. For just as the sun’s image is reflected here in the spring below, so this weariness and sitting of the Lord Jesus refer to another weariness and sitting, which he contemplated in the hidden counsel of his divinity.

What weariness of his own, then, did he contemplate? Above he had said to the Jews: “Destroy this temple, and I will raise it in three days. But he said this concerning the temple of his body” (John 2) [Col. 0353A]. This was indeed to happen; and as they did this, Jesus himself, through the journey of his humanity, would be wearied by a real passion, real sufferings, and real death.

Then, having ascended into heaven, he would come “to the estate which Jacob gave Joseph his son beyond his brothers”: that is, leaving the Jews, he would come to the nations, whom God the Father would give as an inheritance to that true Joseph, of whom the ever-increasing son Joseph bore the type both in name and deeds. The Son of God would come to that inheritance of his; and, after the bitter weariness of death, he would sit in great repose at the Father’s right hand. He would sit over the well of this his inheritance—that is, he would surpass every depth of human desire or philosophical wisdom.

For when he demonstrated that the foolishness of God is wiser than human beings, and by the foolishness of the cross confounded and subdued the wise of this world (1 Cor. 1), and restrained human desires by his fear, what else did he do but sit over the well? Therefore, after he tells the Jews, when they have driven him from his temple, “Destroy this temple, and I will raise it in three days,” he leaves Judaea and sits over the Samaritans’ well [Col. 0353B]. For after he has cast them out of God’s house and kingdom, because they most wickedly destroyed the temple of his body and, when he said in the agony of death, “I thirst,” offered him a drink of gall and vinegar (John 19), he leaves them their house desolate. He comes to drink the faith and salvation of the nations and to give them living water, which, flowing forth from the temple of his body when destroyed, the Jews did not allow to come to them.

When Jesus thus sits, it is the sixth hour, because now, while the Lord of all reigns seated at the Father’s right hand, the sixth age of the world is passing away [Col. 0353C].

It follows: “A Samaritan woman came to draw water.” This is certainly what the thirsty and parched Gentile world did. It ran eagerly to the empty teaching of this world’s philosophers, in the hope either of satisfying curiosity according to the Stoics or of filling every desire according to the Epicureans; it hoped that in them lay a vein of living waters—that is, that the schools of those philosophers proclaimed the path of true and highest blessedness. For what did they suppose the academy of Socrates or Plato, and the other diverse schools of philosophers, to be, except wells of living waters?

Thus the Samaritan woman came to draw water and at last found the Lord seated over the well. That is, the Gentile world, having long admired its philosophers, at last heard, through the apostles, the wisdom of God—Christ—opposing them.

“Jesus said to her, ‘Give me a drink.’ For his disciples had gone into the city to buy food. The Samaritan woman therefore said to him: ‘How is it that you, being a Jew, ask a drink from me, who am a Samaritan woman? For Jews do not associate with Samaritans’” [Col. 0353D].

It was not the woman who first addressed Jesus, but Jesus who addressed the woman; and when he asks to drink from her, he declares that he does not regard her, or any human being, as common or unclean. Yet he could not have been ignorant of the very reason for which the woman was astonished, and which the Evangelist adds: “For,” he says, “Jews do not associate [Col. 0354A] with Samaritans.”

In this a small spark of his condescension shines forth; but in his judgment the immensity of his grace, afterward spread abroad among all nations in the same condescension, is prefigured. For as he then anticipated that woman by speaking to her—though she had no possibility of converse or any communion among the Jews, who despised all nations—and as he deigned first to entreat her, though without her aid he could have drunk not only water but changed the entire well into wine: so his mercy anticipates the merits of all nations, which were regarded as foreign and unclean by that particular people of God, who placed excessive confidence in their own merits or those of their fathers. He deigned to entreat them to share with him, especially as the Apostle acting as ambassador for him says: “We beseech you on Christ’s behalf: be reconciled to God” (2 Cor. 5).

When he sought that reconciliation from the Church drawn from the nations by a spontaneous and gratuitous embassy, he certainly asked to drink from her, because thirsting for her salvation, he truly drew it in amid a great thirst with all the depths of his love [Col. 0354B]. Hearing this, those nations were filled with more astonishment and joy than this woman, as it is written in the Acts of the Apostles (ch. 15): when they had read the apostles’ letter, they rejoiced at its consolation—namely, that they could be saved without circumcision and the remaining works of the law, by faith in Christ alone.

Nor is it without mystery that his disciples went away—of whom it is also said that “they had gone into the city to buy food”—and that the Savior spoke alone with the sinner and foreign woman alone. For when Christ’s grace first addressed the nations, when he sent his angel to Cornelius (Acts 10), Christ’s apostles had gone away and had not spoken anything of the word of salvation with people of that kind. Believing that only the children of the kingdom—that is, the Jews—were to be incorporated into themselves, they were, as it were, going around the city, according to the Psalmist: “They were scattered to seek food; and because they were not satisfied, they murmured” (Ps. 58).

Therefore, when the astonished woman had said, “How is it that you, being a Jew, ask me for a drink, when I am a Samaritan woman?” Jesus answered and said to her: “If you knew the gift of God, and who it is who says to you, ‘Give me a drink,’ perhaps you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water.”

Wisdom now deigns to use the elegance of human eloquence beautifully divided. From visible water, for which the majesty hidden in flesh had stooped to ask, he makes a metaphor, gradually raising the woman’s mind and gently inviting her to seek the grace of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0354D].

“If you knew,” he says, “the gift of God, and who it is who says to you, ‘Give me a drink.’” The sequence and tenor of the words must be carefully noted. He does not say, “If you knew God”; for not only the Samaritans but also many Gentiles could know, in some measure, that there is one Creator God. But he says, “If you knew the gift of God,” which is surely nothing other than the Holy Spirit, the gift of Father and Son, whom this wretched world did not know before the Redeemer’s coming.

Again, he does not say, “If you knew who says to you, ‘Give me a drink,’” which she could certainly have known by sight and hearing, and could have pointed out with an extended finger to her fellow-citizens of Samaria as he sat over the well. Rather, he says, “If you knew who it is who says to you”—that is, what his essence is, how greatly he differs from other mortals: that he is not merely Son of Man but also Son of God, not merely human being but also God.
