The meaning is: If you knew the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; if you had heard the gospel of his name, perhaps you would believe in him and ask from him the gift of God, namely living water—that is, you would be baptized, so as to receive through the grace of the Holy Spirit remission of sins. For many people already knew God the Father in some fashion; but they did not know that the one now speaking these words was the Son of God, nor did they know the Holy Spirit [Col. 0355A].

This was said as a reproach to the Jews from whom he had now returned, knowing them to be unbelieving and having cast them out of the temple. It prefigures what would happen: when they had been cast out, he would introduce foreigners into the kingdom of God through rebirth by water and the Holy Spirit—what he afterward stated plainly to Nicodemus.

It is like what he says in reproaching Jewish cities: “If the mighty works that were done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have repented in sackcloth and ashes” (Matt. 10). What Truth declares concerning this Samaritan woman should be understood universally concerning the idolatrous nations. When they were granted to hear and know, through evangelical preaching, the gift of God and the Christ, Son of God, who spoke to them in his apostles, they repented; and they asked of Christ the Savior for the gift of God, living water, namely the Spirit granting remission of sins. They were baptized in the name of the Trinity; and thus one Church was made from all nations. This woman bore its type, and Truth, giving testimony in her person, testified that she had sinned not through malice, like the faithless Synagogue, but through ignorance [Col. 0355B].

But the woman, still erring in a carnal sense concerning the name of the water for which she had come to draw, “said to him: ‘Sir, you have nothing with which to draw, and the well is deep. From where, then, do you have living water? Are you greater than our father Jacob, who gave us the well and drank from it himself, and his sons, and his livestock?’”

For this woman erred in the expression “living water,” not knowing that “living water” is an equivocal designation for a continuously flowing stream of invisible water and for the unfailing grace of the Holy Spirit. But now it is pleasing to compare her objection with the objections of the Jews. Above, when they asked him for signs and he said something which seemed impossible to their understanding—“Destroy this temple,” he said, “and I will raise it in three days” (John 2)—they irreverently objected: “This temple was built in forty-six years, and will you raise it in three days?” (ibid.). “And you,” they say, are a contemptible man; for by saying “you” they express arrogance and contempt. “So, contemptible man who deserves crucifixion, will you raise it in three days?”

But she speaks not with hostile mockery but with friendly inquiry, having prefaced a reverent address: “Sir,” she says, “you have nothing with which to draw, and the well is deep” [Col. 0356A]. Had she not humbly spoken first, addressing him as “Sir,” perhaps we might think that she was unwilling to lend her vessel to a foreign man, a Jew, for drawing water. But now it is clear that she did not despise the Jew; rather, she feared being despised by the Jew. For the Jews, having a more evident ground for pride, did not even deign to use Samaritan vessels. The Samaritans, however, yielding to the habit of their conscience, although they sometimes consoled themselves through spirited contention, were content not to be despised and not to be excluded from communion with those who trusted in themselves as true Israelites.

Again, the Samaritan woman, seeing no vessel present for that Jew, our Lord, except her own, says: “Sir, you have nothing with which to draw, and the well is deep”—of such depth, namely, that your hand cannot reach it. It is indeed forty cubits deep, measured from a person’s side to the tips of outstretched fingers. Is not, then, the Jews’ pride farther from salvation than the humble conscience of the Samaritans?

Here and there Truth, the President of justice, sits in the temple of his body, weighing the causes of words and things in the balance. From that same temple of his body flows one water, entrusted not to the Jews but offered to the Samaritans; indeed, to the whole Church from the Gentiles, which, as has often been said, this Samaritan woman prefigured [Col. 0356B].

Not yet understanding this, and supposing that the Savior, whom she did not know, despised the Samaritan water itself with Jewish haughtiness, she says: “From where, then, do you have living water? Are you greater than our father Jacob, who gave us the well and himself drank from it, with his sons and his livestock?”

It is as though she said: “Is any ordinary inhabitant of Jerusalem greater, purer, or more religious than our father Jacob? No. Yet he gave us this well—he, I say, not just any foreigner, but our father, so great, so holy, so pure, and beloved by God—‘gave us this well, and himself drank from it, with his sons and his livestock.’ From where, then, do you, or any Jew, have water which, in contempt of this water as though it were dead or unclean, you call living water, or clean water?”

Note that she does not say, “who dug,” but “who gave us the well.” For Jacob is nowhere said to have dug a well there, but only to have bought a portion of the field from the sons of Hamor, Shechem’s father (Gen. 33). The Evangelist reports that estate, in accordance with the truth of the ancient history, as having been given by Jacob to his son Joseph, as has been said above; he then adds concerning this well, “Now Jacob’s spring was there” [Col. 0356C]. Every well is a spring, although conversely not every spring is a well.

Abraham and Isaac are, indeed, recorded to have dug wells at certain places; the Palestinians, out of envy, are also said to have stopped up most of these, and to have disputed over some of them. But neither Jacob nor any of the patriarchs is remembered to have dug this well, concerning which the Savior has so great a conversation with the Samaritan woman [Col. 0357A]. Therefore she rightly did not say, “who dug,” but “who gave us the well”—perhaps bought together with the estate itself from the sons of Hamor. She thought it sufficient for the defense of this water that so great a patriarch drank from it, “with his sons and his livestock.”

In response, our Lord accommodates himself to the woman’s slowness, knowing that he had undertaken the instruction of unlearned souls. The general proposition “living water,” whose distinctions or kinds she could not discern, is defined by the particular differences between the living water which he said he could give and the water known by this woman alone:

“Everyone who drinks from this water will thirst again. But whoever drinks from the water that I shall give him will never thirst” [Col. 0357B].

These differences—thirsting again and never thirsting—are contrary to one another, like extinguishing every thirst and extinguishing no thirst. It is easy to observe these contrary effects in our Lord’s words. For the water which this woman had come to draw, namely elemental water, does not extinguish any thirst whatsoever. Whoever drinks it refreshes the body only; when he thirsts again, he clearly shows that he has not fully overcome nature’s need.

But the water given by Jesus utterly extinguishes the everlasting thirst of body and soul, so that the burning person may not thirst in hell, nor the thirsty person burn, but, with the Lamb who speaks these words as guide, may go to the springs of the waters of life (Rev. 7); and, cleansing every need of body and soul by the draught of eternal blessedness, may never lack any good forever (Isa. 58). Hence it follows:

“But the water that I shall give him shall become in him a spring of water leaping up into eternal life” [Col. 0357C].

What is this living water except, as has been said above, the grace of the Holy Spirit received in Christ’s baptism? This water is the Holy Spirit; this water is God. This water is, in the heart of God the Father, the spring of life; in the mouth of God the Son, the river of grace and peace; in the blessed angels, the torrent of glory; in the chosen human beings, the flood of life.

When it has been drunk by anyone, it springs back to its source, the abyss of eternal divinity—deeper than hell, broader than the earth, wider than the sea, and higher than heaven. There, I say, it springs back; thence it comes; and by its leap into eternal life it raises the soul of the one drinking it even if that soul has descended into hell, where it neither hungers nor thirsts, and heat and sun do not strike it (Isa. 49) [Col. 0357D].

Before it leaps there, it becomes a spring in the drinker. Pouring out streams of wisdom and knowledge through the bosom of the heart, filling the soul’s whole channel, and gradually breaking forth through the passage of the mouth in the word of life, it abundantly waters neighboring gardens and threshing floors far away. Such a soul merits to hear: “A spring of gardens, a well of living waters” (Cant. 4). Rightly, therefore, he says: “Whoever drinks from the water which I shall give him, it shall become in him a spring of water leaping up into eternal life.”

[Col. 0358A] “The woman said to him: ‘Sir, give me this water, so that I may not thirst or come here to draw.’”

Blessed is this foreign woman—or rather, blessed is the Church gathered from foreigners, of which she bears the type. It will deservedly rise in judgment with the evil and adulterous generation in order to condemn it (Matt. 12). “If,” he says, “I told you earthly things and you did not believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things?” (John 3).

Using the analogy of an earthly temple and earthly building, he had said: “Destroy this temple, and I will raise it in three days.” They understood only earthly things in those words and did not believe that he could do it. How would they have believed had he spoken heavenly things? Had he said that he could give heavenly life, that he could carry them in such a way that they might leap into eternal life? [Col. 0358B]

But this woman believed, confessed, and did not deny. This woman said—and the great woman now says it too, expanded throughout the whole world, panting and thirsty, thirsty and crying out—“Sir, give me this water.” Therefore she believed, and thus she speaks (Ps. 106); consequently, as was foretold, that generation is rightly condemned by comparison with her.

What remains at last? Why is so great a good delayed? Why does he who, unasked, said that such a desirable good ought to be sought from him, not immediately grant it to the one simply asking? Hear what follows:

“Jesus said to her: ‘Go, call your husband.’ The woman answered him: ‘I have no husband.’”

See how he calls the sinful woman, whom he knew not to have a husband and knew not to have entered into a lawful marriage, back to her own heart, so that in the testimony of her conscience she may see what must be done in order to deserve to receive that gift of God [Col. 0358C].

He could have said: “Unless you repent and confess your sins—because you are a sinner and have acted thus—unless, I say, you repent, I will not give you this water. For this grace of the Holy Spirit, this gift of God, is granted only to those who repent, confess their sins, and abandon them.” The Lord could have said this. But the wisdom of God, the maker of our salvation, employed its own art, so that it might neither drive her away through burdensome shame nor fail to draw forth the confession of sins necessary for her salvation.

[Col. 0358D] “Go,” he said, “call your husband, and come here.” What could she have supposed, except that her husband ought to be summoned for this purpose: lest a woman receive, without her husband, something like the means of life; and that it was rightly considered by the giver of so great a gift that the husband, with whom the woman was one body, ought to share in such a gift? Indeed, she would immediately have run to fetch him, if she had had anyone whom she could lawfully acknowledge as her husband. But what was she to do, who had no husband, and yet was neither virgin nor widow? How could she fail to fear a deserved rejection, compelled by such a reminder to recognize herself as a woman not lawfully married? Therefore, acknowledging her unworthiness, she stood still and confessed: “I have no husband.” This beginning of confession was enough for the mercy that called her. He neither waited for nor demanded that she say everything; rather, extending the hand of clemency, he spared her shame and aided her wavering conscience. For it follows:

“Jesus said to her: ‘You have spoken well in saying, I have no husband. For you have had five husbands, and he whom you now have is not your husband. This you have said truly.’” The woman understood well that she had spoken truly. The Church too now speaks well and truly: just as that woman had misused five husbands and, though she had no husband, nevertheless had someone whom she could not call her husband, so the Church, when she was once Gentile, had indulged the five bodily senses in every desire of the flesh and of the eyes which is in the world. At last she had fallen so far as to receive the devil as her lawful husband, in place of God, the maker and lover of souls; and, committing fornication with him in wood and stone, she cleaved to one who was not her husband, but the enemy of her nature—not a lover, but a murderer; not a bridegroom of love, but the author of death; a killer, not a physician; the devil, not God.

This, I say, she truly said: by saying this she spoke the truth; and thus, accusing herself at the outset, she was washed in the laver and obtained the living water as a cup of salvation. Therefore the Master and Lord, to be imitated by his disciples, ministers of this water of life, by fitting skill elicited from her who asked for living water a confession of sins, and called her back to her conscience, saying: “Call your husband, and come here.” She immediately did not conceal her sins, but confessed them and did not defend them. For by her answer she makes plain how truthfully she agrees with his account, and with what humble conscience she yields to the truth:

[Col. 0359C] “Sir, I see that you are a prophet.” For what more is it to say, “It is true: I have had five husbands,” than to say, “Sir, I see that you are a prophet”? Finally, this clearly shows how willingly she confesses: she honours as Lord and calls prophet the one who searches her conscience, for no other reason or evidence than that, according to the truth of his declaration, she recognized herself as a sinner. In one and the same answer she confessed concerning herself what she was, and concerning him what she could understand him to be. Certainly she confessed less—and far less—than the reality was; yet by confessing as much as she understood, she made herself worthy for Jesus to disclose to her all that he was.

Meanwhile, this must not be passed over: not only foreknowledge of the future, but also the disclosure to the eyes of things past and present, is properly called prophecy. This woman had heard the Lord foretell nothing about the future; but, perceiving that he spoke truthfully about the past and present secrets of her heart, she declared that he was a prophet. Thus, even then it was customary to call the revelation of hidden things prophecy.

Indeed, since there are these three parts of prophecy—concerning the past, the present, and the future—that aspect gives the greatest proof of the prophetic Spirit by which someone is convicted in the present so that the secrets of his heart are made manifest. For then no doubt remains to a person that in the prophet only God is speaking, besides whom no one else can see through human hearts. Commending this, the Apostle says: “If all prophesy, and an unbeliever or unlearned person enters, he is convicted by all, he is judged by all; the secrets of his heart are made manifest; and so, falling upon his face, he worships God, declaring that God is truly among you” (1 Cor. 14). So certainly this woman, when she heard outwardly from a man what she herself knew inwardly, confidently declared that God was truly in that man, and unhesitatingly said: “Sir, I see that you are a prophet.”

Then, knowing also that prophets were accustomed to speak through figures and tropological interpretations, she removed the carnal understanding from his words. No longer, in the former sense, did she ask him for living water; rather, she intended to seek from him the teaching of truth—as from a prophet, as from one who did not, in speaking from his own heart, vainly exalt himself in disputes, but through whom, as she had learned by experience, God spoke. For beyond the bodily thirst for which she had come to draw water, she had another thirst: the thirst for hearing the word of God. The very one who watered minds, who was speaking to her, knew this well. Did he know only her sins, and not the desire of her soul and the teachable humility of her heart? Why then had he said to her: “If you knew the gift of God, and who it is that speaks to you, perhaps you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water”? Did he speak uncertainly? Or, because he said “perhaps you would have asked,” should he be thought to have doubted? Certainly not. In the speech of one who knows all things and sees all things, “perhaps” does not signify the uncertainty of one doubting, but the astonishment of one affirming—as also there: “If you believed Moses,” he says, “perhaps you would also believe me” (John 5). For there he marvels at the hardness or unbelief of the Jews, and here, to their reproach, at the readiness of foreigners to believe.

Therefore he had foreseen in this woman also a thirst to hear the word of God. As soon as she discovered that he was a prophet, she asked that this thirst be immediately satisfied. For she says to him:

[Col. 0360D] “Our fathers worshipped on this mountain; and you say that Jerusalem is the place where one ought to worship.” As if she said: Lord, since, as I see, you are a prophet, and for many days now no prophet has appeared in Israel, speak to us from the mouth of the Lord; give us who consult you an answer of justice in the Lord’s word. Behold, there is an ancient and longstanding dispute. You Jews do not associate with us Samaritans; and you do not associate with us because we do not worship at Jerusalem. For you say that one must worship only at Jerusalem; yet, when you say this, the authority of our fathers opposes you, and it cannot lightly be despised. For our fathers worshipped on this mountain, and beyond doubt, outside Jerusalem and Solomon’s temple, propitiated God, whom they worshipped in their minds.

Here our father Jacob, having set up an altar, invoked upon it the most mighty God of Israel, after he had returned from Syrian Mesopotamia and dwelt here beside this town; and he bought from the sons of Hamor, the father of Shechem, for a hundred lambs, a portion of this field in which he had pitched his tent (Gen. 33). Therefore, Lord, since you are a prophet, what do you say?

By raising this question the wise woman was surely now asking for living water, and, bending a vessel capacious for great desire over the edge of the eternal fountain, was plunging it in to draw—about to find more living water than she herself could yet estimate. Yet even in this inquiry of her own she does not say everything, nor does she put everything forward. For in saying that from which the place might be venerable—namely, “Our fathers worshipped on this mountain”—she kept silent about the causes of the division and separation. That is, she did not mention that Jeroboam and the ten tribes with him, in order to withdraw from Judah and from the house of David (3 Kings 12), to whom the Lord had said on oath, “Of the fruit of your womb I will set one upon your throne” (Ps. 131), had made golden calves and, worshipping them, said: “These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up from the land of Egypt.” The history of the book of Kings relates that this was done in the same city of Sychar, which Jeroboam rebuilt (3 Kings 12).

Moreover, as was said above, they had intermingled with the nations among whom Shalmaneser, king of the Assyrians, after transporting the ten tribes, had caused their remnant to dwell; and, since each nation made its own god, they learned their practices and thus supplied their Jewish despisers with a greater cause or material for contempt (4 Kings 17). These causes, I say, the woman kept silent in her proposed question. Yet she had confessed the stains of her own fault humbly enough. Therefore it is not a fault but rather a credit to her that she did not hasten to proclaim the common disgrace of her nation, well known to all. But the Lord, judge of equity, being asked, answered thus:

[Col. 0361C] “Woman, believe me: days are coming when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem.” These utterances of the incarnate Word, resounding most sweetly from the holy temple of his body, are to be revered and heard in holy fear: in brief but weighty speech he sets forth a true judgement, worthy of himself, concerning the worship of the Divinity. He reasonably establishes that the Samaritans had been inferior to the Jews in their former dispute; but he also consoles them, indicating that true worshippers of God will soon cease to endure every controversy about the pre-eminence of their places.

He divides the words of this consolation, both at the beginning and at the end, by remarkable art, placing in the middle the parts of his brief discourse by which he most effectively strikes the Samaritans, saying that they worship God without knowledge. For before saying, “You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know, for salvation is from the Jews,” he repeated and continued what he had first said: “But the hour is coming, and now is, when true worshippers will worship the Father in spirit and truth,” and so forth. Thus he took great care, with great condescension, to retain the goodwill of his weak hearer. Now each word of grace flowing from his mouth must be considered.

“Woman, believe me.” To you, he says, O woman, I shall tell what I have not yet told men; to you I shall entrust what I did not entrust about myself to the Jews, scribes, Pharisees, or priests worshipping—indeed, robbing—in that great and beautiful temple of God. What I had only signified to them by my deed, when I cast them with a whip from my Father’s house (John 2), and had not yet entrusted to words to disclose, I now tell you. To you, O woman, I entrust it; I commit it to your faith. Only believe me for the present as a prophet, since you have called me a prophet. Believe me, I say; and I do not yet tell you to believe in me—that will come when you begin to perceive something in me above a prophet, indeed above every rank or dignity.

Believe this of me: days are coming, and they are near. Your fathers who worshipped on this mountain, and many prophets and kings who worshipped at Jerusalem but did not see them, will be followed by your blessed eyes, which shortly will see them. Then you, who are now despised as strangers to God’s temple—you, I say, and all from whatsoever nations who are predestined to life (Luke 10)—will worship God, calling him Father, that is, confessing and worshipping together the Son whose Father he is. Through worship of the Son it will come about that God his Father will also be your Father.

Thus you will worship the Father, not on this mountain nor in Jerusalem, but in every place of his dominion; for not only here or in Jerusalem alone, but “from the rising of the sun to its setting” (Ps. 112), “his name will be great and terrible among the nations” (Mal. 1). But in Jerusalem, where the place of prayer is now renowned, “not one stone shall be left upon another which will not be thrown down” (Matt. 24).

The woman could now have rejoiced at the favour shown to her people, supposing that by the authority of so great a man, whom she believed to be a prophet, the holy city of David and Solomon’s temple were in no way preferred to the mountain of Samaria. Although this was true concerning the future, it was not true concerning the past. Therefore she had to be humbled on account of the sin that had abounded more in Samaria, lest she rejoice improperly in the superabundant grace. It follows:

[Col. 0362D] “You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know, for salvation is from the Jews.” As if he says: You Samaritans, because you withdrew from the house of David and the temple of God, and put your trust in the mountain of Samaria, were not justified because your fathers worshipped on the mountain (Deut. 12), but defiled because Jeroboam, building this city—that is, Shechem—on the mountain, made golden calves here and said: “These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up from the land of Egypt.”

You, I say, who withdrew from God’s temple because of the worship of calves, worship what you do not know, while in worship you say without knowing what you say: “These are your gods, O Israel.” We Jews, who have clung to our king and worship the God of our fathers in the place which he chose, do not speak without knowing what we say, but know very well that salvation is from the Jews: for the promised Saviour is from the tribe of Judah and the seed of David. Knowing this, and clinging for this reason to the same David, and worshipping in the temple built by his son the God who swore to him, “Of the fruit of your womb I will set one upon your throne” (Ps. 131), we surely worship what we know. We ourselves were preserved for David, so that salvation promised to him might arise from us.

But thus far we have worshipped amid this dispute. Days are coming “when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem.” This is what he repeated in what follows:

“But the hour is coming, and now is, when true worshippers will worship the Father in spirit and truth.” The hour has already come and now is: the “acceptable time” and “day of salvation” have come and now are (2 Cor. 6), “when true worshippers”—true, I say, that is, not ignorant of what they worship, but possessing the true knowledge of worship—“will worship the Father, not on this mountain nor in Jerusalem,” as was said before, but “in spirit and truth.”

What is sweeter? What is more beautiful than this definition of a true worshipper? You will worship the Father, he says, receiving from him the Spirit of adoption as sons and becoming members of his only-begotten Son. For what is worshipping the Father in spirit except receiving the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, “Abba, Father” (Rom. 8)? What is worshipping the Father in truth except calling upon him while abiding in his Son, who says, “I am the truth” (John 14)? Thus it is as though he had said: True worshippers, through the manifest and necessary distinction of persons, will worship one God: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

Why in this place did he put “spirit” before “truth,” and not say, “They will worship the Father in truth and spirit,” but say, “in spirit and truth”? Evidently because, just as “no one comes to the Father except through the Son” (ibid.), so no one knows him except through the Holy Spirit. “For no one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (1 Cor. 12). True worship itself is also the proper work of the Holy Spirit: “for we do not know what we ought to pray for, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with unutterable groanings” (Rom. 8).

Therefore a person must receive the Holy Spirit through prevenient grace, so that through him he may know and confess that the Lord Jesus has come in the flesh; this is the straight way of coming to the Father through the Son. Thus he rightly did not say, “They will worship the Father in truth and spirit,” but “in spirit,” he says, “and truth.” Otherwise, wherever he invoked this name in right order and according to evangelical tradition, he consistently named first the Father and Son, and then, as the third person, the Holy Spirit, for the reason that the Holy Spirit proceeds from both, that is, from the Father and the Son. It follows:

[Col. 0363D] “For the Father also seeks such people to worship him.” Believe me, he says, for that hour has now come, and true worshippers will worship the Father in this way. For behold, even now the Father seeks such as worship him; he seeks with a lamp lit, he seeks diligently with the house overturned (Luke 15). Behold, he has placed the light of his Divinity in the earthen vessel of human flesh; and, beginning from his sanctuary, he overturned his house by casting out false worshippers, because they made his house—which is a house of prayer—a den of robbers (Matt. 21). From there he seeks throughout the whole world true worshippers who worship him, not in the flesh but in spirit; not in robbery but in truth.

The temple and city of Jerusalem will be overthrown (Matt. 24); the sacred groves and shrines of the Gentiles will not stand; families of peoples will be divided against one another; the bonds of relatives will be broken; two will be divided against three and three against two; daughter against mother, and daughter-in-law against mother-in-law (Matt. 10). And so, when the house has been overturned by every kind of upheaval, the Father will undoubtedly find such people as worship him. He will not find them already made such as worship him; rather, he will find in sacred groves and idol-shrines those whom he will make such that they may worship him. For he will find idolaters who are greedy, drunken, sexually immoral, and possessed by other vices; but he will wash them, he will sanctify them in his Spirit and in his truth (1 Cor. 6).

“I will not gather their assemblies of blood, nor will I remember their names with my lips” (Ps. 15). They were called idolaters or fornicators, but he will call them by another name, in which whoever is blessed will be blessed upon the earth (Isa. 65). You ask: Why does the Father seek such worshippers? Why shall we worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem? Hear what follows:

[Col. 0364B] “Spirit is God, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth.” Although this may rightly be understood as “The Holy Spirit is God”—that is, with “Spirit” as the subject and “God” as the predicate—yet in this place it is more correctly understood with “God” as the subject and “Spirit” as the predicate. What he said, “Spirit is God,” is no different from saying, “God is Spirit”; just as there: “And God was the Word,” we undoubtedly understand nothing other than, “And the Word was God.”

For here the issue is not against blasphemers of the Holy Spirit, and therefore false and impious worshippers of God the Father, in order to defend the distinct person of the Holy Spirit as God. Rather, the issue is against carnal and bloodthirsty worshippers: the true God, whom they boast of worshipping lawfully, is not flesh but Spirit; and therefore he does not delight in eating bulls’ flesh or drinking goats’ blood (Ps. 49; Heb. 9). Indeed, he is not to be sought in a place, but worshipped in the Holy Spirit and invoked in confession of the truth.

This, then, he establishes: God is Spirit. He is truly Spirit, surpassing not only bodily sense but every spiritual subtlety as well; uncircumscribed Spirit, because he is enclosed in no place and is not, as the Anthropomorphites suppose, bounded by a likeness to human limbs. For he is the mightiest Spirit of all spirits, and the subtlest of all spirits—of which, assuredly, he himself is the Creator—capable of containing nothing, yet, owing to the subtlety of his nature, capable of being apprehended by rational spirits, both angelic and human.

[Col. 0365A] This must be understood equally of the whole Trinity. For Father, Son, and Holy Spirit alike are Spirit. Nor is the Holy Spirit called the third person of the Divinity because this person alone is Spirit, but because he proceeds from both, that is, from the Father and the Son; therefore he receives this name from both, so as to be called the Holy Spirit. For, as has been said, the Father is Spirit and the Son is Spirit; the Father is holy and the Son is holy. Thus, by changing or combining the names, he is called the Holy Spirit.

Therefore, because “God is Spirit” and “those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth,” that is, must cry “Abba, Father” in the Spirit of adoption as sons (Rom. 8), and honour the Father by confessing the Son, as said above. For one must open one’s mouth in confession of the truth and draw in the Spirit, and in him call Jesus Lord and confess that he came in the flesh (1 Cor. 12). Otherwise, “he who sacrifices an ox is like one who slays a dog; and he who offers incense is like one who blesses an idol” (Isa. 66).

Whether Jew, Samaritan, or any schismatic, one who cuts himself off from the unity of the Spirit is not reckoned among the true worshippers of the Father, because the word of truth is not in his heart and mouth (Rom. 10): that is, because he does not believe with the heart unto righteousness, which is to worship the Father in spirit, and does not confess with the mouth unto salvation, which is to worship the same Father in truth. Jew or heretic alike with the pagan is in no way counted among the true worshippers of the Father.

When, then, you ask: If God wished to be worshipped by our fathers in the flesh and blood of burnt offerings or victims, but now prefers to be worshipped in spirit and truth, why did he seek worshippers then other or different from those whom he seeks now? Or why does he now require worshippers other than those of that time? To this I say: God permitted, but did not command, that he be worshipped in sacrifices of this kind. He permitted, I say, but did not prescribe; he endured them, but did not will them. At times he looked upon what had been offered; he never sought what was to be offered.

Long ago the Lord defended himself against every such objection through his prophets. For through Jeremiah he says: “Add your burnt offerings to your sacrifices, and eat the flesh; for I did not speak with your fathers, nor command them on the day when I brought them out of the land of Egypt, concerning the matter of burnt offerings and sacrifices; but I commanded them this word, saying: ‘Hear my voice’” (Jer. 7), and so forth. Likewise through Isaiah: “I have not desired burnt offerings of rams, the fat of fatlings, or the blood of calves, lambs, and goats” (Isa. 1). “When you came before my presence, who required these things from your hands, that you should walk in my courts?”

Therefore, the worshippers he now seeks, and whom he now commands to be such, are those whom God, who is Spirit, has always sought. He never willed, nor did he ever deign, to be worshipped otherwise than in spirit and truth. Yet the Israelites coming out of Egypt were carnal people, accustomed, according to the Egyptians and other nations, to add burnt offerings to sacrifices and to eat flesh. Moreover, the Spirit had not yet been given, nor had truth sprung from the earth, by which they might learn how they ought to worship.

[Col. 0366A] Therefore, for a time and according to the condition of human beings, he allowed worshippers, whatever they might be, to slaughter and eat the flesh of sacrifices. The law concerning sacrifices was laid down because of transgressions, as a pedagogue (Gal. 3), so that the law might restrain the unruly youth until grace should come; the figure might nourish until truth should dawn; the shadow might give favour until the clear reality should follow.

Now the Spirit is given and is near; now truth is present, because “grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1). Now faith has come, through which Abraham our father proved to be a true worshipper. This faith, which is of spirit and truth, is sought when the pedagogue is removed—the faith in which Abraham worshipped, as stated above, and in which all true worshippers must worship. There is neither Jew nor Greek there (Gal. 3); indeed, to speak more closely to the present issue, there is neither Jew nor Samaritan, neither slave nor free, neither male nor female; but truth, with its Spirit, is all things in all (Col. 3). It follows:

“ The woman said to him: ‘I know that Messiah is coming, who is called Christ. When he comes, he will declare all things to us.’” Meanwhile the woman pondered in her remembering mind what he had said: “Days are coming,” and what he repeated: “The hour is coming and now is.” She was not ignorant that he spoke of Christ’s coming, in whose days righteousness and abundance of peace would arise (Ps. 71). For the Samaritans accepted the Law and the Prophets, from whose proclamations they could know that Christ, the teacher of righteousness, was to come.

First, Moses says: “The Lord says, ‘I will raise up for them a prophet from your brethren, like you; and I will put my words in his mouth, and he will speak to them all that I command him. But whoever will not listen to his words which he speaks in my name, I will exact vengeance’” (Deut. 18). Hence she says: “I know that Messiah is coming”—understand, to teach us under another law—Moses also testifying in the passage above and saying: “The Lord will raise up for you a prophet from among your brethren; you shall hear him as you hear me.” “When he comes,” she says, “he will declare all things to us.”

Certainly, the inserted words, “who is called Christ,” were not spoken by the woman but were inserted by the Evangelist to interpret the Hebrew name: Messiah is Hebrew, Christ Greek, and *unctus*, “anointed,” Latin. He is anointed with the fullness alike of royal and priestly grace, anointed above his companions (Ps. 44), that is, above all the children of men. “For God does not give the Spirit to him by measure” (John 3).

“When that one comes,” she says, “he himself will declare all things to us.” See how she probes what she has heard; see how she pretends that she has not heard it, in order to hear again and more fully. She says indeed that she knows days are coming and that Messiah is to come; but she pretends not to have heard, in order to hear again, “for the hour is coming and now is.” Thus, sparing her speech, she asked more effectively; thus, with a modest rather than troublesome question, she knocked more effectively. But he himself says: “Everyone who asks receives; he who seeks finds; and to him who knocks it shall be opened” (Matt. 7; Luke 2). Did not the Jews above seek and knock, saying: “What sign do you show us, since you do these things?” (John 2). Yet they did not find, nor were they worthy to hear openly. Why? Because they sought not with faith but unbelievingly; they knocked not modestly but importunately. But she sought humbly, asked faithfully, and knocked modestly. Therefore it follows:

[Col. 0367A] “Jesus said to her: ‘I am he who speaks with you.’” I, he says, who speak with you, am that Messiah; I will declare all things to you. See how he entrusted himself to this foreign woman, whereas he had not entrusted himself to the Jews. He revealed to her the treasure worthy of honour, his own name, which he had not yet disclosed in his own country, Judea, lest—as was soon to happen—the swine should trample underfoot the precious pearl of that name and, blaspheming this holy thing with canine rage, gnaw at it (Matt. 7).

This was done as a reproach to his own country, in which, as the Evangelist will later say, he declared that he would have no honour—by contrast with the country that was not his own, that is, the Gentile world, in which he was to receive divine honour, not merely as a prophet but as God, the Son of God. He proves this already by the present event. For he was honoured among these foreign Samaritans when he said that he was Christ. He was dishonoured and crucified by his fellow tribesmen, among whom he performed signs and wonders which no one else performed (John 15). It follows:

“And immediately his disciples came, and they marvelled that he was speaking with a woman. Yet no one said: ‘What do you seek?’ or, ‘Why are you speaking with her?’” The Lord Jesus then began to work this miracle in his disciples: though born from Jews, who did not associate with Samaritans, he deigned to enter into conversation with a Samaritan woman. He completed it after his resurrection, when he showed Peter animals, reptiles, and serpents in an ecstasy, saying: “Kill and eat; and what God has sanctified, do not call common or unclean” (Acts 10). In this way he showed that no human being should be called common or unclean.

At that time, reverencing him as Master and Lord, they were silent: “and none of them said, ‘What do you seek?’ or, ‘Why are you speaking with her?’” But when the grace of the Holy Spirit had been poured out upon the nations, when the Holy Spirit had descended upon Cornelius and the other Gentiles, who heard the word while Peter spoke, and they spoke in tongues magnifying God (Acts 10), then the great woman—the Church from the Gentiles, signified by this Samaritan woman—was vindicated by great testimony. Peter said, “Who was I, that I could forbid God?” And they glorified God, saying: “Then God has granted repentance unto life even to the Gentiles” (Acts 11). For could they dare to say to Christ or his Spirit: “Why did you enter in to men having the foreskin?”

[Col. 0368A] “The woman therefore left her water-jar, went away into the city, and said to those people: ‘Come and see a man who told me everything I have done. Could he be the Christ?’” This woman admirably prefigures how the country not his own—that is, the Church from the Gentiles—would honour this Prophet. When she heard him saying, “I am Christ, the one speaking with you,” she immediately forgot, in joy at the living water she had found, the thirst for which she had come to draw water. She left her water-jar in order to run more freely, and made the whole city astonished by crying out what kind of man she had found and what she had heard from him.

For when the primitive Church of the Gentiles heard Christ’s name, it immediately forgot to make provision for the flesh in its desires (Rom. 13); it cast aside its desire or curiosity, which it had striven to fill through empty philosophy (Col. 2) or the pleasures of the transient course of temporal things. Having laid aside every burden and bearing Christ’s name alone in heart and speech, it filled the whole world with the cry of good news, inviting people to faith and hastening to beget a multitude of spiritual children.

At that time, indeed, scarcely a few were amazed or even noticed that, in the haste of joyful happiness, the woman had left her water-jar. But when our mother the Church, which first merited to find Jesus outwardly, received his grace—that is, the Spirit—as the apostles entered, as was said above, and even as certain believers from the circumcision objected to it (Acts 11), she at once cast off every burden of the world so completely that it became a great wonder to all lovers of the world, to all worldly powers, kings, judges, and all nations, and especially to her relatives or connections according to the flesh.

And it was not merely a wonder to all, but to a great part—indeed, to the whole city of the devil, whose head was Rome and whose horn of pride was then Nero—it was a blaze of fury, a cause of tumult and occasion of wrath, an incitement to sedition and most savage persecution. By every punishment and every manner of shedding blood they compelled her to take back the water-jar which she had cast aside. But the power of the living water prevailed, overcoming the flesh sunk in sweet intoxication and making the wakeful mind glad, so that she not only did not desire to drink again the desires which she had cast aside, but wholly surrendered even the earthen vessels of souls themselves, namely, their bodies. Thus the multitude of martyrs was crowned.

Meanwhile, as the cry of those saying, “Come and see a man,” did not cease—“believe in Christ, the Son of God, true God and true man”—the evil citizens of the city of the devil came out and became good citizens of the city of God. Hence it is added:

[Col. 0368D] “They went out of the city and were coming to him.” This too is stated as a reproach to his own country. For his own nation and its chief priests handed him over to Pilate and cast him outside the city; and, rejected by those who had seen many great signs of his, he “suffered outside the gate” (Heb. 13). But these foreign and unknown people, who had not even heard any word from him, much less seen signs—these, I say, because they had heard only one woman saying, “He told me everything I have done,” greatly honouring him, went out of their city and came to him.

Still more now, when he has been dishonoured by his said country even to the end—that is, even unto death, indeed death on a cross (Phil. 2)—we who have not seen him, but have learned only by hearing, that, as the Apostle says, “Jesus, that he might sanctify the people through himself, suffered outside the gate,” go out to him “outside the camp, bearing his reproach” (Heb. 13). Now, I say, those wicked and deservedly ruined tenants must be reproached still more, because they cast the Lord of the vineyard, their Lord, outside the vineyard and killed him (Matt. 21; Luke 20). Therefore the kingdom of God was rightly taken from them and given to a nation—that is, to the Gentile world—producing its fruits.

For from the city “which is spiritually called Sodom and Egypt” (Apoc. 2), or Babylon the harlot—from the city, I say, of the devil, which always opposes the city of God, the heavenly Jerusalem—the people of God have gone out, mourning and confessing that they are strangers and sojourners upon the earth (Heb. 2), crying to one another: “Let us go out to him outside the camp, bearing his reproach. For we do not have here an abiding city, but seek the city to come” (Heb. 13).

“Meanwhile the disciples were urging him, saying, ‘Rabbi, eat.’ [Col. 0369C] But he said to them, ‘I have food to eat which you do not know.’”

This was a feature of Jewish scrupulosity: the disciples of Jesus wondered at him because he was speaking with a Samaritan woman, and yet they offered him for food the provisions which they had bought from the Samaritans. This may indeed have been a carnal, or whatever sort of, righteousness; nevertheless, it was the haughty righteousness of the Scribes and Pharisees to buy things from foreigners, but by no means to receive foods prepared by them or drink poured out by them.

It must not be omitted why this and the other things, as has already been said, were done or written: namely, that although the Scribes and Pharisees held the Gentiles in contempt, and almost all the Jews hated their salvation, they nevertheless rejoiced that kings and princes themselves frequently judged the place worthy of the highest honour, adorned the Temple with very great gifts, and sometimes provided, from their own revenues, expenses pertaining to the ministry of sacrifices. In this, I say, they rejoiced—though their hands were stained with Christ’s blood—by offering sacrifices of this sort. Yet believers who were from the circumcision still disputed with the Gentiles concerning that privilege of theirs, maintaining that the conversion of the Jews alone, as though it were clean food, ought to be offered to Christ; while they regarded the Gentiles, as Peter was shown in a vision, like the unclean four-footed creatures of the earth (Acts IX), as unworthy.

Meanwhile, when certain believers of the sect of the Pharisees arose and said that not circumcision alone [Col. 0370A] but the entire law of Moses must also be observed (ibid.), what else were the disciples of Jesus doing, as they offered him unwelcome food, than saying to him, “Rabbi, eat”? But, on the contrary, he himself cries in the Psalm: “Shall I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats?” (Ps. XLIX). By no means. “I will not take calves from your house, nor goats from your flocks; for all the beasts of the forests are mine, the cattle upon the mountains, and the oxen. I know all the birds of heaven, and the beauty of the field is with me. If I were hungry, I would not tell you; for the world is mine and its fullness” (ibid.). But what then? “Offer to God a sacrifice of praise” (ibid.). Concerning this, certainly, true sacrifice and food fitting for himself, he immediately says: “I have food to eat [Col. 0370B] which you do not know.”

For indeed they did not know that, once foods and drinks, diverse baptisms, and righteous observances of the flesh had been set aside (Mark VII), true worshippers would worship the Father in spirit and truth—which truly is to offer the true sacrifice of praise to God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. They did not know this, I say, for the Lord had said it to the Samaritan woman when they were not present, but absent. Hence, wondering, they said to one another:

“Has someone brought him something to eat?”

They were similarly benighted by a carnal understanding of his words when he said to them, “I have food to eat which you do not know,” just as the Samaritan woman had been when he spoke to her of living water to be requested from or given by him. It is therefore no wonder that she hesitated at the word “water,” [Col. 0370C] when these men were no quicker to understand at the name of “food.”

Here it is surely worth attending to the wonderful condescension of God’s wisdom: it so stoops to little ones that it does not omit any object whatsoever which an occasion places before it, but, eager to introduce them through its likeness, sets the invisible mysteries of the kingdom of God, as it were, before their eyes. For what does he omit, who passes over neither kings’ marriages nor fishermen’s nets, neither merchants’ pearls (Matt. XIII) nor wine-makers’ old wineskins (Luke V), neither fig trees (Mark XIII) nor vineyards, nor the mustard seed (Luke XVII), and surely not even humble vegetables? Thus he explains heavenly realities through individual bodily analogies, so that those whose sick eyes cannot bear the sun’s brightness may see its image as in familiar and common mirrors.

Thus now he spoke to a woman drawing water, under the name of water, concerning the grace of the Holy Spirit, so that from the benefits of the visible water which she was drawing she might estimate the power of the invisible water [Col. 0370D] which she did not know. Likewise, when incorporeal food is offered to him, he speaks of bodily food, so that through the likeness of bodily refreshment he may show that performing the work of our salvation is voluntary for him—indeed, desirable. Since they did not perceive this at his first saying—for they said, “Has someone brought him something to eat?”—he immediately adds: “My food is to do the will of my Father, to complete his work.”

By this saying he plainly indicates with what spontaneous obedience he serves God the Father in working our salvation, and that he takes greater delight in this obedience than a hungry person does when food is offered and he is told, “Eat.” And rightly, greater delight. For by bodily food the flesh alone, which had failed, is refreshed, only to fail again; but through this obedience the mortal and passible human nature in Christ was to be so refreshed that, rising from the dead, it should die no more: “Death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. VI).

For what is the Father’s will except that of which he said a little earlier to the Samaritan woman: “For the Father also seeks such persons to worship him”? What, I say, does the Father will or seek except to have true worshippers who worship him in spirit and truth? But such persons were found through the Son’s passion; such worshippers were acquired for God the Father through the Son’s cross and blood. Therefore, when he says, “My food is to do the will of my Father,” he magnificently expresses, by the fitting analogy already mentioned, how eagerly he is devoted to completing the work of our salvation.

It is certainly established that holy people who have received the Spirit of adoption as sons (Rom. VIII; Gal. IV) work for their brothers’ salvation with great sweetness of love; though they begin from servile fear, they are perfected in the love of sons. This is, according to the Psalmist, to run with an enlarged heart in the way of the Lord’s commandments (Ps. CXVIII). Yet none of them finds the toil of the work so sweet that he can altogether rightly say, “My food is to do God’s will.” For the human substance possesses nothing impassible by reference to which [Col. 0371C] it might say that labour or affliction in God’s work is so delightful to it that it ought to be called its food. For human beings plainly consist of soul and body, both of which are undoubtedly passible.

Accordingly, when someone is afflicted, he bears it patiently and reclines upon the sweetness of his conscience because he lives devoutly in Christ (II Tim. III); but he is not yet rightly said to feed upon his own food, because the reward of the work itself does not yet refresh him. Rather, only the hope of a reward laid up elsewhere consoles him, so that he may not fail or grow weary [OCR: *lacescat*, probably *lassescat*] beneath the force of tribulation which presses upon him wholly, that is, in soul and body.

But Christ was not wholly passible; nor did he consist only of soul and body, both of which were then passible, but he also consists of impassible divinity. [Col. 0371D] When he underwent the bitter passion of death in doing the Father’s will, the force of pain did not pierce through all that Christ is—that is, the divine and human natures together. Rather, the human nature was tortured by real pain, while the divine nature was fed, and is always fed, by its love with the Father.

He was fed, I say, and satisfied by reproaches—not as holy martyrs are in the joy of hope, but as the God of all martyrs and saints, in the presence of an eternal and unchangeable reality. For what did he ever hope for? What did he ever not possess, he through whom all things were made, the Son of God? Was he a hired labourer? Did he preach the Gospel in hope of a reward? Did he ever say anything like the Apostle Paul: “Necessity is laid upon me; for woe is me if I do not preach the Gospel. For if I do this willingly, I have a reward; but if unwillingly, a stewardship has been entrusted to me” (I Cor. IX)?

Therefore nowhere is this said of him: that he received a reward—as it is commonly said of all saints, to whom God rendered the reward of their labours (Wis. X)—because he himself is the rewarder and the reward of all saints, sitting at the Father’s right hand. There, although the human nature was crowned with glory and honour which it had not possessed (Ps. VIII), reverence for the divine nature which exalted that nature rightly binds us to confess that whatever Christ the Lord received according to his humanity, he received not from elsewhere but from the divinity inherent in him; and therefore it is not lawful to say that he was endowed with a reward. [Col. 0372B]

Thus all the saints, so long as they are exiles here, where they mournfully fast away from the banquet of the divine vision, however willingly and however lovingly they perform what is good toward all (Gal. VI), whether they preach unwillingly because of the stewardship entrusted to them, or willingly and therefore have a reward laid up with God (I Cor. IX), nevertheless none of them can rightly say: “My food is to do God’s will.” Only he who did not expect a reward from another source but possessed it in himself—as the prophet says, “Behold, his reward is with him, and his work before him” (Isa. XL)—only he, I say, who was already fed in his work by his own divinity, could truly say: “My food is to do the will of him who sent me, to complete his work.” For the impassible Son of God, in the very passion of the flesh which he undertook by the Father’s will, while completing his work—the work of our redemption, the work of our salvation—was fully and perfectly delighted with him, for our sake, in the fullness of love. [Col. 0372C]

Our good works of whatever kind, our faith and love, and such things, are now meanwhile his food; but hereafter the vision of him will be our food, where he will fulfil what he deigned to promise: “That you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom” (Luke XXII). Hence he speaks in due order in the Apocalypse: “If anyone hears my voice and opens the door to me, I will enter in to him and dine with him, and he with me” (Rev. III). For we feed him whenever we do that same will of the Father to the end—namely, by building one another up—until he who is the head over all the members of the Church, which is his body, his fullness, may be fulfilled all in all (Eph. I).

For just as an emperor is increased if his army grows daily, new provinces are made, and the multitude of peoples increases, so also our Lord Jesus Christ, in that all believe in him and come day by day to his faith, is fulfilled in all things. And whoever do this will of the Father with him feed him; and, according to another Evangelist, they make him advance in age, wisdom, and grace, not only before God but also before men (Luke II).

But why did he first mention this food of his now? For if, when his disciples had previously offered him food, he had been accustomed to speak of these things, they surely would not now have erred concerning his words, saying, “Has someone brought him something to eat?” Why then did he first say now, “My food is to do the will of him who sent me,” unless because now, for the first time, time and place prompted it—namely, as foreigners, the Samaritans, were leaving the city and coming to him? Toward them and toward all the Gentiles this was the Father’s will: that, through the Son’s work, they should become his true worshippers.

For the Son rejoiced in that food of his, in that will of the Father, although with human affection he wept over his own country, in which he was to be dishonoured—namely, the Jews. By their loss that food was being prepared for him, namely, the salvation of the Gentiles; the Jews, I say, false worshippers, were to be cast out when the Temple had been destroyed and the city of Jerusalem [Col. 0373B] overthrown (Luke XIII). Therefore, seeing the Samaritans coming out and approaching him, he remained in the metaphor and rejoiced, like a wealthy man to whom a ripened harvest promises abundant food, and continued what he had begun as follows:

“Do you not say that there are four months, and the harvest comes? Behold, I say to you, lift up your eyes and see the fields, for they are already white for harvest.”

Previously we did not know at what time the Lord, having left Judaea, as was said above, after going up to Jerusalem at the approaching feast of Passover, returned to Galilee and, passing through Samaria, did or said the things recalled by the present Gospel reading. But now, from his saying, “Do you not say that there are four months, and the harvest comes?” we infer that he made this journey about the month which we call February. For the month which we call May is the time of full harvest in those regions. Therefore at the Feast of Weeks, which is also called Pentecost, they were commanded by the Law to offer a new sacrifice—two loaves of firstfruits from two tenths of fine flour, from all their dwellings (Lev. XXIII; Num. XXVIII; Deut. XVI).

Thus, from the time when the Lord changed water into wine at Cana of Galilee until now, when he returns again to Galilee, a year had passed; this was the thirty-first year of his age. John was still alive, of whom it was said above that “he was baptizing at Aenon near Salim, where also a dispute arose between his disciples and the Jews concerning purification” (John III). But when or at what time in the following part of this year that same John was handed over, or how long he was kept by Herod, we do not know with certainty, because we cannot gather it from the Scriptures.

Now let us return to the order of exposition. “Do you not say,” he says, “that there are still four months and the harvest comes?” As though wishing to refute them, he puts the matter more sharply in the form of a question, as one rebuking them—as if, beyond his own spiritual harvest, he knew no other harvest at all. And indeed he judges no harvest worthy of being mentioned by himself or his disciples except that one; though through him through whom all things were made, the harvest of which they spoke also comes each year.

For if, on account of the Gospel, he commands the one who wishes to be worthy of him to forget and leave father, mother, brothers, and sisters (Matt. X; Luke IV), lest he be delayed from heavenly intent by earthly affection, how much more rightly, for the same cause and pursuit, did he not want his disciples to know or remember when that harvest would come? It would certainly not ripen more slowly if they kept silent about it, nor more swiftly if they spoke of it.

For we cannot otherwise truly say, “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III), unless we are so occupied with meditation on heavenly things that we have no leisure to think or speak about earthly matters; so intent upon God’s agriculture that we judge it superfluous to speak of the natural growth of earthly farming; so eager to do God’s will that we neglect bodily food. He therefore rightly rebukes them: “Do you not say that there are still four months and the harvest comes?” And immediately adds: “Behold, I say to you, lift up your eyes and see the fields, for they are already white for harvest.”

“Lift up your eyes,” he says—your inward eyes—from this harvest, which I did not come to eat and for which I did not hire you as labourers; and see, not one region, not Judaea alone, my own country, in which I shall not receive the honour due to a lord or possessor, but see the many regions of the Gentiles, the regions of all nations, how already white they are for harvest. For just as the food of the lords of regions is ready when the regions themselves are white for reaping harvest, so for me, to whom the Gentiles have been given as an inheritance when I ask the Father (Ps. II), abundant food which I have to eat is now at hand, when the Gentiles themselves are ready to receive the faith.

It should be noted that two harvests are found in the Lord’s words. One is that of which he now speaks: the preaching of the Gospel, whose reapers are the apostles (Matt. IX; Luke X). The other, of which he speaks elsewhere, he calls the consummation of the age; its reapers are angels (Matt. XIII). Though they differ in many respects, they clearly also differ in this: the one which he calls the end of the age is only a harvest, while this one is called harvest in one respect and sowing in another.

It is called sowing in relation to the future harvest, that is, the consummation of the age. For just as a householder sows good seed in his field, but while people slept an enemy sows perhaps tares among it, and both are allowed to grow until the harvest, when the tares are bound into bundles to be burned and the wheat is stored in the barn, so the Son of God, preaching the Gospel, made children of God’s kingdom, among whom, as the devil oversows, children of wickedness grow up. But at the end of the age, through the ministry of angels, the evil will be gathered and separated from the good, like tares from wheat.

The same preaching of the Gospel is called harvest in relation to the earlier time, when the holy patriarchs and prophets “went forth weeping, casting their seeds” [Col. 0375A] (Ps. CXXV). For just as the joy of reapers is sweeter than the labour of sowers, so the blessedness of the apostles, who saw Christ present and heard him speaking, and thus announced him to us, was far fuller and more joyful than the blessed hope of the patriarchs and prophets, who prefigured or foretold his coming.

In this harvest, moreover, chaff is carried with the grains to the threshing-floor (Mal. III); but in that other one the Lord of the harvest will hold his winnowing fan in his hand and cleanse his threshing-floor, delivering the chaff to unquenchable fire and storing his pure wheat in his barn (Matt. III). Therefore, his saying that the fields are already white for harvest means the same as if he had said: they are already teachable for receiving the preaching of the Gospel. Of this harvest he also says elsewhere: “The harvest indeed is great, but the labourers are few. Therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send labourers into his harvest” (Luke X).

He wished his disciples to be labourers in this harvest and stirred them to this work when he said: “Lift up your eyes and see the fields, because they are already white for harvest.” And he added:

“And he who reaps will receive a reward and gathers fruit unto eternal life.”

The Lord of the harvest lays down a just rule for his reapers. The labourer, he says, who reaps receives a reward for his labour, “and gathers fruit unto eternal life.” First, he receives a reward; then he gathers fruit unto eternal life. This reward is plainly that of which he says elsewhere: “Into whatever house you enter, remain there, eating and drinking what they have. For the labourer is worthy of his reward” (ibid.).

The mighty reaper Paul defended this rule concerning food, although he did not wish to use his authority, lest he give any stumbling-block to Christ’s Gospel (I Cor. IX): “Who,” he says, “ever serves as a soldier at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruit? Who tends a flock and does not drink of its milk? Does not even the Law say this? For it is written in the Law of Moses: You shall not muzzle an ox when it treads out the grain” (ibid.). And afterward: “If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great matter if we reap your carnal things? Do you not know that those who serve in the sanctuary eat what comes from the sanctuary, and that those who minister at the altar share in the altar?” [Col. 0375D] (I Cor. IX).

Thus the Lord also ordained that those who proclaim the Gospel should live from the Gospel. Therefore, “he who reaps now receives a reward,” namely the sustenance necessary for this present life, “and gathers fruit unto eternal life”; that is, he also receives an eternal reward in the future, “each according to his own labour” (I Cor. III). Otherwise God’s truth would not stand and the promises to the fathers would not be confirmed. Hence, still employing the proposed analogy, he adds:

“For in this the saying is true: one sows and another reaps, so that both the sower and the reaper may rejoice together.”

“In this,” he says, “the saying is true; in this God’s truth remains; in this the promises to the fathers have been confirmed: because another once sowed the seed of the fields which, as I have said, are now white for harvest—that is, the blessing of all nations, which in my coming now possess that same blessing as a present reality—and another now reaps.

“For what is this saying except that which was made to Abraham, Moses, and all the holy prophets: that in their seed all nations should be blessed? (Gen. XVII). And in what is this saying true, except because it has been fulfilled at my coming just as it was promised to them and believed by them? For they, believing and hoping, entrusted their faith and hope, through believing and hoping, to the propagation of their flesh, as to the good soil of God’s grace; they sowed as they went and wept, casting their seeds” (Ps. LXXI).

By weeping and sowing, they confessed that they were strangers and sojourners upon the earth (Ps. CXXV), and that they had no abiding city here but sought one to come (Heb. XIII). Having endured a laborious winter in this way, they sowed and did not reap. For they all died without receiving the promises, but saw and greeted them from afar; and behold, now others reap—namely you, who possess the present fulfilment of the promises made to them.

They did not reap, I say; they did not receive the promises, because God provided something better for you, so that they should not be made perfect without you. This is what follows: “So that both the sower [Col. 0376C] and the reaper may rejoice together” (Heb. XI). Hence, pronouncing them blessed, he immediately adds:

“I sent you to reap what you did not sow. Others have laboured, and you have entered into their labours.”

This saying agrees with that in which the same Saviour says: “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see. For I tell you that many kings and righteous people desired to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it” (Luke X). For blessed indeed were the eyes of the disciples, who now saw that the fields were already white for harvest, and who heard that they had been hired for this work, to reap what others had sown:

“I,” he says, “sent you to reap what you did not sow.” That is: I chose and appointed you for this, that you might go and bear fruit which you did not sow. For did you suffer anything like what Abraham and the other fathers, who sowed, endured? Did you leave land and kindred and become strangers or guests in a foreign land, in the hope that, as you sowed outside your city and home, a harvest might arise—that is, the blessing by which all the families of the earth are blessed? (Gen. XII). Did you possess knowledge or prophecy, or sow the seed of this blessing by prophesying?

It is not so. Rather, others laboured, and you—unlettered and ordinary men (Acts IV), who until now did not know how to cultivate God’s field either by word or deed—have entered into their labours, so that what they sowed may be brought through you into the barn [OCR: *borreum*, for *horreum*]. That is, the blessing of all nations promised to them was to be preached by you as fulfilled and proclaimed throughout the whole world. It follows:

“Now many of the Samaritans of that city believed in him because of the woman’s word, as she testified: ‘He told me everything I had done.’”

This passage should be compared with the one said much earlier: “When he was at Jerusalem on the feast day,” namely, in his own country, among his fellow-countrymen, “many believed in him, seeing the signs which he did” (John II). Here and there, the Evangelist says, many believed in him, but he assigns very different reasons. “Those,” he says, “believed in him, seeing the signs which he did;” these believed because of the woman’s testimony, as she said, “He told me everything I had done.”

This must wholly be read as a reproach to the Jews, just as the Apostle’s saying is: “The Jews ask for signs, and the Greeks seek wisdom” (I Cor. I). For while the Jews sought the vanity of signs, they were deceived; but the Gentiles, delighting in the discourse of rational wisdom, willingly yielded to truth.

What if he had changed water into wine before them, or done among them something such as the many things he did in his own country, namely Galilee or all Judaea? What if, travelling around their towns and cities, he had taught them, instead of commanding his apostles, when he sent them to preach: “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles, and do not enter the cities of the Samaritans” (Matt. X)—lest he give the Jews occasion to despise the Gospel as though reasonably, since this word of salvation had been sent to them?

Hence it is no wonder that some Samaritans later took such offence that one day they did not receive him, because his face was set toward Jerusalem. Yet not all of them were inhospitable to him or his disciples: “They went,” says the Evangelist, “into another village” (Luke IX). Indeed, the Jews omitted no occasion, however slight, for blasphemy. When they began to reproach him by calling him a Samaritan (John VIII), it was because he had spoken with them and now stayed among them for two days, before John had been handed over and he had undertaken the public office of preaching. Much more, if he had remained among them with his disciples, preaching and performing miracles, he would have given them occasion, as though lawfully, to despise the Gospel.

How great a harvest among the Gentiles, then, do you suppose he would have gathered if at that time he had resolved to preach in person to both Samaritans and the other Gentiles? Therefore, when he reproached the cities of his own country, he could equally have said of Samaria what he said of Tyre and Sidon: “If the mighty works which were done in you had been done in Samaria, they would long ago have repented in ashes and sackcloth” (Matt. XI).

Therefore, because they believed in him not on account of signs, which they had seen none of, but because of what has been said, hear what follows:

“When therefore the Samaritans came to him, they asked [Col. 0378A] him to remain there; and he remained there two days.”

This too, like the rest, is clearly said in comparison with Jerusalem (John XII). For when he entered the city of his own accord (Matt. XXI), taught in the Temple, and many believed in him (Luke IV), “seeing the signs which he did, nevertheless Jesus did not entrust himself to them” (John II). We must understand that his poverty was so great, and that he flattered no one, that in the great city he found no host and no lodging, but lived in a small country place with Lazarus and his sisters—that is, in Bethany, their village. Already then, in actual experience, he was receiving proof that in his own country, of which that city was the chief city, he would receive no honour.

For in that city, or his own country, foxes had dens and birds of heaven nests: that is, malicious spirits and evil spirits lifted up on the wings of pride had filled the dwellings of unbelieving minds and lived in those lairs. But the Son of Man had nowhere to lay his head (Matt. VIII): that is, he had no one to whom he might entrust the name or sacrament of his divinity through faith. Therefore, in that same city, where the holy things of his own country were, he rightly never deigned even to lodge for one night.

But the Gentiles, having heard his Gospel, were to drive those foxes and birds from their dens and nests—that is, from their hearts, temples, and altars—and then prepare a resting-place for the head of the Son of Man. Therefore now, among those foreigners, he deigned to remain in such an order, indeed in such a prefiguration.

He remained with them two days. For by making known to his Church the two commandments of love, he remains with it always both in the present and in the future age; and in each age, as in two complete days of his, grace will not fail it.

“And many more believed because of his word, and they said to the woman: ‘We now believe no longer because of your speech; for we ourselves have heard and know that this is truly the Saviour of the world.’”

It was not without purpose that this Evangelist, whose intention was to write the loftier matters, pursued with such care these things which seem more humble. Above he said that they believed because of the woman’s word; now, as the believers increased, they said to the woman, “We now believe no longer because of your speech.” He took care to write both that they believed because of her word and that they now said they believed no longer because of her speech. Why, except because they first heard of him through the woman, but, lest they appear to be led by frivolity and carried about by every wind of doctrine, they carefully tested the Saviour’s own words by the judgment of their own reason (Eph. IV).

Why do we believe, if we now believe no longer because of your speech? “For we ourselves have heard and know that this is truly the Saviour of the world.” The foreigners’ rational readiness to believe must indeed be noted more and more. They claim neither to know nor believe because of the woman’s word, nor because they saw signs: “But we have heard,” they say, “and we know.” For what did they hear except the speech of wisdom from his mouth, the word of truth from his gracious lips? What did they hear except truth, meekness, and righteousness, for which his right hand guides him wonderfully? (Ps. XLIV).

They heard the truth of one teaching, the meekness of one inviting them to believe, and the righteousness of one who did not accept the person of Jew or Samaritan, judging none, from whatever nation, to be despised as unclean. Does not this event, then, plainly accord in every respect with us—us, I say, who have not seen but only “have heard and know that this is truly the Saviour of the world”?

Does not the Saviour himself bear witness concerning us against the hardness of his own country and say: “A people whom I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me”? [Col. 0379B] (Ps. XVII). Does not that country of his now begin, as God foretold through Moses (Deut. XXXII), to be moved to jealousy by a non-nation, by a foolish nation, and to be provoked to anger? For from this they began, in great and evil jealousy, to be angry with foreigners, saying to him, “Is he God of the Jews only, and not also of the Gentiles?” (Rom. VIII)—not only the God of the Jews but also of the Gentiles, not only the Saviour of the Jews but also of the whole world, as the Samaritans have now confessed—“Do we not rightly say that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?” (John VIII).

But let them be jealous as much as they wish; let them rage and curse as much as they have conceived from the devil through hatred of us. For Christ—whom we have not known according to the flesh—rests among us according to the Spirit; and, remaining for two days, that is, in the present and future age, he has laid down his head, because we have heard and, believing by hearing alone, “know that this is truly the Saviour of the world.”

And truly our woman at the well, where she received living water, where she left her water jar and forgot her pleasures—indeed, where she poured out her own blood—sang to him a true song, saying: “My beloved, I will seize you and bring you into my mother’s house and into the chamber of her who bore me. There you will teach me the Lord’s commandments” (Song VIII).

For truly the multitude of our martyrs, who departed from the city of the devil by leaving everything and by despising even bodily life itself, has now brought him into the house of its mother, into the chamber of her who bore it. It brought his name and worship into the common assembly and rite of the Gentiles, into the very secret places of the temples, where the crowd of evil spirits had lain with her; and, crying out, bearing witness, and dying, it prevailed that he should be received after those spirits had been cast out. It follows:

“After two days, however, he departed from there and went into Galilee. For Jesus himself bore witness that a prophet has no honor in his own country.”

This line of reasoning must be carefully considered, as was said at the beginning of this reading, so that it may become wholly clear to which proposition it is attached.
