For it does not answer the verse with which it is joined in the sequence of the text—namely: “After two days [Col. 0380A] he departed from there and went into Galilee.” For if you wish to connect it in this way—why he left there and went into Galilee: “For Jesus himself bore witness that a prophet has no honor in his own country”—you have certainly introduced a reason altogether discordant with, indeed contrary to, the proposition, since Galilee and all Judaea, which did not associate with the Samaritans, were his own country.

It must therefore be connected thus: “I said above,” says the Evangelist, “that Jesus left Judaea and went again into Galilee,” and I added: “But he had to pass through Samaria.” You therefore ask me: Why did he have to pass through there? For this reason, I say: he had to do so for an important purpose, for the proof of a great matter. In the present discourse I have disclosed that matter; I have appended the matter itself in these words: [Col. 0380B] “For Jesus himself bore witness that a prophet has no honor in his own country.” If you attend properly to this matter, it is surely evident that he appropriately and fittingly wished to pass through Samaria, through that country which was not his own; and, remaining two days among those foreigners, he accepted the honor bestowed on him by them as proof of his testimony.

“A prophet,” he says, “has no honor in his own country.” Another Evangelist, to express the sense more fully, altered the words of this testimony a little: “A prophet is not without honor except in his own country” (Matt. 13). It is therefore as though he said: This country dishonors me—a prophet, indeed the Lord of the prophets—for no other reason than that it is my own country. For if I performed in Tyre and Sidon [Col. 0380C] the mighty works which I perform in this my own country, they would certainly honor me in ashes and sackcloth by doing penance (Matt. 11).

Jesus bore this testimony. But they did not receive this testimony, any more than the rest; they did not believe his words. Therefore, just as he says elsewhere concerning another testimony, “If you do not believe my words, believe the works” (John 10), so they too ought to have been able to hear concerning this same testimony in an unanswerable fashion. He had to pass through Samaria and allow room for the experiment by which the truth of his testimony might be proved, and by which it might be shown accordingly that he would receive that honor among the Gentiles—so that those who envied might see and be confounded; see, I say, while envying, and envy still. But those who believed might see and rejoice: see, I say, [Col. 0380D] and, by believing more and more, be justified. It follows:

“When therefore he had come into Galilee, the Galileans received him, having seen all that he had done at Jerusalem on the feast day. For they too had come to the feast day.”

This seems already to conflict with his own testimony, since the Galileans are said to have received him. For this expression suggests honor: “The Galileans,” he says, “received him, having seen all that he had done at Jerusalem on the feast day.” But let us gather the character and end of this honoring from another Evangelist. For this return of Jesus into Galilee is the one from which the other Evangelists, after relating his temptation, begin their accounts. How, or to what end, did they honor him by receiving him?

[Col. 0381A] Luke says: “And all bore him witness and wondered at the words of grace which proceeded from his mouth” (Luke 4). Behold an honorable reception. But immediately it is added: “And they said: Is not this the carpenter’s son?” (ibid.) Again: “How great things we have heard were done by you in Capernaum, do also here in your own country” (ibid.), that is, in the city of Nazareth, where you were born and reared. Because he did not satisfy their curiosity, “they were all filled with anger in the synagogue,” he says, “and they rose up and cast him out of the city, and led him as far as the brow of the mountain, that they might throw him down” (ibid.).

Thus they received him with empty honor—that is, without love—not in order to honor him, but in order that they themselves might feed their curiosity upon his miracles. This too the Evangelist here [Col. 0381B] has not passed over. For when he had said, “The Galileans received him,” he immediately added the reason for this reception: “having seen all that he had done at Jerusalem on the feast day.” On this account, he says, they received him; indeed, as the aforementioned Evangelist Luke says, “all bore him witness.”

Here it should be noted that they did not say, “How great things we have heard were done by you at Jerusalem, do also here in your own country,” lest they seem to wish to rank themselves with so great a city; but rather, “How great things we have heard were done by you in Capernaum,” where, of course, he had remained not many days before ascending to Jerusalem when Passover was near. Yet in whatever manner, they did receive him. What follows, then?

“Therefore he came again into Cana of Galilee, where he made water wine.”

In this statement too we rightly marvel at the most sacred [Col. 0381C] arrangement of this discourse—namely, of the Evangelist John—or rather at the incarnate Wisdom of God, which in this first year of its manifestation proceeded in such an order as he took care, not without reason, to commend here in writing. That year was now almost complete since Jesus had gone up to Jerusalem when Passover was near. For shortly afterward, with the same feast impending, he was to go up there again.

For what during this whole year, in which, before John had yet been handed over, he did not exercise the public office of preaching—what, I say, did he do during this year except prefigure in his deeds the order in which the future preaching, or the salvation soon to come, would proceed from the time of his Passion to the end of the age, as though marking it out with certain extended [Col. 0381D] boundary-lines? For he had set before him, in the eternal counsel of divinity, a fixed and immovable decree: to bring forth the law from Zion and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem (Isa. 2); namely, that he should suffer as was necessary, rise from the dead on the third day, and that thereafter repentance and forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem (Luke 24), so that, because blindness was to come upon Israel, meanwhile the fullness of the Gentiles might enter in, and thus all Israel might be saved (Rom. 11).

He plainly prefigured this in himself throughout this whole year. For when he went up to Jerusalem at the Paschal feast, he signified in advance the Passion and Resurrection which he was to accomplish, by the destruction of the temple and its raising in three days [Col. 0382A] (John 2). Then, speaking with Nicodemus, he defined the repentance and forgiveness of sins which were to be preached in his name, saying: “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God” (John 3), and so forth.

Afterward, remaining in Judaea, when he learned that they spoke against him—for blindness was already happening to Israel—he left Judaea and turned aside to the Samaritans, whom the Jews reckoned among foreigners. Behold, at last he returns into Galilee; at last he comes again into Cana of Galilee, where he made wine from water. Note carefully: he did not return from Samaria to the temple at Jerusalem, where, by casting out those who sold and bought, he rejected the old sacrifice, although that city had also been his first; rather, from the foreigners, among whom he remained two days, [Col. 0382B] he returned into Galilee—indeed, to Cana of Galilee—where, having been invited to a wedding, he turned water into wine.

For salvation will return to Israel when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered in; but Christ will never return to the temple—that is, to receive the blood of victims or the rite of circumcision. Did not, then, the maker of our salvation set forth during this whole year certain shadows, according to this Evangelist, of the things which he was to do? But he will return near the end of the age to his own country, from which the nature of God, taking human nature, made a marriage; and, “like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber” (Ps. 18), he changed the water of our corruption into the wine of incorruption. So now, near the end of this year, he returned to Cana of Galilee. Let us hear, then, what he did there now, [Col. 0382C] and seek the inward mystery in his outward work.

“And there was a certain royal official whose son was ill at Capernaum. When he had heard that Jesus had come from Judaea into Galilee, he went to him and asked him to come down and heal his son; for he was beginning to die.”

This royal official who approached the Lord Jesus, asking him to come down and heal his son, could have known from the preceding year that, for bestowing healing, the result would accompany Christ’s will as he pleased. For the Evangelist here too said above that, before he went up to Jerusalem when Passover was near, he stayed at Capernaum for some days (John 2); and the other Evangelists do not conceal [Col. 0382D] that he performed many mighty works there (Matt. 11), so that his fellow citizens said to him: “How great things we have heard were done by you in Capernaum, do also here in your own country” (Luke 4).

Since he did not doubt the power which had been well established concerning him, why does Jesus say to him, when he says, “Lord, come down, that you may heal my son”: “Unless you see signs and wonders, you do not believe”? For it must not be taken lightly that the most weighty Truth said to his own country what, while speaking to one royal official, he expressed to his whole nation in the plural.

Since believing and having faith are equivalent, or the same, we must first state and explain the definition of faith; and it will immediately become clear how this royal official could seek his son’s healing and yet not yet believe. When the Apostle Paul spoke at length concerning faith, he defined faith itself: [Col. 0383A] “Faith,” he says, “is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen” (Heb. 11). Faith, he says, is not of things which are present and physically seen, but “is the substance”—that is, the possession—of things hoped for; it is the evidence—that is, the certainty—of things which are not visible. “For what a man sees, why does he hope for?” (Rom. 8).

But those signs which the Lord Jesus performed, which this royal official could have seen and which he asked might be granted to him, were present things, visible things. Therefore there was no faith concerning those things: that is, to see those signs, to know those signs, and to be unable to doubt them, was not believing, was not faith. What, then, were the things not present, the things not visible, concerning which he wished faith to be held when he said: “Unless you see signs and wonders, you do not believe”? Clearly, those things of which he was speaking, which he announced to those who did not know them, and for the proclamation of which—because they were not visible, because they could not be seen with bodily eyes—he called himself a prophet: [Col. 0383B] “A prophet,” he says, “has no honor in his own country.”

For example: “The kingdom of God will draw near” (Mark 1); “The Messiah has now come” (John 3); “God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son” (ibid.); “I am he who speaks with you” (ibid.); “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that everyone who believes in him may not perish but may have eternal life” (ibid.). These and similar things were partly present and partly future; but they were not seen with bodily eyes and were therefore not visible.

To hear these matters with the ears of hearing, to receive them with the ears of the heart, and not to waver concerning them when reason’s judgment had gone before—this was believing; this was having faith. But they did not hear; and when he spoke what he knew, when he testified to what he had seen, they did not receive his testimony, although they saw many signs done by him (Matt. 13). He rightly therefore did not merely say, “Unless you see,” but “Unless you see signs and wonders, you do not believe.” He said this, surely, with the bitter rebuke they deserved, because the Samaritans mentioned above were justified in comparison with them. They would not deign to associate with the Samaritans, [Col. 0383D] although he had shortly before been among them not without honor; for they believed in him, not because of signs and wonders—for they saw none—but they began to believe because of the prophecy by which he had told the woman everything she had done. Then, because of his own sound and true word, many more believed, saying: Not because we have seen signs, but because we have heard and know that this is truly the Savior of the world.

Did not his own fellow-countrymen especially hear him—indeed, hear him daily—and consequently have the ability to know? Should not at least the testimonies of John, whom all knew to be a prophet, have sufficed for them? He therefore rightly reproached them at that time, because, as has already been said, the Samaritans had recently been justified in comparison with them; indeed, all the nations were shortly to be magnificently justified.

For they were degenerating exceedingly from the faith of their fathers. Did Abraham believe because of signs and wonders? When God said to him: [Col. 0384A] “Go forth from your land and your kindred, and I will bless you and multiply you, and in your seed all the families of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. 12, 22)—did Abraham, I say, ask: What sign do you show me, that I may believe you because you command this or promise this to me?

But if you object with certain writings that are not authentic, according to which he is said to have been divinely delivered from the fire of the Chaldeans, and say that this might have sufficed as a sign for him, then tell what signs and wonders God had shown him so that, trusting, he would fearlessly permit himself to be thrown into the fire. What sign or wonder had he received, so that when God repeatedly promised him a seed in which all the nations of the earth would be blessed, he did not weaken in faith and did not consider his own body as dead or Sarah’s barren womb? (Rom. 4). Did he at least receive this as a sign, or as a consolation for his hope: that, though both were old, he a centenarian and she ninety years old, they did not grow old or become cold? Finally, did he at least receive this: that the womanly functions—that is, the menses—of barren Sarah did not cease?

Therefore, he says, you are degenerate; therefore unworthy of so great a father; therefore worse than all foreigners, you who will not believe unless you see signs and wonders. But you say: Do you wish us to believe you vainly or lightly? [Col. 0384C] Must we believe every spirit? (1 John 4). If you say that you are the Christ, that you are the Son of God, how shall we ascertain whether you have spoken the truth? To this I say: Certainly test it, but in the manner the Law commands. Prove it, but lawfully. For what is written in the Law? How do you read it?

“The Law says: What a prophet has foretold in the name of the Lord, if it does not come to pass, the Lord has not spoken it; rather, the prophet has fabricated it out of the swelling pride of his own heart, and therefore you shall not fear him” (Deut. 18). Does not the Law likewise say: “If a prophet arises in your midst, or one who says that he has seen a dream, and foretells signs and portents, and what he has spoken comes to pass, and he says to you, ‘Let us go and follow foreign gods,’ you shall not hear the words of that prophet or dreamer” [Col. 0384D] (Deut. 13)?

I acknowledge that it says this as well; but it says it concerning the dreamer, the prophet who urges you to go after foreign gods. The prophet who confesses that he comes in the name of the Lord and prophesies truthfully with this profession has another place, another commandment. For it says: “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from your nation and from among your brothers, like me; him you shall hear, as you asked of the Lord your God in Horeb” (Deut. 18). And afterward: “Whoever refuses to hear his words, which he shall speak in my name, I will exact vengeance” (ibid.). And immediately: “But if,” it says, “you answer in a secret thought, ‘How can I understand the word which the Lord has not spoken?’ you shall have this sign: What that prophet has foretold in the name of the Lord, [Col. 0385A] if it does not come to pass, the Lord has not spoken it; rather, the prophet has fabricated it out of the swelling pride of his own heart, and therefore you shall not fear him” (ibid.).

Thus, according to the commands of the Law, test not by fabrications or wonders, but by a true word, so that you may know, O my country, what you ought to believe. For example, when I say to you: “Destroy this temple, and I will raise it in three days”; indeed, when I say more aptly [more plainly]: after I am killed, I shall rise after three days (Matt. 27)—if what I say does not happen, the Lord has not spoken it; indeed, I who speak am not the Lord.

Meanwhile, before that happens, when I say to you that “you think evil in your hearts” (Matt. 9), and when I say other such things, return to your hearts; if you understand the matter to be in your hearts as I say, know that the Lord has spoken, and that the other things which I speak to you in the name of the Lord are true. In this lawful manner the Samaritans shortly before tested the truth, while one woman preached: “Come and see a man who told me everything that I did.” For who except the Lord God sees through the secrets of hearts?

You pupils of the Law, understand the Law. Both the prophet who speaks indeed in the name of the Lord but lies, and the one whose word which he spoke comes to pass but who spoke in the name of foreign gods—this man, I say, and those things alike shall be despised, indeed put to death. But he who both speaks in the name of the Lord and speaks a true word, he is to be feared; [Col. 0385C] he is to be believed in all things.

But you wish, on the contrary, to test words by signs and wonders. Some of you—indeed almost all—seek signs from heaven: namely, that if I am the Christ (Matt. 24), if I am that prophet of whom Moses said, as mentioned above, “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers; him you shall hear as me” (Deut. 18)—if, I say, I am that prophet, you demand these signs and wonders, and that there should again be done, on your account, the same or something similar to those Roman signs and portents which were done on behalf of your fathers when the Egyptians were destroyed.

And indeed, to this evil and adulterous generation, which seeks such signs by testing, “no sign shall be given except the sign of Jonah the prophet: for as he was in the belly of the whale three days and three nights” (Matt. 12), [Col. 0385D] and only then, when he preached, Nineveh did three days’ penance, and, after it had been spared, the gourd which shaded Jonah’s head withered (Jonah 3), so “shall the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth three days and three nights” (Matt. 12). Then only shall repentance and forgiveness of sins be preached in his name among all nations (Luke 24); and after they have been saved by the threefold immersion of baptism, in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit (Matt. 28), this my own country, this evil generation, shall be destroyed.

Nevertheless, for you few, whoever remain—who seek signs not by testing but because you have need—signs shall be done more numerous and greater than you request, so that the nations, who will be content with hearing alone, may hear and say: “We have heard and know that this is truly [Col. 0386A] the Savior of the world.”

Therefore, when the Lord had said, “Unless you see signs and wonders, you do not believe,” the royal official says to him: “Lord, come down before my son dies.” What else would this royal official say to an expert physician? To a physician, I say, who, being a man and not God, must himself come to the sick man’s bed, discern the kind of illness by the sight of his eyes as well as by touching the veins, and give an antidote suited to the disease. He had come to the Lord, asking him to come down and heal his son; and while Christ delayed, he said: “Lord, come down before my son dies.”

Clearly he did not believe that his son could be raised by him if he died; nor did he have such faith or humility as to say, like that blessed centurion [Col. 0386B] who was not of Israel: “Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof; but only speak the word, and my son shall be healed” (Matt. 8). But Jesus did not come down; he remained in the same place and, as God, who “has done whatever he willed” (Ps. 113), restored health to his son by his will alone, in which all things are established; and, as a Prophet, he spoke a true word, by which, according to the Law mentioned above, it ought to be proved that he fabricated nothing from his own heart.

“For he says: ‘Go; your son lives.’” This one and same statement is both a true prophecy concerning present things and, as the royal official afterward learned from his servants, a command of life. It is clear that the holy Prophets were deservedly held in great esteem, according to the lawful test mentioned above, even for the lesser part of this miracle—that is, for the truth of prophecy. [Col. 0386C] For example, Samuel, when he told Saul that the asses had been found, spoke truly, though he had not found them himself (1 Kings 10). Likewise Elijah told King Ahab that much rain would soon come, and spoke truly, although he neither gave nor made it by his own work (3 Kings 18).

Therefore, since it is incomparably greater to perform a work of life and power by a mighty command and to announce it by a true word, than to announce by a true word only a work not accomplished by one’s own power, this evil and adulterous generation is deservedly reproached: they honored the tombs of the prophets whom their fathers had killed, while dishonoring with blasphemous words the Lord [Col. 0386D] of the prophets, whom, by filling up the measure of their fathers, they were also going to kill (Matt. 23). For how much greater works did he show them, and yet they did not believe!

Nevertheless, this royal official, carefully investigating both the prophecy and the power of this work, had faith, though late. For it follows: “The man believed the word which Jesus had spoken to him, and went his way.” At first he believed his word; shortly afterward, having learned not the power of the word alone but also the power of the speaker, he believed not only his word but also in him himself, as in God, the Son of God. For this too follows:

“But when he was now going down, his servants met him and announced, saying that his son was alive.” [Col. 0387A] From this prior announcement the royal official could already know that Jesus was a faithful prophet of the Lord, since, in accordance with the legal definition (Deut. 13), he said nothing in the name of foreign gods, but rather invited his hearers to love the Creator, and had spoken truthfully to him concerning his son’s life. This, I say, he could have known even if his son had recovered by some chance or through medicine administered in his father’s absence.

But he was not content with this. “He therefore asked them the hour at which he had become better.” He desired, of course, to know whether, by the very word with which Jesus had said to him, “Your son lives”—by that very word, I say—the power of Jesus had conveyed healing, so that the fever was driven away and health had returned so quickly to his son. For he knew that hour and held it in careful memory, having deliberately noted it and fixed it in his mind with firm attention, so that if the hour of restored health were that in which Jesus had said to him, “Your son lives,” he would no longer doubt the divine power of that great Prophet: that he was the Son of God, that he was the King of Israel.

“And they said to him: ‘Yesterday at the seventh hour the fever left him.’ Therefore the father knew that it was at that hour in which Jesus said, ‘Your son lives’; and he himself believed, and his whole household.” It was fitting, indeed, that through the occasion of one son salvation came to the father and to his entire household. But what great thing was it that, because of such a great sign, the whole household of one royal official believed? For this was no small sign, by which he showed sufficiently clearly that he is everywhere present, everywhere able, and accomplishes all things by his will alone. And for that reason it ought not to have been passed over by this Evangelist, [Col. 0387C] who collected almost solely testimonies to the divinity of the Son of God, for the reason often mentioned.

Why then does so great an Evangelist now enlarge this point, declaring to us that the man and his whole household believed, except because that household belonged to the unbelieving country of this great Prophet? “For Jesus himself,” as was said above, “bore witness that a prophet has no honor in his own country” (John 2). But this royal official and his whole household could be led by the light of reason to escape the darkness of envy and, believing, honor the man of their own country not merely as a prophet but as the Lord of the prophets; and, honoring him, believe.

Likewise, when he changed the waters into wine, “his disciples,” he says, [Col. 0387D] “believed in him,” although the fruit, in proportion to the greatness of the miracle, was very small. Thus both what the Evangelist says here—“He himself believed, and his whole household” [Col. 0388A]—and what he says there—“His disciples believed in him”—records a small result in proportion to the works, yet one not to be despised with respect to his own country, which was exceedingly difficult to bring to faith.

This benefit of the Savior, as it is read, was thus performed in the one son of the royal official. Moreover, just as the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, who died at the time when the woman with the issue of blood was healed (Matt. 9), rightly signifies the Synagogue, which abandoned its life through unbelief and envy at the time when the Gentile world, believing in Christ, turned away from its sins; so nothing prevents us from understanding mystically in the royal official’s son the same Jewish people. For the aforementioned Samaritan woman plainly bore the type of the Church from the Gentiles; when she believed in the Lord, this son began to die.

For just as the ruler of the synagogue, falling at Jesus’ knees, prayed for his daughter, so also the royal official rightly signifies the noble faith of the fathers—Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—which, by ancient merits, intercedes with Christ and God the Father for the salvation of that people. When, at the end of the age, he looks upon their faith in the fact that the remnant of Israel shall be saved (Rom. 11), he rightly says to them: [Col. 0388B] “Unless you see signs and wonders, you do not believe.” For unless, when Enoch and Elijah preach, they see signs and wonders of the judgment that is now imminent and immediately to follow—far greater signs than we see, who have neither seen the signs of the Redeemer nor yet see the signs and wonders of the coming judgment—they will not believe (Rev. 11).

Therefore their faith then will be of less praise or grace, so that the same people may rightly be told also what was said to the Apostle Thomas as a type of them: “Because you have seen me, you have believed; blessed are those who have not seen and have believed” (John 20). And the statement, “Yesterday at the seventh hour the fever left him,” together with the fact that the Samaritan woman believed in the Lord sitting beside the well at the sixth hour, accords beautifully with this mystery.

For what is the seventh hour except the descent of the same sun after its ascent? At the sixth hour the sun is highest; it makes the seventh hour only by descending. Therefore at the sixth hour the Samaritan woman recognized the Lord and believed; but at the seventh hour the fever left the royal official’s son, because, when Christ—the Sun of righteousness—ascended into heaven, the Church from the Gentiles believed. But the Jewish people, when he begins [Col. 0388D] to descend—that is, when he sends beforehand the signs and wonders of his descent—will believe.

## BOOK FIVE

[Col. 0387]

[Col. 0387D] It rightly pleased the Holy Spirit that this Evangelist John should be signified by an eagle, as is known to almost everyone. For he contemplated with clear vision Christ, the Sun of righteousness, moving through his circuit and returning into his circles (Eccl. 1)—that is, ordering all things and foreseeing everything in his hidden counsel. In this Gospel he traced Christ’s ways, as on a sundial, with a bright, rational claw [wand], [Col. 0389A] so that the diligent reader might observe the circuit of his wisdom and the circles of his counsels, albeit with somewhat bleary eyes.

For he describes certain journeys and deeds of the Son of Man in order to disclose the counsel of the same Son of God, just as astronomers customarily draw certain geometrical circles in order to investigate the rising or setting of the sun. In this connection one should especially note that he passes over no Paschal feast; and, as if you were to calculate the sun’s successive steps upward from the eastern line, so he always treats from this feast onward, in accordance with Christ’s deeds and words, the greatest and most necessary mysteries of the Christian faith.

There are three feasts belonging to three years which he records, apart from the fourth feast, at which Christ himself suffered and was buried and, rising from the dead, fulfilled the things he had taught in the preceding years and instituted from himself the sacrament of our salvation. Of the Passover of the first year it has already been said that, when he first ascended to Jerusalem, he disclosed only in words the great and most necessary instrument of our life, saying: “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God” (John 3), [Col. 0389B] and so forth. Then, remaining in Judaea while the Jews spoke against him and the Pharisees envied him, turning aside to the city of Samaria and finally returning to his own country, he mystically prefigured to whom, and in what order, he would impart the grace of this same regeneration, as was said above.

Behold, in this second year, ascending to Jerusalem at the same feast and coming to the sheep-pool, he prefigures by deeds too the power of his baptism, which in the preceding year he had commended in words alone. Then, on the occasion of his deeds, as the Jews opposed and calumniated him, while he defended the truth of his divinity, he provides us with the firm word of faith in which the whole power of that baptism consists. In the third year, likewise near the same feast, when a meal had been made from five loaves and two fishes, he commends to five thousand men, on the occasion of that food, another sacrament no less necessary for our salvation, saying: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not [Col. 0389C] have life in yourselves” (John 6), and so forth.

In the fourth year, at the same feast, as was said, he suffers, so that, as he had taught in the preceding years, we might be baptized into his death and receive his flesh to eat and his blood to drink. So greatly does he confirm the holy and true rationale of the old Passover that, at the same feast in which the remembrance of God’s benefits to the ancients shone forth, he established the truth of the new sacraments. Therefore let us contemplate in this mirror of the Gospel reading, as we have begun, what this festive Sun of righteousness did and said in this month, the beginning of months, which is first among the months of the year according to this visible sun.

## CHAPTER V

“After these things there was a feast day of the Jews, [Col. 0390A] and Jesus went up to Jerusalem.”

This Evangelist does not expressly state the Paschal feast when he says indefinitely, “There was a feast day of the Jews, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem”; but it is inferred from what precedes that it was the feast of Passover. For no other reason did he say above, when he spoke to the Samaritan woman, to his disciples: “Do you not say that there are still four months, and the harvest comes?” (John 4). It is certain, moreover, that when no more than four months remain before harvest, the Paschal feast is not more than two months distant. Within that period no other feast occurs at which, according to the command of the Law, every male ought to appear before the face of the Lord (Exod. 23; Deut. 18). Therefore this too is the Paschal feast, at which, as stated, and as will become clearer later, the beginning of our sacraments is repeated.

“But there is at Jerusalem a sheep-pool, called in Hebrew Bethsaida, having five porticoes.”

A pool is not called *piscina* from *piscis* (“fish”), just as neither *fiscina* (“basket”) is named from *fiscus* (“treasury”), nor *mutina* from *mutus* (“mute”), unless perhaps by antiphrasis, because it has no fish at all. It was a body of water marked by two basins: one of them was commonly filled by winter rains; the other was discolored with red waters, [Col. 0390B] in which sacrifices were washed. For this reason it was also called the sheep-pool. For Greek *probata* means “sheep” in Latin. Hence, as stated, this pool is called *probatica* because victims were washed there.

“It is called,” he says, [Col. 0390C] “in Hebrew Bethsaida.” Note that he does not say, “which is called *probatica*.” Had he said this, it would appear that *probatica* in Greek means the same as Bethsaida in Hebrew. Rather, he says, it is a *probatica*—that is, suited for washing victims—a sense which the Latin expression does not convey in a single word; “but it is called Bethsaida,” which in Latin means “house of fruits.” This name contains a great mystery according to the matters which follow.

“Having five porticoes,” he says. The mystery contained in this is only that, although constructed by men, it should rightly be believed that God provided that porticoes of this number should be there. Why were they there? It follows: “In these lay a great multitude of sick, blind, deaf, withered persons, waiting for the moving of the water.” [Col. 0390D] That is, this pool had these porticoes so that the multitude of sick people keeping watch by the pool—the maker of the heavenly remedy—might not lack shelter, and so that it might be possible for them to await the heavenly help without being driven out from beneath its roof by scorching heat, a storm, or rain. For the waiting for the heavenly visitation was long, and it is immediately added concerning this:

“Now an angel of the Lord descended into the pool at the appointed time, and the water was stirred. And whoever first went down into the pool was made well, from whatever sickness held him.”

Thus, at that time heavenly powers were visibly present, presiding over the holy city and the Temple, before all heaven’s protection had withdrawn from them because of the cruel and sacrilegious crime of murder committed against the Savior [the text adds *ob*, “because of”] [Col. 0391A]. When this had taken place, as Josephus too testifies, the same powers were heard crying aloud: “Let us depart from these dwellings” (*The Jewish War*, VII, ch. 12).

It should be observed that one was healed not by eating the sacrifices washed in that pool’s water, but by the very water in which the sacrifices were washed—provided that, after its stirring, he descended first while sick. In these things, as has been said, is contained so great a mystery and so great a prefigured sacrament as was needed by the living sacrifices to be brought into the heavenly Temple—namely, the souls and bodies of the saints—and as is needed by all of us human beings, who have all contracted from our first parent a true languor, a true and complete weakness both of body and of soul [Col. 0391B].

“For we know and believe”—we believe, I say, “and therefore we speak” (John III)—that our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to the prophet is called the Angel of Great Counsel (Isa. IX), came from heaven: that is, not from below like other human beings, but from above; not from earth, like the first earthly man, but the heavenly Man came from heaven (I Cor. IV). He did not, as certain abortive heretics maintain, take His beginning from a mother; rather, He came from God, went forth from the Father, with whom He was before the earth and the world were formed (Ps. LXXXIX).

He came, I say, among the Jewish people, taking flesh from them. And when, by His teaching and proclamation, He announced salvation and peace according to His own mind, that restless nation, unable to bear His most weighty truth, was stirred up and turned to sedition; it delivered to death the Giver of eternal life (Rom. VI) [Col. 0391C]. By that death He established for the world the sacrament of life: the human race was to be baptized in His death—that is, all who, gathered in the various earlier ages, had until then awaited the grace of God testified to by the five books of the Mosaic law (Gen. XLIX; Deut. XXXIII).

That great and divine event plainly bore the figure of this mystery. Therefore John the Evangelist, a careful observer of heavenly charity, rightly judged it not to be passed over. For that sacred pool, in which, as stated above, the sacrifices were washed, signifies the whole body of ceremonies of the Jewish people and the entire rite of the ancient sacrifices [Col. 0391D]. Since these were shadows of things to come (Col. II), before Christ descended and fulfilled the law in Himself, they could justify no one or bring anyone to perfection (Heb. 7), just as that pool could heal no one before the angel’s descent.

And as it was surrounded by five porticoes, in which lay a multitude of sick persons awaiting the movement of the water, so the Law of Moses, whose books are five, held sinners in restraint for the time being, unable to be cleansed by those shadowy sacrifices, until Christ came and truly fulfilled what those sacrifices had prefigured.

Or rather, since Christ the Son of God came to save not only those who were under the Law of Moses, but all who before the Law and from the beginning of the world had pleased God through faith [Col. 0392A], and since Christ’s Passion was necessary for all, there were rightly “five porticoes,” and in all of them lay sick persons awaiting “the movement of the water.” For before Christ’s coming, from whom the sixth age of the world begins, there had been five ages. In none of them, we must believe, were faithful and righteous persons lacking, who, established around that same hope, awaited the saving advent of our Redeemer.

The one man who first descended into the pool and was healed rightly signified the one and same faith of all these persons (Eph. IV). For there is one Lord, one faith, and one Spirit chosen among all; and consequently there is one Church and one body of all the elect—whether dead or living, whether called before or after Christ’s Passion [Col. 0392B] (I Cor. X).

Therefore, with this place so beautifully and brilliantly illumined by the figure of His Passion, let us hear what the Lord did. It follows:

“There was a certain man there who had been thirty-eight years in his infirmity.”

As the holy doctors have rightly expounded, this man, sick for so long, signifies a sinner oppressed by the enormity of his crimes. Because he lacks love of God and neighbor, and therefore cannot recover through repentance, his infirmity fittingly lasts thirty-eight years: it falls short by two of the number forty, which is dedicated to repentance.

Yet, since on his account the Jewish Sabbath is set aside, and the abolition of that carnal Sabbath is defended by a great argument necessary to Christian faith [Col. 0392C], we are not content merely to know that he signifies a sinner. We must also know whom, of what kind, and how great a sinner—that is, how widely spread—he represents. For while he carries his bed on the Sabbath, it is no slight matter that the Lord Himself, who commanded it, became his advocate, arguing against those vigorous Jewish zealots for the Law, who appeared to be zealous for God’s Sabbath but in truth tore themselves apart through envy, disparaging one man’s salvation and begrudging another’s power or glory.

Therefore, just as the one man who could first descend into the pool after the stirring of the water fittingly signifies the earlier people, that is, the Israelites—to whom belong the adoption, the covenant, the giving of the Law [Col. 0392D], the fathers, and from whom is Christ according to the flesh (Rom. IV), who is God over all, blessed for ever—so likewise this man who had no one to put him into the pool when the water had been stirred signifies the people of the Gentiles. Even when they themselves believed in Christ and desired baptism, none of the apostles, as is related concerning Cornelius in the Acts of the Apostles, dared to admit them to the unity of those who were of the circumcision (Acts X).

Since the mystery of this matter concerns us, it must be investigated more carefully in the present reading. “There was,” he says, “a certain man there, having thirty-eight years in his infirmity.” Where that water had been stirred and one person descended into the pool, there this man also was. For where Christ’s Passion was celebrated and the sacrament of baptism was delivered to that earlier people, from that very time the Gentile people, hearing the report of such great salvation, sought the same grace. They had thirty-eight years in infirmity: that is, they had long been without hope, deprived of the temporal and eternal salvation of body and soul, and robbed alike of the reality of the present life and of the future [Col. 0393A].

For by thirty years—the number constituting the full age of a man—the perfection of present life is signified; by eight years, the eternity of the future life, which has eight beatitudes and will be perfected in the eighth age of the world. But the Gentile people knew that they could not preserve the present life and had no hope of the future. Thus this great sick man had thirty-eight years in infirmity: he quickly consumed the present life in labors and burdens and had no hope of the future resurrection [Col. 0393B].

That this sick man might recognize his calamity as truly one far removed from salvation and might groan ever more deeply, the great sound of the stirred water aroused him, together with the great joy of the man who had descended before him and was healed. Nor had he learned this only because that sound had gone forth into all the earth and the descent of that great Angel had been heard unto the ends of the world (Ps. XVIII), but also because the same sick man was present beside that pool and within its porticoes.

For at the time when this messenger of our peace, this Son of God, descended from heaven, and when sedition against Him had been stirred up, so that through His Passion He might save us, “waters entered even unto His soul; He came into the depth of the sea, and the storm overwhelmed Him” (Ps. LXVIII) [Col. 0393C]. At that time, I say, Roman military centurions, commanders of fifty, and commanders of ten were stationed within the borders of Judaea. “There was therefore a certain man there, having thirty-eight years,” as has been said, “in infirmity.”

“When Jesus saw him [the text adds: lying] and knew that he had been a long time, He said to him: Do you wish to be made well?”

With what eyes, do you suppose, did Jesus see that great sick man signified by this man? What and how many eyes has He in His head? Seven. For He is that stone in which the prophet Zechariah testifies that he saw seven eyes (Zech. III): these are the seven spirits of God [Col. 0393D], whose whole fullness dwelling bodily rests in Him (Col. II).

With these eyes of grace or mercy—which is none other than our God, the Holy Spirit—He saw this sick man when He had ascended into heaven, looking forth “from His holy height, looking from heaven upon earth, that He might hear the groaning of prisoners and release the sons of the slain” (Ps. CI). Then, I say, He looked forth; then He saw and knew that he had been a long time—that is, He showed that He had perceived the feeling of His mercy, because the time had come to have mercy on him.

He beautifully indicates this regard for him by familiarly saying to the aforesaid man: “Do you wish to be made well?” Indeed, He had already heard the desire of the poor, and His ear had heard the preparation of their hearts [Col. 0394A] (Ps. IX). How, then, could He fail to know the will of one sick man, open to all? But He asks this, and says only, “Do you wish to be made well?” in order to show that nothing further should be asked of a person: not what sort of person he is or from what nation he comes, but only whether he wishes to leave his sins and practice righteousness. For “in every nation, whoever fears God and works righteousness is accepted by Him” (Acts X).

“The sick man said to Him: Lord, I have no man to put me into the pool when the water has been stirred.”

This necessary man who puts the sick man into the pool—that is, who brings a sinner to the sacrament of the Lord’s Passion—is Christ Himself or one of His vicars, for example Peter or Paul, in whom Christ speaks (II Cor. XIII); indeed, the whole harmonious choir of apostles or priests, whose office is to teach and baptize. This is surely to send the sick man into the pool of Christ’s Passion, fruitful unto eternal salvation.

But the sick man, the Gentile people, truly had no such man, because those believers who were of the circumcision opposed them and contended fiercely that Christ did not pertain to the Gentiles, but only to the race of Abraham to whom He had been promised. This, assuredly, was what this sick man grieved over when Cornelius, praying and giving alms, sought the kingdom of God (Acts XI) [Col. 0394B]. For he neither knew nor dared to send to Simon, who was surnamed Peter; and the creeping things and serpents of the earth had not yet been shown from heaven to Peter, so that in such a pool he ought to wash them and then kill and eat them all (Acts X).

The sick man therefore rightly says: “I have no man to put me into the pool when the water has been stirred.” And as though he were asked why he lacked the man whom he desired, a man so necessary, he immediately adds:

“For while I am coming, another goes down before me.”

According to the literal situation of the man to whom Jesus was then speaking, this does not seem to follow very reasonably. For he did not lack a man because another went down before him while he was coming; rather, because he lacked a man to send him, he could not descend into the pool. But according to what is signified by it, the literal saying proceeds more fittingly. The Gentile people lacked a man to send them into the pool because, while they came, another went down before them: that is, they could not receive Christ’s grace, nor was it permitted to the apostles to admit them [Col. 0394D], because, while they asked that an entrance to salvation be opened to them, those of the circumcision opposed them most harshly, saying: “Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved” (Acts XV), nor admitted to the grace of Christ. Thus they were repelled by a hard condition, since it was said that they did not belong to Christ unless they first submitted to the entire Law of Moses.

But against the envy of that earlier people, the spokesman of Christ and great advocate of the Gentiles, the Holy Spirit, fittingly appears. Before the Gentiles descended into that pool of the Lord’s Passion—that is, into the sacrament of His baptism, in which we are baptized into His death (Rom. VI)—He fell upon them, and they spoke in tongues and magnified God (Acts X) [Col. 0395A]. Thereafter, as seemed good to the Holy Spirit and His apostles, it was determined that no one should any longer attempt to place upon the necks of the disciples a yoke which neither they nor their fathers had been able to bear (Acts XV).

Therefore the Lord, foreseeing these future things—indeed, things arranged by Himself and soon to be done—says to the sick man who could not descend into the pool where another had been healed:

“Rise, take up your bed, and walk. And immediately he was made well, rose, took up his bed, and walked. Now it was Sabbath on that day.”

Why, on the Sabbath, does He command the man whom the almighty Word heals by His command to carry his bed, when this was not permitted among the Jews? For the Law says concerning the Sabbath day: “You shall not bring burdens through your gates” (Jer. XVII). Why, I say, does He command this, unless to show His Jewish enemies that He would soon, as He had foretold through the prophet, cast dung upon their faces—not only from their Sabbath but from all their solemnities (Mal. II)?

This subsequently began to occur through the authority of the Holy Spirit, who wrought signs and wonders, when He released all from service to the Law. The holy apostles, interpreters of His will, said: “For it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to impose upon you no further burden than these necessary things: that you abstain from things sacrificed to idols, from blood, from what is strangled, and from fornication. If you keep yourselves from these, you will do well. Farewell” (Acts XV) [Col. 0395C].

But when the Lord indicates by His commanded action that the carnal Sabbath need not be observed, why did He choose to signify this in such a manner—that is, by the carrying of the bed—rather than in any other way? Clearly He signified something, not little, of good work by this carrying of the bed. For we may not suppose that it signifies any labor or burden such as those borne by persons to whom He says elsewhere: “Come to Me, all who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. XI).

For that labor and burden belongs to sick persons who have not received healing: it is certainly nothing other than love of this world, which bends and weighs down those not yet cured beneath many burdens [Col. 0395D]. Therefore the burden here signifies that which each person bears when he lawfully celebrates the Lord’s Sabbath.

Accordingly, we must first understand that, just as in the man who was healed we understand the people of the Gentiles, once lying in their sins without faith but now standing in faith and walking in good works, so in his bed we rightly understand the whole order of apostles and preachers of Christ. For just as a man carries his bed while sick and, once well, is refreshed by fitting sleep upon it after the day’s labor, so the Gentile people, even while languishing in unbelief, were carried to Christ by the apostles and holy preachers with the great sweetness of love [Col. 0396A]. And once healed through the righteousness of faith, they are nevertheless strengthened in good work, lest they fail, by those men’s merits, examples, teachings, and admonitions, and are released from daily transgressions.

Yet they in turn carry this bed, so that, since the apostles have sown spiritual things, they may rightly reap carnal things (I Cor. IX). Thus when this great sick man, now healed, is told, “Take up your bed and walk,” it is as though he were told: Take care not to appear ungrateful to your bed. Those in whose spiritual preaching you rest you ought to support from your carnal substance. “For the laborer is worthy of his wages” (Luke X).

The man did what he was commanded: immediately made well, he rose, took up his bed, and walked. What could be truer? What more evident? Openly before the whole world he carries his bed and walks. He has received the holy apostles and apostolic men—upon whose faith, merits, and examples he rests—not only during their lifetime, supporting them with appropriate food, but after their death he venerates their memorials with due honor and enlarges them with possessions, so that their successors or imitators may lack nothing bodily [Col. 0396B], since in their spiritual ministry he has laid down his soul.

Jesus therefore commanded this man to carry his bed when Paul—or rather Christ Himself, who spoke through Paul—said to the Corinthians [the printed text has: “Romans”] concerning the ministry performed for the saints in Jerusalem: “It pleased them, and they are their debtors. For if the Gentiles have become partakers of their spiritual things, they ought also to minister to them in carnal things” (Rom. XV) [Col. 0396C].

Therefore, when the Lord had said to that sick man according to the greatness of His power, “Rise,” He rightly added, according to the good pleasure of His will, “Take up your bed and walk.” His command is accompanied by swift healing, and ready obedience accompanies the healing. “Now,” he says, “it was Sabbath on that day.”

“The Jews therefore said to the man who had been made well: It is Sabbath; it is not lawful for you to carry your bed.”

They truly spoke thus as hypocrites, of whom Isaiah rightly prophesied: “This people honors Me with their lips, but their heart is far from Me” (Isa. XXIX; Matt. XV). For unless their heart had been far from God in this as in other matters [Col. 0396D], they would not so wickedly divide His honor, proclaiming with polluted lips the dung of their solemnities while in their hearts begrudging the glory of a splendid divine work.

For what was it? From where had this man received healing? From their Sabbath, or from the power of Him at whose command he carried his bed? Or—to return to the great sick man spread throughout the whole world—from where did the Gentile people receive the Spirit: from works of the Law, or from hearing with faith?

Thus the Apostle groaned over that great and famous bearer of his bed, when Jews and false apostles bewitched him by saying: “Without circumcision and legal ceremonies, even though you are baptized, you cannot be saved.” This man had almost forgotten his healer, from whom he had received health [Col. 0397A]. “O foolish Galatians,” he says, “who has bewitched you not to obey the truth? Before whose eyes Jesus Christ was publicly displayed, crucified among you. This only do I wish to learn from you: Did you receive the Spirit by works of the Law or by hearing with faith?” (Gal. III).

They knew that they had received the Spirit, because this was manifest from the working of miracles. Therefore he immediately added: “He therefore who supplies the Spirit to you and works miracles among you—does He do so by works of the Law or by hearing with faith?” (ibid.). And again, after some intervening material: “You were running well; who hindered you from obeying the truth?” (Gal. V).

They were plainly running after receiving healing, though formerly they had lain down; they carried the easy yoke and light burden (Matt. XI), namely works of righteousness. A healthy person ought by no means to prefer the Jewish Sabbaths, which God hates, to these. For the truthful prophet Isaiah testifies: “New moon and Sabbath and other feasts I will not endure. Your assemblies are iniquitous; My soul has hated your calends and Sabbaths; they have become burdensome to Me” (Isa. I) [Col. 0397B]. And afterward: “For your hands,” He says, “are full of blood” (ibid.).

But this often-mentioned man, namely the Gentile people—now healed, that is, baptized in Christ, but inexperienced and unlearned in the Scriptures, and hence capable in part of being bewitched so as not to believe the truth—did not know these things and was ignorant of the other testimonies of prophecy and Scripture: namely, that Jewish festivals, calends, and all ceremonies were so hateful to God after being polluted by Christ’s blood, with which the Jews’ hands are full. Therefore he could not give an account of the faith which is in Christ, nor could he approach Christ Himself in bodily presence to hear Him, who suffered violence, answer on His own behalf in such a dispute. Thus it is fittingly added:

“He answered them: He who made me well said to me, Take up your bed and walk. They therefore asked him: Who is it who said to you, Take up your bed and walk? But he who had been made well did not know who Jesus was.”

See first how foolish and unjust Christ’s opponents are in their very question. The man who had been made well, and who had so suddenly and perfectly recovered from such a long infirmity that he could carry his bed upon strong shoulders with neck erect, had given them a twofold brief reply [Col. 0397D]: “He who made me well said to me, Take up your bed and walk.” But they excluded one part from their hearing—namely, “He who made me well.” The other part, “He said to me, Take up your bed and walk,” they immediately snatched from his mouth and set up as a mark to be pierced by the arrows of their tongues.

For they did not say, “Who made you well?” but: “Who is the one who said to you, Take up your bed and walk?” They preferred that the manifest benefit of such great power should disappear, since it was no slight cause or matter of His praise and glory. But they strove to have this other matter known, heard, and publicized because they thought they could make it the basis of a seemingly lawful accusation [Col. 0398A].

Likewise afterward, when the healed Gentile people—that is, people justified through faith in Christ—said, “He who made me well, who gave me the Spirit” (Acts XV) “and works miracles in me” (Gal. V), “told me through His apostles: Do not concern yourself with Jewish ceremonies nor observe their Sabbaths; nevertheless love the Lord your God with all your heart, all your soul, and all your strength, and then your neighbor as yourself” (Matt. XXII)—which truly is to rise and take up one’s bed—when, I say, they spoke thus, Christ’s adversaries, Jews or false apostles, did not in turn say: “Who is it that works miracles among you?” They did not wish to hear any explanation or even mention of that. Rather, they dared to say: “Who commands you not to observe Sabbaths or to reject all the ceremonies of the Mosaic Law?” Nor did they fear to detract from Christ’s grace or to despise the persons of the holy apostles.

For example, they said: “Peter is unlearned and without letters” (Acts IV), and “Paul is no apostle of Christ” (Gal. II), and other such things [Col. 0398B]. Because they neither strove to avoid their fables, genealogies, profane novelties of speech, and foolish undisciplined questions—which produce strife and are useful for nothing but overthrowing their hearers (I Tim. I; II Tim. II)—nor could these things be refuted through knowledge of the Scriptures, it is rightly said also that he who had been made well did not know who Jesus was. If they had done so [the text reads *fecissent*, “had done”; perhaps *scivissent*, “had known”], they could by no means have been bewitched into not believing the truth.

The Apostle rebukes this ignorance: “Awake to righteousness, and do not sin. For some have ignorance of God. I say this to your shame” (I Cor. XV), etc. Therefore we rightly say that ignorance of the Scriptures is ignorance of Christ. For without the Scriptures of both New and Old Testament, it is impossible for a human soul to stand firm, so as not to be carried about by every wind of doctrine (Eph. IV).

Thus, although the primitive Gentile people had been made well—that is, baptized in Christ—they did not know who Jesus was: how great He was, how powerful, how truly God, and how truly Lord even of the Sabbath (Matt. XII) [Col. 0398C]. Why did they not know? The Evangelist says:

“For Jesus had withdrawn from the crowd assembled in that place.”

It is especially to be noted that Jesus did not withdraw because the man did not know Him; rather, the man did not know Jesus because Jesus had withdrawn. From where had Jesus withdrawn? “From the crowd,” he says, “assembled in that place.” He had not withdrawn from the place in which He was, nor from the place in which He had worked the healing power, but from the crowd that was in the place. Nothing is truer.

For what place is there in which Jesus works salvation but His holy Church? Yet Jesus withdraws from no place; He withdraws nowhere locally. Being God, He is everywhere, present in every place. How much less does He ever withdraw from His Church, which is His place! “God,” says the Psalmist, “is in His holy place” (Ps. LXVII), that is, in His holy Church. Thus it follows: “God makes those of one manner dwell in a house” (ibid.) [Col. 0399A].

Jesus therefore had not withdrawn from the place. But what does the Evangelist say? “He had withdrawn from the crowd assembled in the place”: that is, He had withdrawn from those who made a crowd in His place, His house, His Church. It is therefore no wonder if the man who had been healed did not know who Jesus was, when Jesus had withdrawn because of the crowd.

For example, when one said, “I am of Paul,” another, “I am of Apollos,” another, “I indeed am of Cephas” (I Cor. I), then because of these schisms and other heresies the simple believer could not know who Jesus was. He could not quickly attain a sure understanding of what he ought to hold concerning Christ or what answer he ought to give against Christ’s true enemies and false zealots for the Law.

What then did Jesus do after the crowd had been calmed? What did He do in peace, He who withdrew from the rending caused by the crowd and tumult of minds? It follows:

“Afterward Jesus found him in the Temple and said to him: Behold, you have been made well; sin no more, lest something worse happen to you.”

Meanwhile, while there is a crowd in the place and the Jews bring an accusation concerning their Sabbath, the man who has been made well enters the Temple, there to see Jesus or to be seen by Jesus. For when the new people of believers are assailed with questions by heretics or false apostles, necessity compels the examination of the treasury of Scripture, the truth of faith is opened, and thus, in the peace of the Church, those who had been strangers and foreigners become fellow citizens of the saints and members of God’s household (Eph. II) [Col. 0399B].

These strangers and foreigners did not lack the gifts of an ardent nature—namely, noble intellects—which, aided by the Holy Spirit, could through reading the Scriptures follow the straight path to the Temple of truth, where they might offer sacrifices of righteousness in sure faith. For as fire sometimes lies dormant and buried beneath its ashes, but glows again when stirred by a breath, and grows stronger the more vigorously it is pressed, so the same good disposition of the new Church advanced more and shone more brilliantly in knowledge of the Scriptures the more and greater disputes of opponents it endured [Col. 0399C].

This too must not be passed over: the Lord Himself made the man well, but did not Himself bring him into the Temple. For He Himself forgives sins and, as stated above, first showed His grace to the Gentiles (Acts X); yet He willed that all those who had already received the Holy Spirit should be admitted into the communion of His Church through water baptism, not by Himself or by His angel, but through the man Peter [Col. 0399D].

Therefore, when He had led that people of His through the midst of crowds of heretics or opposing Jews into the fullness of faith, He said to them: “Behold, you have been made well; sin no more, lest something worse happen to you.” He did not say this at the beginning, when He made them well, because while the faith of the Gentiles was still tender, it was not to be assailed with threats but nourished with encouragements. Much from the old custom had to be tolerated for a time with discerning restraint, in a spirit of gentleness; those matters were more fittingly to be struck with the rod after Christ had been fully formed in them (Gal. IV).

Thus the Lord did not give the Law to the people Israel in Egypt, but delighted them by His signs and wonders, with which He struck their enslaver Pharaoh (Exod. VII), until He led them out through the Red Sea, with the Egyptians drowned (Exod. XIV). Only then did He bring forth the Law, saying: “Whoever does this shall surely die, and his blood shall be upon his own head” (Exod. XXI).

So, indeed, the grace of God, as a nurse or mother, first fed with milk the newborn infancy of souls in Christ, so that they might gratefully receive the preceding remission of sins; afterward it restrained them with firm severity, lest, while confessing that they knew God, they should deny Him by their deeds (Titus I) [Col. 0400A]. Thus He rightly says to the man in the Temple not at the beginning but only now at last: “Sin no more, lest something worse happen to you.” For it would undoubtedly have been better never to know the way of truth than, after knowing it, to turn back (II Pet. II).

It must also be noted that infirmity commonly comes by God’s will for three reasons: either that the patience of a righteous person may be tested and merit increased; or because one has sinned, so that one may be purified in the furnace of bodily suffering; or lest one sin, because the bond of infirmity hinders or resists. This man, of whom the present reading speaks, must be believed to have spent so many years in his infirmity because he had sinned, since the Lord says to him: “Sin no more, lest something worse happen to you.”

This likewise happened plainly in the aforementioned likeness of the Gentile people [Col. 0400B]. For he is that younger son who sinned against heaven and before his father: having received the portion of the paternal estate which fell to him, he went into a far country and squandered everything in luxurious living; finally he attached himself to one of the citizens and fed swine. When he returned and was still far off, his father ran to meet him, fell upon his neck, and embraced him (Luke XV). Thus, as stated above, while the Gentiles were still outside—that is, not yet baptized—God visibly granted them the grace of the Holy Spirit (Acts X).

The man lying in infirmity because of his sins was therefore made well in this manner while the Jews were angry, because this son, who through his own fault had been dead and lost, came to life and was found, despite the envy of his brother (Luke XV) [Col. 0400C].

What then did this man do, who formerly, when questioned by the Jews, did not know how to answer who or how great was the one who said to him, “Take up your bed and walk”—that is, by doing good, do not concern yourself with Jewish Sabbaths? What did he do now, after he had learned that his Savior was true God and true Son of God? It follows:

“That man went away and told the Jews that it was Jesus who had made him well.”

This man divided the matter better and more faithfully than the Jews. When they heard him say: “He who made me well said to me, Take up your bed and walk,” they silently cut away the part which they could not accuse; for they did not say, “Who made you well?” but: “Who is the one who said to you, Take up your bed and walk?” [Col. 0400D].

He, on the contrary, passes over in silence the very part which they had accused, and reports to those plotters the part open to no reproach. In making his announcement he does not say that Jesus was the one who told him, “Take up your bed,” but that Jesus was the one who made him well [Col. 0401A].

This, surely, is what Christ’s faithful people now do and now announce to the Jews: the name and power of their Savior, Christ the Son of God. Even against their will and against their wishes, they press upon them the truth of the Scriptures. And if they do not succeed in converting them, they nevertheless rejoice because, speaking knowingly and steadfastly and convicting them out of their own Law and Prophets, they put to shame and silence the foolishness of the faithless, “that the upright may see and rejoice, and all iniquity may stop its mouth” (Ps. CVI).

It should be noted that the Jews were not in the Temple when the man told them. For it is said: “That man went away and told the Jews.” He went away now; indeed, because he went away, the Jews were not with him in the Temple. For now, when we are in God’s Temple, when we are in the Church of the Fathers and all righteous persons who from the beginning of the world were true worshippers of God, the Jews are outside. By the great scourge of God’s wrath, they have been cast out like evil merchants, like robbers carrying on wicked trade.

We sometimes go out to them and ask them to come with us into the Temple. But it is in vain. For while we are within, eating the fatted calf, they remain outside; hearing the music and dancing, they are tormented even by the sound alone and twisted by obstinate envy, until the Father Himself goes out and deigns personally to entreat them (Luke XV) [Col. 0401B–C].

Now let us return to what was done at that time, and let us who, according to that prefiguration, have been healed in truth gather the supports of the faith by which we have been healed from the mouth of Him who healed us. It follows:

“Therefore the Jews persecuted Jesus, because he was doing these things on the Sabbath. But Jesus answered them: ‘My Father is working until now, and I too am working.’ Therefore the Jews sought all the more to kill him, because he not only was breaking the Sabbath, but was also calling God his own Father, making himself equal to God.”

From this point, the matter demands the deepest silence and the attentive goodwill of every teachable and reverent soul [Col. 0401D]. For in this discourse the supreme wisdom of God, truly providing not for itself but for us, defends itself by its own reasoning for our sake. Indeed, in the common aid of the whole world, it pleads such a defense for us and on our behalf, in a style at once elevated and humble: so that, in the texture of the divine discourse, the wise or eloquent people of this age may not lack artistry to admire, while the majesty and clarity of its meanings may lie open to unlearned believers, suitably building up their childishness or simplicity.

“Therefore,” he says, “the Jews persecuted Jesus because he did these things on the Sabbath,” etc. Behold: in these words the evangelist has constructed a syllogism. It is worth our while to distinguish its parts—not in order to magnify the trifles of syllogistic art in so great a work [Col. 0402A], but that we may somehow attain, by our understanding, its intention and meaning.

“Therefore,” he says, “the Jews persecuted him because he did these things on the Sabbath.” What does the evangelist here put forward, except that the Jews were astonishingly ready and inclined to kill the Saviour—so blind and devoid of true reason that they reckoned such a work of salvation and rest, an evident work of divine power alone, to be a violation of their Sabbath? A violation, I say, not of just any sort, but such and so great that they declared the author of salvation worthy of death, for no other reason than that he worked salvation on the Sabbath day.

For what is the Sabbath except rest? Or for what reason was it given, except that the laborer, wearied during the other days of the week, might rest on one day and yet receive his daily sustenance as his due from the master of the household? Thus it is written in the law: “Six days you shall work; on the seventh day you shall cease, that your ox and your ass may rest, and that the son of your female servant and the stranger may be refreshed” (Exod. 20). Therefore the Sabbath—that is, rest—was given solely for the rest of wretched servants and for restoring their exhausted limbs [Col. 0402B].

But this work of the Lord, and his other works, caused true rest to follow the real toil of fainting sufferers; they supplied refreshment long desired amid genuine anguish. Therefore those blind and cruelly savage, ruined murderers were far removed from true rest and far estranged from compassion, since for such a cause they persecuted the maker of salvation, the grace of God.

Having thus stated the matter, the evangelist immediately supplies the further proposition [Col. 0402C]: “But Jesus said to them: ‘My Father is working until now, and I too am working.’” That he did these things on the Sabbath was already enough, he says, to sharpen their cruelty, so that, like aroused beasts, they rushed forward, intent and open-mouthed to drink his blood. But he said to them something far greater, something much more intolerable to their envious pride: “My Father is working until now, and I too am working.”

Having made this proposition, he immediately concludes: “Therefore they sought all the more to kill him.” If, he says, they persecuted him out of envy because of that former matter, much more had they cause to envy and persecute him if they received from him something greater. But to call God his Father is far greater than to do such a thing on the Sabbath [Col. 0402D]. Consider, then—you who know how to compare greater things with lesser—how greatly this stripped the sons of men, evil sons of evil men, of all humanity: so that their teeth, their weapons, and their arrows clashed against one another in fury, and their tongue, a sharp sword (Ps. 56), thirsting for blood, was thrust far beyond teeth and lips.

But now the words of the reading themselves must be explained.

“Therefore,” he says, “the Jews persecuted him because he did these things on the Sabbath.” Truly, their feet were sufficiently ready for evil, excessively swift to shed blood (Ps. 13). Yet why did the Lord do these things so often on Sabbaths? Was it that he might provoke them, that he gave them this offense? Was it because he knew that his death would be useful and therefore provoked them to shed his blood [Col. 0403A]? Far from it. Rather, he was the lamp, and for that reason had come into the world, that he might shine in the darkness.

For it is certain, as he himself says: “No one lights a lamp and puts it in a hidden place, but upon a lampstand, so that all who are in the house, or enter the house, may see the light” (Matt. 5). It was right, then, that he should reveal the light of his works before the eyes of all; it was right that he should work and teach in synagogues and in the temple, where all the Jews assembled.

But they held their crowded assemblies not on just any day, but on Sabbaths, new moons, and other festivals. Therefore he had to act on Sabbaths, when the house—that is, the temple or synagogue—was full, when all who were at leisure entered, to whom this lamp had been sent [Col. 0403B]. He had to stand then upon his lampstand and perform the work of his brightness, spreading the light of the fullness of divinity bodily dwelling in him (Col. 2). Thus simple eyes might rejoice in his light, while evil eyes might have no excuse for sin (John 15).

For this lamp did not make any eye evil by its presence, but merely distinguished the evil eye from the simple eye. Just as you, any good craftsman, do not make anyone envious by displaying your skill, but by the results discover and distinguish who is envious and who is well-disposed toward you. Therefore, since in the presence of the light evil eyes possessed a wholly dark body (Matt. 6), so that they not only failed to comprehend the light shining in darkness but even wished to extinguish it [Col. 0403C]—for the Jews persecuted him because he did these things on the Sabbath—he says to them: “My Father is working until now, and I too am working.”

The sentence is brief, its rationale wonderful: for he summoned his persecutors to judgment, and enlightened us who are well-disposed toward him, as a lamp illuminates by its radiance. He made us well-disposed toward himself by good works, one of which was this healing of the sick man, performed to win goodwill. For when he says, “My Father is working until now, and I too am working,” it is a concise exposition by the wisdom of God—our advocate pleading for us—bright and brief in words, great and wonderful in meaning. That part, “and I too am working,” argumentative truth steadily and truthfully defends throughout the whole following discourse, for the confirmation of our faith [Col. 0403D].

Hear, Jews; hear the law of equity, which this man whom you persecute, whom you seek to kill for such a reason, advances—a law by which he has made the senate of the world well-disposed toward himself. Rebuked on the Sabbath for some work, he does not defend himself by the quality of the work, though it be praiseworthy; rather, establishing a lawful case from his own right according to his birth, he does not evade your public tribunal—indeed, that of the whole world.

You are all born from Abraham, and all come after Abraham. But this man was indeed born from Abraham, yet he also is before Abraham. Nor does he work on Sabbaths as you do when you water an ox or ass, somewhat disregarding in this matter the Sabbath—that is, the rest—of your female servant or stranger who releases and waters your livestock [Col. 0404A]. And therefore he does not wish to be bound under a law equal to yours (Matt. 12).

You have the law; you are indeed experts in the law. You have judges, if only they are willing truly to speak justice and judge uprightly (Ps. 57). “My Father,” he says, “is working until now.” He does not now first disclose who or where his Father is; rather, since this had long been made known to them, especially through John’s testimony, he intends to defend what follows: “and I too am working.”

And they must plainly grant that point. For you cannot deny that such a Father as you have long heard him to have is “working until now.” Does he not, even on your Sabbaths, cause “his sun to rise upon the evil and the good, and rain upon the just and the unjust?” (Matt. 5). Does he not, on every day without exception for festivals, kill and make alive (1 Sam. 2)? Does he not strike and heal? And on whatever day he finds a man worthy of death, whatever day a sinner falls into his hands, there is no Sabbath able to rescue him from his hand (Num. 13) [Col. 0404B].

Not to mention that he rests no more on the Sabbath from supplying the offspring of animals or nourishing the fruits of the earth than on the first or second day after the Sabbath. Or do you suppose that, while on your Sabbaths you bring burdens of sin through your gates (Jer. 17)—that is, through your senses, which, since they are the gates and windows of the body, admit death through themselves even into the inward parts—while, I say, you carry such burdens and drag them by long cords of iniquity (Isa. 5), while you do these things on Sabbaths and plot murder against me on the Sabbath, my Father meanwhile sits idle (Ps. 68) because he would blot the Sabbath, rather than you, out of his book? Rather, does he write your sin “with an iron stylus and an adamantine point” (Jer. 17), by a mighty work and a deep inscription which no one shall ever erase [Col. 0404C]?
