It is plain, therefore, that “my Father is working until now,” and that he did not rest on the seventh day from every work in such a way as to cease governing on the Sabbath, rather than on another day, all that he created. Therefore I shall defend myself, saying: “And I too am working.” If you resist, true reason, rational truth, will bind your attempts in its chain.

For from John, whom you judged worthy of consultation, as from a proposition, you heard that God is my Father. You cannot refute my inference that this Father is working until now on the Sabbath day. Therefore I conclude by saying: “Accordingly, I too am working.” What then? Will you dare to be so mad as, through hatred or contempt for the Son, to condemn and persecute the Father also because on the Sabbath he does not refrain from works necessary to your life or from governing the whole world?

Again, you will not be able lawfully to establish that the Son is less free than his Father, or that the Son is, even as Lord of the Sabbath, less lawful than his Father. For what son, legitimately born, is placed beneath his father in nature or condition? Could a father generate a son of a substance other or different from that of which he himself is [Col. 0404D]? He can indeed make something other than what he is—as any one of you, when he paints or shapes something, certainly makes something other than himself. But when he generates, nature does not allow him to generate something other than what he is.

But the Father did not merely make me; he begot me. As that same John, whom I cited above, said: “The only-begotten, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared him” (John 1). He testified that I am God’s only-begotten. Therefore I too work on the Sabbath, because I am not less free or less legitimate than my Father.

“Therefore,” he says, “the Jews sought all the more to kill him, because he not only broke the Sabbath, but also called God his Father, making himself equal to God”—namely, by saying: “My Father is working until now,” and making himself equal by adding [Col. 0405A], “And I too am working.”

“Therefore Jesus answered and said to them: ‘Amen, amen, I say to you: the Son cannot do anything of himself, except what he sees the Father doing.’” These words seem to suggest a certain incapacity of an insufficient nature; but, if you attend rightly, they are shown to proclaim the true, certain, and stable omnipotence of the Son of God. Once their true meaning has been perceived, it will be clear how rightly and excellently Jesus thus answered those seeking to kill him.

And first it must be known that the fruitful advocate, the wisdom of God, from this point as far as the much later statement, “but those who have done evil, unto the resurrection of judgment,” employs most firm arguments, speaking to us in order to refute the opposing parties of Jewish or heretical perversity [Col. 0405B] and to confirm the truth of his divinity, which is necessary for every Christian.

“The Son,” he says, “cannot do anything of himself, except what he sees the Father doing.” What angel or human being could ever make such a declaration concerning himself? For what does anyone see God the Father doing except every good thing? And what other thing is there which he does not do except every evil thing? Whoever does evil does it of himself, because he alone does it, because he acts separately, outside God and the Father.

Who, then, whether angel or human, can boast of possessing a heart so pure as to say that he cannot do anything of himself? For angelic nature was able to do evil and does evil; human nature was able to do evil and did evil. Indeed, the holy angels were confirmed because, when the evil angel did something of himself—that is, did evil—they preferred to cleave to God their ruler. They received this as their reward: that henceforth they cannot do evil, because, when they could do it, they refused [Col. 0405C].

Yet this is not through the power of their own nature, but through the rewarding grace of the divine will. Consequently, even if it may rightly be said that they now cannot do anything of themselves, nevertheless it is not true to add that they do whatever they see the Father doing.

Therefore you, Arius—whose name, even among the dead and those buried in hell, is a stench rather than an honor to the whole great and holy city of God—you, I say, are assailed by this present defense of the Son of God. This voice accuses you; this true testimony of his scourges you; this cry of his condemns you to eternal beheading.

For you called that same Son of God a creature; you cried out that he was made; you invented that there was a time when he was not; you alleged that he was mutable—alas, polluted and unclean man!—that is, capable of turning from good to evil, just as angelic or human nature can decline. Finally, when he said these things to the Jews, this dreadful-sounding madness of yours was already in his ears; he already heard you raging and raving amid those tumultuous Jewish crowds; he already perceived that he must defend himself against your blasphemies and aid his faithful people [Col. 0406A].

Therefore he says: “Amen, amen, I say to you: the Son cannot do anything of himself, except what he sees the Father doing.” What is this, Arius, except as if he had said: The Son is not mutable—that is, he cannot bend from good to evil? For what did he ever see his Father doing within or without, in heaven or on earth, except things “very good” (Gen. 1)? Yet he cannot “do anything of himself, except what he sees the Father doing.” Therefore the Son can do nothing except every good thing; therefore he is not changeable or capable of bending from good to evil; therefore he is not mutable.

And so, Jews, do you persecute him merely for your Sabbaths, as though he did anything apart from his Father? Since you do not dare blame his Father, who is working until now, why do you seek to kill the Son? Perhaps you say: God the Father, since he is not bound by the law of Sabbaths, may work always, because he works only good and cannot possibly work evil. “Amen, amen,” he says, “I tell you: neither does the Son ever work except what is good, nor can it happen that he works otherwise or differently than the Father” [Col. 0406B].

Therefore it follows that he too works always in freedom, that he too is bound by no law of the Sabbath, and that he too is Lord of the Sabbath. But this is still insufficient. For, once this first proposition is granted, it is established that the Son can do nothing but good; but it does not yet appear to follow that no good work has been done by the Father without the cooperation of the Son. He therefore adds a reason from which it may be clear that he has excluded nothing whatever in the foregoing proposition.

“For whatever he does, these things the Son also does in like manner.” This must be carefully observed: by this brief statement he writes three magnificent things simultaneously. First, that the Son does the very things the Father does, and no others; second, that he does not do merely some part of them, but all; and third, that he does not do them dissimilarly—that is, what the Father does by natural omnipotence, the Son does not do by accidental or bestowed grace; what the Father does impassibly, the Son does not do passibly; what the Father does by unchangeable command, the Son does not do by mutable craftsmanship [Col. 0406C].

This, I say, must be carefully observed: he did not say, “He does other things,” but “these things”; nor did he say, “similar things,” but “in like manner.” Therefore we do not understand Father and Son as two craftsmen, master and pupil: one working, the other imitating the master’s work in another material. Rather, we understand God the Father as making all things and God the Son, together with him, composing all the same things.

For the Son himself is the wisdom of God the Father. Therefore what the Son now says of himself must undoubtedly be understood no differently from what the wisdom of God says of itself elsewhere: “When he prepared the heavens, I was present; when by a fixed law and circle he enclosed the depths; when he strengthened the upper air and balanced the springs of the waters; when he set its boundary around the sea and gave the waters a law that they should not pass beyond their limits; when he suspended the foundations of the earth: I was with him, composing all things, and I delighted day by day, playing before him at all times, playing in the circle of the earth; and my delights were with the children of men” (Prov. 8) [Col. 0407A].

Therefore all things which the Father does are no less works of the Son than of the Father. But even this has not yet said enough. For it is not yet sufficiently clear why there is such harmonious partnership and such shared concord, that one does nothing without the other—that is, that the Father does nothing without the Son, nor the Son without the Father. Therefore it follows:

“For the Father loves the Son and shows him all things which he himself does.” This was already said elsewhere in the testimony borne by John: the Father loves the Son, namely with no other love than the Holy Spirit, who is the love of the Father and the Son. “The Father,” he says, “loves the Son and shows him all things which he himself does.” Why does he show them to him? Is it that he may know what he did not know before? Far from it [Col. 0407B]. For how can wisdom be instructed in its own things by anyone? It has now been said, and is known to all, that the Son is the wisdom of God.

Why then does he show him all things which he himself does? Clearly, not that he may know, but that he may judge all things. Something else must also be said, but this is true: he shows him all things not that he may know, but that he may judge. For he does not wish to do anything unless it first pleases his Son before he does it.

What then? Is the Father demeaned here, as though awaiting the Son’s judgment upon his works? Far from it. Rather, exceedingly great praise is attributed to him. For who would not judge praiseworthy a wise man who, when a good will suggests a work to be done, or good zeal urges him to undertake it, sits with himself and considers in his mind or reason the work which he knows he is preparing—considering toward what end or fruit he does it [Col. 0407C]? Indeed, even after he has done something which he wishes to be exact or irreproachable, he sometimes brings it again before his own judgment, so that he may bring it to perfection if he finds anything lacking.

But what is the Son of the Father except his wisdom, which, as was said above, was present when he prepared the heavens, composing all things with him? Therefore the Father rightly and praiseworthily shows the Son all things which he does. This must certainly be understood in no other way than the saying of Scripture elsewhere in praise of him: “You have made all things in wisdom” (Ps. 103).

The finger of God expressly sets forth this showing through Moses, the writer of the Law, at the beginning of the book of Genesis [Col. 0408A]. For God first makes each work, then sees each one, and judges of each that it is good. Thus the Father works in his own person; in his Son, who is his wisdom, he sees each thing; and, delighting in his good will—that is, in the Holy Spirit—he says: “It is good.”

Now, although all things shown to his wisdom, that is, to the Son, are pleasing, and the works of the individual days are judged good, in the work of the second day alone there is silence—namely, where the waters above are divided from those below. Above all, the preceding statement, “and he divided the light and the darkness” (Gen. 1), is excluded from the praise of goodness. For before it says, “and he divided the light and the darkness,” the praise of the light alone is set beforehand, Scripture saying: “And God saw the light, that it was good.” Then, without an accompanying praise, it adds: “and he divided the light and the darkness” (ibid.) [Col. 0408B].

Finally, in this visible work of the world’s construction, when God divided light from darkness or waters from waters, he had in view the losses of the invisible homeland, where evil angels, by sinning, became darkness and were divided from the light—that is, from the good angels—and the hostile multitudes were divided by the eternal firmament from the multitude of angels remaining in the heights, just as these elemental waters are divided. That division of waters and that division of visible light and darkness are images of this division.

Accordingly, although the wisdom of God judged good the other things which the Father made and showed to it, it was silent concerning this work of division alone, as has been said, because in the division there was no signification of good. Therefore “the Father loves the Son and shows him all things which he himself does,” because he does all things with every diligence of his wisdom, for the Son’s honor, and orders all things according to his good pleasure.

Yet it should be noticed that he did not say of past time, “and he showed him all things which he had done.” If he had said this, he would be thought to have spoken only of the aforementioned creation, that he showed those things to the Son then, when he created them to exist. But he uses the present tense: “he shows him all things which he does” [Col. 0408C]. We should certainly not suppose that he said this without weighty significance relevant to the present time.

For what is his Father doing now, while the incarnate Son says these things? He is surely bringing about the restoration of all things in heaven and on earth. Through whom, except through the Son himself? God set him forth, as the Apostle says, “to restore in Christ, in the dispensation [or arrangement] of the fullness of times, all things which are in heaven and which are on earth in him” (Eph. 1).

How then does he not show the Son this very work, which he does only through him? How does he not show him our salvation, which he purposed to accomplish through his obedience? Is not giving a command concerning things to be done the same as showing the things to be done? Certainly we do not think that grammarians, orators, or dialecticians can dispute, in accordance with the ordinary meaning of speech, that every instruction is a showing. For we customarily call instructors in the arts “demonstrators” [Col. 0408D].

Much more, therefore, do we say that one who gives commands shows. Everyone who commands or gives an order surely shows; but not conversely: not everyone who shows something gives a precept or command. But the Lord himself says elsewhere: “And as the Father gave me commandment, so I do” (John 14). When he said this, he was surely going to his passion, by which “all things in heaven and on earth in him” were to be restored—namely, the ruin of the angels in heaven through human beings, who are first restored on earth.

Therefore it is rightly and properly said, even according to ordinary speech: “The Father loves the Son and shows him all things which he himself does.” This is no other than to say: through the Son’s obedience he accomplishes the restoration of all things. He also spoke more honorably and more properly when he said “shows him,” as though he had said, “commands him” or “orders him.” For we customarily command those beneath us and those who owe service by right; but regarding equals, a thing which one of us ought to do is more properly said to be shown than commanded or ordered [Col. 0409A].

But the Son is equal to the Father, because in the Trinity which creates and governs all things there is absolutely nothing unequal. Having explained these matters as far as we can, let us consider what follows.

“And he will show him greater works than these, so that you may marvel.” Because, he says, you marvel wrongly at the things which you now see me doing—crazed by foolishness [for *stulta*, perhaps read *stultitia*], and envious with hostility—and seek to kill me because, at my command, a sick man arose healthy on the Sabbath, took up his bed, and walked. Therefore I say to you: “The Father will show the Son greater works than these, so that you may marvel”—that is, that things worthy of wonder may come about in you.

He will show me, I say, now, and all my own, in the evidence of the event, what he once showed me in foreknowledge. For God showed me concerning my enemies: “Do not kill them, lest my people ever forget.” And I shall answer him: “Scatter them in your power, and cast them down, O Lord, my protector” (Ps. 58) [Col. 0409B]. This, I say, he shows; this he showed; this he commanded me. And I answered and asked thus; and he will show me the effect of the same petition—that is, he will bring it about, with me also acting together with him.

“For whatever he does, these things I too, as I said above, do in like manner.” But now hear the greater works themselves. I told you that the Father will show me, his Son, greater works than those which you now see. And they are truly greater: “For as the Father raises the dead and gives life, so also the Son gives life to whom he wills.”

We cannot grasp by our understanding the greatness of this showing—by which the Father shows the Son how to give life to whom he wills—or its greatness, I say, or burden, at which the Jews, unable to bear it, marvel to their own harm, unless first we know who or what sort of dead persons they are whom the Father raises and gives life, and whom he shows the Son to do likewise.

Does he speak of Lazarus, or of the others whom he raised only to die again? Indeed, it was greater that they should be raised than that the man who had endured his infirmity for thirty-eight years should be healed [Col. 0410A]. But far greater are those things to which the continuation of this reading directs us—things which the Jews cannot fail to know and which, whether they wish it or not, they are compelled to wonder at.

For the whole weight of this burden is turned upon them by two clauses which he placed as follows: in the preceding verse, when he had said, “And he will show him greater works than these,” immediately adding, “so that you may marvel”; and in the following one, when he had said, “So also the Son gives life to whom he wills,” immediately appending this reason: “For the Father judges no one,” etc.

Therefore those whom the Father raises and gives life are to be understood as dead by that death (Rom. 5) which entered the world through sin by the envy of the devil (Wis. 2): the death by which all, through one man, are dead in the soul, mortal and daily dying in the body, and in both are born deserving eternal condemnation (1 Cor. 15) [Col. 0410B].

The elect are saved from this twofold death by the grace of God. The Jews knew that Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, their fathers and leaders, belonged among them. Proud of those fathers’ merits, they believed that life was owed to themselves alone and thought that all Gentiles had no share in it. They were already asserting that this same life had been restored to their fathers and laid up for themselves according to the promises of God the Father, whom they said was “our God,” without knowledge or name of the Son, without whom the Father does nothing—for, as said above, “he shows him all things which he himself does.”

Therefore he says: “For as the Father raises the dead and gives life, so also the Son gives life to whom he wills.” By this saying he strikes both parts of their error: both their belief that their fathers had already been perfected without the necessary operation of the Son, and their belief that they alone belonged to God or to hereditary life [Col. 0410C].

It is as though he said: By the same grace and omnipotence by which the Father called to life the dead, and those born from the heap of the dead, before the manifestation of the Son—for the Father was made known to human beings before the Son—the Son, in this time of his manifestation, calls back to life whom he wills from the same ruined mass of humankind.

Attend to what and how I have spoken. For I did not say, “The Son likewise gives life to the children of Abraham” (Gen. 12), lest I confirm your vain opinion that salvation or life belongs only to Jews. Rather I said: “He gives life to whom he wills”—whether Jews or Gentiles. For just as the Father, before the Son’s manifestation, called whom he willed from the Gentiles, from the Chaldeans—namely, your fathers—to knowledge of himself, with no obligation to do so, so also he called the fathers from the common mass, from the Gentiles condemned in the first parent, to his grace [Col. 0410D].

Nor should it be passed over that those who lived before the coming of the Son are rightly said to have been raised and given life by the Father. For although the Father did not call them without the Son, and although some of them recognized the Father’s Son by the prophetic Spirit, they were nevertheless called by such a calling and instructed by such a law that the Son of God could not thereby be openly recognized and publicly preached.

It should also be noted that of the Father he used two words, “raises” and “gives life”; but of the Son one word only: “gives life.” For the Father did not accomplish the work of salvation in the fathers at the same time that he became known to them. “For,” says the Apostle, “he provided something better for us, so that they should not be perfected without us” (Heb. 11). But the Son, at the very time he became known to the world, began and completed our salvation at the same time [Col. 0411A].

Therefore they are rightly said first to have been raised in blessed hope and afterward, much later, to have been given life in actuality. But we, who live in the fullness of time, are rightly said, and are, simply to have been given life. For at one and the same time we believe and, being regenerated by the Spirit through the remission of sins, receive the life which we lost in Adam.

Therefore, speaking of the Father, he fittingly says: “He raises and gives life.” But of the Son he says only: “And he gives life.” And without any exception of Gentile or Jew, “he gives life,” he says, “to whom he wills”: owing nothing to anyone, but by gratuitous will, or voluntary grace, mercifully calling to life those justly consigned to death. He proves by the reason that follows that he does this no differently from the Father.

“For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son.” Accordingly, he says, the Son does not differ from the Father even in giving life “to whom he wills,” without distinction between Gentile and Jew (Mal. 1), circumcision and uncircumcision. For neither does the Father judge—that is, discern or distinguish—anyone according to descent or flesh [Col. 0411B]. This is especially clear because he called Abraham, while uncircumcised, his friend, and hated Esau although he was circumcised (Rom. 9; Mal. 1).

But what then? “He has given all judgment to the Son,” namely, that the Son may preside both in the present and in the future judgment. In the present judgment, his hidden divinity judges; but in the future, the very form of a servant which he assumed, and which can be seen by evil persons as well as good, will judge openly.

By what, then, are we distinguished before him? What is the law of judgment, or what the decree of this judge and king? It follows: “That all may honor the Son as they honor the Father.” Behold with what gentleness of reasoning the wisdom of God declares the strength of his judgment. He now begins to judge the proud and injurious presumption of the Jews, convicting them of dishonoring their God, whom they thought they greatly honored in the filth of their Sabbaths and other solemn observances—filth which, according to the prophet, was now about to be cast upon their faces (Mal. 2) [Col. 0411C].

“Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him.” Before what assembly of men would this proposition fail to stand, if uttered by a senator or advocate: that the honor of sons concerns the glory of their fathers, and conversely that fathers are injured by insults to their sons? For fathers love their sons, and their affections are stored up in them; hence they feel their honor more sweetly in their sons, and in those same sons receive their injuries more bitterly. Yet these men, while saying that they honored the Father in a temple made by hands through the flesh of bulls which they offered and the blood of goats (Heb. 9), and while proclaiming his Sabbaths, [Col. 0412A] pursued with cruel sacrilege and sought to kill the Son dwelling in the temple of his body not made by hands—especially since they themselves had sent to John and, from the testimony he bore to the truth, knew him to be the Son of God. Although he did not receive testimony from men, he had a testimony greater than John’s, from the works which he himself performed in the name of his Father.

They therefore lied, because not only according to heavenly truth but also according to the common sense and custom of humankind, since they do not honor the Son, they do not honor the Father who sent him. Let them therefore by no means suppose that they belong to God the Father—or even to Abraham himself, whom they falsely claim as their father. Let them not say, “It is enough for us [Col. 0412B] to worship as our fathers worshipped” (John 8), who, worshipping the one God without this Son, were called his friends and received heavenly benefits with many great signs and wonders. Let not falsehood say this in blind pride. For did any of the fathers please God without faith and hope in the seed promised to Abraham, in whom all nations were to be blessed? And what is this seed but Christ? Did not those who had faith in this seed receive in their flesh—the part through which seed itself is naturally transmitted—the sign of circumcision, so that in such a sign they might possess testimony that they professed to await this seed of blessing? But this has already been discussed more fully elsewhere.

Let them therefore not deceive themselves. For the Father will not deliver them [Col. 0412C] from the hand of the Son. Indeed, he gave all judgment to the Son, as the Psalmist testifies when he says: “O God, give your judgment to the king, and your righteousness to the king’s son” (Ps. 71), namely by the stated law which he immediately added: “That all may honor the Son as they honor the Father.” All, I say, who wish to be made alive, who desire to be raised from the heap of the dead. Whoever he may be, Jew or Gentile, if he desires to live, let him diminish nothing and take nothing away from the Son’s entire share in the Father’s honor. Nor let him do this injury to the Father, by saying that he begot something other than that which he himself is who begot it.

For he who commanded “that the earth bring forth green grass bearing seed according to its kind, and a tree producing fruit, each having [Col. 0412D] its own seed according to its species; likewise that man should beget according to his own image and likeness” (Gen. 1)—he, I say, who commanded and established these things, and set a commandment which shall not pass away (Ps. 148)—how can it be said without sacrilege that he alone begot a Son outside his own species or contrary to his own kind? For if, as Arius dared to say with unrestrained mouth, he himself being unchangeable and immutable begot a Son who is changeable or mutable, then surely he produced fruit contrary to his kind or species; nor could he retain in himself that which he powerfully granted to all things that he created.

But since all these utterances of malice and wickedness have long since been exploded—utterances which the ancient persecutor of the Son of God, the devil, father [Col. 0413A] of lies, speaking from his own resources (John 8), whispered into the ears of his most wicked hearers—we ascribe jointly to Father and Son every term denoting honor, grace, and truth, every term denoting true wholeness and perfect charity, together with the truth of the meanings involved. Excepting those things which the necessary distinction of the persons requires to be reserved as proper to each, let each be believed by all the faithful who desire life—believed in the heart unto righteousness and confessed by the mouth unto eternal salvation—as true God and Lord, uncreated, immeasurable, eternal, almighty, without beginning and without end, unchangeable and immutable, with equal honor, equal glory, and undissimilar praise (Rom. 10).

Therefore, when the Father’s will has been accomplished and fulfilled through this honoring of the Son, let us approach with confidence the throne [Col. 0413B] of his grace, that we may receive mercy and find grace for timely help (Heb. 4). We possess the testimony necessary for our salvation: that we are not in agreement with the ancient sinner, who rose up against this Son of God and caused the first human being to rise up in the same presumption. For they did not honor that same Son, who alone is truly the likeness of God the Father and who alone is like the Most High, saying: “We too shall be like the Most High” (Isa. 14).

When Adam transgressed the command with this intention, the one God—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—speaks thus in mournful irony: “Behold, Adam has become as one of us, knowing good and evil” (Gen. 3); that is, truly empty of the truth of knowledge and possessing nothing of true wisdom, because he desired to be wiser than he ought to be. The prophet Ezekiel also reproaches the devil with the same irony: “The gold, the work of your adornment, and your sockets were prepared on the day when you were created. You are an outstretched and protecting cherub” (Ezek. 28), etc. For because he presumed himself to be gold—that is, of divine substance—and because his sockets were prepared, that is, the rational capacity by which he could be capable of God, he preferred falsely to seem gold rather than to be a precious stone; and he preferred to be bound to true gold and to appear a cherub—that is, fullness of knowledge—and to be spread out by himself, as though to propagate them, over spirits of the same substance, rather than to be their equal and praise with them the true Wisdom in whom God [Col. 0413D] does all things.

Therefore, as stated above, it is said to him ironically: “You are a cherub, outstretched and protecting,” although in truth he has become foolish and has lost whatever share of true wisdom he might have had with the others. Thus shortly afterward the same prophet reproaches him: “Your heart was lifted up in your beauty; you destroyed your wisdom through your beauty” (ibid.).

For the devil did not first begin now to detract from this Son of God, when through the mouths of Jews and heretics he spews forth such great blasphemies against him. Rather, from the beginning he was a murderer through the hatred by which he killed the Son of God—and which he fulfilled through the Jews (John 8; 1 John 3)—when he found him in that nature in which he could also commit the crime of murder in act.

Likewise, this command is not now given to human beings for the first time: that all should honor [Col. 0414A] the Son as they honor the Father. For what is it that God said to the first man, “Of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat,” except that, beneath the veil of the letter, God said to the carnal people of the time in which these things were written: “Do not exalt yourself against the Wisdom of God, as the devil exalted himself”? For there was not truly in that tree any power such that, once its fruit was tasted, human beings would possess so great a knowledge as to be “like gods, knowing good and evil”—as is made very clear from the outcome. Rather, the father of lies invented and lied about these things. For their eyes were not opened in such a way that they became “like gods”; rather, their eyes were opened only in this respect: they knew themselves to be naked, that is, stripped of their former honor because they had sought to seize [Col. 0414B] divine honor.

But this too is part of the devil’s blasphemy: he did not say, “You shall be like God,” but, “You shall be like gods” (Gen. 1), namely because of his hatred for the inseparable Trinity. With that hatred he still barks, through the mouths of Jews or heretics, against us who confess God the Father and his Son as God, saying that we worship several gods.

The tree may indeed be understood to have been called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil because, through tasting it in disobedience to the command, man was to have experience not only of good but also of evil. Yet man did not eat in the hope of experiencing evils—that is, of being subject to evils—but in order that, according to the serpent’s promise, he might become like God, from whom nothing good or evil can be hidden. For this reason that tree too was called, ironically, “the tree of the knowledge of good [Col. 0414C] and evil.”

Thus it is not by a new plan that people are now for the first time commanded to honor the Son as they honor the Father. Rather, with a remarkable return upon our humility, the command requiring the honor due to the Son of God is given: that we should bend and subject our understanding to God’s supreme Wisdom. For since man disdained to be subject to God’s Wisdom, which creates heaven and earth, sea and all that is in them (Ps. 145; Prov. 8), and orders all things together with the Father, he is now required by that same Wisdom to subject himself to one born of a woman; and thus to honor one hanging upon the cross as he judges that the Father ought to be honored in his majesty, shining without assumption of flesh or suffering of death. But the reward [Col. 0414D] or benefit of this honoring must be weighed more carefully from what follows. For it is not yet sufficiently clear from what has preceded in what manner—that is, into what kind of life—the Son, equally with the Father, makes the dead alive. Yet this is entirely the recompense for honor bestowed upon the Son of God. Therefore it follows:

“Amen, amen, I say to you: whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life, and shall not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life.” We must receive his word—that is, his teaching—against the lie of the devil mentioned above, as the antidote of the true and best physician against the deadly draught of the serpent and the poison already absorbed into every marrow. For that murderer knew that if man, listening to his counsel, [Col. 0415A] did not believe him who had said, “On whatever day you eat of it, you shall die the death” (Gen. 1), then he would die; and knowing this, he persuaded him to eat and infused into the eater, with the bite of the apple, the poison of eternal death.

This one, on the contrary, knowing that if man turns his ear away from that polluted tongue and from that word of falsehood (Ezek. 5; 1 Pet. 5), and humbly under God’s mighty hand believes him who always speaks truth, he can recover the life which he lost in the first parent, says: “Amen, amen, I say to you: whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life.” Behold what honor the Son of God seeks; behold how he wishes to be honored equally or similarly with the Father. He wishes his word to be heard and God the Father to be believed. For what profit or benefit to himself? None; but [Col. 0415B] so that his hearer may have eternal life. Grace, therefore, labors for humankind.

It should be noted that, as though standing in a contest, he produces two witnesses: himself and the Father, saying, “Whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me.” Elsewhere he speaks of them thus: “Is it not written in your law that the testimony of two men is true?” (Deut. 17). “I am the one who bears testimony concerning myself, and the Father who sent me bears testimony concerning me” (John 8). These two witnesses, I say, he now presents for hearing. He was working and speaking truth according to the Scriptures. In his truthful speech he presented himself; in miraculous works, his Father. Thus elsewhere he says: “The Father abiding in me himself did the works.” And again: “The works which the Father has given me to complete, [Col. 0415C] these bear testimony concerning me, that the Father sent me” (John 14).

Or rather, in the present Gospel he presents himself in the ancient Scriptures, which they could not refute, and invokes God his Father as witness. Thus a little further on he will say: “The works which the Father gave me, these bear testimony concerning me”—works which indeed were performed through himself preaching and rising from the dead, and afterward through his apostles preaching the Gospel. Concerning the Father, however, he immediately adds: “And the Father who sent me himself bore testimony concerning me.” What testimony? “Search the Scriptures,” etc.

Therefore, since he is about to state great matters and expound matters great and necessary—those, namely, of which he had said above, “He will show him greater works than these, that you may marvel”—he very fittingly appoints two adequate witnesses against his opponents and promises a sufficiently great and desirable reward merely for hearing the witnesses. Let the whole world, whose judgment against its prince, to be cast out, is now being conducted, hear with attentive ears of the heart the reasoning of this heavenly rhetorician, lawfully defending himself for our sake. “Whoever,” he says, “hears my word,” that is, hears the Gospel now present, “and believes him who sent me,” namely, believes that God the Father sent me as he promised Abraham and foretold through his prophets—whoever hears what I am about to say and, when the Father, who abiding in me himself performs the works, proves that I have spoken the true Word, believes him and receives me as one to be raised from the dead—[Col. 0416A] that person, whoever he may be, “has eternal life.”

And lest anyone suppose that I mean that he will never lay aside his corruptible flesh, let him know with greater certainty what I have said. What I say is more and better: “he shall not come into judgment,” that is, he shall not incur the condemnation owed to the human race because of Adam’s sin. Let him also know that I have not said that he will not come to judgment. For all except those who did not receive the law will come to judgment, distinguished into three classes: some to be judged and condemned; others to be judged and saved; others not to be judged at all, but to sit as judges and assessors with their Lord; while a fourth portion of humankind—those who, as stated above, sinned without the law—will be condemned without the law. But let him know that I have said this: he shall not come into judgment, that is, he shall not incur the condemnation due under the prior judgment arising from paternal transgression.

But what then? He passes from death into life. Nor do I now say that he will pass from death into life; rather, I say that by hearing my word and believing him who sent me, he already passes from the death of the soul. I do not say “to life,” so that he may stand outside it and behold and greet it from afar, as Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the other fathers who beheld and greeted it from afar and all died without receiving its promises. Rather, I say that he passes into life itself by a brief passage, since this passing is nothing other than being born again of water and the Holy Spirit. For when he is baptized in believing, he has passed over and has been regenerated: new from old (Eph. 4), found from lost, and made living from dead (Luke 15). For although the body is dead—that is, mortal—because of sin, the spirit already lives because of justification (Rom. 8).

But you say: “Who will hear you? Or when will what you say happen? Indeed, which of us needs your hearing, which needs life?” To this I say: “Amen, amen, I say to you that the hour is coming, and now is, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live.” If you are dead—indeed, since you are dead—if you recognized your death, you would be the first to hear among the dead and, by hearing, the first to rise from the death of your souls. But now you say that you live; now it must be cried out to other dead people, that they may hear. And this will be wonderful: those who descended more deeply into death because, withdrawing farther from the living God, they worshipped dead gods, will live when they hear; and awakened by one and the same hearing, they will escape the eternal death both of original sin and of all actual sins, and from so distant an abyss of death, by confessing one brief word of faith, they will leap into the citadel of salvation, into the midst of life.

I now speak of such dead persons; I now speak of this passage of theirs into life. Otherwise, if I were speaking universally of the universal resurrection of the dead, I would have said, “All the dead shall hear,” and I would not have so limited it by saying, “Those who hear shall live.” For it is not within their choice to hear and live; rather, by a necessity coming from above, all will hear and rise. But now not all [Col. 0417A] will hear, “for faith does not belong to all” (2 Thess. 3); yet many will hear, “and those who hear will live.” “That hour has already come and now is.” Formerly the Father, speaking in the prophets, said, “It will come”; now, speaking in his Son, he says, “It has come and now is.”

They will hear the voice of the Son of God, but they will not see the form of the servant, the form of the Son of Man. They will hear, I say, not merely the Father’s voice or the voice of God, but “the voice of the Son of God,” that is, the voice simultaneously of the Father and of the Son of God. Therefore I have rightly now said, “the voice of the Son of God,” although elsewhere I customarily call myself the Son of Man; for I shall go to them not according to man, but according to divine majesty present everywhere. And they will believe not merely in God but in me, the Son of God, and thus, hearing the Word of God, “as [Col. 0417B] stated above, they will live.”

“For as the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son also to have life in himself. And he gave him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man.” The meaning of this passage, most lucid in itself, darkens the perverse minds of heretics just as the sun, the more brilliant it is, striking foul eyes and the decayed eyelids of the bleary-eyed, almost blinds them. For what more beautiful or delightful reasoning can shine upon healthy eyes than this, where the power of the Son of God to make the dead alive, having been set forth, is accompanied by such a brief argument? For once this has been carefully perceived, it is also clear how reasonably the Father gave all judgment to the Son.

But the heretic, blinded by the dust of malice, when he reads that the Father gave the Son to have life in himself [Col. 0417C] and gave him authority to execute judgment, says: “How is the Son equal to the Father, when he would not live unless the Father gave him life, and would not judge unless the Father gave him authority and granted him judgment?” One who says this is plainly ignorant of the matter under discussion. He does not know at all the chief point of the intention, nor does he see the body of the whole argument, whose limbs he seeks violently to tear apart.

If you ask him how the Father is said to have life in himself, when he himself is life, he will certainly be able to give no satisfactory answer; and accordingly he will be convicted by his own judgment of not understanding, consequently, how the Father gave the Son to have that same life in himself. Therefore, in order to elucidate the present statement, we must approach it with the aid of the divine reasoning from which it has been drawn: “For as the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son also to have life in himself.” The eye of our consideration must by no means overlook how [Col. 0417D] carefully the features of the text are joined together, since he does not say simply, “As the Father has life in himself.” This plainly indicates to us that this knowledge is consequential upon the preceding statement and is reasonably appended as its proof—a practice especially common among rhetoricians.

The preceding statement was this: “Amen, amen, I say to you that the hour is coming, and now is, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live.” Indeed, in response to this proposition his hearers—or rather his adversaries—could rage because he had not said, “The dead will hear the voice of God,” but, with a careful distinction of persons, “They will hear the voice of the Son of God.” But his point was to prove that the life of the dead depends no less upon the Son than upon the Father, and that no one can be raised unless he honors the Son equally with the Father. This, I say, was his intention—not how the Father himself lived or how he gave life to the Son. To suppose this even in the present statement, where he says, “For as the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son also to have life in himself,” is foolish and erroneous. For the discourse is not about the life of God, who is life to himself; nor about the giving of life to the Son of God, who is equally life to himself; but about the raising and making alive of the dead.

Therefore, when he had said, “The dead will hear the voice [Col. 0418B] of the Son of God,” thus declaring that the voice of the Son, equally with that of the Father, is necessary for making the dead alive, he reasonably added: “For as the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son also to have life in himself.” As though he said: “For this reason I said, ‘The dead will hear the voice of the Son of God’—a phrase in which the distinction between the persons of Father and Son is clear—because, as the Father has life in himself, namely the life of human beings, that is, the effective power or operation of the life of dead human beings, and does not seek it elsewhere nor possess it anywhere except in himself, so he gave the Son to have life in himself”: that is, he laid upon him the greatest share of the same operation, so that he too might make the dead alive in himself. This is not as with Paul, Cephas, or Apollos: although they were granted life, that is, the ability to make the dead alive, none of them was granted to have that same life in himself. Nor can anyone make another alive through the office of life entrusted to him except with God cooperating. Paul expresses this by an analogy: “I planted,” he says, “Apollos watered, but God gave the increase” (2 Cor. 3).

The Son, therefore, is equal to the Father, to whom the Father gave life in himself, that is, whom he sent to make the dead alive from himself. And because he imposed much labor upon him, and the person of the Son labored more in making the dead alive—for “he is the Son of Man,” that is, the Son of God alone became man in his own person—therefore he also gave him authority to execute judgment. [Col. 0418D] For when God made man, not ignorant but perfectly aware that he would die by sinning, the blessed Trinity so apportioned the work concerning this same man among itself that the Father should create, the Son redeem, and the Holy Spirit enkindle.

For not without great counsel—this must be said with the utmost reverence—did the Holy Trinity deem it worthy to make man, assigning to each person its proper share in the work, although the inseparable Trinity works inseparably both in the formation and redemption and in the instruction or illumination of human substance. We ought to understand this distribution in what was said in the counsel of the indivisible Trinity: “Let us make man according to our image and likeness” (Gen. 1; Ps. 103).

The Father’s proper work was the first creation of man, which share of the work he assumed; yet never without the cooperation of the Son, since he made man, as also all things, through Wisdom, who is here the Son of God; nor without the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, since through him he breathed into the face of man’s heart the breath of life (Gen. 2), so that man might be created not only in the image of God—that is, eternal or rational—but also in the likeness of God, that is, with that by which he might be like God or an imitator of God’s goodness.

But the redemption of man, the ministry of which the Father gave to the Son, is the proper work of this same Son of God. For the Son alone was incarnate or made man in his own person; he alone suffered, died, and rose again for the redemption of man, though both the Father and the Holy Spirit cooperated. For the Father sent him from his hidden places into the Virgin’s womb, and the same Virgin conceived him of the Holy Spirit, that is, by the operation of the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit, or his proper operation, will have to be discussed elsewhere in this Gospel.

This distribution of the life of human beings is what is to be understood here: this life, namely, which “as the Father has in himself,” the Son likewise has in himself, needing no one. This is plainly indicated by the words of sacred Scripture. For when it is said that “God formed man from the clay of the earth,” and then added, “and breathed into his face the breath of life” (Gen. 2), what else is indicated except that he made the substance of man from something other than himself, but, possessing good and blessed life in himself, breathed it from himself into the face of man’s heart? But when the Son, redeeming man, poured out from himself the sacraments of his salvation and life—that is, blood and water—and, restored to life, breathed upon the faces of his disciples (John 9), did he not powerfully show that he too has our life in himself?

Therefore, because our life, which is hidden with Christ in God (Col. 3), was restored whole by the Son after the death which had entered the world through the devil’s envy (Wis. 2), just as it had been established by the Father before that death; and because this happened through the Father’s giving—that is, commanding—as the Son says elsewhere: “As the Father gave me commandment, so I do”—it is rightly now said: “As the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son also to have life in himself.”

And because the Son, in his own person, redeemed man through greater works, not without the injury of cross and death—he whose clay he himself assumed, deigning to become man (John 14)—because, I say, he performed a greater work in obediently enduring these things than the Father did in forming man from clay, it is rightly now added: “And he gave him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man.” Hence he is called heir, not of a dead Father but of a dead inheritance. Since it had perished to God the Father, the Son, restoring it to life, possesses it anew; and that inheritance is rightly called and is his, because it was restored at the cost of his life.

But when he says, “And he gave him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man,” [Col. 0420A] the Father’s sovereignty is not diminished in the least. Indeed, authority to judge given to the Son redounds to the Father’s honor, since the Son, by judging, will hand over the kingdom, as the Apostle says (1 Cor. 15), that is, acquire it for God and the Father: first, when the judgment of the world has been carried out, by which the prince of this world is cast out, the Son triumphing over him through his death (John 12); then, when the final judgment has been completed, after which will be the end, as the same Apostle says, when he has handed over and acquired the kingdom for God and the Father (John 21). Then the Son himself will be subject to him who subjected all things to him, so that God may be all in all: subject, I say, not in servile subjection but in inseparable love; not by a difference of nature but in the unity of indivisible charity; inferior indeed according to the nature of man, equal according to the nature of God, and thus always to be honored, as is the Father, with the glory and honor of everlasting dominion.

Of this final judgment he immediately adds:

“Do not marvel at this, because the hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice. And those who have done good will come forth to the resurrection of life; but those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgment.” “Do not marvel at this,” he says, because your amazement is not good. For you do not marvel at these things as words of life and power, but as the madness of one possessed by a demon. Do not marvel, therefore, because these things are small in comparison with the greater things which you will see, that you may marvel, that when you see them you may be disturbed by dreadful fear and astonishment (Wis. 5), and that, according to the prophet, you may see the fire devour the enemies of the Lord’s hand (Isa. 26).

It is indeed great that that hour has come and now is—the hour which many kings and prophets desired to see but did not see (Luke 10). Great, I say, and wonderful it is that the dead hear the voice of the Son of God and live. This is great; but much greater is the coming of the hour of which I do not say, “Now is,” but only say, “It is coming”: that is, it already threatens and draws near and will without doubt occur, “in which all who are in the tombs”—all, I say, dead or living, that is, sinners or righteous—who lie buried in tombs and whose bodies, dissolved or dry, have returned to their dust, “will hear his voice,” in the command of his imperial majesty, in the voice of the archangel and the trumpet of God descending from heaven (1 Thess. 4), with the powers of heaven shaken (Matt. 24), the hinges of heaven and earth convulsed, [Col. 0420D] and with him visibly coming, fire blazing before him and a mighty tempest around him, calling heaven from above and earth to discern his people (Ps. 49).

What then? Will those dead persons who now refuse to hear the voice of the Son of God and live—that is, to rise from the death of the soul through faith, the washing of regeneration, and the invocation of the Holy Spirit (Titus 3; Eph. 4)—then fail to hear his voice, or, because they would refuse to rise, fail to rise? It is not so. Rather, all, unwilling as well as willing, including those longing for that hour and possessing confidence on the day [Col. 0421A] of judgment, will rise and come forth.

A little earlier, when I spoke of the first resurrection, that is, of the conversion of sinners, I did not merely say, “The hour is coming,” but added, “and now is”; likewise, I did not say, “All the dead will hear,” but only, “The dead will hear the voice of the Son of God and will live.” For now not all the dead hear me; not all wish to rise from unbelief to faith, from wickedness to righteousness. And because they do not wish to do so, they do not rise. But now, when I speak of the second resurrection (2 Cor. 5), I say universally that “all will hear the voice of the Son of God, and all who are in the tombs” will come forth.

Those who have done good will come forth to the resurrection of life, because now, having heard the first [Col. 0421B] voice—that is, having received the first coming of the Son of God—they begin to live by the first resurrection; and then they will attain the reality or manifestation of that life in whose hope they now walk by faith. But those who have done evil will come forth to the resurrection of judgment, that is, condemnation, in order to receive the sentence of condemnation, by the same justice and truth by which they were previously condemned in Adam, because they refuse, while there is time, to hear the first voice of the Son of God now inviting them to spring back through faith from that inherited death. It follows:

“I can do nothing of myself. As I hear, I judge; and my judgment is true, because I do not seek my own will, but the will of him who sent me.” Here it seems necessary to take pains to bring the distinct parts of this confirmation or refutation closer before the reader’s eyes, like the clearly distinguished features of a most beautiful body. For behold, he has returned to the beginning and binds together the parts of the argument in one conclusion, when he says: “I can do nothing of myself.” For at the beginning of this defense he had also said: “The Son can do nothing of himself.”

Therefore, so that the whole body of the text and the view of its meanings or intention may be clearer, it should not be passed over that what industrious rhetoricians usually labor to achieve and scarcely attain when they have found a rich subject worthy of every amplification, eloquence—the companion and handmaid of heavenly Wisdom—freely supplies in this present discourse against those vigorous defenders of the Sabbaths and accusers of salvation. Yet it does so so veiled by the majesty of the matters under discussion that it scarcely appears. For the faculty of eloquence does not adorn divine matters in the same manner as it does human affairs, where that pompous and artful mistress displays herself; especially when Wisdom itself, coeternal with God, speaks through itself to those who seem eloquent to themselves and deigns to weave together human words.

Human matters, thin and slight and sometimes obscure or shameful, are illuminated or somehow concealed by brilliant expression; but divine matters, great and flashing with light, conceal any eloquence, however beautiful, beneath their own splendors. Yet, wherever the subject requires it, eloquence is found so strongly equipped that every human eloquence appears mute or foolish when it encounters it.

Consider, therefore, that in the present matter, while he refutes his adversaries by establishing the case, he shows why he ought not to be bound by the law of the Sabbaths, and confirms that he most rightly added, after saying, “My Father works until now,” “and I work.” For he has produced a most complete argument, that is, one perfect in five parts: proposition, reason, confirmation, embellishment, and conclusion.

The proposition is that in which he said: “Amen, amen, I say to you, the Son cannot do anything of himself, unless he sees the Father doing it.” The reason is the statement immediately added: “For whatever things he does, these the Son likewise does.” The confirmation is that which follows at once: “For the Father loves the Son and shows him all things which he himself does.” The embellishment extends from his saying, “and he will show him greater works than these, so that you may wonder,” to the point most recently treated: “But those who have done evil, unto the resurrection of judgment.” This embellishment, I say, is not so much one of words as of matters, not so much of propositions as of heavenly lightnings: it contains no studied elegance, but is wholly terrible and full of divine awe. But the statement in which he says, “I cannot do anything of myself; as I hear, I judge, and my judgment is true, because I seek not my own will, but the will of him who sent me,” is the conclusion of the foregoing parts, briefly gathering again those same parts for the understanding of the teachable, attentive, and well-disposed hearer for whom he knew these things were to be spoken or written.

As though he said: If, then, I do nothing except what I see the Father doing; if whatever he does, I likewise do; if, finally, the Father shows the Son all things which he himself does; and if indeed “he will show him greater works than these, so that you may wonder”—namely, so that “as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so the Son also gives life to whom he wills,” and the rest; and if he knows him to be so utterly unchangeable and immutable that he has given him all judgment, and has demonstrated that it will be safe for his commonwealth to give him authority to execute judgment: then, I say, it is now true, credible, and worthy of faith that, as I said in the first proposition, so now again I say: “I cannot do anything of myself”—that is, apart from God, separately from the true God, with my own will by itself divided from the will of God the Father—“I cannot do anything,” as the apostate angel or the first transgressing man could do and did, since each was a creature and therefore mutable: a made thing, and consequently changeable.

For whether angel or man, so long as he admits any accident while turned away from the essential Good, so long does he act from himself. For example, when he calls evil good and good evil; when he judges unjustly, condemning the righteous and justifying the ungodly—whence does he do these things but from himself, when the essence of things is otherwise? (Isa. V.) And such things, indeed, and others of the same kind, a man, if he is greatly righteous, does not wish to do although he can; but if he is only slightly righteous, or is only now first disposed toward righteousness and has not yet put on the habit of that same righteousness—if, I say, he is only slightly righteous—he does not dare to do them. But God, just as he is subject to no vice and no accidents whatsoever, so, being supremely righteous, cannot at all do such a thing.

Therefore, when I say, “I cannot do anything of myself,” it is as though I said: I cannot do anything unjust; I cannot overturn or subvert judgment. But what then? “As I hear, I judge”; that is, I judge according to the merit of the cause to be judged, or according to the essence of the thing judged; and therefore, since in judging I do nothing from myself, my judgment is true. That is, when, as I have said, I exercise judgment, those will come forth from the tombs: “those who have done good, unto the resurrection of life; but those who have done evil, unto the resurrection of judgment.”

Therefore whoever does good, whether Jew or Gentile, need not fear that, when I judge, anything proceeding from myself will bring him to the resurrection of judgment. And whoever does evil, whether Jew or Gentile, should likewise not deceive himself with empty hope that, when I do anything from myself, he will proceed unto the resurrection of life, “because I seek not my own will, but the will of him who sent me.” Thus now, when I see the wretched city Jerusalem and weep over it with human feeling (Luke XVI), I nevertheless do not seek my own will, that evil days may be turned away from it because of my tears; rather, “as I hear, I judge.” For their cry, more vehement than the cry of the Sodomites (Gen. XVIII; Matt. XI), has ascended to me; and therefore I attend more to what justice requires than to what my human affection desires or laments. So, in that coming forth of the dead from the tombs, I shall not seek my own will, but the will of him who sent me: that is, I do not follow the condescension of human nature, but maintain the rectitude of divine justice.

Therefore, in the minds of those who read or hear this Gospel lesson wisely, falsehood is refuted and truth confirmed. Hence reason agrees and faith judges that, since the Father works until now, being bound by no law of Sabbaths, the Son also works freely and powerfully, who cannot do anything from himself and cannot admit anything evil or unjust.

One thing yet remains for the great oratorical wisdom of God, which makes words for us and on our account, and on our account sets art against art, so that the truth of faith may have a sound discourse not without art against the loquacity of skilful falsehood. One thing, I say, yet remains: the conclusion or epilogue, which immediately follows by amplification of the matter, for the illustration of truth and the enlargement of the Jewish accusation:

“If I bear witness concerning myself, my witness is not true. There is another who bears witness concerning me.” For this, and the other supports of this truth which follow, are chiefly drawn from authority. By them he recalls that the defense or testimony concerning him was and is the concern of God the Father: who testified concerning him before he came, by the testimony of the Scriptures—that is, of the Law and the Prophets—and who now commends and defends him in his presence through the manifest testimonies of miraculous works. At the same time he displays the dreadful crime of the Jews, who did not receive him when he came in his Father’s name, but will receive another coming in his own name.

He says therefore: “If I bear witness concerning myself, my witness is not true.” As though he said: Behold, you have heard all things openly. In speaking these words among you, and saying them that you may be saved, I have not sought, after the manner of you or other men, to win your goodwill or favour by polished speech. Rather, having displayed a work of true virtue, worthy of the goodwill of all men—namely, by healing the whole man from his long-standing infirmity—I sought a hearing. Knowing what sort you were likely to be as hearers, I stated my case not only for your sake but for the sake of those who would hear. “My Father works until now, and I work”; and, dividing the same case, I defended by both the customary strength of human argument and heavenly truth precisely the point at issue: namely, that it is as lawful for me as for the Father to work on the Sabbath.

Now examine lawfully—that is, as the Law commands—the words of this testimony. “If I bear witness concerning myself,” that is, if I come from myself; if I do not come and speak in the name of the Lord, but alone defend myself by my own sole testimony, “my witness is not true”: that is, the words I speak will not have effect; and then, as the Law says, you shall have this sign, that the Lord has not spoken the word which I speak (Deut. XVIII). But it is not so, nor will it be. “There is another who bears witness concerning me”: namely God the Father, the very one of whom I now say to you, “My Father works until now, and I work.” Another, I say—that is, another person of the same substance as I am. Otherwise “another” would not be rightly said; for one and another are not said of individual things of diverse and unequal substances, but “this one” and “this other.” I say that he is another so that, amid a plurality of persons, both unity of substance and plurality of persons may be understood.

That other bears witness concerning me. “And I know that the witness which he bears concerning me is true.” I know, I say; and I bear witness to the one bearing witness concerning me, because he is a truthful witness and testifies truly concerning me. For I am not like other men, of whom no one knows whether he is worthy of love or hatred (Eccl. IX), and for whom all things in the future are reserved as uncertain. Indeed, even if they have received the Spirit of adoption as sons (Rom. VIII), and the Spirit himself bears witness to their spirit that they are children of God, that witness ought to be called not so much true or just as gratuitous and unmerited; for it belongs not to debt but to grace, not to justice but to mercy. It is not the testimony of equals, but a memorial of condescending graciousness.

“But I” was not “conceived in iniquities”—“for” my mother did not “conceive me in sins” (Ps. L); “nor can I do anything of myself, unless I see the Father doing it. Therefore the witness which he bears concerning me is true, just, and due; indeed, it is the witness of equals and therefore lawful. But I have not yet openly said who that other is.

“You sent to John, and he bore witness to the truth.” Perhaps, therefore, you now think that he is the other of whom I have spoken: that I have no testimony from one greater than he. “But I do not receive testimony from men; yet I say these things that you may be saved.” Mark what I say: “I do not receive testimony from men.” What then? Do I say this because I wish to close the mouths of men who bear witness? Do I scorn my angel, sent before my face in order to prepare my way by his testimony? (Mal. III; Mark I.) It is not so. Rather, attend carefully to what I say.

I do not say that I do not receive the testimony of a man, or testimony borne through men; rather, I say, “I do not receive testimony from men.” For the testimony of good and truthful men is not from the men themselves but from God; though borne through men, it is God’s testimony. For what is it to receive testimony from men, or according to men, except to seek praise which has not proceeded from God but has arisen and been fashioned from men?

This testimony of John, when you sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to him to ask him, “Who are you?” (John I), was indeed John’s testimony; but it was not from John: that is, it was uttered through John, but communicated to John by God. Therefore I say: “And I do not receive testimony from men, but I say these things that you may be saved”; that is, I say not for my own glory who my other witness is, but for your salvation, that by believing God’s testimony you may be saved.

It is like the case of a righteous man, free from all hypocrisy, who says: “If your eye is single, your whole body will be full of light” (Matt. VI). I shall not do my righteousness before men in order to be seen by them; but my light shines before men so that they may see my good works and glorify God the Father who is in heaven (Matt. V). Otherwise I should be like you, whose whole Judaism is in the flesh, and whose entire circumcision is manifest in the flesh, whose praise is not from God but from men.

“But cursed,” says the prophet, “is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his arm, so that his heart departs from the Lord. For he shall be like the tamarisk in the desert” (Jer. XVII): namely, trees whose name derives from bitterness and which grow in solitude. He shall be like tamarisks—that is, deprived of the sweetness of divine goodness, cast far outside the fellowship of holy men; he shall not see when good comes, but shall dwell in solitude in the wilderness, in a land of saltness and uninhabitable. This dryness and saltness are far from me. For I, ever green in inhabitable charity and fruitful truth, say these things “that you may be saved”; that is, that you may be saved by believing. Employing a lawful defense, I bring before you, in the public hearing of the whole world, him who bears witness concerning me.

Therefore, as I have already begun, I shall persist in that kind of discourse which is still strongest among you and among other men, making, as it were, a syllogism—that is, an argumentative and indissoluble discourse of truth. And that, furnished with a convincing argument, you may know that “I do not receive testimony from men,” because “I do not receive glory from men,” but bring forward my testimony or my witness for this sole purpose, that by believing you may be saved—not so that you men may hasten to enthrone me upon the seat of your kings—behold, I say to you: “You sent to John, and he bore witness to the truth.”

He was held in such esteem among you that you judged it fitting to consult him, as though you really intended to receive his testimony and would undoubtedly believe whatever he said. Therefore I shall now begin to confront you with that judgment of yours, so that, if you do not believe, you may be without excuse. I say then: “He was a burning and shining lamp.” Truly, it was right to send to him to whom you sent; and by his testimony the present face of truth was to be sought and recognized without doubt. For he was great, and among those born of women none greater than he had arisen (Matt. XI).

Yet his great greatness is from that one who bears witness concerning me, just as an earthen lamp in the darkness of night is illumined for the purpose of finding a road to be followed or an action to be done, through participation in a fiery substance. For as a clay lamp does not shine by its own nature, but receives flame from elsewhere in order to be a lamp, so John was not that other “who bears witness concerning me,” but was sent by him, carrying in his heart, made flaming, and in his bright mouth the words of that same testimony. Thus “he was a lamp,” not the light itself or the substance of the light itself: “a lamp,” I say, “burning and shining”—burning inwardly with love for the truth to be testified, shining outwardly in word and work, so long as the children of darkness permitted him, who have now hidden such a lamp within the confines of a dark prison.

For by his public proclamation of virtue, shining, he invited you to true and eternal rejoicing. “But you were willing to rejoice for an hour in his light.” This at least cannot be denied; this must be conceded: that he was great and bright with faithful speech; that, by your own estimation also, his testimony and baptism were from heaven, not from men. But I rebuke you in this—for I do not pass over your vices in eagerness to gain your goodwill or favour, in order to draw you into agreement with the true testimony—I rebuke you, I say, because, while this lamp invited you to the eternal glory of the kingdom to come, “you were willing rather to rejoice for an hour in his light”: that is, to seize beforehand the temporal happiness of the present kingdom, hoping in a carnal sense that the kingdom of Christ—whom you thought John to be, or at least Elijah, Christ’s forerunner—would be earthly.

Yet whatever your opinion of Christ may be, or whatever rejoicing you may have wished to express toward such a lamp, for the present it is of no concern to me. This point which I have put forward must be granted by you, because it cannot be refuted: since, as I have said, you sent to him, he was certainly held great even in your judgment; and you cannot reasonably judge that one whom you deemed worthy to consult was unworthy of hearing when he answered.

“But I have a greater testimony than John.” The whole palm of victory in this assumption of mine consists in this: when the supports of the arguments have made a contentious hearer either yield or fall silent, I shall immediately conclude by saying: “Because I do not receive glory from men.” This is nothing other than what I said above and began to prove: “Because I do not receive testimony from men”; for I have no need of it.

Therefore I say, intending to prove it by the following reason: “Because I have a greater testimony than John”—“For the works which the Father has given me to complete, the very works which I do in the name of my Father, bear witness concerning me that the Father has sent me.” The Father, who, as I said above, gave the Son to have life in himself as he himself has life in himself, gave to me, the same Son, certain works to complete: works already begun, namely, which, when they have been completed, the deaf will hear and the blind will see (Luke XVIII), if you refuse to hear and see; and the stones will cry out if you refuse to speak (Luke XIX; Ps. X).

What are those works? They are surely great and exquisite works, extending to all the wills of my Father: the work of incarnation; the work of birth; the work of miracles, which I have done among you and which no one else has done; the work of the Passion; the work of resurrection; the work of my ascension and the outpouring of the Holy Spirit. When I have completed all these things, you will not be able to hide them, while the heavens declare this glory of God and the firmament proclaims these works of my hands, so that there are no “speeches nor words whose voices are not heard; their sound goes out into all the earth and their words unto the ends of the world” (Ps. XVIII).

While I do these works in the name of my Father—that is, in the confession that I am the Son of God and that God is my Father—I have true and lawful testimony that he really is, as I say, my Father. Nor will you, in despising me, have any suitable or lawful excuse when whatever word I speak comes to pass in accordance with what I profess in the name of the Lord. Further: “And the Father who sent me, he himself has borne witness concerning me.” When or where he bore witness concerning me, I shall say a little later. First I must describe the person of that Father, set forth the dignity of the witness, and only then explain the antiquity or constancy of the testimony.

For he of whom I speak is not my father Joseph, whom you call my father, whom you could see as a man, whose voice you could hear and make little of (Luke III, IV). But what? “You have neither ever heard his voice nor seen his form.” Behold how much greater he is than John. For you could both hear John’s voice and see his form, as that of a mortal and corruptible man: an articulated voice, formed in the air by the plectrum of the tongue; a circumscribed and visible form; and, apart from the harsh roughness of his desert clothing, almost in nothing unlike yourselves.

But that Father of mine has neither an elemental voice nor a circumscribed or visible form (Exod. XXXIII). For God is not man; he is spirit, not flesh. Even if the patriarchs or prophets heard his voice, and even if some of them saw God face to face (Num. XII), they could never see him in his substance; they never heard his own proper voice or speech except in the mind. Such a one has borne witness concerning me.

“And you do not have his word abiding in you, because you do not believe him whom he sent.” In this lies your guilt; in this your sin remains: because “you do not have his word abiding in you.” This is clear because “you do not believe him whom he sent.” For although “you have neither ever heard his voice nor seen his form,” nevertheless you have heard his word, received his Law, and had prophets sent by him. Reading those prophets, you honour with your lips him of whom I speak—the one who sent them, who spoke through them, and gave the Law—but your heart is far from him (Matt. XV; Mark VII).

For you utter his words with your mouth, but have not written them, as it were, in the book of your heart (Isa. XXIX). Therefore I say that you do not have his word in you—that is, inwardly, in the book of your heart, in the inner faculties of your soul. The evident proof of this is that “you do not believe him whom he sent.” Him, I say—not another, but him; that is, me who am now present, who once spoke with him in the Law and the Prophets and, behold, am here. For I am he whom he sent: not that I might become what I was not, but that I might become visible though I was invisible equally with him; that I might assume a body though I was incorporeal; that I might become man though I was God. Yet “you do not believe him.”

Do not therefore think that you have his Word abiding in you while you defend your Sabbaths against me, having in your hearts the corruption of laborious iniquity. You are therefore like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful to the eyes of those who see them but inwardly are full of dead men’s bones (Matt. XXIII). For as those tombs can be beautiful outwardly and yet within full of corruption, so you can refrain from work on your Sabbaths, recite the entire Law of Moses with your mouths, and yet not have the Word of God abiding in you.

Behold, I have told you who “that other is who bears witness concerning me”: greater indeed than man, incomparably greater than John. You now say to me: When, or what testimony, did he bear concerning you? To this I say: “Search the Scriptures, because you think that in them you have eternal life. And they are those which bear witness concerning me; and you are unwilling to come to me that you may have life.”
