O deaf and blind men, who are led in order to hear and see, and who, sitting in synagogues where that testimony resounds every Sabbath, touch with your hands the passing clouds but do not hear their thunder, and do not see the flashing lightnings that run through them (Isa. IX). Why do you carry the great scroll of the Law on an idle neck and smooth the beautiful codices of the prophets with delicate hands? You do not wish to look within; you do not wish to hear. Indeed, you say to those who see, “Do not see,” and to those who hear, “Do not understand” (Ps. XXXV).

O men liable to judgment, to the heavenly council, to the fire of Gehenna (Matt. V), “search the Scriptures,” false and deceiving men; “because you think that in them you have eternal life”: that is, you think this sufficient for life, that by reading them with your lips you honour God with an alien heart. It is not so. Rather, search them; consult them; seek their will; attend to their intention; hear and see upon what condition, by what way, and under what guide they promise you life. They answer you: “And they are those which bear witness concerning me”; indeed, they themselves are the testimonies which the Father bears concerning me.

But why do I tell you to search them? You have long since searched them and disdain to hear me as your instructor, since among yourselves there are teachers sitting upon Moses’ seat, who have searched the Scriptures most thoroughly, so that not one iota or one point of the whole Law has escaped them, whereby they may hunt their own profits—whether mint, dill, or cumin is to be tithed (Matt. XXIII). You are not so blind as to have no eyes, nor so deaf as to have no ears. Therefore I said through the prophet—and shortly I shall say the same prophecy through the things themselves—“Bring forth the blind people who have eyes, and the deaf who have ears” (Isa. XLIII).

You have therefore searched the Scriptures and know this: “that they bear witness concerning me, and you are unwilling to come to me that you may have life.” O Pharisees, truly, according to your name, separators—but evil separators—who strain out a gnat and swallow a camel: how do you think that you have life in the Scriptures, when you expend all your care upon the petty details of profit-making righteousness, namely tithing mint and dill (Matt. XXIII), enlarging phylacteries and magnifying fringes? Trusting in these things as though you could live from them, you refuse to come to me, the burden-bearing camel, so that, while I carry the dead flesh of your sins, you may have life.

Ungodly and blind men, deserters of life and salvation: where these two things stand—first, that “they,” namely the Scriptures, “are those which bear witness concerning me”; and second, “that you are unwilling to come to me that you may have life”—how can the third stand, namely that you have eternal life in them, as you think? Deaf men, hear; blind men, look in order to see. Otherwise I shall cry to these stones, and they, hearing and seeing, will answer. And I shall say to them: Since these sons of Abraham are silent, at least do you, O stones, cry out; speak righteousness; judge uprightly, so that sons of Abraham may be raised up from you (Luke III; Matt. III). Speak, I say.

Those Scriptures in which these men think they have eternal life “are those which bear witness concerning me.” And if they pretend not to know this, the murderous sacrilege of Herod will convict them: when he sought me in order to destroy me, they showed him the place of my birth, knowing very well how to bring forth testimony from the Scriptures already mentioned (Matt. II). “We cry out,” they say, “that they do not fail to know that those Scriptures are the ones which bear witness concerning you; and, while we endure, they will not be able to deny it. Yet they are unwilling to come to you that they may have life.”

What then? Who, they say, does not know how to draw the conclusion against them here? Who does not see that the empty hope by which they think they have eternal life in the Scriptures has been destroyed by strong opposing barriers, and that, rather, they do not have the Word of God abiding in themselves, as you yourself said a little earlier?

Now I return to the matter. It has plainly and most firmly been established that “I have a greater testimony than John.” Above it had likewise already been said, with no one denying it, that John, to whom you sent, was great even by your own judgment, a burning and shining lamp, and that he bore witness concerning me. But the case had been stated in order to show that I do not delight in vain human glory, when I say: “I do not receive testimony from men,” but say these things “that you may be saved.” Therefore, as I said, “I do not receive testimony from men,” but say these things “that you may be saved”; so now I conclude in the same sense.

“**I do not receive glory from human beings; but I have come to know you: that you do not have the love of God within you.**” Do you suppose that I proclaim myself to be the Son of God in order to be exalted by your votes and commended by your praises? Do you think that [Col. 0430D] zeal has ever consumed me for this reason, or that I rebuke the hardness of your hearts because you have not long ago made me sit upon David’s throne and over his kingdom, and, raising me upon a lofty tribunal—as is customary for earthly kings—have proclaimed with heralds’ voices that I am Christ the King? It is not so. Rather, I lay up for you the wrath stored in reserve, “because I have known that you do not have the love of God within you.”

Do I then contend to receive glory from you? Must the sun be forbidden to shine in heaven and to illuminate the world unless you, miserable human beings—darkness and not light, darkness, I say, and feeble shadows—construct for it the lampstand of heaven? Do I not, as I have already shown, have a testimony greater than that burning and shining lamp, John? Yet he so completely did not receive glory from you that, when you wished to rejoice for an hour in his light and to augment by your flatteries a glory greater than his proper measure—for you supposed that he was the Christ—he drove back your empty breath, saying: “Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the wrath to come?” (Matt. 3; Luke 3).

How much more, then, do I not receive glory from you? Or because, while you deny me, I remain faithful and cannot deny myself, do I therefore not serve empty glory, and will I not please you otherwise than by concealing from human beings the rays of the way of truth and life—which I am? What can be so malicious as your intention? Does a lamp come in order to be placed in hiding, or under a bushel, rather than upon a lampstand, so that it may shine for all who are in the house? (Matt. 5).

Therefore [Col. 0431B] I neither “receive glory from human beings,” nor do I conceal from human beings the glory which the Father gave me; but, like a shining lamp standing upon my lampstand, I shall illuminate every single eye, so that its whole body may be full of light (Matt. 6), and I shall expose every evil eye, so that its whole body may appear to all as dark as it is. Such are you, whom I have known not to have the love of God within you, because: “I have come in the name of my Father, and you do not receive me; if another comes in his own name, him you will receive.”

For this is the fruit of the bad tree; this is the evil treasure of the heart. What then? Unless I had first tasted the evil fruit, would I have known the root of the bad tree? Would I have known the bitterness of the alien vine? (Jer. 2.) Unless you had first said, “This man is not from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath,” and, “He has a demon and is mad”; unless, finally, you had persecuted me and sought to kill me (John 8–9), I would not yet know that you do not have the Word of God abiding in you, or that you do not have the love of God within you. Indeed, even before the grave of your throat opens and your mouth foams forth curse and bitterness, my eyes see what is in your heart, and all things are written in my book (Ps. 5, 13; Jer. 15).

Do I now see and write in my book only this thing—which you do not do, in not receiving me? Certainly I have already seen and written both this and another thing which has not yet happened. For I say: “If another comes in his own name, him you will receive.” So fully do I know you to be without the Word of God, so fully have I known by judgment of hearts that you are deprived of the love of God, that I have long known even this: that, as fiercely as you now persecute and seek to kill me, who “have come in the name of my Father”—that is, in the confession that God is my Father, that he sent me, and that I make this openly known, since I seek not the glory of the world but the glory of God—so greatly will you receive with the rejoicing of your folly the man of sin, the son of perdition, who will come in his own name—that is, will exalt himself by his own presumption, while he opposes and raises himself above everything that is called God or worshipped (2 Thess. 2), so that he sits in the temple of God as though he were God.

For you are of his spirit, “and I have known” that you will quickly yield to falsehood—you who are deaf to truth, untaught [Col. 0432A] and blind, friends of darkness and rebels against light, loving the glory of the world, which he will enlarge for you through murders; while you hate the glory of God, which I proclaim to you in word and example, and so I am hated by you without cause. And one day you will see the greatness of your crime: you who now do not receive me, coming in the name of my Father, coming blessed in the name of the Lord, will receive one who will exalt himself so highly. Yet I say only this, and profess only this with the testimony of your Law: that the name of the Lord is in me.

For I am that angel of whom God, the Lord of Moses’ Law, says: “Behold, I send my angel before you, to go before you and guard you on the way, and to bring you into the place which I have prepared. Observe him and hear his voice; do not think him to be despised, because [Col. 0432B] he will not spare you when you sin, and my name is in him” (Exod. 23). And, I say, I am that angel: the angel of peace and counsel, the angel of life and truth (Isa. 9). And the name of the Lord is in me (Matt. 6; Mark 12).

For apart from the fact that he is Father and I am Son, he begetter and I begotten: whatever his name is, it is in me; and, equally with him, I am called Lord, God Almighty, uncreated, boundless, eternal, and by whatever other name the true God is proclaimed—he whom you say is our God, and whom you have not known. Your sin, therefore, will seize you, and you will find your sin, because you do not receive me, the witness of truth (Luke 16); but you will receive the prince of vanity, since you are wholly given over to flesh and vain glory (Prov. 2).

Accordingly, the accusation of that same vain glory which you falsely hurled against me, I now truthfully turn back upon you together with the punishment of sin. For I say: “How can you believe, who seek glory from one another and do not seek the glory which is from God alone?” It is sin, indeed, that you seek glory from one another—just as your teachers, the scribes and Pharisees, who do everything in order to be seen by people, loving the first places at banquets, the first seats in synagogues, greetings in the marketplace, and being called Rabbi by people (Matt. 23; Luke 11). Indeed, you seek shameful and impure glory from yourselves, like all the Gentiles, whose god is their belly and whose glory is in their shameful parts; whose god is Mammon (Matt. 6), and whose glory is in the worst things. For they rejoice and exult [Col. 0432D] when they have done evil.

This, I say, is your sin; but this punishment of sin is rendered: that, being thus blinded, you cannot believe and “come to me that you may have life.” To believe or come to me, and to seek glory from one another, are utterly contrary and opposed to one another and cannot coexist. But to seek glory from one another and not to seek the glory which is from God alone follow one another; conversely, to believe or come to me and to seek the glory which is from God alone agree with one another and mutually entail one another.

For what is that glory which is from God alone, except the testimony of a good conscience? (2 Cor. 1.) This is indeed true glory, because it cannot deceive. But the glory which comes from one another always deceives; hence it is false and vain. Therefore you cannot lay up for yourselves that true glory—namely, a good conscience—glory and honour, that is, you cannot believe or come to me, so long as you seek glory from one another. Nor do you refuse to come to me for any other reason than because, in vanity, you glory far from God.

You therefore falsely suppose that I desire to receive testimony or glory from human beings; for desire for glory is so far from him that no one who seeks glory from human beings can come to me. And I truthfully and justly turn this accusation back upon you: by seeking glory from one another you have been so blinded that you cannot hear truth; indeed, the glory of God itself is hateful to you.

What next? Do you think, when conscience accuses you, that I shall repay you in kind? [Col. 0433B] For you watch me and go about watching, so that you may find something with which to accuse me; for this you sharpen your tongues like a sword and bend the bow, a bitter thing, in order to shoot secretly at the blameless man (Ps. 7). Yet you find in me no desire at all for your kingdom or glory, nothing that could be struck by an arrow—that is, proclaimed as a legal accusation before your Caesars or governors. But I have much to say and judge concerning you. What then? Shall I also accuse you in equal retaliation? No.

“**Do not suppose that I shall accuse you before the Father.**” Suppose rather—indeed, know—that your cause has fallen much worse, because the Father did not send me to accuse but to judge. You have not given me words as to an accuser; you have not been observed by some ordinary investigator [Col. 0433C] but have fallen into the hands of a judge; before me you are guilty of treason against majesty; you have fallen terribly into the hands of the living God.

This Son of God, in whom you do not believe, to whom you refuse to come that you may have life, to whom the Father has given all judgment because he is the Son of Man—behold, he has come forth to hear cases. For he came into this world for judgment, to cast out the ruler of this world and reserve all his followers for the evil day, the day of slaughter (Jer. 12), as the prophet foretold. Behold, I say, the Judge who is also King has come forth to hear the case, and you, bound by sins, have been brought before his presence.

Do not therefore suppose that I shall accuse you before the Father. The same custom that exists in your courts will be observed for you before me: the accuser and judge will not be one and the same person. But I, as I have already said—what you refuse to believe—I, I say, am the Judge. I await an accuser against whom no defender will appear. For an accuser is not lacking: “There is one who accuses you, Moses, in whom you hope.” With me presiding as Judge, Moses accuses you.

This is a new and unexpected statement from me to you. For you hope in Moses. Why not? You say: “We are disciples of Moses” (John 9); you hang upon Moses’ chair (Matt. 23). Although with deaf ears you hear him saying, “You shall love the Lord your God with your whole heart, your whole mind, and all your strength, and your neighbour as yourself” (Deut. 6), and although you have cast behind your backs the whole Law and the Prophets, which hang upon these two commandments (Matt. 22), you suppose yourselves wholly Mosaic merely by your enlarged phylacteries and magnificent fringes (Matt. 23).

Thus you also hope that, if I accuse you before the Father and the Father devises something severe against you, Moses will stand for you, seize God with his ancient strength, and, when the Father says, “Let me go, that my wrath may be angry against them and destroy them” (Exod. 32), Moses will strengthen his arm and clasp him tightly in an embrace, saying, “Forgive the sins of your people,” until he answers, “I have forgiven according to your word.”

It is not so. For this judgment is not conducted in such a way that the Father judges and Moses excuses while I accuse. Rather, I am Judge, for the Father judges no one. I, I say, am Judge; [Col. 0434B] Moses is the accuser; your cruel and clamorous conscience is one witness; my blood, which you persecute—for you are already seeking to kill me—my blood, I say, crying to heaven from the earth, which will open its mouth (Gen. 4) and receive it from your hand, is another witness; and, conversely, there is no defender.

Yet you hope in Moses, as if he were accustomed to cherish sinners and impious people like yourselves. Did not he also, when he restrained God, as was said above, standing in the breach before him in the excessive humility of his mind in order to turn away his wrath—did he not, I say, before stretching out his hands to God, consecrate his own hands and the hands of all the sons of Levi in your deaths, those alone out of so great a number who came to him when he said: “Whoever is the Lord’s, let him join himself to me”?

Did he not, greatly enraged, break the tablets written by God’s finger? Did he not crush and pulverize your calf, your golden god, before which you leaped and played, and cast it into the stream, giving you from it a drink of cursing; and did he not kill twenty-three thousand of your number? Therefore, he who was so enraged when he saw you dancing, playing, and leading choruses before your calf—how much more will that same Moses shatter you, rebels and unbelievers, a stiff-necked people, by a just accusation now, just as in righteous zeal he broke those stone tablets, to which indeed your hearts are harder?

For you are now to prefer Barabbas, a robber, murderer, and rebel, to me (Matt. 27), more wickedly than you then preferred a molten calf [Col. 0434D] to God, who brought you out from the land of Egypt (Ps. 105), and changed your glory into the likeness of a calf eating grass: then playing and singing, now rioting and shouting, “Crucify, crucify!”

Therefore, just as those first tablets were broken by Moses’ hands and others were cut anew from the mountain after the likeness of the first, so you, the former people, will presently be condemned by Moses’ accusation, and another nation, greater and better, will receive on fleshy tablets of the heart the eternal Scripture of God’s finger (2 Cor. 3). For it was not in vain that Moses was then told: “I see that this people is stiff-necked; let me go, that my wrath may be angry against them and destroy them, and I will make you into a great nation, greater and stronger than this one” (Exod. [Col. 0435A] 32).

For at last another nation will listen to Moses; once you have been cast aside and broken by a just condemnation, he will be the teacher of the world—not in the obscurity of the letter but in the brightness of the Spirit (2 Cor. 2). For just as, with the first tablets, his face did not shine, but upon receiving the later tablets it became radiant through communion with God (Exod. 34), so that your fathers marvelled, feared, and fled, so now, in the teaching of the new people to be preferred before you, the Law will be glorified through the communication of the Gospel, by the rays of grace and truth. While it is preached, you, unable to bear it, will flee wholly in opposition.

And know this: what was then said to him concerning the sin of the calf—“Nevertheless, on the day of vengeance I shall visit this sin of theirs”—will now be fulfilled, so that, together with all righteous blood shed upon the earth, that sin also may come upon this generation. Therefore Moses is one who accuses you: Moses, in whom you hope with proud mouth while in unbelieving heart you depart from him; Moses who cries to you—indeed, to all nations—against you: “Whoever is the Lord’s, let him join himself to me.”

“**For if you believed Moses, perhaps you would believe me also, for he wrote concerning me. But if you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words?**”

See to what concluding end this delightful and victorious discourse of truth has come; see how it has conquered its opposing parties: if not so as to bend them, yet so as to shatter them. They supposed themselves to be children of Abraham; they said that they were Jews; they hoped in Moses—such eager supporters of Moses that they sought to kill the Son of God [Col. 0435C] (Exod. 32; Matt. 13). For this reason they persecuted him, because he did these things on the Sabbath. He shattered them so that they could not stand; he convicted them of not believing Moses and of not being Jews, but of belonging to the synagogue of Satan.

“If,” he says, “you believed Moses, perhaps you would believe me also” (Exod. 32). He explained why, and in what respect, they were to be accused by Moses: namely, because they did not believe Moses. And in a remarkable way he says, “in whom you hope,” adding, “for if you believed.” For one cannot hope unless one believes. It may therefore seem strange that in one respect he does not deny that they believe, while in another he charges the same persons with not believing.

Accordingly, the matter now requires that we not omit the distinction of faith rightly discerned by the holy Fathers. They boldly say that even an unbeliever does not live without faith. For if you ask an unbeliever who his father or mother was, he immediately answers, naming this man and that woman. If you then ask him whether he knows when he was conceived or when born, he will confess that he knows none of these things; and yet he believes what he has not seen. For he testifies without doubt that he had that man for father and that woman for mother. Thus they acknowledge that even an unbeliever has faith.

Unbelievers do indeed have faith—but would that it were faith in God; for if they had that, they would not be unbelievers. Since, then, there is a faith which unbelievers also can possess, and a faith whose possessors are not unbelievers, the Jews are rightly both said to hope in Moses and reproved for not believing Moses.

For according to the faith which unbelievers can possess, the Jews most firmly held then, and still hold now, that they had noble and holy fathers—Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—leaders and guides, kings also and priests. They carried their swollen hope upon the great wind of pride, presuming excessively upon those men’s merits and despising all nations as impure and ignoble with the excessively stiff neck of their hearts. But it is clear enough that they neither had nor have to this day hope in God or the faith through which Abraham and the other fathers were justified.

The Lord therefore rightly added immediately after saying, “There is one who accuses you, Moses, in whom you hope”: “For if you believed Moses, perhaps you would believe me also.” By saying “perhaps,” he expressed most sharply their hardness of heart in believing. For even the elect from among them—the apostles—although rightly believing Moses and awaiting the kingdom of God promised through the prophets, were so difficult to bring to faith that he rebuked even them, saying: “O foolish men, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken” (Luke 24).

Thus, although, once the antecedent “If you believed Moses” has been established, the consequent is “you would believe [Col. 0436C] me also,” nevertheless it could happen even in his disciples that, although they believed Moses, they would not immediately believe him. Great effort was necessary for them to be instructed that he was the one about whom Moses wrote. Therefore he rightly says: “Perhaps you would believe me also.”

Hence, in what follows, he did not say, “But if you do not believe my words, how will you believe his writings?” For it could happen that someone believing Moses’ writings might not yet immediately believe his words. Rather, he said with complete firmness: “But if you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words?” For if they do not believe the writings of the Lawgiver long since dead—for example, when he says, “Behold, I send my angel,” and the rest down to, “and my name is in him” (Exod. 32)—how could they believe the words of him who was present, born from their own people and brought up among them, who professed that that very name was in himself—that is, who declared himself to be God, the Son of God, in relation to whom God is to be called Father, and who uttered a name which belongs to God alone? For example, when he said: “I am the beginning, who also speak to you” (John 8).

## BOOK SIX

[Col. 0435]

[Col. 0435D] The course of the year mentioned above, and what the Lord Jesus did and said thereafter, are passed over by this Evangelist, because very many of those matters are found in the other evangelists. For this is the year in which they begin the account of the Lord’s preaching. He therefore enters upon the narrative of the following year—the final year—of mutable life, directed toward immutable life, ever living in itself: a narrative possessing so much more splendour as it looks more closely upon the everlasting light of the Lord’s passion and resurrection, soon to arrive after the end of that year.

For then, when every cloud had truly been scattered, the gracious brightness of the eternal sun shone forth for us: when this true Lamb, in order to take away the sins of the world, destroyed our death by dying and restored life by rising again (1 Cor. 15). He anticipates the brightness of this benefit in the events of the present year, above all in that our Lord, commending the necessary food of our life—his flesh—and the drink of his blood, says: “Unless you eat the flesh [Col. 0437B] of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6).

Therefore, after the conflict with the Jews in a discourse faithful and worthy of every acceptance, this passage of the evangelical narrative follows.

## Chapter VI

“**After this Jesus went away across the Sea of Galilee, which is the Sea of Tiberias; and a very great multitude followed him, because they saw the signs which he performed upon those who were sick.**”

It should be read not in the prepositional sense, “after these things he went,” but with *post* as an independent adverb: “afterward he went.” For the Lord Jesus did not go across the Sea of Galilee from Jerusalem, where the things mentioned above had been done or said, in order to do or say the things contained in the present reading.

For this Evangelist clearly indicates both when he went there afterward and from where, to where, and why he went and did these things. He says: “Now the Passover, the feast day of the Jews, was near”—that is, about the end of the year mentioned above. The evangelist Matthew plainly explains that he came from his own country, Nazareth, where “he did not perform many miracles because of their unbelief” (Matt. 13). Why did he depart from there, except because they took offence at him? For they said: “Is this not the carpenter’s son? Is not his mother called Mary, and his brothers James and Joseph and Simeon and Judas? And his sisters, are they not all among us? Where then did this man get all these things?” (ibid.)

Herod the tetrarch also, when he heard of his fame, said: “This is John the Baptist; he has risen from the dead, and therefore miraculous powers work in him” (Matt. [Col. 0437D] 14). Departing from his native country because of these things, to what sort of place did he “go across the Sea of Galilee”? “To a deserted place,” he says, “apart.” Mysteries are contained in all these matters; for the moment, let us follow the literal sense.

“He went,” he says, “across the Sea of Galilee, which is that of Tiberias.” First, according to the historical sense, it must be said that the Sea of Galilee, distinguished by many names according to the diversity of neighbouring regions, is called the Sea of Tiberias only in those places where, on the western side, it faces the city of Tiberias, made healthful, they say, by hot waters. For the Jordan flows through it; it extends twenty-two Roman miles in length and five in width.

This is the only miracle, among all those recounted by the others, which this Evangelist has repeated. Why? Namely, so that, in accordance with the author’s intention, he might record both the deed and the reasons for the deed. For when the Lord performed these visible things under the compelling pressure of invisible realities—marvellously constrained, as he himself says, until they should be accomplished—and just as each of us speaks from the abundance of the heart, so he performed outwardly wonderful works according to the works of his divine majesty which he pondered within.

Finally, since his food was to do the will of him who had sent him (Luke 12; Matt. 12; John 5) and to complete his work, could he ever forget that food of his, so as not always to chew it over in words and deeds? But now it was near—near, I say, that is, after a year it was to come to pass—that, according to the Father’s aforesaid will, he would enter the Sea of Galilee, that is, the bitterness of his passage, by passing from this world to the Father through the bitter tribulation of passion and death (John 13). Then he would feed the crowds of peoples who followed him in faith, according to their souls, with the nourishment of the holy Scriptures; and, at once for body and soul, so that each might have life, he would give as food the necessary sacrament of his body and blood.

He openly prophesied this by the present deed, and confirmed it still more openly by the discourse which followed. Hence it is plain that these people, refreshed by so great a miracle, said not of themselves but by divine prompting: “This is truly the prophet who is to come into the world.” The Evangelist himself intends this very point when he prefaces the account by saying: “Now the Passover, the feast day of the Jews, was near,” namely because at the Paschal solemnity, by passing—as has already been said—from this world to the Father, he was to leave to us who follow him, as food and drink, his body and blood.

Therefore this miracle, although narrated by the others, was fittingly repeated by this Evangelist so that he might explain its reasons more fully through the Lord’s subsequent words. But now we must come to the mysteries.

“He went,” he says, “across the Sea [Col. 0438C] of Galilee, which is that of Tiberias.” Behold, it is plain that he went, because he left his house and forsook his inheritance. He forsook, I say, the household of his flesh, false disciples of Moses who deceived themselves, to whom he had said above: “But if you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words?” He went far away where he willed: to raise the dead whom he willed, to give life to all those who know that he is to be honoured equally with the Father (John 5).

“He went across the Sea of Galilee,” that is, he passed over by a bitter way and difficult voyage, borne upon the wood of the cross. Yet by that very crossing he also triumphed in all the fruits of his passion, and this indeed is the Sea of Tiberias: because, as is known to all, he suffered under Pontius Pilate, governor under Tiberius Caesar. And he left to us, the great multitude of the nations, the vessel of that same cross, by which to follow in his footsteps.

For all of us who follow him are baptized into his death; we are buried with him through baptism into death (Rom. 6), so that, as he himself rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, we also may walk in newness of life. Why, then, do we, a people of so great a multitude, follow him? “Because,” he says, “they saw the signs which he performed upon those who were sick.”

Who among all of us who follow him was not sick? Who was not dying in Adam’s original sin, with his own actual sins undoubtedly added? For even though, because of original sin, all of us alike—Jews and Gentiles—were dying, indeed the Apostle says even of the Jews: “We were by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Eph. 2). Although, then, all human beings were sick, we were especially sick when, having no hope, we were far from God. Hence it was rightly said of us: “Their infirmities were multiplied; afterward they hastened” (Ps. 15).

We saw those signs, given not for curiosity but for our salvation—signs of mercy and grace. For where sin abounded, grace superabounded (Rom. 5). We idolaters, whose sins were manifold, received still more numerous gifts of grace through his Holy Spirit, so that, healed and unencumbered, we might run; and running, not grow weary; labouring, not fail.

Indeed, there are many who follow the Christian religion not because they have seen such signs by which weak souls are healed, but because they are more attracted by temporal advantages, which they obtain from the altar as attendants upon Christ’s sacraments, than delighted by the piety of spiritual gifts through which, as has been said, weak souls are healed. In that great multitude also there were very many who did not truly follow the Lord because of the signs which he performed upon the sick. They were not so much delighted by devout rejoicing as drawn, in the Jewish manner, to receive the things which they afterward sought from the Lord while murmuring, or murmured while seeking.

He himself reproved them a little later: “You come to me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate of the loaves and were filled.” Nevertheless, though with differing dispositions, a great multitude followed the Lord Jesus then, and a great multitude follows him now.

“**Jesus therefore went up upon the mountain, and there he sat with [Col. 0439D] his disciples.**” Therefore, he says, because he crossed the sea, he also went up upon the mountain: because God exalted him for this reason, namely that “he became obedient unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. 2); and for this reason [God] exalted his head above all the heavens of heaven, because he drank from the torrent of passion on the way (Ps. 109).

“There he sat with his disciples,” undoubtedly in the great solemnity of contemplation. He had his work before him and expressed by the reverent posture of his body the preparation for the glory and honour in which he was to sit “at the right hand of Majesty on high” (Heb. 1), and that where he was, there his disciples also would be with him.

For if the whole life of a wise man is meditation upon death, although a human being does not know his end (Eccl. 9), how much more did he who knew and arranged according to his will both his course and his end—which could not be hidden from him—keep before himself all the paths of his humanity according to that same end: what profit there would be in his blood when he went down into corruption (Ps. 19)?

The Evangelist also beautifully indicates at what fitting time this was taking place, adding: “Now the Passover, the feast day of the Jews, was near.” For on the Jewish festival called Passover (Exod. 12), that is, “Passage,” when an irrational lamb was sacrificed as a figure of this true and rational Lamb, and the doorposts were consecrated with its blood, and the passage of the children of Israel through the Red Sea was thus celebrated—on that day this same Lord was to be seized. Through his death he was to prepare for all who followed him the way through the Red Sea, that is, baptism, and in himself fulfil all that he now signifies by the preceding miracle and commends in the discourse that follows.

It was therefore fitting, in accordance with the intention of the Lord acting, that the diligence of the writer should say: “Now the Passover, the feast day of the Jews, was near.”

“**When Jesus therefore lifted up his eyes and saw that a very great multitude was coming to him, he says to Philip: ‘Where shall we buy bread, that these may eat?’ But he said this to test him, for he himself knew what he was going to do.**”

To grasp the force of the inserted conjunction, one must remember that he crossed the sea and went up the mountain so that the crowds might follow him; indeed, he endured the bitterness of death and ascended to heaven so that we, following in his footsteps, might confidently approach the throne of grace through him (1 Pet. 2; Heb. 4).

“When therefore,” he says, “Jesus lifted up his eyes.” The lifted eyes of Jesus are the windows of salvation and the open gates of mercy, through which grace and truth are sent forth; the lifting up of Jesus’ eyes is his present compassion for the wretched. Conversely, the Psalmist says of those whose cruel hearts refuse mercy and do not know how to spare: “They have fixed their eyes to turn toward the earth” (Ps. 16).

Indeed, the sins of our fathers—“Our fathers sinned and are no more, and we have borne their iniquities” (Lam. 5)—deserved that Jesus should by no means lift his eyes, justly lowered in anger. Yet, thinking mercifully of us beyond the debt of justice, while he was in the bosom of the Father, “he looked down from his holy height”; and afterward, when received again into heaven, he looked from heaven upon earth, that he might hear the groaning of the fettered and set free the children of the slain (Ps. 101). Hence elsewhere the Psalmist says: “His eyes look upon the nations” (Ps. 65).

Having therefore lifted the eyes of his grace, what did he say or do? “Where,” he says, “shall we buy bread, that these may eat?” At that time he tested one of the disciples whom the master of mercy was training in righteousness, not in order to learn how much faith he already possessed—for, according to this same Evangelist, he knew what was in a human being and “had no need that anyone should bear witness concerning a human being” [Col. 0441A] (John 2)—but in order, by testing him with the hand of inquiry and eliciting his answer by speech, to show him his own ignorance. This is the way a kindly teacher of any art sometimes questions a pupil: not because he doubts the pupil’s ignorance, but so that the pupil may awaken at the question and, now attentive, demonstrate more effectively.

Moreover, even now he questions and tests more sharply the whole order of teachers who preside in his stead over the holy Church. For when he entrusts “his goods” to them, giving “five talents to one, two to another, and one to another, to each according to his own ability” (Matt. 25), or when he appoints someone “over his household, to give them their measure of wheat at the proper time” (Luke 12), what else does he do but question and test—that is, show in actual fact—who is a good and faithful servant and who is a wicked servant?

For if those who are now approved, or who are to be rejected by their own judgment, had received nothing, they would not know themselves. Yet there are many who, because they gladly devote themselves to leisure, blame the slowness of their hearers. Still treating in bodily matters their slight faith, which they have in spiritual matters:

“Philip said to him, ‘Two hundred denarii worth of bread would not suffice for them, so that each might receive even a little.’” This is as though those entrusted with the dispensation of the Gospel were saying: The teaching of all the masters, old and new alike, will achieve nothing by which that foolish and ancient people, long dead through hunger for hearing the Word of God, may receive [Col. 0441C] even a little faith or Christian religion.

“One of his disciples, Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother, said to him: ‘There is one boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish. But what are these among so many?’” Who this boy was, or for whose service—whether that of Christ and his disciples, or of any persons from the crowd—he carried these goods for sale, we do not know from the historical account. Yet wherever, in whatever wilderness or region of the desert—that is, of this present age—the multitude of nations follows Christ across the sea of his baptism, in order to see the signs which he performs upon those weakened by diverse maladies of sin, there is present that boy known to all for the greatness of his folly: namely, that [Col. 0441D] people of the Jews, “which was carried away captive because it had no knowledge” (Isa. 5). That people, I say, scattered abroad; childish in understanding but ancient in malice; defiled by the blood of Christ; it fell beneath the sword under the emperors Titus and Vespasian, and was carried captive among all nations.

Wherever the multitude of believers has followed Christ (1 Cor. 14), that boy has carried himself thither, bearing the five whole loaves of the Mosaic Law, that is, its five books; and also the two fish, that is, all the Prophets and the Psalms, bearing witness together to the Law and the Gospel, or sounding forth with clear proclamations the one and same Christ as both king and priest. He carries those loaves and fish of the Scriptures upon a servile neck, but does not eat them; he sweats beneath the burden of the letter, but does not touch with hand or tooth the marrow of spiritual [Col. 0442A] understanding.

Therefore he bears them not for himself but for the whole world, so that every person and every nation may hear nearby how exceedingly ancient the testimonies concerning Christ are. Thus neither pagan nor heretic may say that whatever testimonies concerning Christ we bring forward against them have been invented by us; nor may that foolish boy, convicted by his own burden—that is, by his own Law—deny whatever the Catholic Church proclaims against all adversaries of truth concerning her king and bridegroom.

For just as the sons of Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, unwilling to cross with the other sons of Israel in order to dwell beyond the Jordan, built sheepfolds and cattle-stalls on this side of it, saying: “We ourselves will go armed and girded to battle before the children of Israel, until we bring them [Col. 0442B] into their places, until they possess their inheritance; nor do we seek anything beyond the Jordan, because we already have our possession”; and they did so (Num. 32): so this people, which refused to cross Christ’s baptism with us, is nevertheless here among us, carrying—not for itself, as has been said, but for us—all the Scriptures of the Law and the Prophets. In one and the same sense these are both food and arms for us; nor do they leave us until our aid has attained victory, whether something must be said or done against pagan, heretic, or even against the very bearer of our armour.

“There is therefore one boy here, having five barley loaves and two fish”: that is, the five books of Moses, containing the grain of the Spirit [Col. 0442C] beneath the most tenacious chaff of the letter, and the Prophets and Psalms bearing witness to Christ. But what are these among so many? Clearly, if they remain as that boy carries them about, they are very little indeed, far too little. For the multitude of those who hunger is great, and among that multitude some are great—that is, capable of great knowledge: rhetoricians and philosophers. Some of these too come to faith in Christ. But those Scriptures, according to their literal sense, are not very great. What great thing, after all, could be offered to a hungry guest—that is, to any philosopher or rhetorician called and seated at Christ’s table—if he read only according to the letter that “Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman [Col. 0442D] and one by a free woman” (Gen. 12; Gal. 4); or that the younger of Isaac’s sons, namely Jacob, by his mother’s contrivance stole the blessing from the elder son while covered with shaggy goat-skins? (Gen. 27.) Thus also in very many deeds, commandments, and burnt offerings, the letter is so meagre that it may generate disgust in the very desire of anyone who hungers or desires God’s Word, unless this Scripture had come to Christ’s hands to be fulfilled.

“Jesus therefore said: ‘Make the people recline.’” The connection of the text, where it says, “Jesus therefore said,” corresponds as a conclusion to the premise set above by the Evangelist when he said: “He said this, testing him; for he himself knew what he was about to do.” Immediately he adds another premise: “Now there was much grass in the place.” Then again the conclusion follows: [Col. 0443A] “Therefore the men reclined.” But how many were there, when the loaves were so few? It follows: “In number about five thousand.” For indeed, because he had said in testing him, “Whence shall we buy bread, that these may eat?” and because he knew what he had purposed, or “what he was about to do,” it followed that, after testing him, he should make the people recline; and because “there was much grass in the place,” the people could recline there more conveniently.

Again the conclusion follows: “Jesus therefore took the loaves.” For because the people were so many and the loaves so few, it was necessary that he himself should take them in his hands, in order to give thanks, or, according to the other Evangelists, to bless them. “And when he had given thanks, he distributed to those reclining.” “When,” he says, “he had given thanks”—that is [Col. 0443B] in order by his example to teach us beforehand to give thanks for the gifts of heavenly grace received or to be received—“he distributed to those reclining.”

Every day indeed the Lord Jesus distributes to those who follow him, to each according to the good pleasure of his grace, the bread of heavenly teaching; commanding all to recline upon the grass, that is, to restrain the vices of the flesh. For “all flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass” (Isa. 40).

But when he took into his hands the sacred Scripture, which, as stated above, is represented by these loaves, is rightly asked and readily found. For then he took into his hands that sacred Scripture by which he feeds us, when, according to John’s Apocalypse, the true Lamb, standing [Col. 0443C] in the midst of the throne and of the four living creatures and the elders—that is, in the midst of the Church—appeared, having become man, in the testimony of all teachers, old and new alike, as though slain—indeed truly slain, but alive again—having seven horns and seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent into all the earth. From his reception into heaven, through the mystery of the Incarnation and the triumph of his Passion and Resurrection, he came as far as the right hand of the One seated on the throne; and thus, in coming or going, he took the book from the right hand of the One seated on the throne and opened it (Rev. 5).

That is, he undertook in himself to fulfil, by divine power, the whole divinely inspired sacred Scripture; and the entire dispensation concerning [Col. 0443D] our salvation in the nature of man which he assumed is the opening of the aforesaid book—that is, the fulfilment of the holy Scriptures. For the Scriptures would not have been understood unless they had been fulfilled in him. Therefore the Lord Jesus took the loaves of the Scriptures into his hands when, according to the Scriptures, he was incarnate, suffered, and rose again. Then, I say, having received the loaves, he gave thanks, when, by fulfilling the Scriptures in this way, as has been said, he offered himself to the Father as a sacrifice of grace and truth.

Therefore, having received the loaves, “when he had given thanks,” he says, “he distributed to those reclining.” “Likewise also of the fish, as much as they wished.” From Moses, from all the Prophets, and from the Psalms alike, he sufficiently instructed his people, “opening their minds that they might understand [Col. 0444A] the Scriptures, first to the apostles, then through them” (Luke 24)—indeed through those who, by the same grace, furnish their successors or hearers with material from the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms, discovered in sufficient abundance to support evangelical faith. Hence in the other Evangelists we read this expressly stated: “When he had blessed and broken [the loaves], he gave the loaves to his disciples, and the disciples to the crowds” (Matt. 14; Mark 6; Luke 9).

“But when they were filled, he said to the disciples: ‘Gather up the fragments which remain, lest they perish.’” The miracle of this outward act of divine beneficence is indeed great; yet it is no more to be wondered at than God’s daily works. For the governance of the whole world is a greater miracle than the feeding of five thousand persons from five loaves. Thus [Col. 0444B] it was not so much to be wondered at, or is not so much to be wondered at, that God could do this, as to rejoice that he who could do these things came into this world and, having become man, was truly God, the Son of God.

This too must be heard reverently and observed diligently when he says, “Gather up the fragments which remain, lest they perish.” Not only in the dispensation of the Word of God—in which one must especially beware lest it be thrust too inappropriately and without discernment upon weak or fastidious hearers—but also in the use or consumption of this visible bread by which the body is fed, care must be taken that, once we have been filled, what may benefit hungry poor persons should not perish. For whose gift is this bread also, by which we are bodily refreshed, if not God’s? Let us not be such heedless assessors of divine [Col. 0444C] sublimity that, when we say to the Father according to the institution of his Son, “Give us this day our daily bread” (Luke 11), we do not judge that this visible bread, by which we are sustained in the body, belongs also to the care of so great a Father and to this solemn petition. For who is to have care in his stead, if he himself does not deign to have care for the sustenance of this wretched life of ours?

Accordingly, when we say, “Give us this day our daily bread,” the humility of our devotion ought to have in view a threefold bread. First, the spiritual bread, namely “every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Deut. 6; Matt. 4), by which our inward person lives. Next, the bread of the Lord’s body, by which the inward and outward [Col. 0444D] person together are strengthened unto eternal life. And then bodily bread, which the same God and Father of all produces from the earth even for undeserving humanity, who works the earth in the sweat of his face (Gen. 3), though, had he not sinned, he could have enjoyed without labour the spontaneous delights of paradise.

Indeed, the Lord himself disclosed before the crowds every abundance of this threefold bread at the same time. For he spoke to them of the kingdom of God, which is to break spiritual bread for the hungry. He refreshed them with bodily food, and then preached to them that they should hunger and thirst for the food and drink of his blood. Therefore what he now says, “Gather up the fragments which remain, lest they perish,” must, as stated above, be heard reverently and diligently observed in every bread which his grace has provided threefold for [Col. 0445A] our life and salvation: namely, that we do not preach things too lofty and strong to the weak; that we do not indiscriminately give the Eucharist of the Lord’s body and blood to the unworthy; and that we neither misuse in excess nor through carelessness allow to perish our abundance of bodily foods, which might relieve the want of others.

“Therefore they gathered them and filled twelve baskets with fragments from the five barley loaves which remained over for those who had eaten.” The slowness and still exceedingly scant faith of the disciples, then, were rebuked: they had said, “Two hundred denarii worth of bread would not suffice for them, so that each might receive even a little”; and concerning the five loaves and two fish: “But what are these among so many?” Indeed, according to the other Evangelists, they gave the unsuitable counsel to almighty mercy and merciful omnipotence that he should dismiss the crowds to go into the neighbouring towns and villages and buy food for themselves (Matt. 14; Luke 9).

But [Col. 0445B] more sharply and far more fully rebuked was that boy of no faith, the Jewish people, little in understanding and exceedingly old in malice, so that he might be provoked to emulation by a non-people, a foolish people, when he saw the loaves of divine Scripture, which he wished to carry alone but did not care to eat, taken from him and shared with the whole world. In accordance with what our same Lord says elsewhere: “Amen I say to you, the kingdom of God shall be taken from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matt. 21), he sees and envies the nations [Col. 0445C] filled with his loaves. He hates their refreshment—that is, their eternal refreshment—and sees the marrow of barley continually grow in mouths and hands as they eat, so that the cupboards of the banqueters are filled with books of exposition; whereas he, hungry and sickly-mouthed, licks and gnaws with childish tooth the exceedingly harsh chaff of that barley.

But why did the abundance of fragments increase into twelve baskets rather than another number? Clearly because there were twelve apostles, who by their number prefigured all the teachers of the holy Church, through whose faithful ministry this life-giving bread of the Scriptures was to be handled (1 Cor. 3). The truth of the promiser establishes and permits no doubt that every “faithful and wise servant, whom the Lord set over his household, to give them food at the proper time” (Matt. 24), when he has done so, will receive a fitting reward. And, according to another parable, because he has something, “it shall be given to him and he shall abound” (Luke 19). Therefore, because “each shall receive his own reward according to his own labour” (1 Cor. 3; Ps. 61), it was fitting that, when all had been filled, twelve baskets of fragments remained, so that each of the disciples [Col. 0445D] who had ministered might carry away his own basket.

“Therefore those men, when they saw the sign which he had done, said: ‘This is truly the prophet who is to come into the world.’” And therefore we, of whom it is written, “The poor shall eat and be filled, and those who seek him shall praise the Lord” (Ps. 21)—we, I say, who sought him [Col. 0446A] by following him across the sea of his baptism, now meanwhile in this desert region, daily refreshed by him with the threefold bread described above—let us praise him with true praise, saying: “This is truly the Prophet who is to come into the world.” For he has done for us a great and evident sign (Ps. 39): he overcame the waters which entered even to his soul—that is, he conquered death, because he rose again and ascended into heaven. To us who hungered he sent the grace of his blessing, namely the Holy Spirit, by whom he made his manifold loaves—that is, the holy Scriptures—edible to us, that is, intelligible; and in this way he put into our mouth a voice of confession, a song of praise, a new hymn of thanksgiving.

For we, the nations from abroad and in pilgrimage—we, I say—are those to whom [Col. 0446B] the Psalm says: “Let them now say” (Ps. 117), those redeemed by the Lord, whom “he redeemed from the hand of the enemy” (Ps. 105), and gathered from the regions. Finally, we wandered in the wilderness, in a waterless place (Ps. 106), alone without God, far from the city of God, in dryness, possessing no water of heavenly wisdom; we did not find the way to the city—that is, the hearing of the kingdom of God—nor did we even know to seek it. We were hungry and thirsty, and our souls were wasting away in evils, unaware of their own need because of the confusion and drunkenness in which all our wisdom was swallowed up.

Let us therefore say: “This is truly the Prophet who is to come into the world.” For not one word of all that he spoke, of all that he foretold concerning himself, or of all that he promised [Col. 0446C] us, fell to the ground. And from those things that have already come to pass we know without doubt also what remains to come: that he “is to come into the world,” namely to judge every age and to reign for ages of ages (2 Tim. 4).

Yet the men who saw this sign and said these things concerning him did not say them in that sense. Being carnal, delighted by his temporal benefit, though he performed it wonderfully, they said, “Who is to come into the world,” as though they were saying: He who is about to receive the glory of this world and the temporal kingdom of the Jews for us who now live. For it follows:

“Jesus therefore, when he knew that they were about to come and seize him in order to make him king [Col. 0446D] over them, fled again into the mountain by himself.” Those who love this world and are wise in the things of the flesh loved in him what they had experienced in the aforesaid miracle: namely, that he could feed his people with every abundance of goods, enrich the kingdom of the Jews, and overcome or acquire the whole world by wealth; and that for this purpose the great King, long ago promised and awaited, had come—the unconquered King, who would rule “from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth” (Ps. 71).

And the crowd of five thousand persons dared, without consulting their rulers—if indeed they ought to have been consulted, and knew how to deliberate according to God—they dared, I say, trusting in one Lamb, who himself intended something altogether different, to conspire to assault the whole [Col. 0447A] world, a great forest of roaring wild beasts. They presumed that they could capture that terrible and exceedingly powerful beast which, according to Daniel, had devoured and crushed, and now was trampling the remainder under its feet with no one daring to resist it (Dan. 7).

But he had not come to kill kings, but to preach to kings the knowledge of ruling justly; not to burden earthly kingdoms with tributes and taxes, but to bring forth from the treasury of the heavenly kingdom the gifts of eternal life that kings and peoples lacked. He was going to defeat an enemy far different from Tiberius Caesar, and capture a beast other than Rome, then mistress of the Jews. Therefore those men did proclaim a true praise when they said: “This is truly the Prophet who is to come into the world”; but “blessed is the people that knows the joyful sound” (Ps. 88).

Those who have tasted the good Word of God signified by that bread with which these men were filled (Heb. 6)—those, I say, who have tasted the powers of the age to come, into which this great Prophet truly “is to come [Col. 0447B]”—utter the same praise in another sense. They run otherwise to God, hasten toward his rule with a far different desire, and in another manner use violence toward the kingdom of God and seize it by force (Matt. 11), saying every day in prayer: “May your kingdom come” (Luke 11).

Yet it is not very surprising that common people of that time—when even the apostles hoped that he was about to restore the temporal kingdom of Israel—should thus have thought concerning that great King of Israel (Acts 1), when, even to this day [Col. 0447C], very many among those who magnificently preach Christ’s spiritual kingdom and know well through learning that his kingdom is not from here, nevertheless frequently run after and seize Christ for the sake only of temporal food which perishes. They cry out that he is their king, quarrelling fiercely and doing violence to his house, which is the Church (Matt. 14; John 15).

For how great a disturbance have such people caused for King Christ and his present kingdom, the Church? One sees very many priests and ministers of the sacred altar in other orders seizing the offices of God’s kingdom with such tumult and uproar as commanders of a thousand, a hundred, or fifty scarcely use in clamouring for temporal honours of the kingdom, opposing and envying one another. Of such persons it may certainly be said most sharply and most truly [Col. 0447D] that all seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ.

What then did Jesus do, knowing that present event then and foreknowing this future one? “When he knew,” says the Evangelist, “that they were about to come to seize him and make him king over them, he fled again into the mountain by himself.” By doing this he certainly delivered those men from the hand of Caesar or his tetrarch Herod, against whom he ought not to have been their advocate if they were doing anything outside their due allegiance, as though on his behalf—especially since he said to them: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matt. 22). And he did not permit himself to suffer the slander which the malice of archers fabricated without any occasion [Col. 0448A], “that they might shoot the blameless in secret” (Ps. 63), when they said to Pilate: “He made himself a king; everyone who makes himself a king opposes Caesar. If you release him, you are not Caesar’s friend” (John 19).

How much more, if he had not forestalled them by fleeing, if he had waited until they seized him and proclaimed him king, would his adversaries have seized an occasion for slander? They would certainly have added that he had led them into a desert place so that they might conspire with him. But by this very flight he signifies something deeper in mystery. For Christ flees from those who follow him for something other than himself; the Spirit of truth flees from them, as he fled from that condemned Simon, offended by what wholly filled him, the gall of bitterness (Acts 8).

But where did he flee from them? Into the mountain, into the highest height of heaven. There he fled; there he hid himself from them; there he keeps himself away from these plunderers and marauders. It is not that he had not ascended there before their assault, but that he does not look down from there upon them with any share of his gifts. [Col. 0448B] Despising those occupied with worthless bundles, namely those given to the belly and shameful gain (1 Cor. 6), he bestows himself only upon those—and does not remove himself too far from them—who can say: “But our citizenship is in heaven” (1 Tim. 3; Phil. 3).

Without delay it is evident to all that Christ has fled from such people, that Christ’s Spirit has left them. For the crowd is thrown into confusion and produces heresies and schisms; but what follows will make this clearer. It continues:

“But when evening had come, his disciples went down [Col. 0448C] to the sea. And when they had entered the boat, they came across the sea to Capernaum.” Another Evangelist relates more clearly that this happened at Jesus’ command. “Jesus,” he says, “commanded his disciples to enter the little boat and go before him across the strait, until he dismissed the crowds. And when he had dismissed the crowd, he went up alone into the mountain to pray” (Matt. 14).

When the disciples enter the boat and are to suffer a storm (Ps. 68), Christ himself, whom they had followed across that very sea, does not enter with them but remains on the mountain. For after he has once crossed the waves of our mortality, and after the waters of death have once entered even to his soul, he does not return again to those waters of suffering: “For, having risen from the dead, he dies no more; death shall no longer have [Col. 0448D] dominion over him” (Rom. 9).

But we who have followed him crossing the waters, having been baptized in his death and buried with him through baptism into death (1 Cor. 10)—we, I say, must still cross many waters and plough the long sea. That is, we must suffer storms of tribulations or indeed of vices, which we are commanded both to bear steadfastly and to overcome, prepared for every temptation. Thus, as the Evangelist Matthew testifies (14), the Lord Jesus himself commanded this, signifying that his disciples and all who desired to imitate him by living devoutly, after he had been received into the mountain of heaven, would labour amid the waves of the age: they would be tested at the waters of contradiction and answered from the hidden place of the storm. To those [Col. 0449A] waves he himself would not return with them except through the present omnipotence of his aid.

And because this Evangelist too was not alone in saying that he went up into the mountain to pray, it must not be passed over that neither then, while still mortal, did he pray, nor now, when he reigns immortally at God’s right hand, intercedes for us (Rom. 8), without the greatest distinction from the entire manner of prayer by which a human being ought—or ever ought—to pray to God (1 Tim. 2). Luke expresses this distinction of prayer in one place: “He was,” he says, “spending the night in the prayer of God” (Luke 6). That is, though he was the Son, he reverently prayed to God the Father; he himself was God, to be reverenced and heard because of his reverence, whose life and death were both sacrifice for us and continual prayer (Heb. 2).

[Col. 0449B] But his present immortality is the fitting advocacy for our confidence. In it he no longer prostrates himself in prayer, but, sitting at the right hand of Majesty on high (Heb. 1), he is rightly said to intercede for us (Rom. 8), because in himself, as a faithful pleader and a righteous and powerful advocate (1 John 2), he always presents our substance to God the Father.

“When,” he says, “they had entered the boat, they came across the sea to Capernaum.” This must be understood according to the rule which Tyconius calls recapitulation. For it is first anticipated that they came across the sea to Capernaum; afterwards it is narrated how they came. Thus Genesis says by anticipation: “God created man in his own image; in the image of God he created him; male and female [Col. 0449C] he created them” (Gen. 1). Later it is narrated how he first formed man from the mud of the earth, and then built one of his ribs into a woman.

Likewise, after Scripture had said, speaking of the generations of Noah’s sons: “From these the islands of the nations were divided in their lands, each according to their languages and families in their nations” (Gen. 10), it narrates below how they were divided, saying: “Now the earth was of one language and the same speech. And when he journeyed from the east” (Gen. 11), and so forth. Thus, I say, in this place too the event is anticipated, and then the event itself is narrated in this manner.

“And darkness had already come, and Jesus had not come to them.” It is as if he said, as I said before: Because evening had come, his disciples entered the boat [Col. 0449D]; and now again I say: Darkness had come when they entered the boat, “and Jesus had not come to them,” because he had remained on the mountain, to which, as I have already said, he had fled by himself because of the crowd.

“But the sea was rising, a great wind blowing.” This happened then and happens often: when an elemental wind blows, the sea rises; and the more fiercely the blast rages, the more it swells and dashes together and rolls about its wandering waves. Then the boat, caught among the waves, is lifted now to heaven, now plunged into the abyss (Ps. 105); and, as someone says:

> The clouds are touched by the sails, and the earth by the keel.

But that storm, stilled by the great miracle of the Lord walking [Col. 0450A] upon the waters, signifies the tempests of the age, which the Saviour now treads down and calms when he restores peace and quiet at the fitting time to the Church crying out to him. Therefore the great wind, the scorching wind, is the devil, whom holy Scripture is accustomed to signify also by the north wind. Then, having great wrath, he blew more violently (Jer. 4) and stirred more deeply with his fury the hearts of the wicked when he saw the boat of Christ’s disciples—that is, his holy Church—driven across the sea of this age.

“Therefore, when they had rowed about twenty-five or thirty stadia, they saw Jesus walking upon the sea and coming near the boat, and they were afraid.” The Evangelist Matthew says that the Lord came thus in the fourth watch (Matt. 14). The fourth [Col. 0450B] watch of the night is approximately the last part; for there are four watches, each assigned three hours, which military guards customarily maintained by changing sentries and keeping watch in turns.

Thus it is also a mystery that the disciples, about to suffer a storm, embark in the evening and are visited by the Saviour’s coming in the morning. For throughout the Scriptures evening signifies the adversity of persecution or sin, while morning signifies the prosperity of peace or righteousness, as the Psalmist says: “Weeping shall remain in the evening, and joy in the morning” (Ps. 29). That is, following Adam’s sin (Gen. 3)—for he was sought when the day had already declined after midday, and was found a sinner—the adversity of mortality shall remain; and following Christ’s righteousness, who by his death destroyed [Col. 0450C] sin (Heb. 2) and rose in the morning, there succeeds the joy of immortality and incorruption.

Certainly, when he says, “When they had rowed about twenty-five or thirty stadia,” he indicates the greatness of the miracle: Jesus had not come to them when they entered the boat, yet had walked upon the sea over so great a distance to them. For since shorelines are curved, and in some places a projection of the mainland extends a narrow tongue into the water, Jesus walked a sufficiently great distance over the waters from whatever part of the coast he entered the sea. If he entered from a recess in the winding shore, he walked thirty stadia; if he kept to a shore projecting further inward, he trod the sea by walking twenty-five stadia.

Again, if one wishes to attend here to a mystical meaning in these numbers [Col. 0450D]: when Christ comes to the aid of those in temptations, whether to visit persons driven away by persecutions from the perfection of good work, or persons driven away from faith in the holy Trinity, he accomplishes a great course of his condescension; and his helping grace runs forth to minds cast down from afar into the deep, from the distant shore of his eternal stability. For the number twenty-five stadia, being a perfect square composed by multiplying five by itself—for five times five makes twenty-five—signifies inwardly the perfection of good work, which is accomplished by the five bodily senses and commended by the five books of Moses. But the number thirty, completed by the second unit, that is, the ten repeated three times [Col. 0451A], fittingly signifies the evangelical faith in the Trinity.

Therefore, when Christ comes to the aid of a Christian driven from good work by the violence of persecution or hidden temptation, he comes to aid as though the person had been removed and drawn away twenty-five stadia. But when in mercy he approaches one who has also suffered loss of faith, he rescues the boat long tossed as though thirty stadia away. “And they were afraid,” he says—indeed, according to another Evangelist, they cried out in fear, because they thought that it was an apparition.

“He said to them, ‘It is I; do not be afraid.’ They therefore wished to take him into the boat, and immediately the boat was at the land to which they were going.”

Here this Evangelist omits what Matthew did not pass over in silence: that Simon Peter, burning with great faith and love toward the Lord Jesus, said, “Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you over the waters”; and when he said, “Come,” Peter, descending from the little boat, walked over the waters to come to Jesus (Matt. 14). Truth usefully provided this against certain heretical enemies of its own—called *Phantastics* from the character of their error—so that Christian faith might not lack a mouth or breath by which it could readily blow away even their phantom-like blasphemy.

There were heretics who said that our Lord possessed not a true and substantial body, but a phantom body, abusing this exceedingly weak argument: because he walked upon the waters. “If,” they say, “he walked upon the waters, his body was phantom and not real.” They said this as ignorant as they were impious, as dull as they were bold. For truth, with the same authority—the authority of one and the same truth—relates that Peter also walked there upon the same waters, and that he did not begin to sink until he became afraid (Matt. 14), seeing a strong wind approaching: perhaps as a sign and portent of his future denial, because, when the great wind of the devil blew in the devil’s courtyard, he would say, “I do not know the man; I do not know what you are saying” (Matt. 26).

It follows, then, that they must deny that Peter too was a real man and had a real body, since he likewise walked upon those same waters. Yet they could not deny that Peter was a real man—indeed, a mere man, that is, man only and not also God. Thus the enemies and deniers of Christ’s true humanity were bound to fall silent, since they could not reasonably assert contradictory things of Christ and Peter on account of one and the same deed: namely, that one walking upon the waters was a true and mere man, while the other, because he did the same thing, was not a true man and did not have a real body.

At last, when tranquillity had been restored to Jesus’ disciples and they had attained the desired shore—for when they wished to take him into the boat, “immediately,” says the Evangelist, “the boat was at the land to which they were going”—we should carefully observe that the fourfold necessities of the wretched, and likewise the fourfold distinction of the Lord’s mercies which they confess—mercies woven together by the prophet in Psalm 106—are prefigured in these deeds of our Lord in the same order in which that same prophet arranged them in sweet-sounding confession.

For the prophet, foreseeing with spiritual sight the grace of God calling, justifying, and glorifying, in the acceptable time, those whom he foreknew and predestined (Rom. 8) to be conformed to the image of his Son; and beholding us, who “from the rising of the sun unto its setting, from the north and from the sea,” had been scattered far from God, confesses to the Lord our first calling:

> “They wandered in the wilderness, in a waterless place;  
> they found not the way to a city of habitation.  
> Hungry and thirsty, their soul fainted within them.  
> And they cried unto the Lord in their tribulation,  
> and he delivered them from their necessities” (Ps. 106).

This happens when, through the regeneration of water and the Holy Spirit, we are led into the straight way, so that we may go to the city of habitation, which we could not otherwise find, as he himself says: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God” (John 3). This was prefigured above when a great multitude followed the Lord as he went away across the Sea of Galilee.

The second division of mercies in the Psalm is this: that “he shattered the gates of bronze and broke the bars of iron” (Ps. 106). That is, he dissolves actual sins, which very many incur mortally after baptism, by stirring sinners to repentance through the Spirit of his power; he receives them back from the way of their iniquity as soon as, because of their injustices, they are humbled and take upon themselves the mourning of repentance. This too was prefigured in that “our Lord performed signs upon those who were sick,” so that the crowds, seeing them, might follow him more readily.

The third confession of those same mercies is that of persons who, suffering at once hunger and weariness in hearing the word of God, after first being justified from every sin through baptism and afterwards from repeated crimes through repentance, again draw near to death, forgetting to eat their bread—that is, through weariness being unable to look upon him in whom man truly lives, the bread of the Scriptures (Deut. 6). Of them the aforementioned Psalm immediately adds:

> “Their soul abhorred all food,  
> and they drew near even to the gates of death” (Ps. 106).

For hunger for that bread by which the outer person alone lives is not like hunger for the spiritual bread, which is the word of God. In hunger for bodily bread there is a grievous desire, and in satiety disgust; but in hunger for that bread—that is, the word of God—there is grievous disgust, and in satiety desire.

It was therefore rightly said of such people: “Their soul abhorred all food,” because they hunger after the husks of pagan poets and the dry, empty hay of Ciceronian eloquence as though they were great delicacies, but disdain the Scriptures of the prophets and holy Fathers as though they were empty chaff. [Note: [Col. 0451D] Words of Jerome.]

One who had already become a great guest at the banquet of the divine word says: “Whenever, after returning to myself, I attempted to read the Prophets, their uncultivated language horrified me, because I could not see the light with blind eyes; yet I thought that the fault was not in the eyes but in the sun.” But from needs and tribulations of this kind as well, the Lord delivered them, so that in these also they might confess his mercies: “And he sent his word,” it says, “and healed them, and delivered them from their destructions” (ibid.); so that, eating the bread of the Scriptures themselves and breaking it for others, they might offer the sacrifice of praise and proclaim his works in exultation.

This is especially signified in the miracle mentioned above, when the people fed from the few loaves praised and proclaimed this work: “This is truly the Prophet who is to come into the world.”

The fourth danger of necessity, or fourth confession of mercies, belongs to the rulers or prelates of the holy Church. As they preside over restless crowds, they are troubled by many waves of cares and persecutions; at length they are visited by the Lord’s help, delivered from their necessities, and rejoice greatly. These are those of whom the Psalmist immediately says:

> “Those who go down to the sea in ships,  
> doing business in great waters,  
> these saw the works of the Lord  
> and his wonders in the deep” (ibid.).

Their danger—the stormy spirit—at the Lord’s word, that is, by his permission, arises and grows strong, so that its waves are lifted up; so that those who now ascend to the heavens through contemplation may suddenly descend to the abyss through the agitation of seditious crowds, be troubled and stagger like a drunken man, and all their wisdom be swallowed up (ibid.).

Moses’ wisdom too was swallowed up by such disturbance, because “they provoked his spirit, and he made a distinction with his lips”: that is, he did not then speak to the waters of contradiction with his customary faith. Their danger, I say, and the praiseworthy miracle of the mercies that came to their aid are signified by the fact that, while the disciples were sailing, as was said above, “the sea rose when a great wind was blowing”; and the Lord, walking upon the waters and coming to them, made its storm a breeze, its waves fell silent, and they rejoiced because they were silent; and he led them into the haven of their desire (Ps. 105). For “immediately,” as stated above, “the boat was at the land to which they were going.”

It follows:
