“On the next day, the crowd which stood across the sea saw that there had been no other boat there except one, and that Jesus had not entered the boat with his disciples, but that his disciples alone had embarked. Other boats, however, came from Tiberias near the place where they had eaten the bread, after giving thanks to the Lord.”

The crowd, he says, saw that no other boat was there except one, and that Jesus had not entered it with his disciples. This is plainly stated. But when did that crowd see this? “On the next day,” he says—namely, when even that little boat was no longer there, since on the preceding evening his disciples had embarked in it and, as was said above, had come to Capernaum. Therefore it saw then not with bodily sight, but with the sight of memory.

Thus, in simple expression but with plain and sufficiently clear meaning, the holy Evangelist indicates to us that this crowd stood across the sea in great astonishment and anxiety; and that, learning from those who arrived that Jesus was across the sea on the other side with his disciples, they investigated by inferential comparison the miracle they had not seen. Looking back upon what had happened, they knew that no other little boat had stood there and that Jesus had not embarked with his disciples. Therefore, either he had walked on foot over the sea, or else, in the manner of Elijah—whom the Spirit of the Lord often carried from place to place (1 Kings 18)—this one too, whom shortly before they had called truly the great Prophet, had been carried across the sea by the Spirit of the Lord.

“When therefore the crowd saw that Jesus was not there, nor his disciples, they embarked in the boats and came to Capernaum seeking Jesus. And when they found him across the sea, they said to him, ‘Rabbi, when did you come here?’”

Therefore, he says, because other boats had arrived and they thus had the means of crossing to seek Jesus, they embarked to seek him; and, having found him, they said, “When did you come here?” They did not dare to say, “Why did you come here so quickly?” For they did not yet judge it safe to reveal in the towns the purpose for which they sought him, or the plan conceived in the wilderness: to seize him and make him king over them. They were not yet established, nor strengthened by his consent, as the undertaking of so great a matter required.

They would have preferred that he had delayed in the wilderness until, after they had acclaimed or raised him as king over themselves, taken military oaths, and arranged the functions of war, they could first bear arms against Herod, tetrarch of Galilee, then against the other tetrarchs of the Jewish kingdom. Thus, having liberated the throne of David’s kingdom, and their king going before them, they would subjugate Rome itself together with the entire world under its dominion, having become such great princes; and so fulfil the prophecy saying, “The house of Jacob shall possess those who possessed them.”

“Jesus answered and said: ‘Amen, amen, I say to you: you have come to me not because you saw signs, but because you ate of the loaves and were filled.’”

Those who seek in faith to understand what Truth begins to say here ought above all to know, insofar as possible, with what intention he said it, and to keep that intention before their eyes. In its light they may recognize its face, and may judge or discern without doubt, against every heretical enemy of Christ’s body and blood, what kind of word this is and what kind it is not.

This must be considered in his intention: he prepares to expel death and restore life to humanity by the same way through which life was excluded and death admitted—namely, through believing something which is known to be invisible and cannot be comprehended by human reasoning. For we know that our first parents assented to the lying devil, who spoke the lie of which he himself is the father, saying: “You shall not die at all. For God knows that on whatever day you eat from it, your eyes shall be opened, and you shall be like gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. 3).

Did they say: “How can this tree open our eyes, bring knowledge of good and evil, and make us gods?” Therefore, this must be understood: just as a skilled physician, knowing the nature of the disease, prepares an antidote and tells the sick person, “Because you drank such poison, or ate such an herb or any harmful thing, you cannot live unless you take its opposite”; so the Author of life, when he says, “Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you shall not have life in yourselves,” intends by highest justice that, to the extent that a human being believed the lie, he should believe the truth; to the extent that he believed deception in proud presumption, he should believe the Redeemer in humble submission; and that with as much faith he should eat the bread and drink Christ’s cup as, with unbelief, he ate the fruit of the forbidden tree. Thus he should believe more of this than he can see, since he believed of that more than he saw—and indeed more and something other than it could possibly be—without being led by any reasoning.

But now we must come to the very words of eternal life: “Amen, amen, I say to you: you have come to me not because you saw signs, but because you ate of the loaves and were filled.”

This king is not made by human beings; rather, he gathers human beings into his kingdom. He does not cast kings down from their thrones so that he himself may sit in their place, but overturns covetousness and builds charity in our hearts. For what he says to these people he says to all the attendants of covetousness: even if they appear to follow Christ or seek God, covetousness truly reigns whenever they seek or follow God for something other than God himself.

Therefore, when we hear this king say, “You have come to me not because you saw signs, but because you ate of the loaves and were filled,” let each of us return to his own heart and question himself with what intention he approaches Christ’s throne or table—that is, desiring what thing he comes to his holy altar. There are the signs which Jesus performed, and there are the loaves by which those who approach are fed; and those who hunger for nothing else are filled.

The signs performed upon the sick are those by which we are healed: the mysteries of the incarnation, birth, passion, resurrection, and ascension of this same Lord Jesus Christ. Those who come for these things, rejoicing and giving thanks that they have deserved to see them—past in time, indeed, but always present in power—and who are fed by holy desire upon them, Christ the king does not reject as robbers of himself. Rather, he recognizes them as his citizens and members of his household (Eph. 2), so that he may cause them to find what they seek; for the kingdom of God is already within them (Luke 17), and they themselves are already within the kingdom of charity.

But the loaves of this same King Christ—the loaves, I say, many loaves, not the one bread—for the question now concerns not that one bread, which is Christ himself, but his loaves. The loaves of Christ the King, then, are those rewards which, established as payment, are owed by just and ancient law to those who serve the altar (Deut. 25). Those who thirst only for this payment and, for this reason alone, thrust themselves into the ministry of the sacred altar are robbers of the king and usurpers of the kingdom: adorning an unsuitable throne and carrying an untimely seat (1 Cor. 9).

The King says to them as sharply as he does wisely: “Amen, amen, I say to you: you have come to me not because you saw signs, but because you ate of the loaves and were filled.” As if he said: You certainly love not me but what is mine; you seek not what I am, but what lies beneath me; you are friends not of me, but of my table. “You eat of my loaves,” and it is enough for you: “you were filled.” For you neither hunger nor thirst for righteousness; you are led only by the belly, and make provision only for the flesh in its desires (Rom. 13).

This is your blessedness and your whole satiety: to enter the house of the Lord with pomp and eat “lambs from the flock and calves from the midst of the herd” (Amos 6). Seeking nothing else, you sing to the sound of the psaltery, as David thought you possessed instruments of song; and you suffer nothing over Joseph’s ruin. For truly you do not suffer with him; neither are you fed by the compassion of charity in contemplating the signs that you see—that is, the mysteries that you commemorate at the altar. You suffer nothing at all over the breaking of the one who says, “As often as you do these things, do them in remembrance of me” (Matt. 26).

What, then, shall I say? By doing what may you seize the King whom you seek, not with rapacious covetousness but with ordered charity?

“Work not for the food which perishes, but for that which remains unto eternal life.”—“Work, I say, not for the food which perishes.”

The food by which you have been filled, and for which you come to me so that you may again be filled, perishes daily for the person who is again hungry. As often as it enters the mouth, so often it goes into the belly—into the belly, I say, and not into the mind—and “is sent out into the privy” (Matt. 15), and thus perishes.

I do not tell you to work for such food; I do not urge you to be concerned about it; I do not invite you to come to me for its sake. For I did not come into this world in order to fill your barns with such abundance, and to make your winepresses overflow with wine, so that your hearts may be further “weighed down with surfeiting and drunkenness and the cares of this world” (Luke 21; Matt. 6). For the evil of your day is already sufficient for it, so that you cannot foresee that day which shall come as a snare upon the whole world.

Rather, I tell you to work for that food “which remains unto eternal life”: that is, food which, eaten in this mortal life, has this power and this effect, that it gives eternal life to the world. Work for such food, “which the Son of Man will give you.” He will give it, I say—he has not given it—lest perhaps you imagine such food or loaves as those which, as I said, you ate and were filled by. For you hunger for nothing else; you do not possess hunger and thirst for righteousness (Luke 21).

He gave you that food, multiplied by his blessing; he will not give it again. You shall not grow accustomed, under this king, to indulge idly in an abundance of food, once the punishment has been removed by which a human being justly works the earth in the sweat of his face (Gen. 3). But he has not given this food; he will give it when you have performed work worthy of that food. Then, I say, and not before, he will give it to you. Why? “For the Father has sealed him” [the text adds: “God”].

Therefore the Son of Man will give this food only to those who work, because “the Father sealed him”: he marked him off from common signs by his own certain and proper sign. Although he has made all other foods common to good and evil persons, active and idle alike, with the same bounty by which he makes the visible sun “rise upon the good and the evil, and rains upon the just and the unjust” (Matt. 5), he wills never to give this bread, this food of which I now speak to you, except to the worthy—that is, to those who perform God’s work.

Thus he sealed it; thus, keeping it with himself behind all the closed gates of heaven, he does not allow it to be found among common foods by dogs or swine. By what sign, then, did he seal it? By a great and reverent sign indeed: namely, by his own name. For he said of this living bread: “And my name is in him” (Exod. 23). The name which is Lord God and Son of God is this bread’s proper sign. For to which of angels or human beings did he ever say, “You are my Son; this day I have begotten you” (Heb. 1; Ps. 2)? These and all similar names which belong to the divine nature are properly the signs of this bread—or rather one proper sign.

Furthermore, he sealed this same bread not yet in actuality but long ago in predestination; and he will soon seal it in actuality by the sign which you shall all see, when this bread is cooked by the fire of passion. Thus it is not given to anyone to eat without its sign, which is its cross; nor can it be recognized, found, received, or eaten by anyone except through that sign.

Therefore, when the Lord had said, “Work for the food which remains unto eternal life,” there seemed to be nothing left for those very eager workers—who had sought to seize him and make him king over them—except, once the work had been assigned, to undertake it so that they might earn the food which could not perish. For in their greedy hope they presumed that they themselves would make no delay in doing whatever the King, giver of so great a reward, commanded.

“The Jews therefore said: ‘What shall we do, that we may work the work of God?’”

Let us hear what not-harsh yoke, what not-heavy burden this King imposes upon these such strong, broad-shouldered workers of the kingdom of God. “Jesus answered and said to them: ‘This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent.’”

This work of God is a yoke or burden of such sweetness and gentleness that no liberty or leisure of this world can be compared with it. Certainly it is a delightful work, sweet to every person—if all the children of Adam knew how to experience its sweetness—once the sense of the flesh, or the swelling of miserable vanity which from the first root, that is, from the first parent, has poured itself with excessive persistence into all branches and fruits of the human race, had evaporated.

For this work, and no other, was given to the first human being when “the Lord took him and placed him in the paradise of delight, that he might work it and keep it” (Gen. 2). What labour, then, do we suppose was imposed upon him by the words, “that he might work it and keep it”? Do we suppose this work was imposed on him so that, by working, he might eat from every tree of paradise in the sweat of his face? Or that he might guard paradise’s fruit, lest some nocturnal thief, breaking down the hedges, should pluck it?

We should therefore understand the statement, “that he might work it and keep it,” to mean that he should bear a faithful heart toward his Creator in praise and thanksgiving, love God more than any creature of God, and by believing God’s counsel preserve paradise for himself, lest by sinning he lose its dwelling.

But that ungrateful man, although he had been granted the reward of work before he received the command to work—for God first brought him, formed outside paradise, into paradise, and then gave him the command to work—cast away, ungrateful as he was, the sweet yoke and light burden of God, his Lord and Creator. What harshness or weight was there in believing the command which said: “From every tree that is in paradise you shall eat; but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat. For on whatever day you eat from it, you shall die by death” (ibid.)?

Therefore the work of God, sweeter than all leisure, is this: “That you believe,” he says, “in him whom he has sent.” The very definition of believing *in* him will make this especially clear. For what is it to believe in God except to love God not for his gifts but for himself? Those who seek God for something other than himself—as these did, who came to the Lord Jesus not because they saw signs but because they ate of the loaves and were filled—are not to be said either to love God or to believe in God.

For it is one thing to believe God (*credere Deo*), another to believe that God exists (*credere Deum*), and another to believe in God (*credere in Deum*). They may indeed believe God or believe that he is God, but they are by no means to be said to believe in God. But those who love God not for temporal gain but for himself are truly to be said to believe in God (Rom. 8). Such persons have tasted—and experienced as sweet—the work of God, which is believing in the Son of God: a work without labour, a yoke without harshness, a burden without weight.

Therefore, when he says, “That you believe in him whom he has sent,” it is as though he had said: That you come to me, not because of the loaves which you ate, but because of myself. But all friends of this world are not led by that Spirit so as to be able, confessing Christ, to say to him: “We seek not what is yours, but you yourself.”

“Therefore the Jews said: ‘What sign, then, are you doing, that we may see and believe you? What work are you performing? [Col. 0458D] Our fathers ate manna in the wilderness, as it is written: “He gave them bread from heaven to eat.”’” Did not Truth therefore speak truly when he said that these people came to him not because they had seen signs, but because they had eaten of the loaves and had been filled—that is, because they sought not the thing for which he performed signs, but the signs themselves, especially those benefiting not the soul but the belly? For when they had said, “What sign are you doing, that we may see and believe you? What work are you performing?” immediately—as though Jesus had asked, “What sign do you want me to perform for you?”—they say, “Our fathers ate manna in the wilderness”: plainly meaning that whatever he might do or say pertaining to true life, they would judge nothing accomplished unless he filled them, of his own accord, with riches to utter [Col. 0459A] surfeit.

See now how irreverently these empty tempters assail the Lord. As though they had already brought him into partnership with their vanity, they begin from their conclusion: “What sign, then, are you doing?” As if they said: You have said that this is the work of God, that we should believe in you whom he has sent. You are certainly claiming great glory, and it ought not to be granted you on the basis of a small sign. “What sign, then, are you doing? What work are you performing? Is it because with five barley loaves you satisfied five thousand persons once? That is far too little for us to believe you. Greater was that which ‘our fathers ate manna in the wilderness’: bread not made from earth, but given from heaven; not four or five thousand persons, but, apart from little children and women, six hundred thousand fighting men; not once or twice, but throughout [Col. 0459B] all forty years” (Exod. 16). What such thing are you doing? Have you commanded the clouds above and opened the gates of heaven, raining manna upon us to eat and giving us the bread of heaven, so that man may eat the bread of angels and we may have food in abundance? (Ps. 77.) Did not Moses bestow these things upon us? And you must bestow still greater things if, as you assert, “God the Father sent you.” You must bring it about that we believe you by signs no less—indeed, greater—than these.

Tempting him in this way, they thought that the pressure of their temptation could extort from him whatever he was able to do, as though, unable to restrain himself and hurrying toward glory, he would immediately perform such signs as their proud desire sought. Certainly, even now that he had become man, the hand of that same Lord [Col. 0459C] who had wrought those marvels before their fathers was not powerless to rain flesh upon them again like dust, and winged birds like the sand of the sea, and to do other such things. But just as those tempters—the fathers of these tempters—could not be satisfied by miracles except through their deaths alone, testing and murmuring until they filled the wilderness with their corpses, so these their children could not have been satisfied by any kind or multitude of miracles except by the sign of Jonah (Matt. 12), by which they were so crushed and destroyed, together with the ancient shadows of their Temple and priesthood, just as the gourd which shaded Jonah’s head withered under a single stroke of the sun (Jonah 4). For if, after the Son of Man had been three days and three nights in the heart of the earth, Judaea [Col. 0459D] or the Synagogue had remained in its former state, they would no more have ceased raging against the Lord and against his Christ than their fathers would have ceased testing, murmuring, and rising against God unless they had been struck down in the wilderness.

What, then, does the Lord of the eternal and necessary banquet say to those who are filled and seek what is superfluous? Let every hungry person listen—every one who desires to approach so great a King and stand always before him, not for perishing food but for that which “endures unto eternal life.” “Jesus therefore answered and said to them: Amen, amen, I say to you: Moses did not give you bread from heaven, but my Father gives you the true bread from heaven.” Not, he says, your fathers—not Moses, the greatest among all [Col. 0460A] those fathers of yours who ate manna—“gave you bread from heaven, but my Father.” I do not say “gave,” but, in the present tense, “gives you the true bread from heaven”: true bread, that is, bread not perishing but enduring unto eternal life.

You say, as it is written, “He gave them bread from heaven to eat” (Ps. 77). Truly I say to you: this was not then accomplished, when your fathers ate manna, as that prophetic Scripture says it was to be accomplished; rather, it was prefigured then, when your fathers were fed with that bread in the wilderness (Exod. 16): namely, that the gates of heaven, closed against the human race because of the ancient sin, should be opened, and that man should eat the bread of angels. For just as the water which then flowed from the struck [Col. 0460B] rock for your fathers to drink (Exod. 17) did not extinguish the sword placed before Paradise (Gen. 3), so that manna neither became the food of angels nor gave your fathers angelic life.

Here we must not pass over in silence the erroneous opinion of certain unknown men, men of concealed name, who maintain in speech and writing that the fathers at that time likewise ate and drank the true bread and drink which we receive at the holy altar; and that this is no more truly the body and blood of Christ than was that manna which that people ate, and that water drawn from the rock, which not the people alone but also the beasts drank. In support of this error they adduce, as their chief argument, the authority of the Apostle, who says: “And all [Col. 0460C] ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and that rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10).

Accordingly, against this detestable presumption, we must reply, however briefly, with the present authority of Truth, who says: “Amen, amen, I say to you: Moses did not give you bread from heaven, but my Father gives you the true bread from heaven.” First, it must be said that the Apostle did not say, “They all ate the same spiritual food and drank the same spiritual drink,” in the sense in which these men understand it. Nor did he employ the relative expression “the same food” or “the same drink” so as to mean that it referred to that food and drink of which the Lord himself said: “This is my body; this is my blood” (Luke 22; 1 Cor. 11). Rather, he says, Dathan and Abiram ate the same food and drank the same drink as Moses and Aaron; Korah ate the same food as Caleb or Joshua. For this is what the Apostle intends by that reading: to make every person watchful, lest he suppose that he has already attained the goal because he has received the sacraments of the Christian faith. “For all these things,” he says, “happened in a figure for us”: namely, that we may learn from ancient examples that, although we are all baptized in the same name of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and all eat the same body and blood of Christ, we must nevertheless not suppose that God is equally pleased [Col. 0461A] with all of us, however we may live and whatever deeds we may perform after baptism. For just as, although all those men were glorified by the same signs—evil men, I say, by the same signs as the good—yet God was not pleased with most of them so as to bring them into the promised land, so certainly he will not be pleased to bring us into the kingdom of God if we desire evil things as they desired them; if we commit fornication as some of them committed fornication; if we test Christ as some of them tested him; if we murmur as some of them murmured.

Therefore the text of the apostolic writing provides no support to one who wishes “the same food” and “the same drink” to be understood as referring to identity with the life-giving food and drink which we receive in commemoration of our Lord Jesus Christ. Nor does the fact that the same Apostle calls the food and drink “spiritual” provide support. For if you wish to understand “spiritual food and drink” otherwise than as occurring in a spiritual figure, and therefore proceeding not by the natural order of things but by spiritual power, the Apostle himself binds you fast in the same epistle, however much you resist. For shortly afterward he says: “Now all these things happened in figures.” If all things did so happen, then that food and drink also happened in a figure. Thus that manna was no more this true bread, nor was that drink any more identical with this life-giving drink, which we believe and confess to be truly Christ’s blood, than “that rock was Christ”—the rock, that is, an inanimate and insensible rock [Col. 0461C] which Moses struck with his rod. For, as has already been said, all these things happened in a figure; and a figure is certainly never identical with the thing itself which it figures, just as a shadow is not identical with the substance of the thing or body itself.

But the opponent says: “Surely this bread which we consecrate on the altar is also a figure of the living bread that came down from heaven, not the living bread itself.” By what canonical authority, I ask, do you force this upon Catholic ears? When the living bread himself said, of the bread which he held in his hands, “This is my body,” was anything said such as Paul said when, after saying, “The rock was Christ,” he added: “All these things happened to them in a figure”? Certainly, if Christ himself, or an Evangelist, or an Apostle had been the author [Col. 0461D] of this expression, you would not be refuted.

Even if someone says that the later saying, “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves,” is figurative speech, he does not oppose us. For such figurativeness of speech does not destroy the truth of the thing, just as the parabolic words in the parable of the sower do not destroy the reality of the one who truly sows. What is the definition of figurative speech? Surely it is figurative speech when one thing sounds in the words and another is to be understood. Therefore, even if the aforementioned saying is figurative—for it sounded one way to the Jews and Christ intended it another way—the figure does not destroy the thing itself. Rather, the figure itself is set aside, while the thing remains, when it is distinctly said of the [Col. 0462A] bread and wine: “This is my body; this is my blood.” For there the Jewish sense is set aside, because it is clearer than light that Christ is not to be eaten as they understood it. They thought that he wished his flesh, in which he exercised the five senses, to be cut up and eaten as the flesh of a lamb is cut up and eaten. There, I say, this figurative understanding is set aside, and the consonant meaning of the words remains: namely, that the bread is changed by divine power into the true substance of his body.

If this seems impossible to anyone—that bread grown from the earth this year should become Christ’s body, and wine pressed from grapes presently before us should be changed into the Lord’s blood—it follows that he will not believe that water which he recently drew from the Rhine, the Tiber, or any spring, when marked with the sacrament of Christ’s cross and passion, is that very water which flowed with blood from his pierced side (John 19), in order that through his baptism he might wash us from our sins. If he denies this also, then, being wholly a pagan and a publican, such a heretical man is to be avoided by all after a first and second admonition (Luke 18; Titus 3).

But why should he not believe it, since all water—whether of sea, rivers, springs, cisterns, or marshes; all water, I say, drawn or produced from any place whatsoever—is one in substance? Therefore, wherever it is drawn, when it has been applied to the sacrament of the crucified Lord, faithful reason admits no doubt that it is that same water which, as stated above, [Col. 0462C] our Lord poured out from his side. And what is it in substance but water? Water absorbed by the roots rises through vines and, gradually nourished by the warmth of the sun, becomes wine. Likewise, since man is composed of the four elements, blood in him is surely from the substance of water. Thus wine and blood are of the same fluid substance, and neither lacks the element of fire: blood is hot, and wine is warm. They differ only in colour and taste; and since these are accidents, they are of no consequence in divine acts. For substances, not accidents, are counted among created things.

Therefore, when the word of Christ’s cross and passion comes to the wine, what reason prevents us from believing it to be that same blood which was shed for many [Col. 0462D] for the remission of sins? Is it because it does not take on the colour and taste of blood, as it does when it is corrupted in the entrails of corruptible man and becomes hideous even to the eye? Surely the incorruptible Word, and Christ now incorruptible and immortal, made wine his blood in such a way that it introduces no corruption into the appearance or taste of the thing. Nevertheless, the substance of bread, composed of the four elements, is much more akin to the truly human body of Christ than manna was, which, at God’s command, formed in the air and descended above the camp of Israel together with the dew (Exod. 16). Grain is born from earth and ripens under the gentle influence of the air, not without [Col. 0463A] water, rain, and the heat of the sun. But, to leave this aside, it was then mixed again with water and baked with fire to become bread; and thus the substance of bread was produced.

Therefore, when that living bread which came down from heaven—whom, as he himself said above, the Father sealed—marks this bread, which, as all of us know, recently grew from the earth, with the same sign which he himself is, and distinctly says: “This is my body, which will be given for you” (1 Cor. 11), do you dare to say that it is other than Christ’s body? Truth says, “This is my body,” and adds, “which will be given for you”; and do you say it is not the same body? Surely, if it is not the same body, if it is not the same living bread that came down from heaven, then this is not the body which is given for you. But it has long been clear to all where your wholly carnal and merely animal understanding [Col. 0463B] clings, and for that reason does not grasp the things of God (1 Cor. 2): namely, because neither bread nor wine has changed anything of its outward appearance, you cannot and will not understand that it has truly become the Lord’s body and blood.

It follows, then, that if perhaps a white bishop baptizes you, a Moor, you will not believe yourself to have become before God what the one baptizing you is—namely, that from a child of the devil you have become a child of God (Rom. 8); from a child of death, a child of life; from a child of wrath (Eph. 2), a child of eternal grace (Gal. 6)—because your black hair has not become fair again and the Ethiopian skin of your face and whole body has not retained [*renituit*: “shone again in”] the colour of the one who baptized you. But if you shudder to concede this, lest you be worse than an unbeliever, and prefer to confess that, although you have changed nothing in outward appearance, you have truly passed from another body of the devil—that is, the whole mass of the lost—into another body of Christ, which is the Church, then believe this also: that this visible bread and wine, by which you live temporally, although nothing in their outward appearance has changed, have passed into another reality and been changed into that food and drink which is the nourishment of angels, by which they are fed immortally. For in both this and that sacrament, the words which the Lord speaks to us are spirit and life: that is, they accomplish our entire renewal and resurrection not carnally, but spiritually; not according to the grossness of flesh, but according to the spirit of our mind.

[Col. 0463D] But what shall we say to the great and splendid teachers of little children, to whom Plato’s Academy sometimes smells sweeter than this life-giving table of the Lord? What, I say, shall we say to them when, wholly intent upon overthrowing the truth of the Lord’s body and blood, they bring forward sayings of great teachers: “Manna signified this bread; the altar of God signifies this bread; those were sacraments, these are sacraments; they differ in signs, but are equal in the thing signified”; and likewise, “They ate one thing, we another under a visible appearance, yet it signifies the same thing by spiritual power”? These and similar statements, they seem to derive from authorities not to be despised.

Accordingly, they say, hear also the Apostle: “Our fathers were all under the cloud, [Col. 0464A] and all passed through the sea; and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea; and all ate the same spiritual food; and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual Rock that followed them, and that Rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10). What, then, shall we answer them? It has indeed already been said above that the Apostle did not intend “the same food” and “the same drink” to refer to this food and this drink which we receive from Christ’s table, and that the indwelling Spirit of truth and grace uttered these words in a wholly different sense: namely, that Dathan and Abiram ate the same food and drank the same drink as Moses and Aaron, and Korah the same as Caleb or Joshua.

Otherwise, if you say—or understand the Apostle to have said—that they ate in those shadows the same food that we eat in this time of grace revealed; and if, on the authority of the persons mentioned above, you say that that manna and this bread of Christ’s table differ in signs but are equal in the thing signified (and likewise the other things stated above), and consequently confess that this bread is no more Christ’s body than that manna was, nor possesses any greater spiritual power, it plainly follows that you must say that the sacrifices of lambs and rams were holier than the new sacrifice of bread and wine, and that the ancient loaves of presentation were worthier than this bread which is placed and consecrated on Christ’s table (Lev. 21; 2 Sam. 12). For those sacrifices were far holier than that manna (Exod. 16), or than the water which flowed from the struck [Col. 0464C] rock, since it was permitted to none but the clean, and priests or men of Levitical descent, to eat of the sacrifices or loaves of presentation; whereas all people without distinction could eat that manna, and could harmlessly drink that water—even beasts and dogs could lap it—since it had been sanctified by no invocation of the divine name, although it was spiritual, that is, produced not by a natural order but by spiritual power, or signifying spiritual drink. For it is written: “Waters came forth in great abundance, so that the people drank, and the beasts” (Num. 20).

But through Christ’s grace may these wise men not be so exceedingly high-minded—these men who lash the Lord’s table with such objections—as to preach that this bread or drink of the Lord ought to be given without distinction to beasts: not merely to brute animals, which also drank that water, but to beasts “rotting in their dung” (Joel 1), to dogs returning to their own vomit (Prov. 26), and to washed swine wallowing in the mire (2 Pet. 2), just as, as stated above, the people and beasts could use in common that bread to which they wish to compare this bread of the Lord, and that water. Nor should they thereby make void the judgment of the same Apostle, who says: “Whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (1 Cor. 11).

In the comparison of opinions concerning the Lord’s body and blood, the judgment has been made that the saying of blessed Ambrose deservedly wins the palm. Among other things he says: “It is clear, therefore, that the Virgin gave birth apart from the order of nature, and that the body which we make is from the Virgin. Why do you seek the order of nature in Christ’s body, when the Lord Jesus Christ himself was born from a Virgin apart from nature? It is surely the true flesh of Christ which was crucified, which was buried; therefore this is truly the sacrament of that flesh.” Likewise: “Just as the true Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, is not so by grace as men are, but is Son as from the substance of the Father, so the flesh which we receive, as he himself said, is true flesh, and the drink is true drink.”

Therefore, even if an angel from heaven should preach to us the Apostle’s words just quoted—“Our fathers were all under [Col. 0465B] the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses” (1 Cor. 10), and the rest—in such a way as to expound that those things which were then done in that shadow or night possessed the same power as these sacraments now performed in the day of salvation, when faith in Christ shines forth; or should say that by the food, drink, or baptism by which they were baptized into Moses, in the cloud, and in the sea, they were made more perfect than those who came later, among whom were Samuel and David, who did not pass through the sea or eat manna—if, I say, even an angel from heaven should preach this, we would not hear him as an angel of light, nor would we hear the Apostle as Christ’s Apostle in this interpretation.

And if any of the holy Fathers somewhere said anything of this kind which presumptuous men might seize upon against the truth—as is their custom, for when hunters catch something they can brandish against the truth, such adversaries rejoice more than a murderer who has cut down a fellow citizen or companion—there are many other writings of the same author which, if a faithful reader carefully compares them, can more quickly aid endangered faith. For example, the very person whom they hold up as the supposed patron of the opposing opinion says, concerning David, that when he changed his countenance he was carried in his own hands (1 Sam. 21): undoubtedly, he says, the true David—that is, Christ—carried himself in his own hands when, holding bread and wine, he said, “This is my body; this is my blood” (Matt. 26). And shortly afterward he says in this same Evangelist: “And the bread which I will give is my flesh for the life of the world” (John 6).

Does not this same Evangelist John say in the Apocalypse: “If anyone adds to these things, God shall add to him the plagues written in this book; and if anyone takes away from the words of the prophecy of this book, God shall take away his portion from the book of life, and from the holy city, and from the things written in this book” (Rev. 22)? Is that curse not equally to be feared here, so that we do not subtract or add anything to the words: “This is my body, which is given for you; this is my blood of the new covenant, which shall be shed for many for the remission of sins” (Matt. 26)? For when he says, “This is my body,” and we add an implied qualification, saying that it is said figuratively or by resemblance; when, I say, he says, “This is [Col. 0466A] the body,” and we say, “This signifies the body,” do we not add much, or subtract by a perverse alteration, and generate a sense which so great an authority—God and man—nowhere spoke, nor ever entered into his heart?

Surely, when someone objects and scribbles in his little papers that the same Truth similarly said, “I am the vine,” he drags this into a false argument as boldly as ignorantly. For the words that immediately follow—“As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you unless you remain in me” (John 15)—plainly compel us to understand it as spoken by comparison. This is especially so because he did not distinctly say, “I am this vine,” as he distinctly said, “This is my body; this is my blood,” immediately adding a description of true propriety: concerning the body, “which is given for you”; concerning the blood, “which is shed for many.”

Therefore, lest the final plagues come upon us, we neither add nor subtract anything from the divine definition or description which the incarnate Word uttered with his own mouth. Rather, because perfect charity casts out fear (1 John 2), we confess—not so much from fear of plagues as from love of truth—that this bodily bread, after the Father has sealed it, and this wine pressed from grapes present before us, as soon as it has been sealed with that same sign through the hands of the Church saying, “That it may become for us the body and [Col. 0466C] blood of your most beloved Son, our Lord Jesus Christ,” and so forth, down to, “Do this in remembrance of me,” are the body and blood of him who is the author of this handing-over; and this sacrifice is Christ himself, who through his passion was truly sealed by God the Father so that he might become a sacrifice.

Someone may now say: What, then, did the saints of old eat in order to have eternal life? If the Father did not give, but gives in the present, the true bread from heaven, which, unless we eat it, we shall not have life in ourselves, how do the blessed patriarchs, holy prophets, and all the elect who came before now have life—those who died before the Father gave this bread, without receiving the promise, and therefore could not eat it? (Heb. 11.) What then? Did not death pass through one and the same sin to all human beings (Rom. 5), and did not all sin in one, both those who preceded and those who followed Christ’s coming? Was sin, therefore, to be cleansed and death abolished in one way for them and another for us, or in one way for us and another for them? Or does “the Lord pervert judgment, or does the Almighty overthrow what is just” (Job 8), so that instead of applying one common medicine of righteousness to all according to the measure of their common guilt, he varies the order or effect of eternal life according to the mutability of his will? For example, that he should say: You first are perfected by faith alone; you others are made complete through circumcision; you third group, unless you are baptized and unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, [Col. 0467A] shall not have life in yourselves?

This objection must be answered aptly. Since, first, there is no one who doubts that all the saints from the beginning of the world awaited this Redeemer of the human race, and that they could not otherwise be restored to Paradise unless this Lamb first came to take away the sins of the world, it must also be known that, for ancient, definite, and known reasons, he had to come with these two necessary sacraments of our salvation: baptism and the food and drink of his body and blood. For when, according to the unchangeable counsel alike of his justice and mercy, he called the first man, fallen through forbidden food, to account, saying, “Why have you done this?” (Gen. 3), he intended nothing else than to pursue his offspring until he himself should abolish by the stream of his grace that same guilt humbly acknowledged and condemned by devout confession, and should finally set before them for eating the true tree of life—which he himself is—in opposition to that food which man had presumptuously eaten. For that sin, in which man believed the devil more than God and ate forbidden food with proud intent, could not otherwise be destroyed than by the same man once again believing God more than the devil and, conversely, eating commanded food in humble submission.

Thus, in order that everlasting justice might destroy sin by a just judgment, inexhaustible mercy followed the sinner immediately upon his expulsion, and did not cease to call him back until it found faith among the children of men and heard voices of humility answering it. For men, taught by their miseries, began to recognize the malice of the deceiving serpent [Col. 0467C] (Gen. IV), to reject it with execration, and, in condemnation of that food which man, persuaded by him, had eaten against God, to offer tithes, sacrifices, and peace-offerings to God the Creator, desiring by the eating of such sacrifices, with invocation of the divine name, to purge away the curse of that food. But a dumb beast—[200] such as, for example, the simple and innocent lamb which Abel offered in condemnation of the malicious and harmful serpent—could not speak in place of the man offering himself; it could not confer upon its offerer the justice which it did not possess, nor eternal life.

Therefore, when those who hungered had thus been prepared, and Abraham’s bosom had already been filled from among them, when, in the fullness of time, the gates of heaven had been opened [Col. 0467D], the Father gave this living and true bread, the sealed bread, the bread of angels. Having the same reason for coming as he had had in Paradise when he sought the first man—namely, to give, in opposition to the food through which man perished, an opposite food—he willed, after the merit of humility and faith had gone before, that he himself, the fruit of eternal life, should hang upon the wood of the cross in accordance with the Father’s command, in opposition to the tree of the knowledge of good and evil; and through the suffering of death he willed to become food for both the dead and the living, so that both dead and living might eat him, each in his own manner.

For, plucked from the tree of the cross by the hand of the Father—he himself saying, “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke XXIII)—the souls of the saints ate him in that manner in which [Col. 0468A] the angels also eat him. They ate, I say, the true divinity; their eyes were truly opened, and thereafter they saw God, whom no one had ever previously seen (John I). Nor did their bodies lying in their tombs lack the power of this food, as soon as his body was received in the same womb in which they too were held, just as Jonah was in the belly of the whale for three days and three nights (John II). For by the power of this food many of them rose again as testimony to the future universal resurrection.

They certainly rose not, as some have supposed, in order to die again. Of them the Evangelist says: “Coming into the holy city after his resurrection, they appeared to many” (Matt. XXVII). This would plainly be absurdly said of persons destined to die again—for example, of Lazarus (Matt. XI) or of the widow’s son—who did not appear to many, but were visible and touchable by all, and were altogether like other mortals, or capable of suffering, under the condition of mortality: eating, drinking, and dwelling in their own houses.

But the living now eat in the manner suited to them, as was said above. They eat the salvation of that same passion according to the tradition of the Lord himself, who marks out bread and wine, that “the poor may eat and be satisfied, and praise the Lord who seek him” (Ps. XXI). The poor, I say, shall eat the great alms of the King of kings, which he gives—none other than himself—though not yet in his own visible form. “For now we walk by faith, not by sight” (II Cor. V), so that, by truly believingly eating the food of eternal life [Col. 0468C], we may escape the fault of our parents, who ate when deceived by a vain hope and an excessive credulity that divinity might be seized.

Accordingly, the saints of old were not perfected by one remedy and new persons aided by another. Rather, by the blood which flowed together with water from Christ’s side, the whole company of those persons was cleansed at the very hour of the Lord’s death (I John I); and by that same blood each of us is cleansed, and by that same element of water, taken from wherever it may be, together with the word of that same cross and blood, “in which,” John says, “he washed us from our sins” (Rev. I). And the lamb which all those placed in hell swiftly ate, roasted upon the altar of the cross on that most holy evening (Exod. XII)—thus fulfilling the prophecy which says, “O death, I will be your death; I will be your bite, O hell” (Hos. XIII).

For the saying is not active, “I shall bite you” or “I shall be biting you,” but passive: “I shall be your bite, O hell.” That lamb, I say, the dead ate in hell; we eat the same lamb, each in his own times and places, in order that we may live with him eternally.

But if someone asks us: How can bread, which is produced from the earth in this year, be the body of Christ which hung upon the cross, and wine, pressed from grapes now present, be that blood which he poured out from his side? (John XIX.) Let us ask him how the Son of Man—who was certainly conceived of a woman and born from the earth—descended from heaven; or how, before he ascended into heaven, he could already be in heaven, according to the truth of his own saying: “No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John III). [Col. 0469A]

Anyone with understanding can surely answer that the statement is entirely correct on account of the unity of the person of Christ as God and man: that one Christ is the Son of Man together with the Son of God, “who descended from heaven,” and who, while he was on earth, was nevertheless also in heaven and everywhere; for no place confines him, because the nature of divinity is uncircumscribed.

Let us therefore, changing the words a little, say to him: “No one raises you into heaven except this bread which descended from heaven”—this body of the Lord which hung on the wood, and this blood of his which was shed for the whole world. Certainly, if he recognizes the former statement, I do not see what he can doubt concerning this one. For the unity of the Word makes one body of Christ, so that what then hung on the cross and what the faith of the Church now effects with a sacred mouth are one body—one flesh, I say, and one blood.

Accordingly, let us not be such unwise flatterers of blessed Augustine that, when he calls the sacrament and the reality of the sacrament the unity of Christ’s body—which is the Church—calling that unity the reality of the sacrament, while calling the Lord’s bread the sacrament of this reality, we immediately assent to those who seize upon this distinction to defend their own opinion. They say that a sacrament is a memorial of a sacred thing, and thus leave no room for the Lord’s definition, which he expressed thus: “This is my body, which shall be delivered for you; this is my blood, which shall be shed for you.”

For the Church is indeed Christ’s body, but not that body which was delivered for you; since the Church was not delivered for itself. And if the bread of the Lord’s table is only a memorial of this sacred thing, namely the Church’s unity, then still less is it itself that body which was delivered for us. Therefore, let them draw from this whatever analogies they wish, saying: Just as one bread of the Lord’s table is made from many grains, and just as the wine of Christ’s cup has flowed together from many grapes, so the one Church of God consists of many human beings. Let them devise and usefully present such analogies, provided that the foundation which has been laid remains (I Cor. III), besides which no one can lay another: he himself says concerning the bread and cup of wine, “This is my body [Col. 0469D] which shall be delivered for you; this is the cup of my blood, which shall be shed for you” (Matt. XXVII).

When this foundation of faith is not properly maintained, some reverse the Lord’s preaching: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him” (John VI). They put it thus: “He who abides in me, and I in him, eats my flesh and drinks my blood.” They are preoccupied with the idea that abiding in the unity of faith is what it means to eat Christ’s flesh and drink his blood; and thus they consider participation in the bodily communion of the Lord’s table unnecessary for salvation. But what if everyone were to say the same and think the same? Would not the Lord’s institution be judged superfluous [Col. 0470A] [201] and be reduced to nothing, so that the manner of eating and drinking which he himself taught with his own mouth at the very moment of his most holy passion would nowhere be observed?

May this notion, introduced by this useless reversal, therefore perish from the Christian heart. Christ plainly did not teach this. Rather, “He who eats my flesh,” he says, “and drinks my blood”—in the manner in which I am about to hand it down, believing in his heart unto righteousness and eating and drinking with his mouth unto salvation—“abides in me and I in him,” so that there are no longer two, but one flesh (Eph. II). For eating and drinking are the efficient cause; the result is that “he abides in me and I in him.” But “he who eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (I Cor. XI). Someone can eat unworthily; no one ought to eat unworthily.

For bread once consecrated never afterward loses the power of sanctification or ceases to be Christ’s flesh; but it benefits the unworthy person nothing (John VI), whose “faith without works is dead” (James II), and who therefore does not possess the Spirit who gives life (John VI), by whom he may receive it with his mouth. For what wonder is there if earth eats earth? And what is Christ’s flesh, apart from divinity, except our earth? Accordingly, we are not alarmed that anyone may eat Christ’s flesh, being certain what the Son of God took from what is ours and what belongs to him as God.

Where, then, does that which the unworthy person eats and drinks go? Certainly, as has been said before us, it is pious and salutary to believe that it is distributed through the members, so that it is not subject to evacuation. Yet this is what the worthy person has more than the unworthy: for the one it avails unto salvation; for the other, unto judgment. [Col. 0470C]

Now let the discourse return to the order begun; and, treating as we have begun the food and drink of the Lord’s body and blood in accordance with the truth of the present Gospel reading, let us eat as we treat it and treat it as we eat it.

“Amen, amen, I say to you: Moses did not give you bread from heaven, but my Father gives you the true bread from heaven.” For that bread of whatever kind which your fathers ate in the wilderness (Exod. XVI)—bread, indeed, or food that perishes and perished daily—Moses did not give to others; rather, he received it together with the others from the same God, “who gives food to all flesh” (Ps. CXXXV).

Why, then, could Moses not give the true bread of which I speak, whereas my Father gives it to you? It follows: “For the true bread of God is that which descends from heaven and gives life to the world.” This is a true and firm argument, fully proving that this bread is truly greater than Moses and could not have been given by him; and it supplies a definition sufficient to show the substance of this bread by three perfect additions: that it is of God, that it descended from heaven, and that it gives life to the world.

If he had said, “For it is the bread of God,” and added nothing more, he would not have distinguished it from ordinary bread; for every bread which the earth produces is God’s gift and God’s creature. “The earth is the Lord’s, and its fullness” (Ps. XXIII). He therefore added: “Which descends from heaven.” Yet even if he had added no more, he would not yet have sufficiently defined this bread. For when the Jews said, “Our fathers ate manna in the wilderness,” they immediately added, “As it is written: He gave them bread from heaven to eat.” Indeed, the Lord rained that bread from heaven, yet not from the ethereal heaven but from the aerial heaven, through which flying birds are customarily called “birds of heaven.” And the very word “descends,” used here, was also said of that bread: for when the dew descended upon the camp in the morning, manna descended with it (Exod. XVI).

He therefore added a third distinction of this bread, which prevents its being understood as common with any other bread: “And gives life to the world.” That it gives life—not to one nation, but to the entire world—most strongly commends the weight and worth of this bread and demonstrates its uniqueness. For what does “gives life” mean except “makes the dead alive”? Certainly manna could no more do this than the bread which the earth produces every year for the sower.

For there was no life in that bread or in the water which the rock produced, although some have fabulously said that the rock followed the camp of the children of Israel from place to place, prompted by the Apostle’s expression: “They drank from the spiritual rock that followed them” (I Cor. X). For it was not an inanimate stone rolling after the camp; rather, a channel of a torrent, produced from the rock and directed by God’s will along the route the people were to travel, followed them (Num. XXI).

Thus the full definition of this true bread which the Father gives has been given; neither more nor less has been said than was necessary. [Col. 0471C] It is the bread of God: that is, it is not from human beings but from God. Indeed, it is food for angels and human beings, yet it is neither the gift of angels nor of human beings, and does not come from them or because of their merits, but from God’s grace. And it freely descended from heaven, where Moses could not ascend in order to bring it down from there; and “it gives life to the world,” that is, to angels and human beings: so that living angels may eat and never die the death by which the devil died; and human beings who are dead may eat and be raised from the twofold death of body and soul. This bread, therefore, is far greater than Moses, and it is sufficiently clear that such bread could not have been given by him.

But these earthly diners, not raising their eyes above the belly and perishable food, did not attend to this bread—the bread of God, “which descends from heaven” and has now come to give life to the world. They were deaf and unteachable hearers of the Law which says: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word proceeding from the mouth of God” (Deut. VIII). Hence they supposed that he spoke to them of something spiritual.

“Therefore the Jews said: ‘Lord, always give us this bread.’” They mean: Give us continually such bread as we understand you to possess, so that we need not turn the earth with the plough in the sweat of our face, entrust seed to furrows, or, amid the security of abundant bread and leisure, have any need to guard against scarcity of anything. Nevertheless, this proposal had made them attentive through some sort of hope. For they had not merely conceded that the bread which the Lord said was given by the Father was true bread; they had also heard with excessive eagerness that the bread of God had come from heaven and would give life to the world.

The order of the teaching now required that he should show clearly and explicitly what the bread itself was, so that those who murmured and did not believe might shut themselves up in eternal hunger, while those who believed and came to him might eat eternal life. “And he says to them: I am the bread of life. He who comes to me shall not hunger, and he who believes in me shall never thirst.”

As though he said: Since, on hearing of the true bread, you opened your bosoms in eager desire, saying, “Lord, always give us this bread,” do not close or constrict them again when I tell you what that bread is and show you something far different from what you hoped. “I am [Col. 0472B] the bread of life.” It is now in your power to receive and possess this bread. “Do not harden your hearts, as in the provocation, according to the day of temptation in the wilderness, where your fathers tempted me” (Ps. XCIV); but come to me and you shall not hunger; believe in me and you shall not thirst. The Father has prepared a table before you (Ps. XXII), if you hunger for the true bread and thirst for the true water of refreshment.

“But I said to you,” [202] “that you have seen me and do not believe.” I said this to you, I say, for I know you: you came to me not because you saw signs, but because “you ate of the loaves and were filled”; and now I say, “Because you have seen me,” and heard the words of eternal life, “you do not believe.” You wish only to see signs; you do not wish to see or believe that for which the signs are done. You care only to eat loaves and be filled with perishable food, rather than to work for the food “which endures unto eternal life.”

What then? What shall this true bread do, since you do not wish to come to eat it? Hear now: “Everything which the Father gives me shall come to me; and him who comes to me I will not cast out.” I could have said, “Everyone whom the Father gives me shall come to me.” But you fastidious Jews, whose fullness and drunken satiety of Pharisaic superstition loathe the true bread, might think that I had spoken of you alone—as though this bread of God must wait for you alone because you are children of Abraham and would have no other eaters besides yourselves.

[Col. 0472D] He therefore said, “Everything which the Father gives me”: everything, I say, whether good or evil, clean or unclean, circumcision or foreskin, every sex and every condition, shall come to me; and “him who comes to me,” from wherever he comes and whatever he may be, provided that he comes—that is, believes—I will not cast out. I will do what that man did who, when he had prepared a great supper and invited many, and they all began together to excuse themselves, said: “Go out into the streets and hedges and bring in here the poor, the crippled, the blind, and the lame” (Luke XIV).

Do you suppose that this true bread descended from heaven in vain unless you eat it, and that, deserted by the diners, it must be taken back to the table of heaven because his purpose has been frustrated on your account? It is not so. The Father will fill his house for me with a multitude of hungry people desiring to be satisfied with this bread; and whoever he gives me, whoever recognizes this bread as it is revealed by him—even if a little dog comes beneath the table to gather crumbs—I will not cast out.

“Because I descended from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me.” That I descended from heaven and am the living and true bread, I have told you; and I added, “Because you have seen me and have not believed” (Matt. XI). You certainly cannot reproach me for this: “not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me,” since you do not doubt that he is God. For even if you do not grant that I descended from heaven, you nevertheless confessed a little earlier that I am sent by God, that is, that I am the great Prophet who is to come into the world.

I say, you do not reproach me for acting “not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me.” For what is it to do not the will of him who, as I truly say, sent me, but one’s own will, except to use one’s own power in making an unjust arrangement; not to weigh the merits of things, but to make prejudgments, to call good evil and evil good, and to put darkness for light and light for darkness (Isa. V)? Therefore you cannot disapprove that I act “not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me.” Accordingly, I shall pursue the matter I began, in order reasonably to show you excluded from the banquet of eternal life and others to be admitted.

[Col. 0473C] “And this is the will of the Father who sent me: that I lose nothing of all that he has given me, but raise it up on the last day.” But perhaps this is still obscure to you, and you do not understand what “everything which the Father gives me” means. I therefore say the same thing more plainly: “For this is the will of the Father who sent me: that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him may have eternal life.” What I said, “that all which he has given me,” is the same as what I now say: “that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him.”

But I have said it in both ways so that you may know that circumcision no more than foreskin is the sign of those “whom the Father has given me,” whom he wills me not to lose and whom he wills to have eternal life. Rather, those whom he has given to me, his Son, to be saved are to be distinguished by faith alone and recognized by love of the Son alone. “Everyone who sees the Son”—who does not close the eyes of his heart against him, but sees and, seeing, rejoices with joy—and believes in him, is that which “the Father has given me.”

And since it is “the will of the Father who sent me” that I lose none of what he has given me but raise it up on the last day, shall I, by contrast, do my own will by rejecting anyone because he is not Abraham’s seed or has not been marked with the character of circumcision? And if everyone who sees and believes has eternal life according to the Father’s will, how much more are those worthy of eternal life who have not seen and yet believed?

Therefore everyone—whether one who sees me bodily present, sees the works which I do in the name of my Father, and believes; or one who shall see by the perception of reason and believe, when it has been proclaimed to him—already has eternal life. By believing, he has already, as I said above, passed from death to life; “and I will raise him up on the last day.” Even now he has eternal life, having been raised in soul; and in the future, when all who are in the tombs hear the voice of the Son of God and come forth, I shall call him by name, raise him, and distinguish him from the mass or heap of those dead in eternal death, who are going forward to the resurrection of judgment. For as I am the bread of life, so I am also the giver of the resurrection of bodies. His coming to me or believing in me will avail him to rise from the twofold death of body and soul and, as I said above, to hunger and thirst no more (John V). [Col. 0474B]

“Therefore the Jews murmured about him because he said, ‘I am the bread which descended from heaven,’ and they said: ‘Is this not Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? How then does he now say, “I descended from heaven”?’”

This is their sin, for which they have no excuse. For it was not so surprising that they did not know that he had descended, or how he had descended, from heaven—especially since common opinion held him to be Joseph’s son. But it was sinful to murmur about him, rather than confer with him or inquire from him, that they might deserve to know. To murmur about him, I say, was the sin by which they deserved never to find the way of truth. For this was not to seek knowledge of him [Col. 0474C], but to kindle against him the flame of envy with a spirit of pride and indignation.

So their fathers did not provoke God because they asked for food, but because they asked for it while testing and murmuring, as the Psalmist says: “They tested God in their hearts, asking food for their souls; they spoke wickedly of God and said, ‘Can God prepare a table in the wilderness?’” (Ps. LXXVII), etc. Therefore these tempters, children of tempters—that is, murmurers, children of murmurers—did not offend Christ the Lord because they supposed him to be Joseph’s son, but because, while he performed heavenly works and said that he had descended from heaven, they preferred to murmur among themselves about him [203] rather than humbly seek from him, with an intention of learning, the mystery of his descent. [Col. 0474D]

For it savors strongly of the contempt of pride that they strike him here by name, saying, “Is this not Jesus, the son of Joseph?” They knew, of course, that these things appeared greatly opposed and contradictory: that he had descended from heaven, as he said, and that he was Joseph’s son, as they commonly believed. Conversely, it was entirely consistent and consequential that he descended from heaven and was the Son of God, and that he had said much to them above about the Father. But, inflamed by that diabolical envy, they pretended not to notice God the Father in his words, whose authority they could not despise; and they importunately and falsely insisted upon what alone they wished to know: namely, that Jesus was a human being and the son of Joseph and Mary.

[Col. 0475A] “Jesus therefore said to them: ‘Do not murmur among yourselves. No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him.’” Rebuking those who murmured, he maintains that he has another Father, greater than Joseph—indeed, one who stands with them and against them—lest perhaps they did not understand this great fact. “No one,” he says, “can come to me”—that is, to him to whom, as I said above, when one comes, he shall not hunger or thirst. No one, I say, can attain the state of not hungering or thirsting unless “the Father who sent me draws him.” This is plainly greater than Joseph. Because they had said, “Is this not the son of Joseph?” Indeed, it is greater than every human being.

For what human being can draw anyone to eat this living and true bread as it ought to be eaten? Let us ask what it is to be drawn, and it will become clear that no one can draw anyone except God alone. To be drawn to Christ, the living and true bread, is to hunger and thirst for righteousness, and to have such distaste or hatred for all unrighteousness as to be able to endure such hunger and thirst. But who is sufficient for these things? In whose hand is anyone’s heart, so that he can bring this about in it? Is it in Paul’s hand? Apollo’s? Cephas’s? Is it in the hand of any of all those who minister God’s word that, while by preaching God’s word he as it were breaks the living bread, he may give the dead a desire to eat and live?

Certainly, just as Paul planted and Apollo watered, but God gave the growth (I Cor. III), and just as “unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain” (Ps. CXXVI), so preachers break the living bread in vain unless God awakens in the minds of the hearers a holy desire for that same bread. Therefore, since to draw someone to Christ—that is, to give someone hunger and thirst for righteousness—can be done by no one except the Father, and is consequently greater than anything human, he begins to prove most impressively from this effect that his Father is far greater than Joseph.

Nevertheless, it should also be known that this drawing is no less a work of the grace of the Son than of the Father. For this same Son says of himself: “And I, if I am lifted up, will draw all things to myself” (John XII). And his bride, the Church, says to him in the Song of Songs: “Draw me after you” (Song I). Why, then, does he now say concerning the person of the Father alone that the one who comes to him must be drawn by him? Clearly because murmuring concerning Jesus’ Father had arisen or was being aired by those saying, “Is this not Jesus, the son of Joseph?” Aptly he first says of the Father: “No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him.” This is the same as saying: No one can have eternal life by eating this bread unless, by believing, he loves—or, by loving, he believes—that not Joseph but God is my Father, and that I was sent by him from heaven to be born of a virgin mother.

Then he immediately adds, concerning his own power not unequal to the Father’s: “And I will raise him up on the last day.” He had also said above that he would do this according to the same will of the Father; for there he said: “Everything which the Father gives me shall come to me,” and “this is the will of my Father who sent me, that I lose nothing of all that he has given me, but raise it up on the last day.” He repeated the same thing with greater force to those who murmured: “No one,” he says, “can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him,” excluding the murmurers and the envious by a terrible pronouncement from those whom the Father would give him.

But those whom this Father did not draw in the manner already stated—for they had come to him not because they hungered and thirsted for righteousness, but because, as he said, they had eaten of the loaves and been filled—could still murmur indignantly and say among themselves: “Who is this Father, or which one of you all, being human, is to be drawn or compelled to this man so as to believe in him?” Against such contempt, he immediately adds this remarkable proposition:

“It is written in the Prophets: ‘And they shall all be taught by God.’” This is written most fully in Jeremiah in these words: “After those days, says the Lord, I will put my law within them, and I will write it upon their hearts; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people. And no longer shall a man teach his neighbor, or a man his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord’; for they shall all know me, from the least of them to the greatest, says the Lord” (Jer. 31), etc.

For now, after what the same prophet had previously declared has been fulfilled, saying: “Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I will make with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah a new covenant, not according to the covenant which I made with your fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt, a covenant which they broke” (ibid.), etc.—now, I say, after he has put his law within us and written it upon our hearts by the Holy Spirit (2 Cor. 3), a Jewish man no longer teaches his neighbor, as when he makes him a proselyte, saying, “Know the Lord.” For all, from the least to the greatest—that is, from the rustic to the learned scribe—know the point now under discussion: that he has God as Father, and that God sent Christ the Son into this world; and thus they are taught by God.

[Col. 0476D] For this is now at issue, as was said above, against those murmurers: that God is Christ’s Father, while they say, “Is this not Jesus, Joseph’s son?” Therefore he says: “It is written in the prophets, ‘And they shall all be taught by God.’” And, so that it may be made clearer in what respect they are to be taught by God, he immediately adds: “Everyone who has heard from the Father and has learned comes to me.” As though he said: All who are taught by God will learn this from him: that they should believe in me.

For everyone “who has ears to hear” (Matt. 13), such as the teaching of God requires, and learns inwardly—where no human voice makes a din, nor flesh and blood penetrates, but only the revelation of the Father who is in heaven—cannot turn away from the Son of God, but “comes to me,” he says: he believes in me; he is bound to me by an unbreakable bond of love; he hastens to be numbered among my members, so that he too may be able, in the Spirit of adoption as sons, to cry “Abba, Father” (Rom. 8), by which prevenient Spirit he has become one taught by God in the manner stated above.

“Not that anyone has seen the Father, except [he] who is from God: this one has seen the Father.” He says: It does not follow, nor ought it to be inferred from my saying, “Everyone who has heard from the Father and learned comes to me,” that my Father is visible, or that he could be approached and heard bodily as a man; as you, steaming with the cloud of indignation and envy, murmur because I said, “I came down from heaven,” since Joseph is my father—a shield you have seized for your heart, lest you be able to hear or learn anything from my Father.

[Col. 0477B] My Father is he “whom no human being has seen, nor can see, who dwells in inaccessible light” (1 Tim. 6). For even if some of the fathers are recorded to have seen God, they nevertheless did not see him, nor could they see him, in his own substance. Thus, when Moses said, “If I have found favor in your sight, show me yourself, that I may see you plainly,” he was answered: “You cannot see my face, for no man shall see me and live” (Exod. 33). Yet the same Scripture had previously said of that same Moses: “The Lord spoke to Moses face to face, as a man is accustomed to speak with his friend” (ibid.).

Certainly this should not be understood of the blessed angels, as though they do not enjoy the vision of God. For the subject here is not they, but human beings, none of whom has ever seen God, [Col. 0477C] because the wall of enmity stood between human beings and God—that is, original sin—which was to be dissolved in Christ’s flesh through the passion of death (John 1), so that God might be seen by human beings.

Therefore he says: “Not that anyone has seen the Father”; and he added, “Except he who is from God: this one has seen the Father” (Eph. 2). This one, he says, who is not from a human being, whose being did not begin from Joseph, as you say while murmuring against me—this one, I say, namely I, alone of all the children of men has seen the Father, because I alone am from him: namely, born, not made.

Otherwise this distinction would have no force when I said, “Except he who is from God,” since all human beings have been made by God, though none of them has seen him. It must therefore be observed that whenever being “from God” or “of God” is found stated thus absolutely, [Col. 0477D] without “made” or “created” being added, “born” must be understood, even if human beings are being discussed. So: “He who is of God hears the words of God; therefore you do not hear, because you are not of God” (John 8). “Born”—indeed, reborn—must be understood: namely, because one unworthy of the birth of regenerating grace cannot hear God’s words.

When, therefore, he says, “Not that anyone has seen the Father, except this one who is from God,” “born” or “begotten” must be understood: by that generation or birth which belongs not to grace but to nature. For he does not say, “Except those who are from God,” but speaks of himself alone: “This one,” he says, “who is from God”—that is, alone born or begotten by nature, alone the coeternal and consubstantial Son.

For unless you understand here the Son of God’s proper generation in the words, “Except he who is from God has seen the Father,” it follows that all who are from God have seen God. But all of us who have received the Spirit of adoption as sons (Rom. 8) have been born of God, and are called and are children of God (1 John 3, 7); yet it has not yet appeared what we shall be, and nevertheless none of us has seen God. Therefore this one who is from God, and consequently has seen the Father, is from God as the only-begotten is, as the one consubstantial Son is: the unique Son, the Son, I say, alone natural. For all the rest are adoptive.

It follows:
