“Amen, amen, I say to you: he who believes in me has eternal life.” After, in the assertion in which he had said, “I am the bread of life; he who comes to me shall not hunger, and he who believes in me shall never thirst,” Truth itself stood firm and refuted the murmurers—who would not yield—until victory; and after he had also beforehand condemned Cerinthus and other heretics not yet existing, because they would say that Christ had not descended from heaven but had begun to exist from Mary, or had even been begotten of Joseph, now at last the majesty of the eternal Word completes what it had begun with a strong conclusion. It confounds the impious and draws the pious to eat himself, the bread of eternal life: “Amen, amen,” he says, “I say to you: he who believes in me has eternal life.”

[Col. 0478B] This surely follows from what preceded; it is evident to the faithful that it is true, but unassailable to the unbelieving. For if “the Father gives the true bread from heaven, which descends from heaven” and gives eternal life, and I am that bread of life, then “he who believes in me has eternal life.” Therefore I had begun above to say to you: “Work not for the food which perishes, but for that which endures unto eternal life: this is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent.” You interrupted, saying: “What sign, then, do you perform, that we may see and believe you? What do you do? Our fathers ate manna in the wilderness.” Therefore I told you, “I am the bread of life.” Now again I say: “I am the living bread [of life]. Your fathers ate manna in the wilderness and died. This is the bread descending from heaven, that if anyone eats of it, he may not die.”

Compare the results; see the differences between the two breads. “Your fathers ate manna and died”: your fathers, I say, evil fathers, fathers of evil men, murmurers, fathers of murmurers, unbelievers, fathers of unbelievers. Although they all ate the same spiritual food and drank the same spiritual drink as the good fathers of good men—such as Moses and Aaron—“they ate manna and died.” Indeed, though they were dead by the evil death of sin, they ate, and by eating did not revive; but, filled with that food, they descended into hell. They were so dead according to the inner person that some of them, though still retaining outward life, were swallowed up by the earth and covered with soil, and perished from the midst of the multitude (Num. 16).

[Col. 0479A] “What then,” you ask, “do those who eat this bread not die? For you said: ‘This is the bread descending from heaven, that if anyone eats of it, he may not die.’ Do not all who eat this bread of which you say, ‘This is my body, which shall be given for you,’ and who drink your cup, of which you say, ‘This is my blood’ (Matt. 26)—do not all these who eat and drink die, indeed all according to the flesh, and many also according to the soul? In what, then, do you prefer this bread to that which the fathers ate, since those eating manna and drinking water from the rock all died according to the flesh, while some also died according to the soul?”

We concede that many of them died according to the soul, as the Holy Spirit says in David: “They did not know my ways; therefore I swore in my wrath: ‘If they shall enter into my rest’” (Ps. 94). Although some say that by the death in which their corpses were overthrown in the wilderness their sin was consumed (Num. 14), understanding thus what is written, “God will not judge twice for the same thing” (Nah. 1, LXX), so that all those punished by temporal death escape eternal death, nevertheless we hold the better opinion of others, who say that punishments condemn some and do not set them free—namely, those of whom it is said through the prophet: “I struck them, and they did not grieve; you crushed them, and they refused to receive correction” (Jer. 5).

[Col. 0479C] These men, they say, begin their punishments in this life and endure them in eternal punishment. Hence the Lord says through Moses: “A fire has been kindled in my wrath, and it shall burn unto the lowest depths of hell” (Deut. 32). Thus, in accordance also with the same prophet, who says, “Destroy them with a double destruction” (Jer. 17), we concede that very many of them perished together in body and soul; especially because, when they provoked God with the provocation of testing in the wilderness and refused to know his ways, he himself swore, as was said above, in his wrath that they should not enter into his rest (Ps. 114).

In what respect, then, do you prefer this bread, whose eaters nevertheless die, to that which their fathers ate and died? To this I say: Consider more carefully whether he made any exception of evil or good fathers. Did he not say in a universal statement, “Your fathers ate manna and died”? “Your fathers,” he says, not only the murmurers and unbelievers, died, but also the righteous: however faithful they may have been, all your fathers died, namely for that reason for which all human beings die in Adam (1 Cor. 15).

[Col. 0479D] I say this because, although they ate manna, they were nevertheless all held in the same death, just as their older fathers, or their younger descendants who did not eat manna because they did not live in those days. Thus I said: Your fathers ate manna and nevertheless died (Gen. 49), just as those who did not eat it were nevertheless held in hell on account of original sin; just as those before or after that manna were brought hence to their peoples by the way of all flesh (3 Kings 2). They were not freed through that manna, nor did they ascend to the banquet of angels, in order to enjoy the vision of God, by which the blessed angels live eternally—a vision which all human beings lost in their father Adam.

“But this is the bread descending from heaven.” And for what purpose did it descend from heaven? “That if anyone eats of it, he may not die.” For whoever does not eat it shall die—or rather, already dead long ago in Adam, he shall not be freed from that inherited death. And indeed a vast multitude of the dead, separated from their bodies, waits for this bread in hell, of which their father deprived them by sinning.

[Col. 0480B] Thereafter a great multitude of the Gentiles will come, demanding this bread while they are still in the body, and they will eat it while still living in the flesh. For both groups—those long since dead and those who are or will be still living in the flesh—behold, a table has been prepared by my Father before them (Ps. 22). For I say to you: “I am the living bread which came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he shall live for ever.”

Because the guests of my Father have been scattered by death through the forbidden food which their father ate—their souls indeed in hell, their bodies in tombs—I too, the bread of angels, shall be broken; and according to that substance by which angels are nourished, I shall go down into hell, where souls hunger. And according to the body, hidden in the same belly of the earth in which their bodies are hidden, I shall be there three days and three nights, as Jonah was in the belly of the whale three days and three nights (Matt. 12; Jonah 2). There souls, refreshed by the vision of God, shall revive; while bodies, many now but all in the future, shall rise again (Matt. 16).

Then this same bread shall be given to the remainder—that is, to those whom the present age still retains in the flesh—in the form appropriate to living persons: namely, in the true sacrifice of bread and wine according to the order of Melchizedek.

“And the bread which I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world.” Let this be the highest consolation for the poor, to whom the Spirit of the Lord, coming upon me, sent me to preach the Gospel (Isa. 16; Luke 4); let this, I say, be the highest and incomparable rejoicing for the Gentiles and the ends of the earth (Ps. 2), whom, asking, I shall receive from the Father as inheritance or possession. For they shall have no less of this bread of life than the ancient fathers, to whom he signified this bread, “and the Father who sent me gave it.”

[Col. 0480D] For when I descend to them so that they may be refreshed from me, when hell has bitten me and I have become its bite (Hos. 13)—death, the death of death, enclosed in its belly—and am added to the hungry saints or righteous, so that all may be made alive: then I shall give bread to these remaining persons, in which there is no lack of the reality of this same flesh or body of mine, which, brought forth from the whale’s belly, shall sit sound and whole for ever at the Father’s right hand.

The living human being shall eat, through my gift and in a manner suited to himself, this same bread of angels, which the Father gives to those who have departed, so that they may eat and rise again: now their souls, but their bodies on the last day. It should be observed at this point that this proposition may be taken either way and is now reversible [or “convertible”]: “And the bread which I shall give is my flesh.”

For whether you predicate flesh of bread in this way—“And the bread, which I shall give, saying, ‘Take and eat,’ is my flesh,” or “is my body”—or predicate bread of flesh in this way—“And my flesh, which is dead and to be swallowed by the belly of the earth, is bread, because, when the dead are refreshed, it will give life and resurrection”—whichever way you turn it, the statement is true. Yet the order of the wording and the change of persons and tenses require that bread be taken as the subject and flesh as the predicate.

[Col. 0481B] For up to this point he had spoken of the Father’s person: that he gives the true bread, and that the Son himself is the bread. Now the living and true bread, by a transition to his own person through the future tense of the same verb, says: “And the bread which I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world.” And indeed, the bread of angels whom the Father gave in order that he might assume flesh and die so as to give life—this heavenly bread gives us earthly bread, and changes it into his flesh so that it may give eternal life to those living persons for whom it can be eaten.

Thus the Word, which is the bread of angels, became flesh—not by being changed into flesh, but by assuming flesh. Thus that same Word, long since made flesh, becomes visible bread—not by being changed into bread, but by assuming bread and transferring it into the unity of his person. Therefore, just as concerning our flesh, which the Virgin Mary bore, we truly confess, on account of the unity of the person, that it is God, so likewise concerning this visible bread, which the divinity of that same invisible Word assumes and transfers into his flesh, we truly and catholicly confess that it is Christ’s body.

[Col. 0481C] Therefore he says: “And the bread which I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world,” so that the redeemed world may eat and live, first cleansed through baptism from the old stain given and urged upon it by the serpent. Thus from the effects it is clear how much better this bread is than that concerning which they had said: “Our fathers ate manna and died.” But this is the bread descending from heaven, so that if anyone eats of it, he may not die.

Certainly, when he says, “He who eats this bread,” or “he who eats my flesh,” “worthily” must always be understood. Just as, whenever “the angel of the Lord” or “the Spirit of the Lord” is said in the Holy Scriptures, and “evil” is not added, a good angel or a good Spirit is undoubtedly understood, so likewise whenever “he who eats and drinks” is said, and “unworthily” is not added, “worthily” must undoubtedly be understood.

Therefore, when he said, “Your fathers ate manna and died,” since he spoke without distinguishing good fathers from evil, it must be understood that however well some of them ate, nevertheless [Col. 0482A] all died: that is, they were not freed by that manna from the inherited death in which all die in Adam. But by this bread all the elect are made alive, whether they died before this bread descended from heaven or were born after its descent, being liable to the same death.

It follows:

“Therefore the Jews disputed among themselves, saying, ‘How can this man give us his flesh to eat?’” Above, when he said, “I am the bread of life,” they murmured; and now, when he says, “And the bread which I shall give is my flesh,” the rebellious and unbelieving Jews dispute among themselves. They have nowhere been taught to bend their stiff necks in order to question the Master of truth in the manner in which those who hunger and thirst for the knowledge of truth are accustomed to inquire. Rather, they murmur; they dispute; they account the words of eternal life, blaspheming them, to be madness.

Would he then tell such men how he could give his flesh to eat? They disputed among themselves, murmured among themselves, and sought the counsel of God’s wisdom not from God’s Wisdom itself but by murmuring and disputing among themselves. What could they learn from one another but evil? “O man,” says the Apostle, “who are you, to answer back to God?” (Rom. 9). To such persons, who question not from love of learning but with an intention to oppose by argument, nothing else should be said except that, being unworthy of wisdom’s answer, they should stand far off.

[Col. 0482C] “Therefore Jesus said to them: ‘Amen, amen, I say to you: unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves.’” Therefore, he says, because you do not hunger at all and do not suspend your souls upward toward heaven, whence this bread descended—so that the Father who is in heaven may reveal to you what flesh and blood cannot reveal (Matt. 16)—but dispute among yourselves with hearts lacking peace, I shall say only this to you: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves.”

But the manner of eating is not for me to disclose to you. For this is holy, and must not be given to quarrelsome dogs; these are pearls, which must not be cast before swine, lest they trample them (Matt. 7). You are not yet even servants, to offer a reverent ear to the Lord; much less friends, to whom alone I ought to make known the rite or order and the divine reasons of this banquet. Know, then, this little thing: “Unless you eat, you shall not have life in yourselves.”

Concerning this food of the Lord’s body and drink of his blood, the holy teachers have given this interpretation, which readers too hasty and teachers too premature have seized upon as though it were the greatest or primary definition concerning that same body and blood of the Lord. This food and drink, they say, signify the fellowship of his body and members, which is the holy Church, in his saints and faithful who are predestined, called, justified, and glorified.

[Col. 0483A] What then? Did those same fathers leave unspoken in the same place that the bread and wine prepared upon and received from the Lord’s table are the sacrament of the unity of Christ’s body which is the Church? And what is a sacrament, or whence is it so called, except from consecrating, because it consecrates this reality—namely, the body of Christ which is the Church—and, by consecrating, brings about unity?

For just as we call this or that an ornament because it adorns, and a garment because it clothes, and similarly in other cases, so the Lord’s body which we receive at the altar and his blood are rightly called the sacrament of the aforesaid unity, because through that visible food and drink we are invisibly consecrated into the one Church of Christ, which is his body, his fullness.

Therefore we by no means accept the aforesaid interpretation as the greatest definition or description of eating the flesh and drinking the blood of the Lord. This is especially so because he himself, with his own mouth, when he willed, to whom he willed, and those whom he judged worthy, gave so careful a definition or description that no dialectician or philosopher could ever define a substance or any individual more carefully.

[Col. 0483B] For when they wish to designate the substance of any primary thing—for example, when defining equivocation against the sophistical importunities of arguments—they say, “Alexander carried off Helen.” We are compelled in so great a matter now to remember such trifles, and to strike back at little archers with little arrows. When, I say, they say, “Alexander carried off Helen,” since one may object, “Alexander did not carry off Helen; Alexander, the Macedonian king, son of Philip, did not carry off Helen,” they specify: “Alexander, the Trojan son of Priam, of whom we are now speaking, carried off Helen.”

The supreme Wisdom did the same when he wished to show how he could give us his flesh to eat: “This,” he says, “is my body.” And he added: “Which shall be given for you.” Likewise: “This is my blood,” and he added: “Which shall be shed for you and for many for the remission of sins.” And, setting forth the entire manner of eating his flesh and drinking his blood, he says: “Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke 22).

[Col. 0483D] Therefore, with all the mists of figures and similitudes removed, we believe without hesitation that we eat not any body whatever, nor the body of Christ which is the Church, but that body of the Lord which was given for us; and that we drink that blood which was shed for us for the remission of sins. And what he himself did, we know—and know well—that we do in remembrance of him: that is, we eat his flesh and drink his blood.

And although the holy Church is Christ’s body and thus consists of many human beings, just as the bread which we truly call Christ’s body consists of many grains, and the wine which we truly call Christ’s blood has flowed together from many grapes, nevertheless the Church is not that same body of Christ which was given for us. The body so often mentioned, which is the bread of eternal life, always retains this proper distinction by Christ’s own authority.

Therefore: “Unless you eat,” he says, “my flesh and drink my blood”—namely, doing what I shall say to do in remembrance of me—“you shall not have life in yourselves.” Certainly those prevented by tender infancy before they depart this life, before they can eat or drink; or those constrained by a moment of time, such as certain confessors whom the imminence of persecution and death did not permit to be baptized with water, are not prejudiced by this saying of Truth.

[Col. 0484A] For before God a person is not judged not to have eaten unless he was unwilling to eat, took no care, or neglected to do so. God judges dispositions and wills, which cannot be evil in toothless infants; and in such confessors, since they are good, they are not deprived of their effect, because they plainly share in Christ’s sufferings. Therefore we do not suppose that infants whom incapacity of age prevents from eating, and who depart this life as soon as they have been baptized, are excluded from eternal life; nor do we doubt that devout confessors overtaken by the persecutor, baptized in their own blood, have partaken of Christ’s body or drunk the Lord’s cup to their eternal profit.

It follows:

“He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I shall raise him up on the last day.” Not you, he says, and those like you, all you murmurers and disputatious persons, shall have life in yourselves; but that one people of mine which is joined to me in unity of spirit—my one Church—which “eats my flesh and drinks my blood, has eternal life.”

[Col. 0484C] For this is the supreme effective cause of eternal life: to eat my flesh and drink my blood. Not to eat my flesh and not to drink my blood is evidence of the ancient unbelief by which the first parents of humankind preferred to believe the serpent rather than God. For there is no difference in guilt between not believing that they would die by eating of the forbidden tree, and not believing that by eating my flesh and drinking my blood in the prescribed order they would be freed from that same death.

Therefore the one who eats and drinks rightly puts off the punishment of ancient death; and the one who does not eat or drink is no less justly left under the ancient judgment of paternal transgression. It should indeed be noted that, whereas above he had said, “This is the will of my Father who sent me: that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him may have eternal life, and I shall raise him up on the last day,” here likewise, in the same order, he first says, “has eternal life,” and then adds, “and I shall raise him up on the last day.”

This is so that no one may suppose that, without the visible food and drink of his body and blood, he has recovered both kinds of life, bodily and spiritual, by faith alone and has no need of this Sacrament. He repeated this very thing, undoubtedly attesting that whoever scorns to eat and drink does not truly believe.

[Col. 0485A] However faithful you may be, and however much you may profess Catholicism, if you refuse to eat and drink this visible food and drink, then by the very fact that you presume it unnecessary for yourself, you cut yourself off from the fellowship of Christ’s members, which is the Church; nor do you rightly believe in him whose authority you disparage in this food and drink so carefully commended by him.

Did not our first parents first become inwardly and invisibly corrupted by the devil’s spirit, swelling up against their Creator, and then, persuaded through the serpent, perish also by visible food? Thus the repentant human being must first submit invisibly to the Creator by faith, believing with the heart unto righteousness and confessing with the mouth unto salvation, and then complete the necessary justification also by the visible food and drink of eternal life (Rom. 10).

Nor is it without the order of justice that, when he eats, he first already has eternal life—namely, living to God in the soul through righteousness—and then, “I shall raise him up,” he says, “on the last day.” For our first parents, so often mentioned, first died inwardly by the eternal death of the soul, and then outwardly by the death also of the body.

[Col. 0485B] “On whatever day you eat of it,” he says, “you shall die by death” (Gen. 2): undoubtedly by the death of the soul. And afterward they received also the sentence of bodily death from God himself, who said: “In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread, until you return to the earth from which you were taken; for you are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. 3).

Rightly therefore, and with the order of justice preserved: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood,” he says, “already has eternal life,” because he already lives according to the soul. Yet according to the flesh he shall indeed die; “but I shall raise him up on the last day.”

“For my flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink.” True food, I say, and true drink, because what it promises is true, because the hope by which it is eaten and drunk is true. Hence it is also clear that this food is opposed in a contrary way to that food which the serpent offered to the first human being: for that food was the food of falsehood, because what that food promised was false and remains false, since it was given with an empty promise and eaten in an empty hope of attaining divine likeness.

[Col. 0485D] Yet this Truth has promised no less to those who eat his flesh and drink his blood than that falsehood promised in persuading them to eat forbidden food. For it promised divinity: “Your eyes,” it said, “shall be opened, and you shall be like gods, knowing good and evil” (ibid.). Therefore it follows: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him.”

Here he plainly promises divinity to those who eat his flesh and drink his blood, and turns into a true effect, speaking earnestly and not without great torment to that same deceiver, the illusion of the most wicked seducer who said, “Eat, and you shall be like gods” (ibid.). For what has the only Son of God promised us here by this statement, unless as if he had said openly: “You shall be gods, all sons of the Most High” (Ps. 81)?

And it should be observed that he did not employ the deceiver’s same words, “You shall be like gods”; nor indeed ought he to have said, “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood shall be like God,” or “shall be like the Most High.” Rather, “He abides in me,” he says, “and I in him.”

[Col. 0486A] For who is, or can be, like God? He needs no one; he is God by no one’s aid or grace. But apart from him, who can be God by the self-sufficiency of his own nature? Thus the angel wished to be God and became the devil. Thus he dared to urge a human being to desire deity, and stripped the human being of the honor proper to humanity. Both the one and the other, when he wished to be like God, wished to be God without the grace or help of one greater; and by this will each separated himself from God. What, then, would he be but God’s adversary?

Conversely, fellowship with God or God’s grace makes gods and sons of the Most High. Therefore, commending God’s grace and communion to the one who eats his flesh and drinks his blood, he says: “Let him abide in me, and I in him.” And who am I but God, God’s Wisdom, the true, supreme, and eternal Divinity? Therefore the one in whom I abide, having divinity poured into him, has become God and has been reborn as a son of the Most High.

He is not “like God,” because God is one and alone, having no one within himself by whom he became God; but he is God by having me abiding within him, by whom he becomes God. For hear what follows: “As the living Father sent me, and I live through the Father, so he who eats me shall live through me.”

[Col. 0486C] Behold the similar dissimilarity and dissimilar similarity of adoptive gods and the one God: “As,” he says, “the living Father sent me, and I live through such a Father, so also he who eats me shall live through me.”

But how did the living Father send me, or how do I live because of the living Father? I say that the living Father sent me—that is, the immortal Father begot me. For in begetting me he sent me. If your uncircumcised ears could endure it, when I say “sent” I would speak more openly and say “begot,” as he himself testifies in the Psalm, saying to me: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Ps. II). I therefore say that he sent me—though you can scarcely endure even to hear this—that “the living Father sent me,” which is nothing other than that he begot me and willed me to be incarnate; “and I live because of the Father” [Col. 0486D], that is, for this reason I am the living God, the immortal God, the impassible God, the unchangeable God: because I have such a Father, because such a Father sent me, because such a Father begot me. And “as I live because of such a Father,” so he “who eats me shall live because of me”; that is, he shall live eternally and blessedly for this reason, and for this reason is God and son of the Most High: because “he eats me, because I remain in him and he in me.” Behold, I say, the likeness of divinity, the likeness of life and eternity, the likeness between adoptive gods and the one God. But, as was said before, this likeness is unlike. In what respect? Clearly, because the causes differ. Why do “I live because of the Father”? Because the living Father himself sent—that is, begot—me [Col. 0487A]. Why shall a human being live because of me? Because he eats me. I did not eat the Father in order to live; rather, I live because the Father, living in himself and needing no one, begot me, likewise living in myself and needing no one. But a human being does not live because the Father begot him; rather, in order to live, he eats me, whom the Father alone begot. Therefore, as was said before, there is an unlike likeness and a like unlikeness between the only Son and the many sons of the Most High: this one lives because he was begotten; but they live because they eat him who was begotten. Yet they lose nothing through this difference; for though they are not gods by birth, by eating me, who am God by birth, they become one body with me.

Therefore let no human being who desires to live eternally lament that God drove away the human being made a transgressor, lest he take from the tree of life and live forever. For behold, he “has the true bread,” of which “if anyone eats, he shall live forever” [Col. 0487B; 0488A]. Indeed, let him rejoice that he was not then permitted to eat from the tree of life and live forever. For had he then eaten, he would have lived forever as that one lived at whose persuasion he had eaten. On the contrary, if he now lives forever, he will live as I live, because of whom he will live, and by whose grant he eats, that he may live because of me.

It follows: “This is the bread descending from heaven, not as your fathers ate manna and died. He who eats this bread shall live forever.” In a brief epilogue he gathers and enumerates the foregoing parts and recalls the matters of which he has thus far spoken, so that their memory may be renewed and restored in the hearer’s mind. For he had expounded above in the same order in which he now recapitulates them in the conclusion: namely, that this true bread descended from heaven; that it was not the manna which their fathers ate and died. Having pursued these matters as far as possible, the rest must be dealt with in the following volume.

## BOOK SEVEN

[Col. 0487]

[Col. 0487B] The Holy Spirit spoke beforehand concerning our Lord Jesus Christ in his servant David, who was also his Father according to the flesh, saying: “The Lord has sworn and will not repent: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CIX). The order of this Melchizedek is almost unknown to no one: namely, that when Abraham returned from the slaughter of the kings, he brought forth not the flesh and blood of he-goats or calves, but bread and wine (Gen. IV). “For,” Scripture says, “he was priest of the Most High, and blessed him”; by this saying it splendidly intimates that, in such an order, he had prefigured the rite of the priesthood of the Most High.

The radiant sacrament of this order, concealed beneath the veil of the Law, when our Lord—the true King and Priest—unveils it in this place, strikes human eyes with such great rays that, unable to look upon it [Col. 0487C–D], they wholly turn away and flee. Thus, as a type of such people, their fathers of old fled because they could not bear the brightness of Moses’ face, since it had become radiant from speaking with God (Exod. XXXIV). For if these murmuring and contentious sons of theirs are struck back by the brightness of this truth, it is not because everlasting brightness is naturally harmful to rational creatures, but because reason in the creature irrationally defiles and soils its own eyes with earthly desires, so that it cannot see its light. But to those who turn away, as far as they can with God’s help, from the lust of the flesh and the lust of the eyes that are in the world (I John II), the brightness of divinity is friendly and sweet. And even if they are partially weakened and dazzled, they nevertheless do not flee, do not murmur, do not dispute, but await until “that which is perfect comes, and that which is in part is done away” (I Cor. XIII).

These things were already prefigured in those people who heard the Lord Jesus, as what follows will show. It follows: “He said these things in the synagogue, teaching at Capernaum.” Great teachers rightly say that this murmuring and contentious synagogue in which our Lord said these things, while those who heard him objected, “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?” was prefigured by King Achish, to whom the aforesaid David came when fleeing Saul. He is also called Abimelech, according to the title of Psalm XXXIII, when David changed his countenance, and he dismissed him, and he departed. For that synagogue said: “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?” [Col. 0488C–D]. This is rightly understood in the name of the aforesaid king, Achish. For *Achish* is interpreted “how is it?” But because that same synagogue, which did not receive the Son of God, professed the very Father of that Son to be its God, the same Son mystically calls it *Abimelech* in the title of the aforesaid Psalm, which is interpreted “the kingdom of my Father.”

That David changed his countenance signifies to us that this true David, our King and Priest according to the order of Melchizedek, was going to change the old order of priesthood according to Aaron. Achish, however—whose name is interpreted “how is it?”—represented, as has been said, the type of this synagogue, which says, as it now says: How did he descend from heaven? How can he give us his flesh to eat and his blood to drink? For, refusing in its heart to admit these things that struck at its faith, it drives David away as one drumming and knocking upon the gates of the city, by the hard unbelief of its resistance [Col. 0489A]. Therefore Achish, or Abimelech, dismissed him, saying: “Why have you brought me a madman? Send him away from here, and let him not enter my house” (I Kings XXI).

For truly he dismissed her and departed: he dismissed the synagogue, I say, and went to the Church from among the Gentiles, because she accounted the change of his countenance—that is, the aforesaid transfer of the old priesthood—as madness. Thus, in what was said there of the same David—“the saliva was running down upon his beard”—nothing can be understood better than that our Lord seemed to them to be speaking childish or foolish things, like children who, while trying to speak, let saliva run down upon their chins, when he said: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves.”

Accordingly, the continuation of this Gospel reading runs thus: “Therefore many of his disciples, hearing, said: This saying is hard; who can hear it?” In the aforementioned Psalm, in whose title the change of the old priesthood is signified to us, as has been said, by David’s change of countenance, those few who, while the others withdraw, remain attached here to the true Priest say: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. XXXIII). But these many—and all those whom Holy Scripture customarily denotes by the name of a multitude, as there: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. XX); and again: “I have announced and spoken; they have multiplied beyond number” (Ps. XXXIX)—these many, I say, and heaps of much chaff, say: “This saying is hard; who can hear it?” [Col. 0489B–C].

Clearly they are moved in their minds by a contrary spirit and resist the Spirit of God, just as they express concerning this sacrament opinions contrary to those of the good. The latter say, “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet”; the former say, “This saying is hard.” See how opposed they are, and how opposed are their words. For a hard saying is contrary to a sweet one, as bitter is to sweet, as harsh is to gentle. Indeed, these contrary utterances, which were then spoken in that synagogue, have not been absent down to the present day.

To them this saying was hard, by which he had said: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves.” First, because, judging according to the flesh—which alone they relished—they understood him to have said that his flesh must be cut up and thus eaten, as they were accustomed to cut up and eat the flesh of a lamb or any brute beast; and that his blood must be drunk, although the Law permits them not even to taste the blood of any animal, saying: “You shall not eat with the blood” (Gen. IX; Lev. III). They understood that, according to his sense or teaching, no one could have life in himself unless he did this. Yet it was evident, both by the authority of divine law and by the common judgment of all people, that this was a horrible and accursed crime [Col. 0489D–0490A], and thus was not merely powerless to attain life, but wholly contrary and opposed to life itself.

Furthermore, with such an interpretation they might have been troubled by this: even if it could in some way have been lawful for him to be cut up and eaten, and for his blood to be drunk, he would scarcely be sufficient for a few, so that each might receive a small portion. Thus scarcely a hundred persons could attain life, whereas the abundant multitude of people belonging to life can be numbered by no one but God alone.

Nor would it have been so very remarkable if untrained disciples had been unable to grasp so great a mystery, since they were still children (I Cor. III; Heb. V) and at that time needed milk rather than solid food. Yet they were blameworthy, and incurred judgment for their rashness, because they accused their Master’s saying of hardness, rather than acknowledging the slowness or incapacity of their own understanding [Col. 0490B].

This saying seemed hard to them in that sense. But to those who still today murmur and contend when we defend the truth of the Lord’s body and blood, we seem to utter great harshness for other reasons. For, beyond the difficulties mentioned above and refuted as far as possible—not difficulties in the saying, but in their own hearts, to whom this good and sweet saying appears hard—when they are constrained by reasoned faith on the authority of the Gospel, so that they cannot deny that this body of the Lord is that which was delivered up for us, and that this blood of his is that which was shed for us; when, I say, we have firmly established this for them, they say: “Therefore, if this bread is called or is Christ not figuratively but truly, then Christ suffers daily and dies as often as this bread is broken in commemoration of him.” And, they say, “this saying is hard.” Even if Paul did not say, “Christ, risen from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. VI), who could bear this saying? We say that we have learned by experience that they say these and similar things [the printed text has *didicimus*, “we have learned”].

On the contrary, all those to whom it is revealed, not by flesh and blood but by the Father who is in heaven (Matt. XVI), all whom he draws to the Son by a sweet drawing—that is, by the revelation of the Holy Spirit—say and feel, as stated above, that this saying is not hard but sweet, because they have tasted and seen. And they say to us: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. XXXIII) [Col. 0490C–D]. Those who were then present, although they did not yet know how the things they heard could come to pass, nevertheless perceived the sweetness of this saying, so that later they said: “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life” (John VI). For, having the palate of their hearts healed by humble goodwill, they understood of him that his words lacked neither the richness nor the abundance of truth and wisdom. The things which the teacher of venerable authority deigned to set before them they awaited with submissive minds, until he should deign himself to explain them.

But after he himself, at the very moment of his passion, delivered to them the manner or order of eating his body and drinking his blood, and afterward sent the Spirit of truth to teach them all truth (Matt. XXVI; Acts II; John XIX), they too tasted the sweetness of this saying, and set it before us to taste in both speech and writing. With the help of that same Spirit, in order that we too may taste and understand, we rightly reject as groundless that aforementioned objection by which they tell us that, if this bread is truly Christ, then—contrary to the saying of the aforementioned Apostle and to all faith—Christ suffers or dies as often as this bread is broken upon the Lord’s table. Our faith has not become so worn out, nor have its eyes become so dim, that it cannot see itself breaking the bread of God while keeping the Son of God whole, just as aged Abraham could see that he struck the ram and did not injure his son laid upon the altar [Col. 0491A–B].

Although this visible bread has become one with the invisible Son of God, that ram could not be, or become, one with Isaac, for whom it was placed upon the same altar (Gen. XXII). For the Son of God—that is, God and man—has within himself the effective power by which he unites this visible bread to himself. But Isaac could not incorporate the ram into himself while preserving both substances. Therefore Isaac was there sacrificed figuratively in the ram; here the Son of God is sacrificed in bread and wine in the truth of his flesh and blood.

Was it not so that, just as Father Abraham with the same sword sacrificed the ram when he had led forth his son to sacrifice him, so the priest, with the people standing by, pierces the bread and wine placed upon the altar with the word of that same cross and passion by which Christ suffered? Let those who do not believe this fail to know that our same Lord is then especially present in our midst. For when he himself said, “Wherever two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in their midst,” he is much more present in our midst and bends over his altar where, not for any random purpose, but to perform this his own and greatest memorial, we assemble, armed with all faith and its instruments [Col. 0491B–C].

For we have tasted and seen; and therefore we have not listened to those who murmur and say, “This saying is hard,” but answer instead: certainly, and truly, “the Lord is sweet.” Thus the same mixture, now endured in the Church, of those who disagree and speak contrary things, heard our Lord then in that small gathering of disciples with very different minds. Indeed, those called disciples murmured more grievously than the other Jews. For they express their unbelief more strongly in saying, “This saying is hard; who can hear it?” than the others did in saying, “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?” What the disciples say is not merely murmuring or contentious dispute, but the despair of rebellion.

“But Jesus, knowing within himself that his disciples murmured about this, said to them: Does this scandalize you?” “Within himself,” he says—that is, needing no informant—he knew who the murmurers were. He did not first know when they had already begun to murmur; but before he spoke this mystery, because of which they murmured, he knew as God which of his disciples were teachable in the things of God, and which bore, in the inward hearing of their hearts, a willingness to learn and a reverence worthy of heavenly instruction [Col. 0491D–0492A]. Yet, to express the greatness of their unworthiness, he asks in astonishment, as though their unbelief had only now first been discovered: “Does this scandalize you?”

For it is indeed worthy of some astonishment that the living and true bread—life-giving and sweet in itself—should be, in their view, a stone and rock, “a stone of stumbling and a rock of scandal” (II Peter II), so that, rushing against it, they are shattered, and thus crushed by that same bread coming down upon them from above; and that by the bread through which they ought to have been nourished unto life, they are scandalized unto death as by a hard stone of stumbling (Matt. XXI; Luke XX). For to be scandalized properly, or most of all, is to turn backward from a good purpose through stumbling at some occasion. They suffered this greatest scandal through being struck by that bread of such sweetness; for, as is shortly added, they went back and no longer walked with him. The sweet Lord therefore rightly marvels: “Does this scandalize you?”

“If therefore you see the Son of Man ascending where he was before.” The discourse fittingly breaks off at this point, as if the movement or recognition of their angry-minded scandal were worthy of such an interruption in speech [Col. 0492B–C]. “Therefore,” he says, “since even you, who were called my disciples, do not approach the teacher with the feet of one drawing near according to the discipline of instruction, so as to be judged worthy to receive the teaching of eternal life with a submissive ear, but instead are scandalized and undisciplinedly criticize my proposition, I shall not disclose to you that same proposition, whose solution you do not deserve to obtain by pressing a worthy question.

“I now say what, by your own admission, is plainly quite contrary to your carnal understanding: namely, that the Son of Man will ascend where he was before. For the Son of Man’s ascending into heaven, and his flesh being eaten and his blood drunk in the manner you understand, are altogether incompatible and cannot in any way coexist or happen. And I say the Son of Man, not the Son of God, lest you suppose that I have said that, once the flesh has been devoured by your bites, what remains—the incorporeal nature alone—will ascend into heaven. But if you see—or rather, because you will see—for though, going backward, you do not deserve to see, I shall ascend into heaven while those disciples who persevered with me to the end look on (Matt. X, XXIV). Yet you will see that I have ascended then, when every eye sees this same Son of Man coming with clouds (Apoc. I), with all his flesh. Then you will understand that you unjustly charged this saying with hardness, that you thought wrongly, and that, worse still, without awaiting the Teacher’s instruction, you were too quickly scandalized and went backward.”

It should be noted that although the nature according to which he is the Son of Man had its beginning from his mother’s womb, and before that Incarnation Christ was in no way man or Son of Man but only God, the Son of God, nevertheless he asserts that the Son of Man was previously in heaven, whither he would ascend. By this saying, as also by the other in which he says, “No one ascends into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John III), he intended to affirm the unity of person in the one Christ, God and man [Col. 0492D–0493A].

Nestorius, ignorant of this and therefore rightly to be ignored, forbade the blessed Mary to be called the Mother of God, because the nature taken from her flesh was, he held, only human and not divine. Thus he wickedly divided the one Christ into two Christs, one God and the other man, whereas the same Son of Man had previously been in the heaven to which he afterward ascended, and was already in heaven according to his divinity while still speaking on earth according to his humanity. “He who descended,” says the Apostle, “is the same one who ascended” (Eph. IV). It follows:

“The Spirit is that which gives life; the flesh profits nothing.” This statement in no way destroys or weakens the preceding one, in which he said, “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man,” and so forth. Rather, it corrects the carnal sense of those who misunderstand, taking nothing away from the reality of eating his flesh, but adding that the spirit of that same flesh must also be eaten together with it. “It is the Spirit,” he says, “that gives life; the flesh profits nothing.” As if he said: “In the manner in which you understand what I said above—‘Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves’—the flesh of no living creature can be eaten with its life, nor can its blood be drunk. For this to be done by a human being, or while it is done by a beast, the animal must, as is known, be slaughtered. I shall give my flesh to no one to eat in this way. For my ‘flesh,’ unless it is eaten alive and with its spirit, ‘profits nothing.’ Flesh alone, flesh without spirit, ‘profits nothing’; for ‘it is the Spirit that gives life.’”

When he says this, does he destroy the meaning set forth in the preceding words? On the contrary, he supplies and completes it, lest we imagine that in the breaking of the Lord’s bread we eat such fragments of his flesh as were the limbs taken down from the wood and placed in the tomb: flesh without soul, without spirit, without life [Col. 0493B–D]. Such “flesh profits nothing.” Indeed, the Jews would have defiled their bellies with a still greater sacrilege if, after crucifying him, they had attacked his lifeless body with their teeth—had he permitted it, he who was not to allow “his Holy One to see corruption” (Ps. XV)—and had thus eaten him in the way these scandalized persons understood, unable to bear what seemed to them a hard saying.

He forbids us altogether to suppose that his flesh and blood in his bread and cup are such lifeless flesh and blood, when he says: “It is the Spirit that gives life; the flesh profits nothing.” But what is the Spirit which gives life to this flesh, so that it may benefit those who eat it? He says: “The words which I have spoken to you are spirit and life.” The words, I say, which I have spoken and speak to you—whatever concerns me, from the time when the Son of Man descended until he ascends where he was before: the words of my incarnation, birth, passion, resurrection, and ascension—are spirit and life: life-giving spirit, living life, and the true word of life. These work invisibly in the bread of which I shall say, “This is my body,” and in the wine of which I shall say, “This is my blood,” so that they are my true flesh and blood without change in their outward appearance [Col. 0494A]. Likewise they work spiritually in individual human beings—that is, without any alteration in the outward accidents of the body—so that they may be my members, renewed in the spirit of their minds; and so that, after many are separated from the body of the devil, one Church may be made, which in another respect is called and is my body, my fullness.

There are three developments in this discourse, for understanding which faith alone is the merit; for their understanding is a fitting reward of true and great faith. The first is that against which these men, lacking faith, stumbled as against a hard stone: “Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you shall not have life in yourselves.” The second is that by which he strikes their carnal understanding, since they supposed that he wished his flesh to be eaten without its spirit, as the flesh of any animal is eaten—a flesh which can in no way benefit the living entrails of its eaters together with its spirit, unless it has been killed: “It is the Spirit,” he says, “that gives life; the flesh profits nothing” [Col. 0494B–C]. The third is that by which he defines the Spirit and life itself, which alone is eatable. For no life other than this life can be apprehended by living persons, and no one but a rational spirit is capable of its spirit or life: “The words which I have spoken to you,” he says, “are spirit and life.”

These three matters which I have mentioned must now be reconsidered more fully, that it may become increasingly evident how beautifully and by what a rational art of truth they are joined step by step. We already understand that “the words which he has spoken are spirit and life.” But what kind of Spirit, what kind of life? First, this too must be said: the many words that he spoke are one Word—one Word, I say, which itself became flesh. He spoke that one Word by many words—that is, by many elementary and articulated sounds—and placed into the mouths of our souls the many mysteries of his incarnation, birth, passion, resurrection, and ascension. These words are of such a kind—or rather, this one Word is of such power—that it may always be eaten and can never be consumed. For the Word of the Lord remains forever (Isa. XL); when it has been eaten, it springs up again from the good soil of the soul and rises into a great harvest. So too that water which is the Holy Spirit, when drunk, immediately springs up as a fountain in the drinker’s breast and flows out into rivers of living water [Col. 0494C–D].

And, as was said, only a rational spirit is capable of this Spirit or life alone, and this life alone is capable of being received by a rational spirit. Therefore it is rightly and truly called his food and drink. But this Word became flesh, and now, in visible flesh exercising the five senses, spoke present words among those many who murmured and contended, and the few who believed (John IV, VII). Therefore neither the Spirit—that is, the Word, for the Word, equally with the Father and the Holy Spirit, is one God, Spirit—nor the flesh can now be eaten separately: neither the Spirit, that is, the Word without flesh, nor flesh without Spirit. For the Word cannot be loved or worshipped without the due praise of his incarnation. But again, as was said above, the flesh of no living creature can be eaten together with its spirit. When it is eaten, or in order that it may be eaten, it is separated from its spirit; that is, it is killed. Therefore he turns his hearers away from such eating: “It is the Spirit,” he says, “that gives life; the flesh profits nothing” [Col. 0495A–B].

There remained, then, in his words, “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man,” and so forth, some manner of eating and drinking to await, by which flesh together with spirit, and spirit together with flesh, could be eaten, so that both might benefit the human being dead in flesh and spirit. They would have understood that this manner was to be awaited if they had believed; but because they were unbelieving, they were impatient to learn. For it follows:

“But there are some among you who do not believe.” As if he said: “It is not because my saying is hard that it scandalizes some of you, but because some of you have hardened your hearts in unbelief, my saying seems to contain hardness. And you do not fail to believe because you do not understand; rather, you do not understand because you do not believe. For Scripture says: ‘Unless you believe, you shall not understand.’ Therefore we too believe, not because we have understood, but in order that we may understand.”

For truly, just as Christ is one God and man, so this consecrated visible bread is one flesh with that flesh which hung upon the cross: it is one body of Christ. And just as divinity suffered nothing in the true death of the flesh, so when the true body of Christ is sacrificed, broken, and eaten upon the altar, that same humanity of Christ—which suffered once and rose again—“suffers nothing; for he dies no more, and death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. VI) [Col. 0495B–C].

So far as we could, with God’s help, we have taken care to prove from its very bleating that the holy bread and cup which we receive from the altar are the true and living Lamb of God, continually presenting himself there in order both to cover us with his wool and to refresh us with his flesh. We have eaten, as far as we could, namely the head with the feet and entrails: that is, we have devoured both his divinity and humanity, together with the subtle sayings of his mysteries, leaving aside nothing at all that we have been able to attain with the firm tooth of faith. If anything remains, however, we burn it with fire—that is, we entrust it to the Holy Spirit—because we are unable in every respect to comprehend by reason all the mysteries of this Lamb. His grace deals well with us if we can attain and hold firmly what is necessary for eternal salvation. It follows:

“But Jesus knew who were believers, and who would betray him” [Col. 0495D–0496A]. Clearly, he knew this not from some outcome, chance, or moment of human conjecture, but from the beginning—that is, from eternity. For before the foundation of the world he foreknew and predestined those who were to be called holy and blameless in his sight (Eph. I; I Peter I). “And he said to them: Therefore I said to you: No one can come to me unless it has been given him by my Father.” “Because,” he says, “there are some among you who do not believe, and I knew this from the beginning, therefore I said above: ‘No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him’; and now I say the same thing again in words slightly changed but with the meaning remaining: ‘No one can come to me unless it has been given him by my Father.’”

He repeated the same thing now because what he then said is plainly now shown true by the disposition with which they are scandalized. For if the Father had drawn them, if it had been given them by the Father to come to the Son—that is, if he had persuaded them by divinely inspired goodwill to become his disciples—then, believing and by believing tasting that sweetness through which all the elect are drawn, they too would have been drawn more and more [Col. 0496A–B].

“From this many of his disciples went back and no longer walked with him.” Let those who especially disparage the heads of local churches—that is, abbots of monasteries—whenever they suffer loss in their flock, hear this. Though these critics themselves are idle, they rashly judge God’s workers when they see some among those whom the workers have, at their exhortation, converted relapse into the world. “See,” they say, “how indiscreet they are, how rashly and thoughtlessly they call people, receive those who come, and compel them to be bound before God by vowed promises. Then, again, by excessive severity or harshness, scandalizing those whom they have received and who are subject to them (Matt. XIII), they force them into a worse ruin. In every respect they are like the Pharisees, who traversed sea and land to make one proselyte, and then made him twice as much a son of perdition as themselves” (Matt. XIII).

What would these people say? How would they insult those who labor and seek the gain of souls whenever they suffer any such loss, if something of this kind had not happened even to Christ? How would they disparage those casting nets and enclosing good fish as though they were bad, if they admitted only good fish? They would blame their imprudence and charge them with admitting such people as those through whose discordant tumults the nets are torn: some causing seditions, others pursuing drunkenness, fornications, and similar things; others cutting themselves off from the unity of faith through heresies and schisms [Col. 0496C–D].

It was therefore good that this happened even to Christ; indeed, Christ willed that it should happen to himself, that he might have good and bad intermingled and endure them until the wind of their own fault should carry the bad away from the good, as chaff from grain. No one should dare to infer from this that, when people of good will, unable to distinguish the good from the bad, admit both good and bad together and endure them until the last judgment separates them from one another, anyone ought to rebuke them.

For it belongs to a human being to cry out and make a sound outside the ear; but it belongs to God alone to grasp the hearer’s heart with an invisible hand and draw it to Christ [Col. 0497A]. Is anyone to be required to be more effective than Christ himself, by word and deed, in gaining souls? Therefore whenever anything of this kind happens to us, because it also happened to Christ, we say with him: “No one can come to me unless it has been given him by my Father.” It follows:

“Jesus therefore said to the Twelve: ‘Do you also wish to go away?’” You too, he says, whom the Father has given me, whom the Father has drawn to me, to whom it has been granted by my Father that you should come to me—“do you also wish to go away?” He certainly does not ask this in order that he may know; rather, under the form of a question he more attentively confirms [Col. 0497B] that he loses none of those whom the Father has given him. At the same time, while others are losing confidence, he fittingly requires from those who believed the necessary confession: for, just as “with the heart one believes unto righteousness,” so “with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. X).

Simon Peter answers: “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life; and we have believed and known that you are the Christ, the Son of God.” Plainly, this was to happen in Christ’s Church: when Antichristians were scandalized and caused scandals—many who went out from us (John IV), but were not of us—the lovers of Christ would shake themselves free and exhort one another; troubled by the seditious importunity of the faithless, they would more abundantly [Col. 0497C] and more resonantly proclaim, in speech and writing, the confession of the true faith to the whole world. Nor would they cease until, by truthful and authoritative writings, they had refuted Satan, “falling like lightning from heaven” (Luke X), together with his attendants, and had slain them through the pious outpouring of their own blood.

Peter here and elsewhere gives expression to the unity and faith of this faithful Church; he is the first to utter its voice. Hence he receives his name from the rock upon which that same Church is founded, and, honoured by the great praise of his confession, he also merits to receive the keys of the kingdom of heaven (Matt. XVI). Thus, the fact that, when the question is addressed to the twelve apostles, he alone answers for all must be ascribed universally to the one Church as a whole.

For the one perfect and beautiful bride, the Church (Cant. I), surrounded by companies of young women, says to her beloved Christ [Col. 0497D]: “Lord, to whom shall we go?” That is: amid such great disturbances of Arian wickedness and of the other plagues, will you not show us where you pasture, where you lie down, as the Spirit of your truth reveals this to us—so that we should begin to wander after the flocks of your companions? “You have the words of eternal life”: that is, you possess words that bear eternal life; “and we have believed and known that you are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” We did not first know and then believe; rather, we first believe, and thereafter know. For knowledge does not precede faith, but faith precedes knowledge. Faith is merit; knowledge of the Son of God is faith’s reward.

“Jesus answered them: ‘Did I not choose you twelve, and one of you is a devil?’” Why does the gentle Lamb, when many disciples have fallen away, inveigh so sharply against the few who remained? They might now rather seem fit to be warmly commended, especially since he had received from them the same confession of great faith which elsewhere he had declared blessed with worthy praise, saying: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, for flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. XVI).

Indeed, what he says—“Did I not choose you twelve?”—is a proclamation of grace that blesses them. Yet it is also an utterance of great severity and rebuke, both because he states even this in question form and because he immediately adds, terrifyingly: “And one of you is a devil.” Why, then, at such a moment, does he strike them all by this dreadful identification of one man? By not naming him expressly, he presses upon all of them, making each exceedingly anxious [Col. 0498A] on his own account.

They could not think that one so often proved to be the judge of consciences could be mistaken; nor could any of them comprehend the consciences of the others; nor, being uncertain about the future and seeing so many fall into folly, did each dare to set a high value on his own merits. Why, I ask, did he wish this, unless because it was expedient for them? Human weakness needs to be mortified by no sin so much as by that into which fell “the workers of iniquity”: “they were driven out and could not stand” [Ps. 35:12–13]. And what is that sin but the foot of pride? “Let not the foot of pride come against me,” says the Psalmist, “and let not the hand of the sinner move me” (Ps. XXXV).

For when that wandering and unstable [Col. 0498B] foot of pride comes—which commonly comes from excessive self-assurance or confidence in one’s righteousness—the hand of the ancient sinner at once finds the empty and unwatchful person outside, where it may swiftly move him from his good resolve, since he has turned away from God, “who resists the proud” (Jas. IV). Therefore, so that “the sons of men may hope under the shelter of the Lord’s wings” (Ps. XXXV), and, thinking humbly of themselves, may not exalt themselves, their souls are fittingly humbled by anxious fear at the fall of others. We all are instructed by the example: when the neighbouring wall is burning, we should fear for our own house; that is, while those who seemed to stand with us fall, we who still seem to stand should humbly consider that a like fall may happen to us.

[Col. 0498D] “Now he was speaking of Judas, son of Simon Iscariot.” Judas Iscariot took his name either from the village in which he was born or from the tribe of Issachar. He is also called “of Simon”—understand, Simon’s son or kinsman—in order to distinguish him from the other Judas, who in turn, to distinguish him from this man, is called Judas of James—understand, James’s brother—and is also known by the other name of Thaddaeus the apostle.

The Evangelist, wishing rightly to prove that this Judas was called a devil, adds a suitable reason, saying: “For he was about to betray him, though he was one of the twelve.” For “devil” is a Greek name not of nature but of a most evil accident, and it means “flowing downward.” By this name that condemned and lost angel is rightly called: though he had been created good and was greatest among the spirits dwelling in the height [Col. 0499A] of heaven, through his own fault he flowed downward in pride and was hurled into the depths of hell; by deed and by name he became a devil.

But Judas flowed downward, and the Evangelist plainly expressed that very descent when he said: “For he was about to betray him, though he was one of the twelve.” Who does not know that the apostolic rank is higher than all orders of saints, both old and new? Again, who is unaware that the treachery by which that unhappy man betrayed the Lord was an exceedingly deep crime? Therefore, since Wisdom also says, “When the ungodly man curses the devil, he curses his own soul” (Ecclus. XXI)—because the soul of the ungodly has flowed downward and became ungodly only by flowing downward—the Lord rightly calls this standard-bearer of impiety a devil. [Col. 0499B] His soul, with all its efforts, was flowing from the lofty honour of the apostolic summit down into the deep place of his own destruction. Thus the Lord calls him a devil, although he was still hypocritically performing the apostolic office, and though no one more wicked had yet withdrawn.

Many dispute why the Lord chose this son of perdition for the apostolate, if he knew that the man’s intention was evil—for he who knows all things could certainly not be ignorant of what he was. Some maintain that Judas was good before his fall, arguing that otherwise our Lord ought not to have called him to the grace of so great an order. For, they say, if in Christ’s ministers and stewards of God’s mysteries it is judged blameworthy and unlawful to lay hands upon those known to be unworthy (1 Tim. V), and they are commanded not to lay hands hastily upon anyone—that is, not unless they see merits previously demonstrated by good works—how much more ought the supremely just One, justice itself, not to entrust the sacred ministries of apostolic rank to anyone unworthy?

Therefore, they say, Judas was good before his fall and was no less worthy of apostolic eminence than his fellow apostles. For Christ could neither have been deceived, so as not to know Judas’s unworthiness, nor act unworthily by entrusting holy ministry to an unworthy man and committing his money-bags to him more intimately.

One answer must satisfy both parties. First, we ask them whether any Judas today attains an apostolic—that is, episcopal—office. Indeed, since some maintain, as stated above, that Judas was good before the apostolate, [Col. 0499D] do they hold that no one except good men enters upon apostolic sacraments? Plainly, they cannot deny that very many evil men are able, with God’s permission, both to be evil and to exercise so great an office. In no respect unlike Judas, they amass for themselves the money for whose desire they cling to Christ; holding the sacred coffers in their power, they carry away the Church’s revenues by sacrilegious plunder.

What then? Does Christ admit such persons and work his sacraments through them in ignorance or by unjust arrangement? Since today he is shown to admit some who are certainly evil, as is clear from their fruits, the argument by which they say Judas was good before his fall because Christ made him an apostle is weak.

Yet one who investigates more carefully is not yet satisfied. For he may still object as follows: Christ rightly endured Judas while he was persecuting him, in order that by Judas’s fall he might more firmly establish the condition of the others in fear and humility. For it is commanded that good persons should patiently endure evil persons whom they cannot correct (Matt. V; Rom. XII). No one chooses to be Abel unless Cain’s malice tests him (Gen. IV). But again, it is commanded that we should not give what is holy to dogs (Matt. VII), and that one who will not receive correction should be to us “as a heathen and a publican” (Matt. XVIII). Yet Christ knew Judas not merely as some ordinary flesh, not merely as someone like a heathen, but as a devil. Ought he then to have entrusted to him the holy sacraments of life?

To this, I say: the sacraments of our salvation were instituted in Christ’s passion, death, and resurrection. In the Passion—that is, at the very moment of his Passion—the eucharist of his body and blood was first consecrated by him in that place. Concerning baptism also, it is clear to those who inquire—as the authority of the holy Roman Church everywhere, and especially against certain Greeks, maintains—that it was instituted in his death and resurrection. In that death and resurrection, according to Paul, we too are baptized and “buried through baptism, so that, as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too may walk in newness of life” (Rom. VI).

Did he send his disciples to baptize before this, or deliver to them the aforesaid sacrament of his body and blood? We read indeed that not Jesus himself but his disciples baptized, while John was still alive and baptizing (John IV). But after John had been delivered up and Jesus succeeded to the work of preaching, neither he himself nor anyone by his command baptized, nor did he establish the rule of baptism before the resurrection.

But Judas did not reach that hour in which Christ suffered for his own, to whom he said: “And I will go to be sacrificed for you”; nor did he receive with them the seal of apostleship—that is, the Holy Spirit—which Christ first gave then for the remission of sins, when, glorified by rising again, he breathed on them and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them” (Luke XXII; John XX). There is no doubt that Judas was absent from this: neither when Christ was sacrificed for his own, nor when, rising again, he gave them [Col. 0500D] his Spirit.

As to participation in his body and blood, someone might suppose that Judas was present. Yet, if one considers more closely the Evangelists’ account and the differing views of the teachers, one may more readily discover that he was not present even at this sacrament. For after he received the morsel by which the betrayer was identified, he immediately went out. No Evangelist or teacher agrees that this morsel was the bread of the Lord’s body. Since he went out immediately (John XIII), it is certainly clear that, as has been said, he did not communicate in Christ’s body and blood.

For only after the typical Passover, by whose morsel he was marked out, had been completed and he had eaten the lamb’s flesh with the apostles, did Christ take bread, “which strengthens the heart of man,” and pass over to the true sacrament of the Passover. Thus, just as Melchizedek, priest of the Most High God, had done in its prefiguration by offering bread and wine, so Christ himself might set forth in truth his own body and blood.

Although this order is manifestly clear from the other Evangelists, Luke alone gave some occasion for another opinion. This was not because he reversed the aforesaid order of the typical Passover (Luke XXII) and the sacred eucharist, or stated it less clearly than the others, but because he alone wrote later than the others the Lord’s words concerning his betrayer at supper. That is, by anticipating the institution of the sacred eucharist, he joined words spoken at the earlier supper with words spoken afterward.

Therefore, since Judas was appointed indeed to the apostolate but attained no actual possession of that order by any sacrament of life, every argument for his prior goodness fails. There is nothing in Christ’s example of temporarily admitting Judas that hinders those who walk rightly.

Thus this son of perdition was never good, nor did he become evil after having been chosen while good. Rather, because he was evil, he was chosen for a necessary work by him who knows how to use evil persons well; and in Christ’s sight he was always regarded as evil—evil, I say, not through natural wickedness but through an accidental vice. If anyone says that Judas was good by reason of the office of preaching and performing signs, we grant it. For even evil bishops, however evil they may be in their morals, so long as they hold the catholic faith, are good trees by reason of the office they perform. Much might be said concerning their election, by which Judas too was chosen by divine judgment; but, avoiding wearisome prolixity, let us proceed with the Gospel narrative.

## Chapter VII

“After these things Jesus was walking in Galilee. For he did not wish to walk in Judaea, because the Jews were seeking to kill him. Now the feast-day of the Jews, the Feast of Tabernacles, was near.”

The Law and the Prophets testify that Christ the Lord, having power over his own life and death alike and over ours, willed to suffer and to enter into his glory at the time and in the order in which he suffered, died, and, rising again, advanced to the right hand of the Father’s glory. He himself set forth beforehand those whom his own Spirit had instructed; and their testimony does not fall silent as long as the Gospel glory of Christ is proclaimed [Col. 0501D]. For the prophets predicted nothing other than what they foresaw in the Holy Spirit as already fixed in his will; nor could his power admit any other manner of death than that which he had long before ordained within himself, as those same holy prophets looked on.

But the Jews, knowing nothing of the mystery of his will and following their blind rage, sought to kill him by any means whatsoever—for example, now to throw him down (Luke IV), now desiring to overwhelm him with stones (John VIII). They cared for nothing else, provided only that he should be taken from their midst; and they said only this: “When will he die, and his name perish?” (Ps. XL).

Therefore, because it pertained to him to foresee the necessary and fitting time and manner of his death, appropriate to our cause, “Jesus,” says the Evangelist, “was walking in Galilee. For he did not wish to walk in Judaea, because the Jews were seeking to kill him.” Certainly, the surface meaning of the letter conveys a not contemptible weakness which his faithful should reasonably imitate, avoiding death when time or circumstance requires. Yet what follows in the reading indicates rather the other intention already mentioned—that of him who withdrew himself—which the Evangelist at once begins to commend, saying: “Now the feast-day of the Jews, the Feast of Tabernacles, was near.”

It is as if he said: not fearing death, but because, as the Psalmist says, “the sun knew its setting” (Ps. CIII), and having another time fixed for his death, he did not wish to walk into Judaea and give place to his killers. Of this his own time he says a little later: “My time has not yet come.”

For he knew that the Feast of Tabernacles—*Scenopegia*, that is, the feast of booths—in the seventh month was not his own time but that of his forerunner John: the time in which John was announced by an angel to his father Zachariah and afterward conceived in a barren womb. But Christ had long foreseen his own time in the paschal solemnity of the first month, when he, the true Lamb of God, was to be sacrificed to God the Father for the whole world; and at that same time he himself had been announced by an angel and conceived in the Virgin’s womb.

For indeed, according to the regular cycles of all computists, it is certain that on Friday—the day on which the first man was created—in the paschal month, that is, when the moon was newly born, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April [25 March], Jesus Christ our Lord, the Lamb of God, was conceived for the restoration of universal salvation, when the angel announced this to the blessed Virgin. Therefore, as the disposer of his own life and death, the Lord rightly awaited this time and did not wish to go up on this feast-day of Tabernacles—that is, to enter the glory of his immortality by passing from this world to the Father at that time (Luke XXIII).

Although the Evangelist says in the singular, “There was a feast-day of the Jews,” we must nevertheless understand that this feast was to be observed not on one day but on several. For thus it is written of it in the Law:

> “Therefore, from the fifteenth day of the seventh month, when you have gathered all the fruits of your land, you shall celebrate the Lord’s feast for seven days. On the first day and on the eighth day there shall be a Sabbath, that is, rest.”

And shortly afterward it adds concerning the reason for this feast:

> “In the seventh month you shall celebrate feasts, and you shall dwell in booths for seven days. Everyone who is of the stock of Israel shall remain in booths, so that your descendants may learn that I caused the children of Israel to dwell in booths when I brought them out of the land of Egypt” (Lev. XXIII).

The Jews therefore made booths resembling the booths in which they had lived when, brought out of Egypt, they wandered in the wilderness; and they kept the feast-day, a great solemnity, as though recalling the benefits of the Lord whom they were about to kill.

“His brothers therefore said to him: ‘Depart from here and go into Judaea, so that your disciples also may see the works which you do.’” These brothers of Jesus are his relatives or kinsmen. Loving the glory of this world and falsely judging, with their earthly understanding, the true glory of the heavenly man, they gave him the vain advice of extending his fame: namely, that, hastening to become known to all, he should take care not to be absent from so solemn a gathering and should not refrain from displaying miracles.

For this feast was one of the three at which the Law commanded every male Israelite to appear before the Lord (Exod. XXIII). Presuming to go before God’s wisdom with their own understanding and to show him the way, after saying this they attempted to establish their sinister intention by perverse reasoning, saying: “For no one does anything in secret and himself seeks to be openly known.”

The statement is indeed true: no one who employs reason so thoroughly contradicts himself.
