For it is truly inconsistent to wish to become known to people and yet conceal one’s noble deeds—just as if someone wished at once to be in the night and to possess the sun, or for the Lord’s lamp to burn brightly and for its light to be seen by no one. Yet this statement was not made at the right time.

For our Lord did nothing in secret, because he did nothing which he wished to be hidden; nor did he seek to be openly known in the way they supposed. He did not wish to receive brightness from human beings, but to give brightness to them; he came not to please human beings, but to train them to please God. The statement was therefore true, but empty—indeed perverse—and uttered in an alien spirit.

They still try to confirm it by adding: “If you do these things, manifest yourself to the world.” That is: if you do not do these things, you do not manifest yourself to the world.

What these men said might still have seemed like the words which good and faithful brothers ought to speak, not unworthy of those brothers whom we know to have been Christ’s apostles, men indeed of apostolic holiness and faith. But hear what the Evangelist adds against this opinion: “For not even his brothers believed in him.” Certainly those brothers of honoured memory whom, as has already been said, we know to have been apostles—James of Alphaeus, surnamed the Just; Simon the Cananaean; and Judas, also called Thaddaeus—believed in him.

For a little above, the voice of Simon Peter was the voice of all the apostles, Judas the devil alone excepted; one man answered for all: “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life, and we have believed and known that you are the Christ, the Son of God.” But these, says the Evangelist, “his brothers did not believe in him.” Their words therefore testify not so much to goodwill as to envy, since they were not greatly concerned if he should be killed—though they could not have been ignorant of the Jews’ hatred against him.

“Jesus therefore said to them: ‘My time has not yet come; but your time is always ready.’” — “There is a time for all things,” says Ecclesiastes, and afterward: “A time to weep, a time to laugh, a time to mourn, and a time to dance” (Eccl. III). Let fools hear this—those who despise wisdom preaching in the streets, who have neither ears nor eyes in their head, and who, at the ends of the earth, do not distinguish these times. For he did not say “a time to laugh and a time to weep,” but first a time to weep and then a time to laugh; first a time to mourn and afterward a time to dance (Prov. I; Eccl. II).

Because they do not distinguish these times, they snatch premature laughter and dance and revel in uncommanded and untimely festivities; and therefore the present condition of things has not yet changed. For the present state must pass away, and another, far different and contrary, must follow. It is necessary to pass from laughter to weeping, from dancing to mourning.

But the King of that future city, whose “kingdom is not of this world” (John XVIII), knows that he and his own must first weep and afterward laugh; first mourn and afterward rejoice. Therefore he says: “My time has not yet come; but your time is always ready.”

What then? When your time comes, will you seek to be openly known and manifest yourself to the world? Indeed I shall, but that manifestation of mine will be of a glory and honour utterly different from your glory and the brief honour of this present time of yours. For you pursue glory by flattering the evil works of the world; I shall advance to glory by detesting the world’s evil works. This is what follows:

“The world cannot hate you; but it hates me, because I bear witness concerning it that its works are evil.” Things that differ cannot differ in any more opposite manner. These are plainly opposites, set against each other when he says: “The world cannot hate you; but it hates me.” And since he gives this reason for its hatred—“because I bear witness concerning it that its works are evil”—it is certainly clear that, conversely, the reason why the world cannot hate them is that they bear witness that its works are good.

Thus the wisdom of God shows, both strongly and gently, that their advisers differ greatly from his own mind—so greatly that no two things could be more different. At the same time, he indicates what is to come: namely, that his manifestation will proceed in such a way as to admit hatred, since before he exalts his head he must drink from the torrent on the way (Ps. CIX).

And he adds that against which, in light of such consequences, nothing can be said: “Go up yourselves to this feast; I am not going up to this feast, because my time has not yet been fulfilled.” O how great a weight of strength lies in the gentleness of this conclusion! Indeed, the wisdom of God here also remembers what it said in Ecclesiastes: “A time to keep silence and a time to speak” (Eccl. III). When the time comes, it will speak to such men.

In the same book it said most sternly: “Woe to you, O land, whose king is a child, and whose princes eat in the morning!” But, conversely, it added concerning itself and its own: “Blessed is the land whose king is noble, and whose princes eat at their proper time, for refreshment and not for luxury!” (Eccl. X).

For what are these lovers of the world, whose time is ever ready in the folly of earthly ambition—what are they, I ask, except the earth which the serpent eats? (Gen. III). And who is the king, the child, of that land but that father of folly, as ancient as he is foolish, whose heart is in no way possessed by the mature wisdom of God? The princes who eat in the morning are the powerful and proud lovers of the world, of whom the Lord says: “Princes arose, and I did not know” (Hos. VIII). Since in this life they receive their good things so that they may be tormented in the future, they eat, as it were, in the morning, in order to be excluded from the fellowship of those eating at the hour of supper.

Conversely, that land—the land of the living (Ps. XIV)—which the Lord established upon the seas and rivers, that is, above the embittered peoples and the raging rulers of the age, grounding it in faith and preparing it in good works, is blessed. Its king is noble: the true and consubstantial Son of God, who is also according to the flesh the son of David and the only son of the Virgin. Its princes were so ordered by the example of that noble king that in the morning they work soberly at the affairs of the kingdom, and at their proper time eat for refreshment, not luxury. For in this alien time they did not indulge themselves but laboured. Therefore, when their king prepares to recline at table in his own time, they hear him say: “And I appoint for you, as my Father appointed for me, a kingdom, that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom” (Luke XXII).

For these men, therefore, and for all those who climb in the morning toward vain glory, since the Scriptures’ declarations are not lacking from which they may hear what awaits them, it is enough that this noble King should have said gravely and sparingly in his own person: “Go up yourselves to this feast; I am not going up to the feast, because my time has not yet been fulfilled.” That is: be exalted, you who will, as much as you can, before you are humbled; and be humbled after you have been exalted. For “I shall not go up” at present, nor shall I be exalted, before I am humbled “unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. II).

“Having said these things, he himself remained in Galilee. But when his brothers had gone up, then he too went up, [Col. 0505D] not openly, but as if in secret.” It is clear that the various actions are denoted here by the one equivocal word “going up”: “Go up yourselves; I shall not go up” was said by the Lord in one sense, and “when his brothers had gone up, then he too went up” is now said by the Evangelist in another.

The Lord spoke according to their meaning, when they had said: “So that your disciples also may see the works which you do; and if you do these things, manifest yourself to the world.” He answered that he would not go up—that is, that he would not furnish an exalted spectacle of himself in pursuit of glory. But the Evangelist, as is his custom, simply expressed the ordinary journey by the same term, in accordance with the lay of the land, because those coming to Jerusalem had to go up into the hill-country of Judaea.

He also took care to add the difference between this ascent and the ascent intended by the brothers, saying: “Not openly, but as if in secret.” Why not openly but as if in secret? Because his time had not yet come; because his time had not yet been fulfilled.

What then—when his time did come, when it was fulfilled, how did he go up? Clearly, not secretly nor as if secretly, but openly. For then, when the great crowd gathered for the feast heard that Jesus was coming to Jerusalem, they took branches of palm trees, went out to meet him, and cried: “Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel.”

At that time his time had indeed been fulfilled, because, after the council had assembled, the chief priests and Pharisees said: “It is expedient that one man should die for the people” (John XII); and from that day they planned to kill him. That is, they determined to put him to death as though by lawful judicial process, and by the death he himself willed: the gibbet of the cross.

Previously the Jews had often sought to kill him, but not in such a way that the Scriptures would be fulfilled; and therefore, as was said a little above, “he did not wish to walk in Judaea, because the Jews were seeking to kill him.” Even when he had gone there and the Jews wished, as will be said later, to stone him, he did not choose to undergo death, because the Scriptures would not thus be fulfilled (John VIII).

Therefore his time was fulfilled then, and for this reason he went up not secretly but openly, with crowds acclaiming the great King, the great Son of God, the great and noble son of David. What then? Did he thereby approve the aforesaid counsel of his relatives and wish, according to their understanding, to manifest himself to the world? By no means, for this praise came not from human beings but from God. To whom else but God was it said in the Psalm: “Out of the mouths of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise” (Ps. VIII)?

This prophecy was fulfilled then. When the indignant Pharisees said: “Do you hear what these are saying?” he answered them: “Indeed. Have you never read, ‘Out of the mouths of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise’?” (Matt. XXI; Luke XIX).

Therefore, even when he went up with public praises, he did so in one respect secretly, but in another respect openly—and not secretly. Since he did not then go up with royal praises as he would do at his own time, he went up secretly. But since he did not go up so as to wish to remain hidden, he did not go up secretly. The qualifying distinction “as if in secret” was therefore aptly used.

“The Jews therefore were looking for him at the feast and saying: ‘Where is that man?’” Therefore, he says, because they did not see him come with his brothers—that is, with his kindred—the Jews who were seeking to kill him looked for him with evil anxiety, saying: “Where is that man?”

See now, brood of vipers (Matt. III), how they rage with the burning poison of their inmost hearts: they do not say, “Where is Jesus?” but, “Where is that man?” Could they have been ignorant of the name of him whom they sought to kill? Thus the homicidal devil, the inhabitant of their hearts, so drove them that, at hatred’s prompting, they could not—or rather would not—utter the name of salvation.

“And there was much murmuring about him among the crowd.” “Much murmuring,” that is, there was much disagreement: much, I say, because it was whispered in the rumours of many people, but not so violent or so spirited that it could properly be called sedition. For sedition is properly said to occur when a state, divided into factions fighting one another, is endangered by hostile discord, so that the tumult cannot be calmed without serious strain upon governing authority. Hence, according to its etymology, *seditio* is said to derive from being “without dominion” (*sine ditione*). When this happens, the person because of whom it arises is destroyed: his enemies are given greater opportunity to accuse him, and the judge is placed under the necessity of hearing the case.

But this chosen servant, upon whom God the Father placed his Spirit so that he might bring forth judgment to the nations, did not contend or cry out, nor was his voice heard outside in the streets (Isa. XLII). With every kind of gentleness he acted and made provision that no cause of sedition should ever arise on his account (Luke IV). Thus no sedition occurred; rather, a timid disagreement murmured beneath the sound of Jewish hatred or envy, while they looked for him as for a man bearing an accursed name, saying: “Where is that man?”

“Some of the Jews, however, said, ‘He is good’; but others said, ‘No, rather he deceives the crowds.’” From this discord of opinions came the much murmuring. What if those who said, “He is good,” had also known how—or dared—to say that he is the Son of God? Then there would surely have arisen not merely some measure of much murmuring, but a spirited sedition. But they said only this, and scarcely dared to say it: “He is good.” For what follows is:

“No one, however, spoke openly about him for fear of the Jews.” No one, that is, among those who said, “He is a good man,” spoke openly about him for fear of the Jews—namely, those who said, “No, rather, he deceives the crowds.” It should be noted that although both groups alike were Jews, the Evangelist is accustomed here, as throughout the account of all the persecutors of our same Lord, to call “Jews” those who sought to kill the Lord, distinguishing them from the crowd which either followed him or [Col. 0507D] devised no wickedness against him.

That the reason for this may be clearer, one must also know that the name “Jews” is rightly used in three senses, and that the Evangelist intends here the worst of these. For all confessors of truth are rightly called Jews, according to the interpretation of this name: *Judaeus* means “confessor.” Hence we do not doubt that it was divinely ordained that the charge written above the head of the crucified Lord should be set down in Greek, Hebrew, and Latin: “Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews” (John 19), because in those three languages above all the catholic faith of Christian confessors proclaims its testimony throughout the whole world.

In the contrary sense, we call Jews [Col. 0508A] those beginning in malice, murderers, the 217 shedders of Christ’s blood, who to this day curse Christ in their synagogues, bearing upon themselves the same blood of Christ as an inheritance from their parents. We call them Jews, not because they are such, but because they say that they are Jews while lying, since they belong to the synagogue of Satan (Rev. 3).

There is also a middle sense, neither good nor bad; for in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision, neither Gentile nor Jew, but faith alone is required (Gal. 5). In this middle sense we call Jews all who are Jewish by carnal descent, together with those who, being of Benjamin’s stock, remained in the portion of David’s kingdom. To distinguish them, the other Israelites were called [Col. 0508B] Samaritans, with whom, as this Evangelist has said, the Jews did not associate. Yet “Jews” cannot be understood in that sense in this great murmuring of the crowds, since, as stated above, those too were Jews, of whom none spoke openly of him for fear of the Jews. It follows:

“Now when the feast was already half over, Jesus went up into the temple and taught.” He who, as was said a little earlier, “did not wish to walk in Judaea, because the Jews sought to kill him,” and who nevertheless went up, though as it were secretly and not openly—behold, he “went up,” not into a remote corner of the city, but “into the temple”; not on an ordinary day, but “when the feast was half over”; not with closed mouth, hidden in silence, but conspicuous in the splendid authority [Col. 0508C] of his teaching.

Is there now any room for that faithlessness to accuse Christ, the Lord of majesty, of timidity or impotence—namely, because, fearing death and striving as far as possible to avoid it, he did not wish to walk in Judaea? Or did he act changeably, so that there was in him “yes and no”: first unwilling to go there, then changed by the words of brothers such as these, so that he went up where he had not wished to go?

Rather, in this deed too let us say of God, the Son of God, that “with him are wisdom and strength” (Job 12). For it belongs to divine wisdom alone, beyond the comprehension of any human being, that he knew the time of his death had not yet come and therefore would not walk [Col. 0508D] in Judaea or grant the ministers of death permission or opportunity for their crime. But it belongs to strength that he goes up into the midst of his enemies and teaches when the feast is half over, in some sense commanding eager death to keep watch outside and await its appointed time—death, held back at the discretion of the one who was to die, and bound by the halter of his sovereignty.

For he will not be mistaken in the secure awareness of his power, by which he had also sent word to Herod when Herod sought to kill him: “Go,” he said, “tell that fox: Behold, I cast out demons and perform healings today and tomorrow, and on the third day I am brought to completion” (Luke 13). And now, teaching in his Father’s house—once his dwelling, but now made for him a hyena’s den (Jer. 12)—he was in some sense saying to importunate death: Behold, I serve the teaching appropriate to [Col. 0509A] the present feast of Tabernacles (*Scenopegia*), and afterward to the future feast of Dedication (*Encaenia*); and at the third feast, Passover, I wrestle with death itself.

“And the Jews marvelled, saying: How does this man know letters, though he has not learned?” This Jewish amazement—punitive impatience at hearing him—is the rancour of slanderous envy. Pressed by it, because they cannot oppose the wisdom of his teaching, they at least attempt, on the presumption of formal instruction, to disparage his person. If those especially who “have taken away the key of knowledge” (Luke 11) could scarcely endure that such a householder possessed “all the treasures of knowledge” (Col. 2), and resented his knowing anything although he had not entered by their means, how much more did he know that his own household would be assailed by them when, in this same miracle of teaching, they should begin to do greater things—though he himself bestowed these gifts upon them?

For while he taught in their temple in one language only, he nevertheless spoke to one nation only. But, going to the Father, he was going to grant those who believed in him that they should speak the mighty works of God in every language of all nations—and not merely speak them, but, what is greater, that men once without letters and unlearned (Acts 2) should proclaim him to the whole world in invincible writings; and after them their followers, orthodox men possessing gifts of grace, distributed by the Holy Spirit to each individually as he wills (1 Cor. 12). Therefore, since his household too would hear such things much more fully from their acquaintances, who despised their outstanding learning, it was fitting that he should give them [Col. 0509C] such an answer as would adequately shape their speech and furnish a worthy defence for those likewise enduring envy. Therefore it follows:

“Jesus answered them and said: My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me.” What could be truer than this answer? What could more powerfully defend the dignity of sound teaching, or more sweetly soothe envy—if indeed it can be soothed? “My teaching,” he says, “is not mine”: it is understood, as the teaching of the Pharisees (Matt. 15) is their own teaching, because in much of God’s teaching they do not share God’s doctrine and understanding, while teaching people to keep human commandments (Rom. 7).

For they have transgressed God’s ordinances for the sake of their own traditions, and compel the holy, righteous, and good law to serve their own profits and pleasures. Likewise, the prophecy of false prophets is their own prophecy, because they have certainly not lent their own spirit as an instrument to God’s Spirit, or their own voice to God’s voice; rather, they prophesy from their own heart, saying, “Thus says the Lord” (Jer. 27), when the Lord has not sent them. In contrast to such persons, it is plain how significant is what he says: “My teaching is not mine.” For he wishes us at once to understand the contrary implication: Your teaching is not God’s, but your own.

And altogether, because he said both, “My teaching,” and, “is not mine,” it must be understood as if he had said: My teaching is not from man, but from God. Otherwise [Col. 0510A] there would be no place for the adversative conjunction by which he added: “But [it is] his who sent me.”

Therefore, whenever anyone of humble station today attains some degree of learning, so as to be able with Jesus to go up into the temple and open his mouth in the midst of the Church, if some, through the Jewish vice, despise him because perhaps he has not traversed long stretches of land to eminent and renowned teachers, nor reread foreign studies in search of them, and on this account say, “Who is this man, or how does he know letters, though he has not learned?”—it is sufficient for his defence, if he can truly say that his teaching is not his own, but belongs to him from whom comes every true teaching. For by professing catholic teaching through this great distinction, he anathematizes every heresy.

For this is not the confession of heretics—such as Arius, [Col. 0510B] Macedonius, or Donatus—or of the rest, to whom, on the contrary, “stolen waters are sweeter” (Prov. 9) than those fountains or waters which, according to the Psalmist, God sends forth and which pass between the mountains (Ps. 103). That is, each of them prefers his own doctrine to the teaching of the catholic and apostolic faith, which is common to all the saints.

Let then the only Son of God, who teaches and does nothing apart from the Father, say this; let him, I say, say what he wishes every teacher of the holy Church to say: “My teaching is not mine”—that is, it does not make heresies and schisms, as do the teachings of those who, loving novelties of expression (1 Tim. 6), forsake God’s traditions 218 for their own traditions (Matt. 15). Moreover, [Col. 0510C] this meaning is made clear from what follows. For he says: “If anyone is willing to do his will, he shall know concerning the teaching whether it is from God, or whether I speak from myself.”

Therefore, that the following statement may agree more plainly with the preceding sentence, we must first see what it means for anyone to speak “from himself.” It is the principle of philosophers that things whose definitions are contrary are themselves contrary; and this can also be reversed: things which are contrary have contrary definitions. Now these are manifestly contrary and cannot coexist: that someone speaks from himself, and that his teaching is from God. For Wisdom itself now sets these alternatives against each other: he shall know, he says, concerning the teaching, “whether it is from God [Col. 0510D] or whether I speak from myself.” Therefore the definitions of one who speaks from himself must be contrary to the definitions of one who speaks from God.

To speak from God is to speak as the Spirit of truth suggests: not to invent anything from one’s own heart, but to utter truth with the mouth as it is perceived in the heart. Conversely, to speak from oneself is to speak falsehood; it is to prophesy from one’s own heart things which the Lord did not command and which did not rise in one’s heart—to speak from oneself (Jer. 23). But when our God had said, “My teaching is not mine,” he gave a means of testing it: “He shall know,” he says, “concerning the teaching whether it is from God, or whether I speak from myself.” Thus, “My teaching is not mine” is the same as saying: My teaching is not deceptive or [Col. 0511A] false.

We must now see what means he gave for testing whether his teaching is his own—that is, deceptive or false—or from God, that is, true and truthful. “If anyone,” he says, “is willing to do his will, he shall know concerning the teaching whether it is from God, or whether I speak from myself.” Let the person seeking a discriminating understanding of truth hear this counsel. Let him desire to do God’s will, that he may be able to know God’s will; let him desire to walk God’s way, that he may deserve to see God’s way. For he is blind unless he first purifies the eye of his heart by simple goodwill: “Anoint your eyes,” says the Lord, “with eye-salve, that you may see” (Rev. 3). For what a person blinded by the brilliance of truth cannot see is the fault of the eyes, not of the sun.

Therefore, those who do not discern God’s teaching have no excuse, because [Col. 0511B] their very error bears witness against them that they have no desire to do God’s will. If they had that desire, they would freely love the teaching which is from God. It follows:

“He who speaks from himself seeks his own glory; but he who seeks the glory of him who sent him is true, and there is no injustice in him.” Each of these statements has its contrary implication. For when one reads, “He who speaks from himself seeks his own glory,” one must understand: But he who speaks from himself because his teaching is from God seeks God’s glory. Likewise one must understand: “He who seeks his own glory is a liar, and injustice is in him”; and then read: “But he who seeks [Col. 0511C] the glory of him who sent him is true, and there is no injustice in him.” For these things contradict one another and cannot coexist: for someone to speak from himself and to be true; likewise, to seek one’s own glory and to have righteousness in oneself. Conversely, for a person’s teaching to be from God and for that person to be a liar; likewise, to seek God’s glory and not to have God’s righteousness in oneself—these are wholly contradictory and can nowhere coexist.

For the devil, who speaks from himself—for “when he speaks a lie, he speaks from his own resources,” because he is a liar and the father of that lie (John 8)—cannot be true in what he says. And because he seeks his own glory, for he did not wish to glory with God [Col. 0511D] but against God, saying, “I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14), righteousness cannot be in him. Similarly, insofar as, or so long as, a human being speaks from himself, he cannot be true; and insofar as, or so long as, Arius or any other heretic seeks his own glory, righteousness cannot be in him.

Conversely, because “Christ does not speak from himself, but testifies to what he has seen and heard” (John 5), he cannot be a liar; and because he does not seek his own glory, but jointly seeks as his own glory equally the glory of the Father and the Holy Spirit, injustice cannot be in him. Likewise, insofar as, or so long as, a human being does not speak [Col. 0512A] from himself, he cannot rightly be called a liar; and insofar as, or so long as, he seeks not his own glory but God’s, he cannot rightly be called unjust.

Therefore, by a proof of divine reasoning as powerful as it is true, our Lord repels those perverse admirers of himself who say, “How does this man know letters, though he has not learned?” He fittingly defends every person who possesses teaching, or a psalm, or an apocalypse, and who speaks mysteries in spirit and mind (1 Cor. 14), however he knows them or wherever he learned them. Let no one dare, in his presence, to say: “Who is this man?” Thus far Wisdom itself, which plainly knows letters though it has not learned them according to their account, has answered their spoken words. Now, however, it took care also to answer their silent thoughts, [Col. 0512B] which could not be hidden from him, in this manner.

“Did not Moses give you the law? Yet none of you keeps the law. Why do you seek to kill me?” For indeed, while they said one thing, they thought another: while marvelling at his learning, they entertained his death in their minds. See what remarkable retaliation he rendered them. While they marvelled at how he knew letters though he had not learned them, he marvelled at how none of them kept the law though they had received the law. What they marvelled at in him was the praiseworthy power of divinity; what he marvelled at in them was the detestable boldness of transgression. For it was praiseworthy to know letters without having learned them; it was detestable not to keep the law after receiving it.

[Col. 0512C] But what could appear more irrational than that, after saying, “None of you keeps the law,” he immediately added, “Why do you seek to kill me?” It would seem unreasonable to charge them with transgression of the law without stating the form of the transgression. Therefore, after rightly saying, “None of you keeps the law,” he immediately continued: “Why do you seek to kill me?” For keeping the law and wishing to kill a human being are contradictory and cannot coexist. The law says: “You shall not kill” (Exod. 20).

Yet the same law again commands that a guilty person be put to death—for example, a deceptive prophet, once convicted of having spoken falsely in the Lord’s name (Deut. 13). Therefore, the provident guardian and defender of the law, who was also its Lord and author, intending to prove the accusation he had made in saying, “None of you keeps the law,” did not assert, “You seek to kill me.” For at times it was permitted and just to put someone to death in accordance with the law, where a condemnable cause preceded it. Rather, he asked: “Why do you seek [Col. 0512D] to kill me?” As if to say: I grant that those who kill may keep the law where there is a valid cause for lawful killing. But for what cause do you seek to kill me? Have you found that I am a prophet corrupted by arrogance, speaking in the Lord’s name what the Lord did not command? (Deut. 13). Or have I spoken to you in the name of foreign gods? Have I foretold in the Lord’s name a word which did not come to pass? Have you such or such a lawful sign that God did not send me?

When I say to the royal official, “Your son lives” (John 4); when I say of the man born blind, “Neither he nor his parents sinned” (John 9), but [this occurred] so that God’s works may be manifested in him; and when all the other things I foretell come to pass—things which I both do while foretelling them, and foretell while doing them—“Why, then, do you seek to kill me?”

“The crowd answered and said: You have a demon; who seeks to kill you?” Behold, these are the dogs of whom he says in the psalm, having for our sake become the reproach of men and the outcast of the people: “For many dogs have surrounded me” (Ps. 21). The intention of one attempting to describe them labours in vain here: no words could adequately convey this barking of most wicked dogs. Yet one may marvel how these foolish and malicious murderers, with the great bitterness of their answer, both confess by denying and deny by confessing the murder which they contemplate in their minds. Thus contrary are they to themselves; with such force of burning poison do they rage.

For what commonly produces murder except hatred? And when was any murder committed with greater hatred than that indicated by this bitter and utterly wicked insult? Therefore it would have been superfluous to strive to convict them by saying, “I do not have a demon, but I truly say that you seek to kill me,” when they themselves so openly, in the violence of their hatred, spewed out their poison in such an answer. Accordingly, what he began by saying, “Why do you seek to kill me?” he continues by adding: “I did one work, and you all marvel.” [Col. 0513C] He himself reveals shortly afterward what work he means, saying: “Because I made the whole man well on the Sabbath.”

They marvelled at this work; that is, they made a great issue of it among themselves, as though it were a great and unheard-of crime, and were indignant with great zeal, as though for God’s law. For what he says here, “And you all marvel,” he soon repeats, calling that same amazement indignation: “You are angry with me because I made the whole man well on the Sabbath.” He says therefore: “I did one work, and you all marvel.”

When he asked and said, “Why do you seek to kill me?”—that is, What charge do you have on which you could accuse me while killing me?—they could, in accordance with their designs, have answered: Because you are not from God, since you do not keep the Sabbath. But long before they had learned by experience that he could turn this very point much more strongly against themselves, since he had often said to them: “Hypocrites, which of you does not untie his ox or ass and lead it to water on the Sabbath day?” and similar things (Luke 13; Matt. 12).

Therefore, in anger they kept silent—indeed, even more frenzied in their silence, they spewed forth the raging flame of hatred. He therefore fittingly states the same cause while they are silent, in order to defend it rationally, and immediately begins the same defence thus:

“For this reason Moses gave you circumcision—not because it is from Moses, but from the fathers—and on the Sabbath you circumcise a man.” The entire defence of the case rests in the final clause: “And on the Sabbath [Col. 0514A] you circumcise a man.” “For this reason,” he says, “because ‘I did one work, and you all marvel and are angry with me’; for this reason, I say, now using a lawful defence, I tell you: ‘Moses gave you circumcision’”—that is, as he commanded you the rest, so he commanded you this also, that you should circumcise a man.

I do not say that it is from Moses, for before Moses it was from the fathers—Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; from the fathers, that is, from their being fathers, because they believed that they would receive the seed in whom all nations would be blessed (Gen. 17). Likewise Moses gave the Sabbath, not because it is from Moses, but from God: that is, because God rested on the seventh day from all his work and blessed the seventh day (Gen. 2).

Although one and the same Moses gave you circumcision and the Sabbath in writing for such different reasons; although the origin of the Sabbath is older than that of circumcision; and although circumcision is from the fathers but the Sabbath from God—yet on Sabbaths you circumcise a man, so that Moses’ law may not be broken; for it commands a man to be circumcised on the eighth day, without any exception for the Sabbath. To this, I say:

“If a man receives circumcision on the Sabbath so that the law of Moses may not be broken, are you angry with me because I made the whole man well on the Sabbath?” I made the whole man well on the Sabbath. True circumcision, though it is a good work and therefore not a violation of the Sabbath, nevertheless does not make the whole human being well. For even if it heals the inner person in those only who possess the reality of which circumcision is the sign—namely, Abraham’s faith—it does not heal the outer person, but rather wounds and afflicts him with pain.

But when I do on the Sabbath this work for which you are angry with me—for example, when I say to one, “Take up your pallet and walk” (John 5); to another, “Stretch out your hand” (Matt. 9); or when I put mud upon the eyes of another, a man born blind (John 9)—I “make the whole man well,” because, while restoring him outwardly, I form him inwardly toward faith, all beholders seeing that I accomplish the matter not by a human or ordinary medical operation, but by divine power.

“Do not judge according to appearance, but render righteous judgment.” Certainly I was regarded as a despised man, the last of men, and “my appearance is not in me” (Isa. 63; the wording is uncertain). But Moses was a great man, of illustrious memory, an ancient man and the first leader of God’s people, whose face was made radiant by converse with God (Exod. 34). Yet the law which that same Moses gave commands that one must not regard the person of the poor or honour the countenance of the powerful; rather, “Judge your neighbour justly” (Lev. 19).

Therefore, “Do not judge according to appearance, but render righteous judgment”: that is, weigh not the face of Moses and the face or present person of the Son of Man, but the merits of the matters themselves. Circumcision, which Moses gave you, as was said above, heals inwardly the children of Abraham (Gen. 17), those who follow his faith, so that that soul may not perish from among [Col. 0515A] its people; but outwardly it wounds them. Therefore it does not make the whole person well.

But the one and only work which I did on the Sabbath heals the human being inwardly and outwardly. The outward healing proves that the Son of Man had authority on earth to forgive sins—the inward healing—for which circumcision prepares hope through Abraham’s promised seed, which is Christ. Why, then, do you seek to kill me, having no other cause except that “I made the whole man well on the Sabbath?” That they were silent at this and, though unwillingly, recognized the weakness of their case and restrained their anger for a time, is plainly indicated by what follows. For it follows:

“Therefore some of those from Jerusalem said: Is not this the one whom they seek to kill? Behold, he now speaks openly [Col. 0515B] and they say nothing to him.” It is as though it were openly said: The Jews to whom Jesus had said, “Why do you seek to kill me?” replied, “You have a demon; who seeks to kill you?” Yet now, while this same Lord Jesus gave a reason on his own behalf, they were silent; and while he spoke openly, they said nothing to him. But that statement was so true that some from Jerusalem—who had surely learned it not by report or hearsay, but knew it because they themselves, being present, had seen with their eyes and heard with their ears the conspiracies and secret meetings of those present—wondered that, with him now present and speaking openly, they said nothing to him.

And they said: “Have the rulers really recognized that this is the Christ?” For so great a change and such silence among the Jews seemed not to have occurred without a very great reason. “Have the rulers, then,” they say, “understood that they were mistaken, and, having come to their senses, ceased saying or doing anything against the one whom they sought to kill?” It was as after a great storm, when the winds have ceased and the savage waves of the sea rest as their boiling is calmed.

These Jerusalemites who said this might still be thought to belong to those who believed in him, and to have said, “Have the rulers really recognized that this is the Christ?” with the implied meaning, “as we too have recognized”—were it not contradicted by what follows: “But we know where this man is from; and when Christ comes, no one knows where he is from.” And shortly afterward it is said of the same persons: “Therefore they sought to seize him, but no one laid hands on him, because his hour had not yet come.” [Col. 0515D]

Therefore they said, “Have the rulers really recognized that this is the Christ?” not because they believed, but because they tried to oppose belief that he was Christ. For, as though fearing that perhaps the rulers had recognized and consented to believe that he was the Christ, they immediately bring forward what seemed contrary to Christ’s nature: “But we know where this man is from; and when Christ comes, no one knows where he is from.” If this premise were granted, a conclusion would immediately be possible: Therefore the rulers too are mistaken, if they think they have recognized that he is the Christ.

But the proposition they advanced is neither consistent nor sound, because they considered one nature only of Christ, namely his human nature, according to which they could say [Col. 0516A]: “But we know where this man is from; and when Christ comes, no one knows where he is from.” For although he truly was a Galilean, a man from the city of Nazareth, he was not, as they supposed, Joseph’s son—concerning which they often reproached him, saying, “Is this not the carpenter’s son?” (Matt. 12)—but the Son of God through the Virgin.

Thus they did not rightly or consistently say, “But we know where this man is from,” since they attended only to his nature of flesh and did not even know that properly. Therefore, lest they should seem inexcusable while pressing on unopposed to their conclusion, they had to be met swiftly. And this occurred. For it follows:

“Therefore Jesus cried out in the temple, saying: You know me, and you know where I am from; and I have not come from myself, but he who sent me is true, whom you do not know.” Jesus did not cry out without reason in saying these things, because the matter was worthy of a cry—that is, of forceful preaching. “You know me,” he says, “and you know where I am from,” and so forth. It is as though he said: According to my humanity, you indeed know both that I am Jesus and that I am a Galilean man; but there is another nature in Christ, that is, in myself, according to which none of you knows where I am from. According to that nature I now say that “I have not come from myself,” as that lawless man, the man of sin, the son of perdition, will come, whose coming will be according to the working of falsehood. But he who sent me is true, and you do not know him, because, as I have already said elsewhere: “You have never heard his voice or seen his form” (John 5).

[Col. 0516C] “I know him, because I am from him, and he sent me.” I know him—indeed, I know him well—from the beginning, before I became such as you can know me to be when you say, “But we know where this man is from.” And why do I know him? Because I am from him—not in the manner in which you too are from him, though, as I have said, you do not know him. For you are from him by being made or created; but I simply and absolutely am, because he did not create or make me, but begot me. And in order that I might become such as you could know, he sent me.

Therefore do not say either that I am only that which you know where it is from, or that Christ is only that which no one knows where it is from. He is neither the Son of Man only nor the Son of God only, but both together: both that whose origin you can know and that whose origin no one can know; that is, both Son of Man and Son of God.

In saying these things, the Lord did not merely leave undiminished their estimate of Christ, but increased it. For they had not said, “When Christ comes, no one knows where he is from,” with the intention, nor were they accustomed to read, “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isa. 63), in the sense that he was the consubstantial Son of God. Rather, just as in many other matters they preferred their traditions to God’s traditions, so they preferred to the prophetic Scriptures this opinion of theirs, expressed by these people: “When Christ comes, no one knows where he is from.”

For their tradition was that Christ would come at midnight, in likeness to the time of Egypt when Passover was celebrated (Exod. 12), when the destroyer came, the Lord passed over the dwellings, and the doorposts were consecrated with the lamb’s blood; and that he would come not as God and man, but as a mere, though great, human being. Occupied with this opinion, they said according to their own understanding: “When Christ comes, no one knows where he is from,” although the chief priests and scribes knew how to answer Herod’s inquiry concerning where Christ would be born: “In Bethlehem of Judaea; for thus it is written through the Prophet” (Matt. 2), and the rest.

Foolish and malicious people! They could know where Christ was from when he was being sought in order to be killed; but now, when he began to be sought in order to be believed, they do not know—and will not know—where Christ is from. But Christ affirms not that he came from unknown or secret regions [Col. 0517B] to which he had formerly been removed, but that he came from him and had been there before he was born of Mary or lived in Galilee—the fact to which they referred when they said, “But we know where this man is from.”

Therefore, he did not diminish their estimate of Christ, but declared of himself more than they could have conceived concerning Christ.

“Therefore they sought to seize him, but no one laid hands on him, because his hour had not yet come.” Although they were blind and deaf, and perhaps therefore could not sufficiently clearly perceive in the aforesaid cry of truth that both Christ’s divine and human natures were alike being set forth—for even today such a statement is not altogether easy for many of us to understand—yet its general meaning or intention was easy to grasp: namely, that he had said that Christ himself ought to be believed in. But this alone was enough to inflame great envy and immense hatred, just as it is enough to throw a very little oil into a burning furnace for a raging flame suddenly to overflow and spread.

“Therefore they sought to seize him”: that is, to prevail by their frenzy, because they were being overcome by his reasoning. But, “because his hour had not yet come”—an hour, I say, not fated, as astrologers suppose, but fixed beforehand by himself, the Lord of life and death—“no one laid hands on him.”

“But many of the crowd believed in him and said, ‘When the Christ comes, will he do more signs than these which this man does?’” By “the crowd” he here means the multitudes who had gathered for the feast from districts or foreign cities, distinguishing them from those who were from Jerusalem. These latter, as was said above, were disputing in this fashion; and, as Jesus cried out, their madness increased and they sought to seize him. Since they were straw, and their rulers or Pharisees were fire, they burned together, kindled against the Savior. But the aforesaid crowd which had gathered, according as it approached this blaze more closely or more remotely, grew more or less heated by the fire of raging hatred.

Thus many, whom that fire of envy had not reached because they stood, as it were, farther off, believed in him and said: “When the Christ comes, will he do more signs than these which this man does?” It is as though they said: When Christ comes, he will surely be recognized by the magnificent signs which he will perform. But will he himself perform signs more numerous or greater than those which this man performs, or will it be necessary to demand more from him? Therefore, since he both says that he is the Christ and proves this by such great signs, we see no reason why one should not believe in him.

“The rulers and Pharisees heard the crowd murmuring these things about him, and sent officers to seize him.” The rulers and Pharisees heard the crowd murmuring: that is, not stirred into sedition, but quietly muttering because they were forming an opinion different from the rulers’ envy. But those rulers themselves gaped at every wind, as though desiring a suitable opportunity by which they might have grounds to accuse him before the Roman governor as if lawfully.

Therefore, hearing that many of the crowd believed in him and that parties, divided by differing opinions concerning him, were murmuring, they took breath again. In the earlier dispute concerning the breaking of the Sabbath, when he defended himself, they had lost their case and had realized that their argument was weak. Now they hoped that they could accuse him of having caused sedition, though the aforesaid murmuring of the crowd was far removed from the kind of sedition from which danger is usually feared by cities or commonwealths.

Thus “they sent officers to seize him.” But Jesus said to them, “I am with you a little while longer, and I am going to him who sent me.”

While the Jews, as has been said, sought to seize him; while the rulers and Pharisees now sent officers; and while the officers themselves came to seize him, Jesus spoke these words, conscious of his unconquered majesty. “I am with you,” he says, “a little while longer.” Conscious, I say, of his power, and not unaware with what chains he held bound, or with what ring in its nostrils he held bridled, the devil, ruler of death, lying in their hearts (Job 40), he said these words and those which follow.

It is as though he said: You wish to seize me so quickly; you are so eager to kill me (Luke 13); and, because I am grievous for you to behold, you already hasten to exclude me from the assembly of the living. You will endure and wait a little while, until I complete healings and fulfill my time. Meanwhile, whether your instigator—the leader of death and hell—wishes it or not, I, living among the living and mortal among mortals, shall be with you and walk among you (Deut. 32). When I have completed my work, your evil will is inborn; it must be given the opportunity. Do as you please. But when you have done it, do not rejoice; do not exult. For, driven from this life by your crime, “I go to him who sent me.” What then? I tell you already now:

“You will seek me and will not find me, and where I am going you cannot come.” You who now seek me, you whose envy now urges you so greatly that you seek me: do not suppose that, after you have killed me, the cause for which you now seek me will cease. It will not be so. Rather, then I shall much more provoke you to jealousy through a nation that is no nation; through a foolish nation I shall provoke you to anger.

Now indeed a single crowd, the little common people of one nation or land, murmurs, with some believing and saying, “When Christ comes, will he do more signs than these which this man does?” But then “from the rising of the sun to its setting the name of Christ the Lord shall be praised” (Ps. 112); all nations shall praise him, all peoples shall praise him (Ps. 116). Then what is written shall be fulfilled: “He shall rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth; Ethiopians shall fall down before him, and his enemies shall lick the dust” (Ps. 71), and so forth.

Then indeed you will seek me with greater envy than now, desiring to extinguish my name—but in vain. For, “where I am going, you cannot come.” Now, “where I am, you can come”; indeed, because I came to you, you can find me, and shortly you will even be able to cast me, once seized, out of your land of the living by crushing me. Yet while you do this, “I go where you cannot come”; you will not even be able to throw a stone there. Nevertheless, you will seek me in most burning persecution: you will kill, scourge, crucify, and stone my servants, and persecute them from city to city (Matt. 23). But you will not be able to reach me. Rather, safe and sound, when you have killed some, I shall appoint others as my witnesses, so that you may increasingly be provoked to jealousy by the foolish nation.

“Therefore the Jews said among themselves, ‘Where does this man intend to go, that we shall not find him? What is this saying that he spoke: “You will seek me and will not find me, and where I am, you cannot come”? Is he going into the Dispersion among the Gentiles, and will he teach the Gentiles?’”

They said this among themselves and did not ask him. For they could not so much as breathe even a little toward the height of humility, which is exceedingly arduous for proud minds, in order to ask him anything with the intention of learning.

“Is he going into the Dispersion among the Gentiles, and will he teach the Gentiles?” O Jews, deserters of life and enemies of salvation: may the fear which you fear come upon you, and may what you dread happen to you! Do you so greatly fear that, if after Christ the whole world should follow him and God become known among the Gentiles, your singular glory would perish? For your prophetic mind proclaimed this to you: that if Christ came according to Jacob’s prophecy (Gen. 49), he who would be the expectation of the nations, your singular pride in the worship of the one God, like that of unicorns, would no longer exalt itself further upon the earth.

Thus, out of the abundance of your heart, you also spoke to yourselves; for what you feared, on account of which you envied Christ and persecuted him not because you did not see but because you envied, you belched forth with malicious mouth, drunk with wickedness. He will go into the Dispersion among the Gentiles and teach the Gentiles; and when you, trying to forestall this and wishing to avert it, kill him, then, mounting upon his horses and chariots of salvation, with all salvation migrating with him away from you, he will ride into the Dispersion among the Gentiles (Hab. 3). Death itself is the road of life as it journeys to the Gentiles.

Thus Jonah did not travel by dry land to Nineveh, the great city (Jonah 2; Matt. 12), but entered the sea, was immediately enclosed by the deep and covered by the waters, and, recalled after three days from the belly of the whale, at length walked into great Nineveh. By preaching he stirred and troubled it, so that it might be healed through three days’ repentance. Thus, when Nineveh had been saved, the gourd which had shaded Jonah’s head withered: a figure, plainly, of you, whose synagogue, temple, and Holy of Holies—the former tabernacle of God—withered when the Church of the Gentiles flourished.

Thus, when the woman with the issue of blood touched the fringe of the Lord’s garment and was immediately freed from her flow of blood, the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue died (Matt. 9). She had surely been born when the aforesaid woman fell into her infirmity. For the girl was twelve years old, and the woman had suffered her infirmity for twelve years. What does this mean? Namely, that the synagogue was born in Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob when the Gentile world was beginning to sink into idolatry. And behold: when the Gentile world was healed from the flow of that same idolatry through faith in Christ—approaching from behind and touching the fringe of his garment, that is, believing in him after his ascension—when, I say, the Gentile world was healed through faith, the synagogue died out in unbelief because of envy.

Therefore it is true that he is going into the Dispersion among the Gentiles and will teach the Gentiles. And because, through fearful envy, you mentioned this matter as though divining it, he did not delay to prefigure already in himself how, or by what means, he would go into the Dispersion among the Gentiles and teach the Gentiles.

“But on the last day of the great feast, Jesus stood and cried out, saying, ‘If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink.’” The last day of this feast is the eighth day. For thus it is written concerning this feast: “The first and the eighth day shall be most celebrated and most holy” (Lev. 23).

In the mystery of the Lord standing and crying out, it signifies the Paschal feast which was to follow in that same year: certainly the last feast of the Old Testament and the first of the New. For after that Paschal evening, on which the Lord, about to be betrayed, ate the typological Passover with his disciples, whatever the Jews celebrated was no longer to be called a feast or solemnity, but, according to the prophet, “the dung of solemnities” (Mal. 2).

At that last great feast, Jesus stood before the Father, offering prayers and supplications, as the Apostle says, with a loud cry and many tears (Heb. 5). Struck by the violence of his Passion, as was prefigured in the rock which Moses struck with the rod (Exod. 17; Num. 20), he poured out from himself for us what we should drink: first water, by which we might be washed; then his blood, by which we might drink. Next, breathing upon the apostles, he gave the Holy Spirit (John 20), and, according to another Evangelist, “opened their understanding, that they might understand the Scriptures” (Luke 24). This is truly to drink the waters of salvation.

Thereafter he continues to cry out mightily, crying to all nations and, as it were, saying: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink.” For, received into heaven and having given the Holy Spirit, he moved the heavens so that they might declare the glory of God: so that there were no languages or speeches whose voices were not heard; so that their sound went out into all the earth and their words to the ends of the world (Ps. 18). Indeed, their whole sound or proclamation was the cry of Jesus, inviting all who thirsted to come to the waters and hasten to receive the grace of the Holy Spirit for the remission of sins; and then, as that same Spirit distributes as he wills (1 Cor. 12), to drink from the Law and Prophets, through the saving faith of the Gospel, the abundance of God’s Word which they had not previously possessed.

Therefore Jesus fittingly stood on the last day of the great feast and cried out, saying, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink,” because from that time he not only opened the way of salvation to all persons of every nation or condition who desired to be saved, but also invited all, by his resounding proclamation, to drink the cup of life and salvation.

And he added: “He who believes in me, as the Scripture says, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water.” It is the Scripture of Proverbs, which says the same thing in slightly different words. Nor only this; what precedes is also consonant with the same Scripture. For what he says here, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink,” is said there thus: “Drink water from your own cistern and flowing streams from your own well” (Prov. 5). And what he adds here, “Out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water,” is added there thus: “Let your fountains be dispersed abroad, and divide your waters in the streets” (ibid.).

Thus Scripture says: “Rivers of living water shall flow from the belly of him who believes in me.” It is as though he said: Why are you anxiously distressed, saying, “Is he going into the Dispersion among the Gentiles, and will he teach the Gentiles?” Do you suppose that, if you kill me in order to forestall this, there will then be no one to announce to the Gentiles the salvation of which you are jealous? It is not so. For he who believes in me, through the very death by which you will kill me, shall receive the Spirit of wisdom and knowledge; and, filling the world with the abundance of Gospel teaching, he will not permit my name to perish, as you wish, nor permit the Dispersion among the Gentiles to lack the knowledge of God.

And this happened. Behold how many believers drank the water of saving wisdom from the cistern of the Law and living streams from the wells of the Gospel; their fountains were sent forth abroad, and in copious expositions they distributed their waters in the streets. Those who first believed in him at that time—the apostles—first drank; and from that paradise of the primitive Church there first flowed the four rivers of the Gospels and the fountains of the Epistles. They filled the whole world with knowledge of the Godhead. Afterwards, so many teachers were filled by drinking and poured it forth again by writing that the Jews, grieving, see plainly enough fulfilled what they foresaw in envy: namely, that Christ had gone into the Dispersion among the Gentiles.

This living water is the grace of the Holy Spirit. For the Evangelist immediately adds: “This he said concerning the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive.” The Holy Spirit is customarily called “water” in Scripture, and sometimes, with an addition, “living water.” The human soul is called “earth,” by reason of the likeness: as water irrigates the earth and, when suitably poured upon it, makes it germinate, so the grace of the Holy Spirit irrigates the substance of the human soul—poor and barren of itself—with the necessary streams of its gifts; and, by the benefit of its visitation, makes the soul into which it is poured fruitful in faith and good works.

Requesting this visitation through this likeness, the Psalmist says: “My soul is like land without water before you” (Ps. 142). And he aptly compared the gifts of the Holy Spirit not merely to living waters, but to rivers of living water, saying: “Out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water.” For just as living water has its own definite vein and springs from its source, while in flowing it receives the name by which it is called a river, so all the distributions of gifts which are in the holy Church proceed from one Spirit as from one source, as the Apostle says: “But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each one as he wills” (1 Cor. 12).

By enduring in the same Church through succeeding generations, from Christ himself to the end of the age, flowing out into others from itself, or through others, by doctrine as well as by laying on of hands—he working by hidden inspiration—they form, like rivers, long channels. When “river” is said in the singular, as the Psalmist says, “The rush of the river makes glad the city of God” (Ps. 45), the very substance or person of the Holy Spirit is understood. But when “rivers” is said in the plural, as here, “Out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water” (John 7), the distributions of his gifts are aptly signified.

Moreover, they are called rivers not merely of water—water which might be understood in any sense whatever—but rivers of living water, so that by this distinctive difference they may be distinguished from the waters of Pharisaic or heretical teaching, which are truly dead. They should more properly be called not rivers but old cisterns. Concerning them the Lord says through the prophet: “They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and have dug for themselves old cisterns, which cannot hold water” (Jer. 2).

“This,” therefore, says the Evangelist, “he said concerning the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive.” For those believing in him, namely in the Son of God, were truly to receive this Spirit in such a way that his gifts would flow from their bellies like rivers—a thing which had not happened from the beginning of the world until then. For although the ancient fathers had gifts of the Holy Spirit, they did not flow from them like rivers into the Dispersion among the Gentiles now under discussion. Rather, the gifts of grace were contained in one nation, as waters collected in one vessel. But those who believed in him—the apostles, and after them apostolic men—received the Holy Spirit in such a way that, by preaching, baptizing, and laying on hands, they poured out from themselves very great rivers throughout the whole world.

“And they shall flow,” he says, “from his belly”: from the belly, I say, that is, from the inmost parts of the soul, where God is felt by inward love, pouring himself into his chaste bride; where the soul drinks this Spirit from the breast of her husband, God, who impregnates her. When this happens, it differs greatly from those from whose mouth alone an abundance of teaching flows in words, while their heart inwardly does not experience in love the words of its own mouth. Of such persons the Lord rightly says: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. 29; Matt. 15).

It should be noted that he did not say, “the Spirit whom they had received,” but “whom those believing in him were to receive.”

“For the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified.” The glorification of Jesus, on account of which the giving of the Spirit was delayed until it had taken place, must be understood as that which is opposed to Adam’s shameful nakedness. On account of that nakedness, this same Spirit of grace had been hostile to the human race (Gen. 3).

We know the cause which filled Adam with shame and made him naked among enemies—indeed, stripped by the enemy—and an enemy of God: presumptuous disobedience, by which he violated the forbidden tree, fleeing subjection to God and desiring likeness to God. Therefore the obedience of Jesus Christ, by which he offered himself to God the Father for the whole world, is his glorification (Eph. 5). For through that Passion human nature, once stripped naked, was truly glorified in the way a person is glorified when, made a high priest, he stands at the holy altar in consecrated vestments (Heb. 5).

Our High Priest indeed stood before the Father, still wearing corruptible clothing—that is, still wearing mortal flesh—and offered himself for a time. But now, having taken up that same flesh made immortal, he stands before that same Father for us. From then on, from the belly of him who says this very thing—“He who believes in me, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water”—from his belly, I say, that is, from his deep Godhead, two rivers of living water began to flow: the two gifts of this Holy Spirit. The first is the remission of sins; the other is the distribution of diverse graces.

For on the very day on which he rose again, appearing to the apostles in the evening, “he breathed upon them and said, ‘Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive are forgiven them’” (John 20), and so forth. But when he ascended into heaven, where he led captivity captive, he gave gifts to men (Eph. 4): not the same gifts to all, but appointing some apostles, some evangelists, some teachers, and some prophets in his Church (ibid.). These rivers of his gifts endure in the same order until the end of the age: first, being baptized, we receive remission of sins through the Holy Spirit—a gift which works equally in all; then come the gifts of diverse graces, which are not the same in all, but “one and the same Spirit distributes to each one as he wills” (1 Cor. 12).

For Christ did not, as many suppose, consecrate the apostles to the apostolic order when, before his Passion, “having called together his twelve disciples, he gave them authority over unclean spirits, to cast them out and to cure every disease and every infirmity” (Matt. 10). That this was not so is proved by many arguments.

First, because the whole definition of the apostolic order is not the possession of power to cast out demons, cure diseases or infirmities, and perform other such signs. Otherwise the other seventy-two disciples were all apostles [fuissent: “would have been”], since they too received the same power; hence, when they returned with great joy, they boasted, saying: “Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name” (Luke 10).

Second, because the apostles of the New Testament are its first high priests or bishops, whereas the New Testament itself was written or confirmed only by Christ’s blood and death (Heb. 10). How, then, could bishops of the New Testament be ordained before the New Testament itself was written? Or how could Christ, the supreme High Priest, consecrate other high priests or bishops as his vicars before he himself had first exercised his own office?

Certainly, if you maintain that they were consecrated before Christ’s Passion, it is as though you said that it would be fitting for any one of our high priests, simply because he himself has already been consecrated, to consecrate his priests or bishops wherever and however he pleased, outside the lawful time or order of sacrifice and without sacred vestments. Certainly our Lord, before he suffered, was indeed the great High Priest, anointed with the Holy Spirit and power from the very beginning of his conception (Isa. 63; Luke 4); but he did not put on the sacred vestments of his priesthood until he himself became the sacrifice—that is, until he clothed himself with the glory of immortality after putting off, through the Passion of death, his corruptible members.

Before this, according to the prophetic type, “Jesus was clothed in filthy garments” (Zech. 3). But at the very hour of his Passion the Father said concerning him: “Take the filthy garments from him.” And it was said to him: “Behold, I have taken away your iniquity from you and have clothed you with changes of garments.” Again: “Place a clean turban upon his head.” “And they placed a clean turban upon his head and clothed him in garments” (ibid.).

Concerning this putting off of filthy garments—that is, mortal members—and this glorious clothing with immortality, Jesus himself, the great Priest, says here: “I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I will but that it be kindled?” (Luke 12). He immediately adds: “But I have a baptism with which to be baptized, and how I am constrained until it is accomplished!” (ibid.). That is, you are to understand that the fire—that is, the Holy Spirit—is not to be given before that is accomplished.

Thus Jesus had not yet put on the sacred vestments. Nor again was it yet the time or fitting order to pour the sacred oil or chrism upon them, just as the rock in the wilderness was not to pour forth flooding rivers or torrents until it had been struck with the rod at God’s command (Exod. 17; Num. 20). Likewise, the apostles had not yet put on such a garment as would permit them to stand at the holy altar and, from that great High Priest, receive the anointing of sacred oil or chrism—that is, the outpouring of the Holy Spirit—according to fitting reason or order.

For, born as they were in the sin of paternal transgression, they had not yet received remission of sins. This is beyond doubt, unless perhaps someone thinks that remission of sins could have been given to any person, Gentile or Jew, otherwise than through Christ’s death. But this is alien to the faith of Christ. It is therefore established that apostolic ordinations, indeed all ecclesiastical ordinations, and altogether all gifts of the Holy Spirit, were poured out not before but after the glorification of Jesus. For this was the necessary order: first they were redeemed by Christ’s Passion; afterwards, from their High Priest, clothed in the holy robe of immortal glory, apostolic grace was conferred upon them through the twofold outpouring of the Holy Spirit already discussed.

Therefore, as the Evangelist says, “The Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified.” It had not, I say, been given in any [illo: “that”] manner by that bestowal through which sins are forgiven. Yet it had been given to prophets and fathers in that bestowal by which divisions of graces are distributed, but not in such a way that it could properly be called a river. For however small that gift was, it could not flow out into the Dispersion among the Gentiles, but was confined within one nation: the spirit of prophecy announcing in advance that abundance which was to be given through Christ.

## BOOK EIGHT

[Col. 0525]

[Col. 0525B] The struggles of our Lord Jesus Christ require understanding from us who are needy; for, says the Psalmist, “Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and poor” (Ps. 40 [41]), desiring, of course, that He Himself be understood—He “who, though He was rich, became poor for our sake” (2 Cor. 8). For He Himself speaks in the same psalm which we have now begun to expound: “My enemies spoke evil against me: When shall he die, and his name perish?” (Ps. 40 [41]). He plainly describes Himself when He says: “He who ate my bread magnified treachery against me” (ibid.).

Who, having the eye of the heart cleansed by mercy or the compassion of charity, does not understand how great and far from slight was this very contest: that this needy and poor one, standing amid His proud and wealthy enemies [Col. 0525C] who spoke evil of Him, despised in their thoughts because of His poverty, was compelled with His own mouth to proclaim the riches of His divinity and to bear testimony concerning Himself? For if He had concealed Himself in silence, He would have come to us in vain; since without one preaching, none of us would have heard, none would have believed (Rom. 10), and thus His coming would have benefited no one. Therefore He labored by enduring to preach Himself.

And in doing this among the proud, to how much envy, do you suppose, was He exposed? Whoever has learned from Him to be meek and humble in heart (Matt. 11), and for that reason finds it all the more burdensome to proclaim his own excellence, the more humbly he thinks and hates the wind of self-display—such a person feels, in some measure, how arduous it was for this needy and poor one [Col. 0525D] to stand in such a temple and, before enemies speaking evil against Him, to declare who He was and whence He would receive the reproaches cast upon Him (Ps. 68 [69]).

Therefore, that we may share in true blessedness, let us strive to understand this needy and poor one; and let us then judge that we have attained the true understanding of the reading when we receive with a compassionate heart the evils which He hears or suffers.

It follows: “Therefore, when they heard these words of His, some of that crowd said: ‘This is truly the Prophet.’ Others said: ‘This is the Christ.’ But some said: ‘Does the Christ come from Galilee? Does not Scripture say that the Christ comes from the seed of David and from Bethlehem, the town where David was?’” (Mic. 5). “Thus a division arose in the crowd because of Him.”

We read that dissension among a multitude has sometimes furnished holy men an occasion of escape. Something nearly similar happened to the Apostle Paul. When he stood amid the multitude, and the priests and the whole council had assembled against him, “knowing that one part were Sadducees and the other Pharisees, he cried out in the council: ‘Men and brothers, I am a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees; concerning the hope and resurrection of the dead I am being judged.’ And when he had said this, a dissension arose, and the multitude was dissolved. And the tribune ordered the soldiers to go down and snatch [Col. 0526C] Paul from their midst” (Acts 23), plainly because the Lord willed him to be preserved: “For,” He says, “as you have testified of me in Jerusalem, so you must testify also at Rome” (ibid.).

Indeed, something similar happened universally to the holy Church: while the whole multitude of iniquity is divided into many heresies and, discordant against one another, attacks itself, the Catholic faith escapes through the midst of the divisions. This too was prefigured by an ancient miracle—while preserving, of course, the understanding of a still higher mystery—when, at the entrance of the children of Israel, the Red Sea was divided (Exod. 14). For it has been handed down by the elders that, in that division of the sea, separate divisions of the waters were made for each tribe of the children of Israel, and a proper path through the sea was opened for every tribe. They demonstrate this from what is written in the psalm: “Who divided the Red Sea into divisions” (Ps. 135 [136]). By this they teach that many divisions were made according to the path of each tribe.

What was to take place in His Church—namely, that amid the dissenting sects of heretics the Catholic faith should remain unharmed—Christ deigned to prefigure in Himself. For when the rulers and Pharisees had sent officers to seize Him, at His aforesaid cry a division arose [Col. 0527A] in the crowd because of Him, and He was not seized. For this also follows: “But some wished to seize Him, yet no one laid hands upon Him.” In truth, those wishing to seize Him feared “lest perhaps a tumult should arise among the people” (Matt. 26), lest He should be delivered from their hands by the people’s aid. Fearing this, and above all restrained by God, they were held back from their attempt until “Judas handed Him over without crowds.”

“Therefore the chief priests and officers came to the Pharisees.” “Therefore,” he says, because the Lord, who did not yet deign to suffer, had said, “Yet a little while I am with you” (Luke 22), and still wished by words and deeds to fulfill what remained—to fill their eyes and ears and make them sufficiently without excuse, though He was burdensome even for them to behold—the officers came, free from guilt and full of amazement.

“And they said to them: ‘Why have you not brought Him?’” The Evangelist indicates no slight expectation or attentiveness on the part of the chief priests and Pharisees by their prompt question: “Why have you not brought Him?” “Him,” they say, considering it superfluous to say “Jesus,” since they thought that, by bringing Him immediately, they would plainly gratify the assembly that stood waiting.

“The officers answered: ‘Never did a man speak as this man speaks.’” Truly, never did a man so speak. For all human beings who have possessed a word of wisdom or knowledge received it from His fullness (John 1). But the Pharisees are all the more inexcusable because they heard such wisdom and did not obey; they saw such a man and envied Him. What recompense, then, will they have? Surely that which the Spirit of the prophets—or of all the righteous, who indeed spoke less excellently than this man, yet spoke what was good and saving—declares through David’s mouth: “Upon the willows in the midst of it,” that is, of Babylon, “we hung up our instruments, because there those who led us captive asked us for words of songs” (Ps. 136 [137]).

For these men think themselves children of Jerusalem; they think they have eyes to see and ears to hear, and can rationally discern or grasp the lawful sound of the Mosaic or prophetic song. But in truth they are Babylonian willows, clinging by a corrupt root to the banks of the river—that is, to the flowing pleasures of this age—having only the greenness of a Jewish profession in the leaves of their words, but barren of the fruit of good works, so that they have also occupied the ground in vain for so long a time (Luke 13). Therefore upon them—that is, because of them—the instruments of the prophets and of all preachers of truth will be hung up in silence, so that they may not hear the words of the songs for which they have vainly asked. And with this instrument of supreme divinity, with this man who speaks as no man ever spoke, they will go to the nations and sing to them. For these men are altogether unable to endure hearing, unwilling to hear any good testimony concerning Him.

Hence it continues: “The Pharisees answered them: ‘Have you also been deceived?’” And you also, they say, who belong to us and whom we suppose to possess some prudent intelligence—have you been so quickly deceived? As though it had already been established by lawful judgment that whatever they had heard from this man, who spoke as no man ever spoke, was deception. Since no force of reason supports this malicious intention, they immediately twist into an indirect question what they wish to have received as a reason—truly deceivers, and themselves deceived by the evil spirit.

“Has any one of the rulers believed in Him, or any of the Pharisees?” As though they said: It is certain from this alone that you have been deceived by delighting in His words: no one among the rulers or Pharisees has believed in Him. No arguments are needed to prove how weak, vain, and foolish this reasoning is.

O blind guides of the blind—blind, I say, offering guidance to the blind, that together they may fall into the pit (Matt. 15)!
