Are not these rulers, as Isaiah testifies, rulers of Sodom, and this people the people of Gomorrah? (Isa. 1). Then must they be awaited as though they possessed the key of knowledge, so that no one, however much he has eyes, may enter; no one, however much he has ears, may hear, unless such rulers first lead him to sight or hearing? “Has anyone,” they say, “believed in Him among the rulers or Pharisees? But this crowd, which does not know the law, is accursed.”

They judge, of course, that precisely because they do not know the law, this crowd lies under those curses which Moses prescribes in Deuteronomy against those who do not keep the law: “Cursed,” he says, “is he who does not remain in the words of this law, nor fulfill them in deed” (Deut. 27), and so forth. But that crowd would more truly have answered them: This counsel of vanity and this assembly of evildoers (Ps. 25 [26]), which does not perform the law, are accursed. For this crowd, as said above, should be understood as the multitude who had come together from cities and regions for the feast-day, whom those false and deceitful Jerusalemites, in whose possession were the temple and the Holy of Holies, regarded as rustic people in comparison with themselves.

“Nicodemus said to them—the one who had come to Him by night, who was one of them—‘Does our law judge a man unless it first hears from him and knows what he does?’” Why did he not here say openly in defense what he thought, and what he had formerly said when he came to Him by night—namely, that He was not a deceiver but a teacher come from God (John 3), and so forth? Plainly because the night of fear was still in his heart and the day of confidence had not yet dawned. Nor is this surprising, since, “as was said before, the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified”; and therefore rivers of living water could not yet flow from his belly—or from that of the apostles—even into the public circuit of a single synagogue, though, when Jesus was glorified and the Spirit given, they were to flow even into the dispersion of the nations.

Thus, not daring openly to defend the cause or the hated person, yet unable to bear that shameless malice should usurp the license of injustice, he said: “Does our law judge a man unless it first hears from him and knows what he does?” Certainly not; on the contrary, it commands that one should not readily believe what one has heard. By saying this he could not be accused of wishing to defend the man, since his words sounded rather as a defense of the just and holy law. For the law would not be just if it commanded or permitted prejudgments. Thus fearful indeed, but prudent, he fled to a safe stronghold: while speaking for the man, he seemed to plead the cause of the law.

Nevertheless, because his intention could not be hidden from the crafty malice of his hearers, he did not wholly escape hostile assault. For it follows: “They answered and said to him: ‘Are you also a Galilean?’” Is it not therefore true that “the unjust man said, so that he might sin within himself” (Ps. 35 [36])—that is, knowingly and deliberately, the Pharisaic assembly resolved to remain in its sin? Is not this also true: that “he was unwilling to understand in order to do good”? (ibid.). Is this their willingness to understand—that they cannot endure a suggestion that they should hear, or even mention of legal judgment? A man who was a Pharisee and a ruler of the Jews dared, in such a case, to make mention of lawful judgment; by a single saying he made his very presence stink before them and exposed himself to hostile slander. For it breathes no small abundance of hatred that he was so quickly called a Galilean merely because he appeared to favor a Galilean man. For by this point, because of hatred for Jesus, they supposed that the very name of Galilee would offend their scornful nostrils.

“Are you also a Galilean?” they say. “Search and see: for a prophet does not arise from Galilee.” Behold: in recompense and stumbling, that too is fulfilled which the Prophet foretold: “Let their table before them become a snare” (Ps. 68 [69]). The Scripture which they appear to have searched foretold the place where this great Prophet, of whom Moses wrote (Deut. 18), would be born: “And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah; for from you shall come forth a leader who shall rule my people Israel” (Mic. 5). But it kept silent about the fact that an edict would go forth from Caesar Augustus for the whole world to be enrolled; that all would go, each to be registered in his own city; that Joseph would go up from Galilee to the city of David, which is called Bethlehem, to be registered with Mary, his betrothed wife, who was pregnant; and that, while they were there, the days would be fulfilled for her to give birth (Luke 2).

In this way their own table now ensnared them, because they shut their eyes lest they see and made their ears heavy lest they hear (Isa. 6). For, not considering the past and looking wickedly only at present appearances, they thus wove a snare for themselves: according to the Scriptures Christ is to be born from David’s seed and in the town of Bethlehem; but this Jesus is a Galilean man; therefore this man is neither prophet nor Christ. Thus their eyes were darkened so that they could not see (Ps. 68 [69]). For what contradiction is there between Christ’s needing to be born of David’s seed and in the town of Bethlehem, and that same Christ now dwelling in Galilee? Let them therefore search the Scriptures themselves, that they may see that the prophet did not write: “For in you the one born shall dwell,” but “For from you shall come forth a leader who shall rule my people Israel” (Mic. 5).

It follows: “And each returned to his own house.” Because they had woven spiders’ webs, their meeting was easily dissolved and scattered; wounded in conscience by the single objection of a weak cause, each returned to his own house, there again to devise another plan in his den, break the eggs of asps, and brood over what would hatch into a basilisk (Isa. 59).

## Chapter VIII

“But Jesus went to the Mount of Olives, and early in the morning He came again into the temple and taught.” This too is a shadow of things to come: after His adversaries had been scattered and gone away into their little houses, Jesus went to the Mount of Olives, returned again to the temple, and taught. For it was to come about that, when the counsels of those who sought His life were frustrated—saying, “When shall he die, and his name perish?” (Ps. 40 [41])—He would ascend the Mount of Olives, indeed from the Mount of Olives into the height of heaven (Acts 1; Luke 24), and from there give the oil of the Holy Spirit—that is, the true light of knowledge and rest from labors and sorrows. Having done this, He would renew through His apostles an open conflict of preaching with His adversaries (Acts 4–5).

“And all the people came to Him, and, sitting, He taught them.” On the preceding day, says the Evangelist, Jesus stood and “cried out”; now He “sat and taught,” because it was to come about that He would first, “standing”—that is, struggling in His Passion—cry out, as said above; and afterward, having entered into His glory and sat at the Father’s right hand, would send the Spirit of truth to teach us all truth (John 16).

“But the scribes and Pharisees brought a woman caught in adultery, set her in the midst, and said to Him: ‘Teacher, this woman has just been caught in adultery. Now Moses commanded us in the law to stone such women. What, then, do you say?’ They said this to test Him, so that they might accuse Him.” Since Nicodemus had earlier, though timidly, raised a powerful legal obstacle against their wickedness by saying, “Does our law judge a man unless it first hears from him and knows what he does?” they now, with their stratagems renewed, strove with utmost zeal to establish Him as an opponent of the law, so that thereafter no one might dare speak against their counsel.

For what did they suppose except that He, anxious to preserve the reputation of His gentleness lest He lose popular favor, would depart from the course of truth and justice and say something like what He was accustomed to say: “Do not judge, and you shall not be judged; do not condemn, and you shall not be condemned” (Matt. 7). By preaching these and similar exhortations to piety and gentleness, He seemed to have won the people’s favor as one who was merciful and gentle; and this, they thought, was why He was daily surrounded by such great crowds that those wishing to seize Him were restrained by fear of the people. They supposed, therefore, that He would say that the sinner should be released, out of concern for this reputation.

But such mercy would immediately expose Him to accusation, so that those vigorous zealots for the law might say: “You are an enemy of the law; you have spoken against Moses—indeed, against Him who gave the law through Moses—and therefore you yourself must be stoned.” Therefore, that in their crime they might declare themselves avengers of the holy law and so silence every mouth, they brought the sinful woman and set her before Him with the stated design.

Yet, while they thus hunted for the soul of the righteous and undertook to condemn innocent blood (Ps. 93 [94]), they were mocked: they could not harm the righteous, and they lost the sinner from their hands; indeed, while the sinner remained in the temple with the righteous one, the wretched woman with Mercy, they themselves went out covered in shame. Who would not marvel at this event? Who would not venerate this victory of truth and mercy?

Thus it was to come about that, after the things written above, the scribes and Pharisees would bring the sinful woman—that is, the Church from the nations—into the temple to Christ, the liberator of her body and soul; and, when she received remission of sins, they would go out with an evil conscience and fall from grace under the torment of their envy. For when they fastened the Lord’s body with nails and pierced it with a spear, what else did they do but open the true temple of God? And when, through the law and prophets, however unwillingly, they preach that this had to happen for the salvation of all nations, what else do they do but bring to Christ the adulterous gentile world, which had abandoned its lawful husband—its Creator—and had committed fornication with the devil?

You therefore, Christ, fair King, proceed and reign prosperously in all things because of truth, gentleness, and justice; and Your right hand shall lead You wondrously (Ps. 44 [45]). And Your enemies are mocked in all things: the Jews, offspring of vipers, together with their prince, the dragon, “whom You formed to mock him” (Ps. 103 [104]). But let us now return to the historical narrative.

“But Jesus, bending down, wrote with His finger on the ground.” What relevance had it that, when questioned by the voices of those present, He wrote with His finger on the ground, something He was not accustomed to do? Plainly this: they were intent upon the prepared snare, seeking to catch the meek and merciful one, tightening the noose immediately after their first statement of Mosaic authority by adding: “Now Moses commanded us in the law to stone such women.” But He knew Himself to be far greater than Moses, since Moses received on stone tablets the law written by His Spirit—or, more clearly for the present point, by His finger—as you have in Deuteronomy. Therefore, to signify that He ought not, and could not, be bound by the authority of Moses, He fittingly and opportunely bent down and wrote with His finger on the ground, indicating both wisely and humbly that He was the Lord of the law and greater than Moses.

“But as they persisted in questioning Him, He raised Himself up and said to them: ‘Let him who is without sin among you be the first to cast a stone at her.’ And again He bent down and wrote on the ground.” It is a well-known saying, celebrated throughout the world, uttered here not by any arch-senator or consul, but by the King and Emperor of the heavenly court Himself: possessing as much truth as gentleness, and a sweetness of compassion no more lightened than the weight of judgment was made heavy by a balanced measure.

But why, before pronouncing the sentence, did He first write with His finger on the ground, and, after giving the sentence, write again? Certainly because He is the one who, as I said before, wrote with His finger—that is, by His command—the precepts of the law upon stone tablets; and, after the first tablets were broken because of the sin of the calf, wrote others again. Here and there the signs of great things differ, but the realities signified are similar.

For what did the first tablets, broken and cast down because of sin (Exod. 32, 34), signify but the hard hearts of the Jews, to be cast away because of unbelief? Likewise, what does His first bending down to write, followed immediately by the sentence, “Let him who is without sin among you be the first to cast a stone at her,” signify except the same law and the Jews who transgressed it? Their mouths are rightly stopped by this, so that they may not boast against the nations (Rom. 2), since they are proved not to have kept the law which they received.

Hence it follows: “But hearing this, they went out one by one, beginning with the elders.” Thus, both the fact that there the second tablets were cut like the first and written by the finger of God, and the fact that here Jesus again bent down and wrote on the ground, signify the Scripture of the new grace, which is now written by the Spirit of God upon tablets of fleshly hearts (2 Cor. 3). Therefore this woman prefigures the new Church gathered from the nations: when the synagogue departed from the temple of eternal light, convicted by an evil conscience in the scribes and Pharisees who went out, she was left alone with the Savior. It follows:

“And He was left alone, with the woman standing in the midst.” But perhaps, while we seek the higher mysteries, some diligent investigator of the letter may say: How did foolish, malicious, impious persons, treasuring up God’s wrath, so quickly leave Jesus alone with the woman standing in the midst? Did they look inwardly upon themselves and, recognizing in humble conscience that they were sinners, release the sinner? Could their minds, amid so great an abundance of wickedness, admit such a thought? Could “their feet, swift to shed blood,” thus stumble against the barrier of piety? (Ps. 13 [14]).

To this I say: They did not stumble so; they did not so cease from their intention; they did not fall silent in that sense when “they went out one by one.” But what then? Certainly, because they heard such an answer from Him as gave them no hope of accusation, they left their undertaking in confusion. Hence, when the Evangelist had said, “They went out one by one,” he immediately added, “beginning with the elders.” For the older and more experienced they were, the more practiced they were in slander and the more perceptive in recognizing a word they could not slander. When they heard His answer, they first understood it to be strong and unassailable, and therefore they were the first to yield.

For, as said above, since they knew Him to be meek and merciful—indeed, knew that He preached repentance, had called a tax collector, and ate with sinners (Matt. 9), and therefore reproached Him by saying that He was “a glutton and a drinker of wine, a friend of tax collectors and sinners” (Matt. 11)—since they knew these things and were not ignorant that, contrary to Pharisaic thoughts, He had previously defended another sinful woman who touched His feet (Luke 7), they supposed that He would defend this adulteress also, a person whom the law had expressly commanded to be stoned. Thus they expected to condemn Him as guilty of seeking to abolish the law.

But He, turning neither to right nor left, gave such a sentence as neither divine law could weaken nor human reason despise. As they considered the strength of this sentence and perceived that they could gain nothing, the woman was left standing alone with Jesus in the midst; as they went out, her case was abandoned like a useless and rightly ineffectual snare. Having had this snare set before Him, Jesus, with one answer of wisdom, like a roe or a young hart (Song 2), had leapt to the heights, so that no cunning of these dogs could pursue Him.

Therefore these Jerusalemites, thought to be zealots for the law but in truth called by the prophet rulers of Sodom, went out and left the wretched woman, not because they recognized their own wretchedness, but because whatever they did to her, they would have no grounds upon which to accuse Mercy (Isa. 1).

“But Jesus, raising Himself up, said to her: ‘Woman, where are those who accused you? Has no one condemned you?’ She said: ‘No one, Lord.’ And Jesus said to her: ‘Neither do I condemn you.’” Although the deceitful tempters had asked Him to judge, nevertheless, because He truly is “the one appointed by God as judge of the living and the dead” (Acts 10), He shows Himself ready at hand; He in no way denies that He is judge, or that the law and authority of judgment belong to Him. For, after pronouncing the sentence and the accusers having departed, He says: “Woman, where are those who accused you?” and so forth.

For “Let him who is without sin be the first to cast a stone at her” was not a refusal of judgment, like that other response when someone from the crowd said: “Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me,” and He answered: “Man, who appointed me judge or divider over you?” (Luke 12). He had not come to distribute or judge earthly profits, but had received from the Father all judgment for forgiving or retaining sins (John 5). Therefore, when He says, “Woman, where are those who accused you?” it expresses the truth of a judge and the maturity of judgment: He does not refuse lawful judgment but proves that unlawful accusers had come.

For, in every just examination, whether according to divine or human law, both accusers and witnesses must be free from every crime. But they confessed themselves criminals by their flight. When the judge sought witnesses free from crime, who according to the law might cast the first stone, all went out. Thus this is the judge who sits upon the throne (Ps. 9 [10]) and judges equity, doing absolutely nothing outside the right and law of judgment. When the accusers failed and abandoned the case they had begun, He finally substituted mercy for the judgment that was thereby withdrawn: “Neither do I condemn you,” He says.

Yet this mercy does not forgive sins so as also to grant permission to sin. Rather, it suspends judgment so that the sinner may have opportunity to withdraw from sins with the fruit of repentance. Therefore He immediately adds: “Go, and sin no more.” In one and the same sentence mercy and truth meet together; righteousness and peace kiss each other (Ps. 84 [85]). For “Go” belongs to mercy and peace; “sin no more” belongs to truth and righteousness.

Thus the most just Judge of the living and dead neither threatens judgment alone nor promises mercy alone; rather, like a just balance, He weighs the case of every human being by mercy and judgment together, as by two scales. Every soul, the whole Church, once subjected through adultery to the devil, trusts that the scale of judgment will be raised above it if, not empty but laden with faith and good deeds, it presses heavily down upon mercy’s side.

It follows:

[Col. 0534C] “Therefore Jesus again spoke to them, saying: ‘I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me does not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life.’” Therefore, says the Evangelist, because the scribes and Pharisees strove so earnestly to destroy God’s present grace and remove from their midst the testimony of truth by silencing everyone—for example, saying, “Have you also been deceived?” and “Are you also a Galilean?” (John 7)—and because all human testimony failed through fear of them, He Himself, of whom it had been foretold through the prophet, “Behold, I have given him as a witness to the peoples” (Isa. 55), persevering alone in testimony, again spoke to them, saying: “I am the light of the world.”

I say that He spoke again: that is, by this saying He repeated what He had said to them the day before, standing and crying out: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me,” and so forth. For these words now spoken fitly adhere to and agree with those sayings: “I am the light of the world,” and so forth. In the psalm, after it had been said, “For with you is the fountain of life,” it was immediately added, “And in your light we shall see light” (Ps. 35 [36]). For Christ, the wisdom of God, is to us in one and the same act both cup and light: whoever is steeped in the water of this wisdom is immediately freed, by illumined understanding, from every darkness of error.

Accordingly, here too, speaking of Himself, after saying, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink,” He repeats the same thing: “I am,” He says, “the light of the world.” And in the psalm the Prophet, after speaking of Him, “For with you is the fountain of life,” immediately added: “And in your light we shall see light.” Therefore the Evangelist does not simply say, “Jesus therefore spoke to them, saying,” but significantly, “Jesus therefore again spoke to them, saying: ‘I am the light of the world.’”

See how briefly and magnificently He expressed that the envy of impious human beings can do no harm to the glory of God (1 Thess. 5). “I,” He says, “am the light of the world.” As though He said: Why do you, impious children of night and darkness, labor to take away from my brightness or great renown the support of mortals? (Matt. 5). Would you not be laughable if you tried, by blowing upon it, to extinguish this visible sun shining on the whole world from its lofty circuits, or by striking the air with fists to cast it down from heaven’s great candlestick and hide it under a bushel? Surely this is like what you are doing in striving to erase my name or extinguish my fame.

For I am the light of the world. Therefore, ridiculous moles or bats, you may indeed close your own eyes and fail to see me, the true light; but you will never prevail in plucking out the eyes of the whole world or extinguishing its light. I am light—not of the Israelite nation alone, but of the whole world: “the true light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world” (John 1); the light without which no angel or human being ever could or can see God. All angels or human beings deprived of that light are darkness.

Therefore I have said and say: “Whoever follows me does not walk in the darkness” of error or ignorance, “but shall have the light of life”; and, having it, will himself also pour forth light upon his imitators, so that such persons may deservedly be told: “You are the light of the world”—light illuminated, not the substance of light itself.

“Therefore the Pharisees said: ‘You bear witness concerning yourself; your witness is not true.’” Truly he was bearing great witness concerning himself (John 3), both now when he said, “I am the light of the world; whoever follows me does not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life,” and above, in different words but with the same sense: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John 7). But they [Col. 0535D] had determined in their hearts to hear no testimony concerning him; and, so far as they could, they strove somehow to block up the fountain of life and extinguish the brightness of this light (John 9). For they acted wickedly and therefore hated the light, and would not come to the light, lest their works—works of night and darkness—should be reproved.

Therefore they said: “You bear witness concerning yourself; your witness is not true.” As though they said: Contrary to Scripture, which says, “Let another praise you, and not your own mouth” (Prov. 27), you praise and magnify yourself by bearing witness concerning yourself, having no witness other than yourself; and therefore your testimony is neither true nor lawful. For this reason the prophet says: “Hear the word of the Lord, mocking men, who rule over my people who are in Jerusalem. For you have said: We have struck a covenant with death, and have made a pact with hell” (Isa. 28). With such zeal do you suppress the mouth of life and truth, as though you were allies of death and hell.

When the officers marvelled at the speech of this man—or rather, of God who was also man—you said: “Have you also been led astray?” To Nicodemus too, your companion, because he had dared to utter a small word concerning the lawful order of judgment, you immediately shut his mouth, saying: “Are you also a Galilean?” (John 7). You anathematized the believing crowd, saying: “Has any one of the rulers believed in him, or of the Pharisees? But this crowd, which does not know the law, [Col. 0536B] is accursed.” Since, while you thus cry out against him, he has no human witness besides himself alone, you now wish to shut his own mouth also and choke his voice, alleging as though it were a charge of vainglory that he magnifies himself with his own mouth.

Thus you strive, helpers of death and hell, lest any of the dead hear the voice of the Son of God and live; lest the world behold its light through the windows of his utterances and abandon infernal darkness. But it shall not happen thus: your covenant with death shall be annulled, and your pact with hell shall not stand.

It follows: “Jesus answered and said to them: Even if I bear witness concerning myself, my testimony is true, because I know whence I came and whither I go. But you do not know whence I came or whither I go.” These unhappy men do not know [Col. 0536C] how forcefully he contends with them here, and with what weight of his greatness he presses upon them, when, in answer to the single objection by which they detest his testimony, he defends both his testimony as true and his judgment as just. They ought, of course, to recognize what kind of witness they were rejecting: namely, the one whom they would see as judge in the same case of their own.

“And even if I,” he says, “bear witness concerning myself, my testimony is true.” The order and meaning of the words is this: My testimony is true, although I bear witness concerning myself.

And indeed, if anyone bears witness concerning himself, it does not immediately follow that his testimony [Col. 0536D] is false. Otherwise the testimony of Moses and the prophets must consequently be said to have been false, since each testified concerning himself that he had been sent by God (Exod. 33; Jer. 3). For no one among men could know this otherwise than through their own testimony.

It must be understood that, although no human being besides this God-and-man Jesus Christ knows concerning himself whence he came or whither he goes—because he does not know how he was made, or for what end he will come—yet, if anyone bears witness concerning himself, his testimony is true insofar as he knows by whom he was called and to what work he was called. For example, when Paul says of himself: “Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called as an apostle, [Col. 0537A] set apart for the Gospel of God” (Rom. 1); or especially what he says elsewhere: “Since many boast, I too will boast” (2 Cor. 1), and other such statements.

Therefore, since both a truthful spirit and a lying spirit bear witness concerning themselves, the argument of those who say, “You bear witness concerning yourself; your testimony is not true,” is defective. Accordingly, the two little propositions which they had wrongly divided into affirmation and negation, as though mutually contradictory and incapable of existing together—“You bear witness concerning yourself; your testimony is not true”—this true defender of himself and reprover of falsehood joins together and reduces to one affirmative proposition, saying: “Even if I bear witness concerning myself, my testimony [Col. 0537B] is true.”

He immediately proves this by the reason added: “Because I know whence I came and whither I go.” By this reasoning, as he confirms the truth of his testimony, so by its opposite—that is, by what follows, “But you do not know whence I came or whither I go”—he attacks the falsity of those who rejected this same testimony of his. For since these are undoubtedly opposites—“Because I know whence I came and whither I go; but you do not know whence I came or whither I go”—as his testimony is true because he knows whence he came and whither he goes, so conversely the testimony which they utter against Jesus is evidently false because they do not know whence he came or whither he goes.

To know concerning himself whence he came belongs properly to him who was not made temporally from nothing [Col. 0537C] or from non-being, as we were, but was born timelessly from the uncreated essence of the Father; through him all of us were created so that we might be. Likewise, to know whither he goes belongs properly to him, because none other than he himself ordained his ways, which, having become man for us in this mortal condition, he deigned to walk.

For we do not know whence we come. We cannot even know how we were conceived and formed in the womb; nor can we know what we shall be hereafter. For “man does not know his end” (Eccles. 9), and all things are reserved for an uncertain future time. Therefore, when he says, “I am the light of the world,” his testimony is true because he knows whence he came. And when he says, “Whoever [Col. 0537D] follows me does not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life,” he surely bears true witness concerning himself, being certain because he knows also whither he goes and where he will lead the one who follows him.

Moreover, no one knows anything concerning him except so far as he has learned it from him. Therefore whoever says anything else concerning him than what he has received from him is a false witness; and because he does not follow him, he walks in darkness—just as those who said, “You bear witness concerning yourself; your testimony is not true.” To stop their mouths, this rebuke alone is sufficient: “But you do not know whence I came or whither I go.”

This was said to refute their carnal opinion, by which they had said above: “We know where this man is from; but when the Christ comes, no one knows where he is from.” Nor, because he had afterward answered them, “You know me, and you know where I am from,” ought he now to be thought contrary to himself in the present passage when he says, “But you do not know whence I came or whither I go.” For it follows:

“You judge according to the flesh; I judge no one.” As though he said: You do indeed know that I am a Galilean man, and you say, “Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph and Mary? And are not his brothers and sisters among us?” (Matt. 13; Luke 4). And because this is partly true, I therefore said above: “You know me, and you know where I am from” (John 7). But how much is this knowledge of yours? For you think this very thing according to the flesh, and judge according to the flesh; that is, according to the poverty and lowliness of my parents Mary and Joseph, and of my brothers and sisters—that is, my carnal kinsfolk—you assess my person. Beyond what is visible in me, you refuse to hear or understand anything; and so you judge me far inferior to your kings and to your prophets, whom your fathers killed, while you, by persecuting me, build their tombs and hasten to fill up the measure of your fathers.

Therefore I say: “You judge according to the flesh.” Yet I too could judge according to the flesh, but “I judge no one.” For I could conversely say that, even according to the flesh, I am greater than Moses (Matt. 23); greater, I say, and nobler than any king or [Col. 0538C] ruler according to the flesh. For unlike all of you, and all your fathers or rulers, who according to the common course of nature were born of a corrupted woman, I was born according to the flesh from virginal nobility, from the royal stock of David.

Thus I too could judge all men according to the flesh as inferior to myself, since they were conceived in sins and born from corruption; but “I judge no one.” For now I have come not to judge, but to be judged.

“And if I judge, my judgment is just, because I am not alone, but I and the Father who sent me.” Even if at last, he says, I judge—namely, after I have been judged, for then I must judge my birth both according to divinity and according to humanity, [Col. 0538D] so that it may be proclaimed throughout the whole world—“even if,” I say, “at last I judge, my judgment is just.” In what respect? Namely, “because I am not alone, but I and the Father who sent me.”

I am not alone, that is, unlike that other one who comes in his own name, whom you will receive, who will truly be alone and will come alone, because God will not send him; he will come from himself, nor will he act with God, but “will oppose and exalt himself above everything called God or worshipped” (2 Thess. 2). But I have not come from myself: the Father sent me, and I remain in communion with him, doing nothing from myself and judging nothing from myself. Therefore whatever I testify, whatever I judge, he confirms my testimony by works present and following; he establishes that my judgment is true and just.

It should be noted, in the true humility and humble truth of the Son of God, that in all his words he maintains this tenor of communion with the Father, of which he now says: “Because I am not alone, but I and the Father who sent me.” Thus he nowhere speaks anything absolutely concerning his person alone, but always confesses what he is in such a way as to direct attention at the same time to the social and undivided love of the Father’s person.

To those who consider rightly, the Sabellian error can raise no cloud of confusion here. We call this the Patripassian heresy. Confessing only one person of the Godhead, it says: The one and same person is Father when he wills, Son when he wills, and Holy Spirit when he wills. Thus confusing the persons, it contends that the Father alone or the Son alone must be confessed. But in this passage the Son fittingly says: “I am not alone, but I and the Father who sent me.” Therefore the Jews who said, “Your testimony is not true,” are refuted; Sabellius too, before he was born, is crushed and cast out.

It follows:

“And in your law it is written [230] that the testimony of two men is true. I am one who bears witness concerning myself, and the Father who sent me bears witness concerning me.” And therefore, he says, “because I know whence I came and whither I go, my testimony is true”; and further must be said concerning the truth of this same testimony. I say, then: “In your law it is written that the testimony of two men is true” (Deut. 17), namely, God saying through Moses in Deuteronomy: “One witness shall not stand against anyone, whatever sin or crime it may be; but every word shall stand by the mouth of two or three witnesses” (Deut. 19).

This is the great and unquestionable proposition which I set forth, to which assent must freely be given, because “it is thus written in your law.” Therefore an assumption may now be made. Behold, this statement which I uttered—“I am the light of the world”—and every such thing which I say or have said, which you reject by saying, “Your testimony is not true,” is defended by two witnesses. For I am one witness, who bears witness concerning [Col. 0539D] myself, by that ground or authority by which I said, “Because I know whence I came and whither I go”; and another also “bears witness concerning me, namely the Father who sent me.”

By this lawful reply he answers their unjust intention (John 9). For their intention was that no one should bear witness concerning him that he was the Christ, or at least that he was a prophet, or indeed that he was in any way from God. Pursuing this intention, they eventually conspired so far that if anyone confessed him to be the Christ, he should be cast out of the synagogue. This most wicked craftiness had to be mocked; and since so great a majesty did not deign even to mention testimony from men, the testimony from above had to be indicated, a testimony which the pack of dogs and the council of malicious men could not silence.

Therefore he says: “In your law it is written that the testimony of two men is true.” He does not say simply, “in the law,” but pointedly, “in your law,” because the same law, though just, holy, and good, was his law in one way and theirs in another. It was his because it was given by him; it was theirs because it was imposed upon them (Rom. 7). As stated above, it had to be granted that the testimony of two men is true, because it is so written in the law; and therefore, by the assumption: “I am,” he says, “one who bears witness concerning me; the Father who sent me.”

And this itself was plain to them: that he bore witness concerning himself, and that the Father likewise bore witness concerning him. For they heard him say [Col. 0540B] that God was his Father; on account of this, as was said above, they persecuted him; and they had heard what he had said a little earlier: “I am the light of the world.” They heard these and similar things, and they saw works no less great than so great a profession. In his words his own testimony sounded forth; in his works the Father’s testimony flashed from above. For if he lied in professing himself the Son of God, he would certainly not have been glorified by the splendour of miracles, but would have been confounded by punishment fitting for the proud.

It was manifest to the Jews that the God whom they professed as their Father had always resisted the proud. For example, Aaron and Miriam, rising proudly against Moses, were struck with the plague of leprosy (Num. 12); Dathan, Abiram, and Korah, puffed up through pride, were with their accomplices—some swallowed alive by the earth, others devoured by flames (Num. 16); and Saul, made the Lord’s anointed, was through pride given over to a demonic spirit (1 Sam. 16).

But God nowhere refuted this man, who said himself to be Christ, the Son of God, and professed God as his Father (John 11); rather, he testified through works that his words were true, so that he also raised him from the dead and from the grave on the third day, and gave the Holy Spirit through his name to those who believed in him (Acts 2, 10). Therefore it is evident both to the Jews and to the whole world that God also bore witness concerning him—the man thought to be Joseph’s son—who bore witness concerning himself and professed God as his Father.

It follows:

“Therefore they said to him: Where is your Father?” He plainly called God his Father to them, but they did not wish to understand this. Therefore they ask: “Where is your Father?” Impious and blind men, why do you seek his Father? Do you wish to kill him too, or cast him out of the synagogue, should he dare in your presence to bear witness concerning his Son?

“He answered them: You know neither me nor my Father.” Rightly he gently but strongly reproves the inquiry of faithless men who importunately interrogate him, and judges it worthy of such an answer. For why, when he had first said, “Because I know whence I came and whither I go, but you do not know whence I came or whither I go,” did they remain silent and not say, “Lord, whence do you come and whither do you go?” But now, when he said, “The Father who sent me bears witness concerning me,” they insolently inquire and say, “Where is your Father?” Why, I say, do they remain silent concerning the former and inquire about the latter, unless because they know not how to seek the glory of true testimony from the Son of God, but how to envy it?

Therefore, when they said, “Where is your Father?” he did not answer what they had asked, for example by saying: Heaven and earth are full of his glory or majesty (Isa. 6); but he said this: “You know neither me nor my Father.” That is: because you do not know me and do not wish to know me, neither do you know my Father. Perhaps you say: We know you; we know you as the son of Joseph and Mary; we seek nothing further concerning you, a Galilean man. To this, I say: “If you knew me, perhaps you would know my Father also.”

For even with individual men, it is no small part of knowing anyone to know whose son he is, or who his father was. But, he says, “You do not know my Father.” For you now say: “Where is your Father?” Therefore, “You know neither me.” Clearly this little word *perhaps* is doubtful in our manner of speech; but in the language of truth, which knows no doubt, it reaches the full force of confirmation with sharper significance, as though it had been said: Certainly you know my Father also. People sometimes use this expression when they seek to affirm something more solemnly and vigorously, as if someone should say: “If perhaps a mother loved herself.”

Nevertheless, it is truer, firmer, and more necessary that whoever knows Christ should know God as his Father. For no one can in any way know what Christ is according to substance unless he also knows that God is his Father. We cannot know what Christ is according to substance as we know what any ordinary human being is, even if we do not know who his human father was. Therefore, since it is not doubtful to us, much less was it doubtful to him; and consequently he must be understood to have spoken not doubting but rather affirming: “If you knew me, perhaps you would know my Father also,” just as in the saying: “If you believed Moses, perhaps you would believe me also.”

It follows:

“Jesus spoke these words in the treasury, teaching in the temple; and no one seized him, because [Col. 0541D] his hour had not yet come.” Jesus, he says, spoke these words of such majesty in the treasury to those who sought to kill him: that is, in a renowned place, accessible almost only to the rulers and Pharisees. For the treasury was not ordinarily frequented by the common people, except individually as they approached and cast in money [231], while rulers and Pharisees sat around, taking delight in the splendid spectacle of very great profits.

Therefore Jesus spoke these words with great confidence and without fear in such a place, “teaching in the temple”: that is, speaking nothing in secret, but establishing a public doctrine to be proclaimed openly to every age. And, he says, “no one seized him.” Why? “Because his hour had not yet come.” Their frenzied minds, then, had by no means been softened; but by his own nod he restrained their impotent malice—he who had power, at the time or hour he himself had appointed, to lay down his life and to take it up again (John 10).

“Therefore Jesus said to them again: I go away, and you will seek me, and you will die in your sins. Where I go, you cannot come.” Therefore, he says, because while persisting in evil they sought his life (Ps. 37), employed violence without any reason, and meditated deceit all day, and restrained their hands for no reason except that their hour had not yet come, “Jesus said to them again: I go away, and you will seek me,” and so forth.

Jesus said this again, I say, for above he had said the same thing to them when “the rulers and Pharisees sent officers to seize him”: “Yet a little while I am with you,” he said, “and I go to him who sent me” (John 7), and “where I go, you cannot come.” Therefore he said to them not for the first time but again: “I go away, and you will seek me.”

I indeed, he says, as I have already said, depart from here; I die through your crime; death which you bring upon me is now at hand, and I shall pass from this world to the Father. But when I have departed, will my name perish from the earth, as you my hostile envying detractors desire? After I have gone hence to my Father, will your eyes be freed from my glory, so that they shall not see in me what is grievous for them to behold? It shall not be so. Rather, then you will most openly see what I said a little earlier: “I am the light of the world”; and, seeing this, you sinners will be angry, will gnash your teeth, [Col. 0542C] and waste away; and your desire will perish (Ps. 111), because my name cannot perish.

Then, with envy stinging you more sharply, restless and wickedly anxious, you will seek—that is, persecute—me; “and you will die in this your sin,” because you will persevere in this wickedness until the end of your lives. You will be unable to accomplish anything harmful to my glory or name, but will merely kill yourselves by evil will and obstinate envy. “For where I go, you cannot come.” Indeed, even those who seek and follow me in love cannot come where I go; but they will be able to come at some time. But you, who seek and pursue me in hatred, can never come where I go.

Now, indeed, you can come where I am, and at some time will even be able to seize and kill me; but when you do this, “I go” there “where you cannot come.” Thus you will die in your sin: namely, that in which you seek me wickedly and persecute me in my faithful ones, in order to erase my name. For you will persevere in this until death.

“Therefore the Jews said: Will he kill himself, because he says, ‘Where I go, you cannot come’?” Above, when he said to them the same thing that he now says again—“Where I go, you cannot come”—they said: “Will he go into the dispersion of the Gentiles and teach the Gentiles?” (John 7). But now, repeating this same statement, he had attacked them more sharply, as was fitting. For he added: “And you will die in your sin.” Therefore, with their bile more bitterly stirred, “the Jews said: Will he kill himself?” What could be more bitter, what more wicked?

O Jews, cruel and criminal murderers, can you perceive nothing good concerning this man who raised your dead, so that you think the sole possibility remaining to him is to kill himself? And are you so incapable of such a deed that you cannot kill yourselves by his example? Rather, once you have killed this man, you will kill yourselves, with such fury and rage that the world will marvel and even your enemies will grieve for you. Let those who wish read of your destruction under Titus and Vespasian, and see that you are the one nation of murderers killing yourselves.

It follows:

“And he said to them: You are from below; I am from above. You are of this world; I am not of this world. Therefore I told you that you will die in your sins.” He gave them a bitter reason why they could not come where he was going and would die in their sin: “You,” he says, “are from below; I am from above.”

This comparison did not yet suffice to define the cause of their inability, since all men, elect and reprobate alike, are from below according to their common nature. Thus John the Baptist also, when he was thought to be the Christ, said in comparison—or rather, in despair—of himself, while he who truly was and is Christ: “He who is from the earth is of the earth and speaks of the earth; he who comes from heaven is above all” (John 3). Therefore it had to be added, so that the whole cause of their inability might be set down, in accordance with what he had said: “Where I go, you cannot come.”

For there were also persons from below, taken from the earthly mass and born of the first earthly man, to whom he said: “That where I am, you also may be” (John 14). Therefore he added: “You are of this world; I am not of this world.” This belongs to the reprobate, and in this they differ from the elect: although all are from below—that is, from the earth—except Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, who came from heaven, they alone are of this world. For to the elect he says: “If you were of the world, the world would love what was its own; but because you are not of the world, and I have chosen you out of the world, therefore the world hates you” (John 15).

Therefore both had to be said: that they were from below by common nature and that they were of this world through their own vice or wickedness, so that both grounds might show them incapable of going where he was going—he who is from above, that is, from God the Father, by the nature of his own divinity, and who is not of this world through the complete innocence of the human nature which he had assumed, or through his heavenly life.

Having given this reason with equal strength and gentleness, he says: “Therefore I told you that you will die in your sin.” He immediately confirms this likewise with another reason, adding: “If, therefore, you do not believe that I am, you will die in your sins.” For truly no one can otherwise be numbered among the members of Christ, and live from the Spirit of God under that head in the one body of the one Church, except by believing that Christ is from above and not of this world: that is, both that he is true God from God the Father above, and that though born in the world he has admitted none of the vices or sins which are in the world.

He himself said elsewhere: “No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3). Rightly, therefore, he says here—he alone who is from above—to those whom he knew would in no way be incorporated into himself through faith: “Where I go, you cannot come”; and therefore I told you: “You will die in your sin. For if you do not believe that I am, you will die in your sins.”

[Col. 0544B] “Therefore they said to him: Who are you?” Until this point the Jews, unwilling to understand and refusing to inquire [232], could somehow pretend that they had not perceived where his aforementioned testimony was directed. But now the light of the world, defending that testimony of his with a terrible flash, and shaking awake the slumber of men dozing—or rather snoring with wakeful noses—had caused their eyes to be opened by saying: “For if you do not believe that I am, you will die in your sins.” They could no longer pretend that something had flashed forth in this saying which they ought to behold or hear. “Therefore they said: Who are you?”

They inquired irreverently and knocked arrogantly, but it was necessary that they should find, fitting that it should be opened to them, so that they might become more and more inexcusable, and that testimonies of the truth might increase more and more for those who would believe. Hear, then, what follows.

“Jesus said to them: The Beginning, who also speak to you. I have many things to say and to judge concerning you.” He was clearly saying this in order that, because he himself had raised the question and stirred them to inquire by the fearful sentence, “For if you do not believe that I am, you will die in your sins,” he might on this occasion declare some great and worthy testimony concerning himself. And indeed what he testified in this answer is great and worthy; for it is as though he had said that he himself is he who was, who is, and who is to come.

For, because he was, he calls himself “the Beginning”; because he is, he immediately adds, “who also speak to you”; and because he is to come, namely to judge the living and the dead on the last day (Rev. 1), he says, “I have many things to say and to judge concerning you.”

Thus the torment of those whom the wise man has already marked—“Envy kills the little man, and anger slays the foolish man” (Job 5)—was greatly increased. They had long envied this man, as they supposed, the son of Joseph, because some of the crowd thought him to be the Christ. For, as was said above, when some in the crowd heard his sayings, “some said, ‘This truly is the prophet’; others said, ‘This is the Christ’” (John 7), although they thought that the Christ would be merely a man.

But he now, when they said to him, “Who are you?” professed concerning himself something far above man: “The Beginning,” he said—understand, “I am”—and immediately added, “who also speak to you.” In one and the same answer he indicated both the timeless and immutable essence of his divinity and the temporal condition of his assumed humanity.

According to the infinite antiquity of his divinity, he is the Beginning: the Beginning in whom all things were created, as it is written at the beginning of Genesis: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Gen. 1). But according to the flesh he is the End, that is, the consummation, because in him all things have likewise been restored (Eph. 1). Hence he says in the Apocalypse: “I am alpha and omega (α and ω), the beginning and the end” (Rev. 1).

From this Beginning, before the ages, he was God alone; but now, when he speaks these things to them, he is God and man, though still passible as man. At the end of the ages, however, the same God and man will come, having many things to say and to judge, and, since he rose from the dead, impassible in both natures.

Therefore, to those who irreverently asked who he was—of whom he had said, “For if you do not believe that I am”—he described his being in a fearful manner, concluding with the fitting end: “I have many things to say and to judge concerning you.”

His being is to be understood as that which is common to the whole Trinity and proper or singular to the same one God. Speaking to Moses, he expressed it more carefully: “I am who I am. Thus shall you say to the children of Israel: He Who Is has sent me to you” (Exod. 3). This being differs greatly from the being of all things or creatures because it is subject to no accidents. For example, man comes forth like a flower and is crushed, flees like a shadow, and never remains in the same state (Job 14). The angelic creature too proves this, especially from those angels who fell: it is one thing for all rational spirits to be what they are by substance; another thing for some to have become evil through an accidental wickedness and for others, likewise, to have become gracious through an accidental grace.

The substance of God, I say, is subject to no accidents, as are these or other things that have been made. Therefore he alone is true because he is immutable; and thus his distinguishing characteristic is to be that which is. Accordingly, both when he spoke to Moses and now when he bears witness concerning himself against his enemies, he aptly employs this substantive verb to describe himself.

Then, because the name “God” appeared common to many gods to the children of Israel, accustomed to serve many gods in Egypt, he said, in order to distinguish them—those who had once indeed been human beings but now were neither gods nor men—“I am who I am; and thus shall you say to the children of Israel: He Who Is has sent me to you.”

Now, however, because his Jewish enemies intended to bring it about that he should no longer be, and that his name should perish, he fittingly employs the same substantive verb in order to show that they labour in vain.

It follows:

“But he who sent me is true, and what I heard from him I speak in the world.” [Col. 0546A] Almost nowhere in the whole testimony which the Son of God bears concerning himself does he pass over the testimony of the Father, so that by this also he may especially confirm what he said elsewhere: “I have come in the name of my Father; another will come in his own name” (John 5). Thus here too, when he was asked who he was, after replying, “The Beginning, who also speaks to you,” he immediately followed this by invoking the Father’s testimony in these words: “But he who sent me is true, and what I heard from him I speak in the world.” It is as if he were saying: I am the Beginning, yet I did not come from myself; I also speak to you, yet I do not speak from myself. I did not, I say, come from myself, nor am I the Beginning from myself; rather, “he who sent me is true.”

This can be understood more clearly by contrast with him, namely the one [Col. 0546B] who will come in his own name. For Satan, who received his name because he lifted himself up against God, and wished to be a beginning unto himself and to sit for himself on the sides of the north (Isa. 14), is a liar because, speaking from what is his own, he disagrees with the Father of truth and produces falsehood, while boasting that he himself is the Beginning. Having entered that condemned man at the end of the age, he will profess that he is God, the Beginning, “so that he may oppose and exalt himself,” as the Apostle says, “above all that is called God or is worshipped” (2 Thess. 2). Indeed, in the Apocalypse his name, according to its numerical value, is read as *Thytan*, which is interpreted, “say, light.”

Therefore this true witness, declaring that the blasphemy of that liar does not belong to him, fittingly forestalls the thoughts of his opponents, who later, because of these and similar words, will say: “We do not stone you for a good work, but for blasphemy” (John 22). For everything said of this true Beginning and true Son of God stands opposed to the deceits of that evil one. “I am the Beginning,” he says, “who also speaks to you”; but unlike that other who will come in his own name, whom you will receive, neither have I come from myself or in my own name, nor do I speak from myself: “but he who sent me is true, and what I heard from him I speak in the world.” For above he said likewise: “Neither did I come from myself, but he who sent me is true, whom you do not know” (John 5).

Thus, lest this adversative conjunction, by which he joins the following statement to the preceding one—“But he who sent me is true”—be empty and in order that it may explain its meaning more fully, what was openly said elsewhere must now necessarily be understood. Yet in a wonderful and ineffable manner, while proclaiming the Father to be true, he who elsewhere says, “I am the truth” (John 14), bears testimony concerning himself. He could have said, “My Father is true”; but, to show that the Father is true from no other source than because he begot him who is Truth, he preferred to say: “But he who sent me is true.” We commonly speak in this way: “This sun, which drives away the night and brings so bright a day into the world, is a luminous substance”; or, “This man, who acted or spoke so wisely, is wise.”

It should be understood that, although he could have said, “He who begot me [Col. 0547A] is true,” with the prophetic authority by which it was said, “The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Ps. 2), he preferred, both here and in most places, to say, “He sent me.” This is equivalent in force, and, because it breathes a more welcome humility in the ears of human beings—especially the envious and proud—it is more tolerable and less quickly exposed to slander.

Therefore, when he says, “But he who sent me is true,” he vindicates the truth of the Father’s testimony; and when he adds, “and what I heard from him I speak in the world,” he likewise vindicates the truth and certainty of the testimony which he himself bears concerning himself. For above he had proposed to defend both when he said: “I am he who bears testimony concerning myself, and the Father who sent me bears testimony concerning me.”

Furthermore, it is not irrelevant to ask how the Son heard from the Father, since he himself is the Father’s Word. We must not immediately take refuge in the humility of his humanity and say that the Son heard the Father according to his humanity, by that hearing of which it is said through the Prophet: “I will hear what the Lord God speaks in me” (Ps. 84). For he did not merely say, “What I heard from him, I speak”; rather, he added, “in the world,” so that you may understand that he said he had heard outside the world—that is, before he came into this world—what he would speak in the world.

Therefore, when he says, “What I heard from him I speak in the world,” it is as if the Truth consubstantial with God the Father said: As I was born from God, so I remain incorrupt in this world [Col. 0547C] and admit no falsehood. This sense is more relevant to the matter, since they had charged Truth with lying when they said: “You bear testimony concerning yourself; your testimony is not true.” It follows:

“And they did not understand that he was calling God his Father.” Since much earlier, when he said, “My Father works until now, and I work,” the Evangelist had added: “Therefore the Jews persecuted him, because he not only broke the Sabbath, but also called God his own Father, making himself equal to God” (John 5), how does he now say, “They did not understand that he was calling God his Father”? Thus he does not so much excuse their ignorance as marvel at their malice, unwilling to understand. They pretend not to have noticed his words, because they did not yet dare to do what, for that very reason, they would later do: run for stones, or finally drag him before the governor and demand his condemnation on the ground of this statement, as though it were blasphemy.

“Jesus therefore said to them: When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am, and that I do nothing from myself; but as the Father taught me, these things I speak. And he who sent me is with me, and has not left me alone, because I always do what is pleasing to him.”

Therefore, he says, since they did not understand that he called God his Father, since they did not receive his testimony, and since malicious accusers did not listen to truth’s defense, he now supplies a conclusion—that is, an artful ending to the discourse. As skilled orators customarily do, gathering together the parts of their enumeration and briefly recalling the matters of which they have spoken in order to move their audience and renew the speech in memory, so he briefly gathers up and in a sense stores within himself what he has said from the point at which they objected: “You bear testimony concerning yourself; your testimony is not true.” Since they now refuse to see and know so as to be saved, let them someday see and be put to shame, “being jealous as a people; and let fire devour the enemies” (Isa. 26).

“When,” he says, “you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am”—understand, “the Beginning, who also speaks to you”—“and that I do nothing from myself,” that is, I do nothing separately from the Father, apart from the Father’s will or outside communion with the Father. “But as the Father taught me, these things I speak in the world; and you will know that he who sent me is with me”—which, although you refuse to know it now, you ask when you say, “Where is your Father?”—and you will know that “he has not left me alone,” as he testified a little earlier: “And if I judge, my judgment is just, because I am not alone, but I and the Father who sent me.” All these things, he says, you will know when you have lifted up the Son of Man.

In another place the Evangelist testifies that he said this, “signifying by what death he was to die” (John 11). It should be noted that he already knows and foretells the future to those who were to do this, although they neither knew it nor yet contemplated doing it; for God’s foreknowledge, which determines all things before the ages, had preceded their counsel, which they afterward assembled. Hence in the Acts of the Apostles the Apostle Peter says: “Jesus of Nazareth, a man approved by God among you by powers and signs and wonders which God did through him in your midst, as you yourselves also know—him, delivered up by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God, you crucified and killed by the hands of the wicked” (Acts 2).

This counsel—both that they should kill him and the manner of death by which they should kill him—was determined when, after Lazarus’s resurrection, the chief priests and Pharisees assembled a council and said: “What are we doing? For this man performs many signs” (John 12), and the rest. For before this they had indeed sought to kill him, but not by settled counsel: rather, with popular uproar and tumultuous fury. Their counsel had not, I say, been settled in a way that involved seeking a judge, alleging some charge, producing accusers and witnesses in something like the legal order of a trial, and requiring a kind of death corresponding, as it were, to the case.

Once this had been determined, when he again said, “When you have lifted up the Son of Man from the earth,” and added—though this is passed over here—“I will draw all things to myself,” then they understood that he was speaking to them, since they were by then considering the deed, and said: “We have heard from the Law that Christ remains forever; and how do you say that the Son of Man must be lifted up?” Now, therefore, when the counsel had not yet been determined, upon his saying, “When you have lifted up the Son of Man,” they made no such reply, perhaps because they did not yet understand what they had not yet contemplated.

“Then,” he says, “you will know that I am.” For then it will not be possible to remain ignorant, nor useful to dissemble. Then the heavens will declare it and the firmament will announce it; day will pour forth this word to day, and night will communicate knowledge of this matter to night. There will be no speech or language whose voices are not heard; their sound will go out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world. Then, I say, you will know in this manner, and, however unwillingly, will hear “that I am”: that I live forever; and it will become evident to you that I am also the resurrection of the dead. Thus it was rightly said of me in the psalm: “In the beginning you, Lord, founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands. They will perish, but you remain; all of them will grow old like a garment; like a covering you will change them, and they will be changed. But you are the same, and your years will not fail” (Ps. 101). You will know this; and unless you also believe and confess “that I am,” you will die, as I said above, in your sins.

Then you will also know that I do nothing from myself, but speak as the Father taught me. You will know this, namely, from the fact that my works, which I have now begun, will, after you have lifted me up, have continual growth; and my words, which I now speak, will have manifest fulfillment. For this is the sign given in the Law of one whom God has sent: “But if,” it says, “you answer in silent thought, ‘How can I understand a word which the Lord has not spoken?’ you will have this sign: whatever that prophet has foretold in the name of the Lord, if it does not happen, the Lord has not spoken it; rather, the prophet has invented it through the swelling of his own mind, and therefore you shall not fear him” (Deut. 18).

This, I say, is the legal sign. But whatever I foretell in the name of my Father, you will see come to pass; indeed, carried captive among all nations, you will yourselves bear round among all peoples an observable proof of my words. Therefore then you will know that I do nothing from myself—not as one who, corrupted by arrogance, makes himself a prophet from himself and, through the swelling of his mind, feigns things which neither are nor will be to be or to be future—but “as the Father taught me,” that is, as I know the Father’s will to be, so I speak these things; “because wickedness did not teach my mouth, nor do I imitate,” as you say, “the tongue of blasphemers” (Job 13). For example, when I say, “I am the light of the world,” or, “My Father works until now, and I work.” Rather, obedience, or the Father’s love and love for the human race, taught my mouth, so that I might make myself known to human beings, whose eternal life is this: to know the true God and Jesus Christ whom he sent (John 17).

“And you will know this: that he who sent me is with me, and has not left me alone”—not as you imagine when you say, “God has forsaken him; pursue and seize him, because there is no one to deliver him.” O how truly spoken, and how broadly this saying extends: “He who sent me is with me, and has not left me alone.” For the Light of the World speaks not to the Jews alone but to the whole world; and Truth bears testimony not for himself alone but also for us, so that each of us, wherever we go and whatever we undertake, may have ready at hand a means of knowing whether God deigns to be with us.

“He who sent me,” he says, “is with me”; thus, by contrast, understand that whoever is not sent by him does not have him with him. This is demonstrable from each person’s effects. For example: when that son of perdition comes, is revealed, and exalts “himself above all that is called God or is worshipped” (2 Thess. 2), it will be clear even to unbelievers from these effects that God has not sent him and therefore is not with him. “For the Lord Jesus,” says the Apostle, “will kill him with the breath of his mouth” (ibid.).

Likewise every “thief” and robber who enters the sheepfold “only to steal and kill and destroy” (John 10), because he is not sent, will therefore not be admitted through the door, nor will the gatekeeper open to him. He is alone, and it is rightly said to him: Because God did not send you, he is not with you. This is especially clear because the sheep do not hear him as a stranger but flee from him.

Likewise, if some Nazarene—that is, one consecrated and professing the contemplative life—wanders abroad contrary to his vocation, goes outward when no necessity of usefulness calls him, and hates the keys and welcome seals of chastity, God does not send him and God is not with him. This becomes clear through sure experience: like Dinah, Jacob’s daughter, who went out to see the daughters of the region and, while still a virgin, was violated by Shechem, prince of the land, so his soul also, found outside by the devil, prince of this world, is corrupted (Gen. 34). It has no God as protector, of whom it may say: “He who sent me is with me.”

The diligent hearer of evangelical truth can, I say, understand these and similar matters by contrast: whatever he does, wherever he directs himself in going out or returning, he should do all things in such a way that amid the waves of the age and the dangers of vices he may console his heart with the true witness of conscience, saying: “And he who sent me is with me, and has not left me alone.”

But let the discourse now return to its present and principal purpose: “He who sent me,” he says, “is with me, and has not left me alone.” Hearts of the devout that have been instructed by true knowledge—that is, schooled in the edification of charity—are worthy in some measure to perceive the cry of this poor man, who also says in the psalm: “Lord, hear my prayer, and let my cry come to you” (Ps. 101 [102]). Its title reads: “A prayer of the poor man, when he is distressed and pours out his petition before the Lord.” For indeed, when this poor man was distressed, he said these things: “He who sent me is with me,” and so forth.

The cause of this distress was as great as one unable to express it in words and marveling with groaning had long before proclaimed among other things through Isaiah: “And we thought him as it were a leper, struck by God and humbled” (Isa. 53). He could not more feelingly signify the greatness of this poor man’s distress and confusion, of which he says to the Father in the psalm: “For your sake I endured reproach; confusion covered my face” (Ps. 68 [69]). Certainly the Scriptures contain groans and mournful complaints, drawn from this distressed and afflicted poor man in many tearful voices and varied images, to instruct the understanding of the devout.

For how many of us are there who inwardly perceive how he became alien to his brothers and a stranger to the sons of his mother (ibid.), while they said: “He calls himself the Son of God, and boasts that God is his Father” (Wis. 2)? Not to mention that, according to Mark, when he chose the twelve Apostles, his own people, hearing of it, went out to restrain him, for they said, “He has gone mad” (Mark 3). Of these he again says in the psalm: “Those who sat in the gate spoke against me, and those who drank wine sang songs about me” (Ps. 68 [69]). How terribly, do you think, did they reject him when he said: “I am the light of the world; and I bear testimony concerning myself, and the Father who sent me bears testimony concerning me”?

He had most keenly felt their proud hatred and cursed cries—“You have a demon,” “This man is not from God,” and similar words—he who, as was said, because of the greatness of his grief, mingling his own person with theirs, said of such people of his nation: “And we thought him as it were a leper” (Isa. 53). “As it were a leper,” he says: that is, because of his iniquity and blasphemy, one to be fled from and rejected by all, just as a leper, according to the Law, was ordered at the priest’s discretion to be separated and dwell alone outside the camp, crying that he was defiled and unclean (Lev. 13).

For when the rulers and Pharisees, hating him, separated him and cast out his name as evil, and wished him to be so solitary that whoever confessed him to be the Christ should be put out with him from the synagogue (John 9), what else were they striving for than that, by their decision, he should be declared and contaminated as a leper, dwelling alone outside the camp? Therefore these words, “He who sent me is with me, and has not left me alone,” must be heard and understood as the cry of a distressed poor man, one who has suffered prejudgment and, without sin of his own, has become “a reproach of men and despised by the people” (Ps. 21 [22]). It is as though a clean man, bald anew, had been judged at the discretion of unrighteous priests to be subject to roaming and spreading leprosy, separated from human company, cast outside, and condemned to live by himself alone outside the camp (Lev. 13).

But elsewhere, when he had already been separated outside the camp—that is, accounted among criminals outside the gates of the city—and was agonizing in death itself, when, according to the prophet just cited, they especially thought him “a leper, struck by God and humbled” (Isa. 53), he said: “Eli, Eli, famma sabacthani,” that is: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matt. 27).

An easy answer to these words would indeed be possible if he said: “Have you forsaken me?” Since a statement uttered in such interrogative form would signify neither truth nor falsehood and therefore would not oppose or contradict the declaration, “He who sent me is with me and has not left me alone.” But now, when he says, “Why have you forsaken me?” he seems to say the opposite, since he plainly asserts himself forsaken when he asks why he was forsaken.

What then? This: as even those hunters after phrases and words cannot deny, in opposites or contraries the negation must deny the very thing which the affirmation affirmed of the same subject. If one person affirms one thing and another denies something else, it is not contrary but different. Here, however, the statement “He has not left me alone” does not deny of the same thing what is affirmed there in the words, “Why have you forsaken me?” The latter concerns the passion of death, as the following words of the psalm plainly testify, down to the verse, “I will declare your name to my brothers” (Ps. 21 [22]); according to this, he was in a sense forsaken by the Father, as the Apostle says: “He who did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” (Rom. 8).

But when he now says, “He who sent me is with me and has not left me alone,” he speaks of that most wretched abandonment in which they wished him to be forsaken, saying, “This man is not from God” (John 9), or, according to the other Evangelists, accusing him of alliance with Beelzebub (Matt. 13; Luke 11)—indeed, an offense even to hear, that he himself was Beelzebub, as he testifies: “If they called the master of the house Beelzebub, how much more those of his household” (Matt. 10).

Thus he does not now deny what he affirmed at the moment of his passion. For he is no less fittingly called as though forsaken than the Apostle says of himself and those like him: “As deceivers and true; as unknown and yet known; as dying, and behold, we live; as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as having nothing, yet possessing all things” (2 Cor. 9).

But he gave the greatest and strongest argument concerning himself, by which it is clear that he was not forsaken, when he said: “Because I always do what is pleasing to him.” Notice that, after saying, “Because I do what is pleasing to him,” he added, “always.” This is proper to the only-begotten Son and distinguishes him from all those pleasing to God: he does what is pleasing to the Father not partly or for a time, but wholly and always. “For what human being is there who does good and does not sin?” (Eccles. 7). This one alone is righteous and holy, who did not commit sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth (Isa. 53; 1 Pet. 2).

He rightly added “always,” in accordance with what was said elsewhere of him: “Upon whom you see the Spirit descending like a dove and remaining upon him” (John 1). These sayings are equivalent in substance and cannot exist without one another. He would not always do what pleased the Father unless the Spirit remained in him; nor would the Spirit remain in him if he ever admitted anything outside the Father’s pleasure.

It was no small marvel that a mortal human being conducted himself with such unchangeableness, constancy, and firmness among so many enemies tempting him and seeking grounds to accuse him, that when he said these things and afterward asked, “Which of you will convict me of sin?” no one among them was given even an occasion for a false accusation. Though they sharpened their tongues long and greatly and aimed the bow in secret, they at last shot him—but they shot one who was spotless (Ps. 63); that is, they condemned him indeed, but condemned him for no fault.

Thereupon all who saw him were troubled (ibid.) at the wonder of such malice and of the wicked saying which they confirmed among themselves by stubbornly crying, “Crucify, crucify” (John 19). They declared the works of God and understood his deeds; even the wicked themselves were compelled to recognize that this was the Son of God, according to his present statement: “When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am,” and the rest. It follows:

“While he was speaking these things, many believed in him.” What sort of people these believers were—that is, how near they came to the true piety of believers or how far they fell short—is not made sufficiently clear by what follows in the evangelical narrative, especially since, after the Lord said, “If you remain in my word,” and so forth, the Evangelist immediately added: “They answered him: We are Abraham’s seed” (John 9), and the rest. For “answer” is properly used when those to whom or concerning whom the discourse is directed answer him.
