Far above, concerning the belief of these people—that is, the Jerusalemites—the Evangelist said: “When he was in Jerusalem, many believed in him, seeing the signs which he did.” He immediately added: “But Jesus himself did not entrust himself to them, because he knew all people and had no need that anyone should bear testimony concerning a human being, for he himself knew what was in a human being.” Perhaps, therefore, these people too, who believed because they saw—or rather, who believed while persecuting out of envy—became “like their fathers, a perverse and provoking generation, a generation that did not direct its heart, and whose spirit was not faithful to God” (Ps. 77).

For how did they truly believe when, after disputing long with the very one in whom they had believed and refusing to endure the testimony to his divinity, they finally ran for stones? The same Evangelist records that, when he said, “Before Abraham was, I am,” “they took up stones to throw at him.” Thus they could believe in the way that Arians and other such heretics say that they believe. Yet Christ never entrusted himself to them, because, however they may have confessed Christ, in their various sects they attacked belief in his divinity with one spirit of malice; unable to endure hearing his true confessors, they made the uproar of their madness heard throughout the whole world.

That the pattern of all these had already appeared in these people is clear from what follows. For, if we follow the letter more closely, we are compelled to understand the same people as answering whom the Lord addresses, as follows:

“Jesus therefore said to the Jews who had believed him: ‘If you remain in my word, you will truly be my disciples; and you will know the truth, and the truth will make you free.’”

This had to be said to Jewish believers, and now must be said to heretics and all whose faith is corrupted: “If you remain in my word, you will truly be my disciples.” For what? Does everyone who confesses Christ already remain in his word and truly belong among his disciples? By no means. Otherwise so many wicked children, growing up together with the children of the kingdom, like tares with the good seed of the master of the house throughout the public field of the whole world, would not have sprung up; nor would so many bad fish, mixed with the good, have torn apart the nets of faith throughout the world (Matt. 13).

For Christ’s word, in which he says that those who believe in Christ must remain if they are truly his disciples—that is, true Christians—is the word of faith, the one rule of belief, from which it is sinful to take anything away or to which it is sinful to add anything. But Jewish believers in Christ, to whom nevertheless, “as stated above, Christ did not entrust himself” (John 2), and all heretics, such as Cerinthus and Marcion, and the rest against whom this Gospel was especially written, together with the many plagues of heresies that afterward arose, depart far from this word and greatly detract from it. Some confess Christ to be a true human being but deny that he is also true God, or assert that he began from Mary; others truly confess that he who is God came in true flesh (Rom. 8), but deny that he is truly human.

Therefore they do not remain in Christ’s word, which he set forth both formerly through his prophets (Gal. 4) and now through himself. Its entire sum is that the one and same Christ existed as true God before all ages and truly became the Son of Man at the end of the ages. Accordingly, they are not true disciples of Christ—that is, not truly Christians; they have not known the truth; and Truth has not freed them from their sins, however much they may have confessed Christ or been baptized in Christ’s name.

Christ therefore rightly says to such people—then to the Jews through himself and now to heretics through his Church—“If you remain in my word, you will truly be my disciples; and you will know the truth, and the truth will make you free.” That is: unless you remain in my word, you will not truly be my disciples; you will not know the truth; and Truth will not make you free. No one, indeed, by the righteousness of whatever deeds, can be redeemed from sins or freed from the ancient slavery of the devil unless he remains whole in the word of faith and holds to the one communion of evangelical confession.

It should also be understood that he promises these believers in himself, in this place, a worthy and true but unexpected fruit of discipleship: “You will truly,” he says, “be my disciples.” What fruit? What reward or prize? “You will know the truth, and the truth will make you free.” For being carnal and thinking carnally about Christ, they imagined that under him as a carnal king they would possess a worldly age, along with the condemnation of all nations; again, wars and triumphs, slaughtered enemies and crowds of captives, a golden and jewelled Jerusalem on earth, the blood of sacrifices, the injury of circumcision, and the glory of an earthly temple. All these things those who still await Christ dream that they will possess under him.

In this way those who, as said above, believed in him nevertheless looked in their very believing “to vanities and false madnesses” (Ps. 39). Nor is this surprising, since the Apostles too, grieving after his passion had been accomplished, said with such a conception: “But we had hoped that he was the one who would redeem Israel” (Luke 4). Therefore, suitably meeting this mistaken expectation, he destroys the believers’ vain hope, teaching with hope of what blessedness and love for what freedom they ought to believe in him: “You will know the truth,” he says, “and the truth will make you free.”

It is worthwhile to consider this fruit, this recompense or reward, in those who then remained in his word and thereby truly became his disciples. Those who remained in his word until his death—the blessed Apostles—afterward received, as a reward for knowledge of the truth, this commendatory remembrance from him: “But you are those who have remained with me in my temptations” (Luke 22). In that same hour, among other things, he said to them: “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. But when that Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all truth” (John 16).

Behold: because they remained in his word, which all had confessed through the one Peter, saying, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16), they deserved to receive the Spirit of truth, through whom they would know all truth. For when that Spirit of truth came, who has not been amazed—and who is not amazed even today—at how perfectly they knew the truth, and how steadfastly those who had been unlearned and illiterate men (Acts 4) defended it against all the excessively talkative wisdom of the world? He truly freed them from all errors; he freed them from all the desires that are in the world, making them desire that true and highest blessedness which they had come to know in truth; he freed them from fear of death, fear of the enemy, and every miserable slavery of sin; and at last he established them in the perfection of freedom, of which the Apostle Paul, who had already begun to be freed, says among other things:

“For creation itself also will be set free from the slavery of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God. For we know that all creation groans and labors in birth together until now; and not only it, but we ourselves also, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan within ourselves, awaiting the adoption as children of God, the redemption of our body” (Rom. 8).

In this way, by matching the statements with the events, the meaning of the saying becomes clearer: “If you remain in my word, you will truly be my disciples; and you will know the truth, and the truth will make you free.” It follows:

[Col. 0556A] “They answered him: ‘We are Abraham’s seed, and have never been enslaved to anyone. How do you say, “You will become free”?’” O cunning men—how nearly they had now caught and entangled the wisdom of God! For what did they suppose he would say, except: What you say, “We have never been enslaved to anyone,” is false, for you are now subject to the Roman empire. Had he said this, with what an outcry, do you think, would they have attacked him, saying: “If we are friends of Caesar, let us not release this enemy of Caesar. For he contradicts Caesar, holding out to us the hope that, if we follow him, we shall be free and shall not serve the Romans.”

Thus they said, “We are Abraham’s seed, and have never been enslaved to anyone,” not through forgetful ignorance, but through treacherous malice. Indeed, it was a privilege of a certain native freedom [Col. 0556B] that they were Abraham’s seed (Gal. IV): that is, that they had been born according to the promise, not of a slave-woman according to the flesh, but of a free woman. For Ishmael too had been Abraham’s seed, the Lord saying: “But I will also make the son of the slave-woman into a great nation, because he is your seed” (Gen. XXI). Nevertheless, those especially who are according to Isaac are counted as the seed: they alone are free according to the flesh [237] and are called Abraham’s lawful seed, as he himself says: “For in Isaac shall your seed be called” (Gen. XXI).

Let us therefore grant that they are Abraham’s seed, and consequently that, in comparison with the Ishmaelites and the rest born from Hagar or Keturah (Gen. XXV), these are free. Yet they are false in adding, “and we have never been enslaved to anyone.” For they could not have been ignorant that they had served the Egyptians in mud and brick; and that, after obtaining the land of promise, because “they mingled among the nations, and learned their works, and served their graven images” (Ps. CV), the Lord delivered them into the hands of the nations; those who hated them ruled over them, their enemies afflicted them, and they were humbled under their hands. He often delivered them; and now, at last, when they said, “We have never been enslaved to anyone,” they were serving the Roman empire under the condition of tribute.

[Col. 0556C] It is therefore clear that, as stated above, they raised this objection with treacherous malice, intent on extracting a word by which they could accuse him before the Roman government—just as, when the hypocrites tested him, they said: “Is it lawful to give tribute to Caesar, or not?” (Matt. XXII).

And observe the zeal of these grammarians, declining in the school of Satan: how quickly, when he said, “And the truth will make you free,” they sprang upon the etymology of this word, saying to him, “How do you say, ‘You will become free’?” He had not said to them, “And you will become free,” but “And the truth will make you free.” They wished to abuse the precise wording in aid of their perversity. But in vain. For he who had shortly before said, “I am the light of the world,” saw all these things clearly: shining indeed upon earth, but walking in the height of heaven. This was as though blind men, pursuing the sun, wished to bind its rays with snares and drag it down from its zodiac into the earth below, as though its feet were bound.

[Col. 0557A] For how far above their understanding moves the intention of him who says, “If you remain in my word, you will truly be my disciples; and you will know the truth, and the truth will make you free,” may be gathered from what follows.

“Jesus answered them: ‘Everyone who commits sin is the slave of sin. But the slave does not remain in the house for ever; the son remains for ever. Therefore, if the Son makes you free, you will truly be free.’”

See what a requital in kind he rendered them. These men, who were of the earth and spoke of the earth, knowing only earthly slavery and freedom, cleverly seized upon the nicety of one little expression—“And the truth will make you free”—in order to catch him in his speech. But he who came from heaven, and testifies to what he saw and heard, considering only spiritual slavery and freedom, fashioned for them a most powerful syllogism, in order that he might “take the wise in their own cunning” (Job V).

“Everyone,” he says, “who commits sin is the slave of sin.” Truth set forth a true proposition; no hearer, however contentious or rebellious, should hesitate to concede it. But if someone should stubbornly harden an impudent brow, then, disdaining to contend with such a person by means of the great weapons of ecclesiastical Scripture, we shall summon a lighter armament: a great host of poets and pagan philosophers. For example, let us recall Flaccus, speaking of a man enslaved by desire:

> “[lacuna] ‘I am free,’ say on: ‘No?’  
> For a master, not gentle but harsh, presses the mind,  
> Drives sharp goads beneath the weary one,  
> And twists him as he resists.”  
> (Horace, *Satires*, II.7)

[Col. 0557C] Or Sophocles, as Cicero reports: when he was already worn out by age and was asked whether he still made use of sexual pleasures, he replied, “Speak more auspiciously! I have escaped from that, as from a savage and frenzied master.”

But for those who know themselves and willingly yield to truth, there is no longer any need to ask whether they are or have been slaves. They themselves confess unprompted and publicly lament that they are not only slaves but captives, singing while weeping and weeping while singing:

> “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept,  
> when we remembered Zion.  
> Upon the willows in its midst  
> we hung our instruments,  
> because those who led us captive  
> asked of us words of song”  
> (Ps. CXXXVI),

and so forth.

Nor could those enemies of the Lord lie to him by saying that they had not committed, or were not committing, sin—especially since their own teachers, the scribes and Pharisees, a little earlier, when they had tested him concerning the woman caught in adultery, heard him say: “Let him who is without sin among you [first] cast a stone at her”; and, on hearing this, they went out one by one, beginning with the elders. At least they could neither deny nor conceal that they were trying by every means to catch him in speech, so that they might kill him. Thus they themselves—indeed, far more than other sinners—were slaves of sin.

[Col. 0558A] Therefore, with the proposition standing firm and secure, he does not hesitate to add: “But the slave does not remain in the house for ever; the son remains for ever.” This had to be said to slaves of sin, who recognize the present misery of their slavery only in its consequent punishment, delighted by the soft yoke and sweet little chains of lusts; indeed, like blind or drunken people, neither seeing nor feeling the horror and frenzied tyranny of every vice, because they attend to their own wills.

“The slave,” he says, “of sin does not remain in the house for ever,” in accordance with the Scripture spoken through the Psalmist: “He who practices pride shall not dwell in the midst of my house” (Ps. C). And elsewhere he speaks to God: “Nor shall the wicked dwell beside you” (Ps. V). “But the Son,” he says, “remains for ever”—that Son, namely, who is called Son uniquely and properly, and is Son, and is in no way called or is a slave, because he is surely free from every sin. For “he committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth” (Isa. LIII); and he says in the Psalm: “I became as a man without help, free among the dead” (Ps. LXXXVII). This one remains in the house for ever.

Let us first set out the law concerning slaves or masters, so that, once the foundation of the familiar comparison has been laid, the visible walls of the mysteries may rise more firmly. In any house, behold these four matters to be considered: the householder; the house itself; the son of that householder; and some hired servant, the slave of another master. For this slave cannot suitably be referred to the Lord whose house this is, since the sin of whose slave the present discussion is concerned is wholly foreign to that Son of whom the discussion likewise now speaks, and to his Father.

[Col. 0558C] We know that a hired servant, the slave of other masters, cannot legally remain permanently in the house into which he has been hired. Indeed, not even the slave of the Lord to whom the house belongs can remain in that house serving his master longer than his master pleases. How much less can the slave of other masters, as stated above, remain in the house, even if he is tolerated through the householder’s patience! When the time comes or the case demands it, upon the demand of his masters he will be drawn away to the places or services due to them.

But the Son remains in the house by legal right, equally with the Father, as its Lord; and he counts as his own everything the Father stores up. The Father’s word to the Son is rightly this: “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours [238], and yours is mine” (Luke XV). Thus, even in human terms, it is truly said that “the slave does not remain in the house for ever; the son remains for ever.”

Further, once this comparison has been laid down, it is easy to perceive how terribly he announces to the Jews that they must go out, while he himself must remain in the things that are his Father’s. For God is the great and illustrious householder, and his house is the holy Church—that is, the holy fellowship of all who believe in and worship God. His Son is this very one who speaks these things, Christ, one and the same God and man. “But every person born from Adam into the service of sin is a slave of sin, and is freed only through this Son”; most especially, however, the Jewish people, who were then already in God’s house, but were not to remain there when this Son spoke these words.

[Col. 0559A] Thus, in saying these things, he first strikes the Jews, as stated above. Although they were in God’s house as laborers in his kingdom, possessing the law and the covenant, the holy place, and the order of sacrifices, they were soon to be visibly cast out, as true slaves of sin. This he had already signified to them also when, having made a whip of cords, he drove them out: “It is written,” he says, “My house shall be called a house of prayer, but you have made it a den of thieves” (John II; Isa. LVI; Jer. VII). In those cords from which he made the whip, he quite fittingly expressed the slavish bonds of their sins.

But he also affirms here that the Son—that is, himself—of whom they said in another parable, “This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours” (Matt. XXI), will, after they have been cast out, remain in the house for ever. He plainly indicates the same thing in that parable when, speaking beforehand of himself, he says: “Have you never read: ‘The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner; this was done by the Lord, and it is wonderful in our eyes’?” (Ps. CXVII). Immediately he added: “Amen, I say to you that the kingdom of God shall be taken from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matt. XXI).

[Col. 0559C] The same saying also applies to the consciences of each of us who, through the profession of Christian faith, are in God’s house. It terribly warns us not to be in this house, which is the Church, as slaves—that is, performing the slavish works of sin—because, he says, “the slave does not remain in the house for ever.” Even if someone has ascended to the chair and throne of liberation—that is, has exercised the office and authority of freeing slaves by preaching, baptizing, consecrating the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood and distributing it to the peoples, and reconciling penitents—although by all these means the enrollment and covenant of Christian freedom are brought into effect, that illustrious maker of freedom will not remain in the house for ever if he himself is secretly a slave of sin. Rather, surrounded and bound by the cords of his own sins, he will be dragged by those same contending and raging masters of his to the prison-houses of hell.

Therefore the inference of him who says, “But the slave does not remain in the house for ever; the Son remains for ever,” is true. The conclusion follows: “Therefore, if the Son makes you free, you will truly be free.” Therefore, he says, since you also—to whom the prophet says, “You were sold for nothing” (Isa. LII)—are, like the rest, slaves of sin; and since “the slave does not remain in the house for ever, but the Son remains for ever,” “if the Son makes you free, you will truly be free.” That is: unless the Son frees you, you will never be free.

[Col. 0560A] Your swelling boast, then—not greatness but mere inflation—by which you proudly say, “And we have never been enslaved to anyone,” is false and deceptive. It is false, I say, not because you are subject to the Romans—which, in your cruelly imbued hatred, you wished to hear from me so that you might accuse me—but because you are sinners and persistently commit sin.

It should also be known that even among human beings it is a lawful rule that no slave, especially no captive slave, is granted freedom except through the son of the king or prince who, by his own labor or prowess, has conquered the tyrant, recovered the slaves, gained the whole kingdom of the conquered enemy, and at the same time received the written and confirmed testament of his paternal inheritance. But concerning this Son, no one doubts that, clothed in glory, clothed in strength and girded with power (Ps. XCII), he reigned: that is, through the assumption of flesh and the passion of death, he condemned the lord of unhappy slaves (Col. II)—namely sin, the lord of all Adam’s children—destroyed the kingdom of sin and death, boldly led it in triumph, and openly triumphed over it in himself (Heb. I).

[Col. 0560B] Therefore this had first to be said to the Jews. They could not deny that God the Father has the Son whom he appointed heir of all things, saying in David: “The Lord said to me: ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance and the ends of the earth as your possession’” (Ps. II), and many similar passages. To the Jews, I say—who boasted in the merits of their fathers, God’s servants—and with the judgment of sensible people likewise not dissenting from the reasoning given above, this had to be said: “If the Son makes you free, you will truly be free”; nor will you be free otherwise.

Then the same must be proclaimed to all the nations, without any distinction between Jew and Greek, as the Apostle says: “For all have sinned and lack the glory of God” (Rom. III).

The sequence of the text must now be carefully observed. Behold, this final conclusion indicates that unless the Son frees us, we cannot truly be free. But the initial proposition had established that Truth would free us. For he says: “And you will know the truth, and the truth will make you free.” While this proposition is defended argumentatively against adversaries who oppose it by saying, “We are Abraham’s seed, and have never been enslaved to anyone,” it reaches, as I have said, the final conclusion that no one is free except the one whom the Son frees.

[Col. 0560D] It is therefore plainly established that in this passage Truth and Son signify the same thing; and that here too the Son of God testifies that he is Truth, a title by which elsewhere he declares himself more plainly to his disciples, saying: “I am the truth” (John XIV).

Now see how far this victorious witness has carried the defense of his testimony. Above, when he said, “I am the light of the world,” his adversaries replied: “You bear witness concerning yourself; your testimony is not true.” Here, by contrast, he stands not only declaring that his testimony is true, but also professing that he himself is Truth. It follows:

“I know that you are Abraham’s children; but you seek to kill me, because my word finds no place in you.” Having disposed of the latter part of their objection, namely their statement, “And we have never been enslaved to anyone,” he now addresses the former part—the part in which, breathing intolerable pride, they had puffed themselves up by saying, “We are Abraham’s seed.” He deferred the dismantling of these parts in this order because he will say more about this great subject of pride.

“I know,” he says, “that you are Abraham’s children.” For who does not know that, as the prophet reproaches you, “you have come forth from the waters of Judah” (Isa. XLVIII), who was Abraham’s great-grandson? That is, you have sprung up not as imitators of paternal virtue, but merely as superfluous offspring of frail flesh. “You are therefore Abraham’s children, but you seek to kill me.” Why? “Because my word finds no place in you”: that is, you are so impatient [239] of hearing my word that, through impatience with it, you desire my death.

[Col. 0561B] This utterly and exceedingly conflicts with your being counted as Abraham’s children in the seed (Rom. IX). Abraham remained in my word—that is, in the word which he heard concerning me when it was said to him: “And in your seed shall all nations be blessed” (Gen. XXII). He remained, I say, in that word, believing and not failing in righteousness; nor was he ever “weakened in faith, nor did he consider his own body now dead, when he was nearly a hundred years old, nor the dead womb of Sarah,” reckoning faithful the one who had promised (Rom. IV). By thus believing and remaining in the word of promise, he deserved both to be called and to be the father of many nations; “and it was reckoned to him for righteousness, and he was called the friend of God” (Jas. II).

This is the noble lineage and noble nobility of father Abraham in which you glory: namely, not from flesh but from faith; not from nation but from virtue; not from a quality inherent in his seed, but from the long-suffering of obedience. For Abraham’s flesh, if it is in question, comes from the transgressing mass; his race is Chaldean. In this respect I know that you are Abraham’s children.

But this is now required of you: that you too be true children and not degenerate ones; that is, that you remain in the same word of mine in which he remained—believing that the seed of blessing has come, which he believed would come, and that that seed is I, who also speak to you. That you may believe this, I am the one who bears witness concerning myself, and the Father who sent me bears witness concerning me by doing among you works which no one else has done, greater works than Abraham saw and believed.

[Col. 0561D] But “my word finds no place in you”: it finds no faith among you, nor even so much good ground in your rocky, stony, and hard hearts as would enable it to put down a slight root. This is readily known from its fruit, since “you seek to kill me,” unable to endure hearing that same word.

Thus, “I know indeed that you are Abraham’s children,” but you are alien children—alien children, I say, grown old and “limping from your paths” (Ps. XVII)—since you exalt the inferior element of Abraham’s stock, namely flesh, while denying the faith in which, or through which, he is noble. Therefore I no longer need discuss that father with you; for your father is surely far other than he, and my Father is far other—and far superior to that same father Abraham. It is likely that I do not degenerate from my Father, nor you from yours. For I say: “I speak what I have seen with my Father; and you do what you have seen with your father.”

[Col. 0562A] The Son of God, beginning to convict Abraham’s children according to the flesh that they cannot glory in the dignity of so great a father, first puts them at the greatest possible distance from communion with himself. Abraham, according to the flesh, is a father common to him and to them. But he openly assigns one Father to himself and another father to them when he says: “I speak what I have seen with my Father; and you do what you have seen with your father.” They could therefore observe that he was calling their father someone other than Abraham.

Given this distinction, it could not consistently follow that they should call God their Father, though they pretended to do so. For what did he say they had seen with their father and done, except what he had just stated: “But you seek to kill me, because my word finds no place in you”? Convicted plainly both by his words and by their own conscience, they could not have failed to know that they had seen this with the devil—that is, had conceived it in their minds by imitating the devil and through a will familiar to them as his. For they did not sin in ignorance.

And they had long since understood perfectly well with what Father he testified that he had seen the things he spoke. For, as the Evangelist says, “They therefore persecuted him all the more because he called God his own Father, making himself equal with God” (John V). Since he thus makes so manifest a division, signifying God as his own Father and the devil as theirs, why do the Jews still hesitate? Why do they ask questions? For it follows: “They answered and said to him: ‘Our father is Abraham.’”

[Col. 0562C] Surely these words, and the others they later object—“We were not born of fornication; we have one Father, God,” and so forth—are snares, tests, traps, and hunters’ nets. What do these laughable captors gape after? What do they now expect, for example, when they say, “Our father is Abraham”? They wished, of course, that this word might fall from his mouth (Rom. IX), so that he would answer in turn: Abraham is not our father. How great an opportunity for slander they would think they had found! They would surely cry out that he denied the adoption, the covenant, the giving of the law, Moses, the Fathers, and everything which that nation believed it possessed from Abraham.

But “in vain is a net cast before the eyes of winged creatures” (Prov. I). If it is cast in vain before the eyes of winged creatures, how much more in vain before the eyes of their leader, the herodion? (Ps. CIII). How then did he frustrate their plots—the very one through whose teaching his saints learned to be “wise as serpents and innocent as doves” (Matt. X), giving no offense to anyone or occasion for just accusation (II Cor. VI)? It follows:

“Jesus said to them: ‘If you are Abraham’s children, do the works of Abraham. But now you seek to kill me, a man who has spoken to you the truth which I heard from God. Abraham did not do this.’”

[Col. 0563A] What then? Once the two unanswerable propositions had been assumed or conceded—first, “If you are Abraham’s children, do the works of Abraham”; and second, “But now you seek to kill me,” which Abraham did not do—the third proposition should at last have been inferred: Therefore, you are not Abraham’s children. The reasoning of the premises established this even against the adversaries’ will.

Nevertheless, since they had not yet wholly lied in saying, “Our father is Abraham,” he still speaks more gently, withholding the conclusion, though it may readily be understood from his silence. For what they said, “Our father is Abraham,” was not in every respect false, as was what they would shortly say, “We have one Father, God.” They were God’s children neither by nature nor by imitation; but they were Abraham’s children, although not by imitation, yet by the nature of the flesh.

And see how just and reasonable the condition is: “If,” he says, “you are Abraham’s children”—that is, if you profess yourselves to be Abraham’s children—then, in order that you may be truthful in this profession, “do the works of Abraham.” For it is not because you are human beings, which belongs to nature, nor because we are born under the corruption of mortality with sin, which belongs to misery—it is not, I say, from this or that—that you are Abraham’s children, but Adam’s children. Nor are you Sarah’s children because your mothers bore you in pain, but Eve’s children. For all these things take their beginning not from Abraham and Sarah, but from Adam and Eve.

[Col. 0563C] “Do,” therefore, “the works of Abraham”: that is, have the faith which Abraham first possessed. For “this is the work of God, that you believe in him” (John VI), whom he sent, imitating father Abraham, who believed the one who promised.

Otherwise, together with your circumcision you will be counted among the uncircumcised of Sodom, and, according to the prophet, you will be “rulers of Sodom and people [240] of Gomorrah” (Isa. I). Your father will not be Abraham and your mother will not be Sarah, but, according to another prophet, “your father is an Amorite and your mother a Hittite” (Ezek. XVI).

For circumcision—without which Abraham was justified and called the friend of God (Gen. XV; Rom. IV)—and legal ceremonies, sacrificial rites, and such things, because they can be done with either a bad or a good spirit or intention, do not make Abraham’s children out of Adam’s children, or God’s friends out of enemies. Rather, faith and the precepts of righteousness do so: they were written on tablets by God’s finger; and even before they were written, Abraham, by observing them under the law of nature while still uncircumcised, became God’s friend.

But now “you seek to kill me”—a man hateful to you not for just any reason, but because “I have spoken the truth to you,” the truth, I say, “which I heard from God”: that is, a good word which I did not devise through the swelling pride of my own mind, like a false prophet corrupted by arrogance (Deut. XVIII), but heard from God before I appeared among you by birth. And you too can recognize this from lawful signs. For everything I say, I say in the name of the Lord; and the law has established for you this sign for recognizing truth: that every word I preach should be in the name of the Lord.

[Col. 0564A] You seek to kill “me,” I say, such a man. Abraham did not do this. In his faith he had a far different mind and a far different spirit—indeed, one opposed to this spirit by which “you seek to kill me.” When he was to be perfected and depart from here without having received the promises, he saw me from afar with the eyes of faith; from afar he greeted me, weeping and confessing that blessed would be the eyes which would see him by faith (Heb. XI), which were to see these times that you see (Luke X) and believe in me, whom you seek to kill.

I could therefore draw this conclusion against you: Your father is not Abraham. But I shall leave this conclusion to the stones, which will become Abraham’s children, and which, being made eloquent while I keep silence and make no reply to you, will judge that you are by no means Abraham’s children (Matt. III). It follows:

“You do the works of your father.” After he had mutilated one horn of Jewish pride, he again proposes, in ordered argument, to break the remaining horn of the ram which he knew would once more charge upon him through its impatience. For they butted against the truth with two horns, boasting that Abraham was their father and God their Father, and falsely claiming that they had no need of the freedom by which Truth would free them (Gal. IV).

[Col. 0564C] Therefore he again presents the case, so that he may wear out and cast down his enemies, whom he saw pressing upon him, by their own exertions: “They then said to him: ‘We were not born of fornication; we have one Father, God.’” Behold, more openly angered and swelling with quarrelsomeness, they poured out all their strength into the wind with bitterness and shouting: “We were not born of fornication; we have one Father, God.”

This may be understood in two ways. First, in accordance with the customs of the Scriptures which they read, they called fornication the soul’s submission, as though prostituted, to many false gods; and thus they answered, “We were not born of fornication,” and so forth. But secondly, since these assertions are separate—they did not say, “We were not born of fornication, but we have one Father, God”—we judge that, thinking carnally of carnal matters, they were still boasting of nobility of flesh. They say, “We were not born of fornication,” so that you should understand: as are the other sons born from concubines.

It is as though they said: “You ignorant man, you have not noticed the unique dignity of our race. We are not like the other sons whom Abraham our father begot: sons of concubines, unworthy of their father’s inheritance, such as Ishmael and the others whom he begot by Keturah (Gen. XXV). Rather, we were born from Sarah’s lawful marriage, and God chose her son alone, that he might be his God, saying: ‘But I will establish my covenant with Isaac, whom Sarah shall bear to you’ (Gen. XVII).”

[Col. 0564D] This one lawful son inherited both the God of his father and everything that he possessed, as it is written: “Abraham gave all that he possessed to Isaac; but to the sons of the concubines he gave gifts, and he separated them from Isaac his son while he himself was still living” (Gen. XXV). Therefore we were not born of fornication; we have one Father, God.

And observe the bitterness mixed with the pride of those who say, “We were not born of fornication.” It would have been enough to say, “We were born from Isaac, and not from any of the sons of concubines.” They hate all human beings and, blinded by hatred of their brothers—that is, of any of Abraham’s sons—they could not even spare the very father in whom they gloried so greatly. They called fornication the intercourse of women which no Scripture condemns, since it was undertaken not so much for lust as for the love of posterity.

Thus the sons of Gilead, through pride, did not see that they were calling their own father an adulterer, when they said to Jephthah their brother: “You cannot be heir in our father’s house, because you were begotten of an adulterous mother” (Judg. XI). And, swollen with the sense of their flesh in such bitterness, they dare to call God their Father, adding, “We have one Father, God,” misusing for pride the statements of God—for example, his saying to Pharaoh: “Let my firstborn son go” (Exod. IV).

[Col. 0565B] To that God Isaiah also says: “For you are our Father; Abraham did not know us, and Israel did not acknowledge us. You, O Lord, are our Father; our Redeemer: from everlasting is your name” (Isa. LXIII). And Moses says to Israel in the song of Deuteronomy: “Is he not your Father, who possessed, made, and created you?” (Deut. XXXII). There are many similar passages in the law and the prophets.

Indeed, the pride of those who say that they are Jews and are not, but are “the synagogue of Satan” (Rev. III), is great and singular. Thus the Son of God rightly says of them: “Save me from the lion’s mouth, and my lowliness from the horns of the unicorns” (Ps. XII), calling these Jews unicorns because of their lion-like cruelty and their singular pride.

Yet there truly is great and singular nobility in this nation. Only let those who, blinded by fury and hatred, say, “We were not born of fornication,” say more honorably, as befits Abraham’s children: “We were not, like the others whom Abraham our father begot, born according to the flesh”—so that they may truthfully add, “We have one Father, God.”

[Col. 0565D] For “he who was born of the slave-woman,” says the Apostle, “was born according to the flesh” (Gal. IV), because it belongs to the nature of flesh that a young woman, such as Hagar was, should conceive by a man, even though aged. The same should be thought concerning Keturah, whom the Hebrews nevertheless maintain to have been the same woman, Hagar—although Scripture plainly suggests that there was more than one concubine when it says: “He gave gifts also to the sons of the concubines” (Gen. XXV).

But for an old woman, especially a barren one, such as Sarah was, to conceive by an aged man—as Abraham was when he begot Isaac—this does not belong to the nature of flesh. Hence the same Apostle rightly says that Isaac was “born through promise” (Gal. IV), that is, through God’s gift, not through the ordinary course of flesh.

Therefore that nation was a nation of unique nobility, which, with reference to its father Isaac, could say: “We were not born according to the flesh; we have one Father, God.” Only the Idumaean nation [241]—that is, the children of Esau—could likewise say, “We were not born according to the flesh.”

[Col. 0566A] But the addition, “We have one Father, God,” separates them, God saying: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Mal. I), because Esau, worthy of God’s hatred and of exclusion from that nobility of lineage, turned aside into the fornication of idols. Therefore these men who now say, “We were not born of fornication,” are no better than they. For although they say this truly, they lie in adding: “We have one Father, God.” Let us hear how forcefully and sweetly the Son—who is also the wisdom of God the Father—refutes these deceivers.

[Col. 0566B] “Jesus therefore said to them: ‘If God were your Father, you would surely love me. For I proceeded from God and came; indeed, I did not come of myself, but he sent me.’” They had irreverently advanced these two separate claims: that they had not been born of fornication, and that they had one Father, God. But regarding that ground of glory on which they gloried in Abraham according to the flesh, they had been sufficiently answered. He therefore proceeds to convict as false the remaining part of their assertion, in which they had said, “We have one Father, God,” saying to them: “If God were your Father, you would surely love me.”

First, it should be noted that when they said, “Our father is Abraham,” he did not answer them by saying, “Abraham is not your father”; nor now, when they object and say, “We have one Father, God,” does he answer by saying, “You do not have God as Father.” For among that people there were some—and there had been very many—who did the works of Abraham, and consequently were not only sons of Abraham according to the flesh, but sons of Abraham and sons of God according to faith [Rom. IX]. Thus he does not pronounce a hasty judgment, so that when they say, “Our father is Abraham,” he immediately retorts, “Abraham is not your father”; or when they say, “We have one Father, God,” immediately says contrariwise, “You do not have God as Father.” Rather, he first identifies the fault, in order to show reasonably and in proper order only those whose fault it is not to be sons of Abraham or to have God as Father.

“If,” he says, “God were your Father, you would surely love me” [Col. 0566D]. Nothing is truer. For these are equivalent: to have God as Father and to love the Son of God. They follow one another and adhere to one another in such a way that neither can stand or exist without the other. Thus they may also be reversed and converted in this manner: “If God were your Father, you would surely love me”; and if you loved me, God would surely be your Father. For all the children of God love one another, since they have one Spirit of adoption [Rom. VIII]; indeed, they could not otherwise be children of God unless they had love toward one another [I John V]. But all of them love still more, and incomparably more, that one and only, proper and consubstantial Son of God, through whom they have deserved to receive that same Spirit of adoption; for what he alone was by nature, he granted to many brethren, that they might be named and be children of God by grace.

By their love for the only Son, God the Father distinguishes his adopted children from the children of the devil. Rightly, therefore, he says: “If God were your Father, you would surely love me,” and adds the reason why he ought rightly to be loved: “For,” he says, “I proceeded from God and came.” I proceeded from God, I say, being made visible though I was invisible; I proceeded from God and came, fulfilling the Scripture which says: “And he himself, like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber” [Ps. XVIII]. “Indeed, I did not come of myself,” as I have often already said—something which false prophets do, who invent all things “out of the swelling of their own minds” [Deut. XVIII], corrupted by arrogance—“but he sent me.” I have already often said this to you: “I have labored crying out; my throat has become hoarse” [Ps. LXVIII]. Therefore I say:

[Col. 0567B] “Why do you not recognize my speech? Because you cannot hear my word.” This is my speech, and this is my testimony: “I am the light of the world; I am not alone, but I and the Father who sent me; I am not from below, nor from this world as you are, but I am from above; I am the beginning, who also speak to you; and I proceeded from God and came. For I did not come of myself, but he sent me.” Why do you not recognize this speech of mine? Why do you not weigh it in the balance of reason, so as to know whether it is true or false? Do you not have the Law, teaching you and giving you a sign by which you ought to recognize the word of a prophet whom God has not sent? You certainly have it; but the point is that you cannot hear my word—namely because of the greatness of your hatred, by which “I am burdensome to you to behold, and my speech to hear.”

It is therefore no wonder that you do not recognize my speech, because, unwilling to understand, you are excessively impatient of hearing. All whose Father is God can hear my word as a hungry person can receive pleasant food. But if my speech is to you like a burden on the road [Ecclus. XXI], and your heavy heart, unable to endure hearing my word, as it were collapses from labor, then who your father is I have hitherto kept silent about. While you assailed me painfully and said, “We are Abraham’s seed; we are free; Abraham is our father,” I was silent. But now, as you falsely boast that God is your Father, I speak like a woman in labor:

[Col. 0567D] “You are of your father the devil, and you wish to do your father’s desires.” Who can worthily admire the truth and gentleness of the Son of God, accomplishing so great a matter with such sweetness and hurling so great a thunderbolt of justice without the storm of contention? Behold, he says, speaking the truth which I heard from God, resisting throughout the whole dispute the falsehood, nowhere opposes a negation to an affirmation or an affirmation to a negation—the usual beginning of strife—but, as though moving in a circuit and avoiding the encounter of a contentious brow, at last strikes the lofty, uplifted head of pride.

They said, “We have never served anyone.” He did not answer contrariwise: “That is false; for you serve the Romans,” or, “You are slaves of sin.” Then they said, “Our father is Abraham”; he did not answer contrariwise, “Abraham is not your father.” Likewise they dared to say, “We have one Father, God”; he did not oppose them thus: “By no means do you have God as Father.” Nowhere does he confront them contentiously; rather, by the circuit of sound and just reasoning, taking those who seemed wise in their own craftiness [Job V], he struck them more sharply than they could have expected, saying: “You are of your father the devil.”

[Col. 0568A] Thus God the Father rightly, when through the prophet he had said of this chosen servant of his, “I have put my Spirit upon him; he shall bring forth judgment to the nations,” immediately added: “He shall not cry out, nor show partiality, nor shall his voice be heard outside” [Isa. XLII], and so forth. Perhaps you will say: How did he not cry out, nor was his voice heard in the streets, when his voice is this great and terrible utterance [Luke IV]: “You are of your father the devil”? To this I say: this is indeed a great and terrible voice, which is heard to this day throughout all lands, as testimony to all who, like the Jews, are enemies of truth. Yet although it has been heard everywhere and was uttered in order that it should be heard everywhere, it was not heard in the streets, it did not sound at the crossroads; for it was delivered so reasonably that the unlearned rabble of the populace had no occasion from it [Col. 0568C] to dispute in streets or at crossings, saying, “This man denies that Abraham is the father of our nation; he denies that we have one Father, God; and he says these and similar things against Moses and our people.”

Thus his voice was not heard in the streets in the manner his adversaries, who tempted him, would have wished; yet it was so heard by the whole world that they are set forth as an example to all people, marked by such a sentence according to their deserts: “You are of your father the devil.” We are also admonished by the mystery of ancient history to imitate this example—namely, to forestall the contentious by useful skill. For we read that when the Philistines had gone up against David and spread themselves out in the valley of Rephaim, the Lord answered David as he consulted him: “Do not go up directly against them, but circle round behind them, and come upon them opposite the pear trees” [II Kings V].

For the Philistines—whose name is interpreted “falling by drink”—are spread abroad in the valley of Rephaim, that is, “of healings,” when contentious persons oppress the holy Church, in which there is true care for souls and in which Truth frees those who acknowledge it from the old slavery of sin. Because of their deserving, the Lord has mixed for them a cup of stupor and a spirit of dizziness [Isa. XIX], so that their way may be darkness and slipperiness, that a snare may seize them, and that they may fall into the very pit which they hid [Ps. XXXIV]. Against these David then does not go directly up, but circles behind them: when an ecclesiastical man, avoiding controversies as far as he can, according to the Apostle’s saying, “If it be possible, as much as lies in you, having peace with all men” [Rom. XII], moderates his words by an appropriate circuit of reasoning, so that he may defend the truth and yet not cause the flames of disputes to grow.

This is, above all human beings, a wondrous indication of gentleness in our Lord: he never abruptly confronts any adversary head-on, but always surrounds his adversaries from afar with ranks of arguments, through which no craftiness can break, as becomes clearer than light to one who attentively considers the present disputation. Observe with what delay he circles them, and how terribly at last he strikes, saying, “You are of your father the devil,” with the cause both preceding and following: first he says, “But now you seek to kill me,” and then adds again:

[Col. 0569B] “You wish to do your father’s desires.” Thus there was no one among that people who could suppose that what he said, “You are of your father the devil,” did not concern him. Having stated this reason, Truth said this to such sons of Abraham not without the authority of Scripture. For if those who bore false witness against the blood of Naboth the Jezreelite were rightly called sons of the devil, as it is written: “They proclaimed a fast, and caused Naboth to sit among the chief men of the people; and bringing two men, sons of the devil, they made them sit opposite him” [III Kings XXI]—and those men, being devilish men, bore witness against him before the whole multitude—how much more rightly were these called sons of the devil, since they sought to kill a man far, indeed incomparably, better than Naboth, while still “calling God their Father”?

Nor, therefore, was such a declaration open to the charge of slander, since the authority of sacred Scripture had long before pronounced it for a similar cause. Nor is there any doubt—as natural reason itself also readily perceives—that it is a matter of greater wrath to be called or to be a son of the devil than a slave of sin. Hence he said above: “He who commits sin is the slave of sin.” For every son of the devil is a slave of sin; but not every slave of sin is properly called a son of the devil. For although “everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin,” it nevertheless makes a great difference whether someone desires to be set free and for this prays to the Deliverer, or loves sin itself and hates the terms of freedom; just as, conversely, it makes no small difference whether someone performs a good work from fear of punishment or from fear of justice.

Therefore, just as it is a greater grace to be called or to be children rather than slaves of God, so conversely it is a matter of greater wrath that Truth now says to his enemies, “You are of your father the devil,” than what he said above: “Everyone who commits sin is the slave of sin” [I John III]. Accordingly, just as those from whose hearts perfect charity has cast out fear are rightly named and are children of God, so conversely it is rightly said to these, because they diligently practice iniquity, hating and seeking to kill the Deliverer:

[Col. 0570A] “You are of your father the devil.” For you do not merely obey him by committing sin as slaves, but, by defending your sin, willingly cleave to him as children; and you wish to do his desires, after the manner of children who willingly seek to do what is pleasing to their father. And what are his desires?

“He was a murderer from the beginning, and did not stand in the truth, because truth is not in him.” It cannot be said how great is the restraint with which here the Son of God passes from the second person to the third, and, turning in a way from the present children of the devil, attacks as it were their absent father—avoiding words closer to shouting and bitterness, as befits the ancient and mature wisdom of God. For it would plainly have sounded more bitter if, after saying, “You are of your father the devil,” he had added, “And by imitation of him you are murderers, and truth is not in you,” than when, passing to the third person, he says in this manner: “He was a murderer from the beginning, and did not stand in the truth, because truth is not in him.”

Thus, by changing the persons, he expresses the judgments more fittingly; yet he spares these children of the devil no more by striking at their father than you spare any man when, having begun to strike him on the back or around the loins, you suddenly turn the club upon his head. “He,” he says—your father, understood as he now is—“was a murderer from the beginning,” that is, from the time when man was created. For it seems improper to say that he was a murderer before there was a man who could be killed.

Yet, if we follow the strict propriety of the word, neither would the devil seem properly called a murderer because he seduced man. For what is properly meant by killing a man except separating the soul from the body? But he separated the human soul not from the body but, what is more serious, from God. The devil did indeed introduce the cause for which it was beneficial that man should be mortal; but God mercifully imposed bodily death itself upon sinful man, so that through that death he might be recoverable, lest there be for man, as for the devil, a miserable immortality—or immortal misery, eternal misery, or miserable eternity.

Therefore, if you consider the strict sense of the word, the devil, corrupter of the human soul and corrupter of the flesh, cannot properly be called a murderer; otherwise we would call every corrupting man a murderer—for example, a man who publicly taught heresy—and demand a public judicial proceeding against him as against a murderer. Accordingly, since the Son of God is now also speaking of the killing of himself, having first said, “You wish to do your father’s desires,” there is no obstacle, for the moment setting aside the strict propriety of the word, to understand by the name “murderer” the devil’s ancient hatred, by which, even before man was created, he directed himself against the same Son of God whom he now desired and hastened to kill when he had become man—especially since what follows, “And he did not stand in the truth,” and the rest, occurred in the devil before man existed.

[Col. 0571A] And indeed, as soon as, swelling with proud hatred against the Son of God, who alone is the likeness of the Father, he said in his heart, “I will be like the Most High” [Isa. XIV], then—because that hatred was to be consummated in murder through the hands of the Jews—he was already a murderer in the sight of the Father and of the Son himself who speaks these things. Therefore, while the murderous father is shown to his murderous children, so that the children’s folly may be reproved through ignorance of their father, one murder is rightly reckoned: begun by the father in evil will, it is consummated by the children in malicious hatred. For the one and same Son of God and man, who had cast their father down from heaven, now offered himself to his children, having become capable of suffering. “He,” he says, “was a murderer.” What follows? “And he did not stand in the truth, because truth is not in him.”

This is what I foretold: the children of the devil are struck by fitting judgments in their father. For because the proposition he had made above—“If you remain in my word, you shall truly be my disciples; and you shall know the truth, and the truth shall set you free”—did not please them, that reproach concerning their father is rightly and aptly brought against them: “Because he did not stand in the truth.” It is certainly known that he did not stand, because his foot—the foot of pride—was moved; he fell and was made a devil from an angel. But what is it to stand in the truth?

First, we understand truth itself to be none other than the very Son of God who speaks these things. For above, when he had first proposed, “And the truth shall set you free,” he finally concluded, “If therefore the Son sets you free, you shall truly be free.” Therefore, his saying, “And he did not stand in the truth,” is the same as if he had said: He did not love the Son of God, the Word of God, through whom he himself was made—“for all things were made through him.” For to stand in the truth is the same as to love the truth; to stand or to be in Christ is the same as to love Christ.

For it must be understood that the preposition *in* always signifies the close adherence of love, so that by the authority of Holy Scripture God is never said to stand or be in anyone except one who is elect and beloved; nor is anyone said to stand or be in God, or in Christ, or, as here, in truth, except one who is elect and beloved. Therefore, after “He was a murderer” has been stated, “and he did not stand in the truth” is immediately added, and the exposition of all his wickedness is begun in its parts—wickedness which is universally expressed under the first designation, “murderer.” So also Paul, speaking of his children, after saying, “Filled with all iniquity,” immediately listed many species of that same iniquity, adding: “malice, fornication, avarice, wickedness” [Rom. I], and so forth.

[Col. 0571D] “And he did not stand in the truth.” Why? “Because truth is not in him.” At this point many people, spinning out a long thread, ask also: Why is truth not in him? Did truth, they say, without any preceding cause in the devil, abandon its creature and refuse to be in him, and therefore he could not stand in the truth? Far be it! Such an idea utterly conflicts with the sequence and order of the present text. For first it is said, “He was a murderer from the beginning,” and afterward added, “And he did not stand in the truth, because truth is not in him.” Thus if you ask why he did not stand in the truth, we answer: “Because truth is not in him.” If you ask why truth is not in him, we say: Because “he was a murderer.”

For the devil’s not standing in the truth because truth is not in him is the same as the failure of these Jews, his children, to remain in the word of the one who says, “If you remain in my word, you shall truly be my disciples; and you shall know the truth, and the truth shall set you free.” They do not remain in his word because of what he afterward rebukes them for, saying: “Because my word finds no place in you.” He himself asked them the reason why his word found no place in them, saying: “Why do you not recognize my speech?” And at once he answered: “Because you cannot hear my word”—that is, because, owing to the immensity of murderous hatred, my speech is burdensome and intolerable for you to hear.

[Col. 0572B] Thus their father the devil “did not stand in the truth, because truth is not in him,” that is, truth finds no place in him; and truth is not in him because “he was a murderer from the beginning,” always abhorring truth—which is the Son of God himself—with ineffable hatred. Accordingly, the speaker’s intent plainly requires that individual matters said of their father the devil should be understood individually of these his children in this way. He, your father, was a murderer from the beginning; and you now seek to kill me through hereditary hatred. He did not stand in the truth; and you, stirred by the same pride, do not wish to remain in my word, so that truth may set you free and you may be truly free. “Truth is not in him; and my word finds no place in you, and you do not recognize my speech.” It follows:

[Col. 0572C] “When he speaks a lie, he speaks from his own resources, because he is a liar and its father.” The preceding clause ended thus: “Because truth is not in him.” It is evident that a rational creature in whom truth is not speaks falsehood. For there is nothing intermediate. Therefore, in whomever truth is not, its opposite—that is, falsehood—must be in him. It was not necessary, then, after saying, “Truth is not in him,” to add that falsehood is in him or that he speaks falsehood. But the matter required only that it be said and heard from where he received or learned falsehood.

Therefore, after saying, “Truth is not in him,” he rightly adds: “When he speaks a lie, he speaks from his own resources, because he is a liar and its father.” “When he speaks a lie,” he says—that is, when he says something which is without doubt a lie. For everything this lying murderer says is a lie, even if something that he has said either is or comes to pass. For he says nothing with a simple heart, nothing at all without an intention to deceive.

The first thing that he said, which we have from the Holy Scriptures, neither is nor will be—namely, “I will ascend above the height of the clouds; I will be like the Most High” [Isa. XIV]. “For who among the clouds shall be equal to the Lord, or who shall be like God among the sons of God?” [Ps. LXXXVIII]. Likewise the second thing he said, “Eat, and you shall be like gods” [Gen. III], neither is nor will be; for, as the Psalmist says, “Who is like our Lord, who dwells on high?” [Ps. CXII].

But what we read that he said—“If you are the Son of God, cast yourself down; for it is written: He has given his angels charge concerning you, and they shall bear you in their hands, lest at any time you strike your foot against a stone” [Matt. IV; Ps. XC]—is indeed written; but he said it with a double heart and an intention to deceive, namely in order to raise the heart of the Son of Man, whose holiness he envied, to vain glory. Therefore everything this murderer says is a lie. But from where did he receive or learn falsehood?

[Col. 0573B] “He speaks from his own resources,” he says, “because he is a liar and its father.” In this brief description he has portrayed the devil as a liar in such a way as to disclose sufficiently to those who understand the origin from which all evil began: “The devil speaks falsehood from his own resources,” that is, he invents it from his own heart, and he is so much a liar that he is also the father of falsehood. As if he said: This is why I said that the lying devil speaks falsehood from his own resources: because he is its father—understand, the father of falsehood. And by “father” I mean author and inventor.

Swelling with pride, he preferred, as an apostate, to become the father of falsehood rather than to remain with the Most High, the Father of truth, among the sons of God. And in this way, as father of falsehood, he seemed to himself to attain what he had said in his heart, “I will be like the Most High” [Isa. XIV]: if, while the Most High had begotten truth from himself, he on the contrary should become the father of falsehood.

What then are we to say to the wicked? Because the devil is called the father of falsehood, must falsehood conversely be called the Son of the devil, just as God is called the Most High and is the Father of truth, while truth conversely is called and is the Son of God? No. For falsehood is not a substance; thus the name “son” cannot be applied to it substantially in the same manner as it is applied to the truth of God, which is undoubtedly a substance. The Most High is called Father of truth in one way and the devil father of falsehood in another; truth relates to the Most High in one way, and falsehood—that is, falsehood to the devil—in another. Truth is substance, born consubstantially from the hidden substance of the Most High; falsehood, however, is an accident of the angelic creature, like rust upon silver.

[Col. 0574A] God is called and is Father of truth because he is truly the begetter of the Son consubstantial with himself, through whom he made all things. The devil is called and is father of falsehood because he is the author and inventor of an accidental defect, through which he made absolutely no substance—not even a fly or the smallest worm—but wickedly infected certain things that God had made.

O foolish and dishonorable father! O worthy imitator of divine fatherhood, fit to be mocked! Was it not better for you, O wanton creature, to conceive truth—the seed of your lawful husband, that is, your Creator—with the love due to him, than to defile the persons of your sex, that is, spirits coessential with you, through imaginary intercourse by the outflow of falsehood? For the entire community of rational spirits, a great part of which you, most foul adulterer, polluted, ought with one mind to have embraced one husband, their Creator, and enriched the substance of their needy nature with the seed of so great a substance, which is truth.

For whence are all the sons of God, unless because they have partaken of the Word through whom they were also made, who is the only Son of God? But you, proud and impure one, despised the love of so great a Father; and, while he uttered from his heart a good word also toward the creature subject to him [Ps. XLIV], you desired to be like him by uttering something of your own from your own heart. But with such a hostile and perverse mind, what could you utter except something contrary to that Word? That Word is truth. What then could you bubble forth except falsehood?

Thus, just as a woman who exchanges the natural use for a use contrary to nature [Rom. I] thereby generates no substance, but only defiles her own and others’ bodies, so you, abandoning God and wishing to generate something of your own from yourself, invented falsehood, which is no substance. Through it you created nothing; but you made those spirits who consented to your lust your children—that is, you made them liars, as you are a liar. For God alone, who grants to all that generate the power of generation, was able without a consort to generate substance from himself. Through this substance he made all things in the beginning, and even now makes certain human beings gods and children of God, like the blessed angels.

## BOOK NINE

[Col. 0573]

[Col. 0573D] Most wise Solomon says: “Just as one who eats much honey is not well, so one who is a searcher of majesty shall be overwhelmed by it” [Prov. XXV]. A searcher of majesty is one who strives to penetrate the great abyss of God’s judgments [Ps. XXXV]. For example, when he reads or hears what is said in the present passage concerning the devil—“He was a murderer from the beginning, and did not stand in the truth, because truth is not in him” [Col. 0574D]—and entangles himself too rashly, and sometimes childishly, in inextricable little questions, saying: “If God made all things very good, whence comes evil?” [Gen. I]. Or, “How could evil be present or arise in a good substance?” Again: “Why,” he says, “did God make that angel, whom he foreknew would become an inventor of evil? Or why did he not create every rational creature in such a way that it would be altogether impossible for it to be corrupted or to fall into vice? Why did he not make them all, like himself, by nature incapable of change?”

Entangling themselves in these and similar little questions, very many excessive searchers have been overwhelmed by the glory of majesty; and, as if satiated with much honey, they have unsettled themselves. Such, for example, are the Manichaeans, who said that from the beginning there existed a race of darkness which God had not made, but with which he fought and overcame, though at loss to himself; and that consequently a part of God—namely, the souls of the elect—is held captive in the exile of this present life; and that those to whom Truth now says, “You are of your father the devil,” and all who are like them, were born from that race of darkness.

Therefore, venerating with the Apostles the depth of the riches of God’s wisdom and knowledge, his incomprehensible judgments and unsearchable ways [Rom. XI], we say only this, according to the saying of the wise man already cited: God made all things for himself, “even the wicked for the evil day” [Prov. XVI]; that is, he also made for himself the one whom he foreknew would become evil by his own fault [Isa. I], knowing also that he could use that person’s malice for good.

Now that the father of the evil seed and of the criminal children has been described, let us hear what the Son says concerning himself. It follows:

[Col. 0575C] “But I, because I tell you the truth, you do not believe me.” You desire, he says, to do the desires of him who was a murderer from the beginning and did not stand in the truth, because “truth is not in him”; but you do not even believe me, and for no other reason than that “I tell you the truth.” What could be more perverse than this? What eye more wicked? What more crooked or distorted than not to believe someone precisely because he tells the truth, when conversely one ought all the more to believe him because he tells the truth?

But do not wonder: these people are of their father the devil. For this is characteristic of devilish generation: that it is a liar and changes the truth of God into falsehood [Rom. I], calling good evil and evil good, making sweet bitter and bitter sweet, calling light darkness and darkness light [Isa. V]. Therefore, since he who said to them, “You are of your father the devil,” is truth and cannot be deceived, it was necessary that they should disbelieve him above all for this reason, because he told them the truth; and that they should call light darkness because he poured out his light upon them against their will. But, in trying to establish this by shameless contention, they quickly lose their case. For they have no defense founded on reason.

Accordingly, he adds: “Which of you shall convict me of sin? If I tell the truth, why do you not believe me?” Great indeed is the gentleness of the Son of God, by which he deigns to ask who would or could convict him of sin, though he himself came to remit sins; great likewise is the justice whose conscience makes such a proposal before ill-willed hearers; and great also is the secure Truth that says: “If I tell the truth, why do you not believe me?”

Therefore the Psalmist rightly, in prophetic testimony, after saying, “Attend, prosper, proceed, and reign,” immediately adds: “For truth and gentleness and justice; and your right hand shall lead you wonderfully” [Ps. XLIV]. But where does his right hand presently lead him? To the victory of judgment: to the confutation of the rebellious consciences of the king’s enemies. For this is his aim: that they may recognize that on the day of judgment they will have no excuse for not believing him, especially since they cannot, even when he makes this proposal, object: “You did or do this or that.”

[Col. 0576B] Nor, therefore, could they cast against him what is now commonly said: when a man’s life is despised, it remains that his preaching too should be despised. In the same way he wishes his disciples also to be steadfastly humble and humbly steadfast in the authority of their preaching, when he says: “And whoever does not receive you, as you go out from that house or city, shake the dust from your feet as a testimony against them” [Matt. X]. For what is it for a preacher to shake off, as testimony against the reprobate, even the dust from their cities that has clung to his feet, except publicly to bewail even the slight sins without which human life cannot be lived at all, and, by cleansing these through daily remedies, henceforth to preserve his garments—that is, the members of his whole body—undefiled by every mire of carnal life?

He who thus commanded his disciples to shake out their garments, so that, as Solomon says, “Let your garments be white at all times, and let oil not fail from your head” [Eccl. IX], they might proclaim peace by holy living, rightly first showed these men that his own garment was clean and needed no shaking out, saying: “Which of you shall convict me of sin?” But concerning those who despise those thus shaken-out servants, he says: “Amen, I say to you, it shall be more tolerable for the land of the Sodomites and Gomorrheans on the day of judgment than for that city” [Matt. X; Luke X]. How much more inexcusable, then, will these men be, who do not receive him though they are unable to convict him of any sin, however slight!

Therefore, after he had said, “Which of you shall convict me of sin?” he immediately added: “If I tell the truth, why do you not believe me?” Thus confronted, they may ask their own consciences what excuse they can possibly have on the day of judgment. And he immediately adds:

“Whoever is of God hears the words of God; therefore you do not hear, because you are not of God.”

It is as though he said: Why do you rage against me, saying, “We have one Father, God”? Everyone who is of God is recognized by this clear sign: that he has ears to hear and hears God’s words. But you do not hear; rather, you are without ears for everything God says. This is plainly evident to all, especially from the fact that you seek to kill me, as I said a little above: “Because my word finds no place in you.” Therefore, “you are not of God, and for that reason you do not hear.” What remains, then, except that it is as I said: “Because you are of your father the devil” [Col. 0577A].

Thus the whole refutation of these men is concluded in brief: while boasting that Abraham was their father, they falsely claimed to have God also as their one Father, having begun their empty defense by saying: “We are Abraham’s seed, and have never been slaves to anyone.” Yet we must consider more carefully what is meant by the saying: “Whoever is of God hears the words of God; therefore you do not hear, because you are not of God.” For what is it to be of God, and therefore to hear God’s words? Or, conversely, not to be of God, and therefore not to hear? There would plainly be no question if it had been said thus: Whoever hears God’s words is of God; therefore you are not of God, because you do not hear. For it is established, and commonly known, that from the time a person receives the word of faith and is reborn in Christ, that person is of God and belongs to God. John bears witness to this same thing: every spirit that confesses that Christ has come in the flesh is of God; and we recognize that anyone is not of God from the fact that he does not hear God’s words, so as to be transferred into God’s rebirth [Col. 0577B] (1 John 4).

But he says: “Therefore you do not hear, because you are not of God.” Accordingly, while seeking with the authority of Holy Scripture what it is to be of God or not to be of God, and thus to hear or not hear God’s words, let us first recall why these things were said, lest the heresy of the Manichees now cast any cloud over you. They are accustomed to say concerning these words of the Lord: “See: because there are two natures, one good and the other evil, the Lord says, ‘Therefore you do not hear, because you are not of God.’”

These words were certainly spoken because of the Jews’ excessive pride, by which, as was said, they presumed that they alone were of God—namely, according to Isaac, whom barren and aged Sarah received from God [Col. 0577C] (Gen. 17); from God, I say, that is, through God’s promise and not through the ordinary course of the flesh, as Hagar received Ishmael. For, as has already been said, it is natural (Gen. 18) that a young woman should conceive by a man, however elderly, such as Hagar was; but that an old woman, especially a barren one, such as Sarah was, such as Elizabeth was (Luke 1), should conceive, is God’s gift. Knowing this, they presumed that they alone were of God, and that they alone were Abraham’s children.

Against such an opinion, the present Truth says: “Whoever is of God hears the words of God; therefore you do not hear, because you are not of God” [Col. 0577D]. That is to say: Whoever is not in that manifold superfluity of nature concerning which God, after the first human being’s sin, said to Eve, the mother of all the living: “I will multiply your sorrows and your conceptions” (Gen. 3), but is from that blessing by which, in Paradise before sin, he blessed them, saying: “Increase and multiply; fill the earth and subdue it; and rule over the fish of the sea, the birds of heaven, and all living creatures that move upon the earth” (Gen. 1)—from which blessing especially our father Isaac came to be, whose noble birth according to the flesh is the subject of your great boast—“this person hears God’s words.”

For it is certain [Col. 0578A] that all the saints and elect now called and justified through Christ’s grace, and made illustrious by diverse merits (Rom. 8)—all of them, I say, though not with the same prerogative of merits, yet are born by the same providence of God by which Isaac too was foreknown and predestined. All are from that blessing with which, as was said, God blessed the first human beings before sin. It is likewise certain that, had sin not been committed, only those would have been born who are now delivered through Christ’s grace. But all those now left in perdition are from that curse spoken to the woman: “I will multiply your sorrows and your conceptions”; for unless sin, as has been said, had preceded, this forest “which is good for nothing except to be cut down and thrown into the fire” [Col. 0578B] (Matt. 3) would never have grown up from the root of our flesh.

Therefore, “whoever is of God,” he says—that is, from that blessing in which God decreed that all who belong to life should be born—“hears God’s words”; that is, prompted beforehand by the inspiration of God’s grace, he obeys the call back to that same life which he had lost through intervening transgression. “And therefore you do not hear, because,” contrary to your opinion, “you have sprung up manifoldly and superfluously not, like Isaac your father according to the flesh, from that blessing, but from the curse which followed sin,” as the prophet testifies: “Because you have come forth from the waters of Judah” (Isa. 48); that is, you have descended not from the faith of the fathers but from flesh alone.

It follows:

“Then the Jews answered and said to him [Col. 0578C]: ‘Do we not rightly say that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?’”
