Having fittingly concluded the preceding argument, the Evangelist appropriately begins what follows by saying, “Then they answered.” For from the point where it was said, “We are Abraham’s seed, and have never been slaves to anyone,” the Jews had held to this: that they themselves belonged to God by the ancient nobility of the flesh, and that God was the God of Jews only, not also of Gentiles. But they were refuted, and their mouths were so stopped that we, the branches of the wild olive grafted contrary to nature into the good olive tree, need no longer be concerned that we have not been natural branches [Col. 0578D] (Rom. 11). That is, we who have been converted from the Gentiles and stand in the faith of the patriarchs need not be troubled that we are not Abraham’s sons according to the flesh.

Therefore, because their case had fallen and they had been overcome by reason, they rush furiously into insults. It is as if an adversary conquered and cast to the ground by a most powerful athlete, unable to strike with weapons, should attack with foaming teeth: “Do we not rightly say,” they ask, “that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?” Behold two supposed proofs that he is a sinner. For he had said: “Which of you convicts me of sin? If I speak the truth, why do you not believe me?” Therefore, lest he should depart untouched, they wound him on these two points: that he was a Samaritan and had a demon. But plainly “iniquity has lied to itself” (Ps. 26), for these are certainly not the words of one who has a demon, as the crowds testify elsewhere when the Pharisees say: “He has a demon and is mad. Why do you listen to him?” [Col. 0579A] (John 10).

Thus, according to the saying of a certain Wise Man, “At the sight of a word, a fool goes into labor, like the groans of a woman giving birth to a child” (Ecclus. 19), they quickly testified through the frenzied birth of their folly that what Truth had said was true: that they were of the father, the devil, who speaks his own lies. For they did not give birth to this blasphemy without a little torment of their bitterness: lying children, adulterous and foolish souls, who had conceived it from their father, the father of lying, and who, at the sight of the Word, at the rebuke of Truth, gave birth to falsehood.

Moreover, where or when they said that he had a demon is found both earlier in this Evangelist and likewise in the others. For above they said: “You have a demon. Who seeks to kill you?” (John 7) [Col. 0579B]. They also called him Beelzebub, as he himself says in Matthew: “If they called the master of the house Beelzebub, how much more his household?” (Matt. 10). But where or when they called him a Samaritan, or from what they obtained an occasion for this insult, we find in none of the Evangelists—unless perhaps because he remained and taught for two days among the Samaritans, with whom the Jews did not associate, as this same Evangelist reports much earlier.

“Jesus answered them: ‘I do not have a demon, but I honor my Father, and you have dishonored me.’”

When he says here, “I do not have a demon,” he never departs from his great meekness, by which, as was said above, he is accustomed to refute no one [Col. 0579C] (John 4). For it is one thing when a person, questioned, denies something, and another when someone, taking the opposite position, denies what another has asserted. They had said this in the form of a question: “Do we not rightly say that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?” But above they said affirmatively: “You have a demon; who seeks to kill you?” (John 7); and a little later they will likewise say affirmatively: “Now we know that you have a demon.” Thus he preserves here also the wonderful tenor of his meekness and truth: he denies the same insult when questioned here, but elsewhere passes it over in silent patience.

Now whatever reason they may have had for calling him a Samaritan—though they certainly knew that by descent he was a Jew and by locality a Galilean, concerning whom they had said above, “Search and see, for no prophet shall arise from Galilee”—it is remarkable how these little ones, slain by envy [Col. 0579D], pronounced judgment against themselves. Thus, according to the Psalmist, it may rightly be said of this too: “The arrows of little children have become their wounds, and their tongues have been weakened against themselves” (Ps. 63).

For if they wished, on account of some externally occurring circumstance—though they indicate none—to make a man naturally a Jew into a Samaritan so readily, how could they themselves, while seeking to kill the man who spoke truth to them, something Abraham did not do, say: “We are Abraham’s seed; Abraham is our father; and we have one Father, God,” and be angry that this was not granted to them? But now let us attend to the answer of Truth and Wisdom itself: “I do not,” he says, “have a demon.” Notice that he does not say, “I am not a Samaritan.” Certainly, by keeping silence concerning this side of their insulting attack, he sufficiently indicates through his silence that to be a Samaritan, a Jew, or indeed a Greek by descent or by association—an association which Jews did not have with Samaritans—is not so important that anyone should take notice of it or exert effort to wash away or remove from himself the reproach of such a designation [Col. 0580A].

Indeed, according to the mystical sense, which the Jews did not perceive, our Lord Jesus Christ truly is a Samaritan, as the interpretation of the name itself plainly shows to all. For Samaritan means “guardian.” And who but he is the true, watchful guardian of humankind, neither slumbering nor sleeping? (Ps. 120). Therefore, in that distinguished parable which begins, “A certain man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and fell among robbers” (Luke 10), he beautifully commends himself under the name and in the deed of that Samaritan who, making his journey, came beside that same man and bound his wounds, pouring in oil and wine [Col. 0580B] (ibid.).

For this our guardian, looking down from his holy height, looking from heaven upon the earth (Ps. 101), saw the human race stripped by robbers and left half-dead after wounds had been inflicted: that is, stripped by the deceiving devil of the dignity of its condition, and deprived not of the image of its Creator but only of the likeness—the meaning of its being left half-dead. Humanity had not lost the reason by which it was made in the image of God, but had lost the imitation of God’s goodness, by which it had been made in God’s likeness. He saw the human race thus half-dead and drew near; for he became our neighbor, being in all things like us except sin, and applied every care which that same parable describes [Col. 0580C].

Therefore our Lord, the guardian of humankind, rightly kept silence about this name, Samaritan, and by keeping silence sufficiently praised it. But concerning the accusation that contains no mark of goodness, he answered when questioned that it was not rightly said: “I do not have a demon.” But what does he say? “I honor,” he says, “my Father.” These things, then, are plainly opposites: to have a demon and to honor God the Father. The author himself shows this, when replying to the contrary proposition, “And you have a demon,” by setting against it: “No, but I honor my Father.”

Further, to honor God and to dishonor the Son of God are opposites, since they are contrary both in meaning and expression. Accordingly, to have a demon and to dishonor God are different in wording but equal in meaning. Therefore, when the meek and truthful one answers thus, “I do not have a demon, but I honor my Father, and you have dishonored me,” he turns the enemies’ insult back upon their own heads, avoiding the dreadful ugliness of the phrase [Col. 0581A]—lest he should say, “You rather have a demon”—while preserving the truth of the matter, because unless they truly had a demon, they would not dishonor the Son of God.

Having said this, he immediately meets the perversity of their thoughts (Ps. 49), saying:

“But I do not seek my own glory; there is one who seeks it and judges.”

For the wicked thought that he was like themselves—that is, that he bore witness about himself because he sought vain glory—and that he said, “Which of you convicts me of sin?” and similar things with the same intention as they did, to whom he rightly said: “You are those who justify yourselves before men, but God knows your hearts” (Luke 16), along with very many things of this kind. Wishing him to be regarded as such, they had said above: “You bear witness concerning yourself; your witness is not true” [Col. 0581B].

But he was so far from flattering anyone that in their great and spacious city he did not even have lodging for one night; rather, he always lodged outside, especially in Bethany (Matt. 21). For unlike those lovers of this world who seek their own glory and hasten to be in kings’ houses (Luke 17; Matt. 11), flattering everyone and therefore rightly said to be clothed in soft garments, he did not desire their favor so that royal acclamations might as quickly as possible be shouted to him by them and it be said: “Long live King Christ!” and thus that he might be raised by human beings, or through human beings, onto David’s throne.

If he expected anything of this sort from them, he would certainly not have rebuked them so truthfully as not to keep silent a little earlier when saying, “You are of your father the devil.” Therefore he says most truly: “I do not seek my own glory.” And immediately adds: “There is one who seeks it and judges.” These are, then, the words of a wholly confident mind. For how would he not seek and judge the glory of his Christ—the glory of his kingdom and the glory of his priesthood? How did they fail to recognize this confidence of his? “The Lord swore truth to David, and will not turn from it: ‘Of the fruit of your womb I will set one upon your throne’” [Col. 0581C] (Ps. 131). The prophetic Spirit said this concerning the glory of his kingdom. Likewise concerning the glory of his priesthood: “The Lord has sworn, and will not repent: ‘You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek’” (Ps. 109).

They were therefore enemies of truth; and with their father, the devil, father of lying, they devise a foolish plan: how they may, as if rationally, reject God’s counsel in themselves by saying, “We do not want this man to reign over us” (Luke 19), and thus fulfill the Scripture that says: “The kings of the earth stood forth, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ” (Ps. 2). For he who swore, as was said above, will indeed properly take care that his oath is not made void.

For he will seek and judge the glory of his Christ, so that you Jewish enemies may be “like a passing storm,” while he is “like an everlasting foundation” (Prov. 10), in the sight and hearing of all; and all will praise the judgment, because the Lord of heaven will judge that you who, through envy, are guilty of treason against the majesty [Col. 0582A] and glory of his Son are to be given over to a double destruction. The King himself will speak to you in his wrath and laugh at your ruin, saying: “But I have been appointed king by him over Zion, his holy mountain, proclaiming his command: ‘The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I shall give you the nations as your inheritance and the ends of the earth as your possession’” (Ps. 2).

It follows:

“Amen, amen, I say to you: If anyone keeps my word, he shall never see death.”

Truth continues in the discourse with which it began—an incomparable model in every respect of complete constancy—and, when his opponents are weary, repeats the first proposition in the same sense, though with a few words altered. Above he had said: “If you remain in my word, you will truly be my disciples; and you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free.” But now he says: “If anyone keeps my word, he shall never see death” [Col. 0582B]. Certainly, to remain in the word—that is, to keep the word—and never to see death, is the very freedom of which it was there said: “And the truth will set you free.”

By this he taught beforehand in his own person that, when the perversity of evil people grows, preaching ought not merely to remain unbroken but even to be increased. Yet this should not be passed over: although earlier, directing his discourse to the second person, he had said, “If you remain in my word,” and the rest, he now preferred to use the third person, saying universally: “If anyone keeps my word.” For it was not fitting that he should again offer a condition of life and salvation to those to whom he had already said: “You are of your father the devil,” since sentence of their destruction had already been pronounced [Col. 0582C].

“Then the Jews said: ‘Now we know that you have a demon. Abraham died, and the prophets; yet you say, “If anyone keeps my word, he shall never taste death.” Are you greater than our father Abraham, who died? And the prophets died. Whom do you make yourself?’”

Truly fools, such as these especially are, show that they do not yet know the elementary beginnings of God’s discourse—the very sin of which they are slaves—when they contend zealously against God’s wisdom. Where had they left their hearts and laid aside their ears, when Scripture cries out so much concerning the most evil death of sinners? For example, when it says: “For Sheol shall not confess you, nor shall death praise you; those who go down into the pit shall not await your truth” (Isa. 38); or: “For in death there is none who remembers you; but in Sheol, who shall confess you?” [Col. 0582D] (Ps. 6); and similar passages.

Truth was speaking of this true death, this evil death, when it said: “If anyone keeps my word, he shall never see death.” But those who had already cleaved to eternal death—and did not see the death to which they had cleaved (Heb. 5; Ps. 33)—were blinded in the discourse of Truth because they saw only the death of the flesh. Therefore they said: “Now we know that you have a demon.” And from where, O little possessors of folly, have you gained knowledge of such a great matter? “We draw the proof,” they say, “from those greater than you. For Abraham and the prophets died; they were greater than you, and kept a better word of God, more authoritative than your word. Whom, then, do you make yourself? How far do you extend yourself above yourself? By whose measure do you magnify yourself, when we all know your measure—namely, that you are a Galilean man, a carpenter’s son?” [Col. 0583A]

Such a question—“Whom do you make yourself?”—is exceedingly insulting. For who makes himself other than he is except one in whom truth is not: a liar and father of lying, every hypocrite and wicked person, one who has used a part? Thus, while biting Wisdom with a decayed tooth and resisting Truth with a false foot, let us also hear by what blunting reply they were repelled.

“Jesus answered: ‘If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing. It is my Father who glorifies me.’”

Lest these words seem to imply any powerlessness in the Son of God, as though the Son of God were less glorious than God the Father, this must first be understood: no one should be considered to glorify himself except one who seizes another’s glory. “For he who boasts and exalts himself, trusting in his own heart” (Prov. 28), follows the example of him who first despised communion with his Creator and spoke to himself in his heart: “I will sit upon the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north; I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the Most High” [Col. 0583B] (Isa. 14). That one, I say, who imitates him by boasting and exalting himself (Prov. 28) is said to glorify himself; and to him it is rightly said: “Whom do you make yourself?” because he is foolish and stirs up quarrels while stretching himself beyond himself, scorning the fraternal love of equals and despising the love of inferiors.

Therefore the Son of God does not glorify himself; for on the contrary, “though he was in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men; and, found in appearance as a man, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the Father unto death—even death on a cross” (Phil. 2). Therefore, when the Son of God says, “If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing; it is my Father who glorifies me,” he is not, as Arius blasphemously alleged, testifying to his own powerlessness [Col. 0583C], but expressing his concordant love with the Father. By this love he never divided himself from the Father, as these slanderers assert when they say: “Whom do you make yourself?” Rather, obedient to paternal love, he assumed that which was beneath him, namely human nature.

Let him therefore say: “If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing”—that is, whoever extends himself above himself, as you slanderously say of me when you ask, “Whom do you make yourself?”—his glory is nothing. For we ought to imitate the harmonious love of Father and Son, by which the Father glorifies the Son and the Son glorifies the Father; as the Son himself says: “Father, glorify your Son, that your Son also may glorify you” (John 17) [Col. 0584A], so that through mutual love there may be fulfilled in us what is written (Rom. 12): “Outdoing one another in honor”; and then our glory will not be nothing.

What he immediately adds gives a sufficiently humble defense, to a prudent heart and one seeking doctrine like gold, against the accusation brought against the Son of God: namely, that he says these and similar things about himself not by seeking vain glory but for a definite reason. For after saying, “It is my Father who glorifies me,” he immediately adds:

“‘Whom you say is our God’; and you have not known him. But I know him. And if I said that I do not know him, I should be a liar like you. But I know him, and I keep his word.”

What then? Certainly, because he says, “And if I said that I do not know him, I should be a liar like you,” the contrary must be understood: if you knew him of whom you say, “He is our God,” you would be truthful like me [Col. 0584B]. Which course should now be chosen? What, except that a fool should dare to offer advice to God’s Truth and Wisdom: that, in order to avoid suspicions of vain glory, he should deny knowing God or deny that God is his Father, and thus, though he is Truth, become a liar like liars?

Is it not much better and incomparably more worthy to bear false suspicions and accusations for a time, and meanwhile testify to what he has seen and heard, until he makes some of those who say that they have God as Father, yet have not known him and are therefore liars, truthful like himself—confessing God and knowing him alike? Indeed, if these men refuse to know, is it not still better to wait until the whole world knows his glory, since there is one who seeks and judges? For Truth would have come into the world in vain if, by denying himself, he had satisfied liars. Rightly, then, choosing what he preferred, he says: “But I know him, and I keep his word” [Col. 0584C]. For this is his word, and this command he gave me: that I should proclaim truth as testimony not merely amid insults but even unto death, because he himself sent me for this purpose: that “whoever keeps my word may never see death.”

It follows:

“Your father Abraham rejoiced that he might see my day; and he saw it and was glad.”

Having refuted the charge of vain glory with which his opponents had branded him by saying, “Whom do you make yourself?” he now at last answers what they had asked with no little indignation: “Are you greater than our father Abraham, who died?” “Abraham,” he says, “your father rejoiced that he might see my day” [Col. 0584D].

This is a great and marvelous saying, by which he declares both the great merit of father Abraham and the much greater testimony to his own greatness. For what does he mean when he says, “He rejoiced that he might see my day,” except what we too rightly marvel at in that same father of our faith: that he was the first, at God’s command, to undergo a long and arduous pilgrimage, not as though it were sorrow or necessity, but truly as the expectation of great joy? For God had promised him, though he had no heir and, what is more, had a barren wife, that “in his seed all nations would be blessed” [Col. 0585A] (Gen. 17).

Nor did he immediately receive the son through whom he could hope for that seed of blessing (Gen. 12), which is Christ (Heb. 13); rather, he first went out, not knowing where he was going, and remained in a foreign land, dwelling in tents, having no abiding city here but seeking the one to come. This is indeed a great merit of the father: that the Son of God calls his obedience rejoicing. Yet much greater is the testimony concerning himself when he declares that his own day was the reward of that rejoicing, saying: “He rejoiced that he might see my day. And he saw it,” he says, “and was glad.”

For Abraham then saw the Lord’s day when, in the figure of the supreme Trinity, he received angels as guests [Col. 0585B] (Gen. 18). Having received them, he spoke to the three as though to one, because although there is a number of persons in the Trinity, there is unity of divinity in nature. “Therefore he saw and was glad.” Who can weigh the joy of that blessed old man when he received the reward of his long-standing rejoicing: the Son, the testimony of the true God, the beginning of his posterity, the foundation of his race, the pledge of salvation, the seed-bed of Christ who was to be born?

Who, I say, except one animated by the same faith, can inwardly perceive the joy of God’s friend—how his soul was enlarged when he stood familiarly with him beneath the tree, beneath which guilty Adam had timidly hidden himself from his presence; when he fed with his food the one whom Adam had offended by the theft of food; and when he saw the root of his old olive tree grow green again [Col. 0585C] so as to bear the fruit that would finally atone for the bite of the forbidden tree? Rightly, therefore, the Son is here greater than Abraham: “Abraham,” he says, “your father rejoiced that he might see my day, and was glad.”

But Abraham’s carnal sons, lifting their eyes no higher than the flesh and considering in him only the age of the flesh, refused to understand these words. “The words of his mouth,” says the Psalmist—the words, I say, of this unjust Jewish people—“are iniquity and deceit; he refused to understand, so that he might do good” (Ps. 35).

“Then the Jews said: ‘You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham?’”

Truth did not fail to know that whatever answer he gave would be turned into slander [Col. 0585D]. For his opponents pressed him as dishonest wrestlers surround a most powerful man whom they cannot overthrow by strength, seeking to make him fall into a pit through deceit. Thus these treacherous men pressed him in order to draw out a word that they could condemn as blasphemy. Nevertheless, he had to answer them, so that the entire world might hear, though they did not—without disregarding the Scripture which says: “Do not pour out speech where there is no hearing” (Ecclus. 32), since this same discourse was uttered not so much for those who persecuted him as for us who were to believe.

“Jesus therefore said: ‘Amen, amen, I say to you: before Abraham came to be, I am.’”

The expression “before Abraham, I am” is unusual indeed, but proper to the reality. For “before” belongs to past time, while “I am” belongs to the present. Since divinity has neither past nor future time but always has the present, he does not say, “Before Abraham, I was,” but “Before Abraham, I am” [Col. 0586A]. Hence it is said to Moses: “I am who I am”; and: “You shall say to the children of Israel, ‘He Who Is has sent me to you’” (Exod. 3).

One who could come through the manifestation of presence and depart through the course of life had a before and after Abraham. But Truth has always had being, because for it nothing begins at an earlier time nor ends at a later one. Yet the minds of unbelievers could not—indeed, would not—endure these words of eternity. As it is written concerning this especially unjust and foolish people, and as was already said: “He refused to understand, so that he might do good” (Ps. 35).

[Col. 0586B] “Then they took up stones to throw at him. But Jesus hid himself and went out of the temple.”

The end and the beginning of this dispute are the same. For its beginning is the passage where it is written: “Jesus said to them again: ‘I am going away, and you will seek me, and you will die in your sin.’” Thus the Evangelist had concluded the preceding material: “And no one seized him, because his hour had not yet come.” There is therefore another beginning in what follows: “Jesus said to them again,” and so forth. But there the Lord Jesus says: “If therefore you do not believe that I am, you will die in your sins.” Then the Jews said: “Who are you?” Jesus answered: “The Beginning, who also speak to you.” Now, however, he says: “Amen, amen, I say to you: before Abraham came to be, I am” [Col. 0586C].

Thus an end corresponding to the beginning has been given. For these statements do not differ but confirm one another: “I am the Beginning,” and “Before Abraham came to be, I am.” Likewise, what he threatened there in words—“You will seek me; and where I am going, you cannot come. For if you do not believe that I am, you will die in your sins”—he expressed here in deeds, when they took up “stones to throw at him” because he had said, “Before Abraham came to be, I am,” and he hid himself and went out of the temple.

For what is it that the Jews are now far from salvation, except that Jesus—that is, the Savior—has hidden himself from them? And what is it that the city and the temple fell over their eyes—indeed, even over their corpses—when the Romans destroyed them, and that whatever they had been accustomed to offer or celebrate there to the God of their fathers—burnt offerings of rams, fat of the well-fed, blood of calves, lambs, and goats, new moons, Sabbaths, and their other festivals—was cast as dung upon their faces [Col. 0586D], God declaring and saying: “Your assemblies are wicked; my soul has hated your new moons and your solemnities; they have become burdensome to me” (Isa. 1)?

What, I ask, is this except that Jesus, hidden, went out of the temple, saying: “Behold, your house shall be left desolate,” or likewise saying through the prophet: “I have left my house; I have forsaken my inheritance; my dwelling has become like a hyena’s den” (Jer. 12)? Therefore the Lord and Teacher (Matt. 23), who in this same matter had said, “If you remain in my word, you will truly be my disciples,” rightly remains first, as is fitting, fixed in his own discourse with an unwavering step: preserving one and the same message with both strength and gentleness from beginning to end among hostile assailants.

And, as the Apostle says, “What is weak in God is stronger than men” (1 Cor. 1), even in this, that he hid himself and departed as though weak, he displayed the completion of the whole victory; for he fled not so much from stones as from the stony hearts of the Jews [Col. 0587A]. Now that he has hidden himself from these people and, as was said, gone out of the temple, let us consider what he did next and how he continued the prefiguration of the things that we now see more clearly than light.

It follows:

## Chapter IX

“And as he passed by, he saw a man blind from birth.” Christ, the true Light, who also said above: “I am the light of the world; whoever follows me does not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life”—that “true Light,” I say, “which enlightens every person coming into this world,” plainly passed from the Jews, who had closed their eyes, to the Gentiles, and enlightened them. This man, blind from birth, signifies precisely the original blindness of the Gentiles.

For although the whole human race was blind from birth—that is, deprived through original sin, inherited from the first parents, of the vision of the Godhead—yet the people of the Gentiles in particular, who according to the prophet walked in darkness [Col. 0587C] (Isa. XIX), were blind. For Christ, the Light of the world, had sent before himself the lamps of the patriarchs and prophets to the Jews, but not likewise to the Gentiles. Hence, immediately after the end of this reading, explaining what he intended by hiding himself and leaving the Temple, he says: “For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John IX).

Thus, before the coming of this Light, the entire human race was blind, without distinction between Jew and Greek, as the Apostle testifies: “We too were by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Eph. II). Yet, in comparison with the Gentiles, who had received neither the illumination of the Law nor that of the prophets, and had no knowledge whatsoever of God, the Jews thought themselves to see; just as, again after the end of this reading, the Lord says to the Pharisees when they ask: “Are we also blind?” “If you were blind,” he says, “you would have no sin; but now, because you say, ‘We see,’ your sin remains.”

Therefore our Lord splendidly prefigured the mystery that he would hide himself from the Jews and illuminate the eyes of the Gentiles, when “hiding himself, he went out of the Temple; and as he passed by, he saw a man blind from birth,” and enlightened him. Accordingly, whoever, from whatever Gentile nation, receives Christ’s preaching, sets aside all Jewish ceremonies in favor of the Gospel, and counts them as dung for Christ’s sake, as the Apostle says (Phil. III), is the one enlightened outside the Jews’ Temple, [Col. 0588A] from whose people the Light of the world hid himself, so that he may deserve to see God, whose vision he lost in Adam.

But let us now pursue the mystical order of this enlightenment. “As he passed by,” it says, “he saw a man blind from birth.” Truly he saw as he passed by: passing beyond those who boasted that they saw, and placing a veil over their hearts so that he might remain hidden from them, he came to us, that we who were blind might see him.

“And his disciples asked him: Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?” The disciples of the Savior do not ask this idly. For children are indeed sometimes born diseased because of their parents’ fault. For example, every month women’s burdened and sluggish bodies are relieved by an outflow of impure blood. If at that time a man has intercourse with a woman, the conceived offspring are said to contract a defect in the seed, so that lepers and elephantiasis sufferers are born from such conception, and the corrupted discharge degenerates into foul bodies of either sex, through deformity or abnormality of the limbs. Hence the prophet Ezekiel, in his description of a righteous man, after saying among other things, “he has not violated his neighbor’s wife,” adds: “and has not approached a menstruating woman” (Ezek. XVIII).

“Jesus answered: Neither this man sinned nor his parents, but that the works of God might be manifested in him.” In its literal sense, our Lord’s authority restrains our rashness, lest whenever we see persons born with such deprivation, diminution, [Col. 0588C] or deformity of limbs, we despise our own flesh in them and presumptuously declare that this befell them because of either their own fault or that of their parents. Rather, reverencing them all, let us minister to them as truly members of Christ, who will say to us: “As long as you did it to one of the least of mine, you did it to me” (Matt. XXV). Let us remember that in such persons the works of God are commonly manifested through the grace of healings, for the edification of Christ’s Church.

In the mystical sense, indeed, the first parents sinned, so that the human race should be born blind. Yet the Gentile world itself and its parents did not sin in such a way that, while the Jewish people were illuminated by the Creator’s righteousness, Gentile humanity should be left in the blindness of ignorance. For if someone says that the Gentiles were left in darkness because of their own sins or those of their parents, it follows that he must say that the Jewish people or their parents were chosen for their own merits. But Paul speaks against this, saying of the fathers: “Not only this, but Rebecca also, having conceived by one intercourse with Isaac our father. For when they had not yet been born, nor had done anything good or evil, so that God’s purpose according to election might stand—not from works, but from him who calls—it was said to her: ‘The greater shall serve the lesser,’ as it is written [Mal. I], ‘Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated’” (Rom. IX).

And Moses says to the children themselves in Deuteronomy: “Know therefore that it is not because of your righteousnesses that the Lord your God has given you this excellent land to possess, since you are a people of most stiff neck. Remember, and do not forget, how you provoked the Lord your God to wrath” (Deut. IX), etc.

Therefore neither did the Gentile people sin more, nor their parents, that it should be born blind. Rather, since both Jews and Gentiles came from one mass of transgression, the fathers of the Jews were chosen by grace, with no preceding merits; while the fathers of the Gentiles—or the Gentiles themselves—were passed over in justice until their appointed time, so that the works of God might be manifested in them more wonderfully in their due time. And immediately it adds:

“I must work the works of my Father while it is day. Night comes, when no one can work. While [Col. 0589B] I am in the world, I am the light of the world.” So that you may know, he says, for what works of God to be manifested in him this man was born blind, behold, I tell you: “I must work the works of my Father”—that is, those works for which my Father sent me—“while it is day,” that is, while the present age runs its course; when it is completed, “night comes, when no one can work.”

Why is the time of the present age called day? Clearly because elsewhere he says: “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII); and now he says: “While I am in the world, I am the light of the world.” Thus Christ, while he is in the world, is the light of the world; and he is in the world “until the consummation of the age.” Therefore, until the end of the age it is day—that is, a time suitable for working. Conversely, that which succeeds the consummation of the age will be night, that is, a time suitable for no one’s working.

Hence Ecclesiastes says: “Whatever your hand can do, do earnestly; for there is neither work, nor reasoning, nor wisdom, nor knowledge in the underworld, whither you are hastening” (Eccl. IX). Therefore what he says, “while it is day; night comes, when no one can work,” is as though he had said: Until the end of the age, after which comes the time “when no one can work,” but each receives what he has worked for. This is the time of working; that is the time of receiving. For then the Lord will render to each according to his works (Ps. LXI).

What then are the works which the Son of God performs throughout this whole day? They are certainly those toward which “through the tender mercies of our God, the dawn from on high visited us” (Luke I): namely, to enlighten those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death, and “to save them,” as the Apostle says, “through the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit” (Titus III). These works, I say, the Son of God performs “while it is day,” and by working so long as he is in the world, he is the Light of the world.

For he does not cease to work through the ministry of those whom he appointed as deputies of his work: namely, through the apostles, apostolic men, and all preachers of the Word of God, to whom he says: “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII).

Therefore that venerable and memorable blind man of old, who neither “sinned himself nor did his parents sin, [Col. 0590A] that he should be born blind,” was nevertheless born so by God’s providence, in order that the works of the Father, which the Son of God had to perform throughout the whole day—that is, throughout the entire time of the present age—might be manifested in him. That is, through the character of his outward enlightenment, the inward enlightenment of our souls might be commended to us more faithfully.

For the Light of the world did not illuminate this blind man merely by a command, as he could have done—for example, by saying: “Look; your faith has saved you” (Luke XVIII). But what did he do?

“After he had said this, he spat upon the ground, anointed his eyes, and said to him: Go and wash in the pool of Siloam, which is interpreted ‘Sent.’” First, it should be noted that this blind man, unlike Bartimaeus (Mark X), is not found sitting by the way or begging from the Lord. Nor did the often-mentioned Light of the world wait for him to cry out like that man: “Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David” (Luke XVIII); rather, he freely accommodated himself to nature’s need and gratuitously came to the silent man’s aid.

For this too belonged to the manifestation of God’s works: the maker of our enlightenment did not wait until, in our darkness, we should long for the brightness of his knowledge. We thought that darkness itself was light; indeed, we had no distinction at all between light and darkness. Rather, he looked upon us freely, saw us freely, freely made known to us his Word made flesh, and thereby anointed the eyes of our hearts.

For what else is manifested to us in that blind man by the fact that “the Lord Jesus spat upon the ground, made mud from the spittle, [Col. 0590C] and anointed his eyes,” except that remarkable and gracious work of divine grace by which he willed that his Word, united to the dusty nature of humankind, should be preached to us Gentiles? For then, as it were, dust was added to the spittle and mud was made from two substances, when the Word or Wisdom—who says, “I came forth from the mouth of the Most High” (Ecclus. XXIV)—assumed our flesh, to which it was said: “You are dust, and to dust you shall return” (Gen. III). By free condescension he joined himself, in the Virgin’s womb, to that nature which was borne and scattered like dust by every wind of the devil, in order to restore a stable condition and the weight of its ancient dignity to a nature light and unstable.

When this great mystery of godliness is preached to the Gentiles (I Tim. III), the eyes of those born blind are indeed most sweetly anointed; for teachable minds are especially delighted that the eternal power and wisdom of God so greatly humbled himself for human salvation. Thus the eyes of those born blind are most sweetly anointed with the mud which the Lord made from spittle, when the once lofty eyes and high-raised eyelids of our race receive the humble faith of the Incarnation of the Son of God. The pride of the eyes is healed by such an antidote of humility, because, when they wished to be opened without adornment, at the devil’s saying, “You shall be like gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. III), they were instead made yet more darkened.

But when this mud has been spread upon blind eyes—that is, when the Incarnation of the Son of God has been preached and believed—the blind person is not immediately enlightened by that hearing, even though it be believing, nor made worthy of the vision of God which he lost in Adam. He must approach the font of washing as a catechumen and be baptized in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Otherwise none of us would receive the light of our eyes, the Holy Spirit, for the remission of sins (Mark III).

Therefore that blind man, in whom these works of God were manifested, did not see immediately when the Lord anointed his eyes. “But go,” he says, “and wash in the pool of Siloam, which is interpreted ‘Sent.’” For it was not merely said: “Whoever believes shall be saved”; rather: “Whoever believes and is baptized shall be saved” (Mark XVI). The child of darkness must be transformed, by a certain likeness to the death and resurrection of him in whom he has believed, and become a child of light. This occurs in Christ’s baptism by a visible act, [Col. 0591B] but by invisible power, as the Apostle testifies: “All of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death; we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too may walk in newness of life” (Rom. VI), etc.

Thus the blind man, his eyes having been anointed, rightly does not see at once, but is commanded to go to the pool to wash. For merely because someone is a catechumen—that is, a hearer of the Word of God—he does not deserve to enter the kingdom of heaven, “unless he is born again of water and the Holy Spirit” (John III).

Now the words “which is interpreted ‘Sent’” were added by the Evangelist himself, not spoken by the Lord in addressing the blind man, because of a sure mystery. You should understand that by this pool nothing other than the water of baptism ought to be understood. It is truly the pool of him whom the Father sent, namely the Son; or certainly of the Holy Spirit, since he himself is the true remission of sins, and his invisible grace constitutes the whole benefit of the visible washing. For he too is rightly understood by the name Siloam, which means “Sent.” Indeed, he also was sent, according to: “But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name” (John XIV); and elsewhere: “Whom I,” he says, “will send to you from the Father” (Luke XXIV).

Siloam is a spring breaking forth at the foot of Mount Zion. It flows southward with alternating access of water; that is, it does not bubble forth in continuous streams, but at uncertain hours and days, and is accustomed to come with a great sound through the hollows of the earth and caverns of the hardest rock [Col. 0591D]. Whoever wishes to understand mystically all the properties of its nature will surely perceive that our Lord did not without reason choose this spring especially to signify the water of baptism.

“So he went and washed, and came seeing.” Do not suppose that this connective word is empty in the phrase, “So he went”: the faith of this blind man must be understood. “Go,” the Lord says, “to the pool of Siloam and wash.” But he had the faith that would save him, like the other man to whom the Lord gave light when he asked: “Look,” he says, “your faith has saved you” (Luke XVIII). “So he went and washed, and came seeing.”

This, then, is that manifestation of God’s works which the Potter himself, the maker of our nature, intended when, though neither this man nor his parents had sinned, he nevertheless willed, with very great benefit, that an imperfect vessel should be brought forth and that the man should be born blind. For it cannot be estimated how much beauty and usefulness this enlightenment of the blind man possesses, since all of us are inwardly enlightened according to this image of external enlightenment. We contemplate the works of God that have been done around us; and because we cannot grasp them in themselves, what he has worked in us is manifested to us through this likeness.

“Therefore the neighbors, and those who had known him before because he was a beggar, said: Is this not the man who sat and begged?” This very external enlightenment of the blind man, in which, as said above, the works of God are manifested by a kind of likeness—the works which his Son “must perform while it is day”—is itself, I say, a great work of the Father, worthy of manifestation. Therefore, by the will of him who sought the glory of his Son, as the Son himself had testified shortly before: “I do not seek my own glory; there is one who seeks and judges,” [Col. 0592B] “his neighbors and those who had known him before” spread abroad the brilliance of this miracle and kindled so great a flame that it reached the Pharisees, his envious enemies, to consume them.

“Not only the neighbors,” he says, “but also those who had known him before.” For many knew him. Why? “Because he was a beggar,” he says. He was known for two reasons: he was a beggar, because he had been blind from birth and publicly begged. Thus his recognizable person did not allow the miracle to remain hidden; and they said: “Is this not the man who sat and begged?”

[Col. 0592C] “But some said, ‘It is he’; others, ‘Certainly not, but he resembles him.’ But he said, ‘I am he.’” Enlightened in mind and body, he returns to his enlightener such gratitude as he can, choosing rather to endure envy with him than, by ungrateful silence, to diminish the praise and glory of God. This writer, a truly faithful recorder, rightly took care first to receive into a remembering mind and then to set down with his pen this man’s words and replies. For he was the first of all mortals to be questioned for Christ’s sake and to suffer persecution; and he answered all things in the same manner as that great blind man spread throughout the whole world, who even today, answering in councils and synagogues, confesses the grace of his enlightener—strong in labors, victorious in persecutions, preaching and testifying opportunely to the willing and importunately to the unwilling that great mystery of godliness which is mystically contained in this blind man’s words: “The Lord made mud from spittle, anointed my eyes; I went, washed, saw, and believed God.”

“Some,” he says, “said, ‘It is he’; others, ‘Certainly not, but he resembles him.’” Thus the splendor of so great a glory of God could be obscured, and the report of so great a miracle could reach certain knowledge more feebly. But this judge and witness of the truth, conscious of his own identity—now no longer blind, but possessing eyes and seeing—does not allow them to remain doubtful, saying: “I am he.”

“Therefore they said to him: How then were your eyes opened?” It is as though they said: The man who sat and begged [Col. 0593A] was blind. But you, when we ask about that blind man, say: “I am he.” “How then were your eyes opened?”

“He answered: That man who is called Jesus made mud from spittle, anointed my eyes, and said to me: ‘Go to the pool of Siloam and wash.’ And I went, washed, and saw [I see].” Let the whole redeemed world now speak—the world long blind and at last enlightened—against the condemned world, which remains persistently blind. Let it say: “The Lord made mud from spittle, anointed my eyes; I went, washed, saw, and believed God”; and let it resound with so great a song that heaven above and earth below echo it.

If the peace of the churches assists those who sing, let that choir be nourished and delight in its gracious songs. If the war of persecution disturbs it, then all the more, amid every kind of death, let it bear witness in proclamation to this most loving and delightful benefit of its enlightener. But against these things all who are from the devil their father, and therefore cannot hear this word, lay their hands upon and persecute everyone who sees and glorifies God, delivering them to councils and synagogues and dragging them before kings and governors for Christ’s sake (Matt. X; Luke XXI). Of such persons it next says:

“And they said to him: Where is he? He said: I do not know. They brought the man who had been blind to the Pharisees.” The enlightened eyes mourn this very thing: although they see their enlightener by faith, they do not yet see him by sight; and, while their adversaries insult them, they cannot see or show Christ’s presence [Col. 0593C] (I Cor. XIII). Hence in the psalm the voice of any faithful soul says: “My tears were my bread day and night, while daily it is said to me: Where is your God?” (Ps. XLI).

Yet we do not wholly fail to know where he is. We know that he ascended into heaven; but we do not know how he is, or what judgment he has concerning us ourselves. While he says this, they bring him, it says, to the Pharisees. What cause did they find in this man, that they should so quickly drag him to judges or to the synagogue? On what issue did they have to establish the dispute in this case? It follows:

“Now it was the Sabbath when Jesus made the mud and opened his eyes.” The weary hunters, persistently pursuing the roe and the fawn of deer, were refreshed by a welcome respite. The one who shortly before had said, “Which of you convicts me of sin?” had stood, as it were, upon a lofty rock which they could not reach; now they thought they had caught him, so that they could say: We know that this man is a sinner, “and he is not from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath,” because “it was the Sabbath when he made the mud and opened the blind man’s eyes.”

“Therefore they again asked him how he had come to see.” Since Jesus made mud, they say, and anointed his eyes; and “it was the Sabbath” when he did this. Therefore, so that the crowds might hear and the people learn from the blind man’s own mouth that this man was a transgressor of the Law because he had not kept the Sabbath, they again asked the man who had been blind how he had come to see, though this had already been reported to them by those who brought him.

“But he said to them: He put mud on my eyes, and I washed, and I see.” An easy proof, not extracted by any questioning, is accomplished in one plain reply; let his adversaries take it as they wish. For this witness, certain of the innocence of his enlightener, is not ashamed to confess what was done. “For it is good to conceal the king’s secret, but honorable to proclaim the works of God” (Tob. XII).

“Some of the Pharisees therefore said: This man is not from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath.” O slaves of sin, riding the horses of pride and judging with lying, unrestrained mouths free persons on foot—indeed, their Liberator, the Truth itself—do you yourselves perform on the first or second day of the Sabbath a work like this, that blind eyes may be opened. But you cannot do this, nor can anyone like you who is a slave of sin. Therefore opening the eyes of the blind is not servile work.

But the Law written concerning the Sabbath does not say that every sort of work is forbidden; rather: “You shall do no servile work on it” (Lev. XXIII). Why then, O slaves of sin, do you dare judge a work of freedom? Is it lawful for lower things to judge higher? Is the work of God, equally with servile work, bound by the law of days or people? For every work is divided in three ways: one work is God’s work, whose fruit is eternal life; another is sin’s work, whose end is death; and another is the hired worker’s work, whose recompense is daily wages (Rom. VI). The work of sin and the work of the hired worker are both rightly called servile work.

Yet one of these, namely the hired worker’s work, may not be done on a holy day—such as the Sabbath then was, and the first day of the Sabbath is now because of Christ’s resurrection [Col. 0594C] (I Cor. IX). The other, the work of sin, ought never to be done.

But its contrary, namely the work of God, ought never to be omitted at any time or on any day: “Blessed are those who keep judgment and do righteousness at every time” (Ps. CV). This is evident from the fathers or instruments of that work: “For the instruments of God’s work are his gifts: the word of wisdom or knowledge, prophecy, kinds of tongues, the grace of healings” (I Cor. XII), and similar gifts. These are certainly subject to no law, since it is not within human choice at what time or on what day they descend from above from the Father of lights.

Therefore one must always abstain from the servile work of sin; one must never abstain from God’s work (James I). But from that intermediate work, namely the hired worker’s work, one must cease on appointed days—not so much because of some great mystery as for the rest of slave or handmaid. God says through Moses: “For six days you shall work; on the seventh day you shall cease, that your ox and ass may rest, and that the son of your handmaid and the resident alien may be refreshed” (Exod. XXIII).

And when one ceases from this servile work, it is by no means permitted to be idle from the work of God. For, if you consider rightly, God did not rest from his work even on the Sabbath; thus it is written: “And on the seventh day God completed [Col. 0595A] his work which he had made” (Gen. II). Therefore we shall expose the Jews, who glory in Sabbath idleness, because already at the beginning the Sabbath was set aside, when God worked on the Sabbath, completing his works on it and blessing that day.

What, moreover, is the completion of God’s work if not that this man enlightened one blind from birth? For it was an incomplete work when the man was born blind, because one of the five bodily senses had been withdrawn from him—senses which belong by nature not only to human beings but also to other animals. Therefore, “in the multitude of your power your enemies lie to you” (Ps. LXV), O Christ, Son of God, when they say: “This man is not from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath.” For by completing on the Sabbath the unfinished work—that is, the work of the man blind from birth—you likewise testify that you are from God and are the Son of him who, as said above, completed his work on the seventh day.

They lie, I say, and to this day persevere in their lie, hating you—that is, not in ignorance, but knowingly and enviously, because of the multitude of your power. But we Gentiles bless you, our God, saying with the firmness of the prophetic voice: “Let all the earth worship you and sing to you; let it sing a psalm to your name, O Most High” (ibid.). For the whole earth has been enlightened by that very multitude of your power concerning which your enemies lie to you. It follows:

“Others said: How can a sinful man do these signs? And there was division among them.” How, they ask, can a sinful man—a man so unfortunate that one may rightly say of him that he is not from God—do these signs? That is, how can he complete or improve works which only God has done or knows how to do? Those who did not suffer the worst torment of envy had some freedom to weigh the true judgment. For that he should not be from God, and should complete works which God unquestionably began, are far more and incomparably more inconsistent with one another than that he should be from God and perform a work of salvation on the Sabbath.

Indeed, there is no inconsistency at all; rather, it truly follows that one who is from God should do God’s work at every time. Nor was it said without reason that “there was division among them.” For since the chief aim of the accusers was that, all inclining to a single judgment, they should unanimously cry out that this man was not from God, they took it very ill that others said the contrary: “How can a sinful man do these signs?”

“Therefore they say again to the blind man: What do you say about him who opened your eyes?” This is not said by just anyone, but by those whose vain assertion was: “This man is not from God.” They strove to draw him into partnership in their blasphemy and to support the weakness of their case by the staff of his tongue. They thought that division greatly useful to them for detesting the one they hated, if even the man who had received so great a benefit from him should think nothing good of him.

By that perversity they still desire above all else to blind the eyes of our hearts which have been enlightened through faith in Christ, just as they had nearly blinded the Galatians, to whom the Apostle says: “O foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you not to believe the truth? Are you so foolish that, having begun with the Spirit, you are now completed by the flesh?” (Gal. III). Thus the blind, wishing to bewitch one who sees, said: “What do you say about him who opened your eyes?”

“But he said: He is a prophet.” He said less than he is, for Christ Jesus, the enlightener of all the Gentiles, is not only a prophet but also God and Lord of the prophets. Yet the man was still an untrained beholder of truth. Nevertheless, in reply to such people—who do not inquire in order to see, but in order to prevent those who see from seeing—against these, I say, “who are in the synagogue of Satan and blaspheme Christ” (Apoc. III), this reply is sufficient for us and for all who have been enlightened: “He is a prophet.”

For since they refuse to hear or know that he is Christ, let them at least know and see that “he is a prophet.” Yet this is not so that we may boast against the natural branches, insulting them because they were broken off while we, cut from the wild olive, have contrary to nature been grafted into the good olive tree (Rom. XI). Rather, content with this alone—that we may stop the mouths of those who say, “This man is not from God”—let us say that it is false. For even in your punishment it is sufficiently manifest to you that “he is a prophet.” Therefore he is from God, and in the name of the Lord he spoke a true word concerning you: the sign by which the Law commands a prophet in whom the Lord has spoken to be recognized (Deut. XVIII).

[Col. 0596C] “Therefore the Jews did not believe concerning him that he had been blind and had received sight [was seeing], until they summoned the parents of the man who had been blind.” Behold how these little foxes strive to escape through another hole, lest they be compelled to behold the glory of the Son of God. At first, as soon as they were offended by the brilliance of so great a miracle, they took refuge in saying: “This man is not from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath.” But this was no free escape for them, because “there was a division among them,” some saying: “How can a sinful man perform such signs?” Moreover, the man who had been enlightened himself dissented from that blasphemy, saying, “Because he is a prophet.” Therefore they sprang back to yet another escape, so as not to believe and, by not believing, to make doubtful, as it were, that he had been blind and had received sight. For the report of so great an event, though perhaps not capable of being wholly [Col. 0596D] concealed, nevertheless seemed capable somehow of being obscured through this pretense. “Therefore,” he says, “they did not believe that he had been blind and had received sight, until they summoned his parents,” so that by terror they might wring from them something that could assist their unjust purpose.

“And they questioned them, saying: Is this your son, whom you say was born blind? How then does he now see?” Behold: the parents are besieged because of their son, so that they might either lie, saying, “This is not our son, but merely resembles him”; or, “Our son was not born blind”; or certainly, “He was enlightened in some other way than the one stated”; or else, if they told what was true, they might incur the Jews’ anger and, together with their son, be put out of the synagogue. Yet, though thus besieged, they escaped as easily [Col. 0597A] as those who besieged them, on account of hatred for the seeing man, were truly blind and at ease [the text perhaps reads “who had besieged them”]. For it follows:

“His parents answered them: We know that this is our son, and that he was born blind. But how he now sees we do not know, nor do we know who opened his eyes. Ask him himself: he is of age; let him speak for himself. His parents said these things because they feared the Jews.” A sufficiently safe answer, open to no accusation. “We know,” they say. What? What you too know. We know and say only as much as you know and say: namely, “that this is our son, and that he was born blind.” But what you do not know, and ask as though you did not know, saying, “How then does he now see?”—we do not know. They said this because they feared the Jews. Although this comes close to a lie, [Col. 0597B] yet because they spoke it not with an intention to deceive but through fear of danger, they are not to be called liars, nor sons of the devil, who speaks falsehood from what is his own—unlike those of whom they were afraid and because of whom they spoke thus.

What, moreover, could be more just than what they added: “He is of age; let him speak for himself”? For it is indeed lawful that neither children be put to death for their parents nor parents for their children. This is also defended by prophetic authority, where it is said: “The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, nor the father that of the son” (Deut. XXIV; Ezek. XVIII). How much more ought parents to be free in a case of this sort? Thus, with constancy no less than wisdom, it was said to the blind by those who saw and by the parents of the seeing man: “He is of age; let him speak for himself.”

The Evangelist adds the cause of their fear: [Col. 0597C] “For the Jews had already agreed that, if anyone confessed him to be the Christ, he should be put out of the synagogue. Therefore his parents said: Ask him himself; he is of age; let him speak for himself.” This conspiracy was wind and flood: indeed a violent wind and a great flood, but one incapable of moving the house of the wise man founded upon the rock (Matt. VII). Yet that the parents of this blind man were afraid at that time is not very surprising, since Peter too not only feared but was almost wholly submerged by denying Christ, had not Christ quickly stretched out his hand and grasped him, turning at the cock’s crow and looking upon him (Matt. XXVI; Luke XII).

But by this same conspiracy the Jews expelled all God’s grace from themselves; and, while they put out of the synagogue those who confess Christ, they separate themselves from the whole synagogue—that is, from the ancient Church of the patriarchs and prophets, and of all the righteous and elect, who awaited Christ and, by that very expectation, confessed him. Thus they themselves were rather made outside the synagogue of God and shut within the synagogue of Satan (Apoc. III).

It should certainly be noted that, in saying, “Therefore they said, ‘Ask him himself; he is of age; let him speak for himself,’” the Evangelist omitted that part of their reply which is not wholly free from fault, because it is not wholly devoid of the stain of falsehood: namely, what they had said, “But how he now sees we do not know, nor do we know who opened his eyes”; and [Col. 0598A] he repeated only what is beyond reproach, as if bearing witness when he says: “Therefore they said: Ask him himself,” and so forth.

“Therefore they summoned again the man who had been blind, and said to him: Give glory to God. We know that this man is a sinner.” Behold how the fabricators of falsehood go about trying to make this man—not a proselyte or a stranger, but a citizen and member of God’s household of grace—a son of perdition together with themselves, compelling him to exchange God’s truth for falsehood. For what are they attempting except to make him testify to their lie and say, though blind, “This man is not from God”; or to deny that the work of his enlightenment was accomplished by divine power, but rather by some magical incantation?

Therefore they summoned the man again. [Col. 0598B] Moving back from the man who had been blind to his parents, and from his parents back to him, “they searched out iniquities and were exhausted in searching with searching” (Ps. LXIII). “Give,” they say, “glory to God.” In what way? By knowing and saying the same thing that we do. And what is that? “We know that this man is a sinner.”

Well said—for like Joshua, they imagined that they were seeking God’s glory while using words opposite in spirit to the prayer of that brave man (Josh. VII). For Joshua, honouring God in heart and lips, when Achan had taken from what was devoted to destruction and the lot had exposed him, said: “My son, give glory to God, and tell us what you have done.” But these men, honouring God with their lips while their heart is far from him (Isa. LIX), say: “Give glory to God”—that is, deny what you have received. Thus the mouth of the ungodly covers iniquity; and thus, while perverting their ways, they are nevertheless manifest to the enlightened man who sees clearly. For it follows:

“Therefore he said: Whether he is a sinner, I do not know; one thing I know: whereas I was blind, now I see.” They concealed hatred with lying lips, pretending that they sought God’s glory by saying, “This man is a sinner.” But he, enlightened both in mind and body and seeing clearly, was free from calling such a thing God’s glory rather than blasphemy. “Whether he is a sinner,” he says, “I do not know”—that is, I know that he is not a sinner. For that one thing which I know is incompatible with it: namely, that whereas I was blind, now I see—something no sinful human being could have accomplished.

[Col. 0598D] “Therefore they said to him: What did he do to you? How did he open your eyes?” Do they not seem, by questions of this sort, to be saying to him: Invent something else for us; for we do not wish to hear what was done to you, which has already been told once and twice? But whom could such questioning terrify—questioning grand in its command to obey with the tongue, yet unjust, demanding submission to lying lips? (Ecclus. LI.) Could it terrify the man who, with enlightened eyes, saw that false witnesses would perish?

Certainly, for those who then saw but did not see the seeing man, and for all other Jews or heretics who wish to hear something concerning Christ other than that signified in this man’s enlightenment—namely, that he has clothed himself with our dust through that wisdom which proceeded from the mouth of God (I Cor. I), and that thereby we have been enlightened—“for all,” I say, [Col. 0599A] “mockers,” to whom this preaching is a stumbling-block or foolishness, “judgments are prepared, and hammers striking their bodies” (Prov. XIX).

It follows, therefore: “He answered them: I have already told you, and you heard. Why do you want to hear it again? Do you also wish to become his disciples?” He does not answer in this indignant manner, nor launch his attack upon them, saying, “I have told you already, and you heard,” and so forth, out of weariness at answering, but by the judgment of reason. Why, then, did he say, “Do you also wish to become his disciples?” Could he have suspected this of men who had so flattered him by saying, “Give glory to God,” and immediately disclosed the evil path by which they wished to lead him away, adding: “We know that this man is a sinner”? Therefore, by his pointed question he drove sharper nails home: he denied that they wished to become Christ’s disciples, and for this reason judged them unworthy of a repeated narration. This is made still clearer by what follows.

“They cursed him and said to him: You be his disciple; but we are disciples of Moses. We know that God spoke to Moses; but as for this man, we do not know where he is from.” That this expression, “You be his disciple,” is uttered as a curse makes clear that their hatred of him of whom the man had said, “Do you also wish to become his disciples?” was no slight hatred—just as one can be sure that there is fire beneath wherever one sees smoke or sparks flying upward.

But where hatred of truth was present, discipleship of Christ could not be received, because “wisdom will not enter a malicious soul” (Wis. I). Rightly, then, this man, no longer blind but seeing, at once marveling and indignant, says: “Do you also wish to become his disciples?” “They cursed him,” says the Evangelist, “and said: You be his disciple; but we are disciples of Moses.”

Nevertheless, even today the Christian urges the Jew to become Christ’s disciple; while the Jew, conversely, curses Christ and every Christian in his synagogues. But may such a curse of theirs be upon us. For by such curses of theirs especially, the Lord blesses us, just as, conversely, he says through the prophet Malachi: “I will curse your blessings” (Mal. II).

“But we,” they say, “are disciples of Moses.” Utterly in vain do these double-tongued and double-minded disciples flatter Moses: defenders of the Sabbath, but deserters of the love of God [Col. 0599D] and neighbour; craftily honouring God’s servant in order, with his authority, to dishonour God’s Son. In vain, I say. For Moses kicks against them and says: “May the Lord strike you with madness, blindness, and frenzy of mind; and you shall grope 255 at noon, as the blind man is accustomed to grope in darkness” (Deut. XXVIII). In accordance with this curse, they now grope in darkness and limp upon slippery ground; but the Gentile people, signified by the man enlightened by Christ, has the broad and radiant path of noon.

“The man answered and said to them: In this, indeed, is the marvel: that you do not know where he is from, and yet he opened my eyes.” He despised their futile wisdom and did not judge their curses worthy of an answer. But what they had said last—“We know that God spoke to Moses, but as for this man we do not know where he is from”—he most forcefully rebukes. “Out of astonishment,” he says, “I did not repeat my reply to your questions, but said only this: ‘Do you also wish to become his disciples?’ For the marvel lies in this: that he is so great [Col. 0600A] that he opened my eyes, and you do not know him”—that is, you disapprove of him; for you do not wish to know that he is from God. In this, I say, lies the marvel: a marvelous crime, astonishing sacrilege.

“For we know that God does not hear sinners.” We indeed “know” this, Scripture bearing witness: “He who turns his ear away from hearing the law—his prayer shall be an abomination” (Prov. XXVIII). Again: “If I have looked upon iniquity in my heart, the Lord will not hear” (Ps. LXV). Therefore God does not hear sinners so long as they remain sinners—especially such as you judge this man to be. “But if anyone is a worshiper of God and does his will, him he hears.”

Having laid down this proposition, since it cannot be refuted, he immediately adds: “From the age it has not been heard that anyone opened the eyes of one born blind.” And this, without doubt, whether opponents will it or not, must be granted: for nothing of this kind is found in Moses or the prophets. Accordingly he immediately concludes: “Unless this man were from God, he could do nothing.”

The structure of this argument should be carefully noted. “We know,” he says, “that God does not hear sinners; but if anyone is a worshiper of God and does his will, him he hears.” God does not thus hear every worshiper of his, nor everyone whatsoever who does his will. For from the age it has not been heard that “anyone opened the eyes of one born blind.” Great deeds are indeed reported of Moses and the prophets; but everything Moses did, he did outside the human person—that is, in the elements of the world. Yet a few of the deeds performed by the prophets, who were certainly nearer to evangelical grace both in time and preaching, occurred within the human person: such as the raising of the dead by Elijah’s prayers (III Kings XVII), and again by Elisha’s (IV Kings IV).

Since, then, God hears not just any of his worshipers but surely his most eminent ones in such a way that they can perform such deeds, the conclusion is indeed true and firm: Unless this man were from God, he could do nothing—that is, he could neither command the elements, [Col. 0600D] nor restore to the dead the life they had lost, nor infuse into a man born blind the light which had never existed in him, something unheard of from the age, even if other great things have been heard of.

Thus the unjust accusers and witnesses—not so much investigators as mockers of judgment—were refuted and shut up by one strong and knotty argument in their own assertion, in which they had said, “We know that this man is a sinner.” Since they could not escape by the path of reason, they burst forth, as usual, into abuse, saying:

“You were born wholly in sins, and do you teach us? And they put him out.” “Blessed,” he says, “will you be when they curse you, reproach you, and cast out your name as evil” (Matt. V). They had already “cursed him,” saying, “You be his disciple”; they had reproached him, saying, “You were born wholly in sins”; and “they put him out of the synagogue”—that is, they anathematized him. Thus in this man the enlightenment of the Gentiles and also the sufferings of the saints have already been prefigured.

They lie, judging from their own heart: “You were born wholly in sins”—that is, because of your own sins or those of your parents, you were born blind. For Truth had already said of him: “Neither this man sinned nor his parents, that he should be born blind, but that the works of God might be made manifest in him.” Yet let us acknowledge that we are all indeed wholly in sins—that is, born blind. But the prophecy has been fulfilled in us which says: “I will lead the blind by a way they do not know, and make them walk in paths they have not known” (Isa. XLII). We have authority to teach, so that they may emulate us and what was said to them through Moses may be fulfilled in them: “I will provoke you to jealousy by that which is not a nation; I will anger you by a foolish nation” (Deut. XXXII).

[Col. 0601B] “Jesus heard that they had put him out. And when he had found him, he said to him: Do you believe in the Son of God?” The words “Jesus heard” may seem lightly spoken, but in truth it is a most serious thing that the cry of sinners should have reached his ears: “I expected him to perform judgment, and behold iniquity; and righteousness, and behold a cry” (Isa. V). Nor is this phrase without weight: “And when he had found him.” For Jesus finds those whom the world loses; salvation finds those whom perdition abandons. And he finds them nearby: “For the Lord is near to those who are troubled in heart” (Ps. XXXIII). Again, concerning the faithful man: “I am with him,” he says, “in tribulation” (Ps. XC).

What follows must be understood simply, that is, without necessary figurative application to that man, as the matter requires. For it does not follow that, just as the man was first sent to the pool of Siloam, washed, and saw, and then was asked, “Do you believe in the Son of God?”, each one of us must first be washed in baptism and afterward asked whether he believes. Therefore we must consider the devotion of the one man who was then being instructed, concerning whom it follows: “He answered him and said: Who is he, Lord, that I may believe in him?”

Until this point, that man signified what now exists. He signified that we were to be catechized and baptized; now he himself is a catechumen. For previously he did not know the Son of God in whom he was to believe, when he says: “Who is he, Lord, that I may believe in him?” He is therefore catechized, and faith in that Son is laid upon the eyes of his mind—he who shortly before had been signified by clay placed upon the eyes of his body. For it follows:

[Col. 0601D] “And Jesus said to him: You have both seen him, and he who speaks with you is he.” About to say something great—namely, “He who speaks with you is he”—he suitably prefaced it with: “You have seen him,” in order that by recalling his great power and great benefit he might make the hearer’s mind well disposed. For to one asking who the Son of God is, what does “You have seen him” mean except: He is the one who opened your eyes so that you might be able to see him?

Having thus gained goodwill, he immediately says, “And he who speaks with you is he”—a manner of speaking certainly more gracious and farther removed from the suspicion of boasting than if he had said, “I myself am the Son of God” (John II). Nor did the Son of God reveal himself to this man in vain when he said, “He who speaks with you is he.” For hear, hear, I say, and see what this man had been, and what he himself knew him to be—the man of whom it is said elsewhere: “For he himself knew what was in man” (ibid.).

“But he said: I believe, Lord. And falling down, he worshiped him.” Two things are to be noted concerning this first worshiper of the Son of God, which you do not read of any other worshiper of him: namely, that he said “I believe,” and that he fell down. For the leper too is said to have worshiped him (Matt. VIII), but not to have said, “I believe in you,” nor to have fallen down; rather, as Mark testifies, he merely knelt (Mark [Col. 0602B] I). This man alone is found to perform the worship due to the Son of God both by the voice of confession and by bodily gesture. He is therefore rightly set forth each year as an example to the catechumens of the holy Church, when the Paschal solemnity draws near and they are to be baptized into Christ’s death. In that baptism he too, after this confession and worship, was undoubtedly worthy to be washed (Rom. VI).

Therefore, after these events, let us hear the subsequent words of the Savior, and consider him as explaining what he accomplished for us when, hiddenly, he departed from the Jews’ temple and enlightened the blind man in such an order; and then as pronouncing judgment upon those shepherds who had put out this sheep—that is, the enlightened man. It follows: “And Jesus said to him: For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind.”

This is a great and just sentence, spoken fittingly and in its proper time. For since an unjust judgment had been rendered—not judgment, but iniquity—when the Pharisees had put out the frequently mentioned man, rightly he to whom all judgment belongs, and whose office it is to correct whatever is done by unjust judgments, says: “For judgment I came into this world.” And because they had put him out for no other reason than that, though he had been blind, he now saw and refused to blaspheme his enlightener, rightly the Judge calls the punishment he is to repay them blindness: “That those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind.”

From the case of the enlightened man who had been blind, and from the manner in which they put him out, the fitting name of their penalty or vengeance is given. Nor did he say only, “That those who see may become blind,” but also that they might have those whom they would emulate as a punishment: “And that those who do not see,” he says, “may see.”

When, therefore, we hear of judgment, the Judge saying, “For judgment I came into this world,” let us expect the order of judgment itself: namely, that he who will judge the guilty should now declare their guilt, and the nature and designation of the guilt they have committed. Their guilt is that they did not enter by the door but came down by another way into the sheepfold. Its manner is that they came not merely to steal but also to slaughter and destroy, and that they seek to kill the good shepherd himself, whose sheep they are—and this they will indeed accomplish. The legal designation of this guilt, with its definition, is that they are thieves and robbers: thieves, because they steal; robbers, because they kill what they steal.

Accordingly, they are to be blinded by those who did not see but now see; and, as it is said elsewhere in different words but with the same sense, “Many shall come from east and west and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt.
