VIII), while they are to be cast out into outer darkness. They proceed to this in the following order:

[Col. 0603A] “And some of the Pharisees who were with him heard this, and said to him: Are we also blind?” Some of the Pharisees—who, as has been said, had already agreed that anyone confessing Christ should be put out of the synagogue—were with him, not as followers but as persecutors; not imitators but spies. The Pharisees are the clergy of the Jews. If, then, the Jews trust that they see, how much more their Pharisees, their leaders?

In what, however, do the Jews trust that they see? “But if,” says the Apostle, “you are called a Jew, and rest in the law, and glory in God, and know his will, and approve the better things of the law, being instructed by the law, and trust that you yourself are a guide of the blind, a light to those who are in darkness” (Rom. II), and so forth. Therefore, when the Lord said, “And those who see may become blind,” recognizing that he spoke of them, they say: “Are we also blind?” Have we too lost the light of our knowledge because you have come?

“Jesus said to them: If you were blind, you would not have sin. But now you say that you see; your sin remains.” He tempers his sentence well and commendably, granting them that they see and showing that this very fact contributes to the fullness of their condemnation and the punishment of eternal blindness. For they are truly blind through hatred of light and truth, yet seeing through knowledge of that same truth, as persons instructed by the law. Hence God says through the prophet: “Bring forth the blind people who have eyes, and the deaf who have ears” (Isa. XLIII). Thus, to their own harm, sight is granted them in the words: “If you were blind, you would not have sin; but now you say that you see; your sin remains.”

What sin? Surely that which is immediately added in these words:

[CHAPTER X.] “Amen, amen, I say to you: He who does not enter through the door into the sheepfold, but climbs up another way, [Col. 0603D] is a thief and a robber.” He might have said: Amen, amen, I say to you: because you see, and in seeing know how to avoid the door and climb up another way into the sheepfold, you are thieves and robbers; and this is your sin—namely theft and robbery. He could, I say, have spoken thus. But lest truth, as if provoked, should sound with any bitterness, holding the balance of a most severe judgment with greater gentleness, he states the weight of sin universally: “He who does not enter through the door into the sheepfold, but climbs up another way, is a thief and a robber.”

A thief, indeed, because he steals what belongs to another; a robber, because he kills what he has stolen. Notice how fitting is the comparison he employs for the time and circumstance. For those men—the Pharisees—who were as if shepherds but abused pastoral power or authority, had put out the enlightened man as a sheep from the sheepfold—that is, from the synagogue. Therefore he fittingly draws his comparison from the sheepfold, and declares to them and to all who, though wolves, wish to seem shepherds, and who do not admit those subject to and entrusted to their power through the door—that is, who condemn or justify by anathematizing, not according to God but according to their own will, in accordance with the prophet’s words: “They gave life to souls that do not live and put to death souls that do not die” (Ezek. XIII)—that all such men have not entered the sheepfold by the door but climbed up another way, and are consequently thieves and robbers.

Now, concerning those especially to whom or against whom this discourse is addressed, it must be said: “Amen, amen, I say to you, he who does not enter through the door into the sheepfold, but climbs up another way, is a thief and a robber.” Here we must understand what he says later: “I am the door of the sheep.”

It is certain that the Pharisees not only refused to enter through him, but also did not wish to acknowledge him, saying: “As for this man, we do not know where he is from.” And, what is worse, they had already agreed that if anyone wished to enter through him—that is, “if anyone confessed him to be the Christ”—he should be put out of the synagogue. Indeed, they had put this man out of the synagogue for that very reason: because he had already begun to enter through him (Luke XI).

Most rightly, therefore, this proverb is addressed to them, by which it is signified that they are thieves and robbers, because they neither enter through the door—that is, through Christ—themselves, nor permit others to enter. “If you were blind,” he says, that is, if you did not trust in yourselves and had not taken away the key of knowledge, neither entering yourselves nor allowing others to enter, “you would not have sin” (John IX): that sin, namely, by which you so greatly avoid and strive to obstruct the door—that is, me—through whom entry into the sheepfold is made. For does a blind person know how to avoid a door? Does he not rather turn aside from it through ignorance and error?

Thus the judgment will be just: those who do not see the door shall be called and led to it and, once admitted, shall see. But those who see the door and, envying or disparaging the door, climb up another way in order, by carrying out the desires of their father the devil, to slaughter and destroy—these shall immediately become blind, expelled in such a manner that they can neither find the door nor be able to climb up another way.

It follows:

[Col. 0604D] “But he who enters through the door is the shepherd of the sheep.” It plainly follows for one “who enters through the door” that he is a shepherd of the sheep, just as, conversely, it follows for one who climbs up another way that he is a thief and robber. But what is entering through the door except imitating Christ, who himself, as he says shortly afterward, is both shepherd and door? Again, what is imitating Christ except that no one comes of himself, but in obedient submission awaits the command of the one who sends or calls him?

For Christ did not usurp for himself the name or office of shepherd, or possession of the sheep; but, commanded and sent by the Father, he obediently undertook the care of seeking the hundredth sheep which had been lost (Luke XV), as he himself testifies: “For I did not come of myself, but he sent me” (John V). The Apostle confirms this in different words: “No one,” he says, “takes the honor to himself, but he who is called by God, as Aaron was. So Christ also did not glorify himself to become a high priest, but he who spoke to him, saying: You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Heb. V; Ps. II). And elsewhere he says: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CIX).

Therefore, whoever does not come of himself, does not commend himself, but waits for God as his recommender in order to become a shepherd, certainly enters through [Col. 0605B] the door, because he thus imitates Christ, the chief shepherd (I Pet. V). Such a person is very unlike those chiefly intended or opposed in these words: Annas and Caiaphas, who had truly climbed up another way. Therefore it is no wonder that they stole, slaughtered, and destroyed, because they were thieves and robbers. For they were not called by God as Aaron was; but, forcing their way in by contention one against another, they divided the venal priesthood into annual portions.

It follows: “To him the doorkeeper opens, and the sheep hear his voice.” To him, he says, who enters through the door—that is, who by lawful order receives the pastoral office for God’s sake—“the doorkeeper opens,” because, in order that his zeal may benefit the sheep, the doorkeeper by the grace of the Holy Spirit goes beforehand into the hearts of the hearers. This was done for Paul the Apostle, a lawful shepherd, when he said to the Corinthians: “I shall remain at Ephesus until Pentecost, for a great and manifest door has been opened to me” (I Cor. XVI).

The same is meant in the Apocalypse, where this is promised to the angel of the church of Philadelphia: “These things says the Holy and True One, who has the key of David, who opens and no one shuts, shuts and no one opens: I know your works. Behold, I give before you an open door, which no one can shut” (Apoc. III), and so forth. For then the Holy and True One, the keeper of the keys of human hearts, opens a great door to the angel of Philadelphia—Philadelphia meaning brotherly love—that is, to the preacher who desires to advance the salvation of his neighbours. Knowing his works, when he has weighed the intention of his heart, he deigns to unfold for him the understanding of the sacred word, and by his grace, both preceding and following, cooperates with his labor so that it may bear fruit.

And now the doorkeeper is he himself who speaks these things. Before he was glorified through victory over death, he appeared as a lowly door; now, I say, he is not only the door but also the doorkeeper, since, “ascending on high and leading captivity captive, he gave gifts to men” (Ps. LXVII). For from this it is also proved that he is the doorkeeper: that he himself gave some as apostles, others as prophets, others as evangelists, others as pastors and teachers (I Cor. XIII).

Nor does it cause—or ought to cause—any confusion that he himself is both door and doorkeeper. For in the fold of irrational sheep, the door and the doorkeeper are different; but in the rational flock, the door is the doorkeeper. For just as our one and same Lord Jesus Christ is the way, the truth, and the life, so he is not only the door but also the doorkeeper, and further, the pasture of the sheep itself (John XIV).

Yet there is some distinction in our advancement between the door and the doorkeeper. When each of us approaches Christ through Catholic faith, Christ is the door to him; but when, having received some grace, the same distributor of graces bestows it, he is now the doorkeeper. So also, for the highest shepherds after him, the apostles, before his passion Christ was only the door; but when he rose from the dead and received authority, as he himself says, “All authority has been given to me in heaven [Col. 0606B] and on earth” (Matt. XXVIII), he became both door and doorkeeper, and, as truly the doorkeeper of heaven, bestowed upon them the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

Therefore, “He who enters through the door—to him the doorkeeper opens.” What follows? “And the sheep,” he says, “follow him.” This is plainly fitting, and it is expedient for the sheep themselves. For Christ’s sheep would not be Christ’s sheep if they did not follow Christ’s apostles and all those to whom this doorkeeper opened, and if they did not know or approve their voice—that is, their teaching. For to such persons he says: “He who hears you hears me; he who despises you despises me” (Luke X). Relying on this authority, Paul says: “Or do you seek proof of Christ speaking in me?” (II Cor. XIII).

Thus, for whomever the doorkeeper opens, the sheep know his voice and follow him; and whoever follow him are sheep. But those who scorn to follow bear witness against themselves by that rebellion: they are not sheep but goats. It follows:

“And he calls his own sheep by name and leads them out.” O how unlike the man who has entered through the door, or to whom the doorkeeper has opened, are those thieves and robbers who avoided the door and climbed up another way! For they do not call sheep by name; rather, they employ perverse names, calling good evil and evil good, calling darkness light and light darkness (Isa. V), in order to justify the ungodly for gifts and take away the righteousness of the righteous—as did the thieves and robbers against whom these words are especially directed. They called by an alien name the man who had been blind and had received sight; they cursed and reproached him and put him out as evil.

Not so this shepherd. Rather, “He calls,” he says, “his own sheep by name.” “His own,” he says, because by an affection of love he has made Christ’s sheep his own; or because the shepherd himself, through his own labor and care, has acquired and nourished for the Prince of Shepherds those sheep which were not his. “And he calls them by name”—that is, since they are sheep, he does not call them goats, but addresses them gently and familiarly as sheep. Even if they have been goats, he does not tyrannically reproach them with this in a cursing voice, especially since the Prince of Shepherds himself says through the Psalmist: “I will not remember their names upon my lips” (Ps. XV), unless perhaps for the useful remembrance of purifying grace.

Thus the Apostle, after recalling their former names by saying: “Neither fornicators, nor idolaters, nor the greedy, nor the effeminate, nor men who lie with males, nor thieves, nor the rapacious shall possess the kingdom of God” (I Cor. VI), immediately, after touching upon these names of their former state, added in commendation of God’s grace: “And such indeed you were; but you were washed, but you were sanctified, but you were justified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God” (ibid.).

Thus he “calls them by name,” that is, by the name which the great shepherd has written upon us, the former names having been erased: the name of his God and the name of the children of God, namely the Christian name. Of this also he says through the prophet: “I shall call my servants by another name, in which he who is blessed shall be blessed upon the earth” (Isa. 65) [Col. 0607B]. And in calling thus, “he leads them out.” From where does he lead them out, or where does he lead them?

Indeed, all of us who are Christ’s sheep have, by the very fact that we are sheep, been led out of the darkness of former errors; and already, through the hand of his shepherds, God has delivered us from this present evil age and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love (Gal. 1). Yet there still remains, and it very often occurs, something from which many of us, who are already Christ’s sheep, must be led out—indeed, summoned forth with a great cry—as was also signified through Lazarus, whom we read to have been raised by the great cry of our Lord Jesus Christ when he had already begun to stink and had been dead four days (John 12) [Col. 0607C].

For sheep are often defiled even after they have been shorn and washed in the health-giving stream. Delighting in the very diseases of their vices, they are shut up in a perverse habit or, what is worse, are stained by heretical error. Here the shepherd of the sheep, who entered through the door and to whom the doorkeeper opened, labours; and he employs words, now indeed harsh, as when the Apostle says: “It is altogether reported that there is fornication among you, and such fornication as is not even among the Gentiles” (1 Cor. 5); now gentle, as when that same Apostle says to the same people: “Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians; our heart is enlarged” (2 Cor. 6); or to the Galatians: “My little children, for whom I am again in labour until Christ be formed in you” (Gal. 4).

Truly, “he calls the sheep by name” [Col. 0607D], until “he leads them out”: that is, until he cleanses out from them the perverse habit of fornication or restores firmness of faith. Since this is accomplished not by the voice of preaching alone but also by the example of action, it is immediately added:

> “And when he has sent out his own sheep, he goes before them, and the sheep follow him, because they know his voice.”

It is fitting, then, that, when he has sent them out through the word of exhortation, he should go before them by the example of good work, lest God say to him in his sin: “Why do you recount my righteous acts and take my covenant upon your mouth? Yet you hate discipline and cast my words behind you” (Ps. 49 [50]), etc. Guarding against this, the Apostle said: “Thus I run, not as uncertainly; thus I fight, not as beating the air; but I chastise my body and bring it into slavery, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should become reprobate” (1 Cor. 9) [Col. 0608A].

Therefore, when the lawful shepherd has sent out his own sheep, “he goes before them, and the sheep follow him.” They follow him, I say, and this is indeed fitting for the sheep. For if, concerning hypocrites and false shepherds, he says: “All things whatsoever they tell you, keep and do; but do not act according to their works, for they say and do not do” (Matt. 23), how much more ought they to follow those who both speak and act. “Therefore they follow him because they know his voice”: because they recognize that his teaching is true and sound.

“But they do not follow a stranger, and they flee from him, because they do not know the voice of strangers.” By “strangers” one must understand not just any hypocrites [Col. 0608B], but thieves and robbers of the kind then present, on whose account this proverb was spoken. Their voice was very much that of strangers, since it incited to blasphemy by saying: “Give glory to God; we know that this man is a sinner and that he is not from God” (John 9). The oft-mentioned man who had been blind and received sight, not recognizing—or rather refusing to recognize—that voice, would not follow them, but fled from them as true strangers; fleeing in mind, he also endured being expelled from them in body.

All heretics, without doubt, are such, whoever refuse to hear intact the mystery of faith contained beneath the words of that same man as he bore witness to his illuminator: “He made clay from spittle and anointed my eyes; and I went and washed and saw” (ibid.) [Col. 0608C]. Therefore whatever sheep are true do not follow a stranger but flee from him, because they do not know the voice of strangers. They do not know, I say: they did not know and were unwilling to know, just as that man did not wish to know when they said to him, “We know that this man is a sinner.” “Whether he is a sinner,” he said, “I do not know; one thing I know: though I was blind, now I see” (ibid.).

This is what simple sheep—that is, faithful and Catholic people who have not known the depths of Satan—say to strangers, namely Jews and all heretics who think wrongly concerning the incarnation of the Son of God: “You say, ‘We know, and possess knowledge.’ As for us, we know whether you are foolish or senseless—of whom it is likewise written: ‘The senseless and the fool shall perish together’ (Ps. 48 [49]) [Col. 0608D]. This one thing we know: whereas we were blind, that is, ignorant of God, we have now, through entering by this door of faith—namely, ‘In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God; this was in the beginning with God; all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made; and this Word was made flesh and dwelt among us’ (John 1)—through this, I say, as through clay made from spittle, which is wisdom ‘that came forth from the mouth of the Most High’ (Ecclus. 24), and compounded with our dust, we have once been illuminated. We have also tasted the heavenly gift, have become partakers of the Holy Spirit, and likewise have tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come.”

It follows:

> [Col. 0609A] “Jesus spoke this proverb to them.”

A proverb occurs when one word is said in place of another, so that one thing may be more forcefully commended and more effectively understood through another. This mode of speech, or ornament of expression, is customary in the sacred Scriptures and divinely provided both to delight the diligent hearer and to subdue pride through labour, and to renew an understanding wearied by distaste, since things easily discovered commonly become cheap.

And he especially taught that this was so in the present place, in order that the pride of those who, presuming upon the brightness or sharpness of their own intelligence and knowledge, had shortly before said, “Are we also blind?” might be convicted. For it is immediately added: “And they themselves did not understand what he was saying to them.” Was not judgment, then, already beginning to come upon their eyes [Col. 0609B], that they should become blind, since they had said, “Are we also blind?” If they truly saw and were not already dim-sighted through hatred of the present truth, could they not have understood this proverb which he spoke to them, at least through the prophetic vision of Scripture in which Ezekiel says:

> “Woe to the shepherds of Israel who fed themselves!”

And thereafter:

> “Are not the flocks fed by the shepherds? You ate the milk, clothed yourselves with the wool, and killed what was fat; but you did not feed my flock.”  

And a little later:

> “Behold, I myself am against the shepherds, and I shall require my flock from their hand. I shall make them cease from feeding my flock any longer; nor shall the shepherds feed themselves any more. And I shall deliver my flock from their mouth, and it shall no longer be food for them” (Ezek. 34) [Col. 0609C], etc.

Again, at the end of the same chapter: “But you, my flocks, the flocks of my pasture, are human beings; I am the Lord your God, says the Lord” (Ezek. 34). If, therefore, they were not already beginning to become blind, how could they have failed to recognize of what sort of fold and sheep he was speaking to them?

> “Therefore Jesus said to them again: Amen, amen, I say to you, I am the door of the sheep.”

Whether unable or unwilling to recognize, “they did not know what he was saying to them.” The door itself, which had been closed, opened itself, so that, willing or unwilling, they might hear; so that those who had been blind might hear and see what door and what fold he meant. “I am,” he says, “the door” [Col. 0609D]. Here it must be understood, for it cannot be unknown, that he said this of himself, having said above: “He who does not enter through the door into the sheepfold, but climbs up another way, is a thief and a robber.”

Accordingly, when the proposition “I am the door” is joined with the understood and assumed statement that he had previously set forth, he rightly concludes: “All who came are thieves and robbers.” For if he is the door—indeed, because he is the door—and everyone “who does not enter through the door is a thief and a robber,” therefore all who came are thieves and robbers. None of those who had then come and were tyrannizing in the fold had entered through him, because they came not by preaching and keeping God’s word, but by denying and blaspheming the Son of God.

And it is clear that he spoke of those then present, because he says in the present tense, “are thieves,” not in the past tense, “were thieves” [Col. 0610A]. Yet whether in the present or past tense, “all who came were thieves and are thieves,” because they came of themselves and were neither sent nor called by God; and this is not to have entered through the door. For it is one thing simply and absolutely to have come, another to have come in the Lord’s name or from God. Thus the prophets and holy priests must be said not merely to have come, but to have come in the Lord’s name or to have spoken in the Lord’s name.

Therefore “all who came”—understand, because they were neither sent nor called and did not come with God’s word—“are thieves and robbers.” “But the sheep did not hear them.” This has already been said above [Col. 0610B]: they do not follow a stranger, but flee from him because they do not know the voice of strangers. They did not hear them, I say, and they will not hear them, so long as that is fulfilled which was prefigured through that man who had been enlightened in the manner and order described above, and who preferred to be cast out rather than hear the blasphemies of thieves or robbers.

Again he says: “I am the door.” Why does he now say this a second time, unless because there are not merely one but two folds? For shortly afterward he will say: “And I have other sheep, which are not of this fold.” Therefore, in order to signify that he is one and the same who gave the ancient shepherds, Moses and the prophets, and who now admits you—namely, the apostles—by his own election, he said once and again: “I am the door.”

And first, when he said “the door,” he added something concerning the past: “All who came are thieves and robbers, but the sheep did not hear them.” A second time, when he says, “I am the door,” he adds something concerning the future:

> [Col. 0610C] “If anyone enters through me, he shall be saved, and shall go in and go out, and find pasture.”

Thus he distinguishes not two doors for one fold, something easily done in common usage, but, what is far more wonderful, assigns one door to two folds, so that what he will say shortly afterward necessarily follows: “And there shall be one fold and one shepherd.” “And he shall go in,” he says, “and go out, and find pasture.”

Formerly, whoever entered—whether an Israelite native or an immigrant proselyte—found the pasture of the Law and the Prophets; but when he went out, since paradise had not yet been reopened—when he went out, I say, from the present life—he did not find pasture. But afterward, “If anyone enters,” he says, “he shall be saved, and shall go in and go out, and find pasture” [Col. 0610D], because, having entered by faith into the fold of the present Church, he shall rightly gather both the teaching of the Law and the grace of the Gospel; and, departing through bodily death, he shall immediately enjoy the delights of paradise. By the mystery of his most holy Passion, the Lord Jesus has made this door passable even to paradise’s innermost parts.

It follows:

> “The thief comes only to steal, slaughter, and destroy.”

Each of the things said here—“to steal, slaughter, and destroy”—has its own proper meaning. By this precise enumeration of parts, the full savagery is set forth not of just any thief, but of him who, as has been said above, is both thief and robber [Col. 0611A]. For what he steals is one thing, what he slaughters another, and what he destroys another.

For what does he steal except gold and silver? He steals the gold of God’s wisdom and the silver of mystical utterance; or, to continue the metaphor more closely, what does he steal except the wholesome pastures of the sheep? He corrupts them secretly when, by perverse traditions, he deprives sacred Scripture of that sense in which the Holy Spirit delivered it to be written and read.

Therefore, when the Apostle had said:

> “If you are called a Jew, and rest in the Law, and glory in God, and know his will, and approve the better things, being instructed by the Law, and are confident that you yourself are a guide of the blind, a light to those who are in darkness,”

he immediately added:

> “Then you who teach another, do you not teach yourself? You who preach that one must not steal, do you steal? You who abhor idols, do you commit sacrilege?” (Rom. 2) [Col. 0611B].

He employed, surely, a worthy invective and an argument of great force. For just as Barabbas the robber, or any such person, was more shameful than that man blind from birth whose eyes, as narrated above, our Lord opened, so this thief is more detestable, who commits such sacrilege by perverting the Scriptures or the works of Christ, than the Gentile whom he judges because, failing to see the door, he goes about an idol that is deaf and dumb in place of the door. “Therefore this man came in order to steal.”

But when such a thief has entered, the sheep are necessarily endangered in either case. If they refuse to consent to the theft of truth or to partake of corrupted pasture, the angry thief immediately slaughters them. Of such persons it was said: “Behold, I send to you prophets, wise men, and scribes; and some of them you will kill and crucify, and some you will scourge in your synagogues and persecute from city to city” (Matt. 23) [Col. 0611C].

They had not yet done this openly, except that they had cast out the oft-mentioned man who had been blind and received sight because he would not follow their blasphemies; but later they acted in public madness, beginning their bloody robbery with the chief shepherd himself who is speaking these words. But if the sheep consent to the theft, follow the thieves, and hear the voice of strangers, they do not indeed slaughter their bodies, but destroy their souls. For by that very consent their souls have already been destroyed; and though their bodies live, those souls have already perished—though their bodies live, those souls have already perished [Col. 0611D].

Therefore it was most rightly said: “The thief comes only to steal, slaughter, and destroy”: to steal, namely, and adulterate or corrupt the true sense of the Scriptures; to slaughter the bodies of those who do not consent to him; and to destroy the souls of those who do consent. Opposed to his cruelty is what follows:

> “I came that they may have life, and may have it more abundantly.”

It might have been said: “I came as the life of human beings, that they may live more abundantly”—which indeed would have been more than what was said, “I came that they may have life.” For every shepherd of sheep who enters through the door comes for this purpose, is called or admitted for this purpose: that the sheep may have life. Yet he is not life itself, but only a participant in life, a herald or minister of life [Col. 0612A].

This, I say, could have been said; but against thieves and robbers, who come to bring death, the fitting and exactly timely contrast is: “I came that they may have life.” But how great is the force of the addition, “and may have it more abundantly”? Surely as great as the difference between his promise and his advent: that is what is now called “more abundantly,” beyond the moderate measure of the former pasture.

For that the Lord’s sheep formerly possessed much less is testified by the Apostle, who, after enumerating the great and foremost rams, finally says of them: “All these died according to faith, not having received the promises, but seeing and greeting them from afar, and confessing that they were strangers and pilgrims upon the earth” (Heb. 11) [Col. 0612B].

This is certain, and no one may doubt it: all the flocks that had hitherto preceded his advent kept watch outside paradise and, with long bleating, desired the pasture of the divine vision, until he came, as said above, and with his blood extinguished the *romphaea*, that is, the flaming sword, he who had been promised to them (Gen. 3). Well, therefore, after saying, “I came that they may have life,” he immediately added, “and may have it more abundantly,” because he gave them to possess in reality the life which they had possessed in hope.

Hence, above, when he said, “If anyone enters through me, he shall be saved,” he immediately added: “and shall go in and go out, and find pasture” [Col. 0612C]. For after his advent worthy sheep, having entered the fold of the present Church through faith, are fed more abundantly than those before them by the knowledge of God; and, after departing through bodily death, they enjoy the vision of the chief shepherd.

Having said these things in judgment or condemnation of those who are thieves and robbers, he now offers himself as an example in this manner to all his vicars charged with his care, who desire to be worthy shepherds:

> “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd gives his life for the sheep.”

While directing his discourse against those who do not enter through the door but climb up another way [the text reads *descendunt*; probably *ascendunt*], and who therefore “are thieves and robbers,” he said once and again, “I am the door.” Now, attending to the statement, “He who enters through the door is shepherd of the sheep,” he adapts his speech further to the purpose or instruction of the one to whom he speaks, saying: “I am the good shepherd.” And he adds the pattern of that goodness which every shepherd ought to imitate: “The good shepherd gives his life for the sheep” [Col. 0612D].

Clearly, this good shepherd could have taken another pattern of this goodness. For, though our Lord was in the form of God, for us—his people and the sheep of his pasture—“he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and being found in appearance as a man” (Phil. 2). And according to the parable of the hundred sheep and the one lost sheep, though he had ninety-nine sheep, that is, the whole multitude of blessed angels, he left them and came to seek the one that had strayed (Luke 15) [Col. 0613A].

In this way, I say, the good shepherd might here have set forth the pattern of his goodness; but this example is imitable by no one. For when people become shepherds of human beings, they cannot descend beneath themselves; on the contrary, they are raised so far above themselves that they are made like the principalities and powers of heaven. Therefore, when he intends to form human beings for imitation of himself, he omits what they cannot imitate at all and proposes only what can be imitated:

> “The good shepherd gives his life for the sheep.”

For this is imitable by shepherds through the spirit of charity; indeed, it is sweet to imitate. Hence one most steadfast man, defending his sheep from thieves and robbers, said: “But I will most gladly spend and be spent myself for your souls, although loving you more, I am loved less” (2 Cor. 12) [Col. 0613B].

How many, do you suppose, have spent themselves for their sheep? Sheepfolds have been sprinkled with the blood of shepherds; fields have been drenched with the slaughter of shepherds; pastures have been made bloody by shepherds’ wounds; earth has been consecrated by shepherds’ bodies; heaven has been enriched by the souls which shepherds laid down for their sheep. It is therefore clear that this pattern of his humility which the good shepherd proposed is imitable by shepherds.

And yet no one is a good shepherd except this one, because no one is good except the one God. For when someone said to him in one place, “Good Master, what must I do to inherit eternal life?” he answered, “Why do you call me good?” (Luke 18) [Col. 0613C]. For this is a conventional form of greeting, customary to the ambition of scribes and Pharisees. Unless you confess me to be God, it follows that you should not call me good.

Accordingly, how are shepherd and teacher, though different in expression, identical in sense? For he is called shepherd of sheep by resemblance; he is teacher of human beings in reality. As the good teacher is such only because he is God, so the good shepherd is so for no other reason than that he is God: good shepherd, I say, good not by an accidental gift but essentially.

Therefore the other shepherds may indeed be called worthy or competent; but he alone is the good shepherd, who alone so laid down his life for the sheep that he transformed his body and blood into our sacrament, and satisfied with the nourishment of his flesh the sheep whom he had redeemed. But what of one who refuses to imitate this example of the good shepherd? By what name—or rather, by what designation—will he be judged? He says:

> [Col. 0613D] “The hireling, and he who is not a shepherd, whose own the sheep are not, sees the wolf coming and leaves the sheep and flees; and the wolf snatches and scatters the sheep.”

Four things are set forth here: namely, the good shepherd who says, “I am the good shepherd”; the one who imitates the pattern of the good shepherd; the hireling; and the wolf. Likewise, above four things had been set forth: the door, the doorkeeper, the shepherd, and the thief who climbs up another way. There, there was one evil, namely the thief; here there are two evils, namely the hireling and the wolf. Yet the wolf, together with the hireling, is more secretly harmful to the fold. For “the thief, while he slaughters and destroys,” is harmful amid an open storm against bodies and souls [Col. 0614A].

Thus the hireling does not himself slaughter and destroy, but by his flight makes room for the wolf—the devil—who destroys, snatches, and scatters. He is not indeed himself a thief or robber, but neither is he to be called a shepherd. For he says: “The hireling, and he who is not a shepherd.” How, then, or by what way did he enter? For above nothing intermediate was set between the door and climbing up another way. “He who entered through the door,” he says, “is shepherd of the sheep”; “he who climbs up another way is a thief and robber.” By what way, then, did the hireling enter, who is not a shepherd and yet does not in turn slaughter or destroy, as the thief does?

For he does not rage or persecute openly, like Arius or any other heresiarch, to kill the bodies of those whose souls he cannot stain by consent to his perversity [Col. 0614B]. It remains, surely, that, if he is not a thief, he is nevertheless an accomplice of thieves. For it was said of such people through the prophet: “Your princes are companions of thieves; all love gifts, they pursue recompense” (Isa. 1). But he is an accomplice of thieves in mind; in body he appeared to enter with the shepherds through the door. He is therefore divided.

Accordingly, it was said elsewhere of such a person: “The master of that servant shall come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour which he does not know, and shall divide him and assign his portion with the hypocrites” (Matt. 24 [the text reads 34]). “He shall divide him,” he says—that is, he shall expose him as divided and double-minded; “he shall divide him,” that is, he shall take away from him the gift of pastoral grace and hand him over to punishments.

Therefore, after showing shepherds the path which they ought to follow in disregard of death and setting before them the pattern after which they should be formed, he rightly describes by contrast the hireling [Col. 0614C]. Although he does not appear to be a thief and robber, but rather to have entered through the door, because he professes the Catholic faith and preaches no gospel other than that preached by true shepherds, he is nevertheless, in accordance with the prophetic sentence already cited. For when the prophet had said, “Your princes are companions of thieves,” he immediately proved this very point by explanation: “All,” he says, “love gifts; they pursue recompenses” (Isa. 1). He, then, is indeed an accomplice of thieves. For because he loves gifts and pursues temporal reward, he is a hireling.

His description must be carefully considered. “The hireling,” he says, “and he who is not a shepherd.” By adding “and he who is not a shepherd,” he impressed the matter keenly upon the hearer’s mind [Col. 0614D], so as to uproot from the heart the common opinion by which he is thought or said to be a shepherd. For truly he is not a shepherd; a shepherd is so called because he feeds the flock. But that man feeds not the flock but himself. Hence the prophet says: “Woe to the shepherds of Israel who fed themselves” (Ezek. 34), etc.

Thus he is called a shepherd, but “he is not a shepherd, whose own the sheep are not.” This too was said with great weight: “The sheep are not his own,” because grace, their mother, did not give them birth in his breast, as in the one whose voice is: “My little children, for whom I am again in labour until Christ be formed in you” (Gal. 4). The spirit of the good shepherd does not possess his soul; and therefore it is no wonder that neither does he gather the lambs in his arm and carry them in his bosom, nor does he bear those with young. But what does he do?

> [Col. 0615A] “He sees the wolf coming, and leaves the sheep and flees.”

The hireling is not accused of stealing, slaughtering, or destroying because he does not lead the sheep into pastures other than those approved by great and proven shepherds, nor destroy them with the poisonous pasture of false doctrine. Thus he cannot quite properly be called a thief, and therefore has no occasion to slaughter. For meanwhile the sheep do not flee from him, since they have no legitimate reason not to hear his voice, necessarily to avoid his communion, or to withhold from him their milk for food and their wool for clothing.

But of what is he accused? “He sees,” it says, “the wolf coming”: that is, the devil lying in wait for souls and drawing them through various crimes toward eternal death. “He sees,” it says, “and flees”: that is, he conceals himself in silence. “He flees”: that is, he withholds the word of exhortation, lest, if he resists the wolf, he lose the temporal advantage that he loves [Col. 0615B].

For sheep often love their own destruction. They love it, I say; they delight in their own ruin, and are wrongly soothed in the present by the pleasantness of their own dangers. Deceived by the sweetness of vices, they do not reflect how great a destruction follows them. And unless they are permitted to perish, such sheep refuse both to come to the shepherd’s hand and to submit again to the same shearer; moreover, in tumult they dare, as far as they can, to strike the shepherd himself with horns and flanks.

The hireling therefore flees silently, lest by fighting for the sheep he suffer the loss of temporal gain.

> “And the wolf snatches and scatters the sheep. But the hireling flees because he is a hireling, and he has no concern for the sheep.”

The sole reason for his flight, therefore, is that he is a hireling: he longs for transient wages, and while he is satisfied with them, the wolf snatches and scatters the sheep. Nor does he flee only when the wolf comes; he also flees when, according to Ezekiel, rams and he-goats clash, striking with their flanks and shoulders and butting all the weak cattle with their horns until they are scattered abroad (Ezek. 34) [Col. 0615C]. The same hireling flees by concealing himself, not judging between sheep and sheep; or rather, more wickedly, he takes for himself what is fat and throws away what is weak—namely, justifying the impious for gifts and taking away the justice of the righteous from him.

To be sure, when he says elsewhere, “If they persecute you in one city, flee to another” (Matt. 10), then the shepherd flees without blame: when, in open persecution by the heretical thief or by the wolf, the devil exercising his malice through Gentile authority, the shepherd himself is sought in order that his sheep may be deprived of protection. We read that the Apostle Paul did this not merely without blame but even praiseworthily: when, at Damascus, the governor of the people under King Aretas was guarding the city to seize him, he was lowered by the brothers through the wall in a basket and thus escaped his hands (2 Cor. 11) [Col. 0615D].

For he did not flee in order to abandon the sheep, but in order to preserve himself for the safety of the sheep. But all who flee without such a cause, who abandon the sheep, are rightly excluded by this shepherd and bishop of our souls from the number of shepherds [Col. 0616A]. Having driven them out, he says again:

> “I am the good shepherd.”

And it should be noted that above he said twice, “I am the door,” and now likewise twice, “I am the good shepherd.” He is the door and he is the shepherd; he is the one door and one shepherd of both the earlier and the later fold. Again, I say, he says, “I am the good shepherd,” and immediately adds the affection of that goodness, saying:

> “And I know my own, and my own know me.”

That this reason and the former reason which he gave above—“the good shepherd gives his life for the sheep”—are one and the same is evident from his immediately adding: “As the Father knows me and I know the Father, and I lay down my life for my sheep” [Col. 0616B].

Having fulfilled in himself the two commandments of charity, without which no one ever was or can be a suitable shepherd—for no one will ever be a true or worthy disciple of this good shepherd unless, as the Apostle says, he sincerely loves Christ’s flock (Phil. 4)—having fulfilled, I say, the two commandments of charity, he shows his goodness tested in one praiseworthy proof: “And I lay down my life for my sheep.”

The first and greatest commandment is love of God, which is understood in his saying, “As the Father knows me and I know the Father.” The second, however, is like it: “You shall love your neighbour as yourself” (Matt. 22). This likewise must be understood in his saying, “And I know my own” [Col. 0616C]. “I know” means, that is, “I love.” Indeed, he expresses his charity more magnificently by saying “I know” than if he had said “I love.” For this word, together with the meaning of love, conveys an affection of compassion. Thus Solomon says: “The wise man knows the souls of his beasts, but the inward parts of the wicked are cruel” (Prov. 12).

Therefore, as in the Psalm, “For he knew our frame” (Ps. 102 [103]), so also now, when he says, “And I know my own,” he indicates together an affection of love and active mercy. “And I know,” he says, “my own, and my own know me.” A sweet saying, but a terrible judgment.

For this answers what his deniers said above: “We know that God spoke to Moses, but we do not know where this man is from.” Therefore, in distinction from them, because they are not his own, because they denied him, according also to what Daniel says, “And the people who shall deny him shall not be his” (Dan. 9), in distinction from them, I say, he declares: “I know my own, and my own know me” [Col. 0616D]. By equal reciprocity he denies his deniers, as though openly saying: “I know my own, and not you strangers; my own know me, but you strangers will not know me.”

Again, they also said: “This man is not from God.” This contradicts what he says: “As the Father knows me and I know the Father.” “The Father knows me” means, “The Father loves me”; “I know” means, “I love the Father.” Thus, as stated above, the good shepherd manifests his goodness in the two commandments of charity: love of God the Father and love of neighbours, that is, of the sheep of whom he now speaks. By assuming flesh and through the greatness of his benefit, he became their neighbour.

And from these words as well as from the rest of his sayings, this is more deeply commended: the whole care of the Lord’s sheep is the work of twofold love. Whoever does not possess it is not a shepherd but a hireling [Col. 0617A].

It follows:

“And I have other sheep, which are not of this fold; them also I must bring, and they will hear my voice, and there will be one fold and one shepherd.” See how greatly the foolish sheep harmed the good shepherd: having entered into counsel with malicious foxes, that is, evil spirits, they had already conspired that, if any sheep recognized him as its shepherd, it should immediately be struck by the shoulders and sides of the others and driven outside the fold. Would this conspiracy annul the shepherd’s grace toward it, or diminish his name or power? Far from it! “For I have,” he says, “other sheep, which are not of this fold,” because they are not descended from the flesh of the patriarchs and prophets, who were the fathers of this fold—the great ram, and certain shepherds also, such as [Col. 0617C] David, Moses, and Aaron. They are not, I say, of this fold, and “I must bring other sheep.” Why? Because these sheep, inflamed against one another by their aforesaid conspiracy, have wasted away with a dreadful pestilence and corrupted themselves. Therefore, when these have been rejected, the number of sheep foreordained before the ages must be made up from other sheep. “I,” he says, “must bring them.”

Did the shepherd himself, who speaks these things, come in person to us foreign-born sheep? Was he not seized in the midst of this fold by thieves and robbers, laid down his life, and then, ascending into heaven—never seen by us—sent only his vicars to us? Certainly; yet in this way we have no less from him than that great flock which the same shepherd, the same God, led out of Egypt [Col. 0617D] (Exod. III). For did not God bring those sheep through men—through Moses and Aaron, I mean, to whom he had appeared? (Exod. IV.) Surely, his visible presence was no more available in bringing them than us, nor less available to us than to them. One of their shepherds then heard God in the bush (Exod. III); our shepherds saw him on the wood of the cross, of whom one equally learned and faithful man says: “Sins are cleansed by blood in sorrow.” Conversely, the bush brings him forth amid dense torments.

He gave those two signs, saying: “If they do not believe the word of the first sign, they will believe even the word of the following sign.” But likewise he gave our shepherds two signs, saying: “If they have not seen the glory [Col. 0618A] of the first sign, they will at least see the power of the following sign.” For if we have not seen the rod turned into a serpent and, after it had devoured the serpents of the Egyptian magicians, turned back into what it had been, a rod (Exod. VII)—that is, if we have not seen Christ the King himself, the royal rod of the Father’s divinity, come into that death which entered this world through the serpent, and, after consuming our sins, rise again to reign in true and eternal life (Luke XXIV)—at least we see the hand drawn from the bosom become wholly leprous: that is, we see that the entire old fold has wasted away from the pestilence of unbelief; that the Synagogue has fallen from the grace of God; indeed, as he himself foretold, “They shall fall by the edge of the sword and be led captive into all nations,” and have long borne their leprosy around the whole world for all to behold [Col. 0618B], while the Prophet laments and says: “How long will you turn away your hand and your right hand from the midst of your bosom, unto the end?” (Ps. LXXIII.) For near the end of the age it shall again be put into the former bosom of grace and cleansed.

Therefore, when through his envoys, in whom he himself undoubtedly speaks, he called us, his other sheep, he brought us in person no less than the sheep of the former fold. Accordingly he says: “And them also I must bring.” But where must he bring them? Not into your synagogue, O foul goats, who both in soul will enter into the lower parts of the earth and in body will be delivered into the hands of the sword, and become portions for foxes; but into the faith of the patriarchs and prophets, with whom you dare to bleat or sing, saying: “But we are his people [Col. 0618C] and the sheep of his pasture” (Pss. LXXVIII, XCIV), though you are fat bulls and wanton calves, born or reared amid the leaping grounds of the Hittites and Amorites. Into their faith, I say, I must bring my other sheep, after rejecting you; “and they will hear my voice,” which you, as I said above, “do not hear because you are not of God.”

“And there will be,” he says, “one fold and one shepherd.” He did not say, “There will be one shepherd and one fold.” For there is already one shepherd; but there will be one fold, which has not yet come to be, and the one shepherd will remain—the one who is now and always is. “There will be, I say, one fold, with no distinction maintained: foreign and native sheep—that is, Jews and Greeks—and he will be the one shepherd of all, of whom it was said through the prophet: “And I will raise up over them one shepherd, who shall feed them, my servant David; he shall feed them, and he shall be their shepherd. But I, the Lord, shall be their God, and my servant David shall be prince in their midst” [Col. 0618D] (Ezek. XXXIV).”

Having said these things, he still persists in commending charity, by which he also laid down his life for his sheep, saying:

“Therefore the Father loves me, because I lay down my life and take it again.” As if he said: This work of great love—to be a good shepherd and to give one’s life for the sheep—the Father loves; and from whatever shepherd he receives this work, he counts that shepherd worthy of his love. For he could have said: “Therefore the Father loves me, because, as he taught me, I speak these things, and I do nothing of myself”; or [Col. 0619A], “because through me he made all things in the beginning, and without me nothing was made.” But here he intends to establish or instruct the lawful shepherd, and to make known that nothing is dearer to God than the profit of souls. He therefore says aptly, in accordance with the subject: “Therefore the Father loves me, because I lay down my life”—understand, for my sheep—so that shepherds of souls may know how great a merit it is to die for their salvation.

But let not the thief rejoice, let not the robber be glad, let not the wolf exult because the good shepherd lays down his life, because the defender and Lord of the sheep is killed, because this bearer of the pregnant and nourisher of the lambs can die. No, I say, let not these little offspring of goats rejoice—those whom envy kills, dying through envy and envying even in death—who had already begun [Col. 0619B] to fear that he would go forth among the nations, teach the nations, and thus bring in the other sheep. For he did not merely say, “I lay down my life”; he immediately added, “and I take it again.” Nor, content with having said this once, does he cease to strengthen himself against his enemies, but says:

“No one will take it from me, but I will lay it down of myself. I have power to lay down my life and power to take it again.” All the sheep have long known this, rightly judging the strength of their shepherd. They know, I say, that thieves and robbers would have sent men with lanterns, torches, and weapons in vain to seize him, unless he himself had willed to lay down his life (Luke XXII). For just as they once went backward and fell when he said, “I am” [Col. 0619C] (John XVIII), so this could have occurred continually, or indeed their everlasting destruction could have been completed by a single fall.

Therefore no one took his life as life is lawfully taken from each of us, whom the first parent deprived of immortality in himself. “But I,” he says, “of myself”—that is, by dying a voluntary death—“lay it down in the Father’s hand,” saying: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke XXIII), having previously stipulated this condition: that if I pay this talent—that is, my life—for the sanctification of the ancient transgression, I shall receive back both it and all the souls of my sheep, with the Father’s assent. Thus, because of an innocence owing nothing to death, I have power [Col. 0619D] to lay down or not to lay down my life; and if I lay it down, then, by the justice of the condition interposed, I have power to take it again: namely, to rise again and cause all to rise again with me [Col. 0620A].

Perhaps you say: Why, then, do you lay down your life for the sheep when you have power not to lay it down? To this he replies: “I have received this commandment from my Father.” What is this commandment but charity? “For,” he says, “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another.” Therefore this commandment is charity, by which, as stated above, the sheep are known—that is, loved—and the Father is known—that is, loved. “But,” he says, “here I have received this commandment from my Father.” Accordingly, this good shepherd is not good merely accidentally, as are all others who are called good shepherds; rather, he received from his Father—that is, from that nature by which God is his Father—the capacity to be good, and his charity is naturally so great that he lays down his life for his sheep. It follows:

[Col. 0620B] “A division again arose among the Jews because of these words.” “Again,” says the Evangelist, “a division arose because of these words.” For one had already arisen because of the work by which he opened the eyes of the man blind from birth on the Sabbath (John IX). “But some [many among them] said: ‘He has a demon and is mad; why do you listen to him?’” O evil foolishness, to say that the Son of God has a demon and lacks common sense. Above they had said, “You have a demon” (John VIII); now, in unrestrained madness, having said, “He has a demon,” they added, “and he is mad; why do you listen to him?” Was this what the householder said concerning those evil husbandmen, rightly to be destroyed wickedly: “They will reverence my son”? (Matt. XXI.) Which of the servants [Col. 0620C] whom he had previously sent did they dishonor so wickedly and assail with such insults? How did the unhappy earth sustain such foul dogs? How was the accursed air not poisoned by the venomous tongues of such vipers? “He has a demon,” they say, “and is mad; why do you listen to him?”

“But others said: ‘These are not the words of one who has a demon; can a demon open the eyes of the blind?’” Guided by the same reasoning, those who disagreed had said above: “Can a sinful man do these signs?” (John IX.) For being a sinner, or not being from God, is mutually opposed and incompatible with doing these signs. Still more incompatible are having a demon or being mad, and uttering words of this kind together with the performance of such signs [Col. 0620D]. Certainly, if they were not blind, they could know that these are words not of madness but of true wisdom, and that opening the eyes of the blind requires not demonic madness but divine power.

## BOOK TEN

[Col. 0619]

[Col. 0619D] When the Prophet had said in the Psalm, “How greatly magnified are your works, O Lord; exceedingly deep have your thoughts become,” he immediately added: “A senseless man will not know, and a fool will not understand [Col. 0620D] these things” (Ps. XCI). Who is more senseless, or more foolish, than the Jewish people, who do not recognize even the Lord’s magnificent works? For example, when they say above, “This man is not from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath,” and do not understand his words; when they say, “He has a demon and is mad; why do you listen to him?” Yet your works, O Lord, ought to have been magnified in their eyes, and your thoughts revealed in their ears, so that we might not see what was shown to them, nor understand what was said to them [Col. 0621A]; in order that by the same fire the eyes of the humble might be enlightened and the pride of the others blinded by its smoke.

Thus, down to this point, the teaching of truth had proceeded safely before its enemies; and afterward, increasingly assailed by questions yet always increasing, it advances in a straight course through words and deeds before their ears and eyes, as the Evangelist continues the narrative in this manner.

“Now the Dedication took place at Jerusalem, and it was winter.” Encaenia was the feast of the dedication [Col. 0621B] of the Temple, and the name derives from the Greek *kainon* (καινόν), which in Latin means “new.” Whenever anything new has been dedicated, it is called *encaenia*. If someone puts on a new tunic, he too may properly be said to “celebrate encaenia.” Thus the Encaenia—that is, the solemn celebration of the Temple’s dedication—was being observed when the Lord spoke the following words in answer to the Jews’ questions: “And it was winter,” he says.

In the literal sense, this indicates the season of the year in which this feast of dedication was observed, from the time of the Maccabees, who, after the nations had defiled the altar, “built a new altar according to the former one, and dedicated it on the twenty-fifth day of the month Casleu” (1 Macc. IV). Judas and his brothers and the whole assembly of Israel decreed that the day of the altar’s dedication should be observed in its seasons, year by year, for eight days, beginning on the twenty-fifth of Casleu [Col. 0621C]. The month Casleu is the same month that the Romans call December; it is the tenth month from March, with which the Romans of old began the year. But from April—which, among the Hebrews according to the Law, is the beginning of months and the first month of the year—it is the ninth. Thus, literally, as has been said, the nature of the season is indicated; but mystically, which is more relevant to the matter, the cold impiety of the Jews is signified, because the devil, like an icy north wind, had blown upon their minds turned away from the divine fire.

“And Jesus was walking in the Temple, in Solomon’s porch.” This porch of Solomon was the very one of which it is written in the Book of Kings: “On that day King Solomon consecrated [Col. 0621D] the middle of the court which was before the house of the Lord, and there he offered holocaust and sacrifice and the fat of peace-offerings” (3 Kings VIII). Therefore, when our Lord walked in such a porch, he was surely walking in the Temple, because that porch had been consecrated by Solomon just as the Temple had.

“Therefore the Jews surrounded him and said: ‘How long do you take away our life? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly.’” Very watchful guardians of their souls, and anxious for their own salvation, they were greatly troubled whenever, on assembling against the Lord, divisions arose among them and their souls were endangered by dissensions—as most recently, when some said, “He has a demon and is mad; why do you listen to him?” while others said [Col. 0622A], “These are not the words of one who has a demon,” and, “Can a demon open the eyes of the blind?” In such disagreements they said that the souls of those were perishing who, by disagreeing with their own purpose, were drawing nearer to salvation. And indeed, because of the division which arose once and again among us concerning the man born blind who was enlightened, their ineffectual assembly was dissolved.

But now, coming to the feast of dedication, he was walking, as has been said, in the Temple, that is, in Solomon’s porch; and they seemed to have found an opportunity to hunt for some accusation against him. “Therefore they surrounded him, like many calves, and fat bulls besieged him” (Ps. XXI). And they said: “How long do you take away our life? If you are the Christ [Col. 0622B], tell us plainly.” O lost souls! If he openly tells you that he himself is Christ, will that opinion of him then cease to be, which you resent and call your destruction when you say, “How long do you take away our life?” What do you desire to hear from his mouth except something by which you may find an unavoidable accusation against him before the authority of the Roman Empire? For since Christ ought to be King of the world—although this would do no harm to earthly kingdoms—you would nevertheless be forceful accusers, able even to pressure the judge, saying: “If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend. Everyone who makes himself king opposes Caesar” (John XIX).

Does he, then, take away your life now, but not take it away when you have carried this out? Far be this blessedness from you—that he should take away your life and possess you! Rather, since this is what you wish, may he grant us [you] that, as the Prophet foretold with groaning: “May your iniquities take you away and possess you apart from him” (Isa. XVI). There are other souls that he will take when you hand him, bound, over to Pilate on the charge of royal title (Matt. XXVIII). For with his hands bound, he who is stronger will bind the armed strong man; with hands and feet nailed, he will conquer his court and take away all blessed souls, for he will plunder his goods. But you shall by no means be taken by that strong one; rather all his wickednesses will possess you, and your last state will be worse than the first [Col. 0622C] (Luke XI).

Now we shall hear how he broke your circle, by which you surrounded him both with intent to harm him and with the crowd pressing around you, declaring himself not only King but also God, consubstantial with the Father:

“I speak to you, and you do not believe. The works which I do in the name of my Father, they bear witness of me. But you do not believe, because you are not of my sheep.” Above, this same one who is now surrounded by the Jews said: “Christ [is] the light of the world; and in your law it is written that the testimony of two men is true” (Deut. XIX). He immediately added: “I am one who bears witness of myself, and the Father who sent me bears witness of me” (John VIII). Now, at the point of answering this present question, he suitably presents the same testimonies—in order to confirm the truth of his answer—which ought to be heard not only in Solomon’s porch or Temple but throughout the world: “I speak [Col. 0623A] to you,” he says, “and the works which I do in the name of my Father, they bear witness of me.” He rebukes them for rejecting both testimonies, contrary to their law, in which it is written: “The testimony of two men is true.” He rebukes them, I say, for despising each testimony separately by adding: “and you do not believe.” For when he said, “I speak to you,” he immediately added, “and you do not believe”; and when he had continued, “The works which I do in the name of my Father, they bear witness of me,” he at once added: “But you do not believe, because you are not of my sheep.”

As if he said: You are no longer to be taught that I am Christ, but to be convicted of sin, because you did not long ago believe clear testimonies. According to the Law’s decree, this is the manner of rebuke and this the sentence of judgment: that I now disown you, as indeed I do when I say, “Because you are not of my sheep.” In vain, therefore, did these captors gape after him, surrounding him and saying: “If you are the Christ, tell us plainly.” For he does not urge them to investigate his relation to Caesar’s rule, nor does he reproach them because they have not already exalted him as king; rather, “You are not,” he says, “of my sheep,” maintaining the metaphor according to which he had above said: “I am the good shepherd,” and so forth.

But why, when he could have said according to the royal title about which he was questioned, “You are not of my citizens,” did he prefer to say according to the title of shepherd, “You are not of my sheep?” [Col. 0623C] Because what he said—“I lay down my life for my sheep”—was indeed enough for the goodness of a shepherd, but too little for his majesty. Accordingly, he adds what remains concerning the majesty or power of his divinity in this manner:

“My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me. And I give them eternal life, and they shall never perish, and no one shall snatch them from my hand. What my Father has given me is greater than all, and no one can snatch them from my Father’s hand. I and the Father are one.” Here more was said than had been asked: for though they inquired only about royal power, an answer was also given concerning the majesty of his divinity. Yet in all this not one word was uttered on which Caesar’s officers or friends could pass judgment. These words do not threaten an assault upon the Roman Empire, but contain the mystery of the kingdom of God; and before Gentile judges they are chiefly words of a sealed book. If, as the Prophet says, “you give it to one who does not know letters and say, ‘Read,’ he will answer, ‘I do not know letters’” [Col. 0623D] (Isa. XXIX).

Thus it happened also to Paul: when he began to open his mouth, Gallio said to the Jews: “If indeed it were some injustice or wicked crime, O Jews, I should rightly bear with you. But if the questions concern a word and names of your law, see to it yourselves. I do not wish to be judge of these matters” (Acts XVIII). Therefore now also the King of heaven, who through the same Apostle commands, “Giving no offense to anyone” (2 Cor. VI), did not answer concerning his kingdom in such a way as to display power over an earthly empire. Rather, using words and names of Sacred Scripture, concerning which Roman judges would not care to adjudicate, he mocked the Jews’ impiety as it gaped after an accusation against him.

“My sheep,” he says, “hear my voice.” When would the proud forces of Roman soldiers fear this, when the man accused professed himself not a destroyer of cities but a shepherd? Indeed, they could more easily laugh than fear at such a charge, so that they might say, while bending the knee in mockery: “Hail, King of the Jews” (Matt. XXVII). Certainly, what he now says, “And I know them, and they follow me,” [Col. 0624B] he had also said above: “I know my own, and my own know me.” The eternal life of which he now says, “And I give them eternal life,” is that pasture of which he had said above: “Through me, if anyone enters, he shall be saved, and shall go in and go out and find pasture.” Yet the manner of speaking differs: “And I give them eternal life”—which assuredly no one but God can say or do.

The sequence of this saying must be carefully noted: “They hear,” he says, “my voice; and I know them; they follow me; and I give them eternal life; and they shall never perish.” The opposites of these things must likewise be understood concerning those to whom he said, “Because you are not of my sheep”: namely, that he does not know them, that they are deprived of eternal life, and that they have perished eternally. For to distinguish them from such goats he said: “My sheep hear my voice,” and so forth.

What he added—“And no one shall snatch them from my hand”—has without doubt long since been demonstrated to the whole world by many arguments. What have thieves and robbers left untried? What have wolves, or all the wild beasts of the forests, not done in order to snatch away the sheep? Yet they have not been able to snatch even one sheep at all from this shepherd’s hand. Rightly, therefore, this most mighty shepherd was called David through the prophet, in whom God speaks these words, as has been said above: “And I will raise up over them one shepherd, who shall feed them, my servant David; he shall feed them, and he shall be their shepherd. I, the Lord, shall be their God, and my servant David shall be prince in their midst” [Col. 0624D] (Ezek. XXXIV).

For David, in tending the flock, bore the sign of this good shepherd: “Your servant,” he says, “was feeding his father’s flock; and a lion or a bear would come and take a ram from the midst of the flock. I followed them, struck them, and rescued it from their mouth. And they rose up against me, and I seized their jaws and throttled and killed them” (1 Kings XVII), and so forth. That flock is the people of God, who say in the Psalm: “But we are his people and the sheep of his pasture” (Ps. XCIV); the lion or bear is the devil. David himself, both in strength and in name—for his name is interpreted “strong of hand”—prefigured Christ the good shepherd, who loses none at all of his sheep.

“And no one,” he says, “shall snatch them from my hand.” For he throttled the devil and delivered us, his sheep, from his mouth; and he punished with eternal condemnation every persecutor—such as Annas and Caiaphas, and the other scribes and Pharisees, who had already conspired that no sheep should follow this shepherd—convicting them, deceived in their futile effort, of theft and robbery [Col. 0625A]. But whence came such strength into his hands? He says: “What my Father gave me is greater than all.” That which my Father gave me—namely, that by which he is my Father, that is, what I am not according to the nature of flesh, received from a human being, but according to that nature by which God is my Father—is greater than all, stronger than all, more powerful than all. And if it is greater than all, it is certainly greater and stronger than the devil, the snatcher of souls.

What, then, is that thing greater than all which your Father gave you? “And no one,” he says, “can snatch from my Father’s hand.” Certainly, this is greater than all: that no one can snatch from my Father’s hand. For nothing apart from God is unconquerable. But, he says, “What my Father gave me is greater than all.” What, then, did the Father give his Son except his own omnipotence, so that no one may snatch from the Son’s hand, just as “no one can snatch from the Father’s hand”? [Col. 0625B]

Accordingly, it is immediately and rightly added: “I and the Father are one.” Upon this chiefly rests that which Catholic faith, sailing between Arius and Sabellius as between Scylla and Charybdis, has long been accustomed to proclaim with one voice through its most valiant rowers: neither confusing the persons nor separating the substance. For the person of the Father is one, that of the Son another, and, further, that of the Holy Spirit another; but the divinity is one, the glory equal, the majesty coeternal.

Sabellius—for he is also called Patripassian—confused the persons, saying that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one and the same. Conversely Arius says: “The Father is one thing; the Son another. The Father is uncreated, but the Son is a creature.” Catholic faith detests both follies, firmly holding both the plural word “we are” and the neuter expression of unity, “one”: “one,” he says, not “one person.” Thus the Son of God said: “I and the Father are one.” By saying “one,” he expressed unity of substance; by saying “we are,” [Col. 0625C] he expressed plurality of persons.

Therefore, when the Son says of himself, “No one shall snatch them from my hand,” and of the Father, “No one can snatch from my Father’s hand,” and immediately adds, “I and the Father are one,” he unquestionably intends it to be understood that the divinity of Father and Son is one, their omnipotence one and the same, their substance one, their nature one—what in Greek is called *homoousion* (ὁμοούσιον), and because we confess this, we are rightly called Homoousians. The Arians vainly slandered this term, saying that, according to the Apostle, “profane novelties of words” are to be avoided (1 Tim. VI), and consequently that this name must be avoided because it is not found [Col. 0626A] in the entire canon of Scripture.

For names or words, being signs of things, are certainly subsequent to the things themselves, since they were invented to signify things. The things themselves must first exist, and then their signs. But it is clear that neither before the Gospel nor except through the Gospel did the Son of God become known to the world. Therefore, once he himself, or his divinity coeternal with the Father, had become known through the Gospel—as, for instance, by what he now says, “I and the Father are one”—then, the reality being established, it was certainly permitted, indeed necessary, to introduce a name for the reality against heretics who opposed it. It was permitted, and will always be permitted, to introduce the name when the thing signified is present and recognizable. But now let us hear what the Jews did in response. It follows:

“The Jews took up stones to stone him. Jesus answered them: ‘I have shown you many good works from my Father; for which of these works do you stone me?’” Above, when they similarly wanted to stone him because he said, “Before Abraham was, I am,” he hid himself and went out of the Temple (John VIII), as though weak and unable to bind his enemies in their very attempts. But now he stands visible in the midst of the raging crowd and speaks as a judge or defender, about to investigate the charges of the seditious. What does this mean except that not only in his great and principal actions, but also in his ordinary deeds, “with him,” as Job testifies, “are wisdom and strength” [Col. 0626B] (Job II)?

It belongs to wisdom that he then hid himself and went out of the Temple, and, passing by, opened the eyes of a man blind from birth: thereby signifying, as has already been said in the same place, the counsel of his wisdom, concerning which he later said: “That those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John XIX). But it belongs to strength that he now remains in the midst of those who rage, thus proving what he had said shortly before:

“No one shall take my life from me, but I lay it down of myself.” For behold, they were able to run as far as taking up stones and to reveal in armed hands the hardness of their stony hearts; but, daring nothing further, they plainly show us that he is the one who says to blessed Job: “I surrounded the sea with my bounds, and set bar and doors, and said: ‘Thus far you shall come, and no farther; here you shall break your swelling waves’” [Col. 0626C] (Job XXXVIII).

Thus this prince of strength both set a limit to Jewish rage, lest they stone him for saying, “I and the Father are one,” and opposed the bar of his omnipotence to heretical persecutors of that same consubstantiality, lest they perniciously harm the faith of the Homoousians. “I have shown you many good works from my Father,” he says. O ungrateful people! For which of these works do you stone me? What is not good? What is not divine? What is not a great and manifest proof of power?

“The Jews answered him: ‘We do not stone you for a good work, but for blasphemy.’” Therefore, unjust judges, you at least count one of the two testimonies as valid, concerning which above, when he had said, “And in your law it is written that the testimony of two men is true,” he immediately added: “I am one who bears witness of myself, and the Father who sent me bears witness of me” [Col. 0627A] (John VIII). You have allowed, I say, that one testimony is true. For you said: “We do not stone you for a good work”; but you rejected the other by saying, “But for blasphemy.”

For the things he says here—“I and the Father are one”—and similar things said elsewhere, “The words which I speak to you, I do not speak of myself,” are the testimony of the Son himself; while the good works which he showed you from his Father, as he likewise says, “But the Father who remains in me does the works” (John XIV)—those works, I say, “are the testimony of the Father himself” (ibid.). But if you are human beings—indeed, if you profess yourselves lawful judges or learned in the Law—how have you judged one testimony to be good without the other? How do you attribute a good work to one man together with blasphemy? Can anyone, while blaspheming God, at the same time perform a good work, especially works such as he performs? Certainly we know, since we were born blind but now see through Christ’s grace, that God does not hear sinners, and especially blasphemers. Therefore you are judged out of your own mouth: for, as the magicians likewise testified before Pharaoh, it is not a spirit of blasphemy but the finger of God that shows you these works [Col. 0627B] (Exod. VIII). What, then, is this blasphemy for which you stone him? You said:

“And because you, being a man, make yourself God.” [Col. 0627C] We may now rejoice, not only against Arius, who refused to understand what you understood in these words, “I and the Father are one,” but also against Valentinus or Apelles, who denied that our Lord Jesus Christ was truly human, maintaining that he had not a real body but a phantom one. For it is remarkable that those who call themselves Christians deny Christ’s true humanity, whereas you, Christ’s adversaries, drew the whole force of your argument to prove that he is not God from the fact that he was truly a man, in the true substance of flesh—a fact which you could also ascertain through his very suffering of death.

But, as the matter requires, let us hear from the sanctuary of the human breast a true and rational defense of the one and everlasting divinity. “Jesus answered them: Is it not written in your Law, ‘I said, You are gods’?” (Ps. LXXXI [82]). What argument, he says, do you draw as though from contraries or incompatibles when you say, “You, being a man, make yourself God”—as though God and man were contrary or incompatible and could not coexist in one and the same person? Has not the authoritative Scripture called human beings gods?
