Is it not written in your Law—that is, in the greatest prophet of your Law; in the Law, I say, not ours, for mine is one thing and yours another—is it not written in your Law: “I said, You are gods”? Certainly it is written; and, as the text of the Psalm itself plainly indicates, this was said to human beings. [Col. 0628A] And for the present you must grant this, because it is written in your Law; you must grant, I say, that it was said without blasphemy. Therefore I say: “If he called them gods, to whom the word of God came—and Scripture cannot be broken—do you say of him whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world, ‘You blaspheme,’ because I said, ‘I am the Son of God’?”

Let this strong and unanswerable argument of wisdom and truth, made by comparison with the lesser matter, be carefully considered. For it is the lesser thing that the word of God should have come to human beings; but it is far greater that the one speaking these things existed before the world was made, and was holy before the Father sent him into this world. Yet this Scripture, which called those persons “gods” because of the lesser matter, “cannot be broken,” he says: that is, no one can rightly say that what such Scripture sets forth or asserts ought not to be admitted. How then, because of the greater matter—namely, “because the Father sanctified me and sent me into the world”—do you not allow me to say, “I am the Son of God”? Indeed, because I say this, do you wish to stone me as a blasphemer?

While he says these things, let envy alone be absent and reason freely consents, with the support also of the firm foundation of secular rhetoric: what holds in the lesser case holds in the greater. But who especially are those to whom the word of God came? Or what is this word of God which, by participation in itself, raised human beings to become gods? Certainly these gods are especially those fathers to whom the word of God—that is, the promise concerning the Incarnation of the Son of God—was made. The first of these was our father Abraham, to whom Christ himself was first promised.

Accordingly, beginning with him, the holy evangelist Matthew wove Christ’s genealogy not as that of men, but as though it were a genealogy of gods: for he traced the line of this generation not to Mary, of whom Christ the Lord was born according to the flesh, but to Joseph. For Joseph is one of the three to whom the word of God concerning the Incarnation of his Son was chiefly made. By a threefold advance, indeed, the promise was made to these three leaders: Abraham, David, and Joseph.

The promise made to Abraham testified that Christ would be a man in the true substance of our flesh: “In your seed,” it says, “all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. XXII). To David, however, it was foretold not merely that he would be the seed of Abraham or of David himself, [Col. 0628D] but that he would also be king: “For the Lord,” it says, “has sworn truth to David, and he will not turn away from it: ‘Of the fruit of your womb I will set one upon your throne’” (Ps. CXXXI [132]). Finally, when the angel spoke to Joseph, he testified that the same Lord Jesus Christ would be not merely man and king, but also God, saying: “For he shall save his people from their sins” (Matt. I). For saving human beings from their sins belongs to God alone.

And these three things, gradually displayed to these gods through so prolonged a course of ages, the wonderful grace of the Holy Spirit suddenly inspired into the Gentiles when the firstfruits of the Gentiles—namely, the magi who came from the East—worshiped him, testifying by myrrh that he was a mortal man, by gold that he was king, and by incense that he was God (Matt. II). [Col. 0629A]

Thus among those fathers whom the divine evangelist included in the genealogy of Jesus Christ, Son of God, these three stand out, as has been said: Abraham, David, and Joseph. Conversely, three others—Ahaziah, Joash, and Amaziah—deserved no place or name among this people of gods. For, following the most impious Jezebel (III Kings XVIII), who had killed the prophets through whom this same word of God came, and whose seed had intermingled with that of Joram, they too killed the prophets, bearers of that same word of God, who had been sent to them (ibid.).

For Ahaziah acted wickedly and impiously in the sight of the Lord, like the house of Ahab and his wife, who, as has been said, killed the prophets (II Chron. XXII). Joash also killed Zechariah the prophet, son of the high priest Jehoiada (II Chron. XXIV). Amaziah likewise, when the Lord sent a prophet to him because he had worshiped the gods of the sons of Seir, said: “Be silent, lest I kill you” (II Chron. XXV). Thus these three, because they killed the prophets through whom the word of God came to them, and did not even repent as Manasseh did, were rightly excluded by the holy evangelist from the genealogy of the gods to whom the word of God came.

Therefore the fathers who received in faith, before receiving in the flesh, the Lord, God’s Son, promised to them, are gods—gods, I say, not by nature but by adoption. Among them stood this God by nature in the synagogue (Ps. LXXXI [82]); that is, he was made like them according to the flesh, [Col. 0629C] and in the midst—that is, publicly—he judges or distinguishes gods. For he shows a great difference between himself and them when he says: “If he called them gods, to whom the word of God came, do you say to him whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world, ‘You blaspheme,’ because I said, ‘I am the Son of God’?”

Perhaps you say: How is it established that the Father sanctified you and sent you into this world? To this, I say:

“If I do not do the works of my Father, do not believe me; but if I do them, then, even if you do not wish to believe my words, believe the works, that you may know and believe that the Father is in me and I in the Father.” This is to say: the authority of your own Law indicates that, for a prophet in whom God has spoken, it ought to suffice as testimony concerning himself if the word which he has spoken in the Lord’s name comes to pass. Thus it says: “What a prophet predicts in the name of the Lord, and does not come to pass, the Lord has not spoken; and therefore you shall not fear him” (Deut. XVIII). [Col. 0629D] It follows, then, that if the word he spoke in the Lord’s name comes to pass, he should be feared, because the Lord spoke in him.

Now every word that I have spoken to you has come to pass, so that at times I have even truthfully prophesied to you concerning your own thoughts, saying: “Why do you think evil things in your hearts?” (Matt. IX), and similar things. Therefore this ought to have been sufficient testimony for you, so that you might also believe what I said: that the Father sent me. But I have wished to be more generous in meeting your slowness. Therefore I say: “If I do not [Col. 0630A] do the works of my Father”—that is, works such as no human being can do unless God the Father belongs to him by nature—I grant that you should not believe me. “But if I do them”—indeed, because I do them—“then, even if you do not wish to believe my words, believe the works.” That is: if you refuse to accept the one testimony of faithful words, accept at least the two testimonies together, of words and works; for your Law judges that even human testimony, which is less than God’s testimony, is true on the testimony of two persons (Deut. XVII, XIX).

Therefore, lest you be convicted of sinning against the laws of God and of men, “believe, that you may know.” For unless you believe, you will not understand (Isa. VII). Believe, I say, that you may know and believe; for by knowing you will believe more firmly. What are you to know? What are you to believe? “That the Father is in me and I in the Father.” This is nothing other than what I said above: “I and the Father are one.” For I and he are one in this: “the Father is in me and I in the Father.”

But how is the Father in me and I in the Father? Is it as a smaller vessel is in a larger vessel? Certainly, even though a smaller vessel can be in a larger vessel, the larger is by no means, nor can be, in the smaller. Yet as I am in the Father, so conversely the Father is in me. Therefore whatever is naturally in the Father in this manner is the same thing, and not another thing, naturally in me the Son; and conversely, whatever I the Son am, the Father naturally is the same. This is what I said: “The Father is in me and I in the Father.” For, apart from the fact that he is properly Father and not Son, [Col. 0630C] and I am properly Son and not Father, whatever he is, I also am by nature: namely God and Lord, almighty, boundless, eternal, creator—or uncreated. And whatever belongs to the Father’s nature is wholly in the Son; and conversely, whatever belongs to the Son’s nature is wholly in the Father. Thus indeed, “I and the Father are one.”

“They therefore sought to seize him, and he went out of their hands.” This is the sequence and connection of the words. They had craftily asked whether he himself was Christ the King. But he had answered that he was not only Christ the King, but also Christ God and Lord, saying: “I and the Father are one, and the Father is in me and I in the Father. They therefore sought to seize him.” [Col. 0630D] But what then? He went out of their hands. Is it doubtful that here God and Lord went out of the hands of the Jews? Surely everything that that homicidal people performs in all its ceremonies is futile: “When you spread out your hands,” he says, “I will turn my eyes away from you; and when you multiply prayers, I will not hear; for your hands are full of blood” (Isa. I). Therefore from the hands of the Jews—that is, from all their works—the Son of God, and God the Father who is in him, went out; and Satan, the ruler of their whole synagogue, applauds himself in the blood with which their hands are full.

Likewise Jesus went out of the hands of heretics, especially those who deny or attack the consubstantiality of the Father and Son which is especially commended in this reading: out of the hands, I say, of heretics such as the Arians. For whatever they consecrate, God execrates; and on whomever they lay hands, not the grace of the Holy Spirit but the plague of the most foul leprosy accompanies him.

“And he went again beyond the Jordan, where John had first been baptizing, and remained there.” “Again,” he says, “he went beyond the Jordan,” for this had been said of him once before, much earlier. “After these things,” it says, “Jesus came into the land of Judea, and there he remained with his disciples and baptized. Now John too was baptizing at Aenon near Salim” (John III), and so forth. Jesus therefore went out again and “went beyond the Jordan”; and by coming there both on his first and on his second departure, he declares in his deeds that, leaving the Jews, he would pass over to the one true baptism of the new Church. In it, whoever is baptized confesses God the Son to be coeternal and consubstantial with God the Father.

“And many came to him and said: ‘John indeed performed no sign; but all things whatsoever John said concerning this man were true.’ And many believed in him.” The sequence is this: John performed no sign, but this man performed such great signs that his present deeds proved true whatever John had said concerning him—for example, “He must increase, but I must decrease” (ibid.)—and similar sayings. Thus they rightly and convincingly confirmed their faith by an argument: namely, that two witnesses have greater force than one in every matter. [Col. 0631C] Now in our Lord Jesus there were two testimonies: word and works (I Tim. I). For he was powerful in work and word; hence he said shortly before: “Even if you do not wish to believe my words, believe the works.” But in John there was one testimony only, namely, his word—faithful indeed and worthy of all acceptance, yet without the working of signs. Therefore they rightly acknowledged that, although John was great, the Lord Jesus appeared greater than he by this comparison. It follows:

## Chapter XI

“There was a certain Lazarus, sick, of Bethany, the village of Martha and Mary his sister. And Mary was she who anointed the Lord with ointment and wiped his feet with her hair, whose brother Lazarus was sick.”

Observe, O Jews—or, if you refuse to understand, let the stones of the whole earth observe and see; let them see and understand, stones harder than yourselves, who have already once and again taken up stones to stone him—what works the Son of God performs, the works of his Father. For shortly before he said: “If I do not do the works of my Father, do not believe me; but if I do them, then even if you do not wish to believe my words, believe the works.” What works are worthier of God or more beneficial to human beings than to raise sinful souls from their sins, and to call dead bodies back from their tombs?

Behold, before your eyes and outside the gates of your great city—for “Bethany is not more than fifteen stadia from Jerusalem”—before your eyes, I say, O scribes [Col. 0632A] and Pharisees, he who is the author of both resurrections performed the works of his Father. First, you know that this Mary (John V), whose brother Lazarus is now sick and will shortly die, when she was among the tombs of the dead heard the voice of the Son of God; and because she heard it, behold, she now lives. For after those tears with which she washed the feet of the Son of God, after the loosening of her hair with which she wiped those feet, after the kisses she impressed upon them, and after the pouring forth of the ointment with which she anointed him, she no longer opens her eyes in desire, nor arranges her hair to please lovers, nor loosens her mouth from the restraint of chastity, nor feeds the stench of sensuality with aromatic scents (Luke VII).

And indeed this is one woman; but afterward, enlarged by the fullness of many nations, the Church has likewise been raised. It is now, before your eyes, a true witness of itself by living justly and piously, because it has come out from the tombs of the vices of its idolatry and fornications at the voice of the Son of God. Then, later, in this brother Lazarus, who is now sick, you will have a proof of the future resurrection of bodies at the voice of that same Son of God, as he himself says: “The hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come forth: those who have done good unto the resurrection of life, but those who have done evil unto the resurrection of judgment” (John V).

These, I say, are the works of the Father in the Son of God; these are the illustrious proofs of both resurrections in Mary and her brother Lazarus, which you have close at hand. What then remains to testify to us concerning the omnipotence of the Son of God, since you believe neither his words nor his so great works? What remains, I say, except that, when the dead rise, you who were said to be living may die in your sins?

But now, in the order of the reading, let us contemplate the glory of so great a miracle. “There was,” he says, “a certain sick man named Lazarus, of Bethany, the village of Martha and Mary his sisters.” The holy evangelist aptly describes the person; rather, the author of the resurrection himself aptly chose a known person, in whom the glory of God might be made manifest to more people through a work of so great power. “And he indeed was sick.” But Mary his sister had already revived and recovered from the worst sickness—indeed, from the very death of the soul, in which she had already begun to stink—through the Lord’s grace. “For Mary herself was she who anointed the Lord with ointment and wiped [Col. 0632D] his feet with her hair.” For where she washed his feet with her tears, there she undoubtedly, who had been dead and buried by evil habit, revived and came out from her tomb.

How completely she recovered we learn from other passages of the Gospels, where her love and devotion are commended by great testimonies. For example, when she and her sister Martha had received our Lord into their house, and Martha busied herself with much service, Mary sat at his feet and heard his word, while the Lord bore witness concerning her and said: “Mary has chosen the better part, which shall not be taken away from her” (Luke X).

“Therefore his sisters sent to him, saying: [Col. 0633A] ‘Lord, behold, he whom you love is sick.’” Therefore, he says, because they were believers and had begun, through hearing his word, to be members of his household, they confidently sent to him. Nor did they ask him to come and heal the sick man; they merely said: “Lord, behold, he whom you love is sick.” For to one who loved, it was enough to bring the news.

“But when Jesus heard it, he said to them: ‘This sickness is not unto death, but for the glory of God, that the Son of God may be glorified through it [variant: through him].’” What is this, Son of God, mighty and truthful revealer of God’s glory? What is this that you said: “It is not unto death”? Will not this sick man’s illness lead to death? Or is it because, once dead, he slept for you—that is, because you could raise him as easily as one person customarily wakes another person sleeping? Yet the separation of body and soul is a kind of death; and when this man was about to undergo it, you later said: “Lazarus is dead.” What then does “This sickness is not unto death” mean, except that the final purpose of this sickness is not that Lazarus should die? For then an illness is unto death when nothing beyond death is sought and the end is fixed in death itself. But here, through sickness or death, the glory of God is sought: namely, that through the one who falls sick and dies, the Son of God may be glorified by raising him.

For the Son of God is God; and therefore, after saying, “but for the glory of God,” he immediately added, “that the Son of God may be glorified.” Truly, then, he says, this sickness is not unto death, “but for the glory of God”—for the glory, I say, of God, that is, for attesting [Col. 0633C] the divinity of the Son of God. For the Son of God is reproached and told, for example, that “he has a demon and is mad,” because he said: “The hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God and come forth” (John V). Therefore, in order that the Son of God may be glorified rather than accused of madness, he must give, in this one man now sick, an experimental proof of his power and truth: that is, he must show in one person what and how he will do in the whole human race.

“Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister Mary and Lazarus.” He truly loved them; for unless he loved them, he would not have displayed such great glory in them, nor would the Son of God have so glorified himself through them. For how great is God’s glory in that he deigned to show in Mary the resurrection of souls, and in Lazarus how truly and powerfully, as has already been said, he will bring about the universal resurrection of bodies. He also wished in Martha and Mary to prefigure the condition of the present Church when, according to another evangelist, “he entered into a certain village, and this same Martha received him into her house. While she was busied with much service, Mary sat beside his feet and heard his word” (Luke X), along with the rest which we now pass over to avoid excessive length.

He therefore loved them as vessels of his glory. He loved them so that in them he might first deign to show a proof of his grace and truth. “Therefore, when he heard that he was sick, he remained [Col. 0634A] in the same place two days.” Why did he remain two days in the same place? Certainly so that, through his delay, the sick man might die and be buried. For he did not wish to heal the sick man, nor to raise one already dead but still lying in the house, as he did the ruler of the synagogue’s daughter (Matt. IX), or one just beginning to be carried to the tomb, as he did the widow’s son (Luke VII). For, as has already been said, he was preparing a demonstration of the saying: “All who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God and come forth” (John V).

Therefore, in order to arrive at this point, he delayed until the dead man was laid in earth’s bosom, where dust turns to dust and all flesh is brought back to its origin, so that he might be called forth from there by Christ’s cry—from where we all are to be summoned “at the command, and at the voice of the archangel, and at the trumpet of God,” when he descends from heaven for judgment (I Thess. IV).

“Then after this he says to his disciples: ‘Let us go into Judea again.’” Then, he says—that is, after he had remained two days in the same place, after those things which he had suffered from the Jews above, who wished to stone him—“after these things,” I say, which was great and far removed from fear of death, “he said to his disciples: ‘Let us go into Judea again.’” “The disciples say to him: ‘Rabbi, the Jews were just now seeking to stone you, and are you going there again?’” They feared, of course, that he would be killed, not knowing that he would not die unless he willed it; and therefore they advised him not to go again into Judea.

“Jesus answered: ‘Are there not twelve hours in the day?’” Why, he says, do you advise me, when it is not you who chose me, but I who chose you twelve; and you ought therefore to follow your master’s will as the twelve hours follow the movement of the sun or day? Alternatively: “Are there not twelve hours in the day?” Is it not written, “The sun has known its setting”? (Ps. CIII [104]). Can this sun of which it is written be shaken by anyone’s attack and set before its hour comes? “I am the light of the world” (John VIII); I am that sun which “has known its setting.” Therefore, just as this sun, by which the air is illuminated and day comes to be, proceeds from east to west, and it is by no means in a human being’s power to make it set before its twelfth hour has come, so know that the Jews will not kill me before my hour comes, the hour in which I have decreed to die.

But if you fear that, while I am being sought, you may be endangered, behold, I tell you:

“If anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble, because he sees the light of this world; but if he walks in the night, he stumbles, because the light is not in him.” You know that it is safe to walk by day, but hazardous to walk by night. Yet I am day for you. For “I am the light of the world”; I am that sun which “has known its setting.” Therefore, while I am with you, do not fear that you will suffer any stumbling block or offense; but be confident, “and let us go into Judea again.” For just as, while someone walks in the day, he does not stumble because he sees this world’s light, but when he walks at night, he stumbles because light is not in him, so you will not stumble while I am with you, because the day of salvation shines for you. [Col. 0635A] But when I arrive at that setting which I have known as my own, when I am seized and handed over to be killed, then all of you will stumble; then, walking as it were by night, all of you will suffer scandal on my account (Matt. XXVI).

“He said these things, and after this he says to them: ‘Lazarus our friend sleeps, but I go that I may awaken him from sleep.’” After this, he says—after saying what he had said in order to strengthen their hearts so that they would not fear to go again into Judea—he gives the reason why they should also wish to go: “Lazarus, our friend,” he says, “sleeps.” For they have a twofold reason for going: Lazarus, their friend, is sleeping with a sleep from which no one can awaken him but Christ the Son of God alone; and his awakening is a great occasion for the glory of that same Son of God, their Lord and teacher.

But with this word, “sleeps,” the Master had not stated the distinction or nature of the sleep. “Therefore his disciples said: ‘Lord, if he sleeps, he will be well.’ But Jesus had spoken of his death; they, however, thought that he spoke of the sleep of slumber.” The Lord’s disciples had not yet advanced sufficiently to know how to speak regularly and properly according to the discipline of faith. For where faith in the resurrection is in question, it is better to speak of the laying down of bodies as sleep rather than death, although both separation of the soul from God and separation of the soul from the body are, by a proper and customary equivocation, called death.

But here, as has been said, the subject was the resurrection of the dead; and Lazarus was to be raised as a testimony to the saying uttered by Christ, God’s Son, who is resurrection and life: “All who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God and come forth.” He therefore rightly preferred here to use a word which may properly be equivocal for both the dissolution of bodies and the sleep of slumber, since he will raise both Lazarus now and, on the last day, all who are in the tombs as easily as you sometimes cannot awaken your equal snoring in deep sleep. But they, as has been said, did not yet understand: “Lord,” they say, “if he sleeps, he will be well.” As though they said: There is no danger in the sleeping of a sick man; indeed, there is hope of recovered health. Therefore there is no reason for you to expose yourself to danger by going to awaken him, so that you may be stoned again. [Col. 0635D] “For, as the evangelist says, when he spoke of his death, they thought that he spoke of the sleep of slumber.”

“Then Jesus said to them plainly: ‘Lazarus is dead; and I rejoice for your sakes that I was not there. But let us go to him.’” Therefore, he says, because they thought he spoke of the sleep of slumber, “then Jesus said to them plainly: ‘Lazarus is dead.’” This, indeed, is plain. But what does he mean when he says, “And I rejoice for your sakes”? There must certainly be a great and reasonable cause for rejoicing, especially for the Son of God, the supreme wisdom of God. He himself immediately added the cause of his joy, saying, “Because I was not there.”

For what, Lord, if you had been there? “If I had been there,” he says, “there would not have been such great material for the glory of God. For the prayers and tears of those who loved him would have pressed me to do this: that he should not die, or at least that I should raise him when dead before he was buried. Now the Son of God will be more magnificently glorified, when, after the corpse has been buried and has already begun to stink, proof will be given that, at the last hour, all who are in the tombs will truly come forth at his voice.”

Moreover, it is also a power of divinity that I know the man to be dead when I was not there. I “rejoice,” however, not for my own sake but “for your sakes.” For I do not seek my own glory; rather, what I teach you when I say, “Let your light shine before human beings, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V), [Col. 0636B] I myself do first, displaying before you the radiant works of my Father, so that seeing you may believe, and believing you may be saved. Then, I say, I was not there; but now let us go to him.

“But Thomas, who is called Didymus, said to his fellow disciples: ‘Let us also go, that we may die with him.’” The disciples’ fear was indeed great: they feared that the whole storm of Jewish fury, rising against their one Master, might sweep them all away together. But, Thomas says, setting aside our own life for the will or command of our Lord and Master, “let us also go,” and, if this must happen, “let us die with him.” Thus he rightly praises them for having endured many dangers with him, saying to them in Luke, when the hour of his Passion was at hand: “You are those who have remained with me in my temptations” (Luke XXII). Nevertheless, the knower of their capacity judged differently when he had said shortly before: “If anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble, because he sees the light of this world; but if he walks in the night, he stumbles, because the light is not in him.”

For while this true day was with them, they were not going to stumble, and they seemed to themselves able to die with him. But in that night of sorrow—that is, in the adversity of his Passion—they would stumble, so that all would prefer to flee, leaving him, rather than die with him.

“Jesus therefore came and found that he had been four days in the tomb. Now Bethany was near Jerusalem, about fifteen stadia away. And many of the Jews had come to Martha and Mary to console them concerning their brother.” All these details contribute to the greatness or testimony of the power: that “he found him already four days in the tomb”; that the place was near Jerusalem, so that the report might not come cold from far away to the scribes and Pharisees; and that many Jews were present, so that many witnesses would not be lacking for the miracle.

But what is the meaning of four days? Why did the divine plan choose to delay his arrival until the fourth day rather than the fifth or sixth? Clearly because the resurrection of the dead is to be completed in its fourfold time, and Lazarus was raised, as has already been said, as a testimony to it. The first time was before the Law, when death reigned so completely that there was no hope of resurrection. The second was under the Law, when the resurrection had already been promised and attested by the Law and prophets. The third was under grace, when Christ, the firstborn of the dead, rose and many bodies of saints rose with him; thus faith in our resurrection was accomplished and consecrated. The fourth time, finally, will be the age to come, at whose dawning, when the Lord appears, all the dead will rise at his command.

Our Lord therefore rightly remained two days when word was brought that Lazarus was sick, so that, setting out on the third, he might arrive there on the fourth. For in the third time, namely, he descended to give us the grace of resurrection; but in the fourth his commanding majesty will arrive at our tombs.

[Martha therefore, when she heard that Jesus was coming, went out to meet him; but Mary remained sitting at home.” [Col. 0637B] That Mary remained at home while Martha went to meet the Lord shows not less love, but greater humility. For it is clear from other passages of the Gospel that these two sisters, Martha and Mary, signify the two lives: the active life through Martha and the contemplative life through Mary. Therefore it rightly belonged to so great an evangelist, in such an important matter, not to omit that, while Martha went to meet the Lord, Mary, waiting for the Lord’s good pleasure and call, remained humbly and quietly at home. This accords with the occasion described in another evangelist, when Martha was occupied with much service and Mary sat beside the Lord’s feet, hearing his word (Luke X). For the contemplative life is quieter; the active life is more laborious.

“Martha therefore said to Jesus: ‘Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.’” She did not dare to complain why he had not been there or why he had not come immediately when the message had been brought by those saying, “Lord, behold, he whom you love is sick.” But preserving reverence toward the Lord and taking care not to offend his love, she merely confesses in humble faith and contrition of heart the omnipotence of the one who loves. For it follows: “But even now I know that whatever you ask of God, God will give you.”

“I know,” she says, not only this, “If you had been here, my brother would not have died,” but also this: that even now, after he has died, “whatever you ask of God,” whether concerning this man or any other, “God will give you.” Yet it is not lawful to know or say this concerning any human being except the only-begotten Son of God, “whose are all things whatsoever the Father has” (John VII). The Father does not give him, as to a servant, some particular gift of grace, but as to a Son gives all that he possesses, all that he can treasure.

“Jesus said to her, ‘Your brother will rise again.’” To one who was faintly panting and sighing in great thirst toward the fountain of mercy, this was said too sparingly—too sparingly, I say. For what was being prepared was not stated plainly: “Today your brother will rise again.” Nor was it said, “Your brother will rise on the last day,” so that a common consolation might seem to have been recalled for mourners, according to what the Apostle says in writing to the Thessalonians: “We do not wish you, brethren, to be ignorant concerning those who sleep, lest you grieve as do the rest who have no hope” (1 Thess. 4) [Col. 0638A].

Therefore the uncertain sister, hastening to know the will of the merciful one and advancing attentively, says: “I know that he will rise in the resurrection on the last day.” This is the Catholic faith that she confesses, so that through its strength she may draw forth from him a great work of power—him of whom she had said: “Whatever you ask of God, God will give you.”

“Jesus said to her, ‘I am the resurrection and the life.’” This alone remained for the completeness of her confession and faith: that she should confess whose power and whose work that resurrection on the last day is. Therefore, like an instructor catechizing a receptive soul, he speaks beforehand, so that he may hear the whole faith of the woman answering him, to whom he may deservedly grant even now the restored life of her brother in addition to the universal resurrection [Col. 0638B]. “I,” he says, “am the resurrection and the life”: the resurrection, certainly, of bodies; and likewise the resurrection and life together of both bodies and souls. For souls cannot now revive from the death of their sins except by receiving me; nor will the resurrection of bodies occur on the last day except at my command (Matt. 22).

Concerning the resurrection of souls he continues: “He who believes in me, even though he has died, shall live; and everyone who lives and believes in me shall never die for ever.” He said two things. He who lives, if he believes, shall not die; he who is dead, by believing shall live again. Who is dead except especially the person who is without God? Conversely, who lives except that blessed person whose Lord is his God? [Col. 0638C] But we know and confess that we Gentiles were without God, whereas God was known in Judaea. Therefore, he says, “He who believes in me, even though he has died, shall live”: because the Gentile people, though dead—that is, alienated from God—shall live by believing in me, with that life, namely, which God is. Conversely, the Jew who lives because the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob is his God—the God who is not God of the dead but of the living—“shall never die for ever.” But what of the one who lives and does not believe? Certainly, through unbelief he shall die; just as, conversely, the one who had been dead lives again through belief.

“Do you believe this?” She said to him, “Certainly, Lord. I have believed [Col. 0638D] that you are the Christ, the Son of God, who came into this world.” He who was asking knew that this woman believed it; nevertheless, because the faith of the mind ought to be commended by the testimony of the voice (Rom. 10)—for “with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation”—the confession of a faithful soul was fittingly to be expressed in a resounding confession (Matt. 16). And what sounds better, what sounds sweeter, in the ears and mouth of the Catholic Church? “I have believed,” she says, “that you are the Christ, the Son of God.”

This is the apostolic confession of blessed Peter; yet this woman added: “Who came into this world.” For truly this one alone, above all the sons of men, the only-begotten Son of God, came into this world: that is, he did not, as Cerinthus and other heretics falsely maintained, receive the beginning of his existence from Mary [Col. 0639A], but came from elsewhere “into this world”—that is, from heaven to earth, from the Father’s heart into the Virgin’s womb.

For good reason, then, “Jesus loved,” as was said above, “Martha and her sister Mary, and Lazarus.” For they possessed faith, the sum of all righteousness, through which our father Abraham too was justified and called the friend of God; without it no soul is worthy of God’s love.

“When she had said these things, she went away and secretly called her sister Mary, saying, ‘The Master is here and is calling you.’” She called her sister secretly, he says. Why secretly, except because of the Jews, many of whom, as was said above, had come to Martha and Mary to console them concerning their brother? For they did not fail to know that they had recently wished to stone him. Thus, lest irreverent enemies assail the Master with their customary insults, or lest, running after them, they impede those desiring to enjoy his conversation, she called her sister secretly.

“But when she heard it, she rose quickly and came to him. For Jesus had not yet come into the village, but was still in the place where Martha had met him. Therefore the Jews who were with her in the house and were consoling her, seeing that Mary rose quickly and went out, followed her, saying, ‘She is going to the tomb to weep there.’” This belonged in the Evangelist’s narrative in order that we might see what caused more people to be present when Lazarus was raised, and so that a miracle so great—the rising of one dead four days—might find many witnesses.

Meanwhile, it should not be passed over that those offering consolation showed greater attentiveness toward Mary than toward Martha [Col. 0639C]. For when Martha rose to meet the Lord, the Jews did not follow; but when Mary went out at Martha’s summons, they followed not Martha who called but Mary alone, saying, “She is going to the tomb to weep there.” Why was this, except because Mary loved her brother with a more tender affection, and, loving more, grieved more deeply? It is therefore not surprising that, when the grace of the Holy Spirit came and was joined to this natural devotion by a heavenly gift, she loved the Lord Jesus with such love—she who, weeping at the tomb, was worthy to see him before all mortals and to announce eternal consolation to the apostles. It follows:

[Col. 0639D] “Therefore, when Mary had come where Jesus was, and saw him, she fell at his feet and said to him, ‘Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.’” The faith in Christ the Son of God which Martha expressed at greater length in words, Mary expressed more swiftly by worship. For, wounded alike by grief for her brother and love for Christ, she fell at his feet; and, speaking briefly—“Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died”—her tongue fell silent, while she accomplished the rest more abundantly with tears.

“Therefore Jesus, seeing her weeping, and the Jews who had come with her weeping, groaned in spirit, troubled himself, and said, ‘Where have you laid him?’” What does this groaning of the most mighty Son of God signify? What is this disturbance of the same Son of Man, mortal and weak? For his groaning belongs to divine strength and most powerful divinity; but his being troubled by that same groaning belongs to human weakness. “He troubled himself.” For who else but he himself would trouble himself? But why did he trouble himself, or with what purpose did he groan and thus trouble himself?

A great matter, to be considered with fear, is prefigured by this groaning and disturbance. Let us look to what happened afterward, or especially after this miracle—namely, what happened because he raised Lazarus. For on account of this sign the chief priests and Pharisees, stirred by intolerable and consummate envy, assembled a council and from that day planned to kill him. In that very killing, human weakness was indeed greatly troubled; but divine strength, threatening everlasting death, ascended like a lion roaring and growling for prey, and despoiled hell (Gen. 49) [Col. 0640B]. Therefore, because that was to occur on the occasion of this miracle, Christ—God’s power and God’s wisdom (2 Cor. 1)—“groaned in spirit and troubled himself.” Some of his sayings are deeds, and his deeds are in a manner words.

“And where,” he says, “have you laid him?” He asks not in order to learn, but in order to make all who were present more attentive to the expectation of God’s glory, or of the glorification of the Son of God. “They said to him, ‘Lord, come and see.’ And Jesus wept.” [272] True humanity condescends even to tears with those who sorrow; and to the one whom, as God, he was about to raise, he first gave devout tears as man—perhaps not so much because he was dead as because, for the building up of the faith of the living, he had to be recalled to endure anew the miseries of this life [Col. 0640C].

“Therefore the Jews said, ‘See how he loved him.’ But some of them said, ‘Could not this man, who opened the eyes of one born blind, have made it so that this man should not die?’” “He who could do the greater thing,” they say, “could not do the lesser?” For it would have been less to heal one who was ill, which has sometimes happened, than to open the eyes of one born blind, which had never been heard of from the beginning of the world. There health is restored, which had formerly been present; here light is bestowed, which had never shone.

“Therefore Jesus, again groaning in himself, came to the tomb.” Again, he says, Jesus groaned. For shortly before he had said that he groaned in spirit. Yet there is no small difference: there, after saying, “He groaned in spirit,” he immediately added, “And he troubled himself.” Who can adequately weigh so careful an observance of mysteries? For when the Lord Jesus first groaned in the spirit of his strength—that is, when he entered in order to overcome hell—he was troubled by the true suffering of death (Mark 15). But when he groans again, namely when he comes to judge, he shall not be troubled, because he is now impassible, “and death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. 6).

“Then he shall cry out, he shall shout, and with a great roaring he shall prevail against his enemies” (Isa. 42). By that groaning, I say, he shall shake the powers of heaven, break the sleep of the dead, snatch to himself in the clouds the companies of men whom one and the same terror of a mighty tempest shall kill and, raising them again in the same moment, make live (Luke 21) [Col. 0641A]. Rightly, therefore, he groaned again in himself, but did not again trouble himself, “and came to the tomb.”

“Now it was a cave, and a stone had been placed upon it. Jesus said, ‘Take away the stone.’” When Jesus groans, and terribly at that second coming of his, when he shall come to judge the living and the dead, the dead lying in graves will not need their tombs opened by the ministry of living human beings or angels in order to come forth (1 Thess. 4). For at that groaning not only the graves, but heaven and the heaven of heavens, shall tremble and open. And indeed, though Christ was still mortal, he could likewise at this time have caused an earthquake merely by groaning; but it was fitting that, with gentleness and delay, the faith of those present should be invited to behold the glory of God [Col. 0641B]. For they did not yet know what he wished to do, because he had not plainly told them that he intended to raise Lazarus. Moreover, since that stone could be taken away by people, it would have seemed done without cause had he cast it aside by divine power. Therefore, so that nothing might be done ostentatiously, and so that the knowing and prudent faith of those present might go before the glory of God: “Take away,” he said, “the stone.”

Martha, the sister of the one who had died, said to him: “Lord, he already smells, for he has been dead four days.” Why was the Evangelist not content to say, “Martha said to him,” but added, “the sister of the one who had died”? Clearly, so that all hearers of this glory of God might judge without doubt that this man had been dead four days [Col. 0641C]. For it was not just anyone who spoke, but Martha; nor was it another woman of the same name, but that same Martha, already frequently named, sister of the one who had died—she whose mind was wounded and whose wakeful memory, unable to sleep, could not fail to know the days of her brother’s burial.

She said, I say, these words: “Lord, he already smells, for he has been dead four days.” As though she said: “Lord, why do you command the stone to be removed? That you may see your friend at least dead, or that you may restore him alive to his unhappy sisters? If you intend the latter, you can do it; for I know, as I have already said, that ‘whatever you ask of God, God will give you.’ But if you merely wish to see him, I tell you, ‘He already smells, for he has been dead four days’; and therefore he is no longer fit to be seen.”

Jesus said to her: “Did I not tell you that, if you believe, you will see the glory of God?” When, he says, you sent to me saying, “Lord, behold, he whom you love is ill,” did I not tell you that this illness is not unto death, but “for the glory of God, that the Son of God may be glorified through it [him]”? What glory of God do you think I promised, except the unprecedented raising of one dead four days? “Only believe, and you shall see this glory of God” [Col. 0641D].

“Therefore they took away the stone. But Jesus, lifting his eyes upward, said, ‘Father, I thank you because you have heard me. And I knew that you always hear me; but I said it because of the people standing around, that they may believe that you sent me.’” You Jews, since you can neither be absent from this spectacle nor conceal this deed, the whole world is assembled. “You said of this man, ‘He blasphemes,’ because he said, ‘I am the Son of God’” (John 10). Is it blasphemy or falsehood that usually raises one dead four days, rather than sends living persons down to hell? For Dathan and Abiram, through pride, went down alive to the lower world (Num. 16). Saul likewise, though he was the Lord’s anointed, deserved through pride to be enslaved to a demon (1 Sam. 16). “For God always resists the proud” (Jas. 4).

But behold: in order to do a work that no one can do except God, he calls his Father Lord and confesses himself to be the Son of God. Therefore either he shall accomplish nothing divine with this promise, or you impious persons are true deniers of the Son of God. But now let us contemplate the words themselves, which were immediately afterward confirmed by the deed. “Father,” he says: carefully consider that he openly called him Father and wishes to perform this work in the Father’s name—that is, to confirm that God is his Father. “I thank you because you have heard me.” How, they ask, does he give thanks to the Father if he is Son not by grace or adoption but by nature? For to give thanks is to remember a freely bestowed benefit. But let not the heretic exult. For he continues: “And I knew that you always hear me; but I said it because of the people standing around, that they may believe that you sent me” [Col. 0642B].

“For this reason,” he says, “I give thanks: so that, through your testimony in the work that follows, the people standing around may know and believe that I am pleasing and acceptable to you, and that I said not presumptuously but graciously above, ‘I and the Father are one.’ I do not give thanks because I have deserved to be your Son, but because you wished this very thing to become known to people who did not know it, so that they might be saved; according to what he says elsewhere: ‘I confess to you, Father, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and have revealed them to little ones’” (Matt. 11).

“You always hear me,” he says: that is, not at a time or hour, as is the case with those who share in me, righteous human beings, in none of whom the Spirit of grace has remained without interruption; and none of whom works a deed of your glory as one possessing authority, rather than as one receiving a gift. For the manifestation of the Spirit is not always present to anyone for usefulness; nor does anyone always feel himself heard, or feel power always present to him. Therefore, “I alone am singular in this: you always hear me.” I knew this; and it was necessary to say it with thanksgiving, not for my own sake but for the people standing around [Col. 0642D].

“When he had said these things, he cried with a loud voice, ‘Lazarus, come out!’ And immediately the one who had been dead came out, bound hand and foot with bands, and his face was bound with a cloth.” [273] Behold now, Jews: “If you do not believe the words, believe the works, that you may know,” he says, “and believe that the Father is in me and I in the Father” (John 10). He said this long ago in words, and you wished to stone him; now he proves it in works, and shortly afterward you will crucify him.

“He cried,” he says, “with a loud voice.” Rightly he cried with a loud voice so that Lazarus might come out: for with the great crash of the heavens and a great stirring of the heavenly powers, he shall shake those sleeping in the tombs. For “our God,” says the Psalmist, “shall come openly; our God shall not be silent. Fire shall burn before him, and a mighty tempest round about him. He shall summon heaven above and the earth, to judge his people” (Ps. 49 [50]) [Col. 0643A]. Thus he fittingly employed a loud voice in this signification.

“And he who had been dead,” he says, “came out.” But in what condition did he come out? “Bound,” he says, “hand and foot with bands, and his face was bound with a cloth.” A marvelous thing! Thus bound, he could neither walk with his feet nor even crawl with his hands; nor could he see with his eyes where he was to come out. What, then, does the Evangelist intimate to us by this description of one coming out, except that the voice or cry possessed great power—a voice which shook a bound dead man out among the living, and by shaking him made a living person from a dead one? If this is great and incomprehensible, how great will be that of which this is the proclamation? How shall the dead leap from their graves at the roar or groaning of the lion who reigns immortally, if this man now leapt forth at the bleating of the lamb, drawing near to the hands and knife of executioners?

Therefore it is incredible only to stones, not also to children of Abraham, that this omnipotent Son of God said: “All who are in the tombs shall hear his voice and shall come forth” (John 5). “Jesus said to them, ‘Untie him and let him go.’” Without doubt, the command of the one calling contains more miracle “in that he came out bound hand and foot with bands, and his face bound with a cloth,” than if he had crawled out with his feet and hands freed and his eyes open [Col. 0643C].

Yet it should be noted that although, even after Lazarus came out, our Lord could by his command have broken the bonds of his feet and hands, shaken off the cloth, and even cast aside the stone which he had commanded to be removed, he preferred first to say, “Take away the stone,” and now, “Untie him and let him go.” Why should he make his word of divine power a miracle in matters that could be done through the ministry of those present? All ostentation is far from the wise one and from his omnipotent nature. For it is fitting that he show his strength usefully only in those things in which human weakness cannot act.

This must also be wisely and discerningly observed by his servants: they should expect divine power only where human skill is plainly lacking. Otherwise they will seem to act against the commandment: “You shall not tempt the Lord your God” (Deut. 6) [Col. 0643D].

Having therefore seen in this Lazarus and his sister Mary two works corresponding to the Son of God’s twofold resurrection—for, as has already been said, she was raised in soul, he in body—let us now briefly touch upon the mystical likeness of these same works. A sinner is like this man dead four days, now already stinking: for the soul, miserably deprived of its life, which is God, is such as this very Mary, Lazarus’s sister, once was, of whom we have already spoken. For what had she been? Certainly a sinner, not hidden but ill-famed, and already stinking through that very notoriety, as though buried in the tomb of evil habit [Col. 0644A]. For a woman who sins in such a manner more commonly becomes offensive to people than a man does.

Therefore any sinner already infamous through evil habit is compared to Lazarus, dead four days and already stinking. When such a sinner begins to stink in the Church, the whole hospitable house of Christ is deservedly turned wholly into mire. Every order laments and prays to Christ for such a brother, whether those devoted to the active life or those devoted to the contemplative life. Those engaged in the active life, who take care of souls, are troubled first; afterward this concern and weariness are conveyed also to those who lie hidden in contemplation. Thus Martha first, then Mary, weeping, rightly approaches the Lord for her brother.

When the grace of God returns to such a sinner, the dead man is found bound hand and foot, because he is surrounded by the cords of his sins and shut beneath a stone (Ps. 118 [119])—that is, he is held guilty under the Law [Col. 0644C]. Jesus cries “with a loud voice, ‘Come out!’” because a sinner who is wrongly secure is brought back to his heart only when terrified by the great dread of God breathing upon him and threatening the future judgment. He immediately comes out—that is, he confesses his guilt—and, because he now lives, Jesus says: “Untie him.” For he said: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. 18).

But those whose office or power this is must take care not to depart from this rule: they must not bind except one who is dead, nor loose except one whom the voice of confession shows to be alive again, brought out of the tomb. For if, according to their own will or disposition, they bind one who lives and loose one who is dead—condemning the righteous and justifying the impious—they deprive themselves of that power, which is not theirs but Christ’s. By binding the living they cannot make him die in that way; and by loosing the dead they not only fail to make him live, but even thrust his stench into everyone’s nostrils [Col. 0644D]. It follows:

“Therefore many of the Jews who had come to Mary and had seen what Jesus did believed in him. But some of them went away to the Pharisees and told them what Jesus had done.” Those who believed acted better; yet those informers contributed more to the spreading of God’s glory. For when they reported abroad an event made certain by their testimony, zeal seized the uninstructed people; and while those men burned and fanned the greatness of the miracle with the strong blast of their envy, the flame of the Son of God’s glory shone more widely [Col. 0645A]. For especially because of this sign, crowds afterward went out to meet him with palm branches, crying: “Hosanna to the Son of David” (Matt. 21). “They told,” he says, “what Jesus had done; and, while they were already sufficiently zealous because of the earlier miracles, by reporting a new event they added oil to the furnace.”

“Therefore the chief priests and Pharisees assembled a council and said, ‘What are we doing? For this man performs many signs.’” [274] This is the council of vanity (Ps. 25 [26]), with which the Psalmist did not sit: that assembly of evildoers into which neither the Law nor any prophet entered. For if they had entered, if they had been consulted by that wicked council or assembly, what would they have answered those who said: “What are we doing, for this man performs many signs?” What, I say, would they have answered these senators of sin and judges of iniquity except, “Hear him; believe in him”? For if they consulted Moses concerning him, they would hear from Moses himself: “If you believe me, believe him also” (Deut. 18), as the Lord himself says: “If you believed Moses, perhaps you would also believe me, for he wrote concerning me” (John 5).

But they did not wish to believe, nor did they seek by consultation to know the truth; rather, they sought to resist the truth. Therefore they were wholly silent concerning the intention of the Scriptures, without which counsel is not lawful; and, indicating what they preferred, they immediately proposed this:

[Col. 0645C] “If we let him go on like this, all will believe in him; and the Romans will come and take away our place and nation.” That is to say: if, as we deliberate, this decision is approved—that we allow such a man, performing so many signs, to continue like this—all will believe in him. They will believe him to be the Christ; they will believe him to be their king. But we have Caesar as king, and, having long since become tributaries under Roman rule, we are a very small province entrusted to this governor Pontius Pilate. For Judaea is not so much a province as a not-large part of the province of Syria.

Therefore, if anyone besides Caesar is called king among us, the avenging “Romans will come and take away both our place and nation.” What then shall we do? Shall we let one man go, so that we all perish? Or rather—what is preferable—shall we destroy one man, so that our place and the whole nation may be preserved? Who, when such a case was proposed, did they suppose could blame their intention, or dare to defend that one man? They were deliberating about the common safety of the whole nation and seeking counsel on preserving fidelity to the Roman Empire. Thus it seemed safe to kill this man before Caesar’s tribunals and necessary, as they pretended, before the judgment-seat of the people [Col. 0645D].

Thus that assembly of evildoers and multitude of workers of iniquity bent the bow (Ps. 63 [64]); thus, I say, they bent the bow for a bitter thing and strengthened for themselves an evil word. Under this pretext of fear or fidelity to the Roman Empire, they hid snares and said, “Who shall see them?” Let that fear be granted them, since the Lord God is not their fear or terror. Let it be granted, I say, by the permission of the Lord our God himself, when he says through the prophet Jeremiah: “Let them be afraid, and let not me be afraid” (Jer. 17). “Bring upon them a day of affliction, and crush them with a double destruction, O Lord my God.”

Let them, I say, fear one destruction—namely this, lest “the Romans come and take away their place and nation”—and incur a double destruction: that the Romans, coming, take away their place and nation, and that evil spirits, flying upon them, take away their souls and cast their bodies also into Gehenna, ever burning. We have heard the proposal of men deliberating prudently, as it seemed to them; now let us listen to their discovery of what is expedient. It follows:

“One of them, Caiaphas by name, being high priest that year, said to them, ‘You know nothing, nor do you consider that it is expedient for you that one man should die for the people and not the whole nation perish.’” The spirit of falsehood appropriated for itself through the mouth of this Caiaphas a little speech signifying a great truth, so that what evangelical faith confesses in truth might sound in the same equivocal words through the mouth of an ignorant murderer striving against every truth [Col. 0646B]. Marveling at this, the Evangelist immediately adds: “But he did not say this of himself; but, being high priest that year, he prophesied that Jesus was to die for the nation, and not for the nation only, but in order that he might gather into one the children of God who were scattered abroad.”

A great spectacle is this high priest of that year: having purchased a high priesthood for one year, he truly entered the sheepfold as a thief and robber, and now intends to slaughter the shepherd of the sheep himself, so that he may more freely carry out his thefts. “He did not say this,” he says, “of himself.” What does “he did not say it of himself” mean except that he did not devise this word from his own heart? For in truth, before Caiaphas came to be, this word already existed—that Jesus should die for the nation; indeed, it was made known to the holy prophets and existed before prophets existed, before Abraham was made, and even before Adam was formed. For it was already in the good pleasure of God saying: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1). Even then this word existed: that Jesus should die for the nation [Col. 0646D]. Caiaphas therefore did not say this of himself. But what then? “Being high priest that year, he prophesied.”

For example, one may say: “Being a great cymbal, he rang out clearly,” since a cymbal is no more aware of the power of its own speech than it feels its own ringing. It does not at all perceive what we humans perceive when we hear the sound of a little bell: namely, that it was truly expedient that this one and unique man, the Holy of holies and the righteous Sun, Jesus Christ, should die for the nation—not only for the nation of Abraham, but also for all the children of God predestined from the foundation of the world, scattered outside the original paradise into the four quarters of the world, and now to be gathered from the mass of humankind up to the last elect person [Col. 0647A].

Thus he indeed perceived a falsehood, which is nothing: namely, that it would be useful for Jesus to die because, if he himself were called Christ the King, the nation would perish through the wrath of the Romans taking vengeance. But he neither perceived nor spoke from himself the truth of the matter that has now been stated. Rather, driven by the hand of God, his foolish heart produced, as God wished, a clear ringing audible far away. Therefore, because he did not say this of himself but prophesied the word, the holy Evangelist—and indeed the whole Church of Christ—rightly seized this word from the mouth of that evil prophet and unworthy high priest. From his polluted mouth and lying lips, I say, it seized this word of truth (Wis. 1), and says: “You know nothing.”

“You impious murderers,” I say, “unwise and wicked treasurers-up of death, whom malice has blinded, do not know the mysteries of God, nor consider that it is expedient for one man to die for the nation”—and not only for the chosen nation of patriarchs or prophets—“but also that he may gather into one the children of God from all nations, who were scattered” and dispersed far away, who had not heard the Lord’s name [Col. 0647B]: into one people, one Church, one body of his own. “This you do not know or consider.”

Nor could even the foxes that have dens in you, nor the birds of heaven that nest in you (Matt. 8)—that is, the evil spirits, foxes and birds which you cherish in your hearts and assemblies—grasp, either by their cunning or by their swiftness, this great mystery of godliness: that through his death the Son of God would gather his scattered brethren into one (1 Tim. 3). “Therefore you do not know this, nor do you consider it.” [275] For you are unworthy to know this counsel of God, revealed to the holy fathers and prophets. It follows:

“From that day, therefore, they planned to kill him.” Therefore, he says, because they had seemingly confirmed their conspiracy rationally by the authority of a council, from that day, once their counsel had been settled, they planned to kill him whom they had earlier wished to stone through crowd and tumult, but now to kill as though by the lawful order of a judicial proceeding.

“Therefore Jesus no longer walked openly among the Jews, but went away into the region near the wilderness, to a city called Ephraim, and remained there with his disciples” [Col. 0647D]. This true sun did not hide himself in a cloud, ceasing to walk openly among the Jews, from fear of his setting—especially since afterward he came to that same setting with such radiant splendor that the eyes of the envious could not endure the brightness of his glory. Rather, both by this action he set before his faithful useful examples, and in his usual manner signified divine mysteries.

By his example, his disciples are permitted humbly to avoid the pressure of persecution; and, mystically, it is likewise given to understand that his house should now be left desolate to the Jews. For by going into the region near the wilderness and remaining there with his disciples, he indicates by the wilderness the abandonment of the Jews, and by the region beside the wilderness the chosen dwelling-place of the Gentiles, among whom he would remain—in the city Ephraim, that is, in the Church producing abundant fruit. For Ephraim is interpreted “fruitful” or “growing” [Col. 0648A].

“Now the Passover of the Jews was near, and many went up from the country to Jerusalem before the Passover, in order to sanctify themselves.” “Jesus,” he says, “was no longer walking openly among the Jews,” but he did not hide for long. “For the Passover of the Jews was near,” and he knew it to be his own time, when he wished and desired to suffer, as he himself testifies: “With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer” (Luke 22).

Moreover, this was the last Passover of the Jews. Whatever the Jews sanctify thereafter is defiled; whatever their priests bless is accursed. For God curses their blessings, as he foretold through the prophet: “And thereafter he cast the dung of their solemnities upon their faces” (Mal. 2) [Col. 0648B]. “In order to sanctify themselves,” he says, “they went up before the Passover.” The Jews’ sanctification, consisting wholly in foods and drinks, various washings, and ordinances of the flesh, was solemnly performed before Passover: that is, from the beginning of the first month, on the fourteenth day of which, at evening, the sacred lamb was sacrificed; and it was commanded in the Law that no unclean person should eat of it (Exod. 12).

“Therefore they were seeking Jesus and talking with one another as they stood in the temple: ‘What do you think? Will he not come to the feast day?’” Behold the cruel hyena, dwelling in that inheritance [Col. 0648C] in which God once dwelt: how it thirsts, how it pants, thrusting out its tongue in haste and impatiently thirsting to shed Christ’s blood. The feast day had not yet arrived, and already, lying in wait in their den, in that house of the Father which they had made into a den of thieves when it ought to have been a house of prayer (Matt. 21; John 2), they said: “What do you think? Will he not come to the feast day?” That is, because he had not come first, or among the first, of those who, as was said above, went up to Jerusalem to sanctify themselves; wickedly anxious and fearing that their intended murder might fail: “What do you think,” they said, “will he not come to the feast day?” O impious men, what should we think except that this is the paschal lamb [Col. 0648D] and the tenth day of this month has not yet arrived? For the Law does not command that the lamb to be sacrificed in the house of the children of Israel be taken on the feast day of the new moon amid the sounding of trumpets, but on the tenth day of the month. Therefore he has not yet come to the feast day because he awaits the time and his lawful day, so that on the lawful—that is, the tenth—day of the month the paschal Lamb may enter the house of the children of Israel, that is, the temple of God; and thereafter may distribute to his hearers the health-giving pastures of heavenly teaching around, or within, the garden of that same temple—while you hear nothing and cannot lay your knife upon him—until the fourteenth day arrives, on whose evening he will sacrifice himself with his own hands, and only then permit himself to be butchered by you, O bloody gladiatorial trainers. Then [Col. 0649A] you will receive him “like a lion ready for prey, and like a lion’s cub dwelling in secret places” (Ps. 17 [Vulgate Ps. 16]). Signifying their evil intention, the Evangelist immediately adds:

“But the chief priests and Pharisees had given an order that, if anyone knew where he was, he should report it, so that they might seize him.” They were not, he says, seeking him rightly, nor were they eagerly desiring to see him come to the feast day for a good purpose; rather, “the chief priests and Pharisees had given an order that, if anyone knew where he was, he should report it, so that they might seize him.” They were concerned lest perhaps for this very reason he might not come to the feast day. Thus each of them was intent on obtaining favor by informing on him, especially since they were ready to give a price—as they did give it to his disciple when he informed them [Col. 0649B] when or in what place they could seize him without crowds (Matt. 26).

[CHAPTER 12.]—“Therefore Jesus came to Bethany six days before the Passover, where Lazarus had been dead, whom he raised.” Therefore, he says, because the rulers and Pharisees had issued such an order, Jesus came not fourteen or twelve days beforehand, but later—that is, “six days before the Passover”—into the neighborhood of Jerusalem, namely Bethany. By this example he foreshadowed that no one should expose himself to persecutors before divine grace calls him, since he himself took care to observe that time or day which had long been ordained through the Scriptures. The sixth day before the fourteenth of the month, on whose evening the lamb was to be sacrificed, is the ninth day of that month. Therefore, when he came to Bethany on the ninth [Col. 0649C] day of the month, and, as follows shortly afterward, entered the city of Jerusalem on the next day—which was certainly the tenth day of the month—the true Lamb of God is plainly shown here also to have fulfilled the Law written concerning the paschal lamb: “He came,” he says, “to Bethany, where Lazarus had been dead, whom he raised,” namely, in order, as has been said, to enter the holy city on the following day.

“Now they made him a supper there, and Martha was serving; but Lazarus was one of those reclining at table. Therefore Mary took a pound of costly pure nard ointment, anointed Jesus’ feet, and wiped them with her hair; and the house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment.” From Matthew and Mark we clearly know that this supper was held in the house of Simon, formerly a leper [Col. 0649D] (Matt. 26; Mark 14). According to Luke also, it was the house of the same Simon, in which this same Mary, first a sinner—this same woman, I say, as more careful interpreters have truly maintained—was received by the Lord, washed his feet with her tears, and had many sins forgiven her because she loved much (Luke 7). Why, then, with so many men present, was the woman Martha serving in another person’s house? Certainly it would not have been surprising had she been serving in her own house, as on the occasion when “Jesus himself entered a certain village, and this same woman received him into her house and was busied with much serving” (Luke 10). But whatever necessity had joined Martha to Simon so that she served in his house, [Col. 0650A] since Scripture is silent, let us now examine more carefully in this supper the holy and mystical ministries of great devotion rendered to our Lord. “They made him a supper there,” he says. The house, as was said, belongs to Simon; Martha serves; “Lazarus is one of those reclining at table”; Mary poured precious ointment upon the Lord’s head and feet. For although in this place the Evangelist relates that ointment was poured over his feet, Matthew and Mark do not conceal that it was also poured over his head.

More abundantly, then, at the time when the Lord’s Passion was imminent, the service of the holy Church was foreshadowed in this supper than when this same Mary, a sinner, was received by our same Lord in the house of that Simon. For then, when this notorious sinner entered the Pharisee’s house and was justified by offering worthy repentance despite the murmuring of the diners, she prefigured the conversion of the Gentiles [Col. 0650B]. For after the Lord’s Ascension this Gentile people came to the riches of the Jews, from whom salvation comes; breaking uninvited into the great banquet of the Scriptures, it reclined behind, at the Lord’s feet (John 4), having formerly been a harlot—that is, prostituted, as it were, to many husbands by many gods. It clung to the footsteps of him whom it had not known according to the flesh, weeping and doing penance for its former error, while those of the circumcision murmured because they judged the Gentiles unworthy of Christ’s grace (Acts 11).

Now, however, the same woman, already justified, together with her sister Martha signifies the one and same Church of Christ, which serves the same Lord in Bethany—that is, in the house of obedience—with the differing offices [Col. 0650C] of the active and contemplative life. “But Lazarus, who had been dead,” whom Jesus raised, “is one of those reclining at table,” because without faith in the resurrection Christ is served in no order of the Church. The house itself belongs to Simon the leper, because, as the Apostle says, to the Jews belong adoption as sons, glory, the covenant, the giving of the Law, worship, promises, and the fathers; from them is Christ according to the flesh (Rom. 9). But we—the Church from the Gentiles—were formerly without Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, strangers to the covenants, having no hope of promise, and without God [Col. 0650D] in this world (Eph. 2). Therefore, when we were admitted so that we are no longer strangers and foreigners but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household, the Church of the Gentiles serves Christ in the Pharisee’s house, although the Synagogue envied and slandered the penitent woman.

Thus, once supper had been made, Martha serves and Mary pours ointment upon the Lord; and this too was no small ministry. Yet it differs from Martha’s ministry, because Martha ministers to the needs of the body, whereas Mary’s service, though great, does not refresh the body through such service. Mystically, the hair with which she wipes the Lord’s feet signifies the proud abundance of the rich, by which they can relieve the lack of the poor without impoverishing themselves, just as they can cut off their hair without pain to the head. Yet, bodily speaking, as has already been said, Mary does not feed the Lord through this service. Therefore Martha’s ministry signifies the diligence of those who serve Christ in the active life, while Mary’s ointment, “with whose fragrance the house was filled,” figures the devotion of those who, worn down by the holy labors of the contemplative life, pour out a good fragrance before God and people.

What was said also accords with their perfection: “She took a pound of costly pure nard ointment.” A pound of ointment, that is, a good and complete measure of devout service. *Pistic* ointment means faithful and unadulterated ointment, or ointment of the finest proof. For πίστις (*pistis*) in Greek is called *fides*, “faith,” in Latin; and faith, joined with humility—which the low-growing and aromatic nard plant signifies—becomes the finest ointment, most sweetly anointing not only the Lord’s head but also his feet [Col. 0651B]. It is not without purpose that this Evangelist, while Matthew and Mark plainly said that she poured the ointment upon the head of the reclining Lord, writes what they leave unmentioned: that she also anointed his feet with it. For indeed, when she first came to the Lord, she anointed only his feet with ointment which she had bought not for the Lord himself but had prepared to preserve the fragrance of her own body. A sinner could not at once be worthy of his head. But now, justified and beloved, she anointed both head and feet with ointment that she had bought for this very purpose.

Therefore, while Martha ministers bodily food, Mary, the model of spiritual ministries, anoints the Savior’s head and feet with precious ointment, before all who see and marvel at the fragrance. Thus, in the hearing of the people serving the Lord, devout ministers of Christ and “stewards of the mysteries of God” (1 Cor. 4) faithfully confess and proclaim, in relation to the six works of mercy mentioned in Matthew’s Gospel—“I was hungry and you gave me food; I was thirsty and you gave me drink” (Matt. 25), and the rest—that “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God; and the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1). To anoint the head is faithfully to proclaim his divinity; to anoint the feet is humbly to believe and steadfastly proclaim the true humanity [Col. 0651D] and true Passion of the same God and man. Acting thus, and not “adulterating the word of God like so many,” they say: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God in every place, among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing” (2 Cor. 2). “Therefore the house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment.” Yet this one and same ointment of the Church is to some a fragrance of death unto death, and to others a fragrance of life unto life.

“Therefore one of his disciples, Judas Iscariot, who was about to betray him, said: ‘Why was this ointment not sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor?’” To this unhappy man the woman’s good work brought the fragrance of death; the sweet fragrance of precious ointment killed him [Col. 0652A]. Indeed, because he was already truly dead while walking among the living—that is, the chosen apostles—he lay dead to God in the tomb of his own wickedness and could not bear the fragrance of life. He could not see without the torment of indignation and envy a service of devotion or honor worthily rendered to his master; he could not contain the poison of avarice with which he was drunk.

The Evangelist described his person by pointedly saying “Judas Iscariot”—a name taken either from the tribe of Issachar or from the village in which he was born—and by adding, “who was about to betray him,” since there was another apostle of this name, Judas also called Thaddaeus. He then explains the intention with which Judas said this: “But he said this not because he cared about the poor, but because he was a thief and, having the money-box [Col. 0652B], carried what was put into it.” This most foul villain, he says, covered with the honorable name of concern for the poor his utterly wicked envy, by which he thought ill of his good Master, and his profound avarice, by which, sparing not the Lord’s money-box, he committed theft. Who would not marvel that he veiled such a conscience with such hypocrisy: that an enemy lying in wait against mercy discoursed about the mercy necessary for the poor? Magnificently the holy Evangelist strikes at this murderer’s atrocity by saying, “Not because he cared about the poor.” This concern, he says, did not belong to him, for his mind, the slayer of piety, had passed far beyond all bounds of human compassion; his heart was so utterly alien that he could deliver to death mercy itself toward the poor.

But why did he say it? “Because he was a thief,” he says. O unhappy man! He would have preferred this ointment to be sold for three hundred denarii because he wished, and was able, to steal from those three hundred denarii. How could he?
