Quite conveniently, since he had the money-box and carried what was put into it. He was, so to speak, the Lord’s purse-bearer, and carried what devout people sent to our poor Lord. For though he had been rich, he became poor for our sake; and although he was Creator and Lord of the earth, sea, and all things in them or springing from them, he nevertheless wished to be supported by people’s alms (2 Cor. 8) and, while proclaiming the Gospel, to live by the Gospel [Col. 0652D]. Judas carried what hearers of the Gospel sent to the Lord, and wickedly abusing his office, carried it away as a thief and sacrilegious man. Not merely any thief, but a thief of money-boxes—of the Lord’s money-boxes, sacred ones. Such was miserable Judas; yet he went in and out with the eleven holy disciples. Indeed, he had been placed in charge of the alms from which both they and the Lord himself lived.

“Why,” you ask, “did our Lord, who knew all things, when he knew him to be such, make him not only an apostle but also the apostles’ provider or purse-bearer?” To this I reply: Why does the same Lord to this day permit many men like him to be placed in authority in his Church? Whoever steals anything from the Church is likened to lost Judas. And how many, do you think, steal from the Church, abusing the ministry in which, by Christ’s permission, they serve? How many commit theft by not distributing the property of the poor to the poor—and not merely theft, but sacrilege? If crimes of ordinary theft and embezzlement are distinguished in court—for embezzlement is theft from public property—and if theft of private property is not judged in the same way as theft of public property, how much more severely must the sacrilegious thief be judged who dared to take not merely from anywhere, but from the Church? Therefore, although even today there are many Judases and we cannot give a certain answer when asked why they have been able to attain ecclesiastical ministry—except that God permits many things that he does not will—let us not rashly examine the Lord’s judgment in the case of that one man. Especially since we do not know whether the Lord entrusted his money-boxes to him by his own choice or whether, more plausibly, Judas forced himself into the position, as very many now force themselves into ecclesiastical offices with such importunity that, unless admitted, they inflict upon souls through discord scandals almost more serious than the losses they would inflict upon Church property if they were admitted [Col. 0653B].

Thus when Judas says, “Why was this ointment not sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor?” there is no fear of God or concern for the poor before his eyes; rather, the words of his mouth are iniquity and deceit, and upon his bed he meditates iniquity.

“Therefore Jesus said: ‘Leave her, that she may keep it for the day of my burial. For you always have the poor with you, but you do not always have me.’” The Lord distributed the words of his response between singular and plural number, saying in the singular, “Leave her, that she may keep it for the day of my burial,” and adding in the plural, “For you always have the poor with you, but you do not always have me” [Col. 0653C]. From this it may be understood that, according to Matthew and Mark, the other disciples also were indignant, saying, “Why this waste?” (Matt. 26), though with a different intention: some said it truly out of concern for the poor, but Judas because of his greed for theft. Rightly, therefore, where intentions were divided, our Lord divided his words, giving to each party what was fitting.

For to Judas the thief, who through his most wicked avarice was shortly to receive the price of his betrayal—or of Christ’s death (Matt. 14)—he announced that same death: “Leave her,” he says, “that she may keep it for the day of my burial.” It is as if he said: Let it not only not be sold for distribution to the poor, but let her retain even what she now has; for she has not yet poured it all upon me. Let her keep, I say, the ointment she now has and buy still more to embalm my body, which through your crime, Judas, will shortly be handed over for crucifixion. But to those who, as has been said, had truly said on the poor’s behalf, “Why this waste? It could have been sold for more than three hundred denarii and given to the poor,” he gave a far different explanation, full of compassion and sweetness: “For you always have the poor with you, but you do not always have me” [Col. 0653D]. It is indeed a good work, he says, to care for the poor and do them good; but first, as I am soon to depart and soon to die, you, my friends, should dutifully bid me farewell. Service to the poor has its own merit, but the duty of devotion offered to the very head of the holy poor surpasses it. Moreover, “you do not always have me”: you will not always be able to pour ointment upon me in this way. The time will come when you will desire to pour out your blood in order to see me, though now you regard as waste the pouring out of ointment which you did not buy.

Thus he rightly spoke the former in the singular and the latter in the plural, responding suitably to the differing intentions of Judas and the other indignant disciples. Yet it may also be understood that he abruptly passed from singular to plural because then there was one Judas, whereas now there are many. Though faithful disciples always have Christ through the presence of his divinity—as he himself says, “Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age” (Matt. 28)—those who are faithful to Judas will by no means have him. For the prophet says, “Let the wicked be taken away, lest he see the glory of the Lord” (Isa. 26), so that, just as Judas did not deserve to see the risen Lord’s face or to be with the blessed apostles when he brought them peace—because the place of perdition had already taken him away—so all who are faithful to Judas may never have him or see his glory [Col. 0654B]. It follows:

“Therefore a great crowd of the Jews learned that he was there, and they came not only because of Jesus, but also to see Lazarus, whom he had raised.” From the time when “the chief priests and Pharisees gathered a council,” and, having resolved to kill the Lord Jesus, had issued the order “that, if anyone knew where he was, he should report it so that they might seize him,” the crowd had not known where he was; for Jesus did not walk openly among the Jews. But now he had come to Bethany, and “they made him a supper there. Lazarus too was one of those reclining at table.” Thus, after a brief period of expectation, the crowd at last learned “that he was there, and they came not only because of Jesus, but also to see Lazarus, whom he had raised.” But had they until then been unable even to see Lazarus, just as they had not known where Jesus was because he was not walking openly? Therefore this crowd [Col. 0654D] was not only made up of inhabitants of Jerusalem; it consisted in large part of those who, as was said above, were going up from the country to Jerusalem before the Passover “to sanctify themselves.” They came to him, he says, desiring not to seize but to see him, and thus causing envy in those who were plotting to kill him. For it immediately follows:

“But the chief priests planned to kill Lazarus too, because many of the Jews were leaving on account of him and believing in Jesus.” Thus those who remained wickedly envied those who came rightly, and envied the Lord’s glory. But whence had this subject nation acquired such audacity as to dare not only to want to kill one man because he raises the dead, but also another because he had come back to life? Clearly from confidence arising out of their own fear, which the chief priests and Pharisees had displayed earlier in their council when they said: “Perhaps the Romans will come and take away our place and nation.” That fear had expressed their loyalty to their masters, namely the Romans themselves. Therefore they dared, relied upon this, and shrewdly and cunningly foresaw that Roman law could not be angry with them. For that same concern had rescued Herod from the loss of his place and from the sword of Roman severity—Herod who had slaughtered so many children because of the birth of the new king (Matt. 2), to whom the prophets in their Scriptures promised not only the Jewish kingdom but the kingdom of the whole world. Accordingly, they readily accepted that in this way he had taken thought not only for himself but also for the Roman rulers, for the interests of Caesar Augustus [Col. 0655A].

“On the next day, when the great crowd that had come to the feast heard that Jesus was coming to Jerusalem, they took branches of palm trees and went out to meet him, and cried: ‘Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel!’” The day on which the events at Bethany now related by the Evangelist took place was a Sabbath: namely, the sixth day before the solemn evening of Passover, that is, the evening following the fourteenth moon, which now according to the Gospel fell on Thursday. But this next day was the first day of the Sabbath, on which the Lord Jesus entered Jerusalem, the eighth before the day on which he would rise from the dead; that day too was undoubtedly the first day of the Sabbath. It was not, therefore, by chance but by the secret ordering of divinity that he entered the city with such honor and display of praise on this day, and, as was said above, that the true Lamb of God came on the tenth moon to undergo his sacrifice on the fourteenth moon [Col. 0655C]. For what was this joy but a heralding of his resurrection, to come eight days later?

Let us therefore examine more carefully the sequence of the Gospel narrative. “The great crowd,” he says, “which had come to the feast, when they heard that Jesus was coming to Jerusalem, took palm branches and went out to meet him.” Palm branches are emblems of victory. A great and wondrous sight! War was now first being prepared; the struggle had not yet begun, and already crowds of people were celebrating the triumph. Did they undoubtedly already know the victory which he was undoubtedly to accomplish? Indeed, they did not even know that the King of Israel had come to fight. This counsel of divinity—that through his Passion and death this King of glory would destroy him who held the empire of death, that is, the Devil, and that he must suffer, rise from the dead, and thus enter into his glory—was hidden from all living persons and even from the apostles themselves. Therefore, according to their understanding of what they were doing, those who sang such great praise were infants and nursing children: they did not know the mystery that they outwardly foreshadowed. Hence, according to another Evangelist, when the scribes and Pharisees said to the Lord, “Do you hear what these are saying?” he answered, “Certainly. Have you never read: ‘Out of the mouths of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise’?” (Matt. 21; Ps. 8).

Therefore he who came to suffer, by his own nod and will moved such infants and nursing children—in comparison with the scribes and Pharisees, among whom were abundance of eloquence and the solid food of legal and prophetic knowledge—to meet him in this way, to bear branches of this kind, and thus to cry aloud to him. And from their mouths he perfected praise of his victory, which they did not know [Col. 0656A]. For what did they say in their acclamations? “Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel.”

*Hosanna* is a Hebrew word composed of two elements, one altered and one intact. Among them *osi* means “save” or “make saving”; but *anna* is an interjection of entreaty, just as among Latin speakers *heu* is an interjection of grief and *papae* an interjection of astonishment. Thus in Psalm 117, where it is written, “O Lord, save me,” the Hebrew reads: *Anna, Adonai, hosanna*. Therefore *hosanna* means, “Save, I beseech you.” The vowel letter *i*, with which the preceding word—properly *osi*—ends, is absorbed through the force of the vowel *a* with which the following word, *anna*, begins. Poets call this *synaloepha* in verse, although when scanning they pass over a written letter. But in the word *hosanna*, the letter *i* is not even written; while the speaker’s intended sense remains unchanged, it is omitted altogether [Col. 0656B].

“Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel.” They took this verse, together with the word *hosanna*, for which, as said above, the Hebrew reads *anna, Adonai, hosanna*, that is, “O Lord, save me,” from Psalm 117, at the prompting of the heavenly will moving them; for there it is written: “Blessed is he who will come in the name of the Lord.” The prophet, so far as belonged to the condition in which he himself stood, wrote “will come.” But these people, confessing him to be the one there foretold, said not “the one who will come,” but “the one who comes in the name of the Lord.” “In the name of the Lord,” that is, seeking the Father’s glory rather than his own; or bearing that name by which he is Lord, as the Lord the Father himself said to Moses concerning the angel of great counsel, namely this his Son: “My name is in him” (Exod. 23).

Thus, as the King of Israel—that is, King of all who live to God, or who are worthy to see God—went forth to war against the devil, he already prefigured the rejoicing [Col. 0656D] which the heavenly city of Jerusalem would have at his victory. For when he rose from the dead and ascended into heaven, the choirs of heavenly citizens would sing, raising branches of victory and receiving their King with due praise and honor. For as, after the Philistine Goliath had been slain by the boy David, David returned carrying his head to Jerusalem and women went out from all the cities to meet him, singing with joyful drums and sistrums (1 Sam. 17), so, once the devil had been overcome by Christ’s Passion, the souls of the saints would go forth with the blessed angels, praising and singing glory to their King; and multitudes of faithful living persons would proclaim his victory throughout the whole world. It follows:

[Col. 0657A] “And Jesus found a young ass and sat upon it, as it is written: ‘Do not fear, daughter of Zion; behold, your king comes, sitting upon an ass’s colt’” (Zech. 9). Here he briefly touches upon what the other Evangelists had already related more fully. But what a meaning this brevity conveys: “He found,” he says, “a young ass.” He spoke magnificently and appropriately; the divine Evangelist expressed the matter forcefully. For what does the tying of the ass, which the other Evangelists narrate more fully, signify except the perdition and captivity of humankind, especially of the Gentile people? Conversely, what does its loosing, which he orders two disciples to carry out, signify except our finding or acquisition? Thus he aptly and briefly, yet properly, says “that Jesus found the young ass and sat upon it,” since through the mystery of his Passion the Savior found lost humankind. Having driven away its rider, the Devil—whom the lowly and foolish ass bore all too patiently, to its great disgrace, bridled with the halter of folly and driven to the stable of death—the noble rider and glorious King mounted it so as to make it a sharer in his nobility and bring it by the salvation of his riding into the heavenly city, Jerusalem [Col. 0657B].

He sat upon it, I say, as it is written: “Do not fear, daughter of Zion; behold, your king comes to you, sitting upon an ass’s colt.” This is written in the prophet Zechariah (Zech. 9); and because it concerns his Passion, to which he was now coming in such a symbolic form, the prophet immediately adds: “You also, by the blood of your eternal covenant, have brought forth the bound ones from the pit in which there is no water” (ibid.). The Hebrew people are called the daughter of Zion; and here, in respect of the elect among them, the Holy Spirit consoles her through this prophet, so that she may not fear but instead rejoice, because her King, bringing in the Gentiles, fills her house and multiplies her children, as is signified by such an advent of his.

“His disciples did not understand these things at first; but when Jesus was glorified, then they remembered that these things had been written about him and that they had done these things to him.” “At first,” he says, before he had risen, before he had opened their minds to understand the Scriptures, they did not understand these things. But when Jesus was glorified, namely by the glory of the resurrection [Col. 0657D], ascension, and outpouring of the Holy Spirit (Luke 24), then they remembered that these things were written about him, the Holy Spirit suggesting all things to them. And, he says, they remembered that “they had done these things to him.” What had they done to him? Certainly those things by which he found the young ass—indeed, by which he sat upon it. For Matthew clearly expresses this: “They put their garments upon it and made him sit upon them” (Matt. 21). He himself indicated where the ass was and ordered it to be brought to him; but in the fixed order of the mystery, though he commanded this with the intention of sitting upon it and thereby fulfilling the prophecy already mentioned, he nevertheless did not wish to sit upon it except when the disciples asked and laid their garments upon it.

Therefore they did this then without understanding; but what was signified then through them while they were unaware, they themselves later did knowingly. For, sent by the Lord throughout the world to loose the Gentile people through the labor of preaching, they added the urgency of prayer, that the Lord might deem worthy to sit upon—that is, protect—the young ass brought to him, the Gentile people believing in him. If he did not do so, they mourned and wept for the unhappy ass, as the Apostle feared might happen to certain Corinthians when he said among other things: “For I fear that perhaps, when I come, I may not find you as I wish, and I may be found by you as you do not wish” (2 Cor. 12); and shortly afterward: “Lest, when I come again, God humble me among you, and I mourn many of those who sinned before and have not repented of the impurity, fornication, and indecency which they have committed” [Col. 0658B].

It follows: “Therefore the crowd that was with him when he called Lazarus from the tomb and raised him from the dead bore witness. For this reason the crowd also came out to meet him, because they had heard that he had done this sign.” This is a summary of what has already been said: namely, that the crowds’ going out to meet him with such cries was a great and true testimony to the Son of God. “Thus,” he says, “the crowd that was with him when he raised Lazarus bore witness in this way; and for this reason the crowd came out to meet him, because they heard that he had done this sign.” He distinguishes one crowd from another: the crowd that had been present at that wondrous sign from the crowd that had not been present but had heard of it. Thus, as those who had seen converged with those who had heard from their report, the crowd increased, the gathering grew, the praise of God was multiplied, and the glory of the Son of God was multiplied in such a great assembly, at such a time, in that preparation for the paschal feast, when, as said above, many had gone up to Jerusalem from the country [Col. 0658C].

“Therefore the Pharisees said to one another: ‘You see that we accomplish nothing. Behold, the whole world has gone after him.’” They groaned together in great torment and breathed out their mutual envy in grievous pain: “You see,” they said, “that we accomplish nothing?” O unhappy straw! Our God is a consuming fire, and would you succeed by crushing him? You will rather fail and be consumed, for straw does not consume fire; on the contrary, fire consumes straw. The more stubbornly you press upon him, the more broadly he will spread the flame of his brightness to your ruin. “We accomplish nothing,” they say. Whence this evil? Whence these groans? “Behold,” they say, “the whole world has gone after him.” They did not say, “the whole crowd,” but “the whole world,” because the children of the Hebrews were singing and the firstfruits of the Gentiles were seeking Jesus. For it follows:

“Now there were certain Gentiles among those who had gone up to worship on the feast day. These therefore came to Philip, who was from Bethsaida of Galilee, and asked him, saying: ‘Sir, we wish to see Jesus.’” What distressed them more deeply was that the Hebrews were already acclaiming Jesus as the Son of David [Col. 0659A], while the Gentiles were seeking him; indeed, in the prescient anguish of their twisted envy, they had long before said: “Where is this man going, that we shall not find him? Is he going into the Dispersion among the Gentiles and to teach the Gentiles?” (John 7). “They were Gentiles,” he says, “and had gone up to worship on the feast day.” Truly they came as poor people to the door of the great rich, desiring to be filled with the crumbs falling from their table; indeed, they had come, like little dogs beneath their masters’ table, to gather the leftover fragments (Matt. 15). How great a humility is suggested by their words, as though standing at a distance: “Sir, we wish to see Jesus.” How contrite must their hearts have been toward the Lord of lords, when, seeking an intercessor [Col. 0659B], they called the servant of the Lord “lord”!

“And Andrew and Philip again told Jesus.” Certainly it was no slight matter, according to custom, for men uncircumcised—strangers to the covenants of promise and without hope—to be admitted even to see the Lord Jesus, whose sight and presence had become wearisome and repellent to the Israelites. For they remembered hearing the Lord say: “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles.” Let us therefore hear what the meek and humble in heart answered to these poor, that is, humble men. “Jesus answered them, saying: ‘The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified.’” The hour has come, he says, in which, so that the Gentiles may see the Son of Man, the Son of Man himself may be glorified—namely, by the glorification of the resurrection and ascension, and also [Col. 0659C] by the outpouring of the Holy Spirit [280]. For from that time—that is, after, according to the Psalmist, “rejoicing as a giant, he has run his course; and as his going forth is from the highest heaven, so his circuit reaches to its height” (Ps. 18)—from that time, I say, like the sun he shall be visible to the whole world, and none shall hide himself from his heat. Then these Gentiles, once foolish, will see me, enlightened by faith; and what is written shall be fulfilled: “Those who did not formerly ask for me sought me; they found me” (Isa. 65); or, according to the Septuagint translators: “I appeared openly to those who did not seek me.”

But what shall be the manner of this glorification, or what efficient cause shall produce so great a brightness? He says: “Amen, amen, I say to you: Unless a grain [Col. 0659D] of wheat, falling into the earth, dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.” At this word, when he said, “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified,” those who desired his kingdom could have rejoiced, as did the apostles, greatly desiring their Master’s glory. They could have rejoiced, I say, as though they were to sit at the right and left hand of the great king upon that earthly throne of David—especially since he had now been hailed by the crowds as King of Israel—without understanding that this was the necessary manner and order of glorification: the humility of the Passion had to precede the height of glory.

Therefore the Wisdom of God, the teacher of his children, immediately introduced an apt comparison, wishing to show that the Incarnation had profited the world nothing unless, through his Passion, he acquired its redemption [Col. 0660A]. The emphatic preface, “Amen, amen, I say to you,” moreover, reflects the slowness of these disciples, which we recognize more plainly from the other evangelists. There, when the Lord said that he must be killed and rise on the third day, Peter took him aside and rebuked him, saying: “Far be it from you, Lord; this shall not happen to you” (Matt. 16). For here and there he gives the same teaching concerning love for one’s soul and its perfect hatred, when he says there: “Whoever wishes to save his soul shall lose it; and whoever hates his soul in this world preserves it for eternal life” (Matt. 9). They had love for their Lord and Master, certainly, but not according to knowledge. Therefore, when Peter—as said above—would offer the Wisdom of God counsel contrary to his own salvation and ours, the Lord said to him [Col. 0660B]: “Get behind me, Satan; for you do not savor the things that are of God” (Matt. 16). He called him Satan—that is, an adversary—because in a carnal will he opposed the divine will.

Therefore, because the disciples’ understanding was then still carnal, he set forth this comparison with the firm assurance of truth: “Amen, amen, I say to you: Unless a grain of wheat, falling into the earth, dies, it remains alone.” O grain of wheat, the remnant of our hope, the consolation of our poverty, happily sprung from your earth which you have blessed, Lord! For according to the nature which he took from the virgin earth, he who came from heaven—the Son [Col. 0660C] of God, who feeds the blessed angels with immortal food—rightly compared himself to a grain of wheat. But from where does he testify that he has a necessity to fall into the earth and die? From this, namely: “Unless, falling into the earth, it dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.”

Therefore the Son of Man was not to die because he was debtor to sin or death, but so that his one death might make the life of many fruitful. A grain of wheat is not cast into the earth because it is defective, but because, so cast down, “when it has died”—that is, when it has lost its solid strength through the moisture of the earth—it rises again by sprouting and brings forth many grains with it. This therefore was [Col. 0660D] the grain of wheat: let it be put to death by the unbelief of the Jews, so that, laid in the tomb, it may grow green again and be multiplied by the faith of the peoples, and thus carry a great harvest into the barns of heaven. Had it refused to die, it could have received only itself; for, apart from the reality of flesh, it had nothing in common with the thorns and thistles which the earth, cursed on account of Adam’s work, brought forth (Gen. 3). “For this,” says the apostle Peter, “he did for us, leaving us an example, that we might follow his footsteps” (1 Pet. 2). Eternal life awaits the person who follows those footsteps; destruction awaits the one who refuses to follow them. This is what follows:

“Whoever loves his soul loses it; and whoever hates his soul in this world preserves it for eternal life.” First it must be defined, according to the words or intention of the Lord [Col. 0661A], what it is to hate one’s soul; for this hatred must be far removed from that hatred of which his Holy Spirit says through the mouth of David: “He who loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Ps. 10). For Christ’s disciples to hate their souls is to conduct themselves among those who afflict them in such a way that they are held in derision and made a likeness of reproach: “so that the foolish may judge their life madness and their end without honor” (Wis. 5). In such people’s estimation, hatred of the soul seems to mean not loving the sweetness of the present life; choosing, in peace, a hard life for God’s sake; and desiring, in persecution, a bloody death for the same sake.

Likewise, to them hatred of father, mother, and children seems to mean setting natural affection for them after God [Col. 0661B]; although Christ’s disciples are not utterly without the good love of nature, but neglect it in comparison with what is better. Thus, according to the understanding of such people: “Whoever loves his soul loses it; and whoever hates his soul in this world preserves it for eternal life.” Behold: that first grain of wheat which fell into the earth and died at that time bore much fruit, because from the root of its faith it produced as many grains as the souls whom, through baptism, it caused to be buried with itself into death and to spring up in newness of life (Rom. 6). Long before, Isaac had prophetically perceived the grace of this shoot by his sense of smell when he said: “Behold, the smell of my son is as the smell of a full field which the Lord has blessed” (Gen. 27).

But see to it that, when you ought to be grain, you are not chaff [Col. 0661C]. “How?” you ask. Certainly by loving your soul wrongly: with that love which the Apostle condemns, saying, “Men shall be lovers of themselves” (1 Tim. 1). It is a time of war; the time of persecution presses; and the whole contest lies in this: either pour out your soul for Christ as though it were worthless and hateful, or, by preserving it, lose your God, your Christ, your Savior. He says therefore: Whoever loves his soul—that is, whoever, enticed by the sweetness of the present life, when given the choice either to lose that life or deny Christ, so values his soul that he puts it before Christ, preferring to live with Christ offended rather than die here with Christ loved—such a person, loving his soul thus, loses it: that is, sends it into eternal destruction.

“And whoever hates his soul in this world”—that is, whoever finds it hateful that denial of Christ should be the price of being allowed to live in this world; whoever, I say, so hates his soul and recoils from keeping silver, a thing cheaper than the promise of gold—which is Christ—indeed miserable mud, which his soul is in comparison with Christ: such a person “preserves it for eternal life,” by the everlasting guardianship of Christ, who is the cause of this hatred for him. Perhaps you say: These ways are hard. By what right or law does he require this [Col. 0661D] [281], that I should hate my soul? To this he says:

“If anyone serves me, let him follow me.” Since, he says, I am to be glorified in the hour now coming by this way and order—first laying down my soul for the salvation of many, as a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies in order to bear much fruit—it is not fitting that one who professes himself my servant and aims at sharing my glorification should, loving his soul excessively, hide himself from the benefit of his neighbors and wish to arrive by barren leisure where I am to arrive through laborious fruitfulness. Let it not be so; rather, “if anyone serves me, let him follow me.” But who serves me except the one who bears my standard on his forehead, my word in his mouth, and who performs or handles my sacraments with hands and mouth? Whoever that person is, then, let him follow me—that is, imitate me.

In what? Namely, if such an hour comes upon him as now comes upon me, of which I said shortly before, “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified” [Col. 0662A] [Col. 0662B], let him prefer, for my sake, to fall into the earth and die, as the grain of wheat is sown, so that he may be a good example to those entrusted to him, rather than, by denying the faith of his ministry, believe the persecutor and so become chaff rather than grain, carried about by a light wind. But if the storm of persecution is absent, even then let him hate his soul: deny his own will, abhor and choke his own desire, hate himself as the person he remembers having been, and bury that self in the deep pit of repentance.

For the Lord commands in the Law that, when someone goes out to attend to nature’s necessities, he should put a stake in his belt and dig a pit in the ground to conceal what has been discharged (Deut. 23). What does that discharge into the pit signify mystically, except renunciation of the old life? Certainly, for one serving in the camp of Israel—that is [Col. 0662C], according to the other evangelists, one who bears the cross set before him and follows Christ—to abhor his discharge and bury it so that others need not be ashamed, means to hate the former desires of his soul and conceal them, beneath the covering of a better life, from the eyes of God and men.

Therefore, not as certain malignant and perverse persons supposed—murderers crueler and more criminal toward themselves—must the one who follows Christ’s footsteps kill himself. Rather, in persecution he must suffer the violence of death from another; but in the peace of the Church, “crucify his flesh with its vices and desires” (Gal. 5), and in this way serve Christ—that is, follow Christ. Consider now whether the sufferings of this present time are comparable with the glory to be revealed in such servants [Col. 0662D] (Rom. 8). For he says: “And where I am, there also shall my servant be.”

But what great thing could it have seemed to those hearing this to be with him? For where was he when he said it? Certainly in the thorny field of this world: one single, naked grain of wheat, soon to fall into the earth and die, as he had said shortly before. Hear, then, what follows:

“If anyone serves me, my Father will honor him.” Taken together with what he had said shortly before—“The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified”—and with what he would afterward say, “Father, glorify your name,” and the rest, this saying teaches that it is no slight thing to be with him; no small honor is indicated in being with the Son of God; it is no cheap thing to be glorified with the Only-begotten of the eternal Father [Col. 0663A]. “But,” you say, “in this sense it seemed that he should have said: ‘And where I shall be, there also shall my servant be.’” To this I reply: Although he spoke these words while still in narrowness and troubled, as he would shortly say, “Now is my soul troubled,” the end of his distress was so near that he could rightly speak as though already elsewhere: “Now I am no longer in the world” (John 17), because of the nearness of his then-imminent departure, though he spoke as one capable of suffering and still mortal in this world. Therefore, “Where I am,” he says—that is, in my kingdom, where I shall afterward be—“there also shall my servant be.”

Thus in the other evangelists, when he had said nearly the same things about hating the soul as he says here [Col. 0663B], he immediately added: “Amen, I say to you, there are some standing here who shall not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom” (Matt. 16; Luke 9). He was indeed then seen by them in that kingdom when, after his resurrection, appearing openly to all his disciples, he showed in many proofs the glory of his immortality; and on the fortieth day, ascending into heaven (Acts 1), as a victorious king, now triumphing and reigning, he led captivity itself captive (Eph. 4; Ps. 67). He foreshadowed the glory of that kingdom when, eight days after these sayings, he was transfigured on the mountain, taking Peter with James and John, the sons of Zebedee (Matt. 26). Therefore the labor of the present ministry is in no way comparable with the future glory or the honor of the Father’s reward [Col. 0663C]. Since that reward cannot be explained in words, he was content to say only: “And where I am, there also shall my servant be; if anyone serves me, my Father will honor him.”

What then, O Son of Man, since the hour has come for you to be glorified by dying and rising again, like a grain of wheat with abundant fruit for our salvation? He says: “Now is my soul troubled. But what shall I say? Father, save me from this hour. But for this reason I came to this hour. Father, glorify your name.” These are the words of one and the same Jesus Christ, both man and possessing both natures, as another evangelist says [Col. 0663D]: “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matt. 26). Because the flesh is weak, he says: “Now is my soul troubled.” And, as another evangelist relates, he began “to be afraid and distressed, and to be sorrowful unto death” (Mark 14). Here “soul,” there “flesh,” is used for the whole human substance. Thus Exodus says of whole persons that Jacob went down into Egypt with seventy-five souls (Exod. 1); conversely, “flesh” is used in the prophet for the whole human substance when he says: “All flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Isa. 40).

Therefore, according to the true human nature—which Eutyches thought had been consumed by the divine nature, and which many other heretics denied to be in Christ—he now says: “My soul [Col. 0664A] is troubled.” And he added: “And what shall I say?” As if saying: “I am constrained by two things: on the one hand, the greatest love urging me to lay down my soul for my friends; on the other, the trembling weakness of flesh pressing me to escape this cup. ‘Father,’ he says, ‘save me from this hour.’” This is the fearful utterance of weak flesh, corresponding to what he says elsewhere: “Abba, Father, if it is possible, remove this cup from me” (Luke 12; Mark 14). But because the spirit is willing, he immediately opposes the will of the flesh and says: “But for this reason I came to this hour.”

As though the Son of God and Son of Man, weak and strong in himself, afraid and trusting, said: “The inclination or weakness of flesh desires that you, Father, save me from this hour by removing this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will but yours be done: that is, not the will of human nature, but that of divine reason. For this reason I came to this hour; for this reason I descended from heaven to earth; for this reason I, who was immortal God, became mortal man; for this reason I have now entered the city, where shortly before the chief priests and Pharisees gathered a council against me: so that I might persevere ‘unto death, even death on a cross’” (Phil. 2).

Therefore, “O Father” [282], according to your will, “glorify your name” [Col. 0664B]: namely, so that, as I said shortly before, the grain of wheat may not remain alone, but may fall into the earth and die in order to bear much fruit. Your name, I say—that name by which I address you when I say “Father,” the name proper to your person—glorify, Father, in the manner now described, so that the world may know why you are called, or are [Col. 0664C], Father.

“Then a voice came from heaven, saying: ‘I have glorified it, and I shall glorify it again.’” Why this fatherly voice came from heaven is afterward declared by the Son himself, to whom the voice came. “And I have glorified it,” he says—“once” must be understood—on account of what follows: “and I shall glorify it again.” For if he had meant many glorifications of whatever kind, “I have glorified it, and I shall glorify it” would certainly have sufficed without the adverb “again.” Thus it is clear that two definite glorifications of the Father’s name are to be understood—not merely any glorifications, given such a time, such a cause, such a speaker, and a voice not from just anyone but from the Father: a voice, I say, coming not from anywhere whatsoever but from heaven [Col. 0664D].

Therefore the two glorifications of the Son which must be understood here, in whom without doubt the Father’s name is glorified, are those which the Apostle expresses to the Colossians in these words: “He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature, because in him all things were created in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones, dominions, principalities, or powers: all things were created through him and in him; and he is before all things, and all things subsist in him” (Col. 1). This concerns the first glorification, of which the Father now said, “I have glorified it.” The Apostle continues concerning the second glorification, of which the Father likewise says, “And I shall glorify it again”: “And he is the head of the body, the Church; he is the [Col. 0665A] Beginning, the firstborn from the dead, so that in all things he may hold the primacy, because in him it pleased all fullness to dwell, and through him to reconcile all things to himself, making peace through the blood of his cross, whether things on earth or things in heaven” (Col. 1).

Thus, by the repeated glorification of the Son—to whom “Father” is said relatively—the very name “Father” is glorified: he through whom the Father made all things in the most glorious work of creation restores all things through him in the most glorious restoration by his blood. Of this same repetition of glorification he says elsewhere: “Glorify me, Father, with yourself, with the glory which I had with you before the world was” (John 17). It follows:

“Therefore the crowd which stood and heard said [Col. 0665B] that there had been thunder; others said: ‘An angel has spoken to him.’” As regards the outward miracle, the greatness of the voice coming from heaven is indicated by the fact that the crowd thought thunder had occurred. As regards the inward mystery, it indicates the differing understanding of the hearers. For others said, “An angel has spoken to him”; this signifies that not all would receive with the same understanding the sound of the foretold glorification, which was to go forth into all the earth. Just as some thought the one and same voice was thunder—a terrifying sound in which nothing is intelligible—while others regarded it as angelic speech, in which there is surely the dignity of rational nature along with understanding, so some would receive the one and same Gospel of Christ’s glorification as foolishness, while others would receive it as the wisdom of God.

Hence the Apostle says: “But we preach Jesus Christ crucified: to the Jews indeed a scandal, to the Gentiles foolishness, but to those who are called, Jews and Gentiles alike, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1). Again: “For the word of the cross,” he says, “is indeed foolishness to those who perish; but to those who are being saved—that is, to us—it is the power of God” (ibid.). Rightly, therefore, with their understandings divided, some said that thunder had crashed, others that an angel had spoken.

“Jesus answered: ‘This voice came not for my sake, but for yours.’” Not, he says, did this voice come so that I might know what I did not previously know—I who shortly before said, “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified”—but that you too might now believe, confirmed by heavenly testimony [Col. 0665D]. But what does this promise of glorification mean? Or what sort of glorification will it be? Hear now: “Now is the judgment of the world; now shall the prince of this world be cast out.”

In these two clauses he embraces all the fruit which he had earlier said would spring abundantly from the grain of wheat put to death: “Now is the judgment of the world, and now shall the prince of this world be cast out.” It must be noted that he said two things separately and distinctly: the judgment of the world and the casting out of the prince of this world. It must also be noted that he varied the tenses of the verbs. For he said, “Now is the judgment of the world,” in the present tense; and, “Now shall the prince of this world be cast out,” in the future tense. Furthermore, it must be understood that he means two worlds: one hostile and the other reconciled; or one condemned and the other saved. For first he says without the article, “There is judgment of the world,” but secondly, distinctly with the article, “the prince,” he says, “of this world.”

What then is the judgment of the world, and what is the casting out of the prince of this world? Certainly the present Passion of the Lord Jesus Christ himself, who speaks these words, is “the judgment of the world”: that is, a salvation separating from the reprobate the whole body of the elect who had existed from the beginning of the age until the hour of that Passion [Col. 0666A]. The casting out of the prince of this world, who holds dominion over all lovers of the world, is the reconciliation of the elect Gentiles, in whom the devil dwells through idolatry, before the aforesaid glorification [Col. 0666B] of the same Lord. For as soon as the Passion then being undergone was completed, the judgment of the world took place: that is, by the victor’s right, the captivity of the whole people of saints who awaited him in the lower regions was loosed. But after his resurrection and ascension and the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, the prince of this world was to be cast out from the hearts—and even the temples or shrines—of the Gentiles, so that, as faith flourished, they might be converted into altars of Christ. Therefore, after saying in the present tense, “Now is the judgment of the world,” he immediately added in the future tense, “Now shall the prince of this world be cast out.”

As if he said: “Until now the strong man armed guarded his courtyard and held in peace, [Col. 0666C] as though by victor’s right, all that he had seized by bold robbery or serpentine deception” (Luke 11). From the time he captured the first man, no one of the whole human race stood against him face to face, summoned him to judgment, or put forward in court a case against his usurpation. But now one stronger than he has come upon him, and, with the case first set out, the question is asked to whom the courtyard of the world which that strong man occupied ought to belong, along with the spoils and weapons in which he trusted. Therefore now is the judgment of the world; and I know that, after the prince of this world has been cast out, the victorious one who came upon him will take away all his weapons and seize and scatter his spoils. How shall this judgment take place? Who will be the victor? Who is that stronger one who will receive the kingdom when the prince of this world is cast out? He says:

[Col. 0666D] “And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself. But he said this, signifying by what death he was to die.” This, [283] he says, is the judgment; and in this way the prince of this world shall be cast out. “If I am lifted up from the earth”—that is, if I am obedient “to the Father unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. 2); if, I say, I am lifted up—indeed, when I am lifted up, for I do not doubt that I shall be lifted up and exalted in this way—then I shall rise against the devil, prince of this world, and having conquered him, “I shall draw all things to myself.”

What things? Certainly the elect, as all members follow their head. All things, I say: the entire multitude of believers, without regard to or distinction among persons or offices [Col. 0667B], so that, as the Apostle says, “there is neither male nor female, Gentile nor Jew, circumcision nor uncircumcision, barbarian nor Scythian, slave nor free, but Christ is all things and in all” (Col. 3). Yet this may rightly be understood not only of grace, by which he draws only the elect to himself, but also of power. By this power he draws to himself not only the elect but also all the reprobate, because the Father gave his Son authority to execute judgment “because he is the Son of Man”; and he has bent every knee to himself—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth (Phil. 2), so that every human being, good or evil, may be subject to his power and rule; all may be judged by him according to their merits; and the devil himself may be cast down by no one other than that Son of Man who was lifted up on the cross, in the sight of all [Col. 0667A].

Why then do you groan together, Pharisees, saying among yourselves: “You see that we accomplish nothing; behold, the whole world has gone after him,” as though, once you have killed this Son of Man, no one will go after him? Lift him up from the earth as quickly as possible, and it will be openly shown to you how much you have accomplished, while he declares and openly demonstrates through the signs which follow: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. 28; Ps. 88). Knowing this without doubt and already foretelling it, he says: “And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself.”

“The crowd answered him: ‘We have heard from the Law that Christ remains forever. How then do you say [Col. 0667C], “The Son of Man must be lifted up”? Who is this Son of Man?’” Are you not then, like the lame, also one-eyed, O Jews, seeing in only one direction? Did he say only that he was to be lifted up from the earth, and did he not add that he would “draw all things to himself”? Why then did you attend only to what signified that he would die, and compare it with the Law’s testimony that Christ remains forever? Surely, for Christ to be lifted up from the earth and to draw all things to himself is the same as for Christ to die and remain forever. But how did you so quickly perceive even this, that he had said, “The Son of Man must be lifted up”? At another time, when he likewise said: “When you have lifted up the Son of Man from the earth, then you shall know that I am,” you showed neither anything of the kind which you now object, nor in any way that you understood what he was saying (John 8).

Whence then, except because, shortly before, the chief priests and Pharisees, having gathered a council, had determined this counsel with you: not only to kill him, but also to kill him by the lifting up of the cross? It is therefore no wonder that you understood in his words what you were devising to do while lying in wait in the hidden chamber of conscience [Col. 0667D].

“Jesus therefore said to them: ‘Yet a little while the light is among you. Walk while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you.’” This Son of Man, he says, is Christ; and, as you have heard from the Law, he indeed remains forever, but he has not yet reached that place [Col. 0668A] where he “remains forever” immortally and impassibly. “Yet a little while the light is among you”: while, with the Scripture of the Law shining, you know that “Christ remains forever,” this is lacking to you, and this you do not see: that the very lifting up of which I spoke is Christ’s passage into the eternal kingdom. Therefore, “while you have the light,” while you are able to use the light of truth, “walk,” so that you also may arrive at Christ’s eternity. For the darkness of death will come, in which no one can now walk, as I said elsewhere: “Night is coming, when no one can work” (John 9).

During this delay of the light—that is, of the present life—there is opportunity to seek from the Law the whole truth concerning Christ: that he indeed remains forever, yet ascends to that eternity only [Col. 0668B] by the way of Passion and death. Walk, I say; run and finish before the outer darkness overtakes you. For after the course of the present life, no lamp of the Scriptures will be available to anyone by which he may arrive at Christ who remains forever. This is what follows:

“And he who walks in darkness does not know where he goes.” For the everlasting darkness is in the lower regions, of which he had said: “Walk while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you”—darkness which overtakes slackened hands and weakened knees; whoever walks in that darkness does not know where he goes (Heb. 12). Hence Ecclesiastes says: “Whatever your hand is able to do, do earnestly, because there shall be neither work, nor reason, nor knowledge, nor [Col. 0668C] wisdom in the lower regions to which you are hastening” (Eccl. 9). Similar to this is what the Lord adds:

“While you have the light, believe in the light, that you may be children of light.” What else does the prophet cry when he says: “Seek the Lord while he may be found; call upon him while he is near” (Isa. 55)? “While you have the light,” he says—that is, while you are in this life, where you have the word of the Law and the Prophets like a lamp shining in a dark place, through which you can find Christ, the true light—“believe in the light, that you may be children of light.” That is: believe in Christ, so that there, where you hear from the Law that Christ remains forever, having the adoption as children of God, you too may remain with him forever.

[Col. 0668D] “Jesus spoke these things, and went away, and hid himself from them.” In the other evangelists, we plainly have that, after his already-mentioned entry into the city, he was teaching daily in the Temple (Matt. 26; Luke 19); but here, seemingly differently from them: “He went away,” he says, “and hid himself from them.” What then does this indicate except, mystically, their blindness? For he makes sufficiently clear in the following course of the reading that by such hiding—that is, their blindness—he signified this. For it follows:

“When he had performed so many signs before them, they did not believe in him, so that the saying of Isaiah which he spoke might be fulfilled: ‘Lord, who has believed our report, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?’ (Isa. 53).” For what else is it that the arm of the Lord was not revealed to them, but precisely what the Evangelist plainly expresses when he says: “He hid himself from them” [Col. 0669A]. The Evangelist very fittingly draws upon this lamenting prophecy at this point. For when the prophet spoke these things, he saw with spiritual eye both the glorification of the Son of Man—by which he was to be glorified among the nations, as said above—and the unbelief of the Jews, now mentioned: that “though he had performed so many signs before them, they did not believe in him,” as the whole passage of the prophet clearly shows.

For he had said: “This one shall sprinkle many nations; kings shall keep their mouths shut because of him; for those to whom no announcement concerning him was made shall see, and those who had not heard shall contemplate” (Isa. 52). This concerns the aforementioned fruitfulness among the Gentiles. Then follows, concerning the blinding [Col. 0669B] of the Jews, the testimony quoted here: “Who has believed our report, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” Here he calls the Son of God the arm of the Lord, because, just as a person works or fights with his arm, so God made all things and defeated the devil in his Son, in his Word. And if you ask the same prophet in what respect he was not revealed, or in what respect he was hidden, he immediately adds: “And he grew up like a shoot before him, and like a root out of thirsty ground. He had neither form nor beauty” (Isa. 53), etc. Having mournfully proclaimed the Lord’s Passion in these words, he again blesses the Gentile people, to whom the fruit of that Passion was to come, saying: “Rejoice, barren woman who does not bear” (Isa. 54 [printed: Isa. VI]), etc.

Again the Evangelist [Col. 0669C] adds: “Therefore they could not believe, because Isaiah again said: ‘He blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, lest they see with their eyes and understand with their heart and turn, and I heal them’” (Isa. 6 [printed: Isa. LIV]). By appending these testimonies of prophetic Scripture, the Evangelist shows quite clearly why he said: “And he hid himself from them.”

Yet it cannot be adequately expressed with how great a rigor the Spirit of wisdom dwelling in this John arranged his words. For what sort of reasoning or cause is this—that, as though you were asking why the Lord hid himself from the Jews, or why the Jews did not believe in him, he added: “So that the saying of Isaiah which he spoke might be fulfilled”; and then, going still further, added: “Therefore they could not believe, because Isaiah again said: [Col. 0669D] ‘He blinded their eyes and hardened their heart’”? Did he think that he had satisfactorily resolved the very question he himself raised?

Indeed, though no one had asked him why the Jews had not believed in the Lord, he himself voluntarily raised a vast question. For even today people do not cease disputing about God’s foreknowledge or predestination; nor are sinners lacking who dare to excuse themselves, saying that they cannot be good because God foreknew and predestined that they would be evil. Such people, excusing themselves and accusing God, find support for their folly in what is written in this passage of evangelical authority: “Unless the foreknowledge or predestination of God,” they say, “exerted force upon human wills, so great an Evangelist would not have spoken in this way and that” [Col. 0670A]. But to such presumptuous reasoners about God’s judgments and ways, the apostle Paul judges that no answer is more fitting than this: “O man, who are you to answer back to God? Can the potter say to the one who formed it: Why did you make me thus?” (Rom. 9).

For this Evangelist answers such persons in the same Spirit when, after saying, “They did not believe in him,” he adds, “so that the saying of the prophet might be fulfilled”; and likewise, “Therefore they could not believe, because Isaiah again says…” For who are they to answer God, or to whom is any account to be rendered of divine judgments? [Col. 0670B]

But to those who are gentle and rightly disposed in the spirit of piety to hear, he proceeds, following the Apostle in the passage already mentioned, to begin giving a profound reason: “God, willing,” he says, “to make known his wrath and to show his power, endured with much patience vessels of wrath fitted for destruction” (Rom. 9), and the rest. And the Lord himself says in another Evangelist: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones. Yes, Father, because thus it was pleasing before you” (Matt. 11).

The Apostle, giving the effective cause of Israelite blindness, called them vessels of wrath; but the Lord called these same people wise and prudent, from whom the Father had hidden these things—namely, his mysteries—which he deigned to reveal to little ones. Both statements signify that pride is the cause of blindness. For why were they called wise and prudent by the Lord [Col. 0670C], except because they were proud? This is especially clear from the contrast with the little ones, that is, the humble, who are worthy of the Father’s revelation. And why were they called vessels of wrath by the Apostle, except because they were children of pride?

Likewise, after the Psalmist had said, “You are terrible, and who can resist you?” he immediately added, “from that time, your wrath” (Ps. 75). For indeed, from the moment God is resisted, his wrath is present. For as long as sin is committed through weakness or ignorance, he overlooks human sins and, sparing people, awaits repentance. Therefore, when the Apostle calls certain persons vessels of wrath, by such a fitting designation he indicates to his hearers that they resisted God; and consequently the just God willed to harden them, as he did Pharaoh [Col. 0670D] (Exod. 10), in retribution for their pride, or to blind their hearts so that they might not recognize Christ.

And when the Lord calls the same persons wise and prudent, in contrast with little ones, that is, the humble, and shortly afterward says to those same little ones, “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble in heart” (Matt. 11), he shows that the cause of the concealment for which he gives thanks to the Father is pride. Thus also in this passage, when the Evangelist says, “He blinded their eyes and hardened their hearts,” and implies, saying, “lest they see with their eyes and understand with their heart,” he certainly thought that attentive hearers would have no doubt why God had done this: for he has never blinded or hardened either the devil or any human being without a preceding sin of pride.

Therefore God’s innocent and holy foreknowledge imposes no necessity upon evil people, just as my seeing a person whom I see walking imposes no necessity of walking upon him [Col. 0671A]. This is the argument advanced with great force by sound and true philosophy when disputing with certain Christian philosophers. But enough of this. Let us now return to the words of the passage itself.

First we must ask what distinction is made between the statement, “He blinded their eyes,” and the following statement, “He hardened their heart”; or between, “lest they see with their eyes,” and the addition, “and understand with their heart” [Col. 0671B]. For does not failing to see with the eyes seem to be the same as failing to understand with the heart? Or are blinded eyes not the same as a hardened heart? Why then are both said?

Clearly, among those who do not deserve to be converted and healed, some do not even see the meaning of the Scriptures, while others do see it but refuse to follow it. Concerning those who do not see: “He blinded,” he says, “their eyes, lest they see with their eyes.” But concerning those who see and refuse to follow: “He hardened,” he says, “their heart, lest they understand with their heart”—that is, lest what they see through knowledge of the plain letter should become pleasing to them through love.

Immediately after the testimony from the prophet just cited, the Evangelist says:

“This Isaiah said when he saw his glory and spoke of him.” It is as though he said: The prophetic vision in which Isaiah said these things displayed his glory—that glory, namely, which the Lord himself was now declaring to be at hand in the words: “The hour has come [Col. 0671C] for the Son of Man to be glorified,” and in the other matters he has discussed so far. This is the vision which the same prophet begins thus: “In the year in which Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting upon a high and exalted throne, and the things beneath him filled the temple. Seraphim stood above it; six wings to one and six wings to the other. And they cried one to another: Holy, holy, holy, the Lord God of Sabaoth; the whole earth is full of his glory” (Isa. 6).

Therefore, the appearance of the seated Lord, with holy spirits standing around him as officials or ministers—who are called *Seraphim* only in this passage of Scripture—mystically proclaims this glorification of the Son of God. Once it had been accomplished, his ministers preached the faith of the holy [Col. 0671D] Trinity throughout the whole world, and thus the Seraphim cried: “Holy, holy, holy, the Lord God of Sabaoth.” The house was filled with smoke: that is, with the smoke of unbelief by which, as has already been said, “he blinded the eyes of the Jews.”

It follows:

“Nevertheless, many even of the rulers believed in him; but because of the Pharisees they did not confess him, lest they should be expelled from the synagogue. For they loved human glory more than the glory of God.” Therefore those did not truly believe who, receiving glory from human beings, preferred their glory to the glory of God. For he himself said elsewhere: “How can you believe, who seek glory from one another and do not seek the glory which is from God alone?” (John 5).

“Not only,” he says [Col. 0672A], “did many from the crowd, who went out to meet him with palm branches, believe in him; but many also from among the rulers—that is, the leading Jews—believed in him. But because the Pharisees, that is, the Jewish clergy, had long ago conspired that, if anyone confessed him to be Christ, they would cast him out of the synagogue, they did not confess him, lest they should be expelled from the synagogue. Nevertheless,” he says—that is, although I said above: “Though he had performed so many signs before them, they did not believe in him”—many of the rulers believed, but, shamefully embarrassed, did not confess him.

“But Jesus cried out and said: He who believes in me, believes not in me, but in him who sent me. And he who sees me sees him who sent me.” This is a great example of steadfast courage, a great and laborious cry [Col. 0672B], if you consider not only that he cried out until now, but also what he cried, what sort of person he still was, and among what sort of people he cried. For what did he cry? “He who believes in me,” he says, “believes not in me, but in him who sent me.”

This is to say: O people, loving the glory of names more than the glory of God, why are you ashamed to believe in me? Or why are you ashamed to confess what you believe concerning me? Do you suppose that the end of your faith or confession is established in that which you see in me with bodily eyes? No, but rather in the one whom the Father sent: that is, in the Word of the Father, which is the Beginning. “For I am the Beginning, who also speak to you.” Therefore it is neither inglorious nor contemptible to believe in me. For no one can believe in me without believing [Col. 0672C] in him who sent me; nor can anyone believe in him who sent me without believing in me. Indeed, “he who sees me sees him who sent me.” Nor can anyone otherwise see or know what substance he is of, how great he is, what he can do, or what he thinks, who sent me, unless he sees me.

This is what he cried, and he had long labored in crying out; already “his throat had become hoarse” (Ps. 69). Thus afterward “he was silent like a lamb before the one shearing him, and did not open his mouth” (Isa. 53). And because of such a cry, those who hated him, blinded by envy, had already become numerous. For what sort of person was he, and among what sort did he proclaim this? Certainly, he was not only mortal and passible, and in nothing according to nature different from the people among whom he walked [Col. 0672D], but also needy and poor, embracing nothing of the kingdom or honors of this world. Yet he said this among fleshly and proud people, swollen with the wind of human glory; and, what is more, among those whose eyes God had blinded and whose heart he had hardened, as was said above, so that they not only did not believe his words and deeds, but moreover blasphemed, saying: “He has a demon and is mad; why do you listen to him?” (John 10).

Therefore he cried out courageously, since the whole spirit of strength was in him; yet he cried out in human vulnerability as well. For he had not lost the bearing of one meek and humble in heart, nor was he free from the constraint of human shame, since he himself says in the Psalm: “Because of you I endured reproach; shame covered [Col. 0673A] my face” (Ps. 43 [citation printed: Ps. XLIII]).

Let us hear what follows in this same cry: “I came as light into the world, so that whoever believes in me may not remain in darkness.” Let a rational person say in response: If Christ is light—indeed, because he is light and the true light—and if he came into the world for this purpose, that whoever believes in him should not remain in darkness, ought he not to bear witness concerning himself? Would he not have come into the world in vain if he remained silent and did not reveal himself? What thief or robber would wish a lighted lamp to be put in a hidden place or under a bushel, rather than placed upon a lampstand so that it may give light to all who are in the house?

Therefore, whether at a fitting time or not, let the Light cry out—not from desire for his own glory, but because our eyes need it—“He who believes in me believes in him who sent me”; and likewise, “He who sees [Col. 0673B] me sees him who sent me.” Thus, in showing himself, let him disregard the envy of evil eyes, provided that he may gladden the goodwill of the simple. “I,” he says, “came as light into the world.” For what purpose? “That everyone who believes in me may not remain in darkness.”

Therefore those who, as mentioned above, believed in him but did not confess him, loving human glory more than God’s glory, acted contrary to the law of faith. For believing in this way, they remained in darkness. It follows:

“But if anyone hears my words and does not keep them, I do not judge him. For I did not come to judge the world, but to save the world. He who despises me and does not receive my words has one who judges him. The word which I have spoken shall judge him [Col. 0673C] on the last day.”

Judgment in the sense of condemnation has already been spoken of in this Evangelist in three ways. There is one sense in which he said: “I came into this world for judgment, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind.” There is another in which he now says: “I do not judge him.” And there is another in which he likewise now says: “The word which I have spoken to you shall judge him on the last day.” The first and third are familiar and self-evident in meaning; but the middle statement—“I do not judge him; for I did not come to judge the world”—is understood from the contrast that he immediately gives: “But to save the world.”

For how did he save the world? Certainly by undergoing judgment—that is, condemnation—when, accused before the judge Pontius Pilate as though guilty of treason, he was delivered to the ministers of Roman power to be crucified [Col. 0673D]. Therefore, from this contrast in which he says, “But to save the world,” it is clear what he means by saying, “I do not judge him.” It is the same as though he said: My kingdom or judgment is not here—that is, not of this world. If it were of this world, my ministers would certainly fight to preserve my words. But now my kingdom or judgment is not from here, and therefore I do not now judge him.

The order or wording of the text is as follows: “But if anyone hears my words, I do not judge him.” “I told you,” he says, “that I came as light into the world, so that whoever believes in me may not remain in darkness. Yet people hear my words carelessly and do not take care to keep them because ‘I do not judge him,’ whoever he may be; because I do not sit as king upon the thrones of tyrants; because I do not demand with swords and axes that my decree be observed. For I did not come to judge the world in this manner, but rather so that, judged in this manner, I might save the world.”

What then? Will those who despise the King of heaven escape unpunished? “Will I always be silent, always hold my peace, always be patient, [Col. 0674A] and bring them into no judgment?” It is not so; it shall not be so; it shall not happen so. “For he who despises me has one who judges him.” He has one, I say; I do not say that he will have one, but that he already has a judge, even if the judge’s sentence or vengeance is not yet apparent.

Who then is that judge? “The word which I have spoken to you shall judge him on the last day.” That word, he says, which they heard and cannot fail to know is true, being confirmed by splendid testimonies of works—that word shall judge him; it shall accuse him; it shall convict him. Where will such a judge sit, and from what throne will he deliver the voices or sentences of his judgment? He will be near; he will sit within; he will resound terrifyingly with just sentences in each person’s conscience. For the Apostle also says: “Their conscience shall bear witness to them, and their thoughts shall accuse or even defend one another, on the day when God shall judge the hidden things of people according to my Gospel” (Rom. 2). Thus “the word which I have spoken shall judge him on the last day.”

Whence does this word have such power? He says:

[Col. 0674C] “Because I have not spoken from myself, but the Father who sent me gave me a commandment, what I should say and what I should speak.” The word which I have spoken, he says, has power to judge because I do not speak from myself; because I have not merely fabricated something from my own heart, in accordance with the presumption of the false prophet whom the Law commands should not be feared (Deut. 18 [printed: Deut. II]). Rather, “the Father who sent me”—by that sending whereby he is my Father—gave me a commandment. He himself commanded me, obedient in the commandment of incarnation and Passion, “what I should say and what I should speak”: what I should now say patiently to those who contradict, and what I shall say terrifyingly at the future judgment, where no one will dare to contradict.

If I had spoken from myself—that is, from a human being or according to the human being whom alone [Col. 0674D] you see in me and whom alone you think me to be—then the word which I spoke would be weak, indeed dead. “But now it is living and effectual, and more piercing than any two-edged sword, reaching even to the dividing of soul and spirit, of joints also and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart. And no creature is invisible in his sight; but all things are naked and exposed to his eyes” (Heb. 4). Therefore he shall judge in truth, therefore in equity. The one who sent me gave me the commandment, and from him I speak such a word.

“And I know that his commandment is eternal life.” I carry out his commandment to speak and act in this manner not with uncertain hope or doubtful expectation, but “I know,” and know well, “that his commandment is eternal life”—that is, it is the effective cause of eternal life for all believers. For I did not speak just before, amid uncertain outcomes: “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified,” and shortly afterward: “And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, shall draw all things to myself,” and similar words. “Therefore, what I speak, I speak as the Father has told me.”

If the beneficial result of [Col. 0676A] this word were not apparent, it would rightly be contemptible, as though not commanded by the Father. But now its fruit is eternal life, and this is demonstrated by many testimonies: while some return through repentance from the death of the soul to life, others also, dead in body, rise again at the command of this same word. Therefore it is true, therefore incontestable, that I do not fabricate what I say as a false prophet; rather, “as the Father has told me”—such is the Father’s will—I speak these things.

BOOK ELEVEN.

[Col. 0675]

[Col. 0675B] For a long time now the Catholic Church has given great thanks to the Holy Spirit dwelling in this Evangelist, because he preserved with such integrity the riches of grace and truth, poured from the mouth of Christ’s fullness into his profound memory, and because he poured them forth again at the fitting time with such faithfulness that heretical poverty, anywhere on earth, has not dared to boast itself rich against us in any substance of truth.

All the things which he has said thus far are indeed the glory and riches of his house—that is, of his breast consecrated to God. But the things which he will say hereafter are precious wealth and a desirable treasure. For their whole sequence, up to the gibbet of the cross, is the reading of the Testament which our Father wrote while dying; it is the designation of the inheritance which, in the very agony of death, he bequeathed with wondrous love to his little children.

Let the orphans stand by—though they were not there—and listen to the one now reading who was present, who received the words of the Testament as the dying man’s finger wrote them upon fleshly tablets of the heart. Let them hear with greater certainty where they should hope for their inheritance and to what Paraclete and guardian they should meanwhile look.

Therefore, just as the words which a most loving father spoke, uttered, commanded, requested, or admonished while drawing his final breath in death are usually sweeter to devoted and loving children, and remain more deeply in their memory, so we must receive with reverent ear, devout heart, and humble spirit, and entrust to faithful memory, the things which he now begins most usefully to pour forth in this manner—things diligently heard by one who was present, faithfully preserved, and now disclosed.

## Chapter XIII

[Col. 0676B]

“Before the feast-day of the Passover, Jesus, knowing that his hour had come for him to pass from this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world, loved them to the end.”

The holy catholic Church confesses that Christ the Lord was the true Lamb of God, sacrificed for the salvation of the whole world, and that he set forth that lamb as his figure—the lamb which, at the Lord’s command through Moses, the whole multitude of the children of Israel sacrificed in Egypt at evening. The whole house of Israel—that is, the universal Church which eats the flesh and drinks the blood of that same true Lamb (Exod. XII)—confesses this.

Nor does it fail to know that the feast-day of Passover, which that people celebrated with the greatest solemnity, was a commemoration of that divine benefit; and that it was called Passover, which means “passing over,” and in Hebrew is called *phase*, because the Lord passed over the dwellings of the children of Israel marked with the blood of the lamb; and, after the firstborn of Egypt had been slain, made those same Israelites pass through the Red Sea, Pharaoh, who pursued them, being drowned together with all the Egyptians.

[Col. 0676C]

It is therefore clear why, when the Evangelist had said, “Before the feast-day of the Passover,” he immediately added, “Jesus, knowing that his hour had come for him to pass from this world to the Father”: namely, in order to signify to the teachable pupil of evangelical truth that the whole shadowy sacrifice of the ancient Passover was holy for this reason: because it prefigured the Lord Jesus, who through the passion of death was to pass from this world to the Father for the salvation of the world.

“For before the feast-day of the Passover” is as though he had said: on that day immediately followed by the feast-day of Passover. It was the fourteenth day of the moon of the first month; and on the following evening of that day, when the moon was already completely full and the fifteenth day begins for us, the lamb, as has already been said, was sacrificed, with great mysteries shining forth: not only because the moon was full, but also because this great solemnity was observed only after the vernal equinox, when the days begin to overcome the night, upon the first occurrence of the full moon.

[Col. 0676D]

For the full moon signifies the fullness of time, when the Church, already multiplied through past generations, awaited in the underworld the redemption to be sent from heaven. The lengthening day, now overcoming the night, signifies that through the mystery of Christ’s passion the bright knowledge of truth would now begin, in reverse of the previous state, to prevail among all nations against the darkness of errors which had hitherto prevailed. But this is not the moment to discuss such matters individually.

[Col. 0677A]

“Jesus therefore, knowing,” he says, “that his hour had come for him to pass from this world to the Father”: that very hour, with reference to which this same Evangelist had earlier said, “And no one laid hands on him, because his hour had not yet come” (John VII). Of it the Lord himself also said elsewhere, “My time has not yet come” (ibid.).

“Having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end.” This is said with great grace. “Having loved his own,” he says: that is, those whom he had chosen from the beginning to be his own. For, lest we should suppose that this means only the apostles, or only the people of Israel according to election—of whom Caiaphas had previously, though unknowingly, prophesied that Jesus would die for the nation (John XI)—he did not merely say “his own,” but added, “who were in the world,” so that we may understand all the elect. For assuredly he was not to die only for the nation, but also to gather into one the dispersed children of God.

[Col. 0677B]
