Therefore, “having loved his own who were in the world” is as though he had said: Having begun to perform the work of great love toward his own, who, driven from paradise because of original sin, were wandering in this world. But how had he begun to love his own, and in what way did he love them to the end? Certainly he had already loved them so as to descend from heaven to earth for their sake, and so that he who was invisible God in the bosom of the Father might become visible man, made from a woman’s womb.

Yet this love was not complete. For it would have profited his own nothing that he had become man, if he had not also suffered for them. Thus he himself had said above: “Unless a grain of wheat, falling into the earth, dies, it remains alone” (John XII), and so forth. Therefore, as was fitting, “he loved them to the end”: that is, he brought his love for them to the point beyond which it could not be increased, namely, to laying down his life for them.

It follows.

“And supper having taken place, when the devil had already put it into the heart of Judas, son of Simon Iscariot, to betray him, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he had come forth from God and was going to God, he rises from supper and lays aside his garments. And having taken a towel, he girded himself.” And “then he pours water into a basin and began to wash the disciples’ feet, and to wipe them with the towel with which he was girded.”

[Col. 0677D]

These words of the Evangelist call for an attentive hearer; the deeds of our Lord Jesus Christ call for an eager spectator. For his deeds are wonderful and most beautiful: he rises from supper before it is yet finished, lays aside his garments, girds himself with a towel, washes the disciples’ feet, and then reclines again, teaching in the bearing of Lord and Master what he had done in the bearing of an inferior and a servant.

The Evangelist’s words, moreover, are most prudent, because he almost explained the cause of what the Lord did in this manner, yet did not wholly disclose it. For before the four clauses concerning the Lord’s acts, he likewise set four clauses, saying: “Jesus, knowing that his hour had come for him to pass from this world to the Father”; and, “knowing that he was going to God.”

He almost explained it, I say, as though he said: “Knowing that his hour had come for him to pass,” he therefore rose after supper had begun, which signified his own passing; for he was eating the Passover. “And knowing that he had come forth from God,” he therefore laid aside his garments; “and knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands,” he therefore washed the disciples’ feet; “and knowing that he was going to God,” he therefore, after washing their feet, took his garments again and reclined again.

[Col. 0678A]

Let us therefore repeat and explain these matters more fully. “He loved them to the end,” he says, and “supper having taken place”: it is to be understood that he chose to perform that act by which he would express his love for his own—how he had begun it and to what end he would carry it. He wished, I say, not only to declare this in words but also to enact it with significance: so that through this present image of great humility he might touch the inward affections of his own; and so that, after his resurrection, when he opened their understanding to understand the Scriptures (Luke XXIV), they might, recalling this deed with wounded memory, understand it more deeply, and understand his same love, in whose signification he, so great a one, had acted thus at such an hour and time.

[Col. 0678B]

“And supper having already taken place,” he says, “when the devil had already put it into the heart of Judas, son of Simon Iscariot, to betray him.” That supper itself which had taken place—that is, the roasted paschal lamb to be eaten with unleavened bread and wild lettuces—could be a cause why the Lamb himself, as will later be said, was troubled within himself. For he knew that the signification of his passion, celebrated by this rite through all the preceding generations from the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt, must now be fulfilled by his death in the present moment.

He knew this after supper had taken place; but he also knew that the devil had already put it into the heart of Judas, son of Simon Iscariot, to betray him—Judas who had gone away on the previous day to the Pharisees and said, “What are you willing to give me, and I will hand him over to you?” (Matt. XXVI).

[Col. 0678C]

Knowing this, and also “that the Father had given all things into his hands”—all things, I say, concerning which he had shortly before said, “And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, shall draw all things to myself” (John XIX)—and knowing “that he had come forth from God,” namely in that, though he was in the form of God, he emptied himself (Phil. II); and “that he was going to God,” namely to sit at the right hand of Majesty on high, as David said of him in the Spirit: “The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand” (Ps. CIX).

[Col. 0678D]

Knowing these things, he rises from supper, namely, in order to signify by bearing and action the ineffable works of love through admirable humility. For what did he do when he rose from supper? “He lays aside,” he says, “his garments.” What next? “Having taken a towel, he girded himself. Then he pours water into a basin and began to wash the disciples’ feet, and to wipe them with the towel with which he was girded.”

It was indeed a great and wonderful spectacle, before angels and human beings alike, to see what the Lord of angels and human beings was doing: the same one man and likewise God; the same one humble and likewise most high.

[Col. 0679A]

But when his disciples came to know who he was—that is, after he rose from the dead and opened their understanding—then, as he himself shortly afterward says, “when it has happened, you may believe that I am”; then, “seeing and understanding, they were astonished, troubled, and shaken, and pangs came upon them as upon a woman in labour” (Ps. XLVIII), because they understood what he had done, or rather what he had signified to them through such an act.

This especially beloved disciple, who at that supper reclined upon his breast (John XXI), understood what he had done for them and to what end; and, indicating this to us, he spoke thus beforehand: “Knowing that he had come forth from God and was going to God, and that the Father had given all things into his hands.”

[Col. 0679B]

Then, I say, they understood; and their souls, wounded by love, perceived how he had loved his own; how for their sake he had risen from his resting-place, from the bosom of the eternal Father, from the throne of unbounded majesty; and, laying aside the garments of his glory, emptied of the splendour which he had before the world existed, appeared so naked—that is, in every respect like us except for sin—among men.

Thus, just as Ham, the cursed servant of servants, a type of him, announced to his brothers that his father Noah lay outside, naked and asleep (Gen. IX), so the heretics Cerinthus and Marcion, and many others, maintained that this same Lord of ours was by no means God born of God before the ages, but only a man, beginning from Mary. They did this especially because, “girded with a towel”—that is, afflicted by the tribulation of the passion—he was demonstrated to be a true man by a true death.

[Col. 0679C]

In this way, they understood, he washed the feet of his own: that is, cleansed their sins. For in the naked humility of his passion he poured forth blood and water from his side (John XIX), by which he does not cease even to this day to cleanse the sins of his own.

But why did he then wash only their feet, when, according to both the outward and the inward person, he washes those who believe in him from their sins in his blood? (Rev. I.) Surely because that hour ought merely to signify the thing, not yet to perform it.

Moreover, he wished to wash feet rather than hands or head because the washing of feet is both a more affectionate gesture of humility and a nearer signification of the love by which he washes us from our sins in his blood (ibid.).

[Col. 0679D]

Finally, he not only washes us in his blood when each of us is baptized, but he also daily washes us from actual sins when we partake at the holy altar of his flesh and blood.

Those sins which even the most religious human life cannot wholly avoid are customarily signified by the dust on the feet. For example, the Lord himself says: “Into whatever house you enter, and they do not receive you, go out into its streets and say: Even the dust which has clung to us from your city, we wipe off against you” (Luke X).

This is to say: We openly remove by daily remedies even the smallest sins, without which the present life of even holy mortality, or mortal holiness, cannot wholly be passed; lest unwise people have some reproach against our life on account of which they might seem to themselves reasonably to despise your preaching.

[Col. 0680A]

The Holy Spirit signifies these stains of sins which are almost unavoidable when, in the Song of Songs, the bridegroom says, “Open to me, my sister, my beloved, my dove, my undefiled one,” and she replies, “I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on again? I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?” (Song III.)

For when the soul has put off the tunic of the active life and composed itself upon the couch in the secret place of the contemplative life, then, because it sees and hears less of the things done in the world, it shrinks, as though its feet had already been washed—that is, as though it had cast away the stains of former worldly actions—from henceforth touching the earth.

[Col. 0680B]

But if the benefit of souls requires it to go forth and, awakened as by the bridegroom’s voice, publicly serve the Gospel of Christ, it does not fail to know that it may again be slightly soiled with dust; and therefore it has greater need for Christ daily to wash its feet.

Therefore it was indeed, as has been said, a great spectacle in that upper room where the disciples had prepared the Passover for the Lord: that so great a Lord and Master rose from supper, laid aside his garments, girded himself with a towel, washed feet, and then, having again taken his garments, reclined and began to teach.

[Col. 0680C]

And far greater is the reality which was there signified most holy and devoutly: the Creator of angels and human beings emptied himself, was made a little lower than the angels, and in the form of a servant was girded with the toil and anguish of the passion, in order to wash us from our sins in his blood. Then, rising from the dead, clothed with the glory of immortality and the honour of incorruption (Ps. III), he reclined in heaven at the Father’s right hand and, having given the Holy Spirit, made us know what he had done for us.

It follows:

“Therefore he comes to Simon Peter.” “He began,” he says, “to wash the disciples’ feet.” Simon Peter was the first with whom he ought to begin.

For though Andrew, having heard John’s testimony, “Behold the Lamb of God” (John I), followed before Peter and came and saw where the Lord Jesus lived, nevertheless, in the order of the calling of the apostles, when they left all things and followed him after John had been handed over, neither Andrew nor any other was before Peter: “But the Lord saw Peter and Andrew his brother first, and called them” (Matt. IV).

Therefore, beginning to wash the disciples’ feet, he comes to Simon Peter.

[Col. 0680D]

Peter says to him, “Lord, do you wash my feet?”

“You,” he says, “whom I have confessed as the Christ, the Son of the living God, King of kings and Lord of lords—you have laid aside your garments, poured water out, and stoop into the mire in order to wash my feet?”

For he was alarmed at such great humility in his Lord and Master, while thinking humbly of himself—as any of the other disciples would have been alarmed had the Lord begun such a work of humility with him.

For they did not yet fully know the teaching of their Master: namely, that in his school the greater one was the humbler, and that the Lord of all himself reigned upon the highest summit of humility.

They did not rightly understand this; hence, according to Luke, there had even then arisen a dispute among them as to which of them seemed to be greatest.

[Col. 0681A]

Indeed, he taught them in words the true order of lordship and authority, saying: “The kings of the Gentiles lord it over them, and those who have power over them are called benefactors; but you are not so. Rather, let the greater among you become as the younger, and the leader as the one who serves; but I am in your midst as one who serves” (Luke XXII; Matt. XX).

Yet, further instructing them by deed, he openly appeared among them as one who serves, by washing their feet; and at the same time, as has been said, he signified what kind of servant he would be in this ministry, namely, that he would give his life as a ransom for many.

Therefore, when Peter had been so alarmed, “Jesus answered and said to him: What I do, you do not know now, but you shall know afterward.”

“The reason,” he says, “for which I do this you do not know now; and even if I told you, you could not bear it now. But you shall know afterward”—namely, “when the Spirit of truth comes, who will teach you both the reason for this deed and all truth” (John XVI).

“Peter says to him, ‘You shall never wash my feet.’ Jesus answered him, ‘If I do not wash you, you shall have no part with me.’”

“Why,” he says, “are you alarmed at this bearing of my humility, at this ministry? Unless I, girded yet more deeply and at greater cost, wash you, you will have no part with me.”

For unless Christ had washed his beloved ones from their sins in his blood, neither Peter nor any other human being would have had a part with him.

[Col. 0681C]

This was therefore said aptly to Peter at this point, because, while he was alarmed by the humility of such a ministry, he recoiled still more from the disgrace of the Lord’s passion, by which both he and the whole world had to be washed.

Simon Peter says to him, “Lord, not my feet only, but also my hands and my head.”

In accordance with his name Simon, he spoke well and obediently. For *Simon* is interpreted “obedient.” Accordingly, the Evangelist rightly does not say, as he had shortly before, “Peter says to him,” but “Simon Peter says to him.”

[Col. 0681D]

Jesus says to him, “He who has been washed does not need except to wash his feet, but is wholly clean.”

Here he plainly gives us to understand that he means another washing of feet, besides the outward one. For who has been washed unless it is the one whom Christ “washed from sins in his blood” (Rev. I), as has already been said?

And what benefit for preserving that spiritual purity comes from this bodily washing of feet? Do we need to wash our feet daily in order to obtain remission of sins, rather than to receive the sacraments of the Lord’s passion?

Peter therefore understands one thing; the Lord hints at another thing to be understood afterward. For when Peter says, “Lord, not my feet only, but also my hands and my head,” he answers: “He who has been washed does not need except to wash his feet, but is wholly clean.”

[Col. 0682A]

It is as though he said: The one who has once been baptized in the death now at hand need not further wash the sins committed before baptism, whether original or actual, but is wholly clean; he need only wash his feet—that is, cleanse by daily remedies the daily or common offences without which human life cannot be lived.

This is like a person who has only feet dirtied by travelling and is clean from dirt in the rest of his body: when going to bed, he needs only to wash his feet.

It follows:

“And you are clean, but not all. For he knew who it was that would betray him; therefore he said: You are not all clean.”

[Col. 0682B]

“You,” he says, “who have remained with me in my trials” (Luke XXII), “are clean, namely because of the word which I have spoken to you, because you have believed. You are clean,” I say, because “I now sanctify myself for you, that you may be holy in truth”: while I sanctify myself—that is, while I offer myself as sacrifice for you.

For I am now going to be sacrificed for you, that you may be clean; “but not all.” For this present sanctification of my passion does not benefit all of you.

“For the Evangelist says, he knew who it was that would betray him; therefore he said: You are not all clean.”

“Therefore, after he had washed their feet and taken his garments, when he had reclined again, he said to them: Do you know what I have done to you?”

Therefore, he says, since he knew the matters said above, he acted thus and thus. After he had again taken his garments and reclined again, the Lord and Master rightly opened his mouth and poured forth from it the words which follow—utterances sweeter than honey and the honeycomb (Ps. XVIII).

[Col. 0682C]

For after, rising from death, he put on the glorious garment of immortality and incorruption, then, through his interpreter the Holy Spirit, whom he sent from heaven, he made his own understand what he had done to them, according to what the Psalmist says in his person: “The right hand of the Lord has wrought power; the right hand of the Lord has exalted me. I shall not die, but live, and shall declare the works of the Lord” (Ps. CXVII).

Accordingly he says, “Do you know what I have done to you?” By this question, the orator of grace and truth awakens his hearers in order to make them attentive. When we are asked what we do not know, we are accustomed to listen more attentively, as though awakened by the hand of one knocking.

Let the toothless tenderness of children now attend to the sweet reasoning by which their mother, grace, commends from his mouth this example of his humility.

[Col. 0682D]

He says: “You call me Master and Lord, and you say well, for I am. Therefore, if I, Lord and Master, have washed your feet, you too ought to wash one another’s feet. For I have given you an example, that as I have done to you, so you also should do.”

If servants and disciples could then have borne it, the Lord and Master might here have said:

“If I, whom you rightly call Lord and Master, did not regard as a thing to be seized upon that lordship by which, with the Father, I stand above all creatures, as do the kings of the Gentiles and those who have power over them, but emptied myself, taking the form of a servant, made in the likeness of men, and found in bearing as a man, and humbled myself, becoming obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. II; Luke XXII)—“if I did this in order to wash you from your sins, it is fitting that you also should regard your apostleship not as lordship but as a ministry of the utmost humility, whose very nature is that you lay down your lives for your brothers.”

[Col. 0683A]

He could have said this. For this is the true imitation of his example.

Yet even those who by no means follow the example of this Lord and Master can physically wash feet. Some, more cruel than kings, lord it most proudly over those subject to them under the religious title of shepherds; they are not only unprepared to lay down their lives for them, but even dare greedily to devour widows and orphans.

Therefore, after setting forth the example of the deed, upon which the whole authority of the discourse depends, he continues:

“Amen, amen, I say to you: a servant is not greater than his lord, nor an apostle greater than him who sent him. If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them.”

[Col. 0683B]

Words cannot explain how weighty it is that he affirms a fact known to all with such solemnity, saying, “Amen, amen, I say to you,” though his utterance, even without an oath, is firmer than heaven and earth, as he himself says elsewhere: “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away” (Matt. XXIV).

For who doubts that a servant is not greater than his lord, nor an apostle than the one who sent him? The apostles already called him Master and Lord, and he says, “You say well, for I am.”

[Col. 0683C]

Therefore, if you know—or rather, because you know these things, for you cannot fail to know that a servant is not greater than his Lord nor an apostle than the one who sent him—“blessed are you if you do them”: that is, if you are content to be as I am, whom you call Master and Lord.

You will be blessed, I say, by acting as I acted toward you. For sown in this humility, as a very few grains of wheat, you too will bear much fruit and fill the face of the world with seed, though you are put to death by harsh but passing tribulation. And in proportion as the humility of your love extends itself into many souls, so will the abundance of your blessedness increase. Therefore you will be blessed as soon as this time of misery has passed.

[Col. 0683D]

“I do not speak of all of you: I know whom I have chosen.”

“You will be blessed,” he says, “but not all. Not all of you,” I say, “will have a place prepared in blessedness.” For there is one among you, a son of perdition, excluded from this saying: a thief, not a minister; a traitor in ambush, not an imitator; darkness, not light; a devil, not an apostle.

Yet it did not happen through an error of mine that such a person is among you. For I know whom I have chosen: whom for glory, whom for flame; whom for honour, whom for disgrace. I did not admit such a one into your number unknowingly.

“But that the Scripture may be fulfilled: He who eats my bread shall lift up his heel against me.”

[Col. 0684A]

For this reason, he says, I endure with much patience that vessel of wrath fitted for destruction (Rom. IX): so that what was ordained concerning me from the beginning may now take place in the manner in which it was ordained, without any new plan intervening; not by chance, but according to a fixed order, foreknown and predetermined from ancient times.

Scripture bears witness, saying in my person: “He who ate my breads made great the supplanting against me” (Ps. XL). Thus it is written according to the Hebrew truth; but this Evangelist, writing in Greek, preferred to employ this form according to the edition of the Seventy Interpreters current among the Greeks.

[Col. 0684B]

This Scripture therefore plainly concerns Judas the traitor. But what does it mean when it says, “He made great the supplanting against me”? It does not merely say, “He supplanted me,” but “He made great the supplanting against me”: that is, he magnificently supplanted me.

Why did it choose to speak in this way, except to prompt us to consider carefully the manner of that supplanting?

For it was truly a great, truly astonishing supplanting, in which this one man, perversely coming upon the buyer—or rather, the Redeemer—of all, dared to sell him.

How, or to whom, did he sell him? To the priests, certainly; to his own ruin he sold the Paschal sacrifice in the very way that at that time the lamb was sought and sold by solemn purchase throughout the households of the children of Israel, for one about to eat the Passover.

[Col. 0684C]

O perverse magnificence! O magnificent perversity of the supplanter! By making the universal victim of our salvation his own possession, he set up for sale, as though it were his private property, the Possessor of the world and the sole, unique Lord of heaven and earth.

He thus raised his heel very high against him—not in order that he himself might buy Christ, but rather in order to sell Christ himself.

Why, then, was this order of the Lord’s passion predetermined: that this Lamb should not only be killed but should first also be sold?

[Col. 0684D]

Surely because the man for whose salvation he came to die had not only died through transgression, but had also been sold in the very transgression. For the first human beings were not persuaded to transgress the command with no hope held out to them; rather, “Your eyes,” he says, “shall be opened, and you shall be as gods” (Gen. III).

And though deceitfully, yet as was said, hope of divinity was proposed as the price of transgression. Hence the prophet says: “You were sold for nothing, and you shall be redeemed without silver” (Isa. LII).

Therefore this order of our salvation was necessary: that the Saviour should not only die for those sold and dead, but should first also be sold.

It follows:

[Col. 0685A]

“From now on I tell you, so that when it happens you may believe that I am.”

“Until now,” he says, “I have not told you—I have not indicated—who that devil is, the one who is among you; but at this hour I tell you who he is and what he is going to do, so that, when it happens”—that is, when, by betraying me, he raises his heel against me—“you may believe that I am” that needy and poor one concerning whom the person who understands shall be blessed, as that Scripture says.

I, I say, am the one who there also says, “Will he who sleeps not add that he may rise?” and afterward, “But you, Lord, have mercy on me and raise me up, and I will repay them” (Ps. XL).

I tell you this from now on. But first I shall state the beginning of that blessedness of which I have already begun to speak, which will immediately begin to come upon you when you do not wish to be greater than your Lord, whose servants you are, nor greater than him who sends you, whose apostles you are.

[Col. 0685B]

I say: “Amen, amen, I say to you: whoever receives one whom I send receives me; and whoever receives me receives him who sent me.”

This, O servants and apostles, who do not go before your Lord who sends you as greater ones but follow him as lesser ones—this is your blessedness.

Behold, I send before you a heralding voice to be heard throughout the whole world, so that those who receive me may then truly be confident that they have received me if they have received you as myself.

And lest you consider the reward for receiving me small because I am now despised, the last of men, a man of sorrows and acquainted with weakness (Isa. LIII), behold, I say this also to you—or rather, I proclaim it concerning you to the entire world: “Whoever receives me receives him who sent me.”

What, then, do you think: when this proclamation has been heard, how will all the scattered children of God receive you, for whose gathering into one you are to be sent? How great, do you judge, will be the honour and glory of your blessedness even in this world, where the devotion of believers is not deceived as they rejoice that in you they have received me “and him who sent me”?

[Col. 0685C]

For he who sends you will indeed be with you and in you.

Accordingly, all the children of men who are born through bloods, the will of flesh, and the will of man according to the old Adam, and through that father the devil come into contact with him, will, through your ministry, be reborn from water and Spirit according to me, the new Adam who sends you; and through me they will come into contact with God the Father, by whom I was sent.

“When Jesus had said these things, he was troubled in spirit, and testified, saying: Amen, amen, I say to you, that one of you will betray me.”

[Col. 0685D]

After he had calmly foretold the blessedness of faithful servants and humble apostles, Jesus was troubled when he was about to speak of the boldness of the unworthy apostle and evil servant; and not merely troubled in some general way, but, he says, “troubled in spirit.”

What then? Is he contrary to himself when he says in Matthew, “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak”? (Matt. XXVI.) This would indeed be harder to resolve if it had been said, “His spirit was troubled.”

But when it is said, “He was troubled in spirit,” it is as though one said, “He was troubled by himself”; and it is equivalent to what is said elsewhere: “He groaned in spirit and troubled himself” (John XI).

[Col. 0686A]

For the weak flesh or soul of Jesus, by which his whole human substance is understood, was troubled by the spirit which groaned and troubled it. For by the spirit through whose groaning the soul is troubled, or through whose willingness the flesh is weak, is understood the strength of divinity.

Since this strength threatens both hell elsewhere and his betrayer here, human weakness is troubled by the present cause of the groaning: that is, by the nearness of death.

Thus, being troubled, he testified: that is, by the event itself he confirmed that the one who ate his breads was truly going to raise his heel against him according to Scripture (Ps. XL). And he said: “Amen, I say to you, that one of you will betray me.”

“Therefore the disciples looked at one another, uncertain of whom he spoke.”

Stunned with astonishment and each assured by his own conscience, they looked at one another and were uncertain: that is, according to another Evangelist, “They were greatly saddened, and one by one began to ask, saying: Is it I, Lord?” (Matt. XXVI.)

[Col. 0686B]

“Now one of his disciples, whom Jesus loved, was reclining in the bosom of Jesus.”

This beloved disciple, most beloved among all the beloved, alone records this about himself: that the Lord Jesus loved him, and that at that time he reclined in his bosom in intimate love.

Why does he do so, except in order to confirm, by the authority of the person testifying—that is, his own authority—the testimony necessary to our faith and salvation, namely the present Gospel?

For although all four writers of the Gospel received by the holy Church are suitable witnesses, and it is impious to doubt the testimony of any one of them, yet this witness is especially worthy of belief because he was so present as a knowing observer of the truth that he relates that he reclined in Christ’s bosom, beloved and intimate, and was admitted nearer than all mortals to that Word which, uttered from the Father’s heart and made flesh, had decreed to resound more deeply through his tongue and pen.

[Col. 0686C]

For the one whom he had summoned from a wedding when he was already taking a wife, he rightly rewarded with so great a grace, delighting his soul with such intimate love; for he had clothed in virginal beauty the flesh which he had recalled from marriage.

Rightly, therefore, since he speaks great things about the Word of God, higher by far than the others, he ought not to have kept silent that in him had been fulfilled the saying of the Wise Man: “He who loves purity of heart shall, because of the grace of his lips, have the king as a friend” (Prov. XXII).

For by reason of the surpassing beauty of chastity, he was worthy to drink from the sacred fountain of the Lord’s own breast the divinity of that Word and the eternal mysteries of the beginning.

[Col. 0686D]

“One,” he says, “of his disciples, whom Jesus loved, was reclining in the bosom of Jesus.”

He adorns the highest truth with accompanying humility, for he does not say, “I was reclining,” but “one of his disciples was reclining”; and likewise he says, “whom Jesus loved,” offering no cause for so great a love, since he wished us to understand only the unprompted grace of the one who loved.

“Simon Peter therefore beckoned to this one and said to him, ‘Who is it of whom he speaks?’” Although he humbly suppresses his own name, he does not altogether conceal his person, since he does not say, “Simon Peter beckoned to him,” but “Simon Peter beckoned to this one.” By speaking thus, as if pointing back at himself, he shows that he was the son of special grace, to whom Peter, in that anxiety and utmost sorrow, beckoned to ask what he did not dare ask the Lord himself: for he rested his head on the Lord’s breast and could exercise greater confidence amid the chief delights of His love. We must understand, moreover, that just as this disciple [Col. 0687A] then rested most intimately in the bosom of the loving Lord, so afterward he was kept in the most watchful guardianship of that same tender love. The Lord later intimated this when, after saying to Peter, “Follow me,” He said of this man: “Thus I will that he remain until I come; what is that to you?” Truly, three times blessed, he rested most sweetly in the bosom of the loving Lord until his end; for just as his body was preserved incorrupt from every defilement, so that love kept him unharmed from every pain. It follows:

“Then, when he had reclined upon Jesus’ breast, he said to Him, ‘Lord, who is it?’ Jesus answered him, ‘It is he to whom I shall give the dipped bread.’ And when He had dipped the bread, He gave it to Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot. And after the morsel, Satan then entered into him.” Everywhere the meek and innocent Lamb ponders the Holy Scriptures [Col. 0687B], and does all things so as both to fulfil the prophetic utterances and Himself first to do what He prescribed in the Scriptures. For why did He choose to identify the wolf present before Him, threatening under a sheep’s skin, by such a sign, when He could sufficiently have indicated him either by his proper name or by pointing a finger at him? Surely in order both to show true the prophecy which He had mentioned above—“The man of my peace, in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has exalted treachery against me” (Ps. 40)—and Himself first to do what He had taught through a certain wise man, saying: “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink; for in doing this you will heap coals of fire upon his head” (Rom. 12).

For who can feed his enemy more patiently? That man of His peace, raging in heart and peaceful in speech, dipped bread with Him in the dish by a shared hand; and because he had not heard the inquiry of the one reclining in Jesus’ bosom, nor the Lord’s quiet answer, this intimate murderer received the morsel from His hand with a flattering mouth. Thus, made the man of His peace, he confidently ate His bread with the same shamelessness with which he was shortly to betray Him by a kiss of peace. So patiently did He feed His enemy as though an innocent child; yet, as the Ancient of Days, He heaped coals of fire upon his head. And although he was not touched by the coals of repentance—whose burning we ought to desire for our enemies, even though, contrary to our wish, they often become worse through kindness—nevertheless he was consumed by the heat of wrath [Col. 0687D]. For immediately after the morsel, Satan entered into the man whom he had already besieged and led bound to the Pharisees, so that he might promise the Lord’s betrayal for the agreed sum of money.

That is, when he understood himself to have been identified by this sign, and said, as the other Evangelists report, “Is it I, Rabbi?” and the Lord replied, “You say it,” he immediately went out, filled with his former greed and, together with it, diabolical frenzy and hatred—speaking in a manner thus: “Since, ensnared by an unexpected judgment, I am driven headlong, I shall extinguish my fire by your ruin” (Matt. 26; Mark 14). Therefore, it is not without divine purpose that the Savior identified His betrayer by a morsel rather than another sign.

We must know that, as was said before us, if Judas went out immediately after the morsel, as the Evangelist says a little later [Col. 0688A], then beyond doubt he was not present when our Lord distributed to the disciples the sacrament of His body and blood. For neither was that dipped bread which He handed to Judas His body, nor was that dish in which the betrayer dipped his hand with Him the cup of His blood; nor did He deliver to the disciples the sacrament of His body and blood before the supper of the old Passover, but after He had supped. Though the other Evangelists say this most plainly, Luke alone seems to have spoken otherwise. That is, Luke so transposed the words which the Lord spoke concerning His betrayer at the earlier meal that, in his narration, he joined the former Passover supper to the following consecration of the Lord’s body and blood, and then at last continued the words which were spoken at both feasts.

Therefore, following the Lord’s example, the good ought indeed to endure the wicked in the Church until, by the winnowing fan of judgment, grain is separated from chaff and tares from wheat. Yet patience should not be so indiscriminate that they hand over Christ’s most holy mysteries to unworthy persons whom they know to be such. But this has already been discussed elsewhere. It follows:

“And Jesus said to him, ‘What you are doing, do more quickly.’ But none of those reclining at table knew for what purpose He said this to him. For some thought, because he had the money-bag, that Jesus had said to him: ‘Buy the things we need for the feast day,’ or that he should give something to the poor.” — “The earth,” says holy Job, “is given into the hand of the wicked man; he shall cover the face of its judges” (Job 9). What then? Did Judas, or the devil who entered into him, receive a command to do what he was not doing? Or was he not rather permitted to do more quickly—that is, to bring to completion—what he was doing? For it is one thing to say to someone already acting, “Do it more quickly,” and another to command someone idle to do this or that.

“Simon,” the Lord says in Luke, “behold, Satan has demanded you, that he might sift you like wheat” (Luke 22). Did not Satan’s perverse desire demand the Lord Himself, as when, as a type of this event, that same Satan stood before the Lord among the sons of God and demanded blessed Job in order to test him? (Job 1.) Therefore, when He says, “What you are doing, do more quickly,” this is no more a command than was the Lord’s reply when Satan, the possessor of unhappy Judas, had said: “Skin for skin, and all that a man has he will give for his life. But stretch out your hand and touch his bone and flesh.” The same Lord replied: “Behold, he is in your hand” (Job 2). This was a concession, not a command; permission, not the sending of a striker.

Therefore, just as then, so now the earth—that is, flesh taken from the earth—was given into the hand of the wicked, by permission, not by command. For the wicked one, that is, the devil, prince of darkness, covered the face of its judges, so that, assailing that same earth, they might think perversely concerning it, judge it unjustly, and condemn it impiously. “But none of those reclining at table,” says the Evangelist, “knew for what purpose He said this to him.” Nor is this surprising. Even when He told them, they could not grasp or bear how great was His desire for the passion then approaching for our salvation [Col. 0689A]. For example, when He said: “I have a baptism with which to be baptized, and how I am constrained until it is accomplished” (Luke 12); and likewise: “My food is to do the will of Him who sent me” (John 4).

Thus none reclining at table—not even that beloved disciple himself, who said, “Lord, who is it that will betray you?” and to whom Jesus answered, “It is he to whom I shall give the dipped bread”—none, I say, knew for what purpose He said it to him. For some, he says, were so ignorant that they thought He had said: “Buy what we need for the feast day,” or “give something to the poor,” because Judas had the money-bag. They were very far from understanding the matter, for they thought He spoke of care or provision for the needy when permission was being granted for the betrayal to death of the Father of orphans and Judge of widows (Ps. 67).

“Therefore, when he had received the morsel, he went out immediately. And it was night.” He went out at once, judged and condemned, abandoning his bishopric so that another might receive it, led forth by the devil who stood at his right hand (Ps. 108). His sinful and deceitful mouth, which he had opened against the Lord and Master, he carried, after the morsel, opened yet wider to the Pharisees. This was not because the morsel was evil, but because, being identified by it, the evil man breathed greater hatred against Him who had identified him. For although he had begun the crime of betrayal solely from love of gain, now at last, as Satan entered into him and hatred was mixed with greed [Col. 0689C], he panted after all cruelty, acting more quickly and hurrying more urgently. “And it was night,” he says: night indeed for one who was a son of night and darkness, who fled the true Light and gladly accepted even bodily darkness as more suitable to wickedness.

“Therefore, when he had gone out, Jesus said: ‘Now the Son of Man has been glorified, and God has been glorified in Him. If God has been glorified in Him, God also will glorify Him in Himself; and He will glorify Him immediately.’” In the time of night which then prevailed, our Lord—the Day of eternity and Sun of righteousness—by a contrast drawn from that likeness, indicates that His glorification was now at hand, by which He would afterward illumine the whole world, while His betrayer and all the wicked remained in the night of sin [Col. 0689D]. By repeatedly using the word “glorification,” He foretells to the grieving disciples, in words henceforth bright and consoling, the splendor of His Passion flashing forth in the underworld; the glory of His Resurrection and Ascension; and also the grace of the outpouring of the Holy Spirit.

“Now,” He says, “the Son of Man has been glorified.” By what glorification, unless that of which He had earlier said: “And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself”; and, “Unless a grain of wheat falling into the earth dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit”? (John 12.) This had not yet indeed been accomplished, but was now being done and was beyond doubt to be completed. Accordingly, He rightly chose to use this word, and many others in this same discourse, in the past tense, saying: “Now the Son of Man has been glorified,” in the same sense in which He would later say, “And now I am no longer in the world.”

But this glorification of the Son of Man is without doubt the glorification of God. For in this way He sought not His own glory, as He says elsewhere, but honored His Father (John 8), namely, by becoming “obedient to Him unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. 2). He therefore says: “And God has been glorified in Him.” Someone may say: How, then, can one know that this Son of Man glorified God by His death? In anticipation of this He says: You shall have this proof: “If God has been glorified in Him”—that is, in His death—“God also will glorify Him in Himself,” namely by raising Him from the dead and placing Him at His right hand in the heavenly places (Eph. 1).

Then He will glorify Him immediately—that is, without delay—by giving the Holy Spirit in His name, who will at once adorn new heavens with great splendor and raise up the firmament of new grace, in which the Sun of righteousness may shine (Ps. 18). That is, this Son of Man will be so splendid and exalted that none can hide himself from His heat. From that time onward, you rational heavens—my Apostles—adorned well with heavenly life, will sound forth with mighty preaching and send frequent flashes of miracles; and the whole earth, watered by your rains, that is, instructed by your teachings, will bring forth works of righteousness and, with attentive faith, receive in heaven the everlasting brightness of the Son of Man.

Having said these things at the beginning, He then begins to expound more fully the greatness of this same glorification:

“Little children, yet a little while I am with you. You will seek me; and as I said to the Jews, ‘Where I go, you cannot come,’ so now I say to you.” Whoever are truly children, and do not degenerate from a good Father in the character of their souls, are not so delighted by the prospect of a great inheritance that they feel no pang of sorrow at their Father’s death, or allow the groans of Him who gave them birth while drawing His last breath to fade from their ears in forgetfulness. There is indeed a great inheritance and a great benefit of the Lord’s death: namely eternal salvation, life, and the resurrection of the dead, which the children would never have obtained unless the testament had been confirmed by the death of the Father.

“For where there is a testament,” says the Apostle, “the death of the testator must necessarily intervene” (Heb. 9). For a testament is confirmed in the dead; otherwise it has no force while the testator lives. Therefore, in order that those who are called might receive the promise of the eternal inheritance, Christ’s testament had to be confirmed by death, because they could not otherwise be introduced into the inheritance of life. Yet the death by which the testament was confirmed was one of grace, not necessity; and for no debt did grace, as a mother, bring forth life for her adopted children through the sharp pain of death.

Therefore, if we are truly children, let us receive with worthy hearing these words, and those which follow, spoken by our Father—holding together with the joy of our redemption sorrow and compassion for the Lord’s death. “Little children,” He says, “yet a little while I am with you.” By calling them “little children,” He indicates at once the grace of His fatherly love and the apostles’ then weak infancy. For when they became strong, armed with the Holy Spirit, they were sons; but now, because they were fearful and could not follow their Father, they were little children.

Whence came it that they were now called little children? Surely from the Lord’s imminent Passion and death, which is for them and for us all the sacrament of regeneration into adoption as children of God. For we must not think that before His Passion they had already been reborn by the baptism of regeneration, or that before His death that baptism had anywhere been celebrated—or ought to have been celebrated—of which the Apostle says: “All of us who were baptized in Christ Jesus were baptized into His death; we were buried with Him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life” (Rom. 6).

Therefore, from this time you are little children, who until now were only servants or disciples; and I say this to you: “Yet a little while I am with you.” A little while, I say—that is, only a very short time—until he who has now gone out reaches the Pharisees and, having received a cohort and officers from the chief priests and Pharisees, returns. From then on, once I have been seized, mocked, judged, scourged, and finally killed, I shall no longer be with you—except that for a time I shall see you again—yet not as I am with you now, a sojourner in the present age, but as Prince and Father of the age to come.

“Therefore you will seek me; and as I said to the Jews, ‘Where I go, you cannot come’—although they will seek me with a far different mind—so now I say to you.” I shall not be so remote that ungodly persecutors cannot come where I am while godly lovers can come; but they, whether living or dead, and you also while you live mortally, can never come “where I go,” or where I am. Thus you will seek me, and those who will believe in me through your word, weeping like turtle-doves and groaning like doves, so that they become what is written in the Song of Songs, each one of you saying separately: “My soul melted when my beloved spoke; I sought him and did not find him; I called him and he did not answer me. The watchmen who guarded the city found me; they struck me and wounded me; the keepers of the walls took away my cloak” (Song 5). “Daughters of Jerusalem, tell my beloved that I am sick with love.”

What then must be done, so that you may come where I go and obtain the whole inheritance? Hear now:

“A new commandment I give to you: that you love one another; as I have loved you, that you also love one another.” Receive this new commandment—new, I say, and to be preferred in comparison with the old commandment. For what is the old commandment? “You shall love your neighbor,” it says (Exod. 20). But I say to you that you should love one another as I have loved you. How then have I loved you? I have loved you when undeserving—“when by nature you were children of wrath, like the rest” (Eph. 2)—and behold, I die for the ungodly; I undergo death for enemies, so that you may be reconciled to God (Rom. 5). This is truly new. For scarcely does anyone die for a righteous person, much less for the ungodly and enemies.

Therefore, He says, “I give you a new commandment,” when I command you to love one another, not in whatever manner, but as I have loved you. Certainly the command is repeated, and the order of the words is this: “As I have loved you, that you love one another; so I give you a new commandment, that you love one another.” For I do not do as the scribes and Pharisees do, “who bind heavy and unbearable burdens and lay them upon men’s shoulders, but are unwilling to move them with their own finger” (Matt. 23). Rather, I first do what I teach: I first love you, so that you may love one another; and then I give you the full commandment that you love one another.

Thus you will not have a just complaint against me such as soldiers may sometimes rightly make against kings of the nations and those who exercise power over them: that they impose harsh commands upon their subjects and, while those subjects shed blood in sweat and dust, themselves remain comfortably amid delights. No, I say, you will not have such a complaint against me. For I first loved you: I who descended for your sake from the most tranquil bosom of the Father into the battlefield of this age to fight, and lay down my life for you. Therefore, with the authority of this deed going before, I give you this commandment: that you too, setting even your rest and your life after the common good, should, if necessary, die for the salvation of your brethren (Matt. 6).

“By this all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.” He does not say: “By this they will know, if you disfigure your faces, or make long prayers, or, with a trumpet sounding before you, give much alms”—all things which hypocrites too can do, with their left hand aware of it. Rather: “By this all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.” This can certainly be done only with a good heart. For no evil, nor any transgression of a commandment, can dwell in the same heart with love.

“The one who loves his neighbor,” says the Apostle, “has fulfilled the law. For, ‘You shall not commit adultery, you shall not kill, you shall not steal, you shall not bear false witness, you shall not covet,’ and if there is any other commandment, it is summed up in this word: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself’” (Rom. 13). Therefore, it will be a true proof and a true, certain testimony of my discipleship if you have love for one another, so that those around you, delighted by the sweet fragrance, may say: “Behold how good and pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity! It is like ointment upon the head, which runs down upon the beard, Aaron’s beard, which runs down upon the collar of his garment” (Ps. 132).

For by the one ointment of the Holy Spirit, the head, the beard, and at the same time the edge of Aaron’s garment will breathe a good fragrance everywhere, for the edification or gaining of many. You, like the beard nearest to the head—that is, to me the Lord and teacher of your love—will be bearded, that is, strong enough to lay down your lives for your brethren; and by your example you will imbue with that same love the whole Church, which, like a garment, spreads out below in devout communities.

“Simon Peter said to Him: ‘Lord, where are you going?’” This man, more ardent than the rest in love for his Lord and Master, stunned by impatient grief, first interrupted the discourse which had begun concerning love. For He had said: “Little children, yet a little while I am with you. You will seek me; and as I said to the Jews, ‘Where I go, you cannot come,’ so now I say to you.” He therefore said: “Lord, where are you going?” Jesus answered: “Where I go, you cannot follow me now; but you shall follow afterward.”

The outcome afterward openly proved this true. Peter, then weak, could not follow the Lord: he denied Him three times lest he should be compelled to follow Him by dying with Him. But afterward he followed, namely when, now old, he stretched out his hands, and, a disciple worthy of his Master, was fastened to the cross after His example.

But at that time, not seeing his own weakness, he had before his eyes his most eager desire to follow the Lord, a desire greater than his own strength. He had not yet experienced what the feeble shoulders of human weakness refuse to bear and what they are able to bear, unless they are strengthened by the Holy Spirit—not yet given—and founded upon Christ the rock. Truly desiring to follow, he said: “Lord, where are you going?” Therefore he had to receive a very different answer from the one who said: “Lord, I will follow you wherever you go,” to whom the Lord replied: “Foxes have dens and birds of the air nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay His head” (Matt. 8).

Thus He says: “Where I go, you cannot follow me now, but you shall follow afterward”—as though saying: You ask because you desire to follow, but you cannot now; for through fear “your faith will fail. Yet you, when you have at last turned back, strengthen your brethren by following me” (Luke 22).

“Peter said to Him, ‘Why can I not follow you now? I will lay down my life for you.’” What Peter says is true, insofar as he speaks in the future tense: “I will lay down my life for you.” For it would happen, and the Lord had said: “You shall follow afterward.” Yet because, in saying this, Peter had in view the present danger then under discussion and thought that he could endure in it, while the Lord foresaw both the present condition of human weakness and the future time of Peter’s strength, it was necessary that the saying of Scripture concerning servant and disciple, in comparison with the Lord and Master, should be fulfilled: “Every man is a liar” (Ps. 115).

For the Lord, knowing Peter’s will and recognizing his weakness, had said: “You cannot follow me now”; Peter, trusting in his own strength, maintained that he could. Therefore he had to be convicted by experience and shown to himself, so that afterward no one might presume upon his own stability when so strong a pillar had fallen. “Jesus answered: ‘Will you lay down your life for me? Amen, amen, I say to you, the cock will not crow this night until you have denied me three times.’” No Evangelist passes over the fact that this was said and afterward done, because it was rightly judged highly useful for restraining the audacity of human weakness.

For it was done by the deep counsel of the Godhead that, during that night of disturbance, when all the Apostles suffered scandal, Peter especially, their chief, should be abandoned for a time to his untried weakness; and, fallen through a threefold denial, he should himself believe by experience and make known to us that unless help comes from the Lord, our foot is quickly moved; and, if He who alone knows and is able to guard us falls asleep, we lose in temptation both sun by day and moon by night—that is, faith in both Christ’s divinity and His humanity.

[Col. 0694B] But concerning disturbances of this kind, the Psalmist, speaking mystically, said: “The waters shall stand above the mountains; at your rebuke they shall flee; at the voice of your thunder they shall fear.” Then he added: “You have set a boundary which they shall not pass over, nor shall they return to cover the earth” (Ps. 103). Therefore the wisdom of God rightly provided this also: that it should set a limit to this denial of the Apostle Peter, which precedes the temptations of the whole Church—namely, the cockcrow, after which he would deny no further, but would wash away the stain of his past denial with bitter tears.

But what does it mean that Peter was allowed to deny three times, and that his denial was corrected and ended by this limit rather than another? We must not suppose that what it pleased Him to be done thus, without whose providence it was not done, lacks mystery. What then does this limit, namely the cockcrow, signify mystically? Certainly it prefigures the good news of the Lord’s Resurrection. For our Lord, rising at midnight, stirred the mouths of the angels to praise and through them sent the good news of His life and victory to the apostles, sorrowing and darkened by the cloud of grief.

But until they heard this message of such great blessedness, the scandal of those same apostles persisted through three continuous nights, namely from the hour when they all fled after leaving Him. Therefore, after the threefold denial had been completed, the cock crowed, and, as Luke relates, “the Lord looked upon Peter” (Luke 22). That is, after the third night of scandal had passed, that most sweet message sounded forth, which the Prophet, striving somehow to express it, addressed to the Lord’s humanity in the person of the Father: “Arise, my glory; arise, psaltery and harp”; and immediately, in the person of the Son replying: “I will arise at daybreak,” He says (Ps. 107).

This message of consolation, I say, brought to the sorrowful apostles after the third night of scandal had passed, touched Peter by name when the angel said: “Tell His disciples and Peter that He goes before you into Galilee; there you shall see Him.” It follows:

[CHAPTER XIV.] “And He said to His disciples: ‘Let not your heart be troubled. You believe in God; believe also in me.’” This should be carefully observed, especially because He does not say, “Do not be troubled,” but “Let not your heart be troubled” [Col. 0695A]. Does a Father about to die immediately demand this fortitude of His orphaned children: that they should not fear being led to death with Him? Or does He now, in the contrary manner, persuade them not to let happen what He had shortly before affirmed would happen—namely, that, when the shepherd is struck, the sheep should not be scattered (Zech. 13), or that Peter should become strong contrary to the declaration of His truth and not deny Him three times before the cock crows?

Therefore, when He says, “Let not your heart be troubled,” it is the same as if He had said, “Let not your faith fail.” And the meaning is: “Because Satan has demanded you, to sift you like wheat” (Luke 22), and the force of that threshing will be so great that all of you will be scattered and leave me alone, this one thing remains to be urged: that, though scattered bodily, you may at least remain with me in heart, untroubled amid my temptations. This is what I prayed for concerning you, Peter: that, while you deny with your voice, your faith may at least not fail in your heart; and that, concerning this very thing over which you stumble in word, when you have at last turned back, you may strengthen your brethren.

Therefore, let not your heart be troubled; but, believing in God, believe also in me. Nor, troubled by the outcome of my temptations, suppose that you have erred in what you have believed until now concerning me. “Believe in me,” I say. And if the harshness of the winter now coming outwardly strips and scatters the green leaves of your confession, let the root of the good tree at least live inwardly, so that after this winter has passed, after this rain has gone and withdrawn, the confession of the mouth may blossom again from the root of faith, which flourishes in the heart unto righteousness, unto salvation. Thus the vineyards of your souls, flowering anew and giving forth fragrance, may openly testify by their beauty that the voice of the revived turtle-dove has been heard in our land, saying to that Church which is to be brought through you from all nations: “Arise, hasten, my beloved, my beautiful one, my dove, and come; come from Lebanon; come, you shall be crowned” (Song 2).

Do you wish finally to hear what the things you are shortly to see mean, the fear of which scatters you; or why I go where you cannot now follow me as I depart? (Rom. 10.) Behold, I tell you:

“In my Father’s house are many dwellings. If it were not so, I would have told you, because I go to prepare a place for you.” Therefore, He says, I go where you cannot now follow me: in my Father’s house are many dwellings, and all who dwell in them—the children of God who have been scattered from the beginning because of the fault of their first parent, who, following the deserting devil, deprived himself and all his race of those dwellings—must be gathered into one through my death, both from the living and the dead, both from Jews and Gentiles (John 11). This is why I go, why through the Passion of death I pass from this world to the Father: because “in my Father’s house are many dwellings.” If those dwellings did not already exist, I would already have said to you, “I go to prepare a place for you.”

“And if I go and prepare a place for you, I come again and receive you to myself, that where I am, you also may be.” I would have said all this to you if those many dwellings in my Father’s house did not already exist. But now the dwellings have indeed been prepared from the origin of the world, while their inhabitants remain unprepared. For all you children of Adam are still in your sins; as even the sons of great Abraham, chosen and faithful, do not despairingly say: “We have all become as unclean persons, and all our righteousnesses are like the cloth of a menstruating woman” (Isa. 46 [probably 64:6]).

Therefore I would indeed have said to you, “I go to prepare a place for you,” if those dwellings in my Father’s house had not been prepared. But now I tell you that I go to prepare you yourselves for those places or dwellings—that is, to wash you from your sins in my blood, so that you may be worthy to enter those starry dwellings, those heavenly holy places of holies [Col. 0696B], so that you may be a kingdom and priests (Rev. 1 and 5). For those dwellings cannot otherwise receive you justly and lawfully, since until now you have been disinherited because of the fault of your common father, unless you are introduced through me, another Father—through me, I say, who regenerate you in my death—the order of justice being preserved.

“And if I go and thus prepare you, I come again to you,” namely by rising from the dead, as a faithful messenger after peace between God and you has been restored. Again, I say, I come, announcing peace and remission of sins to you and saying: “Peace be with you” (John 20). Then I shall receive you to myself. Note the order of the words; consider the distinctions of the times. I do not say to you, “I come and receive you to myself.” For I do not rise from the dead and, by receiving you to myself, take you out of this world at one and the same time. Rather, I come now, in the present time, because I rise quickly; but I do not receive you immediately. I shall receive you at last, after I have invited through you others to the same dwellings, so that where I am you also may be, together with all whom you bring with you, that the many dwellings in my Father’s house may be filled.

Why then are they many? Surely because the merits of those who come are diverse, and the gifts of grace distributed or to be distributed to you and to them are diverse. Thus, “one is the glory of the sun, another the glory of the moon, and another the glory of the stars; indeed, star differs from star in glory” (1 Cor. 15). So also the dwellings are many and differ in glory. Yet all are established in the firmament of immortality and incorruption.

This is the reason why I shall allow such things to be done to me that, seeing them, you will fear and all suffer scandal in me on this night, so that even the most faithful among you, as I said, “will deny me three times before the cock crows.” But afterward, once strengthened, I shall receive you to myself; for then you will follow me, since, as I said to Peter a little earlier, “You cannot follow me now.” Behold, I have told you why I go.

“And you know where I am going, and you know the way.” Thomas said to him: “Lord, we do not know where you are going; how can we know the way?” With the wonderful art of teaching of a heavenly Master, he stirs up his disciples, still little children, to inquire, so that, made more attentive, he may lead them in more effectively, [Col. 0697A] when he says: “And so you know where I am going, and you know the way.” Certainly, when Peter said, “Lord, where are you going?” he did not immediately say, “I am passing from this world,” or, “I am going to the Father,” but only this: “Where I am going,” he says, “you cannot follow me now, but you will follow later.” Therefore, while they were all still in suspense and supposed that they did not know where he was departing, Thomas said: “Lord, we do not know where you are going; how can we know the way?” Since, he says, you have not yet told us where you are going, how do you tell us, “You know the way”? For it follows that if someone does not know a certain country, much more does he not know the road that leads to that country.

Thus, as all became more and more intent on hearing, at last he points out to them the way which they thought they did not know. For it follows: Jesus said to him, [Col. 0697B] “I am the way, the truth, and the life.” You know me, he says; you have believed in me; you have confessed me to be Christ, the Son of the living God. But I—I myself, whom you thus know—am the way by which you must go there, where I am going. I am the way, I say, as you yourselves almost admit when in ready willingness you wish to follow me, though you cannot do so now. Behold, I tell you what kind of way I am: “No one comes to the Father except through me.”

What is meant by, “No one comes to the Father except through me”? What, I ask, except that no one believes in the Father unless he also believes in me? Therefore I said to you: “You believe in God; believe also in me.” For whether one is a Jew or a heretic, he gains nothing by confessing that God is the Creator of heaven and earth and all their adornment (Rom. VIII). For by such a confession he does not attain [Col. 0697C] to the Father, because he does not believe in me. Accordingly, everyone whom the Father deigns to draw to himself, he draws to me, so that, made conformable to the image of the Son, he may receive adoption through the Spirit of adoption and become an heir—indeed, a co-heir with that same Son (Rom. X).

But why did I not merely say, “I am the way,” but add, “and the truth, and the life”? Clearly because, since with the heart one believes unto righteousness and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation, just as I rightly love the believer, so I make truthful in oral confession the one who confesses; and likewise, by showing myself, I make the believer and confessor live eternally. Therefore, because no one walks rightly except by believing in me, I am the way; because no one is truthful except by confessing me, I am the truth; and because [Col. 0697D] no one lives except one who has me, I am the life. For no one has the Father except one who has me; no one comes to the Father except one who sees me. I am the way by which one goes through faith, the truth by which one arrives through confession, the life in which one lives blessedly and eternally.

Therefore, as I have already said, you know where I am going and you know the way, because you know my Father, to whom I am going, and know me by confessing me to be the Son of that same living God. You know, I say, but you have not yet come to know. For knowing is not altogether the same thing as having come to know. A woman, for example, before she marries a man, knows whom she wishes to marry; yet she is not properly or accurately said to have known him until she has married him and been joined to him in the natural manner. Thus you too now know me already, but you have not yet received the spirit of love, [Col. 0698A] by which, having tasted the substance or nature of their husband—that is, the Son of God—your souls may know how to distinguish it from all created things.

“If you had known me, you would certainly also have known my Father.” If, I say, just as you know my person and believe me to be Christ, the Son of the living God, you had known my substance or nature in this manner, “you would certainly also have known my Father.” For the substance or nature of the Father is not one thing and that of the Son another; rather, such as the Father is, such is the Son. For, as I said to the Jews, “I and the Father are one” (John X).

Therefore, if you had known me—if that which, through the revelation not of flesh and blood but of my Father who is in heaven, you have as yet inwardly glimpsed as though from afar, you had received within yourselves, with soul enlarged and understanding opened [Col. 0698B] to understand the Scriptures (Matt. XVI), which all speak of me—“you would certainly also have known my Father”: as those who walk in his way, stand in his truth, and live the life hidden in him with Christ his Son; not ignorant, but recognizing most fully through the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms (Col. III; Luke XXIV) what he willed to be done concerning me, what command he gave me, and how you too must approach him by following my footsteps.

Thus you would have known my Father. “And from now on you will know him, and you have seen him.” For after I have gone away and prepared a place for you, when I come again to you, announcing that reconciliation has been accomplished and saying, “Peace be with you; receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive are forgiven them” (John XX), and [Col. 0698C] open your understanding so that you understand the Scriptures (Luke XXIV), “from then on you will know both me and my Father.” Accordingly, I no longer call you servants, but “my friends, because I make known to you all things whatsoever I heard from the Father”—that is, all things in which I obeyed my Father (John XV).

Moreover, from the time when I again give you the Holy Spirit from heaven, so that you may be eloquent and strong to preach to all nations, you will know me and my Father in such a way that no error of opponents may ever entangle you; from then on you will be enlightened by the knowledge of the Father. Knowing thus, you have already seen him. For to have known in this way is to have seen. Therefore, from then on you have seen him, though not yet face to face, but as through a mirror [Col. 0698D] in an enigma (I Cor. XIII), until I receive you to myself, so that where I am you also may be. Now you will know in part; then, seeing him as he is, you will be like him (I John III).

Philip said to him: “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us.” Philip spoke as though he had already seen the Son as he is: “Lord,” he says, “show us the Father, and it is enough for us.” As though he were saying: You, Master and Lord, Christ the Son of the living God—you, I say, we have already seen and acknowledged, loved and confessed; and we acknowledge that our eyes are blessed because we have deserved to see you. Nothing remains except that you show the Father, for you are enough to us.

In saying this, he certainly confirmed that he did not know the Son, since in the [Col. 0699A] visible man he did not know how to seek, or recognize as present, the invisible riches of divinity—to which Christ had invited them shortly before when he said, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life.” It follows, therefore: Jesus said to him: “Have I been with you so long, and you have not known me? Philip, he who sees me sees the Father.”

What is so astonishing here in Philip’s saying, “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us,” that the majesty of wisdom should marvel so greatly and say, “Have I been with you so long, and you have not known me?” Did he not shortly before indicate the disciples’ ignorance without astonishment, saying, “If you had known me, you would certainly also have known my Father”? Is it then a lesser ignorance or error not yet to know either Father or Son than to suppose that the Son can be seen without [Col. 0699B] the Father, or more easily than the Father, as he is? This indeed is how it must be understood.

For one who knows neither Father nor Son, as the apostles had not known them up to that point, is a child or infant, needing milk rather than solid food. But one who, after the coming of the Holy Spirit—after which the Scriptures ought to be understood with opened minds—asserts that the Son is more visible than the Father is a heretic, because he makes the Son unlike or unequal to the Father. Therefore, against the blasphemies of Cerinthus and Arius, and of all others who dared to deny the consubstantiality of the Father and the Son, let us too, in astonishment, hear this fitting expression of astonishment: “Have I been with you so long, and you have not known me?”

So long a time, he says, instructed by the testimony of such true words and such wondrous [Col. 0699C] works, are you still without understanding, and do you not know me to be not only visible man but also invisible God? For how do you know me, when, seeing me as man, you suppose that you have seen the whole of that which is Christ, the Son of the living God, and say: “Show us the Father, and it is enough for us”? “Philip, he who sees me sees the Father.” For I am not one thing and the Father another—not another thing, I say, although another person. For the Son is not unlike in quality but equal in greatness; not different in form, not distant in place, not later in time. Rather, everything that the Father is, the Son also is, except only this: he alone is Father and not Son; I alone am Son and not Father. Therefore, “he who [Col. 0699D] sees me sees the Father”; and conversely, one who does not see me cannot see the Father.

“How do you say, ‘Show us the Father’? Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?” How, he says, do you say, “Show us the Father,” adding, of course, “and it is enough for us,” as though you had already seen the Son as he is? “Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?” That is: the whole nature of the Father is in the Son, and likewise the whole nature of the Son is in the Father, so that I and the Father are one; and neither is ever seen without the other, speaks nothing without the other, and works nothing without the other.

You would therefore have spoken more rightly if you had said: “Show us God, and it is enough for us”—God, I say, one Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, who is God invisible without any distinction, who dwells in inaccessible light, [Col. 0700A] whom no mortal has seen or can see (I Tim. VI). “For no man,” he says to Moses, “shall see me and live” (Exod. XXXIII). This may rightly be said by the faithful person who is wearied by the present age and loves the age to come, who loves God and despises this wicked world. Let such a person say: “Show us the Father, and it is enough for us.”

“For, as the Psalmist says, ‘As the deer longs for springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God. My soul thirsted for the strong, living God: when shall I come and appear before the face of God?’” (Ps. XLI). “No one has ever seen God,” says John the Baptist; “the Only-begotten, who is in the bosom of the Father, has made him known” (John I).

But it is a very blameworthy ignorance when you say, [Col. 0700B] “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us,” not knowing and not believing that I am in the Father and the Father is in me. Therefore, “as I said to the Jews, if you do not believe my words, believe the works, so that you may know and believe that the Father is in me and I in my Father; and I say this now to you also” (John X).

“The words which I speak to you, I do not speak from myself. But the Father, remaining in me, himself does the works.” Here and there I set together two testimonies, one of words and one of deeds. This is worthy testimony in my speech, because, as you know and have experienced in every way, “the words which I speak to you, I do not speak from myself”—that is, I do not invent them from my own heart like a false prophet. For whatever words I speak truly have their effect.

[Col. 0700C] For the Law says: “This shall be your sign: if that prophet has foretold something in the name of the Lord and it does not happen, the Lord has not spoken it, but the prophet invented it through the swelling pride of his own mind” (Deut. XVIII), etc. Therefore the testimony in my speech is true and worthy; according to the Law it should at least have been sufficient to satisfy you, my friends, for belief: namely, that this also is true which I frequently say both to you who are learning and to the opposing Jews—that the Father is in me and I in my Father.

But behold: alongside this testimony of words, another testimony of deeds openly contends before all. For the Father remaining in me himself does the works. If I lied in speech, would the Father be with me in the display of such great works? Would his Spirit, the worker of wonders, remain—or have remained so long—in me, when he is accustomed to withdraw from the proud, as he withdrew from Saul? (I Kings XVI). Therefore, since it is also written in the Law that the testimony of two men is true, why do you hesitate any longer? (Deut. XVII, XIX).

“Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?” If indeed you follow the legal Scripture, believe because of the speech of truth and wisdom which you have continually heard from me. “Otherwise, believe because of the works themselves.” Otherwise—that is, even if you seek signs instead and are not content with wisdom and truth—believe because of the works themselves, many of which I have shown you from my Father.

But do I alone perform heavenly works as testimony to the things I say? [Col. 0701A] “Amen, amen, I say to you: he who believes in me will also do the works that I do, and he will do greater things than these, because I am going to the Father.” Behold, these very words which I now speak—“Amen, amen, I say to you: he who believes in me will also do the works that I do”—you will later see whether I speak from myself, that is, invent things from my own heart which lack fulfillment, or whether, while the Father remains in me, they occur openly, with the whole world as witness: the whole world rushing, as if to a spectacle, with joyful courses of souls into one faith in my name.

Someone may say: How, or in what respect, will one who believes in you do greater works? What works could be greater? To this I reply: Behold—I pass over the other things which one believing in me will do, perhaps to be preferred to my works by a greatness open to question. For example: what a thing it is that the sick should be laid in the streets on little beds, so that, when one who believes in me comes by (Acts V), even his shadow may overshadow some one of them, and they may be freed from their infirmities. But, not to speak of things of this kind, I tell you this:

I preach the word of saving teaching in one language only—Hebrew, that is—and in one people only, a people not very large; and I convert very few of them.
