But you who believe in me, after receiving the Holy Spirit, will speak the word of heavenly wisdom in every language to all nations—for every kind of language will arise upon your lips—though you were unlearned and illiterate men (Acts IV); and by fruitful labor you will win for eternal salvation an innumerable multitude [Col. 0701C] from all nations. “Therefore, he who believes in me will also do the works that I do, and he will do greater things than these.”

But whence will this come to one who believes in me, that he should do so great a thing? Clearly because I am going to the Father. For by passing from this world to the Father, becoming obedient to him for you unto death, even death on a cross (Phil. II)—by this, I say—it will come about that, receiving forgiveness of sins, you will also be able to forgive the sins of others. For in that very death by which I go to the Father, you will be reconciled to the same God the Father, and then you will be clothed with power from on high (Luke XXIV), so that what is written may be fulfilled: “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the works of his hands. [Col. 0701D] There are no speeches nor words whose voices are not heard. Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. XVIII).

These are indeed greater than those things which I now do by myself, and you will do these shortly. “Because I am going to the Father. And whatever you ask the Father in my name, I will do it, so that the Father may be glorified in the Son.” Now you ask, saying, “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us.” You ask, I say, but not in my name. For you have not yet known me, though I have been with you so long. You have not known, I say, that I am in the Father and the Father in me; that no one comes to the Father except through me; and that no one receives anything from the Father except through me. Therefore, until now [Col. 0702A] you have asked nothing in my name.

Then, taught by the Holy Spirit of truth, you will ask, saying: Lord, show us the Father in yourself, and yourself in your Father. And whatever you thus ask, whatever you request in confession of my name—that is, of the Son of God and your Savior (for this is my name, and in this name you ask whenever you ask for things pertaining to salvation)—“this I will do, so that the Father may be glorified in the Son,” so that the Father may be shown to you in myself.

For then you who now say, “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us,” will know the Son; and by knowing the Son, you will also know the Father. Thus the Father will be glorified; thus he will be shown glorious to you in the Son. And you will see him: now, while you are still in the world, through [Col. 0702B] a mirror and in an enigma, and you will know in part; but afterwards you will know as you are known, and face to face you will see the Father, desired in the Son (I Cor. XIII). This, I say, I will do if you ask the Father in my name. “If you ask the Father anything in my name, I will do it.”

Let neither you nor anyone among those who will believe through you be entangled by this error: that he should suppose every prayer must be directed to the Father through me, Christ his Son, and should think that none ought to be directed to the person of the Son. For “whatever you ask the Father in my name, I will do.”

“And if you ask me anything in my name, I will do it.” The Son of God said this concerning the consubstantiality of the Father and the Son, in order to correct the notion in which Philip had said: “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us.”

Now he returns to what he had begun and continues the discourse concerning love, which Peter, Thomas, and Philip had interrupted: the first by saying, “Lord, where are you going?”; the second, “Lord, we do not know where you are going; how can we know the way?”; and the third, “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us.”

The discourse concerning love, I say, begun thus—“A new commandment I give you, that you love one another as I have loved you, that you also love one another in this manner”—he continues: [Col. 0702C] “If you love me, keep my commandments. And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, that he may remain with you forever.”

For, he says, since I, as I said above, loved you and, because of my great love for you, am going to prepare a place for you—indeed, to prepare you yourselves and make you worthy of those dwellings which are many in the Father’s house—if you are not ungrateful, “love me” in a fitting return, and “keep my commandments”: namely, those which I have already begun to give you when I said, “A new commandment I give [298] you, that you love one another as I have loved you.” For the commandment of love is both one commandment and many commandments. “You shall not commit adultery; you shall not kill; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness,” and the other commandments are renewed in this one: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Rom. XIII).

Therefore keep these commandments of mine, and so love one another “as I have loved you.” Behold, I myself, who give you this commandment of love, am the first to do what I command, loving you unto the end—that is, unto death. Behold, upon the altar of the cross I will ask my Father; behold, on the day of my Passion, “I will offer prayers and supplications, with loud cries and many tears, to him who can save me from death, and I shall be heard because of my reverence” (Heb. V).

By thus asking the Father, as Philip says, I “will show you” the Father: that is, I will show you the Father in myself and myself in my Father. The beginning of this showing will be that the Father will give you another Paraclete, namely the Spirit of truth. For you err, not knowing the Scriptures, when you desire what is not advantageous for you—namely, that I should not go away—yet say, “Show us the Father,” not knowing that the wall [Col. 0703B] of hostilities stands between God and men (Eph. II), and cannot otherwise be broken down unless I go, unless through the Passion of death I pass from this world to the Father.

Therefore, when I ask and offer myself as a sacrifice on the cross, it will happen that I show you the Father; and he, having received me and taken me away from you in bodily absence, will give you another Paraclete, the Spirit of truth. *Paraclete* in Greek is called *consolator*, “comforter,” in Latin. This Spirit of truth is rightly called Paraclete or Comforter because he consoles the children of the bridegroom concerning the death or absence of their Father by the true meaning of the Scriptures, declaring that Christ had to suffer, rise from the dead on the third day, and that repentance and forgiveness of sins had to be preached in his name (Luke XXIV).

He is found never before to have been called by this name, because, although he was given to the holy people of old and even to the apostles before Christ’s Passion, he had not been given to anyone in such a manner that he ought to be called Paraclete. For he had not been given for the forgiveness of sins before Jesus was glorified. For the entire consolation of the Paraclete lies in this: that he wipes away the ancient mourning through the sacred Passion of Christ, since God the Father has been made propitious through the death of his Son; and by a new regeneration he makes, from children of wrath, children of grace; from slaves of sin, children of righteousness; from children of death and perdition, children of life and possession.

From then on we say: “When the Lord restored the captivity of Zion, we became like those comforted; and then our mouth was filled [Col. 0703D] with joy, and our tongue with exultation” (Ps. CXXV). The beginning, therefore, of showing the Father to us is the consolation of the Holy Spirit given for forgiveness of sins. Through this, our high priest who speaks these things, entering by his own blood into the Holy of Holies in order to ask the Father, found eternal redemption (Heb. IX).

Foreseeing long beforehand by the spiritual eye the result of his petition, the Prophet said in an ardent prayer: “May the Lord hear you in the day of tribulation; may the name of the God of Jacob protect you. May he send you help from the sanctuary and defend you from Zion. May he remember every sacrifice of yours, and may your burnt-offering become fat. May he grant you according to your heart, and confirm all your counsel” (Ps. XIX). “May the Lord fulfill [Col. 0704A] all your petitions,” and the rest to the end of the psalm.

Therefore this bridegroom, soon to be taken away from his orphaned children who stand before him, provides a great guardian: “And I,” he says, “will ask my Father, and he, hearing me as I intercede for transgressors—as Isaiah said (Isa. LIII)—so that they may not perish, will give you another Paraclete, that he may remain with you forever; that he may lead you to see the Father face to face; that he may show you the Father in the Son and the Son remaining in the Father; and that, remaining in you himself, he may cause the glorious and eternal majesty of the Father and Son—and his own inseparable and single majesty—to dwell within you.” It follows, and he speaks of the same Paraclete, the Spirit of truth.

“Whom the world cannot receive, because it has not [Col. 0704B] seen him and does not know him. But you will know him, because he will remain with you and will be in you.” Here he calls “the world” those who love the world. Why, then, can the unclean lovers of the world not receive this Paraclete, the Spirit of truth? Clearly, because they have their consolation; because they do not mourn; because they do not grieve for their sins, of which this Paraclete is the forgiver. For *paraclesis*, that is, consolation, is untimely and superfluous to those who are rejoicing.

Therefore this Paraclete is not given to lovers of this world, “who rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst things” (Prov. II), but to those who mourn and say: “Alas for me, because my sojourning has been prolonged; I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar; my soul has been a sojourner long enough” (Ps. CXIX). Likewise: “My tears were my bread day and night, while it is said to me daily, ‘Where is your God?’” (Ps. XLI), and things like these.

Thus the world “cannot receive this Paraclete.” Why? “Because it has not seen him and does not know him.” Its not seeing him belongs to unbelief; its not knowing him belongs to pride. For it belongs to unbelief to look to, or care for, only present things which are seen, and to be occupied or satisfied with them, so as not to think of the eternal things which are not seen. Likewise, it belongs to pride not to know—that is, not to approve—such a Paraclete, and indeed to judge the life of those who seek his consolations to be madness, and their end without honor (Wis. V).

But you, he says, who, while the world rejoices, [Col. 0704D] weep and mourn for the very things in which it rejoices—“you,” I say, “will know him.” And how will you know him? Because “he will remain with you and will be in you.” He will draw near in two ways: because, effecting his consolation, namely forgiveness of sins, through visible sacraments, he will remain with you—that is, he will never be absent from the ecclesiastical assembly; and, by pouring private or particular grace into you, he will be in you, although he will not always remain there.

For, except for him of whom it was said, “He upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining” (John I)—except for him, I say—he does not remain always in anyone, but sometimes withdraws from even a holy dwelling of his; then, invited again by prayer or praise of God, he returns. Although this is plainly evident from many passages of Holy Scripture, sacred history narrates it more clearly in the case of the prophet Elisha. When the king of Israel consulted him, saying: “Why has the Lord gathered us three kings together, to deliver us into the hand of Moab?” he said, “Bring me a minstrel.” And when the minstrel played, the hand of the Lord came upon him (IV Kings III), etc.

Therefore, he says, he will remain with you, because he will never be absent by the power or effect of the sacraments; but in you he will indeed always be by grace, though that grace will not always remain active. It follows:

“I will not leave you orphans; I will come to you.” O wonderful testimony! Through the same death of the Father by which they think they become orphans, children are born and take possession of an inheritance; and, when the same Father rises from the dead, the guardian Paraclete comes with him, testifying concerning him [Col. 0705B] that he lives and undertaking to defend for them, in every tribunal or council, the whole inheritance of the Father’s resurrection.

Because you have heard of another Comforter to be obtained, he says, you grieve, thinking that you will be orphans. [299] It will not be so: “I will not leave you orphans; I will come to you.” Rather, if I did not go away, you would be orphans—namely, with that orphanhood which the Prophet lamented when he said: “Remember, O Lord, and see what has happened to us; behold and regard our reproach: we have become fatherless orphans, and our mothers are like widows. Our fathers sinned and are no more, but we bear their iniquities” (Lam. V).

For what has happened to you, whereby you are orphans, except that your fathers sinned and are no more, while you bear their iniquities? What else is your reproach except the original sin of the human race? Surely because of it you became orphans without God the Father, and your inheritance was turned over to strangers, your house to foreigners; for whereas you ought to have been children of God’s grace and inhabitants of paradise, you are now children of wrath like the rest (Eph. II), driven into the alien inheritance of death and the foreign house of darkness.

Therefore, until now you have been orphans from God because of the fault of the old Adam; you are now about to be reborn to the same God through me, the new Adam. “For I will not leave you orphans,” but I will go and, through my death, give you birth again for God; and, having done this, rising again, I will “come to you” again. When will this happen? He says:

[Col. 0705D] “Yet a little while, and the world sees me no more; but you see me. Because I live, you also shall live.” Only a little, he says, remains. For during the time from now until the ninth hour of the following day this world, which lies in evil, sees me a little longer; but from the ninth hour it sees me no more, neither in this age nor in the future, except on that day when it shall be judged (Zech. XII). For then those ungodly lovers of the world will see; they will see, I say, him whom they pierced.

But you, who are not of this world, whom I have chosen out of this world, will again, after this little while, see me, because I live and, living, appear to you. I live, I say, and you will live eternally because I live—having died for you. Yet first you will follow the traces of my death. Accordingly, I did not say that at the same time [Col. 0706A] “I live and you shall live.” Rather, I live now—that is, at the present time—because I shall rise quickly. But you all will rise on the last day and will live with me forever.

“On that day you will know that I am in my Father, and you in me, and I in you.” On that day, he says, on the day of the great solemnity, the day of the great and true light, in anticipation of which the Psalmist prefaced a song to be sung after captivity at the building of the house, saying: “Sing to the Lord a new song; sing to the Lord, all the earth” (Ps. XCV). On that day, I say, “you will know that I am in my Father and the Father is in me,” which you do not now know when you say: “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us.”

And you will proclaim from day to day—that is, going from the Father to the Son, or from the Son to the Father—you will preach this salvation of God: namely, how I asked the Father and “he gave you another Paraclete.” Thus, according to the prophetic title of the aforementioned psalm, you will build the house after captivity—that is, the new Church from the Gentiles—after the destruction of sin and death.

And then indeed, while I live and shine as the first or chief in the glory of the resurrection, “you will know that I am in the Father and the Father is in me.” But more fully, when you live—when you too have risen—you will know this same thing, because you will see no longer in part nor through a mirror in an enigma, but face to face (I Cor. III). It follows:

“He who has my commandments and keeps them, he is the one [Col. 0706C] who loves me.” Having shown whom he loves as his own unto the end, and how he himself will soon be the first to do what he commands, loving not in word or tongue but in deed and truth (I John III), he next begins more fully to explain to what end this love must be observed by us. “He who has my commandments,” he says, “and keeps them, he is the one who loves me.”

As though he said: I therefore said above, “If you love me, keep my commandments,” because the worth of love lies not in the surface of speech but in truth and deed. Therefore, “he who has my commandments and keeps them, he is the one who loves me.” Otherwise, if he has them but does not keep them, let him know himself by this sign: he is not among those who love me, but belongs to this sinful people, to these hypocrites [Col. 0706D] (Matt. XV), of whom Isaiah rightly prophesied: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. XXIX).

“He,” I say, “will be compared to a man considering the face of his birth in a mirror. He considered himself, went away, and immediately forgot what he was like” (James I). But one who has them and keeps them, his soul will be compared to the king’s daughter, “whose every glory is within,” though outwardly the same glory shines somewhat in golden fringes (Ps. XLIV); and therefore the king also desires her beauty. Hence it follows:

“But he who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and will reveal myself to him.” O how blessed is this love! It does not, like servile fear, have uncertain deliverance as its reward, but has the sure grace of reward, already [Col. 0707A] present in part. For fear of punishment subdues a slave and compels him to hear the commands of his master through threats of blows; and therefore he has not yet deserved to be loved, has not yet been admitted to counsels, nor proved worthy to know his master’s secrets.

But a friend's love has enlarged him in such a way that, when he has accepted the command, he does not reject even the pleasure of counsel. For example, he is not content merely to have avoided adultery, but, occupied with a better love, is even able to disregard permissible marriage. “He,” as the prophet says, “will dwell on high; the strongholds of rocks are his lofty place; bread is given to him; his waters are sure; his eyes will see the king in his beauty” (Isa. XXXIII).

He therefore says: “But he who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him, and will reveal [Col. 0707B] myself to him.” He who loves me, he says, will, because of that very love and because he places even all lawful things after my love, be loved more intimately by my Father, who first loved all in common, as I have already said elsewhere: “For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son” (John III). He will, I say, be loved more intimately; and the bread of the Scriptures—the bread, indeed, of life and understanding—will be given him to eat, and the sure waters of saving wisdom to drink. Thus fed and given drink, as he walks through the broad field of contemplation, he will see with the eyes of his inner person the king in his beauty: him whom, as I said shortly before, you have not known although I have been with you so long.

His eyes, I say, will see—or rather, they will now begin to see—the king in his beauty. [Col. 0707C] For this blessed vision will be perfected in the life to come.

“Judas—not Judas Iscariot—said to him: ‘Lord, what has happened, that you are about to reveal yourself to us and not to the world?’” This Judas, namesake of the one who was the betrayer, has already elsewhere been identified: namely, the brother of James the Less, who is also called Thaddaeus. “‘Lord,’ he says, ‘what has happened?’” Supply: “if you have not yet revealed yourself to us.” For if you are about to reveal yourself to us and not to the world, then neither have you yet been revealed to us. For as we have seen you, so too has the world seen you; the world has seen you, I say, and has seen your wondrous works, which we too have seen. What, then, has happened, if in all these things no revelation of yourself has taken place?

300 “Jesus answered him: ‘If anyone loves me, he will keep my word; and my Father will love him, and we shall come to him and make our dwelling with him. He who does not love me does not keep my words. And the word which you have heard is not mine, but belongs to the Father who sent me. These things I have spoken to you while remaining with you.’” By this answer he indicates that he is at last replying to the question of the aforesaid disciple, who said: “Lord, what has happened, that you are about to reveal yourself to us and not to the world?” “‘These things,’ he says, ‘I have spoken to you while remaining with you.’” As though he said: While I remained with you in bodily presence, I did not yet reveal myself to you, but only announced, spoke, and delivered the word; and whoever keeps it will receive this great reward: that I shall reveal myself to him. This is what he says: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we shall come to him and make our dwelling with him.”

By these words he both confirms what he had already said—“He who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I shall love him and reveal myself to him”—and at the same time expresses more fully the manner of that revelation. For what will be its manner? “‘We shall come to him,’ he says, ‘and make our dwelling with him.’” Therefore one must not suppose that this is the revelation of the Son of God to those who love him: that he will come with the clouds, so that every eye may see him—although this too will undoubtedly happen, in the manner in which those who pierced him will see him. Indeed, that coming, like lightning appearing from east to west, will be visible to all and will be the joy of the righteous who await him [Col. 0708B] (Rev. 1); for, as the Apostle says, “When Christ, your life, appears, then you too will appear with him in glory” (Col. 3). But this revelation now under discussion is expressed more magnificently: “‘Because,’ he says, ‘we shall come to him and make our dwelling with him.’”

Thus the beloved Son is revealed inwardly to those who love the Son of God—inwardly, I say, in the inner parts of the soul—together with the Father. And this is indeed the great reward of love: that the one God, Father and Son through the Holy Spirit, is united inwardly to the beloved soul in the wondrous and ineffable delight of love. But how, you ask, is it said here, “We shall make our dwelling with him,” when elsewhere the dwelling of the Holy Spirit was the distinctive sign by which the Holy of holies was to be recognized? The Holy Spirit is not of another nature than the Father and the Son, of whose persons it is here declared: “We shall come to him and make our dwelling with him.”

Therefore, so long as one lives in this mortal body, the Father, the Son, and likewise the Holy Spirit—the Spirit of both, as has already been said above—do indeed remain in holy souls through the revelation of the Son. But the infusion of their own substance, such that the dwelling may remain eternally, is happily expected to be fulfilled in the recompense of the age to come. For now, indeed, “the beloved puts his hand through the opening, and the inward parts of human weakness tremble at his touch” [Col. 0708D] (Song 5); or, like “the sound of a gentle breeze” (3 Kings 19), the same beloved swiftly plants a kiss and flees. But in that blessed life the friend will be joined to the beloved with full and abiding delight. “The bridegroom,” says the prophet, “will rejoice over the bride, and your God will rejoice over you” (Isa. 62). Such a dwelling of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is especially prepared by the edification of love.

He says therefore: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we shall come to him and make our dwelling with him.” Behold, by the Gospel voice the Lord shows why the Psalmist said: “I have seen an end of every perfection; your commandment is exceedingly broad” (Ps. 118 [119]). For what commandment is broader than this commandment of love, by which the human mind is so enlarged that within the palace of its own substance it can receive the majesty of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit? Let him understand this and, with sweet savour, see it, who leads a heavenly life on earth and, well instructed by the teaching of divine love, knows how to celebrate in the temple of his heart the feast of delightful contemplation. For those who labour and are burdened cannot taste the refreshment of this sweetness so long as they bear their own burdens.

It follows: “He who does not love me does not keep my words; and he who does not keep my words does not love me.” Therefore let no one believe whatever his mind may tell him about love of God without the testimony of works. For love works great things, if it exists; but if it refuses to work, it is not love. And lest anyone think lightly of the Lord’s saying, “He who does not love me does not keep my words” [Col. 0709B]—lest, I say, anyone consider it a small indignity not to keep the words spoken by him—behold, he says again: “And the word which you have heard is not mine, but belongs to the Father who sent me.” For a little earlier he also said: “The words which I speak to you I do not speak from myself.”

Certainly, one who speaks his own word speaks falsehood, and by the authority of the Law, already often stated, is to be rejected because he is a liar. But the word which you have heard is fulfilled and is proved true by its effects. “‘Therefore it is not mine,’ he says; ‘therefore it is not fabricated by me out of my own heart, but belongs to my Father who sent me’”—as the works testify: the works you have seen, those you will see, and those which you yourselves will perform in my name. Accordingly, let him who does not keep my words not suppose this a light matter: for in scorning the word which you have heard, he scorns him whose word it is, namely the Father who sent me.

“These things I have spoken to you while remaining with you.” You were asking, he says, “Lord, what has happened, that you are about to reveal yourself to us and not to the world?” Behold, I tell you what has happened: While remaining with you, I spoke to you of the mystery of the kingdom of God in parables and sayings (Mark 4); and “as to little children in understanding, I gave you milk to drink, not solid food. For you were not yet able, and even now you are not able” (1 Cor. 3; Heb. 5). This alone has happened thus far.

“But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you all things and remind you of all things whatsoever I have said to you.” Therefore, thus far, while I spoke outwardly as a visible man, I planted and watered the new planting; but the Holy Spirit, who is called and is the Paraclete—that is, the Consoler, for the reason I stated above—will give the increase, teaching you all things and inwardly bringing to your remembrance all things whatsoever I have said to you [Col. 0709D]. He will teach you, I say, all things whatsoever I have spoken thus far, and will remind you of all things whatsoever I shall say to you; and he will write them on the fleshly tablets of your hearts (2 Cor. 3).

For I, who thus far have spoken to you as a visible man in elementary speech—I myself, the very same—shall thereafter speak to you by the inward utterance of the aforesaid Holy Spirit. For he will come and will be sent in my name in such a way that he will be Paraclete, that is, he will bring to you the consolation of Israel awaited by all the saints [Col. 0710A]: to you, I say, who heard me speaking and believed, and to those who will believe in me through your word. From that time the revelation will begin which I promised when I said: “He who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I shall love him, and we shall come to him and make our dwelling with him”—a revelation of which, in your ignorance, you say: “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us”; and again, “Lord, what has happened, that you are about to reveal yourself to us and not to the world?” But meanwhile the necessary order of your salvation demands that through 301 my death you be reconciled to God. Therefore I say:

“I leave my peace with you; I give you my peace.” Peace is the fruit of friendship, just as, conversely, war is the work of enmities. This peace comes all the more gratefully and desirably the more grievously the enmities are waged to the loss of the lesser and weaker party. For example, where a victor would condemn all the conquered to death, the name and work of peace are sweeter than where the victor, sparing the conquered, imposes only tributes, though burdensome ones.

Now the enmities between God and human beings were exceedingly grave, nor was there any doubt that in the battle of judgment God would be wholly superior. For even if there were faithful and righteous people, such as Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and all like them, their righteousness, compared with what was owed, was as great as the strength of a king meeting with ten thousand the one who comes against him with twenty thousand (Luke 14). Therefore, the greater the evil in which those enmities were waged against humankind [Col. 0710C], the more necessary peace was to human beings.

But what embassy could we have sent to beg for terms of peace, unless our peace, Christ the Son of God, had freely offered himself? Since he alone was innocent, he alone could plead the case of our peace. “For he himself,” says the Apostle, “is our peace, who made both one, breaking down the middle wall of partition, the enmity in his flesh, abolishing the law of commandments by decrees, in order that he might create the two in himself into one new human being, making peace, so that he might reconcile both to God in one body through the cross, killing the enmity in himself; and, coming, he preached peace to you who were far off, and peace to those who were near. For through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father” (Eph. 2).

Therefore, when the Lord had been questioned by the disciple saying, “Lord, what has happened, that you are about to reveal yourself to us and not to the world?” and had said, “These things I have spoken to you while remaining with you; but the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you all things and remind you of all things whatsoever I have said to you,” he goes on to express more deeply the sum of what has been accomplished: “‘I leave peace with you,’ he says, ‘I give you my peace.’” As though he said: This is what has happened, as I say: through me, in whom it pleased all fullness to dwell, all things are reconciled and made peaceful, whether things on earth or things in heaven.

But “peace” is an equivocal term. Therefore, having said, “I leave peace with you,” he significantly repeats: “‘I give you my peace.’” And he adds: “Not as the world gives do I give to you.” For the peace which the world gives is opposed to the peace which Christ gives. What does the world do in its gift of peace? “‘Come,’ it says, ‘let us enjoy the good things that exist, and swiftly use creation as in youth; let us fill ourselves with wine and perfumes, and let not the flower of time pass us by’” (Wis. 2), and so forth. Of such peace Christ says: “Do not think that I have come to send peace upon the earth; I have not come to send peace upon the earth, but a sword” (Matt. 10).

But what does Scripture say of the peace Christ gives? “How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of the one who proclaims peace, announces good, preaches salvation, and says to Zion: ‘Your God has reigned’” [Col. 0711B] (Ps. 145 [146]). For this is Christ’s peace, which he gives us: once the ruler of this world has been cast out (John 12), O Zion, your God himself has reigned; the kingdom of sin and death has been destroyed (1 Cor. 15; Heb. 2); and “the oppressor has ceased, tribute has rested; the Lord has broken the staff of the wicked, the rod of rulers, which struck peoples in indignation with an incurable wound, subdued nations in fury, and pursued cruelly” (Isa. 14).

Therefore, while I go, he says, I leave you true peace—my true peace; mine, I say, that is, peace obtained through me. When I return, when I rise from the dead, I give it to you by saying: “Peace to you. Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them.”

“Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid. You have heard that I said to you: I go, and I come to you.” Therefore, he says, as I said above, “Let not your heart be troubled; you believe in God, believe also in me”; so now, repeating it, I say: “Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid”—for the sufficient reason has been given why your heart ought neither to be troubled nor afraid. For you have heard that I said to you: “I go, and I come to you.” I go, I say, to prepare a place for you; and if I go and prepare a place for you, I come again and take you to myself, that where I am, you also may be.

But you also “heard that I said to you, ‘I leave peace with you; I give you my peace.’” Therefore, even if your flesh, through weakness, must necessarily be troubled while I go, at least let not your heart be troubled [Col. 0711D] or afraid, as though it had been deceived in its hope and had believed in vain that I am Christ, the Son of God. Rather, amid that trembling, in which the outward beauty of confession fades, let the root of faithfulness live inwardly.

“If you loved me, you would surely rejoice, because I go to the Father; for the Father is greater than I.” You do indeed now love me for the time being as a neighbour, but not yet as God. “For if you loved me thus, if you knew me, if you believed that I am in the Father and the Father in me, you would surely rejoice because I go to the Father.” For how great a cause of joy is this for those who love me? Great indeed, and ineffable. For so long as I am a mortal human being, the Father is greater than I. “You made him,” says the Psalmist, “a little lower than the angels.” But it continues: “You crowned him with glory and honour, Lord, and set him over the works of your hands. You subjected all things beneath his feet” [Col. 0712A] (Ps. 8). Likewise, in another psalm: “The Lord said to my Lord: ‘Sit at my right hand.’” And further: “He will drink from the torrent on the way; therefore he will lift up his head” (Ps. 109 [110]).

This will happen immediately because I go. For you will see me, your Lord and Saviour, crowned with glory and honour because of the suffering of death. Therefore, if you love me—that is, by believing and knowing that “I am in the Father and the Father is in me,” without which knowledge you cannot worthily love me—you would surely rejoice that I pass from the exile of the world and am to sit eternally at the Father’s right hand, entering into the glory of my kingdom. For thus far, since I put on flesh, “the Father is greater than I,” and according to the mortality of that flesh I am a little lower not only than the Father but also than the immortal angels (Heb. 2).

“And now I have told you before it happens, so that, when it has happened, you may believe.” For remembrance of the past strengthens the testimony of present things. For this reason I have now told you before it happens: I have said that I go and come again, so that, when it has happened—when I have gone and come again—you may be confirmed by former words together with present deeds and believe that “I am in the Father and the Father in me”: I who both foretold these things before doing them and, after foretelling them, was able to do them.

“I shall no longer speak much with you; for the ruler of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me.” First, it should be noted that he did not say, “I shall no longer speak many things to you,” but, “I shall no longer speak much with you.” When he says “with you,” one must understand: while remaining in bodily presence. For he then spoke many things to them, and he speaks to us now; yet he neither spoke many things while remaining bodily with them, nor does he now speak bodily with us—that is, by local presence or visible intercourse. Hence after a little while he will say: “Father, when I was with them, I kept those whom you gave me” [Col. 0712C] (John 17). Therefore, “I shall no longer speak much with you,” he says—supply: while remaining bodily. Why? “For the ruler of this world is coming.”

The ruler of this world—the condemned world, namely, which now hates me and opposes me—is the devil. He is called the ruler of the world because he rules over lovers of the world. How does this evil ruler, ruler or overseer of death, and ancient sinner come, except because he enters into conflict with me through death? Thus, I say, he comes, “and he has nothing in me.” He does not come, nor is he permitted to come, because I have seized anything or justly owe what he comes to exact.

“But that the world may know that I love the Father, and as the Father gave me commandment, so I do.” For this reason I admit him, the usurer of death: that the world may know that I love the Father and obey him in all things for the sake of the whole world; as the Father gave me commandment, so I do. Therefore, the coming of that ruler of this world [Col. 0713A] is an act of foolish rashness and rash foolishness; but that, enduring his assault, I die, is the voluntary sacrifice of obedience for the whole world.

“You held my right hand,” says the Psalmist, “and led me according to your will, and received me with glory” (Ps. 72 [73]). For my right arm—that is, my divine power—and my indignation could have saved and assisted me so that I should not die; the same power assists me so that I rise again. But the commandment of the Father, the true and immense love of the Father which he has for the salvation of humankind, holds my right hand so that I do not defend myself or escape death, and will lead me in his will, as I say: “Father, not my will, but yours be done” (Matt. 26). For I judge that I must do not what weak flesh desires, but what the counsel of the Godhead requires.

Therefore let the ruler of this world, who now comes, come, so that, when he finds nothing in me, he may, defeated in the contest by one human being, rightly be cast out—as, conversely, through the one human being whom he conquered, he seemed rightly to have obtained for himself the rule of this world. When this has been done, the world will know by experiencing its salvation that I love the Father and, by his commandment, undergo death, though I acquired from Adam no inheritance of death through any fault.

“Arise, let us go from here.” For, he says, behold, he who will betray me is approaching, and a crowd with him, carrying lanterns, torches, and weapons; lest they seize us in the narrow confines within the walls of this supper-room, and you have no free opportunity to escape. For I do not wish to lose any of you, but I want them to let you go. “Arise, let us go from here,” lest even this man, whose lodging we have enjoyed and with whom we celebrated the Passover, suffer any disturbance because of us.

[CHAPTER XV.] “I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman. Every branch in me that does not bear fruit, he will take away; and every one that bears fruit, he will prune, that it may bear more fruit.” Behold, by the likeness of a familiar visible thing, he shows the benefit of his passion, so that the world may now begin to know why the Father gave him this commandment, why he permits the ruler of this world to come against him, in whom that ruler has nothing: that is, why the Father delivers for crucifixion or death one who has no cause of mortality.

“I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman.” Is it not the case, he says, that the vine, though it is a black, rough piece of wood with dry bark, is planted in the earth by the husbandman’s care so that it may spread its branches more widely and, in its season, bear a sweet cluster which will gladden the human heart with wine (Ps. 103 [104])—after first enduring the horror of winter and the hardships of rains? And I surely am the true vine: the true vine, I say, in distinction from the alien vine, namely that Sodomite people, of which Moses says in his song: “Their vine is from the vineyard of Sodom and from the districts of Gomorrah. Their grape is a grape of gall and their cluster is most bitter. Their wine is the gall of dragons and the incurable venom of asps” (Deut. 32).

Therefore I am a vine so truly such that the one who comes as ruler of this world, as I said shortly before, has nothing in me. For this reason my Father, the heavenly husbandman, judged me worthy to be planted in this world and cultivated with the hoe of passion, so that I might spread my branches, of whom you are the first, more widely; and after the harsh winter of tribulation and death now imminent, might produce the sweet cluster—that is, the grace of resurrection. Having tasted it beforehand by faith, the bride may say in the Song: “My beloved is to me a cluster of cypress in the vineyards of Engaddi” [Col. 0714A] (Song 1).

But just as a vine sometimes puts forth from one and the same stock branches both barren and fruitful, while the husbandman meanwhile cuts off the barren one and prunes every fruitful one, so my Father, the husbandman of this vine, will do where from one and the same faith or confession of my name both many reprobate persons and elect persons spring forth. For “every branch in me that does not bear fruit he will take away; and every one that bears fruit he will prune, that it may bear more fruit.”

Behold Judas, the son of perdition: you see how he cut off the useless branch—indeed the harmful worm clinging to the root of this vine—when he was handed over to Satan, to be immediately carried into the fire of Gehenna (John 18). But you remaining branches, who hitherto bear some small fruit by preaching and healing everywhere (Luke 9), though only among the one nation of the Jews—you, I say, that you may bear more fruit—behold, the husbandman prunes through participation in my passion and death, so that, washed by my blood, you may receive the sweet south wind, that is, the Holy Spirit, whom he gives you [Col. 0714C] for the forgiveness of sins. This is what follows:

“Already you are clean because of the word which I have spoken to you.” For the word which he had then spoken was the word of his passion and resurrection, when he said: “I go to prepare a place for you; and if I go and prepare a place for you, I come again and take you to myself, that where I am, you also may be,” and so forth. Likewise, he had just said: “I leave peace with you; I give you my peace.” For the peace or reconciliation by which we are reconciled to God is the forgiveness of sins.

This word, mingled with faith, cleanses you just as it cleanses them from all sins, because faith in the word is plainly the effective antecedent cause through which the blood of the Son washes us from our sins. Hence the Psalmist, himself to be washed in Christ’s blood, says: “You will sprinkle me with hyssop and I shall be cleansed; you will wash me, and I shall become whiter than snow” [Col. 0714D] (Ps. 50 [51]). By hyssop, through which swelling is removed from branches, is understood faith in this word, by which hearts are purified. “When you first sprinkle me with this,” he says, “then at last you will wash me and I shall become whiter than snow.” Therefore, “because of the word which I have spoken to you, already you are clean,” because through the word of death which I have foretold to you—by which I pass from this world to the Father and am no longer in the world—you are already clean.

“Remain in me, and I in you. As a branch cannot bear fruit from itself unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you unless you remain in me.” Oh, what a terrible declaration of the destitution of all who presume upon human power, and what a true defence and commendation of the unity of the body of the Church by its head, Christ the Lord [Col. 0715A]: “Remain,” he says, “in me, and I in you.” For do not the excessively confident defenders of free will seem to themselves not to need God’s assisting and merciful grace, as though by their own speed, in willing and running, they could attain the fruit of everlasting life? But he says: “As a branch cannot bear fruit from itself unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you unless you remain in me.”

Therefore, presumptuous and proud evil branches, you are rightly to be taken away by the husbandman’s harsh hand, unless you confess that all beauty and all loveliness of fruits proceed not from yourselves but from the innermost root of the vine. Likewise, you schismatics, cutting yourselves off from the body of the Church and severed by the shoots of your own inventions, do not think that you can bear the fruit of life. For who does not know the unity of the vine and its branches? So long as branches remain in the vine, so long do they drink the proper moisture of its root as it rises through their innermost veins; they live, flourish, and their flowers bring forth fruit. But if a branch is cut from the vine, it can no longer share in its good sap; accordingly, it indeed has the appearance of a branch, but neither lives nor has any use except to be cast into the fire and burned.

This fitting comparison is therefore given concerning the Lord himself and his disciples. For so long as, through unity of faith, they agree with the teacher of truth, keeping the commandment of love and all thinking the same thing, they remain in Christ; and each, living from his Spirit, possesses the grace of inward truth (1 Cor. 13; Matt. 10) [Col. 0715C]. And whatever sacrament the Church of Christ celebrates lives for the salvation of those who communicate in it. For Christ speaks in them, and whatever is done by them is rightly believed to be done by God and confirmed by his Spirit.

But where persons dissent and, dividing themselves from the unity of faith through heresies and schisms, cut themselves off from Christ, all their word and sacrament are dead; whatever they seem to do is defiled, whatever they think they sacrifice is polluted. Of such persons the Apostle says: “Having indeed an appearance of godliness, but denying its power” (2 Tim. 3). For example, they can visibly administer water baptism, but they cannot confer the Holy Spirit, in whom the entire power of baptism consists.

Yet for those baptized by them, if they return to the catholic Church, the washing of the flesh is not repeated, provided only that they were baptized in the name of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. This many heretics and heresiarchs have done, though they were nevertheless cut off by another implement of error. I say, their visible water baptism is not repeated; rather, through profession of the catholic faith and reconciliation with the holy Church, they are grafted into the true vine, that is, Christ. Thus, receiving the holy Spirit of love, they grow green and can bear saving fruit.

Therefore, taking the likeness from the vine and its abiding branches, of himself and his disciples abiding with him in one Spirit of love, he says: “Remain in me, and I in you” [Col. 0716A]—just as branches remain in the vine, so that the richness of the vine may remain in the branches. For it is not because the proper moisture of the vine has spread itself into the branches that the branches remain in the vine; rather, because the branches remain in the vine, the vine makes them share in its richness.

So also, it is not because the Spirit of love is poured out from Christ, the true vine, upon all his branches, and loads the whole Church planted throughout the world with fruitful charisms of everlasting grace—it is not, I say, for this reason that individual branches remain in that vine. Otherwise no one would ever be cut off, since this vine is never without the richness of the Holy Spirit. But because we individually remain in Christ through the confession of one true and catholic faith, we all share in his Spirit, and every sacrament lives which we—or rather, he through our ministry—perform.

Rightly, therefore, he does not say, “May I remain in you, and you in me”; but first he says, “Remain in me,” and then, “and I in you.” And, in order to make more fully known how truly necessary it is for us to remain in him if he is to remain in us, he says: “As a branch cannot bear fruit from itself unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you unless you remain in me” [Col. 0716B].

Let, then, the plantings of death and shoots consigned to eternal fires go and eagerly desire to bear fruit—Cerinthus, Arius, and the other impostors, whom the holy Spirit of discipline flees (Wis. 1). For whatever takes place among them, whatever they celebrate as though sacred or sacramental, lacks the true word of life and the Spirit of truth as surely as a branch cannot bear fruit unless it remains in the vine, and as surely as a hand cut off from a body cannot live or act. It follows:

“I am the vine; you, however, are the branches.” For this reason he repeated what he had already said, “I am the vine,” so that he might state more plainly what he had not yet done: whom he intended to be understood as the branches. For above he said: “I am the vine; my Father is the husbandman.” But now he says: “I am the vine; you are the branches.” And he added: “He who remains in me, and I in him, bears much fruit, because without me you can do nothing.”

“For this reason,” he says, “I said, ‘Remain in me, and I in you,’ because ‘he who remains in me, and I in him, bears much fruit.’ For this reason, I say, I said, ‘Remain in me,’ because without me you can do nothing.” But it is too little to say that the branch which does not remain in the vine can do nothing. What then? “If anyone does not remain in me, he will be cast out like a branch; and he will wither; and they will gather him, cast him into the fire, and he burns” [Col. 0716D].

The severed branch not only does nothing, but nothing can be made from it. For example, it is not a little vessel, a peg, or an instrument of any craft or work—indeed, it is nothing that a woodworker would wish to take up for use. Hence the Lord says to the prophet Ezekiel: “Son of man, what will be done with vine wood, compared with all the woods of the groves among the trees of the forest? Will wood be taken from it to make a work, or will a peg be fashioned from it, so that any vessel may hang upon it? Behold, it is given to the fire as fuel” (Ezek. 15).

The Apostle agrees with this prophetic judgment—not, as Novatus imagined, by denying a remedy of repentance to the fallen, but by declaring terribly the difficulty of renewing those who, thinking lofty things, have been cut off from this vine and become heresiarchs: “For it is impossible,” he says, “for those who have once been enlightened, have also tasted the heavenly gift and been made partakers of the Holy Spirit, and have likewise tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come, and have fallen away, to be renewed again to repentance, crucifying again for themselves the Son of God and holding him up to contempt” [Col. 0717A] (Heb. 6).

For what other despair of repentance does the Apostle here teach except that concerning which, writing to Titus, he says: “Avoid a heretical person after a first and second admonition, knowing that one of this kind is perverted and sins, being condemned by his own judgment” (Titus 3)? Therefore, concerning one who has cut himself off from the unity of the true vine—that is, Christ—by becoming a heretic or heresiarch, Christ, prophet, and Apostle agree with one voice and the same meaning.

For Christ says: “If anyone does not remain in me, he will be cast out like a branch and wither. They will gather him, cast him into the fire, and he burns.” But the prophet says: “Will wood be taken from it to make a work, or will a peg be fashioned from it? Behold, it is given to the fire as fuel.” Finally, of one who has never professed the appearance or beauty of the vine—that is, the Christian faith—the same hope may be held as of wild wood: namely, that some vessel may be made, or a peg useful for the Lord God may be fashioned [Col. 0717C].

But of one who, grafted into that same true vine, tasted the good sap of its root and, as the Apostle just cited says, became a partaker of the Holy Spirit by tasting the good word of God and the powers of the age to come—of such a one, I say, when he has been cut off or fallen away, this alone is to be thought to remain: that he be gathered, cast into the fire, and burned. For, according to another passage of the Gospel, his sin is such that it is not forgiven either in this age or in the age to come (Matt. 12). Let these things be said of that branch which has been cut off and condemned by its own judgment. What, conversely, does he say of that branch or those branches which remain in the vine?

[Col. 0717D] “If you remain in me, and my words remain in you, you will ask whatever you wish, and it will be done for you.” A little earlier he said: “Remain in me, and I in you.” Now, by a small change of the wording, he does not say, “If you remain in me, and I in you,” but, “If you remain in me, and my words remain in you.” Thus he disclosed how he himself remains in his disciples. For since Christ is the Word of God and our flesh, if the words—that is, faith in the incarnate Word—remain in us, Christ himself surely remains in us, as the Apostle testifies that Christ dwells by faith in our hearts (Eph. 1 [probably 3:17]).

Therefore, what he had said, “Remain in me, and I in you,” he repeated by saying, “If you remain in me, and my words remain in you,” so that he might add the reward of this unity and mutual abiding in one another: “You will ask whatever you wish, and it will be done for you.”

By this promise, whatever difficulty it may raise for you when you reflect or know that Christ’s faithful ask for many things which nevertheless are not granted to them, it must be kept firmly in mind that, having said, “I am the vine; you are the branches,” he intends this, like the other things already said, according to the analogy [likeness] of the vine and its branches. For what is it? Does a vine deny or withhold anything of its own from its branches? Does it not pour into them all the grace of its vigor, all the power of its root, distributing it through each one, and make its whole fruit depend upon them? But what grace, what power is in the root of this vine—that is, Christ the Son of God—except the entire fullness of the sevenfold Holy Spirit? Therefore, just as branches can expect or receive from a vine nothing other than what the vine has in itself, so these rational branches can either ask from, or receive from, the true vine, which is Christ, nothing except what the vine itself possesses.

[Col. 0718B] Therefore, “If you remain in me,” he says, “and my words remain in you, you shall ask whatever you will, and it shall be done for you”; that is, you shall be rich not in gold and silver, but in every word and in every knowledge; and you shall ask not for the desires of the flesh, but for every gift of the Holy Spirit. For, asking from me for “every perfect gift” which is from above, descending from the Father of lights (James III), you shall receive: the little gems of divine fear, the vine-shoots of piety, the flowers of knowledge, the clusters of fortitude, the ripe grapes of counsel, the winepresses of understanding, and the storehouses of wisdom. Whatever of such things you ask shall be done for you, because they belong to me, the true vine, because they are riches of grace and truth; so that the whole world may be deemed worthy of the fruit of every grace, hanging like clusters from great branches.

Whatever is more abundant than these seven gifts of the Holy Spirit is not fruitful and does not belong to the wine of salvation; rather, it is foreign to the nature of the vine. Therefore it is neither to be desired nor requested by branches remaining in the vine, nor ought it to be granted to them. But whence comes such ready generosity—that whatever you will, you may ask, O good branches, and it may be done for you? It follows: “In this my Father is glorified, that you bear much fruit and become my disciples” [Col. 0718D]. From this, he says, comes the Father’s great liberality in doing for you whatever you ask: namely, because it advances the praise and glory of his name if you, like good branches, bear much fruit.

And for this very purpose you become my disciples: namely, by imitating me, your Lord and Teacher, who, although I am innocent, so that the ruler of this world has nothing in me, as I said above, nevertheless die as my Father gave me commandment, so that, because I am truly the vine, by dying I may bear for the world the finest wine, by which the human heart may be gladdened forever (Ps. CIII). This, I say, accomplishes the Father’s glory and praise: that you too may in the same manner bear much fruit.

[Col. 0719A] He himself is willing and ready to hear in every matter which is requested for the glory of his name. How then will he not do whatever you ask, when you aim at bearing much fruit for his glorification? Indeed, he will do it so abundantly that no instrument of grace will be lacking to you for bringing about the salvation of the world, extending the glory of God, and bearing witness to the grace and truth of the Son of God. Whence is this?

He says: “As the Father has loved me, so have I loved you.” As if he said: As the Father sent me through great love (Rom. VIII), and planted me, the true vine, in this world, so through the same love I send you, my branches, and spread you throughout the world, “that you may bear much fruit.” For the love by which the Father gave the Son the command to come to the contests of suffering, and by which he exalted the same Son—“obedient unto death, even death on a cross”—and gave him the name above every name, “that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. II), is the same love by which that Son sends his disciples into the whole world to preach the Gospel to every creature (Matt. XXVIII; Mark XVI).

[Col. 0719B] They are to go before kings and governors, be dragged away, and put to death, so that, quickened as fellow branches by the sweetness of the same Spirit with which the vine is full, they too may bear the fruit of eternal salvation (Luke XXIII). Therefore, “As the Father has loved me,” he says, “so have I loved you. Remain in my love.” Remain—that is, persevere—by loving one another, possessing one Spirit and one faith which works through love (Gal. V). For I told you that “my Father is the husbandman; every branch in me which does not bear fruit he will take away.” Therefore, lest this husbandman take you away, remain in my love by bearing fruit—that is, by loving one another—and strive not to be cut off from me, the true vine. For what is it?

“If you keep my commandments, you shall remain in my love, just as I have kept my Father’s commandments and remain in his love.” My commandments, though they are many, are restored in this word: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Rom. XIII; Matt. XXII). “If, I say, you keep my commandments, you shall remain in my love.” Perhaps someone may say: since love itself is a commandment, how is it now said, “If you keep my commandments, you shall remain in my love”? He seems to have made a division of all righteousness, so that one part of the whole is love of God and the other part consists of commandments.

[Col. 0719D] To this I say: righteousness truly is one whole, but it has two parts—love of God and love of neighbor. Upon these two commandments the whole Law and the Prophets so depend that the active life wholly depends upon love of neighbor, while the contemplative life depends upon love of God. For love of God belongs more especially to contemplation; love of neighbor attends to the works of the outward life.

God gave Moses two tablets on the mountain. On these two tablets of stone were written the ten commandments of the Law: three on one tablet, pertaining to God, namely, not to have other gods, not to make an idol or any likeness, and not to take the Lord’s name in vain; but seven on the other tablet, pertaining to one’s neighbor. The first of these is, “Honor your father and your mother”; the second, “You shall not kill”; the third, “You shall not commit adultery”; the fourth, “You shall not steal”; the fifth, “You shall not bear false witness”; the sixth, “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife”; the seventh, “You shall not covet your neighbor’s property” (Exod. XX).

[Col. 0720A] Thus three things belong to the first commandment, which is love of God, and the Lord expressed them in the Gospel in this way: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind” (Matt. XXII). But seven look to the other commandment, that is, love of neighbor, teaching how one ought to live among human beings. Therefore, “If you keep my commandments,” he says—that is, those which concern love of neighbor and perfect the active life—and if thus you love one another, “you shall remain in my love,” namely in the love of God, which perfects the contemplative life. One does not arrive at this except through the active life, just as one does not ascend to the love of God except through love of neighbor. Thus, if you keep my commandments, you shall remain in my love.

It is worthwhile, as in the other matters, so also in this saying, to consider carefully the most just authority of the teacher, because he immediately added: “Just as I have kept my Father’s commandments and remain in his love” [Col. 0720C]. For it is fitting and right that the words of that teacher whose deeds are justly praised should also be received; just as, conversely, when someone’s life is despised, it follows that his preaching too is to be despised. How praiseworthily this first Teacher kept the Father’s commandments the whole world now sings with the Apostle, saying: “He humbled himself, becoming obedient for us unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. II).

Concerning this obedience, a little above, after he himself had said, “For the ruler of this world comes, and has nothing in me,” he immediately added: “But that the world may know,” he says, “that I love the Father, and as the Father has given me commandment, so I do” (John XII). Therefore it is right, and fitting for this teacher, that he should command, since the dignity and authority of a command are evident when he himself first does what he orders. Let him therefore say: “If you keep my commandments, you shall remain in my love, just as I have kept my Father’s commandments and remain in his love.”

[Col. 0720D] It should be observed, however, that when he says “just as,” equality of love or obedience is not commanded—something impossible for all human beings to attain—but some likeness, however small, or imitation is required. For how can anyone equal in keeping the Father’s commandments him who “committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth”? (1 Pet. II.) How can an imitator measure the magnitude of the love of him to whom it is said in the Psalm: “You loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions”? (Ps. XLIV.)

[Col. 0721A] Indeed, it is said “above your companions” so that you may understand that no one can attain equally to the obedience or love of the Son of God: he alone loved the Father and was loved by him, and he first loved us, his neighbors—or rather, out of great love became our neighbor (1 John IV). It follows:

“These things I have spoken to you, that my joy may be in you, and that your joy may be fulfilled.” “To you,” he says, “who do not rejoice but mourn and weep over my departure, I have spoken these things,” saying: “If you loved me, you would certainly rejoice, because I go to the Father, because the Father is greater than I,” and the rest; so that, just as the sweetness of the vine is in the branches, so my joy may be in you.

[Col. 0721B] For what is joy amid present tribulation and the sorrow of your souls, in this bloody sweat of my contest—what, I say, is my joy except the Holy Spirit? Through the Holy Spirit I shall offer myself as an immaculate sacrifice to God the Father, so that my blood may cleanse you from dead works to serve the living God (Luke XXII; Heb. IX). And in this offering I rejoice beyond expression, so that it is rightly said of this my joy: “Go forth, daughters of Zion, and see King Solomon in the diadem with which his mother crowned him on the day of his espousal and on the day of his heart’s gladness” (Song III).

Therefore, that this my joy may be in you, that you may know both to suffer with me by rejoicing with me and to rejoice with me by suffering with me, I have spoken these things to you, as a vine eager to pour the gladness of my juice into my branches. And lest your joy be vainly deceived but be fulfilled in the storehouses of eternal delight, you shall reckon the laughter of this world an error, and say to its joy: “Why are you vainly deceived?” (Eccl. II.)

[Col. 0721C] But you shall laugh without error, and your joy shall not be deceived; for it shall not be taken from you. But what are the commandments of which I said to you, “If you keep my commandments, you shall remain in my love”? Behold, I tell you: “This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you. No one has greater love than this, that one lay down his life for his friends.”

In the Song of Songs the bride says: “The king brought me into the wine-cellar; he ordered love within me” (Song II). When do you suppose that this king brought his bride into the wine-cellar, if not when, by dying and treading the winepress (Isa. LXIII), he fulfilled the Scriptures, and, by rising again, opened her understanding to understand those same Scriptures? Behold, having said, “I am the vine, and my Father is the husbandman,” and again, “I am the vine; you are the branches,” he wonderfully ordered love for those who desire to drink his wine.

[Col. 0721D] For there are two commandments of love: love of God and love of neighbor. But, as has already been said above, one does not arrive at love of God except through love of neighbor. Therefore he said a little above: “If you keep my commandments, you shall remain in my love, just as I have kept my Father’s commandments and remain in his love.” And as though you asked what those commandments are whose observance makes us remain in his love, or in the Father’s love, he immediately added: “This is my commandment, that you love one another.”

Love for one another is love of neighbor, through which one arrives at love of God; and such is the order of love that you cannot love God unless you love your neighbor. “For whoever does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” (1 John III.) Therefore, “My commandment,” he says, “of which I told you, ‘If you keep my commandments, you shall remain in my love’—my commandment, I say, is this: ‘that you love one another.’”

[Col. 0722A] But why did he there use the plural, “my commandments,” whereas here he says in the singular, “This is my commandment”? Clearly because every commandment concerns love alone, and all are one commandment: many through the diversity of works, one in the root of love. For “You shall not commit adultery, you shall not steal, you shall not kill, you shall not bear false witness; and if there is any other commandment,” says the Apostle, “it is restored in this word: You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Rom. XIII).

Therefore this wise and eloquent teacher, in a pleasant and properly ordered method of instruction, after proposing, “If you keep my commandments,” and the rest, now adds what you rightly infer, and says: “This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you.” He will next set this forth reasonably and, finally, after the manner of one concluding, will add: “This I command you, that you love one another” [Col. 0722C].

First, he himself defines the love which he commands, briefly yet fully, as is fitting, saying: “As I have loved you.” For the name “love” is equivocal. There is a certain love by which we love our neighbors without command, namely through the affection of kinship and flesh. Although holy Scripture does not oppose that love, it nevertheless differs greatly from this love; for one thing is freely bestowed upon nature, another is owed to obedience to the Lord’s commandments.

Defining, therefore, the manner of love pleasing to God and deservedly crowned, he immediately added: “As I have loved you”; and, as though at once pointing with his finger to the love of which he had said, “As I have loved you,” he continued: “No one has greater love than this, that one lay down his life for his friends” [Col. 0722D]. Thus he made plain how, and how greatly, he loved us—as though he had said more openly: “Love one another unto death, because I loved you unto death.”

O faithful saying, worthy of all acceptance, which truly many kings, prophets, and righteous persons wished to hear but did not hear (1 Tim. I; Luke X). For what is written in Malachi? “I have loved you, says the Lord; and you said, ‘In what have you loved us?’ Was not Esau Jacob’s brother, says the Lord, and I loved Jacob, but I hated Esau? And I made his mountain, Seir, a desolation, and his inheritance a dwelling for the dragons of the wilderness” (Mal. I).

[Col. 0723A] Behold, in his Gospel the same Lord says, “I have loved you.” And as though it were again said to him, “In what have you loved us?” “Have I not laid down my life for you?” he says. For he asserted this in an equivalent way—or rather expressed it more magnificently and affectionately—when he said: “No one has greater love than this, that one lay down his life for his friends.” Therefore this is great and memorable, unheard of in all ages: that the greatness of the Son of God’s love extended toward us reaches even unto death, especially because, although he was immortal, for our sake he assumed the nature in which he could die.

Yet this too must not be passed over: though he could have said “for his enemies,” he preferred to say “for his friends,” so that by the sweetness of his language he might gradually instill in his hearers the sweetness of that very love which he commanded them. For he truly could have said “for his enemies,” as the Apostle testifies: “But God commends his love toward us, because while we were still sinners Christ died for us. Much more, therefore, now justified in his blood, we shall be saved from wrath through him. For if, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, now reconciled, shall we be saved in his life” (Rom. V).

[Col. 0723B] Therefore he said “for his friends,” not because they were already friends, but because by his suffering they were then becoming friends. For, as though someone objected why he had called friends those who, being human beings, were indeed “children of wrath, like the rest” (Eph. II) on account of Adam and needed reconciliation, he immediately added:

“You are my friends, if you do what I command you.” If you, he says, as I said above, remain in me as branches in the vine, and I in you, and if you do what I command you, then henceforth you are my friends; you are reconciled to God; you are children of God; and you have surpassed every servile condition. The words which follow more fully support this meaning: “I no longer call you servants, because a servant does not know what his master does; but I have called you friends, because everything whatsoever I have heard from my Father I have made known to you.”

[Col. 0723C] Therefore, though in gentleness he says, “No one has greater love than this, that one lay down his life for his friends,” he could, by truth and justice, have said “for his enemies.” It was not because we were friends that he laid down his life for us; rather, because he laid down his life for us, we became God’s friends—that is, we were reconciled to God. Accordingly, when he had said, “You are my friends,” lest people should not know that they had become friends by grace rather than merits, he said, “I no longer call you servants.” Why? “Because,” he says, “a servant does not know what his master does.”

It should be observed that he did not say, “Because my servants do not know what I do,” but, “A servant does not know what his master does.” For there is no small difference in Scripture between saying “the Lord’s servant” relationally and saying “servant” absolutely, or without relation.

[Col. 0724A] “It is a great thing for you to be called my servant” (Isa. XLIX), says the same Lord who, when he says, “A servant does not remain in the house forever” (John VIII), certainly does not say “my servant.” Therefore, when he says, “I no longer call you servants,” it is surely as if he said, “I no longer call you enemies,” as is most clearly proved from the opposite expression. For he goes on: “But I have called you friends.”

Thus, when he had also said above, “Amen, amen, I say to you, a servant is not greater than his master” (John XIII), certainly what he now says, “Because a servant does not know what his master does,” concerns that servant of his who “does not remain in the house forever”: that is, the servant of sin, who cannot become a deserter from God. Plainly, that “servant does not know what his master does,” though he remains subjected to his Lord, whether willing or unwilling.

[Col. 0724B] “But you know, because everything whatsoever I have heard from my Father I have made known to you.” What is this: “Everything whatsoever I have heard from my Father I have made known to you”? Since you are human beings, though friends, can you know everything which I, the only-begotten Son of God, know? Certainly this must not be thought. For I do not say, “Everything whatsoever I have known,” but, “Everything whatsoever I have heard from my Father I have made known to you.”

“I have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to you, because you are little ones” (Matt. XI). For while they were blinded and hardened, as Isaiah foretold, lest they should see with their eyes, understand with their heart, be converted, and I heal them (ch. VI), I open your understanding, that you may understand the Scriptures and may know that I heard from my Father the command to act thus: namely, that he placed upon me the iniquities of all of you, so that I might bear your infirmities and carry your sins (ch. LIII); and that, hearing—that is, obeying—him, I became obedient for your sake unto death, even death on a cross (Phil. II).

[Col. 0724C] Rightly, therefore, I no longer call you servants, because you have known the truth, and the truth shall set you free (John VIII). And therefore I say this also to you:

“You did not choose me, but I chose you and appointed you that you should go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain.” “Not,” he says, “for this reason did I call you friends: because you chose me, as the kings of the nations, and those who exercise authority over them” (Luke XXII), are chosen by their friends, to whom they are accordingly indebted because they could not obtain the desired sovereignty except through them. But I chose you first; and in this is love—not as though you loved me, but because I first loved and chose you. Just as branches do not establish the vine, but the vine sends out branches and pours into them that by which they may bear fruit, so “you did not choose me, but I chose you and appointed you that you should go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain.”

[Col. 0724D] This addition made only now, “and that your fruit should remain,” indeed far surpasses the comparison above of the vine and its branch. For the fruit of a vine and of insensible branches does not remain, but quickly passes away; it is stored in a cellar only so that it may grow old and, drunk with pleasure, pass away in the brief, though more agreeable, use of mortals. But the fruit of this vine and of rational branches surely remains glorious unto eternal life.

Therefore a certain joyful branch, great and fruitful—namely the Apostle Paul—says to his enduring fruits: “For you are our glory, as we also are yours, in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ” (2 Cor. I). Thus, lest it be too little merely to say, “that you may bear fruit,” he rightly adds, “and that your fruit may remain”; and further: “And that whatever you ask the Father in my name, he may give you.”

[Col. 0725A] This is the highest benefit of friendship for you, friends whom I now call no longer servants but my friends; this, I say, is the highest fruit or benefit: that whatever you, my branches, ask—while meanwhile you are stretched out for winepresses and ripe fruits, tortured as you weep and groan, with the Spirit pleading for you in unutterable groanings (Rom. VIII), that is, causing you to groan inexpressibly in prayer—“whatever, I say, you ask the Father in my name, he may give you” more abundantly than you ask or understand: namely, what eye has not seen nor ear heard, which God has prepared for those who love me and remain in me, my branches (1 Cor. II).

## BOOK TWELVE

[Col. 0725]

[Col. 0725B] The sum or conclusion of the things thus far said concerning love is at last drawn when it is said: “These things I command you, that you love one another.” For “if you keep my commandments, you shall remain in my love.” But “this is my commandment.” Therefore I command you these things, that you love one another.

Behold, the very surface of the text requires that, as has already been said above, in the one commandment of love the attentive reader should understand together all the commandments for right living. For above he said in the singular, “This is my commandment,” and here in the plural he spoke of the same commandment of love. Indeed, both here and there is added, “that you love one another.”

It follows: “If the world hates you, know that it hated me before you.” Having first given the commandment of love, concerning which he has spoken at length, he now rightly foretells to his chosen and beloved ones the afflictions which they will suffer in the reprobate and hateful world. For steadfast love, laid down as it were in the foundation, bears the weight of afflictions, so that those departing from the council’s presence may rejoice that they are counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus (Acts V).
