[Col. 0725C] Therefore, rightly and in order, after what has already been said about love, he now urges confidence and perseverance upon my friends, hated by this world, in the things which they will suffer from this enemy of theirs, the world: “If,” he says, “the world hates you, know that it hated me before you.” A marvelous exhortation of consolation! For what benefit is this knowledge to Christ’s lovers, that it should rightly be said to them as something important: “Know that it hated me before you”? Benefit in every way and greatly.

For faithful servants of so great a Lord console themselves by the glorious assurance—having a true testimony in the very hatred of the world—that they are not of the world but are of God. For he immediately adds:

“If you were of the world, the world would love what was its own; but because you are not of the world, and I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you.” Accordingly, even if the world wishes to love, its love must be avoided; and its hatred must be sought by Christ’s lovers. For the world’s hatred bears witness to friendship with God.

[Col. 0725D] Hence this same John says in his Epistle: “If anyone wishes to be a friend of this world, he makes himself an enemy of God” (1 John III). For there are two generations, one of God and the other of the world; or two cities, one of God and the other of the devil. Rising together from the beginning, they run on until the end of the age, always opposing one another with implacable hatred. Their hostility was first made manifest in the two brothers Abel and Cain (Gen. IV), and they oppose one another so persistently that no one can at the same time hold the friendship of both.

How often the Apostle says to the Corinthians: “Do not be yoked with unbelievers. For what partnership has righteousness with iniquity? Or what fellowship has light with darkness? Or what portion has a believer with an unbeliever? What agreement has Christ with Belial?” and so forth (2 Cor. VI).

[Col. 0726B] Therefore, “if the world hates you,” he says, know this, and let this knowledge be at once testimony and consolation to you: that “you are not of the world, but I chose you out of the world.” Knowing this, I say, be consoled, because the world will not always have leisure to hate you, nor will this license of hatred endure long. Rather, afterward you shall stand in great steadfastness against those who oppressed you:

“They shall see and be troubled with terrible fear, and shall marvel at the suddenness of an unexpected salvation; and, groaning in anguish of spirit, they shall say within themselves, repenting: ‘These are they whom we once held in derision and made a proverb of reproach. We fools considered their life madness and their end without honor. How then are they numbered among the children of God, and their lot among the saints?’” (Wis. V).

Know these things, and keep them firmly in mind: “the world hated me before you.” What does this have to do with the matter? It follows:

“Remember my word which I spoke to you: A servant is not greater than his master.” For knowledge of the hatred which I first suffered, and remembrance of this saying of mine, will scourge your forgetful impatience and rebuke the tender indulgences of your own will.

[Col. 0727A] For what is it? Knowing or remembering what I said, will you be astonished at the insults and persecutions which will befall you? While your Lord is crowned with thorns and clothed in a mocking purple robe, will you, my servants, dare to desire jeweled diadems and purple garments to be worn in earnest? Is it the order of a lawful court that, while the King is struck with fists, spat upon, and slapped, his servants sit upon lofty seats in the theatre and seek applause for themselves from the same hands which so abuse their Lord? It is not so. But what then?

“If they persecuted me, they will persecute you also; if they kept my word, they will keep yours also.” Certainly this is the usual course of hostilities. For how could those who persecute the Lord fail to persecute his servants striving for faithfulness? It is clear to you that they did not keep my word, since they persecute and kill me. Know, therefore, that they will not keep your word either; but they will persecute you, stone you, crucify you, kill you, and drive you out of their cities. Thus you shall flee from city to city (Matt. XXIII), weeping and confessing that you are strangers and sojourners upon the earth, having here no abiding city but seeking the one to come (Heb. XIII).

[Col. 0727B] Even to your parents, brothers, kinsfolk, and friends you shall be unknown; by them you shall even be delivered over to death; and thus, because of me—such a Lord of yours, hated by them—you shall be hated by all.

“But they will do all these things to you for my name’s sake, because they do not know him who sent me.” Behold again how great is the consolation of the speaker: “But they will do all these things to you for my name’s sake,” that is, because of hatred for my name. It is truly great, and sufficient for those who love him to form their patience. For the hatreds of people distress Christ’s lover; reproaches weary him; curses trouble him; losses of possessions or even bodily torments afflict him. Yet the joyful assurance of rewards moderates and makes light all these things. For the glorious dignity of Christ’s name, for which they suffer these things, adorns reproaches, sanctifies curses, turns losses into gains, and transforms torments into delights of great hope.

[Col. 0727C] Therefore, having foretold the persecutors, he rightly says: “But they will do all these things to you for my name’s sake.” But why do they have, or will they have, such hatred of my name that they do all these things for my name’s sake? Namely, “because they do not know him who sent me.” They do not know, I say—that is, they refuse to know. For lest you suppose this ignorance to be pardonable or excusable, hear what follows:

“If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin. He who hates me hates my Father also.” Lest, I say, you suppose that those of whom he speaks ought to be forgiven as though for ignorance, like those of whom it is written, “Little children asked for bread, and there was none to break it for them” (Lam. IV), he himself explained what he meant by saying, “They do not know him who sent me,” and struck them with the universal judgment: “He who hates me hates my Father also.” Therefore, not to know him is to hate him.

[Col. 0727D] And concerning the sin of this execrable, dreadful, and diabolical hatred—by which they hate both the Father and the Father’s own Son—he said: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin.” For what is it? Did he say that they would have no sin at all? Certainly not. Rather, “they would not have sin,” that is, understand the sin of hatred: the hatred, I say, by which they hate both the Son of God and God the Father. “They would not have this sin,” he says, “if I had not come and spoken to them.”

How great, indeed, is the guilt of their sin, since it arises from the coming and speaking of him whose advent took away the sin of the world (Gal. IV; Rom. X). What a fault it is to hate him for this reason: because he spoke peace and friendship. All who become worse because of good imitate this sin. It is as though you said: Unless Abel had offered gifts pleasing to God, Cain would not have been angry and his countenance would not have fallen. What sort of excuse is that? Indeed, it is not an excuse but a vehement accusation of perversity.

[Col. 0728B] The Apostle Paul, when he says, cautiously sympathizing with them for the humbling of the Gentiles’ conscience, “I bear them witness that they have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge” (1 Cor. VIII), must by no means be thought to excuse their ignorance.

What, then, did he intend to be understood by saying, “They have zeal for God,” and immediately adding, [Col. 0728C] “but not according to knowledge,” except as though he had said: They do not possess true knowledge, which does not puff up—that is, the love of God (ibid.). It therefore follows, according to the same Apostle’s judgement, that they have hatred of God. Thus his saying, “They have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge,” is as if he had said: With mouth or lips indeed they defend the law of God, but in their heart they are empty of the love of God—which is true knowledge. The prophet also agrees, through whom God says: “This people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. XXIX).

Therefore what he says, “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin,” is as though he had said: If I had not spoken, if I had not proclaimed righteousness and stood opposed to [Col. 0728D] their deeds, they would not have burned with envy or hatred—which removes every excuse for sin. For, that you may understand that he spoke of sin, he immediately added: “He who hates me hates my Father also.” This, then, is that which was foretold through the prophet: “Zeal has seized an untaught people” (Isa. XLIII), because, when the Son of God came and spoke to them—the Son of him whose worshippers they seemed to be—and opposed their vices, they flared up with evil zeal.

But it is little merely to say that he came and spoke. For his speaking, as has often already been said, was like the testimony of one man; and the Jews, despising it, said: “You bear witness concerning yourself; your witness is not true. [Col. 0729A] (John VIII)” Therefore, just as he had then said: “It is written in your law (Deut. XVII; XIX) that the testimony of two men is true. I am one who bears witness concerning myself, and the Father who sent me bears witness concerning me” (John VIII)—namely, by performing works. “For,” he says, “the works which the Father has given me to complete, those works themselves bear witness concerning me that the Father has sent me” (John VIII)—so now likewise he sets forth two testimonies. Having first given one testimony when he says, “If I had not come and spoken to them,” and so forth, he immediately adds:

> “If I had not done among them the works which no one else has done, they would not have sin. But now they have both seen and hated both me and my Father.”

“If it was too little,” he says, “that I spoke, although [Col. 0729B] I spoke a true and sound word, and although by the truth of the word the law commands that he whom God has sent should be recognized (Deut. XVIII), behold: by another testimony they are justly sentenced to condemnation: ‘If I had not done among them the works which no one else has done,’” and so forth. What then? Are they not manifestly transgressors of the law in which it is written, “The testimony of two men is true,” when, hating the testimonies—those of his words, namely, and of his deeds—they fulfil the Scripture saying: “They shall lie in wait for the soul of the righteous, and condemn innocent blood” (Ps. XCIII)? For wherever the support of the law is lacking to judges, the condemnation of any person is accounted as homicide.

But how should that be understood which, after saying, “If I had not done among them the works,” he immediately [Col. 0729C] added: “which no one else has done”? What, I ask, is “no one else,” except no evil person—such as I was judged by them to be? For no one other than him is good, especially since in all good persons, whoever performs such things, it is none other than he who acts: “who alone does great wonders” (Ps. LXXI).

Yet this too, like many other things in this discourse, though said in the past tense, may rightly be understood concerning the future. Thus the Lord said, “If I had not done among them the works which no one else has done,” as though he had said: If I had not risen from the dead and ascended into heaven—which indeed no one else has done. “Therefore, if I had not come,” he says, “and spoken, if I had not performed works, they would not have sin. But now I have performed the works of my Father, heavenly works, [Col. 0729D] ‘and they have seen,’ and, seeing, ‘they have hated both me and my Father’; and from this they have a seared conscience” (1 Tim. IV), because they sinned against me through hatred rather than ignorance.

> “But that the word may be fulfilled which is written in their law (Ps. XXIV), ‘They hated me without cause’”—“and they have seen,” he says, “and hated”; therefore they “have no excuse for their sin.”

Yet their own law foretold that this would happen; the word of that law is the word of God, and cannot be dissolved without its coming to pass, as it is written, with the truth of the word in all things preserved—whatever the Holy Spirit has beforehand spoken concerning me (Matt. V). Therefore bear with me in an even spirit their unmerited attacks [Col. 0730A] and gratuitous hatreds.

It should be noted that here the Lord, although he could have recalled a similar example from the Psalms—which are no less ascribed to his person—such as: “Unrighteous witnesses rose up, questioning me about things I did not know; they repaid me evil for good” (Ps. XXXIV); or: “Those who return evil for good spoke against me” (Ps. XXXVII), preferred to take his quotation from this psalm, namely the one hundred and eighth, where it is written: “They spoke against me with a deceitful tongue; they surrounded me with words of hatred and attacked me without cause.” The appropriateness of taking it from that psalm is proved by the fact that, in the first Song of Ascents, every imitator of him, striving through many tribulations to ascend to eternal recompense, likewise says: “With those who hate peace I was peaceable; when I spoke to them, they attacked me without cause” (Ps. CXIX).

For it is clear that in the present Gospel passage he instructs his disciples to become his imitators through patience, saying: “If the world hates you, know that it hated me before you,” and so forth. He therefore aptly recalled this saying of Scripture, in a sense saying, in accordance with the meaning in which he had said the preceding things: If any one of you is hated by the world, just as it hated me before you; if, I say, any one of you, beset by wicked lips and a deceitful tongue, laments and says: “Woe is me, for my sojourning has been prolonged; I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar” (ibid.), and, “With those who hate peace I was peaceable; when I spoke [Col. 0730C] to them, they attacked me without cause”—know that before you, the same was true of me: “The mouth of the sinner and the mouth of the deceitful man were opened against me; they spoke against me with a deceitful tongue; they surrounded me with words of hatred; they attacked me without cause” (Ps. CVIII). It follows:

> “But when the Paraclete comes, whom I shall send you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness concerning me. And you also will bear witness, because you have been with me from the beginning.”

Behold, there are three who bear witness to this Son of Man that he is truly the Son of God; beyond this number of witnesses it is neither necessary nor lawful to demand, according to the law. For it is just and lawful that every word should stand in the mouth of two or three witnesses (Deut. XVII). But his Jewish adversaries had said, as was recalled above: “You testify concerning yourself; your testimony is not true” (John VIII). To this he replied: “I am one who bears witness concerning myself, and the Father who sent me bears witness concerning me” (ibid.).

He had shortly before recapitulated these testimonies in saying: “If I had not come and spoken to them”—which is the testimony of the Son of God concerning himself—and then: “If I had not done among them the works which no one else has done”—which is the testimony of the Father concerning the Son. “For,” he says, “the Father dwelling in me, he himself does the works” (John XIV). Behold now the third witness, the Holy Spirit, concerning whom he says: “But when the Paraclete comes, whom I shall send you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, [Col. 0731A] he will bear witness concerning me.”

Therefore, as this same John says in his Epistle: “There are three who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit” (1 John V): the Father, I say, performing the works; the Word himself, who in the beginning was God with God (John I), speaking concerning his flesh and saying: “I am the beginning, who also speak to you” (John VIII), and similar things; and the Holy Spirit, who would console the apostles amid all the persecutions or hatreds of the world. Therefore let faith glory, hope exult, and love rejoice, because the testimonies of the Trinity are not lacking for this Son of Man, in whom we believe, in whom we hope, whom we love—so that Jewish insolence may no longer have room to say: “You bear witness concerning yourself; your testimony is not true.”

Let us now consider the words of this Gospel reading itself. “But when,” he says, [Col. 0731B] “the Paraclete comes, whom I shall send you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father.” In three distinctions the person or majesty of the Holy Spirit is here described: because he is “Paraclete,” because he is “Spirit of truth,” and because he “proceeds from the Father”; and inserted between these is, “whom I shall send you from the Father.”

Why he has been called the Spirit of truth, or Paraclete—that is, Consoler—has already been said above, namely where he says: “If you love me, keep my commandments; and I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, that he may remain with you for ever: the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive” (John XIV). It remains, then, to consider what is now added: “who proceeds from the Father”; and likewise that which the Son himself, equal to the Father, commending the glory of his majesty, inserted in saying: “Whom I shall send you from the Father.”

Therefore, with his inspiration, let us attempt somehow to express first what has been said: “Who proceeds from the Father.” First it should be noted that, speaking of the Holy Spirit, the Son of God used the present tense, “who proceeds from the Father,” whereas much earlier, bearing witness concerning himself against the Jews, he used the past tense: “For I proceeded from God and came” (John VIII). For when he said this, he had already proceeded, “like a bridegroom from his chamber” (Ps. XVIII), namely, having become visible man who had been invisible God. But this Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, had not yet proceeded to human beings. “For,” says the evangelist, “the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet [Col. 0731D] been glorified” (John VII).

At that time this was being accomplished, that he might proceed, after the worthy preparation of the great repentance which, in the Only-begotten of God, the nature of our flesh had undergone, making satisfaction for the ancient sin of Adam’s transgression; that he might proceed, I say, coming for the remission of sins, as he had never been given to anyone before the saving mystery of Christ’s Passion. The very word “procession” expresses the dignity of his person, namely that he is Lord, equal to God the Father or the Son, who himself, as has already been said, proceeded and came as Lord.

But the characteristic or difference of the procession is this: the Son indeed proceeded and came in order to found the house of the holy [Col. 0732A] Church, which God, who created all things, founded through him; whereas the Holy Spirit then proceeded, and does not cease to proceed until the end of the age, in order to dedicate and illuminate the same house, so that in it God—the one Father and Son—and the Holy Spirit himself, who dedicates and consecrates it, may dwell and walk.

Moreover, when God the Father created all things through his Word, the Son proceeded once, because he created all things once and at once. But the Holy Spirit, from then on and unto eternity, does not cease to proceed into the rational creature subject to him; for without his procession the creature’s need cannot subsist, just as, according to natural philosophers, the moon does not shine without the light of the sun. Indeed, the blessed fellowship of the holy angels [Col. 0732B] is always like a full moon, and neither wanes nor diminishes. From the time when the apostate angels sinned, those angels who refused to sin have been set in the sight of the eternal Sun. Hence they shine with full light, since the Adorner of the heavens—that is, this same Holy Spirit—always proceeds into them.

But the Church of chosen human beings which journeys in this world does not always remain in the same state. At one time, lifted up through contemplation, it shines more brightly with the gifts of this same Spirit; at another, darkened by afflictions or the storms of the age, it shines less, until this circuit of the world is ended and it, like a full moon, sits at rest in the sight of its sun. Rightly, therefore, although the Son said of himself in the past tense, “For I proceeded from God and came,” he says of the Holy Spirit in the present tense, [Col. 0732C] “who proceeds from the Father.”

Accordingly, in the mouth of the Catholic Church the Son is rightly said not to proceed but to be begotten; the Holy Spirit, however, is said not to be begotten but to proceed. Yet certain Greek heretics have held that the Holy Spirit proceeds not from the Father and the Son, but from the Father alone, because the Son seemingly spoke with this qualification: “The Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father.” But present truth resists this perverse interpretation. For when he says, “who proceeds from the Father,” the same Son, who also says in this very passage, “whom I shall send you,” says elsewhere: “I will send upon you the promise of my Father” (Luke XXIV). What else is it for the Paraclete to be sent than for the Spirit of truth to proceed? That sending is indeed procession, except that in his own substance the Spirit always proceeds invisibly; but he was sent for a time in another form, namely when he appeared either over the Lord in the form of a dove (Matt. III), or over his apostles in fire (Acts II).

Again, when the same Son truly says: “Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father in me?” (John X), how can the Spirit who proceeds from the Father not also proceed equally from the Son? Is the Son or the Father spatially confined, so that when the Holy Spirit proceeds from the secret fountain of the Father’s breast, he does not proceed from the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father? Therefore, since elsewhere he has said, “I and the Father are one” (John X), in saying, “whom I [Col. 0733A] shall send you,” and “who proceeds from the Father,” he by no means makes himself unequal to the Father through the Holy Spirit’s common procession; rather, he indicates to his faithful something quite different by these words.

For this statement also vehemently opposes whatever heretics have dared to blaspheme against the Holy Spirit by saying that he is a creature. For if he is a creature, how does he proceed from the Father? Is not every creature created from nothing, and does none of them proceed from God’s substance? For what other than God could proceed from God? Thus it is a testimony to the Holy Spirit’s divine nature and majesty alike that, as the Son bore witness concerning himself, saying, “For I proceeded from God,” so he bears witness concerning him: “who proceeds from the Father.” Let this suffice concerning these matters. For it is not the purpose of the present passage to set out everything that might be said against heretical perversity concerning the true divinity of the Holy Spirit.

Let us now return to the order of the text. “He,” he says, “will bear witness concerning me, and you will bear witness, because you have been with me from the beginning.” The Holy Spirit will bear witness, and you will bear witness. Since “you have been with me from the beginning,” you can preach what you know. What was spoken was also done; as Truth promised, so he fulfilled. For the Paraclete came, the Spirit of truth was sent, and he then proceeded visibly who always proceeds invisibly. He proceeded visibly then, I say, not in his substance, in which he is invisible, but he appeared in tongues of fire, kindled hearts, made mouths eloquent, and thus brought forth into public those instructed witnesses of Christ—the Holy Spirit himself, the unconquered witness.

Then the heavens thundered forth [Col. 0733C] the glory of God: there are no speeches or words whose voices are not heard, proclaiming this glory of the Son of God and announcing these works of his hands, because he “placed his tabernacle in the sun, like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber”; and because “his going forth is from the summit of heaven, and his course unto its summit”—that is, because the true God descended from the highest heavens in order to become man, and, having traversed the way of his Passion, like a giant rejoicing, hastened again to the summit of heaven (Ps. XVIII). What then could the Jews do, who had said, “Your testimony is not true”? What, I ask, could the nations, held captive, say when, yielding to this Son of God, so glorious a witness, kings kept silence over him? It follows:

[Col. 0733D] **[CHAPTER XVI.]** “I have spoken these things to you, that you may not be scandalized.”

This too must be understood in the same way as what was said above, when, having assured his disciples that they would be troubled, he said to Simon Peter: “Amen, amen, I say to you, the cock will not crow this night until you deny me three times,” and immediately added: “Let not your heart be troubled” (John XIII). That is, even if the tongue stammers from fear, let faith not fail in your heart. In the same way, I say, this must be understood: although he said to them, “You will all suffer scandal because of me this night” (Matt. XXIX), he now says, “I have spoken these things to you, that you may not be scandalized.”

For to be scandalized on that night was one thing; to be scandalized absolutely, or without any qualification, is another. They were indeed scandalized on that night, when, through the storm of that night, the shepherd being struck, the sheep were scattered in fear (Zech. XIII). But they were not scandalized without all exception, because in compassionate spirit they remained with him from whom they fled while bodily scattered. Nor did Peter himself, though denying him with a trembling mouth, cease in heart to believe in him whom he had confessed to be Christ, the Son of God. It was therefore not without purpose that he forewarned and fortified them, saying: “I have spoken these things to you, that you may not be scandalized.” And he added:

> “They will put you out of the synagogues.”

That this was done to Christ’s disciples is most fully read in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts V, XIII). For they were scourged in synagogues and even driven out of cities. Therefore, turning to the nations, they established other synagogues—or rather, new churches—for the glory of God; and when God’s law and covenant were transferred to these, those who had put them out of the synagogue would themselves weep outside God’s synagogue and remain excluded in the synagogue of Satan [Col. 0734B] (Rev. III).

But it is little that he says, “They will put you out of the synagogues.” He therefore added: “But the hour is coming when everyone who kills you will think that he is offering service to God,” and so forth. “And these things,” he says, “they have already begun to do; they have already put you out of the synagogues. For they had long since agreed that if anyone confessed me to be Christ, they should put him out of the synagogue” (John IX). “But the hour is coming” when they will do what is greater, namely, kill you, and do so with such authority, with such an appearance of reason, “that everyone who kills you will think”—that is, will seem to think—“that he is offering service to God.”

For although Saul truly thought that he was offering service to God by binding and killing Christ’s disciples (Acts IX), this should not be understood in the same way of those of whom he had shortly before said: “But now they have both seen and hated both me and my Father”—namely, the chief priests and Pharisees, who had taken away the key of knowledge, neither entering themselves nor allowing others to enter (Luke XI). They first killed the Lord himself and then his disciples; they did not truly think, but seemed to think, that they were offering service to God.

Or again, if you attend to the proper sense of the word *to think* (*arbitrari*), from which judges are said *to judge* (*arbitrari*) when they measure any matter by their own judgement, Christ’s enemies—and enemies of God his Father—truly thought, in killing his disciples, [Col. 0734D] that they were offering service to God. That is, although against their own conscience, they judged that it pleased God, pretending a supposedly necessary concern for the place or the nation, as they themselves first did against the Lord, saying: “If we let him go on thus, all will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away our place and nation” (John XI). Indeed, persisting stubbornly in this judgement, they again deceitfully thought themselves to be standing for the place or the nation when they set witnesses against Stephen to say that they had heard him saying that Jesus of Nazareth would destroy this place (Acts VI).

Therefore, “the hour is coming,” he says, “when everyone who kills you will think that he is offering service to [Col. 0735A] God.” The hour, I say—that is, a short time. For they were not allowed for long to kill Christ’s disciples, as though for that temple of God whose ancient worship they zealously maintained indeed, but not according to knowledge, that is, not according to the love of God, which is certainly true—that is, unpuffing—knowledge (Rom. X). For afterward it was overthrown, not by Christ’s disciples but by the Roman nations, fulfilling the prophecy that foretold concerning that corrupt vineyard: “The boar from the forest has laid it waste, and the solitary wild beast has devoured it” (Ps. LXXIX).

This hour of Jewish persecution was plainly a short time. For this cannot be said of persecuting idolaters, who killed Christ’s apostles and martyrs not during an hour, but through long persecutions over many periods, and thought that they were offering service, not to God, but to their gods. It follows:

> “And they will do these things to you because they have not known the Father or me.”

As though he said: Therefore they will not merely put you out of the synagogues, but will also kill you, because “they have hated both me and my Father.” For when above he said, “But now they have both seen and hated both me and my Father”; and likewise, “Now they have no excuse for their sin,” he surely does not excuse ignorance, but condemns the hatred of those unwilling to know, saying: “Because they have not known the Father or me.”

The Apostle, intimating the perversity of such obstinate ignorance to the Thessalonians, after saying, “in a flame of fire, inflicting vengeance on those who do not know God,” immediately added: “and on those who do not obey the Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ, who will pay penalties in destruction from the presence of the Lord” [Col. 0735C] (2 Thess. I). Rightly, therefore, by saying, “because they have not known,” contempt for God and hatred are indicated.

And immediately there follows: “But I have spoken these things to you, so that, when the hour comes, you may remember that I told you.” “They will do them,” he says, “but be consoled. For this is why I now foretell these things to you: that, when the hour comes, you may remember the things that I told you; and, remembering, do not forget that also which I promised: that in all afflictions not a hair of your head will perish, and while enemies kill your bodies, by your patience you will possess your souls” (Matt. X; Luke XXI).

> “But I did not tell you these things from the beginning, because I was with you. But now I am going to him who sent me, and none of you asks me, ‘Where are you going?’ But because I have spoken these things to you, sorrow has filled your heart.”

In this Gospel reading, the first matter to be carefully discerned is with what purpose the Lord said: “I am going to him who sent me, and none of you asks me, ‘Where are you going?’” For truly, when he said this, he was about to go into heaven by an ascent so manifest that none of the apostles needed to ask him where he was going, since “while they watched, he was lifted up, and a cloud received him from their sight” [Col. 0736A] (Acts I). But when he went in that manner, sorrow did not fill their hearts, but joy—as Luke plainly testifies: “They worshipped and returned to Jerusalem with great joy” (Luke XXIV).

The prophet long ago foretold the magnitude of this unspeakable joy, saying: “God ascended with jubilation,” immediately adding, “and the Lord with the sound of a trumpet” (Ps. XLIV), namely, as a dreadful proclamation of his second coming; for the angels said to those looking into heaven: “He will come in the same manner as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts I). Thus joy, not sorrow, filled the disciples’ hearts because the Saviour ascended into heaven before their eyes.

But here he says: “Because I have spoken these things to you, sorrow has filled your heart.” And shortly afterward: “Amen, amen, I say to you, you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice.” Therefore sound reasoning requires that this be understood of the way or passage of his Passion, concerning which the evangelist had previously said: “Jesus, knowing that the hour had come for him to pass from this world to the Father” [Col. 0736B] (John XIII).

Furthermore, it must be known that through Christ’s Passion this was accomplished: the grace of the Paraclete Spirit was poured out upon us. For if Christ had ascended into heaven without suffering, that Spirit of grace, who remits sins through his blood, would certainly not have been given. He himself confirms this by his declaration: “Amen, amen, I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falling into the earth dies, it remains alone” (John XII).

With this meaning guiding us, let us hear what he says: “But I did not tell you these things from the beginning, because I was with you.” The meaning is: These things that I now tell you concerning the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, I did not tell you “from the beginning”—that is, from the time you began to follow me—because I had not yet been wounded for your sins, nor yet cut off or crushed from the land of the living for your iniquities (Isa. LIII). For this reason, I say, I did not speak to you of this Paraclete, this Spirit of adoption as sons (Rom. VIII). But now “I am going to him who sent me”—now, I say, when, delivered over to death, I commend my spirit into the Father’s hands (Luke XXIII).

But what does he mean by saying, “And none of you asks me, ‘Where are you going?’” It is because they had asked him, saying: “Lord, where are you going?” and again, “Lord, we do not know where you are going, [Col. 0736D] and how can we know the way?” (John XIV); and they seemed to themselves ready in spirit to follow him then, prepared to go with him both to prison and to death (Luke XXII). But they were to flee and leave alone him whom they had so urgently questioned. He therefore aptly says, “And none of you asks me,” foretelling with gentle rebuke that solitude of his, concerning which later he would say: “Amen, I say to you, the hour is coming when you will all be scattered and will leave me alone.” For then truly none of them said, “Lord, where are you going?” because their flight showed that none wished or was able to follow him.

He then added: “But because I have spoken these things to you, sorrow has filled your heart.” “You ought to rejoice,” he says, “because I am going to the Father; especially because, as I said to you above, ‘I, going, will ask the Father, and he will give another Paraclete,’ and because ‘in my Father’s house are many dwelling places’ (John XIV), in which, with this Paraclete going before and leading, I shall receive you to myself. But on the contrary, ‘sorrow has filled your heart because I have spoken these things to you,’ because in this human life you desire always to have me present.”

> “But I tell you the truth: it is expedient for you that I go away. For if I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go away, I will send him to you.”

He confirms his statement with great weight in saying: “I tell you the truth.” Why this, except because it is truly expedient for us to know or believe that unless he had suffered, we would not receive the Spirit of adoption as sons [Col. 0737B] (Rom. VIII)? For this reason it was truly expedient that he should go away; and it is likewise expedient for you to believe that we would not have received through him the grace of reconciliation unless, in going away, he had poured out his blood.

He says, therefore: “I tell you the truth: it is expedient for you that I go away.” And, explaining how truly this is expedient: “For if,” he says, “I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you.” Why, if I do not go away, will the Paraclete not come to you? Namely, because there will be nothing by which he may console you. For by what will he console you unless I do as the Father commanded me, and, excluding the disobedience of the first man by the power of obedience, restore to you the life of souls which you lost, and obtain the resurrection of bodies (Rom. V)?

Therefore, if I do not go away, if I do not drink from the torrent on the way (Ps. CIX), the Paraclete—that is, the Consoler—will not come to you. Nor will this Holy Spirit declare himself to be Paraclete, having nothing by which to console you or anything to say to you while you bear the prejudice of ancestral transgression. Moreover, every consolation that this Holy Spirit has spoken through the mouth of his holy prophets from the beginning of the world will be ineffectual (Luke I). For the Scriptures which this same Holy Spirit inspired as consolation for the prophets mourning the common misery will not be fulfilled. For whatever has been written was written for your instruction, so that through the consolation of the Scriptures you might have hope of the life which you lost in Adam (Rom. XV).

Therefore, “it is expedient for you,” he says, “that [Col. 0737D] I go away. For if I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go away, I will send him to you.” “I will send him to you,” that is, I will send him into you. For he is not sent from place to place, since the Holy Spirit, God, is everywhere and is not contained by walls; rather, he is received by the faculties of the mind and by faith.

Our Lord indeed did once and again what he now promises. Once, on the very day on which he rose, when he had indeed already gone away—already passed from his humiliation to glory and honour, from mortal condition to immortality, from this world to the Father. For then, that is, on that very day, “standing in the midst of his disciples, he breathed on them and said: ‘Receive the Holy Spirit’” (John XX). Receive, I say, the Paraclete [Col. 0738A] for the greatest consolation: that is, for the remission of sins and the opening of the Scriptures. Thus the evangelist immediately adds in the same passage: “Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them” (ibid.). And Luke, recounting the same appearance, says: “Then he opened their understanding, that they might understand the Scriptures” (Luke XXIV). The sending forth of the Spirit must be discussed more fully in its proper place.

Then he sent him again on the tenth day after his ascension, when the disciples were gathered together in one place: “Suddenly there came from heaven a sound like that of a violent rushing wind, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting” (Acts II). Then, I say, he again sent this Paraclete, so that he who had been given equally to all for the remission of sins might now distribute diverse gifts of grace to each according to his will, that they might be eloquent for preaching and strong to endure the contests of sufferings. It follows:

“And when he comes, he will convict the world concerning sin, and righteousness, and judgment: concerning sin indeed, because they did not believe in me; concerning righteousness, because I go to the Father, and you will see me no longer; and concerning judgment, because the prince of this world has already been judged.”

The Lamb of God, soon to be sacrificed, foretells the great power of the Holy Spirit and the sum of all those things which that same Spirit, even until now, wonderfully proclaims with his voice—marvellous in its sweetness. For everything which human beings, inspired or inflamed by this Holy Spirit, thereafter preach with strength and sweetness, chiefly treats of these three matters: sin, righteousness, and judgment. Explaining each of them, he says: “Concerning sin, because they did not believe in me,” and so forth.

Two of these are opposites and contrary to one another: namely, sin and righteousness. The third is judgment, in which fitting places or rewards are to be rendered to those two, sin and righteousness. This sin is certainly not to be understood here only of the Jews, who did not believe in him whom they saw and heard bodily present; rather, first of the Jews, then of the Greeks—that is, of all the nations of the whole world. For he did not say, “He will convict the Jews concerning sin,” but “He will convict the world”; and the Holy Spirit will convict not Jews alone, but the whole world also through Christ’s apostles.

How, you ask, was the whole world to be rebuked concerning this sin, because they did not believe in him, when he preached among only the one nation of the Jews? To this I say: the sin of unbelief must plainly be considered more deeply. For every vice and every iniquity of humankind took its beginning from unbelief, because the first human beings believed or obeyed the serpent more than God (Gen. III). Thereafter their corrupted descendants, and the nations believing more in the devil or his idols than in God, and the Jews expecting Antichrist more than Christ, sinned in common; and, the Apostle says, all things were shut up in unbelief (Rom. XI).

Thus, by the sin which he expounded in this way, saying, “because they did not believe in me,” is to be understood every unrighteousness or disobedience of the old man; and by the righteousness which he indicated in this way, saying, “because I go to the Father,” every righteousness or obedience of the new man. Concerning these—sin and righteousness—the Holy Spirit convicts the world in that, through his preachers, he does not cease urgently, in season and out of season, to press them to put off the old man with his deeds and put on the new man, who was created according to God in righteousness and holiness of truth (Eph. IV; II Tim. IV).

For the righteousness of the new man is beautifully indicated in his saying, “Because I go to the Father”; that is, because, obedient to the Father unto death (Phil. II), I leave behind the common way of life of this present existence. That this should be understood thus has already been said above and will still be said later, where he says, “A little while, and you will no longer see me; and again a little while, and you will see me,” immediately adding, “because I go to the Father.”

Therefore the sin to which this righteousness is opposed in the present passage is the root of all sins: namely, original sin. Since we are commanded in Christ’s baptism to renounce it, and the faith of that same new man and the future judgment are entrusted to us as things to be believed, the Holy Spirit truly convicts the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment, so that no one may remain ignorant of what the end of sin is, what the end of righteousness is, and how dreadful the judgment will be at the end for discerning the merit of each.

Moreover, by saying, “Concerning judgment, because the prince of this world has already been judged,” he has terrifyingly expressed the consequent condemnation of those who still cling to him. For once the head has been judged, the members too are believed to be cast down together, as the Judge says: “Go, you cursed, into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV).

Therefore the coming of the Holy Spirit, which follows Christ’s passion, is a worthy reason why his disciples ought not to grieve because he goes to the Father. But they were not yet fit to bear the things he had now said, and the other such things which must be known and believed concerning him. Therefore he immediately says:

“And I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now.”

Therefore what he had said above—“I no longer call you servants, because a servant does not know what his lord does; but I have called you friends, because I have made known to you everything whatever I heard from my Father” (John XV)—must be understood of the future. It is consequently expressed in the past tense because what he promises is without doubt about to occur at once.

He continues: “But when that Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all truth.” For he will teach you every truth which it is necessary to know, opening your understanding so that you may understand the Scriptures and truly know all that is contained concerning me in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms, whether said parabolically or enacted figuratively (Luke XXIV).

“For he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak; and he will announce to you the things that are to come.” He says: This is why he is the Spirit of truth, and why he will teach you all truth: because “he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak.” For a spirit that speaks from itself is not a spirit of truth but a spirit of falsehood; it makes all prophets false prophets (Jer. XXVII), so that they prophesy from their own heart what the Lord has not spoken, invent what does not exist, or declare evil to be good and good to be evil (Isa. V).

This Spirit will not speak thus; rather, “whatever he hears he will speak”: that is, he will speak things that are, things that truly exist, and things having authority in the Scriptures, inventing nothing and perverting nothing. He will make you true prophets, so that you do not speak from yourselves but speak whatever you hear concerning me in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms—making up nothing and corrupting nothing, but expounding the truthful Scripture with a true understanding. Thus, through your mouth, “the Spirit of truth will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak; and he will announce to you the things that are to come,” so that you may be not merely instructed hearers of the prophets, but yourselves knowers of future things and comparable to prophets, moreover tasting beforehand your future blessedness through such a message.

“He will glorify me, because he will receive from what is mine and announce it to you.”—He, I say, such a true and fitting witness, “will glorify me, because he will receive from what is mine”; that is, from that which is written—“he will receive from what is mine and announce it to you”—he will receive, making it plainly known to your understanding.

For example, this saying in the Psalm is mine: “The Lord said to me, ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I shall give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession’” (Ps. II). From this testimony concerning me he will receive and make known to you the authority for bearing witness concerning me: that I am the Son of the Lord God, not adopted but begotten, because he said to me, “Today”—that is, in eternity—“I have begotten you”; and that I now do what he commanded me, namely, ask for the nations.

This, I say, I now do in these days of my flesh, offering prayers and supplications, with loud cries and many tears, to him who is able to save me from death (Heb. IX); and assuredly he will soon hear me because of my reverence: “I shall give you,” he says, “the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession.” This is assuredly mine; and whenever he announces or reveals such a thing to you, “he will receive from what is mine,” because, since I am the Word of God, all God’s Scriptures are mine; they are my testimonies.

And in doing this he will indeed glorify me, bearing witness concerning me, so that you too, having such an advocate or spokesman in every tribunal, in all synagogues, or in councils, may bear witness that I am the Son of God, and that all nations and all the ends of the earth are rightly my inheritance or possession. Perhaps someone may ask why he did not say, “He will receive what is mine,” but “He will receive from what is mine and announce it to you.” But he himself immediately says:

“All things whatsoever the Father has are mine. Therefore I said that he will receive from what is mine and announce it to you.”

You ask, he says, why, receiving not all things but from what is mine, he will announce them? Behold, I say: “All things whatsoever the Father has are mine.” What things does the Father have? “He has immortality and dwells in inaccessible light” (I Tim. VI), and whatever such things sacred Scripture witnesses that he possesses—things which no human being while alive can see or know as they are (Exod. XXXIII; I John III).

For this is laid up for you in the future: that now you may know in part and see through a mirror in an enigma, but then may know as you are known and see face to face (I Cor. XIII). Yet all these incomprehensible things which the Father has are mine because I am of the same nature as he, and with him I possess one divinity, equal glory, coeternal majesty. Rightly, therefore, I did not say, “what is mine,” but “from what is mine”: namely, because in the present life he will not announce to you everything that belongs to the Father and to me, but will enable you to know in part and to prophesy in part concerning things which eye has not seen, ear has not heard, and which have not entered into the human heart (I Cor. II).

He continues:

“A little while, and you will no longer see me; and again a little while, and you will see me, because I go to the Father.”

According to the other Evangelists, while these things were being said, the apostles’ eyes were heavy, and they slept untimely because of sorrow. Yet he, from whom nothing was hidden, knew how meanwhile Judas, the son of perdition and minister of death, driven by the devil, was running about and hastening, obtaining a cohort and servants from the chief priests and Pharisees, lighting lanterns and torches, and procuring weapons. Before all these things happened, Christ our Lord, our salvation, had again set this before them so that he should lose none of those whom the Father had given him (John VI).

Therefore, just as he says in another Evangelist, “Could you not watch with me one hour? Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation” (Matt. XXV), so in this Evangelist, desiring that they be watchful and ready to escape, he says: “A little while, and you will no longer see me.”

Endure with me a little while, and with wakeful eyes consider and attend to me. After this little while—that is, after this imminent hour or day—you will no longer see me. Yet let not your heart be troubled: behold, I tell you this also, that “again a little while, and you will see me, because I go to the Father.”

It should be noted that in saying, “And you will no longer see me, and again you will see me,” he sets almost the same yet contrary things alongside one another, namely seeing and not seeing, in order to commend the truth of the resurrection which after a little while was to occur in him, and at the end of the age will occur in us.

For when in both places he says “me,” he asserts that he himself, and not another, will rise in the true substance of flesh. But when he says, “you will no longer see,” and “you will see,” he promises that the same flesh will be changed—that is, that it will possess another glory. This, I say, should be noted: because “you will no longer see me” means, “You will never again see me such as you now see me”—that is, passible, mortal, living among human beings, acquainted with human infirmities, a man of sorrows and the last of men (Isa. LIII). You will no longer see me thus after this “little while,” that is, after the ninth hour of the following day. But, on the contrary, you will again see me immortal and impassible; thus you will see not another, indeed, but one greatly changed.

Therefore he who, intending to say, “You will again see me,” prefaces it with “You will no longer see me,” plainly asserts not that the truth of his human substance will perish, but that the glory of its nature will be changed through the power of the resurrection.

He continues:

“Then some of his disciples said to one another, ‘What is this that he says: A little while and you will not see me, and again a little while and you will see me, and because I go to the Father?’”

This was because they did not know the power of the resurrection—indeed, they did not even believe that he himself would rise. Though they held great opinions of him, they could not understand even this, that he was to die. It is therefore not surprising that they could not grasp the force of his speech.

“Therefore they said, ‘What is this that he says to us, “A little while”? We do not know what he is saying.’”

Certainly the Lord could have declared in plainer words what he meant to those who hesitated thus; but the event itself, immediately to follow, was going to explain everything more fittingly. This was expedient for their tender minds: that he should neither remain altogether silent nor announce in words the whole matter of their immense grief, but only part of it, lest the storm, suddenly breaking upon them with too great force, utterly overthrow in them the foundation of faith. Rather, grief gradually disclosed would become more bearable.

He therefore continues thus:

“Jesus therefore knew that they wished to ask him, and says to them: ‘Do you inquire among yourselves about this, because I said to you, “A little while and you will not see me, because I go; and again a little while and you will see me, because I go to the Father”? Amen, amen, I say to you: you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice.’”

Behold, it is clear that instructive Wisdom, acting gently according to its counsel, both increases their anxiety and for the most part keeps hidden the cause of their anxiety. For, after first saying, “Do you inquire among yourselves because I said, ‘A little while and you will no longer see me,’” and so forth, he does not immediately say what would have been easy to understand: one little while is from now until the ninth hour of the coming day, after which I shall be buried and “you will no longer see me”; and the other little while is from that hour until the third day, on which I shall rise and “you will again see me.” Rather, he adds: “Amen, amen, I say to you: you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice.”

Here one must understand: but afterward the world too will weep and howl; or its laughter will be mingled with pain, and mourning will seize the end of its joy (Prov. XIV). For immediately afterward, by contrast, follows: “But you will be sorrowful, and your sorrow will be turned into joy.”

The joy, he says, will be that of this unclean world, which hates me because I oppose its impurities: the world, that is, the lovers of the world, will rejoice because I go to the Father, whom nevertheless it does not know. But a double affliction will swallow up such joy. First, because days will come in which they will say, “Blessed are the barren, and the wombs that did not bear, and breasts that did not nurse” (Luke XXIII): namely, when the Romans come and take away their place and nation (John XI), according to their fear. Then, because at last they will see him whom they pierced (Zech. II).

But how great a joy your sorrow will produce, and when it is to be destroyed by joy, behold: I make known to you by a comparison.

“A woman, when she gives birth, has sorrow because her hour has come. But when she has borne the child, she no longer remembers the anguish, because of the joy that a human being has been born into the world. Therefore you too now indeed have sorrow.”

For this conclusion, “Therefore you too now indeed have sorrow,” to fit more appropriately, one ought first to understand, or supply, that the holy Church is a great and illustrious woman; that her man or husband is God, the Father of all; and that her child, whom she conceived by the grace of great true love from that same husband, is he who speaks these things, our Lord Jesus Christ.

For she first conceived him by faith when, already a young woman, she heard in Abraham the promises saying, “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. XXII), and believed. From then on the blessed offspring, pregnant in mind and carrying the word of promise, advanced through the patriarchs and prophets by the increase of that same Word; like a woman with child, she swelled more and more in her womb. At length this same woman—of whom the blessed apostles are a great part—brought forth the long-desired child amid great pain and distress of his passion; and she saw him happily born into the day of eternity, that is, risen from the dead. “And she no longer remembers the anguish, because a human being has been born”—because he has been reborn and lives again—“into the world,” redeemed and saved, so that he might obtain sovereignty over the world, indeed over heaven and earth and all things in them.

Therefore, once the comparison has been set forth—“A woman when she gives birth has sorrow; but when she has borne the child, she no longer remembers the anguish because of the joy that a human being has been born into the world”—what has now been said must be supplied by implication, and so the conclusion will enter with greater force: “And therefore you too now indeed have sorrow.”

“But I shall see you again, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you.”

You, he says, who are now like a woman having in her womb, who cries out in childbirth and is tormented in order to give birth: I shall see again, and I shall appear for you to see, separated indeed from the womb of your mortality, but born for your good and made immortal for the eternal kingdom (Rev. XII). “And your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your sure and true joy from you.”

For you will rejoice steadfastly and say: “Why have the nations raged, and the peoples meditated vain things?” (Ps. II). For they will truly rage in vain and devise empty things when they beat you in the synagogues. There indeed you will rejoice all the more, and will go rejoicing from the presence of the council because you have been deemed worthy to suffer disgrace for my name (Acts XII). Even if they kill the body, your heart will rejoice even then, because your joy will be stored not in flesh, which can be killed, but in the heart or soul, which the persecutor cannot kill (Matt. X). Therefore “no one will take your joy from you.”

“And on that day you will ask me nothing.”

You now inquire among yourselves concerning this because I said to you, “A little while and you will no longer see me, and again a little while and you will see me,” and you wish to ask me. But “on that day” of your joy, “you will ask me nothing” about these matters, for you will know them thoroughly through the present evidence of events and feelings.

Moreover, whatever else it will be necessary to know, having your understanding opened from that day onward, you will inquire of the Scriptures: you will consult the books of the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms, and they themselves will explain to you what I have done or said to you (Luke X).

He continues: “Amen, amen, I say to you: if you ask the Father anything in my name, he will give it to you. Until now you have not asked anything in my name. Ask, and you will receive, that your joy may be full.”

By repeatedly saying and impressing upon his disciples that they must ask in his name if they wish to ask anything of the Father, our Lord beneficially desires to be acknowledged as the mediator between God and human beings (I Tim. II). This is so necessary that no one can come to the Father except through him, and no one can obtain anything from the Father except through his name.

Hence the saving custom and Catholic rule of prayer according to the practice of holy Church is that, in every prayer which it addresses to the Father, it adds: “Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son.” For besides this there is no way and no other door, by looking toward which one may effectively say: “Let my prayer be directed as incense in your sight; the lifting up of my hands as an evening sacrifice” (Ps. CIV). The name alone of this only-begotten Son of God, Jesus Christ, is the necessary vehicle of every prayer, by which it is carried in a direct course to heaven and stands before the Father’s presence, able to draw salvation from his bosom and the grace of forgiveness of sins.

But the apostles did not yet know this. Therefore the Master of life, now about to depart, commended it to them more earnestly in his discourse. Thus, when he says, “Amen, amen, I say to you: if you ask the Father anything in my name, he will give it to you,” the contrary must be understood: that the Father will give you nothing unless you ask in prayer in my name.

The present passage is joined to what precedes in this way: “So that you may know that you now have sorrow with the truly great fruit of joy to follow, like a woman giving birth, I say this to you: ‘If you ask the Father anything in my name, he will give it to you.’” “In my name,” he says, that is, according to my name, which is interpreted Jesus and Saviour. Explaining the reason or meaning of this name, the angel said to blessed Joseph: “For he will save his people from their sins” (Matt. I).

Therefore to ask in the name of Jesus is to ask for that for which he who chose this name for himself “came down from heaven, was incarnate and made man, was crucified, died and was buried, rose on the third day, ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of the Father.” Why was all this done, except that through his name we might receive forgiveness of sins? Therefore, whenever we ask for something which undoubtedly cooperates with this purpose, we should confidently hope to receive it as those asking in the name of Jesus.

This meaning is made clearer from another Gospel passage: “Amen,” he says, “I say to you: if two of you agree on earth concerning any matter whatever that they ask, it shall be done for them by my Father who is in heaven. For where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in their midst” (Matt. XVIII).

Who are these two who agree—these two or three gathered in the name of Jesus—except those concerning whom he had said beforehand: “If your brother sins against you, go and rebuke him between yourself and him alone; if he does not hear you, take with you one more person” (ibid.)? For then the two agree with one another, when the brother who has sinned listens to the brother rebuking him. Then, I say, two or three are gathered in the name of Jesus, when a person either rebukes the sinner alone with him, or, not yet heard, takes with him one more person. They are assuredly then truly gathered and truly agree with one another when the one who sinned is gained and yields to agreement in repentance.

Accordingly, they are given confidence concerning pardon or the salvation of their brother when it is said, “If two of you agree on earth concerning any matter whatever that they ask, it shall be done for them” (ibid.); and from what precedes it must necessarily be understood that you say, “concerning every matter of sin.”

But concerning whatever else we ask for according to our superfluous wishes, God is by no means bound as a debtor in law on account of these or other such promises of his—especially since, in the prayer which he himself composed when the apostles said, “Teach us to pray” (Matt. VI), he set forth in seven petitions the sum of all things that should be requested, corresponding to the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. The first is, “Hallowed be your name”; the seventh, “But deliver us from evil” (Matt. VI).

Therefore, when he says, “Amen, amen, I say to you: if you ask the Father anything in my name, he will give it to you,” we must neither dare to ask the Father for anything except what pertains to our salvation, nor suppose that we can obtain it otherwise than through the name of the only-begotten Son.

Because the apostles did not yet know this, as has been said: “Until now,” he says, “you have not asked anything in my name.” For they did not yet know him perfectly, although they believed or confessed that he was the Christ, the Son of the living God. They had not yet, I say, known him so plainly as to know that he had undertaken the embassy of our peace and had been given as mediator for obtaining for human beings the grace of God the Father (Eph. I). Therefore they had not until then asked anything in his name, since he himself is not found to have commanded this to them before this hour of his passion, though in many places he had spoken much concerning persistence in prayer.

And he added: “Ask and you will receive, that your joy may be full.” The order or sense is: “Ask, that your joy may be full, and you will receive.” But in what can it be full except that we come and appear before the face of God? For every joy of this world is deceptive, and all its laughter is mistaken (Eccles. II); only joy arising from the vision of God and the smile of his present face has fullness and is true. Nor can it be darkened or taken away. Therefore, when he says, “Ask and you will receive, that your joy may be full,” he indicates that only those things are to be asked which advance us toward the vision of God, in whom alone is fullness of joy.

Finally, at the end of his discourse he adds:

“I have spoken these things to you in proverbs. The hour is coming when I shall no longer speak to you in proverbs, but shall announce the Father to you openly.”

What are the things which he asserts that he spoke in proverbs? Did he speak proverbs or parables from the time when he rose from supper, rather than give plain precepts of love and exhortations to patience? Indeed, the apostles themselves, considering only this discourse which he had continued that night until this point, say: “Behold, now you speak openly and say no proverb.”

Therefore, when he says, “I have spoken these things to you in proverbs,” and so forth, he did not intend the words themselves which he was then speaking to be understood; otherwise he would more properly have said, “I have spoken these proverbs to you,” if indeed the things he had spoken to them thus far could fittingly be called proverbs.

But “these things,” he says, “which are now imminent, which are now occurring”—namely, my passion, for which your heart is now filled with sorrow; likewise the resurrection or ascension, at the sight of which you will rejoice and “no one will take your joy from you”; and the outpouring of the Paraclete, whom, as I have said, “if I go away, I shall send to you”—“these things, I say, I have hitherto spoken to you in proverbs.” I have signified them beforehand in various figures until this hour of my passion—indeed, until, as I yield up my spirit, the veil of the temple is torn from top to bottom (Matt. XXVII), testifying by its very rending that the mysteries of the Word of God which had until then lain hidden under figures would thereafter shine forth in truth.

“For from then on I shall no longer speak to you in proverbs, but shall announce my Father to you openly,” so that, through the present events whose figures went before, you may be able not only to understand what I myself have now done or said to you, but also to examine and disclose what happened figuratively to your fathers.

“On that day you will ask in my name.”

On that day, I say—the day of revealed grace, the day of salvation, and the acceptable time (I Cor. X; II Cor. VI)—when the Spirit of truth, receiving from what is mine and announcing it to you, will teach you all truth: “You will ask in my name,” because, knowing me and believing that “I am in the Father and the Father is in me,” true God and human being, equally worthy of worship with the Father, you will ask in my name, as you have not done until now.

“And I do not say to you that I shall ask the Father concerning you. For the Father himself loves you, because you have loved me and believed that I came forth from God.”

He does not say: “On that day I shall ask the Father concerning you.” Lest perhaps a heretic should fail to understand how it was said above, “And I shall ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete,” and from this argue that the Son is less than the Father because asking is the part of an inferior, behold, he adds this also from the contrary: “And I do not say to you that I shall ask the Father concerning you”—namely, “on that day on which,” as I have already said, “you will ask in my name.”

For on this present day which now presses upon us—the day of my tribulation, when they seize my soul and the mighty rush upon me (Ps. LXXVI)—“I shall ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete.” I shall ask, he says, being made a priest and myself the sacrifice, according to the passible nature of a human being. But on that day and thereafter, when you again see me with joy in your hearts, “I shall no longer ask the Father concerning you.”

Why? “For the Father himself loves you”: that is, through this petition of mine he already has you reconciled to himself as friends, and has made you children of his grace from children of wrath (Eph. III). Why is this? “Because you have loved me and believed that I came forth from God.”

“I came forth from the Father and came into the world; again I leave the world and go to the Father.”

“I emptied myself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. II), and came to save the world, keeping hard paths because of the words of the Father’s lips (Ps. XVI), while I do not speak the works of human beings. Again I leave the world, laying aside the yoke of service, and go to the Father, receiving glory and honour because of the passion of death (Heb. II).

For this reason the Father himself loves you on that day, because you believed this. For this faith is the effective cause why my passion benefits you, why you are reconciled to God, why he counts and loves you no longer as children of wrath but as children of grace. Thus from that day onward it is no longer necessary that I ask the Father concerning you, as I now do once only. For I die once, and when I die, I die to sin—not my own, but yours; thereafter I shall live to God, because, as I said to you, “I go to the Father,” from whom I came forth in order to return in this manner.

This indeed is what the Psalmist heard with prophetic ear as the heavens declared it. For after introducing the verse in which he explained what glory of God they declared, saying, “He has placed his tabernacle in the sun; and he, like a bridegroom coming forth from his bridal chamber, rejoiced as a giant to run his course,” he immediately continued: “His going forth is from the height of heaven” (Ps. XVIII).

Therefore Cerinthus and heretics like him lied in saying that Christ did not exist before Mary. “For,” he says, “I came forth from the Father and came into the world,” while the prophet testifies: “I came forth from the height of heaven.”

He continues:

“His disciples say to him: ‘Behold, now you speak openly and say no proverb.’”

For he had said to them: “I have spoken these things to you in proverbs; the hour is coming when I shall no longer speak to you in proverbs, but shall announce my Father to you openly.” They had not noticed that he did not say in the present tense, “I speak these things to you in proverbs,” but in the past tense, “I have spoken these things to you in proverbs.” This has already been said above.

Therefore they said: “Behold, now you speak openly and say no proverb.” Although it is true in part that now—that is, at this supper—he had spoken no proverb, still not everything which he had said was plain to them. For a little earlier they had said: “What is this that he says to us: ‘A little while and you will no longer see me, and again a little while and you will see me, and because I go to the Father’?” “We do not know what he is saying.”

So deeply were they obscured in that great cloud of sorrow, by which not only their eyes but also their inner faculties were weighed down (Matt. XXVI), that they did not even know their own ignorance or slowness. Yet faith lay beneath this error, destined to appear in its own time when the darkness of ignorance had been dispelled and the storms of sorrow or fear calmed.

For it follows:

“Now we know that you know all things, and that you have no need for anyone to question you. By this we believe that you came forth from God.”

This is a venerable profession worthy of God’s wisdom: “Now we know that you know all things.” For to know all things belongs to Wisdom alone—“his wisdom, of which there is no number” (Ps. CXLVI)—which “reaches from end to end mightily and orders all things sweetly” (Wis. VIII). This alone knows all things, searches the hearts of all (Jer. XVII), and understands every thought of minds.

They immediately indicate by what experience they came to know this: “And you have no need for anyone to question you.” This is plainly fitting testimony for so great a matter. For who among teachers is so capable that he can always suffice for questions put to him, let alone anticipate the unspoken thoughts of his hearers? But that Lord and Teacher, with as much power as benevolence in his teaching, held all hearts in his hand, so that he did not fail to know what any person lacked; indeed, no thought of the heart lay hidden from him.

The disciples had been confirmed in this by many experiences, and also by this recent proof. For a little before, when he said, “A little while and you will no longer see me,” and so forth, while some said to one another, “We do not know what he is saying,” he knew that they wished to ask him; nor did he need them to ask, for he anticipated them, saying, “Do you inquire among yourselves about this?”

“Therefore,” they say, “we rightly know that you know all things,” nor do we doubt it. And they rightly spoke thus of him, without whom no one else has stretched lines of knowledge or understanding over each individual person (Job XXXVIII). “And,” they say, “you have no need for anyone to question you,” as anyone who wishes to teach must have disclosed to him in words the point at which the mind of the hearer is stuck.

But what they add—“By this we believe that you came forth from God”—is as though they said: By this we believe that you are Wisdom itself, which said: “I came forth from the mouth of the Most High” (Ecclus. XXIV).

“Jesus answered them: ‘Do you now believe? Behold, the hour is coming—indeed, it has already come—when you will be scattered, each to his own place, and will leave me alone. Yet I am not alone, because the Father is with me.’” “Do you now believe?” he says; “do you now know?” It is indeed good that you believe, and good that you know; but take care lest “your heart be troubled” [Col. 0749A]; take care lest a wind drive this very belief from your hearts, lest a breeze carry it away. For “behold, the hour is coming”—it is not far off, but has already come—of which it was said: “Satan has demanded you, that he might sift you like wheat” (Luke 22). This hour is coming, I say, in which Satan will sift you amid so great a tempest, “so that you will be scattered, each to his own place”: that is, fleeing far away from my distress, each content with his own safety, and leaving me alone, that I may go alone to be sacrificed for you. For where I am going, as I said above, you cannot now follow me.

Thus the Scripture will be fulfilled which says in my person: “I have trodden the winepress alone, and of the nations there was no man with me; I looked around, and there was no helper; I sought, and there was none to assist” (Isa. 63). Thus, as I have already said, “you will all take offense at me, because you will be scattered, because you will take flight and leave me alone” (Matt. 26). Nevertheless, “I am not alone, because the Father is with me.” For I did not so depart from the Father and come into the world that he left me alone. Does my spirit, then, speak falsely when it says in the Prophet: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Ps. 21 [22]). Far from it.

For a little while my God will be silent, will keep silence and be patient, until these men—whose hour, now come, it is, together with the power of darkness—see me and mock me, speak with their lips and shake their heads; “pierce my hands and my feet, number all my bones, divide my garments among themselves, and cast lots over my clothing” (ibid.) [Col. 0749C]. For a little while, I say, he will be silent and will seem to have forsaken me, because he keeps silence; but afterward he will not keep his help far from me. For he will rescue my life from the sword, my only one from the hand of the dog, raising me from the dead; and thereafter I shall openly show that he did not leave me alone, because I shall declare his name to my brothers and praise him in the midst of the Church—that is, I shall make him known as worthy of praise.

“These things I have spoken to you, that you may have peace in me.” What peace, if not the forgiveness of sins? What peace, if not the ending or reconciliation of the enmities that stood between God and humankind? (Eph. 2.) “This peace,” he says, “which is greatly necessary, that you may have it in me—that is, through my death—is why I have spoken these things to you.” I have spoken, that is, I have done them. For my words have already become deeds, since what I have spoken to you is certainly to be; indeed, it is impossible that they should not come to pass. What are these things that I have spoken to you, except the mysteries of my incarnation, already accomplished, and of my passion, soon without doubt to occur, together with my resurrection? “These things I have spoken to you, that you may have peace in me,” as Scripture testifies when it says: “If there be an angel speaking for him, one out of a thousand, to declare a man’s righteousness, he will have mercy on him and say: Deliver him, that he may not go down into corruption; I have found one in whom I may be gracious to him” (Job 33), and the rest.

That “one out of a thousand” is plainly contained in these words: “whatever I have spoken to you, that you may have peace in me” [Col. 0750A]—that you may be delivered and not descend into corruption; that God may be gracious to you in me, who alone was found.
