What is that one? Namely, that I too am, equally with you, a human being capable of suffering and subject to death. The remaining points are dissimilar: for I alone of all human beings was born when and how I willed; I die when and how I will; likewise I rise when I will and ascend into heaven. Therefore, “these things I have spoken to you” is as though he had said: “These things I do for you.” It follows:

“In the world you will have tribulation; but take courage: I have conquered the world.” You will have peace, he says, not in the world but in me; conversely, you will have tribulation in the world. “For they will hand you over in councils and scourge you in synagogues; you will be brought before kings and governors on my account, and some of you they will put to death” (Matt. 10). Not peace, I say, but disputes, wars, and enmities of this kind “you will have in the world. But take courage,” and do not fear those who kill the body and after that have nothing more they can do (Luke 12). For “I have conquered the world,” since, though killed by it, I shall rise on the third day. Therefore, with this confidence do not be afraid, since you have peace in me; for you too, though killed, will rise, and will be companions in victory, fellow-heirs of my kingdom, and sharers in glory (Rom. 2; 2 Cor. 10).

## [Chapter XVII]

“Jesus spoke these things, and, lifting up his eyes to heaven, said: ‘Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son, that your Son may glorify you.’” The title of Psalm 101 [102] aptly corresponds to this prayer of the Savior: “A prayer of the poor man, when he is in distress and pours out his supplication before the Lord.” For in that hour the soul of this poor man was distressed, and he was sorrowful unto death, so that, as another Evangelist relates, “being in agony, he prayed more earnestly, and his sweat became like drops of blood running down to the ground” (Luke 22).

It should be known that he did not pour out this prayer in the upper room where the supper had been held. For above, the Evangelist indicated that he departed from there: after a great part of his discourse had already been completed, when he had said, “I will no longer speak much with you, for the ruler of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me; but that the world may know that I love the Father, and as the Father gave me commandment, so I do,” he suddenly added: “Rise, let us go from here” [Col. 0750D]. Where they then went he does not state; but we learn it more clearly than daylight from the other Evangelists. For they agree in reporting: “And when they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives.” It is clear that this prayer was offered there. For after he went out there, “Then,” Matthew says, “Jesus came with them to a place called Gethsemane, and said to his disciples: ‘Sit here while I go over there and pray.’ And taking Peter and the two sons of Zebedee, he began to be sorrowful and distressed.” And shortly afterward: “And having gone forward a little,” he says, “he fell on his face, praying and saying: ‘My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me’” (Matt. 26) [Col. 0751A].

Mark (chapter 14) clearly relates the same thing. Luke also recounts that he went out to the Mount of Olives and withdrew from his disciples about a stone’s throw, prayed on his knees, and adds that, “being in agony, he prayed more earnestly, and his sweat became like drops of blood running down to the ground.” Therefore, since all agree, he uttered this prayer on the Mount of Olives, with Peter and the two sons of Zebedee present. For he had withdrawn from the other disciples about a stone’s throw. Having instructed the others to sit—“while I go,” he says, “and pray”—he afterward said to Peter and the sons of Zebedee, whom he had taken with him: “Remain here, and keep watch with me.” And advancing, no longer about a stone’s throw, “but a little way,” he fell on his face [Col. 0751B].

It is therefore not so surprising that this Evangelist, the son of Zebedee, wrote down his lengthy prayer (Luke 22), whereas the others wrote it so briefly, since, when going to pray, he took this man alone of all the Evangelists with him, and prayed in his hearing. What, then, this poor man in distress prayed, what cry he uttered to God the Father—a cry that would doubtless reach him—we have more fully set forth in this Evangelist. If we have ears to hear, let us hear what he cried out, what supplication he poured out before his Lord and Father. The Evangelist says that, lifting his eyes to heaven—where he directed the mighty cry of his prayer—he said: “Father, the hour has come”: the hour has come, I say—understand, the hour of great anguish or tribulation—in which “my days vanish like smoke and I am struck down like grass” (Ps. 101 [102]), lightly slain according to the common condition of all mortals. But “glorify your Son,” namely with the great glory of the resurrection, “that your Son may glorify you,” namely by the splendid preaching of his disciples or by the resurrection of the dead. For it follows:

“As you gave him authority over all flesh, that he may give eternal life to all whom you have given him.” “As you gave him authority over all flesh”—that is, over every human being, whether Jew or Gentile. For he is not God of the Jews only, but also of the Gentiles (Rom. 3). As you gave him authority and decreed that he should be King, Prince, and Savior over all nations, to grant repentance and forgiveness of sins (Luke 1) [Col. 0751D], so attend to this, and establish in the reality of events what you have given or purposed: namely, that he may give eternal life to all whom you have given him, that is, the twofold resurrection of souls and bodies.

Thus, when he had said, “Glorify your Son, that your Son may glorify you,” as though you asked in what way he wished the Father to glorify him, or he himself to glorify the Father, he says: “Glorify now in deed, as you have glorified in authority, so that your Son may do that for which he was incarnate or made man: that he may give eternal life to all whom you have given him.” And as though you again asked what the giving of life to the dead has to do with the glorification of the Father, since he said, “that your Son may glorify you,” he immediately adds:

“And this is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent.” Therefore, when you said, “Glorify your Son, that your Son may glorify you,” it is as though he had said: According to the Spirit of holiness, by resurrection from the dead (Rom. 1), bear witness that I am your Son in power; and clear knowledge of this fact is the effective cause of eternal life for human beings. Toward this the whole incense of this prayer, burning with the great fire of love, yearns and is directed—not because this poor man doubts whether his Prophet truly foretold of him: “Will not he who sleeps rise again?” (Ps. 40 [41]). Rather, it is so that those who heard him then, and those who now read or hear this prayer, may know that our salvation, life, and resurrection were the reason that he who “committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2; Isa. 53) died and rose again.

In another psalm also, in accordance with the sense of this prayer, where he now says, “Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son,” his spirit said: “O Lord my God, I cried to you, and you healed me” (Ps. 29 [30]), and so forth. At last, as though asking in doubt: “What profit is there in my blood, when I go down into corruption? Will the dust confess you, or declare your truth?” (ibid.), immediately afterward he confidently declared: “The Lord heard and had mercy on me; the Lord became my helper” (ibid.), and the rest. Therefore both in this prayer the Lord offers prayer without doubt, and in the prophetic Scriptures his spirit does the same: there, after his cry, he says, “The Lord heard,” which indicates great certainty; and here, having first said, “Father, glorify your Son,” he immediately adds, “As you gave him authority over all flesh,” to show that his prayer rests not upon uncertainty but upon authority. It follows:

“I have glorified you on earth; I have completed the work which you gave me to do.” He will later explain how the Son has already glorified the Father, saying: “I have manifested your name to the people whom you gave me out of the world.” Therefore there is no need to ask how he who said, “Glorify your Son, that your Son may glorify you,” can now say, “I have glorified you on earth.” For the attentive reader understands that the Father had indeed already been glorified, in the knowledge of the Son, in the minds of those who believed that he had come forth thus from God, and who had already confessed him to be Christ, the Son of the living God. Yet, because the majesty or goodness of this same Son was not yet well known to them, much still lacked for the glorification of the Father’s name [Col. 0752D]. Therefore he said both, “that your Son may glorify you,” and “I have glorified you.” The later statement corresponds: “I have made your name known to them, and I will make it known.”

What he now adds—“I have completed the work which you gave me to do”—is as though he said: “I have fulfilled your commandment, having become a mortal human being; and now I have willingly come to the height of obedience, that is, to death; now I am in agony.” Accordingly there immediately follows:

“And now, Father, glorify me with yourself, with the glory which I had with you before the world existed.” “And because,” he says, “I have completed the work which you gave me, now—in this hour that has come—glorify me, Father”: that is, raise me. Glorify me, I say, with yourself, namely by setting me at the right hand of your majesty in the heights (Heb. 1), with the same glory that I had with you before the world existed; so that the newly assumed form of a servant may be worshiped by angels, just as the ancient form of God was worshiped by angels.

Alternatively: “And now, Father, glorify me with yourself, with the glory which I had with you before the world existed”: namely, just as my Spirit “in the beginning was borne over the waters,” so that the angelic creation might be created through me, your Word, when you said, “Let there be light” (Gen. 1), so now may the same Spirit be borne over the waters, so that through me, your Son, a new creation of human beings may be born while they are baptized into my death; and so the fallen tenth order of angels may be restored. For in this way too the glorification in which I then shone will now be repeated.

Now, since he had said, “I have glorified you on earth,” he explains how he has glorified him, saying: “I have manifested your name to the people whom you gave me out of the world.” For the instruction of these people is the beginning of the Father’s glorification: through them the Father’s name was to become known to the world. Hence they were rightly called the light of the world [Col. 0753C], since they themselves were first enlightened, in order that the world might be illuminated by knowledge of this name (Matt. 5). What, moreover, is this name of God but “the Father of Jesus Christ”? For the other names of God, whatever names are found in the Law, people could hear or know before the coming of Christ himself. But this name, “Father”—or in relation to which Son God should be believed to be Father—could never have been known unless the Son of Man himself, when he came, had manifested it.

“Therefore,” he says, “I have manifested your name—the name of my Father, or the fact that you are my Father—by works which no one else has done, to the people whom you gave me out of the world, whom you drew to me: chosen out of the world, because flesh and blood did not reveal it to them, but you, my Father who are in heaven. They were yours, and you gave them to me; and they have kept your word.” For unless they were yours, you would not have given them to me. But how were they already yours, and not yet mine, except because they called upon you as God, but did not yet know that I was your Son, or that you were to be called Father in relation to this Son? Therefore, you gave them to me insofar as you revealed to them that I am your Son.

319 Once this was known, behold, they kept your word, since they left all things and followed me (Matt. 19). The Law testifies that such observance of your word is sure, saying: “He who said to his father and mother, ‘I do not know you,’ and to his brothers, ‘I do not recognize them,’ and did not know his children—these have kept your word and observed your covenant: they shall teach your judgments, O Jacob, and your law, O Israel” (Deut. 33) [Col. 0754A]. Therefore those whom you gave me “were yours, and in this they kept your word”: because, leaving everything, they followed me.

“Now they have known that all things which you have given me are from you, because the words which you gave me I have given them. And they received them, and truly knew that I came forth from you, and believed that you sent me.” It truly followed, because you gave them to me, that they should know, receive the words I gave them, know, and believe. For unless you had given them to me, they would never have known; just as lost Judas did not know. From his dispositions it is plain to everyone that you did not give him to me, nor did he follow me on account of being yours; rather, though he was not yours, he was mingled hypocritically among yours, sinful and deceitful (Matt. 12). Therefore he never understood what these men knew: namely, “that all things which you have given me”—that is, whatever works I performed and whatever teachings I spoke—are words from you. Instead he spoke evil, agreeing in his heart with those who said: “He casts out demons by Beelzebub, prince of demons” (Luke 11)—“This man is not from God” (John 9).

It is therefore plain concerning these disciples that you drew them to me, because they knew that they had judged rightly regarding my works. They knew, I say, that I gave them no words other than those which you gave me; and they received them with a worthy reception, namely, so that, as already said, on account of my words they left all that was theirs (Matt. 19). “They truly knew,” he says, “that I came forth from you, and believed that you sent me.” Since the Son’s coming forth from the Father and being sent seem to be the same thing, why did he say both, “that I came forth from you,” and “that you sent me,” except to indicate equal love: both his own, that is, the love of the Son who came, and that of the Father who sent him? For the Father gave the Son the commandment to come and drink for us the cup of suffering; nevertheless, the Son came by his own voluntary love. Thus the Father did not compel him by his command as one lesser because of his own love, but sent him as one truly coequal and willing with equal love. Therefore, in order to indicate the love of both the Father and the Son, he says: “They knew that I came forth from you, and believed that you sent me.”

Having said these things, he says: “I pray for them.” At last he opens the prayer for which, lifting his eyes to heaven, he had hitherto said, “Glorify your Son,” and so forth. This is plainly to be observed, according to the Apostle, in lawful prayer: that entreaties, prayers, petitions, and thanksgivings be made in order (1 Tim. 2). In this passage, the master and guide of all holy prayer himself is shown to have preserved that order. First he offered an entreaty, saying: “Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son,” and so forth. In these words he sought, as it were, the Father’s goodwill, down to the point at which he now says, “I pray for them.” From this place comes the prayer proper: words of supplication indeed, but not yet specifying what he wills or aims at. What he subsequently says, “Holy Father, keep them in your name, whom you have given me,” and the rest, is petition. Then, what he adds, “Righteous Father, the world has not known you,” and so forth, is thanksgiving [Col. 0755A]. Thus, having first made entreaty, he now adds prayer:

“I pray for them. I do not pray for the world, but for those whom you have given me, because they are yours.” Woe, then, to the rejoicing world, while Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, prays for his own—that is, dies and offers himself as a sacrifice upon the altar of the cross. “For I pray,” he says, “for those whom you have given me, not for the world.” Here “the world” means lovers of the world, as different from those for whom Christ prays while crucified as the Egyptians were, in God’s sight, from the children of Israel who marked their doorposts with the sacred blood of the lamb. Woe, therefore, as has been said, to such a world, because what Christ, the true Lamb of God, requests avails it nothing, so that it may sink more swiftly into the depths of hell with its king, the devil, prince of darkness. Only those whom the Father has given the Son escape through his cross and blood.

“Because they are yours,” he says. And, as though we asked how he could say both that you gave them to me and that they are yours, he adds more fully: “And what is mine is yours, and what is yours is mine; and I have been glorified in them.” Those whom the Father gives to the Son therefore do not cease to belong to the Father, because neither the Father possesses anything without the Son nor the Son without the Father. But in what has the Son been glorified in them—in all those things that are the Father’s? Namely, in this: nothing comes to the Father except through the grace of the Son; no one, whether dead or living, can see the Father’s glory except through the Son’s cross and blood. And because this is now being accomplished—namely, that he may die and rise again, and thus be Lord of both living and dead—he says: “I have been glorified in them,” that is, it is as good as done, though it is about immediately to happen. Therefore it follows:

“And I am no longer in the world, but these are in the world, and I am coming to you.” When he said these things, he was certainly in the world, since he was visibly present and lived a mortal life; indeed, he had tribulation in the world. Yet he was not in the world, because he had already been sold by the traitor and was soon to be seized and led to death. Therefore he was not wholly, but in a sense, already not in the world, because he had already set an irrevocable foot at the boundary of this present life and at his departure from the world.

But because, departing in this way and saying, “I am coming to you,” he was crowned with glory and honor and set over the works of the Father’s hands (Ps. 8); because, I say, drinking from the brook by the way, he was therefore immediately to lift up his head (Ps. 109 [110]), he rightly said as though the event had already occurred: “I have been glorified in them.” He also interposed the reason why, departing in this way, he prays for his own: “And these are in the world.” For it is a great and weighty concern, requiring a friend of salvation to provide for it: that he, having gained the firmness of the shore—that is, the peace and security of immortality—should leave his own oarsmen endangered amid the waves of a difficult voyage, surely to perish unless the harbor of salvation is prepared for them by him.

Therefore he now at last asks the Father on their behalf—that is, he more clearly unfolds what he prays for and why he has made entreaty. For he says: “Holy Father, keep in your name those whom you have given me, that they may be one as we are” [Col. 0756A]. He has briefly expressed the substance of his necessary petition in saying: “That they may be one as we are.” He repeats this many times, because it is truly great, splendid, glorious, and desirable to be one. And how great it is we may gather from the likeness of the Father and the Son themselves, for he said, “as we are.” What is it to be one, except always to be the same and to endure unchangeably without alteration? Thus God is indeed one: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one, that is, one and the same. Hence he says to Moses: “I am who I am” (Exod. 3). And the Psalmist: “The heavens will perish, but you remain; they will all grow old like a garment. You will change them like a covering, and they shall be changed; but you are the same, and your years shall not fail” (Ps. 101 [102]).

But after humankind was cast down from the eternity of paradise by sin—where, according to its measure, it could be or become one—it is manifest that it is no longer one. For it “comes forth like a flower and is crushed; it flees like a shadow and never remains in the same state” (Job 14) [Col. 0756B]. The Psalmist also laments this mutability—or rather, this failing—when he says: “In the morning it passes like grass; in the morning it blooms and passes away; in the evening it falls, hardens, and withers, because we have failed in your wrath and have been troubled in your fury” (Ps. 89 [90]). Thus humankind ceased to be one, and in this lost the likeness of God, who is always one and the same.

But the Son of God, who now speaks these things as one about to die, dies now for this purpose: that humankind may be restored to oneness—that is, to the stability of eternity; that the blessed resurrection of both soul, dead in sin, and body, dying in mortality, may restore them, and that thereafter they may be subject to no disasters and troubled by no changes. Therefore, when he says, “Holy Father, keep in your name those whom you have given me, that they may be one as we are,” he asks for the adoption as children of God for those on whose behalf he also suffers. For to be kept in the Father’s name can in no way be better understood than as being adopted as God’s children (Rom. 8). For this reason he invokes the holy Father: that he may sanctify for himself those whom he has as children, not by nature indeed, but by grace.

The precise force of the word “keep” must also be noted. Properly speaking, those are said to be “kept” who have been captured in war and, though they could by the law of war be killed, are granted life through the conqueror’s mercy. So indeed we, justly deserving condemnation together with this world, God’s enemy, are pardoned and kept by the grace of God the conqueror. Hence, according to the reality of the matter, we are servants, although through abundance of grace we are called—and are—children [Col. 0756D].

This too must not be passed over: when it is said, “that they may be one as we are,” equality with God is not given to us, but likeness is set before us. For he does not say, “that they may be one, which we are,” but “that they may be one as we are.” John himself commends this in his Epistle: he does not say “equal,” but “We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3). This, then, is being accomplished: not that we may be equal to God in nature, but that by grace we may recover the likeness of God, so that by seeing him who alone truly is, we may by that very vision become one, just as he himself is one. One, I say: immortal and incapable of suffering, and subject to no shadow of change. It follows:

“While I was with them, I kept them in your name.” “While I was with them,” he says, by my bodily presence, “I kept them”; yet he did not add, “that they might be one as we are.” For this could not have happened while he remained with them exempt from suffering. He shows how he kept them by adding: “Those whom you gave me I guarded, and none of them perished except the son of perdition, that the Scripture might be fulfilled.” Thus he says only that he kept them so that they did not lose their offices of oversight, as that “son of perdition” lost his, “that the Scripture might be fulfilled,” namely the Scripture that says of him: “Let his days be few, and let another take his episcopate” (Ps. 108 [109]), and so forth [Col. 0757B].

That this occurred through his presence—that they were guarded even in this manner—is sufficiently clear from the fact that as soon as he began to be taken away from them, Peter, their greatest, denied him and would have lost his office of oversight, had he not turned and looked upon him. “Therefore, because I kept them,” he says, “so far that, up to the hour of my passion, they remained with me in heart, though fleeing in body and leaving me alone, the outpouring of my blood may be for their salvation and forgiveness of sins. Henceforth, Holy Father, keep them in your name,” he says, “so that, made strong, persevering through all the world’s dangers” (Luke 21), “they may attain that state in which, as has already been said, they are one like us.”

“I guarded them while I was with them.”

“But now I am coming to you, and I speak these things in the world, that my joy may be in them.” He did not say, “Now I come to you and am in the world,” which would contradict what he said a little earlier: “And I am no longer in the world.” “I speak these things in the world,” he says: this is not the same, but different. For after his resurrection too he spoke in the world—that is, to those who were in the world—although he himself was not in the world, since his manner of life was not worldly or mortal. What then are the things he speaks in the world, if not this very prayer, whose purpose, as he dies, is: “I am coming to you, O Father, and am no longer in the world”? Why does he speak these things, and why does he, both high priest and saving victim, offer this prayer? He says: “That my joy may be in them.” This is indeed true and known to our faith: that in order to give us his joy, he suffered for us; for this reason he spoke these things; for this reason “he prayed to the Father for us with a loud cry,” as the Apostle says, “and with many tears” (Heb. 5). It follows:

“And I have given them your word, and the world hated them, because they are not of the world, just as I am not of the world.” The fundamental distinction between them, and the reason why I pray for them, is this: “I have given them your word,” that is, I have left them after me the inherited office of preaching the truth. For this reason “the world hated them” and persecutes them. For this reason, I say: had they not spoken things displeasing to the world, they would not be killed and would not have tribulation in the world. Thus “they are not of the world as I am not of the world.” For this is also why I am not of the world, but “I have become a stranger even to my brothers, and an alien to the sons of my mother” (Ps. 68 [69]), because I speak what displeases them.

What, then, do I pray for them? What do I will when I say, “Keep them in your name, that they may be one as we are”? Do I ask that, their bodies now laid aside, they may leave this world free; or that they be taken away like Elijah and Enoch (Gen. 5; 4 Kings 2)? By no means.

“I do not pray that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from evil.” For if they were now taken out of the world, by what vehicle, what chariots, what teams, or what cavalry would your word go out into all the earth and to the ends of the world (Ps. 18 [19])—your word by which you assign to me, at my request, the nations as my inheritance and the ends of the earth as my possession? (Ps. 2.) For these are the only remaining horses and chariots of yours, of whom it is written: “You ride upon your horses; your chariots are salvation” (Hab. 3). I do not ask—because it is not at all expedient—that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from the world, that is, from sin. For sin alone is evil, because nothing besides sin can harm a rational creature.

Therefore, even if the world that hates them kills their bodies, preserve their souls, so that it cannot kill them; so that Satan, however much he sifts them like wheat (Luke 22), may be unable, when their faith fails, to winnow any one of them like chaff into condemnation [Col. 0758C]. But how I will that they be kept, while also left in the world, I shall now say: “Sanctify them in truth; your word is truth. As you sent me into the world, I also sent them into the world.” This, he says, is what I pray for them: that they may be sanctified in truth and sent into the world as I was sent; that is, as I came to suffer persecution, so they too may go to suffer persecution.

What is it to be sanctified in truth, except truly to be justified by faith in my blood? 321 For up to this point they had indeed been sanctified—sanctified, I say—but not yet in truth. For all the sanctifications written in the Law of Moses were not truth itself, but shadows or figures of the truth, or of the true sanctification by which the sins of the world are now taken away in my blood [Col. 0758D]. The effective cause of this sanctification is your word, which is truth. What is this word of yours, except the Word that was made flesh and now, through the suffering of death, binds hell and rises on the third day? (1 Cor. 15; Col. 1.) Whoever are baptized in this word are sanctified in truth. Therefore, because they believed in this word, in this truth, I do not pray that they, truly sanctified, be taken from the world; but I send them into the world as you sent me into the world: namely, that they may suffer from the same persecutors who persecuted me, while bearing witness to the truth.

“And for them I sanctify myself, so that they too may be sanctified in truth.” If it had simply been said, “[Col. 0759A] ‘And for them I sanctify myself,’” the more immediate meaning would suggest that he spoke of the present sacrifice of his passion, in which he himself, the true Lamb, was offered for the whole world, not by another high priest but by himself. Yet, according to the proper force of the word, the same meaning is at hand: since *sacred* and *holy* mean the same thing, he must be understood to have said nothing other than, “And for them I sacrifice,” or, “I offer myself as a sacrifice.” For he is not only the sacrifice, as he is the high priest of the sacrifice, but also the temple, as the Apostle testifies, who, after speaking at length of shadowy sacrifices, says: “But Christ, having appeared as high priest of the good things to come, through the greater and more perfect tabernacle not made by hands, that is, not of this creation, nor [Col. 0759B] through the blood of goats or calves, but through his own blood, entered once for all into the holy places, having obtained eternal redemption” (Heb. IX).

Therefore, being about to deliver up his soul for sin, so that he might see long-lived offspring: “And for them,” he says, “I sanctify,” that is, sacrifice, “myself, that they too may be sanctified in truth.” If you weigh this properly, he touched the matter more fully and more exactly by saying “I sanctify” than if he had said “I sacrifice.” For when he says “I sanctify,” he implies that he had been defiled. And in saying “for them,” he plainly determines that he was defiled not by his own sins but by those of others. The prophet too expressly states this, when, after saying, “All we like sheep have gone astray; each one has turned aside into his own way,” he immediately adds: “And the Lord laid upon him the iniquities of us all” [Col. 0759C] (Isa. LIII). And Zechariah: “And Jesus,” he says, “was clothed in filthy garments, and Satan stood at his right hand to oppose him” (Zech. III).

Therefore, although in himself he was holy—indeed, the Holy of holies—being conceived of the Holy Spirit; and although throughout his whole life “he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (I Pet. II), yet, according to the iniquities of us all which God had laid upon him, the Lamb of God was clothed in filthy garments. Rightly, then, he said, “I sanctify myself,” significantly adding, “for them.” But why for them? “That they too,” he says, “may be sanctified in truth.” In truth, that is, not in shadow or figure, but in the true remission of sins: “not as the blood of goats or bulls, [Col. 0759D] or the ashes of a heifer sprinkled upon those who are defiled, sanctified them for the cleansing of the flesh; but much more may my blood, who through the Holy Spirit offer myself without blemish to God, cleanse their conscience from works of death, to serve the living God” (Heb. IX).

“But I pray not for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word: that all may be one, just as you, Father, are in me and I in you; that they too may be one in us, so that the world may believe that you sent me.” The meaning is this: I pray, or sanctify myself, not only for those whom you gave me, but also for all who will believe in me through their word, so that, whether Jews or Gentiles, [Col. 0760A] they may all be one and there may be no distinction among them before you.

It should be noted that, in now saying that they may be one, he does not add, as above, “as we are”; though later he will say, “that they may be one as we are one.” For our peace now aims at making both one (Eph. II), and at creating the two in himself—that is, Jews and Gentiles, with no distinction between them—into one new man, making peace and reconciling both to God in one body through the cross, killing the enmity in himself, so that through him both may have access in one Spirit to the Father. Therefore, after saying, “That all may be one,” he immediately introduced a remarkable comparison [Col. 0760B] by saying, “Just as you, Father, are in me and I in you,” so that you may plainly recognize that, just as the Father and the Son are not two gods but one God, so the Gentile and the Jew are not two peoples but one people, one Church, one body. He then repeats the point of unity itself: “That they too,” he says, “may be one in us.” And he adds: “That the world may believe that you sent me.”

Behold, these are the glorious things which the Prophet, admitted in the Spirit to the council of the Godhead, heard and thus proclaimed: “Glorious things,” he says, “have been spoken of you, city of God” (Ps. LXXXVI). And as if you asked what those sayings were, or what the Lord said to his city—namely, to the holy Church—whose foundations he laid upon holy mountains, that is, upon the apostles, through whose word we were to believe: “I shall remember,” he says, [Col. 0760C] “Rahab and Babylon, who know me.” And he adds: “Behold foreigners, and Tyre, and the people of Ethiopia: these were there” (ibid.).

For truly, as he had then promised in the prophets, so now in his passion our Lord remembered Rahab and Babylon—that is, breadth and confusion: the widely spread and exceedingly confused Gentile world. He remembered, I say, this great harlot when he said: “I pray not for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word,” and so forth. In that remembrance of his, we were foreigners, Tyre, and the people of Ethiopia: we, I say, foreigners and strangers to the covenant of the fathers; Tyre, that is, those in distress, imprisoned in the prison and darkness of sins; truly a people of Ethiopia, because of the extreme blackness of vices, [Col. 0760D] blindness, and ignorance. We were there, in that remembrance of him who said, “That they too may be one in us, so that the world may believe”—the world, I say, and not the Jewish nation alone—that you sent me. For he elsewhere says that “whoever believes and is baptized shall be saved” (Matt. XVI). But what reward will there be for this faith and unity? He says:

“And I have given them the glory which you gave me, that they may be one as we are one: I in them and you in me, that they may be perfected into one, so that the world may know that you sent me and loved them as you loved me.” This is plainly what John himself says in his Epistle: “Beloved, we are now children of God, but what we shall be has not yet appeared. [Col. 0761A] We know that, when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (I John III). What glory, indeed, should we understand when he says, “And I have given them the glory which you gave me,” if not that for which the expectation of creation waits—namely, the revelation of the glory of the children of God?

The Father gave this glory to this his only-begotten Son, the firstborn from the dead, by raising him from the dead and setting him at his right hand in the heavenly places, giving him, in himself, what our nature had not possessed: the honor of incorruption and the glory of immortality. For from that point onward, because our substance in the Word of God is not subject to a multitude of accidents, it truly remains one and the same. Hence, after saying, “That they may be one,” he adds, as above, [Col. 0761B] “as we are one.”

This cannot suitably be referred to the consubstantiality of the Father and the Word. For we cannot be one as the Father and the Word are one. Rather, we who have been adopted as sons await that glory which the Father gave the Son—the glory and honor of immortality and impassibility—which he gave because the Son had not previously possessed it according to the flesh, and with which he crowned him when he rose from the dead (Eph. I). Therefore, what he says, “That they may be one as we are one,” does not concern the consubstantiality proper to the Word with the Father, but that blessedness of incorruptible eternity which is common by grace with the blessed and immortal Trinity, not only to the Lord’s human nature but also to all his faithful.

By this unity the Psalmist calls blessed the glorious city spoken of above: “Jerusalem,” he says, “which is built as a city, whose participation is in the Same” (Ps. CXXI). For “the Same” is that which is always the same and remains unchangeably; and this is truly the most splendid and highest good which our substance now has with God, first in Christ and afterward will have in his whole body, which is the Church (Eph. I), not by communion of nature but by participation in grace. [Col. 0761C] And without doubt the Father gave this glory to the Son according to his humanity; but the Son himself, according to his divinity, gave it to his faithful, as he now says: “And I have given them the glory which you gave me.” In accordance with what is elsewhere said: “But as many as received him, he gave them power to become children of God” (John I).

Because this steadfastness of unity begins here, while through faith we are one and of one mind, he therefore prefaced it with what was already said: “I pray not for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word, that all may be one,” and so forth. But he expresses the unity of future blessedness more fully when he adds: “I in them and you in me, that they may be perfected into one.” Yet since the whole Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—is one God, and equally dwells now by faith in our hearts and will dwell hereafter by sight, why did he say and distinguish it thus, “I in them and you in me,” unless he wished to show himself alone as mediator between God and human beings?

For the person of the Son alone, besides dwelling in our hearts through faith, as stated, is in us in another manner: namely, because he descended into our flesh and nature; while the Father is nevertheless in him, because he did not abandon him in his descent. For the Son did not so empty himself as to lose the form of God by taking the form of a servant (Phil. II). Thus, with the mediator between God and human beings intervening, we are restored to eternity and perfected into one, and our participation is in the Same. Hence he now says: “That they may be perfected into one.” What immediately follows—“so that the world may know that you sent me and loved them as you loved me”—requires us to understand that knowledge which will no longer be partial but complete, as Paul testifies when he says: “Now I know in part; but then I shall know, even as I am known” (I Cor. XIII). [Col. 0762B]

Let the world, then—that is, all who have been redeemed, saved, and perfected into one—know, that is, experience through the very fruit of immortality (Rom. VIII), and see face to face, “that you sent me.” They now know this in part and see it as through a mirror in an enigma. Let them know what they now believe and hope: “that you loved them as you loved me,” that is, that you willed them to be made like me. Only this is excepted: that I may be the firstborn among many brothers; in this their blessedness is in no way diminished, but charity is the more delighted. He asks for the sum of all things, and finally gathers it up in a brief conclusion.

[Col. 0762C] “Father, those whom you gave me, I will that where I am, they too may be with me, that they may see my glory which you gave me, because you loved me before the foundation of the world.” It is as if he said: This is the end of their preservation, which I requested when I said, “Keep them in your name whom you gave me.” This, I say, is the end; and in this he judges it worthy of justice that, because the world hated them because I gave them your word, and they received it and truly believed “that you sent me,” therefore “where I am, they too may be with me, that they may see my glory which you gave me,” and may also see “that you loved me before the foundation of the world.”

It should be observed that he does not merely say, “That they may see my glory which you gave me.” For this is the glorification of the assumed humanity, which the wicked too could see when he comes in great power and majesty upon the clouds, so that every eye shall see him, even those who pierced him (Matt. XIII; Apoc. I). But he added, “because you loved me before the foundation of the world”: let them see what only the blessed eyes of the righteous will deserve to see. For only the poor in spirit, the meek, those who mourn, those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, the merciful, the pure in heart, the peacemakers, and those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake will see the form of God in which he was beloved to the Father before the foundation of the world. Therefore they will reign in heaven, possess the land of the living, be comforted and filled, obtain mercy, see God, be called children [Col. 0763A] of God, and possess the kingdom of heaven (Matt. V).

Thus the words, “that they may see the glory which you gave me,” are sufficient to determine future blessedness. For to see is to possess; indeed, the vision of eternal glory is the glory of those who see, and the efficient cause of their glory. So John himself, after saying, “We shall be like him,” immediately adds the efficient cause: “how we shall see him as he is” (John XIII).

Now that these three have been completed—entreaty, prayer, and petition—the fourth finally follows, namely thanksgiving, when he says:

“Righteous Father, the world has not known you, but I have known you; and these have known that you sent me. And I have made your name known to them, and I will make it known, so that [Col. 0763B] the love with which you loved me may be in them, and I in them.” This is plainly a thanksgiving, in which he praises the Father’s justice and mercy. It was justly done that the world, blinded through the fault of pride, should not know its Creator—the world, I say, whose darkest part consists of the murderers of our Lord. But mercy was granted when the world, receiving in humility the light of its eyes, namely the Son of God—that is, the whole body of the elect—lifted up again its face, illuminated to behold the glory of God.

He says, then: “Righteous Father.” Here we must understand: because you turned away your face or hid your grace from the wise [and] prudent (Matt. XI), that is, from the proud. The prophet laments this in the person of your people: “You have hidden your face,” he says, “and crushed us into the hand of our iniquity” (Isa. LXIV). Likewise: “Why, Lord, have you made us stray from your ways, and hardened our heart so that we do not fear you?” (Isa. LXIII), and so forth. “And the world,” he says, “has known you”: blinded, namely, by a fitting recompense, so that they lost knowledge of him whose love they did not receive, and lost the help of him whose counsel they despised.

“But I have known you”—I, whom they say is not from God, have known and loved you—“and these have known that you sent me.” They are my witnesses that the things you gave me, as I said above, are from you; for they confess and say, “Now we believe that you came forth from God” (John [Col. 0764A] IX; XVI). Therefore, since you judged them worthy of the revelation of those things which you hid from the wise and prudent, “I have made your name known to them” already through teaching and the power of signs, and I will make it known more fully through the invisible power of the Holy Spirit, so that their sound may go forth into all the earth (Ps. XVIII), as they declare the glory of your fatherhood.

For in what is knowledge of your name perfected except in the outpouring of the Holy Spirit? Hence it follows: “That the love with which you loved me may be in them, and I in them.” This love is the Holy Spirit, by whom the Son loves the Father and the Father loves the Son. Plainly and beyond doubt, the love of the Father and the Son is the Holy Spirit. Therefore, “that the love with which you loved me may be in them, and I in them,” is the same as saying: May the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, come to them and teach them all truth; and when he is in them, I too may dwell in their hearts through faith and through this Spirit of love (Eph. III).

The supreme high priest—himself propitiator and propitiatory, priest and sacrifice—prayed this for us; and the expression of his countenance has not afterward changed in different directions. For the mighty cry of his heart did not cease when his words ceased; rather, by those words alone he indicated for what cause and with what purpose he would immediately endure bonds, reproaches, blows, spittle, scourges, a crown of thorns, cross, nails and spear, the drink of gall and vinegar—remaining silent through all things and not opening his mouth. “For why, being in agony and praying more earnestly, did he sweat, and did his sweat become like drops of blood falling to the ground [Col. 0764C] (Luke XXII),” unless to show that the prayer which he poured out to the Father with such sweat contained the cause for which he would soon pour out all his blood upon the cross?

Thus, by this prayer, the king and high priest declared, joyful indeed in the Lord’s strength but sorrowful and anxious in the weakness of the flesh, with what desire he was drawn toward the winepresses of the passion. And the Psalmist says: “Lord, you granted him the desire of his heart, and did not deny him the request of his lips; for he asked life of you, and you gave him length of days for ever and ever” (Ps. XX).

## BOOK THIRTEEN

[Col. 0763]

[Col. 0763D] The vesture of this our supreme High Priest is ordered and lawful; and rightly, according to the law and order which he prescribed for those who share in his priesthood, he enters the Holy of holies in a manner worthy of beholding and hearing. For, to omit other matters for the present, the legality of his priestly vesture is plainly shown because he arranged for himself, in spiritual fashion, the hems of the priestly tunic as they were commanded to be made in the letter of the outward law.

“On the lower edge,” it says, “around the hem of the tunic, you shall make pomegranates of blue, purple, and scarlet twice dyed, with bells interspersed among them, so that there shall be a golden bell and a pomegranate; again another golden bell and a pomegranate. Aaron shall wear it when carrying out the ministry, so that the sound may be heard when he enters and leaves the Holy of holies in the presence of the Lord, and he shall not die” (Exod. XXVIII).

What are the hems of the priestly tunic except the final events of our Lord’s life, of which we now speak? What are the deeply red pomegranates except the works of his love, greater than which no one has? He attached these pomegranates to the hems of his tunic because, having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them unto the end: namely, by laying down his life for those same friends. The bells, moreover, are the most illustrious words of his love, by which he instructed them at the aforesaid supper and afterward prayed to the Father for them. Thus, with the bells of his teaching interspersed with the pomegranates of his works, nothing is more beautiful to see, nothing sweeter to hear, nothing more delightful to experience.

Therefore, since we have now seen the beauty of the pomegranates and lately heard clearly the sound of the ringing bells, let us next follow the sequence of the Gospel narrative, considering how, after entering, he stood before the face of God for us and in what order he offered himself (Heb. IX). It follows:

[CHAPTER XVIII.] “When Jesus had said these things, he went out with his disciples across the torrent of Cedron, where there was a garden, into which he and his disciples entered.” It has already been stated where and when he went out from the upper room in which he had eaten supper: namely, after saying, “Rise, let us go from here,” and after a hymn had been sung, as the other Evangelists report (Mark XIV; Luke XXII), he went out to the Mount of Olives. Having told the disciples to remain in the estate of Gethsemane, he withdrew from them about a stone’s throw, taking with him Peter and the two sons of Zebedee; and, going a little farther, he fell down and prayed.

Therefore, when he had returned there and found them sleeping, he said, as Matthew relates in rebuke: “Sleep now and rest; [Col. 0765C] behold, the hour is at hand, and the Son of Man will be betrayed into the hands of sinners. Rise, let us go; behold, he who betrays me is at hand” (Matt. XXVI). He “went out,” as this Evangelist now says—and it must be understood, from the estate of Gethsemane, which is at the foot of the Mount of Olives. He went out, I say, and returned across the torrent of Cedron, drawing near again to the city so that he might voluntarily meet his adversaries.

“Where,” he says, “there was a garden, into which he and his disciples entered.” Beautifully, the second Adam chose to be found obedient in a garden, because the first Adam was found disobedient in a garden—namely, Paradise, which means “garden”—indeed, was outwitted by the serpent.

“For Judas, who betrayed him, also knew the place, because Jesus often met there with his disciples.” He knew it, that man who made the worst possible use of his knowledge of things, a vessel of malicious knowledge, more wicked than all human beings as the serpent was craftier than all animals; and therefore a more suitable attendant for the murderous devil, just as the serpent was formerly a more suitable instrument for the same devil in deceiving the first human being. For as he then used the serpent to kill the earthly man in soul, so now Satan used this traitor to kill in body this heavenly and new man.

For this reason he entered the garden; for this reason, I say, because he approached his passion willingly, he hastened to the place where he would be found sooner by his executioners. For, as though you asked why he entered there, “For Judas,” says the Evangelist, “who betrayed him, knew the place, because Jesus often met there with his disciples.”

“Judas therefore, having received a cohort and attendants from the chief priests and Pharisees, came there with lanterns, torches, and weapons.” A cohort consists of three hundred men. It should be noted that he does not say, “having received a cohort and attendants from the chief priests and Pharisees,” but “having received a cohort, and attendants from the chief priests and Pharisees.” For *cohort*, *legion*, and *tribunes* are terms of Roman military service, not of a Jewish crowd. Judas received this cohort not from the chief priests and Pharisees but from Pontius Pilate, governor of Roman authority; the chief priests and Pharisees added their own attendants, so that any members of the people who might be roused by that nighttime disturbance and wish to defend the Lord would be intimidated both by the Roman name and by armed force on either side.

Thus “sinners drew the sword and bent their bow” (Ps. XXXVI). Rightly, then, it was repaid to them so that their sword entered their own hearts and their bow was broken: their sword, I say, entered their hearts, so that for the one Roman cohort which they hired in arms against their Lord and king, an immense army of Roman power was stirred against their rebellion. And because they went out at night with lanterns, torches, and weapons, as against a robber, therefore the lamp of God—the lamp of the Law and the Prophets, by which their fathers were enlightened—would fall from their hands, as it is written: “Let their eyes be darkened, that they may not see” (Ps. LXVIII); and therefore, under the same arms with which they went out, “let their back always be bent.” It follows:

“Jesus therefore, knowing all things that were coming upon him, went forward and said to them: Whom do you seek?” The Evangelist said this in praise of voluntary love, that is, voluntary passion: “Because, knowing all things that were coming upon him,” as is evident from what has thus far been said or done, “he went forward and, as has already been stated, crossed the torrent of Cedron, entered that garden, into a place known to Judas”; and as his adversaries came, lest they should seize many in an indiscriminate tumult while seeking one, he voluntarily met them and said: “Whom do you seek?”

He did not say, “Here I am, since you seek me,” but, “Whom do you seek?” For truth knows no such manner of persecution; salvation is ignorant of it; light and life recoil from it.

“They answered him: Jesus of Nazareth. Jesus said to them: I am. Now Judas, who betrayed him, was standing with them. Therefore, when he said to them, ‘I am,’ they went backward and fell to the ground.” What wonder is it if, at the single utterance, “I am,” those who are not went backward and fell to the ground? Doubtless he said this according to the divinity which truly is, according to which that which is remains in being: “I am.” The substantive verb most truly declares this of him alone, who also says to Moses: “I am who am.”

And although they sought the essence of divinity in no way, even though coming with lanterns, torches, and weapons, God nevertheless fittingly answered from the temple of his body, saying, “I am”: not with reference to their intention, but to his own name. For when asked what they sought, they answered, “Jesus of Nazareth.” What is Jesus of Nazareth except the holy Savior? The Word, who is God, possessed this name from the time he became flesh, or human; but the reason why this name was assigned when he became human depends not upon human nature but upon divine power. For from what source does he save us, or is he our Savior, except from God—because he is not merely human but also God?

Moreover, because the one true God and the human being whom he assumed are one person, he rightly answered those saying that they sought Jesus of Nazareth with the expression proper to his divine essence: “I am.” I say, the expression proper to his divinity, uttered with definite purpose, as the result showed, because he cast his standing adversaries to the ground. Therefore it is no wonder, concerning those who are not because they are wicked—not loving, and wickedly seeking him who alone truly is, Jesus of Nazareth—that “they went backward and fell to the ground.” This is no wonder compared with greater things yet to come, especially since the devil Judas the traitor stood with them: the standard-bearer of malice, bearing Satan in his breast, had brought forth with his mouth the sign of peace, and had already pressed the knife of a most wicked kiss upon the Lamb of God.

But why, when the Lamb was immediately to be sacrificed, did he already roar a little as a lion, casting to the ground by saying “I am” so great a crowd of lightly armed gladiatorial attendants? So that they might be without excuse and might know that Jesus of Nazareth, whom they sought, is he who is. The wrath of God which awaits those who do not fear was revealed to them; the strength of the avenger who is to come in judgment was revealed. For if he could do this while about to die, much more, when reigning immortally over those same enemies, will he be strengthened.

This was made manifest in them, and his eternal power and divinity were grasped by experience, so that they might be without excuse, because, when they had thus known him saying, “I am,” they did not glorify him as the one who truly is (Rom. I), but seized him, bound him, abused him, and killed him. Therefore heaven will reveal Judas’s iniquities, and the earth will rise against him; and his sin will be manifest on the day of the Lord’s wrath, because he stood with them—indeed, fell with them—and his heart was not terrified. Rather, “according to his hardness and unrepentant heart, he stored up wrath for himself on the day of wrath and revelation of the righteous judgment of God” (Rom. II). Thus, I say, so that they might be without excuse, he said to them: “I am.” But perhaps it was too little to say it once. Therefore they had to be questioned again, and this same thing had to be said again, lest perhaps they had not understood.

“Therefore he asked them again: Whom do you seek? And they said: Jesus of Nazareth. Jesus answered: I told you that I am. If therefore you seek me, let these go.” Again, he says, when questioned, “Whom do you seek?” you insolently answer as before, “Jesus of Nazareth.” “But I told you that I am”; and, when you heard this, you experienced by your fall the prince of power whom you seek, “Jesus of Nazareth.” Therefore, if you still seek me, and having been thus struck you have not been pained, seize me indeed, “but let these go.”

He could nevertheless effectively have said, “Let me go,” and bound Satan, who dwelt in Judas, together with his attendants and weapons, in everlasting chains. But it was necessary that he should suffer; and likewise necessary that those whom the Father had given him should be preserved. Yet the wisdom of God acted both mightily and gently (Wis. VIII), and graciously used the devil’s malice for the end it intended, as it had spoken long before concerning him to blessed Job: “He who made him,” it says, “will apply his sword” (Job XL).

This he does in all his elect, and most of all the Son of God did it in himself. For he so applied—that is, turned to his own use—the sword of the murderous devil, which he could have entirely taken away from him, that he himself might die, without whose death the world would not be saved; and that they might be saved, without whom that same salvation could not be proclaimed to the world. Why he took care that they should be allowed to go, the Evangelist subsequently explains.

“That the word might be fulfilled which he said: Of those whom you gave me, I lost none.” Above, in his prayer to the Father, he said this word concerning the future as though it were past: “Those whom you gave me I have kept, and none of them perished except the son of perdition, that the Scripture might be fulfilled” (John XVII). For if, when captured, they had denied him through fear of death—which surely would have happened, since they were still weak, as was shown in Peter’s denial—if, I say, they had denied him and nevertheless been killed while denying him, they would doubtless have perished in that indiscriminate tumult.

But suppose perhaps that some might be killed without denying him, indeed without even being questioned. Would they not, in a sense, still perish, since they would by no means be allowed to attain the end for which they had been chosen? For why had they been chosen except to bear with great power throughout the whole world the testimony of the resurrection, and thus fulfill the Scripture which says: “Their sound has gone forth into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. XVIII)? For a little earlier he had said to them: “You did not choose me, but I chose you and appointed you, that you should go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain” (John XV). Therefore they would in this way too have perished, since they would not attain what they had been ordained for, and God’s purpose—which was impossible—would be thwarted. It follows:

“Simon Peter therefore, having a sword, drew it and struck the servant of the high priest, cutting off his ear. The servant’s name was Malchus.” This untimely courage of the apostle Peter clearly arose from genuine weakness. He who knew this well, because he knows all things, had said to him: “Where I go, you cannot follow me now.” He now made clear that Peter could not then follow him, because, while the Lord wished not to kill but to be killed, Peter preferred to kill rather than be killed.

Yet in this weakness of his a noble and powerful mystery was figuratively prefigured. For it was later to happen that the sword of apostolic strength—that is, “the word of God, living and effective, and sharper than every two-edged sword” (Heb. IV)—would cut off, or rather would prove to have cut off, the right ear of the Jews or chief priests, and would demonstrate that all they seem to hear from the Scriptures they hear with the left ear, that is, understand perversely. For, as the other Evangelists report, it was the right ear that was cut off (Matt. XXVI).

But that the Lord is read in Luke to have healed that same ear by his touch (Luke XXII) signifies this: that at some time the right hearing and true understanding of Scripture will again be opened to that people—namely, when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered in (Rom. XI); for then the remnant of Israel will be saved.

But when Simon Peter drew such a sword and struck in this way, he had not yet properly understood what sword the Lord used, he who is “strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle” (Ps. XXIII), or what he had said concerning the sword according to Luke: “But now, let him who has a purse take it, and likewise a bag; and let him who has none sell his tunic and buy a sword” (Luke XXII). Neither he nor the others—who answered, “Lord, behold, here are two swords”—had yet properly recognized the sword of the Word of God, habitually employed in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms.

The person who has no purse should buy this sword by selling his tunic, because in a time of persecution, the more stripped anyone is of worldly possessions, the stronger and readier he is to preach the word of God; and, by divesting himself of worldly goods, he girds himself better with the sword of strength. But “let him who has a purse,” he says, “take it, and likewise a bag,” because, in such a time as then existed, when no one listens to the preacher and consequently feeds him much less, each person must provide for himself, since he cannot live by the Gospel.

In these and all other places where the Lord and Master speaks beyond the disciples’ understanding, it is not he who should be charged with obscurity, but the disciple with slowness—like this Simon Peter, who had understood so carnally what he had said about buying a sword. For the Lord honored Holy Scripture, as was fitting, by speaking according to it and commending that sword of which it is written in the Law: “And my sword shall devour flesh” (Deut. XXXI). Likewise in the Psalm: “Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most mighty one” (Ps. XLIV). And there are very many such passages.

“Jesus therefore said to Peter, ‘Put your sword back into its sheath. Shall I not drink the cup which the Father has given me?’” Therefore, he says, because Peter had drawn his sword rashly and without command, and had struck unlawfully: “Put back,” says the leader and master of the righteous battle, [Col. 0770A] “your sword”—“your,” I say, and not mine—“into its sheath,” into its proper place. And the same meaning in which Peter had formerly said, “Far be it from you, Lord; this shall not happen” (Matt. 16), because he had foretold that he would suffer—the same meaning, I say, now raging in the sword, he rebukes, saying, “Shall I not drink the cup which the Father has given me?”

Even in calling the passion of death a cup, he speaks according to the Scriptures, which are accustomed to call tribulation by the name of waters or a torrent, as in the words spoken in his person: “Save me, O God, for the waters have entered even unto my soul” (Ps. 68). Likewise: “He shall drink from the torrent in the way; therefore he shall lift up his head” (Ps. 109). Certainly the Father gave him this cup, because he suffered not by human decision but by the Father’s command. He gave it to him as Father, not as judge: that is, in love, not wrath; by will, not necessity; through grace, not vengeance.

“The cohort, therefore, and the tribune and the attendants of the Jews seized Jesus and bound him.” 326 Therefore, because the cup which the Father had given could not pass away unless the obedient Son drank it, “they seized Jesus,” he says—that is, insofar as darkness could seize him, though it never comprehended the light. They seized him, I say, and bound him, because this alone was the power of darkness: to seize for binding him whom they had not deserved to comprehend in understanding. Thus they seized him in their hour, in one brief hour and a momentary power, because henceforth [Col. 0770C] darkness will nowhere have any power to comprehend the light.

“They seized him,” he says, “and bound him.” O utterly dreadful audacity of sinners! Thus those officers who bound salvation and mercy—those strong madmen, I say, who so tightly confined the physician—howl and lament, wondering that their enemies have taken away their place and nation and have trampled down their sanctuary. For example, when they say, according to Isaiah: “Where is he who brought them up from the sea with the shepherds of his flock? Where is he who put in the midst of him the Spirit of his Holy One, who led Moses at his right hand by the arms of his majesty?” (Isa. 63), and so forth, let it be answered them that both arms of his majesty are bound, and therefore will offer no help.

And because they not only bound the hands of their deliverer [Col. 0770D] but also fastened them with nails, when they likewise read while weeping: “Your holy city has become a wilderness; Zion has become a wilderness; Jerusalem, the desolate house of our sanctification and our glory, where our fathers praised you—will you restrain yourself over these things, O Lord?” (Isa. 64), let it be answered that he must restrain his hands: “For,” he says, “I stretched out my hands to an unbelieving people” (Isa. 65), and the rest.

But for us who believe, those hands, thus bound or stretched out upon the cross, accomplished more: for they bound the strong armed man, who until then had guarded his courtyard (Luke 11) and possessed his goods in peace; and, by openly nailing and triumphantly displaying it, they erased the bond of sin [Col. 0771A] (Col. 2).

“And they led him first to Annas, for he was the father-in-law of Caiaphas, who was high priest that year. Now Caiaphas was the one who had advised the Jews that it was expedient for one man to die for the people.” As the Lord had shortly before said to his disciples: “Amen, amen, I say to you, you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice” (John 16). It was fitting that the enemies of truth should rejoice and should share with one another the joy of victory in this long-desired capture. Therefore they made him, captured and bound, be carried about as an object of reproach: first to Annas, then to Caiaphas, then to Pilate, then, as Luke testifies, to Herod, and then again to Pilate (Luke 23).

They did this, indeed, as though outdoing one another in honor; but in truth they were openly confirming their sacrilege by common agreement, lest, under Roman laws, one person, if he alone appeared to be the author of the crime, should bear the stigma or accusation. The Evangelist gives the reason why they brought him first to Annas, saying: “For he was the father-in-law of Caiaphas, who was high priest that year.” But by further adding, “Now Caiaphas was the one who had advised the Jews that it was expedient for one man to die for the people,” he indicates that it was done at Caiaphas’s will that he should first be brought to Annas—so that Caiaphas himself, who had first given the counsel, might not also be the first to condemn and thus bear the whole odium among men.

“Simon Peter and another [Col. 0771C] disciple were following Jesus. That disciple was known to the high priest, and he entered into the high priest’s courtyard. But Peter stood outside at the door.” Peter followed, but from afar, as the other Evangelists testify: he followed from afar, I say, not so much in the movement of his feet as in the disposition of his frightened mind. For, in accordance with the truth of him who said, “Where I am going, you cannot follow me now,” he was not yet able to imitate the Master and Lord as he went to his passion.

Yet, somehow, he did follow, that he might see the end: fearful indeed, but bearing a pious concern for the Lord. The other disciple (John 13) is perhaps the one who wrote these things, concerning whom some did not hesitate to maintain that he was noble, and hence “was known to the high priest.” Yet we do not know the character [Col. 0771D] of his nobility; but we hold this one thing as certain from the Gospel: that he was a son of Zebedee, called not from the court but from fishing, together with his brother James, and that, leaving nets and father, he followed the Lord. Whatever the reason that he “was known to the high priest,” let us consider what follows.

“Therefore that disciple who was known to the high priest went out, spoke to the doorkeeper, and brought Peter in.” At this point one is pleased to recall a far greater miracle, when the disciples were laboring on the sea—“for the wind was contrary and the boat was tossed among the waves”—and the Lord came in the fourth watch, walking upon the waters. At his voice Peter eagerly ventured out and himself walked upon the sea to come to Jesus; but when a strong wind came, he was afraid and almost sank, until he was held by the Lord’s hand [Col. 0772A] (Matt. 14).

This is truly the Lord upon the waters, though amid a great tempest. He was truly walking upon the waters while the disciples labored on the sea, because, while the apostles suffered scandal and were scattered in flight, he endured tribulation according to his own will, untroubled: weak indeed in flesh, but ready in spirit, and soon also to be victor over death. “Peter too walked upon the waters to come to Jesus” (ibid.), because, mindful of his former love, in which he had said, “I will lay down my life for you” (John 13; Matt. 26), he still followed Jesus from far behind with the daring of little faith. But he saw the strong wind coming and was afraid; in being afraid he denied; in denying he was swallowed up—unless, as Luke says, “the Lord turned and looked upon Peter” [Col. 0772B] (Luke 22), and by that same look, as though taking him by the hand, restored him, weeping, to his former footing. And from what source did he see the strong wind coming? The passage continues:

“Then the servant-girl who kept the door said to Peter, ‘Are you also one of this man’s disciples?’ He said, ‘I am not.’” If you look at the doorkeeper, she is a small cloud; but if you look at that council of the wicked, because of which Peter feared this servant-girl’s insolent outcry, it is a strong wind. Nevertheless Peter’s weakness was exposed, because, while he feared to die, he denied life. Thus Satan, that sifter of the apostles, saw to it that the device of temptation began with a woman—the sex which in Paradise had been the gateway of deception to the first-created man (Gen. 3).

[Col. 0772C] “The servants and attendants were standing by the coals and warming themselves, because it was cold. Peter also was standing with them and warming himself.” It was cold, as sometimes occurs near the vernal equinox; and Peter, growing cold as he denied, was warmed at the fire of cold murderers and enemies of Christ. We consider the vicars of this same Peter—priests or high pontiffs—comparable to such a Peter whenever, sitting amid the riches of sinners, they delight in them greedily, having put away the sword of God’s Word and forgotten what the Psalmist says: “A little is better for the righteous than the great riches of sinners” (Ps. 36).

For they imagine themselves to be like Peter as he was in Nero’s tribunal: strong key-bearers of heaven, with the kingdom of heaven [Col. 0772D] shut or opened at their discretion. Yet, in gladly accepting gifts and rejecting truth on their account, they are rather like that Peter who, sitting by these 327 coals, lost life because he denied the author of life.

“The high priest therefore questioned Jesus about his disciples and about his teaching.” He questioned him about his disciples and his teaching: namely, who his disciples were and what his teaching was. The questioner’s purpose was that, if Jesus openly affirmed before the whole council what he had taught—namely, that he was the Son of God—judgment would immediately follow by concerted decision: “He has blasphemed; he is guilty of death.”

For if false witnesses had been set up, as Matthew says, and had said many things that were not consistent, “the high priest said to him: ‘I adjure you by the living God to tell [Col. 0773A] us whether you are the Christ, the Son of God’” (Matt. 26). Therefore he questioned him concerning his teaching: that is, concerning what he had taught, namely that he was the Son of God.

“Jesus answered him: ‘I have spoken openly to the world; I have always taught in synagogues and in the temple, where all the Jews assemble; and I have spoken nothing in secret. Why do you question me? Question those who heard what I said to them. Behold, they know what I have said.’” It is as though he said: A man is necessarily questioned concerning a case when the fact is known but the manner of the act is not known. For example, Achan was necessarily questioned by Joshua, who said: “My son, give glory to God and tell us what you have done” (Josh. 7), because, though he had perhaps been discovered by lot to be the common cause of evil, the same lot had not also revealed [Col. 0773B] what crime he had committed.

But I, he says, whose case is now known to you on the basis of my teaching, “have spoken openly to the world and have spoken nothing in secret”—namely, concerning those matters about which you now question me. “Why do you question me?” Certainly, “if I tell you, you will not believe me; and if I question you, you will not answer, nor let me go” (Luke 22). Accordingly, by law or judicial custom, because no one is permitted to be his own witness in a lawful trial, question those who heard; behold, they know what I said.

“When he had said these things, one of the attendants standing by struck Jesus with the palm of his hand, saying, ‘Is that how you answer the high priest?’” Behold this mighty striker and feeble flatterer: he displayed himself as the very strongest of those strong men concerning whom the Spirit of the Lord Christ complains through the Prophet in Christ’s own person: “For behold,” he says, “they have seized my soul, and strong men have rushed upon me, though there is neither iniquity [Col. 0773C] nor sin in me” (Ps. 58).

Who are these, if not men falsely strong but truly weak and feeble, who rushed upon God’s strength—raising the dead—as a madman rushes upon a physician who wishes to heal him? This frenzied man, then, is one of the chief among those who were wickedly strong. He rushed so insolently upon the man speaking words of health and truth that he was truly insane; and, zealously but foolishly rather than bravely acting for his lord the high priest, he sought to commend his own guardianship to him.

The arm of the Lord could indeed have struck down the striker (Isa. 40, 44), and could have immediately overthrown not only him but also the whitewashed wall (Acts 23)—that is, the man falsely called his lord, the high priest—whom such a rigid post supported. But he accepted injury, kept patience, and returned instruction. For it follows:

“Jesus answered him: ‘If I have spoken evil, bear witness concerning the evil; but if well, why do you strike me?’” It was spoken gently and meekly, but most justly devised and most weightily uttered. Why, he says, do you strike me, who speak well? Even if I had spoken evil, you would have no authority to strike unless commanded; indeed, it would not be right for you to receive either command or authority unless the case had first been stated and a free sentence rendered by the judges. For if I had spoken evil, it was your duty to accuse me and state the ground [Col. 0774A] on which you would prove that my speech was evil. Therefore, when the act is already unjust in itself, you make this present hearing still more unjust by your disturbance.

“And Annas sent him bound to Caiaphas the high priest.” He had first been brought to Annas by Caiaphas’s will, because Annas was his father-in-law; but Annas sent him to Caiaphas because he was “high priest that year.”

“Now Simon Peter was standing and warming himself.” This had already been said above: “Peter was standing with the attendants and warming himself”; but it is now repeated in order that the account of his threefold denial, which had been interrupted, might proceed in its begun order. “Therefore they said to him: ‘Are you also one of his disciples?’ He denied it and said: ‘I am not.’” He denied for the second time; but the truth of the physician was not yet wholly fulfilled. Knowing well the sickness of the infirm man, he had said: “Before the cock crows, you will deny me three times.” It follows:

“One of the high priest’s servants, a relative of him whose ear Peter had cut off, said to him: ‘Did I not see you in the garden with him?’ Peter denied again, and immediately the cock crowed.” Thus he who had presumed that he could suffer all the waves of tribulation for the Lord, saying, “Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you,” feared at the first wind, because he was sinking, because he denied for the third time. But the Lord stretched out the hand of grace and seized him, turning and looking at him, so that he might quickly repent and weep; and thus, washed by the Lord, might have a share with him.

For unless the faith of repentance had immediately gone before, [Col. 0774C] at the hour when our Lord poured out blood and water from his side, the sin of Peter’s denial would not have been blotted out. For just as even now everyone to be baptized must first believe and confess, and only then be baptized into the death of Christ Jesus, buried with him through baptism, and raised with him (Rom. 8), so Peter, in order to remain an apostle, and the thief, in order to enter Paradise with the Lord (Luke 23), had to repent and confess before Christ, giving up his spirit, poured forth the stream of the foretold blood and water.

For all who, after that hour in which he washed the whole Church gathered from the beginning of the world, are converted to faith in him, are not counted [Col. 0774D] among the children of that Church unless the sacrament of the Lord’s passion is renewed for them individually through baptism.
