“Therefore they led Jesus from Caiaphas into the praetorium.” Through the fault of copyists, it began to be read: “to Caiaphas into the praetorium.” For the praetorium belonged not to Caiaphas but to the Roman governor; and on the day when the Passover was to be eaten, it was unlawful for any Jew—and much more for the high priest—to enter it. Therefore, since it was said above, “And Annas sent him bound to Caiaphas the high priest,” it is better written and read here: “Therefore they led Jesus from Caiaphas into the praetorium.”

“Now it was morning. And they themselves did not enter the praetorium, lest they should be defiled, but might eat the Passover. Therefore Pilate went out to them and said: [Col. 0775A] ‘What accusation do you bring against this man?’” At this point that chapter of the prophet Hosea does not seem fit to be passed over:

“All of them are adulterers, like an oven heated by the baker. The city rested a little from the mixing of the leaven until it was wholly leavened. On the day of our king, our princes began to rage from wine. He stretched out his hand with scoffers, because they had applied their heart like an oven when he lay in wait for them. All night their baker slept; in the morning he himself burned like a flaming fire,” and so forth (Hos. 7).

How this may be referred to Jeroboam son of Nebat and the princes of his time, on account of the fury with which they made calves and, having abandoned God’s Temple and separated from the house of David, worshipped them (3 Kings 41), is uncertain; for no history relates anything to which such an account would suit. Therefore, because the same prophet had shortly before plainly spoken of Christ’s resurrection—“Come and let us return to the Lord, for he has seized us and will heal us; he will strike and cure us; after two days he will revive us; on the third day he will raise us, and we shall live in his sight” (Hos. 6), and so forth—it is not unfitting to apply the foretold chapter to the present place, not as an account of past events but as a prophecy of things truly to come.

“All of them are adulterers,” he says, “like an oven heated by the baker,” and so forth (Hos. 7). Who are these adulterers, more wicked or more inflamed, whose heart was truly heated like an oven by the baker, the devil? The city had rested a little from the mixing of the leaven of its wickedness and malice, until it was wholly leavened: that is, from the day on which they had planned to kill him, saying, “Lest the Romans come and take away our place and nation” (John 11), they had rested until, by persuading the crowds, they had spread their leaven and leavened the entire mass of the city by consent to their malice.

At last came the day on which they cried, saying, “The day of our king,” by saying, “We have no king but Caesar,” and: “If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend” (John 19). And the princes began to rage from wine, because they were already drunken. Having seized the Lord in that great paschal night, they remained awake all night; belching out their late debauchery and breathing out foul drunkenness, they vomited vile insults [Col. 0775D] upon that poor and needy man. Thus was fulfilled the prophecy spoken in his person: “Those who sat in the gate spoke against me, and those who drank wine sang about me” (Ps. 68).

And what of the servant of their king Caesar, Pilate? He certainly slept all night while baking them, because, being a shrewd dissembler and, as someone said of him, “placing falsehood in a small matter,” he remained at home as though ignorant of the affair and gave them a cohort and a tribune. Through these he made the Jewish furies, already sufficiently inflamed, burn still more and more. “Therefore in the morning he himself burned like a flaming fire, going out to them” (Hos. 7), and saying: “What accusation do you bring against this man?” He stretched out his hand with the scoffers—those, namely, who had mocked the Lord all night [Col. 0776A] (Matt. 27)—because they had applied their heart like an oven when he lay in wait for them.

For in everything he said and did—for example, when he said, “What evil has he done?” or when, taking water, he washed his hands before them—he was laying a trap for them, namely, to pour the whole guilt upon them, so that he himself should not face judgment before the Roman emperor for unjustly condemning a man. For if he truly wished to release him, why did he nowhere employ that power of which he later says: “Do you not know that I have authority to kill you, and authority to release you?” (John 19). Therefore, greater indeed was the sin of the man who handed the Lord Jesus over to him; yet Pilate too was not free from sin, because he willingly undertook the service of murder.

Accordingly Herod was rightly compared to a fox, the Lord saying: “Go, tell that fox” (Luke 13; Matt. 14). For, though he gladly beheaded John, he pretended to be grieved because of his oath; likewise this liar, who, as has been said, “placed falsehood in a small matter,” is rightly compared to a fox. Though he gladly accepted the demand for the Lord’s death, he pretended to defend him; and, having taken water, he washed his hands but not his conscience (Matt. 27).

But let us now return to the Gospel words themselves. “They themselves,” he says, “did not enter the praetorium, lest they should be defiled, but might eat the Passover.” Blind Pharisees, you have most carefully cleansed what is outside the dish and cup, while within you are foul and bloody; truly whitewashed tombs, beautiful outwardly to men, but inwardly full of dead men’s bones [Col. 0776C] (Mark 7; Matt. 23). What is this? You take care not to be outwardly defiled by entering the praetorium of a Gentile, but you do not fear to be horribly polluted within by plotting cruel murder. What is more impure than this purity? What more criminal than this holiness?

“Pilate therefore went out to them and said: ‘What accusation do you bring against this man?’”

“They answered and said to him: ‘If this man were not an evildoer, we would not have handed him over to you.’” So, righteous nation and innocent people, are you accustomed to hand over—indeed, to kill—none but evildoers? Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? They killed those who foretold the coming of the Righteous One, of whom you are now betrayers and murderers [Col. 0776D]. Thus, at the beginning of the case, you made a defective submission to the Roman governor.

“Pilate therefore said to them: ‘Take him yourselves and judge him according to your law.’ The Jews said to him: ‘It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death.’” They did not say, “It is not lawful for us to judge anyone,” but “It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death.” For they had already kept watch the whole night and had judged him—not according to their law but against their law; they had mocked, spat upon, and struck him with their fists. Yet it was not lawful for them to put to death one who had been judged unless the Roman governor confirmed the judgment.

Nor is it surprising that during the Babylonian captivity they had been permitted to stone Susanna without consulting the Babylonian ruler (Dan. 13). But now, while living in their own land, they were not permitted to kill a man apart from [Col. 0777A] the tribunals of the Roman governor. For the Roman Empire, stronger and more powerful than the Babylonian, Persian, and Macedonian empires, had subjected to itself all the kingdoms of the earth. This indeed was the kingdom of which Daniel said in his night vision: “Behold,” he says, “a fourth beast, terrible and wondrous and exceedingly strong. It had great iron teeth, devouring and crushing, and trampling the rest under its feet” (Dan. 7).

Therefore the Roman Empire devoured and crushed all the kingdoms of the world; but most especially it broke the Jewish kingdom into fragments, dividing it among four tetrarchs. What remained it finally trampled under its feet, so that not one stone was left upon another (Matt. 24), and they were led captive into all nations. Thus, already much crushed by the teeth of the terrible beast and later also to be trampled beneath its feet, they say: “It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death.”

“That the word of Jesus might be fulfilled, which he had spoken, signifying by what death he was to die.” For he had said: “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and all that has been written through the prophets concerning the Son of Man will be fulfilled. For he will be handed over to the Gentiles to be mocked, scourged, and crucified.” Therefore, for this saying to be fulfilled, it was necessary for him to be handed over to the Gentiles by the Jews saying, “It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death,” because nothing could happen except what he had foretold (Matt. 16, 20). Nor would he have foretold anything except what was immovably to occur.

[Col. 0777C] “Pilate therefore entered the praetorium again, called Jesus, and said to him: ‘Are you the King of the Jews?’” Behold Pilate, in his ignorance, suddenly shows himself to have been privy to Jewish envy. For the Jews had not yet shouted that Jesus had called himself King of the Jews, and already, questioning him, he says: “Are you the King of the Jews?” Therefore, when he said, “What accusation do you bring against this man?” he did not fail to know the charge, 329 but pretended that he knew it not.

Accordingly, immediately “Jesus answered him: ‘Do you say this of yourself, or have others told you about me?’” If he had immediately answered, “I am a king,” before distinguishing his kingdom from human kingdoms, he would have given Pilate an occasion for accusation, as though he had acted against Pilate’s lord Caesar. Therefore, by answering better in this way, “Do you say this of yourself, or have others told you about me?” he both removed the ground for a just accusation and testified that he was king, because he did not deny it.

For it is the same as though he said: It is so true that I am King of the Jews that, if you said this from yourself rather than at another’s prompting, it is evident that you have divined it as a prophet. What then? “Do you say this of yourself,” or have others truly informed you of my case—as you pretend not to know—when you sent a cohort and a tribune to seize me?

“Pilate answered: ‘Am I a Jew? Your nation and the chief priests have handed you over to me. What have you done?’” It is as though he said: The whole case takes its beginning from the Jews. Am I present, since I am not a Jew, at their councils or synagogues in which they condemned you, so that the origin of this charge or title could have arisen from me? It is not so. Rather, your nation and chief priests, accusing you and demanding sentence, have handed you over to me. “What have you done?”

To this the Lord, the great and wise king, did not answer that unworthy man what he had done, since he had done all things well and all things good—indeed, since all things, and all things very good, had been made through him (Gen. 1). Nor did he care to say what had first been asked, namely that he was King of the Jews, because his adversaries had already stated it sufficiently. But what they had said inadequately or perversely, he supplied and corrected in this manner.

“My kingdom is not of this world.” True indeed, he says, your nation and chief priests, who handed me over to you, told you about me, accusing me of being King of the Jews; but they falsely alleged that my kingdom conflicts with Caesar’s kingdom. For my kingdom is not of this world. He did not say, “My kingdom is not in this world.” For he is the exalted ruler in the kingdom of men, giving it to whom he wills, and he is governor and Lord of the whole world (Dan. 4). But, he says, it is not *of* this world: that is, it does not arise from the decision or pleasure of those who are in this world; not from the greatness of cities or wide expanses of lands; not from the multitude and strength of raging soldiers or the blood of battles.

Therefore the Roman Empire, or any other earthly kingdom, suffers no harm from me, because my kingdom seeks nothing of that sort. That this is so needs no proof, because it is clear and evident to all. In what way? He says:

“If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would surely fight that I might not be handed over to the Jews. But now my kingdom is not from here.” I would have servants of this world fighting for me, he says, if my kingdom were of this world. But now there is no servant of this world, no one who fights for me from this world. Therefore “my kingdom is not from here.” Is this what it means to reign in this world: to open blind eyes, give hearing to the deaf, restore walking to the lame, raise the dead, preach the Gospel to the poor (Matt. 11), and for such acts be seized like a robber, bound, struck on the face, mocked, and spat upon?

“Pilate therefore said to him: ‘Then you are a king?’” For, being a rational man, he saw that this followed: if his kingdom was not from here, it was from elsewhere; and a kingdom, wherever it is from, is still a kingdom. Therefore he draws the conclusion: “Then,” he says, “you are a king?” The Jewish accuser proposed it; Christ assumed it; Pilate concluded it.

“Jesus answered: ‘You say that I am a king.’” You say this, he says; you have long since objected this to me as a crime; on this charge you sent a cohort and a tribune, together with Jewish attendants, to seize me. But I have not denied the charge; rather, I have said that “my kingdom is not from here.” If you sought truth, if you loved truth, then, when I said, “My kingdom is not from here,” you ought to have asked and learned whence it is. Since you disdain to do this, behold, I now tell you of my own accord whence it is, lest, in killing me, you boast that you defended Caesar’s frontiers.

“I was born for this, and for this I came into the world: to bear witness to the truth. Everyone who is of the truth hears my voice.” In saying this the Lord plainly accords with the prophecy in which David speaks in his person: “But I have been appointed king by him over Zion, his holy mountain, proclaiming his command” (Ps. 2). To proclaim his command is to bear witness to the truth. There he says: “I have been appointed king by him” for this purpose, that I might proclaim his command. But here he says: “For this I [Col. 0779B] was born king, and for this I came into the world: to bear witness to the truth.” And he adds: “Everyone who is of the truth hears my voice.”

These sayings are of such height and strength that neither Pilate can reach them nor any other enemy of the heavenly kingdom overthrow them. For would this man, however deceitful a partisan of Caesar, say that his lord, the ruler of great Rome, did not wish anyone to be born or to come into the world in order to bear witness to truth, and that it would diminish Caesar’s honor if any of his soldiers listened to the voice of one bearing witness to truth? In this way he would not protect the head of his ruler by a defense, but bury it beneath a great detestation.

For the name of truth is lovable, and it is honorable. Human nature willingly assents to it; and although utterly wicked scoundrels hate what it signifies, yet no one has ever been allowed to detest its name itself. Thus Pilate was overcome and failed.

“Pilate said to him: ‘What is truth?’ And when he had said this, he again went out to the Jews and said to them: ‘I find no charge in him.’” He had learned by experience that there was nothing in Jesus by which, if he killed him, he could defend himself should he be accused before Caesar of unjustly inflicting punishment. For Jesus, prince of all the righteous and king of justice, “had put on justice as a breastplate, had taken certain judgment as a helmet, and had taken equity as an invincible shield” (Wis. 5), so that they could in no way catch him in speech.

Therefore frustrated cruelty, thirsting for blood and punishment, says: “I find no charge in him.” And he added: “But it is customary to release one person at Passover. Do you therefore wish me to release to you the King of the Jews?” He said this, certain of what they would answer; for he knew that they had handed him over out of envy. If he himself had not been of the same will, would he so readily have placed the entire matter at the discretion of those envious men, rather than use the authority of which he would later say: “Do you not know that I have authority to release you and authority to crucify you?” (Matt. 27)?

At the same time one must consider that, when the furnace was already hot enough, he knowingly cast in, as it were, a drop of oil: knowing that they had handed him over out of envy, he threw before them the very title for which they envied him, saying: “Do you wish me to release to you the King of the Jews?” [Col. 0780A]

“Again they all cried out, saying: ‘Not this man, but Barabbas.’ Now Barabbas was a robber.” Again, he says, they cried out—for they had already cried once, saying: “If this man were not an evildoer, we would not have delivered him to you.” And now once more they cry: Do not release this man to us, but Barabbas. They cried this loudly and shouted it on high. This is the outcry of which the Lord speaks through the prophet: “Behold, I expected,” he says, “that he would do justice, and behold, iniquity; and righteousness, and behold, an outcry” (Isa. V). For it was thus to happen: the Savior would be killed and the robber preserved.

The Law of Moses commands—or rather thus prophesies mystically [Col. 0780B]: “The priest shall take from the whole multitude of the children of Israel two goats for sin, and shall set them before the Lord at the entrance of the tabernacle, casting lots upon the two, one lot for the Lord and the other for the scapegoat. The one upon whom the lot for the Lord falls he shall offer for sin; but the one upon whom it falls for the scapegoat he shall set alive before the Lord, that he may pour prayers over it and send it into the wilderness. When these things have been duly performed, he shall offer it and, praying for himself and for his household, shall sacrifice it” (Lev. XVI).

Behold, this prophetic rite was fulfilled. Who are the two goats but Christ, the Savior of the world, and Barabbas, the instigator of rebellion? The Savior indeed, though in accordance with his own innocence he truly was and is the Lamb of God, nevertheless [Col. 0780C], in accordance with the iniquities of us all—which, as the prophet testifies, God placed upon him (Isa. LIII)—appeared as it were a goat. Barabbas, however, was a goat not through others’ sins but through his own, whom that people, casting its lot wickedly, set before him who came to take away the sins of the world.

Thus the lot for the Lord fell upon our goat; but their lot fell upon that foul goat, namely the rebellious Barabbas, who became their scapegoat and was sent into the wilderness and preserved—that is, for that nation desolated by God. But our goat, namely Christ our Savior, praying for himself and for his household, which is ourselves, was willingly sacrificed. “Now Barabbas,” he says, “was a robber,” who also, as the other Evangelists report, had been put in prison for sedition and murder [Col. 0780D] (Matt. XXVII; Mark XV). Setting such a man before the Lord and King, the Son of God, they also cried out when Pilate asked: “What then shall I do with Jesus the Nazarene?” “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. XXVII).

“Woe therefore to the sinful nation, the people laden with iniquity, the wicked seed, the criminal children” (Isa. I), who asked that a murderer be granted to them, but killed the author of life. Rightly, therefore, they were destined to perish by rebellions and murders, because they exchanged the Prince of Peace for the author of rebellion and the Son of God for the son of their master, the devil (Isa. IX). For Barabbas is interpreted “son of their master.” And who is their master [Col. 0781A] except the devil, whom they imitate? Concerning this, when the Lord himself had said: “I do what I have seen with my Father” (John VIII), he immediately added, in contrast: “And you do what you have seen with your father.” They therefore justly inherited rebellions and murderous blood, to be overwhelmed by calamities so great that no abundance of any writer, nor any power whatever of an orator, could adequately declaim them.

[CH. XIX.] “Then Pilate took Jesus and scourged him.” A great spectacle to the world, to angels, and to human beings: that the Prince of freedom should be cut down in slavish fashion by servants of sin. “But,” says the prophet, “by his bruise we have been healed” (Isa. LIII). For it is clear that his soul truly suffered pain for us, and that his body, scourged and torn, bore the marks of injury in welts and bruising [Col. 0781B].

“And the soldiers, plaiting a crown of thorns, placed it upon his head, and clothed him with a purple garment; and they came and said to him: ‘Hail, King of the Jews’; and they struck him with the palms of their hands.” They did these things in mockery and with cruel jesting; but all was received in earnest by the power and wisdom of God, the great King Christ—or rather, it was providentially arranged to occur for a saving purpose (I Cor. I). Each mockery, each wound and blow, had a mighty voice, and all spoke justly on our behalf. For since blood cries to heaven from the earth which opened its mouth (Gen. IV) and received it from the hand of the Jews, the thorns too, the mocking garment, and the other injuries undoubtedly cry out to the heavenly propitiatory [Col. 0781C] and powerfully obtain forgiveness of sins for those who believe in him.

By the thorny crown they visibly signify what the prophet foretold of him: “He himself bore our sins” (Isa. LIII). For thorns denote sins, which pierce and tear the soul. They were given to humankind because of sin, as the Lord said to Adam: “When you work the earth, it shall not yield its fruits, but shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you” (Gen. III).

Nor did he disdain, while he was being mocked, to be clothed in a scarlet cloak. Does this not accord with the ministry of charity which he was exercising on our behalf in his Passion? For scarlet is fiery in color; it was commanded to be offered in the tabernacle of the Lord and to be used double-dyed in the priestly garment [Col. 0781D] (Exod. XXV, XXVIII). It signifies the twofold love of God and neighbor, because whatever we offer must be aflame and, as it were, well-colored to be pleasing before the divine sight. But he himself, because of the exceeding love with which he loved us (Eph. II), drank the cup of the Passion, as he himself says: “That the world may know that I love the Father”; and, “No one has greater love than this: that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John XV).

Therefore the scarlet cloak was fitting for this our King, so that by this very apparel he might show himself to be the one signified in the Law by the red heifer (Num. XIX), whose body was commanded to be burned outside the camp for sin, and whose ashes were sprinkled over the people in water with hyssop. [Col. 0782A] Nor did he refuse to receive in his hand from those mocking him a reed or staff, either to write down the sacrilege of the Jews or to kill poisonous creatures. For he had in his hand the rod—that is, his own soul in his own power—so that he might lay it down willingly and take it up again (John XII).

And as Moses, before Pharaoh, cast down his rod, which became a serpent and swallowed the rods of the magicians that had become serpents, and then returned again into a rod (Exod. VIII), so he himself was now in some manner about to lay down his soul, descending into death, which entered the world through the serpent (Wis. II), taking upon himself the serpents of Egypt—that is, the deaths of sinners—and returning again into the rod, that is, into his former power.

When, in such apparel, the King of the Jews was worshiped or greeted, if this had been a time for speaking and not rather a time for silence (Eccl. III), he could already have declared truthfully that every knee ought in earnest to bow to him and every tongue likewise confess him (Phil. II). Yet, though he himself was silent while suffering, his prophet cried out for him and does not cease to cry: “As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bow to me and every tongue shall confess” (Isa. XLV). Therefore, when the power and wisdom of God was mocked, he received all things seriously and reasonably, and did not turn away his face from those who struck him. It follows:

“Pilate went out again and said to them: ‘Behold, I bring him out to you, that you may know that I find no charge in him’” [Col. 0782C]. However much you feign constraint, condemned man and fuel for eternal fire, Roman severity will not believe you, who brought Jesus forth and spoke thus—leaving aside divine justice—any more than it afterward believed the tribune of the governor Felix, perhaps instructed by your example, who rescued the Apostle Paul from the fury of the Jews not by a mild and cold defense but by military force (Acts XXIII).

“Then Jesus came out, wearing the crown of thorns and the purple garment. And he said to them: ‘Behold the man.’” He came out thus, and “there was no form nor comeliness in him, and his appearance was without beauty” (Isa. LIII). “Behold,” he says, “the man.” We detest the intention of the speaker and the meaning of the mocker [Col. 0782D], but embrace the words and say: truly man; for, though he was God, he was made in the likeness of human beings and was found in appearance as a man (Phil. II).

“When therefore the chief priests and the attendants saw him, they cried out, saying: ‘Crucify him, crucify him.’” Thus the shameless chief priests, no less than their attendants, “opened their mouth wide. ‘Aha, aha,’ they say, ‘our eyes have seen’” (Ps. XXXIV). “So far all has been well done; now carry out what remains: ‘Crucify him, crucify him.’”

“Pilate said to them: ‘Take him yourselves and crucify him, for I find no charge in him.’” For they feared, as has already been said, that when he was summoned to Caesar’s judgment—as indeed would happen—he might endure trouble without having any defense to give concerning Jesus’ killing.

[Col. 0783A] “The Jews answered him: ‘We have a law, and according to the law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God.’” Transgressors of the Law, while you wish to reassure a Gentile by offering, as it were, the Law as a shield, “your iniquity has lied to itself” (Rom. II; Ps. XXVI). For one who asserts himself to be the Son of God ought not to die according to the Law; rather, it is the prophet who speaks falsely in the Lord’s name, convicted of falsehood because the outcome of his word does not follow (Deut. XVIII).

“When Pilate heard this saying, he feared more.” He certainly feared, but he did not repent. He feared, I say, because his mind foreboded the greatness of the evil to come, especially since his wife had already sent to him, saying: “Have nothing to do with that righteous man, for today I have suffered much in a dream because of him” [Col. 0783B] (Matt. XXVI).

“And he entered the praetorium again and said to Jesus: ‘Where are you from?’ But Jesus gave him no answer.” He asked this at an exceedingly inopportune time, since then was most especially a time for silence (Eccl. III), and he was unworthy to hear because he did not wish to believe. Furthermore, because he had already wickedly shorn the same Lamb of God—that is, scourged him—therefore Christ rightly kept silence before him and did not open his mouth (Isa. LIII).

“Pilate said to him: ‘Will you not speak to me? Do you not know that I have power to crucify you and power to release you?’” Therefore, O Pilate, mighty man with such great and vigorous power, you are judged out of your own mouth; and you are held guilty not only before God but also before human beings, because, though you could have released one innocent and just, you preferred to crucify him [Col. 0783C].

Wait a little, and do not hasten to say, “Will you not speak to me?” For he will afterward speak to you and tell you where he is from. For the Lord, who is now held weakly under your power, “will go forth as a strong man; like a warrior he will stir up zeal; he will shout and cry out against you, and against all his enemies he will prevail. ‘I have been silent,’ he will say, ‘I have always kept silence; I have been in travail; like a woman in labor I speak’” (Isa. XLII).

“Then he will speak to you in his wrath and trouble you in his fury,” clearly telling you what you now ask: where he is from. “I,” he will say, “have been appointed King by him over Zion, his holy mountain, proclaiming his commandment. The Lord said to me: ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you’” (Ps. II). He will speak this to you in his fury, and to all the kings and rulers of the earth [Col. 0783D] who assembled against the Lord and against his Christ.

But he who did not wish to tell you where he is from—hear what he answers concerning your power. “You would have no power against me unless it had been given you from above.” It was not, he says, through your lord Caesar, nor through these men who, crying “Crucify,” strengthen your arm against me; rather, you have been given authority against me by him who is above all human beings. For unless that which is my origin held my right hand and led me by its will (Ps. LXXII), I could at least look upon you and, with the iron rod of a single utterance, shatter you like a potter’s vessel (Ps. II).

Therefore, because I have been delivered from above—for the Father delivered me and did not spare his own Son [Col. 0784A] (Rom. VIII)—do not glory, you; for it is not your power but heavenly permission. Moreover, the authority you exercise against me is not truly authority but a kind of robbery. “For there is no authority except from God” (Rom. XIII). Such authority has legal force only where guilt exists. Do you wish, man, not to fear authority? Do good, and you will have praise from it; but if you do evil, fear. If, guilt being absent, you rage and kill, you commit robbery, you commit murder, and therefore become guilty before a higher authority.

If you are permitted from above to abuse authority, do not glory, “because the Lord will not leave the rod” (Ps. CXXIV)—that is, he will not allow the authority of sinners to remain over the lot of the righteous. “Will the axe glory against him who cuts with it? Or will the saw exalt itself against him by whom it is drawn?” (Isa. X). “Behold, strong men have rushed upon me, though there is neither my iniquity nor my sin” [Col. 0784B] (Ps. VII). Therefore this authority, while you crucify me, is not truly authority but truly cowardly robbery, which you could not carry out unless power had been given you from above.

“Therefore he who delivered me to you has the greater sin.” Why? Because he received the Law and, not in ignorance but through envy, abuses God’s permission; whereas you did not receive such a Law, and therefore it is as great a folly or wickedness in you as in him (Wis. II) either to hate wisdom or not to know the mysteries of God. You, shedding the blood of an unknown man, commit murder; he, delivering his King and Lord to death, joins sacrilege to murder against the one promised to his fathers, whom he had until then awaited, and whose expectation he professes by the sign of circumcision that he received. By killing him, he causes the very prophets he reads to accuse him [Col. 0784C]. It follows:

“And from that time Pilate sought to release him.” From that time, he says, Pilate sought to release him; for before that he had not sought to do so. Why then, as though refusing his condemnation, had he so often cried out? Because he was a hypocrite and a liar. But now, when he had learned Christ’s manifest innocence—for he had not been able to trap him at all in speech about the title of king—he feared more, especially because, as was said, “his wife had sent to him.”

“But the Jews cried out, saying: ‘If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend.’” And as though they were asked how releasing him conflicted with friendship for Caesar, these importunate and excessively zealous friends of Caesar—but enemies of God—support their proposition with this judgment: “Everyone who makes himself a king opposes Caesar.” Thus iniquity, as it seems to itself, closed every mouth, so that no one might dare to criticize or call unjust this man’s condemnation. For “everyone who makes himself a king opposes Caesar.” But this man makes himself a king. Pilate therefore may be secure and suppose that in killing him he renders service to Caesar.

“Therefore, when Pilate heard these words, he brought Jesus outside and sat upon the judgment seat in the place called Lithostrotos, but in Hebrew, Gabbatha. [Col. 0785A] Now it was the Preparation of the Passover, about the sixth hour.” *Parasceve* means “preparation.” By this name the Jews living among Greeks called the sixth day before the Sabbath—which we now call Friday—because on that day they prepared what was necessary for the Sabbath, in accordance with the former command concerning manna: “On the sixth day you shall gather double” (Exod. XVI), and so forth. Jews living among Romans more commonly called it in Latin *cena pura* (“the pure meal”).

Because on the sixth day humanity was made and the whole creation of the world completed, while on the seventh day the Creator rested from his work—whence he commanded this day to be called Sabbath, that is, rest—the Lord was rightly crucified on that same sixth day and fulfilled the mystery of human restoration. Thus [Col. 0785B], “when he had received the vinegar, he said: ‘It is finished’” (John XIX): that is, on the sixth day, the whole work he undertook for the restoration of the world was completed.

For those killers of the Lord, indeed, the Preparation was great because of the following great—that is, Paschal—Sabbath; but for us, because of the preparation of eternal life which was prepared for us on that day, it is the greatest Preparation. “And he said to the Jews: ‘Behold your King.’” This mocker had already said: “Behold the man”; now, still mocking, he says: “Behold your King.” He did not know how to speak the third name of the accusation or charge: “Behold your Son of God”; yet the Jews had said, “Because he made himself the Son of God.” These are the three utterly true names [Col. 0785C] of the one Christ our Lord: Man, King, God or Son of God. His enemies confessed him while mocking and worshiping with laughter; but we, his friends, confess him while wounded by compunction and worshiping in earnest.

“But they cried out: ‘Away with him, away with him; crucify him.’” Understand the unhappy Jews to have said: Take away from us the king; take away the prince; take away the priest. From that time was fulfilled what had earlier been predicted through the prophet: “For many days the children of Israel shall sit without king, without prince, without sacrifice, and without altar” (Hos. III). Likewise: “They shall go with sacrifices and gifts to seek the Lord, and shall not find him; he has been taken away from them” (Hos. V). And rightly so, because they said: Take away the Savior, crucify the propitiator; therefore they lost salvation and have no defense [Col. 0785D].

“Pilate said to them: ‘Shall I crucify your King?’” The shameless judge said this as if wearied by jesting, but their madness, impatient of and disgusted by his jest, rejected it and hurried toward a settled conviction. For what follows? “The chief priests answered: ‘We have no king but Caesar.’” Therefore let it be granted them that they have no king but Caesar, since they rejected all others without exception, whether God or human being; and let them receive Caesar’s fitting gifts: the slaughter and captivity of their nation, the overthrow of their city, fire, and the irrecoverable ruin of the Temple.

“Then therefore he delivered him to them to be crucified.” Thus those “sons of men, whose teeth were weapons and arrows and whose tongue was a sharp sword” [Col. 0786A] (Ps. LVI), prevailed; for, strengthening themselves in an evil word (Ps. LXIII), they persisted until he was delivered to them for crucifixion.

“Then they took Jesus and led him away.” He himself expresses through the Psalmist the eagerness of those who took him: “They seized me,” he says, “like a lion ready for prey, and like a lion’s cub dwelling in secret places” (Ps. XVI).

“And bearing his cross for himself, he went out to the place called Calvary, but in Hebrew Golgotha, where they crucified him.” He did indeed go out, but he did not reach the place while himself carrying his cross. For they compelled Simon, a passerby, the father of Alexander and Rufus, to carry the cross after him (Matt. XXVII; Mark XV). “Let us therefore,” says the Apostle, “go out to him outside the camp, bearing his reproach” [Col. 0786B] (Heb. XIII). And not like that Simon, who indeed carried the cross after him but was not himself crucified; rather, let us take up his cross in such a manner that we crucify ourselves with our vices and desires (Gal. V) and, whenever time or circumstance calls for it, follow the footsteps of him who suffered for us, leaving us an example (I Pet. II).

Calvary was the place of the condemned, called “the place of Calvary” from the heads of those punished there, where they crucified him. “And with him two others, one on either side, and Jesus in the middle.” Thus, according to the prophet, “he was reckoned among the wicked” (Isa. LIII); indeed, as though the greatest of criminals, he was crucified in the middle. Yet the cross itself was not merely the punishment of one judged, but in some manner also the judgment-seat of one already judged. For, as Luke explains most plainly, he mercifully received one of those criminals and justly left the other.

“Pilate also wrote a title and placed it upon the cross. And it was written: Jesus the Nazarene, King of the Jews. Therefore many of the Jews read this title, because the place where he was crucified was near the city.” The Holy Spirit dictated this writing with one intention, and Pilate wrote it with another. For Pilate hoped to glory in this wickedness and, by this title, to make it more evident and report it more clearly to Caesar that he had killed for Caesar’s loyalty a man whom a great multitude of that nation, receiving him with palm branches, had acclaimed with royal praises, thinking him to be the Christ promised through the prophets [Col. 0786D] (Matt. XXI).

But the Holy Spirit, making good use of the hand of the malicious writer, made this title one that shall not pass away though heaven and earth pass away (Luke XXI), because Jesus the Nazarene—that is, Savior and truly Holy One—became King of the Jews through his cross. Of the Jews, I say: not of those who say that they are Jews and are not, but are the synagogue of Satan (Rev. III), but of those Jews who are truly confessors of God.

“And it was written in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin.” These three are the chief languages through which Holy Scripture is today celebrated throughout the whole world, testifying that this title is true: namely, that Jesus the Nazarene is truly King of the Jews—King, I say [Col. 0787A], of all who confess in truth. For from the narrow dwelling-place of the Hebrew language, the Law, Prophets, and Psalms have burst forth through Greek and Latin tongues and filled the libraries of the world with their testimonies. Therefore the Word of God fittingly gathered these languages in his title, being neither bound nor destined to die, and made good use of the malicious writer as he wished for his own honor.

What shall we say of the cross itself? Does its form signify nothing mystical? I pass over the point—none would deny it to be most fitting—that the salvation of the human race was established upon the wood of the cross, so that life might rise again from the very place from which death arose, and he who conquered by a tree might also be conquered by a tree; and that, as a certain author says:

> Lest anyone be unaware, the form of the cross is to be venerated,  
> which bore the Lord, triumphing by mighty reason.

From it the squared world gathers its four regions. I must not pass over that the cross upon which he hung also signified, by its own form, the first gateways of the salvation he accomplished: faith, hope, charity, and, as the fourth among these, perseverance. For the cross has length, breadth, height, and depth. Its depth is the point by which it is fixed and adheres to the earth; its length extends from there to the arms; its breadth lies in the outstretching of the arms; its height extends upward from the arms, where the head is raised.

These four aforementioned virtues are signified by these four dimensions. By the depth, faith [Col. 0787B], which, through the hidden calling of God’s will, is first laid in the depth of the heart like a foundation in a building; by the length, perseverance; by the height, hope, which is set for us in heaven; and by the breadth, charity. For we understand the Apostle to have spoken of these: “That you may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the length, breadth, height, and depth” (Eph. III). Therefore, in the form of his punishment, our Savior proclaimed the first teachings of salvation.

Thus Christ’s killers, by their own intention, speak and perform sacrileges; but by God’s dispensation, they speak and perform sacred mysteries. “Many of the Jews,” says the Evangelist, “read this title, because the place where they crucified him was near the city.”

“Therefore the chief priests of the Jews said to Pilate: ‘Do not write, “King of the Jews,” but, “He said, I am King of the Jews.”’” These chief priests are plainly those destroyers or corrupters against whom Christ’s Spirit spoke beforehand in certain Psalm headings: “For the end: do not destroy,” or “do not corrupt,” in the inscription of the title (Ps. LVI). For they wished to destroy and corrupt a good and well-written title by thus truncating it: “Jesus the Nazarene, who said: ‘I am King of the Jews’” [Col. 0787D].

As though Pilate did not know that the crowds had acclaimed him king when, as he came to Jerusalem, they went out to meet him with palm branches, and that many believed him to be the King promised by prophetic oracles. “Pilate answered: ‘What I have written, I have written.’” Thus, Pilate, you have sealed your iniquity in your hand, because you wish it to stand fixed and settled that, by killing Christ the King, you have killed Israel’s expectation and, as you supposed, rendered void the oracles of God’s prophets [Col. 0788A], who said of this King that he would have a great kingdom: for example, that “he shall rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth” (Ps. LXXII).

But it is the will of God, who knows how to use a wicked servant well—it is God’s will, I say—that what you wrote should be written and remain. After the Psalmist had set forth the promises of Christ’s kingdom, God saying: “Once I have sworn by my holiness: if I lie to David, his seed shall remain forever, and his throne as the sun before me, and as the moon perfected forever, and the faithful witness in heaven,” he immediately added the assessment of you and your like: “But you have rejected and despised; you have delayed your Christ” [Col. 0788B]. And shortly afterward: “You have turned away the help of his sword and have not aided him in battle. You have cast him down from cleansing and dashed his throne to the ground. You have shortened the days of his time; you have covered him with shame” (Ps. LXXXVIII).

You could have heard these or similar proclamations concerning Christ in the same way as Herod did, who, when the Magi had come from the east, himself summoned the chief priests and scribes of the people and asked where Christ was to be born (Matt. II). What Herod was unable to accomplish against the Magi, you thought you had prudently accomplished. Your hope will deceive you: for you will not escape the judgment of this slain King of the Jews, nor will you even enjoy Caesar’s table more intimately because of this deed or inscription. For it is reported that, because of this, he was brought to Rome and sentenced to exile by the Emperor Tiberius; and the sentence was so intolerable that, unable to endure hunger, he took his own life with a sword [Col. 0788C]. Thus those manifest curses fell upon him by which divine Scripture condemns the impious, saying: “Let his strength be weakened by hunger, and famine shall invade his ribs, one after another. Let death’s firstborn devour the beauty of his heart and consume his arms” (Job XVIII), and so forth.

“Therefore, when the soldiers had crucified him, they took his garments and made four parts, a part for each soldier, and also the tunic. Now the tunic was seamless, woven from above throughout. They therefore said to one another: ‘Let us not tear it, but cast lots for it, to determine whose it shall be.’” Since they could sell his garments profitably, the soldiers took them by lot as the spoils of a great victory [Col. 0788D]. For the garments were not thought cheap, from the fringes of which power had been accustomed to go forth when they were touched (Matt. IX). Nor, certainly, were there lacking at that spectacle persons who pressed forward competitively to buy them.

For, to say nothing of his mother and the disciple whom Jesus loved, standing beside his cross: “All his acquaintances,” says Luke, “stood at a distance, and the women who had followed him from Galilee, seeing these things” (Luke XXIII). So completely was the Lord treated as an outlawed criminal and sinner that his own dear ones, who would have preserved them as a great treasure, were not allowed to divide his garments among themselves; but, satiated with reproaches in his body, he saw even his garments pass as payment to his killers, so that Scripture might be fulfilled, saying: “They divided my garments among themselves, and upon my clothing they cast lots” [Col. 0789A] (Ps. XXI). As though he said: They were so cruel, and stood watching and looking upon me with so little pity, that they even had leisure to cast lots while dividing my garments. This undoubtedly belonged to the fidelity of imperial rule: Roman soldiers were to kill the King of the Jews not merely obediently but joyfully.

It is permissible to compare the audacity of heretics with this plundering: although they have torn Holy Scripture apart into their perverse interpretations, they have nevertheless not been able to tear apart the faith of Christ or his Catholic Church. For the Lord’s many garments signify the many volumes of the Scriptures in which the one Word of God is clothed; but the seamless tunic, woven continuously from above—such as his beloved Mary had carefully woven by lot—fittingly signifies the one whole and inviolate faith of the Catholic Church [Col. 0789B].

“And the soldiers indeed did these things.” The Evangelist finely brings the deeds of the impious to their conclusion. “These things indeed,” he says, “the soldiers did”—implying that afterward they had nothing more they could do. They crucified the body and took the spoil, but they could not kill with his soul the power of God, the Word of God, God the Word. He next relates what occurred once the soldiers’ hands had ceased.

“Now there stood by the cross of Jesus his mother, and his mother’s sister, Mary of Cleophas, and Mary Magdalene.” His mother, he says, stood by the cross of her Son, undoubtedly grieving and undergoing pains as of a woman in labor. For she was grievously tormented by his cross, just as Simeon had foretold to her: “And a sword,” he says, “shall pierce your own soul also” [Col. 0789C] (Luke II).

“Therefore when Jesus saw his mother and the disciple standing by whom he loved, he said to his mother: ‘Woman, behold your son.’ Then to the disciple: ‘Behold your mother.’” By what right is the disciple whom Jesus loved the son of the Lord’s mother, or she herself his mother? Namely, because she gave birth without pain to the cause of all salvation when she bore God made man from her flesh; and now she was giving birth with great pain, when, as was foretold, she stood beside his cross.

For if in the hour of his Passion the Lord rightly compared his apostles to a woman in labor, saying: “A woman, when she gives birth, has sorrow because her hour has come; but when she has borne the child, she no longer remembers the anguish because of the joy that a human being has been born into the world. So you too will now have sorrow, but I shall see you again, and your heart shall rejoice” [Col. 0789D] (John XVI), how much more rightly did such a Son compare this woman, standing beside his cross, to a woman in labor. Yet why do I say “compare,” when she truly is a woman, truly a mother, and truly has the pains of childbirth in that hour?

For this woman did not receive the punishment of giving birth in pain as other mothers do when her child was born to her; but now she grieves, is tormented, and has sorrow, because her hour has come—the hour for which she conceived by the Holy Spirit, for which she became pregnant, for which her days were fulfilled that she might give birth, and for which God was altogether made man from her womb. But when this hour has passed, when this entire sword has pierced through her laboring soul, “she shall no longer remember the anguish because of the joy that a human being shall have been born into the world”: because the new human being shall have been manifested, he who renews the entire human race and obtains the everlasting dominion of the whole world; “born,” I say, that is, made immortal and impassible, having surpassed the straits of this life in the expanse of the eternal homeland, the firstborn from the dead [Col. 0790A].

Accordingly, because the blessed Virgin truly gave birth to the salvation of us all, with pains as of a woman in labor (Ps. XLVII), in the Passion of the Only-Begotten [Col. 0790B], she is plainly the mother of us all. Therefore what was said to this disciple—that he should most justly have care for his mother—“Woman, behold your son,” and likewise to the same disciple, “Behold your mother,” could rightly have been said of any other disciple had he been present. Yet although, as has been said, she is the mother of all, it was more fitting that a virgin should be entrusted to this virgin, especially because such grace was reserved for this disciple: that he should describe in evangelical writing the very Word whom that mother had borne made flesh, insofar as was possible for a mortal human being—indeed, more than any other mortal could.

“And from that hour the disciple took her into his own.” Into his own, that is, not into estates, which he neither possessed nor would possess—for he was one of those who had left everything to follow the Lord (Matt. XIX)—but “into his own” is said in the sense that, in that community of goods in which distribution was made to each according to need, whatever was necessary for her belonged to his care [Col. 0790C] (Acts II, IV).

“Afterward Jesus, knowing that all things were now accomplished, that the Scripture might be fulfilled, said: ‘I thirst.’” “Knowing,” he says, “that all things were now accomplished”—namely, those things which he had to suffer. For these things were not happening without his knowledge, but with his full knowledge and with him ordering all things—he who had also foretold all things through the prophets—“that the Scripture might be fulfilled, said: ‘I thirst.’” How was Scripture fulfilled by this saying? [Col. 0790D] Hear what follows: “There was therefore a vessel set full of vinegar. And they, putting a sponge full of vinegar around hyssop, offered it to his mouth.” Another evangelist reports that “they gave him wine also to drink, mixed with gall” (Matt. XXVII). Therefore, in order that Scripture might be fulfilled, he said, “I thirst”; and when it was ministered to him in that manner, Scripture was fulfilled not only spiritually but also literally, which says: “They gave me gall for my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Ps. LXVIII). Again: “Their grapes are grapes of gall, and their cluster most bitter; their wine is the gall of dragons” (Deut. XXXII).

It is remarkable that the agents of the Lord’s death—or rather he by whose counsel of divinity all these things had been arranged—performed everything so methodically and completely, as though they had sworn among themselves to fulfil in him every utterance of the prophets. How they could apply a sponge to the mouth of one raised from the ground upon the cross, another evangelist states more plainly: namely, “that they put the sponge upon a reed” (Matt. XXVII). By doing this they sufficiently revealed how greatly their hearts overflowed with the gall of bitterness; and that that house of Israel and house of Judah was truly no longer the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts, his delightful planting, but that their vineyard was of the vineyards of Sodom, and how truly the same Lord had foretold through the prophet that, when he waited for it to produce grapes, it produced wild grapes (Isa. V).

Moreover, by tasting the vinegar mixed with gall offered to him, yet refusing to drink it, he signifies the rejection of that same Sodomite vineyard of his, which mixed for him the bitterness of death when it ought to have brought the sweetness of love. Having tasted it a little—that is, for three days—he no longer wishes to drink from the produce of such a vine [Col. 0791B]: “For, having risen from the dead, he dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. VI).

“Therefore, when he had received the vinegar, he said: ‘It is accomplished.’ And, bowing his head, he gave up the spirit.” What did he say had been accomplished, unless everything that had been proposed or arranged according to the Scriptures for him to suffer? Therefore, he says, it is accomplished: the contest of obedience has been completed; the course has reached its goal; now at last the crown of glory and honour remains. He said this, and then at last, “bowing his head, [Col. 0791C] gave up the spirit.” He gave up, or handed over, the spirit, I say, by the power he possessed of laying down his life; because he suffered only as much as he willed, accepting death at the hour he willed, he gave up the spirit.

“Therefore the Jews, because it was the Preparation, so that the bodies might not remain upon the cross on the Sabbath—for that Sabbath day was a great one—asked Pilate that their legs might be broken and that they might be removed.” The Jews: religious in their lips, but bloody in heart and far from God, they displayed a legal concern for the great day of the paschal Sabbath. Magnificent worshippers of God: although they had stored away the blood of the Just One in an evil conscience, they held firmly in mouth and lips to the commandment of the Law. For what does the Law say? “When,” it says, “a man has sinned in something punishable by death, and, having been condemned to death, has been hanged [Col. 0791D] upon a gibbet, his corpse shall not remain upon the wood, but you shall bury him on that same day, because he who hangs upon a tree is accursed by God; and you shall by no means defile your land, which the Lord your God is about to give you for a possession” (Deut. XXI).

This, indeed, is what the Law says; and these friends of the Law—or rather corruptors of the Law and enemies of God—knowing that the Law had said this, cunningly hung the Lord upon a gibbet, so that it might consequently be established that he was accursed by God and therefore certain that this man, according to their verdict or accusation, was not from God. But, O Jews, blinded by malice: he indeed was—for this too the Apostle says—“our Lord was the curse of the Law, that he might redeem us from the curse” (Gal. III). Yet, according to the words of the Law, is hanging upon a tree the antecedent cause of the curse?

Leaving aside that it does not merely say, when a man “condemned to death has been hanged upon a gibbet,” but introduces the matter thus: “when a man has sinned in something punishable by death,” and only then adds, “and, having been condemned to death, has been hanged upon a gibbet”—leaving aside, I say, that this manifestly clears our Lord of the curse, because he was indeed hung upon wood but did not sin in something punishable by death—does it say, “Accursed by God is he who hangs upon a tree”? Does it say this as an imprecation, “let him be accursed,” with the verb *let him be* understood; or absolutely, “accursed,” so that the imprecator’s word *let him be* may be understood? Or does it not rather say it declaratively: “He is accursed by God,” not because he hangs, but “he who hangs upon a tree”? [Col. 0792B]

For the text of Hebrew truth is not as the Seventy translated it, since they did not perfectly possess the sense of God. They were not prophets, but translators; and therefore, as in many other places, so here they did not translate sufficiently fully: “Accursed is everyone who hangs upon a tree,” whereas the Hebrew reads: “He who hangs upon a tree is accursed by God.” Clearly this translation differs from the truth in three ways. For whereas the Hebrew reads, “He is accursed,” they translated simply, “accursed,” so that *let him be* can be understood. Again, “by God” is added in the Hebrew but lacking in the Seventy; and conversely, “everyone” is added in the Seventy but is not found in the Hebrew.

Why then, you ask, did the Apostle use the translation of those Seventy [Col. 0792C] in this statement? He says thus: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the Law, having been made a curse for us, because it is written: ‘Accursed is everyone who hangs upon a tree’” (Gal. III). Why did he employ this example in that way? Clearly because the edition of the Seventy interpreters had been current among the Greeks to whom he was writing from the time of Ptolemy Philadelphus; and it would have been excessively inconvenient, when he maintained that the Scriptures bore witness to Christ, and would scarcely have been heard, if he had also tried to show that the Scriptures themselves had been wrongly translated, since among them the authority of the Seventy interpreters was held in highest renown. He therefore preferred to recall the meaning in a form that would edify rather than offend readers accustomed to the old text by correcting the Scripture.

Moreover, consider more carefully the purpose of this same proclamation of curse, especially because, on account of his being accursed by God, it commands that he be buried. Is burial not a share of blessing for the dead, and conversely, is deprivation of burial not a share of curse—after the manner of an ass, as it was dreadfully said of a certain king, as he deserved: “He shall be buried with the burial of an ass,” that is, with no burial at all (Jer. XXII)? Did not the holy and great fathers, or patriarchs, carefully give commands concerning the burial or even transfer of their bodies, and consider it a great matter to be buried—not merely anywhere, but in the tombs of their fathers? (Gen. XXXV, L.)

O marvellous and ancient counsel of this crucified one, who, so long before he came, gave a command concerning the burial of his body in such a way that the legal command, written for him alone, benefited all crucified persons. For while it was permitted without penalty to cast out unburied to dogs those killed by beheading, stoning, or some other violence, the prophetic Law, written as it were by the finger of God, forbade burial to be denied only to those crucified, because of the Just One who was to be crucified. Does not, then, the prophetic Spirit concerning crucifixion roar with unutterable groanings in the heart of Moses as he writes such a law (Deut. XXI): so that while all crucified persons are buried by law, this one crucified for the salvation of the world should not lack burial—he who is accursed by God, the Law even adding “by God,” which it does nowhere among all the curses of the Law? For example, when it says, “You shall be accursed in the city, accursed in the field, accursed when entering, accursed when departing” (Deut. XXIII), [Col. 0793B] and likewise in the rest, it nowhere says “by God” except in this one place.

Why is this, unless because this one alone is truly accursed by God, inasmuch as, as the prophet says, God placed upon him the iniquities of us all? (Isa. LIII.) Therefore, it says, let him who hangs upon the tree be buried, because one will hang upon the tree who will be accursed by God—by God, I say, transferring onto him the curses of the human race. But if someone objects that curses were often pronounced by God—for example, when he says to Cain, “Now therefore you are accursed from the earth, which has opened its mouth and received your brother’s blood from your hand” (Gen. IV)—we reply that this is not the outpouring of a curse, but the declaration of a curse already existing; especially since he does not say, “May you be accursed,” but “You are accursed,” and not by me, but by your sins. For Cain is not accursed by God, but by the voice of his brother’s blood crying from the earth and declaring his impiety to God himself.

Therefore this one alone was accursed by God and not by his own sin: by God, I say, who placed upon him the curse of us all which was upon us—that is, all our iniquity. But what the Law added, “And you shall by no means defile the land which the Lord your God is about to give you for a possession” (Deut. XXI), the Holy Spirit spoke and wrote with marvellous art, although the land might rather seem defiled if it received into itself the body of one accursed. What then? What does the writer of the Law intend here also? Certainly this: that the land which God gave to the true Israel for a possession is the body of this one uniquely accursed for us. Israel did not then defile that body given to it—that is, did not permit it to be defiled—when Joseph and Nicodemus buried it that same day (Matt. XXVII; Luke XXIII), in accordance with the common law for all who hang upon wood: namely, lest it should be disgracefully cast away unburied and, by those dogs who had surrounded it while alive, be spat upon while still lifeless. [Col. 0793D] They, however, thought that their land was not defiled by him if the body of anyone thus slain was not displayed before the eyes of the living.

But if anyone further asks why the legislator was so concerned about this, when the most holy body could even have been guarded from heaven while unburied—as many bodies of martyrs too were guarded from injury by dogs or birds—let us ask him why, when the same Lord was dying and the earth was shaking, the tombs of the saints were opened (Matt. XXVII). Certainly either no adequate answer, or only this answer, will be given: that this was expedient for the bodies of the dead, namely, that in the tombs the body of this dead one, which brought the resurrection of the dead, should be joined to them; and for that reason they opened themselves eagerly and avidly to receive it. For just as it was fitting that the soul of the Lord Jesus should descend to the souls in the underworld in order to lead them out from there, so also it was necessary that his body should come to bodies in order to raise them. But enough has now been said on this subject; let us return to the words of the Gospel.

“The Jews,” he says, “asked Pilate that, their legs having been broken, the bodies might be taken away.” Why? “Because it was the Preparation,” because that Sabbath day was great. “That Sabbath day was great,” he says, namely because it was the paschal Sabbath. For since Passover was celebrated for eight days, the Sabbath day was held the greatest and most festive of all days, whether it fell on the first, second, third, or fourth day; and it would be called the paschal Sabbath. Therefore the Jews asked that the bodies be removed, lest so great a day be defiled by the horror of such a spectacle. Indeed, even on any ordinary day the Law commanded that bodies of this kind be buried on the same day. But because of the Sabbath, the Jews wished them to be buried more hurriedly.

“Therefore the soldiers came, and broke the legs of the first, and of the other who was crucified with him.” [Col. 0794C] “The first,” he says—that is, the outer one—and likewise the other outer one, for the Lord Jesus was crucified in the middle: they broke their legs because they had not yet died, so that, when taken down, they might not live, but might expire sooner. “But when they came to Jesus, and saw that he was already dead, they did not break his legs.” Rightly so; for there was no need to add anything to the pain of his wounds (Ps. LXVIII), since no sensation remained in him.

“But one of the soldiers opened his side with a spear, and immediately blood and water came out.” Thanks be to God. By blood we are redeemed; by water we are washed. Our God, pierced by the spear in the midst of the earth, accomplished so great a salvation through which he willed to save us. But the greatness and dignity of this matter demand a very attentive and rightly believing hearer. [Col. 0794D] It follows, therefore: “And he who saw it has borne witness, and his witness is true; and he knows that he speaks truth, that you may believe.” Behold, here is one witness who saw and wrote these things, although there is no doubt that many were present who saw and wished to see. But lest I seem to be a witness alone, he says, I will bring with me two other witnesses: the legal utterance as one witness, and the prophetic utterance as another. “For these things were done that the Scripture might be fulfilled: ‘You shall not break a bone of it’” (Exod. XII). The Law commands this concerning the paschal lamb. Therefore, by a brief but clear judgment he teaches that the legal lamb of Passover was a figure of this true Lamb, who has now at last been sacrificed for us, as the long-exercised faith of the holy Church has long held with certainty.

“And again another Scripture says: ‘They shall look upon him whom they pierced.’” This is the testimony of the prophet Zechariah (ch. XII). Therefore, in the mouth of three witnesses—the Law, the Prophets, and this evangelist—the following word shall stand: “The soldiers, as has now been said, did not break the legs of the Lord Jesus, but one of the soldiers opened his side with a spear, and immediately blood and water came out.” Let us now at last contemplate this great matter more fully. For the mystery of so great a thing must not be passed over, when the holy evangelist has so carefully inserted his testimony and added suitable examples from the Scriptures.

Why, then, did the Lamb who was sacrificed not wish a bone of him to be broken? For this occurred not by chance, but by his own will and ordering; namely, he did not wish his legs to be broken because nowhere does the breaking of bones commend anything good by its resemblance. For bones, which everywhere in the Scriptures are mystically understood as virtues, would communicate no mystery to us in their being broken. But conversely, in the preservation of his legs intact they signify for us that all his ways are rightly inviolable. For his legs signify his ways. Hence it is said in the Song of Songs: “His legs are pillars of marble, founded upon bases of gold” (Cant. V): that is, his beautiful paths are established in uprightness upon the wisdom of divinity.

What, then, did he will to be done by avoiding the breaking of his legs? “But one of the soldiers,” says the evangelist, “opened his side with a spear, and immediately blood [Col. 0795C] and water came out.” Why, then, did he prefer this to be done? Clearly that he might pour out upon us with his blood that water of which, when commending it, he had said: “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot see the kingdom of God” (John III). For the sacrament of this water took its beginning from this miracle. Therefore the Lord, baptized in his passion, when already dead sent forth to us such a participation in his saving death.

It is neither new nor strange that we say he was baptized in his passion. When the mother of the sons of Zebedee asked and said, “Master, say that these two sons of mine may sit, one at your right hand and the other at your left in your kingdom,” he answered: “Can you drink the cup that I am to drink, or be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized?” When they answered, “We can,” he said: “You shall drink my cup, and you shall be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized” (Mark X), and so forth. By the name of cup or baptism he intended to signify the passion of martyrdom, by which both he and they were to be brought to completion. Hence elsewhere too he speaks of his passion: “But I have a baptism with which to be baptized, and how I am constrained until it is accomplished” (Luke XII).

In Greek, moreover, *baptism* is called *ablution* in Latin. What defilements, then, did the Lord possess that he should be washed by the baptism of passion? Certainly our mortality and passibility, because of which he appeared foul and contemptible to human beings, as we also read in Zechariah: “Jesus was clothed in filthy garments. And the Angel said to those standing [Col. 0796A] before him: ‘Remove from him the filthy garments’” (Zech. III). Jesus was clothed in filthy garments: he who, though he had committed no sin, was made sin for us (II Cor. V). And he himself bears our infirmities (Isa. LIII). And we read in the Apostle: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the Law, having been made a curse for us” (Gal. III). In the twenty-first Psalm he says: “The words of my offences are far from my salvation.” And in the sixty-eighth Psalm: “O God, you know my foolishness, and my offences are not hidden from you.” All these things, he says, are called filthy garments, and are removed from him when in his death he blots out our sins.

Therefore, when we see the Lord Jesus, because of the suffering of death, crowned with glory and honour and washed from the sins which he himself had borne [Col. 0796B] for us (Heb. II), we rightly understand him to have been baptized with his own baptism in his death; and, so that he might transmit that same baptism to us, when already dead he poured blood and water from his side. It has already been stated elsewhere that the baptism with which John baptized him did not belong to the same efficacy.

For this reason neither blood alone nor water alone flowed from the Saviour’s side, because the divine order of our salvation required both. For we were not redeemed in order that he might possess us as we were before. Hence the Apostle also says: “For God did not call us to uncleanness, but to sanctification in Christ Jesus” (I Thess. IV). And elsewhere, after recalling former sins: “And such were you,” he says, “but you were washed, but you were sanctified” (I Cor. VI), and so forth. Therefore, so that there might be that by which we might be washed from sins, water, which could wash only bodily stains, was joined to blood, which is the price of our redemption; and through that association it received power and authority, so as to be worthy to cooperate with the Holy Spirit in washing away the invisible stains of sins. Through its association, I say, with the life-giving and precious blood, it received this: that it might be truly compared to the Red Sea through which the people passed and were saved, Pharaoh being drowned with his chariots and horsemen (Exod. XIV). For it carries those fleeing the Egypt of this world, once cleansed, across into the true land of promise, and utterly swallows up the pursuing devil with his former deeds and pomps.

Therefore, as was said above, it was far more fitting that the soldier’s spear should open his side than that his legs should be broken; more fitting, I say, and more worthy of so great an artificer of salvation. It also added greatly to the beauty of the work that, when dead, he should draw forth from his side that from which the Church would be born: he who drew out a rib from the sleeping Adam, from which Eve might be formed (Gen. II). What could be more beautiful, more elegant, or sweeter than this resemblance? For that first Adam fell asleep; this second, as has been said, died in order to rise again. The Lord put sleep upon the former; the Father gave the cup of passion to the latter.

“Go forth and behold, daughters of Zion, King Solomon in the diadem with which his mother crowned him, on the day of his espousal and on the day of the joy of his heart” [Col. 0797A] (Cant. III). Go forth, I say, from those darknesses which came over the earth from the sixth hour to the ninth (Matt. XXVII). Indeed, go forth from those realities signified by them, which now cover the face of the hearts of the Jews. Go forth, then, from these darknesses and behold in intent contemplation him who called you into his marvellous light (I Pet. II): the great King, the peaceable King, in the thorny diadem, which is the ornament of love and of great compassion, with which his mother, the Synagogue, crowned him on this day of his espousal. On that day, as was said, he brought forth, in the joy of his heart, the first elements of the Church, his bride, who was to be born for him. It follows:

“After these things Joseph of Arimathea, because he was a disciple of Jesus—though a secret one, for fear of the Jews—asked Pilate [Col. 0797B] that he might take away the body of Jesus. And Pilate permitted it. Therefore he came and took the body of Jesus.” This man was a secret disciple of Jesus, yet he did not secretly ask Pilate, nor did he secretly take Jesus’ body for burial. Nor was this contrary to the Law; for, as stated above, this was its command (Deut. XXI): that one hanged upon a gibbet should be buried on the same day. The very Word of God, speaking through Moses, had already provided freedom of burial for his own body.

Therefore, when this blessed disciple took up his master’s body, he rightly did not fear Jewish calumny; for anyone who slandered his good service in such a cause would himself act against the Law. Nor was there any ground for suspicion concerning his discipleship, since he seemed to be obeying not love for the Lord Jesus but a commandment of the Law. “And Nicodemus also came, bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about a hundred pounds. Therefore they took Jesus and bound him in linen cloths with the spices, as is the Jewish custom of burial.” Lest we should wonder that they dared to prepare the Lord’s body with spices when they had not dared, except secretly, to be disciples of him while living, the evangelist added: “as is the Jewish custom of burial.”

“There was in the place where he was crucified a garden, and in the garden a new tomb in which no one had yet been laid.” And this too had been provided by him who was buried: just as, when about to be born, he prepared for himself [Col. 0798B] a virgin womb to which no man had come, so, when about to rise again, he was to be placed in a new tomb of stone in which no one had yet been laid. Therefore, because of the Jews’ Preparation, they laid him there. Now then, Jews, you who killed the Just One contrary to your works have been set free. Go now, eat the Passover and celebrate the great Sabbath, so that henceforth the Lord may cast upon your faces the dung of your solemn feasts (Mal. II).

## Book Fourteen

[Col. 0797]

[Col. 0797C] “Judah, from this time your brothers shall praise you” (Gen. XLIX). Judah, I say, great and strong: you who, rising from the dead, have put on the confession and beauty of immortality and incorruption (Ps. CIII). Your brothers and friends, co-heirs and fellow-partakers of your kingdom, shall praise you. How shall they praise you, or what shall they cry in praise? “Your hand,” they say, “is upon the necks of your enemies” (Gen. XLIX). O mightiest of brothers and prince of their confession, the horns are in your hands; and behold, the strength that was hidden there now comes forth. How could the muddy necks of your enemies endure without being made the footstool of your feet? Therefore your enemies shall howl beneath your feet, “but your brothers shall praise you.” It is too little that they shall praise you: “The sons of your father shall worship you” [Col. 0797D].

The reason for this worship shall be “because you are a lion’s whelp”: O Judah, lion’s whelp, that is, Son of the most mighty God, prince of all strength and all virtues, from whom you in no respect degenerate. For you have ascended to the prey, my son, and, fearing no encounter, have valiantly conquered hell. Therefore your brothers, the sons of your father, shall praise and worship you; and those who praise and worship you are equally your brothers and sons of your father, having through the very faith in which they worship you received the grace of adoption as sons.

Now, most beautiful of men, after your labours have been completed, “because you have washed your robe in wine and your cloak in the blood of grapes” (ibid.), that is, you have regenerated your Church in your blood through the Holy Spirit, we shall endeavour, as our pen proceeds and with your grace assisting, to declare how you brought to those same brothers the good news of your strength and victory.

[Chapter XX.] “On the first day of the Sabbath Mary Magdalene came early, while it was still dark, to the tomb, and saw that the stone had been taken away from the tomb.” “One of the Sabbath,” that is, the first day of the Sabbath: namely, the day which follows immediately after the Sabbath. It should be known, moreover, that this woman and the other women devoted to the Lord, who had loved him while living and longed for him when dead, came to the tomb by walking through the night, aided by the moon. For they walked through the night, since they were at the tomb at dawn. Otherwise, unless they had come during the night, how could they have reached the tomb so early? For example, Mary Magdalene, whose house was at Bethany—a village fifteen stadia from Jerusalem—how could she, before the others, come on the first day of the Sabbath, according to John, very early, “while it was still dark,” to the tomb?

For after the Lord was buried, the women who had followed him did not remain in Jerusalem. But after they had seen where he was laid, Luke says, “returning, [Col. 0799A] they prepared spices” (Luke XXIII). But when they prepared or bought them, Mark indicates more plainly: “And when,” he says, “the Sabbath had passed, Mary Magdalene, and Mary of James, and Salome bought spices, that they might come and anoint Jesus” (Mark XVI). For on the Sabbath, as Luke says, they rested because of the commandment—namely, the Law’s commandment—because the Law forbids work (Exod. XX).

It is therefore clear that, wearied by tearful vigils of love and by the exceedingly long delay of the restraining Sabbath, during which Jews were permitted neither to work nor to walk more than a thousand paces, as soon as that burdensome Sabbath had gone, departed, passed, they did not rest, did not give sleep to their eyes, and did not wait for the morning star to set out. They took night for day, desire for guide, and the moon [Col. 0799B] for sun. The moon did not fail the night, for it was in its seventeenth day.
