On the seventeenth day of the lunar month, shortly after evening has closed—that is, about an hour and a half later—it rises, thereafter to provide its light for the whole night.

Therefore some have falsely accused the evangelists of saying contradictory things because Matthew said that the women came to the tomb on the evening of the Sabbath, while the others said that they came at dawn on the first day of the Sabbath. For Matthew, in order to commend their longing, states when they began coming; the others state when they arrived.

Why, moreover, could this evangelist have said “the first day of the Sabbath,” yet preferred to say “one of the Sabbath,” unless because of the singular and unique glory of that day? It is truly a festal day, truly a blessed day: the nobility of the year, the glory of the month, the armour of days. Through the beauty of this day paradise flowered again, heaven was clothed in purple, angels were made white, and human beings were gladdened. The singular grace of this day cannot be expressed in words. Therefore he rightly and properly said, “one of the Sabbath”: “She came,” he says, “to the tomb.”

The evangelist himself makes clear how early she came, saying: “while it was still dark.” But the Lord had already risen. “For,” he says, “she saw that the stone had been taken away from the tomb.” What then is meant by the Father’s saying in the Psalm: “Arise, my glory; arise, psaltery and harp” (Ps. LVI, CVII)? Immediately that glorious instrument of the Father, namely the mouth of the Lordly Man, replied: “I will arise at dawn.” For he did not wait for dawn in order to rise. Indeed, the women came very early, and were then forestalled by the love of the resurrection.

What, then, does he mean when he says, “I will arise at dawn,” except that this dawn does not belong to our bodily eyes? For if all this time from the Lord’s resurrection is one day of salvation, as the prophet says, “At an acceptable time I heard you, and in a day of salvation I helped you” (Isa. XLIX; II Cor. VI), why should not the beginning of that period also be understood by the name of dawn? Therefore there was bodily darkness at the tomb, but for all the holy and elect there was dawn—that is, the beginning of eternal light—already from midnight, when he rose and, like the mighty Samson, carried away the gates of hell; Samson’s name means “their sun” (Judg. XVI).

This is plainly what Mark the evangelist intended, for after saying, “And very early on one of the Sabbaths they come to the tomb,” he immediately adds what is literally contradictory: “when the sun had already risen” (Mark XVI). For when the sun has already risen, it is not very early. Therefore, even if our Lord rose at midnight, it is nevertheless true that, answering the Father, he says, as stated above, “I will rise at dawn.”

“Therefore, coming, she found the stone removed from the tomb,” namely the stone which the angel of the Lord had rolled away in order to show the women who came that it was empty. Accordingly, when Matthew says: “But in the evening of the Sabbath, which was dawning into the first day of the Sabbath, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came to see the tomb. And behold, a great earthquake occurred; for an angel of the Lord descended from heaven, and came and rolled away the stone, and sat upon it” (Matt. XXVIII), it should be understood thus: while they were coming—that is, while they were on the way, having begun to come in the evening, as stated—the Lord rose amid the earthquake; then the angel of the Lord rolled away the stone; and thereafter, when the women had already seen the tomb empty, he sat upon the stone, so that so great a matter might be imparted gradually, not suddenly, to the fearful minds of human beings: first the tomb, then the angel, then the Lord seen.

“Therefore she ran to Simon Peter and to the other disciple whom Jesus loved, and said to them: ‘They have taken the Lord from the tomb, and we do not know where they have laid him.’” Therefore dawn had already come for holy souls in the other world, and also for that thief to whom it was said, “Today you shall be with me in paradise” (Luke XXIII); and, as Mark says, the sun had already risen. Yet for those coming to the tomb, darkness existed not only through the time of night but also through the condition of their minds. For what are forgetfulness and ignorance of truth except blindness or darkness of mind? They were so forgetful and unmindful of the words he had spoken—that the Son of Man had to be crucified and rise from the dead on the third day—that, when they did not find his body, they thought that nothing remained but that it had been taken away. Yet what follows?

“Therefore Peter and that other disciple went out, and came to the tomb. And they ran together.” [Col. 0800D] The other disciple is John himself. What spectacle could be more beautiful than such a race, if one rightly considers the evangelist’s meaning or intention in narrating it? For should we suppose that one who attends so excellently to heavenly matters could have had leisure to write such things carefully without hope of fruit—that is, of spiritual understanding? Therefore, having been admitted to the spectacle, let us now, with eyes lifted up, behold the broad field of this world, and in it two peoples running: the Jews and the Gentiles. Let the prize be the very palm of the cross which Christ ascended; and let Christ himself be the director of the contest, who, as judge, will adorn the victor’s right hand with the palm.

Certainly, when it was heard—and this sound went out into all the earth (Ps. XVIII)—that Christ had risen from the dead, the people of the Gentiles went out [Col. 0801A] and came to the tomb: they went out, I say, from the darkness and gloom of sins, and came to worship the dead and buried Son of God and Man, Jesus Christ, conqueror of death. The other one also went out, namely the Jewish people; but it went out from nearby, because it had already run before, had already drawn near, since it awaited—and indeed had prophesied—the one who would die and rise again. “Therefore they ran together.”

“And that other disciple ran more swiftly than Peter, and came first to the tomb. And when he had bent down, he saw the linen cloths lying, yet he did not enter.” With respect to the same faith—for the faith of the ancients was indeed the same as that of the moderns—we Gentiles ran together with that earlier people. Yet with respect to the distinction of times, we would not run together, were it not that at the beginning of the Gospel a multitude both of Jews and of Gentiles received faith in Christ. Therefore that people came first to the tomb, but, seeing the linen cloths, did not enter; because it was so ashamed of the sufferings of the Lord’s passion, by which he was as it were wrapped and bound in linen cloths, that many even of those from that people who had already believed recoiled. Thus Christ crucified became for them a stumbling-stone and rock of offence, partly because of the carnal ceremonies of the Law, which they saw being abandoned, and partly because of their hatred for the Gentiles, to whom they begrudged the grace of God (I Pet. II).

“Then Simon Peter came, following him, and entered the tomb; and he saw the linen cloths lying there, and the napkin which had been upon His head, not lying with the linen cloths, but folded separately in one place” [Col. 0801C].

A faithful saying. He who came first and did not enter saw only the linen cloths; but he who came later and entered saw not only the linen cloths, but also the napkin which had been upon the Lord’s head. What does this mean, except that we Gentiles, who entered by faith while the Jews remained outside, attend not only to that which the Son of God endured for human beings—that, born of a woman, He toiled in the flesh and was crucified through our weakness—but also to that which He is and was as God before He became, or assumed from what is ours, that in which He might suffer? For the napkin which had been upon His head fittingly signifies that “Word which was in the beginning, which was with God, which was God” (John 1) [Col. 0801D]. Both of these things the later-coming people of the Gentiles sees and worships when it enters: it worships, I say, and confesses that Christ is Lord and the Word of the Father, through whom the world was made, and also flesh, or Son of Man, through whose passion the world was saved.

But he who refuses to enter saw only the linen cloths, because he considers only the affliction by which Christ’s true humanity could be bound or constrained; and this he holds as the shield of his heart, so that, beginning to err, he says that He could not be God who was able to die. Therefore he did not see the napkin. But what follows means: “not lying with the linen cloths, but folded separately in one place”? This is plainly what the Catholic faith confesses: namely, that the one and same Christ was passible as man, but impassible, as He always is, as God [Col. 0802A]. The napkin was not placed with the linen cloths because God, in Himself, did not groan under the sufferings which He bore according to His humanity. He stood separately and apart from every anguish, not through a division of substance or a duality of person, but through the differing condition and great diversity of the two natures.

Moreover, the napkin was folded, plainly signifying that Christ’s divinity has neither beginning nor end; for just as neither beginning nor end can be seen in a thing that is folded, so He neither began nor ceases to be God. But what is meant by “in one place,” except that God is not in a division of minds? “One is my dove” (Song of Songs 6); one is Christ’s body in the Church. And in this sole and single place there is the sacrament of truth, which cannot be torn or divided [Col. 0802B]. Thus that people saw only what is weak in God; being thus offended, it halted with faltering foot and remained outside. But because it follows:

“Then the other disciple, who had come first to the tomb, entered also; and he saw and believed.”

Thus, indeed, after the fullness of the Gentiles, that people too will enter. “For I would not have you ignorant, brethren,” says the Apostle, “of this mystery, lest you be wise in your own conceits: that blindness in part has happened to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter; and so all Israel shall be saved” (Romans 11). The darkness, therefore, was still at the tomb; and the disciples’ minds, still sleeping from grief, did not know what was being done. But day was breathing forth, and the shadows or figures were near to being bent away and driven out by the rays of things that were to follow [Col. 0802C]. “And he saw,” he says, “and believed.”

It will indeed come to pass that that later people, entering, will see and believe; but not yet did this disciple “see and believe” in that sense. For it follows: “For as yet they did not know the Scriptures, that He must rise again from the dead.” Therefore he rather believed—that is, he supposed true—what the woman had said: namely, that they had taken the Lord from the tomb, and that “we do not know where they have laid Him.” Yet the Evangelist preferred to say that “he believed,” remaining closer to the term suited to the matter for which he had so carefully recounted this course of running. And immediately he adds:

“Then the disciples went away again unto their own home” [Col. 0802D].

Therefore, he says, because “they did not yet know the Scriptures, they went away unto themselves.” On the contrary, when they understood the Scriptures, they went beyond themselves, speaking Christ’s mind rather than their own and proving that the Lord had not been taken from the tomb, but that the Lord had risen from the sepulchre, the pains of hell having been loosed; as it was impossible for Him to be held by it. David bears witness, saying concerning Him: “I foresaw the Lord always before my face, because He is at my right hand, that I should not be moved. Therefore my heart was glad, and my tongue rejoiced; moreover also my flesh shall rest in hope. For Thou wilt not leave my soul in hell, neither wilt Thou suffer Thy Holy One to see corruption” (Psalm 15), and similar passages.

“But Mary stood outside at the tomb, weeping” [Col. 0803A].

In his customary manner, the holy Evangelist attends here also to heavenly mysteries; and, while he appears to walk upon the earth with his feet—that is, to weave a simple history—he flies aloft. For he proclaims the morning revelation of the resurrection in such a way that, through his account, the intention of Him who rose may readily shine upon readers. When the disciples had gone away unto themselves, he reports that Mary alone stood outside the tomb weeping; and that, amid her tears, she stooped down and saw two angels, one at the head and one at the feet; then, turning back, she saw the Lord and heard from Him these words: “Touch me not, for I am not yet ascended to my Father. But go to my brethren, and say unto them: I ascend unto my Father [Col. 0803B] and your Father, and to my God and your God.”

Beautifully, indeed, before all other women, this woman was held by the hand of the risen One, bound to His sepulchre by pious longing, so that she might become the messenger of the second resurrection, in which the most famous and celebrated work of the first resurrection was accomplished. For the first resurrection, of which John himself says here, “Blessed is he that hath part in the first resurrection,” is that which the Lord announced to the Jews: “Amen, amen, I say unto you, the hour is coming, and now is, when the dead that are in the tombs shall hear the voice of the Son of God; and they that hear shall live.”

This woman was the first of all, or the best known, to draw breath again by this resurrection. For, when she was a sinner in the city, more foul with the stench of evil repute than her brother Lazarus had been in body after four days, she heard, in the tomb of evil habit, the voice of the Son of God; and because she heard, she immediately came forth (Luke 7) [Col. 0803C]. For by repenting she washed away with tears the stains of her crime, and “many sins were forgiven her, because she loved much” (John 11). The second resurrection is that of bodies, in which Christ, the Son of God, is the firstborn from the dead; and His life was now to be announced to the mourning and weeping disciples.

Mary therefore stood, detained by the will of the Prince of Life and of both resurrections, fittingly about to announce the second resurrection, since the announcement of the first resurrection had rendered her worthy. She stood, I say, and in standing outside and weeping [Col. 0803D], she represented the type of the whole Church drawn from the Gentiles. For the primitive Church—from righteous Abel to the thief who confessed upon the cross—had already been received within the sacrament of the Lord’s passion; but sinful Gentile humanity had remained outside, because Christ’s blood had not washed from sins one that had not possessed faith in Him.

For example, that eunuch who had come to worship at Jerusalem and was returning while reading the prophet Isaiah stood outside at the tomb. For the passage of Scripture which he read was this: “He shall be led as a sheep to the slaughter; and as a lamb before its shearer shall be dumb, so He shall not open His mouth” (Acts 8; Isaiah 53), etc. He certainly stood outside the tomb weeping, because in reading he grieved over the passion of Him whom he did not know. Likewise Cornelius the centurion, praying to God and continually giving alms, stood outside at the tomb (Acts 10) [Col. 0804A]. The whole Gentile world stood outside; and, if it was not yet weeping, it was to weep by confessing its sins, and, through faith in Him who died and rose again, it was to rise in the first resurrection after the example of Mary, abandoning the multitude of many gods—indeed, of demons—just as the Lord had cast seven demons, that is, every vice, out of this woman.

“Therefore, as she wept, she stooped down and looked into the tomb; and she saw two angels in white sitting, one at the head and one at the feet, where the body of Jesus had lain.”

Since John and Luke (chapter 24) report that two angels were seen, how do Matthew and Mark differ from them in recording that only one was seen? Plainly because, though there were two, one spoke. He was seated at the right according to Mark (chapter 16), upon the stone according to Matthew (chapter 23 [probably 28]), and at the head according to John (chapter 20); and no one ought to be troubled by these differing positions [Col. 0804B]. For, as those acquainted with those places testify, the Lord’s tomb is situated on the northern side of the crypt, hewn from the rock, seven feet long, rising three palms’ measure above the floor, with its entrance on the southern side. This being so, he who sits at the right sits at the head, because he sat outside upon the rolled-away stone.

“They say unto her: Woman, why weepest thou? Whom seekest thou? [Col. 0804C] She saith unto them: Because they have taken away my Lord, and I know not where they have laid Him.”

This woman, stooping while weeping, saw angels and deserved to hear their inquiry, because the Gentile world was destined, by mourning over its sins and humbling itself, to become known to the holy apostles or preachers—who are indeed angels of the Lord of hosts—and to receive from them the sweetness of eternal consolation. And rightly all the angels of the Lord of hosts, all priests or preachers of the truth, whose lips preserve knowledge and from whose mouth the Law is sought (Malachi 3), are signified by the two angels sitting in this manner, one at the head and one at the feet. For they preach that the one and same Christ was God before the ages [Col. 0804D] and was made man at the end of the ages; and by the voices of both Testaments they demonstrate that He was incarnate, suffered, died, was buried, and rose from the dead as the true Son of God.

Hence also the two cherubim covering the mercy-seat look toward one another, their faces turned toward the mercy-seat (Exodus 32 [probably 25]). *Cherubim* is said to mean “fullness of knowledge.” And what do the two cherubim signify except the two Testaments? What does the mercy-seat signify except Him who is the propitiation for our sins (1 John 2)? When the Old Testament foretells that which the New Testament proclaims as accomplished concerning the Lord, the two cherubim, as it were, look toward one another as they turn their faces toward the mercy-seat. For those accounts do not diverge from one another, since they harmoniously recount the mystery of His dispensation [Col. 0805A].

But in answering the question why she wept and whom she sought, the woman said: “Because they have taken my Lord from the tomb.” Even today it may rightly be said to this great woman, the Church, and not vainly: namely, that the Jews, so far as lies in them, took the Lord from the tomb, when they lied—having given money to the guards—that He had not risen but had been stolen away, and hired false witnesses (Matthew 28). Yet their lies did no injury to the truth. Hence they are severely mocked by the Prophet, who says: “Their wounds have become as the arrows of little children, and their tongues have been weakened against them” (Psalm 63). For those guards hired with money to lie say: “His disciples stole Him away while we were asleep.”

We reply: O childish archers! If you were asleep, how did you know that His disciples stole Him? But if you were awake, why did you not guard Him? Furthermore, because she did not merely say, “They have taken the Lord,” signifying the part from the whole, although she sought only the body—she did not simply say “the Lord” or “our Lord,” but “my Lord”—this was rightly said by that sinful woman, and likewise is rightly said by the sinful Church from the Gentiles. For Christ is the Lord of sinners: the particular Lord, I say, of repentant sinners. “For I came not,” He says, “to call the righteous, but sinners” (Luke 5) [Col. 0805B].

“Having said these things, she turned back and saw Jesus standing, and did not know that it was Jesus. He saith unto her: Woman, why weepest thou? Whom seekest thou?” [Col. 0805C]

It is remarkable that the woman, occupied by the angelic vision, had leisure to turn back, unless there is mystery in this also: she did not turn back so as to return whence and by what route she had come, but so as to see Jesus standing and gradually recognize Him. Thus, finally, the Gentile world, after recognizing the Saviour, turned back—that is, it confessed its past iniquities—and, looking upon them in repentance, turned its face toward Him to whom it had turned its back.

But because it is insufficient for those seeking the worship or knowledge of the one true God to abandon the filth of idolatry unless they hold the summit of faith, that is, certainty concerning the resurrection—and because whoever doubts the resurrection of the dead does not yet rightly know Jesus—Mary, who did not believe that the Lord had risen, fittingly both saw and did not recognize Him: love showed Him to her, while doubt concealed Him. For it follows:

“She, supposing Him to be the gardener, saith unto Him: Sir, if thou hast taken Him away, tell me where thou hast laid Him, and I will take Him away” [Col. 0805D].

Indeed, because she did not believe that He had risen, she rightly thought that she saw the gardener, rather than the Creator Himself of the heavenly garden or paradise. Yet why should it be surprising that the Lord wished her to entertain the belief that He was a gardener? For the Church of the former people was His garden, of which He says in the Song of Songs: “A garden enclosed is my sister, my bride; a garden enclosed, a fountain sealed” (Song of Songs 4). In that garden the Church of the Gentiles found her Saviour [Col. 0806A], and thus knew Him through the Scriptures of the Law and the Prophets which sprang up there, just as Mary recognized Him, now found in this garden, through familiar speech.

For it follows: “Jesus saith unto her: Mary. She, turning, saith: Rabboni, which means Master.” The address in which He says “Mary,” and the response which says “Rabboni”—which, as the Evangelist explains, means “Master”—most beautifully prefigured that the Gentile world, approaching its calling through the Scriptures, would invoke the Lord Christ as the Master of its faith. Therefore that garden in which our Lord was crucified, died, was buried, and rose again rightly signifies the primitive Church, in which it is plainly found from the Scriptures that “Christ had to suffer, die, be buried, and rise from the dead” (Luke 22 [probably 24]) [Col. 0806B].

The proselyte Church of the Gentiles, which had formerly been sinful, entered; and, not yet recognizing the Lord, it heard its own name from His mouth, immediately recognized Him, and confessed Him as Master, because in reading the Scriptures it found its own name written there. For example, when the Spirit of Christ says concerning Him through the mouth of the patriarch Jacob: “The sceptre shall not be taken from Judah, nor a ruler from his thigh, until He comes who is to be sent; and He shall be the expectation of the Gentiles” (Genesis 59 [probably 49]). Likewise in David: “The Lord said unto me: Thou art my Son; this day have I begotten thee. Ask of me, and I will give thee the Gentiles for thine inheritance” (Psalm 2), and similar passages. And she said, “Rabboni,” because she understands herself to be a disciple and the mysteries of the Scriptures to be owed to her. But this calling of the Gentiles was not to occur before He Himself rose from the dead; whence it follows [Col. 0806C]:

“Touch me not, for I am not yet ascended to my Father.”

Three considerations oppose the thought that this was said on account of His own person. First, He had already passed from this world unto the Father, since by rising He had transcended all our mortality. Secondly, mortals would be far less able to touch Him when seated at the Father’s right hand. Thirdly, before He ascended into heaven—indeed, on the very day on which He rose—the women touched Him, for they held His feet and worshipped Him. Therefore “Touch me not” was said on account of the Church of the Gentiles, whose person she represented. For before He was glorified, He was not to be joined to the Church from among the Gentiles [Col. 0806D].

Hence He said to another woman, representing that same Gentile world, before He suffered: “It is not good to take the children’s bread and cast it to the dogs to eat” (Matthew 15). And He commanded His disciples: “Go not into the way of the Gentiles, and enter not into the cities of the Samaritans” (Matthew 10). And when His passion was imminent, when Gentiles sought to see Him, He said: “The hour has come that the Son of Man should be glorified” (John 12). This is certainly the same as saying: The hour has come for the Son of Man to ascend to His Father—so that you may understand: and then you will see Me; then you will touch Me with the touch of faith.

Mary therefore now bears the figure of such a Church as the Gentile world was before the Lord’s passion, already prepared to receive His faith [Col. 0807A]. Accordingly it is rightly said to her: “Touch me not, for I am not yet ascended to my Father.” But how, O Christ the Son of God, after You have ascended to the Father, will this sinful woman be able to touch You? He says:

“But go to my brethren, and say unto them: I ascend unto my Father and your Father, and to my God and your God.”

As if He said: After I ascend to my Father, O Gentile world, you will not be able to touch or see Me bodily; but “go to my brethren,” namely, the apostles, and confess this faith in their hearing: that I suffered and died for the salvation of humankind, rose again, and ascended into heaven; and they will impart to you concerning Me whatever is expedient [Col. 0807B]. For they are my brethren, not by nature indeed, but by the grace of adoption: they are children of my Father, possessing together with Me the whole inheritance of the sacraments; and nothing is lacking to them by which you may come to touch Me perfectly.

Consider, O woman who desires to touch Me; consider, I say, that you may truly touch Me. For I did not say, “I ascend unto our Father and our Lord,” but “unto my Father and your Father, my God and your God.” For the Father is Father to Me in one way and to my brethren in another; God is God to Me in one way and to them in another. He is my Father because He begot Me; He is their Father because He adopted them as sons to Himself. Likewise, He is my God because He assumed His creature—that is, humanity; but He is their God because they are nothing other than human beings and are only creatures of God [Col. 0807C]. This faith beholds Me in the heart unto righteousness, and confession of the mouth touches Me unto salvation (Romans 10).

“Mary Magdalene came, announcing to the disciples: ‘I have seen the Lord, and He said these things to me.’”

Even to this day—indeed, until the end of the age—the Church does not cease to come after the likeness of that which went before in Mary: now rising in the first resurrection of souls, and announcing to those who do not know the second resurrection of bodies, which shall take place at the last day. Yet many do not believe, and even mock, just as then Mary’s report, “I have seen the Lord,” appeared to the disciples, as another Evangelist testifies (Luke 26 [probably 24]), like idle talk [Col. 0807D].

Meanwhile day gradually dawns, and the night of the apostles’ grief is brightened by repeated reports; as the force of the testimonies prevails, the darkness grows thinner—darkness which, as was said above, still lay at the tomb. For other women came who had seen the Lord, held His feet, and worshipped Him. Two disciples also came, to whom, as they went to the town called Emmaus, He had appeared in another form and been known in the breaking of bread. Moreover, it was heard and spread abroad among them that the Lord had truly risen and had appeared to Peter (ibid.). Thus, after the eyes of those who watched had been prepared and were expectant—though they had slumbered from grief throughout the whole space of the three days (Matthew 28)—at last the Sun of the world Himself emerged visibly from the east with rosy countenance, and, having driven away every remaining trace of darkness, brought a day full of joy upon all who wondered [Col. 0808A]. For it follows:

“Therefore, when it was evening on that day, the first day of the week, and the doors were shut where the disciples had gathered for fear of the Jews, Jesus stood in the midst and said unto them: Peace be unto you.”

First, I gladly consider that which gives especial delight: namely, the utterance of this new salutation, which no human being had hitherto heard from the mouth of God, and which, when He stood in the midst of His disciples, He immediately gave forth, saying, “Peace be unto you.” What is this? Why did the Lord of hosts and King of glory (Psalm 23), upon first entering the assembly of the apostles and of those gathered with them, as Luke says, first sound forth for their joy this utterance as a most sweet consolation? (Luke 24 [Col. 0808B].)

Did the conqueror of death, returned from hell, bring such a greeting by chance? Certainly not. Rather, He uttered this word to signify a definite reality. For had He not then, for the first time, dissolved in His flesh the enmities which had hitherto existed between God and humankind, and endured death for this purpose: to reconcile the human race to God? “For He,” says the Apostle, “is our peace, who hath made both one, and reconciled us unto God in one body through the death of the cross, slaying the enmity in Himself” (Ephesians 2), etc.

Therefore, because He had borne our sins in His own body upon the wood, and because He had removed from the midst the handwriting of sin (Colossians 2), fastening it to the cross, and had stripped principalities and powers, openly leading them in triumph in Himself, this “Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle” (Psalm 23) [Col. 0808C], returning with victory to life, rightly said, when He stood in the midst of the disciples: “Peace be unto you.”

Why, however, were the disciples within, behind closed doors? “For fear,” he says, “of the Jews.” What did they fear? Jews sated with the Lord’s blood. If the Jews still burned and thirsted for their blood, could the disciples protect themselves by doors that could so easily be broken down? Why, then, had they shut the doors? Plainly because they had a conversation among themselves in which they thought it unsafe for anyone except a friend or a sharer in their grief to be present. For not only had they already heard the women say that they had seen the Lord, but two disciples had returned from the town of Emmaus [Col. 0808D], reporting that they had recognized Him in the breaking of bread. Indeed, they had already gathered for this very purpose, saying: “The Lord is risen indeed, and hath appeared to Peter” (Luke 24). While they were speaking among themselves of these matters, it did not rightly seem safe that a Jew should overhear them, and therefore they kept themselves behind closed doors.

“But,” someone asks, “how could a body be real if it entered through closed doors?” Whoever asks this unbelievingly, and will not concede that a true body could thus be brought in, must much less concede that the apostles, still corruptible and mortal, were brought out in the manner written in the Acts of the Apostles: “We found the prison shut with all diligence, and the guards standing before the doors; but when we opened the prison [Col. 0809A], we found no one inside” (Acts 5). Such persons must also assert that these men, who had not yet risen, vanished into winds and thin air, so that they might be blown out through open cracks, if they refuse to receive Holy Scripture. Those who do not receive it are not to be heard, but are altogether to be avoided as unbelievers.

For us who believe, this suffices as proof: God created all things from nothing, and all things are to be reckoned by Him as though they were nothing and void, whether He wishes to do anything or to convey anything wherever He wishes. Indeed, it would be more surprising if He could not do so, since scarcely any craftsman is so unskilled that he cannot himself penetrate or open what he has made.

But when He willed, “the earth opened and swallowed Dathan, and immediately covered the congregation of Abiron” (Psalm 105) [Col. 0809B]—those leaders of sedition, who disparaged God’s promises and said mockingly: “Truly thou hast brought us into a land flowing with streams of milk and honey” (Numbers 16). Yet I shall seem to cast words into the wind if I attempt lengthy replies against such enemies of the Christian faith. For those little foxes, long ago terrified by the thunder of heaven—that is, by the thundering cry of the Church—lie hidden wherever they are, in underground dens, and do not dare come forth to demolish with their foul teeth the flowering vines and fruit-bearing plants, according to their habit. But let us now contemplate what follows in the present joy:

“And when He had said this, He showed them His hands and His side” [Col. 0809C].

Why did He show His hands and side, and also His feet, as Luke testifies (chapter 24), except to demonstrate to disciples who thought they saw a spirit that He had a true body, and that in a true body and true members He presented the true bruise which effected our peace? For “the chastisement of our peace was upon Him, and by His bruise we are healed” (Isaiah 58 [probably 53]). This chastisement was visible in His hands, feet, and side, and was even touchable through the marks of the nails and spear.

These signs of the bruise are everlasting: pearls of the victor, and splendid ornaments or testimonies of the peace which He brought to us. By the power through which He rose and restored a truly living body from a truly dead one [Col. 0809D], He could indeed have utterly removed or smoothed away the marks of nails and spear. But the signs of the love and obedience fitting for the eyes of the Father were to be preserved upon the Son of God; they were the venerable pledges of our cause, eternal incentives to our love, and perpetual fires of terror for the ungodly.

“Then the disciples were glad when they saw the Lord.” How were they glad? How did those exhausted by the greatness of grief then breathe again in joy? Magnificently, as when “they were comforted; then their mouth was filled with joy and their tongue with exultation, and they were made glad” (Psalm 125). “A woman, when she is in travail, hath sorrow; but afterward she forgetteth the anguish for joy, because a man is born into the world” (John 16) [Col. 0810A]. The woman, I say—that is, their soul—had, as though in labour, endured for three days a multitude of pains and continual mourning and weeping; but now what He had promised was fulfilled: “I will see you again, and your heart shall rejoice.”

The disciples, therefore, were glad when they saw the Lord; yet, tossed amid the vehement abundance of this very joy, they did not yet believe. For Luke says: “While they yet believed not for joy, but wondered” (Luke 24), etc.

“Then said He unto them again: Peace be unto you.”

To those hesitating and receiving peace with difficulty, He offers peace: that peace, I say, which no one can receive except by believing. For only by believing are we reconciled to God through the death of His Son (Ephesians 2). Moreover, why He says to them again, “Peace be unto you,” He makes clear when He adds: “As the Father hath sent me, even so send I you.” For how, or for what purpose, did the Father send the Son except that He might make peace between God and human beings? Likewise, how, or for what purpose, does the Son send His preachers into the whole world, except that they may reconcile hostile human beings to God? [Col. 0810B]

Knowing this, the Apostle says to the Corinthians: “But all things are of God, who hath reconciled us to Himself and hath given us the ministry of reconciliation. For God was in Christ, reconciling the world unto Himself, not imputing unto them their trespasses, and hath placed in us the word of reconciliation. Therefore we discharge an embassy for Christ, as though God were exhorting through us. We beseech you for Christ: be reconciled to God” (2 Corinthians 5), etc.

Therefore, if you ask how or for what purpose the Father sent the Son, as pertains to the present passage: “God,” he says, “was in Christ, reconciling the world unto Himself, not imputing unto them their trespasses.” If you ask what is meant by “even so send I you”: “He has placed in us,” he says, “the word of reconciliation; we discharge an embassy for Christ, and we beseech for Christ: be reconciled to God.” Therefore, having said once and again, “Peace be unto you,” in order to signify both that He had made peace for them and that He would send peace to us through them, He says: “As the Father hath sent me, even so send I you” [Col. 0810C]. And if you ask more clearly what that peace is, hear what follows:

[Col. 0810D] “And when he had said this, he breathed upon them and said: ‘Receive the Holy Spirit’;” and immediately: “Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain are retained.” Clearly, the peace spoken of here is the forgiveness of sins, which is the first and greatest gift of the Holy Spirit. Therefore, when he had said, “Receive the Holy Spirit,” as though they were asking, “In what shall we receive him?” he at once added: “Whose sins,” he says, “you forgive are forgiven them,” etc. This peace, then, as has already been said, is forgiveness of sins; and this forgiveness is the reception of the Holy Spirit.

Accordingly, let the mountains receive peace under this king (Ps. 78), under this king’s son, to whom God, when he rose from the dead, gave his judgment and righteousness: first, when he said, “Peace [Col. 0811A] be with you”; let them receive peace for the people—understand, peace to be proclaimed in the Gospel—when he said again, “Peace be with you.” For this King’s Son is not only to judge his people with righteousness, but also his poor with judgment. Therefore he said twice, “Peace be with you,” because both through himself he made peace and reconciled to God the Church of his former people—namely, the patriarchs, prophets, and all the elect, from the first Abel to the thief hanging on the cross—and through the apostles, in whom, as was said before, he himself placed the word of reconciliation (2 Cor. 5), he invited his poor, that is, us Gentiles, us strangers and foreigners to the covenants (Eph. 2), who were without God in this world, to the same peace, saying to them: “As the Father sent me, so I [Col. 0811B] send you.” Thus, in judging, he humbled the slanderer (Ps. 71), because “now is the judgment of the world; now the ruler of this world will be cast out” (John 12); and, coming, he proclaimed peace to the poor of his people who were near—that is, to the apostles and the others who were of the circumcision—and peace to us, the children of those same poor, who were far off (Eph. 2).

But why, when he was about to say, “Receive the Holy Spirit,” did he first breathe upon them?—“For the breath which our Lord, while still a mortal and passible man, drew in and expelled through his mouth, was not the Holy Spirit but common air; and, being now immortal, he had no need of it for breathing 343, nor shall we need it in that age after the resurrection, where corruptible life is absent. Accordingly, [Col. 0811C] although he had the power bodily to breathe, just as he could eat or drink without needing to do so, we nevertheless do not suppose that he walked about breathing individually upon each of the eleven apostles and all who had assembled with them; nor that, standing in their midst, he emitted in one breath so great a blast that he physically blew upon them all at once, and then said to those touched by such a breath, ‘Receive the Holy Spirit,’ etc.

“Rather, he breathed thus not as a man, but as God, who is recorded to have breathed even before he became man. For ‘God formed man from the dust of the earth, and breathed into him’ (Gen. 2); or, as the Septuagint has it, ‘breathed into his face the breath of life.’ He therefore who then breathed, so that man might become a living soul, now breathed again, [Col. 0811D] so that the soul of the living human being might receive the Holy Spirit and have its understanding opened for understanding the Scriptures. Indeed, Luke relates this very thing: ‘Then he opened their understanding so that they might understand the Scriptures’ (Luke 24). By this Holy Spirit they are enabled to forgive sins by acting in the manner now stated: ‘Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them.’

This is shown more plainly in Matthew in these words: ‘All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go therefore, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit’ (Matt. 28). Precisely so: whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain are retained. For this is what he says in Mark: ‘Whoever believes and is baptized shall be saved; but whoever does not believe shall be condemned’ (Mark 16). Upon this authority also depends what is said elsewhere: ‘Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven’ (Matt. 18). Yet he did not give this authority before his passion, but only promised it, as, speaking more plainly to Peter concerning the future, he says: ‘And to you I will give the keys of the kingdom of heaven’ (Matt. 16), etc.

There he promised authority to bind or loose; but here—that is, after his resurrection—he lays down the rule concerning what is prior, or better: namely, baptizing all people for the forgiveness of sins. From that time the one holy Catholic Church throughout the whole world forgives sins by baptizing [Col. 0812B] in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Nor is this faith vain, because sins are no less forgiven to those whom he now incorporates into himself, washing them in baptism through his ministers, than they were forgiven to those who were already in the Church, whether living or dead (2 Cor. 12), at the hour when Christ, pouring blood and water from his body, washed the sins of all who believe in him.

“For as,” he says, “the Father sent me, so I send you”: that is, the authority over forgiving sins which I received from the Father according to my humanity, I give to you in every respect. “For all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me; and whatever sins you forgive are forgiven in heaven and on earth.” This is the first and more necessary gift of the Holy Spirit: namely, for forgiveness of sins. There is another gift, by which, on the day of Pentecost, the same Holy Spirit was given in the adornments of diverse graces. This is given equally to all, so that, baptized, we may all be justified from sins; that other gift is distributed in unequal grace, the same Spirit working in each person and dividing as he wills (Eph. 5).

For as the Holy Spirit proceeds not only from the Father but also from the Son, so he had to be given not once but twice, for different effects. He proceeds from the Son for the forgiveness of sins, as the Evangelist plainly expressed by these words: “He breathed upon them and said: ‘Receive the Holy Spirit.’” For he breathed upon them—that is, he gave him as proceeding from himself. That he proceeds from the Father need not be demonstrated, and no Greek is accustomed to doubt this, although some among them have said that he does not proceed from the Son. Before the Son came into this world, the Holy Spirit was given to the ancient saints in diverse distributions of gifts; but he had not yet been given to anyone for forgiveness of sins, which could never occur unless our same high priest had first offered himself as a sacrifice for us. But this has already been discussed more fully elsewhere, where baptism had to be treated.

Meanwhile, while peace—that is, forgiveness of sins through the Holy Spirit—is bestowed in the great house of the holy Church, in which Christ’s disciples alone are found, the Jewish people is absent. It does not wish to share in the blessed joy of the disciples rejoicing over the Lord’s resurrection. Therefore the Evangelist, whom he who loved him—the wisdom of God, Christ the Lord—had filled from his own breast with a multitude of mysteries, immediately adds: “But Thomas, one of the twelve, who is called Didymus, was not with them when Jesus came.”

Thus it was indeed divinely arranged that this one disciple should be absent from so great a joy, because the Jewish people was destined to withdraw itself from the whole body of the Gentiles, who in unity of faith receive the grace of the Holy Spirit for forgiveness of sins. “Therefore the others said to him: ‘We have seen the Lord.’ But he said to them: ‘Unless I see the mark of the nails in his hands, and put my finger into the place of the nails, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe.’”

If one considers only the letter, why should this apostle Thomas be reproved more, or more justly, than the others, as unbelieving or faithless? Is it because he said, “I will not believe unless I see the marks of the nails in his hands and put my finger into the place of the nails”? Why, the others too would not have believed unless they had seen—indeed, unless they had touched. For according to this Evangelist, after he said, “Peace be with you,” he showed them his hands and side; and according to Luke he not only said, “See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself,” but also, “Touch me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have.” Yet even these things did not suffice to make them believe. For Luke continues: “But while they still did not believe and marvelled for joy, he said: ‘Have you anything here to eat?’” (Luke 24).

In what, then, was Thomas more unbelieving, if you wish to retain a merely plain historical account, except perhaps because he did not believe those who had seen him risen? Yet they themselves did not easily believe their own eyes. Therefore, as was said above, Thomas, in the hand of God’s wisdom wisely ordering its own works, bore the figure of the Jewish people. In the days of the apostles, who were the first witnesses of the Lord’s resurrection and said, “We have seen the Lord”—as they do not cease even now to say through the mouth of the universal Church—the Jews resist with obstinate hardness and do not believe unless they see. Thus it is not so much Thomas, in comparison with the other apostles, as the Jewish people, in comparison with the Gentiles, that is charged with unbelief; for we have not seen, and we believe. “O God, we have heard with our ears; our fathers have declared to us” (Ps. 43). The Jews will not believe unless, with Enoch and Elijah going before, they see the terrible things of the coming judge (Mal. 4; Rev. 11). Hence follows:

“And after eight days his disciples were again inside, and Thomas was with them.” After eight days the disciples were inside—inside, but not inside the same doors 344; they were not in Jerusalem. For it must not be supposed that, though he had repeatedly commanded them to go into Galilee, they delayed for eight days. Where, then, were they inside, except on the mountain in Galilee to which they had gone, as Matthew reports (ch. 28), in accordance with Jesus’ appointment? Hence it has long been said by great teachers: “After his resurrection Jesus is first seen and worshipped in Galilee,” although some doubt it.

Then he shows Thomas more plainly both his side wounded by the spear and his hands pierced by nails. But how were they “inside” if they were on a mountain? Evidently because Nazareth, his city, was situated on a mountain in Galilee, as we have in Luke: “And he came,” he says, “to Nazareth, where he had been brought up. And when they said to him, ‘What we have heard you did in Capernaum, do here also in your own country,’ afterwards, filled with anger, they led him, he says, to the brow of the mountain on which their city was built, in order to throw him down” (Luke 4). Therefore they had both gone to the mountain and were indoors, because perhaps they had assembled in Nazareth, the city of Galilee, in the house of Mary his mother. Mystically, moreover, Thomas was with them after eight days because, after this fullness of time, the remnant of the Israelite people will believe together with the Gentiles (Rom. 11).

“And Jesus came, though the doors were shut, and stood in the midst, and said: ‘Peace be with you.’ Then he said to Thomas: ‘Put your finger here and see my hands; bring your hand and put it into my side; and do not be unbelieving, but believing.’” Because, he says, you declared, “Unless I see and put my hands into his side, I will not believe,” and because I heard you saying this while I was thought absent and unseen, though I was present—behold, put in your finger and see: that is, prove that my hands are not a spirit, but flesh and bones, which a spirit does not possess. And, by touching the substance of true flesh, do not be unbelieving but believing in the substance of the true divinity dwelling fully, or bodily, in it—a divinity which was able to raise its flesh.

“Thomas answered and said to him: ‘My Lord and my God.’ Jesus said to him: ‘Because you have seen me, you have believed. Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed.’” What is said to Thomas alone—“Because you have seen me, you have believed”—could plainly, if one considers only the literal sense, have been said to all the apostles; for unless they had seen, they would not have believed. Before seeing him, they did not believe the women who reported that they had seen him; rather, their words seemed to them like nonsense (Luke 24). Why, then, does he say to one alone, “Because you have seen me, you have believed,” adding, “Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed”? We indeed have not seen and do believe. But are we consequently more blessed than the apostle Thomas, who believed after seeing, and than the other apostles who saw?

[Col. 0814D] Therefore, as has already been said, beneath the outwardly shining silver beauty of this letter there is also hidden the golden radiance of mysteries; and this passage is a kind of parable of him who neither spoke nor acted without parables, as Matthew says (ch. 13), adding the prophet’s testimony spoken in his person: “I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter things hidden from the foundation of the world” (Ps. 77). Thus, in the person of the Jewish people it is said to Thomas: “Because you have seen me, you have believed; blessed are those who have not seen and have believed.” For those too will indeed be blessed who believe, because they will see the brightness preceding his coming; yet they will be less praiseworthy than us Gentiles, because they will believe last, though they ought to have been the first to believe, and will be converted from head to tail.

“Jesus indeed did many other signs in the presence of his disciples which are not written in this book. But these have been written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that, believing, you may have life in his name.” It is as though he said: Of the many signs Jesus performed before his disciples after he rose from the dead, these two have been written in this book, because it is written in the Law that “the testimony of two persons is true” (Deut. 17, 19), so that through these two testimonies “you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God”—namely, he who, though dead as man, rose as God.

The Apostle also teaches that deeds may rightly be accepted as witnesses. After saying to the Corinthians, “Behold, this is the third time I am ready to come to you,” he immediately adds: “Every word shall stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses” (2 Cor. 13). But perhaps a contentious hearer is not satisfied with two witnesses and demands a third. Therefore follows:

## [Chapter 21]

“After these things Jesus manifested himself again by the Sea of Tiberias; and he manifested himself in this way: Simon Peter and Thomas, called Didymus, and Nathanael, who was from Cana of Galilee, and the sons of Zebedee, and two others of his disciples were together.”

Behold, the loving and beloved Evangelist records this third testimony also, so that nothing may be lacking: for, as has already been said, “every word shall stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses.” For, so that you may know that he intends to confirm the hearer of the Gospel in faith in the resurrection of Jesus Christ our Lord by the lawful number of witnesses, he immediately concludes at the end of this reading: “This was now the third time Jesus manifested himself to his disciples after he had risen from the dead.”

The trustworthy account of this miracle is splendid and worthy of hearing: with testimony to the resurrection of the head, it also prefigures the resurrection of the body—that is, of the whole Church. No less venerable and true is the arrangement of this divine Evangelist. Of the many things which Jesus did in the presence of his disciples, as stated above, he selected three signs which, while bearing witness on the historical surface to the Lord’s resurrection, also mystically proclaimed the imminent calling of the fullness of the Gentiles, the salvation at the end of the age of the remnant of Israel, and the universal resurrection of all.

“Simon Peter and Thomas, called Didymus, and Nathanael, who was from Cana of Galilee, and the sons of Zebedee, and two others of his disciples,” he says. The Evangelist gave the number of the disciples not only because it was great enough that the Lord’s appearance to them might properly be called a manifestation, but also because the holy Church is rightly figured by the number seven, as gathered or ordered by the holy sevenfold Spirit.

“Simon Peter said to them: ‘I am going fishing.’ They said to him: ‘We too will come with you.’” For apostles chosen and following in Christ’s footsteps, returning to fishing was not a sin, just as it is not a sin today for those who renounce the world and follow Christ to practice lawful trades and seek sustenance from the labor of their hands (Acts 20). Otherwise the apostle Paul, who had put his hand to the plough, would seem to have looked back: though he could have used the authority granted him, he supported himself by the labor of his hands (2 Thess. 3). For, preaching the Gospel, lest anyone should make his glory void—especially among the Corinthians (1 Cor. 3)—he did not wish to live from the Gospel. Thus the business of fishing, which before conversion had been without sin, did not suddenly become blameworthy for the apostles after conversion. It follows:

“They went out and got into the boat, and that night they caught nothing. But when morning came, Jesus stood on the shore; yet the disciples did not know that it was Jesus.” Before morning came and the Lord stood on the shore, the seven disciples labored and cast their nets 345, but caught nothing. This signifies that, before the acceptable time and day of salvation which dawned for us when Christ, the sun of righteousness, rose from the dead, the Law and the prophets indeed preached, but did not accomplish the salvation of the whole world. They cast nets, indeed, but did not bring the fish they had caught to shore: they wove together holy Scripture, but did not lead people through it to the harbor of eternal salvation.

But morning came, and the Lord Jesus stood on the shore, because after the letter of the Law, which brought nothing to perfection, came the time of helping grace; and after his resurrection our Lord, now immortal and impassible, began firmly to stand beyond the waves of our mortality (Heb. 7).

“Jesus therefore said to them: ‘Children, have you anything to eat?’” Since, he says, they had not yet recognized that he was the one who had called them from the sea to make them fishers of men, he graciously condescended to those who did not know him and first spoke to the fish-catchers as any buyer of fish might speak (Matt. 4). And, in keeping with the purpose of the miracle he was to perform, he appropriately asked for food. “My food,” he says, “is to do the will of my Father” (John 4); and that will is nothing other than to draw people from the false and bitter waves of this age to the harbor of salvation.

“They answered him: ‘No.’” The Lord’s children then have no food, and, in the Psalmist’s words, “they suffer hunger like dogs” (Ps. 58), when, casting the nets of preaching, they catch no one or only a few; and then they complain because they are not filled.

“He said to them: ‘Cast the net on the right side of the boat and you will find.’ They cast it, therefore, and now they could not draw it in because of the multitude of fish.” He certainly did not say, “Cast the net on the right side of the boat,” when he was still amid the waves and was to suffer death and passion; rather, he said only, “Let down your nets for a catch” (Luke 5). Thus they then enclosed such a multitude of fish that their net was breaking and their little boat was nearly sinking.

But now, standing on the shore and having wholly passed beyond the tossing waves of this turbulent age, he says, “Cast,” not just anywhere, but “cast on the right.” And now, says the Evangelist, they could not draw it in because of the multitude of fish. He did not merely say that their net was breaking or their boat sinking. What, then, did he intend here except to prefigure that fishing of people in which all the elect, with all the reprobate separated to the left, will be placed at the right hand (Matt. 25)? The reprobate, like bad fish, tear the net of the present Church by their seditions—a thing especially done by heretics and schismatics. For he had risen and stood upon the safest shore, he “who, having risen from the dead, dies no more; death shall have no more dominion over him” (Rom. 6). Therefore he rightly prefigured only those whom he wished to raise with himself and cause to sit with himself at the Father’s right hand in heavenly places (Luke 24).

“The disciple whom Jesus loved therefore said to Peter: ‘It is the Lord.’” Since, he says, that great caller of his children who stood upon the shore had prophesied so truly in saying, “Cast the net on the right side of the boat and you will find,” it came to the mind of the foremost disciple, the one whom Jesus loved, that it was the Lord. And he told Peter, whom he knew would rejoice above all others. Rightly so: because, like the gentle, who had followed the Teacher of gentleness, they quickly obeyed the command, “Cast on the right,” they at once recognized him. So also those two fittingly recognized him in the breaking of bread, because they had constrained him, saying, “Remain with us, for evening is drawing on.”

That disciple did not say, “It is Jesus,” but “It is the Lord”; and not “our Lord” or the Lord of any specifically designated persons, but indefinitely, “It is the Lord.” Why should he call him his own Lord in particular, when he had openly shown at that moment that he was Lord even of the sea? Indeed, by standing on the shore of immortality he had proved that he was victor over death and lord over the death he had conquered.

“When Simon Peter heard that it was the Lord, he girded himself with his tunic, for he was naked, and threw himself into the sea.” It was not the beloved disciple, who had said, “It is the Lord,” but Peter, who was to be girded and led where he did not wish, who “girded himself with his tunic and threw himself into the sea.” Long ago he had thrown himself into the sea and walked upon the waters in order to come to Jesus, who alone walked upon the waters; but, seeing the strong wind approaching, he was afraid and, in that fear, nearly sank. Now, however, with the Lord standing on the shore, he voluntarily throws himself into the sea; he is not afraid and suffers no danger.

What is this except that Peter, who was to deny the Lord from fear of death during the Jewish tempest which the Lord conquered by walking over it, was now to act courageously amid the waves of the Roman Empire, in the great storm of savage Nero? Therefore he who feared and nearly sank before the Lord’s passion, after his resurrection throws himself into the sea and happily reaches the harbor.

“But the other disciples came in the boat, for they were not far from land, but about two hundred cubits away, dragging the net full of fish.” The order of the sentence is: The other disciples came in the boat, dragging the net full of fish; for they were not far from land, but about two hundred cubits away.

The disciple whom Jesus loved, and the others who came in the boat, signify those rulers of the holy Church who end their lives in peace. But Peter, who throws himself into the sea, signifies all those who, like him, hasten and run to the Lord through the midst of the waves of tribulations, dragging the net of fish—that is, by their writings or labors of every kind containing or defending the faith of the Gentiles. For they are not far from that land of the living where the Lord stands immortal, as were those laboring long ago under the Law before grace came; rather, they are near, about two hundred cubits away: that is, free from all legal ceremonies and needing only love of God and neighbor in order to arrive.

“But when they came down to land, they saw coals laid there, with a fish placed upon them, and bread.” The kingdom of blessedness, which is one eternal breakfast and one perpetual supper, is to be found on that shore—that is, at the end of the age. There all the elect will find coals: that is, the full fire or love of the Holy Spirit, which in this life is somewhat small in the saints, but in that kingdom exceedingly great, as the prophet beautifully proclaims: “The Lord says: ‘Whose fire is in Zion, and whose furnace is in Jerusalem’” (Isa. 31).

They will find also a fish laid upon the coals and bread: that is, the one and same Christ, God and man—according to his humanity, like roasted fish; according to the nature of his divinity, the impassible bread of angels.

“Jesus said to them: ‘Bring some of the fish which you have now caught.’” Well does he say, “Bring some of the fish which you have now caught.” “For he will summon heaven above and earth, to distinguish his people: ‘Gather to him his saints, who establish his covenant upon sacrifices’” (Ps. 49). Who are those to whom this is commanded according to the Psalmist, except the apostles or holy preachers, each of whom 346 will present to the eternal Judge as many good fish as he has gained by his labor?

“Simon Peter went up and drew the net to land, full of large fish, one hundred and fifty-three.” Since it was said above concerning the seven disciples, “They cast it, and could no longer draw it in because of the multitude of fish,” how is it now said, “Simon Peter went up and drew the net to land,” when he could much less have done it alone? Unless Peter, to whom above the others it was especially said, “To you I will give the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 16), signifies the whole body of those whose right or duty it is to handle this net of fish, which is the word of God.

Thus the one faith which all fishers of men preach is rightly represented by the one Peter, to whom the chief authority was granted over all fish belonging to the kingdom of heaven and to the banquet of the holy Trinity. All these fish are large and numbered, because all the elect, though unequal in merits, are nevertheless all great; and their number is certain before God, since they are saints called from the foundation of the world according to his purpose. For how could the number be uncertain to him of those whom he foreknew, predestined, called, justified, and glorified?

Moreover, this divinely provided number of fish is such that it is not confined to one rank but arranged in three consecutive ranks: hundreds, tens, and units. This arrangement is familiar to arithmeticians. Why, unless because the people signified by these fish are distinguished not all in the same order or vocation, but by diverse orders, though within the same faith? Some are married; others are widowed or continent; others lead a virginal life. In the looser order or vocation there are more, but they are less strong; in the stricter order there are fewer, but more precious. For according to the parable of the sower, the hundredfold fruit belongs to fewer persons, namely virgins; the thirtyfold to more, namely married people; and the sixtyfold to those in the middle, namely the continent or widows.

Therefore, if the unit which, as the arithmeticians know better, is placed in the hundred, the five which is placed in the ten, and the three which is placed in the unit had all been reckoned together as hundreds, the number of fish would indeed have been greater, since they would have made nine hundred. But now the mystery is greater, because in the hundred fish are rightly understood the faithful living more freely, in the three those contemplating more highly, and in the fifty those acting in an intermediate manner. For the holy Church resembles the ark which Noah built, because it was broader below and narrower above. Below it extended three hundred cubits in length and fifty in breadth; above it was completed in one cubit (Gen. 6). There are many things already profitably discussed by learned writers concerning the number of one hundred and fifty-three fish, which the diligent reader may readily find in their proper places. It follows:

“And though there were so many, the net was not torn.” It rightly belonged to the Evangelist to say, “Though there were so many, the net was not torn.” For in the present state of the Church, the fish which exceed the number tear the net, as the Psalmist testifies when he says: “I have declared and spoken; they are multiplied beyond number” (Ps. 39). But on that shore of resurrection there will be peace and the net will be sound, because only the numbered fish, all large—that is, all good—will be there.

“Jesus said to them: ‘Come, dine.’” Rightly, when so many great fish, all caught on the right side of the boat, had been drawn to land, Jesus says, “Come, dine.” For when the same Son of Man sits upon the throne of his majesty and sets all the elect at his right hand, then he will most sublimely and sweetly utter these words: “Come, you blessed of my Father; inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25). For what is this dining, except receiving the eternal kingdom? And what is it to dine by reigning, or reign by dining, except to behold face to face, as he is, the king of glory himself—the food of angels, into whom angels desire to look (1 Pet. 1; 1 John 3; 1 Cor. 13)?

Therefore, after the prophet had spoken of the person who walks in righteousness and speaks truth—“Bread is given to him; his waters are sure” (Isa. 33)—as though you asked what bread was given him or what waters these were, he immediately added: “His eyes shall see the king in his beauty” (ibid.).

Accordingly it immediately follows:

“And none of those reclining [variant: saying] dared ask him, ‘Who are you?’ knowing that it was Jesus.” At that time they did not dare; intent only upon seeing or hearing, they showed reverence. But when he invites all his own to that eternal banquet, they will no longer need “to ask him, knowing that it is Jesus”: knowing, I say, and perfectly recognizing what they now know only in part while reading the Scriptures and consulting the Holy Spirit of knowledge, until “that which is perfect comes and that which is in part is done away” (1 Cor. 13).

“And Jesus came and took the bread and gave it to them, and likewise the fish.” From where did he come, or where did he go, in order to serve them bread and fish? According to the letter this would plainly be judged superfluous, but in its mystical sense it has some force. For it is said here, “He came and took bread and gave it to them,” just as elsewhere, concerning servants awaiting their Lord, after it has first been said that he will make them recline, it is immediately added that, passing by, “he will minister to them” (Luke 12).

For when, standing on the shore, he says, “Come, dine”—indeed, when, seated on the throne of his majesty, he says, “Come, you blessed of my Father; inherit the kingdom” (Matt. 25)—then even the evil fish on the left, who in the former fishing were multiplied beyond number and tore the nets, will see him. Then, I say, every eye will see him (Rev. 1, 7), including those who pierced him. But he will pass on; he will come inside, with the doors shut; and after those people have been cast out, he will make his own recline and will minister to them. Of this ministry it is now mystically said: “He took the bread and gave it to them, and likewise the fish.” What is this bread except the sweetness of the divine vision? And what is the roasted fish except the nature of the Son of Man cooked by the fire of suffering? He takes both and gives them to his own, because he will refresh the participants in his kingdom by the vision of both natures, as he promises elsewhere: “And I appoint for you, as my Father appointed for me, a kingdom, that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom.”

“This was now the third time Jesus manifested himself to his disciples after he had risen from the dead.” It was said above that the testimony of two persons is true, and that it is not lawful to require more than a third; for every word shall stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses. The prudent Evangelist has already recorded two testimonies, concluding thus: “Jesus indeed performed many other signs in the presence of his disciples,” and so forth. And lest anything be lacking to the contentious inquirer, he added this third manifestation. Since whoever does not believe these three would not give the hearing of faith even to many others, if they were written, he now at last, content with what is sufficient for believers, concludes: “This was now the third time Jesus manifested himself to his disciples after he had risen from the dead.” It follows:

“Therefore, when they had eaten, Jesus said to Simon Peter: ‘Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these?’ He said to him: ‘Yes, Lord, you know that I love you.’ He said to him: ‘Feed my lambs.’”

The Lord Jesus now begins to disclose to Simon Peter—who did not know what the Lord had accomplished through him when “he girded himself with his tunic and cast himself into the sea,” and likewise when, at His command, “he went up and drew the net to land,” full of so many fish—the mystery, I say, of his action, [Col. 0821B] and what that number of fish, so distinctly divided threefold, signified for him. First, indeed, by imposing upon him for the third time the office of shepherd, saying twice, “Feed my lambs,” and the third time, “Feed my sheep,” He refers to the hidden meaning of the fish. Then, in saying, “When you were younger, you girded yourself and walked where you wished,” and so forth, He foretells what Peter had prefigured by girding himself, though unknowingly.

“Simon, son of John,” He says, “do you love me more than these?” Fittingly enough, invoking his father’s name, He called him Simon, son of John—that is, one obedient to the grace of God (John XVI). For by quickly girding himself and casting himself into the sea, and likewise by drawing the net to land, he powerfully expressed a type of the entire obedience which he was to undergo, whether in living or [Col. 0821C] in dying. Therefore, when He was about to say truly, “Feed my lambs,” He first asked, “Do you love me more than these?”—because the one who undertakes to feed rational lambs needs the work that proceeds from love: that love by which the Prince of Shepherds Himself first laid down His life for His sheep (1 Pet. V). And He beautifully calls them lambs, whose salvation, having recently been sacrificed as a ram, He had begotten in His own blood.

Why, then, when He says, “Do you love me,” does He add, “more than these?” Certainly, in saying this, He most sweetly recalls to Peter’s mind that earlier declaration, as though Peter had then said, in loving more than the others: “Even if all are scandalized because of you, I shall never be scandalized” (Matt. XXVI). At that time, indeed, He checked Peter’s presumptuous confidence in his love, [Col. 0821D] saying: “Before the cock crows, you will deny me three times.” But now, in asking, “Do you love me more than these?” He graciously takes hold of his conscience, knowing well that, fear overcome, he will thereafter openly show how greatly he loves.

“He said to him again: ‘Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these?’ He said to him: ‘Yes, Lord, you know that I love you.’ He said to him: ‘Feed my lambs.’” Here we must understand larger lambs: lambs surpassing the former by as much as the middle number of fifty fish is, according to the spiritual sense stated above, more worthy than the more abundant multitude of one hundred fish. For just as, when the net was drawn to land, fifty-three fish were counted separately, so now [Col. 0822A] in the distinction of pastoral care we should understand first one hundred lambs, then fifty lambs, and finally three sheep when He says, “Feed my sheep.” Thus there are in Simon Peter’s pastures one hundred and fifty-three lambs and sheep together, just as there were as many fish in the net which he drew to land.

For it follows: “He said to him a third time: ‘Simon, son of John, do you love me?’ Peter was grieved because he said to him a third time, ‘Do you love me?’ He said to him: ‘Lord, you know all things; you know that I love you.’ Jesus said to him: ‘Feed my sheep.’” After lambs and lambs come sheep: those, namely, of whom it is said in the Song of Songs, “All are bearing twins, and none among them is barren” (Cant. IV), because they can govern both orders of lambs—those who still need milk, and those who are now [Col. 0822B] rather grown, or yearlings, and know how to gather the fodder of the Scriptures. Thus, indeed, they are more advanced, yet stronger, than those whom they can benefit; just as in the net mentioned above the other fifty fish, counted after the hundred, are admittedly fewer but more worthy.

Therefore, what was signified by Peter’s drawing such a net to land at the Lord’s command is made clear in this command to feed lambs and sheep. The same Lord proceeds to foretell how Peter, who then girded himself with his own tunic, would later be girded: “Amen, amen, I say to you: when you were younger, you girded yourself and walked where you wished. But when you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish.”

[Col. 0822C] The Evangelist immediately explained what He said this to mean. For he says: “He said this, signifying by what death he would glorify God.” The sense is this: When you were young, and as though serving an apprenticeship in military service, before experiencing the perils of war, “you girded yourself”—that is, you trusted very greatly in your own strength—and without a guide you walked where you wished. For you said: “I am ready to go with you both to prison and to death” (Luke XXII); and again: “Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you” (Matt. XXVII). There, as one young and unprovided with foresight, you girded yourself, not thinking that you needed to be girded with God’s help.

But when you have grown old—when the understanding of your inner person has grown grey—then, going with me both to prison and to death (Wis. IV), you will stretch out your hands upon the cross, [Col. 0822D] yet so that another will gird you: you will know that you cannot gird yourself, and He will lead you where you do not wish—that is, He will govern you in the passion of death which, by natural fear, you dread. In that age of old age, when your strength has failed (Ps. LXX)—that is, when you presume nothing upon your own strength—you will say, remembering that by fearing death you denied life; and all who have rightly come to know their own weakness will say likewise: “But we ourselves had within ourselves the answer of death, so that we might not trust in ourselves, but in God who raises the dead; who delivered us from such great dangers and will deliver us, in whom we hope that he will yet also deliver us, while you assist us by your prayers for us” (2 Cor. I).

[Col. 0823A] “And when he had said these things, he said to him: ‘Follow me.’” With wonderful sweetness the true and gentle Lord recalls the former contention, in which He Himself had said, “Where I am going, you cannot follow me now; but you shall follow afterwards.” Peter replied: “Why cannot I follow you now? I will lay down my life for you.” To this the Lord said: “On this night, before the cock crows, you will deny me three times.” Peter, still young, as was said above, answered: “Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you” (John XIII).

The Lord graciously recalls this contention, I say, when He says: “Follow me.” It is as if He said: You have now, by denying me three times, proved me true [Col. 0823B] in what I told you: “Where I am going, you cannot follow me now.” It remains that my word may likewise appear true in what I added: “But you shall follow afterwards.” Therefore follow me—that is, imitate me. Henceforth you will be ready to go for me, both to prison and to death; ready, I say, and strong. And just as a little earlier, girding yourself with your tunic and casting yourself into the sea, you confidently reached the shore, so, girded with the spirit of strength in the labor of preaching, running through the midst of tribulation, you will be established eternally with me upon the shore of peace.

“Peter turned and saw following him the disciple whom Jesus loved, who had reclined at supper upon his breast and said: ‘Lord, who is it that will betray you?’” Peter, still not knowing what was being said, followed the Lord by the movement of his feet; and that other disciple likewise followed, though unbidden. But why did he now add, beyond his customary description of his own person, “this disciple who also reclined at supper upon his breast and said: ‘Lord, who is it that will betray you?’” 348 For although he had already mentioned himself in many places by saying, “whom Jesus loved,” nevertheless here, in identifying himself, he added: “who also reclined at supper upon his breast and said: ‘Lord, who is it that will betray you?’”

Why, then, except that you may understand that when the Lord said to Peter, “Follow me,” He had in view what He had said to him at supper: “You cannot follow me now, but you shall follow afterwards”? For this was said at the time when this disciple, reclining upon His breast, said to Him: “Lord, who is it that will betray you?”

“Therefore, when Peter saw him following, he said [Col. 0823D] to Jesus: ‘Lord, what of this man?’ He says to him: ‘I will that he remain thus until I come; what is that to you?
