Follow me.’” From this saying it was at last perceived why the Lord had said to Peter, “Follow me,” and why He had said to him, as signifying his passion: “When you were younger, you girded yourself and walked where you wished,” and so forth. For immediately it follows: “Therefore this saying went out among the brethren, that that disciple does not die.”

For how could this saying have gone out among the brethren unless the other saying also went out with it: that Peter would follow by dying, or would die by following? That saying indeed went out among the brethren in its true sense; but in the matter that this disciple does not die, there was an error requiring correction by a better understanding. Therefore [Col. 0824A] the prudent Evangelist adds: “Jesus did not say, ‘He does not die,’ but, ‘I will that he remain thus until I come; what is that to you?’”

For what He said with this qualification—“I will that he remain thus until I come; what is that to you?”—is different from merely saying, “I will that he remain thus.” For in the latter way He would have made it understood that this disciple would not die. But now, when He qualifies it by saying, “Until I come,” He plainly declares that he is to die in peace.

Someone may say: If the Lord willed that this beloved disciple should remain thus until He came—that is, should end not by a violent but by a natural death—why did He say, speaking plurally to the two sons of Zebedee, one of whom was this man: “You shall drink my cup” (Matt. XX)? To this, I say: “Did he not drink the Lord’s cup, who, at the hour when the Lord Himself drank, stood beside the cross with His mother?” (John IX). Unless the sword passed through the soul of the Lord’s mother, according to Simeon’s prophecy (Luke II), this beloved disciple too drank His bitter cup. Therefore, even if this disciple did not undergo martyrdom by a material cross or sword, he was nevertheless not without a share in the Lord’s cup.

Moreover, it was not without a great counsel of the Divinity that this beloved disciple, distinguished by the bright purity of his virginity, did not receive the triumphant purple of his own martyrdom. For, once this is observed, who in the Church would judge the triumphs of martyrs alone worthy of honor? Behold, these two, Peter and John, are chief pillars among the saints; in the one shines the strength of the active life, [Col. 0824C] and in the other the beauty of the contemplative life. For what was prefigured in Martha, busied with much service, and in Mary, sitting at the Lord’s feet and hearing His word (Luke X), had already begun to be enacted in those two: care for feeding the Lord’s sheep was entrusted to one; the other, reclining upon the Lord’s breast, was more fully imbued with knowledge of the incarnate Word. Thus Holy Church rightly embraces the red roses of martyrdom, while nonetheless celebrating the white lilies of confession, beloved by Christ. It follows:

“This is the disciple who bears testimony concerning these things and wrote these things. And we know that his testimony is true.” This, he says, is the disciple of whom Jesus said, “I will that he remain thus until I come”; who reclined at supper upon His breast and said, “Lord, who is it that will betray you?” He is the one who bears testimony concerning these things and who wrote them. And if you judge rightly, children of men, such a disciple is a fitting witness. Since, in a lawful assembly, the one who writes and the one who subscribes are regarded as equals, O all you who receive this testimony: let this be your subscription, which I subscribe on behalf of you all: “And we know that his testimony is true,” so that all alike, I and you, may hear it in the assembly of heaven.

“There are also many other things which Jesus did; if they were written individually, I suppose that the world itself could not contain the books that would have to be written.” This [Col. 0825A] is incontrovertibly true. For behold: the world cannot contain even this one book written by this disciple; and though one little man can hold it in his fist, the whole human race cannot contain the entire depth of its mysteries. How much less could the world contain them if all were written—being both weary of seeking and dull in understanding. [Col. 0826A] Therefore, because those for whom these few things are insufficient as testimony will not benefit from many things either, let the witness now sit down, having completed his service; for enough has been done for well-disposed hearers: Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God.

[Col. 0825]

[COMMENTARY ON THE APOCALYPSE.]

RUPERT’S PROLOGUE TO THE APOCALYPSE OF JOHN THE APOSTLE, ADDRESSED TO FREDERICK, ARCHBISHOP OF COLOGNE.

349 That you also, O Frederick, venerable chief bishop of the people of Cologne, may be fully taught by the present and explicit example of truth found in the Scriptures, all who are journeying toward the true land of promise need a spirit of piety in order to be meek. For the Lord Himself says: “Blessed are the gentle, for they shall possess the land” (Matt. V), excluding the ungentle from blessedness, because they shall not possess the land.

A well-known and celebrated example of both those who are gentle and therefore shall possess the land, and those who are ungentle and therefore shall not possess the land, is set forth in the spies whom Moses, at the Lord’s command, sent to inspect the land of Canaan. For those among them who were gentle—that is, who, knowing the truth, did not resist it—namely Joshua son of Nun and Caleb son of Jephunneh, said: “The land through which we have passed is exceedingly good. If the Lord is favorable, he will bring us into it and give us this land flowing with milk and honey. Do not rebel against the Lord.” They possessed the land. But the rest, who were ungentle and rebellious against the truth, speaking against their own conscience and saying, “The land which we surveyed devours its inhabitants” (Num. XIII), did not possess that same land.

What, then, is sacred Scripture to us but the true land of promise? In short, what it was for them bodily to leave Egypt and enter that land of promise, that it is for us to leave the darkness of ignorance and enter, through the truth of the Scriptures, into the knowledge of God. Indeed, this is more abundant for us, by as much as the body or reality surpasses a shadow or figure. To be sure, while we read or understand the Scriptures, we do not yet see the Lord face to face; nevertheless, that very vision of God which will one day be perfected is already begun here through the Scriptures.

And what part of this land—that is, of Holy Scripture—is more fruitful than this book of the Apocalypse of John the Apostle? The delight of your conversations especially stirred me to explore this portion by diligent meditation. For the lord Cuno, abbot of the monastery of Siegburg, a man illustrious in religion and zealous for sacred letters, urged me onward: first presenting separately certain chapters of this book, and afterward presenting them in your hearing as well. His intention was that it might be established to your satisfaction that I could, as he supposed, usefully add something beyond what the earlier Fathers had thought or said in expounding this book.

He acted thus because of the excessive good will of his mind, by which he had long since begun to think more highly of my insignificance than the capacity of my intellect warrants. Both before and after those same discussions, he pressed me to undertake this work; nor did he cease urging until at last he prevailed, as he wished.

What sequence of Holy Scripture is more beautiful on the surface, or richer in meaning, than this Apocalypse? For, as has been said before us, [Jerome, in the argument to this book], it has as many mysteries as words; indeed, even this says too little, and every praise falls below the merit of the volume. Multiple meanings lie hidden in each individual word.

Therefore, that we may possess this land, let us follow the example of the faithful spies who were gentle, saying against the ungentle heretics, who disparage this land, that “the land through which we have passed is exceedingly good.” They say, “The land which we surveyed devours its inhabitants,” but they lie. For this land, God’s land, does not devour its inhabitants; rather, their own inventions devour the proud, just as some of those murmurers were devoured—not by that land of promise which they did not reach, but by the very earth upon which they trod, which, split open beneath their feet, swallowed them.

Therefore, as has already been said, it is expedient that all who enter this land, that is, this Scripture, should be gentle in spirit, and should judge that a higher majesty of divine meanings lies hidden where we understand less as yet. For if the Lord is favorable, He will bring us into it and give us this soil flowing with milk and honey, so that we may find in it the hidden riches of salvation: treasures of wisdom and understanding, counsel and strength, knowledge and piety, and fear of the Lord.

But someone will say: “It is enough already that others, better, holier, and more learned, have found and written such things. It is unlawful and rash to add anything to what has been said by renowned Catholic Fathers, and thereby weary readers by increasing the multitude of commentaries.”

To this I say: Surely the spacious field of the holy Scriptures is common to all confessors of Christ, and no one may rightly be denied liberty to treat them, provided that, keeping the faith intact, he speaks or writes what he thinks. For who would rightly object if, on the same estate, after one or two wells dug by the preceding Fathers, their succeeding children dig more by their own labor? Indeed Isaac dug other wells besides those which the servants of his father Abraham had dug, and which, after Abraham’s death, the Philistines had formerly stopped up. After he had dug those again and called them by the same names that his father had used before, Scripture continues and says: “They dug in the valley and found living water.” Again, they dug another. And afterward: “Moving on from there, he dug another well” (Gen. XXVI).

Accordingly, by this rule, let them grant us too, after those wells which the Fathers and our predecessors dug—that is, after the treatises which they composed—the right to dig other wells with the plowshare of our own intellect, provided that we too may find living water that harms no one who drinks it and causes no scandal or error to anyone who reads it. But now, relying upon the protection of God’s grace and your authority, I shall enter upon the proposed work, judging it good only to place my hope in the Lord God (Ps. LXXII), so that I may receive my reward not here but in the future.

R. D. D. RUPERT, ABBOT OF DEUTZ, COMMENTARIES ON THE APOCALYPSE OF JOHN THE APOSTLE

BOOK ONE.

[Col. 0827]

350 (CHAPTER I.)

[Col. 0827A]

“The Apocalypse of Jesus Christ.” Although the whole sequence of the book was written in Greek and flowed from its Greek source into the stream of the Latin language, its title alone remained untouched, so that among the Latins it is called *Apocalypsis*. This name could have been rendered “revelation,” on account of the excellence of the matters or mysteries contained in this Scripture. Thus *alleluia* and *amen*, Hebrew words, have remained in Greek and Latin writings because of the dignity of their meanings. Thus *Evangelium* has been retained from Greek in Latin codices, in the language in which all the Evangelists except Matthew wrote.

Therefore, “Apocalypse,” that is, a surpassing revelation, full in meaning of majesty worthy of worship, “of Jesus [Col. 0827B] Christ”—that is, of the Anointed Savior. As it is written in the Psalm: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. XLIV). Many, indeed, have shared the name Jesus, but this one possesses the proper rationale of this name. The angel states it when, after saying, “You shall bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus,” he adds: “For he shall save his people from their sins” (Matt. I).

Likewise, many have been *christs*, that is, anointed ones; but this one is anointed above all of them, as one “in whom all the fullness of Divinity dwells bodily” (Col. II); whereas they were, or are, His companions or participants. Thus we must understand that, as in all things, so also in the case of this Apocalypse to be revealed, the humanity of Jesus Christ received as a gift the power which it did not possess by nature. Hence it follows and says: “Which God gave him to make known to his servants the things that must shortly come to pass.”

For what does our nature possess, even in the only-begotten Son, that it has not received? (1 Cor. IV; Rom. VIII.) Moreover, what has it not received, or what was not given to it because He obeyed “unto death, even death on a cross”? (Phil. II.) God left nothing unsubdued to Him, when the Psalmist says: “You have subjected all things beneath his feet” (Ps. VIII). [Col. 0828B] And He Himself says of Himself, His obedience now completed: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. XXVIII). In this book too He says: “I was dead, and behold I am alive [living] for ages of ages, and I have the keys of death and of hell.”

But let this be said concerning authority over all things. The humanity received as a gift the authority now under discussion—namely, to reveal heavenly mysteries to His servants—as is signified in this book, where the Lamb received and opened the sealed book from the right hand of Him who sat upon the throne (Rev. V). Concerning this authority the Spirit likewise says to the churches: “These things says the holy and true one, who has the key of David: he opens and no one closes; he closes and no one opens” (Rev. III).

Thus nothing was not given to, or received by, the humanity of Jesus Christ; but nothing was given into the power of His Divinity which it did not already possess. Let it therefore say: “Which God gave him to make known to his servants.” It would be clearer if it said, “which [things].” But this manner of speaking occurs frequently in the Scriptures. For example: “I have fought the good fight” (2 Tim. IV), instead of “I have fought with a good fight.”

To which servants does He make them known? Surely to those whom, on account of this very manifestation, He already calls friends, speaking thus at the very opening of the sealed book—that is, at the moment of His Passion, by which, in fulfilling the Scriptures, He made them intelligible: “I shall no longer call you servants, but my friends, because I have made known to you all things whatsoever I have heard from my Father” (John XV).

But when He says, “the things that must shortly come to pass,” this should not be understood as though this Apocalypse contained only things that were then future, and not things already then present or things that had occurred before. For John is later told: “Write, therefore, the things which you have seen, the things which are, and the things which must take place after these.” Yet because the chief focus is upon those things which were shortly to come to pass, and because past and present matters are especially woven in for their sake, He was right to be content at the beginning with saying: “The things which must shortly come to pass.”

Jacob the patriarch similarly was not about to remain wholly silent concerning present or future [past] matters in his blessings, yet at the beginning he mentioned only future things, saying: “Gather together, sons of Jacob, that I may announce, 351 what shall happen in the last days” (Gen. XLIX). It follows:

“And he signified it, sending through his angel to his servant John.” Here *signified* is equivalent to *sealed*: that is, He shut it up and made it secure with certain seals of images, so that it might lie open not to everyone, but only to those who love and study it. Nor does this contradict the preceding expression, by which He said, “to make known to his servants.” For there are some to whom He made things openly known, saying, “To you it has been given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of God” (Matt. XIII); while there are others to whom He signified them, concerning whom He immediately added: “but to the rest in parables” (Acts II).

Indeed, the holy apostles, to whom it was granted in their own time to know the mystery of the kingdom of God—namely, when the Holy Spirit came upon them and invisibly taught them (Acts II)—are those who had been servants up to that point, but from then on were friends, to whom He made these things known openly. But those who, owing to the character of their understanding, do not know how to revere or love heavenly things unless they are represented under human forms or images of things that are ordinarily fearful or venerable to fleshly perceptions—these are those to whom He signified the same things.

“He sent,” it says, “through his angel to his servant John.” This angel appeared to blessed John in the figure of Christ. For since the Son is one God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, revealing all things, He undoubtedly filled [Col. 0830A] that angel and, dwelling in his heart, spoke through him to John.

“Who bore testimony to the Word of God and to the testimony of Jesus Christ, whatever things he saw.” This part of the preface establishes the great authority of the whole book, so that it ought not to be despised or regarded as of lower dignity than the other Scriptures which the Church of Christ receives and venerates at the summit of the canon. For if anyone does not receive this Apocalypse, it follows that he does not receive that testimony to the Word of God, that testimony to Jesus Christ—that is, the Gospel of this same John, at the beginning of which he says: “In the beginning was the Word,” and so forth.

For he speaks of that testimony when he adds, “whatever things he saw,” namely, in confirmation of that testimony; because, where testimonies differ in firmness, the most steadfast witness is judged to be the one who himself saw the things of which he testifies. For the same reason, after he had said that “one of the soldiers opened the Lord’s side with a lance when he had already died, and immediately blood and water came forth,” he immediately added: “And he who saw it bore testimony, and his testimony is true, and he knows that he speaks truly, that you also may believe” (John XIX). And elsewhere: “This is the disciple who bears testimony concerning these things and wrote them; and we know that his testimony is true” (John XXI).

Yet he did not bear testimony in writing concerning every individual thing that he saw. For he himself says: “Jesus indeed did many other signs in the presence of his disciples which are not written in this book” (John [Col. 0830C] XX). But even in saying, “he bore testimony concerning all things that he saw,” he does not mean that he wrote everything; rather, he says that there were many things, so that, as he says at the end, if all were written, he does not suppose that even the world could contain the books that would have to be written.

When he says this, however, he refers not to the quantity of codices but to the magnitude of their meanings, which those in the world cannot even now contain in their entirety, although the books are few. Those things which Jesus Christ performed visibly—that is, according to the form of a servant or the condition of humanity—he could see; but the Word itself, to which he nevertheless bore testimony, he could not see with his eyes. Therefore he did not say: “Who bore testimony to the Word of God, whatever things he saw”; [Col. 0830D] rather, lengthening the clause, he first inserted, “and to the testimony of Jesus Christ,” and only then concluded: “whatever things he saw.”

“Blessed is the one who reads and the one who hears the words of this prophecy and keeps the things written in it; for the time is near.” Conscious of what and how great the things were which he had seen, of what punishments for the wicked and what rewards for the good this Apocalypse of Jesus Christ had openly disclosed to him, he fittingly cries out with a mighty voice and vehement intent, declaring that the one who hears the things written here—for example, the seven marvelous trumpets sounding forth in this prophecy—or, if he knows letters, reads [them], and observes them, is truly blessed, and prepares himself watchfully for that trumpet of God, the last trumpet of the archangel, which will sound on the day of judgment.

Thus Moses the lawgiver, who from afar—being much earlier than this man—beheld the blessedness of the saints and foretold it partly through an enigma, suddenly cried out: “Blessed are you, Israel; who is like you, O people that are saved?” (Deut. XXXIII). For the condemnation of the wicked is so great and so terrible, and the glorification of the righteous so great and so terrible, that the observer rightly cries out, and by crying out the spirit signifies what the tongue cannot explain in speech. This is especially so because the time is near, and it is uncertain and cannot be foreseen when [or because] it will arrive, when the last trumpet will sound.

Certainly, when it says “the words of this prophecy,” we must understand or expect prophecy here in every sense—that is, prophecy concerning three times: past, present, and future. For it has been said before us, and it is true, that there are three times of prophecy: past, present, and future. Prophecy concerning the future is: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son” (Isa. VII). Prophecy concerning the past is: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. I). For a human being spoke of that time when no human being existed. Prophecy concerning the present is that of which the Apostle Paul says: “But if all prophesy, and an unbeliever or unlearned person enters, he is convicted by all, judged by all; the hidden things of his heart are made manifest; and thus, falling upon his face, he will worship God, declaring that God is truly among us” (1 Cor. XIV).

Therefore, when it says that the hidden things of his heart are made manifest, it clearly shows that by this mode of prophecy the spirit does not foretell what will be, but reveals what is. Yet it should be known that in two of these times prophecy loses its etymological meaning. For since it is called prophecy because it predicts future things, when it speaks of the past or present it loses the rationale of its name, because it does not prophesy what is future, but either recalls things that have passed or shows things that are.

This prophecy is woven from all these times, or concerning all these times—past, present, and future—because Jesus Christ revealed to this beloved disciple in this Apocalypse what the condition of the Church had been, what it then was, and what it would be, as the blessed reader or hearer can come to know from its wonderful sequence, through the gift of Jesus Christ Himself.

Therefore, with hope in the promised blessedness, let us enter upon the reading of this prophecy with Jesus Christ as our guide; and as we read, let us also hear: outwardly reading the letter, inwardly hearing the mysteries which the Father, hiding them from the wise and prudent, reveals to little ones who apply that ear (Matt. XI) which this prophecy itself frequently requires when it says: “Whoever has an ear to hear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches” (Rev. III).

For what has been said up to this point has been said in order to persuade us to possess or seek such an ear—one attentive, teachable, and well-disposed—something which secular teachers labor with no little effort suitably to produce in their introductions. For [Col. 0832A] in saying, “The Apocalypse [352] of Jesus Christ, which God gave him to make known to his servants the things which must shortly come to pass,” he calls forth the hearer’s attention, as one who promises to speak of great matters soon to occur. He intends to make the hearer teachable by saying, “and he signified it,” for by this he indicates that heavenly mysteries must be sought beneath figures of names or images. He desires the hearer to be well-disposed when he says of his own person: “who bore testimony to the Word of God and to the testimony of Jesus Christ, whatever things he saw.” For such a person, “who bore testimony to the Word of God and to the testimony of Jesus Christ, whatever things he saw,” rightly merits much goodwill from us. Great too is the subject itself, whose fruit for those who read, hear, and keep it is blessedness.

[Col. 0832B] “John, to the seven Churches that are in Asia: grace to you and peace.” All faithful believers everywhere among the nations gladly receive this greeting of grace and peace as truly sent to us from John, freely and truthfully professing that we belong to the seven Churches and are in Asia. For “Asia” is interpreted as “loftiness,” and signifies this world, lifted up and exalting itself, like the waves of the sea, as is sung in the Psalm: “Wonderful are the upliftings of the sea; wonderful is the Lord on high” (Ps. 92). That is to say: Wonderful are the persecutions of the world, but far more wonderful is the Lord in restraining those same persecutions.

In such an Asia are the seven Churches: that is, the one and only Catholic Church, ordered and adorned by the holy sevenfold Spirit. Whatever grace and peace, therefore, are here wished for “the seven Churches that are in Asia,” we who worship Christ among all nations rightly claim for ourselves, even if the Apostle and Evangelist, humble in spirit, seemingly avoids asserting his authority over the whole world and names only that part of the world—Asia Minor—in which he had laboured.

These are the seven women who, in Asia, when the crown of the daughters of Zion has already been made bald, seize one man and say: “We shall eat our own bread and wear our own clothing; only let your name be invoked over us: take away our reproach” (Isa. 4). It is as though all the families of the nations, worshipping him, say: “Behold that nation which, when it had no land, you brought out of Egypt [Col. 0832D] (Ps. 80), and after destroying seven nations in the land of Canaan, allotted their land to it by lot. Behold what repayment it rendered you: it cast you outside the gate of the city and crucified you. At least now turn to us. We do not ask that you give us foreign regions, as the reward for your Gospel, as you gave them the territories of seven nations as the reward for the Law they had received—namely, of the Canaanites, Amorites, Girgashites, Jebusites, Hittites, Perizzites, and Hivites (Josh. 13; Deut. 7). As then, on its account, you destroyed those seven nations, so surely until now, content with love for that one woman as it were, you have disregarded us seven women—that is, the whole body of the nations. Rightly you once complained in the prophet concerning that adulteress, saying: ‘And she did not know that I gave her grain and wine and oil, and multiplied silver and gold for her, which they made into Baal’ (Hos. 2).”

[Col. 0833A] What she has now done is worse: namely, by favouring adulterers, she crucified you. We ask nothing earthly from you beyond what we had before your Gospel: only let your name be invoked over us; take away our reproach, so that the name of demons may no longer be invoked over us.

Therefore, “John to the seven Churches that are in Asia” means the same for us as if he had said: John to all the Churches that are in the world. Beginning in this way, he visibly fulfills in himself that true saying of the Wise Man, which speaks with a splendid promise concerning the one who fears the Lord: “In the midst of the Church he shall open his mouth, and the Lord shall fill him with the spirit of wisdom [Col. 0833B] and understanding” (Ecclus. 15). For behold, in the midst of the seven Churches—which, as has already been said, are all one Church—the Lord opened his mouth; and he speaks so that his discourse is worthy to be heard by all Churches. For his account has a head, namely the Catholic faith, which—or rather, the confession of which—is the head of all sound doctrine.

At this head he makes confession from this point as far as what he later says: “I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end, says the Lord God, who was, and who is, and who is to come, the Almighty.” First he confesses him who was, who is, and who is to come; then his seven spirits; then Christ Jesus, the faithful witness, offering him gold, frankincense, and myrrh. He offers myrrh to him as the man once mortal, [Col. 0833C] saying that he is the firstborn of the dead. He offers gold to him as king, saying that he is ruler of the kings, and that to him belong glory and dominion. Finally, he offers frankincense, saying in his person, or concerning his person: “I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end, says the Lord God,” and so forth.

But no one can adequately grasp how great is the value of a confession poured forth in this manner. For he did not speak as is customarily said by ordinary people or in the public Church: “I believe in him who is, and who was, and who is to come, and in his seven spirits, and in Jesus Christ the faithful witness”—as we confess in the daily creed, not indeed in the same words or syllables, but in the same sense and manner of expression. By one and the same reasoning he both confesses the faith and invokes upon his hearers faith and the fruit of faith. And although he does both, he appears to do only one thing—namely, to invoke grace and peace—unless one attends carefully.

Just as gold melted in fire, and frankincense or myrrh cast upon coals, abandons its former shape, so this confession of faith, set ablaze by the great fire of brotherly love, can scarcely be recognized as a confession of faith, because the force of the prayer of invocation has almost wholly transformed it into itself. But let us now examine the words themselves in order.

“Grace,” he says, “to you and peace, from him who was, and who is, and who is to come.” “Grace and peace” is a very customary greeting of Christ, in the manner of the Apostles, and especially in the manner of Paul, whom the grace poured out upon the lips of Christ himself called his chosen vessel. [Col. 0834A] For in none of his Epistles does he omit a greeting of this kind. The phrase is therefore worthy to be weighed, as though in a balance, and its weight considered; and, if it cannot be wholly defined, at least estimated in some measure.

What, I ask, did the Apostles—of whom this man is one, beloved of Jesus Christ—receive through Jesus Christ himself, if not grace and peace? For they were called by grace, not by works (1 Cor. 15), in order that they might be what they were, namely Apostles; and they were honoured by grace alone as long as the Lord Jesus himself, who had called them, walked with them. But when, dying for us, he paid to the eternal Father Adam’s debt (Col. 2), and wiped away with his gracious blood the bond of the ancient offence, then, rising on the third day, he brought them peace, standing in their midst and saying to them: “Peace to you” (Luke 26 [an apparent citation error]). For through the death of the cross he had reconciled them to God, having broken down the wall of enmity (Eph. 2).

What they had received, therefore—first the calling of grace, then the peace of necessary reconciliation—they ought to wish and offer to us both, not from themselves but from him from whom they had received them, namely “from him who was, and who is, and who is to come.” This, I say, they ought earnestly to remind them of, so that they might know that they had been called by God through grace and might preserve the peace and reconciliation by which they had been reconciled to God through Christ.

Meanwhile, I do not wish to pass over in silence that, while the Apostle Paul just mentioned joins these two in greeting the Churches throughout all his Epistles, saying, “Grace to you and peace,” only in those which he writes to his disciple Timothy does he insert mercy: [Col. 0834C] “To Timothy,” he says, “my beloved son in the faith: grace, mercy, and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Tim. 1). For since in Timothy he was instructing all bishops, the highest and necessary ornament of whose office is mercy—and Timothy, as is reported, was more fervent in zeal—he rightly and fittingly wished him to possess the bowels of mercy, saying among other things: “Do not rebuke an elder, but exhort him as a father” (1 Tim. 5).

Indeed, all of us ought to remember that whatever good we are or possess is the grace of God, not from ourselves; and for this reason we ought to sympathize with those who do not yet seem to be what we are or possess what we possess (1 Cor. 4; 2 Cor. 3), according to the mystical example of the holy Law, in which the Lord says: “You shall not trouble a stranger. For you know the souls of strangers, because you yourselves were strangers in the land of Egypt” (Exod. 23). Yet this is especially to be observed by bishops, who are appointed guardians of souls; but it is very necessary both for them and for their subjects.

Accordingly, it was most beneficially arranged for us that he to whom mercy was especially to say [variant: who was especially about to say mercy], “Feed my lambs,” should first learn in his own fall how merciful he ought to be. But let us return to the path of the letter which we began: “From him,” he says, “who was, and who is, and who is to come.”

Some have thought that these words should be understood of the person of the Son, chiefly because he says last, “and who is to come.” For the Son himself is to come to judge the living and the dead; and here, they say, no mention is made of the person of the Father, but only of the Son and the Holy Spirit—twice of the Son, namely both in what was first said, “from him who was, and who is, and who is to come,” and in what is said later, “and from Jesus Christ, who is the faithful witness”; but once of the Holy Spirit, in the words, “and from the seven spirits who are before his throne.”

But the Apostle Paul already mentioned meets this objection, repeatedly saying and repeatedly distinguishing: “Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.” Certainly the Father of Christ is our Father, as he says: “I ascend to my Father and your Father” (John 20); and he both was, and is, and is to come. [Col. 0835B] Only the final phrase, “and who is to come,” seems to compel the interpretation of these words as spoken of the Son, because the angels said of this person: “He shall so come as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts 1).

Yet the Father too will undoubtedly come—that is, he will manifest himself to the faithful—who now see him “through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face” (1 Cor. 13). There is only this difference: the Son will come in the form of a servant (Phil. 2), so that at last not only the good but also the evil will see his form, as is written below: “Every eye shall see him, even those who pierced him.” But the Father will come—that is, appear—so that only the good shall see the glory of God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

If testimony from Scripture is needed in order that one may rightly believe that the Father is to come in that sense, behold what is written in Daniel: “And I watched until thrones were set in place, and the Ancient of Days sat” (Dan. 7). Again: “And behold, that horn made war against the saints and prevailed over them, until the Ancient of Days came and gave judgment to the saints of the Most High; and the time came, and the saints obtained the kingdom” (ibid.). Who can doubt that, when the Ancient of Days comes, the person of the Father is expressed? For concerning the person of the Son it is written in the same place: “I watched therefore in the vision of the night, and behold, the Son of Man came in the clouds of heaven and reached as far as the Ancient of Days” (ibid.).

Therefore, nothing prevents us from understanding as God the Father him [Col. 0835D] “who was, and who is, and who is to come.” Indeed, it is most beautiful, fitting, and venerable that, when there follows “and from the seven spirits who are before his throne, and from Jesus Christ, who is the faithful witness,” a glorious confession of the whole Trinity should be believed to be proclaimed.

The Father was, that is, he remained immutable in himself before he created these mutable things. He is also, that is, he remains immutable while he governs these same things in their mutable course. He will likewise come, that is, he will appear immutable when this corruptible appearance of mutable things has passed away. But much later it is written of the evil beast that attempts to oppose this purpose: “And the beast that I saw [you saw] was, and is not.” Let John himself, therefore, banished into exile, and all who desire to live devoutly in Christ and suffer persecution (2 Tim. 3), receive consolation in this grace: for it shall come to pass that of every persecution or persecutor it will be said, “It was, and is not.” But of him for whose sake they suffer, let it always be said: “Who was, and who is, and who shall never cease to be.”

[Col. 0836A] “And from the seven spirits who are before his throne.” “From the seven spirits,” that is, from the sevenfold Spirit. In speaking thus, he looks back to the expression of the earlier Scripture, where it is written: “And the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. 11).

And here he appropriately looked to the form of that Scripture, especially because he of whom the prophet spoke—“the flower that rises from the root of Jesse” (ibid.), the Lamb of God and likewise the mighty Lion—signified both the power and glory of these same seven spirits resting upon him: in his seven horns and seven eyes; in the seven lamps burning before the throne of God; and in so many sevenfold signs of mysteries—the seven books sealed with seals, the trumpets of seven angels, and the seven bowls; and, before all else, the seven stars and seven lampstands, that is, the seven Churches.

Therefore, “from the seven spirits,” that is, from the one holy sevenfold Spirit, one must supply the same phrase: grace to you and peace. These seven spirits are before the same throne of the Father—that is, before the holy angels, who are so truly God’s throne, and God sits so truly in them, that some of them are even properly called “thrones.” They have this because these spirits are before them—that is, because they behold these spirits. For unless they were strengthened by this sevenfold Spirit, they could never bear the weight of God who sits upon them.

For this Spirit is love, by which alone a rational creature is made fit for the majesty of God to sit in it; and no one who does not love that majesty can bear it. Conversely, of those before whose eyes or in whose careful remembrance these spirits are not present, the Psalmist says: “As wax melts before the fire, so let sinners perish before the face of God” (Ps. 67). Thus you should understand that no one can stand before the face of God—much less be God’s throne—who does not possess this Spirit of love.

[Col. 0836D] From this sevenfold Spirit, therefore, he says, “grace and peace to the seven Churches,” the fruit of which grace and peace is that they too may be the throne of God with the holy angelic spirits. “And from Jesus Christ, who is the faithful witness, the firstborn of the dead, and ruler of the kings of the earth.” And from Jesus Christ, he says—supply: grace and peace—“since through him grace itself was made, and he is our peace” (Eph. 2). For grace and peace came through Jesus Christ, and “he himself,” says the Apostle, “is our peace, who made both one” (Rom. 8 [an apparent citation error]).

This person did more in obtaining for us this peace and grace, and gave himself up, by assuming our nature and becoming obedient “unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. 2), then raising that same nature of ours from the dead in himself and causing it to sit at the Father’s right hand, where it now is, holding firm authority for us over this grace and peace.

[Col. 0837A] He rightly placed this person last, that is, in third place, both because he is about to say more about him here and because in what follows this same person is seen in diverse figures, speaks the most, and speaks almost everything. For the seven spirits indeed each in turn speak to the individual Churches, as we shall consider more carefully in its place; and concerning each of them, or through each of them, it is said: “He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the Churches.” But that very speaking of the Spirit speaks in this person: “Write to this or that Church, or to the angel of the Church.”

Thus, as the matter [or matters] requires, this same person is adorned and commended with praises, so that in all that he says in this Scripture, as in the others, faith may be given him without doubt. “Who,” he says, “is the faithful witness.” And immediately he adds, “the firstborn of the dead.” He adds further, “and ruler of the kings of the earth.” And still more fully: “Who loved us,” he says, “and washed us from our sins in his blood, and made us a kingdom and priests to God and his Father. To him be glory and dominion for ages of ages. Amen. Behold, he comes with the clouds, and every eye shall see him, even those who pierced him; and all tribes of the earth shall mourn over him. Even so, Amen. I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end, says the Lord God, who was, and who is, and who is to come, the Almighty.”

[Col. 0837C] In this way, as was said above, the Apostle beloved of Christ Jesus, in gracious speech, confesses the Catholic faith and at the same time invokes upon the Churches the grace of that faith. Though he most beautifully does both, he wonderfully appears to do only one thing: to invoke grace and peace. Every expression proceeds with supreme dignity; each contains, in few syllables, the majesty of meanings most expansive.

“Who,” he says, “is the faithful witness.” Truly he is a witness—Greek *martyr* (μάρτυρ)—because he was born to bear witness to the truth and died for the testimony of the truth, as he himself says to Pilate: “For this I was born, and for this I came into the world: to bear witness to the truth” (John 18). The Father too is a witness, of whom Jesus Christ himself says: “The Father who sent me bears witness concerning me” (John 8). And the Holy Spirit is a witness, of whom he likewise says: “When the Paraclete comes, whom I shall send to you from the Father—the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father—he shall bear witness concerning me” (John 13 [an apparent citation error]).

But this alone is the person who suffered death for the testimony of truth; hence the Son alone is fittingly called here “the witness.” Many, indeed, have suffered death as witnesses to the truth, on account of the word of their testimony; and for this reason the holy Church customarily calls them by the Greek name *martyrs* (μάρτυρες). Yet there is no slight difference on account of which this one is splendidly called, with the addition, “the faithful witness.”

For what this witness testified, he saw and heard before he came into this world. Before, I say, he saw and heard; then he was born into this world and “came into the world to bear witness to the truth,” as he himself said before the governor already mentioned. Hence John the Baptist also says: “He who comes from heaven is above all; and what he has seen and heard, that he testifies” (John 3). All others came from the earth and were born before they knew anything; afterwards they received from elsewhere, from another informant, what they might declare in testimony. And even this they knew not perfectly but in part, as Paul the Apostle, one of them, says: “For we know in part, and we prophesy in part” (1 Cor. 13).

[Col. 0838B] Therefore he alone is the faithful witness: that is, such a witness as had seen and heard the matter before coming here to testify, so certain that he knew and prophesied not partially but wholly and perfectly. Add that, having died for this same testimony of truth, he conquered death itself and rose from the dead, something the other witnesses had not done before him. This is what is immediately said: “the firstborn of the dead,” that is, the first of those rising from the dead.

For resurrection will be regeneration for us: since now, being born, we are generated unto corruption, but then, rising again, we shall be regenerated unto incorruption. Hence the Lord says: “In the regeneration, when the Son of Man shall sit upon the throne of his majesty” (Matt. 19). He says “in the regeneration” to mean “in the universal resurrection.” In that regeneration of the dead this witness is beyond doubt the firstborn, because he rose before them all, never thereafter to die. For no one before him rose in such a way as never to die again (Rom. 6). He also granted and effected this for the other witnesses, of whom righteous Abel was the first: that they should rise and never die again.

It is a very beautiful and splendid expression that he should be called “the firstborn of the dead” because he was the first to rise. Delighting in this splendour, we say that in such a birth the blessed souls of the Apostles stood, as it were, as mothers, since they grieved with maternal affection for the Lord Jesus Christ while he was dying, until he rose again. For this reason he used this comparison in speaking to or concerning them: “A woman, when she gives birth, has sorrow because her hour has come; but when she has borne a child, she no longer remembers the distress because of joy that a human being has been born into the world” (John 16).

[Col. 0838D] Finally, what did he do after being thus regenerated to immortality and incorruption? He ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of God (Acts 2). “God,” says Peter, “raised him up and exalted him as Prince and Saviour” (1 Pet. 5 [an apparent citation error]). Accordingly he adds: “And ruler of the kings of the earth.”

Of which kings of the earth, or what kind? Surely not those such as stood against the Lord and against his Christ? He is not ruler of such men here; rather, he is their judge. Such people call themselves kings of the earth, but are not: they are slaves of the earth, since they are slaves of sin, subject to earthly desires. He is ruler of those who, even though they are not commonly called kings, are nevertheless kings of the earth because they know how to govern their earthliness, being free from sin but servants of righteousness (Rom. 6). Thus he is ruler only of kings. For all who wish to belong to him must be such.

O truly beautiful and glorious rule of this ruler, who makes all those subject to him kings—or a kingdom—and a royal priesthood. For this is what is said afterwards: “And he made us a kingdom and priests.” This rule differs greatly from the tyranny of this world. “The kings of the nations,” he says, “lord it over them, and those who have authority over them are called benefactors” (Luke 22). Speaking these and other things to his servants, this ruler of kings even washed their feet (John 13). By performing this act proper to a servant, he confirmed what he had said: “But I am in your midst as one who serves” (Luke 22).

[Col. 0839B] For in what further service could the diligent minister abase himself for kings of the nations? Yet while serving thus, he would still be Lord and Master, for they needed his teaching. But there, where he ascended after his resurrection, just as he had no need of service, they had no need of teaching. Therefore, there still more, he will not be king of those who wage war or Lord of those who serve, but, as it is written, “King of kings and Lord of lords.”

It follows: “Who loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood.” The faithful witness had briefly deferred what was greatest in his work when he said, “who is the faithful witness,” and immediately added “the firstborn of the dead,” because, anticipating the glory of the resurrection, he had passed over the saving mystery of his passion. But now he repeats it more beautifully and splendidly, in gracious speech: “Who loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood.”

Let us linger for a little while in this sweetest honeycomb of thanksgiving, and draw sweet speech for our throats, sweeter to our mouth than honey and the honeycomb (Ps. 18). “Who loved us,” he says: certainly before the ages of the world; and this Son loved us in the Father, and the Father in this Son. Thus the Apostle Paul says to the Ephesians: “As he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him in love; having predestined us for adoption as sons through [Col. 0839D] Jesus Christ unto himself, according to the purpose of his will, to the praise of his grace, by which he made us gracious in his beloved Son” (Eph. 1).

Yearning for the act of this love, the Church says in its first utterance in the Song of Songs: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song 1). What she desired came to pass. The loving and beloved one came, wholly desirable and anointed with every fragrance of all graces; in the secret chamber of the virginal womb he bestowed upon his beloved the long-desired kiss, where God’s nature—the true God—joined itself to human nature, to true flesh and a true rational soul.

Then, “like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber” (Ps. 18), he gave his whole devoted attention to writing into the testament of his bride, and of her whole race, a heavenly dowry. Her race, I say, means all souls which, together with that flesh of his, are through the one faith one race, one Church, one body.

[Col. 0840A] The judgment came, of which he also said: “Now is the judgment of the world; now shall the ruler of this world be cast out” (John 12). In the equity of the judgment he showed that the human nature he possessed was free from the guilt of Adam’s transgression. “For,” he says, “the ruler of this world comes, and has nothing in me.” He showed this also by his obedience in coming to Jerusalem, where he was sought in order to be killed.

For God had commanded in the Law: “Three times in every year you shall celebrate feasts for me. You shall keep the solemnity of unleavened bread, and the solemnity of the harvest of firstfruits, and also the solemnity at the end of the year, when you gather all your crops from the field. Three times in the year all your males shall appear before the Lord your God” (Exod. 24; Deut. 16). Therefore, when he had come to Jerusalem according to the command of the Law, that rash ruler of this world already mentioned rushed upon him; and from him who had no cause of death—that is, no sin—he exacted the penalty of death, forgetting in his folly the tenor of the right he claimed for himself to possess all human beings because of the sin of one man. For if through one offence many were made sinners, why should not through one man’s righteousness many be made righteous?

Loving us, therefore, he died for us and “washed us from our sins in his blood.” How? “One of the soldiers opened his side with a spear, and immediately blood and water came out” (John 19). By that blood he redeemed us; by that water he washed us from our sins. “Us,” says the beloved Apostle of Jesus Christ, counting himself among those who sinned. Do not suppose that he makes any distinction between Jew and Greek (Rom. 10). Another man too, from the Israelite people, says: “We too were once by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Eph. 2). Likewise another, of acknowledged holiness, from that people says: “All our righteousnesses are like the cloth of a menstruating woman” (Isa. 64).

[Col. 0840D] “Therefore he washed us,” that is, the whole Church, “from our sins.” To this extent he loved us. He did not love us as we were, but by loving us he made us different; by washing us in that blood and that water, he regenerated us. Thus by love he made the Church one body with the flesh which he had assumed; thus he gave himself for her, “that he might sanctify her, cleansing her by the washing of water in the word of life, that he might present her to himself a glorious Church, having neither spot nor wrinkle nor anything of the kind, but that she might be holy and blameless” (Eph. 5).

He washed not only those who already were or had been believers, but all who were to be. He did not wash those who were to be then already in act, but in power. For those not yet born, or not yet believing, could not then already be washed. He gave them power to be washed; through the washing of regeneration he gave them power to become children of God. For after rising from the dead, he said to his disciples: “Go, teach [Col. 0841A] all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28).

That way, that rule of baptism, that water which had gone out from the right side of that temple—the temple of his pierced body—and had washed the primitive Church gathered from the beginning of the world, descended into the sea of the nations, according to Ezekiel’s prophecy: “These waters, which go forth toward the eastern mounds of sand and descend to the plains of the desert, shall enter the sea; and they shall go out, and the waters shall be healed; and every living creature that moves shall live wherever the torrent comes” (Ezek. 68 [an apparent citation error]).

This is the great fruit of the love by which he loved us, and by which God the Word joined our nature to himself in the virginal womb. That bond of love, with such an outcome, gathered into one all the children of God who had been scattered abroad.

“And he made us,” he says, “a kingdom and priests to God and his Father.” O wonderful condescension of goodness, greater than our heart and speech: he did not purchase us at so dear a price, by his most precious blood, for slavery, but in order to make us a kingdom and priests—to his Father, a kingdom; to his God, priests. He alone was king and priest; he purposed, by shedding his blood, to make kings and priests from slaves of sin and children of death. Of how great merits is this faithful witness the source, and of how many crowns the head!

The Lord says in the prophet: “You shall take silver and gold, make crowns, and place them upon the head of Jesus son of Josedec, the high priest” (Zech. 6). On this the distinguished man Jerome says: “Crowns are placed upon the head of Jesus son of Josedec, the high priest, because the Lord is crowned through each of our virtues; indeed, when we are crowned through the virtue of repentance, the Saviour receives a crown in each person.” Truly, therefore, “O Lord our Lord, how admirable is your name, because you have crowned with wonderful glory and honour” (Ps. 8) this princely king—with as many and such great crowns as there are kings composing this kingdom, in which all who have been consecrated by his blood are resplendent kings.

[Col. 0841C] “And he made us priests,” namely, of that sacrifice by which he conquered the spiritual Pharaoh, that is, the devil, and destroyed the kingdom of sin. For just as the sons of Aaron were priests of that typical sacrifice because their father, together with Moses, was a minister of that deliverance commemorated by the Paschal feast of the year-old lamb, so the sons of this priest—whom he spiritually begot through the washing of regeneration—are rightly priests of that sacrifice which commemorates not a temporal salvation, as that former sacrifice did, but the eternal salvation of all.

Thus it is rightly of no consequence from what people or tribe someone comes, provided that the person is qualified in knowledge and conduct, because all of us are children in the Spirit of the heavenly priest, who begot no one according to the flesh. Even if we do not all exercise here that priestly order by which we consecrate with sacred speech the body and blood of our Lord, still we must all be priests in this respect: that we offer ourselves to God, as the Apostle says: “I beseech you to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing to God—your rational service” (Rom. 12).

[Col. 0842A] Otherwise we are not permitted to enter into those heavenly Holy of Holies, into heaven itself, where these forms of our sacrifice—the forms of bread and wine—shall not be.

The sacrifice which he will offer forever shall never fail: namely, the sacrifice of thanksgiving, and the voice of praise, the voice of exultation and confession. Such is precisely what he immediately adds here: “To him be glory and dominion for ages of ages. Amen.” For the rule of justice itself requires that, when a benefit has been received, the creature should render praise and thanksgiving to the Creator.

For example: thus Moses and the children of Israel, delivered from Egyptian bondage through the blood of the lamb, after Pharaoh and his army had been submerged in the Red Sea, sang a song of glory to the Lord (Exod. XV). For the beginning of ingratitude [Col. 0842B] is not to acknowledge a benefit, and to keep one’s mouth mute and one’s tongue still when thanks should be returned. Therefore let us all say this brief song of praise and thanksgiving, as he says, “To him be glory and dominion for ages of ages,” “Amen”—“and every tongue,” as the Apostle says, “confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. II).

Thus far this leader of our faith, one among its most illustrious leaders, has himself confessed those things necessary to the perfection of confession, and has given us an example of confession. And although in different words, yet in the same sense in which all the apostles confess in the common Creed what they handed down to us, one thing remains—and it is the greatest of all: namely, that from the place where he now sits as “the ruler of the kings of the earth,” [Col. 0842C] where glory and dominion are his for ages of ages, he will come from that glory of his, from that right hand of the Father, with his great dominion and majesty, to judge the living and the dead.

It follows, therefore: “Behold, he comes with the clouds, and every eye shall see him, even those who pierced him.” “Behold,” he says, that is, because he is near. Hence another Apostle also says: “The Lord is near; be anxious about nothing” (Phil. IV). It is customary in the manner of the prophets and of all the holy watchmen, who vigilantly foresaw that coming, to say: “Behold, he will come; behold, he will appear; he will come swiftly; he will soon appear to you” (Isa. LXVI; Ezek. VII; Joel I).

But the evil servant thinks this will happen only after a long time, and says in his heart [Col. 0842D]: “My lord delays his coming”; and he begins “to beat his fellow-servants, and to eat and drink with the drunken” (Luke XII). But what then? The lord of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him, and at an hour that he does not know; and he will divide him, and appoint his portion with the hypocrites: “there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Luke XIII). Thus to those who sleep, and who through drunkenness have a constricted faculty of perception, the times seem long. But to those who keep watch—whose prudent souls faith has nourished, hope has advanced, charity has enlarged and made great—every span of the present age seems short in comparison with eternity and the age to come. “Therefore, behold, he comes; he comes quickly; he will appear quickly.”

How? In what conveyances? Seated upon what tribunal? “With clouds,” he says. This very thing he also [Col. 0843A] foretold: “From that time they shall see the Son of Man coming in a cloud,” or “in the clouds of heaven,” as it is written in another Gospel, “with great power and majesty” (Luke XXI; Matt. XXIV). The angels too, when he ascended, said: “He shall so come as you have seen him going into heaven” (Acts I). A cloud had received him out of their sight. Therefore he shall so come: that is, he whom a cloud received shall come again with a cloud, or with the clouds of heaven. Of these clouds the Apostle also says: “Together we shall be caught up in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and thus we shall always be with the Lord” (I Thess. IV).

Here it is now asked why he will come thus, and why with clouds. Is it in order that he may be concealed or hidden by clouds? Certainly not. For then he will come manifestly [Col. 0843B], since formerly he came hidden; and, as is written here, every eye shall see him. Why then will he come with clouds? Let us question another Scripture.

When the prophet Isaiah had spoken concerning the wicked in the form of a question, saying: “And he shall not see the glory of the Lord,” he immediately added, by a kind of concession: “Lord, let your hand be exalted, and let them not see.” Then he at once added: “Let them see and be confounded, ye that are zealous for the people; and let fire devour your enemies” (Isa. XXVI). As though he had uselessly granted, “Let your hand be exalted, and let them not see,” he corrects it by saying: “Let them see and be confounded.” Thus, in one way they will not see; yet in another way even the wicked will see him as he comes.

So that the wicked may not see the glory of the Lord, he will come with clouds; so that the wicked, seeing, may be confounded [Col. 0843C], every eye shall see him. For the clouds with which he will come will conceal his glory, so that the wicked may not see it; but they will not conceal the power of his majesty so as to prevent every eye from seeing it. What sort of clouds will those then be? Certainly not such as we now often see, dripping with rain and refreshing the earth, but storm-clouds, breathing fire and hurling lightning. For “fire shall burn before him, and a mighty tempest round about him” (Ps. XLIX).

Paul, striving to express the violence of such clouds, of burning clouds, writes to the Thessalonians: “If indeed it is just with God to repay affliction to those who afflict us, and rest with us to you who are afflicted, at the revelation of the Lord Jesus from heaven with the angels of his power. In a flame [Col. 0843D] of fire, inflicting vengeance upon those who do not know God” (II Thess. IV), etc. This every eye shall see. The wicked shall see it, that they may be confounded; but they shall not see the glory of the Lord, for the purpose of preventing them from seeing which his hand shall be exalted. The brightness of his body—or the body of his brightness—to which, as the Apostle says, he will conform the body of our lowliness (Phil. III), those clouds spread over the wicked will conceal; but they will not conceal the Son of Man himself. Every eye shall see him, and the wicked, seeing, shall be confounded. But the godly shall see his glory: they who, in order to be always with the Lord, as the Apostle says, shall be caught up in the clouds to meet the Lord (I Thess. IV). They shall swiftly pass upward unharmed through fiery clouds, through clouded fires, and thus shall always be with the Lord.

[Col. 0844A] The wicked below shall be astonished and shall see, in order that, seeing, they may be confounded—especially those who pierced him: those, namely, who bored his hands and feet with nails and pierced his side with a spear. Those indeed shall be confounded when they see him; and all who do not obey his Gospel shall share in their confusion. “And all the tribes of the earth shall mourn over him.”

This the Apostle and Evangelist says here on the testimony of the earlier prophet—he who drank wisdom from the breast of the Lord, a Hebrew of the Hebrews, whom the Saviour loved exceedingly. For in Zechariah the person of this ruler of kings speaks thus: “And they shall look upon me whom they pierced, and they shall mourn with mourning as for an only-begotten son, and they shall grieve over him as men are wont to grieve [Col. 0844B] at the death of a firstborn” (Zech. XII).

This same John, in his Gospel, quoted only the portion of this prophetic testimony, “They shall look upon me whom they pierced.” Having first said, “They did not break his legs, but one of the soldiers opened the Lord’s side with a spear,” he adds: “For these things happened that the Scripture might be fulfilled: ‘You shall not break a bone of it’” (John XIX; Exod. XII). “And again another Scripture says: ‘They shall look on him whom they pierced’” (Zech. XII). But what he omitted there—namely, the following clause, “and they shall mourn with mourning as for an only-begotten son”—he added here in this way: “And all the tribes of the earth shall mourn over him.”

What he says here, “all the tribes of the earth,” you likewise find in the same prophet, where it is immediately written as follows: [Col. 0844C] “And the land shall mourn, families and families separately: the families of the house of David separately, and their women, or wives, separately; the families of the house of Nathan separately, and their women separately; the families of the house of Levi separately, and their women separately; the families of Shimei separately, and their women separately. All the remaining families, families and families separately, and their women separately” (ibid.).

For “families” the Septuagint translators put “tribes,” whom John followed elsewhere, since he was writing in Greek, the language into which the same Seventy translators rendered the Scriptures. Therefore, when he now says “all the tribes of the earth,” he speaks on the testimony of the same prophet. For then the tribe of the house of David, the tribe of the house of Nathan, [Col. 0844D] the tribe of the house of Levi, and the tribe of the house of Shimei shall be separated from their wives: that is, they shall be deprived of all their pleasures, in order that they may mourn the only-begotten and firstborn Lord Jesus Christ, concerning whom they said: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. XXVII).

In David the royal tribe is understood, that is, Judah; in Nathan the prophetic order is described; Levi refers to the priests, from whom the priesthood arose; in Shimei teachers are understood, for from this tribe companies of masters sprang up. He passed over the remaining tribes, which possess no privilege of rank. But by saying, “every remaining tribe, tribe and tribe separately, and their wives separately,” he includes them all without naming them.

[Col. 0845A] Now such mourning then occurred as a type [or: as something typical] when the righteous king Josiah was wounded by Pharaoh surnamed Necho. Jeremiah wrote lamentations concerning him, which are read in the Church; and the book of Chronicles testifies that he wrote them (II Chron. XXXV). For what is written there, namely in the Lamentations—“The breath of our nostrils, Christ the Lord, was taken in our sins, of whom we said: ‘In your shadow we shall live among the nations’” (Lam. IV)—far surpasses the person of Josiah, except insofar as, as has already been said, he who was wounded was a type of the Saviour to be crucified.

For as at that time, after sinful kings, all the people’s hope rested in Josiah, and a great mourning arose in the city when he was killed, so at the crucified Saviour a mourning shall then be renewed [Col. 0845B] among all the tribes of the earth: that is, among lovers of the earth, who killed him, speaking and devising deceits, as the Psalmist says, “in the wrath of the earth” (Ps. XXXIV), that is, angry because of the land which they pretended would be taken from them on his account. “If we let him go on thus,” they say, “all will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away our place and nation” (John XI).

And it is to be noted—indeed, it is marvellous—that he said: “They shall mourn him as for an only-begotten son, and shall grieve over him as men are wont to grieve at the death of a firstborn.” I remember having said in a certain work concerning this:

> O Jews, Christ the Son of God did not please you because he was such as he was; because he came in such a manner; because he acted thus and thus; because he spoke thus and thus. He pleased you in no respect; he did not suit your mind [Col. 0845C]. You desire another; you await another. But he—that is, God the Father, who sent this Son—has no other. This Son is his firstborn and only-begotten. He has no other, I say. This one is his first and his last; he will send no other. What then will you do, left desolate? Surely, as he now says, you will look upon him whom you pierced; as, I say, his Spirit now says, with grave truth and true gravity, you shall mourn over him as for an only-begotten son and grieve over him as men are wont to grieve at the death of a firstborn. For this firstborn has died to you, because you yourselves have slain for yourselves the only-begotten; hereafter you will have neither this Saviour nor another, because he alone is the firstborn, he alone the only-begotten.

Intending to reinforce all this with emphatic affirmation, because [Col. 0845D] it shall undoubtedly come to pass, he says: “Yes, amen,” which is the same as saying what he customarily writes in his Gospel when the Lord says: “Amen, amen.” For whereas in the other evangelists *amen* is written only once in individual passages—for example, in Luke: “Amen, I say to you, heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away” (Luke XXI)—in this Evangelist *amen* itself is always doubled. This is because the mouth of this Evangelist is more divine, and the Lord Jesus speaks greater things in him; and therefore, so that the weight of the matters may be felt, the form—or weight—of the expression is likewise doubled, for the force of confirmation: “Amen, amen, I say to thee”; “Amen, amen, I say to you.”

What greater or more terrible thing can be said than what he has said [Col. 0846A] in the present passage? Rightly, then, in this place he doubled the affirmation, saying, “Yes, amen,” so that everyone who hears may awaken to belief. It follows:

“I am α and ω, the beginning and the end, says the Lord God, who is, and who was, and who is to come, the Almighty.”

Everything he has said thus far concerning the person of the Son was little, and insufficient for the salvation of one believing or confessing. For what would offend Cerinthus, Ebion, Arius, or any other heretic hostile to Christ’s divinity, in the designation of the Lord Jesus as the faithful witness, the firstborn of the dead—that is, the first to rise from the dead—and ruler of the kings of the earth; or in saying that he loved us [Col. 0846B] and washed us from our sins in his own blood, and would come with the clouds, namely to judge the living and the dead? Any heretic of this kind would grant and confess these things; but he would not confess that he is God, equal to God the Father, or abiding from the beginning with the Father or in the Father.

Rightly, therefore, not content with saying those things, he adds this supreme point, in which the Christian faith consists: speaking sublimely of Christ’s divinity, at its highest degree, with the same judgment as of the Father—as is fitting—and speaking in Christ’s person, in order that the talkative frogs who contradict him may be crushed by a louder thunder: “I am α and ω, the beginning and the end, says the Lord God, who is, and who was, and who is to come, the Almighty.”

For in saying this—or by introducing him as saying it—he makes him equal to the Father [Col. 0846C], of whom he had said above: “Who is, and who was, and who is to come.” What he says, and what he intends by α and ω, he immediately explains by saying: “the beginning and the end.” These are two Greek letters, and he wrote this book to churches using their language. These two letters, α and ω, are respectively the first and last of that language. Therefore, that there may be no doubt what beginning or what end, or of what thing, he means: reminded by α, which, as has already been said, is the first letter of the Greek alphabet, let us look to the beginning of Holy Scripture, where it is written: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. I); and, reminded by ω, which is the last letter, let us likewise look to the end of the same Scripture in the Gospel volume, [Col. 0846D] where it is written: “And behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII). Thus may we truly believe and confess him to be both the beginning, in whom all things were made, and the end or consummation, in which all things have been restored and perfected.

Moreover, this also should be known: α signifies one, but ω signifies eight hundred among the Greeks. For among the Greeks all letters form words and also make numbers; and the later they are in order, the larger are the numbers denoted by their characters. The first letter, α, as has been said, signifies one; ω signifies eight hundred. And in this, indeed, there is a great and pleasing beauty of mystery, because [Col. 0847A]: he who at the beginning was one Son, the only Son or only-begotten, shall at the end of the ages have with him sons of God—not begotten, indeed, but adopted—like eight hundred, that is, innumerable, rewarded by being distributed among diverse dwelling-places according to the eight beatitudes, and distributed by their reward.

Where else does the Lord God say this besides this passage? Not only in his Gospel, where he says to the Jews: “I am the beginning, who also speak to you” (John VIII); but the person of the Saviour himself also speaks in Isaiah: “Before me no God was formed, and after me there shall be none. I am the Lord, and besides me there is no saviour” (Isa. XLIII).

Further, when, as has been stated, “he comes with clouds, when every eye shall see him, even those who pierced him,” those who spoke evil of him—“When shall he die, and his name perish?” [Col. 0847B] (Ps. XL)—those who, in piercing or transfixing him, wished to bring this about: that he should altogether cease to be, that his memory should altogether be removed from the earth (Matt. XIII; Luke IV)—then the Lord God aptly says here: “Then,” I say, “he shall shout and cry aloud, and prevail against his enemies” (Isa. XLIII), and he shall say this to them: “I am α and ω, the beginning and the end.” As though he said: I am not, as you reproached me, the carpenter’s son; I did not begin to exist from that carpenter Joseph. I did not perish, as you wished me to perish, nor did I cease to be; but I am before Joseph and before all things, and after me there shall be none. For I said to you also in the prophet: “Before me no God was formed, and after me there shall be none” (ibid.).

What follows—“Who is, and who was, and who is to come, the Almighty” [Col. 0847C]—confirms the same utterance: “I am α and ω; I am the beginning and the end.” For it is the voice of John and of all of us who believe and confess, that here the Lord God bears witness to the truth concerning himself: that he is not a recent God or Lord, but is he from whom, or with whom, the prophets who came and were sent used of old to say: “Thus says the Lord God.” He is the same Almighty who was before Abraham, for he spoke to him, saying: “I am the Lord Almighty; walk before me and be perfect” (Gen. XVII); and he himself is to come and shall remain in his glorious being, when his enemies have been reduced to nothing [Col. 0847D] (Ps. CVII)—those who, piercing him, said: “When shall he die?” or: “Behold, he shall die, and his name shall perish” (Ps. XL).

Having thus prefaced his work with this so splendid an array of so great, so catholic, and so apostolic a confession, at last the teacher of holy faith, the venerable confessor, and great herald of heavenly reverence enters upon his narrative. Speaking amid the seven Churches, or amid the one universal Church, he is worthily heard with open mouth:

“I, John, your brother and companion in the tribulation and kingdom and patience of Jesus, was on the island called Patmos, because of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus Christ. I was in the Spirit on the Lord’s Day, and heard behind me a great voice like a trumpet saying: What thou seest, write [Col. 0848A] in a book, and send it to the seven Churches that are in Asia: to Ephesus, and Smyrna, and Pergamum, and Thyatira, and Sardis, and Philadelphia, and Laodicea.”

Behold, this diligent and careful author now for the third time has prefixed the title of his name to this work. First, when he said: “He signified it, sending by his angel to his servant John.” Second, when he said: “John to the seven Churches which are in Asia.” And now a third time: “I,” he says, “John, your brother.” For what reason does he, who is about to speak or narrate, triple the placement of his name in this manner? Was it by chance, or because he sought to make much of his name, that he urges and repeats it? Certainly not. Rather, having our benefit in view, he fortifies and defends the most difficult revelations which he begins to write, lest they be despised; lest, because of its [Col. 0848B] difficulty, the book—which was to come—be criticized and judged to lack worthy meanings; or lest it be denied to belong to him whose it is, namely John, apostle and evangelist beloved of Jesus Christ.

For this happened long after that time. Some, holding a Jewish understanding of future promises and teaching that they would be bestowed bodily, and that for a thousand years the saints would reign with Christ in bodily delights upon this earth, attempted to establish proofs for this doctrine of theirs by taking testimonies from this Revelation. On the other hand, others, as Ecclesiastical History testifies, thought that this book should be wholly rejected from and cast out of the canon of Scripture. They attacked each individual chapter [Col. 0848C] and said that the book’s superscription was not genuine, but that John’s name had merely been affixed to another writing; whence they maintained that this book was neither John’s nor could be considered a revelation, since it was covered by a certain thick veil of ignorance.

Among these was Dionysius, bishop of the Church of Corinth, a man of great learning and grace in the word of God. “I,” he says, “by no means dare to despise and reject the writing of this book. Rather, I judge of it that what is written in it surpasses and rises above the capacity of human hearing, and that in it there is a certain hidden, secret, and in every respect admirable meaning, which I too admire and revere even if I do not understand it. I hold that certain divine mysteries are covered by human words, discerning this not so much by my own judgment as believing it by faith. Therefore I do not reject what I do not understand [Col. 0848D], but admire it all the more the less I attain it.”

After this, discussing the whole body of the little book and examining each part, he clearly demonstrated that it was in no way possible for a worthy interpretation of it to appear according to the letter. He also adds these words: “Therefore, after all prophecy is completed, he calls blessed those who keep these things. But he also calls himself blessed. For he says: ‘Blessed is he who keeps the word of the prophecy of this book.’”

On account of these and similar objections and replies, this book of heavenly revelations was pulled apart and handled roughly.
