And unless the Holy Spirit, who revealed all these things, had prepared men of rational reverence [Col. 0849A] to defend it, swine would have trampled such great and precious pearls underfoot, and heretics would have defiled them. What would have happened if the authority of so great a name had not stood at the entrance of the discourse? Rightly, therefore, because according to the law every word stands on the testimony of two or three witnesses (Deut. XVII), John repeated his designation a third time—he “who bore witness to the Word of God and to the testimony of Jesus Christ, whatever things he saw” (John VIII).

And observe how greatly this authority of his very name shines with the grace of holy humility: “Your brother,” he says, “and companion in tribulation and kingdom and the patience of Jesus.” For he could have said: “I, John, teacher and apostle, your preacher and your evangelist, that disciple whom Jesus loved, whose brothers you have been granted to be.” And he would indeed have spoken rightly [Col. 0849B]. But this manner of speaking would not have belonged so fittingly to a little child—such a little child as the good Master wished each apostle to become or be, when he said: “Amen I say to you, unless you are converted and become as little children, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven. Whoever therefore humbles himself as this little child, he shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XVIII).

What is the restraint or modesty of a little child? “As long as the heir is a little child,” says the Apostle, “he differs nothing from a servant, though he is lord of all” (Gal. IV). By our own judgment we are all servants; but this John, beloved of the Lord Jesus, belongs to the sons to whom the good inheritance of God’s word was bequeathed by testament. Yet from that good Master he had learned to humble himself here [Col. 0849C] in virtue, as among little servants, or among the children of little servants, a child humble by age humbles himself, sitting in the dust with them, “not loving the first places at feasts, not greetings in the marketplace, not the first seats in the synagogues” (Matt. XXIII).

Rightly, therefore, and as becomes the disciple of such a Master, he is content with fellowship with us humble little servants, saying: “I, John, your brother; I, John, your companion.” And if occasion had required it, surely we do not doubt that he could have said what is greater—indeed, what is humbler: “I, John, your servant.” For another too, namely Paul, the chosen vessel, apostle of the same Jesus Christ, did not hesitate to say this: “We preach not ourselves,” he says [Col. 0849D], “but the Lord Jesus Christ; but ourselves your servants through Jesus” (I Cor. IV).

“Your companion in tribulation,” he says: a great expression of sympathetic joy in a meek and humble heart. Someone might have thought him exempt from the tribulation, or tribulations, of the righteous—for they are many—because it is written thus concerning him in the Gospel: “Peter, turning, saw the disciple whom Jesus loved following, and says concerning him: ‘Lord, but what of this man?’ Jesus says to him: ‘If I will have him remain until I come, what is that to thee? Follow thou me’” (John XXI). As though he said: I do not will that he should be brought to his end by the passion of martyrdom, but that without the violence of persecution he should await the last day, when I myself come and receive him into the dwelling-place of eternal blessedness. And what is that to you? Only remember that you must [Col. 0850A] follow in my footsteps by undergoing the gibbet of the cross.

For this reason, as has been said, someone might have considered him exempt from the tribulation of the holy martyrs. But he drank the Lord’s cup, the cup of tribulation, according to the truth of the same Lord speaking to the two sons of Zebedee, of whom this man was one: “Can you drink the cup which I am about to drink?” When they answered, “We can,” he said: “You shall drink my cup” (Matt. XX), etc.

Where did this man drink that cup of the Lord? Surely there, where, according to the prophetic saying of righteous Simeon, a sword passed through the soul of his blessed mother (Luke II). For when all the disciples, having abandoned him, had fled, this beloved disciple stood with Mary his mother by the cross, and himself beheld the nails in his hands and feet [Col. 0850B] and the spear also piercing his side (John XIX). Did not that same sword which passed through the soul of Mary his mother touch the soul of the beloved and loving disciple? It certainly did. And there, drinking the Lord’s cup, he became a companion in tribulation both of Mary and of all Christ’s martyrs.

Moreover, whoever shares in tribulation rightfully also shares in the kingdom. What follows is also a legal right with the heavenly King, for he says: “You are they who have remained with me in my temptations, and I appoint unto you, as my Father has appointed unto me, a kingdom, that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom” (Luke XXII). If he said this generally [Col. 0850C] to them all, though in that moment they were about to flee and Peter too was about to deny him, how much more fittingly was it said to this man, who both stood then by the cross and thereafter was always present.

Having said “in tribulation and kingdom,” he added also “the patience of Jesus.” For after he had shared in that tribulation of Jesus dying and in the kingdom of Jesus rising, he possessed Jesus’ patience, by imitating him in enduring reproaches, mockery, blows with the fist, and scourgings. For example, he himself, with others, was scourged, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles; and under Domitian he was cast into a cauldron of boiling oil, and at last was separated from men (Acts V). He also shared with the saints in the patience of Jesus because, as Christ Jesus endured patiently and prayed, saying, “Father, forgive them” (Luke XXIII), so he too loved those who inflicted evils upon him and prayed for them.

“I, such a man,” he says, “was on the island because of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus Christ.” The history is well known: this blessed John was banished to the island of Patmos because of the word of God to which he bore witness—or which he preached—as having been born from the Father’s heart before all ages; and because of the testimony of Jesus Christ, by which he testified that he is the incarnate Word. Patmos is interpreted “a strait,” for the sea there boils more fiercely because it is narrow. There, to the exile to whom earth was denied, heaven was opened. He is therefore an example to all the saints that the more they are afflicted in the strait of the present age, the more abundantly the secrets of heaven are revealed to them.

[Col. 0851A] Having now identified his person, the place of exile, and its cause, he took care also to indicate the time: “I was,” he says, “in the Spirit on the Lord’s Day.” For the quality of events is customarily shown by the character of times. Thus Abraham, in the heat of his faith, saw angels at midday; Lot at evening, at the destruction of Sodom (Gen. XVIII–XIX); Adam after midday (Gen. III); and Solomon, who would not preserve wisdom, received it in the night (II Kings III). Thus, in this passage the Lord’s Day plainly signifies the faith which was so manifest throughout the whole world when he saw these things.

But in what spirit, or how, are we to suppose that he was? If he was only in his own spirit, the vision is thereby degraded and much is taken away from the seer. In that case neither he himself could properly be called a prophet, nor his words prophecy, nor his visions revelations [Col. 0851B], since he did not understand them if he saw them only in his own spirit.

For example, Pharaoh, who saw seven ears of grain and seven cows—not bodily, certainly, but in spirit, for he slept with the bodily lights closed—was no prophet because, although he saw, he did not understand (Gen. XLI). But Joseph was a prophet because he saw—that is, understood—not in his own spirit but in God’s Spirit. Pharaoh’s spirit was only furnished with images, so that he might see; but Joseph’s mind was illumined by God’s Spirit so that he might understand.

The Apostle briefly distinguishes these modes [Col. 0851C] when, having said, “If I pray with the tongue, and my spirit does not pray, my mind is without fruit,” he immediately adds: “What then? I will pray with the spirit; I will pray also with the mind. I will sing with the spirit; I will sing also with the mind” (II Cor. XIV). What he says concerning prayer or singing must be understood likewise concerning vision. For when images have been perceived in a vision, no revelation, recognition, prophecy, or teaching occurs unless understanding—properly belonging to the mind—has been added.

But was there in John, in this vision, such blindness that signs of things were formed indeed in his spirit, while understanding of those same things did not shine in his mind? Far be this from the “disciple whom Jesus loved.” Otherwise, how could this book be called the Apocalypse, that is, Revelation? Whence would it deserve to be called prophecy, when he himself says: “Blessed is he who reads and hears the words of the prophecy of this book”? Therefore, when he says, “I was in the Spirit [Col. 0851D],” let us understand “the Holy Spirit,” as likewise in the passage: “Jesus was led into the wilderness by the spirit” (Matt. XIV), where we rightly understand the Holy Spirit.

Nor should we hesitate to say that his words, “I was in the Spirit,” mean the same as if he had said: “I was caught up to the third heaven.” For because the apostle Paul alone wrote this concerning himself, it must not therefore be thought that no saint besides him was caught up there. Likewise, when he says elsewhere: “The Gospel which was preached by me is not according to man; for neither did I receive it from man nor learn it, but through the revelation of Jesus Christ” (Gal. I), we must not suppose that no saint besides him learned the truth of Christ through God’s revelation, or that all others received it from man.

We must by no means suppose that, by saying this or that [Col. 0852A], he sets himself above this blessed John, or above the other apostles and prophets. For they all surely learned not from man or through man but through a revelation of God or Jesus Christ; and for all of them to be caught up to the third heaven meant to see heavenly things through the intellectual eye. For there are three heavens, that is, three modes of vision.

There is bodily vision, by which we perceive bodies or bodily things by the mental power through bodily lights. There is spiritual vision, by which, whether in sleep or even in thought, we see certain images but do not yet understand them, as Pharaoh saw seven ears of grain and seven cows, as we have already said above (Gen. XLI). There is also intellectual vision, by which the mind is illumined by the Holy Spirit so that it may understand, as Joseph understood what was signified by those same images.

Are not the words contained in this book [Col. 0852B] words of that sort—secret words which it is not permitted a human being to utter, that is, to entrust to human understanding? (II Cor. XII.) For if a man speaks these things—that is, if anyone wishes to expound or receive them by human understanding—a destructive heresy arises from them. This was done by a certain bishop named Nepos in parts of Egypt, who, taking testimonies from this Revelation, attempted with a Jewish understanding to maintain that God’s promises would be bestowed bodily and that for a thousand years the saints would reign with Christ in bodily delights upon this earth. See *Ecclesiastical History*, book VII, chapter 21.

But someone will say: If this grace belonged to all the apostles—that through revelation they learned the heavenly mysteries of Christ [Col. 0852C], since they were “unlearned and unlettered men” (I Cor. XII)—what need was there for the Apostle so emphatically to assert of himself that he had been caught up as far as the third heaven, and that he had learned not from a human being but through a revelation of Jesus Christ? To this I reply: it was necessary because evangelical faith was in danger among the Corinthians and the Galatians, as though the person of Paul the apostle were at issue. False apostles preached in order to draw believers into circumcision and the Jewish rite (Gal. III), and on this account disparaged Paul the apostle, as though in so great a matter he ought not to be heard—since, they said, he did not know the truth of the Gospel and was not among the great apostles. Therefore he affirmed concerning himself the things mentioned above [Col. 0852D], not preferring himself to the other apostles but making himself their equal, so that the truth of the Gospel might remain.

But let us now enter upon the paths of this same revelation. He says: “And I heard behind me a great voice, like a trumpet, saying: What thou seest, write.”

What was behind John when he was in the Spirit? Surely the whole world—whatever is seen with bodily eyes—and indeed the whole condition of the present Church. These were behind him because he himself was stretching forward, when he was caught upward to behold those things; yet what we are now discussing was future. When, after Domitian’s death, he returned to Ephesus by permission of the pious emperor Nerva, he was urged by almost all the bishops of Asia at that time and by delegations from many Churches to speak more profoundly concerning Christ’s divinity coeternal with the Father [Col. 0853A], because in the writings of the three Evangelists—Matthew, Mark, and Luke—they considered that they had sufficient testimony concerning his humanity and those things which he accomplished as man.

Why was this so? While he was in exile, heretics—like wolves breaking into sheepfolds deprived of their shepherd—Marcion, Cerinthus, Ebion, and the other Antichrists, had invaded the Church and stained the simplicity of evangelical faith with perverse teaching, denying that Christ existed before Mary. Therefore he “heard behind him a great voice like a trumpet,” because it was to happen that he would be urgently compelled by almost all the aforesaid bishops of Asia, so that, rising as though to war, he might confront the faithless heretics and, taking up the sword of the Word of God, defend the boundaries of the Church’s faith. By the great voice we understand that vehement and unanimous urgency [Col. 0853B] by which he was to be compelled.

At the same time, because the truth of faith does not love corners, but desires to speak openly before the whole world rather than in secret, it was fitting that what has now been said should be signified not by just any voice, but by a great trumpet voice. “What thou seest,” he says, “write.” This is to say: “All the bishops of Asia: O John, beloved of Jesus Christ, who, reclining upon his breast, drank the streams of evangelical truth from the very sacred fountain of the Lord’s breast (John XIII), since Marcion, Cerinthus, Ebion, and the other Antichrists, during your absence and exile, invaded the Church and stained the simplicity of evangelical faith with perverse teaching, denying that Christ existed before Mary; [Col. 0853C] and since the other Evangelists—Matthew, Mark, and Luke—have sufficiently established in their writings testimony concerning his humanity: you, concerning the antiquity of his divinity, write in the evangelical style what you see, know, and hold; and by your writing, with the light of truth laid open, drive away every darkness of the heretics.”

“And send it to the seven Churches which are in Asia: to Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea.” Send it to the seven Churches—that is, deliver it to the universal Church, which is spread throughout the whole world and ordered and confirmed by the sevenfold Holy Spirit. For in Asia Minor there are seven metropolitan cities, of which Ephesus is the head. Yet when he speaks to the seven Churches of Asia, he certainly speaks to the whole Church, which, though one, is comprehended by the number seven, by which totality is often designated. He directs his prophecy in particular to those seven Churches of Asia, over which divine grace set him as preacher; nevertheless, he desires to hand down to the universal Church what he knows has been revealed to him, for the common benefit of all, since he says without exception: “Blessed is he who reads and hears the words of this prophecy.”

It follows: “And I turned to see the voice that spoke with me.” When the bishops of Asia, as stated above, asked John to speak more profoundly concerning Christ’s divinity coeternal with the Father, what did he do? Surely he turned to prayer and fasting, replying that he would not act otherwise unless, during the said fast, all of them together prayed to the Lord that he might be able to write worthy things [Col. 0854A]. This he did—or rather, when he saw these things, he was going to do it. Rightly therefore, he says: “And I turned to see the voice that spoke with me.” For one who, asked in some manner to ascend into heaven and show human beings the hidden divinity there, flees anxiously to prayer and fasts, being distrustful of his own frailty, is rightly said to turn, or to have turned, so that he may see the voice speaking with him—that is, so that by the gift of heavenly grace he may obtain the power to utter what is required of him, and may himself first deserve to see or know what he is asked to show or write.

“And when I had turned, I saw seven golden lampstands; and in the midst of the seven golden lampstands one like a Son of Man, clothed with a long robe, and girded about the breasts with a golden girdle.” And thereafter this happened exactly so [Col. 0854B]. For, having turned, as has been said, to prayers and fasts, while the Church also observed the fast that had been proclaimed, he saw—through the revelation of the Holy Spirit—what things concerning Christ’s divinity it was fitting to write. The present text also most beautifully signifies these things: its meaning is golden, while its entire surface is silver.

“And I saw,” he says, “seven golden lampstands. The seven lampstands are the seven Churches.” Therefore, just as there are seven Churches and yet the Church is one, so the seven lampstands are one lampstand. Concerning this lampstand the Lord himself speaks in the Gospel: “No one lights a lamp and puts it in a hidden place, nor under a bushel, but upon a lampstand, that those who enter may see the light” (Matt. VI). He was certainly speaking this against Jewish envy, since before these words he had signified [Col. 0854C], through the comparison with the Ninevites (Luke XI), that his glory would be made known to the Gentiles, and that the Gentiles would repent while the Jews themselves—having an evil eye, that is, being envious and perishing through envy—would not. For he had said: “The men of Nineveh shall rise in judgment with this generation and condemn it, because they repented at the preaching of Jonah; and behold, a greater than Jonah is here” (Matt. XII).

And this is to be understood: just as the men of Nineveh repented at the preaching, or sign, of Jonah, who was in the belly of the whale three days and three nights (Luke XI), so the Gentiles shall repent at my preaching, or my sign, after I have been in the heart of the earth three days and three nights [Col. 0854D]; and likewise they shall rise in judgment with this generation and condemn it. Do you ask why this will be so? Because I am a lamp. And just as a lamp is lit not in order to be placed in hiding, but upon a lampstand, so I came into this world in order that the Gentiles might be enlightened by my light (John XIII). Therefore, what accords with the logic of evangelical truth—that a lamp ought to be, or has been, set upon one lampstand—is, according to this revelation, the Son of Man seen in the midst of the seven golden lampstands: namely, Christ, of whom Simeon said, “A light for revelation to the Gentiles” (Luke II). Already at the time when John saw this mystery, it had been brought forth for the glory of all the Churches.

For the seven lampstands, as has been said [Col. 0855A], are the seven—that is, all—the Churches. These lampstands are rightly seen as golden, because the sacred faith by reason of, or from which, we Gentiles have this privilege of being lampstands—that is, Churches—is likened to gold which passes through fire, as the apostle Peter also says: “That the testing of your faith, much more precious than gold which is tested by fire, may be found…” (I Pet. II).

What kind of one did he see in the midst of such lampstands—golden lampstands? So that Marcion, Cerinthus, Ebion, and the other Antichrists, who detracted from Christ’s ancient glory, might hear; or rather, so that John himself might know more certainly what testimony he would later be asked to give concerning Christ’s divinity: he saw one like the Son of Man, clothed with a long robe, and girded [Col. 0855B] about the breasts with a golden girdle.

In the likeness of the Son of Man we understand the reality of his humanity, as also in the passage: “He was made in the likeness of men, and was found in appearance as a man” (Phil. II). In the garment of the long robe, which is a priestly garment, we understand the dignity or office of priesthood, because he himself is our priest or high priest; concerning him the Apostle says: “Having therefore a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast our confession” (Heb. IV). And the apostle Peter says: “For you were as sheep going astray, but are now returned to the shepherd and bishop of your souls” (II Pet. II).

In that he was girded about the breasts with a golden girdle, we understand royal authority, concerning which the Psalmist says: “The Lord reigns; he is clothed with splendour; the Lord is clothed with strength, and has girded himself with power” (Ps. XCII) [Col. 0855C]. By the golden girdle with which he was now seen girded about the breasts, we understand the splendour and strength with which the reigning Lord clothed and girded himself, after destroying the reign of sin and overcoming death. Why about the breasts, in the midst of which is the place of the heart, unless such a girding signifies the condition of the breasts and heart—namely, the state of vital nature, or life containing itself—because Christ is now an immortal king? “For having risen from the dead, he dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. VI).

Behold, these three things have now been shown: that he is the Son of Man—that is, that he is man—priest, and king. Yet the other Evangelists, Matthew, Mark, and Luke, had already testified to these matters in sufficiently full writings [Col. 0855D], and the aforesaid heretics did not refuse to hear their testimony. For however much they were Antichrists, they confessed that Christ was man, priest, and king. There was one matter from which the controversy had arisen: the most exalted and most ancient divinity of this same man, priest, and king, Jesus Christ. It follows, therefore:

“His head and his hair were white as white wool, and as snow.” What is the head of the Son of Man, if not his divinity? Knowing this, the Bride also says in the Song of Songs: “His head is finest gold” (Song V). That head and the hairs of that head were white, “as white wool and [Col. 0856A] as snow.” This is said of the Son of Man, the Son of God. Moreover, Daniel says of his Father, the Ancient of Days: “His garment was white as snow, and the hair of his head like clean wool” (Dan. V). Therefore that Ancient of Days and this Son of Man, his Son—who in the same Daniel came with the clouds of heaven and came even to that Ancient of Days—are of one and the same antiquity in respect of their head, that is, in respect of their divinity. For the hairs of the head of the one and of the other are equally white.

Each is shown as old by the whiteness of his head, without any difference, because this Son is not younger than his Father, so old, by a year, month, day, hour, instant, moment, or even an atom. He saw in the Spirit one who, struck also in the body—or bodily—for the reason already given, was about to write such things [Col. 0856B]. In what manner or in what writing? “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. The same was in the beginning with God” (John I).

Therefore the Son of Man, clothed with a long robe, girded about the breasts with a golden girdle, and having a white head, is Christ, the Son of God: true man, supreme High Priest, great King, ancient and true God. Meanwhile the oft-mentioned Antichrists fashioned their blasphemies in order to deny that he existed before Mary. But he, providing for himself—or rather, caring for his Church, whose faith was in danger—was now showing this John his head, white through antiquity: a head begotten without time not only before Mary and before Abraham, but even before Lucifer, born of the Father before times [Col. 0856C].

But what are the hairs, white through antiquity in this way, like white wool and snow? The hairs, because they proceed from the head and are many, are the many words of God which have proceeded from the one Word, or through the one Word, which was in the beginning. For the Word, God, in his substance is one Word and one head; but the many words which God spoke to holy human beings or prophets are like the many hairs of one head. Why then are these hairs likened to wool? Just as wool, drawn out into thread and woven, becomes some garment, so by means of these hairs—that is, God’s many words—transferred into the language and voice of the prophets, Holy Scripture has been woven in writing.

And why not wool of whatever kind, but, he says, “white” wool; or, as it is written in Daniel, “clean wool” (Dan. VII)? Because those words are holy and clean, right and irreproachable. Hence also: “The utterances of the Lord are pure utterances” (Ps. XI). Again: “The law of the Lord is spotless,” or irreproachable, “converting souls” (Ps. VIII) [Col. 0856D]—converting souls, I say, and washing them from every sin. Therefore he added, “and as snow.” For snow sometimes signifies cleansing. Thus the Prophet says in the psalm: “Thou shalt wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow” (Ps. L). Again, in the prophet: “Though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be made white as snow” (Isa. I).

Finally, this must be understood: whoever rises before this hoary head and pays reverence to its white hairs—that is, worthily receives his words—by the very fact that he receives and meditates on his words, himself also becomes grey and deserves to be called old, as Wisdom declares: “Venerable old age is not that which is long in time, nor reckoned by the number of years. But the understanding of a human being is grey hairs, and an unstained life is the age of old age” (Wis. IV) [Col. 0857A]. It follows:

“And his eyes were like a flame of fire, and his feet like orichalc, as in a burning furnace.” Certainly, what he was to write in saying, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God; this was in the beginning with God,” and then adding, “What was made in him was life, and the life was the light of human beings; and the light shines in darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it. There was the true light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world” (John I)—what he was to write in this manner was shown to him in this radiant image. For just as that beginning, or the Word which was in the beginning, is signified by the white head, so by these eyes is signified that life, the light of human beings, which enlightens every human being coming into this world.

Therefore “his eyes were like a flame of fire”: that is, his inspiration, enlightening every human being and shining in darkness. Thus it is rightly said to be like a flame of fire, because “our God is a fire” (Deut. IV), and his regard for us is a flame—a flame enlightening us, so that we may not be in darkness, that we may not be children of night and darkness [Col. 0857B], but may be children of light and children of God (I Thess. V). Because of eyes of this kind, he also declares in the Gospel, as we recalled above, that a lamp is to be put upon a lampstand (Matt. V), and here he is seen in the midst of golden lampstands.

Indeed, because if any are enlightened by this light or by these eyes so that they may themselves shine for others also through word and example, they are in a certain sense called light and eyes, according to the saying: “You are the light of the world” (Luke XI). And it is said to the Bride in the Song of Songs: “Your eyes are doves” (Song I), that is, your overseers are simple. Yet there is a difference: those eyes, unlike these, are not enlightening but enlightened—not enlightening light, but light that has been enlightened. Therefore it is said in the aforementioned passage concerning one of the most brilliant of them [Col. 0857C]: “He was not the light, but that he might bear witness to the light.”

Again, what he was to write in saying: “And the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us, and we saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father” (John I)—this same thing he sees signified in the image when he says: “And his feet were like orichalc, as in a burning furnace.” For just as by the white or grey head we rightly understand the ancient one—the Word which “was in the beginning”—so by the feet, which are the final part of the body, we likewise rightly understand that same Word made flesh: that God became man in the end of the ages, and remains man beyond all the ends of the ages. These feet—his humanity—are rightly called like orichalc, because, just as orichalc is brought by many applications of fire from bronze to the colour of gold, so that humanity, through the many tribulations of passion and death, was brought forth to the glory of divinity, which is customarily understood by gold [Col. 0857D], so that it too is now immortal, incorruptible, and incapable of suffering. Hence it is significantly said, “as in a burning furnace,” by which the affliction of the Passion is rightly understood: the affliction in which that humanity had to be consumed by fire, as he says: “Was it not necessary for Christ thus to suffer, to rise from the dead, and so enter into his glory?” (Luke XXIV).

“And his voice was like the voice of many waters.” By the name “waters,” the divine Scriptures are customarily understood; and it would be superfluous to prove this from the Scriptures. It is clear, moreover, that whatever that Son of Man—with a head so white and feet of this kind like orichalc—spoke in his passions and temptations, or speaks even now, harmonizes with the holy Scriptures and agrees with their words and meanings. Indeed, his life and death, resurrection and ascension also proceeded thus and for this reason: that the Scriptures might be fulfilled. Therefore, “his voice was like the voice of many waters” [Col. 0858A]: that is, his teaching, or all his work, is the truth and fulfilment of the Scriptures, which are many—namely, the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms. For, he says, “It is necessary that all things written concerning me in the Law and the Prophets and the Psalms be fulfilled” (Luke XXIV).

Alternatively, “his voice was like the voice of many waters,” that is, like the voice of many peoples, according to that which the Psalmist says in his person: “I will confess thee among the peoples, and sing a psalm to thee among the nations” (Ps. CVII). Finally, many peoples today sing in harmony his voice—the words of the Scriptures spoken in his person; and peoples are customarily signified by the name “waters.”

“And he had in his right hand seven stars.” The seven stars, as is written below, are the angels of the seven Churches—that is, all the bishops of all the Churches. They are called angels—that is, messengers—because they announce to those under them the things which God speaks, according to the saying: “The lips of the priest keep knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. II) [Col. 0858B]. Because they are angels in this manner—that is, because they proclaim the law of the Lord—they are rightly called and truly are stars, according to Daniel: “Those who are learned shall shine as the brightness of the firmament; and those who instruct many unto righteousness, as stars for everlasting eternities” (Dan. XII).

That all who are such are rightly marked by this number, namely seven, is also beautifully demonstrated by the fact that, when he was at his right hand—that is, in his great blessedness, having risen from the dead—he had as companions of his meal no more and no fewer than seven disciples, as it is written: “Peter and Thomas, who is called Didymus, and Nathanael, who was of Cana in Galilee, and the sons of Zebedee, and two others of his disciples, were together” (John XXI). These seven cast the net on the right side of the boat [Col. 0858C], drew it to land full of large fish, and ate with the Lord. Thus they signify all those who, in the universal resurrection, will present all the elect whom they have gained by their zeal or labours, and will sit with Christ at his right hand in the heavens.

Then will occur what is immediately signified in the present passage: “And from his mouth there went out a two-edged sharp sword.” For the sword in this passage signifies the final judgment, just as God says in the Song of Deuteronomy: “If I sharpen my sword as lightning” (Deut. XXXII). Explaining what he meant by “my sword,” he immediately added: “And my hand takes hold of judgment.” Then this two-edged sword of judgment will go forth from his mouth, and will effectively distinguish and judge each of the two sides according to their merits: the right and the left.

The going forth of the sword toward the right will be this: “Come, ye blessed of my Father” (Matt. XXV). For at this word his sword will so consume flesh that there will no longer be flesh and blood; all will be stripped of every corruption of flesh and blood, and, while their nature remains in a marvellous manner, they will be changed into another glory (I Cor. XV) [Col. 0859A]. The going forth of the same sword toward the left will be this: “Depart from me, ye cursed, into eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV). On both sides that sword of judgment will be so effective that these shall go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life. Thus separated from one another, they can no longer be joined or mingled, as good and evil are now mingled in the present Church.

From that time onward he will be seen in his glory by those blessed ones whom he will thereafter have at his right hand. God of gods will be seen face to face in that vision which he promised would be the reward of his love for those who love him: “He who loves me,” he says, “will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him” (John XIV). It follows, then: “And his face shines as the sun in its strength.” His face—his presence—will shine as the sun, because he truly is the sun; and it will shine in its strength, that is, in his majesty and divinity. Then the prophecy of Isaiah will be fulfilled: “And the light of the moon shall be as the light of the sun, and the light of the sun shall be sevenfold, as the light of seven days, in the day when the Lord binds up the wound of his people and heals the stroke of their wound” (Ps. XXX) [Col. 0859B].

What is the moon which will then shine as the sun, without the changes of increase and decrease by which it is now altered in this world, if not the Church, then made like its sun, its God? “We know,” says this same John, “that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (I John III). But how great will the light of the sun itself be? “As the light of seven days,” he says. This means: Of such brightness as God the Word possessed when all things were made during six days and all things were completed through him on the seventh day, of such brightness will he then be in his flesh with God his Father. This is what he himself said in prayer: “And now, Father, glorify thou me with thyself with the glory which I had with thee before the world was” (John XVII).

For what is that day of which the prophet said: “In the day when the Lord binds up the wound of his people and heals the stroke of their wound” (Isa. XXX) [Col. 0860A], if not that vision of the face of this sun, which shall be the health of humankind and the complete healing of its wound—the wound with which all of us were struck and wounded in Adam, namely the twofold death of soul and body? It follows:

“And when I saw him, I fell at his feet as dead; and he laid his right hand upon me, saying: Fear not.” Because the one whom he saw “shines as the sun in his strength,” mortal man could not stand or remain upright in his weakness. Thus also formerly, “when he had been transfigured on the mountain before them, namely Peter and James and this same John his brother, they fell upon their faces and were exceedingly afraid” (Matt. XVII). And just as it is said here, “and he laid his right hand upon me, saying: Fear not,” so there: “And Jesus came and touched them, and said to them: Arise, and fear not” (ibid.) [Col. 0860B].

Unless his right hand here and there had touched this man or those men, they could not bear the light or strength in which that sun shone. Therefore all who are to see him in that heavenly kingdom must be placed at the right hand, so that they may be able to see and endure the sight, according to the Gospel truth which says: “And he shall set the sheep at his right hand, but the goats at his left” (Matt. XXV). For what it is here for the right hand to be laid upon this frightened man, falling through fear, so that he may rise and not fear, that will then be for all the sheep to be placed at the right hand: that they may behold that brightness and not melt away with the goats on the left, “as wax melts before the face of fire” (Ps. LXVII).

“I am the first and the last, and the living one; and I was dead, and behold, I am alive for ages of ages, and I have the keys of death and hell.” Following the authority of the earlier writers, we said above that an angel appeared to this John in the figure of Christ, because of what was said at the beginning: “and he signified it, sending by his angel to his servant John.” But it may now be asked why he who appeared professed himself to be Christ by so great and manifest a description: “I am,” he says, “the first and the last, and the living one,” and so forth. Moreover, when John fell at his feet as dead [Col. 0860C], he was neither forbidden to fall nor reproved for falling at his feet.

Yet near the end of the book John himself says: “I, John, who heard and saw these things, after I had heard and seen them, fell down to worship before the feet of the angel who showed these things to me. And he says to me: See that thou do it not; I am thy fellow-servant, and of thy brethren the prophets, and of those who keep the words of this book: worship God” (John XXII). It is therefore plainly understood that one person was John’s guide and showed him these things, while another was shown or seen by him in such brightness that he could not remain standing to behold the brightness of the one who appeared. The one who showed him was plainly an angel, but the one who was shown is called the Son of Man.

Accordingly, the one whose voice he heard in this place, like a trumpet saying, “What thou seest, write,” must be acknowledged to have been the angel who showed these things, of whom it was also said, “and he signified it, sending by his angel.” But the one who was seen may be understood as the one whom he professed himself to be: namely, the first and the last—that is, Christ the Son of God. Nor is it new or unworthy of belief that a human being saw Jesus Christ after his ascension, since the apostle Paul says, though he had not known him before he ascended into heaven: “Am I not free? Am I not an apostle? Have I not seen the Lord Jesus Christ?” (I Cor. IX) [Col. 0860D]. For he saw him on the road as he was going to Damascus; and because then he was unworthy of that vision, being an enemy and persecutor, he not only fell to the ground, but also, after he rose, saw nothing though his eyes were open. The one sent to him, Ananias, confirms that he saw Jesus: “Brother Saul,” he says, “the Lord Jesus, who appeared to thee in the way by which thou camest, has sent me” (Acts IX).

Elsewhere, moreover, this Son of Man is called an angel, and is the Angel of Great Counsel, the angel in whom is the name of God. For in Exodus God says to Moses, or to his people: “Behold, I will send an angel before thee, to keep thee in the way and bring thee into the place which I have prepared. Observe him and hear his voice; do not think him to be despised, for he will not pardon thee when thou hast sinned, and my name is in him” (Exod. XXIII). This is the distinctive property of this Angel, set down there when God says, “and my name is in him” [Col. 0861A]. He did not say, “and my name is upon him,” which could rightly be said of any frail one of the elect, all of whom share that prophetic voice: “But thou, O Lord, art in us, and thy holy name has been invoked upon us” (Jer. XIV). Rather, he says, “my name is in him”: that is, because of natural divinity, he is designated by the same name as I.

For he is called—and is—equally with me God, Lord, Almighty, invisible, uncreated, immeasurable, eternal, and whatever is substantially predicated of God. The sole distinction in respect of the name is that I am called Father in relation to him, and he Son in relation to me, while this indicates the same dignity. The prophet Malachi also says: “And immediately the ruler whom you seek shall come to his temple, and the Angel of the covenant whom you desire” (Mal. III). Stephen, the first martyr, likewise says in the Acts of the Apostles: “This is he who was in the assembly in the wilderness with the angel who spoke to him.” Further: “And when forty years were fulfilled,” he says, “there appeared to him in the wilderness of Mount Sinai an Angel in the flame of fire of a bush” (Acts VII).

Therefore, if it pleases one to call, or to regard as, an Angel this Son of Man who appeared to John—the one concerning whom it was said above, “and he signified it, sending by his Angel”—then certainly, as in the passage where Stephen speaks, one must understand not just any angel, but the one who could truly say: “I am who I am; I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and of Jacob. This is my name for ever” (Exod. III) [Col. 0861B]. Likewise, in this passage one must understand not just any angel, but the one who can truly say: “I am the first and the last, and the living one; and I was dead, and behold, I am alive for ages of ages.”

He is first, namely because I was “in the beginning the Word, God with God, through whom all things were made,” as is indicated by this head of mine so white through antiquity; and “last,” through whom all things were restored, as is indicated or signified by these feet of mine like orichalc—having, as it were, recently emerged from the burning furnace, the furnace of tribulation or Passion, in which I was so last and appeared so contemptible to human beings as a worm is despised and not a man (Ps. XXI). Another prophet also says: “And we desired him, despised and the last of men, a man of sorrows and acquainted with infirmity” (Isa. LIII) [Col. 0861C].

“And I was dead”: namely, laid in the tomb also for three days and three nights. “And behold, I am alive for ages of ages.” For I rose again and am still with God my Father, and true is what the Apostle says of me: “He dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. VI). “And I have the keys of death and hell.” That is, the power to forgive sins. For by forgiving sins, I shut death against those who believe in me and bar hell. Or “of death and hell” means of the twofold death: namely, of soul and body. By “death,” in the customary sense, the dissolution of the body is signified; by “hell,” the death of the soul, which is eternal, is rightly signified [Col. 0861D]. He has the keys—that is, the power—over both deaths, as the prophetess Anna says in her song: “The Lord kills and makes alive; he brings down to hell and brings back” (I Kings II).

“Write therefore the things which thou hast seen, and the things which are, and the things which must happen after these.” The imperative expression or word by which he says “write” is the bestowal of a gift and grace, as though he said: “Receive the capacity and authority to write.” Hence this blessed John is truly blessed and worthy of honour, since among the twelve apostles he grew and was increased just as, among the twelve patriarchs, that truly blessed Joseph—according to his name, the increasing son—grew and was increased. For just as he received a double portion, his father saying: “I will give thee one portion more than thy brothers” (Gen. XLVIII), signifying Shechem, or Sichem, which in the Gospel is called Sychar [Col. 0862A], so this beloved disciple, beyond his brothers the other apostles, received from the gift of the loving Lord Jesus an outstanding single portion: not only that, being an apostle, he should also become an Evangelist and write so divine a Gospel, but also that he should commit to writing so great and wonderful a revelation.

“Write therefore,” he says, “the things which thou hast seen”: namely, what you have seen while following me with the other apostles, and also what you have now seen alone; so that your Gospel may be such as this form or appearance of mine, which you now see, signifies that it ought to be written; and write the things which now require correction or praise in the seven Churches of Asia; and the things which must happen after these, namely, the various afflictions of the Church.

[Col. 0863A] “The mystery of the seven stars which you saw in my right hand, and of the seven golden lampstands: the seven stars are the angels of the seven Churches.” Having made a threefold distinction of the things to be written, when he said, “what you have seen, and what things are, and what things must take place after these,” he now explains only the middle division, that is, the things which are. And, as one about to enter, he opens the door of understanding, so that authority may not be lacking to the man who is to touch the consciences of those who then were in, or presided over, the Churches. For the Son of Man could indeed have said in the same manner: “The mystery of the Son of Man, thus clothed, thus girded, having such a head and such eyes, is this or such a thing.” But the matter did not demand it so much, nor did so great a necessity of the business press for it. For one who merely teaches what the catholic faith holds, or ought to hold, does not need so great a support of divine authority or will as one who rebukes and chastises morals, who deals with or argues concerning the hidden consciences of men, or especially concerning private life, and writes accounts to be read.

There, when the testimonies of Scripture support him, even a sluggish governor of his own life willingly assents to the faith. Here, where the arbiters of the hidden conscience are absent, even a vigorous champion of the faith resents being reproved concerning the condition of his own life, when outwardly he appears to do everything which an ecclesiastical man ought to do. Thus, for example, there appeared to be the angel of the Church of Sardis, to whom he is commanded to write: “I know your works: that you have the name that you live, and you are dead” (Rev. III). Appropriately, therefore, he expressly opens the understanding of those things which then were or were being done in the Churches, leading the seer through each particular: “Write these things,” he says, “to that angel, and these things to that angel.”

[Col. 0864A] And observe how wisely, in accordance with the practice of a prudent and well-composed orator, he wins the goodwill of those to whom he speaks or writes, so that they may patiently hear what is written, although it may seem burdensome. “The mystery,” he says—“write” being understood—“of the seven stars,” that is, what the seven stars signify, “which you saw in my right hand.” And then: “The seven stars are the angels of the seven Churches, and the seven lampstands are the seven Churches.”

Although some rulers of Churches are blameworthy in their private lives, he chose to call them angels and stars; and although much is dark in certain Churches, he honored all the Churches with the beautiful names, or significant images, of golden lampstands. And rightly so: for priests or rulers, although at times dark because of their own deeds, nevertheless shine by reason of their office, reciting the Word of God and celebrating Christ’s heavenly sacraments; and so they are, as it were, certain stars for signs and seasons. For example, when they say that saying of the Apostle: “The night has gone before, but the day will draw near” (Gen. I; Rom. XIII). Therefore mystical Scripture says concerning stars of this kind: “Who made Arcturus, the Hyades, and Orion?” (Job IX). Again: “Can you bring forth the shining stars of the Pleiades, or can you scatter the circuit of Arcturus?” (Job XXXVIII). And similar things.

Likewise, he rightly said that the Churches themselves are golden lampstands, namely in respect of those who glorify Christ as their light both by confession of voice and by the service of good work, according to the command of him who says: “Let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V).

## 366. PROLOGUE TO THE SECOND BOOK

[Col. 0863]

The soul to which it has been granted, in its desire, to taste the hidden sweetness in the Scriptures rejoices in the Song of Songs when it says: “The king has brought me into his storehouses” (Song I). Again: “The king has brought me into the wine-cellar” (Song II). But behold, our young maiden Faith stands outside and, as it were, peers within through the small crevices of the closed storehouse. As her desire increases, she longs in her poverty, listening to what and how that one who is such as she is—who has already been brought in—rejoices and speaks, as we have in the present Scripture: “That same holy and true king, who has the key of David, who opens and no one shuts, who shuts and no one opens: behold, I have given before you an open door which no one is able to shut” (Rev. III).

This is to say: Behold, I have brought you into my storehouses, or into my wine-cellar, through the open door of understanding; and you draw from within the riches of wisdom and knowledge, which, when I grant them to you, no one can take away. For what reason? On account of what merit? “Because,” he says, “you have little strength” (ibid.); that is, you possess outstanding humility, placing your confidence not in your own strength but in mine.

The angel to whom he speaks these things is the angel of Philadelphia, which is interpreted “brotherly love.” Therefore, so long as we stand outside, until that king opens with his key, we must have little strength—that is, we must retain humility—so that through brotherly love we may willingly spend that little which we have already tasted of that sweetness, if there is anything we have deserved to taste or discover, placing our hope in him who also says elsewhere: “He who seeks finds, and to him who knocks it shall be opened” (Matt. VII; Luke XI).

You, Frederick, most illustrious archbishop, especially strengthen this hope of my soul: you have not merely been well-disposed toward my little works, but, because of the greatness of your goodwill, have even been able to smile upon them, as though you were present and supposed me to be present with you at that great and festive banquet which Abraham, the father of his laughter—the father, I say, of his son Isaac, whose name is interpreted “laughter” [Col. 0865] (Gen. XXI)—made on the day of his weaning. For that banquet belongs to those who, in reading the Scriptures, do not become children in understanding, but are indeed little children in malice and perfect in understanding (I Cor. XIV), so that they need not milk but solid food, which belongs to the perfect (Heb. V).

There already begins laughter and joy: eternal laughter, which Mother Sarah foresaw in mystery when she said, “God has made laughter for me; whoever hears will laugh with me” (Gen. XXI). To such persons this book of the Apocalypse ought especially to be offered, because it is not milk for little children but solid food for the perfect. Everything contained in it in mystery is strong as wine—and wine indeed, as the bride says in the Song of Songs concerning such things, “most sweet and excellent, worthy for my beloved to drink, and for his lips and teeth to chew” (Song VII). Let us therefore seek, as we have begun, that we may find; let us knock persistently, that it may be opened to us (Luke XI).

## 367. SECOND BOOK

[Col. 0865]

[Col. 0865A] In the preceding chapter of the most glorious vision, John saw a remarkable foretokening of the Gospel which he was to write: namely, the Son of Man clothed in a long robe and girded with a golden belt, with a white head, by which was signified the ancient Word that was in the beginning with God—against Cerinthus and other Antichrists, who were beginning to deny that Christ existed before Mary. And after he had seen these things and the rest, it was said to him: “Write therefore the things which you have seen.” Then the mystery of the seven stars and seven lampstands was explained to him: namely, that the seven stars are the angels of the seven Churches, and the seven lampstands are the seven Churches. And immediately there follows:

## CHAPTER II

“And write to the angel of the Church of Ephesus: These things says he who holds the seven stars in his right hand, who [Col. 0865B] walks in the midst of the seven golden lampstands.” Here the seven spirits of God begin to speak, who are before the throne of God. For he who speaks is indeed the Son of Man: he who walks in the midst of the seven golden lampstands; who was dead and lives; who has the sharp two-edged sword; who has eyes like a flame of fire; who has the seven spirits of God; who has the key of David; who is the beginning of the creation of God. But consider that through each of the seven sections of his utterances he cries thus: “He who has ears, let him hear what the Spirit says to the Churches.” Therefore the seven spirits of God speak, while the one Son of Man, or Son of God, speaks here. They speak, I say, from that their dwelling-place in which, dwelling in all fullness bodily, they are before the throne of God (Col. II): that is, as a pattern for the Church of God, because this Son of Man has been set before the Church of God for imitation, having within himself the seven spirits of God.

Here the spirit of fear speaks to the Churches first; the spirit of piety second; the spirit of knowledge third; the spirit of fortitude fourth; the spirit of counsel fifth; the spirit of understanding sixth; and the spirit of wisdom seventh. For the Church, while imitating Christ, begins from fear and, ascending, comes to wisdom, as it is written: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. CX; Prov. I). But where the Son of God ascends to instruct the same Church, the spirit of wisdom is first and [Col. 0866A] the spirit of fear last, as the prophet says: “And the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. XI).

Therefore, with the same Spirit leading, “let him who has an ear hear what each of these spirits says to the Churches,” according to the property of his own dignity—and first what the spirit of the fear of the Lord says: “Write,” he says, “to the angel of the Church of Ephesus,” and the rest. That he who says these things to the Churches is the spirit of fear is shown more clearly by what he says: “Remember therefore from where you have fallen, and repent, and do the first works. Otherwise I come to you and will remove your lampstand from its place, unless you repent.”

The name Ephesus, or the interpretation of the name, indicates the condition of those to whom these things are fittingly said. For Ephesus is interpreted “a great fall,” or “my will is in her.” It is indeed a great fall to have forsaken and fallen away from first love; but it is God’s will that one who has fallen or lapsed in this way should repent. Such was then the angel—that is, the priest—of the Church of Ephesus; and there are even today many priests, or those living under priests in the Church, all of whom the spirit of fear rebukes in this one angel, partly by terrifying them and partly by encouraging praise.

But he begins thus: “These things says he who holds the seven stars in his right hand.” “The seven stars are the angels of the seven Churches,” as was said before. By this statement salutary fear constrains stars of this kind, since these stars are in heaven in such a way that they must be held lest they fall to earth. For very many stars fell from heaven, and from stars became princes of darkness (Isa. XIV). Therefore, in saying, “who holds the seven stars in his right hand,” he at once terribly intimates: let him who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall. For he does not stand by his own strength, but because the right hand of the Lord holds him.

This especially must be guarded against, because he himself who holds those stars watches attentively lest, perhaps because of their very brightness, the foot of pride come upon anyone (Ps. XXXV). Hence there follows: “Who walks in the midst of the seven golden lampstands.” It is the same as if he said: He who, moving among you, searches the hearts [Col. 0867A] and reins of each person (Jer. XVII). For, as was said before, “the seven lampstands are the seven Churches.” Therefore, when he walks in the midst of lampstands of this kind, he observes how brightly each one shines, lest the faith of the dead, without the oil of love and without works of charity, smoke instead.

For where he finds such a thing, he says: “I know your works and your labor and your patience, and that you cannot bear evil men; you have tested those who call themselves apostles and are not, and have found them false; and you have patience, and have endured for my name’s sake, and have not failed.” Certainly these are works: to labor in the rule of the catholic faith and to have patience in this labor, even by disputing against perverse doctrines, whose fabricators are evil men, so many and so talkative that you cannot endure them. It is, I say, a good work to test those lying teachers and convict false apostles; but perfection does not consist in this, however much patience you may have in enduring them and not failing, if you lack the first adornment of love. For the Apostle also says: “If I have all faith so that I remove mountains, and if I deliver my body so that I burn, but do not have love, it profits me nothing” (I Cor. XIII). And the apostle James says: “Do you wish to know, O empty man, that faith without works is idle?” (Jas. II). For faith is idle, however much it may seem to work, unless it works through love.

[Col. 0867C] Therefore he says: “But I have against you that you have forsaken your first love.” It is as though he said: What you do in this way is indeed for you and pleads in your favor; but this is against you: in this work of yours you have forsaken first love. For love is first—that is, the chief good—and, according to the Apostle, “a more excellent way” (I Cor. XIII). It is almost the sole and unique sign of perfection and testimony of true virtue, as he said elsewhere: “By this all shall know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John III).

Stephen the protomartyr was recognized by this sign when, in his labor and patience, unable to endure the evil men whom he had found and convicted as false, he so patiently endured for the Lord’s name that, even while dying, he prayed for them and said: “Lord, do not lay this sin to their charge” (Acts VII), because they do not know what they do. “Remember therefore from where you have fallen, and repent, and do the first works; otherwise I come to you and remove your lampstand from its place unless you repent.”

Just as many testimonies of Holy Scripture do, so this passage teaches us that we ought not hastily pronounce sentence upon the angels of Churches—that is, bishops—or upon any ecclesiastical ranks. For he did not say: “Because you have forsaken your first love, I come to you and remove your lampstand from its place.” Rather, he placed a great interval in his speech and a strong curb upon the running sentence, saying: “Remember [Col. 0868A] therefore from where you have fallen, and repent, and do the first works.” Only then does he add: “Otherwise”—that is, if, in addition to that which I already have against you, in addition to having forsaken your first love, you also add contempt—“I come to you,” and so forth.

This order of God’s judgment shines broadly in the Scriptures; but, for example, let only two men be set forth: Saul and David. Saul was a son of one year when he began to reign, but reigned two years over Israel. This means that he was humble as a child of one year old and little in his own eyes when he was made king, and for two years he reigned over Israel in that same humility. Hence the Lord, speaking through Samuel, says to him: “When you were little in your own eyes, were you not made head among the tribes of Israel?” (I Sam. XV).

He fell from this humility when he offered a burnt offering contrary to the law, since he was not a priest of Aaron’s stock but a man of the tribe of Benjamin. Again, because he had fallen from humility, he spared Agag king of Amalek and the best flocks of sheep, against the Lord’s command. And Scripture says again: “He offered a burnt offering to the Lord from the first-fruits of the spoils which he had brought from Amalek” (ibid.). Rebuked because he had forsaken his first humility, he was not mindful of the state from which he had fallen, nor did he repent; indeed, by offering another burnt offering he increased his sin and repeated his presumption. He did say, “I have sinned,” as though mindful of his fall; but he did not say or feel it humbly. For he added: “But now honor me before the elders of my people and before Israel, and return with me” (ibid.). Thus, by this confession—by saying “I have sinned”—he wished to gain not God’s honor or glory but his own. Therefore his throne rightly had to be removed from its place, because he did not repent.

But David too was little, of whom his father Jesse said to Samuel: “There remains yet the little one, and he is feeding the sheep” (I Sam. XVI). And when he was already reigning, he was still humble. For concerning his humility it is written: “When the ark of the Lord had entered the city of David, Michal, daughter of Saul, looking through the window, saw King David leaping and dancing before the Lord, and despised him in her heart” (II Sam. VI). But he said: “As the Lord lives, I will play, and I will become more contemptible than I have become, and I will be humble in my own eyes” (ibid.).

[Col. 0868D] He fell from this humility when he despised the word of the Lord by sinning with the wife of Uriah, whom he took. Therefore the prophet said to him: “Why then have you despised the word of the Lord, so as to do evil in my sight?” And immediately: “For this reason the sword shall not depart from your house forever, because you have despised me” (II Sam. XII). But he immediately remembered from where he had fallen and that he had forsaken his first love, and he said: “I have sinned against the Lord” (ibid.). Again, in the psalm: “For I acknowledge my iniquity, and my sin is always before me. Against you alone have I sinned and done evil before you” (Ps. L).

Therefore the Lord did not come to him as he had come to Saul, to remove his throne or lampstand from its place. For his kingdom stood, and prophetic grace remained with authority to teach; having recovered it, he says: “I will teach the wicked your ways” (ibid.). Therefore, whenever the angel—that is, the priest—of any Church forsakes his first love, it is right that ecclesiastical law should not immediately remove his lampstand from its place—that is, take away his priesthood or Church. Rather, it is said to him: “Remember from where you have fallen, and repent, and do the first works.” If he hears the rebuker, the one who rebuked has gained his brother (Matt. XVIII). But if, after another person has been brought in and after the public testimony of the Church’s assembly, he still does not amend—indeed, if he refuses to listen—then his lampstand is rightly removed and given to another.

There follows: “But this you have: you hate the deeds of the Nicolaitans, [Col. 0869B] which I also hate.” “I have against you,” he says, “that which I have already mentioned; but you have this with me, and in this you agree with me: you hate the deeds of the Nicolaitans. For I too hate them.”

The Nicolaitans were named after Nicholas, a deacon of the Church of Jerusalem, who was appointed with Stephen and the others by Peter. Because of her beauty, he left his wife and said that whoever wished might use her. Such a custom turned into fornication, so that they exchanged spouses with one another. These are the people whom he condemns here.

And the arrangement of the discourse should be observed, how artful it is. Before he released the severity of rebuke, he praised what was praiseworthy: “I know,” he says, “your works, your labor, and your patience,” and so forth. And afterward, when he had rebuked and threatened punishments, he again praised what was praiseworthy: “Because,” he says, “you hate the deeds of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate.” Thus, lest the bitterness of rebuke offend or terrify too much, he anointed it around with the sweetness of praise.

In this manner too, when speaking with the Samaritan woman, before saying, “For you have had five husbands, and he whom you now have is not your husband,” he first commended her, saying: “You have said well, ‘I have no husband.’” And after he had disclosed that she had had so many husbands, he again commended her: “You have said this truly” (John VI). It is a great and eminently imitable teaching of the Spirit of God: certainly to rebuke matters needing correction, but amid rebuke, both before and afterward, to praise whatever has been rightly said or done by the same person who is rebuked in other matters, so that, as far as possible, the person may remain well-disposed and the soul of the sinner may not flee, ashamed or terrified and unable to endure hearing.

Again, it should be observed that what follows is no less powerful upon an intelligent mind than any attack of a rebuker:

“He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the Churches.” Such an utterance is like a most forceful cry, reaching even to the ear of the heart within. Hence the Evangelist says: “Jesus, saying these things, cried out: He who has ears to hear, let him hear” (Matt. XIII). For by such a declaration he forcefully rebukes the negligent soul, indicating that the person is exceedingly deaf, even if his bodily ears are open, if he does not inwardly hear the force of so great a threat or inwardly feel the necessity of so great a judgment.

[Col. 0870A] Certainly, when he does not say, “what the Spirit says to the Church of Ephesus,” but “what the Spirit says to the Churches,” it must be understood that what he writes to individual Churches he says to all Churches. For in all Churches there are those who worthily hear, or those to whom the things of fear ought to be said; those to whom the things of piety ought to be said; those to whom the things of knowledge ought to be said; those to whom the things of fortitude ought to be said; those to whom the things of counsel ought to be said; those to whom the things of understanding ought to be said; and those to whom the things of wisdom ought to be said. Indeed, the reason why seven Churches are written to, or why the Church is called sevenfold, is that all who are in the Church stand at some degree of these graces.

Accordingly, this verse, as though an intercalary refrain, is pronounced concerning each Church and each of the spirits of God: “He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the Churches.” Another is added to it, which varies in each utterance of these spirits according to the character of the fitting rewards: “To the conqueror I will give to eat from the tree of life which is in the paradise of my God.”

At this degree—that is, in the spirit of fear—to conquer is to yield to the rebuker, repent, and perform the first works. But because the first human beings did not yield to God when he rebuked them—indeed, by proudly defending their sin they increased it—the tree of life, which God had planted in the midst of paradise, was closed to them. For the Lord God said: “Behold, Adam has become like one of us, knowing good and evil” (Gen. III). “Now therefore, lest he perhaps stretch out [Col. 0870C] his hand and take also from the tree of life, and eat and live forever,” the Lord God sent him out from the paradise of delight and placed before paradise the Cherubim and the flaming, turning sword to guard the way of the tree of life.

What was therefore closed to the first man because he did not repent is beautifully promised to this person if he repents: that he may eat of the tree of life “which,” he says, “is in the paradise of my God,” and, having eaten from it, live forever. He said “my God” by reason of the nature of our flesh which he assumed. By reason of his divine nature, it could have been said: “which is in the paradise of my Father.” He defined both matters in the Gospel when he said to his brothers, his apostles: “I ascend to my Father and your Father, my God and your God” (John XX).

But must we eat of that material tree in order to rise again and live forever? Certainly not. Rather, “He who eats my flesh,” he says, “and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day” (John VI). For Christ is the tree of life, by whose vision in the heavenly paradise and whose body in the present Church holy souls are refreshed. That material tree of life would not have given life to a man already dead by the death of the soul—that is, by sin—but would have caused his body to live forever; and this would be most unhappy. For if a person dead in soul lived forever in body, he would never be restored and would be eternally miserable, as demons are.

But this tree of life, which is Christ, while refreshing us with his body and blood, already raises the soul from the death of sin, and on the last day will raise our flesh. Yet one who has not yet conquered—that is, who has not repented—often eats of this tree of life which is in the paradise of God: he eats the body and drinks the blood of the Lord. Christ does not give it to him; rather, he seizes it, and therefore “eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (I Cor. XI).

“And write to the angel of the Church of Smyrna: These things says the first and the last, who was dead and lives: I know your tribulation and your poverty, but you are rich; and you are blasphemed by those who say that they are Jews and are not, but are the synagogue of Satan.” After the spirit of fear, above it is the spirit of piety; and beyond doubt this spirit speaks here, urging endurance of persecution, a purpose or intention to which the Church’s name is especially suited. For Smyrna means myrrh, which signifies mortification of the flesh.

[Col. 0871B] Those who suffer persecution for righteousness especially need the spirit of piety, so that in their sufferings they may be devout, gentle in insults or reproaches, not returning evil for evil or reviling for reviling (Rom. XII), but, on the contrary, blessing; indeed, so that meanwhile they may be sustained by their tears, longing for eternal life in whose hope they suffer, and weeping over its delay. Thus each one of them says in the psalm: “My tears were my bread day and night, while it is said to me daily, ‘Where is your God?’” (Ps. XLI).

And from whom should he more fittingly begin his words, when he intends, in the spirit of piety, to console the afflicted? He says: “These things says the first and the last, who was dead and lives.” He sets before the afflicted person’s eyes the first and the last, who was dead and lives, so that he may not wonder, in the heat that occurs for testing, as though something strange had happened. It is as though this Spirit says to the one whom he wishes to console: You have been cast down from whatever temporal eminence you occupied; because of righteousness, like an obscure man, you burn under reproaches and, beyond this, the lashings of a slave (I Pet. II). But how great is this, if you look to him who suffered for you, leaving you an example so that you should follow his footsteps?

For although, with God, he was first and most precious—according to one nature the Son of God, according to another nature the Son of the undefiled Virgin—although, I say, he was thus first and best and more beautiful than the children of men, among men he was last, that is, most despised. As the prophet says in grief: “We saw him, and there was no appearance; and we desired him, despised and the last of men; and we considered him as though leprous, struck by God, and humbled” (Isa. LIII; Ps. LXXXI). Thus he, the first, God standing in the synagogue of gods, was also “the last,” that is, the most despised, when he went under the judgment of men.

What then is remarkable if you, a man and not God, are cast down from whatever small honor was yours for his sake, if what you suffer as a man not without sin is compared with his passion [Col. 0872A] which he suffered for you—he “who committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (Isa. LIII)? Therefore he fittingly and appropriately began: “These things says the first and the last.” But what was the purpose of adding this: “who was dead and lives”? Surely it was to add a great abundance of consolation, so that one who is put to death by following Christ’s footsteps may know that he will live, just as he “who was dead now lives” (I Pet. II).

And what does he say? “I know your tribulation and your poverty.” The words “I know,” which he now says, must be understood forcefully and with the same weight with which the prophet already mentioned said concerning him: “And we saw him, a man of sorrows and knowing infirmity” (Isa. LIII). He said “knowing infirmity” to mean “having experience of infirmity.” Thus here too: “I know your tribulation and your poverty”; that is, I have experience of the tribulation which you suffer, and I have experienced in myself the poverty which you endure. For who has endured greater tribulation than I? And when I was rich, who descended to such poverty as I did? For the Psalmist says concerning me: “He persecuted the needy and poor man, and the one stricken in heart, to put him to death” (Ps. CVIII).

Mindful of this experience, the Apostle says: “For we do not have a high priest who cannot have compassion on our infirmities, but one tempted in all things according to our likeness, without sin” (Heb. IV). For he was tempted by hunger, thirst, persecution, and death; and hence he says, “I know your tribulation and your poverty.” Therefore do not grieve the less because you know or have experienced these things; for I also know them in such a way, I too have experienced them.

There follows, and he says: “But you are rich, and you are blasphemed by those who say that they are Jews and are not, but are the synagogue of Satan.” What I said about your poverty, I said according to men’s false estimate; for according to the truth of the matter, you are rich. They consider you poor, but you are rich. For I, ascending on high (Ps. LXVII)—I, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden (Isa. IV; Col. II), seated at the right hand of the Father—gave gifts to men, and from this you became rich, possessing a word of wisdom, or a word of knowledge (I Cor. XII), or any other talent from the many divisions of graces.

[Col. 0872D] And although you are so rich, you are blasphemed as though poor, as though you were nothing, had received nothing, knew nothing, had no knowledge of God in any respect, or were not known by God. By whom are you so blasphemed? “By those who say that they are Jews and are not, but are the synagogue of Satan.” It is a great labor and a great affliction of heart for you to be blasphemed in such a way and by such persons. But I too know this and have experienced it. I was rich, having within me the full treasures of the divinity dwelling bodily (Col. II), having resting upon me the Spirit of the Lord: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord (Isa. XI). Hence “I did works which no one else does, and spoke in such a manner that my opponents said, ‘Never has a man spoken in this way, as this man’” (John XV).

“And although I was so rich, I was blasphemed as though poor, as though I possessed nothing good or were not from God” (John VII). For they said: “This man is not from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath” (John IX). Again: “He casts out demons by Beelzebub, prince of demons” (Matt. XII). Further: “They said, ‘He has a demon and is mad. Why do you listen to him?’” (John X). And many similar things.

Thus I was blasphemed by those who said that they were Jews, saying: “We are Abraham’s seed; Abraham is our father; we have one Father, God” (John VIII). Yet they were not Jews or sons of Abraham, but were the synagogue of Satan. Therefore I said to them: “You are from your father the devil, and you wish to do your father’s desires” [Col. 0873B] (ibid.). And you too are blasphemed by such persons: namely, by false brothers, whoever they may be, “who profess to know God, but deny him by their works” (Titus I).

“Fear none of these things that you are about to suffer.” “Do not fear,” he says, so as to yield your ground and lose faith through fear of evils. Yet fear or trembling is allowed to the weakness of nature, provided that the spirit does not yield to fear by departing from God’s will. For it is written even of him who speaks these things, and in whom the spirit of piety speaks them: “And he takes Peter and James and John with him, and he began to be afraid and distressed” (Mark 14). Likewise he himself says of himself: “The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matt. 26).
