What are these things that you are about to suffer? “Behold, [Col. 0873C] the devil is about to cast some of you into prison, that you may be tested; and you will have tribulation for ten days.” Behold, he says, this will not extend over a long period: the present time is allotted to your tribulation, but the future to your joy. Conversely, the present time is appointed for the laughter of the wicked, and their future for mourning and distress.

But why did he not say, “Evil men will cast you into prison,” but rather, “The devil is about to cast some of you into prison”? Plainly because the spirit of piety ought to speak and teach in this way, instructing the devout martyr to attribute wholly to the devil, the inward instigator, what the persecuting human being does outwardly; to pity the persecuting person because the devil has possessed him; and to desire that he be freed from the devil. He should remember him who said: “Pray for those who persecute and slander you” (Matt. 3). Indeed, he who said this prayed for those persecuting and crucifying him: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23). Some were granted this forgiveness, as he asked: having shed his blood in persecution, they afterwards drank it in faith.

Therefore, when the devout martyr is sent to prison, let him know and say that this is done by the devil, by whom his human persecutor is held captive. Thus, amid chains and prisons, let him temper his answers accordingly, and lift up to God a suppliant mind on behalf of his persecutors, so that he may free some of them—which has often happened. “He is about to cast [you],” he says, “into prison.” Why? With what purpose? “That you may be tested.” [Col. 0874A] For he is the tempter, and his whole aim is to deceive some of you, if he can (Matt. 4).

With such an intention he demanded holy Job; and so he struck him outwardly with a grievous ulcer, so that there was no soundness in him from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head (Job 2), in order that he might overthrow inwardly his simplicity and uprightness: that Job might sin with his lips and say something foolish against God, and that the devil might then exult as victor over God, who had proposed him, saying: “Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on earth, a simple and upright man, fearing God and departing from evil?” (Job 1).

With this purpose, he says, “the devil is about to cast some of you into prison”: not so that all of you may quickly die by a sudden stroke of the sword, but so that, wearied by the prolongation of punishments [Col. 0874B] and the delay of death, you may be disturbed in your hearts, collapse while tossed amid the storms of injuries, and, if possible, having lost faith, be swallowed up. Behold, this is what will happen; this is what the devil does through his ministers. “And you will have tribulation for ten days”: that is, until death—namely, as long as you serve under God’s law, as you ought, so as to fulfill the Ten Commandments.

For it follows: “Be faithful unto death.” Clearly, steadfastness in faith needs strengthening by good exhortation for as long as the force of tribulations strives to extract that same faithfulness. Therefore, when he says, “Be faithful unto death,” he sufficiently shows that the ten days of tribulation extend to death: “Be faithful,” he says, “unto death, and I will give you the crown [Col. 0874C] of life.”

In saying this, he himself makes clear why he had first said of himself, “Who was dead and lives.” For he supplied in himself an example of the same perseverance which he urges in saying, “Be faithful unto death,” having “become obedient unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. 2). Likewise, for the certainty and confidence of the reward which he promises in saying, “And I will give you the crown of life,” he presents it in his own head; as the Apostle continues in the same place: “Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (ibid.). And elsewhere: “We see the Lord Jesus, because of the suffering of death, crowned with glory and honor” (Heb. 2). Therefore, he says, be faithful unto death, [Col. 0874D] because after death faithfulness is no longer demanded to be kept, but faithfulness kept is crowned.

“He who has ears, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.” To hear, or to have heard, the utterance of this Spirit—the spirit of piety—is to desire the crown of life which he here promises; and, in hope of it, not merely not to flee tribulation or persecution for Christ, but even willingly to embrace it; following his example, to give one’s cheek to the striker; to be filled with reproaches; and, if an outward persecutor is lacking, to persecute oneself inwardly, crucifying one’s flesh with its vices and desires (Gal. 5), and to weep without ceasing because one is delayed from the kingdom of God, from the vision of him who died and lives for us.

[Col. 0875A] Moreover, this Spirit requires such hearing, or such a hearer, not from the one church of the city of Smyrna alone but from all churches. Therefore he says not in the singular, “Let him hear what the Spirit says to the church,” but in the plural, “Let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.” Finally, suitably to the subject and purpose, he adds this conclusion: “He who conquers shall not be harmed by the second death.” The sense is: Whoever remains faithful until the death of the flesh shall not fear the eternal death of the soul.

He called the death of the soul “the second death.” Yet the death of the soul, which is the death of sin, or which comes through sinning, is so much earlier than the death of the flesh that even the resurrection of the soul—by which it rises through faith in Christ in baptism—comes before bodily death. Whoever desires to see the kingdom of God must attain it before passing from this world through bodily death. Why, then, or in what sense, is it now called the second death, unless because it is experienced later?

For Adam indeed died the death of the soul before the death of the flesh: namely, on the very day on which he rashly violated the forbidden tree, in accordance with the truth of him who said: “On whatever day you eat of it, you shall die the death” (Gen. 2). But he experienced that same death of the soul only when dust returned to dust—which is the death of the flesh—and the soul descended to hell. Thus the death of the soul, which through sin separates the soul from God, is first in cause or origin, but second in perception or experience.

[Col. 0875C] “And write to the angel of the church of Pergamum.” After the spirit of piety, the spirit of knowledge again follows. In this church also he rebukes those who hold bad teaching, the teaching of Balaam and the teaching of the Nicolaitans; and he says accordingly to the angel of this church as well: “Repent.” Certainly, for the destruction of every wicked teaching, the power or grace of the spirit of knowledge and the word of truth are necessary. Of this he says here in the opening: “Thus says he who has the two-edged rhomphaea [sword].” And afterwards: “Otherwise,” he says—that is, unless you repent—“I will come to you quickly and will fight against them with the sword of my mouth.”

Therefore, the two-edged rhomphaea, or this sword of the Lord’s mouth, is the word of God, of which the Apostle also says: “For the word of God is living and effective, and more piercing than any two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit, of joints also and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart” (Heb. 4). [Col. 0875D] For he distinguishes between soul and spirit, since he knows what the natural human being thinks or does for earthly advantages, and what the spiritual person thinks or does for heavenly things.

And, to speak in accordance with the present passage and subject, he distinguishes between the blessings of Balaam and the blessings of Moses. Both indeed bless the children of Israel, but in their remaining teaching they differ greatly. Balaam, with the same mouth by which he blessed, taught Balak to place a stumbling block before the children of Israel, that they might eat and commit fornication; [Col. 0876A] Moses did not do this.

The name Pergamum itself accords with this subject or intention. For *Pergamus* is interpreted as “dividing their horns.” This angel is warned, in accordance with the name of his church, Pergamum, to divide and distinguish the teaching of Balaam, or the teaching of the Nicolaitans, from sound doctrine by the holy Spirit of knowledge.

He says therefore: “Thus says he who has the two-edged rhomphaea.” For what does he have that rhomphaea? To execute vengeance upon all who hold the teaching of Balaam, and upon whoever he may be who teaches Balaam’s doctrine. For we must remember the truthful history in which the Lord says to Moses: “Take vengeance for the children of Israel upon the Midianites.” And shortly afterwards: “When they had fought against the Midianites and conquered them, [Col. 0876B] they killed all the males and their kings—Evi, Rekem, Zur, Hur, and Reba, the five princes of the nation; Balaam also son of Beor they killed with the sword” (Num. 31).

And a little later: “Moses was angry with the commanders of the army, the tribunes and centurions who had returned from the war, and said: ‘Why have you spared the women? Are not these the ones who deceived the children of Israel at Balaam’s suggestion, and caused you to transgress against the Lord in the sin of Peor? Because of this the people also were struck down. Therefore kill every male, even the little ones, and slaughter the women who have known men in intercourse’” (ibid.).

We must, I say, remember this truthful history here, because what was done there literally, he who professes himself to possess the two-edged rhomphaea declares that he will do here spiritually. He says: “I know where you dwell, where Satan’s throne is.” [Col. 0876C] It is a great and vehement reproach of that angel of the church that he dwells there “where Satan’s throne is,” or that Satan’s throne is there where that angel is. The following discourse will show what his negligence is, and how Satan was allowed to have his throne there. Meanwhile, he says: “And you hold fast my name, and have not denied my faith.” This might seem great, if his following negligence or work did not obscure the confession of the name.

“And in those days Antipas, my faithful witness, who was killed among you where Satan dwells.” In accordance with the name Pergamum, interpreted “dividing [Col. 0876D] their horns,” he has thus far praised what was worthy of praise, commemorating, as some relate, a martyr named Antipas who suffered at Pergamum, with testimony to his praiseworthy faith. Afterwards he rebukes what is worthy of rebuke, and thus divides the horn of righteousness from the horns of unrighteousness, according to that verse of the Psalm: “I will break all the horns of sinners, and the horns of the righteous shall be exalted” (Ps. 74).

For it follows: “But I have a few things against you, because you have there those who hold the teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak to place a stumbling block before the children of Israel, to eat and commit fornication. So you also have those who hold the teaching of the Nicolaitans.” The present passage warns us to consider more carefully what Balaam’s teaching was according to the history, and how many, who appear to belong to the Church, still hold or imitate it today.

That Balaam is the same person who is called Elihu in the book of Job: at first a prophet and holy man, afterwards, because of avarice, called by the title of diviner or soothsayer. He, possessing the power or efficacy of blessing and cursing, represented priests who, though wicked, nevertheless possess by their office the power to admit to communion or excommunicate. Thus Balak says to him: “Come and curse this people, for I know that he whom you bless is blessed, and he upon whom you heap curses is cursed” (Num. 22). Balaam also had knowledge of God and knew that a priest heaps curses in vain upon one whom his own cause or guilt does not subject to curses.

Yet, because of avarice, he went and repeatedly inquired whether perhaps it would please God for him to curse this people. He plainly portrays those who sell blessings and curses in the Church and do everything for gain. The summit of his wicked teaching was this: “Yet, going to my people, I will give counsel as to what your people may do to this people.” And he gave the counsel which was carried out: that the people might commit fornication with the daughters of Moab, who called them to their sacrifices; they ate and drank, and were initiated into Baal-peor, and the Lord was angered. This, in short, is the counsel he gave. “Are not these,” Moses says, [Col. 0877C] “the women who deceived the children of Israel at Balaam’s suggestion?” (Num. 31).

He fell into teaching of this kind through avarice, not ignorance. For he himself, professing his knowledge, says: “Balaam son of Beor has spoken; the man whose eye is darkened has spoken; the hearer of the words of God has spoken, he who knows the doctrine of the Most High and sees visions of the Almighty, who, falling, has open eyes” (Num. 24). Certainly, while saying these things, he was falling into the deep pit of avarice and saw his own fall.

Thus divided, thus double, was Balaam: publicly chanting God’s blessings in ringing words, secretly devising deceit and providing counsel to an impious king for the ruin of God’s people. Does he not portray in himself the intolerable hypocrisy of venal priests? Are not all things even today filled with the inward pestilence of such sacrilegious persons?

The violent hand of secular men is sent forth—of those who love this world and are powerful in it—in accordance with the name Balak, for it is interpreted “licking” or “crushing”: licking, that is, the delights of the world, and crushing, so far as it can, chaste souls which do not consent to it. [Col. 0877D] This hand, I say, sends across the Jordan, summons some transgressor of holy baptism, and sets up for itself a bishop inclined toward avarice, observing vanities in accordance with the name Balaam. For Balaam is interpreted “vain people.” Kings and emperors too, who call themselves Christians, have pursued such vanity; and against Aaron the bishop they have set up Balaam the soothsayer; against Peter, Simon Magus; against some lawful bishop of the Roman [Col. 0878A] see, they have sometimes intruded some adulterer to pronounce a curse.

But let us speak of Balaam universally—that is, of all who, anywhere in the world, under the name or office of priesthood, pursue avarice and love the wages of unrighteousness. Whoever he is, therefore, who approaches the priesthood in this manner has indeed been brought in to curse, and in his mind he detests Israel because he loves vices and hates virtues. Yet he does not dare to detest it publicly, nor to curse openly with his voice, so as to teach in the Church otherwise than the rule of faith provides.

Thus Balaam, when he wished to curse Israel because of the rewards promised him, did not dare to do so because the Lord forbade it; rather, he blessed them, truthfully uttering concerning Christ the same things for the felicity of that people which Moses and the other holy prophets piously and faithfully proclaim: “A star shall arise from Jacob, and a rod shall rise from Israel, and it shall strike the leaders of Moab” (ibid.), and so forth. It is not possible now to set forth individually their mystical meanings.

Likewise, these people do not dare, even when they wish to do so, to transgress the rule of faith. Though they desire in their minds to remove from the peoples the fear of future judgment, so that they may have many supporters of their own wickedness and many companions in their destruction, they nevertheless recite readings and sing testimonies concerning the Lord’s passion, resurrection, ascension, and the judgment of the last day. In this faith they bless, baptize, and consecrate. But when they have done these things publicly, they turn secretly to counsel, to evil conversations [Col. 0878C] which corrupt good morals.

The daughters of Midian, prepared beforehand, come forward, playing and walking with studied step in order to deceive Israel. This happens whenever persons tender and soft, given over to flowing vices, possessing no manly strength for constancy of life (1 Cor. 15), receive honors and, though base in character, become conspicuous in the Church under the Christian name. This is the counsel or suggestion of Balaam: that is, of all who, following his life, love the wages of unrighteousness. For they advance the children of the Church to ecclesiastical honors not on account of their virtues, but advance daughters—that is, soft and vicious souls—for gifts.

Do those who are thus advanced not hold the doctrine of the Nicolaitans? Clement relates that Nicholas, reproached for jealousy concerning his very beautiful wife, replied that whoever wished might take her as wife; and that he taught unbelievers that the Apostles permitted indiscriminate and common sexual relations with women for all. [Col. 0878D] Is this not close to the doctrine of those who, unwilling to have lawful marriage—as being forbidden by ecclesiastical laws, so that they may be holy and cleansed because they bear the vessels of the Lord—are nevertheless incontinent? Indeed, they rush more disgracefully into it, imitating marriages whenever they wish; and, having no lawful marriage-bed, while they wander in this way, they believe that they have broken no bond of marriage. Yet they commit fornication [with them] (Lev. 20), and all who through the example of such persons become bolder in incest or adultery [Col. 0879A] are initiated into Baal-peor (1 Chron. 15).

At that time it was indeed a miracle that the Lord opened the mouth of a mute beast of burden, and that an animal speaking with a human voice rebuked the foolishness of the prophet who gave counsel of this kind (Ezek. 44; Num. 22). Yet something almost similar happens now, when the common populace rebukes and upbraids the rulers of the Church with its cries because such a pestilence, so great a stain upon sacred orders, has arisen from their avarice.

He says therefore: “But I have a few things against you, because you have there those who hold the teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak to place a stumbling block before the children of Israel, to eat and commit fornication.” And, explaining what that teaching of Balaam is, he immediately adds: “So you also have those holding the teaching of the Nicolaitans.” Therefore, he calls the fornications which Nicholas is said to have introduced, as has already been stated, contrary to ecclesiastical purity, “the teaching of Balaam”; and he affirms that this is the scandal of God’s Church: “to eat and commit fornication.”

And rightly so. For wherever a hired priest or bishop, following Balaam’s example, loves the wages of unrighteousness, the evil fruits of every vice immediately spring up as from an evil root. First, the Church’s chastity and every adornment of religion perish; there is no concern for learning, no honor for it, scarcely any fervor of sacred study; but avarice—[Col. 0879B] which is service of idols—an abyss that swallows every good thing.

It follows:

“Likewise repent; but if not, I am coming to you quickly, and I will fight against them with the sword of my mouth.” A threat altogether fitting and timely to the matter, from him who said that he has the two-edged rhomphaea. For when that Balaam, hired for a reward, was going on his way, the angel of the Lord stood in the road holding a drawn sword in his hand, and said to Balaam: “I have come to oppose you. And unless the she-ass had turned aside from the road, yielding place to the one opposing her, I would have killed you, and she would have lived” (Num. 22).

And because he did not repent, teaching Balak to place a stumbling block before the children of Israel, to eat and commit fornication, vengeance was completed upon him. To signify this vengeance, the angel of the Lord appeared in such a form—that is, holding a drawn sword in his hand. For in that vengeance inflicted upon the Midianites, “Balaam also son of Beor,” Scripture says, “they killed with the sword” [Col. 0879D] (Num. 31).

Well, therefore, he says: “I will come and fight against them with the sword of my mouth,” namely, in likeness of that angelic vision and of that vengeance upon the Midianites and Balaam himself. For that sword in the angel’s hand, and that vengeance upon the Midianites, signify the judgment of which the Apostle says: “God will judge fornicators and adulterers” (Heb. 13). For he will judge not only fornicators, such as the Midianites with whom Israel committed fornication, but also those adulterers who adulterate the word of God, such as Balaam, who adulterated words of blessing by secretly introducing evil counsel and teaching Balak to place that stumbling block before the children of Israel.

“He who has ears, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.” [Col. 0880A] In this place, to hear what the Spirit says is not to cease from sound teaching, to destroy Balaam’s teaching, to exercise holy knowledge, and always to keep in mind that evangelical saying of the Lord: “Woe to you lawyers, because you have taken away the key of knowledge” (Luke 11). “You yourselves did not enter, and you hindered those who were entering.”

For those who nourish sins, or permit them to be nourished, under the Christian name, supposing that the divine name alone suffices for salvation—like those who trusted in deceitful words and said, “The temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord,” while making it a den of thieves (Jer. 7)—certainly have not entered into true knowledge. For if they had entered it, if they had vigilantly heeded, or been willing to heed, the words of the holy Scriptures (Matt. 21), they would know that a profession of the divine name avails nothing when, as in Balaam, wicked teaching supplants it: the teaching of eating and fornication.

Knowing and observing this, they would not have been cast out of the temple by the scourge of God’s wrath (John 2), while the prophetic Spirit continued and said concerning them: “Therefore my people have been led captive because they had no knowledge” (Isa. 5). Let him who has ears therefore hear this: that breast in which knowledge is absent through voluntary blindness shall be struck with the sword like a brute victim.

“He who conquers, I will give hidden manna.” To conquer at this stage is first to destroy Balaam’s teaching—that is, fornications—in oneself through the virtue [Col. 0880C] of continence, and then in others through the virtue of knowledge. Whoever conquers in this way receives worthily the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood; whereas, conversely, whoever neglects to conquer, approaching this sacrament, “eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (1 Cor. 11).

Rightly, therefore, he says: “To the conqueror I will give hidden manna”; that is, to one who keeps purity of heart and body I will give the true bread, the living bread, of which the manna eaten by the children of Israel was a sign or figure. This manna is called hidden because in this sacrament one thing is seen by the eyes and another understood by faith.

And what benefit will come to the recipient of this hidden manna? He says: “And I will give him [Col. 0880D] a white stone, and upon the stone a new name written, which no one knows except the one who receives it.” Whoever receives this sacrament worthily will rise on the last day with a new body, possessing solid and everlasting brightness; and that person’s body will be like a stone, that is, made firm by a splendid transformation. Of this the Apostle says: “The dead will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed” (1 Cor. 15).

To be changed belongs only to the saints, and means the same as if he had said: “We shall die no more; we shall be incapable of suffering.” To have a new name written on such a stone is to be called and to be sons of God. This new name, namely the name received from the new man Christ, has been given to those redeemed through his blood. For the old name from the old man was our inherited name: that we should be called and should be by nature children of wrath (Eph. 2).

But why does no one know this name except the one who receives it? Plainly because knowledge of this name is produced not by instruction coming from another outwardly, but by one’s own inward experience. Let the inflated and arrogant know, or seem to themselves to know, as much as they wish or can: nevertheless they cannot attain knowledge of this name. For it is written: “They thought these things and went astray, for their malice blinded them, and they did not know the mysteries of God” (Wis. 2).

Therefore no one, however much he knows or noisily blusters with puffed cheeks—such as Aristotle or all the Aristotelians—can know the dignity or nobility of this name by which we are called or are sons of God; nor can anyone know the relation of Father to Son [Col. 0881B] or of Son to Father, except one whom the Spirit of adoption, by regenerating him, has made a son of God the Father, and whom that very regeneration has made knowing in this matter and taught by its own touch.

“And write to the angel of the church of Thyatira: Thus says the Son of God, who has eyes like a flame of fire, and whose feet are like bronze.” Here, in the Son of God, the spirit of fortitude, which follows above the spirit of knowledge, speaks what belongs to it. For he says: “I have against you that you permit the woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess, to teach and seduce my servants.”

In saying this, he directs the angel of Thyatira and every holy person who, according to the name Thyatira, translated “into a sacrifice,” has offered his body to God as a living sacrifice [Col. 0881C] (Rom. 12), to the truthful history in which Elijah the Tishbite was so strong against Jezebel and her prophets, and acted so courageously, that to this day he says in the midst of the Church, in memorable praise of the strength of his zeal: “I have been very zealous for the Lord God of hosts, because they have killed your prophets and dug down your altars” (1 Kings 19). For he had been so courageous in zeal that he killed four hundred men, the prophets of Baal, with the sword (1 Kings 18).

With the same strength of zeal Phinehas also—whom the Hebrews maintain was Elijah himself—at the above-mentioned scandal which Balaam taught Balak to place before the children of Israel, “seized a dagger and entered after the Israelite man into the brothel, where he had gone in to the harlot, and pierced both of them, the man and the woman, in their genital parts; and thus the wrath of the Lord was turned away from Israel” (Num. 25).

This zeal, or this fortitude, is a great thing and necessary for a holy man, because if he lacks it he is endangered in the judgment of the Lord, however great the holiness of his own life may be. The danger of Eli, priest of Shiloh, is an example. For because he knew that his sons behaved unworthily and did not rebuke them with zeal worthy of the law, but with excessively fatherly—indeed, almost womanly—softness, saying: “Do not do so, my sons; for the report which I hear is not good, that you make the people [Col. 0882A] of the Lord transgress” (1 Kings 2), judgment came upon him. The Lord thus concluded the sentence: “Therefore I have sworn to the house of Eli that its iniquity shall never be expiated by sacrifices and offerings” (1 Kings 3).

Let us now discuss the words themselves in order. “Thus says the Son of God, who has eyes like a flame of fire.” This pertains to the purpose: namely, because the one who persuades his angel or priest to possess fortitude, showing beforehand in himself an example of the same fortitude of zeal, instructs his disciple with greater authority as Lord and Master.

For, to explain for the present what is meant by his fiery eyes and “his feet like bronze,” is it not as though he said: His fortitude was tested also in his journeys or actions? For bronze, by long heating in a furnace of fire and prolonged polishing, acquires the quality of retaining the appearance of gold. Thus the Son of God himself who says these things, as it were concerning his feet—that is, his end, of which the Apostle James says, “You have heard of Job’s patience [Col. 0882B] and have seen the Lord’s end” (Jas. 5)—courageously completed that end in the burning furnace of his passion; and, rising again, transformed his flesh into the golden glory of immortality. Then, with great zeal, sparing not the hostile fire, he caused his nation, land, and city Jerusalem to burn.

Therefore, because his feet are like bronze, he rightly demands by this example from the one to whom he speaks that after every good work he also possess strict strength of righteous zeal against others who sin. With this intention he says beforehand of himself: “Who has eyes like a flame [Col. 0882C] of fire.” For his eyes, which are seven in number according to the prophet Zechariah (ch. 4), and according to a later passage in this Scripture, “are the seven spirits” (Rev. 3).

Before the furnace of his passion, the Holy Spirit was seen to descend upon him and remain in him, not like a flame of fire but like a dove (John 1). But when he ascended into heaven, he looked down upon the earth as it were with fiery eyes, sending the same sevenfold Spirit, who appeared above the Apostles in tongues of fire and made those who were weak strong and fervent with good zeal (Acts 2).

What does this Son of God say?

“I know your works, and faith, and love, and [Col. 0882D] your latter works are more numerous than the former.” In his customary way, he first commends what is worthy of praise, and afterwards mentions with fatherly correction what is blameworthy. “I know your works,” he says, “and I know and approve this: that you have progressed from good things to better things.” This is what he means when he repeats: “Your latter works are more numerous than the former.”

For example, that person’s latter works are more numerous, or better, than his former works who, having begun a good work from fear, comes to love, which, once perfected, casts out fear (1 John 4). This appears to be what he indicates when, after saying, “I know your works,” he immediately adds, “and faith and love.” For fear, conceived through faith, is the beginning of good works; but love is their perfection, excluding servile [Col. 0883A] fear. And however many the works of fear may be, which are earlier in time or sequence, the works of love, later in time, are without doubt greater in dignity and merit.

Therefore, in his own person, this angel of Thyatira is honored by the great testimony of the heavenly Judge, because, in accordance with the name Thyatira, translated “into a sacrifice,” he has offered himself to God as a living sacrifice through faith and love.

“But I have this against you,” he says, “that you permit the woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess, to teach and to seduce my servants into committing fornication and eating things sacrificed to idols.” It is as though he said: In your work and faith you are praiseworthy, but in this you are blameworthy: content with your own salvation, you do not rebuke with fitting denunciation the heretical unbelief which destroys others. The name Jezebel, indeed, which signifies a flow of blood, suits heretics. And it is especially conjectured that there was a woman in the aforesaid Church who taught the crimes mentioned, and who was a figure of Jezebel throughout the world.

For that one Jezebel, wife of Ahab king of Israel, prefigured all heretical unbelief both in name and deed: for her name is interpreted, as has already been said, as “flow of blood,” and she herself was the first to persecute and kill the prophets of the Lord. Before her, indeed, no one is recorded to have killed prophets. She stoned the righteous Naboth; she would have slain Elijah with the sword had he not taken thought for flight. Her descendants also imitated the example of their impious parent—namely Ahaziah king of Judah, son of Joram by Athaliah, daughter of that same Jezebel, [Col. 0883C] and Joash and Amaziah. They persecuted and killed the prophets of the Lord and forbade the word of God to be spoken; and therefore, when Matthew wrote of the holy and mystical genealogy of Jesus Christ, they were omitted and deserved neither a place nor remembrance in it.

Long before, indeed, golden calves had been made, and the ten tribes had been separated from the house of David and from the temple of the Lord—an event which was the sign and beginning of every heretical and schismatic wickedness. But this Jezebel, plainly, added the worship of Baal; she added, as has been said, the sword of unbelief, shed righteous blood, and drove the minister of God’s word into flight. Rightly, therefore, both that woman—who, speaking and teaching in the Church beyond the dignity of her sex, led others astray (1 Cor. XIV)—and all heretical unbelief are called and are Jezebel. The name of that Jezebel, whose offspring, as has been said, perished from the holy lineage, is kept as a term of reproach.

“Because you permit,” he says, “the woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess,” and so forth. What did he wish that man to do, to whom he said, “because you permit”? Certainly, to put on the spirit of fortitude (1 Tim. II), and in zeal for the Lord spiritually to do what Elijah did bodily. After rebuking the people, saying, “How long will you limp between two sides?” and after bringing it about through evident signs that those worshipping should say, “The Lord himself is God; the Lord himself is God,” he said: “Seize the prophets of Baal, and let not even one of them escape.” When they had seized them, [Col. 0884A] Elijah led them down to the brook Kishon and killed them there (3 Kings XVIII).

A holy man such as that Angel of Thyatira ought to imitate and do this: he should not be content with his own salvation, since he is an angel, and according to that name ought to announce to others how they may be saved. Rather, taking up the sword of God’s word, he should rebuke the people because they limp between two sides: on the one hand communicating in the body of Christ, and on the other, according to the teaching of this woman, committing fornication or eating things sacrificed to idols. For the Apostle says: “You cannot partake of the table of the Lord and of the table of demons” (1 Cor. X). You cannot drink the cup of demons.

Therefore, let the one to whom these things are written restrain those who teach this and, though they seem to teach, deceive the people, as prophets of Baal and prophets of Jezebel; and with the avenging sword—the sword of God’s word, which is in his mouth (Eph. VI)—let him separate them from the Church, as condemned by their own judgment (Tit. III), lest anyone communicate with them or take food, and likewise lest anyone say to any of them, “Greetings,” or receive such a person into his house (1 Cor. V; 2 John I). Thus he spiritually does what Elijah did with the material sword when he killed the prophets of Baal. He now speaks of Jezebel herself—that is, of the whole heretical synagogue which makes itself a teacher.

“And I gave her time to repent, and she is unwilling to repent of her fornication. And behold, I shall cast her onto a bed; and those who commit adultery with her shall be in very great tribulation, unless they repent of their works. And I shall kill her children into death, and all the Churches shall know that I am he who searches the reins [inmost desires] [Col. 0884C] and hearts; and I shall give to each of you according to your works.”

This entire threat of punishment looks to the likeness of that Jezebel, whose name this woman—or every heretical plague—has received according to her deserts. For thus was that Jezebel, queen or king’s daughter, punished, as the historical narrative teaches. First, God gave her time to repent; Ahab, indeed, repented after a fashion, but she was unwilling to repent. To give time for repentance is to send warnings before punishments. This the Lord did when he spoke through Elijah to Ahab: “Behold, I shall bring evil upon you, and shall cut off your posterity, and shall kill from Ahab everyone who urinates against a wall; and I shall make your house like the house of Jeroboam [Col. 0884D] son of Nebat. But the Lord also spoke concerning Jezebel, saying: Dogs shall eat Jezebel in the field of Israel.” And again concerning Ahab: “If Ahab,” he says, “dies in the city, dogs shall eat him; but if he dies in the field, the birds of heaven shall eat him” (3 Kings XXI).

Therefore God gave each of them time for repentance, that they might repent, since he threatened each with punishment before inflicting it. And Ahab, as has been said, repented in some fashion; and therefore the Lord moderated the sentence of punishment which he had threatened, according to the measure of his repentance. For it follows: “And so, when Ahab heard these words, he tore his garment, covered his flesh with sackcloth, fasted, slept in sackcloth, and walked with bowed head” (ibid.). [Col. 0885A]

For this reason, as has been said, the Lord moderated the punishment and remitted something from the sentence. For what he had said at the beginning of his address or judgment—“In the place where dogs licked the blood of Naboth, they shall lick your blood also”—was indeed fulfilled; nevertheless, neither did dogs eat him in the city, nor birds of heaven in the field. For it was afterwards written thus: “But the king died and was carried to Samaria; and they buried the king in Samaria. They washed the chariot in the pool of Samaria, and the dogs licked his blood and licked the reins, according to the word of the Lord which he had spoken” (3 Kings XXII).

Likewise, what he said, “I shall cut off your posterity and make your house like the house of Jeroboam,” he moderated thus: “Because, therefore, he has humbled himself on my account, I shall not bring evil in his days; but in the days of his son I shall bring evil upon his house” (3 Kings XXI). But from the sentence pronounced against Jezebel he remitted nothing, plainly because she did not repent at all.

“And behold, I cast her,” he says, “onto a bed.” This saying looks most fittingly to the manner of her fault: namely, because by her crime she made her husband rise from his bed, when he was strengthened in wickedness. For when he, angry and raging over the word Naboth had spoken—“I shall not give you the inheritance of my fathers” (ibid.)—had thrown himself upon his bed and would not eat bread, she entered; and when she learned the reason, she mocked him as feeble, saying: “You exercise great authority, and rule the kingdom of Israel well! Rise and eat bread, and be of good cheer; [Col. 0885C] I shall give you the vineyard of Naboth the Israelite.”

Rightly, therefore, she ought to have been cast onto a bed. How, then, was she cast onto a bed? “Jezebel,” says Scripture, “when she heard of Jehu’s approach, painted her eyes with antimony, adorned her head, and looked out through the window as Jehu entered through the gate. But he said to the eunuchs: Throw her down. And they threw her down” (4 Kings IX). Thus, by that mode of speech called sarcasm—that is, hostile mockery—she may rightly be said to have been cast onto a bed, where she was thrown down. For she was cast down into hell, where she has such a bed that not she herself rests, but that madness by which she troubled the earth rests.

In this sense the Psalm sings: “The earth trembled and was still, when God rose in judgment” (Ps. LXXV). For when he who rose—God—appears in judgment, the earth will tremble; that is, everyone who loves the earth will tremble, and will be still, that is, will cease, so as no longer to produce disturbance or unrest. Individually, each sinner now becomes still and ceases, as she ceased when she was thrown down; but then, at the judgment, all together will cease.

It follows: “And those who commit adultery with her shall be in very great tribulation.” This too was abundantly fulfilled in that Jezebel. First, her own husband, who committed fornication with her—the fornication by which God is abandoned and idols are worshipped—and then all his house, and indeed all the people, were in very great tribulation: the tribulation of war and famine. Ahab himself was first wounded in battle against the king of Syria and [Col. 0886A] died in tribulation, and dogs licked his blood (3 Kings XXII). After him, his son Joram and all the people who committed fornication with her were in very great tribulation, when Ben-hadad king of Syria fought and besieged Samaria.

“For there was a great famine in Samaria, and it was besieged so long that a donkey’s head was sold for eighty pieces of silver, and a fourth part of a cab [or kab] of dove’s dung for five pieces of silver. And when the king of Israel passed along the wall, a certain woman cried out to him, saying: Save me, my lord the king.” And further: “This woman said to me: Give your son, that we may eat him today, and tomorrow we shall eat my son. Therefore we cooked my son and ate him” (4 Kings VI), and so forth. They were in that very great tribulation because they had not repented; indeed, Jezebel was still living, and they were still committing fornication with her. Hence later, when her son Joram asked, “Is there peace, Jehu?” he replied: “What peace?” (4 Kings IX). “The fornications of Jezebel your mother and her many sorceries still flourish.”

He says, then: “And those who commit adultery with her shall be in great tribulation unless they repent”—and one must understand, just as it happened to those who committed fornication with Jezebel. And immediately he adds:

“And I shall kill her children into death.” The children of the heretical woman are her imitators. The likeness of their slaughter to eternal condemnation is no less clearly seen in the killing of the children of that Jezebel. First Ahaziah her son, who reigned in his father’s place, fell through the lattice of his upper chamber [Col. 0886C] at Samaria, became sick, and died. Jehu killed his brother Joram, when he reigned in his place: “He drew the bow with his hand and struck him between the shoulders; the arrow went out through his heart, and immediately he fell in his chariot” (4 Kings IX).

Moreover, the nobles of the city, among whom they were being raised, killed by Jehu’s command seventy men, all sons of the king, whether by Jezebel herself or by other wives (4 Kings X). Jehu also killed Ahaziah, king of Judah, son of Jezebel’s daughter, who had come to visit Joram, and his forty-two brothers. For when Jehu found them and asked, “Who are you?” they answered, “We are brothers of Ahaziah, and we have come down to greet the sons of the king and the sons of the queen.” He said: “Take them alive.” When they had taken them alive, they slaughtered them, and he left none of them alive (ibid.).

Athaliah also, mother of Ahaziah, seeing that her son was dead, rose up and killed all the royal seed, who were certainly children—that is, great-grandchildren—of Jezebel. One son of Ahaziah, Joash, was stolen away by Ahaziah’s sister from among the king’s sons as they were being killed (4 Kings XI).

It is therefore clear that the whole punishment decreed against this woman—indeed, against all heretical teaching—is decreed after the example of that Jezebel, so that her just punishment may resemble that woman to whom she made herself like in guilt. It would be far too long to dwell on every part according to the likeness set forth: how every soul that is a teacher of heretical doctrine [Col. 0887A] is cast upon a bed with her husband—indeed, her adulterer, the devil; in what kind of tribulation those who commit adultery with her, that is, who delight to imitate her, will be; and how her children are killed into death—that is, killed in such a way that they remain forever in death and are tortured together in body and soul. Let us proceed with the rest.

“And all the Churches,” he says, “shall know that I am he who searches hearts and reins, and I shall give to each of you according to your works.” So that we may not go too far afield in asking why he says here, “I am he who searches reins and hearts,” let us keep in mind the condition which he inserted among these threats when he said, “unless they repent of their works.” For since some repent in order to attain God’s eternal grace, others in order to retain earthly prosperity, and others do not repent at all, it belonged to the Judge—who declares that he will render to each according to his works—to show how he can know the character and merit of the work of any repentant or unrepentant person.

“And all the Churches,” he says, “shall know this, namely in the future, when each shall be repaid according to his works.” For now few know and discern how fitting recompense is rendered to individuals in what they sometimes suffer in the present by God’s judgment. For example, the often-mentioned Ahab repented, but his whole repentance was not in his heart but about his reins [his carnal desires] (3 Kings XVIII). For in repenting he did not take care or fear lest he become estranged from God’s kingdom; he feared only lest he be deprived of his own kingdom.

Conversely, David, who killed Uriah, did not fear in repentance that he would be deprived of his kingdom, but that he would be abandoned by God’s grace (3 Kings XI). Hence he said: “Do not cast me away from your presence, and do not take your Holy Spirit from me” (Ps. L). But Joram, like his mother, having an unrepentant heart, amid his evils during the siege of Samaria, when he said, “Why is so great an evil from the Lord?” sought to take revenge upon the prophet of the Lord for what he could not do against the Lord himself, saying: “May God do this to me and add this besides, if the head of Elisha son of Shaphat remains upon him today.” And he sent ahead a man to cut off his head (4 Kings VI).

Therefore, he who “searches hearts and reins,” that is, who truly discerns who repents with a carnal and who with a spiritual intention, delayed Ahab’s punishment, restored David to grace, and killed Joram and the other children of Jezebel without delay. Thus he rendered to each according to his works, declaring that all around us should know that it will be so in the future when he concludes: “And I shall give to each of you according to your works.” It follows:

“But to you I say, to the rest who are at Thyatira, who have not known the depths of Satan [those who do not have this teaching, etc.], as they say: I shall not cast upon you another burden; nevertheless, hold fast what you have until I come.”

“You who are at Thyatira,” he says, “whom I have reserved for myself, like those of whom I spoke in Elijah, when he fled in fear of the often-mentioned Jezebel: ‘I have reserved for myself seven thousand men who have not bent the knee before Baal’” (3 Kings XIX). For he now says the same thing about these remaining persons at Thyatira, passing from the second person to the third, in other words: “Who have not known the depths of Satan.”

For to commit fornication and eat things sacrificed to idols, just as to bend the knee, is to know the depths of Satan. To know, however, is to approve. The depth of Satan which he now strikes at is that pride by which he strives to be like the Most High, demanding sacrifices to himself in idols, when sacrifice ought to be offered to the Most High alone. Those who then bent the knee before Baal under that Jezebel knew—that is, approved—this depth; and those whom this woman now taught at Thyatira, who committed fornication and ate things sacrificed to idols, likewise knew it. Those who refused to eat did not know it, like those seven thousand men who did not bend the knee.

That depth is not real, but it seems so to those who love and admire the gold and silver in the images of the nations. They admire the images of the nations because they are gold and silver, because they are exquisitely wrought and artful works of human hands; and they themselves are inquisitive, receiving from them the responses of demons. Therefore, when he had said, “the depths of Satan,” he rightly added, “as they say.” It is as though he said: I do not call Satan’s depth what it truly is, but what foolish admirers call it.

“To you,” he says, “to you remaining ones who are at Thyatira,” whom that woman did not teach or deceive, “I shall not cast upon you another burden; only hold fast what you have until I come.” [Col. 0888C] You already have a burden, he says; you are already bearing your punishment, while Jezebel teaches and deceives, while my servants who have been deceived commit fornication and eat things sacrificed to idols, and you do not dare to forbid them, being oppressed by fear, weak and feeble. That very fear, which even the wise of this world count a suffering, is a burden to you: the burden of slavery, the burden of weakness.

You are not strong; you are not free, as that Elijah was, who had nothing in the world, nor wished to have anything, and feared to lose nothing. He rejoiced in no worldly advantage, grieved over no temporal disadvantage; and therefore, strong and unencumbered, he rebuked the king and killed the prophets of Baal (3 Kings XVIII). He feared Jezebel’s threats only once and fled, but he did not so fear or flee as not to return and openly proclaim by the word of the Lord that dogs would eat Jezebel (3 Kings XIX).

Hold fast, until I come, the burden which you have, under which you labour and are burdened (Matt. XIX), or until I cause you to come with evangelical perfection, so that you may follow me; having left all things, you may proclaim God’s word, and, selling your tunic, buy a sword, that you may fear no one except the Lord (Matt. XIX; Luke XXII). Meanwhile, while you bear this burden and groan under it, consuming in silence your sorrow for those who are deceived, I shall place no other burden upon you; I shall not aggravate the sentence. For you are silent through fear, not consent; through weakness, not malice.

“He who conquers and keeps [Col. 0889A] my works until the end, I shall give him authority over the nations, and he shall rule them with an iron rod, and they shall be shattered like a potter’s vessel.”

At this level, to conquer is to overcome every passion which makes a person weak: to drive joy, fear, hope, and sorrow away and banish them from the mind—that is, not to rejoice in the world, not to fear the world, not to hope for worldly things, and not to grieve for worldly things. Certainly, one who is such, who overcomes all affections of the flesh and these passions and thus keeps the Lord’s works to the end—that is, unto perfection—is worthy and fit to preside, to be another’s guide and ruler, and to command and compel recruits into the Lord’s service.

He says, therefore: “I shall give him authority over the nations”; that is, by my appointment he shall become the teacher of those who, without such instruction, are nations—that is, live as Gentiles. For although converted to the faith, because of evil habit they are inclined to return to the life of the Gentiles. “And he shall rule them with an iron rod,” that is, with the upright and severe discipline of justice, which is not quickly bent by favour or hatred. For he has overcome these things, he is victor over the passions mentioned, and he has good zeal: never hating the person and loving the vice, but always loving the person and hating the vice. This uprightness of mind in a ruler of the Church is the “iron rod,” that is, strong and upright discipline.

Accordingly it follows: “And they shall be shattered like a potter’s vessel.” Those subject to a person of this sort rightly fear him when he rebukes them for their faults; they fall upon their faces and submit to the one seated, having nothing to say in reply, constrained by the authority of the good Spirit speaking in him. And as a shattered potter’s vessel cannot hold water, so they, terrified and unable either to excuse or conceal themselves, confess their own fault. Otherwise they would experience greater force, and thus are utterly shattered by the judicial stone of anathema, so that there does not remain from them even a shard in which a small fire may be carried.

“I shall give him this authority as I received it from my Father [as I too received it from my Father].” For because of the passion of death I have been crowned with glory and honour (Ps. VIII), and according to the assumed humanity, “all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” [Col. 0889D] (Matt. XXVIII): authority to execute judgment, so that “he who believes and is baptized may be saved, but he who does not believe may be condemned” (Mark XVI). “As I received,” he says, “I shall give to him, so that whose sins he remits may be remitted to them, and whose sins he retains may be retained” (John XX).

“And I shall give him the morning star.” That is, after the labour in which, in this present life as though in night, he labours anxiously and watchfully in guarding the souls entrusted to him, I shall reveal myself, who am the bright morning star.

“He who has ears, let him hear what the Spirit says to the Churches.” Let him hear—that is, let him understand; let him delight in zeal for justice through hope in the authority and dignity which God promises; let him be inflamed against all heresies. In this and the following chapters, rewards are promised to those who conquer. Thus the sequence of the text is spoken so that the person of the Son of God is understood to speak, namely when he says: “As I received from my Father,” “and I shall confess his name before my Father” (John XIV), “and I shall write upon him my new name,” and “I shall grant him to sit with me on my throne, just as I also conquered and sat with my Father upon his throne.”

Therefore, it is not without reason that the order is changed in these passages, so that he first says, “To the conqueror,” or “To him who conquers, I shall give this or that,” lest another person be inserted into the words of him whose person had begun to speak; and only then does he conclude: “He who has an ear, let him hear.” For what in the preceding chapters is promised for victory in this way—“To the conqueror I shall give hidden manna”; “He who conquers shall not be harmed by the second death”; “To the conqueror I shall give to eat from the tree of life”—it makes no difference whether the person of the Son or of the Holy Spirit speaks. [Col. 0890B]

## Chapter III

“And write to the Angel of the Church at Sardis: These things says he who has the seven Spirits of God and the seven stars: I know your works: you have a name that you live, and you are dead.”

After the spirit of fortitude, the spirit of counsel follows above; according to its own order it speaks here in the Son of God. And to whom is it more fitting for this spirit to speak than to one who has the name of being alive and yet is dead? For we are accustomed to use counsel in hidden matters. Now hidden and secret is the conduct of one who has the name of being alive and yet is dead. For one whose sin is public or known does not here have a name that he lives; indeed, if he formerly possessed a reputation for life or holiness, then, when his dead works become apparent, he has already lost that reputation or name and is publicly spoken of as dead.

Therefore, to this man who, though dead, had the name of living—that is, whose sin or conduct was not such as publicly to create scandal in the Church by its bad example, but who acted wickedly inwardly while outwardly retaining a good reputation where his office required him to preach—the Son of God rightly ought to use the spirit of counsel: that is, not publicly to describe or proclaim the nature or name of his deadly deed, according to the evangelical rule which he himself prescribed. “If,” he says, “your brother sins against you, go and rebuke him between yourself and him alone” (Matt. XVIII), and so forth.

Yet it may be conjectured that the death of this dead man of whom he speaks was a sin of the flesh. For later he says: “But you have a few names in Sardis who have not defiled their garments; they shall walk with me in white.” And indeed it sometimes happens that an angel—that is, a priest or bishop, a man of good reputation—secretly commits a sin of the flesh and, in doing so, is dead beneath the name of one alive.

Let us now proceed in order. “Write,” he says, “to the Angel of the Church at Sardis.” The name Sardis, certainly that of a precious stone, suits that Angel; but the reality signified by the name of stones in the Church’s ornaments, for the reason already stated, does not suit him. “These things says he who has the seven Spirits of God.” In the others he begins so as to begin in accordance with the particular character of the subject he is about to discuss, and so that the hearer may become attentive, teachable, or well disposed from what he first hears. In this case he begins so that nothing concerning the particular case of this Angel appears. For his case is obscure and ought to be concealed with counsel.

“I know,” he says, “your works: you have a name that you live, and you are dead.” It is as though he said: Human beings, who see what is before their eyes, think that you live; but I, who see the heart and am the knower of the eyes, know that you are dead (1 Kings XVI). By writing and speaking thus, he fittingly does precisely as he had instructed others to do. For he rebukes him between himself and him alone. No one besides himself and that man’s conscience knows what he says, or wherein the man is dead, unless perhaps anyone reading these things conjectures or suspects it. Yet suspicion has no place in law for bringing an accusation, nor should anyone’s standing be endangered because of another’s suspicion.

Therefore he does not wish to linger any longer over the mention of his deadly work, but immediately gives counsel by which he may be saved.

“Be watchful, and strengthen the remaining things which were about to die.” Since his sin is not stated, we ought not indeed to confirm our conjecture; nevertheless, we do not doubt that this counsel is appropriate to anyone who has not possessed or has lost sexual continence: that he should watch, and, girding his loins, strengthen what remains, lest it die beyond recovery. Thus the Lord himself says in his Gospel: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning; and be like men waiting for their lord when he returns from the wedding. Blessed are those servants whom, when he comes, he finds watching” (Luke XXI). Indeed, this care—the care of recovering salvation or preserving continence—requires vigils and great vigilance.

“Strengthen,” he says, “the remaining things which were about to die.” Some things, then, still live and have not altogether died, even in one who is thus dead. For his office lives; the sacred act which he performs in baptizing and consecrating lives. Yet these too will without doubt die—that is, must perish and be taken away from him—if, because he does not receive so secret a rebuke from the Spirit of God, God makes him public and declares his sin to the Church. Then he will be deposed from office with legal severity and will be as a heathen and a tax collector.

“For I do not find your works complete before my God.” For this reason the remaining things were about to die, and for this reason your other works must be strengthened: because I do not find them complete before my God. The acts of holy ministry are complete where they have a saving effect, where they are not performed unto judgment but avail for the remission of sins. They are not performed in, or by, one who is dead through evil conduct with this completeness.

“Therefore remember how you received and heard, and keep it, and repent.” “How,” he says, “you received and heard.” You received by example; you heard by command. For you received the example of the chaste apostles; you heard their command: “A bishop must be blameless, sober, prudent, orderly, chaste, hospitable, a teacher; [Col. 0892A] not given to wine, not a striker, but moderate; not quarrelsome, not covetous, ruling his own household well” (Tit. I). He must also have a good testimony from those outside, lest he fall into reproach and into the devil’s snare.

But in the Law you received this: “Any of the seed of Aaron the priest who has a blemish shall not come near to offer sacrifices to God” (Lev. XXI): if he is blind, lame, has a small, large, or crooked nose, a broken foot or hand, is hunchbacked, bleary-eyed, has a white spot in his eye, chronic scabies, an eruption upon the body, or is ruptured. Likewise: “Every person of your stock who approaches the holy things while uncleanness is in him shall perish before the Lord” (Lev. XXII). As you have received and heard these things, “remember” them, keep them in memory; henceforth observe them; and concerning what you have not observed, “repent.”

“Therefore, if you do not watch, I shall come upon you like a thief, and you shall not know at what hour I shall come upon you.” What I ought to do, I have done for you: I have rebuked you and warned you to watch, while the evangelical trumpet also sounds to all: “Watch therefore, because you do not know at what hour your Lord will come” (Matt. XXIV). If, therefore, you do not watch, I shall come upon you as a thief (Luke XII).

I shall not come to you as to those people who watch and wait. Their Lord comes when he returns from the wedding, thanking them and calling them blessed because they watched for his arrival. I shall not come to you as a joyful and festive bridegroom, but as a thief who, while the householder does not know, breaks into the house and kills the lord of the house whom he finds sleeping. For it follows that death, arriving unexpectedly, seizes one who does not watch as a thief.

“But you have a few names in Sardis who have not defiled their garments.” You are blameworthy in your own person; but it is in your favour that you have not also destroyed others by your example, because, as I said above, though you are dead, you have a name that you live. “A few names,” he says—that is, you have among you a few persons known to me by name and inscribed in the book according to their merits, because they have not defiled their garments, that is, they have kept their bodies uncorrupted.

“They shall walk with me in white, because they are worthy.” “With me,” he says—namely, with the Son of the Virgin; with me, whose virgin flesh dedicated an example of continence; who am the virginal flower, the lily of virginity, and the crown of virgins. “They shall walk with me in white,” that is, in spotless bodies, with which they shall rise shining like newborn lambs. Wherever I go, they shall follow me, the Lamb of God, because they are worthy of my companionship.

“He who conquers shall thus be clothed in white garments; and I shall not erase his name from the Book of Life, and I shall confess his name before my Father and before his angels.” At this level, to conquer is to overcome the incitements of the flesh with the fire of the Holy Spirit and, with his aid, to preserve unspotted the garment of the body. Whoever conquers in this shall, he says, “thus be clothed in white garments,” as I said: he shall walk with me in white.

“And I shall not erase [Col. 0893A] his name from the Book of Life.” He seems to have said less than the dignity of the merit requires, by that mode of speech which in Greek is called *tapeinōsis*, that is, a humble expression of a great thing. For this may truly be said of one who, after fornications and adulteries, has turned back and repented. But what he had said here in lesser terms, he supplied more magnificently by adding: “And I shall confess his name before my Father and before his angels.”

There, therefore, by negation, when he says, “I shall not erase the name of him who conquers,” he at the same time strikes the one who does not conquer; for it follows that he erases his name. Here, however, by the affirmation, “I shall confess his name,” he more abundantly signifies the glory and honour laid up for the one who conquers. For this is as magnificent as that which the Apostle says concerning the fathers, after he had more fully commemorated the faith, obedience, and expectation of those living as pilgrims: “For this reason,” he says, “God is not ashamed to be called their God” (Heb. IV).

Thus here also, when he says, “I shall confess his name,” it must be understood in the same sense as if he had said: I shall not be ashamed to confess his name, to acknowledge that such a one here is my disciple; and when he walks in white garments, I shall not be ashamed before my Father and his angels that, in my way of life, he shares knowledge with me.

“Let him who has ears hear what the Spirit says to the Churches.” To hear what this Spirit says is to do all things with counsel. “Do everything with counsel,” Scripture says, “and after the deed you will not repent” (Ecclus. [Col. 0893C] XXXII). For it did not speak of just any counsel, but of that counsel which Holy Scripture proclaims to us, calling the Holy Spirit the Spirit of counsel—whom we understand also to be speaking here. Pharaoh, indeed, had foolish counsel, as it is written: “The wise counsellors of Pharaoh gave foolish counsel” (Isa. XIX). Therefore this is the counsel which is true, sound, from God and from the Holy Spirit; and whoever does everything with this counsel will undoubtedly not repent after the deed.

The first grace is to do all things with this Spirit of counsel, so as not to defile one’s garments—that is, to preserve bodily virginity. 379 For this is not a command but counsel. Hence the Apostle says concerning virgins: “I have no command of the Lord, but I give counsel, as one who has obtained mercy from God to be faithful” (I Cor. VII). Whoever hears this counsel, or acts with this counsel, certainly will not repent after the deed: for he will not have tribulation of the flesh; he will not be anxious about worldly things, about how to please a wife; nor will he be divided.

The second grace is, after a fall, so to do all things with counsel that one listens to a brother rebuking him (Matt. XIII). For if he does this, he will not repent after the deed, because his sin will not be declared to the Church, nor will he be regarded as a heathen and a publican. Therefore, “let him who has ears hear,” because this Spirit of counsel invites the angel of the Church of Sardis to its second grace, and commends, in respect of the first, the few who have not defiled their garments.

[Col. 0894A] “And write to the angel of the Church in Philadelphia: These things says the Holy and True One, who has the key of David, who opens and no one shuts, shuts and no one opens: I know your works. Behold, I have set before you an open door, which no one can shut.”

To this angel the Son of God pours out his affections more abundantly; and the Spirit whom the Churches must hear here is the Spirit of understanding, who is written above in the order after the Spirit of counsel. The proper work of this Spirit is to open, as he wills, the mysteries of the holy Scriptures, and to reveal to little ones what has been hidden from the wise and prudent (Matt. I), often without human instruction—as he enlightened all the prophets and holy apostles, who had been unlearned and ordinary men, after Jesus had been glorified and this Spirit given [Col. 0894B] to them (Acts II).

He does not cease even now to do this as he wills, revealing hidden things to little ones, as has already been said—that is, to the humble and well-disposed, in proportion to the brotherly love they possess. For they love their lesser brethren, and whatever little wisdom or knowledge they have received, they gladly seek to impart to them. The very name of his Church, namely Philadelphia, shows that this angel was such a one. For Philadelphia is interpreted “brotherly love.”

Writing, therefore, to him, he says: “These things says the Holy and True One.” The Holy and True One is the Son of God, who, loving us, sanctified himself, as he says: “For their sakes I sanctify myself” (John XVII). He was already the Spirit of the saints; but in his Passion for us he sanctified himself—that is, he offered himself as a holy sacrifice [Col. 0894C]. God did this in brotherly love, so that he might make us angels of Philadelphia, that is, messengers or imitators of brotherly love. Thus he himself had said above: “This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you. No one has greater love than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John XV).

He therefore says: “These things says the Holy One.” But the addition, “and True,” likewise pertains to the present matter, in which brotherly love is rewarded with the gift of fuller understanding. For in this he proves himself true, and proves that he spoke truly, when, for example, he says in the Gospel parable concerning the servants to whom a householder entrusted his money for gain: “I say to you, that to everyone who has, [Col. 0894D] more shall be given; but from him who has not, even what he has shall be taken away” (Luke XIX).

Thus he is “Holy and True,” and immediately says of himself: “Who has the key of David.” He might have said, “Who has the key of all the prophets, and admits whomever he wills to their understanding”; but he chose to set one in place of all, because David, first in the order of prophets, prefigured in his deeds the mysteries of his Son, the Son of God, wrote them with his pen, and sang them in the Psalter. So numerous are the prophetic mysteries in David’s deeds and sayings that anyone to whom these have been opened cannot be excluded from the meanings of the other prophets. Thus the expression “who has the key of David” sufficiently fits the matter and intention; and in it is also the illustrious authority of that name [Col. 0895A], according to “the genealogy of Jesus Christ, son of David” (Matt. I). Since, after the Law, David was the first to publish prophetic Scripture, every prophetic utterance can and ought to be understood under this designation.

What, then, is that key but the grace of the Holy Spirit? For he is the illumination of the heart; he is “the unfolding of God’s words, which gives light and understanding to little ones” (Ps. CVIII). Hence the Apostle says: “God has revealed them to us through his Spirit, because the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God” (I Cor. II). Commending the power or efficacy of this key, he immediately adds: “Who opens and no one shuts; who shuts and no one opens.” This must both be known without doubt and, when known, humbly feared.

For truly, when this key-bearer opens through the Spirit of understanding to anyone the truth of God contained in the sacred Scriptures, no one shuts him in or confines him by lies and artifices of false argument. For, always having an open door, he has recourse inwardly and, taking up ready testimonies of Scripture, like a good archer directs sure arrows against the enemy. Conversely, when he has shut the door against someone so that he cannot understand the words of truth, he does so by a just judgment. For example, lest swine trample underfoot pearls cast before them (Matt. VII), no one can make such a person understand, however much clamour and instruction he may raise from outside.

What does this Holy and True One say to this angel of Philadelphia, that is, to one who possesses brotherly love?

“I know your works.” What or what kind of works he knows [Col. 0895C], he will soon teach; but he does not yet say, hastening eagerly first to show something of the reward. For he says: “Behold, I have given you an open door before you.” This is the reward of brotherly love: to have an open door before oneself, opened by David’s key, revealed by the Holy Spirit.

He immediately adds those works when he says: “Because you have little strength, and have kept my word, and have not denied my name.” “You have little strength,” he says, “and you willingly spend even it for the benefit of others.” For this is truly to have; just as, conversely, not to spend is not to have. In accordance with this sense the Lord says in the Gospel, as we have already quoted above: “I say to you, that to everyone who has, more shall be given; but from him who has not, even what he has shall be taken away [Col. 0895D]” (Luke XIX). You have, therefore—that is, you do not hide the strength you possess, but distribute it; and you lay out at interest the talent entrusted to you by me. Yet your strength is still little; it ought to increase, so that I may be true, because I said, “To everyone who has, more shall be given.”

Truly you have kept my word, that is, my commandment: “For this is my commandment, that you love one another” (John XV). In doing this you have not denied my word—which you certainly would have denied had you acted contrary to love, as also of those of whom it is written: “They profess to know God, but by their works deny him” (Titus I). Therefore I have given an open door before you and admitted you, as a friend, to my secrets, so that you may know and understand mysteries which those do not deserve to know [Col. 0896A] who are not prepared, as you are, in this love.

“Behold, I will give some from the synagogue of Satan, who say that they are Jews and are not, but lie. Behold, I will make them come and worship before your feet, and they shall know that I have loved you, because you have kept the word of my patience.”

Do not, he says, grieve or be disturbed because of the multitude opposed to you. Envy follows your glory in the opening of the door which I have opened for you; but do not fear. The same happened especially to me. When I understood, in accordance with what was said through the prophet, “Behold, my servant shall understand; he shall be exalted and lifted up and exceedingly high” (Isa. LVIII), they said among themselves: “How does this man know letters, when he has not learned?” (Matt. XIII). “Is not this the carpenter’s son?” (John VII). “Whence has he all these things?” [Col. 0896B]

These were “of the synagogue of Satan,” who said that they were Jews and were not: who said that they were Abraham’s seed, or that they had one Father, God, but were of the devil as father (John VIII). Those who imitate them—“who say that they are Jews,” that is, confessors of God, “and are not, but lie,” and are rather from Satan’s synagogue—will hear you teaching through the open door, or will read your Scripture, and will say, “Who is this man?” Envying you, they will disparage you. “Do not fear before their face, for I am with you” (Jer. I).

Some of them, when they have become weary, will be converted; they will cease to disparage and will favour you, so that they will come and worship before your feet. If not while you live, then certainly after you have died, they will approve what you have set forth. At least then [Col. 0896C] the reader will not consider whose or what kind of work it is that he is about to read. Then they shall know that I have loved you, and that through abundant love I gave this open door before you. And this is because “you have kept the word of my patience,” that is, the word on account of which I suffered. And what is that, if not love? Therefore, because you have kept love, “they shall know that I have loved you.”

“And I will keep you from the hour of temptation which is about to come upon the whole world, to test those who dwell upon the earth.” This temptation is that of heresies, which, as the Apostle says, must occur “so that those who are approved may be made manifest” (I Cor. XI). Who is preserved unharmed from that temptation except one whom the truth of the Scriptures supports? We understand that this is now promised or given to the angel of Philadelphia, by reason of love, in the open door or key of David, which the Holy and True One possesses. Therefore, because you have kept love, “I will keep you,” he says, “from the hour of temptation, so that you do not fall into temptation, so that you are not led astray, so that you are not deceived; indeed, so that you may be prepared to give an answer to everyone who asks concerning the faith of my name which is in you” (I Pet. III).

“Behold, I come quickly.” The time of temptation from which you must be preserved is not far off; indeed, it is like an hour because it passes quickly. “For behold, I come quickly”: I come to break your bonds, so that, released from the body and a stranger to it, you may be present with God and enjoy in reality that of which you have merited here to possess understanding for consolation.

Thus far the sweetness of grace flowing from the lips of the Holy and True One has made blessed the angel beloved and characterized by love, magnifying the joy and exultation which he has stored up for him. It remains for him to warn that same angel to vigilant care, lest he imagine that he has already attained, or, before the end and completion of his course, confidently become careless. He says, therefore: “Hold fast what you have, so that no one may take your crown.”

As though he said: Stand with firm foot in humility, lest, when your foot is moved, you fall; and falling, lose the crown prepared for you, while another succeeds to your place and receives it. Indeed, it cannot happen that any of those whom God foreknew and predestined to a crown should lose his crown (Rom. VIII). Yet it can happen, and has happened, that someone called by God to a crown should lose it—by a visible calling, or one which people could hear [Col. 0897B]. For example, the Lord called Judas to an apostolic crown, but did not predestine him to the crown, because he foreknew that he would be unworthy of it. Therefore another received his crown, namely the honour of the apostleship, as it is written: “Let his days be few, and let another take his bishopric” (Ps. CVIII).

Therefore, while anyone is still struggling, let him not place great confidence in his crown. For if God, who foreknows all things, knows that your head will at the end prove worthy of a crown, you do not know it.

“To the one who conquers I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God, and he shall go out no more; and I will write upon him the name of my God, and the name of the city of my God, the new Jerusalem, which comes down from heaven from my God, and my new name.”

[Col. 0897C] At this stage, to conquer is, with the inextinguishable lamp of brotherly love going before, always to have an open door; never to be shut in or caught by the snares of heretics; to bring forth for the edification of others whatever one finds through this door; and not to desist from this pursuit of love because of any adversities or hostile criticisms from the envious.

“To one who thus conquers,” he says, “I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God.” It is a worthy and fitting reward for such a victor: one who, possessing this grace, has written or taught what strengthens the Church’s faith shall be a pillar in God’s temple. “And he shall go out no more,” he says.
