As though he said: So long as he is at the door which I have given open before him, let him take care lest he slip; but when by his reward he has been established within as a pillar, [Col. 0897D] there will be no reason for him to fear, because he shall go out no more, nor will his foot stagger in temptation.

But what is the name of God and the name of his city which he promises to write upon him? Certainly, because the Son speaks when he says, “I will write the name of my God”—namely, according to his human condition, in accordance with which our God is his God—the name of God is rightly understood to be the Father, that person whom we invoke in the faithful confession of the divinity. Moreover, the name of his city, Jerusalem, is the mother, as the Apostle also testifies when he says: “But that Jerusalem which is above is free, which is the mother of us all” (Gal. IV).

How can we prove that he writes upon this person the name which is Father and the name which is mother? In the Gospel, when someone said to him while he was speaking to the crowds: “Behold, your mother and your brothers are standing outside, seeking you,” he replied: “Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?” And stretching out his hand toward his disciples, he said: “Behold, my mother and my brothers. For whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, that person is my brother and sister and mother” (Matt. XII).

If, while Joseph—who was called his father—was present, someone had said this to him, or could truthfully have said it, “Behold, your father and your mother are standing outside,” he could have answered in the same sense of truth: “That person is my father and mother who does the will of my Father who is in heaven.” For in the inward person, where Christ’s generation is reckoned spiritually, [Col. 0898B] there is neither male nor female.

Accordingly, Christ’s Gospel genealogy is entirely spiritual; and in the spirit David too is Christ’s father, because, believing in his heart, he brought forth with his mouth the Word of God, which is Christ, and set it forth in writing: first among the prophets and most illustrious among the patriarchs (Col. II). Otherwise, unless he had been a father through faith in Christ, he would have been Christ’s ancestor according to the flesh in vain. Hence Ahaziah, Joash, and Amaziah, who persecuted and killed the prophets—heralds of that same Christ, that same Word of God—were not counted in that genealogy.

Therefore, concerning one who conquers in this way, by having understanding and helping and cooperating so that the Word of God may grow and advance, it is said: “And I will write upon him the name of my God [Col. 0898C], and the name of the city of my God, the new Jerusalem.” This is the same as saying: He is called and shall be my father and my mother, and he shall inherit this name eternally.

He says “new Jerusalem” because of the new life: because it has put off the old man and put on the new (Eph. IV). He also rightly declares that it has descended from heaven, because its manner of life is in heaven on account of brotherly love, from which this angel of Philadelphia receives praise; it descends—that is, it condescends as a little one. For example: “Paul was caught up to the third heaven and heard there secret words which it is not permitted for a human being to speak; but for the weak he descended” (II Cor. XII), when the same man says: “Let the husband render the due to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband” (I Cor. VII). Such descents are innumerable; but this one example sufficiently pertains to the matter or cause of this angel, whose praise or merit is the work of love.

Finally he adds, “and my new name.” The name of the person speaking these things is Son of God. Without doubt, he himself writes this name upon the conqueror, for all the beloved are called and are sons of God. But when he says, “I will write,” this means, “I will cause to appear.” For now, indeed, we are sons of God, says John the apostle, who writes these things at the command of the Son of God, “but what we shall be has not yet appeared. We know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (I John II).

Therefore, to write the name of each of God’s children where it can be read is to reveal it, so that the merits of every individual may be known and seen by all [Col. 0899A]. This name, namely that of the Son of God, shall be inscribed upon all the elect; although where or in whom brotherly love is now greater, the splendour of this name ought also to appear greater. But the name of God, which is Father, and the name of his city, the new Jerusalem, which is mother, are to be written upon those who, as having advanced to the full age of faith, have been able and have earnestly sought through love to propagate the Word of God.

“Let him who has ears hear what the Spirit says to the Churches.” Here to hear is to be stirred to zeal for the Word of God: to draw near to his feet in order to drink from his teaching; to sit with Mary at the Lord’s feet; to apply a submissive soul to hearing the words of his mouth; and to give all one has (Luke X), in order to purchase the one precious pearl [Col. 0899B] of his grace (Matt. XIII). Thus, perceiving the truth with the intellectual eye and being well instructed, one may become able also to instruct others, and possess as an eternal inheritance the inscription of so great a name which this Holy and True One promises here.

“And write to the angel of the Church of Laodicea: These things says the Amen, the faithful and true witness, who is the beginning of God’s creation. I know your works, that you are neither cold nor hot.”

Here, now in the last—that is, seventh—place, he speaks in the faithful and true witness: he who above is the last, that is, the seventh Spirit of wisdom, calling his worker to true Sabbath-rest; so that he may rest in humility and not weary himself by even a single superfluous word or thought, magnifying his own works or attributing them to himself. For what does he have of himself except every evil thing? And from whom, except God, does he have every good thing that he possesses?

He urges this angel to see this, saying: “And you do not know that you are wretched and miserable and poor and blind and naked,” and then adding: “Anoint your eyes with eye-salve, that you may see.” For God had worked some good things in him or through him, and hence he could say: “I am rich, I have become wealthy, and I need nothing.” Such a name as Laodicea suits him: for it is interpreted “a people beloved by the Lord,” namely because of the good works which God had done with him. It is also interpreted “those who were in vomiting.” This interpretation likewise suits him because he gloried to himself in the riches of these good works, so that it might deservedly be said to him: “I will begin to vomit you from my mouth.”

Therefore let us too hear what this seventh Spirit says here; and, hearing it, let us advance to the rest of humility and wisdom. For he says: “These things says the Amen, the faithful and true witness, who is the beginning of God’s creation.” Amen means “truthful,” or Truth itself. This is explained by the words which follow: “the faithful and true witness.”

What is the purpose of such a description of the speaker in these and the following words? It is that whoever is conscious of good works in himself, like this angel of Laodicea, may know and consider that he ought not before the time bear witness concerning himself that he is rich and has become wealthy. Indeed, such testimony does not belong to him, but to the one who has been appointed witness and judge of all, and who is to be revealed in his own time [Col. 0900A]. He should know that the testimony and judgment of all good deeds must be left to him, and that he should testify only against himself concerning evils and accuse himself.

Therefore he says: “These things says the Amen, the faithful and true witness.” Amen—that is, Truth—because he cannot be deceived or ignorant of anything. A faithful witness, because he does not know how to lie by calling good evil and evil good. “True,” because he will render to each according to his works. What purpose, likewise [itidem], is served by adding: “who is the beginning of God’s creation”?

What, indeed, is God’s creation here? Certainly the new person, or the regeneration and re-creation of the human being who walks in newness of life by doing good works. Hence the Apostle says: “For it is the gift of God, not from works, lest anyone should boast. For we are his workmanship, created in Christ [Col. 0900B] Jesus for good works, which God prepared for us to walk in” (Eph. II). What he says here, “in Christ Jesus,” that is, renewed through faith in Jesus Christ, is that very creation of which he says elsewhere: “For the expectation of the creation awaits the revelation of the sons of God. For the creation was subjected to vanity, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it in hope, because the creation itself also shall be liberated from the bondage of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God. For we know that the whole creation groans and labours in birth until now” (Rom. VIII).

Why, then, was it said to this angel concerning this faithful and true witness that he is the beginning of God’s creation, except so that he might know to attribute to him, not to himself, his entire re-creation and whatever holy newness he had or seemed to himself to have? For he is the prince of the new person and of holy newness; from him are the beginning and end, or completion, of this creation in which we now live—by which we have passed from death to life, been transferred from children of wrath to children of grace, been cleansed from works of death, and served the living God.

What, then, does he say? “I know your works, that you are neither cold nor hot. Would that you were cold or hot. But because you are lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will begin to vomit you from my mouth, because you say, ‘I am rich, I have become wealthy, and I need nothing,’ and do not know that you are wretched and miserable.”

I know works of yours of such a kind, and I judge them in this way. You are not cold, in that you are sluggish in good work; nor are you hot, in that you give thanks to God. You ought indeed to have done this, but not as that Pharisee did, who, justifying himself, disparaged the publican (Luke XVIII), but as the Psalmist who humbly praises the Lord at work within him: “Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but give glory to your name” (Ps. CXIII).

“Would that you were cold or hot.” This may fittingly be said, for example, to a proud virgin: Would that you were cold or hot—that is, would that you were either bodily corrupted, or possessed, together with bodily virginity, the oil of love. For it would be a lighter fault to be corrupted in body and thereby humbled, than to remain bodily whole and be puffed up because of the consciousness of one’s integrity.

“Therefore I will begin to vomit you from my mouth,” because of the lukewarmness of pride—like lukewarm water which, because of its unpleasant taste, cannot remain in the nauseated stomach of the drinker [Col. 0901A]. I shall do this because you are such: because, considering your works, you imagine yourself to be something; you suppose that you are rich, have become wealthy, and need nothing, like those of whom the Apostle said: “Already you are filled; already you have become rich. You reign without us—and would that you did reign!” (I Cor. IV).

When he says, “you do not know,” this is true: “that you are wretched and miserable,” needing God’s mercy in many things; “and poor,” because you have nothing that you did not receive, and because many things still lack to you; “because you are blind,” because, to say nothing of other things, you do not yet see God face to face; “naked,” because you are clothed in a frail and slippery body.

“I counsel you to buy from me gold tried by fire [Col. 0901B], that you may become rich, and to be clothed in white garments, so that the nakedness of your shame may not appear.” It is expedient for you to know this: I am rich, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Col. II); but you are poor. If you know this, buy from me the gold of wisdom: gold made fiery by love, gold proved by faith working through love. Buy it at the price of devout confession and the continual remembrance of your own frailty, always recalling what you are from yourself and what you have received from God (Gal. IV). Thus grace may be added to you, “that you may become rich,” and “that you may be clothed in white garments,” not from your own works but from the bounty of that same grace, as the Psalmist says: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin” (Ps. XXXI).

Thus it will happen that the shame of your nakedness will not appear, as happens to some when, through pride of mind, they fall into temptation and the shameful corruption of the flesh. “And anoint your eyes with eye-salve, that you may see.” The eye-salve by which defects of the eyes are cleansed signifies the sweetness of humility, which helps little ones so that the mysteries hidden from the wise and prudent may be revealed to them. “Therefore anoint your eyes with eye-salve, that you may see”—that is, cleanse your heart by true humility, so that you may see your poverty and know the true riches of God’s goodness (Luke X).

“Those whom I love I rebuke and discipline.” As though he said: Receive the things I say to you in rebuking and correcting you as the grace and goodwill of one who loves you [Col. 0901D] (Eph. II). For it is not wisdom’s way to allow a son whom it loves to be exalted and vanish away in youthful pride. Rather, it loves and disciplines; it strikes the unruly; and it beats with a rod the same one whom it nursed as an infant when he becomes excessively talkative and reckless. Therefore, while I discipline you, while I prick you as it were with nails driven deep, I love you more truly.

“Be zealous, therefore, and repent.” Be zealous—that is, imitate with a good fervour of spirit the one who loves you and disciplines you; and you who were lukewarm, through this zeal become warm. Repent of having thus far been ungrateful to the one who loves you by not returning love in kind.

Thus far he has struck down the haughty brow of the one who is as it were rich and wealthy, who vainly seems to himself to abound in good works. Now, from this same person—or from any rich person of this kind—he quite amicably requests that he share the glory of his works with God, or with the Son of God, who gives all things: that he may glory in God, or make God glory in him, and glorify the Holy One in all his works (I Cor. I).

“Behold,” he says, “I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will enter in to him and dine with him.” The meaning is this: What I have said thus far in correcting you is like one standing at the door of a rich person and knocking, so that, being admitted as a guest, he may dine with him upon the wealth stored within. If he is admitted, a banquet of love is celebrated, because love cannot exist with fewer than two persons.

Thus you who say that you are rich glory in a good conscience; but “behold, I stand and knock at the door” [Col. 0902B] of your breast. Admit me and make me a participant or companion in your glory, so that you may not glory alone but with me; and altogether may glory, not in yourself, but that you have become rich in me. If in this way you or anyone, hearing the voice, opens the door to me by referring all the good things he has done to God’s glory, I will enter in to him and have confidence in his breast as in the house of a friend. And now indeed I will dine—that is, delight—with him in the good things of his conscience; but he himself in the future will enjoy my goods with me.

“To the one who conquers, I will grant to sit with me on my throne, as I also conquered and sat down with my Father on his throne.” At this stage, to conquer is through the maturity of wisdom to drive far away every lightness of boasting and vain glory, and, though one appears great to others, to be little in one’s own eyes. As the same wisdom says: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things, and you will find grace before God” (Ecclus. III).

For humility, from whose company wisdom has never been absent, is accustomed to fly to heaven. He therefore says: “To the one who conquers I will grant to sit with me on my throne,” not that he may be made equal to divinity, but that he may share in eternity. “As I also conquered,” he says. How did Christ, who speaks these things, conquer, except through the inestimable greatness of his humility and love? “For although he was in the form of God” (Phil. II), he did not wish to glory alone in that form, but wished human beings—who, when the first man sinned, had become deprived of his glory—to become sharers in his glory. Therefore “he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant; therefore he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross” (ibid.).

This is the highest victory of humility and wisdom, which destroyed the pride and folly of the first man. “I conquered,” he says, “and for this reason I sat down with my Father on his throne.” For this reason God exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name, and said to him: “Sit at my right hand” (Ps. CIX). To desire to imitate this example of his is to hear what this Spirit of wisdom says to the Churches.

Truly, one who has heard these things with those ears which have now seven times been required here in respect of the inward person [Col. 0903A] not only does not glory in his deeds, however good and numerous they may be, but is even pained by his own praises and delights in insults. For he relishes what the prophet said of the victor just mentioned and prince of all conquerors [Col. 0904A]: “He will give his cheek to the one striking him; he will be filled with reproaches” (Lam. III).

## 383. PROLOGUE TO THE BOOKS WHICH FOLLOW

[Col. 0903]

He who has ears has heard from the seven Spirits of God what each of them says or has said to the Churches. Henceforth we must hear what and in what manner each of these Spirits has worked, and will yet work, in Christ or through Christ. For we have examined in order the sayings of the Son of God according to the seven Spirits, advancing from the Spirit of fear to the Spirit of wisdom. Now, with his help, we shall endeavour to unfold in reverse order the wondrous deeds of that same Son of God, marked by mystical figures or images and divided into seven sections according to those same Spirits.

For, beginning with the Spirit of wisdom, we shall proceed in order to the Spirit of fear. This is the order prescribed concerning Christ in the prophet, where “the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon the flower: the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and might, the Spirit of knowledge and piety; and the Spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. II). But when an ascent is set before the Churches, as we said above, this order is reversed: the order appointed is that by which the Lord descended to us, as the Psalmist says: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. CX).

Nor is it a forced exposition to say that this writing of mysteries is arranged according to this order of the Spirits. For in many places the distinctive character of each Spirit shows itself spontaneously through the figurative deeds. To make this clear by a brief survey: after the most orderly throne of God is placed in heaven, in whose arrangement the Spirit of wisdom is rightly proclaimed, the Lamb opens the book sealed with seven seals, loosing its seals; and that is manifestly the praiseworthy work of the Spirit of understanding, who is second in order.

Then the Angel of great counsel is seen standing beside the altar of the temple, and by the mystical sounds of seven trumpets the mystery of God is completed—something which we do not doubt pertains to the Spirit of counsel. In the fourth place, a great red dragon having seven heads attacks the woman. Michael fighting with his angels, the dragon with his angels is cast down to the earth; and there, without doubt, the Spirit of might, which is fourth, is displayed. In the fifth place is the Spirit of knowledge in the bowls of the seven angels. In the sixth place, in the blood of Jesus’ martyrs, by which the woman is shown drunk, is the praise of piety. In the seventh place, in the approaching hour of God’s judgment, when all the dead are given up from the earth, the sea, and hell, the whole vision undoubtedly concerns the Spirit of fear.

Then comes the end, in which Jerusalem is shown adorned: the Lamb’s wife, the city of God. What spectacle of God’s wonders is more beautiful than this, O all you spectators of God who are present? May he who has the key of David, the Holy and True One, now open to us, and may we behold this holiness and truth with clear eyes, without darkness.

## 384. THIRD BOOK

[Col. 0903]

## CHAPTER IV

[Col. 0903B]

“After these things I saw, and behold, a door opened in heaven.” When he says “I saw,” both here and elsewhere, we rightly recall that blessedness of his by which he is truly most blessed among those to whom Truth says: “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see” (Luke 10). For the glory which he had seen with the others—the glory of the incarnate Word, concerning which he says, “And we saw his glory, glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father” (John 1)—whose reality he had seen with the others, namely the glorious signs, and especially at the time when the land was closed and he was in exile because of the word of God, heaven was opened to him; and through its expanse he moved with free spirit to behold these things.

“And behold,” he says, “a door opened in heaven.” Here heaven signifies the heavenly life, to which Christ, recently rising from the dead, had raised the whole Church to rise with him in the first resurrection. But what is this door except he himself, who says, “I am the door”? Thus, when this door is opened, heaven lies open to earthly people entering it: namely, when Christ suffered and his side was opened by the soldiers’ spear (John 10). From that point the kingdom of God is within us, the kingdom of sin—which had hitherto reigned in the world—having been destroyed. By such an opening of this door, the mysteries of the Scriptures were likewise opened. To understand them spiritually and live according to them is already to reign in the kingdom of God and to have one’s manner of life in heaven.

“Therefore,” he says, “I saw a door opened in heaven”: that is, what I knew in reality I saw in an image—namely, that Christ is the gate of the kingdom of heaven, a gate opened to human beings by his passion [Col. 0904C] (Luke 17).

“And the first voice which I heard, as of a trumpet speaking with me, saying: Come up here, and I will show you what must happen soon after these things.”

This first voice is his whose voice it was also that he heard above saying, “Write what you see.” Therefore he did not simply say, “the voice which I heard,” but “the first voice which I heard.” In words or meaning, however, it was not the same as the first. For then it was said, “Write what you see” (Rev. 1); but now he is told, “Come up here.” Both here and there it was like the voice of a trumpet, because he intends to speak to the world not in secret but openly. What he says or shows must be openly proclaimed to Greeks and barbarians, to wise and foolish alike. For no one has reason to be ashamed of the Gospel. For it is the power of God (Rom. 1), and whatever he speaks is strong, beautiful, honorable, rational, true, and altogether necessary for human salvation.

What he meant by “Come up here,” and what it is to ascend there, is understood from John’s own statement: “Immediately I was in the Spirit.” Therefore to ascend there is to rise in the Spirit beyond all bodily senses and to see spiritual things with spiritual eyes. And he who said “Come up” brought about that ascent by speaking, for he says, “Immediately I was in the Spirit.” Yet above he says, “I was in the Spirit on the Lord’s day” (Rev. 1). How then does he now again say, “Immediately I was in the Spirit,” as though he had not been in the Spirit before this voice, or before he saw the door opened in heaven? It is because he did not see all the things contained in this book in one vision.

But it may again be asked: how, after he had seen the door opened in heaven, was he only then, upon hearing the voice, immediately in the Spirit, when the very door he saw could not have been seen except in the Spirit? For heaven is not visibly constructed like a building fitted with doors, locks, and bars. Thus the statement “Immediately I was in the Spirit” is rightly understood as though he said: Immediately I understood by spiritual perception the things shown to me through images. Hence we should not doubt that the voice’s saying, “I will show you what must happen soon after these things,” concerns understanding.

For prophetic visions of this sort did not occur, as certain heretics have claimed, in such a way that the prophets themselves did not understand what realities or meanings their visions contained. Accordingly, it was unnecessary that, just as he had said above, “Write therefore what you have seen, what is, and what must happen after these things” [Col. 0905D], he should also here say to him, “I will show you what you have seen, what is, and what must happen after these things.” For what he had seen and what then existed he knew: he had seen the past while walking with the Lord until his end; he saw the Church’s present condition then; but he did not yet know the future. Therefore, rightly instructing him only about the future, he says: “I will show you what must happen soon after these things.” Yet he saw many highly mystical images of the things which he had seen or which had passed, not so much for his own instruction as for ours.

“And behold, a throne had been set in heaven, and one seated upon the throne.”

Once the door is opened, a throne set in heaven is seen, because, after Christ suffered, the kingdom of God was established or ordered so that God might sit in it, the prince of this world having been cast out (John 12). This throne is the Church: the throne prepared from that point onward, in which God sits and reigns. Hence, after the Psalmist had said, “The Lord has reigned; he has clothed himself with majesty; the Lord has clothed himself with strength and girded himself” (Ps. 92), he immediately added: “Your throne has been prepared from that time; you are from everlasting” (ibid.).

For when the Lord, clothed in majesty and strength, reigned—that is, when, assuming virgin flesh and overcoming death by rising again, he reigned over us—he himself, our righteousness and life, destroyed the kingdom of sin and death (2 Tim. 1; Heb. 2). From that time his throne was prepared; from that time the throne, that is, the Church, was set in heaven (Eph. 2).

How was it set in heaven? The Church of patriarchs and prophets was transferred from hell [the underworld], together with all the elect who had existed from righteous Abel to the last person who then departed from the world. It was placed in heaven, enjoyed paradise, and saw the face of God, the wall of hostility having been dissolved [Col. 0906B]. But the Church itself which was still in exile—or which is now in exile bodily in the world—was already set in heaven through its manner of life and through love of heavenly things.

“The one seated above the throne” is God the Father; for the person of the Son is the Lamb, who, as is related in what follows, “received the book from the right hand of the one seated” (Rev. 5). Yet in the appearance of the seated—that is, reigning—God the Father, the honor and glory of the Son are not absent, since by his humanity he prepared that throne for the one God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, to sit upon. For he has prepared, and does not cease to prepare or acquire until the end, a kingdom for God and Father. The highest and final point of that acquisition will be the day of judgment, on which the Son, in human form, will appear to all seated upon the throne of majesty. Thus the Apostle says: “Then comes the end, when he shall hand over the kingdom to God and Father” (1 Cor. 15)—“when,” he says, “he shall hand over the kingdom to God and Father,” that is, when he has brought believers to the contemplation of God and Father.

“And he who sat was like in appearance to a jasper stone and a sardius.”

Jasper is water-colored; sardius is fire-colored. Thus “he who sat was like in appearance to jasper and sardius,” because God, the Lord of judgment, who once judged the world by water, will finally judge it by fire. Therefore he is said to be like those colors—water-colored and fire-colored—because from both the judgment accomplished through water and the judgment to be accomplished through fire, God, who is invisible to us in his substance, is known to be mighty and jealous (Exod. 20).

Between the two judgments mercy has gone forth: while he brought the flood upon the world and will judge the world by fire, he does not cease in the meantime to proclaim repentance and forgiveness of sins, nor does he repel from his grace those who approach in faith. Therefore he immediately adds: “And there was a rainbow around the throne, like the appearance of an emerald.”

For the rainbow is a sign of propitiation, as the Lord says to Noah: “I will set my bow in the clouds of heaven, and I will remember my covenant which I made with you” (Gen. 9). Thus around the throne there is mercy prepared for all who seek it in the Redeemer’s coming; and this mercy runs before judgment throughout the circuit of the world with the great proclamation of evangelical preaching.

Nevertheless, just as the judgment by water was not without mercy—for it saved eight souls in the ark—nor will the judgment by fire be without mercy toward those who, because of the six works of mercy they performed, are placed at the right hand, the King saying, “For I was hungry and you gave me food” (Matt. 25), and so forth; so also this advent of mercy now under discussion did not occur without judgment. For when mercy was chiefly being established through Christ’s passion, he said, “Now is the judgment of this world” (John 12). And before the very moment of his passion, he says elsewhere: “For judgment I have come into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9).

Since, therefore, mercy there concurred with judgment and saved eight souls from whom the world might be renewed; and since mercy will be necessary at the future judgment; why now, when he says that he has come for judgment, is mercy described in such a way that it is said, “There was a rainbow around the throne,” which, as has already been said, is a sign of propitiation? Clearly because of the greatness, or multitude, of mercy in which he now came: for he so judged, so enacted the judgment of the world, that in that very judgment his whole purpose was to establish repentance and forgiveness of sins through his blood, being himself a merciful and faithful high priest. By rising again, he restored our nature, withered and dried up like grass because of sin, to the unfading state of glory.

Therefore, after saying, “There was a rainbow around the throne,” he added, “like the appearance of an emerald.” For the emerald is of extraordinary greenness, so much so that it tinges with its reflected green the green herbs, leaves, gems, and all the air about it. Thus “the rainbow is like the appearance of an emerald,” because this mercy will refashion our old age into the firm beauty of eternal greenness.

“And around the throne were twenty-four seats, and upon the thrones twenty-four elders seated, clothed around in white garments, and upon their heads golden crowns.”

As in the throne we understand the kingdom of God, so in the seats we understand the judicial authority of the saints, of which it is written: “The saints shall judge nations” (Wis. 3). But why are the elders shown sitting on seats in the number twenty-four? The Fathers have given differing interpretations of this. Some, among whom blessed Jerome is one of the best known, wish the twenty-four books of the Old Law to be understood here as represented by the same number of elders. Others understand in these elders the Church brought forth from patriarchs and apostles through the twofold Testament; or at least those who bring the perfection of work, commended by the number six, to completion through the clear preaching of the Gospel. For four times six makes twenty-four.

Approving both this interpretation and that as not useless, nevertheless let us attempt to offer something certain from the majesty of the Scriptures. That “throne set in heaven,” which, as has already been said, we understand as the kingdom of God, around which these seats stood, began to be established from the time when David, Christ’s father according to the flesh, obtained the kingdom of the Israelite people. For he reigned in the people of God as a type of Christ, his future son. And just as that king of righteousness, mighty of hand and desirable, was to reign after the destruction of the kingdom of sin, so David came to reign after the rejection of Saul’s kingdom, Saul whom God cast away because of pride (1 Sam. 16): David was “like the most tender little worm of wood” (2 Sam. 23), humble in his own eyes, so that in the right order of heavenly rank the kingly father might sit before his son in the people of God.

For, lest we doubt that the throne of that father and of this son is one throne, the Gospel’s authority meets us when the archangel Gabriel says to Mary: “The Lord God will give him the throne of David his father, and he shall reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there shall be no end” (Luke 1). Let us therefore consider that throne set in heaven in this broader sense, upon which David sat and, after him, this son of his. Then it immediately becomes clear what the twenty-four seats around it are, who the twenty-four elders are, and how they are around it.

For after the Son, to whom the Lord God gave the throne of David his father, twelve judges succeeded; and before that father, who first sat upon that throne by God’s election, twelve judges presided over the people of God. The first was Othniel son of Kenaz, brother of Caleb; the second Ehud son of Gera, son of Jemini; the third Shamgar son of Anath; the fourth Barak son of Abinoam, from Kedesh of Naphtali; the fifth Gideon son of Joash; the sixth Jair the Gileadite; the seventh Jephthah the Gileadite; the eighth Abessan of Bethlehem; the ninth Ahialon the Zebulunite; the tenth Abdon son of Hillel the Pharaathonite; the eleventh Samson; the twelfth Samuel (Judg. 3 and following).

These precede that throne, the throne or kingdom of David, and sit around the throne set in heaven, as it were on its front side. The other twelve judges, however—namely, the twelve apostles, to whom it was said, “You also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19)—who succeeded David’s Son in time, sit around that throne as it were on its back side. Thus there are “around the throne twenty-four seats, and upon the thrones twenty-four elders.”

And they are rightly called elders because by the maturity of their faith they restrained the people of God, who played the wanton youth. For it is written concerning the earlier ones: “And the Lord raised up judges to deliver them from the hands of those who were devastating them; but they were unwilling to listen even to them, committing fornication with foreign gods, worshiping them” (Judg. 2). And shortly afterward: “When the Lord raised up judges, in their days he was moved by mercy, heard the groaning of the afflicted, and delivered them from the slaughter of their devastators. But after the judge had died, they returned and did many things worse than their fathers had done, following foreign gods, serving them, and worshiping them.”

Truly, then, they were and are elders whose venerable old age, reckoned not by long duration or number of years but by the gray hairs of the inward person’s understanding, corrected the fornications of a youthful people (Wis. 4). By their wise intercession they moved God to mercy, so that he might hear the groaning of the afflicted. Therefore they are “clothed around in white garments,” that is, in eternal joy. “And golden crowns are upon their heads,” because they share in the crowns of him whose name they inherited and whose office they fulfilled. For they were called saviors, because they saved the people of God from perishing. For example: “And the children of Israel cried to the Lord, who raised up for them a Savior, namely Othniel son of Kenaz” (Judg. 3). The golden crowns signify the precious reward of everlasting glory.

Moreover, concerning the later judges, that is, the apostles of Christ, it is known how truly they were and are elders—that is, wise—and how truly they are clothed around in white garments and received golden crowns upon their heads, because they conquered the world, overcame the devil, delivered the people captive to death, and acquired eternal life through Christ’s grace. It follows:

“And from the throne proceeded lightnings, voices, and thunders.”

After our elders, or their seats, have been placed around the throne, lightnings, voices, and thunders proceed, because after the apostles had been established as judges of the world and received the office of preaching, they did not cease to give the lightnings of miracles, the voices of preaching, and the thunders of threats concerning future judgment and the infernal punishments of evildoers. This is what Mark says: “But they went forth and preached everywhere, the Lord working with them and confirming the word by the signs that followed” (Mark 16).

All these things—namely lightnings, voices, and thunders—proceed from the throne, from him who sits upon the throne. For they did not possess from themselves the power to flash forth, give voices, and make thunders, but received it from above. For “every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (Jas. 1).

“And seven lamps burning before the throne, which are the seven spirits of God.”

The seven spirits of God are before the throne. They illuminate the often-mentioned kingdom of God, the Church of God. There indeed, that is, in heavenly glory, they illuminate it so that it sees the brightness of God face to face. But here, where it still journeys in part in the Church, they illuminate it so that it sees not yet perfectly, but as through a mirror and in an enigma (1 Cor. 13), and knows, sufficiently to expose errors, the truth of God, according to the promise of him who says: “When that Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all truth” (John 16).

From the time when he who spoke these things during his passion rose again and ascended into heaven, the splendor of these lamps has shone more broadly upon the world. These seven lamps shine from one lampstand; these seven spirits proceed from one and the same Christ. Their light appeared upon his disciples on the fiftieth day after his resurrection in tongues of fire (Acts 2). The first lamp is the spirit of wisdom; the second, the spirit of understanding; and then, in order, the remaining spirits, as they are read arranged in the prophet, resting upon one flower. In this place they are called lamps, according to another prophet, shining upon one lampstand.

“And before the throne, as it were, a glass sea, like crystal.”

For what purpose is “the sea before the throne”? Namely, so that whoever wishes to ascend to that throne of God, to enter that kingdom of God, may do so only by passing through this sea and being illuminated by the splendid light of the lamps just described. For Christ’s baptism is called a sea, evidently because of the well-known likeness to the Red Sea, through which the people of God, having sacrificed the lamb, passed from Egyptian bondage to freedom, Pharaoh being drowned with his chariots and horses or horsemen (Exod. 19; 1 Cor. 10).

Thus the sea was before the throne because the sacrament of baptism was established in the very setting-up of the throne, while through Christ’s death the kingdom of God was being prepared, when blood and water came out from his pierced side (John 19). From this came the origin of baptism; and immediately after Christ’s resurrection the rule for baptizing was given. For he said: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28).

There, namely before the throne, is the sea, and there are the lamps, because where Christ suffered, so that God might reign after the prince of this world had been cast out, there also from that point onward were baptism, forgiveness of sins, and the distributions of the Holy Spirit’s gifts.

This sea was glassy, because baptism is pure and bright, requiring a pure and simple confession of sins: the person who approaches must not believe one thing in the heart and confess another, just as glass contains within nothing other than what may be seen outside, and does not pretend outwardly to be other than what it contains within. And if human beings are unaware—as they were unaware of Simon the Magician—the Holy Spirit, through whose light this glassy sea shines through, cannot be unaware (Acts 8). Hence it is written: “For the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit, and will not acquit an evil-speaker because of his lips; for God is a witness of his reins, a true searcher of his heart, and a hearer of his tongue” (Wis. 1). Showing that no one can deceive him by a double confession, after first stating, “Because the Spirit of the Lord has filled the world” (ibid.), it briefly declares: “And that which contains all things has knowledge of speech” (ibid.). For how could he fail to know the voice of one making confession, or be unable to judge that voice, when he is also the true witness of the heart?

Therefore let whoever approaches take care not to approach deceitfully, because the sea is glassy and everything done or said there is transparent to the Holy Spirit. Yet glass, while bright, is also fragile. Will this “sea as glass” always be fragile in the same way? Certainly not. For it follows: “Like crystal.” Therefore the sea is first bright but fragile here; afterward it will be bright and also firm.

Accordingly, confessors, bright because they have been born again of water and Spirit, are now fragile in their mortal bodies; but afterward, in the glory of resurrection, they will be firm, with blessed soul and incorruptible body. This is what the Apostle says: “But if Christ is in you, the body indeed is dead because of sin, but the spirit lives because of righteousness” (Rom. 8). By “is dead,” he meant: it is most certainly going to die because of sin, even though sin has been removed in baptism. For in the soul we are made alive through baptism from the death by which Adam died on the very day when he ate what was forbidden. Therefore he says, “But the spirit lives because of righteousness.” Yet we nevertheless die in body by the death which God ordained when he said to the human being: “For you are dust, and to dust you shall return” (Gen. 3); and when he sent him out lest he take also from the tree of life and thus, dead in soul, live eternally in body—which would be most miserable.

Thus, though the spirit lives because of righteousness, the body is still dead—that is, it will most certainly die—because of sin. Behold: “as it were a glass sea,” because we who are baptized and made bright by living faith are like glass in brightness, and fragile like glass in the mortality of our bodies.

But the Apostle continues: “If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in us, he who raised Jesus Christ from the dead will also make our mortal bodies alive because of his Spirit dwelling in us” (Rom. 8). Behold what he said: “like crystal.” For crystal is a stone transformed from water, through freezing, into stony solidity. Christ’s body, by its condition as fragile and mortal, was water; but now, through the glory of resurrection, it has been made firm with eternal solidity. Divinity now shines in that body as the sun in glass; mortality has perished in that body as water’s movement or fluidity perishes from crystal. Moreover, in conformity with that same Christ, we hope that we too shall rise and be [*immolandos*, literally “sacrificed,” but evidently corrupt or uncertain here], that is, impassible. The sea, then, will indeed be glassy, but like crystal.

“And in the midst of the throne, and around the throne, four living creatures full of eyes before and behind. And the first living creature was like a lion; and the second living creature like a calf; and the third living creature had a face as of a man; and the fourth living creature was like a flying eagle.” [Col. 0911D] These living creatures have long been recognized by the Holy Church, both by their appearance and by their names, as figures of the four Evangelists. Yet, according to the order of the letter, we must first ask how these living creatures are said to be both in the midst of the throne and around the throne, whereas the twenty-four elders, who are certainly more numerous, were above said to be around, and not also in the midst of, the throne.

That this may be established more certainly, one must first also know that, according to Ezekiel, “these living creatures are both four and one” (Ezek. 1). For after saying in the first vision, “From their midst came the likeness of four living creatures” (ibid.), and the rest, he says in the second vision: “This is the living creature which I saw beside the river Chebar. And when the cherubim walked, the wheels also went alongside them” (Ezek. 10). And afterward: “This is the living creature which I saw beneath the God of Israel beside the river Chebar. And I understood that they were cherubim: four; and each had four faces, and each four wings, and beneath their wings the likeness of a human hand; and the likeness of their faces was the very faces which I had seen beside the river Chebar” (ibid.). He himself also explains somewhat how the four living creatures are one living creature, when he says: “Each had four faces and each four wings” (Ezek. 1).

First, therefore, we say that the one living creature is the one Christ; but the four living creatures, or the four faces of the one, are the four principal mysteries of Christ, which a Christian may not be permitted to ignore. The first is the incarnation; the second, the passion; the third, the resurrection; the fourth, the ascension. For a Christian may not fail to recognize these faces, or be ignorant of these mysteries; indeed, he ought daily to look to them in confession, as the apostolic tradition has set forth for us in the Creed. For after the preliminary words, “I believe in God the Father almighty, creator of heaven and earth, and in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord,” these four distinct articles follow:

“He was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary.” This is the first mystery, or first face.

“He suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died, and was buried; he descended to the lower regions.” This is the second face.

“On the third day he rose from the dead.” This is the third face.

“He ascended into [Col. 0912C] heaven, sits at the right hand of God the Father almighty, and from there will come to judge the living and the dead.” This is the fourth face.

The face of the mysteries of the incarnation is that of a man, because the true God was truly incarnate and truly assumed, from the womb of the Virgin and without sin, a human nature. The mystery of the passion, however, is the face of the calf, because the calf which, by the commandment of the Law, was sacrificed for sin (Lev. 4), signified the passion of the Redeemer, who was to be sacrificed for our sins. Other animals indeed were offered—the lamb or sheep, the goat, the dove, and the turtledove—but their principal animal was the calf, especially that calf which, because it was for the sin of the priest or of the multitude, had its body burned outside the camp. Of the mystery of this the Apostle says: “Therefore Jesus also, that he might sanctify the people through himself, suffered outside the gate. Let us therefore go out to him outside the camp, bearing reproach” (Heb. 13).

Moreover, his victorious resurrection is the face of the lion. For the foreknowing patriarch Jacob had said: “Judah is a lion’s cub; from the prey, my son, you have gone up. Resting, you lay down like a lion and like a lioness: who shall rouse him?” (Gen. 49). Finally, the sublimity of the ascension is the face of the eagle. Beholding this beforehand, blessed Job says concerning the faithlessness of the Jewish people: “The bird has not known the path” (Job 28).

We must now say how these living creatures, or the four faces of the one living creature, are both in the midst of the throne and around the throne. By the midst [Col. 0913A] of the throne—which, as we have already said above, is the kingdom of God, begun in David and completed in Christ, to whom the Lord God gave the throne of David his father (Luke 1)—we understand the fullness of time, in which Christ celebrated the already mentioned mysteries of his incarnation, 388 passion, resurrection, and ascension. But by the circuit of the same throne we understand, on the one hand, the four volumes of the Gospel, and on the other the five books of Moses. For both in that midst and in this circuit of the throne we marvelously see these faces appear: the face of the lion, the face of the calf, the face of the man, and the face of the flying eagle.

In the Pentateuch of Moses these faces are arranged in this order. But in the four books of the Gospels the same order is not to be observed, especially since, in the course of the Lord himself, the first face is that of the man—that is, the mystery of the incarnation. It should further be noted that not only four but also five faces are seen in this Apocalypse, since after these faces—the lion, the man, the calf, and the flying eagle—the Lamb also stands in the midst, opening the book and loosing its seals.

The individual faces are shown to have been taken from the individual books of Moses in this order. First, in Genesis, we have the face of the lion, when the patriarch Jacob speaks in blessing: “Judah is a lion’s cub; from the prey, my son, you have gone up” (Gen. 49), and the rest, as above. Then, in Exodus, a lamb on the fourteenth day of the first month, at evening, is sacrificed and eaten in all the houses of the children of Israel, as a type of this same our Redeemer (Exod. 12). Then, in Leviticus [Col. 0913C], a calf is commanded to be sacrificed for the sin of the priest or of the multitude, and its body to be burned outside the camp (Lev. 4).

But because the mystery of one and the same Lord’s passion is prefigured both through the lamb and through the calf, rightly one face of the calf—being the greater one, both here and in the prophet Ezekiel—is counted in place of two. The third face, therefore, that of the man, is taken from the book of Deuteronomy, when Moses speaks from the mouth of the Lord to the people:

“The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from your nation and from your brethren, like me, as you asked on Mount Horeb when the assembly was gathered and you said: ‘I shall no longer hear the voice of the Lord God, nor shall I see this great fire again, lest I die.’ And the Lord said to me: ‘They have spoken well in all that they have said. I will raise up for them a prophet from the midst of their brethren, like you’” (Deut. 18), etc.

For by these words, when he says “from your nation and from your brethren,” and adds “like me,” Christ is promised as a true man, in the reality of human nature. Then we find the fourth face, that of the flying eagle, set forth in the song of Deuteronomy, where Moses speaks thus: “As an eagle urges her young to fly, and hovers over them, she spreads her wings, takes them up, and carries them upon her shoulders” (Deut. 32).

Here John, according to the order of that ancient Scripture, places first the face of the lion; but the prophet Ezekiel, according to the order of the event which he foresaw, placed [Col. 0914A] first the face of the man. For in the Gospel Christ is first man by nature; then calf by his passion; then lion by his resurrection; then flying eagle by his ascension. Of the Evangelists, however, according as the manner of discourse written by each seems to require, one is said to have the face of the man, another of the lion, another of the calf, another of the flying eagle; and each deserves to be proclaimed both in this vision and in that prophetic vision of these living creatures.

Concerning Luke and John there is one opinion among all: namely, that Luke is rightly figured by the face of the calf, and John by that of the flying eagle. Concerning Matthew and Mark, however, opinion is divided: some, among whom blessed Jerome is one and the foremost, assign Matthew to the man and Mark [Col. 0914B] to the lion; others, among whom blessed Augustine is the greatest or best-known, assign Matthew to the lion and Mark to the man.

For Luke, both at the beginning and at the end of his discourse, concerns himself with the temple or priesthood. In his account, it is faithfully related how the Holy of Holies was anointed—that is, conceived by the Holy Spirit (Luke 1)—and likewise at the Jordan, where the Holy Spirit descended upon that same true priest in the form of a dove (Luke 3). This Evangelist, presenting him as priest in the expiation of sins, recounts his generations not by descending but by ascending; and ascending, he passes to Abraham and arrives at God, to whom we are reconciled when cleansed and expiated through the priesthood of Christ himself.

Therefore he prefaces both the beginning and the end of the genealogy which he has arranged with adoptive fathers or sons, saying at the beginning: “Jesus, as was supposed, was the son of Joseph, who was the son of Heli”; and at the end, concerning Adam, “who was the son of God” (ibid.). For neither did Joseph beget Jesus, nor Heli Joseph; rather, each had an adopted son; nor did God beget Adam, but fashioned him. Clearly, because Luke had undertaken to weave the Lord’s priestly character, he rightly proceeded thus: for the priestly generation by which Christ regenerates us is wholly adoptive, and descends not from flesh but from spirit and mercy.

In Luke’s Gospel the fattened calf is also killed for the returning prodigal son (Luke 15), and nearly all the parables resound with mercy. And the merciful priest, being in [Col. 0914D] agony, prays at greater length with a sweat of blood (Luke 22); and at his end receives the repentant thief, saying, “Today you shall be with me in paradise” (Luke 23). Thus throughout its whole course Luke possesses the face of the calf, giving closer attention to our priest and sacrifice; and, writing after Christ’s resurrection, he records from Christ’s own mouth that “the remission of sins must be preached in his name to all nations” (Luke 24).

John, flying in lofty understanding beyond every creature and fixing the opened eyes of his mind upon the ray of the eternal sun, deserved to say and write: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God” (John 1). Thus, proceeding most sublimely through the entire texture of his discourse, he established the testimony of Christ’s divinity with his whole attention.

In John, “as an eagle urges her young to fly, and hovers over them, spreads her wings, takes them up, and carries them upon her shoulders” (Deut. 32), when—as he himself says—“the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1); and, speaking with little children, he raised them on high toward an understanding of the glory of his own or his Father’s majesty. This is indeed what it is for the eagle’s young to be urged to fly. He also showed them that they needed to be carried upon shoulders, saying, for example: “If therefore you see the Son of Man ascending above, where he was before” (John 6). And elsewhere: “No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3). Therefore, if no one ascends except he who descended, it is true [Col. 0915B] that all who are or shall be there have been “carried upon his shoulders like an eagle.” Thus John stands out in the face of the eagle, and concerning him too there is a unanimous opinion among all.

But concerning Matthew and Mark there is, as has already been said, a divided opinion among the Fathers. Blessed Augustine, following the order of this book, understands Matthew in the lion, since he recounts Christ’s royal lineage (Matt. 1): “Because the lion of the tribe of Judah has conquered” (Rev. 5)—“for Judah is a lion’s cub” (Gen. 49)—and in Matthew Christ is feared as king by a king and worshipped by the Magi; there also a king settles accounts with his servants (Matt. 25), a king makes a wedding for his son (Matt. 22), and at last a king separates the sheep from the goats (Matt. 25).

Nevertheless, more agree with the opinion which assigns the face of the man to Matthew, and not without reason. For although, because of a certain likeness to the royal majesty about which he often writes, he rightly seems to imitate the face of the lion, king of beasts, one must nevertheless consider that he writes of man more often than of king and almost nowhere sets king without man. For he says: “The kingdom of heaven is like a man, a king, who made a wedding for his son” (Matt. 22). He does not say merely “a king,” but “a man, a king.” Again, where the king separates the sheep from the goats and says to those standing at the right: “Come, blessed of my Father” (Matt. 25), the face of the Son of Man is expressly indicated. For he says: “When the Son of Man comes in his majesty, and all his angels with him, then he shall sit upon the throne of his majesty” (ibid.).

Elsewhere in the parables, where the title of king is unmentioned, “man” is written. For example: “The kingdom of heaven is like a householder who went out early in the morning to hire laborers” (Matt. 20). And: “A certain man, going abroad, called his servants” (Matt. 25). Besides this, in the prophetic vision where this king who was to reign is shown beforehand to Daniel, the venerable face of the man is set forth in this manner: “I looked, therefore, in the vision of the night, and behold, with the clouds of heaven one like a Son of Man came; and he came even to the Ancient of Days, and they presented him before him. And he gave him power, honor, and kingdom; and all peoples, tribes, and tongues shall serve him” (Dan. 7).

Thus in Matthew, although through the likeness of royal power the face of the lion, king [Col. 0916A] of beasts, may rightly be understood, nevertheless, because of the very name “man,” which he joins to king and more frequently places without the name of king, the face of the man is quite fittingly understood—especially because he begins thus: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham” (Matt. 1), because Christ Jesus is their son or seed according to the flesh.

Mark, for this reason, seems to have the face of the lion: he begins his Gospel as with a terrible roar—that is, the preaching of repentance—and ends it with the threat of judgment or condemnation. For he begins with the preaching of John, saying: “The beginning of the Gospel of Jesus Christ, Son of God. As it is written in Isaiah the prophet: ‘Behold, I send my angel before your face, who shall prepare your way before you: the voice of one crying in the wilderness, Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.’ John was in the wilderness baptizing and preaching a baptism of repentance” (Mark 1; Mal. 3; Isa. 40), etc. At the end also he says: “He who believes and is baptized shall be saved; but he who does not believe shall be condemned” (Mark 16).

Therefore, because he strikes terror into hearts both at the beginning and at the end, he is rightly understood, in accordance with his purpose, to have the fearsome face of the lion, whose roar—that is, the final judgment—no unrepentant person will be able to escape. Moreover, the Lord himself displays something more of a teacher’s severity toward his disciples in this Evangelist. For example: “Why,” he says, “do you reason because you have no bread? Do you not yet know or understand? Do you still have your heart blinded? Having eyes, do you not see; and having ears, do you not hear?” (Mark 8). Likewise, after saying to them “how the Son of Man would be delivered into the hands of men, and they would kill him, and, having been killed, he would rise on the third day,” “they,” he says, “did not understand the word and were afraid to question him. And when they were in the house, he asked them: ‘What were you discussing on the way?’ But they kept silent” (Mark 9).

These men, because in writing they too beheld the four aforesaid faces of the one living creature—that is, the four mysteries of the one Christ—deserved each to derive from them a particular likeness more conspicuously.

But all others who rightly preside in the Church of Christ are, however slightly, like one or another of these faces. For one who administers prudently in outward matters is a man; another who contemplates heavenly things sublimely is an eagle; another who worthily exercises a teacher’s severity and makes good use of the rod of discipline is a lion; another who compassionately bears with inferiors in a spirit of gentleness is a calf. But one who shares in all these virtues, and can conform and adapt himself in all these respects according to time and circumstance, is useful in the house of God; and to him it is permitted to say with the Apostle: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (1 Cor. 4).

“These living creatures,” he says, “were full of eyes before and behind.” Christ, “the light of the world,” whom one who follows “does not walk in darkness but shall have the light of life” (John 8), says to the Jews: “Even if I bear testimony concerning myself, my testimony is true, because I know where I come from and where I go. But you do not know where I come from or where I go” (ibid.). Indeed, he could rightly have said this to them also, and it may rightly be said to all like them: You do not know where you come from or where you are going.

In this respect, finally, unbelieving people—blind and unclean living creatures—differ from devout people, luminous and clean living creatures: the former are unwilling even to attend to these things, while the latter know and diligently attend to where they come from and where they are going. Accordingly, the living creatures are full of eyes before and behind.

First, concerning Christ, who is both one living creature and, as has already been said, four in having four faces—that is, the four principal mysteries of incarnation, passion, resurrection, and ascension, through which or concerning which he must be known—the Catholic faith firmly maintains that in each of these he is full of eyes before and behind, because in each of them he knows where he comes from and where he is going.

When he is conceived by the Holy Spirit in the womb of the Virgin, he knows that he comes forth from God the Father and comes into the world. For that “he came forth from the Father” (John 16)—indeed, that “in the beginning was the Word, God with God”—and that from there he came here, was behind us or is behind us; but before us was that, coming into this world, he appeared visibly, that “the Word made flesh dwelt among us” (John 1).

Likewise, when “he is led as a sheep to slaughter” (Isa. 53), he is nevertheless full of eyes before and behind, knowing where he comes from and where he goes. For he knows that, born from the womb of the Virgin, he neither contracted original sin nor committed actual sin; and thus, conceived by the Holy Spirit, he comes and goes as a new man, to bear the iniquities of us all, foreseeing that, according to the prophet, “if he sets his life as an offering for sin, he shall see long-lived seed, and the will of the Lord shall prosper in his hand” (ibid.).

Likewise, when he rises from the dead, he is similarly full of eyes before and behind: knowing that he comes from the utmost abasement, where he was made lower than the angels (Ps. 8), indeed could be trampled as a worm and a man (Ps. 21); and knowing that he goes and ascends in order to be crowned with glory and honor, set over the works of the Father’s hands, with all things subjected beneath his feet (Ps. 8).

Likewise, when he happily ascends into heaven, he is full of eyes before and behind: knowing that he comes from being judged by men in judgment, and that he goes to judge all men in judgment. Thus in Christ the four living creatures are full of eyes before and behind, because in each of them he can say: “I know where I come from and where I go” (John 8), and accordingly, “my testimony is true” (ibid.).

Moreover, both the Evangelists already mentioned and all imitators of Christ take great care always to be, according to their measure, similarly living creatures full of eyes before and behind—that is, to know where they come from and where they are going. For knowing where they come from greatly helps them preserve profound humility; while knowing where they are going benefits them in guarding their strength lawfully, according to the Psalmist’s words: “I will keep my strength for you” (Ps. 58). [Col. 0918A]

Whence do they come, and where do they go? They come from nothing, because they were created from nothing, and this they look upon with the eyes behind them; but they go toward the revelation of the glory of the children of God (Rom. 8), and this they behold before themselves with the eyes ahead. Likewise, they come from sins and vices and go toward the victories of virtues.

For example, Matthew (chap. 9) came from the tax booth, where Jesus saw him sitting; and, in writing the Gospel or book of Christ’s generation, he goes to this throne to give glory, honor, and blessing with the other living creatures to him who sits upon the throne and lives unto ages of ages (1 Pet. 5). He is full of eyes behind, humbly considering in conscience who and what he had been; he is full of eyes ahead, recognizing with simple thanksgiving what he has received and what he has become.

Thus also the other saints are God’s living creatures, full of eyes before and behind: knowing where they have come from, or from what they have been made, and where they are going, or for what they have been made; knowing also what they were by merit and what they have become by grace; likewise repenting of past evils and guarding against future ones.

“And the four living creatures each had six wings.” In the one Christ this must first be understood thus: each of the things mentioned above—namely, incarnation, passion, resurrection, or ascension—“each,” I say, “of these has six wings,” because in each of these the ancient divinity, the everlasting deity of the eternal Word which created all things in six days, was full, true, and operative in the new man. For in him, both when he is incarnate or born, when he suffers, when he rises, and when he ascends into heaven, true and perfect divinity dwells. And all these things alike, individually, have six wings, so that the perfection of their Scripture sublimely escapes every thought that exalts itself against the knowledge of God (2 Cor. 10), and does not fear to be caught or ensnared by crafty little arguments of vain philosophy. For it does not crawl upon the earth; rather, holding heaven by perfect truth, it despises earth.

The number six of the wings indicates to us by its own perfection the perfection of this truth. For this number is the first of the perfect numbers, because it is the first composed of its own parts. It has its half, namely three; its third, namely two; and its sixth, namely one. These—three, two, and one—make six. Therefore each has six wings: that is, in each the truth of saving doctrine is perfect.

But others too, even those who have no pursuit or ministry of teaching or writing, must have six wings if they are to fly out from distress and escape the wrath to come—that is, the six works of mercy, which he who sits upon the throne enumerates thus to those standing at the right: “I was hungry and you gave me food; I was thirsty and you gave me drink; I was a stranger and you gathered me in; naked and you covered me; I was sick and you visited me; I was in prison and you came to me” (Matt. 25).

It follows: “And around and within they are full of eyes.” By “around” the active life, and by “within” the contemplative life, are rightly understood. For one who serves the works of the active life moves about among many things, as the Lord testifies when he says: “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things” (Luke 10). But one who holds to the contemplative life is within, meditating upon the law of the Lord; within he rests; within, with Mary, he sits at the feet of the Lord.

Therefore these living creatures are full of eyes both around and within, because preachers of the Gospel, or any prelates, if they preside lawfully, are cautious and provident both in external action and in internal contemplation. “And they had no rest day and night, saying: Holy, holy, holy, Lord God almighty, who was, and who is, and who is to come.”

From the time when the throne was set in heaven and the Lord sat upon it—that is, from the time when, with the kingdom of sin destroyed, the kingdom of righteousness was established through Christ’s passion and the Lord reigned in his Church—these living creatures have no rest, that is, no leisure, as they cry aloud “Holy” three times to the Lord, who by evangelical doctrine proclaim the Holy Trinity to the whole world.

The four often-mentioned principal mysteries—incarnation, passion, resurrection, and ascension—principally preach the glory or knowledge of this Holy Trinity in Christ. This was not done before: no one disclosed this name through public preaching.

The first living creature, or first face, namely Christ’s incarnation, gives voice to this blessed Trinity thus: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you; therefore also the Holy One to be born from you shall be called the Son of God” (Luke 1). The Most High, or God, is the Father; he who is conceived is the Son of God; and he who comes upon and overshadows the woman conceiving, in order to fashion or create from the virgin for the Son—that is, the Word of God—a human body, is the Holy Spirit. Therefore this first face, that is, the incarnation, gives voice to the thrice-holy one and preaches the Holy Trinity.

The second face, that is, the passion, likewise commends the same Trinity: “I,” says the Son, “will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete” (John 14). Likewise: “But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things” (ibid.).

Then the third face likewise establishes this same name of the Trinity, when the Son said on the day on which, having risen, he appeared to the disciples: “As the Father sent [Col. 0919D] me, I also send you into the world. And when he had said this, he breathed upon them and said: Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20). And elsewhere: “Go,” he says, “teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28).

Finally, the fourth face, namely the ascension, more loudly proclaims the glory of this blessed Trinity. In accordance with the prophecy saying: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand” (Ps. 109), the Son ascends into heaven and sits at the right hand of God the Father; having said beforehand as he was ascending, “I will send upon you the promise of my Father” (Luke 24), on the tenth day that promise, namely the Holy Spirit, came and filled the hearts of the apostles and at the same time opened their mouths more widely for preaching (Acts 2).

Formed, as it were, by these four principal forms, and inspired by that fire of the Holy Spirit which came upon the apostles on the day mentioned, the four Evangelists preached and wrote in such a way that, as has already been said, one imitated the face of the man, another that of the calf, another that of the lion, another that of the flying eagle. From that time both these and the other preachers of the Gospel “had no rest day and night”: that is, they did not cease in prosperity or fall silent in adversity, preaching faith in the holy and indivisible Trinity—which is what it means to say the third time: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God almighty.”

But when, to complete so splendid a praise, these living creatures add, “who was, and who is, and who is to come,” it is a victorious exultation against all persecutors. For adversaries were not lacking, nor would they be lacking, who would strive by threats and terrors and by every kind of death or punishment to suppress the outcry of this preaching. But let these holy preachers be confident, because he whom they preach “was, and is, and is to come.”

“Do not fear,” he says, “those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. 10); or, “after this they have nothing more that they can do. But I will show you whom you should fear: fear him who, after he has killed, has power to cast into Gehenna. Yes, I say to you, fear him” (Luke 12). Therefore neither should those who are killed be afraid, nor should those who kill mock those who die, [Col. 0920C] because he whom we preach—the true and one God in the Trinity—was before this body came to be, indeed even “before the mountains were made and the earth was formed” (Ps. 89); and now he is, giving to his confessors who stand before kings and governors a mouth and wisdom which none of their adversaries can resist or contradict; and when their persecutors, worn out with killing, cease to kill, he will come to judge the cause of their killing, and then not a hair of their heads shall perish (Matt. 10).

“And when those living creatures gave glory and honour and blessing to him who sits upon the throne, who lives for ages of ages, the twenty-four elders fell down before him who sits upon the throne, and worshipped him who lives for ages of ages, and cast [Col. 0920D] their crowns before the throne, saying: You are worthy, O Lord our God, to receive glory and honour and power, because you created all things, and by your will they existed and were created.”

These living creatures magnificently heightened the wonder at the divine majesty, omnipotence, and goodness of God, by giving glory, honour, and blessing to the same one seated upon the throne, who lives for ages of ages. Behold, this is that wonder at which the Psalmist, long before, astounded in spirit, said: “O Lord, our Lord, how wonderful is your name in all the earth!” (Ps. VIII). And immediately, explaining what he wondered at, he says: “For your magnificence has been exalted above the heavens” (ibid.). By this verse he proclaimed in anticipation the fourth face of these living creatures, namely, the Lord’s ascension.

For afterward he briefly set down the four faces in order, saying: “What is man, that you are mindful of him, or the son of man, that you visit him?” (Ps. VIII). This is the first face, the face of a man: namely, the incarnation of the Word of God, by which he became flesh and the Son of Man. “You made him a little lower than the angels” (ibid.). This is the second face, the face of the calf: namely, the passion of that same Lord, in which he was so made lower than the angels that he could suffer and die, whereas the holy angels are neither mortal nor capable of suffering. Hence, when he underwent his anguished struggle, “an angel from heaven appeared to him, strengthening him” (Luke XXII): as a greater strengthening a lesser—that is, the impassible one strengthening the suffering one, the immortal the dying one. “You crowned him with glory and honour” (Ps. VIII). This is the third face, the face of the lion: namely, the resurrection of that same Lord, in which, after hell had been despoiled through the passion of death, he was crowned as victor with the glory of immortality and the honour of incorruption. “And you set him over the works of your hands” (ibid.). This is the fourth face, the face of the flying eagle: namely, the ascension of that same Lord, by which the flesh ascended to that place from which the divinity that was to assume flesh descended, and sits at the right hand of God.

Having said these things, he again, because of the greatness of these matters, repeats at the end in wonder and exclamation the very thing that he said at the beginning: “O Lord, our Lord, how wonderful is your name in all the earth!” Just as these things inspired wonder above all the works of the Lord in him who foresaw them in spirit before they happened, so, when they occurred and since they were accomplished, they are most wonderful to the whole earth beyond the other works of the Lord God—through the preaching of the apostles, and through the preaching and writing of the living creatures of the same four faces, that is, the evangelists.

“And when those living creatures gave glory and honour and blessing to him who sits upon the throne, who lives for ages of ages.” To him who sits upon the throne, we give glory by gracious words, but honour by dutiful deeds. We glorify him when we worthily and laudably proclaim his goodness; we honour him when, by holy living, we prepare our hearts and bodies as vessels of honour and clean dwellings for his Holy Spirit. Yet we do not have it from ourselves either to glorify God thus or to honour him thus, but from his own gift, as the Apostle also says: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the surpassing greatness may be God’s power in us, and not from ourselves” (II Cor. IV). Again: “Not that we are sufficient to think anything from ourselves, as though from ourselves; but our sufficiency is from God” (II Cor. III).

Therefore we add a third thing: namely, to give blessing, that is, thanksgiving, to him who made us fit to glorify him through our deeds. And with the same Apostle, in the same Epistle, we say: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all consolation, who consoles us in all our tribulation” (II Cor. I).

Thus did these living creatures, possessing the firstfruits of glory and honour. They glorified God by preaching with the word of wisdom and knowledge, and with eloquent speech; they honoured God by doing not their own will but God’s will, and by crucifying their flesh with its vices and desires for God’s honour (Gal.
