V); they blessed God by attributing to him, not to themselves, everything that they could say for his glory and everything that they could do for his honour—him who, by sending the Holy Spirit from heaven, so taught them, though simple and unlearned, that they knew and were able to speak for his glory; and so strengthened them, though hitherto weak, that they could not only live, but also die, for his honour.

They gave these three things to “him who sits upon the throne, who lives for ages of ages,” drawing great refreshment for their own need and great renewal of holy hope from this: that, while they glorify, honour, and bless God, suffer persecution, and are killed, they leave him surviving upon the throne, who lives for ages of ages; and precisely because he survives and lives for ages of ages, he can attend, after them, to their deaths and demand an account of their blood.

As they gave these things, “the twenty-four elders,” he says, “fell down before him who sits upon the throne, and worshipped him who lives for ages of ages.” The chief reason why that one who sits and lives deigns to be worshipped by us is the grace and mercy that he has wrought for us in Christ, or through Christ. For worship offered to him for temporal goods is not so pleasing to him as the worship offered by that carnal Israel, which, when it was told, “I will give you a land flowing with milk and honey” (Exod. XIII; Deut. VI; Lev. XX), and in other sayings of that sort, understood or attended to nothing but earthly promises.

But the holy and perfect fathers—Moses and all such as possessed the Spirit of God—worshipped God because of this future grace of Christ. Therefore, in worshipping or sacrificing, they prefigured these living creatures, or these faces, of which we speak, as has already been said above. Therefore, when those living creatures gave glory and honour and blessing, “the twenty-four elders fell down and worshipped,” because, plainly, once those oft-mentioned mysteries had been celebrated in Christ and proclaimed to the world through evangelical heralds, “every knee bends at his name, in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. II); and among all these, especially those who laboured for his kingdom. Of these, as was already said above, the principal figures in the Old Testament before David’s kingdom were the twelve judges of Israel (Judg. III), and in the New Testament, now that Christ reigns upon David’s throne, the twelve apostles, who will judge the twelve tribes of Israel (Matt. XIX).

“But as they worshipped, they cast,” he says, “their 392 crowns before the throne.” Those who laboured in God’s kingdom or for God’s kingdom have worthily been crowned in the presence of the reigning and enthroned one. Yet these, considering that they obtained their crowns not by their own merits but by the grace of mercy that goes before and follows after, and reflecting that he for whom and through whom are all things, who brought many sons to glory, was perfected through suffering as the author of their salvation—do they not make light of their own dignity and attribute, with humble reverence, to him everything that they have deserved?

“They therefore cast their crowns before the throne”: that is, whatever virtue or dignity they possess, they offer it to God with thanksgiving, saying: “You are worthy, O Lord our God, to receive glory and honour and power, because you created all things, and by your will they existed and were created.” Let the dignity of any saints or righteous persons be compared; let the dignities or merits of the elders be compared with the dignity, work, or merit of this Ancient of Days: what are their dignities or merits? For he created all things, and by his will they existed and were created—that is, they existed and were created by no one’s counsel or merit, but by his will alone.

“You created all things,” he says; and again, “they existed and were created.” He did not repeat the word “creation” superfluously, but intended two creations of the rational creature to be understood. The latter is indeed later, but more beneficial: that by which we have been recreated in Christ through the Holy Spirit, concerning which the Psalmist says: “You will send forth your Spirit, and they shall be created” (Ps. CIII). The former is that in Genesis: “And God created man in his image; in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them” (Gen. I).

Concerning this creation by which we have been recreated through the Holy Spirit, and of which the Apostle also says: “For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared that we should walk in them” (Eph. II)—concerning this creation, I say, he first said: “Because you created all things,” that is, all human beings, or all kinds of creatures; as we also have in the Apostle: “For in him it pleased all fullness to dwell, and through him to reconcile all things” (Col. I). But concerning the earlier creation he added: “And by your will they existed and were created.” It was not enough to have said “they existed,” unless he added, “and were created”: that is, they received the beginning of their existence by your will.

What elder, then, considering such great dignity, would judge himself worthy? In comparison with that dignity, all their own dignities vanish from their eyes, just as, in the presence of the sun over the earth, all the stars are obscured and do not appear. “Therefore you,” he says, “O Lord our God, you alone are worthy to receive glory, honour, and power”: glory, because they were created by you from nothing; honour, because by your will they existed through the succession of generations; power, because through your Spirit they were created in the second creation. Therefore, “Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but give glory to your name” (Ps. CXIII).

## Book Four

[Col. 0923]

## Chapter V

[Col. 0923C]

“And I saw in the right hand of him who sits upon the throne a book written within and without, sealed with seven seals.” In the preceding vision we beheld the praise or work of the Spirit of wisdom in the arrangement of his throne; now, in this following vision, we proclaim—or understand to be proclaimed—the Spirit of understanding in the opening of the book and the unsealing of its seven seals.

In that vision there is one throne or seat, and around it seven signs: namely, “a door opened in heaven; a voice heard like the sound of a trumpet speaking; a rainbow around the throne; twenty-four elders sitting upon seats; lamps burning before the throne, which themselves are also seven in number; before the throne something like a sea of glass; and in the middle of the throne and around it four living creatures full of eyes before and behind” (Rev. IV). In this vision, apart from the Lamb being seen with seven horns and seven eyes, there is one book and its seven seals. We say this so that we may not fail to recognize that, in these revelations of the sevenfold Holy Spirit, and in the other matters which follow, the mystery of the number seven is strongly commended.

“And I saw,” he says, “in the right hand of him who sits upon the throne a book.” The one book is Holy Scripture: all Scripture, I say, divinely inspired. It is called and is one book because it was written by one Spirit and is the treasury or sanctuary of the one Word of God. This book in Isaiah is also unopenable both to one who knows letters and to one who does not know them. Yet there too its opening is proclaimed thus: “On that day the deaf shall hear the words of the book” (Isa. XXIX). Ezekiel also speaks of it: “And I saw,” he says, “and behold, a hand was sent to me, in which was a rolled book; and he spread it out before me, and it was written within and without” (Ezek. II). There he also adds what John left unsaid—namely, what was written in the book—saying: “And there were written in it lamentations, and a song, and woe” (ibid.).

For the entire course of both the Old and New Testaments warns that repentance must be done for sins, the kingdom of heaven sought, and the weeping of hell fled. Therefore, “I saw,” he says, “the book”—that is, all Scripture, the great and holy book—“in the right hand of him who sits upon the throne.” Truly it was in his right hand, according to that saying in Deuteronomy: “In his right hand is a fiery law” (Deut. XXXIII). But Wisdom says: “In his left hand are riches and glory” (Prov. III). “Fiery law” is the same thing as this book, namely, all Holy Scripture, as was already said. For it is the Word or utterance of the Lord, concerning which the Psalmist also says: “Your utterance is exceedingly refined by fire” (Ps. CXVIII).

Let us therefore observe that this one seated upon the throne is very powerful and exceedingly rich, and possesses distinct and different resources on his right and on his left: on the right, this book, the fiery law; on the left, riches and glory. As much better as the right hand is than the left, so much happier a good are this book and fiery law than riches and glory. What are riches in this place, and what glory, but earthly riches and worldly glory? Rightly, therefore, riches and glory are in his left hand, because the good that consists in such riches and temporal glory is of such a kind that it is given not only to the elect; indeed, it is more often absent from the elect, and granted to them later, than it is to the reprobate.

But the fiery law, namely this book, is the good and consolation of the elect alone; and this is the portion which remains forever, as the Lord testifies when he says in the Gospel: “Mary has chosen the best portion, which shall not be taken away from her” (Luke X). Some, indeed—such as David and Solomon—received much from both portions: from the right hand, namely the book; and from the left, riches and glory. For together with knowledge of God’s law, they also possessed riches and the glory of a temporal kingdom, and both gifts came from him who sits upon the throne. Yet it benefits every soul to whom such things are given to delight in what is given from the right hand, but to hold under itself and govern through generous stewardship what is from the left, and to say: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me” (Song II). That is to say: Temporal goods are under my control, but that portion which remains when they have passed away—the best portion, which is the Word of God—to read or hear, and, once understood, to commit to memory, is my highest delight.

“Written,” he says, “within and without, sealed with seven seals.” The book is written within and without because Holy Scripture must surely be read according to its historical or literal tenor and understood according to its spiritual sense. It is also sealed with seven seals, namely, in such a way as to contain in itself the whole fullness of Christ’s mysteries. Unless he had come and fulfilled them, no one would understand them; and anyone wishing to unseal such exceedingly firm seals would labour in vain, because whatever he might endeavour to say by way of exposition would lack coherence.

Indeed, those to whom Christ has not come, or who have not received Christ, still handle a closed and sealed book; indeed, they do not even see that it is sealed, because “a veil is laid over their heart” (II Cor. III), and whatever they eagerly attempt to utter as exposition lacks coherence. It was rightly said, moreover, “sealed with seven seals,” because there are seven mysteries of Christ around which Holy Law and prophetic Scripture revolve: namely, the incarnation, passion, resurrection, ascension, the gift of the Holy Spirit the Paraclete, the calling of the gentiles, and Christ’s second coming to judge. By his gift we shall speak of each in its proper place. Holy Scripture is so sealed by these mysteries that anyone who does not receive them is wholly unable to understand its truth.

“And I heard [saw] a strong angel proclaiming in a loud voice: Who is worthy to open the book and break its seals?” This strong angel, thus proclaiming in a loud voice, signifies the yearning expectation and great desire of the saints of old, concerning whom the Lord says in the Gospel: “Many prophets and righteous persons desired to see what you see, and did not see it” (Matt. XIII). And the Apostle, after enumerating the fathers, says to the Hebrews: “All these died in faith, not having received the promises, but seeing and greeting them from afar, and confessing that they were strangers and pilgrims upon the earth” (Heb. XI). And below: “All these, approved by the testimony of faith, did not receive the promise, God having provided something better for us, lest they should be made perfect without us” (ibid.).

Surely that expectation, their greeting from afar, and their confession were a great cry of great desire, such as was fittingly signified here in this vision by the loud voice of a strong angel proclaiming strongly. For example: those of whom he said last that all, approved by the testimony of faith, did not receive the promises, read what was written in one of them concerning the incarnation of the Son of God: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel” (Isa. VII). And again: “A little child has been born to us, a son has been given to us; and dominion has been placed upon his shoulder, and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, Mighty God, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace” (Isa. IX).

And in another place, concerning his divine birth: “The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Ps. II). Again, concerning his passion: “Truly he himself bore our sicknesses and our sins; the chastisement of our peace was upon him, and by his bruise we have been healed. Like a sheep he was led to slaughter, and like a lamb before the one shearing him he shall be silent and shall not open his mouth” (Isa. LIII). And in another place: “They pierced my hands and my feet” (Ps. XXI).

Again, concerning his resurrection: “Come, and let us return to the Lord, because he has seized us and will heal us; he will strike us and cure us. He will revive us after two days; on the third day he will raise us, and we shall live in his presence” (Hos. VI). And in the psalm: “I slept and was in slumber, and I rose” (Ps. III); and again: “I rose, and I am still with you” (Ps. CXXXVIII). Again, concerning his ascension: “For your magnificence has been exalted above the heavens” (Ps. VIII). And again: “God has ascended amid jubilation, and the Lord at the sound of a trumpet” (Ps. XLVI). Elsewhere: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand” (Ps. CIX).

Again, concerning the coming or gift of the Holy Spirit: “And it shall be in the last days: I will pour out my Spirit upon flesh, says the Lord, and your sons and daughters shall prophesy” (Joel II). And elsewhere: “I will pour clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed from all your defilements; and I will give you a new heart, and put a new spirit within you” (Ezek. XXXVI); or, as he shortly afterward says, “I will put my Spirit within you” (ibid.).

Again, concerning the calling of the gentiles and the rejection of the Jews: “I will call that which was not my people, my people; and her who had not obtained mercy, one who has obtained mercy” (Rom. IX; Hos. II). And elsewhere: “A people whom I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me. Foreign sons lied to me; foreign sons grew old” (Ps. XVII). Again, concerning his judgment: “The Lord will come to judgment with the elders of his people” (Isa. III). Elsewhere: “O Lord, let your hand be exalted, and let them not see; let them see and be confounded, those who are zealous for the people, and let fire devour your enemies” (Isa. XXVI).

They read these things, I say, and many like them, because nearly the entire fullness of the Scriptures revolves around these seven mysteries. Desiring and longing to see their fulfilment, they said: “Who is worthy to open the book and break its seals?” In spirit they surveyed all the seed of Israel; they saw persons being born and dying every day, considered the living, remembered the dead, and absolutely no one appeared so great or such a one as could break these seven seals—that is, in whom or through whom so many and such great mysteries might be fulfilled. This is what follows:

“And no one in heaven, nor on earth, nor under the earth, was able to open the book or to look upon it.” In heaven there were angels; on earth there were living righteous human beings; under the earth there were some—namely, in the underworld, yet in a certain repose—patriarchs and prophets, as well as kings and many righteous dead persons. Yet none of them could or had been able to open the book—that is, to fulfil the aforesaid mysteries of Scripture—nor even to look upon it: that is, not even to hope of himself that he might accomplish so great and divine a work of the salvation of the world.

It follows:

“And I wept much, because no one was found worthy to open the book or to see it.” It was too little for this blessed John to hear the loud voice of the strong angel proclaiming strongly, “Who is worthy to open the book and break its seals?”—a voice or proclamation signifying the great desire of the saints of old—unless also the anointing of which John himself speaks elsewhere, “and his anointing teaches you concerning all things” (I John II), anointed his mind, so that in that very ecstasy he might weep because of the sweetness of the things he had seen, and experience through his own weeping how tearful the desire of those saints had been.

“Therefore I wept much,” he says. “And one of the elders said to me: Do not weep. Behold, the lion from the tribe of Judah, the root of David, has conquered, so as to open the book and break its seven seals.” Such a saying by one of the elders not only consoles the weeping man, but also renders teachable one who sees and is about to see, so that he may better become a knower of the things or images which he sees, being forewarned by words of this kind in that very ecstasy and brought to remembrance of events accomplished: “Behold, the lion from the tribe of Judah, the root of David.”

He calls him a lion, although John was immediately to see a lamb. For it follows:

“And I saw, and behold, in the midst of the throne and of the four living creatures, and in the midst of the elders, a Lamb standing as though slain.” Why this? Plainly because he who, in the gentleness and patience of his passion, was worthy to be “as a lamb silent before the one shearing him, and did not open his mouth” (Isa. LIII), after that passion had been accomplished immediately ascended upon his prey like a lion’s cub, despoiled hell, and, resting in the tomb and lying down as a lion and as a lioness (Gen. XLIX), crushed even bodily death—both in himself and in us—on the third day with a great roar and a great earthquake.

Certainly this lion will roar far more greatly when, coming to judge amid the thunder of a mighty tempest, he causes all the dead, as if asleep, to awaken. Therefore he says: “Behold, a lion from the tribe of Judah”: that is, a man such as, according to the prophetic truth foretold by the patriarch Jacob, was to be born from the tribe of Judah and conquered by his strength the prince of the opposing power; so great and such a one that he was and is worthy “to open the book and break its seven seals.”

But why did he say, “from the tribe of Judah, the root of David,” when he might have said, “from the tribe of Judah, from David’s stock”? For Christ is from David’s seed, just as he is from the tribe of Judah. Why, then, did he not say of David’s stock or seed, as he said from the tribe of Judah? Plainly because such wording would not have touched the matter or cause from which he is a lion and from which he could conquer. For Christ is from the tribe of Judah and David’s seed in that respect in which he is not God, nor in that respect did he conquer death or could rise again; but in that respect he is human and could die or be killed as a lamb.

More magnificently, therefore, it was said, as it ought to have been said: “the root of David.” For it is a splendid and wondrous thing that he should be the root of the one from whose stock he descended. For if you consider Christ according to the flesh, he is not the root of David, just as the vine does not bear the root, but the root bears the vine. Therefore “the root of David” is said according to his divinity: because, just as the root bears the vine or branch (Jer. II), so Christ, according to his divinity, bears David, the father of his flesh.

For why is David and that whole people customarily called “the Lord’s vineyard” in prophetic Scripture (Isa. V), except because through faith it clung to the Christ who was to come, who says, “I am the vine”? (John XV). Finally, just as the apostles are branches, so David is a branch of this vine; nor can or could anyone, ancient or modern, belong to the Lord’s vineyard unless he clings or has clung by faith to this vine.

It follows:

“And I saw, and behold, in the midst of the throne and of the four living creatures and elders, a Lamb standing as though slain, having seven horns and seven eyes.” The one and same Christ who is a lamb in dying innocently also became a lion by conquering death courageously. Both are founded upon the authority of the old Scripture. For the one whom the patriarch Jacob foretold as a lion or lion’s cub (Gen. XLIX), Moses prefigured by a lamb in Egypt (Exod. XII).

But how does this Lamb stand in the midst of the throne and of the four living creatures and elders, unless because, as is said elsewhere, “he is King of kings and Lord of lords”? (Rev. XIX). For he expresses the power and wisdom by which he rules and commands when he says that he has “seven horns and seven eyes.” For the sevenfold Spirit, resting in Christ or upon Christ, which above was compared to seven lamps, is here compared to seven horns because of the pre-eminence of power and strength, and to seven eyes because of the illumination of grace or wisdom. Hence Job says: “With him are strength and wisdom” (Job XII). Again: “With him are wisdom and strength” (ibid.).

Therefore, “I saw the Lamb,” he says, “standing in the midst of the throne and of the four living creatures and elders”: that is, Christ, the Holy of holies, reigning and ruling in the midst of all the saints, “with seven horns and seven eyes”: that is, with the seven Spirits, whose whole fullness he possesses in himself, strengthening and enlightening all who are around him by faith. “As though slain” is added as well. What does “as though slain” mean, except once slain but now living? For he indeed, “having risen from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. VI). Yet the marks of his death—the places of the nails in his hands and feet, and the place of the spear in his side, which after his resurrection he showed to his disciples and offered to their touch—are preserved in everlasting remembrance: for his glory, for our grace, and for the cruel conscience of his enemies, “that they may see and be confounded,” according to that prophetic saying: “They shall look upon him whom they pierced” (Zech. XII).

“And he came and received the book from the right hand of him who sits upon the throne.” Since, as has already been said above, “the fiery law” (Deut. XXXIII), which is this book, is in the right hand of the one seated, while “riches and glory” (Prov. III) are in his left hand, it should be carefully noted that Christ, coming into this world through the mystery of the incarnation, received neither riches nor glory from the left hand, but only the book, or fiery law, from the right. He gave an excellent example to all disciples and believers in him: this poor and needy one neither desired nor sought riches or glory in this world. Indeed, even when it was offered to him—as we read in the Gospel, since those whom he had satisfied with five loaves and two fish “were about to come and seize him and make him king” over them—knowing this, “he himself fled” (John VI).

He deigned only to meditate upon the law of the Lord day and night, only to receive the book from the right hand, intending to open it and break its seven seals. Those who, according to their ability, receive this book by following his example are indeed met with the labours and adversities of this world; but it is also written of him: “He shall be filled with reproaches” (Lam. III), that is, it will be sweet for him to endure reproaches for righteousness.

“And when he had opened the book, the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fell down [Col. 0930A] before the Lamb, each having harps and bowls 395 full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints. And they sang a new song, saying: You are worthy, O Lord, to receive the book and open its seals.” A very great matter and the highest undertaking was being carried out when that Lamb came, received, and opened the book; and good and lawful witnesses were needed to defend and testify that he was worthy to receive and open the book—that is, that the Scriptures, or all the oracles of the prophets, ought to be fulfilled in him.

For who believed him when he said that he had been sent by God the Father for such a ministry? On the contrary, the faithless Jews said: “You bear testimony concerning yourself; your testimony is not true” (John VIII), and much else in this manner. Hence John the Baptist cries out mournfully: “He who comes from heaven is above all, and testifies to what he has seen and heard, and no one receives his testimony” (John III). “No one,” he says—indeed, all stood against him, all called him a false witness, and killed him as a magician and deceiver.

For example, when the high priest said to him, “I adjure you by the living God, tell us whether you are the Christ, the Son of the blessed God” (Matt. XXVI), he answered truthfully; and he, seeing that no one received his testimony, kept silent: “And as a lamb before the one shearing him he was silent, and did not open his mouth” (Isa. LIII). Why say more? They killed him as a false witness, as has already been said, and in this way he most fully opened the book: he fulfilled the oracles of Scripture.

Therefore, lest testimony should be lacking even to him when slain, behold a threefold testimony to his dignity, sufficient and abundant according to the ordinance of the sacred law, because “every word stands in the mouth of two or three witnesses” (Deut. XIX).

The first witness in this place is the whole Church of saints, ancient and new, which is understood here through the fourteen elders and the four living creatures. For the one Church of all the elect preaches through writings and preaches through miracles that all things were fulfilled in that man Jesus Christ who was crucified; and it says: “You are worthy, O Lord, to receive the book and open its seals, because you were slain, and redeemed us to God by your blood from every tribe and language and people and nation, and made us a kingdom and priests to our God, and they shall reign upon the earth.”

The second witness is the entire choir or host of holy angels, who announced that he was to be incarnate (Matt. I); sang of his birth with “glory in the highest” (Luke I–II); ministered to him when tempted in the wilderness (Matt. IV); strengthened him when he was in agony in his passion, as Luke testifies (Luke XXII); appearing to blessed women, proclaimed the glory of his resurrection (Matt. XXVIII); and made known to the holy apostles both the triumph of his ascension and his return to judge (Acts I). Therefore he says: “And I saw and heard the voice of many angels around the throne and the living creatures and the elders; and their number was thousands of thousands, saying in a loud voice: Worthy is the Lamb who was slain to receive power and divinity and wisdom and strength and honour and glory and blessing.”

The third witness is the whole universe of created things, because “all things were made through him” (John I). This is the greatest and most steadfast testimony to his worthiness, since without doubt no one is worthier than he “through whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made” (ibid.). The beauty of heaven and all that is in it, the beauty of earth and all that is in it, and the beauty of the waters and all that is in them, bear witness to his worthiness in a certain natural harmony; because, as has already been said, “all things were made through him,” since God the Father “spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. XXXII, CXLVIII). But he is the Word of the one who speaks, the command of the one who commands.

Therefore he says: “And every creature that is in heaven and upon the earth and under the earth, and those in the sea and all things in it, I heard them all saying: To him who sits upon the throne and to the Lamb be blessing and honour and glory and power for ages of ages.” Now let us consider more carefully both the dignity and reverence of the witnesses, and the faithfulness and steadfastness of their testimonies.

> “When,” he says, “he had opened the book, the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fell before the Lamb, each holding harps and bowls full of perfumes, which are the prayers of the saints.” Before the Lamb opened the book, before by his passion he fulfilled the truth of the Scriptures, apart from very few—apart from the three Magi coming from the East [Col. 0931C] (Matt. II), and apart from the man born blind whom he enlightened (John IX)—almost no one is found to have fallen down and worshipped the Lamb, Christ the Son of God. But after he opened it, after he completed obedience, “every knee bends, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. II). Nor indeed is the knee alone bent: complete worship is performed by falling down, as it is written in the Psalm: “Ethiopians shall fall down before him, and all kings shall worship him” (Ps. LXXI).

The Apostles too had not yet learned either to worship him or to ask in his name. Hence, as the hour of his passion was already approaching, he said to them: “Until now you have asked nothing in my name” (John XVI). And afterwards: “On that day you will ask in my name” (ibid.). Therefore, from the time when, because “he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross, God exalted him” (Phil. II), it is required that we worship and fall down before him, and ask in his name, saying to God the Father: Grant or bestow this or that through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son.

“Therefore, when he had opened the book”—when he had fulfilled all that had been written concerning him—“the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fell down, worshipping before the Lamb,” because all the saints, new and old alike, in heaven and on earth, whoever worship the Father also worship the Son; they worship God and the man Jesus Christ. Each has harps, that is, instruments [Col. 0932A] of unceasing praise—not instruments made by hands, but faithful breasts and bodies sounding God’s praise with the plectrum of the tongue. For harps, in which strings are stretched upon wood, are rightly compared with bodies mortified for Christ.

They also have bowls: vessels open wide at the mouth, that is, hearts not narrow but enlarged through charity. Bowls of this kind are full of perfumes, “which,” he says, “are the prayers of the saints.” Indeed, it is this very breadth of the bowls’ mouths—that is, the ample charity of hearts—which causes the prayers of the saints to be honored under the name of perfumes. Hence the Psalm says: “Let my prayer be directed as incense in your sight” (Ps. CXL). And in the consummation of his virtue and prayer the gracious Master [Col. 0932B] says: “I offered myself as a sacrifice to God for a sweet-smelling odor” (Eph. V).

> “And they sang a new song, saying: You are worthy, Lord, to receive the book and to open its seals, because you were slain, and redeemed us in your blood from every tribe, and language, and people, and nation; and you made us a kingdom and priests to our God, and they shall reign upon the earth.”

They worshipped and played the harp, breathing forth the perfumes of prayers, “and they sang a new song”; and this was, and is, a great and ineffable exultation. “They sang,” he says, “a new song,” for all the singers themselves are new: all have put off the old man (Eph. IV), and are a new creation in Christ [Col. 0932C]. The entire subject of the song was new, because the Lamb, newly slain, had opened the book and redeemed them in his blood, as the singers themselves declare. Therefore they are rightly said to sing a new song.

What is that song? “You are worthy, Lord, to receive the book and to open its seals.” They call the Lamb Lord, for he is King of kings and Lord of lords.

But since it has already been said that he opened the book, how do they now say, “You are worthy to receive and open the book”? For he suffered and died once, and in this way opened the book once—that is, he fulfilled the Scriptures. Therefore, when they say to him who had already opened it—that is, fulfilled it—“You are worthy to receive,” it is as if they said: You are worthy and able to open its sense [Col. 0932D] to readers and to give understanding of the Scriptures. For he accomplished both the one and the other by his worthiness. In dying he fulfilled the Scriptures; in rising he gave the Holy Spirit to the Apostles, who opened their minds to understand the Scriptures and loosed the seals of the book—that is, showed that the mysteries of Scripture had been made unsealed and intelligible.

Whence, Lord, is this worthiness yours? “Because,” they say, “you were slain and redeemed us to God in your blood.” Unless you had been slain, the book could never have been opened. Therefore, when Peter drew his sword, preferring to kill men rather than be killed by men—you, the true Lamb of God, said: “Put your sword back into its place. Can I not ask my Father, and he will at once furnish me with more than twelve [Col. 0933A] legions of angels? How then will the Scriptures be fulfilled, that it must happen thus?” (Matt. XXVI). Therefore, because you were slain, by that very fact you opened the book and fulfilled the truth of the Scriptures.

“You were slain and redeemed us to God in your blood.” It should be noted that this sort of song does not occur in the two following testimonies, those of the multitude of angels and of every creature. For neither the angels, who had not perished, nor any other rational creature, but only the Church of human beings—which is here understood through the twenty-four elders and the four living creatures—has been redeemed in Christ’s blood. Therefore these say, “Because you were slain and redeemed us”; but the angels say only, “Worthy is the Lamb who was slain,” and do not add, “and redeemed us.” Moreover, all the other creatures in heaven, upon earth, beneath the earth, and in the sea say none of these things. Rather, they simply bless in their own fashion him who sits upon the throne, by whom they were made, and the Lamb, through whom they were made.

Human beings alone, therefore, before the angels and before every creature, are the first to bear witness in this song, saying: “Because you were slain and redeemed us.” To whom did you redeem us? “To God,” they say. From where did you redeem us? “From every tribe, and language, and people, and nation.” You gathered us from great dispersal and made us one from great discord. For human beings differ greatly among themselves because they belong to many tribes, speak discordant languages, are unlike peoples, and belong to diverse [Col. 0933C] nations. Moreover, they differ so greatly because, captured by the devil, they are held ensnared in the diverse traps of errors. But you redeemed us to God in order to make us children of God, so that, as it is written in the Gospel, you might “gather into one the children of God who had been scattered abroad” (John XI).

The lamb slain in Egypt as a figure of you redeemed that people in its blood from only one nation: its blood was taken from the threshold and placed upon the lintel and upon both doorposts of the houses in which it was eaten (Exod. XII), so that it did not allow the destroyer to enter and strike. When the firstborn of the Egyptians had been slain, those formerly held by them were not merely released but even compelled to leave; and when the Red Sea was divided, they themselves passed safely through, while the Egyptians pursuing them with their chariots and horses perished amid the waves. In this manner that lamb then redeemed that people; or rather, Lord and sovereign Lamb, through the slaughter of that lamb you redeemed them by a figurative redemption.

But now you yourself have redeemed us to God in your blood in such a way that your blood, poured out for us, taken from the sacrament of your baptism, is imprinted by the sign of the cross upon our foreheads; and likewise, taken from the sacred altar, it is placed upon both doorposts of our houses when it is received by the mouth both of heart and body. Once this has been done, the destroyer, the devil, is not allowed to enter; but the firstborn—that is, original sin—is destroyed within us, and all the actual sins which were against us [Col. 0934A] and pursued us are swallowed up in the waters of baptism.

Thus you redeemed us, freeing us from evil spirits and gathering us from the nations, and you made us a kingdom and priests to our God. This too—that you redeemed us in order to make us a kingdom and priests to our God, though we had been slaves of sin and worshippers of demons—was prefigured in that shadow. You redeemed the children of Israel, reduced to the Egyptians’ slavery and serving their gods, in order to make them some sort of kingdom for God and, from the tribe of Levi, priests of a corresponding sacrifice. Thus you began and thus commanded Pharaoh: “Let my people go, that they may sacrifice to me” (Exod. V).

At last it came about by a mighty hand; and that people was a kingdom for God until, by evil counsel, they said to Samuel: “No indeed, but appoint a king over us”; and again: “Appoint a king over us to judge us, as all the nations have.” But the Lord said to Samuel: “They have not rejected you, but me, lest I reign over them” (I Sam. VIII). Thus also in that figure you redeemed them from the slavery alike of Egyptian men and gods, in order to make them a kingdom for God and priests of God from among them.

In accordance with that figure, you have made us truly a kingdom and priests to our God, so that we may no longer be slaves of sin but a kingdom of righteousness; so that sin may not reign in our mortal body (Rom. VI), indeed so that the body itself may no longer be mortal when death has been swallowed up through the glory of resurrection (I Cor. XV). Behold, even now the kingdom begins here and we are priests of God, now offering [Col. 0934C] the saving sacrifice of your body and blood; but then we shall both reign openly and offer unceasing sacrifices of praise. Truly great is the bounty of the Redeemer, who redeemed slaves of sin for this purpose: not to make or hold them as slaves, but as a kingdom and priests of God.

All the redeemed indeed confess—and speak truly—that they are servants of him who redeemed them. Yet he who redeemed them makes and calls them not slaves but friends, not subjects serving beneath him but fellow rulers. What more need be said? By their condition they are purchased servants; by his condescension they are called and are friends, are called children, and are a kingdom and priests of God.

“And they shall reign,” he says, “upon the earth.” Just as those already mentioned, freed from the prison-house of the Egyptians, reigned [Col. 0934D] over that land of promise, from which the Canaanites and Amorites were driven out because of their sins, so these shall reign over the true land of promise, the land of the living, from which those apostate spirits were cast out because of pride.

It should be noted that they pass from the first person to the third: having said, “and you made us a kingdom and priests to our God,” they add, “and they shall reign upon the earth.” This is a very devout transition, avoiding even in the sound of its expression any likeness to the vainglorious. For although they could truthfully say, “and we shall reign upon the earth,” they chose to say more humbly, “and they shall reign upon the earth.” Therefore, “you made us a kingdom to our God” is the praise of all who make confession together; while “they shall reign upon the earth” is said by individuals humbling themselves in reverence.

Nor should this be passed over: it is not said, “they shall reign in the earth,” but “they shall reign over the earth.” For the saints are on earth by condition, because their spirits are in earthly bodies; but by life and conduct they are above the earth and rule over their earthly and corruptible members. And now, while their bodies are mortal, they govern them with labor and anxiety; but in the future they shall reign over them in peace and security.

> “And I saw and heard the voice of many angels around the throne, and the living creatures and elders; and their number was thousands of thousands, saying with a loud voice: Worthy is the Lamb who was slain to receive divinity, power, and wisdom, and strength, [Col. 0935B] and honor, and glory, and blessing.”

The first witness, to whom this matter especially belongs—namely, the whole assembly of elect human beings—had delivered its testimony in the manner already described. Then, “I saw,” says the witness, “the voice of another,” and this was the whole choir of angels standing around the throne, the living creatures, and the elders, evidently for the great spectacle of humanity’s redemption and salvation. Their number is infinite. He declares this with sufficient wonder when he says, “and their number was thousands of thousands.” For when he says their number was thousands of thousands, without saying how many thousands, he plainly denotes an infinite number.

So also in Daniel, when it is said, “Thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stood before him” (Dan. VII), ten thousand times a hundred thousand is certainly a great but still finite number; whereas “thousands of thousands” is not finite.

It belongs to this whole multitude of angels to bear witness to this Lamb, because, although they were not redeemed through him, since they had not perished, nevertheless they were created through his divinity and reconciled to us through his blood, according to the Apostle: “For in him all things in heaven and earth were created, visible and invisible, whether thrones, dominions, principalities, or powers. All things were created through him and in him” (Col. I). And immediately after: “For in him it pleased all fullness to dwell, and through him to reconcile all things in him, making peace through the blood [Col. 0935D] of his cross, whether things in heaven or things upon earth” (ibid.). And elsewhere: “That he might make known to us the mystery of his will according to his good pleasure, which he purposed in him, in the dispensation of the fullness of times” (Eph. I). He immediately explains what that good pleasure of God is, adding: “To restore all things in Christ, things in heaven and things on earth, in him” (ibid.).

For this was the good pleasure of God: when the time of his ordering was fulfilled, to restore in faith in Christ the things in heaven which were half-full—that is, the number of angels which had been diminished—and the things on earth which had been emptied, namely, human beings who had perished. Therefore, because the angels were both created in him, reconciled to human beings through his blood, and have their number supplied from human beings through him, rightly they stand around the throne, the living creatures, and the elders: behold, they are present to testify, and their testimony is heard with a loud voice, that is, with great affection, saying: “Worthy is the Lamb who was slain to receive power,” and so forth.

Because the angels are those who did not perish, they do not say, “Worthy is the Lamb who was slain and redeemed us,” as human beings said a little earlier: “because you were slain and redeemed us to God in your blood.” Rather, they say only, “Worthy is the Lamb who was slain.” In the number seven they ascribe to the Lamb seven distinguished attributes in testimony: power, divinity, wisdom, strength, honor, glory, and blessing. In this number of praises we understand together all the proclamations concerning the same Lamb, Christ, which are sufficiently contained in the Scriptures. For there are many other names of like majesty and sublimity: kingdom, dominion, salvation, life, authority, and the like.

These things were read scattered throughout the Scriptures. For example, Isaiah says: “For a little child is born to us, a son is given to us. And dominion has been made upon his shoulder; and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, Mighty God, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace. His dominion shall be multiplied, and there shall be no end to his kingdom” (Isa. IX). The Jews read these things, but judged unworthy the one whom they had slain like a lamb. They considered him wholly unworthy and unfit for all these names, since these are proclamations of Christ, while they refused to have this son—as they supposed—of Joseph, this son—as they reproached him—of a carpenter [Col. 0936C] (John VI; Matt. XIII), be or be called Christ in any way.

The witnessing angels contend to the contrary: This Lamb who was slain, “this worm and not a man” (Ps. XXI), who was trampled down and crucified—this Son of Man, indeed son of Mary but not son of Joseph—is worthy to receive all these things; he is worthy to have all these things said and proclaimed concerning him. He is worthy to receive power; he is worthy to be or to be called that king of whom the Psalmist says: “Lord, the king shall rejoice in your power” (Ps. XX). He is worthy to receive divinity; he is worthy of that name “which is above every name” (Phil. II), which name is God. Take this too from the prophet already cited, where God is called in this manner: “And his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, God” (Isa. IX).

He is worthy to receive wisdom; he is worthy to be believed to be the very one of whom Jeremiah says: “Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I shall raise up for David a righteous branch; and a king shall reign, and he shall be wise” (Jer. XXIII). He is worthy to receive strength, so that he may be believed to be that very one of whom Isaiah, after saying, “and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, God,” added, “mighty” (Isa. IX); and of whom the Psalmist says: “The Lord is strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle” (Ps. XXIII).

He is worthy to receive honor, so that he may be believed to be the very one of whom the same Psalmist says: “Among them daughters of kings have delighted you in your honor” (Ps. XLIV). And elsewhere: “The honor of the king loves judgment” (Ps. XCVIII). He is worthy to receive [Col. 0937A] glory together with honor, as has been said, so that there may be no doubt that he is the one of whom the Psalmist likewise says: “You crowned him with glory and honor, and appointed him over the works of your hands” (Ps. VIII). Again: “Great is his glory in your salvation; you shall lay glory and great splendor upon him” (Ps. XX).

He is worthy to receive blessing, so that he may be known and believed to be the one of whom the Psalmist immediately says: “For you shall give him as a blessing for age upon age” (ibid.); and so that he may be believed to be that seed concerning which God spoke to Abraham: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. XXII). And in David: “May his name be blessed for ever; before the sun his name endures; and in him all tribes of the earth shall be blessed” (Ps. [Col. 0937B] LXXI). Again, addressed to him: “Fairer in form than the children of men, grace has been poured out upon your lips; therefore God has blessed you for ever” (Ps. XLIV).

Therefore let the Lamb who was slain receive, as he is worthy, power to cast demons out of the temples or shrines of the nations and out of the hiding places of idols, where they were worshipped and delivered responses of their falsehood, lying that they were gods. Let the Lord of hosts drive them from there, according to the Psalmist: “And in the power of your arm you have scattered your enemies” (Ps. LXXXVIII). Let him receive divinity, as he is worthy, so that, when false gods have been expelled from the hearts of the nations, he alone who is true God may be worshipped; so that likewise what is written in the Psalm may take place: “God shall reign over the nations” (Ps. XLVI); and so that the whole world may now sing, [Col. 0937C] “for all the gods of the nations are demons, but the Lord made the heavens” (Ps. XCV).

Let him receive wisdom, as he is worthy, so that no one belonging to him may be able to be “deceived through philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elements of the world, and not according to him” (Col. II). Let him, I say, receive wisdom and strength, so that by choosing the foolish things of the world he may confound the wise, and by choosing the weak things of the world he may confound the strong (Isa. XXIX; I Cor. I); according to what is written in Job: “I shall destroy the wisdom of the wise, and reject the prudence of the prudent” (Job V). This is to receive wisdom; but to receive strength is according to the Psalm: “Gird your sword upon your thigh, O mightiest one. In your splendor and beauty give heed; proceed prosperously and reign, because of truth and meekness and righteousness; and your right hand shall lead you wonderfully. Your arrows are sharp: peoples shall fall beneath you, in the hearts of the king’s enemies” (Ps. XLIV).

Thus it shall happen that neither the wisdom of philosophers may withstand the eyes of the Lamb, nor the strength of kings and emperors resist the horns of the Lamb who was slain, so as to prevent his being acknowledged as wise and strong God, and all peoples hearing and believing in him. Let him also receive honor, as he is worthy, so that hearts and bodies which had been receptacles of wicked spirits and every vice may become his pure dwellings and venerable temples. And let them be, as the Psalm immediately says: “Your throne, O God, is for age upon age” [Col. 0938A] (ibid.); and let the daughters of kings delight you in your honor—that is, cities built by kings of the world, or churches propagated by the Apostles as daughters of kings, living holy lives for your honor.

Let him receive glory together with honor, as he is worthy, so that the nations which honor him by living well may also glorify him by speaking well, proclaiming the Holy of holies, better than angels, higher than the heavens, seated at the right hand of Majesty. Thus “every tongue,” as the Apostle says, “may confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. II). Let him receive blessing also, as he is worthy: let all his saints bless him, attributing what they are not to themselves but to him (I Cor. XV), giving thanks to God the Father through him.

> [Col. 0938B] “And I heard every creature which is in heaven, and upon earth, and beneath the earth, and those which are in the sea, and all things in it, saying: To him who sits upon the throne and to the Lamb be blessing, and honor, and glory, and power for ages of ages.”

Those creatures to which Christ’s passion brought the benefit of peace and glory—namely, the two assemblies of angels and human beings—put the title of Christ’s death in their testimony: these, namely human beings, saying to the Lamb, “You are worthy, Lord, because you were slain and redeemed us”; those, namely the angels who were not redeemed because they had not perished, saying only, “Worthy is the Lamb who was slain.”

But “the other creatures which are in heaven, upon earth, beneath the earth, and under heaven, and those which are in it”—the sun, moon, and stars; [Col. 0938C] “the waters above the heavens”; and all the rest whom the Psalmist summons to praise the Lord (Ps. CXLVIII)—of all these this is the third testimony. In order that the proposition concerning the Lamb’s worthiness may stand, they make no mention either of their redemption, as the living creatures and twenty-four elders do, or even of the Lamb’s slaughter, as all the angels do. They say only: “To him who sits upon the throne and to the Lamb be blessing,” and so forth.

For the Lamb was not slain for the redemption of such creatures, nor for their restoration in any respect. They sing in harmony with their Creator merely because they have been created—not by rational or vocal confession, but by the natural manifestation of their own condition. And because the redemption of human beings and the restoration of angelic orders took place through the slaughter of the Lamb alone—for the person of the Son alone suffered, whereas the nature or substance of all creatures was created by the Father speaking through the Word, that is, through the same Son—human beings and angels rightly proclaim the Lamb’s slaughter in the confession already mentioned. These creatures, however, praise both him who sits upon the throne, namely the Father, and the Lamb, that is, the Father’s Son.

First in their praise is blessing. Why so? Evidently because among them there are certain creatures which not only exist in their nature by his command, but also subsist in the posterity of their succession through his blessing—namely, every living and moving creature which the waters brought forth according to its kinds, and every bird according to its kind. [Col. 0939A] For it is written: “And God saw that it was good; and he blessed them, saying: Increase and multiply, and fill the waters of the sea; and let birds multiply upon the earth” (Gen. I). They therefore rightly utter first the voice of blessing to him through whose blessing they subsist.

Next they render honor to him as Lord of the great house which he himself established with such great, beautiful, and extensive splendor. For honor is due in the house to its builder, as the Apostle says: “For this one has been judged worthy of greater glory than Moses, inasmuch as he who built the house has greater honor than the house. For every house is built by someone; but he who built all things is God” (Heb. III). We indeed are the house of God, as the same Apostle says immediately afterwards: “But Christ as a Son in his own house, whose house we are” (ibid.). Nevertheless, this fabric of the world too is no less a certain house of God, inhabited by such a diversity of creatures as by his household.

They also give him glory, so that he may glory even in such workmanship and say: “I am the Lord, creating the heavens and forming the earth” (Isa. XLV). And in Isaiah: “Who has measured the waters in his fist and weighed the heavens with his palm? Who has suspended the mass of the earth with three fingers and weighed the mountains in a balance and the hills in scales?” (Isa. XL). And similar things.

They also give him power when, as all the powers of this world vanish, he who sits upon the throne and the Lamb alone retain authority over their creation. This was shown to Daniel in a most clear vision: “And I saw that the beast had been slain, its body had perished and had been given to be burned in fire; and the authority of the other beasts had also been taken away, and the duration of life had been appointed to them until a time and times. Then I watched in the vision of the night, and behold, with the clouds of heaven the Son of Man was coming; and he came even to the Ancient of Days, and they presented him before him. And he gave him power, honor, and a kingdom; and all peoples, tribes, and languages shall serve him. His power is eternal power which shall not be taken away, and his kingdom shall not be destroyed” (Dan. VII).

This power is also given to him by the creature beneath the earth, namely that enclosed in the prison of hell, though not by voluntary confession [Col. 0939D] but by compelled concession. For the wicked spirits themselves, whether willing or unwilling, shall confess the power of him who sits upon the throne and of the Lamb.

> “And the four living creatures said: Amen.”

*Amen* means “truly” or “faithfully.” Therefore to say *Amen* is to confirm true testimony. Here the “four living creatures”—that is, the four Gospels—say and do this: they confirm that every creature in its manner asserts or testifies blessing, honor, glory, and power alike to the Lamb and to him who sits upon the throne, alike to the Son Jesus Christ and to God the Father. Yet the fourth living creature, like a flying eagle, namely John himself, says *Amen* more plainly here by writing: “All things were made through him, and without him was made nothing” [Col. 0940A] (John I).

> “And the twenty-four elders fell upon their faces and worshipped him who lives for ages of ages.”

The end or completion of all testimonies is worship enduring eternally. The twenty-four elders—that is, all churches, or the prelates and judges of the churches—exercise their leadership in this worship as worthily as they exercised the office of teachers in bearing testimony.

## Chapter VI

> “And I saw, when the Lamb had opened one of the seven seals, and I heard one of the four living creatures saying, as with the voice of thunder: Come and see.”

Above he had stated briefly that the Lamb opened the book; now he sets out the opening of that same book in sequence, through the loosening of each seal. We too have already said above that the seven seals of the book are seven mysteries of the same Lamb, Jesus Christ, which were enclosed in the Scriptures: namely, his incarnation, passion, resurrection, ascension, the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, the calling of the Gentiles after the abandonment of Judaism, the final judgment, and the consummation of the age.

Therefore, when Christ Jesus, who was in the form of God, emptied himself, taking the form of a servant and being made in the likeness of human beings (Phil. II), then indeed “the Lamb opened one of the seven seals.” For he then fulfilled a certain part of the Scriptures, whose whole intention concerns the mysteries just mentioned. For example: “He placed his tabernacle in the sun, and he himself is like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber” [Col. 0940C] (Ps. XVIII). Again: “Fairer in form than the children of men, grace has been poured out upon your lips” (Ps. XLIV). And afterwards: “You loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (ibid.). Elsewhere: “A man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her” (Ps. LXXXVI). And in Isaiah: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel” (Isa. VII).

Jesus Christ fulfilled these and other similar things when he took the form of a servant, though he was in the form of God (Phil. II). But one who desires the seal of such sayings to be loosed for him—that is, their meaning to be opened—must first possess the merit of faith.

It follows: “And I heard one of the four [Col. 0940D] living creatures saying, as with the voice of great thunder: Come and see.” For “come and see” means: first believe, and only then understand. This one living creature out of the four is the face of a human being—that is, the incarnation of the same Christ, the Son of God. Principally, as has already been said above, the four living creatures are the four greatest mysteries of Christ, which no Christian may be ignorant of: incarnation, passion, resurrection, and ascension. Secondarily, they are those very persons who wrote the four Gospels.

Therefore the one, or first, of the four living creatures is Christ’s incarnation; and we hear the voices of that incarnation as often as this incarnation is preached to us in the Church. The voice is heard as that of thunder because the fullness of the virginal birth does not whisper like a shameful vanity in corners, but loves to be proclaimed openly to the whole world. It is therefore rightly compared to thundering heavens, according to David’s saying: “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament announces the works of his hands” (Ps. XVIII).

> “And I saw, and behold, a white horse; and he who sat upon it had a bow, and a crown was given to him, and he went forth conquering, that he might conquer.”

“And I saw,” that is, I understood. And indeed everyone who comes—that is, who believes faithfully—understands that the mystery of Christ’s incarnation is like a horse and the one sitting upon it. Such a person understands not merely a human being or merely God, but a human being together with God dwelling in that human being: the human being joined to God, or God to the human being, in unity of person [Col. 0941B]. For just as we call a horse and a man sitting upon it one rider, so we confess this human being and the God dwelling in him as one Christ.

Yet God is joined to this human being far more closely than a person to the horse upon which that person sits. For a person descends from a horse; but God, who assumed this human being, never departs from him. The flesh lay dead in the tomb only once, yet divinity never departed from the soul. The flesh rose again, the soul having been reassumed with the power of divinity; and thereafter both flesh and soul remain with the Word as the one invisible Christ.

Accordingly, we understand the white horse and him who sat upon it as the one Christ; and that this horse is the beast of burden of which, in the parable concerning the man [Col. 0941C] who fell among robbers, it is said: “And drawing near, namely the Samaritan, bound up his wounds, pouring in oil and wine, and, setting him upon his own beast, brought him to an inn” (Luke 10). We understand that Samaritan seated upon his beast as the one God and man, Christ. Certainly, he placed wounded humanity upon his beast because he himself bore the sins of the human race in his body (Isa. 53). And this horse is rightly called white, because, as the Catholic faith firmly maintains, this man was conceived of the Holy Spirit and born of a virgin without sin. He alone is the one who was not conceived in iniquities, whom his mother did not conceive in sins (Ps. 50 [51]): namely, in the sins [Col. 0941D] of Adam’s transgression, in whom, as the Apostle says, all sinned (Rom. 5); but not this one, whom, as has already been said, the Virgin conceived of the Holy Spirit.

“And he who sat upon it had a bow.” He had a bow, for he is the archer of whom it is said against Behemoth in Job: “An archer shall not put him to flight” (Job 41)—that is, with reference to the hearts of the faithless, who yield to no threats of the coming judgment so as to be converted. For the bow, striking from afar, signifies the judgment which is not yet present but is deferred until the last day. He had this bow of judgment because the Father gave him all judgment, or the power to execute judgment; and, being about to exercise it, he came first to proclaim repentance and give remission of sins (John 5).

[Col. 0942A] “And a crown was given to him,” that is, the holy primitive Church in the twelve apostles. Hence the Psalmist says: “You placed a crown upon his head” (Ps. 20 [21]). For you placed upon his head a crown “of precious stone” (ibid.); that is, at the beginning of his preaching, you, Father, gave him the choir of apostles, who, according to the faith, are indeed living stones and precious stones. Hence he says: “Holy Father, keep in your name those whom you have given me. They were yours, and you gave them to me” (John 17).—“And he went forth conquering, that he might conquer.” He went forth, namely, when his thirtieth year began, baptized to preach; and at the very outset he conquered the tempter, the devil. For, immediately led by the Holy Spirit into the wilderness, after fasting forty days and forty nights and afterward becoming hungry, [Col. 0942B] he conquered the tempter in three temptations, as we read (Matt. 3 [probably Matt. 4]); the first man had been tempted and defeated by that tempter. Thus he went forth conquering in order that he might conquer: that is, he conquered his own temptations in order to overcome our temptations, in which we had been defeated. Hence also the Apostle says: “For in that wherein he himself suffered, being tempted, he is able also to help those who are tempted” (Heb. 2). Thus he went forth; thus, in being born and in living, he was without sin and conquered every trial, so that with the whole purpose of love he might hasten to conquer our evils.

“And when he had opened the second seal, I heard the second living creature saying: Come and see.” When Christ Jesus “humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even the death of the cross” [Col. 0942C] (Phil. 2), the Lamb certainly opened a great seal of the book. For by that same passion he fulfilled and made intelligible a very large part of the Scriptures. For example: “Surely he himself bore our infirmities and carried our sorrows” (Isa. 53). Again: “He was offered because he himself willed it, and he did not open his mouth” (ibid.). And further: “He delivered his soul unto death, and was reckoned with criminals; and he himself bore the sins of many and prayed for transgressors” (ibid.). And in the Psalm: “They pierced my hands and my feet” (Ps. 21 [22]). Again: “They divided my garments among themselves, and cast lots for my clothing” (ibid.). These and many other very numerous sayings from the prophets and psalms, and many great sayings [Col. 0942D] or ordinances of the holy and mystical law, were kept shut under this second seal. This Lamb then unsealed it when Christ Jesus, struggling, mounted the gibbet of the cross and, having yielded up his spirit, rested dead in the tomb.

“I heard,” he says, “the second living creature saying: Come and see.” The second living creature—that is, the face of the calf—is the Lord’s passion itself. We hear its voice as often as that passion is proclaimed to us, but especially when we are baptized and when we celebrate or receive the sacrament of his body and blood. “For as many of us as were baptized into Christ Jesus,” says the Apostle, “were baptized into his death” (Rom. 6); and as often as we eat this bread and drink the cup, we proclaim the Lord’s death (1 Cor. 11). We come and see—[Col. 0943A]that is, we believe and understand.

“And another, red horse went forth; and to him who sat upon it was given power to take peace from the earth.” The red horse is the bloodthirsty people of the city of the devil, the city of Babylon; and its rider and driver is the devil. In Zechariah (ch. 1), it is true, we read of the Lord’s rose-coloured horse; but that horse is none other than the white horse seen above. For he is white by his own purity and rose-coloured by his own blood; therefore it is said in the Song of Songs: “My beloved is white and ruddy” (Song 5). But this horse is red with another’s blood, the blood of the saints, which it has shed. This horse went forth in the already-mentioned passion of the Lord (Matt. 23), long since red with every righteous blood, from the blood [Col. 0943B] of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah; and then it went forth in order, with the Gentiles and Pontius Pilate joined to it, to fill up the measure of its murders by putting the Lord to death. For the devil sat upon it. And to him was given power to take peace from the earth: to remove peace from the earthly generation subject to him, so that they should kill one another.

This was given—that is, permitted—to him as he persuaded the Jews, whose rider he certainly was and whom he drove, to ask that the seditious Barabbas be released to them and that Jesus be crucified (Matt. 27). In doing this, he took—indeed, swallowed up—peace from the earth. For from that time onward there was never peace for that people: by a just judgment, since those who had killed the Prince of Peace inherited the seditions of Barabbas, whose release they had requested. Therefore it was given him to take peace from the earth—“so that they should kill one another.” Whoever reads of that destruction of Jerusalem under Titus and Vespasian, as astonishing as it was pitiable, sees and marvels more fully how true this is. We must indeed still recall that destruction when explaining the sixth seal.

“And a great sword was given to him.” By the great sword is meant the great and long persecution: the sword of persecution which that malignant horse is permitted to extend from Christ to his last elect, as from the head of a great body down to its feet. But this must be discussed more fully in its proper place, where Babylon the harlot is shown drunk with the blood of the saints.

[Col. 0943D] “And when he had opened the third seal, I heard the third living creature saying: Come and see.” On the day when Christ Jesus rose from the dead and, standing in the midst of his disciples, said to them: “Peace be to you; receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them” (John 20), the Lamb undoubtedly opened the third seal of the book, because he fulfilled the great proclamations of Scripture which concerned him. For example: “Judah is a lion’s whelp; from the prey, my son, you have ascended. Resting, you lay down as a lion, and as a lioness. Who shall rouse him?” (Gen. 49; the printed “XLV” is evidently an error.) And this in Hosea: “O death, I will be your death; O hell, I will be your bite” (Hos. 13; the printed “III” is evidently an error). And in the Psalm: “Make a way for him who ascends above the setting; the Lord is his name” [Col. 0944A] (Ps. 67 [68]). Again: “I have risen, and I am still with you” (Ps. 138 [139]). By fulfilling these and similar things in rising from the dead, Christ made them intelligible; then, as has been said, the Lamb opened the third seal.

Moreover, the third living creature, or the third face of the one living creature, is the resurrection itself. We hear its voice saying, “Come and see,” whenever the glory of that resurrection is proclaimed to us by the voice of the rejoicing Church. “And behold, a black horse; and he who sat upon it had a balance in his hand.” The black horse is the company of false brethren, such as the Lord formerly endured among his fellow-countrymen, the Jews, who boasted that they had one Father, God. This black horse, with its rider the devil, appeared holding a balance in [Col. 0944B] his hand when this very resurrection of Jesus Christ was first announced to those false brethren. For Matthew relates it thus:

> “Behold, some of the guards came into the city and reported to the chief priests all that had taken place. And, having assembled with the elders and taken counsel, they gave a large sum of money to the soldiers, saying: ‘Say that his disciples came by night and stole him while we slept. And if this comes to the governor’s ears, we will persuade him and keep you free from trouble.’ So they took the money and did as they had been instructed. And this report has been spread among the Jews to this day” (Matt. 28).

Thus he who sat upon the black horse above had a balance in [Col. 0944C] his hand, because the lying devil, directing false men and liars, induced them to procure, with money weighed out, a lie denying and concealing Christ’s resurrection. The balance was not then given to him; rather, “he had,” it says, “a balance in his hand.” For he had acted similarly before, when Judas, one of the false brethren—or their most notorious member—received money from them for betraying innocent blood, namely thirty pieces of silver.

Therefore it is said to this one: “Two pounds (*bilibris*) of wheat for a denarius, and six pounds of barley for a denarius; and do not harm the wine and oil.” Let us calculate how many pounds correspond to thirty silver pieces or denarii: namely, reckoning eight pounds at two denarii each, according to the present exposition which says “two pounds of wheat for a denarius and six pounds of barley for a denarius”; [Col. 0944D] and the total comes to one hundred and twenty pounds. Now this was the number of believers at the beginning, whom Christ, redeemed by that man’s sale, left alive in this world. As Luke says in the Acts of the Apostles: “The multitude of persons together was about one hundred and twenty” (Acts 1).

Let it therefore be said to him “who has the balance in his hand: Two pounds of wheat for a denarius, and six pounds of barley for a denarius; and do not harm the wine and oil.” This means: Even if you harm the multitude of the unbelieving Jews by publishing the lie which you bought with a large payment, yet do not glory entirely, because you are by no means permitted to harm those who belong to me, whom I, though sold, redeemed. Although their number is now small, that same number signifies all who through their word [Col. 0945A] will believe and hold the faith of the holy Trinity.

For, in accordance with the aforesaid number of thirty silver pieces, when “two pounds of wheat” and “six pounds of barley” are sold for a denarius, there are thirty pounds of wheat and three times thirty—that is, ninety—pounds of barley. In all these, the number three, expressing the faith of the holy Trinity, shines forth widely. Together, thirty and ninety make one hundred and twenty, which number, as has already been said, was that of the first believers (John 12 [probably Acts 1]). Their merit was unequal, certainly, just as wheat and barley are not of equal value among a farmer’s produce. Yet all sprang up fruitfully from the one grain of wheat which fell into the earth and died; and they held and proclaimed, as has been said, the same faith of the Trinity.

Whatever may happen, whatever you may do to those brethren who are black because of their falsity, you are not permitted to harm these or lead them into error or falsehood. Nor are you permitted to harm the wine and oil. What wine and what oil? Certainly the twofold gift of the Holy Spirit. The first gift of the Holy Spirit is oil, because he was first given so that there might be remission of sins, as he who gave him said on the very day when he rose from the dead: “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them” (John 20). The second gift is rightly called wine because, in the second giving, the Holy Spirit was given as the strength of believers: to make believers eloquent and steadfast in preaching, so that some said, [Col. 0945C] “These men are full of new wine” (Acts 2).

Therefore, O black driver of the black horse, you who carry the balance in your hand, trade as much as you wish; and, with a large sum of money weighed out, bring it about that it be publicly said, “His disciples came by night and stole him while we slept” (Matt. 21 [probably Matt. 28]), provided that you cannot prevent these one hundred and twenty from remaining in the truth, receiving the twofold gift of the Holy Spirit, so that God’s purpose may not be made void and the glory of the risen Christ may not be obscured or hidden.

“And when he had opened the fourth seal, I heard the voice of the fourth living creature saying: Come and see.” When Christ, with the apostles standing by, ascended into heaven and sat at the right hand of God, as Mark says [Col. 0945D] (ch. 16), and as Luke also testifies, “while they watched, he was lifted up, and a cloud received him from their eyes” (Acts 1), then the Lamb certainly opened the fourth seal of the book. For he fulfilled that part of Scripture in which this fourth mystery was contained. For example: “God ascended with jubilation, and the Lord with the sound of a trumpet” (Ps. 46 [47]): with the jubilation, that is, of the same apostles who saw him lifted up; for Luke says that they worshipped and returned to Jerusalem with great joy. And “with the sound of a trumpet,” that is, with the testimony of the angelic proclamation which said that he would come thus—understand, to judge—“as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts 1).

Again: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand, until I make [Col. 0946A] your enemies the footstool of your feet” (Ps. 109 [110]). And elsewhere: “You ascended on high; you took captivity captive” (Ps. 67 [68]); or, as another edition has it: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive.” By fulfilling these and similar things—when he who descended also ascended above all heavens—“then,” as has been said, “the Lamb opened the fourth seal of the book.”

But against him who sits at that right hand of Majesty on high, the devil’s envy rages, maliciously disparaging through the frothing mouths of blaspheming heretics him who reigns in heaven, upon whom it had inflicted insults in his suffering on earth through the tongues and hands of Jews and Gentiles. “The voice of the fourth living creature is heard saying: Come and see.” But they do not wish to come and see; rather, on the contrary, to stand and envy. For this living creature is heard as often as Christ’s same ascension, or his sitting at the right hand of the Father, is proclaimed by the voice of the confessing Church. But the heretic Arius envies, saying: “The Son is less than the Father.” Therefore it follows:

“Behold a pale horse; and he who sat upon it, his name was Death, and Hell followed him.” Finally, the pale horse is the sickly, envious fury of heretics. Their madness is so great that one hearing them may rightly say, concerning Christ glorified, what the sage said: “Envy always follows glory.” They indeed see, but they envy, according to the saying: “The sinner shall see and be angry” (Ps. 111 [112]). They see that he who sits at the right hand of the Father is called the Son of God, and is God, coequal and coeternal with the same Father. They read and [Col. 0946C] hear the Scriptures by which this is established, and they do not dare say that they are lying. Yet they detract from the equality, although they confess him to be God. Why? Because, they say, the Father granted him his divinity, as the Apostle says: “Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend” (Phil. 2), and so forth.

They do not ask to whom he gave it: to the man or to God. For when he gave it is plainly apparent: “He humbled himself,” it says, “unto death, even the death of the cross. Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name, because he became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross” [Col. 0946D] (ibid.). Was the Son of God, the Word of God, God with God, not exalted before this occurred; but, afterward, because he was exalted “because he became obedient unto the death of the cross,” did he then begin to be the exalted Son of God, the only God of God? Did he then begin to possess the name above every name? Who could say something so utterly foolish?

This, therefore, was given to him as man—the one according to whom “the Son became obedient unto the death of the cross”—which that same Son of God, God born equal to God, already possessed. But the Catholic Fathers have sufficiently argued against that pale horse of the devil.
