Thus it is rightly said concerning that horse: “And he who sat upon it, his name was Death, and Hell followed him.” For “through the devil’s envy death entered into the world” [Col. 0947A] (Wis. 2). The devil himself and his servants are also called, by metonymy (*metōnymikōs*), death and hell, because they are the cause of death and hell for many. It may also be understood simply: that those who are spiritually dead here are followed there by eternal punishment.

“And power was given to him over four parts of the earth, to kill by sword, famine, death, and the beasts of the earth.” Behold Arius’s madness, born in Alexandria, reaching even to the Gallic Ocean, pursuing the pious brutally not only with famine of God’s word but also with the bodily sword. Moreover, this also more fully serves the sense: that we should understand the four parts of the earth to be those which this present Scripture itself enumerates in saying, “to kill by sword, famine, death, and beasts of the earth”; and which the prophet Ezekiel calls the Lord’s own four grievous judgments.

[Col. 0947B] “Even if,” he says, “I send upon Jerusalem my four grievous judgments—sword, famine, evil beasts, and pestilence—to cut off from it man and beast, yet there shall be left in it a remnant bringing forth sons and daughters” (Ezek. 14). These are the parts of the earth: that is, the portions of the earthly mind. For in the usage of Holy Scripture “part” is customarily used for “portion,” sometimes in the singular and sometimes in the plural. In the singular, as there: “Fire, sulphur, and the breath of tempests are the portion of their cup” (Ps. 10 [11]). In the plural, as there: “They shall be given over to the hand of the sword; they shall be portions for foxes” (Ps. 62 [63]). Thus over the four parts of the earth—that is, over those four grievous judgments which are the portions or recompenses of the earthly mind—power was given to this pale horse, that is, to heretical fury, to kill “by sword, famine, death, and beasts of the earth.”

It should be noted, however, that among these four grievous judgments only one name has here been changed: namely, “pestilence,” in place of which the general term “death” has been used. And rightly so, because human fury will never reach the point of having power over pestilence—that is, power to create pestilence—as does the Lord God, in whose person the prophet says: “I am the Lord, making peace and creating evil” (Isa. 45), that is, affliction. Its four parts are these four grievous judgments: sword, famine, pestilence, and evil beasts. Nor does it have the power to create famine, except that, by taking away bread, it may kill someone by hunger. Yet when it does so, Scripture’s statement remains true: “The Lord will not kill the soul of the righteous by famine” (Prov. 10).

For it is one thing when a persecutor confines a righteous person and withholds bread from him, as has often happened; another when bread fails a righteous person faithfully serving God—for example, faithfully preaching the Gospel—and famine kills him while God nowhere provides anything by which he may be restored. No Scripture records that the latter has ever happened. Likewise heretical fury cannot create evil beasts, but can only expose someone to beasts and thus kill the body of a faithful soul. It can make a material sword or whatever iron instrument of death it chooses, and kill by it; but it cannot create the material itself. Of those four, pestilence alone is what God alone can both create and kill by. Therefore, as has been said, the general term “death” has rightly been put here in place of pestilence, embracing or signifying every kind of death which can exist or be conceived, apart from deaths by sword, famine, and evil beasts.

[Col. 0948A] “And when he had opened the fifth seal, I saw beneath the altar the souls of those slain for the word of God and for the testimony which they held; and they cried with a loud voice, saying: How long, Lord, holy and true, do you not judge and avenge our blood upon those who dwell on the earth?” When he who ascended on high and led captivity captive [Col. 0948B] gave gifts to men by sending the Holy Spirit to the apostles, the Spirit of truth, who would lead them into all truth, then the Lamb certainly opened the fifth seal of the book. For he then fulfilled no small number of Scriptural proclamations concerning himself. For example: “And it shall be on that day, says the Lord, that I shall pour out upon the house of David and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem a spirit of grace and of prayers” (Zech. 12). Again: “And it shall be after these things that I shall pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and daughters shall prophesy, your old men shall dream dreams, and your young men shall see visions” (Joel 2), and the rest.

The mystery of these and similar prophetic utterances, closed until then, was now opened so that Peter said: “Men of Judaea and all who dwell in Jerusalem, let this be known to you, and receive my words with your ears. For these are not drunk, as you suppose, since it is the third hour of the day; but this is what was spoken through the prophet Joel: ‘And it shall be in the last days,’ says the Lord, ‘that I shall pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh,’” and so forth, up to the words: “And everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved” (Acts 2).

When this seal had been opened: “I saw,” he says, “beneath the altar the souls of those slain for the word of God and for the testimony which they held; and they cried with a loud voice, saying: How long, Lord, holy and true, do you not judge and avenge our blood upon those who dwell on the earth?” These souls, or these slain persons, demanding judgment and vengeance for their blood, are all those whom the murderous followers of Cain killed. Their cry had to be heard, as the Lord foretold to that most wicked generation: “Behold,” he says, “I send to you prophets, sages, and scribes; and some of them you will kill and crucify, and some of them you will scourge in your synagogues and persecute from city to city, so that upon you may come all righteous blood which has been shed upon the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah, whom you killed between the temple and the altar” (Matt. 23).

“All these souls, all these slain persons, I saw,” he says, “crying”: namely, that all these things might come upon this generation. Why? Because they were filling up the measure of their fathers by killing, crucifying, scourging in their synagogues, and persecuting from city to city those prophets, sages, [Col. 0949A] and scribes whom the Holy Spirit had filled on that day. Why, then, do they appear to cry out or to have been slain beneath the altar of God? Because their first member, Abel, was killed by his envious brother on account of a sacrifice pleasing to God; and all those slain from the blood of that righteous man to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah, whom they killed between the temple and altar, suffered for the same faith, or word and testimony. Thus, deposited beneath God’s covenant as beneath an altar, they cry with a loud voice, as was said of that first man: “Behold, the voice of your brother’s blood cries to me from the earth” (Gen. 4).

A loud voice or great cry is a great desire for those things which they know that the Lord wishes to do. For it is not permissible to believe that those souls desire anything contrary to God’s will, since their desires depend upon his own will. Therefore, as is customary in all solemn prayers or petitions, in crying out and seeking judgment and vengeance they rightly begin with praise, addressing him as holy and true. And he is most fittingly addressed by these names, so that he may be moved by them: for, holy in his own deeds, he is bound to make the truth of judgment concerning the deeds of others.

By saying “those who dwell on the earth,” he expresses with great force the sum of the Jewish crime. For the Jews wholly dwelt upon the earth, clung to earth, and, seeking no heavenly things, looked upon and desired only earthly things with downcast minds. Therefore they killed the saints for the word of God and for the testimony which they bore to God’s heavenly kingdom, a testimony which did not approve but rather reproved their earthly desire. They also killed the Lord himself on account of a fabricated pretext arising from that same earthly dwelling. For they said: “If we let him go on thus, the Romans will come and take away both our place and nation” (John 11). Hence the Holy Spirit rebukes them through the Psalmist: “Speaking in anger against the earth, they devised deceits” (Ps. 34 [35]).

Cain was the father and model of such people: he first shed righteous blood and, first building and dedicating a city in his son’s name, dwelt upon the earth as a wanderer and fugitive from God (Gen. 4). [Col. 0949D] What judgment or what vengeance, then, were these souls seen to demand with a loud cry, except that, after the example of Cain, the Jews should be cast out and hidden from the face of God and should be wanderers and fugitives upon the earth, as is evident today? For Christ himself said in the Psalm: “God has shown me concerning my enemies: Do not kill them, lest my people at any time forget.” But what then? “Scatter them in your strength” (Ps. 58 [59]), he says. For it helps peoples preserve the remembrance [commemoration] of Christ that the Jews were not altogether killed but were dispersed among all nations together with their books, which bear witness to that same Christ.

Thus with a loud voice they cried to that holy and true judge and avenger, that he should now cast them out from the earth and that city [Col. 0950A] and cause them to fall by the sword’s edge and be led captive among all nations. He himself foreshadowed this for them then by a terrible sign, when he made, as it were, a whip of cords and drove all out of the temple; afterward, among other things, he said to them: “Behold, your house shall be left desolate to you” (John 2; probably Matt. 23). For the long whip of cords signified the long “cord of sins” with which they were bound, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah, “whom you killed between the temple and the altar” (Matt. 23).

Since he was the son of Jehoiada, the question is asked why Zechariah is called son of Barachiah rather than son of Jehoiada. *Barachias* means “blessed of the Lord” in our language, and the righteousness of the priest Jehoiada is indicated by his Hebrew name. But again the question is asked why he said, or ought to have said, “up to Zechariah,” or “up to the blood of Zechariah.” For the blood of that Zechariah was not the end but almost the beginning of the righteous blood which that Jerusalem shed, or which was shed in it or around it.

They stoned that Zechariah at the command of King Joash; afterward, however, not a few kings and princes of Judah killed others, especially Manasseh (4 Kings 21), of whom Scripture reports that he even made his own son pass through fire and shed exceedingly much innocent blood, until he filled Jerusalem up to the brim (2 Chron. 23 [probably 2 Kings 21]). But, to pass over them and those who followed, and come to the Gospel times when these words were spoken: the blood of the holy innocents, the blood of Saint John the Baptist, the blood of the Lord himself, of whom they said, [Col. 0950C] “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27); the blood of those prophets, sages, and scribes concerning whom he said, “Behold, I send you prophets, sages, and scribes, and some of them you will kill and crucify” (Matt. 23), and the rest—should this not especially have come upon them?

Let us therefore consider the words, “up to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah, whom you killed between the temple and the altar” (ibid.), lest perhaps the Gospel prophecy concerns James the Just, the Lord’s own brother. For apart from the name Zechariah, all else agrees with him. Moreover, because of the likeness of his cause or death, he may very properly be called Zechariah, just as our Lord, likewise because of the likeness of his cause, called John the Baptist Elijah (Matt. 11). If this is admitted, there is nothing inconsistent; for this man is called son of Barachiah more appropriately than the other, who was the son of Jehoiada. For *Barachias* is interpreted “blessed of the Lord.” But this man’s father—as also the father of James and of the other apostles—is Christ the Lord; and in this same Gospel passage he wished to be called “blessed of the Lord,” saying to them: “For I tell you, you will not see me from now on until you say: ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord’” (Matt. 23).

Without doubt he wishes, or wished, this not without the authority of Scripture; a little earlier the children had drawn from it their words: “Hosanna to the Son of David; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.” For this is a verse of the one hundred and seventeenth Psalm. And observe how great is the likeness also in the place of death, between the man whom that city first killed among the prophets and this man, after whom it was not permitted to that same city to kill anyone. Thus both, fittingly signified by the one name Zechariah, ought to be understood.

Of the former it is written thus: “Then the Spirit of the Lord clothed Zechariah, son of Jehoiada the priest, and he stood before the people and said to them: ‘Thus says the Lord: Why do you transgress the commandment of the Lord, which will not profit you? You have forsaken the Lord, that he may forsake you.’ And, gathered together against him, they cast stones at him by the king’s command in the courts of the house of the Lord” (2 Chron. 24).

But Josephus reports this concerning the latter (*Antiquities*, book 20, chapter 7, “On the death of James”):

> “Ananus, the young high priest, son of Ananus and of priestly stock, having seized an opportunity, convened a council; and, publicly compelling James to deny Christ the Son of God, ordered him to be stoned when he resisted. When he had been thrown down from the pinnacle of the temple, his legs broken, and was still half alive, he raised his hands to heaven and said: ‘Lord, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.’ He was struck in the head and died from a fuller’s club, such as is commonly used to wring wet garments.”

The same Josephus relates that James was of such holiness and renown among the people that Jerusalem was believed to have been overthrown because of his murder. The resemblance is therefore sufficient for this man rightly to be called Zechariah, just as John is called Elijah. Both were also, according to the name Zechariah, which means “mindful of the Lord,” mindful of the Lord at the point of death—except that the one, in accordance with the severity of the Law, said as he died: “May God see and require it”; while the other, in accordance with the sweetness of the Gospel, said: “Lord, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.”

Both were righteous even in these final words, but differently so, according to the character or quality of the two respective times, legal and evangelical. But if these things should perhaps displease anyone, let him say, if he can—since differing accounts are read in different places, as blessed Jerome says—who that Zechariah was whose father was properly called Barachiah, who was himself killed between the temple and the altar, and in whom the righteous blood that came upon the Jews ought to have ended. Let us now consider what follows.

“And white robes were given to each of them, and it was said to them [Col. 0951D] that they should rest yet for a short time, until their fellow servants and their brethren, who are to be killed as they also were, should be completed.” Robes were given to those slain, or to the souls of the slain, because they needed them. For they were naked, with that nakedness which our first parents left to all their descendants, of whom it is written: “And when they knew that they were naked, they sewed fig leaves and made loincloths for themselves” (Gen. III).

But was not the word of God and the testimony which they had, for which they had also been slain, a robe or garment for them? If the word, or the name or worship of God, were not the garment or robe of the soul, Scripture would by no means say: “Moses therefore saw that the people were stripped naked; for Aaron had stripped them for the disgrace of their shame, and had made them naked among their enemies” (Exod. XXXII) [Col. 0952A]. Therefore, since the worship of God and the word of God are the robe of the soul, and since these souls suffered on account of the word of God and the testimony which they had, why are they said to have received individual white robes, as though they were still naked?

But it should be noted that it is not said merely, “robes were given to them,” but “white robes.” For they indeed had robes—that is, the righteousness of the word of God or testimony for which they had been slain—but those robes were not yet white. Unless they were washed in the blood of Christ, they could not be white. One of them, Isaiah, testifies to this; he undoubtedly had the word of God and the testimony for which he was slain, for the Jews also say that Manasseh had him sawn asunder [Col. 0952B]: “We have all become as unclean persons, and all our righteousnesses are like the cloth of a menstruous woman” (Isa. LXIV). And David says: “You shall sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed; you shall wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow” (Ps. L). And Zechariah: “On that day there shall be an open fountain for the house of David and for the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for the washing of the sinner and the menstruous woman” (Zech. XIII).

Nothing is more unclean than a menstruous woman, who, according to the law, makes unclean whatever she touches. All their righteousnesses were to be compared with her, as they themselves testify, unless they were washed in the blood of that Christ in whom they believed and whom they awaited. Therefore, they already had robes, but those very robes were not yet white. Accordingly, the statement, “and white robes were given to each of them,” should be understood [Col. 0952C] as though it said: “And it was granted to them that their robes should be white,” although the robes themselves—that is, whatever righteousness they possessed—had not come from themselves but had been given by God.

And therefore, when we read here, “and white robes were given to each of them,” so as to understand it as though it said, “and their robes were made white,” we must at the same time remember what is later written of them and their fellow servants: “These are they who have come out of great tribulation, and have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb” (Apoc. VII). Meanwhile, it is especially beautiful to observe that, although they were already dead, their robes were made white in the blood of the Lamb at the hour when that same Lamb shed his blood on the cross; whereas the robes of these their fellow servants and brethren, who after that passion of Christ, or after the coming of the Holy Spirit, enter into the same faith while still living, are made white when they are baptized in Christ Jesus, or into the death of Jesus Christ (Rom. VI) [Col. 0952D]. But if after this they also shed their own blood for that same Christ—as many did, and as very many will yet do under the final persecution of Antichrist—their whitened robes shine still more brightly.

It should also be known that “white robes were given to them” not because they cried out, demanding judgment for their blood and vengeance, but because they had been slain for the word of God and for the testimony which they had. For when Christ suffered, then, as has already been said, their robes were made white in the blood of that same Christ [Col. 0953A]. That cry, however, had long since begun to be heard, from the time when the first Abel was slain, God saying: “The voice of your brother’s blood cries to me from the earth” (Gen. IV).

Likewise, the statement made to them, “that they should rest yet for a short time,” was not said so that the blood ceased to cry out. For their blood does not cease, nor will it cease until the end of the age, to cry out. The Apostle says of the aforesaid Abel that, having died through his faith, he still speaks (Heb. XI), as long as, crying out in the Church, he says: “Avenge, O Lord, the blood of your servants which has been shed”; or, “Let the vengeance for the blood of your servants which has been shed, and the groaning of those in chains, enter into your sight” (Ps. LXXVIII). As long, I say, as the earth—which is the Church—cries out and says these or similar things, they do not rest in such a way as to cease crying. Therefore, the words addressed to them, “that they should rest yet for a short time,” must be understood or supplied as meaning: not from that cry demanding vengeance for their blood, but from their labors, as we read in this same book: “From henceforth, says the Spirit, let them rest from their labors” (Apoc. XIV) [Col. 0953B].

That being so, why is it said that they should rest yet for a short time? Will their rest last only for a short time? Certainly not. Rather, it is said thus because, after a short time, when their fellow servants and brethren who are to be slain as they were have been completed, something else great will occur, so that they will receive an abundant increase of their rest [Col. 0953C]. For they will rise again; and to those to whom individual white robes are now given, double robes will then be given, so that they may be blessed both with the immortal blessedness of the soul and with the blessed immortality of the body.

For we know that when Adam sinned—in whom all sinned—all were nonetheless deprived in him of that double robe, namely the felicity of body and soul. Of the first, which is the soul’s, it is written: “And when they knew that they were naked, they sewed fig leaves and made loincloths for themselves” (Gen. III). Such a covering was plainly the nakedness of the soul, because all the shame of the flesh proceeded from within, where the beauty of the soul had perished. The other nakedness is the mortality of the body, concerning which God said: “Because you are dust, and into dust you shall return” (ibid.). Scripture also says that the Lord God made tunics of skins for Adam and his wife [Col. 0953D]. Thus, though clothed in tunics, they were truly naked, deprived of the natural beauty of their bodies—which God had formed, and of which they had formerly not been ashamed even without clothing—and bearing in those very tunics a sign of their nakedness and misery: namely, that their mortal bodies must grow old and fail, just as tunics of skin grow old.

Therefore, those who had lost in the first parent the double robe, that is, both the felicity of soul and of body, are meanwhile to have single robes: they are to be blessed in soul alone, and so to rest until they receive, after a short time, the other robe, namely the glory also of immortal bodies.

[Col. 0954A] “And I saw, when he had opened the sixth seal, and behold, there was a great earthquake; and the sun became black as a sackcloth of hair, and the whole moon became like blood,” etc. Most people refer this earthquake, the blackening of the sun, the bloody redness of the moon, the falling of the stars, and the other portents of evils written here, to the final persecution and to the times of Antichrist. But we are bound by our purpose, and we endeavor, as far as we can, to follow the path marked by the lamp of Scripture and the brightness of the opened book. Let us therefore follow the order we have begun.

When the Jews rejected the word of God and judged themselves unworthy of eternal life (Acts XIV), the apostles turned to the Gentiles. Then Jerusalem was surrounded by the Roman army; its people fell by the edge of the sword [Col. 0954B], and were carried captive among all nations. Then indeed the Lamb opened the book’s sixth seal, because at that time many things written concerning this matter were fulfilled. Hence the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “These are days of vengeance, that all things which are written may be fulfilled” (Luke XXI).

For example, Isaiah says: “Behold, look upon us all, your people. The city of your holiness, Zion, has become a wilderness. Jerusalem has become desolate; the house of our sanctification and our glory, where our fathers praised you, has become a burning of fire, and all our desirable things have been turned into ruins. Will you restrain yourself over these things, O Lord? Will you be silent and afflict us exceedingly?” (Isa. LXIV). And the Lord answered: “Those who did not formerly ask me have sought me; those who did not seek me have found me. And I said: Behold, I am here for a nation that did not call upon your name” (Isa. LXV) [Col. 0954C].

Explaining why, after leaving their house desolate—that is, the house of the Jews—he turns himself to the Gentiles, he says: “I have stretched out my hands all day to an unbelieving people, who walk in a way that is not good, after their own thoughts.” Many things of great force and plainly open to understanding were contained beneath this seal: that is, many things in the Law, Prophets, and Psalms testified in clear utterances that the Jews would be abandoned and the Gentiles called. Let us now range through the broad expanse opened by this same sixth seal.

“When,” he says, “he had opened the sixth seal, behold, there was a great earthquake.” And the meaning is: in order that what was contained in the sacred writings concerning the dispersal of the Jews and the calling together of the Gentiles might be fulfilled, the earth was shaken—the Roman world was stirred—when Vespasian and Titus gathered forces from every side and surrounded Jerusalem with their army [Col. 0954D].

“Then,” he says, “the sun became black as a sackcloth of hair, and the whole moon became like blood, and the stars of heaven fell upon the earth, as a fig tree casts its unripe figs when it is shaken by a great wind.” That Jerusalem, in its earthly estimation of itself, was like the sun and like the moon, since it had been David’s seat, in which that man sat as a temporal king. For they read what David himself sang in the Psalm, in the person of God: “Once have I sworn by my holiness: if I lie to David, his seed shall remain for ever, and his throne as the sun before me, and as the perfect moon for ever, and the faithful witness in heaven” (Ps. LXXXVIII) [Col. 0955A].

But he did not say this about a hand-made seat, nor about a throne of stone or even of much gold, such as a mighty king could make for himself, which should remain like the sun before God or like the perfect moon. Rather, he spoke of holy human beings, who are truly the seat of Christ and the city, and who in the age to come will be like the sun with respect to the soul, and like the perfect moon with respect to the body—the moon which surely emits more light when it is perfect and full.

Therefore Scripture truly said that David’s seat—that is, Christ, “strong of hand”—would be like the sun and the perfect moon. But that city, that synagogue of Satan, was deceived by its presumption, reckoning itself the sun of the world and the moon of the inhabited earth, because of the widely celebrated glory of David’s line and of Solomon’s most august temple [Col. 0955B]. “Such a sun then became black as a sackcloth of hair, and such a whole moon became like blood,” when the intolerable pride and stubborn rebellion of that city provoked all nations’ victorious Romans against itself.

Let us read Josephus narrating the miserable tragedy of that destruction, which, because of its magnitude, is always new to its readers. Where did that quasi-solar beauty go? That sun became black, and the purple pride of its splendor was turned into sackcloth. Indeed, as Jeremiah had also foretold: “Their faces have become blacker than coals; they are not recognized in the streets; their skin has clung to their bones; it has dried up and become like wood” (Lam. IV) [Col. 0955C]. And Isaiah says: “Instead of a sweet fragrance, there shall be stench; instead of a belt, a rope; instead of curled hair, baldness; and instead of a breast-band, sackcloth” (Isa. III).

Not partly, but, as he says, “that whole moon became like blood”: without, through siege; within, through sedition; without and within, through sword and fire; but more grievously within, through sword or blood, terror, and hunger. For “outside the sword laid them waste, and inside terror: young man together with virgin, nursing child with aged man; and they were consumed by hunger” (Deut. XXXII). “The hands of compassionate women,” says Jeremiah, “boiled their own children; they became their food in the destruction of the daughter of my people.” Why? “Because of the sins,” he says, “of her prophets and the iniquities of her priests, who shed in her midst the blood of the righteous” (Lam. IV) [Col. 0955D]. Hardly anyone could number the thousands who were slain.

“The sun therefore became black as sackcloth of hair, and the whole moon became like blood.” Such blackening or discoloration was rightly prefigured by the darkness that came over the whole earth when the true sun, Christ, was extinguished by their crime upon the gibbet of the cross (Luke XXIII). Nor were they blackened only outwardly; what is more serious, they were also blinded inwardly in their hearts. A just sentence pursued that moon, that it should become wholly like blood, by its own judgment, when they said: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. XXVII) [Col. 0956A].

“And,” he says, “the stars of heaven fell upon the earth.” In their own estimation, the Jewish people also might be compared to stars, especially when they heard Moses say: “And he said to you at that time: I cannot bear you alone, because the Lord our God has multiplied you, and today you are very numerous, like the stars of heaven. May the Lord God of your fathers add many thousands to this number” (Deut. I). Moses said this not with human gentleness but by divine authority, since he knew the Lord and had written that he said to Abraham:“Look up to heaven and number the stars, if you can.” And again: “So shall your seed be” (Gen. XV).

Indeed, according to this authority, Abraham’s seed was comparable to the stars of heaven, but not wholly or indiscriminately: only in respect of the elect, that is, those who are children not merely of the flesh but of promise. For, as the Apostle says, “It is not those who are children of the flesh who are the children of God, but the children of the promise are counted as seed” (Rom. IX) [Col. 0956B]. But they were children not of promise but only of the flesh. Prophetic truth also reproached them for this, saying: “You who have come forth from the waters of Judah” (Isa. XLVIII).

Therefore those who seemed to themselves to be stars of heaven fell—not as true stars of heaven, but as the unripe fruit of a fig tree falls when shaken by a great wind, that is, when violently agitated by the spirit of the devil. The comparison with the fig tree and its falling unripe figs is especially fitting, because those too among the Jews who at that time believed in Christ and were, as it were, the first fruits of Christ’s cross, fell away when shaken by the great wind: namely, the wind of envy, hating the salvation of the Gentiles and, in rivalry against their own faith in the Gospel, most of them seeking to maintain circumcision, as the Acts of the Apostles also testify (Acts XV, XXI) [Col. 0956C].

Accordingly, having voluntarily fallen away from the grace of Christ, almost all the Jews rightly also fell by the edge of the sword; and those who survived were led captive among all nations, comparable not to stars, as has been said, but to dust which the wind casts away from the face of the earth.

“And heaven departed as a scroll rolled up.” The heaven in which they seemed to themselves to shine like stars was the knowledge of the Law, in which the Jews gloried as high and bright, despising all Gentiles. “The kingdom of God,” he says, “shall be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits.” Heaven therefore departed because their understanding was narrowed, and the spiritual understanding of the sacred Law disappeared from them—or rather, was not given to them because of the poverty of their heart [Col. 0956D].

How did it depart? “Like a scroll rolled up,” he says. He indicates quite beautifully what he intended by the departing heaven, when he compared that departure to a rolled-up book. For what does it mean to say that heaven departed like a scroll rolled up, except as though it said that all divine and heavenly Scripture was rolled up and closed to them? To those, indeed, from whom this heaven departed, this heavenly book is rolled up—indeed, sealed; but to us, to whom it came by departing from them, it is unsealed and open. For this is what we are now handling in our hands: “The Lamb received the sealed book from the right hand of him who sits upon the throne, and loosed its seven seals,” opening it to us who have faith in him, confessing that he is worthy to receive the same book and to loose its seven seals [Col. 0957A].

“And every mountain and island were moved from their places. And the kings of the earth, and princes, and tribunes, and rich men, and mighty men, and every slave and free person hid themselves in caves and rocks of the mountains. And they say to the mountains and rocks: Fall upon us, and hide us from the face of him who sits upon the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb. For the great day of their wrath has come, and who can stand?”

What else did our Lord say, when he turned to the women who wept and lamented him because he had been delivered by the governor to the will of the Jews and was being led away to crucifixion? “Daughters of Jerusalem,” he said, “do not weep over me, but weep for yourselves and for your children; for behold, days are coming in which they will say: Blessed are the barren, and the wombs which have not borne, and the breasts which have not nursed” (Luke XXIII) [Col. 0957B]. Then “they will begin to say to the mountains: Fall upon us; and to the hills: Cover us.” For he signifies the days of the coming Roman siege and captivity, concerning which he had earlier said among other things to his disciples: “Then those who are in Judea shall flee to the mountains” (Luke XXI), etc. “Then,” he says, “they will begin to say to the mountains: Fall upon us; and to the hills: Cover us.”

Finally, Josephus also reports that, as the Romans pressed them hard, the Jews raced one another to seek caves in the mountains and hills, so that he himself testifies that he was betrayed, discovered, and captured by the enemy with forty companions in a certain more secure cave at Jotapata, a city that had been destroyed [Col. 0957C].

He more clearly expresses who the mountains are and what islands were moved from their places, saying: “The kings of the earth, and princes, and tribunes, and rich men, and mighty men, and every slave and free person hid themselves in caves and rocks of the mountains.” These kings and princes are those of whom it is written in the Psalm: “The kings of the earth stood by, and the princes gathered together as one, against the Lord and against his Christ” (Ps. II). After first citing this verse, the Acts of the Apostles say: “For truly in this city Herod and Pontius Pilate, with the Gentiles and peoples of Israel, gathered together against your holy servant Jesus whom you anointed, to do whatever your hand and counsel had decreed to occur” (Acts IV) [Col. 0957D].

These are called mountains because of pride, and islands because of deep avarice. Herod and Pontius Pilate themselves did not in their own persons reach that evil of the siege; each had first received his own judgment. But all those who were then found to be powerful or rulers—Pharisees and high priests—were moved from their places in the manner already described, the Lord Jesus driving them from his temple and from their place with the scourge of his wrath. They fell by the edge of the sword, while their temple and city alike collapsed before their eyes in the burning of fire; and those who survived were carried captive among all nations [Col. 0958A].

Meanwhile they said in vain to the mountains and rocks: “Fall upon us and hide us from the face of him who sits upon the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb.” In vain, I say, they hid themselves in the mountains and caves of the rocks; equally in vain they placed hope in Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and also in Moses and the other fathers and prophets—great mountains indeed, and living rocks. For these did not then protect them; rather, they accused them. For the Lord plainly says to them concerning Moses: “There is one who accuses you, Moses, in whom you hope” (John V).

And unquestionably this saying applies to them: “Hide us from the face of him who sits upon the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb.” For in their grim conscience they could not fail to know that the Lamb whom they had killed lived again and was powerfully angry with them. “For,” they say, “the great day of their wrath has come; and who can stand?” The day of their wrath—that is, of him who sits upon the throne and of the Lamb, of the Father and the Son, of the Lord and his Christ, “against whom these princes stood and gathered together”—has come and will yet come (Matt. XXIV) [Col. 0958B]. For all these things are the beginnings of sorrows; but the end of those same sorrows, their interminable end and endless consummation, will be in Gehenna. Thus God himself cries out concerning them in the song of Deuteronomy: “A fire has been kindled in my wrath, and it shall burn to the lowest depths of hell” (Deut. XXXII).

“And who can stand?” Truly none can stand; none can resist. Yet it will be well for whoever, because he did not stand or resist, will then be able to flee wrath. Something similar occurred literally in that same destruction of Jerusalem: “For when the Roman war and the extermination of the Jewish nation drew near, all the Christians who were in the province, warned by an oracle, departed farther away, as ecclesiastical History relates, and, having crossed the Jordan, remained for a time in the city of Pella under the protection of Agrippa, king of the Jews, who is mentioned in the Acts of the Apostles; with that part of the Jews which wished to obey him, he always lived subject to the Roman power.”

## Chapter VII

[Col. 0958D]

“After these things I saw four angels standing upon the four corners of the earth, holding the four winds of the earth, so that they should not blow upon the earth, nor upon the sea, nor upon any tree.” Where then was the heaven to go, whither was it to depart, of which he had said above: “And heaven departed like a scroll rolled up”? That heaven, namely heavenly doctrine or knowledge, departed from the Jews when the apostles said—who themselves, according to the Psalmist, are the heavens that declare the glory of God, or the firmament that proclaims his works (Ps. XVIII): “To you indeed it was necessary that the word of God should first be spoken; but since you have rejected it and judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts XIII).

Where did that heaven go, and how was it turned to the Gentiles? “For four angels standing upon the four corners of the earth,” he says [Col. 0959A], “held the four winds”: that is, all the kingdoms of the world restrained the preachers of truth. Here the winds are understood in a good sense, and signify the apostles of Christ or all preachers of the Gospel. Hence the Psalmist says in praise of God’s name: “Bringing forth clouds from the ends of the earth, he made lightnings for rain; he brings forth winds from his treasuries” (Ps. CXXXIV).

And the sense is this: those who are now the heaven of which I said, “Whatever the Lord willed, he did in heaven and on earth” (ibid.)—that is, among the more perfect and the lesser saints—those apostles and apostolic men, I say, whom he brought forth and raised from the ends of the earth, that is, from the lowliness in which they were among earthly people, both in regard to temporal possessions and in regard to knowledge, desiring only worldly things: he made them clouds, imposing on them the office of clouds, that they might rain down abundance of preaching and flash with the most clear and terrible threat of God’s judgment. He raised and extended them according to the swiftness of their understanding, as winds fly when carried aloft; and all this came from his treasuries, from his gifts, from his hidden judgments and counsels [Col. 0959B].

Therefore these winds are the same as the clouds: agile and ready, learned and eloquent preachers of the Gospel. But the “four angels standing upon the four corners of the earth” are all kingdoms, of which the four principal ones were Babylonian, Persian, Macedonian, and Roman. These four—indeed, all kingdoms of the earth—held, that is, wished to hold, the aforementioned winds, so that they should not blow upon the earth, sea, or any tree: that is, so that they should not preach the faith of Christ in any provinces, on any islands, or among people of any rank or condition. By this prohibition they held back these winds [Col. 0959C].

Nor did they hold them back lightly or with small resolve, but through laws and public proscriptions, and through every kind of punishment set forth against the heralds of truth. But observe what follows:

“And I saw another Angel ascending from the rising of the sun, having the seal of the living God; and he cried with a loud voice to the four angels to whom it was given to harm the earth and the sea, saying: Do not harm the earth or the sea or the trees, until we have sealed the servants of our God upon their foreheads.”

This other Angel is the Angel of great counsel, who says to his aforesaid apostles: “And behold, I am with you all days, even unto the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII). He ascended from the rising of the sun, in order to enlighten those who sat in darkness and in the shadow of death: ascending from the lower world, rising from the dead—which resurrection is truly for us the sunrise—and as he ascended saying to them: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (ibid.) [Col. 0959D].

“I saw such a one,” he says, “having the seal of the living God”: that is, openly showing by his words and works that he is the living God, the Son of the living God. Peter, seeing and recognizing this, said to him: “You are Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. XVI). Truly he is “the living God and Son of the living God,” who, though he died according to the flesh, could not be held by death but rose again after the pangs of hell had been loosed, since it was impossible for him to be held by it (Acts II). The Apostle also indicates that he ought to be known by this seal when he says: “Who was predestined Son of God in power according to the Spirit of sanctification, by the resurrection from the dead of Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. I). For that he is truly the Son of the living God was made especially clear by his resurrection from the dead [Col. 0960A].

Having this seal, he cried with a loud voice to the four angels. He cried, I say, and cried aloud together with his crying apostles, so that “their sound went forth into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the inhabited world” (Ps. XVIII). By cooperating with them and by accompanying signs, he confirmed their cry or preaching (Mark XVI). Those angels to whom it was given to harm the earth and sea heard: that is, they perceived the invincible power of Gospel preaching throughout all the kingdoms of the world, which by their dominion choked everything and permitted no one to breathe according to his own right.

“Do not,” he says, “harm the earth or the sea or the trees until we have sealed the servants of our God upon their foreheads.” To say this to them is to hinder their evil will, so that however madly they rage, harm, and tyrannize by persecuting, proscribing, and killing, they are nevertheless unable to obstruct or turn aside God’s purpose, so as to prevent him from calling, justifying, and glorifying those “whom he foreknew and predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son” (Rom. VIII) [Col. 0960B].

The seal of calling and justification, and the merit and hope of future glorification, is the sealing of the servants of that same God upon their foreheads with the sign of the cross: once the reproach and punishment of the condemned, but now the honor and salvation of the righteous. “Do not harm”: do not hinder, O mighty angels, O powerful kingdoms occupying the four corners or regions of the earth. But to such an extent are your dominion ineffective and your rage futile, and to such an extent are your laws frivolous and your decrees empty, though they pronounce every kind of death, that nevertheless we seal the servants of our God with the banner of the victorious cross, not only in the hidden places of their hearts but also openly, upon their foreheads [Col. 0960C].

This Angel said, “the servants of our God,” although he is God and has the seal—that is, the proper characteristic—of the living God, professing the God of all to be his God, just as he says in the Gospel to his apostles: “I ascend to my Father and your Father, my God and your God” (John XX). Here he says “our God,” and there “my God,” namely on account of the humility of the assumed humanity.

“And I heard the number of those who were sealed: one hundred and forty-four thousand, sealed from every tribe of the children of Israel.” All the servants of God who are sealed on their foreheads, with the righteousness of God revealed in his Gospel through the loud voice of this crying angel—although there is no distinction or respect of persons ([Col. 0961A] Col. III), whether they are Jews or Greeks—yet the Jews hold the first place, as the Apostle says: “But glory, and honor, and peace to everyone who works what is good, to the Jew first, and also to the Greek” (Rom. II). Conversely, among those who do not receive this sign of the living God, the Jews are first in condemnation, as he himself says in the same place: “Wrath and indignation, tribulation and distress, upon every soul of man that works evil, of the Jew first, and also of the Greek” (ibid.). Rightly, therefore, here too those “who were sealed, Jews from every tribe of the children of Israel,” are numbered first; and then: “After these things I saw,” he says, “a great multitude, which no one could number, from every nation, and tribes, and peoples, and tongues”—all of whom the Apostle wishes to be understood under the single name of Greeks.

Moreover, if you properly observe the formation or composition of this number of [Col. 0961B] one hundred and forty-four thousand, a beautiful and illustrious mystery shines forth from it. Let us therefore say something which may perhaps be less plain or intelligible to simpler persons, but which the present matter requires; to arithmeticians, however, who especially understand the methods of the abacus, it will at once appear reasonable and pleasing. The number twelve, which was the number of the first children of Israel, is arranged so that a unit is placed in the tens-place and a two in the units-place. But in order that these twelve firstborn may increase to as many thousands—that is, twelve thousand—that unit of the tens-place passes the first and second positions and stands in the third, and thus makes ten thousand. Likewise the two in the units-place, [Col. 0961C] which joined to that unit in the tens-place completed twelve, passes the first and second positions and stands in the third, and thus makes two thousand. These two thousand are counted together with the aforementioned ten thousand, already placed in the second position from its own boundary, and twelve thousand result. Thus the children of Israel, who were only twelve, having now been multiplied into twelve thousand, are again multiplied twelvefold and become “one hundred and forty-four thousand.” This number is arranged so that it is distinguished by three positions. For a unit is placed in the hundred-thousands, a four in the ten-thousands, and likewise a four in the thousands. Observe carefully. The first, or single, twelve ascend through three positions in order to become twelve thousand; and those same twelve thousand, multiplied twelvefold according to the same number [Col. 0961D] of the children of Israel, make one hundred and forty-four thousand—a number, as has been said, distributed through three positions.

What, then, do we suppose the holy grace of this revelation intends, except what all legal, prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic truth attests: that it avails no one for salvation to be Israel or Abraham’s son according to the flesh, unless he is also his son through faith, which is accomplished by the confession of no fewer than three names? For the confession of faith, in this time of grace now revealed, necessarily expresses openly the persons of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. But formerly, under that shadow of the Mosaic law, the same number of paternal names was signified in the secret profession of that people of God, when all openly confessed and invoked the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob [Col. 0962A] (Exod. III). And now the servants of God are sealed on their foreheads with the seal of Christ’s cross and blood, in confession of the name of the one God—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; 408 but then they marked the doorposts of their houses under the aforementioned names Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, confessing one God, instructed beforehand by the authority of that same God. For he said to Moses: “Thus shall you say to the children of Israel: The Lord God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you. This is my name forever, and this is my memorial from generation to generation” (ibid.).

What, therefore, I ask, do we understand in these numbers thus multiplied and arranged, except as though it were said: The sealed servants of our God from among the Jews are those who are sons of Israel, or of their faithful father Abraham, not only according to the flesh but also according to faith? [Col. 0962B] “For,” says the Apostle, “not all who are from Israel are Israelites; nor because they are Abraham’s seed are they all children; but, ‘In Isaac shall your seed be called’: that is, not the children of the flesh are the children of God, but the children of promise are reckoned as the seed” (Rom. IX). Thus, when this number is complete, the innumerable multitude of the whole Church is signified, sprung from the patriarchs either by lineage of flesh or by imitation of faith.

Moreover, in this order of the names of the twelve children of Israel a mystical reason is not lacking; for they are plainly not found arranged here according to the order of their generation, in which they were begotten or born according to the flesh. [Col. 0962C] This did not happen through ignorance, but for the sake of a definite mystery. Therefore, in the same sense and in the same words in which it has been treated before us, let it not be burdensome to set it down here.

“From the tribe of Judah, twelve thousand sealed,” etc. Fittingly he begins with Judah, from whose tribe our Lord arose; and he omits Dan, from whom Antichrist is said to be destined to be born, as it is written: “Let Dan become a serpent in the way, a horned serpent in the path, biting the horse’s hoofs so that its rider falls backward” (Gen. XLIX). For he determined to expound not the order of earthly generation, but, according to the interpretation of the names, the virtues of the Church. From present confession and praise, she hastens toward the right hand of eternal life. For this is what the name Judah, which is first, and Benjamin, [Col. 0962D] which is placed last, signify.

Thus Judah is placed first, since it means confession or praise; for before the beginnings of confession no one attains the summit of good works, and unless through confession we renounce evil deeds, we are not formed in righteous ones. Second is Reuben, which means “seeing a son.” The Psalmist testifies that works are designated by sons, when, among other things, he says in the blessings of the blessed man: “Your sons are like young olive trees”; and below: “May you see your children’s children” (Ps. CXXVII). It is not that one who fears the Lord cannot be blessed unless he has begotten sons and received grandchildren, since a greater reward awaits faithful virgins; rather, by sons he signifies works, and by children’s children the fruit of works—that is, [Col. 0963A] eternal reward. After Judah, then, comes Reuben: that is, after the beginnings of divine confession and praise comes the perfection of action.

But “through many tribulations we must enter into the kingdom of God” (Acts XIV); therefore Gad follows Reuben, and Gad means temptation or being girded. For after beginning a good work, a person must necessarily be tested by greater temptations and girded for graver battles, so that the strength of his faith may be proved, as Solomon says: “My son, when you come to the service of God, stand in fear and prepare your soul for temptation” (Ecclus. II). Likewise the Psalmist says: “You have girded me with strength for battle” (Ps. XVII). And because we call blessed those who have endured suffering (Jas. I), Asher—that is, “blessed”—is consequently placed after Gad, in a thoroughly fitting order. [Col. 0963B] For blessed is the man who endures temptation, because when he has been tested, he shall receive the crown of life.

Since those who are secure in the faithful promise of this blessedness are not straitened, but, rejoicing in hope and patient in tribulation, sing with the psalmist: “In tribulation you enlarged me” (Ps. IV), and again, “I ran the way of your commandments when you enlarged my heart” (Ps. CXVIII), and exulting with the mother of blessed Samuel say, “My mouth is enlarged over my enemies, because I rejoiced in your salvation” (I Kings II), therefore Naphtali follows, which means breadth. Manasseh too follows him, meaning “forgetful” or “necessity.” By the mystery of this name we are warned that, instructed by the distresses of present temptations, forgetting those things which are behind ([Col. 0963C] Phil. III), we should, according to the Apostle, stretch forward to those things which are before, so as to make provision for the flesh not in its desires, but only as constrained by the necessity of the human condition (Rom. XIII). Concerning this the Psalmist, longing for better things, says in prayer: “Deliver me from my necessities” (Ps. XXIV).

Simeon is placed beneath him, that is, “he heard sorrow,” or “the name of a dwelling,” so that even the quality of this word might make clearer both what is to be possessed here and what is healthfully to be expected. For the joy of the heavenly dwelling will be given to those whose spirit is made sorrowful here by fruitful repentance; and to them it is said: “Your sorrow shall be turned into joy” (John XVI). Accordingly Levi follows, that is, “added.” In him we understand either [Col. 0963D] those who merit eternal things amid temporal things, as Solomon says: “A man’s own riches are the redemption of his soul” (Prov. XIII); or those who, by following God’s counsel, receive in this age a hundredfold with tribulations, and in the age to come eternal life (Matt. XIX). To these also applies what is written: “He who adds knowledge adds labor” (Eccl. I). For the bitterness of tribulations was added to holy Job so that, once tested, he might receive a greater reward of prizes.

Therefore Issachar, which means “reward,” rightly follows him in that order; because, as the Apostle teaches, “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that shall be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII). For one fights more fruitfully where a certain reward is hoped for. God works and completes these things in the dwelling [Col. 0964A] of strength, which is called Zebulun, when strength is made perfect in weakness, and when the body, thought weak by enemies—and by means of which they endeavor to bring destruction even upon the soul—is found, through God’s strengthening, to be unconquered (I Cor. XII). Then comes a happy increase, which the name Joseph indicates, signifying the addition of gifts of grace; whether you understand the profitable spiritual interest in the doubled rendering of talents, or receive it in those offerings which, through the vowed devotion of believers, are rendered to God the Redeemer. And so that you may understand that all these, whom both the order and the interpretation of the names here significantly placed indicate, will be at the right hand of Christ the eternal King in the future judgment (Matt. XXV), Benjamin, as I said before, is placed last—[Col. 0964B] that is, “son of the right hand”—as though he were the end of the sequence, when, death the last enemy having been destroyed, the blessedness of eternal inheritance shall be given to the elect (I Cor. XV). Or each one of the faithful may rightly be called a son of the right hand; or the whole assembly of the Church, concerning which we sing: “The queen stood at your right hand in a garment of gold, surrounded with variety” (Ps. XLIV).

It should be known that Antichrist is to be born from the tribe of Dan, according to Jacob’s words: “Let Dan become a serpent in the way,” and the rest down to, “that its rider falls backward” (Gen. XLIX). Dan is therefore cast out from this place, to show that Antichrist must be excluded from every number of the saints. Indeed, just as he is cast out from this spiritual catalogue, so all Israelites who are Abraham’s only according to the flesh and not by faith are judged strangers to every number and assembly of the children and to the inheritance [Col. 0964C] of that same father, Abraham or Israel.

“After these things I saw a great multitude, which no one could number, from all nations, and tribes, and peoples, and tongues, standing before the throne and in the sight of the Lamb, clothed in white robes, and palms were in their hands; and they cried with a loud voice, saying: Salvation belongs to our God, who sits 409 upon the throne, and to the Lamb.” All these are the fellow servants and brothers of those to whom white robes were given above (Rev. VI), and to whom it was said that they should rest yet a little while, until their fellow servants and brothers who were to be killed, as they too had been, should be completed. “For these are clothed in white robes.” Then one of the elders says: “Who are these that are clothed in white robes, and from where have they come?” And he adds: “These are those who came out of the great tribulation and washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.” Therefore those who are from all nations, tribes, peoples, and tongues are sons of Abraham, sons of the holy patriarchs, since they are called and indeed are brothers of those holy and godly men. And rightly so. For the Apostle also says concerning Abraham, the father of the saints: “And he received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of faith which he had in uncircumcision, that he might be the father of all who believe through uncircumcision, so that it might be reckoned to them also for righteousness; and that he might be the father of circumcision, not only to those who are of the circumcision, but also to those who follow the footsteps of the faith which was in the uncircumcision [Col. 0965A] of our father Abraham” (Rom. IV).

But let us now examine the matters already mentioned here somewhat more carefully. “I saw,” he says, “a great multitude, which no one could number.” In the Scriptures the number of saints is understood in two ways: sometimes as their multitude, and sometimes as the manifold progress of virtues. As their multitude, as in the passage: “I shall number them, and they shall be multiplied beyond the sand” (Ps. CXXXVIII). Not that they are more numerous than sand, but it is as though he said: I shall receive not a few but many, and I shall preserve them as a numbered and carefully guarded thing. As the manifold increase of virtues or blessedness, as in the passage: “Make known to me, Lord, my end, and what is the number of my days, that I may know what is lacking to me” (Ps. XXXVIII). It is not that there are more days there, but one day alone is more capacious than all days together, where there is boundless spaciousness, a number not passing away but a condition of life enduring and eternal. [Col. 0965B] In both senses no one could number that multitude. For, in their multitude, those who are already with those who are to receive the robes of martyrdom and palms of victory in Antichrist’s final persecution are numbered, or numerable, to God alone. Nor can it be assessed how great is the number of their days—of whom it is said elsewhere in consolation of the righteous: “I will fill him with length of days” (Ps. XC)—since the number there is infinite.

“From all nations,” he says, “and tribes, and peoples, and tongues.” A nation and a tribe differ in this: one nation has many tribes. For a nation is a multitude sprung from one origin, or distinguished from another nation by its own collective identity; thus from the one Jacob, or Israel, came the one Israelite nation, which had twelve tribes. But the Roman nation was divided into thirty-five curiae, which under another name, though not properly, are called tribes. Moreover, “people” is sometimes used for a nation and sometimes for the inhabitants of one city alone.

Concerning tongues, this should be known: although he first placed nations, tribes, and peoples, and then tongues, tongues did not arise from nations, but nations from tongues. At the beginning, there were as many nations as tongues. Afterwards there were more nations than tongues, because many nations arose from one tongue. [Col. 0965D] There are three sacred languages, Hebrew, Greek, and Latin, which chiefly excel throughout the whole world. For in these three languages Pilate wrote the charge above the Lord’s cross (John XIX). Therefore, because of the obscurity of the holy Scriptures, knowledge of these three languages is necessary, “so that one may have recourse to another if the speech of one language introduces any doubt about a word or its interpretation.”

Therefore, one may no longer boast in carnal Judaism or circumcision of the flesh on the basis of what was first written: “God is known in Judea; his name is great in Israel” (Ps. LXXV); because “from all nations, and tribes, and peoples, and tongues”—behold, there are those among whom God is known, among whom his name is great and victorious. “Standing before the throne [Col. 0966A] and in the sight of the Lamb, clothed in white robes, and palms in their hands.” Certainly this standing before the throne, or this throne itself, is that of which Daniel, after first saying, “I watched until thrones were placed and the Ancient of Days sat,” immediately said: “His throne was a flame of fire; its wheels were burning fire.” Likewise: “Thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stood before him” (Dan. VII).

The throne is not a flame of consuming fire for such persons standing thus before it, but only of illuminating fire; yet for those who killed them it will be a flame of consuming or melting fire, as the Psalmist says: “As wax melts before fire, so let sinners perish before God” (Ps. LXVII). For what is it for these to stand before the throne, except the very thing that it was for those above to cry under God’s altar? Certainly, both these who stand and those who cry behold the same thing; they demand the same judgment and vengeance for their blood. But standing before the throne, they also stood in the sight of the Lamb. Nothing is truer. For this Lamb sits at the right hand of God the Father upon the same throne. For this is what Daniel likewise says: “I watched therefore in the vision of the night, and behold, one like a Son of Man came with the clouds of heaven and came even to the Ancient of Days; and they presented him before him; and he gave him power, and honor, and kingdom” (Dan. VII), etc.

Fittingly, too, those who stand thus are clothed in white robes—understood as made white in the Lamb’s blood—so that they may be like him before whom [Col. 0966C] they stand. For his garment, says the same author mentioned above, was white as snow, and the hair of his head like clean wool (ibid.).—“And palms,” he says, “were in their hands.” For they conquered the four angels mentioned above—that is, the four chief kingdoms of the world—and, though these wished to harm them and resisted, striving with every effort, nevertheless they were sealed and received the sign of the living God upon their foreheads. Hence, after the conflict of the four winds and the course of the four beasts, the same author mentioned above says, “The Ancient of Days came” (ibid.), and gave judgment to the saints of the Most High; the time came, and the saints obtained the kingdom. “Palms, therefore, were in their hands,” and those palms themselves flourish meanwhile and grow, until the fourth beast is utterly slain, all power of the other beasts also is wholly removed, and finally the last judgment sits; then the kingdom, power, and greatness of the kingdom under all heaven shall be given to the people of the saints of the Most High, when the robes they now possess are doubled in that glorious resurrection of their bodies.

“And they cried with a loud voice, saying: Salvation belongs to our God who sits upon the throne, and to the Lamb.” Destruction and death, which had entered this world through one man, passed to all human beings, because all sinned in him. But just as sin entered the world through one man, and death through sin, so, says the Apostle, through the one Christ came condemnation and the death of sin, granting eternal life (Rom. V). [Col. 0967A] Rightly, therefore, the saints, mindful that in the first man they sinned and through his sin died, but were saved by the grace of God through Jesus Christ, confess and say: “Salvation”—that is, 410 because we have been saved—belongs “to our God”; let it not be attributed to us; “and to the Lamb,” that is, to the Son of God, through whose blood we have been restored to salvation.

“And all the angels stood around the throne, and the elders, and the four living creatures; and they fell before the throne upon their faces and worshiped God, saying: Amen.” Just as the number of the great multitude from all nations, tribes, peoples, and tongues cannot be comprehended by anyone, so here and above, when the Lamb first received the book (Rev. [Col. 0967B] III), the number of angels is not defined. It was already said there of these that, although they were not redeemed through him because they had not perished, nevertheless they were created through his divinity and, through his blood—as the Apostle also testifies—were reconciled, or made at peace, with us (Col. I); and their number, diminished by the fall of apostate angels, was restored in humankind. Therefore, their falling before the throne upon their faces and worshiping God, saying, “Amen,” is the congratulation of the blessed to the blessed and glorified—or restored—who had perished, as they rejoice together with them.

“Blessing, and glory, and wisdom, and thanksgiving, and honor, and power, and strength be to our God for ages of ages. Amen.” There are seven terms: blessing, [Col. 0967C] wisdom, glory, thanksgiving, honor, power, strength. Now the number seven customarily signifies universality, both among secular philosophers and ecclesiastical writers. Therefore here also, whatever praise, whatever glorification or jubilation the mind can conceive or utter—whatever that language of angels may be—we do not doubt that these blessed spirits proclaim it to our God under these terms, on behalf of all the saints, because they had died and lived again; they had perished and were found.

“And one of the elders answered and said to me: Who are these who are clothed in white robes, and from where have they come? And I said: My lord, you know. And he said [Col. 0967D] to me: These are they who came out of the great tribulation, and washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb; therefore they are before the throne of God and serve him day and night in his temple.” Although this kind of utterance, “Who are they, and from where have they come?” is not an answer but an interrogation or inquiry, yet he is rightly said to have answered, because he intends to answer: that is, he asks for this reason, so that after making the hearer attentive by the question itself, he may then answer.

“These,” he says, “are those who came out of great tribulation.” Truly all the saints came out of great tribulation, the cause or beginning of which tribulation was original sin (II Tim. III). For all who from that time wished to live piously suffered tribulation or persecution. [Col. 0968A] Yet in that tribulation the martyrs shone more notably and splendidly, like gold in a furnace of fire; and of them he immediately adds, saying: “And they washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb.” For though the whole Church has been cleansed from every sin by Christ’s blood, much more have these been cleansed and made white, who shared so fully in Christ’s blood that they poured out their own blood for Christ.

Therefore they are before God’s throne: namely, because they are clean, because they are white, because in white robes they walk conspicuous and pleasing; therefore they stand as intimates; therefore, joyful, they gaze upon him who gazes on them; and, filled and ineffably possessed with delight, they cannot turn away their reciprocal gaze from the sight of him whom they behold. [Col. 0968B] Nor is there any doubt that by their presence they cry before the throne the same thing as the souls of the godly slain beneath the altar: “How long, Lord, do you not judge and avenge our blood?” (Rev. VI).

“And they serve him day and night in his temple.” Day and night—that is, in eternity—they serve or minister, as Daniel says: “Thousands of thousands ministered to him” (Dan. VII), not with laborious or servile ministry, but with the joyful and free festal dance of eternal love. For while one lives here, God’s service or ministry is labor and work; there, however, God’s service is the reward of labor and the recompense of service. “In his temple,” Christ says. That whole homeland is God’s temple, God’s sanctuary, the Holy of Holies, into which nothing unclean can be admitted. While one lives here, nothing unclean ought to be admitted into God’s temple, where his name is invoked; but into that temple of God not made with hands, where his face is seen, nothing unclean can be admitted. [Col. 0968C]

“And he who sits upon the throne dwells over them.” He who sits upon the throne dwells both in them and over them, for they are both his house and his throne. He dwells in them as their life; he dwells over them as their adornment and glory.

“They shall hunger no more, neither thirst any more; neither shall the sun fall upon them, nor any heat; for the Lamb who is in the midst of the throne shall rule them and lead them to springs of the waters of life. And God shall wipe away [Col. 0968D] every tear from their eyes.” Isaiah speaks in almost the same words and with the same meaning: “They shall hunger no more, neither thirst any more; neither heat nor sun shall strike them, because he who has mercy on them shall rule them and shall give them drink from springs of waters” (Isa. XLIX). For what he said, “Behold, these shall come from afar; and these from the north and the sea; and these from the southern land” (ibid.), is what this passage says: the multitude he saw was from all nations, tribes, peoples, and tongues.

Likewise, when the Lord said, “Do not fear those who kill the body,” he immediately added, “and after this they have nothing more that they can do” (Luke XII). This passage magnifies that statement wonderfully when it says: “They shall hunger no more, neither thirst any more; neither shall the sun fall upon them, nor any heat.” For it was once in the power [Col. 0969A] of those persecutors or murderers to make the saints hungry and thirsty, and to afflict them with heat and cold—“wandering about,” as the Apostle says, “in sheepskins and goatskins, needy, distressed, afflicted, wandering in deserts, and mountains, and caves, and caverns of the earth” (Heb. XI). But it will no longer be in their power to do this.

Yet the saints will no longer hunger or thirst with that praiseworthy hunger and good thirst which they had here, concerning which the Lord says: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness”; for there they shall be satisfied and made drunk (Matt. V). Finally, the springs of waters to which the Lamb, who rules them, shall lead them are those springs—or that spring and torrent—which the Psalmist beheld when he said: [Col. 0969B] “They shall be made drunk from the abundance of your house, and you shall give them drink from the torrent of your delight, for with you is the spring of life” (Ps. XXXV).

Who can suffice to explain these things? Who can worthily treat or expound them? Indeed, who can comprehend them in thought? What kind, or how great, an affection of divine love Scripture endeavors to disclose to us by saying: “And God shall wipe away every tear from their eyes”! We fail in this astonishment, “because eye has not seen, nor ear heard, neither has it entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him” (Isa. LXIV; I Cor. II).

[CHAP. VIII.] “And when he had opened the seventh seal, there was silence in heaven for about half an hour.” When he who ascended into heaven and [Col. 0969C] sits at the right hand of God comes to judge the living and the dead, then the seventh seal will be opened, because no small or slight matter of the Scriptures will be fulfilled. For example, the prophet Zephaniah says of that day of judgment: “Near is the great 411 day of the Lord, near and very swift. Bitter is the voice of the day of the Lord; the mighty man shall be distressed there. That day is a day of wrath, a day of tribulation and distress, a day of calamity and misery, a day of darkness and gloom, a day [Col. 0970A] of cloud and whirlwind, a day of trumpet and alarm, against fortified cities and against lofty corners. And I shall distress men, and they shall walk as blind men, because they have sinned against the Lord. And their blood shall be poured out like earth, and their bodies like dung. Their silver also and their gold shall not be able to deliver them on the day of the Lord’s wrath. In the fire of his zeal the whole earth shall be devoured, because he shall make a swift destruction of all who dwell on the earth” (Zeph. I).

These and similar things which are read throughout the Scriptures will then be fulfilled, and then the end shall come, because then all things shall be completed. He says therefore: “There was silence in heaven for about half an hour.” This silence is rightly understood here to signify that rest of which the Psalmist speaks: “The earth trembled [Col. 0970B] and was still, when God arose in judgment, to save all the meek of the earth.” For he first said: “You caused judgment to be heard from heaven” (Ps. LXXV), using the past tense prophetically for the future. And the sense is: When, coming from heaven, you make judgment heard, saying to the righteous, “Come, blessed of my Father” (Matt. XXV), etc., then the earth trembled and was still; that is, the wicked shall fear and cease from doing evil.

And the saints too, who now cry beneath God’s altar, as written above, saying: “How long, Lord, do you not judge and avenge our blood?” (Rev. VI), shall then rest and put an end to their cry, because it shall then be accomplished, then judgment shall have been rendered, their murderers having been removed from every side so that they can kill no more. Such silence or rest in heaven—that is, in the heavenly Church, to endure without end—was signified by that silence. But his saying “as though half an hour” sufficiently signifies the peace and rest just described, and also serves to distinguish what has gone before from what follows, because now the order is recapitulated from another beginning of the mysteries or revelation.

## BOOK FIVE

[Col. 0969]

[Col. 0969D] “And I saw seven angels standing in the sight of God, and seven trumpets were given to them. And behold, another angel came and stood before the altar, having a golden censer in his hand.” Just as Christ truly said that persecutors kill the body but cannot kill the soul (Matt. X), so Christ’s Apostle truly said: “I labor even unto chains, but the word of God is not bound” (II Tim. II). For behold: while this disciple of Christ labors even to exile, and is shut up bodily on a narrow island, the word of God, free and unimpeded, carries his free soul through the broad expanses of ages; his soul is enlarged in all its breadth, so that through thousands of years, through almost all the Scriptures’ [Col. 0970D] many as it were milestones, he beholds before him the mystical accounts of God’s works arranged in order. It leads and brings him back from the first ages to the last, and from the last to the former ages: namely, from the opening of the final seal, which will be opened on the last day, to the first trumpet which sounded after the Flood for the destruction of sin, to establish that God cares about human sins and will judge all people on the last day.

It is laborious and most beautiful to demonstrate from the Scriptures where, when, or how each of these angels sounded his trumpet; what third part of the earth was burned by fiery hail; what great mountain was cast into the sea, and what third part [Col. 0971A] of the sea or of created life died; what third part of the rivers was made bitter or changed into wormwood; what third part of the sun or stars was struck and darkened, and whose; what the pit of the abyss was, and how the star falling from heaven opened it; from where the smoke rose and the locusts came out; who were the four angels bound in the great river Euphrates but loosed at the voice of God’s command; what the final Woe is; and what are the voices saying: “The kingdom of this world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign for ages of ages.” It is laborious, I say, to demonstrate all these things from definite passages of Scripture, as preceding the final day of the great judgment by clear testimonies.

Moreover, it must now be understood here that when the plagues already mentioned began to occur, there was at the same time no lack of a preparation of mercy, unto faith in, or confirmation of, the coming judgment of God [Col. 0971B]. This preparation of mercy is always at hand for those fleeing that judgment, and meets all.
