Thus, fittingly, where it is said, “And I saw seven angels, and seven trumpets were given to them,” before any one of them sounded a trumpet, “behold,” he says, “another angel came and stood before the altar, having a golden censer,” etc. For this angel—or the act or bearing of this angel—signifies the priesthood of Christ, the merciful and faithful high priest. It had already begun to be prefigured there where the angels’ trumpets and plagues began to occur, as the course of our discourse will, as far as possible, explain.

Therefore, just as in the foregoing seven completed seals of the book we acknowledge that the Spirit of understanding worked, so in these seven trumpets of the angels, and in that other angel having a censer [Col. 0971C], we acknowledge that the Spirit of counsel worked, or works. Hence, after the trumpet-sound of the sixth angel, the mighty angel raises his hand to heaven, swearing by him who lives for ages of ages that, in the days of the voice of the seventh angel, when he begins to sound the trumpet, the mystery of God will be completed. Here “mystery” means the same as “secret counsel.”

And this was truly the great counsel of the great God: that he willed the final judgment by fire not to come so suddenly or unexpectedly as that earlier judgment accomplished through water; rather, he sent beforehand many things pertaining to that same judgment, through which there could be no doubt that it would come—mercy accompanying them everywhere on behalf of those whom he foresaw would repent, or were about to repent, before that judgment itself. Since, therefore, in this recapitulation we have abundant material concerning mercy and judgment, from which a great discourse would rightly arise for us, unless we are too weak for speaking, let us first speak of the instrument of mercy, according to this angel’s manner or bearing. The matter itself now seems to demand that we first inquire who this angel is thought to be in his own person; then we shall say whose figure he bears, or whom he signifies, according to the interpretation long commended by the public usage of holy Church.

Many testimonies of the holy Scriptures commend the devout and kindly concern of all angels toward the human race. For example, there is that evangelical saying: “I tell you, there will be joy before the angels of God over one sinner repenting” (Luke 15). Rejoicing together in our redemption, they solemnize and exult at the Lord’s birth in a great multitude, proclaiming in song and singing in proclamation, “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2; Matt. 2). When the Lord rose again and likewise ascended into heaven (Acts 1), they appeared in white garments, celebrating the feast of our salvation and hastening to announce to our faith that it must be celebrated.

Nevertheless, above all others Michael and Gabriel stand before the Lord for us: they labor for our sake and go to and fro in our assistance, as both the Old and the New Testament testify. For in the Old Testament Daniel heard a voice saying to him [Col. 0972B], “Gabriel, make this vision understood” (Dan. 8). The Jews maintain that this man who commanded Gabriel to speak, so that he might make Daniel understand the vision, was Michael. Then, because the vision concerned battles and conflicts of kings—indeed, the succession of kingdoms—Gabriel, who is set over battles, is assigned to this office. For Gabriel is translated in our language as “strength” or “mighty one of God.”

Accordingly, at the time when the Lord was to be born, to declare war upon demons, and to triumph over the world, Gabriel came to Zechariah and to Mary (Luke 1). Later we read in the Psalms concerning the Lord’s triumph: “Who is this King of glory? The Lord strong and mighty; the Lord strong, he is the King of glory” (Ps. 23). Concerning him the same prophet says in another vision: “While I was still speaking in prayer, behold, the man Gabriel, whom I had seen in the vision at the beginning, flying swiftly, touched me at the time of the evening sacrifice and instructed me” (Dan. 9) [Col. 0972C].

But where prosperity is promised to the people, and propitiation or expiation is necessary, Michael is sent, whose name is interpreted, “Who is like God?” Hence this: “But the prince of the kingdom of the Persians resisted me for twenty-one days; and behold, Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me” (Dan. 10). Likewise, shortly afterward: “Nevertheless I will tell you what is set forth in the writing of truth, and there is no helper with me in all these things except Michael, your prince” (ibid.). Finally, when he says, “Unless Michael, your associate, is my helper,” one must understand [Col. 0972D]: in asking God for you, in offering your prayers to God.

In the New Testament, Gabriel performs the office of announcing the Lord’s incarnation (Luke 1), and Michael is declared, in this very Apocalypse, to be a prince in battle against the devil. For, he says, “There was a great battle in heaven: Michael and his angels fought with the dragon” (Rev. 12), etc. Therefore, since, as has been said, all the angels’ vigilant and benevolent concern for us human beings is devout, this must be judged especially true of these angels, whom the celebrated proclamation of both Testaments—the Old and the New—so prominently identifies by name in matters so great.

Moreover, of these most excellent beings Michael is greatest for us, since by the testimony of the other angel he both is called and is our prince: prince in battle, prince in the aid of prayer. Until the end of the age this prince rules over the people of God, as the same angel testifies when he said to Daniel: “At that time Michael, the great prince who stands for the sons of your people, shall arise; and there shall come a time such as has not been since nations began to exist, even to that time” (Dan. 12) [Col. 0973A]. When Daniel is told, “for the sons of your people,” we rightly understand ourselves, because surely we too, whoever are of Abraham’s faith, together with Daniel and with all who are children of Abraham not only according to the flesh but also according to faith, are and are called one people by the authority of Scripture (Rom. 4).

With these testimonies concurring, we truly acknowledge and say that this angel who stood in such a form beside the altar of the temple is Michael our prince, the archangel. We do not doubt that throughout all the ages before the child who is called, and is, the Angel of great counsel was born to us of the Virgin—before, that is, from the time that nations began, from the time Abraham believed God and it was reckoned to him as righteousness (Gen. 15)—this angel stood for the sons of that people and was their helper [Col. 0973B].

From the time Abraham believed God, as has been said, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness, “this angel stood beside the altar of the temple, having a golden censer in his hand.” We have not yet addressed the significance of his standing, of which we shall speak later; rather, we intend to recount the acts of his assistance, whereby the prince in his own person helped the former people. Beside what altar, then, or beside the altar of what temple, do we understand him to have stood? Surely the holy temple of God is the holy universal Church, and the altar of this temple is Christ.

As the visible altar in a man-made temple surpasses all else in dignity of worship, so Christ, God and man, excels in his Church in divine and royal majesty alike. How did this angel stand beside such an altar? At the very time when that altar was first founded in its temple: when Christ was placed through faith in the hearts of the fathers who believed this word, “And in your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22)—which seed is certainly Christ. From that time this angel was made prince of that nation; therefore he is rightly said to have stood beside the altar [Col. 0973C], because on account of such faith he was given as guardian and helper to that people.

“He stood,” therefore, he says, “having a golden censer in his hand.” The holy, pure, golden faith of that people was the golden censer: faith tested, like gold in the furnace of fire, by the many tribulations of those journeying upon the earth. He held their faith like a censer in his hand—that is, he had it itself as their ground of righteousness for obtaining God’s benefits. Hence it follows:

“And much incense was given to him, that he might offer it from the prayers of all the saints upon the golden altar which is before the throne.” What he wishes to be understood by “incense,” he himself explains by saying, “that he might offer it from the prayers of all the saints upon the golden altar.” Therefore the incense given to him is the prayers of the saints [Col. 0974A]. But what did those saints pray for, over whom this angel was prince in such a ministry, as prophetic truth establishes? What did they pray for, or for what cause did they chiefly make prayers?

The divine pages are indeed full of the cries, rather than prayers, of those who know how to call upon God only in necessity and for temporal deliverance. For example: “The king of Egypt died, and the children of Israel, groaning because of their labors, cried out to the Lord. Their cry concerning their labors went up to the Lord, and he heard their groaning” (Exod. 2). Again: “The Lord was angry with Israel, gave them into his hands, and they served him; and they cried out to the Lord, who raised up saviors for them and delivered them” (Judg. 3) [Col. 0974B]. The divine pages, I say, are full of such cries of theirs.

But were these cries alone all the prayers of the saints, and all the incense given to this angel? If they worshiped nothing else, were their prayers worthy to be called incense and burned before the altar, or before the throne, in God’s sight? Therefore, the prayers of the holy fathers or patriarchs which deserved here to be called incense were those they poured out on account of Christ: for attaining his coming, promised to the great patriarch Abraham, so that in him they might be blessed together with all nations or kindreds of the earth (Gen. 22), and be released from the curse of the first transgression.

Holy David plainly pursues this above all in the Psalms which he sings in prayer. Indeed, because of this very intention, he judges his prayers worthy of such dignity that he utters many psalms in the person of him whose coming he longs for, as their meaning clearly shows to attentive readers. For example: “O God, do not be silent concerning my praise,” etc.—that is, “O God, do not be silent concerning the praise of Christ your Son, because the mouth of the sinner and the mouth of the deceitful man have been opened against him. They have spoken against him with a deceitful tongue; they surrounded him with words of hatred, and assailed him without cause” (Ps. 108) [Col. 0974C].

Accordingly, knowing that these and similar prayers are truly incense, in one place, after saying, “Lord, I have cried to you; hear me. Attend to my voice when I cry to you,” he immediately added: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight” (Ps. 140) [Col. 0974D]. The sense is: Do this, that my prayer may be directed—not in the sight of people, who think a prayer directed when it seeks bodily health, riches, and the like—but in your sight, in that which pleases you. This is the same as saying: Make me pray for what ought to be prayed for. It follows, therefore:

“And the smoke of the incense from the prayers of the saints ascended from the hand of the angel before God.” The smoke of the incense is the most sweet affection of the holy prayers. By faith working through love, it becomes sweet and rises before God, just as incense, melting under consuming fire, produces fragrant smoke, breathing upon open nostrils the sensation of its innate sweetness as it rises upward [Col. 0975A]. By a beautiful ascent, smoke of this kind rises so far: from the prayers of the saints to the angel’s hand; from the angel’s hand, it rises before God. What follows?

“And the angel took the censer, filled it with fire from the altar, and cast it upon the earth. And there were thunders, voices, lightnings, and a great earthquake.” This golden censer, the smoke of incense, and the hand of the mediating angel obtained this: that the censer, filled with fire from the altar, should be cast upon the earth, and that there should be “thunders, voices, lightnings, and a great earthquake.” This, I say, to put it more plainly, was merited by the golden faith of the holy fathers: that such great signs and wonders should be done among that people, by which Egypt was crushed, Pharaoh was drowned with his chariots and horsemen while the children of Israel passed through the midst of the sea (Exod. 14); and that there should occur on Mount Sinai what is written: “The third day had now come, and morning had grown bright; and behold, thunders began to be heard and lightnings to flash, while a very dense cloud covered the mountain, and the blast of the trumpet sounded exceedingly loud; and the people who were in the camp were afraid” (Exod. 19) [Col. 0975B].

With a more sacred interpretation reserved, Moses, the man of God, looking to this when blessing the children of Israel, said: “The Lord came from Sinai, and rose upon us from Seir. He appeared from Mount Paran, and with him were thousands of saints. In his right hand was a fiery law” (Deut. 33). He called it a fiery law, so that you may not doubt that the fire which this angel cast upon the earth should rightly be understood as the law. And what is a fiery law except the law of the Spirit of God—who is customarily signified by fire—written down and burning with most ardent zeal against persistent sins?

That this fire was sent into the earth by the angelic hand, and that this fiery law was administered through angels, Stephen the protomartyr plainly declares in the Acts of the Apostles: “They killed those who foretold the coming of the Just One, of whom you have now been betrayers and murderers—you who received the law by the ordering of angels and did not keep it” (Acts 7) [Col. 0975C]. What could be clearer than this testimony? “You received,” he says, “the law by the ordering of angels.” The Apostle too, writing to the Galatians, says: “Why then the law? It was established because of transgression, until the seed should come to whom the promise had been made; it was ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator” (Gal. 3).

By whose hand, or of what mediator? Surely by the hand of the mediator, the Angel of great counsel, who is now the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus. For the aforementioned protomartyr plainly indicates him in the Acts of the Apostles, saying: “God sent this Moses as ruler and redeemer with the hand of the Angel who appeared to him in the bush” (Acts 7; Exod. 3) [Col. 0975D]. And the prophet Malachi expresses more clearly who or how great this Angel is when he says: “And immediately the Lord whom you seek, and the Angel of the covenant whom you desire, shall come to his temple” (Mal. 3).

Therefore, just as there were several angels through whose disposition or ordering the promise was made to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and the law was given [Col. 0976A], so this archangel Michael—who by prophetic authority is said to have been prince of that people—must by no means be believed to have been absent from so great a work. Although there he is silent concerning clear indications of his own person, elsewhere he is not silent. For when Joshua was in the field of the city of Jericho, “he lifted his eyes and saw a man standing before him, holding a drawn sword. He went to him and said, ‘Are you on our side, or on our enemies’?’ He answered, ‘No; rather, I am the prince of the army of the Lord, and now I have come’” (Josh. 5).

Certainly, his statement, “I am the prince of the army of the Lord,” would not have been an adequate description of the person of this archangel Michael unless it had been supplemented by the prophetic authority mentioned above, in which that other angel said, “There is no helper with me in all these things except Michael, your prince” (Dan. 10) [Col. 0976B]. And elsewhere: “At that time Michael, the great prince who stands for the sons of your people, shall arise” (Dan. 12).

There are very many more things than the scope of our present subject permits us to recount—things accomplished through the ministry of this prince, as the holy Scriptures contain. From all these, this great prince, because they were arranged through him, received the name Michael, which is interpreted “Who is like God?” For what else is indicated by this name except that no one but God can do such things as were done through him? The Psalmist too, seeing this, says: “What god is great like our God? You are God, who works wonders” (Ps. 76), etc. It must finally be understood [Col. 0976C] that this angel was a mediator not in reality, but only in signification.

For the same Apostle, as we have recalled above, said: “The law was established because of transgressors, until the seed should come to whom the promise had been made, ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator” (Gal. 3). Elsewhere he says: “There is one God, and one mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Tim. 2). Therefore we must now say how he was a mediator in signification—that is, how, according to this vision, he signified the mediator between God and human beings: “The angel came,” he says, “and stood before the altar, having a golden censer in his hand.”

That the Angel is Christ, the Son of God—the Angel, that is, messenger, of great counsel (Isa. 9)—is established not only by prophetic but also by legal authority. For God says to Moses: “Behold, I shall send an Angel before you, to guard you on the way and bring you into the place which I have prepared. Observe him and obey his voice; do not think him to be despised, because he will not pardon you when you sin, and my name is in him” (Exod. 23) [Col. 0976D]. For the Angel in whom the name of God must be—that is, who may rightly be called God or Lord—is the one and only God, Christ the Son of God.

“He came,” he says: namely, into this world through the mystery of the incarnation. For because he came in this manner and announced the Father’s will to us, he is called, and is, an angel. “And when he came he stood before the altar, having a golden censer in his hand.” How did he stand before the altar, except by presenting himself as ready to undergo the work of voluntary obedience? Though as God he could have protected himself by his own hand, as man he allowed himself to be found weak and seized; and praying to the Father, he said: “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” (Matt. 26; Luke 22) [Col. 0977A].

Thus, without defending himself, he stood before the altar, namely, “like a sheep led to slaughter,” and did not open his mouth (Isa. 53). In this manner he stood, holding a golden censer in his hand: that is, appearing in the sight of the Church, himself made a censer, so that upon the altar of the cross he might offer to the Father for us his golden censer—his immaculate body, conceived of the Holy Spirit. “And much incense was given to him, that he might offer it from the prayers of all the saints upon the altar which is before the throne.”

He offered incense from the prayers of the saints. For the Church herself offered him her prayers, saying: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight” (Ps. 140). To be said to have received from the prayers of the saints is the same as to have offered them, because through him the prayers of all can sweetly come to the Lord [Col. 0977B]. “And the smoke of the incense from the prayers of the saints ascended from the hand of the Angel before God”: when Christ the Lord offered himself as a sacrifice of sweetness, the compunction of the saints’ hearts was made acceptable. Born from inward fire, it is like smoke that commonly draws forth tears.

“And the angel took the censer and filled it with fire from the altar.” He appropriately presents the censer as full of fire. “For God does not give the Spirit by measure” (John 3). We know this to have been fulfilled properly in Christ’s humanity, “in whom all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Col. 2). “And he cast it upon the earth.” Thus the Lord says in the Gospel: “I came to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke 12).—“And there were thunders, voices, lightnings, and an earthquake.” The thunders are heavenly threats; the voices, exhortations; the lightnings, the splendors of miracles; the earthquake, so that some followed him while others opposed: the former saying, “He is good,” the latter, “No, he deceives the crowds” (John 7) [Col. 0977C].

Now let us return to the sequence. We said above that, just as in the preceding matters, after the seven seals of the book were completed, we acknowledge that the Spirit of understanding worked, so in these seven trumpets of the angels and in that other angel having a censer, we acknowledge that the Spirit of counsel worked, or works. Yet the counsel of God itself was, or is, great and wonderful in this: that he willed the final judgment by fire not to happen suddenly or unexpectedly, as that other judgment by water occurred; but he sent beforehand many things pertaining to the same judgment, through which there could be no doubt it would come, with mercy accompanying them everywhere for those whom he foresaw would repent, or were about to repent, before that judgment itself.

Therefore, when this angel stood, as has already been said, given as prince to Abraham and his seed, holding the censer and prepared to receive the incense of prayers in order to obtain for them the assistance of mercy [Col. 0977D]:

[Col. 0978A] “Then seven trumpets were given to the seven angels, and they prepared themselves to sound the trumpet.” That is, to thunder judgment against the sins of the nations which, at that same time, began to follow their own ways. Trumpets, I say, were given to them in order to stir up the world to fight for God against senseless people, so that by the very things through which they sinned, they might also be punished (Wis. 5).

“And the first angel sounded the trumpet, and hail and fire mixed with blood came to be, and it was cast upon the earth; and a third part of the earth was burned up, and a third part of the trees was burned up, and all green grass was burned up.” The sounding of the first angel, or of the first trumpet, was that cry concerning which the Lord spoke in this way to the aforesaid patriarch Abraham: “The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah has multiplied, and their sin is exceedingly grievous. I will go down and see whether they have completed in deed the cry that has come to me; or whether it is not so, that I may know” (Gen. 18) [Col. 0978B].

Indeed, through the angels appointed for us, our deeds are reported daily, by night and by day, to the Lord our Creator. If, therefore, the deed we do is great, when it is reported, that very report is like the sound of a trumpet, like a great cry. Whether it is an extremely great sin or a forceful prayer, it is a cry before God. For he who said, “The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah has multiplied,” says elsewhere: “I have seen the affliction of my people, and I have heard their cry” (Exod. 3).

Therefore, while the first angel’s trumpet sounded, hail came to be, etc. Who does not know when or how this occurred? “For the Lord rained sulphur and fire upon Sodom and Gomorrah, and overthrew these cities, and all the surrounding region, all the inhabitants of the cities, and every green thing of the earth” (Gen. 19) [Col. 0978C]. Indeed, by “earth,” “trees,” and “grass,” human beings are to be understood, on the well-known authority of Scripture. By “earth,” for example, when God says: “Because you are dust, and to dust you shall return” (Gen. 3), or, “You are earth, and to earth you shall go.” And elsewhere: “Why are you proud, earth and ashes?” (Ecclus. 10). By “trees,” when the Lord himself said: “There is no good tree which bears bad fruit, nor a bad tree bearing good fruit” (Matt. 7; Luke 6). By “grass,” when the Lord says through the prophet: “Cry out: All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass. The grass has withered and the flower has fallen, but the word of the Lord remains forever” (Isa. 40) [Col. 0978D].

Therefore, the earth, trees, and green grass were the Sodomite people: greedy, proud, insolent—indeed, lustful. But why are they called a third part of the earth or trees, that is, of human beings? For a twofold reason: because they were both of Ham’s stock and unrepentant. For the race of Ham is rightly called, and is, the third part of humankind, since there were three sons of Noah who went forth from the ark: Shem, Ham, and Japheth. Now Ham himself is the father of Canaan, among whose descendants the Sodomites were dispersed, as it is written: “Through these the peoples of the Canaanites were dispersed. The boundaries of Canaan extended from Sidon as you come to Gerar, as far as Gaza, until you enter Sodom and Gomorrah, and Admah and Zeboiim, as far as Lasha” (Gen. 10) [Col. 0979A].

Therefore, by nature—that is, by lineage or nation—they were a third part, that is, from the third part of humankind, since they were of the stock of the cursed Canaan, one of Ham’s descendants. Their father said: “Cursed be Canaan; he shall be a servant of servants to his brothers” (Gen. 9). This is one reason why the Sodomites are rightly called a third part of the earth or a third part of the trees.

The other reason is that, as has already been said, they were unrepentant, proclaiming their sin and not concealing it (Prov. 21). Hence, up to the present, the following reason is given why those who rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the most wicked things are condemned by God the judge: “Because,” he says, “they proclaimed their sin like Sodom and did not conceal it” (Isa. 3) [Col. 0979B]. For the unrepentant are the third part of humankind in such a way that the righteous who ought worthily to preach, and the sinners who hear and are converted by their preaching, are not doubted to save their souls; and the sole remaining part, the unrepentant, must without doubt be sent into Gehenna.

“And the second angel sounded the trumpet, and something like a great mountain burning with fire was cast into the sea; and a third part of the sea became blood, and a third part of the creatures which have souls died, and a third part of the ships perished.” Then the second angel sounded the trumpet, when, after the king of Egypt had died, the children of Israel, groaning because of their labors, cried out to the Lord, and their cry concerning their labors went up to God, and he heard their groaning. “But while this trumpet sounded, something like a great mountain burning with fire,” he says, “was cast into the sea.” — “For Scripture says: God remembered the covenant which he had made with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, looked upon the children of Israel, and delivered them” (Exod. 1, 3) [Col. 0979C].

How did he deliver them? “Stretch out your hand,” he says, “over the sea, and let the waters return upon the Egyptians, upon their chariots and horsemen. And the waters returned and covered the chariots and horsemen, the whole army of Pharaoh, who had entered the sea in pursuit; not even one of them remained” (Exod. 2, 4). Therefore something like a great mountain burning with fire was cast into the sea: namely, Pharaoh with his chariots, an exemplar of diabolical pride. For pride is signified by the name of a mountain; burning fire signifies the envy of Pharaoh and the Egyptians.

For Jethro, Moses’ kinsman, likewise spoke of their pride. After saying, “Blessed be the Lord, who delivered you from the hand of the Egyptians and from the hand of Pharaoh, who rescued his people from the hand of Egypt,” he immediately added: “Now I know that the Lord is great above all gods, because they acted proudly against them” (Exod. 18) [Col. 0979D]. Pharaoh himself sufficiently indicates the burning fire of his envy when, at the beginning, he says: “Behold, the people of the children of Israel are many and stronger than we are. Come, let us oppress them wisely, lest perhaps they multiply” (Exod. 1).

By “sea” the nations are signified here, just as in the Psalm where it says: “The mountains shall be moved into the heart of the sea” (Ps. 45). This is the same as saying: the apostles will pass from the Jews into the midst of the nations. By “ships” too the transitory life of human beings is signified, as in Job: “My days have passed like ships carrying apples” (Job 9) [Col. 0980A]. Thus here also by a third part of the sea or ships, just as above by a third part of the earth and trees, the third part of humankind is rightly understood: namely, the progeny of Ham. For the Egyptians arose from Mizraim, one of Ham’s descendants.

For it is written: “The sons of Ham were Cush, Mizraim, Put, and Canaan”; and then: “Mizraim begot Ludim, Anamim, Lehabim, Naphtuhim, Pathrusim, and Casluhim, from whom came the Philistines, and Caphtorim” (Gen. 10) [Col. 0980B]. The ancients report that the Egyptians too, as has been said, descended from this Mizraim. The Psalmist likewise maintains that Ham, their father, was father of the Egyptians when he says: “He struck every firstborn in the land of Egypt, the first-fruits of all their labor in the tents of Ham” (Pss. 77 and 104), that is, where the children of Ham, Noah’s son, dwell.

Nevertheless, the Egyptians were a third part for another reason also: they too were unrepentant, so much so that, when signs and wonders were multiplied before them, they became yet more hardened. For they hated and envied the children of Israel; and therefore, as is characteristic of those who hate and envy, the more signs they saw performed for them—which were Israel’s glory—the harder they became, as the greatness of their hatred increased with each sign [Col. 0980C]. Foreseeing this, the Lord himself said to Moses: “I will harden his heart, and he will not let the people go” (Exod. 7). This is the same as saying: I shall indeed perform signs before him, but these will avail him for nothing else than that the envy of one who hates may grow, and the hatred of one who envies may increase.

Therefore they were unrepentant; and since, as has been said, there are three parts of humankind—some righteous, others repentant, others unrepentant—these, because they belonged to the unrepentant, belonged to the third part. What is said here, that “a third part of the sea became blood,” since the sea, as has already been said, signifies nations—this statement, I say, that a third part of the sea and a third part that had souls died, plainly refers to the fact that he struck the water of the river before Pharaoh and his servants (Exod. 7), so that it was changed into blood; the fish that were in the river died; and he also consumed their cattle with fire and hail (Exod. 9) [Col. 0980D].

Hence the Psalmist says: “He turned their waters into blood and killed their fish.” And then: “He gave their cattle over to hail.” Again: “He made a path for his wrath and did not spare their souls from death, and shut up their cattle in death.” And again: “He struck the firstborn of Egypt, from human being to beast” (Pss. 77 and 104). Therefore, according to the letter, the third part of humankind—that is, Ham’s race, one of Noah’s three sons—was struck a second time. For we chiefly intend to show historical inflictions [Col. 0981A].

“And the third angel sounded the trumpet. And a great star, burning like a torch, fell from heaven; and it fell upon a third part of the rivers and upon springs of waters; and the name of the star is called Wormwood. And a third part of the waters became wormwood, and many people died from the waters, because they had become bitter.” By “rivers” also nations are signified, as there: “The rivers lifted up their waves, at the voices of many waters” (Ps. 92). That is to say: hostile nations shall raise certain disturbances like waves—namely, threats, blows, and such things—and they shall do this because of the voices of many waters: that is, because of the voices of those preaching Christ’s Gospel, or because of the noisy accusations of many persons [Col. 0981B] who say amid popular tumult (Acts 17) that devotees of a new religion and destroyers of their gods have arrived.

Now the third part of the nations, as has been said, was Ham’s race. Therefore the third angel sounded the trumpet when, forty years after the children of Israel departed from Egypt, the iniquities of the Amorites and the other nations or kingdoms of Canaan had been completed. God’s waiting patience indicated this when, after saying to Abraham, “Know beforehand that your seed shall be a stranger in a land not its own,” and the rest, he added: “For the iniquities of the Amorites are not yet complete up to the present time” (Gen. 15).

Accordingly, while the third trumpet sounded—that is, while the cry of these people too rose to God because, by persisting in sin, they had filled up their iniquities, and the time had come when the land ought now to vomit them out [Col. 0981C].

“‘A great star fell from heaven, burning like a torch,’ he says. The star burning like a torch means that the great wrath of God fell from heaven upon those nations: the wrath of God, I say, being a star for us, but for them like a torch. For God’s wrath gives light to us and advances our knowledge of that same God; but it consumed them like a torch, so that they burned in their fury, sought no mercy, and did not surrender to the victors. For it is written: ‘There was no city that surrendered itself to the children of Israel, except the Hivite who dwells in Gibeon. Joshua took them all by war. For it had been the Lord’s judgment that their hearts should be hardened, that they should fight against Israel, fall, deserve no mercy, and perish, as the Lord had foretold Moses’ (Josh. 11) [Col. 0981D].”

“‘And it fell upon a third part of the rivers, and upon the springs of waters’: that is, upon those nations which, as has already been said, belonged to the third part of humankind, namely the race of Ham. They also belonged to the third part of humankind for another reason: namely, because they were impenitent. For three principal divisions appeared there: the righteous, that is, the children of Israel, because of the worship of God; the penitent, such as the household of Rahab the harlot, who received the messengers of the children of Israel (Josh. 2), concerning whom it is written: ‘But Joshua preserved alive Rahab the harlot, her father’s household, and everything she possessed; and they dwelt in the midst of Israel down to the present day’ (Josh. 6) [Col. 0982A]. The impenitent division, however, were those very nations. For they too had heard the mighty acts of God done in Egypt and afterward; and, because of this, ‘all the inhabitants of the land grew faint.’ Yet they did not, like Rahab and her household, turn to repentance.

“‘And the name of the star,’ he says, ‘is called Wormwood.’ *Absinthium* is the Greek name of an herb exceedingly bitter in taste, pleasant in fragrance, beneficial to the bodily constitution; its crushed leaves, by their juice, induce vomiting, and are found most useful for removing pains or bruises of the body. The wrath or judgment of God which came upon those nations is rightly compared with this herb and called by its name: it caused the land to vomit them out and, as though evil humours had been expelled, to be freed by the opening of its breast [Col. 0982B]. For he himself says concerning them: ‘The inhabitants of the land who were before you committed all these abominations and defiled it. Therefore beware lest it vomit you out also, when you do like deeds, as it vomited out the nation which was before you’ (Lev. 18 and 20). Rightly, therefore, as has been said, that falling star—that is, the judgment of God coming upon those nations—is called wormwood, since it produced such a necessary vomiting for that land.

“‘And a third part of the waters became wormwood, and many people died, because they became bitter.’ It became wormwood: that is, the cohabitation of those nations was shown to be most bitter and exceedingly harmful to the children of Israel; ‘and many of them died from the waters,’ that is, through those nations, because they ‘became bitter’ [Col. 0982C]. Thus God himself had foretold this when, through Moses, he warned Israel: ‘Take heed never to make friendships with the inhabitants of that land, lest they become your ruin. Do not make a covenant with the people of those regions, lest, when they have prostituted themselves with their gods and worshipped their images, someone invite you to eat of the sacrifices’ (Exod. 34), and so forth. For they did not heed the Lord’s prohibition, but many drank bitter waters and died: that is, they mingled with the nations, learned their works, served their carved images, and this became a stumbling-block to them.

“‘And the fourth angel sounded the trumpet, and a third part of the sun was struck, and a third part of the moon, and a third part of the stars, so that a third part of them should be darkened, and a third part of the day should not shine, and likewise of the night’ [Col. 0982D]. The hand that struck was raised from the third part of the earth, sea, and rivers to the sun, moon, and stars; and a third part of them was struck: that is, from the third part of humankind or of the nations, the race of Ham, as has often been said—those who love the earth, make themselves bitter, and continually lapse into vices and sins—it was raised against the race of Shem itself, the seed of Abraham itself, the stock of Jacob itself. For just as those who do not seek God and do not look toward heaven are, for that very reason, earth, sea, and rivers; so, conversely, the seed or children of Abraham are sun, moon, and stars.

They are the sun, namely, because of Christ, the true sun [Col. 0983A], the one seed promised to Abraham himself. They are the moon because they are the Church. They are stars because each possessed a distinct grace of the heavenly light. Foreseeing this, Moses said: ‘Today you are as numerous as the stars of heaven’ (Deut. 1). For he knew and had written that God said to Abraham: ‘Look at heaven and count the stars, if you can’; and immediately added: ‘So shall your seed be’ (Gen. 15). Moreover, to establish that under the names of sun, moon, and stars that people—that is, its fathers and mothers and every individual child—must rightly be understood, this testimony alone is sufficient: ‘I, Joseph, saw as it were the sun and moon and eleven stars worshipping me.’ When he reported this to his father, the latter said: ‘What does this dream which you have seen mean? Shall I and your mother and your brothers worship you upon the earth?’ (Gen. 37) [Col. 0983B].

Therefore ‘the fourth angel sounded the trumpet’: that is, the exceedingly aroused murmuring of the children of Israel in the wilderness, in the presence of the angel who went before them in the pillar of cloud, reached the Lord’s ears. Hence Moses said: ‘Come before the Lord, for he has heard your murmuring’ (Exod. 13). That trumpet sounded long; for a long time that terrible-sounding chant painfully struck God’s ears. Accordingly, moved by it, he said to Moses: ‘Go, descend; your people, whom you brought out of the land of Egypt, has sinned. They have quickly turned away from the way which you showed them’ (Exod. 16).

Then that trumpet most grievously struck the ears of the same Lord when the scouts returned and disparaged the land they had inspected before the children of Israel; the entire assembly cried aloud and wept, and all the children of Israel murmured against Moses and Aaron, saying: ‘Would that we had died in Egypt, and not in this vast wilderness. Would that we might perish, and that the Lord might not bring us into this land, lest we fall by the sword and our wives and children be carried away captive’ (Num. 14), and so forth [Col. 0983C]. Then indeed a third part of that sun, that moon, and those stars was struck: ‘For he swore in his wrath: “If they shall enter into my rest”’ (Ps. 94).—‘As I live,’ he says, ‘all the men who saw my majesty and the signs which I performed shall not see the land concerning which I swore to their fathers.’ And afterward: ‘As I live, says the Lord, as you have spoken in my hearing, so I shall do to you. In this wilderness your bodies shall lie, all of you who have murmured, from twenty years old and upward, and have murmured against me. [417] You shall not enter the land concerning which I raised my hand to make you dwell there, except Caleb son of Jephunneh and Joshua son of Nun’ (Num. 14) [Col. 0983D].

It is well known from the sacred histories how they perished and for what further causes they were destroyed: some were swallowed alive by the earth, some were killed by fire issuing from the Lord, and some fell by the sword (Num. 16). By their lives and their end they openly showed that they too belonged to the third part. They did not indeed belong to the third part of the human race by bodily descent—that is, to the race of Ham—as did the aforementioned Sodomites, Egyptians, and Canaanites [Col. 0984A]; but by imitation they belonged to the same division. God testifies to this when he speaks through the prophet to such an Israel: ‘Your father was an Amorite, and your mother a Hittite.’ The Amorite and Hittite belonged to the race of Ham and were children of Canaan. Therefore these persons were the third part of what was thought to be the sun, moon, and stars—that is, the people of the saints; but in truth they were the third part, that is, persons belonging to the third part of humankind or the nations: the part of Ham, the part of Canaan.

Thus it happened that this third part of the day did not shine, nor likewise of the night. That seed of Abraham, or Israelite people, insofar as it was sun and moon, was at once a bright day and a shining night. A bright day, namely, because of Christ, their kinsman, promised to the fathers, the eternal sun. A shining night, because of the favourable course of temporal affairs [Col. 0984B], the promised possession of the land of Canaan, and an earthly kingdom illuminated by many miraculous signs of God. But those unbelieving murmurers—whoever in pride spoke against God and were therefore called by God’s own mouth ‘an evil multitude,’ as when he said, ‘How long will this evil multitude murmur against me?’ (Num. 14)—deserved neither to see Christ the sun in the life to come nor the temporal inheritance of the fathers in this present life. Accordingly, this part of day and night, which was thought to belong to the bright day and shining night, because it instead belonged to that third part in which Canaan was reckoned, as has been said, did not shine and was not made bright, but left behind a dark memory.

“‘And I saw and heard the voice of one flying eagle through the midst of heaven, saying with a loud voice: Woe, woe, woe to those dwelling upon the earth, because of the remaining trumpet-sounds of the three angels who were about to sound [sing]’” [Col. 0984C]. This flying and foretelling eagle is sacred Scripture. It should be noted that no eagle foretold the preceding four strokes. For no Scripture or written law threatened or foretold to the Sodomites that they would perish by heavenly fire or a rain of sulphur; to Pharaoh and the Egyptians, that they would perish in the Red Sea; or to the Amorites, that, once their iniquities were complete, they would be punished and vomited out of their land. They were judged and condemned solely by the natural law.

Likewise, the murmuring children of Israel, whose bodies were cast down in the wilderness, had not heard Scripture foretell, nor learned by the instruction of Scripture, what punishment their murmuring and rebellion would bring upon them [Col. 0984D]. For they began to murmur before Scripture had been established or the law written; before even the first tablets of the Ten Commandments, written by the finger of God, had been made. Those tablets themselves were made before the written law, yet woe already hung over that people. For example, when the Lord said concerning the guilt of the calf made by Aaron: ‘I see that this people is stiff-necked. Let me alone, that my wrath may be angry against them and destroy them’ (Exod. 32). And when he was not left alone, because Moses stood in the breach—that is, in profound humility of mind before him—he finally said: ‘But on the day of vengeance I shall visit this sin of theirs also’ (ibid.).

The law, I say, had not yet been written, or certainly not yet recited; and therefore this flying eagle is not recorded here as having foretold this woe [Col. 0985A]. Sacred Scripture foretold the three woes which remain. The first was that which the children of Israel suffered when, sinning against the Lord, they were delivered into the hands of the nations; those who hated them ruled over them, their enemies afflicted them, and they were humbled beneath their hands. The second was what they endured when they were carried into captivity and miserably bore, because of their sins, the imperious power of four kingdoms: Babylonian, Persian, Macedonian, and Roman. The fourth of these—the Roman Empire—was the beast terrible, wondrous, and exceedingly strong, possessing great iron teeth; it devoured and crushed them and trampled the rest beneath its feet (Dan. 7) [Col. 0985B].

The third woe was the final judgment, when both those to whom the law was written and all the nations receive their due: namely, ‘Whoever sinned without the law shall perish without the law, and whoever sinned in the law shall be judged by the law’ (Rom. 2). Before these three events occurred, God willed to announce them through his Scripture; and therefore woe is rightly proclaimed here for the third time through the flying eagle, ‘because of the remaining voices of the three angels who were about to sound the trumpet.’ And to whom, or to what sort of persons, is the woe directed? ‘To those dwelling on earth,’ he says: that is, those whom the earth wholly drags down, whom earthly affection holds fast so that they do not even look upward. Sacred Scripture is rightly likened to a flying eagle—an eagle flying through the midst of heaven [Col. 0985C]—because its whole intention tends upward and despises earthly things; it fixes clear and open eyes upon the sun of righteousness, who is Christ, and proceeds openly, as something beyond reproach and honourable, with complete freedom.

## Chapter IX

“And the fifth angel sounded the trumpet, and I saw a star fallen from heaven to earth; and the key of the pit of the abyss was given to him, and he opened the pit of the abyss,” and the rest down to “the first woe has passed.” This one great and prolonged woe briefly and wonderfully recounts great and numerous evils: the mockeries of the varied servitudes of the children of Abraham. After Joshua’s death they sinned against the Lord by serving Baals and Astartes; and for this reason he delivered them into the hands of Chushan-rishathaim, king of Mesopotamia, and they served him eight years. Again they did evil in the sight of the Lord; and for this reason he strengthened Eglon king of Moab against them, and they served him eighteen years (Judg. 3). Again they added to their evil-doing, and the Lord delivered them into the hands of Jabin king of Canaan, who grievously oppressed them for twenty years (Judg. 4). Then they did evil, and therefore he delivered them into the hands of Midian for seven years (Judg. 6). Again they forsook the Lord and did not worship him, and therefore in anger he delivered them into the hands of the Philistines and the children of Ammon (Judg. 10) [Col. 0985D].

After they had at last been crushed by long conflict with these peoples, they were so liberated through the might of the victorious king David that he humbled the Philistines and the other surrounding nations, as it is written: ‘David took the bridle of tribute from the hand of the Philistines, and struck Moab’ (2 Sam. 12), and so forth [Col. 0986A]. Yet their iniquity advanced so far that ten tribes were severed from the house of David and the temple of the Lord; they made golden calves for themselves, becoming the first heretics and an example of every heretical perversity (1 Kgs. 12).

Let us now follow the order of the text. “‘And the fifth angel,’ he says, ‘sounded the trumpet, and I saw a star fallen from heaven to earth.’” That fifth angel indeed sounded the trumpet when the truth of God’s words to Moses was fulfilled: ‘Behold, you shall sleep with your fathers, and [418] this people, rising up, shall prostitute itself after foreign gods in the land into which it will enter to dwell. There it shall forsake me and make void the covenant which I made with it’ (Deut. 31). Again Moses says: ‘For I know your contentiousness and your most stiff neck. Even while I am alive and walking with you, you have always acted contentiously against the Lord; how much more when I am dead!’ And afterward: ‘For I know that after my death you will act wickedly and quickly turn away from the way which I commanded you’ (ibid.) [Col. 0986B]. The fifth angel, I say, sounded the trumpet when it was announced to the all-knowing God that Israel would prostitute itself after foreign gods.

“‘And I saw,’ he says, ‘a star fallen from heaven to earth.’” This star fallen from heaven is the devil, to whom the prophet says: ‘How you have fallen from heaven, Lucifer, who rose in the morning’ (Isa. 19). It should be noted that he did not say of such a star, “I saw it fall,” but “I saw it had fallen.” For it had fallen long before and was creeping over the earth when the events which this mystical vision recounts here began to occur [Col. 0986C]. When it fell, no human being existed to see it, except him who speaks in his Gospel, saying: ‘I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven’ (Luke 10). For Christ, who says these things as man, was God before becoming man; he was before that angel, that star, or that Lucifer fell—indeed, before any angel or creature came into being. Thus he rightly says not, “I saw [it] fall,” but, “I saw [it] had fallen.”

“‘And the key of the pit of the abyss was given to him, and he opened the pit of the abyss. And smoke rose from the pit like smoke from a great furnace.’” In mystical signification he briefly touches upon the principal cause or origin of idolatry and of every heresy. For “‘the key of the pit of the abyss was given to him’”: that is, power or opportunity was permitted to that angel, who did not stand in the truth and whose every lie has no foundation—for it rests upon no existing thing. Therefore the lie which he speaks from his own resources, and of which he is the father (John 8), is fittingly called a pit of the abyss [Col. 0986D], that is, of infinite depth, because, as has been said, it has no foundation in existing things and nothing lies beneath it: for he speaks what does not exist. He opened such a pit of the abyss to wretched human beings, saying that he was God and persuading them to worship him as God in images.

“‘And smoke rose from the pit like smoke from a great furnace.’” It rose, indeed, even to the sages of the world, whom it darkened. Of them the Apostle says: ‘They became vain in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened. Claiming to be wise, they became fools’ (Rom. 1), and so forth [Col. 0987A]. This smoke is said to be like the smoke of a great furnace because, just as smoke arises only from fire lying beneath it, so blindness of mind, or the darkening of the foolish heart, arises only from a preceding cause of desire or concupiscence.

“‘And the sun and air were darkened by the smoke of the pit.’” The vision has now reached the matter for which it had first mentioned both the fall of the star and the opening of the smoking pit of the abyss. That sun and air, as has already been said, were Israel: the sun because of the fathers, or the faith of the fathers, from whom Christ, the sun of righteousness, came according to the flesh; the air because of the illumination of that same faith subsequently received. After Joshua’s death this sun and air were darkened, so that Israel forsook the Lord, the God of its fathers, and followed foreign gods, the gods of the peoples dwelling around it (Judg. 2) [Col. 0987B]. The Lord raised up judges for them to deliver them from the hands of those ravaging them. Yet they would not heed even those judges, prostituting themselves with foreign gods and worshipping them. Thus the sun and air were darkened by the smoke of the pit. What follows?

“‘And from the smoke locusts came out upon the earth.’” Locusts came out of the smoke because, through the smoke of error and folly by which they were darkened, enemies were raised against them by divine judgment: Mesopotamians and Moabites, Canaanites and Midianites, together with Amalekites, Philistines, and the children of Ammon. Scripture says of them in one place: ‘For they and all their flocks came with their tents and filled everything like locusts: an innumerable multitude of men and camels, laying waste whatever they touched’ (Judg. 6) [Col. 0987C].

It certainly did not say “like locusts” vainly or without significance; rather, he who dwells in heaven sees and mocks such multitudes exulting in evil, leaping like so many locusts in their lightness of mind and body, foreseeing that what his Wisdom says through a certain author will soon happen to them: ‘The almond tree shall blossom, and the locust shall grow fat’ (Eccles. 12). This is as though he said: He who now walks green and upright, and leaps like a locust, will grow gray and begin scarcely to walk bent over; when his legs swell, he will no longer, light and nimble as now, spring himself into a leap. For the locust grows fat when, after the lightness of youth has passed, its legs swell, as commonly happens to old men [Col. 0987D].

“‘The locusts therefore came out’: that is, Israel’s enemies were multiplied because of its sins. ‘And power was given them, such as the scorpions of the earth have power.’” A scorpion is more a worm than an animal, or a serpent armed with a sting; it is called this in Greek because it pierces with its tail and pours out poison through its curved wound. For this reason he says “scorpions of the earth,” because the scorpion is an earthly worm: it flatters harmlessly with its mouth or head, and only then, turning its tail, strikes the unsuspecting person. Such power was given to those locusts: namely, that after they had enticed Israel into pleasures forbidden by God’s law through the blandishments of women, and had stripped them of God’s help by making them transgressors, they then rose against them with weapons [Col. 0988A].

Balak son of Zippor, king of Moab, first learned to do this through Balaam the diviner, who said to him: ‘Nevertheless, as I go to my people, I shall give counsel concerning what your people will do to this people’ (Num. 24). By his counsel the people prostituted themselves with the daughters of Moab, who invited them to their sacrifices (Num. 25). Hence afterward, when vengeance had been taken, Moses angrily said to the leaders: ‘Why have you preserved the women? Are these not those who deceived the children of Israel at Balaam’s suggestion and made you transgress against the Lord in the matter of Peor, on account of which the people was struck?’ (Num. 31). Thus the Midianite or Moabite scorpions first learned this through Balaam, and afterward other nations also [Col. 0988B].

For after Joshua’s death Scripture says: ‘Therefore the children of Israel dwelt in the midst of the Canaanite, Hittite, Amorite, Perizzite, and Jebusite; they took their daughters as wives, gave their own daughters to their sons, and served their gods’ (Judg. 3). In this act, surely, the scorpions put forward, as it were, a flattering head, but immediately struck with their tails. For afterward, being made the victors over those with whom God was angry, they grievously afflicted them.

“‘And they were commanded not to harm the grass of the earth, nor anything green, nor any tree, but only the people who do not have the sign of God upon their foreheads.’” He plainly shows that he says locusts came out of that smoke not literally but by likeness, since he writes that what locusts ordinarily do was forbidden to them. For it is the nature of locusts to harm the grass of the earth, all greenery, and every tree, as is written among the plagues of Egypt: ‘[419] Thus the vegetation of the land and every fruit of the trees which the hail had left was devoured; nothing at all green remained on trees or herbs of the earth throughout all Egypt’ (Exod. 10) [Col. 0988C].

These locusts, however, were forbidden to harm anything of this sort, but only people, because those called locusts here were themselves human beings. Nevertheless, it would later come to pass, when the sins of that people demanded it, that their enemies would harm not only persons but grass, every green thing, every tree—indeed their whole land—and set their cities on fire; but the time had not yet come. We shall recall that this occurred later, when the sixth angel sounded the trumpet. For when this fifth angel sounded the trumpet, the plague was moderated in such a way that only people were harmed and reduced to servitude.

And indeed at that time, ‘when Israel raged,’ says Scripture, ‘Midian and Amalek and the other eastern peoples came up, filling everything like locusts; just as they did among the herbs, they laid everything waste and left nothing at all pertaining to life in Israel—not sheep, not oxen, not asses’ (Judg. 6) [Col. 0988D]. But in comparison with the injury of which we must speak later, when all things were burned by Babylonian fire, this does not deserve to be called an injury. Finally, when it speaks of the people who were to be harmed, distinguishing ‘those who do not have the sign of God upon their foreheads,’ this is equivalent to saying: those who abandoned the law of their God, who were estranged from the faith of their father Abraham. For what we Christians now mark upon our foreheads as the sign of God, the sign of the cross of Jesus Christ, they had been commanded, according to their custom and time, to do by being circumcised in their flesh and marking the doorposts and lintels of their houses with the blood of the lamb (Exod. 12) [Col. 0989A]. But they scorned to do this, serving foreign gods. Thus they were people without the sign of God upon their foreheads, without faith in their hearts.

“‘And it was given to them not to kill them, but that they should be tormented for five months.’” It would later come to pass that they would be killed or fall by the sword’s edge, but the time had not yet come: this was not yet granted to those locusts. But what was granted? “‘That they should be tormented,’ he says, ‘for five months.’” The five months during which they were tormented were the five changes of servitude in which they were delivered to their enemies and served them, as Scripture sets them forth in this order. First, the Lord delivered them into the hands of Chushan-rishathaim king of Mesopotamia, and they served him eight years. Second, he strengthened Eglon king of Moab against them and joined to him the children of Ammon and Amalek; they served him eighteen years (Judg. 3). Third, he delivered them into the hands of Jabin king of Canaan, who oppressed them for twenty years (Judg. 4). Fourth, ‘he delivered them into the hands of Midian for seven years, and they were greatly oppressed by them’ (Judg. 6) [Col. 0989C]. Fifth, he delivered them into the hands of the Philistines, by whom they were crushed with various afflictions (Judg. 10), until David came, who, ‘as Scripture says, took the bridle of tribute from the hand of the Philistines’ (2 Sam. 8).

The evils which Israel subsequently endured because of its sins, from the time of the Babylonian captivity, belong to the trumpet-sound of the sixth angel. Therefore they were tormented for five months because they were delivered into servitude five times. Why, however, are those periods of servitude denoted by the name or number of months rather than years? Namely, because the months according to the moon—the only months which the Hebrews, of whom the discussion concerns, knew or reckoned—display change through waxing and waning. This signifies also the mutability of fools, as Scripture says: ‘The fool changes like the moon’ (Ecclus. 27) [Col. 0989D].

Did not they change like the moon, so that they were rightly reproved for folly? For it is written concerning them: ‘When the Lord raised up judges in their days, mercy was renewed, and he heard the groans of the afflicted and delivered them from the slaughter of their ravagers’ (Judg. 2). But after the judge died, they returned and did many things worse than their fathers, following foreign gods, serving them, and worshipping them. Therefore the statement, “but that they should be tormented for five months,” is equivalent to saying: that, changed into folly five times, they should in turn be reduced to servitude five times.

“‘And their torment was like the torment of a scorpion when it strikes a person.’” This is the same as what he said above: ‘And power was given to them, such as the scorpions of the earth have power.’ For just as the scorpion first flatters with its head and then, striking with its tail, pours out deadly poison, so they first enticed them to sacrificial pleasures and marriage with their daughters, so that God might be offended; then they rose armed against those who were unarmed and, as it were, naked, when God’s assistance—by which they were protected as with weapons and a shield—was absent [Col. 0990A]. But he now repeats the comparison with scorpions and locusts because he is about to say more concerning it.

“‘And in those days people shall seek death and shall not find it; they shall desire to die, and death shall flee from them.’” You should rightly understand these words as spoken, as it were, by the aforesaid flying eagle, which says: ‘Woe, woe, woe, because of the three angels who were about to sound the trumpet’ (Rev. 8), of which this is the first woe [Col. 0990B]. It is as though it said: This woe shall be so great that ‘people shall seek death and not find it; they shall desire to die and death shall flee from them’: that is, death shall be dearer to them than life, and they shall wish to end their long misery by a short way.

Why? Because they had already begun at that time to store up such wrath for themselves, when they vainly wished for death while no cause existed and nothing harmed them. For they said: ‘Would that we had died in Egypt and not in this vast wilderness. Would that we might perish and that the Lord might not bring us into this land, and that we might not fall by the sword and our wives and children be carried away captive’ (Num. 14). Then they wished for death, as their speech sounded because of the exceeding bitterness and rancour of an impatient spirit [Col. 0990C]. As their sins increased, it would happen that they would wish to die for good reason, and death would flee from them, because the locusts were commanded not to kill them but to torment them for five months.

“‘And the likeness of the locusts was like horses prepared for battle.’” What is more unlike in reality or nature than horses and locusts? What is so unequal and disproportionate? Either the locusts grew to the size of horses, or, more wonderfully, these human beings became so small that the locusts appeared, by comparison with them, to possess the size of horses. Clearly, it is established that what I said second happened by God’s judgment: not through a decrease or diminishment of their bodies, but through a failure of their souls. Those who, by reason of their contemptible life, were locusts in the Lord’s eyes remained what they were—namely, the wanton Canaanite peoples. But those who ought to have been human beings were deservedly diminished and in some sense became locusts of locusts, fearing those whom they ought themselves to have caused to fear [Col. 0990D].

For the Judge repaid them in kind, because they were children of their slanderous and murmuring fathers and followed their sins. Those fathers had disparaged that same land, saying: ‘The people whom we saw are of lofty stature. There we saw certain monsters, the sons of Anak, of the race of giants; compared with them, we seemed like locusts’ (Num. 13). Therefore, as it were in prosecution of their own words, God then said to them: ‘As you have spoken in my hearing, so I shall do to you: in this wilderness your corpses shall lie’ (Num. 14) [Col. 0991A]. Yet this flying eagle, announcing woe, [420] speaks almost the same thing to their descendants and says: As you have spoken, so shall it happen to you. Those locusts, compared with you, shall be like horses; you, compared with them, shall seem like locusts. Again: As you have said, “Would that we had died; would that we might perish,” so shall it happen to you. You shall seek death and not find it; you shall desire to die, and death shall flee from you.

Nor is it without significance that, having said “‘like horses,’” he added “‘prepared for battle.’” He thereby expresses the great confidence of those locusts and the great courage of the hostile peoples: they come voluntarily to battle and seek with weapons those whom they had formerly fled. The histories plainly report that this occurred.

“‘And upon their heads were, as it were, crowns like gold.’” The kings or princes of those nations, who are rightly understood by the heads, were crowned, as it were, and not truly crowned by victories [Col. 0991B]. For they did not conquer by their own strength; rather, these people were conquered because of their sins. The crowns themselves are not said to be truly golden but “like gold,” because whatever they boasted concerning victory, as though they were wise and strong, was false. The gold of their prowess was not the reason for their prevailing; rather, it was the testing judgment of divine dispensation, by which Israel was exercised for its own experience. Scripture itself also foreshadows this: ‘These are the nations which the Lord left, in order that he might instruct Israel through them, and all those who knew the wars of the Canaanites, and that afterward their children might learn to fight against enemies and acquire the practice of warfare’ (Judg. 3) [Col. 0991C].

“And their faces were like human faces. They had hair like women’s hair, and their teeth were like lions’ teeth; and they had breastplates like iron breastplates.” All these things may be understood as diminishing the sons of Israel while setting forth, as it were, the greatness of those locusts; so that, as has already been said, the Israelites themselves, when compared with them, might seem like locusts. More particularly, however, in the human face is the pretence of reason; in women’s hair, loose and effeminate habits; in lions’ teeth—which are accustomed both to tear and to produce a natural stench—the fierceness of mind; and in iron breastplates, every kind of military equipment is rightly understood. Their equipment was so extensive that they even abounded in scythed chariots. For this too is written concerning the king of Canaan: that he had nine hundred scythed chariots and oppressed them grievously for twenty years (Judg. IV).

“And the sound of their wings was like the sound of horses running to battle.” The sound of wings is the exaltation of the pride of such locusts. We have heard their voice, for example, in the First Book of Kings, when they said among themselves: “Be strong, and be men, O Philistines, lest you serve the Hebrews, as they served you. Be strong, and fight” (I Sam. IV). Indeed, to say, “Be strong, and fight,” was like the sound of many horses running to battle.

“And they had tails like scorpions, and there were stings in their tails; their power was to harm men for five months.” Here, for the third time, those locusts—that is, Israel’s enemies—are shown to be like scorpions: harmless, as it were, in appearance, but preserving poisons in their hind parts. Why so? Because on three occasions the sons of Israel are read to have been deceived by the women of those nations, so that, having offended God, they fell before their enemies as though without their weapons.

First, where it is written—as we mentioned above—that the sons of Moab summoned them to their sacrifices: “The people,” Scripture says, “committed fornication with the daughters of Moab; and they worshipped their gods, and Israel was initiated into Baal-peor” (Num. XXIII).

Second, where after Joshua’s death it is written: “Therefore the sons of Israel dwelt in the midst of the Canaanite, Hittite, Amorite, Perizzite, Hivite, and Jebusite; and they took their daughters as wives” (Judg. I), etc. [Col. 0992B]

Third, where it is written of Solomon “that he loved many foreign women, including Pharaoh’s daughter, Moabite, Ammonite, Edomite, Sidonian, and Hittite women; and through women his heart was corrupted, and the Lord was angry” (III Kings XI).

In the first case, the Lord’s anger was severe, when he said: “Take all the leaders of the people and hang them in gibbets before the sun; and let every man kill his neighbours who were initiated into Baal-peor” (Num. XXIII). In the second, it was more severe, “because he delivered them into the hands of the nations, and those who hated them ruled over them” (Ps. CV). In the third it was most severe, because one nation was divided, and one kingdom into two kingdoms; and those schisms themselves, being irreparable, were afterwards handed over to enemies (III Kings XII). “For the king of Assyria came and carried Israel away into Assyria, and settled them in Halah and Habor, by the river Gozan, in the cities of the Medes” (IV Kings XVII).

But that carrying away of Israel into Assyria, just as the removal of Judah into Babylon, belongs to the sounding of the sixth angel’s trumpet, of which we must speak later. He therefore continues by repeating what he had already said: “Their power was to harm men for five months,” that is, to subject them to servitude through five successive periods.

“And they had over them a king, the angel of the abyss, whose name in Hebrew is Abaddon, in Greek Apollyon, and in Latin he has the name Exterminator.” This angel of the abyss is plainly contrary to the Angel of Great Counsel: king opposed to king, king of the children of pride opposed to, or set against, the king of the children of wisdom. For Scripture, having set down the name of this one and the name of that one in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin, declares that the former is evil and the latter good, to be recognized by all nations.

For we know that it was written in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin: “Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews” (John XII). He is in Hebrew *Jesus*, in Greek *Sōtēr* [Saviour], in Latin *Salvator*. But this one, as we now have it before us, is in Hebrew *Abaddon*, in Greek *Apollyon*, in Latin *Exterminator* [Destroyer]. This Destroyer, I say, was to be recognized by those to whom that Saviour had been made known, so that, when it is understood how novel this Destroyer is, it may better be understood how truly and rightly he who saves from this one is called Saviour.

Moreover, divine authority in the Old Scripture had already almost expressed the name “Destroyer” when it says: “For the Lord will pass through to strike the Egyptians; and when he sees the blood on the lintel and on both doorposts, he will pass over the door and will not allow the destroyer to enter your houses and harm you” (Exod. XII). The one and same angel—the king of the abyss, Destroyer or striker—was permitted there to harm no one except in houses that did not have blood on the lintel and both doorposts; and here he is commanded, with his locusts, to torment only those people who do not have the sign of God upon their foreheads.

“And the first woe has passed; behold, two woes are still coming. And the sixth angel sounded the trumpet, and I heard one voice from the horns of the golden altar which is before the eyes of God, saying to the sixth angel who had the trumpet: [Col. 0993B] Release the four angels who are bound at the great river Euphrates.”

The sixth angel had long been sounding the trumpet when the Lord spoke concerning Jerusalem and Judah: “Behold, I will bring evils upon this place and upon its inhabitants, and all the curses written in this book which they have read before the king of Judah, because they have forsaken me and sacrificed to foreign gods, provoking me to anger by all the works of their hands. Therefore my wrath shall drip upon this place and shall not be quenched” (II Chron. XXXIV).

For what wrongdoing, what outcry, concerning that nation—its kings, princes, and priests—from whom the Lord had expected judgment and justice, had he not heard? They had killed his prophets, undermined his altars, and filled Jerusalem up to the brim with the blood of the innocent. They had also placed an engraved and molten image in the house of the Lord, concerning which the Lord had spoken to David and to Solomon his son, saying (III Kings XIX): “In this house and in Jerusalem, which I have chosen from all the tribes of Israel, I will set my name for ever” (II Chron. XXXIII).

Surely because of sins of this kind the Lord brought upon them the king of the Chaldeans, and he killed their young men with the sword in the house of the sanctuary (II Chron. XXXVI). He did not spare young man, virgin, old man, or even the decrepit; but he delivered all into his hands. Their enemies burned the house of the Lord, destroyed Jerusalem’s wall, burned all its towers, and demolished whatever had been precious. Whoever escaped the sword was led into Babylon and served the king and his sons [Col. 0993D].

After this they endured the second kingdom, the Persian, though it was milder toward them; then the yoke of the third kingdom, that of the Greeks, because of the multitude of sins that continued. Finally, under the fourth kingdom, that of the Romans, they filled up the measure of their fathers by killing Christ, the Son of God, so that upon them, or upon that generation, might come all righteous blood shed upon the earth (Matt. XXIII).

He therefore says: “And I heard one voice from the horns of the golden altar which is before the eyes of the Lord, saying to the sixth angel who had the trumpet: Release the four angels who are bound at the great river Euphrates.” The voice which he heard commanding the release of the four angels was a permission and judgment producing and bringing evil—that is, affliction upon men—justly on account of their sins, as he says in Isaiah: “I am the Lord, making peace and creating evil” (Isa. XLV).

Moreover, this golden altar is the same one of which we have above: “An angel came and stood before the altar, holding a golden censer in his hand” (Apoc. VIII), and the rest. This altar, as we said above, is the faith of Christ, founded in the hearts of the holy Fathers, from the time when God first spoke to Abraham: “In your seed,” he says, “all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. XXII).

What, then, are the horns of the altar except the patriarchs and prophets, kings and leaders, or judges of that people: the chief representatives of the same faith, which they both proclaimed in writings and prefigured by mystical deeds? [Col. 0994B] There is indeed one supreme horn of this altar, of which the Psalmist says: “Keep the feast-day in close assembly, even to the horn of the altar” (Ps. CXVII): that is, abstain from the servile works of sin, intent upon a multitude of virtues, until the knowledge of Christ’s divinity. Yet there are nevertheless as many horns of the altar as there are participants in that same Christ, of whom the Psalmist elsewhere says: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. XLIV).

How was a voice heard from horns of this kind, saying, “Release the four angels”? In a prophetic and permissive manner. For, foreknowing, they foretold it; and, assenting to divine justice, they allowed the four kingdoms that were to arise from the earth to be released—that is, not to be restrained by any obstacles raised by holy angels, and especially by Michael the prince—so that they might take captive, kill, enslave, and scatter among all nations the Jewish people, whose prince he was.

For example, Jeremiah, considering within himself the sins of the people who persecuted the prophets, killed many of them, and were going to kill Christ himself, says: “But you, Lord of hosts, tester of the righteous, who see their inward parts, let me, I pray, see your vengeance upon them; for to you I have revealed my cause” (Jer. XI).

Daniel, foreseeing the same four kingdoms under the images of four beasts, expresses them thus: “The first, like a lioness, is the kingdom of the Babylonians. The next, like a bear, is the kingdom of the Persians and Medes. The third, like a leopard, is the kingdom of the Greeks. The fourth, without a name, terrible and wonderful, exceedingly strong, is the kingdom of the Romans” (Dan. VII).

Most writers, omitting the kingdom of the Persians and Medes, or counting it as one with the Babylonian kingdom, place the African kingdom, whose capital was Carthage, in third place. “First,” they say, “was the Babylonian; then the Macedonian; after that the African; and finally the Roman, which remains to this day.” Thus, by an ineffable ordering, the principalities of four kingdoms stood out in distinct ranks at the four quarters of the world: the Babylonian kingdom in the east, the Roman in the west, the Carthaginian in the south, and the Macedonian in the north.

But such a reckoning does not pertain to Sacred Scripture in this matter, since it dealt, or ought to deal, only with those kingdoms which at different times afflicted the Hebrew people, delivered to them on account of their sins. For it is known that the beast in Daniel which was like a bear, and stood “on one side,” and to which they said, “Arise, eat much flesh,” signified the kingdom of the Persians and Medes (Dan. VII). Its standing on one side means that that kingdom committed nothing cruel against Israel. Likewise, the words, “Arise, eat much flesh,” signify the time when, under Ahasuerus, at the prompting of Haman the Agagite, all the Jews were commanded to be slaughtered in one day (Esther III). And fittingly it does not say, “It will devour them,” but “they said to it,” so that there was only an attempt and the outcome was by no means achieved.

Now the reason why angels are written in place of kingdoms, when it says, “Release the four angels,” is that kingdoms have been entrusted to angels, and in the same prophet they are called princes of kingdoms. For the angel who came because of Daniel’s words says to him: “But the prince of the kingdom of Persia resisted me for twenty-one days; and behold, Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me, and I remained there beside the king of Persia” (Dan. X). The prince—that is, the angel of the Persians—resisted, acting for the province entrusted to him, so that all the people of the captives might not be released.
