But while the angel of the Persians was resisting, “there came,” he says, “to help me,” the one who presides over the people of Israel, namely Michael, the prince or archangel.

Afterward he says: “And now I shall return, to fight against the prince of Persia. Therefore, when I went out, the prince of the Greeks appeared, coming” (ibid.). “Appeared” means that he entered into the presence of God, namely in order to accuse the prince of the Persians and Medes, so that the kingdom of the Macedonians might succeed in their place. And indeed, by God’s wondrous ordinances, after the Jewish people had been released from captivity, Alexander, king of the Macedonians, overthrew the kingdom of the Persians and Medes by killing Darius; and the prince of the Greeks conquered the prince of the Persians.

Thus, what he says to the angel who had the censer, “Release the four angels who are bound,” is as though he said: All the horns of the altar—that is, the holy fathers, holy leaders, or prophets of that nation, who once worshipped the true God according to their ancestral faith—do not resist the four kingdoms; do not offer the incense of prayers against them for the Jews; do not prevent by prayer their coming, prevailing against them, and leading them captive.

They are said to have been bound at the great river Euphrates—that is, until then they were not permitted to enter the borders of Israel. For the river Euphrates is rightly put for all the borders of Israel, because, according to the authority of Scripture, this river is one of its borders. For thus the Lord said to them: “From the wilderness and Lebanon even to the great river Euphrates shall be your border” (Josh. I).

Therefore, when the Assyrians or Chaldeans first crossed the great river Euphrates and the people of Israel or Judah was carried by them into captivity, then these angels were released, so that they might no longer be held bound at that great river Euphrates. At that time the Lord spoke to Jeremiah: “Go and procure for yourself a linen girdle, and put it on your loins.” And afterwards: “Take,” he says, “the girdle which you procured, which is around your loins, and rise, go to the Euphrates, and hide it in a hole in the rock.” Jeremiah went and did so.

“And after many days the Lord said again: Rise, go to the Euphrates, and take from there the girdle which I commanded you to hide there. And I went,” he says, “to the Euphrates, dug, and took the girdle from the place where I had hidden it; and behold, it had rotted, so that it was fit for no use. And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Thus will I cause the great pride of Judah and the great pride of Jerusalem to rot, and this most evil people, who refuse to hear my words. For as a girdle clings to a man’s loins, so I joined to myself the whole house of Israel and the whole house of Judah” (Jer. XIII), and the rest.

Finally, the girdle or belt joined to God’s loins was the people Israel, which, taken from the earth in the likeness of linen, unwashed, had neither softness nor whiteness, and yet through his mercy clung to God. When it sinned—for linen and a girdle of this kind are rational—it was led beyond the Euphrates, into Assyria, and was hidden there; that is, it was in a manner swallowed up in the multitude of great and innumerable nations and accounted as nothing. But after a long time the prophet himself, as a type of God, frees the people from captivity; nevertheless, even after their return they did not obey God’s commands, but followed foreign gods, and at last laid hands even upon God’s Son. Thus they wasted away in eternal destruction, just as that girdle had rotted and was fit for no use.

These things have been drawn from the prophet for the present passage, so that it may be neither doubtful nor unknown how, or in what respect, those angels were bound at the great river Euphrates. Namely: as long as that girdle clung to God’s loins, they were kept bound by the same girdle or belt. But when Jeremiah, at the Lord’s command, hid it in the Euphrates, they were released. That is to say: as long as the people Israel or Judah kept the law of their God, those kingdoms did not tear them apart, nor did the Assyrians or Chaldeans take them captive. But when they worshipped foreign gods and served Baal—indeed, also killed the prophets—then, with God’s permission, those peoples crossed the Euphrates and led them into captivity (III Kings XIX).

For who that is wise would think that this happened apart from God’s ordering, or that angels of this kind were released by anyone other than God? Finally, that all authority and all ordering are from God is felt even by those who have not read it, and recognized by those who have. But if authorities are from God, as the Apostle also testifies when he says, “There is no authority except from God” (Rom. XIII), how much more are kingdoms, from which other authorities proceed? And if diverse kingdoms are from God, how much more some greatest kingdom, to which the whole power of the other kingdoms is subject, such as these were, each in its own time? He continues, therefore:

“And the four angels were released, who had been prepared for the hour and day and month and year, to kill a third part of men.” Who could count the killings and slaughters of men which those kingdoms, rising and falling throughout the world, produced? Why was this permitted to happen except because of human sins? For they were sinners and ungodly, all set in the evil one, ready and intent upon nothing but being killed or killing (I John V). They are therefore rightly called a third part of men, that is, all the reprobate, such as Ham was, the third father of men after the flood.

But attention should be directed chiefly to what concerns the present subject: namely, the evils which they inflicted upon the Jewish nation, God judging them for their sins. “Who had been prepared,” he says, “for the hour, day, month, and year.” In connection with this fourfold distinction we must recall what was said above at the sounding of the fifth angel’s trumpet: “And it was said to them not to kill them, but that they should be tormented for five months.” We have shown that those five months of torment were the five servitudes which they endured: first under the king of Mesopotamia, second under the king of Moab, third under Canaan, fourth under Midian, fifth under the Philistines.

Recalling this, therefore, just as those servitudes are signified by the months, so by the hour, day, month, and year we understand the captivities or servitudes which they suffered under the dominion of these kingdoms. These differed in duration, or in extent of time, just as “hour, day, month, and year” plainly have differing lengths. By the hour, namely, we understand the seventy years counted from the Babylonian deportation until the first year of Darius, son of Ahasuerus, of the seed of the Medes, who overthrew the Chaldean kingdom. By the day, the two hundred and thirty years of the Persian kingdom, that is, until the beginning of the Macedonian kingdom. By the month, the three hundred years of the Macedonian kingdom, that is, until Roman rule. By the year, the long duration of the Roman empire, under which the Jews were not merely taken captive as before, but miserably crushed and trampled down; and those who survived the deaths were sold and scattered among all nations, and will remain scattered, as through the whole year—that is, until the end of the age.

How, or for what, were they prepared for such an hour, day, month, and year? Namely, to seize the permission or opportunity of doing evil, as wicked servants stood ready; and as God’s scourges. Yet God the Lord, for their own ruin because of such readiness of evil servants, calls Assyria the rod and staff of his wrath, and calls Nebuchadnezzar—who first came to take the Jews captive and was the first to serve him—his servant: “Woe to Assyria, the rod of my anger; the staff itself in his hand is my indignation” (Isa. X). Likewise: “Behold, I will send and take all the kindreds of the north, says the Lord, and Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, my servant, and bring them upon this land and its inhabitants” (Jer. XXV).

What reward he received for this service subsequently appears from the words of the very God whom he had served: “And when seventy years have been completed, I will visit upon the king of Babylon and upon that nation, says the Lord, their iniquity” (ibid.), and the rest. The same must be thought concerning the other kingdoms: each, after the time allowed for its evil service, received evil rewards for itself.

It must also be noted here that he reckons the Jews in the race of Ham, who—or whose race, as has often been said—is read to be the third part of humankind after the flood, because there were only three sons of Noah who left the ark with him (Gen. VIII). How does he reckon the Jews in him? Namely, by saying, “that they might kill a third part of men.” And rightly so; for at the same time when they deserved to be so killed and carried captive, the prophet, as though giving the reason why it would happen, reproached that nation with this: “Your father was an Amorite and your mother a Hittite” (Ezek. XVI). And who doubts that the Hittite and Amorite sprang not from Shem but from the seed of Ham? He continues:

“And the number of the army of horsemen was twice ten thousand times ten thousand; I heard their number.” The number of the mounted army is not written without reason, because those kingdoms gloried exceedingly in horses and horsemen. Thus Rabshakeh, crying out against Hezekiah, reports the great king, king of Assyria, as boasting extravagantly: “But now give yourself to my lord, the king of Assyria, and I will give you two thousand horses, though you cannot from among yourselves provide riders for them” (Isa. XXXVI).

Now when he says “twice ten thousand times ten thousand,” it is the same as if he had said, conversely, “ten thousand times twenty thousand,” which is two hundred thousand thousand. I say it is the same in quantity, but not in mystical meaning. One may understand something entirely different from the expression “twice ten thousand times ten thousand” than if he had said “ten thousand times twenty thousand.”

So that what we now wish to say may become clearer and more intelligible, let us first say a little concerning the nature of numerical multiplication. The unit, that is, the numeral-character, which, as the abacists know better, signifies one in the first place, also called the singular place, when transferred beyond into the fifth place signifies ten thousand. Likewise the binary numeral-character, which signifies two in the aforesaid singular place, when transferred to the same—that is, the fifth—place, called the ten-thousand place, signifies twenty thousand. Thus, in one and the same ten-thousand place there are both the unit to be multiplied and the binary multiplier: the unit, namely, ten thousandfold, and likewise the binary, twenty thousandfold.

We judge that some mystery lies in the fact that, in this quantity of the mounted army, the unit and the binary lie in one and the same place; and that the unit does not multiply the binary, such that it might be said, “And I heard their number: ten thousand times twenty thousand,” but conversely the binary multiplies the unit, saying: “And I heard their number: twice ten thousand times ten thousand.”

For what does the unit of ten thousand signify except the Hebrew nation, worshipper of one God? And what does the binary ten-thousand number—sometimes infamous in Sacred Scripture, as where it is said of unclean animals, “two by two they shall enter the ark” (Gen. VII)—signify? The unit lies, therefore, in the same place with the binary, because the Israelite nation, which ought to have been the people of one God, was placed in the land of unclean nations doing abominable things. There the Israelite nation did not convert unclean and idolatrous nations to a clean life and to the worship of one God; rather, on the contrary, unclean and idolatrous nations perverted that people toward unclean and abominable things.

For this is what Ezra and Nehemiah, and the rest with them who feared the Lord after returning from Babylon, lament, saying: “For our iniquities have multiplied above our head, and our sins have grown unto heaven” (I Ezra IX). And after some words: “And after all that has come upon us for our evil deeds and our great transgression, because you, our God, have delivered us from our iniquity and have given us deliverance as it is today, shall we turn again and make void your commandments, and join in marriage with the peoples of these abominations?” (ibid.), etc.

Furthermore, while they were under the Greek kingdom, they did not convert the Greeks to the worship of the true and one God; rather, on the contrary, the Greeks perverted them toward laws opposed to the true God. Thus Mattathias, with his sons, laments in the Book of Maccabees, their garments torn: “Woe is me! Why was I born to see the crushing of my people and the crushing of the holy city, and to sit there while it is given into the hands of enemies? Holy things have fallen into the hands of foreigners; her temple is like an ignoble man” (I Macc. II), etc. For many in Israel had consented to abandon the law of God and sacrificed to idols.

Accordingly, the unit does not multiply the binary, but the binary multiplies the unit; and what grows from this is again binary, for it becomes two hundred thousand thousand. Indeed, the unit multiplied by the binary becomes binary in this way: twice one is two. And because the unit is ten thousandfold and the binary twenty thousandfold, the binary which results is placed in the fifth position from that which is multiplied; and, as has already been said, it amounts to two hundred thousand thousand. There the binary, so multiplied, signifies the unclean mixture of Israel and the nations. He continues:

“And I saw in the vision horses, and those sitting upon them had fiery, hyacinth-coloured, and sulphurous breastplates; and the heads of the horses were like lions’ heads, and from their mouths proceed fire, smoke, and sulphur. By these three plagues a third part of men was killed: by the fire, smoke, and sulphur proceeding from their mouths.”

He had first set down the number, not by defining it but by signifying its mystery, saying: “And I heard the number of the mounted army: twice ten thousand times ten thousand.” [Col. 1000A] Now at last he adds a description both of the horses and of the horsemen, saying: “And I saw horses, and those sitting upon them.” Assyrians or Chaldeans, Persians and Macedonians, and Romans, though they were or are human beings by nature, mounting horses and glorying in horses, are nevertheless called and were horses by a certain resemblance; indeed, also asses, according to that prophetic saying: “Their flesh is asses’ flesh, and their emission is horses’ emission” (Ezek. XXIII).

And whose, or what kind of, horsemen were these horses, or those sitting upon them, except evil spirits, drivers of the proud and lustful? These sat upon them; these drove them; and when they leapt upon chariots and horses, the chariots and horses were the devil’s.

“Having,” he says, “fiery, hyacinth-coloured, and sulphurous breastplates.” For evil spirits are clothed in the punishments of those hearts over which they preside; indeed, they appear in the present vision as the kind of people whom they make of those upon whom they sit. And what kind do they make them except greedy, proud, and lustful? What does fire signify except greed? What hyacinth, a colour said to imitate the appearance of the sky, except pride? What foul-smelling sulphur except lust, and especially lust contrary to nature? Such indeed were the nations of those kingdoms: burning with greed, swollen with pride, stinking with lust.

Therefore, after speaking of the horsemen, he fittingly adds nearly the same things of the horses: “And from their mouths,” he says, “proceed fire, smoke, and sulphur.” He merely changes the mention of hyacinth-coloured breastplates, putting smoke in place of that colour which signifies pride; for smoke likewise commonly signifies pride, according to the Psalmist: “But the enemies of the Lord, as soon as they have been honoured and exalted, shall fail; they shall fail like smoke” (Ps. XXXVI).

Thus he testifies that the horses were comparable to the horsemen of whom he had said, “having fiery, hyacinth-coloured, and sulphurous breastplates,” when he says: “And from their mouths proceed fire, smoke, and sulphur.” People of this kind are like the evil spirits that ride and dwell in them, although demons have less in this respect: they are lustful not in act but only in will, since they are without flesh.

And who does not know that the enemies of the Lord there were greedy, proud, and lustful? To proclaim anything about the fire of their greed would be superfluous. It is plainly evident that their fire of this kind set the whole world ablaze, setting kingdom against kingdom and allowing no rest or relief to the earth.

As for their smoking pride, this is sufficient evidence: their kings, mortal human beings, wished to be regarded as gods. For example: “Nebuchadnezzar commanded Holofernes to destroy all gods of the earth, so that he alone might be called god by those nations which could be subdued by his power” (Judith III). Likewise, in the Persian kingdom, the most proud Haman, indignant that Mordecai did not worship him, attempted for this reason to destroy the entire Jewish nation within Ahasuerus’ kingdom (Esther III).

In the Greek kingdom, the illustrious Antiochus went up to Jerusalem with a great multitude, entered the sanctuary in pride, and spoke great proud words, thinking in his pride that he would make the land navigable and the sea passable by land, because of his exalted mind (I Macc. I). In the Roman kingdom, arrogant emperors wished to be honoured as gods even while living (II Macc. V). Thus Flaccus, flattering Octavian Augustus, says among other things:

> To you, present among us, we grant mature honours,  
> And we establish altars at which men must swear by your name.  
> —Horace, *Epistles*, I.1, Book II

Likewise Virgil, speaking of the same man:

> O Meliboeus, a god has made this leisure for us.  
> For he shall always be a god to me; often a tender lamb  
> From our sheepfolds shall stain his altar.  
> —Virgil, *Eclogues*
What need is there to say much more about the lusts of those same kingdoms? For, to pass over the testimonies of the divine Scriptures, what of that saying of the Apostle: “God gave them over to a reprobate mind” (Rom. 1)? What shameful things do the Greek and Latin satirists not sing about them? Besides these things, he adds one point, which especially denotes the fierceness or cruelty of horses of this sort: “And,” he says, “the heads of the horses were like the heads of lions.” This is so plain that, in Daniel, the first of those kingdoms—namely, the Babylonian—was signified by a lioness:

> “The first beast,” he says, “was like a lioness, and it had wings like an eagle’s” (Dan. 7).

For that kingdom is thus figured, on account of its savagery and cruelty, or on account of its luxury and life enslaved to lust: it is called not a lion but a lioness. For those who have written on the natures of animals say that lionesses are fiercer, especially when they are nursing cubs, and that they are always eager for intercourse. That it has eagle’s wings signifies the pride of a most powerful kingdom.

Will you ask why God permitted men—that is, the Israelite people—to be killed by horses or horsemen of this kind? He continues and says: “By these three plagues a third part of men was killed—by fire, smoke, and sulphur—which proceeded from their mouths.” “By these three plagues,” that is, because of these three plagues, just as in the Psalm: “Because of the sound of my groaning, my mouth clung to my flesh” (Ps. 101 [102]). That is, because of the devil’s voice saying, “Eat, and you shall be like gods” (Gen. 3), which was the matter and beginning of my groaning, I wasted away and became mortal. And because that voice was believed, just as in a wasting body bone clings to flesh, so in me reason assents to sensuality.

Likewise: “For I ate ashes like bread, and mingled my drink with weeping, because of the face of your wrath and indignation” (Ps. 101 [102]); that is, because of the face, or presence, of your wrath and indignation. Thus “by these three plagues” means because of these three plagues: “a third part of men was killed by fire, smoke, and sulphur” [Col. 1002A], that is, because of fire, smoke, and sulphur, which, as we have already said, were the sins of those nations or kingdoms—namely, concupiscence, pride, and Sodomite lust. For they themselves did the same things, and those like them were guilty, to whom they were handed over for punishment.

It is more than sufficient for us to prove this from the testimonies of Scripture, as it was for the Apostle when, after recounting the crimes of the Gentiles, he turns to the Jew who rebuked and judged those who had believed from among the Gentiles, and says to him:

> “Therefore you are inexcusable, O every man who judges. For in judging another, you condemn yourself; for you do the same things that you judge” (Rom. 2).

Justly, therefore, was this part of men—namely, the Hebrew nation—killed, because it had been wounded before God by these three plagues of sin. Hence it is also called “a third part of men,” that is, it is reckoned in the portion of Ham, who was one of Noah’s three sons, a sinner, and deserved to be cursed.

These plagues are said to have proceeded from the mouths of the horses because the Jews contracted such practices from intercourse and association with the Gentiles. For example, Jason, brother of Onias, as is read in the book of the Maccabees, favoring Antiochus’s wicked decrees, set aside the lawful rights of the citizens and established corrupt institutions. Indeed, he dared to establish a gymnasium under the citadel itself and to place the most promising youths among the *ephebes* in brothels. This was not the beginning, but a certain growth and advance of Gentile and foreign manner of life, because of the impious and unheard-of crime of Jason, who was not a priest [Col. 1002C], so that the priests were no longer devoted to the services of the altar; rather, despising the temple and neglecting the sacrifices, they hastened to take part in the wrestling-ground and in its unjust provision, and in the exercises of the discus. Holding their ancestral honor in no esteem, they judged Greek glories to be best (2 Macc. 4).

Because of these things, dangerous rivalry held them fast; they emulated their customs and desired in every way to be made like those whom they had had as enemies and destroyers. Thus they were burned by fire, puffed up or darkened by smoke, and corrupted by sulphur—things proceeding from the mouths of horses of this kind. Therefore they were killed and carried captive by them, God being their judge and justly giving power to those horses, so that they might be slain by the swords of those whose empty glories and lusts they followed [Col. 1002D]. Concerning the power given to them, he immediately continues:

> “For the power of the horses is in their mouths and in their tails.”

The sense is this: they received power over them because God gave it, since those people had approached their mouths by accepting their errors. And they clung to their tails—that is, they assented to their prophets, diviners, and magicians. For “the prophet teaching falsehood,” Isaiah says, “is the tail” (Isa. 9): namely, because he in a sense covers filth while adorning, with whatever plausibility he can, the very falsehood which he speaks.

There are very many examples or testimonies of Scripture that Israel had tails of horses of this kind—that is, such prophets, diviners, or Gentile soothsayers [Col. 1003A]. For Elijah alone killed four hundred and fifty men, all the prophets of Baal (4 Kings [1 Kings] 18). Therefore, “the power of the horses is in their mouths and in their tails”: that is, evil conversations and false prophets—enchanters, magicians, diviners, or augurs—by deceiving the people of God gained for those kingdoms the power which they had over that people; the Babylonians and Persians especially abounded in such persons.

And as though you were to ask how their tails came to exercise such power, he immediately adds: “For their tails are like serpents, having heads, and with them they do harm.” They are like serpents: that is, they imitate evil spirits and are full of the spirit of falsehood, which deceived the first human being through the serpent. “They have heads, and with them they do harm” [Col. 1003B], that is, they attach themselves to princes and powerful men, kings and emperors; supported by their patronage, they are able to oppress those whom they cannot seduce, so that such people follow their error even against their will.

For example, in Israel itself Jezebel was the head of the prophets of Baal (ibid.); and because of such a head they were so strong that no one dared oppose them except Elijah alone, although besides him there were seven thousand men who had not bent the knee before Baal. In the same way, the kings of the Babylonians and Persians, and of the other kingdoms, were heads to their magicians and augurs, so that by their force or sword they might accomplish what, by speaking or persuading, they could not achieve among the people who worshipped the true God (4 Kings [1 Kings] 19).

> “And the rest of the men, who were not killed by the plagues, did not repent of the works of their hands, so that they should not worship demons and images of gold, silver, bronze, stone, and wood, which can neither see nor hear nor walk; and they did not repent of their murders, nor of their sorceries, nor of their fornication, nor of their thefts.”

It is certain that the kings of those kingdoms did not kill all those men—that is, the Israelite people or Jews. For even under the last of them, namely the Roman Empire, which like a terrible and wonderful beast devoured and crushed everything (Dan. 7), some survived to be led captive among all nations. It is equally certain that, though thus captive and dispersed, they did not repent of their murders and their other sins; for even to this day they remain rebellious against Christ and blaspheme Christ, whom their fathers killed [Col. 1004B].

What, then, will become of them? What must be understood in such a statement? For he has made an ellipsis—that is, a deficiency of expression—by saying, “and the rest of the men who were not killed by the plagues,” and so forth. What, then, will become of them? Will they be unpunished? Certainly not. Rather, it must be understood that they themselves will drink from the bowls full of the wrath of the living God (Rev. 16). This will be discussed more fully in its place: bodily escape from death will not profit them, when in eternal death their souls must be held so much more deeply as they remain more stubbornly in their sins—those who, worn down by so many plagues or deaths, did not return to him who struck them.

## BOOK SIX

[Col. 1003]

[Col. 1003C] Of the seven trumpets, one trumpet remains—the last trumpet—after which no trumpet of this kind will sound. For six trumpets have sounded; and since only seven were given, one to each of seven angels, the seventh which remains is certainly the last. The Apostle, knowing this, says to the Corinthians:

> “We shall all indeed rise again, but we shall not be changed. For the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall rise incorruptible” (1 Cor. 15).

Likewise, to the Thessalonians:

> “For the Lord himself, at the command, at the voice of the archangel, and at the trumpet of God, shall descend from heaven” (1 Thess. 4).

Here the mighty angel immediately confirms on oath that this seventh trumpet is the last, saying that there will be no more time; but in the days of the voice of the seventh angel, when he begins to sound the trumpet, the mystery of God will be completed, as he proclaimed through his servants the prophets.

This is fear, trembling, and a most terrible expectation. For this trumpet is not to be thought like the others: another crash, another tempest than in the other trumpet-sounds will appear at the blast of that trumpet. Indeed, the prophet labors greatly to describe it, saying:

> “That day is a day of wrath, a day of tribulation and anguish, a day of calamity and misery, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and whirlwind, a day of trumpet and blast” (Zeph. 1).

But why seek many arguments? For as proof of the greatness of that trumpet, this alone suffices: the Son of God took care by his own coming to precede it and to declare to us in his own voice what kind of trumpet it would be, so that we might not be unprepared. For what follows is also relevant.

## CHAPTER 10

> “And I saw another mighty angel descending from heaven, clothed with a cloud, and a rainbow was upon his head.”

And shortly afterwards:

> “And the angel whom I saw raised his hand to heaven and swore by him who lives for ages of ages, who created heaven and the things in it, earth and the things on it, and sea and the things in it, that there will be no more time; but in the days of the voice of the seventh angel, when he begins to sound the trumpet, the mystery of God will be completed, as he proclaimed through his servants the prophets.”

Who is that angel except the Angel of Great Counsel, often called—and to be called again and again—the Angel of God’s covenant: truly another, and far unlike all angels? He calls this angel mighty; for he is truly mighty—indeed, the prince of might. Hence the Psalmist says:

> “The Lord is strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle” (Ps. 23 [24]).

Accordingly, the angel who announced beforehand that this one was coming is called Gabriel, that is, “strength of God.” “I saw him,” he says, “descending from heaven.” From heaven, I say—that is, from where he was before. For where did he descend from heaven, if not into the virgin’s womb? He did not begin to exist from that virgin’s womb, as certain blaspheming heretics said, of whom Cerinthus was the first; but he descended from heaven into that womb, coming from the Father’s bosom. And he who was God became man; and what was the Word in the beginning became flesh—not because divinity was changed into flesh, but because flesh was assumed [Col. 1005B].

This is what he says: “clothed with a cloud.” For a cloud here, as in very many places of the mystical Scriptures, signifies that flesh. The comparison is surely beautiful and fitting: just as the sun, when covered by a cloud, is hidden, yet is known to be present although it does not show its disc, and nevertheless makes day for the whole world; so God was both hidden in that flesh and could be recognized as present. For he kept his divinity invisible, as it always was, yet through visible works illuminated the whole world.

“And a rainbow,” he says, “was upon his head.” The rainbow—that is, the heavenly bow—signifies the mercy of this same most mighty one. For it is a sign, or was given as a sign, of propitiation, the Lord saying to Noah: “No longer shall all flesh be destroyed by the waters of the flood”; and afterwards: “This is the sign of the covenant between me and you: I will place my bow in the clouds, and it shall be a sign between me and the earth” (Gen. 9).

Therefore, “the rainbow was upon his head,” that is, mercy lay in the supreme and governing purpose of his coming. For this is why he came clothed in the cloud of flesh: to prepare us and make us such that we may stand on that day of judgment when the final trumpet sounds. This preparation consists in giving remission of sins—something he did, preaching repentance and washing us from our sins in his blood (Heb. 5). Hence he is called a merciful and faithful high priest, because such was the rainbow upon his head.

> “And his face was like the sun, and his feet like a pillar of fire.”

His face is knowledge of him, which, from the time of his resurrection—when he was glorified with the glory which he had before the world existed (John 17)—shone upon the whole world with clear light. Thus was fulfilled what Zechariah, foretelling the imminent birth of that same one, said: “The Dayspring from on high has visited us, to illuminate those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death” (Luke 1).

Looking toward the rising of this sun, the Apostle Paul says: “The night has passed; but the day has drawn near” (Rom. 13). For night existed before; but from that time, as the sun rises, the day draws near to those who draw near to it. Mark the Evangelist also speaks mystically when he says: “And very early, on the first of the Sabbaths, they come to the tomb, the sun having already risen” [Col. 1006A] (Mark 16). For, understood mystically concerning this Sun of righteousness, who gave a new day to the world by his resurrection, “very early” and “the sun having already risen” would otherwise be contradictory.

“And his feet,” he says, “were like a pillar of fire.” This description differs somewhat from the earlier one, when he who is now described first appeared to John. There the Son of Man is plainly written of first; but in this place he is called the Angel of death. There his head and hair are written as white like white wool and snow (Rev. 1). Here such whiteness is passed over in silence, and this alone is said: “a rainbow was upon his head.” There it is written: “His feet were like fine bronze, as if glowing in a furnace.” Here, however, it is said: “His feet were like a pillar of fire.”

It is not idle to inquire why such differences in description have occurred. We say, then, that the former appearance had a different reason or purpose, which we did not leave unexplained there, and the present one another, which likewise we do not attempt to pass over. There, against Cerinthus and Ebion and the other antichrists, who while John was exiled on the island of Patmos had begun to deny that Christ existed before Mary, Christ was shown to him in such a form or figure as the Gospel which John was going to write, or the testimony he had to bear concerning Christ, required. Here, however, it was signified alike to all believers and unbelievers what business, and how great a business, hangs over the whole world—the reason Christ came into this world: by announcing the terrible sound of the final trumpet, that is, the last judgment, to make every person forewarned and without excuse.

Therefore, there we rightly understand both natures of the one and same Christ to be signified; here, his office. Hence there he is called the Son of Man, which belongs to nature; here he is called Angel, which belongs to office. Again, there his head is described as white with age, signifying the antiquity of his divine nature; here “a rainbow is upon his head,” signifying the mercy and compassion of the office he assumed. There his feet, which are the lowest parts of any body, are said to be like fine bronze, signifying that the lower—that is, human—nature of Christ, while its substance remained, was transformed into the golden glory of divinity [Col. 1006D]. Here, however, his feet are said to be like a pillar of fire: by this expression his preachers are signified, through whom he comes to us, strengthened and illuminated by the Holy Spirit.

For all the bearers and ministers of his Gospel are his feet, concerning whom the Prophet also says:

> “How beautiful are the feet of one who brings good news and announces peace, who announces good, who preaches salvation, who says to Zion: Your God shall reign” (Isa. 52).

These feet became “like a pillar of fire” when the Holy Spirit came upon them like fire. From that time those who had previously been weak and fearful, unlearned and without letters, became strong and confident, eloquent and skilled in all the Scriptures (Acts 2). For example, Peter, formerly cold, sitting by the coals and warming himself, was afraid and denied him because of the voice of one maidservant who kept the door (Luke 22). But afterwards he became a pillar of fire, or fiery pillar: standing firm, he sustained the Church of God like a pillar; burning with good zeal like fire, he scorched princes, kings, and supreme emperors with responses of strength and righteousness; and upon the Church which he upheld as a pillar he shed the light of truth as fire.

> “And he had in his hand an open little book.”

This little book is the same book which John saw sealed with seven seals in the right hand of him who sat upon the throne (Rev. 5). It is now called open because, as was written there, the Lamb opened it and loosed its seals. For the Lamb who is written there to have opened the book is the very angel who is here seen holding the open little book in his hand. He truly has this open little book in his hand because it lies within his power to make known to those who believe in him the secrets of the Scriptures. This power was already in his hand when, after rising and appearing to his disciples, “he opened their understanding that they might understand the Scriptures,” as the Evangelist relates (Luke 24).

> “And he placed his right foot upon the sea, but his left upon the earth.”

All the feet of this angel, from the time they became “like a pillar of fire”—that is, from the time they were strengthened and illuminated by the Holy Spirit—are, by that very fact that they are so strengthened and illuminated, all right feet: that is, good and chosen [Col. 1007C]. But before they were thus strengthened and illuminated, namely before the Lord’s Passion, all were left feet, because many were reprobate and all were weak.

For example, when he spoke and said, “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves” (John 6), and things like these, “Many of his disciples,” says the Evangelist, “when they heard this, went back and no longer walked with him” (ibid.). Among the remaining twelve too, one was a devil. Peter also—now a strong and right foot, a good and chosen foot, and, according to the prophet, exceedingly beautiful—was then almost a left foot, because he fell and fell by denying Christ, whom he ought to have borne—that is, preached.

Thus, before the Lord’s Passion, all feet of this kind were left, as has already been said, because many were reprobate and all were weak [Col. 1007D]. We know, moreover, that before the Passion just mentioned these feet walked only through Judaea—that is, they preached in Judaea alone—because he himself commanded them thus: “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles, and do not enter the cities of the Samaritans; but go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. 10). But after his Passion, when he had risen from the dead, he says to them: “Going into the whole world, preach the Gospel to every creature; go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28; Mark 16).

Therefore he placed his right foot upon the sea and his left upon the earth: that is, he sent his now strengthened preachers to the totality of the Gentiles; but while they were still weak, he commanded them to preach only in Judaea. For Judaea is often signified by the name “earth,” and the Gentiles by the term “sea,” as, for example, in the Psalm:

> “Therefore we shall not fear when the earth is troubled and the mountains are carried into the heart of the sea” (Ps. 45 [46]).

The sense is this: We shall not fear the tribulations to come when the earth is troubled—that is, the Jews, who ought to have been cultivated and fertile earth but are now merely earth, devoted only to earthly things—and when the apostles are transferred into the midst of the Gentiles. He continues:

> “And he cried with a loud voice, as when a lion roars.”

By placing his right foot upon the sea and his left upon the earth, as has now been said, this angel cried with a loud voice because, in appointing his preachers, he wondrously sent forth the Gospel voice which the whole world would hear. How, or with how great a voice, did he cry? “As,” he says, “when a lion roars.” Truly, as when a lion roars. For the patriarch Jacob foretold this in these words:

> “Judah is a lion’s cub; you have gone up to the prey, my son. Resting, you lay down like a lion and like a lioness” (Gen. 49).

And the prophet Amos says:

> “The Lord will roar from Zion, and from Jerusalem he will give his voice” (Amos 1).

And in many other prophetic utterances this very thing is proclaimed which is now said: “as when a lion roars.”

Those who have written on natural history say that at the voice or roar of the lion all things tremble and every kind of living creature is frightened. Hence the prophet says: “The lion will roar: who will not fear?” And immediately, showing what he intends by this comparison: “The Lord God,” he says, “has spoken: who will not prophesy?” (Amos 3).

Thus it must be known and understood that the cry of this angel, crying with so loud a voice “as when a lion roars,” was the cry of his Passion or death: by it hell trembled, heaven was opened, and the gate of heaven or paradise stood open to souls breaking forth after the barriers of hell had been shattered; the earth trembled, the tombs were opened, and many bodies of saints who had fallen asleep arose (Matt. 27) [Col. 1008D]. Every kind of beast—that is, the power of evil spirits—was terrified. And just as was prophetically said there, “The Lord God has spoken: who will not prophesy?” all prophecy and the oracles of all prophets came into harmony and disclosed what they meant at so great a cry of that angel.

Hence it immediately follows: “And when he had cried, the seven thunders spoke their voices.” For what are the seven thunders—by which number universality is frequently, and especially in this book, signified—except the oracles of all holy prophets from the beginning of the world? Their voices had formerly been like thunders: just as thunder sounds terribly but does not give an articulated or intelligible sound, so the voices of the Law and prophets formerly sounded terribly, yet ordinary people did not understand what was signified by those voices.

For example, it is written in the Song of Deuteronomy:

> “I will raise my hand to heaven and say: I live for ever. If I sharpen my sword as lightning and my hand takes hold of judgment, I will render vengeance to my enemies and repay those who hate me” (Deut. 32).

He who spoke there, saying, “I will raise my hand to heaven,” and the rest, is this very angel, concerning whom it is afterwards said here: “And the angel whom I saw standing raised his hand to heaven,” and the rest.

Moreover, as an example, that saying in Hosea shines out here: “He will give us life after two days; on the third day he will raise us up” (Hos. 6). For it aptly accords in sense with what has now been said, “and he cried with a loud voice, as when a lion roars.” For the lion’s roar has this power, according to the natural historians. When a lioness has borne a cub, the cub sleeps for three days and three nights, and only then, when the place of its den is shaken, as it were, by the father’s roar, the sleeping cub is said to be awakened. If this is so, there is certainly a great reason for the comparison why it ought rightly now to be said, “as when a lion roars”: namely, because our nature in Christ had thus slept the sleep of death for three days and three nights, and then at last the place of the tomb was shaken, as it were, by the lion’s roar of divine power; and the man assumed in God, who had been dead, rose again—in whom we all also rose [Col. 1009C].

These things and others like them had formerly been thunders, that is, sounds or voices as though unarticulated, because they contained mysteries not yet intelligible. But after this angel cried in such a manner, they became intelligible, he having opened the understanding of his disciples so that they might understand the Scriptures (Luke 24). He says, therefore: “And when he had cried, the seven thunders spoke their voices.” He continues:

> “And when the seven thunders had spoken their voices, I was about to write. And I heard a voice from heaven saying: Seal up the things which the seven thunders have spoken, and do not write them.”

“I was about to write,” he says. What is it to write the things spoken by the seven thunders except to explain, by treating them with pen and ink, all the mysteries of the Scriptures? This neither John nor the other apostles did. Why? Did they not know or understand them? Far be that from us! On the contrary, they were friends, of the kind from whom nothing ought to be hidden, as he himself says:

> “I no longer call you servants, but my friends, because I have made known to you all things whatsoever I heard from my Father” (John 15).

“I have made known to you,” he said in place of “I shall make known,” because what he was soon to do was, when he said this, as certain as though he had already done it. For soon, by rising again, he was to open their understanding that they might understand the Scriptures (Luke 24), giving the Spirit of truth, who would teach them all truth (John 16), though up to that point they had been unlettered and unlearned persons.

Why then? Did they not wish to do it, or did they shrink from it through impatience with labor? Certainly not. “For I,” this man says, “was about to write,” that is, I wished to write. What, then, prevented it except the precept or rule of holy discretion? For all things could not be fulfilled at once or at the same time, because of the slowness of people, who were then untrained and weak for hearing wisdom of this kind.

Hence the Apostle Paul, after saying, “And, having been made perfect, he became the cause of eternal salvation to all who obey him, called by God a high priest according to the order of Melchizedek,” immediately adds:

> “Of whom we have a great discourse, and difficult to interpret in speech, because you have become weak in hearing. For whereas, by reason of the time, you ought to be teachers, you need to be taught again what are the elements of the beginning of the words of God; and you have become such as need milk, not solid food” (Heb. 5) [Col. 1010B], and so forth.

Therefore, that neither John nor the other apostles wrote the things spoken by thunders of this kind was due not to any lack of ability or will in them, but to the weakness of understanding of those who would then hear or read them. Otherwise, unless there had been such a reason, the time would not then have been unsuitable. As the same Apostle sometimes gave a brief foretaste, according to the time and subject: for example, when he said, “It is written that Abraham had two sons” (Gal. 4), and touched briefly upon their allegorical mystery.

And just as this same John knew or was able fittingly to employ the testimony of the Law and prophets, saying, for example: “For these things were done that the Scripture might be fulfilled: You shall not break a bone of him” (Exod. 12; John 19); and again, “Another Scripture says: They shall look upon him whom they pierced” (Zech. 12), so he and the other apostles would have known and been able to explain the other voices contained in all those thunders of the Law and prophets.

It was therefore a matter of praiseworthy discretion for them only to lay the foundation of faith, knowing or hoping that in the future there would not be lacking those who, as they would build other good things upon it, would also build upon it expositions of the sacred Scriptures. Hence the same Apostle says:

> “For we are God’s fellow-workers; you are God’s field, God’s building. According to the grace of God which was given to me, as a wise architect I laid the foundation, but another builds upon it. Let each one see how he builds upon it. For no one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus. But if anyone builds upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw, each person’s work will become manifest” (1 Cor. 3) [Col. 1010D], and so forth.

He says this concerning those who build upon the foundation. We know, however, that those who build upon it are principally distinguished in two ways: one builds in the active life, another in the contemplative life. If anyone rightly judges the works of the active life—feeding the hungry, giving drink to the thirsty, clothing the naked, receiving the stranger, visiting the sick and those in prison—to deserve to be reckoned gold, silver, and precious stones, how much more worthily ought the splendid marks of the contemplative life—hearing the words of God, meditating upon them, and both uttering and writing the mysteries of the sacred Scriptures—to be understood by such names as gold, silver, and precious stones?

For this is to build with gold, silver, and precious stones: to show that holy Scripture, which outwardly seems somewhat obscure in the letter, is inwardly adorned with splendid meanings. And this spiritual work surely has great merit before that friend of the soul, Wisdom herself, as she testifies: “And those who make me clear,” she says, “shall have eternal life” (Sir. 24) [Col. 1011A].

Indeed, the Apostle himself indicates in the passage cited above that he especially devotes himself to this study when he later says:

> “Thus let a man regard us as ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God. Here it is further required among stewards that a person be found faithful” (1 Cor. 4), and so forth.

He says, therefore: “Seal up the things which the seven thunders have spoken; do not write them.” This is to say: Seal up the mysteries of Scripture which have been given you to know and which you are ready to expound; leave them sealed and closed for posterity to seek out, so that they may not be like unsolicited wares, which, as people commonly say, tend to stink. They will be precious when there is need for them—that is, when they are sought amid the pressure of various heresies, which must needs arise so that those who are approved may become manifest (1 Cor. 11). Then the outstanding intellects of many persons will be exercised in many ways, and what has been won from the treasures of Scripture by laborious study will not seem cheap.

We judge that this saying is likewise addressed to the whole original order of Christ’s disciples, of whom this man was one—and loved above the rest. He continues:

“And the angel whom I saw standing upon the sea and upon the earth lifted up his hand to heaven, and swore by him who lives for ever and ever, who created heaven and the things in it, and earth and the things upon it, and sea and the things in it, that there shall be no more time; but in the days when the seventh angel’s voice is heard, when he begins to sound the trumpet, the mystery of God shall be brought to completion, as he proclaimed through his servants the prophets.”

What he had said a little earlier—“and he cried with a loud voice, as when a lion roars”—he now repeats, expressing more fully and forcefully what he cried, or what he did by crying. [Col. 1011D] “He lifted up,” he says, “his hand to heaven.” The hand of this angel is his majesty, and the lifting up of his hand is the exaltation of that majesty, which the Psalmist, marvelling, declares: “O Lord, our Lord, how wonderful is your name in all the earth! For your majesty has been exalted above the heavens” (Ps. VIII).

But what is that majesty except the Lord’s resurrection and ascension? For he subsequently continues and says to the Father of that same Lord of ours: “You made him a little lower than the angels; you crowned him with glory and honour, and set him over the works of your hands. You subjected all things beneath his feet” (ibid.). Indeed, this lifting up of the hand—that is, of the majesty [Col. 1012A] or omnipotence of so great an angel—began with that exaltation of which he himself said: “And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself” (John XII).

For, lifted up or exalted to the height of the cross, even in the very suffering of death he was raising his hand, because the author of salvation for all was being brought to completion, effecting for us the first resurrection, which is that of souls, since he was blotting out the sins of all by his blood (Rom. VIII). Then, lifted up and rising from the tomb, by that same exaltation of resurrection he became the firstborn of the dead (I Cor. XV), that is, the chief of those rising from the dead, consecrating in himself the second resurrection, which is that of bodies. Then, before the eyes of his apostles, lifted up and ascending into heaven, by that same exaltation of ascension he was established as judge of all the living and the dead, sitting at the right hand of the Father; the angels bore witness in this way: “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? Thus shall he come, just as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts I).

By this complete lifting up of his hand into heaven, “this angel swore by him who lives for ever and ever.” He swore, that is, he established it by unchangeable truth. For he did not swear with words or with the common profusion of oaths, as the entire text of the Gospel discourse testifies, in which nowhere is it found that he swore by word or voice. Indeed, it is clear that he altogether discouraged swearing; for he says: “You have heard that it was said to those of old: You shall not swear falsely, but shall render your oaths to the Lord. But I say to you, do not swear [Col. 1012C] at all.” And immediately afterwards: “Let your speech be: yes, yes; no, no. Whatever is more than these is from evil” (Lev. XIX; Matt. V).

Therefore he swore, that is, as has been said, he established it by unchangeable truth. He inserted only this among his sayings as a confirming sign: “Amen, amen, I say to you”—that is, “Truly” or “faithfully I say to you”—when he uttered something such as deserved the insertion of this truth [429]. For example: “The hour is coming, and now is, when the dead shall hear the voice of the Son of God; and those who hear shall live” (John V). “The hour is coming when all who are in the tombs shall hear his voice, and those who have done good shall come forth unto the resurrection of life; but those who have done evil, unto the resurrection of judgment.”

Thus he swore by him who lives for ever and ever, [Col. 1012D] that is, by himself, who was dead and now lives for ever and ever (Rev. I). “For, having risen from the dead, he dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. VI). Not to seek further: when he says, as we have already said, “Amen, amen,” he swears—that is, he affirms by himself, whom it is certain is the truth, the faithful witness—as the Spirit also testifies much earlier, saying to the churches: “Thus says the Amen, the faithful and true witness” (Rev. III).—“He is the one through whom all things were made, and without him nothing was made” (John I).

Describing himself, therefore, he rightly says: “Who created heaven and the things in it, and earth and the things upon it, and sea and the things in it.” That he himself was the living one by whom he swore—and thus that, in swearing, he swore by himself—is readily understood from the very posture of the one standing. For he stood in such a way as to encompass these three, signifying that he himself is the one who contains all things. He had placed his right foot upon the sea and his left upon the earth, while he had lifted his hand to heaven, which is the third of these, or the first. Therefore, since he created these things and contains them by his hand and feet—that is, by his omnipotence—it is certain that he is able to fulfil the words by which he swore.

What, then, does he swear? “That there shall be no more time, but in the days of the voice of the seventh angel, when he begins to sound the trumpet, the mystery of God shall be brought to completion.” Times vary around or within heaven, earth, sea, and the things in them, [Col. 1013B] succeeding one another as they pass; and therefore he who created them undoubtedly fixed their times as well and is able to end them when he wills.

“For there shall be no more time,” he says—namely, time for repentance, as there has been hitherto, after the preceding angels sounded their trumpets. For after the first angel sounded the trumpet and the ungodly perished in the Pentapolis when fire descended, while righteous Lot escaped, time for repentance remained (Gen. XIX). After the second angel sounded the trumpet, and the people of God passed through the Red Sea while their enemies were drowned, time for repentance remained for those left behind (Exod. XIV). After the third angel sounded the trumpet, and he wished to destroy by the hand of the children of Israel the inhabitants of the land, who had abandoned themselves to hateful deeds, [Col. 1013C] time for repentance was reserved (Josh. I, XII). After the fourth angel sounded the trumpet, and wrath came, as it were, upon the sun—that is, upon the people of God—so that their bodies were strewn in the wilderness, time for repentance was given to the rest (Num. XVI). After the fifth angel sounded the trumpet, and those who had entered the promised land were delivered five times into the hands of the nations (Judg. II, III), because they did not destroy the nations, as the Lord commanded them (Ps. CV), time for repentance remained. And after the sixth angel sounded the trumpet, and the four angels were released—that is, the four principal kingdoms of the world, Babylonian, Persian, Macedonian, and Roman—to kill and lead the Jewish race into captivity because of that people’s sins, there is still room for repentance, so that a remnant may be saved (Rom. IX).

But at last, what will occur when the seventh angel sounds the trumpet—that is, when the final day of judgment comes? There will be absolutely no more time, no place, no interval for repentance thereafter. For those were particular or local judgments; that judgment will be universal. No one will be left for this age in order to be able to repent.

When he begins to sound the trumpet—which will be the last trumpet, of which the apostle Paul also speaks—“we shall all,” he says, “rise in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet; for the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall rise incorruptible” (I Cor. XV), then the mystery shall be brought to completion: that is, the secret counsel of God by which [Col. 1014A] he has hitherto dealt with sinners, chastising them and, amid the chastisements, granting them long intervals for repentance.

In what will that mystery of God be brought to completion? Surely in this: that the ungodly shall go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life, as he proclaimed through his servants the prophets—that is, through the apostles and evangelists (Matt. XXV). For the Lord also calls these prophets: “Behold,” he says, “I send to you prophets, and wise men, and scribes” (Matt. XXIII). They are truly called prophets because they prophesied concerning the highest matters, judgment, and the age to come. So great will that last trumpet be that those who foresee it, speak of it, and proclaim its greatness are rightly called prophets by the Lord himself.

[Col. 1014B] “And the voice which I heard from heaven [And I heard a voice] again speaking with me and saying: Go, take the little book, open, from the hand of the angel standing upon the sea and upon the earth.”

This voice was the voice of another angel, not that of the mighty angel standing upon the sea and upon the earth. For it said: “Go, take the little book, open, from the hand of the angel standing upon the sea and upon the earth.” Whose voice, then, was it, except that of the angel who showed him these things and the rest, and who said to him at the beginning: “What you see, write in a book” (Rev. XI)? Perhaps he now says that he heard such a voice again because what was there signified once in the words, “What you see, write,” is here signified again in the words, “Go, and take the little book.”

Yet because it is subsequently said: “And [Col. 1014C] a reed like a rod was given to me, saying: Rise, and measure the temple of God,” one may distinguish it thus: what was said to him, “Go and take the little book, open, from the angel’s hand,” was shared by him with the other apostles—namely, understanding the Scriptures with an opened sense and undertaking the office of Gospel preaching. But what he says afterwards, “And a reed like a rod was given to me, saying: Rise and measure the temple of God,” signified a gift peculiar to him: the right and power to write the Gospel and to establish the boundaries of evangelical faith, which no one may lawfully transgress.

Hence it will subsequently be said: “And I went to the angel, saying to him that he should give me the book. And he says to me: Take the book and devour [Col. 1014D] it; it will make your belly bitter, but in your mouth it will be sweet as honey. And I took the book from the hand of the angel and devoured it; and it was sweet as honey in my mouth, and when I had devoured it, my belly became bitter.”

For what was it for this John and the other apostles to go to this angel after his very great cry and ask him to give them the little book which he held open in his hand, except what we all know from Gospel truth: that after the ascension of this victor they returned to Jerusalem with great joy, in order to remain there until they were clothed with power from on high and became strong and fit to preach the things written in that little book—indeed, in the great book of the holy prophets, the Law, and the Psalms?

Certainly, as Luke testifies, they all persevered with one accord in prayer, together with the women, Mary the mother of Jesus, and his brethren. This was to ask that great angel [430] to give them the book to devour: that is, to appear to them and make them fit to preach the Gospel by giving the Holy Spirit. Under his activity their inward person could devour such a book, that is, could both store it by reading in the depths of the heart and, by preaching, bring forth the mysteries of the holy Scriptures.

And this happened. For “when the days of Pentecost were fulfilled, there suddenly came from heaven a sound as of a rushing, mighty wind, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting. And divided tongues as of fire appeared to them, and one sat upon each of them. And they were all filled [Col. 1015B] with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in various tongues, as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance” (Acts I).

He therefore says: “And I took the book from the hand of the Angel and devoured it.” As though he said: I received, by the gift of the Son of God and of his Father, the capacity to understand the Scriptures, together with the power and ministry of preaching; and by reading and understanding, as well as by speaking or preaching, I was delighted, refreshed, and strengthened. “And it was,” he says, “sweet as honey in my mouth.” Nothing is truer. For the Psalmist speaks of such a taste: “How sweet are your utterances to my palate, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth!” (Ps. CXVIII).

And holy Scripture itself, the true wisdom of God, says of itself: “Come to me, all you who desire me, and be filled from my fruits. For my spirit is sweeter than honey, and my inheritance sweeter than honey and the honeycomb. My remembrance endures unto generations of ages. Those who eat me shall still hunger, and those who drink me shall still thirst” (Ecclus. XXIV).

These and similar sayings in the Scriptures concerning the sweetness of this little book are best perceived only by whatever blessed soul has deserved to experience what it has tasted, and which through tasting has itself become sweet like a honeycomb, so that the bridegroom himself, delighted by it, says to his beloved: “Your lips, bride, drip honeycomb; honey and milk are beneath your tongue” (Song IV).

But see what follows: “And when I had devoured it,” he says, “my belly became bitter.” This little book brings great sweetness whenever it is devoured; but for the present, while one lives in this world, that sweetness is sprinkled with many [Col. 1015D] bitter experiences. For adversaries are not lacking who at times bring the wormwood of tribulations and death. This is what we know and have learned of those who, in that sweetness of theirs, were at the same time made bitter by its bitterness: they drank the Lord’s cup, according to his own promise: “Can you drink the cup which I am about to drink?” and again: “You shall indeed drink my cup” (Matt. XX), etc.

This John himself, although he was not put to death by a material sword or any human violence, was nevertheless not altogether without that bitterness. For he had been cast into a vat of boiling oil, and now, while seeing these things, was held in banishment on the island of Patmos. Therefore let whoever has been granted this indeed take the book [Col. 1016A] and devour it; but let him know that, when he has devoured it—when he begins to live and teach according to it—his belly, that is, his soul, will be made bitter by persecutors, in accordance with the true declaration of Paul: “All who desire to live piously shall suffer persecution” (II Tim. III). Let us proceed to what remains.

“And he says to me: You must prophesy again concerning peoples, nations, tongues, and many kings.”

What he had thus far seen or heard in the descent or appearance of that angel was shared by him with the other apostles. For they too received the opened little book from the angel’s hand and devoured it; it was sweet as honey in their mouths, but their bellies were made bitter. That is, by the Holy Spirit they received an opened understanding for comprehending the Scriptures and the office of preaching; because of their good will it was sweet for them to do this, but because of the persecution of unbelievers and ungodly people their bellies—that is, their souls—were made bitter.

But the words which he now reports as spoken to himself, “You must prophesy again,” should be understood as said or done with respect to the distinctiveness of his own person. Thus “you must prophesy again” means: you must be released from this exile and write down evangelical truth with pen and ink. For it follows: “And a reed like a rod was given to me.”

Therefore, “You must,” he says, “prophesy again,” as though he said: “For some time I have known that you wish to be released from the body, desiring with all your heart to see my face; my fragrance has awakened in you desires for eternity, and you have repeatedly asked me to come to me. Whenever you asked me, I told you—and now I tell you—wait, so that you may save the people who will believe in me. For this reason you must wait: ‘you must prophesy again concerning peoples, nations, tongues, and many kings’; that is, so that peoples, tongues, and many kings may read and hear with the greatest reverence.

“For while you are in exile, Cerinthus raves in the meantime, Marcion is furious, Ebion begins to blaspheme, and the other Antichrists rage against the word of faith, against the majesty and ancient divinity of the Son of God. They say that he did not exist before Mary and that he is so recent a God that he began to exist from her. Moreover, Arius, the stubborn minion of the devil, will come, declaring and persuading peoples, nations, and many kings that this same Son of God is a creature, that he began to exist in time, and that there was a time when the Son himself did not exist. Because of these people you must prophesy again and provide for peoples, nations, tongues, and many kings, in order to free the Christian people who will believe in me from these plagues.”

How is he to prophesy? He says:

## CHAPTER XI

“And a reed like a rod was given to me, saying: Rise, and measure the temple of God and the altar and those worshipping in it. But cast out the court which is outside the temple, and do not measure it, because it has been given to the nations.”

The reed like a rod signifies the ability to write together with magisterial authority [Col. 1017A]. For the reed is the writers’ instrument; the rod, the teachers’. There are, or have been, some to whom a reed was given, but not one like a rod: that is, ability was given to them, but not with the dignity of teaching authority, such that no churchman may doubt any judgment or statement of theirs. For this teaching authority belongs only to the prophets and apostles, and this rod was given to them alone. Hence it is determined thus in the Psalm: “The Lord shall recount in the writings of the peoples and of these rulers who were in her” (Ps. LXXXVI).

“And of these princes,” he says, “who were in her”—that is, of the apostles and prophets, and likewise of the evangelists. Observe what he says: *who were*, not *who are*, so that, the apostles excepted, whatever is said later may be cut off and have no authority thereafter. Therefore, although someone after the apostles may be holy, although eloquent, let him have no authority, because “the Lord will recount in the Scriptures of the peoples and of these princes who were in her.”

Therefore, “a reed like a rod was given to me”: that is, the power of writing was given to me together with primacy and every authority of teaching, so that I might hold primacy and a teaching-chair in the midst of the Church; so that all the children of the Church might sit at my feet and hang upon my words, having no doubt and daring not to neglect any matter contained in my book, whatever my pen had written—the book of evangelical truth and grace. Such a reed was given to me; and he who gave it commanded, saying thus:

“Rise, and measure the temple of God and the altar and those worshipping in it.”

As though he said: Behold the gathering of bulls among the cows of the peoples—that is, behold the tumult of heretics in the Churches of the peoples, seeking to exclude those proved by silver, to cast out from God’s temple those who hold integrity, who are upright and approved, and who have an approved understanding in every divine word or utterance. Rise: let us rebuke these beasts, these beasts of the reed-bed, these horn-thrusting, stiff-necked ravagers of the Scriptures of truth.

“Rise,” I say, “and measure the temple of God and the altar”: that is, Christ the Son of God, who is both the temple of God and the altar of the holy Church—the temple of God, namely, according to the body which he assumed from the Virgin; but the altar according to the dignity of both natures, divine and human. “For the body which he assumed is the temple of God, in which all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Col. 2). Therefore he said: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up”; “but he was speaking of the temple of his body” (John 2).

Moreover, the altar of the holy Church is this same substance of the now-glorified body, together with that fullness of divinity which dwells in it, according to the truthful authority of the holy and mystical Law, in which God says: “You shall make me an altar of earth” (Exod. 20). That is: confessing Christ to be true God and true man, incarnate—or embodied—in an earthly body, you shall offer me true sacrifices.

Measure this temple of God, this altar. For behold, evil measurers have measured badly and most wickedly; and, by saying that Christ was not before Mary, they begin to create great tumult over his boundaries, which they grievously mutilate by heretical unbelief. You, therefore, measure, and extend his measurements, prescribing with this reed how great his length or breadth is, or ought to be. Extend his length upward—upward, I say, before Mary and before Abraham, indeed before Adam, and also before heaven and earth, unto the Ancient of Days, unto the antiquity of the Ancient of Days—and say: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. This was in the beginning with God” (John 1). Thus measure this temple and altar, and extend its measurements so far.

Measure also those worshipping in it: that is, show whose they are, and how great, who believe faithfully and think rightly concerning him. For example, by saying: “But as many as received him, he gave them power to become children of God.” Measure thus, and show that they shall be of such a measure or greatness that they are named and are children of God.

“But cast out the court which is outside the temple, and do not measure it, because it has been given to the Gentiles.”

What is that court which is now outside, except every conventicle of heretics? Though they contend that they themselves are inside, they are nevertheless outside, and in no way belong or attain to that temple of God—that is, to Christ. Therefore cast them outside: that is, prove that they are outside and have gone out. For example, say: “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (1 John 2).

Do not measure that court, those heretics, who, just as a court is indeed adjacent to the temple but is neither in the temple nor the temple itself, are “having an appearance of godliness, but denying its power” (2 Tim. 3). That is, declare that the measure given to those who received him, who believe in his name—namely, the power to become children of God (John 1)—does not belong to them. Why? “Because,” he says, “it has been given to the Gentiles”: that is, because they are reckoned among the Gentiles. They say that they are Christians and are not, but lie; for they are not Christians, but rage together with the Gentiles in the same spirit of wickedness. They persecute Christians.

[Col. 1018D] For this is what follows: “And they shall trample the holy city for forty-two months. And I will give to my two witnesses, and they shall prophesy for one thousand two hundred and sixty days, clothed in sackcloth.”

It is known from ecclesiastical histories that heretics, with a fury like that of the Gentiles, persecuted the holy city—that is, the Church—not merely for forty-two months, but for very many months and years. Why, then, did he say forty-two months, which are no more than three and a half years? Namely, in order to indicate the magnitude of the persecution of Antichrist, which will be so great that it alone ought almost to be recognized or foreknown, and that it alone should be reckoned as equivalent to all persecutions, as though the other persecutions were not persecutions in comparison with it.

Daniel too heard it said to him that this persecution would endure for so great a time: “And he will think that he can change times and laws, and they shall be delivered into his hand until a time and times and half a time” (Dan. 7). Again: “For a time and times and half a time; and when the scattering of the hand of the people of God has been completed, all these things shall be completed” (Dan. 12).

By “a time and times and half a time” we understand three and a half years. For above in the same prophet we read that seven times passed over Nebuchadnezzar—that is, seven years of his brutishness (Dan. 4). That he means by a time, times, and half a time one year, two years, and half a year, he expresses more clearly afterwards through the number of days, saying: “And from the time when the continual sacrifice has been taken away and the abomination has been set up unto desolation, there shall be one thousand two hundred and ninety days” (Dan. 12).

Indeed, if you divide these days according to the reckoning of lunar months—which alone, together with their intercalations, the Hebrews know—you will find scarcely more than is required for a time and times and half a time: that is, one year, two years, and half a year.

Now it is worth asking why John here, when he could have said, “They shall trample the holy city for three and a half years,” preferred to say “for forty-two months”; and likewise why he says, “They shall prophesy for one thousand two hundred and sixty days,” [Col. 1019C] which are the days of the same period, or of three and a half years, with thirty days assigned to each month. Did he prefer to specify these numbers of months and days by chance or without reason? Certainly not. Rather, as elsewhere in the Scriptures numbers signify a beautiful and delightful excellence of useful meanings, so here too he wishes something beautiful and delightful to be understood beneath these numbers.

To make this clearer, the reasoning concerning the nature of certain numbers requires that something first be set forth which may more quickly open the door of understanding. Of even numbers, some are excessive, others deficient, and others perfect. Those are called perfect which are equal to their divisors: they neither become swollen by excess nor lack through deficiency. For example, six: six has a half, namely three; a third, namely two; and a sixth, namely one. If these are added into one sum, the whole number is found in its parts: that is, the complete six is restored from them.

A deficient number, however, is one whose parts, combined in the same way, are fewer and are exceeded in quantity by the number of which they are parts. For example, eight: eight has a half, namely four; a fourth, namely two; and an eighth, namely one. All these combined make seven, enclosing a sum smaller than eight.

Excessive numbers, on the other hand, are those whose parts extend beyond what is sufficient. For example, twelve: its parts make up a sum greater than twelve itself. For twelve has a half, six; a third, four; a fourth, three; a sixth, two; and a twelfth, one. This entire aggregate rises to sixteen, certainly a greater sum than twelve.

Both secular and ecclesiastical philosophers say that there is in these numbers a great likeness of virtue and vice. The perfect number is a likeness of virtues; the deficient and excessive numbers are likenesses of vices. Clearly, the numbers which this Scripture here presents to us—forty-two and one thousand two hundred and sixty—are excessive.

For forty-two has a half, twenty-one; a third, fourteen; a sixth, seven; a seventh, six; a fourteenth, three; a twenty-first, two; and a forty-second, one. These parts, when added together, produce a sum greater than forty-two: they make fifty-four. Thus the number of forty-two months is excessive, and its parts grow beyond the measure of their origin—as if someone had been born with many hands beyond nature, like the hundred-handed giant, or joined into a triple body like three-bodied Geryon, or whatever monstrous thing nature has ever produced through the multiplication of its parts.

The number of one thousand two hundred and sixty days grows and exceeds still further in its parts.
