For it has a half, six hundred and thirty; a third, four hundred and twenty; a fourth, three hundred and fifteen; a fifth, two hundred and forty-two; a sixth, two hundred and ten; a seventh, one hundred and eighty; a ninth, one hundred and forty; a tenth, one hundred and twenty-six; a twelfth, one hundred and five; a fourteenth, ninety; a fifteenth, eighty-four; an eighteenth, seventy; a twentieth, sixty-three; a twenty-first, sixty; a twenty-eighth, forty-five; a thirtieth, forty-two; a thirty-fifth, thirty-six; a thirty-sixth, thirty-five; a forty-second, thirty; a forty-fifth, twenty-eight; a sixtieth, twenty-one; a sixty-third, twenty; a seventieth, eighteen; an eighty-fourth, fifteen; a ninetieth, fourteen; a one-hundred-and-fifth, twelve; a one-hundred-and-twenty-sixth, ten; a one-hundred-and-fortieth, nine; a one-hundred-and-eightieth, seven; a two-hundred-and-tenth, six; a two-hundred-and-fifty-second, five; a three-hundred-and-fifteenth, four; a four-hundred-and-twentieth, three; a six-hundred-and-thirtieth, two; and a one-thousand-two-hundred-and-sixtieth, one.

All these parts of this number, one thousand two hundred and sixty, added together make three thousand one hundred and eight. To such an extent does this number grow and overflow through its parts.

Since, then, as has already been said, all secular and ecclesiastical philosophers alike hold that numbers of this sort, which are or are called excessive, resemble not virtue but vice, what are we to think the author of this Scripture intends when he prefers to say forty-two months and likewise one thousand two hundred and sixty days, rather than a time and times and half a time, or one year and two years and half a year? What indeed, except to signify by numbers so excessive the abundance of iniquity foretold by the Lord as destined to occur at that time?

For he himself said: “And because iniquity has abounded, the love of many shall grow cold” (Matt. 24). And elsewhere it is written: “I have declared and spoken: they have been multiplied beyond number” (Ps. 39). Truthful Scripture teaches both: that, through the proclamation of Christ the Lord, those who would be called believers or Christians would be multiplied beyond number, many undertaking the empty profession of this name who did not belong to the number of the elect; and that, at the time of persecution, as iniquity abounded, the love of many would grow cold.

Therefore, the highly excessive number of forty-two months, and the far more excessive number of one thousand two hundred and sixty days, are fittingly offered here to readers, so that both the multitude of believers or professing Christians, of which it was said, “I have declared and spoken: they have been multiplied beyond number,” and the abundance of iniquity, of which it is likewise written, “Because iniquity has abounded, the love of many shall grow cold,” may be signified with a beautiful and venerable signification to those judged worthy to know the mystery of the kingdom of God.

Who, moreover, are these two witnesses, or what is meant by them, of whom he says, “And I will give to my two witnesses, and they shall prophesy”? Did this Lord and author of the prophets have, or will he have, no more than two men as witnesses for prophecy? Are not all his apostles and martyrs witnesses of him—not to speak now of the other confessors?

Truly this is a mighty and exceedingly weighty utterance from the mouth of the Mighty One: although he has witnesses so many and innumerable, he declares that he has only two, and is content with this legally sufficient number of witnesses. For sacred law receives the testimony of at least two men, and, if there are no more, is nonetheless content with few. Thus it says: “One witness shall not stand against anyone, whatever that sin or crime may be; but every word shall stand by the mouth of two or three witnesses” (Deut. 19).

Therefore, “I will give,” he says, “to my two witnesses, and they shall prophesy.” This may suitably be understood as though he said: “When you have measured the temple of God and the altar—that is, when you have expanded and extended the bounds of faith, as is fitting, by your reed, that is, by the authority of evangelical Scripture—I shall not permit there to be lacking some who testify that you wrote this concerning me, that you thought this concerning me.”

For what if I said, and said truly, “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 20)? The elect will never be so few, nor will love ever grow so cold through the abundance of iniquity, that evangelical truth cannot find at least two witnesses.

“But,” you ask, “what if only two witnesses arise against so many adversaries?” Assuredly, they provide a just and lawful judgment of condemnation for casting out that “court given to the Gentiles” which I mentioned above. Did not two witnesses—Joshua son of Nun and Caleb son of Jephunneh—suffice against so vast a multitude of Israelites murmuring and disparaging the promised land, so that their bodies deservedly fell in the wilderness? Those two alone spoke to the whole multitude, saying: “The land which we explored is exceedingly good”; and because the whole multitude did not receive their testimony, it fell in the wilderness (Num. 13).

Therefore now also, even if I have no more than two witnesses who bear testimony to truth, the entire multitude of opponents, however great it may be, shall bear judgment. For if, in my Passion, two false witnesses seemed sufficient to my adversaries against me, who arose and said, “This man said: I am able to destroy the temple of God and rebuild it in three days” (Matt. 26), why should two true witnesses not suffice for me in turn against my adversaries?

Yet, since—as I had begun to say or inquire above—we have innumerable multitudes of martyrs, that is, witnesses, even if we choose to count only those who shed their blood in testimony, it must rightly be said that the witnesses of him who speaks these things are indeed many, yet nevertheless, according to a certain rationale, only two: that is, they are distinguished into two orders, just as Enoch and Elijah, both holy and beloved by God, differ from one another.

For Enoch is not recorded to have endured any persecutions; rather, he walked with God in peace, and was not found, because God took him away (Gen. 5). But it is known how great persecutions Elijah endured from the most impious Jezebel (3 Kings 18). According to these two, Christ’s witnesses are distinguished until today and until the end of the age: some witnesses live faithfully in the peace of the holy Church, bearing and ceasing not to bear testimony to the truth alike by speaking and writing; others, fighting in persecution for the standing of the faith, defend the aforesaid measurements of the temple of God, of the altar, and of those worshipping in it, and have shed or will shed their blood in that defence.

These two orders of saints are rightly called two witnesses. Therefore he says: “And I will give to my two witnesses.” What shall I give them? Assuredly, a mouth and wisdom, as I promised when I said: “Settle it therefore in your hearts not to prepare beforehand how you will answer; for I will give you a mouth and wisdom which all your adversaries will not be able to resist or gainsay” (Luke 21).

By this saying he certainly does not remove concern from his witnesses; rather, he commands that they should not prophesy from their own hearts, being content to know and say only those things which holy Scripture has set forth, which the holy Spirit, author of holy Scripture, has suggested.

“And they shall prophesy,” he says, “for one thousand two hundred and sixty days.” They shall prophesy—that is, preach—not in any random manner, but so as to understand and reveal the secret things stored within the Scriptures. And they shall do so for one thousand two hundred and sixty days: that is, even amid that abundance of iniquity, signified above by the excessive character of this number, when not everyone will grow cold.

We have spoken, according to our ability, concerning the excessive nature of this number. But something still remains which perhaps someone may ask: namely, why Daniel wrote one thousand two hundred and ninety days, whereas this writer preferred to say one thousand two hundred and sixty.

The answer may be made that one thousand two hundred and ninety is indeed a little greater than one thousand two hundred and sixty; nevertheless, a much more numerous quantity grows from the parts of this smaller number than from the parts of the greater one. For the accumulated parts of the lesser number, one thousand two hundred and sixty, increase beyond three thousand, as has already been shown; but the parts of the greater number, although it too is excessive, do not reach two thousand.

This too is easy to show here. Daniel’s number, one thousand two hundred and ninety, has a half, six hundred and forty-five; a third, four hundred and thirty; a fifth, two hundred and fifty-eight; a sixth, two hundred and fifteen; a tenth, one hundred and twenty-eight; a fifteenth, eighty-six; a thirtieth, forty-three; a forty-third, thirty; an eighty-sixth, fifteen; a one-hundred-and-twenty-ninth, ten; a two-hundred-and-fifteenth, six; a two-hundred-and-fifty-eighth, five; a four-hundred-and-thirtieth, three; a six-hundred-and-forty-fifth, two; and a one-thousand-two-hundred-and-ninetieth, one.

No one will easily find further or different parts of this number. These parts, accumulated together, do indeed exceed the quantity of which they are parts; nevertheless, they do not grow even to two thousand, as has been said. For they make one thousand eight hundred and seventy-eight, whereas the parts of the smaller number, one thousand two hundred and sixty, which is given in the present passage, when brought into one sum extend beyond three thousand, as has been said.

Therefore both Daniel and this John—or he who speaks to John—use excessive numbers to signify the abundance of iniquity so often mentioned (Matt. 24). But this one, who had heard from the Lord’s own mouth, “Because iniquity has abounded, the love of many shall grow cold,” takes or gives a far more excessive number in order to indicate that same abundance of iniquity more sharply; yet he does not depart very far from the same duration of time which Daniel foresaw.

It should, however, be carefully noted that, after saying, “They shall prophesy for one thousand two hundred and sixty days,” he added, “clothed in sackcloth.” What does “clothed in sackcloth” mean except greatly humbled, wholly devoted to penitence? Sackcloth signifies the harsh austerity of penitence, with which mourners—and especially penitents—are accustomed to cover themselves. Thus it is written of the king of Nineveh that, at Jonah’s preaching, he rose from his throne, cast off his robe, put on sackcloth, and sat in ashes (Jonah 3).

But who would not wonder that witnesses of such dignity should have to be clothed in sackcloth? Yet so it is. For it belongs to them to mourn human sins in sackcloth and ashes, and to humble themselves before the Lord all the more as the abundance of iniquity is greater in their own time.

Thus, when Jezebel and Ahab were killing the prophets of the Lord and overthrowing his altars, Elijah was not clothed softly nor living in royal houses; rather, in deserts, unkempt and shaggy, he led a harsh life (3 Kings 19). For concerning his appearance and dress it is written: “What appearance and clothing,” Ahaziah said, “had the man who met you and spoke these words?” They replied: “A hairy man, with a leather belt girded about his loins.” And he said: “It is Elijah the Tishbite” (4 Kings 1).

With this in view, the Apostle, after saying, “The saints endured mockings and scourges, and moreover bonds and prisons; they were stoned, sawn asunder, tempted, and died by the slaughter of the sword,” added also: “They wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins, destitute, distressed, afflicted” (Heb. 11; printed “II”).

Therefore these faithful witnesses, precisely because they are or will be faithful in that tribulation, will mourn the sins of the peoples, as Elijah and Elisha then mourned the sins of Israel in deserts, solitudes, mountains, and caves, together with the other sons of the prophets. For will those days of tribulation be such without the cause of sin? Certainly not. Rather, as it is written elsewhere: “Affliction does not arise from the ground” (Job 5); so then that tribulation will arise not without cause, but because of sin.

Since there are many sins among the people of Christianity, it is not irrelevant to know or inquire from the examples of Scripture for what sin above all, or for what sort of sin, so great a tribulation will be permitted to arise against the Church.

The blessed Jerome, a man illustrious for well-known learning and faith, discussing the passage in Micah, “Her princes judged for gifts, her priests taught for payment, and her prophets divined for money; and they rested upon the Lord, saying, ‘Is not the Lord in our midst? Evils shall not come upon us.’ Therefore, because of you, Zion shall be ploughed like a field, Jerusalem shall become a heap of stones, and the mountain of the temple shall become high places of forests” (Mic. 3), says among other things:

“Peter the apostle says: ‘Silver and gold I do not have’ (Acts 3). He could certainly have sold to Simon Magus what he sought; indeed, he could have pretended to sell it (Acts 8). For the Holy Spirit can neither be sold nor bought; rather, he condemned the money offered together with the one offering it. Now you may see the prophets of Jerusalem not having prophecy in their mouth, yet resting in the Lord and saying, ‘Evils shall not come upon us.’ Because of them God’s watchtower is divided by the hostile plough; the place once of peace becomes full of ruins; the temple of the Lord is turned into brambles and thorns, and becomes the dwelling-place of beasts.”

And after some further remarks:

“Because of us, who are such people—who build Zion in blood and Jerusalem in iniquity, who judge for gifts, who give answers for payment, who divine for money, and who, claiming a fictitious sanctity for ourselves, say: ‘Evils shall not come upon us’—let us hear the judgment of the Lord which follows. Zion, Jerusalem, the mountain of the temple, the watchtower, the vision of peace, and the temple of Christ, at the consummation and end, when love has grown cold and faith has become rare, shall be ploughed like a field, reduced to mounds, and shall become a forest in the Church; so that where once there were spacious houses and heaps of grain beyond number, there may scarcely be a small hut preserving the appearance of food, without refreshment for the soul.”

When he says these things, we may certainly know and say that the chief cause of so great a future tribulation is the sin of ecclesiastical ranks: the sin of venality and greed, which we now observe and see reigning everywhere. Excessive ambition lays all things waste; greed devours almost all that has been stored within the Churches, where, because it is permitted to live, it is also pleasing to seek office.

Therefore it will then rightly come about that, because it will not be permitted to live, it will no longer be pleasing to seek office—far more extensively and miserably than in the time of the Neronian or Diocletian persecution. For when these persecutors pressed hard, it was neither pleasant to buy ecclesiastical offices nor possible to sell them.

Therefore, “clothed in sackcloth they shall prophesy”: that is, doing penance and preaching it to others, they shall announce the testimony of truth to the people; and with all earnestness they shall entreat God either to make the plague cease or to free them from being led into error.

It follows:

“These are the two olive trees and the two lampstands standing before the Lord.”

As though you were asking what fruit ought to be hoped for from their prophesying clothed in sackcloth: “These,” he says, “are two olive trees and two lampstands.” As though he said: Because they shall prophesy in this way, they will therefore be good trees in their time—olive trees, beautiful and fruitful, abounding in mercy obtained from heaven—so that, for their sake, those days, so evil and calamitous, may be shortened.

For they are those elect of whom he himself, foretelling these future things in the Gospel, says: “Unless the Lord had shortened the days, no flesh would have been saved [variant: *would become* saved]; but for the sake of the elect whom he chose, he shortened the days” (Mark 13). Thus they will be olive trees: that is, causes of mercy then to be hastened. For the olive customarily signifies the Lord’s mercy in the Scriptures, not only because of the likeness of its fruit, by whose sweet and gentle ointment wounds are healed, but also because its very name is derived from the Greek ἔλεος (*eleos*), which in Latin is called *misericordia*, “mercy.”

But in what respect are they lampstands? In that, in those days so black and dark, they will shine with clear prophecy or preaching, so that it cannot happen that any of the elect should be led into error. The danger of this error will be so great that the Lord himself, guardian of the elect, took care to say: “For false prophets shall arise and shall give great signs and wonders, so that, if possible, even the elect may be led into error” (Matt. 24).

Thus these are both the two olive trees and the two lampstands. So, at that time, when Jezebel—the night and great darkness of that ancient Church—had darkened heaven and spread darkness through her agents, the prophets of Baal, Elijah stood forth, both to pour forth fitting light like a lampstand, so that the people might say, “The Lord himself is God; the Lord himself is God,” and to obtain mercy for the people from heaven like an olive tree, so that heaven might give rain and earth yield its fruit (3 Kings 18).

Hence it is said in the praises of the fathers: “Then Elijah the prophet arose like fire, and his word burned like a torch.” And shortly afterwards: “You who are recorded in the judgments of the times, to soothe the Lord’s wrath, to reconcile the heart of a father to his son, and to restore the tribes of Jacob: blessed are those who saw you, and who were adorned in your friendship” (Ecclus. 48).

Elisha at that time was the other olive tree and the other lampstand. With the same purpose of usefulness, in order that he might benefit the wretched people, when given a choice he chose to pray that a double portion of his master’s spirit might come upon him. Of him it is written there: “And in Elisha his spirit was fulfilled. Yet in all these things,” it says, “the people did not repent of him, nor did they depart from their sins until they were cast out from their land and scattered throughout all the earth.” Nevertheless, it continues: “And a very small nation was left, and a ruler in the house [variant: *household*] of David.” Immediately it adds: “Some of them did what pleased God, but others committed many sins” (ibid.).

As though he said: Although they did not correct everyone, they nevertheless benefited many toward correction. Assuredly, it will be so with you also. For while these olive trees and lampstands of which he now speaks stand before the Lord, although many will be scandalized, it will nevertheless be impossible that even the elect should be led into error.

Indeed, what he says of these persons standing before the Lord also accords with the profession of Elijah and Elisha. Elijah says to Ahab: “As the Lord God of Israel lives, before whom I stand, there shall be neither dew nor rain in these years” (3 Kings 17). Elisha says to Joram king of Israel: “As the Lord of hosts lives, before whom I stand, if I did not reverence the face of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, I would not even attend to you or look upon you” (4 Kings 3).

Here and there the word “standing” signifies the disposition of virtue: namely, that faithful witnesses, the Lord’s witnesses, do not lie in sins and vices with those who err and must be cast out, but stand upright and ready with the truth—in the exercise of godliness, in the defence of justice, and in service to God, who sits upon the throne and judges the world in equity.

It follows:

> “And if anyone wishes to harm them, fire will come forth from their mouth and devour their enemies. And if anyone wishes to injure them, thus must he be killed. These have power to shut heaven, so that it may not rain during the days of their prophecy; and they have power over the waters to turn them into blood, 435 and to strike the earth with every plague as often as they wish.”
>
> This entire dignity of the witnesses proceeds together with the majesty of the Scriptures; and, more beautifully than words can explain, while it directs attention to things future—and present—it also compels us to remember things past, if we wish to grasp the true meaning of what is said. For although it could have said: “If anyone wishes to lead them into error and to overwhelm the preaching or rule of truth with the storms of heretical perversity, a judgment of condemnation shall go forth from their mouth, so that they anathematize them and hand them over to Satan for eternal destruction,” why did it prefer to be understood thus: “And if anyone wishes to harm them, fire shall go forth from their mouth and devour their enemies”?
>
> Why, I ask, except because a mystical example of this power had already preceded in that often-mentioned Elijah? For thus it is written: “And Ahaziah sent to him a captain of fifty and the fifty who were under him. He went up to him and said, as he was sitting on the top of a mountain: Man of God, the king commands you to come down. Elijah answered and said to the captain of fifty: If I am a man of God, let fire come down from heaven and devour [Col. 1027C] you and your fifty. And fire came down from heaven and devoured him and the fifty who were with him” (4 Kings 1).
>
> He sent another captain of fifty, with fifty men, and similarly “fire went forth from his mouth”—that is, it descended at the command of his mouth—and devoured them. From this it is clear that they said, with the intention of doing harm: “Man of God, the king commands you to come down”; “Man of God, thus says the king: Hurry, come down.” And therefore he said: “Let fire come down from heaven and devour you,” and the effect followed the word.
>
> Just as visible fire then went forth from Elijah’s mouth and devoured his enemies, who bore the king’s commands with arrogant insolence, so invisible fire will go forth from the mouths of these witnesses—that is, a judgment of dominion [Col. 1027D]—and will devour those who, flattering impious kings and Antichrist, the head of impious kings, wish to harm him or injure them.
>
> Again, although it could have said: “They have power to bind in heaven and on earth, so that propitiation or forgiveness of sins may not come upon their enemies throughout all the days of their ministry or office—that is, until the end of the age, or forever,” why did it prefer to say: “These have power to shut heaven, so that it may not rain during the days of their prophecy”?
>
> Why, I ask, except because in the same Elijah there was also manifest the mystery of such rain, or of the power to restrain rain of this kind? “For he prayed earnestly that it might not rain upon the earth, and it did not rain for three years and six months. And again he prayed, and heaven gave rain and the earth gave its fruit.” Since he undertook this at the Lord’s command, he said to King Ahab with great authority: “As the Lord God of Israel lives, in whose presence I stand, there shall be neither dew nor rain in these years except according to the words of my mouth” (3 Kings 17; James 5; 3 Kings 18).
>
> Thus indeed these witnesses shut heaven against their adversaries, the enemies of Christ and foes of truth: they keep their mouths shut—for they themselves are heaven—so that they may not rain the word upon them, refusing to pour forth speech where there is no hearing; for, according to the Apostle, they must “avoid [such persons] after a first and second admonition, because they are perverted and condemned by their own judgment” (Titus 3).
>
> For such a reason this heaven was first shut against the Jews, perverted and condemned by their own judgment, following God its author, who, foreseeing their guilt, said concerning—or against—them in the prophet: “I will command my clouds not to rain rain upon them” [Col. 1028B] (Isaiah 5).
>
> Again, although it could have said: “They have power to condemn wicked doctrines and to pronounce a sentence of anathema, so that whoever receives them may share a like condemnation,” why did it prefer to say: “And they have power over the waters to turn them into blood,” except in order to send us to the mystical history in which the witnesses Moses and Aaron turned the waters of Egypt into blood (Exodus 7)?
>
> Finally, just as, while they possessed this power, the material waters of the Egyptians were turned into blood, so, when these witnesses exercise the power of divine judgment, the consciences of heretics who pour forth perverse teaching, and of all who agree with them, here hear the dreadful and bloody condemnation of eternal death which they will drink.
>
> It adds here: “And they have power to strike the earth with every plague as often as they wish.” It must be understood in the manner in which the aforementioned Moses and Aaron visibly struck the land of Egypt with so many plagues. Thus, by manifold judgments, they invisibly strike the earth—that is, earthly people—until the rebellious fail and are involved in final condemnation, just as those men visibly afflicted the land of Egypt until, struck by the last plague, the Egyptians with their king were hurled into the depths of the sea.
>
> It follows:
>
> “And when they have finished their testimony, the beast that ascends from the abyss shall make war against them, and [Col. 1028D] shall overcome them and kill them. And their bodies shall lie in the streets of the great city which is spiritually called Sodom and Egypt, where also their Lord was crucified.”
>
> “When,” he says, “they have finished their testimony.” Certainly a fixed time and a fixed number are appointed to each of the faithful witnesses: that is, how long they are to perform the office of bearing witness, or until the full measure of their merits has been completed. Since they do not know this, while still living in the body and absent from the Lord (2 Corinthians 5), they sometimes eagerly desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ (Philippians 1), panting upward toward God through the haste of their desire, without considering whether they have completed their testimony or not.
>
> But He who knows and foresees what and how much yet remains defers the fulfillment of their desire for their own profit. Thus also this John, as we read in his Acts, when he repeatedly begged that he might be allowed to depart from here and come to Christ, received this answer: “Wait until you deliver the people who are to believe in me.”
>
> Likewise, impious persecutors, hating the progress of the word of God and the glory of its testimony, hasten to remove the holy witnesses from the earth; but God preserves them, forestalls and frustrates the efforts of those lying in wait, until they finish their testimony. So Herod hastened to kill Christ himself, the faithful King and chief of the faithful witnesses, but was not permitted to do so until He had finished His testimony. Luke relates this as follows:
>
> “Certain Pharisees came, saying to him: Depart; go away from here, for Herod wishes to kill you. And he said to them: Go and tell that fox: Behold, I cast out demons and accomplish healings today and tomorrow, and on the third day I am brought to completion. Nevertheless, I must journey today and tomorrow and the following day, because it is not possible for a prophet to perish outside Jerusalem” [Col. 1029B] (Luke 13).
>
> Therefore, when they have finished their testimony—that is, not before they finish it—the beast, namely Antichrist, who, as the Apostle says, “has long wrought and is working the ministry of iniquity,” shall make war against them (2 Thessalonians 2).
>
> What sort of war? Certainly the sort that is customarily waged between truth and falsehood. For these witnesses, against whom he makes or will make war, are accustomed to fight not with material steel but only with the word [Col. 1029C] of truth. Therefore he will make war against them: that is, he will attack truth, boldly raising up falsehood.
>
> “And he shall overcome them”: that is, he will press them down almost unto victory, 436 just as what is said elsewhere, “They filled both boats so that they were sinking” (Luke 5), must mean that they were being pressed toward sinking. For, Christ says, “False Christs and false prophets shall arise, and shall give signs and wonders to deceive, if possible, even the elect” (Mark 13).
>
> Then the godly martyr, amid his torments, will not perform signs; but that beast will perform lying signs through his prophets, and in this he will seem superior. What finally? “Behold, he shall kill them,” he says.
>
> [Col. 1029D] Who shall kill except the one who is accustomed to kill? For he himself, in his own person, who is properly called Antichrist, has not yet come, though it is certain that he will come. Yet Nero has already come in his spirit, and after him the rest, in whom that son of perdition, who is to be revealed in his own time, has long and extensively carried out the ministry of iniquity.
>
> “And their bodies shall lie in the street of the great city.” The beast that ascends from the abyss—that is, from the hidden and unknown-to-us depth of malice and darkness, where the devil now is, hostile to God, before he enters that man of perdition and is properly called, and becomes, Antichrist—after he has killed the body, will have nothing further that he can do (Luke 12). But he will do this alone: he will cause the bodies [Col. 1030A] which he has killed to lie unburied in the streets.
>
> How often this has already happened is not unknown to one who has read the acts or passions of the martyrs. Moreover, the great city in whose streets the bodies of these witnesses have lain or will lie is the city opposed to the holy city: the city of the devil, opposed to the city or Church of God. Its first citizen and builder was the fratricide Cain (Genesis 4), and thereafter all the children of pride, whose king is the devil himself. “For,” the Lord says to blessed Job, “he is king over all the children of pride” (Job 41).
>
> The buildings of such a city are all vices, above all lust and pride. Therefore he now says: “Which is spiritually called Sodom and Egypt.” Sodom, namely, because of lust—especially that which is against nature—of which the local Sodom was a dreadful example in its punishment (Genesis 15). Egypt, because of pride; and the Egyptians, drowned with their king in the sea together with chariots and horses, supplied a great and famous lesson to the whole world of how damnable its presumption is (Exodus 14).
>
> Rightly, then, is that city denoted by such names. “Where,” he says, “their Lord also was crucified.” Jesus Christ, the Lord of these witnesses, is the faithful witness; and he was crucified here at Jerusalem, outside the city gate.
>
> Is then Jerusalem—that city in which just kings once reigned, in which stood the unique temple of the one God—called Sodom and Egypt? Certainly, if you look to the prophetic truth by whose prompting Isaiah spoke thus: “Hear the word of the Lord, rulers of Sodom; receive with your ears the law of my God, people of Gomorrah.” But in the heading he had previously said: “The vision of Isaiah son of Amos, which he saw concerning Judah and Jerusalem” [Col. 1030C] (Isaiah 1).
>
> Therefore those who were carnally Judah and Jerusalem were spiritually called Sodom and Gomorrah there. Another prophet also, when he says to the same people, “Your father was an Amorite and your mother a Hittite” (Ezekiel 16), provides a place and reason for applying this other name, so that the same city may be called Egypt; since, namely, just as the Amorites and Hittites, so also the Egyptians arose from the posterity of the accursed Ham.
>
> Let, therefore, that city in which the Lord of these witnesses was crucified bear its reproach: let it be spiritually called Sodom and Egypt—that is, let it be reckoned a part [Col. 1030D] of the great city of the devil, denoted by these names. And as the Lord rained fire and sulphur upon Sodom (Genesis 19), and as in Egypt the waters struck by Moses’ rod were turned into blood (Exodus 7), so those who crucified the Lord shall undergo, with the rest—indeed, above the rest—of the murderers and unclean persons among all nations, the everlasting judgment of fire and blood.
>
> “And they from peoples and tribes, tongues, and nations shall see their bodies for three days and a half, and shall not allow them to be placed in tombs. And those who dwell upon the earth shall rejoice over them, and make merry, and send gifts to one another, because these two prophets tormented those who dwell upon the earth.”
>
> The sin of sins, the worst of all, [Col. 1031A] is that impious persons rejoice when they have done evil, exult in the most wicked acts; and rightly there is stored up for such persons a great and inexhaustible treasury of the wrath of the living God (Proverbs 2). This pronouncement, which now says, “They shall see, and rejoice, and make merry, and send gifts to one another,” most gravely marks this sin in those murderers of the holy witnesses.
>
> What, then, will they see? Certainly their great crime: namely, the bodies of the saints whom they have killed not placed in tombs, and the fact that it lies within their power that they shall not be placed in tombs. And why will they so greatly rejoice and make merry and send gifts to one another? “Because,” he says, “these two prophets tormented them.” It must be understood: because, by killing them, they have freed themselves, as they suppose, from great torment.
>
> It would be easy to bring forward examples from the acts or conflicts of the saints and show where or when savage murderers rejoiced and made merry over the overthrow of legions of martyrs—indeed, reclining amid the funerals, they feasted at lavish banquets, as though they had won immense triumphs over their greatest enemies. But one example from their Lord who was crucified is enough.
>
> When they crucified him, they rejoiced and made merry so greatly that, shaking their heads, they said: “Ha! You who destroy the temple of God and rebuild it in three days” [Col. 1031B] (Matthew 27). Moreover, they sent him to one another as though he were a gift: leading him first to Annas, then to Caiaphas, then to Pilate, then to Herod, and then again to Pilate. Thus they sent him to one another as a gift of spectacle and bestowed impious favor upon this gift of theirs.
>
> Finally, Annas considered that an honor was being done him by their bringing Jesus first to him, because he was Caiaphas’s father-in-law (Luke 23). Pilate and Herod, moreover, became friends on that very day, for previously they had been enemies to one another. Thus they rejoiced and made merry as if freed from immense torment, because, as has just been said, “these two prophets tormented those who dwell upon the earth”; and much more vehemently had the Lord of the prophets himself tormented them, so much so that he was burdensome even for them to behold.
>
> For they were dwellers upon earth—that is, they clung no less in heart than in body to earth or earthly desires—whereas he spoke heavenly things and rebuked their earthly [Col. 1031D] greed. Nevertheless, what is said of these witnesses, that they would not allow their bodies to be placed in tombs, they were not permitted to do to their Lord who was crucified.
>
> For the Holy Spirit had provided for him through this precept of the sacred and mystical law: “When a man has sinned in a matter worthy of death, and, having been sentenced to death, has been hanged upon a gallows, his corpse shall not remain upon the wood, but you shall bury it on the same day, because he who hangs on the wood is accursed by God” (Deuteronomy 21).
>
> In this statement it should be observed that it is guilt, not punishment, which makes a curse; for it first says, and carefully specifies, “when a man has sinned in a matter worthy of death,” and only then adds, 437 “and, having been sentenced to death, has been hanged upon a gallows.” But they wished, by their own judgment, that he who had no guilt should be accursed because of the punishment.
>
> Nevertheless, as has already been said, the authority of the law supporting this, they were not permitted to prevent his burial. Thus, even in this, unknowingly they served our salvation: his soul descended into hell to liberate, through the power of the divinity inherent in it, all the souls of the elect; and his body, whose burial was not prevented, was placed in the earth, so that it might grant dead bodies to leap out from their tombs in the resurrection to come.
>
> Finally, it should be noted that he so defines the periods of time as to say that they will see their bodies for three days and a half, and again: “After three days and a half the spirit of life from God entered into them, and they stood upon their feet” [Col. 1032B]. For the same length of time which he had earlier indicated by saying, “They shall trample the holy city for forty-two months,” and again, “They shall prophesy for one thousand two hundred and sixty days,” he now signifies by saying, “three days and a half”; and again, “after three days and a half.”
>
> Thus he calls a time, times, and half a time—that is, three and a half years—three days and a half here. Why is this? Why, while these witnesses were prophesying, was the time of their prophecy fixed at one thousand two hundred and sixty days, that is, three and a half years, but after they have prophesied, after the beast has killed their bodies and thereafter has nothing that it can do, did he choose to say or write “three days and a half” instead of three and a half years? (John 21.)
>
> Certainly because, for the holy witnesses of God contending for truth in a most grievous struggle, while the time of distress is imminent and present, while they are led where they do not wish, it seems long to the sense of the frailest flesh. But after that time has passed, “when there shall be no more death, neither mourning, nor crying, nor pain, because the former things have passed away” (Revelation 21), then, established in blessed eternity and looking back behind them, what they endured will seem to have been brief. Then they will perceive how truly the Apostle said: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory which shall be revealed in us” [Col. 1032C] (Romans 8).
>
> He says therefore: “And after three days and a half the spirit of life from God entered into them”—that is, after a short time, however long it may seem, it shall happen that the returning spirits, at the command of the Almighty, return to their own limbs, and those who lay dead in tombs, or even cast out unburied, shall rise again.
>
> The tense of the verbs has changed. For although the statement thus far has concerned the future—“they shall trample the holy city”; “I shall give to my two witnesses, and they shall prophesy”; “their bodies shall lie in the streets”; “they shall see, and rejoice”—it is now said in the past tense: “The spirit of life from God entered into them, and they stood.”
>
> Certainly this change of tense indicates a change of speaker. For from what was said above, “But cast out the court which is outside the temple, and do not measure it, because it has been given to the nations, and they shall trample the holy city,” these and all the subsequent words down to this point are the words of the person who gave the reed. But here John himself begins to speak again, using the same verbal tense, namely the past tense, in which he spoke above. This, as is clear, is not unusual in prophetic speech: when they foretell future things, they very often use verbs in the past tense.
>
> “And they stood,” he says, “upon their feet.” It is understood: in great steadfastness. For this is indicated by the added phrase, “upon their feet.” “Then,” as Wisdom says, “the righteous shall stand in great steadfastness against those who afflicted them and who took away their labors. Seeing this, they shall be troubled with dreadful fear” [Col. 1033A] (Wisdom 5).
>
> Concerning this fear of the wicked, and at the same time concerning that state of the saints, he immediately adds: “And great fear fell upon those who saw them. And they heard a great voice from heaven saying to them: Come up here. And they went up into heaven in a cloud, and their enemies saw them.”
>
> This, certainly, their enemies saw—indeed, will see—because they shall hear the great voice saying: “Come up here”; saying: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom” (Matthew 25). “Then,” says the Apostle, “we shall be caught up in clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord” (1 Thessalonians 4).
>
> This is what Wisdom says: “Seeing this, they shall be troubled with dreadful fear, and they shall marvel at the suddenness of an unexpected salvation; and, groaning through distress of spirit, they shall say within themselves, repenting and groaning through anguish of spirit: [Col. 1033C] These are they whom we once held in derision and as an object of reproach. We fools considered their life madness and their end dishonorable. How then have they been numbered among the children of God, and how is their lot among the saints?” (Wisdom 5).
>
> “And in that hour there was a great earthquake; and the tenth part of the city fell, and in the earthquake seven thousand names of men were killed. And the rest were struck with fear and gave glory to the God of heaven.”
>
> Nothing is truer than that in that hour, when the dead rise, there will be a great earthquake, so that all may awaken when they have been lulled as if by so profound a sleep. Moreover, what he above called the great city, which he also affirmed to be spiritually called Sodom and Egypt, he now calls not the city but the [Col. 1033D] tenth part of the city, which he says fell, or will fall.
>
> In truth, what is called the city of the devil is not a city but the ruins of the great and holy city, the heavenly Jerusalem. It has nine orders of angels; and therefore those who fell from it, together with the human beings who share their lot, are rightly called the “tenth part,” the ruinous part of that “city.” Both shall fall—that is, will fall—into hell with the devil and his angels: both his human followers and they themselves.
>
> Therefore he was not content merely to say, “And the tenth part of the city fell,” but added: “And seven thousand names of men were killed in the earthquake.” For “seven thousand men” is the same as saying the totality of impious people. Yet he preferred to say “names of men” rather than simply “men,” by which we understand persons named and renowned in this world, such as those of whom it is written in the Psalm: “Their dwelling places are from generation to generation, and they have called their names in their lands” [Col. 1034A] (Psalm 48).
>
> And in Isaiah: “Therefore hell has enlarged its appetite and opened its mouth without any limit; and their mighty men, their people, their lofty ones, and their glorious ones shall descend into it” (Isaiah 5).
>
> How did, or shall, that tenth part of the city fall, and how shall the names of men be killed in that hour of so great an earthquake? Certainly when the same Lord who will say to his witnesses, “Come up here”—that is, “Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom”—will say, “Fall down there”—that is, “Depart, accursed ones, into eternal fire” (Matthew 25). Then they shall fall and go into eternal punishment.
>
> “And the rest were struck with fear and gave glory to the God of heaven.” Who are, or will be, the rest except all the elect who will stand at the right hand? But will they be afraid or be struck with fear when the devil is cast down before the eyes of all? Certainly they will be afraid, because, as we have heard or read the Lord saying to blessed Job: “When he is raised up, the angels shall be afraid, and, terrified, shall be purified” (Job 41). 438
>
> For they will be shaken by such a weight of terror that the strength even of the holy preachers, whom Scripture is accustomed to call angels, will be troubled. Yet there will in them be, in some manner, a joyful trembling and a secure fear: for they will be certain that they are to be rewarded with the heavenly kingdom, yet because of the weakness of the flesh they will tremble at the fear of so great a convulsion.
>
> “And,” he says, “they gave glory to the God of heaven”: namely, marveling at the power of the Most Strong, who will cast down so strong and so proud an enemy with such strength [Col. 1034C].
>
> In this way the tenth part of the heavenly city, which long ago fell from heaven, while the nine orders of angels remained, as has been said, shall then fall and be cast down also from the earth and from this air—in which those great spirits have hitherto wickedly wandered. This is the part which the Apostle calls “the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 6); and impious human beings shall be sent away with them.
>
> “The second woe has passed; behold, the third woe will come quickly.” This is joined to the earlier passage (Revelation 9), where, after the words, “One woe has passed; behold, two woes are still coming,” it immediately follows [Col. 1034D] that “the sixth angel sounded the trumpet.” A great plague is then described: the four angels are released, and by them a third part of humanity is killed by three plagues—namely, the plague of fire, the plague of smoke, and the plague of sulphur.
>
> Indeed, the matters treated in this following little book, from the place where it began thus, “And I saw another mighty angel coming down from heaven” (Revelation 10), to this present place where it now says, “The second woe has passed; behold, the third woe will come quickly,” belong neither to that second nor to this third woe, but to the praise of Christ and the magnificence of his glory and mercy. For, lest that final woe should come suddenly and unexpectedly upon his unprepared elect, he deigned to come in person and to foretell it.
>
> Noting this, whatever we believe—that Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners (1 Timothy 2)—and whatever we read—that he himself, with his own mouth in the Gospel, foretold that beneath that final woe, that is, the judgment of condemnation for the impious, would come—we should say with the one who speaks or writes these things: “The second woe has passed; behold, the third woe will come quickly” [Col. 1035A].
>
> “And the seventh angel sounded the trumpet, and great voices arose in heaven, saying: The kingdom of this world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign for ages of ages. And the twenty-four elders, who sit before God upon their thrones, fell upon their faces and worshipped God, saying: We give thanks to you, Lord God Almighty, who are, and who were [and who are to come, because] you have received your great power and have reigned. And the nations were angry, and your wrath came, and the time for the dead to be judged, and for reward to be given to your servants, to the prophets, to the saints, and to those who fear your name, small and great, and for destroying those who corrupted the earth.”
>
> This seventh trumpet is, as we have already mentioned above, that last trumpet of which the Apostle also speaks when he writes to the Corinthians: “We shall all indeed rise again, but we shall not all be changed. In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet: for the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall rise incorruptible” (1 Corinthians 15). And likewise to the Thessalonians: “For the Lord himself shall descend from heaven at the command, and with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God” (1 Thessalonians 4).
>
> Who could doubt that the resurrection of the dead belongs, or will belong, to the sound of that seventh or last trumpet—of which the Apostle there also says, “The dead shall rise incorruptible,” and of which this writer has already said here, “The spirit of life from God entered into them, and they stood upon their feet” [Col. 1035C]?
>
> Why then did he anticipate matters in this way, first saying, “The spirit of life from God entered into them,” which is for the dead to rise, and then writing, “The second woe has passed; behold, the third woe will come quickly,” immediately adding, “And the seventh angel sounded the trumpet”?
>
> Why, I ask, except because to rise from the dead and stand upon one’s feet is not a woe but great joy to those witnesses concerning whom, or on whose behalf, he framed that prophecy? Finally, because he said that the tenth part of the city fell when the earthquake occurred, and said this for the glory of those same witnesses, it ought rather to be announced as a joy for the saints. Therefore, at last looking toward the woe of the seventh trumpet, he introduced its sound; and the chief utterance of that trumpet’s sounding is the utterance by which it thus concludes the woe: “Your wrath came, and the time for the dead to be judged, and for reward to be given to your servants, and for destroying those who corrupted the earth.”
>
> This, certainly, is the final woe, and this is the sound of the seventh trumpet, concerning which that mighty angel swore truly “that there would be no more time, but in the days of the voice of the seventh angel, when he begins to sound the trumpet, the mystery of God shall be completed” [Col. 1035D] (Revelation 10).
>
> Therefore, when the seventh angel sounds, “great voices,” he says, “arose in heaven, saying: ‘The kingdom of this world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign for ages of ages.’” These great voices of the blessed angels and of all the saints will never fall silent throughout eternity.
>
> When they say, “The kingdom of this world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ,” we must understand that, from that final trumpet onward, what the Lord Father said to the Lord Son will then have been fulfilled: “Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies your footstool” [Col. 1036A] (Psalm 109).
>
> For the Lord already reigns, and his Christ, who says in the Psalm, “But I have been established by him as king upon Zion, his holy mountain” (Psalm 2), has been in the glory of his kingdom ever since he rose from the dead and ascended into heaven, according to the prophetic proclamation of the same Psalmist: “You crowned him with glory and honor and set him over the works of your hands” (Psalm 8).
>
> But the world, being rebellious in large part, still kicks against him and persecutes his holy ministers. Therefore, when the Apostle recalled this testimony, saying, “You crowned him with glory and honor and set him over the works of your hands; you subjected all things beneath his feet,” he immediately added the future matter of which we speak: “But now we do not yet see all things subjected to him” [Col. 1036B] (Hebrews 2).
>
> Thus, as has been said, the Lord and his Christ indeed already reign, and the present Church is called and is his kingdom. But there are still many stumbling-blocks in his kingdom, which will be gathered out when the last trumpet sounds. When this has happened, then at last it shall rightly be sung with full voice: “The kingdom of this world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ,” because, once all enemies have been bound in the prison of hell, the kingdom shall be at peace, and they shall reign in peace for ages of ages.
>
> “And the twenty-four elders, who sit before God upon their thrones, fell upon their faces and worshipped God, saying: We give thanks to you, Lord God Almighty, who are and who were, because you have received your great power and have reigned; and the nations were angry, and your wrath came, and the time for the dead to be judged, and for reward to be given to your servants, to the prophets, to the saints, and to those who fear your name, small and great, and for destroying those who corrupted the earth.”
>
> Great and everlasting thanksgivings are owed for God’s many good works and his great and eternal benefits. What benefit of this same Lord God Almighty is greater and more beautiful than that which they recall when they say: “Because you have received your power and have reigned” [Col. 1036D]?
>
> What is more magnificent than that the Lord received his power, 439 and reigned? For sin reigned; death had reigned from Adam; the devil reigned, holding the rulership of the world. He was the armed strong man who possessed and guarded his court in peace (John 12; Matthew 12; Luke 11).
>
> Having compassion on humankind because of this, he received his power and reigned: the stronger one came upon him, conquered him, and plundered his goods. This is that receiving of power and kingdom concerning which the Psalmist also foretold: “The Lord has reigned; he has put on splendor. The Lord has put on strength and girded himself” [Col. 1037A] (Psalm 92).
>
> How, or when, did he receive that power of his? Indeed, what is that power of God except the Spirit of God, the finger of God? The one who reigned himself says: “If I cast out demons by the finger of God, then surely the kingdom of God has come upon you” (Matthew 12).
>
> That the Spirit of God is rightly called—and is—his power is also attested by the archangel Gabriel when he says to Mary: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you” (Luke 1). Hence it should be noted that they did not merely say, “You received power”; rather, they say, “You received *your* power.”
>
> For the Son of God, having become human—or in becoming human—received this power in his conception; but before becoming human that same power was his, because the Spirit was one and the same, his and the Father’s. Therefore it was not without great weight that it was said, “You received your power.” For the power, or Spirit, which, as we faithfully believe, he received as a gift in his human nature, was the same power and the same Spirit which the one and same Son of God possessed, consubstantial with himself, in the nature of divinity before the world was made [Col. 1037B].
>
> Rightly, therefore, when such a great benefit of the reigning Lord has been brought to completion, the “twenty-four elders falling upon their faces”—that is, all the fathers, teachers, or rulers of the Churches—worship and say: “We give thanks to you, Lord God Almighty,” and so forth.
>
> That thanksgiving of those falling upon their faces—that is, submitting their souls in ordered reverence—will have no end. Their words, “who are and who were,” strike and endlessly scourge the evil purpose of the condemned adversaries, who strove to bring about his nonexistence, that he should not endure, as the Psalmist testifies against them in his own person: “My enemies spoke evil against me: When shall he die, and his name perish?” [Col. 1037C] (Psalm 40).
>
> For, after the words, “Because you have received your power and have reigned”—that is, incarnate through your Holy Spirit, you cast out the prince of this world—they immediately add:

“And the nations were enraged.” For why were the nations enraged, or what did they seek to accomplish by their anger, except that he should not exist? Certainly the Jews are not excluded here from the name “nations,” since they were the first to be enraged and most bitterly jealous, handing him over to the Gentiles to be mocked, scourged, and crucified (Matt. [Col. 1037D] 20; Luke 18), saying, as we have already recalled: “When will he die, and his name perish?” Therefore in the Psalm the Holy Spirit vehemently and mockingly reproaches them: “Why did the nations rage, and the peoples devise vain things?” (Ps. 2). Truly they devised vain things, because you, Lord, were God even before you became man; and now, after the nations were enraged and raged furiously in killing you, you rose again and are. Hence you likewise say to the Father in David: “I arose, and I am still with you” (Ps. 138 [139]).

Therefore, “the nations were enraged,” that is, they killed you and, as has already been said, in killing you raged furiously. But what follows? “And, they say, your wrath came.” Rightly and in due order: the nations were first enraged; afterward [Col. 1038A] your wrath came. This is the lawful order of justice: God is angry with no one unless that person has first become angry—swelling with pride, resisting, and defending his own guilt after the likeness of the transgressor Adam. Where a person is angry and resists, there at last God is angry and resists, and against the strong man employs his power, which cannot be borne. Thus, when the Psalmist had said, “You are terrible, and who can resist you?” he immediately added, “from then is your wrath” (Ps. 75 [76]). It is as though he said: Not from the moment a person sins, but from the moment, by defending his sin and resisting your justice, he multiplies it—from then is your wrath, which none can withstand, as it is written elsewhere: “God, whose wrath no one can resist” (Job 9).

This order of judgment is observed both particularly in individual persons and universally in the whole human race. They say, therefore: “And the nations were enraged, and your wrath came.” As though they said: Because the nations refused to receive repentance when you preached, but instead “were enraged,” and “raged, and devised vain things, and the kings of the earth stood forth, and the rulers assembled together against the Lord and against his Christ” (Ps. 2), therefore only now did your wrath justly come, as is written there concerning you: “Then he shall speak to them in his wrath, and trouble them in his fury” (ibid.).

For, explaining what they meant by “and your wrath came,” they continue and say: “And the time for the dead to be judged, and to render reward to your servants, and to the prophets, and to the saints, and to those who fear your name, small and great, and to destroy those who corrupted the earth.” The effect of his wrath [Col. 1038C] which came is to destroy those who corrupted the earth. For rendering reward to the saints is not wrath but grace for grace: the grace of blessedness for the grace of calling, or blessedness earned by faith. And rightly the wording is connected and ordered thus: first it is said, “to render reward to his servants,” and afterward, “and to destroy those who corrupted the earth.” For according to the true order, or the ordered truth, of the Gospel, reward will first be rendered to the servants of God at the right hand, and afterward those at the left will be destroyed. For that King will first say to those on the right: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom” (Matt. 25). Then he will say to those on the left: “Depart, accursed ones, into eternal fire” (ibid.). In such a manner reward will be rendered to God’s servants, and the corrupters of the earth will be destroyed.

But who are the corrupters of the earth except corrupters of bodies and souls, serving every kind of their own desire? For in God’s judgment the charge is not brought concerning any corruption except that by which the rational creature is corrupted. Though it ought to be God’s earth and bear the fruit of faith, holiness, peace, and love, it has been so corrupted in itself that it produces the bitter thorns of unbelief and every lust, and is therefore reckoned fit for the curse.

Thus in the days of the voice of the seventh angel, when he begins to sound the trumpet, “the mystery of God will be completed”; and, as that mighty angel who stood upon the sea and upon the earth, raising his hand to heaven, swore (Rev. 10), “time shall be no more.” The time of repentance will no longer be granted to sinners, who have been sufficiently warned beforehand by the many terrifying trumpet-blasts already described. Not partly, as in the sounding of the other trumpets, but all the corrupters of the earth together [Col. 1040A] will perish and be destroyed at the command of the reigning Lord, at the voice of the archangel, at the trumpet of God (1 Thess. 4), so that they may no longer cause any scandal in the kingdom of God.

440. BOOK SEVEN

[Col. 1039]

CHAPTER 12

[Col. 1039B]

“And the temple of the Lord was opened in heaven, and the ark of his covenant was seen in his temple. And there were lightnings, and voices, and an earthquake, and great hail. And a great sign appeared in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun, and the moon beneath her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars; and she was with child, and cried out in travail, and was tormented to give birth.”

Here one must recall the earlier passage, where seven angels standing before God were given seven trumpets and prepared themselves to sound them (Rev. 8). Scripture has thus far set out in sequence what happened and what was done at each separate trumpet-blast. For there, before it says, “and the seven angels prepared themselves to sound the trumpets,” another angel is introduced, “who came [Col. 1039C] and stood before the altar, having a golden censer; and much incense was given to him, that he might offer it with the prayers of all the saints upon the golden altar which is before the throne” (ibid.).

Thus, after the seven angels to whom the trumpets were given had been set in place on the one hand, and the other angel who had the golden censer on the other, it was first explained what was done through each trumpet-blast, and seven punishments for sins were recorded. Only now, resuming the beginning, is written what was done in the ministry of the angel having the golden censer; and the great war and prolonged conflict are recounted of the angel who is now also called Michael, fighting against the great red dragon with seven heads. The splendid victories of the martyrs are proclaimed, as they finally sing, after the labors of battle, something like a new song.

Here the works of the spirit of fortitude are plainly proclaimed. In the order of the seven spirits it is fourth, joined to the spirit of counsel, whose providence we mentioned above in connection with the seven sounding trumpets. He says, therefore: “And the temple of the Lord was opened in heaven.” By this conjunction—“and it was opened”—he brings us back to the foregoing passage, where he had said: “And another angel came and stood before the altar,” and so forth. For at the same time the temple of the Lord was opened and the angel stood by the altar. The temple of the Lord was opened when holy people received in their hearts faith in the Lord and the promises of Christ; and the angel stood by the altar when, on account of this same faith, Michael was appointed prince over the nation of the righteous, as we have more fully shown in its place on the authority of the Scriptures.

Therefore “the temple of the Lord was opened [Col. 1040B] in heaven”; that is, the holy fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob believed, and by believing in the Christ who was to come became the temple of the Lord. “And the ark of his covenant was seen in his temple.” That is, the incarnation of Christ, the Son of God, was beheld in advance and greeted from afar; now it is seen in his temple—that is, in his Church—shining with the great brightness of the purest gold, namely his divinity.

The incarnation of the Son of God is rightly understood by the ark of the covenant because, as a figure of him, Moses at the Lord’s command made in the wilderness both the ark of the covenant and the mercy-seat (Exod. 37). The ark signified the same Son of God who was to be incarnate; the mercy-seat signified that same Son as one who would suffer for human sins.

“And there were [Col. 1040C] lightnings and voices, and an earthquake, and great hail.” Supply: at the place where the angel took the censer, filled it with fire from the altar, and cast it upon the earth (Rev. 8). For there it immediately follows: “And there were thunders, and voices, and an earthquake.” Although this is rightly understood of the Holy Spirit, whom the Lord sent upon his apostles and who rested upon them like fire (Acts 2), nevertheless, as we have said, it is also rightly understood of the giving of the Law to that people on Mount Sinai (Exod. 19), through the ordering of angels, as Stephen the first martyr says (Acts 7). For the lightnings and voices that shone or were heard spiritually through the apostles were not absent in reality on Mount Sinai when the Law was given. Thus it is proper to understand the Psalmist’s words concerning both disturbances, that of the Law and that of the Gospel: “O God, when you went forth before your people, when you passed through the wilderness, the earth was moved” (Ps. 64 [68]), and so forth.

Therefore, returning to those times when the blessed offspring of the saints conceived in promise faith in the coming Christ, while the other nations were permitted to walk in their own ways: just as in the seven trumpets we have seen an equal number of notable and conspicuous punishments for sins, so now in what follows, down to the Lamb standing upon Mount Zion, let us observe the wars and victories of the saints. It begins thus: “And a great sign appeared in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun, and the moon beneath her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars; and she was with child, and cried out in travail, and was tormented to give birth.”

Truly this was a great sign, and a sign of a great matter. For that woman signified the holy Church, whom we find called in many places in the Scriptures of the prophets a woman joined to and loved by her husband, that is, God; indeed, sometimes, with reference to the transgressors who served the vices and sins of idolatry, reproved as an adulteress. This woman is rightly called “clothed with the sun” from the time when she received in promise Christ, the true Sun of righteousness. “The moon beneath her feet”: that is, the splendor of temporal goods under her administration. For the moon, because of its changeableness, rightly signifies the mutable goods of this world, to which the foolish person is subject, but over which the wise person rules.

It is therefore praiseworthy in the holy fathers that, though they were rich, as the sacred histories relate, they did not allow riches to rule their affections. Rather, they ruled their riches, distributing them as private or public need required. In this way such rich persons are commendably excused, because fault lies not in possession but in affection. On the other hand, whoever has indeed believed in Christ but clings to and serves the gains of temporal things in his affection is their slave, not their master. Nor can it rightly be said of his soul that she is “a woman clothed with the sun, with the moon beneath her feet”; rather, in a most perverse manner she is clothed with the moon and strives to have the sun beneath her feet.

It follows: “And on her head a crown of twelve stars.” A crown of twelve stars is seen upon this woman’s head because, at the beginning of the Church’s birth, the twelve patriarchs, and likewise at the beginning of her rebirth the twelve apostles, are numbered as distinguished and shining. For the present, however, following the order of the heavenly marvels, [Col. 1041C] we understand the crown of twelve stars as the number of the twelve sons, or tribes, of Israel. Joseph too, recounting his dream, said: “I saw the sun and moon and eleven stars worshipping me” (Gen. 37). His father was like the sun on account of the Christ whom he held in promise; his mother, whichever woman stood to him as mother—for his natural mother had died—was the moon, shining by faith in that same Christ; and the eleven brothers to whom he recounted the dream were the eleven stars to be. Joseph himself was the twelfth star.

Therefore, “on the woman’s head a crown of twelve stars”: at the beginning of the Church, the choir of the twelve sons or tribes of Israel. “And she was with child, and cried out in travail, and was tormented to give birth.” What was it to be with child except to preserve in the secret place of the heart faith in the promise? For when God first spoke to Abraham, saying: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22)—and that seed is certainly Christ (Gal. 5 [uncertain citation])—Abraham believed the one promising; and from that time, as his descendants hoped in the same faith, the woman began to be with child.

But God, who had promised, was the husband of that woman, and the father and author of her conception—that is, of the faith through which the Christ who was to come already dwelt in the hearts of the believing fathers. As the multitude of believers increased over time, Moses and the prophets followed, and, both speaking and writing, they expressed the faith they had received with intense longing.

[Col. 1042A] It follows therefore: “And she cried out in travail and was tormented to give birth.” What he said, “and she cried out in travail,” he repeated—or rather completed—by adding, “and was tormented to give birth.” For it would have been insufficient merely to say, “and she cried out in travail.” It might seem that he intended nothing more than if he had said: when she was giving birth, she began to cry out. But before she gave birth, before she brought forth the child, she travailed and cried out. For to travail is to suffer before childbirth; “to travail” is a word denoting a process, whereas “to give birth” is a completed word.

Therefore, just as a woman physically pregnant, when the hour of birth draws near, is wholly occupied with the thought of her delivery, remains absorbed in that expectation, and endures suffering until she gives birth, so too that woman, spiritually pregnant, “cried out in travail and was tormented to give birth.” We could produce many of her cries, but by way of example this one passage in the prophet Isaiah is sufficient:

> “Lord, who has believed our report? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed? And he shall rise like a shoot before him, and like a root out of thirsty ground. He has neither form nor beauty. And we saw him, and there was no appearance; and we desired him: despised and the last of men, a man of sorrows and knowing infirmity; and as though his face were hidden and despised, therefore we did not esteem him. Truly he bore our infirmities, and he carried our sorrows” (Isa. 53).

When the holy prophets said these and similar things, crying out and grieving, were they unwilling that the cause of this same cry and grief should occur and be certain? On the contrary, they desired it most earnestly, as the Lord himself testifies when he says: “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see. For I tell you that many prophets and kings wished to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it” (Luke 19 [uncertain citation]). Is not here also a true likeness of a woman in travail, crying out as she travails? For she cries out while in travail because she suffers pain; yet surely she prefers to suffer thus rather than remain barren with a healthy womb.

It follows: “And another sign was seen in heaven, and behold, a great red dragon, having seven heads and ten horns, and on its heads seven diadems; and its tail drew a third part of the stars of heaven and cast them upon the earth. And the dragon stood before the woman who was about to give birth, that when she had given birth he might devour her son. And she gave birth to a male child, who was to rule all nations with an iron rod. And her son was caught up to God and to his throne.”

Truly this was another sign, that is, a sign of another thing. For it was a sign of the devil, who has always exercised and does not cease to exercise enmity against that woman—evil to himself, but good to the woman. For God, who is good, established these very enmities for the woman’s good, as in the beginning, speaking to the serpent, he says: “I shall put enmities between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed. She shall crush your head, and you shall lie in wait for her heel” (Gen. 3).

Accordingly, this dragon was a sign of that serpent—that is, of the devil who spoke in the serpent. Conversely, that woman clothed with the sun was a sign of the whole Church, of which the Blessed Virgin Mary is the greatest portion—indeed, the best portion because of the blessedness of her own womb.

“Therefore,” he says, “another sign was seen: and behold, a great red dragon.” Why great, and why red? Great, namely, because it had “seven heads and ten horns”; red chiefly because “its tail drew a third part of the stars of heaven,” and, thirsting for red blood, “stood before the woman who was about to give birth, so that when she had given birth it might devour her son.” From this it was great; from this, red.

What then did those seven heads signify? To make this clear more briefly, one must first know that such a great and red dragon signified the devil in such a way that it simultaneously signified his entire body: namely, the whole wicked generation, the generation of Cain, which from the beginning opposed the holy generation, the generation of Abel, the generation of those seeking the Lord, seeking the face of the God of Jacob (Ps. 23 [24]); and, as has been said, such a woman was its sign.

Once these matters have been understood, it is easy to see that the dragon’s heads are rightly said to be those who were chief in the devil’s work or purpose: namely, in besieging the woman already mentioned, intending to kill the offspring of God’s Church, to choke the word of God, and to destroy faith in the seed of Abraham—that is, Christ. Such heads are truly seven. For from the time when Father Abraham and his descendants received faith in the seed “in whom all nations shall be blessed,” there have been seven kingdoms of this world, according to the tradition of the Holy Scriptures, which fought against that faith; but the seventh kingdom has not yet come.

The first kingdom after Abraham believed was that of Pharaoh and the Egyptians, who hated the children of Israel (Exod. 1). The second was the kingdom of Jezebel and her impious children or descendants—the kingdom of Israel and Judah—which killed the prophets (3 Kings [1 Kings] 19). The third was Babylonian; the fourth Persian or Median; the fifth Macedonian; the sixth Roman; the seventh will be the kingdom of Antichrist. Apart from these seven kingdoms, Holy Scripture records no other as having stood or standing before that woman to devour her son, opposing the holy Church from the time Abraham believed, in order to destroy faith in his seed.

Let us touch briefly, by way of example, upon the bloody jaws of each of these heads. Pharaoh, the first king of the Egyptians, said to his people: “Whatever is born of the male sex, cast into the river; whatever is female, preserve” (Exod. 1). And again: “You are idle, and therefore you say, ‘Let us go and sacrifice to the Lord’” (Exod. 5), and much else of this kind.

After him, Jezebel, having captivated her husband King Ahab so that he went and served Baal and worshipped him, killed the prophets of the Lord, as Elijah the Tishbite mournfully says: “Lord, they have destroyed your altars, and killed your prophets with the sword; and I alone remain, and they seek my life to take it away” (3 Kings [1 Kings] 19). In Judah also, the offspring of that same Jezebel—King Joash—killed the prophet Zechariah; and from that time the dragon began even in Jerusalem to drink the blood of this woman, killing prophets lest they prophesy, or because they prophesied in the name of the Lord (1 Chron. 30 [uncertain citation]). Nor did it cease until it thought, by crucifying the son brought forth in childbirth, that it would devour him. But this will be discussed more plainly later.

In the third place, Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, carried the prophets of the Lord into captivity together with the rest of the Jews, set up an image, and wished so far to abolish the Lord’s name that he said to the three youths: “If you do not worship, you shall be cast into a furnace of burning fire. And who is the God who shall deliver you from my hand?” (Dan. 3), and so forth.

Then, in the fourth place, the kingdom of the Persians and Medes sought to destroy the entire Jewish race, among whom alone God was then known, through Haman, enemy of the Jews (Esther 3). He was of the stock of Agag, whom Samuel killed and cut to pieces before the Lord (1 Kings 15). For when King Ahasuerus had exalted him and set his throne above all the princes he had, and all the king’s servants who remained at the palace gates bent the knee and worshipped Haman, Mordecai alone did not bend the knee or worship him. Haman was greatly enraged; and, thinking it of no account merely to lay hands on Mordecai, he rather wished to destroy the entire nation of the Jews in Ahasuerus’s kingdom. Hence Esther says: “This Haman is our most evil enemy and foe” (Esther 7). And again: “Now he is our enemy, whose cruelty overflows even upon the king” (ibid.).

The fifth head of this dragon was the Macedonian kingdom. The sufferings and battles of the Maccabees testify how, during the reign of Antiochus, who was called Epiphanes—that is, noble or illustrious—he afflicted this woman by compelling the Jews to abandon the laws of their fathers and of God. Of this Antiochus it is also written that “he sent to defile the temple at Jerusalem, and to name it after Olympian Jupiter, and that at Garizim, according to the inhabitants of the place, after Hospitable Jupiter” (2 Macc. 6).

For the event which especially concerns the dragon’s most wicked purpose begins thus: “Two women were accused of having circumcised their sons. With their infants suspended at their breasts, after they had been led publicly through the city, they were cast down from the walls” (ibid.). What did he intend by this and by the events that follow, except that the conception of the woman—that is, faith in Abraham’s seed, of which circumcision was for them the seal and testimony—might be utterly extinguished?

Concerning the sixth head, that is, the Roman kingdom, who does not know how fiercely it raged to devour this woman’s son? It is surely that kingdom which, together with the second head, namely the Jewish kingdom, gaped with one violently savage mouth—first, to devour that son in his own person, when the Son of Man was handed over to the Gentiles to be mocked, scourged, and crucified (Matt. 20), that Jewish people, namely, saying to the minister of this other great head: “If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend” (John 19).

Then came, as we shall say shortly, the greatest war which the dragon waged against Michael and his angels. Again, when it adds that the dragon made war against the rest of this woman’s seed, by what head was it done except the Roman empire, which, dispatching edicts and public laws throughout the whole world, killed so many thousands of martyrs?
