Finally, concerning the seventh head, when it rises—that is, concerning the man of sin, the son of perdition, Antichrist, when he is revealed, “who opposes and exalts himself above everything called God or worshipped” (2 Thess. 2)—who does not know that he will persecute this woman and the remnant of her seed so severely that, as the Lord says, there will then be tribulation such as has not been from the beginning, is not, and never shall be? For he will be the one of whom the angel says to Daniel: “He shall speak words against the Most High and wear down the saints of the Most High” (Dan. 2 [7]), and so forth.

Elsewhere, after the angel had said to this John, “The seven heads of the beast are seven mountains and seven kings,” he immediately added: “Five have fallen, one is, and another has not yet come. And when he comes, he must remain a short time” (Rev. 17). What is silent here is supplied there: namely, that upon the beast—which is none other than this dragon—sat a woman, another woman, always opposed to this woman whom the dragon attacks: that is, the city of the devil, ever contrary to the city of God.

What does he mean by “five have fallen, one is, and another has not yet come”? Namely, that when these things were seen or written, the kings of the five kingdoms already mentioned, who persecuted the woman so often mentioned, had long since passed away; but the decrees against Christ’s Church of the king of the Roman kingdom—King or Emperor Nero—were raging, and were preserved by his successors. The other, namely Antichrist, had not yet come—and has not yet come. But of these matters elsewhere. Let us now pursue what lies before us.

Having said, “having seven heads,” he added, “and ten horns.” It is also written in Daniel concerning the fourth beast, which signified [Col. 1045D] the Roman kingdom, that it had ten horns. Nearly all ecclesiastical writers have handed down that at the consummation of the world, when the Roman kingdom is to be destroyed, ten kings will arise to divide the Roman world among themselves; and an eleventh, a small king, will rise up and overcome three of the ten kings: the king of Egypt, the king of Africa, and the king of Ethiopia. This is what is written there: “And behold, another small horn arose from the midst of them, and three of the first horns were plucked up before it” (Dan. 7), and this horn will be Antichrist.

But here, where not the fourth beast alone, as there, signifies the Roman kingdom, but the dragon—that is, the devil—is seen, and its seven heads are described, while no mention is made of three horns plucked up, another explanation may be given, joined to the meaning already begun and to the authority of the Scriptures. The dragon has only seven heads, but ten horns appear. This is because one of the kingdoms mentioned above, the Macedonian kingdom, was divided among four kings. For after the death of Alexander the Great, four of his generals arose in his place and divided the empire among themselves. Ptolemy, son of Lagus, held Egypt; Philip, also called Arrhidaeus, Alexander’s brother, held Macedonia; Seleucus Nicanor held Syria, Babylon, and all the eastern kingdoms; Antigonus ruled Asia.

This is what we read in Daniel: “The he-goat became exceedingly great; and when it had grown, its great horn was broken, and four horns arose beneath it toward the four winds of heaven” (Dan. 8). Explaining this, the angel says: “The he-goat is the king of the Greeks, and the great horn between his eyes is the first king. But when it was broken and four arose in its place, four kings shall arise from his nation”; and he immediately adds, “but not in his strength” (ibid.). For none of them could equal Alexander’s power or greatness.

Thus, as has been said, there were seven heads but ten horns: that is, seven kingdoms but ten kings, with which that dragon had armed itself. But it continues:

“And on its heads seven diadems.” If the ten horns are ten kings, why are there not as many diadems as horns? Did not all four of those kings into whom that one kingdom was divided also have diadems? For it is written in the First Book of Maccabees: “His children—that is, Alexander’s—each obtained the kingdom in his own place, and they all put diadems upon themselves after his death” (1 Macc. 1).

Why, then, are not ten diadems mentioned but “seven diadems,” when there were ten horns? Certainly because, although four horns of one head—that is, four kings of the one Macedonian kingdom—existed, the dragon used only one of them against the woman: namely, the descendants of Seleucus, whose allotted portion was Syria, within which Judaea was contained. For from those who ruled in Syria came forth the sinful root Antiochus Epiphanes, that is, the Illustrious. Of those four diadems the red dragon put on this one diadem in its own cause against the woman, and, a cruel murderer, stained it with the blood of the saints.

For although the other parts of the divided kingdom sometimes also ravaged Judaea, it is nevertheless certainly true that the king descended from the one father who possessed Syria and, with it, Judaea, carried on the dragon’s cause against the woman and executed the devil’s purpose against God’s Law. This was, as has been said, Antiochus the Illustrious, concerning whom Daniel, foreseeing, says:

> “From one of them came forth one little horn, and it became great toward the south and toward the east and toward the strength; and it was magnified even to the strength of heaven. And it cast down some of the strength and of the stars, and trampled them; and it was magnified even to the prince of the strength, and took from him the continual sacrifice and cast down the place of his sanctification. And strength was given against the continual sacrifice because of sins; and truth shall be cast down to the earth; and it shall act and prosper” (Dan. 8).

The angel mentioned above again explains it:

> “After their kingdom, when iniquities have increased, a king of shameless countenance, understanding propositions, shall arise. His power shall be strengthened, but not by his own might. Beyond belief he shall lay all things waste, and shall prosper and act; and he shall kill the mighty and the people of the saints according to his will. Deceit shall prosper in his hand, and he shall magnify his heart; and amid abundance of all things he shall kill many, and shall rise up against the Prince of princes” (ibid.).

This king was the Antiochus already mentioned. He raised his grandeur “even to the strength of heaven”—that is, against the children of Israel, who were defended by angelic help—so that he subjected many of the saints to idolatry and trampled them beneath his feet as stars of heaven. Thus it came to pass that he held Egypt and Persia—“the south and the east”—under his power.

The statement, “he was magnified even to the prince of the strength,” signifies that he set himself up against God, persecuted his saints, took away from him the continual sacrifice offered morning and evening, and defiled and threw down the place of his sanctification. This was done not by his own power, but because of the people’s sins. Thus truth was cast down to the earth; and while idolatrous worship flourished, the religion of God—which was the adornment of that woman so often mentioned—fell silent. Let us now continue with the rest.

“And its tail drew a third part of the stars of heaven and cast them upon the earth.” We have already said above that the stars of heaven signify the children of Israel, and that the crown of twelve stars which the woman had on her head was the twelve patriarchs, through whom the Church was propagated in the beginning, according to Joseph’s dream: “I saw the sun and moon and eleven stars worshipping me” (Gen. 37). Joseph himself was the twelfth star.

Moses likewise says to the entire multitude of the children of Israel: “I said to you at that time: I cannot bear you alone, because the Lord your God has multiplied you, and today you are very numerous, like the stars of heaven” (Deut. 1). Who does not know that, in the assault upon that woman, wherever the dragon attacked her, many of that people supported and aided the dragon’s deceitful wickedness?

For example, when this dragon began to rage in the Antiochus already mentioned, it is written:

> “In those days lawless sons came out from Israel and persuaded many, saying: ‘Let us go and make a covenant with the nations around us, because since we withdrew from them many evils have found us.’ And the proposal seemed good in their eyes. Some from the people were appointed, and they went to the king; and he gave them authority to practise the customs of the nations. They built a gymnasium in Jerusalem according to the laws of the Gentiles, made themselves foreskins, withdrew from the holy covenant, joined themselves to the nations, and sold themselves to do evil” (1 Macc. 1).

We omit many further examples that might be given of stars of this kind falling from heaven’s height, from the dignity of God’s covenant, so far as even to assist the devil’s party by attacking those who wished to persevere in the religion of their ancestral faith. The dragon’s tail, therefore, plainly drew a third part of the stars of heaven. “And it cast them,” he says, “upon the earth”: namely, so that those who ought to have directed their attention toward heaven might be bent down toward earth, and those commanded to await the blessed hope of heavenly things might desire only earthly things.

[Col. 1048B] It follows:

“And the dragon stood before the woman who was about to give birth, that when she had given birth it might devour her son.” This was the purpose of the dragon in raising so many heads and brandishing so many horns. This, I say, was the devil’s most wicked desire in stirring up so many kingdoms and inflaming so many kings with hatred for divine religion: that, “when the woman who was about to give birth had given birth,” when the Church had brought forth Christ—when the Virgin Mary gave birth—it might “devour her son”; that is, erase his name from human memory, so that no usefulness or fruit might arise from such a birth. But it follows:

“And she gave birth to a male child, who was to rule the nations with an iron rod.” It is as though he were saying: That baleful dragon, aroused by the cries of the woman in labor, [Col. 1048C] stood watchfully before her in order to devour her son. He raged especially in the bloodthirsty head of Herod, when that man was stirred by the prophetic oracle which he had heard: “And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah; for from you shall come forth a leader who will rule my people Israel” (Mal. XV; Matt. XI). He sought the child in order to destroy him, sent to Bethlehem, and killed all the boys who were in it and throughout all its borders, as though it were impossible that that one should not be killed along with them. But how did that foolish dragon, who raged in Herod, suppose that he could nullify the counsel or purpose of God? For he “was to rule the nations [Col. 1048D] with an iron rod,” and this had been established beforehand in the Scriptures of truth. For example, he himself says in the Psalmist:

> “The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I shall give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession. You shall rule them with an iron rod” (Ps. II).

How, then, did the malicious folly of the dragon hope to devour him so quickly, when it had been written of him that he would rule the nations with an iron rod? Certainly, “an iron rod” means unbending justice. Likewise, when he says “a male child,” it is as though he said “a most mighty one.” For a male—that is, a strong—son was then born to us, as the prophet had foretold: “And his name shall be called Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God” (Isa. IX).

Yet that dragon [Col. 1049A] did all that he could, never ceasing to persecute that son, “in order to devour” him—that is, to erase his memory—uttering what we hear in the Psalm: “When will he die, and his name perish?” (Ps. XL). By saying this, he impatiently brought about his crucifixion; and by doing this he thought that he had devoured him and that his name had perished. But see what follows: “And her son was caught up to God and to his throne.” Who does not know how truly this occurred? Who has not heard? For when he was thought to have been devoured—buried in the earth and enclosed in the earth by a sealed stone (Matt. XXVII)—then, the pains of hell having been loosed, since it was impossible for him to be held by it, he rose and ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of God (Acts II), while the truth of Scripture triumphantly says [Col. 1049B] in David:

> “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand” (Ps. CIX).

Therefore the woman’s son—the son of the Church, of the woman Virgin Mary—was caught up to God and to his throne. From there he looks down upon all the dragon’s heads and mocks them, just as the Holy Spirit likewise spoke in the Psalm:

> “He who dwells in heaven shall laugh at them, and the Lord shall deride them. Then he shall speak to them in his wrath, and trouble them in his fury; but I have been established king by him” (Ps. II),

and so forth. It follows:

“And the woman fled into the wilderness, where she has a place prepared by God, that there they may feed her for one thousand two hundred and sixty days.” Once her son had been caught up to God and to his throne, “the woman fled into the wilderness.” That is, now that Christ the Lord sat at the Father’s right hand [Col. 1049C] and the Holy Spirit had been given, the Church of that time chose a solitary life. For thus we read in the Acts of the Apostles:

> “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul. Nor did anyone say that anything was his own, but all things were common to them. And they were distributed to each according to each one’s need” (Acts IV).

Surely this was the woman’s flight into the wilderness: to possess or desire nothing in this world is the faithful and tranquil solitude of the mind. Conversely, to possess, desire, or covet is not solitude but great anxiety and restlessness. Thus “the woman fled into the wilderness” when the Church resolved to possess nothing in this world, calling her children to imitate her. For example, when she says in the Apostle:

> “For the form [Col. 1049D] of this world is passing away. But I want you to be without anxiety. He who is without a wife is anxious about the things of the Lord, how he may please God” (1 Cor. VII).

Amid these and similar words she says: “But I would have all people be as I myself am” (ibid.).

In such a wilderness, he says, “the woman has a place prepared by God.” What is the woman’s place in this solitude but God himself? Accordingly, the Psalmist too says in prayer: “Be for me a protecting God and a place of refuge” (Ps. XXX). And of the sinner who perishes it is written in Job:

> “As a cloud is consumed and passes away, so he who goes down to hell shall not come up; nor shall he return any more to his house, nor shall his place know him any longer” (Job VII).

For when it says, “nor shall [Col. 1050A] his place know him any longer,” it is as though it said: God will no longer seek him—the God who is the place of all the blessed, outside whom no one is blessed, and in whom, even now while we are away from him, the foot of the soul, that is, Christian hope, is fixed.

She has this place prepared by God; for God can be prepared for us by no one except God himself. And this is in that kind of solitude in which, being free for contemplation, she may know this her place and always guard against her fall, saying: “Let not the foot of pride come upon me, nor let the hand of the sinner move me” (Ps. XXXV).

Moreover, in that solitude a place is prepared for them by God “that there they may feed her.” For the Lord prescribed this law for the children—the children of their mother the Church—who have not yet reached the summit [Col. 1050B] of their mother’s perfection: that they should wish to possess nothing in this world. And he commanded this of them so that they might feed their mother—that is, apostolic perfection, the motherly love which evangelizes them. For he said: “The laborer is worthy of his food” (Matt. X). And elsewhere: “Remain in the same house, eating and drinking what they have; for the laborer is worthy of his wages” (Luke X).

Mindful of this entitlement or obligation, the Apostle says to the Corinthians:

> “Do you not know that those who work in the sanctuary eat what comes from the sanctuary? And those who serve at the altar share with the altar. Thus also the Lord ordained that those who proclaim the Gospel should live by the Gospel” (1 Cor. IX).

Likewise: “If we have sown spiritual things for you, is it a great matter if we reap your material things?” (ibid.).

Thus they feed her [Col. 1050C] “for one thousand two hundred and sixty days,” that is, for as long as she endures persecutions while journeying in this world. Since the final persecution is to rage for such a period, when this dragon, in that son of perdition—namely, Antichrist—pours out all his enmity, we rightly understand by so many days the whole span of all persecutions. This period or number of days has already been treated more fully elsewhere. It follows:

“And there was a great battle in heaven: Michael and his angels fought with the dragon. And the dragon fought, and his angels; and they did not prevail, nor was their place found any longer in heaven.”

A great and wondrous spectacle of such images appeared before the soul of John [Col. 1050D]; wondrous too was the disposition or capacity of his soul, which could conceive, in beholding such great things, such honorable signs of marvelous mysteries. We can scarcely dream of, or imagine for ourselves in meditation, the height of his astonishment—namely, his perception of it with marvelous horror.

How unwillingly that dragon, the devil, was driven from the temples, altars, and images of the nations! This began to occur when that son was caught up to God and to his throne. For, being about to ascend, he said: “Go into the whole world; preach the Gospel to every creature. Whoever believes and is baptized shall be saved” (Mark XVI; Matt. XII; Luke XI). This was the same as saying: Go; drive from his court that strong armed man, now conquered by me; draw that dragon, the devil, now bound by me—indeed, as though caught with a hook, his nostrils pierced with stakes, bound with a ring through his nose and a bracelet through his pierced jaw—from the temples and altars, [Col. 1051A] so that I may draw his vessels to myself, as I foretold: “For if I am lifted up from the earth, I shall draw all things to myself” (John XII).

From this came the terrifying sounds of persecutions throughout the whole world, of which this visionary battle was the sign: a great battle. “A great battle,” he says, “occurred.” Where? “In heaven.” By this was signified the Church: a land far higher, and far superior to earthly people and those who think earthly thoughts, whose “citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III).

For after her Son had been caught up to God and to his throne, [Col. 1051B] the Church did not deem it fitting any longer to fight on earth, as she had formerly been permitted to do, when holy kings and prophets fought many battles with material weapons for land, for earthly goods. Now the condition of the cause was different, and the affection of perfect purpose different: to despise earth and seek heaven, to restrain the hands and set free the instructed tongue, to offer the flesh to swords and defend the faith by the word. Therefore she fought in heaven.

But how was the dragon in heaven, or how did he fight in heaven? He was in heaven, certainly, in his own estimation, and seemed to himself “like the Most High” (Isa. XIV), when what was virtually a divine religion was rendered to him, and he was worshiped as God by the miserable nations whom he had deceived. Thus he too fought as though in heaven, while he contended to be regarded as a heavenly God.

[Col. 1051C] Therefore almost no one is ignorant that this dragon wanders in the air and exercises the authority granted to him until the time of judgment, and that this air itself is customarily called “heaven” in Scripture—as in: “The birds of heaven and the fish of the sea” (Ps. VIII). In this heaven, that is, in the air, we too still have a battle against him today, as the Apostle writes to the Ephesians:

> “For our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, and the rulers of the world of this darkness, against spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. VI).

Therefore there are spiritual forces of wickedness—namely, this dragon and his angels—in the heavenly places: not where the ordered stars shine and holy angels dwell, but in the dark habitation of this frail air, where [Col. 1051D] mist too gathers. Yet it is written that “he covers heaven with clouds” (Ps. CXLVI), where birds do not even fly, and yet they are called the flying creatures of heaven.

Thus these most wicked spirits dwell in these heavenly places, not in that higher tranquility of heaven. Against them spiritual wrestling is enjoined upon us, so that, after the evil angels have been conquered, we may enjoy that reward by which we shall be joined to the good angels in incorruptible eternity. Hence elsewhere the same Apostle, when he indicated the dark dominion of the devil, says: “According to the spirit of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air, who now works in the children of unbelief” (Eph. II). What he here calls “the prince of the power of the air,” there he called “spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places.”

Therefore, even according to the letter, it is rightly understood that [Col. 1052A] John saw the visionary battle occur in this heaven—that is, in the air—as a sign of the battle in which the devil had now begun to be driven from temples and altars, indeed from human hearts. The end of this battle will be that this dragon, with his angels, is cast into eternal fire (Matt. XXV), and thus what follows comes to pass: “And they did not prevail, nor was their place found any longer in heaven.”

In heaven, I say—not only in that spiritual or heavenly manner of life of believers who are pilgrims here, but not even in this air into which he was cast down; for on that great and terrible day of judgment he will be cast down again into Tartarus. But now let us proceed through the words themselves in order.

“Michael,” he says, “and his angels will fight with the dragon; and the dragon fought, and his angels.” Nowhere [Col. 1052B] in the entire course of Scripture do we read that, before the birth of that often-mentioned woman, the archangel Michael fought with the dragon and conquered him. For the son of the woman had not yet crushed the head of that dragon, so that it might be conquered by the angels; but now he did this, and in doing it was caught up to God and to his throne. Hence it is sung of him in the Psalm:

> “You crushed the heads of the dragons in the waters. You broke the heads of the dragon” (Ps. LXXIII).

Indeed, many notable acts of angelic strength on behalf of human beings before this are recorded in Scripture. For example: “And it came to pass that night that an angel of the Lord came and struck one hundred and eighty-five thousand in the camp of the Assyrians” (4 Kings XIX; Isa. XXXVII). But this and other such deeds were not good angels fighting [Col. 1052C] evil angels for the conversion to piety of impious people. Rather, good angels were using the service of evil angels for the destruction of impious people, as the Psalm testifies:

> “He sent upon them the wrath of his indignation, indignation and wrath and tribulation, dispatches through evil angels” (Ps. LXXVII).

Here it is not so. Evil angels are not sent in order that impious people may be killed; rather, battle is joined by good angels against evil angels so that people may be freed from the error of impiety. How was this battle fought, or how is it fought? With what weapons, or weapons of what kind, do those battle lines fight?

Undoubtedly, in John’s vision certain likenesses of material weapons could have been seen; but angels, whether good or evil, being [Col. 1052D] spirits, are not clothed with bodily or material armor. Nevertheless, what that dragon did not have by nature, he acquired for himself by malicious art: every sort of weapon by which wars are waged and killings carried out among human beings—namely, the swords of kings and emperors, the axes of consuls, the chains and prisons of judges, and every kind of torture whatsoever. The first sword he seized or took up in Rome was Nero’s sword, and in it he fought.

But Michael and his angels, fighting in return, possessed or sought none of this kind of weapon. Rather, since they “are ministering spirits, sent into service for those who are to inherit salvation” (Heb. I), they bestowed upon the Christian people, their fellow soldiers—who were or are of the seed of that great woman—[Col. 1053A] signs of miracles given by Jesus Christ through the Holy Spirit. Present with them and cooperating, they healed the sick, raised the dead, stood beside pious martyrs, spoke with them amid tortures and goads, and by their conversation comforted and refreshed them in prisons and chains. They also bound the dragon’s angels and drew them out from the ancient images in temples. Whoever reads the Acts of the holy martyrs or apostles knows that all these things occurred.

For example: a soldier, still a Gentile, says to a martyr struggling upon the rack: “I see a most beautiful young man standing before you with a cloth, wiping your limbs. Therefore I adjure you, by the Christ who sent his angel to you, do not abandon me.” [Col. 1053B] Should we suppose that holy angels were present with pious martyrs only where they appeared visibly? On the contrary, even where they did not visibly appear, they were always present: sympathizing with the sufferers, cleaving to those who labored, counting their wounds, measuring their flowing blood, recording each person’s answers; and amid all this Michael bore before the eyes of the Lord God—and of that victorious Son who had been caught up to his throne—the prayers and groans of the dying, like abundant incense burning in a golden censer.

In this way Michael and his angels fought with the dragon. Yet this side attempted nothing with material weapons for its own defense, even when whole legions of martyrs were sometimes struck down. They held military weapons, [Col. 1053C] with which they had faithfully and bravely armed themselves for the defense of the commonwealth, but in the cause of the Christian faith they disdained utterly to touch them.

Thus, most truly, after the prophet had said, “You have overcome the yoke of his burden, the rod of his shoulder, and the scepter of his oppressor,” he added, “as in the day of Midian” (Isa. IX): namely, when Gideon conquered Midian with three hundred men by a marvelous manner of fighting. How? Lamps were placed inside jars; when the jars were broken, the lamps were revealed, and the enemies, terrified by the flashing light, turned to flight (Judg. VII). The trumpet blasts signified the cry of preaching; the lamps, the brightness of miracles; the jars, the frailty of bodies. Disregarding [Col. 1053D] their own safety, the martyrs overthrew their enemies by dying, and conquered their swords not with arms and swords but with patience.

Surely Michael and his angels rightly delighted to be companions—indeed leaders and commanders—of this battle. The dragon and his angels fought also with material arms, as has already been said. And the bloody diadem of his sixth head, namely the Roman kingdom, drenched in the slaughter of Christians and in abundance of blood, whenever it hurled itself into battle, drenched the world in blood.

“And they did not prevail,” he says, “nor was their place found any longer in heaven.” In what did they not prevail? Certainly, they could not stand any longer against the strength of the stronger Michael and his angels, but were cast out with their prince, the red dragon, just as [Col. 1054A] the woman’s son foretold: “Now the prince of this world shall be cast out” (John XII).

For he was cast out in such a way that Christian religion flourished in the places where his filth had rotted; in the temples where the idol of every shamefulness had stood, the cross of Christ shone; and through mouths accustomed to chant of Jupiter the adulterer, the name of Christ and the praise of the holy Trinity resounded with glory. This is what he means by: “Nor was their place found any longer in heaven.” It is as though he said: No place remained to him in which heavenly or divine worship was rendered to him.

But it will come to pass, as has already been said, that he will not even have leave to appear in this aerial heaven. The battle extends so far, until he is hurled down into the depths of hell, “while all behold” [Col. 1054B] (Job XL), never again to ascend, even to this heaven. Hence it continues:

“And that great dragon was cast out, the ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan, who deceives the whole world; he was cast out onto the earth, and his angels were sent with him.”

For “he was cast out onto the earth,” that is, having lost the lofty reputation by which he seemed to possess heaven while he was worshiped as God, and having lost the elect people—in whose heaven God now dwells—he now possesses only those who, stubbornly loving the earth, are themselves earth; and at last he will be cast with them and his angels into eternal fire. Certainly, when he is thus cast down, he is better known by those from whose hearts he is cast out, or before whose eyes he is hurled down.

Therefore [Col. 1054C] this dragon is now finally described by his names and properties when it says: “And that great dragon was cast out, the ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan, who deceives the whole world.” For, as though you asked, “Who is that great dragon?” it adds: “the ancient serpent.” It is as though it said: This very great dragon is that serpent who, in ancient time, when the first human being was made, entered a living serpent and spoke through its mouth. He deserved to be called a serpent because, through the serpent into which he entered, he worked the deed of iniquity and malice, deceiving God’s creature by saying: “Eat, and you shall be like gods” (Gen. III).

Likewise, as though you asked what his name is, it adds: [Col. 1054D] “who is called the devil and Satan.” *Diabolus* means “flowing downward”; *Satanas*, “adversary.” The reasons for both names are known. He is called *diabolus*, that is, “flowing downward,” because, falling from heaven through pride (Isa. XIV), he flowed downward; and the sinner perished from the face of God as wax flows before fire (Ps. LXXVII). He is called *Satanas*, that is, “adversary,” because, having likewise fallen from heaven, he does not cease to oppose God the Creator.

For what he said or had said—“I will be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV)—was not enough: he still raises himself higher in swelling pride. The Apostle testifies when he speaks thus about the son of perdition, in whom this devil was: “The man of sin, the son of perdition, who opposes and exalts himself above everything called God or [Col. 1055A] worshiped” (2 Thess. II). In what does this Satan oppose God? Namely, in speaking falsehood so as to deceive the creature into committing a second adultery, presenting himself as though he were God, so that the devil himself may be received as God, like an adulterer in place of a lawful husband.

It follows: “Who deceives the whole world.” For to what or from what does he lead the whole world astray, except from the worship due to God to the undue worship of himself? Such a one “was cast out onto the earth,” so that God alone might possess his heaven—that is, the inmost minds and public worship of all the elect—while the devil possesses only the earth, that is, the entirely earthly life of lost people. Of such people God spoke at the beginning of the deception: “You shall eat earth [Col. 1055B] all the days” (Gen. III).

The chief portion of earth of this kind is the Jews, who, as though rivaling the earth, crucified the God of heaven. They spoke with the cunning of this malignant serpent, as the Psalm says in the person of Christ himself:

> “For they indeed spoke peaceably to me, but speaking in the anger of the earth, they devised deceits” (Ps. XXXIV).

Indeed, they devised for themselves a very great pretext of just indignation when, as though fearful and trembling, they said: “If we let him go on thus, all will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away our place and nation” (John XI). Thus the serpent also ate these as his earth, and the prophecy of the Song of Deuteronomy was fulfilled: “I shall send upon them the teeth of beasts, with the fury of those that crawl upon the earth [Col. 1055C] and of serpents” (Deut. XXXII).

It follows: “And I heard a great voice from heaven saying: Now salvation and power and the kingdom of our God and the authority of his Christ have come, because the accuser of our brothers has been cast out, who accused them before the presence of our God day and night. And they conquered him through the blood of the Lamb and through the word of their testimony, and they did not love their life even unto death. Therefore rejoice, heavens, and you who dwell in them.”

That great voice which he heard in the Spirit is this public chorus by which the heaven of God—that is, the Church—today sings praises throughout the whole world, while angels sing, indeed lead the singing, “Glory to God in the highest” (Luke II), according to the prophetic invitation of the Psalm which says to God Most High:

> “Let all [Col. 1055D] the earth worship you and sing psalms to you; let it sing a psalm to your name” (Ps. LXXV).

And immediately afterward:

> “Bless our God, O nations, and make the voice of his praise heard” (ibid.).

Would you therefore hear and know what fruit or benefit has resulted from the casting down of that great dragon, that ancient serpent, the devil and Satan, with his angels onto the earth? The singers of God’s grace, the praisers of the works of Christ the Son of God, say with a great voice: “Now salvation and power and the kingdom of our God and the authority of his Christ have come.”

How is it evident that this has occurred? “Because,” they say, “the accuser of our brothers [Col. 1056A] has been cast out, who accused them before the presence of our God day and night.” Then before he was cast onto the earth, was there no salvation and no power? Was there no kingdom, no authority of our God and of his Christ? Certainly, there was not salvation but destruction and death; not power but weakness and corruption. In human beings there was not the kingdom of our God, but the kingdom of sin and death; there was not the authority of his Christ, but the authority of the prince of darkness, who ruled in this world. These things had not yet come to pass, but were future; they were promised as things to be done, and this hope consoled a few under the old law.

But when, by the very passion and resurrection in which he was caught up to God and to his throne, he passed from this world to the Father and destroyed destruction, death, and even the corruption of mortal bodies, then “salvation and power came.” [Col. 1056B] Salvation means the forgiveness of our sins, which is the resurrection of souls; power means the restoration of our risen bodies. Then, I say, and from then on, “the kingdom came”—indeed, we became the kingdom of our God—and the authority of his Christ came in heaven and on earth. Not before, but after his resurrection, he himself affirmed: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. XXVIII). Rightly therefore, because that Satan was cast out, this was sung.

Why, then, or on what account was Satan called, or should he be called, “the accuser of the brothers”? Clearly because he held the written bond of the decree against us, which was contrary to us, in which Adam’s sin was written. By reciting it he continually accused us, confidently and boastfully asserting that, [Col. 1056C] on the witness of that written bond, the human race was rightfully his possession. But when he was cast out, he lost that written bond, as the Apostle says:

> “God made us alive together with Christ, forgiving us all our offenses, blotting out the written bond of the decree that was against us and contrary to us. He removed it from the midst, fastening it to the cross; and stripping the principalities and powers, he displayed them boldly, triumphing openly over them in himself” (Col. II).

When this was done, the holy apostles and martyrs rushed upon him, that great wounded dragon, as the Psalm sings: “You humbled the wounded proud one” (Ps. LXXXVIII). They rushed upon him, I say, as the present battle also testifies, aided by Michael and his angels. Having struck down their great adversary, [Col. 1056D] they triumphed in Christ’s victory through both their own blood and his. This is what those heavenly singers now say:

“And they conquered him through the blood of the Lamb and through the word of their testimony, and they did not love their life even unto death.”

Who were those who conquered him? Certainly those who were accused by that accuser. In the very accusation, or in the cause for which they were accused, they conquered and silenced him by steadfast contest and their lawful defense. And they did this not by the power of their own righteousness or condition, but “through the blood of the Lamb,” by which they were redeemed, and “through the word of their testimony”—that is, through the faith by which the Spirit bears witness to them that they are [Col. 1057A] children of God (Rom. VIII).

Add that, for this same word of their testimony, for their confession of faith, these victors or combatants gave up their lives. For this is what is now said: “And they did not love their life even unto death.” They did not love it—that is, they hated it with the perfect hatred of which their Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever hates his life in this world keeps it for eternal life” (John XII). By not loving, indeed by hating, their lives, they conquered him.

“Therefore rejoice, heavens, and you who dwell in them.” You heavens, you bright bosoms of the blessed homeland, “therefore rejoice, and you who dwell in them,” O our brothers: you who were formerly accused because you were earth and ought by right to be eaten by that great and ancient serpent, but [Col. 1057B] now dwell in heaven—indeed, are yourselves heavens—from which he was cast out and driven forth. It follows:

“Woe to the earth and the sea, because the devil has come down to you with great wrath, knowing that he has but little time!” While heaven and those who dwell in it rejoice, he looks back, as it were, turning away his right eye and looking with his left: “Woe,” he says, “to the earth and the sea!” For we must remember what was said before: “And that great dragon was cast down to the earth,” and understand that the earth into which he was cast down from heaven is the exceedingly hard and heavy mass of the ungodly and unbelieving, who seek only earthly and vain things. Hence they are rebuked by the voice of the Holy Spirit speaking in the Psalm: “Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? [Col. 1057C] Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?” (Ps. 4).

They are also called “the sea,” because of the restless bitter experiences of every vice and of useless cares which they endure and love; indeed, in Scripture they are called “wild waves of the sea,” according to that saying of the Apostle Jude: “These are stains at their feasts, feasting without fear, feeding themselves; clouds without water, carried about by winds; wild waves of the sea, foaming out their own shame” (Jude 12). And, that with the authoritative witness of ancient divine Scripture we may distinguish more deeply this earth and sea from that heaven from which the dragon was cast down: the earth and the sea are all those who increased and multiplied beyond the blessing given before Adam sinned, when the Lord God said to the woman: “I will multiply your sorrows and your conceptions” (Gen. 3) [Col. 1057D]. For heaven consists of those whom, before sin, he commanded to be born, blessing those first two and saying: “Increase and multiply” (Gen. 1).

And he was cast out of this heaven in such a manner that all those called saints according to purpose—indeed foreknown and predestined, justified and glorified (Rom. 8)—are placed at the right hand, and are told, in accordance with the purpose by which they had been blessed in those first parents: “Come, you blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you” (Matt. 25). Thus they are openly heaven, or the kingdom of heaven. “Therefore,” he says, “woe to the earth and the sea”: that is, to all who do not deserve to be or to be called heaven. Why? “Because the devil has come down to you with great wrath” [Col. 1058A].

He addresses that earth and sea as though they had asked: Why, or whence, is woe to us? “The devil,” he says, “has come down to you”—that is, having been cast down from heaven. But did he not possess that earth and sea before he was cast down from that heaven, from those who are now called heaven or the kingdom of heaven? Indeed he did, and possessed them more securely; and they were much more at peace under his possession—his own peace, a malignant peace. How, then, did he come down to them? Surely by boiling over in greater wrath within them. For this is what he adds: “having great wrath.” Certainly he possessed that earth and sea with wrath even before, since he always had, as though by nature, hatred against the human race. Why, then, does he now say “having wrath,” adding also “great,” unless because from that time onward he made those called earth and sea more wicked? [Col. 1058B]

For example, concerning the Jews—earthly men, that is, lovers of the earth—the Lord speaks mystically thus: “When an unclean spirit has gone out of a man, it walks through dry and waterless places, seeking rest; and, finding none, it says: I will return into my house from which I came. And when it comes, it finds it swept clean. Then it goes and takes with it seven other spirits more wicked than itself; and, entering in, they dwell there, and the last state of that man becomes worse than the first” (Matt. 10). By saying this, he declares with vehement denunciation that, after that dragon was cast down from heaven into that earth, he came down with multiplied iniquity; that is, after Christ suffered and “the prince of this world was cast out” (John 12), he possesses the Jews with greater wickedness than he once possessed them with in the land of Egypt, from which he went out when they embraced the worship of the one true God [Col. 1058C].

Moreover, concerning the Gentiles, who are rightly signified here by the sea, as has already been said elsewhere—concerning those Gentiles, I say, who did not receive the Gospel of Christ—it is likewise evident that he possesses them more wickedly now than he did before, when Christ had not yet been proclaimed to them, as has now occurred. Hence the Apostle says: “But I say, Have they not heard? Indeed, their sound has gone forth into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the world” (Rom. 16; Ps. 18). And what does Scripture say [Col. 1058D] of all who still remain Gentiles, all who, after hearing this, live in a Gentile manner, from which we may infer that the devil came down from heaven to them although he already possessed them? When the Psalmist had said, “Arise, O Lord; let not man prevail,” he immediately added: “Let the Gentiles be judged in your sight” (Ps. 9). He further added: “Set, O Lord, a lawgiver over them, that the Gentiles may know that they are men” (ibid.), that is, and not gods, as some of their rulers wish or once wished to be regarded.

Whom does he allow to be appointed as lawgiver over them, if not the devil, the giver of his own law—not God’s law, not the law of righteousness, but of sin? Therefore the devil has come down to you, O earth and sea, whom before he possessed more sluggishly. In what condition has he come down to you? “Having,” he says, “great wrath” [Col. 1059A]. By what may we discern that the wrath which he now has, coming down and cast down in this manner, is truly great in comparison with the wrath he had before? Namely, because before he caused you to wander through ignorance, but now causes you to blaspheme through envy. This is the great wrath: malignant envy inspired within you. For now, because you have heard Christ’s Gospel, you have no excuse for your sin (John 15); and it is clear that you are not ignorant—that is, wrathful—but envious. With spirits multiplied with himself in wickedness, he now drives such persons as you, “knowing that he has but little time.” For he knows that the day of judgment is near, beyond which he will have no opportunity to persecute that woman. It follows:

[Col. 1059B] “And when the dragon saw that he had been cast down to the earth, he persecuted the woman who had borne the male child. And two wings of a great eagle were given to the woman, so that she might fly into the wilderness to her place, where she is nourished for a time and times and half a time, away from the face of the serpent. And the serpent cast water from his mouth after the woman, like a river, that he might cause her to be carried away by the river.”

This is what he had cried out over when he said: “Woe to the earth and the sea!” and so forth. This is that great wrath of the dragon cast down to earth, who is called the devil and Satan: the wrath which this wonderful vision wonderfully indicates in what was said: “And the serpent cast water from his mouth after the woman, like a river, that he might cause her to be carried away by the river.” Let us recall from ecclesiastical history how, after that dragon “was cast down to the earth,” after, as the Christian faith advanced, idols were abandoned and destroyed and he lost the glory of a worship falsely usurped as divine, Arius, a presbyter and great heresiarch, burst forth most audaciously under the Christian name into blasphemy against Christ the Son of God, with intolerable verbosity.

For when the Roman summit of imperial power worshipped the son of this woman, who “was caught up to God and to his throne,” and when the Christian emperor Constantine bore upon his brow the sign of Christ’s cross, we shall recognize how truly, fittingly, and exactly in accordance with the event this was shown in the vision and so spoken or written [Col. 1059C]. For what could be truer than what is now said: that “after the dragon saw that he had been cast down to earth, he persecuted the woman,” sending after her “water from his mouth like a river”? The devil saw that he could no longer maintain the old idolatry once the highest rulers had inclined toward receiving the profession of the Christian name; so he turned the whole abundance of his malice toward corrupting the truth of the Scriptures, and in this way began to persecute “the woman who had borne the male child.”

Notice what he says: he does not say, “He persecuted the male child,” but, “He persecuted the woman who had borne the male child.” For through the mouth of Arius and other such heretics, pouring forth impious doctrine, he did not openly demand of anyone that he deny Christ or the Christian name [Col. 1059D]; rather, [Col. 1060A] he persecuted that woman by striving—indeed contending—that everyone confessing Christ should receive a rule of confession or faith other than that handed down by apostolic truth, so that Satan might make his own synagogue out of Christ’s Church. Acting thus with excessive loquacity and clamorous contention, that serpent sent “water from his mouth like a river.”

Observe that he did not say, “He sent a river from his mouth,” but “he sent water like a river.” The water which that serpent sends “from his mouth” may indeed resemble a river, but cannot truly be a river. For the true river, the river of living water, is Holy Scripture and true catholic doctrine, which the Church—the woman in question—is accustomed to send forth from the fountain of truth. Possessing that fountain within herself, she is the Lord’s garden, as is said in the Song of Songs: “A garden enclosed is my sister, my bride; a garden enclosed, a sealed fountain” (Song 4) [Col. 1060B]. Likewise in the Gospel: “He who believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly” (John 7).

But the serpent, whose mouth was Arius, sent from his mouth dead water, foul water of wicked doctrine. Yet because he disputed from those same Scriptures and appropriated for himself testimonies from them—the Scriptures which this woman receives and possesses—his water was accustomed to seem a river of living water, a river of sound doctrine. For what purpose? “That,” he says, “he might cause her to be carried away by the river.” Certainly: from faith to unfaithfulness, from truth to falsehood, from light to darkness, from life to death, from height to depth, from heaven to hell. For all who admire and follow the flowing loquacity issuing from the mouth of blaspheming heretics are drawn into things so different—indeed contrary.

“And the earth heard the woman, and opened its mouth, and swallowed up the river which the dragon had sent from his mouth.” This occurred, undoubtedly, when the most famous Council of Nicaea was convened through the zeal of the Christian emperor Constantine, who ordered bishops and those with them to come to the synod in public asses, mules, and swift horses. Then, I say, “the earth heard the woman,” because distinguished men gathered from nearly the whole earth, from the whole world: religious and renowned men from every nation, capable of disputation and trained in every art of eloquence [Col. 1060C]. They sat down to defend [Col. 1060D] the Church of catholic truth.

Among them the most eminent were the great Eustathius, bishop of the Church of Antioch, and Eusebius surnamed Pamphilus, along with many others, through whose merits the sick were healed while alive and the dead were said to be raised. Among them were also some burned with red-hot iron in earlier persecutions, or with their right eyes gouged out, or else with their right hands cut off. One of these was Paphnutius of Egypt. There, indeed, one could see a people of Christ’s athletes and martyrs gathered in one place. Syrians, Cilicians, Phoenicians, Arabs, Palestinians, Egyptians, Thebans, Libyans, Mesopotamians, Persians, Scythians, Pontic men, Asians, Phrygians, Thracians, Macedonians, Achaeans, and Epirots were present together.

The assembled chief ministers of God from all the Churches which filled the whole of Europe, Libya, and Asia were there together; and one house of prayer, as though inwardly enlarged by God, contained them all in one place [Col. 1061A]. There “the earth”—that is, the assembly gathered from the whole earth—“opened its mouth,” namely, for speaking, disputing, and producing testimonies from Scripture; “and swallowed up the river which the dragon had sent from his mouth,” that is, it annihilated and condemned the sect of wicked doctrine which had been formed by a diabolical spirit. There Arius’s doctrine was destroyed.

[Col. 1061B] Likewise, when the Council of Constantinople was celebrated, by which the error of Eunomius and Macedonius was convicted; when the Council of Ephesus was celebrated, in which Nestorius’s impiety was judged; and when the Council of Chalcedon was celebrated, in which the perversity of Eutyches and Dioscorus was rejected—then too “the earth opened its mouth and swallowed up” such a “river,” while the woman escaped and flew upon two wings, as is here foretold:

For “two wings of a great eagle were given to the woman, so that she might fly into the wilderness to her place, where she is nourished for a time and times and half a time, away from the face of the serpent.” The great eagle, as we have already said above elsewhere, is Holy Scripture; and its two wings are the two Testaments. They were given to this woman—that is, made intelligible to her—so that she may have the means to lift her heart to heaven and not fall into the river flowing across the earth: the diabolical river, the river of heretical loquacity, full of snares and sophistical nets [Col. 1061C].

Having wings of this kind, she flies into the wilderness to her place; that is, she pursues holy leisure, in order to devote herself to meditation upon the Scriptures, according to the saying of the Wise Man: “The wisdom of a scribe comes in the time of leisure; and he who is diminished in activity shall receive it” (Ecclus. 38). “He who is diminished in activity” means one less occupied with bodily exercise, such as Jacob, who was a simple man dwelling at home and was not as active as Esau, who, being a hunter, exercised himself physically (Gen. 25). Jacob therefore received wisdom, whereas Esau’s exercise profited him little.

Accordingly, the Apostle, instructing his diligent disciple, says: “Exercise yourself unto godliness. For bodily exercise is profitable for a little, but godliness is profitable for all things, having promise of the life which now is and of that which is to come” (1 Tim. 4) [Col. 1061D]. Flying there, therefore, into that wilderness, into that kind of place of her own and holy leisure, for the exercise of godliness, this woman “is nourished,” he says—understand, by contemplation of truth and sacred reading, and also, as was said elsewhere, by bodily sustenance supplied from the generosity of her children.

“She is nourished,” I say, “away from the face of the serpent,” that is, so as not to fear the serpent, “for a time and times and half a time”: that is, for three years and a half, during which time Antichrist will harass the world by his persecution. Hence this period rightly signifies the whole time during which the Church suffers persecution because it lives devoutly in Christ.

Thus the river, or phantom of a river, of the serpent was swallowed up when the holy Council, the Council of Nicaea, condemned Arius’s impious doctrine. But see what follows: “And the dragon was angry with the woman, and he added [went] to make war with the rest of her seed, who keep the commandment of God and have the testimony of Jesus” [Col. 1062A]. “The dragon was angry with the woman” because, after Arius had been extinguished, his doctrine again sprouted through a certain presbyter. From this there again arose private and public debates, controversies, injuries, enmities, and the many things which commonly occur in such matters.

Nor was there a long delay: heretics, taking advantage of the weakness of the emperor Constantius, stirred up war against Christians, and did no less than the pagan and sacrilegious tyrants of old had done in their persecutions. Therefore he says of the dragon persecuting the woman:

[Col. 1062B] “And he added [went] to make war with the rest of her seed.” That is, because the river which he had sent from his mouth was accomplishing too little, because he could not draw the woman along by that flood of his doctrine, he added outward war; the heretical power cruelly added the sword to its tongue. At first Catholics were expelled from their churches; then they were forced by tortures even to communicate with heretics, so that very many succumbed beneath the dreadful severity of beatings. Some were deprived of their property, others of civic standing; marks were placed on others’ foreheads, that they might be branded with such a sign. These things occurred throughout all the cities of the East, especially in the imperial city of Constantinople.

For the emperor Valens had finally come to the devil’s aid, led astray by the persuasion of his heretical wife. She herself had first been ensnared by the traps of Arian deceit, and persuaded her husband also to fall with her into the pit of blasphemy. Eudoxius was the author of this deception: at that time he held the helm of the Church of Constantinople, sinking his ship rather than steering it [Col. 1062C]. Strengthened by this confidence, the Arians became yet more unrestrained and violently harassed the orthodox, beating them, insulting them, imprisoning them, frequently impoverishing them through financial penalties, and doing every intolerable thing against them.

But why do I speak of small things among great? Since the extent and cruelty of the heretics’ acts against Catholics are contained, scattered—indeed at length—in ecclesiastical histories, the letters of the remarkable Peter of Alexandria alone are sufficient as a shorter testimony. [Col. 1062D] Lamenting the tragedies of those times, he says among other things:

“Lucius, sent as my successor after I had been expelled, hastening to display a wolf’s wickedness and acts, the great and inseparable associate of diabolical impiety, its most bitter standard-bearer and minister, gathered a multitude of people and seized nineteen presbyters and deacons, some of whom had passed their eightieth year. He confined them under Roman laws as though they had been caught in some crime and were enemies of the Romans. Declaring that these actions pleased the ruler Valens, he said: ‘Bow, most wretched men, and agree with Arian doctrines; bow, for the divinity will forgive you.’”

And after some intervening words:

“O great inhumanity of one judging—and rather prejudging! For those who struggled for piety cannot even be compared with murderers. Their bodies, certainly, were left unburied, and those who laboured piously were thrown out as food for beasts and birds. Those who wished, prompted by natural conscience, to be compared with the fathers of sons were, as evildoers, beheaded. What law of Romans, what decree of barbarians, punishes anyone for grieving with fathers? When did any of the ancients commit such an injustice?” [Col. 1063A]

From these and similar cruel deeds it is clear when and how that dragon, together with the river of wrongly dogmatizing loquacity which he poured from his mouth, “also added to make war with the rest of the woman’s seed,” those who had survived the deadly swords of pagan persecutors. But what sort were these remaining ones, and how could they be conquered? For he says: “Who keep the commandments of God and have the testimony of Jesus” [Col. 1064A]. This is as though he said: those who are watchful in good works and strengthened by the Holy Spirit. For that Spirit is the testimony of Jesus, bearing witness, as the Apostle says, “to our spirit that we are children of God” (Rom. 8).

Thus, surrounded by both the river and the war of persecution, they spoke as strong men, as unconquerable men, to every defender of Arian impiety: “Be quiet—now be quiet—about frightening us with such speeches; cease uttering empty words. We worship neither a new nor a recent God. Though you rage vainly and shake yourself like a violent wind, we stand in the doctrines of piety unto death, never confessing a God who is powerless, foolish, or without truth, nor one who only came into existence at some time, as Arius’s impiety proclaims the Son to be temporal,” and things of this kind.

## BOOK EIGHT

[Col. 1063]

## CHAPTER XIII

[Col. 1063B]

“And I stood upon the sand of the sea, and I saw a beast rising out of the sea, having seven heads and ten horns; and upon its horns ten diadems, and upon its heads names of blasphemy.”

What we have thus far considered, as seen or written, concerning the great red dragon with so many heads and horns, who intended to devour the male child of that blessed woman and, after he was caught up to God and to his throne, waged so great a war against those who have his testimony—these things have, more clearly than light, been fulfilled in events before our age and up to the present. One tribulation still remains, to come at the end, by which the others will be completed: harsh and the worst of all tribulations. It will occur when, as the Apostle says, “the man of sin is revealed, the son of perdition, who opposes and exalts himself above all that is called God or is worshipped, so that he sits in the temple of God, showing himself as though he were God; whose coming is according to the working of Satan, in all power, signs, wonders, lies, and every deceitfulness of iniquity among those who perish, because they did not receive the love of truth that they might be saved. Therefore,” he says, “God will send them an operation of error, that they may believe a lie, in order that all may be judged who did not believe the truth but consented to iniquity” (2 Thess. 2) [Col. 1063C].

That one tribulation, I say, now remains; and the Lord himself has most solemnly testified how truly great it will be, saying: “Those days will be such days of tribulation as have not been from the beginning of the creation which God created until now, [Col. 1063D] nor shall be” (Matt. 24). Again: “False Christs and false prophets,” he says, “will arise and give great signs and wonders, so that, if possible, even the elect may be led astray” (ibid.). [Col. 1064B] This heavenly vision now begins to treat of that man of sin, that son of perdition—of his self-exaltation and opposition, his deceitful power, signs, and wonders, and the great tribulation with which he will afflict the elect in order that he may deceive them—when this beholder of marvels says: “And I stood upon the sand of the sea.”

The statement, “I stood upon the sand of the sea,” is fitting for the spectacle. For standing on sand is not secure standing, but is usually a fall or proximity to a fall. For example, in the Gospel: “Everyone who hears these words of mine and does not do them shall be like a foolish man who built his house upon sand; and the rain descended, the floods came, the winds blew, and rushed upon that house, and it fell; and its fall was great” (Matt. 7) [Col. 1064B]. Since a fall commonly occurs upon sand, while he here says that he stood upon sand, [Col. 1064C] what is suggested by this except the difficulty of that time and the extremity of the tribulation? It will be so great that, as he says, “unless those days had been shortened, no flesh would be saved,” when such and so many lying wonders will occur “that, if possible, even the elect may be led astray.”

“I stood,” therefore, he says, “upon the sand of the sea,” signifying the exceedingly uncertain and dangerous condition at that time, when the elect and those who stand will waver, while those who waver will stand; for, seeing signs together with the tribulation, they too will indeed marvel, but it will not be possible for them to be led astray. Thus, standing upon the sand of the sea:

“I saw,” he says, “a beast rising out of the sea.” From what sea? Surely that sea to which belong woe, wrath, and the eternal burning of Gehenna, because the devil—that is, the beast now said to rise—came down to it, as was said above, when the dragon was cast down from heaven: “Woe to the earth and the sea, because the devil has come down to you with great wrath” (Rev. 12) [Col. 1064D].

That dragon, that devil, is now called a beast by another but related name—not without reason, but on account of the greatness of this new reality. For he who was formerly called the devil and dragon will be in a man and armed with a man; and that man will be the man of sin, the son of perdition, as we mentioned shortly before [Col. 1065A]. Therefore the designation is suitably changed so that he may be called a beast; for that man will be hostile to God and every creature by the working of the same Satan. According to the derivation of the name, *bestia* (“beast”) is said as though *festia*, by antiphrasis, because it is hostile (*infesta*).

“Out of the sea”—that is, out of this present wicked age, out of the flowing course of the human race by birth—such a beast rises, from the multitude of the ungodly, from the wave-tossed populousness of evildoers. Some hand down that the place of the sea from which he is to be born is Babylon. [Col. 1065B] For, they say, as our Lord and Redeemer chose beforehand Bethlehem as the place where he would deign to assume humanity for us (Matt. 2; Mic. 5), so the devil knows a fitting place for that lost man called Antichrist, where the root of all evils ought to arise: namely, the city of Babylon.

But since this has no certain authority in the authentic Scriptures, wherever he rises and wherever he is born, we should know that at the very beginning of his conception the devil will enter together with him into his mother’s womb; by the devil’s power he will be fostered and troubled in his mother’s womb, and the devil’s power will always be with him. And as the Holy Spirit came upon the mother of our Lord, overshadowed her with his power, and filled her with divinity, so that she conceived by the Holy Spirit and what was born was divine (Luke 1), so too the devil will descend into the mother of Antichrist, fill her wholly, surround her wholly, hold her wholly, and possess her wholly inwardly and outwardly, so that, with the devil’s cooperation, she may conceive by a man and what is born may be wholly wicked, wholly evil [Col. 1065C].

Therefore he, so conceived in such a manner, is rightly called “the man of sin” (2 Thess. 2), and this is his proper designation. No one anywhere in all the Scriptures is called by such a title. Those who commit sin are called, and may be called, servants of sin, as the Lord says: “Everyone who commits sin is a servant of sin” (John 8; Rom. 6). But this singular sinner, in order to signify that there is in him something beyond the slavery of sin, ought rightly to be called “the man of sin.” For as “Christ,” who, as the Apostle says, “was made righteousness for us” (1 Cor. 1), is called the righteous man and the God of righteousness, so, conversely, that adversary of Christ is rightly called the sinful man and the man of sin [Col. 1065D].

Next, observe that he did not say, “I saw the beast proceeding from the sea,” but “I saw,” he says, “it rising.” What is it for such a beast to be seen or said to rise? Or to where do we think that it rises or will rise? Surely not into the heaven from which it fell, according to Truth saying: “I saw Satan falling from heaven like lightning” (Luke 10). The one who fell does not rise; only he who descended rises, concerning whom the Apostle says: “Now that he ascended, what is it but that he first descended into the lower parts of the earth? He who descended is the same also who ascended above all the heavens, that he might fill all things” (Eph. 4).

Where, then, does this one rise, who did not descend but fell? He rises nowhere; rather, he swells more and more within himself. We must understand it altogether thus: “I saw a beast rising,” as though it said: I saw a beast exalting itself within itself. For its whole ascent is that very self-exaltation which the Apostle intended to declare in these words: “He exalts himself above all that is called God or is worshipped, so that he sits in the temple of God, showing himself as though he were God” [Col. 1066A]. Therefore “I saw a beast rising” was said more fittingly and forcefully than if it had said, “I saw a beast coming out of the sea,” because the name “beast” fittingly reproves the ferocity of its folly and the word “rising” its excessive arrogance.

“Having,” he says, “seven heads and ten horns.” He said above that the great red dragon also had seven heads and ten horns. Certainly, because this beast and that dragon are one and the same devil together with his body, that is, with the entire people of the ungodly. For, as has already been said, the “seven heads” are seven kingdoms, whose persecutions, well known from the Scriptures, aimed to extinguish in the world [Col. 1066C] the holy name of true divinity [Col. 1066B].

Up to this point, those heads have raged separately and successively, each in its turn making war against God. First, the kingdom of the Egyptians, who mocked the children of Israel, Pharaoh saying: “You are idle, and therefore you say: Let us go and sacrifice to the Lord” (Exod. 5). Second, the kingdom of carnal Israel, when Jezebel and her descendants killed the prophets of the Lord (3 Kings 19). Third, the kingdom of the Babylonians, when Nebuchadnezzar compelled the captive people of God to worship the golden statue which he had made (Dan. 3). Fourth, the kingdom of the Persians and Medes, when Haman wished to destroy the entire Jewish race (Esther 3). Fifth, the kingdom of the Greeks, when Antiochus Epiphanes acted with extreme cruelty and impiety, as we read in the book of Maccabees (1 Macc. 1). Sixth, the kingdom of the Romans, when Nero and his successors persecuted Christians (2 Macc. 5). Seventh, the kingdom which is to come, the kingdom of Antichrist, when that same son of perdition will inflict a persecution such as has not been, nor will be, from the beginning of creation (Matt. 24) [Col. 1066D].

Thus, I say, the individual heads of the dragon have raged separately and successively until now. But when what we are now treating comes, when this beast rises from the sea having seven heads, all the heads together will gape with their own jaws and gnash their teeth over Christians, according to the purpose of the seventh and greatest head, which will be Antichrist. For he will send messengers and preachers throughout the whole world. His preaching and power will reach from sea to sea, from east to west, from north to north. He will first convert kings and princes to himself and then, through them, stir up persecution under the whole heaven against all peoples confessing Christ [Col. 1067A].

Accordingly, it should be noted that, after saying “having seven heads and ten horns,” he added: “And upon its horns ten diadems.” Here the number of horns and diadems is the same. Above, however, it was not so: the dragon had ten horns, but seven diadems. We must therefore recall those same kingdoms which we have already enumerated. Although there were seven kingdoms, their kings numbered ten, because the one Greek kingdom, after Alexander the Great’s death, was divided among four successors: Ptolemy son of Lagus, Philip surnamed Arrhidaeus, Seleucus, also called Nicanor, and Antigonus [Col. 1067B].

Syria together with Judaea fell to Seleucus’s share; and only his descendants—among whom that exceedingly wicked Antiochus Epiphanes arose—attacked the name of the Lord, as we have from the memorable deeds of the Maccabees. Therefore, since the seven kingdoms had ten kings, but the rulers of three divisions of the Greek kingdom did nothing against the worship of God, it was fittingly the case above that the dragon with seven heads had ten horns but only seven diadems. Yet when that son of perdition comes, it will not be so. No kingdom and no part of any kingdom will be exempt from persecution of Christians. Thus there are fittingly as many diadems as horns, because as many kings as there will be, so many will be the ministries of this impiety.

“And upon its heads were names of blasphemy.” “Names of blasphemy,” that is, names of divinity arrogated to themselves, or of a pretended likeness to God. Concerning the first of these heads, namely the kingdom of the Egyptians, it is certainly known that it blasphemed—not only by standing against God and oppressing the children of Israel so that they might retain no remembrance of the Lord’s name, but also by aspiring to the very likeness of God itself (Exod. 5). Hence it also bears the type of the devil; and, in reproach of him, the Lord says through the Prophet: “Son of man, say [Col. 1067D] to Pharaoh king of Egypt and to his people: To whom have you become like in your greatness?” (Ezek. 31). And after some intervening words: “To whom have you been compared, O renowned and lofty one among the trees of delight? Behold, you have been brought down with the trees of delight to the lowest earth; in the midst of the uncircumcised you shall sleep with those slain by the sword. This is Pharaoh and all his multitude, says the Lord God” (ibid.).

Concerning the kingdom of the Israelites, it is certain that Jezebel blasphemed, not merely by compelling Baal to be worshipped as God, but also by perverting the oath customarily sworn at that time in the name of the Lord. For, whereas it was customary to swear thus: “May God do these things to me, and add these things” (3 Kings 2), she herself, for example, swore thus against Elijah: “May the gods [Col. 1068A] do these things to me, and add these things, unless by this time tomorrow I make your life like the life of one of them” (3 Kings 19)—that is, of the prophets of Baal whom you killed.

Concerning the kingdom of the Babylonians, it is well known that it gloried magnificently, especially when it set up a golden statue and compelled men to worship it; it blasphemed and said: “And who is the God that shall deliver you out of my hand?” (Dan. 3). Likewise it is written in the Book of Judith: “For Nebuchadnezzar king had commanded Holofernes to destroy all the gods of the earth, namely, that he alone should be called God by those nations which could be subjected to his power” (Judith 3).

Concerning the kingdom of the Persians and Medes, we likewise know that the most proud Haman inscribed upon it the name of pride, because, when he learned that Mordecai [Col. 1068B] would not worship him, he was exceedingly angry (Esther 3). But Mordecai, praying to God, says among other things: “I would gladly have been ready even to kiss the prints of his feet for the salvation of Israel; but I feared lest I should transfer the honour of my God to a man, and lest I should worship anyone except my God” (Esther 13). In saying this he sufficiently makes clear that that proud man demanded of himself not just any reverence, but that worship which is owed to God alone.

For there is a form of reverence by which, without prejudice to God’s honour, it is permissible to do homage and to receive homage. Mordecai would not have rejected this so emphatically, since even a holy prophet did homage to a human king, as it is written: “And they told the king, saying: Nathan the prophet is here. And when he had entered and stood before the king, he bowed down with his face to the ground before the king” (3 Kings 1), [Col. 1068C] and so forth.

Concerning the kingdom of the Greeks, there is scarcely anyone who does not know that it blasphemed and branded itself with the mark of blasphemy—namely when the often-mentioned Antiochus, going up to Jerusalem “with a great multitude, entered the sanctuary arrogantly and spoke great arrogance” (1 Macc. 1). Daniel, foreseeing his proud blasphemy, says: “And he was magnified even unto the host of heaven; and he cast down some of the host and of the stars, and trampled upon them; and he was magnified even unto the prince of the host, and from him he took away the continual sacrifice” (Dan. 8), and so forth.

Concerning the kingdom of the Romans, who does not know that it inscribed the name of blasphemy upon itself yet more loftily, by giving its kings the stolen name of divinity? For—to pass over the others who, after they had died, were enrolled among the gods—[Col. 1068D] Octavian Augustus was called a god while still alive and present in the flesh; and, an excessive pretender, he allowed a temple and image, as well as rites of sacrifice, to be offered to himself by the foolish and utterly senseless crowds of flattering peoples.

Concerning the kingdom of Antichrist, which will be the seventh head, there is no need to seek farther examples or testimonies of the blasphemy by which that unclean head is to be marked—or crowned. For this Scripture later says of him: “And there was given to him a mouth speaking great things and blasphemy; and he opened his mouth in blasphemies against God, to blaspheme his name and his tabernacle.” Therefore, upon the heads of the beast are names of blasphemy, because the individual kingdoms ascribed to their kings the name which is God—or the kings themselves voluntarily snatched it away [Col. 1069A]—and this, surely, is blasphemy.

“And the beast which I saw was like a leopard, and its feet were like those of a bear, and its mouth like the mouth of a lion.” In Daniel’s vision, where four great beasts, different from one another, came up out of the sea, the leopard signifies the kingdom of the Macedonians. It is an exceedingly swift beast, rushing headlong to bloodshed and leaping to death. The Macedonian kingdom, Alexander’s kingdom, is therefore compared to it; for nothing was swifter than his victories. From Illyricum and the Adriatic Sea as far as the Indian Ocean and the river Ganges, he traversed the world not so much by battles as by victories, and in six years subjected to himself part of Europe and all Asia.

The beast which I saw was like such a leopard—that is, according to the wickedness [Col. 1069B] of the aforesaid Antiochus, who, as Daniel likewise foretold, “was magnified unto the host of heaven,” or unto the prince of the host, and took from him the continual sacrifice. Finally, most teachers refer this to Antichrist in such a way that they say what was done typologically under Antiochus will be fulfilled in truth under Antichrist. Therefore, “it was like a leopard”: that is, Antichrist will fulfil that which was prefigured of him through Antiochus.

“And its feet,” he says, “were like those of a bear.” In the same vision of Daniel, the bear signifies the kingdom of the Persians and Medes, because of that kingdom’s hardness and ferocity (Dan. 7). The feet of this beast are compared with the feet of that bear. Who, then, will be the feet of this beast, if not the attendants of his wickedness, bearers throughout the whole world of his most evil commissions for the shedding of blood? [Col. 1069C] And who were the feet of that bear—that is, of that Persian and Median kingdom—if not the accomplices of Haman the Agagite, enemy of the Jews, who hurried to carry the cruel letters, indeed letters obtained from the king, containing savage commands that the Jews should be killed? (Esther 3).

Thus, when he says, “and its feet were like a bear,” it is as if he said: His ministers, like Haman, will be swift to shed blood.

“And its mouth was like the mouth of a lion.” In the same vision of Daniel, not a lion but, more savage still, a lioness signifies the Babylonian kingdom, on account of its savagery and cruelty, or because of its luxury and a life enslaved to lust. Therefore its mouth is like the mouth of a lion, when it speaks proud and cruel things—as that king of Babylon did when he said: “And who is the God that shall deliver you out of my hand?” (Dan. 3).

Notice that there, in Daniel’s vision, the lioness is placed first, then another like a bear, then another like a leopard, and then a fourth beast, unnamed, terrible, wonderful, and exceedingly strong (Dan. 7). Here, however, in reversed order, the kingdom of Antichrist is first called “the beast,” by a general designation without a particular name; then it has the likeness of a leopard; then its feet have the likeness of a bear; then its mouth the likeness of a lion.
