By this is mystically signified how obstinate will be the apostasy of the diabolical spirit, which will overflow wholly in that man: it reverses its evils and turns itself back [Col. 1070A] upon its own tracks. It continues:

“And the dragon gave it his power and great authority.” We are wonderfully brought back and held again in that same vision of Daniel, so that when it says, “The dragon gave it his power” (Dan. 13), we may see this as the opposite of what the Ancient of Days gave to the Son of Man—his power and great authority. For there, after the ascent of those 453 great beasts—the lioness, the bear, the leopard, and the unnamed fourth—there immediately follows: “And I looked until thrones were set, and the Ancient of Days sat.” And shortly thereafter: “I looked in the vision of the night, and behold, with the clouds of heaven there came one like the Son of Man; and he came even to the Ancient of Days, and they presented him before him. [Col. 1070B] And he gave him authority, honour, and a kingdom; and all peoples, tribes, and tongues shall serve him. His authority is an everlasting authority, which shall not be taken away, and his kingdom one which shall not be destroyed” (Dan. 7).

Here, on the contrary, after he has called that savage creature “the beast” by a common or general term, and said that it was like a leopard, that its feet were like those of a bear, and that its mouth was like a lion’s, he indicates that the man of sin comes as far as the ancient dragon when he says: “And the dragon gave it his power and great authority”; and later he repeats: “And authority was given to him over every tribe, people, tongue, and nation.”

But whereas there it was said: “His authority is an everlasting authority, which shall not be taken away, and his kingdom one which shall not be destroyed,” [Col. 1070C] here, in this opposite figure, we find nothing even falsified to resemble it, as the other things are. For the authority which this one gave to the son of perdition cannot be or be called eternal or incorruptible.

What, then, does this ruinous tyrant of sin mean—this governor of death? How does he here imitate the Most High? Is this what he once promised himself when he said in his heart, “I will be like the Most High”? (Isa. 14). O lethargic father of lies, how does he wish to boast that he is truthful precisely in that wherein he is most false? What could be more unlike than this likeness, or more remote than this imitation? Let all heaven, the whole earth, all generations of the ages, turn wondering eyes toward such a spectacle.

The Most High [Col. 1070D] begot from his heart truth—the true and good Word—and willed that he should be incarnate; and to that man, on account of his perfect obedience in humility, he truly gave his great authority in heaven and on earth. But this imitator of him, remembering that he had said, “I will be like the Most High,” as though wishing to act likewise, begot falsehood from his heart; and he will gather it whole and establish it in that man who is to come. He will also give him all his power, namely all the kingdoms of the world. Yet he will not give even that from what is his own, but from robbery.

For when, in the Gospel, he showed the Saviour all the kingdoms of the world and their glory while tempting him, and said: “All these things will I give thee, if thou fall down and worship me,” he adds: “All these things have been delivered to me, and I give them to whom I will” [Col. 1071A] (Matt. 4; Luke 3). He lies, because they have not wholly or truly been delivered to him; rather, he seized them. The beginning of this seizure was the deception by which he deceived the first human being. For in truth, “The earth is the Lord’s and the fullness thereof” (Ps. 23), and there is absolutely nothing which ought not to belong to him, except only the vice of rational creatures.

Therefore understand that, when he added “great” in speaking of power or authority, it was said not according to reality but according to its estimation. Let us still consider what follows:

“And I saw one of its heads as if slain unto death, and its deadly wound was healed.” The one and same man of sin, Antichrist, was shortly before called the beast with seven heads, and here is called one of the beast’s heads: the beast with so many heads in respect of its body, which is the whole generation of the wicked; but one head in respect of his own person and of the sovereignty of his time, when he will be revealed—the king of all the children of pride.

But what he here says, that “this head of the beast was as if slain unto death and its deadly wound healed,” he repeats later, calling it the beast’s very head: “That they should make an image of the beast which has the wound of the sword and lived.” Where, I ask, was this head slain? Where did it receive the wound of the sword? How was its deadly wound healed? How did it live? Indeed, how does this concern the name Antichrist—that is, one contrary to Christ? Truly, in a manner both marvellous and execrable.

For the true Christ received the wounds of the nails and the wound of the lance, and died to sin; but now his death has been healed and he himself lives to God. This one, however—O marvellous thing!—in heaven before the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, subjected to judgment before the entire court of the assemblies and the holy senate of blessed angels, received a capital sentence for the crime of pride and was struck by the sword of eternal condemnation. Thus he died to God and lived to sin, and still lives. [Col. 1071C] He lives—certainly he lives—because he most stubbornly defends himself, and wishes to be regarded not as dead but as God; indeed, he exalts himself above every being called god or worshipped (2 Thess. 2).

Was his deadly wound, then, truly healed? It was not healed; rather, rebellious against the sword and rebellious against God’s sentence, he maintains that the wound has done him no harm. For even before the devil enters into him, his own vessel, the son of perdition—though he has been struck in heaven—has procured temples, altars, priests, and sacrifices for himself as though he were a living god. After the devil has entered that man, he will obtain the kingdoms of the world and sit in the temple of God, displaying himself as though he were God.

How will he admit, even in agreement with his own conscience, that he has ever been slain or wounded, or that he ever ought to be wounded or slain? O tyrant, tyrant! We wonder whence comes such foolish hardness, such hard foolishness. Yet within our race we read and see many persons conformed to you, schooled beforehand by you, hardened and made foolish after your example. For whoever, convicted of a crime and sentenced by judgment, acts against his own conscience and, conscious of his crime, defends himself, resists the sentence.

For example, when some powerful person, guilty and rebellious in adultery or homicide, by his own power resists the sword of anathema by which he is justly struck, we rightly and truly judge of him that he has the wound of the sword and lives: that is, he has been condemned in conscience by his own judgment, yet through contumacy defends himself as though he were righteous. It continues:

“And the whole earth marvelled after the beast, and they worshipped the dragon which gave authority to the beast; and they worshipped the beast, saying: Who is like the beast, and who can fight against it?” Here that generation which will receive such a man is especially blamed, according to the grave and truthful complaint of that man who “comes blessed [Col. 1072B] in the name of the Lord,” when he says: “I came in my Father’s name, and you did not receive me; another will come in his own name, and him you will receive” (John 15).

For they are earth, and savour earthly things; and that reception by which they will receive him is this very amazement of which he now says: “And the whole earth marvelled after the beast.” They are blamed in this, and it is reproached to them, because if they were not earth—if they savoured anything of the things above—they would not marvel, they would not esteem highly his earthly exaltation, earthly power, or earthly glory. The true Christ so despised these things that, when he was first greeted by the crowds as king of Israel, who said, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Matt. 21), he chose to sit upon a donkey, in contempt of every earthly [Col. 1072C] height.

Moreover, he strikes them further by adding: “And they worshipped the dragon which gave authority to the beast, and they worshipped 454 the beast, saying: Who is like the beast, and who can fight against it?” Being about to say, “and they worshipped the beast,” he first said, “and they worshipped the dragon which gave authority to the beast.” Why? Clearly because the prior cause whereby they worshipped the dragon, the parent of such a beast, brought about their worship of the beast.

For as the Apostle says: “Because they did not receive the love of the truth so that they might be saved, therefore he will send them an operation of error, that they may believe a lie” (2 Thess. 2). Likewise one may rightly say: Because they worshipped the dragon, that is, the devil, they are consequently permitted to err so that they may worship the beast, that is, Antichrist.

But you say: How can even the wicked be said to have worshipped the devil, when they often curse the devil? To this I say: Certainly—to pass over other matters for now—they worshipped the devil at least in this, that they served Mammon. For the Apostle also says of covetousness that it is the service of idols (Eph. 5). Therefore, since they had long been servants of Mammon, and in serving Mammon worshipped the devil, why are you surprised that afterward they worshipped the beast, who possesses riches and is able to give gold and silver, since the dragon gave him authority over all that belongs to himself?

Thus, marvelling and worshipping, they will say: “Who is like the beast?” They will ask this question and answer themselves: No one. They will say further: “And who can [Col. 1073A] fight against it?” Speaking foolish things in their foolishness, they will not remember that Pharaoh with his chariots and horsemen, while God fought for Israel, was drowned in the sea (Exod. 14); that dogs devoured Jezebel (4 Kings 9); that Nebuchadnezzar was driven out from among men and ate grass like an ox for seven seasons (Dan. 4); that Haman was hanged on the gallows (Esther 7); that Antiochus rotted inwardly while still alive (1 Macc. 4), and, as Daniel foretold, was broken without hand; or that Nero, minister of the devil, as he lived disgracefully, so perished more shamefully (Dan. 8). They will not remember these things; indeed, if anyone reminds them, they will not endure to hear them. For concerning them above all will be true what the Apostle says: “And they shall indeed turn away their hearing from the truth, but shall be turned unto fables” (1 Tim. 4).

We may observe an example of such foolish amazement also among those of whom it is written in the Acts of the Apostles: “And upon an appointed day Herod, clothed in royal apparel, sat upon the tribunal and made an oration to them. But the people cried out: The voice of a god, and not of a man” (Acts 12). Now, “Who is like the beast, and who can fight against it?” are words proper to God and not to a human being—that is, words which may be addressed to God alone, not to a human being.

For example, in the psalm the righteous man says: “All my bones shall say: Lord, who is like thee?” (Ps. 34). But these men say: “Who is like the beast?” That is, who is like Christ? For from John’s standpoint he is called the beast, but by those deceived he will be called Christ. Likewise, the righteous man says to God: “Thou art terrible, and [Col. 1073C] who shall resist thee?” (Ps. 75). But these men, on the contrary, say of the beast: “And who can fight against it?”

This is what we have just said: Herod too was an example of it, to whom a crowd, excessively given to flattery, cried out, “The voice of a god, and not of a man.” And how small was the occasion for which they acclaimed words of this sort to Herod! It was surely slight, and far less than the greatness which this beast will possess. Josephus, in the nineteenth book of the *Antiquities*, recounts that ridiculous vanity more fully:

“When,” he says, “he was presenting spectacles for the citizens in honour of Caesar, on a day apparently vowed for Caesar’s safety, and when men distinguished both by rank and wealth had gathered there from the whole province, on the second day of the spectacles he came into the theatre at the beginning of the day, clothed in a shining garment wondrously interwoven with gold and silver. When the first rays of the sun had been received in the folds of the silvery garment, its reflected brilliance cast forth before the spectators a doubled light, flashing with the gleam of the vibrating metal. The terror of the sight struck the eyes of those who looked, and by this an artificer’s arrogance falsely asserted that he possessed something more than human nature. Immediately the cries of the flattering crowd resounded, proclaiming honour but bringing destruction; and from one side and the other they called him God and simply entreated him to be propitious, the people saying: ‘Until now we have feared you as a man, but henceforth we confess that you are above human nature.’”

Therefore, if, because a silver garment reflected the sun’s radiance, they attributed so much to a petty ruler of one province, how greatly, do you suppose, will “the voice of a god” resound for so great a beast, possessing all gold and all silver, together with the shining light of miracles? Or will the people of that time be less inclined to flatter? For what will people be like in those last days, those perilous times? Certainly, as the Apostle says: “Lovers of themselves, covetous, proud, arrogant, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, ungrateful, wicked, without natural affection, without peace, accusers, incontinent, unmerciful, without kindness, traitors, rash, puffed up, lovers of pleasures more than of God” (2 Tim. 3). If God sends to such persons an operation of error, why are you surprised that they cry, “The voice of a god, and not of a man”? (2 Tim. 2; Acts [Col. 1074B] 12).

And concerning Herod it was said only slightly, because he had not given glory to God—namely, by assenting to the people’s excessive applause. But concerning this beast, what this Scripture says is far greater. For it continues:

“And there was given to it a mouth speaking great things and blasphemy; and authority was given to it to act for forty-two months.” Then, in order to explain the greatness of that mouth, or the great things which it would speak, it adds: “And it opened its mouth in blasphemies against God, to blaspheme his name and his tabernacle, and those who dwell in heaven.” Likewise, explaining what authority is given to it, and how it exercises the authority received during the forty-two months, it further adds: “And it was given to it to make war [Col. 1074C] with the saints and to overcome them. And authority was given to it over every tribe, people, tongue, and nation.”

This is the distinctive mark of the sin of him of whom it is written: “He himself is king over all the children of pride” (Job 41): he will not merely consent to the excessive applause of those saying, “Who is like the beast?” Rather, he will have a great mouth, a mouth speaking great things, arrogating to himself God’s majesty and demanding from everyone words proper to God and not to a human being, so that all may say: “Who is like thee?” He will demand this not only by speech but also by military power.

For this reason he will open his mouth in blasphemies against God: namely, as the Apostle says, by exalting himself above every being called god or worshipped (2 Thess. 2). For this reason he will wage war with the saints and overcome them: those whom he cannot subdue by blaspheming speech he will vindicate himself against by waging war and killing them.

Observe carefully that he will do all these things according to his name—or rather, that his name, Antichrist, that is, “contrary to Christ,” has already been imposed upon him because of these things. For all that is said here is contrary to what we read concerning Christ.

First, the fact that “there was given to him a mouth speaking great things” is contrary to Christ’s mouth. Christ’s mouth, indeed, was small and silent. For it is written: “He was offered because he himself willed it, and he did not open his mouth; he shall be led as a sheep to slaughter, and as a lamb before its shearer shall be silent, and he shall not open his mouth” (Isa. 35 [materially uncertain citation; apparently Isa. 53]). Likewise in the Prophet whom the Evangelist also mentions: “He shall not contend nor cry out, nor shall anyone hear [Col. 1075A] his voice in the streets” (Isa. 42; Matt. 12).

This beast will open that boastful mouth in blasphemies against God; Christ, however, opened his mouth in confession and praise of God. For example, he says: “I confess to thee, Father, Lord of heaven and earth” (Matt. 11). These are altogether contrary.

Likewise, Antichrist will blaspheme not only the Lord’s name, but also his tabernacle and those who dwell in heaven. Christ, however, not only confessed the Father, Lord of heaven and earth, but also honoured and pronounced blessed his tabernacle—that is, the Church—and those who dwell, or shall dwell, in heaven; and for this he opened his mouth, as it is written in the Gospel: “And opening his mouth, he taught them, saying: Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. [Col. 1075B] 5), and so forth; which he concludes thus: “Rejoice and exult, for your reward is great in heaven” (ibid.). These are plainly contrary.

Likewise, “his authority is to make war with the saints for forty-two months”; Christ’s authority, for an equal period, was to procure peace for the saints, as he says: “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you” (John 14). These, indeed, are contrary.

Likewise, “this one’s authority extends over every tribe, people, tongue, and nation”; but Christ received no authority from God over anyone, not even to judge the smallest fields. Rather, “when one of the crowd said to him: Master, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me, he said: Man, who made me a judge or divider over you?” (Luke 12). And when he knew that those whom he had fed with five loaves and two fishes, about five thousand in number, were going to come and seize him and make him king, “the Evangelist says, he fled alone to the mountain” (John 6), because, as he later told Pilate, “his kingdom was not, and is not, of this world” (John 18). These too are contrary.

For it continues:

“And all who dwell upon the earth, whose names are not written in the book of life of the Lamb who was slain from the foundation of the world, shall worship it.” He has made a great and true distinction concerning those who will worship him, saying: “whose names are not written in the book of life of the Lamb.” The book of life is in heaven, as it is said in the Gospel: “But rejoice in this, that your names are written in heaven” [Col. 1075D] (Luke 10). Where, then, are the names written of those who will worship him? On earth, as the Prophet testifies: “Those who depart from thee shall be written in the earth” (Jer. 17).

This too is not left unstated in the present distinction. For, about to say “whose names are not written in the book of life,” he first said, “all who dwell upon the earth.” To dwell upon earth is to yearn with one’s entire desire for earthly things. Whoever does this departs from God and is written in the earth, according to what is said elsewhere in prophetic confession: “Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and let them not be written with the righteous” (Ps. 68).

But he admits only those worshippers “whose names have been written in the book of life from the foundation of the world.” This book is God’s foreknowledge and the blessed certainty of predestination, as the angel says distinctly to Daniel: “And at that time all your people shall be saved who are found written in the book” (Dan. 12).

These are writings of opposites; the books themselves are opposite, and the reasons why persons are written in the books are opposite. For the cause of the good book, the book of life—in which all and only those who are to be saved are written—is God’s purpose, of which the Apostle says: “We know that all things work together for good to those who love God, to those who are called saints according to his purpose. For those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son” (Rom. 8), and so forth.

Having said here concerning this book, “whose names are not written in the book of life of the Lamb who was slain,” he added: “from the foundation of the world.” It should not be read or understood thus: “in the book of life of the Lamb who was slain from the foundation of the world”; but thus: “whose names have not been written from the foundation of the world in the book of life of the Lamb who was slain.” The sense is: They have not been written in the book of life from the foundation of the world—that is, they were not in God’s purpose at the very foundation of the world, namely when, after creating the first humans, he blessed them and said: “Increase and multiply and fill the earth and subdue it” (Gen. 1).

Finally, all and only those whom he commanded to be born by that blessing are written in the book of life. The book of life is rightly called the Lamb’s, because all the elect, whose names are written in it, were or are able to recover, only through the Lamb Jesus Christ, through the blood of that same Lamb Jesus Christ, the blessing by which they were commanded to be born or multiply and which they lost in Adam.

That they might be born and live for his glory, they were in God’s purpose, foreknowledge, and predestination. Thus, in the passage already cited above, when the Apostle had said, “those who are called saints according to his purpose; for those whom he foreknew and predestined,” he immediately added that they were “to be conformed to the image of his Son,” and that through the humility of his death they were called, gathered into one from dispersion, justified, and glorified.

But the cause of the evil book, the book of death—in which all and only those who do not belong to that purpose of God are written—was sin, when it first entered this world through the envy of the devil (Wis. 2). Scripture testifies to this because God says to the woman not before but after the act of that sin: “I will multiply your sorrows and your conceptions” (Gen. 3).

This multiplication or excess of conceptions has always, from the beginning, greatly oppressed by its multitude the children of blessing, who are born more slowly and sparingly. It began with Cain, Eve’s firstborn, who killed his righteous brother Abel (Gen. 4); and in those last days now under discussion, while worshipping and saying, “Who is like the beast, and who can fight against it?”, it will persecute and kill the remaining children of the same blessing. It continues:

“If anyone has an ear, let him hear. He who leads into captivity shall go into captivity; and he who kills with the sword must likewise be killed [by the sword].” He wished powerfully to rouse us and make us attentive to hear by prefacing: “If anyone has an ear, let him hear.” Who would hesitate at this declaration? Who would not immediately grant the truth of the proposition which says: “He who leads into captivity shall go into captivity; and he who kills with the sword must likewise be killed”?

For this is the same as when, having said to Peter, “Put your sword back into its place,” he immediately added: “For all who take the sword shall perish by the sword” (Matt. 26). Here it must also be understood: unless they repent. Likewise in the Law, where it is said, “Whoever wilfully strikes a person to kill him shall surely die” (Exod. 21), it must be understood: unless he repents. Otherwise, the rule of sound doctrine would not stand.

Therefore, having heard or granted this true proposition, look and consider that this beast, this man of sin, who calls himself Christ but is a beast, has taken the sword, led into captivity, and killed with the sword, making war with the saints so that, as this Scripture later says, “whoever does not worship his image may be killed.” Thus all who worship such a beast will be without excuse. For they possess the sign by which they may know with certainty that he is not the son of God but the son of the devil: he is a murderous man, a bloodthirsty man.

For “in this,” the same John says here, “the children of God and the children of the devil are manifest” (1 John 3). In what are they manifest? After immediately adding, “Everyone who is not righteous is not of God,” he adds: “and whoever does not love his brother” [Col. 1077C]. Then at once, having said, “For this is the message which you heard from the beginning, that you should love one another,” he goes on and says: “Not as Cain, who was of the evil one and killed his brother” (ibid.).

This is the sign by which those who are of God may know that this wicked man is of the evil one: because he will kill, as has already been said, and lead into captivity—things which no one who is of God does or has done. Let anyone who has an ear hear this; let whoever possesses faithful reason call this to mind. When he sees him leading into captivity and killing with the sword, even if he lacks abundant knowledge or a wealth of Scriptural testimonies, let him know at least from this fact alone—that he is a murderer—that he is not of God and therefore will not stand.

But as other people receive their recompense, so that those who take the sword perish by the sword, so this man too shall receive captivity for captivity and killing for killing: eternal for temporal punishment, double for single; so that he who captured and killed only the bodies of the saints may himself receive captivity and the killing both of soul and body.

What if this does not happen immediately? Indeed, if it happened immediately—if that great mouth were checked at its first blasphemy, and if, at the beginning of the war or sword which he will take up, he immediately perished by the heavenly sword—where and in what would the patience and faith of the saints be tested? It continues:

“This is the patience and faith of the saints.” As if he said: In this the faithful patience and patient faith of the saints must be tested: that beast will indeed act, prosper, and deceit will be directed in his hand. Yet they will nevertheless believe and steadfastly hold as true what has been said: that he who leads into captivity shall be taken captive, and he who kills with the sword shall himself likewise be killed.

Nor will this patience and faith of the saints be disappointed; for after the end or completion of the beast’s slaughter, which will be prolonged—or rather shortened—to forty-two months, the Lord Jesus will slay him with the breath of his mouth and destroy him by the radiance of his coming (2 Thess. 2). It continues:

“And I saw another beast rising from the earth. It had two horns like a lamb, but it spoke like a dragon; and it exercised all the authority of the former beast [Col. 1078B] in its presence. And it caused the earth and those dwelling in it to worship the first beast, whose mortal wound had been healed. And it performed great signs, even making fire come down from heaven to earth before men.” We have already said that the seven-headed beast is the whole race of the ungodly, and that its seven heads were, or are, the seven kingdoms of the world, whose power at different times crushed the saints of the Most High; the seventh of these heads will be Antichrist. What, then, is this other beast which he saw rising from the earth? Or how are there two beasts, when there is one body of the depraved and perverse generation, just as, conversely, there is one body of the one holy and elect generation?

In reply, it must be understood that, although the wicked generation is one, it is nevertheless called one beast and another beast [Col. 1078C], because of its twofold force—warlike or royal, and magical. This Scripture now begins its account in the divine vision of the magical force when it says: “And I saw another beast rising from the earth.” When do you suppose that this other beast rose, which he saw rising? Clearly, at the very same time as that former beast rose, having seven heads, of which the seventh head will be the kingdom of Antichrist.

For as soon as the generation of the ungodly subjected and afflicted the generation of the saints in slavery, and brought it to bitterness through the hard works of mortar and brick, Pharaoh moreover commanding all his people and saying, “Whatever male child is born, cast it into the river; whatever is female, preserve” [Col. 1078D] (Exod. 1), then, together with that royal or hostile power, the magical force also rose against God. How? Namely, when Moses and Aaron entered before Pharaoh in order to perform the signs which the Lord had commanded: “Pharaoh summoned the wise men and sorcerers, and they too did likewise by Egyptian enchantments and certain secret arts” (Exod. 7).

Thus, he says, “I saw another beast then rising.” But what has this to do with the present subject, where he was plainly speaking of the open persecution of Antichrist which will occur in the last days? Certainly this: magical deceptions and assaults against God began earlier, but then they will abound more greatly. “For,” Christ says, “false Christs and false prophets will arise, and will give great signs and wonders, so that, if possible, even the elect may be led astray” [Col. 1079A] (Matt. 24). The sequence of this Scripture will declare the same concerning this beast in the present chapter.

This most evil power has never been absent from the company of the cruel sword: from the Egyptian, Israelite, Babylonian, Median and Persian, Greek, and Roman kings—who persecuted and crushed the saints of the Most High—nor will it be absent from the power of Antichrist; indeed, it will be present more abundantly and powerfully. The Roman emperors used it more secretly; Julian the Apostate applied himself to that art with particular malice and zeal. The Greeks and Macedonians likewise used it less openly. But the earlier Persians, Babylonians, and Egyptians employed it publicly and, as it were, without restraint; their magicians publicly called themselves such and did not conceal it.

The Israelite kings, however [Col. 1079B], covered their magicians with the name of prophets. Elijah killed four hundred and fifty such men in one day—all prophets of Baal (3 Kings 18). What kind of beast did he see rising? “It had,” he says, “two horns like a lamb, and it spoke like a dragon.” As the seven-headed beast, previously described through ten horns, so this beast too has two horns. For just as the first kings of the ten kingdoms were especially well known, and have been mentioned above, so there are two especially well-known and conspicuous founders of magical art—the two whom Pharaoh summoned against Moses and Aaron, as has already been said. They were Jannes and Mambres, as the Apostle also recalls.

After saying, “For among these are those [Col. 1079C] who enter houses and lead captive little women burdened with sins, driven by various desires, always learning and never able to arrive at knowledge of the truth,” he immediately adds: “Just as Jannes and Mambres resisted Moses, so these also resist the truth: men corrupted in mind, reprobate concerning the faith. But they shall make no further progress; for their folly will become plain to all, as theirs also did” (2 Tim. 3).

Thus this beast had two horns when it first rose: that is, magical art had two leaders of its efficacy when it first took its stand against God. And these horns were like a lamb in a proud and contrary likeness, performing similar miracles to those done through the Word of God, who is the Lamb of God. Even if you consider the historical letter, where this beast first rose it is most aptly and properly said to have horns “like a lamb.” For all the signs which Moses and Aaron performed before Pharaoh and the Egyptians are rightly called signs of the Lamb, because all those things were completed through the blood of the lamb which the people of Israel sacrificed at evening, so that Pharaoh and Egypt might be struck by the final plague (Exod. 12).

There, indeed, the horns of the beast seemed like the horns of the Lamb, where it is written: “The sorcerers also did likewise by their Egyptian enchantments and certain secret arts; each threw down his rod, and they were turned into dragons” [Col. 1079D] (Exod. 7). Again: “When Moses, raising his rod, struck the water of the river and it was turned into blood, the Scripture says that the Egyptian sorcerers did likewise by their enchantments” [Col. 1080A] (ibid.). A third time they did likewise by their enchantments, bringing frogs up over the land of Egypt (Exod. 8). Thus far they were able to feign a likeness to the horns of the Lamb; beyond this they could not, and, confessing themselves defeated, said: “This is the finger of God” (ibid.).

In the same way, throughout the succeeding ages under the other kingdoms mentioned above, magical art always sought an imitation of God and wished to appear to perform signs no less great than those done through the Word of God. Of this presumption of the beast he immediately says: “And it spoke like a dragon”—that is, like the devil, who spoke thus: “I shall be like the Most High” [Col. 1080B] (Isa. 14). We also read in many ancient histories that they required people, through certain magical tortures, to worship them as gods.

“And this beast exercised all the authority of the former beast in its presence.” It is as though he said: Magicians performing signs strengthened royal hearts in unbelief and resistance to the signs and powers of God, so that those rulers might not consider themselves less powerful than the God proclaimed amid such great miracles, since they themselves had persons with them who did similar things. This was to exercise all the beast’s authority in its presence: to reinforce the estimation of its proud heart, lest it should seem powerless to itself.

“And it caused the earth and those dwelling in it to worship the first beast, whose mortal wound had been healed.” [Col. 1080C] Omitting the other things done since the appearance of those two horns like a lamb, already mentioned—things performed by magical art allied against God with the swords of the kingdoms described above—the present text brings us back to the last days of which it had spoken shortly before. For the beast “whose mortal wound had been healed” will be Antichrist, the seventh head of the beast. Above, as far as we were able, it has already been said how his wound will be received, and how it will be healed—or how he will wish it to seem healed.

Therefore it caused—that is, it will cause—the earth and all who dwell in it, namely earthly people, who store up treasure not in heaven but on earth, to worship with sacrilegious desire the first beast: that is, the chief power of Antichrist, and to accept his beastly [Col. 1080D] exaltation, by which he exalts himself above everything called God or worshipped (2 Thess. 2). How did it do this? He says: “And it performed great signs, even making fire come down from heaven to earth before men.”

Great power; great and astonishing efficacy of the spirit of deception. But for whom will this be great? Certainly for “those who are perishing,” as the Apostle says, “because they did not receive the love of the truth, that they might be saved” (ibid.). This must be carefully observed. For when the Apostle says, “whose coming is according to the working of Satan, in all power and signs and lying wonders, and in every deception of unrighteousness,” and then adds, “for those who are perishing, because they did not receive the love of the truth, that they might be saved,” he clearly maintains [Col. 1081A] that unless they had already perished, they would not now be deceived; unless they had first abandoned inwardly the brightness of truth, they would never assent outwardly to lying wonders.

Is this not the customary and ancient order of perishing? For we all know approximately the same thing concerning the first human beings: unless they had first perished inwardly through pride, unless they had abandoned the love of truth, they would not so easily have yielded when tempted from without, nor so quickly bowed themselves to the astonishing speech [address] of the brute animal, the serpent, or believed its promises.

Therefore what the Apostle now says universally—“because they did not receive the love of the truth, that they might be saved; therefore God will send them an operation of error, so that they may believe a lie, so that all may be judged who did not believe the truth but consented to unrighteousness” [Col. 1081B]—is, by a most lamentable and ruinous example for us, a certain and unquestionable truth: for this is what happened to our first parents, to whom, because they did not receive the love of truth, God sent an operation of error in that serpent.

Let us not, then, wonder as though it were something new which will happen to them—that such a beast should perform great signs before them and deceive them—as the Scripture immediately adds: “And it deceives those dwelling on the earth because of the signs which it was given to perform in the presence of the beast, saying to those dwelling on the earth that they should make an image of the beast which has the wound of the sword and lived. And it was given to it to give spirit to the image of the beast, so that the image of the beast might speak.” It will deceive no one except one who has perished, one who has abandoned the love of truth.

But what true or unheard-of greatness do these greatest signs possess, which it will be able to perform and which Scripture here sets forth because of their excellence? One is in its saying that it would make fire come down from heaven before men. Another miracle is in its saying: “And it was given to it to give spirit to the image of the beast, so that the image of the beast might speak” [Col. 1081C]. Are these things of such a kind or magnitude as the devil has ever done? Did he not also make fire come down from heaven before men, when authority was given him to test Job? “The fire of God,” said the messenger, who did not know what was being done or what Satan was plotting, “fell from heaven and consumed the sheep and servants; and I alone escaped to tell you” (Job 1).

Did not the same devil likewise give spirit to his image and cause his image to speak, when the serpent spoke wicked words, deadly words? For through whatever image the devil may speak at that time, it is evident that the serpent which deceived the first human being was his image, especially because the human race has, as though naturally, hated that reptile kind ever since [Col. 1081D] (Gen. 3). How then will those be excusable who, deceived by such signs, worship that beast? Can they be excused on the ground of ignorance? Certainly, if they do not know—if they have not read—that such an image of the beast, namely the serpent, spoke to the first human beings, and that the devil made fire come down from heaven upon the sheep of blessed Job, they are foolish. But if they know, if they have read, and nevertheless do not guard themselves, they are stupid. Yet the Psalmist says: “Both the foolish and the stupid shall perish together” [Col. 1082A] (Ps. 48).

But if you wish to understand a handmade image, to which it will give spirit so that it may speak, because Scripture, after saying, “It deceives those dwelling on the earth because of the signs which it was given to perform in the presence of the beast,” immediately adds: “saying to those dwelling on the earth that they should make an image of the beast”—if, I say, you wish here to take “image” in the ordinary sense, like those which people can make from wood, stone, or any metal, this miracle of diabolical malice, that such an image should speak, was much more familiar. Such images spoke in temples through the skill of an evil spirit entering through open cavities before the cross of Christ was raised on high [Col. 1082B].

If, therefore, this beast by its persuasion causes men to make an image of that greater beast—for example, as Isaiah says, “The carpenter stretches out a measuring line, forms an idol with a plane, makes it with an angle-tool, rounds it with a compass, and makes it into the image of a man, like a handsome man dwelling in a house” (Isa. 44)—and if in this way that man of sin, the son of perdition, sits in the temple of God, in the place from which he has cast down the sign of Christ’s cross, will not the one who bows down and worships it be much more foolish or stupid? Certainly, as the same Prophet says, “A foolish heart shall worship it and shall not deliver itself; indeed, it shall give its soul over to perdition” (ibid.).

The true Christ performed no sign of this kind, nor ought he to have performed one [Col. 1082C]. He nowhere made fire come down from heaven before men, although Elijah had done this before his coming by Christ’s power (4 Kings 1); nor did he ever cause an image to speak, nor ought he to have done so. What use is there in signs of this kind? Indeed, when his disciples James and John said, “Lord, do you wish us to command fire to come down from heaven and consume them”—that is, the Samaritans, who did not receive him because his face was set toward Jerusalem—he turned and rebuked them, saying: “You do not know of what spirit you are. The Son of Man did not come to destroy souls but to save them” (Luke 9).

Likewise, when he was sent back by Pilate to Herod, who was greatly delighted to see him because he hoped to see some sign performed by him, he gave him no answer. He preferred to be despised and mocked by Herod rather than feed his curiosity with useless signs [Col. 1082D], since Herod was not seeking signs of mercy but miracles of vanity (Luke 23). But Christ briefly declares what signs he deigns to perform or make known, and only in a fitting cause or time. For example, speaking to John’s disciples, he says: “Go and report to John what you have seen and heard: the blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead rise, and the poor receive the Gospel” (Matt. 13).

The adversary of piety will not be a worker of such merciful signs—namely, “the beast which has the wound of the sword and lived”—nor will the other beast, its prophet, do them, just as its two horns, Jannes and Mambres, of whom we spoke above, did not [Col. 1083A]. For they could not even follow or imitate the signs of Moses which were beneficially performed at that time; they failed, and their folly became manifest to all. The wound of the sword which the beast bears has already been discussed above. It follows:

“And it will cause all who have not worshipped the image of the beast to be killed.” Christ did not do this; neither did his prophets nor his apostles teach it; nor did Christian kings, once converted, receive this command—that they should kill and suppose Christ’s service must be heaped up with blood. For the true God desires service freely rendered, not compelled (2 Cor. 9). Thus, in this especially—indeed, above all in this—it will openly show those who possess understanding and reason that it truly is Antichrist, truly not Christ but, according to its name, opposed to Christ [Col. 1083B]. This is Christ, who shed his own blood; this is Antichrist, who shed another’s blood.

“And it will cause all, small and great, rich and poor, free and slave, to receive a mark on their right hand or on their foreheads, and that no one may buy or sell except one who has the mark, or the name of the beast, or the number of its name.” This is that perverse imitation; in this respect it is dissimilarly like the Most High. For the Most High “will cause all, small and great, rich and poor, free and slave,” without distinction of persons or origins—Jews or Greeks—all alike, I say, to receive his mark on their foreheads and in their hand [Col. 1083C], alike through the authority of Law and Gospel.

For in the Law he says: “The words which I command you, you shall meditate upon while sitting in your house, while walking on the road, while sleeping and rising; and you shall bind them as a sign upon your hand” (Deut. 6). But in the Gospel he says: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28). For when all are baptized, whether small or great, they receive on their foreheads the mark of Christ’s name, that is, the seal of the cross, and the number of the Lord’s name: the number of the three persons, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

They also receive this number in order to confess the one Christ: for Christ is not merely man or merely God, but both God [Col. 1083D] and man, subsisting in one person from a rational soul and human flesh and the divinity of the Word. The false prophets will endeavour to remove this number from the foreheads, hearts, and mouths of all, so that, conversely, the mark of the beast’s name and the number of its name may be inscribed.

“Here is wisdom. Let him who has understanding calculate the number of the beast. For it is the number of a man, and its number is six hundred and sixty-six.” He wishes the hearer to be alert when, as if pointing with his finger to the place and looking about him, he says: “Here is wisdom.” Then immediately: “If anyone has wisdom, let him calculate the number of the beast.” What number, or why should he calculate the beast’s number? “For,” he says, “it is the number of a man, and its number is six hundred and sixty-six.” What is this—that he himself specifies the number and yet says [Col. 1084A], “Let him who has wisdom calculate the number of the beast”? Does he mean that, calculating wisely, you should investigate how many units or perhaps tens are in this number? Who possessing wisdom would seek, or propose for inquiry, something so plainly written? Therefore, since no one is summoned here to calculate except one who has wisdom, perhaps there is a problem contained in the number.

Indeed, illustrious interpreters of this Scripture before us, diligently considering this number, have noticed certain names: three Greek and one Gothic—ΑΝΤΕΜΟΣ, ΑΡΝΟΥΜΕ, ΤΕΙΤΑΝ, ΓΕΝΣ ΗΡΙΚΟΣ. The first is interpreted “opposed to honour”; the second, “I deny”; the third, “sun”; the fourth, “deceiver of nations.” The letters of each of these names contain the number six hundred and sixty-six.

For the first letter of the name ΑΝΤΕΜΟΣ, Α, signifies one; Ν, fifty; Τ, three hundred; short Ε, five; Μ, forty; short Ο, seventy; and Σ, two hundred. Likewise in the other name, ΑΡΝΟΥΜΕ: Α signifies one, Ρ one hundred, Ν fifty, short Ο seventy, Υ four hundred, Μ forty, short Ε five; together these make six hundred and sixty-six [Col. 1084B]. In the name ΤΕΙΤΑΝ, Τ signifies three hundred, short Ε five, Ι ten; again Τ three hundred, Α one, Ν fifty; joined together, these make six hundred and sixty-six. Finally, the Gothic name written in Greek letters is ΓΕΝΣ ΗΡΙΚΟΣ: Γ signifies three, Ε five, Ν fifty, Σ two hundred, Η eight, Ρ one hundred, Ι ten, Κ twenty, Ο seventy, and Σ two hundred [Col. 1084C].

This examination by the Fathers deserves praise; nevertheless, something still remains to be investigated with care. Will that beast wish to be called by such names, addressed by such terms? Will it reward with its favour those by whom it is called “opposed to honour” or “deceiver of nations,” so that they may be able to buy or sell? For this is what you have here: that no one might be able to buy or sell unless he has the mark, the name of the beast, or the number of its name. Will it command that it be called “the adversary,” which is Satan, or ΑΝΤΕΜΟΣ; or “denier,” or “deceiver of nations,” and that the one who pronounces this should be free and able to buy or sell? Or will it be content with the giant’s name ΤΕΙΤΑΝ [Col. 1084D], when it exalts itself above all that is called God or worshipped, showing itself as though it were God?

Among us, DICLVX is written, containing the same number. For D signifies five hundred, I one, C one hundred, L fifty, V five, X ten; gathered together, these likewise make six hundred and sixty-six. But even if Scripture in this place openly ascribed that name to it, and said that the number of this man was six hundred and sixty-six, would there not still remain an inquiry into what relation this number had to that man?

Therefore, since this number is given here, and yet wisdom is required for calculating it—“If anyone has understanding, let him calculate the number [Col. 1085A] of the beast”—let us seek wisdom and consult Holy Scripture, without which we can find or say nothing firm or certain either concerning the number of God or concerning the number of the beast which exalts itself against God. For just as Samson could truly say: “If you had not ploughed with my heifer, you would not have found my riddle” (Judg. 14), so our Lord Jesus Christ, whose riddles or problems are all the profound mysteries contained in this book, may truly say to us: If you have not ploughed in the other Scripture, you will not find the solution of this number which the present Scripture has marked.

First, it must carefully be observed that when it first said that no one might be able to buy or sell unless he had the mark or the name of the beast or the number, it significantly added “of its name”; but afterward, when it says, “If anyone has wisdom, let him calculate the number,” it makes no mention of the name, but only says, “Let him calculate the number of the beast”; and then, “its number,” without inserting “name,” it says, “is six hundred and sixty-six” [Col. 1085B].

Why this, unless the beast’s name means one thing and the beast itself another? For the beast itself is a human being, and the devil dwells within him; but its name—the name it arrogates to itself, which no one can refuse to confess and still buy or sell—is God. For it opposes and exalts itself, as has often been said, “above all that is called God or worshipped, so that it sits in the temple of God, showing itself as though it were God” [Col. 1085C] (2 Thess. 2).

Thus two numbers must be understood here: one, the number of its name, which that beast arrogates to itself, namely God; the other, the number of the beast—that is, of the human being which it will be. For the number of God is one thing and that of man another; indeed, the number of every rational creature which does not attain the grace of the Creator, whether human or angelic, is another. The Creator and creature ought to have had one number, but the creature chose another number for itself by dissenting from the Creator.

What is the Creator’s number? The number seven, as Scripture says: “God completed on the seventh day his work which he had made, and rested from all his work which he had accomplished. And God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it, because on it he had ceased from all his work which God created to make” [Col. 1085D] (Gen. 2). What, then, is the creature’s number? The number six, because Scripture comprehends the entire creation in the six days, and on the sixth day—indeed, the sixth day itself is the creature of man.

Man was created for this purpose: that, after the work of obedience had been completed, he might keep Sabbath with God on the seventh day—that is, rest—and thereby be completed in the good signified by the words, “God completed on the seventh day his work which he had made.” For the seventh day signifies the reward of good work, as the Apostle also testifies when he says: “For we who believe shall enter into rest, as he said: ‘As I swore in my wrath, they shall not enter into my rest’” (Ps. 94).

And after works had been completed from the foundation of the world, he said somewhere concerning the seventh day: “God rested on the seventh day from all his works” [Col. 1086A] (Gen. 2), and again in this passage: “They shall not enter into my rest.” “Since, therefore, it remains for some to enter into it, and those to whom it was first proclaimed did not enter because of unbelief, again he appoints a certain day, ‘Today,’ speaking in David after so long a time, as has been said above: ‘Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts’” (Heb. 4; Ps. 94), and so forth.

Man was created, I say, to enter into that rest of the day, to keep Sabbath with God in the Sabbath-rest of that number seven. Yet neither man then entered nor will the devil, who deceived him, ever enter. For both wished to glory apart from God—indeed, against God—in the creation of the world and in themselves.

Therefore he says: “For it is the number of a man.” But he had first said: “If anyone has wisdom, let him calculate the number of the beast.” It is as though he said: If anyone has wisdom, when he sees that man of sin, the son of perdition, powerful and rich, exalting himself, killing those who resist him, and glorying magnificently in everything, let him consider and reflect that whatever he says and whatever he does does not belong to that rest, is not of that seventh day of the Creator, of the Word of God, or of the kingdom of charity, but is all concerned only with the creation of the world, with the lust of the eyes [Col. 1086B] (1 John 2), and with the pride of life. Therefore, as though confirmed by a certain proof, let him know and say that that man is not what he claims to be: he is not God, but falsely presents himself as though he were God.

When, therefore, he said, “For it is the number of a man,” the simple or single six may be understood, if that man were only a human being and not also the devil. But that man will indeed be human by nature; yet the devil, with all his power and his whole fullness, will be wholly in him. And the coming of that man, as the Apostle says, will be according to the working of Satan (2 Thess. 2). Therefore it follows: “And its number is six hundred and sixty-six.”

Behold, the number six is repeated three times—indeed, multiplied tenfold and then a hundredfold. What we say is very well known to arithmeticians and abacus-calculators: the numeral six, passing from the first or unit place to the second, the tens place [Col. 1086C], makes sixty; and carried into the third, the hundreds place, makes six hundred. When, then, it says, “And its number is six hundred and sixty-six,” the six which was the number of man—as has been said, of man not reaching the seventh day, the Sabbath, that is, the rest of God, because of his transgression—is multiplied by passing into the second and third places.

What does this mean except that the devil Satan, according to whose working that man will come and who will dwell wholly within him, after once casting himself out from the rest of God and from the heavenly Sabbath-rest, has multiplied his labour a second and third time? Let us note again where, when, and how the ancient transgressor, the laborious multiplier, thus multiplied his number.

First: when heaven and earth and all their adornment had been completed, and “on the seventh day God completed his work which he had made and rested from all the work which he had accomplished” [Col. 1087A] (Gen. 2), he did not rest with the Creator resting on his seventh day. Rather, already long before, because of the restlessness of his pride, he had been cast from heaven into this dark air; the wicked one walked about in a circuit and laboured (Ps. 11). Thus he was in the number six, in this six-day creation. In this six, the penitent man, grieving that he is held there and sighing for the seventh day, says in the Psalm: “Make known to me, Lord, my end and what is the number of my days, that I may know what I lack” (Ps. 38).

But that wicked and transgressing angel did not do so. Though outside the rest or seventh day, and though his six was still simple or single, he was not content with his own labour, but through envy added to it by drawing the human race with him into the same labour, deceiving the first-formed human being. In doing this he increased his transgression, and rightly the labour of man, as well as his own, is charged to him. Therefore his first six was multiplied, and his number became sixty-six [Col. 1087B].

Yet not even with this content, he will further add that he may wholly enter that man of sin, the son of perdition, and through him do what we now wonder at in this passage concerning the evil beast. There, by the third transgression, his six will be multiplied: when the one who first deceived humankind by fraud without force will employ both fraud in lying wonders and force, or the sword, openly an enemy of God and men, persisting in the envy by which he brought death into the world, and persisting also in the pride—indeed, a pride increased for the worse—by which he exalted himself in heaven against God.

Rightly, then, after saying, “For it is the number of a man,” he added: “And its number is six hundred and sixty-six,” because the labour of sin, which is simple in a human being who does not keep Sabbath with God, is increased a second and third time in that beast by marked increments [Col. 1087C].

With these points observed, no one should think it irrelevant that this Scripture mentions its mortal wound three times. First, when it says: “And I saw one of its heads as though slain unto death, and its mortal wound was healed.” Second, when it says: “And it caused the earth and those dwelling in it to worship the first beast, whose mortal wound had been healed.” Third, when it says: “That they should make an image of the beast which has the wound of the sword and lived.”

For that evil one was wounded three times. First, when, judged in heaven, he received the sentence of condemnation (Isa. 14). Second, when, in the serpent through which he deceived humankind, he was punished by a curse (Gen. 1). Third, when the Lord Jesus will slay him with the breath of his mouth and destroy him by the brightness of his coming (Luke 10). This is the true number of the beast: six hundred and sixty-six [Col. 1088A].

But the number of its name, without which no one may buy or sell, is as falsely attributed to it as the very name in which it boasts, showing itself as though it were God (2 Thess. 2). For the number seven belongs to God and to the Lamb: to God, I say, who rested on the seventh day (Gen. 2), and to the Lamb, whose seven horns and seven eyes are in this very book. Thus the beast’s display of seven heads is violent and contrary. In opposition to God’s resting on the seventh day, its seventh head has a mortal wound, a wound of the sword; it does not rest but always labours and lives in labour, as the Psalmist says: “And he shall labour for ever, and shall yet live unto the end” [Col. 1088B] (Ps. 48).

Therefore also, as has been said above, there are names of blasphemy upon its seven heads, because its name is not God, although it has inscribed that name upon its heads, as we mentioned there (Rev. 5). And if that is not its name, then certainly neither is it the number of its name. This is the number of its merit, and it is truly attributed to it, as has been said: “six hundred and sixty-six.” It never reaches the seventh, because it has never repented and never will repent, so that it might rest [Col. 1088C].

## Book Nine

[Col. 1087]

## Chapter XIV

[Col. 1087D]

“And I saw, and behold, the Lamb stood upon Mount Zion, and with him one hundred and forty-four thousand having his name and the name of his Father written upon their foreheads.”

Where now shall we go, whither shall we direct the course of our discourse? The bright order of the seven spirits of the Lord clearly shows us, as we proposed to follow it; without it, we judged that we could see nothing and could nowhere keep to a straight path. For it is not without purpose that this John, at the beginning of the book, writes grace and peace from the seven spirits who are before the throne of God to the seven churches. Now in the order of these same spirits, according to Isaiah’s prophetic proclamation, the fifth is the spirit of knowledge [Col. 1088D] (Isa. XI), following that spirit of fortitude whose great works we beheld in the preceding vision—namely, in the battles of the martyrs. The highest or final contest of those battles will be that which the first beast itself shall wage, whose number we calculated a little earlier. This beast, undoubtedly, will be Antichrist, who is to be revealed in his own time.

Therefore, we do not know where we are now going; but this bright order of the spirits, as has been said, leads us to perceive that a recapitulation takes place here, and to contemplate from this point the deeds which the holy Spirit of knowledge performed in this world [Col. 1089A], where the Lamb is seen standing upon Mount Zion. For where the knowledge of God first began to be given or written down, there too Christ, the Lamb of God, began to be prefigured. Indeed, where Moses, the first writer of God’s knowledge, wrote the Law, there a lamb began to be sacrificed as a type of Christ; and the doorposts of the children of Israel were marked with its blood (Exod. XII).

Accordingly, in these one hundred and forty-four thousand, singing as it were a new song before the throne, before the four living creatures and the elders; in the four angels flying through the midst of heaven and having the everlasting Gospel, the fourth of whom is John himself, who said: “And I heard a voice from heaven saying: Write: Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord!”; and in the seven bowls of the seven angels—in these, I say, we understand all the builders or writers of heavenly knowledge, that is, of holy Scripture [Col. 1089B], and in accordance with them or with their labours we begin to proclaim the wondrous holy Spirit of knowledge.

“And I saw,” he says, “and behold, the Lamb stood upon Mount Zion.” This vision carries John’s eye back from the end of the ages, where shortly before he had seen the beast, or the malignant head of the beast, Antichrist, struck down by the sword of eternal condemnation, upward to the beginnings of the ages: namely, to the times of the patriarchs’ promise or faith, from which all these recapitulations run and return.

Certainly this Lamb is Christ, who now indeed stands in his own person upon Mount Zion, above [Col. 1089C] every dignity of the Church, above every principality and all the powers of heaven. But when the promise was being made, or had recently been made, he stood in a figure, as has already been said: when, or from the time when, the lamb was sacrificed in the houses of the children of Israel (ibid.). Once their doorposts had been marked with its blood, while its flesh was eaten, the firstborn of the Egyptians died; the children of Israel passed through the Red Sea; and Pharaoh, pursuing them with his chariots and horsemen, was drowned.

This Lamb wrote his own name and the name of his Father upon our foreheads with the seal of the cross. But then blood was taken from the lamb which was at the threshold, and put upon the lintel and upon both doorposts (ibid.). In this arrangement there was, indeed, a divine foreshadowing or mystery of the cross [Col. 1089D], which would profit them in the fullness of time, in the time of blessing, when the true Lamb, Christ, the seed of Abraham, “in whom all nations were to be blessed” (Gen. XXII), was to be sacrificed upon the altar of the cross.

“I saw these standing with the Lamb,” because all who were signified according to Abraham’s faith or God’s promise were blessed by that blood with Christ and live with him. But what does this number of theirs, one hundred and forty-four thousand, mean? It indicates to us, surely, that the children of Israel, or children of Abraham, who were to be saved through the Christ to come, had to be children not merely of flesh, but of faith or promise. “For,” says the Apostle, “not all who are of [Col. 1090A] Israel are Israelites; nor are all who are Abraham’s seed children; but ‘In Isaac shall thy seed be called’: that is, not the children of the flesh are the children of God, but the children of the promise are reckoned as the seed” (Rom. IX).

The fullness of this number mystically signifies this faith together with Abraham’s works. For the number of the first children of Israel according to the flesh—namely, twelve—if multiplied tenfold once, twice, and a third time, produces twelve thousand, as calculators know. Again, if twelve thousand are multiplied by the same number twelve, the result is one hundred and forty-four thousand.

It is pleasing to explain this still more plainly. Twelve, the number, as has been said, of the first children of Israel, multiplied tenfold become one hundred and twenty. Again, one hundred and twenty multiplied tenfold [Col. 1090B] become one thousand two hundred. Again, one thousand two hundred multiplied tenfold become, as has already been said elsewhere, twelve thousand sealed ones. This threefold multiplication by ten fittingly suggests to us faith in the holy Trinity, with whose mystical confession those men marked their houses, confessing the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob (Exod. III).

But since faith alone, without works, is insufficient for perfection or life, let the twelve thousand again be multiplied by twelve and become one hundred and forty-four thousand: by this number both the confession of faith and the abundance of good works are signified. Therefore, all those holy persons standing with the Lamb, “having the name of the same Lamb and the name of his Father written upon their foreheads,” are the perfect children of Abraham from that time when Christ, who was to suffer for the whole world, was being prefigured by the annual sacrifice of the paschal lamb. The present passage immediately commends their perfection magnificently and wonderfully. For it continues:

“And I heard a voice from heaven, as the voice of many waters and as the voice of great thunder; and the voice which I heard was like that of harpists playing upon their harps. And they sang as it were a new song before the throne, and before the four living creatures and the elders; and no one could sing the song except those one hundred and forty-four thousand who were purchased from the earth. These are they who were not defiled with women, for they are virgins. These follow [Col. 1090D] the Lamb wherever he goes. These were purchased from among human beings as firstfruits to God and to the Lamb; and no lie was found in their mouth. They are without blemish before the throne of God.”

First, concerning this passage, the subject requires us to set forth beforehand this point: when he had said, “And no one could sing the song except those one hundred and forty-four thousand who were purchased from the earth,” he immediately answers, as though questioned concerning what merit made them alone capable of singing such a song: “These,” he says, “are they who were not defiled with women, for they are virgins.”

This praise may certainly, and not unprofitably, be understood of bodily virginity. For that sweet purpose of virginal beauty [Col. 1091A], in which one may think of the things of the Lord (I Cor. VII), has great power to exhort, strengthen, and confirm. Bodily virginity joined to virginity of mind truly possesses a great prerogative.

Nevertheless, in order to maintain the proposed order, something else must also be said, against which no authority or reasoning from Scripture can be shown to object. For no one would lightly dare to attribute so much to bodily virginity as to judge that some song, to be sung by holy virgins, would be impossible for all others to sing, however great they may be—for example, the apostle Peter in the New Testament, and Moses in the Old—of whom it is certain that, according to the flesh, they did not embrace a virginal calling. Having briefly set these things forth, let us now pursue the order.

“And I heard,” he says, “a voice from heaven, like [Col. 1091B] the voice of many waters and the voice of great thunder.” When the Lamb stood upon Mount Zion with his sealed ones, a voice from heaven began to be heard like the sound of many waters and like the sound of great thunder. That is, when the Passion of Christ the Son of God began to be prefigured through the typical sacrifice of the paschal lamb in Egypt, the voice of God also began to be heard through Scripture. For then Moses wrote the Law, which he received not from earth but from heaven, not from a human being but from God.

After him the other righteous persons and prophets wrote the knowledge of God, and they too spoke not from earth but from heaven. Hence the saying: “For holy Scripture was not at any time brought by human will, but holy men of God spoke, inspired by the Holy Spirit” (II Pet. [Col. 1091C] I).

“I heard therefore,” he says, “a voice from heaven.” Holy Scriptures are sometimes signified by the name of waters, as in: “All you who thirst, come to the waters” (Isa. LV). They are likewise compared to thunder, namely because of the terrible threat of future judgment, according to: “And the Lord thundered from heaven, and the Most High uttered his voice” (Ps. XVII). The first judgment has indeed already been made through water; but those same Scriptures, as though sounding together in thunder beforehand, testify that the second will come through fire (Gen. VII; Isa. LXVI). Rightly, therefore, he calls that voice—the voice of the heavenly Scriptures—“like the voice of many waters” and “like [Col. 1091D] the voice of great thunder.”

Yet that voice proclaims not only judgment and the punishments of the wicked, but also mercy and the everlasting rewards of the saints, things which are sweet and delightful to hear or understand. It follows, therefore:

“And the voice which I heard was like that of harpists playing upon their harps.” For just as the harshness of terror is in thunder, while sweetness of delight is in sounding harps, so in the holy Scriptures the threat of judgment terrifies and beneficially disturbs sinners, while the promise of rewards soothes and gladdens those who do good.

It should be noted that the sounding strings of harps delight those who hear them, but they themselves are, as it were, strained in their stretching. Thus those through whom holy Scripture was composed delighted good hearers in their respective times by promising good things; but they themselves laboured inwardly and were often worn out. [Col. 1092A] Hence Moses, the first of them, said to the Lord: “Why hast thou afflicted thy servant? Why have I not found grace before thee? Why hast thou laid the burden of this entire people upon me?” And afterward: “But if it seems otherwise to thee, I beseech thee, kill me, that I may find favour in thy eyes and not be afflicted by such great evils” (Num. XI).

Moreover, those holy people were wearied in many different ways, as the Apostle, remembering them, says among other things: “Others experienced mockings and scourges, and moreover bonds and prisons; they were stoned, sawn asunder, tempted, died by the slaughter of the sword. They wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins, destitute, oppressed, afflicted” (Heb. XI), [Col. 1092B] and so forth. Therefore they were like harpists playing upon their harps, because while they gave voice to the testimonies of truth, they were stretched by many tribulations.

They also afflicted themselves by voluntary restraint, so that they might deserve to receive the grace of the heavenly song of blessedness. Thus we read of Daniel and his companions that, when royal food was set before them, they chose rather, for God’s sake, to eat vegetables. “And God gave these youths knowledge and instruction in every book and wisdom; but to Daniel he gave understanding of all visions and dreams” (Dan. IV).

It follows, therefore:

“And they sang as it were a new song before the throne, and before the four living creatures and the elders.” They played and sang: that is, they afflicted themselves and gave voice to God’s glory. But what does it mean that he did not say, “They sang a new song,” but “as it were a new song”? What is a new song? Once this is known, what “as it were a new song” means will immediately become clear.

The New Song is the New Testament, in which we have put off the old human being and put on the new (Eph. IV); in which, renewed, we have escaped the likeness of our earthly parent [Col. 1092C] (I Cor. XIV), and have been transformed into the form of our heavenly Maker. The Old Testament, however, is as it were a new song, because by certain likenesses and many figures it signifies the same things contained in the New Testament.

They therefore sang “as it were a new song”: that is, by the wonderful power of the prophetic Spirit they foresaw the mystery of evangelical grace. In accordance with this pattern they performed and taught the ministry of the Law, and through fitting figures declared that Christ, the Lamb of God, would suffer for the salvation of the world and would renew the world by his Passion (II Pet. I). Thus “they sang before the throne and before the four living creatures”: that is, in preparation for the kingdom of God, in service to Christ’s Gospel, for the instruction of those whose venerable old age—that is, whose blameless life—governs the Church of God. For it follows:

“And no one could sing the song except those one hundred and forty-four thousand who were purchased from the earth.” Why could no one else sing it? Because such a song was never brought by human will; rather, the singers, that is, the authors of the Scriptures, sang while inspired by the Holy Spirit [Col. 1093A]. And for what merit of theirs could they sing that song? He says: “These are they who were not defiled with women, for they are virgins.”

How, or with what women, were they not defiled? Surely with foreign women, concerning whom the Lord had commanded the children of Israel, saying: “You shall not go in to them, nor shall any of them go in to yours. For most certainly they will turn away your hearts, so that you follow their gods” (III Kings XI; Deut. VII). Is not this a great reason why the song of the Lamb is rightly taken from the mouths of all who are defiled with women of this kind? For along with bodily defilement, their souls also committed fornication with demons because of their love [Col. 1093B] for women (Num. XXV).

First, because of these women, “they were initiated into Baal-peor” (Ps. CV); and, as it is written, “the stain of this crime remains among them to the present day” (Josh. XXII). Then defilements with such women multiplied; and the most impious Jezebel holds the foremost place among them all (III Kings XVI). “Who has bound such fire in his bosom, and his garments have not been burned?” (Prov. VI). Solomon too, though most wise, did not escape unburned, because he joined himself to such women with most ardent love (III Kings XI). For his heart was corrupted by them when he was already old, and he went and served their gods and goddesses.

Therefore let it be said as the highest praise: “These are they who were not defiled with women; [Col. 1093C] they remained virgins.” For they alone were able to present themselves as a chaste virgin to the true God, and to escape the corrupters of the nations, who are not gods but demons: they who kept themselves undefiled by the women belonging to those corrupters (II Cor. XI).

Such virgins laid up for themselves a good song, while, clinging to their one husband, their one God, they conceived a good word in their minds from his breast, uttered it with their mouths, and some of them also wrote it down with a pen for us to read.

“These,” he says, “were purchased from the earth.” Again: “These follow the Lamb wherever he goes.” And again: “These were purchased from among human beings as firstfruits to God and to the Lamb.” These four splendid statements must be considered in their order with watchful and open eyes, since they are proclamations, most pure, of grace, merit, and reward [Col. 1093D]. It is especially to be noted that the first and fourth proclaim grace, the second commends merit, and the third reward. The first says, “They were purchased from the earth”; the fourth, “These were purchased from among human beings as firstfruits to God and to the Lamb.” Both proclaim the same thing: the grace of the Redeemer.

Who can be unaware that these same saints had been children of wrath and were redeemed through grace? One from that people, Saint and great Paul, says: “For we too were by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Eph. II). Thus, after the proclamation of grace has been made, merit is at last stated: “These are they who were not defiled with women, for they are virgins.” And rightly so. For each of them says, and ought to say: “I laboured and was diligent not to be defiled—yet not I, but the grace of God with me” (I Cor. XV).

The reward immediately follows: “These follow the Lamb wherever he goes” [Col. 1094A]. They follow the Lamb, namely their purchaser or Redeemer, by whose blood they were redeemed. Hence the apostle Peter says: “You were redeemed from your vain manner of life handed down from your fathers, with precious blood, as of Christ, an undefiled and spotless Lamb” (I Pet. I).

The repetition, “These were purchased from among human beings,” indicates great emphasis, lest we forget that they are what they are by the Redeemer’s grace (I Cor. XV). For “from the earth” and “from among human beings” are the same, as if he had said: from the earthly mass of humankind, which as a whole sold itself under sin in the first parent [Col. 1094B].

Further, it should be noted that when he had said, “These follow the Lamb,” he added, “wherever he goes.” Does the Lamb, then, necessarily go from place to place to arrange the affairs of his kingdom, taking some into his retinue while making himself absent from others? But, setting aside any such changeability, they “follow the Lamb wherever he goes” in two ways: by investigating his judgments contained in the sacred Scriptures, concerning which one of these saints says, “With my lips I have declared all the judgments of thy mouth” (Ps. CXVIII); and by imitating his examples, concerning which likewise one of them says, “I have kept thy ways and have not departed from his commandments” (Job XXIII).

They therefore follow the Lamb wherever he goes while they understand his judgments through the Spirit, praise them through charity, and justify him in all those judgments; and while they imitate the example of his love unto death, as John says: “Because he laid down his life for us, we too ought to lay down our lives for the brethren” (I John III).
