This too must not be passed over: when he had said, “These were purchased from among human beings,” he added, “as firstfruits to God and to the Lamb.” For this also makes clear that the earlier saints are meant, concerning whom the holy and mystical Law says: “If you offer a gift of the firstfruits of your crops to the Lord, from ears still green, you shall parch them with fire, crush them in the manner of grain, and thus offer your firstfruits to the Lord, pouring oil over them and putting incense upon them” (Lev. II).

The earlier holy people of the age were ears still green [Col. 1094D], from whom we then offer a gift to the Lord when we resolve to live well after their example. Yet in their actions some things are found that were then allowed but are now cut off by the sickle of the Gospel in its more mature age. Thus afterward it is said to the Son of Man seated upon the cloud: “Send forth thy sharp sickle, for the hour to reap has come, because the harvest of the earth is dry” (Rev. XIV).

Therefore parch them with fire: that is, by the holy Spirit of discernment, distinguishing the condition of the two ages, you will neither condemn nor imitate things which you have learned are not to be imitated under the Gospel. And thus you will offer them with the application of oil and incense: that is, you will imitate their good deeds in charity for the honour of God [Col. 1095A].

Therefore, “these were purchased from among human beings as firstfruits to God and to the Lamb.” This is as though he said: Christ, the Lamb of God, redeemed these from the mass of the human race, having found them approved by the testimony of faith in the earlier age, still recent. He next speaks of this testimony of faith: “And no lie was found in their mouth.” For they were faithful; they did not worship falsehood, but the one living and true God.

Elijah believed that none of such people remained except himself alone, and said: “Lord, they have killed thy prophets, dug down thy altars, and I alone am left; and they seek my life” (III Kings XIX). “I have left,” says the Lord, “seven thousand men who have not bent the knee before Baal” (ibid.). Thus, because they were not defiled with the women mentioned above, and did not utter the lie of their gods, “They are without blemish,” he says, “before the throne of God [Col. 1095B].”

“And I saw another angel flying through the midst of heaven [Latin *coeli*, ‘of heaven’], having the everlasting Gospel, that he might preach the Gospel to those dwelling upon the earth, and to every nation and tribe and language and people, saying with a loud voice: Fear the Lord and give him honour, because the hour of his judgment has come; and worship him who made heaven and earth and sea and all things that are in them and the springs of waters. And another angel followed, saying: Fallen, fallen is that great Babylon, which has made all nations drink of the wine of the wrath of her fornication. And the third angel followed them, saying with a loud voice: If anyone worships the beast and its image, and receives its mark upon [Col. 1095C] his forehead or upon his hand, he too shall drink of the wine of God’s wrath, mingled with pure wine in the cup of his wrath, and shall be tormented with fire and sulphur in the presence of the holy angels and before the presence of the Lamb; and the smoke of their torments shall ascend for ages of ages; and they have no rest day or night, those who worship the beast and its image, and anyone who receives the mark of its name. Here is the patience of the saints, who keep the commandments of God and the faith of Jesus. And I heard a voice from heaven saying to me: Write: Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord! From henceforth, the Spirit says, let them rest from their labours; for their works follow them.”

[Col. 1095D] After the song of the one Mount Zion, these four do not stand upon any one mountain or place, but fly through the midst of heaven and proclaim to the whole world with a loud and public voice. The fourth is John himself, who, thinking more humbly of himself, did not say, “A fourth followed the three others flying through the midst of heaven,” but: “I heard,” he says, “a voice from heaven saying to me: Write: Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord!” For just as he had said, “I saw an angel flying through the midst of heaven, preaching the Gospel, saying: Fear the Lord”; and another followed him, saying, “Fallen, fallen is Babylon”; and a third followed them, saying, “If anyone worships the beast,” and the rest—so he could have said: “And I, the fourth, was following them, saying: Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord.”

But he rightly preferred to speak thus, both to report more humbly of himself [Col. 1096A] and to express the matter somewhat. For by these evangelists, or those having the everlasting Gospel, among whom he puts himself in the fourth place, the four Evangelists are now to be understood. He himself is the fourth, because he wrote the Gospel last.

Meanwhile, it must be remembered that we said above, in view of the order of the seven spirits before God’s throne, that under the images of this present vision the proper works or gifts of the Spirit of knowledge are proclaimed. Whatever grace had been given before Christ’s coming, whatever heavenly knowledge was in the Law and the prophets, was celebrated on only one Mount Zion, in only one temple, which was in Jerusalem; for there alone were the holy things of that people.

[Col. 1096B] But when Christ came, his Gospel immediately sounded publicly throughout the world, joined to the Law and the prophets; and then the knowledge of God was multiplied, fulfilling what Daniel foretold: “Many shall pass through, and knowledge shall be multiplied” (Dan. XII). Rightly, therefore, according to these visions, the song was first heard only upon Mount Zion; but these four angels fly through the midst of heaven preaching the Gospel. For the Law and prophets first sounded in the narrow place of one nation, whereas now, as the apostles preach Christ’s Gospel with the testimony of the Law and prophets, the whole world has heard, because “their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the world” (Ps. XVIII).

Moreover, scarcely anyone doubts that preachers of the Gospel, or any holy priests, are rightly called angels, since it is written: “The lips of the priest preserve knowledge, and they seek the Law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. II). The Lamb himself, from whose mouth all the Law is undoubtedly sought and ought to be sought, is called the Angel of Great Counsel. “Angel” is the name not of a nature but of an office; it is a Greek word, which in Latin we call *nuntius*, “messenger.” [Col. 1096C] Therefore, after saying above, “And I saw, and behold, the Lamb stood upon Mount Zion,” he now says, “And I saw another angel flying through the midst of heaven.”

Let us now examine the individual statements and consider together whether each speaks according to its own face. Their faces and the order in which they were earlier designated in this Apocalypse are well known. [Col. 1096D] For the first living creature is like a lion, the second like a calf, the third has a face as of a human being, and the fourth is like a flying eagle. We have said something in its place concerning the difference of this order from that written in Ezekiel (Ezek. I).

Certainly, what he now says of the first—“flying through the midst of heaven, having the everlasting Gospel, to preach the Gospel to those sitting upon the earth and to every nation and tribe and language and people”—must likewise be understood concerning the other who followed him, the third who followed them, and the fourth who expresses his own person.

First, his statement, “flying through the midst of heaven,” is almost opposed to the preceding statement, where he said that “one hundred and forty-four [Col. 1097A] singing as it were a new song” stood with the Lamb upon Mount Zion. Those who sang stood upon one Mount Zion, but these and the others who followed flew through the midst of heaven. That is to say: before the Lamb of God suffered in himself, while an irrational lamb was still sacrificed as his figure, the knowledge or understanding of God existed only in Zion or Judaea. But once he suffered, that knowledge immediately flew to all nations, in that flight of which the prophet, after saying, “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob; and he will teach us his ways, and we will walk in his paths,” added: “For from Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isa. II).

It was flying, therefore: that is, going out from one nation to the entire world, through the midst of heaven—that is, in the hearing of all. The word of God was no longer confined to one language as before, but expanded into all languages, especially Greek and Latin, just as Pilate wrote this title above the head of that same Lamb upon the cross in Greek, Latin, and Hebrew: “Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews” (John XIX).

This flight through the midst of heaven also signifies the freedom of those who preach the Gospel. Nothing that they proclaim has been done in a corner, nor is there anything to be ashamed of. Hence the Lord himself says: “What I tell you in darkness, speak in the light; and what you hear in the ear, preach upon the housetops” (Matt. X). Hence Paul says: “I am debtor to Greeks and barbarians, to wise and foolish alike. Thus, so far as lies in me [Col. 1097C], I am ready to preach the Gospel to you also who are at Rome. For I am not ashamed of the Gospel; for it is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek. For in it the righteousness of God is revealed from faith unto faith, as it is written (Hab. II): ‘But the righteous lives by faith.’ For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of people who hold the truth of God in unrighteousness” (Rom. I).

Thus, “flying through the midst of heaven” means having one’s heart set on things above, proceeding publicly with contempt for earthly things, not ashamed of one’s ministry because one does or teaches nothing shameful or weak. For this is what follows: “Having the everlasting Gospel.” It is God’s power; it is God’s truth, which cannot pass away or grow old. [Col. 1097D] “For,” he says, “heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away” (Matt. XXIV; Luke XXI).

And where or for what purpose was he flying?

“To preach the Gospel,” he says, “to those sitting upon the earth, and to every nation and tribe and language and people.” The meaning is: to preach among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem, without respect of persons, without distinction between Jews and Gentiles, tribes, languages, and peoples.

“Fear,” he says, “the Lord, and give him honour, because the hour of his judgment has come; and worship him who made heaven and earth and sea and all things that are in them, and the springs of waters.” Above in this book we recalled that the four living creatures were designated in such a way that the lion’s face is first [Col. 1098A]. For the first living creature is like a lion. The nature of a lion, moreover, strikes fear into other animals; at its roar all animal nature trembles. Hence: “The lion will roar: who will not fear?” (Amos III). And immediately: “The Lord God has spoken: who will not prophesy?” Therefore the first rightly demands fear, saying: “Fear the Lord, and give him honour.” A fitting reason for fear is given: “Because,” he says, “the hour of his judgment has come.”

This is penal fear, caused by expectation of judgment: not yet perfect wisdom, but the beginning of wisdom, as it is written: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. CX). Yet it has some justice in it, because it proceeds from faith. For unless someone believes in the judgment to come, that person [Col. 1098B] does not fear. Therefore it is useful, since it makes the sinner anxious and compels repentance. Thus, after saying, “Fear the Lord,” he immediately adds: “And give him honour.” In what way? Namely, by abandoning idols and turning to him. For it follows: “And worship him who made heaven and earth and sea and all things that are in them, and the springs of waters.”

“And another angel followed him, saying: ‘Fallen, fallen is that great Babylon, which has made all nations drink of the wine of the wrath of her fornication.’” This second angel also speaks according to his own face, the face of a calf; for the second living creature is like a calf. A calf was offered as a sacrifice for sin; its blood was brought into the sanctuary by the high priest, but its body was burned outside the camp (Lev. IV), signifying our Lord [Col. 1098C] Jesus Christ, who was offered for the sin of the human race and suffered outside the gate. Recalling this, the Apostle goes on to say: “Let us therefore go out to him outside the camp, bearing his reproach” (Heb. III).

He says, therefore: “Fallen, fallen is Babylon.” Babylon, which is interpreted “confusion,” is the kingdom of sin, the dominion of the world, and the devil’s brigandage. This was undoubtedly wholly destroyed in the elect through Christ’s Passion, as he himself, about to suffer, said: “Now is the judgment of the world; now shall the prince of this world be cast out” (John XII).

Whatever defilement, whether through force or persuasion, the city of the devil inflicted upon the city of God—from the time when Cain first built that city with bloody [Col. 1098D] hands (Gen. IV), and from the time when the sons of God, that is, those of Seth’s line, saw that the daughters of human beings were beautiful, namely those of Cain’s line, and took wives for themselves from all whom they chose (Gen. VI)—all iniquity and every sin which the elect had contracted through association with the reprobate were together blotted out by Christ’s death along with original sin. And the rulers of this world of darkness (Eph. VI) fell from their former power, so that they might not deceive the nations, and so that the nations might be free to turn to the true God, repent, and receive forgiveness of sins.

Therefore “Babylon has fallen, fallen—the Babylon which made all nations drink of the wine of the wrath of her fornication”: that is, judgment has been enacted, the prince of this world has been judged through Christ’s death [Col. 1099A], and every confusion of error has been emptied, because the intoxication of committing fornication against God caused all nations to be given over to wrath. Certainly, it is called “great” in reproach, because in pride it magnified itself.

“And a third followed them, saying in a loud voice: ‘If anyone worships the beast and its image, and receives its mark upon his forehead or upon his hand, he too shall drink of the wine of God’s wrath, mixed with unmixed wine in the cup of his wrath; and he shall be tortured with fire and sulphur before the holy angels and before the Lamb. And the smoke of his torments shall ascend for ages of ages; and those who worship the beast and its image have no rest by day or by night, nor does anyone who receives the mark of its name.’”

This third one speaks according to his face, according to the face of a man. For, he says, “the third living creature had a face like that of a man.” What, then, does he say? After the first, who had said, “Fear the Lord and worship him,” he lays down the law and prescribes the sentence for those who worship another besides that same God. For, when those who have done this are judged, the face of the man shall appear to all.

Concerning this beast and its image, its name—indeed, the number of its name—and its mark, without which no one can buy or sell in that final persecution, enough has been said above. Further, when it says, “he too shall drink,” it says this because the preceding angel had said, “Babylon has fallen, has fallen”; and for her, surely, to fall is to drink the cup of damnation. The punishment of damnation itself is called wine, or unmixed wine, with the gravest irony; for it would more properly be called the bitterest gall. In another sense, however, it is truly unmixed wine, because the judgment is just and irreproachable. There, judgment shall be altogether without mercy. For who will show mercy where even the Lamb himself will no longer remember his mercies?

It should indeed be observed that, when it had said, “he shall be tortured with fire and sulphur,” it added, “before the holy angels”; and, not content with this, it further added, “and before the Lamb.” Here it calls the Judge himself the Lamb; yet it further adds: “And the smoke of their torments shall ascend for ages of ages, and they have no rest by day or by night,” and so forth. It is great and wonderful that he who judges or punishes is himself the Lamb, and yet is—and is said to be—unyielding to mercy for ages of ages. Here a deep abyss of his judgments lies hidden from us.

Many have borne the ignorance of this depth impatiently; and, fleeing from the thought of attributing excessive severity to God, they have denied that torments will be eternal. They have not considered their own folly: while striving to make him merciful, they have not feared to make a liar of him who said: “These shall go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matt. 25). But the saints believe the truthful Scripture and nevertheless without doubt judge God to be merciful. Rather, they reckon it their own deficiency that they cannot penetrate the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God (Rom. 11), comprehend his judgments, or trace out his ways [Col. 1100A]. They bear this deficiency most patiently, knowing in part until that which is perfect comes (1 Cor. 13).

Therefore it immediately adds: “Here is the patience of the saints, who keep the commandments of God and the faith of Jesus.” “Here,” it says—that is, in the statement that they are to be tortured for ages of ages before the Lamb; in the statement that the Lamb shall be unyielding toward them in mercy for ages of ages—is the patience of the saints. They do not murmur as though at excessive severity: they keep God’s commandments, knowing that judgment is to come; they keep the faith of Jesus, not doubting that Jesus, who foretold and threatened so terrible a judgment, is faithful and true. It follows:

“And I heard a voice from heaven saying to me: Write: [Col. 1100B] Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord. From henceforth, says the Spirit, let them rest from their labours; for their works follow them.”

This fourth one hears and writes according to his face, according to the face of the flying eagle. For, he says, “the fourth living creature was like a flying eagle.” This is John, who hears and writes in the fourth place. After the other evangelists, at the request of the churches and instructed by revelations from heaven, he received the face, as has already been said, of “a flying eagle.” Beginning from the hidden height of the eternal Beginning, he wrote, beginning there, those things which are almost all laid up in the world to come—that is, in heaven. This, surely, is the end and sum of all that he wrote: “Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord,” and so forth.

[Col. 1100C] “And I saw, and behold, a white cloud, and upon the cloud one seated like the Son of Man, having upon his head a golden crown and in his hand a sharp sickle.”

He whom he had indicated above when he said, “And I saw, and behold, he stood upon Mount Zion,” he now declares more plainly that he saw, calling him “like the Son of Man.” For he who was formerly prefigured in the Law by the spotless lamb himself spoke in the Gospel, having become Son of Man and been incarnate of the Virgin Mary. That virginal flesh—the spotless flesh assumed without any stain of original sin—is here signified by the white cloud, according to the prophet who says: “Behold, the Lord ascends upon a white cloud and shall enter Egypt” (Isa. 19), that is, he shall assume flesh from the Virgin and enter this world.

For just as the sun upon a white cloud makes daylight for us but does not reveal all its brightness, gives light but withdraws its own form, does not put forth all its fires, and yet sufficiently overcomes the chill of the preceding cold night, so the most brilliant divinity, in the flesh, enlightened us by miracles and by the word of wisdom. Yet it did not reveal itself as it is. He spoke and acted as God, but did not show the form of God or exercise all his power; nevertheless, he was sufficient to overcome spiritual wickedness. Thus the likeness of the Son of Man sat upon the white cloud; indeed, even that upon which he seemed to sit was not a real cloud [Col. 1101A], but the likeness of a cloud. For he saw these things not bodily, but in the spirit.

Although this sitting of the Son of Man may rightly seem to refer to his second advent, nevertheless, if we are to maintain as far as possible the intended sequence of events, we may not inappropriately understand it of his first advent. In the Lamb standing upon Mount Zion, and in his singers, the one hundred and forty-four thousand, we have understood the typical sacrifice of the Law and the unblemished believers of that time; in the four heralds of the eternal Gospel, we have understood the Gospel chariots of this Son of Man. We must now say how, in his first advent, he used his twofold sharp sickle, according to the present chapter of this vision. For here he is said to have a sickle for reaping; and later another angel—through whom the same one is signified, the Son of Man, the Angel of Great Counsel—is said to have a sickle in his hand for gathering grapes.

“I saw,” he says, “one seated, as has already been said, like the Son of Man, having upon his head a golden crown and in his hand a sharp sickle.” For a twofold reason this Son of Man is said to have a golden crown on his head: because he is both king and priest. That the dignity of priesthood possessed a crown is attested by the Wise Man, who, in praising the fathers, says of Aaron the priest: “A golden crown upon his mitre, engraved with the sign of holiness, the glory of honour and a work of power” (Ecclus. 45 [printed 46]). He says this concerning the holy plate, on which was written the ineffable tetragrammaton—the name of the Lord of four letters.

For it signified the crown of this Son of Man, concerning whom the Psalmist, after saying, “What is man, that you are mindful of him, or the son of man, that you visit him? You have made him a little lower than the angels,” immediately added: “You have crowned him with glory and honour” (Ps. 8) [Col. 1101C]. And it signified that name of his of which the Apostle says: “Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name” (Phil. 2). Let him therefore have “upon his head a golden crown, and in his hand,” he says, “a sharp sickle”—understand, for reaping. For it follows:

“And another angel came out of the temple, crying with a loud voice to the one seated upon the cloud: Send forth your sharp sickle, because the hour has come for reaping, because the harvest of the earth is dried up. And he who sat upon the cloud sent his sickle upon the earth, and reaped the earth.”

We must therefore seek the harvest which this Son of Man reaped at his first advent. For it is certain that the harvest of which he spoke when he said, “Let both grow until the harvest; and at the time of harvest I shall say to the reapers: Gather the tares and bind them into bundles to burn; but gather the wheat into my barn” (Matt. 13)—that harvest, I say, is the end of the age. For he said: “The harvest is the consummation of the age, and the reapers are angels.” Where, then, is another harvest found?

Surely, where this same Son of Man, weary from the journey and seated by the well, seeing that the faith of the Gentiles was ready to hear, said to his disciples [Col. 1102A]: “Do you not say that there are still four months and then the harvest comes? Behold, I say to you: Lift up your eyes and see the fields, for they are already white for harvest. And he who reaps receives wages and gathers fruit unto eternal life, so that he who sows and he who reaps may rejoice together” (John 4). “I sent you to reap what you did not sow; others have laboured, and you have entered into their labours” (Luke 10).

Who are those who laboured, or who sowed, except Moses and the prophets, who foretold that Christ would come? Others entered into their labours and reaped what they had sown, because they did not see in their own time the Christ whom they prophesied, whereas the blessed eyes of the apostles saw him. Therefore, when Christ came, the time of harvest had already arrived: just as, when full grain in the ear is reaped, it is separated from dry straw, so, in receiving Christ, the life-giving spirit is separated from the killing letter.

Thus the other angel came out of the temple and cried with a loud voice: “Send forth your sharp sickle, because the hour has come for reaping, because the harvest of the earth is dried up.” The evangelical authority of the Son of Man tells us who this other angel is, when he says of his forerunner John: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet. For this is he of whom it is written: Behold, I send my Angel before your face, who shall prepare your way before you” (Matt. 11; Mal. 3). Therefore John is an angel, and is rightly called here the other angel, because this Son of Man, to whom he cries out and whose herald or forerunner he is, is also called an angel—as does the prophet in whom the passage concerning John is written, immediately saying: “And at once the ruler whom you seek, and the Angel of the covenant whom you desire, shall come to his holy temple.”

This other angel came out of the temple—indeed, out of the shadowy priesthood of that handmade temple. For his father Zechariah was a priest, and by the Law a priest’s son ought by right to succeed his priestly father. But he departed: he went into the wilderness and preferred a leather belt and camel hair to the splendid vestments of that priesthood. There he went to cry with a loud voice, to pray with great longing that he might be worthy to see and show to the world him whom, while enclosed in the womb, he had greeted by leaping for joy [Col. 1102D]. For he did not know him by sight, although through the spirit of prophecy he knew that he had come (Matt. 4 [probably Matt. 3]). What, then, did he say? “Send forth your sharp sickle.” That is: reveal yourself in Israel; preach through yourself; and by preaching teach people to leave outside the killing letter and gather the life-giving spirit, and to understand what the Law and the prophets have hitherto prophesied.

Why? “Because the hour has come for reaping, because the harvest of the earth is dried up.” Just as in the fields, while grain in the ear has not yet fully formed and matured, it remains outside with the straw; but when it has fully ripened, it is finally cut, the straw being left outside and the grain carried within—so, while you were awaited as the one to come, the Law was observed carnally. But now that you have come and are preaching, the letter of the Law must be left outside with the carnal Jews, and the spiritual sense must be gathered within. Thus, for example, they may remain celibate and yet nevertheless—indeed, far better—attend to what was said: “Cursed is everyone who does not make seed in Israel.”

He cried until the answer was given him: that the one who was to come baptizing in water should receive this sign: “Upon whom you see the Spirit descending like a dove and remaining upon him, this is he who baptizes in the Holy Spirit” (John 1). This came to pass; and, having been made known in Israel by this sign, from then on he began to preach and say: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. 3, 4). It follows, therefore: “And he who sat upon the cloud sent his sickle upon the earth, and reaped the earth.”

The first fruits of that harvest were the apostles, and after them all those who, believing from that people and leaving behind the dry straw of carnal ceremonies, strove spiritually to fulfil the spiritual Law. But concerning all those who, carnally emulating that straw—that is, the killing letter of the Law—and envying the evangelical Spirit, persecuted Christ’s apostles with the same impiety by which they killed Christ himself, the following words of the vision immediately signify what judgment occurred.

“And another angel came out of the temple which is in heaven, himself also having a sharp sickle. And another angel came from the altar, who has power over fire, and cried with a loud voice to him who had the sharp sickle, saying: Send forth your sharp sickle and gather the clusters of the vine of the earth, because its grapes are ripe. And the angel sent his sickle upon the earth, and gathered the vine of the earth, and cast it into the great winepress of God’s wrath; and the winepress was trodden outside the city, and blood came out of the winepress up to the horses’ bridles for one thousand six hundred stadia.”

This other angel signifies Christ himself, now possessing through the passion of death the authority acquired in heaven and on earth, just as he said after rising again: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. 28). In his hand he had a sharp sickle—that is, in that same authority, an unavoidable sentence to be pronounced in just judgment against his Jewish enemies. This was to happen to them, as he had foretold: they would fall by the edge of the sword and be led captive into all nations (Luke 23 [probably Luke 21]). Having such a sickle, he came out of the temple that is in heaven. For when his wrath came upon the unhappy Jews, while the Roman army surrounded them, he had already ascended into heaven and entered that temple of his not made by hands, where now, as the Apostle himself says, “he stands before the face of God, having been made High Priest for us forever” (Heb. 9).

“And another angel from the altar, who had power over fire, cried with a loud voice to him who had the sharp sickle, saying: Send forth your sharp sickle and gather the clusters of the vine of the earth, because its grapes are ripe.”

The angel who cries these things is rightly understood as Moses, who accuses the Jews. For the Lord himself said to them in one place: “Do not think that I shall accuse you before the Father; there is one who accuses you, Moses, in whom you hope” (John 5). This Moses surely cried out and accused the most bitter clusters, namely the Jews, who had given the Lord of the whole vineyard vinegar mixed with gall to drink (Matt. 27). Even to the present day he does not cease accusing them, for example whenever that passage from the Song of Deuteronomy is read or sung: “Their vine is from the vine of Sodom and from the territory of Gomorrah; their grape is a grape of gall and their clusters are most bitter. Their wine is the gall of dragons and the incurable poison of asps” (Deut. 32). When he says these things, he certainly cries out and accuses the vine which is to be gathered to its ruin.

But what does it mean that he is said to cry from the altar and to have authority over fire? This same Moses had first made the tabernacle, the altar, and the holy of holies for them (Lev. 9); and at that altar he had such authority over fire that, when he called upon God, fire descended from the Lord upon the burnt offerings. Likewise, when he was angered against the violators of the priesthood and said to God, “Do not look upon their sacrifices,” no fire of propitiation descended upon the burnt offerings; rather, the fire of God’s wrath consumed those presumptuous men—namely Korah and his whole company.

The rite of that altar, delivered to the Jews by Moses himself, was indeed propitiatory until their sacrilege in killing the Lord (Num. 16). But from that time onward, while Moses cried out and said to God, “Do not look upon their sacrifices,” all their sacred things were irrecoverably burned by the fire of destruction while the Romans resisted them. “Send forth, therefore,” he says, “your sharp sickle and gather the clusters of the vine of the earth.” Why? “Because its grapes are ripe”: that is, because its iniquities are complete. So he himself, shortly before being killed, said by way of concession: “Fill up the measure of your fathers.” And shortly afterward: “Behold, I send to you prophets, wise men, and scribes; and some of them you shall kill and crucify, and some of them you shall scourge in your synagogues and persecute from city to city, so that upon you may come all righteous blood shed upon the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah, whom you killed between the temple and the altar” (Matt. 23).

It follows: “And the angel sent his sickle upon the earth and gathered the vine of the earth, and cast it into the great winepress of God’s wrath.” That vintage—that most unhappy destruction, in which a heap of every misery was piled upon them—is known throughout the world; even the accounts themselves are full of horror and astonishment.

But what does it mean that, after saying, “And he gathered the vine of the earth,” it added, “and cast it into the great winepress of God’s wrath”? Surely it is the same thing that was joined in Moses to the preceding words, “A fire has been kindled in my wrath”: “and it shall burn to the lowest depths of hell” (Deut. 32). For they were not only cut down by the material sword or captured by bodily captivity, but were condemned alike to temporal and eternal damnation. Hence the prophet speaks in confession: “Crush them with a double destruction, O Lord my God” (Jer. 17).

Thus it further adds: “And the winepress was trodden outside the city.” What is “outside the city” except outside the kingdom of God, outside the Church of Christ? For they were cast out from the city whose ruler they killed, and from the kingdom whose king they crucified. They were cast out because this was their will, when they said: “We do not want this man to reign over us” (Luke 19). Therefore, when those unwilling to have the King of the eternal city reign over them were crushed by the surrounding Roman army, the winepress was surely trodden outside the city.

And, O incalculable calamity, inconsolable misery! Those clusters were not treated like others which are trodden within the city walls and therefore sing concerning the winepresses: they are pressed by the afflictions of this world, yet do not flow down into the pool of hell, but into the Lord’s storehouse, into those most beloved tabernacles of the Lord, into those courts of the Lord for which they fail with longing and, even in failing, continue to long (Ps. 84 [printed 83]).

He marvellously signified—or saw signified—their double condemnation or destruction: “And the winepress,” he says, “was trodden outside the city; and blood came out of the winepress up to the horses’ bridles for one thousand six hundred stadia.” The order of the words is: The winepress was trodden outside the city for one thousand six hundred stadia, and blood came out up to the horses’ bridles.

“It was trodden,” he says, “for one thousand six hundred stadia, far outside.” Surely this is more than a Sabbath-day’s journey. For according to the Law, it is not permitted to go more than one thousand paces beyond one’s place on the Sabbath. But one thousand six hundred stadia are two hundred thousand paces. Therefore it is far more than a Sabbath-day’s journey.

Now the Lord, with whom the whole Law is spiritual, intends the name “Sabbath” to signify the state or age which follows this present life. Foretelling both the tribulation and wrath predicted for that people and that which shall come upon all under Antichrist, he says: “Pray that your flight may not take place in winter or on the Sabbath” (Matt. 24). The meaning is: Pray that death, the end of all things, may not overtake you in the winter of unbelief; or that you may not first wish then to be converted and escape God’s wrath by repentance, when it is not permitted to work.

O then, miserable people, who shall never obtain mercy! Their winepress has been trodden so far outside the city that they can no longer return into it, because there is Sabbath there, when it is not permitted to proceed more than one thousand paces—that is, to obtain pardon except for lesser sins. And who are the horses to whose bridles the blood came, except evil spirits? Now they are borne through the air like unbridled horses, untamed; at the last judgment they will at last be bridled. Surely the blood of such men came up to the horses’ bridles because they shall be companions and fellows of demons in eternal punishments. For the sentence has already been written which shall be spoken: “Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25).

## Chapter XV

“And I saw another sign in heaven, great and wonderful: seven angels having the seven last plagues, because in them the wrath of God is consummated.”

After the song sung with the Lamb upon Mount Zion, and after the flights and loud voices of the three angels—to whom John himself was added as a fourth—while the Son of Man sits and gathers the vine of the earth, seven angels “having seven last plagues” are seen in seven bowls, as is written later. For after the ancient songs of the Law and the prophets, once Christ’s Gospel had been established and Christ himself had sat at the Father’s right hand—the Christ by whose judgment the Jewish people were gathered as grapes in the manner described above—holy preachers were multiplied and filled the whole world with the knowledge of the Lord.

For here also one should remember that, in dividing the parts of this book according to the seven spirits of the Lord, we have already said that he whose works are represented in the preceding vision is the Holy Spirit of knowledge. Therefore the bowls rightly signify that outpouring or abundance of which it is written in Daniel: “Many shall pass through, and knowledge shall be multiplied” (Dan. 12); and likewise that abundance of languages of which David, after saying, “Day utters speech to day, and night declares knowledge to night,” immediately added: “There are no languages or speeches in which their voices are not heard” (Ps. 19 [printed 18]).

For bowls are broadened outwardly by a large mouth, from which they take their name. Indeed, *phy* in Greek means “mouth” in Latin, while *alin* means “glass”; hence vessels of this kind are so called because, made of that glass and containing only a moderate belly, they broaden outwardly with an open mouth, as has been said. Such vessels, then, fittingly resemble the preachers of the New Testament, apostles or apostolic men: the Holy Spirit filled their minds inwardly with his knowledge and broadened their mouths outwardly, so that, as has already been said, there might be no languages or speeches in which their voices were not heard—that is, so that every kind of language might arise in their mouths.

Conversely, the aforementioned singers, among whom the Law and the prophets lay hidden in only the one Hebrew people and who sang or read those songs in only one language, Hebrew, are compared to cups: vessels swollen in the belly but narrowed by a very small mouth. Therefore he says: “And I saw another sign in heaven, great and wonderful.” Truly, after that sign in which he saw the Lamb standing upon Mount Zion with the one hundred and forty-four thousand standing with him and singing a new song, this is a great and wonderful sign: namely, that while the Son of Man gathers the vine of the earth, those seven angels possess the seven last plagues and in them consummate the wrath of God.

For who are these seven angels, if not all the preachers of the Gospel, messengers of the truth? Since the Holy Spirit, who gave them the bowls already mentioned and to be mentioned later [Col. 1107A], is sevenfold, they are rightly comprised under the number seven and are understood collectively to mean all such preachers. Moreover, he calls them the last plagues in relation to the first plagues—namely, the seven first plagues mentioned above, where seven angels sounded seven trumpets. Concerning each of these last plagues it will later be necessary to explain in order how those are called and are first, while these are last. Yet this must briefly be anticipated here: those plagues are called first because they struck bodies; these are last because they reach as far as souls. Hence one should note what he says: that in them the wrath of God was completed. For God’s wrath begins by killing bodies, and, after it has killed them, is completed by sending souls into Gehenna [Col. 1107B].

It follows: “And I saw, as it were, a glassy sea mingled with fire; and those who had conquered the beast and its image, standing upon the glassy sea mingled with fire, having the harps of God; and they sang the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb, saying: ‘Great and marvellous are thy works, Lord God Almighty; just and true are thy ways, King of the ages. Who shall not fear thee, O Lord, and glorify thy name? For thou alone art gracious; because all nations shall come and worship before thee, because thy judgments are manifest.’”

These have been preserved in vessels of mercy; singing of their salvation and playing upon the harp the grace of their Saviour, they have happily escaped from the earth and the sea; from the rivers and springs of waters; from the heat, or fire, of the sun; from the dark throne or kingdom [Col. 1107C] of the beast; from the great river Euphrates; and from the air, or the powers of this air. Into all these things the bowls of God’s wrath, already mentioned, are afterwards said to have been poured out. For these are they who, when the wrath of God from heaven was revealed through the Gospel against all the impiety and unrighteousness of human beings, believed, repented, and were baptized for the remission of sins (Rom. 1). Therefore, in the sequence of the narrative, they are separated from those children of wrath who refused to believe; first the salvation of these is related, and then the destruction of the others.

He says, then: “And I saw, as it were, a glassy sea mingled with fire.” This sea is the sacrament of Christ’s baptism: that water which visibly flowed together with blood from his side, pierced by the lance as he hung on the cross. It blots out and cleanses all sins [Col. 1107D], but not without the power or presence of the invisible Holy Spirit. Thus, having said, “And I saw, as it were, a sea,” he rightly added, “mingled with fire,” because in baptism, as has already been said, visible water could do nothing without the power of the invisible Spirit.

And, though he could have said, “And I saw water,” he preferred to say, “And I saw, as it were, a sea,” because there is no slight or obscure likeness between Christ’s baptism, in which sins are swallowed up, and the Red Sea, in which Pharaoh perished with his chariots and horsemen (Exod. 14). Catholic faith also knows that those earlier harp-players or singers, who were seen standing with the Lamb upon Mount Zion, stood together with these younger ones upon this sea: that is, they too were saved or brought to perfection not [Col. 1108A] without the water of baptism, the blood of Christ’s Passion, and the fire of the Holy Spirit.

For those shadowy sacraments—for example, their baptism in Moses in the cloud and in the sea, their eating manna, and their drinking water from the rock (1 Cor. 10)—not these, I say, nor the other figurative miracles of God brought them to perfection. Rather, being, as it were, instructed through all these things, they were at last regenerated by the Passion of the Saviour when he came; and all together at that time, when, as already said, his side was opened and water flowed out with blood, the sacrament of baptism was instituted. We, indeed, are baptized individually because we had not been incorporated into the Church that was then regenerated—indeed, we did not yet exist at all.

[Col. 1108B] Therefore, when he now says, “And I saw those who conquered the beast and its image standing upon the glassy sea,” we rightly understand this of all the saints of both the Old and the New Testament. For those believed that Christ would come, while these believe that he has come; and, in that very faith, while believing and being baptized, they conquered the beast and its image—that is, the devil and every ungodly human being who imitates him. Finally, every offence and all sins, both original and actual, whatever that beast and its image have instilled in them by persuasion or example, are overwhelmed in this sea. But they themselves stand above the sea—that is, they survive, so that they may pass over to the true land of promise, which the letter of the Law then concealed by promising it, but which the Spirit of the Gospel now reveals [Col. 1108C].

For this reason the sea is beautifully called glassy: as what is contained in glass shines through, so in this sacrament of the Gospel nothing is now hidden. What was first enacted in figure is now enacted in reality, and everything is manifest. But you rightly understand it to be called a glassy sea in order that you may know that all who approach must be glass-like—that is, simple, through the truthfulness of a pure confession. For it is written: “The Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit”; and God, “who searches hearts and reins” (Wis. 1; Jer. 17), sees with what mind and disposition each person stands upon this sea; with what kind or degree [Col. 1108D] of thanksgiving he receives or regards the sea which he has crossed; what sort and how many pursuing enemies he has escaped; and how, standing upon it, he trembles or dances in humble rejoicing to the praise of God, not ungratefully.

Accordingly he immediately adds: “Having the harps of God, and singing the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb.” Certainly, the harps of God are not made by hand, like those upon which a person, by art, stretches strings measured out in due proportion. Rather, they are the harps of faithful hearts, in which through faith heavenly music—that is, the word of truth—dwells; and whose strings are the stretched-out commandments of God. Of such harps the Psalmist says: “Give thanks to the Lord with the harp; sing psalms to him upon the ten-stringed psaltery” (Ps. 32). For the commandments of the Law are ten, and no one who has crossed this sea can avail before God without observing them.

For when he had said, [Col. 1109A] “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit,” he added further: “Teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you” (Matt. 28). To observe these things is, while standing upon this sea, to sing first [469] upon the harp, and then upon the more clearly sounding psaltery: that is, first in fear, then in perfect love. “Having therefore the harps of God,” he says—that is, doing good works for God’s glory, not so as to be seen or heard by human beings, but so that their Father who is in heaven may be glorified (Matt. 5).

[Col. 1109B] Moreover, when he says, “and singing the song of Moses, the servant of God,” it is historically known what, or what sort of, song Moses the servant of God sang with the children of Israel after crossing the sea, when Pharaoh was drowned with his chariots and horsemen: “Let us sing,” he says, “to the Lord, for he has been gloriously magnified; horse and rider he has cast into the sea” (Exod. 15), and so forth. In the mystical understanding of Gospel truth, scarcely anyone is ignorant how this song befits those who have come up from the laver of regeneration. Therefore, having said, “Singing the song of Moses, the servant of God,” he rightly added, “and the song of the Lamb,” because what was historically enacted in figure under Moses in that crossing of the sea was spiritually fulfilled here by Christ, the Lamb of God, in his baptism, by which he regenerated us.

And Scripture aptly calls the Son of God, into whose death we have been baptized (Rom. 6), the Lamb of God in this place. For when Moses sang that song, the very event for which he sang had occurred through the sacrifice of a lamb, slaughtered by the Lord’s command on the fourteenth day of the first month, toward evening (Exod. 12), as a type of the same Christ, the Son of God, who was to be sacrificed for our sins in order to take them away [Col. 1109C].

“They say: ‘Great and marvellous are thy works, Lord God Almighty; just and true are thy ways, King of the ages.’” This is, to be sure, the song of Moses, the servant of God, if not in its words, nevertheless in its meaning. For in that song they repeatedly, not merely once, praise the Lord’s magnificence in those works. “For he has been gloriously magnified,” he says; again, “Thy right hand has been magnified in strength” (Exod. 15, 17); and again, “Who is like thee among the mighty, O Lord? Who is like thee, magnificent in holiness?” (ibid.). Thus it is the song of Moses, for it is sung both in Moses’ meaning and after Moses’ example.

[Col. 1109D] There are two supreme things which this brief verse plays upon the harp in a voice of exultation and confession: God’s power and the justice of the eternal King. For when they say, “Great and marvellous are thy works,” it is praise of his power; when they add, “Just and true are thy ways,” it is confession of his justice. Yet these two things do not have equal merit in the soul that makes this confession. For one indeed merits well who, seeing the marvellous works of God, the strongest of spirits, fears, praises, and confesses. But he merits best who, in those same works, strives to defend God’s justice against the slanderer where he understands it; and where his understanding fails, being inferior in understanding, nevertheless reveres it with love and says what the Apostle teaches each of us to say: [Col. 1110A] “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments, and unsearchable his ways!” (Rom. 11).

For example, when Pharaoh was drowned with his chariots and horsemen, concerning whom the aforesaid song of Moses, the servant of God, is sung—“Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously magnified” (Exod. 15)—it is easy to know why the Lord is sung of as truly mighty, since the marvellous work of his power is evident. But where God says concerning that same Pharaoh, “I will harden his heart” (Exod. 7), and likewise says to Moses, “I will have mercy on whom I will” (Exod. 33), there undoubtedly, even though it appears less plainly, the justice of his ways must be believed and confessed. For by this means the humility of subjection, which was formerly hidden, sometimes deserves to know something in part, until that which is perfect comes (1 Cor. 13).

The Lord’s ways themselves are two: one mercy, the other truth. Thus Scripture says: “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. 24). Of mercy these conquerors sing: “For thou alone art gracious, because all nations shall come and worship before thee.” For it is the work of free mercy, or merciful grace, [Col. 1110B] that the Gospel has been preached to all nations without distinction of persons, so that they might come, and those who had been far off might become near (Eph. 2). Therefore, having said, “For thou alone art gracious,” he added the work of mercy itself: “Because all nations shall come and worship before thee.”

[Col. 1110C] But concerning the second way, which is truth, these immediately say: “Because thy judgments are manifest.” It is understood that they are true. For by a true judgment it came about both that he said to the aforementioned Pharaoh, “For this very purpose I raised thee up, that I might show my power in thee,” and that, as said just above (Exod. 7), he harvested the Jewish nation, so that not only did those who formerly saw become blind, but they also fell by the edge of the sword and were led captive among all nations (Rom. 5). Judgments of this kind are manifest—not indeed to everyone, but to those to whom he himself has revealed them by his Spirit (1 Cor. 2); and not yet perfectly, but in part, until that which is perfect comes (1 Cor. 13). Their meaning might here have been treated more fully, had we not been carried onward by the desire to proceed.

[Col. 1110D] Amid works of this sort—works of the Lord’s power and justice—these singers say in wonder: “Who shall not fear thee, O Lord, and glorify thy name?” When they say, “Who shall not fear?” it must be understood: “and have peace?” Thus another Scripture says: “Who has resisted him and had peace?” (Job 9). And elsewhere it is written: “Thou art terrible; and who shall resist thee?” (Ps. 75). The implied answer is: no one. And the most weighty reason why none could resist is immediately given: “From then on is thy wrath.” The meaning is: from the time when the sinner sins not by falling through weakness or erring through ignorance, but by resisting thee through pride, from then on is thy wrath—so that thou no longer overlookest him or callest back one who has turned away, but strikest and powerfully crushest him [Col. 1111A].

Thus, “Who shall not fear thee, O Lord, and glorify thy name?” is as though he said: Since thy works are so great and marvellous, O Lord, and thy ways so just and true, where will the proud and ungrateful appear? Whoever does not fear now, when subject, will fear—indeed, will be thrown into turmoil when oppressed—according to that which is said in a prophetic denunciation through Isaiah: “Enter into the rock; hide thyself in a pit in the ground from the face of the Lord and from the glory of his majesty” (Isa. 2), when he arises to strike the earth.

“After these things I saw, and behold, the temple of the tabernacle of testimony in heaven was opened; and seven angels, having seven plagues, came out of the temple, clothed in clean, white stone, and girded about their breasts with golden girdles. And one of the four living creatures gave [Col. 1111B] the seven angels seven bowls full of the wrath of God, who lives for ages of ages.”

“After these things,” he says, “I saw”—that is, what I had already begun to relate above. For he had said: “And I saw another sign in heaven, great and marvellous: seven angels having seven last plagues, because in them the wrath of God was completed.” But after beginning to say this he immediately set it aside and made a beautiful digression, so that he might first write what he had seen at the same time: namely, the glassy sea, and those who, by standing upon it, escaped those plagues by Christ’s grace; and then the order of those same plagues, showing how they were, or are, poured out upon those who did not believe and neglected to stand upon that sea. For this is the Gospel order: “He who believes and is baptized shall be saved; [Col. 1111C] but he who does not believe shall be condemned” (Mark 16). First salvation is set forth for believers, then condemnation for unbelievers.

“I saw therefore,” he says, “after these things, and behold, the temple of the tabernacle of testimony in heaven was opened.” [470] The temple of the tabernacle of testimony was the Church of the former time, whose whole figurative rite or order began from the tabernacle of testimony, which Moses made in the wilderness (Exod. 36). This temple—that is, this Church—was confined to the one Jewish nation, in which alone God was known (Ps. 65). It was enclosed by the narrowness of place; it was enclosed because the mystical and figurative reasons of its ceremonies were not understood.

But when the Lord Jesus gave up the spirit, instituting in his death the aforesaid sacrament of baptism [Col. 1111D], the veil of the temple was torn from top to bottom; and he himself, rising from the dead, opened his disciples’ understanding so that they might understand the Scriptures (Matt. 26; Luke 24). Therefore the temple of the tabernacle of testimony was opened. Where? “In heaven,” he says. Heaven, or the heavens, means all the saints in whom God dwells, and especially the apostles. For it is written concerning them: “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the works of his hands” (Ps. 18). Thus it was opened in heaven—that is, in the hearts of the apostles—for he opened their understanding, as already said above, that they might understand the Scriptures.

Accordingly, once the temple had thus been opened, “seven angels, having seven plagues, came out of the temple.” How did they come out, or where did they go? Certainly, [Col. 1112A] by abandoning the carnal ceremonies of the Law they came out of the temple; indeed, by shaking the dust from their feet against the unbelieving Jews, they went out to the Gentiles (Matt. 20; Acts 15). “Having,” he says, “seven bowls”—that is, commanded to preach wrath and indignation and tribulation upon every soul of a human being who does evil (2 Tim. 4), first of the Jew and also of the Greek; and conversely glory and honour and peace upon every soul of a human being who does good, first of the Jew and also of the Greek. Such, indeed, were those whom he shortly before described as standing upon the sea and singing the song of Moses, the servant of God.

Yet those who bore plagues of this kind and were to announce, in season and out of season, the evils soon to come upon this wicked world needed to be secure amid adversities and well prepared to endure temptations. It follows, therefore: [Col. 1112B] “Clothed in clean, white stone, and girded about their breasts with golden girdles.” The clean, white stone is Christ: holy, innocent, and undefiled. But the Apostle says: “All you who have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. 3). The golden girdle about the breast is perfected love in their hearts. For the same Apostle says: “The love of God has been poured out in our hearts through his Spirit dwelling in us” (Rom. 5). Thus, well prepared and fortified, they went forth: outwardly stony against persecutions; inwardly girded against temptations.

“And one,” he says, “of the four living creatures gave the seven angels seven bowls full of the wrath of God, who lives for ages of ages.” [Col. 1112C] These bowls were given to these angels when those who had been unlettered and ordinary men received, as we have said above, understanding of the Scriptures and abundance in every language. One alone of the four Evangelists, Luke, writes when and how this happened: “And when,” he says, “the days of Pentecost were fulfilled, all the disciples were together in the same place” (Acts 2), and so forth. Therefore one of the four living creatures rightly gave the bowls, because only one of the four Evangelists narrated how the disciples’ hearts were enlarged by knowledge and their mouths by every kind of eloquence, like the bowls already discussed above.

It was also said above that the Holy Spirit who filled them is sevenfold. Thus, although there were twelve apostles—indeed, one hundred and twenty disciples—upon whom the Holy Spirit descended, both all of them and all the preachers whom that same Spirit has never ceased to send from that time until the end of the age are rightly signified by the number seven, his own number: seven angels [Col. 1112D].

He calls such bowls, a most terrible thing, full of the wrath of God who lives for ages of ages. For what is the wrath of God who lives for ages of ages, except the sentence of eternal judgment, the eternal vengeance upon sins? These bowls are assuredly full of that wrath for those who do not believe, who oppose the truth, and who commit works of iniquity (Rom. 2). This wrath of God is revealed from heaven against them through the ministry of these preachers of the Gospel. Formerly the holy heralds did not have bowls so full of wrath, as was said above: [Col. 1113A] “They constrained their mouths within only one nation and one language; they were cups rather than bowls, speaking to few persons and, speaking to those same persons through figures and enigmas, withholding very much.”

The mouths of these preachers have been enlarged in every language throughout the whole world, so that they might openly announce to kings and nations the impending wrath of the judgment to come, together with the person who will judge—the one who will say to those at his left hand: “Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25). It follows:

“And the temple was filled with smoke from the majesty of God and from his power. And no one could enter the temple until the seven plagues of the angels were completed.” When the angels came out of the temple, the temple itself [Col. 1113B] was filled with smoke. That is, when the preachers were abandoning, and teaching that the carnal ceremonies of the Law must be abandoned, the Jews, exceedingly impatient, were blinded by their own fury; and this came from the majesty of God and from his power—that is, because of the preaching of the holy Trinity and because of the miracles powerfully performed along with the preaching of this faith.

Isaiah likewise writes that, when the Seraphim cried, “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts,” the house of the Lord was filled with smoke (Isa. 6). For where the one majesty of the Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—began to be preached, together with the kingdom of the Lord seated, as the same prophet says, “upon a high and exalted throne,” namely at the Father’s right hand, above every might and dominion and power, [Col. 1113C] Jewish hearts were blinded by their own envy. This is the smoke by which the temple was filled from the majesty of God. Nor did that smoke arise for any but unbelievers.

When Stephen stood in the midst of those making such smoke for themselves, he nevertheless saw clearly—indeed, he deserved to see much more clearly—when, looking into heaven, he said: “Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God” (Acts 7). Finally, he belonged to the fellowship of these angels who came out of the temple, and he was accused on this ground by those who said: “For we have heard him say that this Jesus of Nazareth will destroy this place and change the traditions which Moses handed down to us.” He also had a bowl full of the wrath of God when he said to them: “Stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in hearts and ears, you have always resisted the Holy Spirit,” and so forth [Col. 1113D].

“And no one,” he says, “could enter the temple until the seven plagues of the seven angels were completed.” This means: no one can convert the Jewish people until Christ’s Gospel, by which a punitive judgment is announced as impending, is preached throughout the whole world.

## Chapter XVI
“And I heard a great voice from the temple saying to the seven angels: Go, pour out the bowls of God’s wrath upon the earth.” This voice is great because it proclaims great wrath. It is heard from the temple because, when they were about to depart from the ceremonies of the Jewish temple, as has already been said, the Lord Jesus, who was soon to suffer, foretold to these same angels: “And when the Paraclete comes, [Col. 1114A] he will convict the world concerning sin, and righteousness, 471 and judgment: concerning sin, indeed, because they did not believe in me; concerning righteousness, because I go to the Father, and you will no longer see me; and concerning judgment, because the ruler of this world has already been judged.”—“Go, therefore,” he says, “and pour out the bowls of God’s wrath upon the earth”; that is, openly convict the world and declare for what reasons human beings—who are earth because they love the earth—deserve the wrath of the living God.

“And the first went and poured out his bowl upon the earth; and there came a cruel and exceedingly grievous sore upon the people who have the mark of the beast and who worshipped its image.” Here we must recall the sequence of the first plagues, namely those which occurred above at the voices of the seven angels sounding their trumpets [Col. 1114B]. In relation to those, these plagues are called the last. At the sound of the first angel, a third part of the earth was burned; at that of the second, a third part of the sea became blood; at that of the third, a third part of the rivers was turned into wormwood; and at that of the fourth, a third part of the sun, moon, and stars was darkened. At the sound of the fifth angel, warlike locusts came out of the pit of the abyss onto the earth; at that of the sixth, the four angels bound at the great river Euphrates were released; and at that of the seventh, victorious voices arose in heaven.

In the same sequence, through the same regions of the world, these final plagues are poured out. The first is upon the earth; the second upon the sea; the third upon the rivers and fountains of waters; the fourth upon the sun; [Col. 1114C] the fifth upon the throne of the beast; the sixth upon the great river Euphrates; and the seventh is poured into the air. In place of the pit of the abyss, he has written “the throne of the beast” in this sequence; the remaining things he has expressed under the same names. These final plagues must therefore now be compared with those first ones, each with its corresponding one; and we must likewise see, as truth deigns to reveal itself, why these are called—or are—the final plagues after those.

“And there came,” he says, “a cruel and exceedingly grievous sore upon the people who have the mark of the beast and who worshipped its image.” The mark of the beast—that is, of the devil—is pride; and anyone who sins knowingly and contemptuously is rightly judged to bear it. Thus the Apostle says of some that, “although they knew [Col. 1114D] God, they did not glorify him as God or give him thanks” (Rom. 1); indeed, as the same Apostle says, “they did not see fit to retain God in their knowledge” (ibid.). Accordingly, in what follows—“and upon those who worshipped its image”—the crime of idolatry is readily understood; for the Apostle says in the same place of them: “They exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of an image of corruptible man, and of birds, and beasts, and four-footed creatures, and serpents” (ibid.).

Upon such persons, surely, there came a cruel and exceedingly grievous sore. What is that cruel and exceedingly grievous sore? “Therefore,” he says, “God gave them over to dishonourable passions, to do things that are unfitting. For their women exchanged the natural use for that use which is against nature [Col. 1115A]; likewise also the men, abandoning the natural use of the woman, burned in their desire for one another, men committing shameful acts with men and receiving in themselves the recompense due for their error” (Rom. 1). What could be worse or more cruel than this sore? Therefore, when he had said “a cruel sore,” he added, “and exceedingly grievous.” For it is not only sin, but also the most grievous punishment of sin.

Thus the first angel poured out his bowl upon the earth—that is, upon those who committed the sin of the Sodomites, whose sin was fullness of bread and idleness. The earth received them, an earth which, as Scripture reports, had formerly been watered like the paradise of the Lord (Gen. 13). He reproved and convicted them, I say, of being so grievously ulcerated because they did not see fit to retain God in their knowledge; and he openly declared [Col. 1115B] that, for this sin—indeed, because of this punishment of sin—they should rightly be transferred to the punishment of eternal fire.

In this way he poured out his bowl; yet a cruel and exceedingly grievous sore came upon them nevertheless, for they persisted in ulcerating themselves with such passions, adding contempt after hearing of the future judgment. In this respect this first bowl differs from that first trumpet, so that the trumpet is rightly called one of the first plagues and this bowl one of the final plagues. That is, the Scripture in which that trumpet sounded—that is, in which the cry of Sodom is read to have ascended to God—uttered no sentence or teaching concerning damnation or judgment to come on the last day, but narrated only what was then visibly and presently done: namely, that they were punished with bodily death through a rain of fire and sulphur [Col. 1115C]. Here, on the contrary, where the preachers of the Gospel reveal wrath from heaven, no bodily, visible, or present vengeance descends from heaven upon similar sinners; rather, a threat is made concerning the future, concerning invisible and eternal damnation: “Those who do such things are worthy of death” (Rom. 1).

The future punishment of sinners, which was there silent because of the character of that time, is here openly declared; and conversely, the bodily or present punishment enacted there is here recalled as an example but is not inflicted. Therefore that is rightly called one of the first plagues, and this one of the final plagues. Moreover, it should be noted that there only a third part of the earth or of the trees [Col. 1115D] is said to have been burned; by the trees, in figurative speech, human beings are signified. Here, however, not a third part of human beings but human beings themselves are said to have been struck by a cruel and exceedingly grievous sore.

Finally, both the Sodomites and the Egyptians, as well as the Canaanites—nations that endured different judgments in those times—were all from the third part of humankind, namely from the stock of Ham, one of Noah’s three sons, whom his father also cursed (Gen. 9). But on the final day of the great judgment, will only that portion of the human race which proceeded from Ham be judged according to its works? Certainly not. “Without distinction of persons or nations, wrath and indignation and tribulation [will come] upon every soul of a human being who does evil,” says the Apostle, “of the Jew first and also of the Greek” [Col. 1116A] (Rom. 2). Neither is descended from Ham: one is descended from Shem, the other from Japheth. Therefore vengeance follows not, as there, upon a third part of humankind, but upon human beings.

“And the second poured out his bowl upon the sea; and it became blood like that of a dead man, and every living soul died in the sea.” The sea comprises all those who, puffed up by worldly power, imitate the swelling pride of Pharaoh and Egypt. Pharaoh indeed, and his Egyptian servants, swelled like the sea and lifted up their waves against the Lord (Exod. 14). For just as a swollen sea is thrown into turmoil by its recurring waves within itself, rising now with its advances and now with its recessions, until at last, exhausted within itself, it is checked and calmed; so Pharaoh or Egypt, contending against God, changed back and forth, now saying, “I have sinned,” now again hardening his heart. This resembled the ebb and flow of the sea; and finally, in the element suited to his character, he perished in the midst of the sea [Col. 1116B].

All, therefore, who similarly fluctuate within themselves by contending against the Lord—for example, those of whom the Psalmist says: “When he slew them, they sought him, and returned, and came early to him; and they loved him with their mouth, and lied to him with their tongue. But their heart was not right with him, nor were they faithful in his covenant” (Ps. 77)—all, I say, who persevere in such unbelief are rightly understood 472 under the designation of the sea. Upon them the bowl of God’s wrath is poured out in such a way as to constitute, in the manner stated above, a final plague.

For when the second trumpet sounded—by which we understand the cry of the children of Israel, which ascended to God because of the pride of the Egyptians—no threat concerning the judgment of the last day or the punishments of hell sounded in it. Rather, having been struck ten times with various plagues of present evils, they are finally read and sung to have been drowned in the Red Sea (Exod. 14). Their pride, burning with the fire of envy, is signified there where, when the second angel sounded, “a great mountain burning with fire,” he says, “was cast into the sea” (Rev. 8). But the preaching of the Gospel inflicts nothing of this kind upon similar ungodly persons; rather, it dreadfully consigns them to future judgment. Thus the drowning of the burning mountain at the second angel’s [Col. 1116D] trumpet is called the second of the first plagues; and this pouring of the bowl upon the sea is called the second of the final plagues.

“And it became,” he says, “blood like that of a dead man.” That is, the condemnation of such ungodly persons will be like the condemnation of the devil, who is truly already long dead—that is, opposed to the living God. For they will be joined to him, as the Judge says: “Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25). “And,” he says, “every living soul died in the sea.” For not merely the third part of humankind, from which the Egyptians came—for they too sprang from one of Ham’s descendants, as has already been said—but every soul without distinction will be judged, whoever is in such a sea, whether it be the soul of a Jew or of a Greek. And a soul that thus dies is rightly said to die while living, because whoever knowingly, and out of envy for what is good, does evil, is said to live in sin; as did Pharaoh, who persecuted the children of Israel not through ignorance but through envy [Col. 1117A].

“And the third poured out his bowl upon the rivers and the fountains of waters; and they became blood.” By the designation of rivers, here are to be understood those who also persecuted the saints with the material sword. Upon rivers and fountains of this sort, when the third angel sounded the trumpet, a great star burning like a torch fell from heaven: that is, the wrath of God which destroyed the seven nations when the children of Israel entered under the leadership of Joshua. For those nations hated Israel from the time it came up from the land of Egypt, as you have in the Song of Moses. For when he had said, “You led in mercy the people whom you redeemed, and carried them in your strength to your holy dwelling-place,” he immediately added: “The peoples rose up and were angry; pains seized all the inhabitants of Philistia” (Deut. 32), etc. The children of Israel had not yet passed through, and they were already tormented.

Hence it is said in imprecation: “Let them become immovable like a stone, until your people passes through, O Lord, until this people whom you have acquired passes through” (Exod. 15). Amalek was the first to attack them in war, and Moses conquered him in battle by prayer. Thus Balaam son of Beor says: “Amalek is the first of the nations, whose end shall be destruction” (Num. 24). I have chosen to recall these things now so that you may not say that all those who took up arms against Israel were prompted by zeal and necessity on account of their own land, which Israel would take away [Col. 1117C]. Israel was claiming again, by God’s promise, only that land in which Abraham had purchased for himself a right of burial, where Isaac and Jacob had been buried with him and with Sarah their mother (Gen. 23). Why, then, did Amalek, who was from Edom, Jacob’s brother, come and fight against Israel? Why did Edom itself go forth armed to meet its brother?

Therefore, upon the rivers and fountains of waters—upon a third part of which God’s wrath then fell when the third angel sounded the trumpet—this third angel poured out his bowl. “And they became,” he says, “blood.” Then it did not happen in this way; rather, a third part of the waters became wormwood, and many people died from the waters because they became bitter. For many of the Canaanites, who belonged to that often-mentioned third part of humankind, then survived. Among them also “the children of Israel mingled, and learned their works, and served their idols, and it became a stumbling block to them” (Ps. 108). This, surely, was for the waters to be turned to wormwood for them: waters which became so bitter to their drinkers that they thereby incurred the wrath of their God.

But here, where the third of the final plagues is poured out—that is, the third bowl—it is not so: not a third part of the waters becomes wormwood, but universally they become blood. For not only the descendants of Ham, who, as has often been said, was one of Noah’s three sons, but the whole body of persecuting nations is consigned to eternal judgment by this third bowl of God’s wrath, so that there may no longer [Col. 1118A] remain among them anyone able further to persecute or trouble his saints.

It follows: “And I heard the angel of the waters saying: You are just, you who are and who were holy, because you have judged these things; for they shed the blood of saints and prophets, and you gave them blood to drink, as they deserve.” Who is this angel of the waters? Or rather, what kind of waters are these? Surely, the faithful, of whom it is written in Isaiah, “His waters are faithful”: “He who walks,” he says, “in righteousness and speaks truth, who rejects gain from oppression and shakes his hands free of every bribe, who stops his ear lest he hear of blood, and shuts his eyes lest he see evil—he shall dwell on high; the fortresses of rocks shall be his high place; bread is given him; his waters are faithful” [Col. 1118B] (Isa. 33).

Faithful waters, moreover, are living waters, which flow from the belly of the believer, as the giver of those waters says: “He who believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly” (John 7). Therefore this angel of the waters is the one whose those waters are, to whom they have been given, from whose belly they flow: namely, every scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 13), every faithful interpreter or author of the holy Scriptures. Because his lips preserve knowledge (Mal. 2), he deserves in this place especially to be called the angel of the waters—not because he is only one man in person, but because there is one understanding shared by all according to faith.

For all who truly dwell amid the waters of the holy Scriptures have one Spirit and one faith; and if you consult those waters properly, they all speak in harmony and agree in this: that God is a righteous judge. Therefore the angel of the waters says: “You are just, you who are and who were holy, because you have judged these things; for they shed the blood of saints and prophets, and you gave them blood to drink, as they deserve.”

This description of the eternal God has already frequently occurred in this Scripture: “who were, and who are, and who are to come.” But this third phrase, “and who are to come,” is not said here because this confession of God’s justice belongs to that time after which he will no longer come. Thus, “you who are and who were” means: you who now endure through the ages and who were before the ages, against whom all the rivers that attempted to swallow up your name have failed. For you are who you were, [Col. 1118D] and that prophetic truth stands and endures in its firmness: “In the beginning, O Lord, you founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands.
