They shall perish, but you remain; and all shall grow old like a garment; and like a covering you shall change them, and they shall be changed. But you are the same, and your years shall not fail” (Ps. 101).

“You,” he says, “who have judged these things, are just.” What, then, did you judge? That because they shed the blood of saints and prophets, you gave them blood to drink; and in this recompense you judged murderers and bloodthirsty persons worthy of it. 473 Certainly, in such condemnation the Jews are, before all nations, worthy to drink first, since they not only shed the blood of saints and prophets [Col. 1119A], but also killed the Lord himself, the Holy One of holies and of prophets. Therefore, even while still alive, wretched people everywhere already taste the drink of blood, carrying, in a strong and cruel conscience, from their fathers the inheritance of blood, as though by this written testament: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 16).

Therefore whatever they think they drink from the waters of the Scriptures in their synagogues becomes blood to them, because they corrupt those waters for themselves by a deadly understanding, the Spirit of prophecy permitting and judging it when he says: “Let their table before them become a snare, and a recompense, and a stumbling block. Let their eyes be darkened so that they do not see, and bend their back continually” (Ps. 68).

It follows: “And I heard the altar saying: [Col. 1119B] Yes, Lord God Almighty, true and just are your judgments.” In some copies it is read, “And I heard another saying”; and in reading “another,” it is understood that a word or response is supplied. But in more corrected manuscripts “the altar” is written; and this is not without reason, if you recall that the saints and prophets, whose blood these people are accused of shedding, had previously cried to God from beneath the altar, where it is written: “And when he had opened the fifth seal, I saw beneath the altar the souls of those slain for the word of God and for the testimony which they held; and they cried with a great voice, saying: How long, O holy and true Lord, will you not judge and avenge our blood upon those who dwell on the earth?” (Rev. 6).

That it may be said, “I heard the altar saying,” with the sense, “I heard those beneath the altar saying,” is not an unfamiliar manner of speaking among grammarians. It occurs through the trope called metonymy, signifying what is contained by means of that which contains it. Thus, “I heard the altar saying” means: I heard beneath the altar those whom I had previously heard, not now crying out and demanding judgment or the vengeance of their blood, but, now that the vengeance they sought had been accomplished, praising the justice of the one judging and avenging and saying: “Yes, Lord God Almighty, true and just are your judgments” [Col. 1119C]. True in word, just in deed.

“And the fourth angel poured out his bowl upon the sun, and it was given him to afflict people with heat and fire.” There, where the fourth angel sounded the trumpet, a third part of the sun, a third part of the moon, and a third part of the stars was struck (Rev. 8). Both here and there, by the sun is understood that seat of God of which it is said in the psalm: “And his seat is like the sun before me” (Ps. 88), namely the Church, concerning or within which Christ is, the Sun of righteousness.

But we have learned that the difference is this: there the Church is signified as it was when, already possessing the promise that Christ the sun would be born from it, it came up from Egypt; and that part of it which murmured was struck and laid low in the wilderness. Here, however, the Church is signified as it comes up from baptism after Christ’s passion; and within it are condemned false brethren, false Christians, who profess to know God but deny him by their deeds (Titus 1). Finally, upon these also [Col. 1120A] the bowl is poured out in full measure, because they neglect to redeem their sins by almsgiving (Dan. 4), and do not perform the six works of mercy: feeding the hungry, giving drink to the thirsty, clothing the naked, receiving the stranger, visiting the sick, and coming to the person in prison (Matt. 25). Those who do not do these things—and indeed who disparage those who do them—do they not also drink from the bowl of God’s wrath, so as to go into eternal fire?

“Therefore he poured out his bowl upon the sun, and it was given him to afflict people with heat and fire.” This was given to the angel: namely, that by reproving carnal people—among whom, for example, are jealousy and strife (1 Cor. 3)—for being merely human, he should afflict them with a twofold evil, heat and fire; that is, the power of judgment both present and future [Col. 1120B]. For “of those who are outside,” the Apostle says, “what is it to us to judge?”—with “at present” understood. “But do you not judge those who are inside?” he says (1 Cor. 5), and this must be understood of both present and future judgment.

For rulers already judge those who are within, for example when the same Apostle says: “Though absent in body, yet present in spirit, I have already judged that such a man should be handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord” (ibid.). To judge in this way is surely to afflict people with heat. For they burn with a certain heat of shame when they are separated from the assembly of the Church, so that one may neither say “greeting” to such a person nor eat with him (2 John 1). But if, struck by such heat, they are not corrected, then it will at last be just that they should be afflicted with fire in the future, so that by their judgment, since they have proved rebellious and contemptuous, they may be handed over to the fire of Gehenna [Col. 1120C].

It follows: “And people were scorched with great heat, and they blasphemed the name of God, who has power over these plagues; and they did not repent to give him glory.” Such people, proud, arrogant, insolent, overbearing, slanderous, murmuring, lovers of pleasures, despisers of holy teaching, have often done and still do this in every order of the Church. An example of them all was Dathan and Abiram (Num. 16), together with the other children of Israel who were children according to the flesh and not according to faith, whose bodies, as we mentioned above in the sequence of the seven trumpets when the fourth angel sounded, were laid low in the wilderness in different ways.

When people of this sort are rebuked for their transgressions, they burn with great heat: that is, by becoming angry, contradicting, and conspiring against their rulers, raising the flame of contention, quarrelling, and implacable hatred (Rom. 10), after the pattern of the aforementioned Dathan and Abiram and the others who rose up against Moses and Aaron (Num. 16) [Col. 1120D]. The seriousness of their bitterness and their evil words, which they utter from an abundance of gall, is indicated by the addition: “And they blasphemed the name of God.”

For whatever madness they direct against prelates or fathers all rebounds upon God, as Moses and Aaron, already mentioned, testify: “What are we,” they say, “that you murmur against us? Your murmuring is not against us but against the Lord.” The present passage expresses this even more deeply when, after saying, “and they blasphemed the name of God,” it adds, “who has power over these plagues.” It is as though it said: By blaspheming prelates and despising their judicial sentence, they blaspheme not them but the name of God; and therefore this guilt will rightly be reckoned to them as blasphemy against God, because what prelates do or judge for the sake of discipline, they do not by their own power or authority but by God’s.

Considering this, Paul does not hesitate to say that he knew Christ to be stern, namely by the power of him who spoke in him. For he says: “Do you seek proof of Christ, who speaks in me?” (2 Cor. 13). Rebellion against discipline is therefore rightly reckoned to them as blasphemy against God, especially because it is further said of them: “They did not repent to give him glory” [Col. 1121B]. For the impenitent heart is convicted of blaspheming God—indeed, the Holy Spirit—because, while it defends its iniquity, it undoubtedly fights against God and opposes the judgment of the Holy Spirit.

This is why Samuel says to Saul: “For refusing to obey is like the sin of divination, 474 and refusing to submit is like the crime of idolatry” (1 Sam. 15). “And the fifth poured out his bowl upon the throne of the beast, and its kingdom became dark; and they gnawed their tongues because of pain, and blasphemed the God of heaven because of their pains [Col. 1121C] and sores, and did not repent of their deeds.”

Where the fifth angel sounded the trumpet, the smoking pit of the abyss was opened; but here, where the fifth angel poured out his bowl, the throne of the beast is darkened. In the other trumpet-soundings and bowl-pourings alike, the things or parts of the world are named by the same terms: earth, sea, rivers and fountains, sun, and the river Euphrates. Here the designation changes, since “the throne of the beast” is written in place of “the pit of the abyss.” What, I ask, is the throne of the beast except that upon which the beast rests? And what is that except falsehood? For just as God’s authority is nothing but truth, so the devil’s support is nothing but falsehood. Therefore, as falsehood is rightly understood there in the pit of the abyss, so it is rightly understood here in the throne of the beast.

Certainly, from the time that the devil’s falsehood disclosed itself through the tongues of heretics, the venerable order of holy Fathers rose up in opposition and convicted their perfidy by ready testimonies from the Scriptures, then condemned it with an eternal anathema; from that time this angel poured out his bowl upon the throne of the beast [Col. 1121D]. But what did the heretics do in response? Did they rest and submit to victorious truth? Certainly not. Rather, they raged more fiercely, spread their impiety more widely, and in their fury made the whole world labour.

It follows, therefore: “And its kingdom became dark, and they gnawed their tongues because of pain.” For they themselves are, or were, the kingdom of the beast, since the throne of the beast—that is, falsehood—found in them a prepared place. Once the bowl had been poured out, therefore, the kingdom of the beast became dark because, when judicial sentences had been rendered upon the perfidy of heretics, they, smoking with fury and envy, were more deeply blinded. But how did they gnaw their tongues? Surely by thinking against themselves, saying things contrary to themselves, and fighting against themselves through the conflicts of opposing sects. For against the Catholic Church they wage war indeed in an equal and apparently united spirit of malice; but by conflict among themselves they produced heresies divided in many directions. Thus, each defending his own party, contending and quarrelling, gnaws his own tongue [Col. 1122A].

Why? “Because of pain,” he says—that is, because of envy. For pain here is not to be understood otherwise than where it is written: “Behold, he has conceived injustice, and conceived pain, and brought forth iniquity” (Ps. 9). Again: “His mouth is full of cursing, bitterness, and deceit; beneath his tongue are toil and pain” (Ps. 7). Because of such pain they gnawed their tongues—that is, by making sects opposed to one another because of envy, they made themselves enemies through their own tongues.

It is further added: “And they blasphemed God because of their pains and sores.” A remarkable thing: “And they blasphemed God,” he says. Why? “Because of their pains and sores”: that is, because of private envies and hatreds, which are wounds not of the body but of the heart. This is remarkable, yet true. For, as ecclesiastical writings testify, Arius the presbyter, because of hatred for Alexander his bishop, broke out into blasphemy against God; and, to raise scandal against him because he hated and envied him, he began to teach doctrines contrary to the truth concerning the Son of God [Col. 1122C]. Therefore it may truly be said universally of heretics: “They blasphemed God because of their pains and sores.”

Finally, he further says: “And they did not repent of their deeds.” How could those people repent who spoke words against the Holy Spirit? For, as the authority of earlier Fathers also teaches, that person speaks a word against the Holy Spirit who contradicts holy Scripture not through ignorance but through envy; and Scripture is without doubt the voice and words of the Holy Spirit. But the Lord says: “Whoever speaks a word [Col. 1122D] against the Holy Spirit shall not be forgiven, neither in this age nor in the age to come.” For it is the judgment of the Holy Spirit that one who has sinned in this way shall never be inspired to perform worthy repentance. Where repentance does not come first, forgiveness cannot follow. Therefore those who did not repent, and could not repent of their deeds, will not be forgiven: abandoned by the judgment of the Spirit, because they blasphemed God not through ignorance but, as has already been said, “because of their pains and sores”—the pains of envy and the wounds of hatred.

“And the sixth poured out his bowl upon that great river Euphrates, and dried up its waters, so that a way might be prepared for the kings from the rising of the sun. And I saw three unclean spirits, like frogs, proceeding from the mouth of the dragon, [Col. 1123A] and from the mouth of the beast, and from the mouth of the false prophet.”

When the sixth angel sounded the trumpet, the four angels bound at the great river Euphrates were released, and the plague struck the people of God through the four chief kingdoms of the world, under which the children of Israel, or Judah, were afflicted by God’s judgment. That was not among the last plagues, in which the wrath of God is consummated, because it delivered not souls but bodies to such angels—that is, to earthly kingdoms. But this bowl of God’s wrath is poured out into the river: not so that such angels may be released, but so that its waters may be dried up and a way prepared for the kings from the rising of the sun.

Therefore the bowl of God’s anger is poured into the water of the river; and accordingly we must understand such water as something to which [Col. 1123B] God’s wrath may reasonably be said to be due. Moreover, since the preceding bowls condemned the sea, the rivers, and the springs of waters to become blood, why does the river Euphrates receive a bowl of its own, unless the waters of this river signify some evil among the other evils done under the sun? There is indeed an evil whose condemnation we have not yet encountered in the preceding bowls, which is rightly understood here to be signified first by the waters of that river and then by the three unclean spirits creeping forth in the likeness of frogs. This evil is plainly threefold, and its parts are the tricks of magicians, the inventions of philosophers, and the fictions of poets. Their profound malice and turbid verbosity are suitably signified by the waters of the Euphrates. For [Col. 1123C] Euphrates is the river of Babylon; flowing through it, it divides into many channels. By its very name too it commonly signifies in Scripture the whole race of the ungodly, opposed to the race of the righteous: the city of the devil, opposed to the city of God. For Babylon is interpreted “confusion.”

Thus, after bowls have been poured out upon the sea, the rivers, and the springs of waters, this bowl too is poured out upon Euphrates, because tyrants or ungodly kings, together with the nations subject to them, have earned condemnation; and wrath is also owed to those who drove them mad and increased their error by empty talk—indeed, by their malicious, lying, fabulous writings. Before the wrath of God from heaven against waters of this kind was revealed through the Gospel of Christ, [Col. 1123D] the holy kings could not cross them: namely, those who were rulers or authors of the Scriptures of truth, some of whom were also kings in worldly rank. They are rightly said to have come from the rising of the sun, 475 because they did not come or speak from themselves, but received from the illumination of the Godhead both that they should speak and what they should speak.

These kings could not cross those waters; with the single Hebrew language they could not meet the eloquent Greeks and learned Latin grammarians, rhetoricians, dialecticians, and so many poets—tragic, comic, and satirical. But “when that Spirit of truth came, to convict the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment” (John 16), by convicting it he also brought this about: that the waters of so great a river were dried up. For he made the wisdom of this world foolish. As the wisdom of God went forth and gave an account of that which appeared to be God’s foolishness, as the Apostle says: “But we preach Jesus Christ, and him crucified: to the Jews indeed a stumbling-block, to the Gentiles foolishness” (1 Cor. 1), then, by comparison with him, what had hitherto seemed great and profound appeared foolish and dry.

How cheap, detestable, and contemptible that worldly wisdom was—or appeared—in the eyes of those enlightened by truth, he finely indicates in his own person when he says: “And I saw three unclean spirits proceeding from the mouth of the dragon, from the mouth of the beast, and from the mouth of the false prophet, like frogs.” By “unclean spirits” he means [Col. 1124B] sects that appear to be wisdom and knowledge—magical, poetic, and philosophical—which the unclean spirit of this world, opposed to the Holy Spirit, inspired.

For magicians chiefly adopted unclean spirits as their patrons, by I know not what unhappy compact; poets too, under respectable names, attached themselves to the same spirits and asked these unclean spirits to inspire them, sacrilegiously presuming to call them gods when they were demons. Moreover, the spirit which inspired philosophers was likewise, without doubt, unclean. Does not the Apostle say of them: “Claiming to be wise, they became foolish, and they became futile in their reasonings?” (Rom. 1). And see to what degree of uncleanness they became futile: serving the creature rather than the Creator, they were therefore handed over to dishonourable passions or to the uncleanness of the desires of their hearts. They are therefore rightly called unclean spirits.

Moreover, by the name “dragon” the devil is rightly understood; by the title “beast,” the beastly kingdom of the devil is here signified. For in Daniel the four chief kingdoms of the world are signified by four beasts: namely, the Babylonian, Persian or Median, Macedonian, and Roman kingdoms. Therefore the first spirit proceeded from the mouth of the dragon, because human curiosity learned the magical art from converse with the devil. The next spirit came out of the mouth of the beast, because the baseness of the human mind, flattering the beastly kingdom of this world, raised earthly kings—mere human beings—to the status of gods by poetic fictions, and sang in fabulous ditties of their translation into heaven and the spheres of the stars.

Philosophy too proved to be a false prophet, [Col. 1124D] for it referred the filthy acts attributed to the gods by fanatics—for example, Jupiter’s adulteries, the jealousy of Juno, his sister and wife, Venus’s prostitution, and the like—to the elements of the world. It wished to contrive allegorical interpretations for things of which people could by then be ashamed in their gods. Such an interpreter was truly a false prophet, because he prophesied from his own heart (Ezek. 13), vainly consoling human shame by adorning the adulteries of the gods with fictitious and useless mysteries, while nevertheless remaining in the condition of serving the creature rather than the Creator (Rom. 1), who is blessed for ever. Amen.

“I saw,” he says, “three unclean spirits go forth from the mouth of the dragon, from the mouth of the beast, and from the mouth of the false prophet”; [Col. 1125A] and he adds further: “Like frogs.” Frogs are unclean, ugly, small, and as it were talkative. Dwelling in mud, they take away quiet by their importunate and, as it were, chattering croaking. Thus those who seem to themselves great and eloquent are fittingly compared with frogs, or said to resemble them. For example, poets who think that they utter great things: yet all their material is fabulous mud, and their greatness is inflation. Therefore, since their knowledge, being no knowledge at all (2 Cor. 10), exalts itself against the knowledge of God, the story from Aesop’s fable aptly suits their spirit: when it tried to puff itself up to the size of an ox, it vainly stretched its skin and at last burst by puffing beyond its strength. [Col. 1125B]

Where now are those grandiloquent men who exalted themselves against the true greatness of the knowledge of God? “Their memory has perished with a noise, but their Lord remains for ever” (Ps. 9). Who believes the talkativeness of those men? Indeed, who does not laugh at their shameful theologies when reading or hearing them?

Moreover, the magicians whose leaders in Egypt were Jannes and Mambres brought forth frogs before Pharaoh against Moses and Aaron by their incantations, and could do no more. They are rightly said to have the character of frogs, so as to resemble those which they produced against God, beyond which their tricks had no power.

It follows:

“For they are spirits of demons, working signs, and they go forth to the kings of the whole earth, to gather them [Col. 1125C] for battle on the great day of the Almighty.”

Truly, he says, I have called those spirits unclean, for they are spirits of demons. Since their doctrines are in fact contrary to truth, no one can doubt that all such supposed greatnesses—indeed, inflations—are inspirations of demons. “And they go forth,” he says, “to the kings of the whole earth, to gather them for battle.” The first to do this, as Holy Scripture relates, were the aforementioned sorcerers Jannes and Mambres. For the spirit of deception that was in them went forth to the king of Egypt; through confidence in signs they worked as though similar to the signs of God’s power, they increased his folly, so that, fighting against God on behalf of Israel, he dared to wage battle.

In the same or a similar way the other sorcerers, poets, and philosophers gathered the kings of the whole earth—not in one place, certainly, [Col. 1125D] but in one and the same disposition of utterly evil will—that they might battle against the Lord. Captivated by their great reputation, the kings of the earth might disdain or neglect to esteem the great miracles worked by the servants of the Lord, or to marvel at the wisdom which they preached, since their opponents had been accustomed both to do wonderful things and to speak magnificently as men who were wise.

They have therefore fought, and do not cease to fight, by persecuting all who desire to live devoutly in Christ—but to their own harm. For, having thus been gathered for battle, they will be gathered for judgment. Thus, having said here, “to gather them for battle,” he added: “for the great day of the Almighty.” For the day of the Almighty will be the day of judgment, undoubtedly great, [Col. 1126A] as the prophet says: “The great day of the Lord is near, near and exceedingly swift; the voice of the day of the Lord is bitter; there the mighty man shall be afflicted” (Zeph. 1), and so forth.

“It is near,” he says, and this is true. For although some delay may appear between the time when he prophesied and that great day of the Almighty, death—the end of this present life—is certainly near to each person, and it is unknown when it will come. Therefore he says at once: “Behold, I come like a thief” (Luke 12). The evil servant says in his heart: “My master delays his coming”; but the Lord says: “Behold, I am here; I come quickly.” He adds, “like a thief,” that is, to be feared by the negligent and sleeping.

For he himself deigned to use the likeness of a thief for himself, when, having first commanded his servants [by a command?] to watch, he said: “For you do not know [Col. 1126B] at what hour the Son of Man will come”; and he says: “But know this: that if the master of the house knew at what hour the thief would come, he would certainly watch and would not allow his house to be broken into” (ibid.). With the same purpose or reason for which he says there, “Let your loins be girded; blessed are those servants whom the Lord, when he comes, finds watching,” he immediately adds here: “Blessed is he who watches and keeps his garments, lest he walk naked and they see his shame.”

The Almighty added this because of his great day, when it had been said before that the kings of the earth were to be gathered for battle on the great day of the Almighty. It follows:

“And he gathered them for battle in the place which is called in Hebrew Harmagedon.”

Whom did he gather? Certainly the kings, for this gathering began to be written of concerning kings. But [Col. 1126C] there are here diverse—indeed, opposed and contrary—kings. For it had previously been said of the good kings that a way would be prepared for the kings from the rising of the sun; but of the evil ones it was then added: “and they shall go forth to the kings of the whole earth, to gather them for battle.” Which of these kings, then, did he gather in the place called in Hebrew Harmagedon? Or who gathered them in such a place? For he had not introduced any single person, nor does he explicitly distinguish whether he gathered the evil or the good.

It may therefore be said that the gathering of evil and good is here prefigured—that gathering of which we know that, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, not only kings but all nations will be gathered before him. There they will be gathered for a wondrous battle, [Col. 1126D] because there the wondrous and terrible end of the battle between the evil and the good has been fixed. That condition is rightly designated by the name Harmagedon used here. For it is interpreted “a rising together into former things,” or “a rounded mountain.” It fittingly signifies that gathering in which the holy kings who came from the rising of the sun will rise together into former things and sit in judgment; while the evil kings, like a rounded mountain, will be lifted up with the devil their prince. For then this mountain will truly be commanded to be lifted and cast, no longer into the sea, but into the depths of Gehenna.

“And the seventh poured out his bowl into the air. And a great voice came forth from the temple, from the throne, saying: It is done.”

And there, where “the seventh angel sounded the trumpet, great voices arose [Col. 1127A] in heaven saying: The kingdom of this world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ” (Rev. 11). Thus, here too, when it is said, “It is done,” the same thing must be understood: namely, “the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ”; but with this distinction, that we perceive more of the wrath of the living God in this seventh bowl than in that seventh trumpet. For these plagues are the last, whereas those were the first; and they differ in that those concern visible evils, while these concern the varieties and distinctions of invisible evils.

Therefore, in the seventh trumpet, the visible conflagration of this whole world is understood; in this seventh bowl, the fullness of condemnation by which demons are to be punished, who now wander through this air after being cast down from heaven. This is what he means when he says: “And [Col. 1127B] the seventh poured out his bowl into the air”—that is, upon the aerial hosts or powers. The seventh bowl is rightly poured out upon them, because whatever evils are punished by the preceding six bowls redound upon those who instigate those same evils. Hence the Apostle calls them principalities, powers, and rulers of this world of darkness (Eph. 6).

Therefore, when that great voice says, “It is done,” it is as if it said: In the elect the kingdom of God has been fulfilled, and in the reprobate the wrath of God has been consummated, because the devil too has been hurled with his angels into the depths of hell.

“And there were lightnings, voices, and thunders; and there was a great earthquake, such as had never been since men were upon the earth, so great an earthquake, so mighty.”

Not after that great voice saying, “It is done,” but meanwhile, while the angels pour out their bowls, “there were lightnings, voices, thunders, and an earthquake.” [Col. 1127C] Lightnings are miracles; voices, the testimonies of the Scriptures; thunders, threats of future evils. By all these things the angels who poured out their bowls—that is, the preachers sent into the whole world to proclaim the coming judgment of God—confirmed their message.

Moreover, the earthquake that was so great was an earthquake of our hearts, moved when they heard the preaching of the Gospel in which the wrath of God is revealed. Of this earthquake the Psalmist says: “The earth was moved and trembled; [Col. 1127D] the foundations of the mountains were troubled and moved, because he was angry with them” (Ps. 17), and so forth. Such a great earthquake, he says, had not existed since human beings were upon the earth, because before Christ’s advent it had never happened that preachers sent out should shake the whole world: that, as the heavens declared the glory of God, their sound should go forth into all the earth and their words to the ends of the world (Ps. 18).

He intends us to understand the magnitude of this earthquake from what follows, when he says: “And the great city was divided into three parts, and the cities of the nations fell.” The great city here is the whole human race. For, lest we suppose that he means here only that division in which the reprobate alone are assigned, [Col. 1128A] he immediately adds concerning it: “And great Babylon came into remembrance before God, to give her the cup of the wine of the wrath of his indignation.” Therefore both points must be observed, and each distinguished according to its own likely meaning.

That the universality of the world was, before Christ’s advent, not merely one city but as it were one courtyard of one strong man, mingled from elect and reprobate alike, is conveyed by the well-known authority of our Lord Jesus Christ in this way: “When a strong man armed guards his courtyard, all that he possesses is in peace; but when a stronger one comes upon him and conquers him, he will take away all his weapons in which he trusted and distribute his spoils” (Luke 11).

Moreover, [Col. 1128B] that this city was to be divided into three parts by the preaching of the Gospel—by which, as by the outpouring of these bowls, the wrath of God is revealed—the Lord himself foretold in this manner: “Do not think that I have come to bring peace upon the earth; for I have not come to bring peace, but a sword. For I have come to set a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; and a man’s enemies are those of his own household” (Matt. 10). These are the three parts, which Luke expressed yet more distinctly in these words: “Do you think that I have come to give peace on earth? No, I tell you, but division. For henceforth five in one house will be divided: three against two, and two against three. Father against son, and son against his father; mother against daughter, and daughter against her mother; mother-in-law against daughter-in-law, and daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law” (Luke 12).

It should be noted that the two are father [Col. 1128C] and mother—that is, husband and wife—against whom the three are divided. But the two themselves, namely husband and wife, are in no way divided against one another because of the Gospel. A husband is not permitted to depart from his wife, nor a wife from her husband, on account of the Gospel—indeed, for no cause except fornication alone.

Thus, when the bowls of God’s wrath have been poured out, the great city is divided into three parts: that is, when the wrath of God has been revealed through the Gospel, some fleeing to repentance and others remaining in repentance, 477 the common human relationships, naturally so great, are divided threefold when they do not agree with one another in the way of the Lord: son departs from father, daughter from mother, and daughter-in-law from her mother-in-law.

When these divisions have taken place, as these are converted and become Jerusalem, [Col. 1128D] the city of God, while those others remain turned away, Babylon, the city of the devil, as they were, they undoubtedly become inexcusable. Then at last God remembers their sin, by which they persecute the faithful, as it is written: “For he who avenges their blood remembered; he did not forget the cry of the poor” (Ps. 9).

It follows: “And great Babylon came into remembrance before God, to give her the cup of the wine of the wrath of his indignation.” He calls the sentence of condemnation “a cup of wine,” adding “of wrath and indignation,” in contrast to the good and splendid cup concerning which God says in the psalm: “And my cup which intoxicates me—how splendid it is!” (Ps. 22). For just as that cup of grace happily intoxicates, so this cup of wrath, on the contrary, unhappily intoxicates: the city of the devil is lulled into eternal folly, as [Col. 1129A] Ecclesiastes says: “For there is neither work, nor reasoning, nor wisdom, nor knowledge in hell, whither you are hastening” (Eccl. 9).

He gives a further and greater reason why that city came into such remembrance before God. For he says: “And every island fled, and the mountains were not found.” This is as if he said: That city roused remembrance of itself to its own harm, because persecutions like waves of the sea drove the servants of God into hiding in remote places. Thus Paul too says, mourning over the saints of earlier times: “They wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins, needy, distressed, afflicted—of whom the world was not worthy—wandering in deserts, mountains, caves, and holes in the earth” (Heb. 11).

Moreover, islands commonly signify Churches in Scripture, [Col. 1129B] and mountains signify the more eminent saints. Did the preaching of the Gospel fall silent through the flight of the saints? Certainly not; rather, it gained strength. It follows therefore: “And great hail, like a talent in weight, came down from heaven upon men.” The sense is: the greater the persecutions endured by the saints, the more they preached and [Col. 1130A] revealed from heaven the wrath of God against all human ungodliness.

“This,” he says, “was great hail, like a talent.” By this statement he signifies that each person receives what he deserves, as if by weight according to the measure of his sin (Deut. 25). But those who are such people—ungodly and rebellious against righteousness and truth—become worse the more they are rebuked. Indeed, at times they even resist and contradict the word, and curse. It follows therefore: “And men blasphemed God because of the plague of hail, for it had become exceedingly great.” This means: the ungodly turned to blasphemies because of the unconquerable constancy of preaching; and because they could not defend themselves by reason, they raged in curses, because there was in the preachers such a spirit of wisdom and strength that they could not possibly be overcome.

[Col. 1130B] Such were first the Jews, concerning whom Luke says in the Acts of the Apostles: “When Silas and Timothy had come to Macedonia, Paul was occupied with the word, testifying to the Jews that Jesus was the Christ. But as they opposed him and blasphemed, he shook out his garments and said to them: ‘Your blood be upon your own heads; I am clean. From now on I shall go to the Gentiles’” (Acts 18).

# BOOK TEN

[Col. 1129]

[Col. 1129C] Thereafter, by fitting images and appropriate sayings, the Spirit of piety is shown—what he does or will do for his elect. For it is the work or office of the Holy Spirit, according to this very name, “the Spirit of piety,” to console all the saints who are pilgrims in this age and who endure persecutions while living devoutly (2 Tim. 3), so that they may not be wearied by adversities or envy evildoers when they are lifted up and exalted in the glory of this world and enjoy the riches they desire.

This is done in this part of the Scripture which we are now entering in two ways. First, it is shown that the power of the wicked who persecute the saints is soon to be taken away; then, that the glory of the kingdom of God will follow, in which God will be eternally praised with rejoicing by his saints frequently saying Alleluia. Therefore, as in the outpouring of the preceding seven bowls we rightly perceive the Spirit of knowledge to be proclaimed, so in these we do not doubt that the Spirit of piety is commended through his works, since he follows that Spirit in the often-mentioned order of the prophetic reading. For this is the sixth of the seven Spirits by whom grace is conveyed to the Churches at the beginning of this book. He says:

## CHAPTER XVII

“And one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls came and spoke with me, saying: ‘Come, I will show you the condemnation of the great harlot, who sits upon many waters, with whom the kings of the earth committed fornication, and those who inhabit the earth were made drunk with the wine of her fornication [prostitution].’”

[Col. 1130C] This one of the seven angels having seven bowls signifies one faith and one Spirit speaking in them. For all these angels—that is, all writers or expositors of the Scriptures whom the holy Church receives—say the same thing, think the same thing, and have no schisms among them.

John, who says that one of them came to him and spoke with him so many and such great words of consolation, here bears in his own person the figure of all the saints who, while pilgrims in this age, have merited or do merit to be strengthened in blessed hope through the consolation of the Scriptures. For when John saw these things, he had become their companion in tribulation, since he was in exile on the island of Patmos, sent there by the emperor Domitian because of the Gospel; and [Col. 1130D] therefore he deserved to experience in a personal vision their common consolations. 478

“Come,” he says, “I will show you the condemnation of the great harlot.” As though he said: Whoever you are, seeker of the eternal city or homeland whose one king is God, its founder, why do you look with such great sighs upon the advancing course of the earthly homeland, or city of the devil? It hastens to reign while the kingdom of the one King, God, is delayed a little: a harlot of many kings, like a hydra with many heads, and like a woman with many lovers. Do not grieve or grow weary in spirit as though because of the great good fortune of one who is now reigning and insulting your exile. Come, and I will show you her condemnation, though she appears great to herself.

“Because she sits upon many waters.” This harlot truly sits upon many waters, [Col. 1131A] because many are the nations over which desire rules. For waters here are peoples or nations. Thus a little later the angel explains to John: “The waters,” he says, “which you saw, where the harlot sits, are peoples, nations, and tongues.” Therefore, because this harlot sits upon many waters—that is, because many peoples or nations are ruled by desire—when he said, “I will show you the condemnation of the harlot,” he added “the great.” Yet such greatness is certainly deceptive, because it does not endure.

Nor is it without reason that nations or peoples are here signified by waters. Nations flow through generation of the flesh, and flow downward from their birth to the setting of death; they never attain a fixed place where they may be made firm and stand—that is, God. She is a great harlot, not by true greatness but by her own estimation.

He gives the reason why he called her a harlot, immediately adding: “With whom the kings of the earth committed fornication.” For it is true and great fornication for a rational creature—that is, a human being—to remove himself from God and cling to worldly desire. Thus the Psalmist, after saying, “For behold, those who remove themselves from you shall perish,” immediately adds: “You have destroyed all who commit fornication away from you” (Ps. 72).

This was done especially by the kings of the earth, for whose desire to rule no expanses of land were sufficient; indeed, for the enlargement of their borders they committed countless human slaughterings. By such fornication they came also to such madness that, having lost the dignity of reason, human beings [Col. 1131C] worshipped demons through different kinds of images and compelled the peoples subject to them to worship them.

It was therefore fitting that, after saying, “with whom the kings of the earth committed fornication,” he immediately added: “And those who inhabit the earth were made drunk with the wine of her prostitution.” By committing fornication with the desire of this world, they were made drunk: that is, just as those drunk with wine lose the power of discernment and say and do everything without reason, so they, utterly bent down toward the earth by desire, could not look upon the true Godhead in heaven, and imagined that the power of divinity was in their idols.

“Come,” he says, “and I will show you the condemnation of this harlot.” When he says, “Come,” we must understand that the elect soul is, as it were, called inward, [Col. 1131D] lest it too wander outside after the desire of the flesh and the desire of the eyes (1 John 2), but gather itself inward to the secret place of contemplation, where it may carefully weigh within itself, with the judgment of reason, the things which are and those which will be hereafter. This is what follows: “And he carried me away into the wilderness in the Spirit.” Because of its solitude, the wilderness here signifies the withdrawal of a solitary mind when it removes itself from the tumult of cares in order to investigate God’s truth. Thus, after saying, “he carried me away into the wilderness,” he aptly adds “in the Spirit,” because whoever seeks solitude of this kind is led not by flesh but by Spirit.

It follows: “And I saw a woman sitting [Col. 1132A] upon a scarlet beast full of names of blasphemy, having seven heads and ten horns.” A little earlier, the one speaking said that the harlot sat upon many waters; here he says that she sits upon the same scarlet beast. Therefore the multitude of waters itself—that is, of peoples or nations—is the beast. This is truly so, because the harlot woman sitting upon such a multitude of waters—that is, desire—drives it to live beastially.

This beast is called scarlet, a fiery colour, because every multitude ruled by desire burns for slaughter and lust. What its seven heads and ten horns are or were has already been said above, where the dragon stood before the woman who was about to give birth (Rev. 7), and where this same beast was seen rising from the sea. Something has already been said there also about the names of blasphemy with which it is said to be full. Nevertheless, the account of these heads, horns, and names of blasphemy must briefly be renewed.

The seven heads are the seven kingdoms of the world which, even in the time of the promise when Christ, the seed of blessing, was promised to our father Abraham (Gen. 22), assailed the faith of that seed and sought to extinguish it by attacking the faithful people: namely, the kingdom of the Egyptians, the kingdom of carnal Israelites, the kingdom of the Babylonians, the kingdom of the Persians and Medes, the kingdom of the Macedonians, the kingdom of the Romans, and the kingdom of Antichrist, which will be the last. These seven kingdoms of the world are the seven heads of the beast (Dan. 8).

Moreover, the ten horns [Col. 1132C] of the seven heads are understood as ten kings of those same seven kingdoms. For one of those kingdoms—the Macedonian—which while Alexander the Great lived had only one horn, that is, one king, Alexander himself, was divided after his death into the four winds of heaven and began to have four kings in one kingdom. In this way the horns become ten—that is, ten kings.

The names of blasphemy were names of usurped divinity, because the kingdoms or nations of the world, flattering their kings, wished them to be regarded as gods, and especially exalted the dead to heaven by false praises. “I saw,” he says, “a woman sitting upon such a beast”—that is, desire, and the corruption of all vices, reigning.

[Col. 1132D] “And the woman was clothed in purple and scarlet, and adorned with gold, precious stone, and pearls, having in her hand a golden cup full of the abominations and uncleanness of her fornication; and upon her forehead a name written: Mystery: Babylon the Great, mother of the fornications and abominations of the earth. And I saw the woman drunk with the blood of the saints and with the blood of the martyrs of Jesus.”

Intending to see the condemnation of the woman or harlot, in accordance with the angel’s promise, who said: “Come, I will show you the condemnation of the great harlot who sits upon many waters,” he first testifies that he saw the causes of that same condemnation. The first is that she openly professed the fornications and abominations of the earth. For when it is said, “And upon her forehead [p. 479] her name was written: Mystery: Babylon the Great, mother of fornications and abominations,” she is plainly accused of public profession: namely, that the city of the devil does not merely sin or commit fornication in some ordinary way, but even glories in its very sins and fornications.

[Col. 1133A] The second cause of her condemnation is that she shed the blood of saints who did not agree with her. This is what he repeats concerning his vision: “And I saw,” he says, “the woman drunk with the blood of the saints and with the blood of the martyrs of Jesus.” Let us therefore look more carefully at these two causes of her condemnation set forth here.

“And the woman,” he says, “was clothed in purple and scarlet.” Purple is royal apparel, and signifies the courtly power or pride of all the kingdoms or kings of this world. Who, moreover, does not know that murderous cruelty has almost always accompanied royal power? Books are full of it—indeed, the theatres of the whole world have by now been satiated with the tragedies of kings who, out of desire to rule, bore arms not only against foreigners but even cruelly ran the sword through kindred, brothers, or parents, lest they should endure them as partners or rivals in the kingdom.

[Col. 1133B] Scarlet is therefore rightly joined with purple, when it says, “And the woman was clothed in purple and scarlet,” because the fiery cruelty of murders has surely always accompanied the purple of kingdoms. And it is aptly said that “she was clothed in purple,” a phrase which calls to the attentive hearer’s mind how much vanity there is in the royal attire of the proud. For outwardly they may be coloured with beautiful appearances, the finest of which seems to be royal purple; but inwardly, or beneath that same purple, mortal bodies—of kings no less than of peasants—are miserable and wasting, not only through the ulcerations of unrestrained desire but also through various kinds of incidental disease.

It continues: “And adorned with gold, precious stone, and pearls.” All these are the woman’s riches; all these are the fruits of false and deceptive human covetousness. For human presumption seeks beauty outside itself, and desires an alien splendour as though it were its own. Unable to change its nature, namely that it is itself mud, it surrounds itself with glittering gold, precious stones, and pearls, so that, though sometimes foul with scabs and pallid leprosy, it may shine most proudly from above by means of such ornaments that do not belong to it.

[Col. 1133D] Yet this also sometimes greatly troubles the reasonable purpose of the elect and wearies their minds with manifold temptation. Therefore it continues: “Having in her hand a golden cup, full of the abominations and uncleanness of her fornication.” For why is she said to have a cup in her hand, except in order that she may offer drink and proffer her potion to all who pass by? And what is her potion but error and forgetfulness, by which the human mind, smeared with the enticements of vices, departs from God?

The woman, then, is said to have a cup “in her hand, full of the abominations and uncleanness of her fornication.” This cup is surely the entire fruit or effect of covetousness: it overthrows the rational human being and utterly overwhelms his mind, so that he commits fornication from the living and true God both in mind and body, handed over in soul to idolatry and subjected in body to every uncleanness and all shameful passions.

[Col. 1134A] The urgency of this most wicked intention should be noted. For, to allure more effectively and deceive more quickly, she is said to hold in her hand not a wooden or bronze cup but a golden one. This woman seized such a cup when the kings of the world, in order more easily to seduce the covetous and ambitious eyes of human beings, set up not only stone or wooden images but golden ones as well. To worship these was indeed the height of abomination and the beginning of all uncleanness and fornication.

For example: “When Jeroboam made calves not of wood or stone but of gold, placing one in Bethel and the other in Dan” (3 Kings [1 Kings] 12), then indeed the woman “had a golden cup in her hand, full of the abominations and uncleanness of her fornication.” For the desire to reign, which sat excessively over that man, deceived the eyes of the people by the beauty of gold, so that they might drink the fornication of the one who said: “These are your gods, Israel, who brought you out of Egypt,” and thus might commit fornication away from their God, depart from the house of David and from the temple of the Lord in Jerusalem (ibid.). Especially since among such gods they were permitted to eat and commit fornication, to defile and be defiled, and to subject their bodies in themselves to every abomination and uncleanness.

[Col. 1134B] The nations practised outrages of this kind not merely in secret but, worse still, frequented them publicly and everywhere with boasting. Hence it is written in the Book of Maccabees concerning a sacrilegious man of the Jewish people (1 Maccabees 7): “Because, following the example of the nations, he dared to establish a gymnasium and an ephebate in Jerusalem, and to place the finest of the ephebes in brothels” (2 Maccabees 4).

It therefore continues:

“And upon her forehead a name written: Mystery: Babylon the Great, mother of the fornications and abominations of the earth.”

This is as if one were to say: the citizens of the devil’s city do not even conceal the works of their shame; indeed, “they rejoice when they have done evil, and exult in the worst things” (Prov. 2). In short, what is it to have the name Babylon written upon one’s forehead except to attest publicly, by one’s profession, works of confusion?

[Col. 1134D] Accordingly God reproaches prostituted Judah through the prophet: “You have acquired the forehead of a harlot; you refused to be ashamed” (Jer. 3). This woman is therefore rightly said to have written upon her forehead the name “Babylon the Great, mother of the fornications and abominations of the earth,” because she is the body or totality of the ungodly, who have invented fornications and abominations and proceed brazenly in those very inventions. Of such persons it is likewise written: “They proclaimed their sin like Sodom; they did not hide it” (Isa. 3).

But if this is so, and she has this written on her forehead, glorifies herself in the worst things, and says that she is Babylon the Great, magnifying her fornications, how can what is written openly be called—or be—a mystery? For he says: “And upon her forehead a mystery written.” Therefore it is either said ironically, or for this reason: that nature itself wishes every act of fornication, in which this harlot glories, to be a mystery—that is, a secret. Although harlot-like impudence proclaims it, natural shame nevertheless strives to keep it hidden.

[Col. 1135A] This, as was said above, is the first cause given for the demonstration of her condemnation. It proceeds to declare another cause: “And I saw the woman drunk with the blood of the saints and with the blood of the martyrs of Jesus.” He had just seen the attire of this harlot, such that, even if it stood alone, it could have sufficed for her condemnation. But she, not content merely to be what the foregoing description signifies, added this further evil: she shed the blood of the saints because she saw that they did not consent to the uncleanness of her fornications.

The repeated word of vision, “And I saw,” is therefore rightly inserted, for he saw not another woman or harlot, but another iniquity of the same woman. Moreover, it should be observed that he distinguished between “saints” and “martyrs of Jesus,” saying: “with the blood of the saints and with the blood of the martyrs of Jesus.” He properly calls those “martyrs of Jesus” [p. 480] whom the same harlot killed after Christ’s coming for confessing the name of Jesus.

[Col. 1135C] Therefore, when he says “with the blood of the saints,” the reference should be understood as to the prophets and others who were killed for God’s covenant before Christ Jesus came in the flesh. When he adds, “and with the blood of the martyrs of Jesus,” he plainly denotes those who, as has been said, were killed for the testimony or confession of this name, Jesus.

Accordingly it is clear that the first and chief portion of this harlot was the Israelite people, which killed the holy prophets. Thus it deservedly bears feminine names and is convicted of having committed fornication with kings, such as those of whom it was written above in the condemnation of this harlot, with whom the kings of the earth committed fornication. For the Lord says through the prophet:

“Son of man, there were two women, daughters of one mother; and they committed fornication in Egypt; in their youth they committed fornication. There their breasts were handled and the breasts of their virginity were crushed. Their names were Oolla [Oholah], the greater or elder one, and Ooliba [Oholibah], her sister; and I had them—or they became mine—and they bore sons and daughters. Their names were Samaria, Oolla, and Jerusalem, Ooliba.

[Col. 1135D] Oolla therefore committed fornication against me, and raged—or went—to her lovers, the Assyrians, who approached her, clothed in hyacinth-blue garments, princes and magistrates, young men of desire—or all chosen men—horsemen riding horses. And she bestowed her fornications upon them, all the chosen sons of Assyria; and with all those for whom she raged, she was defiled by her uncleannesses—or inventions. Moreover, she did not forsake her fornications which she had practised in Egypt. For they had lain with her in her youth and had crushed the breasts of her virginity—or they themselves had deflowered her—and had poured their fornication upon her” (Ezek. 23).

So far is carnal Israel from being excluded from the name or body of this harlot, called Babylon here, that by divine authority it is thus designated by women’s and harlot’s names and reproved for raging in feminine lusts. “For,” he says, “their names are Samaria, Oolla, and Jerusalem, Ooliba.” You readily see how rightly this is said if you remember that the woman Jezebel raged in Samaria and her daughter Athaliah in Jerusalem, causing Israel and Judah to commit fornication with Baal and killing the holy prophets.

[Col. 1136A] Thus the woman drunk with the blood of the saints is also the Israelite people, as are the other nations—indeed, more than the other nations, because it shed the blood of saints; rather, because it shed the blood of Christ, the Holy of Holies. It is drunk because it neither understands nor sees, and has neither reason nor perception of truth. Rather, ensnared in every net of error by that drunkenness, it fulfils the prophecy which, yielding to divine justice, after first saying, “They gave me gall for my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink,” immediately added: “Let their table before them become a snare, a recompense, and a stumbling-block. Let their eyes be darkened so that they cannot see, and bend their back continually” (Ps. 68).

“Of the martyrs of Jesus” also—that is, of those who received or bore witness to Jesus by believing his Gospel—she first shed the blood, because she stoned Stephen the protomartyr (Acts 7), and Herod, to please her, killed James the brother of John with the sword (Acts 12). At that time she also scourged the other witnesses of Jesus in her synagogues and persecuted them from city to city (Acts 14).

[Col. 1136C] These things have been said so that there may be no doubt, nor any possibility of excusing carnal Judaism from being the first or chief portion of that great city Babylon—indeed, as it is written here, “the great harlot”—whose first foundations Cain laid when he killed his righteous brother.

It continues:

“And I marvelled when I saw her, with great amazement.”

This amazement belongs to an imperfect heart. A perfect heart does not greatly marvel at or esteem the harlot’s purple, scarlet, gold, precious stones, and pearls. Was this John, then, of an imperfect heart? Certainly not; rather, he bears in himself the figure of imperfect persons. Thus the great and holy prophet David expresses such amazement, not in his own perception but in the person of those whose hearts are imperfect, when he says: “But as for me, my feet were almost moved, my steps almost poured out, because I was envious of the wicked, seeing the peace of sinners” (Ps. 72).

[Col. 1136D] These things, and the rest that follows, he says not in his own sense but in that of others who still suffer weakness of mind, are still tempted, and long after the vanities of the age: they see themselves afflicted all day long, while sinners prosper and enjoy peace in their pleasures. For in his own voice he had said beforehand: “How good is the God of Israel to those who are upright of heart!” (Ps. 62).

So too this John, in the person of those who, still weak in heart, looked upon the splendour of the great harlot while they themselves were afflicted, testifies that he marvelled with great amazement. In his true understanding he would by no means have considered such things worthy of wonder. Yet for God’s elect, whoever through weakness marvel at or have marvelled at that harlot, consolation from the Holy Spirit has not been, and cannot be, lacking: the Spirit suggests to them that they ought not to have marvelled, or ought not to marvel, at her, and that she possesses nothing worthy of admiration as though it were happiness.

[Col. 1137A] It continues:

“And the angel said to me: Why do you marvel? I will tell you the mystery of the woman and of the beast that carries her, which has seven heads and ten horns. The beast which you saw was and is not, and is about to ascend from the abyss and go to destruction. And the inhabitants of the earth, whose names have not been written in the book of life from the foundation of the world, will marvel when they see the beast which was and is not.”

This speech of the angel rebuking admiration that is unworthy is an instance of the whole truth which instructs us in the holy Scriptures that we ought not to attend to “the things which are seen, but to those which are unseen; for the things which are seen are temporal, but those which are unseen are eternal” (2 Cor. 4). For example, when it says: “Do not emulate evildoers, nor be envious of those who work iniquity; for they shall quickly wither like grass and fade swiftly like the green herbs” (Ps. 36), and so forth.

[Col. 1137C] He says, then: “Why do you marvel?” As though he said: You who know eternal things and hope for eternal things, why are you envious? Why are your feet moved when you see such a beauty of the harlot—not true beauty, but phantom beauty?

And at the same time, as he had said above, “Come, I will show you the condemnation of the great harlot who sits upon many waters,” he begins to console those in whose blood she does not cease to intoxicate herself. He says: “I will tell you the mystery of the woman and of the beast which carries her.” This mystery—that is, secret—is the evil awaiting her, presently hidden from her eyes while she gleams and shines in purple, scarlet, gold, precious stones, and pearls. For the present she does not believe, nor does she wish to know, that anything evil can happen to her; rather, she says: “I sit as queen; I am not a widow, and I shall not know barrenness” (Isa. 47).

[Col. 1137D] The mystery, then—that is, the secret—is the judgment of condemnation which is to come upon her. This is revealed to saints and prophets, of whom John now bears the type, so that they may be consoled in God, their feet may not be moved, and they may not envy, as already said, the apparent peace of sinners. This also should not be passed over: the condemnation of this same woman or beast began especially to be revealed when the people of God was led into Babylonian captivity, so that the citizens of God’s delayed kingdom should not be moved from their hope when they saw the advancing and, as it were, morning glory of the kingdom of this world under which they were held captive.

For at that time Daniel saw visions and such images of events, as he says among other things: “And I saw that the beast had been slain, that its body had perished, and that it had been delivered to the fire to be burned” (Dan. 7).

[Col. 1138A] The phrase “the mystery of the woman and of the beast that carries her” may also be understood in another way, as signifying this: “I will tell you the mystery of the woman and of the beast that carries her, which has seven heads and ten horns”—that is, “I will tell you what the beast’s seven heads and ten horns signify.”

For it continues: “The beast which you saw was and is not, and is about to ascend from the abyss and go to destruction.” Let the captive children of Zion be greatly consoled, however tyrannically cruel and beastly Babylon may oppress them in captivity, because “the beast which you saw,” he says, “was and is not.” But the God in whom you, captives and exiles, have placed your hope “was, and is, and is to come.” For this same intention was expressed at the beginning of this book: “Grace to you and peace from him who is, who was, and who is to come.”

[Col. 1138B] Be consoled, then, because God, who is for you, always is; whereas the beast which is against you was and is not. It does not exist always: all that it does, avails, or can do is transitory. It ceases to be; the Lord, however, remains for ever.

“And it is about to ascend,” he says, “from the abyss and go to destruction.” This is as though he said: It will revive, in Antichrist, the power of its cruelty, which was and is not; but after raging for a little while, it will go to destruction, “because the Lord Jesus will slay him with the breath of his mouth” (2 Thess. 2). And now it may truthfully be said only that it was and is not; but then it will be said that this beast indeed was, but now is not and never will be.

“And the inhabitants of the earth,” he says, “whose names have not been written in the book of life from the foundation of the world, will marvel.” At what will they marvel? Clearly, at what I do not want you to marvel at, when I rebuke you and say, “Why do you marvel?” Let those marvel who do not look toward heaven but dwell upon the earth in mind as well as body.

[Col. 1138C] “Whose names have not been written in the book of life”: that is, those whom God did not predestine for life from the foundation of the world, namely, when God established the world or the human race; when, having created the first human beings, he blessed them and said: “Increase and multiply.” Those whom God did not then write in his book, whom he did not then command to be born by that blessing—because they do not belong to that blessing of the Creator—will marvel, just as they have marvelled hitherto, at such a beast.

Who are they? Surely all those for whose birth the sin of the first transgression was the cause; for on account of it all those superfluous persons were born, God saying to the woman: “I will multiply your miseries and your conceptions” (Gen. 3). They will marvel, and have always marvelled, at the greatness of the beast or the beauty of the harlot—at her purple, scarlet, gold, precious stones, and pearls.

[Col. 1138D] “Seeing the beast which was and is not.” In this they are already reproved for folly when it is said, “which was and is not.” By contrast, marvel at and proclaim as wonderful him “who was, and who is, and who is to come.”

“And here is the understanding which has wisdom.” This is as if he said: In the things you have seen and those which I say, meaning and benefit lie hidden; and the one who perceives them is the one who has wisdom—that is, one practised in the holy Scriptures.

“The seven heads are seven mountains upon which the woman sits, and they are seven kings.” We have already said above that the seven heads are the last seven kingdoms of the world. Each in its own time, as the sacred Scriptures testify, stood against God’s kingdom and oppressed its citizens, sojourning in this world, with various tribulations.

[Col. 1139A] First, the kingdom of the Egyptians afflicted the children of Israel (Exod. 1); second, the kingdom of the Israelites killed righteous people (Exod. 5) and, beginning with Jezebel, the prophets of the Lord (3 Kings [1 Kings] 19); third, the kingdom of the Babylonians burned Jerusalem with fire, carried its people captive, and sent the three youths into the furnace of fire (Dan. 3); fourth, the kingdom of the Persians and Medes, at the instigation of most proud Haman, nearly destroyed the entire Jewish race on account of Mordecai (Esther 5); fifth, the kingdom of the Macedonians, through Antiochus Epiphanes, cruelly afflicted that same people, under whom the brothers called Maccabees were crowned with remarkable martyrdom (1 Macc. 1); sixth, the kingdom of the Romans filled the world with Christian blood (2 Macc. 3); the seventh kingdom, that of Antichrist, will afflict the faithful with such tribulation that, if possible, even the elect may be led into error (Matt. 24).

[Col. 1139C] “These are the seven mountains,” that is, the seven kingdoms. Finally, he called these kingdoms mountains because of their pride, by which they swelled upward against God. Hence, after saying, “The seven heads are seven mountains,” he explained what he had said by adding, “and they are seven kings.” He used “kings” as equivalent to “kingdoms”; indeed, more properly, because it is not so much the kingdoms or tracts of land as the kings who are guilty, so as to be called and to be the heads of the beast.

Although many reigned in succession in the individual kingdoms, he nevertheless rightly sets down as many kings as kingdoms, because the present matter requires the numbering not so much of the persons who ruled as of royal powers.

It continues: “Five have fallen, one is, and another has not yet come.”

[Col. 1139D] For when John saw these things, in that age of the world the Egyptian king who oppressed the children of Israel, the Israelite king Ahab or Jezebel, she or whose posterity killed the prophets, the Babylonian king who carried the people of God captive, the Persian king—or rather Haman, the enemy of the Jews who incited him—and Antiochus of the Greek kingdom, who committed so many and such abominable acts against that people of God: these five had fallen and been buried in hell.

It should indeed be observed that such heavenly judgments were carried out upon every one of them that, if you consider each person’s end, you will not hesitate to confess that it was properly said that they fell. The Egyptian king fell into the sea with his chariots and horsemen (Exod. 14); dogs licked Ahab’s blood and ate Jezebel (4 Kings [2 Kings] 9); Nebuchadnezzar was expelled from his kingdom and ate grass like an ox (Dan. 4); Haman was hanged on the gallows (Esther 7); Antiochus, rotting away, ended his impious life by a miserable death (1 Macc. 6).

[Col. 1140A] Thus five had already fallen, and “one is,” he says. Who is this one? Clearly, the Roman king or emperor who then existed and raged against Christians when these things were spoken. Nero, disgraced, had already perished shamefully; yet the persecution which he had first decreed against Christians was then active in the Roman principate. Although many rulers of that empire persecuted Christians, the whole body of them is one king in relation to the one kingdom, as has already been said.

“And another,” he says, “has not yet come”: namely, the one who will be Antichrist. The one whom he said then existed and the other whom he asserts had not yet come are added to the five who had fallen, and thus become seven. Having said, “And another has not yet come,” he immediately added: “And when he comes, he must remain a short time.”

[Col. 1140B] Why must he remain a short rather than long time? Namely, because of the elect. “For,” the Lord says, “those days will be days of tribulation such as have not occurred from the beginning of the creation which God made until now, nor shall occur. And unless the Lord had shortened the days, no flesh would be saved. But for the sake of the elect whom he chose, he shortened the days” (Matt. 24). Thus, “when he comes, he must indeed remain, but for a short time.”

Here, because we are proud and weak, the Lord’s mercy, joined with truth, both terrifies us by the magnitude of adversity and restores us by the shortness of the time.

It continues: “And the beast which was and is not, she herself is an eighth and is of the seven, and shall go to destruction.” In this place the beast must be understood as one head of the beast, namely, the head which is Antichrist. “This beast,” he says, “is both an eighth and of the seven.” This is as if he said: Antichrist, one and the same head of the beast, is both the eighth and the seventh.

[Col. 1140C] This could not stand or be understood unless it were clear that there are two things together in one and the same Antichrist. For that son of perdition is at once man and devil. Thus, if you attend only to what is outwardly visible in Antichrist, he is of the seven, because he belongs to the race or nature of the other kings or ungodly persons. But if you look to that which is hidden within, he is the eighth head, because he is the devil, who, before entering the dwelling-place of that lost man, exalted himself in heaven against God and remains proudly invisible even now.

Nevertheless, “he shall go to destruction,” because it is as easy for God to send both man and devil to destruction as to send a mere or solitary human being. Thus it may truthfully be said of each: he was and is not; but God always is.

It continues:

[Col. 1140D] “And the ten horns which you saw are ten kings, who have not received a kingdom, but will receive authority as kings for one hour after the beast.”

This has already been said above: there are indeed seven most notable kingdoms from the sequence of the holy Scriptures which exercised hostility against the saints of the Most High; but there are ten kings of those same kingdoms, because one of them—the kingdom of the Macedonians—was divided after Alexander’s death, by the four winds of heaven, among his four successors. Each placed a diadem upon his own head, and in this way ten kings came into being (Dan. 8).

He said above, “And they are seven kings,” but now says, “They are ten kings,” because three of Alexander’s successors are not recorded as having done anything against the people of God, but only the fourth, who held Syria. Thus they are ten in number; but with respect to the action belonging to the present matter—that is, the persecution of the martyrs—they are only seven.

[Col. 1141A] But since a little earlier he said, “Five have fallen, and one is,” how does he now say, “who have not yet received a kingdom”? By a remarkable irony, as though he said: They appeared indeed to reign and arrogated to themselves royal pomp and title, but they never truly reigned. Their kingdom is not truly a kingdom, for the kingdom belongs to the Lord alone (Ps. 21; Ps. 101).

This bears upon the rebuke above: “Why do you marvel?” Kings of this sort truly are not to be admired but judged miserable: in order to rule, they committed so many murders, yet they fell, died, and have not received the kingdom. But what then? “They will receive authority,” he says, “as kings for one hour after the beast.” They will receive not a true kingdom but a certain power as if they were kings; and they will receive it for one hour after the beast.

[Col. 1141B] It is as though he said: Do not call, or suppose that one ought to call, their exaltation a kingdom. For kingdom implies enduring power; but they received, or will receive, not enduring power but power for one hour. He said “will receive” in the future tense because, when Antichrist comes, he will restore the strength or kingdoms of those kings who have already fallen for the persecution of the saints.

What kind of authority they will receive, he briefly indicates when he says, “after the beast.” This is as if he said: for the shedding of the blood of the saints, because the beast’s power is not truly for ruling but for raging, for shedding blood. It was therefore aptly and truly said that they have not yet received a kingdom.

It continues:

“**These have one purpose, and they will hand over their strength and power to the beast. These will wage war with the Lamb, and the Lamb will conquer them, because he is Lord of lords and King of kings; and those who are with him are chosen, called, and faithful.**” These, he says, have one purpose—understand, when Antichrist comes and remains for a short time; for all will conspire in agreement with that son of perdition. But what of those kings before the coming of that Antichrist? Did they not already have one purpose with him who was to come? Did they not have the same intention? the same will? Indeed, by the purpose, intention, and will with which he will persecute the saints when he comes, the king of Egypt and the others already mentioned afflicted the people of God in their own times [Col. 1142A]: namely, so that no one might remain mindful of the one true God. In them and through them the devil strove to make void the faith in the promise—namely, the promised seed, which is Christ, whom God promised beforehand to the patriarchs.

This was the ancient purpose of that serpent when he first deceived humankind: that no human being should be saved. With this same purpose he armed all those whom we have repeatedly named: Egyptians, carnal Israelites, Babylonians, Persians or Medes, Macedonians, the Antiochene kings, Roman Caesars; and finally he will raise up the head of this same design in that oft-mentioned man of sin, Antichrist. Truly, therefore, these have one purpose.

“**And they will hand over their strength and power to the beast**” [Col. 1142B]. This is as though he said: What they intended, they could not, or will not, accomplish; but the devil, whom they serve, will make his own man Antichrist heir to their strength and power, so that what he could not achieve through them, he may perhaps at least accomplish through this outstanding instrument. But what follows? “These will wage war with the Lamb,” he says, “and the Lamb will conquer them.” All have long ago been conquered, each in his own time; and still all together will be conquered in the one Antichrist.

Although he could have said, “They will fight against Christ, and Christ will conquer them,” he preferred to say, “They will fight against the Lamb, and the Lamb will conquer them,” because their first representative, the Egyptian king, was conquered by the sacrifice of the lamb, so that he let the children of Israel go; and, pursuing them, he was drowned in the Red Sea [Col. 1142C] (Exod. 12). Therefore, although he speaks in the future tense—“These will fight against the Lamb, and the Lamb will conquer them”—it must nonetheless also be understood of the time before John: they fought against the Lamb, and the Lamb conquered them.

For John here bears the type of all those who, from ancient times, when the people of God began to be afflicted under the kingdoms named above, deserved to be divinely comforted. This is wonderful—indeed praiseworthy—and true: before this Lamb came into the world, they fought against the Lamb, and he himself conquered them. Thus the prophet is quite elegantly commanded to call his name, “Quickly take the spoil; swiftly plunder,” or, “Hasten to take the spoil; hurry to plunder” (Isa. 8). Why? [Col. 1142D] “Because,” he says, “before the child knows how to call his father and his mother, the strength of Damascus and the spoil of Samaria will be carried away before the king of the Assyrians” (ibid.).

This is as though he said: This child, who is the Savior, before he comes into this world by birth, knowing or experiencing his mother—the Virgin, certainly—and Joseph, his most excellent father, will himself deliver Israel from the hand of its enemies. A marvelous speed, a wondrous haste: that the child, not yet born, should deliver the people possessing or awaiting the promise of his birth. Yet this is so true that whoever does not believe it is not faithful. For one must believe that, before this child was born of his mother, he was almighty God with the Father.

Accordingly, after saying, “And the Lamb will conquer them,” he immediately added [Col. 1143A], “**Because he is Lord of lords and King of kings.**” Did he not, before he was born, also conquer the Babylonians, Persians or Medes, and Macedonians, who fought against him—that is, against his own people who held faith in his future coming—and held them captive? For what else is shown to King Nebuchadnezzar or to the prophet Daniel when the stone cut out without hands struck the great statue, and gold, silver, bronze, and iron were shattered together? (Dan. 2). What, I ask, except that Christ, who is called the Lamb, before he was born, hastened with the marvelous swiftness already mentioned to conquer, and did not permit his elect, held captive under those kingdoms, to be tested beyond what they could bear?

For he who, after being born of the Virgin, finally conquered and broke the iron—that is, the Roman Empire—by the word of evangelical preaching, himself before his birth shattered the gold and silver: that is, the great and strong Babylonian, Persian, and Macedonian kingdoms. Prophetic truth had gone before. For example, Daniel foretold concerning Antiochus Epiphanes: “And he will be broken without hand”; and so it came to pass (Dan. 8; 2 Macc. 6). Struck by God with an invisible and incurable plague, he wasted away and ended his miserable life miserably, as he deserved.
