Therefore “the Lamb,” he says, “will conquer them,” since even before his birth he conquered the first of them. Hence there is no doubt that he will conquer the rest as well. The saints, or his elect, share in his victory; for while they labor, the Lamb conquers by aiding them. Therefore he added [Col. 1143C]: “**And those who are with him are chosen and called and faithful.**” These, indeed, fight and conquer; but they attribute victory to the Lamb, without whom they know that they neither could nor can conquer. Thus one of them, after saying, “Because I labored more abundantly,” immediately added: “Yet not I, but the grace of God with me” (1 Cor. 15).

“The chosen, called, and faithful” are those of whom the Apostle says: “Those whom he predestined, them he also called; and those whom he called, them he also justified; and those whom he justified, them he also glorified” (Rom. 8). Those whom he predestined are here called chosen; for to be predestined is to be chosen, or chosen beforehand. Likewise, “those whom he called” are here called called. And “those whom he justified” are here called faithful [Col. 1143D], because the righteousness or justification of the chosen, predestined, and called is faith. Thus the same Apostle, after many arguments of truth, says: “Therefore, having been justified by faith, let us have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ” (Rom. 5). Likewise, “those whom he glorified” are here said to fight and conquer with the Lamb. For to have conquered such a beast is true glory.

It follows: “**The waters which you saw, where the harlot sits, are peoples and nations and tongues.**” Peoples and nations over whom the harlot sits are rightly designated by the name of waters, because, precisely because such a mistress presides over them, they are fluid and unstable. But when he says, “peoples and nations,” the Israelite tribes of whom Balaam the diviner speaks are undoubtedly not excluded [Col. 1144A]: “The people shall dwell alone and shall not be reckoned among the nations” (Num. 25). Therefore, by “peoples” in this place are meant the carnal tribes of Israel, while the term “nations” designates the other peoples.

For who can doubt that this harlot sits, or has sat, even over Israel—that is, the Jewish people? They especially committed fornication with worldly desire, since they killed the saints and prophets who rebuked their fornication. Thus they too are waters, through their own fault, as the prophet says: “Hear this, house of Jacob, who are called, and who have come forth from the waters of Judah” (Isa. 48): that is, you who are children only of flesh and not of faith (Rom. 10).

When he said, “They are peoples and nations,” why did he add “and tongues”? This would necessarily follow even if he had not said it, since only peoples and nations speak in tongues. Why then did he add “and tongues,” unless perhaps to recall to us that the pride of this great harlot deserved that tongues should be divided and multiplied in the very time of her infancy or wanton youth [Col. 1144B]? For when the tower of Babel was being built by the pride of people wishing to ascend into heaven—a tower from whose name this harlot herself is now called Babylon—God, seeing this, confused their language; and, divided from one another, they withdrew from one another (Gen. 6). Thus it was not without reason that, after saying, “The waters upon which the harlot sits are peoples and nations,” he added, “and tongues,” so that he might not omit that the divisions of languages also were a loss or plague inflicted upon us by the pride of this harlot.

It follows:

“**And the ten horns which you saw, and the beast [in the beast], these will hate the harlot, and will make her desolate and naked; they will eat her flesh and burn her up with fire.**” A remarkable assertion; a remarkable and vehement detestation of the wicked. How are the kings designated by the horns said to hate their harlot, with whom they themselves commit fornication? For these kings, and no others, are those of whom it was said above: “Come, I will show you the condemnation of the great harlot, who sits upon many waters”; and it was added: “With whom the kings of the earth committed fornication.” Therefore these very persons, who commit fornication with her, are said to hate her, make her desolate and naked, eat her flesh, and burn her herself with fire [Col. 1144D]. This is astonishing, yet true.

For who does not know with what great hatreds the kings of the world have always been troubled? And against whom were they hostile in their unrest except against the very desire or glory of the world with which they committed fornication, preferring it to their Creator? The instruments of their fornication were the beauties of cities, the abundant wealth of the nations over which they ruled, and all other such things in the world that provoke the lust of the eyes. Yet they never allowed these things to flourish in peace: they laid all waste by wars, killed crowds of people by the sword, and burned cities and fortresses with fire.

Nor did kings merely do these things to one another—kings against kings and kingdoms against kingdoms—in hostile fashion. Individual kings very often inflicted these evils upon their own peoples and cities [Col. 1145A]. For, to say nothing of others, who was a crueler or more wicked enemy to the city, people, and senate of Rome than its own emperor Nero? He made the city desolate; by slaughtering its people and senate, he in some manner ate its flesh. He also burned the city with material fire, merely that he might delight in the beauty of the flames, watching in them a likeness of how Ilium had once burned. Sitting in the highest Maecenatian tower, dancing with delight at such a spectacle, he sang the *Iliad*.

One who remembered and lamented such cruelty sang thus:

> We know what ruin he brought,  
> When the city was burned and its fathers slain—  
> He who, fierce after killing his brother,  
> Was drenched with his mother’s outpoured blood.  
>
> Alas for the grievous lot, etc.

(Boethius, *The Consolation of Philosophy*, bk. 2, met. 6.)

It is therefore true that the kings of the earth, having abandoned God and committed fornication with the beauty of worldly creatures, hate their own harlot; and the price of their fornication was the fierce hatred that they rendered to her. “For there is no peace for the wicked, says the Lord” (Isa. 57). O wretched condition of Babylon, the earthly city, which commits fornication away from God with her lovers! For she not only commits fornication with lovers, but with enemies; and whatever love exists among them is so mixed with the gall of bitterness that they savagely tear apart the very one with whom they commit fornication.

The devil is the cause or instigator of these evils. Therefore he did not merely say, “And the ten horns which you saw will hate the harlot,” but: “And the ten horns which you saw, and the beast,” he says, “will hate their harlot,” and so forth [Col. 1145C]. He immediately adds: “**For God gave it into their hearts to do what was pleasing to him, to give their kingdom to the beast, until the words of God should be fulfilled.**”

“To do,” he says, “what was pleasing to him.” To whom? This seems to refer to God, because it was previously said, “For God gave it into their hearts,” and may thus be understood: “that they should do what was pleasing to him”—that is, to God. Yet, since he had said before, “And the ten horns which you saw and the beast will hate the harlot,” and then, after saying, “that they should do what was pleasing to him,” added “that they should give their kingdom to the beast,” it is more correctly referred to the same beast: that they should do what was pleasing to him—that is, to the beast—and then, “that they should give their kingdom to the beast”; that is, that they should devote all the strength of their kingdom to the devil, doing his will, which always opposes God’s good purpose.

For what do they do but evil? Yet evil does not please God; indeed, he hates those who work evil, as Scripture testifies concerning him: “You have hated all who work iniquity” (Ps. 5). Likewise: “For you are not a God who wills iniquity” (ibid.). But Scripture again says: “Making peace and creating evil” (Isa. 45). Within these considerations, according to the logic of truth and the truthful authority of the orthodox Fathers, it must be said and believed [Col. 1146A] that the evil which is affliction or war, contrary to peace—the evil of which it is said, “making peace”—God sometimes creates for correction. But evil in the sense of iniquity or sin he neither creates nor finds pleasing.

It is indeed his will that, when war or another such affliction comes upon those who deserve to suffer it because of preceding sins, they should not be able to escape it. But that human beings should do evil or become evil has never been and is never pleasing to him. The question therefore arises: if the evil they do, or their very being evil, is not pleasing to God, how is it said here beforehand, “For God gave it into their hearts”? When this is asked, one must consequently, or at the same time, ask also concerning what the Psalmist says: “He turned their heart so that they hated his people and dealt deceitfully with his servants” (Ps. 104).

This must be understood in such a way that no suspicion can ever find a place in the human heart that God is in any respect the author of hatred or deceit—a notion even to suspect which is utterly mad and impious. For God neither hardened Pharaoh nor turned the heart of the Egyptians to hatred by willing their hardness or hatred. Rather, he merely did good to the children of Israel, multiplying them in that land, as he had promised Abraham, saying: “I will bless you and multiply your seed” (Gen. 22). But Pharaoh and the Egyptians, being proud, were also envious; and according to the habit of the envious, the more and greater the benefits of God which they saw bestowed upon those whom they envied, the more fiercely they raged against them with greater hatred [Col. 1146C].

Foreseeing this, God said to Moses: “I will harden Pharaoh’s heart” (Exod. 7). This is as though he said: I will indeed perform signs and wonders for the children of Israel before Pharaoh and his servants; but because they are envious, this will avail them for nothing except that they become hardened against them in still greater hatred. Father Augustine explains the verse cited above in this sense.

Thus what is said here—“For God gave it into their hearts”—must likewise be understood so that we never suppose that God put into the hearts of any of those kings the impulse to do anything evil or to become evil. Rather, he did the good he willed for individual kingdoms in their proper times; but the kings of the world, being proud, were also envious, and envied one another’s prosperity [Col. 1146D]. For example, God made the Babylonians prosperous so that they might be stronger than other nations. And, lest there be any doubt that this was given to them by God, God himself says in the prophet: “I have placed an iron yoke upon the neck of all these nations, that they may serve Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon; and they shall serve him. Moreover, I have given him even the beasts of the earth” (Jer. 28).

This gift of God stirred the hearts of the Medes and Persians—who were envious and equally proud—to rise up and inflict upon them whatever evil they could, God not resisting them but indeed permitting it because of Babylon’s sins. In the same way, later the prosperity of the Persians and Medes stirred up the Macedonians; and that prosperity was brought to them not by chance but by God’s ordering. Therefore, he says, “God gave it into their hearts to do what was pleasing to him, to give their kingdom to the beast” [Col. 1147A]: that is, prosperity granted to some by God’s gift stirred the hearts of other envious persons to hatred; and, incited against one another by envy, they devoted all the powers of their kingdoms in rivalry to the service of diabolical malice.

Until when? “Until,” he says, “the words of God should be fulfilled”: that is, until the judgments which God foretold through his saints and prophets would come upon those kingdoms should be accomplished. For what was going to happen to them had not the word of God, spoken to humankind, predicted beforehand? Or what did the word of God predict about them except what ought justly to happen to them?

Indeed, it was to happen, and ought justly to happen, that the Egyptians, after oppressing the children of Israel, should themselves pay the penalty for their iniquity; and God himself foretold this beforehand when speaking to Abraham [Col. 1147B]. For he says: “Knowing beforehand, I know that your seed will be a stranger in a land not its own; and they will reduce them to servitude and afflict them for four hundred years. But I will judge the nation which they shall serve, and afterward they shall come out with great possessions” (Gen. 15).

Likewise, it was to happen that the kings of Israel and Judah, because of the abominations they committed and the innocent blood they shed, should receive their deserved recompense; and finally that both Israel and Judah should be led away captive into Assyria and Chaldea. God repeatedly foretold this through the prophets: the books of the prophets are full of it—Isaiah (ch. 10), Jeremiah (ch. 27), and also Ezekiel, proclaiming the Lord’s words in this manner (ch. 12). Likewise, Babylon was to be overthrown by the Medes and Persians, and God foretold this beforehand through the same prophets and through Daniel (Dan. 7). Likewise, the Persians and Medes were to be conquered by Alexander the Macedonian, and God showed and foretold this beforehand through the Daniel already mentioned (Dan. 8).

Likewise, both the Macedonians and the other nations were to be crushed and trampled down by the power of the Roman Empire; and God showed this beforehand to the same Daniel through the fourth beast, great, terrible [Col. 1147C], and exceedingly strong, having iron teeth, devouring and crushing, and trampling the rest under its feet. Likewise, Antichrist is to surpass all these kingdoms through the working of the devil dwelling in him, and to crush the saints of the Most High more than all of them; and this the Son of God predicted beforehand not only in the prophets but also himself in his Gospel.

Therefore it is rightly and truthfully said, “until the words of God should be fulfilled,” because the kingdoms of the world have done and can do nothing as though against God’s purpose which God did not foreknow—indeed, did not also foretell. Yet the boundless perversity of all must be noted. For it is said first, “These will fight against the Lamb,” and then that they will hate the harlot and make her desolate, and so forth. They fight together against God, agreeing in this through one spirit of malice; but with regard to their own desires, or because of desire for the things of the world, they rage discordantly and savagely against one another. In every manner these serpent heads disagree among themselves [Col. 1148A].

Finally the same angel says: “**And the woman whom you saw is the great city which has dominion over the kings of the earth.**” In a brief recapitulation he renews what he said above, or what Scripture itself inscribed on the woman’s forehead: “Babylon the great, mother of fornications and abominations of the earth.” Moreover, what he there said, “with whom the kings of the earth committed fornication,” he has here altered slightly by saying, “which has dominion over the kings of the earth.”

What was said there indeed says much to signify the shame of the kings of the earth; but this says much more to disclose their servile folly, when it is said, “which has dominion over the kings of the earth.” What then? Do not earthly kings walk with head held high and trust that they are free? Yet behold: they are proved to have a kingdom over themselves; and, what is most shameful, a harlot woman is asserted, reasonably and irrefutably, to reign over them and press upon their necks [Col. 1148B]. Therefore they lie when they declare themselves free, for they are slaves: bearing the harlot’s yoke, always panting, bent under its burden, slaves of as many masters as they are captives of vices.

## Chapter XVIII

“**After these things I saw another angel coming down from heaven, having great authority; and the earth was illuminated by his glory. And he cried out with a mighty voice, saying: Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great; and she has become a dwelling-place of demons, a prison of every unclean spirit, and a prison of every unclean and hateful bird, because all nations have drunk of the wrath of her fornication, and the kings of the earth have committed fornication with her, and the merchants of the earth have grown rich from the power of her luxuries.**”

The angel who was speaking does not yet seem to have fulfilled the promise by which he had said, “Come, I will show you the condemnation of the great harlot.” Yet another angel is now introduced, crying in a mighty voice; and he especially sets forth the condemnation of the same harlot, whereas the former only identified what she was and described her heads and horns. You will rightly and properly understand this according to the reality if you recall that this harlot had first been denounced by the entire prophetic order, especially by Daniel, who spoke much against her lusts and cruelty; and then the Son of God himself came, the great and mighty Angel, of whom the prophet says: “Behold, the Lord whom you seek will come to his temple, and the Angel of the covenant whom you desire” [Col. 1148D] (Mal. 3). He cried in a mighty voice that her condemnation was now at hand in the hearing of the whole world, and proclaimed it by evangelical manifestation.

He now says that he saw another angel descending beautifully from heaven, because this one descended from heaven through humility, whereas another fell through pride. “He has great authority,” he says; and this has much bearing on the present matter, namely the condemnation of the harlot here displayed. For he himself, speaking of himself in one place, after saying, “As the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son also to have life in himself,” immediately added [Col. 1149A]: “And he gave him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man.” Likewise: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5). Thus he rightly said, “having great authority”: authority to execute judgment or condemnation upon the harlot.

“**And the earth was illuminated by his glory.**” This too was truly said, just as the prophet Zechariah sang at his coming: “The Dayspring from on high has visited us, to give light to those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death” (Luke 1). And when he came, he said of himself: “I am the light of the world; whoever follows me shall not walk in darkness” (John 8, 12). Likewise: “As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world” (John 9). This illuminating Angel “cried with a mighty voice, saying: Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great” [Col. 1149B].

Where or when did this Angel cry this out? Surely before a great crowd of Jews, when the moment of his passion was at hand; for through that passion the city of the devil was made to fall. For he said: “Now is the judgment of the world; now the prince of this world will be cast out.” And he cried this not in any ordinary manner, but “with a mighty voice”: that is, strengthened against the weakness of the flesh by the power of his divinity. For his flesh was weak, so that he said: “Now my soul is troubled; and what shall I say? Father, save me from this hour” (ibid.). But he immediately strengthened himself, saying: “But for this reason I came to this hour. Father, glorify your name” (ibid.). This strengthening or power is indeed memorable and praiseworthy. Therefore it was rightly and fittingly said that he cried with a mighty voice.

But how do the parts of this cry or utterance not contradict one another? For after saying, “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great,” he added: “And she has become a dwelling-place of demons, a prison of every unclean spirit, and a prison of every unclean and hateful bird.” How has she both fallen and nevertheless become so closed and fortified that birds cannot fly? To this it must briefly be said that, when this Angel cried—that is, when Christ suffered, whose passion was indeed a great cry [Col. 1149D], concerning which the Apostle says, “Who, in the days of his flesh, offering prayers and supplications with a mighty cry and many tears to God who was able to save him from death, was heard because of his reverence” (Heb. 5)—the city of the devil fell in such a manner at his cry that all and only the elect could escape and pass over its ruins, their bonds of both original and actual sins broken, because of the righteousness of their faith.

Therefore he rightly says both “Babylon has fallen” and nevertheless “she has become a dwelling-place of demons and a prison of every unclean and hateful bird,” because in the elect alone every structure of sin and every power of death and hell has fallen. In the reprobate, the condemnation of sin and the penal prison of hell remain. What he called “a dwelling-place of demons,” he repeated in saying, “a prison of every unclean spirit.” Demons, indeed, are unclean spirits. And why did he repeat it? Because the condemned angels, who are demons or malignant spirits, will pay penalties for two causes [Col. 1150A].

One cause is that in heaven they grew proud against their Creator. The other is that they defiled the human race, deceived through its first transgression by the serpent, with every filth of vice. On account of the former, demons—that is, beings aware that they exalted themselves against the knowledge of God—are so called; on account of the latter they are called unclean spirits, because they are utterly foul. For, as has already been said, by their suggestions they afflicted the human race with manifold passions of impurity and disgrace.

Moreover, by unclean and hateful birds are rightly understood all the proud, both demons and human beings. For the flight of birds signifies the lightness and vanity of the proud [Col. 1150B]. Nor are they compared with just any birds, but with unclean ones—for example, owls or hoopoes, which delight to perch upon human excrement and are therefore rightly considered unclean and hateful. Babylon has become a prison for such birds, and, as it is said through Isaiah, “It will not be able to fly away from distress” (Isa. 8).

The cause or explanation of the fall which follows is clear and has in part already been expounded: “Because all nations drank of the wrath of her fornication; and the kings of the earth committed fornication with her; and because the merchants of the earth became rich from her luxuries.” Three things are said here: that all nations drank of the wrath of her fornication; that the kings of the earth committed fornication with her; and that the merchants of the earth became rich from her luxuries.

In sum, the entire reproach of fornication is laid upon the kings, and they are repeatedly marked in this passage by the crime of that fornication. And rightly so, because they not only received what that harlot taught but also enforced it by the decree and sword of their empire [Col. 1150C]. The nations, however, which, subject to kings, worshiped monsters either at their rulers’ command or voluntarily in place of God, rightly “drank,” he says, “of the wrath of her fornication.” He does not merely say that they drank of her fornication, but “of the wrath of her fornication,” because immediately after the fornication by which they worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, God’s wrath followed: he abandoned them and gave them over to passions of disgrace, gave them over to the desires of their hearts unto uncleanness (Rom. 1), and gave them over to a depraved mind, to do what is unfitting.

But is it really being positively asserted that “the merchants of the earth” became rich through “the power of her luxuries,” rather than that those merchants are blamed for falsely supposing this? For Babylon itself—that is, desire itself, the root of all evils—and all who preside over desire, malignant demons and perverse human seducers of the world (1 Tim. 6), the whole company of whom is here called Babylon and the great mother of fornications—this perversity, I say, did not create and give the goods by which the merchants of the earth became rich. Rather, the goodness of the one God did so; but they supposed otherwise.

Therefore God rightly says through the prophet about such persons [Col. 1151A]: “I will not have mercy on her children, because they are children of fornications; for their mother has committed fornication. She who conceived them has been put to shame, because she said: ‘I will go after my lovers, who give me my bread and my waters, my wool and my flax, my oil and my drink’” (Hos. 2). “And she did not know that I gave her grain, wine, and oil, and multiplied silver for her, and gold, which they made into Baal.”

Moreover, the fact that he did not merely say “from her luxuries,” but “from the power of her luxuries they became rich,” marks their folly: among them poverty is regarded as a reproach and despised as if it were a monstrous vice, while abundance of riches is judged a virtue. Yet, on the contrary, even a pagan says:

> Silver is more worthless than gold; gold than virtues.

[Col. 1151B] It must nevertheless be noted that he was not content to say once only, “Babylon has fallen,” but with the word for falling or ruin repeated, he says: “Babylon has fallen, has fallen.” Repetition is indeed affirmation; but one must also understand that this Babylon, when this Angel uttered the cry mentioned above—that is, when Christ suffered for the salvation of all—fell in both places: among those below and those above, that is, it fell among the dead and the living.

For her infernal power was broken and lost the dead, so that the people of the saints, held captive in death, might go out from those prisons and bonds. And her falsehood was exposed and overthrown here among the living, in the temples and images of demons, so that those whom the devil held captive in various errors might be called through evangelical preaching from their darkness to the true light, and might go forth to the living God. Therefore the word is rightly doubled, because both there the power of death and here the worship of demons fell.

“And I heard another voice from heaven saying: ‘Come out of her, my people, lest you share in her sins and receive of her plagues, because her sins have reached as far as heaven. And the Lord has remembered her iniquities.’” After that angel cried out, “I heard another voice from heaven,” he says, because after Christ himself preached the Gospel and suffered, the Holy Spirit came from heaven and gave other tongues to Christ’s apostles. From that time the triumph of the Lord’s Passion began to be proclaimed [Col. 1151D] throughout the whole world; from that time repentance and the remission of sins began to be preached among all nations (Acts 2). “Therefore come out,” this voice says, “from Babylon, my people”—that is, repent, and let each one of you be baptized in the name of the Lord. For this is truly to come out of Babylon. “My people,” he says—that is, every one of you who has been foreordained to eternal life. For outwardly the Gospel is preached to all, and often even the reprobate are brought, as it were, to faith; but within the purpose of God only the elect are sought.

And what he intends in saying, “Come out,” he aptly defines in adding: “lest you share in her sins and receive of her plagues.” Thus they are not commanded to go from one place to another, but to change their manner of life, so that, having abandoned sins and her above-mentioned fornications [Col. 1152A], they may consequently and deservedly be kept free from her plagues also. “For,” he says, “her sins have reached as far as heaven”—that is, by committing fornication and making herself drunk with the blood of the saints, she has advanced so far as to kill the very King and Lord of heaven. “And therefore,” he says, “the Lord has remembered her iniquity”—that is, he has appointed the day of universal judgment, on which her iniquities shall be punished. Hence it follows: “Render to her as she herself rendered to you, and repay her double according to her works. In the cup in which she mixed, mix double for her. As much as she glorified herself and lived in luxury, give her so much torment and mourning.”

Who are those commanded to render to her as she rendered to them and to double the recompense according to her works [Col. 1152B], except those who, when the Lord sits in judgment upon the throne of his majesty (Matt. 9), will themselves sit upon judicial thrones—namely, the saints and martyrs of Jesus, with whose blood this harlot is shown above to be drunken? “Render to her,” therefore, he says, “as she rendered to you”—that is, condemn her as she condemned your innocent blood. It would have been too little merely to say, “as she rendered to you,” unless he had immediately added, “and repay her double according to her works.” For it is clear that, while she persecutes the saints and martyrs of Jesus, she kills only the body, “and after this has nothing more that she can do”; but they have this power at the judgment together with the same Lord Jesus, to cast body and soul into Gehenna (Luke 12). Rightly, therefore, he says: “Repay her double according to [Col. 1152C] her works.” Likewise, in the cup in which she mixed, “mix double for her.” And immediately he says: “As much as she glorified herself and lived in luxury, give her so much torment and mourning.” For the boasting by which she exalted herself, give her mourning; for the luxuries in which she indulged without restraint, give her torment.

These are the two causes of her condemnation: one, because she returned evil to the saints and martyrs of Jesus by shedding their blood; the other, because she abounded in her luxuries and fornications. These causes were indeed set forth above and are here repeated in reversed order. The chief mark of her guilt is her boundless pride in sin: she does not merely sin or commit fornication in some ordinary way, but glories in her sins and fornications, [Col. 1152D] or glorifies herself. Hence it is further added: “Because she says in her heart: ‘I sit as queen [or: I sit, a queen], and I am not a widow, and I shall not see mourning. Therefore in one day her plagues shall come: death, mourning, and famine; and she shall be burned with fire, because God who judged her is mighty.’”

That she should speak thus in her heart, “I sit as queen,” and so forth, and that she must therefore suffer these plagues, prophetic truth had long before confirmed. For in the prophet Isaiah, among other things, it is said to her: “Come down and sit in the dust, virgin daughter of Babylon; sit upon the ground” (Isa. 47). “Virgin” is said there with the most severe irony; here she is truly declared to be a harlot. Then it is said to her: “You said: ‘I shall be mistress forever.’ You did not lay these things upon your heart, nor remember your latter end. And [Col. 1153A] now hear this, you luxurious one, who dwell securely, who say in your heart: ‘I am, and besides me there is no more. I shall not sit as a widow, nor know barrenness.’ These two things shall come upon you suddenly in one day: barrenness and widowhood” (Isa. 47), and so forth.

Therefore, because of her pride—because this harlot does not merely sin, but sins proudly, and in sinning is proud and exults that she is not a widow, as is the city of God which is a pilgrim in this world, since she is a harlot and many kings commit fornication with her, as though this were the lawful marriage of a blessed queen, powerful and ruling—for this reason, I say, it is a just and irreproachable judgment “that these plagues should come upon her: death, mourning, famine, and that she should be burned with eternal fire.” Nor is this judgment doubtful [Col. 1153B] in that it must certainly take effect: “because,” he says, “God who judged her is mighty,” and having once pronounced the sentence by voice or in writing, he is not unable to fulfill it.

“And the kings of the earth who committed fornication with her and lived in luxury shall weep and mourn over her. And when they see the smoke of her burning, they shall stand far off for fear of her torments, and shall say: ‘Woe, woe, that great city Babylon, that mighty city, because in one hour your judgment has come.’”

Here it is helpful to recall that writing or volume concerning which it is written in the prophet Ezekiel: “And I looked, and behold, a hand was sent to me, in which was a rolled-up book; and he spread it before me, and it was written within and without, and in it were written lamentations, and [Col. 1153C] song, and woe” (Ezek. 2). That book is all Scripture inspired by God; it is spread out before the prophet because, through the grace of Christ opening it, it is made intelligible to the faithful person. In that book “lamentations, song, and woe” are written. Of these three, song and woe are opposites, while lamentations hold, as it were, the middle place. For the holy Scriptures promise an eternal song to the saints and elect in the age to come; but woe to all the ungodly—such as the kings of the earth denoted in this passage, who committed fornication with the harlot and lived in luxury, and the merchants of the earth who became rich from the abundance of her luxuries. Lamentations, however, belong to penitents, who temporarily mourn their sins in the present life lest they come to that eternal woe.

All these things—namely, “lamentations, song, and woe”—the present passage of this Scripture displays together to diligent readers. For when it says, “Come out of her, my people, lest you share in her sins and receive of her plagues,” repentance, as has already been said, is preached to all nations; and this is assuredly to lament. But the woe which belongs more plainly to the ungodly is expressed here when they themselves say: “Woe, woe, that great city Babylon, that mighty city, because in one hour your judgment has come.” And again: “Woe, woe, that great city, which was clothed in fine linen, purple, and scarlet, and adorned with gold, precious stones, and pearls, because in one hour such great riches have been laid waste [Col. 1154A].” Likewise, for the third time: “Woe, woe, that great city, in which all who have ships at sea became rich through her wealth, because in one hour she has been desolated.”

“Woe” is repeated twice on the third occasion, and thus “woe” is said six times. And throughout the same reason is given for saying “Woe, woe,” though with a few words altered: “because in one hour your judgment has come”; “because in one hour such great riches have been laid waste”; “because in one hour she has been desolated.” For then the crimes of all the ages of the world—which are six in number, having no seventh, that is, no Sabbath—will be punished together in them. And it will be a strange and most wretched thing for those who love this wicked age so greatly to see that the evil works of so many days and times, of so many ages of the world, are judged [Col. 1154B], and that their joys perish when an endless magnitude of torments succeeds: one hour of judgment, one hour of destitution, one hour of desolation. Then all things will perish together in which the lustful lovers of the world reveled with the oft-mentioned harlot: “gold and silver, precious stones and pearls, fine linen, purple, silk, scarlet, every kind of thyine wood, every vessel of ivory, every vessel of precious stone, bronze, iron, and marble”—all of which belong to the fornication of the eyes.

Then follow “cinnamon and amomum,” and the other kinds of incense and fragrant substances, which clearly are referred here to the lustful sense of smell. Then there are also kinds of ointment, which concern luxury. Then, he says, “wine, oil,” [Col. 1154C] fine flour, and wheat, which, or things like which, are referred to taste. After many items there follows the sound of harpists and musicians, of flute-players; and the trumpet will no longer be heard in you. These concern the fifth bodily sense, hearing. Thus all instruments of fornication which entice through the five bodily senses are condemned, through which senses every adultery of the soul that commits fornication away from God is practiced. “The services of beasts of burden and sheep, horses, chariots, slaves, and human lives” are likewise numbered among the household goods of the perishing world. Fruits too are expressly named, because they themselves must perish from disordered desire, when it says: “And your fruits, the desire of the soul, have departed from you.” Likewise there are included among these [Col. 1154D] “whatever things are provocations to gluttony or trials of the kitchen,” when it adds: “And all rich and splendid things have perished from you.”

Almost all the instruments of pleasure, whatever and however great they may be, which are taken in through the five senses of the body and through which the nobler part of the human being languishes and is enslaved, are expressly named as destined to perish, by the fitting diligence of the one who saw and wrote. For in that hour, when this world begins to be consumed by the final fire, it will present a wretched spectacle to all its lovers, who will see, not without great pain, the destruction of whatever they possessed with excessive love. Therefore, to show that the violence of their grief will be no small matter, he sets forth once, twice, and a third time the inconsolable misery of those who weep and mourn [Col. 1155A]. For he says: “And the kings of the earth shall weep and mourn over her.” Again: “And the merchants of the earth shall weep and mourn over her, because no one will buy their merchandise any longer.” And then: “And every helmsman, everyone who sails to a place, sailors, and those who work the seas stood far off; and seeing the place of her burning, they cried out, saying: ‘What city is like this great city?’ And they cast dust,” he says, “upon their heads.”

Dust upon their heads signifies the sadness of repentance. But that repentance is no longer useful or fruitful, because it is too late. At the same time, it must be understood that among these very penitents there is now no reason or wisdom. For what rational measure of repentance is there in this woe, where, weeping [Col. 1155B] and mourning, they cry out and say, “What city is like this great city?” Even now they suppose that the image of transient glory which they had seen was a great city. Thus they grieve not so much that they admitted harmful pleasures as that those same pleasures perish irrecoverably for them. Indeed, if they could rescue from the fire and retain for themselves all these perishing incentives of desire, which are here individually named together with their torment, they would wish to do so. But without doubt they will be unable; and, as these things perish, help will be far from those who perish with them.

Hence, with a great indication of their weakness, it is said here once, twice, and a third time that they stood far off. “When,” he says, “the kings see the smoke of her burning, standing far off for fear of her torments [Col. 1155C], they shall say: ‘Woe, woe.’” Again: “And the merchants of men, who became rich from her, shall stand far off for fear of her, weeping and mourning, and saying: ‘Woe, woe.’” And a little later: “And every helmsman and the sailors stood far off, and cried out weeping and mourning and saying: ‘Woe, woe.’” All alike—kings as well as sailors and helmsmen, sailors as well as merchants—will stand far off, not so much in place as through a failing heart and feeble spirit. For kings will then have neither weapons nor armies to fight; sailors, no oars with which to sail; merchants, no shops in which to collect their wares. For all assistance from beasts of burden, horses, and chariots will be lacking.

Meanwhile, note that shepherds or country-dwellers are not written as having this weeping and mourning, because the occupations of a simple life serve necessary use rather than superfluous desire. Sailors are rightly not excluded from such weeping and mourning, because they too laugh and glory somewhat as they row and are carried across the seas on a favorable course. That this is so, anyone who has ever seen ships successfully sailing with full canvas, and heard the boisterous *celeuma* of sailors—that is, a nautical song—can have no doubt. Nor can these be considered as excusable as country-dwellers or shepherds, with some of whom God spoke from the beginning, since ships not only for trade but also for war have run under the strength of their arms [Col. 1156A], and have often stained the waves of the sea with the blood of war. It follows:

“Rejoice over her, O heaven, and apostles and holy prophets, because God has judged your judgment upon her.” We have already spoken in its place of lamentations and woe; of the song, which was the third thing written in the above-mentioned volume, we shall speak later in its place. For the present, let us pursue what remains concerning the condemnation of the great harlot, and what still belongs to her woe. “Rejoice over her,” he says, “O heaven, and apostles and holy prophets, because God has judged your judgment upon her.” And immediately it follows: “And one mighty angel lifted up a stone like a great millstone and threw it into the sea, saying: ‘With such violence shall that great city Babylon be thrown down, and [Col. 1156B] shall be found no more.’”

It must be held in memory that this whole condemnation of the harlot was revealed for consolation not only to John here, but also to the earlier prophets, as we said at the beginning of this vision: so that they might have consolation amid adversities and patiently endure tribulations, knowing that the opposing party which persecutes them will not remain so forever, will not prevail forever by speech, but will be removed from the midst, leaving God’s kingdom at peace and causing it no further stumbling-block. When this has happened, as the preceding discourse indicated with vehement proclamation, there will indeed be full joy for angels and holy human beings. He says therefore: “Rejoice over her, O heaven”—that is, you heavenly company of angels now completed from among human beings—“rejoice, apostles; rejoice, holy prophets; and all you martyrs of Jesus, because God has judged your judgment upon her,” because what your cry demanded has come to pass, when you said: “How long, O Lord, holy and true, will you not judge and avenge our blood upon those who dwell on the earth?” (Rev. 6).

Here the words of that voice heard above from heaven come to an end, which began thus: “Come out of her, my people.” But this mighty angel, who is immediately said to have lifted a great stone like a millstone and thrown it into the sea, saying: “With such violence shall that great city Babylon be thrown down and [Col. 1156C] shall be found no more,” signifies the strong and mighty Lord himself. Sitting upon the throne of his majesty, with all nations gathered before him, he will say with his own mouth to those at his left: “Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25). For then the whole city of the devil will truly be thrown with great violence into the abyss; and as a great stone thrown into the sea does not float and does not spring back again, so she, once cast down, will no more emerge from hell.

And he fittingly said not merely some stone but “like a millstone,” to express the likeness: because this Babylon is as heavy with the weight of sin as she is unstable through the agitation of error. A millstone suitably indicates both things, since it is heavy in weight and constantly turns in performing its grinding work. And immediately it follows:

[Col. 1157A] “And the sound of harpists and musicians, of flute-players and trumpeters, shall no more be heard in you.” We anticipated this above in order to continue the account of the pleasures of the five bodily senses, because the other things mourned there serve the other senses in their luxuriance, whereas hearing is soothed by these—that is, musical instruments. Nor without reason is all the music of so great a harlot condemned. For the things sung by her are slippery and wanton—indeed, even shameful phantasms of demons—and this harlot especially misuses their sweetness as incentives to lust. But in the true praises of the true God, the rational service of the art of music is most beautifully and praiseworthily received; and for those who sing lawfully and make psalmody wisely, the reward or prize will be the eternal song, concerning which this Scripture shortly afterward, declaring good hearing, magnificently consoles the patience of the saints.

“And every craftsman and every craft shall no more be found in you. And the sound of a millstone shall no more be heard in you. And the light of a lamp shall no more shine for you. And the voice of bridegroom and bride shall no longer be heard [Col. 1157B] in you, because your merchants were the princes of the earth, because all nations were led astray by your sorceries. And in her was found the blood of prophets and saints, and of all who were slain on the earth.”

Here all things are as they are said to be. For not only will no crafts of any kind remain—for instance, those of planting or building—but even the things which had been planted and built will be wholly taken away. For it is further written (1 Cor. 7) that the form of this world passes away; and they will neither grind nor seek or find other services for the belly, and thus they will lack every lamp’s light, so that the ungodly may remain in the eternal horror of darkness. And as it is true what was promised to them above, that they will say, “Woe, woe,” so it is certain and unchangeable what is now said: “And the voice of bridegroom and bride shall no longer be heard in you.”

What is added—“Because your merchants were the princes of the earth”—is as though he said: Therefore no convenience of any kind will remain in you, because, even if you seemed to possess something of some sort of justice, you received your good things in your own time, the things you sought; and in order to acquire or safeguard them, you had and observed certain laws, outward or inward, not inconsistent with reason [Col. 1157C]. For you did not observe anything of the kind for the sake of true life, but so that your princes might trade more safely in the acquisition of gold and silver, estates and maritime regions, and so that nothing might be lacking for the fulfillment of pleasures. You have therefore received your reward; henceforth the condemnation stored up for you is now due and is now rendered to you by eternal judgment.

This is for those two reasons: because through your sorceries they were led astray, and because in you was found the blood of prophets and saints—causes which have already been discussed more fully above. Nor is the blood of prophets and saints alone demanded from you, but also that of all who were slain on earth, because what was the cause of all wars and homicides except covetousness, the root of all evils? We have now spoken of the lamentations of penitents [Col. 1158A] and of the manifold woe of the ungodly and impenitent. Let us now, with more careful understanding, gather the great and desirable voice heard from heaven concerning the song of the righteous.

## CHAPTER XIX

“After these things I heard as it were a great voice of many trumpets in heaven, saying: ‘Alleluia; praise and glory and power are to our God, because his judgments are true and just, because he has judged the great harlot who corrupted the earth by her prostitution, and has avenged the blood of his servants from her hands.’ And again they said, ‘Alleluia.’ And her smoke rises unto ages of ages. And the twenty-four elders and the four living creatures fell down and worshiped God who sits upon the throne, saying: ‘Amen, alleluia.’ And a voice came forth from the throne [Col. 1158B], saying: ‘Give praise to our God, all his servants, and you who fear him, small and great.’ And I heard as it were the voice of a great trumpet, and like the sound of many waters, and like the sound of great thunders, saying, ‘Alleluia.’”

This is the hearing of consolation; this is the song written in the above-mentioned book: a song of exultation, your song, O pilgrim citizens of the heavenly homeland, who are pilgrims and mourn in this world. When those kings, those merchants, those helmsmen and sailors weep and mourn as they see the vanities and false madnesses in which they trusted perish, and say, “Woe, woe,” then you will sing “Alleluia.” For *Alleluia* is a Hebrew word, interpreted, “Praise the Lord”; and many psalms bear this title. In one of them it is thus inscribed: “Alleluia: the return of Haggai and Zechariah.” The prophets Haggai and Zechariah foretold that the captivity of the children of Israel brought about by Nebuchadnezzar would be ended, and [they foretold] the destruction of the temple; they themselves also took part in their return to Jerusalem and the rebuilding of the temple. This is a likeness, plainly, of all the elect returning from this pilgrimage—where that condemned harlot Babylon inflicted evils upon them—to their eternal and heavenly city, Jerusalem.

“After these things,” therefore, he says, “I heard as it were a great voice of many trumpets in heaven, saying: ‘Alleluia.’” A remarkable contrast must be noted: those people, lamenting, say three times, “Woe, woe, that city”; but these, rejoicing, say three times, “Alleluia.” First, he says, “I heard as it were a great voice saying, ‘Alleluia’” [Col. 1158D]; second, he says again, “They said, ‘Alleluia’”; third: “And they worshiped God seated upon the throne, saying: ‘Amen, alleluia.’” Nor content with this, he repeated again what he had said: “And I heard as it were the voice of a great trumpet, and like the sound of many waters, and like the sound of many thunders, saying: ‘Alleluia.’” Thus *alleluia* is said four times.

And if one wishes to take the interpretation or meaning of this word as equivalent in force, then, just as “woe” was said six times there, so here *alleluia* is said six times. For after *alleluia* is first said, there follows: “Praise and glory and power are to our God.” Again, after it is said, “And they worshiped God seated upon the throne, saying: ‘Amen, alleluia,’” there follows [Col. 1159A]: “And a voice came forth from the throne, saying: ‘Give praise to our God, all his servants.’” Therefore, just as there one hears “woe” six times, so here one hears six times *alleluia*, or praise to God: because those whose portion is woe stored up that woe for themselves through the six ages of the world, succeeding one another in those fornications; while these, whose portion is *alleluia*, likewise through the six ages of the world, succeeding one another, exercised themselves in holy virtues to the praise and glory of God.

Therefore they sing and praise, and praise is beautiful in their mouths. What do they praise in singing, and what do they sing in praising? Judgment and mercy, in which the whole subject of divine song and praise consists, as the Psalmist says: “I will sing of mercy and judgment to you, O Lord” (Ps. 100). Before judgment occurs, mercy is first sung, then judgment; but after judgment has occurred, the truth of the judgment will first be praised, then mercies will be sung forever. For now mercy is first withdrawn, and then judgment is rendered to those who despise mercy; but then judgment is first performed once and for all in act, and afterward mercy, as already said, is sung forever.

They therefore first praise judgment when they say: “Because his judgments are true and just, because he has judged the great harlot who corrupted the earth by her prostitution and avenged the blood of his servants from her hands.” They praise the truth of judgment for the two reasons for which, as we said above, the harlot was condemned: one, because she corrupted the earth by her prostitution [Col. 1159C]; the other, because she shed the blood of the saints. Then, in sweetest harmony, they praise mercy when they say: “Because the Lord our God Almighty has reigned, let us rejoice and exult, and give glory to him, because the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his wife has prepared herself, and it was given her to clothe herself with shining white fine linen.”

From this comes praise and glory; from this, joy and exultation; from this, *alleluia* so often repeated: because, while that woman, the harlot and prostitute, is judged, the Lamb and his wife—another woman, a blessed woman—celebrate their marriage. Thus they answer with *alleluia*, “because the Lord our God Almighty has reigned.” What Lord, or what God? The very Lamb with whom those fornicating kings fought, and who conquered them, “because,” he says, “he is Lord [Col. 1159D] of lords and King of kings.” Therefore let us rejoice and exult, because he conquered and reigned; and let us give glory to him—we who are “chosen and called and faithful,” who are with him and have conquered with him. As conquerors, or participants in his victory, let us give glory to him in him, so that we attribute our victory not to ourselves but wholly to him alone, the sole conqueror, the sole Almighty One.

And not merely because he conquered and reigned, but because his marriage has come and his wife has prepared herself, she whom the Father betrothed to him, saying in David’s bridal song: “Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever; the rod of uprightness is the rod of your kingdom. The queen stood at your right hand” (Ps. 44). In what did she prepare herself? “In a garment embroidered with gold, clothed round about with golden fringes and varieties” (ibid.) [Col. 1160A], of all which the first is shining and white fine linen. “For,” he says, “the fine linen is the righteous deeds of the saints.”

Moreover, the first justification, or the beginning of justification, is faith (Gen. 15), which, as it was reckoned to Abraham for righteousness (Rom. 4), so also, the Apostle says, “will be reckoned for righteousness to us who believe” (Eph. 2). This was given to her, namely to his wife, because faith is undoubtedly the gift of God. Hostile to this shining and white fine linen was the scarlet of the condemned harlot: not given, but seized; not shining, but dreadful; not white, but blood-red. This voice of those singing was like the sound of many waters and great thunders—indeed, like the sound of many trumpets—because it will be the voice and harmonious sound of many peoples, resounding with the great thunder of hearts, that is, with great devotion; and of many thousands of saints, as if sounding trumpets, arousing in their hearts not war but peace and love, ever coming to meet and ever to come to meet the Holy Trinity.

“And he said to me: ‘Write: Blessed are those called to the marriage supper of the Lamb.’” To every faithful soul this is so firm and certain that it is more fitting to sigh over it than to dispute the truth of the saying. It is true; and this truth is now known as if ancient, yet must always be known as if new. “Write,” therefore, he says, “because blessed are those called to that supper”—not a supper of just any calendar observance or festival, but of the marriage of the Lamb. For there the whole supper is love, where the wife—that is, the soul—is joined to the husband, God, not for an hour [Col. 1160C] but eternally, because this nuptial and conjugal love is eternal life. Hence comes that saying in the Psalm: “They shall be intoxicated with the abundance of your house, and you shall give them drink from the torrent of your delight” (Ps. 35).

“—And he said to me: ‘These words of God are true.’” The one who says this is one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls, who spoke above with him, saying: “Come, I will show you the condemnation of the great harlot who sits upon many waters” (Rev. 17), and so forth. He showed more than he promised, since he showed and enabled him to hear not only the condemnation of the harlot, but also the glorification of the blessed woman, the wife of the Lamb, and the hearing of the heavenly song, which is *alleluia*. “And these words,” he says, “are true words of God,” so that we may receive all these things not as the words of any human being, or even of an angel, but truly as God’s words, and judge them true and reasonable even if we are less able to understand or expound them.

Moreover, how gladly John received, and how highly he valued, such disclosures is clear from his saying: “And I fell at his feet to worship him.” And immediately it follows: “And he said to me: ‘See that you do not do it. I am your fellow-servant and of your brothers who have the testimony of Jesus. Worship God. For the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy.’” Thus John here, who could not have been ignorant that the one God alone ought to be worshiped by humankind, for a moment, because of the ecstasy of mind in which he was, attended to this less clearly. Yet he did not stray far from [Col. 1161A] sound judgment. For we read that before him some of the ancient saints prostrated themselves before angels and were not forbidden (Gen. 12). Why, then, did this angel forbid him so emphatically, saying, “See that you do not do it”?

Plainly because from the time when God became human, assumed the true nature of humanity, raised that same nature—given over to suffering and death for the whole world—and placed it at the Father’s right hand, and gave the Holy Spirit of reconciliation to human beings, now his brothers and friends, the dignity of human nature has risen above itself and been brought to the measure of angelic dignity. Therefore, after saying, “See that you do not do it,” he immediately gave this reason for the prohibition: “I am your fellow-servant and of your brothers who have the testimony of Jesus.” Therefore, he says, “Worship God [Col. 1161B], whom I too, your fellow-servant, worship.”

And immediately, as though you were asking what he meant by “having the testimony of Jesus,” or what the testimony of Jesus is, he took care at once to make it clear: “For,” he says, “the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy.” And what is the spirit of prophecy except the Holy Spirit? This is plainly our testimony, as the Apostle says: “You did not receive the spirit of slavery again in fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father.’ For the Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit that we are children of God” (Rom. 8).

Therefore, because the Holy Spirit is the testimony of Christ’s faithful people, and bears witness to them not about some insignificant matter but that they are children of God, they are rightly instructed in the person of John not to worship anyone except the one and only God, having regard to the dignity of their condition and grace received. Although it could properly have been said thus: “For the testimony of Jesus is the Holy Spirit,” or “the Spirit of adoption as sons whom they received,” yet for John’s person he more beautifully said: “The testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy,” because this Apocalypse is prophecy, as was stated in the opening of the book when it says: “Blessed is he who reads and he who hears [Col. 1162B] the words of this prophecy.” Therefore, in saying, “The testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy,” he wished John himself to be reminded of the more excellent grace which he had received; because, while all who have received the Holy Spirit have testimony that they are children of God, much more does this beloved disciple of Jesus Christ, who received such a great and lofty prophecy.

**BOOK ELEVEN**

[Col. 1161]

[Col. 1161C] The citizens of the kingdom of God, who are consoled while sojourning here among the children of this age, ought to rejoice and exult. The voice heard a little earlier from heaven sang this because the Lord has judged the great harlot, because the Lord our God Almighty himself has reigned, and because the marriage of the Lamb has come. They receive this consolation, instilled in their minds by the Holy Spirit, as an example of devotion, when they themselves say in David: “When the Lord restored the captivity of Zion, we became like those who are consoled. Then our mouth was filled with joy and our tongue with exultation. Then they will say among the nations: ‘The Lord has magnified his dealings with them’” (Ps. 125).

Therefore let us also rejoice and exult like those who are consoled—but in such a way that the fear of the Lord moderates and, [Col. 1161D] together with its discipline, directs that joy and exultation. For in the same David the very Spirit of the fear of the Lord says: “Serve the Lord in fear, and exult before him with trembling” (Ps. 2).

There are two kinds of fear: one servile or penal, which “perfect love casts out” (1 John 4), concerning which the Apostle says: “You have not received the spirit of bondage again in fear” (Rom. 8); the other free and sweet, concerning which the Psalmist says: “The fear of the Lord is holy, enduring for ever and ever” (Ps. 18). That servile fear has no place here. For where God’s elect are so consoled, after hearing and understanding the works of the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and strength, the Spirit of knowledge and devotion—works which, just as they are expressed here and there in the holy Scriptures, are also gathered beneath such great images in this mystical revelation—how could penal fear have any place? Therefore those who are consoled ought indeed to fear, but with holy fear, with chaste fear: namely, that they may humbly stand upon the foundation of humility, having been deemed worthy of the consolation of the Holy Spirit.

Accordingly, the salutary exposition is again taken up from another beginning; and he who has often in these revelations been seen or called the Lamb, Christ the Son of God, is beheld in this form once, again, and a third time, so that even those who are consoled may not forget that something still remains for them to fear. For it follows:

> “And I saw heaven opened, and behold, a white horse; and he who sat upon it was called Faithful and True, and with justice he judges [with justice he judges and [Col. 1162D] fights]. His eyes were like a flame of fire, and upon his head were many diadems; he had a name written which no one knows except himself. And he was clothed in a garment sprinkled with blood, and his name is called the Word of God. And the armies which are in heaven followed him on white horses, clothed in clean white linen. And from his mouth proceeds a sharp sword, that with it he may strike the nations; and he shall rule them with a rod of iron. And he treads the winepress of the wine of the fury of the wrath of God Almighty; and he has written upon his garment and upon his thigh: King of kings and Lord of lords.”

All these matters, carefully considered as far as the passage saying, “And I saw a great white throne, [Col. 1163A] and him who sat upon it, from whose presence earth and heaven fled; and books were opened; and the dead were judged; and judgment was rendered concerning each according to their works; and hell and death were cast into the lake of fire”—all these matters, I say, when attentively observed, are full of fear and fittingly and profitably instruct the prudent soul in holy fear. For no wise person dares boast that on that day, at that hour, he will be found duly prepared, with a chaste heart and a perfect conscience.

Nowhere among all that is revealed in this Apocalypse by the seven spirits who are before the throne of God is Jesus Christ, who is the faithful witness, seen beneath an image so terrible—from the place where he who sat upon the throne “was like in appearance to a jasper stone and [Col. 1163B] a sardius, and there was a rainbow around the throne” (Rev. 4), down to the present passage.

There we considered the revelations and adornment of the Spirit of wisdom. In the second place, the Lamb was seen in the midst of the throne; and when he received from the right hand of him sitting upon the throne the book, opened it, and loosed its seven seals (Rev. 5), we proclaimed the Holy Spirit of understanding in his works. In the third place, where an angel is written to have stood before the altar in his figure, holding a golden censer in his hand, while seven trumpets sounded in their order, the angel is again seen before the sounding of the last trumpet, with a rainbow upon his head (Rev. 8); there we surveyed the works which the Holy Spirit of counsel accomplished through him concerning us. In the fourth place, the male child born from the great woman in labour is seen, [Col. 1163C] who was to rule all nations with a rod of iron and who was caught up to God and to his throne; and there, amid the ensuing battles and the celebration of manifold victory, we recognized the Holy Spirit of strength at work (Rev. 12). In the fifth place, the Lamb is seen standing upon Mount Zion, while his companions play a new song upon harps; then the same Son of Man is seen with a sharp sickle in his hand, after whom come seven angels possessing and pouring out seven bowls full of God’s wrath (Rev. 14). There we observed what works, and works of what kind, the Holy Spirit of knowledge carried out concerning humankind. In the sixth place, or sixth recapitulation, after the harlot and the beast bearing her were shown, and after the statement concerning her horns—that is, the kings [Col. 1163D] of the earth, because they will fight with the Lamb and the Lamb will conquer them—an angel descending from heaven with great authority is likewise seen, and the earth is illuminated by his glory (Rev. 17). There we recognized, in the Spirit of piety speaking from his mouth, the deeds that pertain to consolation.

Nowhere did such a terrible countenance of his appear as in this seventh part of the vision, where he is first seen judging and fighting with an army and the sword of his mouth, and at last sitting in judgment while earth and heaven flee away. Therefore here, not inappropriately, he who is last in descending order among the number of the seven spirits—the Spirit of fear—is recognized in his proper order from the characteristic images of his works. Let us now follow the course of the Scripture.

“And I saw,” he says, “heaven opened, and behold, a white horse.” Here heaven opened signifies the gaze of God and our Lord descending toward us, according to that prophetic saying: “For the Lord looked down from his holy height; from heaven he looked upon the earth” (Ps. 101). Likewise: “Truth has sprung up from the earth, and righteousness has looked down from heaven” (Ps. 94). Finally, this is what immediately follows: “And behold, a white horse.” For the white horse is the Lord’s spotless body, assumed from the Virgin; of this we spoke more fully in the place where, as the Lamb opened one of the seven seals of the book, a white horse went forth, and he who sat upon it had a bow, and [Col. 1164B] a crown was given to him, and he went out conquering in order that he might conquer—the same one who there had a bow and went out with a crown, conquering in order that he might conquer (Rev. 6).

Here he is called Faithful and True: “and,” it says, “with justice he judges and fights; and his eyes are like a flame of fire; and upon his head are many diadems; and the armies which are in heaven followed him upon white horses; and from his mouth proceeded a sword sharp on both sides.”

First, how worthy and true are the names Faithful and True. For he is Faithful, namely to God the Father, whom he faithfully obeyed, as the Apostle says: “Consider Jesus, the apostle and high priest of our confession, who was faithful to him who made him, just as Moses also was in his house. For this man was deemed worthy of greater glory than Moses. And Moses indeed [Col. 1164C] was faithful in all his house as a servant, for a testimony of those things which were to be spoken; but Christ as a son in his own house, whose house we are” (Heb. 3). God himself also says through the prophet: “And I will make with you an everlasting covenant, the faithful mercies of David. Behold, I have given him as a witness to the peoples, a leader and commander to the nations” (Isa. 55).

Likewise, he is True—or rather, Truth itself: “I am,” he says, “the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14). And John the Baptist says: “But he who has received his testimony has set his seal that God is true” (John 3). Scripture indeed says: “Every man is a liar” (Ps. 115). But this one, because he is not only human but also God, is rightly called and is the true God—the man whose truth alone, or rather who, being Truth itself, sets us free.

He who gave these names also added their operative grounds, saying: “With justice he judges and fights.” For because he fights with justice, he attacks no one except for the cause of justice and conquers no one except justly. Indeed, he takes up the weapons of war only against the proud, as it is written: “God resists the proud” (Jas. 4). Certainly he is Faithful because he judges with justice and does not call evil good or good evil (Isa. 5); and undoubtedly he is True. And because he can never be deceived through ignorance, so as to judge unjustly, “his eyes,” it says, “are like a flame of fire.” He sees all things clearly and, as has already been said, cannot be deceived into judging unjustly.

His eyes are all seven in number: the graces of the Holy Spirit. Hence in this same book the Lamb, and in the prophet Zechariah the one stone, are written to have seven eyes (Zech. 3). Likewise, because “with justice he judges,” or fights justly, he always conquers and triumphs in battle both in his own person and in each of his faithful ones. Therefore it immediately adds: “And upon his head are many diadems.” That is, because the victories or crowns of all the saints are attributed to his glory and grace, there are many diadems upon his head.

Thus God speaks concerning him through the prophet Zechariah under the name of Jesus son of Josedec, the high priest: “Take from the captivity—from Boldai, Tobiah, and Idaiah—and on that day you shall come and enter the house [Col. 1165B] of Josiah son of Zephaniah, who have come from Babylon; and you shall take silver and gold and make crowns, and you shall place them upon the head of Jesus son of Josedec, the high priest; and you shall speak to him, saying: Thus says the Lord of hosts: ‘Behold, the man whose name is the East’” (Zech. 6), and so forth.

Finally, according to the mystical sense, crowns are placed upon Jesus son of Josedec, the high priest, from silver and gold taken from the captivity—that is, from those who have come from Babylon—because, as we advance and return to better things, the Lord is crowned through each of our virtues; indeed, when we are crowned through the virtue of repentance, the Saviour receives a crown in each individual, in accordance with what Paul also says: “Henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the righteous judge shall give me; and not to me only, but also to all who love the coming of our Saviour Jesus Christ” (2 Tim. 4).

Therefore, because in truth there are many diadems upon his head, and, as the Apostle says, “he himself is fulfilled all in all” (Eph. 1), it rightly follows: “Having a name written which no one knows except himself.” For apart from him no one knows by how great a name, or how greatly, he himself has been named or will be named; since apart from him no one knows the number of those by whose crowns he is crowned, and of whose salvation he is called the author. Where, then, does he have this name written, if it is not known? Certainly in the great book of life, which is nothing other than the secret of his knowledge or foreknowledge. For where the names of all the elect are written, there cannot be absent the number of those whose salvation he is the author; and that number is surely the definition of a certain name of his, unknown to all.

“And he was clothed in a garment sprinkled with blood, and his name is called the Word of God.” This is as though he said: This one, both as a passible and mortal human being, suffered and died, and is the impassible and immortal God. For in his passion his garment—that is, his flesh—was sprinkled with his own blood. Therefore the prophet, marvelling intensely, asks and says: “Who is this who comes from Edom, with garments dyed from Bosra?” And when he answers, “I who speak righteousness, and am a defender to save,” he asks: “Why then is your garment red, and your clothing like that of those who tread in the winepress?” (Isa. 63). Why, he says, did they make your garment red? Why did they shed your blood, if you speak righteousness, if you committed no sins and no deceit was found in your mouth? Therefore the garment sprinkled with blood is the innocent flesh which endured death and the shedding of its own blood.

Moreover, “his name [Col. 1166B] is called the Word of God”: the Word through whom “all things were made, and without whom nothing was made” (John 1), who could not die, and through whom even the flesh which had died was restored to life. Thousands of saints follow the example of his suffering and death. Therefore it says: “And the armies which are in heaven followed him on white horses, clothed in clean white linen.” His armies are the martyrs and all the saints—whoever in this world have contended for him in any manner. They are called armies because of the struggles which they endured.

How did they “follow him”? “On white horses,” it says, “clothed in clean linen.” “On white horses”: that is, in bodies made white by baptism, fittingly adorned by the righteousness of good works, signified by the clean white linen [Col. 1166C]. Thus they went and followed him, especially those who over and above the purity of their lives put on the sprinkling of their own blood through martyrdom. For he himself first sat upon a white horse and afterwards was likewise sprinkled with his own blood. Hence his bride rightly speaks in glory in the Song of Songs: “My beloved is white and ruddy, chosen out of thousands” (Song 5): white, namely through virginity; ruddy through suffering.

Furthermore, his armies are all the powers of heaven; and he is the one who is so often called in the prophets and Psalms “the Lord of hosts, the Lord of powers” (Isa. 6; Ps. 23). Here there is now much to fear, when it is said that “with justice he judges and fights,” and that he is the Lord of hosts or powers. For he is that king whom one must not rashly meet in battle: that is, before whom, or in whose judgment, one must not readily presume upon one’s own righteousness.

Indeed, according to that Gospel example, he has double the force against our force, whatever it may be. If ours is an army of ten thousand, his army is twenty thousand: that is, if we trust in our works of righteousness, he will set both our works and our thoughts against us for judgment. Therefore he urges and says: “Or what king, going to wage war against another king, does not first sit down and consider whether he can meet with ten thousand the one who comes against him with twenty thousand? Otherwise, while he is still far away, he sends an embassy and asks for terms of peace” (Luke 14).

Knowing this, the holy man says: “Truly I know that a man is not justified when compared with God. If he wishes to contend with him, he will not be able to answer him one thing in a thousand” (Job 9). And shortly afterwards: “How great, then, am I, that I should answer him and speak my words with him? Even if I have something just, I shall not answer, but shall plead with my judge” (ibid.). This means: Even if I have performed some righteous work, nevertheless I shall send an embassy and ask for terms of peace, because he plainly has at least double an army against me. That is, if I justify myself by works, he also brings thoughts into judgment, because he searches hearts. Hence it further adds:

> “And from his mouth proceeds a sword sharp on both sides, that with it he may strike the nations; and he shall rule them with a rod of iron.”

This is the sword of which the Apostle speaks: “The word of God is living and effective, and more penetrating than any two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit, joints also and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart; and there is no creature invisible in his sight” (Heb. 4). Therefore the sword is rightly said to be “sharp on both sides,” which “proceeds from his mouth,” because, since his name is and he is called the Word of God, he discerns not only deeds and words but also penetrates and strikes the innermost thoughts.

For example, when he says to the Pharisees: “Hypocrites, Isaiah rightly prophesied concerning you, saying: ‘This people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me’” (Matt. 15; Isa. 29). Likewise: “Why do you think evil in your hearts?” (Matt. 9), and many similar things.

For what purpose does such a sword proceed from his mouth? “That with it,” it says, “he may strike the nations.” This has already happened, is happening, and does not cease to happen until the end of the age, until he separates the good nations at his right hand from the evil ones set at his left, where he will exercise the final and irrevocable force of the sword—that is, the judicial sentence—upon either group according to their merits. For the present, the blow of him who strikes is indeed delayed, but the sword of him who threatens is already brandished. Hence the Psalmist says: “Unless you are converted, he will brandish his sword” (Ps. 7). Likewise, in the Song of Deuteronomy he himself says: “If I sharpen my sword like lightning, and my hand seizes judgment, I will repay vengeance to my enemies” (Deut. 32).

Thus it is truly said, “that with it he may strike the nations.” But it further adds: “And he shall rule them with a rod of iron.” Whom will he rule except repentant persons from among the nations? For because it is said that a “sword sharp on both sides” proceeds from his mouth, because it has been preached and is preached that he will strike the nations with the inevitable word of judgment, the nations who believe the Gospel have repented; and “he shall rule” these “with a rod of iron,” that is, with inflexible righteousness. So the Father says to him in the Prophet: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I shall give you the nations as your inheritance and the ends of the earth as your possession; you shall rule them with a rod of iron” [Col. 1168A] (Ps. 2).

What was immediately added there—“You shall break them like a potter’s vessel” (ibid.)—and what is said here, “that with it he may strike the nations,” can in part rightly be understood in a favourable sense.
