For there is a salutary striking and a profitable breaking: when the nations—that is, those from among the nations ordained beforehand for life—are shaken with fear upon hearing through the Gospel of the coming judgment, and are broken in heart unto repentance. But all who remain in unbelief will be struck to their harm and broken to their harm; they will be like an irrecoverable potter’s vessel, whose pieces cannot again be joined or glued together.

Someone may ask: But what of the Jews? Does this sword not reach them, though it strikes the nations in this way? Hear what follows:

> “And he treads the winepress of the wine of the fury of the wrath of God Almighty, and he has written upon his garment and upon his thigh: King of kings and Lord of lords.”

He who strikes or will strike the nations and rules them with a rod of iron already “treads the winepress of the wine of the fury of the wrath of God Almighty.” That is, he is already preparing a blow for that people; the causes are already stirred up on account of which the weight and pressure of the Roman Empire will come upon and press them, so as to enclose their multitudes and squeeze their armies into a narrow place by the forces of Titus and Vespasian. This pressure is certainly rightly and very fittingly signified by the winepress. For that nation was, or ought to have been, the Lord’s vineyard; and because, when it ought to have produced grapes, it produced wild grapes (Isa. 5), God himself foretold through the prophet that this evil would befall it: “For their vineyard is from the vineyard of Sodom, for their grape is a grape [Col. 1168C] of gall” (Deut. 32). Therefore God foretold in the Song of Moses that these evils were stored up with him and sealed in his treasuries to be repaid to them.

In the prophet Isaiah, after he had first said in his own person: “I will sing to my beloved the song of my cousin concerning his vineyard” (Isa. 5), and so forth, God finally says: “Now therefore, inhabitants of Jerusalem and men of Judah, judge between me and my vineyard” (ibid.). A few words later: “And now,” he says, “I will show you what I shall do to my vineyard: I will remove its hedge, and it shall be for plundering; I will tear down its wall, and it shall be for trampling,” and so forth. After threats of this kind, he again says: “For the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel, and the man of Judah his beloved plant” (ibid.).

David the prophet likewise, after saying, “You transplanted a vine from Egypt; you cast out the nations and planted it” (Ps. 79), and so forth, foresaw this winepress and this pressure: “The boar from the forest has destroyed it,” he says, “and the solitary wild beast has devoured it” (ibid.). For “the boar from the forest,” or “the solitary wild beast,” signifies the Gentile emperor and the Roman army. Therefore, after saying, “And he shall rule the nations with a rod of iron,” he fittingly adds, wishing to signify what was to happen to the unbelieving Jews: “And he treads the winepress of the wine of the fury of the wrath of God Almighty”—as though to say: The Jews will fall by the edge of the sword, they will be led captive into all nations, and there will be great distress upon the land and wrath upon this people.

Why, however, was he not content to say only “fury,” or only “wrath,” but joined both fury and wrath, saying, “the winepress of the wine of the fury of the wrath of God Almighty”? Surely because the wine of the Jews—which may more truly be called gall and poison, as Moses testified when he said, “Their wine is the gall of dragons and the incurable poison of asps” (Deut. 32)—that poisonous and bitter wine of the Jews, who gave the Lord of the vineyard himself gall and vinegar to drink while he hung upon the cross (Matt. 27), gained for itself not fury alone or wrath alone, but both fury and wrath together. That is, it acquired for itself condemnation not only in the present or only in the future, but in the present and future together: so that the Roman army might slaughter and take captive their bodies here, while the devil might possess their souls there and hell might torment them.

Moses expresses both acts of vengeance in one brief verse: “A fire,” he says, “has been kindled in my fury, and it shall burn unto the lowest depths of hell” (Deut. 32). Having said beforehand, “And he treads the winepress of the wine of the fury of the wrath of God Almighty”—words of the utmost gravity, for it is no light thing that God Almighty should be named in such a context—he suddenly adds, remarkably:

> “And he has written upon his garment and upon his thigh: King of kings and Lord of lords.”

In this subtle and weighty saying he strikes at the heart of the Jewish people’s guilt, for which they are trodden in the winepress of the fury of the wrath of God Almighty. For they are those citizens who, when this king, or nobleman, went away into a far country, according to the Gospel parable, to receive a kingdom for himself and return, sent an embassy after him, [Col. 1169C] saying: “We do not want this man to reign over us.” But when he had returned, having received the kingdom and settled accounts with his servants (Luke 19), he finally turned to his own people and said: “Nevertheless, bring here my enemies, who did not want me to reign over them, and kill them before me.”

Therefore, after they are killed before the king whom they denied, and are, according to the present passage of Scripture, trodden in the winepress of the fury of the wrath of God Almighty, it is suddenly added: “And he has written upon his garment and upon his thigh: King of kings and Lord of lords.” For they deserve ridicule and mockery, having rejected him in the belief that he could not be king except according to their own pleasure—unless they themselves wished it, unless they themselves received him.

With the same indignant rebuke the Prophet says in the Psalm, after stating: “Why have the nations raged, and the peoples imagined vain things? The kings of the earth stood forth, and the rulers assembled together against the Lord and against his Christ: ‘Let us break their bonds and cast their yoke away from us.’” He immediately adds: “He who dwells in heaven will laugh at them, and the Lord will mock them. Then he will speak to them in his wrath, and in his fury he will trouble them: ‘But I have been appointed king by him upon Zion, his holy mountain’” (Ps. 2), and so forth.

But upon what garment, or upon what thigh, does he have this name written: “King of kings and Lord of lords”? The garment of this king, Christ, must be understood differently according to the diversity of the passage. At times it signifies the holy Church, or the Catholic faith; at other times, holy Scripture. Both meanings may be understood from one verse of the Psalm, where he himself says: “They divided my garments among themselves, and cast lots over my garment” (Ps. 21). For the Lord’s divided garments signify the sacred Scripture, often corrupted by heretics, as the Psalmist says elsewhere: “They have destroyed what you have made perfect” (Ps. 10). His seamless upper garment, over which they cast lots (John 19), signifies the Church or Catholic faith, given to the faithful by divine election, which no one can corrupt.

Likewise, his garment signifies the Church when the Psalmist again says: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity: like ointment upon the head, which descends upon Aaron’s beard, which descends to the hem of his garment!” (Ps. 132). The meaning is this: the grace of the Holy Spirit, which dwells fully in Christ our head, first descended from him upon the strong men, the apostles, who are signified by Aaron’s beard; then upon the martyrs and the other children of the Church—great indeed, but inferior to the apostles—who are understood in the hem of the garment, because after the apostles they are foremost in the Church. Christ himself is adorned by that Church’s faith and virtues, as a person is adorned by putting on a precious garment.

In the present passage, however, the garment rightly signifies holy Scripture. Moreover, so that the garment and also his thigh, bearing this inscription, may be especially pleasing and shine with greatest beauty, both are one and the same holy Scripture: that Scripture which the fathers of his flesh—signified by the thigh—wrote. This is especially the Scripture of the Psalms, which is truly the Scripture of Christ’s thigh, because it is the Scripture of David, his father according to the flesh.

Indeed, that he is King of kings is written there in this way: “O God, give your judgment to the king, and your righteousness to the king’s son” (Ps. 71). This verse does not yet call him King of kings, but only king. Yet it later follows: “And he shall rule from sea to sea and from the river unto the ends of the earth. The kings of Tarshish and the islands shall offer gifts; the kings of Arabia and Sheba shall bring offerings; and all kings [Col. 1170D] shall worship him” (ibid.). Without any contradiction, the king to whom other kings offer gifts and bring offerings, and who is not only thus honoured but also worshipped by them, is King of kings. And human kings rightly worship this king, who, although human, is also God. This is indicated briefly and magnificently when it is said in the same Psalm: “His name endures before the sun.” This is as though one said: This king was God before he was born as a human being, because he existed before the world was made, of whose life and fair portion this sun that we see is a part.

But “Lord of lords” is not so explicitly expressed in this passage of Scripture, except where it says: “And he shall rule from sea to sea.” Let us therefore look elsewhere. The same father of his flesh, certainly lord of many servants, who by a public and solemn form of address, according to the honour due to kings, was called Lord—as you readily find in the history of his deeds—said elsewhere, I say, that same king and lord: “The Lord said to my Lord: ‘Sit at my right hand’” (Ps. 109). That reigning and ruling man called him his Lord, equally with God the Father. Likewise, in the same Psalm: “Rule,” he says, “in the midst of your enemies.” Many of those enemies surely are or have been lords, and have ruled and do rule over broad regions of the earth; yet, whether willing or unwilling, they cannot escape the dominion of this Lord.

Therefore it is true and evident that he has written upon his garment and upon his thigh—that is, attested in the Scripture which the fathers of his flesh wrote—that he is King [Col. 1171B] of kings and Lord of lords. His citizens who hated him could indeed deny him and send an embassy after him, saying: “We do not want this man to reign over us” (Luke 19). But they cannot annul or conceal this Scripture.

It follows:

> “And I saw another angel standing in the sun, and he cried with a loud voice to all the birds flying through the midst of heaven: ‘Come, gather yourselves to the supper of the great God, that you may eat the flesh of kings, and the flesh of tribunes, and the flesh of mighty men, and the flesh of horses and of those seated upon them, and the flesh of all, free and slave, small and great.’”

Here too this “other” angel—and indeed a third angel—signifies the same Christ, because of a different time and a different matter. For what was said earlier—“And I saw heaven opened, and behold, a white horse, and the one seated upon it, who will be called Faithful and True”—means Christ, true God incarnate from the Virgin. But this other angel standing in the sun is the same Christ, true Son of Man and of God, manifested in Israel in the appearance of a dove.

Moreover, what has already been said—“and upon his head were many diadems, and he was clothed in a garment sprinkled with blood,” and the rest—was said by anticipation. For from this point the same matters begin to be explained more fully through fitting figures and according to the order in which events accomplished or yet to be accomplished present themselves down to the end of the age.

Therefore, “I saw another angel standing in the sun”: that is, I saw Christ manifested in Israel by the great manifestation of the Holy Spirit, or dove, and the paternal voice. What it says—“standing in the sun”—is wonderful indeed, but not altogether unprecedented; for it was also said earlier in the more ancient Scripture: “He has placed his tabernacle in the sun” (Ps. 18). That is, openly he said and preached that he is God, the Son of God, made human for the sake of human beings, and that he truly assumed a human body.

He began to do this with the cry of a loud voice, calling the birds that flew through the midst of heaven: that is, with the calling of the apostles, by which he called them to leave everything and follow him (Matt. 4). For birds in this passage are understood in a good sense and signify the life of spiritual people, as in the saying: “Man is born for labour, and the bird for flight” (Job 5). And in the Gospel, after the Lord had said, “One will be taken and one left” (Luke 17), and the apostles asked, “Where, Lord?” he said: “Wherever the body may be, there the eagles will be gathered” (ibid.).

Thus the birds, with the favourable specification now given—those “which flew through the midst of heaven”—are the apostles. Yet this is said by anticipation: not because they were already spiritual beforehand, but because through that calling they became spiritual and knowers of lofty mysteries. These are the birds whose example or imitation should lead us to lay aside every anxiety about food or clothing, as the Lord says: “Look at the birds of heaven: they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and your heavenly Father feeds them” (Matt. 6).

For because the apostles, to whom this freedom of birds was first and immediately set forth for imitation, so that they might devote themselves to the contemplation of heavenly things, left behind all earthly things, they are rightly called birds of heaven. In this passage their calling is understood to be signified by the name of birds. Where, or when, did this angel say to such birds: “Come, gather yourselves”? Certainly by the Sea of Galilee, when he saw Peter and Andrew casting nets into the sea and called them, saying: “Come after me, and I will make you fishers of men” (Matt. 4). Likewise, calling the others from different places or occupations (Matt. 9), he surely said to the birds: “Come, gather yourselves.”

To what did he command them to come, to what did he command them to gather? “To the supper of the great God”: to that supper which he, having become human, prepared for us, according to the Gospel parable: “A certain man made a great supper and invited many. The people, however, excused themselves: one said, ‘I have bought an estate and must go out and see it’; another, ‘I have bought five yoke of oxen and am going to test them’; another, ‘I have taken a wife, and therefore I cannot come’” (Luke 14).

But these birds, or fowls, just as they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, do not buy estates, acquire yokes of oxen, or cultivate pleasures, which are signified by the wife. That is to say: greedy lovers of the world, such as the scribes and Pharisees especially were at that time, despised him who called them; but those who had been granted a heart free from desires followed him. What, then, is the meaning of his saying:

“‘That you may eat the flesh of kings, and the flesh of tribunes, and the flesh of mighty men, and the flesh of horses and of those seated upon them, and the flesh of all, free and slave, small and great?’ Clearly, in accordance with the metaphor by which the apostles are signified through birds, he fittingly designates the force and purpose of the apostolic office. For just as birds eagerly attend to eating flesh, and do not care whose corpses they devour, or of what rank—noble or ignoble—provided that they find on a great field a slaughter of the slain, so it belongs to the apostles, by evangelical authority, to make or maintain no distinction among any kinds of human beings, but, whether they are Jews or Greeks, to receive all alike into the faith and bring them into the body of the Church. For this is what it is to eat, according to what was signified to the apostle Peter. For he “saw,” in an ecstasy, “heaven opened, and a certain vessel descending, like a great sheet, let down from heaven to earth by its four corners; in it were all four-footed creatures and creeping things of the earth, and birds of heaven. And a voice came to him, saying: Rise, Peter; kill and eat” (Acts 10). Certainly, those who there were signified by the four-footed creatures and creeping things of the earth and the birds of heaven are here more plainly expressed as human beings, and all are commanded to be admitted alike to the Christian faith: kings, tribunes, mighty persons, weak persons, slaves, free persons, great and small—[Col. 1173A] in short, Jews and Greeks alike.

Yet there is one point here that must be understood still more figuratively: namely, where he says, “the flesh of horses.” For at this supper of the great God the flesh of horses is not eaten as is that of human beings, because Christ’s sacrament is preached not to horses but to human beings; and they are required to put to death, and utterly to abandon, the evil habits of works of the flesh. Now the horse is an animal of war. Therefore those who at one time opposed Christ’s faith are rightly understood by horses. Those seated upon them are the kings and powerful men of this world, who, abusing the services of such men, were at times driven by edicts and proscriptions to the killing of Christians. Who does not know that such persons too were often recalled and [Col. 1173B] converted to Christ by the apostles and apostolic men, and repented of the blood of the saints which they had shed? Rightly, therefore, he says: “And eat the flesh of horses and of those seated upon them”; that is, bring persecuting people and their instigating rulers into the unity of your body, into the fellowship of your faith.

“And I saw the beast and the kings of the earth and their armies gathered together to make war against him who sat upon the horse and against his army. And the beast was seized, and with it the false prophet, who performed signs before it, by which he deceived those who received the mark of the beast and worshipped its image. These two were cast alive into the lake of burning fire and sulphur.”

When the angel called or cried out, and the birds already mentioned came together for the supper, the beast and the kings of the earth with their armies are reported to have assembled for battle against the rider on the horse. For when Christ was preaching, and many disciples were following him and proclaiming the Gospel through cities and villages, the devil and the kings of the earth—namely Herod, Pontius Pilate, and other rulers of that sort with their supporters—were stirred up (Luke 23), and, as the Psalmist says: “They stood and gathered together as one against the Lord and against his Christ” (Ps. 2). This is what he now says: that he saw them gathered to make war against him who sat on the horse—that is, against Christ, God incarnate—and against his army, his faithful people and preachers.

And the devil is rightly called the beast in this place, since the Roman Empire, to whose authority the Jews, at the devil’s prompting, then handed over our Lord, was that great, strong, and exceedingly dreadful beast which Daniel saw, having iron teeth, devouring and crushing, and trampling the rest under its feet (Dan. 7). The devil put it into their hearts to hand him over to the authority of this beast, namely Pontius Pilate; and therefore both the devil and Roman power itself are rightly understood here under the name of the beast. “And the beast,” he says, “was seized, and with it the false prophet.” Christ indeed suffered; but by the very power of his passion the devil was seized, judged, and cast out, to be punished in eternal fire. For this is what he himself, shortly before suffering, said: [Col. 1174A] “Now is the judgment of the world; now shall the prince of this world be cast out” (John 12).

Who, then, was the false prophet who was seized with the beast at that time? Surely the Pharisaic body, and above all Caiaphas, who was high priest that year. For he was a false prophet, although what he prophesied was true. Indeed, when the council had assembled against the Lord Jesus, he prophesied, saying: “You know nothing, nor do you consider that it is expedient that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation should not perish” (John 11). He prophesied truly, for Jesus was to die for the nation, and not for the nation only, but also to gather into one the children of God who had been scattered abroad (ibid.). Nevertheless, he was a false prophet, because, if you consider his meaning or intention, he lied altogether. For this was what he intended, and what he wished the wretched people to understand and believe: that unless Jesus died—he whom the crowds already regarded as Christ the king—the Romans, under whose rule they then were, hearing that they had accepted a king without their command, would send an army against them as rebels and take away both their place and their nation (ibid.). Thus he was a false prophet, and he was caught in his own cunning by him “who catches the wise in their cunning” (Job 5; 1 Cor. 3). For in Job it is written especially concerning such people: “With him are strength and wisdom; he knows both the deceiver and him who is deceived. He brings counsellors to a foolish end, and judges to stupefaction” (Job 12), and so forth. This was the deceiver who thus prophesied; but the foolish people, prone as they were to murder, were deceived and gladly accepted his prophecy. Hence it follows:

“He performed signs before it, by which he deceived those who received the mark of the beast and worshipped its image.”

It is not, indeed, recorded that Caiaphas and the other high priests and Pharisees of that time performed any signs. But just as all persecutors who killed or kill with the material sword are reduced to one body and called one beast, so all who deceive by the word of falsehood, reduced to one body, are rightly called one false prophet. Yet many among those same deceivers performed lying signs, as Jannes and Mambres, who resisted Moses before Pharaoh [Col. 1175A] (Exod. 7, 8). Therefore, when the discourse concerns the persons of those who deceived the people into killing the Lord, it is not unfitting to impute to them that they performed signs before the beast—that is, in service of the beast—for, as has already been said, they are one with all deceivers, some of whom performed signs, if not altogether in deed, yet in every respect in will.

Most especially Caiaphas, of whom we have already spoken, deceived “those who received the mark of the beast”: that is, those who carried out the ministry of Satan by crying, “Crucify, crucify” such a man; “we have no king but Caesar” (John 19). In saying this truthfully, they “received the mark of the beast”: that is, an excessive and altogether voluntary profession of Caesar against the Lord and against his Christ. Likewise, by accepting Barabbas, the instigator of sedition, and rejecting the Prince of Peace—when, of these two, they had the option of choosing whom they wished—they “received the mark of the beast,” having been deceived by the high priests already mentioned into accepting him. For what was Barabbas but the mark of the beast? Finally, in his own person he was pre-eminently a great and principal example of Antichrist: they were to receive him who would come in his own name, though they did not receive the Son of God, blessed as coming in the name of the Lord. For “I,” he says, “have come in my Father’s name, and you have not received me. Another will come in his own name; him you will receive” (John 5).

Moreover, what he had said—“those who received the mark of the beast”—he repeated in saying, “and worshipped its image,” because from that time onward, however much they may suppose that they worship God, they are proved to worship not God but the one whom they accepted, or will accept, after rejecting the Son of God. It follows:

“And these two were cast alive into the lake of burning fire and sulphur, and the rest were killed by the sword of him who sat upon the horse, which proceeds from his mouth.”

“These two,” he says, namely the beast and the false prophet, “were cast alive into the lake of burning fire.” He seeks to awaken us to wonder and understanding when he says “alive.” For what does “alive” mean but knowingly? Thus, whoever knowingly resists the truth goes down alive into hell. But whoever, having ignorance of God, serves iniquity goes down there as though dead. Hence that saying in the Psalm: “When men rose up against us, perhaps they would have swallowed us alive” (Ps. 123). For unless the Lord had been in them, strengthening them by the power of the Holy Spirit, although they were alive, although they had knowledge, they would have denied Christ when overcome by torments.

As for the beast, that is, the devil, it is certain that he knew him to be Christ; yet he himself put it into the hearts of the Jews that they should kill him. But concerning the prophet whom he here calls the false prophet—that is, that assembly of wicked high priests and Pharisees, one of whom, Caiaphas, as has been said, prophesied—someone may perhaps doubt whether they knew him or not. Yet he speaks whose word is beyond doubt: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin” (John 15). Again: “If I had not done among them works which no one else did, they would not have sin; but now they have both seen and hated both me and my Father” (ibid.).

Therefore, knowingly, both beast and false prophet, both devil and the faithless Synagogue gathered with its false prophet Caiaphas, assembled “to make war against him who sat upon the horse and against his army”; that is, they “stood against the Lord and against his Christ” (Ps. 2). Consequently they are most rightly said to have been cast “alive” into the lake—to have gone down “alive,” I say, into hell. And it should be noted that he was not content to say “into the lake [Col. 1176A] of fire,” or, as you often find it said in the Gospel, “into the Gehenna of fire” (Mark 9), but added, “of burning fire and sulphur,” or “of fire burning with sulphur,” as some manuscripts have it. Both expressions mean the same thing: sulphurous fire. Why this, unless because of the deserts of those lost men? For their private life was wicked and so corrupt that they deserved to be burned with sulphurous fire in the lower world. Were they not those whom the prophet, foreseeing from afar with spiritual vision and execrating their utterly evil life with fitting severity, addressed: “Hear the word of the Lord, rulers of Sodom; give ear to the law of my God, people of Gomorrah” (Isa. 1)? And indeed it must be believed, nor should it be doubted, that their hidden life was abominable, since they were able openly to commit so great a crime against the Lord of majesty.

“And the rest,” he says, “were killed by the sword of him who sat upon the horse, which proceeds from his mouth.” Those two already mentioned—the beast, that is, the devil, and the false prophet, namely Caiaphas, high priest of that year, together with the whole assembly of scribes and Pharisees—because they knowingly committed so great an impiety, are said to have been “cast alive into the lake of fire burning with sulphur.” But were the rest, understood to be those deceived by that false prophet—the ordinary Jews who, persuaded by the high priests, cried, “Crucify, crucify” (John 19)—therefore to be excused or left immune from punishment? Certainly not. Rather, as the Psalmist had foretold of them, “They shall be delivered into the hands of the sword; they shall be portions for foxes” (Ps. 62), so it came to pass. For the Romans came and, as the whole world heard, they were delivered into the hands of their sword; foxes came—that is, evil spirits—and the unhappy souls of those people fell to their portions.

“They were therefore killed by the sword of him who sat upon the horse, which proceeds from his mouth”: that is, according to the word which he himself had spoken concerning them with his own mouth: “They shall fall by the edge of the sword and be led captive into all nations” (Luke 21). Jeremiah too had earlier said of this very vengeance, by way of concession: “Therefore give their children to famine, and deliver them into the hands of the sword. Let their wives become childless and widows, and let their men be slain by death; let their young men be pierced by the sword in battle. [Col. 1177A] Let a cry be heard from their houses, for you shall bring a robber suddenly upon them” (Jer. 18), and so forth. This was for them the treading of the winepress, as was said above by anticipation: “And he treads the winepress of the wine of the fury of the wrath of God Almighty.”

Nevertheless, just as, as has been said, the stroke of the sword proceeding from his mouth is sometimes understood in a favorable sense, so here too this must be referred to that same sword: some of them repented when the apostles preached. “For they were pierced to the heart and said to Peter and the other apostles: What shall we do, brothers? But Peter said to them: Repent, and let every one of you be baptized” (Acts 2). And afterward: “Save yourselves,” he says, “from this crooked generation” (ibid.), meaning, lest that sword likewise overtake you. For all whom it does not strike unto temporal repentance, it undoubtedly strikes unto temporal punishment; indeed, wrath will strike most of them so as both to kill the body and send the soul into Gehenna. It follows:

“And all the birds were filled with their flesh.”

The birds already mentioned were the holy apostles of that time. Truly, all they, or their successors, “were filled with their flesh,” but not in the manner they wished. For they converted exceedingly few of them, and bore this with great difficulty. Hence it is written in the prophetic Psalm: “They shall return at evening, and suffer hunger like dogs, and go around the city. They shall wander abroad for food; and if they are not filled, they shall murmur” [Col. 1177B] (Ps. 58). They were filled in another manner, namely that of which it is also said in the Psalm: “The righteous shall rejoice when he sees vengeance; he shall wash his hands in the blood of the sinner” (Ps. 57). Certainly a certain joy is fitting in such matters, on account of the glory of the righteous judgment of God’s justice. Yet that same joy is mingled with a reasonable bitterness; for example, when one of them says: “I speak the truth in Christ, I do not lie, my conscience bearing me witness in the Holy Spirit, that I have great sorrow and continual pain in my heart for my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh, who are Israelites” (Rom. 9).

After that battle had been joined, in which he who sat upon the horse proved so much the stronger and those who fought against him so much the weaker, what was done next is mystically set forth by the following discourse in this manner.

## Chapter XX

“And I saw an angel descending from heaven, having the key of the abyss and a great chain in his hand. And he seized the dragon, the ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan, and bound him for a thousand years, and cast him into the abyss. And he shut and sealed it over him, that he should deceive the nations no more until the thousand years should be completed. After these things he must be released for a little time.”

This angel is Christ himself, but performing another action—or rather, powerfully bringing to completion the work begun above. For what was signified a little earlier in the words, “And I saw heaven opened, and behold a white horse” (Rev. 6), is not simply repeated now in the words, “And I saw an angel descending from heaven.” Rather, what was begun there is here shown as having been accomplished, and also as still to be accomplished until the end of the age.

There Christ was descending from heaven into the Virgin’s womb in order to destroy the dominion of death and free those who were held in hell. Here likewise Christ is signified as descending from heaven in order to destroy the rule of the prince of the darkness of this world, and to free those who, in ignorance, were being led as they were led to dumb idols (1 Cor. 12). Someone may perhaps say: Did Christ, after conquering death and ascending victoriously into heaven, descend here again? Certainly he descended, but invisibly. He descended not in his former passible humility, but in impassible and invisible majesty. The whole world heard that descent; the sound of that descent went out into all the earth.

Or when “there suddenly came from heaven a sound as of a violent rushing wind, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting” (Acts 2), did Christ not descend from heaven? Did Christ not visit this world? Or is the substance or majesty of the Son separable from that of the Holy Spirit, so that when the Holy Spirit descended upon human beings, the Son of God did not descend? Certainly, even if he did not descend through the circumscribed form of his humanity, nevertheless without doubt he descended through his uncircumscribed divinity: through the Holy Spirit whom he gave, and through the apostles whom he inspired to visit the nations.

If the authority of this word, “descended,” which we employ is sought, the Prophet, after speaking in the Psalm about the preaching of the apostles and the repentance of the nations, said: “The earth was shaken and trembled; the foundations of the mountains were disturbed and shaken, because he was angry with them. Smoke went up in his wrath, and fire burned from before his face; coals were kindled by him.” Then immediately, as though you asked how this had happened or could happen, he added: “He bowed the heavens and descended” (Ps. 17). That is, by the gift of the Holy Spirit he made his apostles into heavens, caused them to stoop down to human beings, and descended through them to the nations and made himself known to the nations.

Therefore, “I saw,” he says, “an angel descending from heaven”: that is, Christ visiting the world anew through the gift of the Holy Spirit. Already in that descent, because of the suffering of death, he had been crowned with glory and honor (Heb. 2); already he had all authority in heaven and on earth (Matt. 28); already he was Lord of life and death. He says, therefore: “Having the key of the abyss and a great chain in his hand.” For he who had long since returned victorious from the lower world was rightly and truly said to possess the key of the abyss. This is why, at the beginning of this Apocalypse, after he had said: “And I was dead, and behold, I am alive for ages of ages” (Rev. 1), he then added: “And I have the keys of death and hell” (ibid.). For according to his will, by that descent into hell he brought out his elect, but left the reprobate shut in so that they could not come out.

“And a great chain in his hand,” he says: that is, the power to bind and [Col. 1179A] cast out the devil, who, dwelling in the shrines of the nations, caused himself to be worshipped as God. This is what immediately follows:

“And he seized the dragon, the ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan, and bound him for a thousand years.”

It is obvious, and proved as such by its effects, that he seized and bound him, so that it is madness to doubt this even slightly. For if he was not bound by Christ, how does he lie so powerless since Christ suffered? How do so many people escape from him? How has he been mocked by so many—not merely by mature and wise men, but by little children and tender girls? Let us consider what and how great things have been done against him by persons of weak age or condition, especially as we recall the deeds and sufferings of the martyrs, and we have a delightful spectacle. For he has not only been bound but also made foolish. Not only are his hands and feet held fast by a great chain, but also, as the Lord had promised that he would do to Job, he has his nostrils pierced with stakes, his tongue bound with a cord, a ring in his nostrils, and his jaw pierced by a bracelet (Job 41).

Hence it is that he is mocked by those who are not only servants but also handmaids of the Lord; that friends cut him to pieces; that merchants of whatever kind divide him—those who seek good pearls and, having found the one precious pearl of evangelical truth, purchased it by giving all that they had (Matt. 13). Who can number the thousands of martyrs, the multitudes of confessors, the choirs of virgins, and the company of all the elect who, from that time onward, while he looked on and envied, flew up into heaven, burst forth from the filth of his temples while he could not hold them back, shook that very filth into his eyes, and fled to the true God? Truly, then, it is said that he seized and bound him.

What these many dreadful names mean, by which this Scripture defames him—calling him “the dragon, the ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan”—has already been stated elsewhere and must here be briefly repeated. He is called serpent because he deceived the first man by entering into a living serpent (Gen. 3). He is dragon because from that time his malice grew and was multiplied in envy, and so from an ordinary serpent, as it were, he became a great dragon, an old or ancient dragon. He is devil, which is interpreted “flowing downward,” because he did not keep his own principality but, leaving his dwelling place—that is, heaven—flowed down into this dark air. He is Satan, which is interpreted “adversary,” because with evil intention he always opposes the will of the Creator.

“He bound him for a thousand years,” that is, for some period or for many years, since in Holy Scripture a finite number is often set down for an infinite one.

“And he cast him,” he says, “into the abyss.” This very thing was said much earlier: “And he was cast down to the earth” (Rev. 12). There, under the name of earth, and here, under the name of abyss, wicked and reprobate persons are signified: those who, desiring only earth or earthly things, are themselves earth, and who by stirring up evil have made themselves more deeply an abyss, because their life is a secret place of wickedness.

His power was diminished, and he was cast down, as it were, from on high into the abyss, in that the name he claimed as divine—or rather, his usurpation of the divine name—is no longer publicly celebrated in temples, as formerly, nor is the solemn rite of sacrifices performed. Rather, only those captive people who remain in his miserable slavery serve him in secret, practicing filthiness in hidden places and the remnants of ancient sorceries. He says, therefore: “And he shut and sealed it over him, that he should deceive the nations no more”: that is, that the counterfeit spirit, who is not God but the devil, should no longer be celebrated with sacred rites and sacrilegious sacrifices; nor should Saturn with his sickle, adulterous Jupiter, or Venus the harlot be worshipped as of old—those to whose impious worship the nations had been led in wretched error and deception.

Thus, bound as he is, the devil will be held “until the thousand years are completed”: until all the times appointed beforehand for evangelical liberty are fulfilled, times which we do not know, but which God the Father has placed in his own power (Acts 1). “After these things,” he says, “he must be released for a little time.” The release of the dragon, or ancient serpent—the devil—will be the coming of Antichrist. For then the devil will truly come released in that son of perdition, whose persecution of Christ’s servants will be so great and such that they will be forbidden to dare confess not merely any word of righteousness, but the very name Christian. And this will be not for long but for a little time, namely only three and a half years. He will have so short a time for the sake of the elect, because “unless those days had been shortened,” the Lord says, “no flesh would be saved” (Matt. 24).

We have already spoken of this above, where it is written thus concerning the seventh, and likewise final, head of the sevenfold beast, or the seventh king: “And when he comes, he must remain a short time” (Rev. 17). Here and there alike he used the same word, saying, “must.” The question therefore arises: Why must he be released for a little time, or remain for a short time? People are accustomed to debate questions of this sort and almost to make God’s will suspect to themselves: that he wills evils to happen, and that they must happen because he himself—an impious thing even to say—wills iniquity. “For,” they say, “it could not happen in this way unless God willed it.”

But the Apostle, repelling with abhorrence such an objection born of wicked suspicion, says: “O man, who are you to answer back to God?” (Rom. 9). And immediately, having repelled the slanderer who multiplies questions more from a desire to argue than to learn, he turns gently to the one who asks with friendly intent, not in order to dispute but in order to be found worthy to know in some small measure the truth of divine judgment, without doubting that the cause of our evils is in ourselves: “God,” he says, “willing to show wrath and to make known his power, endured with much patience vessels of wrath fitted for destruction, in order that he might show the riches of his glory upon vessels of mercy, which he prepared in glory” (ibid.).

When, therefore, the question is asked concerning that seventh head of wickedness, Antichrist, why he must be released, let the same question be asked also concerning the other heads of the beast: why each of them had to remain in its own time. For example, concerning Pharaoh, whom the Apostle mentions in this way because of the adversary who speaks against him: “For Scripture says to Pharaoh: For this very purpose I raised you up, that I might show my power in you and that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth” (ibid.). For just as it is now said of this one that he must be released, so of that one you may truly say that he had to be raised up.

Let the question therefore be asked concerning these and all the rest, and we shall answer what the Apostle teaches us to answer: namely, that these things must happen because God wills to show wrath and make known his power; and because he wills this, he therefore endures “vessels of wrath fitted for destruction.” It must be noted how he says that what God wills is good—namely, to show wrath and make known his power—whereas the things he endures are evil, namely “vessels of wrath fitted for destruction.”

Him—Pharaoh—whom the apostles have now set before us as an example, let us take as a “vessel of wrath, fitted for destruction,” so that the reason may become clearer why God wills to show His wrath, and in what respect it is good that He then showed, or now does not cease to show, His wrath. Men who love pleasures and are inclined to every vanity—such as the children of Israel already were then in Egypt—unless some present affliction is at hand, do not understand, indeed do not wish to understand, that the good, merciful, and gracious God knows how to be angry, or that He can endure to behold judgment exercised with severity or the condemnation of His creature. [Col. 1181C] For at that time the children of Israel committed fornication with the gods of the Egyptians no less than did the Egyptians themselves. Hence through the prophet Ezekiel, under the figure of the women Oholah and Oholibah, He speaks against Samaria and Jerusalem: “Thus Oholah committed fornication against me, with her lovers, the sons of the Assyrians” (Ezek. XXXII); moreover, she did not abandon the fornications which she had practised in Egypt. And, after some intervening words: “Oholibah multiplied her fornications, remembering the days of her youth, in which she committed fornication in the land of Egypt” (ibid.). Again, to her He says: “You have visited the wickedness of your youth, when your breasts were subdued in Egypt and the breasts of your puberty were crushed” (ibid.).

Therefore, lest the untrained children of Israel at that time should fail to know [Col. 1181D] that, although God is a gracious and merciful Father, He nevertheless possesses a most powerful jealousy, will judge with severity, and has wrath stored up by which He will at some time punish all sinners universally, an experiential demonstration was necessary: it was expedient that His wrath should be displayed to those whom His goodness desired to save. For they could not otherwise be saved unless, already knowing by some experience the wrath to come, they fled from that coming wrath. It was therefore necessary that Pharaoh should be raised up; necessary that God should permit that vessel fitted for destruction—that impious and proud man—to sit upon the royal throne, which indeed was what it meant for him to be raised up. For one must note that Scripture does not say, “For this very purpose I made you wicked,” but, “For this very purpose I raised you up”: that is, when you were wicked, I caused you to ascend [Col. 1182A] to the kingdom.

For what purpose? “That I may show my power in you”; that I may show in you the wrath which I will to show: so that, while you afflict the children of Israel according to your habitual wickedness and your boundless malice, the present affliction may give them understanding, and they may perceive and experience that wrath exists with me; and, knowing this, may flee my wrath and take refuge with me—their God, the God of their fathers—from whom they had departed (Isa. I). For the same reason it was afterwards necessary that the Assyrians and the other enemies of Israel should be raised up, as the Holy Spirit speaking in the prophets testifies everywhere; and for that reason God endured all the “vessels of wrath fitted for destruction,” that they might make bitter to His elect the enticements of pleasures through which they forgot God, so that, even if compelled by necessity, they might return [Col. 1182B] to Him.

Moreover, the whole multitude of these is reckoned as one spirit of wickedness, in one body; and that body is the beast which in this book is so often said to have seven heads, of which Antichrist himself is the seventh. Therefore, when it is said, “After this he must be loosed,” let us understand the same reason for which God had to endure the often-mentioned beast, in order that it might ascend and its six heads might already devote themselves to the persecution of the saints: namely, that His wrath might be made known to the utmost, that He might possess evident and sufficient testimony that He does not will iniquity but hates it; and that consequently it is fitting for Him to sit on the throne of judgment on the last day and judge all who are found uncorrected. For it will be manifest that He greatly hates evil—that is, sin—who could endure that evil—that is, affliction—should be inflicted even upon His own elect, or could Himself inflict it.

It follows: “And I saw thrones, and they sat upon them, and judgment was given to them; and the souls of those beheaded for the testimony of Jesus and for the word of God, and those who did not worship the beast or its image, nor receive its mark on their foreheads or in their hands; and they lived and reigned with Christ for a thousand years. The rest of the dead did not live until the thousand years were completed. This is the first resurrection.” With the dragon, the devil, bound; with Christ’s Gospel proceeding freely in public; with men who had been his vessels transformed into vessels of God, sons of God; and with temples of idols changed into churches of Christ—he foresees in the vision what the condition of the holy Church throughout the world [Col. 1182D] began from that time to be, saying: “And I saw thrones, and they sat upon them, and judgment was given to them.”

These thrones are ecclesiastical dignities: namely, those of Catholic bishops, and also of priests or prelates of the lower order. Their authority is indeed so great that it may rightly be said that judgment has been given to them, since by the authority of Him to whom the Father gave all judgment, this has been granted them: whatever they bind on earth is bound in heaven, and whatever they loose on earth is loosed in heaven (Matt. XVIII). The supreme tribunal of this judgment has been established in the Roman Church, where the apostolic see of blessed Peter has been founded both in name and bodily presence; to him it was specially said: “You are Peter, and upon [Col. 1183A] this rock I will build my Church; and to you I will give the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XVI). Through the devout and venerable tradition of that holy see, the memorials of Christ’s martyrs have been made so renowned and splendid that their anniversary days are solemnized with every honour throughout the whole world, and the solemnities of Mass are celebrated over their sacred bodies.

He therefore says: “And the souls of those beheaded for the testimony of Jesus and for the word of God, and those who did not worship the beast or its image, nor receive its mark on their foreheads or in their hands, lived and reigned.” That is to say: as the Church of Christ sits in its proper order, and as the rulers and kings of the earth obey its judgment, the souls of the holy martyrs—who shed their blood in persecution for the faith of Christ, refusing to obey pagan rulers by denying Christ and sharing in the sacrifices of demons—proved by outstanding powers that they lived; and thus they reigned among men, though they had been unjustly condemned, so that kings and emperors themselves, ungirded and having laid aside their diadems, prostrated themselves bareheaded at their venerable memorials. This happens, and does not cease to happen, for a thousand years—that is, as has already been said, until the coming of Antichrist: “They will reign with Christ so long that all who confess Christ will also humbly venerate Christ’s martyrs.”

“But,” he says, “the rest of the dead did not live”: the rest of the dead, that is, those who are dead in another way, who live to the world and are dead to God, being far [Col. 1183C] different from those who are dead to the world for the testimony of Jesus and live to God. These did not live, nor were they judged worthy to live; rather, they were reckoned among the dead, and truly are so, until the thousand years are completed—that is, until Antichrist comes, who, conversely, will surely make such persons live, but will put to death those who are living, that is, the righteous who live to God.

“And this,” he says, “is the first resurrection.” Namely: this binding of the dragon; this judgment of those seated upon thrones; this life of the souls of holy martyrs reigning with Christ—this is the first resurrection. For there are two resurrections, just as there are two deaths: one of souls, the other of bodies. By the resurrection of souls, through believing in Christ, we have risen through baptism. With this in view, the Lord said to the crowds of Jews: “Amen, amen, I say to you, the hour is coming, and now is, when the dead shall hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear shall live.” But by the resurrection of bodies we shall all rise on the last day. Indicating this likewise, the Lord immediately continued: “Do not marvel at this, for the hour is coming in which all who are in the tombs shall hear his voice and shall come forth: those who have done good, unto the resurrection of life; but those who have done evil, unto the resurrection of judgment” (John V).

It follows, therefore: “Blessed and holy is he who has a share in the first resurrection. Over these the second death has no power; but they shall be saints of God and of Christ, and shall reign with him for a thousand years.” “For he who has believed and has been baptized shall be saved,” not merely [Col. 1184A] for a thousand years, but through all years and days of eternity. For, says the Psalmist, “You will add days upon the days of the king; his years unto the day of generation after generation. He remains for eternity, and for age upon age” (Ps. LX). But because Antichrist, when he comes, will unsettle that faith in many, he has for this reason set a kind of limit: “And they shall reign with him for a thousand years.” He immediately adds: “And when the thousand years are completed, Satan shall be loosed from his prison. And he shall go out and deceive the nations which are at the four corners of the earth, Gog and Magog.”

He will be loosed and will go out: that is, he will avail himself of permission and stir up a public persecution against Christians throughout the world. “And he will deceive all nations”—the elect, of course, excepted, for it will not be possible for the elect to be led into error (Matt. [Col. 1184B] XXIV). This was also expressed above in these words: “The inhabitants of the earth shall marvel, whose names have not been written in the book of life from the foundation of the world” (Apoc. XVII). “Nations,” therefore, means those living as Gentiles; by that designation all who belong to Christ are, of course, counted as above them.

Furthermore, all who are not Christ’s are here strikingly denoted when they are called Gog and Magog. Gog is interpreted “roof”; Magog, “from the roof.” What then do we understand by these except hidden and open adversaries alike? For by Gog—that is, “roof”—we understand false brothers who are within and profess the Christian name with us. Because they have not yet revealed themselves, since an opportunity of circumstance or time is lacking to them, they are rightly called “roof.” But by Magog, which means “from the roof,” are rightly signified those who oppose us in deeds as well as word: namely, pagans, Jews, and heretics. Yet, when they receive an opportunity and Antichrist comes, false Christians will join them in no dissimilar fury, and together with them will use violence against true and simple Christians.

He says therefore: “And he shall gather them for battle, whose number is as the sand of the sea; and they went up over the breadth of the earth and surrounded the camp of the saints and the beloved city.” He will gather them, certainly not into one place, but into one and the same purpose of impiety, one and the same zeal for doing harm. He rightly calls their number “as the sand of the sea,” because they are not those who should in any way [Col. 1184D] be likened to the stars of heaven—unless perhaps as a sign of falling and perdition, as in the passage: “His tail, that is, the dragon’s, drew a third part of the stars of heaven and cast them down to earth” (Apoc. XII). This can rightly be said only of those who might once have been called brothers, but went out from us—such as are here signified by Gog, that is, “roof.” Therefore they are “as the sand of the sea,” because their names are written not in heaven but on earth, as the prophet says: “Lord, all who forsake you shall be confounded; those who depart from you shall be written in the earth” (Jer. XVII).

“They went up,” he says, “over the breadth of the earth.” From the future time of events, of which he had said, “Satan shall be loosed, and shall go out, and shall gather,” he suddenly returns to the past time of the vision, saying: “And they went up and surrounded the camp of the saints.” They went up, then—understand, in the image of that vision; for in reality they are yet to go up. Their ascent is their pride. At that time, indeed, their time will come to go up, glorying in chariots and horses; the locusts will leap up and spread themselves over the breadth of the earth, exercising wide power and dominion under such a great prince of the lands. Thus going up, thus exulting in pride, they “surrounded the camp of the saints and the beloved city.” What he had called “the camp of the saints,” he more plainly repeated by saying, “the beloved city.” For the beloved city is the camp of the saints: a camp of peace and love, founded upon faith, not material stone; armed with the word, not iron. Such a camp, such a city, they surrounded; they did not [Col. 1185B] break into it. They attacked it; they did not breach it. The wicked are outside, and walk about its circuit, because, even if they harm the body, they do not touch the soul; if they tear the flesh, they do not injure faith. What follows at last?

“And fire came down from heaven and devoured them. And the devil, who deceived them, was cast into the lake of fire and sulphur, where the beast and the false prophet shall be tormented day and night for ages of ages.” All these things have been said by anticipation. For how they are to happen, how the fire will devour the devil and all whom he deceived, and how they are to be cast into the lake of fire and sulphur, he explains more fully by repeating it in the following chapter. For he says: “And I saw a great white throne, and one sitting upon it, from whose presence earth and heaven fled, [Col. 1185C] and no place was found for them. And I saw the dead, great and small, standing before the throne. And books were opened; and another book was opened, which is the book of life. And the dead were judged by the things written in the books, according to their works.”

This session and all this solemn array are what He who is to sit foresaw when, as He was already hastening to His Passion, He spoke in this way: “When the Son of Man comes in his majesty, and all the angels with him, then he shall sit upon the throne of his majesty; and all nations shall be gathered before him, and he shall separate them from one another, as a shepherd separates sheep from goats” (Matt. XXV), and so forth. The great throne is that great seat of the highest majesty. That throne, as it is great, is also white, because nothing in that judgment is or shall be rightly open to reproach. He says, “one sitting upon it,” without giving any name, indicating that person all the more majestically through silence: for He is neither unknown nor may be unknown, and it is impossible that He should not then be recognized. Indeed, one must take care that, when He is seen seated, the person who is to behold Him may have an eye prepared for goodwill. For the prophet speaks of Him against malicious eyes: “Lord, let your hand be exalted, that they may not see; let the peoples who are jealous be confounded, and let fire devour your enemies” (Isa. XXVI). For how shall jealous peoples, how shall malevolent eyes, endure Him?

For he says that earth and heaven fled from His face, and no place was found for them. How, then, will earth or heaven flee? Assuredly, [Col. 1186A] the earth, utterly consumed in a great conflagration, will lose its former appearance; at the same time earthly works will disappear: the works of kings and rulers will collapse together and burn together. Not one stone upon another will remain of cities or fortifications, whatever men have built beginning with Cain; nor will even a little residue of their dust remain from the fire. In this manner the fleeing earth will also yield back all the blood by which it has been defiled, ever since the aforesaid Cain killed his brother Abel (Gen. IV), and all the bodies of men with which it has been filled from the beginning. For this is what he says: “And I saw the dead, great and small, standing before the throne.”

Heaven, moreover, will flee in the manner foretold by the Psalmist concerning both earth and heaven: “In the beginning, O Lord, you founded the earth, and the heavens are the work of your hands. They shall perish, but you remain; they shall all grow old like a garment, and like a covering you shall change them, and they shall be changed” (Ps. CI). What here is signified in the singular as “heaven,” there in the plural as “heavens,” means the aerial heaven; for this denser and more bodily air is also customarily called heaven. Thus birds, which in their flight do not rise beyond the lowest air, are nevertheless called birds of heaven. Although the air is one, there are diverse qualities of air according to its different places and regions; consequently both one heaven and many heavens are spoken of. Hence one of the pagans says:

> Those who hasten across the sea change their sky, not their mind.  
> —Horace [Col. 1186C]

There is no doubt that these heavens will perish, namely, dissolved by excessive heat when He who sits upon His great throne appears. For the apostle Peter also says in his epistle concerning them: “But the heavens which now are, and the earth, by the same word have been stored up, reserved for the day of judgment and destruction of ungodly men” (2 Pet. III). That flight of heaven or of the heavens will be marvelous and terrifying. It will not happen silently; rather, the tearing apart of those that flee—or the flight of those torn apart and tearing themselves apart—will be heard with terror, like the tearing of an old garment. For fire, commanded then to exercise its power, will not merely cause the heavens to crackle a little, as they sometimes crackle now when summer heat grows intense (a crackling which natural philosophers call thunder); rather, there will be a mighty tempest and a mighty fire burning round about Him who comes, sent out for vengeance upon the ungodly and for the examination of the merits of good and evil persons.

Moreover, sinful men may rightly be understood by the fleeing earth, and demons by heaven—that is, by the air—in which they have the power of wandering. For he continues: “And no place was found for them.” We may rightly understand by that earth and that heaven those who indeed desire to flee but can find no place to hide from the presence of Him sitting upon the throne: namely, impious human beings and evil spirits. They will not be able to flee the sight of so great a Judge, nor will they obtain what they desire by hiding themselves in clefts of rocks and saying [Col. 1187A] “to the mountains, Fall upon us; and to the hills, Cover us from the face of him who sits upon the throne” (Apoc. VI). Rather, they will all stand before Him; all will be brought into public view.

Therefore he immediately adds: “And I saw the dead, great and small, standing before the throne.” By “great and small” he means the same as if he said that no one can hide from being present before Him, whether great or small. Nor will faces alone appear, but consciences also. This is what he immediately adds: “And books were opened.” For the opening of the books will be the disclosure of consciences. “For we must all,” says the Apostle, “be manifested before the judgment-seat of Christ, so that each may receive according to what he has done in his body, whether good or evil” (2 Cor. V).

“And another book was opened, which is the book of life.” This book is the certainty of divine foreknowledge and blessed predestination. This book will contribute greatly to the truth of judgment, because it is not lawful that any should be saved except those written in this book of life—that is, those ordained beforehand for life—whom God had already written then, and whom He commanded to be born when, after forming the first human beings, male and female, our parents, He blessed them with a gratuitous blessing, saying: “Increase and multiply” (Gen. I). For the cause of the birth of all the rest was the sin of the first transgression, as the text or sequence of the narrative indicates. For after sin had already been committed, the same God said to the woman: “I will multiply your hardships and your conceptions” [Col. 1187C] (Gen. III).

This book, opened—which is the book of life—will therefore, as has been said, contribute greatly to the truth of judgment and at the same time to the praise of mercy, when it becomes clear to all that none of those who acquired destruction for themselves by evil works was predestined; and likewise, that none of those predestined to life, who were commanded to be born by that blessing, will fail of salvation or then appear with works such as should require condemnation, being saved by the grace of that blessing which endures and perseveres. Therefore Mercy, rejoicing in victory, will say to those standing at the right hand: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. V). Surely, as He says this, the victorious blessing of God will be celebrated or commemorated in no small triumph, because amid so many thorns and thistles of the ensuing curse it was able to grow and be brought to perfection, to the praise of Him who became man for our sake, removed the curse, and recovered the former blessing.

“And the dead,” he says, “were judged by the things written in the books, according to their works.” This is so certain that no one may fail to know by whose mouth whatever is written in those books will be recited. The King Himself, sitting upon the throne, declared that He would recite it in this way, first to those who will be at His right hand: “For I was hungry and you gave me food; I was thirsty and you gave me drink” (ibid.). Conversely, from the consciences of those at His left hand He will pronounce [Col. 1188A] that they did not do these things, and therefore, “Depart,” He will say, “you cursed, into eternal fire” (ibid.). There nothing can be absent, wherever a person may have been consumed and by whatever end.

Therefore he immediately adds: “And the sea gave up its dead which were in it, and death and hell gave up their dead which were in them.” The sea gives up bodies; death and hell give up souls. Indeed, not the sea alone, but the earth also will restore all bodies from graves. Yet he is content aptly to mention the sea alone, because it was especially possible for unbelievers to doubt concerning it. Since it seems incredible to them that our bodies can be restored whole from the dust of the earth, it is judged much more impossible that they can be called back from the sea and all rivers, when so completely consumed that not even a small particle of dust appears anywhere to survive. Moreover, death and hell differ in this: hell is only for the wicked, but death may be said to exist also for the good. For “precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. CXV). Thus “death and hell gave up their dead”: that is, the souls of blessed dead persons who died in the Lord, and of the condemned who have been assigned to hell (Apoc. XIV), will return to their own bodies, wherever those bodies may be—even those consumed in the depths of the sea by the voracity of beasts. 502 It follows:

“And each was judged according to his works; and hell and death were cast into the lake of fire. This is the second death. And whoever was not found written in the book of life was cast into the lake [Col. 1188C] of fire.” He had already said this: that the dead were judged by what was written in the books according to their works. Then, after inserting that “the sea gave up its dead which were in it,” and that “death and hell gave up their dead which were in them,” he finally repeats: “And each was judged according to his works.” Surely because the ungodly, concerning whom he immediately adds, “and hell and death were cast into the lake of fire,” undergo a double condemnation. Before they rise with their bodies in the resurrection in which the sea also gives up its dead, the souls of the ungodly are judged and tormented in hell; and after they have risen, their souls together with their bodies will then be judged and tormented for ages of ages.

Then hell and death—that is, impious people who will stand at the left hand with the devil and his angels—will be cast into the lake of fire. “And this,” he says, “is the second death.” Namely, the death of which he had earlier said, after declaring, “Blessed and holy is he who has a share in the first resurrection”: “Over these the second death has no power.” Therefore, since the first resurrection is rising from sins through faith in Christ, the first death is rightly understood as sin; and the second death as the eternal punishment of sin. Of this he again adds: “And whoever was not found written in the book of life was cast into the lake of fire.” He seems to repeat this because there was a twofold reason why they should be cast into the lake of fire: both for original sin, from which they were not freed through faith in Christ, and for the actual sins which each person added in his own life to that transgression.

Thus, what he had said earlier by anticipation—“And the devil, who deceived them, was cast into the lake of burning fire and sulphur, where the beast and the false prophet shall be tormented day and night for ages of ages”—has been shown from that point up to the present conclusion, as to how it will happen. From here onward, the following vision indicates what will be the blessed state of immortality for those at the right hand, to whom it will be said: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom.”

## Chapter XXI

“And I saw a new heaven and a new earth. For the first heaven and the first earth passed away, and the sea is no more. And I saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem, [Col. 1189B] coming down from heaven, prepared by God as a bride adorned for her husband.” After those who corrupted the earth had been destroyed, “I saw,” he says, “a new heaven and a new earth”: that is, the appearance of heaven and earth made new and changed for the better. For the first heaven and the first earth—that is, the former appearance of heaven and earth—passed away or fled, as was said above: “Earth and heaven fled from the presence of Him sitting upon the throne.”

As for his saying, “And the sea is no more,” teachers have debated whether the fluid substance of the sea will be wholly dried up and annihilated by the greatness of the conflagration by which the whole world will be burned, or changed for the better, so that its substance indeed remains but its appearance is different. When all things, therefore, have been made new, “I saw,” he says, “the holy city, the new Jerusalem.” It was fitting that the whole company of saints and elect should be exalted with so venerable a proclamation that he should call it a city—holy by merits, Jerusalem by name, new in condition. For this city is holy; but that other city which he had seen above, its enemy, is called and is the harlot and mother of fornications. This Jerusalem signifies by its name its own true peace and that of its God; Babylon, by its own title, signifies its confusion. This one is new and remains in eternal youth; that one, its youth rapidly spent in fornications and consumed in a short time, thereafter grows wrinkled with everlasting old age.

What is this city’s newness except the twofold grace of holy [Col. 1189D] regeneration? For now, regenerated through the first resurrection—that is, through Christ’s baptism—it walks in newness of life (Rom. VI); but then, when what the present vision describes has come to pass, it will be regenerated through the second resurrection, of which Christ Himself says: “In the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits upon the throne of his majesty” (Matt. XIX), and so forth. Then it will truly be new, both in body and in soul.

“Such,” he says, “I saw coming down from heaven”; and explaining what he had said, he adds: “Prepared by God.” For that holy city does not claim for itself what it is, but remembers that it received itself from God, not by its own merits but by heavenly grace, and gives eternal thanks. How prepared by God? “Like a bride,” he says, “adorned for her husband.” [Col. 1190A] In every respect this city is proclaimed greatly unlike that great city, the harlot. For the latter, seated in the garb of a harlot upon a scarlet beast full of names of blasphemy, is openly accused of prostitution and fornication—prostituted to demons, fornicating with kings. But this city is declared to be modestly adorned for her one husband, her one God, like a bride already prepared to enter the marriage, while that adulteress undergoes the penalties of death and hell which she has deserved.

It follows: “And I heard a great voice from the throne saying: Behold, the tabernacle of God is with men, and he dwelt with them; and they shall be his people, and God himself shall be with them as their God.” Truly great and delightful is this voice, by which He who sits upon the throne shows and commends the holy city as worthy, and as His bride. For she has never commended herself; and therefore it is fitting that her husband, her God, should commend her. Conversely, that harlot commends herself to those who are corrupt and who corrupt her; with her own heart and mouth she magnifies herself among them in her own evils. For on her forehead the name is written: a mystery, “Babylon the great, mother of fornications and abominations of the earth.” Again, she herself says in her heart: “I sit as a queen, and am no widow, and shall see no mourning.” But this city does not commend herself: her God, her husband, sitting upon the throne, commends her with a great voice.

“Behold,” he says, “the tabernacle of God with men, and he shall dwell with them.” “Behold,” an adverb of pointing, is a great sign of great rejoicing, uttered by a joyful mouth, because, as the Psalmist says, “The Lord shall rejoice in his works” (Ps. CIII). For this tabernacle is the work of the Lord; all its ornaments, inward and outward, are beautiful works of the Lord, worthy of the praise of the Lord who points it out and worthy of the joy of the Lord’s heart, so that, as has already been said, in the prophet’s testimony He may rejoice in them. From the time when He formed the first man, took a rib from his side, and built it into a woman (Gen. II), God has not ceased, nor does He cease, to build this His tabernacle until He completes it and says: “Behold, the tabernacle of God.”

Moreover, when he adds “with men,” it is the same as saying “from men.” For this whole tabernacle has been built from human beings. Hence they are also called living stones, polished by cutting and pressure, each well set in its own place by the hand [Col. 1190D] of God the builder. But how shall “God dwell with them,” except because “the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us”? God, made man according to the truth of nature, is and always shall be one of us. And because the author of our salvation was perfected through suffering, it is rightly said: “And they shall be his people.” And because He who possesses them is also the possession of those whom He possesses, he further adds: “And God himself shall be with them as their God.” It follows.

“And God shall wipe away every tear from their eyes; and death shall be no more; neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain any more, for the former things have passed away.” A wonderful affirmation of truth: “God,” he says, “[Col. 1191A] shall wipe away every tear from their eyes.” The abundance of consolation laid up there for the saints and elect of God who weep in this world could not have been expressed more magnificently. For this manner of speech is drawn from the likeness of a mother who, unable to bear the weeping of her little child, wipes his eyes and face with her hand and soothes him with kisses. To make known to us the greatness of his affection, God himself says among other things through the prophet: “Their children shall be carried upon shoulders, and they shall be comforted upon knees” (Isa. 66). And immediately he turns in address to the little children themselves, and the same Spirit of grace says to them: “As a mother comforts her children, so I also will comfort you, and you shall be comforted in Jerusalem” (ibid.), etc. But it would seem pointless for tears to be wiped from their eyes unless the very cause of weeping were also removed. [Col. 1191B] Accordingly it follows at once, and he says: “And death shall be no more.” By the name of death he briefly comprehends all the afflictions of mortality. It is as though he were saying: And that harlot, whom you saw drunk with the blood of the saints, will no longer be able to drink anything of their blood, since they will in no way be able any longer to die. Once death has been removed, mourning is consequently removed as well. He says therefore: “Neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain any more, for the former things have passed away.”

And immediately follows: “And he who sat upon the throne said: Behold, I make all things new.” This is said by him for whom to speak is to do: “All things shall be new,” because they shall be such things “as eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the heart of man, which God has prepared for those who love him” [Col. 1191C] (Isa. 64; 1 Cor. 2). Those former things—namely, all old things, all evil things—have passed away: death, mourning, crying, and pain; and all these new things, all good things, succeed them in proper order.

But the course of that harlot was not so. What then? All her former good things passed away: her purple, her gold, her precious stones, all her citron wood, her pearls, all her ivory vessels, and her other riches, which above are described as perishing. Then, in their order, death, mourning, famine, and the burning of sulphurous fire succeed; and over all these things “Woe, woe, woe” is cried out against her once, twice, and a third time.

“And he says to me: Write, for these words are most faithful and true.” He who sits upon the throne, who speaks in making all things and makes them by speaking with his mouth, “says to me: Write.” By his gift he brings it about that I may know and may be worthy to write with both apostolic and evangelical authority. And he gives the reason why I should write: “For these words,” he says, “are most faithful and true.” They are most faithful in the promise of good things, true in the threat of evils—whatever things were written in the preceding passage in the fearful and yet desirable display of him who sits upon the throne.

“And he said to me: It is done.” He who, at his first coming, had sworn—or seemed above to have sworn—“by him who lives for ever and ever, that there shall be time no longer” (Rev. 10), but that in the days of the voice of the seventh angel, when he begins to sound the trumpet, the mystery of God will be completed, as he proclaimed through his servants the prophets—this same one [Col. 1192A] here, in the prefiguration of his second coming, says: “It is done.” For what is it to say, “It is done,” except that the mystery of God is completed? Therefore it is done: the time of repentance is completed, and there shall no longer be any change. For a great chasm has been fixed between that condemned harlot Babylon and this holy city Jerusalem, God’s bride, so that neither her torment or mourning may ever again be diminished, nor the joy or adornment of this city ever be lessened (Luke 16). Having said this, he immediately employs a most beautiful sort of epilogue, saying thus:

“I am α and ω, the beginning and the end. I will give freely to him who thirsts from the fountain of living water. He who conquers shall possess these things, and I will be his God, and he shall be my son.
