But for the fearful and unbelieving and accursed, and murderers, [Col. 1192B] and fornicators, and sorcerers, and idolaters, and all liars, their portion shall be in the lake burning with fire and sulphur, which is the second death.”

For he briefly recounts the matters of which I have spoken hitherto, or whose images he displayed to him, and which he pronounced words both most faithful and true: namely, the good things of those who will stand at the right hand, and the evil things of those who will be placed at the left in that judgment. For when he says, “I will give freely to him who thirsts from the fountain of living water; he who conquers shall possess these things, and I will be his God, and he shall be my son,” these are most faithful words laid up for those who will be on the right. What follows—“But for the fearful and unbelieving, and accursed, and murderers, and fornicators and sorcerers, and idolaters, and all liars, their portion shall be in the lake burning [Col. 1192C] with fire and sulphur, which is the second death”—are true words concerning those who will be on the left. So that no one may doubt the faithfulness and truth of all these matters, Truth itself, which speaks, interposes its own authority with wonderful gravity, saying: “I am α and ω, the beginning and the end.”

Something has already been said at the beginning concerning this description of himself, where he likewise says: “I am α and ω, the beginning and the end” (Rev. 1). Truly, all the things said in this final section are said in such a way as to be full of fear; and according to these works, or judgments, the Holy Spirit is rightly called, and is, the Spirit of the fear of the Lord (Isa. 11). This fear of the Lord is holy (Ps. 18), because it makes all the saints and elect of God reverently fearful. I say reverently fearful, not cowardly: for however greatly they may have advanced in holiness, when they consider the truth and severity of the dreadful judgment, they still fear and tremble. Nor do they think that they have already attained it (1 Cor. 9); nevertheless they are strong and run in order to attain it—which the cowardly do not do.

For those are called, and are, cowardly who have neither faith nor hope in future things; and they are rightly called cowardly when, doubting God’s promises, they undertake nothing brave in hope of life, nothing difficult in confidence of rewards. Therefore, in this passage the cowardly are rightly joined with the unbelieving; and, like that of the unbelieving, the portion of the cowardly also is declared to be in the burning lake. This indeed is the recompense of justice; but that which is promised to the saints in reward is the gift [Col. 1193A] of grace. Therefore, when he had said, “I will give to him who thirsts from the fountain of living water,” he added, “freely,” because certainly this very fact—that he thirsts in acting, acts in thirsting, and desires God, “as the deer longs for fountains of waters” (Ps. 41)—is wholly a divine gift, a free gift. For he made us freely, and freely, before we existed, predestined all his saints to life; and when we had perished in Adam, he likewise freely called us and, by the regenerating grace of Christ, justified us from [Col. 1194A] sins (Rom. 8). Consequently, it will also be—or is—an act of grace that he glorified those whom he called and justified with that glorification by which they are made sons of God, as he says: “And I will be his God, and he shall be my son.” And they shall drink “from the fountain of living water,” so that they are made drunk, as the Psalmist says: “They shall be intoxicated with the abundance of your house, and you shall give them drink from the torrent of your delight; for with you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light” (Ps. 35).

## Book Twelve

[Col. 1193]

[Col. 1193B] We have considered the works of the seven Spirits of God—what works, and of what kind, they performed with the human race from the beginning to the end of the age—each in its own order, from the first, the Spirit of wisdom, to the last in that same order, the Spirit of the fear of the Lord. For, as has been said elsewhere, for us ascending to God the Spirit of the fear of the Lord is first in order, as Scripture testifies when it says: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110). But for heavenly grace descending to us, another order of the same Spirits of the Lord is enumerated by the prophet, when he speaks of the flower rising from the rod that springs from the root of Jesse and says: “And the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and strength, the Spirit of knowledge and piety; and the Spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill [Col. 1193C] him” (Isa. 11).

Having sought the works of these Spirits according to the authority of the holy Scriptures, we have considered them, and, as far as we were able, explored seven sections, distinguishing them according to these same Spirits. For it was from them that the writer of this book announced grace and peace to us in Christ Jesus, saying at the beginning: “Grace to you from him who is, and who was, and who is to come, and from the seven Spirits who are before his throne, and from Jesus Christ” (Rev. 1), etc.

Now at last, at the end of this vision or revelation, the totality of the work which Jesus Christ built with so great an expenditure, with so many graces or gifts of his Spirits, is shown to this John: namely, the holy city Jerusalem, which is the Church of God—not as it is in this pilgrimage [Col. 1193D], nor as it will stand at the right hand in the final judgment, as was said shortly before, still not without some fear until the wrath of the Lord passes, by which those at the left shall be cast into eternal fire—but as it shall be after judgment, alone and entire in eternal glory, all outsiders having been cast forth, enjoying the vision of God. It begins thus:

“And one of the seven angels having bowls full of the seven last plagues came, and spoke with me, saying: Come, I will show you the bride, the wife of the Lamb. And he carried me away in the Spirit to a great and high mountain, and showed me the holy city Jerusalem coming down from heaven from God, having [Col. 1194B] the glory of God.”

This one of the seven angels is the one Christ, who speaks in all these angels—that is, in the holy preachers—as one of them, the apostle Paul, says: “Do you seek proof of Christ who speaks in me?” (2 Cor. 13). This one was to come in the future to his beloved John and appear to him with his disciples, as you read in the widely circulated account of his assumption, saying: “Come, my beloved, to me, for it is time for you to feast at my banquet with your brothers.” Prefiguring this, this one of the seven angels, he says, spoke with me, saying: “Come, I will show you the bride, the wife of the Lamb.” For he who says these things plainly indicates that there is a wedding feast there, concerning which, as has already been said, he was to be told: “It is time for you to feast at my banquet with your brothers.” For the bride is at the wedding feast.

But why did he use both terms, “bride” and “wife of the Lamb”? Clearly because the marriage of the Lamb and his one Church is virginal, even there where she will already be a wife in the fullness of delight. Nevertheless, she will remain a bride, because in that blessed union she will forever be wife with children and forever virgin, the marriage and bridal festivities enduring. “And he carried me away,” he says, “in the Spirit to a great and high mountain.” Truly, the one who is borne up to the vision of divinity—which, as we have said, was to happen to him—is lifted to the great height and lofty greatness of the eternal mountain.

For this mountain is Christ, who, like “a little stone cut [Col. 1194D] from the mountain without hands”—that is, born from the Virgin in the humility of our condition—grew, “and became a great mountain and filled the whole earth” (Dan. 7). He grew by ascending above the choirs of angels, Lord of all things heavenly, earthly, and infernal (Phil. 2). “He carried me away to this great and high mountain,” he says, “and showed me the holy city Jerusalem.” Therefore the city of Christ is founded or built upon this Christ. This is so true that we also read God saying of him through the prophet: “Behold, I will lay in the foundations of Zion a chief stone, a precious cornerstone, founded in the foundation” [Col. 1195A] (Isa. 28). And this stone himself, in the Gospel against the scribes and Pharisees (Matt. 21; Luke 20), employs the Psalmist’s testimony concerning himself, when he says: “The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner” (Ps. 117).

Therefore the city is rightly shown upon the mountain, since the Church of Christ is known to be founded upon Christ himself, with a wonderful building and a wonderful arrangement of foundation and stones. For every building—every structure of cities or houses whatsoever in this world—has its foundation stone below at the lowest point and its wall above. But this building or city, shown here in the Spirit, has its loftiest foundation above, from which depends all the framework of its walls, all the hope and love of the faithful peoples, both the Jews who came first and the Gentiles who were built afterward. He calls this city holy and names it Jerusalem, because it is the holy Church of the Bridegroom, consecrated by his blood, possessing and destined to possess the vision of eternal peace. Therefore the Holy Spirit speaks to her in the Psalm: “Praise the Lord, Jerusalem; praise your God, Zion. For he has strengthened the bars of your gates; he has blessed your children within you; he has made your borders peace” (Ps. 147).

He calls her “coming down from heaven from God.” As he had already said above: “coming down,” I say, not falling, as that angel fell and became the devil and Satan. For to fall belongs to pride; to come down belongs to humility. Holding herself always in this descent, [Col. 1195C] that Jerusalem shall stand forever, knowing that what she is comes not from her own strength or merits but from the grace of God (1 Cor. 15), which came down from heaven with Christ. Such a descent is glorious and sublime in great brightness. Therefore, when he had said, “coming down from heaven,” he rightly added:

“Having the glory of God.” She comes down beautifully indeed, she who in that very descent, in the very humility of her descent, has the glory of God—that is, is like the charity of God. For by seeing God, who is most dear, she too shines according to his likeness and is most bright. Thus this same John says in his Epistle: “Beloved, now we are sons of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be; we know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” [Col. 1195D] (1 John 3).

Nor indeed shall she have the glory of God only in her soul, but also in her body: that is, the glory by which the body of the Son of God was glorified after his resurrection. For thus the Apostle says: “From there also we await the Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, who shall transform the body of our lowliness, conformed to the body of his glory” (Phil. 3). He establishes this more fully in the present passage when he immediately adds: “Its light was like a precious stone, like a jasper stone, like crystal.” For, as though you asked how he could say that she has the glory of God, her light is like a precious stone—that is, Christ, who is indeed called a stone and is precious.

Moreover, this likeness is divided between two stones of different kinds when he says, “like a jasper stone, like crystal.” For the Church is made like God or Christ not by one thing but by two: not by faith alone, but by faith together with works of virtue. By jasper, therefore, we understand the beauty of virtues; by crystal, the purity of faith received in baptism and preserved. “And it had a great and high wall, having twelve gates, and at the gates twelve corners.” Its great and high wall is the eternal firmness of incorruptible protection, where each of the faithful may safely lay up his treasures. Thus the Lord himself, the king of this city, says in his Gospel: “Lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where a thief does not draw near, or where thieves do not [Col. 1196B] dig through and steal” (Matt. 6; Luke 12).

This wall is that chasm concerning which the patriarch Abraham most truly says to those buried in hell: “And in all these things a great chasm has been fixed between us and you, so that those who wish to pass from here to you cannot, nor can they cross from there to us” (Luke 16). Its twelve gates, moreover, are the twelve apostles, who, because in this world they opened the kingdom of God to us by preaching and became for us gateways to life, shall have greater honor there, inasmuch as gates possess greater honor and beauty in cities than the rest of the circuit of the walls. At these gates, the twelve corners are all teachers whatsoever who, laboring for the building up of the Church and serving her by voice and writings, have steadfastly adhered and relied upon the faith and authority of the [Col. 1196C] twelve apostles.

“And names were written, which are the names of the twelve tribes of the sons of Israel.” For the twelve apostles themselves are the named and illustrious sons of spiritual Israel—that is, of Christ—of whom the patriarch Jacob, or Israel, as a type, physically begot twelve sons, the fathers of the twelve tribes. Therefore both the twelve apostles of Christ and the twelve tribes of Israel are the twelve gates of this city, but in different ways: the apostles in reality, the tribes of Israel in signification. To make this clearer in brief, see what follows:

“On the east three gates, on the south three gates, on the north three gates, and on the west three gates.” This must be understood of the spiritual arrangement which is completed through the apostles. In the arrangement of the twelve tribes of the sons of Israel coming up from Egypt, however, the camps were positioned at the Lord’s command in such a way that three tribes camped toward the east, three toward the south, three toward the west, and three toward the north [Col. 1196D] (Num. 2). Thus, when he says of the sealed twelve gates, “And names were written, which are the names of the twelve tribes of the sons of Israel,” he beautifully directs the attentive reader to that symbolic arrangement of the camps, recalling at the same time what he says in the Song of Songs to this his bride, this holy city Jerusalem: “You are beautiful, my friend, sweet and lovely as Jerusalem, terrible as an army drawn up in battle array” (Song 6). Again: “I have likened you, my friend, to my cavalry among Pharaoh’s chariots” (ibid.).

But to pursue the spiritual arrangement of the gates which we have begun: what does he mean when he says, “On the east three gates, on the south three gates, on the north three gates, and on the west three gates,” except that the holy apostolic faith, established in the name of the Trinity, received through their ministry persons coming from every people and nation, of every sex and age? Moreover, this division of the regions of the world may usefully be understood in terms of the ages: childhood, adolescence, youth, and old age. Thus, the three gates open from the east, south or noon, west, and north for every age: at whatever age a person is converted, the evangelical and apostolic rule has without distinction opened admission into the holy city—that is, the Church—through faith in the holy Trinity. For childhood is understood through the east; fervent adolescence or youth through the south; mature age through the west; and decrepit old age, rightly, through the north. Hence a distinguished poet of the Christian school says:

> Whether the first sun guides children, whether heat  
> Kindles young men, whether the full light of mature age  
> Perfects men, or whether the cold age of the north wind  
> Calls decrepit old age to sacred rites:  
> The triune Deity meets them at the four crossroads.

These things are not said because, after the judgment, there will then be a future reception of those who come; rather, although the office of receiving will cease, the rank and merit remain of those who preached to the whole world and, through their labor, gathered and received all nations and all ages into the one faith. [Col. 1197C] It follows:

“And the wall of the city had twelve foundations, and on them the twelve names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb.” The same apostles who are the gates of this city are also its foundations. For the Church of God is founded upon their faith, yet in such a way that Christ is their foundation. Thus, deriving from that one foundation, they are called foundations in the same manner as their first and chief member, from the rock—which is without doubt Christ—was called Peter. Therefore, when he had said, “and on them,” the foundations, “the twelve names of the twelve apostles,” he fittingly added, “of the Lamb.” For whatever they wrote—and upon their writings as foundations the whole structure of Christian faith and ecclesiastical doctrine rests—they did not write from themselves, but received from the fullness of the Lamb and adhered to and relied wholly upon his evangelical words.

These are the foundations and these the gates concerning which the Holy Spirit says in the Psalm: “Its foundations are in the holy mountains; the Lord loves the gates of Zion more than all the tabernacles of Jacob” (Ps. 86). The meaning is this: the holy mountains, that is, the apostles, shall by faith and teaching be the foundations of God’s glorious city; and they are also its gates, because through their preaching and miracles entry shall be made into that Zion. “The Lord loves these gates more than all the tabernacles of Jacob,” that is, more than all those serving him among the former people. For although Moses and the other prophets lived holy and righteous lives and possessed exceedingly great holiness and faith, the dignity of the apostles surpasses their merits. The apostles not only lived rightly, but also saw the Lord himself—whom the prophets had foretold from afar—with bodily presence, deserved to be nourished by the inward food of his most sweet preaching, took up their own cross and followed his footsteps, and proclaimed throughout the world the peace granted to humankind in his death.

Although here only the names of the apostles, and not also those of the prophets, are said to be written upon these foundations, nevertheless the prophets too are foundations of this city. For in one of these foundations, namely the apostle Paul, we read written: “Now you are no longer strangers and foreigners, but fellow citizens of the saints and members of God’s household, [Col. 1198B] built upon the foundations of the apostles and prophets” (Eph. 2). They were indeed earlier in time than the apostles; but for us who are built upon the foundation, or in our building upon it, it always has been and is necessary to build in such a way that, whether reading or discussing the prophets, we diligently refer everything they wrote or said to the apostolic foundations and understand nothing from them except what evangelical truth, written through the apostles in both Gospel and Epistle books, approves and receives as evangelical. Therefore the prophets too are foundations, but the apostles are foundations of foundations, and Christ is the foundation of all foundations. He is here called the Lamb because all these foundations rest most especially upon the foundation of his passion, for which reason Christ the Lord is called the Lamb. It follows:

“And he who spoke with me had a golden measuring rod, that he might measure the city and its gates and wall. And the city was laid out in a square. Its length is as great as its breadth; and he measured the city with the rod for twelve thousand stadia. Its length, breadth, and height are equal. And he measured its walls: one hundred and forty-four cubits, according to the measure of a man, which is that of an angel.”

This measurer is surely the distributor of graces and the rewarder of them. For he is the one of whom John the Baptist says: “From his fullness we have all received, grace for grace” (John 1). In this life he first gives grace, bestowing diverse gifts upon those who believe in him [Col. 1198D] (1 Cor. 12); afterward, in that age of which we are now speaking, he grants the rewards of eternal recompense in return for grace well employed. Therefore it should be noted that in the present passage this measurer’s rod is called both reed-like and golden.

Above, when John said: “And a reed like a rod was given to me, saying: Rise and measure the temple of God” (Rev. 11), he did not say that the reed was golden. For there was signified the Gospel which he was necessarily to write for Christ’s Church; in that ministry of writing there is present labor, but future reward, when grace is hoped to be repaid for grace well employed—not merely any grace, but golden grace, that is, most rich grace—so that the one who faithfully wrote or taught here may there perfectly know what he knew only in part. This is what the reed measure and golden measure signify in this passage.

Certainly, when grace or authority to preach or write was first given to the apostles of whom we are now speaking, indeed to the prophets and to many holy Fathers, the measure was only reed-like. But then, when, as has been said, grace is returned for grace, the measure is rightly both reed-like and golden. But will only those be rewarded who received skill to use in the holy Scriptures? For the reed commonly signifies Scripture, as there: “Rebuke the beasts of the reed” (Ps. 67), that is, restrain the heretics who fiercely corrupt the Scriptures of truth; for books are written [Col. 1199B] with a reed. Shall only those chief persons who wrote be rewarded in that city, and not also the rest who did not receive such grace? Rather, all others too who obeyed the holy Scriptures shall be rewarded. For he says: “That he might measure the city and its gates and wall.”

For the wall, whose gates and foundations these are, is the whole body of the elect, who, as living stones, have been built upon these foundations (1 Pet. 2), after the likeness of material stones joined together by suitable cement in a humanly constructed edifice. Absolutely all shall receive their own reward, each according to his labor and according to the grace of the measurer with which he labored (1 Cor. 3).

“And the city,” he says, “was laid out in a square”; that is, there is there the complete peace and concord of all, and it will no longer be necessary to exhort them concerning peace—for example, that they all speak the same thing and that there be no schisms among them (1 Cor. 1). All there are harmonious voluntarily, as though by nature, just as all the walls or corners of a square building are equal. He repeats this in other words when he immediately says: “Its length is as great as its breadth.” Moreover, when he adds at once, “And he measured the city with the reed for twelve thousand stadia,” he further adds, so that you may understand an equal number of stadia on each of the four sides: “Its length and breadth are equal.” He nevertheless adds its height also, of which we shall speak later.

Thus, when you see twelve thousand stadia in the circuit of the city, and the city itself is square, you can easily perceive how many stadia each side measures, namely three thousand. But how can what follows stand: “And he measured its walls, one hundred and forty-four cubits,” which is far less than three thousand stadia? This might seem to have been said of the height of the walls—that is, that the walls rise one hundred and forty-four cubits high—[Col. 1199D] if he had not said that the city’s length, breadth, and height were equal. But, as we have said, both its length and breadth were three thousand stadia, which far exceeds the measure of one hundred and forty-four cubits.

Therefore this wall is another wall; for its size is far different and far smaller. Nor may we even suppose [Col. 1200A] that when he says here, “And he measured its walls, one hundred and forty-four cubits,” he means any one side of the square city, while when he said, “And he measured the city for twelve thousand stadia,” we should understand the area of the same city. For the principle of geometrical science is that every quadrilateral having equal sides multiplies one side by itself and by that one multiplication yields its area. But this quantity of one hundred and forty-four cubits, multiplied by itself, scarcely amounts to anything more than fifteen stadia. How much less is that than twelve thousand stadia? Therefore, as has been said, this wall of the city is one thing and that wall another. That a narrower wall may be enclosed within a larger wall in human-built cities needs no demonstration from us.

Indeed, no one would build unfittingly if within a city whose circuit is twelve thousand stadia he constructed a citadel whose each side was one hundred and forty-four cubits. We must seek the spiritual meaning, because the plain surface of the letter itself compels us to understand that another, shorter wall is enclosed within the wider wall. What, then, shall we say, except that although there is one city, one Church, there are nevertheless two ranks in the city: one consisting of those who suffered persecutions outside and fought bravely; the other, of those who, by doing good works in the peace of the Church, completed the course of this present life. Stadia signify the labor of those who fight; cubits signify the peace of those who work.

“He therefore measured the city with the reed for twelve thousand stadia”: that is, he rewarded that great and strong order of the holy Church which ran in the stadium and fought, bearing witness to the faith of the holy Trinity through the four quarters of the world. The numbers four and three are components of twelve—for four times three, or three times four, is twelve. This order shed its blood for that testimony; it includes the apostles and martyrs of Christ. Certainly the wider wall of this order contains within it the shorter wall of one hundred and forty-three cubits, because the merits of such great defenders brought it about that the multitude of the weak, confirmed in Christ’s faith, might arrive at dwelling in the same city by persevering in good works. Therefore nothing conflicts with the statement: “Its length, breadth, and height are equal.” Through this figure of the most beautiful square is signified the harmonious and inseparably united confession of all the tribes that have ascended or shall ascend there, the tribes of the Lord, “to confess the name of the Lord” [Col. 1200D] (Ps. 121). The city’s length signifies harmony of faith; its breadth, sufficiency of charity; its height, the perseverance of hope which shall be rewarded there.

“The measure,” he says, “of a man, which is that of an angel.” “For,” the Lord says, “they shall be equal to the angels, and are sons of God, being sons of the resurrection.” In the literal sense, when he says, “the measure of a man, which is that of an angel,” he indicates that the angel appeared to him in human form.

“And the construction of its wall was of jasper stone; but the city itself was pure gold, like clear glass.” When he distinguishes between the wall and the city, saying, “and the construction of its wall was of jasper stone, but the city itself was pure gold,” by the name of the wall he signifies the more steadfast faithful of a more spiritual calling; by the designation of the city, the streets of the city—that is, the multitude of a less strict manner of life, especially of the lay order. Nor is it surprising that he proclaims the streets of the city to be pure gold, or paved with pure gold. He adds that this gold will be so pure as to be like clear glass, because among those in secular life there are also some adorned with the highest virtues, who shine both with purity of mind and with the radiance of their work.

For because they retain the truth of faith, they are rightly called pure gold, since faith is a golden virtue—indeed, more precious than gold—as the apostle Peter says: “That the testing of your faith may be found much more precious than gold which is tested by fire” [Col. 1201B] (1 Pet. 1). But because they frequently make holy confession and do not defend their sins, but disclose them by confessing, this gold is rightly said to resemble clear glass. If anything blameworthy still remains in them, it is to be hoped that after the purgatorial fire this gold will be more splendidly pleasing, so that it may all be gold; for, as the Apostle says: “The fire shall test what sort each person’s work is; and if anyone’s work is burned”—that is, if it is a remissible sin—“he himself shall be saved, yet so as through fire” (1 Cor. 3). It follows:

“**The foundations of the wall of the city were adorned with every precious stone** [Col. 1201C]. The first foundation, jasper; the second, sapphire; the third, chalcedony; the fourth, emerald; the fifth, sardonyx; the sixth, sardius; the seventh, chrysolite; the eighth, beryl; the ninth, topaz; the tenth, chrysoprase; the eleventh, hyacinth; the twelfth, amethyst.”

The foundations of the city, as has already been said, are the apostles, “because,” he says above, “the wall of the city has twelve foundations, and upon them the twelve names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb.” See how beautiful these foundations are, how beautiful these stones: holy stones which, when they were rolled about upon the earth, seemed contemptible to the rich of this age. For their beauty was not then apparent in the eyes of human beings [Col. 1201D], when they were beaten and struck; but they were beautiful in the eyes of the Lord, and, that they might become more beautiful, they were polished by the blows of tribulations. There their beauty and radiance are, and shall be, manifest to all, so that at some time the ungodly, seeing them, will say: “These are those whom we once held in derision and made a byword of reproach; we fools accounted their life madness and their end dishonourable” (Wisdom 5).

How, then, have they been numbered among the sons of God, and how is their lot among the saints? Certainly, just as all these stones are beautiful and precious, yet with differing beauty, so that none of them is altogether like another; so all the holy apostles are indeed illustrious and glorious, yet with differing glory, according as the Holy Spirit, coming upon them [Col. 1202A], bestowed upon each. Thus, in the distribution of the graces which they received in a wondrous manner, likeness is unlike and unlikeness like; and the disposition of the mind—that is, of the inward person, in which they are established in Christ—is in none of them altogether the same.

Many have written with considerable care about the natures of the individual stones, diligently matching almost every merit of the saints with the particular qualities or colours of the respective stones. It continues:

“**And the twelve gates are twelve pearls; each of the gates was made from a single pearl.**”

The apostles, as has already been said, are called both foundations and gates; and, in a wondrous manner, they are proclaimed glorious both in the foundations by the names of precious stones and in the gates by the likeness of precious pearls. For Christ [Col. 1202B] is the precious stone and the precious pearl which the wise merchant, having found it, bought by giving all that he possessed (Matt. 13). Making them conformed to himself, he granted them this: that they should be pearls of beauty in the foundations and in the gates.

For the adornment or beauty and glory of the gates through which we entered that city, coming from the four quarters of the world, could not be signified more beautifully or fittingly than by the name or appearance of pearls. Certainly, just as a noble woman, arrayed in precious pearls, is accustomed to glory before human eyes, adorned for her husband, so that city which is the Church may glory in such leaders, such great fathers, such glorious apostles—adorned thus as a bride for her bridegroom, Christ.

Thus the apostle Paul, conscious that he was indeed one of these ever-open gates [Col. 1202C], says to the Corinthians: “For you are our glory, as we also are yours in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Cor. 1). This is as though he said: The Holy Spirit has bestowed such gifts of grace upon us, and the grace of God has worked so greatly and so fruitfully with us, that you may rightly glory in us against the false apostles. Nevertheless, after saying, “for you are our glory,” he adds, “as we also are yours.”

The present text fittingly and harmoniously declares the same thing, when, after first saying, “and each gate was made from a single pearl,” it immediately adds:

“**And the streets of the city are pure gold, like transparent glass**” [Col. 1202D].

And above, when about to say, “The foundations of the city wall were adorned with every precious stone,” it first stated: “Its wall was built of jasper, while the city itself was pure gold, like clear glass.” Therefore it is truly said: “You are our glory, as we also are yours”; that is, you may glory in the grace bestowed upon us, and we in your faith and manner of life, won through our labour. Nor are we unseemly or unfitting for one another. Rather, as foundations adorned with every precious stone befit walls of jasper or a golden city, and as gates made of pearls likewise befit a golden city, so the primacy of the apostles adorns the Christian people; and conversely, it is not unfitting for such great apostles to profess leadership over such a people.

[Col. 1203A] It continues:

“**And I saw no temple in it; for the Lord God Almighty is its temple, and the Lamb. And the city has no need of sun or moon to shine in it, for the glory of God illuminates it, and its lamp is the Lamb.**”

By this magnificent hope he consoles the poverty or need of the spirit of truth which is ours in this pilgrimage, when it is said: “And I saw no temple in it, and the city has no need of sun or moon; for the Lord God Almighty is its temple, and the Lamb; and the glory of God illumines it, and its lamp is the Lamb.”

For how great is, or will be, this in comparison with what we now possess concerning God, or what we now see concerning God and God’s Son Jesus Christ? We pile up stones; we bring together material stones without feeling and without life; and, constructing a house from them, we call upon the name of the Lord in them or upon them, so that, since we cannot see his face, we may at least know where or how we ought to invoke his holy name.

Then, because we have had—or have—ignorance even of that name, we employ a little light, that is, Holy Scripture, so that in it or through it we may somehow perceive, not now what or how God is, but only what he is not, and that God is not to be likened to any creature. But where “in that Zion the God of gods shall be seen” (Ps. 83), “face to face, and as he is” (1 Cor. 13), and he himself shall be present within us, the divinity dwelling and overflowing in the very substance of our souls will be perceived [Col. 1203C] like the rushing of a river, like a torrent of delight. And with outward eyes also—leaving aside the substance of divinity itself, concerning whose vision the holy Fathers have disputed in various places, whether it ought or can be seen by bodily eyes—with outward eyes, I say, that temple of divinity will be seen as present, which is beautifully signified when it is said: “And the Lamb is its temple.”

For truly the Lamb is and shall be the temple of God, the temple of the Holy Trinity, according to the fabric of his body, “in which the fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Col. 2). For he himself said: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I shall raise it up.” But, says the Evangelist, “he spoke of the temple of his body” (John 2).

What need, therefore, shall we have there [Col. 1203D] of a handmade temple, such as we make here to invoke the name of the Lord, when there the face of the Lord and the beauty of the temple not made by hands—that is, the glorified body of Christ—are seen as present? What need shall we have there to seek the sun or moon of the Scriptures, where God the Word is in himself and in the heart of the Father—the Word for whom the Scriptures are necessary here as signs?

For, just as in the psalm, through the words, “Day pours forth speech to day, and night makes knowledge known to night” (Ps. 18), so here too by the greater and lesser lights, the sun and moon, we rightly understand the knowledge of the Scriptures, which will not be necessary there. In another sense, that city truly will not need these visible sun and moon either, where there will be no night, nor even day in such a way that it will need the abiding presence of this sun which now circles in its course.

[Col. 1204A] For, to say nothing further of the city’s light, the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “Then the righteous shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. 13). What, then, can the sun contribute there to illumination, where there will be as many suns, as it were, as there are elect human beings or angels? Yet the radiance of the angels themselves will derive from the light of the one God. Hence he says: “For the glory of God illumined it, and its lamp is the Lamb. And the nations shall walk by its light, and the kings of the earth shall bring their glory and honour into it.”

“The nations shall walk,” he says; and by this statement he touches upon and recalls the magnificent benefits or works of the Lord’s mercies. For it is no slight matter or significance that he calls those who walk in the light of such a glorious city “nations.”

[Col. 1204B] It is as though he said: “Those who were formerly Gentiles, going to mute idols as they were led,” as the apostle says (1 Cor. 12)—people of whom he also says: “Therefore remember that you were once Gentiles in the flesh, called the uncircumcision by that which is called circumcision made in the flesh by hands; that at that time you were without Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in this world” (Eph. 2), and so forth. These persons, I say, shall walk in such a city and in such light of the city, having become members of God’s household and having been built upon the foundation of those apostles of whom we have already spoken.

They will indeed marvel, and their mouths will always be full of praises for God’s grace, because from so far away they were gathered into that city: those whom, as the Psalmist says, “he gathered from the regions, from the rising and setting of the sun, from the north and from the sea,” adding: “They wandered in the wilderness in a waterless place; they found no way to a city of habitation” (Ps. 106), and so forth.

[Col. 1204C] As they walk through the expanse of that great city, it will delight them then to remember this; and because they have found such a city, they will sing the mercies of the Lord forever. For this is what he immediately adds here: “And the kings of the earth shall bring their glory and honour into it.” For the kings of the earth are the same persons as the nations: all shall reign there; all shall be kings and priests of Christ; and they shall reign for ages of ages. They shall bring into it the glory and honour of their own kingdom, always offering everlasting thanks to him who did these things for them, who glorified them with the immortal blessedness of their souls and honoured them with the blessed immortality of their bodies.

“**And its gates shall not be shut by day, for there shall be no night there.**”

It is a great proof of great security that “its gates shall not be shut.” For this sufficiently indicates that neither enemies nor thieves will be feared there. “For the thief,” says the Lord, “does not draw near” (Luke 12). So long as we are pilgrims here, the apostolic gates must very often be shut against Jewish and pagan enemies and against thieves and heretics, and secured with the strong bars of authoritative judgments. But then these people shall appear nowhere, for they shall already have been sent with the devil and his angels into [Col. 1205A] eternal fire.

Why, then, should the gates be closed by day? If you ask whether they will at least be closed by night: by no means, he says, “for there shall be no night there.” There shall be no night at all there: neither the spiritual night suffered here by the eyes of the heart, nor the night of the heart, nor the bodily night that surrounds the eyes of the body here.

“**And they shall bring into it the glory and honour of the nations. And nothing defiled, nor anyone practising abomination and falsehood, shall enter it, except those written in the book of life and of the Lamb.**”

Who are those who bring into it the glory and honour of the nations, if not those who laboured and whose labour bears as fruit the salvation of the nations, unto the glory and honour of the Lord? They are the apostles so often mentioned, whom Christ, their teacher and Lord, instructing them to bear fruit for the honour and glory of the nations, said among other things: “You did not choose me, but I chose you and appointed you that you should go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain” (John 15).

[Col. 1205B] They shall bring into that city the glory and honour of the nations—that is, the glorious and honourable fruit which they bore among the nations—and shall present it forever to the King and Lord of that city, God and the Lamb. In that glory and honour of the nations they themselves shall be glorious, according to the promise of prophetic truth: “You shall consume the strength of the nations, and you shall glory in their glory” (Isa. 61).

“They shall bring,” he says, “the glory and honour of the nations,” and not the vicious manner of life of the nations, on account of which they were called nations. Therefore he adds:

“**And nothing defiled, nor anyone practising abomination and falsehood, shall enter it**” [Col. 1205C].

Such was the former life of the nations. Therefore, when he says, “They shall bring the glory and honour of the nations,” it is understood that only those from among the nations shall be presented there who have transformed the reproaches of Gentile life into the glory and honour of God.

So that he might bring into that city the glory and honour of the nations, and not also anything defiled, the apostle Paul says to the Corinthians: “Do not be deceived: neither the sexually immoral, nor idolaters, nor effeminate men, nor men who lie with males, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor robbers shall inherit the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6). These are defiled things and works of abomination and falsehood; none of these shall enter there [Col. 1205D], because those who do them shall not possess the kingdom of God.

But what follows: “And these indeed you were; but you were washed, but you were sanctified, but you were justified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the power of the Holy Spirit and in the Spirit of our God” (1 Cor. 5)—these are the glory and honour of the nations which shall be brought into that city.

Therefore they shall bring only the glory and honour of the nations; and these glorious and honourable persons are those whom God foreknew and predestined, called and justified (Rom. 8). These are those chosen out from all unclean nations, with reference to whom he says: “Except those written in the book of life and of the Lamb.” This is as though he said: None shall enter it except those whom God foreknew and predestined, whom the Lamb—that is, the Son of God—called, though condemned in Adam, and justified through his passion.

[Col. 1206A] For this reason the book of life is rightly also called the book of the Lamb: although they had been inscribed in God’s purpose when God blessed the first parents, saying, “Increase and multiply” (Gen. 1), after Adam’s transgression they could not attain the inheritance for which they had been inscribed unless they were redeemed through the blood of this Lamb.

## Chapter 22

“**And he showed me a river of living water, bright as crystal, proceeding from the throne of God and of the Lamb, in the midst of its street. And on either side of the river was the tree of life, bearing twelve fruits, yielding its fruit each month. And the leaves of the tree are for the healing of the nations; and there shall be no more curse.**”

These things which he shows here in the final place are the ineffable riches and inestimable delights of the glorious city, which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the human heart (1 Cor. 2) [Col. 1206B]. This river is the abundance of gladness and delight, of which the Psalmist says: “The rush of the river makes glad the city of God” (Ps. 45). And elsewhere: “They shall be filled with the abundance of your house, and you shall give them drink from the torrent of your delight” (Ps. 35). And Isaiah, consoling the children of this Jerusalem, says: “For thus says the Lord: Behold, I shall turn toward them like a river of peace and like an overflowing torrent of the glory of the nations” (Isa. 66).

Therefore this river is the Lord, and truly so because it is the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit is this river of peace, this torrent of glory, this river of gladness, this torrent of delight, and the abundance of God’s house. [Col. 1206C] For he is the love of bridegroom and bride in that glorious city. What indeed is the entire blessedness of that life or city except this love? By this love all the holy angels and all the souls of all the saints live.

Therefore, after saying, “and he showed me a river,” he fittingly adds, “of living water.” And because such water gives life, illumination, and strength, he fittingly says “bright,” adding, “as crystal.” For in crystal there are at once brightness and firmness, which are beautiful marks of that life, where our hearts shall be transparent and our bodies shall be made firm by blessed immortality and immortal blessedness.

And because the Holy Spirit is said to proceed according to the Gospel tradition of our Lord—for he says: “When the Paraclete comes, whom I shall send to you, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father” (John 15)—he did not leave this unspoken here either. For he says of this river: “proceeding from the throne of God and of the Lamb.” This is what we profess in the catholic faith: that “the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son.”

But when he says, “**In the midst of its street**,” this is fittingly and properly said to express the delights of the city, because the Holy Spirit does not proceed outwardly, outside that city, but only “in the midst of the street” of the city, that is, in the greatly enlarged hearts of the elect. Indeed, since Jesus was glorified, this river has begun to flow to us; but it has not yet appeared, nor can it appear here in the present life, what it has accomplished for us. The whole fruit of its procession, by which it deigns to proceed to us [Col. 1207A], shall appear there. This is what he now says: “**On either side of the river, the tree of life bearing twelve fruits**”: that is, Christ, who chose and sent the twelve apostles.

Finally, that Christ was made human and born of a virgin came from the abundance of this irrigating river, because the virgin conceived by the Holy Spirit, who caused such a tree to rise for us from the earth of the virgin womb. Likewise, that this tree bore twelve fruits—that is, that Christ ordained the twelve apostles—came from the fullness of this river, because he gave them the Holy Spirit. Thus we have in the psalm: “And he shall be like a tree planted beside streams of waters, which shall yield its fruit in its season” (Ps. 1).

What is said there, “in its season” [Col. 1207B], is what is said here, “each month”: that is, without failure and forever. For it shall never cease to bear fruit, because the reward of the saints which comes from it shall never fail. And because the salvation of the nations, which the fruitful twelve apostles brought forth, is attributed to Christ, who bore fruit among the nations through their ministry, it is rightly said: “**And the leaves of the tree are for the healing of the nations.**”

For the leaves of the tree are the words of the Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ; by receiving them, the nations obtained for themselves the eternal healing of souls and bodies. Such leaves shall neither fail nor fall away there, because the words of God shall not be absent from the heart and mouth of the nations; rather, love prompting them more fully, they shall always break forth into everlasting praise. And because the curse was acquired beneath the fig leaves with which those first parents of ours covered themselves (Gen. 3), it is fittingly added in contrast, after first saying that the leaves of this tree shall be for the healing of the nations:

“**And there shall be no more curse.**”

Such a tree and such fruit are said to be on either side of the river, by likeness to some visible delightful river whose watered banks display, on this side and that, fruit-bearing or otherwise verdant trees, not without pleasure.

“**And the throne of God and of the Lamb shall be in it, and his servants shall serve him.**”

Those who are his servants and who shall serve him shall be the throne of God and of the Lamb in that city; and he, the King of kings and Lord of lords, together with God the Father and [Col. 1207D] the Holy Spirit, shall sit in them, dwelling in their hearts. Glorious and sweet shall be that service, in which they remember in their consciences that they are servants of him from whom, through whom, and in whom they were redeemed. Yet that Lord presents himself not so much as the lord of servants or king of those who serve, as the father of children and friend of friends, demanding no service other than ineffable love, unable to be silent in praise, and offering unbounded thanksgivings for the highest and ineffable delights. For how could they rest from such service?

It follows: “**And they shall see his face, and his name shall be upon their foreheads.**” Therefore silence cannot exist there, where they shall see so desirable a face; but, as it is written, “A voice of rejoicing and salvation [Col. 1208A] is in the tents of the righteous” (Ps. 117): service consisting everlastingly in perpetual jubilation.

And, that you may perceive how great an honour and how great a liberty that service is: “And his name,” he says, “shall be upon their foreheads.” What or what sort of name is his, except “God”? For they shall be called and shall be gods, according to the words: “I said, You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High” (Ps. 81). And this same John says: “See what grace he has given us, that we should be called and be sons of God” (1 John 3). Therefore, “his name shall be upon their foreheads”; that is, they shall be called and shall be sons of God.

“**And night shall be no more; they shall need neither lamplight nor sunlight, because the Lord God will illumine them, and they shall reign for ages of ages.**”

“They shall see his face,” he says; and in order to see that face, there shall be no need for light to be supplied, as here light of the sun—or of a lamp, if the sun is beneath the earth—must be supplied in order to see any human face. For “night shall be no more”; another sun shall not make the day there, but the Lord God himself, “who will illumine them,” who is the true and everlasting sun. He will not rise and set, now shine above the earth and then hide himself beneath it, but will always shine upon their faces and always illuminate their minds.

And lest you suppose that the service by which they serve him is something other than liberty and kingship:

“**And they shall reign,” he says, “for ages of ages. And he said to me: These words are most faithful and true. And the Lord God Almighty of the spirits of the prophets sent his angel to show his servants what must shortly come to pass.**”

Just as he wished the beginning or head of this book to be helmeted, so also its end, so that the entire body of these revelations might be fortified, lest anyone dare reject as contemptible, or cast aside, any of the things written in this book [Col. 1208C]. For, as we said at the beginning, it was to happen that some would despise it, especially because of its difficulty; irreverent people commonly despise whatever they read all the more easily the more difficult it is to understand.

Therefore, just as at the beginning he had said: “The Revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave him to make known to his servants what must shortly come to pass” (Rev. 1), so here, after first saying, “These words are most faithful and true,” he says: “And the Lord God Almighty of the spirits of the prophets”—that is, the Holy Spirit who spoke in the prophets, who is certainly almighty Lord and almighty God—“sent his angel to show his servants what must shortly come to pass.”

Likewise, just as, with this purpose or intention, he had said there: “Blessed is the one who reads and the one who hears the words of this prophecy and keeps the things written in it, for the time is near” (ibid.); so also with the same intention or sense he says here: “And behold, I come quickly. Blessed is the one who keeps the words of the prophecy of this book.”

These words are certainly spoken in the person of the Lord Jesus, who, though he may appear to delay, shall come quickly and fulfil the words of the prophecy of this book. Likewise, just as, to commend the book, at the beginning he carefully identified his own person once, twice, and three times—first saying [Col. 1209A], “and he made it known by sending through his angel to his servant John, who bore witness to the Word of God” (Rev. 1); secondly, “John, to the seven churches which are in Asia”; and thirdly, “I, John, your brother and companion in tribulation” (ibid.), and so forth—so here too he clearly identifies his person, which has deserved well of the Church of Christ: “And I,” he says, “John”—understand, *am he*—“who heard and saw these things.”

Therefore, whoever receives the holy prophets, in whom or through whom the Holy Spirit has spoken, and the Gospel of the Word of God which John wrote, receive also this Scripture: for the Spirit of the prophets sent his angel to show these things to his servants, and the one who heard and saw them is John himself.

[Col. 1209B] “**And after I had heard and seen, I fell down to worship before the feet of the angel who showed me these things. And he said to me: See that you do not do this. I am your fellow servant, and of your brothers the prophets, and of those who keep the words of this book. Worship God.**”

This has already been done and said once and twice: first, namely, when the angel showed him the condemnation of the harlot; and now secondly, when he shows him the blessedness of the glorious city. Accordingly, it is sufficiently confirmed that no one besides God—whether human being or angel—ought to be worshipped, because “every matter shall stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses” (Deut. 19).

And he says to me: “**Do not seal the words of the prophecy of this book, for the time is near.**” From here until the end, all is spoken in the person of the Lord Jesus, and the prophecy is confirmed by his mouth, so that no one who wishes to belong to the Lord Jesus may dare despise it. “Do not,” he says, “seal the words of the prophecy of this book.” What is said to John alone is also said to every person who understands the mysteries of this book: that he should not seal or close them, but rather, as far as he can, open and explain them for the edification and instruction of hearers, because the time is near; that is, what is written in it shall quickly be fulfilled. Since this is so, what further decree or command is necessary? It follows:

“**Let the one who does harm do harm still; let the one who is in filth become filthy still; let the righteous do righteousness still; and let the holy be sanctified still.**”

It is as though he said: Since such great punishments are laid up for the ungodly and such great rewards for the godly as the course of this book signifies, let the ungodly not doubt that punishments sufficient to their deserts shall be repaid, however much further harm they do; and let the righteous and holy not doubt that rewards proportionate to their deserts shall be given, however much further righteousness they do or holiness they attain.

But how are we to understand the statement: “Let the one who does harm do harm still, and let the one who is in filth become filthy still”? Does the fact that “do harm” and “become filthy” are imperative expressions mean that the creature has harmfulness and filthiness by the will of the Creator? Certainly not. The Creator does not will his creature to be harmful or filthy; but there is a time when he ought to take no concern about what it does or how greatly it becomes filthy, as it is written: “According to the multitude of his wrath, he will not seek” [Col. 1210A] (Ps. 9).

When is that? Certainly when one who is sinful or filthy provokes God by love and defence of his sins and defilements. For sin is committed in three ways: through ignorance, weakness, or pride. If sin is committed through ignorance, and God foresees that the person will be corrected once the truth is known, God comes to the aid of ignorance, so that the ignorant and erring person may know what is true.

An example is this: “God came to Abimelech at night and said: Behold, you shall die because of the woman whom you have taken, for she has a husband.” To this he replied: “Lord, will you destroy an ignorant and righteous nation? Did he not himself say to me, ‘She is my sister’? And she said, ‘He is my brother.’ I did this in the simplicity of my heart and the cleanness of my hands.” God said to him: “I too know that you did this in the simplicity of your heart, and therefore I kept you from sinning against me, and did not permit you to touch her” (Gen. 20).

[Col. 1210B] The apostle likewise obtained mercy, and heavenly compassion came to his aid, “because,” he says, “I acted ignorantly in unbelief” (1 Tim. 1). But if someone sins through weakness, such is the person in whose person the same apostle speaks: “I delight in the law of God according to the inward person; but I see another law in my members resisting the law of my mind and leading me captive in the law of sin which is in my members. Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. 7).

God patiently bears the sin of such a person—indeed, he even overlooks it—as Wisdom says in praise of his mercy: “You have mercy upon all, Lord, and hate nothing that you have made, overlooking human sins for the sake of repentance” (Wisdom 11).

But if someone sins with pride, God hands him over and leaves him to the uncleanness in the desires of his heart. You must not say that it is the Lord’s will that he be harmful or filthy; rather, God takes no concern for one who is such, and is greatly angered with him, and “according to the multitude of his wrath, he will not seek.”

[Col. 1210C] Such is certainly the person meant here when it says, “Let the one who does harm do harm still, and let the one who is in filth become filthy still,” especially because it does not say, “Let the one who did harm do harm still, and let the one who was in filth become filthy still,” but, “Let the one who does harm,” he says, “and the one who is in filth.” This is as though he said: Whoever has a purpose of doing harm and stubbornly loves his own filth—after anyone has heard him defending himself and despising the plagues written in this book—let no one hope anything good for him. For it is written: “For three transgressions, and for four, I shall not turn him back” (Amos 1), because, after someone has passed through three transgressions and reached the fourth, there is no longer hope of conversion.

The first transgression is to entertain the filth of crimes in thought and desire; the second is to commit the same filth in deed; the third is to make a habit of such filth; the fourth transgression is to defend that same filth. Therefore let the one who does harm do harm [Col. 1211A], and let the one who is in filth become filthy still, because God takes no concern for him and he has been justly abandoned: not because he has become filthy in merely any way, but because, proudly defending his filth, he is in filth.

Conversely, “the one who is righteous and holy”—that is, the person who has a zeal for the good of righteousness and holiness—“let him do righteousness still and be sanctified still,” God providing well that he not depart this present world before his crown is completed and his dwelling in his Father’s house is adorned with the jewels and pearls of merits (John 14).

After this has been said—“Let the one who does harm do harm still, and let the one who is in filth become filthy still, and let the righteous do righteousness still, and let the holy be sanctified still”—there immediately follows:

“Behold, I come quickly, and my reward is with me, to render to each according to his works.” [Col. 1211B] He plainly speaks thus as one well aware that he possesses great strength and inexhaustible power: to punish the harmful and defiled, however much harm they have done or however much they have defiled themselves, so that they will receive punishments no less than their deserts; and to reward the righteous and holy, however much righteousness they have practised or however much they have been sanctified, so that they will receive rewards no less than their deserts. Therefore he says: “Behold, I come quickly, and my reward is with me.”

Although to the evil, harmful, and defiled servant, who makes himself drunk and beats his fellow servants (Matt. 24), this may seem deferred for a long time, I say: “Behold, I come; I come quickly.” And lest anyone doubt concerning the reward: “My reward is with me.” It is not in another hand [Col. 1211C] or in another’s power; it is in my hand and in my power. And when I come, with me comes, in my mighty power, the whole reward, to render to each according to his works.

Whence comes to you such power, such sufficiency? He says: “I am Alpha and Omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the end.” As though he said: My hand is not powerless to render to each according to his works, because I am God before all things and before the ages, and after me there shall be no other. This is signified by Alpha and Omega, of which letters in the Greek alphabet one is first and the other last. For what he meant in saying, “I am Alpha and Omega,” he explains by saying, “the first and the last,” adding also, “the beginning and the end”: namely, he from whom every creature has its beginning [Col. 1211D] and in whom the rational creature is perfected.

He had said the same at the beginning of the book: “I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end” (Rev. 1). He repeats it here so that, in view of what has already been said, no one may still slumber, excuse himself on grounds of ignorance, or, as though this Scripture’s trumpet were insignificant, pretend not to hear it because of love for his own 512 defilements. He adds further:

“Blessed are those who wash their robes, that they may have authority over the tree of life, and may enter through the gates into the holy city. Outside are dogs, sorcerers, the unchaste, murderers, idol-worshippers, and everyone who loves and practises falsehood.”

Certainly, since the marriage of the Lamb and of the holy city Jerusalem—of which splendid things have been shown up to this point—is a marriage of holiness, [Col. 1212A] and since, as was said above, nothing defiled shall enter there, only those are blessed “who wash their robes,” so that they may have “a wedding garment” (Matt. 22), and above all that “their loins may be girded” (Luke 12): that is, that they may possess the adornment of chastity, not from a desire for human praise, but in expectation that they may have authority over the tree of life—that is, that they may enjoy the truly life-giving vision of the supreme divinity—into which one enters through the gates of righteousness, which are the gates of the holy city.

He appropriately called it the holy city at this point, since he was about to add: “Outside are dogs,” that is, all fools who return to folly as a dog returns to its own vomit (Prov. 24; 2 Pet. 2); and sorcerers, who destroy human life with poisons; and the unchaste, who are ashamed of no disgrace; [Col. 1212B] and murderers, who are indeed stained with human blood and bloody in the Lord’s sight; and idol-worshippers, who certainly have no communion with him who is the one and only true God; and everyone who loves and practises falsehood, such as heretics especially are. All these things are contrary to the holy city; therefore, he says, they are outside. For one who commands, it is enough to have said, “outside.” He immediately adds:

“I, Jesus, have sent my angel to testify these things to you in the churches.” As though he said: If you seek this book’s authority, I, Jesus, am the author and giver of this Apocalypse. This Scripture is not from John, nor is it from a human being; for he did not receive or learn it from a human being, but through my revelation—I who am Jesus—and through my sending it by my angel, so that, just as all Scriptures [Col. 1212C] possess divine authority, these writings too may bear witness, be read to you in the churches, and hold a place at the summit of the canon.

Do you ask who I, Jesus, am, who by my authority wish this Scripture to be commended for testimony in the churches? “I am the root and stock of David, the bright morning star.” As though he said: I am that Jesus who am both David’s Lord and David’s son, who suffered and was buried according to humanity, and rose from the dead in the morning. For because I am David’s Lord and creator, as he himself testifies when he says in the Spirit: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand” (Ps. 109), I am therefore the root; and because I am David’s son, born or made from his seed according to the flesh, I am therefore David’s stock.

And now indeed, to you who have long lived in this world and walk by faith, [Col. 1212D] I am the bright morning star, because I rose from the dead. But then you shall have me as the sun, when you have entered the city of which you have heard: the city illuminated by God’s glory, which needs neither sunlight nor moonlight, precisely because God’s glory has illumined it.

“And the Spirit and the bride say, ‘Come.’ And let him who hears say, ‘Come.’ And let him who thirsts come; and let him who wishes receive the water of life freely.”

“I,” he says, “sent [my angel] to testify these things to you in the churches.” Along with this testimony, the spirit addresses the consciences of each one of you and says to each, “Come”: that is, believe those who testify these things to you here. The bride, that is, the Church, says this outwardly to the bodily ear when, by reading, she presents the literal sound; the Spirit says it inwardly to the ear of the heart, [Col. 1213A] suggesting the meaning, so that one may understand that whatever is said here is reasonable, true, trustworthy, and worthy of hearing.

Let each person hear this Spirit—or bridegroom, as some manuscripts have it—and bride saying, “Come”: that is, let him obey those who call and follow the saving call, so that he may enter into the blessedness of so glorious a city. Moreover, let the one who hears, or obeys, say, “Come”: that is, let him not be content merely with his own salvation, but work so that by a word of exhortation he may gain his neighbour and bring him with himself. And whoever thirsts, whoever desires salvation, need only come. For that river of living water which was shown to you is denied to no thirsty person; rather, whoever wishes may receive it, because good will alone is sufficient for receiving the water of life, which [Col. 1213B] grace has prepared. It is given freely to all, provided that there is a seeker or recipient of good will. It follows:

“I testify to everyone who hears the words of the prophecy of this book: If anyone adds to these things, God will add to him the plagues written in this book. And if anyone takes away from the words of the prophecy of this book, God will take away his share in the tree of life, and in the holy city, and in the things written in this book.”

This punishment of condemnation is undoubtedly that of heretics: their share is taken away from the tree of life, which is Christ, and from the holy city, the heavenly Jerusalem, and from all the good things whatever that are written in this book; and the plagues written in this book are added to them. For they corrupt the holy Scriptures, [Col. 1213C] adding something of their own or subtracting something, as people intent upon constructing their doctrine, who would not wish anything that contradicts it in the holy Scriptures to remain anywhere in any manuscripts.

Thus he most firmly defends this Scripture as one that ought to possess divine and canonical authority, since he strikes its corrupter, whoever he may be, with the same condemnation as heretics. He immediately adds: “He who bears testimony to these things says: ‘Yes, I come quickly.’” This writer could here have said, “Jesus says”; but he preferred to say, “He who bears testimony to these things says,” because at the conclusion of the volume he is wholly intent upon defending this book as written with divine authority and the truth of the Holy Spirit, and upon rescuing it from contempt, [Col. 1214A] taking precautions against what was to come: namely, lest fools should dare to despise or judge rejectable the sacred writing whose meaning they did not deserve to grasp.

“Yes,” he says, “I come quickly.” What I have said, I say again; repeating it, I affirm: “I come quickly, to render to each according to his works.” This is surely sweet and desirable to the devoted soul that loves not this world but God, and gladly receives this announcement that the Lord’s coming is near. Therefore the loving and chaste bride immediately replies: “Amen. Come, Lord Jesus.” In a sense she raises her head, according to the Gospel saying: “When these things begin to happen, look up and lift up your heads, because your redemption draws near” (Luke 21).

Therefore she says, “Amen”: that is, let your promise [Col. 1214B] prove true, that you may come quickly, Lord Jesus, knowing my sighs as I say: “Alas for me, for my sojourning has been prolonged; I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Cedar; my soul has been a long-time sojourner” (Ps. 120). Likewise: “My soul thirsted for God, the living fountain: when shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Ps. 42).

Finally, that we may desire to see the Lord’s face, and that this place of our pilgrimage may be a cause not of delight but rather of sorrow, the writer speaks in this way, saying what he wishes us to say: “Come, Lord Jesus.” And so that we may never hesitate to say this, let us be ready to meet him, according to the saying: “And you 513 [be] like people awaiting their master when he returns from the wedding, so that, when he comes and knocks, they may immediately open to him.”

The final greeting follows, the same as the first: [Col. 1214C] “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen.” For thus he had said at the beginning: “John, to the seven churches which are in Asia: Grace to you and peace,” etc. Clearly, loving the Lord and beloved by the Lord, at the beginning, at the end, and throughout the entire course of his discourse, he speaks from the abundance of his heart of the grace and love overflowing within him, desiring them to be not separately in a few but commonly in all—especially that, as the apostle Paul also desires, we may all say the same thing and there may be no schisms among us, through the grace by which we are redeemed (1 Cor. 12). Amen.

[Col. 1215]

## ON THE VICTORY OF THE WORD OF GOD

### PREFACE TO THE WHOLE WORK, ADDRESSED TO CUNO

Teaching on what occasion he undertook to write these books *On the Victory of the Word of God*.

514 Recently, when you, most desirable hope, Cuno, father of the monastery of Siegburg, graced our dwelling by your presence, we withdrew from the others as usual and discussed certain matters concerning the majesty of the holy Scriptures. At that time our chief discussion concerned the four great beasts and Daniel’s vision. The first, like a lioness, was the kingdom of the Babylonians; another, like a bear, was the kingdom of the Persians and Medes; another, like a leopard, was the kingdom of the Greeks; the fourth, terrible, wondrous, and exceedingly strong, having great iron teeth, devouring and crushing and trampling the remainder under its feet (Dan. 7), was the kingdom of the Romans. Each of these kingdoms, in its own time, held supremacy over the other kingdoms of the nations.

We said that these kingdoms were rightly represented by most ferocious beasts, thirsty for blood, because they were full of cruelty, filled the world with blood by raging in bestial fashion, and crushed the saints of God Most High. But the kingdom of God is a kingdom of peace, a kingdom of love and brotherhood; its rule is mercy, and its dominion is truth, justice, and gentleness. Therefore, by reason of the contrast between the things themselves, it ought also to have an unlike image; and in truth it does. For it follows: “I watched until thrones were set in place, and the Ancient of Days sat.” Again: “I watched therefore in the vision of the night, and behold, one like a Son of Man came in the clouds of heaven; and he came even to the Ancient of Days, and they presented him before him; and he gave him power, honour, and a kingdom, and all peoples, tribes, and tongues shall serve him” (ibid.).

What, I ask, could be more unlike than beasts of this kind ascending from the sea, and the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven, arriving at the white Ancient of Days, whose hair shines in utmost purity because of his antiquity, seated amid thrones that had been placed, and judging those beasts that had hastened to reign in defiance of the wisdom of his ancientness?

While we were speaking of those kingdoms and of the saints of the Most High whom those kingdoms had crushed in bestial fashion, you suddenly raised a question about the Maccabees. They repelled with many battles and material weapons the bloody cruelty of the leopard—that third beast, namely the kingdom of the Greeks—and thereby acquired for themselves an illustrious memory in the Church of God. You said: “I should like to know more certainly why, in the holy Church, we celebrate by reading and singing their martial defence no less than the undefended patience of the holy martyrs.”

I answered that their struggle and military courage, with God’s help, greatly benefited us and every age. For the devil was working through Antiochus, who was called Epiphanes, that is, “illustrious,” so that there might be no remembrance, expectation, or faith in the promise made to Abraham, when God said: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22).

For what did that Antiochus do? He built the abominable idol of desolation upon God’s altar; throughout the surrounding cities of Judaea they built altars; before the doors of houses and in the streets they burned incense and sacrificed; and they burned the books of God’s law in fire, tearing them apart. Wherever books of the Lord’s covenant were found, and whoever observed the law of the Lord, they killed him according to the king’s edict (1 Macc. 1). Certainly the effect of this was that the good tree might be cut down and uprooted, lest good fruit should arise from it: that is, that the Jewish people might be destroyed, so that all nations might not be blessed in Abraham’s seed, which is Christ, and what God had purposed and promised might be made void (Gal. 3).

The root was defended so that such great fruit might arise from it and God’s truth be fulfilled. Therefore the Maccabees, through whom this was accomplished, rightly hold a celebrated name in the Church of God. Esther and Mordecai should be viewed similarly. For when it was said to that bear, “Arise, devour much flesh”—that is, when Haman said to Ahasuerus, king of the Persians and Medes, “Decree that the Jewish nation perish, and I shall pay ten thousand talents into the treasuries of your treasury”—they stood for their lives and for their people. The outcome was reversed: Haman was hanged upon the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai; his ten sons were crucified; and when one day of vengeance had been appointed throughout all the provinces, the Jews took vengeance on their enemies (Esther 3).

When I had answered these and similar things concerning them and the other ancient saints, through whose labours and necessary wars the Word of God won mightily, so that the people from whom he had purposed to assume flesh for the salvation of humankind might not perish, you were exceedingly delighted with this reasoning and suddenly broke out with these words: “Write me a book *On the Victory of the Word of God*.” Repeating this frequently, you urgently insisted—and still do not cease urgently to insist—thinking that from this, namely from the ground of my understanding, you may dig out the treasure of a good work worthy of the title 515 which you have prefixed: that the book may be called *On the Victory of the Word of God*.

Truly, the matter is great and difficult to express; indeed, it is impossible to attain it with fitting words, because the victory is great and the God who conquered is great. For the Word is God—great, I say, and mighty—the one who conquered; great too is the enemy who was conquered, great the contest, and great the causes of the contest. Yet I will add this also: great is your love, which compels me to this undertaking, and great ought to be the zeal of holy devotion to please the Word of God, through whom we were made and delivered, without whose grace no one lives.

Therefore may the Word itself be present, that Wisdom which opened the mouth of the mute and made infants’ tongues eloquent; and may it fill my mouth with its praise, so that I may sing its glory and greatness, in a manner profitable both for you who gave the prompting, for me who obeyed, and for anyone who reads. Now, entering upon this work, I judge it fitting to begin from the very title: that is, first to state the substance of the matter—why this work is called, or what is, the Victory of the Word of God—and then the rest.

## OF R. D. D. RUPERT, ABBOT OF DEUTZ, ON THE VICTORY OF THE WORD OF GOD

# BOOK ONE

[Col. 1217]

### CHAPTER I. [Col. 1217A]

What the victory of the Word of God is; why, and because of what adversary—namely, the devil—he has given this work this title.
