By the victory of the Word of God we mean the accomplished effect and perfect work of God’s purpose, to the praise of that almighty and unconquered one: a purpose which “neither death nor life, nor angels nor principalities, nor things present nor things to come, nor strength, nor height nor depth, nor any other creature, could or will be able to turn aside” (Rom. 8), so that what he himself purposed and decreed should be done has indeed been and is being done.

How truly praiseworthy and great this victory of the Word of God is will cause us to marvel more and more when we consider more carefully what sort of and how great an enemy he is who wished, and still strives, to turn aside that purpose, though he has fallen and been conquered so often. For what sort of and how great is that “great red dragon, having seven heads and ten horns” (Rev. 12)? That is, the great dragon, the ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world. This is the adversary of the Word of God. Though he is so constituted and so great—a rebel who fights and resists—he nevertheless could not and cannot turn aside God’s purpose.

This is the victory of the Word of God: that, according to the Apostle, “those whom God foreknew and predestined to be conformed to the image of that same Word, that same Son of his, he also called, justified, and glorified” (Rom. 8), through his Word made flesh, through his Son, God and man, Jesus Christ. His victory is so great and noble that, now that the aforesaid dragon has been conquered and put to shame, he sits at God’s right hand. In the course of this discourse it will be necessary to say concerning that adversary why or whence he is called and is a dragon; whence he is great; whence red; what his seven heads are and what his ten horns are; whence or through what he received the name serpent; whence he is devil; and why he is called Satan—that is, adversary. But now it is preferable to state what the Word of God itself is, so that the beginning, or head, of the discourse may fittingly be adorned with holy confession and adoration.

### CHAPTER II. [Col. 1218A]

That the Word of God is the Son of God, and that the reward for knowing him is God’s protection, for which we give thanks.

The evangelist, a most loving witness of this Word, when he had said, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God,” immediately added, “and the Word was God” (John 1). According to the wholly secure faith of this Gospel, we believe and confess to God that the Word of God is God, consubstantial with God with whom he was in the beginning. Believing and confessing, we worship this God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, giving thanks because we have deserved to know him, since the knowledge of him bears a great reward.

For it is written concerning the righteous man who knew him by faith: “I will protect him, because he has known my name” (Ps. 91). [Col. 1218B] Clearly, knowledge of his name is worthy of a great reward: namely, that the one who knows him may be protected by him. Wisdom speaks in Proverbs, desiring to be known attentively: “Who has established all the ends of the earth?” (Prov. 30). When you undoubtedly answer, “God,” it immediately asks and says: “What is his name, and what is the name of his son, if you know?” (ibid.).

When Wisdom thus asks, surely at that time the answer failed among most people; indeed, apart from the very few who possessed a divine and prophetic spirit, scarcely anyone knew how to answer that the name of that same God was Father and that his Son was called the Word or Speech (*sermo*). Therefore Wisdom itself, which had asked the question, answers its own question wisely, discerningly, and with great restraint, “so as not to cast pearls before swine” (Matt. 17). For it follows: “Every word of God is fiery; he is a shield to those who hope in him” (Prov. 30).

This is as though it said: The name of his Son is the Word of God, and whoever knows and loves this name is protected by it as by a fiery shield. Therefore, encouraging the one who knows him, he rightly says: “I will protect him, because he has known my name” (Ps. 91). Since knowledge of him bears so great a reward, we therefore give thanks to him, as has now been said, because we have 517 known and deserved to confess this Word. We desire to know him more and more, because while we are pilgrims in this body we cannot perfectly know the vision of divinity. Rather, as the Apostle says: “Now I know in part; then I shall know as I also am known” (1 Cor. 13).

### CHAPTER III

The Word of God is known magnificently through his works, but more magnificently through himself.

How, then, is he now known in part? He is known not in one manner only but in two ways. He is known through his works, and he is known through himself. He is indeed known magnificently through his works, but far more magnificently through himself. Through which works is he known? Certainly through all things that have been made, because “all things were made through him” (John 1): angels, archangels, thrones, dominions, principalities, powers, virtues, cherubim, and seraphim; heaven, earth, sea, and whatever is in them—all were made through this Word. For God the Father himself spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created (Ps. 150). If he spoke and they were made, they were surely made through the Word.

This Word is known through all these things, just as the skill of any craftsman is known through his work. Hence the Apostle says: “For his invisible things, from the creation of the world, are understood and seen through the things that have been made” (Rom. 1). Among the things made through which he is known, since they were made through him, the adversary of this same Word itself occasions no small wonder. For he too was made through him, such and so great as may be understood from many passages of Scripture, especially from those words addressed to blessed Job, in which he is wondrously described by the very one who, just as he made all other things through the Word, made him too: “Behold Behemoth, whom I made with you,” etc. (Job 40), down to: “There is no power on earth to be compared with him, who was made to fear no one” (Job 41).

Among the other things through which this Word ought to be known, that wondrous creature and the celebrated victory of the Word over him afford a magnificent demonstration of its omnipotence and strength. Intending, as far as we can, to narrate that victory, we first endeavour to set forth the persons of conqueror and conquered.

But, as has been said, the Word is known more magnificently through himself when, by surpassing grace, he visits some beloved soul and powerfully yet sweetly affects it through contact with his own substance. This sort of knowledge or experience belongs to very few. Indeed, apart from apostles, prophets, and apostolic men, whose lives shone with the highest virtues, one can scarcely judge that anyone has attained [Col. 1220A] the lot of this blessedness: that while the soul still dwells in the flesh, it should, at least for a moment and on several occasions, perceive the force and sensation of that most mighty substance.

And one who has felt it, one whose human spirit has been touched by that strength, remains silent about such a matter, reverently concealing his treasure in silence, because what he feels is ineffable. Any one of them says, “The word of the Lord came to me,” but does not say how the mind or soul that deserved the coming of the Word of the Lord to itself was affected in that hour. Moreover, a human being would labour in vain to explain it to another human being.

### CHAPTER IV. [Col. 1220A]

Only those taught by God can worthily utter the words of God.

Blessed is the one who has deserved in this way to taste the good Word. Blessed is the one who has deserved in this way to learn how truly it was said: “And the Word was God” (John 1). For it is written: “Blessed is the man whom you instruct, O Lord, and teach from your law” (Ps. 94). The Lord instructed him, and he was instructed; he taught him, and he was taught—taught for warfare, instructed for battle.

That man is, by comparison, a horse, as is said to blessed Job: “The noble horse, whose Lord gave him strength, whose neck he clothed with neighing, whose nostrils’ glory is terror, who, trusting in so great a rider, exults boldly, despises fear, and does not yield to the sword” (Job 39). Indeed, he goes forth to meet the armed men: namely, all the dragon’s heads and all the members of the same adversary of the Word of God.

For God is strong, who touched him; indeed, the Word of God is strength itself. Nor is that one and same Word merely strength: it is also wisdom. Hence, whoever has deserved such an advent of the Strong One becomes both strong and wise—strong, so that he even despises death; wise, so that he speaks a sound and fitting discourse. Nor is this surprising: how could one fail to know how to speak when God has communicated his Word to him, when he has tasted the very substance of the Word? Therefore it is fitting that his words should customarily be called God’s words, and God’s words his words.

Nevertheless, this one singular Word is called, and is, the Word of God alone, and not the word of any person. It must be carefully observed that there is some difference when we read or hear “the Word of the Lord” in the singular and “the words of the Lord” in the plural. This singular Word is the divine substance, unmade and uncreated substance; hence it is called the Word and is the Word of God alone.

But the words which we read or hear in the holy Scriptures were brought about by God through this Word and administered through human beings. Therefore, in one way they are called God’s words, and in another they are rightly called the words of some human being. Thus it should be noted that Scripture says, “The words of Jeremiah son of Hilkiah” (Jer. 1), and “The words of Amos, who was among the shepherds of Tekoa” (Amos 1). But nowhere is it written, “The Word of Jeremiah,” “the Word of Amos,” or “the Word of any of the others,” except only in this sense: “the Word of the Lord that came to” this or that man. For the Word is God and belongs to no one except God alone.

### CHAPTER V. [Col. 1221A]

The magnificence of the victory of the Word of God exceeds all praise.

We have not yet deserved to know this Word in that manner by which, as already stated, it is known through itself. Would that we might at least deserve to know it in the former manner, namely through its works. You, most loving father, have increasingly stirred me by diligent encouragement toward this intention and pursuit, that I might be more fervent, urging me to undertake this work, *On the Victory of the Word of God*.

For this part of his works is the best and most illustrious part, a work for whose praise and thanksgiving no language whatever can suffice. As for his other works—the creation of the world, the legal, prophetic, and evangelical mysteries of this Word, and the grace of the Holy Spirit—I have long ago treated them as I could, judging whatever I could do to be slight and utterly inadequate 518 in proportion to the magnitude or dignity of the matters I undertook, according to the saying of the wise man:

“Glorifying the Lord, however much you can, he will still surpass it, and his magnificence is wonderful. Blessing the Lord, exalt him as much as you can; for he is greater than all praise. When you exalt him, be filled with strength; do not weary yourselves, for you will not attain. Who has seen him and described him? Who has magnified him as he has been from the beginning? Many things greater than these are hidden; for we have seen few of his works” (Ecclus. 43).

Since he says this and it is so, what should I judge concerning myself, whether in that part of his works which I mentioned—in which I undertook to glorify, bless, and exalt him—or in this part which you have now proposed to me, namely the victory by which he conquered the devil? I confess that I am exceedingly feeble and without eloquence for so great a matter. But because the subject concerns the Word itself, I fittingly hope that words will be born to me.

Therefore I shall act according to the wise man’s exhortation just cited: I shall indeed exalt the Word of God in his victory as much as I can and as he himself grants. Yet I know and confess that his victory is greater than all praise, and I shall not labour in the expectation that I can attain to equalling the matter with words or magnifying him as he is.

### CHAPTER VI. [Col. 1221C]

By what names and why the enemy of the Word of God is named in the Scriptures, and what the dragon’s seven heads are.

The adversary of this Word must now be recognized from his names. In the Apocalypse he is called: “the great dragon, the red dragon, having seven heads, the ancient serpent, and he is called the devil and Satan” (Rev. 12). These names are interconnected. For the cause on account of which he is called “dragon” did not arise before that in view of which he is called “the ancient serpent”; nor did the reason why he was “called devil” occur before he became “Satan,” that is, adversary. Rather, the reason why he was called Satan came first; then the reason why he was called “devil”; then the reason why he was called “the ancient serpent”; and then the reason why he was called the dragon with so many heads, “the great dragon, the red dragon.”

Accordingly, he is called and is Satan from the time when he began to oppose the Word of God, caused sedition among the angels as a disturber of peace and rebel against the light, and then—or consequently—received the sentence by which he is called devil, that is, “falling downward.” Hence the Lord says: “I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10).

After this he did that by which he deserved to be called “the ancient serpent,” namely when, having entered the serpent, he first deceived the human being. Then, advancing to worse things, he did that by which he is called “dragon”—and not merely any dragon, but “the great red dragon having seven heads.” For he who had formerly been accustomed to deceive the whole world by fraud added force also to fraud, inciting kings, princes, and proud people to persecute and kill the elect because of the Word of God.

He first began this as soon as the promise had been made to Abraham concerning the blessed seed, which is Christ, in whom all nations hoped to be blessed (Gen. 22). [Col. 1222B] This began to be done through Pharaoh, king of Egypt, who first ordered the male children of the Hebrews to be killed in the water (Exod. 1). Therefore the kingdom of Egypt was the first head of this dragon.

The second head of the dragon was the kingdom of Israel, divided because of Solomon’s sin. In its times Jezebel with King Ahab, Athaliah their daughter, and other kings both in Samaria and Jerusalem killed the prophets of the Word (3 Kings 18).

The third head was the kingdom of the Babylonians, who burned Jerusalem and the temple—which at that time was the sole temple of the Lord’s name—and cast the three youths into the fiery furnace and Daniel into the lions’ den because of the Word of God (Dan. 3, 6).

The fourth head was the kingdom of the Persians and Medes, who wished to destroy in one day the entire Jewish people, from whom the Word was to be incarnate (Esther 3).

The fifth head was the kingdom of the Greeks. Its shameless king Antiochus (1 Macc. 1), seeking to erase every remembrance of the Word or law of God, among other cruel crimes killed seven brothers and their mother with extreme brutality (2 Macc. 7).

The sixth head was the kingdom of the Romans, under which this incarnate Word mounted the cross through Pilate, and through whose hands innumerable martyrs of his were killed. The seventh head will be the kingdom of Antichrist.

### CHAPTER VII

Why the devil is called a dragon, when he first began to put forth a horn, and that the Lamb—that is, the Word of God—had the same number of horns.

[Col. 1222D] Therefore, from the time of Pharaoh, he began to be regarded as a dragon, though he had already been a serpent from the time when he deceived the first man through the serpent. If authority is required, the Lord says in Ezekiel: “Behold, I am against you, Pharaoh king of Egypt, great dragon, who lie in the midst of your rivers and say: ‘The river is mine, and I made myself’” (Ezek. 29), etc. Clearly, while rebuking the devil in the person of Pharaoh and calling him “great dragon,” He makes it sufficiently clear that from the time of that Pharaoh he began to do that by which he deserved to be called a dragon. For until then he had not violently persecuted, but only deceitfully seduced. Conversely, it must be considered at the same time that then too was celebrated that for which the Word of God is customarily called [Col. 1223A] the Lamb. For that Pharaoh, a type of the devil, the great dragon, worn down by many plagues and at last overcome by the immolation of the Lamb, let the people of God go.

Having observed these things, it is most fitting also to recall that as many as are the heads of that dragon, so many are the horns of this Lamb, as is written in the same book of the Apocalypse in which the dragon is read to have so many heads: “And I saw in the midst of the throne, and of the four living creatures and the elders, a Lamb standing as though slain, having seven horns” (Apoc. 5), etc. Great and wonderful are these mysteries of the holy Scriptures, of which we shall speak in order, as the Word Himself grants grace. Now it is permissible to go back more deeply, namely to the beginning of the conflict in which that Satan first rose against the Word [Col. 1223B] of God and, conquered, fell from heaven. It is fitting first also to inquire, so far as may be inferred from the sacred Scriptures, what was the cause of the enmity, or what material that enemy had for pride.

## CHAPTER VIII. That pride was the cause of the rebellion, and what were the causes for pride.

Satan had no true causes of enmity against God’s Word, but fabricated false ones. He did, however, have material for pride: beauty, knowledge, and the greatness of his own condition. For he was created beautiful and most fair, as the Creator Himself testifies when He says in Ezekiel: “Behold, Assyria is like a cedar in Lebanon, beautiful in its branches and thick with foliage. And it was most beautiful in [Col. 1223C] 519 its greatness; no tree in the paradise of God was like it in its beauty, because I made it beautiful” (Ezek. 31). This concerns his beauty.

Moreover, the same passage signifies his great knowledge in this manner: “The waters nourished him; the deep exalted him; its rivers flowed around his roots, and it sent forth its streams to all the trees of the region” (ibid.). More plainly, in the same prophet, while he is denounced under the name of the prince of Tyre, God declares that knowledge—customarily understood through waters—was in him, together with the beauty already mentioned: “Full,” He says, “of wisdom and perfect in beauty, you were in the delights of the paradise of God; you were a Cherub, extended and protecting” (Ezek. 28). For *Cherub* is interpreted “fullness of knowledge.”

The third thing, namely his greatness, is sufficiently expressed by its being said there that he was “extended” and “protecting.” It is further expressed by the fact that, in the passage cited above, after saying, “Behold, Assyria is like a cedar in Lebanon, beautiful in its branches and thick with foliage,” He added, “and lofty in height.” And shortly afterwards: “The cedars,” He says, “were not taller in that paradise of God; the fir trees did not equal its summit, and the plane trees were not equal to its foliage” (Ezek. 31). By metaphor, without doubt, the cedars, plane trees, and fir trees that did not equal his summit signify angelic or archangelic ranks.

He was therefore fairer and more beautiful than the others: “because,” He says, “no tree in the paradise of God is like it in its beauty, because I made it beautiful.” He was also greater and higher, because “the fir trees did not equal its summit.” And he was more knowledgeable, because this Cherub sent forth his streams, by which knowledge is signified, to all the trees of the region. Whoever considers these three things—his greatness, knowledge, and beauty—more clearly recognizes why, when the prophet attacks him in the person of Tyre, God says: “You,” He says, “are the seal of likeness” (Ezek. 28). Of what likeness, unless of the holy and adorable Trinity, was he a seal according to these three things? For the Holy Trinity itself is greatness, wisdom, and beauty. The Father is the greatness of the Son and the Holy Spirit; the Son is the wisdom of the Father and the Holy Spirit; the Holy Spirit [Col. 1224B] is the beauty of the Father and the Son. For, as Scripture testifies, he participated more than the rest in greatness, wisdom, and beauty. By this itself it becomes somewhat clear why he was called the “seal of likeness.”

But that foolish being, though he was in such great honour, did not understand, and turned all these things into material for pride. Such great generosity from the Creator did not suffice him unless the same should be said or thought of him as of God; unless he should be called God; unless he should be worshipped by the angels as God; unless he also should be proclaimed uncreated. For he denied that God was his Creator and said that he was God. Thus, in the prophet mentioned above, after the Lord God had reproached him under the name of Pharaoh, saying: “Behold, I am against you, Pharaoh king of Egypt, great dragon, who lie in the midst of your rivers,” He immediately added: “And [Col. 1224C] you say: ‘The river is mine, and I made myself’” (Ezek. 29). He said that he was uncreated; he denied that God was his Creator. Under the name of the prince of Tyre the same Lord God says against him: “Your heart was lifted up, and you said, ‘I am God, and I sat upon the throne of God,’ and you set your heart as though it were the heart of God” (Ezek. 28).

## CHAPTER IX. That through pride he became the father of falsehood, and what that falsehood was according to the prophetic writings.

Behold, this is the falsehood that this devil begot, of which the Lord Jesus Christ, Truth and Word of God, declared him to be the father, saying to the Jews: [Col. 1224D] “You are of your father the devil, and you wish to do the desires of your father. He was a murderer from the beginning and did not stand in the truth, because truth is not in him. When he speaks falsehood, he speaks from his own resources, because he is a liar and its father” (John 8)—that is, the father of falsehood.

This was the beginning of the conflict, the origin of the contest: that he uttered such a falsehood from his own resources. “From his own resources,” I say, because matters were not as he said: “I made myself; I am God” (Ezek. 28). This offspring of his heart is contrary to the offspring of the heart of the one and only God, contrary to the Word of God and to the truth of God. This is the beginning of enmity, and this enmity is natural. For truth and falsehood are naturally opposed. Truth is the Word of God; falsehood is [Col. 1225A] nothing. Yet this nothing brought about this result: that he who was something, who possessed much greatness, wisdom, and beauty, was changed into another so completely that he could no longer be or be called great, wise, or beautiful.

Indeed, he ceased to be so great that he is as ashes. For the Lord says: “I will make you, O Cherub, into ashes upon the earth before the eyes of all who see you” (Ezek. 28). He ceased to be wise: “You have destroyed your wisdom,” says the Lord (ibid.). He ceased to be beautiful: “You have defiled your sanctification,” He says (ibid.). But let us return to the order of the argument. For we have not yet heard the whole sacrilege of his pride, which he committed while still conspicuous in that greatness, wisdom, and beauty, and on account of which he was made so wretched [Col. 1225B] and stripped of those goods.

## CHAPTER X. That Satan, deceived by his own falsehood, despised the other angels and aspired to God’s majesty and equality.

When that liar uttered the falsehood, “I made myself, and I am God” (Ezek. 29), he further deliberated within himself and purposed, saying in his heart: “I will ascend above the height of the clouds; I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14). Clearly, by the name “clouds” he called all the other angels, perhaps on account of his own greatness and beauty. For he was not small in his own eyes, judging all the angels inferior to himself by as much as clouds, even if somewhat white or bright, are darker than the beauty of Lucifer. For he wished to be regarded as Lucifer. Hence he is reproached: “How you have fallen from heaven, Lucifer, you who rose in the morning!” (ibid.).

Certainly, because he is read there to have said, “I will ascend above the height of the clouds,” it is thereby understood—where he is called Lucifer in reproach—that he esteemed the other angels in his heart as clouds, thinking himself to be like the light that clouds need in order to be illumined. But it occurs that in the same place he said both: “I will exalt my throne above the stars of God, and I will ascend above the height of the clouds” (ibid.). To this one must answer that neither these visible stars nor clouds yet existed; therefore, under the names of stars and clouds, the ranks of angels must be understood. Though they were stars of God, he considered them [Col. 1225D] clouds in comparison with himself.

But however he said these things, this is certain: he held all in contempt, for “he sees every high thing, and he himself is king over all the children of pride” (Job 40). What, then, does he mean when he says: “I will ascend into heaven, above the stars of God, above the height of the clouds”? Was he not in heaven, and did not that Satan fall from heaven because of this pride? Had he not ascended above the height of such clouds when, as has already been said from another prophet, the fir trees and plane trees—by which the heights of angelic dignity are understood—were not equal to his foliage and did not equal his summit in the paradise of God (Ezek. [Col. 1226A] 31)?

Another ascent, therefore, must be understood: the ascent of the heart, not of the body; an ascent in honour, not in place. To establish further that an advancement in honour is rightly called an ascent, even schoolboys read a noble leader saying to his soldiers:

> To the height to which a free people could raise a citizen,  
> I ascended; and above me I left nothing but kingdoms.

His statement, “I will ascend,” was the swelling of ambition. For he who said, “I made myself; I am God” (Ezek. 29), consequently sought to ascend into heaven in such a way as to hold dominion over heaven; he wished so to exalt his throne above the stars of God and so to ascend above the height of the clouds that he might be worshipped and honoured by the chorus of angels as their God [Col. 1226B] and Lord. For this is the highest assertion, or the conclusion, of his declaration. As if someone asked, “To what will you ascend?” he says: “I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14).

## CHAPTER XI. That Satan also preached his own falsehood to the other angels and persuaded some to regard him as God.

How, moreover, could this come about except by the consent of the angels themselves? Therefore, in order to carry out the plan he had formed within himself, he began to preach himself to all the angels. Being full of wisdom, he trusted that he had the power to persuade them to believe him when he said: “I made myself; I am God” (Ezek. 29). Whatever those angelic languages may be, it is certainly clear that he preached concerning himself what the prophetic Scriptures of truth testify of him. Nor did he do so casually; rather, with the great skill of knowledge with which he was filled, he proclaimed to every assembly of angels that he was God.

For what else is signified by what, in the passage mentioned above, the Lord says among other things against him under the name of Assyria? “Its rivers,” He says, “flowed around its roots, and it sent forth its streams to all the trees of the region; and its thickets were multiplied, and its branches were lifted up because of many waters” (Ezek. 31). For he sent forth his streams to all the trees of the region because, pouring out his abundant wisdom, [Col. 1226D] he laboured to ensnare all the multitudes of angels and bring them over to his opinion, so that he might be regarded among them as the Most High and worshipped as God. “And its branches were lifted up because of many waters,” because, through the great abundance of wisdom by which he commended himself, he began to be regarded by the greater part of the angels as greater than he had been. Of them, shortly afterwards, He says: “And all the trees of delight that were in the paradise of God envied him” (Ezek. 31).

Notice what, and how, He says it. He does not say, “All the trees of the region envied him,” but “All the trees of delight envied him.” He did indeed send forth his streams to all the trees of the region, but only all the trees of delight envied him, because he attempted through his wisdom to deceive all the angels and draw them to [Col. 1227A] his favour. But only those spirits flattered him who sought their own glory, not God’s; who delighted rather to serve the creature than the Creator. That this was so is especially clear from what is finally said to him: “Behold, you have been brought down with the trees of delight to the lowest earth; in the midst of the uncircumcised you shall sleep with those slain by the sword” (Ezek. 31).

## CHAPTER XII. That Satan thought no one knew of his creation and condition, and therefore feared no testimony against himself.

Whom among all the angels did he think could, when he said, “I am not a creature of God; I was made by no one; rather, ‘I made myself’” (Ezek. 29), oppose him and say: “You speak falsely”? [Col. 1227B] Whom did he fear might be found as a witness of God, testifying and saying: “He made you”? For he is a true and certain witness who “testifies to what he has seen and heard” (John 3). But none of all the spirits or angels saw or heard when God made him. For none of them had yet been created; all were younger, while he was first.

God Himself testifies to this, wonderfully describing him to blessed Job: “He is the beginning of the ways of God” (Job 40). Eliphaz the Temanite likewise, while he judges that righteous man most wrongly, supposing him to be proud against God and to imitate the language of blasphemers, says: “Are you the first man, and were you formed before the hills?” (Job 15). This is as though he said: “Does your heart lift you up, and does your spirit swell against God, so that you seem to imitate Adam, who perished when deceived by a spirit of pride—or rather the devil, who was formed before the hills, that is, before the other angels, and grew proud against the Creator?”

Since, therefore, he had none among all the angels aware of his creation who could say, “I saw” or “I heard,” because he himself had been created first, whom did he think could stand against him as God’s witness? “Who can uncover the face of his garment? Who can enter within his jaws? Who can open the gates of his face?” Clearly, in his judgment, there was no one who could convict him of lying and pronounce judgment upon his created condition.

## CHAPTER XIII. [Col. 1227D] That Satan was convicted by the testimony of the Word of God alone, and that the testimony of the same Word of God was not hidden from the other spirits.

But behold: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God; this was in the beginning with God” (John 1). This Word, this God, ought to be and could be a true and competent witness that that Satan was false and spoke falsehood. For He “is above all; He is before all; and He testifies to what He has seen and heard” (John 3). What did He not see or hear, He who saw all things when they came to be—indeed, who saw and heard all things before they came to be? For “all things were made through Him, and what was made in Him was life” (John [Col. 1228A] 1; printed “XI”). He therefore saw that highest Angel too when he was made; He saw and heard him before he was made, and that angel was made through Him. Accordingly, He could testify of that proud being that he had spoken falsely, that he had been made or created.

Therefore, while he sent forth his streams, as was said above, to all the trees of the region, this Word—the living and true fountain who was with God, according to the saying, “For with you is the fountain of life” (Ps. 35)—was, conversely, sent to water the same trees of the region, that is, to instruct the ranks of spirits in the knowledge of truth. For this Word is such a fountain that He is also the light of hearts, enlightening the eyes of the mind so that they may be illumined and see not only present things, but also things past and things to come. Hence, after the words quoted above, “For with you is the fountain of life,” there immediately follows: “And in your light we shall see light” (ibid.).

We have a sufficient example of this in holy human beings to whom the word of the Lord came, and who were consequently called Seers, because in this light they so saw light that some of them—though until then unlettered men, indeed shepherds, such as Amos and David—suddenly became learned, prudent in mystical discourse, and wondrous and magnificent interpreters of heavenly secrets. Did not such men also see, among other things, the condition and presumption of that Satan—that is, the adversary—whom they described through remarkable figures and tropes, now under the name of Pharaoh, now of Assyria, now of the princes [Col. 1228C] of Tyre, and of the other proud rulers of this age who imitated him?

Thus, at least from the example of human prophets of this Word of the Lord, let it be clear to us that the elect angels, through the infusion of the same Word, knew and did not regard as uncertain, but saw in clear light, that which was past: namely, that the one God had made him first, just as He had made them, who were younger. This was the Word, and the faithful testimony of the Word, who was God, who speaks nothing uncertain but “testifies to what He has seen and heard” (John 3). One part of the spirits received His testimony; another part did not receive it. The part that received His testimony sealed its confession that God is true, saying: [Col. 1228D] “See that I alone am, and there is no other God besides me” (Deut. 32). And that Satan is a liar, who said: “I am God, and I sat upon the throne of God; and the river is mine; I made myself” (Ezek. 28; 29), and other such things.

## CHAPTER XIV. That a portion of the spirits, corrupted by pride and envy, did not receive the testimony of the Word of God; but that another portion, humble and obedient, remained in truth.

The part that did not receive His testimony is as inexcusable as that prince and father of falsehood himself, who lied against his own conscience by saying that he was what he was not and denying that he was what he was. For all of them likewise could have known that the testimony of God’s Word was true; but, through pride or envy, they rebelled against the light—that is, against the same Word. Of this pride or envy there remains even now the customary proverb: “Always, to disparage the better, favour the worse.” Those spirits who are called, and are, evil undoubtedly did this.

For envying the better—indeed, the only good—Creator, they exalted by their favour wicked and lying Satan, that is, His adversary; and they hated and rejected His witness, His Word. In this they resemble those malicious human beings who are accustomed to say to the same Lord God: “Depart from us; we do not desire the knowledge of your ways” (Job 21). The Jews were especially imitators of such spirits. Concerning them, because they did not receive His testimony, the very Word of God says: [Col. 1229B] “But now they have both seen and hated both me and my Father” (John 15).

Someone has eloquently declaimed their pride and folly. After first saying, “O Israel, how great is the house of God, and how vast the place of His possession! Great, and without end; high and immeasurable” (Baruch 3), he continues: “There were those renowned giants who were from the beginning, great in stature and skilled in war. The Lord did not choose these, nor did they find the way of discipline; therefore they perished, and because they did not have wisdom, they died because of their folly” (ibid.). He fittingly signified their pride by the name of giants, and expressed their folly by its proper term. He also set forth the magnitude and monstrosity of their rebellion against truth in a wonderful manner, both precisely and briefly, by saying: “Skilled in war.”

Then he most beautifully expresses the wisdom, humility, and obedience of the holy spirits who, as has been said, received the testimony of the Word of God: “But the stars gave light in their watches and rejoiced; they were called, and said, ‘Here we are,’ and they shone for Him with gladness” (ibid.). Then, against that prince of the wicked who said, “I am God” (Ezek. 28), he truthfully adds: “He who made them is our God, and no other shall be compared with Him” (Baruch 3).

## CHAPTER XV. [Col. 1229D] That Satan was condemned by God because of the testimony of the Word, defeated by the holy angels through the sword of the Word of God, and cast out of heaven.

Therefore, because they were giants, because they were skilled in war—that is, because they were proud and rebelled against the Creator with their entire purpose—it befitted Him who made them to pronounce a just sentence both against them and against their prince, and to display His power in them. In the passage mentioned above, the prophet signifies this sentence by the name of a sword against Assyria, saying: “To whom are you likened, O glorious and lofty one among the trees of delight? Behold, you have been brought down to the lowest earth; in the midst of the uncircumcised, you shall sleep with those slain by the sword” (Ezek. 31).

That the same sentence is a sentence of condemnation, though understood there through the sword, is clear when it is said in the Apocalypse of the beast rising from the sea that “it has a wound from the sword, and lived” (Apoc. 13). For the beast has the wound of a sword and lives because the devil received a sentence of condemnation in heaven and yet still grows proud and defends himself. Thus he was struck by the sword with the trees of delight; that is, he was condemned by the sentence of the Word of God with his angelic followers.

But when condemned by the most just judgment of God’s Word, he was immediately cast from heaven through the ministry of the holy angels, soldiers in the victory of God’s Word. What, then, were or are the weapons used by those spirits in that battle? They certainly were not material weapons; rather, all their armour was and is the very Word of God. The Word of God, exerting His force against those rebellious spirits through the holy angels, achieved victory through Himself.

For the Word of God is fire—so intolerable to the wicked and evil spirits as visible fire is to infirm bodies. Hence it is written in Proverbs: “Every word of God, refined by fire, is a shield to those who hope in Him” (Prov. 30). And the Psalmist says: “Your word is exceedingly refined by fire” (Ps. 118). Again: “As wax melts before fire, so may sinners perish before God” (Ps. 67). Therefore the holy angels defeated the devil and his [Col. 1230C] 522 angels not with ordinary weapons but with burning fire; for the Word of God is in them.

This fire is intolerable indeed to the ungodly and to those who hate it, but gentle and sweet to the godly and those who love it. Therefore, in the prophet mentioned above, the holy angels are called fiery stones. Thus it is written: “And I set you upon the holy mountain of God; you walked in the midst of fiery stones” (Ezek. 28). And immediately He says: “And you sinned, and I cast you from the holy mountain of God, and destroyed you, O protecting Cherub, from the midst of the fiery stones” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER XVI. On what is written in the Psalms: “You are terrible, and who can resist you? From then is your wrath.”

From this it is sufficiently clear how truly the Psalmist says: “You are terrible, and who can resist you? From then is your wrath” (Ps. 75). This is as though he said: It is not from the time anyone sins, but from the time the sinner resists You—which that first one did—that Your wrath exerts its force, and no one can resist it. Who, rightly considering so great a wrath of the terrible God, would not fear it? He who seemed to himself strongest was found among the angels whose lord he wished to be as powerless as wax or straw amid flames. Who would not marvel at this in praise of the Word of God?

Let the prophetic text be considered more carefully, how it declaims against him. It had first said: “Every precious stone was your covering: sardius, topaz, jasper, chrysolite, onyx, beryl, sapphire, carbuncle, and emerald” (Ezek. 28). After this it continues: “Your inward parts were filled with iniquity, and you sinned; and I cast you from the mountain of God, and destroyed you, O protecting Cherub, from the midst of fiery stones” (Ezek. 28). The nine precious stones, by which we understand the nine orders of angels, whom he appropriated to himself as a covering for his adornment and service, are called fiery stones. Does not this saying foretell a wonderful outcome? It is as if a thief or robber should seize and put on a cloak or tunic, only for it at once to be transformed for him into a fiery breastplate or cuirass.

Truly, therefore, You are terrible, O God, and no one resists You. For wherever someone dares to resist You, from then begins Your wrath, which cannot be borne. That great and strong being, when he melted away from before Your face, “as wax melts before fire” (Ps. 67), experienced this terribly in himself; and he sufficiently demonstrates to all that no one can resist You.

Nevertheless, when we read or hear “from then is your wrath,” or anything else of this sort, we do not understand—and ought not understand—such language of the impassible God as though the movements of mind denoted by the words “wrath” or “anger” could occur in Him. For He always gently orders all things in tranquillity; but creation, corrupted and disturbed by its own fault, experiences the Creator’s very gentleness and tranquillity badly and punitively. Thus, at one and the same time or moment, He illumines and does not burn those aforesaid stones that are incorrupt, while He burns and does not illumine their adversaries, who are corrupt and fallen away from a good nature. Although this is sufficiently intelligible in itself to every sensible person, it is nonetheless helpful to see it still more clearly by examining a familiar comparison.

## CHAPTER XVII. [Col. 1231C] By a most beautiful comparison he shows that movements and affections of mind do not apply to God, but that He is unchangeable.

Take some shining stone among the brightest stones of such a kind as those whose names, as has been said, the Lord God uses in the prophet to signify the nine orders of angels. Often, if you wish, you hold it up before the face of the sun shining in a clear sky, and the stone immediately receives, within its small compass, the image of the great sun. Then place beneath it combustible dry fuel. Does not the one and same solar brightness both cast a harmless ray in the stone and produce, in the material just mentioned, a burning fire painful to the touch? The same fire shines in the stone and does not burn; in the fuel it smokes and burns.

It is therefore not strange that our God, who, as the Apostle says, “is a consuming fire” (Heb. 12), should in one and the same act render the holy angels so fiery that this is their beauty and delight, while touching His adversaries in such a way that, struck, they are consumed punitively. Thus, “I destroyed you,” He says, “O protecting Cherub, from the midst of fiery stones” (Ezek. 28): that is, because you could not endure their fire. Your pride and their humility are opposed by such a natural opposition that what is glory to them is itself punishment to you.

Meanwhile, it must be understood that wherever he turns, he carries his punishment with him, and that the wound of the fire of the fiery stones, by which he was once struck as by lightning, continues inwardly within him. This punishment may be understood from these words of the Lord to blessed Job, subject to a more sacred interpretation: “From his mouth lamps proceed like torches of burning fire; from his nostrils smoke proceeds as from a heated pot, and his breath, glowing hot, makes coals burn, and flame goes forth from his mouth” (Job 41).

Until, then, the day of the universal judgment comes, when he “will be hurled down before all who see him” (Job 40) into “the eternal fire prepared for him and his angels” (Matt. 25), he already has the punishment of the lightning-flame by which, struck like lightning, he fell from heaven. Nothing does he fear so much as the thunderbolt of the Word of God. He has no strength to stand wherever he perceives it—in the heart, or proceeding from the heart and mouth, of a human being or angel who possesses love for that same Word.

## CHAPTER XVIII. That from the conflict in which the devil was defeated, one of the princes of the heavenly host returned bearing both primacy and a glorious name, so that he is now called Michael, that is, “Who is like God?”

From that great and wonderful conflict, one who was first among the princes of the heavenly host returned gloriously endowed with a beautiful name and honour: namely, that thereafter he should be called Michael, and that he should be prince not only of angels but also of human beings who possess the Word of God. Thus an angel said of him to Daniel: “And behold, Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me” (Dan. 10). Again: “Yet I will declare to you what is set forth in the Scriptures of truth, and there is no one who assists me in all these matters except Michael, your prince” (ibid.). And, shortly afterwards: “At that time Michael shall arise, the great prince who stands for the children of your people; and there shall come a time such as has not been since nations began to be until that time” (Dan. 12).

When he says, “who stands for the children of your people,” speaking to one whose people alone had then been entrusted with and knew the Word of God, and calls him “your great prince,” it is surely evident that he is prince until the end of the age over all who believe and confess the Word of God. He was endowed with this honour or primacy because he resisted the devil when the latter said, “I am God,” so as to say, “Who is like [Col. 1232D] God?” And in conquering him he proved that “there is no other like God.” Hence, as already said, he was also endowed with the name Michael; for Michael means “Who is like God?”

He shone victorious then in heaven, and he now conquers that ancient enemy in the Church that tends toward heaven. The Church itself is therefore called heaven because it lives the heavenly life. The mystical Scripture of the Apocalypse records this: “And there was,” it says, “a great battle in heaven: Michael and his angels fought with the dragon; and the dragon fought, and his angels” (Apoc. 12), etc. This great prince, then, is the prince of the divine war, while the Word of God is the power of that war. For the Word Himself both crushed that Satan in heaven as God and, now made flesh in [Col. 1233A] this world, bound that same strong one as the stronger man does (Luke 11).

Accordingly, this archangel, fighting with his angels, was then able to cast him out of heaven, where he said: “I am God, and I sat,” or “I shall sit, upon the throne of God” (Ezek. 28). And now, fighting against him not only with his angels but also with holy human beings—and especially with the devout martyrs of Christ, for whom to die was to conquer—he has prevailed to drive the same enemy out of the temples or shrines of idols, where he was worshipped by us Gentiles.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the words spoken to blessed Job: “Who released the cornerstone of the earth, when the morning stars praised me together and all the sons of God rejoiced?”

Thus, when he had been cast down, the holy angels praised and rejoiced [Col. 1233B]—participants with Michael and fellow-workers in the victory of the Word of God—as God and Lord himself, speaking to blessed Job, beautifully indicates. For after saying: “Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth? Tell me, if you have understanding: who set its measures, if you know? Or who stretched the line over it? Upon what were its bases founded?” (Job 38), he added: “Or who laid its cornerstone, when the morning stars praised me together and all the sons of God rejoiced?” (ibid.).

Certainly, in these words we discern a prophecy of future things, and rightly understand the establishment, measuring, and strengthening of the spiritual earth—that is, the holy Church—whose cornerstone is Christ, as [Col. 1233C] blessed Pope Gregory teaches. Yet, if it pleases us to attend to the narration of past events: truly God laid the foundations of this earth which we tread—marvellously—upon nothing, and established its bases, that is, its firmness, by his command alone.

Another stone, namely Satan, is to be understood as the cornerstone of the earth, that is, the prince of this world. For without doubt Job himself, above, using a parable, said of him: “The torrent separates the stone also of darkness and the shadow of death from the travelling people—those whom the foot of the needy man has forgotten, and the pathless” (Job 28). There can be no doubt that in this place Satan must be understood as the stone of darkness: that is, possessing nothing of the illumination of the seven eyes which the prophet Zechariah saw in another stone (Zech. 4). A stone, [Col. 1233D] I say, “of darkness and shadow,” not of just any shadow, but “of the shadow of death.”

“The torrent” of divine judgment separated this stone “from the travelling people,” so that he might not darken or envelop in his own gloom those who know themselves to be strangers in this world, who have here no abiding city but seek the one to come (Heb. 13). With such a stone it separates from that same people also “those whom the foot of the needy man has forgotten, and the pathless,” that is, all ungodly people whom, because of their unbelief, “the foot of the needy man” has forgotten and abandoned—that is, the grace of Jesus Christ, “who, though he was rich, became poor for our sake” (2 Cor. 8). He abandoned them, I say, as “pathless,” because they were unwilling to prepare, or to have prepared within themselves, the way of the Lord.

Therefore that exceedingly hard stone, the hostile stone, the cornerstone of the earth—that is, the proud prince of this world—may rightly be understood in this way. And God truly “laid him down,” that is, cast him downward; nor could anyone but God cast him down. Therefore, when he had cast him down, “the morning stars,” he says, praised together, and “all the sons of God” rejoiced. What he had said—“the morning stars praised”—he repeats by saying, “and all the sons of God rejoiced”: namely, the holy angels, who, because they remained in the brightness of grace, are rightly called “morning stars,” that is, angels of light, angels possessing love and knowledge of God; and this shone upon them more brightly through the overthrow of the defeated devil.

## CHAPTER XX. On what was said to the same blessed Job: “Power and terror are with him who makes peace in his high places.”

What, then, do we suppose was the beginning of this praise or rejoicing? What is more beautiful than what the very name Michael sounds forth? What is more resonant for thundering praise than this: “Who is like God?” Surely the event itself required that, thundering forth thus, they should praise and rejoice, so that at the very beginning of praise and rejoicing they might rebuke the one defeated for his great folly—he who thought himself to be like God—and might worthily magnify the true and only God, because no other can be like him.

At the same time, I say, that victory, having banished the great discord involving the devil and his angels, brought about great concord among all the remaining blessed spirits. [Col. 1234C] Every cause of stumbling had been removed from their assembly. Hence those words to blessed Job: “Power and terror are with him who makes peace in his high places” (Job 25). This was indeed truly said, but it was neither well nor suitably introduced.

For Job had said at the end of his speech: “But if it is not so, who can convict me of lying and set my words before God?” (Job 24). One of his friends, who interpreted all his words very badly, thinking that he had said this through excessive pride of mind, replied: “Power and terror are with him who makes peace in his high places”—as though he meant: He can convict you of lying who was able to rebuke the terrible devil and, after casting him down [Col. 1234D] because he caused discord in his high places, to establish indissoluble peace in those same high places. “Power and terror are with him,” I say, as has been proved in the case of that one and of all proud persons, and in your own case—you who, struck because of pride and stripped of every good, now sit upon a dungheap.

He spoke badly and inappropriately, as has already been said, because he spoke against a man simple, upright, fearing God, and departing from evil. Nevertheless, it was a good and true statement, which could rightly have been said against someone such as the man he supposed Job to be. Therefore, when it says that the morning stars praised or rejoiced together, it indicates that great discord was banished and great concord was made in heaven when the devil fell. This should not be understood lightly, as though that adversary had produced only a small disturbance of discord amid that vast multitude of spirits when he falsely wished to be regarded as God against the true and living God.

## CHAPTER XXI. Satan did not fall immediately upon being created.

To one possessed by the opinion that Satan fell immediately when he was created, it does not appear, nor does it enter the heart, that the tumult of that diabolical sedition and discord was great—although such a person does not fail to recognize the great rage of demons and, correspondingly, the great and good zeal of the holy angels. One must therefore first know that he did not fall as soon as he was created. For thus it was said of him through the aforementioned prophet: “You walked in the midst [Col. 1235B] of fiery stones; perfect in your ways from the day of your creation, until iniquity was found in you” (Ezek. 28).

Surely the expression, “from the day of your creation, until iniquity was found in you,” does not permit that understanding or opinion by which anyone says or thinks that, once he had been created, he immediately fell. That suspicion would also imply that he was created by God as he now is, namely evil. But the present discourse proves both that he was created innocent and upright and that he remained for no brief period among the holy angels, when it begins thus: “You walked in the midst of fiery stones, perfect in your ways,” then adds, “from the day of your creation,” and afterwards, “until [Col. 1235C] iniquity was found in you.”

We do not understand “the day of creation” as we now understand the course and return of the sun, for that visible sun did not yet exist; but the meaning of the prophet—or of God speaking to a human being—could not have been expressed better. It must therefore not be thought that he fell immediately upon being created. Rather, the truth is that he was first created and only then placed in that heavenly paradise. For thus it is written in the same place: “On the day,” he says, “when you were created, your settings were prepared; you were a cherub stretched out and protecting, and I set you on the holy mountain of God” (Ezek. 28).

This also gives us to understand that he was not cast out of heaven immediately at the beginning of his sin, but that the patience of God waited even for him. Yet he, according to [Col. 1235D] his hardness and unrepentant heart, stored up wrath for himself (Rom. 2). For after the words, “until iniquity was found in you,” there immediately follows: “In the multitude of your commerce your inward parts were filled with iniquity”; then immediately, “and you sinned”; and only then, “and I cast you out from the mountain of God.”

These are three stages in the growth of sin, through which at length the just judgment of God overtakes human beings also: first, conceiving iniquity in the mind; then carrying out that iniquity not once or in a single act, but repeatedly; and then sinning by defending the works of iniquity. Therefore, because “iniquity was found in you,” because “your inward parts were filled with iniquity through the multitude of your commerce,” and because “you sinned,” no brief delay in the iniquity of that ancient sinner is to be understood—a delay intended to instruct the elect angels, so that, seeing that sinner to be incorrigible, they might know God’s judgment to be just.

## CHAPTER XXII. Satan disturbed peace in the high places of God.

Therefore, in the high places of God a great tumult of discord arose between the great rage of the demons and the great and good zeal of the good spirits. We should observe, then, that he disturbed peace exceedingly in God’s high places. For this reason he is rebuked under the names of men who troubled the earth—namely Asshur, Pharaoh, the king of Tyre, and Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon—and it is said to him: “Is this the man who troubled the earth, who shook kingdoms, who made the world a wilderness and destroyed its cities?” [Col. 1236B] (Isa. 14). Again: “For you scattered the earth; you killed your people” (ibid.), and other such things.

Otherwise, if we are not to understand of him, by analogy with these persons, that he disturbed the angels by himself as those proud human beings disturbed nations by seizing tyrannical power over peoples, why is he designated by their names and deeds? There is therefore no doubt that already then the powers of heaven were moved because of him, as they are to be moved against him at the last judgment. How great that movement was, when he finally fell cast down from heaven, is briefly indicated by the Word of God—God himself who cast him down—saying: “I was watching Satan fall like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10).

How does lightning fall? Certainly when clouds have been stirred and collided with such a crash—that is, thunder—that the frame of heaven seems shaken and the earth seems to tremble. Then the lightning, struck forth, shines briefly and immediately disappears. Thus, when he says, “like lightning,” he indicates the astonishing movement of the heavenly powers, the great battle of the angels with Michael as leader against him, and, above all these things, the great thunder of the omnipotent Word, which he himself is: the devil was to be struck out so as to fall from heaven with his vain light, immediately extinguished in misery; and, once he had been cast down, the serenity of peace returned to heaven.

It is known why he said this and why he made such mention of Satan: namely, because of the ill-considered joy of the seventy-two disciples whom he had sent and who, returning, said: “Lord, even the demons are subject [Col. 1236D] to us in your name” (ibid.). He set before them such an example so that they might beware lest they too, deceived by vain glory, fall away and turn backward.

## CHAPTER XXIII. When Christ said, “I was watching Satan fall,” he indicated that he was not merely man but also the Word of the Father from eternity.

In saying these things, he also gently suggested his antiquity to the believing hearer in few words. For how ancient is he who was watching that event? Certainly, according to the humanity which was visible, he was a little more than thirty years old when he said these things. But long before thirty years—indeed, before all years, and before the creation of the sun, whose revolution makes the year—that Satan fell. Therefore he who was watching this was long before the years of his flesh. And this is true: for “in the beginning was the Word,” and in the beginning “the Word was God” (John 1).

This also deserves attention: he did not merely say, “I saw Satan,” but “I was watching Satan fall from heaven.” He would rightly and truly have said, “I saw”; but “I was watching,” a verb in the imperfect tense, though referring to the past, contains more and conveys a fuller meaning to the attentive ear. For Michael too, and any other angel, could say, “I saw Satan falling from heaven,” since he fell before their eyes—and not merely before their eyes, but while they were also fighting against him. Yet none of them can say, [Col. 1237B] “I was watching”; they can only say, “I saw him falling.”

He alone not only saw him falling when he fell, but was watching him fall before he fell, indeed before he was formed or made. For he was being made through him, just as all things were made through him; nor could God the Word be ignorant of what was to happen to him, especially since he is the Word who makes human beings prophets, that is, knowers beforehand of future things.

This must certainly be known and confessed: while that angel was being made, while that great stone was being formed and his settings were being prepared, as is said of him through the prophet, “The goldwork of your adornment and your settings were prepared on the day you were created” (Ezek. 28)—while, I say, his settings were being prepared, God the Word was watching that [Col. 1237C] this rebellious and exceedingly hard stone would not receive in those settings the fastenings of gold.

To state this more plainly: while he was being magnificently endowed with talent, intellect, memory, and full and perfect rationality, God the Word was watching that he would by no means receive the love of his Creator, by which he ought to be bound to him alone. Therefore, more fittingly and more magnificently, he says, “I was watching him fall”—with the implication, even before he fell. For any of the angels might say, “I saw him falling,” with the implication, while he was falling.

It is even permissible to add that he alone watched secure in himself; the angels, however, saw while placed in great fear. For the Lord himself says to blessed Job: “When he is lifted up, the angels will fear, and, terrified, they will be purified” (Job 42).

## CHAPTER XXIV. He resolves the question why God created Satan although he knew he would be evil, and defends the irreproachable justice of God.

Someone may say: if he was already watching him fall, why did he form him so magnificently? Why did he prepare his settings so carefully? If this matter troubles anyone, the same answer given concerning Pharaoh must also be given concerning Satan: “For this very purpose I raised you up, that I might show my power in you and that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth” (Exod. 9).

When a faithful mind hears this—a mind that thinks well of the Lord—it does not suppose that God wished Pharaoh to be evil or made him evil. Rather, it understands “for this very purpose I raised you up,” or, as it is read elsewhere, “I set you” (Rom. 9), as though God said: I made you king, or willed you to be such. For making a human being evil is very different from raising to a kingdom one who was already evil. A person becomes evil through himself; but when an evil person rises to a kingdom, this happens by God’s ordering: sometimes because of the sins of a people, sometimes as a test so that the elect may be made manifest, and sometimes to declare and magnify the glory and praise of God’s name, so that it may benefit hearers to have learned God’s omnipotence through the destruction of such persons. This is plainly proclaimed by the divine voice concerning Pharaoh: “For this very purpose,” it says, “I set you, that I might show my power [Col. 1238B] in you and that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth” (Exod. 9; Rom. 11).

What else ought sound faith to think concerning Satan, especially since all the holy Church of Christ knows Pharaoh to have been his type? Thus, concerning him too one may most rightly say: although his Creator knew, while making him—or before making him—that he would become evil, as he foresaw him, so he condemned evil. And in order to show his power in him, he made him great, wise, and beautiful, as has already been shown above from the prophet. He bestowed upon one who would freely become evil such preeminence above the other angels as Pharaoh, who is called his likeness, could not have possessed above other human beings, though he was evil before being raised to kingship.

For some human being in Pharaoh’s own kingdom could have been greater in stature, more capable in wisdom, and more beautiful in form than Pharaoh. But among the angels none was higher, wiser, or more beautiful than Satan. For, as was mentioned above, God himself says through the prophet: “No tree in the paradise of God was comparable to him” (Ezek. 31). Nevertheless, because the Lord says, “Do you know the ordering of heaven, and will you establish its rule upon the earth?” (Job 38), let us restrain ourselves on this question and say with the Apostle: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments and unsearchable his ways!” (Rom. 11).

## CHAPTER XXV. From where and to where the devil was cast down; from what kind of heaven and into what state of hell he fell even then.

What Truth had been watching came to pass: “Satan fell.” From where did he fall? “From heaven,” he says. From heaven, certainly not his own, but the Lord’s; for he was not even created in heaven, but after he was created he was placed in heaven by him who created both heaven and himself. Just as man was not made in paradise but, after he had been made, his Maker took him “and placed him in the paradise of delight” (Gen. 2), so God did not make Satan in heaven but placed him there after making him.

Thus, after first saying, “The goldwork of your adornment and your settings were prepared on the day you were created; you were a cherub stretched out and protecting” (Ezek. 28), he then added: “And I set you on the holy mountain of God” (ibid.). He therefore rightly fell from heaven, because he regarded the heaven given him as plunder and did not preserve it through humility.

But where did he fall? Do you suppose, onto the earth? Certainly, onto the earth—but not such earth as we now see. “For then the earth was empty and void, and darkness was over the face of the abyss”; indeed, “the earth itself was covered with waters” (Gen. 1), nor was it distinguished from the other elements. It was a great chaos, signified there by the name “earth”: not merely the one element which God first called “dry land” and afterwards “earth,” but the whole confused mass of the four elements.

O wretched one, though not one to be pitied! From what blessedness into what misery did he fall? From what riches into what poverty did he descend? Here he found nothing but the abyss and darkness upon the face [Col. 1239B] of the abyss. The kingdoms of the world and their glory did not yet exist, which he later showed to the Lord Jesus, saying: “If you worship me, I will give you all these things, because they have been handed over to me and I give them to whomever I wish” (Luke 4; Matt. 4).

Why do I say that the kingdoms of the world did not yet exist? The sun and moon, stars and light, and everything else made on the second day and afterwards did not yet exist. There existed only, as has been said, chaos and the darkness of gloom upon the face of the abyss. For one must know, on the authority of Scripture, that there are three heavens. The first and highest is that which God created in the beginning: the invisible homeland of blessed spirits. The lowest is this air, which is customarily called heaven; hence birds are called “birds of heaven” (Ps. 103). The middle heaven is the firmament which God made on the second day [Col. 1239C] and called heaven.

This middle heaven had not yet been made when the devil fell, but that invisible heaven had been made—the dwelling of holy angels and human beings, ever bright to them through the vision of God. Nor did this lowest heaven, namely the air, possess even bodily light, but, Scripture says, “darkness was upon the face of the abyss” (Gen. 1). These two heavens, the middle and the lowest, are earth in comparison with the third, because they are seen by earthly eyes. But that which cannot be seen by earthly eyes before those eyes are changed through the glory of resurrection is called the heaven of heaven, according to David: “The heaven of heavens belongs to the Lord, but he gave the earth to the children of men” (Ps. 113).

Did he not, then, already fall into hell? Truly, although he had not yet been sent into the lower hell. This very place is hell to him in comparison with the breadth of the dwelling he abandoned, and in comparison with the dominion he did not preserve; and he is held under gloom in eternal chains, as the apostle Jude says in his Epistle: “The angels who did not preserve their own principality, but abandoned their own dwelling, he has reserved under gloom in eternal chains for the judgment of the great day” (Jude 1). The apostle Peter also confirms the same thing in these words: “For if God did not spare angels when they sinned, but, drawing them down with the cords of hell, handed them over to Tartarus to be tormented and reserved for judgment” (2 Pet. 2).

## CHAPTER XXVI. Why he is called devil, why Satan, and why his spirits are called demons.

He therefore rightly received the name by which he is called *diabolus* [devil], as David was the first to utter through Scripture, speaking in the Spirit: “Set a sinner over him, and let the devil stand at his right hand” (Ps. 108). For *diabolus* in Hebrew means “flowing downward” or “shut in a prison.” The name already mentioned, namely Satan—meaning “adversary,” and the name on account of which he fell and became the more anciently named devil—was first brought forth by the book of Job: “One day,” it says, “when the sons of God came to stand before the Lord, Satan also was present among them” (Job 1).

From the time he began to be proud, he has been Satan, that is, God’s adversary; and from the time he fell after being cast down because of that same pride, he is called and is the devil. For then he flowed downward and was shut in prison, because he fell into the great chaos, far from God’s height, and is held as though in a prison while, depressed in the air, he recognizes that it is impossible for him to return to the place from which he fell. Indeed, he does not fail to know that he will be hurled still lower, handed over to the lower hell, and reserved for this until the day of judgment.

Nor did he flow downward merely in place; he also continually flows downward in intention. For he always desires the vilest things—now as vile a scoundrel as he was at first a glorious archangel. Whoever can should consider this from the fact that in sacred Scripture he is customarily called an unclean spirit. In Greek too, *diabolus* has the same meaning as the Latin *criminator* or *accusator* [accuser]; and this sense truly suits him for a double reason. For he always casts all the blame upon God, and from the beginning did so, daring to call himself just and God unjust; and he accuses the innocence of the elect with fabricated accusations. Hence in the Apocalypse it is said by an angelic voice: “The accuser of our brothers has been cast down, who accused them before the presence of our God day and night” (Rev. 12).

His angels are called in Greek *daemones*, that is, “knowing ones.” For they foresee many future things, and thus they are accustomed to give certain responses. They possess knowledge beyond human weakness, partly through a keener subtlety of perception, partly through experience of an exceedingly long life, and partly through angelic revelation by God’s command. They possess bodies by an aerial nature. Before their transgression they indeed bore heavenly bodies; but having fallen through pride, as has been said, they were changed into an aerial condition.

## CHAPTER XXVII. By what terms the nine orders of angels are represented in the prophets, and that evil spirits cannot rise again.

By contrast, those blessed spirits who remained in love for their Creator and stood in truth are fittingly distinguished by venerable orders and adorned with splendid names. Some are called and are angels, others archangels, others thrones, others dominions, [Col. 1241A] others principalities, others powers, others virtues, others cherubim, and others seraphim.

These nine orders of angels are the precious stones—sardius, topaz, jasper, chrysolite, onyx, beryl, sapphire, carbuncle, and emerald—whose “settings,” just as “your own,” were prepared, he says, “on the day you were created, you cherub stretched out and protecting” (Ezek. 28). But not in the same manner as these did you receive in your settings the fastenings of gold; rather, you rejected the hand of God the goldsmith or craftsman.

What fastenings of gold did they receive? Gold is the Word of God; that gold is the spirit of the Lord’s mouth. By that gold the precious stones, the fiery stones, are so bound that they stand eternally in their orders and none of them can ever fall away. This is what the Psalm sings: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the spirit of his mouth all their power” (Ps. 32). They are the stones; they are the heavens: stones because of their everlasting stability and firm eternity; heavens because of the holy Trinity dwelling in them.

This is already the victory of the Word of God: against the prince of wickedness, they were forestalled and held back by the Word itself, lest they fall with him—the Word through whom they had also been created. And the robber who strove to seize them was himself seized and paid the penalty of a vast fall. God the Word fulfilled in them what he willed—the Word which God spoke: “Let light be made,” and light was made (Gen. 1). By that same Word, God divided light from darkness. For judgment was made firm and an unchangeable sentence pronounced: the devil and Satan, fugitive from the light, shall never again become light, nor shall any of his apostate angels ever rise again into fellowship with the light, that is, the holy angels.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Those who suppose that angels were created before heaven and earth are mistaken.

Now I wish briefly to answer the opinion of some who suppose that angels existed immediately before heaven and earth were made. What else must be answered but that such an opinion has no support either from the testimony of any Scripture or from any reasoning? For Scripture does not say, “In the beginning God created angels”; rather, “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (ibid.). Then, after a few intervening words: “But the earth was empty and void [Col. 1241D] and darkness was upon the face of the abyss, and the Spirit of God was borne over the waters” (ibid.). Only then is added: “And God said: Let light be made; and light was made” (ibid.).

A number of doctors, especially blessed Augustine, hold that this light is the angelic nature; and not only reason, but also—what is greater—the intention of Scripture when carefully considered, strongly supports his view. But if anyone wishes to doubt, let that person say: since there was no place outside heaven and earth, in what place could angels—who are certainly localized and circumscribed—have existed if they had been created before heaven and earth? If it is asked from what they were made, since they are so glorious and splendid, it can at least be answered that they were made from the substance of air. For they have bodies of air, and this has not been left unmentioned by the doctors; in the holy angels, however, those bodies have been happily transformed so that they are called and are heavenly bodies.

The apostate angels, having fallen from that blessedness, were again changed into an aerial condition. They have not been allowed to inhabit even the purer regions of that air, but these gloomy regions, which are as a prison to them until the day of judgment. Perhaps this statement offends some who think it unfitting to angelic dignity that angels should be said or believed to have been made from an aerial substance. Yet they firmly maintain, as is necessary, that the true body of Christ was assumed from earthly substance; and this body ascended above all angels and all heavens and now sits at the right hand of Majesty on high.

Who does not know that the mass or substance of earth is much heavier, lower, and more impure than the element of air? For earth is a kind of dregs of the other elements. Again, who does not know that humankind, formed from the clay of the earth, will at the resurrection attain fellowship with and equality with the holy angels? And already the man Jesus Christ, from that same mass, one person with the Word in the blessed Trinity, sits and reigns above all the choirs of angels. Therefore, no one should imagine that anything is detracted from the blessed angels if they are said to have been made from air, since it is certain that their king and lord, whom they worship, has a body of earthly clay.

Finally, the fall of the apostate spirits, by which, as has been said, they have now fallen from heaven into the air, similarly proves that they were by nature from air, but that God transferred them thence to heaven. Just so Scripture says that God, because of a similar sin, subjected humanity to a nearly similar, though much gentler, sentence: “The Lord God sent him out of the paradise of delight, to work the earth from which he was taken” (Gen. 3). It was surely an equitable judgment that each, because he lost grace, should be cast back into that from which he had taken the beginning of his existence: man into the earth, worse than paradise; the devil into the air, lower than heaven.

But leaving these matters aside for now, the end of this first little book must be set in the blessedness of the angels.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Angels were not created so that they could not advance; God alone has always been perfect without advancement.

Those heavens, established by the Word of the Lord (Ps. 32), and distinguished, as has been said, into nine orders, advanced greatly in knowledge of their Creator and of the Word through whom they were made. Their hearts enlarged and filled with love, they praised with unceasing praise his awe-inspiring power, which they had seen in the judgment and overthrow of so great an adversary.

For holy angels too have advanced and still advance in the knowledge of their Creator, as the Apostle testifies.
