Having first said that the riches of Christ were “unsearchable” and that there was “the dispensation of the mystery hidden from ages in God, who created all things” (Eph. 3), he added: “that the manifold wisdom of God might be made known through the Church to the principalities and powers in the heavenly places” (Eph. 3). Through the Church—that is, through the things which God made and accomplished in the Church or with the Church when he became man: the Bridegroom suffering for the bride, dying and rising from the dead, having conquered the prince of death.

He says that the manifold wisdom of God, or the dispensation of the mystery hidden from ages in God who created all things, is made known to the principalities and powers in the heavenly places, so that, marvelling at the sight of such power, they say: “Who is this king of glory? Who is this king of glory?” (Ps. 23). But of this elsewhere.

For the present, the point was that angels, contrary to what some suppose, were not created in such a state that, once created, they immediately lacked nothing of complete perfection. For surely the Creator alone must be believed always to have been and to be perfect without advancement. Otherwise, if angels had been perfect from the beginning of creation and lacked nothing, God could have had many counsellors in his other works. But prophetic Scripture says: “Who has helped the Spirit of the Lord, or who has been his counsellor and shown him?” (Isa. 40). The Apostle too says: “For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counsellor?” (Rom. 11).

Certainly, as he continues: “For from him and through him and in him are all things” (ibid.). The Creator alone knew and made all things. But when angels had been created by him and admitted to behold his other works, those who saw with a good and simple eye, who did not envy but praised the wisdom of so great a craftsman, were worthily advanced into his friendship. Those, however, who had an evil eye, envied and hated, were justly driven away and removed far off.

## CHAPTER XXX. The good angels, knowing the power revealed in Satan’s overthrow and the goodness of the Word of God in their own confirmation, burst forth into the eternal praise of the holy Trinity.

Therefore, once Satan or the devil and his angels had been removed and terribly cast down, the holy angels immediately made this advance: having new material for divine praise, they began to sing a new song. For they had seen the power of their Creator in the overthrow of a great creature; and they recognized in themselves the grace and mercy of that same Creator, by which they knew they had been forestalled lest they too should fall.

Since they were of the same created condition, they could and can give no slight consideration to their own salvation preserved in the destruction of the others and to their own stability maintained. [Col. 1244B] The settings of the precious stones were loosened—loosened and enlarged—and they received more gold within themselves; they accepted thicker and stronger fastenings of indissoluble gold and were bound to their Creator by eternal love. From that time they cannot cease from praise and rejoicing; glorifying the holy Trinity, they have no silence and shall have none for ever.

Truly, therefore, they are blessed, because they were so established by the Word of the Lord and all their power so established by the spirit of his mouth (Ps. 32) that they can never fear any event of instability. This is the victory of the Word of God, already then casting demons out of heaven in the Holy Spirit. For as it had been purposed in him, so it came to pass, when these his intellectual heavens were established in him and in the Spirit of God’s mouth.

**528. BOOK TWO.**

[Col. 1243]

## CHAPTER ONE. What the Lord said to the prophet Ezekiel: “Son of man, raise a lament over the king of Tyre.”

Meanwhile, while the human mind strives to contemplate the joy and exultation of the angels who praise and rejoice over the victory of the Word of God, behold: the Word itself, speaking to the prophet, makes itself heard in words that deserve no slight attention: “Son of man, raise a lament over the king of Tyre, and say to him: Thus says the Lord God: You are the seal of his likeness, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty; you were in the delights of God’s paradise” (Ezek. 28), etc. Great and wonderful is the discipline of the Word of the Lord, whose command is that the prophet should lament the irrecoverable ruin of so great an adversary [Col. 1243D]. For while those blessed spirits in heaven were exulting over the victory of the Word itself, he commanded that a lament be raised over such a creature, because iniquity had been found in it and it had now lost the Word itself by everlasting perdition. No living human being knows what the praising and rejoicing angels say; and if anyone has heard anything of their utterances, he has not declared to men all that he “heard, because their sayings are secret, and it is not permitted to a man to speak them” (2 Cor. 12).

Yet after that same Word had become incarnate and had again triumphed over that adversary through his cross and blood, there was no longer any reason why he should be lamented or a lament raised over him. Before this, the victorious army of the Word of God, the whole victorious host of heaven, could have had joy thus incomplete, just as, after a civil war has been concluded and many citizens slain, the victorious party cannot celebrate in complete triumph the festal rejoicing of its victory. For it has something to lament: the city, bereft through the loss of so many or such great citizens, has been diminished, and the commonwealth reduced. It is fitting to offer an example from sacred history.

## CHAPTER II. [Col. 1244D]

How the children of Israel lamented when the tribe of Benjamin had been destroyed; and how it is likewise credible that the holy angels lamented when the number of citizens of God’s kingdom was diminished.

When, because of the crime of the city of Gibeah, which was in the tribe of Benjamin [Col. 1245A], the children of Israel undertook a common war against the children of Benjamin, and, having engaged once and twice in vain, finally in the third battle conquered and slew them so that no more than six hundred men remained, “all came to the house of God at Shiloh, and, sitting before him until evening, raised their voices and began to weep with a great wailing, saying: Why, O Lord God of Israel, has this evil happened among your people, that today one tribe should be removed from among us? And again, rising on the next day and offering burnt offerings to the Lord, they wept and said: One tribe has been taken away from Israel” (Judg. 21).

Certainly they did not repent that they had conquered and killed their brothers by the law of war, but that a cause or evil had arisen for which it had been necessary that this should happen [Col. 1245B]. Finally, amid their very weeping, while seeking counsel as to how they might restore the removed tribe, they said: “Who did not go up into the army of the Lord from all the tribes of Israel? And behold, it was found that the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead had not been in that army. Therefore they sent ten thousand of the strongest men and commanded them: Go and strike the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead with the edge of the sword, both their wives and their little children; but preserve only the virgins” (ibid.). As it was said, so it was done.

Therefore they did not weep because they had destroyed one tribe, but because a cause had arisen for which they had deservedly had to act in this way. In accordance with this analogy, it can be believed neither absurdly nor incongruously that the earlier holy angels did what the human prophet and helper of the Word of God is commanded to do [Col. 1245C]: namely, to raise a lament over that king of Tyre—that is, the prince of this world—so that they might indeed rejoice that, once he had been cast down, concord had been established among the high things of God, yet grieve that the heavenly city had been diminished and that the citizens of God’s kingdom were fewer.

## CHAPTER III

Why the Son of Man is commanded to lament the prince of Tyre.

There was a similar cause, though not altogether the same, for the prophet—or for any human being—to raise a lament over the fall of the first man. For when he fell through transgression, it is clear that not the loss of some small part but the ruin of the whole mass, of the entire human race, occurred [Col. 1245D]. Therefore the prophet both ought to have done, and was commanded to do, this: to raise a lament, or take up mourning over the human race, when it is said to him: “Therefore, son of man, take up a lament over Tyre, and say to Tyre, which dwells at the entrance of the sea, trading with peoples on many islands: O Tyre, you said, I am of perfect beauty” (Ezek. 27), etc.

For Tyre signifies the human race, or the present age, not only because of its situation and its encircling waters and abundance of commerce, but also because of the interpretation of its name. For it is interpreted as “narrowness.” And what is the present life of the human race except wretched narrowness and narrow wretchedness? But for a man to raise a lament over the king of Tyre—that is, the devil [Col. 1246A], prince of this age—there was not the same reason as has already been said to have existed for the holy and blessed angels. Why, then, is he commanded to lament him, being told: “Son of man, raise a lament over the king of Tyre”? How ought he to lament him whose fall diminishes not human multitudes but angelic ones? Yet he left vacant, through falling, dwellings in heaven which human beings may ascend to and possess. This inquiry is not idle, and it can be resolved with profit.

That this may become clearer, we must first see what sort of lament that is about which God sees fit to be concerned, saying: “Son of man, raise a lament.” This lament is humility of mind and contrition of heart, considering and seeing the works of the Lord—how “terrible he is in his counsels,” not only [Col. 1246B] “over the children of men” (Ps. 65), but also over the orders of angels. He truly laments usefully; he raises a rational lament over the king of Tyre, who, with contrite heart and humble spirit, searches out and weighs what must be done by himself, dust and ashes, when that highest angel—so great, so wise, so beautiful—was so terribly cast down because he refused to be subject to his Creator, and was made so base, so foolish, so deformed, that, according to prophetic truth, “all who see him will be astonished at him, because he has become nothing and will not be for ever” (Ezek. 28).

Whoever, considering these things, humbles his soul under the mighty hand of God with true humility and the true spirit of humility—which, wherever it touches the heart, certainly stirs up unutterable groanings [Col. 1246C] (Jas. 4)—has truly raised a lament over the king of Tyre. He grieves for himself, because he has either admitted something wicked in imitation of him, or may admit it if he has not yet done so. To this belongs what the Psalmist says: “Serve the Lord with fear, and rejoice in him with trembling” (Ps. 2), and whatever similar language sounds in the holy Scriptures, by which a human being is warned to be vigilant and very watchful, “lest, lifted up in pride, he fall into the judgment of the devil” (1 Tim. 3).

## CHAPTER IV

That the mystery of the Word’s incarnation, through which the number of God’s citizens would be restored, was known to God alone.

The holy angels, indeed, could lament in the spirit of pity the loss of their multitude, as has already been said [Col. 1246D]; but God, in himself, in his Word—in whom was life, whatever had been made—had long possessed and seen what he would do for the glory and praise of his name. He alone knew it, and it was hidden from all the angels. Thus the Apostle, when he had seen what “the dispensation of the mystery” was, added: “hidden from ages in God, who created all things, so that through the Church the manifold wisdom of God may be made known to principalities and powers in the heavenly places” (Eph. 3).

What was hidden, or what was that mystery? Surely this: that the abundance of supreme benevolence, the most lavish benevolence of the Creator, would bring forth from the poor and lowly material of the earth, then lying hidden under the waters, a glorious creature [Col. 1247A] like the brightness of angels; and that he would give to one person from the multitude of that same creature his own power, honor, and kingdom, so that that creature itself should lack nothing that the Creator of all things has and should possess the entire sovereignty of his commonwealth. Truly a great mystery of godliness: then, as has been said, hidden, but now “manifest in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, seen by angels, preached among the nations, believed in the world, taken up in glory” (1 Tim. 3).

That person is known: he is not only creature but also Creator; that is, not only man but also God. The devil presumptuously sought that exaltation through pride, saying: “I will ascend above the height of the clouds, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14). But the Most High, of course, repelled and condemned so great a presumption, not because he considered his own same exaltation to be a thing seized by robbery or wished to glory alone, but because he knew that a creature could not humbly bear the weight of such blessedness unless that creature were assumed in such a way that, with the unity of person preserved, he was also Creator—that is, God [Col. 1247B].

This matter, so great and so wonderful, was contested in a mighty battle and at last brought to effect, the devil being conquered and confounded; he had always labored with most audacious impudence to turn aside the purpose of God. And this is the victory of the Word of God whose triumph the present work intends to proclaim, etc.

## CHAPTER V. [Col. 1247C]

After the world was made, man was made, on whose account the devil undertook the conflict against the Word of God.

Why delay longer? The field of battle was established, and man was made the lawful possession of God; and the cause of the whole conflict was set forth in this manner: “God said, Let there be a firmament; and a firmament was made in the midst of the waters. And he divided the waters that were under the firmament from those that were above the firmament. And God said: Let the waters under heaven be gathered into one place, and let dry land appear. And it was so” (Gen. 1).

From these three parts—the firmament, that is, heaven; the gatherings of waters, that is, the sea; and the dry land, that is, the earth—a place was made, namely this world. It was then adorned, so that it is rightly called *kosmos* in Greek, which means “ornament” in Latin. For God said: “Let the earth bring forth,” and so forth; “and it brought forth green grass, bearing seed according to its kind, and trees making fruit, each having seed according to its own species. And God said: Let lights be made in the firmament of heaven; and it was so. God also said: Let the waters bring forth; and they brought forth creeping things having living souls, and birds over the earth under the firmament of heaven. And God said: Let the earth bring forth living souls according to their kind: cattle, creeping things, and beasts of the earth according to their species; and it was so” (ibid.) [Col. 1247D].

Finally, so that man might exist—who, as has been said, is God’s possession and the cause of the whole conflict—God did not say, “Let man be made,” but said: “Let us make man in our image and likeness.” Concerning this part of God’s creation, that is, the human race, the accounts of how the Word of God contended for it and conquered through himself are plainly known from the sacred writings—not only evangelical and apostolic, but also legal and prophetic [Col. 1248A]. But concerning the other creation, the angelic, what conflict there was in heaven is known only as much as can be learned from such prophetic utterances, which the argument of the preceding book required us in some measure to touch upon or explain.

For the writer of sacred history—or rather, he who wrote through him, the finger of God—judging sufficient those things which concern the affairs of the human race, has narrated almost nothing about the condition of angels and the transgression of reprobate spirits, except only this: “God said, Let there be light; and there was light. And God saw the light, that it was good, and divided the light from the darkness. And he called the light day and the darkness night” (ibid.) [Col. 1248B]. How rightly the foremost teachers have understood this to have been said of angels need not be passed over here, were it not that it has already been treated in another work and the course of the undertaking now begun restrains us.

## CHAPTER VI

That the devil retained his ancient ambition for the divine name, while God persisted in his purpose of advancing man to likeness with himself.

A beautiful place, and beautiful was the possession of God, where formerly “there was an abyss, and darkness upon the face of the abyss” (Gen. 1). Yet all these things, made through the Word, were very good, because, as has already been stated [Col. 1248C], God said of each: “Let it be,” and it was so. Therefore all things ought justly to belong to the same Word, the same God.

But O infinite ambition of the devil! Cast down from heaven, this raging tyrant presumed to seize dominion in this world. Breathing the same craving for the divine name by which he had said in heaven, “I will exalt my throne above the stars of God” (Isa. 14)—that is, above every dignity of the holy angels—and thus “I will be like the Most High” (ibid.), he desired at least in this way to fulfill his audacious purpose: to raise his name above these visible stars, above the sun, moon, and stars, so that he might be worshipped by human beings as God under the names of sun, moon, stars, ether, earth, sea, birds [Col. 1248D], quadrupeds, and serpents (Rom. 1).

Breathing this horrible ambition, he pursued three aims together: first, by deceiving man, to make him like himself; next, as far as lay in him, to despoil the Creator of the honor and service of every creature; and finally to usurp for himself the incommunicable name of Deity. But this was the merciful intention and holy purpose of God and his Word: to make man like himself—that is, an imitator of his goodness and capable of his divinity—so that man might behold his invisible things, understood from the creation of the world through the things made; and that, beholding or understanding, he who was not God by nature might become God by grace (ibid.).

Intending and purposing this, he had said through the great abundance of his goodness: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1) [Col. 1249A]: in the image, namely, in that man would be a rational creature; in the likeness, in that he would be an imitator of his Creator and, by imitating him, would advance to the glory of the vision of God. Thus it was purposed, and thus it has now at last been fulfilled. “Beloved,” says John, “we are now children of God, but it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that when Christ appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3).

## CHAPTER VII

That the devil wished to hinder God’s purpose, and why God laid a commandment upon man.

Satan—the same devil, the eternal adversary of the Word of God, which is truth—dared to attack this purpose in order to overthrow it, so that it should not come to pass as God had purposed [Col. 1249B]. Of the two terms of his purpose he intended to remove one, namely divine likeness. For two things had been said: “in our image and likeness.” He intended to render man wretched so that he retained from God only the image and did not attain the likeness, as though he said: “Let man indeed be made in God’s image, so that he may be rational and eternal; but let him be like me, a despiser of God and made my imitator.”

God began first to do what belonged to him: when he had created man in his image, he began to form him into his likeness. For it is thus written—and must be carefully noted—that after the words, “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1), it is added: “And God created man in his image; in the image of God he created him” (ibid.) [Col. 1249C]. Here nothing at all is said of likeness. For God brings man to his likeness not by creating but by forming him.

After several things, this follows: “And he commanded him, saying: From every tree of paradise eat; but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil do not eat. For on whatever day you eat from it, you shall die by death” (Gen. 2). If he had kept this word, this commandment, he would certainly have stood well formed in the likeness of him who said, “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1). For God, who said, “Let us make,” is the Trinity: Father, Word, and Holy Spirit. And had the impress of his commandment been received, it would have formed three things: charity, hope, and faith—though Christian teaching now, not without reason, recites them in the reverse order: faith, hope, and charity.

To the words, “From every tree of paradise eat,” charity ought to have responded, so that man might love God, who offered him sufficiency with great generosity [Col. 1249D]. To the words, “But from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil do not eat,” ready hope ought to have arisen, so that he might consider that greater things would be bestowed upon him because of obedient submission by him who had already freely bestowed such great generosity. To what he added, “For on whatever day you eat from it, you shall die by death,” human faith ought to have been present, so that he might believe the Word of God as truth. Therefore, if these three had not been lacking in man, he would already then have been made in the likeness of God, because in these three he would have had the seal of the Trinity [Col. 1250A].

## CHAPTER VIII

That, by entering the serpent and deceiving man, the devil deserved now to be called the ancient serpent.

On the contrary, that enemy of God acted so that man might not receive God’s commandment, but might become like himself rather than God. For, having entered the serpent, he said to the woman: “Why did God command you not to eat from every tree of paradise?” But she said: “Lest perhaps we die.” And he said: “You shall by no means die by death” (Gen. 3). But why did he command it? Do you wish to know better why he so commanded? “Behold, I tell you: God knows that on whatever day you eat from it, your eyes will be opened [Col. 1250B], and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil” (ibid.).

The woman believed the devil more than God, the serpent more than the Creator; and both ate, the woman and the man. Thus they lost God’s likeness and were made like him instead, whom they believed, because they committed a like sin. For why did he fall from heaven except because he said: “I will ascend into heaven, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14)? And what else did he persuade them to presume in their transgression, when he said: “Eat, and you will be like gods”? Therefore the adversary of God gained, as it were, the palm of victory over man, and gloried magnificently as though he had conquered and wholly turned aside the purpose of God—saying, as it were, in his heart: “It was not God who made man in his likeness; I made man in mine.”

In addition to the causes he formerly had for being called devil and Satan, he now has a third cause for being called by another name as well: the ancient serpent [Col. 1250C]. It is his everlasting reproach that he is designated by such a name. The Word of God, the truth of God, casts this reproach upon him: because, in order to commit such sacrilege, wholly burning with poisonous envy, he entered the serpent. For he who, intending this while he had been the highest angel, entered a lowly reptile in order to make his lie creep from the serpent into the woman and from the woman into the man, to the destruction of all posterity and the death of the whole human race—did he not rightly inherit the serpent’s name?

## CHAPTER IX. [Col. 1250D]

Why the devil is called the ancient serpent, but God is called and proclaimed the Ancient of Days.

Nor should it be passed over that he is surnamed not merely “serpent,” but “ancient serpent.” He is rightly so proclaimed, because he is much older than that visible animal or reptile serpent which he entered, and through which he poured out the venom of deception by speaking. For that serpent was created on the sixth day of the world’s creation among the other animals, when God said: “Let the earth bring forth the living soul according to its kind: cattle, reptiles, and beasts of the earth according to their species” (Gen. 1). But how ancient is the devil himself? “He is the beginning of the ways of God,” God himself says to blessed Job (Job 40). Therefore that serpent is very ancient [Col. 1251A].

Nevertheless, he is not proclaimed—or to be proclaimed—as ancient in the manner in which God is. God alone is proclaimed “Ancient” in such a manner that the adjective itself is used in place of a proper name, as there: “I looked until thrones were set up, and the Ancient of Days sat” (Dan. 7). Likewise: “And behold, one like the Son of Man came in the clouds of heaven and came even to the Ancient of Days” (ibid.). Such an expression is used by a trope which grammarians call antonomasia: that is, when something else is preeminently predicated in place of a name.

Therefore let the serpent be called ancient indeed, ancient from the beginning, harmful and persecuting—but ancient adjectivally. God alone, however, because he is from eternity and unto eternity, because he is without beginning and without end, is properly and gloriously proclaimed the Ancient of Days, or so proclaimed in place of a proper name [Col. 1251B]. Such a victor, as he seemed to himself! What a fitting title for his victory he acquired: that thenceforth he should be called the ancient serpent, the devil, and Satan; whereas God alone is called and is the Ancient of Days, alone the Most High, and his Word alone is Truth.

## CHAPTER X

That, when he deceived man, the devil employed the same deceits which sophists now employ.

Moreover, the victory in which he gloried, as has been said, was of the kind commonly won by hateful sophists. For first he ensnared the unwary and imprudent through equivocations, saying: “You shall by no means die by death” (Gen. 3), intending bodily death to be understood—the separation of soul and body [Col. 1251C]—whereas God, saying, “On whatever day you eat from it, you shall die by death” (Gen. 2), intended death of the soul from God.

Next, when he said, “Your eyes will be opened” (Gen. 3), he most wickedly equivocated concerning the opening of the eyes. For there is one opening of the eyes by which they were to know, to their shame, that they were naked; and another called illumination, so that nothing can remain hidden. That traitor intended the former kind of opening, but the deceived woman understood the latter.

Likewise he said equivocally: “You will be like gods” (ibid.), thinking of himself and his angels, whom he intended to thrust upon the human race so that the human race would offer them divine worship. But he wanted them to understand that they themselves would become gods in true divinity, equal to God the Creator [Col. 1251D]. Again, when he said, “knowing good and evil” (ibid.), he meant experience of good and evil. But he wanted them to understand knowledge of all good and evil things: knowledge, I say, of all things, whether past, present, or future. Therefore he was unwilling to say “knowing all things,” but said, “knowing good and evil,” so that, when everything happened contrary to their expectation and understanding, he could nevertheless defend himself as truthful and as having said everything truly.

Therefore Wisdom rightly says: “He who speaks sophistically is hateful and will be deprived of everything. For grace has not been given him by the Lord; for he has been deprived of all wisdom” (Sir. 37). When it says these things, we rightly understand the implication: namely, that ancient serpent, who truly “has been deprived of all wisdom” [Col. 1252A]. Thus it is said to him among other things through the prophet: “You destroyed your wisdom in your beauty” (Ezek. 28). For whoever is of this sort is likewise deprived of all wisdom, as that serpent was; he cannot truly be called wise, but malicious.

## CHAPTER XI

That man sinned not through ignorance or weakness, but through pride.

Nor did that most unjust enemy of God and man glory only in victory; he also was pleased with himself because of justice, or a just victory. For he had conquered man not unwillingly, but willingly. Indeed, man could be excused neither on account of ignorance nor on account of weakness [Col. 1252B]. How could he be excused on account of ignorance, when God had made the matter known to him in person? How on account of weakness, when he suffered no struggles of body or flesh? Lest he should so much as hunger, all the other trees of paradise, abundantly bestowed by the grace of the Giver except for one, could suffice. “From every tree of paradise eat,” he said, “but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil do not eat” (Gen. 2).

It remains, then, that he should be believed to have sinned through pride and contempt: unwilling, that is, to endure command; unwilling to acknowledge that he ought to have as teacher and Lord the same one whom he had as Creator and giver of so delightful a paradise. The letter itself plainly declares that this was so. For when the Lord God said to the woman, “Why have you done this?” [Col. 1252C], she replied with no word of submission or humility, but said only: “The serpent deceived me, and I ate.” Adam too made no other reply than this: “The woman whom you gave me as companion gave me from the tree, and I ate” (Gen. 3).

Certainly these answers are not those of persons agreeing with the Lord, nor of humble persons, but of rebels and the obstinate. For these words plainly show that they had not been captured by force, but had defected like deserters from the authority of their lawful Lord and Creator. Therefore, by a certain right, the hostile invader thereafter held the human race in his power; yet the whole cause of human perdition nevertheless falls back upon him. Nor was his victory any more truly just than it was the cunning malice and malicious cunning of an envious being [Col. 1252D].

## CHAPTER XII

That not God’s providence but the instability of the creature is to be blamed, when one considers that neither angel nor man could bear the greatness of divine beneficence without becoming proud.

To this day inquisitive and restless human beings, excessive and suspicious searchers into God’s secrets, dispute: “Why,” they say, “did God Almighty, God who knows all things, not prevent, not guard against the occurrence of those things? If he wished the angel to remain in heaven and man in paradise, why did he not foresee it? Why did he not beforehand bring it about that neither angel in heaven nor man in paradise should sin?”

O man, whoever you are, who turn over questions of this kind! Cease thus to strike at the height of the Creator’s majesty [Col. 1253A]. Instead strike at and accuse the instability of each rational creature—angel and man alike—because neither bears God’s immense benefits, and each turns God’s great gifts into material for pride (Rom. 9). For what gift of the Creator did pride not raise up both man and angel? He established the one at the summit of angelic height; he placed the other in paradise, intending that he should be the father of a multitude of human beings, a multitude of saints and children of God. Certainly great was the exaltation of each: of the one in angelic dominion, of the other in propagating the human race. Neither could humbly bear the weight of so great an honor, since each was a light creature.

And whence is the lightness of either creature except from its own condition? Or, to put it more plainly, whence is either light except because it was created from nothing, or from non-existent things? Man was indeed created from some material, namely earth, but earth itself was created from nothing. Likewise, whatever material the angel was created from, that material itself was created from nothing. Therefore, because both angel and man are creatures created from nothing, each is a light creature; and unless he receives in love that Word of the Lord by which he was created—the uncreated Word—he has no weight and can bear no gift or benefit of God humbly [Col. 1253B].

What then, man, do you accuse God of, if he withholds all his gifts from the creature and bestows nothing, lest the creature—whether angelic or human—have occasion for pride? What would result? But if he should bestow on one creature all that he bestows on each creature, the creature, overthrown by pride, cannot bear it. Behold, it has been proved by two cases—namely, by the highest angel and by the man who was created first and established as father of all—that no one can humbly bear dominion over all except the uncreated God.

## CHAPTER XIII

That it was useful for what God knew by knowledge to be revealed through experience: namely, that dominion over creatures cannot be humbly sustained except by the incarnate Word.

This has been proved, I say; and it is very useful for this to be known by the elect, both angels and human beings. For the Apostle says: “We know that all things work together for good to those who love God” (Rom. 8) [Col. 1253D]. If all things do, does not such an experience among all things work for their good? Certainly no slight cooperation for good is an event through which they have been instructed, and are still instructed, in the knowledge of the Creator.

For we know, and still learn by recalling these things which we ought never to forget, that it was necessary that neither angel nor any human being should obtain dominion over the whole creation, but God alone, who can truthfully say: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11). Clearly, when he placed the highest angel in heaven and the first-formed man in paradise—the former above the other angels, the latter as the sole propagator of the human race—he knew within himself that neither could preside over the others in the mastery of such instruction [Col. 1254A] as to say: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart.”

He knew it, I say, but not in the manner in which he wills things to be known when he must pronounce a judicial sentence concerning them. For example, he knew what sin existed in Sodom and Gomorrah, and yet he said: “I will go down and see whether they have fulfilled in deed the cry which has come to me, or whether it is not so, that I may know” (Gen. 18). Therefore in one way he knew, namely by knowledge; in another way he did not yet know, namely by experience. Thus, before he exalted the angel in heaven and the propagator of the human race in paradise, he already knew each by knowledge, but not yet by experience. He did not wish to pronounce judgment before the experience, waiting to have the elect—both human beings and angels—as participants in his knowledge. This was accomplished by experience and is exceedingly useful to both.

But now we must proceed in order to recall the conflict itself and the victory of the Word of God according to the events accomplished.

## CHAPTER XIV

That God seemed to sleep while the serpent deceived man, and then, awakened like a strong man overcome with wine, struck his enemies.

The Lord God had seemed to slumber a little, had in some manner slept, while that event occurred by which the serpent thought himself victorious—that is, thought that he had turned aside the purpose of God. For unless he had slumbered or slept, his adversary could have accomplished nothing. Scripture indicates that he slept with a certain sleep—the sleep for which we are accustomed to say, “Arise; why do you sleep, Lord?” [Col. 1254C] (Ps. 43)—when it says: “And when they heard the voice of the Lord God walking in paradise in the breeze after noon” (Gen. 3).

For walking in the breeze after noon is a human custom: after a hot sleep, one who perhaps fell asleep after drinking heavily breathes in the mild air and refreshes and relieves his body. Therefore he slept with a certain sleep—that is, with silence—permitting the serpent to approach, the woman to converse with the serpent, and the man likewise to die together with her through disobedience, by the death of the soul. But that God slept in this way was the fault of man, because man did not awaken God either by giving thanks or by calling upon him.

What, then, had the devil done except a sort of robbery? Just as a thief is accustomed to boast when he has departed after stealing, so that deceiver could for a time boast of his crime. But as at a much later time it was done and written: “The Lord awoke like one asleep, like a mighty man overcome with wine, and struck his enemies” (Ps. 77) [Col. 1254D], so it can rightly be said of that time also: he then “awoke like a mighty man overcome with wine,” that is, as though he had become neglectful of man because of the audacity of pride by which man had sought to become like God.

He awoke, I say: that is, he sought the lost and struck his enemies, namely the serpent, the man, and the woman. With what did he strike them? Surely with his Word, the victorious Word. He struck each according to deserts, but not with the same punishment [Col. 1255A]. For as one strikes an enemy in order to kill him, so he struck the ancient serpent in order to condemn him—indeed, to confirm upon him the sentence of condemnation. And as one strikes a son or servant in order to correct him, so he struck proud man in order to bring him back to humility, which is the beginning of salvation.

## CHAPTER XV

With what words, and why, God rebuked the serpent, the man, and the woman.

For he says to the serpent: “Because you have done this, you shall be cursed among all the living creatures of the earth; upon your breast you shall go, and earth you shall eat all the days of your life. To the woman also he said: I will multiply your hardships and your conceptions. In pain you shall bear [Col. 1255B] your children; you shall be under the power of your husband, and he shall rule over you. But to Adam he said: Cursed is the ground in your work; in labours you shall eat from it,” and so on, down to: “until you return to the earth from which you were taken; for you are dust, and to dust you shall return” (Gen. III).

Certainly, he said neither to the woman, “You are cursed,” nor to the man, “You are cursed,” but only this: “Cursed is the ground in your work.” The curse of that ground, plainly, is nothing other than the manifold and frequent affliction by which humanity is afflicted through the various contingencies of the earth, corrupted and made worse since then. To the serpent alone he said, “You shall be cursed”; and by this utterance a fixed and unchangeable sentence of eternal damnation must be understood. For although the letter sounds as though it could be understood of the animal serpent, nevertheless the whole must be understood also—and much more so—of the serpent who is the devil. [Col. 1255C] Otherwise, how could that which was said to it, “Upon your breast you shall go,” be reckoned as a curse or the punishment of a curse, when it possessed this from nature before the devil used it for humanity’s ruin?

Rather, it is laid upon that ancient serpent as a curse that it should go upon its breast and eat earth all its days: that is, that it should seek out and devour with insatiable hatred only those human beings who are so wholly earthbound that they neither desire nor look toward heaven. Given over with an unrepentant heart “to a reprobate mind” (Rom. I), it thus, against its own intention, always furthers and [Col. 1255D] assists God’s good purpose toward the elect while striving to obstruct it. This is the wondrous manner in which it goes upon its own breast.

Moreover, whatever was said to the woman and the man, including bodily death itself—which the merciful God imposed when he said, “For you are dust, and to dust you shall return”—is the language of one reproving and desiring to save. Even then he was hedging in the paths of the errant human being with thorns, so that affliction alone might at least give understanding to the hearing and make a person mindful of his condition, that, humbled, he might be corrected and saved.

## CHAPTER XVI. Why the first promise of crushing the serpent—which was the chief point of the Word’s victory—was made not to the woman but to the serpent.

We postponed a chapter which is of the greatest importance and bears especially [Col. 1256A] upon the argument of the present work: namely, that which God said to the serpent, after the other matters mentioned above: “I will put enmities between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed. She shall crush your head, and you shall lie in wait for her heel” (Gen. III).

What should gracious faith most wonderfully admire first in this saying? The truth of the Word, or the goodness of the Word and of his Father? Let it praise both; let it desire worthily to proclaim both. For with truly great goodness he spoke thus, and with great and unwavering truth his utterance was fulfilled. “I will put enmities,” he says, “between you and the woman,” as though he said: Now the woman and likewise the man are allied to you; they have made a pact with you and struck a covenant with death. For, having fled and hidden themselves from my presence, when I ask why they have done this, they despise the voice that admonishes them; and, by defending their sin, they openly show that they favour you, consent to you, and are your friends. But I shall dissolve friendships of this kind: “I will put enmities between you and the woman.”

Why did he not say this to the woman herself? For where he said to the woman, “I will multiply your hardships and your conceptions,” and so forth, he could have said this very thing to her: “I will put enmities between you and the serpent, and between your seed and his seed.” Why, then, did he not say it? Doubtless for two reasons. First, because on account of sin and the defence of sin the woman did not deserve that God should then make to her promises of such a kind, promises of so great a grace. Secondly, [Col. 1256C] because he who spoke did not mean Eve herself, but another person of the same sex: the blessed Virgin Mary. Rightly, therefore, the promise of assisting grace was made not to the woman who had merited evil, but rather the hostile and warlike threat was addressed to the serpent.

What did God do by this saying except testify that he wished to remain steadfast in his purpose? For the serpent lay in wait lest that which God had purposed should come to pass when he said: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. I). It boasted that it had won and had diverted this purpose. But God, holding the victory of this same purpose in his own power, threatened the serpent.

## CHAPTER XVII. That by the woman and her seed all the elect are indeed understood, but especially the blessed Virgin Mary and her seed, who is Christ; just as by the serpent’s seed we understand those who are of the devil their father.

The blessed Virgin Mary, principally, is that woman between whom and the serpent God said that he would place—and did place—enmities; and her seed is her Son, Jesus Christ. Yet because “woman” is a universal name for the female sex, by the woman we understand all elect persons of the female sex, and by the woman’s seed all elect persons of the male sex. Of all these persons, namely persons of both sexes, Jesus Christ is prince and head, together with the woman from whom [Col. 1257A] he was made.

If a reason is sought why persons of the male sex should be understood by the woman’s seed, those who wrote on natural matters say that girls are born from the paternal seed and boys from the maternal seed, because every offspring consists of a double seed; whichever part prevails assumes the likeness of its sex. Therefore, when he says, “I will put enmities between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed” (Gen. III), we understand by the woman and her seed all the elect, of both female and male sex. Conversely, just as the devil is understood by the serpent, so all wicked and malicious persons, his imitators, are rightly understood by the serpent’s seed, although he has begotten or created no one.

For if wicked and ungodly people were not the seed of the serpent—that is, of the devil—then the Lord would by no means say to the Jews: “And you do what you have seen with your father” (John VIII); and again: “You do the works of your father” (ibid.), plainly intending the devil. For he immediately continues in the same discourse: “You are from your father the devil, and you wish to do the desires of your father” (ibid.). The cause why those who are so consistently called the serpent’s seed—that is, the devil’s children—came to be born was sin, God having said to the woman after she sinned by consenting to the devil: “I will multiply your hardships and your conceptions” (Gen. III). But the cause why those understood by the woman’s seed came to be born was God’s blessing, by which, before the transgression, he blessed the first human beings, as it is written: “Male and female [Col. 1257C] he created them, and blessed them, and said: Increase and multiply” (Gen. I).

## CHAPTER XVIII. That this enmity was the head and beginning of the wars of the Lord; and that Holy Scripture is called the book of the wars of the Lord and the book of the righteous.

This chapter is the beginning of the book of the wars of the Lord, which Moses mentions thus: “For Arnon,” he says, “is the boundary of Moab, dividing the Moabites and Amorites; whence it is said in the book of the wars of the Lord: As he did at the Red Sea, so he shall do at the torrents of Arnon” (Num. XXI). For what is that book of the wars of the Lord, or what are the wars of the Lord?

Certainly, before the Mosaic Law itself, in which this is written, there were no material or handwritten books of the wars of the Lord. Nor do we know of any other wars of the Lord than those in which, from the time enmities were placed between the woman and the serpent, between the woman’s seed and the serpent’s seed, conflict has continued and will continue until the end of the age. And the serpent’s head has been crushed; “and he shall be cast down while all behold” on the day of judgment (Job XL). This is the victory of the Word of God.

Therefore the book of the wars of the Lord is the whole of Holy Scripture. Moses himself wrote its chief part, namely the Pentateuch, and, being a prophet such as “there arose no more in Israel”—as it is written of him—“whom the Lord knew face to [Col. 1258A] face in all signs and wonders” (Deut. XXXIV), he was not ignorant that the other sacred books of the Old and New Testaments were to be written. And who can doubt that such a book, namely Holy Scripture, is—or is rightly called—the book of the wars of the Lord? For what else is contained or enacted in the Holy Scriptures except the war and contest of the Word of God for the destruction of sin and death?

The same Holy Scripture is also called the book of the righteous. For it is written: “David made a lament over Saul and over Jonathan his son, and commanded that they should teach the children of Judah the bow, as it is written in the book of the righteous” (II Kings I). This means: because they had fought badly on account of Saul, who had not kept the word of the Lord, David “commanded that they should teach the children of Judah” in what they ought to place their hope for strength in war, which is understood by the bow—that is, that they might learn to fight and hope for victory in the manner taught by every book of the righteous, every text of Holy Scripture.

Therefore, from this beginning of the book of the righteous, the book of the wars of the Lord, in which God thus proclaimed: “I will put enmities between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed. She shall crush your head, and you shall lie in wait for her heel” (Gen. III)—from this beginning, I say, let us behold, as from a lofty mountain, the power of the Word of God descending as it were into the level plain against the malice, or falsehood, of the devil, the ancient serpent: how it fought, how it conquered and triumphed, so that, his purpose fulfilled, he who blessed the first human beings at the foundation of the world may at last say: “Come, blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared [Col. 1258C] for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. XXV).

## CHAPTER XIX. That the Lord immediately placed enmity between Cain, the serpent’s seed, and Abel, the seed of blessing; and that Abel foreshadowed the victory of the Word by his death.

Cain was the first seed of the serpent. Hence John says in his Epistle: “Not as Cain, who was of the evil one” (I John III). Therefore he was the serpent’s seed—by imitation of envy, not by nature. But Abel was the first seed of the woman, the seed of God’s blessing. I call him the woman’s seed because he came to be not from the sin on account of which it was said to the woman: “I will multiply your hardships and your conceptions” (Gen. [Col. 1258D] III), but from the good of the blessing by which, before sin, God had commanded all saints to be born, blessing them and saying: “Increase and multiply” (Gen. I).

Between this seed of the woman and that seed of the serpent, God, mindful of his purpose, immediately placed enmities. Their beginning was that they differed from one another in pursuits that were diverse—indeed contrary. Cain was unbelieving and a tiller of the ground; Abel was faithful and a shepherd of sheep (Gen. IV). Of Abel the Apostle says: “By faith Abel offered to God a more abundant sacrifice than Cain, through which he received testimony that he was righteous, God bearing testimony to his gifts” (Heb. IX). God especially placed enmity between them in this manner: by bearing witness to Abel’s gifts. For thus it is written: “And the Lord looked upon Abel and his gifts; but upon Cain and his gifts he did not look. And Cain became exceedingly angry, and his countenance fell” (Gen. IV).

God therefore placed enmities between the two, because God’s regard for Abel became for the wicked seed a cause of hostility and hatred. Moreover, it should be considered that in his very offering the devout Abel enacted visible enmity against the serpent, offering a lamb, a simple and innocent animal, against the malicious and harmful serpent. But what happened? What was then the outcome of the enmity? The impious man killed the devout. The envy of the wicked seed extinguished the good seed. Behold the beginning of the wars of the Lord. Here, first, by the prefiguration of a devout death, he manifested the victory of that same Word in the presence of the Word of God.

## CHAPTER XX. [Col. 1259B] That Abel, through the righteousness of faith, was made according to God’s likeness; and, though dead to human beings, lives more truly—even speaks—to God.

Behold: already he had advanced one man from that mass whose first beginnings were Adam and Eve, in accordance with the good intention which he had set forth when saying: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. I). For this man was not only made in the image of God—that is, rational, which is not denied even of malicious Cain—but also in the likeness of that same God, in that he became his imitator through the righteousness of faith.

Moreover, this especially pertains in him to the likeness of God: that he bore in himself a most beautiful figure of the Word of God, the Word to be incarnate and, through suffering, to accomplish the victory over sin and death. It is known to almost all pupils of Holy Church what we mean: in Abel, Christ; in Cain, who killed him, the Jewish people who were to kill Christ; in the voice and cry of Abel’s blood, the accusation of the inexcusable crime of the Jews; and in the earth which opened its mouth and received Abel’s blood, the Church which was faithfully to drink Christ’s blood in the sacrament—all were signified by a devout likeness.

Therefore the Word of God, God’s purpose, was beginning not to be defeated but to conquer in the death of the righteous man. He was truly made perfect in God’s image and likeness when he fell in such a manner. For though he died to human beings, [Col. 1259D] he lives to God; he speaks to God—indeed, he speaks also to us (Heb. I)—and his blood sounds forth the word of God. God himself says: “The voice of your brother’s blood cries to me from the earth” (Gen. IV). And the Apostle of God, after saying, “By faith Abel offered a more abundant sacrifice,” continues: “and through it, though dead, he still speaks” (Heb. XI).

Does not the Lord himself also testify to this in the Gospel? When he gave proof of the resurrection from the dead, citing God’s words, “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob,” he immediately added: “God is not the God of the dead but of the living; for all live to him” (Matt. XXII; Luke XX). It is superfluous to establish that Abel, the first of all to die, nevertheless lived to God after dying to humanity—except that it is delightful to mock the ancient serpent, who is so foolish that, while desiring himself to be victor, he already makes God victor in his good purpose. For the one whom he caused to be slain in relation to humankind he made to live better for humankind and for God, truly going upon his own breast and effecting that which is wholly contrary to his most wicked intention.

## CHAPTER XXI. That Cain’s generation, the serpent’s seed, sprang up more quickly and established cities and kingdoms; likewise, that Cain was the beginning of the generation of the reprobate, Abel of that of the elect; and that their subsequent intermarriage according to the flesh deserved the vengeance of the Flood.

Meanwhile, the serpent’s seed, Cain, sprang up quickly, following the imitation of his father—that is, of the ancient serpent, a murderer and envier—since Cain himself also killed through envy. This seed, I say, sprang up quickly and was already hastening to rule, founding cities and towns, as it is written: “Cain built a city and called it by the name of his son Enoch” (Gen. IV).

But the seed of the woman, or the seed of God, came more slowly; indeed, it seemed to have perished from its root when Abel, leaving no seed—that is, having no children—was slain. For it must be known that Cain and Abel were the beginnings of two generations: one the generation of the reprobate, the other that of the elect. These generations were indeed intermingled according to the flesh; but this occurred through sin. For “when human beings began to multiply upon [Col. 1260C] the earth, and daughters were born to them, the sons of God saw that the daughters of men were beautiful, and took wives for themselves from all whom they chose” (Gen. VI).

This occurred contrary to God’s ordinance, just as much later the children of Israel, contrary to the Lord’s command, took the daughters of the Canaanites as wives and gave their own daughters to the Canaanites’ sons. As a result, being led astray by women, they did evil in the sight of the Lord by serving foreign gods. So too, I say, it was against God’s command that the sons of God—that is, men of the elect generation—took as wives the daughters of men, that is, women from the reprobate generation of which Cain was the beginning. Hence they were so corrupted that God brought in the Flood and destroyed them: “For,” he says, “it repents me that I made them” (ibid.).

Therefore, when righteous Abel had been removed, the serpent, swelling as though with victory, applauded himself because, with the nursery of the good generation destroyed, his generation alone sprang up in the world: an evil and adulterous generation.

## CHAPTER XXII. That, after Abel’s destruction, the generation of the elect was restored more slowly through Seth and Enos; and that it has no abiding city here but seeks the city to come.

“But Adam knew his wife again,” Scripture says, “and she bore a son, and called his name Seth, saying: God has given me another seed in place of Abel, whom Cain killed. A son was also born to Seth, whom he called Enos; this man began to call upon the name [Col. 1261A] of the Lord” (Gen. VI). From this seed of the woman, the other generation of the righteous, which had failed according to the flesh in Abel, was raised up again. Therefore his father gave him a name quite fitting in calling him Seth; for Seth means “resurrection.”

Doubtless Adam was taught beforehand, either by prophetic spirit or by whatever experiences, so as to know that Seth was from God the Father and that through his generation God’s purpose would be fulfilled, so that the predestined elect might be born. Accordingly he said: “God has given me another seed in place of Abel, whom Cain killed.” How long a delay there had been before this beginning of the good generation was raised up again! “Adam lived,” Scripture says, “one hundred and thirty years, and begot a son in his own likeness and image, and called his name Seth” (Gen. V).

During so many years Adam could have begotten sons and daughters; nor Adam only, but Cain himself, who was already founding a city. Rightly, therefore, and truly the Wise Man said: “An inheritance hastily acquired in the beginning shall lack blessing in the end” (Prov. XX). This is made clear by certain examples not only in any individual person but also in the human race as a whole. For Cain’s generation—that is, the serpent’s seed—both came quickly and founded cities quickly. But the generation of Abel or Seth, God’s seed, which God set in place of Abel, came more slowly and had no abiding city here, but sought the city to come.

## CHAPTER XXIII. That the generation of the sons of God was again corrupted through women by the cunning design of the ancient serpent.

What was the ancient serpent to do? Where was he to turn, when God’s seed, contrary to his own seed, was multiplying? He found what to do, by which he hoped still to be able to overcome the Word of God and divert his purpose. He knew that he had first begun with the man through the woman. Now many beautiful and desirable women had sprung up, and men—even though righteous—were inclined to lust, being born from a corrupted root.

Knowing, therefore, that unions with foreign women—that is, women sprung from Cain’s generation—would further the occurrence of the men’s death, he brought it about that what Scripture records should happen: “When human beings began to multiply upon the earth and had begotten daughters, the sons of God, seeing that the daughters of men were beautiful, took wives for themselves from all whom they chose” (Gen. VI).

Behold the first effect and first proof on account of which it was truly said of him to blessed Job: “His strength is in his loins, and his power in the navel of his belly” (Job L). Through lust, which is in men’s loins and women’s navel, he accomplished so great a thing that he seemed to himself strong and powerful. For he thought he had advanced his own purpose not a little in making the sons of God conform to the sons or daughters of men, so that there was no distinction, or little distinction, between Cain’s generation and Seth’s generation.

Did he not seem to himself to have done much when he caused him who had purposed, saying, “Let us make [Col. 1262A] man in our image and likeness,” to utter such a saying, so wholly different: “It repents me that I made man” (Gen. VI)? For thus it is written: “I will destroy,” he says, “man whom I created from the face of the earth, from man even to beasts, from creeping things even to birds of heaven. It repents me that I made them.” Thus, if you rightly weigh the vanity of the blasphemous serpent and the frivolity of the presumptuous enemy, there is no doubt that this event greatly increased his swelling pride, so that he thought he had utterly diverted God’s purpose and made his word return empty to him.

## CHAPTER XXIV. How the words God spoke—“It repents me that I made man” and “I will destroy man whom I created from the face of the earth”—are to be understood.

Meanwhile, I ask: what does it mean that the writer, speaking of God, says, “It repented him that he had made man upon the earth” (Gen. VI)? Or that God himself, after saying, “I will destroy man whom I created from the face of the earth,” added, “for it repents me that I made them” (ibid.)? If he says that he will destroy humanity because it repents him to have made humanity, why does he preserve even one human being with such great care and by so great a miracle, from whose offspring both good and evil people are again multiplied—few good, but many evil?

This wholly conflicts with the meaning which the letter seems to signify when it says that God repented. Nor does this fact alone conflict with interpreting God’s repentance as a passion, according to the letter’s sound; Scripture in another place also says: “For God is not as a son of man, that he should change” (Num. XXIII); and again, concerning repentance: “He shall not be turned aside, for he is not a man, that he should repent” (I Kings XV). If, then, God is not like a human being or son of man, so as to change; and if he is not bent by repentance so that, for example, even now when he says, “It repents me that I made” humanity, he should destroy humanity altogether—how shall we preserve in this saying both the truthfulness of the speaker and the unchangeable majesty of one who does not repent?

Here, first, it must be known that there is a great difference between the repentance ascribed to God and that which happens to a human being. Since the human being is mutable, one sometimes repents of evil or unjust deeds, and sometimes even of good and just deeds. Neither mode of this—that is, of human repentance—belongs to the wise person. For among the philosophers of this world, the wise person is held to be one who has admitted nothing evil or unjust which repentance must correct, and who has not perverted into evil anything good or just that he has done. If such repentance does not belong to a wise person, how much less can it ever happen to God? For he has never repented, nor could repent, of anything but good or just things, because he never can or could commit anything evil or unjust.

God’s repentance, then, differs greatly from human repentance. It is nothing other than a transition either from mercy to judgment or from judgment to mercy. For these are [Col. 1263A] “all the ways of the Lord: mercy and the truth” of judgment (Ps. XXIV). Sometimes, when passing from mercy to judgment, he is not in any way turned by repentance so as to pass again from judgment to mercy: namely, when a sinful person persists unrepentantly against God. Thus, concerning Saul, after the Lord had said, “It repents me that I have made Saul king” (I Kings XV), Samuel later says of that same man: “Moreover, the Victor in Israel shall not spare and shall not be bent by repentance; for he is not a man, that he should repent” (ibid.).

At other times, after mercy—or amidst the very abundance of mercy—he exercises judgment, yet is not by any repentance turned aside from his merciful purpose. An example is David, upon whom, after much mercy, he exercised severe judgment on account of Uriah the Hittite (II Kings XII), yet did not cast him from his presence as he had cast Saul away. According to this dispensation of mercy and judgment, it did indeed repent him that he had made humanity: that is, from mercy bestowed or to be bestowed upon the sons of God he passed to judgment. Yet he was not bent by that same repentance so as to abandon the good purpose for which he first made humanity.

## CHAPTER XXV. What Moses meant in writing of God, “And looking ahead to the future, he was touched inwardly by pain of heart.”

What shall we say of the fact that Scripture testifies not only that the Lord repented, but even that he was touched inwardly by pain? For it is written: “It repented him that he had made man upon the earth,” and, looking ahead to the future, “he was touched inwardly by pain of heart: ‘I will destroy,’ he says, ‘man’” (Gen. VI).

Someone says: Scripture speaks in a human fashion because it speaks to human beings. We agree that this is so. Yet what Scripture—the speaker of truth—says must be true. It declares that the Lord was touched by pain of heart. But pain is a passion, one of four passions, whose names are these: pain or sadness; joy or excessive gladness; pity or fearfulness; hope or desire. We read these four passions, indeed vices, expressed very briefly by the distinguished poet:

> “Men fear, desire, rejoice, and grieve.”  
> (VIRGIL, *Aeneid* VI.)

Since, therefore, the Godhead is impassible, some are offended whenever reference is made to this passage in which sacred Scripture recounts that God was touched inwardly by pain of heart. But, on the other hand, it must be known that Holy Scripture proclaims to us another pain, another joy, another hope, another fear: not passions or vices, but, as those who are spiritual understand spiritually, the highest virtues.

There is pain, that is, pity, which the Holy Spirit produces; hence he is called the Spirit of pity. Joy too is a fruit of that same Spirit, as the Apostle says: “But the fruit of the Spirit is joy” (Gal. V), and so forth. Hope also is the middle one of the primary virtues, as the same Apostle says above: “But now remain faith, hope, and charity—these three” (I Cor. XIII). There is also holy fear, a virtue and guardian of virtues, which the same Holy Spirit produces. Therefore, among the order of seven spirits, just as the Spirit of pity has already been mentioned, so also the Spirit of the fear of the Lord is proclaimed.

Thus a faithful mind is not offended, as though it were incongruous to proclaim concerning the impassible God that, as sacred Scripture declares, he was touched inwardly by pain of heart. For truly, as prophetic truth also testifies elsewhere: “God is zealous and the Lord avenges” (Nahum I). Nor does anyone truly imitate God at all unless he shares in his good zeal or emulation.

## CHAPTER XXVI. [Col. 1264B] In what pain God is said to have been touched inwardly.

The pain of heart by which so strong, so merciful, and impassible a God was touched inwardly is good zeal. Therefore we call his pain, as it truly is, not a passion but a virtue. Conversely, the devil’s envy, through which death entered this world, is evil zeal; and that zeal is a great and wretched passion, indeed the highest vice. It is pleasant to define both kinds of zeal.

Good zeal is to love human beings but hate human iniquities. Conversely, evil zeal is to hate human beings but love human iniquities. The former is God’s zeal; the latter is the devil’s. For God first and above all loves humanity, but hates human iniquity. Those imitate him who so love their fellow human beings that they hate and persecute their evil deeds. Conversely, the devil first and above all hates humanity, while loving human iniquity. Those imitate him who so hate human beings or their brothers that they love their iniquity: that is, they do not love them unless they consent to them or become like them in committing iniquity.

This opposing contrast of zeal makes the devil contrary to God and the enemy of human beings. The continual duel of the two zeals endures from the beginning to the end of the age: the zeal of the Lord of hosts always conquering, and the devil’s zeal always falling into shame and reproach. When, in the zeal of bitterness, the devil cannot entice a human being into iniquity, which is the death of the soul, he rises up through his servants to kill the body. But God sends into Gehenna both body and soul of that sinful or impious person from whom his zeal has withdrawn because that person is incorrigible in iniquity. The person for whom he deigns to show zeal, however, he punishes temporally so that he may not punish eternally. Of such persons the Apostle says: “But when we are judged by the Lord, we are corrected, that we may not be condemned with this world” (I Cor. XI).

## CHAPTER XXVII. Concerning the Flood—or rather, the three judgments of God.

Therefore, touched by repentance and inward pain of heart—that is, stirred by good zeal—what did the Lord God say and do? “My spirit,” he says, “shall not remain in man forever, because he is flesh; and his days shall be one hundred and twenty years.” Then to Noah: “Make for yourself an ark,” he says, “of smoothed timbers. Behold, I will bring the waters of the Flood upon the earth, to destroy all flesh in which is the spirit of life under heaven. Everything that is on the earth shall perish” (Gen. VI).

This judgment is a great part of the victory of the Word of God, and is the middle one of his three judgments. It is well known that there are three judgments of his dreadful majesty. The first was that by which the devil, that Satan, was cast from heaven. This second was that by which the world, cleansed through water, perished. The third is that which shall take place on the last day through the conflagration of fire. In the first judgment angels alone were judged; in the second, human beings alone; in the third, at last, both human beings and angels shall be judged.

Likewise, the penalty of the first judgment has been prepared for angels alone; that of the second, for human beings alone; and the penalty of the third, suitable and sufficient according to each one’s condition, has been prepared together for angels and human beings, by the wondrous and terrible ordering of the Creator. For the substance of air bears angels—and not human beings—into which angels, having become demons, were cast down from heaven. Conversely, the substance of water can or could drown the life not of angels or spirits, but of human beings; when the waters overflowed, human beings were then terribly destroyed. Yet the substance of fire shall be able to burn angels and human beings together, as the Lord himself testifies when he declares that he will say to evil people: “Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV).

Thus it was not without reason stated beforehand that God repented and was touched inwardly by pain of heart, because he was about to inflict the punishment of so great a judgment (Gen. VI). He is the one who does not delight in the punishments of the wretched, yet cannot in turn be negligent or unjust so as not to punish sins according to the measure of each. Hence he himself says in the Gospel: “I can do nothing of myself; but as I hear, I judge” (John V). For a person acts and judges of himself when, having heard the merits of cases, he overturns them and leaves disorderly things in place—for example, when he calls good evil and evil good, and, for his own favour, lets both the righteous and the unrighteous go unpunished. Whoever, being human, does not dare to do this is in some measure just; whoever does not wish to do it is just and holy; but he who never can or could do it is God alone, who is just by nature.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. What the Lord meant when he said: “My spirit shall not remain in man forever, because he is flesh.”

Why, then, before carrying out this judgment, did he preface it by saying: “My spirit shall not remain in man forever, because he is flesh” (Gen. VI)? Did not God, even before saying this, take away the spirit from man, so that they failed and returned to their own dust? (Ps. CIII.) Did he not first say to man: “Until you return to the earth from which you were taken, for you are dust, and to dust you shall return?” (Gen. III.) [Col. 1266A] Indeed, was it not for this reason that he sent him out of Paradise, lest he should live forever? For, with most grave irony, now “stricken inwardly with grief of heart,” he said: “Behold, Adam has become like one of us, knowing good and evil”; and immediately added: “Now therefore, lest perhaps he put forth his hand and take also of the tree of life, and eat and live forever,” the Lord God sent him out of the Paradise of delight (Gen. III).

What then does it mean that, when the sons of God took the daughters of men as wives, and they bore giants—that is, men famous and mighty from ancient times—when the earth was already corrupted and all flesh had corrupted its way, and when, for this reason, he intended to bring on the flood, he said, as though deciding this for the first time: “My spirit,” that is, [Col. 1266B] “the spirit given by me, or made in my image, shall not remain in man forever”? What, I ask, does he mean except that, by these experiences through all ages, he wishes it to be acknowledged that he acted wisely and beneficially, reasonably and mercifully, in doing precisely this: namely, that he did not wish man, already dead in soul through sin, to be immortal in body—when he declared to him, “for you are dust, and to dust you shall return”—forestalling him and casting him out of the Paradise of delight, lest perhaps, putting forth his hand, he should take and eat from the tree of life and live forever.

Therefore, when he says, “My spirit shall not remain in man forever” (Gen. VI), we judge that his purpose is that we should approve and praise his good counsel: because truly, in forbidding man, dead in soul, to be [Col. 1266C] immortal in body, he acted mercifully, providing for us and, as it is written, making provision beforehand for the future. For what if, because of the rather long life which men then lived—one nine hundred and thirty years, another nine hundred and five, another nine hundred and sixty-two, another nine hundred and sixty-nine, as Methuselah—what if, I say, on account of such a brief delay in dying, which compared with eternity has not even the measure of a moment or an instant, men were so proud: those men famous from ancient times, mighty and gigantic, that is, men who held God in contempt, most proud in mind and most corrupt in flesh, as Scripture itself, pressing and repeating the point once, twice, three times—indeed four times—plainly asserts? What [Col. 1266D] would they have done, or what kind of men would they have been, if they had known that they would never die?

Let him who can reflect upon this: for truly it was not said lightly, “making provision beforehand for the future”; nor was the obstacle to salvation, against which God made provision for those predestined to eternal glory, slight or small—God desiring to bring his good purpose through to victory. For one may suppose that the evil of pride in human beings would have been no less incurable than in demons, with the corruption of the flesh added beyond the misery of demons, who are not fleshly.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Why Noah, after receiving the sentence for the destruction of all flesh, did not intercede for humankind as Moses did.

Accordingly, when God said: “The end of all flesh has come before me, and I will destroy them with the earth; make yourself an ark” (Gen. VI), and the rest, Noah, a just and perfect man, heard and was silent. He offered no prayer for the unjust, to restrain God or suspend his wrath, as, for example, Moses restrained the same Lord when he said to him: “Let me alone, that my anger may be kindled against them and that I may destroy them; and I will make you into a great nation” (Exod. XXXII). Moses did this as one truly meek and just, in no way desiring that he himself should become a great nation, [Col. 1267B] but providing more for others than for himself.

Yet Noah was not therefore harsh or unjust, though, while he prepared the ark with his sons for the restoration of the world, he is not recorded to have interceded or laboured to restrain the same God when angry against all living creatures and intending to destroy them all. For Moses had another reason in the faith and love of his heart than that which the letter alone seems to convey when it says: “Remember Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, your servants, to whom you swore to give this land” (Exod. XXXIII), and the rest. For he did not attend so much to the multiplication of the seed or to possession of the land of Canaan, into which they were then about to enter, as he looked to the honour of God and the salvation of humankind: that God might be true and victorious in his purpose, [Col. 1267C] according to the saying, “that you may be justified in your words, and prevail when you are judged” (Ps. L).

For God had promised Abraham—indeed, had promised him again with an oath—that “in his seed all nations would be blessed” (Gen. XXII); and this seed is Christ. And the Spirit of truth had foretold through Jacob’s mouth that Christ would be born from the tribe of Judah: “The sceptre,” he says, “shall not be taken from Judah, nor a leader from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent” (Gen. XLIX). If, therefore, God had fulfilled his threats against that people, saying to Moses, “Let me alone, that my anger may be kindled against them” (Exod. XXXII), and the rest, God would not have appeared justified in his words, nor would the word of truth have accomplished the victory of its purpose.

For Moses, although of Abraham’s race, was nevertheless not of the tribe of Judah. Therefore, even if God had made him into a great nation, so that Christ might be born from his line, the Word of God would not have prevailed completely. For Christ had been promised to the tribe of Judah, not to the tribe of Levi, so that he might be born from it. Therefore, the same God whom Moses faithfully restrained when he was angry against one nation, Noah reasonably allowed to proceed when he intended to destroy all flesh. For the destruction of the multitude did not hinder the victory of the Word of God, or God’s purpose, provided that even one person remained through whom the seed of the woman, destined to have enmity against the seed of the serpent, might be raised up.

## CHAPTER XXX. What is meant by the words: “Noah found grace before the Lord.” Likewise: “Noah was a just and perfect man in his generations.”

At that time he alone was just, as Scripture says of him: “But Noah found grace before the Lord.” Likewise: “Noah was a just and perfect man in his generations” (Gen. VI). Now his generations were descended from him whom God appointed in place of Abel: Seth begot Enos; Enos begot Cainan; Cainan begot Mahalaleel; Mahalaleel begot Jared; Jared begot Enoch; Enoch begot Methuselah; Methuselah begot Lamech; and Lamech begot Noah (Gen. V). For these were Noah’s generations, the generations of the sons of God; whereas the generations of Cain are called the generations [Col. 1268B] of the sons of men. Thus Scripture says: “When men began to multiply upon the earth and had begotten daughters, the sons of God, seeing that the daughters of men were beautiful, took wives for themselves from all whom they had chosen” (Gen. VI).
