Since, then, Noah alone was just and perfect in his generations—that is, in the generations of the sons of God—a great and lamentable corruption of the sons of God through mingling with the daughters of men is shown to have occurred. Their beauty captivated minds and eyes and, beyond doubt, perverted hearts, just as in more recent times Solomon also, though most wise, is known to have been corrupted by foreign women (III Kings XI). But what was one man in number amid that immense multitude of men, who lived long and begot children in abundance? [Col. 1268C] Yet that one man sufficed for the almighty Word of God to preserve or accomplish the palm of its victory, so that it might nevertheless at some time fulfil the good purpose which it had intended in saying: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. I).

For what was before God all that multitude of a flourishing and blooming age except “grass and the flower of the field”? (Isa. XL.) Truly the people are grass (Ps. CII); truly “all flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass” (Isa. XL). And as grass easily dries up and the flower falls when the wind blows, so it was easy for the Word of God to destroy so great a multitude. But the Word of the Lord, abiding forever, caused one man obedient to it to remain, guiding him by means of contemptible wood.

## CHAPTER XXXI. That Noah, because he had kept the Word of God, was himself preserved by that Word.

Imagine, therefore, that God already said to him then: “Because you have kept the word of my patience, I also will keep you from the hour of trial which is to come upon the whole world, to test those who dwell on the earth.” For it contributes greatly to the praise of the victorious Word of God that its keeper, precisely because he kept it, was preserved from the hour of trial—indeed, from the entire year of judgment, that is, of the flood, which occupied the whole earth for a full year.

What was that word of God’s patience? “Behold,” he says, “I will bring the waters of a flood upon the earth, to destroy all flesh in which is the spirit of life under heaven” (Gen. VI), and the rest. This word is rightly called the word of God’s patience because, after God spoke it, he still endured patiently for a long time. Nearly a hundred years passed after this utterance before the flood overflowed; and those who refused to believe and remained in impiety, by despising God’s patience, stored up irrevocable wrath for themselves. Hence the Apostle Peter says: “Those who had once been unbelieving waited for the patience of God in the days of Noah, while the ark was being built” (I Pet. III).

Therefore, to one who attends carefully, it is clear that God’s patience was long and great, and that this just and perfect man truly kept the word of God’s patience, namely, [Col. 1269B] by building the ark for “a hundred years,” as has already been said (Gen. VI). He endured mockery and perhaps many hardships from unbelievers, while by word and deed he proclaimed that the waters of the flood would overflow the whole earth (Gen. VII). Finally, when he was five hundred years old, God spoke to him, saying: “Make yourself an ark of smoothed wood” (Gen. VI). And according to the testimony of the same Scripture, he was six hundred years old when the waters of the flood overflowed.

How many assaults from men do you suppose he endured during so long a period, when prophets in their own times, foreknowing through the Word of the Lord whatever scourge was imminent, so offended people that they even risked their lives? Hence one of them says: “Prophecy and destruction have become terror and a snare to us.” Who would find it incredible that this just man deeply offended those proud and gigantic men, in that recent age, so exceedingly stiff-necked and luxurious, by building the ark and foretelling the coming flood for so many years? Therefore, how did he keep the word of God’s patience, and how did God himself, or the Word of God, preserve him from that severity of judgment by a great miracle suited to his faith? As he overcame in mind the corruption by which all flesh had corrupted [Col. 1270A] its way, and deserved the praise of righteousness or perfection, so, by overcoming the violently overflowing waters of the flood through contemptible wood, he became known to all ages.

## CHAPTER XXXII. That the Lord sufficiently declared his purpose by blessing humankind so often.

After that judgment, the Word of God had—or rather, caused itself to have—new and notable heralds in the world. The first of these was Noah himself, who with his sons received the same blessing that God had formerly pronounced when he created the first human beings, male and female. For as God then blessed them and said: “Increase, multiply, and fill [Col. 1270B] the earth” (Gen. I), so after the flood he blessed these survivors with the same word (Gen. IX).

Thus it is written: “Come out,” he says, “from the ark—you and your wife, your sons and your sons’ wives with you; bring out with you all things that are with you, and go forth upon the earth; increase and multiply upon it” (Gen. VIII). And afterwards: “The Lord smelled the sweet savour, and blessed Noah and his sons, and said to them: Increase and multiply and fill the earth; and let fear and dread of you be upon all the animals of the earth” (Gen. IX). Then, a third time: “But you, increase and multiply; go forth upon the earth and fill it” (ibid.).

This threefold repetition of the same words is a great confirmation of God’s purpose, which he set forth in his Word, knowing, foreknowing, and having predestined all his saints [Col. 1270C] and elect—those whom he wished to be born to him from the human race, with what merits they should increase and to what number they should multiply from that time to the end of the age. Then, when they have been gathered at his right hand, the incarnate Word itself, Jesus Christ, victorious in its purpose, will say: “Come, blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. XXV).

# BOOK III

[Col. 1269]

## 540 CHAPTER I. [Col. 1269D] Concerning Noah’s three sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth; and what is meant by, “May God enlarge Japheth, and may he dwell in the tents of Shem.”

Now the discourse, proceeding by a shorter course—that is, passing over the long paths and great circuits of mysteries or allegories—comes to the tents of Shem, as Noah the father says: “May God enlarge Japheth, and may he dwell in the tents of Shem” (Gen. IX). By the tents of Shem we understand the adoption as sons of God, the glory, the covenant, the giving of the law, worship, and the promises. All these things were given to the seed of Abraham, who was descended from Shem. For Shem begot Arphaxad; Arphaxad begot Salah; [Col. 1270D] Salah begot Eber; Eber begot Peleg; Peleg begot Reu; Reu begot Serug; Serug begot Nahor; Nahor begot Terah; and Terah begot Abraham (Gen. XI).

The tents of Shem, therefore, are the aforesaid benefits of God, which God bestowed upon the seed of Abraham, descended from Shem. We rightly understand those benefits as tents, because Abraham and the other fathers through whom, or with whom, they were administered did not seek to have an abiding city here, but awaited that city whose architect and builder is God (Heb. XI). They lived in tents, confessing that they were strangers and sojourners upon the earth. We must therefore enter these tents of Shem, to which our discourse has led us, and reverently consider how the Word [Col. 1271A] of God, undertaking our pilgrimage, served from that point onward, not disdaining to have human beings as companions in the same tent, through whom it might order the whole campaign of our salvation—dwelling with them so long and sounding through their voices—until, taking flesh also from among them, the warrior and commander of the whole war should himself come forth openly against the ancient serpent.

## CHAPTER II. Concerning the confusion of languages, the birth of Abraham, and the second word of promise: that in his seed all nations were to be blessed.

The islands of the nations had already been divided into their regions, both from the sons of Japheth and the sons of Shem, and also from the sons of Ham. For, after the sons of Japheth had been enumerated, it is immediately added: “From these the islands of the nations were divided in their regions, each according to his own language, and according to their families in their nations” (Gen. X). Likewise, after the sons of Ham had been enumerated: “These,” it says, “are the sons of Ham in their nations, languages, generations, lands, and peoples” (ibid.). Then, after the sons of Shem had been enumerated according to their kindreds, languages, and regions among their nations, Scripture immediately prefaces: “These are the families of Noah according to their peoples and nations. From these,” it says, “the nations were divided upon the earth after the flood.”

The reason why these same nations were divided into differing languages Scripture immediately relates: namely, because in excessive pride they wished to build a city and a tower whose summit would reach heaven. Scripture marks this pride there by calling them sons of Adam. For it says: “The Lord came down to see the city and tower which the sons of Adam were building” (Gen. XI). When it calls them sons of Adam, undoubtedly it must be understood as though it said: imitators of Adam, who sought the likeness of God not through obedience to the Word of God, but through the pride of their own minds.

That division or confusion of languages occurred in the days of Peleg, who was called Peleg for this very reason: because in his days the earth was divided, as has already been said. About one hundred and ninety years after that division of human languages, Abraham was born. To him the one and indivisible Word of God made the desirable promise of its incarnation, when God said to him: “Go out from your land, [Col. 1271D] from your kindred, and from your father’s house, and come into the land which I shall show you. I will make you into a great nation; I will bless you and magnify your name; you shall be blessed, and in you all the kindreds of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. XII). Or, as he said elsewhere: “In your seed all nations of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. XXII).

## CHAPTER III. That the confusion of languages served to conceal the treasure of the divine promise.

Here it is fitting to say that, just as the Apostle says, “All things work together for good to those who love God” (Rom. VIII), so that confusion of languages also worked for good both for the holy fathers to whom this word was spoken and for God, the Word of God himself. For at that time such a mystery had to remain hidden and not be publicly debated, because the world was unworthy of it: nearly all everywhere was wanton and licentious, excessively fierce and proud, although it had recently been struck by the severity of the overflowing flood and consumed in a single destruction down to a small remnant. Such a treasure of so great a promise had, I say, to remain hidden for a time: first, lest those foreigners to whom this good had been entrusted should already then suffer intolerable envy; and second, lest the pearl of the divine calling and heavenly hope, cast before swine, should be trampled underfoot (Matt. VII).

Thus the Word of God had to take precautions for the holy fathers against the envy of impious [Col. 1272B] or worldly people, just as one takes precautions for a young root while it has scarcely put forth a single shoot, from which one hopes or desires good fruit. For as the uprooting of the root comes before the hope of receiving fruit, so if an untimely injury of death had been inflicted upon the fathers by persecutors, it would have prevented the fulfilment of the promise. Therefore the Word itself guarded the fathers of its future flesh, as the psalm testifies when it says: “He did not permit anyone to harm them, and for their sake he rebuked kings: ‘Do not touch my anointed ones, and do not deal wickedly with my prophets’” (Ps. CIV).

And what was more suitable for this precaution than the preceding confusion of languages? It was indeed expedient and useful that, when God confused the languages of those building that tower, no one heard the voice of his neighbour and they ceased building. But it was more expedient and more useful that, while the nations were ignorant because of the confusion of languages, Holy Scripture, the true tower truly reaching to the height of heaven, was to be constructed, containing the mysteries of the promise already mentioned.

## CHAPTER IV. That the mysteries of God were hidden not only from foreigners through the confusion of languages, but also from unworthy Israelites through riddles and figures. Likewise, concerning the invention of the letters of three languages.

Would there not also be, within the multitude of Abraham’s, Isaac’s, and Jacob’s seed—that multitude, namely, of the twelve tribes, which became one nation or one people—people of this kind, people as unworthy as the Gentiles or the uncircumcised, to whom the mystery of the Word of God should not be shown openly? Certainly there would be such people. Indeed, there would be in that nation a multitude of carnal persons whose folly would wear out the wisdom of the few spiritual ones. The Word of God himself was not ignorant that this would happen when, as was necessary for our salvation, he willed to set forth beforehand to humankind through the Scriptures of the law and prophets his counsel.

Therefore, the Word of God rightly hid himself not only in one language, but also, within that very language unknown to the other nations, so tempered his sayings and decrees and so shaded them with mystical likenesses and figures that scarcely a few—scarcely the spiritual alone—could perceive what counsel he had and by what order he intended to restore the salvation [Col. 1273A] of the world. For this reason letters were first invented: so that in them and through them the mystery of the Word of God, who would come to conquer the enemy of humankind through the sacrament of the flesh he assumed and his passion, might be signified, enclosed, and sealed until its appointed time.

This was the reason why the first letters—that is, Hebrew letters—were to be invented, and were invented. For first Hebrew letters were invented through Moses and handed down to the Hebrews. Secondly came Greek letters, which Cadmus gave to the Greeks, at the time when the judge Othniel ruled the children of Israel. In third place among the principal languages, the younger Latin language began to have letters, invented by Carmentis, at the time when Jair judged the people of Israel (Judg. III). Those later letters, Greek and Latin, were invented to signify human matters, but by God’s grace were afterwards admitted to signify divine matters. The first letters, however—that is, Hebrew—were invented or handed down to signify divine matters. But now let us return to the order of the narrative.

## CHAPTER V. That the ancient serpent, moved by envy on account of the Word of promise, acted against Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, yet could not harm them.

Once the promise of the blessed seed had been made to the fathers, as has been said, how could that ancient serpent have learned something of it? Or rather, how could that crafty one have failed to learn, being wickedly concerned for his own kingdom, the kingdom of this world? For he went about the earth and walked through it, like a strong armed man guarding his court, watching lest anything perhaps arise against his dominion (Job I; Luke XI), in accordance with what he had heard God say to him: “I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed” (Gen. III).

Thus, at nearly the same time, the Lord questioned him, saying: “Where do you come from, Satan?” And he answered: “I have gone about the earth and walked through it.” And the Lord said to him: “Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him upon the earth—a simple and upright man, fearing God and departing from evil?” (Job I). Now Job was descended from Uz, the firstborn of Nahor, Abraham’s brother. Scripture in the book of Genesis mentions this Uz in this way: “After these things it was reported to Abraham that Milcah also had borne sons to Nahor his brother: Uz the firstborn, and Buz his brother” (Gen. XXII). Elihu the Buzite, who is also called Balaam in the book of Numbers, was descended from Buz.

Moreover, the aforesaid Job, who lived in the land of Uz and was, as has been said, descended from Nahor’s firstborn, was also the husband of Dinah, Jacob’s daughter, as Philo reports. Satan had observed him while going about the earth and walking through it, seeing that “he was a simple and upright man, fearing God and departing from evil.” How, then, would he not also have observed Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, who held the faith of the promise and, on account of that hope, journeyed from nation to nation and passed from one kingdom to another people? Certainly he observed them and knew that they were citizens of God’s kingdom, opposed to his own kingdom; and he perceived that from them the seed of the woman, opposed to his seed, was to be born. But what could he do? How could he corrupt that good root, or through whose hands among men could he uproot it?

The Word of the Lord, frequently visiting them, both kept their faith uncorrupted inwardly and rebuked kings for their sake outwardly, and did not permit anyone to harm them. Abraham feared death because of Sarah’s beauty; Isaac because of Rebekah’s beauty; and Jacob because of the blessing that he had taken from his brother; he also fled Mesopotamia because of Laban. Yet, as has been said, the Word of the Lord did not permit anyone to harm them: “Do not touch my anointed ones,” he says (Ps. CIV), and so forth. Thus it came about that the enemy never prevailed in harming them. That ancient serpent could injure none of them, either in soul or in body, and so forth.

## CHAPTER VI. That Joseph afterwards endured the serpent’s first assaults through his brothers on account of his dream.

While Jacob his father was still living, holy Joseph endured the first assaults of the devil, the serpent; and in that growing son, beautiful in appearance, the loving father suffered no little, for with a father’s suffering heart he sympathized with his wounded son. [Col. 1274C] That envious one hurled all the force of his malice against the young man. Nevertheless, what he wished did not happen—the deed which he incited Joseph’s brothers, stirred by envy, to perform. Rather, what God willed happened, or what the Word of God willed, which was with Joseph and in him, as it is written: “For the utterance of the Lord kindled him” (Ps. CIV).

For what did that serpent wish to happen? Clearly, he wished Joseph to be killed; and from the will of that same murderous devil, from his prompting, there came forth that cry, when Joseph’s brothers saw him and said: “Behold, the dreamer is coming. Come, let us kill him and cast him into an old cistern” (Gen. XXXVII). But what did God will? Certainly, since he was about to call a famine upon the earth and break all the support of bread, he willed to send this man before them, and willed Joseph to be sold as a slave rather than killed, so that his feet might indeed be humbled in fetters and iron might pass through his soul (Ps. CIV), yet his soul might not be humbled under sin, nor iron pass through his body. He was to have patience until the Word of God should come, until the utterance of the Lord should kindle him, so that the king might send and release him, the ruler of peoples set him free, and appoint him lord of his house and ruler of all his possessions.

Thus the utterance of the Lord prevailed in him even then: for what they first said, according to the prompting of the malignant serpent—“Come, let us kill him”—did not happen. Instead, what was surely the utterance of the Lord sounded through one of them, saying: “What profit is it to us if we kill our brother and conceal his blood? It is better that he be sold, and that our hands not be defiled; for he is our flesh and brother” (Gen. XXXVII).

## CHAPTER VII. [Col. 1275A] What is meant by Jeremiah’s saying: “A voice was heard in Ramah,” and so forth: “Rachel weeping for her children.”

I have called those the serpent’s first assaults because, from the time when the promise of the blessed seed was made to Abraham, Joseph was the first person to suffer persecution and to have his blood demanded on account of righteousness. Hence one may observe that the holy and truly divine evangelist spoke very fittingly and very wisely concerning the death of the innocent little children: “Then was fulfilled what was spoken through the prophet, saying: ‘A voice was heard in Ramah, weeping and great lamentation; Rachel weeping for her children, and she would not be comforted, because they are not’” (Matt. II; Jer. XXX; Lam. I).

For is not such a powerful testimony able to make every son who is killed for the cause of that blessed seed, which is Christ, be regarded as Joseph? And to make every mother who mourns a son killed for such a cause—whether she is an individual woman, his bodily mother, or the Church, his spiritual mother, grieving in devotion with mothers at their children’s death, as has often happened—be regarded as Rachel? Rightly and reasonably, the mother of each of those innocent little children is called Rachel in such a cause, and likewise the whole Church, mother of Christ’s martyrs, because Rachel is said to have been the mother of him through whom iron first passed.

This pleases the Holy Spirit, in whom both the prophet sang and the evangelist understood: for just as Jacob the father then would not be comforted, and as Rachel the mother, had she still been alive, would not have been comforted because Joseph was not there—yet he was there, and not only lived but was also powerful and prospered (Gen. XXXVII)—so the Church, or any faithful mother, does indeed weep in tender affection for a slain son as though he were not, but he is; and he not only is, but is better off and lives more truly, precisely because what happened to him for such a cause is not in this world.

Therefore the Lord immediately says to Rachel, weeping for her children and unwilling to be comforted over them because they are not: “Let your voice cease from weeping, and your eyes from tears, because there is a reward for your work, says the Lord. They shall return from the land of your enemy; there is hope for your latter end, and your children shall return to their own borders” [Col. 1275D] (Jer. XXXI). The Catholic faith firmly holds this: that the children shall return to their own borders, because the devout martyrs, or those innocents who were mourned because they were not and had left no bodily remembrance in the world, shall rise again and appear in Christ’s kingdom—their own kingdom—in likeness to that Joseph who, though thought to have been devoured by a beast, lived and was found living and powerful.

## CHAPTER VIII. That the ancient serpent stirred against Joseph not only his brothers’ plots, but also the enticements of a woman’s desire, and yet did not prevail.

Meanwhile, it should be noted that the ancient serpent attacked [Col. 1276A] Joseph not in only one way, but in two. For he did not rise up only through fraternal envy in order to kill him bodily, as Abel had been killed; nor did he seek only through a woman to ensnare him in order to kill his soul, as he had ensnared Adam. Rather, he attempted both, and in both his attempt was frustrated. The envious brothers said: “Come, let us kill him” (ibid.), and it did not happen. His mistress said: “Sleep with me,” and it did not happen. A great struggle, a great spectacle: the serpent was defeated. Because he could not inflict a true crime, he fabricated a false accusation, on account of which “they humbled his feet in fetters, and iron passed through his soul” (Ps. CIV).

But was not the serpent, in doing these things, going upon his breast? [Col. 1276B] (Gen. III)—that is, trampling down his own purpose, acting against himself? For by such a way and such a course the utterance of the Lord which tested Joseph advanced toward victory; and it was brought about that Joseph’s dreams, consonant with the Word of the Lord, should benefit him (Gen. III): namely, that when famine had been called upon the earth, his sheaf should arise and stand, while his brothers’ sheaves stood round about and worshipped his sheaf. Likewise, that the sun, moon, and eleven stars should worship him upon the earth.

Joseph’s brothers indeed did this. His father, however, is recorded to have done nothing other than worship God, turned toward the head of his bed, when Joseph made him swear concerning the transfer of his body. That father was figured by the sun, just as his brothers were figured by the eleven stars. His mother, signified by the moon, had already died; but certainly, if she had still been alive at that time, she would joyfully have worshipped God in her son.

Therefore, in praise of conquering Wisdom, which is none other than God, the Word of God, it has truly been said, and should often be said, that Wisdom “did not abandon this righteous man when he was sold, but delivered him from sinners; it descended with him into the pit and did not abandon him in chains, until it brought him the sceptre of a kingdom and power against those who oppressed him, and showed false those who had stained him.”

## 543 CHAPTER IX. Concerning the third word of promise: “The sceptre shall not be taken from Judah until he comes who is to be sent.”

After these proofs of divine power, behold now for the third time the word of promise—the invincible word—has issued forth its oracle through the mouth of the patriarch Jacob: “Judah is a lion’s cub; from the prey, my son, you have gone up. Resting, you have lain down like a lion and like a lioness. Who shall rouse him? The sceptre shall not be taken away from Judah, nor a ruler from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent; and he shall be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. XLIX). This was the third proclamation concerning the blessed seed, which is Christ. The first had been that addressed to the serpent: “I will place enmities between you” (Gen. III), etc. The second, that addressed to Abraham: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. XXII). And accordingly this is the third, whose truth accomplishes and completes the two preceding ones. For if Christ—indeed, because Christ—is of the tribe of Judah, therefore he is Abraham’s seed; and when he is foretold as about to go up to the prey, the truth is confirmed of that which God had foretold, namely, that he would place enmity between the seed of the serpent and the seed of the woman.

Thus the house of Jacob, in which the word of promise had been deposited, was shaken by the prompting of the malignant serpent and defiled by a crime committed against a brother; Joseph laboured even unto chains. Yet the word itself was neither shaken nor bound. Rather, what God had foretold once and again, he confirmed a third time, repeating and declaring it more plainly through the mouth of the patriarch living as a stranger in Egypt and dying in that very sojourn. Add also that he marked out the time of his coming by a definite sign. “The sceptre shall not be taken away from Judah,” he says, etc. For by this sign—the fact that not only a king but also a ruler was to be taken away, and was taken away, from Judah, that is, from the Jewish people—in the time of the Roman Empire, when a king was to be given and Herod the foreigner was given, namely one whose father was an Idumaean and who was born of an Arabian mother: by this, I say, if by no other sign, the time of his coming has been recognized and is to be recognized, as now appears, since they have lost not only king and ruler, but also place and nation.

## CHAPTER X. On the sign of the woman clothed with the sun, travailing and crying out to give birth; and likewise on the sign of the great red dragon, etc.

How shall we then pursue in speech, by what sort of words shall we endeavour to follow, how shall the diligent student awaken and make attentive the spectator of this wondrous contest by what sign or trumpet-sound, the manner in which the oft-mentioned enmities proceeded? Behold, John says in the Apocalypse of Jesus Christ: “A great sign appeared in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun, and the moon beneath her feet, and upon her head a crown of twelve stars; and being with child, she cried out in labour and was in anguish to give birth. And another sign was seen in heaven: and behold, a great red dragon, having seven heads and ten horns, and upon his heads seven diadems; and his tail drew a third part of the stars of heaven and cast them to earth. And the dragon stood before the woman who was about to give birth, so that, when she had brought forth, he might devour her son” (Apoc. XII).

These signs are great by virtue of their significance; they are able both to direct the discourse now begun and to make the hearer attentive. These signs strike, awaken, and open the eyes of the mind, so that they may recognize the character of the things of which we speak. That woman is the Church; that dragon is the devil. The woman began then to have a child in her womb, when the faith of the patriarchs of whom I was just speaking, possessing the promise, began to await Christ. The devil, however, began then to be a dragon, when he began to rage against that faith and hope by open persecution: namely, after Joseph and all his brothers had died, when a new king was set over Egypt who did not know Joseph and said to his people: “Behold, the people of the children of Israel are many and stronger than we. Come, let us oppress them wisely, lest perhaps they multiply” (Exod. I), etc.

Then, I say, he began to be a dragon, and as a dragon not merely to deceive fraudulently but also to fight violently; not merely to deceive souls but also to kill bodies. For that king said: “When you act as midwives for the Hebrew women and the time of birth has come, if it is a male, kill him; if a female, preserve her” (ibid.). Again, to his people: “Whatever is born of the male sex, cast into the river; whatever is female, preserve” (ibid.). Before such a thing was ordered or done at his instigation, he was a serpent and deserved to be called a serpent, because he secretly and craftily insinuated himself into minds by deception. From that point he is a great dragon, a red dragon, raging openly and persecuting manifestly: great by the greatness of kings and the multitude of impious men who kill; red with the blood of the pious who die.

## CHAPTER XI. That the crown of twelve stars upon the head of the same woman was the twelve princes of the tribes, and that what she had in her womb was the Word of promise.

Both signs—the woman and the dragon—appear and are seen in heaven, because they are seen only by those who meditate on heavenly things, who can say: “But our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III). By such persons, I say, it is seen and felt in the mind how great was the woman’s pain and how great is or was the horror in that dragon.

That woman was “clothed with the sun,” because the faith of the patriarchs was endowed [strengthened] by the heavenly promise. “The moon [was] beneath her feet,” because the holy Fathers used the temporal goods of this world in such a way that those goods did not rule their minds through desire, but they themselves ruled those goods through generous stewardship. “Upon the woman’s head [was] a crown of twelve stars,” because at the beginning of that primitive Church the sons of Jacob were fathers of the twelve tribes, according to that faithful and true dream: “I saw in a dream as it were the sun and moon and eleven stars worshipping me” (Gen. XXXVII). Without doubt, the twelfth star is he who saw the dream. Certainly, according to their merits at that time, the eleven brothers did not shine; but according to the hope of things to come and the election that was to be drawn from them, they were bright stars. The bright stars are the twelve apostles, princes of that same election.

“And having in her womb,” he says. Having what, and from whom? “Having,” he says, “the seed in which all nations were to be blessed” (Gen. XXII). And the rational creature has this from God the Creator, as a lawful wife has it from her own husband. From the time when God promised that seed to Abraham, and the soul of Abraham and of every one of the others received faith in the promise, that same woman began to have a child in her womb, that is, to be pregnant. “And she cried out in labour and was in anguish to give birth.” Women who have brought forth bodily children and experienced those pains in giving birth know well how truly Truth says: “A woman, when she gives birth, has sorrow, because her hour has come” (John XII), etc. So surely every soul that loves the Word of God, God the Word, Christ Jesus the Son of God, and, desiring to live piously in Christ, suffers persecution, well perceives what is said of that woman: that “she cried out in labour and was in anguish to give birth.”

As we continue the course undertaken, let us chiefly maintain among the great and illustrious proofs of the victory of the Word of God the fact that, after all the dragon’s heads had been overcome, the woman’s male child was caught up to God and to his throne, to rule all nations with a rod of iron.

## CHAPTER XII. When she first began to travail, cry out, and be in anguish so as to give birth.

When, as has already been said, a new king arose over Egypt who did not know Joseph, and began to afflict the growing people of the children of Israel and ordered the males to be killed or drowned in water because he envied their increase and multiplication (Exod. I), then that woman who had a child in her womb began to cry out. For then the first head of the dragon first raised itself up, both in that king and in the one who succeeded him when he died. For then “the children of Israel, groaning because of their works, cried out; and their cry rose up to the Lord because of their works, and he heard their groaning” (Exod. II).

All indeed cried out, but not all possessed the knowledge of crying out; that is, not all knew how, in crying out, to seek or desire the deliverer of their bodies and souls alike, who had been promised to their fathers. For almost all, concerned only for the safety of their bodies, did not know how to take care or be concerned for their souls. Hence one must observe that it greatly benefited the woman that she saw the first head of the dragon standing against her: for, warned by that danger, she recognized that she had a child in her womb and learned to hope in the blessed outcome of her birth. For if the tranquillity of that time in Egypt had smiled upon her, she would have lain in evil security amid the fornications of idolatry, of which it is said figuratively through the prophet: “Son of man, there were two women, daughters of one mother; and they committed fornication in Egypt; in their youth they committed fornication; there their breasts were pressed and the bosoms of their virginity were bruised” (Ezek. XXIII).

It was well, therefore, that affliction at least gave understanding to hearing, so that, though few, still some might sigh and long for that seed which God promised to Abraham (Gen. XXII). For Moses was the first then to say to the Lord: “I beseech you, Lord, send whom you are going to send” (Exod. IV). For he perceived that nothing could be brought to perfection by himself or another unless he came who was to be sent—he of whom the patriarch Jacob said in his blessings upon Judah: “The sceptre shall not be taken away from Judah” (Gen. XLIX), etc. And he said this not without a great cry of longing, since he is also recorded elsewhere to have cried out with silent mouth, the Lord saying: “Why do you cry out to me?” (Exod. XIV). The woman, therefore—that is, she who was now beginning to be the Church, which the woman signifies—“cried out and was in anguish to give birth,” since some, together with the temporal liberation of their bodies, were already desiring the one promised to the fathers to come, the deliverer alike of souls and bodies.

## CHAPTER XIII. That the lamb which the children of Israel sacrificed was a type of the Word to be incarnate; whereas Pharaoh king of Egypt was the first head of the serpent.

“But Scripture says that the Lord was angry with Moses: ‘Aaron your brother, the Levite—I know that he is eloquent; behold, he himself shall come out to meet you, and I will show you what you must do’” (Exod. IV). He said that in this very matter the Lord was angry with him: because he delayed his Christ and did not immediately send the one who would turn away the wrath that had come upon account of Adam’s sin. Yet he did not leave him wholly unheard: even if he did not immediately send the one whom he was to send, he at least sent beforehand some sign of him—a great sign, a great sacrament.

“Let every man take a lamb for his family and household, and let the entire multitude of the children of Israel sacrifice it at evening” (Exod. XII). That lamb was a sign and sacrament of the Christ who was to come, who was to be sent; longing for him, as has already been said, Moses said: “I beseech you, Lord, send whom you are going to send.” John the Baptist, who was sent before him, had this in view when, seeing him walking, he said: “Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world” (John I).

Conversely, Pharaoh, then king of Egypt, bore the sign and likeness of the aforesaid dragon—that is, of the devil. The Spirit of God indicates this when he says against him through the prophet: “You have been likened to a lion among the nations and to a dragon that is in the sea” (Ezek. XII), etc. In that likeness of himself, in that sacrifice of the lamb, how the Word of God fought, how it conquered and crushed that first head of the dragon—that is, the kingdom of Egypt—who does not know? That head raised itself up against the woman so as to remove all expectation of the blessed seed, abolish the name of God, destroy faith in the promise, and swallow up hope of the kingdom to come. Conversely, through Moses the Word of God—or Moses in the Word of God—struck that head with many plagues, saying: “Let the people go, that it may sacrifice to me in the wilderness” (Exod. V).

But Pharaoh not only did not let the people go; he even mocked and said: “They are idle, and therefore they cry out, saying: ‘Let us go and sacrifice to the Lord’” (ibid.). He oppressed them still further with labour, so that they said to Moses and Aaron: “You have made our smell stink before Pharaoh and his servants, and have given him a sword to kill us.”

## CHAPTER XIV. That the almighty Word of God struck the firstborn of Egypt.

Why say more? After the frogs and gnats, after the flies and locusts by which that head of the dragon had been stung and gnawed, after the swelling blisters and hail mingled with fire, by which it had groaned, ulcerated and battered with hail, since it still yielded neither to these nor to the other plagues, the destruction of the firstborn vindicated the victorious Word of God, together with the aforesaid sacrifice of the mystical lamb.

“For while all things kept profound silence,” says Wisdom, “and night in its course had reached the middle of its journey, your almighty Word, O Lord, leaping from heaven from the royal thrones” (Wis. XVIII), “a harsh warrior, sprang into the midst of the land of destruction, bearing your unfeigned command as a sharp sword; and standing, filled all things with death, and while standing upon the earth reached unto heaven.” Scripture said this of that midnight when God “struck every firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh, who sat upon his throne, to the firstborn of the captive woman who was in prison, and every firstborn of cattle. Then Pharaoh rose in the night, and all his servants and all Egypt; and a great cry arose in Egypt. For there was not a house in which no dead person lay.”

Therefore, since the earlier Scripture said, “It came to pass at midnight that the Lord struck every firstborn in the land of Egypt,” while this later passage says, “While night in its course had reached the middle of its journey, your almighty Word” (Wis. XVIII), etc., there can be no doubt that the Lord who struck those firstborn of Egypt is the very person of the Word of God, the Son of God, the almighty Word, the victorious Son. Hence it must be attentively observed that, after saying, “The Lord shall pass through to strike the Egyptians; and when he sees the blood upon the lintel and on both doorposts, he shall pass over the door and shall not permit the destroyer to enter,” he immediately added: “Keep this ordinance for yourself and your children for ever” (Exod. XII).

For what is it here to say, “Keep this ordinance for yourself,” except as though he said, “Keep this Lord for yourself for ever”? For this Word, this almighty utterance, is the Lord, as has already been said, and he must be kept for ever, rather than the rite of sacrificing that lamb, which certainly ought not to remain or be kept for ever, but only until that fullness of time in which this Word, to be incarnate, was to come—the Word who must be kept for ever.

## CHAPTER XV. That it was said of the same Word: “He rejoiced as a giant to run his course.”

The description of him already given deserves closer consideration. “Your almighty Word, O Lord,” it says, “leaping from heaven from the royal thrones, a harsh warrior, sprang into the midst of the land of destruction, bearing your unfeigned command as a sharp sword; and standing, filled all things with death, and while standing upon the earth reached unto heaven” (Wis. XVIII). Do you not recognize in these words a great and mighty giant—the giant of whom the Psalmist sings: “He rejoiced as a giant to run his way; his going forth is from the highest heaven” (Ps. XVIII)?

For who else descended from heaven by the incarnation and, having overcome the dominion of death, ascended victoriously into heaven? Whom did the Psalmist sing of in the prophetic Spirit except “your almighty Word, O Lord, who then from heaven, from the royal thrones, as a harsh warrior sprang down to earth and, standing on earth, reached unto heaven”? Great indeed was that giant who, standing on earth, reached unto heaven—what the Psalmist, prophesying of the future, said: “His going forth is from the highest heaven, and his course unto its highest point” (ibid.). And what the Wise Man there says in recollection of the past: “Leaping from heaven from the royal thrones, he sprang down to earth and, standing on earth, reached unto heaven.” They magnificently proclaim alike the swiftness and gigantic greatness of one and the same being: he who was to come incarnate into the world, and who, not yet incarnate, had come upon Egypt.

But since the work presently undertaken or proposed is not to investigate mysteries of this kind, but to weave something like a history of the wars of the Word of God, this must now be said briefly in praise of his victory: this almighty Word of the Lord made himself worthy of the manner in which he then leapt from heaven, from the royal thrones—so that as a harsh warrior and sharp sword he sprang into the midst of the land of destruction and, standing, filled all things with death. That is, there was no “house in which no dead person lay, from the firstborn of Pharaoh who sat upon his throne to the firstborn of the captive woman who was in prison, and every firstborn of cattle” (Exod. XII).

## CHAPTER XVI. That the same Word of God was a sharp sword to the Egyptians, but a gentle and meek lamb to the children of Israel.

Certainly he wrought a wonder between the houses of the Egyptians and the houses of Israel at one and the same time, on one and the same night. There, that is, in the Egyptians’ houses, he was like a harsh warrior and brandished judgment like a sharp sword. But in the houses of the children of Israel he signified by the lamb—a simple and gentle animal which he commanded to be sacrificed—that he was meek and humble by nature.

For God is meek and humble; the Son of God did not learn to be such among us when he assumed our flesh, so as to say: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. XI). Rather, he was such before heaven and earth were made, by his own nature and not through imitation of anyone. He did not come among us to learn this, but to teach it. The impiety of sinners, in rebelling, deserves that he should appear such as he was called at that time: “a harsh warrior and a sharp sword”—namely, toward those whose hard heart abuses his meekness and patience, as did that hard and proud Pharaoh.

For when Pharaoh first heard, “Thus says the Lord God of Israel: Let my people go, that it may sacrifice to me in the wilderness,” he said: “Who is the Lord, that I should hear his voice and let Israel go? I do not know the Lord, and I will not let Israel go” (Exod. V). Beginning thus, and hardening and burdening his heart more and more, he deserved that this meek and humble one should restrain his meekness and display his strength against him.

Nevertheless, this harsh warrior did not conquer Pharaoh himself or the other Egyptians by personally striking the firstborn, but by giving authority to the destroyer, namely an evil angel. Of this he himself said to Moses and Aaron: “When he sees the blood upon the lintel and upon both doorposts, he shall pass over the door and shall not permit the destroyer to enter your houses and harm you” (Exod. XII). And when the Psalmist had said, “He sent upon them the wrath of his indignation,” etc., he immediately added, “a sending forth through evil angels” (Ps. LXXIII).

For this almighty Word is life and has in himself no bitterness of that worst death which belongs to sinners; but he holds in his power the evil angels, ministers of that same death. He therefore justly permits them to strike, because guilt accusing sinners does not allow them to live in righteousness.

## CHAPTER XVII. For what reason the firstborn of the Egyptians were struck.

And what could be more just, what more beautiful in the order of justice, than that the firstborn of such people should be killed? For Pharaoh and the Egyptians wished utterly to take away the Lord’s firstborn; and therefore, by just requital and beautiful order, they received the final plague in the destruction of their firstborn, as had been prescribed and predetermined by the Lord himself.

For when the Lord sent Moses to Pharaoh, he said to him: “You shall say to him: Thus says the Lord: Israel is my firstborn son. I have said to you: Let my son go, that he may serve me; and you have refused to let him go. Behold, therefore, I shall kill your firstborn son” (Exod. IV). The order of justice is clear in this: he killed that man’s firstborn who refused to release the Lord’s firstborn.

But how was that people the Lord’s firstborn or son? Had God begotten it? Or before that people or man whom he called Israel, had he had no one chosen from the beginning of the world, or no son of his grace? Certainly that people could in some manner be called firstborn in comparison with the Gentile people whom he would later regenerate through the Gospel of Christ his only-begotten Son. Nevertheless, one must still inquire why that people was called a firstborn son at such a time: namely, because the same Son of God, truly firstborn and truly only-begotten, was to assume flesh from that people.

The devil was pressing this purpose and aiming at it: that the people from whom the only-begotten Son and “firstborn among many brethren” (Col. I) was to be born should not remain. Therefore, whatever he did against that people through Pharaoh and his servants is rightly referred to that Son, whose bodily lineage he was hastening to cut off so that he should not be born. The firstborn, then, were not slain for a trivial or slight cause.

But if you ask, Why were also the firstborn of the cattle slain? A brief answer must be given: because Pharaoh held their cattle and herds by force. For when Moses said, “You shall also give us victims and burnt offerings, which we may offer to the Lord our God; all the flocks shall go with us” (Exod. X), and again said, “We shall go with our little ones and our old men, with sons and daughters, with sheep and cattle,” Pharaoh said: “Depart from me, and take care that you see my face no more.” And immediately they were cast out from Pharaoh’s presence (ibid.).

## CHAPTER XVIII. Why, likewise, after the slaughter of the firstborn, all the Egyptians were overwhelmed by waters.

By that plague—that is, by the death of the firstborn—that head was crushed and overcome, so that Pharaoh spoke softly and said: “Arise and go forth; go and sacrifice to the Lord as you say and as you have asked; and when you depart, bless me” (Exod. XII). He spoke so while still wounded by fresh pain. But afterward, when he had dismissed the people and was told that they had fled, envy revived, pride swelled, and with all his chariots and his whole army he pursued departing Israel to the sea, not so much to retain them in his service as to kill them utterly.

“For the enemy said,” Moses says in the song, “I will pursue and overtake; I will divide the spoils, and my soul shall be filled. I will draw my sword; my hand shall kill them” (Exod. XV). Therefore, just as, when he refused to release the people who were the Lord’s firstborn, he justly lost his own firstborn son, so likewise, by a just judgment, when he desired to kill them all, he himself in turn perished with all his people, covered by the waters; not even one of them remained. Thus the Word of God conquered the first head of the dragon through the figurative sacrament of his future flesh or passion—that is, through the evening sacrifice of the Lamb. And that woman who “cried out while having a child in her womb rejoiced”: that is, the people destined one day to bear Christ, with Moses leading the song, sang a hymn of glory to the Lord.

Therefore Wisdom says: “He submerged their enemies in the sea and brought them out from the depth of the underworld. Therefore the righteous carried away the spoils of the impious, and they sang: ‘O Lord, your holy name’; and together they praised your victorious hand” (Wis. X).

## CHAPTER XIX. That God foretold all these things to Abraham, and that the children of Israel justly despoiled the Egyptians.

Is this not the just and true word which was spoken to Abraham their father? “Know beforehand,” he says, “that your seed shall be a stranger in a land not its own; they shall subject them to servitude and afflict them for four hundred years.” And immediately he added: “Yet I shall judge the nation whom they shall serve, and after these things they shall go out with great substance” (Gen. XV).

It is most beautiful and worthy of expectation that this almighty Word, leaping from heaven from the royal thrones as mentioned above (Wis. XVIII), a sharp sword and harsh warrior, should fight and conquer in judgment not only there but in everything whatever that he overcomes or strikes. He strikes no one at all without judgment, because he is the supreme judge—indeed, because he is judgment, because he is the truth of judgment. Hence it was said of him in the Apocalypse, not as a new assertion but in ancient truth: “He who sat upon the white horse”—that is, concerning this very Word having an immaculate body—“was called Faithful and True, and in righteousness he judges and fights” (Apoc. XVI).

But if judgment, or the justice of that judgment, is sought concerning the fact that the righteous took the spoils of the impious, that they went out with great substance and despoiled Egypt at his command—“that each man should ask of his friend and each woman of her neighbour vessels of gold and silver” (Exod. XII)—if, I say, an explanation is sought of this, to demonstrate that it was done with judgment, the just and well-known sentence is at hand: “The labourer is worthy of his wages” (Luke X).

And who does not know that the children of Israel were labourers of the Egyptians? Pharaoh had set taskmasters over them to afflict them with burdens, and they built the store-cities Pithom and Ramesses (Exod. I). What wages did such workers receive for those labours, or amid those labours? Certainly no good wage; on the contrary, bitter punishment. As it is written: “The Egyptians hated the children of Israel, and afflicted them, mocking them; and they brought their lives to bitterness by hard works of clay and brick and every service by which they were oppressed in the works of the land” (Exod. I).

The wage which those unjust men had unjustly withheld, these men justly took. And in taking the spoils of the Egyptians they cannot be accused of injustice, since the Word himself—God who is Faithful and True, who, as already said, judges and fights in righteousness against the nation to whom they were enslaved—judged justly that they should go out with great substance.

## CHAPTER XX. That the dragon is the same as Behemoth, and that he can be conquered by the Word alone, so that he multiplies prayers and speaks softly.

After this victory had been achieved, and the victorious truth of the Word of God fulfilled against that first head of the dragon, at the same period the same Lord said to blessed Job concerning the same dragon, whom he called Behemoth, who was conquered in that Pharaoh and through whom he had assailed the word of promise: “Will he multiply prayers to you, or will he speak soft words to you?” (Job XL). Again: “He who made him shall apply his sword to him” (ibid.).

Certainly it was fitting that he should now say this, because he had already done it to the first head and would do it to the remaining heads, so that each should speak soft words to him. For he who had spoken hard words with hardened heart, saying, “Who is the Lord, that I should hear his voice? I do not know the Lord, and I will not let Israel go” (Exod. V), and the like, was at last humbled like a wounded man. After once and twice falsely saying, “I have sinned even now; pray to the Lord. I have sinned, but forgive me this sin also this once,” at last, unable further to deceive, he said: “Arise, go forth, and when you depart, bless me” (Exod. X, XII). When in the sea, with his hardness broken, he also said most softly: “Let us flee from Israel, for the Lord fights for them against us” (Exod. XIV).

Likewise, concerning the other heads of the dragon—that is, the kingdoms which fought, or through which the dragon himself fought, against the Word of God—this must briefly be said here: each, in its own times and places, after much pride and hardness, multiplied prayers and spoke soft words. For Nebuchadnezzar, the head of the Babylonian kingdom, after being cast out from among men and eating grass like an ox, said: “I lifted my eyes to heaven, and blessed the Most High” (Dan. IV), etc. Likewise Haman, the head of the pride of the Persian kingdom, when he believed that he was about to destroy the whole Jewish race, finally multiplied prayers and spoke soft words to such a degree that he fell upon the couch, entreating Queen Esther for his life (Esther VII).

Similarly, examples will be found in their own places concerning the other heads, showing how truly it was said of the devil, the dragon who drives them: “Will he multiply prayers to you and speak soft words to you?” And likewise: “He who made him shall apply his sword to him,” so that the attempts of his sword may be frustrated (Job XL). So it happened to this first head, which, though it had said, “I will draw my sword; my hand shall kill them” (Deut. XXXII), was impeded by the suffocating waters and could not draw its sword from its sheath.

## CHAPTER XXI. That the Lord delivered the people of Israel for the praise and glory of his name, in order to make them higher than all peoples.

Truly this is a great and praiseworthy spectacle of the victory of the Word of God, if you rightly consider the aim and purpose of this warrior, or harsh combatant. What did he intend? What did he have in view when “your almighty Word, O Lord,” leaping from heaven from the royal thrones, conquered that first head of the dragon? What fruit did he seek from his war or victory?

Though nearly all of us know this, still we take greater delight at this point in hearing it from the oracle of Sacred Scripture itself. After Moses had first said to Israel: “The Lord has chosen you today, that you may be his peculiar people, as he has spoken to you, and that you may keep all his commandments,” he added the sum of that intention: “That he may make you higher than all the nations which he created, for his praise and name and glory” (Deut. XXVI). What could be more beneficent, sweeter, or more lovable than this intention?

A people few in number, most miserable in slavery, more worthless and despised than all other peoples, serving the most proud, and in that very service exposed to Egyptians who afflicted and mocked them amid the hard work of clay and brick—he intended so to console them that he proposed to make them higher than all nations. Intending and saying, “I have indeed seen the affliction of my people in Egypt” (Exod. III), he came down to deliver them and undertook this contest so great.

But what that exaltation was, or in what respect he wished and did make that people higher than all peoples, we declare in the words of the Apostle: “The adoption as sons is theirs, and the glory, and the covenant, and the giving of the law, and the worship, and the promise; theirs are the fathers, and from them is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed for ever. Amen” (Rom. IX). Is this a slight exaltation? And elsewhere, after asking, “What advantage then has the Jew, or what profit is there in circumcision?” he immediately answers: “Much in every way. First, because the utterances of God were entrusted to them” (Rom. III).

He deigned to make that people pre-eminent above all peoples by so great an exaltation. How or when did he entrust his utterances to them? On the fiftieth day he said to Moses: “Come up to me on the mountain and remain there; I will give you two tablets of stone, and the law and commandments which I have written, that you may teach the children of Israel” (Exod. XXIV). God entrusted his utterances to them with such great and particular care that he gave Moses also the signs of those utterances, namely letters, by giving him tablets written with the finger of God.

## CHAPTER XXII. That the utterances of God were not only entrusted to the people of Israel, but were also written, and this by his own finger.

For who else, finally, will be regarded as the author or inventor of signs of this kind—that is, of letters—except God himself? Moses himself testifies thus: “The Lord said, ‘I will give you two tablets of stone, and the law and commandments which I have written’” (Exod. 24). When he says “the law,” adding “and commandments,” he surely means not the law of ceremonies but the law of the Ten Commandments. Again it is written: “Moses returned from the mountain, carrying in his hands the two tablets of testimony, written on both sides, and made by the work of God” [Col. 1287C] (Exod. 32). The writing of God was engraved upon the tablets; and, when the ten commandments are set out again in Deuteronomy: “These words,” he says, “the Lord spoke, and wrote them upon two tablets of stone, which he gave to me” (Deut. 5). Likewise, concerning the second tablets, which he made after the first had been broken: “When I had cut two tablets of stone like the former ones,” he says, “I went up the mountain holding them in my hands, and he wrote upon the tablets, according to what he had written before, the ten words” (Deut. 10). Again, in Exodus: “When he had finished such words on the mountain, he gave Moses two tablets of stone, tablets of testimony, written by the finger of God” (Exod. 31); and afterwards: “Cut for yourself,” he says, “two tablets of stone like the former ones, and I shall write upon them the words which the tablets that you broke contained” [Col. 1287D] (Exod. 34).

Why so many testimonies? Clearly, so that it may plainly be established that the God who gave this capacity and voice, or language, for speaking, was himself also the first to write letters—that is, the very shapes of the alphabet—by his own hand, and gave them written to Moses, the first of all human beings deemed worthy to write. For Moses himself had not yet written anything when God said to him: “Come up to me on the mountain and remain there, and I shall give you two tablets of stone, and the law and commandments which I have written” (Exod. 24).

Certainly Cadmus gave letters to the Greeks at the time when Othniel was ruler over the children of Israel; and Carmentis gave Latin letters at the time when Jair judged the people of Israel. 548 But this could have been accomplished by human ingenuity, in imitation of the earlier Writing and divine work: thus it was no longer impossible for something to be made in another language which God had himself shown to a human being in one language, namely Hebrew. [Col. 1288A]

## Chapter XXIII. Nothing is more useful than the invention of letters for the knowledge of God the Creator

It should therefore be noted that among all works made by human hands, this alone is a work which humanity possesses through the craftsmanship of God the Maker; and among all the works of God, though they are many, this alone is a work which he commanded human beings to perform with their own hands. For on tablets he wrote his own Writing by his own work, and he commanded humanity to write in a book.

For example: “Write this,” he says, “as a memorial in a book, and deliver it to the ears of Joshua: for I shall blot out the memory of Amalek from under heaven” [Col. 1288B] (Exod. 17). Did he command Moses to write only that Amalek, the beginning of the nations—that is, the first among all the nations—had come and fought against Israel, and that therefore its memory was to be erased? Rather, it is certain, and ought rightly to be understood, that he commanded him to write this further statement: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. 1), although the words “The Lord said to Moses, Write this” are not prefixed to “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.”

If you weigh rightly the usefulness of this work, namely writing by hand, you will surely confess that it was fitting, or had to be fitting, for the God of majesty to be the first author of such figures—that is, letters—and no other. For what is there in the whole world, among the entire multitude of things or visible signs, which offers the human mind so effective and useful, so certain an aid for knowing its Creator? Is it the order of heaven, sun, moon, and stars? All these are beautiful and are certain signs of creative omnipotence; yet they do not instruct our senses, or are not able to instruct them, as these signs of words do. These signs tell of the past, show the present, and announce the age to come; and, what is greatest of all, they affirm not only the Creator’s omnipotence but also make his will known to us. Whenever we wish, God speaks with us through these signs. It is therefore a work worthy to be believed to have been made by God himself, as Scripture plainly testifies. For, as has already been said, he himself first wrote upon tablets by his own work, by his own finger—certainly in an ineffable manner—and afterwards commanded humanity to write. [Col. 1288D]

## Chapter XXIV. As Moses’ first two tablets were broken, so we judge that the characters of the letters were changed under Ezra

The Hebrews have twenty-two letters. Their characters indeed were changed, since it is certain that Ezra, a scribe and teacher of the law, after Jerusalem had been captured and the Temple restored under Zerubbabel, discovered other shapes, while the sound remained the same. What is remarkable, then, if God wished the forms of the alphabet, which he himself had given, to be changed through the prophet Ezra—whom we understand to be Malachi himself, the last in the order of the twelve prophets [Col. 1289A]—when he also willed that the very tablets upon which the letters of God’s Writing had been engraved should be broken? Those tablets, certainly, were not cut by Moses, but were given to Moses by God himself; and Moses himself made others, although he did not write upon those either. For the Lord said to him: “Cut for yourself two tablets of stone like the former ones, and I shall write upon them the words contained by the tablets which you broke” (Exod. 39).

For regarding the first tablets, Scripture’s authority plainly declares that Moses did not cut them, but that the Lord himself both wrote them and gave them to Moses. It says: “The Lord said to Moses: Come up to me on the mountain and remain there, and I shall give you tablets of stone, and the law and commandments which I have written” (Exod. [Col. 1289B] 24). Again, elsewhere: “When he had completed such words upon Mount Sinai, he gave Moses two tablets of stone, tablets of testimony, written by the finger of God.”

It is therefore no wonder if, at the restoration of the city or Temple, it pleased him that letters written by the finger of God should be changed through a human being, since, in the construction of the tabernacle that was one day to be destroyed, tablets prepared by God himself were broken by a human being, and others were cut at God’s command. Could both events—the alteration of the tablets and the change of the letters—have been portents of the same reality? Namely, that everything instituted then by God, before he became man, was destined to pass away. For behold, the old things are old and have passed away, and all things had to be made new, as now they have been made new by that same God made man, Priest forever, of whom the Apostle says: “But Christ, appearing as High Priest of the good things to come, through the greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made with hands” [Col. 1289C] (Heb. 9), and so forth.

## Chapter XXV. It is a gift of God that a human being can meditate upon the Word of God, then speak it, and finally write it and read what others have written

See with how small an aid God and his Word have brought such great help to the human race. There are only twenty-two letters, as has already been said. See what a great structure has been built from such slight outlay. First, upon them was laid the foundation of writings—that is, those writings called canonical Scripture, composed through the Holy Spirit. [Col. 1289D] Then how many people, from every nation and people, especially Greeks and Latins, built upon it while using no more letters.

Hence it has come about that the Word of God has been brought into our public assembly, and that we can always possess it. Until then, only a few persons had been instructed by this Word, among whom Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are especially known. The Word of God came to them not through a reading of this kind but through hidden inspiration; and therefore very few received the Word, because not many were worthy of such instruction. Once letters had been given, they immediately opened a way for the multitude to receive the Word of God.

Accordingly, I should rightly say that the first author or inventor of letters ought not to have been any human being but God himself, whose third gift effective for the knowledge of his Word was that he gave letters to humanity. The first gift of God is that a human being, as rational, can meditate upon that Word. The second is that, alone among all living creatures, possessing an articulate tongue, one can express one’s meditation in speech. The third is that, after learning letters, one can write by hand and understand what others have written, and so can know the Word of God, the wisdom of God. [Col. 1290A]

Under these visible signs, the divine utterances were first entrusted to that people; and it was instructed concerning the majesty to be worshipped of the one and only true God: 549 that he alone created all things—heaven, earth, sea, and all that is in them; that he created humanity in his own image; that he spoke to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; that he chose their seed as his own peculiar people. Under the same signs it received his laws, whose entire sum lies in the precepts of the Decalogue, which he himself wrote upon the tablets; and under the same signs it received his ceremonies—that is, the rite or order of sacrificing to that same God. [Col. 1290B]

## Chapter XXVI. The heavenly mysteries hidden beneath the surface of sacred letters are like a treasure hidden in a field

How much splendor of wisdom, how many treasures of wisdom, do you suppose lie concealed beneath these signs—that is, letters? Who could unfold the riches of salvation which the woman mentioned above received, stored under those letters, in that first victory—namely, where the first head of the dragon was conquered and crushed?

For this is why, in Ezekiel, the Lord says to that same woman: “I entered into a covenant with you, and you became mine; and I washed you with water, cleansed your blood from you, anointed you with oil, clothed you in many-colored garments, shod you with hyacinth-colored footwear, girded you with fine linen, clothed you in delicate fabric, and adorned you with ornaments. I put bracelets on your hands, a necklace around your neck, an earring upon your mouth, rings in your ears, and a crown of beauty on your head. You were adorned with gold and silver, and clothed with fine linen, embroidered work, and many colors” [Col. 1290C] (Ezek. 16).

By so many splendid names of riches, what are we to suppose is signified except heavenly mysteries concealed under the coarse covering of that sacred Scripture? For, if you attend to the preceding and following portions of that prophecy, it is certainly clear that these words were spoken about the institution of the sacred law, which the primitive Church then received from the Lord through the hand of Moses—indeed, through the ordering of angels—full of heavenly mysteries.

Whoever considers these things surely sees that the parable of the incarnate Word is true and fitting when he says: “The kingdom of heaven is like a treasure hidden in a field, which a man who finds it hides; and for joy over it goes and sells all that he has, and buys that field” (Matt. 13). For that body of letters is, in a certain way, recognizable upon the surface; but in such a field there is hidden a treasure—the noble treasure of heavenly wisdom. Whoever finds it—that is, understands it rightly—rejoices and truly says to the Lord: “The law of your mouth is good for me beyond thousands of gold and silver” [Col. 1291A] (Ps. 118).

Delighted by this discovery, they sold everything that they had and bought such a field, in order that, freed from secular occupations, they might be at leisure to give their attention to and meditate upon that law of the Lord. Although they had not yet been able, nor would they be able except in part, to know it, they perceived that the Lord lay hidden there in figurative deeds and mystical sayings.

## Chapter XXVII. This treasure was hidden so that little children, who needed milk, might not be unable to bear solid food, and swine might not trample pearls cast beneath their feet

Certainly, by thus hiding a treasure of such value, he himself at that time first did what he teaches elsewhere when he says: “Do not cast your pearls before swine, lest perhaps they trample them and, turning upon you, tear you to pieces” [Col. 1291B] (Matt. 7). Wisdom also teaches that solid food is not to be offered to little children, but milk. This, I say, he did then, when he marked out the treasure of his Word and the pearls of heavenly secrets in such a manner that neither swine could find them nor little children collapse under the weight imposed upon them.

Indeed, if you consider the condition of that time, people were either excessively contemptuous or simple, apart from the very few whom the prophetic Spirit—which was more abundant in Moses—deigned to make privy to his counsel. For example, Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, and the other leaders of the synagogue, who stood against the Lord and against Moses, scoffing and saying: “Indeed, you have brought us into a land flowing with streams of milk and honey, and have given us possessions of fields and vineyards” [Col. 1291C] (Num. 16). Were they not swine, who, had they seen the pearls of the kingdom of heaven laid before them, would have trampled them underfoot?

It should therefore be carefully noted that, although the whole intention of Holy Scripture tends toward the kingdom of heaven, scarcely anywhere in the whole Pentateuch is there any mention of the glory of that kingdom or any threat of the fire of Gehenna in explicit words, except the saying in the Song: “A fire has been kindled in my wrath, and it shall burn unto the lowest parts of hell” (Deut. 12). The threats intended to deter sin concern the sword, famine, pestilence, and evil beasts. The promises intended to stimulate good zeal concern fields and vineyards, towns or villages, fortified cities, fig trees and olive trees, and a land flowing with streams of milk and honey. By these names, and by whatever else is commonly understood, lighter things are meant than those perceived spiritually by spiritual persons; yet they affect much more effectively the minds of those who attend to or await not the things which are unseen, but only the things which are seen. [Col. 1291D]

Certainly, if at that time the sweetness of eternal life in the world to come, and the rest of paradise—understood under the name of the land flowing with milk and honey—had been announced more explicitly in its own terms, little children, who needed milk, would have rejected it as solid food; whereas the proud, like swine, would have trampled the pearls. [Col. 1292A]

## Chapter XXVIII. Examples prove that it was not expedient for the mysteries of Scripture to be disclosed in plain words until they had been fulfilled in deed

What shall I say of the mystery of the mystical tabernacle, which the Lord undoubtedly commanded to be made according to a heavenly pattern? For he says: “See, and make it according to the pattern shown to you on the mountain” (Exod. 25). If he had commanded that the reality itself be openly described then in words—namely, the mysteries of his incarnation, passion, and resurrection, of which those things were patterns—who could have borne it?

To offer one example out of many: in Deuteronomy it is said thus: “Your life shall hang, as it were, before you, and you shall not believe in your life” [Col. 1292B] (Deut. 28). If it had pleased him to state this a little more plainly, Isaiah would, as we understand it, have been sawn asunder, as though condemned by a just judgment of the law, 550 because he had said, “I saw the Lord sitting upon a high throne” (Isa. 6). For in saying this he was judged contrary to the Lord himself, who said of himself: “No human being shall see me and live.”

If, then, Isaiah was condemned by human beings because he said, “I saw the Lord sitting,” what would have happened to Moses if, where he said, “Your life shall hang before you, and you shall not believe in your life” (Deut. 28), he had said more plainly: “You will crucify and cause your Lord to hang before you, and you will not believe that the same author of life has risen”? [Col. 1292C]

The providence of the Word is therefore praiseworthy in that through Scripture he both made himself known to the world and concealed himself from the world, tempering that same Scripture in such a way that, like a sealed book, it escaped the carnal eyes of that age and was preserved for future spiritual persons, for whom it could usefully be opened in its own time. To its guardians he immediately gave, with a generous hand, the reward they desired, as it is written: “He gave them the regions of the nations, and they possessed the labors of peoples, that they might keep his ordinances and seek his law” (Ps. 104).

Thus it happened that, although most of them were unwarlike, nevertheless they bore weapons for those who would fight in the warfare of the Word of God; and in a wonderful way they became forerunners and armor-bearers of combatants who would come much later. Foreseeing this, the Lord said to Moses: “I will strike them with pestilence and consume them; but I will make you ruler over a great nation, stronger than this one” [Col. 1292D] (Num. 14). Though this did not happen immediately, because Moses intervened, we now see it fulfilled: the Jews were struck, and Moses has been established, with unveiled face, as ruler and teacher over another nation—namely, over the whole holy Church.

# Book Four

[Col. 1293]

## Chapter I. Which animals the dragon’s seven heads resembled

Concerning the first head of the dragon, which stood before the woman about to give birth, so that when she had borne her child it might devour him (Apoc. 12)—that is, concerning the first kingdom which aroused persecution against the Word of God and the promises, so that his purpose might not be accomplished—it has already been said how the Word of God, God the Word, triumphed. Now, as we are about to recount the destruction of the second head, we judge it appropriate to distinguish, by clear contemplation, the individual forms of the individual heads: how there are seven heads and how they have differing appearances.

Behold, from the testimony of the Scriptures it may plainly be observed that the first head was like a dragon; the second was like a calf; the third like a lion; the fourth like a bear; the fifth like a leopard; the sixth unlike the other beasts; and the seventh like a human being. “You have been likened to the dragon that is in the sea,” the Lord says through Ezekiel concerning Pharaoh, king of Egypt [Col. 1293B] (Ezek. 32).

There is no need to prove this by lengthy evidence, since it is known and most celebrated everywhere throughout the whole Church that the carnal Pharaoh who subjected God’s people to servitude, pursued them as they crossed the sea, and was drowned in the sea with his chariots and horsemen, was a type of the devil. After the servitude of sin, the people who flee to Christ renounce him along with all his pomps. Therefore the first head is rightly like a dragon.

The explanation of the other heads or faces is equally ready to hand. We observe that the face of the second head—that is, the character of the Israelite kingdom—was like a calf because, immediately after their departure from Egypt, that people fashioned the head of a calf and worshipped it. At that time the head was indeed suppressed for a while; but when an opportunity came, that kingdom, divided from the house of David, immediately remade the same face in twofold form—that is, two calves (2 Kings 12)—and, in worshipping and defending them, killed the heralds of the Word of God. [Col. 1293C]
