Daniel then describes the faces of the third, fourth, fifth, and sixth heads. “The first,” he says, “was like a lioness,” because the Babylonian kingdom abounded in two evils after the likeness of a lioness: pride and luxury. “Another beast,” namely the kingdom of the Medes and Persians, “was like a bear,” namely because of the cruelty of Haman the Agagite, enemy of the Jews. “The third beast,” or kingdom of the Macedonians, “was like a leopard,” he says, certainly because of the diversity of the Greeks, and the ferocity of Alexander the Great and of Antiochus, who raged impiously against the Jews. The fourth beast, namely the Roman kingdom, is not said to have been like anything, because that kingdom proved unlike all others in magnitude and power, and raged more than all others, and more terribly, against faith in the incarnate Word. [Col. 1293D]

After those two earlier and these four later heads or kingdoms, there will be a seventh head, whose face will be like a human being: namely, the kingdom of Antichrist, who will be the man of sin and son of perdition. Let us now continue in order.

## Chapter II. The face of the second head was the face of the calf which Aaron made, and how the woman with child then cried out

Meanwhile, while the Lord spoke with Moses on the mountain—or Moses with the Lord—the ancient serpent, disarmed in its first head, hastened to raise another head against God and his Word. For when the people saw that Moses delayed in coming down from the mountain, they fashioned and made a molten calf. “These,” they said, “are your gods, Israel” [Col. 1294B] (Exod. 32). Again, they said to one another: “Let us appoint a leader for ourselves and return to Egypt” (Num. 14).

Who contrived this except the devil, the ancient serpent? 551 His intention was that God, offended by the people’s guilt, might forget his Word and promise and turn away from his purpose. But the woman with child cried out—namely Moses, whose soul was a part of that woman, the Church—crying and praying to the Lord his God and saying: “Why, Lord, is your fury angry against your people? Remember Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, your servants, to whom you swore by yourself, saying: I shall multiply your seed like the stars of heaven” (Exod. 32). By saying this and the rest, he surely longed intensely that God should be justified in his words and overcome by the victory of truth; and by the force of such an intention he held fast the Lord when he said: “Let me be, that my wrath may grow hot” (ibid.). [Col. 1294C]

A strong person was able to hold him, because truly strong before God and human beings is whoever is a faithful hearer of the Word of God: that is, one who desires, as David did, that God may be justified in his words and prevail when judged. Thus, as has already been said, the face of the second head was like a calf; but then that head could not have a sword, because they did not appoint a leader for themselves. Rather, they immediately experienced their leader—and their avenger against their calf—as their God: how strong was his zeal for justice, though he was the meekest of all human beings.

For, greatly angered, he threw from his hands the tablets and broke them; and, when the calf had been burned and ground to powder, he said: “Whoever belongs to the Lord, let him join me” (ibid.). When all the sons of Levi had gathered to him, he said: “Let each man put his sword upon his thigh, and let each kill his brother, friend, and neighbor” [Col. 1294D] (ibid.).

## Chapter III. The same head, removed for a time, was raised again under Jeroboam

At that time the dragon’s head, namely the calf, was removed from sight; but it was never wholly removed from the people’s heart. They always desired such a god, but were kept from it by severe judges until the time of Rehoboam, son of Solomon, son of David. When he succeeded his father, the ten tribes were divided from the house of David and made Jeroboam their king. Having devised a plan, he made two golden calves, placed one at Bethel and the other at Dan, and spoke the very words which the children of Israel had spoken in the wilderness after fashioning the calf, as already related: “Behold your gods, Israel, who led you out of the land of Egypt” [Col. 1295B] (3 Kings 12; Exod. 32).

Then the dragon’s second head, having, as has been said, the face of a calf, rose with all its force against the woman. It began to use swords, and to kill and persecute especially the prophets of the Word of the Lord. Until then, since Pharaoh had perished, none of the kings had wielded swords in this cause so as to prevent sacrifice being offered to the true God and the Word of the Lord being proclaimed. Whatever it did in the meantime by turning the people away from God’s worship, it did not do as a dragon at war but as a deceiving serpent, deceiving the people through the same sex through which it had first deceived humankind, without violence. For they took their daughters as wives, gave their own daughters to those men’s sons, and served their gods (Judg. 3).

For this the angered Lord handed them over to their enemies, and, afflicted by them, they cried to the Lord. The Lord too was moved by mercy, heard the groans of the afflicted, raised up judges for them, and delivered them from the slaughter inflicted by the ravagers. But after a judge died, they returned and did far greater evils, following foreign gods, serving and worshipping them [Col. 1295C] (Judg. 2). Thus the serpent was unarmed and unable to wage war as a dragon, because it possessed no judge or ruler among them whose power it could use to deter them from worshipping the Lord. On the contrary, nearly all the judges acted courageously in their respective times, binding the people to observe the law of the Lord.

## Chapter IV. Through the judges the Lord restrained the people from idolatry and defended them from enemies, the Word of God conquering through them

The entire victory of those judges is certainly the victory of the Word of God, because they conquered not by a multitude of troops but by the Word of the Lord, delivering Israel from the oppression of enemies. Of Othniel, the first of those twelve judges, it is written: “The Spirit of the Lord was in him, and he judged Israel. He went out to battle, and the Lord delivered Chushan-rishathaim, king of Syria, into his hands, and he subdued him” (Judg. 3).

After him came Ehud, who delivered Israel from the hand of Moab when he struck King Eglon. “I have a word from the Lord for you,” he said [Col. 1296A] (ibid.). The event immediately proved true his statement that he had the Word of the Lord with him: Moab was conquered and humbled under Ehud’s hand, and the land rested.

After him Shamgar defended Israel, doubtless not by human strength but by the power of that same Word. Evidence for this lies in the sign that he struck down six hundred Philistines with a ploughshare. Then, as Barak went to battle against Sisera, commander of the army of Jabin king of Canaan, the prophetess Deborah said to him: “In this campaign victory shall not be credited to you, because Sisera shall be delivered into the hand of a woman” (Judg. 4). And so it happened. For Jael, wife of Heber the Kenite, struck him in the head, seeking a place for the wound and piercing him with force at the right moment.

Who does not know that the victory by which Gideon conquered Midian, Amalek, and the other eastern peoples was the victory of the Word of God? He went to battle with three hundred men, holding lamps in their left hands and sounding trumpets in their right; and when they cried out, “The sword of the Lord, the sword of Gideon” [Col. 1296B] (Judg. 7), each standing in his own place, the Lord set a sword throughout the entire camp, and they cut one another down in mutual slaughter. Such a battle and victory is plainly not a human being’s but God’s.

It is not so clear in Jephthah’s case that the Word of God fought in him without military strength, except for the statement written concerning him: “The Spirit of the Lord came upon Jephthah; he passed through Gilead and Manasseh, made a vow to the Lord, crossed to the children of Ammon, and the Lord delivered them into his hands” (Judg. 12). In Samson’s case there is no doubt that his strength was the Word itself, whose most illustrious mysteries of future coming into this world through the mystery of the incarnation he prefigured by illustrious deeds [Col. 1296C] (Judg. 15).

## Chapter V. Judges were raised up only when the people cried to the Lord

These judges were raised up by the Lord to deliver the children of Israel from the hands of ravagers, not in silence, but after the people’s cry had gone before. Which of these things is more worthy of reverence? Which more greatly commends the power or wisdom of the Word of God advancing toward victory? Was it that he handed them over into the hands of enemies 552 so that they might cry out, or that, when they cried, he raised up judges to deliver them?

Certainly in both cases your almighty Word, Lord, fought like a stern warrior, so that it might not return to you empty—the Word in which you had purposed the salvation of the human race and promised it to Abraham. But he directed the course of this salvation especially by handing Israel over to its enemies. For affliction gave understanding to hearing, so that the woman often mentioned, warned by adversities, might reflect and remember what conception she bore in her womb, and how necessary it was for her that this conception should come to birth.

For what are we to suppose that the young woman—the Church of that time or age—cried out? Whenever we read or hear: “The children of Israel cried out to the Lord, who raised up for them a savior and delivered them” [Col. 1297A] (Judg. 3), we surely understand that some did not cry out in vain but, by crying, asked that this Savior might now come, the one promised to Abraham and designated through Moses by the sign by which he would be recognized: “The Lord your God shall raise up for you a prophet from your own nation and from among your brothers, like me” (Deut. 18), and so forth.

Are we to think that no one cried out to him in the same or subsequent age merely because we plainly read that Moses alone cried out to him? Certainly, when Moses was sent to Pharaoh in Egypt, desiring rather that the one who would accomplish full salvation should already be sent, he said: “I beseech you, Lord, send the one whom you are going to send” (Exod. 4). Again, after they had made the calf, when praying for the same people, he said among other things: “You command me to lead out this people, yet do not tell me whom you will send with me, especially since you have said: ‘I know you by name, and you have found grace before me’” [Col. 1297B] (Exod. 33).

Accordingly, one should note that this same Moses is rightly called hasty in this respect: “Moses hastened, bowed down to the ground, and worshipped, saying: ‘If I have found grace in your sight, Lord, I beseech you, walk with us’” (Exod. 3), and so forth. For he was greatly hastening, because Jacob had said: “The sceptre shall not be taken from Judah, nor a ruler from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent” (Gen. 49); and Moses already desired the coming of the one who was to be sent, paying too little heed to the fact that not only leaders and judges but kings also had to arise from Judah before he came.

## Chapter VI. Why those judges were called saviors

What is plainly written concerning Moses must without doubt also be understood concerning certain others. For at no time did faith so fail in Israel that there was not someone who held the hope of that coming one and awaited the promise. Therefore I should rightly say that the very fact that the Lord handed the children of Israel over to their enemies was part of the purpose of the Word of God, advancing toward victory and a completed work: namely, that the woman with child might cry out and suffer more and more so as to give birth.

To one who considers this attentively, it appears very beautiful and venerable that Holy Scripture calls the judges thus given “saviors.” For example: “They cried to the Lord when they were in distress, and he raised up for them Othniel as savior” [Col. 1297D] (Judg. 3). Again: “And afterwards they cried to the Lord, and he raised up for them a savior named Ehud” (ibid.). For what did they cry to the Lord for, except that the Savior who was to be sent might already come? That each of them might, for example, utter Moses’ words: “I beseech you, Lord, send the one whom you are going to send” (Exod. 4).

But because the time of his coming had not yet arrived, those who were sent in the meantime to deliver the people temporally deserved rightly to be called so, because they were representatives of the one and true Savior. Salvation was administered through them in two ways: judging and fighting. By judging, they restrained the people from the service of idols; by fighting, they themselves, marching at the front, courageously avenged them upon the enemies whom Israel had served. They were therefore judges in discipline, leaders in battle, and saviors in both, prefiguring by splendid deeds and mystical victories the mysteries and victories of the eternal Savior. For as a mirror placed before the sun reflects a similar image, so the bright faith of those saviors and judges presented in their deeds a beauty like that of the eternal Savior and Judge whose representatives they were. [Col. 1298A]

## Chapter VII. The twelve judges and the twelve apostles are the twenty-four elders
The judges, however, are twelve in number: the first, [Col. 1298B] Othniel, son of Kenaz, brother of Caleb; the second, Ehud; the third, Shamgar; the fourth, Barak; the fifth, Gideon; the sixth, Tola; the seventh, Jair; the eighth, Jephthah; the ninth, Ibzan; the tenth, Elon; the eleventh, Abdon; the twelfth, Samson. After these follows the kingdom of David, whom, after Saul had been removed, Samuel anointed as king while still a youth, by the Lord’s command and choice. This kingdom of David is the kingdom of the incarnate Word, Christ the Son of God; for the angel likewise said of him to Mary: “The Lord God will give him the throne of David his father, and he will reign over the house of Jacob for ever, and of his kingdom there will be no end” (Luke 1).

If, therefore, to the twelve judges already mentioned you add an equal number of other judges, namely the apostles—to whom the King himself said, “You also shall sit upon twelve thrones, [Col. 1298C] judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19)—behold, you have twenty-four judges. These may surely be understood to be the twenty-four elders of whom it is written in the Apocalypse: “And around the throne were twenty-four seats, and upon the thrones twenty-four elders sitting, clothed about with white garments, and golden crowns upon their heads” (Rev. 4).

For what more splendid thing can be understood by that throne than the kingdom of David just mentioned, the kingdom of Christ the Son of God, to whom the Lord God gave the throne of David his father? Thus: “Around the throne were twenty-four seats, and upon the thrones twenty-four elders.” For before the beginning of David’s kingdom there were those twelve judges; and at the consummation of that same [Col. 1298D] kingdom, where Christ the King sits upon the throne of his Father, there are those other twelve judges, who are to sit for ever upon twelve thrones and judge the twelve tribes of Israel.

They are rightly called elders—not only the latter, but also the former—because through the maturity of their faith they restrained the people of God in its youthful wantonness; and because, insofar as they could, they wiped away by judicial authority the fornications of that same people, by which Israel committed fornication with foreign women and with their gods, they are rightly said to be clothed about with white garments. Likewise, because through them it was brought about that the Word of God should run its appointed course and that the promise should not perish, and that the stock of Abraham should be preserved, from which the seed of blessing, Christ, would come in his own time, rightly were there “golden crowns [Col. 1299A] upon their heads.” For they were deservedly crowned with the victorious Word of God, since God deigned to make use of their battles and victories in order that, with Abraham’s line preserved, the word of promise might be fulfilled.

## CHAPTER VIII. Why the apostles, unlike the judges, were not permitted to use the sword.

The later judges or elders, namely the apostles, did not have the same reason or cause as those earlier men to use material weapons while fighting for the word or testimony of God. For in their time the One who was to be sent had come; nor could any other coming from Abraham’s flesh, in whom salvation should be found, now be hoped for. Why then should men fight with a material sword in order to protect the flesh?

Therefore he who had come, awaited from that flesh, when in his Passion [Col. 1299B] he said to them: “And I appoint unto you, as my Father has appointed unto me, a kingdom, that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom, and sit upon twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel,” etc. (Luke 22), and they replied to this, “Lord, behold, here are two swords,” immediately forbade them such swords; for he said: “It is enough.” Then, when one of them immediately struck with the sword, he said: “Suffer ye thus far” (ibid.). And to Peter who had struck, he said: “Put thy sword back into its place” (Matt. 26).

Surely by saying “It is enough,” or “Suffer ye thus far,” he indicates that the use of the sword before his coming, up to that point, had pleased him—as it was used by those first twelve judges now under discussion. But it would no longer please him that the latter judges should use it; indeed, that they should put it back and lay it aside entirely, content with the better sword which had now come, which had now been given: the Word of God itself. Therefore, just as the latter praiseworthily abandoned the material sword altogether because it was no longer necessary, so the former undoubtedly used it praiseworthily because at that time it was necessary, lest the good root perish before its fruit came.

Therefore there are rightly golden crowns upon the heads of all those elders: for, according to the differing requirements of the times, both the martial prowess of these men and the unarmed patience of those men served the Word of God.

## CHAPTER IX. [Col. 1299D] In how many dangers the judges of Israel were involved.

And since, as has been said, such was their intention in fighting, it must be considered that, in that good intention, they were worn down by great and grievous danger. For in almost every battle, as Scripture testifies, they were very few in number; and therefore some weakness of fear could not be absent, even with the support of faith or hope, however firm.

Hence one of them, Barak son of Abinoam, sings with Deborah: “You who freely offered your lives from Israel to danger, bless the Lord” (Judg. 5). And again: “You who of your own will offered yourselves to peril, bless the Lord” (ibid.). For they were not, nor are, strangers to endurance or suffering in that very use of the sword for which those judges were crowned [Col. 1300A] from whom, as has been said, Christ the incarnate Word took away the use of the sword because of the circumstances of the time.

It is therefore pleasing and greatly delightful that, just as both these and those—that is, all the twenty-four elders—are said in the same Apocalypse to have golden crowns, so they are also said to have harps and golden bowls: “When the Lamb had opened the book, the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fell down before the Lamb, each having harps and golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints” (Rev. 5). Is it not the case that, as was recalled from the hymn just cited, when they offered their lives to danger and voluntarily offered themselves to peril, they also offered necessary prayers in their distress and affliction?

Accordingly, just as their victories are recognized in the golden crowns, and the blessings with which they bless the Lord after their victories in the harps, so also may the prayers by which they entreated God in time of distress be reverently recognized in the golden bowls. For their distress was so great that, while they were fighting, not to bring them aid was a great crime, as the same hymn testifies in these words: “Curse the land of Meroz, said the angel of the Lord; curse its inhabitants, because they did not come to the help of the Lord, to the help of his mighty ones” (Judg. 4 [probably 5]).

## CHAPTER X. Why Eli does not belong to the number of the twelve judges.

Someone may perhaps say: Eli, the priest of the Lord, also judged Israel, as it is written: “For the man was old [Col. 1300C] and advanced in years, and he himself judged Israel forty years” (1 Sam. 4). Why then is he not counted among the other judges? Is he removed from the number so that you may make a pleasing comparison and count as many judges before David’s kingdom as there are other judges—namely, the apostles—once Christ, David’s son, reigns?

To this I say: we do not remove Eli already mentioned from the number merely in order that we may count only twelve judges; rather, because he is removed from the number, we have only twelve judges. Their deeds are the subject of the book itself that is called Judges, and we have set out their names above. How, or for what reason, is he removed from the number? Clearly, because of contempt for the Word of the Lord. For in his days nearly everyone had excessive liberty to spurn the law of the Lord.

It should be noted that after Samson died—he who judged Israel twenty years—the authority of sacred Scripture did not think it worthy to say, “After him Eli was,” or, “Eli succeeded him,” although, as has been said, he judged Israel forty years. Instead, amid the unhappy histories of those days, this complaint recurs: “In those days there was no king in Israel, but every man did what seemed right to himself” (Judg. 12 [probably 17:6; 21:25]). What does this say except that it charges the folly of such a priest and judge? It is the same as saying: He who judged Israel in those days, though according to title and person he was someone, according to reality and merit was no one.

At last the Word of the Lord was sent against him—the Word with whom, or through whom, all judges or elders, both ancient and new, deserved to sit crowned: “For I have foretold,” says the Lord, “that I would judge his house for ever because of its iniquity, since he knew that his sons were acting unworthily and did not correct them. Therefore I have sworn to the house of Eli that the iniquity of Eli’s house shall not be expiated with sacrifices and offerings for ever” (1 Sam. 3).

After these words, the outcome proves how far his merit differed from that of all the crowned judges or elders, who, as has been said, sit upon seats. The man who had fled from the battle line brought him this report: “Israel has fled before the Philistines, and a great slaughter has taken place among the people. Moreover, your two sons Hophni and Phinehas have been slain, [Col. 1301B] and the ark of God has been captured. And when he mentioned the ark of God, Eli fell backward from his seat beside the gate, and, his neck having been broken, he died” (1 Sam. 5 [probably 4]). Clearly, by falling backward from his seat and dying with his neck broken, he openly showed that he deserved neither a seat nor a golden crown among the other judges.

Accordingly Scripture at once adds, in pity: “For the man was old and advanced in years, and he himself judged Israel forty years” (ibid.). For he is to be lamented because, though he judged Israel for so many years, he performed nowhere anything memorable or worthy of a judge’s office.

## CHAPTER XI. What Isaiah means by “call his name, ‘Hasten to take the spoils; make speed to plunder.’”

What or how great are the mysteries of the eternal Judge, the Word of God Jesus Christ, signified in the deeds of those judges is not the purpose of the present inquiry. Nevertheless, let this be said briefly in praise of that same Word of God, that same Jesus Christ: his name was rightly called in Isaiah, “Hasten to take the spoils; make speed to plunder” (Isa. 8). For he who made those judges victorious, and conquered through them, is Christ Jesus, the Word of God.

For this reason he was called “Hasten to take the spoils; make speed to plunder”: before he became a boy and knew how to call his father and mother—that is, before he was born of a woman and, being subject to parents, experienced [Col. 1301D] our weakness—he took away the strength of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria. Damascus and Samaria had then joined forces against Judah, from which that child was to be born, and wished to wage war upon and destroy it.

Clearly it is a great hastening and a great speeding to take spoils from someone before being born from one’s mother, to plunder in war before being conceived in the womb. But did he do this beforehand only himself? Did he beforehand take only the spoils of Samaria and the strength only of Damascus? On the contrary, earlier still, in the judge Samson, he both plundered and took spoils, so that Samson might destroy a thousand men with the jawbone of an ass, the jawbone of a colt of asses, and at last kill more men in dying than he had previously killed while alive.

Likewise, in the other judges he himself took spoils, he himself plundered, and he defended Israel, not yet made a boy or a man, but from eternity God, the Word of God.

## CHAPTER XII. That the same Word of God conquered through David as he had previously conquered through the judges.

If this is rightly—indeed, because it is rightly—understood concerning the judges mentioned, how much more must the same be understood concerning the victories of King David, who after them sat upon the royal throne? For who achieved those victories by David’s hands other than the same son of David, not yet born from him, whose name, as has been said, is called “Hasten to take the spoils; make speed to plunder”?

He is David’s son, the Son of God, God the Word, the Word of God, who hastened greatly, made great speed, took spoils most swiftly, and plundered quickly. For before he knew how to call David his father and the Virgin of David’s line his mother, he struck down the Philistine Goliath by the hand of David himself, still a boy and not yet having any son. And through David he performed the other deeds which we admire to this day in David’s three mighty men, namely in his wisdom, humility, and strength, in which none of the rest could be his equal.

For David was “the wisest, sitting in the seat” (2 Sam. 23): this is the praise of his wisdom. “He is like the tenderest wood-worm” (ibid.): this is testimony to his humility. He killed eight hundred in one assault: this is proof of his strength. Who, I say, worked in David and through David’s mighty men of this kind [Col. 1302C] except God the Word, who was to become the son of David’s flesh? He was so present to David that David already spoke in his person, and in David himself foretold in his own words concerning himself things to come as though they were already past.

For example: “But I have been established as King by him over Zion, his holy mountain, proclaiming his command. The Lord said to me: You are my Son” (Ps. 2). Again: “They pierced my hands and my feet” (Ps. 21 [22]). There is no need to establish what is known to all: these are the proper utterances of him who, though he was in the form of God, was to humble himself so as to be crucified (Phil. 2)—that is, to have his hands and feet pierced. It is therefore no wonder that the Word himself already fought and triumphed through David’s hand, since he spoke in his own person through David’s mouth.

## CHAPTER XIII. Why David did not build the house of the Lord.

But here there arises the point that David himself said to Solomon his son, as Scripture relates in the book of Paralipomenon: “My son, it had been my intention to build a house for the name of the Lord my God; but the word of the Lord came to me, saying: You have shed much blood and fought many wars; you shall not build a house for my name, because so much blood has been shed before me” (1 Chron. 22).

Again, to the people he said: “Hear me, my brothers and my people: I planned to build a house in which the ark of the covenant of the Lord and the footstool of [Col. 1303A] our God’s feet might rest; I made all preparations for building it. But God said to me: You shall not build a house for my name, because you are a man of war and have shed blood” (1 Chron. 28).

Someone therefore says: If the battles David fought diminished his merit or dignity so that he did not deserve to build a house for the name of the Lord, how do you say that these same battles of David were battles of the Word of the Lord and therefore rightly celebrated in the Church’s praises? Or if the Church rightly celebrates his battles or victories as truly the Lord’s wars, why did the Lord say on their account: “You shall not be able to build a house for my name, because so much blood has been shed before me”?

To this I say: we do not ascribe to the Word of the Lord every war that David fought, but only those which he fought in the Word of the Lord, with zeal for the Lord, in defense of the Lord’s people. The first or greatest of these was his striking down of the Philistine who blasphemed the God of Israel and removed reproach from Israel. But the deeds he performed as a man of war in military exercise are not commended by God, except where the power of the Lord’s name plainly worked. Above all, he could reckon to himself Uriah the Hittite’s blood as sin and as a diminution of great merit (2 Sam. 10 [probably 11]).

Hence it should be noted that, before he had shed that man’s blood, the event reported in Scripture had indeed occurred: Nathan came to David, with the Lord saying, “You shall not build me a house for habitation” (2 Sam. 7). Yet the reason was not then given: “because you are a man of war and have shed blood,” as he spoke in this manner to Solomon his son or to the people, as we have said. Uriah’s blood had long since been shed, and especially then he could regard that as having diminished such merit in himself.

Therefore, if he had killed no one except from zeal for the Lord, with the Word of the Lord working with him, this must be known without doubt: the shedding of blood would not have hindered him from building the house of the Lord. For Moses too killed an Egyptian and nevertheless was found worthy to make or ordain the tabernacle of the Lord in the wilderness and the whole rite of the sanctuary. And Phinehas, in good zeal, pierced through together an Israelite man and a Moabite woman committing fornication; and on that account the Lord said: “Behold, I give him the peace of my covenant, and it shall be for him and for his seed a covenant [Col. 1303D] of everlasting priesthood” (Num. 25).

## CHAPTER XIV. That, when Saul was cast aside and David chosen, the saying was fulfilled: “The Lord makes poor and makes rich; he humbles and exalts.”

In this event the truth of the word of the Lord was first fulfilled magnificently, which shortly before Hannah had sung in prophetic speech: “The Lord makes poor and makes rich; he humbles and exalts; raising the needy from the dust and lifting the poor from the dungheap, that he may sit with princes and hold the throne of glory” (1 Sam. 2).

For then, when Saul was rich and exalted, while David was poor and humble, so great a reversal occurred that this poor and humble man became rich and exalted, was raised from the dust, and held the throne of glory. But Saul became so poor and humbled that, delivered to an evil spirit, he became powerless over himself.

These matters are such that anyone considering them may rightly say: “I will sing to you, O Lord, of mercy and judgment” (Ps. 100 [101]). For there was great mercy in David, great judgment in Saul, and in both a great example that men should obey the word of the Lord. For, if you weigh the matter rightly, Saul was rejected because of the sin of disobedience, Samuel saying: “Does the Lord desire holocausts or sacrifices, and not rather that the voice of the Lord should be obeyed? For obedience is better than sacrifices, and hearkening more than offering the fat of rams; because rebellion is like the sin of divination, and unwillingness to submit like the worship of idols. Therefore, because you have rejected the word of the Lord, [Col. 1304B] the Lord has rejected you from being king” (1 Sam. 15).

With this earlier testimony, that later saying of the same incarnate Word is true, when he says: “He who is not with me is against me, and he who does not gather with me scatters” (Matt. 12). That is to say: however much a person may offer, however many virtues he may seem to possess, if he despises the Word of the Lord, the Word of the Lord in turn despises him, and he becomes worthless and contemptible; even those things which seem to have been rightly done by him will be imputed to presumption and empty glory, not to reward.

## CHAPTER XV. How Saul and David despised the word of the Lord.

But how Scripture also rebukes David for contempt of the word of the Lord is clear from the Lord’s saying to him: “Why then have you despised the word of the Lord, to do evil in my sight? You have taken the wife of Uriah the Hittite and killed him with the sword of the sons of Ammon” (2 Sam. 12).

A careful distinction must be made, lest Saul appear equal to David in the magnitude of sin, in contempt for the word of the Lord. We say, therefore, that all sinners indeed—for example, adulterers or murderers—by the very fact that they commit adultery or kill, despise the word of the Lord. For written law and natural law say to every human being, without distinction of persons: “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery” (Exod. 20); and “What you do not wish done to yourself, do not do to another” (Tob. 4).

Thus David also in some way despised the word of the Lord, because he did not fail to know Scripture and the will of the Lord, or of the Word of the Lord, and nevertheless committed adultery and killed. Yet the manner of sin or transgression differs very greatly when the very thing which the law or word of the Lord commands generally to all is individually enjoined by the Lord, or by the Word of the Lord, upon a particular person; and then the Lord’s gracious condescension is also despised, and he is not obeyed.

Saul was guilty of this very grave crime, contempt. For in Exodus the Lord said to Moses: “Write this for a memorial in a book and deliver it to the ears of Joshua: for I will blot out the memory of Amalek from under heaven” (Exod. 17). And immediately it is added there: “Moses built an altar and called its name, ‘The Lord is my exaltation,’ saying: Because of the hand of the Lord alone, there shall be war of God against Amalek from generation to generation” (Exod. 7 [probably 17]).

In this way it had been said generally to all, that they should be enemies of Amalek and desire to blot out its memory for the Lord’s sake. But after many years the Lord wished Saul personally to be the minister of this same war of his, commanding him in his gracious condescension: “I have reviewed all that Amalek did to Israel, how he opposed him on the way when he came up from Egypt. Now therefore go and strike Amalek; or, go and kill the sinners of Amalek, and you shall fight against them until they are utterly destroyed” (1 Sam. 15).

He, now no longer small in his own eyes, made light of this gracious condescension of the Lord and despised this word of the Lord. David was by no means guilty of such contempt. Rather, in all things that were commands personally addressed to him in the word of the Lord, he fulfilled them vigorously; and where he was rebuked for transgression of the common law, he made humble confession, saying: “I have sinned” (2 Sam. 12), not with a double heart.

## CHAPTER XVI. That both confessed themselves to have sinned, and why this man’s confession was accepted while the other’s was rejected.

It is now fitting to compare their confessions: how Saul said “I have sinned” in the same words as David. The reasons that distinguish the same verbal confession in the two need not be sought far away. They are immediately found in their subsequent words.

When Samuel said to Saul: “I will not return with you, because you have rejected the word of the Lord, and the Lord has rejected you from being king over Israel. Moreover, the Victor in Israel will not spare and will not be moved by repentance; for he is not a man, that he should repent,” Saul said: “I have sinned; but now honor me before the elders of my people and before Israel, and return with me, that I may worship the Lord your God” (1 Sam. 15).

But David says: “Have mercy on me, O God, because against you alone have I sinned. Have mercy on me, that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged” (Ps. 50 [51]). Consider now how utterly opposed these motives are, since in saying “I have sinned,” one sought his own glory and the other the glory of God.

When Saul said “I have sinned,” and added, “but now honor me before the elders of my people”—by whom we should understand the men of his tribe, namely the sons of Benjamin—“and before Israel, and return with me that I may worship the Lord,” did he not seek his own glory? For a man of worldly spirit, wholly given to ambition, accustomed even to approach the worship of the Lord with pomp, grieved that, at such a time and amid the celebration of so great a triumph, so great a prophet should withdraw himself from his retinue. And therefore once and again he said, “I have sinned.”

Certainly, by a confession of such intention, the almighty word of the Lord does not permit itself to be overcome; hence Saul deserved to hear: “Moreover, the Victor in Israel will not spare and will not be moved by repentance.” But when David said: “Have mercy on me, that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged,” did he not, as has been said, seek the glory of God?

For, being humble in spirit, he joined concern for his own salvation with the greatest anxiety for God’s glory. He saw that glory in this: that God should be proclaimed faithful to his promise, true and just in the oath by which David testified that God had promised and sworn to him, saying: “The Lord swore to David a truth, and he will not disappoint him: Of the fruit of your womb I will set one upon your throne” (Ps. 131 [132]).

Anxious, therefore, lest God, overcome by David’s iniquity, should revoke what he had promised and make his oath void, David—most desirous of God’s glory—said: “That you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged.” That is, that you may remain, O God, faithful; that your word made to me may not be in it “yes and no,” but may be in it “yes”; and that you may not be judged to have acted out of fickleness or changeableness. And so, concerning this promise or oath made to me as concerning the others, every sex and every age may truly say—and I with them—“For however many promises of God there are, in him is ‘yes.’ Therefore also through him is the Amen to God for our glory.”

Accordingly, when he said, “I have sinned against the Lord,” he immediately deserved to hear this in the word of the Lord: “The Lord also has taken away your sin. You shall not die” (2 Sam. 12).

## CHAPTER XVII. David was heard because he asked according to God’s will.

[Col. 1306C] David, therefore, was heard—and rightly—because he asked according to the will of God, saying: “That you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged” (Ps. 50 [51]). “This,” says John, “is the confidence that we have toward him: that if we ask anything according to his will, he hears us” (1 John 5).

For it was God’s will that his word be fulfilled, that the word of promise first made to Abraham and then made to David be brought to completion. For God, willing and providing the salvation of the world, had determined that his Word should become incarnate from their seed. But if David’s iniquity had rendered void the faithfulness of the Promiser, so that God, repenting of the promise, changed his decree and did not fulfill what he had promised, could we today proclaim so confidently with the Apostle: “But God is true, every human being a liar, as it is written: That you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged” (Rom. 3)?

Indeed, what would now have become of the human race if God were angry every day; if his gifts and calling were not without repentance; if, as soon as anyone’s iniquity abounded, his grace withdrew itself? God’s will, therefore, was that the purpose or word of his promise should be brought to victory; that, though every human being should be found a liar before him, he should nevertheless remain true. And because David asked according to this will, as has been said, he deserved to be heard, as one of God’s best helpers—one who sought God’s glory, loved God’s righteousness, and desired God’s purpose.

## CHAPTER XVIII. That God would not have appeared justified in his words unless David had received mercy.

What complaint, do you think, would have been available not only to David but to all who know how to judge concerning God’s words, unless God had had mercy upon him when he repented, so as to preserve inviolate the faithfulness of his promise? Observe what is said. God had to take a different precaution concerning the words spoken to David in promising than concerning those words spoken to many others. Why? Because when speaking with many others, he promised them his good things conditionally, as to Saul and to the people who demanded him as their king:

“If,” he says, “you fear the Lord and serve him, and hear his voice, and do not provoke the mouth of the Lord, you and the king who rules over you will follow the Lord your God. But if you persist in wickedness, both you and your king shall perish together” (1 Sam. 12).

Likewise to Solomon: “If you walk,” he says, “in my ways and keep my precepts and commandments, as your father walked, I will make your days long” (1 Kgs. 3).

But to David, as to Abraham, he spoke without conditions: “Of the fruit,” he says, “of your womb I will set one upon your throne” (Ps. 131 [132]). He did not say to Abraham, “If you keep my ways, I will bring upon you all that I have spoken to you.” Rather, he said: “Can I hide from Abraham what I am about to do, since he is to become a great nation and all nations of the earth are to be blessed in him? For I know that he will command his children and his household after him to keep the way of the Lord and to do righteousness and judgment, so that the Lord may bring upon Abraham all that he has spoken to him” (Gen. 18).

Likewise concerning Isaac, Jacob, and Moses, to whom the Lord God said: “I will show you all good things, and I will call upon the name of the Lord before you” (Exod. 33).

It must, I say, be carefully observed that these are not conditional utterances or promises. Therefore God, wishing to be justified in his words and prevail when judged, had to remember his spontaneous promise, so that he himself might be true, however much the iniquity of the seed to whom he had promised and sworn should abound. Knowing this, the legal experts Moses and David held God to it: the former by saying, “Remember Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, to whom you swore” (Exod. 32); the latter by saying, “Have mercy on me, that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged” (Ps. 50 [51]).

## CHAPTER XIX. That the promises of the law were made with a condition, but the promises to Abraham and David without condition.

To this sense belongs the Apostle’s statement to the Romans: “For the promise to Abraham or to his seed, that he should be heir of the world, was not through the law, but through the righteousness of faith. For if those who belong to the law are heirs, faith has been emptied and the promise abolished; for the law works wrath; for where there is no law, neither is there transgression. Therefore it is of faith, that according to grace the promise may be firm to all Abraham’s seed, not only to the one who is of the law, but also to the one who is of Abraham’s faith, who is the father of us all, as it is written: ‘I have made you the father of many nations before God, whom you believed’” (Rom. 4).

In saying these things, he truly justifies God in his words, so that among those to whom he gave the law, or who are of the law, God is not held as though a debtor and prevails when judged. Yet among those who are of Abraham’s faith, it cannot be denied that he was a debtor.

For the whole law is conditional, and it began to be given under condition on Mount Sinai, in the third month after the children of Israel departed from the land of Egypt. For, after first saying: [Col. 1308B] “You yourselves have seen what I did to the Egyptians, how I bore you upon eagles’ wings” (Exod. 19), he immediately begins, intending to give commands and law: “If, therefore, you hear my voice and keep my covenant, you shall be my special possession above all peoples. For all the earth is mine, and you shall be to me a priestly kingdom and a holy nation.”

Under this tenor of condition the whole law proceeds: “If,” he says, “after you have heard these judgments, you keep them and do them, the Lord your God will keep for you the covenant and mercy that he swore to your fathers” (Deut. 6), and the rest.

Therefore, when so great a multitude of those who are of the law, or who wish to be, are excluded from being the Lord’s special possession according to his stated pledge, should God be called to judgment on this account? Let him indeed be judged, since he himself stands ready, saying in Isaiah: “Who is there to be judged with me? Let him come.” Let him be judged, I say—but he immediately prevails, because they did not keep what was laid down as a condition: they did not hear his voice or keep his covenant. Rather, “all have turned aside; together they have become useless; there is none who does good, not even one” (Ps. 52 [53]).

And thus the law works wrath, while in judgment it recites what God laid down as a condition. Accordingly, better is the promise made without condition and the reiterated promise confirmed with an oath. For God did not say to Abraham: “If you do this or that, if you walk in this or that manner, if you keep these or those commandments of mine, all nations shall be blessed in your seed.” Instead, without any condition, as has been said, and entirely silent about future observances, he said: “By myself I have sworn: because you have done this thing and have not spared your only son, I will bless you, and all nations of the earth shall be blessed in your seed, because you have obeyed my voice” (Gen. 22).

Hence the Apostle says to the Romans: “Where there is no law, neither is there transgression” (Rom. 4). For how, on account of an abundance of iniquity, could the righteousness of God withdraw from Abraham himself or from his descendants, as from transgressors, what he had promised in this manner? There was no law there—that is, no condition concerning anyone’s future observance of a commandment—and therefore in any sin no transgression could be named by which God, because he is true, might be permitted to alter the word of his promise (John 3 [citation uncertain in the source]).

## CHAPTER XX. What the Apostle means when he says: “For if those who are of the law are heirs, faith has been emptied and the promise abolished.”

It is also worth considering how wisely and truthfully the Apostle said in the passage mentioned: “For if those who are of the law are heirs, faith has been emptied and the promise abolished” (Rom. 4). That is to say: if you think that it came about through the merit of the law subsequently received that all nations should be blessed in the seed of Abraham—which is Christ—when the promise had preceded the giving of the law by four hundred and thirty years, [Col. 1309B] do you not make God changeable and alterer of his promise? For it is a great changeability, a profound alteration, to offer after so many years, as the reward for future service, what he had previously promised freely with an oath—especially since, in promising thus, he had already given it. And what faithful human being could make a reward for future service out of what he had long before freely given to his friend? How much more, then, did God neither act thus, nor was it fitting that God should act thus. For this would be to empty faith and abolish the promise, if, after so many years, when the fathers had died, he should speak thus to their children, saying: “If therefore you hear my voice and keep my covenant,” I will fulfil my promises, so that in Abraham’s seed all nations may be blessed. This seed, of course, is uniquely Christ.

It would not be fitting, would not be appropriate—indeed, would be unbecoming for the truthful God, who, as another Scripture testifies, speaks once and does not repeat or alter the same thing a second time, but says one thing and adds another: “If you hear my voice and keep my covenant, you shall be my special possession among all peoples” (Exod. 19); I will give you a land flowing with milk and honey; I will keep for you my covenant and the mercy which I swore to your fathers. Even if I do not keep it for you when you transgress, nevertheless I shall keep it for your fathers, to whom I swore, and for all nations or peoples who are or shall be of their faith; for I promised the blessing in his seed not to you alone, but to all nations. The same holds in David’s case.

[Col. 1309D] Likewise, it would be to empty faith and abolish the promise if he were to destroy by the law, on account of sins that crept in, what he had promised and sworn by grace. But because he did not do this, and remained faithful in all his words: “Once,” he says, “have I sworn by my holiness: if I lie to David, his seed shall remain for ever” (Ps. 88). Therefore he is justified in his words and prevails when he is judged, because he cannot be accused of changeability.

## Chapter XXI. What the Apostle means in saying that “the righteousness of God is revealed in the Gospel from faith unto faith,” and what that righteousness is.

What other righteousness of God do we suppose is revealed in the Gospel, as the Apostle says: “For in it the righteousness of God is revealed from faith unto faith, as it is written: But the righteous shall live by faith” (Rom. 1)? The righteousness of God is the incarnation of the Son of God, who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh. The incarnation, I say, or coming of Jesus Christ, son of David and son of Abraham: this righteousness is revealed in the Gospel.

Is this righteousness of God a small matter? It is not small, but truly great and highly praiseworthy; for through that incarnation, in his being made from David’s seed, God is justified in his words, fulfilling what he promised and keeping what he swore, as the truthful and faithful God. Observe this very beautiful definition of this righteousness: “Righteousness,” he says, “from faith unto faith.” From whose faith, unless that of him who promised and swore? Unto whose faith, unless that of the one who believed the promiser and trusted the one swearing—namely Abraham or David?

[Col. 1310B] This righteousness is one thing; that of those Israelites who are not true Israelites is another. For, seeking to establish their own righteousness, they are not subject to this righteousness. What then is their righteousness? Surely a righteousness not from faith unto faith, but, as it were, from works unto works: as though Abraham had been justified by works, though Scripture says, “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Rom. 4; Gen. 15); and as though they themselves could be justified by works, though Scripture likewise says, “No living person shall be justified in your sight” (Ps. 142).

Therefore the righteousness of God which is revealed in the Gospel is well defined by the phrase, “Righteousness from faith unto faith,” because the incarnation of God’s Son and the blessing of all nations in this seed proceed from the faithfulness of God, of whom it is written: “God is faithful in all his words” (Ps. 144). Neither David’s sins nor those of the others offended or diverted him so that he should fail, in great faithfulness, to fulfil what he had promised in great grace. And this righteousness tends unto faith, because it is possible for someone to be justified before him not through works but through faith, Scripture saying: “If you mark iniquities, O Lord, O Lord, who shall endure?” (Ps. 129).

[Col. 1310D] Therefore it is written thus: “The righteous lives by faith” (Rom. 1). For every righteous person lives through God alone, who alone is holy in all his works; the righteous person has this very fact—that he lives as righteous by faith—not from works but from faith. For if anyone wishes rightly to judge the righteousness of works, not outwardly, before the eye, but in the secret of his conscience, he will never reject as inapplicable to himself what someone said: “All our righteousness is like the cloth of a menstruating woman” (Isa. 64).

## Chapter XXII. The Word of God won the palm of truth both in Saul and in David.

Therefore, because it is from faith unto faith, the promise to David himself is firm; and behold, he now lives—and not merely lives, but remains in more abundant grace—as patriarch, king, and prophet. He is patriarch because, after Abraham, a promise was specifically made to him, that he should be the father of the blessed seed, which is Christ, who is not ashamed to be called son of David, although he himself is David’s Lord: son according to the flesh, Lord according to divinity. He is also king, not merely in any manner whatever, but according to God’s election—and, what is greater and more magnificent, according to God’s heart.

[Col. 1311A] “The Lord has sought for himself,” Samuel says to Saul, “a man according to his own heart; and the Lord has commanded him to be leader over his people, because you have not kept what the Lord commanded” (1 Sam. 13). Paul too recalls this in the Acts of the Apostles: “And after removing Saul, he raised up David as their king; and bearing witness concerning him, he said: I have found David son of Jesse, a man according to my heart, who will do all my wills” (Acts 13).

This statement sharply distinguishes David’s election from Saul’s election. For the Lord too is said to have chosen Saul, when Samuel said to all the people, as Saul stood among them, taller than all the people from the shoulder upward: “Surely you see the man whom the Lord has chosen, for there is none like him among all the people” (1 Sam. 10). Thus the Lord indeed chose him, but not according to his own heart; rather, according to the empty and proud heart of the people, and according to his wrath. For Saul was especially, or among the foremost, an occasion for the rebuke which Hosea directs at Israel: “Where is your king, that he may now save you in all your cities? And your judges, of whom you said: Give me a king and a ruler? I will give you a king in my wrath and take him away in my indignation” (Hos. 13).

[Col. 1311C] Indeed, he gave Saul in such wrath that he said to Samuel: “They have not rejected you, but me, lest I should reign over them” (1 Sam. 13), and so forth. Likewise he removed him in such indignation that he became possessed, as Scripture says: “But the Spirit of the Lord departed from Saul, and an evil spirit from the Lord tormented him” (1 Sam. 16).

I have recalled these things now so that, even in Saul’s case, the Word of the Lord may not seem to have fallen from its purpose or to have lost the palm of righteousness by choosing one who was unworthy of election. David himself was a prophet—not merely any prophet, but so peculiarly and intimately related to the Word of God that the person of that same Word spoke, through David’s mouth, the mysteries of his future incarnation, passion, resurrection, and ascension more clearly and more resonantly than through the mouth of any of the others, with the sweetness of harmonious melody. Did he lack even this grace after his fall? Certainly not. For “I will teach,” he says, “the wicked your ways” (Ps. 50)—that is, by the same prophetic grace as before.

## Chapter XXIII. How the saying of Wisdom, “It is better for two to be together than for one,” is shown to be true in those two men.

It is now apparent in these men how truthfully Wisdom said: “It is better for two to be together than for one; for they have benefit from their partnership. If one falls, he will be supported by the other. Woe to one alone, because when he falls he has no one to lift him up. And if two sleep together, they will keep one another warm; but how will one be warmed? And if anyone prevails against one, two withstand him” (Eccl. 4).

In these men, I say—in Saul and David—it is apparent how true and beautiful these words are. For what is it to be one, or alone, except to have cast away the word of the Lord? And what is it for two to be together except to have the word of the Lord as a companion on the journey of this life, or in the bedchamber of one’s conscience? This is far better. For, he says, “Woe to one alone, because when he falls he has no one to lift him up.”

[Col. 1312A] Woe, then, to Saul, who when he fell was alone, having no one to lift him up—namely, the word of the Lord; for he had cast it away. Hence it was said to him: “I will not return with you, because you have rejected the word of the Lord, and the Lord has rejected you from being king over Israel” (1 Sam. 15). David, on the other hand, had the word of the Lord as companion in the house of his breast, in the bosom of faith. Thus there were two: David himself and the word of the Lord. One fell and was supported by the other. What could be truer?

David fell, and was supported by the word of the Lord, which does not know how to fall. Firmly leaning upon it, he said to God: “Have mercy on me, that you may be justified in your words” (Ps. 50). He was raised up; and the two slept together, and to the end of David’s life they kept one another warm. For the word of the Lord warmed David by meditation upon itself, both nightly and daily, as he says: “At night I meditated with my heart” (Ps. 76); and again: “My meditation is all the day” (Ps. 118). This was David’s being warmed—that is, being delighted. For he says: “I remembered God and was delighted” (Ps. 76).

[Col. 1312C] The word itself was warmed—that is, delighted—by resting in David’s most sweet humility, when he said to God: “Remember your word to your servant” (Ps. 118); and again: “Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but give glory to your name” (Ps. 113). As though neglecting himself, he was concerned only for the word of God, the word of promise which he possessed, lest it be consigned to oblivion. He knew that, if God guarded and glorified this word, he himself would likewise be guarded and become a sharer in glory, in accordance with what is there said: “They have benefit from their partnership” (Eccl. 4).

Someone had prevailed against one, but two withstood him. David was one at the time when, rising from his bed after midday and seeing another man’s wife, he fell into desire for her (2 Sam. 11). He was one because his mind had withdrawn from its customary meditation on the word of God. Thus the one whom Nathan calls “the traveller”—that is, the devil, alien from the city and kingdom of God—prevailed against him. But the two of whom we have spoken withstood him, and one was supported by the other; for David was raised up by the aid of God’s word, so that he continued in manifold grace: prophet, as already said, king, and patriarch.

## Chapter XXIV. Solomon indeed had the word of God, but did not rest with it so as to be warmed; and therefore he fell and was not raised up.

But Solomon the king, David’s son, through whom Wisdom had spoken in this manner, fell much more grievously. For zeal for idolatry is much more grievous than the crime of adultery or homicide. He loved many foreign women, and through them his heart was so corrupted that he followed foreign gods; he worshipped Astarte, goddess of the Sidonians, Chemosh, god of the Moabites, and Molech, god of the Ammonites (1 Kgs. 11).

What then shall we say? Were not the two together in the manner described above? It is plain and cannot be denied that the word of the Lord was with him, and that it manifested itself from his breast and mouth as from its temple, in words and deeds. How then did he fall as though he were alone and had no one to lift him up? To this I say: the two were indeed there, but he did not have peaceful sleep, so that they might sleep together and keep one another warm. Another was present between them, always clamorous, restless, and hostile: love of this present age, which is far at variance with the word of God.

[Col. 1313B] Hidden in a corner, it did not permit those two to be well together, or to keep each other warm in peaceful sleep. That such love of the world was familiar there and had long dwelt in the abode of Solomon’s heart is sufficiently suggested by the Lord’s angry words concerning Solomon’s turning away: “Because you have had this with you, and have not kept my covenant” (1 Kgs. 11), and so forth. By saying, “You have had this with you,” he sufficiently indicates that no sudden temptation had come upon him, but that his faulty inclination had been an inveterate disease.

This may also be plainly observed in the fact that, when at the beginning the Lord appeared to him with great condescension and said, “Ask what you wish me to give you” (1 Kgs. 3), Solomon could, by one request, have obtained the eternity of heavenly glory, which is supreme blessedness. Yet, delighted with temporal glory and wishing to be accounted glorious among men, he asked for a slight or mediocre good: “You will give,” he said, “to your servant a teachable heart, so that he may judge your people and discern between good and evil” (ibid.). What he asked was indeed good, and better than if he had asked for many days or some such thing that is good indeed but small and very lowly. And this request pleased the Lord more than if he had asked for anything of that kind—for many days, riches, or the lives of his enemies. But why did he not say, as his father David had said: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I shall seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life” (Ps. 26)? Namely, because his heart was not perfect with the Lord his God, as Scripture testifies, like the heart of David his father.

## Chapter XXV. God’s purpose was not turned aside by the sins of David’s sons, because he had sworn to David.

Did the word of God, then, fall even in this case, and could what God had purposed be turned aside? Certainly not. Rather, it gains the palm of righteousness still more splendidly, as Scripture determines in these words: “Nevertheless,” says the Lord, “I will not do it in your days, for the sake of David your father; I will tear it from the hand of your son. Yet I will not take away the whole kingdom, but will give one tribe to your son for the sake of David my servant and Jerusalem, which I have chosen” (1 Kgs. 11).

[Col. 1314A] Again, to Jeroboam: “I will not,” he says, “take the whole kingdom from Solomon’s hand, but I will make him ruler all the days of your life, for the sake of David my servant whom I chose. But I will take the kingdom from the hand of his son and give you ten tribes. And I will give one tribe to his son, so that a lamp may remain for David my servant before me all the days in Jerusalem, the city which I chose for my name to be there” (ibid.).

When almighty God says these things, he is assuredly bound by the strength of his word, mindful of his promise, in order that he may be truthful and faithful, according to the reason cited above, which David himself set forth: “That you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged” (Ps. 50). Thus the word of God retains the palm of truth even in Solomon’s fall. But as for David himself, how great is his praise, how great the proclamation of his merit, since God declares that for David’s sake he preserves the city of Jerusalem and the tribe of Judah in order to fulfil the promise of truth—the incarnation of that same Word of God from David’s seed.

For he speaks as though he were a man deeply offended, who, though he has grounds for anger and for withholding what was hoped for, is nevertheless bound as a debtor to give, however unwillingly, because he promised, because he swore. But God was not unwilling to fulfil what he had freely promised and confirmed by oath. To what end, then, does he so often remember David amid the transgressions of David’s descendants and people, who so often provoked God to anger, saying that he spares them for David’s sake and does not wish wholly to destroy them? Clearly, so that the abundance of his grace may become ever more manifest where iniquity abounds and there is no righteousness from works. But this has already been discussed more fully above.

## Chapter XXVI. Why God, who cannot lie even in what he says without an oath, had to and wished to swear.

But why did God have to swear, or what usefulness did he envisage in his oath—he whom it is impossible to lie, even in whatever he says without the addition of an oath? The Apostle expresses it more plainly in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “Because,” he says, “he had no one greater by whom to swear, he swore by himself” (Heb. 6). For human beings swear by one greater than themselves, and an oath is the end of all their disputes for confirmation. “In this, God, wishing more abundantly to show the heirs of the promise the immovability of his purpose, interposed an oath, so that through two immutable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we may have the strongest consolation.”

This is as though he said: God requires faith from everyone before all else, “and without faith it is impossible to please him” (Heb. 11). Yet human beings are hard and slow of heart to believe. The greater part consists of unbelievers, who do not believe at all. And although this is no great surprise in others—though it is a condemnable evil—it is all the more astonishing in those who ought to have been heirs of the promise, whose fathers received the promise and had it confirmed by oath, that they are or were so unbelieving that it is especially of them that Scripture says: “A perverse and provoking generation, a generation that did not set its heart aright, and whose spirit was not faithful to God” (Ps. 77).

[Col. 1315A] Moreover, God knew that even those who would at some time believe would be difficult to bring to faith, as indeed they were—those very men whom the Lord himself rebuked so severely: “O foolish and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken” (Luke 24). Therefore, because an oath is the end of all human controversy for confirmation, he interposed an oath, so that they might thereby put an end to unbelief, so that people might thereby be alert to hear, and perceive God’s purpose to be unchangeable.

Accordingly, when he himself says: “Let your word be yes, yes; no, no; what is more than these is from evil” (Matt. 5), it is rightly understood as referring to the evil of the one whose unbelief or mistrust compels another to swear. By understanding his words, “is from evil,” in this way, we humbly blame our own slowness to believe even in God’s oath—which is certainly evil—because, although it is impossible for God to lie even when he does not swear, few in comparison with unbelievers believed him when he swore by himself.

## Chapter XXVII. The principal reasons why Abraham and David were worthy of the word of promise reaffirmed with an oath.

To whom, or with whom, did he swear in the promise concerning the seed, which is Christ? There are two great patriarchs, Abraham and David, and he swore by great grace. First of all, we must know that he acted more out of his grace than out of their merits. Nevertheless, as that same grace went before them, they were in some manner prepared for this dignity, so that God should deign to bind himself to them by oath.

[Col. 1316A] This is clearer in Abraham’s case: by faith he offered Isaac when he was tested, offering his only-begotten son, he who had received the promises; and to him it had been said: “In Isaac shall seed be called to you” (Gen. 22), “considering that God is able even to raise from the dead” (Heb. 11). For this reason, by righteous grace, God reaffirmed with an oath what he had long before promised without an oath: that all nations would be blessed in Abraham’s seed—the seed being Christ.

But regarding David, we must inquire for what particular virtue God judged him especially worthy that he should swear to him, as David himself testifies and as has already been mentioned above. Scripture does not report this as plainly concerning David as it does concerning Abraham: it does not say that God told him, “I have sworn by myself, because you did this or that thing: I will place one from the fruit of your womb upon your throne” (Gen. 22). But reason teaches that sparing an enemy for God’s sake is a merit not much less than not sparing one’s only-begotten son for God’s sake.

David did this to his most hostile enemy, who sought his life: to the enemy king, whose kingdom he knew without doubt that he himself would receive. He spared him when he sought David’s life—something unheard of until then, as Saul himself testifies, wondering and saying to him: “For who, when he finds his enemy, lets him go safely on his way?” (1 Sam. 24). We judge that it was chiefly on this account that God swore to him that his seed or flesh would be assumed into the Son of God. For this above all makes people children of God, as the Lord himself testifies when he says: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you, that you may be children of your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5).

[Col. 1316C] David loved his enemy and did him good, not only by sparing him when he could have killed him, but also by mourning him after he had been killed. And, as already said, it was especially for such a reason that he was found worthy of such an oath from God.

# Book Five

[Col. 1315]

## Chapter I. How the calf—that is, the dragon’s second head—was set up anew under Jeroboam.

Meanwhile, that great dragon, the ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan, seeing the word of promise prosper—now confirmed after Abraham by an oath a second time in David—was consumed by a great blaze of raging envy, and, stirred by the great heat of his poison, raged wholly within himself. But what could he do? Long since stripped of the head which he had first raised up, namely the kingdom of Egypt, when Pharaoh was drowned in the sea with his chariots and horsemen [Col. 1316D] (Exod. 12), he had no other head to raise—that is, no other kingdom through whose power he could rage for the destruction of the people from which the aforesaid word of promise was to be fulfilled. Indeed, the Word itself, which was to become David’s flesh, already reigned in David the father; and David, its father, holding the sceptre of rule, mighty and warlike, was engaged in battles and glorified by victories. Therefore that psalmist played the harp more confidently, adorning the Word of God with musical sounds.

The dragon therefore burned with the poison of envy, by which he nearly set all David’s own house ablaze: David himself fell at once into the crimes of adultery and homicide, while one of his sons, Absalom, bloody from killing his brother, took up arms against his own father, drove him from the kingdom, and sought his life in order to reign in his place. If this had been accomplished, the serpent would indeed then have possessed that head through which he hoped to attack the Word of God and abolish its remembrance. But it did not happen so. Absalom died, David completed his life in peace, and his wise son Solomon succeeded him, reigned in peace, and built for the name of the Lord a house of peace.

At last Solomon’s sin assisted the malignant design of the same serpent, so that the kingdom of Israel was torn away from the house of David. Jeroboam son of Nebat was received as ruler; and he immediately made two golden calves and said: “Behold your gods, Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt” (1 Kgs. 12). There the dragon raised up his second head, and the face upon that head was that of a horned calf; and the devil began to be a horn-goring beast, acting and compelling through royal power so that images of calves should be worshipped as God.

## Chapter II. Although they also served and worshipped Baal, the calf was nevertheless the head of idolatry.

How greatly do you think that calf—or rather, the devil in the calf—raged madly against the word of the Lord, brandishing its horns? Elijah says: “Lord, they have destroyed your altars and killed your prophets with the sword; and I alone am left, and they seek my life” (2 Kgs. 19). Israel already worshipped Baal too, through Jezebel’s agency. And Scripture adds: “Ahab provoked the Lord in his deeds,” namely because he served Baal and worshipped him.

[Col. 1317C] Yet the head of all idolatry in Israel was the worship of the calves. Baal and the other monstrous objects of demonic worship had been adopted from other nations, but the kings of Israel devised the worship of the calf for themselves, and all persisted in that crime. Thus in Hosea, after the Lord had said concerning those kings and rulers, “How long will they be unable to be cleansed?”, he immediately adds this reason: “For it is from Israel itself; a craftsman made it, and it is not God”—understanding the calf, concerning which he had previously said: “Your calf, Samaria, has been cast away” (Hos. 8).

The meaning is this: the kings and rulers of Israel cannot be cleansed or recalled from the worship of the calf, because they sin in it not through ignorance but through wickedness. They did not adopt its worship because foreign nations deceived them; they devised it themselves. Thus it is fittingly said: “A craftsman”—namely Jeroboam—“made it,” as Scripture says: “Jeroboam said in his heart: Now the kingdom will return to the house of David if this people goes up to offer sacrifices in the house of the Lord in Jerusalem; and, having devised a plan, he made two golden calves” (1 Kgs. 12). “Therefore a craftsman made it,” because Jeroboam made it after devising a plan.

Thus, although Baal and many other monstrous forms of idolatry existed in Israel, I rightly call that calf the head of idolatry, because Israel received the other monstrosities from foreign nations and could sometimes be restrained from worshipping them. Jehu even destroyed Baal from Israel, as already said; but Israel devised the calves for itself, and neither Jehu nor any king of Israel ever departed from their worship.

## Chapter III. Although this head appeared gentle, it was nevertheless as destructive to God’s people as the rest.

What face, among all the heads or faces of the oft-mentioned adversary, could seem so gentle as this face of a calf? [Col. 1318A] The other faces are fierce: the face of the dragon, the lion’s face, the bear’s face, the leopard’s face, and the face of a dreadful and powerful beast with iron teeth, devouring and crushing, and trampling the rest beneath its feet. By these, as we have already said, are signified the kingdoms which persecuted the Word of promise: the kingdom of the Egyptians, the kingdom of the Babylonians, the kingdom of the Persians and Medes, the kingdom of the Greeks, and the kingdom of the Romans.

The face of this calf is gentle, and by it, as stated, is denoted the kingdom of Israel, in which Jeroboam made golden calves. Is the kingdom of Israel then, just as this face is gentler than those faces, gentler in its conduct and less harmful than those kingdoms? On the contrary: the more domestic it was, the greater the damage it caused and the more it overthrew the household.

For what, or how much, had been done when the prophets of the Lord had been killed, and all the people followed the command of Jezebel and Ahab, so that Elijah thought himself left alone—even though seven thousand men remained whose knees had not bent to Baal? Jehu indeed destroyed Baal from Israel, as already said; but the worship of the calf held the people with their kings irrevocably captive in mind, and accomplished so much that Israel, removed from its own land, was also made captive in body, in an unbreakable captivity. The Lord foretold this in Hosea: “For I will no longer have mercy upon the house of Israel, but I will utterly forget them; and I will have mercy upon the house of Judah” (Hos. 1). That is: the ten tribes would remain in perpetual captivity under the Assyrians, while I shall bring the tribe of Judah back from Babylonian captivity after seventy years.

[Col. 1318C] The other kingdoms struck Israel in body; the kingdom of Israel killed itself in soul, killing the prophets of the Lord on account of the calves, which none of Israel’s kings was willing to abandon. It also possessed, together with royal force, a certain hypocrisy. In what respect? Namely, because it retained and commemorated God’s benefits with its mouth. It sinned most wickedly by ascribing those benefits to the mute and lifeless images of calves, saying: “Behold your gods, Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.” “And he celebrated a solemn day on the fifteenth day of the eighth month, in imitation of the feast which was celebrated in Judah” (1 Kgs. 12).

## Chapter IV. What was the first battle of the Word of God against this head?

The more wicked the enemy, then, the greater and more prompt had to be the assistance of the Word of God; and so it came about. For then the word of the Lord caused more numerous and more frequent trumpets of its battle to be heard: namely, prophets, whom it sent, adding to their voices power in signs and wonders.

The beginning of the duel, and the first encounter between the word of the Lord and this head—that is, the Israelite kingdom—was as follows. As Jeroboam went up to the altar to burn incense, behold, a man of God came from Judah in the word of the Lord and cried out against the altar: “Altar, altar, thus says the Lord: Behold, a son shall be born to the house of David, named Josiah, and he shall sacrifice upon you the priests of the high places.” And thereafter: “This shall be the sign that the Lord has spoken: behold, the altar shall be split apart, and the ashes which are upon it shall be poured out.”

[Col. 1319A] But when Jeroboam stretched out his hand from the altar and said, “Seize him,” his hand withered, and he could not draw it back to himself. The altar also was split and the ashes were poured out from it, according to the sign which the man of God had foretold in the word of the Lord (1 Kgs. 13).
