After this, Ahijah the Shilonite was still living—the one who had told Jeroboam that he would reign over Israel. As the Lord spoke within him, he said: “I am sent to Jeroboam with a harsh message: those of Jeroboam who die in the city the dogs shall eat, and those who die in the field the birds of heaven shall devour, because the Lord has spoken,” and so forth. After him came Jehu son of Hanani, to whom the word came against Baasha, who had struck down Nadab, the son of that same Jeroboam, in accordance with the same judgment: “Whoever of Baasha dies in the city, dogs shall eat; and whoever of his dies in the countryside, the birds of heaven shall eat” (1 Kgs. 10 [citation as printed]).

After him Elijah raised the banner of the Word of God and triumphed in a fiery chariot; then Elisha, and with them many sons of the prophets, of whom Obadiah, servant of the Lord, fed one hundred men in caves when Jezebel was killing the prophets of the Lord. Then came also those whose own books date from that time. If you consider their times according to the narratives and the titles prefixed to the books, you plainly perceive that at no time under any king did the word of the Lord neglect its purpose; the devil’s falsehood in idols was always refuted by God’s truth in the prophets.

## Chapter V. That Jehu was the first to die for testimony to the Word of God.

[Col. 1319D] Who first shed his blood in that conflict and died for testimony to the word of God is less widely known from the writings of venerable teachers than an attentive observer of such a battle would desire, although Scripture does not pass over his name in silence. This was Jehu son of Hanani, whom Scripture mentions as already said: “And the word of the Lord came against Baasha, saying: Since I exalted you from the dust” (1 Kgs. 16), and so forth. It then adds: “When the word of the Lord came by the hand of Jehu son of Hanani the prophet against Baasha and against his house, and against all the evil that he had done before the Lord, provoking him by the works of his hands, so as to become like the house of Jeroboam, for this reason he killed him”—that is, Jehu son of Hanani the prophet (ibid.).

Sacred Scripture splendidly named him, repeating a third time, “he killed him”—that is, Jehu son of Hanani the prophet. And it should be known that before him, from the beginning of the promise, Scripture records no one by name as having been killed for the word of the Lord. An attentive observer of the conflict of the Word of God would therefore wish that, just as after Abel there is “Zechariah son of Barachiah, whom they killed between the temple and the altar” (Matt. 23), this man too were widely known by his own name. For his merit is truly not small: from his blood that great dragon first received the ground for deserving to be and to be called red.

The course of our argument has now made him better known to us, because where there is discourse or work concerning the victory of the Word of God, one ought not to pass over the man who is first read to have shed blood in the battle of the Word of God while advancing against the ancient enemy, sent as the faithful envoy of the Word of God.

## Chapter VI. That it is not without mystery that the prophet was killed on the road by a lion.

Since this man is the first of those who spent their own blood, in the office of prophecy, for the word of God, consider now how beautiful and fitting a mystery preceded this, a mystery pertaining to the glory of that same Word. The man of God who came from Judah, at the word of the Lord, to Bethel—as stated above—while Jeroboam stood upon the altar, said: “Altar, altar, behold, a son shall be born to the house of David, Josiah by name, and he shall sacrifice upon you the priests of the high places” (3 Kings 13 [1 Kings 13]). That man, I say, had received a command through the word of the Lord, which directed him: “You shall not eat bread, nor drink water, nor return by the way by which you came” (ibid.); but an old prophet dwelling at Bethel deceived him, so that he ate bread and drank water in his house. Therefore a lion found him on the road and killed him; and his corpse lay cast upon the way, while the ass stood beside it and the lion stood beside the corpse (ibid.). This is a mystical figure of the aforesaid holy prophet Jehu son of Hanani, and of all the saints and prophets who have been killed or are killed for the testimony of the same Word of God. To them the incarnate Word himself says: “Do not fear those who kill the body and after this have nothing further that they can do” (Luke 12). For that lion which killed him and stood beside the corpse signifies the devil and his impious human servants. Through them, when he has killed the bodies of the saints, he stops and cannot proceed further to harm them, because the devil, being a spirit, does not know how to eat bodies; nor can he reach souls outside the body, whom he persecutes while they are in the body. Therefore, if the servants of God have incurred any sin through their bodily sojourn, and for this reason the enemy is sometimes permitted to kill their bodies, let him be content with that punishment and stand beside the corpses; that is, let him know that he is unable to inflict any further injury either upon their souls or even upon their bodies, so as to prevent their resurrection. For he cannot bring it about that even their bodies, by dying, perish to God. This is beautifully signified [Col. 1321A] by the fact that the lion did not devour the slain man, but stood beside the corpse.

## CHAPTER VII. What the twelve tearings of the cloak of Ahijah the Shilonite signified

Moreover, just as the Word of God has authority, after it has killed, to cast into Gehenna, so it had authority, after the prophets had died or been killed, nonetheless to fulfil their prophecy: that is, to reap the later descendants of impious kings, so that whoever of them died in the city should be eaten by dogs, and whoever died in the open country should be eaten by the birds of heaven. Thus the aforementioned prophet Jehu son of Hanani had foretold concerning Baasha, and Ahijah the Shilonite concerning Jeroboam.

This deserves no slight attention. For it contributes greatly to the glory of the Word of God, ever true and ever victorious—for the victory of that Word consists in whatever it has said becoming true—and that manifold division of the Israelite kingdom, which then took place, beautifully commends its truth. The aforesaid Ahijah the Shilonite gave Jeroboam, soon to be king, this omen concerning the kingdom: he took hold of the new cloak with which he was covered, tore it into twelve pieces, and said to him: “Take for yourself ten tearings. For thus says the Lord God of Israel: Behold, I shall tear the kingdom from the hand of Solomon and give you ten tribes” (3 Kings 11 [1 Kings 11]).

What did this mean: that he did not make merely two tears from one cloak, just as only two kingdoms arose from one people? It meant that the kingdom torn away from the house of David and entrusted to Jeroboam was to be torn ten times; and so it happened. The first tearing occurred in Jeroboam himself; the second in Baasha, who struck down Jeroboam’s son Nadab and reigned in his place; the third in Zimri, who struck down Baasha’s son and reigned in his place; the fourth in Omri, who pursued Zimri to death; the fifth in Tibni son of Ginath, whom the same Omri, father of Ahab, struck down; the sixth in Jehu son of Nimshi, who struck down Joram son of Ahab and reigned in his place; the seventh in Shallum, who struck down Zechariah, Jehu’s great-grandson; the eighth in Menahem, who struck down Shallum and reigned in his place; the ninth in Pekah son of Remaliah, who struck down Pekahiah son of Menahem and reigned in his place; [Col. 1321D] the tenth in Hoshea, who struck down Pekah son of Remaliah and reigned in his place.

Or rather, since Tibni—whom we said constituted the fifth tearing—is recorded not to have reigned even for a single day, but only to have been followed by half the people in an attempt to establish him as king, and did not prevail: omitting him, the fifth tearing was in Jehu, the sixth in Shallum, the seventh in Menahem, the eighth in Pekah son of Remaliah, the ninth in Hoshea, and the tenth in the king of Assyria, who tore Israel, already torn away from God, even from its place and land, and transported it into Assyria.

Thus it is as the Word itself says: “Every kingdom divided against itself shall be laid waste, and house shall fall upon house” (Luke 11). And, as the truthful Scripture foretold: “But the word of the Lord remains for ever” (Isaiah 40). For it fulfils the words of its prophets after they have withered like grass by dying or being killed; and it will make them themselves rise again, strong and lofty above the trees of cedars.

## CHAPTER VIII. That God, by a just judgment, established Jeroboam as king over Israel, not in order that he might cause them to sin, but because they were going to sin

Someone asks: How will this be justified? How will this Word obtain the palm of truth even in that it appointed such a man as Jeroboam king over Israel? Did it know, or did it not know, that he would make Israel sin? If it knew, why did it appoint him, and by what right did it punish them? If it did not know, how is it always victorious with justice? Or do error and ignorance contribute nothing to victory?

To this I reply: the Word and Wisdom was not ignorant, but knew exceedingly well; and yet in judging it retains the unimpaired palm of truth and justice. For it did this by judgment, and its judgment in this matter is not wholly hidden. Although its judgments are a great deep, although incomprehensible, nevertheless some of them may in part be known—those, namely, whose causes it deigns to disclose by its own mouth. Of these the Psalmist says: “With my lips I have proclaimed all the judgments of thy mouth” (Psalm 118 [119]).

For what cause was it judged that such a king should be given, who would make Israel sin? Clearly because Israel wished to sin. From when, do you suppose, did Israel possess the will to sin? “From the day,” says Moses, “on which you came out of Egypt until this place, you have always contended against the Lord” (Deuteronomy 9). Since in saying this and other such things he accuses them concerning the guilt of the calf which they made at Horeb, it is plain that they had always been inclined to the same idolatry; especially since God himself also says through the prophet: “Did you offer sacrifices and offerings to me in the wilderness for forty years, house of Israel? And you carried the tabernacle of Moloch, your idol, and the image of your idols, the star of your god, which you made for yourselves” (Amos 5).

For this they wished to stone Moses and Aaron. For this they rejected Samuel—or rather, in Samuel, the Lord himself—as he testifies (1 Kings 8 [1 Samuel 8]). For this they persecuted David and drove him from the kingdom. Therefore they so often said: “We have no portion in David, nor inheritance in the son of Jesse” (2 Chronicles 10 [2 Samuel 20; 1 Kings 12]), because they had the will to sin but, under holy rulers, did not have the opportunity to sin. Therefore their being given Jeroboam, under whom or with whom they set up for themselves a calf as their god—as they had begun to do when they came out of Egypt—was a true judgment, the judgment spoken of in another prophet: “Ephraim is a companion of idols; leave him alone” (Hosea 4). And if you ask why he says, “Leave him alone,” he immediately gives the reason: “Their thoughts will not allow them to return to the Lord” (Hosea 5). It was therefore a just judgment that he left them to the desires of their heart, to go in their own devices. But it was gratuitous mercy that he spoke solicitously through the prophets for those who erred in ignorance; and the word of the Lord came to them armed with signs and wonders, so that from its works they might know that the Lord himself is God.

## CHAPTER IX. That Elijah the prophet was sent by God so that those who were ignorant might not err together with the impious

For it was with signs and wonders, and with the strength of zeal, that the Word of the Lord then manifested itself more forcefully in Elijah. Of him it is truthfully said in the praises of the fathers: “Then Elijah the prophet arose like fire, and his word burned like a torch. By the word of the Lord he shut up heaven, and brought down fire from heaven. Thus was Elijah magnified in his wonders; and who can glory like you?” [Col. 1323B] (Ecclesiasticus 48).

Why does it say that Elijah arose like fire and that his word was like a burning torch? That wise man was moved to admiration because it is so abruptly written concerning Elijah: “And Elijah the Tishbite, from the inhabitants of Gilead, said to Ahab: ‘As the Lord God of Israel lives, in whose presence I stand, there shall be neither dew nor rain in these years except according to the word of my mouth’” (3 Kings 17 [1 Kings 17]). Elijah is introduced so suddenly that, just as the Apostle said concerning Melchizedek, so he could have said concerning this man, had occasion presented itself: “Without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life” (Hebrews 7). For Scripture is silent concerning his father and mother, genealogy, and number of years, just as it is concerning Melchizedek; and he had no end of life because, as the same author cited above says, “he was taken up in a whirlwind of fire, in a chariot of fiery horses” (Ecclesiasticus 48).

If you consider his reception rightly, you may add also what was said of Melchizedek: “But made like the Son of God, he remains a priest for ever” (Hebrews 7). For it is clear that this man was a priest, because Scripture records where, when, and how he offered a burnt offering; and, as has already been said, he was received “in a whirlwind of fire.” Thus “he was made like the Son of God,” the true and eternal Priest, as he ascended into heaven. More might be said about this; nevertheless, for the present purpose I shall say only this: the Word and Truth of God showed itself worthy of itself in making its power known through him in such a manner at such a time, when Baal had joined Jezebel and Ahab together with Jeroboam’s calves. It did so for those who were ignorant and astray, lest they fall with the impious into the same pit of perdition.

## CHAPTER X. The miracles Elijah performed, and how the double spirit of Elijah in Elisha is demonstrated by the doubled number of miracles

This must be carefully observed: for such a cause he readily offered himself to work miracles, beginning in this manner: “As the Lord lives, in whose presence I stand, there shall be neither dew nor rain in these years, unless according to the word of my mouth” (3 Kings 17 [1 Kings 17]). The same cause must be considered in Elisha when he says: “I pray that your spirit may be doubled in me” (4 Kings 2 [2 Kings 2]). Their purpose was, by working wonders, to convict the impious that neither the calf nor Baal is God, but that the Lord himself is God.

And indeed it happened so. The spirit of Elijah—that is, the working of miracles which had been given to Elijah in the Spirit of the Lord—became double in Elisha. For Elisha performed twice as many miracles as Elijah. Indeed, if you count rightly, Elijah worked eight miracles, and Elisha sixteen.

Elijah’s first was that by his word he shut up heaven so that it did not rain. The second, that ravens fed him. The third, that with the widow who fed him, at his word the jar of flour did not fail and the flask of oil was not diminished. [Col. 1324B] The fourth, that he raised the dead son of that same widow. The fifth, that when he offered the burnt offering, the Lord answered by fire, while the people watched and said: “The Lord himself is God.” The sixth, that as he prayed, a great rain came. The seventh, that striking the waters with his cloak, he divided them and crossed over with Elisha. The eighth, that a fiery chariot and fiery horses separated the two, and Elijah ascended into heaven in a whirlwind.

Elisha’s first, immediately, was that he struck the waters with Elijah’s cloak and they were divided. The second, that he healed bad waters and barren ground. The third, that bears tore apart boys who mocked him. The fourth, that when the three kings—of Israel, Judah, and Edom—had gathered, and there was no water for the army, he commanded ditches to be made and the ground was filled with water. The fifth, that for a widowed woman he filled many vessels from a little oil. The sixth, that the woman who had ministered to him and had no son conceived and gave birth at the time and hour he foretold. The seventh, that he raised that same boy from the dead. The eighth, that in the hermits’ pot he made the most bitter flavours sweet. The ninth, that a hundred men ate, according to his word, from twenty barley loaves, and some remained. The tenth, that he cured Naaman, commander of the army of the king of Syria, of his leprosy by the washing of water. The eleventh, that Jehu, leaving him, became leprous as snow. The twelfth, that when he sent wood, the iron which had fallen off floated upon the water. [Col. 1324D] The thirteenth, that when Syrians were sent against him, the Lord, at his prayer, struck them with blindness until he brought them into Samaria. The fourteenth, that when the siege of Samaria was lifted, two measures of barley cost one shekel and a measure of fine flour one shekel, according to his word at the gate of Samaria. The fifteenth, that while sick, he foretold to the king of Israel that he would strike Syria three times. The sixteenth, that when he was dead, a man’s corpse was thrown into his tomb, and when it touched Elisha’s bones, the man came to life and stood upon his feet.

## CHAPTER XI. What progress Elijah and Elisha the prophets made among the people, and to what extent

Yet in all these things the people did not repent and did not depart from their sins—that is, from the calves which Jeroboam made—until they were cast out of their land and scattered throughout every land. Nevertheless, Baal was destroyed from Samaria and Jerusalem. For Jezebel’s sacrilege had also spread into Jerusalem, since Athaliah, daughter of Jezebel and Ahab, was the wife of Joram, son of Jehoshaphat king of Judah. Concerning her it is thus written in Chronicles: “For most impious Athaliah and her sons had destroyed the house of God, and from all the things that had been consecrated to the temple of the Lord they had adorned the shrine of Baal” (2 Chronicles 24).

Baal was destroyed from both: that is, from Israel and from Judah. From Israel through Elijah and Elisha, when they worked the miracles described above. From Judah through Elijah, who was there too a minister of the Word of God, as it is written: “There were brought to him”—namely, to Joram son of Jehoshaphat—“letters from Elijah the prophet, in which it was written: ‘Thus says the Lord God of Israel, the God of David your father: Because you have not walked in the ways of Jehoshaphat your father, but have walked in the way of the kings of Israel, and have made Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem commit fornication: behold, the Lord will strike you with a great plague, together with your people, your sons, your wives, and all your possessions; but you shall suffer from a most grievous disease of the bowels, until your vital organs come out little by little, day after day’” (2 Chronicles 21).

[Col. 1325C] It happened according to this word. For that Joram, son of Jehoshaphat and king of Judah, was consumed by so prolonged a wasting illness over two years that he even expelled his entrails; he lost both health and life. After his wife Athaliah had been killed by the sword, the high priest Jehoiada and all the people entered the house of Baal and destroyed it; they shattered its altars and images. They also killed Mattan, priest of Baal, before the altars.

Moreover, in Israel that same Elijah had killed four hundred and fifty men, prophets of Baal, in a single day; and Jehu killed all the remaining prophets, every servant, and all the priests of Baal, destroyed his temple, and burned and crushed his statue. Elisha had anointed Jehu king over Israel in Elijah’s stead. For the Lord had commanded Elijah to anoint that same Jehu; and Elisha carried out this office concerning which the Lord had commanded Elijah: “You shall anoint Elisha son of Shaphat, who is from Abel-meholah, as prophet in your place” (3 Kings 19 [1 Kings 19]). Thus Baal was destroyed from Judah and Israel through the most powerful zeal of the Word [of the Word] of the Lord, blazing from Elijah’s mouth; for Elijah, as it is truly said of him, “was like fire, and his word burned like a torch” (Ecclesiasticus 48).

## CHAPTER XII. Why the Lord’s zeal blazed more fiercely in Elijah against Baal than against the golden calves

Whoever rightly weighs the causes reveres still more the fire of that so fiercely burning torch: the zeal of the Word [of the Word] of the Lord, so powerfully avenging itself upon the worshippers of Baal. What were the reasons why it was less zealous because of the calves which Jeroboam made, but more zealous because of Baal? Clearly, because the worship of the calves was confined within Israel. But the worship of Baal, from the house of Jezebel and Ahab, had spread through the aforementioned Athaliah as far as Jerusalem, as far as the house of David, from which the fulfilment of the promise—namely, the incarnation of the Word of the Lord—was hoped for, a promise secured by God’s own oath.

There faith in, or expectation of, the promise was more endangered by the sacrilege of Baal. For none of the kings of Judah worshipped Jeroboam’s calves; consequently their worship was less harmful to the promise, being confined only to those tribes from none of which Christ was to be born. Therefore, when Baal came in, the Word of the Lord rightly, justly, and praiseworthily blazed like fire in its prophet, took up the sword, and shed the blood of the impious.

For Baal himself had taken up the sword in order to kill all the seed of David, from which, according to the promise, the aforementioned incarnation of the Lord was to come. For it is written: “Indeed Athaliah, seeing that her son was dead, arose and killed all the royal seed” (4 Kings 11 [2 Kings 11]). By “all the royal seed” it means all the kings, that is, the males of David’s line, from whom the seed of Abraham—that is, Christ—had been foretold and preordained to be born, the Lord having sworn it. Accordingly, we must consider that Baal’s sacrilege was no small or tolerable impiety: through its worship souls in both Judah and Israel were perishing, and the ancient dragon, the devil, was seeking to remove the seed-bed of our salvation by inciting Athaliah, a worshipper of that same Baal, to kill—and by killing, to eradicate—the holy line of Davidic descent.

## CHAPTER XIII. That the Lord visited the sins of the house of David with rod and lashes, but did not scatter his mercy from him

Having considered so great a cause for most just zeal in Elijah, the mighty and most holy proclaimer of the word of the Lord, that reasonable and illustrious saying of Davidic prayer returns again to mind: “Have mercy on me, that thou mayest be justified in thy words and prevail when thou art judged” (Psalm 50 [51]). It is pleasing here to recall the words in which David wished God to be justified, victorious, and to gain the palm of truth. What are those words?

“But if,” he says, “his sons forsake my law and do not walk in my judgments; if they profane my statutes and do not keep my commandments, I will visit their iniquities with a rod and their sins with lashes. But I will not scatter my mercy from him, nor will I harm my truth, nor profane my covenant, nor make void the things that proceed from my lips. Once have I sworn by my holiness: Shall I lie to David?” (Psalm 88 [89]).

In these words God the Truthful One was then magnificently justified and splendidly victorious. For then David’s sons had most greatly forsaken God’s law and did not walk in his judgments. They had profaned his statutes and had not kept his commandments when the aforementioned Joram son of Jehoshaphat, after killing all his brothers, walked in the ways of the kings of Judah—as the house of Ahab had done—whose daughter Athaliah he had as his wife, and served Baal.

The Lord visited such iniquities and sins of David’s sons with rod and lashes; but he did not scatter his mercy from him—David is understood. In what did he not scatter his mercy from him? In what was it preserved? Certainly in this: Athaliah, seeing—as has been said—that her son Ahaziah was dead, arose and killed [Col. 1327B] all the royal offspring of the house of Joram (2 Chronicles 22). But Jehosheba, the king’s daughter, took Joash son of Ahaziah, secretly carried him away from among the king’s sons as they were being killed, and hid him with his nurse in the bedchamber. Jehosheba, who hid him, was the daughter of King Joram, the wife of the high priest Jehoiada, and the sister of Ahaziah; therefore Athaliah did not kill him.

What a rod, what severe lashes: according to the word of the Lord, according to the truth of the letters which Elijah, as mentioned above, had sent, the Philistines and Arabs came up into the land of Judah, laid it waste, and plundered all the wealth found in the king’s house, together with his sons and wives. Beyond all this, Joram was struck by the Lord with an incurable illness of the belly and consumed by a long wasting disease; Jehu killed his son Ahaziah, who had succeeded him; and thereafter a woman more savage than all evils killed all the royal seed.

Yet under that very rod, amid those very lashes, with what care was mercy for David himself preserved: that Jehosheba, a true daughter of the king, truly a daughter of David, and a wife worthy of the high priest Jehoiada, should secretly take away one-year-old Joash from among the king’s sons while they were being killed! For the Lord, Scripture says, did not wish to destroy the house of David because of the covenant he had made with him and because he had promised to give him a lamp, to him and to his sons for all time (ibid.). That lamp which the Lord promised David is Christ, “the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1). He would not have given David that lamp, as he had sworn, if at least that least one, Joash, had not survived the slaughter of David’s line. For no other male survived through whom the Davidic succession could have been carried down to its fulfilment in Christ.

## CHAPTER XIV. How great Elijah’s zeal was, and how great his dignity

How great, do you suppose, was the dignity of having exercised zeal in view of so great a matter, as he himself says: “With zeal I have been zealous for the Lord God of hosts” (3 Kings 19 [1 Kings 19])? Do not ask a human being. The fiery chariot with fiery horses, in which he ascended to heaven in a whirlwind, answers you. A chariot is the vehicle of lords, the chariot of those who triumph. Therefore understand in that chariot the dignity of a ruling spirit and the distinguished power of a friend of God: he truly ruled, exalted above every age; and he was powerful in the word by which he shut heaven and opened it again; powerful in anointing kings to power, while deeming it worthy to reverence the whole power of the kingdom of God alone.

He therefore sat in the chariot as one ruling: a vigorous champion of the Word of God and a victorious despiser of worldly vanity. And that you may recognize the greatness of his zeal, the chariot was not ordinary but fiery. It cannot be expressed, though it may in some manner be conjectured, how greatly Elijah’s heart burned when he saw that human beings—so far as lay in them—were making the world unworthy of that mercy, which is Christ, promised long ago and confirmed by an oath. Certainly what the good and omnipotent One had promised could not be turned aside, because he who had sworn was faithful and true. Yet people, as has been said, so far as lay in them, acted so that God might regret the great mercy he had promised and sworn: enemies of divine grace, foes of human salvation, evil toward all humanity, and worst toward themselves.

O perfect hatred, then, and holy blaze of good zeal, whose dignity the heavens testified to by withholding rain at his command and then granting the earth the benefit of rain; and still more by sending a fiery chariot with fiery horses to lift up the victorious, deservedly rewarded, and mighty friend of God. From his glorification, so great and so astonishing, let everyone take an example and conceive hope that he will not lack a reward if he diligently strives to render faithful service to the Word of God.

## CHAPTER XV. That Elijah, having been taken up, is to be sent before the great and terrible day of the Lord, and that this was fulfilled in John the Baptist

The opinion of very many teachers concerning this man is that near the end of the age he will come with Enoch, and that, they say, under the persecution of Antichrist he will have to pay the common debt by undergoing the death which he did not escape but postponed.

Jerome, however, one of no mean rank among illustrious men, seems to hold another view at the end of the prophet Malachi, where the Lord says: “Behold, I shall send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes” (Malachi 4). After some remarks he says: “We have said these things concerning Elijah, following the teachers, although many even among our own believe that he will come literally, restore all things, and pay the debt of death. But when the Lord was asked by the apostles about Elijah’s coming, he answered: ‘Elijah has already come, and they did not recognize him, but did to him whatever they wished’” (Matthew 17), intending John to be understood in Elijah. Hence he added: “If you are willing to receive it, John himself is Elijah who is to come” (Matthew 11).

In saying this, he plainly indicates agreement with other teachers who understand Elijah’s coming not according to the letter but according to the Spirit, when he says: “Although many even among our own believe that he will come literally and pay the debt of death.” Yet he sufficiently indicates that he wishes Elijah already to have been freed from the necessity of death. If this is so, it is truly great and magnificent, and highly praiseworthy among glorious men, that the Lord has worked his magnificence in him. For if he still awaits death, one may judge that he has attained less blessedness than the other saints, who, having laid aside all the corruption of mortality, have been freed from a great debt and grievous usury. For awaiting death undoubtedly entails punishment; and therefore all those may be called more blessed who have neither fear of death nor uncertainty concerning the glory of resurrection. It was therefore more magnificently done for him, and for blessed Enoch, if they did not postpone death but escaped it—if they were translated while living and suffer no torment from the long anxiety or expectation of death.

## CHAPTER XVI. That it is plausible that Enoch and Elijah, having been translated, were freed from the necessity of dying

And since there are two, and it is lawful that “by the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may stand” (Deuteronomy 19), we might rightly wish that they had therefore been translated and would not die, so that through them that word which we possess concerning the whole human race might be confirmed for us. What is that word? Namely, that sin is the cause of death or mortality for the human race; and that it would have been easy and voluntary for the omnipotent Creator to transfer the human being placed in paradise, and the entire human race, at his own good pleasure and at the time pleasing to himself, without bodily death, into the kingdom of immortality, where death neither exists nor can ever occur.

This is indeed a great word, and difficult for those slow to believe, especially concerning matters of which they have received no experience. What then, if it pleased almighty God to transfer at least two persons born from the corrupted mass as a testimony, so that he might have two witnesses “by whose mouth this word may stand”: namely, that he nevertheless would have wished, and could have been able, to transfer all human beings without bodily death, if the mass had not been corrupted through sin? Certainly this is a measure of wisdom, in view of which the wise man could say in praise of the fathers: “Enoch pleased God and was translated into paradise, that he might give wisdom to the nations.”

The same must be understood and said concerning Elijah: that he was translated in order to give wisdom to the nations, so that the nations, hearing of their translation, may be stirred up by their example to walk with God and obey the word of God. For just as he translated them alive, so he would have translated all people without the difficulty of death, had death not entered this world through sin. But because both opinions have been handed down by great and catholic teachers, we do not dare determine anything certain on this matter; let us continue our subject.

## CHAPTER XVII. That after Elijah and Elisha the same Word of God did not fail through the succession of other prophets

After Elijah was translated—he who was the chariot of Israel and its charioteer—and Elisha died, to whom likewise, when he was sick, the king of Israel had said: “My father, my father, the chariot of Israel and its charioteer” (4 Kings 2 [2 Kings 13]), the Word of God, the omnipotent Word, nevertheless maintained its course and purpose, appointing other chariots and other charioteers to its service.

For other heralds of the Word of the Lord immediately arose, those whose own books still exist. At that time Hosea arose in Israel and Isaiah in Judah, both contemporaries, as may readily be known from the titles of their books. They read as follows: “The vision of Isaiah son of Amoz, which he saw concerning Judah and Jerusalem in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah” (Isaiah 1).—“The word of the Lord which came to Hosea son of Beeri in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam son of Joash, king of Israel” (Hosea 1).

This is Joash, grandson of Jehu, in whose days Elisha died; and, as the present title has it, Hosea prophesied “in the days of Jeroboam his son.” I have said this in order that it may be plainly evident that the Word of the Lord left none of those kings unrebuked or excusable; it maintained an unbroken course of rebuking prophecy, and more prophets succeeded prophets than kings succeeded kings.

For the title of the prophecy indicates that Amos too prophesied in the days of that same Jeroboam, and especially this passage written there: “Amaziah, priest of Bethel, sent to Jeroboam king of Israel, saying: ‘Amos has rebelled against you in the midst of the house of Israel; the land cannot endure all his words. For Amos says this: Jeroboam shall die by the sword, and Israel shall be led captive away from its land’” (Amos 7).

What more beautiful or more resonant thing can be said from this? The Psalmist foretold it, and the Apostle echoes it: “You, O Lord, in the beginning founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands. They shall perish, but you remain; and all shall grow old like a garment; and like a cloak you shall change them, and they shall be changed. But you are the same, and your years shall not fail” (Psalm 101 [102]). The Apostle recalls that this was said to the Son, who is the Word of God (Hebrews 1).

The aforementioned Elijah and Elisha, like David and Abraham and the other saints, were earth in respect of their created condition and heaven in respect of their worthiness of faith; for God sat and dwelt in their minds through faith, and they are rightly called heavens. Such heavens perished—that is, passed away—because they were mortal and died, and at some time must be changed and renewed, having grown old in this manner. But you, O Word of the Lord, are the same: when they failed, you did not fail, nor will you fail.

## CHAPTER XVIII. What is meant by the saying through Hosea: “I will no longer have mercy on the house of Israel, but I will utterly forget them; and I will have mercy on the house of Judah.”

“In those days,” says Scripture, “the Lord began to grow weary of Israel” (2 Kings 10), plainly because that carnal Israel was incorrigible, as were its kings, so that not one of them departed from the sins of Jeroboam [Col. 1331A]—that is, from the worship of the calves which Jeroboam made, he who caused Israel to sin. For “the Lord began to grow weary of Israel, and Hazael struck them throughout all the borders of Israel” (ibid.). This was the beginning of His weariness. Later, however, the Lord’s complete weariness came when the king of Assyria captured Samaria and carried Israel away into Assyria, placing them in Halah and Habor, by the river Gozan, in the cities of the Medes. I say, the Lord’s weariness was complete—not toward Judah, but only toward Israel, that is, toward the ten tribes—according to what He Himself had foretold through the prophet mentioned above: “For I will no longer, He says, have mercy upon the house of Israel, but I will utterly forget them; yet upon the house of Judah I will have mercy” (Hos. 1).

This belongs to the steadfastness of the truth [Col. 1331B] of God: “That thou mayest be justified in thy words, O God, and prevail when thou art judged” (Ps. 50 [51]). Certainly He had to have mercy upon the house of Judah and the house of David; that good root of this stock, from which Christ was to be born according to the truth of the promise and oath made to David himself, had to be preserved and defended. And so it came to pass. For in the eighth year after Israel had been carried away from its land, Sennacherib king of Assyria came up against all the fortified cities of Judah, captured them, and besieged Jerusalem. But the Lord said: “He shall not enter this city, nor shoot an arrow into it, nor take it with shield, nor cast up a mound around it; and I will protect this city and save it, for my own sake and for the sake of David my servant. For out of Jerusalem shall go forth a remnant, [Col. 1331C] and that which is saved from Mount Zion.” Therefore, in that night the angel of the Lord came and struck one hundred and eighty-five thousand in the camp of the Assyrians (2 Kings 18–19). Clearly, the forgetting by which He forgot the ten tribes could do no harm to God’s purpose, provided that the tribe or house from which Christ had to be born remained.

## CHAPTER XIX. That the Word of God, not yet incarnate—that is, Emmanuel, not yet born—delivered the land from the king of Assyria.

Did He not provide for Himself? Did not the Word of God accomplish this for His own sake? Indeed, He provided for Himself for us and on our behalf, so that He might preserve the lineage from which the Virgin would come, conceive, and bear Him who would be called Emmanuel (Isa. 7). He was not yet called so, but He was going to be called Emmanuel. Yet Isaiah called upon Him as Emmanuel, that He might deliver Jerusalem from the Assyrians already foretold.

For after he had said, “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel” (ibid.), he also later spoke these words: “The Lord shall bring upon them the strong and abundant waters of the river—the king of Assyria and all his glory—and he shall rise over all his channels and flow over all his banks; and, overflowing and passing through Judah, he shall come up to the neck; and the spreading of his wings shall fill the breadth [Col. 1332A] of thy land, O Emmanuel” (Isa. 8).

The words, “thy land, O Emmanuel,” are a great cry of the heart, intended to remind the Word of God that the land of Judah was His own land according to the purpose of grace. For it had been predestined and foretold that from the land of Judah and the house of David a Virgin would conceive and bear Him, and He would be called Emmanuel. And because this was to come about with such complete certainty—because this Emmanuel, not yet born according to the flesh, was going to strike the camp of the Assyrians—he immediately cries out in triumph: “Gather yourselves together, O peoples, and be defeated; hear, all ye lands afar off; strengthen yourselves and be defeated; gird yourselves and be defeated; take counsel, and it shall be brought to nothing; speak a word, and it shall not come to pass, because God is with us” (Isa. 8).

This is spoken with great confidence [Col. 1332B] and certain assurance, because it was not uncertain to Him that there was nothing able to overturn God’s purpose. Against whose counsel every human counsel is vain, he therefore triumphs in safety, according to what is written: “He who dwells in heaven shall laugh them to scorn, and the Lord shall mock them” (Ps. 2). By laughing and mocking He challenges them; by challenging them He ridicules and mocks the nations that rage in vain and the peoples who devise empty things—those who even then stood together and gathered as one against the Lord and against His Christ, Emmanuel.

## CHAPTER XX. That the same Word, “before the child knew to call his mother,” hastened to strip away spoils and hurried to plunder.

[Col. 1332C] We should also observe the beautiful and remarkable name which He is there commanded to receive: “Call his name,” He says, “Hasten, strip away the spoils; hurry, plunder” (Isa. 8). Why? “For before the child knows to call his father and mother, the strength of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria shall be taken away,” He says, “before the king of Assyria” (ibid.). Truly a beautiful and fitting name! For what could be more astonishing than this haste, more marvelous than this speed: to strip away spoils before knowing or calling one’s father, to plunder before being born from one’s mother?

This Emmanuel did it. Before He knew to call the man who was His father in name alone, Joseph; before He was born of His mother, namely the Virgin Mary, He provided this benefit for His people as He provided the rest [Col. 1332D]: He gave aid also to the house of Judah, from which He was to be born, so that the strength of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria might be taken away before the king of Assyria. How? “For,” says Scripture, “the king of Assyria went up to Damascus, devastated it, carried its inhabitants to Cyrene, and killed Rezin. Then the king of Assyria captured Samaria and carried Israel away into Assyria, placing them in the cities of the Medes” (2 Kings 16).

For what reason did Emmanuel thus take away the strength of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria? Plainly because Syria and Ephraim, and the son of Remaliah, had entered into an evil design against Judah, saying: “Let us go up against Judah, stir it up, tear it away to ourselves, and set in its midst a king, the son of Tabeel” (Isa. 7). Therefore [Col. 1333A] Israel’s own deportation into Assyria is rightly attributed to the victory of the Word of God, because Scripture plainly testifies that Emmanuel did this before He knew to call father and mother—that is, that the Word of God did this before He assumed flesh.

And rightly did He not spare Israel, because ever since Israel had been severed from Judah and the house of David, it had envied that tribe of Judah more than the other nations and had fought against it more often. Jeroboam, the first king of Israel, fought against Abijah king of Judah; and Abijah, standing on the mountain, said: “Hear me, Jeroboam and all Israel! Do you not know that the Lord God of Israel gave the kingdom over Israel forever to David and to his sons, by a covenant of salvation?”” (2 Chron. 13). And shortly afterward: “Now therefore you say that you are able to resist [Col. 1333B] the kingdom of the Lord, which He possesses through the sons of David?” (ibid.).

I have recalled these matters so that no one may fail to understand whence the ten tribes could have drawn a fiercer flame of envy against Judah. For from this passage and similar ones it is plainly evident that frequent disputes of this kind occurred between the two sides: the tribe of Judah said that the kingdom of David alone was the kingdom of the Lord, while the kingdom of the ten tribes was not a lawful kingdom but rebellion against the Lord’s kingdom.

## CHAPTER XXI. Once the ten tribes had been carried into captivity, the Word of God’s war against the golden calves came to an end.

At length the duel, prolonged over a long time, came to an end between the living God—the Word of God—and Jeroboam’s god, a metallic god, the image of a horned calf. Nearly two hundred and sixty years elapsed from the time when the aforesaid Jeroboam made such a god for himself until the ninth year of Hoshea, when the king of Assyria carried Israel away from its land. Nor did the Word of God cease to contend through words such as these: “Thy calf has been cast away, O Samaria. A craftsman made it, and it is not God; for the calf of Samaria shall become spiders’ webs” (Hos. 8). And in another prophet: “Hear and testify against the house of Jacob: for in the day when I begin to visit the transgressions of Israel, I will visit them upon him and upon the altars of Bethel; and the horns of the altar shall be cut off and fall to the ground” (Amos 3).

And because Israel, or any of its kings, neither did depart nor would depart [Col. 1333D] from the sins of Jeroboam—that is, from the same calves which Jeroboam made—He also said: “The house of Israel has fallen; it shall not rise again. The virgin Israel is cast down upon the ground; there is none to raise her up” (Amos 5). Hence the justice of Him who likewise said in Hosea is manifest: “For I will no longer have mercy upon the house of Israel, but will utterly forget them; yet upon the house of Judah I will have mercy” (Hos. 1). For, as has already been said, none of the kings of Israel departed from the sins of Jeroboam, although throughout every one of their reigns the Word of God did not cease to call them back to repentance. But some kings of Judah were righteous, and some of those who sinned repented. Just, therefore, is the judgment: “I will no longer,” He says, [Col. 1334A] “have mercy upon the house of Israel”; and not unjust is the mercy in the words, “Upon the house of Judah I will have mercy.”

## CHAPTER XXII. That the Assyrians were more righteous than Israel, and therefore Israel was handed over to them into captivity.

We should not know how to weigh this justice unless the Word Himself had given us a demonstration that any nation whatsoever was more disposed and more receptive to repentance, and therefore more righteous and more worthy of pardon, than Israel. Hence the providence of God is truly praiseworthy: before He pronounced judgment upon Israel and issued the sentence He had foretold—“For I will no longer have mercy upon the house of Israel, but will utterly forget them” (Hos. 1)—He sent His Word [Col. 1334B] to a nation which at that time was harsher and stronger than the other nations.

It was as though He said to any one of His prophets: “Even if I sent thee to many peoples of deep speech and unknown language, whose words thou couldst not understand, they would hear thee; but the house of Israel will not hear thee, because they will not hear Me” (Ezek. 3). He said this, indeed, to one prophet, Ezekiel. But before He said it to him, the truth of this saying had been established by a great demonstration through another prophet: “For the word of the Lord came to Jonah, saying: Arise and go to the great city Nineveh, and preach in it, because the cry of its wickedness has come up before me” (Jonah 1). And it came to pass that, when he preached, the men of Nineveh believed in the Lord, proclaimed [Col. 1334C] a fast, and clothed themselves in sackcloth, from the greatest to the least (Jonah 3).

Did Jonah alone preach to Israel about the coming captivity? Far from it. Hosea proclaimed much, and Amos resounded in that same time—leaving aside Elijah and Elisha, whom I mentioned above, who performed many magnificent and great signs. Yet Israel did not repent, and none of Israel’s kings departed from the sins of Jeroboam. Who, then, can censure—or dare to censure—the judgment of the Word of the Lord, by which He handed Israel, unbelieving toward Himself, over to Assyrians who believed and were therefore more righteous? Indeed, it is praiseworthy, because it is reasonable and altogether fitting that He should have wished, by such a demonstration, to show that particular nation to be more righteous [Col. 1334D] to which He had resolved to hand over the transgressing people.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Why the house of Judah was preserved when Israel was carried into captivity, although there were some righteous persons in both.

Here someone may perhaps object that among Israel too, which was carried away, there were some who pleased God; and this cannot be denied. For example, Tobias, of the tribe and city of Naphtali, was taken in that captivity; and while captive he remained holy and of praiseworthy life. For it is written of him that “when he had been taken captive in the days of Shalmaneser king of Assyria, even in captivity he did not forsake the way of truth” (Tob. 1). He held to it so firmly that he was found worthy of a new miracle: the marvelously novel visitation of an angel.

Why, then, did the Lord not continue to have mercy at least upon him and the others mentioned in that history, so that they might be released from the yoke of captivity, as He had mercy upon Judah and the house of David? Yet that house of Judah, or house of David, had not only this claim before the merciful God—that some righteous people were found there—but also this, which must certainly be known and remembered: the truth of the word or promise of God had necessarily to be fulfilled by Christ’s birth or incarnation from the tribe of Judah, from the seed of David. Israel, carried captive into Assyria, did not possess this reason, because, as was mentioned above, Christ had been promised to be born not from any tribe of Israel but from the tribe of Judah.

This reason, not merit, assisted the tribe of Judah; the truth [Col. 1335B] of God, necessarily to be fulfilled, not its own righteousness, preserved the house of David. Consequently, we should no more complain about Tobias and the other righteous persons who may have existed in those days because the Lord did not bring them back to their own land, than we now complain about Jews who are converted to faith in Christ because they are not immediately brought back to the land from which they were led captive. Then the ten tribes, from which Christ was not to be born, might be wherever they were; now Jews may be scattered everywhere, even though converted to the faith, because Christ has already been born. It was sufficient for God, and is sufficient for the human race, that He was so careful and provident as faithful David forewarned when he said: “That thou mayest be justified in thy words, and prevail when thou art judged” (Ps. 50 [51]).

## CHAPTER XXIV. Why it is written in the Law, “The Lord spoke to Moses,” but in the Prophets, “The Word of the Lord came,” and so forth.

[Col. 1335C] The matter itself now strikes the mind and makes us hear and understand more clearly the expression customary in the prophets: “The word of the Lord came.” For “the Word of the Lord came to me” and “the Lord spoke, or said, to me” may indeed appear equivalent or of equal force. But they are not so. And, to make it plainly clear that they are not, first consider this point, which I think most pleasing to an intelligent mind: nowhere in the Law do you find it said or written in this way, “The Word of the Lord came to Moses” [Col. 1335D] or to Aaron; rather, it says only, “The Lord spoke to Moses, saying,” or “The Lord said to Moses.” But among the prophets this expression is frequent: “The word of the Lord came,” or “the utterance of the Lord came.”

This is a most beautiful consideration, and it gives great delight to contemplate why this was carefully observed. Why, then, do you think? Clearly because it was fitting for this to be declared only in those cases where all things spoken are irrevocable and unavoidable, as though they had already happened. The Law, however, was given with a conditional promise; for example, at the beginning when that Law was being given, or had been given. For after the words, “You yourselves have seen what I have done to the Egyptians, how I bore you upon eagles’ wings,” it immediately adds in a conditional [Col. 1336A] manner: “If therefore you hear my voice and keep my covenant, you shall be my peculiar possession above all peoples, and you shall be to me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation” (Exod. 19).

Certainly they were not going to hear the Lord’s voice or keep His covenant, and consequently they were not going to remain in God’s peculiar possession or kingdom. Therefore it was not fitting in such a matter for it to be declared, “The word of the Lord came,” and then for promises to be made unconditionally: “You shall be my peculiar possession; you shall be to me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation.” Likewise, regarding other matters, especially the ceremonies of sacrifices, because they were temporary and destined to change, it was not fitting to say, “The word of the Lord came to Moses.”

That this is so, as we say, becomes immediately clear to one who considers that nowhere in Moses, but only in or to the prophets, do you find written, “The word of the Lord came.” [Col. 1336B] And it was and is impossible that anything foretold under such a declaration, without the introduction of a condition, should remain unfulfilled. Therefore, when we hear or read anywhere of a prophet that the Word of the Lord came to him; when we hear any prophet saying, “The utterance of the Lord came to me,” let us receive it as confident joy, as triumphant exultation—as though, leaping from darkness into light, from slavery into freedom, from captivity into their homeland, from death into life, they should leap, saying—say as they leap—“It has come to pass, it has come to pass.”

And what has come to pass? That which is future has come to pass, because we have heard His word; we have seen, without seeing, the word of Him for whom to speak is to do.

# BOOK SIX

[Col. 1337]

## CHAPTER I. That kings and kingdoms are called the heads of the ancient dragon.

[Col. 1337D]

Kings and kingdoms deserved to be called the heads of the ancient dragon because of the greatness of their wickedness. For all wicked persons are called, and are, members of the devil, because they are filled with the devil’s spirit; they hated the Word of God. But those kingdoms, or the kings of those kingdoms, so surpassed wicked human beings as a head [Col. 1338D] surpasses the limbs in a body; and all the wicked served them against God just as limbs serve the head. Woe to them, therefore: as much as they excelled in power, so much more heavily shall they be weighed down in judgment; as much as in glory, so much in punishment. Thus the justice of God says of each one of them: “As much as she glorified herself and lived in luxury, give her so much torment and mourning” (Rev. 18).

Likewise, understand that the words spoken to the first of them—namely Pharaoh, king of Egypt—were spoken, or could have been spoken, to each one of those heads: “For this reason I have set thee up, that I may show in thee my power, and that my name may be proclaimed in all the earth” (Exod. 9). Let us now enter upon the discussion of the battles of the Word of God and of the third head.

## CHAPTER II. That the kingdom of the Assyrians and the kingdom of the Chaldeans together were the third head of the dragon, like a lion.

After Israel—that is, the ten tribes, which closely threatened the tribe of Judah and the house of David as a deadly enemy—had been carried into Assyria, that great dragon, the devil, did not delay. He immediately clothed himself with the kingdom of Assyria, supposing that this head had been added to him so that he might destroy that tribe or house [Col. 1339B] in which the faith of God’s covenant and promise was deposited. But he did not prevail; he could not use that kingdom as such a head, because, as has already been mentioned, “the angel of the Lord came in the night and struck one hundred and eighty-five thousand in the camp of the Assyrians. And when he rose early in the morning, he saw all the bodies of the dead; and Sennacherib king of Assyria departed, returned, and dwelt in Nineveh. And as he worshiped in the temple of Nesroch his god, his sons Adrammelech and Sharezer struck him with the sword” (2 Kings 19).

Thus was fulfilled the consolation of the Lord God, who said to Hezekiah: “I will deliver thee and this city from the hand of the king of Assyria, and I will protect this city for my own sake and for the sake of David my servant” (2 Kings 20). Therefore that kingdom was not counted among the dragon’s heads, because it did not tear apart the seat of the promise, though it desired to tear it apart. But because afterward the kingdom of Babylon arose from the same region, it is rightly counted as the third head of the dragon, and it has the face of a lion, as we read in Daniel’s vision. Or certainly, because the Assyrian kingdom, through the greatness of its proud power—or powerful pride—opened wide its mouth and blasphemed the true God and Lord, it was truly a deadly enemy and should be counted together with the kingdom of the Chaldeans as one head of the dragon.

For in the prophet, where it is said, “What the caterpillar left the locust has eaten; what the locust left the cankerworm has eaten; and what the cankerworm left the rust has eaten” (Joel 1), we understand the caterpillar, on the authority of ancient teachers, to signify both the Assyrian and Chaldean nations, because, coming from the same region, they devastated the land of Judah; the locust signifies the kingdom of the Persians and Medes, the cankerworm the kingdom of the Macedonians and Greeks, and the rust the kingdom of the Romans.

## CHAPTER III. How God pursued the house of David with zeal for good, while the devil did so for evil.

The contest, therefore, was waged on both sides with the greatest zeal: here good zeal, there evil zeal. Good zeal is the zeal of the Lord of hosts; evil zeal is the zeal of the devil, the ancient dragon, the head of the enemies. The zeal of both these parties burned in relation to humankind, and especially then in relation to the tribe of Judah and the house of David: the one for good, the other for evil.

Let us now define both. Good zeal is to love people but hate their vices. Evil zeal is to hate people but love their life. You have a great fervor of that good zeal in its hatred of human vices in the passage where, after the words, “There was no king like Josiah before him, who turned to the Lord with all his heart, nor did any like him arise after him,” Scripture immediately adds: “Nevertheless, the Lord did not turn from the fierceness of his great wrath, with which his anger was kindled against Judah because of the provocations by which Manasseh had provoked him. And he said: I will remove Judah also from my sight, as I removed Israel” (2 Kings 23).

But concerning His love for people, the fervor of the same good zeal at about the same time is expressed through the prophet: [Col. 1340B] “If my covenant with the day can be made void, and my covenant with the night, so that day and night should not be in their season, then my covenant with David my servant can be made void, so that he should have no son to reign in the house of his [David’s] line” (Jer. 33). Without doubt, on the contrary, the devil’s evil zeal devised means by which the house of David might fail and there might be no son from it reigning upon its throne. And his members, namely all the wicked, thought this had been accomplished when Judah was removed from its land as Israel had been removed; yet Judah’s captivity was not to have a similar end.

For the prophecy spoken in Hosea was to be fulfilled: “For I will no longer have mercy upon the house of Israel, and upon the house of Judah I will have mercy” (Hos. 1). The son from David who reigns on his throne is certainly Christ, of whom the angel said to Mary: “The Lord God shall give him the throne of David his father” (Luke 1). But concerning the temporal and fleshly kingdom of the succession of David’s sons, neither was this said nor did it occur. And God’s truth remains intact: for a long time now no one has sat in this manner upon David’s throne, though God’s covenant with day and His covenant with night have not been annulled, and day and night still remain in their season.

## CHAPTER IV. That by this third head the dragon opposed the Word of God in intention, but cooperated with Him in effect.

At the beginning of the conflict it must now be said that the combatants were very unequal. On one side was God, or the Word of God; on the other, the dragon, or the kingdom already called the dragon’s third head. How utterly unequal were those who met in combat! It was as though a servant fought against his master and, in fighting him, rendered the obedience he had sworn.

The Lord Himself beautifully indicates this when He declares both the devil himself and his servant, the king of Babylon, to be His servants. For He says of the devil to blessed Job: “Will he make a covenant with thee, and wilt thou take him as an everlasting servant?” (Job 40). For we must understand: as he made a covenant with Me and as I received him as an everlasting servant. We must also understand: not by his will, but in effect; for in will he is always an adversary, but in effect, He says, he always cooperates for good with Me and with My elect.

For example, he has now cooperated for good with Me in thee and with thee in Me: so that thou, who wast unknown, may be held known and renowned both in the present time and in all succeeding ages, on earth and in heaven; and that I may have in thee an example of patience to set forth, useful to all My elect who are to be afflicted in the world by various tribulations.

Likewise He says in Jeremiah concerning his servant, the king of Babylon: “Have I not given all these lands into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, my servant?” (Jer. 27). And again: “Behold, I will send and take Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, my servant” (Jer. 25). We must understand this in the same way as with the devil, whose type he bore: “my servant,” not in intention indeed, but nevertheless in cooperation; a servant not by will, but still serving Me in effect and advancing My purpose.

## CHAPTER V. For what sins in the house of David that dragon, His servant, inflicted punishment.

Who has not heard how that evil servant cooperated at that time with the Word of God, God the Word? Who has not heard it? Who does not know that voice of God, that oath of the Word of God: “Once,” He says, “have I sworn by my holiness: if I lie unto David” (Ps. 88 [89])? What have You sworn, O God? And in what do You not lie unto David? “I will establish,” He says, “his seed forever and ever, and his seed shall remain unto eternity. But if his children forsake my law and do not walk in my judgments,” and so forth, as was mentioned above.

That truth of God, that sworn threat of the Lord, was assisted by that evil servant so that it might be fulfilled and accomplished in deed. And we have mentioned above how it had already been partly accomplished: the Lord had visited with a rod and struck with scourges the flood of iniquity which, through Jezebel, wife of Ahab king of Israel (1 Kings 11), had flowed even into the house of David. He struck Jehoram, son-in-law of Ahab and Jezebel, and exterminated all his house except one little child, namely Joash, whom his aunt Jehosheba had stolen away, lest Athaliah, his most cruel grandmother, should kill him with the rest.

But those remnants of David’s house, though struck in this way, did not grieve or accept correction. Joash himself, preserved when so little, did not remember the mercy which Jehoiada the priest had shown him, but killed his son Zechariah the priest, who said: “Why do you transgress the commandment of the Lord?” Likewise the others sinned, except Hezekiah and Josiah. Moreover, Manasseh, the son of that same Hezekiah, provoked the Lord and led the people astray so that they did evil beyond the nations whom the Lord had destroyed before the children of Israel.

It was therefore necessary that the rod should still be raised, the blows multiplied, and the iniquities and sins of David’s sons thus visited. For they had not slightly forsaken the law of the Lord, nor moderately profaned the Lord’s ordinances; indeed, they had done so more than the ten tribes whom the same God, their Judge, had handed over to perpetual captivity.

## CHAPTER VI. That when Jerusalem was besieged and captured and its people carried away, Nebuchadnezzar gloried that he had accomplished it by the strength of his own hand.

How at last, in this affair, did that evil servant serve the Lord God? He came, besieged Jerusalem, captured it, and Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard, burned the house of the Lord and the king’s house; he burned all the houses of Jerusalem, destroyed the entire wall surrounding Jerusalem, and Judah was carried away from its land. Woe to such a servant; woe to him for such service: he was the rod of the Lord’s anger and the staff itself, as was said of Assyria; and it is likewise written concerning the king of Babylon himself: “The Lord has broken the staff of the wicked, the rod of rulers, which struck peoples in indignation with an incurable blow, subjected nations in fury, and persecuted cruelly” (Isa. XIV). Yet he did not think so, nor did his heart judge thus: namely, that through his action the Lord was visiting the iniquities of the sons in the rod, and their sins with blows. Rather, he said, “By the strength of my hand I have done it, and by my wisdom I have understood.” This was as though an axe should boast against him who cuts with it, or a saw exalt itself against him by whom it is drawn; or as though a rod should raise itself against the one who lifts it, and a staff—which is surely wood—should exalt itself. For that he boasted against the Lord, and that his heart was exceedingly exalted and lifted up, is sufficiently indicated by the fact that, in his person, the devil is rebuked—he who, on account of pride and disordered self-exaltation, is known to have fallen from heaven, the king [Col. 1342C] over all the children of pride. “Take up,” says the Lord, “this parable against the king of Babylon, and say: How has the oppressor ceased? How has tribute come to rest? How have you fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, you who rose in the morning?” (ibid.)

## 573 CHAPTER VII. Nebuchadnezzar bore the type of the devil; in effect he served God, but in intention he was a lieutenant of the devil.

Appropriately indeed, just as the power of the Word of God vehemently attacks that man as though he were the devil, so it attacks the devil as though he were a man; for the son of pride performed deeds greatly resembling, by a certain special likeness, those of his king, the devil. For the devil [Col. 1342D] carried the human race captive, in its first parents, from the heavenly Jerusalem; and Nebuchadnezzar carried captive the one people of God then existing from that earthly Jerusalem which bore a great and well-known likeness of that heavenly city. For in the heavenly Jerusalem God is seen; in this earthly Jerusalem there was only the temple in which God was worshipped. Therefore, just as that one city of David then possessed the worship of God, so it shared the name of the heavenly city of God, being called Jerusalem—that is, “vision of peace.” Yet that earthly city did not possess, as it did the name, so also the reality signified by the name; otherwise it would no longer have been a likeness, but the same thing.

Thus, as David, king of this earthly Jerusalem, prefigured Christ, [Col. 1343A] king of the heavenly Jerusalem, so Nebuchadnezzar, king of that Babylon, signified the devil, prince of this world and possessor of everlasting confusion. That Babylon and the earthly Jerusalem exhibit in themselves an image or likeness of the two divisions of the whole rational creation: one is the city of the living God; the other is called, and is, the city of the devil. One consists of good human beings and good angels; the other, of evil human beings and evil angels.

Therefore, when we hear David saying in the Spirit, “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept” (Ps. CXXXVI), we rightly perceive that he also says this truly concerning himself. He did not, indeed, live to the time of that Babylonian captivity; rather, he long preceded it. Yet he was in that captivity, as were all [Col. 1343B] God’s elect, whose likeness he spiritually understood in that captivity which he foresaw was to come upon that people. Therefore Nebuchadnezzar was, in effect, as was said above, the Lord’s servant; but in intention, a foremost attendant of the devil.

## CHAPTER VIII. Although the Lord chastised the people, he did not forget his promise, but raised up prophets and broke the rod.

While the sons of David were under that rod and amid those blows, did not God preserve the invincible truth of what he had promised, what he had sworn by his Holy One: “But my mercy,” he says, “I will not scatter from him” (Ps. LXXXVIII)? He certainly preserved it. And though [Col. 1343C] he delayed that mercy—namely, his Christ—he nevertheless did not allow them to despair or to suspect that he had been so angered by their iniquities and sins that he wished to profane his covenant and make void the things that had gone forth from his lips (Ps. XXXV).

The good Word and faithful utterance came to the captives and went forth with the captives; and he made his heralds and prophets conquerors and standard-bearers of his victory. Thus, just as he said to Moses, “Behold, I have made you a god of Pharaoh” (Exod. VII), so also he might say, and make, one of them a god to the king of Babylon. “For King Nebuchadnezzar fell upon his face and worshipped Daniel, and ordered sacrifices and incense to be brought, that sacrifice might be offered to him” (Dan. II). This the good Word, [Col. 1343D] the Word of God, accomplished by showing himself to Daniel and his companions through wonderful and magnificent visions. By these the faith of the godly was confirmed, the hope of the captives revived, and the love of those who longed for him was strengthened; according to the multitude of sorrows in their hearts, the consolations of the Lord gladdened their souls (Ps. XCIII).

Before that captivity, we rarely find imaginative visions of the Word of God—who was to come in the incarnation and triumph over the devil, prince of this world—shown to the prophets. During the captivity itself, however, we read not only that the word of the Lord came to them, but also that they saw venerable images and consoling visions of the invincible King, the conquering King who would reign: the Word of God, the Word to be incarnate, the Son of God, the Son of Man. In Ezekiel the discourse is [Col. 1344A] more difficult; Daniel, however, the clearer he is, the more delightful he is to read and the sweeter to understand.

It is not the purpose of the present discussion to investigate those visions, but only to consider how, and in what order, the Lord broke that rod or staff with which he had visited the iniquities or sins of the sons, and by what plan the conception of the blessed woman, who had in her womb and cried out, crushed that third head of the dragon—that is, the king or kingdom of Babylon—which sought to devour that conception, namely the faith of Abraham’s seed, the faith in the Word to be incarnate.

## CHAPTER IX. How and in what order the Word of God struck Nebuchadnezzar and at last conquered him.

[Col. 1344B] First it must be noted that the Word of God struck King Nebuchadnezzar himself three times. Since by the first and second blows he was not brought down from the height of his pride, the third time it struck him in such a manner that, cast down from his throne, deprived of reason, and driven outdoors from human company, he lived with beasts, ate fodder with beasts, consumed grass like an ox, was drenched with the dew of heaven, and seven times passed over him.

After this, God numbered and completed his kingdom, the Babylonian kingdom; it was weighed in the balance and found deficient. It was divided and given to the Medes and Persians (Dan. III). For Belshazzar, king of the Chaldeans, was killed, and Darius the Mede succeeded to the kingdom. [Col. 1344C] To whom should this share of victory be ascribed, if not to God—to God’s Word? Every faithful soul carrying him in her womb, as Daniel did, “cried out in travail and was tormented to bring forth” (Apoc. XII). That Word, the mystery of that Word, crushed the dragon’s head; it made that king mad as though he were an ox; it overthrew that kingdom by righteous judgment. The very words of Scripture plainly bear witness to this.

It is pleasant to linger a little and triumphantly proclaim each of these blows against the head of pride, in praise and glory of the victorious Word of God, whose person is declared in the events themselves, whether accomplished or signified, by manifest words.

## CHAPTER X. For many reasons Nebuchadnezzar’s dream was worthy of attention.

[Col. 1344D] “Nebuchadnezzar saw a dream; his spirit was troubled, and the dream fled from him” (Dan. II). In that dream there is a manifold rationale pertaining to the wisdom of the Word of God, who wished to confirm the promises 574 of his coming and console all who awaited that same coming of his—especially those who at that time were held captive under the very king who saw the dream.

First, one must consider the mystery of the dream itself. Next, that not Daniel himself, nor any other holy prophet of the Lord worthy of a vision of God, but Nebuchadnezzar, a man without God, saw such a dream: an unjust and most wicked man, as the three youths sent by him into the burning furnace testify in their prayer. “You have delivered us,” they say, [Col. 1345A] “O Lord God, into the hands of our unjust and most wicked enemies, transgressors, and into the hands of a king unjust and wicked beyond all the earth” (Dan. III).

Further, this too must be considered: Daniel, who would reveal the dream and disclose its interpretation, was not found until the sentence had gone forth that the wise men should be killed, because they could not make known to the king the dream and its interpretation. Nor was it revealed to Daniel himself until he had first gone in and asked the king to grant him time to declare the solution.

Finally, this also should not be absent from our admiration and the Lord’s praise: through this occasion he so honored his captives that Nebuchadnezzar, their very captor, fell upon his face and worshipped Daniel, a mortal man [Col. 1345B] though a wonderful prophet of the wonderful God.

## CHAPTER XI. What Nebuchadnezzar’s dream signified.

We have now learned the mystery of the dream not only by reading, but have also recognized it by seeing. For we were born and reborn in the days in which the God of heaven raised up “a kingdom which shall never be destroyed, and its kingdom shall not be handed over to another people” (Dan. II). Through it, the golden kingdom then belonging to Babylon, the silver kingdom of the Medes and Persians which succeeded it, the bronze kingdom of the Macedonians that followed, and the Roman kingdom, once iron but now in great part beginning to become [Col. 1345C] clay, evidently are being broken up and consumed.

We see that this has happened and is happening as he saw: a stone was cut from the mountain without hands and shattered the clay, iron, bronze, silver, and gold. And the stone which struck, and which at the last judgment will still strike these kingdoms so that no place is found for them, “became a great mountain and filled the whole earth” (ibid.), because it has openly become known to the entire earth that the Word was made flesh—that is, was made man from a Virgin, without the hands of those embracing her—and is King of kings and Lord of lords.

That mystery, then revealed through Daniel and his companions, afforded great and timely consolation to the humility of the captives, who in their captivity sighed in hope of God’s promise. For how great, do you suppose, was their grief and weariness of heart at that time? How [Col. 1345D] full of sighing, when they saw God’s kingdom delayed, while meanwhile the kingdoms of the world—and the head of kingdoms, Babylon’s kingdom—seemed, beneath the morning sun, prepared to sit enthroned, to leap upon towers and horses? A dream of this kind, containing so great a mystery, therefore came opportunely to relieve the exhaustion of the sorrowful, so that they might then possess their souls in patience (Luke XXI), looking not at present things but toward those to come, and consoling the condition of their imminent evils through hope of future goods.

## CHAPTER XII. [Col. 1346A] Why Nebuchadnezzar, rather than someone else, saw this dream.

That not Daniel himself, nor another man worthy of God, but Nebuchadnezzar—a man unjust and most wicked—saw so great a dream, might rightly astonish us because of his unworthiness, if he had not been troubled by the dream itself and if his dream had not fled from him. But now, since “his spirit was troubled and the dream fled from him” (Dan. II), we are not astonished, knowing the order of justice: for just as there is truly no participation of light with darkness, no agreement of Christ with Belial (II Cor. VIII), so there is no share for an impious soul with the Word of God, no fellowship of the foolish and unjust with God’s counsel.

Yet in such a dream there was, and is, a true word and a profound counsel of God. How, then, could the soul of a foolish and impious man—a soul torn apart and not held together by even the least reverence for the divine name—contain the reality of so great a mystery which it had seen? Let no one object that Pharaoh saw a dream and retained it in memory, and say that God showed Pharaoh what would come to pass. For that Pharaoh was not yet as impious as Nebuchadnezzar, and the prediction in his dream of the coming famine in no way corresponded to Nebuchadnezzar’s dream, which was a prediction of God’s eternal kingdom.

Thus, in a certain way, he did see the dream; but, as he says, “Confused in mind, I do not know what I saw.” Let us not suppose that he was admitted to the Word or counsel of God; rather, let us know that he was driven away in righteous indignation from a sight of which he was unworthy. [Col. 1346C] For the very fact that he says, “Confused in mind, I do not know what I saw” (Dan. II), and that it is said, “the dream fled from him,” sufficiently suggests that, in dreaming thus, he provoked wrath against himself, as though it were said to him in his dream: “How have you presumed to dream anything of this kind?”
