For truly a presumptuous and proud thought was the cause of this dream, as Daniel himself testifies: “You, O king, began to think upon your bed what should come to pass hereafter” (ibid.). As though something had already been achieved merely because he had become king, and as though nothing greater or better could come about than his own kingdom, he thought what should be after these things. God answered his thoughts as he deserved: namely, so that he should neither understand nor be able to bear it, though, astonished and confused, he should remember that something had happened around him.

## CHAPTER XIII. The king’s cruelty secured Daniel the interpreter a favorable and attentive hearing.

For his part, in seeking and obtaining the dream which had escaped him, he was cruelly eager and eagerly cruel, when in great wrath and anger he commanded that all the wise men of Babylon should perish because they could not tell him the dream. But God and his Word, without his knowing it, mercifully made use of that cruelty. In what way? Namely, that before revealing so great a mystery, he might first make everyone [Col. 1347A] attentive.

For the mysteries of the Word of God are pearls; but diviners, magicians, sorcerers, and Chaldeans, together with their king and all the Babylonians, were swine, before whom pearls of this kind are not to be cast. But if Daniel, or one of his companions or fellow captives, had seen that dream and expounded its interpretation before the Babylonians, for the consolation of the captives whose hope depended upon the future kingdom of God, would they not have cast pearls too freely before swine? And assuredly they would not merely have trampled them underfoot, but, turning upon those who dared to hope, would cruelly have torn them to pieces (Matt. VII).

God’s wisdom, therefore, rightly made use of the excessive curiosity of the furious king. For by his urgent power, by his powerful urgency and great wrath, [Col. 1347B] the decree for execution of the wise men went forth. Meanwhile Daniel and his companions were sought in order that they too might perish; and during the respite requested by him, all the wise men hung beneath the sword, doomed to die unless he, at least, by recounting the dream, should bring protection from their common danger. By these means, I say, all—from greatest to least, including the king himself—became attentive to hear, ready to receive, most eager and very teachable in understanding, and well disposed to praise.

Thus at last the Word of God judged it fitting to set himself forth in their midst, because surely the occasion and circumstances did not allow so great a pearl of mystery to be trampled underfoot.

## CHAPTER XIV. King Nebuchadnezzar could not hear the Word of God from Daniel’s mouth without falling upon his face.

[Col. 1347C] Who, then, would not marvel that King Nebuchadnezzar, fierce as a lion—or like a lioness—upon hearing the truth of the dream, fell upon his face and worshipped Daniel? (Dan. II). Did he do this, pierced by true devotion? Did he honor the true God in his servant by loving him, or love him by honoring him? What follows strongly contradicts this: for he made a golden statue of wondrous size and commanded that the three youths who refused to worship it—Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego—be thrown into the blazing furnace. “And who,” he says, “is the god who will deliver you from my hand?” (Dan. III).

We must therefore rather understand that, just as when he saw the dream “his spirit was troubled and his mind confused,” so when he heard it and, in hearing, felt the power of the present Word of God from the mouth of a man to whom the Word of the Lord had truly come—whose heart it truly inhabited and from whose mouth it wonderfully sounded—he could not endure the Word of the Lord. He could not remain seated or standing, but fell; and thus he worshipped, thus he confessed, just as demons trembled and confessed when Christ himself was incarnate and present.

Thus Daniel, captive of the king who had captured him, became a god to that king. But that fierce captor, foolish worshipper, still had to be conquered, until he ate grass like an ox. For no small pride belonged to that madman, nor small madness to that proud man. Although he had been so terrified and had so fallen upon his face in worshipping Daniel as to say, “Truly your God is God of gods and Lord of kings” (Dan. II), and though he [Col. 1348A] raised that same Daniel to high rank and appointed his companions over the works of Babylon, Scripture immediately adds what he did next:

## CHAPTER XV. Nebuchadnezzar was still so proud as to command that his statue be worshipped.

“King Nebuchadnezzar made a golden statue, sixty cubits high and six cubits broad, and set it up in the plain of Dura in the province of Babylon. Then King Nebuchadnezzar sent to assemble the satraps, magistrates, judges, commanders, tyrants, prefects, and all the rulers of the regions, that they might come to the dedication of the statue which King Nebuchadnezzar had erected” (Dan. III).

See how the evil servant of the Lord helps fulfill the truth of God and the true interpretation of his dream. See the reason why he had been designated in the dream by the golden head of the statue, when the interpreter said: “The head of this statue was of finest gold, and you, O king, are the golden head” (Dan. II). Nebuchadnezzar truly became a great head of idolatry by making such a statue and summoning a multitude of peoples and rulers to its dedication, while a herald loudly proclaimed: “To you it is commanded, peoples, tribes, and tongues: at the hour when you hear the sound of the trumpet, pipe, lyre, sambuca, psaltery, symphonia, and every kind of musical instrument, fall down and worship the golden statue which King Nebuchadnezzar has set up. But whoever does not fall down and worship shall, in that same hour, be cast into the blazing furnace” (Dan. III).

[Col. 1348C] Nowhere does Scripture recall that before him anyone had so great a zeal for founding idolatry, had fashioned—or seen—a statue so dreadful, not to say so costly, or had imposed so cruel an edict for the worship of an idol. Babylon is therefore rightly called by the prophet a golden cup intoxicating all the earth; and likewise the whole body of the impious devoted to idolatry is written of or shown as follows: “Holding a golden cup in her hand, full of the abominations and uncleanness of her fornication; and upon her forehead was written: Mystery, Babylon the Great, mother of fornications and abominations of the earth” (Apoc. XVII).

By Babylon’s cup or goblet, we understand its sweet deception, of this sort or like that which the king of Babylon then literally offered under that name, when he employed the sound of trumpet, pipe, lyre, sambuca, psaltery, symphonia, and every kind of musical instrument to entice the peoples. Thus, intoxicated by the festive sweetness of the sounds, all peoples, tribes, and tongues might fall down to worship the golden statue of a corruptible man—which truly is to fall.

## CHAPTER XVI. Why Scripture attributes a golden cup to the Babylonian harlot.

The reason, I think, sufficiently appears why Nebuchadnezzar himself was called the golden head and why there was a golden cup in Babylon’s hand: namely, because he elevated the capital madness of idolatry by making a golden statue so immense and laborious, bringing it to completion at such expense and through such foolish toil. At its golden appearance, combined with the sweetness of music, as has already been said, the souls of covetous mortals could be intoxicated or maddened as by a full cup.

The matter itself now prompts us to ask why the kingdom of the Medes and Persians, succeeding that kingdom, was signified by the silver breast and arms of the statue Nebuchadnezzar dreamed of; why the kingdom of the Greeks was signified by the bronze of the belly and thighs; and why the Roman kingdom was marked or signified by iron legs and feet partly of iron and partly of clay.

It has indeed already been said before our time, and is customary to say, that the kingdom of the Medes and Persians was signified by silver because it was so much inferior to the Babylonian kingdom as silver is judged inferior to gold—something not difficult to establish from histories. They say, moreover, that the Greek kingdom was signified by bronze because bronze is both hard and very resonant, while the Greeks were strong and especially eloquent.

576 Yet although this interpretation is true and good, the purpose of our present argument suggests still other reasons. For it is agreeable, according to one’s ability, to give or discover particular reasons why those kingdoms provoked against themselves that stone which “was cut from the mountain without hands, struck the statue, shattered it, and broke it to pieces.” For the Word of God, whose victory this little work intends to celebrate, was a stone before he became flesh, and is one now after he was made flesh; and through him, with him, and in him, each kingdom has in its own time been struck and broken. At the end they are to be broken so utterly that they will be reduced as it were to dust, and, like dust caught up by the wind, no place will be found for them.

## CHAPTER XVII. For what reasons the Babylonian kingdom was signified by gold, and the Persian and Median kingdom by silver.

Let us therefore observe that, as the Babylonian kingdom—or King Nebuchadnezzar—provoked that stone, namely the Word of God, the Son of God, by its gold (and we rightly marvel that he confessed him to be this, saying, “The appearance of the fourth is like a Son of God” [Dan. III]), so the pride of the Median kingdom—namely, the exceedingly proud Haman—stirred the same stone against itself [Col. 1349D] by its silver. For he said to King Ahasuerus: “If it pleases you, decree that the Jewish nation perish, and I will weigh out ten thousand talents to the treasurers of your treasury.” And the king said to him: “The silver which you promise is yours; deal with the people as you please” (Esth. III).

Surely the silver weighed out or offered for the universal destruction of the Jewish people is, or ought to be, no small matter for reflection: it was contrary to God’s purpose, contrary to the word of promise, which could not be fulfilled if the intended effect of the devil—raging in Haman—had been attained. Indeed, when Daniel said to Nebuchadnezzar, “You are the golden head,” and afterward, “A kingdom inferior to you shall arise” (Dan. II), we willingly understand this as referring implicitly to the work of wickedness or malice. That kingdom, namely, acted less against the word of promise than Babylon’s kingdom did.

Even if that kingdom surpassed the Persian and Median kingdom by as much as gold exceeds silver, was the Persian and Median kingdom correspondingly more abundant than the Greek and Roman kingdoms by as much as silver is more precious than bronze and iron? Therefore, for the same reason that Nebuchadnezzar or his kingdom is signified by gold, the kingdom of the Medes and Persians is rightly understood to be signified by silver: in the former case the devil strove, armed with gold; in the latter, with silver, to prevent fulfillment of the word of promise.

## CHAPTER XVIII. [Col. 1350B] Why the kingdom of the Greeks was signified by bronze.

For the same reason we rightly understand the Greek kingdom to be signified in the same statue by the metal bronze. For what did that kingdom do? What did the dragon, the devil, and Antiochus, the devil’s attendant, do there? He cruelly used his frying-pans and bronze pots. For when seven brothers with their mother had been seized, he ordered frying-pans and bronze pots to be heated, and, after the skin of each of their heads had been stripped off with the hair and the extremities of hands and feet cut off, ordered them, while still breathing, to be roasted in the frying-pan (II Macc. VII).

Thus the impious man used his bronze against God, with the devil acting through him, in order to erase from their hearts the word of promise and covenant of God, to whom the promise had been given or to whose fathers it had been made. For Antiochus, driven by the devil, wrote throughout his entire kingdom that all the people should be one. The Jews, indeed all Syria, were under his rule. What then did the spirit of the devil intend by this, except that, when the Jews passed over into one body with the other peoples subject to his kingdom, the promise might perish, since there would nowhere remain an expectation of the promise?

Because a very few refused to do this, among the other evils he brought upon them, this was the greatest: he cruelly applied heated frying-pans and bronze pots to the seven brothers just mentioned and to their mother. Is this not a sufficient reason why that kingdom should be understood through the bronze belly and bronze thighs of the statue? Moreover, in the bronze thighs let indecency be understood together with cruelty: for while these things occurred, the temple was full of luxury, revelry, and men consorting with prostitutes; women even intruded themselves into the sacred precincts, bringing in things which were forbidden (II Macc. VI).

## CHAPTER XIX. Why the Roman kingdom was signified by iron legs, and feet partly iron and partly clay.

Concerning the Roman kingdom, the reason why it was signified by iron legs and feet partly iron and partly clay is plainly given in the words: “As iron breaks and crushes all things, so the fourth kingdom shall break and crush all things.” Yet the fact that one part of the feet was seen to be iron and another clay still requires investigation if it is to become clearer, although the same interpreter almost explains it, saying there: “But because you saw part of the feet and toes to be pottery and part iron, the kingdom shall be divided, though it shall arise from the stock of iron. According as you saw iron mixed with pottery made from clay, and the toes of the feet partly iron and partly clay, the kingdom shall be partly strong and partly broken. But because you saw iron mixed with pottery and clay, they shall indeed mingle by human seed, but they shall not adhere to one another, just as iron cannot be mixed with pottery” (Dan. II).

We can by no means discover more fittingly the definite time in which these things are known to have occurred than by following the prophetic text immediately added: “But in the days [Col. 1351B] of those kingdoms the God of heaven raised up a kingdom which shall never be destroyed, nor shall its kingdom be handed over to another people.” Therefore the time in which God raised up the eternal kingdom—when the stone was cut from the mountain without hands and shattered clay, iron, bronze, silver, and gold—was the time, I say, when Jesus Christ, God and man, was conceived and born from a Virgin without conjugal intercourse.

Let us consider the condition of the Roman kingdom at that time, which was undoubtedly signified by iron. For when it says, “In the days of those kingdoms,” this is as if it said: When these kingdoms have succeeded one another in sequence, the God of heaven shall raise up a kingdom which shall never be destroyed.

## CHAPTER XX. [Col. 1351C] What the mixture of iron and clay signifies.

Therefore, in the feet of the statue, by the incompatible signs of iron and clay, one may suppose that there was signified what had happened to the Romans when Christ was born of the Virgin. What had happened? This, indeed: through the greatest civil discords Roman power had come to a kingdom and monarchy. Who has not heard of those discords? Who is ignorant of those civil wars? The world was wearied, and is still wearied, as scholars read them, historians recount them, and even boys repeat them: the fierce, irreconcilable conflicts of nearly all the Romans, but especially of Pompey and Gaius Caesar; likewise the civil wars of Antony and Octavian Augustus, through [Col. 1351D] and amid which Octavian Augustus himself became monarch of the Romans. In his days the stone was cut without hands from the mountain; while he reigned, Christ was born from a Virgin; and in the times of both him and his successor Tiberius Caesar, God’s eternal kingdom was raised up through the passion and resurrection of the same Jesus Christ.

By the iron and clay in the statue’s feet, then, we willingly understand those discords and civil wars to be signified. This is what is written: “Because you saw part of the feet and toes to be pottery and part iron, the kingdom shall be divided, though it shall arise from the stock of iron”—that is, from excessive strength, rising envy will cause the kingdom to be divided. And this same point is repeated: “Because you saw iron mixed [Col. 1352A] with pottery made from clay, they shall indeed mingle by human seed, but they shall not adhere to one another, just as iron cannot be mixed with pottery” (Dan. II).

This must be understood with great astonishment, because they were not merely fellow citizens but even kinsmen: Pompey was the father-in-law of Gaius Caesar, and Antony the brother-in-law of Octavian; yet they were no more able to cleave together in harmony than iron can be mixed with pottery. And they disagreed until the weaker party, defeated, withdrew. There one part of a single and identical Roman strength overcame the other so swiftly and powerfully that the defeated part may be compared to earthen pottery and the victorious part to iron:

> One battle-line suffers the war; the other wages it . . . .

says the distinguished author, describing those civil wars (Lucan, *Pharsalia* VII, 501). Likewise, he refers to the one who was superior—that is, to the aforesaid Gaius Caesar (*ibid.*, *Pharsalia* I, 82–85):

> Gaul held you warring through two five-year periods—  
> What part of the world is that? If a few battles  
> Fell to a favorable outcome, Rome would have subjected the world to you.

And so it happened. The sum of what has been said is this: through the disparity of clay and iron, the civil discords of the fourth—that is, the Roman—kingdom may rightly be understood. Let us now return to the sequence.

## CHAPTER XXI. Why Nebuchadnezzar exclaimed: “Behold, I see four men unbound, and the appearance of the fourth is like a Son of God.”

[Col. 1352C] A matter of great wonder in the golden head, Nebuchadnezzar, set against the golden statue which Nebuchadnezzar erected, is this: he cries out, “Did we not,” he says, “cast three men bound into the midst of the fire?” And when his nobles answered him and said, “Certainly, O king,” he said, “Behold, I see four men unbound, walking in the midst of the fire, and there is no harm in them; and the appearance of the fourth is like a Son of God” (Dan. III).

The whole world heard this utterance of great exclamation from the mouth of a Gentile and impious king. And who can sufficiently marvel where that man had seen the Son of God, so that he could recognize his likeness in the midst of the fire? For he said: “The appearance of the fourth is like a Son of God.” Those speak in this way who recognize, at another time or in another place, in some person, a form formerly seen somewhere, observed and retained in the mind, marked in memory. “This man,” they say, “is like that one whom I saw”; “this is like that which I observed there or there.” “How like this young man is to my cousin,” someone says, looking at the younger Tobias (Tobit VII). For he had seen the father and observed a similar appearance in the son, as commonly happens.

But where had this man seen the Son of God, that he could recognize his appearance in the one who had descended with Azariah and his companions into the furnace, into the midst of the fire? He had never seen the Son of God; nor had he ever learned by reading or hearing who or what the Son of God was. Did he not, therefore, speak with a mind not his own? Did he not utter these words in a great ecstasy? Truly, in a great ecstasy and great amazement. The astonishment was not slight which Scripture expressed almost lightly when, in the passage cited above, it said: “Then King Nebuchadnezzar was astonished and rose up quickly” (Dan. III).

## CHAPTER XXII. Why the designation “Son of God” ought first to have been used by an enemy and persecutor.

The fair portion of the victory, and the distinguished proclamation of the Word of God, the Son of God, is that an enemy confessed him first in open confession before a friend did; a persecutor before an executor; an unjust man before a just man; a Gentile before a Jew. For which among all the prophets even expressed this name, “Son of God,” so openly? Throughout the prophetic Scriptures we have “Word of God,” and this Word of God is the Son [Col. 1353B]; but the world did not know him, so that not even among the Jews, to whom the Word of God had been entrusted, was it safe to preach this name, which is “Son of God.” “He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him” (John 1); and not only did the world not know him, but even the Jew could not bear the proclamation concerning him. Hence the prophets had to close, bind, and seal his testimonies in the Scriptures. For, as has already been said, not even worshippers of God could endure it, nor would they allow it to be heard that there was any generation of God, any Son of God.

Through this chief among his princes—whom neither Jew nor Gentile could accuse, whose mouth the world would not dare suppress—the world first heard this name, “Son of God.” Yet perhaps even this great preacher was asleep and dreaming when he proclaimed that name. For we should not suppose that he slept only now, when he dreamed that great statue, of which mention has already been made above, and lost the dream, not knowing what he had seen. Rather, his whole life was a dream, insofar as he uttered anything good concerning God; whatever blessing and praise he uttered was a dream. For just as he lost that dream of the statue, so everything of praise that he declaimed concerning God swiftly vanished altogether from his heart.

Finally, after the interpretation of the dream—or statue—which he had seen, he worshipped Daniel, saying: “Truly, your God is God of gods and Lord of kings” (Dan. 2). Yet afterward, when he dedicated a golden statue, [Col. 1353D] he sent the servants of that same God into the furnace of fire. “And who,” he said, “is the God who will deliver you from my hand?” (Dan. 3). Again, he who said, “Blessed be the God of Sidrach, that is, Misach and Abdenago” (ibid.), etc., afterward, in proud defiance of God’s decree which he had seen or heard, answered: “Is not this great Babylon, which I have built as the house of my kingdom, by the strength of my power and for the glory of my majesty?” (Dan. 4). Immediately, because of his pride, he deserved to become like an ox.

## CHAPTER XXIII. That Nebuchadnezzar’s confession and praise were, because of pride and swollen vanity, reprehensible.

Now, then, so that it may become increasingly clear how rightly those declamations are approved, consider that “praise is not fitting in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclus. 15) [Col. 1354A]; for it is wholly sprinkled with the leaven of swollen vanity. For how did he give praise when he wrote: “Nebuchadnezzar the king, to all peoples, nations, and languages that dwell in all the earth: Peace be multiplied to you. The Most High God has wrought signs and wonders with me. Therefore it pleased me to proclaim his signs” (Dan. 3)? How great he considers himself in his own eyes when he says, “The Most High God wrought signs with me”! And then, “Therefore it pleased me”! For what does “he wrought them with me” and “it pleased me” mean, except: He wrought them for my sake, and it turned out well for that God because it pleased me?

Truly, just as the Most High God does not deem praise worthy unless it comes from a humble spirit, so it was just and fitting that he should reject the exaltation of that man’s lofty eyes [Col. 1354B], who, while praising the One worthy of praise, lied in the very act of praise. For the Most High God had not wrought signs with him, since he was not a friend; rather, he had wrought them against him, because he was an enemy of the Most High God and of his servants. And which of the righteous kings or patriarchs who saw God’s mighty works ever said—or ought to have said—while recounting them: “God wrought signs with me”? Likewise, when speaking of those saints, we do not say, nor ought we to say, “With him” or “with them”; rather, God performed wonders through him and through them, or before them—for example, in the land of Egypt.

Therefore, just as the Most High God says of the king of all the children of pride, “I will not spare him mighty words, framed for entreaty” (Job 41), so one may rightly say of this son of pride [Col. 1354C] that God did not spare him, nor ought to have spared him—that is, on account of his loud praise and lofty magnificence.

## CHAPTER XXIV. That, as the Son of God was present with the three boys in the furnace, so he will be present with all who confess him.

Nor should this be passed over: even if that foolish man had not said, “The appearance of the fourth is like the Son of God” (Dan. 3), we who now live and endeavor to contemplate the mysteries of the eternal kingdom in events performed in time could knowingly and in the true sense say—and do now say—that “the appearance of the fourth was like the Son of God.” That is: he who appeared fourth in the furnace of fire and wonderfully preserved the servants of the Most High God was a sign, and in himself signified [Col. 1354D] what the Son of God, the Word of God, would do and had already begun to do.

For when has he been absent from his servants as they struggle for the Word of God? Above all, this was to happen in the times of his Gospel: the king of great Babylon, the devil, would assail faith in the holy Trinity by public edicts and proscriptions. And so it happened under the pagan kings of the Roman Empire, who served the devil. Was the Son of God not always present with devout martyrs, both in the flames and in their other struggles? For example, when the distinguished martyr Lawrence was placed upon fires for faith in the Son of God: because he was roasted and gave up his spirit upon a gridiron and over a fire, would you therefore say that the Son of God was absent and stood far away from his fires? Rather, he was more present to him and triumphed more gloriously in him [Col. 1355A] than if he had shaken away the coals and made his burning gridiron like a breeze blowing with dew. He passed through fire, and the flame did him no harm; nor was there the smell of fire upon him, because his faith was not injured—indeed, like gold, it was tested through fire.

Thus we perceive in that Babylonian furnace the appearance of the fourth, like the Son of God: for just as those three boys were preserved through the appearance that was seen there, so through the invisible presence of the Son of God faith in the eternal Trinity remained unharmed in the holy martyrs. And the Roman Empire deserved at length to confess Christ, the Son of God, more loudly and sweetly than that Babylonian king had done.

## CHAPTER XXV. Why God did not defend the temple from being burned, as he defended the three boys.

Could this Most High God not keep his temple, which was in Jerusalem, unharmed from the flames of Babylonian burning—he who preserved the three boys so in the furnace of fire that the fire had no power over their bodies, the hairs of their heads were not singed, their trousers were not altered, and the smell of fire did not pass over them? [Col. 1355B] Certainly he could. But the world had to be taught that the Most High God does not delight in fine stones or golden walls of a handmade temple, but in the brightness of faith and pure hearts; that is the place desirable to him.

For since Moses constructed the tabernacle by God’s authority, and Solomon built and adorned the temple with such labor, gold, and jewels, covetous people, thinking wrongly about God, could suppose that he was like themselves; and, taking no care for the religion of righteousness, they might think that they honored God sufficiently with gifts of gold and might reinforce their own covetousness as though by God’s example. He took care worthily to remove this suspicion from himself by fulfilling in deed what he said to Solomon when Solomon had completed the building of the Lord’s house: “But if you and your sons turn away in turning away, not following me nor keeping my commandments, I will remove Israel from the face of the land which I gave them, and the temple which I sanctified to my name I will cast away from my sight” (3 Kings 9) [Col. 1355C].

“Solomon,” says Stephen the first martyr, “built him a house; but the Most High does not dwell in things made by hands, as he says through the prophet: ‘Heaven is my throne, but earth the footstool of my feet. What house will you build for me, says the Lord, or what is the place of my rest? Has not my hand made all these things?’” (Acts 7).

Rightly, therefore, he showed that for a time and in the given matter he cared little for the temple, or for the gold of the handmade temple; but he has never ceased to glorify and spread abroad his name and the Word of promise, in which is life.

## CHAPTER XXVI. Though Nebuchadnezzar was defeated so often, he was never humbled from the heart.

Nebuchadnezzar the king had now been warned once and twice to subside from his loftiness [Col. 1356A] and, though a mortal man, to think humbly of himself. The first warning was terrible, but the following one was more terrible and severe. For in the first he was merely frightened; in the second he also suffered loss among his own men, since the flame of fire killed those very strong men from his army who, at his command, had cast the servants of the Most High God into the furnace.

Therefore a just sentence afterward came upon him, preceded by a vision whose interpretation foretold the sentence itself; yet the untamable pride of his heart nonetheless persisted. For, that we may know how great was the arrogance in his heart and the exaltation in his eyes, it is significantly said: “At the end of twelve months”—that is, after he had seen the dream concerning the tree to be cut down and had heard its interpretation—“he was walking in the palace of Babylon, and the king answered and said: ‘Is not this great Babylon, which I have built as the house of my kingdom, by the strength of my power and for the glory of my majesty?’” (Dan. 4) [Col. 1356B].

To whom, or against what, is he said to have answered, except against what he had heard: “This is the interpretation of the Most High which has come upon my lord the king: They shall drive you from men; your dwelling shall be with the beasts; and you shall eat grass like an ox” (ibid.)? Thus the exceedingly great fault of pride is clear in that place: considering the greatness of Babylon, the strength of his power, and the breadth, as he supposed, of his glory, he judged impossible what he had heard upon divine authority. He thought it easier for the word of the Lord, according to the interpretation of the dream, to pass away unfulfilled than for anything adverse to come upon himself, so great a king of great Babylon.

Therefore, when it is immediately added, “While the word was still in the king’s mouth, a voice fell from heaven: ‘To you it is spoken, King Nebuchadnezzar: your kingdom has passed from you’” (ibid.), etc., it is openly proclaimed that, as omnipotence is just, so too is the justice of the Almighty: for the Holy and Just One punishes no one with humiliation unless that person stubbornly exalts himself.

## CHAPTER XXVII. That Nebuchadnezzar ate grass like an ox.

Finally, it should be noted that this same Nebuchadnezzar became like the devil, the captor of the human race, both in fault and in punishment. For the Lord had said of him to blessed Job: “Behold Behemoth, whom I made with you: he will eat grass like an ox” (Job 40) [Col. 1356D]. Therefore, when Nebuchadnezzar, cast out from among men, ate grass like an ox, it is plainly given to understand that in his punishment he became like the devil: for what the latter did spiritually, the former did bodily; what the latter does without ceasing, the former did for seven years—a number by which universality is customarily signified.

For the devil eats grass: that is, he incorporates into himself carnal people, of whom it is written: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory like the flower of the field. Truly the people are grass: the grass has dried up and the flower has fallen” (Isa. 40). He eats only such grass as an ox, because there is nothing in those over whom that Behemoth has prevailed except the greenness of flesh. And what more is there in those who strike against his teeth than what follows: “But the word of the Lord remains for ever” (Isa. 40)? [Col. 1357A]

Therefore, how just and how beautiful is the judgment by which that once most powerful king ate grass like an ox—as if the voice which fell from heaven upon him were saying (Dan. 4): “To you it is spoken, King Nebuchadnezzar: you wished to destroy the Word of the Lord, which remains for ever, by setting Jerusalem on fire and the temple of the Lord, the only place in which the Lord’s name was invoked. But neither you nor Behemoth, your father, nor any who belong to his party, will be able to bring it about that the word of promise should pass away in vain, however much you afflict or devour grass or the flower of grass—that is, carnal people or the glory of carnal people. Some of these are permitted to you, although descended from Abraham, because they are indeed children of the flesh but not children of the promise, and therefore do not deserve to be counted in the seed.”

## CHAPTER XXVIII. In what sense it was true that Nebuchadnezzar said: “Is not this Babylon which I built?”

Do you think Nebuchadnezzar spoke truly when he boasted: “Is not this Babylon which I built?” (Dan. 4). For, as Pompeius Trogus reports, Semiramis founded Babylon and surrounded the city with a wall of baked brick, with sand, pitch, and bitumen laid between the materials. Did he therefore speak truly, being so much later than Semiramis, wife of Ninus, in whom the kingdom of the Assyrians began? [Col. 1357C]

Nevertheless, sacred authority prevails: Babylon existed before Semiramis, and the cause of its name is set forth in the most ancient sacred writings. “Cush,” it says, “the son of Ham, begot Nimrod; he began to be mighty on the earth. And the beginning of his kingdom was Babylon. From that land Asshur went out and built Nineveh” (Gen. 10). The reason for the name Babylon was that there God confused the language of those who were building, and they ceased to build the city. For “therefore,” it says, “its name was called Babel, because there the speech of the whole earth was confused” (Gen. 11).

Therefore that vainglorious man, of whom Wisdom says in the case of any such person, “Clouds and wind and rain that do not follow: a vainglorious man who does not fulfill promises” (Prov. 25)—that vainglorious man, I say, full and swollen with the wind of vanity, perhaps because he had enlarged Babylon by his own resources and expenditures, valuing highly, or wishing others to value highly, his own undertaking or work, loudly declaimed the answer of a proud heart and stiff neck: “Is not this Babylon which [Col. 1358A] I built?”—rather than saying, “which I advanced” or “enlarged.”

And what then, vainglorious man, if you had built Babylon from its foundations? Even so, could you have made void the word you had heard, namely the interpretation of the dream? Therefore, because the word of God is as just as it is almighty, the voice of judgment rightly fell upon you, even if in some fashion you had followed the counsel of the holy prophet, who said: “Redeem your sins by alms, and your iniquities by mercies to the poor; perhaps he will forgive your offenses” (Dan. 4).

## CHAPTER XXIX. That Nebuchadnezzar lost not only his mind but also his form when he ate grass like an ox.

Finally, it must be said concerning this man that the question is commonly asked whether he lost only his mind and not also his bodily form. Indeed, when he himself says, “I, Nebuchadnezzar, lifted my eyes to heaven, and my understanding was restored to me” (Dan. 4) [Col. 1358B], our elders maintain that, when he says his understanding was restored, he shows that he lost not his form but his mind.

But there still arises what seems to oppose this: later he repeats, “At that time my understanding returned to me, and I came to the honor and splendor of my kingdom; and my appearance returned to me, and my nobles and magistrates sought me” (ibid.). Among other things, when he says there, “my appearance returned to me,” it is certainly given to understand that he lost something of the form, or uprightness, of the human condition. Even if the shape of his hands and feet, and the distinction or distinct number of his fingers, remained, he nevertheless walked on all fours—especially since it was said expressly, “You shall eat grass like an ox” (ibid.) [Col. 1358C].

And he ate grass like an ox, for an ox is a quadruped which uses no hands, since nature did not create hands for it; rather, bent down to the ground, it cuts grass with its teeth and eats as it drags its mouth along the earth. Moreover, the statement in the sentence, “Your dwelling shall be with beasts and wild animals” (ibid.), proves to some extent, as has been said, that his form was changed—especially because he said, “My appearance returned to me,” and because beasts or wild animals would not readily associate with him unless he bore some likeness to them.

Yet whatever the state of his form may have been, this is to be admired in praise of the almighty Word of God: that he altered so powerful a king by a transformation greater than any transformation of a human being that sacred Scripture anywhere records, except that of Lot’s wife, who, looking back behind herself, was changed into a pillar of salt.

# BOOK SEVEN

[Col. 1357]

## CHAPTER I. That King Belshazzar was already defeated by the Word of God when the hand of a man appeared writing on the wall.

After the victorious action of the Word of God, by which it strongly cast down a human king, a proud man and an exalted king, and powerfully humbled him [Col. 1358D], it came also to overthrow the kingdom itself. It first sent an astonishing sign of itself, or of its presence, while King Belshazzar was celebrating a banquet and was already drunk with his nobles, his wives, and his concubines.

“While they drank wine in the sacred vessels of the temple of the Lord and praised their gods of silver and gold, bronze, iron, wood, and stone, in that very hour there appeared fingers like the hand of a man writing opposite the lampstand, on the surface of the wall of the royal hall; and the king saw the joints of the writing hand. Then the king’s face was changed, and his thoughts troubled him; the joints of his loins were loosened and his knees knocked one against another” (Dan. 5) [Col. 1359A].

That writing was a sign of the Word of God, now about to rise, now about to rush upon and overthrow the pride of the tyrannical kingdom—the kingdom of the Assyrians and Chaldeans—which, from the times of Ninus and his wife Semiramis, had for nearly thirteen hundred years pressed the necks of peoples beneath a harsh yoke. That king of a most powerful empire could not bear even the small signs of that same Word, the few letters of its judgment, the true judges, while he could not yet understand them or anyone read them. He could not endure seeing them. His face changed and his mind was disturbed; the lustful loins of the man sitting among his wives were loosened, and the knees of the lustful man drinking among his concubines knocked against one another. Thus it was openly made plain how weak he was who seemed strong and commanding.

## CHAPTER II. That Daniel was not disturbed, but confidently looked, read, and interpreted.

But he to whom and for whom—or for whose like—God, the Word of God, came and contended, did not turn pale and was not disturbed. Called to read and asked to interpret, he stood before them in familiar confidence [Col. 1359C], looked confidently, read knowingly, and interpreted wisely: “Mane, Thecel, Phares.” “Mane: God has numbered your kingdom and completed it. Thecel: you have been weighed in the balance and found wanting. Phares: your kingdom has been divided and given to the Medes and Persians” (Dan. 5).

How brief were the words, yet how much length, breadth, and height they displayed to the soul of the man who possessed love for the Word of God! Its lofty and deep hidden counsel was contained in those three words, six syllables, and fourteen letters. From what was written, “Mane,” which means “number,” he saw in the breadth of his heart the narrow duration of the Assyrian or Babylonian kingdom: it had not happened by chance, but by the just judgment of God, that it could press so many nations beneath its yoke for, as has been said, thirteen hundred years [Col. 1359D].

Let us read this Scripture carefully and follow its divine interpretation. Since it is reported to have been written opposite the lampstand, it urges us to approach the lampstand so that we may see clearly. Our lampstand is Christ; our light is the Word of God. “Your Word,” says the Psalmist, “is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths” (Ps. 118). Therefore, that we may obtain a fuller interpretation of the brief writing, let us follow the teachings of the Word of God which we possess in the holy Scriptures.

## CHAPTER III. What the first word, Mane—that is, “he has numbered”—means.

“Mane,” he says, “God has numbered your kingdom and completed it” (Dan. 5). When or how did God number it? When or how did God complete that kingdom? Surely before Nineveh was founded, before Babylon was built, before Ninus was born, before Asshur or Nimrod son of Cush existed—Nimrod whose kingdom began with Babylon—“God numbered that kingdom” [Col. 1360A]. As he placed all things in number, weight, and measure, so he numbered that kingdom also.

How, then, did he number it? Certainly, he knew the causes among the nations for which he would allow the rod of the wicked, the staff or yoke of rulers—that kingdom of which we have spoken—to be raised over them, so that it might strike peoples in indignation, subdue nations in fury, and persecute them cruelly. He knew those causes, I say, and according to the measure of the causes he numbered and measured the times or years of that kingdom, so that it would persecute, subdue, and strike to that extent or for that length of time.

That staff or rod of wicked rulers had come as far as the children whose iniquities and sins had to be visited, because they had forsaken the law of the Lord and had not walked in the judgments of the Lord. Thus the time had come; the years had passed according to the number he had fixed, and what had been foretold through the Psalmist had to happen: “For the Lord will not leave the rod of sinners upon the lot of the righteous, lest the righteous stretch out their hands to iniquity” (Ps. 124) [Col. 1360C]. “Therefore I have completed it,” he says—that is, the appointed and elapsed number of years or days—and behold, as another Scripture says: “The yoke shall rot away from before the oil” (Isa. 10): that is, the power which long behaved proudly shall cease when God’s mercy comes.

## CHAPTER IV. What the second word, Thecel—that is, “it has been weighed”—means.

“Thecel: it has been weighed in the balance and found wanting” (Dan. 5). It is a right and lawful order that, after that evil servant has served, he should be judged concerning his service or the recompense for his service. Once the kingdom is complete, let it receive what it deserves. For judgment is between God and kingdoms, or the kings of kingdoms. He who ordered kingdoms judges them.

What do you suppose is the subject of this judgment? Imagine God the judge saying: “I raised you up; I gave you power, so that you might strike the peoples who sinned against me. You fulfilled your service, but there is less in your deed than in my purpose” (Zech. 1) [Col. 1360D]. For in my purpose there is a good intention, but this was absent from your deed. Therefore, “your kingdom,” he says, “has been found wanting,” because all you kings of the Assyrians did not have the good intention that I had; rather, you fulfilled only your own pride and cruelty. I was angry; you added a little to the evil.

Thus much is lacking in the weight, because everything that would have been praiseworthy is lacking: namely, every intention of justice, the will to rebuke, the intention to correct, to restrain vices, and to establish lawful ordinances among nations. Moreover, it was found greatly wanting in this also: that the kingdom, or the kings of that kingdom, did not glorify the Most High God who had given them their power, nor give him thanks. Rather, they exchanged truth for a lie, exalted themselves against God, and praised their unpraiseworthy gods.

“The heart of Nebuchadnezzar,” Daniel says, “was lifted up, and his spirit was hardened unto pride” (Dan. 5). “You also, Belshazzar his son, did not humble your heart, though you knew all these things which befell him. But you were lifted up against the Lord, ruler of heaven; the vessels of his house were brought before you, and you and your nobles, your wives and your concubines drank wine in them. And you praised your gods of silver, gold, bronze, iron, wood, and stone, which neither see nor hear nor perceive. But you did not glorify the God who holds your breath in his hand and all your ways” [Col. 1361B].

Therefore, because it was found so greatly wanting, the judgment of the One writing is just, and the sentence of the One speaking is just.

## CHAPTER V. What the third word, Phares—that is, “it has been divided”—means.

“Phares: your kingdom has been divided and given to the Medes and Persians” (Dan. 5). Pompeius Trogus records that the one in whom that long-lasting kingdom of the Assyrians first ended was Sardanapalus, a man more effeminate than a woman; and he writes that the man who succeeded him after his death, having fomented a conspiracy and brought war against Sardanapalus, and who transferred the empire to the Medes, was Arbactus, governor of the Medes [Col. 1361C].

In a remarkable way, the last kings—Sardanapalus, in whom the Assyrian kingdom ended, and Belshazzar, in whom the Chaldean kingdom was divided—were alike in disgrace as they were comparable in pride. For the former man, as has been said, more effeminate than a woman, spun purple thread on a distaff amid troops of prostitutes; and, wearing female clothing, while he surpassed all women in bodily softness and wantonness of eyes, he endured the yarns among maidens. For this reason a conspiracy was formed, and he was put to death by his own people. The latter, prolonging his night-time banquet amid crowds of wives and concubines, was killed that same night, glutted and drunk.

Josephus, indeed, relates it thus: “Not long afterward both Belshazzar and the city were captured.” But this text says that Belshazzar king of the Chaldeans was killed that same night, and Darius the Mede succeeded to the kingdom. Since Josephus adds, after the preceding narration concerning the writing and its interpretation, “Not long afterward he was captured,” he appears to say that he was not killed that same night [Col. 1361D].

If the histories are contradictory—for the multitude of secular writers differs in many things—without doubt greater credence is due to this man who was present, who read and interpreted the writing, who received from it the purple and the golden chain about his neck, who was proclaimed third ruler in the kingdom, and who, with such honor and such authority, was transferred from kingdom to kingdom (Dan. 5): from the conquered Chaldeans to the victory of the Medes and Persians [Col. 1362A]. He was a faithful interpreter, bearing the known and conspicuous triumph of truth.

“Your kingdom has been divided,” he says—understand, “against you”—because, with a conspiracy formed by those over whom you should have ruled, you are surrounded by siege and will die this night in gluttony and drunkenness. “And it has been given to the Medes and Persians,” in accordance with the proclamation of him who before you, praising and magnifying the One who lives for ever, said: “His ways are just; he can humble those who walk in pride, and he rules in the kingdom of men and gives it to whomever he wills” (Dan. 6).

## CHAPTER VI. That what was then written and spoken against one kingdom, Babylon, must be understood of all kingdoms of the world.

This Scripture, “Mane, Thecel, Phares” (Dan. 5), extends more widely than has yet been said. We must think similarly concerning the other kingdoms: the kingdom of the Persians and Medes, that of the Macedonians or Greeks, and that of the Romans. God had already numbered each of them, and would complete each in its own time; he would weigh each in the balance and pronounce the judgment of division because he found it wanting [Col. 1362B].

Yet it is still too little to consider this in its parts. If it is proclaimed concerning the whole, it has greater wonder, benefit, and terror. Those kingdoms are or were parts; the whole, however, is the entire age, the totality of creatures—only those, of course, which are rational—namely angels and human beings, concerning whom the judgment of the Lord Creator is and shall be. Therefore, returning to the highest level, let us set forth the world and the devil, prince of the world. Asshur bore his type; among the Medes and Persians, the most proud Haman; among the Greeks, Antiochus; among the Romans, Nero, the worst emperor of evil emperors; and in the last days the one called Antichrist shall be revealed.

In this prince of the world and in the whole world, let us contemplate God’s numbering, God’s weighing in the balance, and God’s dividing judgment, according to this Scripture: “Mane, Thecel, Phares.”

## CHAPTER VII. What Mane signifies against the prince of this world.

“Mane: God has numbered the kingdom which you call ‘yours’” (Dan. 5) [Col. 1362D], O prince of the world, king of darkness, tyrant of sin and death. He has numbered it, I say, in the six-day period and completed it on the seventh day. For in six days he made all things: light, or the distinction of light and darkness; the firmament; the waters, dividing them from the waters; dry land—that is, earth—and the gatherings of waters, which he called seas and restrained within fixed boundaries; the sun, moon, and stars; birds and every swimming creature; human beings and cattle; and the remaining things that move upon the earth. He completed these works of the six days on the seventh day; and he blessed and sanctified the seventh day itself. You strive to reign over these things; you claim that these are your kingdom; you lie that all these things are yours or were entrusted to you.

## CHAPTER VIII. What Thecel signifies against the same prince of the world.

“Thecel: it has been weighed in the balance and found wanting” (Dan. 5). The true and just balance is the Word of God—God the Word, the wisdom of God—in which your kingdom is weighed when judgment is passed upon you. We have all heard that judgment spoken by him in whose hand is the balance, indeed who is the balance itself: “Now is the judgment of the world; now shall the prince of this world be cast out” (John 12) [Col. 1363A].

How was it “found wanting”? Namely, because you did not reach the seventh day, on which God completed all his work. You did not wish to arrive at the Sabbath—that is, the rest of blessing and sanctification. Therefore, truly, according to the holy and mystical Apocalypse, your number is six hundred and sixty-six. By being proud among angels you labored; in deceiving humankind you began to go around and walk through the earth; in Antichrist you will be wearied. Thus your labor increases, just as these sixes are multiplied tenfold: six, sixty, six hundred. But “God,” as has already been said, “rested on the seventh day.”

Therefore, once weighed, your kingdom certainly has been and shall be found “wanting,” because it has not attained the Creator’s rest, but continues empty and vain labor concerning creation (1 Pet. 5).

## CHAPTER IX. What Phares signifies against the same prince, and what the Persians and Medes are, to whom his divided kingdom is given.

“Phares: your kingdom has been divided and given to the saints of the Most High” (Dan. 5) [Col. 1363C]. In the destruction of Babylon, the Persians and Medes bore their type, particularly because Cyrus their king was also called the Lord’s anointed one (*christus*) in the prophetic utterance. “Thus says the Lord to Cyrus my anointed one, whose right hand I have taken hold of, that I may subject nations before his face and turn the backs of kings” (Isa. 45). He had first given the reason for this expression: “Who says of Cyrus, ‘You are my shepherd and will fulfill all my will’; who says, ‘Jerusalem shall be built and the temple shall be founded’” (Isa. 44). For Cyrus was to grant permission and means for rebuilding Jerusalem and the temple of the Lord.

“Your kingdom,” I say, “has been divided,” while the kingdom of the saints remains undivided. For the number six, which is your number, is divisible and capable of being cut; but the number seven, which is the number of God because he rested on the seventh day, is indivisible and incapable of being cut. So your kingdom is divisible and has undoubtedly been dissolved, and you yourself must be cast down before the sight of all; but the kingdom of God and of his saints remains for ever.

“For the figure of this world passes away” (1 Cor. 7), and you shall pass from the dominion of the world and the power of this darkness into Tartarus; you shall be drawn down by the cords of hell, while to those to whom your kingdom must be given are reserved those dwellings which you lost in heaven. [Note: [Col. 1363D] Something appears to be missing.]

Here Daniel alone is clothed in purple [Col. 1364A], bearing about his neck a golden chain taken from the condemned king. Just as the authority of the Word of God tore the purple and golden chain away from the sorrowful and condemned king and transferred them to this holy interpreter of his, so every adornment of heaven and every service of creation which you arrogated to yourself shall be torn away from you and given to the holy people of God.

## CHAPTER X. That this appearing hand signified the hand of God, concerning which David said: “Let your hand be strengthened and your right hand exalted.”

Let us finally recall how fingers appeared in such a way as though it were the hand of a man writing, and how one normally writes with the right hand. Indeed, let us suppose that God remembered what David had sung in rejoicing and giving thanks because he had deserved to hear, with an oath, [Col. 1364B] the Lord’s word of promise: “Let your hand be strengthened, and your right hand exalted” (Ps. 88 [89]:13). The hand of the Lord, that right hand of the Lord, which he had desired with supreme longing and the greatest cry of his heart to be strengthened and exalted, was signified by the hand that appeared visibly. What was to be done universally by the hand of the Lord, by the right hand of almighty God—which is none other than the Word of God, the Son of God—was now being done in part. For what was happening to that particular Babylon except what was to be done to the whole body of the ungodly through the promised and sworn grace of the Word of God? And what was that, except what immediately follows: “Righteousness,” he says, “and judgment are the preparation of your throne. Mercy and truth shall go before your face. Blessed is the people that knows jubilation; [Col. 1364C] O Lord, they shall walk in the light of your countenance” (ibid.), etc.

This, I say, was already being done in that part, because the hand of the Lord, abiding in its purpose, was being firmly exalted. Righteousness and judgment were already present in the preparation of his throne: righteousness, in that he had delivered his people, deprived of city and temple, into captivity; judgment, in that he was numbering, weighing in the balance, and dividing the kingdom of their captivity, giving it to the Medes and Persians. By doing these things his throne was prepared, and mercy and truth went before his face: mercy, that that captivity might quickly be ended; truth, that “the sceptre shall not be taken away from Judah, nor a ruler from his thigh” (Gen. 49:10), [Col. 1364D] until that throne should be fully prepared, until the promise should be fulfilled, until Christ should be born. Blessed is the people that knows this jubilation. Blessed Daniel, who, reading that Scripture and walking in the light of your countenance, O Lord, both gave a sure interpretation and held in his breast the faithful consolation of the Lord’s hand.

## CHAPTER XI. On the four beasts seen by Daniel, and why God is called “the Ancient of Days.”

The plan of our present undertaking does not require us to dwell upon every, or even individual, mystery of the revelations by which that blessed man was joyfully comforted amid [Col. 1365A] tribulation, in the affliction of captivity. Yet there is one thing which the mind does not allow to pass untouched: the most delightful mystery of that most beautiful vision which he saw before Babylon’s bestial savagery had fallen, before the fingers—or hand—of a man writing appeared upon the surface of the wall, announcing the cause or sentence of God’s judgment soon to come upon it.

“For in the first year of Belshazzar king of Babylon,” he says, “I saw in my vision by night, and behold, the four winds of heaven strove upon the great sea, and four great beasts came up from the sea, diverse one from another” (Dan. 7:1–3), etc. It is pleasing to pause here for a little, since it is beautiful to consider the tyrannical ferocity of the kingdoms of this age under the likeness of the fiercest beasts, and conversely the dignity, gentleness, [Col. 1365B] and piety of the kingdom of God in the appearance of the Ancient of Days seated upon a throne, and in the coming of “the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven, and coming even to the Ancient of Days, and being presented before him, who gave him power, honor, and a kingdom; and all peoples, tribes, and tongues shall serve him. His power,” Daniel says, “is an everlasting power, which shall not be taken away, and his kingdom shall not be destroyed” (ibid.; Dan. 7:13–14).

First, we wish to ask why, or with what purpose, God is thus called “the Ancient of Days,” a designation which we had nowhere found before this delightful passage of noble prophecy. Throughout all the holy Scriptures we indeed understand that this God, the Father of the eternal Word, is ancient—being the uncreated God, having neither beginning nor destined to have an end. [Col. 1365C] We faithfully understand the same concerning his Word, who is God. Nevertheless, as has already been said, it is here that we first find this name, “the Ancient of Days,” employed. We therefore do not idly inquire into its reason.

## CHAPTER XII. The four kingdoms did not reign from God.

Look now upon the faces of the beasts rising from the sea, on whose account judgment is said to have sat because of their savagery. “These four great beasts,” he says, “shall be four kingdoms which shall arise from the earth” (Dan. 7:17). But he whose judgment it is says: “They have reigned, and not from me; princes have arisen, and I knew them not” (Hos. 8:4). Truly they did not reign in him; indeed, the kingdoms of which we have spoken were not so much kingdoms as certain enormous and public robberies.

[Col. 1365D] What beginning did the first of these—the kingdom of the Assyrians and Chaldeans—have before Ninus, king of the Assyrians? Even if there were earlier kings who waged wars, they nevertheless sought glory not for dominion over themselves but for their peoples; content with victory, they abstained from empire. He was the first of all to alter the old and, as it were, customary practice among the nations by a new lust for empire, and to secure the greatness of the dominion he sought by continuous possession. Truly, then, “they reigned,” he says, “and not from me.” And what business have they ruling in the world while he reigns who alone ought to reign, the Creator of the world?

Therefore, that we may recognize and abhor the outrage of excessive presumption in humankind, he fittingly called him here [Col. 1366A] the Ancient of Days, since it is clear that an injury had been done to him by their reigning. For he who made the world ought himself also to have ordered it; and no one should have exercised rule except according to his judgment. If it is disorder and irreverence not to rise before a gray head, how great is the disorder, how great the irreverence, to have torn apart the kingdom of so gray a head, of one so ancient in days, by seizing the royal title? Among human beings, young and old, comparison of ages is easy; but there is, and can be, no comparison whatever between the days of that Ancient One and the days of men who seized his royal name. For who can say or imagine how much longer the duration or antiquity of the uncreated One is than the times, years, or days of men of yesterday, who were, as it were, created or born only yesterday?

[Col. 1366B] When the most ancient of those beasts rose from the sea, when the Assyrian kingdom arose from the earth, this “Ancient of Days” was already speaking with Abraham and was as ancient then as he is now.

584

## CHAPTER XIII. Supreme dominion and kingship belong to God; yet the four beasts seized for themselves as much as each was able.

He was speaking, and was framing a judgment mature and worthy of his own gray head: that he would entrust the sovereignty of all things and the monarchy of his kingdom to no other than his Son, his Word, so that all things might be governed through him through whom all things were made. This was the decree of the wise Ancient One; this was the immutable [Col. 1366C] counsel of infinite antiquity.

But those recent, newly born beasts, which by being born had contributed nothing to this world, presumed to leap against this decree and to rebel against this counsel. Without reverencing so great an elder, they plundered such parts, however many or however small, of his kingdom—of this world—as they could: they invaded human beings, claiming kingship over human beings, although in the sight of that wise Lord one human being could no more naturally precede or excel another than one mouse another mouse.

Those beasts were indeed great in human estimation: the first like a lioness, another like a bear, another like a leopard, and the fourth exceedingly terrible. Nevertheless, in comparison with the majesty of that Ancient One, they scarcely deserve to be called mice; they scarcely deserve comparison with the caterpillar, locust, cankerworm, and rust, [Col. 1366D] because they are of no account. It was, and is, far easier for the Word of God to kill those beasts and give their bodies to destruction, or deliver them to be burned in fire, than for the beasts themselves to stand against a caterpillar or overtake the leap of a locust—unless it was because the sins of the nations deserved that, with God permitting it, they should be torn apart by beasts.

For who finally killed those beasts but the Word of God? “Your almighty Word, O Lord,” says a certain Wise Man, “leaping from heaven, from the royal thrones, as a fierce warrior, sprang into the midst of the land of destruction, bearing your unfeigned command; and standing, he filled all things with death, and, while standing on the earth, reached to heaven” (Wis. 18:15–16).

## CHAPTER XIV. [Col. 1367A] Only the Word of God possesses true sovereignty; all human dominion is counterfeit.

Without doubt, he who made so great a plague in the land of Egypt—of which the author of those words speaks—he, the same “almighty Word, O Lord,” also did whatever he willed in these beastly kingdoms, and especially these things: that Nebuchadnezzar should become like an ox; that Haman should be hanged on the gallows; that Antiochus should be broken without human hand; that Nero, because he had lived disgracefully, should die still more disgracefully.

Concerning this almighty Word of the Lord, I do not wish to pass over what was said among the other things: “bearing your unfeigned command.” What is an unfeigned command except a command that is not counterfeit? And what is a command that is not counterfeit [Col. 1367B] except a true command? When this is said or understood, are not human dominions, by contrast, declared counterfeit? Truly counterfeit and not true are the dominions of beasts, the dominions of bestial human beings, who for a time possessed the power of killing like beasts, but could not benefit either themselves or others unto life.

This almighty Word bears an unfeigned command; he holds the true kingdom, whose kingdom and dominion endure without end for ages of ages. He already bore such a dominion, but it had not yet appeared. The pride of that man appeared, and he who possessed, in the form of God, unfeigned dominion received the form of a servant, according to the most beautiful spectacle of that great vision: “And behold, one like the Son of Man came in the clouds of heaven, and came even to [Col. 1367C] the Ancient of Days; and they presented him before him, and he gave him power, honor, and a kingdom, and all peoples, tribes, and tongues shall serve him. His power is an everlasting power, which shall not be taken away, and his kingdom shall not be destroyed” (Dan. 7:13–14).

Let us now return to the order of our subject.

## CHAPTER XV. The kingdom of the Medes and Persians was the dragon’s fourth head.

When the dragon’s third head had been overcome, the fourth immediately raised itself. For, with the Babylonian kingdom crushed and the kingdom of the Persians and Medes raised up, the same devil at once began to act against God’s purpose, against the word of promise, desiring to exterminate the people from whose flesh that which God promised the fathers—and confirmed by oath—had to be fulfilled.

On this head was the face of a bear, and three rows of teeth in its mouth; by these are understood the three kingdoms of one empire: the kingdom of the Babylonians, the kingdom of the Medes, and the kingdom of the Persians, which were reduced into one kingdom or empire. The kings of that empire were not, indeed, by their own purpose unmerciful toward the people of God; but through the princes who were subject to the kings, and especially through Haman, as the history of the Book of Esther records, the devil wished to accomplish this: that that people should be utterly exterminated.

This was prefigured in the aforementioned vision of Daniel by the fact that, after he had said, “And behold another beast like a bear stood on one side, and three rows were in its mouth and in its teeth,” [Col. 1368A] he immediately added: “And they said to it: Arise, devour much flesh” (Dan. 7:5).

## CHAPTER XVI. The satraps of the Medes and Persians dug for Daniel the pit into which they themselves fell.

For it was proposed to the kings—first to Darius, that he should destroy Daniel; then to Ahasuerus, who is also called Artaxerxes, the second king of this name—that he should blot out the entire Jewish nation. Envious of Daniel because he was one of the three princes appointed by Darius, to whom the satraps were to render account, and because Daniel surpassed all the princes and satraps, since the Spirit of God was more abundant in him, and because the king intended to appoint him over the entire kingdom, they brought the king to this point. Having taken [Col. 1368B] counsel with the princes of the kingdom, magistrates, senators, and judges, they caused an imperial decree and edict to be issued (Dan. 6): that everyone who should make a petition to any god or human being for thirty days, except to the king, should be cast into the lions’ den.

They knew with complete certainty that Daniel, knowing the law had been established, would nevertheless ask of his God, pray, and worship his God, and that in this way he would fall under the judgment of that great, mighty, and—as they supposed—provident law and inescapable decree. And so it happened, but not as they wished. For Daniel, entering his house with the windows of his upper chamber open toward Jerusalem, [Col. 1368C] three times a day bent his knees and worshiped, confessing before his God, as he had previously been accustomed to do (ibid.), namely, firmly adhering to his holy purpose 585 according to that saying of David: “Evening and morning and at noon I shall recount and declare, and he will hear my voice” (Ps. 54 [55]:18).

Nor was he ignorant what this meant, or how true it was: “They dug a pit before my face, and fell into it” (Ps. 56 [57]:7). They did not know this, but they ought to have known that the God of Daniel was the very God of his three young companions, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, and that he could no less command the lions on Daniel’s behalf than he had been able to temper for them the flames of fire.

## CHAPTER XVII. [Col. 1368D] Daniel’s prayer toward Jerusalem, for which he was accused and, though the king could not save him, cast into the lions’ den.

O foolish envy of the devil! O foolish envy of the ancient dragon, who so quickly raised and directed his fourth head, the power of the Median or Persian kingdom—that is, his newly born head of iniquity—to this end: that Daniel might not call upon his God or remember the Word of his God which he bore in his mind. Can a woman with child forget her pain and not cry out while she is tormented and gives birth? So certainly the blessed soul of the most holy prophet, carrying within itself the conceived good word of blessed promise, could not be silent.

Engaged in expectation of salvation, he cared nothing for the laws of princes rushing to destruction, and admitted none of their counsels. He fixed his spirit upon Jerusalem, where the promise had been sworn; he was mentally present where he was bodily absent in exile; there faithful David had received the oath, and from there the Word—or the fulfillment—of the promise had to proceed. For the prophetic Spirit said: “The law shall go forth from Zion, and the Word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isa. 2:3).

Therefore, with the windows of his upper chamber open toward Jerusalem, the “man of desires” bent his knees, at times mourning, not eating desirable bread, and afflicting himself in many ways, so that, exerting all his strength, he might raise a mighty prayer to heaven and draw down from there consolation suited to him. He was watched, accused, and came to judgment as a transgressor of the great law, as one guilty of treason. O truly blessed soul! When not even the king himself could save you—though he set his heart on saving you and labored until sunset to deliver you—you then indeed had sorrow, pains like those of a woman in labor: “A woman, when she gives birth, has sorrow because her hour has come” (John 16), says the incarnate Word himself (John 16), in whose service you suffered so vehemently. That Word knows well such pain in holy souls, especially because he himself is in them and is the cause of their sufferings.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Daniel was not inferior to the three youths in martyrdom for the Word of God.

Therefore, martyr for the Word of God, you possessed nothing less than your three holy companions, the youths. Perhaps, O man of desires, [Col. 1369C] when you saw, “Behold, I see four men loose and walking in the midst of the fire, and there is no harm in them; and the appearance of the fourth is like the Son of God” (Dan. 3:25)—when, I say, you heard these things, when you saw your three companions coming triumphantly from the furnace of fire for the glory of God, and heard praises and blessings proclaimed to your God on this account—perhaps you sighed, perhaps you groaned because so much was lacking to your happiness: that you had not deserved to become a sharer or participant in their suffering and glory.

You were not neglected; you were not worthless or despised in the sight of the Son of God, whose likeness was recognized there. For behold, alone without your companions, alone with the angel of the same grace, you remained safe and unharmed through the whole night among the mouths of lions: “Your God sent his angel [Col. 1369D] and shut the mouths of the lions, and they did not harm you, because righteousness was found in you before him; and also before human beings you committed no offense” (Dan. 6:22).

Therefore, receive also the titles of triumph inscribed upon the banner of your faith, not inferior to your companions. Receive the titles earned by your merits, proclaimed by a royal voice: “Let all in the whole empire fear,” he says, “and tremble before the God of Daniel. For he is the living God, eternal for ages, and his kingdom shall not be destroyed, and his power endures unto eternity. He is deliverer and savior, working signs and wonders in heaven and on earth, because he delivered Daniel from the lions’ den” (ibid.; Dan. 6:26–27).

## CHAPTER XIX. [Col. 1370A] When the number of years of captivity was completed, not prophets alone but also the angels rejoiced at the rebuilding of Jerusalem.

Meanwhile, “the number of the years was completed, concerning which,” he says, “the word of the Lord came to Jeremiah the prophet, that seventy years of Jerusalem’s desolation should be completed. And I set my face toward the Lord my God, to seek him in prayer and supplication, with fasting, sackcloth, and ashes” (Dan. 9:2–3).

Then Zechariah also, who is eleventh in the order of the twelve prophets, relates that the angel of the Lord answered and said: “O Lord of hosts, how long will you not have mercy on Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, against which you have been angry? This is the seventieth year.” And “the Lord,” he says, “answered the angel who spoke in me with good words, consoling words” (Zech. 1:12–13).

It is remarkable how not only human beings, the children of captivity, but also the holy angels, citizens of another age, rejoiced exceedingly that the rebuilding of Jerusalem was now imminent. The highest angels consoled Daniel; holy angels, rejoicing, moved to and fro between God and Zechariah, ready like attendants upon great preparations and a great festival: “And I lifted up my eyes,” he says, “and saw, and behold, a man, and in his hand a measuring line. And I said, ‘Where are you going?’ And he said to me, ‘To measure Jerusalem and Judah, how great its breadth is and how great its length.’ And behold, the angel who spoke in me was going out, and another angel was going out to meet him. And he said to him: [Col. 1370C] ‘Run, speak to this young man, saying: Jerusalem shall be inhabited without walls, because of the multitude of human beings and cattle in its midst’” (Zech. 2:1–4).

What is the meaning of so great a rushing to and fro of angels, such urgent commission? In the building of an earthly city and temple, the angels too wish to appear as workers, and eagerly present themselves in rivalry. Do they devote such great zeal to building the city for the city’s own sake? Certainly not for the city itself, but for the hope once laid up in David’s breast; and they rejoice that, through the people of that city and the worship of that temple, the Word of the Lord had not failed, the word of promise had not fallen away—since the virgin Israel would soon return to her cities, [Col. 1370D] where she was to bear the Lord Savior.

586

## CHAPTER XX. Not only the rebuilding of the temple, but also the future course of all kingdoms, was revealed to Daniel.

Nor did divine visions and angelic conversations promise only the rebuilding of the city and temple and the spacious dwelling of a multitude; they also foretold the troubles and miseries that would come upon hostile nations as vengeance: “Cry,” says the angel to Zechariah, “Thus says the Lord of hosts: I am exceedingly jealous for Jerusalem and Zion, and with great anger I am angry against the wealthy nations” (Zech. 1:14–15).

[Col. 1371A] By the wealthy nations we understand the nations of the kingdoms often mentioned, which crushed Judea. He immediately indicates why he is angry against those nations with great anger: “For I was angry a little, but they added to the evil” (ibid.). The sense is: “I intended to visit their iniquities with a rod and their sins with scourges” (Ps. 88 [89]:33), which is a slight anger. But they added their own anger and hatred, seeking to destroy them utterly, whereas I did not intend the extermination of the nation but its correction.

But to Daniel angels spoke thus, and such visions were shown to him, that the hidden future of these same kingdoms was disclosed to him—an exceedingly remarkable thing—in such a manner as nowhere appears from the sayings or writings of the prophets to have been disclosed or foretold to any other prophet. [Col. 1371B] For he learned and wrote through angels the condition of kingdoms and kings, now their prosperous outcomes and now the unhappy deaths of certain persons, in such a way that he cannot be doubted to have woven a history of the future—except that he did not identify the kings themselves by their proper names.

## CHAPTER XXI. The house of God, which Cyrus had decreed should be built, was finally built under Darius, as the Word of God thus prevailed.

Whose word was that, finally, except the Lord’s word, of which it was said to him: “From the going forth of the word for the city to be built” (Dan. 9:25)? What was that going forth of the word, and from where did it go forth? “The Lord stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of the Persians, and he caused a proclamation to pass throughout his whole kingdom, and also in writing, saying: ‘Thus says Cyrus king of the Persians: The Lord God of heaven has given me all the kingdoms of the earth, and he himself has commanded me to build for him a house at Jerusalem, which is in Judea’” (1 Esdr. [Ezra] 1:1–2), and so forth.

This word of the king was the Lord’s word. Just as he saw fit to call Cyrus his “anointed one” [*christus*] in Isaiah (Isa. 45:1), so he also willed to place his word in Cyrus’s mouth. But afterwards, when Cyrus had died, the neighboring nations, or enemies of Judah and Benjamin, heard that the children of captivity were building the city and temple to the Lord God of Israel. They wrote an accusation against Artaxerxes, saying: “Let it be known to the king that the Jews who came up from you to us have come to Jerusalem, that rebellious and most wicked city, which they are building, [Col. 1371D] erecting its walls and joining together its masonry” (1 Esdr. [Ezra] 4:12).

Thus, by beginning and pursuing their accusation against the inhabitants of Judah and Jerusalem, they achieved the result that the king sent an order forbidding the city to be built. “Then the work of the house of the Lord in Jerusalem was interrupted, and was not done until the second year of the reign of Darius king of the Persians. But Haggai the prophet and Zechariah prophesied to the Jews who were in Judea and Jerusalem.
