Then Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and Joshua son of Jozadak rose up and began to build the temple of God; and the prophets of God were with them, helping them” (1 Esdr. [Ezra] 4:24–5:2).

When their adversaries asked and said, “Who gave you counsel to restore the walls and build this house?” (1 Esdr. [Ezra] 5:3), they replied, among other things: [Col. 1372A] “But in the first year of Cyrus king of Babylon, King Cyrus issued an edict that the house of God should be built” (ibid., 5:13). Therefore the aforesaid enemies of the Jews sent a letter to King Darius, saying after other matters: “Now therefore, if it seems good to the king, let search be made in the king’s archives which are in Babylon whether King Cyrus commanded that the house of God in Jerusalem should be built; and let the king’s will in this matter be sent to us” (ibid., 5:17).

“Then King Darius commanded, and they searched in the library of the books which had been deposited in Babylon; and one scroll was found, in which this memorandum was written: ‘In the first year of King Cyrus, King Cyrus decreed that the house of God which is in Jerusalem should be built’” (1 Esdr. [Ezra] 6:1–3), etc. When these matters had been read: “Now therefore,” Darius says, “you who are beyond the river, withdraw far from them, and let the temple of God be built by the leader of the Jews and their elders … I, Darius, have issued a decree which I wish to be diligently carried out” (ibid., 6:6–8).

## CHAPTER XXII. The time that elapsed from the going forth of the word until the completion of the work was not only brief before God but also beneficial to human beings.

Such was the going forth of the word, undoubtedly protracted and difficult for human beings or servants of God. For from the reign of King Cyrus—whose will while living, and whose written word after his death, the authority of the Lord’s word served—until Nehemiah and the twentieth year of King Artaxerxes, the work remained unfinished; [Col. 1372C] during that period one hundred and fifteen years of the Persian kingdom elapsed: “and it was the one hundred and eighty-fifth year of Jerusalem’s captivity.”

Yet the same captivity is rightly said or counted as only seventy years, because it is rightly said to have been ended not when the work that had been interrupted was completed, but when the first permission was granted, Cyrus proclaiming: “Who among you belongs to the whole people of the God of heaven? May his God be with him. Let him go up to Jerusalem, which is in Judea, and build the house of the God of Israel; he is the God who is in Jerusalem” (1 Esdr. [Ezra] 1:3). When he said these things, he also brought out the vessels of the Lord which Nebuchadnezzar had taken from Jerusalem and gave them to those “whose spirit God stirred up to go up to build the temple of the Lord” [Col. 1372D] (ibid., 1:5–7).

Then the captivity of the people was truly ended, because then everyone who wished to leave Babylon’s delights behind and go up did go up. Moreover, that adversaries caused delays to the word thus going forth for the rebuilding of Jerusalem and the Lord’s temple is of no account before the Lord’s word itself, before whose eyes “a thousand years are as yesterday which has passed, and as a watch in the night” (Ps. 89 [90]:4), that is, one of the four watches of the night. How much more could the slightly more than one hundred years during which the work of the Lord’s house was interrupted by hostile impediments be of little—indeed, of no—account before his eyes!

Thus that delay was nothing to the Word or purpose of the Lord, since such things are reckoned as nothing: “their years,” he says, [Col. 1373A] “shall be”—that is, they shall be reckoned on earth, understood 587 as before his eyes. But for the children of captivity, who bore those years and the delays of the interrupted work with great distress and faithfully groaned before the Lord, the merit of faith was increased, the crown of hope grew, and the rewards of love were multiplied. For they labored so that we might enter into their labors; hence we ought to give thanks for their devout efforts, because what they sowed in tears we shall reap in joy.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Whence Cyrus, a Gentile, received such goodwill toward the God of heaven and toward his captive people.

Whence, do you suppose, did Cyrus, a Gentile, receive such goodwill toward [Col. 1373B] the God of heaven and toward his captive people? Whence but because it is written and truly said, “The heart of the king is in the hand of God” (Prov. 21:1)? Truly, what the almighty Word of the Lord accomplished in Cyrus’s heart, he could have accomplished in the heart of any other king—not less in Nebuchadnezzar’s heart, preventing him from leading the people into captivity, than he accomplished in Cyrus’s heart, preventing him from keeping the captive people.

It is pleasing now to observe the very manner in which the Lord’s hand deigned to win the goodwill of Cyrus’s heart. Long before this Cyrus was born, before the fathers of his fathers came into being, the Word of the Lord that came to the prophets deigned to retain the memory of him in its counsels and promise him its benefits. For it was written in Isaiah: “Thus says the Lord to Cyrus, my anointed one, whose right hand I have grasped, that I may subdue nations before his face, turn the backs of kings, open doors before him, and that gates may not be shut. I will go before you, humble the glorious ones of the earth, break bronze gates, shatter iron bars, and give you hidden treasures and the secret things of mysteries, that you may know that I am the Lord, the Holy One of Israel, who calls you by your name” (Isa. 45:1–3).

Had Cyrus not heard so great and such a prophecy concerning himself? Can there be any doubt that those captives hastened to bring this Scripture of the Lord and these promises of their God to his attention, since they could hope that this prophecy made concerning him would become for them a great occasion of relief before that king? [Col. 1373D] The Lord’s hand itself, in which is the king’s heart, intervened and effected this: that he should not prove ungrateful for so great a word and promise of God, but should make a proclamation throughout his whole kingdom, a proclamation also in writing—that is, a written proclamation—saying: “The Lord God of heaven has given me all the kingdoms of the earth,” understood: he who, long before I was born, promised that he would give them to me and called me also by my name. He immediately added: “And he himself commanded me to build for him a house at Jerusalem, which is in Judea” (1 Esdr. [Ezra] 1:2), as though saying: For this reason he gave me all the kingdoms: that I might release his people, among whom is written that prophecy about me, freely to build the house in Jerusalem which is in Judea.

For when God had said, “I who call you by your name,” he immediately added, “for the sake of my servant Jacob and Israel my chosen one” (Isa. 45:4). Therefore, for this reason he gave me all kingdoms: that I might repay him a favor in his own people by restoring them to freedom.

## CHAPTER XXIV. [Col. 1374A] Cyrus was made king so that he might recognize divine providence toward himself.

And indeed, the aforementioned man, reading or hearing the prophecy just cited and recalling his own infancy, could observe or consider that it was not by chance but through divine providence that he became king. Pompeius Trogus writes concerning him that, when he was born as the child of Astyages’ daughter, he was handed over to be killed because of his grandfather’s jealousy. [Col. 1374B] His grandfather feared a dream by which seers had foretold that the infant would become king.

But the man to whom the infant was entrusted to be killed, fearing that the child’s mother might someday exact vengeance from him for the child’s death, handed the boy over to a shepherd of the royal flocks to be exposed. By chance, at that very time the shepherd too had a son. When the shepherd’s wife heard of the royal infant’s exposure, she earnestly begged that the child be brought forth and shown to her. Wearied by her entreaties, the shepherd returned to the forest and found beside the infant a little bitch giving her teats to the child and protecting him from wild beasts and birds.

Moved himself by the pity which he had seen move even the dog, he brought the child to the sheepfolds, the dog anxiously following. When the woman received him in her arms, such vigor and such a sweet, winning smile appeared in the infant [Col. 1374C] that she spontaneously begged the shepherd to allow her to nurse him. The lots of the little children were exchanged: this child was brought up as the shepherd’s son, while the shepherd’s child was exposed as the king’s grandson.

Afterwards, while among the shepherds, the boy received the name Cyrus. When, after an interval, he had grown up, he learned from Harpagus, a friend of his grandfather, how his grandfather had ordered that little child to be killed and how he had been saved. Harpagus urged him to prepare an army and take the path that lay open toward kingship, promising the transfer of the Medes’ dominion. And it came about that Cyrus became king of the Medes and Persians. If such a story is true, he could certainly knowingly say: “The Lord God of heaven has given me all the kingdoms of the earth” (1 Esdr. [Ezra] 1:2), especially since such a prophecy had gone before, in which he was designated and called by name by that same Lord God as a great and [Col. 1374D] powerful king.

## CHAPTER XXV. Whether the freedom granted by Cyrus to the captive Jews could avail him to attain eternal salvation.

Do you suppose that such a repayment of grace could have sufficed for that same Cyrus to attain eternal salvation? We call it a repayment of grace because, knowing or recognizing that the kingdom had come to him through the ordering of God, whose temple was in Jerusalem, he did not prove wholly ungrateful; rather, “He himself,” he says, “is God, who is in Jerusalem,” and he issued an edict throughout his whole kingdom that the children of the captivity should go up and should have permission to rebuild the temple and the city. Do you therefore think that this sort of return for a benefit was sufficient for him unto eternal salvation? By no means sufficient. For it cannot be perceived that he hoped for or sought that same eternal salvation, although he was indeed of some account in comparison with other kings, who were or are altogether ungrateful to the Creator, who by just ordering gives kingdoms to them. Yet it is no very great thing to give thanks for present benefits while, carelessly or without concern, one lacks eternal ones. You may reckon him among those of whom the Psalmist says: “For his soul shall be blessed in his lifetime; he shall praise you when you have done him good” (Ps. XLVIII [Vulgate numbering]). For when he says, “his soul shall be blessed in his lifetime,” one must understand: and he will be content with that blessing, taking no thought for the future, provided that in the present age, while he lives, his soul—that is, his sensual nature—may be exalted or prosper; for this is plainly the blessing with which Esau was content. It is not, I say, a very great thing then to praise God when God has done good to a man in this respect, unless he also praises him when some adversity befalls him. True confessors praise more earnestly when they are worn down by adversity. Thus Daniel and his companions extended themselves more fully to confessing the Lord when they underwent the adversity of captivity. They undertook so great a devotion to holy confession that they resolved continually to maintain a praiseworthy frugality in food and drink, imitable by few, so that the beauty of sobriety might render their confession more acceptable to God.

## CHAPTER XXVI. [Col. 1375C] What true confession is, and what Cyrus lacked in respect of true confession.

Nor should it readily be conceded that that rejoicing of one who praises God when God has done him good is confession; indeed, let it be called what it is: flattery. For what is the confession of which the Psalmist speaks: “Confession and beauty are before him” (Ps. XCV [Vulgate numbering]), and of which he likewise says: “Enter into his gates with confession, into his courts with hymns; give praise to him” (Ps. XCIX [Vulgate numbering])? It is surely praise that is whole, devout, and rightly ordered. In what order, or of what sort, unless a man first accuses himself and then justifies God? “For the righteous man is first the accuser of himself” (Prov. XVIII); and, when this accusation goes before, he justifies God, for example by saying: “The Lord is faithful in all his words, and holy in all his works” (Ps. CXLIV). Thus he accomplishes confession—that is, praise.

Examples need not be sought far away. Daniel himself, an exile or captive of those days, makes confession in this manner: “I beseech you, O Lord God, great and terrible, keeping covenant and mercy toward those who love you and keep your commandments. We have sinned, we have acted wickedly, we have behaved impiously, and we have departed and turned aside from your commandments and judgments. To us belongs confusion of face—to our kings, our princes, and our fathers, who have sinned; but to you, O Lord our God, mercy and propitiation” (Dan. IX), and so forth. This is the lawful order of confession: first to accuse oneself, then to justify God, and to seek from him remission of sins. But did men of the world, such as this man was, deign to descend to such confession? Rather, they said: “We will magnify our tongue; our lips are our own; who is lord over us?” (Ps. XI). All proud and utterly untamed in the matter of the soul, they either wished themselves to be regarded as gods, or to serve gods of such a kind as could give no counsel concerning care of souls or the concern that must be exercised over sin, which is the death of souls. Therefore the chance praise of such men ought to be called not so much a health-giving confession as barren flattery.

## CHAPTER XXVII. That there is a greater occasion for praising God in the restoration not only of the temple at Jerusalem but also of the whole human race than in its preservation.

Therefore let the faithful and diligent praiser wrest praise from their mouths, and say more knowingly than he said: He is God who is in Jerusalem. Let us say, both because of the many—indeed, innumerable—wonders he has done and also for this one: “He is God who is in Jerusalem, because he performed this marvel: that the prey which a lioness had carried away should be brought home by a bear.” That is, this king of the Persians and Medes should restore and send back to Jerusalem the captives whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had carried away from Jerusalem, and the vessels of the Lord which he had taken away—gold and silver bowls, gold and silver cups, and other vessels, five thousand four hundred gold and silver vessels in all.

Did the glory and power of God shine forth less through this deed than if the temple had been preserved from heaven so that it should not be plundered or burned by the Babylonians? Rather, it possesses greater honor and provides greater proof for knowing the power and providence of the Word of God. As it is more admirable to restore a dead man than to preserve him from being killed, so it is more miraculous to restore in this way the condition of a people and a place than to defend it so that it should not be abandoned.

So it is plainly established concerning the whole election of the human race, concerning all the saints or elect, foreknown and predestined to conformity with the image of the Son of God: they are now raised from the death of soul and body with greater glory for God and a more glorious triumph of the Word of God, and return to that heavenly Jerusalem, the city of the living God, than if they had never been brought captive from there, had never died, and death had never entered this world through the envy of the devil.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. How the statement concerning Cyrus, “I have made you like [another], and you did not know me,” is to be understood.

Did the Word of God itself fail to know or pass over the fact that, as we have said, the praise in the mouth or action of Cyrus would be imperfect? For when it uttered such an oracle concerning him—“Thus says the Lord to Cyrus my anointed, whose right hand I have grasped,” and the rest—it finally concluded: “I have made you like [another], and you did not know me. I am the Lord, and there is no other; apart from me there is no God. I girded you, and you did not know me” (Isa. XLV).

Is it no reproach, or only a small one, when he says, “And you did not know me”? And how did he not know him, when he had said, “He is God who is in Jerusalem”? Truly he did not know him, though he had made such a confession. Much was lacking in that confession or knowledge, because the words spoken there by God who girded him—“I am the Lord, and there is no other; apart from me there is no God”—he passed over with a deaf ear. Cyrus refused to hear or understand this; indeed, he persisted in the folly of those fools who serve the creature rather than the Creator.

Therefore it may rightly be said to him: “If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, is it not evil?” For he offered or rendered certain things to God, and in this he did rightly. But he retained himself for himself, because he did not subject his heart to the worship or religion of him to whom he offered external things. It is therefore no wonder that, having ranged through the world in pursuit of his own greed, he met a miserable end to his life. For histories relate that Tomyris, queen of the Scythians, by an ambush destroyed his whole army together with the king himself—two hundred thousand Persians—cut off Cyrus’s head, and cast it into a skin filled with human blood, reproaching his cruelty in these words: “Satisfy yourself with the blood for which you thirsted and of which you have always been insatiable.”

## CHAPTER XXIX. That the title of the sixty-fourth psalm pertains to the release from this captivity.

It bears somewhat upon the present matter to recall that, in the title of the sixty-fourth psalm, the prophetic Spirit joined Jeremiah and Haggai. The one, namely Jeremiah, foretold that captivity and saw it present; the other, namely Haggai, was present at the return to their country when the captivity had been released. The title reads thus: “Unto the end: a psalm of David, a canticle of Jeremiah and Haggai, concerning the word of pilgrimage, when they began to set out” (Ps. LXIV [Vulgate numbering]). The psalm follows: “A hymn is fitting for you, O God, in Sion, and to you shall a vow be paid in Jerusalem.”

I say it pertains to the present matter to recall the preceding canticle or title, because it resounds with great joy over the triumph of the Word, for whose truth to be fulfilled the people, freed from captivity, ascended to the place where that very Word, through whom all things were made, had to be incarnate, from the tribe of Judah and the seed of David. It is indeed sweet to meditate upon the allegory in the psalm itself, or in its title: namely, to understand the heavenly Sion and celestial Jerusalem, and here the universal pilgrimage of the human race, from which all the elect will ascend when the end of the world has come.

Yet it also has some sweetness that, historically, that people returned free from captivity, and that the prophet Haggai was present at their return. For that return was not merely a type but also a very necessary preparation for the beauty or hymn fitting for you, O God, in the heavenly Sion; a preparation for the payment of the vow which is or shall be paid to you in the eternal Jerusalem, to which all flesh shall come, when you have been propitiated for all our iniquities through the redemption of Jesus Christ your Son. His coming birth required that captivity to be released, so that, according to the prophet, the virgin Israel might return to her land or her cities, there to bear the same Lord and Savior: a great and just cause of joy and gladness for the prophets of that time, and a great and beautiful subject for triumphal rejoicing.

## CHAPTER XXX. According to Haggai’s prophecy, the latter temple had greater glory than the former because of the incarnate Word.

Did not Haggai already behold this with prophetic eye? For he says: “Who is left among you who saw this house in its former glory? And how do you see it now? Is it not as though it were nothing in your eyes?” Then, after a few intervening words, he gives encouragement: “Do not fear, for thus says the Lord of hosts: for the glory of this latter house shall be greater than the former, says the Lord of hosts; and in this place I will give you peace, says the Lord of hosts” (Hag. II).

What kind of glory do you suppose he announces with so great a proclamation to be greater in the latter house than in the former? Worldly glory, namely abundance of gold and silver? Even if it was to be, or could have been, that more gold should glitter in the latter house than Solomon had expended in the former, would he deign to reckon this so greatly as glory, and would the Lord of hosts proclaim it so vehemently on that account? The glory to be understood is rather that which is true glory: namely, the presentation of the incarnate Word, Christ the Son of God, who was not to be presented in that first house but was to be presented in the latter house, while Simeon waited for him and received him in his arms with this canticle of thanksgiving: “Now you dismiss your servant, O Lord, according to your word, in peace” (Luke II).

Does not the same prophet there declare this very thing: “And the desired one of all nations shall come, and I will fill this house with glory, says the Lord of hosts” (Hag. II)? Truly the glory of the latter house was to be greater than all the glory of the former, because in it, according to the law concerning firstborn sons and with the legal sacrifices, was to be presented that firstborn among many brethren, this desired one of all nations (Apoc. I).

## CHAPTER XXXI. That Ezra, Nehemiah, Jozadak, and Zerubbabel were illustrious at the time when the captivity was released.

Memorable was that return and splendid ascent, if you consider that chariot—or four-horse chariot—of the Lord, seated upon which the Word of the Lord, the Word of the promise that had necessarily to be fulfilled, hastened to his place. By that four-horse chariot of the Lord we mean the four men who were the principal authors and, as it were, heads of that return: Ezra, Nehemiah, Jesus the high priest, and Zerubbabel the governor. Zerubbabel was so called because he was born in Babylon during the years of captivity. It is pleasing to regard the prophets Haggai and Zechariah, who, as mentioned above, were with them and helped them, as charioteers before the four-horse chariot.

To these—indeed, to the Word of God dwelling in them—every wise man who follows his triumph gives thanks, because they were happily born in order to be prepared for such a time. “How shall we magnify Zerubbabel?” he says. “For he too was like a signet on the right hand of Israel; and Jesus son of Jozadak, who in their days built the house and raised up the holy temple, prepared for the Lord unto everlasting glory; and Nehemiah, of long remembrance, who raised up for us our ruined walls, made the gates and bars stand, and rebuilt our houses” (Ecclus. XLIV).

What it says, “unto everlasting glory,” is rightly understood as stated above: that house was to stand until Christ should come, the true and everlasting glory of the saints, as Simeon declared: “A light for the revelation of the Gentiles and the glory of your people Israel” (Luke II).

## CHAPTER XXXII. [Col. 1380A] That Ezra was eminent because he renewed the law in new characters.

They say that Ezra is Malachi, who is twelfth in the order of the twelve prophets. How great ought he to be for us! For we ought not to be ignorant that he renewed the law: the holy Scriptures, which are the very words of the Word of God, scattered and scarcely surviving the Babylonian fire, he gathered and restored. How great is this, or ought it to be, in every age? Great and memorable though it may be that by the labor both of him and of the others that city and that handmade temple could be restored or rebuilt, this indestructible edifice—the restoration of Holy Scripture—is and always will be of more enduring memory, greater glory, and loftier excellence.

He also discovered letters or characters more convenient and easier than the old ones; handing the written law to the people, he then deserved to be called “a swift scribe,” and now and forever he is a learned scribe in the kingdom of God.

# BOOK VIII

[Col. 1379]

## CHAPTER I. [Col. 1379C] That Mordecai’s dream was not vain.

A great spectacle in heaven and on earth followed after the favor shown by the kings of Persia. It is pleasing to begin the narrative with Mordecai’s dream, which, although it is not found in the Hebrew, as the illustrious man Jerome says, nevertheless formed the beginning of the book of Esther in the Vulgate edition and bears somewhat upon the matter. In the second year of the reign of Artaxerxes the Great, Mordecai, a Jewish man of the tribe of Benjamin, who lived in the city of Susa—that city being the beginning or capital of the kingdom—saw a dream.

“Voices,” he says, “appeared, and tumult, thunderings, earthquakes, and disturbance upon the earth. And behold, two great dragons, ready for battle against one another; at their cry all nations were stirred up to fight against the nation of the righteous. And that day was one of darkness and peril, tribulation and anguish, and great terror upon the earth. And the nation of the righteous, fearing its evils, was troubled and prepared for death, and they cried out to the Lord. And while they cried aloud, a little fountain grew into a great river and overflowed into many waters. Light and the sun arose; the lowly were exalted, and they worshiped the illustrious” (Esther XI).

Moreover, after the end of the same book this chapter was transmitted: “And Mordecai said: These things were done by God. I remembered the dream which I had seen, signifying these very things, and none of them was void: the little fountain that grew into a river, and was changed into light and sun, and overflowed into many waters. Esther is she whom the king took as wife and wished to be queen. But the two dragons are I and Haman; the nations that assembled are those which attempted to destroy the name of the Jews” (Esther X).

## CHAPTER II. That Mordecai and Haman were signified by the two dragons, but for different reasons.

From this sort of dream, I say, it is pleasing to begin the narrative of the things contained in the same book of Esther, in order that an awakened mind may perceive that the evil which Haman devised came from the devil, the ancient dragon, having his throne in Haman’s breast. For behold, Haman is called a dragon: “The two dragons,” he says, “are I and Haman.” Mordecai too was seen as a dragon, but for a very different reason.

Haman was a dragon for a true cause: because he truly had in his breast the devil, the ancient serpent. The fourth head of that dragon having seven heads has already been said to be the kingdom of the Persians and Medes, especially because of Haman and the peoples of that empire. When Haman was raised over them, he wished to destroy the people from whom Christ was to be born, according to the promise Abraham had received. Mordecai, on the other hand, was a dragon not in truth but through the false accusation of enemies—namely Haman and his accomplices—who said that his race, the Jewish race, was a race of seditious men, hostile to the kingdom.

Nor is it surprising that a simple and upright man should be represented in a dream by a malicious and crooked dragon because of a false opinion, when Christ himself, King of the simple and Lord of the upright, was prefigured by the bronze serpent. The Lord said to Moses: “Make a bronze serpent and set it up as a sign; whoever has been struck and looks upon it shall live” (Num. XXI). For just as that bronze serpent was without venom, so Christ, when accused of being a magician, was without sin. Likewise Mordecai, because of Haman’s accusation, was seen in the dream as a dragon; but in the reality of the matter he was a worshiper of God, not possessing the malice of the ancient dragon, which raged most arrogantly in that Haman.

## CHAPTER III. [Col. 1381B] As Haman prepared a cross for Mordecai and was hanged upon it, so the devil, prince of this world, prepared a cross for Christ and was defeated upon it.

And since mention has now arisen of the likeness whereby holy men deserved, in diverse ways and for diverse merits, to be likened to the Son of God—as he says, “I have been likened in the hand of my servants the prophets”—it is fitting at once to speak of the height of this likeness, because he deigned to be likened also in the hand of this Mordecai, as had been foreshadowed in the aforementioned dream.

The two dragons fought against one another: that is, Mordecai and Haman rose up against each other. Haman prepared a gallows for Mordecai; and, Mordecai happily escaping, Haman was hanged upon the gallows which he had prepared. So it was necessarily to be that the incarnate Word, God made man, Jesus Christ King of all ages, should proceed against the prince of this world and engage with him. Thus it came about that that dragon, the devil, caused the cross to be prepared for him through his agents; but he was not pierced upon that gallows. The Word triumphed, being the impassible God, and, having resumed the flesh into immortality after it had suffered death for a brief time, the living God strangled that murderer in his own contrivance.

The Apostle says: “Blotting out the handwriting of the decree that was against us, which was contrary to us, he took it out of the way, fastening it to the cross; stripping principalities and powers, he made a public display of them, triumphing over them confidently in himself” (Col. II). Let us now enter upon the order of the events.

## CHAPTER IV. That the little fountain which grew into great rivers was Queen Esther.

“The little fountain grew into a great river and overflowed into many waters” (Esther X): that is, Esther, a captive and poor little woman, orphaned of both parents, became queen of many nations and mistress of many provinces on the day appointed by God, at the favorable time, carefully preserved by the providence of the Most High. By what path or mercy?

“Scripture says: ‘There was a Jewish man in the city of Susa, named Mordecai, son of Jair, son of Shimei, son of Kish, of the stock of Jemini, who had been carried away from Jerusalem at the time when Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon carried away Jeconiah king of Judah. He was foster-father to the daughter of his brother, Hadassah, who by another name was called Esther; she had lost both her parents and was exceedingly beautiful and fair of face. When her father and mother had died, Mordecai adopted her as his daughter’” (Esther II).

A pious work, active compassion: it had a pious Judge and Observer in God, to whom, in such a deed, alms were surely offered with a sweet fragrance in so generous a grace. Truly the Lord smelled an odor of sweetness, and truly he blessed both them: her who had been adopted and him who had adopted her. He blessed them, I say, so that both might increase unto the salvation of the people, unto the deliverance of their nation, against which a most wicked enemy was rising—namely Haman son of Hammedatha, who was of the stock of Agag.

Let us not suppose that he first began to be an enemy of the Jews when Mordecai refused to worship him. He had long been an enemy, carrying in his breast an ancient cause of hatred and breathing forth the old fuel of enmity with burning wrath. For Agag, of whose stock this Haman was, was king of Amalek and was killed by Samuel. The Lord had commanded Saul king of Israel to destroy that sinful people. But Saul and the people spared Agag, the best flocks of sheep and herds, garments, rams, and everything beautiful, and were unwilling to destroy them. Therefore, when the Lord was angry, Samuel said: “Bring Agag king of Amalek to me”; Agag, very fat, was brought to him, and Samuel cut him in pieces before the Lord (I Kings XV).

## CHAPTER V. [Col. 1382C] That by God’s providence Mordecai remained in captivity, although those who wished had received freedom to return to their homeland.

Did it then happen by chance, and not rather through God’s providence, that this man—or his father, or his father’s brother—remained in captivity and did not go up to Jerusalem after the edict which granted permission to return to their homeland? There is no doubt that the same Spirit who stirred up the spirit of those going up, as it is written, “And the chiefs of the fathers’ houses of Judah and Benjamin, the priests and Levites, and everyone whose spirit God stirred up, arose to go up to build the temple of the Lord”—there is no doubt, I say, that the same Spirit, the same God, inspired the mind of this man so that he might remain there, in order that his adopted Esther might be prepared at such a time.

He who “foreknew, predestined, called, justified, and glorified all the saints” (Rom. VIII), foreknew and prepared Mordecai as the worker of great kindness toward his little niece. He foreknew this, I say, before Mordecai’s great-grandfather Kish was taken captive to Babylon with Jeconiah. It was not without purpose that one should here be reminded that it is not Mordecai himself but Kish, his great-grandfather, who must be understood where, after the words, “There was a Jewish man in the city of Susa, named Mordecai, son of Jair, son of Shimei, son of Kish, of the stock of Jemini,” it immediately follows: “who had been carried away from Jerusalem at the time when Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon carried away Jeconiah king of Judah” (Esther II).

For from that earlier deportation to Babylon until the third year of King Ahasuerus, when he held the banquet, rejected Queen Vashti in anger, and Esther pleased him in her place, nearly two hundred years are reckoned. Thus, before his great-grandfather Kish was carried there, God had foreknown the coming elevation of Haman, enemy of the Jews. He had also foreknown and predestined, in opposition to him, the Jew Mordecai and his little niece, that at such a time the Word of God might have prepared in those lowly persons a safeguard for his future flesh, lest the tree which was to bear such fruit—Christ, the salvation of all nations—should be cut down.

## CHAPTER VI. [Col. 1383B] That Haman, when exalted and commanded to be worshiped, also coveted the kingdom, and became Mordecai’s enemy because Mordecai had saved the king.

What God foresaw came to pass: King Ahasuerus exalted Haman son of Hammedatha, who was of the stock of Agag, and set his throne above all the princes whom he had; and all the king’s servants who stood at the gates of the palace bent the knee and worshiped Haman, for so the emperor had commanded them. The king’s liberality was excessive and undiscerning: thinking that he was advancing a faithful friend, he was in truth raising up against himself a cruel enemy. “We even cherish him in the place of a father,” he says in the same letters which he sent to the princes and governors of the one hundred and twenty-seven provinces.

A foolish exaltation: to command a man to be worshiped, which is due to God alone. Yet worship was customarily offered to the kings of Persia. Alexander the Great, following the Persian example in his royal pride, tolerated it for a time; but at last, when he believed that he had overcome the resulting envy, he ordered that he should be worshiped, not merely greeted. Callisthenes the philosopher was the most vehement among those refusing; this matter proved fatal both to him and to many Macedonian nobles. For all were killed under the pretext of conspiracy. Yet the Macedonians retained their custom of greeting the king, abhorring worship.

What, then, except the royal title itself, was lacking to that most proud man in the eminence of Persian royalty? His insatiable greed wickedly coveted even that title, as may be seen from the prefatory section of the book in the Vulgate edition, set before it, as Jerome the faithful translator says. Mordecai remained at the king’s court with Gabatha and Thara, the king’s eunuchs, who were gatekeepers of the palace. When he had understood their plot and learned that they were attempting to lay hands upon the king, he reported it to the king, who, after investigating both men, ordered them, when they confessed, to be led to death. “But Haman son of Hammedatha, a Bugaean, was most highly honored before the king, and wished to harm Mordecai and his people because of the two eunuchs who had been put to death” (Esther XII).

He therefore coveted the royal title too, not content with honor, however excessive; ungrateful to men and an enemy of God, he wished to harm Mordecai because he had saved the king’s life by guarding it beforehand.

## CHAPTER VII. [Col. 1384A] That Haman, being Mordecai’s enemy when he saw that Mordecai did not bend the knee to him, conceived the plan of exterminating the whole Jewish people.

Yet the greater and more certain cause of his hatred and great wrath was that which the truth of Scripture reports in this manner: “Mordecai alone did not bend the knee or worship Haman” (Esther III). When Haman had heard and tested this, that Mordecai did not bend the knee to him or worship him, he became greatly enraged and considered it beneath him to lay hands on Mordecai alone. For he had heard that Mordecai was of the Jewish nation and preferred to destroy the whole people of the Jews who were in the kingdom of Ahasuerus.

This was the cause of the war; this was the beginning of the duel. In this manner the two dragons began to fight one another: Mordecai, a dragon in the eyes of men by whom he was condemned; Haman, a dragon first judged before God and all his saints, and then condemned by men. Never did the dragon, the devil, raise his own head against the woman of whom we have often spoken with such cruelty and fury. For his other heads, lifting themselves up and opening with wide jaws, aimed to devour her son. But this head sought to devour the woman’s whole body itself, as must be said more plainly.

The other kingdoms, serving diabolical cruelty, sought by vexing that people to take away God’s law and every hope of the promise; this kingdom, at Haman’s urging, wished to destroy the people itself. Therefore that woman, with child and in labor, never cried out more than at this time and was never more violently tormented (Apoc. XII): that is, that people never had such public and universal mourning throughout all the provinces, towns, and places to which the king’s cruel decree had reached. There was great mourning and lament among the Jews, fasting, wailing, and weeping; many used sackcloth and ashes as their bed.

## CHAPTER VIII. Why Mordecai did not worship Haman.

Mordecai himself first tore his garments, put on sackcloth, sprinkled ashes upon his head, and in the middle street of the city cried out with a loud voice, displaying the bitterness of his soul. In this wailing he proceeded as far as the gates of the palace. You may truly say of this man as well: “Iron pierced his soul” (Ps. CIV [Vulgate numbering]); and he is truly blessed. For “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake” (Matt. V).

For it was righteousness that he refused to worship Haman, seeing the just cause. “You know all things, O Lord,” he says, “and you know that I did not do this from pride or from any desire for glory, in refusing to worship the most proud Haman. For I would gladly be prepared, for the salvation of Israel, even to kiss the prints of his feet; but I feared to transfer the honor of my God to a man, and to worship anyone except my God” (Esther XII). Therefore the righteous man is shown in this action to obey the holy law justly and well, whose command is: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve.” Accordingly, he possesses blessed memory and is eminent among those blessed persons who suffer or have suffered persecution for righteousness’ sake; and such a son of captives worthily obtained possession and the civic crown in the kingdom of heaven.

## CHAPTER IX. Why certain men could be worshiped without blame.

But someone says: If it is against the law to worship any human being, how did holy David, the most diligent defender of the holy law, permit himself to be worshiped, and why is the deed not reproved as contrary to the law? For Ahimaaz, crying out and bearing the good news of victory over Absalom, said to the king: “Hail, O king”; and, worshiping the king, prostrate before him upon the ground, he said: “Blessed be the Lord your God” (II Kings VIII), and so forth. Again it is written: “Bathsheba bowed herself and worshiped the king”; and again: “Bathsheba, her face bowed to the ground, worshiped the king” (III Kings I).

And lest the gesture of worship appear lesser, so that you might say it is far less to bow the face or incline oneself prostrate than to bend the knee, as was done to Haman, there is the case of the woman of Tekoa, sent by Joab, who, when she had entered before the king, fell upon the ground before him and worshiped. Why, then, is this deed in David not reproved as contrary to the law, while Mordecai considered it sacrilege to worship a man?

The brief answer is that it is one thing to worship a man without God, such as Haman was, and another to worship a man of God, such as David was. For when a man without God, a man serving the devil, is worshiped, the devil in him is undoubtedly worshiped; conversely, when a man of God, a man honoring and worshiping God, is worshiped or received, God in him is worshiped, God in him is received. There is also this great difference: proud Haman wished and demanded to be worshiped. David, or any holy man, a humble servant or representative of God, takes no delight in worship and does not demand it for himself. And if religious observance sometimes requires this to be done, it is clearly done not to dishonor but to honor God; it is clearly not done to the man, because it is done for the name of the Lord.

## CHAPTER X. [Col. 1385D] Why access to the king was so difficult that one who approached unbidden was put to death.

Why, then, was access to the king so difficult? That it was extremely difficult is evident from Esther’s reply, conveyed to Mordecai: “All the king’s servants and all the provinces under his dominion know that, whether man or woman, whoever enters the king’s inner court unbidden is immediately put to death without any delay, unless perhaps the king extends to him the golden scepter as a sign of clemency, so that he may live. Go again, gather all the Jews whom you find in Susa, and pray for me. Eat nothing and drink nothing for three days and nights; and I, with my maidservants, will likewise fast. Then I shall enter the king’s presence, acting against the law, unbidden, and surrendering myself to death and peril” (Esth. 4).

Why, I ask, was access to the king so difficult? Surely it arose from the excessive vanity of miserable emptiness: a king of a great empire was thought to possess something more than humanity, and was not to be diminished by being commonly seen. Especially among the Persians, this custom was established by law, that the king’s person should be concealed beneath an appearance of majesty. The devil wished to exploit this law through Haman: while that accuser, so intimate with the king, pressed his charge, and no one had access to make a defense, nor any approach by which to entreat him, the king’s sentence, once extracted, might run irrevocably. Thus that dragon might be allowed to devour not merely the conceived child but the entire body of the woman with child—that is, to destroy the whole nation in whose keeping was the promise—as Mordecai himself says in prayer to God: “And now they wish to alter thy promises, to destroy thy inheritance, to shut the mouths of those who praise thee, and to extinguish the glory of thy temple and thine altar” (Esth. 14).

## CHAPTER XI. Haman foolishly sought by lots the time of the Jews’ destruction, although he did not yet know whether they were to be destroyed.

Let us consider the height of a proud heart in the very preparation of its malice. In the first month, called Nisan, in the twelfth year of Ahasuerus, a lot was cast into an urn, called in Hebrew *Phur*, before Haman, to determine on what day and in what month the Jewish nation should be put to death; and the twelfth month came out, called Adar (Esth. 3).

The fool did not yet know whether the Jewish nation ought to be put to death, and already by lot he sought on what day and in what month it ought to be put to death. Perhaps he imagined himself to be such a great man—and he was so great in his own eyes—that human death and life should be believed to lie in his hand. Therefore, judging his own will decisive, he thought the lots need be consulted concerning the killing only as to its time. But He whose birth according to the flesh that man was preparing, by those lots, to foretell, had long before said through the prophet’s mouth: “My lots are in thy hands” (Ps. 30).

For the words of that thirtieth Psalm are the words of the incarnate Word. Faith and hope in his incarnation, according to the promise, were in the heart of that nation as an infant is in a woman’s womb. Whatever or however many his lots were or are—of which he speaks to God the Father, saying, “My lots are in thy hands”—there is no reason to exclude the lots cast by Haman from belonging to those same lots. And indeed, as he was already saying in another Psalm: “They cast a lot upon my garment” (Ps. 21), so it was fitting that he should say with equally steadfast truth: They cast a lot also upon my mother, upon the nation from which I was to be born.

Thus that ruined man, deceived by his own pride, believed that in a single consultation of lots he had received an answer, or satisfaction, concerning two matters: both the slaughter itself and the time of the slaughter. But, “My lots are in thy hands,” he says; which may rightly be understood as though he said: This malignant caster of lots, Haman, my worst enemy and foe, has now cast lots in order to kill me. But thou, holding in thy hands the power of life and death, hast changed those same lots into his destruction and the deliverance of my people.

## CHAPTER XII. Haman, deceived by lots, gave the Jews time to obtain God’s help.

Truly, in this member of the devil there was already accomplished what was signified in the devil himself as head, when the Lord said to blessed Job: “Wilt thou put a ring in his nostrils? Wilt thou mock him as a bird?” (Job 40). For he was made foolish and mocked by the very lots. When he cast the lot in the first month to determine on what day and in what month the Jews should be killed, the twelfth month came out: that lot demanded, in effect, an entire year’s postponement.

God required this lot, governing it and holding it, as has been said, in his hands. First, Haman was made foolish and mocked in this: although he did not know whether the nation was to be killed, and sought only the time of its killing, when the lots answered that the killing itself must be deferred from the first month to the twelfth—that is, for nearly a full year—he supposed that this was the same as having both things in his own hands: the killing and the day of the killing.

Then he was mocked in this also: while, during so great a delay, the sentence of death hung suspended, he provided the entire nation an opportune period sufficient for sending embassies into the far distance—that is, into the height of heaven—from which auxiliary forces might be summoned: namely fasts, tears, and prayers. These indeed were, and are, fitting embassies for inviting or invoking the Lord’s help from heaven.

Certainly, even though the Lord was near—as he is near to all who call upon him in truth (Ps. 144)—nevertheless this long period of delay, granted by the lots, was necessary. It allowed sufficient time for letters to travel and return among the rulers and peoples of so many provinces, so that new letters might correct the earlier letters of Haman, plotter and enemy of the Jews, by which he had commanded that they perish in all the king’s provinces, before the allotted limit of time was reached.

Indeed, the sacred choir of the Church wishes every generation to recognize and not forget how great were the cries by which they cried to heaven. Accordingly, each year on appointed days it proclaims before the Lord, in their person: “Turn his heart”—that is, the king’s—“to hatred of those who oppose us, and of those who agree with them; but deliver us into thy hand, O our God, for ever” (Esth. 14).

Truly, one who weighs how great a matter it was to cry to heaven lest that one nation be exterminated—from which the salvation of the world was hoped for—will judge that cry worthy to be uttered in such high-sounding words, and worthy of lingering contemplation upon the distress of that time, when the aforesaid woman with child, even before she brought forth our salvation, was almost swallowed up.

## CHAPTER XIII. There have always been those who, mindful of the divine promise concerning Christ, desired its fulfillment.

Do you suppose that there was then no one in that nation or among that people whom this concern touched, or who knew that the Messiah was to come? On the contrary, since God spoke to Abraham, no age has existed which did not have some persons holding the faith and meaning of that promise and awaiting his coming. Such persons were very few, namely those who understood spiritually the coming or kingdom of Christ.

Yet all had to hear the Law and the Prophets, which contained and bore witness to his promise, though they did not understand it spiritually—that is, though they hoped for a kingdom of his that was earthly rather than heavenly. And there is no doubt that, though in prosperity they were more negligent, in adversity they became attentive to that hope and expectation, and then desired the coming of him whom they believed able to bring aid: a great king, a powerful king.

Moses himself, when he was sent to Pharaoh, said: “I beseech thee, Lord, send whom thou art to send” (Exod. 4). The same judgment must be made concerning the remaining ages and times whenever we read: “And the children of Israel cried to the Lord because of this or that tribulation.” We must understand that their cries did not lack remembrance of the aforesaid promise, by which they heard from the Law and the Prophets that a Savior had been promised.

At the same time, it must be observed that whenever God raised up a savior for those who cried in this way, he accomplished through that person something which signified or prefigured the one awaited and desired: Christ, the one true Savior. This has already been said, and must still be said, concerning Mordecai as well. I have said these things now so that there may be no doubt that at least this affliction gave understanding to their hearing: when they heard the decree of their death, they remembered to flee to God and to cry for Christ’s coming, in words such as those of David: “That thou mayest be justified in thy words and prevail when thou art judged” (Ps. 50).

## CHAPTER XIV. Esther was endowed with those four most celebrated virtues.

It is pleasing to linger and contemplate at greater length the deed of this good woman, of whom one may rightly say: “Blessed is the husband of a good wife; for the number of her years is doubled” (Ecclus. 26). For both in the present age and in the age to come she possesses good remembrance, eternal remembrance.

It is pleasing, I say, to contemplate how good she was, with what good qualities she was adorned, and how the work of salvation proceeded through her hands. Behold, in her deed and course we observe the four principal virtues, celebrated by both divine and human schools, and most highly extolled by philosophers, whether secular or ecclesiastical: prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice. The difference is that the ecclesiastical philosophers reckon them in spiritual and eternal fruits, the secular philosophers in secular and transitory ones.

It is easy to recognize these virtues, adorned together by heavenly grace, in this good and sensible woman and in the deeds of this good woman. First, we should consider her temperance; next, her justice; third, her prudence; fourth, her fortitude.

## CHAPTER XV. How the virtue of temperance shone in Esther.

The virtue of temperance shines in her, because at the summit of royal dignity, in the king’s great chamber, she appears chaste and humble. For after Scripture had related that the royal diadem was placed upon her head, it says: “Esther had not yet disclosed her country and her people, in accordance with his command”—namely, Mordecai’s. “For Esther observed whatever he commanded, and did all things as she had been accustomed to do when he was raising her as a little child” (Esth. 2).

Again, she herself says in her prayer: “Thou knowest, Lord, my necessity: that I abhor the sign of my pride and glory which is upon my head on the days of my display; I detest it as the cloth of a menstruous woman, and do not wear it on the days of my seclusion” (Esth. 14). Here a truly outstanding proof of temperance appears, because these words breathe a great sweetness of humility.

Again she says: “Thou, Lord, who hast knowledge of all things, knowest that I hate the glory of the wicked and detest the bed of the uncircumcised and of every foreigner” (ibid.). Here too is surely a great glory of temperance: though made queen in captivity, this woman has God as witness that she is chaste in heart.

## CHAPTER XVI. How justice was found in her.

We first observe justice in this, that she confesses and says: “We have sinned, Lord, in thy sight, and therefore thou hast delivered us into the hands of our enemies; for we worshiped their gods. Thou art just, O Lord” (Esth. 14). Here is justice; for “the righteous man is the first accuser of himself” (Prov. 18).

Moreover, justice appears also in this: as has already been said, she has God as witness that she hates “the glory of the wicked” and has detested “the bed of the uncircumcised and of every foreigner.” For at that time—and since God, making a promise, spoke to Abraham, saying: “Every male among you shall be circumcised, and you shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskin, that it may be a sign of the covenant between me and you” (Gen. 17)—from then until the coming of Christ, the beginning of justice was to be circumcised with the faith of Abraham, who believed in the promise of the blessed seed.

Hence the Apostle also says: “He received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of faith” (Rom. 4). Nor should it be passed over that it was highly fitting for that sign or seal of the righteousness of faith to be in the part of the body by which seed is born, because the promise which Abraham believed was a promise of seed, of the one seed, which is Christ.

Thus circumcision was a testimony of faith, a testimony to believing in Christ who was to come; without that faith no one can be justified. Therefore justice gains the palm—the justice which is from God—when Esther detests the bed of the uncircumcised, knowing that apart from faith in Abraham’s seed, of which faith circumcision was the sign, that king, though merciful to her, remained unjust toward God.

## CHAPTER XVII. It was also an act of justice that she endured union with an uncircumcised man because of necessity.

Do you suppose that she possesses less justice now by enduring what she hated, the bed of the uncircumcised, than if she had refused so as never to be joined to him? By no means. “Thou, Lord,” she says, “knowest my necessity” (Esth. 14). And it is a true saying: necessity produces a crown; truly her necessity was a necessity that produced a crown.

“And who knows,” says Mordecai, “whether you have come to the kingdom for this purpose, that you might suffer in such a time?” (Esth. 4). She ought not to have valued the safeguarding of her own body so highly as to set it before the common salvation of her nation—indeed, before the salvation of the whole world. That union of captive Esther and King Ahasuerus wonderfully cooperated in the salvation of all. For through that occasion the Jews were delivered, who were to become the fathers of salvation, the fathers of Christ according to the flesh.

Even if she did not yet know all this when she was first brought to the bed of the uncircumcised man, nevertheless it was to happen thus. And who would accuse Moses of injustice for saying to God: “Either forgive them this sin, or, if thou dost not, blot me out of thy book which thou hast written” (Exod. 32)? Likewise, who would accuse the Apostle of injustice for saying: “I myself wished to be anathema from Christ for my brethren, who are my kinsmen according to the flesh” (Rom. 9)?

So Esther too cannot be accused of injustice even if she had wished to be joined to an uncircumcised king for the salvation or consolation of her nation. Even if the great danger that afterwards occurred through that union had not occurred, captivity’s necessity alone could have excused her.

## CHAPTER XVIII. How prudence was displayed in her counsels.

The virtue of prudence in her must now be proclaimed as worthy of praise to God. For she acted so prudently that one cannot doubt that she acted at the prompting of the Spirit of wisdom. Just as it is said of blessed Joseph, “The word of the Lord inflamed him” (Ps. 104), so one may truly say of her also: “The word of the Lord inflamed her.”

When the king said to her, “What do you wish, Queen Esther? What is your request? Even if you ask for half my kingdom, it will be given you” (Esth. 5), she answered: “If it pleases the king, I beseech you, come to me today, you and Haman, to the banquet which I have prepared” (ibid.).

She did not immediately state her request or disclose her desire at once, but invited both to the banquet, friend and enemy, king and Haman. Prudently she intended to disclose the hostility where the murderous enemy could not escape. Nor did she reveal the matter even at the first banquet. She allowed the enemy, destined for death, to enjoy the illusory security of one day and to boast of the greatness of his wealth, saying proudly: “Queen Esther has invited no one but me to the banquet with the king; and tomorrow also I shall dine with the king at her house” (ibid.).

Thus she made him ill-secure, but made the king more favorably disposed and more attentive. “If,” she says, “I have found favor in the king’s sight, and if it pleases the king to grant what I ask and fulfill my request, let the king and Haman come to the banquet which I have prepared for them, and tomorrow I shall reveal my desire to the king” (ibid.).

To give over a savage beast, a fierce bear, to punishment, she entices it to food, lest it hear the report before it undergoes its punishment, lest it see the pit before it falls into it. She was prudent, knowing that it is more expedient to crush a beast once caught indoors than to pursue it in uncertainty with dogs when frightened and fleeing through the woods.

## CHAPTER XIX. She prudently set forth her request before the king.

Furthermore, when at last she disclosed her desire to the king and made known her petition and entreaties, what was the manner of her speech? When for the third time the king said, “What is your request? Even if you ask for half my kingdom, you shall obtain it,” she replied: “If I have found favor in thy sight, O king, and if it pleases thee, give me my life, for which I ask, and my people, for whom I entreat. For I and my people have been delivered up to be crushed, slaughtered, and destroyed. Would that we had been sold as male and female slaves! The evil would have been tolerable, and I would have groaned in silence. But now our enemy is one whose cruelty rebounds upon the king” (Esth. 7).

The prudence in such speech is praiseworthy: sound prudence, taught by holy and mature humility. Did she not know that she was queen, she who implored the king in such a manner? Did she not perceive herself to be loved, she who entreated with so great fear? Surely the king himself could marvel. He was ready to give her half his kingdom if she asked it; and yet his queen, his beloved, judged worthy of rule above all women and more pleasing to him than all other women, begged for her own soul—that is, her life—as though she were a captive, an outlaw, as if the king himself had condemned her.

These things have been said to make known her prudence, which is so great that no one can adequately attain its magnitude in words.

## CHAPTER XX. Her prudence was more truly divine providence.

But is it enough to call it prudence? Rather, it was divine providence. Let us consider what happened during the delays while she postponed disclosing her desire to the king; it will be plain that divine providence directed the queen’s prudence.

When Haman first came with the king to the banquet, he had not yet prepared for himself the punishment intended for him. For by God’s judgment it had been preordained that he himself should prepare the gallows devised for another but due to himself. This, as has been said, he had not yet prepared.

Therefore we do not doubt that it was an act of divine providence that, postponing her disclosure at the first banquet, she said: “Let the king and Haman come to the banquet which I have prepared for them, and tomorrow I shall reveal my desire to the king.” Haman went out that day joyful and cheerful. “Command,” his wife said, “that a high beam fifty cubits high be prepared; and in the morning tell the king that Mordecai should be hanged upon it. Then you shall go joyfully with the king to the banquet.” But that night the king passed sleeplessly, and while the histories and annals of former times were being read or heard (Esth. 5–6), an occasion arose for Haman himself to set upon the royal horse, clothed in royal garments, the man whom he was preparing to hang upon the gallows, going before him and crying: “This honor is due to whomever the king wishes to honor” (Esth. 6).

Thus through those delays the king’s favor was greatly increased. This was divinely provided, because the king who was to hear Esther’s request needed also to become favorably disposed toward Mordecai; and this was wonderfully brought about that night by the rereading of the memory of his merits.

## CHAPTER XXI. Haman was caught at the banquet as with a hook.

Moreover, what I still wish to say is praise both of Esther’s prudence and of divine providence. For it is said of the devil to blessed Job: “In his eyes he shall catch him as with a hook” (Job 40). Again: “Canst thou draw out Leviathan with a hook?” (ibid.). Surely that which is drawn out with a hook is caught by bait: the bait is displayed, the iron is concealed.

It is a familiar and customary understanding that, in persecuting Christ’s humanity, the devil was seized by that same Christ’s divinity. Haman was undoubtedly a servant and chief satellite of that devil; and the devil dwelling in him contrived this great crime. Is it not therefore wonderful and delightful to contemplate that he was caught at a banquet, when the queen said: “This Haman is our worst enemy and foe” (Esth. 7)?

Thus he was caught as a man in his own eyes; he was seized, he who found punishment at the table while feasting. Manifestly and in a wonderful way Haman bore the figure of the devil, while Mordecai, conversely, bore the type of Christ. For just as Haman was fixed to the cross which he had prepared for Mordecai, and Mordecai mounted the royal horse—the honor which Haman thought the king would bestow upon himself—so the devil was condemned on the cross which he brought about for Christ, while Christ, living, sits at the Father’s right hand, the likeness of which the devil had presumptuously claimed for himself.

Therefore I may gratefully say that the Word of God, the Word who is God, the Word not yet incarnate, God not yet made man, not only prefigured there his victory but already won it there. There already his prudence struck down the proud one, and there already “by his hand the twisting serpent was brought forth” (Job 26).

## CHAPTER XXII. How great was the strength of her good zeal.

What had been vigorously—indeed divinely—provided through the three virtues already mentioned, temperance, justice, and prudence, was promptly completed with unsluggish fortitude. Such great fortitude was in the breast of this humble woman, and it overflowed even to her whole nation, that after Haman was hung on the gallows and the king’s anger had subsided, the queen’s zeal did not subside. Rather, she said: “If it pleases the king, let authority be given to the Jews, so that as they have done today, so they may do tomorrow also in Susa; and let Haman’s ten sons be hanged upon the gallows” (Esth. 9).

For the king had said to her: “In the city of Susa the Jews have killed five hundred men and the other ten sons of Haman. What slaughter, do you suppose, are they carrying out in all the provinces?” (ibid.). How great was the fortitude of zeal which said, “As they have done today, so they may do tomorrow also in Susa,” and which hanged on gallows the ten sons of Haman who had already been killed.

If this had not been for God or for justice, it would seem cruelty. But now, when its cause is considered, such vengeance is not only excused but justified: it was not a fury of cruelty but an ardor of fortitude, not a movement of savagery but a movement of justice, not an excess of anger but a regard for life.

We have already considered the cause and proposed to consider it: from that nation the world’s salvation was hoped for; Christ, who was to be born, was expected. Accordingly, by inspiring humble and tender minds, the Holy Spirit made them worthy to employ, according to time and circumstance, a harsh justice, a just harshness, defending the root of the good olive tree, and the olive tree of the good root, so that it might stand and remain until it yielded its fruit, until by bringing forth Christ it poured out the true oil.

When this had come to pass, he said to Peter: “Put thy sword back into its sheath” (Matt. 26), because Peter no longer had a necessary cause for using the sword. Therefore, when we read that the Jews stood for their lives and killed their enemies and persecutors, so that they brought the slain to seventy-five thousand, while no one touched anything of their property, we should bear the aforesaid cause before our eyes and judge the deed worthy of a festival. Mordecai proclaimed the festival by written edict, and Esther established it, so that the day of that slaughter should thereafter be solemnly observed with all care and, as each year returned, celebrated with solemn honor.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Whenever the Word of God conquered one of the dragon’s heads, he bestowed signs of victory upon the person through whom he conquered.

Here we must note concerning the Word of God that, as he conquers each of the dragon’s heads, he lays royal signs of victory upon those persons through whom he conquers. Joseph and Moses, through whom he conquered the first head, the Egyptian head, triumphed in chariots and became lords and princes. Of Joseph the king said: “Behold, I have appointed thee over all the land of Egypt”; he received the royal ring, a linen robe, and a golden chain, and sat in the royal chariot (Gen. 41). Moses, after Egypt had been subdued and Pharaoh drowned, sang the song of victory and held the leadership of the whole people.

Elijah, through whom the second head was judged and cut down, as has been related in its proper place—after he had cast down kings to destruction and broken their power, after he had anointed kings to authority and made prophets his successors—was received in a whirlwind of fire, in a chariot with fiery horses.

Daniel and his companions, through whom the third head was humbled, were made princes, especially Daniel. King Nebuchadnezzar fell on his face before him and worshiped him, exalting him to high rank; afterward Belshazzar clothed him in purple and placed a golden chain around his neck.

Mordecai and Esther, through whom the fourth head was strangled and cut down by the hanging of Haman and his sons and, as has been said, by seventy-five thousand, were glorified with some title of victory. Queen Esther bore the royal diadem upon her head. Mordecai, coming out from the palace and the king’s presence, shone in royal garments—hyacinth-colored and bronze-colored—bearing a golden crown on his head and clothed in a silken and purple mantle.

Who struck down the fifth head, the most wicked head? The Maccabean brothers, after great wars and frequent victories, were adorned in royal fashion with purple, a sacred robe, and a golden clasp; and their descendants recovered and possessed the kingdom and priesthood with no small glory.

But he who conquered the sixth head and will conquer the seventh, when Christ Jesus kills Antichrist with the spirit of his mouth, was no ordinary champion of the Word of God, but the very Word of God, the Word who is God, made man. In this world he received crown and purple only in mockery: a crown of thorns, a scarlet cloak, and a reed placed in his right hand as a scepter. Yet what was given him in this world for mockery he transformed so truly into reality that he now appears to holy angels and men in his Father’s glory and honor, possessing the purple of resurrection, the crown of glory, and the scepter of everlasting dominion.

Let only this mention be made now of the last three heads, so that at this point one spectacle may be presented of all the heads together, a spectacle that pertains to the praise of the Word of God: those who labored for him and awaited his kingdom received, in their respective times, royal insignia of victory, visible in this present age also, after labors and distresses. Let us now return to our order.

## CHAPTER XXIV. What mystery is contained in Haman’s being hanged on the gallows which he had prepared for Mordecai.

It was a great spectacle then for the eyes of those who saw it, and it is one now for the minds of those who remember it: that a powerful and proud man, accustomed up to that point to be adored, was hanged before the city gates upon the gallows which he had prepared for Mordecai, together with all his kindred. “Not to us,” says the king, “but to God, who repays him what he deserved” (Esth. 16).

Josephus also greatly marvels at this, though he did not know how to marvel at it wholly, because he did not know the sacrament of Christ, of which this event was enacted as a type. “Hence,” he says, “it befell me to marvel at the name of God and to acknowledge his wisdom and justice: not only because he punished Haman’s malice, but also because he turned upon Haman the torments he had devised for another, and allowed others to perceive this—that whoever has been troublesome to another discovers that these things were first prepared for himself.”

As has been said, he did not know how to marvel at the whole. But let us know and marvel, to the praise of the Word of God, because there he set forth a most beautiful likeness of his future triumph, by which the whole world was to be redeemed. For, as was said above, it was not the Word of God, the Word who is God, who perished on the wood of the cross; rather, the devil, whose likeness Haman bore, received the judgment of condemnation. And this occurred outside the city gate, so that it is not without mystery that the same king says: “Before the gates of this city”—that is, Susa—“Haman and all his kindred hang upon the gallows” (ibid.).

The miracle is greater because God effected so great a sacrament, so full of profound mystery, not through a human prophet or one who knew his name, but through a Gentile man.

## CHAPTER XXV. What mystery is contained in the house of Haman being given to Queen Esther.

The fact also has some bearing upon the mystical likeness that, after Haman was hanged on the gallows, “on that day,” Scripture says, “King Ahasuerus gave Queen Esther the house of Haman, the adversary of the Jews” (Esth. 8). In giving it to Esther, he surely gave it to Mordecai; for shortly afterward it is written: “Esther appointed Mordecai over her house” (ibid.).

How much beauty there is in this deed, if you recall what Truth says in the Gospel, signifying that the devil would be cast out of his house: “When a strong man armed guards his court, all that he possesses is in peace. But when one stronger than he comes upon him and conquers him, he takes away all his weapons in which he trusted, and distributes his spoils” (Luke 11).

Thus it was to be, and thus it came to pass. The devil, like a strong armed man possessing power over the human race through sin, held the world as his house or court; but the incarnate Word, coming upon him with a stronger hand, conquered him and made his court his own. It was fitting, then, that Mordecai with Esther, having escaped the gallows, should possess alive the house of Haman who had been hanged. For thus it was to be: Christ, the Word of God, whose lineage according to the flesh was defended through Esther and Mordecai, would, after the prince of death was condemned on the cross, himself hold dominion with his Church, joined in the public religion of this present age to the secular empire and ecclesiastical priesthood in celebration.

## CHAPTER XXVI. Mordecai’s dream, in which he sees a little fountain become a great river and then the sun, was fulfilled in Queen Esther.

Who, then, does not see that the dream’s outcome was true, as it is said: “The little fountain which grew into a river, was changed into light and sun, and overflowed into many waters, is Esther, whom the king took as his wife and wished to make queen” (Esth. 10)?

But perhaps you say that the whole city rejoiced and was glad because a new light seemed to rise for the Jews, bringing honor, joy, and dancing; that among all peoples, cities, and provinces, wherever the king’s commands reached, there was marvelous exultation, feasting, banquets, and a festive day; and that, after so great a night of sorrow, they had so great a light of joy. Perhaps you say that this is insufficient reason to judge that the vision of the little fountain growing into a river and changing into the sun was fulfilled there.

It must be granted that no transitory joy, however great, deserves to be called the sun or compared to the sun, whose light or form does not change like the moon’s but remains full. Therefore neither Jacob in Joseph’s dream nor Esther in Mordecai’s dream was likened to the sun on account of his or her own person. Rather, each was marked by the sun because of Christ, the one and only sun of righteousness.

Joseph was so marked because he already possessed Christ in promise; Esther, because she preserved the lineage from which Christ would be born, aided by the gracious beauty of her body and preceded by the merit of faith and a chaste mind. Christ is the end and final cause of the things done then; and therefore you speak truly in saying that “the little fountain was changed into the sun.”

## CHAPTER XXVII. The captivity of the people for the sake of the Word of God was far more glorious than the imperial liberty of the Gentiles.

Let that captivity of the people of God now be compared with the liberty of the nations under whom, or among whom, that people was held captive. What is more glorious, what more fortunate: the imperial liberty of the nations that were without God, or the captivity of a people whose hope rested in the word of promise? But, if you would give a certain judgment, look to the prosperity—indeed, the misery—of the nations and of the kings who ruled over them, as it is recorded in histories and annals. How did they reign? How did they exercise dominion? They reigned amid bloodshed; they ruled amid death: falsely living and truly dying, thirsting for glory and drinking calamity. For did those 598 heads of the dragon, of which we spoke, while they stood open-mouthed and gaping against the woman with child, spare even themselves, or cease from tearing one another apart by mutual biting? On the contrary, by their own bites they made themselves far more bloody. For though, in evil accord with one spirit of malice, they always opened their jaws and gnashed their teeth against the woman, yet, divided against themselves in a strange manner, they hated one another and sprang upon one another [Col. 1397A]. Kings of kings, friends of friends, relatives of relatives, sons of fathers, fathers of sons, drenched the earth with their blood as with abundant rain. Sons, sparing not even their mothers’ breasts, greedily drank blood, sometimes provoked merely by divided favouritism because of their beastly desire to reign. A mother was sometimes slaughtered by one son because she was thought to favour another son more; a father was cut down by his son. Hundreds of thousands, and more than hundreds of thousands, slain daily in war, are doubtless reckoned by the devil as sport.

It is not our present purpose to recount the horrible and devilish tragedies of the wars of the nations. Whoever wishes, or has leisure, may read the many histories. Our purpose here is to affirm what is true: that the nations [Col. 1397B], or the kings of the nations, who held God’s people captive were more wretched even in respect of this present age than the captive people of God. For to the latter, who looked to the word of promise, all things worked together for good, not only in the future but sometimes even in the present age; whereas for the former, who had nothing to do with the Word of God, all things worked together for evil.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. After the Persian and Median kingdom had been overcome by the Word of God, the Macedonian kingdom—signified in Daniel by the he-goat—succeeded it.

At last what had been ordained in the word of the Lord had necessarily to occur, as Daniel had foreseen: namely, that the he-goat, coming over the face of the whole earth [Col. 1397C], should rage against the ram, strike it, and shatter its horns, so that no one could rescue the ram from its hands. The he-goat was the kingdom of the Macedonians, and the conspicuous horn which it had between its eyes was Alexander the Great. The ram, moreover, was the kingdom of the Persians and Medes. Darius, son of Arsames, reigned as the fourteenth king; in him was fulfilled what had been signified by the prophetic Spirit’s forewarning: “When he had cast the ram to the ground,” he says, “the goat trampled it, and no one was able to rescue” it—namely, “the ram—from its hands” (Dan. 8).

Concerning this man, I have chosen not to pass over something both remarkable and pitiable, in view of the previously mentioned unhappy prosperity of the kings or kingdoms of the nations [Col. 1397D]. For he became a great spectacle and a striking proof of how unstable is the condition of this age, how untrustworthy the world’s security.
