Defeated in three battles by Alexander, he was bound by his own kinsmen with golden fetters and chains to win the conqueror’s favour. Carried out in a closed carriage, pierced by many wounds, and still breathing, he was found by Alexander’s soldiers and brought before Alexander. “I have found you,” he said, “a happier enemy than my own relatives and kinsmen. For you, though an enemy, gave life to my mother and children; my relatives took mine away—those to whom I gave both life and kingdoms.”

Let these things be recalled because the chance of worldly prosperity is uncertain and slippery: the kingdoms of the world always have been, and are, deceitful. But true is the word: “For the kingdom is the Lord’s, and he himself shall rule the nations” (Ps. 21 [22]:28) [Col. 1398A].

## CHAPTER XXIX. Why the Macedonian kingdom was signified in the earlier vision by a leopard and in the later vision by a he-goat.

It is worth observing also, since it bears somewhat upon the purpose of the present work, that in the earlier vision the Macedonian kingdom is signified by a leopard, and in the following vision by a he-goat. Was so different an image of one and the same kingdom shown without reason? Certainly not. Rather, because the matters were different, the kinds of vision were varied. The Holy Spirit, the prophetic Spirit, just as he foreknew the events to come, knew how fittingly to assign beforehand figures appropriate to those future events [Col. 1398B].

For it was to come about that the Macedonian kingdom, possessing both the beastly ferocity of the leopard and the effeminate lustfulness of the he-goat, would brandish its horns against the Most High and harden its cruelty against the true and truly firm word of the oft-mentioned promise. From the sacred histories it must be recounted—and shall later be recounted—how savage and how lustful it was: most fierce and cruel in the leopard’s ferocity, crushing the saints of the Most High with cruel ferocity and fierce cruelty; lustful and effeminate in the he-goat’s always lustward-inclined wantonness, contaminating the people and the temple of God with frenzied lust and lustful frenzy; cunning and crafty according to the leopard’s variegation; unstable and uncontrolled [Col. 1398C] according to the immoderate heat of goat’s blood.

By these very different vices, ferocity and lust, that Macedonian or Greek kingdom laboured against the word of promise. This will later have to be stated fully in its proper place; and therefore it was fitting that in the preceding vision it should be foreshown by a leopard, and subsequently by a he-goat.

## CHAPTER XXX. Why the kingdom of the Persians and Medes was signified in the earlier vision by a bear and in the later by a ram.

Likewise, concerning the kingdom of the Persians and Medes, it is worthy of inquiry why in the earlier vision it was denoted by the likeness of a bear and in the subsequent one by the form of a ram. A fitting answer [Col. 1398D] may be given: the kingdom had different—indeed contrary—relations toward God’s people and toward the word of promise, so often mentioned, which was preserved among that people.

I would not hesitate to say that those causes were as far apart as are the natures of the bear and the ram: one lives by plunder and bloodshed; the other is harmless, neither thirsting for blood nor living by plunder. This is easy to distinguish if you consider how cruel that kingdom was in the person of Haman, and how kindly its kings devoted themselves to that people. For Haman, truly a bear in his character, wished with savage fury and monstrous rage, gaping with open mouth, to devour the entire race of the Jews. But the kings, especially Ahasuerus, after the manner of a ram, cherished and enriched that same people with their fleeces—that is, with the great wealth in which that kingdom abounded [Col. 1399A]. They inflicted no tooth of malice, just as a ram attacks no one with its tooth; indeed, through the favour of Queen Esther and Mordecai, they greatly gladdened the life of that nation.

But perhaps someone will say that the person of King Ahasuerus himself ought to be understood by the bear in that vision, because it is written: “And they said to it,” namely to the bear, “Arise, devour much flesh” (Dan. 7:5). And this corresponds to what was said to King Ahasuerus: “If it pleases you, decree concerning the people that it perish” (Esther 3:9). To this I say that the bear signified not only the king’s person but the whole body of the kingdom. Nor was the command, “Decree that the people perish,” given to the king alone; rather, instructions were sent throughout all the provinces to all the satraps and judges of the provinces [Col. 1399B], that they should kill and destroy all the Jewish people. Therefore, in Haman and in all who wished to harm the Jews, that kingdom was a most savage bear; in the king and in all who did not possess that spirit of malice, it was as it were a ram.

## CHAPTER XXXI. Why the he-goat was seen to have only one horn, but the ram two.

If you also ask why the same he-goat was seen to have only one horn between its eyes, while the ram had two horns, the answer is readily apparent. The bodies of the animals signify individual kingdoms, while the horns [Col. 1399C] are understood as the kings of those kingdoms. It is certain that Alexander alone was king of the Macedonian kingdom, and, having defeated Darius, as has already been said, he alone held the kingdom in his own time.

But it was not one king who raised the Babylonian heads of the Persian and Median kingdom: there were two conquerors of Babylon and two kings at the same time, sharers in one empire—namely Cyrus and Darius the Mede, his uncle, son of Astyages. Thus the one horn of the he-goat and the two horns of the ram were rightly seen, because one king strengthened the dominion of the Macedonian kingdom, but two kings the empire of the Persians and Medes. Cyrus, younger than Darius in time or age, grew greater in victories and power, and also became greater than Darius in wealth. This the aforementioned vision aptly indicates [Col. 1399D], when, after saying, “And behold, one ram stood before the marsh, having lofty horns,” it adds, “and one was higher than the other and grew up afterward”—that is, Cyrus was more powerful than Darius and advanced more in victories than he did (Dan. 8:3).

## CHAPTER XXXII. A great part of the Word of God’s victory lies in this: that, as it foretold kingdoms would change, so it also changed them.

Finally, does not a beautiful part of that same victory of the Word of God, which we have undertaken to praise, shine forth in these very changes of kingdoms? For to speak the truth and be incapable of error is without doubt to conquer; and victory of this kind belongs especially to the Word of God [Col. 1400A]. God said these things before they occurred, and the word of the Lord concerning future events came to human beings, so that, when they took place, people might undoubtedly recognize that they happened not by chance but proceeded reasonably by God’s ordered providence and came about according to a justly arranged judgment.

Therefore one of the prophets, having first said, “Will there be evil in a city which the Lord has not done?” immediately added: “For the Lord God will do nothing unless the Lord has revealed his secret to his servants the prophets” (Amos 3:6–7). For example, with regard to these kingdoms which were to change and fight against one another, the Lord did nothing without first revealing his secret: first under the images of beasts—a lioness, a bear, a leopard, and the terrible fourth beast, described without a name—and then under the likenesses of the ram and the he-goat, which the discourse most recently mentioned [Col. 1400B].

Therefore, when the secret is first revealed to the prophets in the word of the Lord, and then all things happen exactly as they were revealed or foretold, the Word of God simultaneously gains the palm of truth and refutes the opinion of those who think this world is governed by causes and not ruled by God’s providence. Against them the very Word of the Lord says through the prophet Jeremiah: “Who is he that has said it, so that it came to pass, when the Lord did not command? Do not good and evil proceed from the mouth of the Most High?” (Lam. 3:37–38).

Rightly indeed is he indignant against people of this sort, because nothing happens unless the Lord commands it. Nothing is without cause under the sun. The world is not governed apart from God’s providence; rather, good and evil proceed from his mouth. Evils do so when the world is afflicted by a just judgment because of its deserts; goods do so when it finds consolation and rejoices in some prosperity [Col. 1400C]. Whoever thinks otherwise is rightly unknown; whoever holds the contrary view is justly rejected, and it is said of him: “Who is this?” This is as though God said: “I do not know who this man is; I do not wish to know who he is. Let him depart from me. I have not known him; I do not wish to know him.”

# BOOK NINE

[Col. 1399]

## CHAPTER I. Preface to Cuno, in which he complains that he is cold and negligent, and asks to be helped by prayers.

As I set my mind to the conflicts of the fifth head against the Word or purpose of God, I have long had cause to remember that saying in Job: “From the north gold will come, and fearful praise to God” (Job 37:22). This cause, dearest Father Cuno, must be disclosed to you. Since you began to embrace as gold the praise of the Lord spoken by my mouth, I confess that I have felt more than I had previously felt that I am in the north—that is, that I do not possess, as I ought, the fervent power of divine love or a lively and burning concern for my own salvation [Col. 1401A].

I confess that I have found in myself the truth also of that saying: “They made me a keeper in the vineyards; my own vineyard I did not keep.” Especially now, while I pursue the individual heads of the dragon and am eager to describe the sins and bloody crimes of each, it seems to me that he turns against me in wrath, devises his fury against me, and, as against his accuser, seeks the vengeance he desires. Thus he covers me with the snow of temptations and the hail of anxieties, and binds me with the frost of negligence. So, while you gladly read my writings aloud and embrace them as gold of praise, you may truly say as well: “This gold came from the north.”

It remains, then, and is needful for me, that this praise should be fearful to me—that I should fear precisely this: lest a writing that praises the Lord be reckoned to presumption and empty glory rather than reward, because I have shamelessly seized upon a pursuit that belonged to holy people, though I am not holy [Col. 1401B]. I desire to be helped by your prayers and the prayers of all who love you, lest I remain in the land of the north, whence the gold comes, but may deserve to set out with the gold itself for the region of the most radiant south, shining with the midday sun.

## CHAPTER II. A pleasing answer to Cuno, who had asked that the preface to the Second Book of Maccabees, explained, be inserted into this work.

From this head, great as it was, and from those who struck it—the brothers Maccabees—an occasion arose for you to say to me: “Write me a book on the victory of the Word of God,” as I mentioned in the prologue, which I prefixed to this work as I spoke with you. Yet you persist, asking—or rather, by the force of affection commanding—that I apply some effort to explain the long preface of the Second Book of Maccabees, almost difficult, as you say, and as it seems to me; as though I could satisfy, or were obliged to satisfy, the whole of your demand [Col. 1401C].

You also say in jest that you dreamed this very thing long ago, and that in your dream you both begged and commanded me to insert and fittingly adapt this part—namely, an elucidation of the prologue—to this work; and that I seemed at first to refuse strongly and then to promise compliance. And I dare say to you, though concerned lest the eye of some scoffer see this and receive it without goodwill, that I once seemed to myself to be engaged in a long struggle with the devil and at last to say to him as he despised me: “When it pleases the Most High, let him establish his seat in me, and he will speak judgments against you.”

If what seemed to be was not vain, and if it is now fulfilled in fact, while with diligent discourse we strike the individual heads of the dragon, the Word itself will help, so that your dream too may prosper through my obedience [Col. 1401D].

## CHAPTER III. The fifth head of the dragon was the kingdom of the Greeks.

My mind was already eagerly prepared to begin with what must first be said concerning this head: that one little horn among the many horns of the he-goat, through which the kingdom of the Greeks was signified, as was touched upon at the end of the preceding book—namely, the horn which was magnified even to the host of heaven, cast down some of the host and stars, received power against the continual sacrifice because of sins, and cast down the place of sanctification—was Antiochus, called Epiphanes, that is, “Illustrious,” under whom the seven young brothers Maccabees suffered with their mother [Col. 1402A].

My discourse was hastening toward this matter, which is surely a great part of the battle waged by that great dragon, the ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan, against the oft-mentioned conception of the blessed woman (Rev. 12)—that is, against the word of promise received in faith by the ancient Church from the time of Abraham. But my mind is still held above by that utterance of the angel speaking to Daniel: “Daniel, man of desires, understand the words that I speak to you, and do not fear. For from the first day when you set your heart to afflict yourself before your God, your words were heard, and I came because of your words; but the prince of the kingdom of Persia resisted me for twenty-one days. And behold, Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me, and I remained there beside the king of Persia” (Dan. 10:11–13).

And again he says: “Do you know why I have come to you? Now I shall return to fight against the prince of Persia. For when I went forth, the prince of the Greeks appeared, coming; and no one is my helper in all these things except Michael, your prince” (ibid.) [Col. 1402B–C]. Such an utterance, I say, turns the hearing mind to itself like a mighty trumpet; and by its marvel it warns us not to pass over the fact that not human beings alone, but even angelic powers, were moved and became leaders in the battle which we have undertaken to proclaim in writing this work on the victory of the Word of God.

## CHAPTER IV. The princes of Persia and Greece must be understood as evil angels resisting the good princes, that is, the angels.

What sort of beings these princes of Persia and Greece were is briefly indicated by one of the most eminent teachers, Blessed Jerome [Note: [Col. 1401] Jerome, *Commentary on Daniel*, ch. 10, v. 13, ed. Migne.]: “These,” he says, “are the princes of whom the Apostle Paul also speaks: ‘We speak wisdom among the perfect, which none of the princes of this age knew; for if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory’” (1 Cor. 2:6, 8).

Certainly, even if such authority were lacking, a prudent reader would not doubt that evil princes means evil angels, against whom good princes had to fight—those who oppose the prayers of holy people and the embassy of holy angels. For the devil is called by the Lord the prince of the world; and “the world,” says apostolic truth, “lies in the Evil One” (1 John 5:19) [Col. 1403A]. If this is certain of the whole, who can doubt it of the parts? If the devil is prince of the entire world, are not the princes of parts of the world—namely, Persia and Greece—rightly understood as evil powers serving the greater prince, the devil?

For the Persians and Greeks were not worshippers of God. Rather, they served the creature rather than the Creator; they worshipped demons, not God, but demons in God’s place. The Persians worshipped the sun, which they also called Apollo; the Greeks, under the name or pretext of their wisdom, Minerva; and other nations other monstrous demons. Each nation singularly worshipped its own above the rest; but all, under the universal name of Jupiter, worshipped the prince of demons, the devil, prince of the world. Before the images of such princes—such evil spirits—they prostrated themselves [Col. 1403B]; and those whose gods these were were all the more rightly called their princes.

## CHAPTER V. Michael is the prince of God’s people; all good princes agree with one another, but evil ones agree neither with the good nor among themselves.

Michael was the prince of Daniel and of the entire people who worshipped the true God: a holy prince, a good angel, a great archangel. For the same angel says: “No one is my helper in all these things except Michael, your prince” (Dan. 10:21). And again he says: “At that time Michael, the great prince who stands for the children of your people, shall arise” (Dan. 12:1).

Human beings and kings of nations, placed under such diverse—indeed contrary—princes, moved in divergent and contrary directions. Their evil princes, princes of evil people, undoubtedly resisted the good princes of good people and worshippers of God. For one of the good princes here says: “The prince of the kingdom of Persia resisted me for twenty-one days” (ibid.) [Col. 1403C]. Good princes always agree with one another; evil ones always resist the good as far as they can, always disagree among themselves, and are always in contention with one another, because they are proud.

Likewise, the evil people under them always differ from the good, and are no less divided against themselves: kingdom against kingdom, city against city, house against house, man against man. And though some are at times joined by blood relationship, nevertheless:

> No trust abides among partners in a kingdom,  
> and every power will be impatient of a fellow ruler.  
> —Lucan, *Pharsalia* 1.92–93

## CHAPTER VI. What sort of battle exists between good and evil princes.

Whence do evil princes derive any power to fight against good princes? Whence their strength to resist? Whence their capacity to oppose? From causes: from the sins of human beings or peoples. For they fight in the field of justice, in the conflict of judgment. The evil fight by accusing; the good fight by defending; God is the judge. In proportion as the accusation is great and true, the defense is slow and powerless.

For example, great and true was the accuser’s charge against the ten tribes of Israel [Col. 1404A], called Samaria, which had been divided from the house of David and from the tribe of Judah. Great, I say, was the accusation of the prince of the Assyrians—whoever that evil angel was—that they had never departed from the sins of Jeroboam, who caused Israel to sin; and that they had proved incorrigible although they had so often heard the word of the Lord through the prophets and had witnessed among themselves so many signs and wonders performed by Elijah and Elisha.

Great indeed, but not so great, was the accusation of the prince of Persia against the Jews held captive under the Persian king. For the tribe of Judah in Jerusalem had sinned, just as the ten tribes had in Samaria, but not so stubbornly. Some of the kings of Judah repented, such as Manasseh; some were also righteous and corrected the people, such as Hezekiah and Josiah. But, as has already been said, none of the kings of the ten tribes departed from the sins of Jeroboam [Col. 1404B].

Therefore the accusation of the prince of Assyria was great, and so great that no one could defend those who were justly to be held captive in perpetual captivity. But the accusation of the prince of Persia was indeed great, though not so great as to require the Jews’ captivity under the Persian king to be irrevocable. For neither they nor their kingdom had committed an irrevocable fault—that is, one without any public or common repentance by certain kings and by the people. Thus, “the prince of the kingdom of Persia resisted me,” he says—understand, but he will not be able to resist me altogether. For our cause and the measure of sin give Michael, our prince—who alone is my helper in all these matters—a just ground for defense: that you ought not to be held in perpetual captivity, because you have not departed from the Lord forever; indeed, you have at times offered, and now offer, repentance as satisfaction [Col. 1404C].

## CHAPTER VII. How the prince of Persia resisted for twenty-one days.

What, then, is the significance of this number: “The prince of Persia resisted me for twenty-one days” (Dan. 10:13)? Clearly it was because Daniel had waited and longed for the divine answer for that many days, with such desire that he deserved to be called “a man of desires” (Dan. 10:11). For that many days the answer had been awaited. “In those days,” Daniel says, “I mourned for three weeks; I ate no pleasant bread, nor did flesh or wine enter my mouth; neither did I anoint myself with oil until the three weeks were completed” (Dan. 10:2–3) [Col. 1404D].

The days of three weeks are twenty-one. Thus, as though Daniel complained of delay and charged the angel with tardiness, the angel offers unprompted an explanation of why he had not come from the first day of mourning and fasting. “From the first day,” he says, “when you set your heart to afflict yourself before your God, your words were heard” (ibid.)—for you personally, because righteousness was found in you before God. Yet I did not come on the first day because of your words; and this was the reason for my delay, because the prince of the kingdom of Persia resisted me: opposing me, that is, and asserting that release from captivity was unjust. Thus, while he resisted and you persisted in prayer and affliction, twenty-one days passed; and now at last I have come to teach you what is to happen according to the mercy and truth of God the Judge.

Beginning in this way, he announces to Daniel many great and wonderful future things as though recounting history, and the conclusion is this: “Those who are wise shall shine like the brightness of the firmament; and those who instruct many unto righteousness, like the stars for everlasting eternities” (Dan. 12:3) [Col. 1405A].

## CHAPTER VIII. How evil spirits fight with the good while we pray.

From this we receive a terrible and lamentable lesson: we must know that there is a cause before God’s judgment whenever, amid any public or private affliction, we are not quickly heard when we cry out to the Lord. We should know that holy angels are ministers between God and God’s servants, that we sing psalms and pray in their presence, and that they are always ready to offer God the prayers of the Church. We should also know that evil angels come in opposition, contradict and resist them, and, though themselves unjust, plead against us the causes of our injustice: namely, that we ought not to be heard because we neither pray in full faith nor observe the conditions prescribed to us for being heard.

These conditions are as follows: “Loose the bonds of wickedness, undo the bundles that oppress, let the crushed go free, and break every yoke. Break your bread for the hungry; bring the needy and homeless into your house; when you see the naked, cover him, and do not despise your own flesh. Then you will call, and the Lord will hear; you will cry, and he will say, ‘Behold, I am here’” (Isa. 58:6–9) [Col. 1405B–C].

Therefore, when we call and the Lord does not hear, when we cry and he does not say, “Behold, I am here,” we should know that evil spirits resist and contradict the holy angels who offer God our invocations and cries. They hold in their hands the accusation, the weapons which are our sins—not redeemed by the aforementioned works of mercy, which the Lord made a condition if we desire to be justly heard. But let us proceed with what we have begun.

## CHAPTER IX. How the saying should be understood: “Behold, Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me, and I remained there beside the king of Persia.”

“Behold,” he says, “Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me, and I remained there beside the king of Persia” (Dan. 10:13). And afterward: “Now I shall return to fight against the prince of Persia. For when I went forth, the prince of the Greeks appeared, coming” (ibid.). This wording should be noted. He says, “I remained,” not beside the prince of Persia, but “beside the king of Persia” [Col. 1405D].

For the king of Persia was a human being—Darius or Cyrus—beside whom, or with whom, as it is better expressed, the good angel had to remain, because the cause of the captives required this. But the prince of Persia was an evil angel, beside whom the good angel ought not to remain, but against whom he ought to fight.

There is no need to ask what advantage or good fruit came from the fact that this good angel remained beside the king of Persia and fought against the evil angel, prince of Persia. For it is known, and has already been discussed above, how the king of Persia, by God’s prompting, released the Jews from captivity and issued a decree for rebuilding the temple of the great God; and then how another Persian king, Ahasuerus, was restrained from allowing the most wicked plan of Haman the Agagite, enemy of the Jews, to be carried out, and instead turned the devices of his malice back upon his own head [Col. 1406A].

Whence did these things so happily come to pass, except because this good angel remained beside the king of Persia, administering good counsel? For, says the Apostle, they are ministering spirits. And he fought against the evil angel, the prince of Persia, who resisted him, by offering prayers to God and defending the cause of the captives. These matters are great and worthy of the holy princes of heaven fighting for their accomplishment, if you remember what we have often said: that the preservation of that nation was a preparation for the advent of Christ Jesus, so that, when he was born, there might be a people from whom the word of promise would be fulfilled. Therefore not only this angelic warrior and Michael his helper, but all angels, archangels, thrones, dominions, principalities, powers, virtues, cherubim, and seraphim, together with all people of good will, had cause to rejoice and be glad [Col. 1406B].

## CHAPTER X. How the saying should be understood: “For when I went forth, the prince of the Greeks appeared, coming.”

But behold another evil: “For when I went forth,” he says, “the prince of the Greeks appeared, coming” (Dan. 10:20)—understand, in order to obtain or acquire empire for the Macedonians, under whose dominion the children of your people would suffer many things. Already then he appeared; already then the Greek kingdom was coming, while this one whom he calls the prince of the Greeks was stirring up the peoples of Greece.

Nor is it remarkable that the good angel, standing in God’s presence, going forth from him and returning to him, already saw this prince beginning to come. For the Greeks were already then beginning to do great things [Col. 1406C–D]. Anyone who wishes may readily recall from histories how much the Greeks, especially the Athenians, afterward both did and suffered. They were preeminent, indeed first, among the Greeks in military affairs; and, as Pompeius Trogus says, their deeds were greater in accomplishment than in narration, achieved beyond not only the expectation of success but even the credibility of what had been accomplished.

During the same period when these visions were revealed to Daniel, the Athenians defeated Darius, the third Persian king after Cyrus, in whose time the angel spoke these things to Daniel in the vision. For when Darius learned that the Athenians had supplied aid against him to his enemies, he directed the entire force of war against them. Hearing of his approach, the Athenians sought aid from the Lacedaemonians and advanced against the enemy with great eagerness of spirit [Col. 1407A]. The battle was fought with such courage that you might have thought men on one side and beasts on the other. The Persians lost two hundred thousand in that battle or shipwreck.

Thus it is clear how it could be said, “For when I went forth, the prince of the Greeks appeared, coming”: for the Persians were already beginning to be defeated by the Greeks. Then, after Darius died, when his son Xerxes entered Greece with seven hundred thousand men—so that it has not without reason been recorded that rivers were dried up by his army and that all Greece could scarcely contain it—they were defeated in two land battles and a third naval battle, in which they are said to have had one thousand ships. The entry of their king into Greece was as terrifying as his departure was shameful and disgraceful.

It is wonderful to say, and clear to readers of the ancient histories, how cruelly those evil princes, savage angels, played with human blood in those very times: now making Greeks strike down Greeks, now likewise making Greeks strike down and kill Persians in implacable fury [Col. 1407B]. Thus you should not fail to understand why it was said that the world lay, or lies, in the Evil One. Those aforementioned beings were subordinate princes of that evil devil; and because they ruled their subjects, there could be no peace for the wicked.

## CHAPTER XI. How the kingdom of the Greeks had its beginning.

We think we have spoken of the prince of the Greeks and of how he began to come. Now it must be said how he arrived: how the kingdom of the Greeks or Macedonians—for the Macedonians certainly are Greeks—grew into an empire, held Judea along with other nations, and brought about those things which the earlier vision showed would be done through the little horn that arose from the four horns of the aforementioned he-goat [Col. 1407C].

After about two hundred and twenty years of Persian rule, Alexander of Macedon succeeded to the kingdom when Philip died. He was born, as was thought, of the same Philip, but was greater than his father in prowess and wealth. Yet, if those who wrote of him record the truth, that aforementioned evil prince of the Greeks truly led him to the kingdom; and when Alexander attained it, that prince arrived, by God’s permission. God’s permission is always just, although the will or intention of evil princes is always unjust.

For the writers of Alexander’s deeds report that a certain magician, Nectanebus, transformed by magical arts into the demon of horned Jupiter, whom they call Hammon, had intercourse with Olympias, Philip’s wife, and that Alexander was generated from this union. Others report also that on the night in which his mother Olympias conceived him, she saw herself in a dream entwined with a huge serpent. These two accounts of the writers agree well enough with one another, except that one says more and the other less [Col. 1407D]. We gladly receive them both, since either account testifies that the cooperation of evil spirits was not lacking where such a man was conceived: a man destined to become such a plunderer of lands and, as one distinguished author says,

> … brought forth, no benefit to the world,  
> an example that so many nations  
> could lie beneath one man.

## CHAPTER XII. [Col. 1408A] King Alexander wished to be regarded as the son of Hammon; and this was signified to Daniel by the he-goat which did not touch the earth.

Because of the success of his plundering, by which he plundered the world, and because of the unconquered strength and swiftness of his victories, he was prefigured by the conspicuous horn which, Daniel says, the he-goat had between its eyes (Dan. 8). For he is said to have been a most keen youth, educated in literary studies, and then to have matured for five years under Aristotle, the most renowned teacher of all philosophers. Having gained empire, he commanded that he be called king of all lands and of the world. Such was his pride that he ordered people to think of him as more than a man, and turned to his own glory that shameful circumstance of his mother’s [Col. 1408B] conception, unheard of before.

For, as those same writers say, Philip, near the very end of his life, had publicly declared that Alexander was not his son; for this reason he had repudiated Olympias, as though convicted of adultery. Olympias herself had confessed to Philip that she had conceived Alexander not by him but, as already stated, by a serpent of immense size—nothing other than the adultery of Nectanebus, transformed by magical arts and claiming to be Hammon. Therefore, when Alexander went to Jupiter Hammon to seek responses concerning future events and his own origin, desiring to acquire a divine ancestry and at the same time clear his mother of disgrace, he arranged beforehand through intermediaries what answer he wished the priest of the temple to give him. [Col. 1408C] As he entered the temple, the priest at once, as he had been instructed, greeted him as Hammon’s son. Delighted as though by divine adoption, Alexander ordered that he be regarded as having this father.

He then asked whether he had avenged himself upon all the murderers of his parent—for Philip had been cut down at public games by a certain noble youth, whom no one suspected. He was answered that his father could neither be killed nor die; that the vengeance for King Philip was almost complete; and his companions received this answer: that they should worship Alexander as a god, not as a king. On account of such great pride of heart, I think this was so seen and so said: “The he-goat came from the west over the face of the whole earth, and did not touch the ground” (ibid.). The meaning is that he wished his generation to be thought not earthly but divine. For even when he finally died, he ordered that his body be embalmed in the temple of Hammon, as though of his father, a god.

## CHAPTER XIII. How Alexander came to Jerusalem and venerated the high priest clothed in sacred vestments.

The reason had not yet arisen why that he-goat—that is, the Greek kingdom—should ravage Judah and Jerusalem, and the Temple lately restored from the ruin and fire of the Chaldeans. Nor had that conspicuous horn been appointed for this purpose: to do what was to be done by another horn of the same goat, according to the mystery of the vision mentioned above. One must know, indeed, [Col. 1409A] that it happened only for manifest causes, only for great crimes, that Nebuchadnezzar first, or Antiochus later, rendered that place desolate. We have spoken in its place of the causes of the former, that is, Babylonian, tempest; we shall speak later of the causes of the latter.

The devil did indeed intend to hurl against God, against the word of God’s promise, that great horn of the goat; but he was not permitted to do so. Rather, that place was defended by manifest divine power. “When this same Alexander came to Jerusalem,” Josephus says, “the Phoenicians and Chaldeans with him reckoned that whatever the imperial rage might be able to do to the city, he himself would do and would allow them to do; and that he would afflict the high priest with the greatest indignities. But the same high priest, named Jaddi, had been forewarned by a divine vision to take courage, adorn the city with garlands, and immediately open the gates. The others were to go out in white clothing; he himself and the remaining priests were to go out in their lawful vestments, hoping to suffer nothing cruel under God’s providence.”

When this was done, the outcome was the opposite of what the aforesaid Phoenicians and Chaldeans supposed. For Alexander, seeing the multitude dressed in white garments, the priests in linen vestments, and the high priest in a blue tunic and golden robe, with a mitre upon his head and a golden plate on which God’s name was written, approached alone, worshipped the Name, and was the first to venerate the high priest. [Col. 1409C] When the kings of Syria and the others were astonished at this and thought the king’s mind had been corrupted, one of them asked him: “Why, when all worshipped you, did you yourself worship the high priest of the Jewish nation?” He replied: “I did not worship this man, but the God whose high-priestly office he holds; for I saw him in a dream in such attire.”

A splendid part of the victory—the victory of God’s Name or Word—was that, in order to fulfill the truth of the promise, preserving and defending that nation, it humbled to itself the heads of kingdoms: Babylon’s head, Nebuchadnezzar, fell down and worshipped His prophet; the diadem of the Macedonians, great Alexander, likewise worshipped God’s Name in the priestly adornment; and, between them in time, the most powerful king of the Persians and Medes celebrated, though unknowingly, the mystery of His victorious Passion by hanging Haman on the gallows, as has been said in its proper place. [Col. 1409D]

## CHAPTER XIV. How that horn was broken—that is, how Alexander the Great died.

How, then, was that horn broken? “For the he-goat,” Scripture says, “became exceedingly great; and when he had grown, the great horn was broken” (Dan. 8). How was it broken? How did the great Alexander die—he who was thought, and wished to be thought, immortal?

He came to Babylon and there received through a treacherous plot a cup of poison. The poison is said to have been so powerful that it could be contained neither by bronze, iron, nor pottery, and could be carried only in a horse’s hoof. Having received the cup, in the middle of drinking he suddenly groaned as though pierced by a dart. Half alive, he was carried away from the banquet and so bitterly tormented that he called for a sword as a remedy; and the touch of human beings caused pain like wounds. Alexander died on the sixth day, at the age of thirty-three years and one month.

We mention this very brief span now so that you may reflect what sort of—or how great—a figure this young man can be in the judgment of the Ancient of Days, seated upon the throne and judging those beasts, of which this leopard was the third beast: that is, he was signified by the leopard, fierce and proud. [Col. 1410B] For what is it, when viewed in relation to that Ancient One, to see a youth of so few years snatching a kingdom which that same Ancient One was to dispose, and commanding himself to be called king of all lands and of the whole world? Surely it is such—indeed, far more ridiculous—than if a grasshopper were to leap up and, because of its brief jump, wish to be considered a giant so great as to touch heaven.

Long ago it had been said of this man and of the rest who show irreverence and seize kingdoms in the commonwealth of that same Ancient of Days: “Their memory has perished with a sound, but the Lord remains for ever” (Ps. 9). And He who remains says: “My counsel shall stand, and my will shall be done” (Isa. 46): that is, so that He alone may conquer, alone reign, and rule, who was chosen beforehand by the Ancient One—because the judgment of my antiquity is true and paternal—that He alone may be King of all, through whom alone all things were made. [Col. 1410C]

## CHAPTER XV. After the horn was broken, four others grew up; and thus the dragon, although it has only seven heads, nevertheless wears ten diadems.

After the great horn of the goat was broken, “four horns arose over it toward the four winds of heaven” (Dan. 8). That is: after Alexander the Great died, his kingdom was divided into four parts, and was also torn apart among outsiders, apart from these four kingdoms: Macedonia, Asia, Syria, and Egypt.

In Egypt Ptolemy son of Lagus first ruled—that is, in the south. In Macedonia, Philip, who was also Aridaeus, Alexander’s brother—that is, in the west. In Syria and Babylon, Seleucus, also called Nicanor—that is, [Col. 1410D] in the east. In Asia and Pontus, Antigonus—that is, in the north. This is according to the regions of the whole world. Yet Judaea has Syria to its north and Egypt to its south.

Here the occasion suggests the following point: in the Apocalypse, this dragon or beast—whose wars against the Word of God this present work has undertaken to recount—has indeed seven heads and seven diadems on its heads, but is written to have ten horns. For: “Behold,” it says, “a great red dragon, having seven heads and ten horns, and seven diadems upon its heads” (Rev. 12). Why this is so is indicated by a careful observation of the present passage: when, in one of the seven kingdoms which are the dragon’s seven heads, four successors arise in place of one departing king, Alexander, and all set diadems upon themselves, the number of kings increases, and ten kings come to belong to seven kingdoms. Through these kingdoms, as has often been said, the devil-dragon set himself to make void the Word of God’s promise.

For even though the Macedonian kingdom was divided into four parts, it was nevertheless counted as one empire down to the Roman Empire; and only one part, namely the kingdom of Syria, through Antiochus Epiphanes, cruelly carried out the malice of its dragon—that is, persecution savage against God’s covenant. [Col. 1411A]

## CHAPTER XVI. How Antiochus was signified by the little horn which came forth from one of the four.

[Col. 1411B] As has been said, Seleucus, surnamed Nicanor, was the first to rule Syria after Alexander’s death; the second was Antiochus, called Soter; the third, likewise Antiochus, was called Theos, that is, “God”; the fourth, Seleucus, was surnamed Callinicus; the fifth, Seleucus, surnamed Ceraunus, that is, “Thunderbolt”; the sixth, Antiochus, Seleucus’s brother, was called the Great; the seventh, Seleucus, son of Antiochus the Great; the eighth, Antiochus, Seleucus’s brother, was called Epiphanes, that is, “Illustrious.”

[Col. 1411C] This is the sinful root of which the First Book of Maccabees begins thus: “And from them came forth a sinful root, Antiochus the Illustrious, son of King Antiochus, who had been a hostage at Rome; and he began to reign in the one hundred and seventh year of the kingdom of the Greeks” (1 Macc. 1). This is he whom the prophetic vision designates thus: “From one of the four horns there came forth one little horn” (Dan. 8). That is, from Seleucus surnamed Nicanor, as stated above, came this eighth king, Antiochus: small in royal power, great in arrogance.

“And that horn became great toward the south, and toward the east, and toward strength; and it was magnified even unto the strength of heaven, and it cast down some of the strength and of the stars, and trampled them; and it was magnified even unto the prince of strength, and it took away from him the continual sacrifice, and cast down the place of his sanctification” (ibid.), as is narrated in the books of the Maccabees. It belongs to our purpose to recount this portion of evils. The other evils of that kingdom, which Alexander’s princes, commanders, or companions—soon made kings—committed against one another, do not concern the present matter. They did not raise their hands or weapons against God’s covenant, but wickedly drank one another’s blood with reckless wastefulness.

Anyone who reads the histories can plainly observe that Alexander did not fail to resemble the serpent—indeed, the demon—from whom he himself boasted that he had been conceived under the name of Hammon. Alexander’s pride, falling swiftly into death, became a seedbed of very many massacres and divided his own household against itself by viperish hatreds and serpentine discord. [Col. 1411D]

## CHAPTER XVII. How this fifth head of the dragon was first drenched with the blood of Onias and made red.

[Col. 1412A] The beginning of the blood by which this head, the dragon’s fifth head, was drenched and began to become red was the killing of the high priest Onias, a pious man who hated evil. Because of his piety, while the laws were still being most excellently kept and the holy city dwelt in complete peace, the kings and rulers themselves considered the place worthy of the highest honor and adorned the Temple with the greatest gifts. Thus Seleucus, king of Asia, supplied from his own revenues all expenses pertaining to the ministry of sacrifices.

Seleucus had died, and Antiochus—called Epiphanes, that is, “Noble”—had assumed the kingdom. [Col. 1412B] While that falsely noble and truly ignoble king ruled, Menelaus, who had been called Onias but, emulating Greek glory, had among the other marks of pagan custom adopted a Greek name, so as to be called Menelaus, that is, “strength of the people,” stole certain golden vessels from the Temple, gave away some, and sold others. When Onias rebuked him for this, he arranged that Onias should be killed by Andronicus, to whom he had given part of the vessels; and so it happened.

Thus Onias was killed for righteousness: the first in the line of the holy Maccabean martyrs, of whom, God granting, there will now be speech. In life and after death he bore a venerable testimony: that he was a good and kindly man, modest in appearance, restrained in conduct, graceful in speech, and trained in virtues from childhood. [Col. 1412C]

The first to persecute him was his own brother Jason. His ancestral name had been Jesus; but, like Menelaus, as has already been said, preferring Greek glories to the law of his native land, he had first adopted a Greek name, so as to be called Jason. This man, impiously seeking the high priesthood, easily obtained it from an impious king by offering money. Afterwards Onias, as already stated, also lost his life for righteousness.

## CHAPTER XVIII. By what sins the people deserved that God should afflict them through Antiochus.

First it must be said what sins made it permitted and just before God that that most wicked head should have such great power against God’s covenant that the hope of the promise was nearly [Col. 1412D] endangered. As has often been said, the Church then held this promise in mind under the likeness of a woman with child. Their first evil proceeded from themselves, so that justice demanded the fulfillment of what God, righteous in His words and victorious when judged, had said in David: “I will visit their iniquities with a rod, and their sins with stripes” (Ps. 88).

For after arranging that the pious high priest Onias should be killed—he through whom, as already stated, the laws had been most excellently kept—the aforesaid Jason and Menelaus, with many whom they had persuaded, approached Antiochus and informed him that they wished to abandon their ancestral laws and way of life and observe Greek customs. [Col. 1413A] They therefore asked him to permit them to build a gymnasium in Jerusalem (1 Macc. 1).

A gymnasium is an exercise-place for the naked, in which young men trained by wrestling naked. *Gymnos* is Greek; in Latin, “naked.” When Antiochus had granted this, Josephus says, they concealed their circumcision so that they might not appear unlike the Greeks. What he says—“they concealed their circumcision”—is what the Scripture of the Book of Maccabees says: “They made themselves foreskins” (ibid.). For it was impossible for circumcised persons to make foreskins for themselves except by concealing their circumcision, lest it appear that they did not have foreskins.

By doing this, he says, they withdrew from the holy covenant—namely, the covenant which God made with Abraham, in which was the promise of the seed, which is Christ. They denied faith in that promise by concealing circumcision, the seal of faith, and making foreskins for themselves; and so they truly withdrew from the holy covenant. [Col. 1413B]

## CHAPTER XIX. By what successes the people’s crimes were increased.

This was the beginning of sorrows: they had indeed summoned it upon themselves. This beginning was immediately followed by advancement, and an increase ensued. For Jason dared to establish a gymnasium beneath the citadel of Zion itself; he even dared to place the best of the youths in brothels.

[Col. 1413C] “For,” Scripture says, “this was not a beginning, but a kind of increase and advance of pagan and foreign ways of life, through the impious and unheard-of crime of Jason, who was no high priest. Thus the priests were no longer devoted to the services of the altar; but, despising the Temple and neglecting the sacrifices, they hastened to take part in the wrestling-ground and its unlawful distribution, in the exercise of the discus; and, holding ancestral honors in contempt, they judged Greek glories best” (2 Macc. 4).

Where the priests were such, what do you suppose the people were? Where, after the pious high priest Onias was killed, the impious Jason, a non-priest installed in his place, placed the best youths in brothels, what do you suppose the youth were like, pupils of so excellent a high priest? Surely it was now the place and time for that sentence of curses in the Book of Deuteronomy to come upon them (Deut. 28), so that they might become an example of the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah, [Col. 1413D] Admah and Zeboiim, which the Lord overthrew in His anger and wrath (Gen. 19).

Had not the Lord God been held by His oath, which He had sworn to Abraham and David concerning the seed that was Christ, who was to be born from them—as Isaiah too testifies when he says: “Unless the Lord of hosts had left us seed, we would have been like Sodom and would have resembled Gomorrah” (Isa. 1)—these things have been said in order that the equity of God’s just judgment may appear to some extent. For unless He had wished by grace alone to preserve that nation in order to fulfill the truth of the promise, it would have been just to subject them not only to the criminal hands of impious Antiochus, but even to such punishment as overwhelmed Sodom or Gomorrah. For the sin of these people, who possessed the written Law, was even more grievous than that of the Sodomites, who had no such Law. [Col. 1414A]

## CHAPTER XX. What it means that the Lord said through Zechariah: “For I was a little angry,” but they “added unto evil.”

Here, however, we encounter what the Lord of hosts says through the prophet Zechariah. Having first declared, “I am jealous for Jerusalem and Zion with great jealousy, and I am greatly angry with the wealthy nations,” He immediately gives this reason: “For I was a little angry” (Zech. 1), but they “added unto evil.” The meaning is: led by good zeal, I visited “their iniquities with a rod and their sins with stripes” (Ps. 88), granting the nations power to afflict them a little. [Col. 1414B] But those to whom I permitted power, abusing the permission, exceeded the measure.

It must now, therefore, be carefully considered and attentively distinguished what the just God, being a little angry, wished to be done to that people, and what the nations—such as the Greeks then were—added unto evil by doing more. To make this easier, we must first say in what God’s small anger consists, according to which He says, “For I was a little angry”; and in what His great anger consists, according to which He says, “And I am greatly angry with the wealthy nations” (Zech. 1). At the same time it will be considered why He calls His small anger “zeal,” saying: “I am jealous for Jerusalem and Zion with great jealousy.” Conversely, it will be appropriate to distinguish His great and small mercy; for as great mercy is opposed to great anger—mercy which David asks for when he says, “Have mercy on me, O God, according to Your great mercy” (Ps. 50)—so it is evident that small mercy is opposed to small anger. We have heard what this is in Hosea, God saying: “What shall I do to you, Ephraim? What shall I do to you, Judah? Your mercy is like a morning cloud and like dew passing away in the morning” (Hos. 6). [Col. 1414C]

## CHAPTER XXI. What it means for God to be a little angry.

God’s small anger, according to which He says, “For I was a little angry” (Zech. 1)—with Jerusalem and Zion understood—is the rod of discipline, namely temporal affliction or vexation. It has power to give understanding to the hearing, [Col. 1414D] lest Jerusalem or Zion—that is, any chosen soul—become drunk on temporal goods and fall asleep, and its hearing lack the understanding of God’s Word, in which is eternal life.

Such anger is rightly called zeal, He Himself saying: “I am jealous for Jerusalem and Zion with great jealousy” (ibid.), as when a loving husband is strongly jealous for his beloved when she goes after her lovers. “Behold,” He says, “I will hedge up your way with thorns, and I will enclose it with a wall; and she will find her paths. She will pursue her lovers and not overtake them; she will seek them and not find them; and she will say: ‘I will go and return to my former husband, for it was better with me then than now’” (Hos. 2).

But God’s great anger is when He is not jealous, [Col. 1415A] as He Himself says in Jeremiah: “When my zeal has departed from you,” and He does not seek the cursing soul, nor hedge its way with thorns so that, struck by adversity, it may return to its Creator. In accordance with this it is said in the Psalm: “According to the multitude of his anger, he will not seek” (Ps. 8). Great mercy is opposed to this great anger. After saying to David in His oath, “I will visit their iniquities with a rod and their sins with stripes”—namely, the sons of David—He immediately added: “But I will not scatter my mercy from him” (Ps. 88).

What is that mercy, unless the promise then to be fulfilled, but now fulfilled? Elsewhere it says: “God is my protector; my God is my mercy” (Ps. 58). “My God,” I say—namely Christ, “who is God blessed above all for ever” (2 Cor. 11). David, speaking in his own person, that is, concerning himself, could certainly call Him his protector, because it was to happen, and did happen, that his God, the Word of God, God the Word, would take up David himself: would take up our flesh, a true human being from David’s own seed. [Col. 1415B]

This very great mercy is the fruit of that blessing in which the father Isaac, blessing his younger son Jacob, said: “Let peoples serve you and tribes worship you. Be lord of your brothers, and let the sons of your mother bow down before you. Whoever curses you, let him be cursed; but whoever blesses you, let him be filled with blessings” (Gen. 27). That blessing was directed to this end: that our God, our mercy—Christ, God and man—should be born from Jacob’s line. For Rebekah had received this answer: “Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples shall be divided from your belly” (Gen. 25). Therefore it could not happen that He should be born from both, since Jacob and Esau were divided.

That blessing which the weeping Esau received when his father said: “In the fatness of the earth and in the dew of heaven above shall be your blessing” (Gen. 27), is a small mercy, opposed to the small anger of God already discussed. [Col. 1415C]

## CHAPTER XXII. What Antiochus added “unto evil.”

[Col. 1415D] We must now return to the point proposed: namely, to distinguish what the just God, being a little angry, wished to be done to that people, and what that sinful root, Antiochus the Illustrious, added “unto evil” by doing more (Zech. 1).

Esau had received only one and small mercy, as already stated: that he should abound in the fatness of the earth and the dew of heaven above, that is, in earthly goods and temporal riches. But Jacob had received in the blessing both small and great mercy: that “from the dew of heaven and the fatness of the earth” there should be given him abundance of grain, wine, and oil—which is small mercy; and that “peoples should serve” his seed, that is Christ, “and tribes worship him”—which is great mercy.

God took away that small mercy by small anger [Col. 1416A] whenever He handed that people over to be devastated by the nations because of their sins, as is written: “And He delivered them into the hands of the nations, and those who hated them ruled over them; their enemies afflicted them, and they were humbled under their hands” (Ps. 105). “But they added unto evil” whenever they sought to take away from them great mercy, eternal mercy—not that they themselves might possess it, but that it might come to no human being and that there might be in no human being faith in God or the Word of promise. Thus the devil, the ancient dragon, moved, for example, King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon to cast the three youths into the furnace of fire because they would not worship the statue which he had made. But enough has already been said about him and the others; the discourse now comes to the deeds of impious Antiochus. [Col. 1416B]

## CHAPTER XXIII. How the things Antiochus did in Jerusalem belong to God’s small anger.

After the kingdom had been established before Antiochus, and he began to reign in Egypt so as to rule over two kingdoms; after he had captured fortified cities in Egypt and taken the spoils of Egypt, he turned and went up against Israel. He went up to Jerusalem with a great multitude, entered the sanctuary in arrogance, and took the golden altar, the lampstand of light, all the vessels and ornaments which were before the Temple, and shattered everything; and so on, as far as the saying: “According to his glory his [Col. 1416C] dishonor was multiplied, and his exaltation was turned into mourning” (1 Macc. 1).

All these things—every devastation and destruction of holy treasures of this kind, the plundering of treasuries, the slaughter of human beings, great mourning in Israel and in all their places, the groaning of rulers and elders, the weakening of young men and virgins, the lamentation of husbands, and the mourning of married women; the great blow to the city and destruction of much of the people—for Antiochus also burned the city with fire and destroyed the houses and walls around it (ibid.)—all these, I say, belong to the small anger, according to the Lord’s saying: “For I was a little angry.”

For these were small things because all concerned the body: they took away temporal, perishable goods, which were sooner or later to be lost. It is not the business of the present work to recount the cause or desire for which he entered Egypt to wage war against his nephews, the sons of his sister—Ptolemy Philometor and his brother Ptolemy Physcon, sons of Ptolemy Epiphanes—or how, restrained and frightened by the authority of Rome, he withdrew from there. Especially so because the mind, holding to the path of its purpose, looks to worthier matters and presses toward them. [Col. 1416D]

## CHAPTER XXIV. That his compelling the Jews to adopt pagan observance was an addition unto evil.

What follows is rightly called their addition, as He says: “But they added unto evil” (Zech. 1). [Col. 1417A] King Antiochus wrote to all his kingdom that all the people should be one, and sent letters by messengers into Jerusalem and all the cities of Judah, commanding that they follow the laws of the nations of the earth; that they forbid burnt offerings, sacrifices, and propitiations to be made in God’s Temple; that they forbid the celebration of Sabbaths and feast days. He ordered altars, temples, and idols to be built; swine’s flesh and common cattle to be sacrificed; their children to be left uncircumcised; and whoever did not act according to King Antiochus’s word to be put to death.

He built the abominable idol of desolation upon God’s altar. Throughout the surrounding cities of Judah they built altars; before the doors of houses and in the streets they burned incense and sacrificed. They tore up and burned the books of God’s Law. Wherever books of the Lord’s covenant were found, and whoever observed the Law of the Lord, the king’s edict commanded that he be slaughtered (1 Macc. 1). [Col. 1417B]

Who can doubt, or be unable to distinguish, that all this was added beyond the anger of the Lord and Father, who wished not to destroy His servants or children but to correct them? “For I,” He says, “was a little angry” (Zech. 1), namely, visiting “their iniquities with a rod and their sins with stripes” (Ps. 88). “But they added unto evil”: that is, with the devil, their instigator, aiming to take away My mercy from them and make void the Word of promise, by abolishing the Law, removing the covenant and the books of the covenant, and even removing the nation itself—so that, if the nation from which salvation was hoped should no longer survive, Christ Himself, the salvation of the world, would consequently not be born.

## CHAPTER XXV. Why the devil is called Leviathan on account of additions of this sort.

Consider now how rightly, and for what great reason, this great dragon, the ancient serpent called the devil and Satan, is also called Leviathan, which is interpreted “their addition.” The addition of whom, indeed, if not of the seven heads often mentioned? From the time when the Lord, a little angry with the human race, said to Adam: [Col. 1417C] “Cursed is the earth in your work; in labors you shall eat bread all the days of your life. Thorns and thistles shall it bring forth for you, and you shall eat the herbs of the earth. In the sweat of your face you shall eat bread until you return to the earth from which you were taken; for you are dust, and to dust you shall return” (Gen. 3), and drove him out of the paradise of delight.

From that time, I say, when He was a little angry even with His own elect in this way—willing them to be mortal, to live briefly, and to spend their short life in labors—the devil always strove [Col. 1417D] that great anger should also be added to them: that is, that they should remain dead through the death of the soul.

But after the Word of promise was given to Abraham, by which the blessing was promised—which blessing is indeed the destruction of sin and death—the same devil began to rage. Against that same promise, so that what had been promised might not come to pass, he raised more furiously those heads of his of which we are now speaking. So far as lay in them, whenever God was a little angry with that people especially, they “added unto evil,” so that, after taking away their freedom in this present life, they might take away God as well. This is their addition, on account of which he who added, or wished to add, was called Leviathan.

It is clear that God Himself first used this name of none other but him in Job, when He says: “Can you draw out Leviathan with a hook, or bind his mouth with a rope?” (Job 40), and so forth. Then in Isaiah: “On that day the Lord shall visit with His hard, great, and strong sword Leviathan, the bar-serpent, and Leviathan, the twisting serpent; and He shall kill him who is in the sea” (Isa. 27). [Col. 1418A]

## CHAPTER XXVI. What God’s great anger is.

[Col. 1418B] What is more just than that visitation? What harder than that sword? For the hard, great, and strong sword is God’s great anger, which this Leviathan wished to add to the human race and especially to that chosen people which had received the Word of promise: that mercy might be taken away from it and what was promised might not come to pass.

Hence it is easy to see that it is altogether just for that ancient serpent himself and all his heads—all the impious without exception, who are called and are the devil’s members or body—to undergo the hard, great, and strong sword, that is, the great anger of God. For they wished to add this anger to God’s elect, who endured the small anger already described.

It is at once very beautiful and terrifying to perceive this sense [Col. 1418C] where the Spirit says in John’s Apocalypse: “Woe to the earth and the sea, because the devil has come down to you, having great wrath!” (Rev. 12). It is proper to understand this “great” wrath by comparison or relation to the lesser anger already mentioned. For the devil’s wrath is great, or is called great, in this respect. Reason teaches this, and the Aristotelians also maintain that “small” and “great” are terms of quantity not in an absolute sense, but in relation: for example, when one says “a great mouse” and “a small mountain,” these are understood as spoken in relation to other things, because a mountain is small in relation to a larger mountain, and a mouse is without doubt great in relation to a smaller mouse.

Therefore, when it says, “Woe to the earth and the sea, because the devil has come down to you, having great wrath,” signifying all the impious by the names “earth” and “sea,” the small anger is aptly understood: it has come to an end, and all the elect have passed through it, suffering such things as can be understood by God’s saying, “For I was a little angry” (Zech. 1). [Col. 1418D]

For the devil has great wrath laid upon him: namely, the irrevocable sentence of eternal condemnation. He brings it upon earth and sea—that is, upon all the impious. When God had been “a little angry” with His own, they “added unto evil,” in order to take from them the hope of mercy and bring upon them forgetfulness of God. Woe to them, because the devil who has great wrath shares it with them, so that they may have what they added, or wished to add, to God’s elect!

## CHAPTER XXVII. [Col. 1419A] God’s small anger can be appeased; His great anger cannot.

How, then, was that wrath of God, with which at that time He had been somewhat angry, removed by sacrifices and offerings? This, then, is the difference between the small wrath of God and the great wrath of God: the great wrath of God is not expiated by victims and offerings for all eternity. Thus also, concerning the aforesaid Leviathan—that is, the devil, upon whom great wrath rests—the Lord says to blessed Job: “I will not spare him for his mighty words, nor for words composed for entreaty” (Job 41).

But the small wrath of God can be appeased by sacrifices and offerings, both those appointed under the Law and those appointed in grace; above all, however, by those which anyone freely adds beyond law or commandment through voluntary devotion—for example, by giving up his body for the covenant of God. By what sacrifices, then, by what offerings was that wrath, with which God had now been somewhat angry, appeased or removed? Not by whole burnt offerings of rams and bulls, nor by thousands of fat lambs; but as the three youths cast into the Babylonian furnace were received with a contrite heart and humble spirit, so the seven brothers together with their mother, by suffering, deserved that an acceptable sacrifice should be received—one through which it was fitting that the Lord’s wrath should be appeased for the place and for the whole people.

Hence, immediately after their sufferings, it is added: Judas Maccabaeus and those who were with him, summoning their kinsmen, taking with them those who had remained in Judaism, and calling upon the Lord that He might have mercy on the temple and city, hear the voice of blood crying to Him, and remember also the most unjust deaths of innocent little children, began to take up arms, God, surely, strengthening them and granting success. “For,” Scripture says, “the wrath of the Lord was turned into mercy” (2 Macc. 8).

## CHAPTER XXVIII. The woman who had a child in her womb gave birth again and cried out.

Who has not heard the cries of that time—the cries of the woman who had conceived and who cried out in giving birth? It has often been said, and must often be said, nor should it cause weariness, because the chief concern of this present little work looks to the mystery of the great and wondrous sign: namely, the red dragon having seven heads, standing before the woman who was about to give birth, so that when she bore her son he might devour him.

“The woman who had conceived cried out and was in labor” [Col. 1419D]: the Church of that time, holding faith and hope in the word of promise, cried out; “and she was tormented in giving birth” (Rev. 12), that is, she desired, and was wearied by desiring, that God might fulfil His promises concerning the seed of Abraham. Who, I ask, has not heard the cries of that time?

“Woe is me,” says Mattathias, “why was I born to see the crushing of my people and the crushing of the holy city, and to sit there while it is given into the hands of enemies? Its temple is like a dishonored man; its vessels of glory have been carried away captive” (1 Macc. 2).

Likewise: “They fasted, put on sackcloth, scattered ashes upon their heads, tore their garments, and brought forward the Nazirites who had completed their days [Col. 1420A]; and they cried with a loud voice to heaven, saying: What shall we do with these, and where shall we take them? Your holy things have been trampled down and defiled. Your priests have been made into mourning and humiliation; and behold, the nations have gathered together against us to destroy us. You know what they are devising against us” (1 Macc. 3).

For armies of many thousands had assembled to come into the land of Judah and destroy it. But although they were few, they said: “Now let us cry out to heaven, and our God will have mercy on us and crush them before our face today” (1 Macc. 4). The history of those days and the succession of their deeds are full of cries of this kind—cries which truly, according to the mystery set forth above, were the cries of the woman who had conceived, was giving birth, and suffered great torment in childbirth [Col. 1420B].

## CHAPTER XXIX. That the seven Maccabaean brothers, and especially their mother while they suffered, cried out.

If the longing and groaning of individual souls—which are one in the person of that great woman—constituted a great cry to God, what do you think, what do you suppose, of the mother of the seven sons, who was exceedingly admirable and worthy of blessed remembrance, and beheld her seven sons perish within the course of a single day? Indeed, she bore it with good courage because of the hope she had in the Lord, and encouraged each of them: “It was not I,” she said, “who gave you spirit and soul in my womb, nor who joined together the limbs of each of you; but the Creator of the world, who formed human birth and discovered the origin of all things, will in mercy give you back hope and life again” (2 Macc. 7).

With good courage, I say, she bore the tortures and deaths of her children because of her hope in their future resurrection; yet nature nonetheless grieved with maternal affection, and with great sorrow cried out to God. Each of her children cried out in his own anguish and punishment. But the mother, who was herself consumed last after her sons, suffered more abundantly in the deaths of all and in the pains of each; she cried more deeply, and bore each one for God with no less agony of mind than she herself suffered when she bore each into the world.

Therefore, at least in this one mother, consider the whole Church of those days [Col. 1420D], and how fitting, how full of divine terror, was—or is—the mystery that the dragon with so many heads stood before the woman who had conceived, that is, who awaited by faith the coming Christ, in order to devour her son, in order to remove from her heart faith in the promise. The fifth kingdom of that dragon was the kingdom wickedly established under the reign of Antiochus to assault the woman; and this appeared almost visibly in that mother of the seven sons.

Before the sufferings of these—that is, the mother and her seven sons—much blood had been shed by Antiochus, crying out to God, as it was later said: “that He might hear the voice of blood crying to Him” (2 Macc. 8). But their blood had a louder voice [Col. 1421A], and, reaching the hearing of heaven, put an end to wrath.

## CHAPTER XXX. That their refusal to eat pork was the cause of their suffering, and that all things are clean to the clean.

Do not regard the cause of their suffering as slight when you read only that they, together with their mother, were seized and compelled by the king to eat unlawful pork, tortured with whips and scourges (2 Macc. 6). For those meats were not merely pork, but also sacrificial meats—that is, they had been offered to demons. For, as you have in the preceding passage: “The altar also was full of unlawful things forbidden by the laws. They were led by bitter necessity on the king’s birthday to the sacrifices; and when the rites of Bacchus were celebrated, they were compelled, crowned with ivy, to march in procession for Bacchus” (2 Macc. 6). And in the First Book of Maccabees it is said more plainly that “Antiochus commanded pork and common cattle to be sacrificed” (1 Macc. 1).

When, therefore, you hear of pork, understand also meat sacrificed to idols. There was a twofold cause for their contest: first, because the Law had reckoned pork among unclean things and forbidden its consumption; second, because it had been sacrificed to demons. “What the Gentiles sacrifice,” says the Apostle, “they sacrifice to demons and not to God” (1 Cor. 10).

Yet concerning one cause—namely, that the letter of the Law reckons these things unclean—the life-giving Spirit sets us free through the grace of the Gospel. The Apostle says: “Eat whatever is sold in the market. But if anyone says: ‘This has been offered to idols,’ do not eat it” [Col. 1421C] (ibid.). Again, to Timothy: “Every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving; for it is sanctified through the word of God and prayer” (1 Tim. 4). Again, to Titus: “To the clean all things are clean; but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is clean” (Titus 1). Likewise, in the Acts of the Apostles: “It seemed good,” they say, “to the Holy Spirit and to us to impose upon you Gentiles no further burden beyond these necessary things: that you abstain from things sacrificed to idols, from what is strangled, and from fornication; and that you do not do to others what you do not wish done to yourselves” (Acts 15).

## CHAPTER XXXI. Why God distinguished between clean and unclean things in the old Law.

[Col. 1421D] It is not from fickleness or changeability, but from judgment and reason, that the one and same God both gave the Law concerning clean and unclean things and, in the Gospel or through the ministers of the Gospel, says that all things are clean to the clean. Consideration of this matter proceeds usefully if you properly weigh both what He Himself says concerning His commandments in the prophets and what had then happened when He gave commandments of this sort.

In Ezekiel He says: “I brought them out of the land of Egypt and led them into the wilderness; and I gave them my commandments and showed them my judgments, which, if a man does them, he shall live by them” (Ezek. 20). Having said this, He immediately rebukes them because they rejected His commandments and their eyes followed idols: “Therefore,” He says, “I too gave them commandments that were not good [Col. 1422A], and judgments by which they shall not live; and I defiled them in their offerings, when they offered everything that opens the womb” (ibid.).

See how great is the difference among the commandments: some commandments and judgments are good, “which, if a man does them, he shall live by them”; others, He says, “are not good, by which they shall not live.” In order that we may clearly distinguish one set from another, the good from the not-good, let us return to the times and to their sequence: how and through what intervening causes He gave commandments so different.

He had come to Mount Horeb and spoke through Moses commandments that were indeed good: “You shall have no strange gods before me,” and so on, down to: “You shall not make a covenant with the nations or with their gods” (Exod. 20, 23). Meanwhile, while He was speaking with Moses, they made for themselves a molten calf, worshipped it, and offered sacrifices [Col. 1422B] (Exod. 32). Up to that point Moses had given the people God’s good and life-giving commandments with unveiled face. Then, after the guilt of the calf had intervened, his face had to be veiled when he spoke to the people (Exod. 34); and the commandments he gave thereafter were not good commandments by which they might live—such as those concerning clean and unclean animals, bodily leprosy, leprosy of garments, leprosy of houses, and other such matters. Their letter, certainly, kills; but the Spirit now gives life when the face of Moses is unveiled.

These things have now been said in order that it may be clear that disputes about distinctions of foods are rightly regarded as superfluous in apostolic teaching, since, as has already been said, God Himself plainly declares that commandments of this kind were not good [Col. 1422C], and that the preceding transgression was the reason they were given, and so forth.

## CHAPTER XXXII. That the seven Maccabaean brothers are especially worthy of veneration because they openly confessed the resurrection of the dead.

Let the discourse concerning the devout martyrs conclude in such a way that we judge them more venerable to us in the Gospel of Christ than the rest. For what reason? Because in their sufferings, when they gave up their bodies for the covenant of God and submitted them to most grievous tortures, they confessed and testified with resounding voice to faith and hope in the blessed resurrection.

“One of them said: ‘You most wicked man, indeed, destroy us in this present life; but the King of the world will raise us up, who die for His laws, in the resurrection of eternal life’” (2 Macc. 7). Another, when his tongue was demanded beforehand and he steadfastly held out and stretched forth his hands, said: “I possess these from heaven; but for God’s laws I now despise them, because I hope to receive them back from Him” (ibid.). Then the next, when he was tortured and already near death, said: “It is better, when put to death by men, to await the hope given by God that we shall be raised again by Him. But for you there will be no resurrection to life” (ibid.).

Their mother also, a martyr and more than a martyr, who beheld her seven sons perish within the course of one day and bore it with good courage because of the hope she had in the Lord, encouraged them: “The Creator of the world,” she said among other things [Col. 1423A], “who formed human birth and discovered the origin of all things, will in mercy give you back hope and life again” (2 Macc. 7). And, bending toward the last surviving son, she said among other things: “Become worthy of your brothers; receive death, so that in that mercy I may receive you with your brothers” [Col. 1424A] (ibid.).

Therefore, since the sum of our faith is the resurrection of the dead through Jesus Christ, it is not without reason that among all the saints of the Old Testament these are to be venerated—men who, in their precious deaths, sang forth such a devout and clear testimony to the holy resurrection.

# BOOK TEN

[Col. 1423]

## CHAPTER I. Saints conquered kingdoms through faith.

“The saints,” says the Apostle, “through faith conquered kingdoms, practised righteousness, obtained promises. They stopped the mouths of lions, quenched the violence of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, were strengthened out of weakness, became mighty in war, put to flight the armies of foreigners” (Heb. 11).

In that holy assembly of such victors, in that illustrious army of such strong men, we gladly behold the Maccabaean warriors—Judas and his brothers and companions.
