Their martial courage, their labors and glorious struggles, in a manner of speaking, gave birth for us to Christ the Savior, because they magnanimously defended their people—of whom Christ was to be born and was born—when the nations wished to destroy it. They manfully struck that already mentioned fifth head of the dragon in King Antiochus and his commanders, the Word of God, God the Word, cooperating with their labors, so that the impious king might be crushed without hand, as had been foretold of him to Daniel [Col. 1423C] (Dan. 8).

These are that little help which had already been foreseen and promised in the words: “When they have fallen”—understand, many of the people—“they shall be aided with a little help” (Dan. 11). For if you consider the multitude of their adversaries and recall the thousands of hostile camps, what or how much was Mattathias, from the village or mountain of Modin, with his five sons, a few kinsmen, and those of his countrymen who had remained in Judaism? Truly, in number they were a little help [Col. 1423D]; but through their faith and the mercy of God, they brought forth for themselves and for the whole age the greatest assistance.

## CHAPTER II. Saints, needy, distressed, and afflicted, wandered in deserts and mountains.

He who has the anointing from God—an anointing which, as the Apostle John says, teaches us concerning all things (1 John 2)—says that they groaned together, and groans with them, because they endured many evils: “needy, distressed, afflicted, wandering in deserts, in mountains, in caves, and in holes of the earth” (Heb. 11).

In one day as many as a thousand human beings were killed in the wilderness on the Sabbath, because they feared, for the sake of religion and observance, to bring assistance to themselves by force. “Let us die,” they said, “in our simplicity; and heaven and earth shall be witnesses over us that you unjustly destroy us” (1 Macc. 2).

But what follows? “A man said to his neighbor: ‘If we all do as our brothers have done, and do not fight against the Gentiles for our lives and our ordinances, they will quickly destroy us from the earth.’ And on that day they took counsel, saying: ‘Every man who comes against us on the Sabbath day, we shall fight against him, and we shall not all die as our brothers died in hiding’” [Col. 1424B] (ibid.). “And even to the present,” says Josephus, “there remains among us the custom of fighting if wars arise even on such a day.”

Therefore, he who, as has been said, has the anointing from God, and whom “His anointing teaches concerning all things,” knows, understands, and weighs matters in the balance of reason. In these people the Apostle’s saying shows itself to possess abundant experiential proof: “needy, distressed, afflicted, wandering in deserts, in mountains, in caves, and in holes of the earth.” Considering these things, he gives profound thanks for their afflicted faith, because they truly gave birth for us in pain; their souls labored in childbirth for the whole age, bringing forth the eternal fruit of salvation, the birth of Jesus Christ, the true and eternal Savior.

We do not say, nor can we say or maintain, that all those slain in such a storm, of whatever sex or age, had or could have had knowledge of so great a hope, of so great an expectation in the promise made to Abraham concerning the blessed seed—the coming Jesus Christ [Col. 1424D] (Gal. 3). But this we admire in praise of God’s word, in the firmness of God’s purpose: that even into many who did not know, He deeply poured the love of preserving and defending their own race, from which the salvation of the human race, Christ the Son of God, had to be born according to the truth of the promise—the promise of truth, because God is truthful. And the humility of sinners cried out to Him through the mouth of David: “That You may be justified in Your words and prevail when You are judged” (Ps. 50).

## CHAPTER III. How great was the joy at the cleansing and renewal of the temple.

What shall I say of the great joy which arose among the people at the cleansing and renewal of the temple, which had stood defiled for three years? Josephus too testifies how great their joy was in hymns and confessions blessing the Lord: “From that time,” he says, “we celebrate this feast of the renewal of the temple for eight days, calling it Lights, because beyond hope this bright light of religious worship appeared to us.”

Who but God poured into their minds so great a love of His name that they celebrated with such joy the recovery of the place where His name was invoked, regarded it as so luminous, and decreed that it should be celebrated every year for eight days, though this had not previously been done? Solomon indeed celebrated the dedication for eight days, and on the eighth day dismissed the people. But it is not written that he appointed a feast of that dedication to be celebrated yearly for the same number—that is, eight—days [Col. 1425B].

Therefore this too must be ascribed to the great praise of God, in whose hand are the hearts of the children of men: mindful of His promise, in order to fulfil it by sending His Son, His Word, in the fullness of time, He acted by instilling desire and supplying aid, so that the very people through whom the promise had to be fulfilled might defend themselves and the place.

## CHAPTER IV. How earnestly Cuno requested an interpretation of the prologue of Second Maccabees, and that the author will now undertake it.

Now this present discourse turns itself to what you have urgently requested and insistently demanded, Cuno, a very close friend of the bride and beloved of the eternal King, for whom her friends make little chains of gold: to elucidate, as far as possible and as God grants, the Scripture which stands before the Second Book of Maccabees as a kind of prologue or preface. In one and the same treatise, a diligent mind seeks to accomplish two things: to proclaim the greatness and dignity of the joy at the renewal of the temple, which I have just briefly mentioned, and to elucidate to some extent the Scripture of the aforesaid preface.

For that Scripture is especially concerned with the joy at the renewal of the temple, and its purpose is that every Jew, wherever he may be, and every true confessor—one who is a confessor both in name and in reality, as the interpretation of the name *Jew* indicates—may rejoice over that restoration of the temple with a great heart and willing mind, with heart opened to the Law of God and His commandments [Col. 1425D].

And truly, if the Jew considers the cause at hand—if the true confessor of God considers the great work God had with humankind in order to fulfil His promises—he has reason to rejoice, reason to be glad that that temple was repaired by the labors of the Maccabees, and to mingle his voice with theirs in blessing God through hymns and confessions.

We know that the holy Church of Christ does this even today throughout the whole world: wherever the name of the Lord is invoked, wherever an altar or temple is dedicated, or is being dedicated, to the name of the Lord, there the memory of these memorable Maccabees likewise gives forth its fragrance and flourishes [Col. 1426A]; and the chorus of the Church solemnly echoes and harmoniously celebrates the voices of their souls, which labored in childbirth for our eternal salvation. Therefore we must proceed, following that preface, to magnify a matter so gracious and so glorious. And if its elucidation proves less than you request or desire, you will rightly attribute this not to my negligence but to impossibility.

## CHAPTER V. That Onias went to Egypt with many Jews and there built a temple.

First it must be said why, or from what cause, there were then Jews throughout Egypt, to whom the letter begins thus: “The brothers, the Jews who are in Jerusalem and in the region of Judaea, send greetings and good peace to the Jewish brothers who are throughout Egypt” (2 Macc. 1).

In the one hundred and forty-ninth year of the Greek kingdom, King Antiochus had killed Menelaus, the younger brother of Onias, to whom the father of this same Antiochus had granted the high priesthood. There were three sons of the high priest Simon: Onias, who succeeded his father in the high priesthood and whom Andronicus killed; Jesus; and another Onias. Jesus caused himself to be called Jason, while Onias caused himself to be called Menelaus. Both professed delight in Greek names and a wish to imitate Gentile customs.

A little son of Onias, also named Onias, was left behind. When Onias, as has been said, had been killed by Andronicus, [Col. 1426C] Antiochus Epiphanes granted the high priesthood to his aforesaid brother Jason; but afterward he took away that dignity again and granted it to Menelaus. When Antiochus died and his namesake son succeeded him, this son killed Menelaus at Lysias’s suggestion, on the ground that he was the cause of all evils.

But the son of the high priest Onias, of whom we have spoken, who had been left a little boy after his father’s death—seeing, says Josephus, that the king had killed his uncle Menelaus and, at Lysias’s instigation, had transferred the high-priestly office from that family to another house by giving it to Alcimus, who was not of priestly descent—fled to Ptolemy, king of Egypt. He won favor from him and from his wife Cleopatra and requested a place in the region of Heliopolis [Col. 1426D], where he might build a temple like that of Jerusalem.

That temple remained until the reign of Vespasian for two hundred and fifty years. The city itself, called the City of Onias, was later razed to the ground when the Jews fought against the Romans; no trace of either city or temple remains.

On the occasion of this high priest Onias, then, innumerable multitudes of Jews fled to Egypt. For Onias maintained that he was fulfilling Isaiah’s prophecy: “There shall be an altar to the Lord in the midst of the land of Egypt, and a pillar of the Lord near its border” (Isa. 19). Yet even previously no small multitude of Jews had gone down into Egypt. For Ptolemy son of Lagus, carrying off many captives from the hill country of Judaea and from places neighboring Jerusalem, transported them to Egypt; and Ptolemy Philadelphus, who succeeded the aforesaid Ptolemy son of Lagus, released from the bonds of slavery up to one hundred and twenty thousand Jews serving in Egypt, as Josephus records [Col. 1427A].

## CHAPTER VI. How often and at what times the Jews of Jerusalem wrote to their brethren in Egypt.

There were, then, Jews throughout Egypt; and the Jews in Jerusalem and in the region of Judaea wrote to them in about the one hundred and ninth year, after Menelaus, as has been said, had been killed, Alcimus had obtained the high priesthood, and the younger Onias with an innumerable multitude of Jews had fled into Egypt. [Col. 1427B]

For it is established that Antiochus Eupator killed Menelaus in the one hundred and forty-ninth year of the Greek kingdom. But in the one hundred and eighty-eighth year, the people in Jerusalem says—this Scripture says—“To the Jews in Egypt, greetings and health” (2 Macc. 1).

Nevertheless, the matter requires us to observe also that we read in connected and continuous narration: “In the one hundred and sixty-ninth year, while Demetrius was king, we Jews wrote to you in the tribulation and assault which came upon us in these years, after Jason had departed from the holy land and kingdom. They burned the gates and shed innocent blood; and we prayed to the Lord and were heard, and we offered sacrifice and fine flour, lit the lamps, and set out the loaves [Col. 1427C]. And now celebrate the days of the Feast of Tabernacles in the month Casleu. In the one hundred and eighty-eighth year, the people in Jerusalem and Judaea, the senate, and Judas, send greetings and health to Aristobulus, teacher of King Ptolemy, who is of the race of anointed priests, and to the Jews in Egypt. Having been delivered by God from great dangers, we give Him magnificent thanks, since we have fought against such a king” (ibid.), and so forth.

The plain text of this letter clearly shows that the Jewish brothers in Jerusalem and Judaea wrote not merely once but twice to their brethren throughout Egypt; and almost eighteen years elapsed between the two letters. It must also be known that the one hundred and sixty-ninth year, in which they wrote first under the reign of Demetrius, was the fourth and final year of the leadership of Jonathan, brother of Judas. The one hundred and eighty-eighth year, in which they wrote the second time, was the eleventh year after the death of Simon, brother of that same Jonathan and Judas—Simon whom his own son-in-law, Ptolemy son of Abubus, killed by treachery [Col. 1427D].

These facts make clear which Antiochus was the one over whose death they rejoice, relating how he fell in Persia: namely, Antiochus son of Demetrius, who persecuted and defeated the impious Tryphon, but also afflicted the Jews in many ways, both while Simon still lived and after Simon, when his son Hyrcanus held the leadership.

## CHAPTER VII. That the author will discuss the subject matter, purpose, and usefulness of the prologue to Second Maccabees.

[Col. 1428A] Now, in order that I may rise in some measure to meet your most devout request—by which you desire and ask that a discourse attentive and studious in the Word of God might clarify for you the sequence of this letter, which seems somewhat obscure—I wish to descend to what we once heard as little schoolboys, where teachers, when undertaking a reading, customarily set before their hearers its subject matter, purpose, and usefulness.

It is worth while to explain the subject matter, purpose, and usefulness of this preface in distinct chapters, so that in such order it may become somewhat clear what that Spirit says in this letter—the Spirit who is present in every Scripture divinely inspired and speaks to the churches [Col. 1428B]. I think that the subject matter, purpose, and usefulness of this Scripture, though brief, are such that they deserve to be heard fittingly by the wise: by those wise who are not wise in their own eyes, indeed who, in order to become wise, deem it fitting to become foolish—that is, to be disciples before they become teachers.

Therefore, as we are about to speak and hear of these three things which we have proposed, we first seek or set forth the subject matter around which the Scripture of this Second Book of Maccabees is chiefly occupied.

## CHAPTER VIII. What was the subject matter, or argument, of this prologue.

Observe that the whole Scripture of this book is concerned with God’s Law, and especially with the temple of the Lord, which was then regarded as the sole and unique temple throughout the whole world dedicated to the Lord’s name. The beginning of the narrative concerns Heliodorus and the guarding of the treasury: how utterly impossible it was that those who had entrusted themselves to the place and temple, which the whole world reverenced because of its sanctity and venerability, should be defrauded (2 Macc. 3). [Col. 1428C]

The end likewise concerns the temple, where Nicanor, stretching out his hand against the temple, swore: “Unless you hand Judas over to me bound, I will level this sanctuary of God to the plain, dig up the altar, and consecrate this temple to Father Bacchus.” Having said this, he departed (2 Macc. 14). He began battle, in which the commander himself was the first to fall in war; and all, by common counsel, decreed that this day should by no means pass without celebration. The celebration was to be held on the thirteenth day of the month Adar, called in the Syrian language the day before Mordecai’s day [Col. 1428D].

“The middle of the same book, moreover, contains this: that on the very day on which the temple had been defiled by foreigners, its purification took place, on the twenty-fifth day of the month Casleu; and for eight days they kept the celebration with joy in the manner of the Feast of Tabernacles, remembering that a short time before they had observed the solemn day of Tabernacles in mountains and caves like wild beasts. Therefore they carried *thyrsi* [Bacchic wands] and green branches before Him who had caused their place to be cleansed prosperously, and by common command and decree they ordained that the whole Jewish nation should observe these days every year” (2 Macc. 10).

These are the days of the Feast of Tabernacles (*Scenopegia*), concerning which the brethren, or Jews, in the region of Judaea wrote once and again, as has already been said, to the Jews throughout Egypt, saying: “And now celebrate the days of the Feast of Tabernacles”—saying this, I mean, in their second letter. Therefore, as they were about to perform the purification of the temple on the twenty-fifth day of the month Casleu, they judged it necessary to inform them, so that they too might observe the day of the Feast of Tabernacles; and they add also the day of the fire that was given when Nehemiah, after building the temple and altar, offered sacrifice.

We shall speak again later concerning these days. For the present, it seemed proper first to say that the temple and the holy things in Jerusalem, for which the Maccabees fought, constitute the subject matter of this book’s Scripture [Col. 1429A]. Hence it is not surprising that the text of this Scripture, or book, proceeds no further than the event concerning the death of the impious Nicanor, who had again sworn with outstretched hand to defile that temple and consecrate it to Father Bacchus. For after his death, although Judas and his brothers fought many battles, nothing of the kind happened concerning the temple that is contained at the beginning, middle, and end of this book. [Col. 1429B]

## CHAPTER IX. What was the purpose of this prologue.

We must now speak of its purpose. The purpose of this Scripture is to maintain that the temple in Jerusalem was holy, lawful, and pleasing to the Lord; and that it was the only place of prayer chosen by God, the place in which sacrifice ought to be offered to Him.

The circumstances then required that they write to the Jews in Egypt with this purpose. For, as has already been said, Onias fled to Egypt to Ptolemy Philometor. Wishing to leave behind an everlasting memorial and glory of himself, he requested from King Ptolemy and Queen Cleopatra permission to build in Egypt a temple like that of Jerusalem. Having obtained and completed this, he appointed Levites and priests from his own lineage, relying upon the prophecy of Isaiah, who two hundred years earlier had foretold that an altar of the Lord must be in the land of Egypt.

Because of that temple disputes arose among the Jews in the region of Judaea and those throughout Egypt, both before Onias and among those who had departed with Onias: some taken away captive, as has already been stated [Col. 1429D], others voluntarily drawn by the abundance of the country and Ptolemy’s generosity.

Likewise, in the time of Alexander of Macedon, the Samaritans built a temple on Mount Gerizim, through the agency of Sanballat the satrap and his son-in-law Manasseh, brother of Jaddus, high priest of Jerusalem, as Josephus writes more fully. Thus disputes arose because of the temples, so that they even contended before kings: the Jews of Judaea maintaining that they had built their temple in Jerusalem according to the Law of Moses, and the Samaritans maintaining that theirs was on Gerizim.

Those in Egypt, meanwhile, defended their own temple or strove to prefer it, as though by the testimony of prophetic authority—plainly misunderstanding the truth of the prophetic word and being far from the sense or meaning of so great a prophecy [Col. 1430A]. The circumstances therefore required, as has been said, that they write to the Jews throughout Egypt concerning the deeds performed by the manifest power of God around the temple in Jerusalem, with the purpose that it might be established that this temple, as it was ancient, was also the sole lawful temple.

The other temples, whether on Gerizim or in Egypt, had been built through transgression, as the prophetic vision of Daniel testifies: “The sons also of the transgressors of your people shall exalt themselves, that they may fulfil the vision—and fall” (Dan. 11). This signifies Onias and those with him; and they are called sons of transgressors because they abandoned the Law of the Lord, wishing to offer sacrifices to God in a place other than that commanded. “They shall exalt themselves,” he says, in pride and in vision—that is, they shall boast that they are fulfilling prophetic truth [Col. 1430B].

## CHAPTER X. That the temple of Jerusalem alone was lawful because God’s promises had to be fulfilled there.

In controversies of this kind it was useful that the Jews who were in the region of Judaea should prevail, and that the holy temple which was at Jerusalem should remain, for the truth of God, to confirm the promises concerning the coming of Christ the Son of God, attested from the Law and the Prophets, as in that saying: “For from Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isa. 2). This cause, this final cause, and this great benefit ought always to be before our eyes, in the sight of our heart; and then there will be no need for the question: What advantage, or what greater benefit, was there at that time in worshipping God at Jerusalem rather than on Mount Gerizim; on Mount Zion rather than at Heliopolis; in Judaea rather than in Egypt; in the temple of the descendants of faithful David rather than in the temple of the transgressor Onias? The time had not yet come for it to be said: “The hour is coming when you will worship the Father neither on Mount Gerizim nor in Jerusalem, but in spirit and truth” (John 4). For the salvation which is from the Jews had not yet come; and that temple had to stand until this salvation should come, until Christ should be brought to that temple by his parents, with the sacrificial offerings prescribed by the Law. In accordance with that saying of the prophet Malachi: “And immediately the Ruler whom you seek, and the Angel of the covenant whom you desire, shall come to his holy temple” (Mal. 3).

## CHAPTER XI. Why, in place of a greeting, it was written: “May he open your heart in his law.”

Having observed these things, you may at the same time consider what sort of greeting this is: “May God deal well with you and remember his covenant, which he spoke to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, his faithful servants; and may he give to you all a heart to worship him and to do his will with a great heart and willing spirit. May he open your heart in his law and in his commandments, and make peace. May he hear your prayers and be reconciled to you, and not forsake you in the time of evil. And now we are here praying for you.” As fraternal charity required, so it greeted and prayed for its Jewish brethren, whose hearts had certainly not been opened in the Law and commandments of the Lord, when it said: “And now we are here praying for you.” For if their hearts had been opened in the Law and commandments of the Lord, they would by no means have done what was contrary to the Law and the Lord’s commandment: namely, built a temple and altar in the land of Egypt, with hearts closed and ears wrongly opened to that prophecy of Isaiah: “And there shall be an altar of the Lord in the midst of the land of Egypt” (Isa. 19). By doing this they had made themselves transgressors of the Law and the Lord’s commandments, in accordance with the previously mentioned prophecy of Daniel, where it was said: “Even the sons of the transgressors of your people shall be exalted, that they may fulfil the vision, and they shall fall” (Dan. 11). Therefore they say, “May he be reconciled to you, and now we are here praying for you”; it must be understood: because you are transgressors, or sons of transgressors, in making or possessing a temple in the land of Egypt such as the Lord neither commanded through Isaiah nor caused to enter into his heart. Concerning this matter, they say, may he be reconciled to you.

## CHAPTER XII. What that affliction and assault were which had come upon the Jews.

After such a preface, by which the goodwill of the brethren in Egypt was plainly sought, so that they might become well-disposed, attentive, and receptive to hearing, the narrative follows: “In the one hundred and sixty-ninth year, in the reign of Demetrius, we Jews wrote to you concerning the affliction and assault that came upon us in these years.” It has already been said that this one hundred and sixty-ninth year of the Greek kingdom—in which the Jewish brethren in Judaea report that they wrote to their Jewish brethren in Egypt—was the fourth and also the final year of the leadership of Jonathan, brother of Judas. At that time the temple had already been restored and cleansed of the defilement by which the nations had polluted it, and defended against the impious Nicanor, who wished once more to defile it, swearing and saying: “Unless you hand Judas over to me bound, I shall level this sanctuary of God and dig up the altar, and consecrate this temple to Father Liber” [Dionysus] (2 Macc. 14).

After the blasphemous Nicanor had been killed, and the God of heaven praised, who preserved his place undefiled, a common decision and decree were made that this day should by no means pass without annual celebration. “We Jews,” they say, “have written to you, who ought yourselves to be Jews, not only by nation but by the faith of Abraham and faithful David, to whom the promise was made and confirmed in the place chosen by God, namely Jerusalem. We have written to you, I say, concerning the affliction and assault that came upon us in these years.”

“What was that affliction, or what was that assault?” (2 Macc. 1). “After Jason had withdrawn from the holy land and kingdom, they set fire to the gates and shed innocent blood,” as we said much earlier. This was the beginning of sorrows: Jason, who was also called Jesus by his ancestral name, brother of Onias the high priest, whom Andronicus killed at Menelaus’s request. Jason, I say, impious and no priest, but set over his brother unlawfully by an impious king, withdrew from the holy land. How did he withdraw? First willingly in mind, then unwillingly and as a fugitive in body as well. For when the king had consented to his suit and his promises of money, and he had obtained the high-priesthood, he immediately began to transfer his fellow-countrymen to Gentile customs. Thus he began by withdrawing from the holy land and kingdom with his whole mind. Then, advancing in wickedness and inflicting many massacres upon his fellow citizens, he received confusion as the end of his plots and fled into the region of the Ammonites. “Finally, hated by all, as a deserter from the laws; abominable as an enemy of his country and citizens; driven into Egypt, and thence making his way to Lacedaemon, he was at last cast out unburied” (2 Macc. 5). “After such a man had withdrawn,” they say, “they set fire to the gates and shed innocent blood.” Before his withdrawal, or apostasy, however, the holy city was inhabited in complete peace; and even kings and rulers declared the place worthy of the highest honour and adorned the temple with the greatest gifts.

## CHAPTER XIII. Why they called Judaea the holy land.

One must remember what we have already said above: the entire course and purpose of this book or writing looks to the veneration of the city of Jerusalem and to the singular dignity and honour of the temple which was in it. At the same time, the reason must be known which we likewise mentioned above: they were troubled by temples made contrary to the Law, where they ought not to have been, in imitation of that temple. Throughout this book the whole Scripture proclaims with its entire intention that that holy temple, and the sacrifices celebrated in that temple, were holy and legitimate, and that the city of Jerusalem was holy. This was fitting, namely in order to destroy confidence in the adulterous temples, one of which had been built on Mount Gerizim and the other in Egypt. Once this is observed, you will not wonder when they speak of “the holy land” in this manner: “after Jason withdrew from the holy land.”

Then, when they add: “And we prayed to the Lord, and were heard; and we offered sacrifice and fine flour, and lit the lamps, and set forth the loaves” (2 Macc. 1), we rightly understand all these words as the strongest defences of the legitimate privilege of the temple already mentioned, which was at Jerusalem: namely, that it belonged, or ought to belong, to those who served that temple to offer sacrifices, set forth loaves, and in doing these things to be heard there—not in the temple on Mount Gerizim, not in the temple of Heliopolis, which were rival temples.

## CHAPTER XIV. How the words “Celebrate the days of the Feast of Tabernacles in the month Casleu” are to be understood.

Moreover, what follows also looks to this: “And now celebrate the days of the Feast of Tabernacles in the month Casleu” (2 Macc. 1). Scenopegia was the feast of tabernacles, celebrated by that people in the seventh month, called Theseri among them and October among us. We must therefore consider how they say, “Celebrate the days of the Feast of Tabernacles,” adding “of the month Casleu,” which among them is the ninth month, counting from April, but among the Romans is called December, since it is the tenth from March. Without doubt they institute for the Egyptians another Feast of Tabernacles besides that which they had customarily celebrated from the giving of the Law: namely, that while they themselves observed in Jerusalem during Casleu the Encaenia—that is, the solemnities of the dedication or purification of the temple—the Jews in Egypt should likewise celebrate that same purification, not as Encaenia, which certainly did not concern their temple, but as a Feast of Tabernacles.

Let us now produce evidence for this from the Scripture itself. “But on the day,” it says, “on which the temple had been polluted by foreigners, it happened that purification took place on that same day, the twenty-fifth of the month Casleu. And for eight days they celebrated with joy in the manner of tabernacles, remembering that a short time before they had spent the solemn day of tabernacles in the mountains and caves like wild beasts. Therefore they carried thyrsi [ivy-wreathed staffs], green branches, and palms before him who had prospered the cleansing of his place. And by a common command and decree they ordained that the whole nation of the Jews should observe these days every year” (2 Macc. 10).

It plainly says that for eight days they celebrated in the manner of tabernacles, and gives the reason why they did so not in the manner of the ancient dedication made by Solomon, but in the manner of the feast of tabernacles, which, as has been said, was celebrated in the seventh month for another reason. What was that reason? “Remembering,” it says, “that a short time before they had spent the solemn day of tabernacles in mountains and caves like wild beasts.” It is therefore clear what they mean by saying: “And now celebrate the days of the Feast of Tabernacles in the month Casleu.” It is as though they said: In the manner of Scenopegia—that is, of the feast of tabernacles, which for an ancient reason was celebrated in the seventh month—celebrate also in the ninth month this festival of purification of the temple. It is called a purification because the temple had been polluted by foreigners.

“But Maccabaeus and those who were with him, with the Lord protecting them, recovered both the temple and the city; they demolished the altars which foreigners had built in the streets, and likewise the shrines; and, after cleansing the temple, they made another altar and offered sacrifices and incense, lit lamps, and set out the loaves of presentation” (2 Macc. 10).

## CHAPTER XV. Why they wrote twice for the same reasons, and why the second admonition is harsher than the first.

In accordance with the common command and decree by which they had ordained that the entire nation of the Jews should observe these days every year, they wrote once and again to their Jewish brethren in Egypt: first in the one hundred and sixty-ninth year, and then in the one hundred and eighty-eighth. From the fact that they wrote once and again, with nineteen years intervening between the two occasions, we may understand that the recipients did not comply on the first occasion. Since they possessed another temple which, as stated above, they boasted that they had built in accordance with Isaiah’s oracle, they were unwilling to regard the temple at Jerusalem as belonging to them; and for this reason they refused to accept its festival of dedication or purification.

It should therefore be noted that the following admonition is somewhat harsher than the first. For the greeting on the first occasion is so gentle, as may be seen from their words: “Jewish brethren to Jewish brethren: May God deal well with you and remember his covenant,” and the rest. But in the second, the sweetness of the fraternal name is absent. It says instead: “The people who are in Jerusalem and Judaea, together with the senate and Judas, to Aristobulus, teacher of King Ptolemy, who is of the race of anointed priests, and to the Jews who are in Egypt.” The name “senate” is, indeed, a sign of judicial intent. But who this Judas was cannot easily be known from the histories, unless perhaps he was Judas the Essene by descent, who lived in those times and who, as Josephus says, was never false in the things he predicted.

Likewise, who this Aristobulus, teacher of Ptolemy, was cannot easily be discovered from the histories, except that in calling him “one who is of the race of anointed priests,” they signify that he was someone among the descendants or relatives of the aforementioned Onias. Onias, the son of Simon the high priest, had built a temple in the land of Egypt, as it were by high-priestly authority and under the protection of a prophetic proclamation which he evidently misunderstood. This Aristobulus was one of the relatives or descendants of that Onias, and was teacher of King Ptolemy Philometor. Nor is it surprising that a Jewish man should be called teacher of an Egyptian king, since from the days of Ptolemy Philadelphus, who had the Law translated for himself by the seventy interpreters, the kings of Egypt had customarily had Jewish teachers.

## CHAPTER XVI. For the same reason the city was called holy as the land was holy.

“Having been delivered,” they say, “from great dangers by God, we give magnificent thanks to him, as men who fought against such a king. For he caused those who fought against the holy city to boil up from Persia.” See how, in accordance with the intention which we have stated, their venerable language proceeds in calling the land holy and the city holy. This ornament of fine speech is maintained from such a beginning almost throughout the whole body of the book, undoubtedly against the rival claims of those who wished, contrary to the Law, to possess elsewhere a temple or a Holy of Holies. We willingly accept that there was a holy land, a holy city, and a holy place—surely on account of him who, not from elsewhere but from there, was to come: the Holy of Holies.

We have already said above who King Antiochus was; nor is it tiresome to say again that he was the same man concerning whom the narrative began, though was not completed, near the end of the first book of Maccabees: how he committed many evils against Simon and John Hyrcanus. Josephus relates that he shut up Hyrcanus in the city, surrounded him with seven divisions, and severely afflicted them. This passage of Scripture explains more plainly how he died: while he himself was a commander in Persia, he and his immense army fell in the temple of Nanea, deceived by the counsel of Nanea’s priest.

“In every way blessed is God,” they say, “who delivered up the impious.” This rejoicing too at the destruction of the impious serves to commend the holy place and the temple of God—the temple whose likeness they had made in Egypt, but which ought truly to have been regarded as the only holy one. For in it manifest divine power had appeared so often, exacting vengeance from whoever dishonoured it; and although, because of the sins of its inhabitants, contempt for the place sometimes occurred, nevertheless those who held the place in contempt did not go away unpunished.

## CHAPTER XVII. For the same reason, why the fire given from heaven is recalled.

The account of the fire which, they say, was given when Nehemiah, after the temple and altar had been built, offered sacrifices, is sufficiently clear and is better received if the reader does not lose from memory the cause or purpose which we have stated: namely, that all these things tend to defend the privilege and attest the singular dignity of the holy city and temple, in imitation of which a temple had been made in the land of Egypt which ought not to have been made. For the fire so given is a great and memorable testimony to that temple’s legitimate holiness. The narrative, as we have already said, is indeed clear; nevertheless, for simpler readers something must be said concerning this altar-fire itself.

## CHAPTER XVIII. What kind of fire this altar-fire was.

“The fire,” says the Lord to Moses, “shall always burn upon the altar. The priest shall feed it, laying wood upon it every morning, day by day; and after placing the whole burnt offering upon it, he shall burn the fat of the peace offerings. This is a perpetual fire, which shall never fail upon the altar” (Lev. 6). But from where had this fire, to be fed with such care and guarded lest it should fail by the concern and diligence not of another but of the priest, been given or received? From the Lord himself, certainly, by a great and evident miracle.

For after the tabernacle had been anointed and the rite of priesthood and sacrifices arranged according to the Lord’s command, Moses said: “Today the Lord shall appear to you.” Again: “Do this, and his glory shall appear to you.” Then it immediately follows: “But Moses and Aaron entered the tabernacle of testimony; and afterwards, when they came out, they blessed the people. And the glory of the Lord appeared to all the multitude; and behold, fire went out from the Lord and devoured the whole burnt offering and the fat which were upon the altar. When the crowds saw this, they praised the Lord, falling upon their faces” (Lev. 9).

The fire was therefore worthy to be tended by the priest and never to fail from the altar; and the place, the temple, and the holy altar were worthy to possess the gift of so great a privilege—a privilege which neither existed nor ought to have existed in that rival Egyptian temple. It was possible for the fire never to fail upon the altar until the time of the Babylonian captivity, because, however many storms had arisen up to that point, none was so great that the fire necessarily had to be extinguished. For nowhere does any Scripture before Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, mention that anything of this kind happened: that the fire could not be maintained or guarded. But when both the temple was destroyed and the city was burned by Chaldaean fire, how or where could the priest take care that the fire should not fail upon the altar?

They therefore did what they could, having faith and hope toward God, according to the evident sense of this letter: “When our fathers were being led away into Persia, the priests who were then worshippers of God secretly hid the fire taken from the altar in a valley where there was a deep dry well; and there they concealed it, so that the place was unknown to all” (2 Macc. 1). What could be more beautiful in contemplating their faith? They entrusted for revival a dying fire which could not be fed, which had no place in which it might be fed. In this there is an image of the resurrection of the dead. Nor did their hope deceive them. How?

## CHAPTER XIX. For the same reason, why the miracle of the fire and Nehemiah’s prayer are recalled.

“When many years had passed and it pleased God that Nehemiah should be sent by the king of Persia, he sent descendants of those priests who had hidden it to seek the fire; and, as they reported to us, they found not fire but thick water” (ibid.), and so forth. The narrative is clear, as is the indication of divine providence; and it greatly bears upon the often-mentioned cause which must always be remembered, a cause which this letter also beautifully states when it says: “And the same fire was given when Nehemiah, after the temple and altar had been built, offered sacrifices” (ibid.).

For Nehemiah did not build the temple and altar. Zerubbabel the governor and Jesus son of Josedec the priest had already built it before Nehemiah was sent by the king of Persia; Nehemiah rebuilt the walls of the city. Therefore, when they say, “when Nehemiah, after the temple and altar had been built, offered sacrifices,” the phrase “after the temple and altar had been built” must certainly be understood as an insertion occasioned by the completed rebuilding of the walls. It is a commendation of the aforementioned temple, which alone was holy and legitimate: the temple upon whose altar this perpetual fire had existed before the Babylonian captivity and was recovered after the captivity by so great a miracle. Truly this was a great and splendid testimony among the other authoritative evidences by which that temple is known to have been adorned.

For what sort of thing was it that, after wood and sacrifices had been placed upon it, and likewise great stones drenched with water, a great fire should be kindled from the contrary element? The same purpose is served by their statement that Nehemiah’s prayer had this form: “Lord, God, Creator of all things” (2 Macc. 1), and so forth. Among these words the following must be noted: “Gather our dispersion and establish your people in your holy place, as Moses said.” How, then, did Moses say this? “When,” he says, “a king has been established, he shall not multiply horses for himself, nor lead the people back into Egypt, relying upon the number of horsemen, especially since the Lord commanded you that you should never return by that same way” (Deut. 17). Yet they had not returned to Egypt.

Again Moses said: “You shall not do so before the Lord your God, but you shall come to the place which your God shall choose from all your tribes, to put his name there and dwell in it; and in that place you shall offer your whole burnt offerings and your sacrifices.” The place which the Lord chose (Deut. 12) was Jerusalem, as Scripture narrates: “When the angel of the Lord stretched out his hand over Jerusalem to destroy it, the Lord had mercy and said to the striking angel: ‘It is enough now; restrain your hand.’ And the angel of the Lord was near the threshing floor of Areuna the Jebusite. Then Gad came to David that day and said to him: ‘Go up; establish an altar to the Lord on the threshing floor of Areuna the Jebusite’” (2 Sam. 24). Yet they were offering sacrifices in Egypt.

See, therefore, how subtly and moderately they rebuke and accuse them as transgressors of the Law, by citing from Nehemiah’s prayer this saying: “Establish your people in your holy place, as Moses said.” They wished, of course, the holy place of God to be at Jerusalem, against whose election a place presumptuously declared holy in Egypt could surely not be holy. Nehemiah called that day or that sacrifice Nephthar, which means “purification.” This was a different purification, and for a different reason, from the purification of the month Casleu, of which we spoke above and which they called the purification of the temple. But they did not need to announce to them the day of this fire—what month it was or what day of the month—because they knew it and had long celebrated it.

## CHAPTER XX. For the same reason, the recollection of the tabernacle and ark, and the excuse given.

While they contended, with such true statements, that the chosen place and the holy and legitimate temple could not be possessed by those in Egypt, but were to be found in Jerusalem, they perceived that they lacked something: namely, the tabernacle, the ark, and the altar of incense made by Moses. To their rivals, that is, the Jews who had their own temple in Egypt, this undoubtedly seemed to mean that great glory had departed from Jerusalem—as though there were no other sufficient reason, nor could there be, for commending or preferring the dignity of the Jerusalem temple, since it did not possess those insignia: the tabernacle, ark, and altar of incense.

They console themselves concerning this apparent loss of glory by adding the following: “It is found in the writings of Jeremiah the prophet that he commanded those who were being carried away to take the fire, as has been indicated. But in that same writing was the account of how the prophet, in response to a divine oracle given to him, commanded the tabernacle and ark to accompany him until he went out to the mountain upon which Moses ascended and saw the inheritance of God. Jeremiah came and found there a place in a cave; and he brought the tabernacle, ark, and altar of incense into it, and shut up the entrance. And he said that the place would remain unknown until God gathered the assembly of the people and became merciful; and the Lord will reveal these things, and the majesty of the Lord will appear, and there will be a cloud, as it was also manifested to Moses, and as when Solomon asked that the place might be sanctified for the great God. He made these things manifest; and, being endowed with wisdom, he offered the sacrifice of the dedication and completion of the temple, just as Moses prayed to the Lord and fire descended from heaven and consumed the whole burnt offering” (2 Macc. 2).

## CHAPTER XXI. How the statements about the tabernacle and ark should be understood.

This consolation was then timely. It raised high a great crown of hope for God’s legitimate temple at Jerusalem, lest it should seem unable to be preferred over the Egyptian temple merely because it did not possess the tabernacle, ark, and altar of incense. Nevertheless, they say that these matters are found in the writings of Jeremiah the prophet which we now have. If you consider the dignity and majesty of the Holy Spirit who spoke in the prophets—of whom Jeremiah was one of the best known and most eminent—the letter indeed sounds loudly of the glory of that man-made temple, but any spiritual person finds far greater glory in the Spirit of present prophecy.

Thus the natural Jewish person, whose circumcision consists not in spirit but in flesh alone, thinks that Jeremiah said that, at some unknown time, the Jews who had been carried captive among all nations ought to be gathered together, and that the temple and city ought to be restored, with such a cloud appearing as was present where Moses received the Law and where Solomon dedicated the temple he had built for the great God. But after the time when these things were written, after the victorious battles of the Maccabees, we know of no gathering of God’s people except that which the same Spirit who spoke in the prophets declares to us through John the Evangelist (John 11): that Jesus was to die for the nation, and not for the nation only, but that he might gather into one the children of God who were scattered abroad.

Then, surely, the glory of God appeared: the glory of the Son of God shining forth in the resurrection of the dead. And from then on there has been a cloud, as it was manifested to Moses when he received the Law, and as there was a cloud where Solomon built the temple of the Lord. From then on, I say, there has likewise been a cloud: namely, the blindness of the Jews, of which those clouds became a sign. “Until that time,” Jeremiah says, “the place where the tabernacle, ark, and altar of incense are will remain unknown”—that is, it will not be known to the peoples or nations of which, or of what kind, those things were copies of the heavenly realities.

## CHAPTER XXII. Whatever sense Jeremiah wrote those things in, the Jews adapted them to their own purpose.

Someone says: “Do you suppose that those who wrote this prologue, or those to whom they wrote it, understood the prophetic sayings of Jeremiah as you now speak, and as the Church of Christ now understands them?” To this I say: Do you suppose that the Jews who wrote from the region of Judaea, or the Jews in Egypt to whom they wrote, were prophets or possessed prophetic understanding? If they were prophets, or had the understanding of the prophetic Spirit, they surely understood the things hidden under the veil of the legal or prophetic letter: what the construction and rite of the tabernacle intended; what the altar of incense signified; what the ark, the mercy-seat, and the two cherubim signified; and, in short, what or of what kind was that which the Lord intended when he said to Moses: “See, and make according to the pattern which I showed you on the mountain.”

But in those days there were almost no prophets, from the time when the temple was rebuilt after the Babylonian captivity. Malachi, the last of the twelve prophets—whom the Hebrews say was Ezra himself—prophesied. Hence it is written in the first book of Maccabees: “And there was great affliction in Israel, such as had not been since the day when no prophet had appeared in Israel” (1 Macc. 9).

Therefore, however they understood what they said was found in the writings of Jeremiah the prophet—whether Jeremiah himself spoke of a gathering of the people, an appearance of the Lord’s majesty, or a future cloud resembling the cloud manifested to Moses on Mount Sinai or that manifested to Solomon at the temple’s dedication—we should maintain in the present writing the intention of those who wrote it. They wrote these deeds or sayings of Jeremiah to their brethren in Egypt, who possessed an illegitimate temple, for their own appropriate consolation: namely, that the dignity of the place or temple ought not to seem less because at that time they did not possess the tabernacle, ark, and altar of incense.

## CHAPTER XXIII. For the same reason as above, the prayer of Moses and the fire given from heaven.

What is finally added—“Just as Moses prayed to the Lord, and fire descended from heaven and consumed the whole burnt offering”—and what Moses said, “Because that which was for sin was not eaten, it was consumed,” have the same object: namely, testimony to holiness or sanctification, that the temple should rightly be regarded as holy, since it was clear that sins were consumed by fire divinely given, just as when Moses prayed.

For it was no less a miracle that, after water had been sprinkled upon the sacrifice, a great fire was kindled than that, when Moses prayed, fire went out from the Lord and consumed the whole burnt offering. They wish it to be maintained by heavenly authority that no less holiness or dignity should be ascribed to that temple than to the tabernacle of Moses.

When they say, “Moses says, because that which was for sin was not eaten, it was consumed,” it is as though they said: Why was the sacrifice for sin not eaten but burned? Namely, because it was not cleansed, being for sin; for just as sin is unclean, so the sacrifice which was for sin did not belong to eating as did the peace offerings. It was fitting that it should be wholly burned, just as we need our sin to be burned by the fire of the Holy Spirit.

They do not recall this saying of Moses idly, in accordance with their often-mentioned purpose: namely, that it may be clear that the temple was made in which sin is consumed, as attested by fire given divinely and by the sacrifice for sin. Let this now be the end for us of such a treatment of the letter of the preface which you imposed upon me for explanation. If it has been done in any way usefully, you too ought to receive the favour of blessing from all to whom it seems useful, because you have been its prompter and exactor.

## CHAPTER XXIV. How many enemies of the Word of God swiftly passed away like a shadow.

Meanwhile the treasure of father Abraham and of faithful David remained safe and unharmed: namely, the word of promise which the truthful God had stored up for them under oath. For the place and nation from which it had to be fulfilled still stood. One generation passed away and another came; but he to whom it is truly said, “But you are the same, and your years shall not fail” (Ps. 101 [102]), remained in his purpose.

In that year, as has already been said, when the brethren in Jerusalem and the region of Judaea wrote to the brethren in Egypt—in that year, I say, 188—John, surnamed Hyrcanus, governed the place and nation, and it was the eleventh year of his rule. Where then were those who, pursuing that place and nation with such hatred, had wished to exterminate them? They had passed away swiftly like a shadow, dying one after another by different disasters. If you consider the swiftness of their destruction, you may rightly say that their name was wiped out in one generation.

For scarcely had one generation of the Maccabees passed when Hyrcanus was governing, in the eleventh year of his leadership. Through Hyrcanus’s father Simon and his uncles Judas and Jonathan, God had preserved the place and nation; yet so many hostile kings had successively died within a period of little more than forty years. After the sinful root, Antiochus Epiphanes, who was broken without hand, died his son Antiochus Eupator; after Eupator, his cousin Demetrius son of Seleucus; after Demetrius, Alexander son of Antiochus; after Alexander, Demetrius son of Demetrius; then Tryphon, tyrant of the kingdom, who, having treacherously killed Jonathan and Antiochus, the young son of Alexander, placed the diadem upon himself; then Antiochus, son of Demetrius, who fell in the temple of Nanea.

There had been seven, and now they were no more: plainly, they had swiftly been erased in the one generation of the Maccabees, as has been said. And God was blessed and praised according to the Psalmist’s words: “But the enemies of the Lord, as soon as they have been honoured and exalted, shall fail; they shall fail away like smoke” (Ps. 36 [37]).

## CHAPTER XXV. Why God did not wish to subject the other kingdoms to his people.

The terrible God, who so swiftly took away the spirit of the princes and with such slight aid sustained the nation and its place—could not the Word of God, God the Word, have done this: that His nation and His place should rule over all kingdoms, as the kingdom of the Greeks [Col. 1441B] had shortly before ruled under Alexander of Macedon? Could He not have brought it about that Jerusalem should be regarded as the head of the kingdoms of the world, whether through the victories of the Maccabees or earlier under David, whom God by His election had established as king after His own heart?

Certainly He could, had He wished to concern Himself with such things—more than His own purpose required. But His purpose was not that the blessed men, heirs of His blessing, should already leap about on horses and chariots in this valley of tears, in this place appointed for their weeping and hunger, and for the pursuit of holy poverty; nor that they should possess power among the nations after the manner of the kings of the Gentiles, or exercise dominion. But what was His purpose? Namely, that His saints and all His elect should in this world be pilgrims [Col. 1441C] or exiles, and should await His kingdom, whose king or emperor is God and Lord Himself.

Accordingly, in keeping with this purpose, God was content to grant His people only such small help that, among the nations, one nation and one place might be preserved until God’s truth—that is, the word of promise—should be fulfilled from it. Beyond this safeguard or providence, the King of the humble, God, had no reason to exalt an exiled people, the children of the sojourning Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. For the nations—the nations of the Gentiles—had kings, while kings themselves had emperors over them. It was sufficient for Him to provide that nation and that place with kings or princes, such as David and these Maccabees, whose wars or victories were not meant to establish [Col. 1441D] any worldly supremacy, but to defend the nation from which the salvation of the world would come.

But when, or at what time, the kingdom and dominion of that nation over all nations would arise, He foresaw who sat upon the throne in Daniel as the Ancient of Days, already extending kingdom and authority to the Son of Man who was to come from that nation, so that all peoples, tribes, and languages might serve Him for ever.

## CHAPTER XXVI. That the Maccabees ought not to have entered into alliance with the Romans, and why they were taken away by so swift a death.

Something dark befell the victorious brothers in the midst of their glory—Judas, Jonathan, and Simon: namely, glorified by their victories, they voluntarily sent to establish alliance and friendship with the powerful and renowned Romans. Although Scripture, which records their deeds, does not blame them for this, it is nevertheless easy to perceive that it was neither safe before God nor permitted by the Law for the Jews to seek the friendship of the Gentiles. Yet, as they were glorious in their lives, so they were glorious after death; for if they admitted any dust, or dust of vanity, in this manner, it was wholly wiped away by the swift ensuing [Col. 1442B] death of each.

For Judas had first sent to Rome to establish friendship and alliance with them; and meanwhile King Demetrius, after the fall of Nicanor and his army, set Bacchides and Alcimus to go again into Judaea, and in that battle fell that mighty man who saved the people of Israel (1 Macc. vii). Then Jonathan sent to Rome to establish and renew friendship with them, and afterward was ensnared and killed by the deceits of Tryphon. Likewise Simon sent to renew friendship with them, and not long afterward was murdered by treachery by his son-in-law Ptolemy.

Such outcomes seem to cast a shadow over the end of each of them: namely, that they diminished heavenly help for themselves when they sought from worldly men something like a foundation of peace and security. Yet a thoughtful mind prefers to judge another cause: that they died so soon because, as the Apostle says of the saints, “of whom the world was not worthy” (Heb. xi), so that people at that time was not worthy of leaders such as these, so great that they should remain long. For it had already become, as it were, an old man, nearly altogether deranged, except for a few righteous persons, having grown exceedingly cold in the worship of divine religion.

Thus after Hyrcanus, Simon’s son, it deserved to have as ruler Aristobulus, Hyrcanus’s son, the murderer of his mother and brother; then the brother of that same Aristobulus, Alexander, himself also a parricide and murderer of many of the Jewish populace; then the sons of that Alexander, Hyrcanus and Aristobulus, [Col. 1442D] who tore the principality apart with dreadful contention; and, much later, Herod, alien in descent, eminent in cruelty, standard-bearer of every domestic and public murder, attendant of death, destined for everlasting perdition.

Blessed, then, was their lot, whatever manner of death they endured. For “their bodies were buried in peace, and their names live for ever” (Sirach xliv).

# BOOK ELEVEN

[Col. 1443]

## CHAPTER I. How the word of the Lord through Isaiah, “If it be not as I have thought, so shall it be,” is to be understood.

For it is written in Isaiah: “The Lord has sworn, saying: If it be not as I have thought, so shall it be; and as I have planned in my mind, so shall it come to pass”; and thereafter: “For the Lord of hosts has decreed, and who can weaken it? And His hand is stretched out, and who shall turn it back?” (Isa. xiv).

What, I ask, did the Lord think, and what did He plan in His mind? What did He decree, and toward what is His hand stretched out? Did He merely think, plan, or decree this: that He should crush that fleshly Assyrian in his own land and trample him down upon his mountains? No. “This,” he says, “is the counsel which He has devised over all the earth, [Col. 1443B] and this is the hand stretched out over all nations”—of whom, indeed, the devil was prince, who was signified by the Assyrian.

Concerning that ancient dragon, the Lord thought this and planned this in His mind concerning His elect: that his yoke should be removed from them and his burden lifted from their shoulder; that all his heads—his seven heads, concerning which, or against which, the present little work is composed, and the sixth of which, the Roman Empire, we now approach—should bite one another and consume one another; and that at last the whole wicked beast, together with its heads, should be delivered up to be burned with fire.

## CHAPTER II. [Col. 1443C] How God may properly be said to “think” something.

How did the Lord think, before it existed, that it would exist? Did He think as prophets were accustomed to think or dream? For example, as Joseph said to his brothers: “Hear,” he said, “my dream which I saw: I thought that we were binding sheaves in the field, and that my sheaf, as it were, rose and stood, while your sheaves stood around and worshipped my sheaf” (Gen. xxxvii).

Certainly the Lord thought far better. The thinking of man and the thinking of God differ greatly—indeed, incomparably; far apart are a human dream and God’s word, the prophetic grace of any individual and the very substance of supreme wisdom. “A man thinking or dreaming sometimes, and very often, does not know what the images of his dreams [Col. 1443D] signify—as Pharaoh, who said: ‘I thought that I stood upon the bank of the river, and seven cows rose out of the stream’ (Gen. xlii),” and so forth. Certainly he did not know what was signified by those things, nor was there anyone to interpret them.

But how did the Lord think? Namely, as the Evangelist says: “Because what was made in Him was life”—concerning all things before they were made, He was as certain that they should be made (John i) as He is now, after all things have been made. Therefore He could swear, saying: “If it be not as I have thought, so shall it be.”

Why, then, did He say, “I have thought,” if He was certain? Clearly because they did not yet exist in actuality, although they were certain in predestination. Therefore He did not improperly say “I have thought,” though He could have said “I have foreknown,” even though “to think” signifies less than “to foreknow.” But what wonder is it if in divine speech something is sometimes said less fully and means more? This mode of expression is called by grammarians *tapeinōsis*, that is, humility of expression, when the word does not attain to the magnitude of the thing.

All modes, tropes, and figures—all the ornaments of speech of which secular masters have boasted as though they were their inventors—are found scattered throughout the divine Scriptures, and existed before those supposed inventors [Col. 1444B] were born. And if any man or prophet, such as Daniel, could sometimes delight wonderfully in thinking something in dreams, almost as though in images were real things, how greatly, do you suppose, did God delight while He still “thought” in His own manner, before He made anything, before the earth existed, or anything else of all things that were made?

Therefore Wisdom herself says: “Before He made anything, before this thing or that came to be, I was with Him, arranging all things; and I delighted day by day, playing before Him at all times, playing in the circle of the earth; and my delights were to be with the children of men” (Prov. viii).

## CHAPTER III. [Col. 1444C] Among all that God thought, the chief thing was the Son, whom the dragon wished to devour, but who was to be caught up to God and His throne.

Among all things whatsoever that God thought, planned in His mind, or decreed, the greatest and most beautiful in predestination—and now in actuality—was that which we have in hand: namely, what was fulfilled under the Roman Empire; what God promised to the fathers and swore to Abraham and Isaac—that Christ, the Son of God, should be born of a virgin, suffer, rise again, ascend to heaven, and sit at the right hand of God the Father, according to the aforesaid revelation, where “the dragon stood before the woman who was about to give birth, in order that, when she had borne her son, he might devour him” (Rev. xii).

“And she bore a male child,” Scripture says, [Col. 1444D] “who shall rule all nations with a rod of iron” (Ps. ii); “and her son was caught up to God and to His throne.”

O delightful sport of Wisdom: to foreknow and predestine a definite number of angels and human beings, and to inscribe each one’s name in the book of life; to think that out of the multitude of creatures or spirits to be created someone would arise who would try to frustrate so good a purpose—whence he is rightly called the great dragon, the ancient serpent, the devil, and Satan—and, on the other hand, to plan in the mind how he should be mocked through the Word who was with God, with whom He held His ancient counsel; and to decree concerning that dragon what no one could weaken: the decree of eternal judgment.

There already were the delights of the same Wisdom with the children of men, and indeed with angels also, but especially with the children of men, because He was nowhere to take hold of angels, but of the seed of Abraham—that is, human nature—as has now come to pass. Hence apostolic faith rejoices also when it says: “For He nowhere takes hold of angels, but He takes hold of the seed of Abraham” (Heb. ii).

From this point, our discourse, begun in praise of the victorious truth of God, must now be brought forward [Col. 1445B].

## CHAPTER IV. He invokes Wisdom, meanwhile explaining what this means: “Do not give wine to kings, but to those bitter of heart.”

Let that same Wisdom, once invoked, be present, since we now come upon the most beautiful part of the subject undertaken. Let her be present when invoked, and count me among those to whom, or of whatever kind, she judges wine ought to be given to drink.

“Do not,” he says, “give wine to kings, O Lemuel; do not give wine to kings, for there is no secret where drunkenness reigns, lest perhaps they drink and forget judgments, and change the cause of the sons of the poor. Give strong drink to those who mourn, and wine to those bitter of soul; let them drink and forget their poverty, and remember their pain no more” (Prov. [Col. 1445C] xxxi).

What sort of wine is this, which, if given to kings to drink, makes them forget judgments and alter the cause of the sons of the poor; but if given to those who mourn, makes them forget their poverty and remember their pain no more? Certainly, since it is a parable, it must be understood mystically according to the laws of parables.

This wine, then, is the word of wisdom or the word of knowledge. If it is given to kings—that is, to the proud, among whom drunkenness reigns, namely those whom knowledge puffs up—they forget judgments and alter the cause of the sons of the poor: that is, they wrongly examine the meaning of the Scriptures while they defend their own views through contention, yield to no one, and reckon as vain glory and presumption the sound words of others, who are sons of the poor—that is, humble according to Christ and lovers of truth.

Therefore, O Lemuel, whose name means “in whom is God”; O Christ, in whom all the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily: do not give the wine of Your knowledge to such persons. Give it instead to those who mourn, that is, the humble, and to those who are bitter of soul because they have a humble consciousness of poverty and sins. For when this wine is given to such people, it gladdens their hearts, and by a kind of good forgetfulness they forget their poverty, strengthened by the Apostle’s saying: “God has chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God has chosen the base things of the world and the despised things, and things that are not, to destroy the things that are” (1 Cor. iii).

And if You give wine to us also, then we likewise, strengthened and forgetful of all [Col. 1446A] our poverty, no longer mindful of the pain or sadness of the world, shall proclaim as foolish, weak, and ignoble the wise, mighty, and noble kings of the earth, and the princes who stood against the Lord and against His Christ, imagining that they could weaken God’s decree or turn back the Lord’s outstretched hand. We shall proclaim this in praise of the victory of God’s Word, following the triumphal chariot of so great a conqueror.

## CHAPTER V. It cannot be said to what the dragon’s sixth head was like.

Concerning the individual heads of the dragon, it could be shown, with the testimonies of holy Scripture, what sort of faces they bore, or what kinds of beasts they resembled. But concerning this sixth head, intensely red, it cannot be shown what sort of appearance it had or to what beast it resembled, because Scripture did not say. When Daniel saw the vision of the four beasts, he said only this concerning future things: “The beast was terrible and wonderful and exceedingly strong, having great iron teeth; it devoured and crushed, and trampled the rest beneath its feet; it was unlike the other beasts which I had seen before” (Dan. vii).

He said that this beast was unlike the others he had seen earlier—namely the lioness, bear, and leopard—but did not say that it resembled any of the many beasts besides those. He expressed its terrible strength in terrible terms when he said, “having great iron teeth”; by these, undoubtedly, we understand the consuls or warlike and exceedingly powerful emperors of Roman might, and its armies ordered in battle with stern strictness and rigorous severity.

To pass over for the present the other nations, this beast devoured and crushed the Jewish nation and trampled the rest beneath its feet, because it destroyed the place, struck the nation with the sword, and sold and scattered into captivity those who remained. We do not, therefore, recognize the Roman Empire as one of the heads of the red dragon because it exacted a just vengeance, though unknowingly, for the blood of Christ; rather, because the power of that empire killed Christ and Christ’s martyrs, it became a great head among all the impious persons who then lived and who were, indeed, the body or members of the devil.

## CHAPTER VI. [Col. 1446D] That what the Hebrews suppose to be said of the sixth head—“The boar from the forest laid it waste,” etc.—is inappropriate.

The Hebrews suppose that what is silent in Daniel is said in the Psalm: “The boar from the forest laid it waste, and the solitary wild beast fed upon it” (Ps. lxxix). They maintain that the fourth terrible beast bore the likeness of a boar or a solitary wild beast.

This seems contrary to their opinion: horns are ascribed to that terrible beast. “It had,” he says, “ten horns. I considered, and behold, another little horn sprang up from their midst” (Dan. vii), and so forth. This, I say, seems contradictory, for a boar has no horns. Therefore, to suppose or say that beast was a boar seems to us as unsuitable as to attach a dolphin to forests or a boar to waves.

At the same time, it should be noted that, in another vision concerning the future kings of the same kingdoms—the Persian and Median kingdom, which in the same vision were signified by the bear and leopard—those kings, who had to be signified by horns, were represented by the appearances of other animals: namely, a ram and a goat, to which horns are known to belong by nature’s gift. Therefore, what Scripture has left unspoken concerning the name of the fourth beast, let us also leave unspoken, so that whatever we can conceive fiercer among beasts, we may understand to be that fearful empire of the Romans.

## CHAPTER VII. [Col. 1447B] How the fourth beast rose from the sea and constituted the dragon’s sixth head in order.

How did this terrible beast come from the sea? How did it rise from the sea? How did this head stand before the woman about to give birth, as part of that bloody succession of the seven-headed dragon? Namely, through great and unspeakable discords, through civil wars—wars worse than civil.

The spirit of discord breathed by this beast troubled the world, afflicted nations, drenched cities and kingdoms with slaughter, and filled almost all lands—Europe, Africa, and Asia—with its own blood and that of nearly all nations. Histories exist: let those who wish read the tragedies of the human race, the sufferings of the world truly, as John says, “set in the evil one.” This has been sufficiently evident from effects of this kind [Col. 1447C] and is evident to one who reads and understands.

We proceed toward that supreme point of madness in which this head raised itself against the woman so often mentioned and still to be mentioned, who had a child in her womb; and it prepared its iron teeth in order to devour her son when she had borne him.

## CHAPTER VIII. Herod, born of an Idumaean father and an Arabian mother, was decreed king of Judaea by the Roman Senate.

In the reign of Augustus Caesar, in the one hundred and eighty-fourth Olympiad, when Gaius Demetrius and Gaius Asianus were consuls, Herod was decreed king of Judaea by the Roman Senate, through the favour of Caesar Augustus and the support of Mark Antony. He was not a Jew by descent; indeed, he was born of an Idumaean father [Col. 1447D] and an Arabian mother.

Nevertheless, Nicolaus of Damascus, as Josephus relates, says that this Herod’s father Antipater was a Jew of very noble descent, one of those who returned from Babylon to Judaea. But he says this—that is, reports it—in favour of Herod his son, who happened to become king of the Jews despite being neither of royal nor even Jewish lineage. For Antipater was Idumaean by descent; and, possessing great wealth, he received from Caesar authority and guardianship over all Judaea, being a friend of Hyrcanus, king and chief of the priests.

But when he saw that Hyrcanus was slow and indolent, he appointed his elder son Phasael commander in Jerusalem, and his second son Herod governor of Galilee; afterward, as has already been said, Herod came to the kingdom.

A certain righteous man named Sameas foretold this in the council, in Herod’s presence, when he had been summoned on a charge and stood surrounded by purple and attended by armed guards: “I accuse you,” he said, “or the Law, because you have given him such license. Know that the man whom you now wish to acquit for Hyrcanus’s sake will someday torture us and the king himself.” Nor did he speak falsely in saying this. For once Herod had gained the kingdom, he killed all those then found in the council, together with Hyrcanus himself.

## CHAPTER IX. Discords between the Roman Senate and the Jewish people brought Herod the kingdom.

Utmost discord, bloody discord, both in the Roman [Col. 1448B] Senate and among the Jewish people, brought him the kingdom. For when Gaius Caesar and the great Pompey contended with the forces of the whole world, and in Judaea the brothers Hyrcanus and Aristobulus struggled fiercely for the principality, Antipater, powerful and, as already said, possessed of great wealth, supported Hyrcanus in Judaea—more just indeed, but more sluggish—and in the Roman commonwealth purchased the favour of Caesar, now victorious and pursuing the defeated Pompey even into Egypt, by many services and still more expenditures. Thus he gained great authority for himself in Judaea and opened for his son Herod, through great services rendered to the victorious Roman faction, a path to obtaining the kingdom.

It should also be known that through that discord of Hyrcanus and Aristobulus, the Temple at Jerusalem was violated once and again with great calamity. First, Pompey, having defeated Aristobulus, attacked the city against Aristobulus’s allies; being admitted into the city through sedition, he broke into the Temple when a great tower was shaken and fell, opening a part of the Temple through which the enemies rushed in; and all was filled with the slaughter of Jews. Some were killed by the Romans, while others killed themselves; and thus twenty-two thousand Jews fell, while very few Romans died.

Nor were small offenses committed in the Temple, when Pompey entered those places which in an earlier time were invisible or inaccessible, and he with no few others saw what only priests were permitted to behold. Then, as already said, when Herod gained the kingdom [Col. 1448D] and Antigonus, Aristobulus’s son, held the city, the city suffered the same fate, and many were slain in the Temple while the Romans strove on Herod’s behalf.

This suffering befell the city of Jerusalem, Josephus says, when Marcus Agrippa and Callidius were consuls, in the one hundred and eighty-fifth Olympiad, in the third month during the observance of fasts—as though the calamity inflicted upon the Jews under Pompey had returned. For it is known that the captivity occurred twenty-seven years later on the same day. While the city was still being besieged by Herod and the legate Sosius, the aforementioned Sameas persuaded the people to accept Herod, saying that, because of their sins, he could not be avoided.

## CHAPTER X. Neither sceptre nor ruler was to be taken from Judah until Christ came.

Therefore, when the foreigner Herod had obtained the kingdom through so many and such bloody discords as I have chosen to recount, it was time for the truthful God to fulfill the word of His promise. For it had been foretold: “The sceptre shall not be taken away from Judah, nor a ruler from his loins, until He comes who is to be sent” (Gen. xlix).

He who was to be sent is the same Christ who came: He “in” whose “seed,” God said to Abraham, “all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. xxvi), as Jacob added in the same place: “And He shall be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. xlix).

But behold: the sceptre had truly been taken away from Judah and [Col. 1449B] from his loins when Herod, a foreigner, was thrust into the kingdom. He killed all who seemed to be of royal lineage, including Hyrcanus himself, by whose gentleness and mildness he had been advanced. Therefore, that God might be justified in His words, the seed promised to Abraham and promised again with an oath—likewise sworn to David—had now to come and could not be deferred any longer. For the sceptre had been so taken from Judah and the ruler had so failed from his loins that, contrary to Jewish law, a king—or rather, a tyrant—sat upon the throne: an alien man, a plunderer, a newcomer, an outsider, a murderer.

## CHAPTER XI. Besides Zacharias, Elizabeth, Simeon, and Anna the prophetess, there were many who awaited Christ’s coming.

What, do you suppose, was then the disposition of righteous souls? And whom should I call righteous persons of that time except those who had faith and hope, or expectation, in the promise to Abraham, the promise to David, the oath to Abraham, and the oath to David? David himself, faithful and strongly holding fast to God, said: “Have mercy on me, that Thou mayest be justified in Thy words and prevail when Thou art judged” (Ps. l).
