One of such persons, or the best known to us from that time, was Simeon. While proclaiming in this faith and seeking God’s truth—the truth of the promise, in which God, greater than man, freely swore to human beings—he deserved to receive the answer that he should not see death until he had first seen the Christ of the Lord (Luke ii).

Was Simeon alone at that time an expectant of this same promise? Certainly there were Zacharias and Elizabeth, both righteous; there was Anna the prophetess; there were Joseph and Mary (ibid.). I ask further: because the Gospel has made only these persons known to us, was there no one else who awaited God’s faithfulness and victory, that He might be justified in His words and prevail when judged?

Certainly, although the dreadful cloud of Herodian wickedness darkened the sky, there were not a few stars in the sky, shining with the brightness of the same light, resplendent with the beauty of the same faith, and longing for the fulfillment of the promise. Many souls cried out that the truthful and faithful God might appear in His words. I think that the woman with child in her womb, as has often been said, never cried out more intensely in labour, and was never more grievously afflicted that she might give birth (Rev. xii).

Do not suppose, however, that the body of this woman whom we say was with child consists only of the faithful people of that time who were alive in the body. Rather, it is the Church of all days or ages: when the whole multitude of faithful souls, from the beginning of the world—both those living in the flesh and those, having laid aside the burden of flesh, awaiting blessed hope in the underworld—uttered cries of such longing. This whole company, because of one and the same expectation, was one woman with child in her womb.

## CHAPTER XII. Christ cannot be set forth worthily either by demonstration or by narration.

What now remains to be said, except that the woman bore a male child? In saying this, how the mind wishes to linger and dwell in contemplation of a great—indeed, truly great—festival and triumphant joy, because God, who promised this seed of blessing, has proved true! Yet to what shall it give itself? In what direction will our discourse turn: demonstration or narration?

If it turns to demonstration, if it wishes to point out that birth, that son, that male child, it would be like someone, today at midday, under a clear sky, when the sun shines most brilliantly at the height of its ascent, pointing a finger to one who has eyes and sees, and saying: “Look: behold the sun.” For it is written: “He has set His tabernacle in the sun” (Ps. xviii).

But if it turns to narration, we fear that we shall be superfluous, because we shall say nothing new. We do not deposit or write these things among strangers, nor do we set them forth to the ignorant or in company with the ignorant. Let, therefore, the whole intention of this discourse turn toward delight, and strive to possess some dignity together with delight, so that the discourse itself may be founded in full faith and uttered with a full voice, with the grace of necessary humility; so that whoever deigns to read it may delight and rejoice because of the praise of such a Son, the honour of so great a male child, the glory of God the Father, and the honour of the Holy Spirit, by whom that blessed woman conceived and bore Him.

This delight of discourse has in it that laughter which Isaac, the son of blessed old age and of faith that had earned its reward, signified by his own name. He was a type of this Son or male child, of whom the aged mother—the ancient Church—giving birth through the womb of the Virgin Mary, may truly say, and always says and will say: “God has made laughter for me” (Gen. xxi), because such a Son is truly eternal laughter to His mother.

We shall borrow dignity from the prophetic faculty of the Holy Spirit; we shall take it from the fullness of prophetic grace, where the eminent prophet Isaiah speaks against the pride of Assyria.

## CHAPTER XIII. How the saying through Isaiah, “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse,” is to be understood.

“And those lofty in stature shall be cut down, and the high shall be humbled; [Col. 1451A] and the thick places of the forest shall be overthrown with iron, and Lebanon shall fall with its lofty ones” (Isa. x).—“And a rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root; and the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon Him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and godliness; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill Him” (Isa. xi).

See what an opposition this is. Look here at the thick places of the forest and Lebanon with its lofty trees; there, at the rod with its flower. What is a single flowering rod compared with the dense forests and Mount Lebanon with its lofty things, strong or tall—as, for example, the wood of cedars? Yet what do the thick forests and Lebanon with its lofty trees amount to compared with this rod and the flower rising from it? The thick places of the forest shall indeed be overthrown with iron, and Lebanon shall fall with its lofty trees; but this rod and its flower has received, bears, the whole weight of the heavenly Majesty, and does not fall or suffer overthrow.

Let us speak more plainly, although the whole world does not fail to know what realities are conveyed under this metaphor, nor does the chorus of the Church throughout the world remain silent. Consider, on this side, the tyrants and leaders, emperors and consuls of the nations, whom we understand through the thick places of the forest; on that side, the kings, tetrarchs, and high priests of the Jewish nation, understood through Lebanon; and among these heights and magnitudes, the humble Virgin Mary, sprung from the house of David and giving birth to Christ—God and man. You perceive the great wonder of the victory of God’s Word: entering this world, He did not seek to have any parent of high or exalted station, knowing that He alone sufficed for Himself, without human agency, against the pride of that Assyrian—that is, the devil—in order to obtain for Himself a kingdom and possess the throne of David His father, indeed the eternal dominion of God His Father.

## CHAPTER XIV. The heights of Lebanon fell when the foreigner Herod reigned and rebuilt the demolished Temple anew.

To say nothing of the forest of the nations, whose thick places were then everywhere being overthrown and had been overthrown by the iron of the Roman Empire, so that the whole world already lay silent under that empire when this flower rose from the rod [Col. 1451D] or root of Jesse: how did the heights of Lebanon, or Lebanon itself, fall around the rising of this flower?

Understand the very summit of Lebanon as the Temple itself, because it is written in the prophet Zechariah: “Open your gates, O Lebanon, that fire may consume your cedars” (Zech. xi). Understand the cedars, or the lofty things of Lebanon, as the leaders of the nation, whose glory had the Temple itself as its head—the most august place in the world.

How, then, did this Lebanon fall, or begin to fall, with its lofty things? I would not hesitate to say that the beginning of its great and irreparable fall was when Herod reigned. For in his reign a great height of royal dignity had fallen: the sceptre had been removed from Judah and the ruler from his loins.

Herod, I say—manifoldly a murderer, indeed a parricide, a tyrant rather than a king—after six hundred years removed the old Temple which the children of the Exile had built upon returning from Babylon and which the victorious Maccabees had purified, [Col. 1452A] and constructed another. Whence came this man’s presumption to undertake such a work? Was that work destined to stand, or could it please God?

If faithful David, king of the tribe of Judah, found and chosen after God’s own heart, was not permitted to build a house for the Lord, the Lord saying to him: “You shall not build a house for My name, because you are a man of war and have shed much blood” (1 Chron. xxviii), how ought this man—no mere shedder of blood, but also murderer of his sons and wives, and the furious killer of household members and friends—to have built a house for the Lord?

It is not surprising, therefore, that what was made by an impious man from the plundering and despoiling of regions came to so miserable and horrible a destruction, being, as is known, irrecoverably devastated by the Romans after Christ’s Passion. Let this suffice for the present: Lebanon began to fall when Herod removed the old Temple and built another, indeed larger, twice as large as that made by the children of the Exile; but he did this seeking his own glory, not God’s.

## CHAPTER XV. Herod, in rebuilding the Temple, wished shamelessly to compare himself with David and Solomon.

Well, he says, you know that our fathers built this temple for the most great God when they returned from Babylon, and that it lacks sixty cubits in height [Col. 1452C] to equal the size of that which Solomon constructed. No one charges our fathers with negligence in piety. The temple was made shorter through no fault of theirs; Cyrus and Darius ordered that a building of such dimensions should be made. He said “our fathers” and “the fathers of our fathers” because, although he was not of Jewish stock, he wished to be considered one of them. Continuing, he said this as well: Now, since by God’s will abundant peace has been granted to my rule, together with possession of riches, an abundance of revenues, and—what is greatest—the friendship and favour of the Romans, who are held to be masters of all things, why do we not strive to repair the work left incomplete in the time of slavery and necessity, and render it whole to God in return for the benefits bestowed upon [Col. 1452D] my kingdom?

Having said this, he hastened on, and the temple was completed in one year and five months. Did not that man—or rather, that beast—by thus speaking and acting so hastily, endeavour to compare himself, or even to prefer himself, to faithful David and peaceable Solomon, legitimate kings of the tribe of Judah? Yet faithful David, plainly, robbed no one, nor did he set about building a house to the Lord’s name from plunder. Rather: “Behold,” he says, “in my poverty I have prepared the expenses for the house of the Lord: one hundred thousand talents of gold, and a thousand thousand of silver; but there is no weight for bronze and iron, for their quantity is surpassed by their magnitude; I have prepared wood and stones for all the costs” (1 Chron. 22). Saying this, he also gave to Solomon his son the plan of the temple and of every work: [Col. 1453A] “And all these things,” he says, “came to me written by the hand of the Lord, so that I might understand all the works of the pattern” (1 Chron. 28). When we read or hear him saying this, should we not suppose that he too, being a prophet, saw a revelation of this kind, so that it might be said to him as it was said also to Moses concerning the making of the tabernacle: “See, and make according to the pattern which I showed you on the mountain” (Exod. 25)? Solomon likewise possessed gold and silver not from plunder, but as God’s gift. 624 Was Herod the rascal to compare himself with such men and such greatness?

## CHAPTER XVI. That the people ought by no means to have rejoiced over that man’s work, nor flattered so great a sinner.

[Col. 1453B] The whole people ought not to have been carried away with joy over that man’s work, nor should they have flattered so great a sinner. Yet they were filled with foolish joy: first they gave thanks to God for its speed of completion; then they exalted in praise the king’s eagerness displayed at the dedication. Their laughter therefore deserved to be turned into weeping, and their joy into mourning.

Nevertheless, it must be understood that, although Herod changed the walls and amassed huge stones to be admired for his own glory—stones which even Christ’s disciples could admire, saying, “Master, see what stones and what buildings!” (Mark 13)—the altar had not, however, been removed or altered. Had that occurred, you might wonder much more that so much was permitted to a murderer—or rather, a parricide—that he himself should set up the head of religion, that is, the altar, [Col. 1453C] upon which Christ—or in which the Son of God, having become man—was immediately to be presented to God the Father together with the animals prescribed by the Law.

Let these brief remarks on the temple suffice, so that the prudent admirer of God’s judgments may now see that, besides the other reasons for which that temple ought not to have remained, this reason too may have contributed to its falling—not in any ordinary way, but exceedingly badly, indeed with a crash heard by the whole world: the work constructed by that enemy of humankind, the enemy of God. Now let the discourse return to the chapter of prophetic truth which it undertook.

## CHAPTER XVII. Why God permitted Herod to rage so fiercely against the royal and priestly line that he did not spare even his sons.

[Col. 1453D] “And Lebanon,” he says, “shall fall with its lofty ones” (Isa. 10). We have already said that the great height of that Lebanon had fallen, namely because the sceptre had departed from Judah and from his loins. Ill-fated Herod was extirpating the royal line by the sword and did not cease to extirpate it. Wherever he had detected any royal element—whatever household, even his own household, indeed especially his own household, or royal descent, had suggested to him someone of consequence; whenever, among many other wives, he had married Mariamne, daughter of Hyrcanus the high priest, herself of royal stock, and had begotten by her Alexander and Aristobulus—wherever, in short, whether from without or within, he foresaw that something royal might be hoped for, that monstrous beast raged. At the same time he slaughtered high priests and his own royal sons, plainly [Col. 1454A] so that no person might disturb his excessively eager reign by any such suspicion.

For the royal family had indeed become intermingled with the priestly family; consequently his murderous savagery was directed alike against both, sparing no sex, withholding the sword neither from his own wives nor, when occasion arose, from his sons, since his sons touched the royal line through their mother’s blood. From what source, then, would you prevail, O faithful God who makes promises? From what source would you be justified in fulfilling what you promised and swore to David, whose spirit did not cease to cry in your ears: “Have mercy on me, that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged” (Ps. 50)?

Certainly you knew and ordained that you should be justified and prevail from a lowly place—from which impure Herod, or rather the devil whom [Col. 1454B] Herod served, could suspect nothing that might rise to the height of the throne. This is what you immediately added through the prophet: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root; and the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom” (Isa. 11), and the rest.

## CHAPTER XVIII. That the rod is the Virgin Mary, Christ the flower; and why it is said “from the root of Jesse,” not “from the root of David.”

Wherever Christian or Catholic faith itself has heard with its ears and sees with its inward eyes, it recognizes that this rod—a slender and beautiful rod, humble indeed but straight—is the blessed Virgin Mary. And the flower rising from this rod, the fruit of her womb, [Col. 1454C] is Christ, the Son of God and son of the Virgin. In him God, who promised, has been found faithful and true; God, who swore, has been proved just and holy.

But we must ask here why the Holy Spirit chose to say, “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse,” rather than “from the root of David” or Abraham, to whom God promised and swore. To this I say: had it said “from the root of David,” it would indeed declare the triumphant truth of the promise, but the expression itself would contain less mystery. Now it has more mystery, because, while proclaiming the truth extending to the seed of David, it also sends us back into the hidden setting of his father’s house, to the occasion or day on which the prophet Samuel was sent to anoint the king whom the Lord, having rejected Saul, had provided for himself among the sons of Jesse, who is also called Isai.

For how was it said, and how was it done? “The Lord says: ‘You shall take a calf from the herd in your hand and say, “I have come to sacrifice to God.”’ For Samuel was afraid: ‘Saul,’ he says, ‘will hear and kill me.’ And he filled a horn with oil according to the Lord’s command and went. ‘I have come,’ he says, ‘to sacrifice to the Lord; sanctify yourselves and come with me, that I may sacrifice.’ Therefore he sanctified Jesse and his sons and called them to the sacrifice. When they had entered, he saw Eliab and said: ‘Is his anointed one before the Lord?’ And the Lord said to Samuel: ‘Do not look upon his countenance or the height of his stature, because I have rejected him; nor do I judge according to human sight: for man sees the things that appear, but the Lord [Col. 1455A] looks upon the heart.’ Jesse called Aminadab and brought forward Sammah, and likewise his other sons, seven in number; but the Lord chose none of them. Samuel said to Jesse: ‘Is the number of your sons complete?’ Jesse said: ‘There remains still the little one, and he is tending the sheep.’ Therefore, at Samuel’s command, he sent and brought him. When he came, ruddy and fair to look upon, and of handsome face, the Lord said: ‘Rise and anoint him, for this is he’” (1 Sam. 16).

## CHAPTER XIX. What mystery lay in the events concerning Jesse’s root—that is, David—and how they pertained to Christ.

What mystery is hidden in those events, unless it is what we have heard and understood in these prophetic words: “Those lofty in stature shall be cut down, and the high shall be humbled; the dense forest [Col. 1455B] shall be overthrown by iron, and Lebanon shall fall with its lofty ones” (Isa. 10)—“And a rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root, and the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him” (Isa. 11)?

For, since this is the meaning—namely, that the proud and the rich 625 shall be left behind, and the promise of truth shall be fulfilled from a humble or poor young woman—the phrase “from the root of Jesse” at the same time recalls to our minds the ancient precedent: what happened to Jesse when his elder sons were rejected and humble or little David, the least, was chosen. It is therefore as if he said: Why are you astonished that I said, “Those lofty in stature shall be cut down, and the high shall be humbled,” and that humility shall be exalted? The same happened in Jesse’s days. Eliab was imposing in appearance and tall in stature, but “I have rejected him,” says the Lord (1 Sam. 16).

Likewise, when this prophecy is fulfilled, there will be many corresponding to his other great sons: “lofty in stature and exalted in glory,” both of royal and priestly descent, powerful in strength and able to field armed armies. But the Lord chose none of them, nor did he need human exaltation to fulfil the word of his promise: not the height of courtiers exulting in chariots and horses, who trust in manifold human favour and the fickle applause of the populace rather than in the Lord. Then the least of Jesse’s sons, little David, pleased him; and afterwards the humble handmaid of the Lord, sent forth before all human beings in the spirit [Col. 1455D] of humility, will please the Most High, so that the promise may be fulfilled from her at Christ’s birth, as though a splendid flower rose from a slender rod.

Further, just as there, the pretext of a sacrificial festival and the calf brought from the herd—when the elders of the city met Samuel and wondered at his arrival—provided a reason so that Saul might not hear, so here the Virgin’s betrothal, or the customary solemnity of marriage, and Joseph’s being named the girl’s husband deceived the devil and all his followers, such as Herod and his accomplices, so that they should not know the mystery before its time for being known.

## CHAPTER XX. [Col. 1456A] That God’s plan was praiseworthy in deceiving the devil and Herod through humility, and in having art outwit art.

In Maro [Virgil], some vaunting person speaks in jest and says:

> It makes no difference whether victory is gained by arms or by stratagem.

[Note: [Col. 1455] Perhaps the author alludes to *Aeneid* II, verse 390: “… who would ask, in dealing with an enemy, whether it is stratagem or courage?”]

Certainly this maxim does not hold for the manner of this victory or triumph. It matters greatly: it was much better and highly beneficial that God, or God’s Word, should conquer in this way, or advance in order to proceed, so that throughout the whole encounter of battle art deceived art, rather than that, having assumed flesh from noble and powerful persons, he should fight impious people with their material weapons—as the invisible one, not yet made man, fought through the [Col. 1456B] Maccabees and other strong and faithful men, and often slew many thousands with the weapons of a few.

He could likewise have done this: incarnate from the daughter either of Hyrcanus, high priest at that time, or of one of the others, he could have employed martial instruments in defence of truth, with better success than either the Maccabee or David himself had ever fought; so that, for example, one might pursue a thousand and two put ten thousand to flight (Deut. 32). It was much better, I say, that art deceived art than that the matter should have been accomplished by such weapons: “Not by an army nor by strength, but by my Spirit, says the Lord of hosts” (Zech. 4).

This was the word of the Lord to Zerubbabel in the prophet Zechariah, where he saw seven eyes upon one stone and seven lamps [Col. 1456C] upon one lampstand. These were nothing other than the seven spirits of the Lord resting upon this one flower.

## CHAPTER XXI. How beneficial it was for us that Christ was born of a poor Virgin mother.

No tongue can attain by words, indeed no human mind can comprehend even in thought, how great are the benefits that have come to us because the humility of the Godhead, the humility of the Word of God, chose for himself not a rich but a poor Virgin as mother; because he looked upon his handmaid, so humble before him in comparison with the rich or proud, as any rod issuing from an ancient root is known to be smaller than the lofty cedars of Lebanon [Col. 1456D].

For if Christ had chosen wealthy parents, what place would there be today for the poor in Christ’s Church? But now both “God does not reject the mighty, since he himself is mighty” (Job 36), and he has more often chosen the poor in this world, acknowledging them in his blessings—that is, bestowing upon them the eminent gifts of his Spirit, such as he grants more rarely, doubtless, to the rich who have their consolation. “See,” says the Apostle, “your calling, brothers: not many wise according to the flesh, not many powerful, not many noble. But God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; [Col. 1457A] and God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong; and God chose the ignoble and despised things of the world, and things that are not, in order to destroy the things that are, so that no flesh may glory in his presence” (1 Cor. 1).

Therefore God more abundantly and more often bestows upon the poor and weak the heavenly gifts of his calling. This consideration has also given us a most beautiful reflection from an excellent father, who bears the known and true testimony that he was filled with the spirit of all the righteous: “Let him who needs less give thanks to God and not complain. But let more be given to him who needs more, and let him humble himself because of weakness, not exalt himself because of mercy.” Certainly, when he says this, we recognize an imitation of God, who is accustomed to give his spiritual gifts more abundantly to those who need more—namely, to the poor, weak, and low-born—so that, according to the multitude of their sorrows in their hearts, their souls may be gladdened by consolations of this kind (Ps. 93 [94]).

[Col. 1457B]

## CHAPTER XXII. He praises the incarnation of the Word from David’s psalm: “My heart has uttered a good word.”

With what voice, with what or how great praises, shall we proclaim the beauty of this flower rising from such a rod? From where shall we take words? We are almost mute, almost infants, in relation to the dignity of so great a thing, where beauty flourishes and thrives with strength, strength with beauty; the Holy Spirit himself is its praiser. What shall we say such that he may delight to hear it in accordance with the intention of our mind?

Let us take something not from our own store, which is nowhere to be found, but from the fullness of him who fills all the saints: from the treasure of the good heart, the treasure of delight and exultation, which he stored up in his prophet of this Word—prophet, patriarch, and king—who speaks in the person of God the Father: “My heart has uttered a good word; I speak my works to the King. My tongue is the pen of a swift-writing scribe.” Immediately the Prophet himself responds in his own person: “You are fair in form above the children of men; grace has been poured out upon your lips; therefore God has blessed you for ever. Gird your sword [Col. 1457C] upon your thigh, O most mighty one. In your splendour and your beauty, press on, proceed prosperously, and reign,” and so forth (Ps. 44 [45]).

[Col. 1457D] Let the poor little soul now think itself come to a fountain of discourse, from which it may draw what to say, for the grace of this fair and beautiful flower, with the good intention of delighting rather than teaching. O whoever you are who read or hear these things, think that I linger here, because it is sweet, beautiful, and devout to repeat and dwell frequently even upon familiar things: upon the form of the fair one; the splendour and beauty of the beautiful one; the one most mighty, girded with his sword upon his thigh; the one who proceeds prosperously and reigns; whom his right hand leads wonderfully in truth, meekness, and justice. Peoples fall beneath him in their heart, because they have been pierced with his sharp arrows—the saving arrows of his sayings—so that they may grieve that they were once [Col. 1458A] enemies of the King, and may fall down to adore him, falling on their faces in worship of him.

## CHAPTER XXIII. How David’s words, “My tongue is the pen of a scribe,” are to be understood.

Taking together the two testimonies, Isaiah’s and David’s, we first wish to contemplate this saying of God the Father: “My tongue is the pen of a swift-writing scribe” (Ps. 44 [45]). It is natural to understand the Holy Spirit as the tongue of God the Father, because, just as the tongue of flesh administers words to a human being, so the Holy Spirit suggests God’s words to the believing soul.

Thus also, when he descended upon Christ’s apostles—men whom he came to make, until then unlettered and unlearned, henceforth learned and eloquent—he appeared in fiery tongues (Acts 2:3–4). The subsequent result immediately showed why he wished to appear thus. For they became strong servants of God through charity and holy zeal, which the fire signified. They became eloquent in diverse languages and skilled in the Scriptures, which the division of tongues foreshadowed.

Therefore, when in the one passage he says, “My tongue is the pen of a swift-writing scribe,” and through the other, “And the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. 11), it is clear concerning Christ both that he is truly God and that the fullness of divinity truly dwells bodily in him (Col. 2). Although Christian faith is firm in this age and does not need this [Col. 1458C] assertion, along with necessary faith it is pleasant and useful to possess fitting knowledge as well.

Human nature, from the substance of virginal flesh, was assumed like a clean and carefully prepared little parchment, suitable for the work of writing; and the tongue of the Father itself, that is, the Holy Spirit, swiftly ran across it, swiftly inscribed the whole of it like a scribe’s pen, filled it with the entire substance of the Word. Nothing remained over; rather, everything that was in the Father’s heart he inscribed upon that soul: all wisdom, all understanding, all counsel, all God’s strength, all knowledge, all God’s piety, and all fear of the Lord—so that there might be nothing he did not know, nothing he could not do; nothing in God the Father [Col. 1458D] which the human nature of this child did not possess. Hence he is God.

## CHAPTER XXIV. How “My heart has uttered a good word; I speak my works to the King” is to be understood.

This is what we understand to be said by the person of the Father himself: “My heart has uttered a good word; I speak my works to the King” (Ps. 44 [45]). The thing is great, but the expression is not very great in comparison with the thing. For what is this word, “uttered”? What is magnificent about it? Among us, I say, each of us belches when he is full; but a hungry person is not filled by another’s belch. Someone speaks of his work; but the hearer does not immediately attain the result of the work heard, so as to do likewise whatever that person has done.

But he who [Col. 1459A] speaks these words, “My heart has uttered a good word,” who says, “I speak my works to the King,” brought forth into the Virgin’s womb, in complete fullness, that good Word—the very substance of the good Word—and imparted his works to the King, that is, to the man whom he was forming from the womb of that same Virgin, in such a way that he too might be a maker or craftsman not unlike him. Great and wondrous things are proclaimed through these two small words: “My heart has uttered a good word; I speak,” and so forth.

Grammarians commonly call *tapeinosis* the trope that is an expression of humility for a great thing—for example, if, intending the sea, one calls it a “whirlpool,” or, intending a vast mountain, calls it a “mound” or “hill.” I would not dare to declaim these trifles in the majesty of so great a matter; nevertheless, I think that nowhere is there an expression in which the words [Col. 1459B] are so unequal to the things they signify as in the present phrase.

Why then was it said in this way? Or rather, how could it have been said otherwise than it was said, when words sufficient for the thing understood could nowhere be found? Let there indeed be a deficiency in the words; but, if you weigh it rightly, the very smallness of the terms instructs the attentive mind through that deficiency. In what? Namely, in making it observe that the work is great, but not difficult for God. For what human being, full of food, is wearied by belching? Thus God the Father, full of the good Word, did not labour in implanting it in human nature.

## CHAPTER XXV. Why God chose to become incarnate, rather than save the human race through an angel.

This good work was done by God, supremely powerful and supremely [Col. 1459C] good: this is what he promised, what he swore to Abraham, what he swore to David. As supremely good, he promised freely and swore freely; as supremely powerful, he fulfilled it. For just as it belongs to supreme goodness that he wished to do this, so it belongs to supreme power that he was able to do it.

This must be carefully observed. Some are accustomed to say: Why did God, the Word of God, come in person and become man to save the human race, when this same thing might have been done through another? Why did he not instead send some envoy? Why did he not send an angel or archangel? To this I say: because it was ever possible for no other—not for any except the divine nature alone—to assume what it was not and remain what it was.

And why was this possible for it? Because the nature or [Col. 1459D] substance of divinity is so much subtler than the rational soul that it can penetrate it. Among other arguments for the truth against heretics, the Catholic Fathers faithfully adopted and wrote that the Holy Spirit is God equally with the Father and the Son, because he too is capable of the human soul and able to contain that same rational soul. For unless he were God, he could not be capable either of a human or of an angelic spirit.

Accordingly, it should be noted that, although a person is said to be full of a demon, that spirit does not fill the human being so as to penetrate the soul. It can enter into the cavities of the body, where drunkenness or fever may enter, and agitate and afflict the soul caught within its own dwelling-place. [Col. 1460A] God alone—the one God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—when he wills and as he wills, pours himself into the rational soul or spirit and makes his dwelling in it. Therefore one speaks or asks in vain why God, the Word of God, did not send an envoy or angel, but came in person to save the human race: plainly, because no nature except the nature of God alone could put on human nature. Therefore, just as we proclaim him good because he willed it, so we proclaim him omnipotent because he was able to do it.

## CHAPTER XXVI. That Christ was born while his Mother’s virginity remained intact.

What shall we say, to his praise, concerning his Mother’s preserved virginity? “Contrary to nature,” says the Jew, “a virgin could not give birth.” But we believe—and therefore speak—that above nature a virgin could give birth to such a son [Col. 1460B]. We do not say “contrary to nature,” because there is no injury to nature; rather, we say “above nature,” because it is nature’s glory.

What sense is there in saying that he who made nature could not do something above nature? All things were made through the Word; and if all things, certainly female nature as well. Would nature, then, be stronger than he through whom nature was made? A rational person rightly judges in saying that he who made all things, including nature itself, consequently overcomes all things, including nature itself.

But if the greatness of the miracle leads a Jew or a Manichaean to unbelief, I ask: which is more wonderful—that a human being was assumed or formed from living and sentient earth, or that a human being was fashioned from lifeless and insentient earth? Indeed, I would call Mary [Col. 1460C] living and sentient earth, since both she and we were made from earth. But the earth from which the first human was fashioned was undoubtedly lifeless and insentient. Was not, then, the formation of the first Adam more wonderful than the formation of the second? For living and sentient material—that is, woman—although virgin, is closer to this work than that material which was neither living nor sentient. Therefore the former formation was more wonderful, but this latter more venerable.

## CHAPTER XXVII. What it means that he is “fair in form above the children of men,” and girded with a sword upon his thigh.

Behold, fair in form; behold, most mighty, girded with his sword upon his thigh (Ps. 44 [45]). We must recognize [Col. 1460D] him whose victory we proclaim and whose triumphal chariot we desire to follow with praise: once the Word, now also flesh; once God, now also man. “Fair,” he says, “in form.” What is “form”? Divinity.

For divinity is form: form which gives form, form lacking matter. The divine substance, as has been said before us, is form without matter; and therefore it alone is what it is, while other things are not what they are. For each thing has its being from the things of which it consists. Thus, since the earthly human being consists of soul and body, he is body and soul, not body alone or soul alone in part; therefore he is not simply what he is. But that which is not from this and that, but is only this, truly is what it is; and [Col. 1461A] it is most beautiful and most strong, because it depends on nothing. Therefore he is “fair in form,” that is, fair according to divinity.

Only his lovers see this beauty by which he is “fair above the children of men,” who certainly are not gods by nature; only they will see the King in his beauty, the eyes of those who love him will see him. “And I,” he says, “will manifest myself to him” (John 14). But what is the sword with which this fair one, this most mighty one, is girded? Certainly it is the one and same Word of God: the Word which is God is the form of the fair one and the sword of the most mighty one. For the word of God is one, effective and sharper than every two-edged sword (Heb. 4).

Thus, as has now been said, behold the fair one; behold the most mighty one: fair as a flower, most mighty as a giant, whose “going forth is from the highest heaven, and his course [Col. 1461B] unto its height” (Ps. 18 [19]). He enters this world having become visible, to fight visibly—the one who previously, invisible, fought invisibly—fighting with a new mode of war: namely, not by army or strength, but by his Spirit (Zech. 4), able to cast out demons.

Elsewhere Holy Scripture proclaims this fair flower and this most mighty King: “A Lamb,” it says, “having seven horns and seven eyes” (Rev. 5), namely the seven spirits resting upon the flower. But concerning the Lamb, who is also the conquering Lion, something must later be said in its proper place.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. As the sevenfold Spirit rested upon the flower, so this psalm sings of Christ the King [Col. 1461C] in sevenfold praise.

Now it is pleasant briefly to consider whether, just as all these spirits rest upon the flower, so something proper to each of them is said in the psalm or hymn previously cited concerning the fair King, the most mighty King.

“I speak my works to the King. My tongue is the pen of a swift-writing scribe” (Ps. 44 [45]). That these words are said according to the spirit of wisdom and understanding needs no proof from us; for plainly, where God the Father speaks his works to the Son the King, there wisdom and his tongue act as a scribe’s pen, and there is understanding.

“Grace has been poured forth upon your lips; therefore God has blessed you for ever. Gird your sword upon [Col. 1461D] your thigh, O most mighty one,” and so forth; “and your right hand shall lead you wonderfully” (ibid.): we understand these to be sung according to the spirit of counsel and strength. For it belonged to counsel that, seeing we could not be justified by our own works and that all were shut up under sin, God poured out grace—that is, free remission of sins—upon the lips of this fair one. Therefore he blessed him for ever and caused him to be born holy and free from every sin, so that this grace might be effectively poured out from his lips and he might say to the sinful woman, who was the one universal Church: “Her many sins are forgiven,” not because she did much, but “because she loved much” (Luke 7).

To be girded with a sword upon the thigh, to proceed prosperously and reign, and to be led wonderfully by his right hand, is without doubt a work or effect of strength. “Your arrows are sharp” (Ps. 44 [45]): what is this except, “In teaching or preaching you always have ready the sayings of the Scriptures, by which the hearts of those who were enemies are pierced; they believe, yield to truth, and fall in worship before you, having become friends”? Therefore that these words belong to the spirit of knowledge is beyond doubt.

“God, your God, has anointed you [Col. 1462A] with the oil of gladness above your companions” (ibid.). This oil is surely the spirit of piety. *Eleos* in Greek is “mercy” in Latin. Likewise, “and the King desires your beauty” (ibid.) pertains to the same spirit of piety. For the desire of this King is nothing other than piety. This is the oil with which this fair King is anointed, so that he might come [Col. 1462B] blessed in the multitude of mercy, desiring the souls of the lost and summoning them by the allurements of mercy to his banquet of eternal salvation.

The spirit of the fear of the Lord is not in him so that he may fear, but so that he may be feared, and that religious holiness and holy, reverent worship may surround him. To this belongs: “All the rich of the people shall entreat your face. Virgins shall be brought to the King; they shall be brought in gladness and exultation; they shall be brought into the temple of the King; and peoples shall confess you for ever and unto ages of ages” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER XXIX. Why it is not said “shall remain,” but “the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him.”

There remains one word of the same chapter in which [Col. 1462C] we are engaged, lest we proceed already to follow the progress of the King, lest we now recount how that dragon wished to devour the birth of the blessed woman. What is that word? “And,” he says, “the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him” (Isa. 11). He did not say “shall remain,” but preferred to say “shall rest”; and there is no doubt that this signifies something more than if he had said “shall remain.”

Let us observe that this is prophetic speech. “You do well,” says the apostle Peter, “to attend to it as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts” (2 Pet. 1:19). Behold, we encounter a certain place that is dark indeed; yet the little flame of this lamp, that is, of prophetic speech, makes it bright for us and, like the morning star, brings the day of understanding.

When the Lord [Col. 1462D] spoke to Moses in the wilderness and Aaron exercised the priesthood, Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, with other leaders of the Synagogue, stood against Moses and Aaron; their whole company stood against the Lord. Therefore, because of the evil of their detestable pride, they did not die the ordinary death of human beings. Rather, the Lord did a new thing: opening its mouth, the earth swallowed them, and they went down alive into hell because they blasphemed the Lord. Moreover, fire went out from the Lord and killed two hundred and fifty living men who offered incense (Num. 16).

Then: “The Lord says, ‘Speak to the children of Israel, and take from them one rod for each of their families: twelve rods from all the leaders of the tribes; and you shall write each man’s [Col. 1463A] name upon his rod. But Aaron’s name shall be on the rod of Levi. The rod of him whom I choose shall sprout, and I shall stop the complaints of the children of Israel against me,’” and so forth (Num. 17).

That event in the Law, in which Aaron’s rod sprouted, the swelling buds burst into flowers and then fruit with leaves, and thus the pride of those contending over the priesthood ceased—that event, I say, is compared with this utterance of the prophet. For while the prophet inveighs against Assyria’s pride—“Those lofty in stature,” he says, “shall be cut down, and the high shall be humbled; the dense forest shall be overthrown by iron, and Lebanon shall fall with its lofty ones” (Isa. 10)—one may understand: just as Korah, Dathan, Abiram, and their accomplices were cut down or humbled, overthrown and fell, [Col. 1463B] he immediately adds: “And a rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root; and the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him” (Isa. 11).

Certainly here too it is fitting to understand: just as the flower rose from Aaron’s rod, and just as the Spirit of the Lord rested—that is, ceased from his wrath and was appeased—whom the murmurers and the proud had provoked.

## CHAPTER XXX. That apart from Christ there was no one of whom it could be said that the Spirit of the Lord rested upon him.

Accordingly, what he says must be understood according to that likeness: “And the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him” (Isa. 11). There was indeed some likeness there; but here the reality is far more extensive. [Col. 1463C] There an insensible rod, producing blossoms and leaves beyond the ordinary course of nature, and also nuts, put an end to the complaints of a few rebels. Here a sentient rod—the rod, that is, the Virgin or the virginal womb—bearing the beautiful King already mentioned as its flower, struck down the pride of the devil, corrected the fault of pride throughout the whole human race, turned away the wrath of God which had consequently come upon it, and rendered God favourable toward us.

Therefore, he says, the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon this flower; that is: “For Christ’s sake, O Lord, thou wilt temper all thy wrath and turn away from the anger of thy indignation” (Ps. 84). For this flower will never disturb thee: indeed, he is meek and humble of heart. Moses, certainly, was meek above all men [Col. 1464A] who dwelt upon the earth (Num. 12), but not as this one was—not so always, not so impassibly. For, troubled and provoked, “he made a distinction with his lips” (Ps. 55); he made a distinction, and did not glorify the Lord. Speaking amid those contradictions, he did not speak as a meek man, nor in the manner in which the Spirit of the Lord would have wished to hear him, because he spoke words of unbelief. Therefore the Lord said to Moses and Aaron: “You shall not bring this people into the land for which I swore to their fathers” (Num. 20). This one never made a distinction with his lips; rather, when he was harshly treated, he did not open his mouth, and, “like a sheep, like a lamb before its shearer, he was silent” (Isa. 53). He was therefore worthy to bring the people into the true land of promise.

## Chapter XXXI. As Aaron’s rod, so also Jesse’s rod put an end to a proud contention.

Much is made clear from the Scriptures by applying the lamp of this prophetic saying: “And the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him” (Isa. 11); but it is not the purpose of the present work to linger longer over matters of this kind. Nevertheless, in order that the proposed likeness may be more fittingly explained, I should still like to say this alone: just as it befell those proud men against whom, as has been said, the rod blossomed in the wilderness, that they perished by a new and unheard-of destruction, so it befell those lofty and exalted men in whose times the rod came forth from the root of Jesse and the flower rose from his root, that they should fall by a different calamity and, in their destruction, prove unlike [Col. 1464C] all other men who perished in war.

Josephus bears witness to this. Describing their pitiable ruin, he says of them: “I cannot recount their wicked deeds one by one. But, to speak briefly, I think that no other city ever suffered such things, nor that any nation, within the memory of humankind, was fiercer in wickedness.” And elsewhere: “Finally, I do not doubt that all adversities since the beginning of ages would be surpassed if compared with the calamities of the Jews; and no foreign power was the author of these things.”

For these men were chiefly of their father Assur, that is, the devil, against whose loftiness this rod rose with its flower—that is, the humble Virgin with her meek and humble son.

# Book Twelve

[Col. 1463]

## Chapter I. That the Blessed Virgin Mary was no small part of the woman who has a child in the womb, is in labour, and cries out to give birth.

[Col. 1463D]

It has already been said, and must still be said, that “the dragon stood before the woman who was about to give birth, so that, when she had borne a child, he might devour her son” (Rev. 12). Here the name *woman* has a double meaning. Before there was the Blessed Virgin Mary, there was—before her, I say, and long before her—the woman whom we understand in the mystery, namely, the Church: and she was certainly pregnant, a woman pregnant in mind, bearing the Word of promise, as has often been said already.

But in its proper and customary meaning, according to sex, Mary was a woman, though a virgin, as the Apostle says: “God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the law” (Gal. 4). This woman, or this individual member of the human race, is a part of that woman whom we call [Col. 1465A] the Church, that is, the universal gathering of believers. Therefore, when this woman, the Virgin Mary, gave birth, who does not know that the whole Church gave birth? Hence we all say: “A child is born to us, and a son is given to us” (Isa. 9).

## Chapter II. That the dragon also wished to devour Mary’s son.

What, then, would it have meant for her son to be devoured? Surely, to die or be killed in such a way that his name should perish. But that sixth head of the dragon—that terrible beast—could not in this case satisfy its own instigator, the devil, through Herod, mentioned in the preceding little book, as it could with its great, iron teeth consume, crush, and trample things belonging to the body, whether of good men or evil men. Who does not know, and who has not heard, how he sought the child in order to destroy him?

Certainly that impious agent of the Roman Empire—and Augustus himself was not free from the guilt of impiety—was so readily persuaded by Herod’s suggestion that he granted him permission, by whatever means, to destroy the king whom he had heard was born, as though that king were going to take away human kingdoms; which was not so. Against this foolish cruelty, against his cruel folly, the woman often mentioned, secure in the safety of her son, long ago reproached him and does not cease to reproach him:

> No, he does not take away mortal things,  
> Who gives heavenly kingdoms.

The cruelty of Herod, made king by Roman power, quickly recoiled upon the Roman Empire. [Col. 1465C] For he could not have slain so many children with impunity unless he had possessed the licence of Roman power, or the consent of Caesar Augustus. Just as, when he wished, he received permission from that source to slaughter his own people, so, under the pretext of fearing that neither he nor Augustus could trust himself concerning a change of kingdom or empire, he obtained leave to kill all the children born within two years in Bethlehem and throughout all its borders.

It was indeed to come about that this king would be killed by Roman hands; but the time for that had not yet arrived. Nor was it to be done in such a way that the male child would be devoured; that is, he was not to die in such a way that his name should perish.

## Chapter III. Why the devil could not reveal Christ to Herod.

[Col. 1465D]

Herod thus acted, and wished to accomplish this, as truly one or a chief son of the devil—of the kind to whom the Son, or this male child, says: “You are of your father the devil, and you wish to do the desires of your father” (John 8). What desires, or what sort of desires? “You seek,” he says, “to kill me” (ibid.); this is the desire of your father. For this desire, “he was a murderer from the beginning” (ibid.), because from the beginning he hated the truth—that is, myself—and now, since I have become a mortal man, he desires to fulfil that hatred by murder.

This was his desire; Herod wished so quickly to do the desire of his father, the desire of the devil. Someone may say: If his father the devil had long desired this, why did he not immediately betray the child? [Col. 1466A] Why did he allow himself to be deceived by the Magi? Did he not know? Could that spirit, not clothed in flesh, not perceive that this king had been born unless men came from afar and caused disturbance and fear in Herod and all Jerusalem, saying: “Where is he who has been born King of the Jews?” (Matt. 2).

To this I say: certainly he knew, but the child himself, who was born, did not permit him to speak. This may easily be proved from another place. “Demons,” says the Evangelist, “were coming out from many, crying out and saying: ‘For thou art the Son of God.’ And rebuking them, he did not permit them to speak, because they knew that he was Christ” (Luke 4). And rightly he did not permit them to speak, because they were certainly speaking for evil, namely in order to stir up hostility against him.

Thus the devil knew even then that he had been born, and wished that his son Herod should know it; but the newborn infant did not allow him to speak. For, unless he had been prevented, he could have said to Herod in his distress, by means of a possessed person, just as elsewhere he says, “I know who thou art: the Holy One of God” (Mark 1): I know where the Holy One of God is; or, I know where that king is whom you seek.

## Chapter IV. That Christ was tempted by the devil, not in order that he might be known, but in order that he might be corrupted.

But someone says: If the devil knew him, why did he persist in seeking a test and saying: “If thou art the Son of God, command that these stones become bread” (Matt. 4)? Whoever is troubled by this matter ought to know [Col. 1466C] that he acted as a tempter, or as a corrupter. For he is one who always tempts with this intention: to corrupt. He was certainly not seeking to know one unknown to him, but to corrupt one known to him.

What is it to corrupt, except to make someone like or conformed to oneself? This is dreadful to hear; but he went still further into evil, saying at last: “All these things I will give thee, if, falling down, thou wilt worship me” (ibid.). Does not the Apostle also say of him: “Who opposes and exalts himself above all that is called God or is worshipped?” (2 Thess. 2).

Let not a devout and faithful mind shrink from considering how great a presumptuous person the devil is; for he must be recognized by men, who is to be judged by men. “Do you not know,” says the same Apostle, “that we shall judge angels?” (1 Cor. 6). Therefore, when he says, as tempter—that is, corrupter—“If thou art the Son of God, command that these stones become bread,” consider that Satan intended to conform God to himself, to make God like himself.

How would he make him like himself by making him command that those stones become bread? Clearly because both those who falsely say of themselves what they are not, and those who boastfully display for vain glory what they are not, are like him. The Lord himself testifies to this. When the seventy-two returned and joyfully said, “Lord, even the demons are subject to us in thy name” (Luke 10)—which was certainly true—he immediately touched them, as strongly as sweetly, saying: “I saw Satan falling like lightning [Col. 1467A] from heaven” (Luke 4). By this saying he briefly indicated that many of them would fall or turn back according to Satan’s likeness because of vanity. “For many of his disciples,” John says, “went back and no longer walked with him” (John 6).

Moreover, the devil falsely said of himself in heaven, and still strives to say upon earth, that which he is not: namely, that he is God. But the Lord was and is the Son of God; yet he had no reason to demonstrate this to the devil through miracles except boasting or vain glory. For would the devil worship him in order to be saved, if he proved to him in such a manner that he was the Son of God?

The devil’s presumption is therefore astonishing. Not content long ago to have said, “I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. 14), he sought by temptation to make the Most High like himself. Let whoever can marvel at this: that he advanced to the worse point of urging a fall, and then sought by tempting and persuading to cast that one also beneath himself, so that he might worship him; and let him observe that the devil’s judgment is truly great.

## Chapter V. Why Christ forbade not only demons but also apostles to reveal him.

Now I return to what I had begun: namely, that, rebuking the demons, he did not permit them to speak what they knew, namely that he was Christ. Did he forbid, rebuke, and prevent from speaking only demons in this matter? On the contrary, he also forbade human friends concerning the same matter. [Col. 1467C]

For example, when he had asked his disciples, “Whom do men say that the Son of Man is?” and again, “But whom do you say that I am?” Simon Peter answered him, “Thou art Christ, the Son of the living God.” He pronounced him blessed, saying: “Blessed art thou, Simon Bar-Jonah, for flesh and blood has not revealed this to thee, but my Father who is in heaven,” and so forth (Matt. 16). But “then he commanded his disciples that they should tell no one that he was Christ” (ibid.).

Why? Because it was to come about that, once this royal title had been publicly proclaimed of him, he would immediately be killed, while his Jewish enemies rejoiced, armed as they were with a powerful argument and supported by a strong pretext: that they were Caesar’s friends in killing one who, by calling himself Christ the King, opposed Caesar; and if they did not kill him, they would not be Caesar’s friends.

But he did not wish to give place or furnish an opportunity to those murderers before he had established all the instruments of blessing that were to come to us Gentiles, according to the word of promise to Abraham: “And in thy seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22). Therefore he commanded death, or the ministers of death, to wait. For example, concerning Herod the tetrarch: “On a certain day some Pharisees came to him, saying: ‘Go out and depart from here, because Herod wishes to kill thee.’ And he said to them: ‘Go, tell that fox: Behold, I cast out demons and perform healings today and tomorrow, and on the third day I am consummated’” [Col. 1468A] (Luke 13).

This was to say: This year and the next I proclaim the kingdom of God, and in the third year, by the passion of death, I shall be crowned with the highest glory and the highest honour. For it is not within the fox’s power to decide when he shall devour the lion; it is not within the power of a deceitful little man to decide when he shall kill the Lord of life and death.

Therefore, as wise, he privately disclosed to friends, but concealed from enemies until the time, that he was Christ—as wise, indeed as Wisdom itself, which says: “Conduct thy cause with thy friend, and reveal not thy secret to a stranger, lest perhaps, when he hears it, he insult thee and never cease reproaching thee” (Ecclus. 25). Again: “Golden apples in silver settings is one who speaks a word in its season” (Prov. 25).

## Chapter VI. Why the Jews asked whether he was Christ, and why before his Passion he always answered obscurely.

[Col. 1468B]

If you run through the whole sequence of the Gospel, nowhere will you find that he named himself Christ in public; nowhere will you find that before the appointed time of his Passion he called himself, or allowed himself to be called, king. Nevertheless, because he had to bear witness to the truth—for to this he was born and for this he came into the world—he was silent concerning the title Christ, or Anointed, in such a way as to bear witness concerning himself to something much greater than his adversaries could have conceived from that title.

For example, on one occasion the Jews surrounded him and said to him: [Col. 1468C] “How long dost thou keep our souls in suspense? If thou art the Christ, tell us plainly” (John 10). He did not say, “Behold, I tell you plainly: I am Christ,” lest he comply with their evil purpose; for they questioned him maliciously, so that either he might deny that he was Christ—which could not happen, for, as the Apostle says, “he remains faithful; he cannot deny himself” (2 Tim. 2)—or, if he professed himself to be Christ, they would then undoubtedly have the desired basis for a great accusation against him: that he had called himself king against the Roman Empire. For if he were Christ, he would certainly admit that he was also king.

What did Wisdom itself do against this? It both prudently mocked their quibbling and faithfully proclaimed of itself more than it had been asked. The shepherd began to speak concerning his sheep—terms which Roman legions would not greatly fear or heed in their arms. “I tell you,” he says, “and you do not believe, because you are not of my sheep. My sheep hear my voice” (John 10). See how great is the humility of these words, at which the Roman loftiness of that time did nothing but laugh; but see how great is the majesty of the realities in such humility of words. “And I know them,” he says, “and they follow me, and I give them eternal life” (ibid.). Surely to give this belongs to God alone.

Thus, beginning in this way and concealing the title maliciously demanded, he finally spoke thus: “I and the Father are one” (John 9). This is certainly more than that for which he could have been accused among the Romans had he answered openly that he was Christ.

## Chapter VII. That Christ, when the time had come, not only did not forbid, but even wished himself to be proclaimed king.

When the time had come which the work, or the order of our salvation, required, then, preceded by the trumpet of a great miracle—namely the raising of Lazarus, already four days dead and already stinking (John 11)—he accepted this title, publicly receiving the royal title with praises. The crowds came to meet him with palm branches, the emblems of a victor, crying and saying: “Hosanna! Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord! Blessed is the kingdom of our father David which comes! Hosanna in the highest!” (Mark [Col. 1469B] 11). Or, according to Luke: “Peace in heaven and glory in the highest!” (Luke 19).

By this saying the children echoed the angels who, on the night when he was born, announced him by secret revelation to the shepherds, saying: “A Saviour is born to you, who is Christ the Lord in the city of David”; and suddenly they praised God and said: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will!” (Luke 2).

This alone had been lacking to the public praise: that Christ did not publicly proclaim himself king or allow himself to be proclaimed so. But the children supplied this; the children made the praise complete—indeed, without being ordered, but inspired by God, reasonably allowed, and fittingly admitted. Hence, when the chief priests and scribes were indignant and said to him, “Dost thou hear what these say?” he answered very subtly: “Certainly; have you never read: ‘Out of the mouth of infants and nursing children thou hast perfected praise’?” (Ps. 8; Matt. 21).

This is the same as saying: Until now you have importuned me that I should plainly tell you whether I am Christ; but I delayed this title for the proper time and occasion of my praise. Behold, now these, who are infants and nursing children compared with your learning, have perfected praise by acclaiming for me the royal title; they have fulfilled prophecy. For what I was silent about on your account, my friends, they have proclaimed.

And when some of them said, “Master, rebuke thy disciples,” he said: “I tell you that if these are silent, the stones will cry out” (Luke 19). It is understood: that I am King, that I am Christ; and because you say, “We do not want this man to reign over us” (Luke 19), “there shall not remain one stone upon another that shall not be thrown down” (ibid.).

## Chapter VIII. That Christ, riding upon an ass, displayed contempt for the kingdoms of this world.

Indeed, on hearing the title King acclaimed by the crowds, and seeing that he did not forbid it, they rejoiced that the opportunity they had desired had been offered them, so that they might press this charge upon the Roman authorities with seditious voices: “We found this man subverting our nation, forbidding tribute to be given to Caesar, and saying that he is Christ the King”; and: “If thou release this man, thou art not Caesar’s friend. Everyone who makes himself king opposes Caesar” (Luke 23).

But he, wise and provident—truly King, yet not like the Caesars—greatly weakened their accusations in the very acclamation of the crowds, and gave satisfaction to Caesar and to all the kings of the age that he neither desired nor sought the kingdom of any one of them, esteemed no worldly honours at all, such as Roman pomp, and never intended to take up iron weapons or military standards. [Col. 1470A] For he sat not upon a bridled, foaming horse, but upon a small and lowly ass. Around him were not swords or axes, but palm branches and olive boughs. The olive branch, it was agreed, was also among the Gentiles a sign of peace.

What, then, was the Spirit of Christ the King doing in the crowds, or in the children, except hastening to excuse by deeds rather than words the King who had been falsely accused, or was to be accused, of seeking to seize the Roman kingdom or empire?

## Chapter IX. That it was sufficiently proved that Christ’s kingdom is not of this world, though it could have been proved more fully.

The King, meek and humble of heart, also excused himself in words when before Pilate the accusation concerning the royal title was being examined as though it were a great crime: “My kingdom,” he said, “is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would certainly fight, so that I should not be delivered to the Jews. But now my kingdom is not from here” (John 18).

With the same lips of grace he could have said: If my kingdom were of this world, not the little ass upon which I sat the day before yesterday, but a horse or chariot would have been provided for me; and those who acclaimed me king would have displayed not olive branches but the equipment of military arms. And if these were insufficient for them, I would have asked my Father, and he would have furnished me at once with more than twelve legions of angels.

He could also have said: When I fed five thousand people with five loaves, and for that reason they wished to seize me and make me king over them, I would not have fled from them unless it were true that my kingdom is not of this world. These and many other such proofs of his innocence—he who wished to do Caesar no harm—he could have set forth in answer to Pilate; except that Pilate had no hearing, and Christ had spoken beforehand through a certain wise man: “Do not pour forth speech where there is no hearing” [Col. 1470D] (Ecclus. 32).

He reserved these things for us to know; and it is ours to cry out even to his adversaries after their death that he does not take away mortal things, because he gives heavenly kingdoms; that, desiring to be deceived, they were deceived by their own wickedness; and that iniquity lied to itself when it said: “We found him forbidding tribute to be given to Caesar” (Luke 23). For he did not make himself such a king, nor did he thus oppose Caesar. Rather: “Render,” he says, “the things that are Caesar’s to Caesar, and the things that are God’s to God” (Matt. 21).

## Chapter X. That the devil, deceived by plotting against Christ’s life, did not hinder but advanced God’s counsel.

Christ had to die. The oft-mentioned dragon stood upon this and dwelt in this: that he might die; and this he thought was his devouring. [Col. 1471A] He thought, I say, that through death he could devour him—that is, annihilate the counsel or purpose of God—so that what had been foretold might not happen: “He shall be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. 49); and: “In him all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22).

Already long fearing this, when Christ said to the Jews, “You shall seek me and shall not find me; and where I am, you cannot come” (John 7), he spoke through their mouths as they said among themselves: “Where will this man go, that we shall not find him? Will he go into the dispersion of the Gentiles and teach the Gentiles?” (ibid.).

But the Psalmist truly sang: “This dragon, which thou hast formed to make sport of him” (Ps. 103); and the Lord himself says of him to blessed Job: “Wilt thou make sport of him as of a bird?” (Job 40). Again: “Behold, his hope shall disappoint him” (ibid.). He was indeed mocked; his hope disappointed him. For Christ was by no means to be devoured, nor was he devoured, by dying. Rather, by his death it was brought about—and could only have been brought about through that death—that he should go into the dispersion of the Gentiles and teach the Gentiles.

Let us consider the sacraments through which all nations were to be, and shall be, blessed in him according to the promises. Then we shall be able to marvel at the greatness of the deception played upon this dragon, to the praise of God who formed him to be mocked: because, while he wishes to oppose, he serves God’s purpose; while he thinks he is devouring such a son of the blessed woman, he renders an exceedingly profitable service to her counsel.

## Chapter XI. That through Christ’s death we have received the sacraments of baptism, the Eucharist, and the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 1471C]

What and how many are the chief sacraments of our salvation? Holy baptism; the holy Eucharist of his body and blood; and the twofold gift of the Holy Spirit—one for the remission of sins, the other for the divisions, or manifold distributions, of graces. These three sacraments are necessary instruments of our salvation. Yet they were to be established, or were established, only through his death and resurrection.

First, concerning the sacrament of baptism, we believe and know that it flowed from his death, when he was thought to be devoured—that is, when he was already dead. “For when they came to Jesus,” says the Evangelist, “and saw that he was already dead, they did not break his legs; but one of the soldiers opened his side with a lance, and immediately blood and water came out” [Col. 1471D] (John 19). By that blood we were redeemed; by that water we were washed, both Jews and Gentiles. And first the Jews, then the Gentiles—or rather, first the dead, then the living.

For all the faithful who had existed from the beginning of the world, and who were awaiting the blessed hope in the underworld, first received the fruit of this salvation. They had not yet, as it were catechumens, communicated in the heavenly altar—that is, in the vision of the Godhead—because the dividing wall of enmity had not yet been removed. “For we also,” they say, “were once by nature children of wrath, as were the rest” (Eph. 2); and: “All our righteousnesses are like the cloth of a menstruous woman” (Isa. 64).

Then, washed and cleansed in that stream, they entered the sanctuary of God, into the kingdom of God, which is wholly holy. And because at that time the entire Church of all former ages was baptized at once, this sacrament was placed, as it were, at the doors of that same Church, so that whoever thereafter wishes to be incorporated into the Church may be baptized in his own person, because the Church was baptized together and universally in the death of Christ.

For when water is taken and the word of the cross is spoken with the invocation of the Holy Spirit, the sacrament of Christ’s death is present. Hence the Apostle says: “All of us who have been baptized in Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death” (Rom. 6), and so forth.

There was a long contest of the holy Roman Church against the custom of the Greeks, who wished the solemn sacrament of baptism to be celebrated on the day of Epiphany because on that day the Lord himself is known to have been baptized by John in the waters of the Jordan. The Roman Church, and the great Leo writing in reply, reasonably demonstrate that John’s baptism did not belong to the same efficacy, because it was not for the remission of sins but for repentance. Christ’s baptism took its beginning from his death, when, as has been said, his side was opened with a lance and blood and water came forth; and therefore this sacrament is to be celebrated in his death and resurrection.

## Chapter XII. For what use the sacrament of the Eucharist was left to us.

[Col. 1472C]

Concerning the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, it is certain and does not need our assertion that it is indeed the proper and singular commemoration of his Passion or death, and that it took, or ought to have taken, its beginning from his Passion or death. This sacrament was instituted as near to his death as possible: namely, when he had already been sold unto death, and on the night in which he was betrayed.

This sacrament was preserved and sent for us who live and remain, in which, under the appearance of bread and wine, is hidden the benefit of his death and resurrection. For those faithful persons who had died were, in a wondrous manner, fed or given food in that appearance in which he hung upon the cross: so that his soul descended to their souls in hell, and his body to their bodies, and he was three days and three nights in the heart of the earth, in that same womb of the earth into which their bodies had been received or taken.

It is not now my purpose to treat this great mystery at greater length. Yet, lest it be left altogether untouched, I should like to say something concerning the reason why it is necessary for us. This reason was that the first human beings were unbelieving toward God and excessively credulous toward the devil. Since they saw only a fruit however sweet, fragrant, and beautiful to the eye, they believed that it had the effect of divinity in it; they believed the devil saying: “It shall by no means be as God said: ‘If you eat, you shall die the death’; but it shall be as I say: ‘If you eat, you shall be like gods’” (Gen. 3).

In opposition to that food, which was food of death, reason itself declaring it, another food had to be given by justice, a food which should be food of life, and in a similar order: so that the mind should believe something to be in it which the eye does not see; should believe that the flesh and blood of Christ are food and drink truly effecting participation in divinity. This the senses of flesh and blood cannot perceive. By this faith God judges that satisfaction has been made to him by man, since man believes God no less than he had believed the devil.

## Chapter XIII. That the Holy Spirit is first poured out upon us for the remission of sins, then in the divisions of graces.

Who does not know that we all who believe receive, or have received, the first gift of the Holy Spirit for the remission of sins through his death or blood? Therefore, on the day on which he rose from the dead, when it was evening, standing in the midst of the disciples, [Col. 1473B] “he breathed upon them and said: ‘Receive the Holy Spirit.’” And immediately he added: “Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them” (John 20).

Moreover, they received the second gift of the same Holy Spirit, for the divisions of graces of which the Apostle speaks in writing to the Corinthians—“To one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom, to another a word of knowledge” (1 Cor. 11), and the rest—on the fiftieth day. These are the gifts concerning which it is written: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; he gave gifts to men.” The greater of these gifts are that he “appointed some apostles, others prophets, others evangelists, others pastors and teachers” (Eph. 4).

These are the consolations of the Paraclete, concerning which, when he wished to depart, he said to them: “Because I have spoken these things to you, sorrow has filled your heart. But I tell you the truth: it is expedient for you that I go away; for if I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go away, I will send him to you” (John 16).

When he says, “if I go away,” it is rightly understood as though he were saying: if I ascend into heaven, if I withdraw my bodily presence from you. Nevertheless, since they were not to grieve at his ascension but, rather, to rejoice with great joy, as Luke records, saying: “And they, worshipping him, returned to Jerusalem with great joy” (Luke 24), whereas they were sorrowful over his Passion—for “because I have spoken these things to you,” he says, “sorrow has filled your heart”—it is nonetheless rightly understood that he spoke of his Passion or death when he said that he would go away.

For the Evangelist means it so, saying: “Before the feast day of Passover, Jesus, knowing that his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father” (John 13). For he did not first pass from this world then; rather, he had already done so when, having risen from death, he ceased to live among men and to suffer worldly labours.

## Chapter XIV. That neither the devil nor impious people knew these sacraments.

These three things had to be done; and for their sake his death was necessary to the Gentiles, because these are the blessings by which all nations were to be blessed in this seed, which is Christ. [Col. 1474A] The great dragon did not know this, although he hoped through death to be able to devour that son, or male child. He did not know it, I say; nor did those over whom he presided know it—those of whom, or of what kind, Wisdom says: “They thought these things and went astray; their wickedness blinded them, and they did not know the mysteries of God” (Wis. 2). And the Apostle says (1 Cor. 2): “For if they had known”—understand, the wisdom which is from God, “which we also speak among the perfect” (ibid.)—“they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.”

This is altogether true. If Leviathan, or the great whale that is in the sea, had known that an iron hook lay hidden beneath the flesh, he would never have bitten the flesh by which the iron was covered. He did indeed know that he was Christ, the Son of God, and that he had come for the salvation of humankind; but he did not know the mystery hidden from the ages, the counsel of God’s wisdom, that from the death of one the life of all should be reborn.

He knew his own counsel, but this counsel had been hidden through all ages and was so unthinkable to human minds that even the apostles, when he spoke privately to them concerning these things, understood none of them, as the holy Gospels attest in many places. For the time had not yet come for them to understand these things, before he himself had been glorified with the glory of the resurrection (Luke 18).

## Chapter XV. That the dragon rose seven times against Christ through impious people, and was seized on the seventh occasion.

Who, moreover, can understand—who can feel with inward sympathy—the disposition in the mind of this male child, from the time when the oft-mentioned woman bore him, while that dragon so often gaped in order to devour him, that is, while impious men sought to kill his flesh and erase his name (Matt. II)? For, if you count correctly, seven times it gaped with open mouth, seven monstrous jaws it opened; and, frustrated in the others, at last with the seventh jaw it seized the flesh—but to its own harm, because, as has already been said, it feels the iron hidden in the flesh as most grievous.

The first gape of this dragon was when, according to Matthew, the deadly Herod sought the life of the child newly born, as has already been said above, and killed the infants because of him. [Col. 1474D] The second was when, according to Luke, after he had come to Nazareth, where he had been brought up, and was teaching in the synagogue, they rose up, drove him out of the city, and led him to the brow of the mountain upon which their city had been built, in order to throw him down. But he, passing through their midst, went on his way (Luke IV).
