The third was when, according to John, he fled from the face of the mocking Jews when he said: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have eternal life” (John VI).

For truly, in saying this he fled and hid himself from them, according to the title of the thirty-third Psalm, which is inscribed thus: “A Psalm of David, when he changed [Col. 1475A] his appearance before Abimelech, and he dismissed him and went away; and he drummed at the doors of the city gate, and saliva ran down into his beard, and he was carried in his hands” (1 Sam. XXI). Abimelech is the very one who above is called Achish. Now Abimelech is interpreted “the kingdom of my father,” whereas Achish means “how is it?” Therefore it signifies the Jews, whom Christ had rightly first called the kingdom of his Father—this is denoted by Abimelech. But now they are Achish, from the time when they said, “How can this be?”

In what respect did he “change his appearance” before these men? Namely, in that he changed the rite of the old sacrifice into a new one. Likewise, “saliva ran down into his beard” because, when he said, “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood” (John VI), and the rest, he seemed to them to utter childish [Col. 1475B] words. For it belongs to infants to dribble saliva. Then too he drummed at the city gate when, to those unwilling and refusing to hear, he proclaimed the mystery of his Passion, knowing that some would open it by believing. “He was also carried in his hands,” namely when, holding bread and wine in his own hands, he said: “Take and eat; this is my body. This is my blood of the New Testament” (Matt. XX), and so forth. Yet according to the Hebrew truth we now read: “and he collapsed in their hands.”

The fourth persecution was when the chief priests and Pharisees sent officers to seize him. When these returned and were asked, “Why have you not brought 634 him?” they replied: “Never has a man spoken as this man speaks” (John VII). But they, persisting in their purpose, brought before him a woman caught in adultery, testing him so that they might accuse him (John VIII). The fifth persecution was when he said: “Amen, amen, I say to you, before Abraham came to be, I am”; they took up stones to throw at him (ibid.). The sixth was when he said: “I and the Father are one”—“they took up stones to stone him” (John X). The seventh and last was when “they gathered a council against him and did not cease until they crucified him” (John XI).

## CHAPTER XVI. Why it was said: “I waited for one who would grieve with me, and there was none.”

Who, I say, understands his meek and humble spirit in so prolonged a struggle with death? [Col. 1475D] “Blessed,” says the Psalmist, “is he who understands concerning the needy and poor man” (Ps. XL), whom, according to a verse of another Psalm, that dragon pursued in Judah, pursued among the Jewish people: “to put to death the poor and needy man, and the one pierced in heart” (Ps. CVIII). We, almost unteachable, or too slow to learn from him who says: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. XI), understand far less than we ought concerning that poor man, that meek and humble one, grieving for us and wounded for us. “Behold,” says the prophet, “how the righteous man dies, and no one takes it to heart” (Isa. XVII).

He himself also says in the Psalm: “And I waited for one who would grieve with me, and there was none” (Ps. LXVIII). But did not blessed Mary, standing beside his cross and seeing how he died, take it to heart and grieve with him? Indeed, she took it greatly to heart; she grieved greatly; and, as Simeon had foretold, “a sword passed through her soul” (Luke II). Likewise the beloved disciple did not see him die without inward perception or without sorrow. The other disciples too, although all fled after abandoning him, were not wholly without shared grief; indeed, sorrow filled their hearts.

Therefore “no one takes it to heart,” and “there was none who would grieve” [Col. 1476B] are said not according to the judgment of reason, but according to the force of pain, which sometimes admits no reasoning. And you observe that this was fittingly said, since, in comparison with so great a multitude of scoffers and mockers, those who grieved were, because of their fewness, of no account or number.

But because elsewhere he says, “I looked around, and there was no helper; I sought, and there was none to assist; and my own arm saved me, and my indignation itself aided me” (Isa. LXIII), this is not a similar complaint, but a most true statement of fact: absolutely no one, even had anyone wished, could help or assist him in a battle or encounter of this kind, in which the prince of the world was coming—the ancient sinner and ruler of death. For there was no one who could say of him, “And he has nothing in me.” Apart from him there was no one in whom there was, together with human innocence, the arm and indignation of the divine nature—that is, zeal or strength.

## CHAPTER XVII. That there were two wills in Christ, divine and human: one willed death, the other shrank from it.

What then? In looking around for a helper, did he seek one with such an intention—that he might not die—when he had come for this very purpose, to die? Certainly, as he was God and man, so, at the very point of the Passion, he had two wills: one of divinity and the other of humanity. For humanity naturally feared and recoiled from the taste of death; the soul was held by its natural love for the body and wished to remain in the flesh. But divinity, by rational judgment, intended something else—namely, that which was necessary for the salvation of the human race. Humanity set the will of that nature before its own will when, in his prayer, after first saying, “My Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me,” he immediately added: “Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” (Matt. XXVI); or thus: “Nevertheless, not my will but yours be done” (Luke XXII).

Thus, according to the reasoning of divinity, he looked around seeking one to help; but according to the natural feeling of the flesh he willed this very thing which holy men would prefer, saying with the Apostle: “Because we do not wish to be unclothed, but to be clothed upon, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life” (2 Cor. V). [Col. 1477A] But did he merely look around, and, looking around, seek a helper? Indeed, he also cried out in a loud voice: “Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani,” that is, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matt. XXVII).

This is rightly understood as though he were saying: “O you in whom all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily in me” (Col. II), why do you restrain yourself within? Why are you silent while I am dying? A little earlier, when those who were to seize me came, you uttered one brief word, saying, “Whom do you seek? I am he”; and immediately “they went backward and fell to the ground” (John XII). Recently too, shining forth from these eyes which now grow dim in death, you terrified a great multitude; and what an infinite army could not have done, you did with one whip made of cords, driving them from [Col. 1477B] the Temple and reminding them of this prophecy: “My house shall be called a house of prayer; but you have made it a den of thieves” (Matt. XXI). Why, O divinity of the Word so mighty and strong, have you forsaken me, your flesh, while containing yourself within like a sword unwilling to come out of its sheath?

## CHAPTER XVIII. Why it was said: “With him are wisdom and strength.”

Here it is now fitting to recall that it is written: “With him are wisdom and strength.” Likewise: “With him are strength and wisdom” (Job XII). Let us say therefore this too: he is himself the lamb; he is himself the lion; and all things have their season. So also the things signified by the lamb and the lion ought to have had their own seasons. There was a time when, as wise, he maintained the patience of a lamb; there was a time when, as strong, he gave forth the lion’s roar. While strength still restrained itself within, he was not utterly forsaken; for wisdom consoled him as though forsaken.

For he did not fail to know what was being done around him. Therefore he not only restrained his disciples when they struck and said: “Lord, behold, here are two swords” (Luke XXII); but he even went out to meet his adversaries and allowed himself to be seized. Nor did the Lord of angels disdain to be strengthened by an angel, having entered into agony, 635 and to sweat drops of blood running down upon the earth. He allowed his face to be veiled by those who struck him; he did not reject the reed [Col. 1477D] given him in mockery as a sceptre for his hand, nor the scarlet cloak placed about him, nor the crown of thorns set upon his head; nor did he oppose the Roman soldiers as they bent their knees before him and, with a bitter laugh, hailed or worshipped him as King of the Jews. For he knew that all these cruel sportings would be turned for him into realities, joyful and sweet.

## CHAPTER XIX. Why Christ commanded the sword to be put back into its sheath.

We cannot, while avoiding wearying readers, set forth in this place the explanations handed down by the holy Fathers concerning these matters, all the rest besides, and the cross itself—which, “for the joy set before him,” as the Apostle says (Heb. XII), he endured, despising shame—in order to demonstrate that in all these things there is great praise of the wisdom that is with him. But there is one point which, although it has already been briefly mentioned elsewhere, I do not wish to pass over here: what is the meaning of his saying to Peter, as he drew his sword and struck, “Put your sword back into its place”; or of his saying, when they said, “Lord, behold, here are two swords,” “It is enough” (Matt. XXVII); and, according to another Evangelist, “Allow it as far as this” (Luke XXII).

For it greatly concerns the line of our argument to know or state what sense is contained in his saying “It is enough” at such a moment and in so weighty a matter, when they showed him only two swords. For this is plainly not the same as if he had said: “These two swords are enough for us; let us use them.” It is quite inconsistent with that that he commanded one of them, once drawn, to be put back into its sheath, and said, “Allow it as far as this.” Surely we perceive that these two sayings, “Put your sword back into its place” and “Allow it as far as this,” are equivalent in the speaker’s intention. Therefore it is now enough, in our judgment, if reasons are given why, and with what in view, he fittingly said, “It is enough,” and what he intended or meant by saying, “Allow it as far as this.”

What was it to say “It is enough” to those showing two swords for his defence, unless it was as though he said: “Before I came—the promised one—a sword was needed to defend the people from whom alone it was necessary that I be born, lest, if that people were destroyed, as the devil wished, the salvation which is now from the Jews should not come to pass, because the word of promise has been fulfilled. It is enough: they have laboured enough and used material swords. They existed long before you. [Col. 1478C] Allow it now—that is, put the sword back into its sheath—as far as this”: understood, a sword of this kind was necessary, that it might serve the kingdom of God, until he came. Now, because he has come, now because “the kingdom of God is within you” (Luke XVII), the swords must be changed.

From this point onward, for citizens or soldiers of the kingdom of God, let the sword be the word of God. For it was of such a sword that I spoke to you just now when I said: “Let him who has none sell his tunic and buy a sword” (Luke XXII)—that is, let him put off the encumbrances and possessions of the world, so that he may be free to learn or teach the word of God.

## CHAPTER XX. What is meant by: “Go forth and see, daughters of Zion, King Solomon in the diadem with which his mother crowned him on the day of his betrothal and on the day of the gladness of his heart.”

Why delay with many words? “Go forth,” says the Holy Spirit, “go forth and see, daughters of Zion, King Solomon in the diadem with which his mother crowned him on the day of his betrothal and on the day of the gladness of his heart” (Song III). See this king of wisdom, this mighty king, and learn by experience how true is the judgment we recalled above concerning him: how “with him are wisdom and strength” (Job II). We strive to proclaim wisdom in him as he suffers and dies, and then to say something concerning strength; but speech fails, while the reality, for a mind contemplating it more diligently, rises and shines ever more brightly.

See this crowned king; see the [Col. 1479A] sceptre in his hand; see the purple garment; see those who salute him; see the Romans who worship him. Do not see in his crown only that it is made of thorns. See in those thorns him for whom the thorns are a preparation—a crown of glory and honour—as the Psalmist sang: “You made him a little lower than the angels; you crowned him with glory and honour” (Ps. VIII). See not only the reed given in place of a sceptre, but see the true reality of which it is the foreshadowing: the highest sovereignty of heaven and earth. For with that reed, and because of that reed, on that very day “all power in heaven and on earth was given to him” (Matt. XXVIII).

See not only that man-made purple cloak mockingly placed around him, but in that purple meditate upon the purple Church, cleansed by his blood and destined to shed its own blood for him. And in those soldiers of Roman power, bending their knees in laughter and worshipping in laughter or jest, see what is portended; and let the thought of him who is silent sound in the ears of your heart, as though he said: “As I live, the knee of the Roman Empire shall bend before me, and the Hebrew tongue, the Greek tongue, and the Latin tongue shall confess that I am King of the Jews—indeed, King of kings and Lord of lords. Nor shall it be void, though you wrote it in irony and hostile mockery: ‘Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews’ (John XVIII), that is, the holy Saviour, King of all who confess God.”

Seeing such a King Solomon, know that this was the day of his betrothal and the day of the gladness of his heart: the day of his betrothal, indeed, by which [Col. 1479C] he betrothed the Church to himself through his blood—a betrothal greatly unlike betrothals of the flesh or of this world, since these begin in pleasure and end in pain. But this betrothal began in pain, so that he said, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matt. XXVII), and is consummated in everlasting pleasure and the gladness of his heart, because after overwhelming pain he said, “It is finished” (John XIX).

## CHAPTER XXI. What the bloody sweat portended.

What, moreover, will you see in his agony, in his sweat which, while he prayed more earnestly, became like drops of blood running down upon the earth? (Luke XXII). What will you see in so great [Col. 1479D] a miracle? For it is not so great a miracle that blood flowed from his wounds, since it is customary and natural for blood to flow when flesh is wounded. 636 This is unusual, beyond nature: while the flesh was whole and the skin sound, blood ran down upon the ground as sweat from his entire body. The miracle should make you more attentive to the matter, that you may see what it means.

What then is it but a vehement accusation of Jewish unbelief, but a terrible condemnation of the parricidal people? “You have come,” says the Apostle, “to Jesus the mediator, and to the sprinkling of blood that speaks better things than Abel” (Heb. XII). “What have you done?” the Lord said to Cain. “The voice of your brother Abel’s blood cries to me from the earth. Now therefore you shall be cursed upon the earth, which opened its [Col. 1480A] mouth and received your brother’s blood from your hand; you shall be a wanderer and fugitive upon the earth” (Gen. IV). Would not the same God say to the Jews concerning his Son what he said to that Cain concerning Abel, seeing the blood of one agonizing and praying earnestly in agony—the blood crying more effectively, speaking more effectively than Abel, as the Apostle says (Heb. XII)? Truly, therefore, so great a miracle of sweat was not purposeless, because it ran down upon the earth against the unhappy and impious Jewish murderers as a portent of terrible judgment.

## CHAPTER XXII. Why it was said: “Horns are in his hands; there his strength is hidden.”

In all these things, the wisdom which is with him openly performed its office, while strength—which is likewise with him—remained hidden, yet not idle, and held itself within, as had been foretold in Habakkuk: “Horns are in his hands; there his strength is hidden” (Hab. III). By the horns in his hands we understand the arms of the cross, to which they fastened his hands. How was his strength hidden there? Namely, where no strength of his was thought to exist. For a man’s strength is especially powerful in his arms and hands; but he hung nailed to the cross by his hands. Thus it seemed that he had no strength, but he had some—indeed, great strength—and it was already working secretly.

Already the invisible teeth of the dragon, which thought itself to be devouring him, were invisibly being broken, and the abyss of its throat was being strangled, as it were, by an iron hook. Certain visible signs of this operation at once shone forth, and “we have heard with our ears, O God” (Ps. XLIII). For when he gave up the spirit, behold, the veil of the Temple was torn in two from top to bottom; the earth shook, the rocks split, the tombs were opened, and many bodies of saints who had fallen asleep arose. Going out from their tombs—not indeed before, but after his resurrection—they came into the holy city and appeared to many (Matt. XXVII).

Words fail when we desire to speak of the strength of the Word: the strength of the Word which was and is in that spirit or soul which Christ Jesus sent forth in dying. Why do words fail, except because we do not perceive—and do not deserve to perceive—how powerful, and in what manner powerful, that Word is? Or even if some saints have felt his Word drawn into their inmost hearts, by what words could they recount it? Let this alone now be said: that then, in accordance with the event, the mighty Word—the Word who is God—roared in the spirit or soul as it departed from the body of Jesus; and hell trembled when that spirit of Jesus came, when the soul of Jesus came united with the Word. No one can endure the strength of that Word unless he has love for it. Hence the Psalmist says: “As wax melts before fire, so let sinners perish before the face of God” (Ps. LXVII).

## CHAPTER XXIII. [Col. 1481A] Why it was said: “Judah, a lion’s whelp; from the prey, my son, you have ascended.”

Let the prophetic proclamation of the patriarch Jacob support our weak discourse concerning this matter. “Judah,” he says, “is a lion’s whelp; from the prey, my son, you have ascended. Resting, you lay down as a lion, and as a lioness” (Gen. XLIX). “Who shall rouse him?” Judah, which is interpreted “confession,” is Christ Jesus, the leader of our confession, born from the tribe of Judah. He is the lion’s whelp—that is, the Son of God most mighty. Until this point he had been a lamb, and like a sheep led to slaughter; but when all that he had to suffer according to the likeness of a lamb or sheep had been completed, this same lion’s whelp immediately roared.

“For from the prey, [Col. 1481B] my son, you have ascended”: you rose up mighty to plunder hell. The first spoil which this plunderer of death seized from hell was that thief who, as he was now drawing near to the very jaws of hell, was held back by one brief confession and heard from him: “Amen, I say to you, today you shall be with me in paradise” (Luke XXIII). How great a prey did he at once ascend to, beginning in this way? Who besides him could have brought out of hell so many thousands of the elect, as the prophet Zechariah says: “You also, by the blood of your covenant, have sent forth your prisoners from the pit in which there is no water” (Zech. IX)?

A desirable plunderer, restoring to life those whom he took from death, restoring to heaven those whom he snatched from hell. He knew this would occur not uncertainly: “And I, if I am lifted up from the earth,” he says, “will draw all things to myself” [Col. 1481C] (John XII). When he says “all things,” we understand the elect, or all authority in heaven and on earth. For because of the suffering of death he was crowned with glory and honour; because of the cross’s gibbet he was appointed judge of the living and the dead; and all things were subjected beneath his feet. Those enemies of his who still rebel will without doubt experience in fact that they are already under his feet in power. Hence, after citing this testimony of the Psalm, the Apostle says that what we are discussing is still to come: “But now we do not yet see all things subjected to him.”

## CHAPTER XXIV. What is meant by: “Resting, you lay down as a lion, and as a lioness”; and how necessary it was that he who had died should not lack burial.

“Resting,” he says, “you lay down as a lion, and as a lioness” (Gen. XLIX). When the work was completed, immediately—as soon as it was said, “It is finished”—you gave up your spirit; you rested from your labours; you rested with the prey which you took from the lower world, having also with you in the delights of paradise the thief who confessed devoutly. There, while the spirit rested, the flesh also rested in the tomb.

Is the repose of the tomb—the repose of the buried body—a small or negligible part of rest? Certainly not small, but great, and greatly beneficial to the entire human race. For by the three-day burial of the dead man the Trinity of divinity, hitherto offended against the human race, had to be appeased; and by the burial of one righteous man the resurrection of bodies was also obtained for us all. Whoever rightly considers this reason should greatly approve the counsel of the Lord’s Word, the Word which thus went beforehand in the Law through the mouth of Moses:

“When,” he says, “a man has sinned in a matter deserving death, and has been condemned to death and hanged upon a gibbet, [Col. 1482A] his corpse shall not remain on the wood, but you shall bury him on the same day; for he who hangs upon the wood is accursed by God, and you shall in no way defile your land which the Lord your God has given you as a possession” (Deut. XXI).

What is the intention of the Law—indeed, of the Holy Spirit—in decreeing such an ordinance through the Law? Is it not so that, since by the Law’s command all who had been hanged upon a gibbet, however guilty or however deserving of death, were buried, consequently this man also, whose burial was necessary to the world, could not lawfully be left unburied? Otherwise, why would it be wholly silent about those stoned or otherwise put to death for their crimes, and decree the benefits of burial only for those hanged upon a gibbet?

Consider at the same time how wisely it concealed this very intention, lest the impious should perceive it, by saying: “For he who hangs upon the wood is accursed by God, and you shall in no way defile your land which the Lord your God has given you as a possession.” What then? Can the earth which the impious understand here be more defiled by an unburied body than by a buried body received into its womb? Therefore understand this as said to righteous Joseph: “You shall bury him”—as he did—“and you shall in no way defile your land,” [Col. 1482C] namely, the flesh of Christ, the God-bearing flesh given to you as a possession of resurrection and life. “You shall not defile it,” I say, that is, you shall not leave it unburied, lest it be defiled or treated unworthily by some indignant approach of that kind, by which bodies are customarily handled in any burial.

Those foolish and malicious men, ignorant of the mysteries of God, calmly permitted him to be buried—something desirable even for dying saints—content that they had made him, as it were, accursed, the Law saying: “For he who hangs upon the wood is accursed by God.” But wisdom is justified by her children, because the well-devised law of wisdom made provision for the fact that it placed someone under a curse not because of punishment, but because of guilt. For it did not here make punishment alone the ground; it first stated guilt. Having first said, “When a man has sinned in a matter deserving death,” it only then added, “and, having been condemned to death, has been hanged upon a gibbet.”

And this too should not be lightly overlooked: it says in this manner, “For he who hangs upon the wood is accursed by God,” although the Apostle, writing to Greeks and, for the need of the time, following the translation of the Seventy Interpreters which had long been accepted among them, said: “Accursed is everyone who hangs upon the wood” (Gal. III).

## CHAPTER XXV. Why it was said: “Accursed by God is he who hangs upon the wood.”

It is sufficiently clear that there is some difference between the two translations, but how great may be inferred from the three differences in wording. For in the Greek, “everyone” is added, which is not found in the Hebrew; conversely, in the Hebrew we have “by God” and the substantive verb, which the Greek does not have. Thus we know what the impious thought concerning the curse, wishing by it to destroy in him the praise which they had heard proclaimed from the mouths of infants and nursing children in the verse of the one hundred and seventeenth Psalm: “Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Ps. CXVII; John XII). We indeed know that they thought as they wished to think, they whose wickedness had blinded them; nevertheless let us receive for praise what was said: “For he who hangs upon the wood is accursed by God,” so that the sense may be this (Deut. XXI): every person who has sinned in a matter deserving death, [Col. 1483B] has been condemned to death, and hangs upon the wood, is accursed—understood, by his own sin.

But this one righteous man, who was indeed condemned to death and hung upon the wood, yet did not commit a sin deserving death—indeed, never committed any sin—was not accursed by his own sin. Rather, he was sufficiently afflicted by God as though accursed—that is, as though a sinner—not truly a sinner, but truly bearing the sins of all. “For,” says Isaiah (ch. LIII), “he placed upon him the iniquities of us all.” To state this most emphatically: in the holy Scriptures it is not easy to find anyone expressly said to be “accursed by God” except in this passage, where it is said thus: “Accursed by God is he who hangs upon the wood.”

If anyone objects that the same God says to Cain, “Now therefore you shall be accursed upon the earth,” or says to the serpent itself, “Because you have done this, you shall be accursed among all animals and beasts of the earth,” one must know that nowhere is “by me” added. One must carefully distinguish between cursing and declaring someone accursed. For sin alone is a curse, and certainly is not from God. Therefore, in this sense, the one “accursed by God” is the one upon whom, as has already been said, God placed the iniquities of us all—iniquities which truly are curses—through an exchange, a gracious exchange: so that, bearing or taking upon himself our curses, he might give us his blessing, which truly is from God.

## CHAPTER XXVI. What is meant by: “A woman, when she gives birth, has sorrow”; and that Christ kept Sabbath in the tomb.

[Col. 1483D]

Meanwhile the male child was thought to have been devoured; and the oft-mentioned woman who had borne him had sorrow on this account, and was grieving almost inconsolably in those few who still lived in the flesh and who, though few in number, formed a great part of that blessed woman. Therefore he had foretold to them that their sorrow would end happily, under this comparison: “A woman, when she gives birth, has sorrow, because her hour has come. But when she has borne a child, she no longer remembers the distress because of joy that a human being has been born into the world” (John XVI). For he immediately explained [Col. 1484A] why he said this: “And so you indeed now have sorrow; but I shall see you again, and your heart shall rejoice, and no one shall take your joy from you” (ibid.).

He was thought, I say, to have been devoured. While they had sorrow, those murderers—the members, of course, of the oft-mentioned dragon—rejoiced; and perhaps, as it is elsewhere written of such people, “rejoicing, they sent gifts to one another, because this greatest of prophets tormented them,” for he was burdensome to them even to look upon. But now, dead and buried, he lay in such a way that, with the stone sealed and a very great stone placed over him, the pit of his tomb was shut and blocked, lest he rise; lest even there the soul might enter again into the body, or, should the body revive, might crawl out from it. Guards also had been stationed because of his disciples.

But he who dwells in heaven laughed at them and mocked them; meanwhile, however, he kept Sabbath—that is, he rested as a lion and as a lioness, secure in his prey, because he had rescued the dead and held death captive. “As a lion,” he says, “and as a lioness”: surely because he is God and man in one and the same person. According to the divine nature, he is the lion of whom it is elsewhere written: “The lion will roar; who will not fear? The Lord God has spoken; who will not prophesy?” (Amos III). But according to his human nature, a little earlier he was a sheep when he was led to be sacrificed; now, however, from the moment he said, “It is finished,” he was a lioness—a fierce lioness, placing her cubs, that is, all the elect whom she had borne to eternal life by her blood, in her den; in her paradise, [Col. 1484C] nourished by the strong and free soul, which was to return immediately after the Sabbath to its flesh and bring it back to her cubs. From the sight of that flesh, surely, a richer nourishment of life-giving milk was to flow to those cubs, and now does flow.

Meanwhile, that Sabbath was beautiful as it looked toward the Sabbath of which it had been written at the creation of the world: “And God rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had accomplished” (Gen. II). He who then completed the creation of the world in six days and rested on the seventh is the same one who, on the first day of the Sabbath—which we call the Lord’s Day—entered the city; and, having finally died on the sixth day in order to regenerate human creation, rested according to the flesh in the tomb on the seventh day, while his soul rested in paradise. [Col. 1484D]

## CHAPTER XXVII. That “Arise, my glory; arise, psaltery and harp” was spoken concerning Christ’s resurrection.

The hour had come of which he himself had said elsewhere to the Jews: “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified” (John 12). That hour had come, I say, with the proclamation of the word sounding from the Father’s mouth in David: “Awake, my glory; awake, psaltery and lyre” (Ps. 56 [57]). What was that psaltery, or what lyre? The one and same body resting in the tomb was the psaltery; it was the lyre. It was the lyre whose strings, stretched by love, had sounded forth and modulated the sweet tones of preaching, and which the Jews had broken. Yet the breaking of that lyre became for it a cause of increase, [Col. 1485A] a cause of the greatest success: so that the ten-stringed psaltery might arise—that is, the sweet-sounding psaltery—never again to be broken, ever to give forth the voice of confession among the peoples and of a psalm among the nations; a psaltery whose strings no hand could thereafter snap, whose wooden frame no force could henceforth prevail in breaking. As the Apostle says: “Christ, having risen from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. 6). This is the glory of God the Father: namely, that in this work he glories through the great abundance of love. “Therefore,” he says, “awake, O my glory; awake, psaltery and lyre.” Did not that soul hear, did it not perceive, this voice of the Father, this purpose of the Word—this soul united to that same Word as bride to bridegroom by an unending [Col. 1485B] kiss and joined by an unremitting embrace? Certainly it heard; fully it perceived. For it knew, by a right more than matronly, all things belonging to that same Word; it comprehended all things. Therefore it answered with joy: “I will arise at dawn.” What could be more delightful than such an answer? What heart could be readier than that of one so answering? Thus the reason should not escape us why the beginning of the same psalm had sounded in this manner in her person: “My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready” (Ps. 56 [57]). O heart, how delightfully ready, how willingly raised to receive the command of divinity—the sweet command that says, “Awake.” Indeed, this is to have a ready heart: to answer thus, “I will arise at dawn.” But was her heart ready only, or had it been ready only, for this? Surely it was ready also [Col. 1485C] to obey unto death. It was altogether ready to give its body to those who struck it, its cheeks to those who plucked them, not to turn its face away from those reproaching and spitting upon it, and to endure all things unto death—even death on a cross (Phil. 2). “But I,” it says, “do not resist; I have not turned backward.” It was fitting, therefore, that the heart which had been ready to obey its Father, who did not spare it for our sake, should be ready to answer, “I will arise at dawn.” Thus, I say, the reason should not escape us why the psalm’s beginning had sounded thus, “My heart is ready,” and why, not content to say it once, it said both once and again: “My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready” (Ps. 56 [57]; 107 [108]).

## CHAPTER XXVIII. “An obedient man speaks victories”: said concerning Christ.

Is this man, then, not he of whom Wisdom says: “An obedient man speaks victories” (Prov. 21)? Indeed, although there are or have been many men who are sons of obedience, this is the one man, unique and singular, to whom there has not been, is not, nor will be any other like him—obedient in a similar or equal matter. He alone is an obedient man in this: although wholly without sin, he humbled himself by the will of the Father for the sins of others, and humbled himself unto death—even death on a cross (Phil. 2). It is fitting, therefore, that he, now the obedient man, should speak victories; and behold, he speaks them in a speech [Col. 1486A] unceasing and everlasting. What sort of speech is this? Surely it is exceedingly clear and exceedingly resonant, because he himself is the display of his wounds, which he received in that very obedience. His five wounds are like five tongues; he retained and preserved in his body the scars of his wounds in order that he might always speak his victories through them as though through tongues. To whom does he speak? Truly, first to God the Father; then to angels and human beings, to all the saints and all the elect. God the Father sees and delights in these beautiful testimonies of victory. The angels see and are stirred to praise and glory. Redeemed human beings see, and their thanksgivings are extended without ceasing.

## CHAPTER XXIX. The five wounds of Christ are seals of righteousness.

We say with the Apostle, and understand the meaning of the Apostle as he says it, that the patriarch Abraham received and handed down to his descendants the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of faith. For he believed, as one faithful to God who said: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22), although he had no son and was already an old man, while his wife was old and barren. That circumcision was a testimony to a great matter, a great seal of faith; and it proclaimed before God the palm of great righteousness for Abraham himself and for his descendants, reminding God of his promise, lest, ever offended, he should somehow evade giving the seed in whom “all nations would be blessed,” when he saw the memorial seal [Col. 1486C] of that promise, which declared him faithful and true.

But behold, here are several seals—seals of righteousness and faith—namely, the five wounds which this obedient man, the righteous and faithful man, received for the condition of human salvation. For the condition, I say, of human salvation: for the prophet himself well knew that such a condition had been laid before him: “If he shall lay down his soul as an offering for sin, he shall see a long-lived seed, and the will of the Lord shall prosper in his hand. Because his soul has laboured, he shall see and be satisfied. By his knowledge the righteous one himself shall justify many of my servants, and he himself shall bear their iniquities” (Isa. 57 [53]). Does not righteous divinity therefore rightly grant to us, his descendants, the palm of justification and salvation [Col. 1486D] when it sees not merely one seal, or one wound as a seal of righteousness, such as was the wound of circumcision, but the five wounds of the righteous one, suffering for whatever our flesh had sinned through its five senses? For we have gently received in baptism these seals of righteousness or faith which he received painfully; and just as, with the testimony of the one seal—that is, circumcision—he was awaited as the one who would come to redeem humankind, so now he is awaited by us, bearing the seal of the five wounds—that is, of the cross—imprinted upon our foreheads, as one who will return to judge the living and the dead.

# BOOK THIRTEEN

[Col. 1487]

## CHAPTER I. How the woman’s son was caught up to God and to his throne.

See how this dragon, who for so many years and generations stood before the woman who was to give birth, in order to devour her son when she had borne him, was deceived. He was deceived because the woman bore the one whom she was to bear, and her son was caught up to God and to his throne. How was he caught up? Who caught him up? He was caught up when the pains of hell were loosed, since it was impossible that he should be held by it. God caught him up, God raised him; the Word of God caught him up to God the Father. From where did he catch him up? From the confines of hell; from beneath the great stone of the tomb. Beneath the stones God put his hand; God brought in his word, and [Col. 1487B] caught up that body, the body restored to life, as easily from a closed tomb as he could have caught it up from a tomb unclosed or open. O foolish and blind men, who said that they knew God and had set a stone against God! For if they had known the Lord God, they would never have hoped that a single stone could resist God’s will. And he said: “My Father, who glorifies me, whom you say is our God—and you have not known him” (John 8). But let us return to the matter.

## CHAPTER II. What it is to be caught up to God and to his throne; and what is meant by “Paul, an apostle, not from human beings nor through a human being, but through Jesus Christ.”

[Col. 1487C] “He was caught up,” it says, “to God and to his throne.” Two things were said, and had to be said: for he was caught up to God, and he was caught up to his throne. For he both rose again and ascended into heaven. By rising again he was caught up to God; by ascending into heaven he was caught up to his throne. Indeed, by rising again he became in flesh, as he was in divinity, immortal and incapable of suffering; and the fullness of divinity dwelling in that flesh was established for that same flesh with such firmness that, as the Apostle recalls, “having risen from the dead, he dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. 6). Therefore now not only according to the divinity of the Word, but also according to itself, the assumed humanity is proclaimed God, as is likewise proved from the same [Col. 1487D] Apostle, writing thus to the Laodiceans: “Paul, an apostle, not from human beings nor through a human being, but through Jesus Christ.” For what follows if it is not through a human being, but through Jesus Christ? Does it not follow that he says that Jesus Christ, at the time when he called him or made him an Apostle, had already ceased to be human and was God? Yet the orthodox Fathers, in saying these things, do not remove human nature from him, but confess the surpassing divine glory of human [Col. 1488A] nature. For since Jesus Christ rose again, he is truly human by nature, as he was; but he is God in glory. Moreover, when, in the presence of his disciples, he was taken up from them, ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of God, what is this but the Son’s being caught up to the throne of God?

## CHAPTER III. Although he was caught up to God and to his throne, the promise “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” had not yet been wholly fulfilled.

Therefore, according to the faithful and humble prayer of David confessing and repenting, you are justified, O God, in all your words and prevail when you are judged: for as you swore to him, you fulfilled truth and did not disappoint him, because his seed was caught up to [Col. 1488B] you and to your throne. Yet what you swore to Abraham you had not completed unto consummation. For this word was a promise—indeed, a reiterated promise—to him: “By myself I have sworn, because you have done this thing and have not spared your only-begotten son for my sake, I will bless you and multiply your seed like the stars of heaven and like the sand upon the seashore. Your seed shall possess the gates of its enemies, and in your seed all nations of the earth shall be blessed, because you have obeyed my voice” (Gen. 22). All these things, indeed, except one, had been fulfilled when Jesus Christ, the seed of Abraham, was taken up into heaven to God’s throne; for Abraham’s seed had truly been multiplied in the holy patriarchs and prophets like the stars of heaven. For they are the stars which that same eternal Sun, raised into heaven, took up with himself; and that seed possessed the gates of its enemies, namely, evil spirits, as he says: “I was dead, and behold, I am alive, and I have the keys of death and hell” (Rev. 1). Yet a great part remained—a part desirable and necessary for us—which was set aside for us Gentiles in this declaration, repeated once and again: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22). To fulfill this part, the twelve apostles had been chosen and preserved, as he himself says: “If, therefore, you seek me, let these go.” So that the word might be fulfilled, [Col. 1488D] says the Evangelist, which he had spoken: “Of those whom you gave me, I have lost none” (John 18). Where had he said this? At the supper itself, shortly before that very hour in which, when he was seized, all the disciples deserted him and fled. “Those whom you gave me,” he says, “I have kept, and none of them has perished except the son of perdition”; and immediately he added: “That the Scripture might be fulfilled” (John 17). Although this may rightly be understood thus—that the one man perished in order that the Scripture might be fulfilled, since it did not pass over his perdition in silence—yet in view of the present argument it is more pleasing to understand it as though he had said: I preserved these men, none of them perished, and they are all unharmed, not only in soul but also in body, so that they might be those through whom Scripture would be fulfilled, through whose ministry the blessing promised in Abraham’s seed might be bestowed upon all nations. From what sacraments, and from what sources, the work of that blessing was to be accomplished—and is accomplished even now—has already been said above. It remains now to say how, against the will and resistance of the oft-mentioned dragon, the omnipotent divinity, the divine omnipotence, of the incarnate Word conquered also in this part of its work or purpose, casting out in the Holy Spirit the gods of the nations, who all were and are demons.

## CHAPTER IV. How the woman fled into the wilderness.

“And the woman fled into the wilderness, where she has a place prepared by God, that they might feed her there for one thousand two hundred and sixty days. And there was a great battle in heaven: Michael and all his angels fought with the dragon; and the dragon fought, and his angels” (Rev. 12), and so forth. After the woman’s male child was caught up to God and to his throne, she fled into the wilderness. That is: after Christ ascended into heaven, his mother—that portion of his people from which he is according to the flesh, namely, the Church of apostolic or apostolically perfected character, wholly gathered from the Jews—left worldly business behind, as the Acts of the Apostles testify, so that no one called anything his own, but all things were held in common among them. For this is to flee into the wilderness: to leave behind every care of the flesh or worldly concern apart from food and clothing. Those who were and are such persons needed, or need, to be supported by common alms for one thousand two hundred and sixty days, for the sake of the Gospel, or by the example of the Lord himself, who, while preaching the Gospel with his disciples for so many days, lived from the Gospel.

With such a beginning was commenced this battle, concerning which it says: “There was a great battle in heaven.” For the apostles and all who shared in apostolic grace, full of grace and strength, full of faith and the spirit of wisdom, undertook a great battle against the dragon, who was exulting as though in heaven, going into the whole world and preaching the Gospel to every creature. This indeed was for a battle to take place in heaven: that is, in those who had been foreordained or predestined to become heaven, or a seat, for God their Creator. For when the dragon, the devil, reigned in them or over them, demanding divine honours from them as though he were God, when he was worshipped by them in temples or before images, he foolishly supposed that he was in heaven and was like the Most High. And this was done so that he, expelled from altars and dragged from shrines, should first give place to God in the minds of persons deceived by error—just as happened long ago, when, on account of pride, he was cast out from the higher and invisible heaven.

## CHAPTER V. How Michael and his angels fought against the dragon.

Let us consider the great miracle of this great battle: what kind of battle it was, what forces stood against one another, and with what weapons they fought. “Michael,” it says, “and his angels fought with the dragon; and the dragon fought, and his angels” (Rev. 12). With what weapons did these men, and those men, fight? Surely the former—Michael and his angels—with the weapons of heavenly powers; the latter with the laws of kings, decrees of emperors, the fury of Gentiles, and the cruel hands of executioners. With such instruments the dragon and his angels fought. But Michael and his angels, being ministering [Col. 1490B] spirits, supplied the preachers of the Gospel with every kind of working of miracles: so that in Christ’s name they might cast out demons, take up serpents, lay hands upon the sick and heal them, raise the dead, and perform whatever other signs appeared necessary or suitable to confirm the word. When these were fighting, the dragon and his angels who fought against them did not prevail; nor was a place found for them any longer in heaven. For they could retain none of those who had been foreordained to life. Although kings and priests, persuaded by them—ungodly kings and priests, themselves dead, of the dead—killed their bodies, although in zeal for demons, lest I say their gods, they scattered their bodies with countless punishments, they could not harm Christ’s souls or assist the dragon and his angels in preventing their defeated fall from this heaven also: that is, in preventing them from losing the worship that resembled divine religion. Hence comes that voice, the great voice of praise which we heard in heaven—that is, in the Church: “Now have come salvation, power, the kingdom of our God, and the authority of his Christ, because the accuser of our brethren has been cast down, he who accused them before the presence of our God day and night. And they conquered him because of the blood of the Lamb and the word of their testimony, and they did not love their lives even unto death” (Rev. 12).

## CHAPTER VI. How the dragon, cast down to the earth, sent water from his mouth.

“And when the dragon saw that he had been cast down to the earth, he persecuted the woman who had borne the male child.” And afterwards: “The serpent sent from his mouth after the woman water like a river, to make her be swept away by the river” (Rev. 12). When or how did the dragon see that he had been cast down to earth? Surely when Roman emperors, abandoning the profane worship of ancient idolatry, submitted themselves to the kingdom of our God and to the authority of his Christ, and when the other kings and rulers of the earth, together with the peoples subject to them, became Christians. Then the dragon saw; then the devil perceived that he had been cast down to earth—that is, that he had no power to defend for himself the vain glory of a divinity he had presumptuously claimed. Therefore he changed the manner [Col. 1491A] of his persecution and began to persecute otherwise than he had previously persecuted the woman who bore the male child: that is, the Church, which, according to the promises repeatedly mentioned, brought forth from its flesh the man Christ. For although, in one respect, the Church of the one Israelite people before Christ’s coming is different from the Church of the nations after Christ’s coming, nevertheless in faith the Church of Jews and Gentiles, those preceding and those following, is one and unique Church.

How did he persecute her? He sent water from his mouth like a river, in order to make her be swept away by the river. This is the same as saying more plainly that he devised heretical doctrines through whose evasions the ecclesiastical faith might be corrupted. Whoever knows or reads ecclesiastical histories does not doubt that this happened as it is said. Arius, the very well-known founder of a heresy, was nothing but the serpent’s mouth at the time when Constantine, Helena’s son, had taken refuge in faith in Christ. Through that mouth the serpent sent water like a river—that is, the doctrine of a most evil heresy—like speech living and effective and flowing from the living fountain of the Scriptures. He was not the first or the only mouth of the serpent of this sort; but among all those through whom that serpent poured forth the abundance of his iniquity, he was the most foul and harmful.

## CHAPTER VII. How this water first crept in secretly, then gained strength by degrees and spread through the four quarters of the world.

This monstrous evil of that utterly perverse doctrine first crept in secretly; then, gaining strength by degrees, it spread through the four quarters of the world—east, west, north, and south—and nearly filled Asia, Europe, and Africa. It also armed itself with the swords of kings and emperors against the Catholic faith, and brutally shed much blood of those who had gone before. Scripture seems to indicate this when, in connection with this affair, it first calls the devil, the father of lies, a serpent, and then, as it had previously done, calls him a dragon. For it says: “The serpent sent from his mouth after the woman water like a river”; and then, it says, “the earth opened its mouth and swallowed the river, and the dragon was angry with the woman” (Rev. 12). For at first heretical treachery, such as this Arian teaching—which taught that the Son is less than the Father and the Holy Spirit less than the Son—arose secretly at Alexandria. Through Arius’s disciples or accomplices it moved by slippery turns and sophistical windings; then, bringing forth its head publicly for the people’s hearing, it hissed. When Alexander, the bishop, resisted its wickedness, it poured from its mouth the water of evil doctrine upon neighbouring cities and the bishops of those cities. It was not truly a river, but like a river: that is, it possessed eloquence or copious, overflowing verbosity, but did not know the fountain of truth. It misused the words of Scripture and thereby showed simple people a certain likeness to a river—that is, to sound doctrine. At last, as has been said, the devil, father of lies, having gained the favour of kings and queens, emperors and empresses, began to rage with tongues; strengthened thereby with swords, he stirred more violently, as a dragon—that is, being made greater—the water which he had sent from his mouth as a serpent, so as to make the woman be swept away by the river: that is, to compel the Church to agree with him.

## CHAPTER VIII. How the earth helped the woman and swallowed the river.

“But the earth helped the woman; the earth opened its mouth and swallowed the river which the dragon had sent from his mouth.” This occurred as it is said. For then the fervour of Emperor Constantine convened that most famous council at Nicaea, commanding bishops and those with them to come to the synod by public asses, mules, and swift horses. You may rightly understand that council, which strengthened the Catholic faith, as the earth that helped the woman: for they assembled from the whole earth, and in a certain sense the entire earth changed its place by sending suitable persons from all its regions to the appointed location. From all the Churches which had filled all Europe, Libya, and Asia, the leading men among God’s ministers were gathered together; and one house of prayer, as though borne there by God, received them all within itself: Syrians together with Cilicians; Phoenicians, Arabs, and Palestinians; Egyptians and Thebans; Libyans, and also those who came from Mesopotamia. A Persian also came, nor was Scythia absent; Pontus and Asia, Phrygia and Pamphylia provided most excellent men. Thracians and Macedonians were present; and, to put it briefly, devout men were gathered and present from every nation under heaven. The multitude of bishops numbered three hundred and eighteen, followed by presbyters, deacons, and acolytes, whose number could not be reckoned. What else, then, but that the earth, as has been said, “opened its mouth and swallowed the dragon’s river,” when so many men summoned from the entire earth, adorned with wisdom, eloquence, and other virtues, opened their mouths in united defence of the truth, destroyed the impious doctrine, and unanimously formulated and confirmed by subscriptions the faith and glory which has remained in the Church to this day?

## CHAPTER IX. The dragon’s seventh head, wounded to death by the stroke of a sword.

Concerning the dragon’s six heads, it is therefore established that in all of them he has long since been conquered; and God, righteous in his words and victorious in his judgments, has obtained the palm of truth. For, as he promised and swore, David’s seed remains for ever; as he promised and swore, “in Abraham’s seed all nations shall be blessed.” And the dragon has not been able, nor can he be able, through pagans, heretics, or Jews to prevent the blessing of all nations. But who can sufficiently wonder at the madness of the devil’s obstinacy and burning envy? “And the dragon,” Scripture says, “was angry with the woman and proceeded to make war with the rest of her seed, those who keep the commandments of God and have the testimony of Jesus. And he stood upon the sand of the sea” (Rev. 12), says the same man who saw the preceding things: “and I saw a beast rising from the sea, having seven heads and ten horns, and upon its horns ten diadems, and upon its heads names of blasphemy. The beast that I saw was like a leopard, its feet like a bear’s, and its mouth like a lion’s mouth. And the dragon gave it his power and great authority. And one of its heads was as though slain unto death, and its mortal wound was healed” (Rev. 13). This seven-headed beast is the dragon himself. The preceding discussion has treated of his six heads as overcome while warring against the Word of God; here the seventh head is marked with a remarkable weight of expression when it says: “And one [Col. 1493B] of its heads was as though slain unto death, and its mortal wound was healed, and the whole earth marvelled after the beast” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER X. How its mortal wound was healed.

That head will without doubt be Antichrist, in whom will blaze forth the dragon’s final wrath, of which it was said: “And the dragon was angry with the woman and proceeded to make war with the rest of her seed” (Rev. 12). What, then, does it mean that this head is said to be as though slain unto death, and that “its mortal wound was healed”? Again, Scripture later says “that it has the wound of a sword and lived.” Where did it receive the sword-wound? How was its wound healed, or how did it live? (Rev. 13). Certainly, though other things may suitably be said, because definite testimonies of sacred Scripture are lacking, this understanding is more pleasing: long ago it received in heaven the sentence of eternal condemnation. This is the wound of sword and death in that head. For that man of sin, the son of perdition, will not be merely a human being, but also the devil; his coming will be Satan’s working, the working of error. I mean the devil, or Satan, who opposes and exalts himself above everything called God or worshipped, so that he sits in the temple of God, displaying himself as though he were God. When this being fell from heaven through pride, without doubt he received the wound of the sword, the wound of death. As Ezekiel says against him under the name of Asshur or Pharaoh: “Behold, you have been brought down with the trees of delight to the lowest earth; in the midst of the uncircumcised you shall sleep with those slain by the sword” (Ezek. 31).

But how was its mortal wound healed? How does it have the wound of so great a sword and yet live? Its wound was surely healed falsely, and it lived falsely. The healing of its wound is the defence of its fault; and to live in the sword-wound is for it to be proud in punishment itself. For the marvel and the abomination of this presumptuous being consist in this: though struck down and made a devil, he exalts himself and presents himself as though he were God. For when the devil wishes to show himself to be God, what does he do but claim, though dead, to be alive? One may take an example of this marvel from any imitator of his. When someone is expelled from the Church by a just judgment because of his fault, and then, lifted up in pride and defending his deeds, accuses the judges themselves of being unjust while he is righteous, then surely his wound has been unhappily healed and he lives deceitfully: unrighteous in God’s judgment, but righteous in his own.

## CHAPTER XI. That this head is Antichrist, to whom the dragon gave his power and great authority.

Words do not suffice to grasp the matter, especially when we hear that the dragon gave him his own power and great authority. What does this mean? To what does the devil tend even in this? Does he suppose that by this he will become like the Most High? For the Most High, the Ancient of Days, when, as we read in Daniel, “thrones were set, and he sat; and behold, one like a Son of Man came in the clouds of heaven, came even to him, and they presented him before his presence, and he gave him power, honour, and a kingdom” (Dan. 7)—does the perverse imitator, by giving his power and great authority to that beast or man of sin, still say, “I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. 14)? That is: as God did what was his own in Christ, so I shall do what is mine in Antichrist.

Who, observing this, would not marvel what kind of purpose has proceeded from the human race unto the end or consummation: on this side, God’s good purpose; on that, the opposing evil of the resisting devil? From one and the same mass one has arisen who is God and human; and another will come who is devil and human. In the former God’s goodness is proclaimed; in the latter the devil’s perversity is recognized. Nothing is better than the former; nothing worse than the latter. The former is God, blessed above all; the latter is devil, cursed beneath all. In the former God was well pleased with himself and will be well pleased for ever; in the latter, the devil, pleased with himself, will appear foolish after he has been raised on high. The former descended from heaven and rose from lowly things like a shoot, and like a root from thirsty ground. The latter fell from heaven and will rise from all the children of pride like a beast from the sea.

## CHAPTER XII. What the Apostle means by “And now you know what restrains, so that he may be revealed in his own time”; and concerning the mystery of the woman riding the beast.

The devil does not delay of his own will, nor does Antichrist come late by his own choosing; rather, against his will he is restrained, though he is inclined and swift toward every evil. “And now you know what restrains,” says the Apostle (2 Thess. 2). What is this? Namely, that his time has not yet come. This must be understood: God has placed times in the power not of this being or of any other, but in his own power alone. For the passage continues: “So that he may be revealed in his own time” (ibid.). This is as if he said: heavenly power restrains one impatient of delay and already desiring to be revealed, so that he is revealed only in his own time. To show how unwillingly he is restrained, how quickly he would wish to be revealed: “Already,” he says, “the mystery of iniquity is at work” (ibid.)—that is, as far as it can, especially through Nero’s cruelty. Though Nero was evil, the devil was nevertheless able to do less in him than he will be able to do in this one, “with every power and signs and lying wonders, and with every seduction of iniquity” (2 Thess. 2).

How long is he delayed, or what marks his time? “Only,” says the Apostle, “let the one who now restrains restrain, until he is taken out of the way” (ibid.). When the Apostle wrote this to the Thessalonians, who was restraining, and what was being restrained? Surely the Roman king, or Caesar, held the empire of the world. He does not speak of one individual man—for example Nero—but of all the rulers of the Roman Empire, who, although many in number, are nevertheless one in imperial authority. This interpretation is established not only by reason but also by authority. For later the angel says to the same John: “Why do you marvel? I will tell you the mystery of the woman and of the beast that carries her, which has seven heads and ten horns. The seven heads are seven mountains upon which the woman sits, and they are seven kings. Five have fallen, one is, and another has not yet come; and when he comes, he must remain for a short time” (Rev. 17). For the seven-headed beast, both here where the woman—that is, desire—sits upon the beast, and there where the beast rose from the sea, is the whole body of the ungodly. As has already been demonstrated above, in the lengthy treatment of the seven-headed dragon, the seven heads are seven kingdoms through which this beast or dragon exercises its force against the word of promise. Therefore, when it says, “The seven heads are seven kings; five have fallen, one is, and another has not yet come,” the seven kings must be understood as all the rulers of those same kingdoms, or “seven kings” is written in place of the seven kingdoms. “Five have fallen,” it says: namely, the Egyptian, Israelite, Babylonian, Persian, and Macedonian; “one is,” the sixth, namely the Roman; and “another has not yet come”: he will be Antichrist.

## CHAPTER XIII. Why the Apostle spoke so obscurely: “Only let the one who restrains now restrain, until he is taken out of the way.”

Thus enough was said for the wise in the words, “Only let the one who now restrains restrain, until he is taken out of the way” (2 Thess. 2); and the foolish were given no opportunity which they might have seized if he had said more plainly: “Let Rome, which now holds power,” or “let the Roman Empire, which now holds power, hold the nations subject to itself until it is taken out of the way, or until the falling-away occurs.” For human pride wished Rome to be an eternal city and the Roman Empire everlasting; and consequently nowhere would any devout person hear blasphemy against God with greater impatience than would Roman rulers or soldiers if the end of the Roman Empire were proclaimed through Christ’s Gospel. The Gospel’s preachers offended them sufficiently—indeed, more than sufficiently—even while “giving no offence to anyone” (2 Cor. 6); how much more if they had publicly proclaimed in advance that future falling-away?

Let these brief remarks suffice concerning the difficulty of the apostolic expression. Moreover, how long the one who restrains must continue to restrain, after how many years he must be taken out of the way or the falling-away must come, ought not to have been written—especially because of the same caution. Perhaps it was not even revealed to the Apostle when this would occur, or after how many years that lawless one must be revealed; just as it was not revealed to Daniel. When Daniel said to the man clothed in linen, “How long until the end of these wonders?” (Dan. 12), and again, “My lord, what will be after these things?” he was not given the answer he sought, but heard this: “Go, Daniel, for the words are closed and sealed until the appointed time” (ibid.). The Saviour himself likewise says to the disciples asking about times: “It is not for you to know the times or seasons which the Father has placed in his own power” (Acts 1).

## Chapter XIV. How great a wrath the dragon will stir up through Antichrist, and that the Lord Jesus will slay him by the breath of His mouth

No one can adequately set forth in words the dragon’s wrath, which he will exercise through that man of sin, that son of perdition—being enraged against the woman so often mentioned, and going forth to make war upon the rest of her seed. For the event will surpass human speech, indeed even human thought; especially since the Lord Himself foretold it in His own words: “For then,” He says, “there will be great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning of the world until now, nor ever will be. And unless those days had been shortened, no flesh would have been saved; but for the sake of the elect those days will be shortened” (Matt. XXIV).

Therefore, since this discourse too, now prolonged, is drawing toward its end, and one speaking or writing must take care lest excessive length produce weariness in reader or hearer, we must come to that in which lies the completion of the conflict recounted: the completion of the victory of the Word of God. What is that? Surely, the destruction of that wicked one, and the judicial throne or session of the Son of Man, Jesus Christ, as He Himself briefly indicates after foretelling that great tribulation: “And then,” He says, “they shall see the Son of Man coming in the clouds with great power and majesty, with abundant might and glory” (ibid.).

What, then, will be the destruction of that wicked one? “The Lord Jesus,” says the Apostle, “will slay him with the breath of His mouth” (II Thess. II), just as it had been foretold through the prophet: “And with the breath of His lips He will slay the wicked” (Isa. XI). Indeed, we read that the Lord has slain many people; yet we do not now recall that this was said of any person—that He slew him with the breath of His mouth or the breath of His lips—except that ungodly, wicked one.

Must the Holy Spirit, who is the Spirit of the Lord Jesus, therefore be sent against him because of his unique greatness and excessive strength, so that the wicked one cannot otherwise be slain unless the Spirit of the Lord Himself rushes upon him? But this Holy Spirit, the Spirit of the Lord Jesus, does not ordinarily exert Himself to kill; He is customarily sent only to give life. For death is not in Him, since He is rather life itself.

The phrase “the breath of the mouth,” or “of the lips,” of the Lord Jesus must therefore be understood otherwise. This will be done more fittingly if we bring forward here also that prophetic utterance: “Cry.” And I said, “What shall I cry? All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of the field. The grass has withered, and the flower has fallen, because the Spirit of God has blown upon it” (Isa. XL).

Every living human being—and what, I ask, is easier for you than to blow? What is weaker before you than that which you can cast down merely by blowing? Thus, from your own example, it is easy to observe how truly mighty is the Lord Jesus, whose name is the Word of God, the Word who is God; and how truly even that living man will be sheer vanity (Ps. XXXVIII)—the greatest tyrant of the entire human race, a diabolical tyrant. For as easily as you disperse by blowing a strand of a spider’s web, so easily—indeed, more easily—will He slay that wicked one, notwithstanding the many conjectures customarily made on this point. By this interpretation, I think, one may be set free.

## Chapter XV. After Antichrist has been slain, the victory of the Word of God is complete

After Antichrist has been slain, and a few—namely forty-five—days have intervened, as is inferred from Daniel’s vision, the Lord will come in His majesty; and “the last enemy of all, death, shall be destroyed” (I Cor. XV).

How will it be destroyed? “The Lord Himself,” says the Apostle, “at the command, and at the voice of an archangel, and at the trumpet of God, will descend from heaven; and the dead who are in Christ will rise first. Then we who live, who remain, shall together with them be caught up in the clouds to meet Christ in the air; and so we shall always be with the Lord” (I Thess. IV).

That destruction of death will be the consummation of the victory of the Word of God, the consummation of God’s purpose, when the triumphant Word of God says: “Come, blessed of My Father; inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. XXV).

When He says “from the foundation of the world,” this means from that time or day when the world was being established in the creation of the human race, when, after the first two had been created, He said: “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” (Gen. I). For, since there were only two, in saying to them, “Increase and multiply,” He had in view that multitude which will stand at the right hand; and He was then preparing for them a kingdom whose predetermined number would receive the kingdom of God.

For those multiplied beyond that number, who will stand at the left hand, do not belong to the Creator’s blessing and would not have been born had not the cause of sin intervened. After sin had been committed, He said to the woman: “I will multiply your sorrows and your conceptions” (Gen. III). Thus there will be an apt remembrance of the world’s foundation and of the blessing by which He blessed all His elect, saying: “Increase and multiply.” And the saying of the triumphant One will furnish a great and ineffable subject of praise for angels and holy human beings alike: “Come, blessed of My Father; inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.”

Then every soul will truly be praised in the Lord, and then the meek who hear will rejoice (Ps. XXXIII). Rejoicing, they will marvel that the first blessing, amid so many thorns of curses, concerning which or against which we have treated in this present little work, could not perish or be rendered empty. They will see that none of all God’s elect is lacking, through the care and providence of Him who foreknew them, predestined them, called and justified them, and glorified them through the grace of that same Son (Rom. VIII), through the incarnation, passion, and resurrection of that same Word, to whose image they were predestined to be conformed (ibid.).

## Chapter XVI. What is meant by the saying addressed to blessed Job: “Behold, his hope shall deceive him”

Then that saying concerning the dragon so often mentioned, addressed to blessed Job, will appear true: “Behold, his hope shall deceive him, and in the sight of all he shall be cast down” (Job XL). At the same time all the wicked will be cast down with him, when the triumphant One and Judge says to those who will be at His left hand: “Depart from Me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV).

How will He cast them down? Certainly, what the Apostle said concerning the one man of sin, the son of perdition, Antichrist—“The Lord Jesus will slay him with the breath of His mouth” (II Thess. II)—He intends, and we must nonetheless understand Him, to mean also of the devil and his angels and of all wicked human beings: even if He has not said it in the same words or syllables, He will cast them down by the breath of His mouth; that is, as easily as you disperse into the air a small amount of dust or smoke merely by blowing.

For, as has already been said above regarding the ease of the Almighty, who does not labor in doing anything, the Apostle said that “the Lord Jesus will slay that wicked one with the breath of His mouth”; and the prophet had said, “With the breath of His lips He will slay the wicked.” If authority is sought for the condemnation of all the wicked—that they are to be cast down with the same ease—behold, another prophet also said, as was mentioned above: “All flesh is grass; the grass has withered and the flower has fallen, because the Spirit of God has blown upon it” (Isa. XL). And it is written in Job: “Indeed, I have seen those who work iniquity and sow sorrows reap them; they perish by the blast of God and are consumed by the breath of His wrath” (Job IV).

## Chapter XVII. What it means for something to be done by the breath of the Lord’s mouth

The almighty Word also made, and makes, all good things with the same ease; He will also accomplish the resurrection of the dead. Yet the Holy Spirit of Scripture is not accustomed to use such language of blowing or exhaling concerning these things. Rather, it is against pride that He customarily speaks in this way, as there: “Your spirit blew, and the sea covered them” (Exod. XV).

If someone objects that it is also written: “His spirit blew, and the waters shall flow” (Ps. CXLVII), the answer is readily given: this is not said of the spirit of wrath, but of the Spirit of grace. Although it is easy for God to pierce a sinner’s heart, “His spirit blew” is not said so much to indicate that ease as to suggest the sweetness of the divine fire: when it touches a cold heart by breathing upon it, it tempers and softens it as a warm south wind melts ice.

For He had first said: “Who can endure before His cold?” Then He immediately added: “He will send forth His word and melt them; His spirit will blow and the waters shall flow” (Ps. CXLVII).

## Chapter XVIII. He proves by examples how easily the Word of God can do all things

Why do we say more, as though anyone could doubt this ease? The One who is to judge has supplied sufficient proofs of how easily, when He comes as Judge in His majesty, He will do the things that have been said.

First, this is proof of the ease with which He will raise the dead: Lazarus had been in the tomb four days, and He uttered only one cry: “Lazarus,” He said, “come forth”; “and immediately he who had been dead came out” (John XI). When did he come out, or in what condition? “Bound hand and foot with bandages, and his face was bound with a cloth” (ibid.).

The Evangelist fittingly recorded this, and it somewhat serves our present purpose: namely, because the voice of Him who called had a most effortless power, which both gave Lazarus life and drove him from the tomb at the same time. For, bound hand and foot with bandages, he could crawl out neither with his feet nor with his hands.

If proof is sought also concerning the forgiveness of sins, which is the first resurrection—how easy it is for that same Word, the Son of God, the Son of Man, Jesus Christ, to accomplish both in the present age and in the age to come—behold it appears in Mary Magdalene, sister of that same Lazarus. While she too was still mortal, still subject to judgment, dead in soul and already stinking with infamy, He brought her out of the tomb of an evil conscience. He did so without uttering even the voice by which He called Lazarus from the tomb; indeed, He was bodily absent from her.

For unless she who had been dead had come out from the tomb, she would not have come before His presence in that wonderful manner. And where He said to her, “Your faith has made you whole; go in peace,” the Evangelist immediately said “that seven demons had gone out from her” (Luke VII).

Therefore, since in speaking of the ease with which He works salvation and performs judgment we have used the support of Holy Scripture concerning the word “exhaling,” would I not rightly say also that He expelled those seven demons from her by exhaling—that is, with the greatest ease—while He was still a human being subject to suffering, mortal, and destined for judgment?

Because it was equally easy for Him to blot out the sins of the whole Church, of which she bore the type, it may be supposed that, when He rose from the dead and stood in the midst of His disciples, He breathed upon them and immediately said: “Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them” (John XX).

Not that, without breathing, He could not give the Holy Spirit; but the Word who is God, in accordance with His omnipotence, wished deliberately to signify Himself also in that manner, always and everywhere seeking to fulfill and to prove true whatever had been foretold concerning Him in the Holy Scriptures. Was this not also foretold concerning Him in Isaiah’s person? “You are My servant, Israel; do not forget Me. I have blotted out your iniquities as a cloud, and your sins as a mist” (Isa. XLIV).

For how is a cloud or mist wiped away except most easily, by the passing breath of a clearer breeze? Therefore He did not breathe idly when He gave the Holy Spirit to the disciples with authority to forgive sins; nor do His disciples or ministers breathe vainly while baptizing, as the ecclesiastical custom has it. Rather, they render Him a laborious ministry, so that through their act He may now also say to each person being reborn what He foretold: “I have blotted out your iniquities as a cloud, and your sins as a mist.”

## Chapter XIX. With what ease He will cast down those at the left hand with the devil and his angels

Further, concerning the casting down by which He will cast down those at the left hand—that is, the wicked—with the devil and his angels: concerning this, as has already been said, the Lord says to blessed Job, “And in the sight of all he shall be cast down” (Job XL). The word “breathing” indicates that this will be as easy for Him to do as it is to breathe.
