Likewise, this is a true proof: while He was still subject to suffering and death, and was continually about to suffer and die, He cast down merely by His look the armed cohort of the governor and the servants of the chief priests and Pharisees. For when He said to them, “I am He,” they went backward and fell to the ground.

But perhaps someone will say that they were few. At the resurrection of the dead, however, when He judges the world, there will be innumerable multitudes. Will He then cast all of them down as easily as He cast down those few? Such a suggestion, if it touches anyone, is rightly convicted of excessive folly.

Both things are reasonable enough if the Lord had cast down that cohort merely by laying a hand upon them, or by doing something like what Samson, one man, did when he struck and cast down a thousand armed and strong men with an ass’s jawbone. But since He cast them down merely by saying, “I am He,” reason agrees that the whole world has only as much power against Him as that cohort—or as one human being.

And if it is asked what proof He gave, while still mortal and subject to judgment, that He will cast the devil and his angels into hell with the same ease as human beings, behold: that legion is sufficient proof. Possessing one man, it begged that same Lord not to torment it and not command it to go into the abyss. With the same ease, surely, He will execute judgment upon all the legions of demons, upon the devil, and upon his angels. They will not even have time to beg that they not be sent into the abyss or into hell, because the almighty Word will swiftly cast them down in chains.

## Chapter XX. What is meant by the saying in Isaiah: “The light of the moon shall be as the light of the sun, and the light of the sun sevenfold, as the light of seven days”

What will follow these things except the everlasting festivity of triumph and the joy of God, rejoicing in His works, a joy that will never end? What will be the joy or festivity of that triumph? What will the triumphant One be like—the Word who is God, God and man, Jesus Christ—seated in His majesty? What will the company of His nobles, His veteran soldiers, be like around Him? With what splendor will His whole triumphant court shine? Who can now proclaim to us, even in some small measure, that condition, unless the Word of the Lord, revealing Himself through the prophets, does so?

Behold, something from His prophetic revelations occurs here which accords with all proclamations of that eternal blessedness, that blessed eternity which follows the great and terrible judgment and will remain forever for that King who is God and man, and for all angels and human beings united through Him. In Isaiah, after the preceding words, “For the Lord is a God of judgment; blessed are all who wait for Him,” there follows shortly afterward: “And the light of the moon shall be as the light of the sun, and the light of the sun sevenfold, as the light of seven days” (Isa. XXX), on the day when the Lord “shall bind up the wound of His people and heal the blow of their stroke.”

What, I ask, is the wound of the Lord’s people, and what is their stroke or blow, except the wound of the soul’s death—that is, sin—and the stroke or blow of bodily death, by which the soul departs from the body, together with the wound of that death? The Lord will then heal perfectly both the wound and the stroke or blow of this death, when He says: “Come, blessed of My Father; inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. XXV).

Then the light of the moon will be as the light of the sun. The moon is the Church; the sun is Christ Himself. Now, in the present age, the moon’s light is not as the sun’s light; that is, the Church’s brightness is not like Christ’s brightness. For Christ the sun always shines with His own unfailing light. But the Church, the moon, has no light of her own; she borrows light from Christ the sun. Now she rejoices in increase, now she suffers diminution; but then she will always shine, because she will always have Christ in open vision. This will be for the moon’s light to be as the sun’s light.

“For,” says John, “we know that when He appears, we shall be like Him, because we shall see Him as He is” (I John III). But how great will the light of the sun be? Lest the promise concerning the moon should appear small, when He says, “Its light shall be as the light of the sun,” we must know how great the sun’s light will be. Therefore He says: “And the light of the sun sevenfold, as the light of seven days” (Isa. XXX).

What sort of light, or how great a light, is the light of seven days? “All things,” says the Evangelist, “were made through Him”—all things, I say, “very good,” which were completed on the seventh day. Such will now be the light of the sun, because it will then be manifestly disclosed what the Word is, through whom God made all things in six days and rested on the seventh day.

# ORDER OF THE MATTERS CONTAINED IN THIS VOLUME

## RUPERT, ABBOT OF DEUTZ

Prolegomena to Volume III, 9.

# ON THE GLORIFICATION OF THE TRINITY AND THE PROCESSION OF THE HOLY SPIRIT

## BOOK ONE

**Chapter I.**—That the mystery of the Holy Trinity is a desirable treasure, and that the treasure is hidden in a field, 13.

**Chapter II.**—That the holy Scripture of the Old Testament is that field, and for what reason it is appropriately signified by the name of a field, 15.

**Chapter III.**—How, or to what sort of persons, such a treasure is hidden in such a field; and by what sort it may quickly be found, 16.

**Chapter IV.**—That this treasure, throughout the entire field of Holy Scripture and not in one part of the field only, is hidden from the unworthy and is found, or quickly may be found, by the worthy, 16.

**Chapter V.**—On the opening of the book, “In the beginning God created heaven and earth”: what concealment of this treasure is there, and that the Son is the beginning, as he himself said, “I am the beginning, who also speak to you,” 17.

**Chapter VI.**—Why the Son, or Word of God, ought to be called the beginning, 18.

**Chapter VII.**—On that which the Father says to the Son in the psalm: “With you is the beginning in the day of your power, amid the splendors of the saints; from the womb before Lucifer I begot you,” 19.

**Chapter VIII.**—Likewise, on the reason for the name “beginning,” and on what the Apostle says: “For whom are all things, and through whom are all things,” 20.

**Chapter IX.**—That the title “beginning,” when spoken to the Jews, conveys something higher than if he had said, “I am the Son of God,” or “I am Christ,” 21.

**Chapter X.**—How Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one beginning, and why it was more necessary to know that the person of the Son was seen to be the beginning, 22.

**Chapter XI.**—On the Holy Spirit, or the procession of the Holy Spirit: that it occurred in three ways. First, in creating all things, as was said, “And the Spirit of God was borne over the waters”; second, in order that rational creation might be adorned with spiritual gifts; third, in order that he might be given for the remission of sins, which was not done before Christ’s coming, 23.

**Chapter XII.**—Since both the Father is Spirit and the Son is Spirit, why this substantial name itself—namely, Spirit—is more frequently assigned in Holy Scripture to this one person, 24.

**Chapter XIII.**—On the procession of the Holy Spirit: that the beginning of this procession was the statement that “he was borne over the waters,” and how far this Spirit of God proceeded in his work, 25.

**Chapter XIV.**—Likewise, on the procession of the Holy Spirit: how it differs from the procession of God, since the Son said, “For I proceeded from God and came,” 26.

**Chapter XV.**—What procession, or proceeding, is; and why, speaking of himself, he said in the past tense, “I proceeded,” but of the Holy Spirit he said in the present tense, “He proceeds,” 27.

**Chapter XVI.**—That neither did the Son proceed to create all things without the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, nor does the Holy Spirit proceed to sanctify without the cooperation of the Son, 28.

**Chapter XVII.**—Against those who said that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone and not also from the Son: the statement of Wisdom, “Behold, I shall bring forth my Spirit to you and make my words known to you,” 29.

**Chapter XVIII.**—That the statement which the Son made on the night when he was betrayed strongly supports the same argument of truth: “But I tell you the truth: it is expedient for you that I go away; for if I do not go, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go, I shall send him to you,” 29.

**Chapter XIX.**—Likewise, on the same saying: that the Holy Spirit was then first called the Paraclete, that is, Comforter, because he himself is the remission of sins—which remission of sins he did not formerly give, since Jesus had not yet been glorified, 31.

## BOOK TWO

**Chapter I.**—On the treasure of the Lord’s name, those who treasure it up for themselves being, according to blessed Job, kings and consuls or princes, 31.

**Chapter II.**—That the Spirit proceeds no less from the Son than from the Father; and on the Son’s words, “Whom I shall send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father,” 32.

**Chapter III.**—Likewise, on the same saying against heretics: because it does not follow that the Holy Spirit does not proceed from the Son on account of the statement, “who proceeds from the Father”; rather, it follows that the Holy Spirit is God, who proceeds from the Godhead, 34.

**Chapter IV.**—Likewise, on the same statement: to what end it served that, at that most sacred supper when he was betrayed, not content with saying, “Whom I shall send to you,” he added, “who proceeds from the Father,” 35.

**Chapter V.**—Likewise, that the Son is a fountain of this procession, as is also the Father, the Psalmist saying, “For with you is the fountain of life,” 36.

**Chapter VI.**—That the same argument of truth is served by the cry of that fountain: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink,” and on the opening of that same fountain, 37.

**Chapter VII.**—On the property of that fountain which is with you, O Lord, and on the equivocal uses of “fountains” in Scripture, so that there one may draw waters in joy from the fountains of the Savior, 37.

**Chapter VIII.**—On the Evangelist’s saying, “But this he said concerning the Spirit, whom those believing in him were to receive,” 38.

**Chapter IX.**—That from the belly of one believing in the Son of God proceed only the mysteries of the Scriptures administered through the Holy Spirit; but from that fountain, namely the Son of God, proceeds also the very substance of the Holy Spirit, 39.

**Chapter X.**—On the Holy Spirit himself as proceeding, and on his divine power, according to which it is said: “The Spirit breathes where he wills,” 40.

**Chapter XI.**—On that mode of his breathing by which, breathing where he wills, he penetrates the very substance of the soul and traverses its abyss; and that it is the experience of very few people in this life to feel this condescension, 41.

**Chapter XII.**—That this Paraclete may breathe where the consolation of the present age is neither sought nor received; and on the Lord’s saying, “I shall ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete,” 42.

**Chapter XIII.**—Likewise, on the same condescension of one breathing where he wills, according to that passage in Proverbs: “Do not give wine to kings, O Lemuel; do not give wine to kings. Give strong drink to the sorrowful, and wine to those who are bitter in spirit,” 43.

**Chapter XIV.**—That the sorrow of the saints and their bitterness of spirit arise from great strength of faith, and that for this reason they are worthy of the consolation of the Holy Spirit, 44.

**Chapter XV.**—On the degrees of faith: why great faith, little faith, and least faith are so called for definite reasons in the Lord’s words, 45.

**Chapter XVI.**—Likewise, on the sorrow or bitterness of great faith, and on Solomon’s statement that a heart which knows the bitterness of its own soul is not mingled with a stranger in its joy, 46.

**Chapter XVII.**—On the fact that, after first saying, “The Spirit breathes where he wills,” the Lord adds, “And you hear his voice, but do not know whence he comes or whither he goes”; and that, when he comes, the same Spirit displays some sign appropriate to the grace which he brings, 47.

**Chapter XVIII.**—An account of certain signs with which, in our own days, the Holy Spirit graciously bestowed the visitation of himself upon certain persons, 48.

**Chapter XIX.**—Likewise, on his saying, “And you hear his voice”: that the voice of an inspired person is full of groaning; what it is not to know whence he comes, and what it is not to know whither he goes, 49.

**Chapter XX.**—That in one who groans under inspiration is proved what Truth promised when it said, “Amen, amen, I say to you: if you ask the Father for anything in my name, he will give it to you”; and on the Apostle’s threefold prayer to the Lord, 50.

**Chapter XXI.**—Whether, after this Paraclete has once infused himself by a familiar visitation, it can happen that he withdraws himself and utterly and irrecoverably abandons that soul which he has kissed, 51.

[Col. 1531]

**Chapter XXII.**—That no one ought to have excessive security; and on the Apostle’s words, “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God”; and that David, because he had grieved him, said: “Restore to me the joy of your salvation,” 52.

## BOOK THREE

**Chapter I.**—That we ought to bless the Lord as much as we can, and that he is greater than praise; for many things are hidden and we have seen few of his works, 53.

**Chapter II.**—On the angelic creature: that it was made when God said, “Let there be light”; and on the judgment of the Holy Spirit in condemning the darkness, or the prince of darkness, the devil, 54.

**Chapter III.**—On the Lord’s words to blessed Job: “Do you know the order of heaven, and will you establish its reason upon the earth?” 54.

**Chapter IV.**—What the order of heaven, or the order of the heavens, is; and on the verse of the psalm: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the spirit of his mouth all their power,” 55.

**Chapter V.**—That first, in that holy order of blessed spirits, one must contemplate the order of the Holy Trinity; that the glorious city so often mentioned by Holy Scripture has God as its lover with ineffable love—this lover, indeed, complains through Jeremiah that he has been despised by the unfaithful soul, 56.

**Chapter VI.**—That, according to the likeness of a lover—in whom these three things are found, the lover himself, his love, and the increase for whose sake he is led by his love to propagate offspring—God the Father is one, his love is the Holy Spirit, and his Word is the Son, 57.

**Chapter VII.**—On the Apostle’s words: “For it was fitting for him, for whom are all things and through whom are all things”; and that it is too little for us to know that the angelic creature and every creature were made through him, unless we also know that they were made for him, 58.

**Chapter VIII.**—Likewise, on the procession of the Holy Spirit: that, in human beings, it is poured forth in two gifts—one for the remission of sins and the other for distributions of graces—but in the holy angels in one gift only, namely the distributions of graces, 59.

**Chapter IX.**—That the Holy Spirit rightly and by the just judgment of God judged the devil unworthy of his regard, guilty of an eternal offense; and on the fall of that devil, who had been set upon God’s holy mountain, 60.

**Chapter X.**—A reply to one who perhaps asks: Why did he set the devil upon God’s holy mountain? And why did he confer so much upon him, when the Holy Spirit, who searches all things, even the depths of God, knew him? 61.

**Chapter XI.**—Why he was condemned by so terrible a judgment; and on what is said in the Apocalypse: “One of the heads of the beast which had seven heads, as though slain unto death, and the wound of its death was healed,” or, “it has the wound of a sword and lived,” 62.

**Chapter XII.**—On what was said to blessed Job: “His Spirit adorned the heavens, and by his midwifing hand the twisting serpent was brought forth,” 63.

**Chapter XIII.**—On what was said to the same blessed Job: “Who has set forth the order of the heavens?” And why not even Moses ought to have described the order of the heavens—that is, the holy ranks of angels—although he was the first to set forth the orders of the earth, the generations of the children of men, 64.

**Chapter XIV.**—On what was said to the same blessed Job: “And who causes the harmony of heaven to sleep?” and what, or of what kind, that sleep is, 65.

**Chapter XV.**—Likewise, on that harmony and on the words of that harmony—or that chant—which we heard in Isaiah: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God,” 66.

**Chapter XVI.**—The opinion of blessed Pope Gregory concerning those heavenly orders of holy angels: what human beings, or persons of what kind, attain fellowship with each order, 67.

**Chapter XVII.**—A reply to those who say that multitudes fell from each individual order, because, according to that opinion of blessed Gregory, some people are assumed, or will be assumed, into one order and others into another, 68.

**Chapter XVIII.**—Another teaching on the likeness between the nine orders of angels and the nine charisms of the Holy Spirit, which, according to the Apostle, are given to human beings, when he says, “To one indeed through the Spirit is given the word of wisdom,” etc., 69.

**Chapter XIX.**—On the Apostle’s statement: “For nowhere does he take hold of angels, but he takes hold of the seed of Abraham,” 70.

**Chapter XX.**—Likewise, the opinion of blessed Gregory on that verse from the Song of Deuteronomy: “He established the bounds of the nations according to the number of the angels of God.” But we, following the Hebrew truth as translated by blessed Jerome, read: “He established the bounds of the peoples according to the number of the children of Israel,” 71.

**Chapter XXI.**—That it may more plausibly be said that not so much human beings were made to supply the number of angels, as angels and human beings alike were made for the human being Jesus Christ, 72.

**Chapter XXII.**—What meaning this text may have, which, according to the Hebrew and in blessed Jerome’s translation, we read: “He established the bounds of the peoples according to the number of the children of Israel,” 73.

## BOOK FOUR

**Chapter I.**—A proposal to say something about human creation in praise of the Holy Trinity, in honor of the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father and the Son, whose goods shine forth very clearly in this creature, 75.

**Chapter II.**—On God’s purpose in saying, “Let us make man in our image and likeness,” 75.

**Chapter III.**—On what blessed Job—and after him David—says: “Your hands made me and formed me,” 76.

**Chapter IV.**—That there are not hands or feet in God as there are in us, as those who were called Anthropomorphites because of rustic simplicity supposed; and on what is written in Isaiah: “Who has measured the mass of the earth with three fingers, and weighed the mountains in a balance and the hills in scales?” 77.

**Chapter V.**—On the Lord God’s words, “Behold, Adam has become as one of us, knowing good and evil,” and his words to Adam himself: “Because you are dust, and to dust you shall return,” 79.

**Chapter VI.**—An exclamation concerning the prophet who, after the foregoing statement, “Who has measured the mass of the earth with three fingers?” immediately added: “Who has helped the Spirit of the Lord, or who has been his counselor and shown him?” 80.

**Chapter VII.**—Likewise, on the same exclamation, “Who has helped the Spirit of the Lord?” and on the obedience of the Son: that it helped the Spirit of the Lord, 81.

**Chapter VIII.**—Likewise, on what is written there in the prophet: “With whom did he take counsel, and who instructed him, taught him the path of justice, taught him knowledge, and showed him the way of prudence?” And a reply to that inquiry according to the Apostle, who says, “We speak wisdom among the perfect,” and elsewhere, “But God has revealed it to us through the Spirit,” 82.

**Chapter IX.**—On that irony of God, or of the Holy Trinity, in saying, “Behold, Adam has become as one of us, knowing good and evil,” after he had already said, “Because you are dust, and to dust you shall return”; and how that irony was turned into earnest when the new Adam, Jesus Christ, became one person among the three persons of the Holy Trinity, 83.

**Chapter X.**—On faith, which is one and the chief of the gifts of the Holy Spirit: that in the first holy fathers of old it was the preparation for so great a mystery and so great a salvation, 84.

**Chapter XI.**—That at that time not only faith but prophecy also was given by the Holy Spirit to those holy persons before the flood, as he willed; and on the mystery of the number in which Lamech says: “Sevenfold vengeance shall be given for Cain, but for Lamech seventy times seven,” 85.

**Chapter XII.**—Likewise, on the charisms of the Holy Spirit: that at that time, and afterward before the coming of the Spirit given for remission of sins, he was not so given; that the gifts then given were preparations for the regeneration by which people are now children of God; and on blessed Job’s statement concerning them, that those conceived did not see the light, 86.

**Chapter XIII.**—On Noah’s three sons, from whom the world was restored; and that it is very noteworthy that the word of blessing which God pronounced over the first human beings was renewed over them by a threefold declaration; and that Canaan, rather than Ham himself, was cursed by the father, 87.

**Chapter XIV.**—On the divine purpose in the judgment, namely the flood: that the splendor of the Holy Trinity shines within it to one who examines the letter of the text more closely, 88.

**Chapter XV.**—On the first pronouncement of that judgment: “My Spirit shall not remain in man forever, because he is flesh”; that it suits the person of the Father, 89.

**Chapter XVI.**—On the second pronouncement: “Seeing, God repented that he had made man on the earth; and, looking ahead to the future and touched inwardly by sorrow of heart, ‘I shall destroy,’ he said, ‘the man whom I created’”; that it suits the person of the Son, 89.

**Chapter XVII.**—On the third pronouncement: “And when God had seen, he said to Noah, ‘The end of all flesh has come before me; make yourself an ark’”; that it suits the person of the Holy Spirit, 91.

**Chapter XVIII.**—On God’s words, “Come, therefore, [Col. 1533] let us descend and confuse their languages there”: that this is the voice of the Trinity, like the plural statement, “Behold, Adam has become as one of us,” 91.

**Chapter XIX.**—On his saying, “Nor will they desist from their designs until they accomplish them by deed”: how they accomplished them by deed, 92.

**Chapter XX.**—On that plague of confusion: in what way it was beneficial, and to which person it more fittingly belongs to say to the others, “Come, let us descend and confuse,” etc., 93.

**Chapter XXI.**—On the faith of the father Abraham, who believed the promises of the blessed seed; and on the fact that he saw three and worshipped one, 94.

**Chapter XXII.**—On the three fathers—Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—and how in the three angels who dined and promised Isaac’s birth the mystery of faith in the Holy Trinity was prefigured, by which the world was enlightened through Christ’s coming, 95.

## BOOK FIVE

**Chapter I.**—On Solomon’s statement in Proverbs: “The name of the Lord is a most strong tower; the righteous runs to it and shall be exalted”; and that the righteous person is one justified by faith in this name, 95.

**Chapter II.**—On God’s words, when he began to speak to Moses: “Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: The Lord God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you”; and on the name Adonai, of which he says, “I did not make my name known to them,” 97.

**Chapter III.**—That it was no diminution of glory or merit for those fathers that he said, “And I did not make my name Adonai known to them,” 98.

**Chapter IV.**—On the Lord’s answer to the Sadducees concerning the resurrection of the dead: why he appropriately recalled these fathers when God said, “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob,” from which he drew the conclusion: “He is not the God of the dead but of the living, for all live to him,” 99.

**Chapter V.**—On the chapter of the prophet Hosea: “And I have spoken,” says the Lord, “through the prophets, and through the hand of the prophets I have been made like”; how the Holy Trinity was prefigured in these fathers: God the Father in Abraham, God the Son in Isaac, and God the Holy Spirit in Jacob’s supplanting, 100.

**Chapter VI.**—Likewise, on Rebekah’s counsel, which he adopted with a beneficial result: why we rightly understand the grace of the Holy Spirit to be prefigured in it; and on the very good garments with which she clothed him, and on the verse of the psalm, “He chose for us his inheritance, the beauty of Jacob whom he loved,” 101.

**Chapter VII.**—On the charisms of the Holy Spirit signified by those good garments; on the mystical dimness of the eyes of Isaac as he blessed; and on Moses’ words: “Either forgive them this sin, or blot me out of your book which you have written,” 102.

**Chapter VIII.**—Likewise, on the charisms of the Holy Spirit: that the blessing by which our Isaac blessed us is the grace of the Holy Spirit proceeding from him; and, against the Monothelites, on that wondrous mystery in which Isaac blessed not the one whom he himself wished, but the one whom Rebekah his mother preferred to be blessed, 104.

**Chapter IX.**—On the working of miracles, which is great among the charisms of the Holy Spirit: that it is according to this that it is said, “And no prophet thereafter arose in Israel whom the Lord knew face to face”; and that to work miracles was to make known the name Adonai, 105.

**Chapter X.**—Likewise, on that grace of the Holy Spirit which is the working of miracles: how the magicians before Pharaoh imitated it and, unable to persist, said, “This is the finger of God,” 106.

**Chapter XI.**—On the threefold blessing of the Lord’s name, which, after the tabernacle had been completed, the Lord commanded Moses, saying, “Thus you shall bless the children of Israel”; and on his saying, “They shall invoke my name over the children of Israel, and I shall bless them,” 107.

**Chapter XII.**—On the blessing by which Jacob blessed his son Joseph under a threefold invocation of the holy name: “The God in whose sight my fathers walked; the God who has fed me from my youth; the angel who rescued me from every evil”; and that this angel is the person of the Son, 108.

**Chapter XIII.**—That in those ancient blessings the relative names—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—had to be kept silent, and the utterance closed, so that they did not bless as openly as we now bless or baptize in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and on what is written in Isaiah: “To us the vision of all things shall be like the words of a sealed book,” 109.

**Chapter XIV.**—On the statement, “Hear, Israel: [Col. 1534] the Lord your God is one God”; and on the three things immediately added: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength”; and that love is threefold and one—not three loves, but one love, 110.

**Chapter XV.**—That there are three operations of the one love, which Moses immediately set in order; that the first operation, corresponding to “You shall love with all your heart,” begins thus: “And these words shall be in your heart”; and that this operation is the contemplative life, 112.

**Chapter XVI.**—The second operation of love, corresponding to “with all your soul,” is the active life, which he begins to set forth thus: “You shall fear the Lord your God and serve him alone, and swear by his name,” 113.

**Chapter XVII.**—The third operation of love, corresponding to “with all your strength,” is to overthrow altars and break images; this operation is the crown of martyrs, though in a different manner, because they did not fight with the material sword, 114.

**Chapter XVIII.**—That, by the likeness of these three operations of one love, we ought to be helped to understand that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three persons and one God, 115.

**Chapter XIX.**—That the Son of God and the Holy Spirit proceeding from him are prefigured in what the Lord said to Moses: “Gather for me seventy men, and I shall take from your spirit and give it to them,” 116.

**Chapter XX.**—That those seventy men received a share of Moses’ glory, namely prophecy, but not also the working of miracles, as did Joshua, of whom the Lord said, “And you shall give him a share of your glory”; and that this was what he meant in saying, “I shall take from your spirit,” 117.

## BOOK SIX

**Chapter I.**—On what is written in Micah: “And we shall raise up against him seven shepherds and eight chief men.” Who these shepherds and chief men are; what it is to raise them up over Christ; and that Moses is one of those shepherds, 118.

**Chapter II.**—Likewise, on the word “raising,” since that which had been dead and comes to life again is said to be raised, 119.

**Chapter III.**—How this mystery of the shepherd was raised up over the Lord Christ in the fact that Moses was ordered to gather seventy men at the entrance of the tabernacle of the covenant, so that some of his Spirit might be given to them, 120.

**Chapter IV.**—That the Lord had patiently endured until that point, but after so many people received of Moses’ spirit, he began to strike the murmuring people; and in the figure of what matter this occurred, 121.

**Chapter V.**—On the Pharisees’ saying, “This man does not cast out demons except by Beelzebub, prince of demons,” and the Lord’s answer: “But whoever speaks a word against the Holy Spirit shall not be forgiven, neither in this age nor in the age to come”; and that this event occurred as a figure of this judgment, 122.

**Chapter VI.**—That David was the seventh of the aforesaid shepherds; and that in him are found not only the name of God repeated threefold, as in Moses, but also the expressly stated relative names of the Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—and that he was the first to name the Holy Spirit, who had previously been called the Spirit of God or Spirit of the Lord, 124.

**Chapter VII.**—On the promise made to him with an oath: “Once have I sworn by my holy one”; and on the threefold name of the Lord when he says to him, “I shall give you rest, and the Lord shall declare to you that the Lord will make you a house,” 125.

**Chapter VIII.**—On the fact that when the Paraclete, the Spirit of truth, was sent to the apostles—and before he appeared in tongues of fire, which occurred on the day of Pentecost—after he had opened their understanding to comprehend the Scriptures, the first testimonies concerning Christ were taken from David’s psalms, 126.

**Chapter IX.**—Likewise, on his saying, “That Spirit will glorify me, because he will receive from what is mine and declare it to you”; and on the verse of the fourth psalm, “The light of your countenance, O Lord, is marked upon us; you have given joy in my heart,” 127.

**Chapter X.**—That through the understanding of the first psalm the Spirit of truth declares this to us concerning Christ: that he came into this world without original sin and lived in this world without actual sin, 128.

**Chapter XI.**—That through the understanding of the second psalm the Spirit of truth declares this to us concerning Christ: that through obedience he suffered for our sins, namely by obeying the Father who said, “Ask of me”—surely by dying. For this was the asking: “And I shall give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession,” 129.

**Chapter XII.**—That through the understanding of the third psalm the Spirit of truth declares this to us concerning Christ: that he rose again and ascended into heaven, and that this is what he says: “I slept and was overcome by sleep, and I rose again”; and, “But you, O Lord, are my protector,” 130.

**Chapter XIII.**—That through the understanding of the fourth psalm, which begins, “When I called, the God of my righteousness heard me; in tribulation you enlarged me,” the Spirit of truth declares this to us concerning Christ: that he did as he promised, saying, “Your heart shall rejoice, and no one shall take your joy from you,” 130.

**Chapter XIV.**—Again, on the verse of the fourth psalm: “The light of your countenance, O Lord, is marked upon us”: that the Lord’s countenance is the Son of God, and the light of the Lord’s countenance is the Spirit of the Father and the Son, 131.

**Chapter XV.**—On the variation between singular and plural in the same psalm: that the singularity is that of believers possessing one Spirit and one faith, whereas the plurality, or multitude, is that of those who are against or outside this unity, 132.

**Chapter XVI.**—Again, that unity says, “You have given joy in my heart”; and that where the Holy Spirit dwells, there is everlasting and inexpressible joy, 134.

**Chapter XVII.**—Wonder at how wisely the book was sealed until the Lamb opened it; and on blessed Job’s statement: “He who moves the earth from its place, who commands the sun and it does not rise, and seals up the stars as under a seal,” 135.

**Chapter XVIII.**—On Solomon’s statement: “Who has raised up all the ends of the earth? What is his name, and what is the name of his Son, if you know?” Likewise: “Woe to one alone, because when he falls he has no one to lift him up,” etc.; after which he adds, “A threefold cord is not easily broken,” 126.

**Chapter XIX.**—That there are three things—faith, hope, and love—through which a human being is brought to the likeness of God, according to his purpose in saying, “Let us make man in our image and likeness”; and that in accordance with these three Solomon made three books: Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs, 137.

**Chapter XX.**—On his statement in Proverbs: “Wisdom has built herself a house; she has cut out seven pillars”; and that “The Lord possessed me at the beginning of his ways,” and the remainder down to “I was with him, arranging all things,” and “In the beginning was the Word; all things were made through him,” have one and the same meaning, 138.

**Chapter XXI.**—That, by the likeness of a weary traveler, the frequent division of books relieves the weary mind of the writer, 140.

## BOOK SEVEN
### Chapter I

Again, on the treasure of faith, hope, and charity in Solomon’s three books: that one ought indeed to rejoice over that treasure of wisdom, yet fear that so wise a man fell, or could fall. 141

### Chapter II

On the co-eternity of the Father and the Son, according to these words of Wisdom: “Before anything was made, I was already conceived,” etc.; and on the Incarnation of that same Wisdom, according to these words: “Wisdom built herself a house,” and the rest. 141

### Chapter III

On what follows in the same book of Proverbs: how nearly the entire discourse is, as it were, in conflict through the opposition of the righteous and the wicked, mutually opposed and contending, in accordance with what incarnate Wisdom itself says: “I came not to bring peace, but a sword.” 143

### Chapter IV

Again, on the opposition between the righteous person, namely one who lives by faith, and the wicked person, that is, one without faith; and what, according to the same book of Proverbs, is the end of each. 144

### Chapter V

Again, on faith: that it is the valiant woman of whom it is written at the end of the same book: “Who shall find a valiant woman? Her worth is far beyond the utmost bounds.” 145

### Chapter VI

Again, on the dignity of that same faith: how it is said, “The heart of her husband trusts in her, and he shall not lack spoil; she renders him good and not evil all the days of her life.” 146

### Chapter VII

What or what sort of good faith—or the faithful Church—renders, so that her husband’s heart rightly trusts in her, according to the Hebrew alphabet, whose individual letters are prefixed to individual verses. 148

### Chapter VIII

On the wondrous power of faith, especially in this saying: “She made fine linen and sold it, and delivered a girdle to the Canaanite.” 149

[Col. 1536]

### Chapter IX

How the following book, Ecclesiastes, pertains to the instruction of faith: “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity.” 150

### Chapter X

How all things which God made in six days are rightly charged with vanity in comparison with the seventh day, on which He rested. 151

### Chapter XI

That it is not so much creation itself as the immoderate use of creation or perverse love which is rightly charged with vanity; and how Scripture says: “And God saw all things that He had made, and they were very good.” 152

### Chapter XII

On the saying: “Fear God, and keep His commandments, for this is the whole man”; and that without the fear of God every living human being is vanity. 154

### Chapter XIII

That these two—faith, which is instructed in Proverbs, and hope, which is strengthened in Ecclesiastes—work through the third, namely charity, which speaks in the Song of Songs. 155

### Chapter XIV

How, in these three—faith, hope, and charity—we may profitably contemplate how we are instructed ever more fully toward the fellowship of the Holy Trinity. 156

### Chapter XV

That in the ancient Scriptures these names—faith, hope, and charity—are found almost so rarely, though the realities themselves are proclaimed everywhere; just as the relative names Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are either unspoken, or uttered very rarely and with caution. 157

### Chapter XVI

Again, on faith, hope, and charity: that through these three the Holy Trinity is represented in the sacred Scriptures; and on the Apostle’s passage, “Then I shall know, even as I am known”: what it is to know or to be known. 158

### Chapter XVII

In what sense or with what intention the Apostle said: “But now faith, hope, charity, these three remain; but the greatest of these is charity”; and that these three are inseparable, just as the Trinity itself is. 159

### Chapter XVIII

We must pray that, since through these three we are re-formed into the likeness of the Trinity, the Blessed Trinity may increase faith in us, increase hope, increase charity. 160

## Book Eight

### Chapter I

That the confession or praise of the Holy Trinity is the song of the Lord, which ought not to be sung, in response to the question of heretics, “in a strange land, by the rivers of Babylon.” 161

### Chapter II

On the three victorious youths in the midst of the Babylonian furnace: that in them the Holy Trinity both displayed and signified the presence of its aid against the chief of idolatry. 161

### Chapter III

How both the words and mystical meanings of Psalm 136, “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept,” accord with that history or event. 162

### Chapter IV

That the cause of such lamentation is not equally great for us as it was for the saints of old: “Upon its willows, in its midst, we hung up our instruments. How shall we sing the song of the Lord in a strange land?” 164

### Chapter V

On great Rome: that it was great Babylon for as long as it carried out persecution against the worshippers of that same Trinity, which was glorified in the earlier Babylon through those three youths. 164

### Chapter VI

How beautiful is the mystery in the saying: “Then these three, as though with one mouth, praised and glorified and blessed God”; and, concerning the furnace heated sevenfold beyond its customary heat, what the number seven signifies there. 166

### Chapter VII

On the four beasts which Daniel saw—the lioness, the bear, the leopard, and the other, unnamed, terrible and wondrous beast—that against each was set the aid of the Trinity under the mystery of the number three. 166

### Chapter VIII

On the bear, that is, the kingdom of the Persians and Medes: how there the Most High glorified His power under the same mystery of the number three—that is, through three kings—in the rebuilding of the temple or city. 167

### Chapter IX

Again, how through only three persons the aid of the Holy Trinity against Haman was foreseen, lest he destroy the Jewish race, from which Christ had to be born. 169

### Chapter X

That for this cause the Holy Trinity called Cyrus, king of Persia, by name and likened him [to itself]; that it gave so great a goodwill in the hearts of the other Persian or Median kings; and that our Lord Jesus Christ, for whose future birth those things were done, is first taught in the Scriptures. 170

### Chapter XI

What thanksgiving is; and when, how, and where our Lord Jesus Christ gave thanks. 171

### Chapter XII

On the third beast, namely the leopard—that is, the kingdom of the Greeks—how the Holy Trinity displayed the presence of its aid against it through three men, the three brother-leaders Judas, Jonathan, and Simon. 172

### Chapter XIII

On the rectitude of the judgment expressed through the prophet Hosea: “For I will no longer have mercy on the house of Israel, but I will have mercy on the house of Judah”; and that the house of Judah had three righteous kings, but the house of Israel not even one. 173

### Chapter XIV

An epilogue of deliverances: that from the word of promise until the Nativity of Christ that people from whom Christ had to be born was delivered seven times; and that this pertains to the mystery of the Holy Trinity, because each deliverance came about on account of, or through, three men found in their midst. 174

### Chapter XV

That it is not now so with that people after Christ’s birth, but: “If,” says the Lord, “these three men—Noah, Daniel, and Job—were in its midst, as I live, they alone by their righteousness would deliver their own souls.” 175

### Chapter XVI

From what sword and famine, from what beasts, and from what pestilence the apostles did not save their kinsmen according to the flesh, the Jews; and that they were among them as Noah, Daniel, and Job. 176

### Chapter XVII

What, or of what kind, was the sin of that land which Noah, Daniel, and Job could not save; and how the Jews blasphemed, or spoke, against the Holy Spirit. 177

### Chapter XVIII

On Jerusalem: which Jerusalem is meant when the Lord says in the same place, “If I send my four grievous judgments into Jerusalem, nevertheless there shall be left in it a deliverance bringing forth sons and daughters.” 178

### Chapter XIX

On those three men whose proper names were Noah, Daniel, and Job: how each departed in his own time. 179

## Book Nine

### Chapter I

On what is written: “As one who eats much honey, it is not good for him; so one who is a searcher of majesty shall be overwhelmed by glory”; and that searching the Scriptures is not the same as being a searcher of majesty. 180

### Chapter II

That the house which Wisdom built for herself is the body of Christ; and that the procession of the Holy Spirit into this house was celebrated three times: first to build it, second to adorn it, third to dedicate it. 181

### Chapter III

On the seven pillars of that house, and who was the first author to write of the seven Spirits of God. 182

### Chapter IV

On the first seven days; and that the Spirit of the Lord “who was borne over the waters” should be understood from them to be the sevenfold Spirit: first, the Spirit of fear, according to the division of darkness and light; and, at the summit, the Spirit of wisdom, according to the seventh day on which God rested. 183

### Chapter V

Why the same mystery of the sevenfold Spirit was fittingly designated by the name of the seven pillars; and why Isaiah, adorning those same Spirits in reverse order, descended from the Spirit of wisdom to the Spirit of fear. 185

### Chapter VI

On the building of this house of the Lord; and that there came about in it what the Psalmist said: “Mercy and truth have met each other; righteousness and peace have kissed.” 186

### Chapter VII

Again, on the same matter: for what purpose mercy and truth met each other, and what counsel they had there concerning the salvation of humankind, according to Blessed Job: “Would that my sins, by which I have deserved wrath, and the calamity that I suffer, were weighed in a balance.” 187

### Chapter VIII

Again, on the building of the same house: what mystery is contained in the saying, “When the house was built, it was built of stones hewn and made perfect.” 189

### Chapter IX

On the adornment of that house: with what gold it was adorned when the Holy Spirit descended upon the Lord in the form of a dove as He was baptized by John. 190

### Chapter X

What was meant by the Holy Spirit’s appearing, as He proceeded to this work, not in any form whatsoever, but in the form of a dove. 191

### Chapter XI

On that day which the Holy Spirit determined through David, saying: “Today, if you hear His voice.” 192

### Chapter XII

On the dedication of that house, that is, its resurrection, according to Psalm 29, whose title is “A psalm of David, a song at the dedication of David’s house.” 192

### Chapter XIII

Again, in the same psalm, on the threefold invocation of the Lord’s name: “I will exalt You, O Lord; O Lord, I cried to You; O Lord, You brought up my soul from hell”; and on the title of another psalm: “Unto the end: a song of a psalm of the resurrection.” 193

### Chapter XIV

Why from that feast of dedication, that is, from the glory of the resurrection, the Holy Spirit appeared not in the form of a dove but in the form of fire; and on the spirit of blasphemy, whose sin “shall not be forgiven, neither in this age nor in the age to come.” 194

### Chapter XV

Again, on the same judgment of the Holy Spirit, together with the Apostle’s sentence: “For if we sin wilfully after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins.” 195

### Chapter XVI

How we ought to sing psalms and, in singing psalms, confess the memory of His holiness; and that this memory itself is the mission of the Son of God, who says in Isaiah: “Before they came to be, I was there,” etc. 196

### Chapter XVII

On the procession of the Holy Spirit according to the following chapter of Isaiah: “They did not thirst in the wilderness when He led them forth; He brought forth water for them from the rock, and split the rock, and waters flowed”; and on the voice of exultation by which we are commanded to proclaim this. 198

### Chapter XVIII

That the dedication of this house not made by hands was the repudiation of the old house made by hands, according to Isaiah’s vision in which, while the seraphim cried, “Holy, holy, holy,” etc., the house was filled with smoke. 198

### Chapter XIX

On what is written in praise of the valiant woman, that is, holy faith: “Her husband praised her,” and “Give her of the fruit of her hands.” 201

Fourteen Books of Commentaries on the Gospel of St John. 204

Commentaries on the Apocalypse of John the Apostle. 827

# On the Victory of the Word of God

Prolegomena. 1215

## Book One

### Chapter I

What the victory of the Word of God is; why, and on account of what adversary—namely, the devil—this work bears this title. 1217

### Chapter II

That the Word of God is the Son of God; and that the reward of knowing Him is the protection of God, for which we also give thanks. 1218

### Chapter III

That the Word of God is known magnificently indeed through His works, but more magnificently through Himself. 1219

### Chapter IV

That only those taught by God can worthily speak the words of God. 1220

### Chapter V

That the greatness of the victory of the Word of God surpasses all praise. 1220

### Chapter VI

By what names, and why, the enemy of the Word of God is named in the Scriptures; and what the dragon’s seven heads are. 1220

### Chapter VII

Why the devil is called a dragon; when he first began to put forth a horn; and that the Lamb, that is, the Word of God, had as many horns. 1222

### Chapter VIII

That pride was the cause of rebellion, and what the causes of pride were. 1223

### Chapter IX

That through pride he became the father of lies, and what that lie was according to prophetic writings. 1224

### Chapter X

That Satan, deceived by his own lie, despised the other angels and aspired to God’s majesty and equality. 1225

### Chapter XI

That Satan also preached his own lie to the other angels and persuaded some to regard him as God. 1226

### Chapter XII

That Satan thought no one was conscious of his creation and condition, and therefore feared no testimony against himself. 1227

### Chapter XIII

That Satan was convicted by the testimony of the Word of God alone; and that the testimony of that same Word of God was not hidden from the other spirits. 1227

### Chapter XIV

That some spirits, corrupted by pride and envy, did not receive the testimony of the Word of God, while others, humble and obedient, remained steadfast in truth. 1238

### Chapter XV

That Satan was condemned by God because of the testimony of the Word, was defeated by the holy angels with the sword of the Word of God, and was cast from heaven. 1229

### Chapter XVI

On what is written in the Psalms: “You are terrible, and who shall resist You?” 1230

### Chapter XVII

By a most beautiful comparison he shows that movements and affections of mind do not apply to God, but that He is immutable. 1231

### Chapter XVIII

That from that conflict in which the devil was defeated, one of the princes of the heavenly host gained both a principality and an illustrious name, so that he is now called Michael, that is, “Who is like God?” 1232

### Chapter XIX

On what was said to Blessed Job: “Who laid the cornerstone of the earth, when the morning stars praised Me together,” etc.? 1233

### Chapter XX

On what was said to the same Blessed Job: “Power and terror are with Him, who makes concord in His high places.” 1234

### Chapter XXI

That Satan did not fall immediately upon being created. 1235

### Chapter XXII

That Satan disturbed peace in God’s high places. 1236

[Col. 1539]

### Chapter XXIII

That when Christ said, “I saw Satan falling,” He indicated that He was not only man but had also been the Word of the Father from eternity. 1236

### Chapter XXIV

He resolves the question why God created Satan, though He knew that he would be evil, and defends God’s justice as irreproachable. 1237

### Chapter XXV

Whence and whither the devil was cast: from what kind of heaven, and into what kind of hell he then fell. 1238

### Chapter XXVI

Why he is called the devil, why Satan, and why his spirits are called demons. 1240

### Chapter XXVII

By what words the nine orders of angels are represented in the prophets; and that evil spirits cannot rise again. 1240

### Chapter XXVIII

That those are mistaken who suppose the angels to have been created before heaven and earth. 1241

### Chapter XXIX

That angels were not created in such a way that they could not advance; but that God alone was always perfect without advancement. 1242

### Chapter XXX

That the good angels, having learned in Satan’s downfall the strength, and in their own confirmation the goodness, of the Word of God, burst forth into the eternal praise of the Trinity. 1244

## Book Two

### Chapter I

What the Lord said to Ezekiel the prophet means: “Son of man, raise a lamentation over the king of Tyre.” 1248

### Chapter II

That, just as the sons of Israel lamented when the tribe of Benjamin was destroyed, so the holy angels probably lamented when the number of citizens of God’s kingdom was diminished. 1244

### Chapter III

Why the son of man is commanded to lament the ruler of Tyre. 1245

### Chapter IV

That the mystery of the Word’s incarnation, through which the number of God’s citizens would be restored, was known to God alone. 1246

### Chapter V

That after the world was created, man was made, on account of whom the devil undertook conflict against the Word of God. 1247

### Chapter VI

That the devil retained his ancient ambition for the divine name, but God remained steadfast in His purpose of advancing humanity to His likeness. 1248

### Chapter VII

That the devil wished to hinder God’s purpose, and why God imposed a command upon man. 1249

### Chapter VIII

That the devil entered the serpent and, having deceived man, deserved thereafter to be called the ancient serpent. 1250

### Chapter IX

Why the devil is called the ancient serpent, while God is called and proclaimed the Ancient of Days. 1250

### Chapter X

That when the devil deceived man, he employed the same deceptions now used by sophists. 1251

### Chapter XI

That man sinned not from ignorance, nor from weakness, but from pride. 1252

### Chapter XII

That God’s providence is not to be blamed, but the instability of the creature is to be accused, when one considers that neither angel nor man could endure the greatness of divine beneficence without becoming proud. 1252

### Chapter XIII

That it was useful for it to be revealed by experience what God was not by knowledge: namely, that the rule of creatures cannot be humbly borne except by the incarnate Word. 1253

### Chapter XIV

That God, as though asleep while the serpent deceived man, then awoke and, like a mighty man made drunken with wine, struck His enemies. 1254

### Chapter XV

With what words, and why, God rebuked the serpent, the man, and the woman. 1255

### Chapter XVI
